Marcus is listing qualities he learned from his mother. These are devotion to the gods, kindness to others, and restraint, which includes refusing even to think of evil. He also names a simple way of living, free from the habits of wealthy people.

Marcus is thanking his great-grandfather for two things: not sending him to public schools, and giving him good private teachers at home. He also learned from him that money should be spent freely on such education.

Marcus is recalling what he learned from his governor, a teacher in his youth. The governor taught him to stay out of the rival factions at the chariot races and gladiator fights, to bear hard work, to need little, to work with his own hands, to avoid meddling in others' business, and not to listen eagerly to gossip.

Marcus is thanking Diognetus, his teacher, for the lessons he learned from him. These include avoiding trivial pursuits, being skeptical of charlatans who claimed to cast out spirits, and not becoming absorbed in cockfighting. He also credits Diognetus with teaching him to accept open speech, to study philosophy, and to live simply, sleeping on a plain bed.

Marcus Aurelius says that his teacher Rusticus taught him to improve his character and to avoid showy behaviour. He lists things to avoid: rhetorical display, speculative writing, flashy speeches, and performing good deeds for show. He also says Rusticus taught him to write plain, simple letters.

Marcus Aurelius lists qualities he learned from others. He is quick to make peace with people who have insulted or wronged him once they show they want reconciliation. He reads carefully, does not accept shallow understanding, and does not quickly agree with talkative people. He also thanks a teacher for sharing the teachings of Epictetus.

Marcus says he kept "notes" of Epictetus, a Stoic teacher, and the Greek word used here should not be rendered as "writings," because Epictetus wrote nothing himself. The notes were made by his pupil Arrian, who recorded Epictetus's thinking and preserved it for others.

Marcus is listing what he learned from Apollonius, a teacher he admired. The main lessons are to keep a free and steady purpose, to rely only on reason, and to stay calm through pain, grief, and illness. He also learned to be firm yet gentle in teaching, to treat his own skill as a small matter, and to accept friends' favors without feeling humbled or ignoring them.

Marcus Aurelius here lists qualities he learned from Sextus, a teacher he knew. These include kindness, a household run with a father's care, living according to nature, dignity without showiness, care for friends, and patience with ignorant or hasty people. Sextus could adapt to anyone, so that spending time with him was more pleasant than any flattery.

Marcus is praising a teacher he admired, Quintus Junius Rusticus, for his character. The passage says he was greatly respected by those around him, could find and order the principles needed for living, stayed free of anger and strong emotion, was warm, and showed approval or knowledge quietly rather than showily.

Marcus is describing what he learned from Alexander the grammarian. When someone uses a wrong, clumsy or odd word, Alexander did not scold them. Instead he quietly used the correct word in his reply, or turned the talk to the subject itself rather than the wording.

Marcus learned from his teacher Fronto to recognise envy, deceit and hypocrisy in a tyrant. He also learned that men of noble birth, called Patricians, are often lacking in affection for their children.

Marcus is thanking Alexander the Platonist for teaching him not to keep saying he is too busy. He should not often make that excuse, and not without real need, nor use constant business to avoid the duties he owes to the people he lives with.

Marcus lists qualities he learned from people in his life. From Catulus he took care not to ignore a friend who criticizes him, even unfairly, and a wish to bring that friend back to his normal mood. He also names speaking well of his teachers and loving his children sincerely.

Marcus says his brother Severus taught him to love family, truth and justice. Through Severus he came to admire certain Roman men who resisted tyranny, and he received the ideas of a state under one law for all and a king who values the freedom of his people.

In this part of the Meditations, the writer lists qualities he learned from a teacher. These include steady devotion to philosophy, generosity, good hopes, and trust in his friends' affection. He also notes that the teacher was open about his views, so friends never had to guess what he wanted.

Marcus Aurelius lists qualities he learned from a teacher named Maximus. These include self-control, not being pulled off course, staying cheerful in all conditions including illness, balancing gentleness with dignity, and doing assigned tasks without complaint. He also notes that people trusted Maximus's words and saw no bad intent in his actions.

Marcus describes the character of Maximus, a man he admired. Maximus never showed amazement, haste, or hidden irritation, and was never passionate or suspicious. He was generous, forgiving, and honest, and seemed naturally fixed on what was right. No one felt looked down on by him, and no one felt superior to him.

Marcus describes the qualities he saw in his father. These include a calm, steady temper, firm and deliberate decisions, modesty about public honours, hard work, willingness to hear others' suggestions for the common good, fair treatment of each person, and good judgment about when to act and when to rest. He also notes that his father had mastered sexual desire for boys and regarded himself as an ordinary citizen.

This passage lists qualities the author admired in a teacher or friend. He let friends off duties like dinner invitations or escorting him, and he stayed the same toward those who could not come. He examined matters carefully and did not accept first impressions. He kept friends steadily, without tiring of them or overdoing affection, and stayed content and cheerful.

This passage lists the qualities Marcus Aurelius admired in his adoptive father, Antoninus Pius, as the emperor's example. Among them are careful planning, sound management of public money, and quiet firmness. It also says he did not chase popularity, flattery, or gifts, was not superstitious, and avoided novelty.

Marcus describes a man who used the comforts that came his way without pride or apology, and went without them calmly when they were absent. Nobody could call him a show-off, a slave to fashion, or a pedant. People saw him as mature, sincere, not swayed by flattery, and capable of running his own affairs and those of others.

Marcus Aurelius describes a man he admired, who respected true philosophers but did not scold those who only pretended to be philosophers, and was not easily swayed by them. This man was pleasant to talk to without being showy. He looked after his health with moderate care, neither obsessed with living nor careless, so he rarely needed doctors or medicines.

This passage describes a man who was glad to help others with their talents, such as skill in speaking or knowledge of law, so they could earn the reputation they deserved. It also says he kept to his country's customs without seeming to try, disliked change, stayed with the same places and work, and returned to his usual tasks right after severe headaches.

Marcus describes the qualities of a good ruler, who kept few secrets, spent public money with care, and cared more about doing what was right than about public praise. He also avoided luxuries such as fine houses, rich food, expensive clothes, and handsome slaves.

This section praises the character of a man described by Marcus Aurelius, who is his adoptive father, Antoninus Pius. It says he was gentle, not harsh, angry, or violent, and that he weighed every matter calmly, in order, and without rushing, yet with firm consistency.

Marcus says that a person who can both go without pleasures and enjoy them moderately, as Socrates was said to do, shows a strong and unbeatable soul. He gives Maximus's illness as an example of this kind of strength.

Marcus thanks the gods for the good people around him, such as his family, teachers and friends. He also thanks them that he was never pushed into wronging them, though he had a nature that might have done so. Circumstances never tested him in that way.

Marcus gives thanks to the gods for several things from his upbringing. He was not raised with his grandfather's concubine, he kept his youth chaste and did not start sexual life early, and he had a ruler and father who taught him that a man can live in a palace without guards, fine clothes, torches, or display.

Marcus describes a man, probably his adoptive father or a relative, who could live close to the simple manner of a private citizen while still doing his public duties as a ruler well. He then thanks the gods for his brother, whose character spurred him to self-discipline and whose respect and affection pleased him, and for children who were neither foolish nor physically deformed.

Marcus is listing things he is grateful for from his upbringing. He says he did not pursue further study in rhetoric and poetry, even though he might have, if he had seen real progress. He also says he quickly gave honor to his teachers, instead of postponing it until they were older.

Marcus thanks the gods for clear teaching about living according to nature, which is the Stoic ideal of living in line with the natural order. He says that, with divine help, nothing has stopped him from living this way, though he still falls short through his own fault. He also says his body has lasted this long in such a life.

Marcus lists things he is thankful for in his life. These include his own good conduct, his mother's company in her last years, his ability to help others, his obedient and affectionate wife, and good teachers for his children.

Marcus says he is grateful that dreams showed him remedies for his illnesses, and that when he turned to philosophy he avoided showy teachers, historical writing, logic puzzles and astronomy. He notes that these pursuits depend on help from the gods and fortune.

This note is about the text's editing history, not Stoic ideas. It says that the first book may have been written during a war with the Quadi, if the words are genuine. It also says that some editors placed the first three sections of Book 2 at the end of Book 1, while Gataker moved them to the start of Book 2.

Marcus tells himself each morning that he will meet annoying, ungrateful and unkind people. He says these people act badly because they do not know what is truly good and bad. He adds that he himself knows the good and the bad, and that the wrongdoer is related to him, that is, akin to him.

Marcus says that people share the same reason and a portion of the divine, so they are related in more than blood. Because of this, no one can really harm him, he cannot stay angry with or hate a fellow human, and working against one another goes against nature, since people are made to work together like hands, feet, eyelids and teeth.

Marcus says that he is made of three parts: flesh, breath, and the ruling part, meaning the mind that directs him. He tells himself to look down on the body as blood, bones and nerves, and to see breath as air that is constantly taken in and sent out. The mind, he says, must not be a slave to impulses or fear of the future.

Everything that comes from the gods is guided by providence, meaning a divine plan. Even what seems to happen by chance belongs to nature and is tied to that plan. Whatever the whole of nature brings is good for each part, so the reader is urged to hold these ideas firmly, give up the craving for books, and die thankful rather than complaining.

Marcus is telling himself that he has long delayed doing what matters and has had many chances to act. He must recognise that he is part of a larger universe, governed by a divine order, and that his time is limited. If he does not use that time to clear his mind, it will pass and not come back.

Do each task of the day as if it were your last, with dignity, sincerity, kindness, freedom and justice, and without carelessness, resentment, hypocrisy, self-love or discontent. Few things are needed for a calm life, and the gods ask nothing more.

Marcus is speaking to his own soul. He says it is harming itself and will soon lose the chance to respect itself. He adds that a person's life is enough, and his own is nearly over, yet he has put his happiness in what other people think of him instead of in his own soul.

If outside events pull your attention away, give yourself time to learn something good and stop being spun around by them. But do not swing to the opposite extreme either: people who keep busy without any aim for their actions or thoughts are also wasting their effort.
People rarely become unhappy by failing to notice what is in another person's mind. Those who fail to watch the movements of their own minds, however, are bound to be unhappy.

Keep in mind what the whole of nature is, what your own nature is, how the two are connected, and what kind of part you are of that whole. No one can stop you from always doing and saying what fits the nature you are a part of.

Theophrastus, a philosopher who followed Aristotle, argued that wrongs done out of desire are worse than wrongs done out of anger. His reason is that a person driven by anger turns away from reason with a kind of pain and involuntary tension, while desire is the more deliberate fault.

Wrongdoing done out of desire, driven by pleasure, is judged worse than wrongdoing done in anger caused by pain. The angry person is often reacting to a wrong already done to them, while the person driven by desire acts purely from their own impulse.

Since death could come at any moment, a person should guide each action and thought with that in mind. Leaving human company is nothing to fear if the gods exist, because they will not harm him. And if the gods do not exist or ignore human affairs, the writer asks, what does a world without them matter to him?

The passage argues that the gods exist and care for human affairs. They have given people the means to avoid true evils, and if anything were evil, they would also have made it fully avoidable. Since something that does not make a person worse cannot make his life worse, the things outside his control cannot harm him.

The passage argues that the nature of the universe cannot have overlooked or badly mishandled things. It could not be through lack of knowledge, nor through lack of power or skill, that good and bad things fall on good and bad people alike.
Death, life, honor, dishonor, pain and pleasure happen to good and bad people alike. Since these things do not make a person better or worse, they cannot be good or evil in themselves.

Everything passes away quickly: physical bodies fade from the universe, and their memory fades over time. The passage says the mind should look closely at worldly things, such as pleasure, pain and fame, and see how worthless and temporary they are, and also ask who the people are whose praise gives reputation.

Death, if you break it down into its parts and look at it plainly, is just a natural process. Being afraid of it is childish. It also serves nature's purposes. The passage adds that one should notice how a person draws near to God, and through which part of the self.

The most wretched person, the passage says, is one who searches everywhere, even under the earth, and guesses at what others think. It is enough to attend to the inner daemon, or guiding spirit, and honor it sincerely by keeping it free from passion, carelessness, and resentment toward what gods and people send.

Things that come from the gods deserve respect for their excellence. Things that come from other people should be loved because we are kin to them. Sometimes we even pity people, because they cannot tell good from bad, a failing as real as being unable to tell white from black.

Whether a person lives thousands of years or only a short time, each person loses only the life they are living now, and gains only that same present moment. The present is the same for everyone, so a long life and a short one come to the same thing. A person cannot lose the past or the future, because they never hold them.

Marcus is saying that living a long time gains a person nothing, because all things repeat in endless cycles and the longest life and the shortest lose the same thing. The only thing a person can lose is the present moment, and a person cannot lose what they never had.

Marcus is reminding himself that everything is a matter of judgment or opinion. He points to a saying of the Cynic Monimus that is plain on its face, and says its value lies in taking from it whatever is true.

The passage says that a person harms their own soul in two ways. First, by resenting whatever happens, which cuts them off from nature, the whole order of things that every other thing belongs to. Second, by turning away from others or moving against them with intent to hurt, as angry people do.

The soul harms itself when it is ruled by pleasure or pain, when it pretends or speaks falsely, and when it acts without purpose or without thought. Even small actions should aim at an end, and the end for rational beings is to follow reason and the law of the ancient city, meaning the natural order of the world.

Human life is brief, the body is always changing and decaying, and the mind, luck and fame are all unreliable. Marcus asks at the end what can guide a person through all this. The question is left open in this line.

Philosophy is one thing: keeping the inner guiding spirit, or "daemon," safe from harm and violence, and not ruled by pain or pleasure. It means acting with purpose and honesty, not needing others to act in any particular way, and accepting whatever happens as coming from the same source a person came from.

Death is simply the breaking apart of the elements that make up every living thing. Since these elements change into other things without harm to themselves, there is no reason to fear their change. Nature brings this about, and the speaker holds that whatever accords with nature is not evil.

Life is shrinking every day, and a person who lives longer may lose the mind's ability to understand and reflect on divine and human things. Bodily functions like breathing, eating and desire may still continue even if the mind fails in old age.

Marcus is saying that the ability to use our own reason, to do our duty, to judge clearly what we see, and to decide whether to leave life is fading. Our understanding fails before we die, so we should hurry to live well.

Even things that come after what is natural can have a charm. Bread splits open as it bakes, figs gape when fully ripe, and olives near rotting gain a special beauty. Such features are not what the baker or the process intended, yet they still appeal.

Things like bent ears of corn, a lion's eyebrows, or boar foam look unattractive when examined one by one. Yet they follow naturally from the way nature forms things, so they add to the whole's beauty. A person who looks deeply at everything nature produces will find almost all of these by-products pleasing.

A person who truly knows nature can find pleasure and beauty in things that others overlook. Even real wild beasts' open jaws, or the signs of age in old people, can be seen with appreciation, and young people's beauty can be looked at without desire. Only those who know nature well see these things this way.

Even the famous and skilled die in the end. Hippocrates, a physician, fell ill and died, and great generals like Alexander and Caesar also died despite their power. The passage lists such figures to show that skill, learning and power do not protect anyone from death.

Marcus is saying that life is like a voyage that is now over, so it is time to step off the ship. If death leads to another life, the gods are there too. If it leads to a state without feeling, then pains and pleasures no longer hold you, and you are freed from the body, which he calls a vessel, and which is lower than the mind that uses it.

Do not spend your remaining life thinking about other people unless those thoughts serve a useful common purpose. Such idle wondering about what others do, say, or plan pulls the mind away from watching its own guiding reason. Useless thoughts should be stopped, especially nosy and spiteful ones.

A person should train their mind to think only about things they could openly name if someone asked what they were thinking. Their thoughts should be simple, kindly, and fitting for a being that lives in society, with no thoughts of pleasure, rivalry, envy, or suspicion that they would be ashamed to admit.

A person who has decided to be among the best is described as a kind of priest of the gods, guided by the divine spirit inside him. Such a person is not swayed by pleasure, pain, insult or passion, accepts whatever happens to him, and rarely concerns himself with what others say, do or think, except when truly necessary or for the common good.

The passage says a person should focus on their own part in life, the share of things given to them, and act well within it, trusting that this portion is good. It adds that every thinking being is a kinsman, so caring for all people is natural. A person should value the opinion only of those who live according to nature.

The speaker keeps in mind what kind of people those are who do not live well, both in public and in private. Because such people are not even content with themselves, their praise means nothing to him.

Work with a willing heart, for the common good, and with careful thought and full attention. Keep your mind inner-focused, not showy, and do not talk too much or take on too much. Above all, stand on your own inner strength, ready to face death, needing no outside help or approval.

If you find something in human life better than justice, truth, temperance, and courage, meaning a mind content with doing what right reason requires within the circumstances given to it, then pursue that thing wholeheartedly and enjoy it. The point is that these virtues are the highest good.

Marcus says that if you find nothing better than the inner guiding part of yourself, the part that rules your desires, judges what appears to your senses, and stays faithful to the gods and to humankind, then you should give nothing else first place. Once you turn toward other things, you will no longer be able to keep choosing this inner good, which is your own.

Marcus says that things like public praise, power, or pleasure must not be allowed to compete with what is good in reason and in practical life. These things may seem to fit in at first, but they quickly take over and sweep a person away. He urges choosing the better path and sticking to it, and he takes "useful" to mean useful to us as rational beings.

If something is useful to you only as an animal, a living creature with bodily needs, you should say so plainly and hold to your view without pride. You must also make sure your examination of the matter follows a reliable method.

Do not count any gain as worthwhile if it forces you to break promises, lose self-respect, hate or deceive others, or hide your actions. Someone who puts their own reason and inner guiding spirit first will not act a part or complain. Such a person needs neither isolation nor crowds, and faces death without running toward it or away from it.

A person who lives by these principles does not care whether the soul stays in the body for a long or short time. If he must die at once, he goes as calmly as he would start any other decent and orderly task. His one concern through life is to keep his thoughts on what belongs to a reasoning being and a member of a community.

A mind that has been cleansed and purified contains nothing corrupt, diseased, or shameful. Such a person's life is complete when death comes, not cut short like an actor who leaves the stage before the play ends. Nothing in them is servile, pretended, over-attached, or cut off, and nothing needs to be hidden.

Marcus says we should respect the mind's power to form opinions. Whether our inner guiding part holds opinions that go against nature and against the rational animal (a human being) depends entirely on this power. When it works well, it brings freedom from rash judgment, friendship with others, and obedience to the gods.

Set aside everything except a few essentials. Each person lives only in the present moment, and the rest of life is already past or not yet known. Our lives are brief, the place we live is small, and even long-remembered fame lasts only briefly among people who soon die and do not truly know themselves, let alone those who lived before.
When something appears to you, make a clear definition of it. Look at what it is in itself, stripped of extras, and name it, along with the parts it is made of and the parts it will break down into.

Looking at each thing in life carefully, and asking what it is within the whole universe, what role it plays there, and what worth it has both to the whole and to a human being as a citizen of the greatest city, raises the mind more than anything else. The universe is treated as one city, with all other cities like its households.

Marcus says that when something affects him, he should ask what the thing is, what it is made of, how long it will last, and which virtue he needs to meet it, such as gentleness or truth. He should see every event as coming from god or fate, and see other people, even those who act against their own nature, as kin he understands better than they understand themselves.

The writer says he treats other people fairly and kindly because of a natural bond that people share. At the same time, when dealing with things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, he tries to work out how much each one is actually worth.

If you do your present task carefully, reasoning rightly, and keep your inner reason clean, expecting and fearing nothing, and speak truthfully, you will live happily. Marcus says no one can stop you from doing this.

Just as doctors keep their tools ready for sudden emergencies, one should keep guiding principles ready to understand divine and human matters. Even small everyday actions should be done with awareness that humans and gods are connected. Nothing human is done well without reference to the divine, and the reverse is also true.

Stop drifting from one thing to another. You will never get to read your old notes, the histories of Rome and Greece, or the books you were saving for old age. Hurry toward the end that is ahead, drop empty hopes, and help yourself now while you still can.

Marcus says that people do not understand what many everyday words really mean, such as stealing, sowing, buying, keeping quiet, and seeing what ought to be done. Seeing what ought to be done is not a matter of the eyes but of a different kind of inner perception.

Marcus says humans have three parts: body, soul and intelligence. Receiving sense impressions is shared with animals, and being driven by desire is shared with wild beasts and with bad rulers such as Phalaris and Nero. Even intelligence that picks what seems suitable can belong to people who reject the gods, betray their country and act wrongly in private.

The good man's own possession, unlike the things shared by everyone, is to accept whatever happens to him as fate assigns it. He keeps the divine reason inside him clear of disturbing images, follows it as a god, and speaks truth and acts justly.

If people refuse to believe that a man lives simply, modestly and contentedly, he does not become angry with them. He also does not leave the path that leads to the end of life, which a person should reach pure, calm, ready to go, and fully accepting of his lot without being forced.

The mind, when it is in line with nature, adapts easily to whatever happens and turns it to its own use. It needs no particular material to work on. Like a strong fire that feeds on what is thrown onto it, it uses obstacles to grow stronger.
Every action should have a clear purpose and be done in the best possible way, following correct principles of skill. Nothing should be done carelessly or without a reason.

People look for quiet places such as country houses, the seaside, or mountains. Yet the author says a person can withdraw into their own mind at any time, and that the mind offers more peace than any such place, especially when its thoughts bring calm at once.

Tranquillity is simply a well-ordered mind. The writer advises keeping short, basic principles to return to, which clear the mind and remove discontent with the world, including the wrongdoing of other people.

Rational beings exist for one another, so enduring others' wrongs is part of justice, and wrongdoers act without meaning to. Think how many people have died in feuds and fights, and let the quarrel go. If you are unhappy with your share of the universe, remember there is either a providence guiding everything or only random atoms.

Marcus lists things a person can recall to calm the mind and stop being troubled. These are the Stoic idea that the world is like one political community, the view that the mind is separate from breath and bodily sensation, and the view that pain and pleasure should not decide one's peace. He ends by naming the wish for fame as another worry to be dealt with.

Everything is quickly forgotten, and the praise of others is empty, since those who give it are changeable and poorly judging. Fame is also limited: the earth is a tiny point in vast time and space, and few people live in your small corner of it, so few could praise you.

Outside things cannot really disturb the mind; only our own judgments about them cause upset. Everything we see is constantly changing and will pass away, so we should keep that in mind. In short, the world is constant change, and life is what we make of our own opinions.

Marcus argues in a chain of "if this is so" steps. If human minds share one reason, then we share one law, are fellow citizens, and belong to one community. So the whole world is, in a sense, one state.

Marcus asks where human reason and the capacity for law come from. He argues that, as the body's earth, water and fire each come from a source, the thinking part must also come from some source, since nothing comes from nothing.

Death is a natural process, like birth: the body is put together from the same elements and then broken apart into them again. Because it is not against the nature of a reasoning living being, or against the reason that shapes human beings, no one should be ashamed of it.

Marcus is saying that people who act badly do so by nature, as a matter of necessity, just as a fig-tree produces juice, and it is foolish to expect otherwise. He adds that you and such a person will both soon die, and your names will not survive.
If you remove your judgment that you have been wronged, the complaint "I have been harmed" goes away. And without that complaint, the harm itself is gone. The harm exists only as you judge it.
Whatever does not make a person morally worse also does not make his life worse. Such a thing harms him neither from outside nor from inside.

Everything that happens is just, and a careful observer will see this. It is as if each event were done by someone who gives each thing its proper worth. So a person should keep to being good in every action, in the true sense of what it means to be good.
Do not judge things the way the person who wrongs you does, or the way he wants you to judge them. See them as they really are.

Marcus says a person should keep two rules ready. First, act only as reason, the ruling part of the mind, directs for the good of people. Second, change your opinion when someone shows you are wrong, but only for good reasons such as justice or the common good, not because the new view is pleasant or brings fame.
Marcus asks whether a person has reason, the faculty of thinking. If the answer is yes, he asks why that person does not use it, since if reason does its own work, nothing more is needed.
You were a part of the whole, and when you die you return to the source that produced you. You are taken back into its seed-like origin and changed into something else.

Some grains of incense are burned on the same altar. One falls a little earlier than another, but the order makes no difference to the result. The image suggests that small differences in timing do not matter.

If you go back to your guiding principles and honor reason, people who now see you as a beast and an ape will, within ten days, see you as a god. The point is that a change in how one lives can change how others regard you.
Do not behave as though you will live for thousands of years, because death is always close. While you are still alive and able to choose, be good.

Marcus says that a person avoids much trouble by watching only his own actions and keeping them just and pure, not watching what others say, do or think. He compares this to the saying of Agathon: do not look around at others' bad conduct, but run straight along your own line.

Wanting fame after death is pointless, Marcus argues, because the people who remember you will die too, and their memory will fade. Even if memory lasted forever, he asks, what good would it do the living? Praise is only worth something for its usefulness, and chasing it throws away the natural gift of living well now.

Something truly beautiful is beautiful in itself and does not depend on praise. Praise does not make a thing better, and blame does not make it worse. The same holds for objects such as an emerald, gold, or a flower, and for qualities like law, truth, and modesty.

Marcus asks how the air can hold souls forever. He answers by comparing it to burial: bodies decay in the earth and make room for new ones. In the same way, souls in the air are changed, spread out, and taken into the universe's fiery reason, making room for new souls.

Marcus argues that if souls survive death, the number of souls would be huge, since we must also count the countless animals eaten daily. Yet the earth still receives all these bodies, because they are changed into blood and into air or fire.

The passage asks what the real inquiry is into the matter at hand. It answers that the key distinction is between what is material and what gives a thing its form, the formal cause. The bracketed note and reference are the translator's, pointing to a related passage in the same work.
Do not let yourself be swept around by every change. Keep justice in mind in all you do, and when something strikes your mind, keep your power to judge it clearly and understand it.

Everything that fits the universe also fits Marcus, and nothing comes too early or too late for him, since all timing belongs to nature. All things come from nature, exist in it, and return to it. He ends by asking why one should not call the world "dear city of Zeus," as a poet called Athens "dear city of Cecrops," its legendary founder.

Marcus says that the advice to do few things is good, but he would put it differently: do what is necessary and what the social nature of a human being requires, and only as much as it requires. Doing less brings calm, and cutting out unnecessary acts and thoughts means fewer useless acts follow.

Marcus is urging himself to test whether the life of a good man fits him. That kind of life means being content with his share of the whole world, and with his own fair deeds and kindly attitude toward others.

Stay calm and simple, and do not let outside events upset you. If someone wrongs you, the harm falls on that person, since they are the one who does wrong. Whatever happens to you was assigned from the start, and life is short, so use the present well through reason and justice.

Marcus is asking whether the universe is either a well-ordered whole or a jumbled mass, yet still a single universe. He then asks how order could exist in a person while disorder rules the whole, since everything is linked together.

Marcus Aurelius here lists a series of bad character traits, such as stubbornness, childishness, deceit and cruelty. The list is a set of labels for the kinds of people or behaviour he wants to name and set aside, without any argument attached.

The main point is that a person who does not understand the world, or who cuts himself off from its shared reason by resenting what happens, is cut off from the whole. Such a person is like a runaway, a blind man, or a diseased limb torn from the body, since the same nature produces both the world and him.

Marcus is mocking men who call themselves philosophers but lack the outward marks of the trade: one has no plain cloak, another no book. A third says he has no bread yet keeps to reason, though his learning does not earn him a living.

Be content with the skill you have learned, even if it seems humble. Live the rest of your life trusting all you have to the gods, and do not make yourself either a ruler over others or a slave to them.

Marcus asks the reader to imagine past times, such as the reign of Vespasian, and to picture the ordinary human activities of those days: marriage, war, work, ambition and death. He then says that all of those lives are now gone, and the same is true of the times of Trajan.

Think of past nations and people who strove hard and soon fell apart, and of those you knew who wasted effort on trivial things instead of doing what suited their own nature. Give each matter only the attention it deserves, and you will not be dissatisfied.

Even famous names from the past soon fade. Words, and the people once remembered for them, become old and then turn into mere stories, and total forgetting covers them, even those who once shone in remarkable ways.

Once people die, they are soon forgotten, and even lasting fame amounts to nothing. So the only thing worth serious effort is living well: thinking justly, acting for the common good, speaking truthfully, and accepting everything that happens as natural and coming from the same source.
Accept your fate without resistance. Clotho is one of the three Fates in Greek myth, the spinners who spin each person's life thread. The point is to let her spin it into whatever shape she chooses.

Everything in the universe is constantly changing, and nature loves to turn what exists into new things like it. Every existing thing is, in a way, the seed of what will come next. Thinking of seeds only as things planted in soil or a womb is too narrow a view.

You will die soon, yet you are still not simple, calm, free from fear of outside harm, or kind to everyone, and you do not yet find wisdom only in acting justly. The writer is pointing out how far he still has to go in these qualities.
Look closely at what drives people's choices, even wise people, by noticing what they run from and what they chase. The idea is to understand the inner motives behind their actions.

Evil does not lie in other people's minds or in changes to the body. It lies in the part of a person that judges things to be evil. If that part refuses to judge, all is well, even when the body is harmed. Things that happen equally to good and bad people are, by this reasoning, neither good nor bad.

Think of the whole universe as a single living creature with one body and one soul. Everything in it is linked, moves together, and helps cause everything else. The passage asks the reader to keep this picture in mind, comparing the connection to a thread spun into a woven cloth.
Changing is not bad for things, and lasting on because of change is not good for them either. Things are neither harmed by changing nor helped by continuing through change.
Time is compared to a fast-flowing river made of the things that happen. As soon as something is seen, it is swept away and replaced by something else, which will also be swept away.

Everything that happens is as ordinary and predictable as roses in spring or fruit in summer. Illness, death, slander, betrayal, and everything else that pleases or upsets foolish people are all of this kind.

Marcus says that the events of the world follow one another in a fitting order. The sequence is not a random list of separate things but a reasoned connection, so each thing that comes into being is linked to what came before it.

Marcus urges himself to keep several thoughts in mind: the elements change into one another, as Heraclitus taught; people forget where their life is heading and quarrel with the universal reason they share; and they should not act or speak as if asleep or merely copy what they were taught as children.
If a god told you that you would die tomorrow or the day after, the gap of one day would hardly matter. So dying in many years is no great matter compared with dying tomorrow.

Many people who once had great skill, knowledge, or power are now dead, including doctors, astrologers, philosophers, warriors, and tyrants, as are whole cities such as Helice and Pompeii. The reader is told to count everyone they have known who has also died.

Human life is brief and its affairs are worthless: one person buries another, and soon the living are dead too. Marcus urges living this short span in line with nature and accepting death calmly, as a ripe olive falls from its tree, grateful for the life it was given.
A headland stays firm while waves keep breaking against it, and in doing so it calms the rough water around it. The passage asks the reader to be like this headland, steady under constant pressure.

Marcus argues that a hard event is not a misfortune in itself. Anyone can suffer such an event, but staying free from pain while it happens is rarer and is the real good. Something counts as misfortune only if it goes against human nature, and suffering an event that human nature allows does not do that.

Misfortune cannot take away the virtues that make a person good, such as justice, courage, self-control and wisdom. Bearing a hardship well is a good thing, and whenever something upsets you, you should remember this rather than call the event a misfortune.

Reflecting on people who clung hard to life is a common but useful way to become less afraid of death. Those long-lived people end up in their tombs just as the early dead do, and the time between birth and death is short for everyone.

Life is a short interval, passed with hardship, among difficult people, in a weak body, so the writer tells us not to value it highly. Looking at the endless time before and after, he asks what difference there is between living three days and living three generations.
Take the most direct route, which is the natural one. Say and do everything in line with the soundest reason, because doing so frees a person from trouble, conflict, and pretence.

Marcus urges himself to get up and work each morning, because people exist to act, not just to seek comfort. He asks whether he was made to stay in bed for warmth and pleasure, and points to plants, birds, ants, spiders and bees, which all work to do their part of the world.

Marcus argues that rest has natural limits, as eating and drinking do. People overindulge in food and drink, yet hold back from their real work, which he says is their natural duty. He concludes that this shows a failure to love oneself and one's nature, while craftsmen who love their skills will work even without washing or eating.

The speaker says you care less for your own nature than craftsmen, dancers, misers and the vain care for their own pursuits. Such people will go without food and sleep to perfect what they value. The question is whether acts that serve society deserve less of your effort.
It is easy to push away any troubling or unfitting thought or impression, and at once be calm again. "Impression" here means a thought or feeling that comes to the mind from outside.

Judge whatever you say or do by whether it fits your nature, and do not let other people's blame change that. Others act from their own reasons and follow their own course, so their criticism should not stop you. Keep to your own nature and the nature shared by all, which the passage says are one and the same path.

The speaker accepts that he will die and return to the natural world. He will breathe out his last breath into the air he has breathed all his life, and his body will fall back into the earth that gave him his food, his drink, and his very substance.

Marcus says that people may not admire how quick your mind is, but you cannot claim you lack natural ability for many other good qualities. Sincerity, self-control, hard work, kindness and similar virtues depend only on your own choice. He asks why you still fall short in them when no natural limit stops you.

Marcus asks whether nature forces a person to complain, be stingy, flatter, fuss over the body, seek approval, show off, and stay anxious. He answers no: these faults could have been dropped long ago. If the only real fault is slowness to understand, he says one must work at that too and not enjoy one's dullness.

Some people, after doing a kindness, count it as a favor they are owed. Others do not announce it but still keep it in mind as a debt the other person owes them. The best kind does not even keep track, and is like a vine that asks nothing more once it has borne its grapes.

A good person, like a horse after a race or a bee after making honey, does not stop to show off the good deed. He simply moves on to the next one, as a vine produces grapes again each season, and does this without noticing he is doing anything remarkable.

Marcus says that people, as social beings, naturally notice how their work serves others and want others to notice it too. He replies that the listener misunderstands what has just been said, and so falls into the same error as others he described earlier, who are misled by a plausible-sounding argument.

If you choose to understand what is said, do not worry that this will stop you from taking part in any duty owed to others. The point is that careful thought does not have to make a person withdraw from social life.
Marcus quotes an old Athenian prayer asking Zeus for rain on the fields. He says that people should either not pray at all, or pray in this simple way.

Marcus says that when we hear that the god of medicine, Aesculapius, prescribed a remedy such as riding, cold baths or going barefoot, we understand it as a means to health. In the same way, when we say the nature of the universe assigned someone illness or loss, it means that what happens to each person is fixed for them to suit their destiny.

Marcus says that things fit together as stones do in a wall, forming one harmony. In the same way, the universe is made of all bodies, and necessity or destiny is made of all causes, so each thing belongs to the whole. Even ignorant people speak this way when they say that necessity brought something to a person.

Just as a patient accepts unpleasant medical orders because they aim at health, we should accept whatever happens, even when it seems unpleasant, because it serves the health and well-being of the whole universe. The good that nature intends is treated as the same kind of thing as bodily health.

Marcus says that what happens to a person is not sent at random. It serves the good of the whole, and nature does not cause anything unfitting for the thing it governs. So there are two reasons to accept what happens: it was arranged for you, and it is tied to your fate from ancient causes.

Everything that happens to a person, even what comes to them individually, serves the universe's governing power as a source of its completeness and even of its continued existence. The whole is damaged if any part or cause is cut away from its connection with the rest. When you are dissatisfied and try to push something out of the way, you are doing that cutting.

Do not be upset or give up when you fail to act fully on right principles. Return to them, be satisfied if most of your conduct fits human nature, and treat philosophy as a gentle remedy, not a harsh master. Philosophy asks only for what your nature already requires.

Marcus argues that pleasure can mislead us into choosing what is not in line with nature. He suggests that qualities such as generosity, freedom, simplicity, calm, and piety are more pleasant than ordinary pleasures. He adds that wisdom itself is the most agreeable thing, since it brings security and a good course of events.

Things are so wrapped up that even leading philosophers, the Stoics included, find them hard to grasp. Our agreement with what we believe also keeps changing. So Marcus tells himself to look at things directly and see how brief and worthless they are, since they may end up in the hands of anyone, even a criminal.

Marcus says that people around us are hard to put up with, even the pleasant ones, and that a person can barely bear himself. Given how dark, impure and constantly changing everything is, he cannot see anything worth highly valuing or seriously pursuing.

A person should accept death calmly, waiting for it without impatience, and rely on two beliefs. First, nothing happens to him that does not fit the nature of the universe. Second, he alone decides never to act against his inner guiding spirit, and no one can force him to do so.

Marcus asks himself at every moment what his soul is currently busy with. He tells himself to check which kind of soul he is using, such as a child's, a young man's, a tyrant's, or a wild beast's, so he can notice when his inner ruling part has become something lesser.

Marcus says we can see what the many think is good by looking at how they react. A person who truly holds virtues such as prudence, temperance, justice and fortitude to be good will not patiently hear anything that goes against them. A person who holds the popular goods to be good will happily accept a line from a comic writer that fits those goods, and so the many can tell the difference.

Marcus is saying that people happily accept jokes about wealth and luxury, such as the comic writer's line about a rich man having so much he has no room to relieve himself. He asks whether things that deserve such mockery should really be counted as good.

Marcus argues that he is made of form and matter, and neither can be destroyed, because neither came from nothing. His parts will change into other parts of the universe, which change again, endlessly. So he, and the people who produced him, have always existed in an unending chain of change, even if the universe runs in fixed cycles.

Reason and the art of reasoning (philosophy) are complete in themselves and can do their own work. They start from their own first principle and reach the goal set for them. That is why such acts are called katorthoseis, or right acts, meaning they follow the straight road.

Marcus says that things which do not belong to a man as a human being should not be called his. Such things are not required of him, human nature does not promise them, and they do not help him reach his purpose. So the good of a person lies elsewhere, and if these things were truly his, he would not be right to scorn them.

Marcus is saying that externals like wealth, comfort and reputation are not really good in themselves. If they were good, a man who gave them up would not be admirable. The more calmly a person goes without them or loses them, the better that person is.

Your habitual thoughts shape the character of your mind, so the mind should be stained with a steady run of helpful thoughts. One example given is that wherever a person can live, they can also live well, even in a palace. Each thing also has a purpose it was made for, and its end lies in that purpose.

Marcus argues that each thing's good lies in its purpose, and that the good for a reasoning being is living in society with others. He supports this by saying that lesser things exist for the sake of greater ones, and that beings with reason rank highest.
It is madness to try for what cannot happen, and it cannot happen that bad people will avoid doing such things. In other words, people who are bad will inevitably act in this foolish way.

Nothing happens to a person that they are not naturally made to bear. Others suffer the same things either because they do not notice what has happened, or because they want to appear strong, and so they stay unharmed. Marcus calls it shameful that ignorance and vanity should prevail over wisdom.

The soul is not moved by outside things at all, because they cannot enter it or change it. It moves only itself, and whatever judgment it chooses to make about things is what those things become for it.

Other people are close to us in that we must treat them well and bear with them. When some people block what we must do, they count as one of the indifferent things, like the sun, wind or a wild beast. Such obstacles can hinder outward action, but the mind turns each hindrance into a help for acting.
Respect what is highest in the universe, the force that uses and directs all things. In the same way, respect what is highest in yourself, because it is of the same kind and it directs your life.

If something does no harm to the state, it does no harm to the citizen, so when something seems harmful, ask whether the state is harmed. If it is not, the person is not harmed either. If it is, do not be angry at the one who caused the harm; instead, point out his mistake.

Everything passes away quickly, like water in a flowing river, and nothing stays still for long. Since all things vanish into the endless past and future, the author asks why anyone would be proud of such things or troubled by them, since they bother us only briefly.

Think of the whole of matter, of which you hold only a very small share, and of all of time, of which you have been given a brief moment that cannot be divided. Think also of fate, and how small a part of it you are.
If someone wrongs me, that is their concern, since they have their own character and their own actions. My task is to accept what universal nature gives me and to do what my own nature asks of me.

The ruling part of the mind should stay separate from bodily pleasure and pain and not join them. Physical feelings may still reach the mind, since body and mind are linked, and resisting them is not needed because they are natural. The mind should simply avoid judging them as good or bad.

To live with the gods, a person must show constantly that his soul accepts what has been given to him, and that he follows the inner guide (the daemon) that Zeus gave each man. That guide is his own understanding and reason.

Anger at someone for a bad smell or foul mouth makes little sense, since such things come naturally from the body. A person with reason can be shown his fault and corrected by calm instruction, so anger is not needed.

If other people block your life, Marcus says you may leave it calmly, as if no harm were done. He compares this to leaving a smoky house. While nothing forces him out, he stays free and chooses to live as a reasoning, social being is meant to live.

The universe's reason is described as sociable, arranging lesser things to serve greater ones and fitting the greater ones together. Each thing is given its proper place, and the best things are brought into harmony with one another.

Marcus asks himself how he has treated the gods, his parents, siblings, children, teachers, nurses, friends, relatives and slaves. He tells himself to check whether he has treated all of them in a way that could be said of him without fault.

Remember the hardships you have endured, the pleasures and pains you have set aside, the honors you have refused, and the kindness you have shown to ill-minded people. The passage says your life's history is now complete and your service ended.

The passage asks why people who lack wisdom should trouble someone who has it. Its answer is that a wise soul is one that understands how the universe begins and ends, knows the reason running through all things, and governs the cosmos through its fixed cycles of time.

Soon the speaker will be dust or bones, and perhaps not even remembered by name. Life's prized things are empty, petty and like children squabbling, while virtues such as faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth have gone away.

Since the senses are unreliable, things keep changing, and the soul is short-lived, a good reputation in such a world means little. So one should calmly wait for death, whether it ends everything or leads elsewhere. Until then, the task is to honor the gods, do good to others, be patient and self-controlled, and accept that anything beyond the body and breath is not in one's power.

A calm, happy life is possible if a person follows the right path and thinks and acts rightly. Two things belong to God, to humans, and to every reasoning being alike: not being blocked by others, and treating goodness as lying in a just character and just conduct, where one's desires come to rest.

The writer asks why he should be troubled by something when it is neither his own fault nor caused by his own wrongdoing, and when the common good is not harmed. If none of those things are true, he sees no reason for his distress or any harm to the community.

Do not be swept along by outward appearances. Help others as far as you are able and as they deserve. If they lose something that does not really matter, do not treat it as a real harm. Marcus compares this to an old man who, leaving, asked for back a child's toy top, remembering it was only a toy.

Fortune is not luck or outside success. A man is fortunate only when he has a good state of mind, good feelings and good actions. Public honours and worldly concerns, which other people care about, do not make a person fortunate.
The universe's basic stuff yields to the reason that governs it, and that reason has no motive to do harm. It has no malice and harms nothing, and all things are formed and completed by it.

It is about doing one's duty whatever the conditions: cold or warm, tired or rested, praised or criticized, and even when dying. Death is just one more act of life, so it is enough to do well the task at hand in that moment too.
Everything that exists soon changes. Either it turns to vapor, if all matter is one substance, or it scatters into separate parts.
The governing reason, meaning the mind that directs a person, knows three things: what its own state is, what it is doing, and what material it is working on.

Find your enjoyment and peace in one thing: moving from one act done for others to the next, while keeping God in mind. "Social act" here means an action that serves other people. Stoics held that such acts are a natural part of human life.
The "ruling principle" is the mind or inner reason that a person has. It shapes itself into what it chooses to be, and it also makes whatever happens to it appear to it in the way it chooses.

Everything happens according to the nature of the universe. It cannot happen according to any other nature, whether one that contains the universe, one that is contained within it, or one that exists outside and apart from it.

Marcus sets out two possibilities: the universe is either random disorder that scatters everything, or it is an ordered whole guided by providence (a divine plan). If it is disorder, he asks why he should care about anything except returning to earth, since his elements will scatter anyway. If it is ordered, he says he will revere, stay steady, and trust the one who governs it.

When outside events have pushed you into being upset, return to yourself quickly and do not stay upset longer than the event forces you to. By often returning to inner calm, you will gain more control over that calm.

Marcus compares the royal court and philosophy to a step-mother and a real mother. He says that a person should respect the court's duties as one does a step-mother, but should often return to philosophy for rest and comfort. Philosophy makes court life bearable and keeps the person bearable there too.

Marcus says that when we look at food or luxury goods, we should see them for what they really are: a dead fish or pig, grape juice, or sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Stripped of the names and appearances we attach to them, these things are revealed as they are.

Marcus says we should strip admired things of their praise and see how little they are worth, because outward show can mislead the mind most when we feel most sure we are chasing something worthwhile. He then refers to a saying by Crates about Xenocrates, a fellow philosopher.

Marcus says that people value things according to how much life they seem to have. Most people admire inanimate objects held together by simple structure, such as stones, wood and trees. Slightly more reasonable people admire living things, such as flocks and herds.

Marcus says that people with more learning admire things that are held together by a reasoning soul. But he means a soul that is only clever at a craft, skilled in some other way, or reasoning enough to own many slaves. The person who values a universal reasoning soul, one fit for life in a community, cares about nothing else.
A person who is good above all keeps his mind working in line with reason and with living together in society. He also works together with other people who are like him, toward that same end.

Everything in the world is constantly coming into being or passing away, as time and change keep renewing it. Since nothing stays in this flowing stream, the speaker asks what among these passing things is worth valuing highly.

Life is fleeting, like a sparrow that flies out of sight after you have grown attached to it. Each person's life is just a breath taken in and then given back to the air, a process that repeats every moment and that we received at birth.

Marcus Aurelius lists ordinary bodily and animal functions, such as breathing, eating, feeling impressions, and following desires, and says none of them is worth valuing. He asks what is worth valuing and answers that praise from others, even applause, is not it either.

Praise from the crowd is just empty noise, like clapping of tongues. If a person gives up fame, Marcus says the only thing worth valuing is to act and hold back according to one's own nature, which every skill aims at: making a thing suited to its purpose.

Marcus compares tasks: the vine-grower, horse-breaker and dog-trainer each aim at a specific end, and education aims at its own end. If education reaches its proper goal, a person will not seek anything beyond it. Otherwise, he will still value many other things, and so will not be free, self-sufficient, or free from passion.

If you want things that others can take away, you will inevitably envy and plot against those who hold what you value, and you will be disturbed and blame the gods. Honoring your own mind instead brings contentment, harmony with others, and acceptance of what the gods give.

Marcus says that the movements of the natural elements, whether up, down or around, are not the movement of virtue. Virtue moves in a more divine way, advancing quietly and almost unnoticed on its course.

People often refuse to praise those who live beside them, yet they want praise from future generations whom they will never meet. Marcus says this is no different from being upset that people who lived long ago did not praise you.
If something is hard for you to achieve, do not assume it is beyond human ability. If something is possible for a human being and fits human nature, you can take it that you too can reach it.

Think of a wrestling partner who scratches you or hits your head by accident in training. You do not get angry, hold a grudge, or treat him as a traitor. You simply keep out of his way without hostility. Marcus says to act the same way toward people in everyday life, overlooking their faults and avoiding them without hatred or suspicion.

Marcus says he will gladly change his mind if anyone can show him that he is thinking or acting wrongly. He seeks the truth, which harms no one. Only the person who stays in error and ignorance is truly harmed.
The speaker says he attends to his duty and is not troubled by other things. Those other things, he says, are either lifeless, or lack reason, or have wandered off and lost their way.

Animals and other things lack reason, so you may use them generously. Humans have reason, so you should treat them with a spirit of fellowship. Call on the gods on every occasion, without worrying about how long this takes, since even three hours of it is enough.
Death makes no difference between a great king and his stable servant. Either both return to the universe's seminal principles, the source of all things, or both scatter into atoms.

Many things happen in a person at the same moment, both in the body and in the soul. So it should not seem strange that everything that exists in the whole universe, which the Stoics called the Cosmos, exists together at once.

Marcus says that a duty, like spelling a name, is made up of separate parts. He asks whether a person who is asked to spell "Antoninus" would shout or get angry if others grew angry at them. He concludes that one should calmly work through each part and finish the task without being upset by those who are angry.

It is unkind to stop people from pursuing what seems good and useful to them, and being angry at their wrongdoing amounts to doing exactly that. People act because they think something suits their nature and benefits them, but that belief is mistaken. So they should be taught and shown the error calmly, without anger.

Death, in this view, is the stopping of several things: sense impressions, the urges that drive desire, the back-and-forth of reasoning thoughts, and the serving of the body. Each of these ends when a person dies.
It is shameful when the mind gives up in life before the body does. The Stoic view is that the soul should stay firm and not collapse first while the body is still holding on.

Marcus is warning himself not to become like a ruler who has been corrupted by power, as "Caesar" stands for an emperor. He urges himself to stay simple, good, honest and kind, to honour the gods and help others, since life is short. He should act as Antoninus, his adoptive father, would have.

Marcus is recalling the qualities of a man he admired, presumably a teacher or relative, listing traits such as steadiness, calm, patience with critics, careful thought, and avoiding haste, gossip, fault-finding, and suspicion. The list describes the character he wants to keep in mind.

Marcus is listing the qualities of a man he admired, such as being content with simple lodging, food and clothing, being steady in friendship, accepting criticism, welcoming better ideas, and being devout without superstition. He ends by urging the reader to copy these traits so that his own conscience will be clear at death.

Wake up to your real senses and look at your present surroundings the way you looked at your dreams. Once you see that the troubles in a dream were only dreams, treat the troubles of waking life with the same clear eye.

Marcus says he is a small body joined to a soul. The body cannot tell one thing from another, so nothing matters to it. The mind is indifferent only to things it does not cause itself. It controls what its own actions are, but only those done in the present, since past and future actions are also indifferent to it now.

Work is not against nature as long as each part does its own job: the foot walks and the hand grasps. In the same way, a person's labor is not against human nature when it does what a human being is meant to do. Work that fits human nature is therefore not an evil.

Craftsmen like builders and doctors will adjust to non-experts only so far, and they hold firmly to the principles of their craft. Marcus asks why people should respect their own reason, which they share with the gods, less than craftsmen respect the reason of their arts.

Everything in the universe is small, changing and temporary, including lands, seas and the present moment. All things come from one ruling power, so harmful things such as a lion's jaws or a thorn are part of the same source as what is good and beautiful. The reader should not think of them as coming from a different source.
Whoever has seen the present clearly has, in effect, seen everything, past and future alike. The reason given is that all things share one origin and one pattern.

Everything in the universe is connected and related to everything else. Because of this, all things are, in a way, friendly to one another. Things follow one another in order, through shared movement and the single unity of their substance.

Accept the circumstances your life has given you, and love the people you have been placed among, but do so sincerely. The advice is to adjust to your situation and to care for others in genuine, not pretended, good will.

Tools work well when they do their job, even though their maker is no longer present to guide them. Natural things are different: the power that made them stays inside them. So we should respect that power, and if we live by its will, our whole being agrees with reason, as the universe does.

If we count only the things within our control as good or bad, we have no reason to blame the gods or hate other people for misfortune or loss. Treating outside things as good or bad is what leads us to blame and resent others, and so to do injustice.
All people contribute to one common end, whether they understand it or not. Even those who complain about events or try to resist them still help bring the outcome about.

Marcus says the universe needs people of all kinds, so each person should see what role they play in it. The ruler of all things will use a person well and place them among those who work toward one shared end. He warns against being like the petty, foolish character in a play that Chrysippus mentioned.

The passage asks rhetorical questions: the sun does not do the rain's work, and Aesculapius (the Greek god of healing) does not do the earth's work of bearing fruit. Each of the stars is different from the others, yet all work toward the same end. The point is that different beings have different roles but serve one common purpose.

If the gods have decided what will happen to him, Marcus says they have decided well. He argues that a god without foresight is hard even to imagine, and that the gods would gain nothing by harming him or the whole world they care for.

If the gods have not planned each detail of my own life, they have at least planned the whole order of things. So I should accept with pleasure whatever follows from that general order and be content with it.

Marcus says that if the gods decide nothing about our affairs, then we should not act as if they were present and involved in our lives. Instead, he can decide for himself what is useful, and what is useful for each person is what fits their own nature.
My nature is reasoning and social, so I belong to two cities: Rome as Antoninus, and the whole world as a human being. Only what benefits those cities is truly useful to me.

Whatever happens to a person serves the good of the whole universe, and that alone may be enough. Further, what benefits one person also benefits others. Here "profitable" means only in the ordinary sense, applied to things that are neither good nor bad in themselves.

Just as watching the same sights again and again in the amphitheatre becomes tiresome, so life as a whole becomes wearisome, because everything above and below is the same and comes from the same source. The closing question, "How long then?", asks how long this sameness must be endured.

Marcus tells himself to picture all people, of every nation and trade, as already dead, down to minor figures like Philistion and Origanion. He then asks him to turn his mind to famous past men: great speakers, philosophers such as Heraclitus, Pythagoras and Socrates, heroes, generals and tyrants, all now gone.

Even famous thinkers and scholars such as Eudoxus, Hipparchus and Archimedes are long dead, and their fame does not help them now. The one thing that matters is to live honestly and justly, and to be kind even to liars and unjust people.

When you want to cheer yourself up, think of the good qualities of the people you live with, such as one person's industry, another's modesty, and a third's generosity. Examples of virtue give more delight than anything else, so these should be kept in mind.

You should not be unhappy about your body's weight, since you do not expect to weigh three hundred litrae. In the same way, be content with the number of years you have been given, just as you accept the amount of bodily substance you were assigned.

When someone blocks you, try to persuade them, but act justly even against their will. If force stands in the way, accept it calmly and use the obstacle to practise another virtue. Your aim was conditional, not an impossible demand, so you succeed if the effort itself is carried out.

People who love fame treat other people's actions as if they were their own good. People who love pleasure treat their own feelings that way. A person of understanding treats their own actions as their own good.
We can choose not to form an opinion about a thing, and so keep our minds undisturbed. Things by their own nature have no power to force us to judge them in a certain way.

Listen closely to what another person says, and try as far as you can to enter into the speaker's thinking. "Thyself" is an old form of "yourself," so the instruction is to train yourself in this habit.

Marcus asks a pair of questions. If sailors insulted the helmsman, or patients insulted the doctor, would they still listen to anyone else? And how could the helmsman keep the ship safe, or the doctor keep his patients healthy, without that trust?

Things look bad or good to us because of our own state, like honey tasting bitter to someone with jaundice. The passage asks why anger should be any different: a false judgment about events is as strong a force as bile or poison. It implies that anger rests on a false opinion, which can be as misleading as those physical conditions.
No one can stop you from living by the reason that belongs to your own nature. And nothing will happen to you that goes against the reason of the whole universe.
Marcus asks what kind of people others want to please, what they seek by doing so, and by what actions. He then notes how quickly time buries everything, and how much it has already buried.
Badness is nothing new, the passage says. Whatever bad thing happens, one has seen the same kind of thing before, as old histories and present cities show. All things are familiar and short-lived.

Marcus says that our guiding principles fade only if the thoughts that match them are allowed to go out, and that we can keep those thoughts burning. He argues that outside things have no bearing on the mind, so if we hold the right view, we have no cause for disturbance. Recovering one's life, he says, means looking at things again the way one did before.

Marcus lists busy human activities, such as shows, games and labor, and calls them all empty and alike. He says the right response is to stay cheerful and not proud, and to remember that a person's worth matches the worth of what they spend their time on.
In speech, you should attend to what is being said. In action, you should watch what is being done. For speech, look at what the words aim at; for action, look closely at what it means.

Marcus asks whether his understanding is enough for a task. If it is, he should use it for the work, as a tool given by universal nature. If it is not, he should either step aside for someone more capable, unless there is a reason not to, or do his best with the help of another person. All his efforts, alone or with others, should aim at what benefits society.

Many people who were once famous have been forgotten, and many who praised the fame of others have themselves been dead for a long time. Fame does not last, and even those who spread the names of others are soon gone.

Do not feel shame at needing help, because your duty is to do your part like a soldier storming a town. If a lame man cannot climb the walls alone but can with another's help, then he can still do his duty by accepting that help.
Do not let future events worry you. If they come, and it is necessary to face them, you will meet them with the same reason you now use for present troubles.
All things are linked to one another, and the link is sacred. Everything is arranged together to form one universe, with one god, one substance, one law and one reason shared by all thinking beings.

Everything physical soon dissolves back into the whole of matter. Everything that gives a thing its form or cause is soon taken back into the universal reason. And the memory of everything is soon buried under time.

Rational beings, though separate, are made to work together, like the limbs of one body. Calling yourself a "member" (melos) of this whole, rather than a mere "part" (meros), helps you feel that doing good to others is also good for yourself. Saying only "part" means you still help others out of duty, not from genuine care.

Whatever happens to the outside of a person, such as the body, may hurt those parts that feel it and can complain. The person himself is not harmed unless he judges the event to be an evil, and he can choose not to make that judgment.

Whatever others do or say, Marcus says he must stay good. He compares this to gold, emerald, or purple, which keep their color and nature no matter what is said about them. He must keep his own character in the same way.

The mind, which Marcus calls the ruling faculty, cannot be harmed by outside things unless it harms itself through its own judgment. Only its own opinions can make it afraid or in pain. The body may suffer, but the mind stays free if it does not disturb itself.

Marcus is speaking to his own imagination, which keeps returning to trouble him. He tells it to leave, though he is not angry, because he does not want it here. The passage is his way of dismissing an unwelcome thought.

Change is a natural and necessary part of the universe, so there is no reason to fear it. Just as heating wood for a bath or digesting food requires change, changing yourself is equally necessary and part of nature's order.

Everything in the world, all bodies, is swept along by the universal substance, the single stuff that makes up all things. Each thing is joined to the whole, the way parts of the body work together. Time has already swallowed great thinkers like Chrysippus, Socrates and Epictetus, and the same is true of every person and thing.
Marcus worries about one thing: that he might do something human nature does not allow. This covers the act itself, the manner of doing it, and the timing.

It is part of human nature to love even wrongdoers, if you remember that they are relatives, that they act from ignorance, that you both will die soon, and that their wrong has not harmed your inner reason, the ruling part of the mind.
