Nature takes one material, like wax, and shapes it into a horse, then breaks it up and reshapes it into a tree, a man, or something else. Each form lasts only a short time. Breaking up a shape is no more hard than forming it in the first place.

A frown is unnatural, Marcus says. If a person often wears a scowl, their good looks fade until they cannot be restored. He urges the reader to see from this that frowning goes against reason, since losing the awareness of doing wrong would leave no reason to keep living.
Nature, which governs everything, will soon change all the things you see. It will turn their substance into other things, and those into others again, so that the world is always renewed.

When someone wrongs you, look at what they believe is good or bad that led them to do it. Seeing this, you will pity them rather than wonder at or resent them, since you either share that belief or one like it, and so pardoning them is your duty. If you do not hold such beliefs yourself, you will be even more inclined to be kind to someone who is mistaken.

Be grateful for what you already have rather than dwelling on what is missing. Pick the best of your possessions and consider how much you would want them if you lacked them. Enjoy them, but do not come to value them so highly that you would be upset to lose them.
Withdraw into your own mind. The reasoning part of a person, which guides him, is content when it acts justly, and in that contentment it finds calm.

Stop letting impressions pull you about, and keep your attention on the present moment. Understand clearly what happens to yourself or to others, and break each thing into its form and its matter. Remember that your life will end, and leave another person's wrong where it was done, without carrying it with you.

Pay close attention to what is being said, and try to understand both the events that happen and the causes that bring them about. The passage tells the reader to look beneath the surface of things, to grasp both what occurs and what produces it.
Be simple and modest, and do not care about things that fall between good and bad conduct. Love other people, follow God, and remember that a universal law governs everything.
Death is either the scattering of the body, its break-up into atoms, or total annihilation. In each case it is either the end of existence or a change into something else.

Severe pain either overwhelms a person quickly or, if it lasts a long time, becomes bearable. The mind can stay calm by withdrawing into itself, so its guiding part is not harmed. Any bodily part that pain hurts may state its own view of the pain.

Look closely at what people who chase fame are really like: what they avoid and what they pursue. Just as new heaps of sand cover the older ones, later events in life soon bury the earlier ones, so fame does not last.
A person with a wide view, who considers all of time and all of reality, cannot think human life is very great. For such a person, death is not an evil either.
It is shameful for the face to obey the mind and arrange its expression as the mind directs, while the mind fails to arrange and control itself. The point is that the mind should govern itself first.

Marcus quotes Plato's answer to a man who thinks a good person should weigh the risk of death. Plato replies that this is wrong. A good man should look only at whether his actions are just or unjust, and whether they are the deeds of a good or bad person.
A soldier should stay at the post he has chosen or been given, and face danger there. He should not count death or anything else as a reason to leave, since deserting one's post is shameful.

Marcus says that what is noble and good may be different from simply staying alive or being saved. A real man should not cling to how long he lives. He should leave such matters to the gods, accepting that no one can escape fate, and focus on living well in the time he has.

Picture yourself moving along with the stars as you watch them, and keep thinking about how the basic elements change into one another. The writer says such thoughts clear away the dirt of everyday earthly life.

Marcus quotes Plato's advice that a person thinking about human affairs should look down on earthly life from a height. Seen that way, all the varied human activities, from wars and markets to births, deaths and festivals, appear as one mixed whole of opposites arranged in order.

Looking back at past shifts of power shows what the future will be like, because events keep the same pattern. So watching human life for forty years is the same as watching it for ten thousand, since nothing new will appear.
Everything that grew from the earth goes back to the earth, and everything that came from heavenly seed goes back to the heavens. Each thing returns to the place it came from.

Marcus is listing the two possible explanations for what happens to the body at death, as the Stoics and their rivals saw it. Either the tiny particles that hold the body together come apart, or the lifeless material parts scatter in the same way. Both options end with the body breaking up into its parts.

Trying to escape death with food, drink, or magic is pointless, as the passage sees it. Instead, we must accept what fate sends and work through it without complaint. "The channel's course" is an image from sailing: a ship's path being steered away from death.

Someone may be more skilled at defeating an opponent in wrestling, yet not be more sociable, more modest, better able to accept whatever happens, or more forgiving of others' faults. Skill in fighting, the passage says, does not make a person better in these qualities.

Where a task can be done in line with the reason shared by gods and humans, there is nothing to fear. If we can gain something through action that succeeds and fits our nature, no harm is to be expected.

You can always, in any place and time, accept your present situation with devotion, treat the people around you fairly, and examine each thought carefully so that no unchecked idea gets in. The passage says these three things are always within a person's power.

Do not study what other people's guiding principles are. Instead, follow what nature requires, both the nature of the whole world through the events that happen to you, and your own nature through the duties you must perform. Every being should act according to its own make-up, and rational beings exist for one another.

Marcus names three basic features of a person's nature: a drive toward other people, control of the mind over bodily urges and feelings, and freedom from error and deception. If the ruling part of the mind keeps hold of these three, it stays on its proper course and has what belongs to it.
Imagine you have already died and your life up to now is over. Then live the time that is still left to you in agreement with nature.
Accept and love whatever happens to you, because it is woven into your personal destiny. The passage asks what could be more fitting than that.

Marcus asks why we should copy people who once got upset by events and now are gone. He suggests leaving other people's agitations to them and focusing on using what happens to us well. His advice is to attend to yourself and try to be a good person in every action.
Good is found inside a person, not outside. Like a spring, it keeps flowing if one keeps digging into it.

The body should be firm and steady, with no awkward movements or poses. Just as the mind shows intelligence and good order in the face, the whole body should show the same, and all of this should be done naturally, without pretense.
The art of living, he says, is like wrestling rather than dancing. A wrestler must stay steady and ready to meet attacks that come suddenly and without warning.

Look closely at the people whose approval you want, and at the principles that guide them. If you understand where their opinions and desires come from, you will neither blame those who wrong you without meaning to, nor crave their approval.

People, according to the philosopher, lose truth against their will, and so they also lose justice, self-control and goodwill in the same way. Keeping this in mind, Marcus says, makes a person kinder toward everyone.

Pain does not dishonor a person or harm the rational mind, which stays unaffected by it. Epicurus's point helps too: most pain is neither unbearable nor endless, provided you do not add to it in your imagination. Some unpleasant states, such as heavy drowsiness, heat, or lack of appetite, are not pain at all, so when you feel discontent over them, you are really yielding to pain.

Marcus asks how we can know that Telauges was not better in character than Socrates. Socrates' famous acts, such as his noble death and his skill in argument, do not by themselves prove that he was the superior man. Telauges is otherwise unknown here; the passage gives him as a comparison to Socrates.

The passage asks what kind of soul Socrates had. It suggests he was content to be just to people and devout toward the gods, without being upset by others' wickedness, enslaved to their ignorance, or troubled by what life gave him, and without letting his mind be swayed by bodily feelings.

Human reason is not so tied to the body that a person cannot govern themselves and master what belongs to them. A person can be truly good and divine without anyone noticing, and little is needed for a happy life. Even if you cannot master logic or natural science, you can still aim for freedom, modesty, kindness to others, and obedience to God.

The main point is that a person can keep their mind calm and free from outside control, even when others criticize them or when the body is attacked. Nothing stops the mind from judging things clearly and seeing each thing for what it really is, whatever others think it looks like.

Whatever comes to hand, the person should treat it as the very material needed for practicing virtue and skill. Everything that happens relates to God or to people, so it is never new or too hard to deal with; it is ordinary material to work on.

Moral perfection, in this view, means living each day as if it were your last. It also means avoiding three things: being overly excited, being numb or sluggish, and pretending to be what you are not.

The gods live forever and are not annoyed at having to put up with so many bad people, and they still care for them in every way. Mortal humans, who will die soon, should ask whether they are tired of bearing with the bad, when they are bad themselves.
It is foolish to try to escape other people's badness, which cannot be done, while not trying to escape one's own badness, which can be done.
The rational and social part of the mind ranks anything that is neither intelligent nor social as lower than itself. In other words, the mind judges what lacks reason or community to be beneath it.
When you have done a good deed and someone has received it, the passage asks why you still want something more, such as a reputation for goodness or a reward. It calls such wanting foolish.
Nobody gets tired of receiving what helps them. Acting according to nature is useful, so one should not grow tired of doing good to others, which is also a useful thing to do.

Everything that happens either follows from a chain of cause and effect, or the highest directing power of the universe acts without any reason at all. Keeping this in mind, the passage says, will bring calm in many matters.

Marcus is saying that if a passage is not corrupted, it is worth working hard to find the writer's real meaning. He believes the writer did mean something, even if readers disagree about what it was. If he has explained this author's meaning correctly, he has reached an answer to an important question.

Marcus is telling himself that he can no longer have lived his whole life, or even his life since youth, as a philosopher should. Others and he himself can see he is far from philosophy, so he has lost any easy claim to the name of philosopher, and his way of life now works against it.

Once you have seen clearly what really matters, stop worrying about how others see you. Be content to live the rest of your life as your nature wills, and let nothing else pull you away from that. Wealth, reputation, pleasure and clever argument have not brought happiness, so the author asks where happiness is to be found.

A person does what human nature requires by holding certain basic beliefs about good and bad, which then shape their feelings and actions. Those beliefs are that only what makes a person just, temperate, manly and free is good, and that only what works against these qualities is bad.

Before each action, Marcus asks himself whether he will regret it, since he will soon be dead and everything will be gone. He concludes that the right course is to act as a rational, social being who shares the same law as God.

Marcus Aurelius contrasts famous conquerors with the philosophers Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates. He says the philosophers understood the nature and causes of things and lived by principles that matched their work. The conquerors, by contrast, had many concerns and were slaves to many things.

People will keep acting the same way no matter what you do, even if you were to burst with anger or frustration. The point is that other people's behaviour is outside your control, so trying to force change through your own distress achieves nothing.

Do not be upset, because everything happens according to the nature of the whole universe, and everyone is soon forgotten, as the emperors Hadrian and Augustus were. Keep your mind on your duty: act as a good person should, and speak honestly and modestly, without pretending.

Nature, the universal order, constantly moves things from one place to another and changes them. Everything is in flux, yet nothing new should frighten us, since all things are familiar and their arrangement stays the same.

A rational being is content when it goes well, which means four things: it accepts only what is true and certain, it acts for the good of others, it wants and avoids only what it can control, and it accepts what the whole of nature gives it. Each being is part of that whole, as a leaf is part of a plant.

Human nature is part of a larger nature that cannot be blocked and is both reasoning and just. This nature gives each thing its share according to its worth, timing, substance, cause, activity and circumstances. So one should compare whole things with whole things, not single parts, when judging whether two things are equal.

You may not have time to read, but you do have time to curb arrogance, to rise above pleasure and pain, to be free of the desire for fame, and to stay calm toward foolish and ungrateful people, even to care for them.

Stop complaining, in anyone's hearing, about the life of the imperial court or about your own life. The sentence is an instruction to the writer himself, telling him not to let others hear him criticise his surroundings or his circumstances.

Regret is blame for having neglected something useful. What is truly good must be useful, and a perfectly good person would take care of it. Such a person would never regret turning down a sensual pleasure, so Marcus concludes that pleasure is neither good nor useful.

Marcus is listing questions to ask about any thing you meet: what it is in itself, what it is made of, what its cause or form is, what role it plays in the world, and how long it lasts. The passage is a set of questions for examining things closely, not a set of answers.

When you get up from sleep unwillingly, Marcus reminds himself that doing social duties fits human nature, while sleep is shared even with animals. What belongs to each person's nature is more truly their own and more agreeable to them.

Whenever something strikes the mind, he says, one should always try to examine it using three fields of Stoic study: physics (the study of nature), ethics (the study of how to live well), and dialectic (the study of reasoning and argument).

When you meet someone, ask what they believe about good and bad, about pleasure, pain, fame, shame, life and death. If their beliefs are of a certain kind, their actions will seem unsurprising, since they are driven by those beliefs.

Just as it would be odd to be surprised when a fig-tree bears figs, it is equally odd to be surprised when the world produces the things it naturally produces. A doctor should not be surprised by a fever, nor a sailor by an unfavorable wind.

Changing your mind when someone corrects your error is as much an exercise of freedom as holding on to the error. Either way, the action comes from your own movement, judgment and understanding, so it is yours.

Marcus says that if something is up to you, you should fix it, and if it is up to someone else, you should still not blame the atoms (chance) or the gods, since both are foolish. If you cannot change the cause or the thing itself, blaming gets you nothing, and nothing should be done without a purpose.

When something dies, it does not leave the universe. Its parts stay here, changing and breaking down into the elements that make up the universe, including the elements that make up a person. These parts change too, and they do not complain about it.

Everything exists for a purpose, such as a horse or a vine, and even the sun and the gods have one. So the question is what purpose a human being has. The writer doubts that pleasure is the answer and asks whether common sense accepts it.

Nature cares about how a thing ends as much as how it begins and how long it lasts, just as a person who throws a ball cares about its landing. Asking whether a thrown ball rising, falling, or landing is good or bad, or whether a bubble is harmed when it bursts, shows that such changes are not good or bad in themselves. The passage says the same of a light.

Look at the body closely, inside and out, and see what it really is. Think about what it becomes when it grows old and when it falls ill. The point is that the body is a plain physical thing that decays.

Praise and fame do not last. Both the one who praises and the one who is praised will soon be gone, and so will anyone who remembers them. All of this happens in one small corner of the world, where people do not even agree with themselves, and the whole earth is only a point in the larger scale of things.
You are being punished fairly, the passage says, because you choose to become good tomorrow instead of being good today. The point is that putting off goodness to a later day is itself the fault.
Whatever I do, I do for the good of humankind. Whatever happens to me, I accept it and trace it back to the gods, the source from which all events come.

Things that seem pleasant or proper at first, like a bath, can look disgusting when you see what they really are: oil, sweat, dirt and dirty water. The passage says the same is true of every part of life and everything in it.
Each person named saw someone close to them die, and then died too. Marcus uses these cases to say that this is how everything is: the living always follow the dead.

Marcus asks where clever men are now, naming a few who were once known for their wit. His answer is that they are all gone: some were forgotten quickly, some became figures in stories, and some have vanished even from those stories.

Your body, which the passage calls this "little compound," will either break apart, or your breath will stop, or your soul will be moved somewhere else. Death is one of these three outcomes, and the passage asks the reader to keep this in mind.

A person finds satisfaction in doing what is proper to a human being. The passage names these proper acts: showing goodwill to other people, not being ruled by sense impressions, judging appearances fairly, and understanding the nature of the universe and what happens in it.

Marcus says a person has three kinds of connection to other things. The first is to the body that surrounds them, the second is to the divine cause that all things come from, and the third is to the people they live with.

Pain is either harm to the body or harm to the soul. If it harms the body, the body can speak for itself. The soul, though, can keep its calm and refuse to judge pain an evil, since judgment, desire and aversion all happen inside it and no outside evil reaches that high.

Marcus tells himself to clear his mind of harmful imaginings by repeating that he has the power to keep his soul free of wrongdoing, desire and disturbance. By seeing things as they really are and valuing each one accordingly, he holds that this power comes from his own nature.
Speak in the senate and to anyone else in a way that fits the moment and the listener, without pretense. Keep your speech plain and direct.

Marcus lists the people around Augustus, the first Roman emperor, and notes that all of them are dead. He asks the reader to think of whole families ending, not just single deaths, and points out that someone must always be the last of his line.

Your duty is to act well in each action, and if each act does its duty as far as it can, you should be content. Outside things may block a particular action, but nothing can block acting justly, soberly and thoughtfully. If another action is blocked, you accept it and turn your effort to what is allowed, and a new opportunity appears in its place.

A severed hand or foot lying apart from the body is the image. Marcus says a person who refuses to accept what happens, cuts himself off from others, or acts against the good of the community makes himself like that severed part.

A person who has separated from the natural whole, of which they were made a part, can still reunite with it. Marcus says this is a privilege given to humans alone, since no other separated part can come back together. Humans also have the power never to be cut off at all.

The passage describes a part being separated from a whole and then allowed to return, rejoin it, and take its place again. In Stoic thought, this image stands for a person's relation to the universe, which the passage presents as a whole of which each being is a part.

Just as the universe takes every obstacle opposed to it and turns it into part of itself, a rational being can take any hindrance and use it as material for its own purposes. The passage presents this as a power given to humans by universal nature.

Do not burden yourself by imagining your whole life's troubles at once. Deal with each moment by asking whether it is truly unbearable, since you would be ashamed to admit it if so. Remember that only the present causes pain, and it is small if you limit your mind to it.

Marcus asks whether anyone still sits at the tombs of the emperors Verus and Hadrian, and says it would be absurd. Even if mourners did, he argues, the dead would not know it, would not be pleased, and would not gain immortality. Everyone grows old and dies in the natural order, and the body is only foul matter.
In Marcus Aurelius's view, human nature shows no virtue that works against justice. It does show one that works against the love of pleasure, and that virtue is temperance, or self-control.

If you drop your judgment about what seems to cause you pain, your inner self stays completely safe. When asked what this self is, the answer is reason. If another part of you suffers, that part may form its own judgment about itself, while reason stays untroubled.

Anything that blocks a creature's natural function harms that creature. For animals, blocking sense perception or desire is an evil, and for plants, whatever hinders their growth is harmful. So whatever blocks the mind is harmful to the rational nature. Marcus asks the reader to apply this to himself: pain and pleasure are for the senses to deal with, and obstacles to his aims are a matter for his reason.

Marcus says that an obstacle is only a harm to a person as a reasoning being if the effort was made without any reservation. Looking at the normal course of events, nothing has yet been damaged or blocked. Only the mind's own proper activities are beyond the reach of others: fire, iron, tyrants and abuse cannot touch them. Like a sphere, the mind keeps its shape once formed.

I will not cause myself pain, because I have never meant to cause pain even to another person. The writer holds that he has always refused to harm others on purpose, so harming himself would go against that same rule.

People enjoy different things, but the writer's own delight is to keep his inner guiding part (his "ruling faculty," meaning his mind or reason) healthy. He wants to face every person and everything that happens with an open, welcoming attitude, and to treat each thing according to its worth.

Focus on living well in the present, rather than chasing fame after death. People who want a good reputation later do not realize that future people will be just as hard to please as the people they already dislike, and both groups will die. So what future people say or think about you should not matter to you.

Marcus speaks to the body, saying it can be sent anywhere. He says his inner, divine part stays calm and content wherever it is, as long as it acts according to its own nature. He asks whether a change of place alone could make the soul unhappy, and what could be a good reason for that.

Everything that happens to a thing is natural for that kind of thing: a man meets human troubles, an ox acts like an ox, a vine like a vine, a stone like a stone. So if nature brings only what is usual for each thing, there is no reason to complain, since nature brings nothing that a person cannot bear.

Our distress comes from our own judgment about things, not from the things themselves, and we can change that judgment. If we cannot do what we think is right because of an obstacle outside our control, we should not grieve over it. If that leaves life seeming not worth living, the passage says we should leave life calmly, accepting even the obstacles.

The main point is that the ruling part of the mind cannot be defeated when it is calm, content with itself, and acts only by its own choice. A mind free from passions is like a fortress, a safe place to retreat to. Someone who sees this and still fails to retreat there is unhappy.

Stop at what you directly perceive and add no judgment of your own. Hearing that someone insults you is not the same as being harmed, and seeing a child is sick is not the same as seeing the child is in danger. Keeping to bare appearances means nothing harms you, though Marcus adds that one should judge like someone who knows all that happens in the world.

Marcus says that when something is unpleasant, such as a bitter cucumber or thorns on the road, you should simply get rid of it or avoid it, without asking why such things exist. He compares complaining about them to a carpenter being mocked for complaining about wood shavings, since workers have places to put their waste. Nature, he notes, has no outside space to throw things into.

Nature, the force that produces and orders all things, is described as self-sufficient. It takes whatever decays or grows old within itself and turns it into new things, so it needs no outside material and no place to throw its waste. It has its own space, matter and skill.

Do not be lazy in what you do, careless in what you say, or scattered in your thinking. Keep your inner mind free of conflict and not spilled out in show, and do not be so busy that you have no time to yourself.

Even if people kill, mutilate, or curse you, they cannot make your mind impure, wise, self-controlled, or just. Marcus compares the mind to a clear spring that stays pure however much mud or abuse is thrown into it. He says the way to keep such a spring is to train yourself each hour toward freedom, contentment, simplicity, and modesty.

Someone who does not know what the world is, or what it is for, does not know who they are or where they stand. So the passage asks what one should think of a person who seeks praise from others who themselves lack this knowledge.

Marcus asks whether anyone should want praise from a person who constantly condemns himself, or wants to please someone who is not pleased with himself. His point is that a man who regrets most of his own actions cannot be a reliable source of approval.

Your breathing already matches the air around you, and the passage urges that your reason should likewise match the universal reason that holds all things together. Just as air fills everything for anyone able to breathe it, this reason is spread through all things and is available to anyone willing to take it in.
Wickedness does not harm the universe as a whole, nor does one person's wickedness harm another person. It harms only the person who has it, and that person could be free of it whenever they chose.

Marcus says that another person's free will is no more part of his own choices than that person's breath and body are. Although people are made to live for one another, each person's inner ruling power has its own job. If it were otherwise, a neighbor's wrongdoing would harm him, and God did not intend that his unhappiness depend on someone else.

The sun's light spreads out in every direction, but it is not poured out or lost from the sun. Its rays are called "extensions" because they stretch outward. A ray can be seen by letting sunlight pass through a small opening into a dark room: it travels in a straight line and is broken up when a solid object blocks it.

Marcus compares the mind's understanding to a steady light. It should spread outward calmly, without rushing or crashing into obstacles, and it should shine on whatever receives it. A body that refuses this light cuts itself off from it.

Someone who fears death fears either losing the ability to feel, or feeling something different. But if there is no feeling, there is no harm to feel. And if the feeling changes, the person is simply a different kind of living being, still alive.
The mind moves in a different way from an arrow, yet it still goes straight toward its goal. It does so even when it is being careful or when it is busy investigating something.

Acting unjustly is, in this view, a kind of impiety, because nature made rational beings to help one another and never to harm one another. Lying is also impiety, since nature is the reality of all things and is itself called truth.

Lying on purpose is wrong because it is unjust, and lying by mistake still goes against the natural order of the world. Someone who lies cuts against nature, which gave people the ability to tell truth from falsehood. Chasing pleasure as good and avoiding pain as bad is also called impiety.

Marcus is saying that a person who judges the universe by pleasure and pain will end up blaming it. He sees the bad enjoying good things and the good suffering, which seems unfair to him. Fearing pain or pursuing pleasure, he says, leads to impiety, meaning a lack of reverence toward the universal order.

Things that nature treats equally, such as pain and pleasure, life and death, or honor and dishonor, should be met with equal calm by anyone who wants to follow nature. Whoever reacts to them unequally is, Marcus says, acting against nature's will.

Marcus says that universal nature (the whole ordering of the cosmos) treats all things equally. He rejects the view that events simply happen alike to a series of beings, or that they follow from an original plan of Providence (a divine ordering) that set the world in motion and fixed its powers from the start.

The best fate would be to leave life never having been tainted by lying, pretence, excess or pride. If that is not possible, leaving life after having had enough of these is the next best thing. The ruin of the mind is a worse plague than bad air, because bad air harms animals while the ruin of the mind harms human beings as humans.

Do not look down on death, and do not be upset by it. Death is part of nature, like growing up, aging, and other natural changes of life, so a thoughtful person should wait for it calmly as one of nature's processes.

Just as a child is about to be born, we should be ready for the moment our soul leaves the body. For comfort about death, Marcus suggests thinking about the people and things we will leave behind, and remembering that we should bear with others patiently rather than be angry at them.

Marcus says the only thing that could make us want to keep living is being able to live with people who share our principles. He notes that quarrels among people who live together are so troubling that one might wish for death, lest one lose one's own sense of self.
Doing wrong harms the person who does it, not only the victim. The wrongdoer makes himself bad by acting unjustly, so the wrong falls on himself.
A person can be unjust by failing to act, not only by doing wrong. Refusing or neglecting to do what is right counts as injustice just as much as committing a wrong deed.

The passage says that three things are enough for a good life: a judgment based on reason, actions aimed at the good of others, and acceptance of whatever happens. The writer asks for nothing more than these three present states.

Stop letting passing impressions take hold of you, hold back your desires, and put out your cravings. Keep your governing mind under its own control, so that outside things do not rule it. "Ruling faculty" means the reasoning part of the mind.

Creatures without reason share one kind of life, and reasonable creatures share one intelligent soul. Just as all earthly things share one earth and all seeing creatures share one light and one air, reasoning beings are bound together by a single soul.

Things that share a common nature tend to move toward others of their own kind. Earth falls toward earth, liquids flow together, and air-like things rise in the same way. Without some outside force, they would need something to hold them apart.

Fire rises toward the fire of its own kind, and dry things catch light easily because little in them resists burning. Marcus compares this to rational beings: whatever shares in the common reason is drawn toward what is like itself, and more strongly the higher it stands.

Marcus says that a drawing-together power is found at different levels of nature. Animals show it in swarms, herds and care for their young. Humans show it in communities, friendships, families and treaties. The highest things, such as the stars, stay apart yet are still joined in some way.

Marcus says that people are naturally drawn to one another, even though they often try to avoid this. Things in nature tend to join together, and humans are no exception. He concludes that a person completely cut off from other people is harder to find than a piece of earth that touches no other earth.

Man, God and the universe each bear fruit in their proper seasons, just as a vine does. If the word "fruit" is usually applied only to plants, that does not matter. Reason bears fruit for others and for itself, and it produces more things like itself.

If you can, correct wrongdoers by teaching them; if you cannot, remember that you were given patience for exactly this situation. The gods are patient with such people too, and even help them gain health, wealth and reputation. Nothing stops you from doing the same, he asks.
Work without treating yourself as miserable or wanting pity or praise. Aim your will at one thing: moving yourself to act and restraining yourself as the reason of the community requires.
Today the writer says he has freed himself from all his troubles. He corrects himself: he did not remove them from outside, because the troubles were inside him, in his own judgments.
Everything in life is the same and familiar, lasts only a short time, and has little real value in its substance. Things are now just as they were for the people who have already died.
External things exist on their own. They know nothing about themselves and make no judgments. So the thing that judges them is the ruling faculty, the mind's leading part.
For a rational social being, good and bad both lie in what he does, not in what he passively undergoes. Virtue and vice are likewise found in action rather than in inaction.
A thrown stone is not harmed by falling back down, and it gains nothing from having been thrown up. The point is that rising and falling are neither good nor bad for a thing in itself.

Look closely at people's guiding principles, and you will see what kind of judges they really are, the ones you fear. Their judgments reflect their own inner standards, and those standards are often poor.
Everything is constantly changing, and that includes you and the whole universe. Each thing is always being altered and, in a way, always breaking down.

Stopping activity, ceasing to move or hold opinions, and in a sense dying are not evil, Marcus says. He points out that each stage of a person's life ended in a kind of death, such as childhood giving way to youth. Since those changes were not frightening, the final end of life should not be feared either.

Examine three things quickly: your own inner guiding faculty, so you can make it just; the universe, so you remember that you are a part of it; and your neighbor, so you can tell whether he acted knowingly or in ignorance, and recall that his inner faculty is like yours.

Every action should serve the good of the community, as you are part of a social whole. An act with no connection to that common purpose breaks your life apart and works like a mutiny, like a man in an assembly who stands alone against the general agreement.

Marcus compares ordinary human pursuits to children's squabbles and games, and to weak spirits hauling corpses around. He says the world's real nature shows more clearly in pictures of the dead, a reminder of how little these pursuits matter.
Look at the form of a thing by itself, apart from the matter it is made of. Then consider how long a thing of that particular form is naturally meant to last.

You have suffered endless troubles because you were not satisfied with your ruling faculty (the mind, or reason, that guides you) when it did what it is naturally made to do. The writer then says enough of this.

When others blame, hate, or speak ill of you, look inside them to see what kind of people they are. Their opinions of you are not worth worrying about. Still, you should be kind to them, since they are by nature your fellows, and the gods help them toward what they value.

Marcus says the universe moves in repeating cycles. He offers three possible causes: a universal intelligence acting on each event, a single first movement that sets everything in sequence, or indivisible particles (atoms). His conclusion is that if there is a god, all is well, and if chance rules, one should not let oneself be ruled by chance either.

Everything in the world keeps changing, and the earth itself will one day cover us all and will change too. If a person thinks about how quickly these changes follow one another, like waves, he will look down on whatever can perish.

Everything is swept along by the universal cause, like a flooded winter stream. Marcus criticizes people busy with politics who think they are philosophers. He tells himself to act as nature now requires, without seeking applause or hoping for an ideal state, and to count small good results as worthwhile, since no one can truly change others' opinions.

Without changing one's opinions, a person is only a slave who groans while pretending to obey. Marcus says famous rulers like Alexander, Philip and Demetrius must judge for themselves whether they lived by the common nature, and that he is not bound to copy them as if they were tragic actors. Philosophy, he says, is simple and modest, so he does not want to be pulled toward arrogance and pride.

Imagine looking down on all of human life from above: its crowds, festivals, voyages, births and deaths. Then consider how many people, past, future and foreign, will never know or will soon forget your name, and how quickly praise turns to blame. Fame after death, and reputation, are worth nothing.

Be undisturbed by things that come from outside you, and act justly in what comes from your own inner reasoning, directing your actions toward acts that benefit others. This, the passage says, is what fits your nature.

You can drop many useless worries, since they exist only in your own judgment. Then you gain room for yourself by thinking of the whole universe, the endless span of time, and how brief a single life is between the endless time before birth and the endless time after death.
All that we see will soon pass away, and those who watch it fade will soon die too. Whether someone dies very old or very young, they end up in the same state.

Marcus asks what drives other people: what their guiding principles are, what occupies them, and why they love and honor certain things. He tells himself to imagine their inner selves stripped bare. Seen that way, he suggests, the idea that their blame can harm or their praise can help him is absurd.

Loss is just change, and nature takes pleasure in change. Everything happens rightly under nature's order, and things have always been and always will be much the same. The closing question asks whether the world is therefore doomed to endless evil with no god able to fix it, a view the passage rejects.

Everything solid or valuable, such as water, dust, bones, rock, gold, clothing and dye, is traced back to a base matter that is decaying or crude. Even breath, the life-force, is described as the same kind of thing, constantly changing from one form to another.

Marcus is telling himself to stop complaining and fretting over life. He says that whatever upsets him is either its outward form or its underlying matter, and he should look at each closely, since nothing else is involved. He adds that studying these things for a hundred years or three would bring no different result.

Marcus argues that either the universe is one reasoning whole, in which each part should accept what serves the whole, or it is only random atoms mixing and scattering. Either way, he asks why the mind should be upset. He then challenges his own inner reason, asking whether it has died, decayed, turned hypocritical, or become like an animal grazing with the herd.

Marcus argues that praying for outside things makes no sense. If the gods have no power, prayer is pointless. If they do have power, he asks why people do not pray for inner strength, such as freedom from fear, desire and pain, instead of asking that particular events be avoided or happen.

Marcus argues that if people can work together with others, they can also work together toward these ends. He says it is better to use what lies within our control as a free person would, rather than craving what is beyond it. He suggests that the gods may help even with things within our control, so one should try praying for such help and see.

Marcus says that people pray for the wrong things, such as getting what they desire or escaping what they dislike. He advises changing the prayer so that it asks for freedom from the desire or fear itself, and then seeing what results.

Epicurus, while ill, said he did not talk about his bodily pain with visitors. He kept discussing the nature of things, focusing on how the mind can stay free of disturbance and keep its own good even while the body suffers.

The speaker says he never let doctors make a show of solemnity over his illness, and his life went on well and happily. He advises the reader to act the same way when sick or in any other situation. Never giving up philosophy and avoiding idle talk with ignorant people or those who do not understand nature is, he says, a rule shared by all philosophical schools.
Keep your attention on the task you are doing right now, and on the tool you are using to do it. The passage does not say more than this. It asks for focus on the present action and its means.

When you feel angry at someone's shameless behavior, remember that shameless people must exist in the world. Since that cannot be otherwise, do not expect the impossible. The same reasoning applies to dishonest, faithless, and wrongdoing people.

Marcus says that remembering people who do wrong is unavoidable should make you kinder to each person. Nature gave humans a remedy for each kind of wrongdoer: for example, gentleness against a foolish person. Wrongdoers can also be corrected by teaching them, since anyone who errs has missed his aim.

Marcus says that other people cannot make your mind worse; the harm you feel comes only from your own mind. If an uninstructed man acts like one, that is not strange, so you should blame yourself for expecting better from him.

When someone lets you down, Marcus says, you should first look at yourself. You had reason to expect the mistake, or you gave your kindness expecting something back, so the fault is yours. Once you have done a favor, he asks, what more is needed?

Doing something that fits your nature is reward enough, so there is no need to ask for payment. The writer compares this to the eye, which needs no payment for seeing, or the feet for walking. Humans are made for kindness and service to the common good, so a kind act already gives them what is theirs.

Marcus asks his own soul whether it will ever become good, simple, unified and open, and whether it will ever be content and lack nothing. He asks whether it will stop longing for pleasures, for more time, for a better place or climate, or for pleasant company.

Marcus asks whether a person can be content with their present situation and with everything around them, trusting that all comes from the gods and is good. He asks if they can live in harmony with gods and humans, neither blaming them nor being blamed by them.

Marcus Aurelius says a person should first do what their nature needs as a physical thing, then what it needs as a living being, then what it needs as a rational, social being. Each step is allowed only if it does not harm the higher nature. He concludes that these rules are enough and nothing else needs worrying about.

Whatever happens either fits what you are naturally able to bear or does not. If it fits, you should bear it without complaint. If it does not, it will end once it has worn you down, so complaining is pointless. You can also make hard things bearable by judging them to be in your interest or duty.
If someone is wrong, correct them gently and point out the error. If you cannot do that, blame yourself, or blame no one at all.
Whatever happens to a person was determined from eternity. A chain of causes has been spinning out the thread of a person's life, along with everything that befalls it.

I am a part of a whole run by nature, and so I am closely tied to the other parts of that whole. Remembering this, I should not be discontented with what is given to me from the whole, because nothing that helps the whole can harm a part.

Every nature shares a common principle, but the nature of the universe has the extra feature that no outside cause can force it to produce anything harmful to itself. Marcus concludes that, remembering he is part of this whole, he will accept whatever happens.

Because I am closely bound to other people, who are of the same kind as myself, I will do nothing antisocial. Instead I will direct my efforts toward the common good and away from what works against it.
If a person does things in the right way, life can go on happily. Marcus compares this to a citizen who keeps doing what helps his fellow citizens and accepts whatever the state gives him.

The parts of the world must change, and in that sense they must perish. But if this change were a natural evil for the parts, the whole could not stay in good condition, since its parts would be constantly breaking apart in various ways.
Marcus asks whether Nature deliberately meant to make her own parts suffer evil and fall into it, or whether these outcomes happen without her knowing. He says both possibilities are hard to believe.

It is foolish to say that change and breaking apart are natural, and yet be shocked when things change or fall apart as if something unnatural had happened. Each thing dissolves back into the parts it was made from.

Marcus says that at death the body breaks back into its basic elements, which return to the universal reason, whether the world ends in fire or renews itself. He adds that the solid and airy parts of the body are not really yours from birth, since they were gathered only recently from food and breath.

The body, which takes in additions such as food, changes, but not the body a mother bore. Even if this changing body is closely bound to the other part, which has the power to change, that is no real objection to what has been said.

Marcus is saying that once a person has taken on these qualities (good, modest, true, rational, even-minded, and noble-hearted), they should keep them and quickly return to them if they lose them. He explains two of the words: "rational" means paying careful attention to each thing and not being careless, and "equanimity" means willingly accepting what the common nature assigns to you.

Magnanimity means raising the thinking part of yourself above bodily pleasure and pain, and above fame, death and similar things. If you keep hold of this quality without wanting other people to call you by its name, you become a different person and begin a new kind of life.

Marcus says it is foolish to keep living the same damaged way, torn and defiled, just to hold on to life. He compares this to wounded gladiators who beg to be spared until tomorrow, only to face the same beasts again. Instead, he tells the reader to settle on a few core principles and stay with them, as if living on the Islands of the Blessed.

If you find you are losing your hold on these principles, withdraw to some quiet place to keep them, or else leave life calmly, not in anger. Remembering the gods helps, because they do not want flattery but want reasonable beings to become like themselves.

Each thing is what it is by doing its own work: a fig-tree does the work of a fig-tree, a dog the work of a dog, a bee the work of a bee, and a man the work of a man. The passage says that a man should keep in mind that his work is that of a human being.
The passage describes a place where human life is easiest. There is no snow, storm or rain there, only gentle west winds blowing in from the Ocean, the river that was thought to surround the earth.

A note in this edition says the Odyssey's author likely repeated an old legend rather than describing real places. It suggests the two islands Sertorius heard of may be Madeira and a nearby island, and refers to Pindar for comparison.

Marcus says that mimicry, war, astonishment, dullness, and slavery will daily wear away his sound principles. He then urges that he should observe nature closely while acting, so that his practical skill grows, his contemplation is exercised, and his confidence rests on knowing each thing, shown quietly rather than displayed.

Marcus is asking when he will find time for simplicity, seriousness, and a full understanding of every thing. That understanding would cover what each thing is made of, where it fits in the universe, how long it lasts, what it is composed of, who might own it, and who can give or take it away.

Marcus compares people who feel proud of their catches to spiders and hunters. A spider is proud of a fly, a hunter of a hare, a fish, a boar or a bear, and a conqueror of Sarmatians (a people from the east). He asks whether, judged by their own reasoning, these proud people are no better than robbers.

Watching how all things turn into one another is said to produce greatness of mind. A person who sees this clearly accepts that he must soon leave the body and the world, so he acts justly in everything he does and accepts whatever happens as part of universal nature.

A person who is truly good does not worry about what others say, think, or do against him. He is content with two things: acting justly in what he is doing now, and accepting what has been given to him. He sets aside distracting pursuits and aims only to follow the straight course set by the law, which means following God.

If you can see what should be done, follow that path calmly without looking back. If you cannot see clearly, stop and seek good advice. When other obstacles arise, keep going as far as you can, holding to what is just. Someone who follows reason in everything stays both calm and active.

On waking, Marcus asks himself whether it matters to him if someone else acts justly and rightly. His answer is that it makes no difference to him, because another person's conduct does not change his own.

Marcus asks whether the reader has not noticed that people who act proud when praising or blaming others behave just as badly in private, in their daily habits. He says such people steal and rob with their mind, the most valuable part of a person, rather than with their hands. The mind is also what produces fidelity, modesty, truth, law and happiness.

The wise and humble person accepts that nature gives and takes back everything. Such a person says, in effect, "Give what you will, and take back what you will." This is said without pride, out of obedience, and with contentment.

Life is short, so live as if on a mountain, apart from the crowd. Where a person lives does not matter if they live in the wider world as a citizen of one community, and living truly according to nature is better than living as most people do, even if others oppose it.

Think of all of time and all of matter as a whole, and see each single thing as tiny by comparison. Measured against the whole, a thing is no bigger than a fig seed in substance and lasts no longer than one turn of a drill in time.
Everything that exists is already breaking down and changing, decaying or scattering apart. Nature has made all things so that they die.

Marcus is asking the reader to picture people in their ordinary bodily acts, such as eating and sleeping, and then in their proud or angry moods of power. He points out that they were once slaves to others and to their own desires, and that before long they will be in a different state. The point is that status and power are temporary.

Each thing receives what is good for it, because the universal nature (the natural order of the whole world) brings it to that thing. Whatever nature brings is good for the thing at the moment it arrives.

Nature is shown as loving what it does: the earth loves rain, the sky loves, and the universe loves to bring new things into being. Marcus answers that he loves as the universe loves, and he notes that people also speak of things as wanting to be produced.

Whatever happens, one of three things holds: you are living in a place you have grown used to, you are leaving by your own choice, or you are dying after doing your duty. Beyond these there is nothing else to fear, so take heart.

Any place is much the same as any other, whether a hillside, the seashore, or a particular plot of land. Marcus says that wherever a person chooses to live, they will find what the philosopher Plato described: a settled life, like a shepherd's fold on a mountain, even inside a city's walls.

Marcus notes that the Greek verb "philei" means both "loves" and "is accustomed to" or "does." He takes this everyday double meaning as a philosophical truth. His point is that great truths often sit in ordinary speech, and many people use them without grasping their full meaning.

Marcus is asking himself a set of questions about his mind, which the Stoics called the "ruling faculty." He asks what state it is in now, what it is being shaped into, and what it is being used for. He also asks whether it has lost its reason, been cut off from community with others, or been merged with the body so that it moves only with bodily desires.

Someone who flies from his master is a runaway, and the law is the master. Anyone who breaks the law, or who feels grief, anger or fear because of what has happened, is happening, or will happen, is also a runaway. Such feelings mean rejecting what the ruler of all things has assigned.

Marcus says that a child forms from seed placed in the womb, with other unseen causes doing the work after the father leaves. Similarly, food eaten becomes perception, movement and life through hidden causes. He asks us to notice these hidden powers, which we can see working even though we cannot see them directly.

Marcus says that everything happening now has happened before and will happen again. He suggests picturing past rulers' courts, such as Hadrian's, Antoninus's, Philip's, Alexander's and Croesus's, as the same kind of play as today, with only the actors changed.

A person who is upset or unhappy about something is compared to a pig being sacrificed, which kicks and screams as it is killed. The point is that such distress is useless and undignified, like the animal's struggle.

Marcus is saying that a person who lies quietly in bed complaining about the limits on life is like a pig. Only a reasoning being can accept what happens by choice, while all other things are simply forced to go along with events.

Before each thing you do, stop and ask whether death is frightening because it would take that thing away from you. The idea is that you should check whether losing the action is really a reason to fear death.

When someone's fault angers you, turn to your own faults first, such as valuing money, pleasure or reputation. Remember that the wrongdoer is compelled to act as he does. This should calm your anger, and if you can, remove the compulsion itself.

Marcus tells himself to picture a series of people he has seen, each paired with a person who has already died, and to think of himself the same way. His point is that all these people are gone, and no one knows where they are.

Marcus is telling himself that if he keeps viewing human affairs as smoke, of no lasting worth, and remembers that what has changed never returns in endless time, then he should see how brief his own life is. He asks why he does not live this short time in an orderly way, and what chances to act he is wasting.

Everything that happens in life is a training exercise for reason, which examines what happens and its nature. Keep at it until these lessons become fully your own, just as a strong stomach digests all food and a fire turns whatever is thrown into it into flame and light.

Marcus says no one can truly claim that you are not simple or not good, and anyone who says so is lying. Being good and simple is entirely up to you, since no one can stop you from it. He adds that if you are not such a person, reason does not allow you to go on living.

Marcus asks what can be done or said that best fits reason in our present circumstances. He says it is always within our power to do or say it, so we should not claim we are prevented. He adds that we will keep complaining until we take such right action as pleasure-seekers take delight in their luxuries.

A person should take pleasure in whatever he can do in line with his own nature, and that is possible everywhere. Objects like a rolling cylinder, water, or fire are blocked by obstacles, but reason can get past any obstacle and act as it is made to act by nature and as it chooses.

The main point is that reason moves through everything as easily as fire rises, a stone falls, or a rolling cylinder goes down a slope, so nothing further is needed. Outside obstacles can only harm the body, which is lifeless, or harm the mind if the mind itself gives way through judgment.

Things with a fixed nature get worse when harmed, but a person who responds well to misfortune becomes better and more worthy of praise. A true citizen is not harmed by anything that does not harm the state, and nothing that harms the state harms the law or order. So none of the events called misfortunes actually harms the law.

A person who truly holds sound principles needs only a very short saying, even an ordinary one, to remember that he should be free from grief and fear. The passage then gives an example of such a saying, though the example itself is not shown here.

Human praise, blame and fame are like leaves: they come and go, and each generation replaces the last. Everything has a brief life, so it is foolish to chase things as if they lasted forever. Death comes soon, and others will mourn you in turn.

A healthy sense or mind takes things as they come, without wanting only what it likes. The eye should see whatever is there, and the mind should be ready for whatever happens. Wanting your children to live or everyone to praise you is like a sick eye that craves particular colours.

Even a good and wise man, when he dies, will have some people glad to see him go. Some will feel relieved to be free of his quiet judgment, since he never openly scolded them but seemed to silently disapprove. Marcus then suggests that many people want to be rid of us, even if we are not good men.

Marcus says that when you are dying, you can leave more peacefully by thinking that even the people you worked for, prayed for and cared about now want you to go, perhaps hoping to gain something from your death. So there is no reason to cling to staying longer in life.

When you must leave other people, Marcus says, do not become cold toward them. Keep your own kind, friendly and gentle character, and part from them calmly, as a soul leaves the body in a peaceful death. Nature joined us to others, so the separation should be without force or resistance.
Whenever you see someone do something, ask yourself what purpose the person has in doing it. Start by asking this about yourself, and examine your own purpose first.

The passage says that a person is the hidden inner part that moves the body, not the body itself. The body and its organs are compared to tools like an axe, a weaver's shuttle, a pen or a whip, which are useless without the hand or cause that works them.

The rational soul, the thinking part of a person, can examine itself and shape itself as it chooses. It gets its own result, the way a plant bears fruit, and it is complete wherever life ends. Unlike a dance or play, it is not spoiled if cut short.

The passage describes the mind, which can reach across the whole universe and through all of time. It claims that nothing truly new happens, since the same patterns repeat forever. So a man of forty who thinks clearly has, in effect, already seen everything that has happened and everything that will happen.

Marcus Aurelius says that love of one's neighbor, truth, and modesty belong to the rational soul, and that the soul values nothing above itself, just as Law does. Because of this, right reason is the same as the reason of justice.

Marcus suggests that you can lower the value of pleasures like singing, dancing and wrestling by splitting them into their separate parts. Examine each sound or movement and ask whether you are controlled by it; you would likely feel ashamed to admit that you are. Apart from virtue and virtuous acts, he says, apply this same method to your whole life.

A soul is praised here for being ready to leave the body at any moment, whether it ends, scatters, or lives on. The readiness must come from the person's own reasoned judgment, calmly and with dignity, not from stubbornness like that the writer attributes to Christians.

The writer asks whether he has done something for the common good, and answers that if he has, that act is already his reward. He tells himself to keep this in mind and to keep doing such good without stopping.

The main point is that a person's whole task is to be good, and this can only be done well by knowing general principles. These principles concern two things: how the universe is built, and what the right make-up of a human being is.

Tragedies were first staged to remind people that events happen as nature brings them, so that a person who is moved by a stage play should not be troubled by the events of real life. The passage adds that even those who cry out on stage must still endure what happens to them.

Old Greek comedy, which spoke with bold, open frankness, was introduced after tragedy. Its plain speaking warned people against arrogance, and the Cynic Diogenes also drew on these writers for that purpose.

The writer asks what purpose the middle and new comedies served, since they gradually became mere imitation. Some good lines appear in them, but he questions what the whole aim of such plays and poetry is.
The writer says it is clear that no other way of life suits the study of philosophy as well as the one he is living now. He speaks to himself, using "thou," an old form of "you."

A man who cuts himself off from another person, by hating him and turning away, separates himself from the whole human community, as a severed branch falls from a tree. But it is still in his power to grow back and rejoin the others as part of the whole.

Marcus compares a person who often breaks away from others to a branch. Once cut off, it is hard to rejoin the tree and become whole again. A branch that was never cut and still shares the tree's life is different from a grafted one, which may grow with the tree yet not share its mind or spirit.

Keep doing what reason says is right, and do not let opponents turn you from it. Also do not let them turn you against them: staying kind to those who oppose you is part of the same duty. Being angry at them is a weakness, just as giving way out of fear is, since both leave your post, and the one who turns against a fellow human, who is a kinsman by nature, does so too.

Nature is never worse than human skill, since art copies nature. Just as all arts serve higher ends, the universal nature does too, and justice comes from this. The other virtues rest on justice, which fails if we care about indifferent things or are deceived, careless, or changeable.

If things you desire or fear do not come to you, you still go toward them in your mind. If you let your judgment about them rest, they will stay quiet, and you will be seen neither chasing nor running from them.

The soul keeps its round, balanced shape when it does not reach out toward outside things, shrink inward, scatter, or sink. It is lit by a light that lets it see the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

If others despise or hate him, that is their concern. Marcus says he will focus on his own conduct, avoiding anything worthy of contempt, and will stay gentle and kind toward everyone, correcting others honestly and without showing off.

A person should be inwardly content and should not complain, since acting in line with their own nature and with the nature of the universe is no harm. Each human has a place in the world and a task that serves the common good.
People look down on each other and flatter each other at the same time. They want to rise above others, and they also bow low before them.

A person who announces that he has decided to deal fairly with you is unsound and insincere. Honest character needs no announcement, because it shows itself in actions and even in the eyes, as a lover's feelings are plainly read by the beloved.

A good and honest person should be obvious to others without any effort, the way a strong smell reaches a bystander whether he wants it or not. Pretending to be simple is crooked and false, and a fake friendship is the worst thing. Goodness and kindness show plainly in a person's eyes.

The soul can live well when it stays indifferent to things that are themselves indifferent, meaning things that are neither good nor bad. It achieves this by looking at each such thing, and all of them together, and remembering that none of them forms a judgment about itself in us or comes to us on its own.

Things outside us stay as they are; the distress comes from the judgments we make about them and write into our minds. We can choose not to write them, or wipe out any that slip in unnoticed. Since our life is short, the effort is not much to make.

If things are in line with nature, accept them gladly and they will be easy to bear. If they go against nature, pursue what fits your own nature, even if it earns no praise, since everyone has the right to seek his own good.
Think about where each thing comes from, what it is made of, what it will turn into, and what it will be after that change. Seen this way, the change does it no harm.

Marcus argues that people are made for one another and that nature arranges all things, with lesser things serving greater ones and those serving each other. If the world were only random atoms, that order would not hold. So when someone wrongs him, he starts by reminding himself that humans are bound together by nature.
Marcus tells himself to look closely at other people's ordinary habits, such as how they eat and sleep. He asks him to notice what opinions force them to act, and how proudly they do what they do.

If people act rightly, there is no cause for displeasure. If they act wrongly, they do so unwillingly and out of ignorance, just as no soul is willing to lose the truth. People are pained when called unjust or ungrateful, because they do not see themselves as wrongdoers.

You do wrong things too, and you are no different from other people. Even when you avoid a fault, you still have the tendency to commit it. You hold back only out of cowardice, fear of reputation, or some similar base motive.

Marcus is saying that we often cannot tell whether another person is actually doing wrong, because many actions depend on circumstances we may not know. Judging someone's acts correctly takes a great deal of learning.
When you are deeply troubled or sad, remember that human life lasts only a moment, and soon everyone is laid out dead. The point is that even great distress is brief against the shortness of life.

Other people's acts do not upset us directly; our own opinions about those acts do. If we drop the judgment that an act is grievous, our anger goes away. The reason is that another person's wrong act cannot bring shame on us, since only what is shameful in itself is bad.
Anger and annoyance at someone's wrongs often cause more pain than the wrongs themselves. The passage asks the reader to notice this by comparing the two.

A kind attitude that is sincere cannot be defeated, even by a violent man. If you stay gentle toward him, and calmly correct his wrongs while he is attacking you, he can do you no real harm. He only harms himself.

The speaker advises gently showing someone, using general principles, that they are wrong to act against their nature, as even bees and social animals do not. This should be done kindly and without mockery, and privately rather than to show off in front of others.

Be a true man by avoiding both flattering others and being angry at them, since both harm social life. Remember that giving in to anger is not manly, while mildness and gentleness are both more natural to people and more manly.

A person who is free from strong emotions is stronger. Like the feeling of pain, anger is a sign of weakness, because both the person who gives way to pain and the one who gives way to anger are wounded and yield.

It is foolish to expect bad people not to do wrong, since that asks for something impossible. To let people treat others badly while expecting never to be wronged oneself is also unreasonable and domineering.

Marcus says there are four main lapses of the mind to guard against. For three of them, he advises rejecting the thought, the idea of harming others, or the insincere speech. The fourth is self-reproach, which he treats as a sign that the higher part of a person has given way to the body and its lower pleasures.

Marcus says that the elements in a person's body each have a natural direction: air and fire rise, earth and water sink. Yet within the body they are held in positions against that nature, because they follow the order of the whole universe.

Marcus is saying that things in nature stay where they are placed until the universe signals their dissolution. He asks why the human intellect alone resists its place and is discontented with it, even though it is forced only into what suits its nature, yet still moves the opposite way.

Injustice, excess, anger, grief and fear are described as a turning away from nature. The ruling part of the mind also leaves its post when it resents what happens. Its proper duties include piety towards the gods and justice, and both rest on accepting how things are arranged.

Someone who does not aim at one fixed goal cannot stay consistent throughout life. The goal, Marcus says, should be something shared and public, concerning the common good of people living together. A person who directs all their efforts toward that goal will act consistently and so remain the same.

The passage is a short reminder to picture the fable of the country mouse and the town mouse, focusing on how frightened the town mouse was. The point is that a life full of fear and unrest is shown by the town mouse's anxious state.
Socrates called the opinions of most people "Lamiae," which were bogeys used to frighten children. The point is that common opinions are like childish scares, not real dangers.

The Spartans, at public shows, gave strangers the shaded seats, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to be. Spartans were the citizens of Sparta, a Greek city known for its strict discipline.
Socrates declined to visit Perdiccas, a king, because he did not want to be placed in debt. He said that accepting a favor he could not repay would be the worst way to end up.

The Ephesians, people of the city of Ephesus, had a rule for their writings: keep calling to mind some person from the past who lived virtuously. The passage recalls this rule as something Marcus once read.
Marcus says the Pythagoreans advised people to look at the sky each morning. The heavenly bodies always do the same work in the same way, and they are pure and bare, with nothing covering them.

Marcus recalls that Socrates, after his wife Xanthippe took his cloak and left, put on a skin instead. When his friends were embarrassed by him and kept their distance, Socrates spoke to them in a way the passage does not record here, so the point is to picture his calm in that humiliating moment.
You cannot set rules for others, in writing or in reading, until you have first learned to follow rules yourself. The same holds even more strongly for how you live.

Looking for figs in winter is foolish, because the season for them has passed. The passage compares this to searching for a child who is no longer allowed to be yours, meaning a child who has died. Both are seeking what the world no longer gives.

Epictetus said that a man kissing his child should silently remind himself that the child may die tomorrow. Someone objects that such words bring bad luck, but Epictetus replies that no word is unlucky if it names something natural, just as speaking of harvesting ripe grain is not unlucky.

Stages of a grape, from unripe to dried, are all changes. Each one turns into a new state that does not yet exist, not into nothing. The point is that change is always a passage from one thing to another, never a ceasing to be.

Epictetus taught that a person should learn rules for agreeing to things, the mind's act of assent. Actions should suit the situation, serve the common good, and match what the thing is worth. Desire should be avoided altogether, and aversion should be shown only toward things that are not up to us.

Socrates asks what kind of souls people want, and the answer is sound rational souls. He then asks why people fight if they already have such souls. The point is that people already possess reason, so their quarrels make no sense.

Marcus says that what you want to reach by a long, roundabout route you can have now, if you do not refuse it to yourself. To get it, set aside the past, leave the future to providence (the divine order that governs the world), and act in the present with piety and justice. Accept the lot given to you, since nature assigned it to you and you to it.

Act in line with justice: speak the truth openly, do what the law requires and what each person deserves. Do not let other people's wrongdoing, their opinions or their words, or the pains and pleasures of the body stop you. The body's feelings belong to its own passive part, which will deal with them.

Marcus says that when death is near, a person should set aside everything else and honor only the inner guiding part of the mind and the divine spirit within. The fear that matters is not of dying, but of never having lived in accordance with nature. Such a person becomes at home in the universe and stops being surprised by daily events or dependent on outside things.

God sees each person's inner reason, stripped of the body and its outward covering, because the divine mind touches only the intelligence that came from itself. The writer adds that if a person also learns to look past the body, they will free themselves from much worry about clothing, housing, reputation and outward show.

Marcus says a person is made of three parts: body, breath, and intelligence. Only intelligence is truly one's own. If a person separates the mind from everything outside it, including bodily sensations, other people's words and deeds, past actions, and future worries, the mind can stay pure and free, acting justly and speaking the truth.

Living only in the present, the only life a person really has, lets a person spend the rest of life undisturbed, nobly, and obeying the inner divine guide, or daemon, that the Stoics believed each person carried.

Men love themselves more than anyone else, yet they care more about what others think of them than about their own opinion of themselves. Even a god or wise teacher telling a man to think or plan only what he would be willing to say aloud, he could not bear it for a single day.

Marcus asks how the gods could have arranged everything well for humanity yet overlooked one thing: that good, pious men who were closest to the divine are, once dead, never to exist again and are completely extinguished. The question expresses doubt that such a fate fits a well-ordered world.

Marcus argues that if something in the world seems wrong, it cannot really be wrong. If it were unjust, the gods would have prevented it, since they are just and all-powerful over nature. So arguing against how things are amounts to arguing against the gods, who would not allow a real injustice.
Keep practising even at things you think you cannot achieve. The left hand is weaker than the right at most tasks, but it holds the reins more firmly, because it has been trained to do that job.

Think about the state your body and mind should be in when death comes, and remember how short life is. Also consider the endless stretch of time before and after us, and how weak all physical things are.

Look at things stripped of their outer wrappings, and examine their underlying forms and the purposes behind actions. Ask plainly what pain, pleasure, death and fame are, and see that no one else can harm you and that everything depends on judgment.

Apply your principles the way a pancratiast does, not the way a gladiator does. A gladiator can drop his sword and be killed, but a pancratiast (a wrestler-boxer in ancient Greek contests) always keeps his hands, so he has only to use them.
