Man is able to do only what God approves and to accept whatever God gives him. The passage presents this as a power he has, which is the point it makes.

Things that happen according to nature should not be blamed on the gods or on people. The gods never do wrong, on purpose or by accident, and people do wrong only by accident. So no one should be blamed.

Anyone who is surprised by something that happens in life is, in this view, absurd and out of place in the world. Nothing that happens should be unexpected to him, because such things are ordinary parts of life.

Marcus sets out three possibilities for the universe: fate that cannot be resisted, a caring providence, or random chaos with no guide. Whichever is true, he argues, the mind is still yours to govern. If chaos rules, your reason can still steer you, even if your body and breath are swept away.
A lamp keeps its brightness until the moment it goes out. Marcus asks whether the truth, justice and self-control within a person should likewise stay bright until death, rather than go out earlier.

Marcus says we cannot be sure a person has really done wrong, and even if they have, they may already be punishing themselves for it. Blaming them is like wounding one's own face. He compares wanting bad people never to act badly to wanting figs without sap, or babies never to cry: it is natural and cannot be helped. So if you feel anger, you should cure your own temper.

When something gives you an impression, examine what it actually is by breaking it into four parts: its form, its matter, its purpose, and the time it will last. "Appearance" here means the impression or image a thing creates in the mind. "Resolve" means to analyze or take apart.

Marcus is telling himself to recognise that there is a part of him better and more divine than the feelings that tug at him like puppet strings. He then asks himself what is in his mind right now, whether fear, suspicion, desire, or something similar.
Act with thought and a clear purpose, never carelessly. Let every action aim only at the good of society, meaning the community of people.
Everything you see will soon be gone, and so will you and everyone now alive. Nature makes all things change, decay and pass away so that other things can keep coming after them.
Everything we experience is a matter of opinion, and we have control over our opinions. If we drop an opinion, we can find calm, like a sailor who has rounded a headland and reaches still water.

Any action, when it ends at its proper time, is not harmed by ending, and the person who did it is not harmed either. In the same way, a whole life that ends at its proper time suffers no harm from ending, and the one who lived it has not been wronged.

Death comes at a time and in a way that nature sets, and nature as a whole keeps the universe renewed through constant change. Since the end of a life is useful to the whole, it is not an evil. It is neither shameful nor against the common good, and it is good because it fits in its season.

Marcus is saying that a person is moved to act in the same way that the divine moves, and is turned in his mind toward the same goal. In Stoic thought, the Deity is the rational order of the universe, so living by reason means sharing its direction.

Marcus lists principles to keep ready. In your actions, act carefully and always as justice would act. Accept what happens to you from outside as either chance or providence (a divine ordering), blaming neither. Also, consider how every living thing comes into being, lives, and breaks back into its parts.

If you rose high above the earth and looked down at human affairs, you would see how varied and large they seem. You would also see how many other beings live in the air and sky, and that each time you rose you would find the same things: similar forms and short lives. So, the passage asks, is there anything here to be proud of?

When you are troubled by something, you have forgotten that everything happens according to universal nature, that another person's wrongdoing is not your concern, that events have always happened this way and always will, and that all humans share a bond through reason, not just blood.

Every person's reason is a portion of the divine, and nothing belongs to a person outright, since even children, body and soul come from god. Everything is a matter of opinion, and each person lives only in the present moment, which is the only thing they can lose.

Marcus tells himself to keep in mind people who were once famous, feared, or unfortunate, and to ask where they are now. All have become smoke and ash, or at most a story, and so have people of this kind who lived in the country or gardens.

Marcus says that eagerly chasing things with pride is pointless, since men strain hard for things that are worth little. He holds that it is wiser to act justly, temperately and obediently toward the gods, and to do so simply. Pride even in one's lack of pride is the worst kind of pride.

Someone asks how Marcus knows the gods exist and why he worships them. He answers that the gods can be seen with the eyes, and that he honors his own soul though he has never seen it. He knows the gods through the power he constantly experiences from them.

This is not Marcus Aurelius speaking; it is the translator George Long's own editorial note on the Meditations. He says that the scholar Gataker has good notes, quotes Calvin and Seneca on how God shows himself through the visible world, and lists other parallel writers. He ends by saying he believes his reading of Antoninus is correct.

Living safely, in this view, means examining each thing thoroughly: what it is in itself, its matter and its form. It also means acting justly and speaking the truth with all one's soul. Beyond that, the passage says, life is simply enjoyed by linking one good thing to the next without gaps.

Marcus argues that many things can still be one whole. The sun's light is one though walls and mountains break it up, and the soul is one though it seems divided among many beings. Other parts of the world, such as air and matter, have no sensation, yet the intelligent principle holds them together. Intellect joins with what is like itself.

Marcus asks whether ordinary things like sensation, movement, growth, and speech are really worth wanting to keep. He says that if these can be valued lightly, one should turn to following reason and God. It makes no sense to honor reason and God and yet be troubled by losing these everyday things at death.

Human life is a tiny span within endless time, and a tiny part of the whole of existence and the earth. Given this, the passage says the only thing worth counting as great is acting according to one's own nature and accepting what the universal nature brings.

The ruling faculty means the mind or reason that directs a person. The passage says that everything depends on how this faculty uses itself. Other things, whether or not they are within one's will, are worthless, like ash and smoke.
The passage says that thinking about death is especially useful for making us scorn it. Even people who believe pleasure is good and pain is bad have still looked down on death.

For this kind of person, only what arrives at the right time counts as good. Whether he has done more or fewer right actions, or looked at the world for a longer or shorter time, makes no difference to him. So death is not a terrible thing to him.

Marcus says that a person's life is like a citizen's stay in the world, or like an actor's part in a play. Death is the end set by nature, which brought us in, so it is not a wrong done by a tyrant or unjust judge. Like a complete drama, a life counts as whole when its author ends it, even if it is short.

Some things depend on us, such as our judgments, goals, desires and aversions. Other things, such as the body, property, reputation and public office, do not. The passage warns that if we treat things outside our control as our own, we will be hindered, distressed and will blame gods and people.

If you claim only what is truly yours and see other things as they really are, no one can force or restrict you, and you cannot be harmed. To reach these great goods, you must drop any pull toward outside things like power and wealth, or put them aside for now. Chasing them may cost you the inner freedom you are seeking.

Epictetus advises that when something unpleasant appears to us, we should tell ourselves it is only an appearance, not the thing itself. We should then test it by asking whether it is within our control. If it is not, we should treat it as none of our concern.

Wanting something means you expect to get it, and dreading something means you expect to avoid it. Those who fail to get what they want are disappointed, and those who meet what they dread are miserable. So you should only avoid things that are within your control, since then you will never meet what you avoid; avoiding sickness, death, or poverty risks misery.

Stop disliking things you cannot control, and turn that dislike toward the things you can control that are bad. For now, hold back desire altogether, since wanting what is outside your control leads to disappointment. When you must pursue or avoid something, do it calmly and moderately.

Things you love or find useful are mortal and can be lost, so the passage advises keeping in mind what each thing really is. A cup is only a cup, and a child or wife is only a mortal, so their loss is easier to bear when it comes.

Before any action, Epictetus advises picturing what it will involve, including the annoyances that usually come with it. If something goes wrong, the aim is to remember that the real goal is to keep one's will in line with nature, and that anger at events would undo that.

People are upset not by things themselves but by what they think about those things. Death is not terrible in itself, or it would have seemed terrible to Socrates; the fear comes from the idea that it is terrible. So when we are hurt or troubled, we should blame our own judgments, not other people. Someone untrained blames others, a learner blames himself, and a fully trained person blames neither.

Do not feel proud of qualities that belong to something else. A horse may be handsome, but pride in owning a handsome horse rests only on the horse's merit. What is truly yours is how you use your impressions of things, and pride in that is justified.

Epictetus compares life to a ship at anchor. While ashore, you may enjoy small things like a shellfish or a truffle, including a wife or child, but your mind should stay on the ship. When the captain calls, you must drop everything and go at once. Older people should stay close to the ship so they can answer the call.
Do not insist that events turn out the way you want. Instead, want them to happen as they actually do, and things will go well for you.
Sickness hinders the body and lameness hinders the leg, but neither hinders the will unless the person lets it. Whatever happens may block something else, but it does not truly block you.

When something happens to you, ask which of your own abilities can deal with it. Meeting a handsome person calls for self-control, pain calls for endurance, and insults call for patience. With this habit, events will not overwhelm you.

Nothing we have is truly ours, so when something is taken away we should not say it is lost but that it has been returned to the one who gave it. Possessions and even loved ones are held only for a time, like a traveler staying at an inn.

Epictetus says that to become better, you should drop the reasoning that you must control every loss and every servant's fault. He argues that losing money or a servant's goods is a small price for peace of mind, and that it is better for a servant to be bad than for you to be upset. Start with small losses, accepting them calmly, and do not let others have power to disturb you.

To make progress, be willing to seem foolish or dull about outward things, and do not want a reputation for knowledge. Even if others think well of you, do not trust that opinion. Keeping your inner will in line with nature and gaining outward things are hard to do together, so attention to one means neglecting the other.

Wanting things that depend on other people, such as children, friends, or servants never being harmed or dying, is foolish, because those things are not in your control. What you can control is your own wanting and avoiding. Whoever wants nothing that others can give or take away is free; otherwise, that person is a slave.

Treat life like a dinner party: take a modest share of what is offered, let go of what passes you by, and do not crave what has not yet arrived. Being able to give up even what is set before you is what makes a person worthy to share the gods' feast and rule with them, as Diogenes and Heraclitus did.

When someone weeps over a loss, the Stoic advice is not to be carried away by how bad the event seems. The upset comes from the judgment the person makes about the event, not from the event itself. You may still sympathize aloud and even groan with him, but without feeling the grief inside.
Your life is like a role in a play that someone else assigns. Whether the part is short or long, poor or powerful, your job is to perform that given role well. Choosing the role is not up to you.

A raven's croak is taken as a bad omen, but the speaker refuses to be frightened by it. He says that the bird predicts nothing about his body, property, reputation, children, or wife. Whatever happens, he can choose to make good use of it.

You can only be unbeatable if you take part only in contests you can win on your own terms. So do not judge people who hold honors or power as happy, because real good lies only in what is within your control. Freedom comes from not caring about things outside your control.

Insults and blows do not hurt by themselves; what hurts is the judgment we make about them as insults. So when someone provokes you, the provocation comes from your own opinion. Gaining a pause before reacting makes it easier to stay in control.
Keep death, exile, and other frightening things in mind every day, death most of all. Then you will never have a low, fearful thought, and you will not want things too eagerly.

If you seriously take up philosophy, expect people to mock you and call you arrogant. Do not act superior, but keep to what you judge best, as if God had placed you in that role. If you stay firm, the same people will later admire you; if you give in to their mockery, you will be ridiculed twice over.

Epictetus says that if you care about outward things just to please other people, you have spoiled your way of life. Be satisfied simply with being a philosopher, and if you want others to see you that way, it is enough that you see yourself that way.

Epictetus tells the reader not to be troubled by fears of losing reputation or being unimportant. Loss of standing is not a real evil, since no one can be made bad by what other people do. Real worth lies in what is within your own power, not in power, status, money, or the fortunes of friends, which belong to others.

Epictetus argues that he will not give up his own honor, faithfulness and self-respect to get things for others. He says that a friend of good character is worth more than money, and that he would rather help others by keeping his integrity than by losing it. Even if his country gains nothing from him, he asks what that loss really amounts to, since public buildings like porticos and baths are not the true good.

Each person should do their own proper work and be useful to the community in that way, just as a smith cannot do a shoemaker's job and the state still needs everyone in their own role. The question is what place you hold in the state, and the answer is whatever place you can hold while keeping your loyalty and honor. Losing these in the name of service makes you unable to serve your country at all.

Epictetus says that if others get honours, favours or close friendships you lack, you should not envy them when those things are good, and should not mind missing them when they are bad. You cannot have the same rewards without paying the same price, which means flattering and servility. Wanting them for free is unreasonable.

Epictetus says that if someone pays for lettuces and you do not, he gains nothing over you, since you keep the coin you did not give. Likewise, a dinner invitation has a price: praise and attendance on the host. If you want the dinner without paying that price, you are foolish. You still keep your freedom: you need not praise someone you dislike or put up with his servants' insolence.

Nature's way can be seen in things everyone agrees on. When a neighbor's cup breaks, we call it a normal accident, so we should take the same view when our own cup breaks, and when a stranger's child dies, we say it is a fate of mortals, yet we cry out when our own child dies.
Just as a target is not set up so that it will be missed, evil does not exist in the world as part of its natural design. The point is that evil is not something the world was made to contain.

Epictetus says it would be foolish to let any insulter upset your mind, when you would be angry if a stranger were allowed to hurt your body. He also urges you to think ahead about what an undertaking involves before you start it, so you do not quit halfway. His example is an athlete who wants to win at the Olympic Games and must accept strict training rules and a restricted diet.

Epictetus says that a person who wants to enter a contest must first accept strict training: set hours, hot and cold conditions, restricted drinks, and obedience to the trainer. He adds that the fighter may still be injured or lose. Only after weighing all this should one decide to compete.

Epictetus warns that a person who copies whatever impresses them, like children playing at wrestlers or gladiators, never really commits to anything. Each new interest pleases only until it becomes familiar. He says this happens because the person never thinks a matter through or tests it before starting, and comes to it with only half-hearted effort.

Epictetus warns that seeing a philosopher and admiring his speech is not enough to become one. A person should first consider their own nature and what they can bear, as a would-be wrestler considers his body. Philosophy demands watchfulness, hard work, self-control, and accepting scorn from others, which a person living as they do now may not be able to face.

Epictetus says that a person who wants calm, freedom and peace of mind must give up outside things such as office, honor and public success. He warns against trying to be a philosopher and also a tax collector, orator or official at the same time, because these roles do not fit together. A person must choose one path: either develop their own reason and inner life, or pursue external things and be one of the crowd.

Our duties come from the relationships we have with others, such as father, brother, neighbor or citizen. A bad father or unjust brother does not cancel the duty that comes with the bond. What matters is keeping your own conduct in line with nature, since no one else can harm you unless you let them.

Piety toward the gods, the passage says, means holding correct beliefs about them: that they exist and govern the universe justly and wisely. Accepting their rule without complaint, you will never blame them. This is possible only when you treat as good or bad just the things that are within your own control.

If you believe that things outside your control are good or bad, then when you fail to get what you want or get what you dislike, you will naturally blame whoever you think caused it. Every creature is built to avoid what seems harmful and to seek what seems beneficial, so a person who feels hurt cannot take pleasure in the one who seems to hurt them. A son, for example, will blame his father for withholding what seems good to him.

Epictetus says that people blame the gods when their own interests are hurt: the farmer, the sailor, the merchant, or someone who has lost a loved one. Piety follows self-interest, so whoever controls his desires and aversions will also be careful in matters of piety. Still, everyone should make offerings as their country's customs require, sincerely and without greed or excess.

Epictetus says that when you consult a diviner, you learn the outcome only from him, but you should already know that the outcome cannot be good or bad for you if it lies outside your control. So do not go to him wanting something or fearing something, because that will make you anxious. Instead, accept that every event is neutral and does not matter to you.

Epictetus advises that when you face a choice, you should consult the gods as your advisers and remember them when their counsel comes to you. When a matter depends only on how events turn out, and reason or skill cannot settle it, he says to seek divination, as Socrates recommended.

When a friend or country is in danger and we have a duty to share that danger, we should not ask an oracle whether to do so. Even a bad omen only warns of death, injury or exile, and our own reason tells us to stand by them. The passage cites the god at Delphi, who expelled a man who had failed to save his friend.

Epictetus advises keeping a calm, quiet manner in both private and social settings. Speak little and only when needed, and avoid common gossip such as sports, food, drink, and criticizing or comparing people. Keep laughter moderate, avoid oaths, and stay away from crowded public entertainments.

Epictetus advises keeping your attention on your goal when you meet people who might pull you toward common, vulgar behavior, since a good person is corrupted by close company with a corrupted one. He also says to limit bodily needs to what is necessary, avoid show and luxury, and avoid sexual relations before marriage without judging or boasting about those who fail.

If someone reports that another person criticises you, do not defend yourself. Instead, reply that the critic must not know your other faults, or would have named them too. At public shows, do not cheer, mock, or get carried away, and afterwards do not talk much about what you saw.

Epictetus advises that when you must deal with a powerful or superior person, you should picture how wise men like Socrates or Zeno would act, and accept whatever follows without complaint. Even if you are ignored or turned away, you should not say the visit was not worth the trouble. He also says not to talk too often or too much about your own deeds and dangers in company.

Do not talk too much about your own dangers, since others may not enjoy hearing about them. Avoid trying to get laughs, because it can slide into coarseness and lower you in others' eyes. If talk turns indecent, rebuke the speaker when you can, or at least show your displeasure through silence, blushing, or a serious look.

When a pleasure looks attractive, do not act on it at once. Delay, and picture both the moment of enjoying it and the later regret that follows. Then set against it the satisfaction of having resisted and won that victory over yourself.

If you act on a clear judgment that something is right, do not hide it, even if others misunderstand you. If the act is wrong, avoid it. If it is right, there is no reason to fear people who unfairly blame you.

Epictetus uses a logic comparison: "either day or night" works in an either-or argument but not in an "and" argument, so each situation has its own rules. He applies this to dining. Taking the biggest share suits the body's appetite but clashes with the courtesy owed to the host, so when eating with others, one should weigh courtesy as well as physical benefit.
If you take on a role that is beyond your ability, you fail at that role and also give up one you could have carried out well. The point is to choose roles that match what you can really do.

Just as you watch your step on a walk so as not to step on a nail or twist your foot, you should guard your mind's ruling part (its governing faculty, the part that judges and chooses) from harm. Doing this in every action makes acting safer.

Just as a shoe should fit the foot, a person's possessions should match what the body actually needs. If you stop at that limit, you stay in proportion. If you go past it, there is no natural stopping point, and the excess keeps growing, like a shoe that becomes gilded, then purple, then jewelled.

Once girls reach about fourteen, men begin to flatter them as mistresses. The girls then come to see themselves as valued only for pleasing men, so they focus on their appearance. The passage says they should instead want to be honored for good conduct and modesty.

Spending a lot of time on bodily matters, such as too much exercise, eating, drinking, and other bodily functions, is a sign of a weak mind. Such things should be done only as side matters, and one's main effort should go to reason.

When someone wrongs or insults you, they act on what seems right to them, not what seems right to you. If they judge by false appearances, the harm falls on them, because they are the one deceived. So you can bear their insults calmly, saying to yourself, "It seemed so to him."

Every matter can be grasped in two ways, one that makes it bearable and one that does not. When a brother wrongs you, take hold of the situation by the fact that he is your brother and was raised with you, not by his wrong, which is the harder way to bear it.

Being richer or more eloquent than someone does not make you their superior, because those facts only show that your possessions or your style are greater. Your real self, the author says, is not made of property or style, so such comparisons do not measure you as a person.

Epictetus says that when someone bathes quickly or drinks a lot of wine, we should describe what they did, not judge it as bad. We cannot know whether an action is wrong unless we understand the reasons behind it. So we should only accept an impression of something once we fully understand it.

Do not call yourself a philosopher or talk much about your principles to people who do not understand them. Show your principles through your actions instead, and when discussion of them arises among the ignorant, mostly stay silent.

A student should not repeat half-understood ideas to outsiders in order to show off what he has learned. Like sheep that digest grass before turning it into wool and milk, he should let his principles become part of him and show them through his actions. Being told he knows nothing should not upset him, a sign that his training has begun.

Do not boast about your simple habits, such as drinking only water or eating plainly. Remember that poor people live with less and endure more hardship than you do. If you train yourself through hardship, do it privately and modestly, without showing off.

Epictetus contrasts two kinds of people. An ordinary person expects help or harm only from outside things, while a philosopher looks to himself for both. A person who is making progress blames and praises no one, does not boast of himself, and when hindered, blames only himself.

The passage describes how a person who has made progress in Stoic discipline behaves. He does not defend himself when criticized, and he holds back his desires and his dislikes, keeping them only for things that interfere with his own will. He treats his own mind with constant wariness, as if guarding against an enemy.

Being able to interpret Chrysippus's obscure writings is not worth pride in itself. Understanding him is only a means to living according to nature, and the real value lies in putting his teaching into action. Someone who only admires the interpretation is merely a scholar of texts, and Epictetus says he feels ashamed when he cannot show his actions matching what he reads.

Keep the rules you have chosen as binding laws, and ignore what others say about you, since it is none of your concern. Epictetus asks how long you will keep putting off the best self-improvement and failing to follow reason. You already have the philosophy you need, and you are an adult, so you need no further teacher to begin.

Epictetus warns against putting off self-improvement again and again, which leads to achieving nothing. He says a person should start now, treat the best course as a fixed rule, and face each pain, pleasure, honor or shame as a contest that cannot be postponed. He offers Socrates as an example of someone who became perfect by following reason alone.
You may not yet be as wise as Socrates, but you should live as someone who is trying to become like him. The point is to act on that aim now, even before reaching it.

Epictetus says philosophy has three parts. The most important is applying principles in daily conduct, such as "we ought not to lie." The second is proving why those principles hold, and the third is the logic that supports such proofs. He complains that people spend nearly all their effort on logic and neglect the first, most necessary part.

Epictetus says that, when people are tempted to lie, they should instead keep ready sayings about accepting fate and the will of the gods. He gives examples: following destiny willingly, yielding to what the gods decide, and Socrates' words that his accusers can kill him but cannot harm him. The rest of the text is a publisher's book list and is not part of the teaching.

Most of our mental abilities cannot examine themselves, so they cannot approve or disapprove of their own workings. Epictetus gives grammar and music as examples: grammar judges written and spoken words, and music judges melody, but neither judges itself.

Grammar can tell you which words to use in a letter, but not whether you should write at all. Music can tell you how to play, but not whether to play or stay silent. Only the reason, the faculty that examines both itself and everything else, can decide that.

The main point is that the mind is the only faculty we have that can examine itself, along with every other faculty. Gold does not say it is beautiful, so something else must judge that, and the passage says that something is the faculty that judges appearances. Likewise, that same faculty judges music, grammar and the other skills, and shows when and how to use them.

A person facing death, chains or exile should keep in mind only what is in his own control and what is not. Dying, being imprisoned or being exiled are not in his control, but his inner attitude is, so he can face them calmly. Threats to his body cannot take that inner calm away.

A person threatens Epictetus with chains, prison and beheading, and he answers that these can only reach the body, not the will, which not even Zeus could overpower. He ends by saying that philosophers should constantly think about and practise this distinction.

Agrippinus, a Stoic, refuses to let bad news disturb his routine. Told he has been condemned to banishment, he calmly asks about his property, then proposes going to Aricia to dine. The point is that outside events do not stop him from acting as he chooses.

Humans are troubled only by what seems unreasonable to them, and they accept what seems reasonable, even if it is painful. Physical pain is not intolerable in itself. The Spartans endured whipping because they judged it reasonable, and a person who judges suicide reasonable may act on it.

Epictetus says we should think about the price we accept for giving up our own will, and at least not sell it cheaply. He suggests that greatness of this kind belongs to people like Socrates. He asks why, if we are naturally able to be like him, so few are, and compares this to saying that all horses are fast or all dogs are good trackers.

Epictetus argues that being slow to learn is no reason to stop trying. He says he does not need to match Socrates to be satisfied, just as a man does not stop caring for his body because he will never be as strong as Milo, or stop managing his money because he will never be as rich as Croesus. People keep working at things even when they cannot reach the very top.

If people truly accepted that God is the father of all humans, Epictetus argues, they would not think meanly of themselves. He compares this to being adopted by the emperor: people would find the resulting pride unbearable, so why would someone who knows he is Zeus's son not feel elated?

Humans are made of two parts: a body, which they share with animals, and reason, which they share with the gods. Many people pay attention to the bodily side, which is mortal and miserable, while only a few turn toward the divine side, which is happy.

Everyone acts according to what they believe about things. A few people see themselves as made for loyalty, self-control and sound judgment, and so they think highly of themselves. Most people think of themselves as poor, miserable bodies, but Epictetus says each person has something better than the body.

Epictetus says that because we are bound to the body, people who lean toward the flesh turn into animals. Some become wolves, treacherous and harmful, some become lions, savage and wild, and most become foxes or worse creatures, such as slanderers. He warns the reader to avoid becoming such creatures.

A person who is making progress in philosophy has learned that desire aims at good things and aversion at bad ones, and that peace of mind comes only from not failing to get what one wants and not falling into what one wants to avoid. So he drops desire for things outside his control and directs aversion only at things that depend on his own will.

Epictetus argues that trying to avoid things outside our control leads to unhappiness, because we will sometimes meet what we want to avoid. If virtue brings good fortune, tranquillity and happiness, then moving toward virtue moves us toward those same goods. Progress is simply getting closer to the goal that a thing's perfection would reach.

Epictetus asks what the result of virtue is, and answers that it is tranquillity, a calm state of mind. He then argues that reading many books by Chrysippus, an early Stoic philosopher, cannot be the measure of progress, since virtue is not the same as knowing his writings.

Epictetus says that virtue itself produces one result, while getting closer to virtue is a separate thing he calls progress. He mocks a man who only shows he can read the philosopher Chrysippus alone as having made progress. He tells the teacher to show the man where real improvement lies, which is in his own moral work.

Epictetus asks where a person's real work lies: in managing their desires, their likes and dislikes, what they pursue and avoid, and whether they accept or withhold judgment about things. He says these are the most basic tasks. If someone is only anxiously trying to avoid what they fear, he asks how that person is making progress.

Epictetus compares a student to an athlete who shows his weight-lifting weights (halteres) instead of the results they should produce. He says the real test is not what a student has read about the mind's impulses, but how he actually handles wanting, avoiding, planning and acting, and whether this agrees with nature.

Epictetus is saying that someone who only explains philosophy books, without living by what they teach, is not making real progress. He asks what such a person gains, since a whole book costs only five denarii, so an expounder is worth no more than that. Real progress must show in how one lives, not in talk about the teaching.

Epictetus says that a person who turns away from outside things and works on their own will (proairesis) can make it natural, free, and steady. He adds that anyone who wants or avoids things beyond their control cannot be free. Such a person is pushed around by events and depends on others who control those things.

The main point is that real progress comes from applying one's guiding principles to everything that happens, each day, in the same way a runner trains for running or a singer trains the voice. Someone who does this, from morning routines onward, is the one who has truly improved and whose journey was not wasted.

Epictetus says that travelling only to read books is worthless, so a person should go home and attend to their own affairs. What really matters is learning how to live without lamentation, misfortune or fear, and how to face death, exile or prison calmly, as Socrates did when he accepted his fate.

Epictetus says that complaints like "I am a wretched old man, and I kept my gray hairs for this" are the voice of tragedy, spoken by kings such as Priam and Oedipus. Tragedy shows people who care about external things being upset by them. Yet if a fiction can teach that nothing outside our control truly concerns us, he would gladly accept that fiction, since it lets him live calm and untroubled.

Epictetus says that Chrysippus teaches people to know that certain basic truths are not false, and that happiness and calm come from knowing them. He praises Chrysippus's books for showing that these truths agree with nature and free the reader from disturbing emotions. He compares Chrysippus to Triptolemus, a figure who taught farming and was honored with temples.

Epictetus says that people honour gods for gifts like wine and grain, but do not thank them for the truth that teaches how to live well. He asks why no one builds altars or temples to honour the person who first found and shared this truth, or to thank God for it.

When someone denies obvious truths, it is hard to find arguments that will change his mind. The difficulty does not come from the man being strong or the teacher being weak. It comes from the man being so hardened, even after being refuted, that argument has no effect on him.

Epictetus says there are two kinds of hardening. One is a hardening of the mind, where a person refuses to accept what is plainly true or to give up contradictions. The other is a hardening of shame. People fear bodily pain but not harm to the soul, and they count a loss of shame as strength.

It is easy to praise Providence (the divine order that governs the world) for everything that happens, if a person can see how things serve the whole and is grateful. Without those two qualities, a person either fails to see the use of things or does not give thanks for them, even when he knows about them.

Epictetus argues that the parts of the world fit together for a purpose. Colors would be useless without the power to see them, sight would be useless without visible things, and both would be useless without light. So he asks who arranged each thing to match the others.

Epictetus argues that animals share many bodily functions with humans, but they do not understand what they do. Using things and understanding their use are different. God gave animals the ability to use appearances (sense impressions), but gave humans the ability to understand that use. For animals, eating, drinking and mating are enough.

Humans, unlike animals, have reason, so simply having what they need is not enough. They must act in a proper and orderly way, matching the nature of each thing, or they will not reach their true end. Animals whose nature is made only for use need nothing more than use.

Animals exist for practical uses such as food, farm work, or cheese, so they need no understanding of appearances. Humans, however, are made to understand and to observe God and God's works, and so they must exercise their reason to reach their proper end.

Humans should not live and die the way animals do, merely taking in the world. Instead, they should start from the same point as animals but go further, ending in contemplation, understanding, and a way of life that follows nature. The passage warns against dying without having looked closely at these things.

People travel far to see the famous statues of Phidias, a Greek sculptor, and think it a loss to die without seeing them. Yet, the speaker says, the works of God are present wherever a person is, so one should want to see and understand them. Those works show what a person is and why they were given sight.

Epictetus asks a series of questions about the discomforts of the Olympic Games: heat, crowds, poor bathing, rain, and noise. He suggests that a person puts up with these for the sake of the spectacle. He then asks whether humans have not been given the ability and greatness of soul to bear whatever happens.

Epictetus asks why he should worry about any event, since he has received manliness, endurance and greatness of soul. He argues that he should use these qualities for their purpose and not grieve or lament over what happens.

Epictetus urges the reader to look at the inner abilities they have and to face whatever happens with confidence, trusting that these abilities let them meet it with honor. Instead, he says, people sit in fear of future events, weep and groan over what has already happened, and then blame the gods. He calls this weakness of spirit a form of impiety.

God has given people mental powers that let them endure whatever happens without being crushed. God gave these powers freely, as a good king or father would, and kept no power to block or limit them. The passage says people fail to use these gifts and do not even recognize where they came from.

Some people fail to see the giver of their good things and do not thank their benefactor. Others, out of a small spirit, blame God. Epictetus says he will show that people have the means for greatness of soul, and asks what means they have for finding fault.

Epictetus says he would rather a teacher guard against young students who, having learned they are kin to God, decide to throw off their bodies and possessions as painful burdens and go back to their divine kinsmen. His concern is that they will treat the body and daily life as something to escape, not something to manage.

The speaker imagines a student going to his teacher and asking to be released from the body. He says the body must be fed, cleaned and rested, which he finds a burden, and that such things are indifferent and death is not an evil. He says humans are kin to God and came from him, so he asks to be allowed to return to that source.

Epictetus describes people who want to be freed from the body, which he calls bonds that weigh them down. Such people want to show tyrants, thieves and judges that they have no power over the self. He advises waiting for God's signal to leave life, and until then staying in the place where God has put them.

Life here is short, and easy to bear for anyone who has come to see the body and possessions as worthless. Such a person has nothing to fear from tyrants, thieves or courts. So one should wait for a proper reason before leaving life.

Epictetus lists four views about whether gods exist and care for the world: that they do not exist, that they exist but ignore everything, that they care only for heavenly matters, and that they care only in general. He names a fifth view, held by Ulysses and Socrates, that nothing happens without the god's knowledge, quoting Homer's Iliad.

Before accepting any belief about the gods, one must first check whether it is true. If the gods do not exist, or do not care for the world, or never communicate with people, then following them would not make sense. The wise person therefore accepts the will of the one who governs the whole, as a good citizen obeys the law.

A student of philosophy should come to lessons asking how to follow the gods in everything, how to accept the divine order, and how to become free. Freedom means that things happen as one wills and no one can stop them. Wanting everything to go exactly as one likes is not freedom but madness.

Epictetus says it is wrong to want things to happen just as we happen to like. In writing, music and every other skill, we learn to do things the correct way, not the way we fancy. If knowledge bent to each person's whim, it would be worthless.

The main point is that true freedom does not mean wanting whatever you like at random. Learning means coming to want things to happen as they actually do, because the divine ordering of the world, which Epictetus calls the disposer, arranges everything, including seasons, plenty and want, and good and bad, for the good of the whole. Each person is given a body, possessions and companions within that order.

Epictetus says that if we complain about being alone or about being with other people, the fault lies in how we name our situation. Being alone should be called calm and freedom, and being with many should be called a festival, so that we accept both with contentment.

Epictetus says that refusing what life gives is its own punishment: a person simply becomes what they are, such as a lonely man or a bad parent. A prison is any place a person is in against their will, so Socrates, who stayed in prison by choice, was not truly imprisoned. He asks whether a person should blame the whole world for one lame leg, or give up that part willingly for the good of the whole.

Epictetus says that a person should willingly give back life to the god who gave it, and should not resent what Zeus and the Fates have set in order. He adds that in body a person is only a small part of the whole, but in intelligence a person is equal to the gods, since intelligence is measured by thought, not by size.

Eating acceptably to the gods means eating justly, contentedly, calmly and temperately. Epictetus then gives an example: when a slave brings lukewarm water or fails to appear, not losing your temper is also pleasing to the gods. He ends by asking how one can put up with such a slave, and answers that the slave is a brother, since all people share a divine origin.

Epictetus tells a person in power not to become a tyrant over those beneath him. He reminds them that these people are their kin, equal by nature and children of Zeus, the chief god. He says the ruler has bought them, but they have not bought him, and he criticizes the ruler for following human laws rather than divine ones.

Philosophy does not promise to get a person any outside thing, such as land, health, reputation, or another person's behaviour. Its only material is each person's own life, so a man's brother's anger belongs to the brother's own art, not to his. Philosophy only promises to keep a person's governing part (the mind or will) in line with nature.

Epictetus tells a man who wants quick peace with his estranged brother that good things do not come suddenly. He compares it to a fig, which must flower, bear fruit and ripen over time. A person's mind matures in the same slow way, so the man should not expect it to happen quickly or easily.

Epictetus argues that people who do wrong are not really wicked on purpose but are mistaken about what is good and bad. So they should not be destroyed for their faults. He compares them to people who are blind or deaf, who are harmed rather than deserving of punishment.

Epictetus argues that the greatest harm is losing one's own inner will or choice, and that this loss is not caused by other people's wrongs. So anger at someone who wrongs us makes little sense. He asks whether we are angry only because we value the things such people take from us, such as property or status.

Epictetus says that if you value fine clothes, you give thieves a reason to steal them. A thief thinks, as you do, that having fine things is what makes a person good, so he will come and take them. Keeping such things out of sight, rather than airing them, avoids the temptation.

Epictetus describes a lamp being stolen and says the loss is no surprise, since a person can only lose what they own. He suggests that a loss means the thing was once possessed, and that pains and losses only touch what belongs to us. Losing a garment or having a headache follows the same reasoning. Nothing lost was ever truly ours, so it is not a cause for distress.

A tyrant can chain only the body, such as the leg, and take away only the neck, meaning life. He cannot touch the will, which is the mind's choice. So a person should practise self-control in small matters, like not complaining about a headache, and work up from there.

Epictetus says you may groan aloud if you must, but you should not torment yourself inwardly over small troubles, such as a slave being slow with a bandage, or by thinking everyone hates you. Trust your own judgment instead, and stand upright and free, not relying on physical size or strength, which he compares to an ass's unbeatable bulk.

A person who thinks he has some advantage, even when he does not, will become proud of it if he lacks learning. Epictetus gives the example of a tyrant who boasts of his power. He then asks whether the tyrant can guarantee that his desires will not be blocked, or that he will always avoid what he fears and move toward what he wants without mistake. He compares this to a ship, where people trust the helmsman, not themselves.

Epictetus asks what real power a person has if they rely on others, such as a charioteer, for their safety. He answers that he respects his own tools and animals only because they meet his needs, not because they are better than him. He suggests that respect shown to him by others is of a similar kind.

Epictetus is mocking a tyrant who thinks he commands respect through fear. He says people value the tyrant only as they value a donkey or a sickness, and no one admires him as a person or wants to copy him as they copied Socrates. The tyrant's only power is the threat of execution, so people honour him as they would a fever.

Epictetus argues that a free person cannot be disturbed by outside forces, only by their own opinions. A tyrant can threaten the body, but the person who values their own will, rather than their leg or comfort, is not troubled by the threat and accepts whatever the tyrant decides.

Epictetus is answering a tyrant who claims power over him. He says the tyrant cannot control his inner self, since Zeus made him free. The tyrant can only take his body, and his own sense of self stays his own. He treats the tyrant with no more regard than he gives a cheap clay pot.

Epictetus says that people give power over their opinions to tyrants only because they wrongly believe that things outside their control are good or bad. He wishes people would not also give that respect to the emperor's servants. He mocks how a minor court attendant, once given a post by Caesar, suddenly seems wise, and he says Felicion would look foolish again if he lost that position.

People cheer and honor a man when he is made tribune, with kisses, torches and sacrifices at the Capitol. Epictetus asks who ever gave thanks to the gods for good desires or for living according to nature. His point is that people thank the gods for the things they count as good, such as office and status, not for virtue.

Epictetus argues that seeking fame through public office is pointless. A man who wants to be named as a priest of Augustus will only be remembered in documents that no one reads for long, and even a stone inscription will not carry his name far beyond his own town. If he wants a crown, he might as well wear roses, which look better.

Epictetus argues that a person should be content with the role nature has given them and should act according to nature, without showing off. He mocks the wish to be admired and pointedly asks whether anyone wants to be admired by people whom he himself calls mad.

Everyone starts with the same basic ideas, such as that good is worth pursuing and justice is admirable. People only disagree when they apply these shared ideas to particular cases, for example whether a specific action was brave or foolish.

Epictetus says that people of different nations argue not over whether holiness should be put above everything, but over whether a particular act, such as eating pork, is holy or not. He says the same kind of quarrel appears between Agamemnon and Achilles, who both agree that what is right should be done but still disagree about the specific case.

Agamemnon and Achilles argue over who has the right to decide what is owed. Agamemnon says he must give Chryseis back to her father, and Achilles tells him he must. Each man reads the idea of duty differently, and the quarrel starts from that difference, which turns into a dispute over who keeps a prize.

Education, for Epictetus, means learning to apply our natural basic understanding to real situations, and to separate what is within our control (our will and our choices) from what is not (the body, possessions, family, and country). He then asks whether good should be placed in things outside our control, such as health, children, and country, and implies that people would not accept denying that these are good.

Epictetus argues that if a person counts wealth, land or goods as "good," then losing them makes happiness impossible and leads to bad conduct. Someone who believes his own advantage lies in taking his neighbor's land or another's garment will steal, and that, he says, causes wars, civil strife, tyranny and conspiracy.

Epictetus argues that if a god does not protect people from harm, or allows them to suffer, there is no reason to value him. He then asks why people build temples and statues to gods like Zeus and to Fever, and why they call Zeus a saviour or giver of rain, if they place the good in such things. Each claim leads to absurd results.

The speaker asks what he should do, since he cannot see what is truly good or bad. He admits this makes him seem mad. If he placed the good in things that depend on the will, he expects that everyone, including a wealthy old man, would laugh at him and tell him to go on with philosophy.

The speaker is scolded by someone who says he knows logic but acts better than the philosophers who teach it. He asks why he is blamed for knowing how to act well. He says that, since he cannot silence the critic without the critic bursting with anger, he must answer by asking to be excused, as lovers are, because he is not his own master and is mad.

Hard times show what a person is really like. When a difficulty comes, Epictetus says to see it as God matching you with a tough opponent, as a trainer does with a wrestler, so that you can grow strong. He adds that the difficulty can be very useful if you face it the way an athlete faces a young rival.

Epictetus compares a frightened messenger to a scout who runs back from a noise or shadow, shouting that the enemy is close. He says that a person who reports dangers such as death, exile, poverty or slander, and urges flight, is like that scout. The speakers reply that the only mistake was sending such a messenger in the first place.

Epictetus compares Diogenes, the Cynic, to a scout who has come back with a report. Diogenes says death is not an evil and that fame is only the noise of madmen. He also says going naked is better than a purple robe and that bare ground is the softest bed.

Epictetus describes a man who proves each claim by pointing to his own courage, calm, freedom and healthy body. He says there is no enemy nearby, so all is peaceful. Epictetus answers that such a man is like a scout who should report only what he has actually seen, and he tells him to go back and look again once his fear is gone.

Epictetus asks why people still feel disturbed and afraid if they truly believe that good and evil lie only in their own will. He says the things people worry about are not in their power, and the things that are in others' power they do not care about. So he asks what trouble is left.

Zeus, the highest god, has already given each person what is truly theirs: their own choices and character, which nothing outside can block. Other things, such as possessions, are not ours and can be taken away. So a person should keep hold of what is their own and not reach for what belongs to others, because reaching for it costs them what they already have.

Epictetus argues that the reader already has what they need to know their duty. He says the "promptings and commands" come from Zeus, the highest god, and that the reader's own innate ideas, the teachings of philosophers, and what they have heard, said, read, and thought all show this. Therefore, he says, these all come from God.

If you set your admiration on your body or your possessions, you make yourself a slave, because those are the places where you can be caught. Whatever part you guard is the part your master will attack, so there is no one left to flatter or fear.

Epictetus is speaking to someone who wants a seat among the senators at the amphitheatre, and who feels cramped where he is. He says the discomfort comes from our own choices: we crowd ourselves by wanting to watch the show from a particular place. His advice is to stop being a spectator, or to wait until the show ends and then take the senators' seat.

Epictetus says that being insulted hurts only because our own opinions make it hurt. Insulting a stone achieves nothing, and an insult gains the insulter something only when the person insulted is weak enough to react. He then jokes that the insulter may keep his insult, since it does him no good.

Epictetus says people would rather study anything than the means to inner freedom, and that Socrates lived by such means. He argues that philosophy, like other arts, has statements that sound strange to outsiders. Surgery seems absurd to the untrained too, since cutting an eye seems a way to harm it, yet it helps sight.

Things can seem to us in four ways: they may be as they appear, not be and not seem so, be but not seem so, or not be yet seem so. In each case, the educated person's task is to judge rightly, and whatever troubles us needs a remedy.

Epictetus says that whatever troubles a person must be met with its own cure. If the trouble is clever arguments, such as those of the Sceptics (Pyrrho and the Academics), use argument against them. If it is false appearances that make things look good when they are not, look for a remedy to that. If it is habit, the cure is the opposite habit.

Epictetus tells the reader to stop speaking in the way just quoted, which describes a death as untimely and far from home. Instead, he says, take up the opposite habit of speech, and set reason and its training against clever arguments. Against misleading appearances, one should keep clear, ready ideas that are free of error.

When death seems evil, we should keep in mind that death is necessary and that we should avoid evil things. There is no place to escape death, so the speaker resolves to act bravely himself, or to let another person have the chance to do so. If brave action is beyond our power, we can at least think this way.

Epictetus is saying that people fear death because they want something that death will take away, and they cannot have it. He asks whether anyone can find a way to avoid death altogether. He notes that people try to control outside events, and if they cannot, they grow angry at whoever blocks them, because humans cannot bear to lose what is good or to fall into what is bad.

Epictetus describes a person who, unable to change events or stop an obstacle, groans and blames the gods. He asks what the gods are to him if they do not care for him. When told this makes him impious, he asks how his situation would be any worse. His conclusion: piety can only last in someone whose own good lies in the same thing as piety.

The mind agrees to something only because it seems true to it. It cannot agree to what seems false. The understanding is naturally drawn to the true, rejects the false, and holds back agreement when things are uncertain.

Epictetus says we cannot make ourselves believe something we see is false, such as night being day or the stars being an even number. When someone accepts a falsehood, they do not do it knowingly; the false thing simply looks true to them. He adds, following Plato, that no soul is willingly cut off from the truth.

In actions, the things that count are what is fitting or not fitting, useful or harmful, and suitable or unsuitable, not true or false. Epictetus holds that a person cannot think something is useful for him and still refuse to choose it. He cites Medea, who admits she knows the evil she will do but gives in to passion.

Epictetus argues that a person acts on what she believes is best, so a woman who wrongly thinks revenge on her husband is worth more than protecting her children will act on that false belief. Since she cannot see her error, anger at her makes little sense; he says she should be pitied, as one pities the blind or the lame.

Each person judges an action by how it appears to them, as good or bad. If it appears good, the doer is not to blame; if it appears bad, the doer suffers for it, since the one deceived and the one who suffers are the same person. Remembering this stops a person from being angry at, blaming, or fighting with anyone.

Epictetus says that great and terrible actions come from opinion, meaning how things appear to a person. The Trojan War, the subject of the Iliad, is in his view just a result of appearances. Had Menelaus judged losing his wife a gain, there would have been no war and no Iliad or Odyssey.

Epictetus asks whether great events like wars and the destruction of cities are really so different from the deaths of animals and the burning of birds' nests. His answer is that they are very alike: bodies are destroyed, and dwellings are burnt, in both cases.

Epictetus asks what is so grand or frightening about a human house, since a stork's nest serves the same basic purpose as a dwelling. Men build with beams, tiles and bricks, storks with sticks and mud, so in body the two are much alike.

The passage asks whether humans differ from storks in basic animal matters like eating and reproducing. Its answer is no: those matters are shared. Humans differ in understanding what they do, in social bonds, fidelity, modesty, steadfastness and intelligence, and that is where good and evil lie.

A person is harmed only by what happens within their own character. If modesty, fidelity, and intelligence stay intact, the person stays intact, just as a city stays safe when its walls hold. Epictetus says that Alexander suffered no real loss from the war, the fall of Troy, or his brothers' deaths, since those were external events, not his own actions.

A person is ruined not by losing a great friend or a city, but when they lose their right opinions. Epictetus says Alexander was ruined when he gave up modesty, loyalty and respect for guests, and Achilles when he let anger and a love for a girl take over from his duty to fight at Troy. Ruin, in his view, is the corruption of right judgment.

The main point is that good and bad belong to the will itself. External things are only the material the will works with. The will becomes good or bad depending on whether our opinions about those things are right or distorted, and it becomes good by not over-valuing them.

The main point is that good things must come from within a person, not from others. Threats from a tyrant can only reach the body, such as hands, feet, head or the whole body, and not the person's own good.

Epictetus argues that a threat only works if the person feels fear. If a tyrant threatens banishment and the listener feels that such things do not concern him, then no threat has been made against him. He asks whom he would fear: a master of things within his own control, of which there is none, or a master of things outside his control, which in his view mean nothing to him.

Epictetus has an objector ask whether philosophers teach people to despise kings, and says he hopes not. He argues that philosophy does not teach people to claim power over the things kings hold, such as body, property, reputation and companions. The only thing he admits to commanding is opinion, and he asks who gave anyone the power to control another person's opinion.

Epictetus argues that a person's own judgment or will can only be overcome by that person's own will, not by outside force. He then says the law of the strong, that the stronger rule the weaker, is only about physical power: chains, killing, and taking property.

Epictetus is saying that a group of ten can beat one person only where they are stronger, such as in physical force. In matters of right opinion, the one who holds the correct view has the advantage, and numbers do not change that. He compares this to a scale, where the heavier side always sinks.

Epictetus argues that it is wrong to call the Athenians' treatment of Socrates strange or unjust, or to blame God for it. Socrates had a good that the Athenians could not take away: they could kill his body but could not harm him. He accepted whatever God allowed.

Epictetus says that the superior always overpowers the inferior, by nature and by God's law, but only in the area where it is superior. A stronger body beats a weaker one, and many beat one. He lost his lamp because the thief was more alert than he was.

Epictetus is saying that a man who gains a lamp by becoming a thief and a traitor has made a bad trade, whatever he thinks. He then imagines a stronger man seizing him and dragging him to prison or death, and asks what philosophy could protect him from that. The point is that no teaching can stop a stronger person from using force.

Epictetus argues that a person who has learned the Stoic lesson should not be upset by outside events. If ten men seize and imprison him, he is not harmed, because such things are outside his will and so are nothing to him. He asks why anyone would look for gain in anything other than what they have learned truly benefits them.

Epictetus urges a student to stop merely debating the fine points of Stoic philosophy, which he calls small arguments that lazy people rely on. He says what is needed is someone who puts these teachings into practice, so that his actions prove his words.

Philosophical study belongs to people with free time, since humans naturally enjoy contemplation. Epictetus says it is shameful to study like a runaway slave, who half-watches a show while glancing around. Instead, a person should sit calmly and attend fully, as in a theatre.

The main point is that no person is truly anyone's master. Only death, life, pleasure and pain have real power over a person. A slave fears his master only because he has not understood this, and a philosopher should not be frightened in the same way. The speaker says he would stand firm even before Caesar, the emperor, because he does not fear those things.

The speaker says that when fearful things such as thunder and lightning come, he acts like a runaway slave caught by his master, afraid even when he seems at ease. He argues that if he frees himself from the things that make masters frightening, he will have no master left to fear.

Epictetus says we should not share these teachings with everyone. Instead, we should adapt to people who do not understand, excusing them as people acting from their own view of good. He gives Socrates as the example: Socrates excused his weeping jailer and spoke about the matter only to friends who could understand it.

Epictetus begins by raising a question: can a person act with both caution and confidence at once? Caution seems opposed to confidence, and opposites cannot go together. He says the philosophers' view on this may look like a paradox to many people, and he proposes to examine whether it is true.

Epictetus argues that caution and confidence are not contradictory when applied to different things. Good and evil lie only in how we use our judgments about events, while things outside our will have no good or evil in themselves. So we should be confident about things outside our control and cautious about things within it.

Epictetus argues that caution should be applied only to things under our control, since the real bad is a wrong use of the will. Things outside our control are not bad for us, so we should feel confident about them. Caution about what truly matters therefore produces confidence about everything else.

Epictetus compares us to deer that flee from feathers, the huntsmen's lure, and run into the nets instead. We fear things outside our control, such as events and other people's actions, and feel safe about things that depend on our own choices. We therefore mistake what is dangerous for what is safe.

Epictetus says that mistakes in small matters, or in things we cannot control, do not really matter to us. What matters is fear and flight when faced with death, exile, pain or disgrace. When people go wrong in these greatest matters, they turn natural confidence into recklessness and shamelessness, and natural caution into cowardice and fear.

If you direct your caution toward what lies within your own will and choices, you can avoid what you choose to avoid. If you direct it toward things outside your control, you will fear, be unstable and be disturbed. Death and pain are not themselves frightening; the fear of them is.

Epictetus says we should face death with courage and be careful about fearing it. Instead, people try to run from death and treat their own view of it with carelessness and indifference. He compares life's events to the tragic masks in a play: children find masks frightening only because they lack experience, and people are frightened by events for the same reason.

Epictetus says that a child is only ignorant, and that a child who knows these things is no worse than an adult. Death is like a theatre mask that looks frightening but cannot hurt anyone when examined closely. Since the body must be separated from the spirit sooner or later, there is no reason to be troubled that it happens now.

Pain is compared to a mask: look at it closely and it is not what it seems. The body is pushed about roughly and then gently, and things are accepted as part of the universe's completed course. If a person is not satisfied, the door is open to leave. If they are satisfied, they should endure what happens. Either way, the exit is always available, so there is no trouble.

The passage argues that the real fruit of learning is freedom from disturbance and fear. It claims that only educated people are truly free, not those who are merely born free, because freedom means being able to live as you choose. Since no one chooses to live in error, the educated are the ones who can live as they really want.

Someone who lives in error, fear, sorrow or disturbance is not free, and freedom from these inner troubles is the same as freedom from slavery. So Epictetus asks how the lawmakers can claim that only free people should be educated, when philosophers hold that only the educated are truly free.

Epictetus says that a legal ceremony of manumission, where a master formally frees a slave before a Roman magistrate, does not by itself make a person free. The man who frees a slave has only done a legal act and paid a tax. He is still ruled by his own desires and fears, such as money, a lover, or a powerful patron, so he has not become free in the inner sense.

Epictetus asks why a person should worry before facing danger. His answer is to keep certain principles ready that show which things to be careful about and which to face bravely. Things outside one's control call for courage, while things within one's control call for care.

Epictetus says that if a person keeps their own will in line with nature, and keeps what is truly up to them, they have nothing to fear from others. No one can take away one's own choices, such as being modest and faithful, or force one to want what one should not want.

Epictetus argues that no one can force you to avoid what you do not think you should avoid, and a judge can only threaten outcomes, not make you suffer in your choosing. If your choice of what to pursue and what to avoid is up to you, nothing else needs to matter, since that choice is all the rest depends on.

Socrates, asked to prepare for his trial, says he has been preparing all his life. He means that he kept hold of what was in his own power, which for him was never doing anything unjust in private or public life.

Epictetus is telling a student who wants to keep his body, property and reputation that he must prepare for the trial, which means considering the judge and the opponent. He adds that if he must beg, weep or groan before the judge, he should do so.

Epictetus says that if you have handed over what is really yours to outside things, you should either fully accept being a slave or refuse it completely, not switch back and forth. He urges a clear choice: endure punishment to the end, or give in at once, rather than resisting for a while and then yielding. He asks where good and evil truly lie, meaning in choices rather than outward conditions.

Epictetus says it is foolish to ask a teacher for a set answer to every situation. Instead, one should train the mind to adapt to whatever happens. He compares this to an unskilled writer who asks what to write for each name given to him, when he should simply learn to write any name.

Epictetus says that a person who has trained in a skill is ready for whatever it requires, so no extra advice is needed. Anyone who instead chases external things must wander about, obeying whoever controls the things they want or want to avoid.

Things outside us, such as possessions, health and events, are neither good nor bad in themselves. What matters is how we use them, and that lies within our control: our own choices and will. Good and bad belong only to what we control, not to external things.

Epictetus says we should use external things with care, because how we use them is up to us and affects our will, even though the things themselves are neither good nor bad. We should act with firmness and calm, since the things we handle do not matter in themselves. Only our use of them can be good or bad, and that use is in our power, while obtaining such things is not.

Epictetus says it is hard, but not impossible, to combine careful concern for what happens to us with a calm indifference to it. He compares this to a sea voyage: you choose the captain, crew and day, and once a storm comes, your part is done and the outcome belongs to the captain. Even then, he asks what you should do if the ship is sinking.

Epictetus says that since he is only a mortal part of the whole, like one hour of a day, he must pass away like everything else that is born. So it makes no difference how he dies, whether by drowning or by fever, because every death is a way of passing away.

Some things are "according to nature" or "contrary to nature" only in relation to the whole they belong to. A foot is naturally clean when considered alone, but as part of a body it may need to step in mud or be cut off for the body's good. People should see themselves the same way, as parts of a larger whole.

Epictetus says that if a person thinks of himself as separate from others, then long life, wealth and health seem natural. But if he thinks of himself as a part of a larger whole, then illness, danger, poverty and early death can also serve that whole. So he asks why such a person would be troubled by them.

Epictetus argues that a person is only a whole being as a member of a larger community. Just as a foot stops being a foot when cut off from the body, a man is not fully a man when cut off from other men. He says each person is part of the state of gods and men, and of the smaller community close to it. So he asks why he should be spared the trials and losses that others suffer.

Epictetus says that in a world with so many people living together, wrongs will inevitably happen to some and not to others. His point is that each person should do their own part well, such as speaking and arranging things properly, and then leave it to others to do theirs. If someone accuses you of wronging them, you have still done your own duty, but you should check whether you have done yours, since you may not notice your own failings.

Epictetus is saying that some things are indifferent, meaning neither good nor bad in themselves, such as a hypothetical argument or life itself. What matters is the judgment we make about such things and how we use them. So when someone calls these things indifferent, do not become careless, and when someone urges caution about them, do not become overawed by material things.

Know what you are prepared for and what you are not. Where you lack training, stay quiet and do not be upset when others do better. In the matters you have studied, such as logic (syllogisms), you may claim the advantage yourself, and if others are annoyed, you can answer that you learned these things and they did not.
Where a skill is needed, do not look for the benefit that comes from having that need. Instead, defer to people who already have the practice, and be content with a steady mind yourself.

Epictetus says that when you visit someone, you should not act in a demeaning way, and that if you fail to get what you want, the outcome belongs to the other person, not to you. The lesson is to keep clear what is yours to control and what belongs to others, so that you are not disturbed.

Chrysippus said that while the future is unknown, he keeps to what helps his natural well-being, since God gave him the power to choose. But if he knew that illness was fated, he would move toward it, as a foot would walk into mud if it could think. Crops grow so they can dry and be harvested, so each thing serves the larger order.

Epictetus compares people to ears of corn. A corn stalk that was never cut down would be cursed, so not dying would be a curse for people too, just as not ripening or not being harvested would be. We are upset about our death because we do not know what we are, and we have not studied what belongs to human nature, as horse experts know what belongs to horses.

Epictetus contrasts Chrysantas, a soldier who stopped his own attack when the retreat was sounded because he preferred to obey his general, with most people. Most people obey necessity only with weeping and groaning, and they call the things that happen to them "circumstances." He asks what kind of circumstances these are, since by that name everything around us would count as one.

Epictetus argues that dying is not a real hardship, since whatever causes death, whether a sword, a fever, the sea or a tyrant, leads to the same end. The way a person dies makes no real difference, and a tyrant's killing is not even slower than an illness. The words for these harms are only empty names.

Many people neglect their duties because they rely too much on fortune-telling. A diviner can only foresee death, danger or illness, so Epictetus asks why one would need him. If duty requires facing danger for a friend, one already has an inner guide that knows what is good and what is evil.

Epictetus asks why he should accept advice from reading animal entrails or bird flights when told it serves his interest. He asks whether the diviner really knows what is good for him, and whether someone who reads omens also knows what is good, bad, beautiful, ugly, just, or unjust.

A speaker is asked to say whether a sign means life or death, poverty or wealth. He refuses to ask whether these things are good for him, and he asks why the diviner gives opinions on such disputed matters when he does not give opinions on grammar, a subject where people agree.
