People turn to fortune-tellers because they are afraid of what the future holds. So they flatter the diviners, thank them for good news as if it were a real gift, and so the diviners end up controlling them.

Good is to be sought in the rational animal, meaning human beings, since it cannot be found in plants or other animals. Plants and animals are God's works but not superior things, while humans are superior because each person carries a portion of the divine within. The passage asks why people do not remember this noble origin.

Epictetus says that a person carries a god within themselves, so every social act, bit of exercise, or discussion is done in the presence of that god. The god is not a statue of silver or gold but something inside the person. Thoughts and deeds that are impure or dirty stain this inner god, and the speaker says a person would not act that way if a divine image stood in front of them.

Epictetus argues that a person who believes God is always present and watching should not need outside fears about behavior. He asks why teachers worry that a young man leaving school will misbehave, dress badly or act proudly. The young man who does so, he says, does not know his own God or who is with him as he goes out into the world.

Epictetus asks why a person would look for guidance elsewhere when God is already within them. He compares a human to a statue made by the sculptor Phidias: a statue of a god would be made carefully and presented with dignity, so a person made by Zeus should likewise act in a way worthy of their maker.

Epictetus contrasts human-made art with God's work. A statue like Phidias's Athena stays fixed in its pose and has no life of its own, but God's works can move, breathe, and judge what they perceive. He then asks whether a person who has been made this way dishonors their maker, and notes that God also left each person in their own care.

Epictetus says that God has put a person in your care like an orphan child, asking that they be kept modest, faithful, upright, fearless, and free from passion and disturbance. The speaker's point is that the listener fails to keep the person as they were given.

A student replies to critics who think his stern looks show arrogance. He says he has not yet gained the calm confidence of a true philosopher, because he still fears his own weakness. Once his beliefs are firm, he will show a fitting face and bearing. He compares himself to the statue of Zeus at Olympia, whose calm, fixed look suits a god.

Epictetus says he can show himself faithful, modest, noble and free from disturbance, and can die and fall ill as a god would. He cannot make himself immortal or free from old age and sickness. What he can show, as a philosopher, is a desire that is never disappointed, an aversion that never lands on what it wants to avoid, and a sound, careful judgment.

Epictetus says a human being is a rational, mortal creature, set apart from animals by reason. If a person acts like a wild beast or a sheep, they fail to live up to what a human being is meant to be. He then asks what we do when we act like sheep.

Epictetus says that when people act greedily, lustfully, rashly, or dirtily, they have fallen to the level of sheep and lost their reason. When they act with quarrelsome, harmful, passionate, or violent behavior, they have fallen to the level of wild beasts. A person who fails to act as a human being has broken what being human promises, just as a complex statement is true only when it does what its nature requires.

Things are kept in being by doing what they are meant to do. A disjunctive statement (an "either/or" claim) holds only when it fulfils what it promises, and flutes, a lyre, a horse or a dog are kept whole when they perform their own work. In the same way, a person is improved and preserved by acts that fit his craft, and is corrupted when he acts against it, as a writer who keeps writing ungrammatically loses his skill in grammar.

Actions keep a person's character as it is: modest acts keep a modest person modest, and faithful acts keep a faithful person faithful. Acts of the opposite kind destroy those qualities and strengthen the opposite ones, so that shameless, faithless, angry, or greedy acts make a person more so.

Philosophers urge people to go beyond learning ideas and to practice them, because people often act against the true ideas they know. Without putting right ideas into action, a person only repeats what others have taught. Anyone can easily state the teaching that some things are good, some bad, and some neutral.

Epictetus is scolding students who can recite Stoic teaching about what is good, bad and indifferent, yet lose their composure when someone makes a noise or laughs at them. He says their philosophy stays in their mouths and is not put into practice, like bread and wine stored away instead of eaten.

Epictetus says that doctrines should become part of a person, the way food becomes flesh and blood. Knowledge that is only stored up, and can be recited on demand, gives no real benefit beyond looking like one has it. He points out that someone could explain Epicurus's views as well as Epicurus did, yet still not live as a Stoic, and he asks why such a person calls himself a Stoic.

Epictetus asks why someone who is a Greek would act like a Jew. He says people are called Jews only when they truly hold Jewish teaching and belong to that group. A person who only half follows it is said to act like a Jew, but is not one.

Epictetus says that a human being is above all other things in one way: the will, or power of choice, is the only thing that is fully one's own and cannot be controlled by others. He adds that reason separates humans from wild beasts and from tame animals.

You are, the passage says, a citizen of the world and a part of it, and not a lesser part that serves but one of the ruling parts, since you can understand the divine order of things and how they connect. From this the passage asks what a citizen of the world commits to, and its first answer is that he counts nothing as advantageous to himself alone.

The main point is that a person should not make choices as if he stood alone, apart from the community. He should act the way a hand or foot would if it had reason and understood how nature is ordered. Such a limb would never move or want anything except for the good of the whole body.

Epictetus says that a good person who knew the future would accept sickness, death and injury as parts of the universal order, since the whole matters more than any one part. Because we cannot know the future, our duty is to choose what is naturally more suitable, which is what we were made for.

Epictetus says that being a son means treating the father's possessions as the father's, obeying him in everything, never blaming him to others, never harming him, and cooperating with him as far as possible. He then adds that being a brother means being willing to give way to others.

Being easy to persuade, speaking well of your brother, and giving up things outside your control (such as a lettuce or a seat) rather than fighting over them. In return you keep more of what is under your own will, which is your goodness of character. Epictetus says this trade is a large gain.

Epictetus says that each role a person holds, such as senator, young man, or old man, comes with its own duties. If someone forgets their role, for example by blaming a brother, they have forgotten who they are. A smith who misuses his hammer has likewise forgotten what a smith is.

Epictetus argues that the worst loss is not money but the loss of one's human nature. If you stop being a brother and become an enemy, or stop being a social human and become a treacherous beast, you have lost something far more important than any possession. He asks whether losing a skill like grammar would count as damage, implying that losing one's humanity counts for more.

Epictetus says that losing modesty, moderation and gentleness is a real loss, not a small matter. Other things, such as wealth or health, can be lost through causes outside our control, so losing them is not shameful. These inner qualities are lost through our own fault, so failing to keep or losing them is shameful.

Epictetus asks whether he should hurt someone who has hurt him. He argues that, by Stoic teaching, harm to a person lies in their own choices and intentions, not in outside losses. So the wrong done to him would be a wrong done by the other man to himself, and returning it would harm only the one who returns it.

Epictetus says people think it does no harm when the will goes wrong, since being deceived or acting unjustly does not hurt the body or cost property. People care only about bodily and material safety, not whether their will is modest and faithful. Their learning in the school goes no further than the words they use about it.

Philosophy begins when a person admits they are weak and unable to know necessary things. We are not born knowing things like geometry or music theory; we learn them through teaching and skill. People who have not learned these things do not think they know them.

Everyone is born with basic ideas of good and evil, beautiful and ugly, right and wrong, and happiness and misfortune. Because of these built-in ideas, we all use such words and apply them to particular situations, such as calling an action good, bad, just, or unjust.

Epictetus says that people start with some natural grasp of what is good and bad, but they assume they already apply it correctly without learning how. He says the real question is whether we apply that understanding properly, and that self-conceit gets in the way of asking it.

Epictetus is saying that people start from shared basic ideas but then fit them wrongly to particular cases, and so they disagree. He asks why, if they could fit the ideas correctly, they would not already be perfect. When someone claims a correct fit, another person can claim the same thing, and neither can prove it.

Epictetus asks whether two people with opposite opinions can both apply their basic ideas correctly, and answers no. He then argues that a madman acts on what seems right to him, but that this is not enough to judge truth. So something beyond mere appearance is needed as a standard.

Philosophy begins when people notice that others disagree with them, and then look for the cause of the disagreement. It also means distrusting mere appearances, testing whether they are right, and finding a standard to test them by, like a balance for weights or a rule for straight lines. The passage then asks how all opinions can be right when they contradict each other.

Epictetus argues that what merely seems right to each person cannot be the standard for what is true. Just as weights and measures need a fixed rule rather than appearance, he says there must be a rule for judging truth, since the most necessary matters cannot lack a means of discovery.

Epictetus asks why people do not look for a standard of judgment and then hold to it closely. He says that finding such a standard cures those who trust mere appearances as their guide. Once basic principles are clear, we can then apply our fixed ideas to particular cases.
Epictetus uses a question-and-answer test. Something is put on the scale to see whether it can be trusted. Pleasure fails, because it is not secure, so it is excluded from what counts as good.

Being elated by what is good is fitting, but being elated by present pleasure is not. Epictetus says that philosophy means testing and confirming the basic rules for judging things, and that a wise and good person then applies those rules once they are known.

The Stoic philosophers have clearly laid out what a person must learn before they can argue well. But people are not practiced at actually using those skills. Give most of us an uneducated person to debate, and we cannot work out how to handle them.

When a debater's opponent answers off the point, the debater mocks him or calls him ignorant and gives up. Epictetus says a guide does not mock a traveler who has strayed but leads him back to the right road, and so the debater should show the untrained man the truth and expect him to follow.

Socrates' main quality was that he never got angry in an argument and never used insults, even when others insulted him, and he ended quarrels instead. Epictetus points to Xenophon's Symposium as proof of how many quarrels he settled, and notes that poets also praise this skill.

Anxiety comes from wanting something that is not up to us. The lute player sings well alone without worry, but in the theatre he fears for the applause, which he cannot control. He is confident where his skill lies, and he does not care about listeners who know nothing of music.

Epictetus says a person who has never practised facing a crowd gets anxious, because he does not know what crowd praise is or how much power it has over life. Such fear is not about real evils, and it is not about evils that are within his control and may not happen. The fear comes from inexperience.

Epictetus argues that if only our own will is in our power, and outside things like the body, property and the wishes of rulers are not good or bad in themselves, then there is nothing inside us to worry about. He notes that we still worry about external things, but not about our own judgments or actions.

Epictetus compares a doctor's diagnosis to a judgment about the mind. Just as a doctor reads a pale face as a sign of a disordered spleen or liver, a person whose desire and aversion are disordered is said to be sick in the same way, like a man with a fever. Only an inner disorder, he argues, would produce such visible signs as pallor, trembling, and shaking knees.

Zeno was calm before meeting Antigonus because Antigonus could not affect the things Zeno valued. Antigonus was anxious, because he wanted to please Zeno, and that depended on someone else. Zeno had no wish to please Antigonus, since a skilled person does not seek the approval of someone without that skill.

Epictetus asks why he should try to please someone who does not know what makes a man good. He says a good man does notweep, tremble, or fear how others will receive him. He suggests that how another person treats your words is that person's responsibility, not yours.

Epictetus argues that a fault belongs to the person who has it, not to someone else, so worrying about what other people do is misplaced. He then compares fear of speaking to someone with writing or reading a familiar name: a person is not disconcerted by what they have practised, and speaking can be practised in the same way.

Epictetus asks what the study of logic (syllogisms and sophistical propositions) was for. His answer is that it was for speaking skilfully: speaking at the right time, with care, intelligence, no mistakes, and confidence.

Epictetus says that a rider on a horse has no reason to fear a man on foot, since the rider has the advantage in a contest. A person who answers that the other man can kill him is told to speak the truth and stop claiming to be a philosopher. As long as a person's body can be harmed in this way, he should yield to whoever is stronger.

Epictetus says that Socrates and Diogenes trained in speaking, and so they could face tyrants, judges, kings and pirates with confidence. He criticises his listener for doing the opposite: going off to private matters, sitting in a corner making logical arguments, and never acting in public life.

Epictetus stopped a reading and said that this was the method of teaching. When asked to continue, he said that every skill is hard for a beginner to learn, though the products of skills show their use and often please.

Watching someone learn a craft is unpleasant, but the finished work is useful or pleasing. A shoemaker's or smith's training looks tedious to a bystander, and music's practice sounds harsh to a learner's listeners, yet the results please everyone.

The philosopher's task, as described here, is to shape his wishes to match what actually happens. Then nothing will happen against his wish, and what he wants not to happen will not happen. The result is that he will not fail in what he desires and will not run into what he wants to avoid.

Epictetus says a philosopher's work is to live without anxiety, fear, or disturbance while keeping up all his ordinary relationships, such as son, father, citizen, husband, neighbor, and ruler. He then says the next question is how this can be done.

Just as a carpenter or a pilot becomes skilled only by learning specific things, Epictetus argues that wanting to be wise and good is not enough in philosophy either. Certain things must be learned first, and the Stoic philosophers say the first lesson is that God exists, provides for all things, and sees even our intentions and thoughts.

To please and obey the gods, a person must learn what they are like and then copy them. If the divine is faithful, free, beneficent and magnanimous, a person must be the same, acting and speaking in line with that.

Epictetus says some people take the idea that one should be firm, and that only the will is free, to mean they must stick to every decision they have made. He replies that a decision must first be sound, or true. He compares this to bodily strength, which is only good when the body is healthy.

Epictetus says that a man who boasts of his own "tone" (mental strength) while acting like a frenzied person needs a physician, since what he shows is a lack of right tone. He then describes a companion who, without reason, decided to starve himself, and he asks him what led to the decision.

Epictetus says that a person should keep only those decisions that are right, not every decision made. If a decision is unreasonable, it should be changed. Before holding firm to a choice, one should first test whether it is sound, and only then build firmness on it.

Epictetus is saying that a faulty starting point makes any structure built on it collapse sooner the more weight is added. He then asks whether someone who kills a harmless friend can still claim to be bound by his own earlier decisions, and suggests that a person should not feel bound by such decisions if he decided to kill him.

Epictetus says that some people cannot be persuaded to change their minds, and he compares them to fools and madmen. The more firmly such people hold a false belief, the stronger the cure they need. He ends by describing the ideal reply of a sick person who asks a doctor for help and accepts that he must obey.

Epictetus is showing a person who refuses to examine a question because he has already made up his mind. The teacher says that holding to a decision without ever being open to change is a sign of madness, not sound mind. The speaker's stubborn replies, such as "I will die if you compel me," are presented as examples of this rigid attitude.

A person who says "I have decided" to refuse money may, with the same firm tone, later give in without reason and still say "I have decided." Epictetus compares a weak mind to a sick body, where fluids flow first to one part and then another. If a stubborn resolve is added to that unsteady leaning, the condition becomes beyond cure.

Epictetus says that good and evil lie only in the will, the power to choose, while things outside our will are neither good nor evil. He asks whether people practise these lessons outside the classroom, as they practise answering simple questions. He asks whether they have trained themselves to answer that money is not a good, or only to answer clever arguments.

Epictetus asks why a student who has trained in a skill still feels anxious. A public speaker may have written well, memorized his speech, and have a pleasant voice, yet he still worries. His worry comes from wanting the audience's praise. He trained for the speaking itself, but he has not trained himself to deal with praise and blame.

Epictetus asks why anyone should be surprised that a person is skilled only in what he has been taught and studied. Someone who has never learned or practised what praise and blame really are will act like ordinary people in those matters. He compares this to a lute player who plays and sings well yet trembles when he steps onto the stage.

Epictetus says that a person who understands the technical matters of a craft still does not understand crowds, their shouts, or ridicule. Such a person does not know what anxiety is or whether he can control it. So he swells with pride when praised and deflates when mocked, like a punctured bladder.

Epictetus says people fear and worry because they treat outside things, things not under their control, as good or bad. He then mocks the idea of praying to be spared a runny nose, arguing that a person already has hands to wipe it and the endurance to bear troubles.

Epictetus says that people do not care about how well they act or think. They care only about getting the result they want. He asks who cares about the quality of their own walking or deliberating, and notes that when a plan succeeds, people praise the outcome rather than the care they took.

Epictetus says that when we expect something to happen a certain way, and it does not, we feel humbled and confused. He asks who among us has consulted a seer about such matters, or has acted without concern, and then says he is looking for one truly noble person.

Epictetus says that what weighs on people and upsets them is not events themselves but their opinions about them. A person who leaves friends, home, and familiar habits is burdened only by what he thinks about leaving. He compares this to a child who stops crying when given a cake, and says he wants to be comforted by right opinions instead.

A person should spend the day not being moved by things outside his control, including other people, places, and even his own body. He should keep the divine law in mind: hold to what is his own, use what he is given without desiring what is not, and give up what is taken away willingly, being grateful for the time he had it.

Epictetus mocks people who grieve over losing familiar comforts, such as a favorite gymnasium, its porticos, or a particular water supply. He says attachment to such things is no better than a child's crying over a girl. Any water, he suggests, becomes familiar, so the loss matters only because of the attachment.

The speaker asks why anyone would long to see Athens and its Acropolis when the sun, moon, stars, earth and sea are already in view. If a person understands the power that runs the whole universe and carries it within themselves, they would not still want stones and a rock.

The first task of a student of philosophy is to drop self-conceit, the belief that one already knows. A person cannot start learning something he thinks he already knows. People come to philosophers to learn about right and wrong, yet they judge these matters freely, even though they do not really know them.

Epictetus says it is foolish to expect to gain skill in something one does not actually learn. People take philosophy either for its clever sayings or for practical benefit, so they should expect to be taught what they study. He notes that the orator Theopompus made the same mistake when he criticised Plato for trying to define every term.

Epictetus asks whether people before Theopompus used words like "good" and "just" without knowing their meaning. He says everyone has natural ideas of such things, called preconceptions. These ideas can only be applied to real cases after they have been analyzed and each one matched to the right object.

We all have a general idea of health, as we did before Hippocrates, the famous physician. The trouble is applying that idea to a particular case. So doctors give opposite advice (fast, eat, bleed, use cupping), because people cannot fit the general idea of health to the specific situation.

Habits grow stronger through repeated action and weaken through neglect. Reading makes a reader, writing makes a writer, and walking strengthens the legs, while long rest weakens them. So if you want something to become a habit, do it, and if not, do something else in its place.
When you feel anger, the passage says, it is not only a harm that has happened to you. Each time you give in to it, you also strengthen the habit of anger, like throwing fuel on a fire.

Once you desire money, the desire can be stopped if reason shows you its harm, and the mind's guiding power is restored. If that cure is not applied, the desire returns more easily each time, until the mind becomes hardened and the love of money is fixed.

A recovery from a fever is not complete until the illness is fully gone, and the same holds for faults of the mind. Old marks remain, so a man who is struck again in the same place will develop sores, not mere blisters. To stop anger, a person should not feed the habit, and should first simply count the days without anger.

The passage describes how a bad habit of anger weakens over time. If a person goes longer and longer without giving way to it, the habit first loosens and then disappears. Going two or three months without being vexed, while still guarding against provoking events, shows real progress.

Epictetus says that when troubling thoughts or "appearances" come, a person should aim to be approved by their own conscience and pleasing to God, and keep their inner self pure. When such thoughts arise, he advises turning to noble and just people, whether living or dead, and measuring oneself against them.

Epictetus says that when a strong impression or appearance comes to mind, we should not let it sweep us away. We should pause, examine it, and not let it paint vivid pictures of what might follow. Instead, we should set against it a better, nobler impression. He adds that practicing this would show our real strength, while for now our efforts are only empty words.

Epictetus says that the true struggle is to resist harmful appearances, meaning the impressions that shake a person and cloud their reason. He urges the reader to hold firm, calling on God for help as sailors in a storm call on the Dioscuri (twin sea-gods). He argues that a storm is itself only an appearance, so the real danger lies in these impressions.

Remove the fear of death, and the mind stays calm even when frightening events come. If you keep losing and keep promising to do better later, you will end up so weak that you stop noticing your wrongs and start defending them. Epictetus says this proves the old poet Hesiod right: the person who keeps delaying struggles with constant troubles.

People readily admit to some faults, such as timidity, but refuse to admit others, such as foolishness, intemperance, injustice, envy or meddling. The passage asks why people confess some faults and not others.

The main point is that people are inconsistent and confused about what is good and bad. They call timidity and compassion virtues, treat foolishness as the mark of a slave, and refuse to admit that they do wrong by harming others.

People admit to some faults more readily when they think the fault came upon them against their will, such as timidity, pity, or jealousy. Injustice, by contrast, is not seen as involuntary, so people are less ready to confess it.

Epictetus says that, living among people who are confused and do not know what their troubles are or how to be freed from them, a person should constantly check whether he is one of them. He should ask whether he behaves wisely and calmly, and whether he knows that he knows nothing.

Epictetus is rebuking a student who comes to his lessons not to learn humbly, like a pupil ready to obey, but to sit in judgment over the teacher's explanations. The student has just been quarrelling at home and arrives envious and empty-handed, yet behaves as if he were already wise.

The speaker is a student who sits in class worrying about what his father and brother think of him back home. He hopes they believe he is making progress and will return knowing everything. Yet he admits he has not learned much, that he gets no help from home, and that he finds fault with his surroundings wherever he is.

Epictetus argues that people naturally love whatever they devote themselves to. Since people do not devote themselves to what is bad or to what is irrelevant, they devote themselves only to what is good. So only someone who can tell good from bad, and from what is neither, is able to love, and that ability belongs only to the wise.

Every animal, the passage says, cares most about its own interests. Anything that seems to block those interests, even a close relative, a lover or a god, is hated and rejected. The passage gives Alexander burning the temples of Aesculapius after his friend died as an example of this.

If a person puts his own interest at the center of his life, his friends, country, family and justice all give way to it. Whatever he places the "I" and the "Mine" in, he naturally leans toward that thing, whether it is the body, the will, or outside possessions.

Epictetus says that a person is truly a good friend, son, or father only when his will is set on being good. Then he will want to keep up faithfulness, modesty, patience, and other virtues. If instead a person puts his own interests in one place and honesty in another, he supports the view of Epicurus that honesty is either not real or is only what people happen to approve of.

Epictetus says that wars between peoples, from Athens and Sparta to the Trojan War, came from ignorance about what is truly good. He gives the example of Paris and Menelaus, who seemed close friends until a woman and some goods came between them, and then war broke out.

Epictetus says that brothers who look like close friends cannot be trusted to be friends, even if they swear it. A bad person's inner guiding principle is unstable and easily swayed by outside impressions. To judge real friendship, one should not look at shared parentage or upbringing. Instead, look at what each person values: external things or their own choices of will.

Epictetus says that people who base their bonds on external things, such as money, status or pleasure, should not be called friends, trustworthy, brave, or even men. He argues that human nature does not make people attack, slander, rob, and corrupt one another. Such conduct comes only from the mistaken belief that their well-being lies in things outside their control.

Epictetus says that if people hold that the only good is found in the will and in the right use of impressions, then they should be called friends for that reason alone. Family ties or long companionship do not matter. Friendship exists wherever there is faithfulness, justice, modesty, and shared honest aims.

Epictetus argues that past kindness or a long relationship does not prove that someone truly loves you. He compares a person who treats you well to how a man cleans his shoes or cares for his animal, meaning they may value you only for what you are useful for. He gives Eriphyle, who lived with Amphiaraus and had children, as an example that a long life together can still end in betrayal.

A necklace came between a husband and wife, and Epictetus says the real cause is the opinion people hold about such possessions, which he calls a beastly principle. That opinion broke their friendship and stopped the woman from being a proper wife and mother. Anyone who wants to be a friend, or to have one, should drive such opinions out of the soul.

The wise person does not blame, contradict or punish himself, and he is a full friend to anyone who is like him in wisdom. Toward someone unlike him, he stays patient, kind and ready to forgive, because that person is ignorant and wrong about matters of the greatest importance.

The speaker says a wise person is never harsh toward anyone, since people go wrong only against their will, following Plato's idea. He adds that sharing meals, a home, a voyage, or even parents does not make people friends. Without this shared understanding, they remain as far apart as snakes that share a birth.

Epictetus argues that good, fitting words help people read and listen more easily, so eloquence is worth having. He says that denying that people have the ability to express themselves is a mark of an irreverent person, who scorns God's gifts, as if he rejected the gift of sight or hearing.

The speaker asks a series of rhetorical questions about the senses: the power of sight, the air that carries vision, and light. Each question implies that none of these would exist for no reason, so their existence points to a purpose behind nature.

Be thankful for the senses, life, food and wine, but remember that the greatest gift is the ability to use these things, test them, and judge their worth. The passage asks what it is that tells us the value of each of these powers.

The main point is that the senses, and things like grain or animals, cannot judge themselves or anything else. They serve the mind, the faculty that uses appearances, and it alone can judge the value of each thing. So no other faculty can be more powerful than the mind, since it uses the rest and evaluates them.

The passage asks what controls our senses: which faculty decides when to open or close the eyes and ears, and where to direct them. Its answer is that this is not the sense itself (vision or hearing) but the faculty of the will, the power of choice.

The passage says that the will is the one faculty in a person that can see clearly. The other faculties are like blind senses, able only to perform their own functions for the will. Because of this, the will alone can judge what each faculty is worth, and the author asks whether it would name anything other than itself as the highest good. He compares this to an open eye, which by its nature simply sees.

Epictetus asks who decides how we should respond to things we see or hear, such as looking at another man's wife or believing a report. His answer is that the faculty of the will decides these things.

The passage says that the most excellent thing a person has is not the power of speech but the power of the will when it is right. The will uses speech and all other faculties. When the will is set right, a bad person becomes good, and when it fails, a good person becomes bad. Happiness or unhappiness depends on how it is cared for.

Epictetus says people often behave like a traveller who, on the way home, stops at a pleasant inn and forgets to move on. They forget that they were only passing through. Pleasant places, like inns and meadows, are meant only as stops on the journey.

Epictetus is telling a listener that his goal is to go home and take up ordinary life there: caring for family, doing civic duties, marrying, having children, and holding public office. He is not looking for a more pleasant place to live, but for the place where he was born and made a citizen. He then says the same kind of reasoning applies to the matter under discussion.

Epictetus says that speech and teaching are meant to help a student improve his character and judgment. Some people, however, get stuck on the means themselves: one is caught by fine wording, another by logical arguments, another by clever tricks of reasoning, and so on. They stay at these stopping places instead of moving on to the goal.

Epictetus tells a person that their true purpose is to deal with what happens to them in line with nature, so that their desires are not thwarted and they do not meet what they wish to avoid. They should be free, accept the will of Zeus (the Stoic name for the divine order of the universe), blame no one, and willingly say, "Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny."

Epictetus asks a man who has been ignored by him for a long time whether speaking is an art, like other skills, so that only the trained speak well. The man agrees that it is. The passage sets up the idea that skill in speech must be learned before it can be used.

Speaking well means being able to help yourself and others by it. Epictetus argues that some people are harmed by their own speaking and harm others, and that some listeners are helped while others are harmed. He concludes that both the speaker and the listener can gain or lose.

Epictetus argues that hearing well is a skill, just as speaking is. He compares it to music and sculpture: making music belongs to musicians, making statues to sculptors, and judging a statue well also needs trained skill. So judging what one hears well needs skill too.

Epictetus argues that if speaking well is the mark of a skilled person, then hearing well is too. He says he will not go further on perfect speaking and hearing, since he and his listeners are far from it. Still, anyone who wants to hear philosophers needs some practice in listening.

Epictetus says that a person who does not know who they are, what the world is, or what is good and bad cannot properly desire, act, judge, or choose. Such a person goes through life blind and dumb, falsely thinking they are someone important. He adds that all human errors and misfortunes have come from this same ignorance.

Epictetus says he speaks only reluctantly because his listeners have not stirred him. He compares this to a rider who needs a spirited horse to be roused. He says the listeners' bodies, dress, and manners give him nothing to respond to. He asks them to show they are worthy of hearing, and then the teacher will be moved to speak.

Epictetus is asked to prove that logic is necessary. He agrees to give a formal proof, but then asks how the listener could tell whether he was tricking them with his argument. The listener cannot answer, and Epictetus points out that this shows the listener already needs logic to judge whether logic is necessary.

Epictetus uses a question-and-answer exchange with a young speaker who has styled his hair and dressed elaborately. He asks whether dogs and horses can each be beautiful, and whether people are beautiful for the same reason or for qualities special to each. The point is that beauty depends on what kind of thing is being judged.

A thing is beautiful when it is at its best according to its own nature. Since dogs, horses and nightingales have different natures, each is beautiful in its own way. What makes one beautiful can make another ugly.

A thing is beautiful when it has the excellence proper to its kind. A pancratiast, wrestler, or runner each needs a different build, so a body that suits one event looks wrong for another. Since a dog is beautiful through dog-excellence and a horse through horse-excellence, a man is beautiful through human excellence.

Epictetus tells a young man that real beauty comes from human excellence, meaning justice, moderation and self-control. He points out that people admire these qualities in others, so a person who has them is beautiful. A person who lacks them is ugly, however much he tries to look attractive.
Epictetus says that a person who wants to become wise and good should train in three areas. The first is desire and aversion: getting what one wants and not falling into what one does not want.

Epictetus lists the areas of a person's inner discipline that a wise person must attend to. He names three: how one moves toward or away from things, so that one acts in an orderly and reasoned way; avoiding deception and rashness in judgment; and above all, controlling the strong emotions, which he calls "perturbations."

In this passage, Epictetus says that strong negative feelings arise only when a person fails to get what they want or meets what they want to avoid. These feelings bring disorder, misfortune, sorrow, envy and jealousy, and they keep people from listening to reason.
Epictetus says he should not be free from emotions (affects) in the way a statue is. Instead, he should keep his natural and chosen roles: being devout, a son, a father, and a citizen.

Epictetus says that students who are making progress need a third kind of training: guarding the mind so that no unexamined impression catches them off guard, even in sleep, drunkenness, or sadness. He admits this may be beyond human power. He then criticizes the philosophers of his day for skipping the first two topics, the emotions and duties, and spending their time on the third, using clever word-games, trick questions and even lies.

Epictetus is saying that a wise and good person must guard against being deceived in these matters. He asks his listener whether he has already mastered money, desire, and envy, and whether anything remains except a steady, unchanging firmness of mind.

Epictetus scolds a listener who gets anxious about what others think of him. When someone praises him as a philosopher, his small soul swells with pride, and when someone belittles him, it shrinks. The point is that his mood depends on other people's opinions.

Epictetus says that a true philosopher does not need to announce himself, because his conduct already shows what he is. He asks why a person would want to prove it through others. He tells the story of Diogenes, who pointed out a sophist by raising his middle finger, which only enraged the man. A person is shown by his principles, not by a finger pointed at him.

Epictetus says that his listener cares little about his own will, the inner power to choose, and cares instead about outside matters. He asks whether the listener worries what others will think, whether he is seen as learned, and whether he has read certain Stoic philosophers. He suggests the listener is still anxious about how he appears to others.

Epictetus is scolding a student who has shown himself to be petty, complaining, cowardly and vain. He tells him to stop studying Archedamus, a teacher of Epictetus's time who sounds like a scholar of some note, and to drop concerns that have nothing to do with him. He warns that a student who gets too proud of such study can die as Crinis did, a man who also fancied himself a Stoic scholar, and that the lesson is for him to listen to.

Epictetus says that calm study of logic and argument suits only those who are already free of anger, grief and envy. Lighthearted pleasures suit people who are happy. A person in real trouble, like a ship going down, should not ask for those things, so he compares that to asking for sails to be raised in a sinking boat.

The wise person's task is to respond to impressions in line with nature. Every mind naturally accepts what is true, rejects what is false, and withholds judgment on what is unclear. It moves toward what is good, turns away from what is bad, and stays indifferent to things that are neither.
Just as a money-changer or seller must accept genuine Caesar's coin, the soul cannot refuse what clearly appears good. Good naturally draws the soul toward itself, and evil pushes it away.

Epictetus advises a habit of checking everything you meet each morning against one test: is it within your control or not? Beauty, a child's death, and a high official's rank are all outside our control, so they should be set aside and treated as nothing to us.

Epictetus says that people are easily swayed by first impressions and only wake up a little during lessons. Outside the classroom, they judge others by outward circumstances: a mourner is "undone," a consul "happy," an exile "miserable," and a poor man "wretched."

Epictetus says that things like weeping, misfortune, quarrels, blame and accusation are only opinions, not real goods or evils. They are judgments about things outside our control, which we wrongly treat as good or bad. If a person moves these judgments onto things within their own will, they will stay steady whatever happens around them.

Epictetus compares the soul to a dish of water and appearances to a ray of light falling on it. When the water shakes, the light seems to shake, but the light itself does not move. Likewise, when a person becomes dizzy, the skills and virtues are not really disturbed; the mind or nervous power they rest on is. Once that is calm again, they return to order.

Epictetus is answering a question about why earlier thinkers made more progress even though reason is now studied more. His answer is that progress follows whatever reason is now studied for. Today it is studied to solve logical puzzles (syllogisms), and so progress is made in that skill.

Epictetus says that in earlier times people studied philosophy to keep their governing mind in a state that agrees with nature, and they made progress. He tells the reader not to mix different aims or expect progress in one area while working on another. He adds that anyone who focuses only on living in agreement with nature will make progress.

It is hard to encourage weak young men, just as soft cheese is hard to hold with a hook. Young men with a good natural character, however, hold on to reason more firmly when someone tries to turn them away from it.

Epictetus asks the Epicurean visitor to tell him what the highest good is, as a stranger asks a city's residents for the best sights. He points out that nearly everyone agrees human life has three parts: soul, body, and external things.

Epictetus asks what is best for a person. He tells the story of Maximus, who sailed in bad weather with his son, and says that pleasing the body cannot be the aim. When Maximus agrees, Epictetus concludes that one should be busy with what is best, and that this is the soul, which is better than the flesh.

Epictetus argues by question and answer that the best good things are better than lesser ones, and that they lie within our own will. He then asks whether the soul's pleasure is also within the will. He concludes it cannot rest on itself. Pleasure needs a prior good, a real substance or nature, to be obtained first.

Epictetus is arguing against the view that pleasure is the highest good. If the soul's pleasure comes from things of the soul, then the good must lie in the soul itself. Good cannot be one thing while the pleasure that comes from it is another, and what follows from something can be good only if what comes before it is good too.

Epictetus is pressing an Epicurean to see the consequences of his own view. If the soul's pleasure depends on bodily pleasures, then bodily things must come first and make up the nature of the good. Epictetus argues that this follows from Epicurean teaching, and that the Epicurean would contradict himself by denying it.

Epictetus says that a person should look for teachings that agree with his own, so that they guide him away from pleasures that pull and overpower people. He warns that a philosophy which instead pushes people toward those pleasures is harmful. He compares this to a silver object: the workmanship, which shapes and leads the result, matters more than the material, just as a hand's skill matters more than its flesh.

Epictetus says that duties come in three kinds: those concerned with a thing simply existing, those concerned with it existing in its proper kind, and the chief or leading things themselves. In the same way, a person should value not the body, the "poor flesh," but the leading part, the guiding faculty that governs the person.

Epictetus says that people should carry on ordinary life, such as public duties, marriage, children, honoring the gods, and caring for parents, in the right way and in keeping with human nature. He describes human nature as free, noble and modest, and points out that only humans can feel shame.
Humans are made by nature so that pleasure serves other ends. It is like a servant that encourages us to act and keeps us steady in actions that fit nature.

Epictetus says we should train ourselves daily against first impressions, just as we train against tricky arguments. His examples are a son's death, a disinheritance, and a condemnation by Caesar. In each case, the thing is outside our control and is not in itself an evil, so the upset a person feels comes from how they judge it.

Epictetus says that trouble is bad only if we judge it so, because the will decides what is good or evil. Events themselves are just facts: a son dies, a ship sinks, a man is imprisoned. Adding "this is bad" comes from our own opinion.

Epictetus is answering the complaint that Zeus, the highest god, treats people unjustly. He lists the gifts Zeus gave: the ability to endure hardship, greatness of spirit, the power to stop suffering from becoming evil, the power to be happy even in pain, and a way out when life is unbearable. If these gifts are there, he says, a person should simply leave rather than complain.

Epictetus reports that a respected Roman figure named Italicus, when annoyed with his friends, said that they would make him become like Epictetus, pointing at him. The remark shows how Romans saw philosophers: as people whose company was feared or looked down on.

Epictetus tells a man going to Rome over a lawsuit that he cannot say whether the man will win or lose. He can say how the man will fare: well if his opinions are right, badly if they are false. He adds that a person's opinion is the cause of what he does.

Epictetus argues that every action comes from an opinion, so a person's choices are only as sound as the opinions behind them. He points out that opposing sides each believe their own opinions are right, and even madmen think so, so feeling certain proves nothing. He asks the rhetorician to show that he has actually examined his opinions.

Epictetus asks a rhetorician who is travelling to Rome to seek a post as governor that he has never made a journey to examine his own mistaken beliefs. He asks when, whom, and at what age he planned to do this, and tells him to recall his youth to see whether he ever looked at his opinions at all.

Epictetus asks a rhetoric student, now going to Rome for a lawsuit, what he lacked when he was young and trained in public speaking, and whether he ever accepted being shown his opinions were wrong. He says he has no formal rule to offer for this kind of problem. He adds that the man came to him as if to a market seller or cobbler, not to a philosopher, and asks what use philosophical rules would be in that case.

The aim is that, whatever happens, a person's inner guiding part stays in agreement with nature. Epictetus calls this the greatest thing, not a small one, and asks whether it takes only a short time to achieve. He suggests that if it can be grasped as one passes by, one should grab it.
Meeting a philosopher, Epictetus says, means more than being seen by him like a stone or statue. Both sides share their opinions and test each other's views, correcting any mistakes they find.

Epictetus is addressing a visitor who plans to hear him only while waiting for a ship, then leave and mock his speech as clumsy and unpolished. He asks what such people come to judge. He then imagines the reply that if he cared about such things, he would lack the land, silver and fine animals that his critics have.

Epictetus says that he needs nothing that the rhetorician has, because the rhetorician owns many things and so needs more. Whether he chooses it or not, the rhetorician is poorer. What Epictetus needs is firmness, a mind in agreement with nature, and freedom from disturbance of the mind, which the rhetorician lacks.

Epictetus says that a person should have the right principles ready for each everyday situation, such as meals, bathing, or going to bed. The verse adds that before sleep one should review the day's actions, noting what was done wrong, what was done right, and what was left undone, then criticising the faults and rejoicing in the good.

Epictetus says we should keep useful sayings ready so we can actually apply them, not just recite them. In a fever, we should already have the right thoughts about illness, and not drop everything when it starts. He mocks the person who, when sick, decides philosophy is pointless and only cares for the body.

Epictetus is saying that preparing yourself to endure whatever happens is a kind of training. He compares someone who complains about hardship, and wants to quit, to a fighter in the Pancratium, a Greek combat sport, who gives up after being hit. The fighter could simply choose not to take blows in the first place, but once he is in the contest, he must keep going.

Epictetus asks what someone gains by giving up philosophy when painful things happen. He says that training in philosophy prepares a person to face pain, just as athletic training prepares an athlete for a contest. He asks whether someone who has trained should then show weakness when the test comes.

Epictetus says that a person can always choose how to bear fever, thirst or hunger, even when illness takes away other freedoms. A doctor can stop a sick man from drinking or eating, but cannot stop him from enduring those discomforts well.

Epictetus argues that a philosopher's studies exist to keep the mind in harmony with nature, so fever should not stop that harmony. Being sick is just one part of life, like walking or sailing, and a philosopher should handle it as calmly as he handles those other activities, without needing his books.

To bear a fever well means facing the illness calmly. You do not blame God or other people, and you do not panic about death. You also do not get too excited or too down when the doctor speaks, because being ill or well is not the real measure of a person's worth.

Epictetus asks whether it matters that the soul is close to parting from the body, since death will come to everyone sooner or later. He questions why a sick person would flatter the doctor, call him master, or give him a chance to look self-important.

Epictetus says a sick person should treat the doctor the way people treat a shoemaker or builder: as an expert doing a job on something that is not really the person's self. A philosopher's real concern is his inner ruling power, not outside things like his body, wine, or oil. He should not be careless about such things, but he has no reason to fear for them.

Anger and fear make no sense about things outside our control, since only our own will can be good or bad. We should not try to direct events but accept them as they come. If a brother wrongs us, his conduct is his affair, while how we act toward him is ours.

Epictetus says that philosophers should not train with stunts that go against nature and are meant only to amaze people, since that would make them no different from jugglers. Difficult or dangerous feats, like walking a tightrope, are not good practice. Good practice is whatever helps them reach the goal set for them.

The passage says the goal of training is to live with desire and aversion (wanting and avoiding) without being held back by them. In practice, this means never being disappointed in what you want and never falling into what you wish to avoid.

If you want your desires never to be disappointed and your dislikes never to land on what you wish to avoid, you need steady, hard practice. Your desire and aversion must be aimed only at things within the power of your own will. If they reach for things outside that power, you will fail to get what you want and fail to avoid what you dislike.

Epictetus says that our habit is to give desire and aversion only to things outside our control, so we should build a opposite habit of practice. Where appearances are most slippery and easily mislead us, we should train against them. Only later, when a chance arises, should we test ourselves, and at first we should avoid whatever is stronger than we are.

Epictetus says a contest between a pretty young girl and a beginner in philosophy is unfair from the start. He uses the old saying that a clay pitcher and a rock do not match, meaning the beginner, like the pitcher, will be broken by the stronger one.

Being alone is not the same as being solitary. Solitude is a state of helplessness, the feeling of having no one to rely on and being open to harm. People can feel solitary in a crowd, as when they lose a close person, even though others are all around them.

Being alone in a place is not the same as being in solitude. A traveler feels lonely among robbers even though other people are present, because they are not trustworthy or kind. Epictetus adds that if mere absence of others were enough, even Zeus would be solitary during the world's fiery destruction, since he would lack his family and companions.

Epictetus says that people who think solitude is hard do not understand how a person spends time alone. They assume humans naturally seek company, affection and conversation. He argues that a person should also be ready to be alone, able to be self-sufficient and his own companion, just as Zeus keeps himself company and thinks about his own governance.

A person should be able to talk with himself and never feel he needs others. He should use solitude to think about the divine order, his place in the world, his past and present reactions, and how to fix his faults by reason. If someone attacks him while alone, Epictetus says the attacker can only harm the body, not the person himself.

Epictetus asks why a person left alone should feel miserable, since children left alone never run out of things to do with shells and ashes. Children play this way out of ignorance, he says, while adults are unhappy because they know better and still choose misery.

Strong abilities can be risky for beginners, so they should bear only what they can, and in a way that fits their nature. The passage advises practising a simpler, more restrained way of living, as someone who is ill does, so that they can later live well, as a healthy person does.

Just as poor tragic actors cannot sing alone and need a group around them, some people cannot go about by themselves. Epictetus tells the reader to stand on his own, to think for himself, and to look inward until he understands who he really is.

Epictetus says two faults must be removed from people: pride, meaning the belief that you lack nothing, and distrust, meaning the belief that happiness is impossible given your circumstances. Pride is removed by refutation, which Socrates was the first to practise. Searching for how to use desire and aversion without hindrance is, in a sense, philosophy.

Epictetus says that boasting about family rank, offices held, or wealth is like horses boasting about their speed or fodder. A man's real superiority lies in qualities such as modesty, fidelity and justice. Pride in a skill like kicking hard is, he says, pride in something an ass does.

Before starting any action, think through what comes before it and what will follow from it. Otherwise you may begin with enthusiasm, then give up when the difficulties appear. The Olympic example shows this: first weigh the costs and whether the goal really serves you, then decide.

Epictetus describes the hard training an athlete must accept before a contest: strict rules of diet, forced exercise in all weather, and total obedience to a trainer. In the contest itself he must endure injuries and defeat is still possible.

Epictetus says that if you have weighed the costs first and still want to train as an athlete, you may go ahead. If you have not weighed them, you are like children who copy whatever they have just watched, switching from wrestler to gladiator to actor. He says that people who move from one pursuit to another, such as athlete, gladiator, philosopher and orator, are committed to none of them and merely imitate what they see, like an ape.

The main point is that the listener keeps chasing new things and loses interest once they become familiar. He never takes up a task after careful thought or testing, but acts on a whim with a weak desire. So some people want to be philosophers just because they have seen and heard a striking speaker like Euphrates, a famous Stoic teacher.

Before taking on a task, look at what it demands and whether your own nature can meet it, as a wrestler checks his body for wrestling. Epictetus asks whether someone can become a philosopher while living as he does now, eating, drinking, and getting angry as before.

Epictetus says that philosophy costs a lot. A person must work hard, control their desires, leave their family, accept scorn from slaves and mockery from strangers, and give up public office and honors and legal standing. Only after weighing all this should they take it up, if they want freedom from disturbance, liberty, and calm in return.

Epictetus warns that a person cannot be a philosopher one day and a tax collector, speaker, or government officer the next, because these roles do not fit together. He says a person must choose one path: either work on their inner character and reason, or work on outside things, which makes them one of the ordinary crowd.

Someone asked the philosopher Rufus, after the emperor Galba was murdered, whether the world was still ruled by Providence (divine order). Rufus answered that he had never reasoned from Galba's fate to the claim that the world is so ruled. His point is that the murder does not count as evidence either way.

Close, frequent social contact with others will shape you in one of two ways: you either become like them or they become like you. Epictetus compares this to two pieces of charcoal, where a cold one placed next to a burning one either cools it or is set alight by it.

Epictetus warns that close friendship with ordinary people is risky, because spending time with them can make you pick up their faults, much as being near someone covered in soot leaves you dirty. He gives examples of common talk: gossip about gladiators, horses, athletes, and other people, along with mocking or unkind behaviour.

Epictetus asks whether anyone is ready to tune a lute as soon as he touches it, or has the skill of Socrates to lead his companions wherever he wants. He concludes that, lacking such skill, people are necessarily swept along by the crowd.

Epictetus says that ordinary people are stronger than his listeners because they speak what they really believe. The listeners only speak fine words with their lips, so their words have no force, and their talk of virtue sounds empty. A firmly held belief, he says, is strong and cannot be defeated.

Until your good opinions are firmly set and you have gained some strength to keep them safe, the advice is to avoid close company with ordinary people. Otherwise, like wax left in the sun, what you have learned in the school will melt away. Keep away from that influence while your opinions are still soft as wax.

Philosophers advise people to leave their home country, because old habits get in the way of starting new ones. People who knew you before will not let you change, saying you are still who you once were. Doctors likewise send long-term patients to a new place and climate. The speaker then urges his listeners to adopt new habits and hold to new opinions, but says they do not.

Epictetus describes a routine of going from one public entertainment to another, such as gladiator shows, exercise grounds and the circus, always with the same people. He says this leaves no good habit or care for oneself. He then asks whether one meets the things that come before the mind in line with nature, and whether one accepts that things outside one's control do not concern one.

When someone blames Providence (the divine order that governs the world) for letting an unjust person prosper, the answer is that the outcome still follows reason. The unjust man may gain money, since he flatters, feels no shame and watches for chances. But the passage asks whether he is ahead in faithfulness or modesty, and says you will not find that he is.

Epictetus tells of a man who envied Philostorgus for his wealth. Epictetus asks him whether he would sell himself for that wealth, the way Philostorgus apparently sold something to gain it. The man says no, so Epictetus asks why he envies someone who got his fortune by means the man himself despises.

Epictetus argues that God, or Providence, gives the better things to the better people, so there is no wrong in it. Modesty is better than wealth, and people should not be upset when they have the better thing. The superior person naturally has an advantage in whatever area they excel, and keeping this in mind prevents vexation.

Epictetus says that events like a bad wife or a father who gives nothing are only facts in themselves. Calling them evils is an extra judgment that we add, and it is false. So the cure is to change that opinion about hardship, not to remove the hardship itself.

Epictetus tells a student who asks what a Cynic should be that he will answer later, since he has more urgent things to say. His main warning is that a person who tries such a great task without God is hateful to God and only aims to behave shamelessly in public.

Epictetus tells the Cynic philosopher that he must change his own conduct first. He must stop blaming gods or people, remove desire, and direct his aversion only at things he can control. He must also avoid anger, envy, pity, attraction to beauty, love of fame, and pleasure in small treats.

Other people hide their private actions behind walls, doors, guards and darkness. The Cynic has no such hiding places. Instead, his protection is modesty, and he should not want to conceal anything he does.

A true Cynic who fears being discovered, and so needs to hide, has lost the Cynic's freedom and his open life under the sky. Such a man cannot be bold enough to teach and guide others. Epictetus argues that this is impossible.

Epictetus says a person must first purify their ruling faculty, meaning the mind or reason, and their way of life. The mind's true work is judging appearances correctly, while the body and its parts are not his concern. Death may come whenever it chooses, and no one can banish him from the world, since the sun, stars, and gods are everywhere.

A true Cynic, in this view, is a messenger sent by Zeus to show people where good and evil really lie. They are looking in the wrong places. He is like a spy who must examine things carefully, report the truth, and not be frightened into calling harmless people enemies.

The Cynic should be ready to speak out loudly in public, as Socrates did, and call people to account. He asks why they search for happiness in the wrong places, such as the body, and do not accept guidance toward the true path.

The main point is that wealth and power do not bring happiness. Epictetus asks where happiness is found and points to Myro, Ophellius and Croesus, a famous rich king, whose lives are full of grief despite their riches. Even men who held high office twice or three times are not happy, so the people who actually live those lives are the ones to ask.

Epictetus says that power and public honor do not make people happy. He points to Nero and Sardanapalus, who had royal power and were not happy, and to Agamemnon, who was a better man but still suffered anxiety. He quotes Agamemnon's own words from the Iliad to show his distress.

Epictetus asks a man what is wrong with him, since his money, possessions and body are fine. His answer is that the part of him that chooses and avoids things has been neglected and is corrupted. That part is neglected because he does not know what good and evil are, or what is his own and what belongs to others.

Epictetus criticizes a person who grieves over the misfortunes of others, such as the Greeks in danger from the Trojans. He argues that whether people die together or one at a time, death is equally an evil only if it is an evil at all. He concludes that death is simply the separation of soul and body, so the grief over others' deaths lacks reason.

Epictetus is speaking to a man who grieves over the fall of the Greeks, as if he were a king with a god-given authority. He says that no king is unhappy in a way a god is not, and that the man is really a shepherd weeping over lost sheep. He asks whether the man's own desires or aversions were threatened, implying that his grief comes from misplaced attachment to things outside his control.

Epictetus uses the Trojan War to question the value of anger and pride over a stolen wife. He asks whether losing an adulterous wife was really a loss, and whether the opinion of the Trojans matters. His dilemma: if the Trojans are wise, why fight them; if they are foolish, why care what they think.

Epictetus argues that the body is not truly free, since it can be overcome by illness, pain, rulers, fire or iron. So nothing belonging to the body can be free from hindrance. He suggests the one thing that is free is your power to judge what seems true or false. No one can force you to accept a falsehood or reject a truth.

Epictetus says that a person has a natural inner freedom. Desiring, avoiding, moving toward or away from things, planning, and deciding all depend on first seeing something as useful or as a duty, and this part of us cannot be blocked. He urges people to focus on this inner power and to look for good there.

Other people's troubles should not disturb you, because you are not made to share their misery but to be happy alongside them. If someone is unhappy, the cause lies with him, since God meant all people to be happy and free from disturbance. God gave each person some things that are his own and others that are not, and only the first kind is fully within his control.

Epictetus says that only our own choices and judgments are truly ours, while things like other people and their company are not. A person who grieves at parting from a friend has treated that friend as his own possession, forgetting that the friend is mortal and may leave. The grief is therefore the result of his own mistaken thinking.

Epictetus scolds someone who enjoyed people and places as if they would last forever, and who now weeps because those people and places are gone. He says such a person is more wretched than crows and ravens, which move freely and leave their old homes without grief, though he notes that birds do this only because they lack reason.

Epictetus asks whether reason was given to humans just to make them miserable. He points to absurd results: people must never travel, must sit and weep when a friend leaves, and must dance like children when the friend returns.

A speaker says that his mother grieves because she does not see him, and he does not want to act to stop her grief by any means. He holds that only his own sorrow is fully in his control, so he will stop his own grief completely, while he will try to ease another's grief only as far as he can. Going further would mean opposing God, or Zeus, who governs the universe.

Epictetus says that a person who fights against God and disobeys him will suffer for it, and so will his descendants. He will be anxious and fearful, dreading every piece of news, so that his peace of mind depends on other people's letters. Wherever he is, some place or some report can become a cause of trouble for him.

Epictetus is saying that misfortune follows people wherever they go, so it makes no sense to expect safety by moving away. Friends who die far off have only suffered what all mortals suffer. A person who wants a long life cannot also avoid losing those they love, since over a long time fever, robbers, or tyrants will strike many people in different ways.

Outside things such as weather, travel, hardship and the demands of public duty can ruin one person or send another far from home. Epictetus warns against sitting in anxious lament over these events, since doing so leaves a person dependent on countless other people and conditions.

Human life is compared to an army at war, where each person has a different duty: one keeps watch, one scouts, one fights. Not everyone can or should be in the same place. The speaker criticizes those who refuse their assigned task and complain when their duty is harder than usual, while ignoring how their own conduct weakens the whole army.

Epictetus argues that a person who refuses every duty would be useless, like a soldier who will not dig trenches or a sailor who will not climb the mast. Such a person would be thrown out of the ship as a burden. He concludes that human life is like a long and varied military campaign, in which each person has tasks to perform.

A good person acts for the sake of doing right, not to be seen doing it, and the doing itself is the reward. Epictetus compares this to a soldier obeying a general, but says a true teacher is not like that general. Writing a name correctly is its own benefit, so nothing more is owed.

Epictetus tells his listener that being good and happy is a worthy goal, even more than winning an Olympic crown. He asks why, as a grown man with a duty to live like one, the listener still wants comfort and coddling like a child. He warns that an adult who acts like a child looks more ridiculous the older he gets.

When you kiss a child, brother or friend, do not let the feeling of pleasure run freely. Hold it back, the way a triumphing general was reminded by an attendant that he was mortal. Remember that the person you love is mortal and is not truly yours.

Your son, friend, or other things you have are lent to you only for a time, and they can be taken back at any moment. Wanting them when they are not available is like wanting figs or grapes in winter: it is foolish, because each thing comes and goes in its own season, as the nature of the universe decides.

Epictetus advises that when you are happy with something, you should picture the opposite. He says there is no harm in telling a child you are kissing that they will die, or telling a friend that you will part and never meet again. He argues that such words are only "of bad omen" if they point to some evil, and he does not mind them being called that if they are useful.

Epictetus argues that words such as cowardice, grief and shamelessness should not be avoided just because they sound unlucky. He compares this to harvest and seasonal change: reaping grain or leaves falling destroys only a particular form, not the whole world, so calling these things bad omens makes no sense.

Death is presented as a change from one state into another, not a destruction. The passage asks whether the self will still exist after death and answers that it will not exist as it is now, but will become something else that the world needs, just as the person came into being when the world needed them, not when they chose.

The main idea is to keep certain thoughts ready at all times, so that bad news does not come as a shock. Epictetus gives the example of a father who knows his son is mortal, and says the same should be true of oneself: knowing in advance that one may die, lose one's home, or be imprisoned makes such events less surprising.

When something unpleasant happens, Epictetus says we should look at where it came from: things outside our control and not our own. So it is not really ours to be troubled by. If someone asks who sent it, the answer is the commander, the state, or its law, and a person must accept what that authority sends.

Epictetus says that when painful thoughts come, you cannot stop them from appearing, but you can resist them with reason and not let them grow. He gives an example: a man exiled on the bare island of Gyara should not picture the pleasures of Rome, but should live well where he is. Likewise, someone in Rome should think about Rome, not Athens.

Epictetus says that in place of other pleasures, a person should take delight in knowing they are serving God, and that they are acting like a wise and good person in what they do, not just in what they say. He describes the satisfaction of being able to tell oneself that one is doing this, while others talk about one's virtues in the schools.

Epictetus says that Zeus has chosen to use him as a demonstration. Zeus shows him to others as poor, powerless and sick, so that he can witness that outside things are not under our control. He urges people not to fear or desire things without reason, and to look for the good within themselves rather than in external things.

Epictetus says that God sends him to exile on Gyara and into prison, not from hatred or neglect, but to train him and to use him as a witness to others. Given such a task, he asks whether he still worries about his place, his companions, or what people say, or whether his whole attention is fixed on God's instructions and commands.

The passage says that if you keep these principles ready and practise them, you will always have something to comfort and strengthen you. Going hungry is not shameful; what matters is having the reason to keep fear and sorrow away. Once fear and sorrow are gone, a tyrant, his guards, or Caesar's attendants no longer have any power over you.

The speaker asks whether a Cynic should be upset that others win court posts or public honours, since he has received great authority from Zeus. He tells him not to show off this authority or boast of it, but to show it through his actions. If no one notices, he should be content that he is healthy and happy within himself.

Epictetus tells people who have given up their goals to look at what they set out to do. They should notice which aims they reached and which they missed, and try to recover the ones they failed. He adds that one must not shrink back in the greatest struggle but must accept blows.

The passage says that the real contest is not an athletic one like wrestling, where winning or losing says little about a person. The real contest is for good fortune and happiness themselves. If someone gives up this contest, nothing stops them from starting it again straight away, without waiting four years for the next Olympic Games.

If you fall back in the struggle, you can recover, get back into the contest, and keep trying. Winning once makes you as if you had never given up. The warning is not to let giving up become a habit that you enjoy, like a bad athlete who keeps running away from the games.

Epictetus asks whether people should feel shame for being more timid and stingy than runaway slaves. He points out that runaways have no estates or household to support them, yet they steal enough to start, move on, and find ways to keep alive, and none of them is known to have starved.

Epictetus tells a worried man that lacking necessities leads only to death, like a fever or a falling stone would. He points out that the man has often said and written that he is not afraid of death. He concludes that the man should first learn what is truly shameful before calling himself a philosopher.

Epictetus asks whether it is shameful to have things that are not your own doing, such as illness, or poverty caused by parents who left their money to others. He argues that shame belongs only to what you yourself do wrong, so blaming someone for something they did not do makes no sense.

Epictetus is asking whether you can change your father or the things outside your control, and whether you should be ashamed when you cannot. He then describes the fear of someone who looks to others instead of relying on himself, worrying about food and about slaves stealing, running away, or dying.

Epictetus is scolding people who call themselves students of philosophy but use it only for clever arguments. They have never sought calm, freedom from disturbance, or control of their passions, and they have never tested their own impressions by asking whether they can bear them.
