Epictetus says that his listener has been relying on the idea that things stay unchanged, so as to keep hold of things that are bad: cowardice, meanness, admiring the rich, unfulfilled desire, and avoidance that fails. He suggests the listener has been anxious about keeping these secure.

Epictetus is asking a student what he has actually gained from reason. He points out that the student practises logic and argument, yet has no firm possession to protect, like a walled city with a guard, and no clear measure of anything. He concludes that reasoning should show what makes people happy, why no one should be blamed, and how to accept the way the universe is run.

Freedom, the passage says, means living as you wish, without being forced, blocked or thwarted, so that your desires reach their goal and you do not run into what you want to avoid. It then argues that no one chooses to live in error, deceived, unjust or discontented, so no bad person lives as they wish.
No one who lives in sorrow, fear, envy, pity, or unmet desire is free, and nobody chooses such a life. Epictetus argues that since no bad person escapes these troubles, no bad person is free.

Epictetus argues that freedom is something great and valuable, so a person who has it cannot be mean or low. He says that anyone who submits to another or flatters someone against his own judgment is not free. This holds whether the reason is a small meal or a high public office.

Epictetus says that a person is free only if no one else can stop or force them. Someone who can be hindered or compelled by another is not free, whatever his family or rank. If he calls another person "Master" from his heart, he is a slave, even if he holds high office.

A person is not free just because he is not complaining at the moment. Epictetus says that you must look at his beliefs: if he thinks his desires can be forced, blocked, or harmed by bad luck, he is still a slave, even if he is enjoying a holiday like the Saturnalia, when slaves briefly had freedom.

Epictetus asks what makes a person free from hindrance and their own master. Wealth, high office and royal power do not do it. He answers that it is knowledge: the skill of writing frees a writer, the skill of playing the lute frees a lute player, and so the science of life frees a person in life.

Epictetus argues that a person who wants things that depend on other people or on outside events cannot be free, because those things can be blocked. He then asks which things are fully in our control. His examples are that bodily health, good looks, and even life or death are not in our power.

Epictetus lists things that are not under our control: the body, property, slaves, clothes, house, horses, and even the lives of children, wife, brother and friends. Each is held only for a while and can be taken away, so none of them is fully in our power.

Epictetus argues that some things are fully in our control. No one can force us to agree to something false, so our judgment is free. Others can threaten us into wanting to move toward something, but if we despise death and bonds, their threats lose their hold, and that choice of ours is our own act.

Epictetus says that once a person has learned to separate what is their own from what is not, they have nothing to fear from other people. Only one's own choices and judgments are one's own, and no one else controls them. So, he asks, what is there left to be afraid of?

Epictetus argues that no person can take away or block the things that are truly within a person's control, just as no one can block God. He asks why someone who has studied philosophy would still fear for their body or possessions, which are not their own and do not really concern them. The point is that learning to separate what is in our power from what is not should bring freedom from fear and disturbance.

Fear comes from expecting bad things in the future, and grief from bad things that are already present. The passage says that if you desire only what is in your own power to choose, and not what lies outside it, then no unreasoning, impatient, or hasty feeling has room to take hold.

Epictetus asks why you would be angry when God takes back what he gave. Everything you have, including your own life, was received from God, who brought you into the world, gave you reason and senses, and placed you here as a mortal to watch his order and share in it for a short time.

Epictetus says that a person who has been allowed to live and see the world should leave gracefully when the time comes, thankful and modest, as one leaves a festival or ceremony. He points out that others must be born and need room, houses and supplies, so the earlier ones must step aside. Otherwise nothing would be left for the newcomers.

Epictetus asks why a person is never satisfied and wants to keep what is not truly theirs, such as children and a wife. He says these belong to the giver, meaning God or nature, so one should give them up when asked. If one does not accept the terms of life, one may leave, since the giver wants no unhappy spectator.

The passage uses a festival as a picture of life. Those who take part should join in gladly and praise the occasion. Those who cannot bear hardship and complain about the god, fortune, and their companions do not do their part, so the speaker is content to see them leave.

Epictetus says that people are given certain powers, such as greatness of mind, a generous spirit and freedom, to use only for as long as the giver allows. He adds that things stop being necessary to us once we stop clinging to them and stop telling ourselves that we need them.

Epictetus says that a man may admit he is not free yet, because he still fears his masters and values his body too much. He points instead to Diogenes as a free man. Diogenes was free not because of his birth but because he had removed every hold that could be used to enslave him.

The speaker describes a man whose possessions, body, family, friends and country are all held loosely, so he would give up any of them if asked. He accepts this because he knows they were given to him, by whom, and under what terms.

The speaker means that a person's true parents are the gods and his real country is the whole universe. He would never abandon that country or disobey its commands, and he would not ask whether a deed was done for the whole of things. He simply accepts that everything done comes from the universe and is done for it, under the direction of the one who governs it.

Diogenes says he can speak freely with the kings of Persia and Sparta, and the reason is not his birth. Other Greeks, even free-born ones, were afraid of such kings. Diogenes is free because he does not treat his body as his own, wants nothing, and regards only the law as binding on him.

Epictetus says that real freedom is worth any cost, since people have died or lost whole cities for the sake of lesser forms of liberty. He asks whether a person would not give back to God, when asked, the things God gave, in order to gain true and secure freedom.

Epictetus asks whether a person should learn to accept death, torture, exile and loss of possessions, as Plato taught. He says that if someone refuses, they remain a slave even if they hold the highest office or serve at the emperor's court. He adds that philosophers may say things that seem strange to ordinary opinion, but they do not say things that go against reason.

Getting the things people eagerly want does not bring the peace they expected. Once obtained, they bring the same restlessness, craving and dissatisfaction as before. Freedom comes not from possessing what you desire but from removing the desire itself.

Epictetus urges the listener to put the effort once spent on wealth into gaining a belief that will make them free. He says to attend a philosopher rather than a rich patron, and that trying is worthwhile even if it fails.

Epictetus warns against becoming so close to old friends that you join in their habits and actions. If you refuse, they may feel you have turned away from them, but he says nothing comes without cost. You must choose: stay the same and keep their love, or improve yourself and accept that they may no longer treat you as before.

If you lose something external but gain something of greater worth, you should not call it a loss. Examples given are trading an ass for a horse, or money for a good action. Keeping this in mind helps a person keep their character as it should be.

Epictetus says that a person's chances to improve are running out, and that all their effort can be wasted through a small departure from reason. He compares this to a ship: a steersman does not need much to wreck it, only a slight turn toward the wind or a little carelessness in his duty.

Epictetus says that a moment of carelessness can cost you everything you have built up. He says the real treasures to guard are modesty, faithfulness, steadiness, freedom from strong emotions, a calm mind, freedom from fear, and inner liberty. He asks what could be worth trading these for, and tells the reader to weigh whatever is received in return.

Epictetus says that others may hold offices, status or honours, but he keeps his own good: his decency and modesty. He does not seek outward things like wealth, office or reputation, because God has not made them good for him. He accepts God's will willingly and so stays free.

Epictetus says that a person should deal with other things only as far as reason allows, and be satisfied with that. If he does not, he will fail and be blocked in everything. These laws come from God, and a person should explain them and obey them, not the rules of the lawyers Masurius and Cassius.

Even wanting calm, leisure, travel or learning can make a person a servant to others, as wanting wealth or power does. Epictetus says that whatever outside thing we value places us under the control of others. So, for him, being a senator or a private citizen makes no real difference if we still crave the post.

Epictetus says that complaining about having no time for books is no different from complaining about being tied to them like a corpse, since books, like honours and power, are outside our control. What matters is why you read. If the aim is only amusement or learning, the reader is foolish. If reading serves a calm and happy life, it is worthwhile.

A man says reading would give him a calm, happy life, and that he is upset to be cut off from it. Epictetus replies that a calm life can be stopped by almost anything, even a crow, a flute player or a fever. He holds that a calm life depends on steady flow and freedom from being blocked.

Before going out to a task, the speaker resolves to keep the proper rules: to act with modesty and steadiness, without craving or rejecting outside things. When watching other people, he means to look at himself first and ask whether he makes the same mistakes, not to find fault or mock. He notes that he once erred but no longer does, and gives thanks to God.

Epictetus says that people study and write only to learn words, explain them to others, and solve logical puzzles, not to act well on the impressions that come to them. Because this is their aim, their study itself blocks them from living well.

Epictetus asks whether we want things that are outside our control. If so, we should expect to be blocked and to fail. He says that reading about action, desire and aversion is useful only if it helps us act well and avoid what we fear, not just to know what is said.

If we read about duty so that we remember how things relate to one another and act in line with those relations, then being kept from our reading should not upset us. We should measure our progress not by counting how many verses we read or wrote, but by whether our actions match those relations.

The speaker looks back on a day and judges it by Stoic standards. He says he used his actions as philosophy teaches, kept his desire in check, and avoided only what lies within his own control. He did not fear others or give in to their pleas, and he practised patience, self-restraint and cooperation. For these things, he says, we should give thanks to God.

Happiness, the passage says, comes from one rule: do not concern yourself with things outside your power of choice. Treat nothing as your own except what cannot be taken from you, and leave other things to God or Fortune. Keep this rule in mind at all times, including while reading, writing and listening.

Reading and writing alone do not make a person industrious. What matters is the purpose behind the work. A man who studies for fame loves fame, one who studies for money loves money, and one who studies for learning itself loves learning.

Epictetus says a person deserves praise for their effort only when they work to keep their own inner reasoning in line with nature. People should not be praised for shared things like the body or possessions, but for their judgments, since those judgments make their actions good or bad. He ends by urging contentment with the present and with what comes at the right time.

Epictetus says that when you notice a lesson you have studied showing up in your daily actions, you should be glad. If you have given up a bad temper, harsh speech, haste, or laziness, or no longer react as you once did, you have reason to celebrate. Each good act can be a reason for a daily festival.

Epictetus argues that a person's happiness and closeness to God do not depend on the place where they live. He points out that the gods are equally distant from all places and see everything from anywhere, and that the good things a person has come from themselves and the gods, not from public office.

A wise and good person does not fight with others and, as far as he can, stops others from fighting too. Epictetus offers Socrates as the model: Socrates avoided quarrels himself, settled quarrels between others, and patiently put up with difficult people, including his wife and son.

The main point is that no one can control another person's inner guiding principle, so a wise person wants only what is within his own power: to act according to nature himself. He does not demand that others act according to nature, since that belongs to them. Epictetus then asks whether being a military commander would be the goal, implying it is not.

Epictetus says that a person's aim in any matter, such as marriage, is to keep his own ruling principle, meaning his reason and will, in a state that fits nature. Wanting a son or wife to behave well is wanting what belongs to others to be otherwise. Learning means knowing which things are one's own and which belong to others.

A person who holds this Stoic view should not be surprised when bad things happen, and should expect the bad to do worse than they actually do. So any harm short of the worst is seen as a gain. Insults, blows and wounds are each met with thanks that something worse did not happen.

Epictetus asks why someone who has never learned that people should love one another, or that injustice harms the doer, should not pursue what seems to benefit him. He then argues that a person hit by a neighbor's stones has not been wronged, since he is a free will, not a piece of household property. If you answer like a wolf, you bite back and throw more stones.

A creature is wretched when it lacks the abilities that are natural to its own kind, not when it lacks abilities belonging to other animals. A horse is unhappy when it cannot run, and a dog when it cannot track game. The passage asks whether a person's natural faculties include a wild beast's urge for revenge after an injury.

Epictetus argues that a man is truly unhappy not because he lacks physical strength, such as the ability to strangle lions, but because he has lost his honesty and loyalty. Such a man deserves pity, but not for being born or dying. His misfortune is losing what is truly his own, not property like land, houses, or slaves.

Epictetus says that a person's external possessions belong to others and can be taken back at any time. What truly belongs to a person is the mental "stamp" they are born with, much as a coin is judged by its stamp. A coin bearing the wrong emperor's stamp is counterfeit and must be rejected.

Epictetus says that a person's character is judged by the qualities they show, not just by their outward form. If someone is gentle, sociable and tolerant, he is accepted as a fellow citizen and neighbor. If he is violent and quick to strike, as Nero was, then calling him a man proves nothing about his worth.

Being a human is not a matter of outward form alone, as a wax apple has the look and smell of an apple but is not one. A person must also have a human mind and judgment. Someone who refuses reason, feels no shame, and attacks others becomes, in turn, an ass, a worthless creature, or a wild beast.

Epictetus asks whether he should be despised, and then argues that the only people who could despise a gentle and modest man are those who know him, who would not. Being despised by strangers matters little, since no craftsman cares what people ignorant of his craft think. Even if others turn hostile, no one can harm a person's own will or stop them from responding naturally to what happens to them.

Epictetus asks why a person still feels troubled and shows fear, and urges that such a person should openly declare peace with everyone and laugh at those who think they can harm him. The speaker says those who try to hurt him do not know who he is or where his real good and evil lie, because they cannot reach what is truly his.

A city under siege may mock its attackers, confident its walls and supplies will hold. Epictetus says that a person's opinions are the only thing that can make the soul truly secure. No wall, body, property or reputation is as safe from attack as one's opinions.

Everything outside us can be lost or taken away, so anyone who clings to such things will be troubled, fearful, and disappointed. Epictetus asks whether we should not instead secure the one safe refuge we have and turn toward what cannot perish and is free by nature.

Nobody really harms another person; what harms a person is his own opinion about things. Epictetus gives the example of Eteocles and Polynices, who fought because they judged royal power the greatest good and exile the worst evil. People naturally seek what they think is good and avoid what they think is bad, so they treat anyone who blocks the good or brings the bad as an enemy, even a brother, son, or father.

Epictetus argues that if outside things like money, status or health were truly good or evil, people would be enemies to their own families and everyone else. But if only a person's own will, or purpose, is good or evil, then there is no reason to quarrel. Quarrels, he says, are about things that do not really matter, and are with people who do not understand what matters most.

Epictetus describes a man who is upset that others pity him. He asks whether the pity is really his concern or theirs, and whether he can stop it by showing he does not need it. The man believes he does not deserve pity for his faults, since others pity him only for poverty, lacking public office, illness, and death.

The speaker asks whether his listener is ready to convince ordinary people that being poor, having no public office, and having no honor are not evils, and that a man can still be happy without them. The alternative, he says, is to pretend to be rich and powerful, which belongs only to a boastful, foolish, useless person and needs constant pretense to keep up.

Epictetus is describing what a person must do to avoid being pitied if they choose the "second path," which is living for outward show. This means owning slaves and silver, displaying them as if they were more than they are, dressing grandly, seeking invitations to rich men's dinners, and using tricks to look more attractive and noble than one really is.

Epictetus says that trying to convince all people of what is good and bad is both impossible and slow, even for Zeus. The only person you can really persuade is yourself, and you have not yet done that. He asks why, since you know yourself best and are closest to yourself, you still have not taught yourself what you need to learn.

Epictetus says the only way to be free from grief and disturbance is to let go of things that are not up to us, and to accept that they belong to others. What other people think of you is one such thing, so it is nothing to you. If you are still upset by it, you have not truly grasped what is good and bad.

The passage asks what really makes a tyrant frightening. People usually point to his guards, their swords, and the attendants around him. But a small child brought before the tyrant is not afraid, the speaker suggests, perhaps only because the child does not understand what these guards mean.

A man who wants to die will not fear the tyrant's guards, because wanting death removes the power that makes the guards frightening. Likewise, a man who neither wants to die nor to live at any cost, but accepts whatever happens, has nothing to stop him from approaching the tyrant without fear.

A person who values the enjoyment and activity of things more than the things themselves, and who does not care whether they keep their property, body, children or wife, has nothing to fear. Like children who argue over a game but ignore the shells they play with, such a person has no reason to dread a tyrant, guards or swords.

A person who has clearly understood what is and is not within his control can live calmly, accept whatever happens, and bear hardship well. He says he will meet poverty, power, or exile with the same steadiness, because each can be handled well wherever he is.

Epictetus says that his well-being never depended on where he was, but on his opinions, which no one can take from him. So he is content wherever he is. As for dying, he says it is simply the body returning to the parts it was made from, and that it should not be called a tragedy.

Epictetus asks what there is to fear: nothing in the universe will perish or change in a way that threatens him. He says a tyrant and his armed guards hold no power over him, because he has made himself free and knows his own duties. He claims he has his own proper judges and defenders of that freedom.

A speaker is answering a threat. He says that his body, his property, his exile and his chains do not matter to him in the way the threatener supposes. He will give up his body whenever the threatener chooses, and invites the threatener to test how far that power goes.

The speaker asks what he should fear from court officials who could bar him from the emperor's bedchamber. He says that if they shut him out, he accepts it, because he does not enter unless allowed. He trusts that what God chooses is better than what he would choose, so he aligns his own wishes with God's.

Epictetus says he wants the same things as the emperor's court, but he does not push his way in, since he knows nothing good is handed out to those who go inside. When he hears of someone honored by Caesar, he asks what that person actually gets: a province, a prefect's office, and then whether he gains the wisdom and skill to use them well. Since the answer is no, he sees no reason to seek entry.

Epictetus compares public honours and offices to dried figs and nuts thrown to a crowd. Children fight over them, but a sensible adult sees them as trivial and does not chase them. Provinces, money, and magistracies are treated the same way. If such prizes are handed out by the emperor and you miss them, the passage says you should not be troubled.

A dried fig that falls in your lap is fine to eat, since it is a small thing you can enjoy. But if you must bend low, flatter people close to Caesar, or be pushed around by others to get it, the fig is not worth the trouble. Epictetus says the same goes for anything that is not truly good.
When you see someone with power or wealth, you can set against it that you do not desire these things. If you lack that desire, you have something more valuable than what the other person has.

People's troubles and feelings of helplessness come from worrying about things outside their control, such as what will happen or how things will turn out. Epictetus says that questions like these show a focus on what is not up to the will. He tells a person who is anxious about such things that the matter is in their own power, so they need not worry.

Do not accept an idea too quickly, before you test it against the natural rule (reason). The passage then praises a person who worries about whether his own desires and avoidances will succeed. Such a person drops the concerns that trouble others and focuses on his own affairs and condition.

If you want to avoid failure and disappointment, desire only what is within your own control, and do not try to avoid things outside it. Anyone who desires what others control, or tries to avoid what is out of their hands, will inevitably fail and suffer what they hoped to escape. Once this is accepted, there is no room for anxious questions about how things will turn out.

Good and evil lie only in what we control, our own will and choices. Nothing outside that can stop us from responding well to whatever happens, so we need not ask anxiously how events will turn out. The passage compares this to Hercules, who did not fear the lions and boars he met, since facing them was his task.

Epictetus says that if a person dies while doing something brave, such as fighting a wild boar or ridding the world of bad men, that death is a good one. Since everyone must die while doing something, he asks what a person would most want to be doing when death comes.

Epictetus says he would prefer to do great, useful, noble deeds for others. If he cannot, he will at least do what no one can stop him from doing: improve himself, train his judgment about how things appear to him, aim for calm of mind, and fulfill his duties to the people around him.

If death comes while he is busy with his philosophical work, the speaker says it is enough. He can raise his hands to God and say he has used the faculties God gave him to understand and follow God's ordering of the world. He has not dishonored God by his actions and has never blamed God.

The speaker asks whether he has ever complained about what happens to him or wished things were otherwise. He thanks God for the gift of life and says he is content while he has used what belongs to God. He accepts that God may take everything back, since all things were God's to begin with. He concludes that leaving life with this attitude is the best and most fitting end.

Epictetus argues that love of cleanliness is part of human nature, and that it is what sets humans apart from other animals more than anything else. When we see an animal clean itself, we call it acting like a man. When we blame an animal for being dirty, we excuse it by saying it is not human.

Humans have something superior in them, which comes from the gods. The gods are pure, and people come closer to them through reason, which draws them toward purity. Because human nature is mixed with impure material, it can never be fully pure, so reason works to make human nature love purity as far as it can.

The passage says the highest kind of purity belongs to the soul, and impurity too. Unlike bodily dirt, soul impurity cannot be seen, so it can only be found in the soul's own acts: movement toward or away from things, desire, aversion, preparation, purpose, and assent.
The soul is made impure only by its own wrong judgments or opinions. It is purified when it holds correct opinions, and only then is it free from disturbance and pollution.

A philosopher should not put people off philosophy by looking miserable. Epictetus says he should appear cheerful and calm, including in his body. He points to his own poor, homeless life, saying he lacks nothing and is freer and happier than the rich, and that his hard living has not harmed his body.

Someone asks why he should take up philosophy if it makes men look like condemned prisoners, with neglected dress and face. The speaker says he would not want that, and he prefers a beginner who shows care for his appearance. Such care, he says, shows a sense of beauty and a wish for what is fitting.

Beauty, Epictetus says, is found in the reasoning part of a person, not in the body. The body is only earth, and a person who works hard on it for no purpose will eventually learn from time that the body amounts to nothing.

Epictetus says that a man who is covered in filth and neglects his appearance gives him nothing to work from. There is no sense of beauty in him to appeal to, so telling him that beauty lies in reason is pointless. He compares trying to reform such a man to telling a pig not to roll in mud.

Epictetus warns that losing attention for a short time is a mistake you cannot simply undo later. Each lapse builds a habit of not attending and a habit of putting attention off. Over time this pushes away a good life, proper conduct, and living in line with nature.

Epictetus argues that putting off attention is no better than dropping it altogether, so if attention helps, it should be kept constant. He asks whether playing or singing would go worse with attention, and whether anything in life is done better without it.

Epictetus argues that no craft, such as woodworking or steering a ship, is done better by carelessness. He then warns that once the mind is allowed to wander, a person cannot easily bring it back to propriety, modesty or moderation, and acts only on whatever desire comes up.

Epictetus says we should keep our minds fixed on a single aim: to pursue only what is within our own will, and not things outside us or belonging to others. Other things we should accept as far as they are allowed, that is, as the one who has power over them permits.

Epictetus says we should remember who we are and what our roles are, and shape our conduct to fit them. That means judging when to sing or play, who is present, what an action will lead to, how others will regard us, and when to join in or hold back, all while keeping our own character.
Whenever a person breaks any of these rules, the harm comes at once. It does not come from outside events. It comes from the wrong action itself.

Complete freedom from faults is not possible. What is possible is to keep working steadily toward being faultless, and to be satisfied if this constant attention lets you avoid at least a few errors. Saying "tomorrow I will start paying attention" amounts to saying "today I will be careless."

Epictetus is warning that if you put off paying attention to your own mind, you let others gain power over your feelings, and you allow yourself to become angry and envious. He argues that if attention is good tomorrow, it is even better today, so you should not keep postponing it.

Epictetus describes how people, after a friend openly shares his own private affairs, feel pressed to share their own secrets in return. They do this for two reasons: it seems unfair to take without giving back, and staying silent would make them look less open and honest.

People tend to trust someone who has already shared his own private affairs, thinking he will keep ours secret out of fear of being exposed himself. Epictetus gives the example of Rome, where a soldier in plain clothes may criticise the emperor to draw out a listener's own views, and the listener who speaks freely is arrested.

Epictetus describes how careless talk spreads. If someone confides in a person who cannot keep quiet, that person passes the secret on, and the one who told it is disturbed by what follows. The thinker says that a man who remembers that no one harms another, but each person's own acts harm or help him, will not act this way, though he still suffers from his own foolish talk.

Epictetus is objecting to a one-sided exchange of confidences. He asks why someone who shared private matters should expect the listener to share his own in return, when the speaker is simply a chatterer who treats everyone as a friend. He argues that it is not fair to demand openness from someone who has not earned it.

A person with a leaky cask should not expect a person with a sound cask to share their own wine in return, since the leaky one cannot keep it. The point is that trust is not equal when one side cannot hold what it is given. Here, the speaker says the other person trusted him with their affairs because he is faithful and modest, and believes only his own actions can harm or help him.

Epictetus asks why he should trust his own affairs to someone who has corrupted his own will and would chase money or court favour, even at the cost of murdering his children as Medea did. He says that person must first show he is faithful, modest, steady, and sound, like a cask without a hole.

The speaker says he will not wait to be asked for advice. He will go to people himself and ask to hear their troubles. He argues that everyone wants a good, faithful adviser, and that someone who shares the weight of another's difficulties eases that person's burden.
Our whole being comes from our thoughts, and is built on them. If a person speaks or acts with a bad thought, suffering follows them, like a cart wheel following the foot of the ox that pulls it.

Our present state is shaped by our thoughts; everything we are rests on what we have thought. If a person speaks or acts from a pure thought, happiness follows them closely, like a shadow that never leaves.
Holding on to thoughts such as "he insulted me, he hit me, he beat me, he stole from me" keeps hatred alive. As long as a person dwells on these grievances, the hatred does not end.
Hatred ends for those who stop holding on to thoughts like "he insulted me, he hit me, he beat me, he stole from me." The verse says that when such thoughts are not kept, hatred fades away.
Hatred is never ended by more hatred. It is ended only by love, and the speaker calls this an old rule.
People do not usually realize that everyone must die. Those who do realize it stop their quarrels at once.

A person who lives only to seek pleasure, with unrestrained senses, eating without moderation, lazy, and weak, will surely be overcome by Mara, the tempter, just as a strong wind knocks down a weak tree.

Someone who lives without chasing pleasures, keeps the senses under control, eats in moderation, and is faithful and strong cannot be overthrown by Mara, the tempter. Mara is not able to defeat such a person, just as wind cannot topple a rocky mountain.
A person who wants to wear the yellow robe of a monk, but has not cleansed himself of wrongdoing and ignores self-control and truth, does not deserve it.

The verse says that a person who has become free of sin, stands firm in all good qualities, and keeps to self-control and truth, truly deserves to wear the yellow robe. The yellow robe is the dress of a Buddhist monk.
People who take what is false to be true, and what is true to be false, never reach the truth. They only follow empty desires.

Those who see truth as truth, and untruth as untruth, reach the truth and follow right desires. The verse says that clear seeing of what is true and what is false leads a person to the truth and to good aims.

Just as rain leaks through a badly thatched roof, strong desires break into a mind that does not think carefully. The point is that a mind without careful thought is open to passion, much as a poorly roofed house is open to rain.
Just as rain cannot leak into a house with a good roof, strong passion cannot enter a mind that is well trained in reflection. The verse uses this image to say that a mindful mind keeps out desire.
An evil-doer suffers grief in this life and in the next. The pain comes from seeing the evil he has done.
A good person finds joy both in this life and in the next. He is glad when he sees that his own actions are pure.
The evil-doer suffers both in this life and in the next. He suffers when he remembers the wrong he has done, and he suffers even more while he keeps walking the path of wrongdoing.
A good person is happy in this life and in the next. He feels happy remembering the good he has done, and happier still while continuing on the good path.

A careless person may know many teachings by heart, but if he does not practice them, he does not truly share in the religious life. He is like a herdsman who only counts other people's cows, gaining nothing for himself.

A follower of the law who knows only a little of it still shares in the priesthood, if he has given up desire, hatred and foolishness, and has true knowledge and a calm mind. Such a person cares for nothing in this world or the next.

Being earnest, meaning careful and mindful, leads to immortality, which here means Nirvana, the end of suffering and rebirth. Being thoughtless leads to death. Those who are earnest do not die, while the thoughtless are already as good as dead.
Those who have become firm in earnestness, and who clearly understand this, take delight in earnestness. They also rejoice in the knowledge of the Ariyas, the noble or elect ones.
Wise people who meditate, stay steady, and keep strong inner powers reach Nirvana, which the verse calls the highest happiness. Nirvana is the Buddhist goal of release from suffering.

A person who is earnest, meaning diligent and mindful, and who stays alert, acts purely, thinks before acting, controls themselves, and lives by the Dhamma (the Buddha's teaching) will see their good reputation grow.
A wise person can build a kind of island for themselves through effort, care, and self-control. Once built, this island cannot be swept away by any flood.
Foolish people chase empty things, and people with poor judgment do the same. A wise person treats earnestness, meaning careful and serious attention, as the most valuable thing they own.
Do not chase empty pleasures or the enjoyment of desire. A person who is serious and thoughtful finds great joy.

A wise person who drives away vanity through earnestness rises to the heights of wisdom. From there he looks calmly down on foolish people working hard below, as a man on a mountain looks down on people standing on the plain.

A wise person who stays attentive while others are careless is compared to a fast racehorse passing a slow old horse. The image shows him moving ahead of others by being more alert and diligent than they are.
Earnestness, meaning careful and diligent effort, is said to have raised Indra to rule over the gods. People always praise earnestness, and thoughtlessness is always blamed.

A monk who enjoys earnestness and fears carelessness moves through life like a fire, burning up all his bonds, whether small or large. In this verse, "earnestness" means careful, diligent effort in the spiritual path, and "fetters" are the attachments that keep a person bound.
A monk who enjoys careful reflection and fears carelessness cannot fall from his spiritual state. Such a monk is close to Nirvana, the end of suffering.
A wise person straightens their thoughts in the same way a fletcher (an arrow-maker) straightens an arrow. Thoughts are described as shaky and restless, and hard to control.
Our thoughts are compared to a fish pulled out of water onto dry land. Like the fish, the mind jumps and shakes as it tries to get free of Mara, the tempter who leads people away from the good.
The mind is hard to control. It is restless and moves wherever it wants. The verse says that taming it is good, and that a tamed mind brings happiness.
A wise person should watch over their thoughts. Thoughts are hard to see, very cunning, and they go wherever they like. When thoughts are well guarded, they bring happiness.

Those who control their mind, which wanders far, moves alone, has no body, and hides in the heart, will be freed from Mara, the tempter. Mara is a figure in Buddhist teaching who tries to lead people away from the path to liberation.

A person whose thoughts are unstable, who does not know the true law, and whose mind is disturbed will never have complete knowledge. In this verse, a steady mind and knowing the true law are presented as needed for full understanding.
A mind that is not scattered or confused, and has stopped weighing good against evil, has no fear while it stays alert. The verse ties freedom from fear to calm, unclouded attention.

One should see the body as fragile as a clay jar and make one's thinking as firm as a fortress. With the weapon of knowledge, one should fight Mara, the tempter, and keep watch over him once he is defeated, never resting.
The body will soon lie dead on the ground, ignored and without awareness, like a useless piece of wood. The verse uses this image to point out how short and empty physical life is.
A mind that is pointed the wrong way does more harm to us than any hater or enemy could do to us. The verse says that our own misdirected thoughts can hurt us more than other people's hostility.
A well-directed mind can do more for a person than a mother, father, or any other relative can. The verse says the mind's own right direction is the greater help.

Who will conquer this earth, the realm of Yama (the lord of the dead), and the world of the gods? The verse asks who will find the plainly shown path of virtue, the way a skilled person picks the right flower. It is a question, not a statement, so it poses the challenge rather than answering it.

A disciple, or follower of the Buddha's teaching, will overcome the earth, the realm of Yama (the god of death), and the realm of the gods. He will find the clearly shown path of virtue, just as a skilled person picks out the right flower.

The verse says that whoever understands the body is like foam and as empty of lasting substance as a mirage will defeat Mara, the tempter or god of death, and so will not face death. Mara is the figure who stands for desire and death in Buddhist teaching.

Death takes a person who is busy gathering flowers with a distracted mind, just as a flood sweeps away a village while its people are asleep. The point is that death can come at any time, when people are not paying attention.

Death overtakes a person who is busy picking flowers, with a distracted mind, before that person has had enough of pleasures. The verse says that desire is never fully satisfied, and death can come at any time.

A bee gathers nectar from a flower and leaves it unharmed, without damaging its colour or scent. The verse says a wise person should live in his village in the same way, taking what he needs without harming the people around him.
A wise person should not focus on the wrongs other people do or fail to do. Instead, they should pay attention to their own wrong actions and their own carelessness.
Words that look fine but have no effect are compared to a flower that is bright but has no scent. Such words are empty when the speaker does not act on them.
Words that are fine and fruitful are compared to a beautiful flower, bright and fragrant. They belong to a person who acts in line with what he says.

Just as many different garlands can be made from a pile of flowers, so a person, once born, can accomplish many good things. The verse stresses that a single human life offers wide room for doing good.

Flowers, sandalwood and other fragrant plants give off their scent only in the direction the wind blows. A good person's reputation, the text says, spreads even against the wind and fills every place.
Among fragrant plants such as sandalwood, tagara, lotus and vassiki, the scent of virtue is said to be the best. Virtue is compared to a perfume that is greater than all the others.
Fragrant tagara and sandalwood give off only a small scent. The good conduct of virtuous people, the passage says, rises even to the gods and is the highest fragrance.

Those who have these virtues, live without carelessness, and are freed through true knowledge cannot be found by Mara, the tempter. Mara is a figure in Buddhist teaching who stands for the forces that pull people away from liberation.

A lily growing on a heap of rubbish by the road still gives off sweet scent. In the same way, a disciple of the Buddha shines with knowledge among ordinary people who live in darkness, meaning those without that knowledge.

Time seems long to those who are restless or weary: a sleepless night, a short walk made hard by tiredness, or a life lived by a fool who does not know the true law. The verse says that the same length of time feels different depending on the state of the person experiencing it.
If a traveller cannot find a companion who is better than him or equal to him, he should keep going alone. A fool makes no true companion.
A fool worries because he thinks his children and his money are his own. The passage says that he does not even own himself, so he can own them even less.
A fool who knows he is a fool is wise at least to that extent. A fool who thinks he is wise is a fool in the full sense.
A fool can spend his whole life with a wise person and still understand little of the truth. He is like a spoon, which tastes nothing of the soup it stirs.

A person of understanding who spends even one minute with a wise person will quickly come to see the truth, much as the tongue quickly tastes soup. The point is that contact with a wise person brings understanding fast.
People who lack understanding are their own worst enemies. The evil they do produces bitter results for them.
A deed is not well done if the doer must later regret it, and if its result brings him weeping with a tearful face. The verse measures a good deed by whether it leaves no regret and no sorrow behind.

A deed is well done, the verse says, when the person does not regret it and receives its result gladly and cheerfully. The test is whether the doer feels no regret afterward and welcomes what follows from the act.
A fool thinks an evil deed is sweet, like honey, while its results have not yet appeared. When those results arrive, the fool suffers.

A fool may eat only as little as an ascetic does, taking food on the tip of a grass blade each month, yet he is still worth far less than those who have carefully considered the teaching. Kusa is a sacred grass used in Indian ritual.
An evil deed does not sour right away, just as fresh milk does not turn at once. Like a fire hidden under ash, it keeps smouldering and then follows the fool, who did it.
A fool's evil deed, once it comes to light, brings him sorrow. That sorrow destroys whatever good fortune he had, and it breaks his head, a figure for severe harm.

A fool, the verse says, may want a false name, first place among the monks, control over the monasteries, and honour from other people. The verse lists these wants as the kind of thing a foolish person chases.
A fool wants both householders and monks to believe that he alone has done their work, and to obey him in all matters. Thinking this way only makes his desire and pride grow.
A monk who knows that wealth and Nirvana lie on two different roads will not seek public honour. Instead, he will work to leave worldly life behind.
If you meet a wise person who points out true treasures, shows what to avoid, and corrects your faults, follow them. Those who do so will be better off, not worse.
A wise person should warn others, teach them, and stop them from doing wrong. Good people will love him for this, while bad people will hate him.
Choose friends who are good and virtuous, and avoid friends who do evil or are of low character. The verse says to keep company with the best people.

A person who takes in the teaching (the "law," or Dhamma) lives happily with a calm mind. The wise person always takes joy in the teaching as taught by the noble ones (the Ariyas, those who have reached spiritual attainment).

Just as craftsmen shape water, arrows and wood to their purpose, wise people shape themselves. The verse says that a wise person can train and change his or her own character, much as a craftsman shapes materials.
Wise people remain steady when others criticize or praise them, just as a solid rock stays in place when the wind blows against it. Praise and blame do not move them from their course.
Wise people, after hearing the teachings, become calm. The verse compares them to a deep, smooth, still lake.
Wise people stay steady whatever happens to them. They do not chase pleasure or talk endlessly about it. Joy or sorrow does not make them overly excited or low.
A wise and good person does not want a son, wealth, or power, whether for himself or for others. He also does not seek his own success by unfair means.

Only a few people reach the other shore, meaning they become Arhats, people who have reached full spiritual freedom in Buddhism. Most others stay on this side, running up and down the bank without crossing over.
Those who follow the teaching once it has been properly explained will cross beyond death's power, even though that power is very hard to overcome.

A wise person should give up ordinary household life and become a homeless monk, living apart from the world. There he should find joy in a place where joy seems absent, leave all pleasures behind, claim nothing as his own, and cleanse his mind of its troubles.

Those whose minds are firmly rooted in the seven elements of knowledge (the seven factors of awakening), who cling to nothing and delight in being free of attachment, who have overcome their desires, and who shine with inner light, are already free in this life.
For a person who has reached the end of the spiritual path, who has let go of grief and freed himself from every bond, there is no suffering.

Those who have reached this stage leave their homes with their minds fully composed. They do not feel at home where they live, and they leave house and family behind, as swans leave a lake they have outgrown.

Those who own nothing, eat only what is given to them, and have grasped emptiness and unconditioned freedom (Nirvana) are hard to follow, as hard to trace as birds flying in the air. Nirvana is the state of freedom from craving and suffering in Buddhism.

A person whose desires are calmed, who is not caught up in pleasure, and who has understood emptiness and unconditioned freedom (Nirvana), is hard to follow. Their way is as hard to trace as the flight of birds through the air.
The gods themselves envy a person whose senses are under control, like well-trained horses, and who is free from pride and from desire.

The verse describes a person who has done his duty (the Arhat, one who has reached the goal of Buddhist practice). Such a person is patient like the earth, firm like Indra's thunderbolt, and clear like a lake free of mud. For him, there will be no further rebirth.
A person who has truly known and so gained freedom is calm in thought, speech and action. Having become quiet in this way, he is called a quiet or peaceful person.

A person who is free from credulity (blind belief), who knows the uncreated (nirvana, the state beyond conditioned things), and who has cut all attachments, removed temptations and given up desire is called the greatest of men.
Wherever holy people called arhats live, that place is pleasant, whether it is a village, a forest, deep water, or dry land. The place itself is made good by the presence of these people.
Places where people find no pleasure, such as forests, can delight those who are free of desire. They are happy there because they do not seek pleasures.

A thousand words of empty talk are worth less than one meaningful word that, when heard, brings a person to calm. The verse says a single sensible word is better than a long speech made of meaningless words.

A thousand verses made of empty, meaningless words are worth less than one single line of verse that, once heard, brings a person peace of mind. The point is that meaningful words matter more than sheer quantity.
A hundred verses made of empty words are worth less than one word of the Dhamma (the Buddhist teaching). Hearing that one word brings a person to calm.
Winning a battle against a thousand times a thousand enemies is less than the victory of someone who conquers himself. The one who masters his own self is the greatest conqueror.

Conquering oneself is greater than any other victory. Even a god, a Gandharva (a heavenly being), Mara (the tempter) or Brahman (the supreme power) cannot turn the victory of a self-mastered person, who always lives with restraint, into defeat.

A person who makes sacrifices for a hundred years, month after month, is still worth less than one who, for a single moment, honours a man whose mind is firmly rooted in true knowledge. The honour paid to such a wise person is said to be greater than all that long offering.

A man might worship the fire god Agni in the forest for a hundred years, yet a single moment of honoring someone whose mind is firmly rooted in true knowledge is worth more than that hundred years of sacrifice.
Any offering a person makes for a whole year to earn merit is worth less than a quarter of a farthing, a tiny coin. Showing respect to people who live rightly is worth more.

Whoever always greets and respects elders will gain four things: long life, beauty, happiness, and strength. "Power" here means strength or ability, and the verse says these gains come to such a person.

A person who lives a hundred years without self-control and without virtue is worse off than someone who lives just one day while being virtuous and thoughtful. The verse says that moral character and reflection count for more than the length of a life.

A person who lives a hundred years without wisdom or self-control is worse off than someone who lives only one day but is wise and thoughtful. The verse says that a short life guided by understanding is better than a long life without it.

A life of one day is better than a hundred years of idleness and weakness, if in that one day a person has gained firm strength. The point is that the quality of a life, not its length, decides its worth.

A person who lives a hundred years without seeing how things begin and end is worse off than someone who lives only one day but sees how things begin and end. The verse values understanding the rise and fall of things over the length of life.

A man who lives a hundred years without seeing the "immortal place" is worse off than a man who lives only one day but does see it. In Buddhist terms, the immortal place means the deathless state, nirvana.

A person who lives a hundred years without seeing the highest law is worse off than someone who lives only one day but does see it. The verse says that understanding the highest law matters more than how long a life lasts.
If someone wants to move quickly toward good, they should keep their mind away from evil. If someone does good only half-heartedly, their mind takes pleasure in evil.
If a person has done wrong, they should not repeat it or take pleasure in it, because suffering is what evil leads to.
If someone does good, the verse says they should do it again and take pleasure in it. Happiness, it says, comes from doing good.
An evil-doer may feel happy while his wrongdoing has not yet had its effect. Once the evil he did ripens, meaning it comes back to him as its results, he begins to experience the evil.
A good person can still suffer hard times while his good deeds have not yet matured. When those deeds ripen, he then experiences happy days.
Do not think that evil is small and will never reach you. Just as a water-pot fills drop by drop, a foolish person fills with evil by gathering it little by little.
Do not think that good deeds are unimportant, or that they will never reach you. A water-pot fills drop by drop, and a wise person becomes full of goodness by collecting it bit by bit.

A person should avoid evil deeds in the way a merchant avoids a dangerous road when he has little protection but much wealth, or the way a person who wants to live avoids poison. The comparison stresses that evil is a serious danger to be kept away from.
Poison cannot harm a person whose hand has no wound, and evil cannot harm a person who does no evil. The verse uses the image of poison to say that a person who does no wrong is not hurt by wrong.
If someone harms a gentle, pure, and innocent person, the harm returns to that foolish person. It is like dust thrown into the wind, which blows back onto the thrower.
People who do evil are reborn in hell, and people who do right go to heaven. Those who give up all worldly desires reach Nirvana, a state beyond rebirth and suffering.
No place in the world can free a person from the results of an evil deed. The verse says this is true even in the sky, under the sea, or deep inside mountains.
No place in the world is safe from death. The verse says that not in the sky, not in the middle of the sea, and not deep inside mountains can a person find a spot where death cannot reach them.

All living beings fear punishment and death. Because you share this fear with them, the verse says, you should not kill or have others killed. Wait: the rules say not to address the reader as "you" unless the passage does. The passage does use "you" ("remember that you are like unto them"), so that is allowed. The explanation should stay within what the verse says.
All beings fear punishment and love life. Since one is like them, one should not kill or cause killing.
Someone who hurts or kills other beings, while seeking their own happiness, will not find happiness after death. The point is that those others want happiness just as they do.
A person who wants happiness for himself, and who does not punish or kill other beings that also want happiness, will find happiness after death.
Do not speak harshly to anyone, because people will answer harshly back. Angry words cause pain, and hitting back will bring blows in return.
If a person stays silent like a broken metal gong and does not speak, they have reached Nirvana, the state of freedom from craving and suffering. In this state they know no quarrels.
Just as a cowherd drives his cows into the pen with a stick, old age and death drive human life toward its end. The verse says that people are moved along by these forces, as animals are herded.
A fool does not notice that he is doing wrong while he does it. But the wicked person is harmed by his own actions, as if he were burned by fire.
The verse says that a person who hurts innocent, harmless people will soon reach one of ten states. The passage breaks off here, so the list of those states is not given in this verse.

This verse lists the harms that come to a person who harms others: cruel suffering, loss, bodily injury, heavy affliction, and loss of mind. It is the second part of a verse about the results of violence, and the full verse is not given here.

Misfortunes listed here include harm from the king, a frightening false accusation, the loss of family, or the destruction of one's wealth. The verse names these as kinds of suffering that can come to a person.
Lightning or fire may destroy the wicked man's house, and when his body dies, the fool goes to hell. The verse says that a fool's wrongdoing brings punishment both in this life and after death.

Outward practices such as going naked, matted hair, fasting, lying on the ground, covering oneself in dust, or sitting still cannot make a person pure if they have not overcome their desires. The point is that purity depends on inner control, not on these bodily acts.

A person is a true holy man, whatever clothes he wears, if he is calm, self-controlled, pure, and has stopped finding fault with other living beings. Such a person is called a Brahmana, a sramana (ascetic), or a bhikshu (monk).

Is there anyone so humble and self-controlled that he takes blame calmly, as a well-trained horse takes the whip? The verse suggests that very few people do this, since a person who is truly restrained accepts rebuke without resentment.

Just as a well-trained horse responds to the whip, the listener is urged to become active and lively. Through faith, virtue, energy, meditation and understanding of the teaching, one will overcome the great pain of reproof and become perfect in knowledge and conduct, never forgetful.

Just as well-makers guide water, fletchers bend arrows, and carpenters shape wood, wise people shape themselves. The verse says a person can train and discipline their own character, as craftspeople shape their materials. A fletcher makes arrow shafts straight by bending them; "fletcher" means an arrow-maker.
Why laugh or feel joy when the world is always burning? The verse asks why people surrounded by darkness do not seek a light. It is a question about looking for a way out of that darkness.

It asks the reader to look closely at the human body and see it as a decorated bundle of flesh that is wounded, held together, sickly, and full of changing thoughts. It has no real strength or lasting grip on anything.
The body is weak, full of sickness, and easily broken. It is a heap that decays and falls apart, and life always ends in death.

Bones left after death are compared to gourds thrown away in autumn. The verse asks what pleasure anyone could find in looking at them. It points to the body's decay as something not worth delighting in.
The body is described as a fortress built of bones and covered with flesh and blood. Old age, death, pride and deceit are said to live inside it.
Even the finest royal chariots and the human body decay and pass away. Good people's virtue does not decay, and the good say this to one another.
A person who has learned little grows old like an ox: his body gets bigger, but his understanding does not grow with it.

The speaker has been searching for the builder of the body, which is compared to a house, and has passed through many rebirths in the search. Now the builder is seen, so the house will not be built again. The mind has reached nirvana, the end of all desire.
People who have not trained themselves properly and have not gathered good qualities while young end up dying helplessly, like old herons left in a lake with no fish to eat.
People who in youth neither trained themselves nor built up any inner wealth end up in old age like broken bows, lying useless and sighing over the years they have lost.
If a person cares for himself, he should guard himself closely. A wise person should stay alert at least during one of the three watches of the night.
A person should first put himself on the right course, and only then teach others. Done in that order, a wise person will not suffer.

A person who wants to guide others should first train himself the way he teaches them. Only when he has mastered himself can he rightly master others. The verse adds that controlling one's own self is hard.
Self is the master of self, since no one else could be. When a person has tamed the self well, he gains a master that few people find.
Evil that a person does to himself, arising from his own actions, crushes a foolish person. The image is of a diamond breaking a precious stone, meaning the harm is as hard and sure as that.

A person whose evil is very great drags himself down to the state his enemy wants for him, just as a creeper that wraps around a tree brings the tree down. The image is of a vine whose growth weakens the tree it clings to.
Harmful deeds, the kind that hurt oneself, are easy to commit. Good and beneficial deeds are very hard to do.

A foolish person who looks down on the worthy, holy and virtuous people, and follows false teaching, produces a harvest that destroys himself. The verse compares this to the fruit of the katthaka reed, which dies once it has borne fruit.

Evil is done by a person, and that person suffers for it. Evil is avoided by the same person, who is then made pure. Purity and impurity depend on each person alone, so no one can make another person pure.

A person should not neglect their own duty for the sake of someone else's, no matter how important that other duty is. Once a person has understood what his own duty is, he should keep paying close attention to it.
Do not follow evil ways, do not drift through life carelessly, do not follow false teachings, and do not become a friend of worldly attachments. The verse urges a person to avoid these four things.
Make an effort and do not be lazy. Live by the law of virtue, and the virtuous person finds happiness both in this life and in the next.
Follow the way of virtue and not the way of sin. A virtuous person rests in happiness both in this life and in the next.

Seeing the world as a bubble or a mirage, something empty and passing, is said to make a person invisible to the king of death. The verse claims that whoever looks at the world this way is not seen by death.
The verse compares the shining world to a royal chariot. Foolish people sink into it and get caught up in it, while wise people do not get attached to it.
A person who was careless in the past but later becomes sober and mindful lights up the world, the way the moon shines once the clouds have moved away.
A person whose bad deeds are covered over by good deeds lights up the world, the way the moon shines when it comes out from behind clouds.
Most people in this world cannot see clearly, and only a few reach heaven. Those few are like birds that have escaped from a net.
Swans travel along the sun's path through the sky by their own power. In the same way, wise people leave this world after overcoming Mara, the tempter or god of death and desire in Buddhist teaching.
A person who has broken one moral law, tells lies, and mocks the idea of another world will, according to this verse, be capable of any wrong act.
The stingy do not reach the world of the gods, and only fools fail to praise generosity. A wise person delights in giving and, through it, is blessed in the next world.

The verse says that reaching the first step on the path to holiness is worth more than ruling the earth, going to heaven, or ruling all worlds. The first step is the reward itself, and it outweighs these greater-seeming goods.

The verse describes a person whose victory over the inner passions can never be undone, and whom no worldly defeat can reach. It asks how such a person, the Awakened one who knows all, could be followed or traced, since he leaves no path behind.

A person whom no desire can lead astray cannot be led by any path or trail. The verse calls such a person the Awakened, the all-knowing, and "trackless," meaning no trail can be followed to him or traced in him.

Even the gods envy people who are awake, mindful, given to meditation, wise, and content in quiet withdrawal from worldly life. Here "awakened" means enlightened, and "the gods" are beings of the heavens in Buddhist belief.
Human birth is hard to obtain, human life is hard to live, hearing the true teaching is hard, and the arising of a Buddha is hard. The verse lists four things that are rare.
The verse gives the core teaching of the Buddhas, the "Awakened" ones. It says that a person should avoid wrongdoing, do good deeds, and keep their mind pure.
Patience is called the highest form of self-discipline, and patient endurance the highest peace. A true monk, the verse says, is not someone who hits or insults others.

The verse lists the core of the Buddha's teaching: avoid blaming and harming others, live with self-control under the rules, eat moderately, sleep and sit in solitude, and keep the mind focused on the highest thoughts. "The Awakened" is a title for the Buddha.
Desires cannot be satisfied, even by a rain of gold coins. The verse says that a person who understands desires give only brief pleasure and bring pain is wise.
A fully awakened disciple finds no satisfaction even in the pleasures of heaven. His only delight is in the ending of all desire.
People who are afraid go to many places for protection, such as mountains, forests, groves and sacred trees. The verse describes this as a common human reaction to fear.

The passage says that some kinds of refuge are not safe and not the best. A person who turns to such a refuge is not freed from all suffering. The verse is contrasting these weaker refuges with a truer one.

Whoever seeks refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma (his teaching), and the Sangha (the community of followers), and who clearly understands the Four Noble Truths, is described here. The verse is the first half of a pair, and its second half is not included in this excerpt.
The passage lists the Four Noble Truths in brief. It names four things: suffering, its origin, its ending, and the Eightfold Path that leads to the stilling of suffering.
The "refuge" here is the Buddha's teaching of awakening, which the verse calls the safest and best place to turn to. The verse says that a person who goes to this refuge is freed from all suffering.
A Buddha, an awakened teacher, is rare and does not appear in every place. Where such a wise person is born, the people of that family or community do well.

Good fortune comes with the arising of an awakened one, with the teaching of the true Law, with peace within the community, and with the devotion of those who are at peace. The verse calls each of these happy, or blessed.
Whoever honors those worthy of honor, such as the Buddha, his disciples, and those who have overcome evil and sorrow and are free from fear, gains merit that no one can measure.
Let us live happily without hating those who hate us. Even among people who hate us, we should stay free from hatred.
Let us live happily and free from suffering, even among people who are suffering. Let us stay healthy in mind while others are troubled.
Let us live happily, free from greed even among greedy people. The verse says that one can stay free from greed while living among those who are greedy.
Even though we own nothing, we can live happily. Such a life, the verse says, will be like that of the bright gods, who feed on happiness.
Winning over others creates hatred, because the loser is left unhappy. A person who gives up both winning and losing, and is content, is happy.
Passion is like a fire, and hatred is like a losing throw in a game. The body is the greatest pain, and rest, meaning peace from craving, is the highest happiness.

Hunger is the worst sickness and the body the greatest source of pain. If a person truly understands this, the verse says, that understanding is Nirvana, the highest happiness. Nirvana is the Buddhist term for the end of suffering.
Good health is the greatest gift, and contentment the best wealth. Trust is the best kind of friendship, and Nirvana, the state of liberation from suffering, is the highest happiness.
A person who has enjoyed quiet solitude and calm is free from fear and from wrongdoing. That same person also enjoys taking in the law, meaning the Buddha's teaching.

Being with wise and noble people brings lasting happiness, and not seeing foolish people brings true happiness. The verse says that the company of the wise, the "elect" (Arya, the noble ones), is good, and that avoiding fools leads to real contentment.
Spending time with foolish people brings long suffering, much like being with an enemy. Spending time with wise people brings joy, like a reunion with family.

One should follow the wise, the learned, the patient and the dutiful, and follow a good and wise person the way the moon follows the path of the stars. The verse uses the moon's steady path across the sky as its image for such following.

A person who chases pleasure and vanity, and neglects meditation and the true goal of life, will eventually envy the person who has worked hard at meditation. The verse warns that the pursuit of pleasure leads to regret.
Do not seek out what is pleasant or what is unpleasant. Missing what you like causes suffering, and having to face what you dislike causes suffering too.
Attachment causes suffering, because losing what you love is painful. Someone who loves nothing and hates nothing is free of the bonds that hold a person in suffering.
Pleasure leads to both sorrow and fear. A person who is free from pleasure has neither sorrow nor fear.
Grief and fear come from attachment, meaning strong affection or clinging to people and things. A person who is free from such attachment knows neither grief nor fear.
Lust leads to both sorrow and fear. A person who is free from lust feels neither sorrow nor fear.
Grief and fear arise from love, according to this verse. A person who is free from love knows neither grief nor fear.
Greed leads to both sorrow and fear. A person who has no greed experiences neither sorrow nor fear.
Someone who has goodness and wisdom, who is fair, tells the truth, and attends to his own duties, is the person the world will value. The verse says that such a person is loved by others.

A person who longs for Nirvana, the unspeakable state of liberation, whose mind is content, and whose thoughts are not confused by desire, is called "urdhvamsrotas," meaning one carried upward by the stream.
Relatives, friends and loved ones greet a man who has been away for a long time and comes back safe from a distant place. The verse describes how people welcome a returning traveller.

Someone who has done good deeds in this life is welcomed in the next world by those deeds, just as relatives welcome a friend coming home. The good works act like friends who greet the doer after death.

A person should give up anger and pride and break free from every kind of attachment. Someone who does not cling to name and form, meaning the self and things, and who claims nothing as his own, does not suffer.
A person who stops anger from rising, as one would stop a runaway chariot, is the true driver. Others only hold the reins without really controlling the horses.
A person should defeat anger with love, evil with good, greed with generosity, and lies with truth. The verse says that the right response to each wrong is its opposite virtue.
Be truthful, do not give way to anger, and give even when asked only for a small thing. Following these three steps, the verse says, brings a person close to the gods.
Wise people who harm no one and always keep their bodies under control reach the unchangeable state called Nirvana. Once there, they suffer no more.
Those who stay alert, study day and night, and work toward Nirvana (the state of freedom from suffering and craving) will see their passions come to an end.
People will be blamed whatever they do. Whether a person stays silent, talks a lot, or speaks only a little, someone finds fault. The saying holds that no one on earth escapes blame.
No person has ever been, will ever be, or is now, someone who is always blamed or always praised. Everyone receives both kinds of judgment at different times.

The verses say that a person whom wise people praise day after day, as faultless, wise, and rich in knowledge and virtue, is hard to blame. Like a gold coin from the Gambu river, such a person is valued beyond criticism. Even the gods and Brahman praise him.
Be careful of anger that shows in the body, and keep the body under control. Give up bodily wrongdoing, and use the body to do good.
Be careful of angry speech, and keep your tongue under control. Stop speaking wrongly, and use your words for good conduct.
Be on guard against anger that arises in the mind, and keep the mind under control. Give up wrongs that come from the mind, and train it in goodness.
Those who are wise keep control of their body, their speech, and their mind. Because they do this, they are truly well controlled.
The speaker tells a person that they are like a dry, fallen leaf and that death is close. They stand at the door of leaving life with no preparation for the journey ahead.

Be your own refuge, work hard, and stay wise. When your impurities are blown away and you are free from guilt, you will enter the heavenly world of the noble ones (Ariya), meaning the spiritually elect.
Your life is nearly over and you are close to death, the figure called Yama. There is no place to rest on the road ahead, and no provisions for the journey.
Work hard to become your own refuge, like an island, and become wise. Once your impurities are blown away and you are free from guilt, you will not be reborn again into birth and decay.
A wise person should remove the faults in their own mind bit by bit, the way a smith cleans impurities out of silver. The work is done gradually and repeatedly, one fault at a time.
Just as rust forms on iron and eats away at the metal it came from, a wrongdoer's own deeds lead him toward a bad path. The harm comes from within, from what he himself has made.
Each kind of thing has its own fault, or "taint": prayers are spoiled when they are not repeated, houses when they are not repaired, the body when it is lazy, and a watchman when he is careless.
Bad conduct is named as the flaw of women, and greed as the flaw of a giver or benefactor. The verse adds that all evil ways are impure, both in this life and the next.
Ignorance is the worst kind of taint, or stain on the mind. The verse urges monks to get rid of this taint so that they become free of all taints.
Living is easy for a person who has no shame. Such a person acts like a boastful crow, causing trouble, insulting others, and bold in his wrongdoing, yet still wretched.
Life is hard for a modest person who always seeks what is pure, is free from selfish desire, and is calm, spotless, and wise.
It lists four wrongs: killing living beings, lying, taking what is not freely given, and sexual relations with another man's wife. The verse names these as the actions that mark a person as impure.
A person who keeps drinking intoxicating liquor harms himself even in this life. The verse says he "digs up his own root," meaning he destroys the basis of his own well-being while still alive.
People who do not control themselves are in a bad state. Greed and wrongdoing can cause suffering for a long time, so a person should be careful about them.
Food and drink are given out according to each giver's faith or pleasure. A man who frets over what others receive finds no rest, day or night.
Someone who has completely uprooted a certain feeling finds rest both day and night. The verse does not name that feeling.

Passion burns like fire, hatred is as dangerous as a shark, folly traps like a snare, and greed sweeps a person away like a torrent. The verse names four mental states that are each compared to a natural danger.

It is easy to see other people's faults but hard to see one's own. A person sorts out others' faults like chaff from grain, yet hides his own, the way a cheat hides a loaded die from the gambler he is playing.
A person who keeps watching the faults of others and is always easily offended lets their own passions grow. Because of this, they are far from ending those passions.
A person is not a true seeker, or Samana, merely because of outward acts, just as there is no path through the air. The world takes pleasure in empty show, but the Buddhas are free from it.
Outward acts do not make someone a holy man (a Samana), and no path to a spiritual goal lies through the air. All living beings pass away, but the awakened ones (Buddhas) are not shaken by this.

A person is not truly just merely because he forces his will on a matter. The one who judges rightly and wrong, who is learned, and who leads others by fair law and equity, guided by wisdom, is the one called just.
A person is not wise just because he talks a lot. Someone who is patient and free from hatred and fear is the one who counts as learned.
