A person does not uphold the law just by talking a lot about it. Someone who has learned little but actually lives the law, and never neglects it, is the true upholder of the law.
A grey head does not make someone an elder. A person may be old in years and still be called "Old-in-vain," meaning old to no purpose.
A person is called an "elder" not because of age but because of inner qualities. These are truth, virtue, love, self-control, moderation, freedom from impurity, and wisdom.
A person who is envious, greedy and dishonest does not earn respect just by talking a lot or by having a handsome appearance. Good looks and words alone do not make such a person worthy of respect.

"All this" refers to the faults listed earlier in the chapter, such as craving and hatred. When these are destroyed completely, down to the root, and the person is free from hatred and wise, he is called respectable.
A shaved head does not make a man a Samana, a religious ascetic, if he is undisciplined and tells lies. Someone still ruled by desire and greed cannot truly be one either.
A person who keeps calming down evil, whether small or great, is called a "Samana," meaning a quiet or calm person. The name is given because they have stilled all evil.
A monk, or bhikshu, is not one who only begs for food. He is one who takes on the whole teaching, or law, of the Buddha.
A bhikshu is a Buddhist monk. This verse says that a true one is someone who has risen above good and evil, lives chastely, and moves through the world with knowledge.
A person is not a sage (muni) just because he keeps silence, if he is foolish and ignorant. The wise person, who weighs good and evil like a balance and chooses the good, is the true sage.
A man is not called noble (Ariya, meaning "elect" or "noble one") for harming living beings. He is called Ariya because he feels compassion for all living beings.

The speaker says that discipline, vows, much learning, trance and sleeping alone do not by themselves bring the happiness of release. He tells a monk not to feel secure until he has ended his desires.

The best path is the eightfold one, the best truths are the four noble truths, and the best virtue is freedom from passion. The best person is one who can see clearly, meaning who understands these things.
The Buddha says that one path alone leads to purifying the mind. Everything else is a trick of Mara, the tempter, a figure who tries to pull people away from liberation.
Following this path leads to the end of suffering. The speaker taught it after he had understood how to remove the "thorns," a figure for the inner troubles that cause pain.
You must make the effort yourself. Buddhas only teach the way, and thoughtful people who follow it are freed from Mara, the tempter or power of death and delusion that holds people in bondage.
Everything that is made or formed will come to an end. A person who truly sees this stops being driven by suffering, and this is the path to purity.
Everything created or conditioned is suffering. A person who clearly sees this becomes calm and detached from pain, and this path leads to purity of mind.
One who knows and sees that all forms are unreal becomes free from pain and no longer reacts to it. The verse calls this the path to purity.

A person who does not get up and act when it is time, even though young and strong, but stays lazy with weak will and thought, will never reach knowledge. The verse says laziness blocks the way to wisdom.
A person should guard their speech and mind, and never do wrong with their body. If they keep these three paths of action clean, they will reach the way taught by the wise.
Knowledge grows through effort and is lost through neglect of effort. Someone who understands this two-sided path of gain and loss should set themselves in a way that lets knowledge increase.

Cut down the whole forest of lust, not just single trees, because danger grows from it. Once both the forest and its undergrowth are removed, the monks will be free of it. In this image, "forest" stands for lust or craving, and "undergrowth" for its smaller roots and traces.
A person's mind stays tied down for as long as any desire for women remains, even a small one. The passage compares this to a calf that depends on its mother's milk.
Give up self-love, the way a person pulls off a dead autumn lotus flower with the hand. Keep to the path of peace, since the Buddha has shown the way to nirvana, the state of release from suffering.
A fool plans to stay in one place through every season, saying he will live there in the rain, winter and summer. He makes these plans without thinking that he will die.

Death takes away a man who is praised for his children and herds, even though his mind is busy and scattered. The image is of a flood sweeping away a village while its people sleep, meaning death comes without warning.
Death takes a person, and family cannot help. Sons, a father, and other relatives give no protection once death has seized someone.
A person who is wise and good and understands this teaching is said to clear the way to Nirvana, the state of freedom from suffering, quickly.
If giving up a small pleasure leads to a greater one, a wise person should give up the small one and aim for the greater.
Whoever causes pain to others in order to gain pleasure for himself is tied up in hatred. Because of this, he will never be free of hatred.
People neglect what they should do and do what they should not. Those who are careless and undisciplined keep wanting more and more.
Wise, watchful people who keep close watch over their body, avoid what they should not do, and steadily do what they should will see their desires come to an end.

A true Brahmana, meaning a truly holy person, is not harmed by consequences even after killing his parents, two warrior kings, or destroying a whole kingdom. The verse says that such a person remains untouched by these deeds.

A true Brahmin, meaning a holy person, is not harmed by his deeds even if he has killed his parents, two holy kings, and a distinguished man. The verse says such a person is free from the consequences of these acts.
Those who follow Gotama (the Buddha) stay alert at all times. Their minds, day and night, keep returning to the Buddha.
Those who follow Gotama (the Buddha) stay alert at all times. Day and night, their minds are fixed on the Dhamma, his teaching of the way to end suffering.

Followers of Gotama (the Buddha) are always alert, and their thoughts, day and night, stay fixed on the community of believers. The translation's word "church" stands in for the Buddhist monastic community, the sangha.
Gotama's followers stay mentally alert at all times. Day and night, their attention is fixed on the body, meaning close awareness of their own physical existence.
Those who follow Gotama (the Buddha) stay fully alert at all times. Their minds, day and night, find joy in compassion, which means caring for the suffering of others.
Followers of Gotama (the Buddha) stay alert at all times. Their minds, day and night, take pleasure in meditation.

Leaving the world to become a monk is hard, and living in the world is hard too. Monastery life, living among equals and wandering as a beggar all bring pain. So the verse says a person should not become a wandering beggar, and then will not suffer that pain.
A man who is faithful, virtuous, famous and rich is respected in whatever place he chooses to settle. His respect comes from these qualities and his wealth, wherever he goes.
Good people are visible from far away, like snow-covered mountains that can be seen at a distance. Bad people go unnoticed, like arrows shot in the dark that no one sees coming.
A person who constantly practises sitting and sleeping alone, and who controls himself, will find joy in the end of all desires, living alone as if in a forest.
Liars go to hell, and so does anyone who does wrong and then denies it. After death they are equal, both people whose evil deeds follow them into the next life.
Many monks wearing the yellow robe are undisciplined and lacking self-control. Such people, through their wicked actions, go to hell.

It is better to swallow a red-hot iron ball than to be an undisciplined wrongdoer who lives on the alms of the people. The verse says that a person who lacks self-control and depends on public gifts is worse off than one who suffers the most painful death.

A reckless man who desires his neighbour's wife gains four things: a bad reputation, an uncomfortable bed, punishment, and hell. "Wreckless" is an old spelling of "reckless," meaning careless about consequences.
Adultery brings a bad reputation, leads toward hell, and gives only brief pleasure, which is followed by fear. The king also punishes it severely. So a man should not desire his neighbour's wife.

Just as a blade of grass cuts the hand if it is grasped the wrong way, a harsh discipline done the wrong way leads to suffering after death. "Asceticism" means strict self-denial, and "hell" here means a painful state of rebirth.

Acting carelessly, breaking a vow, and obeying the rules only half-heartedly do not bring much good result. The verse says these habits lead to little reward, so careful action, kept vows, and wholehearted discipline are what count.
If something needs doing, a person should do it with full energy. A careless seeker only stirs up more of his desires and passions, like dust scattered by the wind.
It is better not to do a bad deed, because a person later regrets it. It is better to do a good deed, because after doing it a person does not regret it.
A person should guard himself as carefully as a fort is guarded on every side. He should not let any moment slip by, because those who waste the right moment suffer pain in hell.

People who feel shame where they should not, and feel no shame where they should, take up false teachings and go down the evil path. The verse says shame is wrong when it is aimed at the wrong things and missing when it is needed.
People who fear the wrong things, and fail to fear what they should, are said to hold false beliefs and so take the path of evil.
People who ban things that are not wrong, and fail to ban things that are wrong, hold false teachings and walk the path of evil.
People who correctly recognize what is forbidden as forbidden, and what is not forbidden as not forbidden, follow the true teaching and walk the good path.
A person says they will bear insults quietly, just as a war elephant bears an arrow shot from a bow. They give the reason that the world is ill-natured, meaning people are often unkind.
Elephants that have been trained are the ones taken into battle and ridden by kings. In the same way, the person who has been trained, and who bears insults quietly, is called the best of people.
Tamed mules, noble horses and large elephants are useful animals once they are trained. The verse says that a person who trains himself is better still.
Nobody reaches Nirvana, the untrodden country, by riding ordinary animals. A tamed person reaches it by riding their own well-tamed self, meaning self-mastery.

The verse compares a strong, wild elephant to a restless mind. Once tied up, the elephant refuses food and longs for its home in the forest, just as an untrained mind longs for its old habits. The image is about craving for what is familiar and free.

A man who grows fat, eats greedily, sleeps too much and rolls about in bed is called a fool. The verse says such a person is reborn again and again, like a pig that keeps feeding on kitchen leftovers.
The speaker says that their mind used to wander wherever it wanted. Now they will hold it firmly, the way a rider uses a hook to control a wild elephant.
Do not be careless, and keep watch over your thoughts. Pull yourself out of wrong conduct, as an elephant pulls itself out of deep mud.
If a person finds a sensible, wise companion who lives moderately, he may walk with that companion through all dangers, happy yet careful.

If a person cannot find a wise and sensible companion to travel with, the verse says they should go alone. It compares this to a king who has left a conquered land behind, or to an elephant roaming the forest by itself.
It is better to live alone than to keep company with a fool. A person should walk alone, avoid wrongdoing, and want little, like a wild elephant living in the forest.
Friends, enjoyment and good deeds are pleasant when the right moment comes, and at death a good deed is pleasant too. Giving up all grief is also pleasant.

Being a mother, being a father, being a samana (a wandering monk), and being a brahmana (a member of the priestly caste) are each called pleasant in the world. The verse simply lists these four states as pleasant.
Good qualities are pleasant when they last a whole life, such as virtue and a firmly rooted faith. Gaining wisdom and avoiding wrongdoing are also called pleasant.
A person without careful thought has craving that spreads like a climbing vine. Driven by it, he moves from one life to the next, the way a monkey jumps through the forest looking for fruit.

Whoever is overcome by this fierce, poisonous craving in the world will see their suffering grow, like the thick growth of the birana grass. "Birana" is a kind of fragrant grass, so the image is of suffering spreading fast.
Whoever overcomes this fierce craving, which is hard to conquer in this world, has his sufferings fall away from him. They drop off like water from a lotus leaf.

Those gathered are told to pull out the root of craving, the way a person seeking the fragrant usira root must first dig up the birana grass that covers it. Doing so keeps the tempter, Mara, from crushing them again and again, as a stream flattens reeds.
A tree that has been cut down will grow again if its root is still alive. In the same way, suffering keeps returning unless the things that feed craving, or thirst, are destroyed.
Whoever's thirst for pleasure runs strongly through thirty-six channels is carried away by waves. These waves are his desires, which are set on passion.
Desire runs through the mind like channels of water and grows like a creeper. When it starts to sprout, the verse says it should be cut at the root by knowledge, meaning clear understanding.
People who chase pleasure, sunk in desire, keep going through birth and decay again and again. The verse says that craving for enjoyment keeps the cycle of rebirth turning.
People driven by craving run about like a trapped hare. Bound by chains of desire, they suffer for a long time, again and again.

People, driven by craving, dart about like a trapped hare. So a monk should drive out craving by working toward freedom from passion for himself. "Mendicant" here means a Buddhist monk, and "passionlessness" means freedom from strong desire.
Someone who has escaped desire, called the "forest" in this verse, and then goes back into it runs into bondage again, even though he was free.
Wise people do not count iron, wood, or hemp chains as the strongest bonds. A stronger one is the attachment to jewels, rings, sons, and a wife.

A fetter is a chain or bond. The verse says that the bond wise people call strongest pulls a person down and gives way easily, yet is hard to undo. Once it is cut, people leave the world, free of worry, and give up their desires and pleasures.
Those who are ruled by desires are carried along by them, like a spider running down the web it has spun. Wise people cut this web, leave the world free of worries, and let go of all attachment.
Let go of the past, the future, and the present, if you want to cross to the far side of existence. When the mind is completely free, it will not be reborn again into birth and decay.
A person who is shaken by doubts, driven by strong desires, and wanting only pleasant things will see his craving grow. In this way he makes the chains that bind him stronger.

If a person enjoys calming doubts and keeps reflecting on what is unpleasant, such as the impurity of the body, he will loosen and fully cut the fetter of Mara. Mara is the tempter, a figure who holds people in the cycle of craving.
A person who has reached the goal, who does not tremble, has no thirst (craving) and no sin, has removed every thorn of life. For such a person, this body will be the last one.

A person who is free from thirst (craving) and from attachment, who understands the words and their meaning, and who knows the order of the letters, has reached their final body. Such a person is called a great sage, a great man.

The speaker says he has overcome everything, knows everything, and is free from defilement in every state of life. Having given up all attachments and ended craving, he is free. Since he has come to know himself fully, he asks whom there is left to teach.
The gift of the teaching is greater than any other gift, and its sweetness and joy are greater than any other pleasure. Ending craving, or thirst, overcomes all suffering.
Pleasures ruin the foolish person who does not seek the other shore, meaning liberation from suffering. Driven by his craving for pleasure, he harms himself as if he were his own enemy.
Just as weeds ruin a field, passion ruins people. So a gift given to someone free of passion brings a great reward.
Just as weeds harm a field, hatred harms people. So a gift given to those who are free of hatred brings a great reward.
Just as weeds harm farm fields, vanity harms people. So a gift given to those free from vanity brings a great reward.
Just as weeds harm a field, lust harms people. So a gift given to those who are free from lust brings great reward.
Holding back the senses is good: restraint of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue is each named as good. The verse lists these senses one by one, saying that controlling each of them is a good thing.
Self-control is good in body, speech, and thought, and in everything else. A monk who is restrained in all these ways is freed from all suffering.

A bhikshu is a monk or mendicant. The verse says such a person is one who controls his hands, feet and speech, and who is well restrained overall. He finds joy within, stays focused, and is content while alone.

A monk who keeps his speech under control, speaks wisely and calmly, and teaches the meaning and the law (the Buddha's teaching) has words that are sweet. The verse links good speech with wise teaching.
A monk who lives in the law, takes joy in it, reflects on it, and follows it will never fall away from the true law. Here "law" means the Buddha's teaching (Dhamma), and "Bhikshu" means a monk.
A mendicant, a monk who lives on alms, should not look down on what he has been given, and should never envy others. The verse says that someone who envies others does not gain peace of mind.
A monk who receives only a little and does not look down on what he gets is praised even by the gods, provided his life is pure and he is not lazy.
A bhikshu, or Buddhist monk, is defined here as someone who does not take themselves to be their name and bodily form, and who does not grieve over things that have passed away.
A monk who acts with kindness and stays calm in the Buddha's teaching will reach Nirvana. Nirvana is described here as a quiet place, the ending of natural desires, and happiness.
A monk is told to empty a boat so that it will move quickly. Once he has cut off passion and hatred, he will reach Nirvana, the state of liberation from suffering in Buddhist teaching.

Cut off the five senses, give up the five, and rise above the five. A monk who has escaped the five fetters, the bonds that tie a person to the world, is called "saved from the flood," meaning he has crossed over the river of rebirth.
Meditate and do not be careless, monk. Do not let your mind dwell on pleasant things, so that you do not later suffer in hell, swallowing a red-hot iron ball and crying out in pain as you burn.

Knowledge and meditation depend on each other: there is no meditation without knowledge, and no knowledge without meditation. Someone who has both is close to Nirvana, the state of liberation from suffering in Buddhism.
A monk who has entered an empty dwelling and has a calm mind feels a joy beyond the ordinary when he clearly sees the Dharma, the Buddhist teaching or law. "Bhikshu" means a Buddhist monk.

When a person has understood how the body's parts (the khandhas, the five groups that make up a person) arise and pass away, they find joy and happiness. This is the joy of those who know the deathless state, Nirvana.
A wise monk starts his training by guarding his senses, being content with little, and keeping the monastic rules. He also keeps good companions who live purely and are not lazy.
A person who lives with kindness and fully carries out his duties will, through deep joy, bring suffering to an end.
Just as the Vassika plant drops its dead flowers, a monk should let go of passion and hatred. The verse uses the plant as an image for giving up these two states of mind.
A monk is called "quiet" when his body, speech and mind are calm, he is self-controlled, and he has turned away from the worldly things that tempt people.
A monk is told to wake himself up and examine his own conduct, relying on no one else. By guarding himself and staying alert in this way, he will live happily. "Bhikshu" is a Buddhist monk.

Each person is their own master and their own refuge, so a person should restrain themselves the way a merchant holds back a fine horse. The verse urges self-control, using the image of a skilled trader reining in a valuable animal.
A monk who takes delight in the Buddha's teaching and stays calm in it will reach Nirvana, the quiet state where natural desires stop and happiness is found.
A young monk who devotes himself to the Buddha's teaching lights up the world, as the moon does when it is free of clouds.

Stop the flow of craving and drive out desire. Once you understand that everything made or formed is impermanent and comes to an end, you will understand what is unmade, the state that is not formed or conditioned.

A person who has crossed to the far side of both disciplines, restraint and meditation, is free of all bonds once he has gained knowledge. Here "the other shore" means the state of freedom reached beyond ordinary life, and "Brahmana" means a holy person.

A person who has no attachment to "this shore," "that shore," or both is called a Brahmana here. Such a person is fearless and free from bonds. In Buddhist usage, a Brahmana means a holy person who has reached liberation, so the verse defines a true Brahmana by inner freedom rather than by birth.
A true Brahmana, meaning a holy person, is defined here by inner qualities rather than birth. He is thoughtful, blameless, calm, dutiful, free from passions, and has reached the highest goal.

The verse compares several sources of brightness: the sun by day, the moon by night, a warrior in his armour, and a Brahmana (a member of the Hindu priestly class) in meditation. It says the Buddha, the Awakened One, shines with a brightness that lasts both day and night.

A person is called a Brahmana because he is free from evil, a Samana because he walks calmly, and a Pravragita, or pilgrim, because he has sent his own impurities away. The verse gives three names and explains each by what the person has done.

A Brahmana is a member of the priestly class in ancient India, and here the term refers to a spiritually advanced person. The verse says that no one should attack such a person, and that the person attacked should not strike back. Both the attacker and the one who retaliates are described as suffering harm, with the retaliator's fault called greater.
A Brahmana, meaning a member of the priestly class, gains a great deal by holding back from worldly pleasures. Once all wish to harm others is gone, suffering will also end.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who does no harm through body, speech, or mind, and who keeps control over all three. A Brahmana here means a holy person, not a member of the priestly class by birth.
Once a person has understood the teaching of the Buddha, he should honour it with care, just as a Brahmana (a Hindu priest) honours the sacred fire at a sacrifice.
A person does not become a Brahmana, a member of the priestly class, because of matted hair, family, or birth. Instead, someone who has truth and righteousness is a Brahmana.

Outward signs of holiness, such as matted hair and goat-skin robes, are of no use if the inner self stays greedy or cruel. The speaker says the person cleans only the outside while the inside remains corrupt.
A man in dirty robes, thin, with visible veins, who lives alone in the forest and meditates, is the one the speaker calls a brahmana. The verse names these outward signs of the person it describes.
A Brahmana, a title for a holy person, is not defined by birth or by the mother who bore him. A man who is arrogant and rich does not qualify, while a poor man who is free from all attachments does.

In this verse, a "Brahmana" means a person who is spiritually worthy, not a member of the priestly caste by birth. Such a person has cut all the bonds that hold the mind, never trembles with fear, and is free and unbound.

In this verse, a "Brahmana" (a person worthy of the name, in the sense used here) is someone who has cut off the straps, thongs and chains that bind him, along with everything attached to them, broken the bar that holds him, and become awakened.
A true Brahmana, meaning a worthy person, is one who bears blame, chains, and beatings patiently even though he has done no wrong. His patience is his strength, and it serves him as an army would.

A "Brahmana" here means a man who has reached spiritual perfection, not a man of priestly birth. The verse says such a person is free from anger, dutiful, virtuous, without craving, self-controlled, and in his final life.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who does not cling to worldly pleasures. Like water on a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed on a needle's point, such a person does not stick or hold on to them. A Brahmana is a member of the priestly class in Indian tradition.
A person is called a Brahmana, a holy person, here meaning someone who in this life knows the end of suffering, has set down the burden they carried, and is free of their chains.

A Brahmana, a person of high spiritual standing, is defined here by inner qualities rather than birth. Such a person has deep knowledge and wisdom, can tell right from wrong, and has reached the highest goal.
A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who stays apart from both ordinary householders and other monks and wanderers. He visits no homes and wants very little.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who does not blame any living being, weak or strong, and neither kills nor causes others to kill. The word "Brahmana" here means a person of spiritual worth, not a member of the priestly caste by birth.
A true Brahmana, in this verse, is a person who stays patient with those who are intolerant, gentle with those who criticise him, and calm when others are driven by desire or anger.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone from whom anger, hatred, pride and envy have fallen away completely. The image is a mustard seed slipping off the tip of a needle, so that nothing is left behind. A Brahmana is a member of the priestly class in traditional Indian society.
A "Brahmana" here means a person of true worth, not a man of a priestly caste. The verse says such a person speaks truthfully, in a way that teaches and is gentle, and so hurts no one.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is a person who takes nothing that is not freely given to him. This holds whatever the thing is, whether long or short, small or large, good or bad. "Brahmana" here means a holy person, a member of the priestly class.
A Brahmana, meaning a truly worthy person in this context, is one who has no desire for either this life or any future life, has no leanings or attachments, and is free from bonds.

A Brahmana, meaning a holy person, is someone who has no worldly attachments. Once he understands the truth, he no longer asks endless questions like "How, how?" and has reached the deep state of the Immortal, meaning nirvana.

A "Brahmana" here means a truly worthy person, not a member of the priestly caste by birth. The verse says such a person is beyond both good and evil, free from the chains of each, and free from grief, sin and impurity.

The verse says that a true Brahmana (a holy person) is one who is bright like the moon, pure, calm, and untroubled, with all joy gone from him. "Brahmana" here means a person of spiritual worth, not a member of the priestly caste by birth. Word count: about 48.

A "Brahmana" here means a truly worthy person, not a member of the priestly caste. The verse says such a person has crossed the muddy road of the world and its emptiness, reached the far shore, and is thoughtful, honest, free from doubt and craving, and content.
A true "Brahmana" (a holy person in this text's sense) is someone who gives up all desires in this world, lives without a fixed home, and has no craving left at all.
A "Brahmana" here means a person of true worth, not a member of a priestly caste. The verse says such a person gives up all desires, lives without a fixed home, and has no greed left in them.
A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who has freed himself from every bond. He has left behind ties to other people and has risen above ties to the gods as well.
A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who has let go of both pleasure and pain. He is calm, free from the seeds of future rebirth, and has overcome the whole world.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who knows how beings die and are reborn everywhere, who is free from bondage, and who is "Sugata" (well-gone or welfaring) and "Buddha" (awakened). The verse defines the title by inner knowledge and freedom rather than by birth.
A true Brahmana, here meaning a holy person, is one whose path is unknown even to gods, spirits and men. Such a person has no passions left and is an Arhat, a fully enlightened, venerable figure.

A true Brahmana, in this verse, is someone who owns nothing and claims nothing, whether in past, future, or present. He is poor in this sense and free from attachment to worldly things. "Brahmana" here means a holy person, not a member of the priestly caste.
In Buddhist teaching, a "brahmana" is a holy person. This verse says that the true brahmana is the one who is manly, noble, heroic, a great sage, a conqueror, unshaken, accomplished, and awakened.

A Brahmana, in this verse, is a person who has reached a high spiritual state. Such a person knows his past lives, sees heaven and hell, has ended the cycle of rebirth, and has complete knowledge and perfect qualities.

Those who are dutiful to parents and respectful to elder brothers rarely offend their superiors, and those who do not offend superiors almost never cause disorder. The gentleman focuses on the root, since good conduct grows from it. Filial piety and brotherly respect are therefore seen as the foundation of all kindness.
People with smooth speech and a charming manner rarely have true virtue. The saying warns that a pleasing surface is not a sign of real goodness.

Tseng, a disciple of Confucius, says he checks himself every day on three things. He asks whether he has been unfaithful when acting for others, whether he has been insincere with friends, and whether he has failed to learn and practise his teacher's teachings.

To govern a state of a thousand chariots, a ruler must attend to his duties with care and be sincere. He must spend carefully, care for the people, and call on them for work only at the right times of year.

A young person should first show duty to parents at home and respect to elders outside the home. He should be sincere and truthful, love people widely, and make friends with good people. Only after doing these things should he spend any spare time on learning and the polite arts.

Zixia says that a man who turns his love of beauty toward love of virtue, serves his parents and ruler with all his strength, and keeps his word with friends has learned, even if others say he has not. Learning here means moral conduct, not book study.

A scholar who is not serious will earn no respect, and his learning will lack firmness. He should hold loyalty and sincerity as his basic principles, keep friends who are his equals, and not hesitate to give up his faults.

Tseng Tzu, a disciple of Confucius, says that people should carefully hold funeral rites for their parents and keep up sacrifices to them after they have died. If this is done, the virtue of the people will return to its proper excellence.

Tsze-ch'in asks whether Confucius gets information about a country's government by asking for it or by having it offered to him. Tsze-kung answers that Confucius is gentle, upright, courteous, moderate and agreeable, and that these qualities are how he gets the information.

A son's character can be judged by how he behaves. While his father is alive, look at what he intends to do. After his father dies, look at what he actually does. If for three years he keeps to his father's ways, he can be called filial, meaning dutiful to his parents.

Yu, a disciple of Confucius, says that ease and naturalness are valuable in following the rules of proper conduct, and that following the ancient kings' ways in all matters is the best course. But ease should not be shown without being guided by those rules; ease alone is not enough.

Agreements that rest on what is right can be kept, and respect shown in line with what is proper keeps a person away from shame. A person who relies on others should rely only on those worthy of close trust, and then they can serve as his guides.

A person who wants to be truly virtuous does not chase comfort or fine food. Instead, he works earnestly, speaks carefully, and seeks out people of good principle to correct himself. Such a person, the saying goes, truly loves learning.

Confucius says that a poor man who is cheerful, or a rich man who loves good manners, is better than a poor man who does not flatter or a rich man who is not proud. Tsze-kung links this to a line of poetry about cutting, filing, carving and polishing, which describes self-improvement. Confucius praises him for understanding the idea quickly.
Confucius says he does not mind if others fail to recognize his worth. He says he would be troubled instead by his own failure to understand other people.

A ruler who governs through his personal virtue, or moral goodness, is compared to the North Star. The Star stays in its place, and the other stars turn toward it, so the ruler's example draws people to him without force.

Confucius says that the three hundred poems in the Book of Poetry can all be summed up in one phrase: "Having no depraved thoughts." In other words, the whole collection aims at keeping the mind free of corrupt desires. "Depraved" here means morally corrupt.

Leading people by laws and punishments may make them avoid wrongdoing, but they will feel no shame. Leading them by virtue and proper ritual conduct gives them a sense of shame, and so they become good.

Confucius describes his life in stages. At fifteen he began to focus on learning, and by thirty he was settled. Over the following decades he gained certainty, understood Heaven's decrees, and at seventy his desires matched what was right without his having to force them.

Filial piety, respect owed to parents, is explained here as not being disobedient. When Confucius's student asks what he meant, he says it means serving parents properly while they live, burying them properly when they die, and making proper offerings to them afterward.

Asked by Meng Wu what filial piety (respect and care for one's parents) is, Confucius replies that parents worry constantly that their children might fall ill. The point is that a child should avoid causing parents that worry by taking care of their own health.
Filial piety, or respect for one's parents, is not just providing for them. Dogs and horses also provide for their keepers. Without reverence, the two kinds of support cannot be told apart.

Zixia asked what filial piety (respect and care for one's parents) is. Confucius replied that the hard part lies in the expression on one's face. Doing chores and serving food for elders is not enough, he suggests, if the attitude behind those acts is missing.

The Master says that Hui listened to him all day without objecting, so Hui seemed dull. But after Hui left, the Master saw him on his own and found he could apply the teachings well. So Hui is not stupid.

Confucius says that a person can be understood by three things: what he does, why he does it, and what keeps him content. Hiding one's true character is therefore not possible, as he repeats in the closing question.
A person who keeps old knowledge close while always gaining new knowledge is fit to teach others.
A "utensil" is a tool made for one fixed job. Confucius is saying that a truly educated person is not like this. Such a person is not limited to one narrow use but can take on many different duties.
A "superior man" is a person of good character. According to this saying, such a person acts first and only then speaks, so that his words follow from what he has done.

A good person is fair to all and does not take sides, while a petty person takes sides and is not fair to all. "Catholic" here means broad-minded or universal, not the church. "Partisan" means belonging to a faction or clique.
Studying without thinking about what you learn gets you nothing, and thinking without studying is dangerous. Good understanding needs both careful study and personal reflection on it.

Studying strange or heterodox teachings is harmful, according to this saying. "Strange doctrines" refers to ideas outside the accepted teachings of the time. The Master is the title used for Confucius here.
Knowledge means admitting what you know and admitting what you do not know. Confucius says this is true knowledge, and he speaks to his disciple Yu, asking whether he wants to be taught it.

Confucius advises a student who is studying for a salary to be careful in speech and action. He should set aside doubtful points, speak cautiously about the rest, and avoid risky things. Doing so leads to few blames and few regrets, and that is the way to gain an official post.

Duke Ai, a ruler of the state of Lu, asks how to win the people's obedience. Confucius answers that the people will obey if upright men are promoted and crooked men are set aside. If crooked men are promoted instead, the people will not obey.

Chi K'ang asks how a ruler can make his people respect him, be loyal, and strive for virtue. Confucius answers that the ruler should govern with dignity, be filial and kind to everyone, and promote good people while teaching those who lack ability. Then the people will respect, trust, and eagerly pursue goodness.

Someone asked Confucius why he did not hold government office. He replied that the Shu-ching, an ancient book, says that filial piety and brotherly duty, shown within the family, are already a way of governing. So, in his view, holding an official post is not required for a person to take part in government.

A person without truthfulness cannot function in life, the Master says. He compares this to carriages: a large cart needs its yoke bar for the oxen, and a small one needs its fittings for the horses, and without them neither can move.

Zi Zhang asked whether the affairs of the next ten generations could be known in advance. Confucius replied that each dynasty copied the rules of the one before it, adding or removing parts, so the changes can be traced. By this reasoning, even a dynasty a hundred generations later could be known from what came before.
To honour a spirit that is not one's own is flattery, and to see what is right without doing it is a lack of courage.

Confucius criticized the head of the Chi family for using eight rows of dancers, a privilege reserved for the ruler, in his own household. He asked what other improper acts such a man would be willing to commit, since he could do this.

The three families sang the Yung ode while the sacrifice vessels were being cleared away, a use Confucius criticizes. He asks what the lines about princes assisting the Son of Heaven could possibly mean in the hall of these three families, who were not royal. The point is that the lines describe the ruler's court, so using them there is out of place.
A person who lacks inner goodness, the virtues proper to being human, has no real use for ritual forms or for music. Ritual and music only mean something when they come from genuine humaneness.

Lin Fang asks which matters most in ceremonies. Confucius replies that in festive rites, simplicity is better than excess, and in mourning, genuine grief is better than careful attention to every formal detail.

Confucius observes that the uncivilized tribes of the east and north still have their rulers, while the states of China, though far more cultured, are now without them. He is pointing to a contrast between the barbarians' order and the disorder of his own land.

Confucius asks his disciple Zan Yu whether he can stop the head of the Ji family from performing a sacrifice on Mount Tai, a rite reserved for rulers. When Zan Yu says he cannot, Confucius implies that the mountain spirit would be less discerning than Lin Fang, a man who asked about the basis of ritual.

A person of virtue does not quarrel. If there must be contest, the Master says it is found in archery, and even there the gentleman bows politely to his rivals before and after the contest, and the loser drinks the penalty cup. Even while competing, he remains a true gentleman.

Zixia asks what a poem line means: a plain background comes first, and the colours are added afterward. Confucius replies that painting colours on follows the preparing of the plain ground. Zixia then concludes that ritual comes after inner qualities, and Confucius praises him for understanding, saying they can now discuss the odes together.

Confucius says he could describe the ceremonies of the Xia and Shang (Yin) dynasties. But the states of Qi and Song cannot confirm his words, because they lack enough written records and learned men. If those records existed, he could use them to support what he says.

Confucius says that at the great sacrifice, once the libation (a ritual pouring of wine or liquid as an offering) has been poured out, he does not want to watch the rest of the ceremony. The passage gives no reason for this.

Someone asked Confucius what the great sacrifice meant. He said he did not know. He added that a person who truly understood it would find ruling the kingdom as easy as seeing something in his own palm, which he pointed to.

The Master honored the dead and the spirits by acting as if they were really present when he made offerings to them. He added that if he himself could not be present at a sacrifice, it was as though he had not made the offering at all.

Wang-sun Chia asked what a common saying meant: it is better to court the furnace than the south-west corner. Confucius replied that this was wrong, since a person who offends Heaven has no one left to pray to. The saying is rejected, and the reply points to Heaven as the higher power that matters most.
Confucius says that the Zhou dynasty had the benefit of seeing the two earlier dynasties, Xia and Shang, and so its rules are full and graceful. He says he follows the Zhou.

Confucius entered the grand temple and kept asking questions about everything there. Someone criticized him, saying that a man of his background could not really know proper ritual. Confucius replied that asking about everything is itself the proper ritual.
In archery, the main thing is not piercing the leather target, because people do not all have the same strength. This was the old way of doing it.

Zigong wanted to stop the custom of sacrificing a sheep at the monthly ceremony marking the start of each month. Confucius replied that Zigong cared about the sheep, while he himself cared about the ceremony. The point is that the ritual itself mattered more to him than the animal offered in it.

Confucius says that when a person serves his ruler by carefully following all the proper ritual rules, others regard it as flattery. "Propriety" here means correct ritual conduct and good manners, the set of formal rules Confucians valued.

A duke asks Confucius how a ruler should treat his officials and how officials should serve their ruler. Confucius answers that a ruler should employ officials according to the rules of proper conduct, and officials should serve the ruler with loyalty.
The Kwan Tsu is a poem from the Book of Songs. Confucius says its feelings stay in balance: its joy does not become wild, and its sorrow does not become harmful.

Duke Ai asked about the trees planted around the altars to the spirits of the land, and Tsai Wo gave the different dynasties' choices. Confucius replied that past actions should not be discussed, criticized, or blamed, since they cannot be changed.

Confucius says that Guan Zhong, a famous minister of the state of Qi, had a small mind. When asked whether he was stingy or knew proper ceremony, Confucius answers that Guan Zhong lived above his rank. He had a screen at his gate and a stand for cups, which only princes were allowed, so Confucius says he could not have known the rules of ritual.

The Master tells the chief music teacher of Lu how music should be played. All the parts should begin together, then stay in harmony while each stays distinct and the sound flows without break until the end.

A border warden at Yi asked to meet Confucius, and his followers brought him in. Afterwards he told them not to grieve over their master's loss of office. He said the kingdom had long lacked right principles, and that Heaven would use Confucius to awaken it, as a bell is struck with its wooden tongue.
Confucius judged two ancient music pieces. The Shao was both beautiful in sound and good in its moral spirit. The Wu was beautiful in sound but lacked the same moral goodness.

Confucius says that people in high positions who lack generosity, who perform rituals without respect, or who mourn without real grief are things he cannot bear to think about. He finds such behavior hard to look at or accept.

A neighborhood is good because of its virtuous manners, meaning good moral conduct among its people. So a man who chooses where to live without picking a place where such conduct is found is not acting wisely.
People without virtue cannot stay long in either hardship or ease. Those who are truly virtuous remain steady in virtue, and the wise seek it.
Only a truly virtuous person is able to love others or to hate them. In this view, a person who is not virtuous cannot love or hate in the right way.
If a person's will is fixed on virtue, that person will not do evil.

A person should seek wealth and honour only by proper means, and should not keep them if they come improperly. Poverty and low standing should be accepted if they cannot be avoided honestly. The true gentleman never departs from virtue, even briefly, whether in haste or in danger.

Confucius says he has rarely or never seen anyone truly devoted to virtue. Someone who loves virtue puts nothing above it, and someone who hates what is not virtuous keeps such things away from himself. He also claims that anyone who applies full effort to virtue for even one day will find their strength is never insufficient.

A man's faults tend to match the kind of people he belongs to, so each group has its own typical failings. Because of this, looking closely at someone's faults can show whether he is good: the faults of a virtuous person reveal that virtue.
A person who hears the Way, meaning the right way of living, in the morning could die that evening without regret. The point is that learning the Way matters more than how long one lives.

A scholar who is committed to truth but feels shame about poor clothing and food is not yet ready for serious discussion. The point is that caring more about comfort than about the Way (the moral path) shows the scholar is not yet worth talking with seriously.
A person of high moral character does not commit himself either for or against anything in advance. Instead, he simply follows whatever is right.

A person of high moral character focuses on virtue, while a petty person focuses on personal ease. The superior man attends to the penalties the law sets out, while the petty person attends to the favours he might gain.
Acting always with an eye to one's own gain will bring a great deal of complaint from others. The saying warns that a person who keeps pursuing personal advantage will be widely resented.

A ruler who can govern with the courtesy that proper ritual demands will have no real trouble doing so. A ruler who cannot govern in that way has no use for ritual at all. Ritual and good government, in this view, go together.
A person should not worry about lacking a position or being unknown. He should worry about becoming qualified for a position and about being worthy of recognition.

Confucius tells his disciple Shan that his teaching rests on one all-pervading unity. When the other disciples ask what this means, Zeng Shen explains that it is being true to one's own nature and showing care for others, and nothing more.

A person of high moral character keeps his mind focused on what is right. A petty or small-minded person keeps his mind focused on personal profit. "Superior man" and "mean man" refer to these two kinds of character rather than to social rank.
When we meet people of good character, we should aim to be like them. When we meet people of the opposite kind, we should look inward and check our own conduct.
A son who disagrees with his parents should advise them gently. If they do not accept his advice, he stays respectful and keeps his purpose, and if they punish him, he does not complain.
While a child's parents are alive, he should not travel far from home. If he must go away, he should always let them know exactly where he can be found.

A son who does not change his father's way for three years may be called filial, meaning dutiful and respectful to his parents. The sentence says nothing about the father's death, only about keeping his father's way over that time.
Parents' ages should always be kept in mind. Their years are a reason for joy, because they are still living, and for fear, because their remaining time is limited.

The ancient sages were slow to speak because they worried that their actions would fail to match their words. In other words, they held back from speaking so that they would not promise more than they could do.
A person of high moral character, in Confucius's view, wants to speak slowly and carefully, but to act with seriousness and sincerity. Words should be measured, while deeds should be earnest.
Virtue, or moral goodness, does not exist in isolation. Anyone who practises it will gain companions, people who share and support it.
Zi You says that when serving a ruler, too many warnings bring disgrace on the servant. Between friends, too many rebukes cause the friendship to grow distant.

Confucius says that Kung-ye Ch'ang would make a good husband, even though he was once jailed, because he had done no crime. So Confucius gave him his own daughter in marriage. He praises Nan Yung as a man who would always keep out of trouble, whether the state was well or badly governed, and gives him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
Confucius praises Zijian, a disciple, for his virtue. He adds that Zijian could only have gained such character because other good men lived in the state of Lu.
Zigong asked Confucius what he thought of him. Confucius replied that he was a utensil, and when asked which kind, said a jeweled vessel used in sacrifices.

Someone praised Yung as truly virtuous but said he was slow with words. Confucius replied that quick, clever talk is of little value, since those who meet people with it usually make themselves disliked. He said he did not know whether Yung was truly virtuous, but saw no reason for him to be quick with his tongue.
Confucius wanted his student Ch'i-tiao K'ai to take up a government post. The student said he did not yet feel sure enough of himself to do so. Confucius was pleased by this answer.

Confucius says his teaching is not getting anywhere, and he jokes that he might sail away on a raft, taking only Yu, his disciple, with him. When Zilu is pleased at this, Confucius says Yu loves daring more than he does and does not weigh matters carefully.

Confucius is asked whether three of his disciples, Zilu, Ran Qiu and Gongxi Hua, are perfectly virtuous. For each, he names a practical role they could fill, such as managing an army, governing a town, or receiving guests, but says he does not know whether they are perfectly virtuous.

Confucius asks his disciple Zigong whether he or Hui is the better student. Zigong says Hui understands everything from one point, while he himself understands only a second point after one. Confucius agrees that Zigong is not Hui's equal.

Confucius scolds his disciple Zai Yu (Tsai Yu) for sleeping in the daytime, saying he is like rotten wood or a dirty wall that cannot be worked. He then says he used to trust people's words, but now he judges them by their actions, and Yu taught him this change.
Confucius says he has never met a truly firm, unbending man. When someone names Shan Ch'ang, he replies that Ch'ang is ruled by his desires, so he cannot be called firm.

Zigong says he wishes not to do to others what he does not want done to himself. Confucius replies that Zigong has not yet reached this level. The exchange suggests that the rule is a goal Zigong has not yet achieved.

Zigong, a disciple of Confucius, says that the Master's teachings on conduct and everyday matters can be heard and understood. His talk about human nature and the Way of Heaven, however, cannot be heard in the same way, meaning it was rarely given to his students.

Zilu, a disciple of Confucius, would not take in new teachings while he still had not put the earlier ones into practice. He was so eager to avoid having more to live up to that he feared hearing something new.

Zigong asks why Kong Wen was given the posthumous title "Wen," meaning cultured or civil. Confucius answers that he was diligent and loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those beneath him for knowledge.

Confucius praises Tsze-ch'an, a statesman of the state of Zheng, as having four qualities of a superior man (a person of high moral character). He was humble in his own conduct, respectful toward his superiors, kind in caring for the people, and just in governing them.
Yan Pingzhong was good at keeping up friendships. Even when a friend had known him for a long time, he still treated that friend with the same respect he had shown at the start.

Confucius criticizes Zang Wen, a official of the state of Lu, for keeping a large tortoise in a house decorated with carved hills on its pillar capitals and duckweed patterns on its beams. He asks what kind of wisdom that shows, implying it showed none.

Zi Zhang asks about Zi Wen, a minister who took office three times and showed no pleasure, and left office three times and showed no anger. He also briefed each new minister on how he had run the government. Confucius says he was loyal, but he will not call him perfectly virtuous.

Ch'an Wan, a nobleman, gave up his wealth and left three states because each one reminded him of the regicide-minded officer Ch'ui who had murdered his prince. Confucius calls him "pure" for refusing to serve wrongdoers, but he will not call him perfectly virtuous, since that would require more than this one act.

Chi Wan, a man of the state of Lu, thought carefully three times before acting. When Confucius heard this, he said that two thoughts would have been enough. The point is that thinking twice before acting is sufficient.

Ning Wu was wise when his state was well governed and pretended to be foolish when it was in chaos. The Master says others could match his wisdom, but few could match the skill of his feigned foolishness in hard times. Ning Wu was a minister of the state of Wei.

Confucius, while in the state of Ch'an, says he wants to go home to his students. He says they are eager and hasty, and though they are talented, they do not yet know how to restrain and shape themselves.
Bo-yi and Shu-qi did not hold on to the wrongs men had done them in the past. Because of this, few people held resentment against them.

Confucius asks who would call Wei-shang Kao upright. When a man asked him for vinegar, Kao did not have any, so he got it from a neighbor and passed it on as if it were his own. The point is that this small act of pretended generosity does not show true uprightness.

Confucius says that fine words, a smooth false manner, and too much outward respect are things he and Tso Ch'iu-ming both feel ashamed of. He also says the same of hiding resentment toward someone while acting friendly toward them.

Confucius asks his disciples to state their wishes. Zilu wants to share his horses and fine clothes with friends, even if they damage them. Yan Yuan wants to avoid boasting of his virtue or his achievements. Confucius says his own wish is to give rest to the old, be sincere with friends, and treat the young with care.
The Master laments that he has never met anyone who could see their own faults and blame themselves inwardly. For him, this is a sign that true self-examination is rare.
Confucius says that even in a small village of ten families, one person may be as honest and sincere as he is. But that person may not love learning as he does.

Confucius praises Yung (Zhonggong) as fit to rule. When Zhonggong asks about Zisang Boizi, a man who ignores small details, Confucius says he is acceptable. Zhonggong then argues that such easygoing conduct in government could be too lax if carried into practice. Confucius agrees that Yung's view is right.

Duke Ai asked which of Confucius's disciples loved learning. Confucius named Yan Hui, who loved learning, did not vent his anger on others, and did not repeat his mistakes. Yan Hui died young, and Confucius says he has not met anyone since who loves learning as he did.

The main point is that a person of good character should help those in real need rather than add to the wealth of those who already have plenty. When Zan asks for grain for a disciple's mother, Confucius gives a small amount, but when Yen asks for more, he refuses. He tells a disciple to share a large grant of grain with the poor in his district instead of keeping it.

Confucius says that a fine animal can still be used for sacrifice even if people do not want it, because the spirits will still accept it. The point is about Chung-kung, a disciple, whose merit is meant to be recognized despite a poor background. Chung-kung's father was considered of low status, so the image is that good qualities are not rejected because of their origin.
Hui, a disciple, could keep his mind free of anything against perfect virtue for three months at a time. Others, the Master says, manage this only for a few days or months at most.

Chi K'ang asked Confucius whether three of his disciples could serve as government officers. Confucius said yes for each one, naming a strength: decisiveness, intelligence, or wide ability. He saw no difficulty for any of them in holding office.

Min Tsze-ch'ien, a disciple of Confucius, is asked by the head of the Chi family to become governor of Pi. He tells the messenger to refuse politely, and says that if they come again with another invitation, he will leave and live across the river Wan rather than accept.

Confucius visits his sick disciple Po-niu and takes his hand through the window. He says the illness is killing him and calls it the decree of Heaven, lamenting that such a good man should suffer such a disease.

Confucius praises his disciple Hui for staying cheerful while living in deep poverty. Hui had only a basic meal and a poor home, hardships others could not have borne, yet he did not let them spoil his joy.

Ran Qiu says he does enjoy the Master's teachings but lacks the strength to follow them. The Master replies that people who lack strength stop halfway, while Ran Qiu is setting his own limit before he has tried.

Confucius tells his disciple Tsze-hsia to be a scholar in the way of the "superior man," a person of moral virtue, and not in the way of the "mean man," a petty or base person. Here "superior man" means a morally admirable person, and "mean man" means a morally small one.

Zi-yu, governor of Wu-ch'ang, is asked by Confucius whether he has any good men there. He names Tan-t'ai Mieh-ming, a man who never takes shortcuts and visits his office only on official business. The point is that Zi-yu judges his man by strict personal conduct and honesty.

Confucius praises Mang Chih-fan for not boasting. During a retreat, he was at the back of the army, and when they reached the gate, he claimed that he was not trying to be last, but that his horse would not go forward.

Confucius says that, in his own age, it is hard to get by without the smooth talk of T'o, a ritual official, and the good looks of Prince Chao of Sung. The remark is a joke about how much those two gifts were valued. Here the reader needs to know that "litanist" means a keeper of ritual prayers and "specious" means smooth and deceptive.

The Master asks why people do not follow the proper way, using the image of going out of a house. Since no one can leave a room except through the door, he is saying that people should naturally take the correct path in life, yet they refuse to.

A person with too much natural substance and too little polish seems rough and uncultured. A person with too much polish and too little substance seems like a mere clerk, all form and no real character. Only when the two are evenly balanced does one become a truly virtuous person.
Uprightness, or moral integrity, is what a person is born for. Someone who loses it and still stays alive owes that survival only to luck, not to anything they did.

Knowing the truth is not as good as loving it, and loving it is not as good as delighting in it. Each step is higher than the one before. The saying ranks three ways of relating to what is right, with full enjoyment at the top.

Confucius says that the highest teachings can be told to people of above-average ability, but not to those of below-average ability. The idea is that a teacher should match what he teaches to the student's capacity.
Wisdom means working hard at one's duties to other people and respecting spirits while keeping a distance from them. Perfect virtue means tackling the difficulty first and putting success second.
The wise person is compared to water: they enjoy it and are active and joyful. The virtuous person is compared to hills: they enjoy them, stay calm, and live long.

Confucius says that the state of Qi could become like the state of Lu with one change. Lu, in turn, could become a state where true principles prevailed with one change. The point is that Lu is closer to the ideal than Qi, and only one change separates each state from the next.
The Master remarks that a "cornered" vessel without corners is a strange thing, and he repeats the complaint to stress it. The saying is about a thing that no longer has the form its name implies.

A man asks whether a kind person would jump into a well if told someone was drowning there. Confucius replies that such a person can be led to the well, but will not be tricked into going down, and can be deceived but not fooled.

A person of high character who studies widely and also keeps himself within the rules of proper conduct will not go beyond what is right. "Superior man" means a morally admirable person, and "propriety" means correct ritual and manners.
Confucius visited Nan-tsze, a woman of the court of Wei. His disciple Tsze-lu was unhappy about this, so Confucius swore an oath: if he had done anything wrong, he asked Heaven to reject him.
Confucius says that the virtue of following the Constant Mean, the balanced middle way, is perfect. He adds that people have practised it rarely for a long time.

Zigong asks whether someone who gives wide benefits to the people and can help everyone would count as perfectly virtuous. Confucius replies that such a person would be more than virtuous, a sage, and that even the legendary rulers Yao and Shun were concerned with this. He adds that a person of perfect virtue helps others to succeed as he wishes to succeed himself, and judges others by what he finds in himself.

Confucius says he only passes on the teachings of the ancient sages and does not create new ones. He trusts and loves the ancients, and he compares himself to an old figure named P'ang, a man of long ago known for the same devotion.

The Master lists three things: quietly storing up knowledge, studying without ever feeling satisfied, and teaching others without tiring. He then asks which of these he can honestly claim as his own. He is modest about his own achievement.

Confucius names four things that worry him: failing to cultivate virtue, failing to talk through what one has learned, failing to act on righteousness once it is known, and failing to correct what is wrong. The passage is a list of personal faults he fears most.
When Confucius had no official duties to attend to, he was relaxed and appeared cheerful. "The Master" is the title his students gave him.
The Master says that he has grown very old and weak. He has not dreamed, as he used to, of the Duke of Zhou, a figure from the early Zhou dynasty whom he admired and wished to follow.

The Master urges four things: set your will on the right path, hold firmly to whatever good you have gained, practise complete virtue, and find rest and pleasure in the arts of good manners and culture.

Confucius says he has never turned away any student, even one who came with only the smallest gift. The "bundle of dried flesh" was a modest traditional payment for teaching. He means that he taught anyone who offered this much.

Confucius says he will not teach someone who is not eager to learn, nor help someone who is not trying to express their own thinking. If he shows one corner of a subject and the student cannot work out the other three, he will not repeat the lesson.
Confucius shows respect for mourning. When he ate beside someone in grief, he did not eat his fill. On a day he had wept for the dead, he did not sing.

Confucius says that serving in office when called, and withdrawing into private life when not, is a skill he and his disciple Yan Yuan share. When Zilu asks whom he would choose as a companion for leading an army, Confucius rejects a reckless man who fights tigers or crosses rivers without a boat. He prefers someone who acts carefully, plans well, and then carries the plans out.
Confucius says that he would take up even a humble job, such as a groom's, to gain wealth if success were certain. Since wealth is not certain to come, he will instead pursue what he loves.
The Master was most careful about three matters: fasting, war, and sickness. The passage lists these three things and says nothing about why he was careful.

Confucius heard the Shao, an ancient court music, while he was in the state of Qi. It was so moving that for three months he forgot the taste of meat. He said he had not imagined music could be so perfect.

Yan Yu asks whether Confucius supports the ruler of Wei. Zigong goes to ask Confucius about Bo Yi and Shu Qi, two ancient men who refused to take power. Confucius says they sought virtue and achieved it, so they had no regrets. Zigong then concludes that Confucius does not support the ruler.

Eating plain rice, drinking water, and sleeping with an arm as a pillow still brings joy, the speaker says. Wealth and rank gained by wrongdoing mean nothing to him; he regards them as a passing cloud.

Confucius says that if he had a few more years to live, he would spend fifty of them studying the Yi (the Book of Changes, an ancient divination text), and then he might be free of major faults. The short note that follows says he often talked about the Odes, the History, and the proper observance of ritual rules.

Confucius asks his disciple Zilu why he did not simply describe the Master to the Duke of Sheh as a person who loses himself in eager study, forgets his meals, forgets his worries in the joy of learning, and does not notice that he is growing old.
Confucius says he did not have knowledge from birth. He learned by studying the past and by searching earnestly for the wisdom of ancient times.

Confucius did not talk about four kinds of subject: strange or supernatural events, displays of physical strength, social disorder or rebellion, and gods or spirits. The line lists what he avoided discussing, rather than explaining why.
When Confucius walks with two other people, he can learn from either of them. He copies their good qualities and avoids their bad ones.

Confucius says that Heaven gave him his virtue, so a man named Huan Tui cannot harm him. Huan Tui was an official who had tried to kill Confucius. The point is that Confucius trusts his virtue, given by Heaven, to protect him.
Confucius tells his disciples that he hides nothing from them. He says everything he does is open to them, and that this openness is simply how he teaches.
The Master taught four subjects: learning and literature, moral conduct, devotion of the heart, and being true to one's word. "The Master" is the title his students gave Confucius.

Confucius says he has not met a sage or a good man, and would be content to meet someone with real talent and virtue, or someone steady and constant. He adds that people who pretend to have what they lack, to be full when empty, or to be at ease when hard-pressed, find it hard to stay constant.

Confucius fished with a line but not a net, and shot at birds in flight but not at ones perched and easy to hit. The point is that he took only what was fair and did not catch more than he needed or take unfair advantage.

Confucius says that some people act without understanding why they act, but he does not. For him, real knowledge comes from listening widely, choosing what is good and following it, and remembering much of what he sees. He calls this the second kind of knowledge.

Confucius received a young man from a town with a poor reputation. When his disciples doubted this, he said he accepts people who come to him cleanly, without judging or vouching for what they did before or will do afterward.
Virtue is not far away. The speaker says that when he wants to be good, goodness is right there, so it can be reached by simply choosing to pursue it.

Duke Chao of Lu was asked whether he knew proper ritual behavior. Confucius said he did. A minister then pointed out that the duke had married a woman of his own surname, which ritual forbade, so the minister questioned Confucius's view. When Confucius heard this, he said he was fortunate, since any mistakes he made would be noticed.
Confucius would ask a singer to repeat a song he sang well, and then join in singing it with him. The point shown is his enjoyment of good singing and his willingness to take part in it.

Confucius says he may be as good as others at learning, but he has not yet reached the point where a truly good person's conduct matches what he says he believes. In other words, he admits he still falls short of living out his own words.

Confucius says he does not count himself a sage or a person of perfect virtue. He says he only keeps striving toward that goal without tiring and teaches others without growing weary. His disciple Gongxi Hua replies that the students cannot match him in this.

When Confucius was very ill, his disciple Zilu asked to pray for him. Zilu quoted an old text that allows prayer to the spirits. Confucius replied that he had been praying for a long time already, so he did not need Zilu's prayer.
Going to excess in spending leads to disorder and rebellion against proper order, while stinginess leads to meanness. Of the two, the author says, meanness is the lesser fault.

A person of high moral character stays calm and content, while a petty or small-minded person is always anxious and troubled. The contrast is between inner peace in the first and constant worry in the second. "Superior man" means a person of good character, and "mean man" means a person of low character.

Confucius's manner is described as a balance of opposite qualities. He was gentle but still dignified, commanding but not harsh, and respectful but relaxed. Each quality is held together with its opposite, so neither one goes to excess.

T'ai-po, a figure from early Chinese history, is praised as having reached the highest level of virtue. He three times refused the throne, and because the people did not understand his reasons, they had no way to openly praise him.

Good qualities turn bad when they lack proper ritual conduct: respect becomes busy fussing, caution becomes timidity, boldness becomes disorder, and honesty becomes rudeness. The passage adds that rulers who fulfil their duties to family and keep old friends inspire ordinary people toward virtue and away from meanness.

Tseng, a disciple of Confucius, lies dying and asks his students to uncover his hands and feet so they can see them whole. He quotes a poem about walking carefully near danger, and says he now knows he has kept his body unharmed.

Tsang, a disciple of Confucius, is dying, and he tells a visitor that a dying man speaks good words, as a dying bird sings mournfully. He then names three things a man of high rank should mainly attend to: calm, non-violent bearing; a sincere facial expression; and careful, proper speech. Ritual vessel matters are left to specialist officers.

Tsang, a disciple of Confucius, says that he once had a friend who acted in a particular way. The friend was skilled and did not look down on those less able, asking them questions. He had much but acted as if he had little, counted himself empty though full, and did not argue when wronged.

Tseng, a disciple of Confucius, says that a man who can be trusted with a young prince, given authority over a small state, and who cannot be moved from his principles even in a great crisis, is indeed a superior man (a person of high moral character).

A scholar-official, according to Tsang, needs a broad mind and firm endurance. His task is heavy and his road is long, because he must carry the duty of perfect virtue all his life, until death ends it.
The Master says that the Odes (ancient poems) stir up the mind, the Rules of Propriety (proper ritual conduct) give a person firm character, and Music brings the final polish or refinement.
Ordinary people can be led to follow a way of acting, but they cannot be made to understand the reasons behind it.
Two kinds of people are likely to turn to rebellion. One is the bold person who resents being poor. The other is the person without virtue, when others push their dislike of him too far.
A man may have talents as great as those of the Duke of Chau, an early model of wisdom and skill, but if he is proud and stingy, those talents are not worth much attention.
Studying for three years without becoming good is rare, the Master says. In other words, a person who has kept at learning for that long is hard to find who has not also grown good.

A person of firm faith and love of learning, who holds to the right course even to death, will not enter an unstable state or stay in a state in disorder. He comes forward when good government prevails and withdraws when it does not. In a well-governed state, poverty is shameful; in a badly governed one, wealth and rank are shameful.
A person who holds no particular office should not make plans for how that office's duties are carried out. Outside a post, one should not take up its administration.

The Master praises the music at the start of the music master Chih's term of office. The closing piece, the Kwan Tsu, was splendid and filled the listeners' ears. Chih is a music official, and the Kwan Tsu is a piece of music.

Confucius says he cannot understand people who show a quality but lack its partner: those who are ardent but not upright, stupid but not attentive, or simple but not sincere. Each good trait needs its matching virtue to be real.
Learning should be pursued as if the goal is always just out of reach. A learner should also keep worrying about losing what has already been gained.

Shun and Yu, two early rulers of China, held power over the whole empire in a way that seemed to them of no importance. The Master admires this calm, unattached manner of ruling. Shun and Yu are legendary sage-kings in the Confucian tradition.

Confucius praises the ancient ruler Yao as the only ruler who matched Heaven in greatness. His virtue was so vast that people had no name for it, and his achievements and fine institutions were equally splendid.

Confucius says that able people are hard to find. King Wu boasted of ten capable ministers, but Confucius notes that one of the ten was a woman, so only nine were men. He adds that King Wan, Wu's father, served the Yin dynasty even though he held most of the empire, and praises the house of Chau for its virtue.
Confucius praises Yu, a legendary ruler, for living frugally himself while giving his best to honoring the spirits and to public works like ditches and irrigation channels. He finds no fault in him.
Confucius seldom talked about three things: profit, the decrees of Heaven, and perfect virtue. The passage simply records these as the topics he rarely raised, without giving his reasons.

A villager praised Confucius for having wide learning but no single skill that made him famous. Confucius replied that he would practise charioteering, a fairly humble skill, rather than archery, and so kept his choice modest and practical.

Confucius says that he follows the common custom of wearing a silk cap, which is cheaper than the linen cap the ritual rules require. But he refuses the common custom of bowing only after climbing the hall, because that is arrogant. He keeps bowing below the hall as the rules say, even though it goes against common practice.

The Master, meaning Confucius, was free of four faults: he did not jump to conclusions, did not decide things in advance without reason, was not stubborn, and was not self-centered. "Foregone conclusions" means judgments made before the facts are known.

Confucius was threatened while in the town of K'wang. He said that the moral tradition of the dead King Wen was carried on in him, and that Heaven would not let that tradition die. So, he reasoned, the people of K'wang could do nothing to harm him.

A high officer praises Confucius as a sage with many talents. Confucius replies that he gained his skills when he was poor and young, so they were humble matters. He adds that a superior man does not need such a variety of abilities.
Confucius says he does not really know much. Yet when even an ordinary person who seems empty-minded asks him a question, he answers it fully, explaining every part of it.

Confucius laments that the signs of a good age have not appeared. In his time, the phoenix-like fang bird did not come, and no diagram emerged from the river, so he says his hopes for the world are finished.
