Confucius would stand up when he saw a person in mourning clothes, a person in formal dress, or a blind person approaching, even if that person was younger than he was. If he had to walk past them, he would hurry.

Yan Yuan, a devoted disciple, describes how Confucius's teaching seemed to grow ever higher, firmer and more elusive the harder he tried to grasp it. Still, the Master guided him step by step, broadening his learning and teaching him proper conduct, though he could never fully keep up.

Confucius, gravely ill, rebukes his disciple Zilu for wanting them to act as his ministers. He says that pretending to have ministers would deceive no one but Heaven, and he would rather die among his disciples than among pretend officials, even without a grand funeral.
Zigong asks whether a beautiful gem should be kept locked away or sold for a good price. Confucius answers that it should be sold, but that he would wait until a buyer offers the right price.

Confucius says he would be willing to live among the nine wild tribes of the east. When someone objects that these people are rude, he answers that a superior man living among them would remove any rudeness.

Confucius says that after he came back from the state of Wei to his home state of Lu, the music was put in order. The songs from the court and the ceremonial hymns each returned to their correct place.

Confucius asks which of these duties he manages to fulfil: serving high officials and nobles abroad, serving his father and elder brothers at home, doing his utmost in funeral duties, and not being overcome by wine. He does not claim to have fully met any of them.
Standing by a stream, the teacher observes that the water flows on like this, never stopping, day or night. The words suggest that time keeps moving in the same way, without pause.

Confucius says he has never met anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty or good looks. He is pointing out how rarely people give moral goodness the same eager devotion they give to what is attractive.

Learning is like building a mound of earth. If you stop just one basket short of finishing, the failure to finish is your own doing. If you keep adding basket after basket, even small amounts, the progress is also your own doing.
Confucius praises his disciple Hui for never growing weary when the teacher explains something to him. In the Analects, this is a remark about Hui's eagerness to learn.
Confucius praises his student Yan Yuan for steady improvement. He says he always saw Yan Yuan moving forward and never saw him stop getting better.
Some plants sprout but never flower, and some flower but never bear fruit. The saying uses these cases to point to something that can fail to reach its full development.

Young people deserve respect, because their future may match or surpass the present of their elders. But if a person reaches forty or fifty without having become known for anything, then he no longer deserves that respect.

Stern warnings and gentle advice are only worth something when they change how a person actually behaves. A person who agrees with such words but does not change their conduct or pursue their aim cannot be helped.
Confucius gives three rules for a good life: keep loyalty and sincerity at the center, choose friends who are your equals in character, and be willing to give up your faults when you find them.

A large army's commander can be seized by force, but a person's will cannot be taken away, even if that person is an ordinary man. The point is that a person's inner resolve is beyond the reach of an outside power.

Confucius praises a disciple named Yu, who stood calmly among rich men while wearing shabby clothes, feeling no shame. He also quotes an old poem about not disliking others or wanting what they have. When his disciple Zilu kept repeating those lines, Confucius replied that they alone do not make someone truly excellent.

When cold weather comes, the pine and the cypress are the last trees to lose their leaves, and this shows which plants keep their green longest. The saying uses this natural fact to point to a quality that shows only in hard times.

The wise are not confused, the virtuous do not worry, and the bold are not afraid. Each quality removes the feeling that goes with a lack of it: knowledge clears away doubt, goodness clears away anxiety, and courage clears away fear.

Some people can study alongside us but cannot follow us to fundamental principles. Others can reach principles with us yet cannot stand firm in them, and others can stand firm but cannot weigh changing circumstances as we do.

The poem describes flowers swaying in the wind and a speaker longing for someone far away, who says the distance is too great to visit. Confucius replies that the distance is not real: the problem is that the speaker has not really thought of the other person. If the thought were there, the distance would not matter.

Confucius acts differently depending on the setting. At home in his village he seems plain and unassuming, and hardly able to speak. In the ancestral temple or at court he speaks fully and carefully. At court he talks frankly to junior officials, politely and exactly to senior ones, and with respectful, dignified unease when the ruler is present.

This describes how a court officer behaved when the ruler called on him to receive a visiting guest. He showed great care and formal correctness in every movement, and once the guest had left, he reported to the ruler that the guest was no longer looking back.

Confucius shows how he behaved with great respect at the ruler's palace. He bowed low at the gate, avoided standing in the middle of the entrance or stepping on the threshold, and became visibly reverent when passing the empty place of the prince.

Confucius describes how he behaved when entering the ruler's audience hall: very careful and respectful, holding his breath and bending his body. After leaving the hall, he relaxed and looked satisfied, and when back at his own place he still seemed respectfully uneasy.

The passage describes how a court official behaved while carrying his ruler's scepter on a formal mission abroad. He held it low and carefully, looked anxious, and walked cautiously. When presenting gifts he looked calm, and in a private audience he looked pleased.

The passage describes how the superior man (the ideal gentleman in Confucian thought) dressed. He avoided certain colours, such as deep purple and reddish tones, even at home. He also matched the colour of his outer robe to the fur worn underneath it, and he dressed in ways that were practical and orderly.

Confucius describes how he dressed in different situations. At home he wore warm fur, and after mourning he wore full ceremonial belt ornaments. He avoided lamb's fur and a black cap when visiting someone in mourning, and on the first day of the month he wore formal court robes to attend the ruler.
When preparing for a fast, Confucius kept his clothes clean and made of linen. He also changed his usual food and the place where he normally sat in his room.

Confucius was particular about his food. He would eat only rice and meat that were fresh, properly cooked, correctly cut, and served with the right sauce. He refused food that was spoiled, discoloured, badly flavoured, or out of season.

Confucius ate moderately and carefully. He did not eat much meat in proportion to his rice, and he set no fixed limit on wine but never let it confuse him. He avoided store-bought wine and dried meat, always had ginger with his food, and ate little.

Confucius describes his own rules for eating and sacrifice. He does not keep sacrificial meat overnight or, for family rites, beyond three days, because it would spoil. At meals he does not talk, and in bed he does not speak. Even plain food gets a small offering made with solemn respect.
The passage describes a rule of good manners: the sage would not sit on a mat that was not laid out straight. It shows that he cared about proper order and care in small matters.

Confucius shows how he behaves at village customs. When the villagers drink together, he leaves right after the elders carrying staffs go out. When they perform rites to drive away evil influences, he puts on his court robes and stands on the eastern steps, the place of honor in a house.

Confucius shows careful good manners in two situations. When he sent greetings to someone in another state, he bowed twice as he saw the messenger off. When Chi K'ang sent him medicine, he accepted it respectfully but said he did not know its effects, so he would not take it.
When the stable caught fire while he was at court, the man returning home first asked whether anyone had been hurt. He did not ask about the horses.

Confucius describes how he behaved toward his ruler, the prince, in many small matters. He treated each gift with the respect due to it: he tasted cooked meat before passing it on, offered raw meat to his ancestors, and kept a live animal alive. When the prince summoned him, he went at once without waiting for his carriage.
Confucius, on entering the ancestral temple of his home state, asked about every detail of the ritual. The point is that he did not assume he already knew the proper ways, and he checked each step.

Confucius would bury a dead friend himself if the friend had no relatives able to arrange the funeral. He did not bow to a friend's gift, even a carriage and horses, but he did bow to a gift of meat from a sacrifice.

Confucius describes how he behaved in everyday situations. He showed respect and strong feeling in small, specific ways: he changed his expression and bowed to people in mourning, to those in formal dress, and to the blind. He also reacted with caution to abundant food and to sudden thunder or wind.

Before getting into his carriage, the speaker stood upright and held the cord. Once inside, he did not turn his head fully around, speak in a hurry, or gesture with his hands. These are the quiet, careful manners he kept when riding.

Confucius sees a hen pheasant on a hill bridge and remarks that it is at the right time, meaning it is choosing the right moment to act. When Zilu (Tsze-lu), one of his disciples, moves toward it, the bird circles, smells the air three times, and then flies off. The meaning is unclear, but the bird seems to sense danger and leaves.

Confucius says that people of earlier times were called rustics in ceremonies and music, while later people are seen as refined in them. Still, when he needs to use these rites and music himself, he follows the earlier people.

Confucius says that his followers who were with him during hard times in the states of Ch'en and Ts'ai are no longer around to join his school. He then names his best disciples by their strengths: Yen Yuan, Min Tsze-ch'ien and others for virtue, Tsai Wo and Tsze-kung for speech, Zan Yu and Chi Lu for administration, and Tsze-yu and Tsze-hsia for learning.

Confucius says that his student Hui does not really help him, because Hui takes pleasure in everything Confucius says. The remark is a mild complaint that Hui simply agrees rather than questioning or adding to his teaching.

Confucius praises Min Tsze-ch'ien for being devoted to his parents. Other people speak of him in no way that differs from what his parents and brothers say, so his family's account of him is confirmed by everyone else.

Nan Yung often recited a poem about how a flaw in a white jade tablet can be polished away, but a flaw in speech cannot. Confucius took this as a sign of his careful speech and gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
Chi K'ang asked which of Confucius's students loved learning. Confucius named Yen Hui, who loved learning but died young, and said that no one since has loved learning in the same way.

Yen Yuan, Confucius's favorite disciple, had died, and his father asked Confucius for his carriage to buy an outer coffin for the son. Confucius refused. He said that when his own son Li died, he had only an inner coffin, and he would not walk on foot to get a better one, because as a senior officer he could not go on foot.

Yan Yuan, the Master's favorite disciple, has died. The Master cries out twice that Heaven is destroying him, expressing grief at the loss. In this line, "Heaven" refers to the heavenly power that the old Chinese tradition believed governed events.

Confucius grieved greatly when his disciple Yan Yuan died. His followers told him his sorrow was too much, but he replied that if he could not mourn this man so deeply, he did not know who he should mourn for.

When Yen Yuan, Confucius's favorite disciple, died, his students gave him a grand funeral against Confucius's wishes. Confucius said he had not been able to treat Yen Yuan as a son, and blamed the students for the grand burial.

Confucius tells his disciple Chi Lu that he should first learn to serve the living and understand life before asking about serving the spirits of the dead or about death. The point is that human duties in this life come before questions about what lies beyond it.

Confucius watches four disciples standing near him, each with a different manner, and is pleased by them. He then says of Tsze-lu, whose name here is given as Yu, that he will not die a natural death, meaning he will die violently.

Some people in the state of Lu wanted to tear down and rebuild the Long Treasury. Min Tsze-ch'ien suggested simply repairing it in its old style instead. Confucius praised Min for speaking rarely but always hitting the point.

Confucius asks why Zilu, a disciple, plays the lute in his house, since that music is not suited to it. The other disciples then stop respecting Zilu. Confucius replies that Zilu has reached the main hall of learning but has not yet entered the inner rooms.

Tsze-kung asks whether Shih or Shang is the better student. Confucius says Shih goes too far past the right middle way and Shang does not reach it. Confucius then holds that going too far is as much a fault as falling short.

Confucius criticizes his disciple Ch'iu for helping the head of the Chi family collect taxes, which made the already wealthy family richer still. He says Ch'iu is no true follower of his and tells his other students to publicly denounce him. The Chi family was a powerful clan in the state of Lu, and the Duke of Chou was a historical figure of great wealth and rank.

Confucius gives four short judgments on his disciples: Ch'ai (Gaozi) is simple, meaning earnest but plain; Shan (Zizhang) is dull, meaning he lacks some quickness; Shih (Zizhang's rival, Zishi) is specious, meaning showy; and Yu (Zilu) is coarse, meaning rough.

Confucius praises his disciple Hui as nearly perfect in virtue, though Hui is often poor. He says Zi Gong (Ts'ze) does not accept Heaven's decrees passively and grows rich by trade, yet his judgments are often right.

Zichang asked what makes a good man. Confucius replied that such a man does not simply follow in others' footsteps, yet he also does not reach the full depth of the sage's understanding. The saying describes a person who is good but has not yet become a sage.
Confucius asks whether a man who seems solid and sincere in his speech should be called a good man. He wonders if such a person is truly superior, or whether his seriousness is only outward show.

Two students asked the same question: should they act at once on what they had just heard? Confucius gave opposite answers. To Zilu he said that family elders must first be consulted, so he should not act at once. To Ran Qiu he said to act at once.

Gongxi Hua asks why Confucius gave opposite answers to two disciples who asked the same question: whether to act at once on what they had learned. Confucius explains that he adjusted each answer to the man: he urged Ran Qiu, who was shy and slow, to act, and held back Zilu, who had too much energy, by pointing to his duties to his father and elder brothers.

Confucius was frightened while surrounded at K'wang, and his disciple Yen Yuan (Hui) had fallen behind. When they met again, Confucius said he had thought Hui was dead. Hui answered that, as long as his teacher lived, he would not presume to die.

Confucius says that Yu and Ch'iu are only ordinary ministers, not great ones. A great minister serves his ruler only while the ruler acts rightly, and leaves office when he cannot. Asked whether Yu and Ch'iu would always obey their chief, he says no: they would refuse to join a murder of a father or a ruler.

Zilu had Zigao appointed governor of Bi, though Zigao was not yet ready for the post. Confucius said this would harm the young man. Zilu replied that serving people and the gods of the land and grain was itself a form of learning, so books were not needed. Confucius answered that he disliked such smooth talkers who excuse skipping study.

Confucius asks his four students what they would do if a ruler recognised their abilities. Zilu answers first, describing a large state squeezed between powerful neighbours and attacked by armies, and says he would set it in order.

Confucius asks two disciples what they would do if given charge of a state. Zilu (Tzu-lu) promises to make the people brave and able to follow right conduct within three years, and Confucius smiles at him. Ranyou (Ch'iu) promises only to bring plenty to the people in that time.

Confucius asks his disciples what they would like to do. One says he would wish to learn ritual and music, and to serve as a small assistant at ancestral ceremonies and court audiences. The passage then turns to the last disciple, Tien, whose answer is not given here.

Tien, one of Confucius' students, sets aside his lute and says his wishes differ from those of the other three students. Asked to speak them, he describes an outing in late spring: bathing in a river, enjoying the breeze at a ceremonial altar for rain, and walking home singing with a small group of young men and boys.

Confucius sighs and says he approves of Tien, who had been talking with three disciples. When asked about the others' words, he says each simply stated his own wishes. He smiles at Yu because Yu spoke of governing a state without humility, which Confucius thinks is wrong, since governing requires proper ritual conduct.

Confucius is asked whether Ch'ih, one of his disciples, wanted a small territory that was not a full state. He says Ch'ih's ambition was to hold a state, because only princes handle ancestral temple rites and audiences with the ruler. Even as a minor assistant in such rites, Ch'ih would be too grand for a lesser role.

Yan Yuan asks how to reach perfect virtue. Confucius says it means overcoming the self and returning to propriety, the proper observance of social rites, and that it depends on the person himself. He gives four rules: look, listen, speak and move only in accordance with propriety.

Confucius defines perfect virtue as treating everyone with the respect due to an honored guest, handling public duties with the care of a solemn ceremony, and not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself. Doing this means no one complains about you, at home or in the wider community.

Sze-ma Niu asks what perfect virtue is, and Confucius answers that a truly virtuous person is careful and slow in speech. When Niu asks whether that is all it means, Confucius replies that someone who finds action difficult will naturally speak carefully and slowly.

A superior man, a person of high moral character, has no anxiety or fear. When Niu asks whether that alone makes him superior, Confucius replies that if a person examines himself inwardly and finds no wrong, there is nothing to worry about or fear.

Sze-ma Niu worries that he has no brothers, while others do. Tsze-hsia replies that life, death, wealth and rank are fixed by Heaven, so a person should instead act respectfully and properly toward others, and then all people within the seas will be like brothers to him.

Confucius says that a person is intelligent, or even far-seeing, when slander that slowly seeps in and sudden alarming accusations both fail to affect him. The point is that he cannot be swayed by either kind of false talk.

Confucius says a ruler needs three things: enough food, enough weapons, and the trust of the people. When forced to give up one, he would drop weapons first and food second. Without the people's trust, he says, a state cannot survive, even if people still have food.

Chi Tsze-ch'ang argues that a gentleman needs only inner substance, not outward refinement. Tsze-kung replies that substance and refinement are equally necessary, comparing it to tiger and leopard hides, which are valued only for their markings, and dog or goat hides, which are not.

Duke Ai asked how to meet a shortfall in revenue during a bad harvest. His adviser suggested taxing the people at a lower rate, and when the duke objected that even the old rate fell short, the adviser argued that a ruler cannot prosper while his people suffer. Prosperity and hardship are shared between ruler and people.

Confucius says that virtue is raised by holding to loyalty and sincerity and always moving toward what is right. He gives delusion as an example: loving someone and wanting them to live, then hating them and wanting them to die, so that one's wishes swing back and forth without reason.

Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius how to govern. Confucius said good government means each person acts in his proper role: the ruler as ruler, the minister as minister, the father as father, the son as son. The duke replied that if these roles fail, he could not enjoy his wealth.

Confucius praises Yu for being able to settle lawsuits with only a few words, because others trust his judgment. He also notes that Zilu was quick to keep his word, never delaying a promise overnight.
The Master says that when he judges lawsuits, he does it no better than anyone else. The real goal, he says, is to make sure the people have no lawsuits to bring.

Asked by a disciple named Zizhang about government, Confucius says that governing means keeping its affairs in mind without growing tired of them, and carrying them out steadily without changing course.
Broad study of all kinds of learning, combined with holding oneself within the rules of proper conduct (li), will keep a person from straying from what is right.
The superior man, meaning the morally excellent person, helps others develop their good qualities and does not dwell on their faults. The mean man, meaning the petty or base person, does the reverse.

Chi K'ang, a noble official, asked Confucius how to govern. Confucius said that governing means setting things right. If a ruler leads the people by being upright himself, nobody will dare to act wrongly.

Chi K'ang, a ruler troubled by thieves in his state, asked Confucius how to stop them. Confucius replied that if the ruler himself were not greedy, people would not steal, even if he paid them to stop.

Chi K'ang asks whether killing wrongdoers would help good government. Confucius replies that killing is unnecessary. If the ruler wants good things, the people will become good, just as grass bends when the wind blows over it.

Confucius contrasts fame with true distinction. Being well known across the state or clan is only notoriety, he says. A truly distinguished man is solid and straightforward, loves righteousness, and judges others carefully by their words and their faces.

Confucius contrasts two kinds of men. The first is truly humble and so becomes respected in his country and clan. The second only pretends to be virtuous, acts against that show, and feels no doubt about himself; such a man is only famous, not respected.

Fan Ch'ih asks how to raise virtue, correct hidden wrongs, and recognize confusion. Confucius answers that virtue grows when a person puts duty first and worries about results second. Wrongs are corrected by blaming oneself, not others. Anger that risks one's own life and one's parents' lives is a sign of confusion.

Fan Ch'ih asks Confucius what benevolence and knowledge are. Confucius says benevolence is loving all people and knowledge is knowing all people. When Fan Ch'ih does not follow, Confucius adds that choosing upright people and setting aside crooked ones can make the crooked become upright.

Zi Xia answers a question about a saying: when a ruler promotes the upright, the crooked are made upright too. He gives two examples. Shun chose Gao Yao and T'ang chose I Yin, and after that the people without virtue disappeared.
Asked about friendship, Confucius says to advise a friend sincerely and guide him with skill. If the friend will not accept this advice, stop trying, so that you do not bring shame on yourself.
A follower of Confucius named Tsang says that a noble person uses learning and the arts to bring people together. Through these friendships, he improves his own moral character.
Asked how to govern, the Master said to lead the people by example and to work hard at their affairs. When his student asked for more, he said never to tire of these things.

Confucius advises a minister on government: use your officers, overlook small faults, and promote people of virtue and ability. When the minister asks how to recognise such people, Confucius says to promote those you already know, since others will bring forward the people you do not.

Confucius says the first task in government is to "rectify names", meaning to make names match what things really are. His student Zilu doubts this is needed. Confucius replies that when names are wrong, speech does not fit reality, and then affairs cannot succeed.

Confucius says that if affairs fail, rites and music decline, and then punishments are unfair, so people do not know how to act. For this reason, a gentleman makes sure his names for things are correct and that his words match his actions.

Fan Ch'ih asked Confucius to teach him farming and gardening, and Confucius said older farmers and gardeners knew more. After Fan left, Confucius said that a ruler who loves propriety, righteousness and good faith will be obeyed by his people, who will come to him freely. Such a ruler does not need to know farming.

Knowing the three hundred odes by heart is of little use, the Master says, if a man cannot handle a government post or answer for himself when sent on a mission. Learning counts for nothing without the ability to act in practical affairs.
A ruler who behaves well does not need to give commands, because his government works on its own. A ruler who behaves badly may give orders, but people will not obey them.

Confucius says that the rulers of the states of Lu and Wei are alike in their faults. Lu and Wei were neighboring small states in ancient China, and the saying is a short remark that they resemble each other. The passage gives no further detail.

Confucius praised Ching, a member of a noble family, for knowing how to manage a household's money. Ching's attitude grew with his wealth: at first he was pleased to have a small collection, then pleased it was complete, then pleased it was admirable.

Confucius, travelling to the state of Wei, remarks on how many people are there. His disciple Ran Qiu asks what should be done next, and Confucius answers in order: first make the people prosperous, then teach them.
Confucius says that if one of the rulers would hire him, he could achieve something significant within a year. Within three years, he says, he could bring the government to a complete state of order.
Confucius says that if good people governed a country for a hundred years in a row, they could reform even violent wrongdoers and end the use of the death penalty. He agrees that this saying is true.

A true king would need a full generation to bring about good government, and only after that would virtue become widespread. The saying suggests that moral change is slow, even when a good ruler takes power.
A minister who behaves correctly will have no trouble helping to govern. A minister who cannot correct his own conduct has no right to try to correct others.

Zan comes back late from the court and says it was government business. Confucius doubts this and says it must have been family affairs. He reasons that if it had been government business, he would have been consulted, even though he no longer holds office.

Duke Ting asks Confucius for one sentence that could make a state prosperous. Confucius says no single sentence does that, but offers one: being a ruler is hard, and a ruler who understands this might bring prosperity. Asked for a sentence that could ruin a state, he replies that a ruler who thinks being a ruler is easy, with no one to check him, could bring ruin.

Confucius says that one sentence cannot decide everything, but he points to a saying: a ruler who enjoys having no one oppose him. He argues that if the ruler's words are good, no opposition is fine, but if they are bad, unopposed rule could ruin the country.

Good government, in this view, is shown when people nearby are content and people far away are drawn to come and live under it. The Duke of Sheh is the ruler who asked the question, and the Master is Confucius.

Zixia, who was governor of a small town, asked how to govern. Confucius advised him not to rush things or chase small gains. Wanting quick results stops work from being done well, and focusing on small advantages stops large tasks from being completed.

The Duke of Sheh praised a man who would testify against his own father for stealing a sheep. Confucius disagreed: in his view, true uprightness means a father hides his son's wrongdoing and a son hides his father's. The loyalty of family comes first.

Fan Ch'ih asks what perfect virtue is. Confucius replies that a person should be serious and composed when alone, careful and respectful in their work, and sincere in dealings with others. These qualities must be kept even among uncivilized peoples.

Zigong asks what makes a man worthy of the title "officer." Confucius replies that he must keep a sense of shame in his own conduct and must not disgrace his ruler's commission when sent on a mission. For the next rank, he names a man whose relatives call him filial and whose neighbours call him respectful toward elders.

Confucius describes a lower rank of people. Those who keep their word and follow through on their actions are called obstinate little men, though they may still reach the next higher class. Asked about present-day officials, he dismisses them as mere containers, not worth considering.

Confucius says that since he cannot find people who follow the middle way, he will teach those who are either eager or carefully cautious. The eager will go forward and grasp the truth, and the cautious will hold back from doing wrong.

Confucius quotes a southern saying that a man without steady character cannot be a wizard or a doctor, and he approves of it. He adds that someone inconsistent in virtue will meet disgrace. He says this happens only because such a person ignores the divining, meaning the reading of the omens or signs.

A person of good character is friendly without flattering others. A petty or base person flatters others but is not truly friendly. "Superior man" and "mean man" refer to moral character, not social rank.
Being loved or hated by everyone in one's neighborhood does not, on its own, show whether a person is good or bad. Confucius says the best case is when good people love a man and bad people hate him.

A superior man is hard to please by improper means but fair in assigning work, matching tasks to each person's ability. A mean, or petty, man is easily pleased even by improper means, yet he demands that everyone be able to do everything.

A person of good character is calm and dignified without being arrogant. A petty person is arrogant but lacks that calm dignity. The contrast is between being at ease with oneself and being proud without real composure.
Qualities of character that are firm, enduring, simple, and modest are close to being fully virtuous. Someone who has these traits is not yet perfect in virtue, but is near to it.

A disciple asks what qualities make a man worthy of the name "scholar." The teacher answers that such a man is earnest and urgent with his friends, and mild or bland with his brothers and close relatives.
A good teacher who trains the people for seven years prepares them to be sent to war. The point is that after such training, ordinary people can be used as soldiers.
Sending people to war without first training them in what they need to know is, in effect, abandoning them. The saying means that an untrained army is lost before the fighting begins.
Hsien asks what counts as shameful. The Master answers that it is shameful to think only of one's salary, whether the state is well governed or badly governed.

A student proposes that holding back four faults (wanting to be above others, boasting, resentment, and greed) counts as perfect virtue. Confucius agrees that this is a hard thing to achieve, but he does not accept that it amounts to perfect virtue.

A scholar who is fond of ease and comfort does not deserve to be called a scholar. The point is that a person who seeks personal comfort above all else does not meet the standard of a true learned person.
In a well-governed state, a person may speak and act boldly and openly. In a badly governed state, a person may still act boldly, but should speak more carefully.
A person of virtue will always speak well, but a person who speaks well is not always virtuous. Likewise, a person of principle is always brave, but a brave person is not always principled.

Nan-kung Kwo notes that archery skill and great physical strength did not keep Ao and others alive, while Yu and Chi, who worked the fields, gained the kingdom. Confucius says nothing to him, but after he leaves, praises him as a superior man who values virtue.
A superior man may fail to be virtuous, but a petty or mean man is never virtuous. In other words, a person of low character cannot also be truly good.

Real love and loyalty, the Master asks, always lead to some strictness and some teaching toward the one loved or served. The question form makes the point that the two cannot be separated: true care includes correction and instruction.

Confucius says that a government document was produced by four men, each doing one stage of the work. P'i Shan drafted it, Shi-shu reviewed its content, Tsze-yu polished the wording, and Tsze-ch'an gave it its final elegance. Each man's contribution was needed to finish the notice well.

Confucius is asked about three men of the past and gives a short opinion of each. He calls Tsze-ch'an kind, says little about Tsze-hsi beyond an exclamation, and praises Kwan Chung for a case where a man who lost his city to Kwan Chung accepted poverty without complaint.
Being poor without complaining is hard, while being rich without becoming proud is easy. The saying contrasts the two, and says the first is the harder of the two to achieve.

Confucius says that Meng Gongchuo is fit to serve as chief officer in the great families of Zhao and Wei, but not fit to be a senior minister in the small states of Teng or Xie. The point is that a man can be well suited to one role and unsuited to a higher one.

Zilu asks what makes a complete person. Confucius first lists the talents of several famous men, such as knowledge, freedom from greed, courage, varied skills, and knowledge of ritual and music. He then says that a complete person today needs only three things: to think of what is right when offered gain, to be ready to give up life when facing danger, and to keep old promises.

Confucius asks whether it is true that Kung-shu Wan never speaks, laughs, or takes gifts. His student Kung-ming Chia says the reports are exaggerated: Kung-shu Wan speaks, laughs, and takes only at the right times and in the right way, so people never tire of him. Confucius answers with doubt, asking whether that is really so with him.

Zang Wuzhong, the lord of Fang, asked the duke of Lu to name a successor for his family, holding Fang as a base to press his demand. Confucius says that although Zang did not use force against his ruler, he still did so in effect.
Confucius compares two rulers of old China. Duke Wen of Jin was clever and sly but not honest. Duke Huan of Qi was honest but not sly.

Zilu criticizes Guan Zhong, a minister who served Duke Huan of Qi, for not dying with his master's rival Prince Jiu, who was killed, as his fellow minister Shao Hu did. Confucius defends Guan Zhong. He says Guan Zhong helped Duke Huan gather the other states peacefully, not by war, and so brought great good to the realm.

Tzu-kung criticizes Kwan Chung for not dying with Duke Huan's murdered brother and then serving Huan as chief minister. Confucius defends him: Kwan Chung helped unite and order the kingdom, and its people still benefit, so his service outweighs a small personal loyalty like that of ordinary people who die unnoticed.

Hsien, a former family steward to Kung-shu Wan, went up to the prince's court together with Wan. When Confucius heard this, he said Hsien deserved to be called "Wan," meaning accomplished, a title the name of Wan carried. The remark praises Hsien for the act described.
Ch'i K'ang asks how Duke Ling of Wei keeps his state despite his bad conduct. Confucius replies that capable officers handle guests, the ancestral temple, and the army, so the state stays secure.
A person who speaks boldly, without humility, will have trouble making his words come true or be backed up by his actions. The point is that arrogant talk is hard to make good in practice.

Chan Ch'ang (Chen Heng) killed his ruler, Duke Jian of Qi. Confucius went to Duke Ai of Lu and asked him to punish the killer. The duke sent him to the heads of the three great families, but they refused to act. Confucius reported that he had done his duty as an official by bringing the matter forward.
Zilu asked how one should serve a ruler. Confucius answered that one should not deceive him, and should oppose him openly to his face when needed.
A person of high moral character moves toward what is higher, while a petty or base person moves toward what is lower. Each kind of person advances in the direction of their own character.
In the past, people studied to improve themselves. In the speaker's own time, he says, people study to win the approval of others.

Confucius praises a messenger sent by Chu Po-yu. The messenger reports that his master wants to have few faults but has not yet managed it. Confucius's remark, repeated twice, is an approving one that suggests the messenger spoke well and faithfully on his master's behalf.

The main point is that a superior man, meaning a person of high moral character, keeps his thoughts within his proper role. He does not let them wander beyond the duties and position that belong to him.
A person of high moral character speaks with modesty but acts beyond what he says. In other words, his deeds are greater than his words.

The Master says that a superior man (an ideal person of moral character) has three qualities: virtue frees him from anxiety, wisdom frees him from confusion, and courage frees him from fear. He adds that he himself does not match this. Zigong replies that the Master is describing himself.
Zigong often compared other people with one another. Confucius replied that Zigong must have reached a high level of excellence, but that he himself had no time for such comparisons.
Confucius says he will not worry when others fail to recognize him. He will worry instead about his own lack of ability.

A man who does not expect to be deceived or doubted, yet still notices deception or disbelief as soon as it happens, is described as a person of superior worth. The point is that he is alert in the moment without being suspicious beforehand.

Wei-shang Mau, a critic, asks Confucius why he keeps moving from place to place, and suggests he is a smooth-talking persuader. Confucius denies being a persuader and says he dislikes stubbornness, which is why he keeps trying to change minds.
A "ch'i" is a name for a fine horse. The Master says the horse earns this name not for its strength but for its other good qualities.
Asked whether injury should be repaid with kindness, Confucius replies by asking what, then, would repay kindness. His answer is that injury should be repaid with justice, and kindness with kindness.

Confucius laments that no one understands him. When his disciple Zigong asks what he means, he says he does not blame Heaven or complain about people. He works at ordinary learning while his understanding reaches higher, and only Heaven knows him.

Confucius hears that a man named Kung-po Liao has slandered his disciple Tsze-lu, and that another disciple offers to have Liao killed. Confucius replies that whether his teaching succeeds or fails is decided by fate, so Liao cannot change that.

Men of worth, according to the Master, withdraw from public life in different ways. Some leave the world altogether, some leave a particular state, some leave because of rude looks, and some because of contradictory speech.

The passage is a short remark that refers back to people named earlier in the chapter, saying there were seven of them who had done a particular thing. The passage does not name the act, so its exact meaning depends on the surrounding text.

A gatekeeper at Shih-man asks Tsze-lu, a disciple of Confucius, where he comes from. When Tsze-lu says he comes from Mr. K'ung (Confucius), the gatekeeper remarks that this is the man who knows the times cannot be set right, yet keeps trying to act in them.

A man with a straw basket hears Confucius playing a stone chime and says the player must be full of purpose. He then criticizes that single-minded stubbornness and says that if no one notices you, you should give up seeking office. Confucius replies that the man is determined, but that his position is not hard to hold.

Zizhang asks why King Gaozong stayed silent for three years after his father's death. Confucius replies that this was not special to Gaozong, since in ancient times, when a ruler died, the officials simply carried on their duties and took orders from the chief minister for that period.
When a ruler loves to follow the rules of propriety (proper ritual and good conduct), the people willingly answer when the ruler calls on them to serve.

Zilu asked Confucius what makes a superior man. Confucius said he cultivates himself with reverent care. When pressed, he said this is so he can bring peace to others, and finally to all the people, a goal even the legendary sage-rulers Yao and Shun were still concerned with.

Confucius rebukes Yuan Rang, a man who sat squatting when the Master approached. He says a person who is not respectful as a young man, achieves nothing worth remembering as an adult, and still lives on into old age is a nuisance to others. Then he strikes Yuan's shin with his staff.

Confucius is asked whether a young messenger in his service is making good progress. He replies that the boy only wants to look and act like an adult, sitting in adult seats and walking beside his elders. In Confucius's view, this means the boy is not really trying to learn; he simply wants to grow up fast.

Asked about military tactics, Confucius said he had only learned about ritual vessels, and he left Wei. Later, in Chen, his followers ran out of food and fell sick. When Zilu complained that a gentleman should not have to suffer like this, Confucius replied that a gentleman can bear hardship, while a petty person becomes lawless when in want.

Confucius asks his disciple Zigong whether he thinks he is a man who learns many things and remembers them all. Zigong says yes. Confucius replies that he is not, because he seeks one principle that runs through everything.
Confucius tells his disciple Yu (Zilu) that few people truly know virtue, meaning moral goodness. The saying is short and gives no further explanation.

Confucius says that Shun, an early legendary ruler, governed well without active effort. He did nothing more than sit respectfully on his throne. The point is that a ruler's proper, dignified presence can be enough to govern.

A student asks how to be respected everywhere. The teacher answers that a person should be sincere and truthful in speech and honourable and careful in action, since this works even among distant, uncivilized peoples, while without it, one is not respected even at home. He adds that these two qualities should always be kept in view, as if before the eyes or fixed to a carriage yoke. The student writes these words on his sash so he will remember them.

Confucius praises two men for different ways of living under good and bad rule. The historiographer Yu stays straight like an arrow whether the state is well or badly governed. Chu Po-yu serves in office when government is good, but when it is bad he keeps his principles hidden within himself instead of acting on them.

A person who can be spoken to should be spoken to, and failing to do so is a mistake about that person. A person who cannot be spoken to should not be addressed, since speaking to them wastes one's words. The wise avoid both mistakes by judging whether a person is ready to listen.
A determined scholar or a good person will not save his own life by harming his virtue. If keeping his virtue whole requires it, he will give up his life.

Zigong asked how to practise virtue. Confucius replied that a craftsman must sharpen his tools before he can do his work well. Likewise, wherever you live, serve the most worthy officials and make friends with the most virtuous scholars.

Confucius advises Yen Yuan on how to govern a state by adopting the calendar of the Xia dynasty, the carriage of the Yin, the cap of the Zhou, and the music of Shun. He says to banish the licentious songs of Zheng and to keep away from smooth-talking people, whom he regards as dangerous.
Someone who does not plan ahead for the future will face trouble soon. The saying warns that neglecting distant concerns brings sorrow close at hand.
The master laments that he has never met anyone who loves moral goodness as much as they love beauty or fine appearance. He sees this as a sign that real moral devotion is rare.

Confucius says that Zang Wenzhong was like a thief who held his office unjustly. He knew that Liuxia Hui was a man of great virtue and talent, yet he did not get Liuxia Hui a place at court beside him.

A person who demands much of himself and little of others will avoid drawing resentment from people. The point is that strict standards for oneself, combined with leniency toward others, protect a person from being resented.

A person who never asks himself, "What should I make of this?" is someone the teacher says he cannot help. The point is that a person must keep questioning and reflecting on things, or he cannot be taught.

Confucius says that when a group of people spends a whole day together without talking about righteousness (doing what is right), and they prefer acting on clever, petty schemes, they are in a difficult state. "Shrewdness" here means cleverness in small, self-serving matters.

A superior man, meaning a person of high moral character, treats righteousness, or doing what is right, as the basis of everything he does. He carries it out following proper ritual conduct, expresses it with humility, and finishes it with sincerity.

A person of high character worries about lacking ability, not about whether others recognize him. He does not feel distress when people fail to know or appreciate him. The "superior man" is the Confucian ideal of a morally admirable person.
A gentleman, or person of high moral character, is troubled by the idea that he will be forgotten after he dies. He wants his name to be remembered once he is gone.

A person of good character looks for what he needs within himself, while a petty person looks for it in other people. The contrast is between self-reliance and depending on others. "Superior man" and "mean man" refer to moral quality, not social rank.
A "superior man" (a person of good character) is dignified without quarrelling, and friendly without forming factions or taking sides in groups.

A person of good character judges by two separate things. He does not give someone a higher position just because that person speaks well. He also does not reject a good idea just because of who said it.
Zigong asked whether one word could guide a person's whole life. The Master answered that reciprocity does: do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself.

Confucius says he does not blame or praise people beyond what is fair. If he sometimes praises someone more than usual, he has first examined that person's conduct to justify it. He adds that the people of his day follow the straight path, as the three ancient dynasties did.

Confucius says that in earlier times, a historian would leave a gap in his record when he was unsure of a fact, and a man with a horse would lend it to someone else. He regrets that such practices no longer exist.
Clever, smooth talk damages goodness, and an inability to hold back in small matters ruins large plans. Both small failings can undo bigger and more important aims.

When many people hate a man, or when many people like him, one should look into the matter for oneself before accepting their judgment. Popular opinion alone does not settle whether a person is good or bad.

A person can widen the principles he follows through his own effort. The principles themselves do not make the person bigger. The point is that people must act on their principles, because principles alone do not change them.

Having faults is not the real problem; the real fault is having faults and refusing to change them. Confucius says that a person who keeps a fault without correcting it is the one who should be called faulty.
The Master says he spent a whole day and night thinking without eating or sleeping, and it got him nothing. He concludes that studying is the better course.

A gentleman should care most about truth, not about food or wealth. Farming can still leave a person hungry, and study can bring a reward, but his worry is about failing to grasp truth, not about being poor.

Knowledge alone is not enough to keep what one gains; virtue is needed to hold it. Even with knowledge and virtue, a ruler must also govern with dignity, or the people will not respect him. And even then, if he moves the people against the rules of propriety, he does not reach full excellence.

A person of high character is not judged by small matters but can be trusted with great responsibilities. A person of low character cannot be trusted with great responsibilities but can be judged by small matters.

Virtue matters more to people than water or fire, which can kill. Confucius says he has seen people die from stepping into water or fire, but has never seen anyone die from following the way of virtue.
Each person should see virtue as his own personal duty. He should not hand over the practice of it, even to his own teacher.

A superior man is firm in doing what is right, not just stubborn or hard-headed. Firmness counts as a virtue only when it is correct, and mere firmness is not enough. "Superior man" means a person of good moral character.
A government official, when serving his ruler, should carry out his duties with care and treat his salary as less important. The point is that the work comes first and the pay second.
Teaching should be open to everyone, whatever their social rank. Confucius holds that a person's class or status should not decide who receives instruction.
People who follow different paths cannot make plans together. Their goals and ways of living are too far apart for either to work out a course of action for the other.
Language only needs to get the meaning across. Its job is to convey what is meant, and polish or show is not required. The line is a plain statement of that standard.

Confucius guides a blind music-master, Mien, by naming each step, the mat and the people present as they reach them. When his disciple Tsze-chang asks whether this is the proper way to treat a music-master, Confucius says yes, since it is the correct way to help anyone who is blind.

Ji Kang, head of the Ji family, plans to attack the small state of Zhuanyu. His two officials tell Confucius. Confucius blames them, saying Zhuanyu was long ago given a religious duty by a former king, lies inside their own state, and its ruler serves the duke directly, so the attack has no proper cause. The officials reply that their master wants it.

Confucius rebukes his disciple Zan Yu, who is helping a powerful noble plan an attack on the small state of Chuan-yu. Confucius argues that the disciple is at fault, since a guide who cannot support a blind man is useless, and a keeper who lets a tiger escape is to blame. Zan Yu replies that the state is strong and close to the city of Pi, the target of the plan.

Confucius tells his disciple that rulers should not worry about having few people or being poor. They should worry that people do not stay in their proper places, and that the people lack a settled, contented order. The passage is part of a rebuke of a minister who makes excuses for seizing more land.

Confucius says that when each person keeps to their proper place, poverty and disorder end, and when people are at peace, the state does not lose its people. If distant people refuse to submit, the ruler should first attract them through culture and virtue. He then rebukes his two disciples, Yu and Ch'iu, for failing to help their lord do this.

This is Confucius criticizing Ran Qiu, a disciple working for the Ji family, for helping them plan an attack on Zhuanyu, a small state. He says the Ji family's real trouble will not come from Zhuanyu but from inside their own household.

When the empire is well governed, the Son of Heaven (the emperor) decides on rites, music and punitive wars. When it is badly governed, these decisions pass to the feudal lords. Once they do, the lords usually lose their power within ten generations.

Power that passes from a ruler's chief officers usually lasts only five generations before it is lost. Power held by their own subordinates usually lasts only three. When right principles rule the kingdom, the great officers do not govern, and the common people do not debate.

Power over the state's revenue and government has slipped away from the ruling duke's family and the ruler's own line. First the duke lost control of the money, then the great officers took over the government. As a result, the families of the three Hwan, the powerful clans who held these officer posts, have declined.

Confucius says there are three kinds of friends who help you and three who harm you. Helpful friends are upright people, sincere people, and people of wide experience and knowledge. Harmful friends are those who put on a show, those who flatter in a soft way, and those with smooth but empty talk.

Confucius names three kinds of enjoyment that are good for a person and three that harm them. The helpful ones are studying ceremonies and music carefully, speaking well of others, and having many worthy friends. The harmful ones are extravagant pleasures, idleness and aimless wandering, and indulgence in feasting.

Confucius names three mistakes people make when they are in the presence of a superior man. Speaking when it is not their turn to speak is rashness. Staying silent when they should speak is concealment. Speaking without first watching the face of the superior person is blindness.

A superior man, meaning a person of good character, must watch against a different fault at each stage of life. In youth, when the body is still developing, the danger is lust. In strength, it is quarrelsomeness. In old age, when the body weakens, it is covetousness, or greed.

The superior man, meaning the person of true virtue, respects three things: the decrees of Heaven, great men, and the words of the sages. The mean man, the opposite kind of person, ignores Heaven's decrees, shows no respect to great men, and mocks the sages' words.

Confucius sorts people into four classes by how they come to knowledge. Those born knowing are highest, then those who learn quickly, then those who are slow but still learn. Those who are slow and do not learn are lowest.

Confucius lists nine areas where the "superior man" (an ideal person of good character) gives careful thought. He should see and hear clearly, look kind, act respectfully, speak sincerely, and work carefully. He should ask when unsure, think of the trouble anger may cause, and think of what is right when he sees a chance for gain.

Confucius says he has seen people who pursue good as if they could never reach it, and who recoil from evil as they would from putting a hand into boiling water. He has only heard of people who live in seclusion to study their aims and practise righteousness, and he says he has never met such people.

Duke Ching of Qi was rich and had a thousand four-horse teams, yet when he died no one praised him for any virtue. Po-i and Shu-ch'i starved to death on a mountain, and people still praise them. The point is that wealth does not win lasting praise, while virtue does.

Ch'an K'ang asks Po-yu whether his father, Confucius, ever taught him anything different from what others had heard. Po-yu says no. He recalls that his father twice asked him, in private, whether he had studied the Odes and the rules of Propriety (correct ritual conduct), and told him these were necessary for speaking well and standing properly in society.

Confucius's son Li, asked whether he had learned anything special from his father, said he had not, but had been told to study the rules of proper conduct, without which a person's character cannot be formed. Ch'ang K'ang, a disciple who had asked the same question, took from this three lessons: the Odes, the rules of proper conduct, and that a gentleman keeps a certain distance from his son.

The passage explains the titles used for a ruler's wife, and who uses which one. The prince calls her Fu Zan, she calls herself Xiao Tong, and his own state's people call her Chun Fu Zan. People of other states call her Gua Xiao Jun, or sometimes Chun Fu Zan.

Yang Ho, a powerful official, asks Confucius whether a man who keeps his talents hidden while his country is in disorder can be called good, and whether a man who wants office but keeps missing it can be called wise. Confucius says no to both. Yang Ho then warns that time is passing, and Confucius agrees to take up office.
People are born very much alike, but their habits and training make them very different from one another.

The highest-class wise people and the lowest-class stupid people are the only ones who cannot be changed. Everyone in between can be changed, so the statement sorts people by whether they are fixed in their nature or can still be shaped.

Confucius visits a small town and hears music and singing, and he jokes that such a large effort is wasted on a small place. His disciple Zi You reminds him of his own teaching: educated rulers love the people, and educated common people are easy to govern. Confucius agrees the disciple is right and says his joke was only meant in fun.

Gongshan Furao, who held the city of Bi in revolt, invited Confucius to visit him, and Confucius was inclined to accept. Zilu objected, asking why he should go to such a man. Confucius replied that the invitation must have a reason, and that if someone gave him employment, he could build a new and better kingdom in the east.

Confucius says that being able to practise five qualities everywhere makes a person perfectly virtuous. The five are gravity, generosity, sincerity, earnestness, and kindness. Each one brings a result: respect, the support of others, trust, achievement, and the ability to direct others' service.

Confucius is tempted to visit Pi Hsi, a rebel official. His disciple Tsze-lu objects, citing the rule that a gentleman should not associate with wrongdoers. Confucius replies that a truly hard or white thing cannot be harmed by grinding or dyeing, so he will not be corrupted by going. He adds that he is not a bitter gourd, meaning he should not be left hanging unused.

The Master tells his disciple Yu that six virtues each lead to a fault when they are pursued without learning. Benevolence without learning becomes foolish simplicity, and love of knowledge without learning becomes a scattered mind. The passage breaks off before naming the remaining faults.

Each good quality, when pursued without love of learning, turns into a fault. Being trustworthy without learning leads to harm through ignoring consequences, straightforwardness leads to rudeness, boldness to disobedience, and firmness to extravagance.

Confucius urges his students to study the Book of Poetry, listing its benefits. He says the poems stir the mind, help self-reflection, teach social grace, and manage resentment. They also teach duty to parents and rulers, and give knowledge of birds, animals, and plants.

Confucius tells his son Po-yu to study the Chau-nan and Shao-nan, two sections of the Book of Odes, a collection of ancient songs and poems. He says that someone who has not studied them is like a person standing with their face against a wall, unable to see anything beyond it.

Confucius asks whether propriety (correct ritual conduct) and music are only their outward objects. Gems and silk alone do not make up propriety, and bells and drums alone do not make up music. He implies that the outward forms are not the real thing.
Someone who looks strong and firm on the outside but is weak inside is compared to a petty person. The speaker likens such a person to a thief who breaks into a house through a wall.
Confucius says that the careful, respectable people of the village, who seem good, actually harm virtue. "Village worthies" are men who look upright to their neighbours but are not truly virtuous.
Repeating gossip or half-heard talk as soon as you pick it up is, in this view, a way of throwing away one's virtue. The saying warns against passing on news without thought.

Mean people, Confucius says, are hard to serve as a ruler's officials. Before they get what they want, they worry about how to get it. After they get it, they worry about losing it. Driven by that fear, they will go to any lengths.

Confucius says that each of three traits has decayed over time. Ancient high-mindedness ignored small matters, but today it becomes wild lawlessness. Ancient dignity was grave and reserved, but today it turns into quarrelsome stubbornness. Ancient simplicity was straightforwardness, but today it has become outright deceit.
Smooth talk and a charming manner are rarely found together with real virtue. The saying warns that a person who speaks very pleasingly and tries hard to please is seldom a good person.

The Master says he dislikes three things: purple cloth that dulls the brighter red of vermilion, the lively songs of Zheng that spoil the correct music of the Ya, and people with clever, sharp speech who bring down states and families. In each case, something false or showy takes the place of what is proper.
Confucius says he would prefer not to speak. His disciple Zigong asks what they would then record. Confucius replies that Heaven does not speak, yet the seasons turn and things keep being produced.

Zu Pei asked to see Confucius, but Confucius refused, saying he was ill. As the messenger left the door, Confucius played his lute and sang loudly enough for Pei to hear, so Pei would know he was not really sick.

Zai Wo argues that mourning for parents need only last one year, not three. He points out that if a gentleman stays away from ritual and music for three years, both will be lost. He also notes that in one year the seasons turn, with old grain used up, new grain grown, and new fire made from wood.

Zai Wo argues that the mourning period for a parent can end after one full year. Confucius asks whether Wo would feel at ease eating fine food and wearing embroidered clothes so soon. Wo says he would. Confucius replies that a gentleman does not feel at ease doing these things during mourning, so Wo should not do so.

Confucius is answering Zai Wo (Tsai Wo), who argued that the three years of mourning for a dead parent could be shortened to one year. Confucius says that a child is carried in its parents' arms for its first three years, and that three years of mourning is the common practice everywhere. He asks whether the disciple Yu (Zai Wo) had himself received three years of parental care, implying that he lacked proper feeling.
Confucius says it is hard to deal with someone who eats all day and never applies his mind to anything good. He adds that even playing games like chess would be better than doing nothing at all.

Zilu asks whether the superior man values courage. Confucius replies that the superior man places righteousness first. Courage without righteousness leads a person of high rank to rebel against authority, and a common person to commit robbery.

Confucius and his disciple Zigong discuss what a gentleman hates. Confucius names people who publicize others' faults, inferiors who slander their superiors, brave men without good manners, and bold people who lack understanding. Zigong names those who pry out facts and claim them as their own wisdom, those who are rude but think themselves brave, and those who expose secrets and call it honesty.
Women and servants are the hardest people to deal with, the speaker says. If you get too close to them, they become disrespectful. If you keep your distance, they become resentful.

The Master says that a man who is disliked at forty will stay that way for the rest of his life. He does not change for the better. The saying is about how a man's character is fixed by the time he reaches middle age.

Three men of the late Yin dynasty responded differently to the wicked last ruler, Chau: one left the court, one pretended to be a slave to avoid harm, and one protested and was put to death. Confucius says all three were men of virtue, though they acted in different ways.

Liu-hsia Hui, a judge, was dismissed three times. When someone suggested he leave his post, he answered that serving honestly would bring dismissal anywhere, and that serving dishonestly would mean he had no reason to leave his homeland.

Duke Ching of Ch'i said he would not treat Confucius as well as the head of the powerful Chi family, but better than the head of the lesser Mang family. He also said he was too old to use Confucius's teachings. So Confucius left.
The state of Ch'i sent a gift of female musicians to the ruler of Lu. The ruler, Chi Hwan, accepted them and stopped holding court for three days. Confucius then left Lu.

A wandering man called Chieh-yu sang past Confucius, warning that the times were dangerous for anyone serving in government and urging him to stop chasing his goals. Confucius got down from his carriage to speak with him, but the man hurried away and they never talked.

Two farmers, Ch'ang-tsu and Chieh-ni, are working in a field when Confucius's disciple Tsze-lu comes to ask them the way to a ford, a place to cross a river. Ch'ang-tsu answers that Confucius, whom he recognizes, already knows the ford, and Chieh-ni asks who Tsze-lu is and then gives no direct answer to the question.

Chieh-ni, a hermit, asks a disciple of Confucius whether he should follow Confucius, who tries to reform a disordered world. Chieh-ni argues that changing the world is hopeless and that it is better to withdraw from society completely. The disciple says nothing of the kind and goes back to his farm work, covering seed in the ground.

Confucius sighs at the idea of giving up human company for the company of birds and beasts. He says he must live among people, and that he would not try to change the world if right principles already ruled the empire.

Zilu, lagging behind Confucius, meets an old farmer and asks if he has seen his master. The old man rebukes him for not working with his hands and not knowing the grains, then goes back to weeding without answering. Zilu respectfully stands before him with his hands folded.

Confucius's disciple Zilu meets an old man who hosts him and introduces his sons. When Zilu returns to see him again, the old man has gone. The Master calls the old man a recluse, a person who withdraws from public life. Zilu then argues that refusing to take office is not right.

This is a reply to a hermit who refused to serve in office. The speaker argues that a person who withdraws from public service to keep himself pure is neglecting the duty between ruler and minister. A gentleman, he says, takes up office and does its proper duties, even knowing that right principles may not prevail.

Confucius names seven men who withdrew from public life and says which of them kept their principles intact. Po-i and Shu-ch'i refused to bend their wills or accept any stain on themselves. Hui of Liu-hsia and Shao-lien did bend and accept such stains, but their words matched reason and their conduct was admirable.

Confucius says that two recluses, Yu-chung and I-yi, withdrew from public life and spoke freely, kept their persons pure, and adjusted their conduct to the times. He says he is different: he has no course he has fixed in advance, either to follow or to reject.

The passage lists court musicians who left their posts and scattered to other states and remote places. Each named musician is shown leaving, which in the Analects is taken as a sign that the state's music and order had collapsed. The main point is the breakdown of the court's ritual music, shown through the departure of its staff.

The Duke of Zhou advises his son, the Duke of Lu, on how a good ruler should act. He should not neglect his relatives, should not leave senior ministers feeling passed over, and should not dismiss members of old families without a serious reason. He should also not expect one man to have every talent.

The passage is a list of eight officers who served the Duke of Zhou, the founder of the Zhou dynasty's ruling house. Their names are given as a record of who held these posts. The passage does not explain their roles or add any comment.

A disciple, Zizhang, describes the ideal scholar. When danger threatens, he is ready to give up his life. When gain is offered, he considers whether it is right. In sacrifice he is reverent, and in mourning he feels the grief he should feel.

Zizhang asks what worth a man has if he holds fast to virtue without trying to grow it, and believes good principles without true sincerity. His point is that such a man hardly seems to matter, whether he is alive or not.

Tsze-chang disagrees with the rule of associating only with people who can benefit you. He says a superior man honours the talented and virtuous, tolerates everyone, and pities the incompetent. He adds that how others treat him is not his concern to push away.
Zixia says that minor skills and crafts have some value. But if a person pushes them too far beyond their proper scope, they may fail to fit the real need. So the gentleman does not pursue them.

Zixia says that a person who each day learns what he does not yet know, and each month keeps hold of what he has already learned, can truly be said to love learning. The point is steady progress: gaining new knowledge while not losing old.

Zixia says that virtue is found in a course of four activities: studying widely, holding a firm and sincere aim, asking questions earnestly, and thinking about what one has learned and applying it to oneself.
Zixia compares craftsmen to scholars. Craftsmen stay in their workshops to do their work well, and the gentleman studies so that he can fully carry out his principles.
A petty person, according to Zixia, always tries to cover up or excuse his faults. Instead of admitting a mistake, he makes it look smaller or explains it away.
Tzu-hsia says that the superior man, or gentleman, shows three changes. From afar he looks stern, up close he is gentle, and when he speaks his words are firm and clear.

Zixia says that a gentleman must first win his people's trust before asking them to work hard, or they will feel oppressed. Likewise, he must first win his ruler's trust before criticizing him, or the ruler will think he is slandering him.

Zixia says that a person who stays within the limits set by the great virtues may move across the lines of the small virtues. In other words, the small matters can be handled with some flexibility, as long as the main principles are kept.

Ziyou says that Zixia's students are skilled in minor tasks, such as sweeping, answering, and moving properly, but they do not learn the essentials, so they cannot be called truly educated. Zixia replies that Ziyou is wrong, meaning he disagrees with this judgment.

The passage is a saying by Zixia, a disciple of Confucius, about teaching. He says a wise teacher ranks subjects by importance, teaching the main ones and treating minor ones more loosely, and sorts students by their abilities, as one sorts plants by kind. Only a sage, he adds, can master both the start and the finish of learning.
Zixia says that an official, once his duties are done, should use his spare time to study. A student, once he has finished his studies, should go on to serve as an official.

Mourning should go only as far as real grief reaches, and then it should stop. Tsze-hsia, a disciple of Confucius, is saying that once the deepest sorrow has been fully expressed, the mourning should end there and not go on further.
Zixia says his friend Zhang can accomplish difficult tasks, but he is still not fully virtuous. Zixia is pointing out that doing hard things is not the same as having complete moral goodness.

Zengzi (Tsang) says that Zhang's manner is very grand, and that it is hard to practise virtue alongside him. The saying suggests his showy dignity makes genuine goodness difficult to reach in his company.

Zeng Zi reports the Master's teaching that people may not fully show their inner worth in ordinary life, but they do show it fully when mourning their parents. Mourning is named as the occasion when this inner sincerity becomes visible.

Zeng Zi reports the Master's praise of Meng Zhuangzi's filial piety. Other parts of his filial conduct were things others could also do, but keeping his father's ministers and methods of government after his father's death was hard to match.

Tseng Tzu advises a new chief judge that when he finds the truth in a case, he should feel grief and pity for the people involved, not pride in his own skill. He blames long-standing failures by rulers for the disorder among the people.

Zigong says that the wickedness of King Zhou, the last ruler of the Shang, was not as great as his bad name suggests. A good person therefore dislikes being placed in a low position, where all the world's evil would collect on him.

A gentleman's faults are compared to eclipses of the sun and moon. Everyone sees his faults when they occur, but when he corrects himself, people respect him all the more. The speaker is Zigong, a disciple of Confucius, and the "superior man" means an ideal person of good character.

Asked where Confucius learned his wisdom, Zigong answers that the teachings of the early kings Wen and Wu are still alive among the people. Those with great talent keep their main principles, and others keep the smaller parts, so the Master could learn them anywhere and never needed one fixed teacher.

Shu-sun Wu-shu said that Tsze-kung was greater than Confucius. Tsze-kung answered with a comparison: his own wall is low, so anyone can see his worth, but his Master's wall is so high that few can find the door and see the full richness inside. He suggests the chief's remark is only what one would expect.

Shu-sun Wu-shu insulted Confucius, and Tsze-kung, his disciple, replied that the insults achieve nothing. Other men's talents are like small hills that can be stepped over, while Confucius is like the sun or moon, which cannot be stepped over. Insulting him only shows that the insulter does not know his own limits.

Ch'an Tsze-ch'in suggested that Tsze-kung was being too modest, since Confucius was surely greater than he was. Tsze-kung replied that a single word can make a person seem wise or foolish, so speech must be careful. He added that the Master (Confucius) is as impossible to reach as the sky is to climb by a staircase.

This passage is a disciple's praise of Confucius, saying that if he ran a state or a family, people would follow him at once. It describes such a ruler as making people settled, willing to follow, happy and harmonious, so that he is honoured while alive and mourned when dead.

Yao hands power to Shun and tells him to hold fast to the due Mean, warning that if the people within the land fall into distress, the state's revenue will end for good. Shun gives Yu the same charge. T'ang then addresses Heaven, saying he does not pardon wrongdoers and leaves the judging of his ministers to God.

This passage is a ruler's speech, given in the old Chinese tradition as the words of King Wu, who founded the Zhou dynasty, and it describes how he governed. He takes the blame for any wrongs, saying that faults of the people rest on him. He then rewards the good, appoints capable officials, sets standard weights and measures, and reviews the laws, and the kingdom is well governed.

This passage describes the qualities and deeds of a ruler, ascribed to the sage-king of the ancient Zhou era. He restored fallen states and families and brought back retired men to office, which won the people's hearts. His main concerns were food, mourning rites and sacrifices, and he gained support through generosity, sincerity, diligence and justice.

A ruler should honour five good qualities and reject four bad ones to govern well. The five good qualities are: being kind without wasteful spending, giving tasks without making people resent them, seeking what he wants without greed, being calm without pride, and being dignified without cruelty.

A ruler can show kindness without spending much. He helps the people by building on the benefits they already have, and he assigns them only fitting work. He wants good government, not personal gain, and he treats everyone, great or small, with respect, while staying calm and never proud.

Confucius lists four faults a ruler should avoid: killing people without first teaching them, demanding full work without warning, and giving orders casually then punishing harshly when the deadline comes. Each one is a failure of fair treatment. He also says a leader can be dignified and awe-inspiring without being fierce.

Giving rewards stingily is called acting like a mere petty official. The passage then says three things are needed: knowing Heaven's decrees to become a superior man, knowing the rules of proper conduct to establish one's character, and understanding the force of words to know other people.

The Tao, the way or underlying reality, cannot be fully described in words or known through ordinary paths. Seen without desire, it is its deep, hidden source; seen with desire, only its outer edges show. Both views come from one thing, which is called the Mystery.

Each thing we name only makes sense in contrast with its opposite. Knowing beauty means having the idea of ugliness, and knowing skill means having the idea of lack of skill. Existence, difficulty, length, height and sound work the same way: each is known through its partner.
