The sage acts without forcing anything and teaches without words. Things arise, grow and complete their courses without being claimed or rewarded, and the work is done without anyone seeing how, which keeps its power lasting.

The passage says that a ruler keeps people peaceful by removing the things that stir up competition, theft and desire. Avoid honoring talented men, prizing rare goods, and showing tempting things. The ruler also keeps people simple, without much knowledge or desire, and does not let the clever act on what they know. Order then comes without active interference.

The Tao is described as an empty vessel that must never be filled, deep and hidden, and older than all things. The passage says we should blunt our sharpness, settle our tangles, soften our brightness, and match the plainness of others. The Tao is pure and still, and its origin is unknown, seeming to come before even God.

Heaven and earth treat all things without any intent to be kind, just as people treat straw dogs, which are used briefly and then discarded. The sage treats people the same way. The passage then compares the world to a bellows: it stays strong when emptied and gives out more air when moved, so too much speech quickly wears out, and one should keep one's inner self free.

The passage describes a mysterious source it calls the valley spirit or female mystery. This source never dies, and it is the origin from which heaven and earth came. Its power lasts forever and works gently, without force or harm.

Heaven and earth last a long time because they do not exist for their own sake. In the same way, the sage puts himself last and treats his own person as if it were not his own, and so he is kept safe and his aims are reached. The point is that letting go of self-interest leads to lasting results.

Water is the model of the highest goodness: it benefits all things and settles in the low places that people avoid, without contending for them. That is why it is close to the Tao, the natural Way. Each thing is good in its own proper way, and the person who does not argue for a higher position is not blamed.

Stopping before things are full or sharp is wiser than pushing them to the limit. Wealth, status and fame can bring downfall when they are held too tightly or lead to pride. When success is reached, stepping back out of view is described as the natural way.

The passage describes how a person can live in harmony with the Tao, the natural Way. It lists qualities such as keeping mind and breath gentle, ruling without forcing action, and acting without claiming credit. It then says the Tao itself works this way: it creates and nurtures all things, claims nothing, and controls nothing, and this is called its mysterious quality.

Things are useful because of their empty spaces, not their solid parts. A wheel works through the hole for the axle, a pot through its hollow, and a room through its open doorways and windows. So what exists gives convenience, and what is empty gives the actual use.

Too much colour, sound, flavour, racing and hunting, and rare goods dull the senses and unsettle the mind, leading people astray. So the sage meets basic bodily needs and turns away from the endless craving of the eyes.

Favour and disgrace both bring fear: getting favour brings worry about losing it, and losing it brings fear of worse harm. Great honour and great calamity are both tied to the body, since calamity can only reach a person who has one. So a ruler who cares for the kingdom as he cares for his own body can be trusted to govern it.

Tao, the way underlying all things, cannot be seen, heard, or grasped, so it has no fixed description. It is named the Formless and the Invisible, and it is known by following its ancient origin to guide present affairs.

The old masters of the Tao were so subtle and deep that their understanding could not be easily known, so the author describes them by their outward looks: cautious, humble, plain and empty. They stayed still and let things settle, as muddy water clears when left alone. They did not want to be full of themselves, so they seemed worn rather than new.

Keep the mind empty and still, and things will be seen to return to their roots. Returning to the root is stillness, and knowing this unchanging rule brings understanding. Whoever knows it grows in tolerance, becomes fit to lead, and so lasts long and avoids decay.

The passage describes a decline over ages. In the earliest times people barely knew their rulers existed, and later rulers were loved, feared, then despised, as trust in the Tao weakened. The best rulers were quiet and sparing with words, and their work succeeded so that people said they had done it themselves.

When people stopped following the Great Tao, the Way of nature, virtues like benevolence and righteousness began to be praised. Cleverness and hypocrisy followed. Filial piety and loyal ministers appeared only after family and state life had broken down.

The passage says that giving up cleverness, moral display and profit-seeking would benefit people more than these things do. The last lines add that the old ways of ornate rules hid a lack of real worth, and that simple, honest conduct would curb selfish desire.

The speaker says that giving up learning frees him from worry. Ordinary people seem happy and content, while he feels calm, quiet and unmoved, like a baby who has not yet smiled, and even lost. He sets himself apart from the crowd.

The speaker feels that everyone else has plenty and understands things, while he seems to have lost everything and appears dull and lost. Even so, he sets himself apart from others because he values the Tao, which he calls the nursing-mother, the source that nourishes all things.

Great active force comes only from Tao, the Way, which is the source of all things. Tao cannot be seen or touched, yet all forms of things are contained in it and it endures through all time. The writer says we know all things are like this because of Tao's own nature.

Things that are incomplete, bent, empty or worn can become whole, straight, full or renewed. The passage says that a wise person, by holding to humility and avoiding self-display, self-assertion and self-boasting, is recognized and rises above others. Because such a person does not compete, no one can compete with them.

Sudden wind and rain do not last long, because Heaven and Earth do not keep up such brief actions. People who follow the Tao naturally find others who agree with them, whether those others pursue it, show it, or fail at it. If a person's own faith is not enough, others will not trust him.

Those who push themselves forward, boast, or insist on their own views do not gain the standing they seek. Such behaviour is like spoiled food or a diseased growth, which people dislike, so followers of the Tao avoid it.

The passage describes the Tao, a formless and complete source that existed before heaven and earth and is called the mother of all things. It moves on, becomes remote, and returns, and it is the model for heaven, earth, and the sage king. Each follows the one above it, and the Tao follows only its own nature.

Heaviness is presented as the base of lightness, and stillness as the master of movement. A wise ruler should stay steady and not be carried away by distractions. If he acts recklessly, he loses both his foundation and his throne.

The passage says that truly skilled people leave no obvious trace of their work, so their skill is hard to see. A skilled traveller leaves no tracks, a skilled closer needs no bolts, and a skilled binder needs no knots. The sage, or wise person, uses this same quiet skill to save people and things, so he discards none of them. Skill and lack of skill depend on each other, and the whole thing is called a deep mystery.

Someone who knows strength but keeps to weakness, brightness but keeps to darkness, and honour but accepts shame becomes like a valley that all things flow to, and returns to a childlike simplicity. The last lines add that raw material, once divided into vessels, becomes useful, and that the sage who is put in charge of officials governs without harsh measures.

Trying to seize the kingdom by force of effort will fail, because it is a spirit-like thing that cannot be grasped. Gripping it tightly destroys it. Things naturally reverse: strength gives way to weakness, and stored wealth falls to ruin. So the sage avoids excess effort, extravagance and indulgence.

A ruler who follows the Tao should not use armies to gain power over the land. Force brings its own bad results, and a skilled commander uses force only when needed, stops after one decisive blow, and does not seek to dominate. Anything that grows strong and then declines is said to be against the Tao, and what goes against it does not last.

Weapons, even when they seem fine, bring bad luck and are hated by people, so those who follow the Tao avoid them and use them only when forced. A victory in war is treated like a funeral: the winner takes the place of mourning, because killing many people is a cause for grief.

The Tao is described as nameless and unchanging, yet powerful: if a ruler could hold to it, people would submit to him on their own. Once it acts and takes a form, it can be named, and people who rest in it avoid failure. It stands to the world as great rivers and seas stand to streams.

Knowing others shows judgment, but knowing yourself shows true understanding. Overcoming others shows strength, but overcoming yourself shows real power. Contentment makes a person rich, steady effort shows will, and keeping to one's place lasts long. Dying yet not perishing means lasting on in a way that does not end.

The Tao is present everywhere and gives all things their being without claiming credit or ruling over them. All things return to their source without knowing it is the Tao that guides this. The sage achieves great things by not making himself great.

Whoever holds to the Tao, the unseen way underlying all things, draws the world to him, and people come to him safely and find peace. Music and fine food only hold a passing guest for a while, but the Tao itself, though it seems plain and tasteless, never runs out in its use.

The passage says that to get what you want from someone, you should first give them what they seem to want. You weaken a rival by strengthening him, and overthrow him by first raising him up. This is called "hiding the light" of one's plans. It ends by saying that the soft overcomes the hard, and that a state's tools of advantage should stay out of the people's sight, as fish should stay out of deep water.

The Tao, the natural way of things, works without forcing anything, so nothing is left undone. If rulers could hold to it, all things would change on their own. Stillness without desire lets everything go right by itself.

The highest virtue, in this view, is not displayed or worked at, so it is held fully and needs no effort. Lower virtue is always trying to show or keep itself, and so falls short. Benevolence and righteousness, which are lower still, must be actively practised.

The passage says that when people lose the Tao, the natural way, they fall back on virtues like benevolence, then righteousness, then formal propriety, and that propriety is a thin form of loyalty and good faith that starts disorder. Quick cleverness is likewise a surface bloom of the Tao that leads to foolishness. The wise person therefore holds to the solid root and not to the flimsy surface.

Heaven, earth, spirits, valleys, living creatures and rulers all get their order and strength from the Tao, the One. Without it, each would fail: heaven would tear, earth would crack, and the rulers would fall.

Rulers gain their high position from a lowly base, so they call themselves "orphans" and "men of small virtue." The passage says they prefer to look plain, like ordinary stone rather than polished jade, and it compares their humility to the hub of a carriage wheel, the empty centre that makes the carriage useful.

Movement of the Tao (the Way, the source of all things) turns back on itself, so that weakness is how it works. Everything under heaven came from the Tao as something that exists and has a name, and that existence in turn came from the Tao as non-existence, which has no name.

People respond to the Tao in three ways: the highest class practise it, the middle class follow it unsteadily, and the lowest class laugh at it. The passage says the Tao looks weak, plain or even foolish, yet it is hidden, nameless, and able to give all things what they need.

The passage describes how everything comes from the Tao, through One, Two and Three, and returns from darkness toward light, held in balance by a breath of emptiness. It then says that loss can bring gain, and that violent, strong people do not die natural deaths. The speaker says this will be the basis of his teaching.

The softest thing in the world wears down the hardest, and what has no solid form gets into places with no gaps. From this the speaker concludes that acting without forcing has real benefit, and that few people grasp this teaching, which needs no words.

Is fame or life more precious, and is life or wealth worth more? The passage says that clinging to fame or possessions costs you your life, while being content and knowing when to stop keeps you safe from shame, blame and danger, so that you live long.

The passage says that what seems lacking or imperfect is often the strongest. Great achievement that looks modest lasts, and great fullness that looks empty never runs out. It ends by saying that action overcomes cold, stillness overcomes heat, and calm purity sets the right order for everything.

When the Tao, the natural way of things, guides the world, horses are used for farm work instead of war. When it is ignored, war horses are bred on the frontiers. The chapter says that wanting more and being discontented are the worst faults, and that contentment brings lasting sufficiency.

The passage says that real understanding comes from within, not from travel or looking outward. The farther a person goes from himself, the less he knows. Wise people therefore know the world without going out, name things without seeing them, and reach their aims without trying to.

Learning adds something each day, but following the Tao reduces effort day by day until a person reaches doing nothing on purpose. From that stillness, nothing is left undone. Whoever wins the whole world does so by taking no forced effort; striving to win it does not succeed.

The sage does not hold a fixed mind of his own. He takes the people's minds as his own, and treats everyone with goodness and sincerity, whether or not they treat him the same way. Through this, the people become good and sincere, and he regards them all as his children.

Life and death follow each other, and many people die because they work too hard to keep themselves alive. The passage says that a person who manages life well, without anxious effort, is safe from wild beasts and weapons, because nothing in him is open to death.

The Tao gives rise to all things, nourishes them, and guides them to completion, yet it claims no ownership and exerts no control over them. All things honour it naturally, without being ordered to. This quiet, unforced working is what the passage calls the Tao's mysterious operation.

Tao is the source of everything, like a mother to her children. A person who knows this and keeps to its quiet, soft ways avoids harm. Keeping the mouth closed and not striving brings freedom from toil, while talking and pushing one's affairs brings danger.

If the speaker were ever given power to rule by the Great Tao, he would most fear showy display. The Tao is plain and easy, but rulers prefer side paths. They keep their courts neat while fields go untended and granaries stay empty, and they live in luxury while the people suffer. Such rulers are called robbers and boasters, and their conduct goes against the Tao.

Whatever is firmly planted or held by Tao cannot be pulled up or taken away. If Tao is cultivated in a person, in a family, in a neighbourhood, in a state, and in the whole kingdom, its good effects will grow at each level. The author says this can be known by observing these different cases.

A person who has the Tao fully within is compared to a newborn infant. Such a person is not harmed by insects, beasts or birds. The closing lines say that forcing life or strength too hard leads to decline, because whatever goes against the Tao soon ends.

He who truly knows the Tao does not talk about it, and the one who talks about it readily does not know it. Such a person stays quiet, dulls his sharpness, and blends in with others. Passing beyond gain, loss, praise and blame, he is called the noblest person under heaven.

The passage argues that a ruler should rule best by not interfering. Laws, prohibitions, tools for profit and clever schemes tend to make people poorer, more disorderly and more prone to crime. When the ruler acts without purpose and keeps still, the people reform, prosper and return to simplicity on their own.

A government that looks unwise and hands-off often serves the people well, while one that meddles in everything tends to fail. Good and bad outcomes keep switching places, and no one can say where they will end. So the sage, the ideal ruler, acts without harshness, cutting or wounding no one.

Moderation is the key to governing oneself and serving heaven. Through it a person returns early to their natural state, and by repeatedly building up the Tao's qualities they can overcome every obstacle. Such a person can rule a state and last long, like a plant with deep roots and firm stalks.

If a country is ruled by the Tao, the spirits of the dead do no harm. The ruler also does no harm to the people, and so neither side hurts the other. Their good effects then come together in the Tao's power.

A great state gains the support of smaller states by lowering itself to them, the way a low stream draws everything toward it. Small states gain favour by humbling themselves before a great one. Each gets what it wants, but the great state has to be the one that learns to be humble.

Tao is the most valued thing in the world. It helps good people, protects bad people, and does not abandon even those who are not good. A gift of jade or a team of horses is worth less than a lesson in Tao, which can be received humbly. The ancients valued it because anyone can seek it, and the guilty can be freed from their guilt through it.

The passage says the Tao works by acting without strain and handling small matters before they grow. Big difficulties start as small, easy things, so the sage deals with problems early. He does not make rash promises, and by treating even easy things as hard, he avoids difficulties.

Things are easier to manage when they are still small or calm, so it is best to act before problems appear. Large results come from small beginnings. Forcing action with a hidden aim causes harm and loses control, but the sage, the ideal wise person, does not act that way and so causes no harm.

The sage, or wise person, does not grab at things, so he does not lose them. People often ruin their affairs just as they near success, because they stop being careful at the end. So the sage wants what others ignore, learns what others overlook, and lets all things develop naturally without forcing his own purpose on them.

The old masters who practised the Tao did not try to make people clever. They kept people simple and unlearned, because too much knowledge makes government hard. A ruler who governs by cleverness harms the state, while one who does not is a blessing.

Rivers and seas hold the highest place among waters because they lie lower than the streams that flow into them. In the same way, a wise ruler leads by placing himself below the people. Because he does not compete with them, people honor him gladly and no one can rival him.

The Tao is great, and its greatness is why it looks inferior to other teachings. Its three treasures are gentleness, economy and not pushing ahead of others. People who drop these and chase boldness, generosity and first place end in death, while gentleness wins in battle and is protected by heaven.

The chapter says that the best leader in war does not show anger or force. He wins without fighting, keeps apart from his enemies, and still men follow him willingly. Such a person is like Heaven, which does not contend, and so his strength comes from not contending.

The passage advises against starting wars and prefers defending to attacking. It says that the one who regrets having to fight, and avoids rash action, is the one who wins when weapons actually clash. Making war lightly is called the greatest disaster.

The speaker says his teaching is simple to understand and simple to follow, yet almost no one manages either. People fail to grasp it, so they fail to know him, and the few who do know him are therefore valuable. The wise person outwardly wears plain coarse cloth but keeps something precious hidden inside.

To know that you do not know is the highest state. Thinking you know when you do not is a sickness. Feeling pain at that sickness keeps a person free of it, and the sage, who feels this pain, is free of it for that reason.

If people refuse to fear what they should fear, something they dread will overtake them. They should not indulge carelessly in ordinary life or grow weary of the very things that life rests on. The sage knows himself without showing off, and values himself without seeming to, choosing the second path over the first.

Bold defiance of the law leads to death, while bold restraint leads to life, yet which outcome is good or bad is hard to judge. The sage finds this hard to grasp. Heaven acts without striving or calling, yet it overcomes all, and nothing escapes its net.

The people no longer fear death, so threatening them with it does no good. Killing wrongdoers will not stop wrongdoing, because death is controlled by a higher power. Anyone who takes on that power is like an untrained man trying to do a master craftsman's work, and is likely to get hurt.

The passage says that the people's hardships come from those above them. Heavy taxes cause famine, excessive interference makes the people hard to rule, and the strain of struggling to make a living leads them to treat death lightly. It concludes that not making life a matter of great concern is better than valuing it highly.

Living things start out soft and weak and become hard and stiff as they die, so firmness goes with death and softness with life. From this the passage concludes that force does not win, and that what is firm and strong belongs low while what is soft and weak belongs high.

Heaven works by balance: it lowers what is too high and raises what is too low. People often do the opposite, taking from the poor to add to their own excess. Only someone who has the Tao can use what he has to serve everyone, and such a ruler acts without claiming credit or wanting to show his superiority.

Water is the softest thing in the world, yet nothing surpasses it at wearing down what is hard and strong. Everyone knows the soft overcomes the hard, but few put it into practice. So the sage says that the one who takes on a state's shame becomes its lord, and the one who bears its misfortunes becomes its king.

After a bitter quarrel is patched up, resentment usually lingers. So the wise person holds the left half of the contract, the creditor's share, and does not press the other side to pay up. Heaven's way is impartial and always sides with the good.

The passage describes an ideal small state where people need little. They have no use for tools, boats, carriages, or weapons, and they go back to knotted cords instead of writing. They are content with plain food, clothes, and homes. Neighbouring states are close enough to hear, yet the people never visit them.

True speech is plain rather than showy, and those who truly know the Tao do not argue or show off their learning. The sage keeps nothing back for himself: the more he gives to others, the more he has, and his way of acting brings no harm and no struggle.

In the northern sea lives a huge fish called the Leviathan, thousands of li long. It changes into a giant bird called the Rukh, whose back is thousands of li wide. When it rises with great effort, its wings block out the sky like clouds.

The passage describes a huge bird that rises high on a storm wind and flies south for six months. It compares this bird's view of the sky to dust motes seen in a sunbeam. From that height, the blue of the sky looks the same whether it is its true colour or only the effect of distance.

Big things need enough room or depth to carry them. Water cannot float a large ship in a shallow hole, and air cannot hold up a large bird unless it is deep enough. So the great bird needs ninety thousand li of air, with nothing above but clear sky, before it sets off south.

A cicada mocks a young dove for wanting to fly up ninety thousand li and then south. The cicada says it can barely fly from tree to tree and sometimes falls short, so such a long journey seems pointless to it. The passage breaks off before any reply.

Small creatures cannot grasp what larger beings know, just as a short life cannot hold the span of a long one. The mushroom that lives a morning does not know day and night, and the chrysalis does not know spring and autumn. Their years are simply short.

The passage says that a tortoise in Ch'u lives for spring and autumns of five hundred years each, and an old tree lived for eight thousand years each. Even so, P'êng Tsu, a legendary man said to have lived very long, is still envied by everyone. The text then breaks off, so its full point is not clear.
The passage describes a huge fish called the Leviathan in a northern sea and a giant bird called the Rukh. The bird rises high on a storm and flies south, showing creatures of enormous size.

A quail laughs at a great bird (the Peng) that is about to fly far. The quail says it can only rise a few yards and land among the reeds, so it cannot see where such a creature could possibly be going.

Small minds are satisfied with small achievements, like the quail that thinks it has flown far. The philosopher Yung laughs at such people. He is not moved by praise or blame, since he knows what is inward from what is outward. Even so, the passage says, he has not fully achieved his goal.

Lieh Tzu could ride the wind and travel freely, yet the passage says he still depended on something. A man who rides the eternal order of Heaven and Earth would depend on nothing at all. Therefore the perfect man ignores self, the divine man ignores action, and the true Sage ignores reputation.

In the passage, a man asks a ruler to take over the government. He argues that a torch is pointless when the sun and moon shine, and watering is wasted in the rainy season. He says the ruler alone can bring peace, and he himself is unfit and asks the ruler to take the throne.

Hsü Yu refuses to take over the empire from the ruler. He says the ruler's good name is only a shadow of the real achievement, which the ruler already has, and that he himself needs only a little, as a bird needs one twig or a tapir needs only enough water. He adds that a person should not do another's job when that person is able to do it himself.

Chien Wu says he was greatly astonished by what he heard. The account seemed to him vast, like the Milky Way, and far beyond ordinary human experience. The passage breaks off before it gives the details of what was said.

The speaker describes a divine man who lives on air and dew, rides clouds, and is completely still, yet keeps things from decay and makes crops grow. The speaker calls this nonsense and says they do not believe it.

Lien Shu tells his listener that he is like a blind man judging a picture or a deaf man at a concert, unable to appreciate what is in front of him. He says the listener's own mind is blind and deaf in this way. He adds that a great man's good influence already fills the world, so it is wrong to ask him to deal with the small affairs of a government.

The main point is that outside things cannot hurt the person described. He stays unharmed by a great flood or a severe drought, and even the dust left from him could make two sage-kings like Yao and Shun. So the speaker finds it absurd that such a person would concern himself with external goals.

A man from Sung took sacred caps to sell in Yüeh, where people cut their hair and painted their bodies, so the caps were of no use to them. Likewise, after Emperor Yao visited four sages on a mountain, he felt his great empire meant nothing to him. The point is that value depends on what a person wants and what they have become.
A man tells Chuang Tzu that he grew a huge gourd, but it was too big to be useful. It was too heavy to hold liquid and its halves made poor ladles, so he smashed it.

Chuang Tzu tells a story to show that the same thing can be worth little or much depending on how it is used. A family had a salve for chapped hands and only earned a little from silk-washing with it. A stranger paid them a large sum for the recipe, so they sold it, seeing that it could bring far more money that way.

The same salve that protects hands from chapping was used by two different people in different ways. One used it to wash silk and gained nothing. The stranger who sold the recipe to the Prince of Wu used it to win a naval battle and was rewarded with land and a title. The point is that the same thing can be worth very different amounts depending on how it is used.

Someone has a large gourd that is too big to hold much, so it is no use as a container. The speaker asks why they did not turn it into a boat to float on rivers and lakes. He suggests the listener's mind is muddled, since the gourd's uselessness as a vessel was a problem only because it was used the wrong way.

Hui Tzu tells Chuang Tzu that his words are like a large tree that is useless: its trunk is too knotted for planks and its branches too twisted for carpentry, so no one wants it. He is saying Chuang Tzu's teaching is big but of no practical use to anyone.

Chuang Tzu answers a critic with two images: the wild cat that is caught because it is always hunting, and the yak that is too big to catch mice. He then suggests that a useless big tree could be planted in an open space where no one needs it, and left alone to rest in its shade.

Yen Ch'eng Tzu Yu, a disciple standing nearby, asks the man leaning on the table why his body looks as dry as wood and his mind as dead as ashes. He says the man now seated is not the same person who was there a moment ago.

Tzŭ Ch'i tells his friend that human music is only one kind of sound. There is also the music of earth, and above it the music of heaven. He says the breath of the universe is wind, which sometimes lies still and sometimes blows, and then every hollow in the land roars.

Wind blowing through the hollows of hills, forests and large trees makes many sounds, from shrill to deep, loud to soft. Each hollow is compared to an opening such as a nostril, mouth or ear. Then the wind dies down and silence returns.

Tzŭ Ch'i answers his student that the music of Heaven is the wind blowing through the many holes, which all sound differently. He asks what gives each opening its own voice and gives all of them the power to sound. He then says great knowledge covers everything, while small knowledge covers only a part.

The passage describes how the mind changes through a day and through a life. It moves from quick judging of right and wrong, to firm holding of what is secured, to gradual decline, and finally to a closed, dead state from which it does not recover.

Our feelings of joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, caution and regret rise and pass in turn, and we cannot tell where they come from. The passage asks whether we could ever pinpoint their exact cause in a moment.

The speaker says that the emotions depend on the self, and the self has no effect without the emotions. He admits he does not know what sets them in motion. He suspects some soul or power is behind them, though it has no visible form and he cannot prove it exists.

The passage asks whether a person prefers one part of the body over the others, and whether the body's parts rule themselves. It concludes that some single controlling principle, called a soul, must govern all the parts.

The speaker says that whether or not we understand the soul's functions does not really matter to the soul, since the soul's task ends when the body dies. He then describes life as a hard, rushed struggle that ends in death, with no chance to enjoy its results, and asks whether this is not a reason for grief.

The speaker asks whether not dying is any real gain, since the body decays and the mind decays with it, which he calls the true cause for sorrow. He then argues that people who trust only their own private judgment have no real guide. Accepting contradictory ideas without any fixed standard, he says, is as absurd as claiming to have reached Yüeh today after arriving there yesterday.

Speech only means something because it carries meaning; without that, it is no different from birds chirping. The passage asks how the Way (Tao) could be clouded enough to be called true or false, and says it is obscured by our limited understanding and by the worldly polish of speech. This clouding, it suggests, is why rival schools, the Confucians and the Mohists, argue with opposing claims.

The passage says that people who argue for opposite views each deny what the other affirms. Someone who wants to reconcile these opposites must do so by natural insight. It claims that every object is also a subject, so one cannot start from the object alone; knowing must begin from the subjective and move on to the objective.

The passage says that opposites depend on each other, so one cannot exist without the other: when one thing is born, its opposite dies, and what is possible or affirmed has its negative in the same way. Because of this, the sage drops the distinction between "this" and "that" and rests in what is beyond such distinctions.

Every "this" is also a "that," and every "that" is also a "this," so opposite viewpoints mix together. Because of this, the text asks whether the difference between subjective and objective can be said to exist at all.

The passage claims that when opposites such as subject and object, or positive and negative, are set aside, they merge into one whole, which it calls Tao, the Way. It then argues that showing a finger is not a finger, by pointing to something that is not a finger, works better than using a finger itself as the example. The same holds for a horse.

Everything is what it is because of its own nature, and it is named and known through its relation to other things. Seen from the viewpoint of Tao (the Way, the natural order of things), even a beam and a pillar, which seem different, are one and the same.

Opposites such as beauty and ugliness, or building and breaking, are treated as one and the same. From this view, nothing is truly built up or destroyed, because these states are joined into a single whole. Only the wise, it says, see all things this way by putting themselves in the place of the things they observe.

Placing oneself in harmony with things without treating them as separate objects is called Tao, the Way. Wearing out the mind by clinging to the separateness of things, instead of seeing that all things are one, is called "Three in the Morning." The passage then asks what that phrase means.

The keeper of monkeys gives them the same total of chestnuts either way, three in the morning and four at night or the reverse. The monkeys only accept the change because the order suits their feelings. Tzu Ch'i uses this to show that adjusting to how people feel can leave the real situation unchanged.

The Sage accepts opposites as one and goes along with the order of Heaven. The passage then describes three stages of human knowledge: first, a time before matter existed; second, matter without conditions; third, matter with conditions but no awareness of opposites. Once opposites appeared, Tao declined and personal bias began.

The passage uses three skilled performers to make a point about talent and pursuit. Chao Wên's music rises and falls only as a result of his playing, and the other two men were also known for their arts. Hui Tzŭ, a debater, was eager to teach his unusual views but failed to get them across, and so he ended up known only for the "hard and white" argument.

The passage says that a man's son searched his father's writings for a key to the father's principle and never found it. The author then argues that if the principle could be fixed, the speaker could be fixed too, and if it could not, nothing in the universe could be fixed. The true Sage, it adds, looks at things from their own position rather than from his own, and this is called "using the light."

The passage asks whether speech can be placed in either of a pair of opposites, such as "is" and "is not." Whichever way it is placed, it ends up counted as something real. The speaker then offers a sample of speech that belongs to neither side: if there was a beginning, there was an earlier time before it, and an earlier time before that.

The passage argues that the ideas of existence and non-existence cannot be fixed. If something exists, there must have been a time when it did not, and before that even the idea of nothing did not exist. So the speaker cannot say whether even his own words count as spoken or not.

Big and small, long and short are relative: the tip of a spikelet counts as the greatest thing, and a child who died in infancy as the oldest age. The speaker says that since all things are one, speech seems pointless. Yet speaking itself suggests speech exists, and counting "one" plus "speech" already makes two, so the logic breaks down.

Counting up from nothing never stops, so the passage says one must relate oneself to external things to avoid this endless progression. Before any conditions or definitions existed, the Tao (the Way) already was, and before definitions there was Speech. The distinctions we perceive are called the Eight Predicables.

The passage says that the true Sage (a wise ideal person) knows things beyond the bounds of the visible world without claiming to recognise them, and within those bounds he states distinctions without arguing for them. He classifies and argues only in the sense that he does not press his views. Tzŭ Yu asks how this can be.

The true Sage keeps his knowledge inside himself, while ordinary people argue to persuade one another. The passage then says that the highest things do not show themselves openly: the Tao, perfect argument, charity, honesty and courage are not displayed in words, deeds or rigid firmness.

Fixed, showy versions of virtue defeat themselves. The Way that is displayed is no longer the Way, argument misses its goal, and absolute honesty or courage loses its effect. The wisest knowledge is knowing where your knowledge ends.

The passage says that the Way (Tao) cannot be argued in words and does not announce itself. Knowing it is compared to pouring in and out without filling or emptying, done without knowing how it works. Then it turns to a story: the Emperor Yao asks Shun whether he should attack three small peoples he has long wished to subdue.

Shun tells a companion that virtue should outshine even the suns, since ten suns once shone together and lit everything. Then Yeh Ch'üeh asks Wang I whether all things are truly the same, and Wang I replies that he cannot know. Yeh Ch'üeh then asks whether anything can be known at all.

Wang I asks how anyone can be sure that knowing is not really not knowing, or the reverse. He then gives examples: damp ground harms a man but not an eel, and trees suit monkeys but not men. Since each creature has its own preferred living place and food, he asks which is the right one in an absolute sense.

Wang Ni is asked whether the Perfect Man, the ideal sage, also cannot tell what is good or bad. The question is put by Yeh Ch'üeh after Wang Ni has said that moral standards are too blurred to know for certain. The question presses the point: if ordinary people cannot know, does the sage know?

The Perfect Man, a being beyond ordinary life, is unaffected by extreme heat, cold, thunder or storms. He can rise above the world, where death and life no longer control him, so lesser harms cannot touch him at all.

Someone reports that Confucius called a true sage's way of living "wild words," but the speaker thinks they perfectly express the Tao, the Way. Chang Wu Tzu then replies that even the Yellow Emperor doubted such points, so Confucius could not know them.

The speaker tells a listener that he is rushing ahead. He points to an egg and a crossbow as examples: the listener expects a rooster to crow from the egg and roast duck from the crossbow, which are results that are far too early. The speaker asks the listener to take in what he says without fixing on any one meaning.

The Sage, a model of wisdom, stays calm and unified, ignoring rank and the changes of ages, so that even the end of the universe would not disturb him. The passage then asks whether loving life and fearing death are mistaken, comparing the fearful man to a lost child. The final line, about the lady Li Chi, is a separate story fragment.

A woman taken as a bride by the Duke of Chin first wept bitterly, but after she lived in the palace and enjoyed rich food, she regretted her tears. The speaker asks whether the dead may likewise regret having clung to life.

Waking and dreaming cannot be told apart from inside either state. People who dream of feasting wake up grieving, and people who dream of grief wake up to go hunting. Life itself may be a great dream that we only recognise as one at a final awakening, so the speaker calls even his own claim a dream.

Winning an argument does not prove that the winner is right. The passage lists the possibilities: one side is right, both are partly right, or both are wholly wrong. It concludes that no one can know which is true, so people stay ignorant of the truth.

The speaker asks who could judge a dispute between himself and another person. Anyone who shares either side's view would be biased, and anyone who shares neither would be unable to decide. So, he concludes, people cannot settle it themselves and must look to something beyond them.

Relying on something is treated as if it were not really reliance, because all things are held within one undivided unity. By adapting fully to whatever happens, a person lives out the full span of life given to them.

The passage says that if a thing is really positive or really true, it must differ from its opposite, so there is no room for argument about it. It then advises setting aside time and the distinction between right and wrong, and resting in the Infinite.

The Umbra, the faint outer shadow, is asked why it keeps changing between moving and resting. It replies that it depends on something else, which itself depends on something further, so it cannot say why it does what it does.

Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly and, on waking, cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming it is a man. He concludes that a clear boundary separates man from butterfly, and that moving between them is called metempsychosis, the passing of a soul into another body.

Human life is short, but knowledge is endless, and chasing endless knowledge with a short life wears a person out. The passage advises avoiding both fame when helping others and disgrace when looking after oneself, and taking a middle path. Doing so keeps body and mind healthy and lets a person finish their natural lifespan.

A cook is praised for his skill at butchering an ox. He replies that his skill is more than technique: he follows the Tao, the natural Way of things. At first he saw whole oxen, but after years of practice he saw only the natural joints and gaps.

The speaker says he works by mind rather than by sight. When his senses want him to stop but his mind pushes on, he relies on fixed natural principles. He follows the natural openings and gaps in the animal's body and does not force a way through joints or large bones.

A skilled cook keeps his knife sharp for years because he cuts along the natural gaps between the joints of the animal, never forcing the blade through bone. The thin edge slips into these openings, which widen as he works, so the blade meets no resistance.

The cook describes his method of carving an ox: at each hard spot he slows down, works gently, and lets the joint give way on its own. The Prince says he has learned from this how to care for his own life.

Hsien argues that a man who has lost a foot was made that way by heaven, not by people, since humans normally have two feet. He compares this to wild birds, which would rather go hungry and be free than be fed in a cage. Ch'in Shih's reply is short, and the passage does not say clearly what he means by it.

Ch'in Shih visited a dead man's funeral and found mourners grieving as if for their own parents or children. He concludes the man was not as great as he thought, because he must have encouraged that attachment, which goes against natural principles and forgets where life comes from.

Death and birth are natural events that come at their proper time, so grief has no place for those who accept them this way. The passage compares a life to fuel burning down while the fire passes on, so the fire itself never visibly ends.

Yen Hui, a disciple, says the Prince of Wei is headstrong and blind to his own faults, so his people are dying in large numbers. He recalls his teacher's view that a well-governed state may be left alone, but a badly governed one should be visited. He decides to go and try to help that state, as a doctor treats disease.
Confucius warns that Tao, the Way, must not be spread out or divided. If it is split up, it loses its unity, becomes uncertain, and brings mental disturbance that cannot be escaped.

The sages first gained Tao, the Way, for themselves before helping others. The speaker asks how someone who lacks this can concern himself with the wicked. Virtue leads to a craving for fame, and wisdom leads to quarrels, and both can harm others.

Preaching charity and duty to wicked men, before one's own virtue and sincerity have won them over, only makes them hate the preacher. Such preachers are "evil speakers," and those who speak evil of others tend to be spoken evil of in turn.

The passage warns a would-be adviser about a ruler who already loves good and hates evil. Preaching to such a prince will fail, because he will take control of the exchange and the adviser's own composure will break down. Giving way to him at the start only leads to more concessions, so the adviser will end up harmed by the violent man.

Kuan Lung Feng and Prince Pi Kan were both virtuous men who tried to help the people. Their rulers saw this as a threat and killed them to protect their own reputations. Their good conduct was the very reason they were destroyed.

Ancient rulers Yao and Yu waged wars that ruined families, yet still fought for fame and victory. If even sages failed to resist this urge, the speaker asks whether his disciple Yan Hui can succeed. Yan Hui offers his plan: a grave, calm manner, energy, and a single purpose.

Confucius warns his disciple Yen Hui that a ruler who is used to having his way may resent a show of perfection, and may not take well to higher virtues if he has already failed at basic ones. He says that insisting will get nothing, and that Yen Hui would be right outwardly but wrong inwardly. Yen Hui replies that he will stay inwardly straight but outwardly bent, following the ancient models.

The passage contrasts two kinds of service. Serving God means accepting whatever people do to you, as a child would, without worrying whether it is good or bad. Serving men means outward bowing and ceremony, done only because everyone else does it and so no one will blame you.

Yen Hui asks Confucius how to advise a ruler, and offers a plan: he will speak warnings but credit them to the ancient Sages, so he stays safe. Confucius replies that the plan has too many schemes and too little care. It may keep Yen Hui from harm, but it will not change the ruler's own heart. Yen Hui then admits he has no other idea and asks for a method.

Stop perceiving with the senses and stop the mind's own activity, so that the self becomes empty and simply responds to outside things. In that emptiness only the Tao, the Way that underlies all things, can remain. Yen Hui asks whether this is the "fasting of the heart," and the point is that giving up one's individual self is what makes this state possible.

The Master tells a disciple that success comes from entering another person's world without wounding his pride, and living there with complete indifference, without cleverness or tricks. He compares this to walking without touching the ground, and says it is easy to deceive as a human agent but not as an agent of Heaven. People know of flying with wings and wisdom with wisdom, but never of flying without wings or wisdom without wisdom, meaning true skill comes from having no conscious method.

The passage uses a window as an image. Light and scenery come into an empty room through the opening, but the landscape stays outside. The idea is that the senses can take in the world while the mind stays empty of knowledge and cleverness. Yu, Shun, Fu Hsi and Chi Chü are named as earlier sages who used this method.

A minister about to be sent on a mission to the state of Ch'i tells Confucius he is afraid. His ruler's task is important, and he expects the Ch'i ruler to take less interest in it than he does, so he feels deeply uneasy.

The speaker says that Tao alone brings a good result in any undertaking. Otherwise, failure brings punishment from outside, and success brings punishment from inside. Only a person with the needed virtue escapes punishment, whether the task succeeds or fails.

A man given a dangerous mission speaks of his distress. He says he is hot inside before he has even begun the task, and he fears punishment both if he fails and, through worry, while he works. He asks for advice on what to do.

Confucius says there are two sources of safety: Destiny and Duty. A child's love for its parents is destiny, and a subject's loyalty to his ruler is duty; neither can be escaped. The highest form of each is to serve without regard to circumstances, and the highest Virtue is to keep the heart free of joy and sorrow by accepting what cannot be changed.

A minister often serves in situations he cannot control. If he simply does his duty and forgets himself, he has no time left to care about living or dying. The point is that a person who is wholly absorbed in his task is not troubled by life or death.

Personal dealings should be sincere, and distant ones should be stated in honest, faithful terms. A go-between who carries messages of goodwill or ill will tends to exaggerate them, whether with fine phrases or harsh ones. Such exaggeration fails to convince, and the envoy is blamed for it.

Things that start out well often end badly once they are pushed too far. Contests turn from friendliness to hostility, and feasts turn from order to riot. The passage says this is true of all things: trust at the start can end in contempt, and small beginnings can lead to great endings.

Speech and action can stir up anger and conflict, much as wind stirs waves. When one side pushes the other too hard, resistance follows, often for no clear reason. Going beyond the proper limit leads to excess.

Once a settlement is made, it cannot easily be changed, so a go-between should not stray from his instructions. Instead, he should go along with events without fear and leave the outcome to Destiny. The passage is spoken as advice to Yen Ho, who is about to become tutor to a prince's son.

A man of poor natural character is described as a problem either way. If he is left to act on his own unprincipled impulses, he endangers the state. If he is restrained, the speaker's own safety is at risk. He notices other people's faults but not his own, so the speaker says he does not know what to do.

Chü Poh Yü advises a man who must serve a difficult ruler to adapt outwardly while keeping his inner standard intact. He warns that outward adaptation must not sink inward, or the inner standard must not show outwardly, since either path leads to ruin or to being disliked. The safest course is to match the ruler's behaviour, so the man reaches him without giving offence.

The praying mantis raises its arms to block a passing chariot, not realizing it is far too weak for the task, and it thinks its own boldness is admirable. The point is a warning: if you keep showing off your superiority to others, you are likely to come to harm.

Keepers of tigers avoid feeding them live prey or whole animals, because these stir up the tigers' fury. They watch feeding times closely to keep the animals calm. The passage says people, like tigers, can be managed if handled properly but become dangerous when enraged.

The passage gives a story about a groom who, meaning well, brushes flies off a horse and so makes it break its bridle and hurt itself. The point is that good intentions do not help if they are not joined with real care. The passage then turns to an artisan who sees a sacred tree on his journey, a scene the excerpt leaves unfinished.

A carpenter walks past a huge, impressive tree without looking at it. His apprentice is amazed and asks why. The question is left open in this part of the passage, so the reader sees only the apprentice's wonder and the master's indifference.

The master says a certain tree is worthless for any use. It would sink as a boat, rot as a coffin, break as furniture, sweat as a door, and rot as a pillar. Because it has no use, it has been allowed to live to its great age.
A carpenter dreams that a tree speaks to him. The tree says that fruit trees are harmed because their usefulness brings them abuse, so they die before their natural time.

The speaker, a sacred tree, says he long aimed to be useless and so survived dangers and became useful in his own way, since being useful earlier would have harmed him. He tells the critic that a person still in danger should not judge a useless tree. The apprentice then asks how a tree that aimed at uselessness became sacred.

The master is answering a student who has judged something he does not understand. He says the tree's odd survival came from a different kind of safety, not ordinary means. Testing it by normal standards would miss the point. The tree was made sacred so people would not cut it down.

Tzŭ Ch'i looks at a large tree and finds it useless: its branches are too crooked for rafters, its wood too irregular for coffins, and its leaves sting and intoxicate. He concludes that its uselessness is why it has grown so big, and that a wise man might follow its example.

The point is that useful trees are cut down because of their usefulness. Each tree is taken for a purpose tied to its size, such as monkey cages, house beams, or coffins, so none lives out its natural years. The author uses this to say that worth brings a person or thing to an early end.

Animals with white cheeks, large snouts, or people with piles were barred from sacrifices to the River God because soothsayers judged these traits unlucky. The wise, the passage says, saw these same traits as very lucky.

A hunchback named Su is described as so deformed that he is hard to imagine. Still, he earns a living by sewing and washing. Because of his deformity, he is passed over for army service and public labor, and he even gets extra grain when it is handed out.

Chieh Yü, a wandering eccentric, mocks Confucius as a fallen phoenix who can neither look ahead nor back. He says a sage's work depends on the times: when the Way prevails, sages carry out their mission, and when it does not, they only save themselves and barely escape harm.

Useful things get cut down. Fat burns because it can be burned, and cinnamon trees are felled for their food. So people know the value of what is useful, but not the value of what is useless. The lesson is that being valued for use can bring harm.

Wang T'ai, a man with a maimed body, teaches without speaking, yet people who visit him leave full. Confucius, the famous teacher, concludes that Wang T'ai's mind is complete even though his body is not, and he resolves to learn from him and bring others along.

Ch'ang Chi asks how a mutilated man can still be called a master, and Confucius answers that his mind is not touched by life or death, or even by the collapse of heaven and earth. It stays whole and unchanged, and it can change other things without losing its own nature.

Seen as sameness, all things are one, so differences like the liver and the gall, or two rival states, do not matter. Wang T'ai, a man missing a foot, ignores what the senses report and sees all things as one. To him, losing a toe is no more than losing a little mud.
Ch'ang Chi asks why people admire a man who only works on perfecting his own mind. Confucius replies that a person should look for stillness, not movement, because only what is still can calm others.

Pines and cedars are the only trees that stay green in winter and summer, which is how the earth's favour shows in them. Heaven's favour, the passage says, went only to the sage-kings Yao and Shun, who ordered their own lives and so ordered the lives of everyone else.

Physical courage, trained by discipline, can remove fear so completely that a man will face an entire army alone. The passage argues that someone who understands that all things are one, and that the soul lasts forever, goes further still. He waits for his time, and people come to him without any effort on his part.

Shên T'u Chia, a man who had lost his toes as a punishment, was studying with the same teacher as Tzŭ Ch'an, a statesman of Chêng. Tzŭ Ch'an proposed that whoever left the lesson first should let the other stay behind, which shows he thought himself above a man with a mutilated body.

Tzŭ Ch'an, a state minister, confronts a fellow student in the lecture-room. He says they should take turns leaving first, and he accuses the other of showing no respect to a minister. He asks whether the other thinks himself Tzŭ Ch'an's equal.

Shên T'u Chia is answering a man who thinks his rank as a minister should give him precedence among the students. Shên T'u Chia says a clear mirror gathers no dust, so any dust means the mirror was not clear. He adds that a person who long keeps company with the wise becomes faultless, so the other man's fault must lie in himself.

Tzŭ Ch'an answers a man sarcastically: he says the man will soon be copying Yao, a legendary sage-king, and that he should first deal with his own faults. The speaker is mocking someone who presumes to judge others' virtue while having faults of his own.

Shên T'u Chia says that many people hide their faults to avoid losing their toes, a punishment for wrongdoing, while few admit their faults and so lose them. Only the virtuous man accepts what cannot be avoided and calmly accepts his fate.

A man who has lost his toes says he no longer minds being mocked, because years of study with his Master have taught him to stop caring about outward things. He tells his companion Tzŭ Ch'an that they are now studying the inner life, so bringing up his missing toes is a fault. Tzŭ Ch'an becomes uneasy and asks the other man to stop speaking.
A man named Shu Shan No-toes, who had lost his feet as a punishment, comes to Confucius on his heels. Confucius tells him that his injury came from his own carelessness and asks why he has come.

No-toes, who lost his toes through his own carelessness, says he now values something more precious than his toes, which is his inner self. He had expected Confucius to be like Heaven and Earth, which cover and support all people, so he is disappointed. Confucius apologises and invites him in, but No-toes leaves.

Confucius tells his followers that a toeless criminal studies to atone for past wrongs, so how much more should those with no wrongs study. The toeless man then complains to Lao Tzu that Confucius seeks a reputation for clever argument, which real sages see as a prison. Lao Tzu replies that he should free Confucius from that prison by teaching him that life and death, and yes and no, are one.

Duke Ai of Lu tells Confucius about a man in Wei named Ai T'ai T'o, who has leprosy. Men who live with him like him and do not try to drive him away, and many women who have seen him say they would rather become his concubine than marry an ordinary man. A concubine is a secondary wife.

Zhuangzi describes a man who draws people to him without the usual tools of influence. He does not lecture, offers no official position or protection, and has little learning beyond his own state. Even so, many people gather around him.

The speaker, a ruler, first found a deformed man unattractive, but came to trust him completely and offered him the post of chief minister. The man accepted reluctantly and then left, and the ruler grieved over him as a lost friend.

Young pigs leave their dead mother once she no longer seems to be the mother they knew. They loved what made her who she was, not just her body. Likewise, a dead soldier's arms are not buried with him, and a man without toes has no use for boots, because the purpose of those things has ended.

Zhuangzi compares a man of perfect virtue to a father who keeps his marriageable daughter from menial work so she can focus on her beauty. The passage then praises Ai T'ai T'o, a man who says nothing yet is trusted, does nothing yet is sought after, and whose virtue shows no outward form. The Duke asks what it means for his talents to be perfect.

Life and death, success and failure, wealth and poverty, and the other pairs of opposites all come and go like the turning of a wheel of fate, and no one can say where each begins. So they should not upset a person's inner balance or enter the mind. Go along with circumstances without offending others, and this is said to make one's abilities complete.

Confucius compares a still water-level to a model for the inner mind. Still water stays calm inside and does not overflow, and calm inner harmony produces virtue. If virtue shows no outward sign, people will still be drawn to it.

A ruler says that after hearing about a perfect man, he now fears he has failed, since his rule has only harmed his state. He calls Confucius a friend rather than a subordinate. The passage then shows the Duke's taste being misled: he favours a hunchback over well-formed men.

Duke Huan of Ch'i favored a man with a large goitre, a swelling on the neck, and thought well-formed men had necks that were too thin. The point is that the Duke valued the hunchbacked man's odd appearance over ordinary good looks.

Real virtue means forgetting outward form, but people forget the wrong things and hold on to the wrong things. The truly wise need none of the usual tools: they make no plans, so they need no wisdom; they keep nothing apart, so they need no glue of sincerity; they want nothing, so they need no virtue; and they sell nothing, so they need no trade skill.

Zhuangzi says that certain people, given special qualities by Heaven, live on what is divine rather than human. They have human shape and mix with people, but lack human passions, so likes and dislikes do not affect them. When Hui Tzu asks how a man can lack passions, Zhuangzi says it is possible, and Hui Tzu cannot see how.

Chuang Tzu says a man without passions is one who does not let good and evil disturb his inner balance. He accepts whatever happens naturally and does not add to his own mortality. Hui Tzu replies by asking how a person could then have a body at all.

Tao gives a person his appearance, and God gives him his shape. Such a person does not let good and evil upset his inner nature. The speaker says the listener wastes his mind on outside things, leaning against a tree or a table and muttering with half-closed eyes.

A person who understands both what Heaven is and what humans are has reached the highest understanding. Such a person knows they came from Heaven. Knowing human limits, they accept what is known and wait for what is unknown, living out their natural lifespan without dying early. Heaven, the passage adds, works by its own nature, spontaneously and without showing itself.

The speaker says there is a weakness in their view. Knowledge depends on being fulfilled, but that fulfilment is uncertain, so one cannot be sure which parts of oneself are divine and which are human. To have reliable knowledge, one must first have pure people.

The pure men of old did not plan or aim for results, so they felt neither regret after failure nor pride after success. Because of this, they were unafraid of danger, and they slept and woke calmly. The passage presents this freedom from calculation as a sign of their closeness to Tao, the Way.

The ancient pure men accepted both life and death calmly. They neither loved living nor feared dying, and they did not try to hurry or delay either one. They played their assigned roles and waited for the end, letting nature follow its course rather than forcing it with human effort.

The passage describes the perfect man as calm and inwardly free, responding to events naturally, as the seasons change. Such a man is not moved by ordinary human affection. His benefits to later generations do not come from love of his fellow men, and a man who merely delights in people is not yet perfect.

The passage names several legendary figures and says they served rulers and carried out other people's orders rather than their own wishes. It adds that the pure men of old fulfilled their duties toward their neighbours but kept apart from them socially.

The passage describes people who lived by their inner qualities rather than outward show. They seemed modest and humble without flattering anyone, and they were independent without being extreme. They treated laws as a mere trunk and ceremonies as mere wings, meaning these were only supports for something deeper.

Those who were admired had a view of these things that turned them upside down: penal laws were seen as mercy, social ceremony as a way to get through the world, and wisdom and morality as tools to justify conforming to others. Because of this, people praised them as worthy.

Those described here saw all the things they cared about as one, and all they did not care about as one too. Within the One they belonged to Heaven, and outside it to Man, so they never fell into conflict between the two. Life and death, like day and night, follow Destiny, a law beyond human control.
A person will give up their life for a ruler they see as better than themselves. The passage asks why they would not do the same for the Supreme Ruler of Creation, the force behind all things.

Moistening stranded fish with breath or spit is far worse than letting them live in their own water. Likewise, it is better to drop praise of the sage-kings Yao and blaming the tyrant Chieh, and instead follow the Tao, the natural way of things. Tao gives life and death, so it is the best guide for both.

The point is that hiding something inside a bigger thing still leaves a chance it will be taken, since a strong man can carry off the container by night. Only if everything is hidden within the whole universe is there no place left where it could be lost.

Being born in human form is a cause for joy, and the wise take delight in what never ends. If early death, old age, and the end of life can be accepted, then so can Tao, the underlying Ultimate Cause of all things. Tao has laws and signs, yet it has no action or shape and can be passed on but not received.

The passage says that Tao, the Way, existed before heaven and earth and never changes or ages. Spiritual beings and the visible universe came from it. Figures such as Hsi Wei and Fu Hsi obtained it, and through it they ordered the universe and set up lasting principles.

The passage lists mythic and legendary figures, along with the Great Bear and the sun and moon, who each "obtained" a single thing, called "it" here. Because of it, each one achieved a lasting result, such as staying on course, ruling a region, or rising to heaven.

Nü Yü, an old man who looks young, says he gained his youthful look by learning Tao, the Way. When Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei asks whether Tao can be gained by study, the passage leaves the question open, so the main point is the idea that Tao is something one learns and may reach.

Nü Yü says he could not simply pass on the Tao, the Way, to Pu Liang I, even though Pu Liang I had the qualities of a sage and Nü Yü had the Tao but none of those qualities. Nü Yü taught him carefully and slowly, and within three days Pu Liang I had lost all concern for worldly life.

Zhuangzi describes a disciple who, through a stage-by-stage process of letting go, loses awareness of the outside world and of himself. He reaches a state beyond life and death, where he moves in step with whatever happens around him. Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei then asks how he achieved this.

Nü Yü is saying that he learned the Way from books, and that the chain of sources behind books goes back step by step: learning, investigation, application, desire to know, the unknown, the great void, and finally infinity. The chain ends at a source with no beginning or limit.
Four men agree to befriend anyone who can treat non-action as the head of his life, life as its backbone, and death as its tail. Without speaking further, they accept this and become friends at once.

A sick man, Tzŭ Yü, is badly deformed, with his back hunched and his organs out of place. Yet he says his mind is still calm. When his friend Tzŭ Ssŭ asks if he is afraid, the question is left as the closing line.

Tzu Yu, who is dying, says he has nothing to fear. He accepts death as part of nature's order: his body will change into other things, and his coming and going in life happened by the same natural law. Since he is content with this, he feels neither joy nor sorrow.

Tzŭ Lai lies dying, and his family weeps. His friend Tzŭ Li scolds the family for disturbing the body's natural change, then wonders aloud what form Tzŭ Lai will take next. Tzŭ Lai replies that he accepts whatever nature decrees, as a son obeys his parents.

A man says that if his mother ordered him to die, refusing would make him an unfilial son, since she can do him no wrong. He holds that Tao gave him his life and its stages, so the force that guided his life is also the best judge of when it should end.

Asking the maker of things for a particular form is like metal asking to become a sword: it would be refused. The speaker accepts whatever he is sent to be, forgetting the past as a man forgets a dreamless sleep.

Three friends talk about who could roam beyond the limits of space and forget existence forever, and they agree to be friends. When their friend Tzŭ Sang Hu dies, two of them sing and play the lute beside his body. Tzŭ Kung, sent by Confucius to join the mourning, objects that singing beside a corpse is improper.

Tzu Kung reports to Confucius about a group of men whose aim is nothingness and who have separated themselves from their bodies. They can sing beside a corpse without being moved, and Tzu Kung asks what kind of men they are, since no ordinary category fits them.

Confucius says these men go beyond the normal rules of life, while he stays within them, so their paths do not meet. He admits he was wrong to send a disciple to mourn with them. They see life as a growth they are freed from by death, yet they do not know where they were before birth or where they go after death.

Zhuangzi describes people who rise above worldly concerns: they set aside their senses and feelings, ignore ordinary social rules, and do not care what others think. Tzu Kung asks why, then, they should keep to the rules. Confucius replies that Heaven has fixed him to those rules, though he and Tzu Kung may still find a way out.

Confucius says that people need the Tao, the Way, just as fish need water, so that they can live in peace. He also says that divine men seem divine to people but ordinary to heaven, and the reverse holds too.

Mêng Sun, a man in the state of Lu, was praised as the best mourner even though he did not truly grieve, did not wail, and only wore mourning clothes. Confucius replies that Mêng Sun did what was required and had moved toward wisdom, since he could not do less, even though he was in fact doing less.

Mêng Sun, a man in the story, does not know where life comes from or where it goes, or when death will come. He accepts life and death calmly, the way one accepts a passage into the unknown. The living and the dead cannot know each other, and waking and dreaming may not be so different. He treats death as a return home, and he weeps with others when they weep.

A person cannot be sure that the self they feel themselves to be is their true self. Dreams show the problem: you may dream you are a bird or a fish, and you cannot tell while dreaming whether you are awake. The passage then urges giving up awareness of change to reach the one, the divine.

Hsü Yu asks why I Erh Tzŭ wants to stay in a place where the sages' rules of charity, duty, right and wrong have been cut away. I Erh Tzŭ says he would still like to be near its edge. Hsü Yu replies that a man who has lost his eyes, or whose eyes are clouded, cannot appreciate beauty or tell colours apart.

I Erh Tzŭ says that the famous cases of disregarding beauty, strength and wisdom came about through a process of being worn down and reshaped. He then suggests that God might likewise remove his mutilations and give him a new face, making him fit to be a follower of the speaker.

Hsü Yu says the Master he serves helps all things without thinking of it as duty, blesses generations without calling it charity, and shapes all things without counting himself skilled. Yen Hui then says he has got rid of charity and duty, which Confucius asks him to explain.

Yen Hui says he has dropped his body and his reasoning and so become one with the Infinite. Confucius responds that if this is true, he wishes to follow him. The passage then turns to a separate story: the friends Tzu Yu and Tzu Sang, where Tzu Yu hears his friend is gravely ill after ten days of rain and brings food to visit him.

Tzŭ Sang, who is in great poverty, tries to find someone to blame. He decides neither his parents nor Heaven and Earth would single him out for suffering. So he concludes that Destiny, or fate, must be the cause.

Zhuangzi contrasts two kinds of rulers. Shun worked hard at charity and succeeded in government, yet he never got beyond artificial effort. T'ai Huang, by contrast, was natural and unforced in sleep and waking, and never became artificial, even with genuine wisdom and virtue.

Chieh Yü says that ruling people by fixed laws and regulations is a false method and cannot work, as hard as wading through the sea. The truly wise ruler does not focus on outward rules. He first improves himself, and his inner virtue then lets him achieve his aims.

A bird flies high to escape traps, and a mouse digs deep to escape being smoked out. The speaker asks whether a person is less clever than these creatures, a question put to a man who asked how to govern the empire.

A sage sends away a visitor who has asked him about governing the empire. He says he has just been made a man, which is enough for him, and he would rather float off to a place beyond all directions, a realm of nothingness, than be bothered with rule.

A ruler is advised to quiet the mind, stop forceful action, and go along with the natural course of things without putting himself first, and then the empire will be well governed. When Yang Tzu Chu asks whether a man who is bold, understands the order of things, and works hard at following the Tao would make a wise ruler, the passage leaves the answer open.

Lao Tzu says that a wise ruler is not admired for skills or talents, since those bring the holder trouble. He gives examples: a tiger's beautiful skin, a monkey's cleverness, and an ox's obedience all lead to their being caught or tied up. Yang Tzu Chü then asks what a wise man's government does consist of.

A wise ruler's goodness spreads across the whole land, yet he does not seem aware of it, and the things it touches do not notice it either. It works in many forms, gives joy to all things, and rests on no firm foundation.

Lieh Tzu visits a fortune-teller in Cheng who can predict people's fates exactly, and people there avoid him. After seeing him, Lieh Tzu tells his teacher Hu Tzu that he now sees something more perfect than the Tao he used to admire.

Hu Tzŭ tells his student Lieh Tzŭ that he has only taught surface matters, not the core of Tao, and that forcing Tao on people only exposes the teacher. He then lets Lieh Tzŭ bring a friend to see him. Afterward the friend, Chi Han, says Hu Tzŭ is doomed and will die within ten days, because he looks like wet ashes, which means lifeless and without spirit.

Lieh Tzu's teacher, Hu Tzu, is a seer who appears to be dying. Hu Tzu says he showed only a still, calm surface and hid the living power within. On the next visit, Chi Han says the teacher will recover, because he saw that Hu Tzu's inner vitality had returned.

Hu Tzŭ, a physiognomist who reads character from faces, tells his student Lieh Tzŭ to bring the man back. He claims he showed a calm, grand look but let a little life-force show at his heels, so the visitor could see he had some. Chi Han, a fellow reader of faces, then says he cannot read Hu Tzŭ because his appearance changes from day to day, and asks that he become steady first.

Hu Tzu, a seer, tells a visitor that his mind was calm and still, like deep water, and that the abyss has nine names, of which he gives three: the whale's depths, still water and moving water. When the visitor Chi Han saw him the next day, he panicked and ran off. Hu Tzu sent Lieh Tzu after him, but Lieh Tzu could not catch him.

Hu Tzu says he showed himself to a man as the Tao, the force behind all things, looked before time began: an empty, self-existing blank. The man did not recognize him, grew confused and frightened, and ran away.

Lieh Tzu, convinced he still lacked real knowledge, withdrew from the world for three years. He lived simply at home, dropped artificial ways, and stayed calm amid confusion. The passage adds that fame comes to such inaction as spirits come to the boy who plays the dead man in ritual.

The passage says that a ruler gains authority by doing nothing active, letting others act while staying unmoved himself. The ideal person is like a mirror: he takes in things without grasping or refusing them, keeps nothing, and so can master outward matters without being harmed.

Two rulers of the seas, Shu and Hu, wanted to repay the kindness of Hun Tun, the ruler of the centre. Since he had no openings for seeing, hearing, eating and breathing like other beings, they bored one each day. On the seventh day, Hun Tun died.
