Natural growths such as joined toes and extra fingers are useless additions to the body. In the same way, adding charity and duty to others to a person's inner nature is not the true Tao (the natural Way). Such additions are harmful, and they get in the way of clear thinking.

Those with unusually sharp eyesight get confused by the five colours, and fuss over fine shades and differences between greens and yellows. Those with unusually sharp hearing do the same with the five musical notes and the pitch-pipes. Li Chu and Shih K'uang, famous for their senses, are given as examples.

Those who force virtue such as charity, or who argue over fine verbal distinctions, do useless work that wins them fame or empty debate. Tsêng and Shih are given as examples of the first kind, and Yang and Mih of the second. Anything added to or turned away from nature is therefore not part of the highest perfection.

The main point is that a person who reaches this perfection accepts things as they naturally are and does not try to change them. Just as a duck's short legs or a crane's long legs cannot be altered without causing suffering, nothing in a person's nature should be cut off or stretched, and so sorrow is avoided.

Deliberate charity and duty to others, the passage argues, are not part of our natural human makeup. They cause suffering: the charitable grieve over the world's troubles, while the uncharitable damage natural order in pursuit of rank and wealth. Yet people have made much of them for centuries.

Tools and outside aids, such as measuring instruments, cords, glue, ceremonies, music and moral teaching, damage the natural state of things. The passage claims that people who rely on these to make things right or satisfy the mind spoil what is naturally there.

Things have their own nature, just as curved things need no arc and straight things need no line. Nothing has to be fixed on from outside to make it what it is. So the writer asks why charity and duty to others should be attached to the Tao from outside, since that would only cause people doubt.

Shun, a legendary ruler, promoted charity and duty to one's neighbour to win control of the empire, and people have spent their lives chasing these virtues ever since. The passage asks whether these virtues are what change human nature.

Outside influences, not man's own nature, have changed people since ancient times. Each kind of person dies for what they value most: a petty man for gain, a superior man for fame, a man of rank for his family's honours, and a Sage for the world. Their goals differ, but each sacrifice harms their nature in the same way.

Tsang was reading and Ku was competing in feats of strength when their sheep were lost, yet both lost them. Poh I died for fame and Robber Chê died for gain. The author argues that both men harmed their lives in the same way, so there is no reason to praise one and blame the other.

Dying for charity or duty is called noble, while dying for gain is called low, even though the death is the same. Yet in harm done to life and nature, the robber Chê and the sage Poh I are alike, so the difference between noble and low makes no real sense. Zhuangzi says that even matching the moral virtue of Tsêng or Shih, or the taste of Yü Erh, would not count as true perfection.

Perfection, in this view, is not about caring for others or doing one's duty to them. It comes from following TAO, the natural way of things, and yielding to their natural conditions. True keen hearing or sight means perceiving one's own nature, not merely perceiving other people.

A person who looks to others rather than to himself, and takes what belongs to others, ends up becoming someone else. The speaker says that, aware of his own lack of Tao (the Way), he neither practises charity and duty to others nor falls into this error.

Horses are naturally suited to open land: their hoofs and coats protect them from cold, and they graze, drink and run freely. Palaces are of no use to them. The passage then introduces Poh Loh, who claims he knows how to manage horses.

Trainers branded, bound, starved, and whipped horses until many died. A potter then says he shapes clay as he wishes, using compasses and squares, which sets up a contrast between forcing a creature and working with a material.

The passage argues that people praise skilled craftsmen for shaping horses, clay and wood, yet those materials may not want such shaping at all. The writer says good government should instead rest on the basic instincts all people share, such as making clothes and growing food, which he calls "Heaven-sent."

In this passage, people in an early age lived simply and in harmony with nature. They had no roads, boats or bridges, and they lived alongside birds and beasts as one whole. Without knowledge or evil desires, they stayed in their natural, good condition.

In this passage, the sages are blamed for bringing trouble to the world. Their promotion of charity and duty to others is said to have created doubt among people, and their excessive attention to music and ceremony is said to have split the empire apart.

The main point is that the arts of civilisation, such as ritual vessels, court regalia, charity, ceremony, decoration and music, would not be needed if natural things were left whole. The passage argues that these man-made practices only exist because nature has been damaged or abandoned.

Breaking up the natural wholeness of things to make useful objects is the mistake of the craftsman. Destroying the Tao, the natural way, in order to practise charity and duty to others is the mistake of the sage. Both are seen as harmful interference with what is natural.

Horses live naturally on grass and water, and they show their moods only by rubbing necks or kicking. Once bridled and bitted, they learn spite, biting and resistance, so their natural ways are corrupted. The text blames this on Poh Loh, a horse trainer.

In the passage's view, people were content when they were simple: they rested without purpose, ate, and were satisfied. The sages then imposed ceremonies, music, charity and duty, and this made people want knowledge and compete for gain. The sages are blamed for causing this.
Locks and cords only protect against small thieves. A strong thief simply carries off the whole chest, so the careful precautions that people call clever end up helping the strong thief.

The writer claims that what the world calls cleverness and wisdom only helps strong thieves. To show this, he gives the example of the State of Ch'i, where a large area was full of fishing nets, traps and ploughed fields, so that its people and land were widely used and kept under control.

Within a state's borders, every temple, shrine, district and village was run by the rules set down by the Sages, the ideal wise rulers of old. The sentence then turns with "Yet one morning," so the passage breaks off just as a sudden change is about to come.

T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ killed the ruler of Ch'i and seized the state, along with the sages' methods of government. He then lived as comfortably as the legendary rulers Yao and Shun, and his descendants held Ch'i for twelve generations. The passage asks whether this theft was really a way of protecting himself from the consequences of the theft.

The main point is that the wisdom and cleverness the world admires serve only to protect strong thieves, not to protect the good. Four famous sages were executed anyway, so their wisdom did not save them. A follower of the robber Chê then asks whether thieving also has a Tao, or way.

Chê, a notorious robber, argues that the Tao, the Way, is present even in robbery, since robbers need wisdom, courage, shrewdness and a sense of fair shares. From this the passage concludes that the Sages' teachings serve robbers as much as good men, and that because good men are few, the Sages do little good and great harm.

The passage claims that trouble often comes from the things meant to prevent it. It gives examples: when the lips are gone, the teeth suffer; a weak wine from Lu led to the siege of Han Tan; and the rise of sages brought the rise of great robbers.

The passage argues that sages' rules and skills help thieves as much as they help rulers. Robbers become more dangerous when the sages' tools of government are used by them. It concludes that removing the sages would end robbery, and that more sages would only increase the gains of great robbers.

Tools meant to make things fair or honest, such as scales, seals and moral virtues, can be stolen or abused too. The passage suggests that the same means used to protect order can also be used by thieves.

The passage says that a small thief who steals a purse is punished, while a man who steals a whole state becomes a prince. The rulers, it argues, also take charity, duty and the wisdom of the Sages along with the state, so the sages' virtues end up serving the thief.

The passage argues that the tools of government, such as rules, standards and punishments, only help thieves and robbers do more harm. Punishments and rewards do not stop such men, and the Sages (wise rulers) are blamed for this. The closing saying compares government tools to fish in water: they cannot be handed over to others.

The passage argues that the troubles of society come from its rules and tools, such as wisdom, valuables, tallies, measures and music. Remove these, the author says, and people will return to their natural goodness, stop fighting over things, and be ready to receive the Tao, the natural way of the universe.

The passage argues that people act best when left to their own nature, not guided by outside rules. It names skilled or moral figures, such as Li Chu (keen-sighted), Kung Ch'ui (a master craftsman) and the teachers Tsêng, Shih, Yang and Mih, and says that removing their influence lets each person's natural ability and virtue come out.

If each person kept their senses and knowledge to themselves, the world would avoid confusion and doubt. The passage criticizes named thinkers and skilled men for putting their own virtue on show, which stirs up arguments that settle nothing. It ends by pointing back to an earlier age when people used knotted cords for records, meaning a simpler time with less display of cleverness.

The passage praises an earlier time when people were content with simple food and clothing and lived peacefully, so that they never visited even close neighbours. It contrasts this with the present, when anyone can stir people up by claiming a sage is nearby.

The passage says that when rulers want knowledge too much and neglect the Tao (the Way, the natural order that Taoists value), people rush off on errands, neglecting their families and duties. Rulers who chase knowledge while ignoring the Tao will bring the whole empire into confusion.

Clever tools for catching birds, fish and beasts require much skill, yet they bring chaos to the creatures they catch. In the same way, the subtle word-games of debaters, about hardness, whiteness and similar qualities, need much skill, yet they plunge the world into doubt.

Great disorder, the passage says, comes from people wanting to know more. Everyone reaches for what they do not yet know and ignores what they already know. Everyone also tries to belittle what they are not good at, and never what they are good at.

The passage says that the pursuit of knowledge has thrown the world into disorder. Heaven, earth and the seasons are disturbed, and living things no longer keep their natural state. Simple, honest people are pushed aside, while clever deceivers are raised up. Quiet non-action has been replaced by arguing, and the arguing has brought confusion.

Government that "lets alone" is meant to guard people's natural character and virtue from being spoiled. The argument is that if nature is not spoiled, there is no need for rulers to interfere. The passage gives two examples: Yao's rule made people too happy, and Chieh's made them too sorrowful, and both left people unsatisfied or discontented. Such feelings, it says, undermine virtue, and without virtue an empire cannot be stable.

The passage says that when people are pushed around by joy and sorrow and lose their inner balance, they fail in both thinking and acting. From this came the urge to outdo others, and then figures like Robber Chê. Rewards and punishments could never be enough to set things right.

Men have spent their time fighting over rewards and punishments, leaving no leisure to fit themselves to the natural conditions of life. The passage adds that over-refining the senses or virtues, such as sight, hearing, charity and duty, leads to excess and distortion.

Excessive refinement of ceremony, music, wisdom and cleverness each produces its own harm, such as losing sight of the true goal or spreading vice. These eight things do no damage if people live in line with their natural condition. If they do not, the same eight things become obstacles that throw the world into disorder.

The passage argues that the perfect man, if forced into power, should rule through inaction, letting things follow their natural course. Only someone who treats the state as his own body, respecting and loving it, is fit to support or govern it.

The speaker says that if he can avoid harming his body and senses, and sit still in silence, then the natural powers of heaven will respond and all things will grow without effort. With such inaction he has no time to govern the world. The passage then records a question to Lao Tzu about how hearts can be kept in order if the empire is not governed.
Lao Tzu warns against interfering with the natural goodness of a person's heart. He says that pressing the heart down or stirring it up both lead to disaster.

Gentle treatment can soften even a hard heart, but forcing it by cutting or polishing makes it swing to extremes, burning hot or freezing cold. The heart moves swiftly and freely, and no barrier or bond can hold it.

The Yellow Emperor is said to have first mixed charity and duty to others into people's natural goodness. Yao and Shun then worked so hard at feeding people and making laws that they wore themselves out, yet still failed. Their punishments of rebels and officials did not fix matters either.

Once rival schools of thought appeared, such as the Confucianists and Mihists, the empire fell into conflict, deceit and slander. People then lost their original goodness and rushed after knowledge. The passage blames the rise of these teachings for the decline.
Forcing people through physical torture, the passage says, throws the whole empire into chaos. It places the blame on those who meddle with the natural goodness of the human heart.

Zhuangzi says that when rulers and people suffered chaos, punishment and death, the Confucian and Mohist teachers still preached their doctrines, even while people were in chains. He asks that the wisdom of the sages and charity be shown not to be tools of punishment. Until then, he says, Tsêng and Shih may be seen as forerunners of the tyrants Chieh and Chê.

A ruler comes to a hermit on Mount K'ung-t'ung and asks how to reach perfect Tao, the Way. He wants to use the powers of heaven and earth to grow harvests, feed his people, and protect all living things.

Kuang Ch'eng Tzu tells the ruler that he wants to use the original, whole nature of things while trying to control the forces that break it apart. Since the ruler has governed, he says, nature has been disturbed: rain falls early, leaves drop early, the sun and moon dim, and flatterers speak everywhere. So perfect Tao cannot be spoken of.

The Yellow Emperor, a legendary ruler of China, gave up his throne and retreated to a simple hut to live in seclusion. After three months he went back to visit Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ, a sage he had sought out before.

The Yellow Emperor asks the hermit Kuang Ch'eng how to preserve the self so that it lasts. Kuang Ch'eng is pleased by the question and begins to teach him about perfect Tao, the Way, saying its essence is deep and hidden.
Stop looking, listening and thinking, and keep the mind still and pure. The passage claims that by doing this the body takes its proper form, keeps its vital energy, and lives for ever.

Look after your inner self and shut out outside distractions, since too much knowledge is harmful. Do this, and everything else will thrive on its own. The speaker says that by keeping to this for twelve hundred years, his body has not decayed.

The speaker says that the self is eternal and infinite, though people wrongly think it is mortal and limited. He adds that those who follow Tao, the Way, rule in this life and after death, while those who do not return to earth as dead matter.

In this passage, the Spirit of the Clouds says that living things come from dust and return to it, but he himself lasts forever. When he meets the Vital Principle, a figure of life energy, the Principle is slapping his ribs and hopping about. He says he is only strolling and does not stop.
The Spirit of the Clouds had asked a question and let it drop. Three years later he met the Vital Principle again on the road and, delighted, asked whether the other had forgotten him.

A questioner bows and asks the Vital Principle for guidance. The Principle replies that it drifts along without aim, simply waiting for events, so it has nothing to teach. The Spirit of the Clouds says it too drifts, but people depend on its movements, so it asks for advice.

The Vital Principle blames the troubles of nature and society on bad government. The Spirit of the Clouds asks what he should do about it. The Vital Principle tells him to go back, saying the trouble lies in his own meddling. The Spirit then asks for advice.
Stop acting, and the world will set itself right on its own. Let go of knowing and of distinctions, merge with the infinite, and empty the mind until it is nothing.

Things do best when they return to their natural state without deliberate knowledge, since knowledge leads them away from their original simplicity. Leave names and classifications alone, and everything will flourish by itself. The closing line adds that people like others to be the same as themselves and dislike differences.

People who choose friends only from those they like, and reject those they dislike, are doing so because they want to set themselves apart from others. The passage then asks how such people can manage to do this at all.

Ambitious men who want to rule a kingdom follow the majority to get personal gain, and that is worse than letting each person manage his own affairs. Rulers chase the rewards of power without seeing its dangers, so they are far more likely to ruin the kingdom than keep it.

Ruling people as if they were objects is not the right way to govern them, even though leaving them completely alone can also end up treating them that way. Those who see this are not limited to ruling the empire. They can move freely across the world, and this freedom sets them apart from others, which the passage calls the highest thing a person can reach.

The passage says that the perfect man's teaching responds to people's needs like a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound, without fixed aims or effort. His body, though, is ordinary and unremarkable. The closing question asks: if he is not set apart in any way, what is left of the distinction that sets him apart?

The passage sorts people by how they see. The perfect men of old saw what could be seen in the ordinary way. Those who saw what cannot be seen by ordinary eyes are called the chosen of the universe. The lower kinds, such as matter and the humble, still count and are not to be ignored.

Each item in this list is paired with a qualification that limits it. Human affairs, the law, duty, charity, ceremony, virtue, the Tao, and God are each described as needing attention, action, or some modification. The passage seems to say that every concept, even the highest, still has some practical side that cannot be ignored.

The sage is described as doing many things without grasping at them: he looks up to God without asking for help, follows virtue and duty without hoarding them, and takes part in affairs without clinging to them. The closing line sums up the idea: he neither acts nor refrains from acting in a fixed way.

Without divine enlightenment a person cannot be truly pure, and without a clear grasp of Tao (the Way, the natural order of things) that purity stays out of reach. Someone enlightened by neither is in a bad state.

The passage says there are two kinds of Tao, or way: the way of Heaven and the way of man. The way of Heaven rests on not acting and going along with things, while the way of man rests on acting and getting tangled up. Heaven's way is basic, and man's way is incidental, and the gap between them is large.

The passage says that the universe, however large and full of things and beings, runs by fixed laws, and that rule over all of it comes from sovereignty. Sovereignty starts in virtue and ends in God, so it is called divine. In the past, the empire was ruled by inaction, which the passage calls simply the virtue of God.

When words, boundaries, abilities and outlook each match the Tao (the natural way of the universe), the ruler governs rightly, duties are clear, officials do their work well, and all things respond. The passage says that order in society follows from order in these things when they are aligned with the Tao.

In this passage, Tao and virtue are presented as a chain running from God down to human life. Virtue links God and people, and Tao spreads through all creation. People act on outward circumstances and use their natural skill to build civilised life, which is tied to duty, then virtue, then Tao, and finally God.

Rulers of old who had no desires of their own kept the realm in good order by doing nothing forced, and so the people lived in peace. The passage says that a unified, unforced way of acting can accomplish everything, and that Tao, the Way, covers and supports all things.

Each term is redefined in terms of inaction and following the natural way. Acting without deliberate effort is what "God" means, and speaking without forcing is "Virtue." Real strength, completeness and perfection come from holding to virtue, following Tao (the Way), and not opposing the natural tendencies of things.

A person who fully grasps these ten points widens his heart and so takes in all creation. Such a person does not care for wealth, fame, long life, early death, success, or failure. His greatest glory is knowing that all things are one and that life and death are only two stages of the same existence.

Metal and stone can ring only when struck, and so all things need an outside cause to bring out what they hold within. The man of complete virtue stays passive toward events around him, keeps his original nature, and his virtue opens his heart so that others come to him for shelter.

Form needs the Tao (the Way, the underlying order of the universe) to have life, and life needs virtue (inner power or character) to have intelligence. The passage says that keeping one's form, living out one's life, and realising the Tao is complete virtue. Such a person acts naturally, without planning, and others follow him.

The passage describes a figure, here called the Tao-like being, who sees and hears where others cannot, perceiving light in darkness and harmony in stillness. Because this figure stands in right relation to all things, it can meet their needs and bring every thing, large or small, to rest. A short story about the Yellow Emperor losing his magic pearl follows.

Hsü Yu says that Yeh Ch'üeh, though clever and good by nature, is misguided. He tries to reach the divine through human effort, and he does not know the source of wrong. He relies on the artificial, lacks inner unity, and is controlled by his surroundings and by things.

Yao, a legendary ruler, visits Hua, and the border-warden offers him long life, wealth and many sons. Yao refuses each blessing. The point is that he rejects the usual goods a person might wish for, so the warden's good wishes do not move him.

The passage tells how a border official (the warden) answers the sage Yao, who has refused the gifts of many sons, wealth and long life. The warden argues that sons, wealth and long life bring no trouble if each is given his proper role and wealth is shared. He ends by saying the true sage lives simply and without care, like a quail or a young bird.

The passage describes a wise man who moves through the world without leaving a trace. If the Tao (the natural way of things) prevails, he lives in harmony with all things; if not, he quietly cultivates virtue in seclusion. After a thousand years he rises on white clouds to a realm beyond the three evils, where he rests in eternity. The border-warden then walks away when Yao, a legendary emperor, asks him a question.
Poh Ch'êng Tzŭ Kao was a minister under the legendary ruler Yao. When Yao passed the empire to Shun, and Shun passed it to Yü, Poh Ch'êng Tzŭ Kao gave up his fief and became a farmer.

Yü, a legendary ruler, visits a man he finds farming and politely asks why he gave up his position as a vassal lord when power passed from Yao to Shun and then to Yü. The man has stepped away from office and taken up farming.

Tzŭ Kao says that under the ruler Yao, people worked and behaved well without rewards or punishments, but now, with rewards and punishments, they still are not good. Its last lines say that before anything existed, even nothingness did not, and then came a time without names.

In this passage, the One is the first stage of existence. It has no form. When things receive what allowed them to come into being, that receiving is called virtue. The formless force that divides into separate things without gaps is called destiny.

Life-giving movement produces living things, and each takes a form. When the form holds its spirit, the result is that thing's nature. Cultivating that nature returns a person to virtue, and perfecting it makes one like all things at the beginning, free of conditions.

Confucius asks Lao Tzu whether people who follow the Way by fixed rules of right and wrong, possible and impossible, should be called sages. The rules are compared to the schoolmen's habit of separating hardness from whiteness, as if these qualities could be hung on different pegs. The first part says that being joined with the universe without thinking about it is divine virtue.

Lao Tzu says that skill in a craft wears out both body and mind. Hunting dogs get caught because of their abilities, and monkeys are captured because of their cleverness. He adds that Ch'iu cannot understand what he means and cannot put it into words.

Many people have a head and feet but no real mind or perception. Life, death, and movement are not under human control, but self-cultivation is. Whoever is unaware of outside things and of the divine is also unaware of their own self, and so joins the human with the divine.

Confucius (here called Kung) describes the advice he gave the Prince of Lu, which was to be decorous, thrifty, and fair in choosing officials. He says this should leave the prince unopposed. Chi Ch'ê mocks the idea, comparing it to a mantis trying to stop a moving carriage, which would never succeed.

In this part of the dialogue, one speaker warns that a person who acts in a showy way is like someone who builds a high tower and displays his riches for all the neighbours to stare at. The listener, Chiang Lü Mien, admits he is foolish and asks to be taught the right way to act.

Chi Ch'ê says the perfect Sage rules by shaping people's hearts so that they improve their conduct and work for the common good, without them noticing. Such a ruler needs no lessons from the ancient sage-kings Yao and Shun, because he lines the people's desires up with virtue.

In this story, Tzu Kung, a disciple of Confucius, sees an old gardener hauling water by hand in a pitcher. He offers a machine that would water far more land with less work, and the gardener asks what it is.

Tzŭ Kung is describing a device to someone who asked about it. It is a wooden lever, heavy at the back and light at the front, that lifts water from a well in a continuous flow, and it is called a well-sweep.

A gardener refuses to use a labour-saving machine. He says his teacher taught that clever tools lead to clever dealings, then to a scheming heart, then to a restless spirit, which cannot carry the Tao. He says he knows this, but would be ashamed to use such tools.
Tzu Kung, a disciple of Confucius, was embarrassed and fell silent after a gardener spoke to him. When the gardener asked who he was, Tzu Kung answered that he was a follower of Confucius.

A teacher rebukes his student Tzu Kung for chasing fame, showing off his learning, and trying to be seen as a sage. He tells him to forget himself and first govern his own self before trying to govern others. Tzu Kung is embarrassed and leaves, and only recovers his composure after a long journey.

The speaker says he had not known about this other man. He reports the Master's view that a plan is judged by whether it can be carried out and whether it will certainly succeed. In the Sage's way, the least effort brings the greatest success.

A person who aims at Tao first perfects his virtue, then his body, then his spirit, and this is the Sage's way. Such a man does not seek success, profit or skill, and he does not act or react to the praise or blame of others.
Praise and blame from the world do not help or harm the person described. Such a person is called perfectly virtuous, while the speaker says he himself is only driven by his impulses.

Confucius says that a man who studies the "ante-mundane," meaning what came before the world, knows only a little. Confucius calls that knowledge not worth having for himself or his listener. When asked where he is going, the man replies that he is heading to the ocean.

Chun Mang describes how a sage rules: officials stick to their own duties, capable people are kept in work, and the people's views are heard and acted on. People manage their own words and deeds, so the realm stays peaceful. When Yüan Fêng then asks about the man of perfect virtue, the sage's government is the answer's starting point.

Chun Mang describes the man of perfect virtue as someone who has no worries and no fixed ideas of right, wrong, good or bad. He is at peace when others prosper, and people turn to him as lost children turn to a mother. He has plenty but does not know where it comes from.

Chun Mang says the divine man, unseen, follows his destiny and nature and is at one with heaven and man. Two onlookers judge the king Wu Wang inferior to the legendary sage-king Yü, and blame him for the troubles that follow.

Mên Wu Kuei asks whether the empire was already well governed when Yü the Great began to rule, or whether Yü first had to end disorder before governing. The question is a request for information, and it is put to a teacher.

The speaker argues that if the world had been well governed, there would have been no need for Yü, the legendary flood-taming king, to fix anything. Just as wigs are for bald men and doctors for the sick, such heroic remedies only show that something was already wrong.

In this old golden age, people did good things without knowing they were doing good. Rulers were like guiding lights, not active governors, and people lived free and natural. Their goodness left no record, because they never thought of it as a virtue.

A true son does not simply agree with his parents, and a true minister does not simply praise his ruler. Blind agreement and praise are what the world calls disloyalty, yet the world itself is never called a flatterer for agreeing with whatever it says. The author suggests the world is therefore harsher than a father and more to be respected than a prince.

People dislike being called wheedlers or flatterers, yet everyone is one of these. Because the world favours such pretence, people overlook in others what they do themselves. To adjust one's dress or manner to win favour, and agree with everyone, while refusing to admit it, is described as deep foolishness.

A person who knows he is foolish is not truly a great fool, and one who recognizes his mistake is not greatly mistaken. Great error is hard to escape, and the speaker says that since the whole world is in error, he cannot lead people even though he knows the true way.

Great truths fail to move ordinary people, so they are not taken up. Common, familiar sayings win out instead. The passage compares this to two clay instruments drowning out one metal instrument, which produces no harmony.

The speaker asks how he can guide a world that is all in error, when he knows the true path. He reasons that forcing a result he cannot achieve would only add to the error, so he should stop trying. Yet he then asks who would act if he did not, and answers with the image of an ugly father rushing to light a lamp so he can check whether his newborn son looks like him.

The main point is that two things can be treated very differently yet suffer the same loss. A tree cut into ceremonial vessels and decorated is honoured, while its stump left in a ditch is not, but both have lost the tree's original nature. Likewise, the deeds of the robber Chê and of the model men Tsêng and Shih differ greatly, yet each has lost his original nature.

Five things harm a person's natural state: the five colours dull sight, the five sounds dull hearing, the five scents dull smell, the five tastes dull taste, and likes and dislikes cloud the mind. The passage says these are life's banes, yet Yang and Mih treated them as the highest good.
Zhuangzi rejects the idea that a life of confinement can be the highest good. He argues that if fettered people count as having reached it, then caged birds would too, which he takes to be absurd.

Filling yourself with likes, dislikes, sounds and colours, and dressing up outwardly in fine clothes, is, the passage says, no sign of reaching the highest good. A bound prisoner or a caged tiger could claim the same achievement on the same grounds.

Things come about through the steady working of the Tao, the natural way. Rulers and sages gain loyalty the same way, without effort. The sage's repose is an inner calm that nothing in the world can disturb, not simple inactivity.

Still water reflects clearly, and a still mind does the same. A sage whose mind is at rest mirrors the whole universe. Stillness and inaction are the highest order of the Tao, so wise rulers rest in them, and from that rest comes good order in the world.

Repose, stillness and inaction are said to be the source of everything. Whoever understands this well, whether ruling the empire or living in retirement, gains power, wisdom and honour. Because such a person does not compete, no one in the world struggles with them for display.

Being in accord with Heaven (called God in this translation) is the secret by which a ruler governs so that people are also in accord. Agreement with people brings human happiness, and agreement with Heaven brings the happiness of Heaven.

The speaker praises a higher power, here called "my exemplar," for acting without any of the usual labels. It destroys things without seeming cruel, benefits all ages without seeming kind, is older than the oldest times without counting that as age, and shapes all things without counting it as skill. The speaker calls this the happiness of God.

Those who find happiness in the Way, or "God" in this translation, see their birth as carrying out their natural role and their death as only a physical change. They hold no grudge against heaven or people, and nothing harms or punishes them.

Calm and stillness, like the steadiness of earth, let a person hold authority over the world and be at peace with all things. Such inner repose is described as the happiness of God, and it lets the sage care for the whole empire.

A wise ruler takes the universe as his model and follows the Tao, the natural way of things. By doing nothing forced, he governs the empire with energy to spare, while active interference would exhaust him. So the ancients valued non-action.

Rulers should do nothing, and the people should do the work. If the rulers acted and the people also acted, the rulers would become like the people and lose their place over them. Each side keeps its own role, and the passage calls this an unchangeable law.

The passage says that the ancient sages did not feel troubled even though their knowledge was limited, and did not act even though their abilities were wide. It compares this to Heaven and Earth, which produce and nourish all things without effort, and to a ruler who does nothing yet is praised by the empire.

The passage says that the wise ruler is as great as heaven and earth. He is like a driver riding through the world with all creation as his team. The ruler holds the essential power and has the final say, while the minister's job is to represent the ruler.

The passage ranks five things from lowest to higher: force, rewards and punishments, formal rules, music and fine clothes, and loud weeping. It says each of these is the weakest form of its kind. It ends by saying these five should come from the inner movements of the mind rather than being forced from outside.

Ancient sages studied minor matters only after the basic principles, not before them. The passage says that rank and order, such as prince before minister, father before son, and elder before younger, belong to the natural order of the universe, and the Sage accepts them for that reason.

Heaven ranks above earth, and spring and summer come before autumn and winter. Things go through stages of growth and decay in an unending cycle. If even heaven and earth have rank and order, the passage says, then people certainly do too.

Each setting has its proper order of rank: parents in the family temple, the most honoured at court, elders in the village, and the most trustworthy in matters of business. This order belongs to Tao, the Way. Someone who ignores this order while thinking about Tao ignores Tao itself, and so cannot reach it.

The passage says that the early sages first grasped the Tao, which they linked to God. After that came a sequence of lesser things: kindness to others, public duties, names and forms, work suited to each person's ability, moral distinctions, and finally rewards and punishments. Each thing had its proper place in this order.

Names and categories arose once people with different abilities needed to be sorted for government and daily life. When knowledge and plans fail, the passage says people should rely on their natural way, which it calls perfect peace and the best government. The ancients had names for forms but did not put them first.

Early thinkers who studied the Tao went through five stages before they reached forms and names, and through nine before they could talk about rewards and punishments. The passage says that understanding the Tao comes in ordered steps, with names and judgments coming only at the end.

Jumping straight to forms, names, rewards and punishments means ignoring their source and beginning. Such government handles only the tools of rule, not its great principle. Those who argue against the Tao in reverse end up needing to be governed by others rather than governing themselves.

Ceremonies and laws were once meant to serve the people who were ruled, not to be used by rulers to feed them. Yao tells Shun that he cares for the weak, the poor, the grieving, orphans and widows, and does nothing beyond this.

Shun advises being passive, like the way heaven works without effort: the sun, moon, seasons and rain simply follow their course. Yao admits he has been muddling things by following human rules, while Shun follows heaven. The old rulers, the passage says, copied heaven and earth and did nothing more.
Confucius visits Lao Tzu to persuade him of his teachings on charity and duty to one's neighbour. Lao Tzu dismisses them as nonsense and asks whether these virtues are part of man's original nature.

In this exchange, Confucius defines charity and duty to one's neighbour as joy in all things and universal love free of self. Lao Tzu replies scornfully that universal love contradicts itself, so he rejects the definition.

The speaker urges a man to be like the regular natural world: the universe, sun, moon, stars, animals and plants all keep their own steady ways. He says the man should follow Tao, the Way, and so become perfect. He criticizes the effort to practise charity and duty to others, comparing it to beating a drum to find a runaway, and says such effort has confused people's minds.

Shih Ch'êng Ch'i visits the old sage Lao Tzu and bluntly accuses him of failing at kindness and generosity. Lao Tzu says nothing. The next day Shih Ch'êng Ch'i returns, apologizes for his rudeness, and asks why his view has changed.

Lao Tzu tells Shih Ch'êng Ch'i that he claims no special cunning knowledge or divine wisdom. He says he would accept any label others gave him, such as ox or horse. He adds that his humility is natural, not put on to appear humble. Then Shih asks him about self-cultivation.

Lao Tzu tells a visitor that his looks and manner show arrogance and haste, so people will not trust him. He then says the Tao is not too small for the greatest or too large for the smallest, and that it holds all things within its boundless depth.

The passage says that form, virtue, charity and duty to others are secondary to the spirit. Only a perfect man can judge where they belong. Such a person is not drawn into conflict, temptation or the struggle for power, and he keeps to what is essential.

The passage describes a person who stands apart from the world and its affairs, so his mind is untroubled. He follows the Tao, the natural Way, and lives in line with its inner power. He sets aside human duties of kindness to others and treats ritual and music as unimportant extras.

The world treats books as the carriers of the Tao, but books are only words. The real value lies in a thought that words cannot fully express, so the world prizes the wrong thing when it prizes the words.

The passage says that seeing and hearing only show outward form, colour, sound and noise, so they cannot reveal the essence of Tao, the Way. It adds that those who truly know do not speak about it, and those who speak do not know. The frame story then introduces a wheelwright who questions a duke reading in his hall.

The wheelwright says skill in his trade cannot be put into words or passed to his son. Working too fast or too slowly both spoil a wheel, and the right touch comes from a feel that cannot be taught. He concludes that the ancient sages' unspoken knowledge is gone, so the books the ruler studies hold only leftovers.

The passage asks what causes the regular movements of sky, earth, sun, moon, clouds and rain, and who directs them. It offers two views: that a mechanical arrangement moves them, or that they turn endlessly without stopping. It does not give a final answer.
Wu Han Chao does not explain the wind. He says a ruler's rule is good when he keeps in harmony with the Six Influences and Five Virtues, and follows the nine chapters of the Lo book.

Tang asks whether perfect charity must include filial piety, since love and affection lead to it. Chuang Tzu says it does, because charity is the broader term, so filial piety need not be named separately. He compares this to a traveller going south who cannot see a mountain in the north because he is too far away. He ends by saying it is easy to be respectfully filial but hard to be affectionately filial.

Forgetting one's duties is hard, and making others forget them is harder still. Likewise, forgetting the world is hard, and making the world forget one's influence is harder. True virtue acts without effort and works quietly across generations, so striving after human kindness and duty to others seems pointless.

Filial piety, brotherly love, charity, loyalty, truth and similar virtues are presented as deliberate efforts meant to help virtue grow. On this view, they are only pieces of a larger whole rather than the whole itself.

Perfect honour, wealth, or ambition each contains everything of its kind, so the Way (Tao) cannot be divided into parts. The speaker then recalls that the Yellow Emperor's music first frightened him, then amazed him, and finally left him speechless and overwhelmed.
The Yellow Emperor, a legendary ruler, says he is close to the truth. He claims his own work came from inspiration he received from God, and that he carried it out with great care and skill.

Perfect music develops in stages: first following human standards, then the patterns of heaven, then the five virtues, and finally natural spontaneity. Once there, it brings the seasons and all creation into harmony, with its loud and soft, full and fading tones matching the balance of Yin and Yang.
The passage describes a sound of thunder that never stops or starts, rising and falling without pause. It says the listener was frightened by this endless, shifting noise.

The speaker describes playing music that seems to fill the whole world. The sound rises and falls, moves through valleys, and affects all things, while spirits, sun, moon and stars keep to their own courses. The speaker stops only when the music naturally ends.

The speaker tells someone that, if that person had been present, they would have wanted to share the speaker's experience but could not grasp it, see it, or keep up with it. The listener is left dazed and helpless, leaning on a tree and amazed at being left behind.

The speaker describes a kind of music that is natural and spontaneous, without a fixed start or set pattern, so different listeners call it dead, alive, real or ornamental. The Sage, a wise person, responds to the world's changes while keeping to the same unchanging natural order.

The passage describes a kind of music that comes from no played instrument, so that the mind enjoys it without being called. It is said to be too subtle to hear or see, filling heaven and earth. The listener cannot grasp it and becomes confused, and the speaker's own music is said to have first caused fear, then respect, then amazement.

The main point is that a straw dog is treated with great care before it is used in a sacrifice, but once the sacrifice is over, people trample it and burn it as fuel. Someone who tried to keep the discarded dog in the same honored way would only have bad dreams.

The speaker tells a teacher that he treats the ancient sages like a dog already offered in sacrifice, something no longer of worth. He makes his disciples keep watch and sleep beside these old remains, so his teaching stays stuck in the past.

The speaker lists misfortunes that befell Confucius: being driven out of Sung and Wei, and being trapped without food near the Ch'ens and Ts'ais. He asks whether these were a dream or a nightmare. He then starts a comparison: a boat suits water and a cart suits land, and each fails on the wrong ground.

Old times and new are like water and land, and the states of Chou and Lu are like a boat and a cart. Trying to apply Chou customs in Lu is like pushing a boat over land: it brings great effort, no result, and harm to oneself. The speaker says the listener's master has not yet learned to adapt to outside circumstances.

The main point is that a well-sweep (a pole used to lift water from a well) is worked by the man who moves it, not the other way round. In the same way, the ancient rulers' rites and laws were not meant to be identical everywhere. They were meant to govern well, and they changed with the times, like different fruits that each taste good.

The fragment says that the gap between the past and the present is like the gap between the Duke of Chou, a famous ancient sage, and a monkey. It breaks off mid-sentence, so its full argument is unclear.

A village ugly woman copies the frowning of a beautiful woman, and people flee her, so she only copies the look without understanding why it was admired. The speaker says this shows that Confucius, who had not yet heard the Way, is not a success. Confucius then goes to see Lao Tzu.

The main point is that the Tao cannot be handed from one person to another like an object or a lesson. It takes in the listener a fitting inner nature, and in the teacher an outward correctness that lets it work. Where either is missing, the wise person does not try to pass it on.

Fame belongs to everyone, so a person should not take more of it than is fair. Kindness and duties to others are like inns set up by ancient wise rulers: you may stay one night, but staying long brings criticism.

The old sages, it says, used charity and duty to others only as a brief stop on their way to a free, effortless state. They lived without forcing things, owed nothing to anyone, and expected nothing back. Their inner calm showed outwardly.

People who make wealth, fame or power the center of their lives cannot bear to lose them. They hold on anxiously and never learn from the past that their pursuit is foolish, and the passage calls such people accursed by God.

Eight things, such as resentment, gratitude, giving, and power over life and death, are called tools of what is right. Only a person who can accept changes of fortune without being swept away can use them well. Anyone who cannot do this has not yet opened the door of divine understanding.

Lao Tzu says that talk of charity and duty to one's neighbour is as irritating as chaff in the eyes or mosquitoes at night. He urges people to leave the world in its original simplicity and let virtue establish itself naturally, without forceful effort.

Natural things are what they are without effort: geese are white and ravens black without washing or dyeing. Fame and reputation are not worth pursuing. Helping fish stranded on dry land with a little moisture is far worse than having them in their own waters from the start.

Confucius came back from visiting Lao Tzu and stayed silent for three days. A disciple then asked what advice he had given Lao Tzu during the visit, expecting that Confucius had criticised or instructed him.

Confucius says he was so amazed by Lao Tzu, whom he compares to a dragon, that he could not speak. Tzu Kung, Confucius's disciple, responds that a man who can sit still like a corpse yet have such power and influence must be worth seeing, and he wants to go visit him.

Tzu Kung, a disciple of Confucius, visits Lao Tzu and asks why he does not count the early rulers of China as sages. Tzu Kung says their methods differed while their reputations were the same. Lao Tzu does not answer yet. He asks Tzu Kung to explain what he means by "not uniform."

Tzu Kung says the ancient rulers did not all act the same way: each handed power on or took it by different means. Lao Tzu replies that he will explain the earlier sage-kings, starting with the Yellow Emperor, whose rule made people's affections universal and so calm that no one mourned their parents or blamed anyone.

Sage rulers Yao and Shun, in this passage, are blamed for harming the people. Under Yao, people's loyalties were turned into narrow channels, so a son who killed his parents' killer was not blamed. Under Shun, the people began to compete with one another, and the passage says early death came into the world as a result.

The passage says that after the rule of Yü, a legendary ruler, people began to act for themselves and use force. Killing robbers was no longer seen as murder, society split into classes, and the Confucianists and Mihists appeared in response. It ends by asking what has become of the proper relationships in the author's own time.

The speaker says that the rulers of the ancient Three Kings and Five Rulers held power in name only, since their order was really chaos. He argues that their cleverness disturbed the sun, moon, land, water and seasons, and harmed animals too, yet they still called themselves sages. He calls this shameless, and his listener Tzu Kung becomes uneasy.

Confucius tells Lao Tzu that he studied the six classic texts deeply and used them to advise seventy-two rulers. None of the rulers accepted his advice, and he laments how hard it is to persuade people and to teach wisdom.

Lao Tzu tells a visitor that the Six Canons, the classic texts, are only the traces left by ancient sages, much as footprints are left by a shoe. Words are such traces too, and they are not the thing that made them.

The passage says that living things reproduce in different ways, such as by mutual gazing, by answering sounds, or by self-fertilisation. These differences are fixed by nature, fate and time, which cannot be changed, stopped or blocked. The Tao, the Way that runs through all things, gives success to anyone who follows it.

Confucius says he has finally understood, pointing to how birds, fish, insects and mammals each reproduce and raise their young in their own natural way. He admits he was not enlightened for a long time, and asks how someone unenlightened could enlighten others. Lao Tzu replies that he has now attained it.

Self-conceit and showy certainty, which lead people to withdraw from society and boast and disparage others, are described as mere self-importance, the pose of hermits who have cut themselves off from the world. Preaching charity, duty, loyalty, truth, respect, thrift and humility is called ordinary moral training, put on by peacemakers, teachers and scholars.

Zhuangzi lists three kinds of talk and says each is only a surface display. Preaching about service, fame and proper rank is called mere government, done by officials who want to expand their state. Living idly by marshes and fishing is called mere inaction, done by people who have left the world. Breathing exercises and stretching are the last item, and the passage gives them no verdict.

Zhuangzi says that true self-esteem has no self-conceit, moral culture has no charity or duty to others, and government has no rank or fame. In such a state, a person forgets everything yet gains all things, and this calm is the Tao of the universe and the virtue of the Sage.

The sage is described as a kind of "negative quantity": he stays passive and does not act forcefully. Because he is still and passive, sorrow, worry and bad influences do not gather around him, so his virtue stays whole and his spirit is undamaged.

The sage is described as accepting birth and death as part of the natural order, with his life moving in step with the forces of Yin (rest) and Yang (activity). He takes no side in happiness or misfortune, does not act until moved by outside forces, and leaves past and future aside to follow the laws of God.

The passage describes a person who is free from harm, worry and planning, and who lives calmly and without strain. Such a person is said to share in the "virtue of God," meaning a natural, unforced state. The passage ends mid-quotation, with the idea that sorrow and happiness are distortions of this state.

Joy and anger lead a person away from the Tao, and love and hate destroy virtue. Perfect virtue means a heart that feels neither sorrow nor happiness. The passage ends by warning that a body that works without rest will die, and a mind that never stops will wear out and lose its power.

Still water is clear and smooth when left alone, but it becomes cloudy and stops flowing when blocked. The passage uses this as an image of inner purity: a mind that is undisturbed and does not act by force stays clear, in line with the Tao.

Keep one's special powers hidden and unused, because they are very precious. The spirit reaches everywhere, and it cannot be given a fixed form. Following the Tao means keeping the spirit whole, and then the spirit works freely and comes into right relation with God.
The pure means having nothing mixed in. The simple means nothing that harms the spirit. A person who keeps both within himself is called a divine man.

People who train their minds only in worldly learning, hoping to return to their original nature, and people who bury their higher aims in everyday concerns, hoping to reach enlightenment, are both called dullards of the earth. The passage says both approaches fail to reach their goal.

According to this passage, the ancients began with repose (stillness) and then knowledge came from it, and knowledge in turn gave rise to repose. When the two worked together, harmony and order appeared. Harmony is virtue, and order is the Tao, the Way.

Virtue, Tao, charity, duty and loyalty are presented as a chain: each comes from the one before. Music and ceremony follow, and if they are badly managed, the whole realm falls into disorder. Trying to correct others while your own virtue is clouded only harms the one you are trying to correct.

The passage describes an early age when people lived in perfect harmony with nature: yin and yang were at peace, death was unknown, and everything happened naturally without being forced. Over time virtue declined, and the original unity was lost, first under legendary rulers and then under later ones.

Over time, people's natural goodness declined. Once the sage-kings Yao and Shun ruled, laws and moral teaching were introduced, and these pulled people away from the Tao, the natural way, harming their inner virtue.

Man gave up natural instinct for reasoning and cleverness. Minds clashed, and people still could not bring order to the world, so skill and learning were added. These in turn damaged his original nature, and confusion followed, leaving people unable to return to their first, natural state.

The main point is that the world and the Way (Tao) work against each other, so neither can raise the other up. Even so, sages, the wise people who follow the Way, keep their goodness out of sight, though not by choice of their own.

Retired scholars of old were not people who hid themselves or their wisdom on purpose. They withdrew only when the times did not suit their work. When the times suited them and their work succeeded, they blended into the unity of the empire; when it failed, they relied on themselves and waited.

The ancient people who kept themselves whole did not show off their learning, drain the world with it, or wear out their virtue. They stayed within their own roles and returned to natural instinct. Tao, they say, does not concern itself with small details, so trifles harm virtue and detail harms Tao. Self-reform is enough, and the person whose happiness is complete has got what they wanted.

Long ago, getting what you wanted meant gaining nothing extra in happiness, not winning public office. Office is outside a person and comes and goes beyond our control, so the passage holds that real freedom from sorrow means staying content whether you hold office or not, rather than seeking office or flattering others when poor.

People who value outward things too highly and lose their natural instincts in worldly concerns are described as living upside down. The passage calls them the "people of topsy-turvydom," meaning people whose values are reversed.

In autumn, when floods swell the river, the water spreads so wide that the far banks are too distant to see clearly. Even the difference between a cow and a horse cannot be made out from one side to the other.

The River Spirit, having reached the sea and seen how vast it is, admits his own earlier conceit. He says that a person who has heard only part of the truth thinks himself the equal of all others, and he confesses that he was such a person.
The speaker admits he did not believe in the vast, endless nature of the sea-god's domain. Now that he has seen it, he says he would have been a laughing-stock to wise people had he never come there.

The Spirit of the Ocean says that people can only understand what fits within their own limited experience. A frog in a well cannot grasp the sea, and an insect that lives one season cannot grasp ice. Only after the speaker has seen the great ocean can he recognise how small he is and be taught great principles.

The speaker says the ocean is greater than any river, since it never overflows or runs dry and is unaffected by seasons, floods or droughts. Yet he claims no credit for this, because he knows he takes his form from the universe and his life force from yin and yang, the two opposing forces of nature. Compared with the whole universe, he sees himself as a small stone or tree on a huge mountain, so he has nothing to boast about.

Human affairs are tiny when set against the whole universe. The Four Seas are like puddles in a marsh, China is a grain in a granary, and one person is no more than the tip of a hair on a horse. So the famous rulers, wars, and labours of reformers and administrators amount to very little.

The passage has the River Spirit answer a critic. He says that Poh I, a legendary sage who refused the throne, and Confucius, who taught to win a reputation for learning, both overrated themselves. The Spirit then asks whether he should treat the whole universe as big and a hair's tip as small, meaning he judges his own size by comparison.

The Spirit of the Ocean says that size, time, and circumstances have no fixed limits. A wise person therefore does not think small things are too small or large things too big, does not grieve over distant events or rejoice over near ones, and does not celebrate success or mourn failure, because nothing stays the same.

Human knowledge is small compared with what people do not know, and a human life is short compared with the time before and after it. Trying to measure the very great or the very small with limited human measures leads only to confusion. The River Spirit then asks whether the claims of the day's debaters about the smallest and largest things are true.

The Spirit of the Ocean says that size depends on what it is compared with. Something large has no limit when set against smaller things, and something small becomes hard to see when set against larger things. The tiniest is a division of the small, and the vastest is an extension of the great, so the two belong to different kinds.

Every thing, large or small, must have a form, because the mind can only grasp what has a limit. Something that can be neither discussed nor imagined cannot be called great or small. So the truly great man does not injure others and does not take credit for kindness or mercy.

The passage describes a person who does not judge others by his own choices. He neither looks down on people who chase gain, status or wealth, nor takes pride in refusing those things. Honors and disgrace do not move him, because he sees that good and bad cannot be cleanly separated.

A person who follows the Tao seeks no fame, perfect virtue does not try to gain anything, and a truly great person forgets the self. The River Spirit then asks how, if this is so, anyone can tell what is valuable or worthless, great or small.

From the view of Tao, the Way that underlies all things, nothing is ultimately high or low in value. People rate themselves highly and others poorly, while society as a whole does not let any individual judge his own worth.

Size is only relative. If a thing is called great or small just by comparison, then everything is both great and small. The universe looks as tiny as a tare seed, and a hair-tip looks as large as a mountain, when measured against something else.

Whether a thing is said to exist or not depends only on the role it plays or fails to play. Seen this way, nothing is simply existent or non-existent. East and west are like this too: each depends on the other and can change places, and knowing this is seeing how functions fit together.

Judging something good or bad only from one's own view makes every thing both good and bad, so nothing is fixed. Seeing that Yao and Chieh were each good and bad from opposite points of view is what sets up a true standard. The rest gives examples: rulers who gave up power sometimes succeeded and sometimes failed, and rulers who took power by force sometimes succeeded and sometimes failed too.

Whether to give up power or to fight, and whether to act like the good ruler Yao or the tyrant Chieh, depends on the situation and is not a fixed rule. Each thing has its own use: a battering-ram breaks walls but cannot mend them, and fast horses are poor at catching rats.

The owl can catch fleas at night and see the tip of a hair, but in daylight it cannot see even a mountain. The point is that each creature is built for its own conditions, so what works for one may fail for another.

Right and wrong, or good and bad government, only make sense together, since each needs its opposite. Someone who wants one without the other misunderstands how the universe works. Such people, the passage says, are either fools or liars if they refuse to be persuaded.

Rulers and dynasties rise and fall under different circumstances. Those who failed to match their time were called usurpers, and those who fit their age were called patriots. The speaker tells the River to stop judging what is valuable or small. The River asks how it should then decide what to accept or refuse.

The passage says that treating either of two opposites, such as few or many, as absolutely true harms the Tao, the natural way or underlying order. Few and many are relative, like giving and receiving gifts: each depends on the other. Looking at only one side causes confusion about the Tao.

The passage says that a wise person should treat all things alike, as an impartial ruler or a fair deity does, and embrace everything without favour. Once all things are seen as equal, the usual distinctions between long and short no longer apply.

Everything except the Tao (the underlying way of the universe) has no lasting form. Things are born, change and die, and time cannot be held back. The passage ends by asking what a person could do except let this natural decay continue.
Someone who understands the Tao, the Way, must grasp the eternal principles mentioned earlier and know how to apply them. Because of this, such a person is not harmed by outside things.

A person of perfect virtue cannot be harmed by fire, water, cold, sun, or wild animals. This is not because he ignores such dangers. He knows which situations are safe and which are dangerous, stays content in good and bad times, and is careful about what he rejects and what he accepts. For that reason, nothing can harm him.

The passage says that what is natural lies inside a person, and what is artificial lies outside. Virtue rests in the natural, and true knowledge of both comes from the natural and grows through virtue. Whatever one does, one always returns to the essential and the ultimate. The River asks what "natural" and "artificial" mean.

The Spirit of the Ocean says that horses and oxen having four feet is natural, while a halter or a nose-string is something people add. So people should not let human additions wipe out what is natural, or let will override destiny, or give up virtue for fame. Keeping these, one returns to the divine. The final lines then show envy passing from one creature to the next, from walrus up to mind.

In this exchange, the centipede says its many legs move by a natural process it does not control, like saliva falling in countless drops. The snake, having no legs, says a creature's natural make-up cannot be changed and it has no need of legs.

The snake tells the wind it has a definite shape, while the wind blows about without one. The wind replies that anyone who can point at or kick it can overcome it, but it can break huge trees and wreck great buildings. So it takes pride in the one great thing it can do, and the wind keeps on blowing regardless.
Confucius explains to his listener that his long efforts have brought him nothing. He blames fate for his failure and says that his time for success has not yet come.

In the age of the sage-kings Yao and Shun, everyone succeeded, and no one noticed any gain. In the age of the tyrants Chieh and Chou, everyone failed, and no one noticed any loss. The passage says that the times and circumstances made each age what it was.

Courage comes in levels, the passage says. Fishermen face sea monsters, hunters face wild beasts, and heroes face death in battle, but the highest kind is the Sage's: accepting failure as fate and success as opportunity, and staying fearless in great danger. The speaker then tells Yu to rest in this and accept his own destiny.
A group of soldiers had surrounded Confucius, mistaking him for Yang Hu, a man who had once wronged the people of the area. Once they realised their error, their captain apologised and withdrew.

Gongsun Long, a famous debater, tells Mou of Wei that he had mastered the arguments of all the schools and thought he had reached the goal. After hearing Zhuangzi, he is so amazed that he cannot speak and asks Mou to reveal the secret.

The frog in a well boasts to a sea turtle about how happy and well off it is. It can hop, swim and rest in its small world, and it sees no equal among the creatures around it. It invites the turtle to visit, not seeing how small its well is compared with the ocean.

The turtle of the eastern sea describes its ocean as unaffected by floods or droughts, neither growing larger in floods nor smaller in droughts. It says this lack of change, whether of time or water, is the sea's great happiness.

The well-frog, a frog that lives in a well, is astonished by what it has just heard and cannot find a reply. The sentence then starts to say that a person whose knowledge does not reach the "positive-negative" domain, meaning the realm of opposites such as yes and no, is in a similar position, but the passage breaks off there.

The speaker says that trying to understand Chuang Tzu is as hopeless as a mosquito carrying a mountain or an ant swimming a river. He adds that someone whose knowledge rests only on ordinary achievements is like a frog in a well, seeing only a small part of the world.

The speaker says Chuang Tzu has risen beyond ordinary distinctions like north, south, east and west, and has returned to Tao, the Way, which is the source of all things. Trying to test his teachings with argument is compared to looking at the sky through a tube or poking the earth with an awl: it gives only a small, limited view.

A youth who went to Han-tan to learn forgot what he knew and came home in disgrace. Kung Sun Lung, warned the same will happen if he stays, is struck dumb and leaves. Chuang Tzu is fishing when Ch'u's prince sends officials to offer him government office.

Zhuangzi, fishing, tells two officials that he would rather be a living tortoise wagging its tail in the mud than a dead sacred tortoise kept in a temple chest. The officials agree the living animal is better, and Zhuangzi says he will likewise choose to live in the mud.

Chuang Tzu tells Hui Tzu a story about a noble bird that eats only the finest food. An owl with a rotten rat sees it and screeches, as if afraid it will take the rat. Chuang Tzu asks whether Hui Tzu is doing the same over his kingdom of Liang, which Hui Tzu feared losing. Then, at a bridge, Chuang Tzu remarks that the minnows are enjoying themselves.

Hui Tzu argues that Chuang Tzu cannot know what fish feel, since he is not a fish. Chuang Tzu replies that Hui Tzu's own question shows he already knew, and that he knew it from his own feelings while standing on a bridge.

The passage asks whether perfect happiness can be found in this world, and whether some people can truly enjoy life. If they can, it asks what such people do, avoid, accept, reject, like and dislike. It raises these questions without giving answers here.

The passage says that the world values wealth, rank, long life, and kindness, and enjoys comfort, good food, fine clothes, beauty, and music. Those who lack these things are very unhappy. Yet the author calls this folly when judged by the needs of the body.

The passage argues that many things people chase, such as wealth, office, and public virtue, do not serve the body's real welfare. Piling up more money than one can use, working through the night for rank, or living long in weakened old age is, from the body's point of view, excess or going astray. Even admired patriots, it says, do not thereby gain a happy life.

The speaker is unsure whether the moral goodness of loyal advisers helps them live well or only helps others. He cites Tzu Hsu, who resisted his ruler's will and was killed, though his resistance made his name. He asks whether such goodness is real at all.

The speaker doubts that the happiness most people pursue is real happiness, since they simply follow the crowd and call themselves happy. He holds that true pleasure lies in inaction, which the world sees as pain. So perfect happiness, he says, is the absence of ordinary happiness.
Good and bad cannot be fixed as absolute in this world. Yet they can be fixed when a person does nothing. Lasting happiness and staying alive are found only in not acting.

Heaven and earth do not act, yet they are clear, at rest, and bring about everything that happens in the world. The passage says that all the changes of things come from this non-action. It then asks who among people can reach such non-action.

Hui Tzu visits Chuang Tzu after his wife's death and finds him singing and drumming on a bowl. Hui Tzu thinks this is too much, since Chuang Tzu does not even weep for her. The passage shows Hui Tzu's shock at this behavior.

Chuang Tzu explains why he does not mourn his wife's death. He believes she passed through stages from formless spirit to substance, to form, to birth, and now to death, much as the seasons change. Weeping would show that he did not understand these natural changes, so he holds back.

In this story, a hunchback and a one-legged man are looking at old tombs when sores break out on their left elbows. The hunchback asks the other man whether he is disgusted by them, which sets up the question of how one feels about bodily misfortune.

Life is described as a loan that the borrower only adds more dirt to, and life and death are compared to day and night. So the speaker says he has no reason to hate death, even if it comes to him as it has to others.
Chuang Tzu finds a dry, bleached skull and asks it how it came to die. He lists possible causes: ambition, political disaster, shame, starvation, or simply old age. He does not say which one is true.

In a dream, a skull speaks to the man who had been talking to it. It says his words only concern the troubles of living people, which do not exist in death, and asks whether he wants to hear about death.

In this scene, Zhuangzi has asked a skull whether it has suffered, and the skull answers that the dead have no rulers or subjects and do not follow the seasons. It says their lives last forever, and that a king's happiness is no greater than theirs.

Chuang Tzu offers to ask God to restore a dead man's body and return him to his family, and asks whether he would want that. The skull refuses, saying a dead man's happiness is greater than a king's and he would not return to mortal troubles. The passage then shifts to Confucius, who grows sad when his disciple Yen Yuan leaves for another state, and Tzu Kung asks whether that is the reason.

Zhuangzi says that fate is fixed in advance, just as the body has its limits, and nothing can be taken from or added to either. He fears that his friend Hui, if he preaches the sage-kings' way to the prince of Ch'i, will leave the prince searching inside himself, finding nothing, growing doubtful, and then violent.

The passage is cut off mid-sentence, so its full point is unclear. It begins an anecdote: a sea-bird lands outside the capital of Lu, and the prince welcomes it with wine and music in a temple. The story continues beyond this excerpt.

A sea bird, brought to a state ruler's capital, was given wine, music and meat to please it, and it died within three days. The point is that people treated the bird as they would want to be treated, not as a bird would want. A bird would have been left in a forest, a plain or a river, to live as birds do.
Even when a famous piece of music is played in the wilds, animals and birds flee or dive away from it. Only people gather to listen.

Water is life for fish but death for humans, because each kind of creature is made differently and has its own likes and dislikes. So the wise men of old did not force everyone into one skill or one way of life. The passage then turns to Lieh Tzu, who sees an old skull by the road and talks to it, asking whether the dead is at peace or whether he himself is happy.

Living things, the passage says, change step by step into other forms. Duckweed, lichen, plants, grubs, butterflies and insects all arise from one another in this way, with no fixed boundary between kinds.

Things in nature are said to change into one another over long periods, passing from one form to another, until man is reached. Man then returns to the great Scheme, the source from which all things come and to which they return.
People who understand what life can do do not spend their effort on things life cannot achieve. Likewise, people who understand fate do not worry about things that knowledge cannot control.

Nourishing the body does not always keep a person alive, and caring for the body does not guarantee life. Life comes and goes beyond human control. The world wrongly believes that feeding the body is enough to preserve life, and the passage asks what people should do if it is not.

Even if the effort is never enough, it still must be made and cannot be dropped. Neglecting the body is worse than leaving the world altogether, since withdrawing from the world frees a person from worldly cares. That freedom brings a natural state, which the passage calls a rebirth.

Giving up worldly affairs and caring little for life keeps the body and vital force unharmed. Someone whose body and vital force are whole is one with God. Heaven and earth produce things by uniting and return them to their origin by parting.

Kuan Yin is asked how the perfect man can walk through solid objects, pass through fire unharmed, and climb great heights without fear. He answers that the perfect man is in a state of absolute purity, and that courage from cunning plays no part in these feats.

Everything with form, sound, or colour counts as a mere thing. Humans seem set apart from other things because those things are only what they appear to be. Humans can reach formlessness and overcome death, and so they stand above mere things.

The passage describes a person who settles into what is naturally right and lasting, and who moves freely through all of existence. By unifying his nature, building his strength and balancing his virtue, he joins with the divine. Once this is secure, nothing outside can get inside him.

A drunk man who falls from a cart is hurt but does not die, because his spirit is calm and he is not aware of the fall. If wine can give that kind of security, the Sage gets far more from God, and so he is kept from harm.

The passage says that a wronged person does not take revenge on the object that caused harm, such as a weapon or a falling tile. Carried further, this attitude would bring peace to the whole empire, ending war and execution.
