The passage contrasts two kinds of mind. A mind that develops natural, inborn understanding brings virtue, while one that develops artificial cleverness brings only cunning. It then shows this with a hunchback who catches cicadas skillfully because he has practised steadily, balancing balls on one another.

A hunchback who catches cicadas with a pole explains how he does it. He says that when he focuses on one thing, he shuts out everything else, and so he rarely misses. Confucius replies that single-minded focus brings this kind of skill.

A boatman told Yen Yüan that a skilled boatman rows as if the boat were not there, and that keeping a person afloat can seem like sinking them. When Yen Yüan asked what this meant, the boatman would not say, so Yen Yüan asks Confucius to explain.

A man who stays calm in danger, like a swimmer in rapids or a rider in a cart upset, can go anywhere without harm. Likewise, a gambler who cares about the value of the stake loses his skill, because anyone who cares too much about outside things loses his inner steadiness.

T'ien K'ai Chih, asked about his master's study of how to live, says only that keeping life is like herding sheep: you watch for the stragglers and drive them back into line. The Duke asks what this means, so the saying is left unexplained.

The passage gives two examples of men who died in ways that did not match their lives. Shan Pao lived apart from worldly concerns and stayed youthful, yet a hungry tiger killed him. Chang I mixed freely with rich and poor, yet he died young from an internal illness.

Shan Pao cared only for his inner self and was eaten by a tiger, while Chang I cared only for his outward self and was struck by inner disease. Both neglected to attend to what was lagging behind. Confucius adds that avoiding both obscurity and fame, and resting naturally in the middle way, brings lasting renown.

The passage compares two kinds of warning. People advise each other to take an escort on dangerous roads, and warning others against the dangers of passion and feasting is equally needed. The Grand Augur, dressed for a ceremony, then speaks to pigs at the slaughterhouse, a reversal of that concern.

The speaker offers a dying man an elaborate sacrifice: months of fattening, fasting, and a fine ceremonial dish. He then imagines how a pig would judge such a choice, preferring to live on bran rather than face slaughter. Finally he says a person might accept death for honour, such as dying in battle or by execution, to be honoured while alive.

Duke Huan once saw a ghostly figure while hunting, and his charioteer Kuan Chung said he saw nothing. Afterwards the Duke fell ill and could not go out for many days. The passage breaks off as a new figure, Huang Tzu Kao Ngao, is introduced.

The Duke's illness is blamed on himself, not on a ghost. The speaker says that vital strength, if spent in anger and not restored, weakens the body. Where it rises, it makes a person angry; where it sinks, it causes forgetfulness; where it stays stuck in the middle of the body, it causes disease. The Duke then asks whether ghosts exist at all.

Huang answers the Duke's question about spirits by naming a list of them, each tied to a place or thing: mud, fire, the dust-bin, the north-east and north-west winds, water, hills, mountains, the moor and the marsh. The Duke then asks what the last of these, the Wei I of the marsh, is like.

A duke tells Huang about a strange creature he saw, the Wei I, a round being with purple clothes and a red cap. Huang says that whoever sees it will become a leader among men. The duke, delighted that he saw it, gets up and his illness leaves him without his noticing. The story ends with a note that Chi Hsing Tzu was training fighting cocks for the prince.

A prince keeps asking his trainer whether his fighting cock is ready. Each time the trainer says no, because the bird still reacts to other cocks' sounds, shadows and sight. The point is that the bird is not yet calm and unmoved by rivals.

The passage gives two images of control. A trained fighting cock looks like wood, so calm that rival cocks flee from it. Confucius watches a huge waterfall so violent that no fish or other creature can enter it.

Confucius saw an old man go into a waterfall-like torrent and feared he meant to drown himself, so he sent a disciple to rescue him. The old man came out about a hundred paces downstream, singing as he walked on the bank. Confucius asked him how he could handle water in this way.

The old man explains his skill at swimming in rapids. He says he began with a natural ability, grew used to the water until it felt natural, and then accepted what must happen. He adapts himself to the water rather than forcing the water to suit him.

The old man says he simply adapts to his surroundings: born on land, he lives as land-dweller, and raised on water, he adapts to water. He calls this his nature, and doing it without effort is what he calls destiny. Then the carpenter Ch'ing, whose carved stand seemed supernatural, is asked by a prince about the secret of his craft.
Before a difficult task, the speaker keeps his inner energy from draining away and first calms his mind completely. As the days pass, he forgets rewards, then fame, and finally his own body.

The speaker is a craftsman who makes a stand for bells or drums. He forgets the court and outside distractions, finds a suitable tree in the mountain forest, and shapes it by matching his own ability to the wood's natural form. He then compares this to a charioteer whose driving was so precise it looked ruled and compassed.

Yen Ho told the Duke that Chi's horses would break down because Chi was forcing them to do a task beyond their strength. When the Duke heard that the horses had broken down and Chi had left, he asked how Yen Ho knew. Yen Ho said he had seen that the horses could not manage the work.

Ch'ui, a craftsman, drew circles more skillfully freehand than with a compass. His fingers moved so naturally with the work that he did not have to concentrate on it, so his mind stayed whole and was not held back.

The passage says that when a person forgets their body, such as feet in good shoes or a waist in a comfortable belt, the comfort is complete. Likewise, a mind that does not notice positive and negative, and is not moved by outside influences, stays at ease in all conditions, and so does not even notice that ease.

A man complains to heaven that he has done nothing wrong. He behaves properly in peace and bravely in trouble, yet his crops fail, he fails in office, and he is cast out of both his village and his state. He asks what offence he has committed to deserve such treatment.

Pien Tzŭ tells the listener that the perfect man ignores his body and the senses, and acts without relying on self-confidence or authority. He then accuses the listener of showing off his knowledge to dazzle fools and of setting himself above others.

Sun Hsiu complains about his lot, and Pien Tzu tells him he should be content: his body is whole and he still has a place among people, so he has no cause to blame heaven. After Sun Hsiu leaves, Pien Tzu worries that the teaching about the perfect man might have startled him and led him into doubt.

A disciple replies to his teacher that the teacher need not worry about the dispute. If the other man was right and the teacher wrong, the wrong view cannot push out the right one. If the other man was wrong, the fault lies with him, not with the teacher.

Pien Tzu says that the prince of Lu harmed a bird by treating it as a person would want to be treated, with ox meat and music, when it needed quiet woods and water. He says that speaking of the perfect man to the simple-minded Sun Hsiu is the same mistake, so Sun Hsiu is bound to be alarmed.

Chuang Tzu sees a huge tree that woodsmen leave alone because it is useless, and he says that its uselessness is why it lives out its full natural life. Later, at a friend's house, a servant asks which goose to kill, the one that cackles or the one that does not. The two stories make the same point: being useless can keep a thing safe.

A host's master tells a servant to kill the goose that does not honk. A disciple then asks Chuang Tzu which is better: the useless tree that lives out its years, or the useless goose that dies. Chuang Tzu says he would take a middle position between the two, since either choice avoids neither trouble nor death.

Someone who rides on the Tao and rises above ordinary life is not troubled in this way. Such a person neither seeks praise nor fears blame, and moves with the times without forcing effort. They go along with their surroundings and are moved by nothing outside themselves. The passage says this was the method of two legendary rulers, Shen Nong and Huang Di.

In human passions and relationships, every good thing comes paired with its opposite: union with separation, completion with destruction, honour with disparagement. So nothing in the human world stays fixed. The passage says that only the Tao, the Way, offers such a fixed point.
The prince of Lu looks sad. He says he follows the ancient sages, respects religion and honours the good, yet misfortune still comes to him. That is why he is sad.

Zhuangzi's passage says that a fox or leopard avoids danger by hiding in the mountains, coming out only at night, and staying hungry rather than risking open ground. The speaker calls this a shallow way to avoid misfortune, using these animals as the example.

Trees like the cassia are cut down because their wood or bark is valued, so they suffer for what they are. The speaker applies this to the ruler: his own land of Lu is his "skin," the thing that makes him a target. He advises him to let go of both body and land, clear his heart of desire, and go to a place beyond death.

The speaker describes a far southern district called Established-Virtue, whose people are simple, unselfish and free of desire. They make things without keeping them, give without expecting return, and act without rules, yet still follow the way of the wise. He urges the prince to go there, leaving power and the world behind and trusting in Tao, the Way. The prince objects that the road is long and empty.

A ruler is told that if he cuts down his desires, he will have enough even without supplies. He can then journey across rivers and seas into endless space, where his escorts must turn back at the border and he must go on alone.

The speaker says that our own human side blocks us, and the human side in other people brings us sorrow. Yao, a legendary ruler, had neither trait, and the speaker urges the listener to drop this hindrance and sorrow and move freely with the Tao, the Way, in the realm of pure emptiness.

Two boats meet on a river. If the other boat is empty, no one gets angry, but if someone is aboard, anger follows. The point is that people are hurt by others only when they stay occupied, so a person who goes through life with no fixed self, like an empty boat, could not be harmed.

Shê says that in the realm of the One nothing needs managing, because shaped things return to their natural state. So he showed no reaction to people coming, going, or giving, and no one was harmed. Those who hold the Way, he suggests, would do even more so.

The birds called i-êrh act modestly and never push ahead, whether flying, eating or retreating. They take what is left by others, so they stay at peace among themselves and outsiders cannot harm them.

Showy cleverness and self-display bring trouble, just as straight trees get cut first and sweet wells run dry first. The passage says that praise and achieved merit or fame lead to loss, and that the wise person gives up both to become one with everything. Tao, the Way, pervades all things but cannot be seen.

The passage describes a way of acting that is quiet and unseen, seeking neither power nor credit. Such a person does not criticise others and so is not criticised. It ends by asking why someone who wants nothing from fame would take pleasure in it.

Confucius responds approvingly, then leaves his friends and students and lives alone in the wilds, dressed in rough skins and eating nuts. Animals and birds ignore him, and he asks Tzŭ Sang Hu whether people would treat him any differently.

The speaker lists a run of misfortunes: he was driven out of Lu twice, his tree was cut down in Sung, he was shunned in Wei, failed in Shang and Chou, and was surrounded between Ch'en and Ts'ai. He asks why his friends have left and his disciples are gone.

Lin Hui, fleeing the state of Kuo, abandoned valuable jade regalia but carried his child on his back. Asked why, he said the regalia was only a matter of money, while the child was a gift from heaven. The point is that a natural bond outweighs material value.

In times of trouble and danger, people stop worrying about money and hold more tightly to what comes from God. The passage says the gap between letting go of money concerns and clinging to the divine is large.

The passage compares two kinds of friendship. A superior man's friendship starts plain, like water, and grows warm over time. A mean man's friendship starts rich, like wine, and fades to nothing, because it began without good reason. Confucius accepts this, gives up his studies, and his disciples stop calling him teacher, yet his affection for them grows.

Sang Hu quotes Shun's last advice to Yü: act according to the body and speak according to one's feelings, so one needs no outward show. Zhuangzi then dresses in patched cotton and goes to see the Prince of Wei, showing he lives by that advice.

Chuang Tzu says that being poor is not the same as being miserable. A person who has Tao, the Way of nature, cannot be miserable, even in ragged clothes. His own hardship, he says, comes from being out of step with his time. He compares himself to a monkey that is free and at ease in the trees, where archers like Yi and Fêng Mêng cannot reach it.

A creature placed in a bramble bush cannot use its skill, so it moves nervously and fearfully. The passage says a person under foolish rulers and wicked ministers cannot avoid misery, even if he wishes to, and gives Pi Kan, who was disembowelled, as an example.

Confucius, trapped between two states and starving, sings and beats wood with sticks, though his music is crude. His disciple Yen Hui looks around, and Confucius worries that Yen Hui will either boast or fall into grief over their safety. The passage is cut off at this point.

Zhuangzi says it is easy to escape harm that comes from heaven, meaning nature or fate, but hard to avoid the benefits and honours people give, which can trap you. Human and heavenly are one, and he asks who was singing, prompting his student Yen Hui to ask what he meant.

Confucius says that hunger, thirst, cold and heat are like chains on the path of life, but they are natural laws of the universe, and he accepts them and keeps to his set course. He compares this to a subject who must obey his prince, and so a person must obey God. Yen Hui then asks what it means to find it hard to escape the benefits of humans.

Confucius says that if a man begins by adapting to his surroundings, rank and power come to him steadily. He sees these as outside gifts, not something a man creates himself. He says his own life depends partly on such outside things, and he simply accepts them as they come rather than taking them by force.

Swallows avoid bad places, yet they nest among people because they find their natural home there. When Yen Hui asks about endlessness and the unity of man and God, Confucius replies that no one knows the cause of the work or its beginning or end, so we can only wait.

Chuang Tzu sees a large bird with huge wings and eyes fly close past his head and land in a grove. He asks what kind of bird it is, then remarks that although its wings are strong it does not fly away, and although its eyes are large it does not see. The remark is a puzzle: the bird has great abilities but does not use them.

Zhuangzi sees a cicada, a mantis hunting it, and a bird about to eat the mantis. Each creature is so absorbed in its own gain that it fails to notice the danger behind it. He sighs that creatures harm one another and that pursuing gain brings loss, then leaves without hunting.

Chuang Tzu explains why he has not gone out. Gazing at a park or muddy water, he lost track of his true self, and a bird flying past forgot its nature. The grove keeper then took him for a thief, so he stayed indoors.

Being aware of one's own beauty or ugliness makes others see it as the main thing about a person, and so they stop judging the person as beautiful or ugly. Yang Tzu concludes that a person should be good without being conscious of their goodness, and then they will be loved wherever they go.

Tzŭ Fang says the person he describes is perfect: outwardly an ordinary man, inwardly something divine. Though he is free from conditions himself, he mixes with ordinary people, and he is patient with others. When people lack the Tao (the Way), he gently shows them their mistakes, so they give up their wrong aims. Praise, he says, cannot do such a person justice.

A prince has just spoken with Tzŭ Fang and is deeply moved. He says that the teaching of his own tutor, which he had thought the highest, now seems like mere undergrowth. He feels calm, has no wish to move or speak, and sees his own kingdom of Wei as a source of harm.

Wen Po Hsueh Tzu, a traveler, twice refused to meet a man from Lu. The first time he said the Lu people knew ceremonies but lacked understanding of the human heart. The second time he wondered why the man kept asking, suspecting he had something to say.

The passage describes a man who sighs after each meeting with a visitor. His servant asks why he always sighs after receiving this stranger, and the question sets up the explanation that follows in the story.

Wen Po Hsueh Tzu says that people of the Middle Kingdom (China) know ceremony and duty well but lack understanding of human feeling. His visitor behaved correctly in form, yet was fierce one moment and stern the next, scolding him as a son would a father and lecturing him as a father would a son. That is why he sighed.

Confucius says nothing when he meets Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, because with such a man one only needs to look and the Tao (the Way) is present, so speech is not needed. Yen Yüan then says he can follow Confucius at every pace until Confucius outruns him beyond ordinary life, and Confucius asks him to explain.

Yen Yüan says he can only follow Confucius, copying his speech, arguments and teaching, and he admires how Confucius wins belief and love without effort. He asks how this works. Confucius replies that the death of the mind is a greater sorrow than the death of the body.

The passage uses the sun as an image: it lights everything, and things depend on it to see and move, and its rising and setting mean existence and non-existence. The speaker then says that people also depend on something for life and death. He worries that, living in a body with a mind and being worn down day by day, he may end up as a mere thing without knowing where he is going.

Someone is grieving over a dead friend, and the speaker answers that the friend has changed as he always does, yet something in him does not change. The grief looks for the friend's old self, as if it were still there, when that self has already gone, and the speaker asks why there should be grief at all.

Confucius visits Lao Tzu and finds him sitting still, with wet hair, looking like a lifeless body. Lao Tzu says he has been wandering in the unborn, a state beyond ordinary knowing and speech. He says he cannot clearly explain it, but will try to describe what is probably true.

The passage describes how the world works through two forces, a passive principle from above and an active one from below, whose interaction produces all things. It says a First Cause may exist but cannot be seen, and that its effects are visible everywhere, through day and night, life and death. It ends by asking what else could explain these things if not such a cause.
Creatures do not mind small changes in their surroundings, such as a new field of grass or a new pond. Minor change is acceptable as long as the essential part stays the same.
A person who sees all things as one feels no joy, anger, sorrow or happiness. Life and death, and even gain or loss, cannot disturb his inner peace.

Real honour, the passage says, lies within a person and cannot be taken away by a change in social position or by the ups and downs of life, so nothing can truly grieve such a person. Confucius then praises the speaker, saying his virtue matches Heaven and Earth.

Lao Tzu replies that water flows, heaven is high and the sun shines without any effort, and the perfect man is likewise natural, needing no cultivation to hold sway over things. Confucius, humbled, tells his disciple Yen Hui that he has been like a tiny creature in vinegar, unable to see how vast the universe is until his teacher opened his eyes.

A scholar does not need to wear scholars' robes to have the Tao (the Way), and wearing the robes does not prove that he has it. To test this, Duke Ai ordered death for anyone wearing robes without the Tao. Only one old man in the state of Lu dared to wear them, and he went to stand at the Duke's gate.

The passage argues that a person who does not care about rank or power is harder to trap and more useful to others. A duke tries to catch a scholar with political questions and fails. Po Li Ch'i, who ignores office, tends cattle so well that a ruler gives him power anyway. Shun, who did not fear death, could move people's hearts.
A prince wants a map drawn. Most officials eagerly get ready, but one late arrival bows, leaves for home, and is later found sitting bare-backed at ease. The prince calls him a true artist.
The old man is fishing, but he is not trying to catch fish. He fishes only for his own amusement, which the story presents as his real purpose.

King Wen wanted to appoint an old man to run the government. He held back, afraid that his own ministers and relatives would object. Yet he also could not bear to let the old man leave, since the people would then lose his influence.

A ruler named Wên Wang reports a dream in which a strange sage tells him to hand the government to a man of Tsang. His ministers say the dream is a command from his dead father, so it must be obeyed. When he suggests divination to check it, they say no divination is needed.

King Wen of Zhou gave the old man of Tsang a government post. The old man changed no existing laws and made no new unjust rules. After three years the state was orderly: dangerous groups were gone, officials did their jobs, and people agreed with one another. Wen then made him Grand Tutor.

Yen Yüan asks Confucius how King Wen could have done his mission by a dream if he could not do it by himself. Confucius rebukes him, saying Wen Wang did succeed, and that the dream was only there to satisfy ordinary minds. The old man of Tsang, who had been asked for guidance, leaves silently and vanishes.
A master archer draws his bow fully and sets a cup of water on his elbow, then shoots. One arrow leaves before the next is nocked, and he stays as still as a statue while doing so.

Po Hun Wu Jen says that shooting on flat ground is ordinary, not a true test of skill. He proposes climbing a high mountain and standing at the edge of a thousand-foot cliff, where the archer can then be tested.

Wu Jên stands at a cliff edge and tells his companion Lieh Tzŭ to come closer, but Lieh Tzŭ lies flat in fear. Wu Jên says a perfect man would stay calm whether he rose to the sky, sank into the underworld, or went to the farthest point of the compass, while Lieh Tzŭ is terrified and his inner health is weak.

A speaker praises a man who has been appointed to office three times and dismissed three times without showing joy or distress. He asks how the man controls his feelings, noting that his breathing stays steady.

Sun Shu Ao says he is no better than others. He accepts an official post when it comes and does not refuse it, and gives it up when it goes without trying to keep it. Since gaining and losing office do not touch his true self, he feels no disappointment.

Office and rank are not worth worrying about, the speaker says. Holding office would mean losing his own self, and busy thinking leaves no time for rank. Confucius admires sages who were untouched by danger, temptation, or even death, so rank and power matter even less to them.

The passage describes perfected people who pass through hardship without harm and give freely without losing anything. It then gives a dialogue: an official of Ch'u names signs that the state of Fan is being destroyed, and the Prince of Fan replies that its ruin cannot harm his own existence.

The speaker argues that the fall of his state, Fan, did not harm his own existence, so the survival of Ch'u would not secure the existence of the Ch'u people. In his view, the Fans were never truly destroyed, and the Ch'us have never truly existed, meaning both states are equally unreal in the sense that matters.

Knowledge travels north and asks Do-nothing Say-nothing how the Tao (the Way, the underlying order of things) can be known, approached, and reached. He asks by what thoughts, what resting place, and what pursuit this can happen.

Knowledge asked a figure named Do-nothing Say-nothing three questions about the Way, but got no answer. The silence was not a choice; he simply could not answer. Knowledge then went to another figure, All-in-extremes, who claimed to know and offered to explain.

Knowledge asks the Yellow Emperor how to know the Tao, the Way. The Emperor replies that it is known through having no thoughts, resting on nothing, and pursuing nothing. Knowledge then asks who is right, since he and the Emperor understand this while the others who failed to answer do not.

The Yellow Emperor says that the best teaching is the one that cannot be put into words, since those who understand the Way (Tao) do not talk about it. He adds that the Way cannot be forced or reached by effort, and that virtue, charity and duty, as taught by people, are easily misdirected or become empty show.

Each virtue depends on the one before it, so losing Tao means losing all the rest, down to ceremonies. Ceremonies are called a showy decoration of Tao that often causes trouble. The passage then says that practising Tao means losing things day by day, and that when this loss reaches non-action, nothing is left undone.
The passage says that once a person has become a particular kind of being, it is very hard to go back to their original state. Only the very greatest people are able to make that change.

Life and death are two stages of one process, not opposites that cut life off. Life is the gathering of a vital fluid, and death is its scattering, so there is no reason to grieve. All things are one, and the world is filled with a single vital fluid.

In the story, Knowledge asks three figures about the Way. Do-nothing Say-nothing cannot answer, and All-in-extremes forgets what he was going to say. The Yellow Emperor says the first was right because he did not know, the second came close because he forgot, and he and Knowledge are wrong because they claim to know.

The universe is beautiful and orderly, yet it does not explain itself; the seasons follow fixed law without speaking. The sage therefore just observes it, since human intellect, however sharp, cannot reach the root of things, which has always been there.

Tao, the central principle of the Taoist tradition, is present everywhere: in the farthest reaches of space, in the smallest autumn seed, and in all things. Everything on earth rises and falls, but nothing is ever completely destroyed.

The passage says that the cosmic forces of Yin and Yang and the seasons follow their fixed order. Things can seem to vanish while still existing, and the material can pass away while the immaterial remains. This pattern is called the root from which one can get a partial view of the divine, and it is said to be beyond full understanding.

Ideas are passed between figures in a story about getting the Tao, the Way. One speaker advises keeping the body controlled, the gaze fixed on One, and knowledge set aside, so that peace and inner spirit come and the Tao settles in. Asked whether the Tao can be owned, Shun answers that even the body is not one's own, so the question has no clear sense.

Movement, rest and taste happen without our knowing how or why, and these are the workings of God's laws. Confucius asks Lao Tzu how to grasp Tao. Lao Tzu replies that one must purify the heart, discard knowledge, and then he gives a brief outline: light comes from darkness, the soul from Tao, and the body from vital essence.

Living things come into being in their own kinds: those with nine bodily openings from the womb, those with eight from the egg. Their coming leaves no trace and their going has no fixed end. They move freely, as at a crossroads, with no gate or house. Those who enter this way gain strength, clear thought, and sharp senses, without tiredness or obstruction.

Heaven, earth, the sun and moon, and all things act as they must, and this necessary way of acting is their Tao (the Way). The Tao is not reached through much learning or clever argument. The sage (wise person) does not rely on these, and so loses nothing and gains nothing. The Tao of the perfect person works on its own, and it can shape all things without running out.

Some people in the Middle Kingdom (China) do not separate good from bad. They live between heaven and earth, play their human part, and then return to their source. Life is seen as a gathering of breath or vital fluid, so the difference between long and short life is tiny, not enough to tell the sage Yao from the tyrant Chieh. Plants and fruit fall into orderly kinds, and human relations, though harder to handle, can also be put in order.

Human life is brief, like a white horse glimpsed through a crack, and everyone is subject to birth and death. Birth is one change and death is another. At death the soul leaves the body, which follows it, and both return home.

The passage says that the true nature of reality is formless, and that people who have reached it do not talk about it, since talking about it shows they have not reached it. Tao, the Way, cannot be put into words, so silence is better. Asked where Tao is, Chuang Tzu answers that it is everywhere, even in an ant.

Chuang Tzu says the question misses the real point. Just as an inspector judging pigs' fatness checks the leanest parts, the Way and ideal speech cover everything without exception, so one should not fix on any single direction. Words like "whole," "entire," and "all" differ in sound but share one meaning.

The speaker invites a companion to join him in a state of effortless stillness, where the mind is free of worry and does not notice either rest or movement. In this state the mind moves freely through an endless realm that no great intellect could fully explore.

Tao, the Way that underlies all things, is not itself limited by the things it produces. It brings about fullness and emptiness, growth and decay, beginning and end, gathering and scattering, yet it is none of these opposites.
Shên Nung was sitting alone, head on the table, lost in daydreams. A visitor, O Ho Kan, came in and told him that Lao Lung had died. The passage gives no further comment on this news.

Shên Nung, leaning on his staff, speaks to his dead master. He says the master left him because he was seen as worthless and self-sufficient. Now that he has no one to talk to, he says he too will die. The passage breaks off before the story continues.

Tao, the Way, cannot be seen or heard, so anyone who merely talks about it is not really grasping it. The speaker says that even someone with only a tiny share of Tao would do better to stay silent. Asked whether he knows Tao, Without-end admits he does not.

The Empyrean (a name for the sky or heaven, here a character) asks No-beginning which is right: the ignorance of Without-end or the knowledge of Inaction. No-beginning says not knowing is deep and inward, while knowing is shallow and outward. The Empyrean then asks whose knowledge it is that knows not-knowing, a question that turns the contrast back on itself.
Tao cannot be heard, seen, or spoken, because once it is perceived or named, it is no longer Tao. It gives form to all things but has no form itself, so it cannot have a name.

Those who claim to answer questions about Tao do not know it, and those who ask about it do not truly hear it. Such questions cannot really be asked or answered, so a question and answer about Tao are both empty. Anyone who deals in such empty exchanges lacks true perception of the world and of existence's origin.

The speaker says his skill came from single-minded focus: from age twenty he made only swords and ignored everything else, putting all spare effort into that work. The passage then ends with Confucius answering a question about the time before the universe by saying time has always been just as it is now.

Jen Ch'iu returns to Confucius, saying he was clear the day before but is confused now. Confucius replies that his clarity came from his own natural intelligence, and his confusion comes from something that has crept in besides that intelligence. He adds that there is no past, present, beginning or end, and asks whether someone can have descendants before they have any.

Confucius tells Jen Ch'iu that life and death depend on each other: without birth there would be no death, and without death no life. Before the universe there was Tao, the Way, which shapes things without being a thing itself. Everything contains Tao and keeps producing it, and the Sage's endless love for others rests on this same principle.

Confucius tells his disciple Yen Yüan that people of old changed their outward conduct but kept their inner character fixed. Modern people, he says, change inwardly while keeping outward forms. The way to adapt is to adjust only externals, while staying constant within, and to avoid splitting the two.

Perfect men, the passage says, would not have fought over scholarly arguments even if trained by Confucian or Mihist teachers, so people today are even less likely to avoid such quarrels. The true sage harms nothing and is harmed by nothing, and only such a person can be trusted to adapt. Joy and sorrow come and go, and the speaker has no control over them.

Human life is only a short stay, like a night at an inn. People know only what they experience and can do only what is within their power, and they always have limits they cannot pass. Trying to erase those limits is a source of sorrow. The passage adds that the best speech is unspoken, and that knowledge spread too widely stays shallow.

Kêng Sang Ch'u, a disciple of Lao Tzu who had fully grasped the Tao (the Way), sent away his helpers who were clever or charitable by design. He kept only those who seemed useless or unskilled. Within three years the district where he lived prospered.

Some people in a town praise the newcomer Kêng Sang Ch'u so highly that they suggest worshipping him as a spirit or local god. When Kêng Sang Ch'u hears this, he turns his face to the south, a gesture of disapproval or unease in the passage.

Kêng Sang, a follower of Lao Tzu, answers his astonished disciples. Seasons work without any visible agent, which he calls the operation of Tao, the Way. He says a perfect man could be hidden away like a corpse and people would still become natural and free of care. He is ashamed that the people of Wei-lei praise him as wise, so he feels he is a shallow vessel.

The disciples reply that a place unsuited to big creatures suits small ones, like eels and foxes. They argue that since ancient times rulers have honoured the virtuous and promoted the able, so the people of Wei-lei should be given the same chance to try this.

Kêng Sang Ch'u warns his disciples that a large creature leaving its safe place, such as a beast in open ground or a fish on dry shore, is easily caught or killed. So wise beings keep to high or deep places and hide themselves. He then says that the praised rulers Yao and Shun achieved little, comparing their fine distinctions to patching a wall hole with brambles.

The speaker says that the wise rulers Yao and Shun are the root of great evil, such as murder and theft, which will spread for ages to come. When Nan Yung Ch'u asks what someone of his age can do to reach this state, he is asking how to avoid this evil.

Kêng Sang, a teacher, gives advice to his student: keep your body whole, keep your life force strong, and let no worries get in. Do this for three years, he says, and you may reach the goal he describes.

Nan Yung says he sees no difference in the shape of eyes or ears, yet blind and deaf people cannot see or hear. He implies that the same is true of hearts: a difference in understanding exists even though the form looks the same. The passage breaks off before he states the point.

Kêng Sang's listener argues that people with the same bodily form and senses still differ in what they can do, so keeping one's body whole and free of worry is not enough. He says he has only heard about the Tao, the Way, and not grasped it himself. Kêng Sang agrees, comparing himself to a small wasp that cannot transform a large caterpillar.

Bantam hens cannot hatch goose eggs, while the hens of Lu can. The difference lies not in their hatching power but in their natural scale: one suits large work, the other small. The speaker says his own talents are of the small kind and he cannot change another person, so he sends the visitor south to Lao Tzu.
Nan Yung, a visitor, lowers his head in embarrassment and admits he has lost the words for his question because he has forgotten what he came to ask. Lao Tzu asks him what he means.

Nan Yung says that whatever he does, he harms either himself or others. If he does not know, people call him a fool; if he knows, he harms himself. Being charitable or doing his duty leads to the same result, so he asks Kêng Sang for advice on how to escape these three dilemmas.

Lao Tzu tells Nan Yung that he is confused and lost, like a lost child, and that he is trying to return to his true nature without knowing how. Nan Yung then works for ten days to cultivate good and remove evil in himself, and returns still troubled. The passage ends as he begins to ask about disturbances that may come from outside.

Laozi's disciple Nan Yung is told that if disturbances come from inside and outside, he cannot even hold on to the Way, let alone practise it. Nan Yung replies with a comparison: if a sick man can name his illness, he is not seriously ill, but his own search for the Way is like swallowing drugs that make the sickness worse. So he asks only how to preserve life.

The passage says that the ideal is to know when to stop, to be content with enough, to leave others alone and look to oneself, and to be free of worry and of deliberate knowing, like a child. It gives the example of a child who can cry all day without losing its voice, because its inner nature is in perfect balance.

Lao Tzu describes how a person who has gained a kind of inner unity keeps a firm grip and steady gaze without effort, and moves or rests without thinking about it, adapting to circumstances as they come. Asked whether this is the virtue of the perfect man, he says no, and calls his words only a first step, like breaking the ice.

The passage describes the "perfect man" as someone who eats ordinary food but enjoys a godlike happiness. He avoids trouble from people and things, takes no part in blame, scheming or flattery, and lives without worry. Such a person, it says, has mastered the art of preserving life.

Lao Tzu says the sage must become like a child: acting without knowing its purpose, with a body like dry wood and a mind like dead ashes. Good and bad fortune then cannot take hold, so the troubles of human life cannot reach him. A mind at rest shines with a light that lets a person see himself clearly, and only such calm lets one reach what is constant.

Those who keep to their true nature attract the loyalty of other people, and heaven gives them its help. People who are followed by others belong to heaven's people, and those whom heaven helps are its chosen children.

Knowledge is best when it stops at what cannot be known. Studying, practising and debating "this" means working at things that can never be learnt, done or proved. The passage says that anyone who ignores this will be destroyed.

If troubles come despite careful conduct, they are fate, not human fault, and they should not disturb one's inner self. The passage adds that speech not spoken in sincerity is wrongly spoken, and failing to correct this only leads toward ruin.

Wrongdoing done openly will be punished by people, and wrongdoing done in secret will be punished by God. The passage then says that whoever fears both human and divine judgment is fit to walk alone. The sentence breaks off before it finishes its thought about those devoted to the internal.

The passage contrasts two ways of living. Quiet practice without seeking fame gives even humble people a kind of dignity, while those who strive to stand above others look like a tired seller who pretends to be cheerful. It also says that people who are truly sympathetic with others attract them, but those who force themselves to fit in have no room even for themselves, so they end up isolated.

Going out and never coming back is a kind of growth in the spirit-power. Reaching one's end is death. Being wiped out yet still existing means the spirit gathers into oneness. Making formed things seem formless is the total of all things.

Birth and death are not true beginnings and ends, since existence has no limit in space or time. All things come out of Non-Existence, which the passage calls the Portal of God and says is the same as Nothing. The Sage rests in this Non-Existence.

The passage ranks kinds of knowledge. The highest knowledge goes back to the time before anything existed, and nothing can be added to it. The next best starts from existence, where life is seen as a misfortune and death as a return home, and where separation has already begun.

A group of thinkers held that existence began from nothing, then life, then death, and that life, death, existence and non-existence are all one. Human life is like soot on a kettle, and the subjective point of view cannot withstand testing or be reached as knowledge.
A "subjective point of view" is a way of seeing from one's own standpoint. The passage says this view begins with living, and that knowledge then guides it toward judging things as right or wrong.

People who hold their own view of right expect others to conform to it, and some will even die for it. They call what is useful wise and what is useless foolish, success honourable and failure shameful. The passage says such people, like the cicada and the young dove, see only from their own limited standpoint.

People show less formal courtesy the closer they are to us: a stranger gets an apology, a brother a sympathetic word, and a parent nothing at all. From this the passage concludes that true virtues, such as courtesy, duty, wisdom, charity and trust, arise without effort, calculation or pledges. It urges dropping deliberate purpose, mental disturbance and attachment to virtue in order to reach Tao, the Way.

If the twenty-four faculties are kept from running wild, the mind becomes orderly, calm, clear, and free of conditions, and so able to act without strain. The passage then defines a chain: Tao rules De, life shows De, nature is life's substance, and action comes from nature. Error is action gone wrong.

Feelings that arise on their own are called passive virtue, and feelings not caused by outside things are called active virtue. The names seem opposed but mean the same. The archer Yi hit the mark well but could not stop others praising him. The sage follows nature and drops the artificial.

The passage says that the Perfect Man, a sage in Taoist thought, does not reject what is natural. He rejects only what is natural in appearance but made by human effort. It then asks how much more, then, a person should be wary of mixing natural and artificial ways.

Getting people or things depends on skill and on being able to catch them. Yi is an archer who never misses. If the whole world were a cage, nothing could escape. Rulers T'ang and Duke Mu won their wise advisers only because they were themselves skilled at winning them.

People who stop caring about outward appearance, status, and their own sense of self, like a one-legged man or a condemned criminal, become indifferent to praise, insult, life and death. The passage says only those who have entered a state of harmony with God can be this way.
Anger that comes only from outside you is really a kind of calm, not real anger. Action that comes only from outside you is really a kind of inaction, with no inner striving behind it.

To reach peace, you must lower or flatten your emotions. To gain spiritual insight, you must train your mind to adapt. To act rightly, you must go along with what circumstances require, because this is the Way of the sage.

Hsü Wu Kuei tells the Prince that the Prince is the one who should be pitied, not himself. He says that if the Prince lets his passions and likes and dislikes rule him, his natural life will be harmed, and if he suppresses them, his seeing and hearing will be harmed.

Hsü Wu Kuei tells the Prince how he judges dogs by three levels: the lowest eat until full and stop, the middle stare at the sun, and the highest seem to have lost their own individuality. He says he judges horses more surely, by whether their lines, curves, squares and circles match the true tools of measure.

The speaker says that the best horses of the whole realm are not like the horses of a single state. Those horses move as if they were lost or had given up their own will, and so they leave every rival far behind, leaving the dust unstirred.

The Prince is delighted when Hsü Wu Kuei simply talks about how he judges dogs and horses. Nü Shang, who has offered him learned texts and military plans, is puzzled, because those talks never earned a smile.

The point is that the longer a person is away from his own kind, the more eager he becomes for any sign of them. A man exiled from his home state grows glad to meet first people he knew, then people he had only seen, and finally anyone who merely resembles his countrymen.

A hermit alone in the wilderness would be glad to hear any human footstep, and even more glad to hear a relative's voice. The speaker then says the ruler has long gone without hearing the voice of a pure, honest person beside him.

Hsü Wu Kuei, a hermit, visits a Prince who asks whether he has come for food, wine, or because the state is well run. Hsü says he came to sympathise with the Prince's soul and body, and when the Prince asks what he means, Hsü offers to explain. The main point is that Hsü's visit is an expression of concern, not a request for a reward.

The speaker tells a ruler that his position does not make him truly high or low. He says the ruler harms his people to satisfy his desires, while his inner self prefers harmony and dislikes disorder. The ruler replies that he wants to love his people and end war.

Hsü Wu Kuei tells the ruler that love for the people and duty to others, meant to end war, will cause the very harm they aim to prevent. Good things, once made into fixed standards, turn bad, and such virtues would be fake, because inner intention shows through in outward behaviour.

The speaker warns a ruler that disorder inside his state will bring fighting from outside. He asks whether the ruler would turn a pleasant garden or a place of worship into a battlefield, implying that he should not let his own land become one.

Do not try to win over others by trickery, scheming or war. Conquering a nation only feeds one's desires, so true victory lies elsewhere. The ruler need only refrain from aggression, keep his inner sincerity, and respond to circumstances; then the people are spared and war has no reason to continue.

The Yellow Emperor and his companions lose their way and ask a boy herding horses for directions to the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain and to where Tao dwells. The boy says he knows both, and the passage sets up his answer as the point of the story.

The Yellow Emperor, a legendary ruler, is impressed that a boy knows where the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain is and where Tao (the Way) dwells. When asked how he would govern the empire, the boy answers that he would do it as he looks after his horses. He then starts to tell of his youth, when his eyes grew dim and an old man advised him to ride the sun's chariot.

A young boy, asked how he would govern the empire, answers that it is no different from looking after horses: just make sure no harm comes to them. The Yellow Emperor bows to him and calls him a Divine Teacher.

People who make plans, argue logic, or criticize others need something to worry about, argue over, or attack before they feel content. Without these outside targets, they are unhappy, and so the passage calls them slaves of external things.

Each kind of person pursues the thing that matches their nature or skill. Those who win sympathy found dynasties, the strong take on hard tasks, and soldiers love war. Scholars, lawmakers and moralists each devote themselves to their own field.

Each group of people is tied to its work, and people feel lost or unhappy when they cannot do it. Men of every kind keep busy and cannot stop acting. They rush toward ruin, wasting their life energy for good, and the passage asks whether this could really be so.

Chuang Tzu argues that if everyone had his own standard of right, everyone would be like the sage-king Yao. He asks which rival school is right, then gives the example of a man who claims to make ice in summer.
Lu Chü tells his listener that what he is doing is only using hidden heat and cold, which is not what he means by Tao, the Way. He says he will show what his own Tao is.

Two lutes are tuned to the same pitch, so when one note is struck on one lute, the same note sounds on the other, even when they are in separate rooms. The matching comes from the shared tuning, not from any contact between the instruments.

A musician tunes a zither (a stringed instrument with twenty-five strings). If one string is moved out of its proper place in the octave and then played, all the strings clash. The notes still sound, but they lose the harmony that the key-note gives them. The speaker asks whether the listener is in the same condition.

Hui Tzu says his rivals have not proved him wrong, so Chuang Tzu should not either. Chuang Tzu replies with a story: a man sent his maimed son away to be a door-keeper but carefully wrapped up a vase he valued. The point is that a person who guards small valued things while neglecting what matters most is like someone who loses a stray child by refusing to leave home.

The passage uses a comparison: a man from Ch'u who is sent off as a door-keeper and starts a fight in the dead of night is already in serious trouble before his boat leaves the shore. The point is that trouble can be seen coming from the start, before any action takes place.

A man asks a stone-mason to remove a scab from his nose, and the mason does it without the man moving at all. When the prince of Sung asks for the same service, the mason says he can no longer do it, because his partner, the man who trusted him and sat still, is dead. The mason says he now has no one to speak with.
A duke, speaking to his sick adviser Kuan Chung, asks who should run the state if the adviser's illness gets worse. When Kuan Chung asks whom the duke has in mind, the duke suggests Pao Yü.

Kuan Chung, a minister, warns the Duke against hiring a certain man. He says the man is too pure and strict: he will not mix with people unlike himself, and he never forgets a wrong once he hears of it. Employed in government, he would soon quarrel with the prince and the people. The Duke then asks whom they can have instead.

Kuan Chung names Hsi P'êng as the man to blame. Hsi P'êng forgets the authority of those above him and makes those below forget his. He is ashamed he is not equal to the Yellow Emperor, and he grieves over people who are not equal to him.

Sharing one's virtue is true wisdom, and sharing one's wealth is merit. Showing greater merit does not win people's hearts, but showing lesser merit does. The text names Hsi P'êng as the only one who fits the person who neither hears nor sees the affairs of state and family.

The prince of Wu hunts monkeys on a mountain. Most flee, but one plays about carelessly in front of him to show off. The prince shoots it, but the monkey catches the arrow in its hand. When the prince orders his guards to shoot, the monkey is killed.

A prince tells his friend Yen Pu I not to show off his superiority, after a monkey that showed off its skill was killed. Yen Pu I then studies with a teacher to lose his superiority, drops his pleasures, and avoids fame, and within three years he is widely praised.

Nanguo Tzu-chi, sitting lost in thought, is asked why he looks like dead wood and dead ashes. He answers that he once hid in the hills, but when he showed himself, a ruler (T'ien Ho) noticed him and honoured him. He concludes that he must have given himself away, like goods sold to a buyer, and he laments that people bring about their own loss.

Grieving over someone who grieves for another only pushes a person farther away. At a banquet, Confucius refused to speak, calling his teaching wordless, while I Liao settled a quarrel between two houses simply by playing with a ball.

The sea is great because it accepts all the streams that flow into it, and the true Sage likewise embraces everything and benefits all people equally. He seeks no rank, credit, or fame. The second part adds that being good at barking or talking does not make a dog or a man good, so greatness and virtue cannot be earned by showy achievement alone.

The first part says that a person who understands true greatness wants nothing, loses nothing, and is not harmed from outside, because he relies on his own inexhaustible nature. The second part is a story: Tzŭ Chi asks a physiognomist which of his eight sons will prosper, and the reply is that K'un will dine at a prince's table and so end his days.

A diviner, Chiu Fang Yin, says that dining with a prince brings a family good fortune for three generations. He adds that weeping for a person can drive away one's luck. Tzŭ Chi asks how Yin can call K'un fortunate, since rich food only pleases the taste and Yin does not explain how it comes.

Lambs or quails appearing in one's hall would be strange, since the speaker is neither a shepherd nor a hunter and has no reason to keep such animals. The speaker asks what else could such an event be called other than uncanny, meaning something beyond ordinary explanation. The point is that such unusual events are wondrous signs, not ordinary occurrences.

A man says that he and his sons live by going along with nature and circumstances, without scheming or opposing them. Now the world rewards them in a strange way. Since they have done nothing to cause it, he concludes it must be the will of God, and he weeps.

The passage makes two points through short stories. A man named K'un is captured and sold for his value, and the brigands cut off his feet first so that he is easier to sell. Hsü Yu then says he is leaving Yao, a sage-ruler, because Yao cares only about charity and Hsü Yu fears this will bring ridicule and, in later ages, cannibalism.

Winning people over is easy: show them love, profit, or praise and they will come close and compete for it, but they leave once they dislike something. Love and profit come from charity and duty to others, and few ignore these while many turn them into gain. Such virtues are never disinterested, so one man lecturing the whole empire on them is like splitting something with one blow.

Yao, a legendary ruler, sees that good men help the empire, but not that they can also harm it. Only those above good men see this. The passage then describes a "nincompoop" as someone who follows one teacher and feels satisfied, unaware that there was a time when nothing existed.

Parasites are compared to lice on a pig. They settle in bald spots and treat the pig's body as their home, not knowing that the butcher will one day singe the pig and kill them too. Their fate matches what they have done.

Shun is given as an example of a man who draws followers because of his own qualities. The point is made with a comparison: ants are drawn to mutton, not the other way round, so people gathered around Shun. After he moved three times, a large crowd of families came with him to Têng.

Yao gave Shun a poor, barren region, expecting Shun's presence to make it prosperous. Shun was old and his mind was failing, yet he refused to stop working or retire, which the passage calls being an enthusiast, meaning someone carried away by zeal.

The spiritual man avoids crowds, because a crowd brings differences of opinion and no real gain. He keeps a middle distance from people, holding to virtue and seeking harmony with others. The passage ends with a saying that people should leave wisdom to ants and pursue what fish desire.

The passage says that people should let things follow their own nature rather than force them. Use the senses and mind to observe how things naturally work, and the wise person accepts events as they come. Whether life or death is called a gain or a loss makes no real difference.

Some substances that are normally poisonous become cures in the right circumstances, and the list of such cases is endless. The passage also says that a person can see one outcome clearly and still fail to foresee harm to himself. Each thing is suited to its own nature, so changing it would do harm.

The river is not harmed by wind or sun, because it keeps flowing from its source. Things that have fixed, settled connections, like water and earth, are fine. But the connection between the eye and what it sees is harmful.

The passage says that the link between the senses and what they perceive, between the mind and its objects, and between a person's abilities and his inner self all cause harm. Men still prize these abilities as valuable, and this blindness, it claims, leads to the ruin of states and endless killing.

The passage makes two points. A walk is good because of the ground the foot does not touch, and a person's knowledge grows by relying on what he does not know. Perfection is knowing the great One, the Infinite Void, and the underlying order of all things.

The passage lists "great" qualities and says each one reaches everything in its own way: the One is everywhere, the Negative has all power, and the Law binds all things. It then says the ultimate end, God, shows itself in natural laws, yet its origin cannot be known. Inquiry should neither stop short nor go without limit.

Behind this vague, undefined state there is a real existence that time cannot change or reduce. The speaker asks whether this can serve as a great guide, and suggests examining our doubts through it, so that certainty ends doubt and we return to a state free of doubt.

Wang Kuo says that a man who fishes for turtles in winter and rests in a mountain grove in summer, and tells passers-by that this is his home, is beyond the reach of Wang Kuo himself. Wang Kuo admits he could not match such a man's way of living.

The speaker warns that a man with knowledge but no virtue, and with an arrogant manner, may do harm when he tries to help others. He compares this to giving cold people clothes in spring, which is useless. The prince of Ch'u is harsh and cruel in punishing, so only a very skilled or perfect man could sway him.

The true Sage, a person who has fully understood the Tao (the Way, the natural order of things), makes others forget their troubles whether he is poor or powerful. Even rulers come to forget their rank. He is glad to see the Tao spread among people, and he loses nothing by it.

A sage who says nothing can still bring peace, and his mere presence makes people treat one another like father and son. His calm, inactive nature produces this good effect, and this shows how far his heart is from ordinary people's. That is why the speaker said to wait for Kung Yüeh Hsiu, a figure of this kind.

The passage describes the true sage as free from difficulties and as seeing all things as one, without even knowing it, since this is simply his nature. He stays steady in action and follows nature, which others then follow too. He regrets that human wisdom reaches only a short way and sometimes stops completely.

A beauty sees herself through other people, so she needs their praise to know she is beautiful. Yet her joy does not depend on whether she knows or hears it, and people will keep taking pleasure in her. The writer calls this nature, meaning it is simply how things are.

A sage loves other people whether or not he knows he does, and whether or not anyone tells him so, and that love never ends. The passage compares this to a wanderer who is glad to see his old home even when it is mostly wilderness. Jen Hsiang Shih, the person named at the end, reaches the centre and attains understanding.

The passage says that the wise person does not strive to follow God, beginnings, or matter. Instead he moves with the changing world, accepts whatever comes, and so is not harmed or overwhelmed. It asks how one could become like him.

The passage makes a set of separate points about rulers and advisers. A ruler who leans on a tutor's counsel while staying free of it gains both a good name and a sound way of governing, but a famous name for the tutor breaks the natural way and leads into endless choices. Other examples follow, such as a treaty that one prince broke, and a remark that time and space depend on each other.

Prince Hui wanted a man killed out of anger. His Captain-General objected that a ruler should not seek revenge through a common killer. He offered instead to invade the man's country with an army and seize it, so the prince could punish him at will.

Chi Tzŭ, hearing a proposal, protests in shame. He compares it to building a wall and then tearing it down just before it is finished, which would waste the workers' effort. He says the ruler's long peace is the foundation work, and he urges the ruler not to listen to the Captain-General, whom he calls a mischievous fellow. The passage breaks off before Hua Tzŭ's reply.

Hui Tzu's critics are angry at both sides of a quarrel over whether to punish the Ch'i State, and at anyone who judges either side. The prince asks where right action can be found, and the answer given is "In Tao alone," meaning the Way, a Taoist term for the natural order of things.

Tai Chin Jen tells the prince of two kingdoms, ruled by Aggression and Violence, that fight over a small patch of ground on a snail's horn. He asks whether the prince sees any limit to space, and the prince says space is boundless, which is the point of the story.

Tai Chin Jen argues that a ruler's kingdom looks tiny when compared with boundless space. He then asks the prince whether a prince of a small city differs from Violence, and the prince agrees that he does not.

Hui Tzu says that the sages Yao and Shun, though praised by all, are like a faint whoosh next to Tai Chin Jen, a far greater figure. Confucius, seeing a servant climb onto a roof, says that he is a sage disguised as a menial, hiding among ordinary people.

The passage describes a man who withdraws from society. He keeps out of public view, seeks no fame, and avoids living among people, though he keeps going with steady effort. The last line is a speaker naming himself as Liao of Shih-nan, the figure the description is said to fit.

Confucius tells his disciple Tzu Lu not to call on a hermit named Tzu Tsang (Tzu Lu's wording is cut off here). Confucius thinks the man would despise him as a flatterer seeking favor from a ruler, so he should not be approached.

A ruler's administration must be thorough, and his carrying out of duties must be efficient. The speaker gives his own farming as proof: careless ploughing and weeding gave poor crops, but deep ploughing and careful weeding gave a harvest too large to use in a year.

Zhuangzi says that most people today, in trying to regulate and organise themselves, hide their inner divine nature, give up their natural tendencies, and drop their feelings and spirit to follow whatever is fashionable. He adds that when a person is not thorough about their natural tendencies, something harmful takes their place.

Lao Tzu, the teacher, is answering his student Poh Chü, who wants to travel the world. The first lines say that certain things, such as learning or ambition, seem useful at first but later harm a person's natural state, like sores that burst out. Lao Tzu then tells Poh Chü that the world is already just as he sees it here, and asks where he would begin.

Poh Chü says he would start by going to the Ch'i State and looking at the bodies of executed criminals. He would push them to make them rise, cover them with his robes, and mourn them, saying they were the first to fall into the world's trouble.

The passage says that once people set up honour and disgrace, wealth grows and quarrels follow. These troubles keep wearing people down without rest, and the speaker asks how anyone can escape them. The opening line, about asking whether people are robbers or murderers, is a sharp question aimed at those who divide people by such labels.
The ancient rulers gave credit for every success to their people and took the blame for every failure themselves. When something went wrong, they looked to their own faults rather than to others.

Today's rulers hide things and then blame people for not seeing them. They give dangerous or heavy tasks, and punish those who cannot do them. Because of this, the people, feeling unable to meet these demands, turn to fraud.

People turn to fraud, deceit and theft when they lack strength, knowledge or means, so the passage asks who is really to blame. It then notes that Chü Poh Yü changed his views at sixty, and asks whether his new view of right might also prove wrong.

Things arise around us, yet no one knows where they come from. People prize only what they already know and fail to use the unknown to reach knowledge. The author calls this a mistake and says that people cannot escape it, which leads to what he calls "elective affinity," meaning the tendency of things to be drawn to one another by choice or preference.

Confucius asks three court historians why Duke Ling was given the posthumous name "Ling," which means something like "disorderly." Ta T'ao answers that the name was given for exactly those faults: his drinking, pleasure-seeking, hunting, and neglect of government and of other rulers.

The Duke bathed with his three wives when a man named Shih Ch'in arrived. The Duke covered himself and the women, yet he showed great respect to a virtuous man. For this mixture of bad conduct and respect, he was given the posthumous name Ling, which means something like "disorderly."

A dead duke's grave was chosen by divination. An old stone coffin dug up there warned that later generations cannot be trusted. Its claim about Duke Ling makes no sense, since that name had been his long before. Shao Chih then asks what society means.

Society is a joint agreement of many families and individuals to follow shared customs, so separate elements make up one whole. Just as a horse is the combination of all its parts rather than any single part, a just person judges each part by looking at the whole.

A person holds his own view without stubbornness and respects others' views without dropping his own. The passage compares this to the four seasons, which differ but are all equal, so together they make a full year.

Each group of officials or each kind of thing has its own duties, but the ruler, the great man, and the Tao each stay impartial toward them. Because of that impartiality, government works, the civil and military roles achieve their results, and all things can be done. Tao cannot be pinned down, so it acts by not acting.
Things in nature and human life keep changing in cycles. Seasons begin and end, generations pass, and good and bad fortune take turns, bringing sorrow at one time and happiness at another.

The passage says that someone who insists on seeing things only from his own viewpoint may be right in one case and wrong in another. Human society is compared to a jungle or mountain where many different things grow mixed together. Shao Chih then asks whether this mixed whole could be called the Tao, the Way.

Tao is greater than all of creation, the ten thousand things, the vast universe, the forces of yin and yang, and human society. These are only conditioned and limited things, and Tao embraces them all. The difference between them and Tao is as great as that between a horse and a dog.

Shao Chih asks where the life force of all things comes from, everything between the four directions and between heaven above and earth below. The question is posed to Tsê Yang, and the passage opens with this question only.

The speaker says that opposite forces act on and shape each other. He gives examples: the seasons follow and replace one another, love and hate alternate, danger and safety alternate, good and bad fortune produce each other, and gathering and scattering go together. These pairs of opposites are presented as facts that can be observed.

Things have a fixed pattern: they move forward, bend, wear out, and begin again. Words and knowledge cannot go beyond this pattern, so the follower of Tao does not try to probe what comes before or after it. Shao Chih then asks which of two rival teachers, one of chance and one of fate, was right.

The speaker says that people know that cocks crow and dogs bark, but cannot explain why. He then argues that the very small and the very great cannot be measured, so chance and predestination, which apply only to conditioned things, are both wrong.

Things that have a name and a form exist as material beings, while what has neither can be discussed, though the more one talks about it the further one drifts from it. Life's origin and end cannot be traced or fully known, and chance and fate are only convenient explanations invented in advance.

The passage argues that time has no real beginning or end, since looking backward or forward always shows only endless time. Ideas like fate and chance can only apply to physical things, so they cannot reach the infinite. The Tao, it says, cannot be called existent or non-existent; its name is just a convenient label.

Words cannot fully express Tao, the Way. Even a full day of speech would not be enough. Tao is beyond physical things and cannot be conveyed by either speech or silence, so it can only be grasped in a state between the two.

The passage says that events cannot be predicted, and that good conduct does not guarantee a good result. Loyal ministers are still sometimes killed, and dutiful sons are still not always loved by their parents. Examples from old stories are given to show this.

The passage uses fire as a picture of conflict. When opposing forces in nature or in people clash, heat builds up and burns the inner harmony of a person. Once the mind is burned up in this way, the Tao, the natural way of things, comes to an end in that person.

Zhuangzi answers the prince's promise of future money by telling a short story. A stickleback begs for a pint of water now, and Zhuangzi says he will bring water later from a distant river. The point is that a promise of help that comes too late is no real help.

A small fish, the stickleback, is angry because it is stranded and needs only a little water to survive. It says that being spoken to in such a way is as bad as being put in a dried-fish shop, where it would die.

A man baits a huge hook with fifty oxen and fishes in the eastern sea for a year without a catch. Then a great fish takes the bait and thrashes so violently that the sea churns and the noise frightens people for miles.
Jên Kung Tzŭ caught a huge fish and cut it up and salted it, so that people across a wide area all had enough to eat. Later generations kept repeating the amazing story of this catch.

Small catches and minor posts are not the same as big achievements. Those who do not follow the example of Jên Kung Tzŭ, a great fisherman in an earlier story, will never lead their age. As an example, Confucian scholars digging a grave by their books are told, with mockery, that day is breaking and they are still not finished.

Confucians are mocked here as people who pry open a dead man's jaws with force in the name of ritual care. The passage then sets up a meeting: a disciple of Lao Lai Tzu sees Confucius from afar and describes him as a sorrowful-looking man, and Lao Lai Tzu tells him to call Confucius over.

Lao Lai Tzu tells a man who wants to take on the world's sorrows that he will wear himself out. He says using goodness to win influence by pleasing others brings lasting shame, and that it is better to forget both the praise of good rulers and the blame of bad ones. Such efforts, he adds, harm the self.

The passage says a true Sage acts without feeling that his own effort brings success; success seems to come from outside him. It then gives a dream story: a prince dreams of a messenger from the River God, caught by a fisherman, and the soothsayers identify it as a divine tortoise.

The prince cannot decide whether to kill or spare a tortoise, so he asks a divination, which tells him to kill it for good fortune. He kills it, and the seventy-two omens he then takes are all correct. The point is that the tortoise, once killed, was used for divination, which the story treats as a kind of use it could not avoid.

Confucius says that a divine tortoise, though it can appear in a dream to a prince and give seventy-two perfect omens, still gets caught in a fisherman's net and is cut up. His conclusion is that wisdom has limits and cannot reach everything that spirit can.

The passage argues that trying hard to be wise or good can backfire, because wisdom brings its own traps. It says that if you drop small cleverness and conscious goodness, great wisdom and natural goodness will come on their own, as a child learns speech by living among speakers. The closing exchange adds that understanding the useless comes before discussing the useful.

Zhuangzi uses the earth as an example: people use only the small patch under their feet, and only that much is needed while they live, so the rest is of no use to them. Hui Tzu agrees. Zhuangzi says this shows that the useless can have a use. He adds that a person who could go beyond human limits would do so, but since no one can, he cannot succeed.

The passage says that choosing to withdraw from the world is not a sign of perfect wisdom or flawless virtue. Such people do not turn back from coming disasters, and they ignore even deadly danger. Social rank matters only for a time and means nothing in a changed situation. The passage then turns to the idea that a perfect man leaves no trace, and to scholars who praise the past and criticize the present.

The passage says that the perfect man goes beyond ordinary human limits without leaving the world. He lives among people without being harmed by them. He takes nothing from the teachings of the world, because he has an inner source that keeps him independent of others.

Each sense works well when nothing blocks it, and the mind gives wisdom, and wisdom gives te (inner power) when unblocked. Blocking the Tao (the Way) chokes life at its root and brings evil. Breath comes to all beings freely; any shortage is caused by people who stop its flow, not by God.

The passage says that a person's mind needs room to range freely, and that without it, conflict follows, both inside a person and in a household. It also says that trying to help others by withdrawing to remote places does not relieve this strain. Finally, it lists how badly managed virtue, reputation, scheming and knowledge each lead to trouble.
Things grow and heal in their own time, and remedies help only those who need them. Plants are weeded only after they are well grown, and those without illness do not bother with cures.

Each level of person is impressed only by things within a narrower sphere, and those wider or higher things do not draw their notice. The example given is the keeper of the Yen gate, who harmed himself in grief for his parents and was rewarded with office. His relatives copied him, and about half of them died.

A fish-trap is only useful for catching fish, and a snare only for catching rabbits. Once the goal is reached, the tool can be dropped. Language works the same way: it is a tool for conveying ideas, and once the idea is understood, the words can be set aside. The speaker wishes he could find someone who would look past the words to the meaning.

Speech attributed to others, or backed by famous authority, is believed in varying degrees: nine parts in ten for the first, seven for the second. Words that pour out freely, like wine from an overfull cup, are said to agree with Heaven, meaning the natural Way.

Words spoken through other people's mouths carry more weight than a person's own praise of himself. Just as a father cannot arrange his son's marriage by praising the son himself, since an outsider's praise counts for more. So the speaker says any failure lies with others, not with him.

People accept views that match their own and reject those that differ, calling their own view right and the other wrong. Appeals to authority end debate, but an authority is only a true superior if he has real knowledge and experience, not merely age. Without that, no one listens to him, and he becomes irrelevant.

The passage says that the deepest truth cannot be fully captured in words. A thing and its verbal expression are never exactly the same. So speech that is never expressed in words is the true kind, and constant talk is no better than silence, while constant silence still means something.

From a personal point of view, things seem possible or impossible, suitable or unsuitable. This comes from each thing's natural pull toward what it is and its natural clash with what it is not, since every thing has its own nature and abilities. The closing question asks how anything lasting could be reached through language that keeps flowing and changing like liquid poured from a full cup.

All things come from seeds or germs, and they keep reproducing in many forms. The process turns like a wheel with no fixed starting point. The passage calls this balance "the equilibrium of God," and says God is the one who holds the scales.

Zhuangzi points out that Confucius changed his views at sixty, so what he once called right he later called wrong. He asks whether today's right view might also be wrong. Hui Tzu replies that Confucius kept working hard and grew wiser each day.
