Chuang Tzu says Confucius gave up trying to state the Way in words. Confucius instead spoke of following established laws, fixed order, and duties to others, while admitting he had not yet succeeded in bringing men's hearts to submission and so securing the empire.

Tsêng Tzŭ, a disciple of Confucius, was happy on a small salary while his parents lived and sad on a large one after they died. Confucius explains that Tsêng Tzŭ had cares, and that his salary, small or large, meant little to him compared with his parents' loss.

Over nine years, a disciple describes a steady growth in understanding, ending in perfection and the end of his fear of death. He then argues that life has differences but death makes all equal, and asks why death should have a beginning while life has none. He closes by saying Heaven keeps a fixed order.

We cannot know what comes after death or what came before birth, so we cannot firmly say that fate does or does not act in our lives. Whether events go well or badly, no one can say for certain whether a supernatural force caused them.

The Penumbrae (faint outer shadows) ask the Umbra (the main shadow) why it keeps changing its posture and state. The Umbra replies that the question is hardly worth asking, implying that such changes are not something to be concerned about.

The speaker says he acts without knowing why, and that he depends on something beyond himself, much as a cicada's shell seems independent but is not. He follows other things in coming and going and in living, and he asks who gives life, a question he doubts can be answered.
Lao Tzu, travelling west, meets a man who had hurried out to greet him. Lao Tzu sighs and says he once thought the man could be taught, but no longer does. The man is judged to be beyond teaching.

Yang Tzu Chu comes humbly to ask Lao Tzu a question, washing and kneeling as a student would. Lao Tzu rebukes his arrogant manner and says that the truly pure seem stained, and the truly virtuous seem to lack virtue.

Yang Tzu Chu was welcomed warmly at an inn, with guests giving up their seats and the innkeeper's household serving him. When he came back later, the same guests pushed to get the best seats for themselves.
Someone offers the empire to Tzu Chou Chih Fu, who replies that he has no objection to becoming emperor. But he is busy curing a troublesome illness and has no time to govern the empire.

The main point is that a man who refuses to let power harm his life is the one fit to hold it. Shun offered the empire to Tzŭ Chou Chih Poh, who refused because he was busy curing an illness. For the Taoist, not giving up one's life for the empire is what separates the true follower of Tao from ordinary men.

Shun offered Shan Chüan the rule of the empire, but Shan Chüan refused. He said his simple daily life of work, rest and seasonal clothing satisfied him, so he had no need for power. He then hid in the mountains, and Shun offered the empire to a labourer instead.

A ruler's advice to Shun, a legendary sage-king, is that he should save his strength rather than work so hard. The speaker means that Shun had not yet reached true virtue. The couple then left with their household goods and children for the sea and never returned.

Faced with attackers who wanted his land, the ruler T'ai Wang offered them skins, silk, dogs, horses, and jade, but they refused everything except the territory itself. The passage is cut off before his answer, so the rest of his reasoning is not given.

A ruler refuses to rule a people if that means harming his own family, such as killing a brother or a son. He says that a thing meant to nourish life should not harm life, so he leaves with his staff, and his followers go with him to found a new state.

T'ai Wang Shan Fu is praised for valuing his life. The passage says that people who truly value life do not let wealth or rank harm their bodies, and do not let gain wear them down if they are poor. By contrast, powerful men of the author's time fear losing their position yet drop all care for their bodies once they see a chance of gain, which the author calls confusion.
The people of Yüeh had killed three princes in a row. Shou, the son of the last prince, became frightened and fled to a place called Tan Hsüeh, so Yüeh was left without a ruler.

Shou was reluctant to take up the role of ruler when the men of Yüeh finally found him and forced him into the royal carriage. He did not object to being a prince itself, but to the dangers that came with the position. The people wanted him because he would not risk his life for the state.

Two rival states, Han and Wei, were fighting over land. Tzŭ Hua Tzŭ asks Prince Chao Hsi whether he would cut off one of his own hands to become emperor of all, even if losing a hand meant losing the other too. The prince says he would not.

Tzŭ Hua Tzŭ argues to a prince that his two arms are worth more than an empire, his body worth more than his arms, and the State of Han far less than the empire. So the prince is wearing himself out with worry over a small prize, which the prince accepts as sound.

Messengers from a ruler arrive with gifts for Yen Ho, but he tells them they may have the wrong man and should check again. When they go back to make sure, Yen Ho has vanished, and the passage says this is how such men shun wealth and power.

The passage ranks the uses of the Tao: the best part is for cultivating oneself, the remainder for governing a state, and the lowest for governing the empire. So the deeds of rulers are only leftovers of the Sage's wisdom. Such deeds do nothing for keeping the body alive or nurturing life, yet people still risk their lives chasing worldly gain.

The passage makes two points. A wise person weighs the reason and purpose of an action first, and people who use something very valuable for a trivial goal, like shooting a bird with a priceless pearl, are rightly laughed at because they give up the greater for the lesser. Life is worth more than any treasure. The passage then shows Lieh Tzu, a wise man, living poor and hungry in a ruler's state, which a visitor takes as a sign that the ruler does not value scholars.
Tzŭ Yang ordered that food be sent to Lieh Tzŭ. When the messengers arrived, Lieh Tzŭ bowed twice and refused the gift.

Lieh Tzu refused a gift of food from a official because the gift was based on what others said about him. His reasoning is that if the same people spoke ill of him, the official would act against him just as readily. He would rather not depend on another person's opinion, even when that opinion brings him something good.

Yüeh, a butcher, says he lost his trade when the prince lost his kingdom and regained it when the prince got it back, so he wants no reward. He also refuses the punishment, because the loss was not his fault, and refuses the reward, because the recovery was not his doing.

Yüeh refuses to be called to an audience with the prince. He says the law of Ch'u allows an audience only to a subject who has deserved special merit, and he admits he has none, since he failed to save the kingdom and fled when the Wu army took the capital. He adds that summoning him against that law would be improper for the prince.
A prince tells his horse-master, Tzŭ Chi, that a man named Yüeh holds a humble post but has very high principles. So the prince orders that Yüeh be made a San Ching, a high rank in the state.
Yüeh refuses an offer of a more honoured post, saying that accepting would make his prince look unwise in choosing people. He would rather return to his work as a butcher and keeps to that refusal.

Yüan Hsien lives in a poor, leaky hut with a wad of old clothes for a window, yet he sits calmly playing his guitar. When the wealthy Tzŭ Kung visits in a grand chariot, Yüan Hsien greets him in worn, shabby clothes, leaning on a stick. The scene contrasts poverty with wealth.

Yuan Hsien says that a man without wealth is only poor, while a man who has learned but cannot put his learning into practice is the one who is truly sick or troubled. He claims that he is poor but not unwell.

Yuan Hsien, responding to Tzu Kung, lists what he will not do: push himself forward among people, seek friendship through flattery, learn to impress others, teach for personal gain, use kindness and duty as tools for bad ends, or show off with fine horses and carriages.

Tsêng Tzŭ, a disciple of Confucius, was living in great poverty: torn clothes, no fire, no new garments for years. Even so, he sang loudly and grandly, his voice filling the sky as if from a bell or stone chime. The point is that his poverty did not stop him from singing with full joy and dignity.

A man who has gone deep into his purpose forgets his body, and one who looks after his body forgets wealth. One who has reached the Tao forgets his own mind. So rulers cannot win him as servant or friend. Confucius then invites Yen Hui to take office, though Yen Hui is poor.

Yen Hui is refusing an offer of public office. He says his land outside the city feeds him, his land inside the walls clothes him, and his lute and his study of the master's teachings give him enough pleasure. So he has no wish to take up government service.

Confucius praises a disciple's view that contented people avoid chasing gain, do not fear loss, and feel no shame without a post, and says he has now seen this lived out. Prince Mou then admits his body is in his country while his heart is in the city, and asks what to do.

Chan Tzŭ tells a reader who cannot meet a task to follow his natural inclination, since forcing oneself to a task one cannot manage doubles the harm and shortens life. He then notes that Prince Mou of Wei, heir to a large state, found it harder to become a hermit than an ordinary scholar would, yet was still moving toward the Tao.

Confucius was trapped between two states, the Ch'ens and the Ts'ais, and went a week with almost no food, eating only herb soup. Although he looked worn out, he sat inside playing the guitar and singing.

Two disciples complain that their master has been driven out of several states, has nearly been killed, and is now surrounded by enemies. Yet he keeps playing and singing, and they ask whether this is proper conduct for a superior man.

Yen Hui, returning from a failed exchange, reports to Confucius, who puts down his guitar and sighs. He calls his disciples Yu and Tzŭ Lu "ignorant fellows" and asks them to come in so he can speak to them. Tzŭ Lu then says they seem to have failed completely.

Confucius answers that a true gentleman who follows the Way cannot really fail, even when he falls into trouble in a disordered age. Inner cultivation keeps his virtue intact through danger, just as frost and snow bring out the strength of pine and fir. He sees his hardship as a benefit.

Tzu Lu, one of Confucius's disciples, grabbed a shield and started dancing along with the music. Tzu Kung, another disciple, said he had not realized how high heaven is and how deep the earth goes. Both men are reacting to something they have just heard.

The passage says that people who have reached the Tao are equally content whether things go well or badly, because success and failure are just passing events, like weather. Shun offers the throne to Pei Jen Wu Tsê, who refuses, saying Shun's offer is an insult to him.

T'ang offers the throne to Pien Sui, who refuses. Pien Sui says that T'ang first treated him as a robber for helping plan an attack, and now treats him as greedy for power. He finds this insulting twice over and drowns himself.

T'ang offers to give the throne to Wu Kuang. He says the old way was that the wise plan, the brave carry out the plan, and the good rest in the result. He asks why Wu Kuang should not take the throne himself.

Wu Kuang refuses to accept the throne offered to him. He says it would be wrong to overthrow a ruler, to harm the people, or to take power and profit while others suffer. He believes a man should not take office or live in a land without Tao, the right way. He then drowns himself in the river Lu.

Two men hear of others said to have the Tao, the Way, and go to meet them. The king's envoy offers them official rank and a blood-sealed treaty, and they smile at each other. One says this is not what they mean by the Way.
Shên Nung, a legendary ruler, is described as serving God and his people without seeking any reward or personal gain. He never rose by harming others or took chances for his own advantage.

The speaker says that the Zhou rulers, who took power by condemning the wrongs of the Yin dynasty, have ended up doing the same kinds of things. They use plots and bribes, wage war to protect their image, and display virtue only to please the people. The result is that one kind of disorder has simply replaced another.

Two men argue that in times of disorder a wise person should not serve, since the ruling house has lost its virtue, and that it is better to leave and keep their conduct clean. They go north to Mount Shou-yang and starve themselves to death.

Poh I and Shu Ch'i, two figures from old stories, are described as men who would have accepted wealth and honour if these had been properly offered. They would not have taken extreme action or simply pursued their own way, but would have served their age. The passage praises their purity.

Robber Chê led a band of nine thousand men who raided the whole land. They stole property, seized other men's wives and daughters, and showed no respect for parents, brothers or ancestors. Wherever he went, states prepared for war and the people suffered greatly.

Confucius tells Liu Hsia Chi that an elder brother should be able to teach a younger one, and that if he cannot, these family duties mean nothing. Liu Hsia Chi is a scholar, but his brother is Robber Chê, a notorious bandit, so Confucius offers to speak to him for Liu.

Liu Hsia Chi replies to a visitor's argument about fathers and elder brothers by asking what happens to that argument if sons will not obey their fathers and younger brothers will not obey their elder brothers. He suggests the argument falls apart in that case.

Someone warns Confucius that the robber Chê has fiery passions, a whirlwind of thought, great strength, and a sharp tongue, and that his moods turn on whether he is agreed with or opposed. Confucius ignores the warning and goes to visit Chê anyway.

Robber Chê, angry at being told that Confucius wants to see him, sends back a scornful message. He calls Confucius a clever talker who spins empty words about the old kings, lives off work he never did, and muddles the rulers and scholars so they cannot return to the basic truth of things.

Confucius, a famous teacher of moral duty, visits the robber Chê and is received with mocking words. Chê tells him that his teaching of filial piety and brotherly love is only a way to win wealth and power, and that he deserves the worst. When Confucius sends a second message, Chê agrees to see him, and Confucius bows humbly before him.

Robber Chê, furious, confronts Confucius and threatens to kill him unless what Confucius says agrees with his own wishes. Confucius is addressed by his personal name, Ch'iu, and Chê is a notorious bandit leader.

Confucius says the world recognizes three kinds of virtue. The highest is outward beauty that wins admiration from everyone. The middle is wide wisdom that can explain all things. The lowest is courage that holds up under testing and attracts followers.

Zhuangzi's passage is a speech by a man who tells the robber Chê that his fine appearance and voice should make him fit to rule, yet he is known only as a robber. The speaker is shocked that such a man has a bad reputation despite these gifts.

A robber's captive, Robber Chê, is being urged by a speaker to give up raiding and become a lawful ruler. The speaker promises to win him lands, a walled state, and respect, and says this is how sages and capable men behave and what the world wants.

Robber Chê rebukes Ch'iu, who has been trying to win him over with praise and offers of wealth and office. He says such flattery is for ordinary people, not for him, and that flatterers to his face speak ill of him behind his back.

The point is that holding the whole empire did not keep the rulers' families safe. Yao and Shun were rulers whose descendants lost even a small piece of land, and the founders T'ang and Wu Wang had heirs who were wiped out. The speaker suggests that the size of the prize itself is the cause.

In this old account, early people lived in a world where animals outnumbered humans. They built shelters in trees, gathered nuts by day, and slept in branches at night. They were named for these ways of life, such as "Nest-builders" and "Provident."

In this passage, people of the early golden age lived simply and without worry. They slept and rose without planning, lived among animals, farmed for food, wove their own clothes, and had no wish to harm others. The writer calls this the result of perfect virtue.

The Yellow Emperor, the speaker says, did not reach true virtue, because he waged war and spilled much blood. Later rulers such as Yao, Shun, T'ang and Wu Wang are also linked to conflict and seizure of power. The speaker concludes that since T'ang and Wu Wang, the strong have oppressed the weak and rulers have only caused disorder.

Robber Chê is accusing Confucius (here called Robber Ch'iu) of being a bigger thief. He says Confucius preaches old teachings of King Wen and clever arguments, wears modest clothes, and speaks grandly, all to deceive rulers and gain wealth and power. Chê says that if he is called a robber, Confucius deserves the name even more.

Robber Chih's speech is addressing Confucius here. He says Confucius was praised for being able to stop violence, yet his own disciple Tzu Lu tried to kill the prince of Wei, failed, and was chopped up and displayed at a city gate. The speaker blames Confucius for not teaching Tzu Lu properly.

The speaker is mocking Confucius, who is called a man of talent and a sage. He points to Confucius's exile, his failures at court, and the death of his disciple Tzu Lu, and asks what use his teaching can be. Even the revered Yellow Emperor and Yao are said to have fallen short in virtue.

Zhuangzi argues that six famous men, admired for their reputation, were in fact driven by a desire for personal gain that corrupted their original purity. He gives Poh I and Shu Ch'i, who refused a throne and starved, and Pao Chiao, who died clinging to a tree, as examples.

The passage mocks men who died for loyalty or a promise, such as Chieh Tzŭ T'ui and Wei Shêng. It says they are no better than animals that go to slaughter, because they cared about reputation, ignored death, and failed to look after their own lives.

Zhuangzi says the world calls Wang Tzŭ, Pi Kan and Wu Tzŭ Hsü the most loyal ministers. Yet two of them died terrible deaths, Wu Tzŭ Hsü by drowning himself and Pi Kan by being disembowelled, so the world now laughs at them instead of honouring them.

Robber Chih tells Confucius's messenger, Ch'iu, that the ancient sages, even figures like Tzu Hsu and Pi Kan, did not deserve honour. He says he will not understand a sermon on spirits, and a sermon on human affairs holds nothing new for him, since he already knows it all.

The passage lists four kinds of desire: for beautiful sights, for music, for good flavours, and for success or power. It then notes that a human life lasts at most about a hundred years, and often much less. The point is that these desires are pursued within a short span of life.

Robber Chih speaks to Confucius's disciple Ch'iu (Confucius, in the Chuang Tzu's story). He says that illness, death, and grief leave little time for joy, and that human life is brief compared with Heaven and Earth. He then tells Ch'iu to stop preaching, since his teaching is false and cannot keep people's natural purity.

Confucius has just left Robber Chê, and he is badly shaken. He nearly fails to take the reins, cannot see clearly, and looks deeply upset. When his friend Liu Hsia Chi guesses where he has been, Confucius admits he has visited Chê, sighing as he does so.

Confucius says he has nearly been harmed by a tiger, a fierce man, by trying to tame him. Tzu Chang then argues to Man Kou Te that without virtue no one trusts you, and without trust you gain no position or wealth, so duty to others is the key to success.

Man Kou Tê answers that giving up reputation and wealth would leave the virtuous man with nothing to do beyond himself. He argues that wealth and fame usually come from shamelessness and from winning others' trust, so people who chase them are the ones who do the most.

Tzŭ Chang points out that the ancient tyrants Chieh and Chou ruled the whole empire, yet even a common thief would be insulted to be compared to them. Chieh and Chou are thus looked down on, even by thieves.

Confucius and Mih Tzu were poor and humble, yet a powerful minister would be proud to be compared to them, which the passage presents as a sign of how highly learned men are regarded. The passage then says that power does not make a man worthy, and poverty or low rank does not make him unworthy. A person is judged by his actions.

The speaker points out that small wrongdoers are punished while great wrongdoers become rulers, and that good men still serve them. He gives two cases: Duke Huan, who killed his brother, had Kuan Chung as minister, and T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ, who killed his prince, was served by Confucius, who took his pay. He asks whether this shows that what people condemn in words is not what they do in practice.

Tzŭ Chang asks how the family and social duties can be told apart if a man ignores them. Man Kou Tê answers with famous rulers and their acts: Yao killed his own son, Shun exiled his uncle, and T'ang and Wu overthrew their rulers. Each act breaks a bond or rank, so he asks whether such acts count as keeping those duties.

Robber Chê is scornfully asking whether the teachings of the Confucians and the Mohists, with their talk of duty and universal love, help people tell apart the Five Bonds and Six Ranks, meaning the basic social relationships and ranks. He then proposes that he and his opponent, one chasing fame and the other wealth, settle which of their pursuits is wrong by appeal to Wu Yoh, a judge.

Wu Yoh says that a man who chases wealth and a man who chases reputation end up with different moral results, but both would be the same if they stopped their striving and did nothing. He advises that one should return to one's natural self and follow heaven's laws, and that one should view straight and crooked, right and wrong, from a wide standpoint rather than hold to fixed judgments.

The speaker warns against virtue, wealth and success, since these can cost a person their true nature. He gives examples of famous loyal, honest and dutiful men who came to grim ends, and says such were the results of their goodness. The point is that moral virtue brings harm rather than reward.
Learned men from long ago, whose stories are still told, are said to have stressed their teachings by acting on them. Because they did so, they suffered misfortune.

Discontent challenges Complacency: most people chase fame or wealth, since the rich attract followers and respect, which seems to bring long life and happiness. He asks whether Complacency lacks sense, or is too weak to compete and so pretends to be virtuous while still wanting these things.

Complacency, a figure in the text, answers that his critics judge people as all alike only because they share a time and place with them. He says they see him and his fellow scholars as cut off from the world, guided only by old records and empty word-disputes.

Living as ordinary people do would mean giving up the basic conditions of life, and so moving away from long life, comfort and happiness. The speaker also says that the other side does not treat bodily ease or hardship as something that matters.

The speaker says that feelings such as fear and joy do not come from the mind itself. A person may know that these feelings happen but not understand how they arise. Even someone as powerful as the emperor, owning the whole realm, would still not be free from worry.

Discontent, a speaker in this exchange, argues that wealth is very useful to a man. With it he can do more good and wield more power than even a perfect man or a wise sage could, borrowing others' courage, wisdom and virtue, and holding authority without a throne.

The speaker argues that people do not need to learn how to enjoy music, beauty, rich food, or power. The mind and body know these pleasures naturally, and no teacher is needed to tell us what to like or avoid. He adds that, though the world may disagree, no one is free of this natural drive.
The wise man, the speaker says, acts for the common good and keeps within proper limits. He takes what he needs and no more, and he does not call his taking greed or his refusing of extra honesty.

The passage says that a certain kind of person refuses power and wealth because he sees the troubles that come with them as harmful to his own nature, not because he wants a good name. It then describes how Yao and Shun, legendary ancient rulers, governed: they did not try to act as benevolent rulers, and so they did no harm.
People chose what benefited them over what harmed them. The world then praised them as virtuous, though they had never sought that reputation.

Two speakers argue about how to live well. Discontent says a good name must be guarded, and that a life stripped of pleasure for the sake of health would be a long sickness. Complacency answers that happiness lies in contentment, and that wealth and its pleasures bring confusion.

Greed is described here as a kind of sickness. The man wants money for comfort and power to beat rivals, but his wealth brings him illness, and even a huge fortune does not stop his craving. Hoarding it while it does him no good makes his heart burn, and the passage calls this unhappiness.
Someone at home fears thieves, and when out travelling fears bandits, so he guards his house closely and never goes out alone. The passage calls this fear.

The passage says that the six things just named are the worst curses in the world, yet people ignore them until trouble arrives. Then, with desires satisfied, strength spent, and only wealth left, they cannot find even a day of peace. It ends by pitying those who wear out their minds and bodies chasing fame and riches.

King Wen of Chao, a ruler of long ago, loved sword fights. He kept over three thousand swordsmen at his court, who fought before him day and night. Each year a hundred or so were killed or hurt, yet the prince still was not content.

The Heir Apparent, Li, offered a large reward to anyone who could persuade the prince to get rid of his swordsmen, and his officers named Chuang Tzu. Chuang Tzu refused the silver. When the messengers returned it, the Heir Apparent is left asking what more he can say.

Chuang Tzu is asked to cure a prince of a strange weakness, which here means his obsession with swords. He doubts the job is worth the risk of death, but says that success would win him great rewards. When the young prince says the king only receives swordsmen, Chuang Tzu replies that he is one himself.

The Heir Apparent warns Chuang Tzu that the king likes swordsmen with wild hair, rough caps and fierce looks, and that a scholar's dress will go badly. Chuang Tzu agrees to change his clothes and practises the new dress for three days before going back to the court.

Chuang Tzu enters the court of a prince who loves sword-play, and the prince, angry, draws his sword and waits for him. Chuang Tzu does not bow or hurry, and offers to show his skill. He says that if he met an opponent every ten paces, he could walk a thousand li without being stopped.

In this part, Chuang Tzu tells a prince how he fights. He pretends to be weak, attacks hard, starts last and still arrives first. He offers to be tested, and the prince tells him to wait until a day is set.
A prince tests his swordsmen and finally summons Zhuangzi, who offers to let the prince choose from three swords he owns. The prince asks what those three swords are.

The passage describes an imaginary sword of the Son of Heaven, the ruler of all China. Its edge, back, hilt and sheath are the mountains and states of the empire, and it is linked to the seasons, the five elements and the forces of Yin and Yang. A single flash of it makes the rulers of the realm submit.

Chuang Tzu describes a sword made of virtues: wisdom and courage form its point, incorruptibility its edge, virtue its back, loyalty its hilt, and heroism its sheath. Such a sword cannot be pushed, raised, lowered or turned, and it follows heaven, keeping in step with the sun, moon and stars.

The passage describes the "sword of the Princes" as one that follows the square earth and the four seasons, and that brings peace so that everyone in the state obeys the ruler. The prince then asks about the "sword of the People," which is the subject that follows.

Zhuangzi tells a prince that the "sword of the People," a crude fighter's blade, is like a game-cock: it brings quick, brutal fights and a short life, and is useless to the state. He is ashamed that a ruler with sovereign power should prize such a sword.
After this, the prince stayed inside his palace for three months. The swordsmen, having given up their fighting way of life, died peacefully at home.
Confucius rests in a forest grove. His students study their books while he plays the lute and sings. The scene shows him relaxing instead of teaching.

An old fisherman, after listening to a song, calls over two of Confucius's disciples, Tzŭ Kung and Tzŭ Lu, and asks what the man near them is doing there. When told he is the Sage of Lu, from the K'ung family, he begins to question who this sage is.

Tzu Lu describes Confucius as a man devoted to loyalty, charity, ceremony and music, who serves the state and the people. The old fisherman then asks whether Confucius holds any office, such as ruler or minister, and Tzu Kung answers that he holds neither.

An old fisherman tells Confucius's disciple Tzu Kung that Confucius's care for others wears down the mind and body and harms people's natural purity. When Confucius hears this, he decides the fisherman is a Sage (a wise, enlightened person) and goes after him to bow and ask for guidance.

Confucius, having failed to understand the old fisherman's words, humbly asks to be taught. The old man replies that like things follow like things and like sounds answer like sounds, a saying that suggests people are drawn to what matches their own nature. Confucius says he has studied all his life without hearing the true teaching and is ready to receive it.

Each level of society does its own job, and then government works well and no one harms another. When people leave their proper places, the result is complete disorder. The passage then lists the common troubles of ordinary people: poor land, bad housing, hunger, unpaid taxes, and family quarrels.

The passage lists the troubles that trouble ministers and princes. For ministers, the sorrows are being unable to do their duties, being careless, and not being recognized or promoted. For princes, they are disloyal officials, a weak state, poor craftsmanship and tribute, and displeasure from the emperor.

Heat and cold come at the wrong times, rulers fight each other, and people die. Music and ritual are badly kept, wealth is wasted, family duties are ignored, and the common people fall into immorality. The passage says these troubles are the sorrows that belong to the Son of Heaven, the emperor.

The old fisherman is rebuking Confucius for stepping outside his proper role. Neither ruler nor minister, Confucius tries to set rules for music, ceremony and social roles to reform the people, and the fisherman asks whether he is overstepping. He then lists faults such as prying, pushing in, and flattery.

The passage lists faults that make a person disturb others and harm himself. It names ambition as loving to take charge of great affairs and change established order for fame. It names greed as trying to seize what belongs to others, and obstinacy as refusing to correct known faults or heeding criticism.

The passage says that four things get in the way of important work, and that only someone who sets aside eight other things and avoids those four is ready to be taught. In short, a person must first clear away these faults before they can learn.

Confucius sighs and asks why he has suffered so many misfortunes: being driven out of two states, being shunned, having a tree cut down, and being surrounded. The old fisherman answers that Confucius is slow to understand, meaning the cause lies in something Confucius has not yet seen.
A man tried to escape his shadow and his footsteps by running faster, but they kept following him. He wore himself out and died. He could have lost them by standing in the shade or by keeping still.

The speaker tells someone that busy efforts at charity, duty, and managing feelings still bring the very troubles they hope to avoid. He advises keeping one's own body and inner purity in order and leaving outside matters to others. Trying to reform other people, he says, is only dealing with what is external.

The fisherman says that true feeling comes from an inner purity, a truth without mixture. Forced displays do not carry real weight: fake tears do not show grief, feigned anger does not command awe, and a smile without feeling does not create real agreement. Real grief, anger and friendship need no outward show, so the inner purity is what he values most.

Ritual forms matter less than the feeling or purpose behind them. Serving parents, serving a ruler, feasting and mourning are judged by whether their aim is met: a parent gratified, real grief shown, a successful service. How it is done, and any outward trace or ceremony, is of no importance.

Ceremony is a human invention, while original purity is given by Heaven and cannot be changed. The wise person follows Heaven and values this original purity, so human pressures do not control him. Fools do the reverse, relying on human rules and so never reach the goal.

A speaker tells an older man that meeting him is a great stroke of luck. He asks to serve him as a servant, to learn from him, and to be told where he lives so he can begin and learn the great teaching.

The old fisherman says that a man who is a fit companion can be taken along even into the deepest parts of Tao (the Way), but a man who does not know Tao should be avoided so that no harm comes to you. He then leaves in his boat. Confucius does not move until the water is calm and the sound of the boat has faded.

Tzu Lu, a disciple of Confucius, asks why his master bowed deeply and prostrated himself before an old fisherman. The master treats powerful rulers with respect but was humble to this man, which puzzles the disciples.
Confucius speaks to a student who has studied ceremonies and duty to others for a long time. He says the student still has not got rid of his old, faulty nature, and he calls him over to explain.

Showing no respect to an elder or a sage is a failure of courtesy and of goodwill toward others. Without that goodwill, a person cannot humble himself before others, and so cannot reach original purity. The speaker says there is no greater evil than lacking goodwill toward people.

Tao is the source of all things. People who keep it live, and people who lose it die. Actions that go against it fail, and actions that follow it succeed. So the speaker respects the old fisherman, because he holds Tao.

Lieh Tzŭ turned back halfway to Ch'i because restaurant keepers, out of ten, would not take his payment, and he feared what this meant. He thought that people's free gifts showed that his inner truth had not yet fully settled in him, and that such outward appeal could lead to a lack of respect for authority and age, which brings trouble.

A restaurant keeper earns little from selling soup, and the speaker says that a ruler of a large state, worn out by his duties, would be a worse position still. The speaker fears being given such a burden, even though a ruler offers rewards. Poh Hun Wu Jen replies that good inner lights will still draw people to him if he stays where he is.

Poh Hun Wu Jen tells his disciple that people will gather around him whether or not he wants them to, and that trying to control this only makes him lose his natural balance. He says the clever tire and the wise grieve, while those without ability have no ambitions and drift freely, like boats without a set destination.

A man named Huan studied Confucianism for three years and became a scholar of it, and his influence reached three families. He got his younger brother to study Mohism, but when their father sided with the Mohists in the dispute between the two schools, Huan killed himself after ten years.

The father dreams that the ancestor Huan tells him he, not the son, made the younger son a Mihist (a follower of Mozi). People are not rewarded for their deeds but for their nature, and abilities come from one's background, not from oneself alone. A man who claims his gifts as his own is like a well-digger who blocks others from his well. So people today are all like Huan, meaning they take credit that belongs to others.

Real virtue is not aware of itself, and the person who follows the Tao (the Way, the natural order of things) is even less so. Knowing the Tao is easy, Chuang Tzu says, but talking about it makes it hard. Knowing it silently is natural, while knowing it through words is artificial.

People tend to treat things that are uncertain as if they were certain, so they are always ready to fight. Getting used to taking up weapons makes a person reach for them at every provocation, and relying on weapons leads to ruin.

The passage contrasts two kinds of people. The petty person's mind is clouded by small concerns like bribes and recommendations, so he cannot grasp the Tao, the underlying way of the universe, or reach back to the time before anything existed. The perfect person looks back to that earliest time and rests in it, merging with the infinite.
A man from Sung named Ts'ao Shang went to the court of Ch'in as an envoy. He arrived with only a few carriages, but the prince of Ch'in was so pleased with him that he gave him a hundred more.

A man returns to Sung and visits Chuang Tzu, boasting that he could never live in poverty making sandals, but he excels at visiting powerful rulers with a large train of carriages. The remark is a contrast between two ways of life, one humble and one grand, and the speaker says which one suits him.

Chuang Tzu mocks a visitor by saying the man must have licked a prince's piles to earn so many carriages, since the more degrading the service, the greater the reward. In a second story, Yen Ho warns Duke Ai of Lu that making Confucius a pillar of the state would be dangerous, because Confucius relies on outward show and fine words and confuses the branch with the root.

Zhuangzi here criticizes a man who tries to impress people with a proud, commanding manner, not seeing that it is empty. He says that if such a man is trusted with running the state, he will succeed only by accident. He adds that teaching people to abandon the true for the false harms later generations more than the present one, so it would be better if Confucius had never existed.

Punishment can come from outside, through weapons or prisons, or from inside, through worry and regret that tear the mind apart. Fools suffer the outer kind. Only the pure and perfect person escapes both.

Confucius says that the human heart is harder to understand than mountains, rivers, or Heaven itself. People hide their true motives behind their outward behavior, so a man may seem withdrawn while he is really pushing forward, or seem useless while he is capable.

People who rush to do their duty to others, as if they were thirsty for it, drop it quickly, as if it were hot. The passage says a truly good person is tested in nine ways, such as by distant or dangerous tasks, money, or wine, and that these tests show what a lesser person really is.

Chêng K'ao Fu grew more humble with each promotion, bowing lower each time, while ordinary men grow prouder and more arrogant. The passage concludes that deliberately displayed virtue, when the mind looks outward for approval, is the most harmful thing of all.

The passage gives a list of qualities that lead to failure and qualities that lead to success. Beauty, height, strength, courage and similar gifts that set a man above others are called causes of failure. Modesty, compliance and humility are called sure roads to success.

The father's point is that the pearl was valuable only because it came from under a sleeping dragon's nose. He tells his son to smash a stone rather than the pearl's source, since the dragon would wake and the boy would be in danger.

The speaker warns a man who has taken valuable chariots from the prince of Sung. The prince is described as more dangerous than a dragon, and the danger is so great that the man would only have got the chariots if the prince had been asleep. If the prince wakes up, the man will be crushed to powder.

Chuang Tzu turns down a prince's invitation to serve him by comparing himself to a sacrificial ox. The ox is decked out and well fed, but it is led off to be killed. Chuang Tzu suggests it would rather swap places with an ignored calf, so he prefers a humble life that keeps him out of danger.

Chuang Tzu, near death, tells his disciples that heaven and earth, the sun, moon and stars, and all creation already serve as his coffin and funeral. When they fear birds will eat his body, he replies that whether birds or insects eat him, something is fed, so there is no reason to take food from one to give to the other.

Relying on fixed standards that are only relative leads to results that are not truly fair or right. Those who depend on their senses serve outside things, while those guided by inner intuition find the true standard. Fools trust the senses to judge what is good, and they reach only outward results.

Many systems of government exist, and each person thinks his own is best. The passage asks where the old "Tao" (the Way) fits among them, and answers that it is present in all of them. Sages are born, rulers are made, yet all come from one original source.

Those who stay joined to the Source, the essence, and the reality reach higher levels: one with God, a spiritual man, a perfect man. The true Sage takes God as source, Te (inner power) as root, and Tao as gateway, and goes along with circumstances. A superior man is only kind, dutiful, ceremonial, and musical in a more ordinary way.

The passage lists men who follow law, value reputation as something outside themselves, test their ideas, and judge by proof. It says these men are ranked like officials, and that they still serve good government by doing their duty, providing food and clothing, and caring for the old, the weak, orphans and widows. Such was the reach of Tao among the ancients.

The passage praises a single all-pervading principle, here the Tao (the Way). It says this principle works with the gods, cleanses the universe, feeds all creatures and reaches every direction and every size of thing. Nothing lies outside it.

The passage says that a single underlying principle, called "it" here (the Way, in Taoist thought), shaped the ancient classics and government. Each classic reflects a different quality of it: poetry shows vigour, history usefulness, rites adaptability, music harmony, the Changes mystery, and the Spring and Autumn annals careful distinctions. All schools of learning honour its power.

When the world falls into disorder, sages no longer appear, and the Tao is no longer one unified whole. Each person knows only their own special abilities. The passage compares this to the senses and to craftsmen: each is good at its own task, but none is shared by all.

Narrow specialists claim to know the principles of the universe, and each school insists its own path is the only correct one. The schools split apart and never reunite, so the original Tao, the way of inner wisdom and outer strength, is scattered and no longer visible as a whole.

The passage names the old Way (Tao) as a life of not seeking fame after death or public show, not posing as a helper of humanity, and being strict with oneself but forgiving toward others. It says two followers, Mih Tzu and Ch'in Hua Li, took this too far, and it names one essay each by Mih Tzu, Against Music and Economy.

The passage describes Mo Di (Mozi) and his teachings: he rejected singing and mourning, taught universal love without quarrelling, and set aside the music and rites of the ancient sage-kings. It then lists the ancient rulers' musical pieces, which he did not follow.

The passage contrasts old funeral customs, where the number of coffins matched a person's rank, with the rule of Mih Tzu (Mozi), who wanted one thin coffin for everyone and no mourning. The writer says this simple, equal burial does not fit Mozi's teaching of universal love.

The passage says that following certain rules does not prove a man respects himself, and such rules may not wreck his whole system. It adds that it would be unreasonable to ban ordinary human acts like singing, weeping and rejoicing at the right times.

The speaker criticizes a teaching that asks people to work hard all their lives and despise death. He argues it is too harsh and unnatural, going against human feelings, so ordinary people would not accept it. Only a single austere follower like Mih Tzu could live by it, and that would make building an ideal state unlikely.

Mih Tzu praises the legendary ruler Yu, who controlled the great floods. Yu channeled waters into rivers and streams across the empire and worked with his own hands, using bucket and dredger, to bring order out of chaos.

This is a fragment about Yü, a legendary sage-king, and the Mohists, a rival school. It says Yü wore himself down working for the common good, so later Mohists copied his hardship, wearing plain clothes and working without rest, and judged themselves by whether they matched it.

The passage describes later followers of Mo Tzu (Mih Tzu), a school of thinkers. Though they all studied his writings, they disagreed with each other, called one another heretics, and argued over logic puzzles such as "hard and white" and "odd and even." Their leader Chü Tzu was honored as a sage so his teachings would last, and the disputes are still unresolved.

Zhuangzi says that Mo Tzu (Mih Tzŭ) and his follower Ch'in Hua Li had sound ideas but their practice was wrong. Their teaching would have set people competing in harsh self-denial, so its harm would outweigh its good. Still, Mo Tzu meant well and kept to his doctrine despite failure, so he is called a man of genius.

The passage describes an ideal way of living that the ancients followed, called the Tao. It means staying clear of worldly affairs, empty show, and personal ambition, while wanting peace for everyone, taking only what is needed, and keeping the heart pure.

Sung Hsing and Yin Wên were followers of Tao who wore a cap shaped like a mountain as their sign. They treated all things kindly, and they taught that a person who could bring joy to people and peace to the world should be made their ruler.

Zhuangzi describes a group who worked to stop fighting and ended wars across the land. People mocked them and often rejected them, yet they kept going. The passage concludes that they gave too much to others and too little to themselves.

Starving disciples asked for only five pints of rice, which was not enough to satisfy their master. Even so, they kept working day and night for the world. They asked whether they must go on living and whether they should copy the so-called saviours of mankind, which seems to question whether such service is worth the cost to themselves.

The passage describes the ideal "superior man" as someone who does not criticise others or claim their achievements. He sees those who bring no benefit to the world as worthless. He treats stopping violence and disarming as outward matters, and controlling one's own desires as the inner matter.

The passage describes the Tao, the Way, as the ancients understood it. It means being impartial, not acting only for oneself, going with circumstances rather than fixed plans, and not dwelling on past regrets or future worries. Such a person is friendly toward everyone.

These three followers of Tao held that all things are one and that Tao embraces everything but cannot deal with each particular thing. Because selection and training cannot reach everywhere, they taught that Tao is complete. Shên Tao then gave up knowledge and self-interest and accepted fate.

Under torture, even a man who mocks virtue and the wise will give up his fixed opinions on right and wrong. Once he is freed, he stops caring about knowledge and planning, and past and future no longer matter to him.

The passage describes a person who responds to outside pushes and pulls without resisting, moving like wind, a feather, or a millstone. Such a being is harmless, because it acts only as much as is needed, so it cannot be blamed.

Shên Tao is praised for being like an inanimate thing: it has no worries, no tangled knowledge, and so it never gets praise. The passage says a clod of earth can be said to follow the Tao, the Way. A rival mocks this, saying Shên Tao's Way suits only the dead. T'ien P'ien studied under P'êng Mêng and gained nothing.

The passage criticizes three thinkers, P'êng Mêng, T'ien P'ien and Shên Tao, for having only a partial grasp of Tao, the Way. It then gives the older Way: put the root (the inner, essential) first, treat outward things as secondary, see piling up goods as a lack, and accept what Heaven sends.

Zhuangzi describes a school of thinkers who built their teaching on "nothingness" and the idea of oneness, and who valued gentleness, humility and not harming anything. He then quotes two sayings: Kuan Yin advises not taking fixed positions, staying flexible, calm and yielding, and not leading; Lao Tzu says that one who is strong but chooses to act weak will be looked up to by others.

The passage praises those who seek little and hold back. It says such people store nothing, yet have plenty without effort, and laugh at others' tricks. People who worship lesser gods, with a focused but limited mind, get only the small rewards those gods can give, and these soon fade. Those who come to the highest reality reach it directly. Those who think the unmanifested (formless, unseen) has become visible, and do not grasp the true nature of the divine, are blind.

The speaker, a divine figure addressing Arjuna, says he is eternal and unseen, hidden behind his magic veil of appearances. Most people do not see or know him. Yet he knows all things past, present and future, while none of them know him.

Attachment to the "pairs of opposites," such as liking and disliking, traps people and leaves almost all creatures confused. Only a few are freed from these pairs, from sin, and from confusion through right action, knowledge and steady faith, and they turn to the speaker, Krishna.

Those who take refuge in Krishna (speaking as the god) from the cycle of birth and death are said to know the truth. They know him as Brahma, the Soul of souls, the work of action, and the lord of life, of the gods, and of sacrifice. Worship him with love and faith, and he can be found and held at the hour of death.

Arjuna asks Krishna a series of questions about sacred terms. He wants to know what Brahma is, what the Soul of Souls (Adhyatman) is, what action (karma) is, and what the other terms mean. He also asks how Krishna is present in a body, and how good people find him at the time of death.

Krishna names himself with a series of divine titles. He says he is Brahma, the one eternal God, and the soul of all souls. He also says he is the Lord of all living beings, of the gods, and of sacrifice, and that he dwells within the body of the listener.
A person who thinks only of the divine at the moment of death goes to join it. Whatever a person is focused on at death, the soul goes to that, because the soul becomes like what it is set on.

Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna to keep him in mind and to keep fighting. Whoever fixes heart and mind on him, with unwavering faith and no other gods, will surely come to him. He is described as the supreme, eternal being who holds up all three worlds and gives life to every atom.

Whoever knows Krishna's divine form, which is beyond ordinary understanding, and sees his radiance, brighter than the sun and dispelling darkness, has lived rightly. If such a person dies with a steady mind and firm devotion, they die in peaceful faith.

A person who dies calmly, with the senses shut off, desire held in check, breath steadied, and the sacred syllable OM murmured, reaches the highest goal. This goal is called Akshara, the Ultimate, and it is the same destination sought by saints and ascetics. The dying person's final thought is fixed on the god Krishna, who speaks these lines.

Krishna says that a yogi who keeps his thoughts on him alone, with no other gods in view, can easily reach him. Those who reach him are not reborn into this world of suffering. Instead they take the path to the highest bliss.

Even the world of Brahma, the creator god, cycles back into birth and death. Those who reach Krishna, speaking here as God, are not reborn. The passage then describes Brahma's day and night as vast cycles, with creation appearing at dawn and dissolving at night.

Creatures come into being again and again at the dawn of Brahma, a cosmic day, and vanish at his nightfall, without choosing to. Beyond them lies a deeper, unchanging life that does not pass away with them. It is called the Unmanifest.
The verse says that the wisdom it describes is worth more than the fruit of Vedic rituals, more than gifts, and more than prayer or fasting. A yogi who understands this reaches the highest peace.

Krishna, the speaker, says he will now reveal his deepest secret teaching to a listener who is open to it. He says this knowledge frees a person from troubles and sins, and that it is easy to follow and never runs out.

Those who do not accept this teaching, and lack faith to grasp the deeper wisdom, do not reach Krishna, the speaker. They fall back into the cycle of rebirth in the material world, where everything changes. The speaker says he spreads through the whole universe and contains all beings, yet is not contained by them, and remains beyond all things.

Krishna tells Arjuna that all things exist within him, yet he is not identical to them, much as air moves within space without being space itself. At the end of each cosmic age (kalpa) all things return to him, and at the start of the next they emerge again from him, through his power called Prakriti, which is nature or material energy.

Krishna, speaking as God, says that his acts of creation do not bind him or tie him down. He stands apart from them as higher and free. Through him, the material of the world produces all beings, living or lifeless, and the world keeps going.

Untaught people fail to recognize the divine presence hidden in the visible form, so they chase empty hopes and empty knowledge and follow a harmful path. Those of noble soul, by contrast, worship with steady hearts, knowing the divine as the source of all things.

Krishna, speaking in the Gita, says that people who worship him with steady devotion are doing so, and that even those who make offerings to other gods with an awareness of one divine power in all things are, in fact, worshipping him. He then declares that he himself is every part of the ritual: the sacrifice, the prayer, the offerings, and the healing herb.

The speaker, in this part of the Gita, names himself as the source and support of everything. He says he is the sacred syllable OM, the three Vedas, the goal of learning, the father and mother of the world, its judge, witness, refuge and friend, and the source to which all life returns.

The speaker, who is God in this chapter, claims to be the source of all things: the seed, the sun's heat, the rain, death and life, both the visible and the unseen. He says that people who study the Vedas, drink soma and perform sacrifices earn entry to heaven, called Swarga.

Those who follow the three Vedas and their rituals may rise to heaven, the realm of the god Indra, and enjoy its pleasures. But when their merit is used up, they return to the world of death and rebirth. The gain they seek is temporary.
Krishna, the speaker, promises that he will bring complete happiness beyond this life to those who worship him. They worship him with steady minds and do not turn to anything else.

Even those who worship other gods in sincere faith are, in fact, offering their prayers to Krishna, though they do not know it. Each goes where their worship leads: to the gods they follow, to the ancestors (Pitris), or to evil spirits (Bhuts). Those who love Krishna come to him.

Whatever you do, such as eating, sacrificing, giving, or fasting, should be offered to the speaker, as if it belongs to him. Doing so frees a person from karma, the chain that binds people to good and bad results, and leads them to him after death.

Krishna, the speaker, says he treats all beings the same, with no hatred and no special favour. Everything that exists belongs to him. But he loves those who worship him with devotion, and they are united with him, and he with them.

Even someone who has lived an evil life, if they turn their thought wholeheartedly to God, should be counted among the good. Such a person will soon become righteous and reach lasting peace. Birth, sex, or caste does not stop anyone who turns to God.

Krishna, the speaker, tells people in this fleeting and false world to fix their hearts and thoughts on him, worship him, bring him offerings, and make him their highest joy. Doing so, he says, will lead their spirits to his rest.

Krishna says that the gods and sages do not truly know his nature, since he created them. Only a person who sees him with faith, as the unborn and eternal Lord of all worlds, is free from sin and wise. All the different natures found in human beings also come from him.

The speaker, who is God in this chapter, says that many human qualities come from him. These include intellect, self-control, truthfulness, fear and courage, honour, mirth, generosity, and the states of birth and death. The verse then begins to name the great sages and ancient lawgivers, which are also said to come from him.

The speaker, a divine figure, says that he brought into being the rulers of the worlds, the sages, the ancestors and the first lawgivers, along with all human races. Whoever truly understands this hidden power becomes firmly devoted to him, and the wise, knowing he is the source of all beings, come to be united with him.

Those who keep their hearts fixed on the god Krishna, living and praising him with devotion, are given by him a mind that draws them closer to him. Out of love for them, he dwells within their dark, ignorant souls and removes that ignorance with the light of wisdom.

Arjuna addresses Krishna as the supreme God, the eternal source and highest reality, and says that the sages have all declared this. He accepts Krishna's own words as true, and says that not even gods, humans or demons can fully understand Krishna's mystery.

Arjuna speaks to Krishna, the god he is addressing. He says only Krishna truly knows himself and can describe his divine qualities that fill the worlds. He asks how he, Arjuna, can come to know Krishna, even though he thinks about him constantly.

Arjuna asks Krishna in what forms he can best be known, since Krishna has countless forms. He asks Krishna to describe again his great appearances and hidden glory, saying he never tires of hearing these words.

Krishna tells the prince Arjuna that he will reveal some of his divine glories. He says he dwells in the heart of every creature, and all beings come from him, live by him, and return to him. He then gives examples: he is Vishnu among the Adityas, the sun by day, and the moon by night.

The speaker, who is Krishna in the Gita, lists the things in which he is present or which he is among the best of. Each item is a kind of thing with a leader or finest example, such as the Sama-Veda among the Vedas, the Sea among waters, and the Himalaya among hills.

Krishna, speaking in the Gita, lists the greatest or best of each kind of thing. He names the fig-tree among trees, Narada among the sages, and Airavata among elephants. Each item stands for the finest example of its group.

In this part of the Gita, the speaker, Krishna, says that he is the greatest or most powerful example within each kind of thing. He names gods, sea and river beings, animals, birds, winds, warriors and rivers, and says he is the best of each.

In this passage, the speaker is Krishna, who describes himself to Arjuna. He says he is the beginning, middle, and end of all things, and the wisdom within every wise thing. He also names life, death, birth, and fame as parts of himself.

In this part of the Gita, the god Krishna lists examples of his own presence in the world. He names qualities such as memory, patience and constancy, and things such as the best hymns, the month, the spring, and victory. He ends by saying that Arjuna is among these things, because Arjuna belongs to him.

The speaker, who is God in this chapter, says that every excellent thing in the world comes from him. He names examples such as the best poets, saints, and rulers, and says no living or lifeless being exists apart from him. He adds that his greatness is too vast to be fully described.
Krishna tells Arjuna that everything comes from him and that he is both all things and their separate lord. Arjuna is asked how he could possibly grasp this vast truth.

Arjuna says that he has now understood, from Krishna's teaching, where human beings come from, where they go at death, and the nature of God's eternal rule. He asks Krishna to show him his full divine form.

Krishna shows Arjuna, his disciple, his divine form. He says he reveals countless shapes, the gods of the sky and storm, and the whole universe, living and dead, gathered into himself. He tells Arjuna to look, since Arjuna asked to see him as God.
Krishna tells Arjuna that his ordinary human eyes cannot bear or see his true form. So Krishna gives him divine sight, which lets him see his full glory.

Sanjaya, the narrator, describes how the God stood before Arjuna and showed his full form. The God appears with countless eyes, mouths, forms, glories and weapons, crowned with stars and robed in light, filling the scene with awe.

Krishna shows Arjuna his divine form. It fills all space, with faces turned everywhere and a brilliance like a thousand suns rising at once. The speaker says even that image could hardly match the majesty of this holy being.

Arjuna, son of Pandu, sees the whole universe with all its many parts gathered into one vast form. This form is a single body, shining and without a name, the God of gods who never ends. Overwhelmed, Arjuna kneels, bows his head, and speaks.

Arjuna says he now sees that everything is contained within the Lord. He describes the gods, all creatures of earth, heaven and hell, and all features as existing inside the Lord's divine form and face.

Arjuna describes what he sees when the god Krishna shows his true form: Brahma on his lotus throne, sages, and serpent beings, all seen within this one vast form. Krishna has countless arms and faces and eyes on every side, with no visible end, beginning, or fixed center, so that wherever one looks, his central self appears.

Arjuna is overwhelmed by a vision of the god Krishna in his full divine form. He sees Krishna crowned and holding a club, a conch shell and a discus, blazing with light that fills earth, heaven and hell. Arjuna worships him as the undivided, supreme being and the protector of all worlds.

Arjuna addresses Krishna as the source and protector of all things: the eternal, unchanging being from whom all life flows. He describes the divine as having sun and moon as its eyes, with its face warming the universe, so that the worlds are filled with wonder.
Krishna's divine form is shown as present everywhere, in space, among the stars and in every place. At the sight of it the three worlds tremble, and the lesser gods bow down in worship.

Heavenly beings and sages praise the speaker as the highest majesty. Their hymns of glory rise up, and many groups of gods and spirits join in, including the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Maruts, Aswins, Gandharvas and others.

The speaker describes how the worlds react to seeing a vast divine form with many faces, eyes, arms and mouths. Both the beings who see it and the three worlds worship it and tremble in fear at its splendour.

Arjuna describes what he sees when the god Krishna shows him his vast, divine form. The sky is filled with a huge, shining figure whose faces and eyes look in every direction over all worlds. Overwhelmed, Arjuna says his courage and mind have failed before this awesome sight.

Arjuna, overwhelmed by the vision of Krishna's vast form, sees the flaming mouths of the god swallowing the world and the heroes of the opposing army. He sees the sons of Dhritarashtra, along with Bhishma, Drona and Karna, being crushed in that open jaw. He begs for mercy.

Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies rushing headlong into the jaws of a vast, flaming mouth. He compares them to rivers flowing helplessly into the ocean, all being destroyed in that fiery opening.
Warriors are compared to moths drawn to a flame and destroyed by it. The speaker addresses God, who creates men and then devours them, great and small alike, and says his terrors strike with fear.
The speaker addresses Vishnu, whose form now looks terrifying and seems to be destroying all life, and asks who he is. He begs the god to explain why his face is so fierce and frightful.

Krishna tells Arjuna that he appears to him as Time, the force that destroys everything. Arjuna's enemies will all die, and none of the opposing warriors will survive the battle. Arjuna should not be afraid, but rise, fight, and win the kingdom.
Krishna tells Arjuna that the enemy warriors are already doomed and will fall by Krishna's own power. Arjuna is only the instrument, so he will kill those already slain and win the battle.
Arjuna, trembling, folds his hands and speaks to Krishna in awe. He says the world rejoices and obeys Krishna's great power, while demons flee in terror in every direction.

Arjuna praises Krishna, the god speaking in the Gita, as the greatest being. He calls him the infinite creator, the god of gods, and the soul of all souls. He says Krishna is the maker of both formed and formless things and the source of all life.

Arjuna addresses Krishna in awe, saying Krishna knows all and is the source of everything. He lists many forces and beings, such as the wind, fire, the sea, the moon and the stars, and says they are all Krishna's forms.

Arjuna praises Krishna in this verse, calling him the first of all beings and bowing to him again and again. He offers greetings and worship from every side, above and below, wherever the god goes or comes, and calls him the one present in all things.

Arjuna speaks to Krishna, asking forgiveness for past casual behavior. He says he treated Krishna as an equal friend, calling him by his human names, and failed to see his greatness, whether out of carelessness, affection, or joking.

Arjuna, the speaker, asks for forgiveness for having treated the god Krishna carelessly, whether alone or in company. He now recognizes that Krishna is the father and teacher of all beings and worlds, greater than anything worthy of worship, with no equal.

Arjuna, overwhelmed after seeing the god Krishna's vast cosmic form, bows low and asks for mercy. He asks Krishna to be gentle with him, as a father or friend would be. He admits that he is glad to have seen the form but also afraid, and asks Krishna to return to his ordinary human shape that earthly eyes can bear.

Arjuna asks Krishna to stop showing his vast, terrifying cosmic form and to appear again in the familiar form he knew before. Arjuna says his frightened heart wants to see Krishna once more as his charioteer, the human-looking guise Krishna took on.

Krishna tells Arjuna that he has been shown Krishna's hidden, vast and wonderful form out of love. He says no one else has seen it before, and that it cannot be gained through the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, good deeds, penance or prayer.

Krishna tells Arjuna, the prince of the Kurus, that he has been granted a rare sight of God's full, unveiled form. Krishna says Arjuna should not be troubled by the terrifying vision. He reassures him that he will appear again in his familiar form as Krishna.

Krishna, who had revealed his vast divine form to Arjuna, now takes back that form and appears again as his ordinary charioteer. Arjuna says he is relieved and calm, and his heart beats steadily again.

Krishna tells Arjuna that the vision he has just seen is rare, and that the gods themselves long to see it. It cannot be gained through the Vedas, sacrifice, penance, gifts or prayer. Instead, Krishna is known and reached through devoted service, complete faith, and loving surrender to him.
Arjuna asks Krishna which group has the better path: those who worship God in a visible, revealed form, or those who worship God as unseen, without a body and far away.

Krishna says that those who worship him in a visible form, with steady and full devotion, are very holy. He also says that those who worship him as the invisible, unnamed, unthinkable supreme reality, while controlling their senses and staying even-minded and glad in all good, also come to him.

Reaching the formless, unmanifest reality by the mind alone is very hard for an embodied person. The passage says the one who dedicates all actions to the god Krishna, the speaker, and keeps his mind fixed on him will be quickly saved from the ocean of death and suffering.

Krishna tells the listener that those who fix heart and mind on him will dwell with him. If that is too hard, they may seek him with steady effort, or else work for him through actions that please him. Whoever labours in this way for love of him will finally reach him.

If you find devotion too hard, the passage says, give up your hopes for the results of your work and place them in God. It ranks three things: knowledge is better than mere effort, worship is better than knowledge, and giving up the fruits of action is better still. That giving up brings lasting peace.

The speaker says he loves the person who hates no living being, is kind and compassionate, and is free from pride and self-love. Such a person stays steady whether things go well or badly, is patient, firm in faith, and devoted to the speaker. He does not upset others and is not upset by them, and he rises above joy, grief, and fear.

The speaker, a god, says he loves the person who stays calm and even-minded in every situation. That person does their work without clinging to its results, has steady faith in the god, and treats friend and foe, shame and glory, good and bad fortune with the same equal peace.

The speaker says he loves the person who stays calm through heat and cold, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, free of desire and attached to nothing worldly, and who stays steadfast in him. He loves most of all those who live in single, devoted faith and love, drinking the blessed "Amrit," or nectar of his divine being.
Arjuna asks Krishna, here called Kesava, to explain three things: the life that appears to exist, the soul that sees beyond it, and what can actually be known, or what people only think they know.

Krishna says the body is the "field" (kshetra) where life plays out, and the soul is the "knower" of that field (kshetrajna). He says he himself is the knower in every field. True knowledge means knowing the field and the knower, and he promises to explain what the field is and how it works.

The passage lists the parts of a living being: the basic elements, consciousness, mind, the unseen life force, the body's nine openings, the five senses, desire, dislike, pleasure, pain, thought, and the steady sense of continuing to exist. It says all of these are produced in matter by the Soul.

This is a list of qualities that the Gita describes as marks of true knowledge. They include humility, honesty, not harming others, patience, purity, self-control, giving up sensual pleasures, and seeing clearly that birth, death, age, sickness and sin bring suffering. It also names loosely holding on to home, family and other ties, and keeping a calm mind in good times.

True wisdom, according to this verse, is steady devotion to God alone, a love of solitude, a dislike of noisy crowds, and a firm effort to know the highest soul and to understand the value of reaching it. Anything other than this is ignorance.

The speaker promises to teach the knowledge most worth having: the truth of God, called Para-Brahm, the supreme reality that is all things. This reality is not created, is neither existent nor non-existent, neither with form nor without form, yet it is both and more. It is present everywhere, acting, seeing and hearing in every place.

The verses describe the divine as present in everything yet beyond it. It is the source of the senses and yet beyond them, sustains all things without being attached to them, and is within and outside all beings. It is still and moving, close to everything yet infinitely distant.

The passage describes the divine as one reality present in all living things, the sustainer who ends and renews the world at its close. This divine light shines in the darkness of the heart, and it is wisdom and the guide of wise people. Whoever knows this and worships the divine will come to it.

Nature (prakriti, the material world) and Spirit (purusha, the conscious self) both have no beginning. Nature produces qualities and changes and acts through the body, while Spirit gives awareness, so that pain and pleasure are felt. When Spirit joins with matter, it is bound to Nature's qualities and is reborn into good or evil wombs (yonis).

Even while held in the body, which is like a prison, the Spirit remains pure and supreme. It watches over, governs, and guards the body, and it is the Lord and Master, identical with the Supreme Being (Purusha) and one with the speaker, Krishna.

Whoever comes to know the self and its soul, which is Purusha, separate from the workings of nature, is freed and will not be reborn into a body again. People reach this knowledge in different ways: through meditation, through study and a holy life, through action, or by hearing the teaching from others and faithfully holding to it.

Everything that lives or does not move, whether plant or seed, comes into being through the joining of matter and spirit. The one who truly sees the same living Supreme Soul in all beings, which does not perish while everything else does, does not harm himself.

The passage says that a person reaches the highest goal when he understands two things. First, that actions are simply the normal way of Nature, while the Soul acts without being the real doer. Second, that all separate living beings come out of one source and return into it. Such a person then attains Brahman, the ultimate reality.

The Supreme Spirit stays pure even when it enters the body, because it is subtle and unaffected by actions, like air or sunlight that are not stained by what they touch. Those who see clearly the difference between matter and spirit, and the conflict between them, reach the path that leads to life.

Krishna says he will reveal the highest wisdom. Those who possess it and rely on these truths reach perfection and join with him. They are not reborn at the start of a world-cycle (kalpa), nor changed at its dissolution (pralaya).

Krishna, speaking in this verse, says that the universe is like a womb in which he places the seed of all life. All beings are born from it, and the great creator Brahma is their mother. Krishna says that he himself is the father, who gives the seed.

The passage says that three qualities of nature, called Sattwa (goodness or truth), Rajas (passion), and Tamas (ignorance), tie the unchanging Spirit to the changing body. Sattwa binds the soul to happiness and knowledge, Rajas binds it through desire and action, and Tamas binds it through ignorance.

Darkness (tamas) makes people dull, lazy and drowsy. Goodness (sattva) binds the soul to happiness and knowledge, while passion (rajas) binds it through restless effort. When goodness and passion are overcome, the other two qualities rule. The passage is one of the Gita's descriptions of the three qualities that shape human nature.

When knowledge shines through all the gates of the body, a person can clearly see that truth is settled in them. Restless longing, desire for gain, and greed come from the quality of passion. Darkness, dullness, laziness and stupor come from ignorance.

The passage says that the state of a soul at death decides where it goes next. A soul that dies firmly grounded in truth goes to the realm of those who know the highest truth. A soul that dies in restless desire goes to the world of beings bound to action. A soul that dies in hardened ignorance is reborn in a dark womb.

Each of the three qualities, called modes, produces its own result. Goodness (Light, or Soothfastness) brings clear, sweet fruit and lifts a person upward. Passion brings pain and toil and keeps a person in the middle. Darkness, which is ignorance, brings deeper gloom and drags the soul down.

A person who sees that only the three Qualities (the forces of nature in Hindu thought) act, and knows what lies beyond them, is said to draw close to the divine. Such a soul, passing beyond the Qualities, escapes birth, death, sorrow and old age. Arjuna then asks how such a person can be recognised and how he lives.

Krishna describes a person who watches the three qualities of nature (goodness, passion and ignorance) without being moved by them. Such a person does not get angry when they appear or crave them when they are absent. Grief and joy seem the same to him, and he calls the qualities simply the qualities when trouble comes.

He who sees a clod of earth, a stone and gold as the same, who stays even-minded toward pleasant and unpleasant things, and who is unmoved by praise, blame, honour, shame, friends or enemies, is said to have risen above the three Qualities. Such a person, through steady devotion to the god Krishna, reaches Brahman.

Krishna describes the Aswattha, a sacred fig tree (the banyan), as an upside-down tree with its roots above and branches below. Its leaves are like hymns that speak truth. Whoever knows this tree is said to know the Vedas, the sacred scriptures, and everything else.

The passage compares the world to a great tree whose branches reach upward and whose roots spread downward. Like the tree, human deeds grow out of the three qualities (gunas) that make up nature, and people's lives spring to life when drawn toward the pleasures of the senses.
