The passage says that actions done in this world bind a person more and more tightly. It says that if a person truly understood the sacred fig tree image, its roots, its growth and its end, they would sharpen the axe of detachment and cut away the roots of worldly desire. The fragment breaks off before its conclusion.

Those who leave behind passion, illusion and attachment to the body reach a higher realm where they do not die or decay. They reach it by worshipping the Highest, the Father and First who created the world.

Those who are free from the pull of pleasure and pain, like trees that are no longer moved by wind, go to a higher world. It has its own light, with no sun, moon, dusk, dawn or noon. Once there, they never return, because they have reached the speaker's rest, the highest reward of life.

The Spirit, which comes from the divine Self, takes on a body in the world. When it enters a body or leaves it, it gathers the senses and the mind with it, as wind carries scents from flowers. It then connects itself to the objects of the senses.

The passage says that people without spiritual insight cannot see the Spirit (the inner self) when it moves in the body or when it enjoys the world bound up with qualities. Only those with true understanding can see it, and even foolish people who try cannot perceive it, while enlightened people find it within themselves.

The speaker, who is God in this chapter, says that his power is the source of light and life everywhere. He shines in the sun and moon, gives shape and life to the earth and plants, and gives warmth and breath to living bodies, feeding them.

Beings in the world are of two kinds: the divided, meaning all living things, and the undivided, meaning that which stays apart. Above both is the Highest Lord, who holds and sustains all worlds. Speaking as this Lord, the speaker says he is called the Supreme Person, the Purushottama.

Krishna lists qualities that belong to a person born with a divine nature. These include fearlessness, purity of heart, steady pursuit of wisdom, generosity, self-control, humility, honesty, avoiding harm to any living thing, patience with anger, and kindness.

The passage lists the qualities of a person who is set on the path to a heavenly birth. These include compassion for those who suffer, a content heart free of restless desires, a mild and dignified manner, patience, courage, purity, and freedom from the urge for revenge or pride.

Krishna tells Arjuna that deceit, arrogance, pride, quick anger, harsh speech and ignorance mark a person born for the lowly, demonic state (the Asuras). A divine birth leads to liberation, while the demonic birth leads to bondage. Arjuna is told to rejoice because his lot is divine.
Every living person bears one of two marks, the divine or the undivine. The speaker has already described how to recognise the divine kind and now promises to describe the undivine.

The passage describes people who deny that the world has any lawful order, cause, or divine lord. They hold that it exists only as a place of desire, and it says such people, lacking wisdom, are ruined. The speaker, Krishna, rejects this view as false.

Those who follow evil ways are driven by endless desires, pride, and deceit. They believe that pleasure is the highest good and that nothing lies beyond it. The passage calls this belief a lie that leads to death.

The passage describes people who are driven by desire and anger. They chase wealth through wrongful acts to satisfy their appetites, and they boast of their wins, their killed enemies, and their status as lords and proud, rich people. The passage is cut off before the speech ends.

The speakers in this passage are people driven by ignorance, greed and pride. They are caught in their desires and wealth, and they make offerings that look religious but lack true faith. The passage says they are heading toward a dark fate called Naraka, a hell-like realm.

Krishna says that people who blaspheme him, hate him, and act cruelly and evilly are the lowest of men. He casts them down into devilish wombs again and again, from birth to birth. They stay on this path until they turn to worship him.
Three gates lead to ruin: lust, wrath, and greed. A person who avoids all three is said to reach peace and then enter heaven (Swarga). Narak is the word for hell.

Arjuna asks what happens to people who set aside the holy rules but still worship with faith in their hearts, and whether their faith falls into one of the three qualities: goodness, passion, or darkness. Krishna replies that faith is threefold, arising from these qualities, and can be true, passion-stained, or dark.

People become like what they worship: a person's faith matches their inner nature. Those who are truthful honour true gods, while the restless and passionate honour spirits of power, and those ruled by darkness honour ghosts and goblins. Penance done out of pride and show, without proper rule, is also condemned.

The passage says that people who harshly torture their own bodies, driven by passion and ignorance, are devoted to devils rather than to heaven. The speaker, Krishna, then turns to a threefold division, starting with food: some foods bring strength, health and joy, and similar threefold divisions apply to worship, self-restraint and giving.

Foods that are too spicy, hot, salty or sharp cause pain, restlessness and grief, and people crave them. Stale, tasteless, rotten food is also named, and it suits those who love the "Darkness," meaning ignorance.

Sacrifice is judged by the motive and the manner of performing it. A rite done as a duty, with a devout heart and proper form, is called pure. A rite done to gain reward or reputation is called passionate. A rite done against the rules, without food offerings, hymns, or gifts to priests, and without faith, is called dark and worthless.

Bhagavad Gita 17 lists what counts as true religious conduct. Acts of worship include honouring gods, respecting the twice-born (higher castes), teachers and elders, living purely and honestly, keeping celibacy, and not harming any defenceless creature. Speech counts when it is kind, truthful, pleasing, and includes reciting sacred texts.

Faith and worship done with calm, kindness and purity, and with no wish for reward, belong to the quality called sattva (goodness). Worship done to show off and to win honor, praise or status belongs to rajas (passion), which the passage calls rash and vain.

Gifts are sorted by the spirit behind them. A gift given freely, at the right time and place, to a worthy receiver, with no return expected, belongs to sattva, the quality of goodness. A gift given to get something back, to reach some goal, or grudgingly belongs to rajas, the quality of restless desire, and is called poor.

A gift given grudgingly, at the wrong time or place, to an unworthy receiver, or out of scorn or harshness, belongs to the quality called tamas, which means darkness or ignorance. Such a gift brings no blessing.

Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the difference between two kinds of renunciation, sannyas and tyaga. Krishna answers that sannyas means giving up all actions that come from desire, while tyaga means giving up the fruit, or result, of one's actions.

Some holy teachers say all action is sinful and should be given up, while others say worship, penance and charity must still be done. Krishna settles the question: giving up is of three kinds, and worship, penance and charity must not be abandoned. They should be done gladly, because they purify the soul.
Even the high works should still be performed, but without attachment and without wanting their fruit. The speaker, addressing the prince, states that this is his firm and unchangeable decision.

Giving up a duty that is required is never right; abstaining from it comes from darkness, meaning ignorance. Giving up a task only because it is painful or unpleasant is a form of passion and gains no true renunciation. Real renunciation is giving up attachment to the work and its rewards while still doing it faithfully.

The passage says that real action means doing one's duty because it is right, without caring whether the result succeeds or fails, and without seeking praise or reward. Since no embodied person can avoid acting, true renunciation is giving up the desire for the fruits of one's actions. Results in future lives are of three kinds, and work done without fruit-seeking has none.

Krishna says every action has five causes: the basic force, the doer, the various tools, the particular effort, and the god. Whoever thinks he alone is the doer does not understand. A person who acts without self-attachment and with a pure mind is not bound by the act, even when that act is killing.

The passage says that every action has three parts: the knowledge, the thing known, and the knower. It also says that the act, the doer, and the tool make up three parts of the deed itself. Knowledge, doer, and act are then divided into types by three qualities, which the speaker will explain next.

Three kinds of knowledge are described. True knowledge sees one unchanging life in all beings, and one whole that cannot be divided. Imperfect knowledge sees beings as separate and treats them as real. False knowledge clings blindly to one thing as if it were everything, and looks for no cause.

The passage sorts action into three kinds. Right action is done because it is one's duty, without attachment and without love, hate or personal gain. Action driven by desire and self-interest is called vain and belongs to the quality of Rajas, while action done carelessly, without regard for harm to others or to oneself, is dark and belongs to Tamas.

The passage sorts doers of action into three kinds. The first acts without selfish motive, stays steady whether luck is good or bad, and acts rightly. The second acts from impulse and desire for gain, swings between sorrow and joy, and belongs to the quality called rajas. The third is loose-hearted, fraudulent, and dull, and is called a child of darkness.

Krishna is about to explain how intellect and steadfastness (firmness of will) are divided into three kinds. The divisions depend on the three qualities (gunas) that the Gita describes as shaping all things: goodness, passion and darkness.

The passage divides understanding into two kinds. Intellect that grasps how life comes and goes, what must and must not be done, what to fear and what not to fear, and what binds or frees the soul, is called good and belongs to sattwa, the quality of truth and goodness. The passage then begins to describe the opposite kind, the flawed intellect, which is cut off at the point where it knows right and wrong.

Understanding that cannot tell what should be done from what should not, and misreads truth, is classed as rajas, or passion. Understanding clouded by gloom, which takes wrong for right, is classed as tamas, or darkness.

Steadfastness, or firmness of mind, comes in three kinds, based on the three qualities (gunas) of nature. Firmness that controls breath, senses and heart in faith is of Sattva, the good quality. Firmness driven by desire for duty's rewards and gain is of Rajas, passion. Firmness held to laziness, fear and despair is of Tamas, darkness.

Pleasure comes in three kinds, and the passage ranks them. Pleasure that comes from inner peace lasts and is bitter at first but sweet later. Pleasure from the senses is sweet at first but bitter at the end, and belongs to the quality called Rajas. Pleasure from laziness, wrongdoing and folly harms the soul from start to finish, and belongs to Tamas.

Nothing in existence, on earth or in heaven, is free of the three Qualities that nature produces. Because of these Qualities, each class of people (Brahmans, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas, and Sudras) has its own fixed duties.

Each social class has duties that come from its own nature. A Brahman's duties are calm, self-control, religion, purity, patience, honesty, and knowledge. A Kshatriya, or warrior, has courage, skill in fighting, generosity, and a lordly bearing. A Vaisya, or farmer and merchant, tends the land, cattle, and trade. A Sudra, or servant, serves others.

A person who does the work assigned to them, whatever it is, and is content with it, reaches perfection. This perfection comes through worship carried out by doing one's work, offered to the God who is the source of all life and who spread out the universe.

It is better to do your own work, even if it is done imperfectly, than to do another's work well. Every work has some fault, as every fire has smoke, so a person should not give up the duty that comes from their own nature. Freedom from work comes to one who acts with a calm mind, a controlled self, no lingering desires, and no attachment to results.

Krishna tells Arjuna, the son of Kunti, that he will now explain how a person who reaches perfect peace attains Brahman, the highest reality. Brahman is the supreme being or ultimate truth in Hindu thought.

A person who has become pure, self-controlled, free from desire, hatred, pride and anger, and who lives quietly and simply, grows into unity with Brahman, the ultimate reality. Once united with Brahman, that person becomes calm and untroubled.

Through love and devotion to God, a person who loves all living beings is freed from sorrow and desire. Such a person knows God as he truly is and enters into him, reaching eternal rest by God's grace. The passage tells the listener to do all actions for God and to give them up for God.

Krishna tells Arjuna that if he relies on his own will and refuses to fight, his refusal will fail. His own nature will drive him into the battle anyway, and he will end up doing what he tried to avoid.

A Master dwells inside every person and moves their actions as if pulling strings. Arjuna is told to trust him wholly and take him as refuge, which brings lasting peace and the eternal state. The speaker says this is the deepest truth, and then tells Arjuna to meditate and then act as he chooses.

Krishna, the speaker, tells the listener to give him their heart, worship and serve him with faith and love, and to drop formal rites and prescribed duties. In return he promises to free them from all their sins.

Krishna asks Arjuna whether he has listened closely and whether his confusion and ignorance, the cause of his distress, are gone. Arjuna replies that they are gone, that he now has clear understanding by Krishna's grace, and that he will act as Krishna has said.

Sanjaya tells the blind king Dhritarashtra that he has faithfully recounted the words of Krishna, which Vyasa had recorded. He says that Krishna himself revealed the Yoga, the highest truth, and that he keeps remembering the talk between Krishna and Arjuna.

Sanjaya, speaking to the blind king Dhritarashtra, says he is filled with joy at recalling the visible form of Krishna, who is God. He says no words can express his wonder and love. He hails Krishna and Arjuna, and declares that blessing, victory and power will follow wherever this conversation is told.

The Preacher says that everything is empty and without lasting gain. People work hard but are soon replaced by new generations, while the earth stays put and the sun rises and sets in a repeating cycle, going back to where it started.

Wind and water keep moving in circles, and the sea never overflows, since rivers return to their source. Everything is wearisome, so people cannot express it, and neither eyes nor ears are ever satisfied.

Everything that happens has happened before, so nothing under the sun is truly new. People do not remember earlier events, and later generations will not remember those who come after them. The speaker, called the Preacher, introduces himself as a king of Israel in Jerusalem.

The speaker set out to study everything done under the sun using wisdom, and found it a painful task that God gave people. He concludes that all of it is empty and frustrating. What is bent cannot be straightened, and what is missing cannot be counted.

The speaker says he has gained more wisdom than any earlier ruler in Jerusalem. He tried to understand both wisdom and foolishness, and found that this too is futile. More wisdom, he concludes, brings more grief and sorrow.

The speaker sets out to test pleasure, laughter, wine and folly to see what good they bring people in their short lives. He calls the pleasure itself empty, and he goes on to build houses, plant vineyards and make great works.

The speaker lists the large projects and wealth he built up for himself: gardens, orchards, fruit trees, water pools for irrigation, many servants, and large herds of livestock, more than anyone before him in Jerusalem.

The speaker describes gathering great wealth, servants, music, and every pleasure he wanted, and says he refused his heart no joy. He states that his heart found joy in all his hard work, and that this was his reward for it.

The speaker looks back at all his work and finds it empty, with no lasting gain from anything done under the sun. He then compares wisdom with folly and concludes that wisdom is better, as light is better than darkness, though both lead to the same end: what a later king could only repeat has already been done.

The speaker notes that the wise and the foolish share the same fate: both are soon forgotten and both die alike. This leads him to conclude that wisdom gives no lasting advantage, which he calls vanity, meaning emptiness or futility.

The speaker has come to hate his life and all his hard work done under the sun, because he must leave everything to a successor. He cannot know whether that heir will be wise or a fool, yet the heir will control all that he built with his own wisdom. He calls this vanity, meaning emptiness or something without lasting value.

The speaker has given up hope in all the hard work he has done under the sun. A person may work wisely and fairly, yet leave the results to someone who never labored for them. He asks what a person gains from all this toil, since his days are full of pain and his heart finds no rest even at night.

Eating, drinking and finding enjoyment in one's work are presented as the best a person can have, and this comes from God. God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the person who pleases him, but gives the sinner the task of gathering wealth, which then goes to the one who pleases God. The writer calls all of this futile and frustrating.

Every event in life has its own fixed time. The passage lists pairs of opposite actions, such as birth and death, planting and uprooting, weeping and laughing, and says each has a set season under heaven.

Everything has its season: a set time for gaining and losing, keeping and discarding, tearing and mending, silence and speech, love and hate, war and peace. The speaker then asks what gain a worker gets from his labour, and says he has seen the hard toil that God has given people to be busy with.

God has made everything fitting for its time, and he has put a sense of eternity in people's hearts, yet no one can fully grasp what God does from start to finish. So the writer concludes that people should rejoice, do good, eat, drink, and enjoy their labour, since this is God's gift.

The speaker says that whatever God does lasts forever, and nothing can be added to or removed from it. He adds that what has happened returns, and that he saw wickedness in the place of judgment and wrongdoing in the place of justice.

The speaker thinks that God will judge both good and bad people, and that God lets people see they are no better than animals. Humans and beasts share the same fate of death and the same breath of life, so people have no advantage over animals. The speaker concludes that all of this is vanity, meaning empty and without lasting value.

People and animals alike end up in the same place, both returning to dust. No one can know whether a human spirit rises upward while an animal's goes down. So the speaker concludes that the best a person can do is enjoy his own work, since no one can show him what will happen after he dies.

The speaker looks at the oppression happening under the sun and sees that the oppressed have no one to comfort them, while the oppressors have power. So he says the dead are better off than the living, and someone not yet born is better still, since they have not seen the evil done.

The writer sees that hard work often makes people envious of their neighbours, and calls this empty and troubling. A fool, he says, folds his hands and harms himself. He concludes that a small handful with peace is better than two full hands with toil and striving.

A lone man works without end, has no child or brother, and never asks who he is working for or what the work costs him. The writer calls this pointless and a heavy burden. Two people are better than one, because together they share the reward and can help each other up when one falls.

Two people together stay warmer and stronger than one alone, since a threefold cord is hard to break. The passage then says a poor but wise young man is better than an old, foolish king who will not accept advice. Even such a young man can rise from prison to rule, and a king's heir can fall into poverty.

The verse says that crowds of people never end, and that even those who come later will not find joy in the leader or ruler mentioned just before it. The writer calls this vanity, meaning emptiness or pointlessness, and a vexation of spirit, meaning a torment of the mind.

Guard your steps when entering the house of God, and listen more than you offer sacrifice, since fools offer without realizing they do wrong. Do not speak hastily before God, who is in heaven while people are on earth, so keep words few. Many words reveal a fool, just as much busy activity brings dreams.

When you make a vow to God, pay it without delay, because God takes no pleasure in fools who break their word. It is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay. Do not let your mouth lead you into sin, and do not excuse a broken vow as a mistake before the messenger of God.

Injustice against the poor in a region should not be a surprise, because a higher official watches over each official, and even the highest authority has someone above it. The land's produce benefits everyone, the king included. Those who love money never get enough of it, and this too is empty.

Wealth brings more people to consume it, so owners gain little beyond looking at their possessions. A worker sleeps soundly whether he eats little or much, but the rich often cannot sleep. Riches kept by their owners can harm them, and they may be lost through bad business, leaving a son with nothing.

A person comes into the world with nothing and leaves it the same way, taking none of the wealth he worked for. The passage calls this a serious evil and asks what he gains from toiling for something as empty as the wind. It adds that he lives his days in gloom, with much grief and anger tied to his illness.

The speaker says it is good to eat, drink, and enjoy the fruit of one's work during the short life God gives. When God grants wealth and the power to enjoy it, that enjoyment is itself a gift from God, and such a person does not dwell much on the length of life, because God keeps him occupied with joy.
A man may have wealth, honour and everything he wants, yet not be allowed to enjoy any of it. A stranger takes and eats what he has earned. The writer calls this pointless and a sickness.

A man may have a hundred children and live a very long life, yet if he never finds satisfaction in good things and has no proper burial, the writer says a stillborn child is better off. Both die and go to the same place, so the long life brings him no real gain.

People work hard to feed themselves, yet they are never satisfied. The wise man has no clear advantage over the fool, and the poor man gains little either. Wanting more than one has is called vanity, and the passage asks what good man gains when there are so many such things.
No one can say what is good for a person in this life, during the short days he spends like a shadow. Nor can anyone tell him what will happen after he is gone, under the sun.

Good reputation is worth more than expensive perfume, and the day of death is said to be better than the day of birth. The passage claims that visiting a house of mourning is better than attending a feast, because death comes to everyone and the living should take it to heart. It says sorrow leads to a better heart than laughter does, and that wise people think about mourning while fools think about pleasure.

It is better to be corrected by a wise person than to listen to fools laughing and singing. The laughter of fools burns quickly and leaves nothing, and a patient, calm spirit is better than pride or quick anger.

Do not ask why the past was better than the present, since that is not a wise question. Wisdom is as good as an inheritance and helps people who live under the sun. Wisdom protects, as money does, but it gives life to those who have it. Accept that God made things crooked and no one can straighten them.

Good times and bad times both come from God, so people cannot know what will happen after them. The writer has seen a righteous man die young and a wicked man live long. He advises against being excessively righteous or wise, asking why someone would ruin himself.

Do not be excessively wicked or foolish, the speaker advises, since dying before your time is the risk. Holding on to this balance and fearing God brings a person through all extremes. Wisdom gives more strength than many powerful men, because no one on earth is wholly righteous. So one should not pay too much attention to every spoken word, including a servant's curse.

The speaker admits that his own heart knows he has also cursed others. He says he tried to become wise, but wisdom stayed far away and too deep to find. He still set his heart to search for wisdom, the reason of things, and the nature of folly and madness.

The speaker says he finds a certain kind of woman more bitter than death, one whose heart is like traps and whose hands are like chains. He says he has rarely found a good person of either sex, and his conclusion is that God made people upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

Wisdom makes a person's face shine and softens a hard look, so the wise person is hard to match. The speaker advises keeping the king's command, out of respect for God's oath, and not leaving the king's presence or taking part in something bad. Because a king's word carries power, no one can ask him to account for what he does.

The writer says a wise person knows that every matter has its proper time and judgment, yet this knowledge does not remove human suffering. People cannot know what will happen or when. No one controls the spirit or can hold it back at death, and wickedness offers no escape from that fate.

The writer observes that people sometimes rule others to their own harm, and that wicked men are buried with honour and forgotten in the city where they did wrong, which he calls vanity. Because punishment for evil deeds is not carried out quickly, people feel free to do evil.

Even if a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives long, the writer says it will go well for those who fear God. It will not go well for the wicked, whose days are short like a shadow, because they do not fear God.

The Teacher observes that good people sometimes suffer as if they were wicked, and wicked people sometimes prosper as if they were good, and he calls this pointless. So he recommends simple enjoyment of eating, drinking and gladness during the life that God gives under the sun, since that is the only good a person can count on.

The speaker set out to understand wisdom and the busy work done on earth, and saw that people cannot find out the work of God, which happens under the sun. Even hard seeking and the claims of a wise person to know it do not succeed.

The writer concludes that the righteous and the wise, and all their works, are in God's hands, so no person can tell from what happens to them whether God favors or rejects them. Good and bad people, clean and unclean, worshippers and non-worshippers all meet the same fate.

The writer says that one fate comes to everyone, good or bad, and that people live with foolishness in their hearts until they die. He argues that a living person has some hope, since the living at least know they will die, while the dead know nothing and are soon forgotten.

The dead no longer have any share in anything done under the sun, so their love, hatred and envy are gone. Because of this, the speaker tells the living to eat and drink with joy, to keep their clothes clean, and to take care of themselves.

Enjoy life with the wife you love, for these days under the sun are your share, along with the work you do. Do whatever your hand finds to do with full strength, because there is no work or wisdom in the grave where you are going.

Success does not always go to those who seem best suited for it: speed, strength, wisdom, understanding and skill do not guarantee the result. Instead, unforeseen time and chance overtake everyone. People cannot know when disaster will strike, like fish or birds caught suddenly in a net or trap.

A small city was attacked by a great king, but a poor wise man saved it with his wisdom. Afterward nobody remembered him. The speaker concludes that wisdom is better than strength, yet a poor man's wise words are still despised and ignored.
Quiet words from wise people are better heard than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom is stronger than weapons of war, yet a single sinner can undo a great deal of good.

Just as dead flies spoil a perfumer's ointment, a small foolish act can ruin the good name of a person known for wisdom and honour. The passage adds that a wise man's heart leans to the right and a fool's to the left, that a fool shows his lack of sense when he speaks, and that calm yielding can soothe a ruler's anger.

Foolish people are raised to high positions, while rich people are put in low ones, and servants ride horses while princes walk on foot. The writer also says that whoever digs a pit, breaks a wall, moves stones or splits wood risks being harmed by that same work.
Wisdom makes hard work easier, as sharpening a dull blade saves strength. A fool's speech is harmful from start to finish, full of empty words, and no one can know what will happen next.

Fools tire themselves out with work because they do not know the way to the city. Rulers who are children or who feast early in the day bring trouble on a land, while a land with noble rulers who eat at proper times, for strength, is blessed. Laziness lets buildings fall into ruin, and feasting and wine are followed by the statement that money answers all things.
Do not speak evil of the king, even in your private thoughts, or of the rich, even in your bedroom. Word of it may travel, as a bird carries news, and what is said will come out.

Give generously and widely, because you cannot know what will come back or what harm may come. The verses also say that nature follows its own course: rain falls from full clouds, and a fallen tree stays where it lands. Waiting for perfect conditions can mean doing nothing at all.

Just as a person cannot know how life forms in the womb or how the spirit works, they cannot know what God does across all things. So they should keep sowing seed from morning to evening, since they cannot tell which work will succeed. Light and sunshine are pleasant to see.

Even a long life should be remembered as full of dark days, and everything that comes is empty or fleeting. A young person is told to enjoy youth and follow his heart and eyes, but to know that God will judge him for all of it. So he should put away sorrow and evil, since youth is also vanity.

Young people are urged to honor their Creator before old age arrives, when life brings hardship and little enjoyment. The rest of the passage describes that age in images: failing light, returning clouds, trembling household guards, weakened men, few teeth left for grinding, and dimmed eyes at the windows.

Ecclesiastes 12:4–5 describes old age as a slow decline. Hearing fades, sleep is broken by birdsong, the singers grow quiet, and fear of heights and small obstacles grows, until desire fails. The passage ends with the image of a person going to his "long home," meaning the grave, while mourners walk the streets.

Before death, the body's fragile parts break down, like a cord snapping, a bowl cracking, or a wheel failing at a well. Then the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God, who gave it. The writer ends by calling everything empty and says he taught wisdom and collected proverbs.

The Preacher sought pleasing words that were honest and true. Wise sayings are like goads and firm nails, given by one shepherd. Writing many books never ends, and much study wearies the body. The final conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments, which is the whole duty of man.
God will judge every deed, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil. The passage's last words, "The Song of Solomon," are a stray label from the book's heading, not part of the verse.

The book opens by saying it contains the proverbs of Solomon, and gives its purpose: to teach wisdom, discipline, and sound judgment, especially to the simple and the young. It also says wise people will grow in learning, and that the book helps readers understand proverbs and the hidden meanings in wise sayings.

The passage says that respect for the LORD is the start of real knowledge, while fools reject wisdom and teaching. It then tells a son to keep his parents' teaching, which will bring him honor. It warns him not to join sinners who plan to kill innocent people for no reason.

Sinners invite a young man to join them in robbery and share the loot. A father's voice warns his son to refuse, since their violent schemes trap the very people who make them. Greedy gain, the passage says, ends up costing the greedy their own lives.

Wisdom is personified as a woman calling out loudly in public places, such as streets and city gates. She asks simple people, scorners and fools how long they will love their foolishness and reject knowledge. She offers to share her words and spirit if they turn back, but says that people have ignored her calls.

Those who have ignored wisdom's advice and rejected its correction will face disaster. When trouble comes, they will call out for help, but wisdom will refuse to answer, because they hated knowledge and did not choose to fear the LORD.
People who reject wisdom will suffer the results of their own choices, and their own ease will destroy them. But whoever listens will live safely and without fear of harm.

If a son accepts his teacher's words and searches for wisdom as eagerly as for silver or buried treasure, he will understand the fear of the LORD and find knowledge of God. The passage says that wisdom and understanding come from the LORD, who gives them.

Sound wisdom is stored up for the upright, and God guards the paths of justice and his faithful ones. If a person takes wisdom into the heart, discernment and understanding will protect them from evil men who speak twisted words.

Those who leave the right path for the way of darkness, enjoying evil and crooked living, are described as dangerous. The passage warns that the "strange woman," a seductive stranger, leads people toward death, and those who go to her do not come back to the path of life.
Those who walk the way of good and upright people will live securely in the land. The wicked and the transgressors, by contrast, will be cut off and removed from it.

Keep this teaching close and do not forget it, and it will bring long life, peace, favor, and good understanding. Trust the LORD fully rather than relying on your own judgment, and he will guide your path.

Do not think you are wise in your own eyes. Fear the LORD and turn away from evil, and give him part of your wealth and first produce. Do not reject his discipline, because he corrects those he loves, as a father corrects a son he delights in.

Those who find wisdom and understanding are called happy. Wisdom is described as worth more than silver, gold, rubies, or anything else one could desire. It offers long life, riches, honour, pleasant ways, peace, and is compared to a tree of life for those who hold on to it.

The LORD made the earth and the heavens through wisdom and understanding, and he controls the waters and the rain. The speaker then tells his son to hold on to wisdom and discretion, promising that these will bring life, safety, and restful sleep.

Do not fear sudden danger or the ruin of the wicked, because the LORD will keep you safe. Be fair and generous to others when you can help them now. Do not delay payment, plan harm against a neighbour who trusts you, or quarrel without cause.

Do not envy violent people or copy their ways. The LORD detests the crooked, but he is close to the upright and blesses their homes. He mocks mockers and gives favor to the humble, while fools end in shame and the wise gain honor.

A father urges his children to listen closely and hold on to wisdom and understanding. He says he was taught the same way as a boy, and that keeping his words and commandments brings life. He tells them to get wisdom, not forget it, and to love it, since it will protect them.

Wisdom is the most important thing, so a person should acquire it and, along with everything else they gain, gain understanding. If one honors wisdom and holds to it, it brings honor, grace, and glory, and a long life. The speaker, addressing a son, says he has taught him this way.

Walk through life safely by holding firmly to wisdom, which the passage calls your life. Stay out of the path of wicked people and turn away from it. The wicked cannot rest unless they have done harm, and they live on wrongdoing and violence.

The righteous path grows brighter, like light that increases until full day, while the wicked walk in darkness and do not know what they stumble over. The speaker urges a son to keep his words close and guard his heart, because they bring life and health, and the heart is the source of life.
Keep away from dishonest speech and deceitful words. Keep your gaze fixed straight ahead, think carefully about where you are walking, and do not swerve to either side. Stay clear of evil.

A father urges his son to hold on to wisdom and understanding. He warns against a "strange woman," meaning a seductive outsider, whose words are sweet at first but end in bitterness and death. He says her paths are unstable, so they cannot be known or followed safely.

A father warns his children to keep away from a certain woman and her house. If they do not, they will lose their honour, their strength and their wealth to others. In the end they will regret having rejected teaching and correction.

The speaker warns that ignoring wise teachers led to near-ruin in public. He then urges a man to find satisfaction in faithfulness within his own marriage, using the images of his own well and cistern, and to keep his love for his wife alone rather than for outsiders.

The speaker tells a son to stay devoted to his own wife and not to be drawn to a strange, unfaithful woman. He says that God sees every person's actions, and that the wicked are caught by their own sins and die without wisdom, lost in their foolishness.

If you have promised to pay a debt for a friend, or shaken hands to guarantee a stranger's debt, you are trapped by your own words. The passage urges the son to free himself at once: go humbly to the friend, and do not rest until the matter is settled.

The passage tells the lazy person to watch the ant, which needs no leader to store food in summer and harvest. It asks how long the lazy person will keep sleeping. It warns that poverty and want will arrive suddenly, like a traveler or an armed attacker, and it ends by describing a wicked man as one who speaks with a crooked mouth.

It describes a man who secretly signals with his eyes, feet and fingers while plotting harm and stirring up quarrels. Disaster will suddenly overtake him. The LORD hates these things, which include pride, lies, violence against the innocent, wicked plotting, and eagerness to do evil.

A false witness who tells lies and a person who stirs up quarrels among brothers are named as things the speaker hates. The speaker then tells a son to keep his parents' teaching close, carry it everywhere, and let it guide him, since it is a lamp and a light that lead to life.

A father warns his son against an adulterous woman and her seductive words and looks. He says that getting involved with her is as dangerous as carrying fire in your clothes or walking on hot coals. Anyone who touches another man's wife will not go unpunished.

People may not scorn a thief who steals to feed himself when starving, though if caught he must repay sevenfold, even giving up his whole household property. The verses then say that a man who commits adultery lacks sense and ruins himself, earning wounds and lasting shame. A husband's jealousy is fierce, so he will show no mercy when he takes revenge.
The verse speaks of a jealous husband who will not accept any payment to excuse a wrong done to him. Even many gifts will not satisfy him or make him calm.

A father urges his son to hold fast to his teaching and treat wisdom and understanding as close family. The aim is to keep him from a seductive "strange woman," a stranger who flatters with her words. The speaker then says he watched this from the window of his house.

The speaker watches from a window and sees a young man with no sense walk toward the corner where a woman lives, heading to her house at night. She meets him dressed as a prostitute and crafty in her heart. She is noisy and restless, always in the streets, waiting at every corner.

A woman seizes a young man, kisses him, and invites him to her bed. She says she has just made her offerings and fulfilled her vows, so there is a feast to share. She has prepared her bed with fine cloth and perfumes and proposes they make love until morning, since her husband is away on a long trip.

A young man is lured by a seductive woman who uses smooth words and flattery. He follows her at once, like an ox led to slaughter or a bird flying into a trap, not realizing it will cost him his life. The speaker then calls on his children to listen.
Do not let your heart turn toward her ways or wander onto her paths. She has brought down many people, even strong men, and her house leads down to death.

Wisdom is personified as a woman calling out publicly from high places, roads, city gates and doors. She addresses ordinary people, especially the simple and the foolish, urging them to understand and listen, because she will speak of excellent and right things.

Wisdom speaks in the first person here, claiming that her words are always true, right and clear to anyone who seeks understanding. She asks that her teaching be valued above silver and gold, since wisdom is worth more than rubies and nothing desirable can equal it.

Wisdom speaks in this passage and says that fearing the LORD means hating evil, such as pride and dishonest speech. She claims that counsel, understanding and strength belong to her, and that rulers govern through her. She promises that those who seek her will find her, along with lasting riches, righteousness and value greater than gold or silver.

The speaker, here personified Wisdom, claims to walk in the paths of righteousness and promises wealth to those who love her. She says the LORD brought her into being before anything else was made, before the deep waters, springs, mountains and hills.

Before the earth, fields, and dust existed, a figure speaks of being present as God created the heavens, clouds, springs, sea, and earth's foundations. It says this figure was beside God as a close companion, delighting in him at all times.

Wisdom, speaking in the first person, says she delights in people and calls her hearers to listen to her. She says those who follow her ways are blessed and that whoever finds her finds life and favour from the LORD. Those who turn against her harm themselves, and those who hate her love death.

Wisdom is pictured as a host who has prepared a feast in her house and sent servants to call the simple and those lacking understanding to eat and drink with her. The invitation ends with a command to leave foolishness behind and follow the way of understanding, so that one may live.

Correcting a mocker brings the corrector insult, and rebuking a wicked person brings him harm. Mockers resent correction, while wise people accept it and grow wiser. The fear of the LORD is the start of wisdom, and wisdom leads to a longer life.

Wisdom benefits only the wise person, while a scorner alone bears the cost. A foolish woman, loud and ignorant, sits at her door and calls to passers-by who lack understanding, saying that stolen water and secret bread taste sweet.

The guest who accepts the foolish woman's invitation does not know that the dead are in her house, and that those who go to her end up in the depths of the grave, or Sheol, the place of the dead. The verse warns that her invitation leads to death.

Wise children bring joy to their parents, while foolish ones bring grief. Wealth gained by wrongdoing does no good, but righteousness saves from death. Hard work brings riches, laziness brings poverty, and whoever works at the right time earns respect.

Good people are blessed and remembered well, while the wicked bring violence and are forgotten or ruined. The passage sets wisdom and honest walking against foolish talk and crooked ways, saying the righteous stand secure and the wicked are exposed and fall. "Prating" means chattering or empty talk.

Hatred starts quarrels, but love covers over wrongs. The passage contrasts wise and foolish speech, the wealth and poverty of the rich and poor, and the work of the righteous and the wicked. It says that whoever accepts instruction stays on the path of life, while whoever rejects correction goes astray.

Lying and slander are called foolish, and too many words lead to sin, so the wise person holds back their speech. Good speech is valued like fine silver and helps many people, while fools die from lacking wisdom. The passage ends by saying that the LORD's blessing brings riches without sorrow, and that mischief is a game to a fool but wisdom to a person of understanding.

The wicked will be overtaken by what they fear, and their hopes will fail, while the righteous get what they desire and their hope brings gladness. The wicked pass away like a whirlwind, but the righteous stand firm. A lazy person is as irritating to his employer as vinegar to the teeth or smoke to the eyes.

The way of the LORD gives strength to the upright, while those who do evil face ruin. The righteous will never be uprooted, but the wicked will not remain on the earth. The just speak wisdom and what is pleasing, while the wicked tongue is destroyed.

Honest dealing pleases God, and cheating displeases him. Pride leads to shame, while humility brings wisdom. Integrity guides people safely, but wickedness destroys them. Wealth cannot save someone on the day of judgment, but righteousness does.

The righteous are saved by their own uprightness, while the wicked are caught by their own wrongdoing and their hopes die with them. The righteous escape trouble and the wicked take their place. When the righteous prosper, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish, there is shouting.

Proverbs 11:11–15 gives several contrasts. A city rises through the blessing of good people but falls through the talk of the wicked. Gossip spreads secrets, while a trustworthy person keeps them. Without guidance people fail, but many advisers bring safety. Finally, whoever guarantees a stranger's debt will suffer for it, and whoever avoids such pledges is secure.

A gracious woman keeps honour, and strong men keep riches. Kindness benefits the one who shows it, while cruelty harms the cruel person. Righteousness leads to life and a sure reward, evil leads to death, and the LORD delights in the upright but detests the crooked of heart.

Proverbs 11:21–25 contrasts the fates of the wicked and the righteous. The wicked will not escape punishment, while the righteous and their descendants are delivered. It also says that generous people prosper, while those who hold back their goods end in poverty.

Those who hold back grain will be cursed by the people, while those who sell it are blessed. Good-seeking brings favour and evil-seeking brings harm, trust in riches leads to a fall, and the righteous flourish like a branch. Troubling one's own household gains nothing, and the wise are served by fools.
The righteous, meaning good people, will be repaid on earth for their deeds. The wicked and sinners will be repaid even more, meaning they will certainly face consequences in this life.

Those who accept teaching gain knowledge, while those who reject correction are foolish. Good people win the LORD's favour, but schemers are condemned. Wickedness does not make a person secure, while the righteous stand firm. A good wife brings honour to her husband, but a shameful one is like decay in his bones. The thoughts of the righteous are upright, but the plans of the wicked are false.

Good speech from the wicked aims at harming others, while the honest speech of the upright protects people. The wicked fall and disappear, but the righteous family endures. Wisdom earns praise, a twisted heart earns contempt, and a righteous man cares for his animals while the wicked are cruel even when kind.

Hard work brings enough food, while chasing empty pursuits shows a lack of sense. The wicked are trapped by their own words and deeds, while the righteous are rescued and bear good fruit. A fool thinks he is right, but a wise person listens to advice.

Proverbs contrasts the wise with the foolish. Fools show their anger at once, while the sensible hide an insult. Truthful speech is honest and lasting, but lies are brief and deceitful words can hurt like a sword. Wise speech brings healing, and those who plan peace find joy, while the wicked meet harm.

Lying lips are hateful to God, while honest people please him. Wise people keep their knowledge to themselves, but fools announce their foolishness. Diligent hard workers will rule, lazy people will serve others, and a kind word lifts a heavy heart. The righteous are better than their neighbours, but the wicked are led astray by their own way.

A lazy man does not even cook the game he catches, so he loses what he has. A hard-working man keeps his wealth, which is valuable. The second line says that the path of righteousness leads to life and does not lead to death.

A wise son accepts his father's teaching, while a scoffer ignores correction. The passage contrasts the wise and the foolish: careful speech and hard work bring good things, while loose talk, laziness and lying bring ruin and shame.

Righteousness protects the upright, while wickedness brings down the sinner. Wealth and poverty are not always what they seem, since some pretend to be rich while having nothing, and others pretend to be poor while owning much. Pride causes quarrels, but wisdom is found among those who take advice.

Wealth gained by emptiness or dishonest means fades away, while wealth gained through hard work grows. The passage also says that wise living, respect for instruction, and understanding bring life and favour, while foolishness and disregard for wisdom lead to ruin.

A wicked messenger gets into trouble, while a faithful one brings healing. Those who ignore correction end in poverty and shame, and those who accept it are honored. Wise company makes a person wise, while fools' companions come to ruin, and evil follows sinners while good comes to the righteous.

The passage contrasts the good and the wicked. A good person leaves wealth to future generations, while the sinner's wealth ends up with the just. It adds that discipline shows love, and that the righteous are satisfied while the wicked go hungry.

Wise people build up their households, while fools tear them down. Those who live honestly respect God, while those who live crookedly despise him. The passage also says a clean stable means no oxen, but a large harvest needs the ox's strength, and that a true witness does not lie.

Wisdom comes easily to people who understand, but a mocker looks for it and never finds it. The passage advises leaving a fool when he shows no real knowledge, says a fool's folly is deceit, and ends by saying that each heart alone knows its own pain, and an outsider cannot share its joy.

The wicked will be overthrown, while the upright will prosper. A path that seems right to a person can lead to death, and laughter can hide sorrow. The simple trust every word, but the prudent watch where they are going.

Wise people fear wrong and turn away from it, while fools act recklessly and stay sure of themselves. The passage contrasts the two: quick anger and wicked schemes are foolish, the poor are disliked by their neighbours while the rich attract friends, and despising a neighbour is sin. Showing mercy to the poor is called blessed.

Those who plan evil go astray, while those who plan good receive mercy and truth. Hard work brings gain, but idle talk leads only to poverty. The passage also praises honest witnesses, and says that reverence for the LORD gives strength, a refuge, and life.

Proverbs 14:28–32 lists contrasts between wise and foolish conduct. It says a large population brings a king honour, while a lack of people brings ruin. A slow temper shows understanding, and a quick temper promotes foolishness. Oppressing the poor insults their Maker, while kindness to them honours God. The wicked are cast out in their wickedness, but the righteous have hope even in death.

Wisdom rests in the mind of a person who understands, while fools openly show what they are. Righteousness raises a nation up, but sin brings shame on any people. A king favors a wise servant but is angry with a servant who brings shame.

A gentle reply calms anger, while harsh words stir it up. Wise people speak knowledge well, but fools pour out foolishness. The LORD sees everyone, good and evil. The wicked lose their wealth to trouble, and the righteous keep their treasure.

The passage contrasts wise and foolish, wicked and upright people. Wise speech spreads knowledge, while a foolish heart does not. God rejects the sacrifices and way of life of the wicked but delights in the prayers and righteousness of the upright. Those who reject correction will die, and God sees even hell and destruction clearly, so how much more the human heart.

A mocker dislikes being corrected and avoids wise people. Understanding seeks knowledge, while fools feed on foolishness. A cheerful heart brings a steady feast, and a little with reverence for the LORD is better than great wealth with trouble.

Peace and love matter more than wealth or a rich meal. Anger starts quarrels, while patience calms them. The lazy person's path is blocked with thorns, but the upright person's path is clear. A wise son brings joy to his father, and folly is pleasure only to someone who lacks wisdom.

Plans fail when no one is consulted but succeed with many advisers. A well-timed, apt answer brings joy. Wisdom leads upward, away from death, while the LORD tears down the proud and protects the widow, and he despises wicked thoughts but delights in pure words.

Greed brings trouble on one's own household, while refusing bribes leads to life. The wicked speak evil, and the LORD is far from them, but he hears the prayers of the righteous. Those who accept correction gain understanding, and those who reject instruction harm themselves.
Respect for the LORD is what teaches wisdom, and humility comes before honour. The verse says that a person who is humble is honoured only after that humility, not before it.

Human plans and spoken words both come from God, according to this passage. People may think their own ways are pure, but God judges their inner motives. Those who trust their work to God will find their thoughts steady. Proud people are hateful to God and will not escape punishment, even if they band together.

Proverbs 16:6–11 says that wrongdoing is cleansed through mercy and faithfulness, and that a person who pleases God can even reconcile enemies. It states that a little gained honestly is better than much gained unjustly. It adds that people plan their ways, but God directs their steps, and that a king's judgments should be just, with honest scales belonging to the LORD.

Wrongdoing is hateful to kings, because a throne stands firm only on righteousness. Kings delight in honest speech and value those who speak what is right. A wise person can calm a king's anger, and wisdom is worth more than gold or silver.

The passage contrasts wise and foolish conduct. It says that turning away from evil keeps a person safe, that pride leads to ruin, and that humility is better than sharing in stolen goods with the proud. It adds that careful handling of matters and trust in the LORD bring good, and that wisdom and pleasant speech increase learning.

Understanding is described as a source of life, while foolish teaching brings only folly. Wise speech is pleasant and healthy, and a path that seems right to a person may still lead to death. A wicked person stirs up trouble, and his words burn like fire.

Troublemakers cause quarrels and split close friends, and violent men lead others into wrongdoing. Gray hair is honored when it comes with a righteous life. A patient man is better than a warrior, and a self-controlled man than a conqueror. Though lots are cast, the outcome is said to come from the LORD.

Peace with a little food is better than a large house full of feasts shared in quarrels. A wise servant can gain authority over a shameful son and share in the inheritance. God tests hearts as fire tests metal. Liars listen to wicked talk, and whoever mocks the poor insults their Maker, and the one who rejoices in disaster will not go unpunished.

Grandchildren are described as the pride of old men, and children bring honor to their fathers. The verses then contrast wise and foolish people: fine speech does not suit a fool, and lies do not suit a prince. A wise person accepts rebuke more readily than a fool accepts any punishment, and forgiving an offense builds love while repeating it breaks friendships.

Proverbs 17:11–15 warns that trouble tends to follow from evil conduct and from quarrels. It says a stubborn fool is more dangerous than a bear robbed of her cubs, that repaying good with evil brings lasting harm, and that starting a quarrel is like letting out water, so it is best stopped early. It also says that judging the wicked to be innocent, or the innocent to be guilty, is hateful to the LORD.

A fool cannot buy wisdom, since he has no desire for it. The verses then contrast true friendship, which lasts in hard times, with the harm that comes from quarrels, reckless promises, boasting, and a crooked heart or tongue.

A foolish child brings sorrow to the parent who has him, and a cheerful heart is healthy while a broken spirit weakens the body. The passage also says that taking bribes twists justice, that a wise person is aware of understanding, and that punishing the innocent or the righteous is wrong.

A person who knows a lot uses few words, and a person of understanding has a calm, even-tempered spirit. Even a fool is thought wise if he keeps quiet, and someone who closes his lips is seen as sensible.

The passage contrasts wise and foolish speech and conduct. A person who withdraws to pursue wisdom is praised, while a fool takes no pleasure in understanding and only shows what is in his heart. Wicked people bring contempt, the wise speak deep and flowing words, and a fool's lips start quarrels that bring blows.

The passage contrasts ruin with safety and pride with humility. A fool's speech leads to his own downfall, gossip hurts deeply, and laziness is linked to waste. The righteous find safety in the LORD, while the rich trust their wealth, and pride comes before destruction, humility before honour.

Answering a matter before hearing all of it brings shame and folly. Wise people seek knowledge by listening. The passage also says that a person who argues his own case first may seem right, until his neighbour examines him, and that casting lots can settle disputes between powerful people.

Proverbs 18:19–23 says that quarrels between people are hard to end, like the bars of a castle gate. It claims that words bring either life or death, and that a man's speech affects what he gains. It also says a good wife is a blessing, and that the poor speak humbly while the rich answer harshly.
A man with friends has to show himself friendly first. Yet there is a friend who stays closer than a brother.

A poor man who lives honestly is better off than a fool whose speech is crooked. The verses also say that acting without knowledge is not good, that a person's own foolishness can ruin his path while his heart blames the LORD, that wealth brings friends while the poor are left alone, and that liars will be punished.

Proverbs 19:6–10 says that people flatter the powerful and befriend anyone who gives gifts, while the poor are shunned even by their own relatives. Wisdom is good for the one who seeks it, and liars will be punished. It also says that luxury is unfitting for a fool, much less a servant ruling over princes.

Wise restraint keeps anger in check, and forgiving an offence brings honour. A king's anger is dangerous, but his favour is refreshing. The verses also say that a foolish son brings ruin on his father, a quarrelsome wife is a constant annoyance, and a sensible wife is a gift from the LORD. Laziness leads to deep sleep and hunger.

Keeping the commandment protects one's own life, while despising one's ways leads to death. Giving to the poor is like lending to the LORD, who will repay it. The passage also urges discipline for a son while there is still hope, warns that a violent-tempered man will be punished again and again, and urges listening to advice so that one becomes wise later in life.

Human plans are many, but the LORD's purpose is the one that lasts. Fearing the LORD leads to life and safety from harm, while a lazy person will not even lift his hand to feed himself. Punishing a mocker teaches the simple, and correcting a wise person adds to his knowledge.

A son who wastes his father's goods and drives out his mother brings shame. The verses then warn against listening to teaching that leads away from wisdom, and say that mockers and wicked witnesses will face judgment and punishment.

Strong drink makes people foolish, and a man who is fooled by it is not wise. Angering a king is dangerous, and avoiding quarrels is honorable, while fools keep stirring up trouble. A lazy man who will not work in the cold will have nothing at harvest time. Good advice in a person's heart is hidden like deep water, and a wise person can bring it out.

Many people claim to be good, but a truly faithful person is hard to find. A just person who lives with integrity leaves a blessing to his children. No one can honestly say his heart is fully clean from sin. God rejects cheating in weights and measures, and a child's conduct shows whether he is pure and right.

The passage gives a mix of short sayings. It says that the ability to hear and see comes from God, and that too much sleep leads to poverty while watchfulness brings enough food. It warns that a buyer may run down goods before a sale and then boast once he has gone. It adds that wise speech is worth more than gold or rubies, and ends with advice to take a pledge from anyone who guarantees a stranger's debt.

Gain got by deceit may taste sweet at first but later brings pain. Plans succeed when they rest on advice. Gossips reveal secrets, so avoid flatterers. Cursing one's parents ends in ruin, and an inheritance grabbed too quickly will not bring blessing.

Do not seek revenge; wait for the LORD to act. The passage also condemns dishonest weights and scales, says a person cannot fully understand his own path, and warns against rashly vowing and then reconsidering what is holy. It ends by saying that the human spirit is a lamp of the LORD that searches a person's inner self.

Mercy and truth keep a king safe, and mercy holds up his throne. Strength is the pride of young men, and grey hair is the honour of old men. Just as a wound's bruise removes evil, so do harsh blows cleanse the inner parts of a person.

A king's heart is controlled by the LORD, as a stream of water is directed wherever the one who guides it chooses. People think their own ways are right, but the LORD judges their inner motives. Justice is valued above sacrifice, while pride and wicked actions are sin.

Wealth gained by lying is empty and fleeting, and it leads to death. Wicked people who refuse to act justly are destroyed by their own robbery. The passage also says it is better to live alone on a rooftop than share a wide house with a quarrelsome wife, and that the wicked desire evil and show no kindness to their neighbours.

When a scornful person is punished, the simple learn wisdom, and the wise gain more knowledge. The passage also says that the just think carefully about the wicked, who will be overthrown by God. It adds that those who ignore the poor will themselves cry out unheard, and that justice brings joy to the just but ruin to evildoers.

Proverbs contrasts wisdom with folly. A person who strays from understanding ends up among the dead, and a lover of pleasure, wine and oil stays poor. A quarrelsome, angry wife is worse than living alone in the desert. Wise people keep their treasure, while a fool wastes it.

The passage contrasts two ways of living. Those who pursue righteousness and mercy find life and honour, and wisdom can overcome even strong defences. The slothful, who refuse to work and crave greedily, are destroyed by their own desire, while the righteous give generously and keep nothing back.

The passage says that offerings made by wicked people are hateful to God, and even more so when the giver has a wicked heart. It contrasts the fate of liars and the wicked with the upright, and states that no human wisdom or plan can stand against the LORD. Victory in battle, it says, depends on the LORD, not on horses or armies.

A good name matters more than great wealth, and good standing more than silver and gold. The passage also says a wise person sees danger coming and avoids it, while the foolish go on and suffer. Humility and reverence for the LORD bring riches, honour and life.

The passage sets out a series of contrasts: the rich rule over the poor, and borrowers serve lenders. It says that wrongdoing brings empty results, while a generous person is blessed for sharing bread with the poor. It also says that the LORD watches over knowledge and overturns the words of the wrongdoer.

The passage gives a series of warnings and sayings. A lazy man makes up dangers, like a lion in the street, to avoid work. It warns against a seductive woman, calls foolishness in a child something a firm hand should correct, and says that exploiting the poor or favoring the rich leads to poverty. It ends by urging the listener to listen to wise teaching.

It says that keeping these sayings inside you is good, and that they should also be ready on your lips. The teacher has written them so the reader will trust in the LORD, know true words, and be able to answer those who ask. It ends with a command not to rob the poor or oppress the afflicted at the city gate.

Proverbs 22:23–28 gives a series of warnings. It says the LORD will defend the poor and punish those who wrong them. It advises avoiding angry people, since their habits can become your own. It warns against guaranteeing other people's debts, and against moving old boundary markers that earlier generations set.
A person who works hard at his job will be given a place before kings. He will not be given a place before common or lowly people.

Proverbs warns a guest at a ruler's table to be careful and self-controlled. Do not crave the ruler's rich food, since it is deceptive. Do not strive to get rich, because wealth quickly disappears, and do not accept hospitality from a stingy host.

A stingy host says one thing but thinks another, so his food and kind words are worthless to the guest. The passage warns against speaking to a fool, who will scorn wise words. It urges not moving ancient boundary stones or taking land from orphans, since their defender is strong. It ends by urging close attention to learning.

The speaker urges a father to discipline his son with the rod, saying this will not kill the child and will save him from death. He hopes his son will grow wise and speak rightly, and urges him not to envy sinners but to stay in the fear of the LORD, trusting that his hope will not be cut off.

Do not join heavy drinkers and gluttons, since they end in poverty and sleepiness leaves a person in rags. Listen to your father, do not despise your mother in old age, and get wisdom and understanding even at cost, never giving them up. A wise child brings joy to parents.

A father urges his son to pay close attention to his teaching. He warns that a loose woman is a deep trap that catches men, and that heavy drinking of wine brings trouble, quarrels and bloodshot eyes. The son is told not to look at wine when it is red and sparkling in the cup.

Wine, the passage warns, ends by biting like a snake and stinging like a viper. The drinker sees strange things and speaks foolishly, lies helpless as if at sea or atop a mast, feels no pain from blows, and only wakes wanting more.

Do not envy wicked people or wish to be among them, because they plan harm and speak of trouble. Wisdom builds a house and understanding makes it firm, and knowledge fills it with riches. A wise man is strong, and wise counsel and many advisers bring safety in war.

Wisdom is out of reach for a fool, who has nothing useful to say in public. Someone who plans evil is called a troublemaker, and a mocker is hated by people. The passage also warns that giving up in hard times shows weak strength, and that refusing to rescue those facing death is condemned.

God knows the heart and the soul, so he sees what people really know, and he repays each person by their deeds. The passage then compares wisdom to sweet honey: finding wisdom is good for the soul, and it brings a reward that will not be lost.

Do not plot against a good person's home or rob their peace, because a righteous person may fall many times but always gets up, while the wicked fall into ruin. Do not celebrate when an enemy stumbles, since the LORD may see it and turn away from you. Do not be upset or envious of wicked people.

The wicked will get no reward, and their light will go out. Fear God and the king, and do not join those who seek change, since their downfall comes suddenly. Judges must not favor persons, and whoever tells the wicked they are righteous will be cursed by people and nations.

The passage gives a set of short sayings about wise conduct. It says that honest correction is valued, that people should finish outside work before building a house, and that one should not lie about a neighbour or take revenge. It ends by describing a field and vineyard belonging to a lazy, foolish man, which is left neglected.

A field the writer passes is overgrown with thorns and nettles, and its stone wall has fallen down. He concludes that a little more rest and idleness will bring poverty on a person as fast and as surely as a traveller or an armed attacker arrives.

Some sayings say that God hides matters, while kings are honoured for uncovering them. Heaven is high, earth is deep, and a king's mind cannot be fully searched. Removing impurities makes silver ready for use, and removing wicked men from the king's presence makes his rule secure and just.

Do not push yourself forward before a king or take a high seat among great men. It is better to be asked to move up than to be made to step down in front of a ruler. Do not rush into a quarrel, and settle disputes directly with your neighbour without revealing private matters to others.

Warnings about speech and promises: a word spoken at the right time is precious, like gold apples in silver settings. A wise rebuke is valued by a listener willing to hear it. A faithful messenger refreshes those who send him, while a person who boasts of a gift he never gives is like clouds without rain.

Patience and gentle speech can win over even a powerful ruler. The verses then warn against excess, such as eating too much honey, and against wearing out your welcome at a neighbour's home. They also say that lying about a neighbour does great harm, and that trusting an unfaithful person in trouble is like a broken tooth or a dislocated foot.

Singing to someone with a heavy heart is like taking away their coat in cold weather or pouring vinegar on soda. Feeding and watering an enemy is said to bring God's reward. Like a north wind driving off rain, an angry face drives off a backbiting tongue. Living on a rooftop corner is said to be better than sharing a wide house with a quarrelsome wife.

Good news from a distant land is as refreshing as cold water to a thirsty person. The passage then warns that a good person who gives way before the wicked is like a muddied spring, and that seeking one's own honour is not honour. Finally, a person who cannot control his own spirit is like a city with broken walls.

Honour given to a fool is as out of place as snow in summer. A curse without cause does no harm, like a bird that flies away. Fools need correction, as horses and donkeys need a whip or bridle. Answer a fool, but be careful not to become like him, and the proverb also says to answer him so he does not think himself wise. Sending a message through a fool harms the sender.

Fools handle wisdom badly. A proverb in a fool's mouth is as useless as lame legs or a thorn in a drunkard's hand, and honouring a fool is like tying a stone in a sling. A fool keeps returning to his folly, like a dog to its vomit. The last point is that a man who thinks himself wise is more hopeless than a fool.

The passage mocks the lazy man, who invents dangers like a lion in the street as excuses to stay in bed. It says he is stuck in his idleness, too tired even to lift his hand to his mouth, and wrongly thinks himself wiser than sensible people. It ends by comparing a meddler in other people's quarrels to a madman throwing firebrands and arrows.

Proverbs 26:19–24 compares deceit and gossip to fuel for a fire. A person who tricks a neighbour and then claims it was only a joke is like a madman. Gossip and quarrelsome people keep conflict going, and hateful people hide their malice behind friendly words.

A smooth-talking enemy should not be trusted, because his heart holds hatred. Hidden hatred covered by lies will eventually be exposed. Those who set traps for others fall into them themselves, and a lying, flattering tongue brings harm to the people it targets.

Don't boast about tomorrow, since you cannot know what it will bring. Praise is better when it comes from others than from yourself. The passage also says a friend's honest criticism is better than hidden affection, and that an enemy's kisses cannot be trusted.

A full person finds even honey unappealing, while a hungry person finds anything sweet. The passage then compares a man who leaves his home to a bird leaving its nest. It praises a friend's sincere advice, and says a near neighbour is better than a distant brother in times of trouble.

The passage is a set of short sayings. A wise son brings joy to his father, and a prudent person sees danger coming and avoids it. It also warns against guaranteeing a stranger's debts, blessing a friend too loudly and too early, and quarrelling constantly, which is compared to steady rain on a wet day.

The passage is a set of short sayings about character and reputation. It says that a hidden thing cannot stay hidden, that people improve one another through contact, that faithful service brings honour, and that human desire is never satisfied. It ends by comparing a person's worth to the tests used to refine silver and gold.

A fool stays foolish even when beaten hard, so correction does not change him. The passage then urges careful attention to one's flocks and herds, since wealth does not last forever and a crown does not pass unchanged to every generation. Plants grow, and the lambs and goats provide clothing and the price of a field.

Proverbs 27:27 says that a person who looks after their flocks will have enough goat's milk. It will feed the household and provide for the female servants. "Maidens" here means young women who serve in the house.

The wicked run away even when no one chases them, while the righteous stay bold and fearless. The passage also says that a land suffers when it has many rulers, but stays stable under one wise leader. It adds that those who abandon the law praise evil, while those who keep it oppose evil. Only those who seek the LORD truly understand everything.

A poor man who lives honestly is better than a rich man who lives crookedly. The passage says a son who keeps the law is wise, while one who keeps riotous company shames his father. It adds that wealth gained by usury or injustice will go to someone who pities the poor, and that a prayer from someone who refuses to hear the law is detestable.

The passage contrasts good and bad conduct. Whoever leads the upright into evil will fall into his own trap, while the upright will prosper. A rich man may think himself wise, but a poor man with understanding sees through him. Hiding one's sins brings no success, but confessing and turning from them brings mercy.

The verses contrast two kinds of people. Those who stay reverent and upright are blessed or saved, while those who harden their hearts, act wickedly, or live crookedly come to ruin. A wicked ruler is compared to a lion or bear that preys on the poor, and a man who commits violence against another's life will be destroyed.

Hard work brings enough food, while chasing empty pursuits brings poverty. A faithful person is richly blessed, but someone in a hurry to get rich is not innocent. Honest correction is valued more than flattery, and favoring people for gain leads to wrongdoing.

A man who robs his parents and says it is no wrong is a partner of a destroyer. The verses then contrast the proud and the self-reliant, who stir up conflict or fall into folly, with those who trust the LORD, act wisely, give to the poor, and see the righteous grow when the wicked fall.

A stubborn person who ignores repeated warnings will be suddenly destroyed with no cure. The verses then contrast good and bad rulers, wise and foolish children, honest and corrupt kings, and flatterers who trap others.

The passage contrasts wicked and wise people. An evil man's sin becomes a trap for him, while the righteous sing with joy. The righteous care for the poor, but the wicked do not care to know their cause. Fools speak out all their thoughts, while wise people hold them back until the right time.
