A ruler who listens to lies makes his whole staff wicked. A king who judges the poor fairly keeps his throne secure. Discipline brings wisdom, while an undisciplined child shames his mother, and a child who is corrected brings his parents peace and joy.

The verses give a string of short sayings about wisdom and character. They say that a people without guidance or vision falls apart, a servant who does not listen to words cannot be corrected, and a hasty speaker is less promising than a fool. They also warn that anger causes strife, pride brings a man low, and humility is upheld by honour.

A person who shares a thief's crime harms himself, since he hears the curse on the thief and keeps silent. Fearing people leads to a trap, but trusting the LORD keeps a person safe. Each person's judgment comes from the LORD, not from seeking a ruler's favour. Good and wicked people each find the other hateful.

Agur confesses that he is very foolish and has no wisdom or knowledge of the holy. He then asks a series of questions: who has climbed into heaven or come down, who holds the wind and the waters, who set the earth's boundaries, and what the name of this being and his son is. The questions imply that only God can answer them, and that no human has done these things.

The speaker says God's words are pure and protect those who trust him, so nothing should be added to them. He asks for two things: to be kept from lies and empty talk, and to get neither great wealth nor poverty. He fears that riches could make him deny God, and that poverty could make him steal and misuse God's name.

The passage warns against slandering a servant to his master, then lists kinds of people it calls a "generation." These include those who curse their parents, those who think themselves pure but are not, those who are proud and arrogant, and those who prey on the poor and needy.

The passage lists things that never stop wanting more: the grave, the barren womb, dry earth, and fire. It also warns that a child who mocks a father or refuses a mother will be eaten by birds. The closing lines say the speaker finds some things beyond understanding.

The passage lists things that leave no trace or are hard to understand, such as an eagle in the air, a snake on a rock, and a ship at sea. It then describes an adulterous woman who eats, wipes her mouth, and claims she has done no wrong. Last, it names four things that unsettle the earth: a servant who becomes king, a fool who is full of food, a hated woman who marries, and a maidservant who inherits from her mistress.

Small creatures can still be wise. The passage lists ants, conies, locusts and spiders, each small and weak, yet each doing something sensible, such as storing food or building in rocks. It then starts a list of animals that look impressive in their movement, beginning with the lion.

Three things are called stately or unbeatable: a greyhound, a male goat, and a king no one can rise against. The passage then advises that if you have acted foolishly or thought evil, you should be silent. It ends by comparing angry force to churning milk or wringing the nose: it produces strife, as butter or blood comes from those acts.

A queen mother gives her son, King Lemuel, advice. She warns him not to give his strength to women or his conduct to what ruins kings. Kings and princes should avoid wine and strong drink, because drinking may make them forget the law and wrong the afflicted. Strong drink is for those who are dying or deeply sad.

The passage first says that strong drink should be given to those in misery, so they forget their poverty. It then urges speaking up for the voiceless and the poor, and judging fairly. Last, it praises a capable wife, whose worth is above rubies, who is trusted by her husband and works willingly with her hands.

It describes a capable woman who works hard for her household. She brings food from far away like a trading ship, rises before dawn to feed her family and servants, buys and plants a vineyard, and spins and weaves cloth late into the night.

It describes a capable woman who helps the poor and needy and makes sure her household is warmly clothed. She makes fine cloth and goods to sell, and her husband is respected among the town leaders. She is described as dressed in strength and honour, and will rejoice in the future.

A woman of strength speaks wisely and kindly, runs her household well, and works hard rather than living in idleness. Her children and husband praise her. The passage says that charm and beauty do not last, and that a woman who reveres the LORD deserves praise, and that her own work should bring her praise publicly.

A man named Job, living in the land of Uz, is described as blameless, upright, fearing God and avoiding evil. He has seven sons, three daughters, large herds of animals and many servants, and he is the richest man in the east.

Job's sons hold feasts in their homes, each on his own day, and invite their sisters. When the feasting period ends, Job makes offerings for each of his children. He does this because he fears they may have sinned in their hearts by cursing God, and he does it regularly.

One day the heavenly beings gather before the LORD, and Satan, a figure who moves around the earth, comes with them. The LORD asks Satan where he has been, and then points out Job, a blameless man who fears God and turns from evil.

Satan tells the LORD that Job only serves God because God has protected him and blessed his wealth. Satan says that if his property is taken away, Job will curse God. The LORD gives Satan permission to test Job's property, but not Job's own body, and Satan leaves.

A messenger brings Job news of a sudden disaster on the same day his children are feasting. Raiders called Sabeans take his oxen and donkeys and kill the servants tending them, and only the messenger survives to report it.

Messengers arrive one after another to tell Job that his livestock and servants have been destroyed. The first says fire from God fell from heaven and burned his sheep and servants. The second says raiding Chaldeans took his camels and killed the servants with the sword. Each messenger is the only survivor.

A messenger tells Job that a great wind struck the house where his sons and daughters were feasting, killing all of them, and that only the messenger escaped. Job responds by tearing his robe, shaving his head, and falling to the ground in worship.

Job, after losing his property and children, says he came into the world with nothing and will leave it with nothing. He accepts that God gave and God took away, and he blesses God's name. The text states that he did not sin or blame God foolishly in this.

In this scene, the sons of God gather before the LORD, and Satan comes among them. The LORD asks Satan where he has been, and Satan replies that he has been roaming the earth. The word "Satan" here means something like "the accuser" or "adversary," a role rather than a name.

God says Job is blameless and still keeps his integrity, even though Satan has stirred God to harm him for no reason. Satan replies that people give up anything to save their own lives, and says Job would curse God if his body were struck.

The Lord gives Satan permission to harm Job's body, but not to take his life. Satan covers Job with painful boils, and Job sits among the ashes scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery. Job's wife then urges him to curse God and die.

Job answers his wife that they must accept evil as well as good from God, and he does not sin with his words in this. Then three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, hear of his trouble and come from their homes to mourn with him and comfort him.

Job's three friends see him from a distance and fail to recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, throw dust on their heads, and sit silently with him on the ground for seven days and nights, because they see how great his suffering is.
Job curses the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He wants that day to be dark, unseen by God, and filled with gloom and terror.

Job wishes that the night of his birth had never happened. He asks that it be dark, silent and removed from the calendar, and that those who curse days would curse it. He gives as his reason that the night did not prevent his birth or hide the suffering that followed.
The speaker wishes he had died at birth, or had never been born at all. He says that then he would be at rest, like kings, rulers and wealthy men, or like a stillborn child that never saw light.

Job says that in the grave the wicked stop causing trouble, the tired rest, prisoners and servants are free, and great and small are equal. He then asks why light and life are given to people in misery who long for death and dig for it, rejoicing when they find the grave.

Job asks why life is given to a man whose path is hidden and whom God has fenced in. He says his groaning comes before his food and his cries pour out like water. The trouble he feared has come, and he has known no peace or rest.

Eliphaz speaks to Job, who is suffering. He says Job has helped many people in trouble, but now that trouble has come to Job himself and he is shaken. He asks whether Job's fear, confidence, hope and righteous living are now failing him.

Eliphaz asks Job to recall any innocent person who was destroyed, and he says that those who plow wickedness and sow iniquity reap the same harm. God's breath destroys such people. Strong lions, young and old, are also shown losing their strength and their prey.

Eliphaz, a speaker in the book of Job, describes a frightening night vision in which a spirit stands before him without showing its form. The voice in it asks whether a mortal man can be more just or pure than God, its maker.

Even God's servants and angels are not fully trusted, so how much less can humans, who live in houses of clay and are crushed like moths, be trusted. People are destroyed from morning to evening and die without anyone noticing, dying without wisdom.

Eliphaz speaks to Job and says that anger and envy destroy a foolish person. He once saw such a fool seem to prosper, but his home was suddenly cursed. His children have no safety, are crushed at the city gate with no one to help, and their harvest is eaten by the hungry and the robbers.

Trouble does not grow out of the ground by itself, yet people are born into it as surely as sparks rise from a fire. So the speaker says he will turn to God and leave his case with him, since God does great and unsearchable works, such as sending rain and lifting up the lowly and the mourners.

God frustrates the schemes of the cunning, so their plans fail. He traps the wise in their own cleverness, and the plots of the devious rush to ruin. Meanwhile he rescues the poor from the sword and from the powerful, so the poor have hope and wrongdoing is silenced.

Eliphaz tells Job that a person whom God corrects is blessed, so Job should not reject God's discipline. He says God wounds but also heals, and will rescue the person from many kinds of trouble, including famine, war, and slander.

Eliphaz tells Job that a person who is corrected by God will be kept safe from disaster, famine, and wild animals. Such a person will have peace, a large family, and will die at a ripe old age, like grain gathered at harvest.
Eliphaz, a friend of Job, says that he and his companions have investigated the matter carefully and found it to be true. He tells Job to listen and to take the lesson for his own benefit.

Job replies that his grief is so heavy it would outweigh the sand of the sea, which is why his words feel swallowed up. He says God's arrows and terrors are inside him and drain his spirit. He compares his complaint to animals that bray or low only when they lack food, and to bland food that cannot be eaten without salt.

Job says his suffering is so bitter that he has no appetite; the things he once refused now feel like his only food. He wishes God would destroy him quickly, since that would at least bring him relief. He has no strength or future left to hope for, so there is no reason to keep living.

Job complains that he is not made of stone or brass, so he cannot endure endlessly. He says a friend in trouble should receive kindness, but his own brothers have failed him. Like seasonal streams that dry up in the heat, they have vanished when he needed them.

Job speaks to his friends, who have come to comfort him. He compares them to desert travelers who went looking for water at the caravan routes of Tema and Sheba and found nothing, leaving them disappointed. He says he never asked them for money or rescue, and he asks only that they teach him where he has gone wrong, and he will be silent.

Job, in pain and despair, answers his friends. He says their correct words do not prove him wrong, because his speech is only the cry of a suffering man. He accuses them of cruelty toward the weak and their friend, and insists he has not spoken falsely or wickedly.

Job complains that human life is fixed and hard, like a worker's labour that he waits to end. He has been given long months of emptiness and restless nights, and he lies awake longing for dawn. His body is covered with worms and dust, and his skin is broken and sore.

The speaker, Job, describes how quickly his life is passing and how little hope he has left. He compares life to wind and a cloud that vanishes, and says that once a person goes down to the grave, they never return home or are seen again.

Job says he will speak freely about his suffering. He asks why God watches over him as if he were a dangerous sea monster. Even his sleep brings terrifying dreams, so he says he would rather die than keep living, and asks God to leave him alone.

Job speaks to God, asking why God pays such close attention to humans, testing him every morning and every moment. He asks how long God will keep watching him without letting him rest, even long enough to swallow his spit. He admits he has sinned and asks what he can do to God, and why he has been made a target so that he is a burden to himself.
Job asks God why he does not forgive his sin and remove his guilt. He says he will soon die and lie in the dust, and that God will look for him in the morning but find him gone.

Bildad rebukes Job, saying his words are as empty as a strong wind. He argues that God does not act unjustly, so if Job's children died for their sins, Job should seek God and live pure and upright, and then God would restore his prosperity.

Bildad, speaking to Job, says that a small beginning can lead to a great future. He urges Job to ask earlier generations, since people today know little and their lives are brief. He then compares a plant that grows without mud or water: it dries up quickly, before any other plant does.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, says that those who forget God end up with nothing. Their hope fails and their trust is as weak as a spider's web. Such a person may seem flourishing for a time, but his roots are in stony ground, and when he is removed, his place will deny he ever existed.

Bildad, speaking to Job, says that God will not reject a blameless person or help those who do evil. If Job is upright, God will fill his mouth with laughter, and his enemies will be covered in shame while the homes of the wicked are destroyed.

Job replies that a person cannot argue his case against God, because God is too wise and too powerful to answer. He describes God's power: moving mountains, shaking the earth, commanding the sun and sealing up the stars. No one who opposes God is shown to succeed.

Job describes God as the one who stretches out the heavens, walks on the sea, and makes the stars and constellations. He does great works that cannot be traced or counted. Job says he cannot see God pass by or stop him, and no one can ask God to account for his acts. Even the proud helpers bow beneath him.

Job says he cannot argue with God, even if he were innocent. He would only beg his judge for mercy, and he doubts God would really listen. God, he says, batters him with storms and wounds him without cause. God is too strong for any trial, and no one can set a time for a hearing.

Job says that claiming innocence only condemns him, since his own words would prove him guilty. He argues that God destroys both the perfect and the wicked, mocks the suffering of the innocent, and lets the wicked take control of the earth, hiding the faces of its judges. He asks who else could be responsible if not God.

Job says his days are passing fast, like swift ships or an eagle diving on prey, with no good in them. If he tries to put his complaint aside and comfort himself, he fears his sorrows anyway, because he knows God will not count him innocent. Even if he washes himself perfectly clean, God will still throw him into a pit, and his own clothes will feel disgusting to him.

Job says God is not a man like himself, so the two cannot meet in court and no mediator stands between them to lay a hand on both. He asks that God lift his rod and stop frightening him, and then he would speak without fear. He admits this is not his situation.

Job, in distress, tells God he is tired of living and will speak openly in his bitterness. He asks God why he is being judged and punished, and whether it pleases God to oppress the work of His own hands. He asks whether God sees as humans see, and whether God's time is like human time, since God is searching out his sin.

Job speaks to God, saying he is innocent and that no one can save him from God's power. He argues that God formed him with care, shaping him like clay, pouring him out like milk, and curdling him like cheese, so it seems strange that God now wants to destroy him.

Job speaks to God and says that God has kept his true thoughts hidden, yet Job knows God is watching him closely. Whether he is guilty or innocent, Job feels he cannot escape his suffering, and God keeps adding to it, hunting him like a lion.

Job speaks to God in deep distress. He asks why he was born at all, and wishes he had died at birth or had never been born. He asks God to leave him alone so he can find a little comfort before he goes to the land of darkness, the place of the dead, where there is no order and not even light.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, answers Job sharply. He says Job's many words should be answered, that Job's talk should not make him right, and that Job's claim to be pure and innocent is false. He wishes God would speak and show Job his faults.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, tells Job that God's wisdom is far greater than Job can grasp, and that God punishes him less than his sins deserve. God cannot be fully searched out: he is higher than heaven, deeper than the grave, and bigger than earth and sea. No one can stop him if he chooses to act.

Zophar tells Job that God knows empty, foolish people and sees their wrongdoing. If Job turns his heart toward God, puts sin far from his home, and lets go of wickedness, he will hold up his face without shame, stand firm, and forget his trouble as quickly as flowing water passes away.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, tells Job that if he turns back to God, his life will be bright and full of hope, with safety and rest, and people will seek his favour. The wicked, however, will lose their hope and find no escape.

Job answers his friends with sarcasm: he says they must think wisdom will die with them, since he has understanding as good as theirs. He says he is mocked by his neighbours, even though he calls on God and God answers him, and that the upright man is scorned by the comfortable, who look down on someone who is about to fall.

Robbers and those who defy God often prosper, and God gives them plenty. Yet the speaker says that any living creature, from beasts and birds to the earth and fish, would show that the LORD controls all life and breath.

Job says that just as the ear tests words and the mouth tastes food, wisdom comes with age and understanding with long life. He then says that wisdom, strength and counsel belong to God, who can destroy, shut in, hold back waters or send them out to flood the land. He ends by saying that both the deceived and the deceiver are under God's control.

God is shown reversing human status and wisdom: he strips counsellors and judges of their wisdom, unbinds kings, humbles princes and the mighty, takes speech from the trusted and understanding from the old, and brings hidden things out of darkness into light.

God raises nations up and brings them down, enlarging them and then narrowing them again. He takes understanding away from the leaders of the earth, leaving them lost in a trackless wilderness, groping in darkness and stumbling like drunken men.

Job says he has seen and understood everything his friends know, so he is not less wise than they are. He wants to argue his case directly with God. He accuses his friends of speaking falsely on God's behalf and of being poor healers of his trouble, and he asks whether they will take God's side by defending him with lies.

Job speaks to his friends, who have been defending God with empty words. He asks whether God would be pleased with their searching and flattering, warns that God will rebuke them for secretly taking sides, and says their arguments are as weak as ashes. He then tells them to be silent so he can speak, even if it costs him his life.

Job says he will keep trusting God even if God kills him, and he will defend his own conduct before God. He expects God to save him, since a hypocrite cannot stand before God. He asks others to listen closely, states that he has prepared his case and expects to be found right, and says he will speak rather than stay silent.

Job asks God to lift His hand and stop frightening him, so that he can speak and be answered. He asks what his sins are and why God hides His face and treats him as an enemy. He compares himself to a leaf or dry stubble, and says God writes bitter things against him and makes him bear the sins of his youth.

Job tells God that God has placed his feet in stocks, a wooden restraint for prisoners, and watches closely every path he takes. Job says that he himself is wearing away like rotting wood or a moth-eaten garment.

Human life is short and full of trouble, passing quickly like a flower or a shadow. Job asks God why he should be judged such a frail being, and then asks God to turn away and let him rest until his appointed time ends, like a hired worker finishing a day.

A tree cut down may still sprout again from its roots when it smells water. A man, however, dies and wastes away, and no one can say where he has gone. Just as seawater or a river can dry up, so Job says man does not return.

Job says that a man who dies lies down and does not rise until the heavens are gone, so he will not wake from sleep. He wishes God would hide him in the grave until God's anger passes, then call him back at a set time and remember him. He will wait for his change to come, and hopes God will call and he will answer.

Job speaks to God, saying that God watches every step and sin closely, and seals up and sews shut his wrongdoing. He observes that even mountains, rocks and stones wear away, and that God destroys human hope. In the end God overcomes a person, changes his face, and sends him away, meaning death.
A dead man, the speaker says, does not know what happens to his children. They may rise to honour or fall into poverty, and he is unaware of it. Only his own body and inner self feel pain and sorrow.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, accuses Job of talking empty nonsense that does no good. He says Job's own words show his guilt, and he asks whether Job is the first man ever born, implying Job claims a wisdom he does not have.

Eliphaz speaks to Job and asks what secret wisdom Job has that others lack. He says older, wiser men are present, and asks whether God's comfort is too small for Job. He then asks why Job's heart and eyes have led him to turn against God with such words.

Eliphaz, a speaker in the book of Job, argues that no human can be pure or righteous before God. Even the heavens are not clean in God's sight, so people, who drink in wrongdoing like water, are even less so. He says he will pass on what wise men have taught from their ancestors.

The wicked man suffers constant fear and distress, and he expects disaster even when things seem to be going well. He does not believe he will escape, and he is pictured as wandering in search of food, while trouble overwhelms him like an army attacking a king.
Eliphaz is describing the fate of a wicked man who defies God. Though he is proud and well fed, he will live in ruined cities and empty houses, and he will not keep his wealth or his prosperity.

Speaker Eliphaz says that the wicked man will never escape darkness. His plants wither as if burned, and his hope in emptiness will bring him nothing. His life ends early, and the homes of the deceitful and corrupt will be destroyed by fire.

Evil plans lead to empty results, and their inner heart is ready to deceive. The verse, spoken within Job's friend Eliphaz's speech, uses the image of pregnancy: wicked people "conceive" harm and "bring forth" worthless things.

Job replies to his friends that they are miserable comforters and asks why they keep talking. He says he could speak against them in the same way, but he would rather encourage them. Yet whether he speaks or stays silent, his own grief is not eased.

Job describes how God has worn him out and taken away his friends. His thin, wrinkled body now seems to show his suffering to everyone. He says God attacks him in anger like a wild beast, and his enemies mock him and gang up against him.
Job says God has handed him over to wicked people and attacked him violently. He describes being broken, shaken, used as a target, and left in mourning, covered in sackcloth and lying in the dust.

Job, suffering and weeping, insists he has done no wrong and that his prayer is sincere. He asks that his blood not be hidden in the earth, believing a witness in heaven will vouch for him. Since no human advocate speaks for him, he wishes someone could plead his case before God, as one person pleads for another, before he dies.

Job, near death, says his life is almost over and that people mock him. He asks God to give a pledge on his behalf, since no one else will stand surety for him. He says God has kept his accusers from understanding, so they will not be raised up, and that false flattery will bring ruin to those who practise it. He ends by saying he has become a common saying among people, though he was once respected.

Job describes his own suffering: his eyes are weak from grief, his days are over, and his plans have failed. He says the upright will be shocked by his fate and will stand firmer in their ways, while he finds no wise person among his friends who have come to comfort him. He also says that night feels like day to him, since his darkness is so deep.

Job says that if he waits, the grave will be his only home, and he has already made his bed in darkness. He calls decay his father and the worm his mother and sister. He asks where his hope is, and concludes that his hope will go down with him into the dust of death, where all rest together.

Bildad, one of Job's friends, scolds Job for talking too long and for treating his friends as if they were stupid animals. He says Job's anger will not change the natural order of the world. He then declares that the light of the wicked will be put out, and their home left in darkness.

The speaker, Bildad, describes a wicked man whose own plans and steps trap him. Snares, nets and traps lie in his path, terrors chase him, and hunger and ruin wait close by. The image is of a person caught by his own actions and surrounded by danger.
Bildad, speaking to Job, describes the fate of a wicked man. Disease and death take his strength, his home is destroyed, and his family line and memory vanish, so that no one remembers his name.

The speaker, Bildad, describes the fate of a wicked person who does not know God. He is pushed from light into darkness and removed from the world, leaving no children, relatives, or home behind. People who come later will be shocked at his fate, as earlier people were frightened by it.

Job answers his friends, saying their repeated accusations hurt him badly. He says that even if he has done wrong, the error is his own concern, and he claims God has trapped and overthrown him. He cries out against this wrong, but no one hears him or gives a fair judgment.

Job describes how God has blocked his way, stripped him of honor, and destroyed his hope like a felled tree. He says God treats him as an enemy, sending troops against him, and his relatives and friends have turned away from him.

Job describes how everyone close to him has turned away. Relatives, friends, household servants, his wife, and even young children treat him as a stranger or speak against him, and the servant will not answer when he calls. The people he loved now reject him.

Job, in great pain and near death, begs his friends to pity him, since God has struck him. He wishes his words could be carved permanently in rock, because he is sure that his redeemer lives and will stand on the earth in the end.

Job says that even after his body is destroyed by worms, he will still see God with his own eyes, not as a stranger would. He then warns his friends that they should fear punishment for persecuting him, since the true cause of his trouble lies within him.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, answers Job with a claim that the joy of wicked people does not last long. He says even someone who rises very high, with his head in the clouds, is still limited in this way.

The speaker, Zophar, says a wicked man will vanish completely, like a dream, with no trace left, and that people who saw him will no longer find him. His children will have to make amends to the poor, and the sins of his youth will lie with him in the grave.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, says that wickedness may taste sweet to a wicked person, who hides it and keeps it in his mouth. But the sin turns sour inside him like poison. The riches he swallows will be vomited back up, and he will never enjoy the rivers of honey and butter that were promised to the righteous.

Zophar, speaking to Job, says that a wicked man will have to give back everything he gained. He will not enjoy the gains, because he oppressed the poor and seized houses he did not build. He will find no peace or lasting satisfaction, and nothing will be left of what he had.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, says that a wicked man will lose everything just when he feels safe and full. God will send his anger on him while he eats, and he will be struck down by weapons he cannot escape.

Job's friend Zophar describes the fate of a wicked man. Hidden darkness awaits him, a fire no one has to fan will consume him, and his household and wealth will vanish on the day of God's anger. Heaven and earth will expose and turn against him. This, he says, is the share God assigns to the wicked.

Job answers his friends, asking them to listen closely and let his words be their only comfort. He says his complaint is not really against men, and he is troubled and afraid when he thinks about it. He asks why the wicked live long and grow powerful.

The speaker describes wicked people who seem to prosper: their children and herds thrive, they live without fear, and they enjoy music and dancing. Yet they spend their days in wealth and then suddenly die and go down to the grave.

The speakers say they do not want to know God's ways, and they ask what good serving or praying to God would do. Yet the passage then asks how often the wicked are actually destroyed, and answers that God brings their ruin like wind blowing away chaff.

Job is quoting a view he questions: God may store up a man's wrongdoing for his children, and the wicked man will feel the punishment himself. He then describes a different case, where a man dies comfortably and prosperously in old age, which seems to contradict that view.

Job says some men die bitter and never enjoy their lives, yet all lie alike in the dust. He claims his friends are wrong to ask where the wicked live, since anyone who travels can see the signs. He says the wicked are kept for a day of destruction and wrath.

Job asks who will ever call the wicked man to account or repay him for his deeds. Yet the wicked man dies, is buried, and is honored by the valley clods, with many going before and after him. Job says his friends' comfort is empty, because their answers are false.

Eliphaz speaks to Job and argues that God gains nothing from human goodness, so God would not punish Job for being righteous. He then accuses Job of great wickedness, citing that Job took pledges from poor brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothes.

Eliphaz accuses Job of cruelty: refusing water and bread to the tired and hungry, and sending widows away empty-handed. He says that is why trouble, fear and darkness have come on Job. He ends by pointing to God's great height above the stars, as if to say God sees everything from far above.

Eliphaz is speaking to Job and accuses him of thinking God cannot see through the dark clouds. He points to wicked people of old who said to God, "Depart from us," and were destroyed by flood or sudden ruin, though God had filled their houses with good things. He ends by saying he will not follow their counsel.

Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, speaks here. He says the righteous will see the fall of the wicked and rejoice, and that the wicked's wealth is burned. He urges Job to submit to God again, promising restored prosperity, safety, and wealth as plentiful as dust.

If you turn back to God and pray, the passage says, God will hear you, protect you, and bring prosperity, light, and rescue. It speaks of God lifting up the humble and those who have been brought low.

Eliphaz tells Job that God will rescue even a land that is not guilty, and that such a land is saved because of the clean conduct of the people's hands. "Island" here probably means a land or dwelling place, and "pureness of thine hands" means a blameless way of acting.

Job says his complaint is still bitter and his suffering is heavier than his groans. He wishes he could find God, so he could state his case before him and hear God's answer. He believes that God would not oppose him with great power, but would give him strength, and that an honest man could argue with God and be freed from his judge.

Job says he searches in every direction for God and cannot find him, yet God knows his path. He trusts that after being tested he will come out like pure gold. He claims he has kept God's way, obeyed his words, and valued them above his daily food.

Job says God is fixed in his purpose, and no one can change it; he does whatever he has decided, including many things planned for Job. This leaves Job troubled and afraid in God's presence. Yet Job notes that God has not destroyed him before the darkness of death, nor hidden that darkness from him.

Job asks why God does not set a time for judging the wicked, since those who ignore him still see no reckoning. He describes wrongdoers who move boundary stones, steal livestock, take a widow's ox as a pledge, and push the needy aside. The poor are forced to hide, and they go out to scrape a living in the wilderness like wild donkeys.

The passage describes wicked people who take the harvest and wine of others while the poor suffer. The poor are left naked and cold, sheltering among rocks in the rain, and the hungry are robbed of their grain. Even though the wicked make oil and wine, the poor go thirsty.

Job describes people who do evil and hide from the light. Murderers kill the poor at dawn and act like thieves at night, and adulterers wait for twilight and disguise their faces so no one sees them. Job says that God does not charge them with folly, even though their crimes are plain.

Job describes thieves who break into houses at night, having marked them during the day, and who avoid the light. He says their fate is ruin: like drought melting snow water, the grave takes those who have sinned.

The passage describes the fate of a wicked man: he is forgotten, eaten by worms, and his evil is broken like a tree. It also says he harms the childless and the widow, and that though he may feel safe, God still watches his ways.

Job says that the proud and powerful rise for a short time, then are brought low and cut off like ears of corn. He asks who can prove him a liar if this is not true, since he would then have spoken for nothing.

Bildad argues that God has complete power and rules in the heights, with countless armies and light over all. Because even the moon and stars are not pure before him, no human being born of a woman can be justified or clean before God. Humans are called worms, far less pure than the heavenly bodies.

Job answers his friend with a series of sarcastic questions, asking how he has helped someone powerless or given wisdom to someone without any. He then describes God's power over the dead, the underworld, and the earth, which hangs over empty space with nothing holding it up.

God is shown as controlling the sky, the seas and the heavens. He holds the waters inside thick clouds, sets bounds on the waters, and divides the sea by his power. The heavens and their pillars shake at his rebuke, and he made the sky's beauty and the crooked serpent by his spirit and hand.
These are only parts of God's ways, and we hear only a small whisper of him. Who can understand the full thunder of his power?

Job swears by God, who has denied him justice and troubled his soul, that he will never speak falsely. He refuses to admit his friends are right, and he says he will keep his innocence and integrity until he dies.

Job wishes his enemies the fate of the wicked. He argues that a hypocrite gains nothing in the end, because when God takes his life, his hope is gone and God will not hear his cry in trouble. Job says he will teach what he knows of God and accuses his friends of empty talk, since they have seen the same things.

Job says that a wicked man's fate, given to him by God, is that his children will die by the sword and his family will go hungry. His dead will not be mourned, and his wealth, however large, will be taken by the just and innocent.

Job says that the rich man's wealth is as fragile as a moth-eaten house or a watchman's temporary hut. Sudden disaster, sent by God, will strip him of everything, and people will mock him and drive him away.

Miners dig deep into the earth for silver, gold, iron and brass, going into dark places to find them. The passage also describes flowing water that has run dry, and it says that bread comes from the earth above while the ground below seems to burn like fire.

Job 28 describes miners digging deep into the earth for precious things. The passage says that the rocks hold sapphires and gold, and that the path to them is hidden from birds, beasts and predators. Human hands break open rock and mountains, cut channels through stone, and bring hidden treasure into the light.

Wisdom cannot be found by any human means. People do not know its price, and it is not in the depths, the sea, or the living world. No amount of gold, silver, jewels or other precious things can buy or equal it.

Wisdom is worth more than coral, pearls, rubies, topaz or gold, and no precious thing can match it. The speaker asks where wisdom can be found. It is hidden from all living things, even from birds and the realm of death, but God knows its way and its place.

God sees everything across the earth and sky, and he sets the weight of the wind, the measure of the waters, and the paths of rain and lightning. Having done so, he tells people that fearing the LORD is wisdom, and turning away from evil is understanding.
Job wishes he could return to the past, when God protected him, his family was around him, and he was honored in public. He describes a time of blessing and respect that he now misses.

Job recalls how people once treated him. Young men hid, elders stood up, and princes and nobles fell silent in respect. Everyone who saw or heard him spoke well of him, because he rescued the poor, the orphaned, and the helpless, and brought joy to widows.

Job recalls his former life, when he was respected and helpful. He describes himself as righteous and just, helping the blind, the lame and the poor, and punishing the wicked. He expected to live long, prosperous and honored.

Job recalls how men once listened to him in silence and waited for his words as eagerly as farmers wait for rain. He was their leader, sitting at the head and living like a king among his people, and he comforted those who mourned.

Job complains that younger men now mock him, though he once would not have let the fathers of these men work beside his sheep dogs. He describes these men as poor and starving, living in the wilderness on desert plants, and driven out from human society as if they were thieves.

Job describes men he sees as worthless, living in caves and among thorns and nettles, and says they now mock him and spit at him. He blames God for loosening his cord, meaning his good fortune, and says this has let these men lose all restraint toward him.

Job describes how young people, on his right hand, turn against him. They attack his path and push his misfortune forward, with no one to help. Terrors chase his soul like wind, his prosperity has vanished like a cloud, and his suffering now overwhelms him.

Job describes his suffering: pain keeps him awake at night, his body is wasted, and he feels cast down into dirt and ash. He cries out to God and feels ignored, even treated as an enemy. He says God has lifted him up only to be carried away by the wind and broken down.

Job speaks to God, saying he knows he is headed for death, the place where all living things go. He says he has wept for people in trouble and grieved for the poor, but good things he hoped for turned into evil, and light into darkness. His suffering leaves him mourning and crying out in public.

Job describes his suffering. He says he has become a companion to wild creatures like dragons and owls, his skin is dark and his bones feel burning hot. His music, once joyful, has turned into the sound of mourning.

Job declares that he has made a pact with his eyes not to lust after a young woman. He argues that God would punish wickedness and sees all his steps, so he invites God to weigh him fairly to prove his innocence.

Job lists sins he says he has not committed: straying from the right path, lusting after what he sees, deceit, and adultery. For each, he calls down a fitting punishment on himself, such as losing his crops, his children, or his wife. He ends by saying such a crime would deserve punishment by the judges.

Job, speaking in his own defence, says that wrongdoing would bring ruin on his wealth. He asks what he could answer to God if he had wronged his servants, since God made both master and servant alike in the womb. He also denies having refused help to the poor or having worn out the eyes of widows, that is, left them in tears.

Job lists things he says he has never done. He has not eaten his food alone while orphans went without, has not let anyone die for lack of clothing, and has not raised his hand against an orphan when he had power to harm them.

Job says that he would accept a broken arm if he had done any of the things listed. He names trusting in gold, rejoicing in great wealth, and worshipping the sun or moon, and he says he feared God's power too much to do such things.

Job lists things he says he has never done. He has not rejoiced when an enemy fell, has not cursed anyone, and has welcomed travelers into his home. He has not hidden his sins as Adam did. He presents these as proof that he is innocent before God.

Job, speaking in his own defense, says he has not hidden from public opinion or feared the scorn of others. He wishes that God would answer him, or that his accuser would put his charges in writing, so he could wear them proudly and give an account of every step he took. He adds that he would approach God like a prince, and that he would accept it if his land and its furrows testified against him.

Job swears that if he has taken the produce of land without paying for it, or has caused the landowners' deaths, then his fields should grow thistles and weeds instead of wheat and barley. The verse then closes Job's final speech.

Job's three friends stop arguing with him because he insists he is right in his own eyes. A younger man, Elihu, grows angry at Job for defending himself rather than God, and at the three friends for condemning Job without having an answer. Elihu had waited to speak out of respect for their greater age.

Elihu, a young man, explains why he stayed silent while three older men argued with Job: he expected age to bring wisdom. He now says that wisdom comes from a spirit in people, given by God, and that great or old men are not always wise.

Elihu, a younger man, speaks after three friends have failed to answer Job. He says he waited for them to argue, but none of them proved Job wrong. He says God, not human reasoning, has brought Job low, and he will not reply with their arguments. The friends fall silent.

Elihu, a younger man, explains why he finally speaks after waiting for the older men to finish. He feels full of words and says he must answer. He also promises not to favour anyone or flatter people with empty titles.
The speaker says he does not know how to give flattering titles to people. He adds that if he did, his maker would quickly take his life away.

Elihu speaks to Job and asks him to listen closely. He says his words will be honest and clear, and that God made him and gives him life. He tells Job that, before God, he is no different from Job, since both were formed from clay.

Elihu speaks to Job. He tells Job that he will not frighten him or press him hard. He repeats Job's claim to be innocent and sinless, and says God treats him as an enemy, blocking his paths. Elihu replies that Job is wrong in this and that God is greater than man.

God, the speaker says, is not required to explain himself to people who argue with him. He speaks to humans through dreams and night visions, often when they are asleep, to warn them. The aim is to turn them from wrongdoing, stop their pride, and keep them from death.

Elihu describes a man who is punished with pain in bed, so ill that he cannot eat and is close to death. He then says that if a heavenly messenger, an interpreter, speaks for him, one in a thousand, that messenger can show the man what is right for him.

In this speech from Elihu, God is gracious to a man who is near death. God tells the angel to free him, since a ransom has been found. The man's body becomes young again, and he prays to God, sees God's face with joy, and is restored to his righteousness. God does this when a person admits his sin.

Elihu, the speaker, says God often acts this way with people: he keeps a person from dying and brings them back to life. He then asks Job to listen in silence, offering to answer any reply Job has or otherwise to teach him wisdom.

Elihu, a speaker in the debate, asks the wise men to listen and test his words as the mouth tastes food. He then accuses Job of claiming he is righteous while God has denied him justice, of refusing to admit a wrong, and of mocking God and keeping company with wicked people.

Elihu, a speaker in the book of Job, argues that God cannot act wickedly or pervert justice. He says God repays each person according to their deeds, and asks who gave God authority over the earth, implying that no one else sets the terms of God's rule.

This is Elihu speaking to Job in the book of Job. He argues that if God chose to take back the breath and spirit he gave humans, all flesh would die and return to dust. He then asks how a ruler who hates justice could be condemned as unjust, and whether it is right to call kings and princes wicked.

God does not favor princes over the poor, because all people are his creation. He sees every human action, and wrongdoers cannot hide from him, even in darkness or in the shadow of death. The mighty can die suddenly, without any human hand causing it.

God does not put on a person more than is just, so no one can bring a case against him in judgment. He overthrows powerful people, sometimes secretly at night and sometimes openly, because they turned away from him and ignored his ways. Their harm to the poor reaches him, and he hears the cry of the oppressed.

God is shown as the one who alone can bring peace or trouble and who cannot be seen when he hides his face. The speaker asks God to teach him what he cannot see and says he will sin no more if he has done wrong.

Elihu, a speaker in the book, argues that God repays people by their own choices, and he asks wise listeners to judge his case. He accuses Job of speaking without knowledge and of adding rebellion to his sin by arguing against God. He wants Job tested to the end because of these answers.

Elihu asks Job whether he is right to claim his own righteousness is greater than God's, and to ask what he gains from being cleansed of sin. Elihu argues that God is too high to be harmed by human sins, or helped by human goodness.

Elihu asks what good or harm a person's righteousness or wickedness does to God, since God is not changed by it. He says people cry out under oppression, yet few ask where God is, the maker who gives songs in the night and gives humans more wisdom than animals.

Elihu, speaking in the book of Job, says that people cry out to God in distress but get no answer because of the pride of evil men. He claims God does not hear empty talk, and he tells Job to wait and trust God, accusing Job of speaking foolishly without knowledge.
Elihu says he will speak for God and argue that God is just. He claims God is mighty and does not despise anyone, and that God does not keep the wicked alive but gives justice to the poor.

God does not take his eyes off the righteous, and he sets them on thrones with kings. If they are bound in chains of suffering, he shows them their wrongs and calls them to turn from evil. If they obey and serve him, they will live out their days in prosperity and pleasure.

Elihu, speaking to Job, says that those who refuse to listen will die violently or without understanding, and that the hypocritical in heart store up anger and do not cry out to God when he binds them. He says God rescues the poor in their suffering and opens their ears through hardship. He adds that God would have brought Job out of distress into a wide, prosperous place.

Elihu warns Job that his suffering is a judgment he has brought on himself by siding with the wicked. Wealth cannot buy his way out, so he should not long for the night of death or choose wrongdoing over affliction. God is great in power and no one teaches like him.

Elihu, speaking in Job, says no one can tell God what to do or accuse him of wrong. He asks people to honor God's works, which everyone can see from far off. He points to rain forming from water drops and clouds, and asks whether anyone can understand how clouds spread or how the thunder sounds.

God spreads his light over the clouds and the sea. He uses the rain-bearing clouds to judge peoples and give food in plenty. He covers the light with cloud, and the thunder and the storm announce his coming, even to the animals.

The speaker is shaken as he listens to thunder, which he sees as God's voice. The thunder rolls across the whole sky and reaches the ends of the earth, and no one can hold it back. God does great things here that people cannot understand.

God speaks of his power over the weather: he tells the snow and the rain where to fall, and sends cold winds and frost. Living things retreat to shelter, and the clouds are made to pour out or scatter, so that people see his work.

The speaker says that God directs the weather and the clouds to carry out his purposes on earth. These purposes may be punishment, blessing for the land, or mercy. He calls Job to stop and consider God's wonderful works, asking whether Job knows how God arranged the clouds and light.

The speaker, Elihu in the Book of Job, asks Job whether he can help spread out the sky or explain God's works. He says humans cannot speak properly before God, since they cannot see God's light clearly. He ends by saying that God comes in fair weather from the north and is awesome in majesty.

The Almighty cannot be fully understood by people. He is great in power, judgment and justice, and he does not oppress. Therefore people fear him, and he does not favor anyone who thinks himself wise.

In a storm wind, God speaks to Job and challenges him. He asks who is this that speaks without understanding, and where Job was when God set the earth's foundations and measured it. Job is asked to answer, since he cannot.

In this part of Job, God speaks out of a storm and asks Job whether he was present at the creation of the world. God describes shaping the sea, the clouds and the darkness, setting limits for the waves, and ordering the morning to rise on time.

The speaker asks Job a series of questions he cannot answer. Could he take hold of the ends of the earth, or shake the wicked out of it? Has he entered the sea's springs, seen the gates of death, or measured the earth's breadth? The point is that Job lacks the knowledge and power that only God has.

God asks Job a series of questions he cannot answer. Can Job find where light lives and where darkness dwells, or enter the stores of snow and hail that God keeps for times of trouble and war? The point is that Job has no knowledge or control over these hidden things.

The speaker asks Job a series of questions about nature that no human could answer. He asks who divides the light, sends rain on empty wilderness where no one lives, and who gave birth to the dew, ice and frost. The point is that these works belong to a power beyond human reach.

The speaker asks a series of questions that only a power over nature could answer: whether a person can bind the stars, guide the constellations, command the clouds or send lightning. The point is that the reader cannot do these things, so the questions show the limits of human power.

The speaker asks a series of questions that only God could answer. Who gives wisdom to the heart, controls the rain clouds, feeds the lions, and provides food for young ravens? The implied answer is that God does these things.

The speaker asks Job whether he knows when wild goats and deer give birth, and whether he can count the months of their pregnancy. He then describes the young animals growing up in the open and leaving their mothers. The passage ends by asking who has set the wild donkey free.

The passage describes the wild ass, and in the King James translation the "unicorn," as a creature that lives free in the wilderness and mountains, far from cities and human work. God asks Job whether this untamed animal will serve him, be tied to a plough, or be trusted to do his labour.

The passage describes the ostrich, which lays its eggs in the ground and leaves them. It forgets they may be crushed or broken, and is harsh toward its young, so its effort seems wasted. The reason given is that God has denied it wisdom and understanding.

The passage describes a warhorse, speaking as if God is asking Job whether he gave the horse its strength and fearlessness. The horse charges eagerly into battle, mocks fear, does not turn back from the sword, and remains calm while arrows and spears clash around it.

The passage describes a war horse, which charges eagerly toward battle and seems to scorn the sound of the trumpet. It then describes a hawk and an eagle, asking whether human wisdom or command guides their flight. These birds nest high on rocks and spot prey from far away.
The verse is about an eagle. Its young feed on blood, and the bird is found wherever there are dead bodies.

God asks Job whether someone who argues with the Almighty can teach him, and whoever blames God should answer. Job replies that he is worthless, puts his hand over his mouth, and says he will not speak again. God then speaks from the whirlwind and tells Job to prepare himself to answer questions.
God speaks to Job, challenging his right to judge God's justice. He asks whether Job has power like God's, and then tells him to display majesty and wrath and bring down the proud and the wicked.

God speaks to Job, saying that Job's own strength could not save him unless he admitted it. He then describes behemoth, a huge creature he made alongside Job, as strong, powerful in body and bones, and "the chief of the ways of God," able to be overcome only by its maker.

The speaker describes Behemoth, a huge creature, resting among reeds and willows by the water. It drinks a whole river without hurry, feels sure it could drink the Jordan, and is not caught even when a snare is set for it.

The passage asks a series of rhetorical questions about Leviathan, a huge sea creature. It asks whether a person could catch it with a hook, tame it, make it a servant or a pet, or sell its flesh. The implied answer is no, which shows that humans cannot control such a creature.

The speaker asks whether anyone can capture the sea creature Leviathan with hooks or spears, and says that anyone who tries will be defeated just by seeing it. No one is brave enough to rouse it, so no one can stand against the speaker, who claims everything under heaven as his own. He will not hide the creature's strength or its fine form.

This part of Job describes a huge sea creature, often called Leviathan. It describes its armour-like scales, packed so tightly that no air can pass between them, and its fiery breath and eyes. The creature is shown as too fierce for anyone to approach or control.

Job 41 describes Leviathan, a huge sea creature, as almost unstoppable. Smoke and fire come from its nose and mouth, its flesh is solid and cannot be moved, and its heart is as hard as stone. When it rises up, even the mighty are terrified and withdraw in fear.

The passage describes Leviathan, a huge sea creature, as nearly unbeatable. Swords, spears, arrows, slingstones and darts cannot harm it, and it treats iron and brass as straw and rotten wood. It stirs the deep waters into a boiling pot and leaves a shining trail behind it.
On earth there is nothing equal to this creature, which is made without fear. It looks down on all that is high and rules over all the proud creatures.

Job replies to God that he now knows God can do anything and that no plan can be hidden from him. He admits he spoke of things he did not understand. Having now seen God directly, not just heard of him, Job rejects himself and repents in dust and ashes.
God tells Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, that he is angry with him and the other two. They have not spoken what is right about God, as Job has.

God tells Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, Job's three friends, to offer a burnt offering and have Job pray for them. God says he will accept Job's prayer, because the friends did not speak rightly about him as Job did. The friends obey, and God accepts Job.

After Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes and gives him twice what he had before. His relatives and former acquaintances come to his house, eat with him, grieve with him over the troubles the LORD had brought on him, and comfort him. Each gives him money and a gold earring.

After Job's trials, the LORD gave him back more than he had before: sheep, camels, oxen, donkeys, seven sons and three daughters. The daughters are named, are called the most beautiful women in the land, and receive an inheritance along with their brothers.

Job lived another 140 years after his trials ended. He saw his children and their children, four generations in all. Then he died, old and full of days, a phrase meaning he had lived a long, full life.

Those who avoid the advice, company and seat of the ungodly are called blessed, because they delight in God's law and study it constantly. They are compared to a healthy tree by a river that bears fruit and does not wither, while the ungodly are like chaff blown away by the wind.
The wicked will not stand firm when judged, and sinners will not belong among the righteous. God watches over the path of the righteous, but the path of the wicked will come to ruin.

Kings and rulers of the nations plot together against the LORD and his chosen king, wanting to throw off their restraints. The LORD mocks them from heaven, then answers them in anger. He declares that he has set his own king on Zion, his holy hill.

The speaker says that the LORD has declared a king to be his son. The LORD promises this king power over the nations and the whole earth, to crush rebels. The passage then warns the kings and judges of the earth to be wise, and to serve the LORD with fear and trembling.

Readers are told to pay homage to a king called "the Son" so that he will not become angry and they will not be destroyed on their path, since his anger can flare up quickly. Those who put their trust in him are called blessed, or fortunate.

The speaker says many enemies rise against him and claim that God will not save him. He trusts that the LORD protects him, answers his prayer, and keeps him safe through the night, so he is not afraid of any number of enemies.

The speaker calls on the LORD to rise up and save him from his enemies. He says God has already struck down those enemies and broken the teeth of the wicked. He ends by saying that salvation belongs to the LORD and that God's blessing rests on his people.

The speaker prays to God for help, having been relieved from trouble before. He challenges people who chase empty things and lies, and says God sets apart the godly and will hear him. He urges awe, avoiding sin, and quiet reflection.

Trust in the LORD and offer right sacrifices, the speaker says. Many people ask who will show them any good, but the speaker asks God to show his favor. He says God has given him more joy than people have from full harvests of grain and wine, and that he can rest and sleep safely because God alone keeps him secure.

The speaker asks the LORD to hear his prayer, and says he will pray to him every morning. He states that God takes no pleasure in wickedness, that evil cannot stay in God's presence, and that God will destroy liars, the bloody, and the deceitful.

The speaker says he will enter God's house because of God's great kindness, and worship with reverence. He asks God to guide him straight because of his enemies. He describes those enemies as liars whose words are deceitful and whose inner nature is evil.

The speaker asks God to destroy the enemies, who have rebelled against him, and let them fall through their own plans. Those who trust in God are told to rejoice, because God defends them and blesses the righteous like a shield.

The speaker begs the LORD not to punish him in anger, and asks for mercy and healing because he is weak, in deep distress, and near death. He asks how long the trouble will last, and pleads to be saved. He argues that the dead cannot praise God, and he is worn out with weeping through the night.

The speaker is worn down by grief and by enemies. He tells evildoers to leave him, because the LORD has heard his weeping and prayer. He asks that his enemies be shamed and confused, turned back and humiliated suddenly.

The speaker prays to the LORD for rescue from enemies who are hunting him like a lion. He then calls on God to witness that he has done no wrong, saying that if he has repaid peace with evil, his enemies may crush his life and dishonor him.

The speaker calls on God to rise up against his enemies and judge the wicked. He asks to be judged by his own righteousness and integrity, and ends by trusting that God, who tests hearts and inner thoughts ("reins" means the kidneys, seen as the seat of feeling), will make the just secure.

God protects those who are upright in heart and judges the righteous, while he is angry with the wicked every day. If the wicked do not turn back, God will sharpen his sword and bend his bow. The wicked man who plans harm and lies ends up falling into the pit he dug himself.
The wicked man's harm will fall back on his own head, and his violence will land on himself. The speaker responds by promising to praise the LORD for His justice and to sing to His name.

The speaker praises the LORD's name, which is great across the whole earth and whose glory is above the heavens. Looking at the sky, the moon and stars, he asks why God pays attention to humans at all, a small and weak creature.

God has made humans only a little lower than the angels, crowned them with glory and honour, and given them rule over all living creatures on land, in the air, and in the sea. The speaker then praises God's name across the whole earth.

The speaker promises to praise God with a whole heart and to tell of his wonderful deeds. He says that God has defended his right and cause, has judged justly from his throne, and has overthrown his enemies and the wicked so that their names are erased forever.

The enemy's ruins have come to an endless end, and the cities he destroyed are forgotten. The LORD, however, lasts forever and sits on his throne to judge the world fairly. He is a refuge for the oppressed, and he does not abandon those who seek him.

The writer calls people to sing praise to the LORD, who dwells in Zion (Jerusalem). God remembers those who shed blood and does not forget the cry of the humble. The writer asks for mercy from enemies, trusts that God lifts him from death, and promises to praise God publicly and rejoice in his rescue.

The nations and wicked people fall into the traps they set for others, so their own actions bring them down. God shows his justice in this, and the needy will not be forgotten forever. The psalm ends by calling on the LORD to rise up and judge the nations.
The psalmist asks the LORD to frighten the nations, so that they will learn that they are only human. The word "Selah" is a musical or liturgical marker whose exact meaning is unclear.

The psalmist asks God why he seems distant in times of trouble, while the proud wicked man hunts down the poor. He praises his own desires and greedy people, yet he does not seek God and has no room for God in his thinking. The psalmist asks that the wicked be caught in the traps they have planned.

The speaker describes a wicked man who believes he will never be shaken or face trouble. He speaks lies and violence, hides in villages, and secretly traps and kills the poor and innocent, as a lion waits in its den to catch its prey.

The passage describes a wicked man who crouches and pretends humility so that the poor fall into his hands. He tells himself that God has forgotten and will never look. The speaker then calls on God to act, to remember the humble, and to punish such cruelty, trusting that God helps the poor and the fatherless.

The psalmist asks God to break the power of the wicked and remove their evil completely. He declares that the LORD rules forever and that the nations have disappeared from his land. He trusts that God hears the humble and will defend the fatherless and the oppressed, so that oppression ends.

The speaker says they trust in the LORD, and rejects advice to flee like a bird to the mountains. Wicked people are preparing to shoot the upright in secret, and the speaker says the LORD sees all and tests the righteous. The LORD hates the wicked and those who love violence.
God will send snares, fire, brimstone and a terrible storm on the wicked, and this is their lot. The righteous Lord loves justice, and he looks favorably on those who are upright.

The speaker cries out for help because faithful people seem to be disappearing. Liars speak empty words with flattering lips and a double heart. The speaker says the LORD will cut off these flattering lips and proud tongues, which boast that their words are their own power and that no one rules over them.

God says he will rise up to protect the poor and needy from those who oppress them. He calls his own words pure, like silver refined seven times, and says he will keep them safe forever. Meanwhile the wicked spread everywhere, and the vilest people are raised to high positions.

The speaker feels abandoned by God and asks how long this will last while enemies gain the upper hand. He asks God to look and answer, so that he does not die and his enemies do not claim victory. Yet he says he trusts in God's mercy and expects to rejoice in being saved.
The speaker vows to sing praise to the LORD (God) because God has been generous and good to them. "Dealt bountifully" means treated them with great kindness.

The fool says in his heart that there is no God. The passage claims that people have become corrupt and do no good. It says the LORD looks down from heaven to see whether anyone understands and seeks God, and finds that none do. It asks whether the evildoers who devour God's people have no knowledge, since they do not call on the LORD.

There, the wicked are seized with great fear, because God is with the righteous. The poor, whose refuge is the LORD, are shamed by the wicked's plans. The psalm then hopes that salvation will come from Zion and that Israel will rejoice when the LORD restores his exiled people.

The psalm asks who may live in God's tent and dwell on his holy hill, and answers with a list of qualities. The person walks honestly, speaks truth from the heart, does not slander or harm a neighbour, and despises wicked people while honouring those who fear the Lord. He also keeps his word even when it costs him.

Whoever does not lend money at interest, and does not accept a bribe against the innocent, will never be shaken. "Usury" here means lending money at interest, and "taketh reward against the innocent" means taking a payment to harm someone who has done no wrong.

The speaker asks God for protection and says the LORD alone is their Lord and their good. They say their goodness does not reach to God, but belongs to the holy people on earth whom they delight in. They refuse to take part in the worship of other gods, and say the LORD is their portion and their share of life.

The speaker describes a happy, secure life lived close to God, who guides him and keeps him steady. He trusts that God will not abandon him to death or let his body decay, and so he rejoices and rests in hope.
The speaker trusts that God will show him the way to life. In God's presence there is complete joy, and at God's right hand there are pleasures that last forever.

The speaker asks God to hear and judge a just case, since the prayer comes from honest lips. He says God has tested his heart and found nothing wrong, so he has kept his mouth and steps away from wicked paths. He asks God to keep his steps steady.

The speaker calls on God, asking to be heard and kept safe. He asks God to protect him like the pupil of an eye and to hide him under God's wings. He describes his enemies as proud, wealthy, and surrounding him.

The speaker says enemies have surrounded him and wait to attack like a lion hunting its prey. He asks the LORD to stop them and save his life from these wicked men. He also says these men prosper in this life, have plenty of goods, and leave wealth to their children.
The speaker says that he will see God's face in a righteous way. When he wakes up, he will be fully content with God's likeness.

The speaker declares love and trust in the LORD, calling him his strength, rock, fortress and deliverer. He says that calling on God will save him from enemies. He then describes being surrounded by death, floods of wicked men and the snares of death, which left him afraid.

A person in trouble calls out to God, and God hears from his temple. In answer, God comes down in a storm: the earth shakes, smoke and fire come from him, darkness lies under his feet, and he rides on a winged creature (a cherub) through the wind.
God is shown hidden in darkness, surrounded by dark waters and clouds, and he appears in storm. Thunder, hail, fire and lightning come from him, and he scatters his enemies with them.

The speaker describes God's power, shown when the waters and the foundations of the world are revealed at God's rebuke. God then reaches down, pulls the speaker out of deep waters, and rescues him from strong enemies who were too powerful for him in his time of trouble. God brings him into a wide, safe place because God takes pleasure in him.
The speaker says the LORD has rewarded him because of his own righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. He claims he has kept God's ways and laws, stayed upright, and avoided wrongdoing.

God responds to people in kind: he is merciful to the merciful, upright to the upright, pure to the pure, and crooked toward the crooked. He saves the humble and humbles the proud. The speaker says God gives him light in darkness and strength to overcome enemies.

The speaker praises God as perfect and trustworthy, a shield for all who rely on him, and the only true God and rock of safety. He says God gives him strength, sure footing, skill in battle, protection, and honour.

The speaker says that God made his steps firm so he would not fall. With God's help he chased his enemies, defeated them, and put them under his feet. He credits God with giving him the strength for battle and the victory over those who rose against him.

The speaker says his enemies cried out for help and got none, not even from the LORD. He describes scattering them like dust and dirt. He credits God with making him ruler over other nations, who will obey him once they hear of him.

The speaker praises the LORD, the living God, as his rock and saviour. He says God gives him victory over his enemies, and he promises to thank God among the nations. The psalm closes by saying God grants great deliverance to his king, David, and his descendants forever.

The heavens and the sky show that God is great and that he made them. Day and night pass on this message to everyone, with no need for spoken words. The sun is pictured as a bridegroom leaving his room, and as a strong man happy to run a race.

The psalm first describes the sun crossing the whole sky, with nothing hidden from its heat. It then praises the LORD's law, testimony, statutes, commandments and judgments, saying they are perfect, sure, right, pure and true, and that they bring wisdom, joy and light.

The writer says the laws of God are more precious than gold and sweeter than honey. Keeping them brings great reward and warns the servant of wrong. The writer asks God to cleanse hidden faults, keep him from deliberate sins, and so be blameless of serious wrongdoing.

The speaker asks God to find the words spoken by the speaker's mouth and the thoughts of the speaker's heart pleasing. God is called the speaker's strength and redeemer, meaning the one who saves and frees them.

The passage is a prayer or blessing for a person in trouble, asking the LORD to answer, protect and strengthen them from the holy place in Zion. It hopes their offerings will be remembered and their wishes granted, and says the speakers will rejoice in the person's victory and raise banners in God's name.

The speaker is confident that the LORD will save his anointed king from heaven. Others rely on chariots and horses for strength, but the speaker trusts in the name of the LORD, and asks that the king be heard when he calls.

The king rejoices in the LORD's strength and salvation. The psalm says God has granted the king what he wished for, given him long life, placed a golden crown on his head, and bestowed honour and majesty upon him.

The psalm says that God has blessed the king and filled him with joy. Because the king trusts in the LORD, he will stand firm. God will find all the king's enemies and destroy them with fire, as a furnace burns.

The speaker asks God to wipe out the enemies and their descendants, because they plotted evil against him with schemes they cannot carry out. God is asked to drive them back with arrows, and the speaker vows to praise God's power once this happens.

The speaker feels abandoned by God and asks why help is so far away, even though he prays day and night. He recalls that earlier generations trusted God and were saved, yet he describes himself as a worm, scorned by others.

People who see the speaker mock him, saying he trusted God and should now be rescued, since God delighted in him. The speaker answers by recalling that God has cared for him since birth, and pleads for God to stay near while trouble and enemies surround him.

The speaker describes being surrounded by enemies who threaten and mock him, like lions and dogs. He feels weak, drained and close to death, as if his strength has gone and his body is falling apart. He says his enemies pierce his hands and feet and stare at him.

A speaker in danger describes enemies dividing his clothes and casting lots for them, then pleads with the LORD not to stay far away. He vows to praise God publicly and calls on all who fear the LORD, the descendants of Jacob and Israel, to praise and honor him too.

God did not despise or ignore the suffering of the afflicted person, and he listened when that person cried out. The speaker promises to give praise and fulfil vows in the assembly. The humble will eat and be satisfied, and all peoples of the earth will turn to the LORD and worship him.

The LORD rules over the nations. The rich and powerful of the earth will eat and worship him, and even those who have died, and no one can keep himself alive. Future generations will serve him and tell of his righteousness to people not yet born.

The speaker trusts the LORD as a shepherd who provides rest, food, guidance and safety. Even in the darkest valley and in the presence of enemies, the speaker says he will not fear, because the LORD is with him and cares for him.
The speaker is confident that God's goodness and kindness will go with them every day of their life. They also say they will live in the LORD's house forever, meaning in God's presence.

The earth and everything in it belong to the LORD, who set it on the seas and rivers. The psalm then asks who may come into his holy place, and answers: the person with clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lie or swear falsely. That person receives blessing and righteousness from God.

The people who seek God, the descendants of Jacob, are described here. Gates and doors are told to lift up so that the King of glory may enter. The question "Who is this King?" is answered: the LORD, strong and mighty in battle, the LORD of hosts.

The speaker turns to God in trust, asking not to be shamed or defeated by enemies. He asks God to teach him God's ways and lead him in truth, because God is his source of rescue. He also asks God to remember his past mercy and steadfast love.

The speaker asks God not to remember the sins of his youth, and to forgive him for the sake of God's own mercy and name. He trusts that God is good and upright, that he teaches sinners and the humble his way, and that his paths are mercy and truth for those who keep his covenant.

The psalmist says that the LORD teaches and blesses those who fear him, giving them peace and a lasting line of descendants. He then turns to God for help, asking for mercy and rescue from his troubles and from a trap.
