The speaker asks God to see his suffering and forgive his sins, and to protect him from many enemies who hate him. He says he trusts God and waits for him, so he asks not to be put to shame. The final line asks God to rescue Israel from all its troubles.

The speaker asks the LORD to judge and test him, because he claims to have lived honestly and trusted God. He says he avoids liars and wicked people, and he promises to worship at God's altar with clean hands.

The speaker vows to give thanks and tell of God's works, and says he loves the place of worship. He asks not to be lumped together with sinners and violent, bribe-taking men. He states that he will live with integrity, asks for rescue and mercy, and promises to bless the LORD in the assembly.

The speaker says that the LORD is his light, his rescue and his strength, so he has no reason to fear. Even when enemies attack him, and even if an army camps against him or war breaks out, he stays confident because of God.

The speaker asks for one thing: to live in the LORD's house all his life, to see the LORD's beauty and to seek guidance there. He trusts that in trouble God will hide him and set him high on a rock. Then he will lift his head above his enemies and offer joyful sacrifices and songs of praise.

The speaker calls on the LORD to hear, show mercy, and answer him. He says his heart has answered God's call to seek his face, and he asks not to be turned away or abandoned. Even if his parents forsake him, he trusts the LORD will take him up. He asks to be taught God's way, because of his enemies.

The speaker asks not to be handed over to enemies, who are false accusers and violent people. He says he would have lost heart without his trust that he will see the LORD's goodness while still alive. He ends by urging waiting on the LORD, with courage, believing that God will strengthen his heart.

The speaker calls on the LORD for help and begs him not to stay silent, fearing he will end up like those who die and go down to the grave. He asks not to be dragged away with evildoers, who speak friendly words to their neighbours while planning harm in their hearts.

The speaker asks that the wicked be repaid for their deeds, because they ignore what the LORD has done, so he will tear them down rather than build them up. The speaker then praises the LORD, who heard his prayer, is his strength and shield, and has brought him help, so his heart rejoices.
The LORD is the source of strength for his people and for his chosen king, his "anointed." The speaker then asks God to save his people, bless them, care for them, and raise them up forever.

The psalm calls on the mighty to give the LORD glory and strength and to worship him in holy splendor. It then describes the LORD's voice over the waters and in thunder, as so powerful that it breaks cedar trees and makes the mountains of Lebanon and Sirion leap like young animals.

The psalm describes God's voice as powerful over nature: it splits fire, shakes the wilderness, and strips the forests bare. God sits enthroned over the floodwaters as king forever, and he gives strength and peace to his people.

The speaker thanks the LORD for rescuing him from enemies, illness and near-death. He calls on others to sing praise as well. He says God's anger lasts only briefly, while his favour gives life, and sorrow may last a night but joy comes with morning.

The speaker once felt secure in good times and believed nothing could shake him. When God hid his face, he was thrown into distress, so he cried out for help. He asks what good his death would do, since the dead cannot praise God. God then turned his mourning into joy.
The speaker says that they will praise God so that their inner self, here called "glory," will sing and never stay silent. They promise to give thanks to God forever.

The speaker trusts the LORD and asks not to be put to shame. He begs for quick rescue from enemies who have set a hidden net for him. He calls God his rock, fortress and strength, and gives his spirit into God's hands, trusting that God has already redeemed him.

The speaker says he rejects those who trust in worthless idols and puts his trust in the LORD. He describes being in deep distress, with grief wearing down his body and spirit, and he asks God for mercy. He also says God has rescued him from enemies and given him room to move freely.

The speaker is shunned and feared by neighbours, friends and enemies alike, and feels forgotten, like a dead man or a broken pot. Enemies plot to kill him, yet he trusts God and asks to be saved from them.

The speaker asks God to show favor and save him, so he will not be shamed for calling on God. He asks that the wicked, who speak proud lies against the righteous, be silenced and shamed. He ends by praising God's great goodness, which is kept for those who fear and trust him.

The speaker says God hides those who trust him from human pride and from harmful slander. He thanks God for kindness shown in a time of danger, when the speaker felt cut off but was still heard. The closing call is to love the Lord, because he protects the faithful and repays the proud doer.
Those who put their hope in the LORD are told to be brave, and the verse promises that he will make their hearts strong. "LORD" is the traditional English rendering of God's name in the Hebrew Bible.

Happy is the person whose wrongdoing is forgiven and whose sin is covered. The speaker says that while he stayed silent about his sin, he felt worn down and drained. When he admitted his sin to God, God forgave him.

The speaker says that every faithful person should pray to God while he can be found, and that great floods of trouble will not reach such a person. God is described as a hiding place who protects, surrounds with songs of rescue, and guides with his eye.

Do not be like a horse or mule, which have no understanding and must be controlled with bit and bridle. The wicked will suffer many sorrows, but whoever trusts in the LORD will be surrounded by mercy. So the righteous should rejoice in the LORD.

The righteous are called to rejoice and praise the LORD with music and song. The psalm gives as reasons that God's word is right, his works are true, he loves justice, and the heavens were made by his word and the breath of his mouth.
God holds the seas and deep waters as if stored in containers, and his word alone brings things into being and makes them last. Human plans against him fail, but his purpose lasts forever.

Happy is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people he has chosen. The LORD watches all people from heaven and knows all they do. No king is saved by his large army, and no strong man by his strength. A horse cannot bring safety.

God watches over those who fear him and hope in his mercy, saving them from death and keeping them alive in famine. The speakers say they wait for the LORD as their help and shield, trust his holy name, and ask for his mercy in the same measure as their hope.

The speaker promises to praise the LORD at all times and invites others to join him. He says he prayed, was heard, and was freed from his fears. Those who looked to God were lit up with joy and not put to shame, and a poor man who cried out was saved from his troubles.

The passage says that God protects and provides for those who fear and trust him. It claims they lack no good thing, even when strong animals like young lions go hungry. It then invites listeners to learn the fear of the LORD and asks who wants a long, good life.

The verses urge avoiding evil speech and wrongdoing, and seeking peace. They promise that God watches over and hears the righteous, rescuing them from trouble. God is near to those who are crushed in heart or humbled in spirit.

The righteous suffer many troubles, but the LORD rescues them from all of them, and keeps their bones unbroken. Evil brings death to the wicked, and those who hate the righteous are left desolate. The LORD redeems the souls of his servants, and none who trust in him will be left desolate.

The speaker asks the LORD to argue his case and fight against those who attack him, using weapons as images of help. He asks that his enemies be shamed, turned back, and scattered like chaff before the wind, with an angel of the LORD driving them away.

The speaker asks God to bring ruin on enemies who secretly set a trap for him without cause. He wants their own net to catch them and their path to become dark and slippery. The speaker then says he will rejoice in the LORD's rescue.

The speaker praises the LORD, who saves the poor from those stronger than them. False witnesses have accused him of things he did not do, and they repaid his kindness with harm. When those men were sick, he mourned with sackcloth and fasting, but his prayers seemed to bring him no reward.

The speaker says he acted kindly toward people who were like friends or family, even mourning for them as for a mother. When he was in trouble, they rejoiced, gathered against him, and mocked him at feasts. He prays to the Lord to ask how long he must endure this and to rescue his life from them.

The speaker promises to thank and praise God in public. He asks God not to let his enemies gloat over him, since they attack him without cause and plot against peaceful people. He says they mock him openly and asks God to see this and not stay silent.

The speaker calls on God to wake up and judge his case, asking to be vindicated by God's justice. He asks that his enemies, who are glad at his troubles and boast that they have defeated him, be put to shame and disgrace.

Those who side with the speaker's just cause are invited to shout for joy and keep saying that the LORD is great, because he delights in the well-being of his servant. The speaker vows to speak of God's righteousness and praise all day long.

The wicked person, in the speaker's inner thought, has no fear of God. He flatters himself until his sin is exposed, speaks deceit, plans harm even in bed, and does not turn from evil. The closing lines contrast this with the LORD's mercy and faithfulness, which reach to the heavens and the clouds.

God's righteousness is as firm as the great mountains and his judgments as deep as the ocean. He keeps both people and animals alive, and people find safety under his protection. He gives them abundant provision and life, and they see clearly because of him.

The writer asks God to keep showing love and justice to those who know him and are honest in heart. He asks not to be overrun by proud people or pushed out by the wicked. He states that evildoers have already fallen and cannot get back up.
Do not worry about wrongdoers or envy them, because they will soon wither like grass. Trust in the LORD and do good, and he will reward you. Your righteousness will be made clear as light.

Trust in the LORD and wait patiently, without being upset by people who succeed through wicked schemes. Stop anger and wrath, because evildoers will be cut off, while those who wait on the LORD will inherit the earth.

The humble will inherit the land and enjoy peace. The wicked plot against the righteous and poor, drawing swords and bows to kill them. But God will laugh at them, and their own weapons will turn against them and be broken.

The righteous, even with little, are better off than the wicked with great wealth. The wicked will be broken and destroyed, like fat burned into smoke. The LORD supports the righteous, who will keep their inheritance and be fed in times of hunger.

The wicked borrow and never repay, while the righteous are generous. The passage promises that those blessed by the LORD will inherit the earth, and that a good person, even if he stumbles, will not be utterly cast down because the LORD holds him up. The speaker says he has never seen a righteous person abandoned or left begging for bread.

The righteous person is generous, avoids evil and does good, and is promised that his descendants will be blessed and that he will keep the land. The wicked, by contrast, will be cut off, and they plot to kill the righteous.

The Lord will not leave the righteous person to his enemies or let him be condemned. The writer says he has seen the wicked seem powerful, but they vanished and could not be found. So the upright person, who waits on the Lord, will end in peace.
Wrongdoers will be destroyed and the wicked cut off. The righteous, however, are saved by the LORD, who is their strength in trouble and rescues them from the wicked because they trust in him.

The speaker begs God not to punish him in anger. He feels crushed by God's arrows and hand, and he says his sins and foolishness have weighed him down. His body is sick, his bones have no rest, and he goes about mourning all day.

The speaker describes severe illness in body and heart, and says that God knows all his longing and groaning. He feels weak, his eyes have lost their light, and even his loved ones and relatives keep their distance from his sickness.

The speaker is attacked by enemies who set traps and plot harm. He chooses not to answer them, like a deaf or silent man, and trusts that the LORD will hear him. He asks for help so that his enemies do not gloat when he stumbles.

The speaker is close to collapse and constantly aware of his suffering. He admits his sin and feels sorry for it. Meanwhile his enemies are strong and growing in number, paying evil back for his good. He asks God not to abandon him and to hurry to help.

The speaker decided to guard his speech so he would not sin with his tongue, and kept silent even about good things while the wicked were near. The silence grew painful, and his inner heat finally broke out in words. He then asks the LORD to show him how short his life is and how frail he is.

Human life is very short, and even a person at his best is, in the writer's words, "vanity," meaning empty and without lasting worth. People rush about and gather wealth without knowing who will get it. So the writer puts his hope in God, asks to be forgiven, and stays silent, accepting that God has done this.

The speaker asks God to stop punishing him, because the punishment is destroying him. He says that when God corrects people for wrongdoing, their beauty fades like a moth-eaten cloth, and that every person is empty and short-lived. He pleads to be spared so he can regain strength before he dies.

The speaker says he waited patiently, and the LORD heard his cry and pulled him out of a deep, muddy pit. He set him on firm rock and gave him a new song of praise. Others will see this and trust the LORD, and the speaker calls blessed the one who trusts the LORD and does not side with the proud or with liars.

The speaker praises God's countless works and thoughts toward people, then says that God does not want sacrifices and burnt offerings. Instead, the speaker says they come ready to do God's will, which is written in the book and kept in the heart.

The speaker says he has openly proclaimed God's righteousness, faithfulness and salvation to the large assembly, keeping none of it hidden. He then asks the LORD not to hold back His mercy, and to let His steadfast love and truth keep him safe.

The speaker feels overwhelmed by countless troubles and by his own sins, so that he cannot even lift his eyes and his courage fails. He asks the LORD to rescue him quickly, and he prays that those who mock him and seek his harm will be shamed and brought to ruin.

Those who seek God are asked to rejoice in him, and those who love his salvation are to keep saying, "The LORD be magnified." The speaker admits he is poor and needy, but trusts that the LORD thinks of him, is his help and deliverer, and asks God not to delay.

Blessed is the person who cares for the poor, the passage says, because the LORD will protect and sustain that person in trouble and sickness. The speaker then prays for healing for his own sins, while his enemies hope he will die.

The speaker is sick, and his enemies are gossiping about him. They say his illness will finish him, and even a close friend who shared his food has turned against him. He asks the LORD to be merciful, heal him, and let him repay them.

The speaker takes it as a sign of God's favour that his enemy does not gloat over him. God keeps him whole and in his presence forever, so the speaker closes by blessing the LORD, God of Israel, for all time.

The speaker longs for God as a deer pants for water. He weeps day and night while others mock him, asking where his God is. Remembering past festival trips to the temple with joyful crowds makes his longing and grief sharper.

The speaker asks his own soul why it is so low and troubled, and tells it to put its hope in God, because he will yet praise God for help. He then says he remembers God from far off, across the Jordan region, and feels overwhelmed, as if by deep waters and huge waves.

The speaker trusts that the LORD will show his steady love by day and that his song and prayer to God will continue at night. Yet he asks God why he has been forgotten, and why he must mourn under an enemy's attack. Enemies mock him daily, asking where his God is.
The speaker asks his own soul why it is sunk in sadness and troubled inside him. He tells it to put its hope in God, because he will yet praise God, who is his help and his God.

The speaker asks God to judge his case against an unjust, deceitful enemy and to rescue him. He wonders why God seems to have rejected him and why he must mourn. He hopes God will send light and truth to lead him back to the holy hill and the altar, where he will praise God with the harp.
The speaker asks his own soul why it is down and troubled. He tells it to put its hope in God, because he will yet praise God, who is his help and his God.

The speaker says that the people have heard from their ancestors how God gave them the land. God drove out other nations and planted Israel there, and the people did not win it by their own strength. The speaker asks God, as king, to bring deliverance to Jacob (Israel).

The psalmist says that victory over enemies comes through God, not through weapons. He says the people trusted God and were saved, so they praise him. Yet now God has rejected them, so they lose to their enemies and are shamed.

The speaker tells God that he has handed his people over to suffering, like sheep sent to be slaughtered, and scattered them among other nations. God has sold them cheaply, gaining nothing from it. The people are now mocked by their neighbours and are a common saying among the nations, and the speaker is overwhelmed with shame.

The speakers say that enemies mock and curse them, and that disaster has struck them. Yet they insist they have stayed loyal to God and his covenant, never turning from his way or worshipping another god. They even claim that if they had forgotten God, they would have deserved this punishment.

The speakers say they have not turned away from God, since God knows the heart. Yet they are being killed daily, like sheep led to slaughter. They beg God to wake up, stop hiding his face, and rescue them for the sake of his mercy.

The poet says he is composing a poem about a king, speaking as fast as a skilled scribe writes. He praises the king as more beautiful than other men, blessed by God forever, and calls him to ride out in battle for truth, meekness and justice.

The psalm praises a king in strong images. His arrows defeat his enemies and people submit to him. His throne is God's throne and lasts forever. God has anointed him above others because he loves justice and hates evil. His garments smell of fragrant spices, and the palaces he lives in bring him joy.

The verse addresses a bride being brought to a king. It describes her royal companions and wealth, then urges her to leave her own family, since the king desires her beauty and is her lord. Foreign peoples, including the rich of Tyre, will bring her gifts and seek her favour.

The bride is led to the king in embroidered robes, with her attendant maidens following, all with joy. The king's sons will become princes across the land, and his name will be remembered for all generations and praised forever.

God is a safe place and a source of strength in trouble, so the speaker will not be afraid even if the earth shakes and the mountains fall into the sea. A river brings gladness to God's city, which stays firm because God is in it and will help it at dawn.

God speaks and the nations and the earth shake, yet the LORD is said to be a refuge for his people. He is shown ending wars by breaking weapons and burning chariots, and he tells the reader to be still and know that he is God, exalted over all nations.

The LORD of hosts, the God of Jacob, is said to be with the speaker and to be their place of safety. "Selah" is a word of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical marker meant to pause or emphasize the line.

People are called to clap and shout in praise of God, who is described as a great King over all the earth. The psalm says he will subdue the nations, choose the land as an inheritance for Jacob's people, and has gone up with a shout and trumpet sound.

God rules over the nations and sits on his holy throne. The leaders of the peoples gather together as the people of the God of Abraham, because the protectors of the earth belong to God, who is highly exalted.

The psalm praises God as great and says Mount Zion, his holy city, is a place of joy and safety. Kings gather against it, but when they see it they are struck with fear and flee. The last line says God wrecks the ships of Tarshish with an east wind, showing his power over distant enemies.

The psalm says that the people have seen with their own eyes what they had heard about Zion, the city of God, and that God will keep it safe forever. They think about God's love in his temple, and they call on Zion to rejoice and on its people to walk around the city and count its towers.
Look closely at the city's walls and its great buildings, so that they can be described to the next generation. The speaker says this God is theirs forever and will lead them even to death.

The speaker calls on all people, high and low, rich and poor, to listen. He says he will speak wisdom and explain a hidden saying, and he asks why he should fear hard days when wrongdoing surrounds him. He then turns to those who trust in their wealth and boast of their riches.

No one can pay to buy back another person's life from death, because the price of a life is too high. Wise people, fools and senseless people all die and leave their wealth to others, yet they still believe their houses and lands will last forever.

People who are rich and honoured do not last; in death they are like animals that perish. Their descendants still praise their sayings, but they end up in the grave, while the upright rule over them in the morning. The speaker trusts that God will rescue his soul from the grave and receive him.

Do not fear when a man grows rich and his household's wealth rises, because he takes nothing with him at death and his glory does not follow him. Even if others praise him while he lives, he goes to his ancestors and never sees light again. A person who has honour but no understanding is like an animal that dies.

God speaks and calls the whole earth, from east to west, to come before him. He appears from Zion, shining, with fire and storm around him. He summons heaven and earth to judge his people and orders his faithful, who made a covenant with him through sacrifice, to be gathered to him.

God calls on heaven, and on his people Israel, as witnesses that he is the judge. He says he does not rebuke them for their sacrifices and burnt offerings, because he does not need them. Every animal in the forest and on the hills already belongs to him.

God says he needs no sacrifices, since the world and everything in it already belong to him. He asks for thanksgiving and kept vows instead, and he condemns the wicked who recite his laws yet reject his teaching and ignore his words.

God accuses the wicked of stealing, adultery, lying and slandering their own brother. He says he stayed silent so they thought he was like them, but now he will confront them. He warns those who forget God that he will tear them apart with no one to rescue them.
Whoever offers thanks honors God, and God will show his saving help to the person who lives his life in the right way. "Conversation" here means way of life or conduct.

A speaker asks God for mercy and asks to have his wrongs wiped away and washed clean. He admits his wrongdoing is always on his mind, says he has sinned against God alone, and says that God is right to judge him. He adds that he has been sinful since birth.

The speaker asks God to make him inwardly honest and wise, to cleanse him from sin so he is pure, and to restore his joy. He asks God to hide his sins, to create a clean heart and a right spirit in him, and not to send him away or take away God's holy spirit.

The speaker asks God to restore his joy, support him with a willing spirit, and free him from guilt for bloodshed. In return he promises to teach sinners God's ways and praise God aloud. He adds that God does not want sacrifices or burnt offerings, so worship of the heart matters more.

A broken spirit and a contrite heart are what God accepts as sacrifice, and God will not despise them. The speaker then asks God to do good to Zion and rebuild Jerusalem's walls, so that God will again be pleased with the burnt offerings and bullocks offered on the altar.

The speaker confronts a powerful man who boasts of his wickedness, saying his tongue plans harm and deceit and that he prefers lies to truth. The speaker declares that God's goodness lasts forever and that God will destroy and uproot him.

The righteous will see the fall of a man who trusted in his riches and his wickedness instead of God. The speaker contrasts himself with that man: he is like a green olive tree in God's house, trusting in God's mercy forever and praising God for what God has done.

The psalm says that a foolish person claims there is no God, and that people in general have become corrupt and do no good. God looks down from heaven to find anyone who understands and seeks him, but finds none. The workers of evil, it says, devour God's people and do not call on God.

Enemies who were terrified when there was nothing to fear are shown to have been scattered by God, who has put them to shame. The speaker then prays for Israel's salvation to come from Zion and expects that, when God restores his exiled people, Jacob and Israel will rejoice.

A plea for rescue from strangers who want to destroy the speaker. The speaker asks God to save and judge him, trusts that God is his helper, and expects God to punish his enemies. He then promises to offer thanks and praise to God.
The speaker says that God has rescued him from every trouble. He has also seen his enemies receive what he wanted for them, meaning their defeat.

The speaker begs God to listen and not hide from him. He is in distress because enemies and wicked people are oppressing him, slandering and hating him. Overwhelmed by fear and terror, he wishes he had wings like a dove so he could fly away and rest.

The speaker wishes he could flee to the desert, away from a storm of trouble. He asks God to confuse and divide the enemies' speech, because he sees violence and strife in the city. Wickedness, deceit and trickery never leave its streets.

The speaker says an open enemy's insults would have been easier to bear. The real pain comes from a close friend, someone he once shared counsel and worship with, who has turned against him. He ends by asking that death take these betrayers and that he himself will call on God for rescue.

The speaker says he will pray aloud morning, noon and evening, and that God has rescued him in peace from a battle fought against him by many enemies. He asks God to punish these enemies, because they do not change their ways and do not fear God. They have also attacked people who were at peace with God and broken their covenant.

A man speaks smoothly and pleasantly, but he is planning violence and his words are as sharp as swords. The speaker says to hand one's troubles over to the LORD, who will support the righteous and destroy bloody and deceitful men. The speaker ends by saying he will trust in God.

The speaker asks God for mercy because many enemies are daily attacking and plotting against him. He says that when he is afraid, he trusts in God, and he will not fear what humans can do to him. He adds that his enemies twist his words and secretly watch his steps, waiting to harm him.

The speaker asks God to punish wrongdoers, then trusts that God knows his suffering, keeps his tears in record, and will turn his enemies back. Confident in God's protection, he will not fear human harm and promises to give thanks.
The speaker thanks God for saving his life from death, and asks that God also keep his feet from stumbling. The purpose is so he can live and walk before God among the living.

The speaker asks God for mercy and says they trust in him, taking refuge in the shadow of God's wings until their troubles pass. They believe God will send help from heaven, rescuing them from enemies who want to destroy them, and will send his mercy and faithfulness.

The speaker feels surrounded by violent enemies, who are like lions and whose words hurt like weapons. He asks God to be exalted over all the earth, notes that his enemies have set traps and fallen into their own pit, and declares that his heart is steady and that he will sing praise.

The speaker wakes early and calls on his own spirit, the harp and the lyre to wake too, so he can praise the Lord among the peoples and nations. He says God's mercy reaches the heavens and his truth the clouds, and asks that God be exalted above the heavens and his glory fill the earth.

Psalm 58 asks a group of rulers or judges whether they really speak and judge justly. It says they plot wrong in their hearts and act violently, and that wicked people go astray from birth, speaking lies. It compares them to a deaf snake that blocks its ears so it cannot hear skilled charmers.

The speaker asks God to break the teeth of wicked people and to wipe them out completely. He compares them to melting water, a melting snail, a stillborn child that never sees the sun, and thorns swept away by a whirlwind.

The righteous will rejoice when they see the wicked punished, so fiercely that they wash their feet in the blood of the wicked. People will then say that there is a reward for the righteous and that God judges on the earth.

The speaker asks God to rescue him from enemies who are plotting to kill him. He insists he has done nothing wrong to deserve this. He calls on God, the LORD of hosts and God of Israel, to wake up, act against these enemies, and show no mercy to the wicked.

The writer describes enemies who prowl around the city at evening like snarling dogs, boasting that no one can hear them. He then trusts that the LORD will laugh at them and bring them to nothing, and that God will be his protection and let him see them defeated.

The speaker asks God not to kill his enemies outright, so that the people will not forget the lesson. Instead, he asks God to scatter them and bring them low, punishing them for their lies and cursing, so that everyone knows God rules over Israel. He pictures them wandering the city at evening like hungry dogs.

The speaker asks that his enemies wander around hungry and grumble when they are not fed. He then says he will sing of God's power and mercy each morning, because God has been his protection and refuge in his time of trouble.

The speaker tells God that he has rejected and scattered his people and that the land has been shaken and broken. He asks God to restore them, save them with his right hand, and hear his plea. The people have endured hard times, but God has also given a banner to those who fear him, so they can rally to the truth.

God promises victory and claims the tribal lands, including Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, Judah, Moab, Edom and Philistia, as his own. The psalmist then asks who will lead him into the fortified city of Edom, and ends by asking God, who had rejected the people, to go out with their armies again.
Help from other people is useless in trouble, the speaker says. Victory comes through God, who will trample their enemies.

The speaker calls on God from far away, when his heart is overwhelmed, and asks to be led to a rock higher than himself. He trusts God as a shelter and protection, and says God has heard his vows and given him an inheritance. He ends by asking that the king's life be long.

The speaker asks that God's mercy and truth be prepared to protect the king, who is said to remain before God forever. In return, the speaker promises to keep singing praise to God's name and to carry out his vows every day.

The speaker says their trust rests only on God, who is their rock, salvation and defence, so they will not be greatly shaken. They address enemies who plot to bring down a man, warning that they will be destroyed like a leaning wall. They also tell their own soul to wait quietly on God.

The speaker says that God alone is his rock, salvation and refuge, so he will not be shaken. He tells the people to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to him. People of every rank are worthless as a support, and they should not put their trust in oppression, robbery, or growing wealth.
God has spoken once, and the speaker has heard it twice: power belongs to God. Mercy also belongs to the Lord, because he repays each person according to what that person has done.

The speaker longs for God with body and soul, especially while stuck in a dry, waterless land. He remembers seeing God's power and glory in the sanctuary (the temple) and says God's steadfast love is better than life itself. So he will keep praising God and blessing him all his life.

The speaker remembers God at night and rejoices in God's protection, trusting that God holds him up. He says his enemies, who seek his life, will die by the sword and go down to the grave. The king and all who swear by God will praise God, while liars will be silenced.

The speaker asks God to hear his prayer and protect him from enemies. He describes wicked people who plot in secret, sharpening their words like swords and aiming hurtful speech like arrows at an innocent target. They plan their traps openly among themselves, believing no one will see.

God will turn the plotters' own schemes against them. He will strike them suddenly with an arrow, and their own words will bring them down. People who see this will fear and recognize God's work, while the righteous will rejoice and trust in him.

Praise is owed to God in Zion (Jerusalem), and vows made to him will be kept. The psalmist says God hears prayer, so all people will come to him. Although sins overwhelm him, God will cleanse the people's wrongs. Blessed are those God chooses to draw near and live in his temple, where they will be satisfied with its goodness.

God answers his people with awe-inspiring acts done in justice, and he is trusted by people across the whole earth, even those far away on the sea. He holds the mountains firm, calms the roaring seas and the restless crowds, and his signs fill people far away with fear, while morning and evening rejoice.

God is shown caring for the land: he waters it, enriches it with abundant water, and makes the ground soft so crops grow. The harvest year is blessed by his goodness, and even the wild pastures and hills flourish under his care.
The fields and valleys are full of life and growth: the grassland is covered with flocks, and the valleys with grain. The land seems to celebrate, shouting and singing for joy.

All the earth is called to praise God loudly and to honour his name. The psalm says God's works are awe-inspiring, that his power makes enemies submit, and that he once turned the sea into dry land so people could cross on foot.

God rules forever by his power and watches the nations, so proud rebels should not lift themselves up. The people are called to praise him, because he keeps them alive and steady. He has tested them as silver is tested in fire, though he also brought them into a net and laid hardship on them.

The speaker says that people rode over their heads and they went through fire and water, but God brought them out into a place of plenty. In thanks, the speaker promises to bring burnt offerings to God's house, keep the vows made in trouble, and invite all who fear God to hear what God has done.

The speaker says they prayed aloud and praised God. They claim that God would not hear someone who keeps wickedness in their heart, but says God did hear them, and so they bless God for not rejecting their prayer or withholding mercy.

A prayer that God will show mercy and blessing to the people, so that his way and saving help are known among all nations. It asks that all peoples praise God and rejoice, because he will judge fairly and rule the earth. The writer expects the land to produce its harvest and God to bless his people.
God will bless the speaker's people, and as a result people in every part of the earth will fear, or revere, him. The verse expresses a hope that divine blessing will lead all nations to honour God.

God rises up, and his enemies scatter and flee before him, like smoke or melting wax. The righteous are told to rejoice and sing praise to him. God is also described as a father to orphans and a judge for widows, who lives in his holy dwelling.

God gives lonely people a home and frees prisoners, while rebels are left in a dry land. The psalm then recalls God leading his people through the wilderness, when the earth shook at his presence and Sinai trembled. God also sent rain to strengthen his tired inheritance, meaning Israel.

God provides for the poor, and the Lord gives a word that brings a great host of messengers to announce it. Kings and armies flee in haste, and even the women at home share in the plunder. The people, once lying among pots, are promised they will shine like a dove with silver and gold wings.

God chose the hill of Zion as his dwelling place, and the high hills around it are told to stop their rivalry. God's chariots of angels travel with him, as at Sinai. He has taken captives and received gifts, even from rebels, so that God may dwell among people.

God is praised as the one who daily provides for his people and saves them from death. He will punish his enemies, and he will bring his people back from distant places, so that their enemies are destroyed.

The psalm describes a religious procession into the sanctuary, with singers, instrumentalists, and dancing women leading the way, and tribes such as Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun and Naphtali taking part. It calls on the people to bless God and asks God to make strong what he has already done for them.

Kings will bring gifts to God's temple in Jerusalem. The psalm asks God to rebuke hostile nations, which are compared to a herd of bulls and calves, so they bring silver in submission and scatter those who love war. Egypt and Ethiopia will turn to God, and all the kingdoms of the earth are called to sing praise to the Lord.

God, described as riding across the highest heavens, sends out a powerful voice, like thunder. The people are told to give God strength, since his majesty is over Israel and his power is seen in the clouds. God is feared from his holy places and is the source of strength for his people.

The speaker feels overwhelmed, as if sinking in deep water or mud, and is worn out from calling to God for help. Enemies attack him without cause, and he asks God to save him. He admits his foolishness and sins, while saying that God already knows them.

The speaker prays that those who trust in God will not be put to shame because of him. He says he has suffered insults and rejection, even from his own family, because he is devoted to God's house and bears the insults aimed at God. Even his weeping and fasting brought him scorn.

The speaker is mocked and shamed, wearing sackcloth and becoming a figure of gossip and drinking-songs. Even so, he turns to God in prayer, asking to be heard and rescued from his enemies and from drowning in deep waters.

The speaker is in deep distress, sinking as if under floodwaters and about to be swallowed by a pit. He asks the LORD to hear him quickly, not to turn away, and to rescue him from his enemies. He says the LORD already knows his shame and disgrace.

The speaker says insults have broken him, and that he looked in vain for pity and comfort. Enemies gave him bitter gall and vinegar instead of food and drink. He then asks that their own feast become a trap for them, and that they be blinded and left trembling.

The speaker asks God to punish his enemies: to pour out anger on them, leave their homes empty, and remove them from the book of the living. He says they attack him, whom God has already struck, and he asks God to save him, since he is poor and sorrowful.

The speaker says that praising God with song and thanks pleases the LORD more than a sacrifice of an ox or bull. The humble will see this and rejoice, and God hears the poor and does not ignore his prisoners. Heaven, earth and seas are called to praise him, because God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah.
The servants' descendants will inherit the land, and those who love God's name will live in it. "Seed" here means children or offspring, and "dwell therein" means live there.

The speaker asks God to act quickly to rescue him. He prays that those who want to harm him will be shamed and turned back, while those who seek God will rejoice. He ends by describing himself as poor and needy and asking God not to delay.

The speaker places all their trust in the LORD and asks never to be shamed or defeated. They ask to be rescued from wicked and cruel people, calling God their rock, fortress, hope, and trust since youth.

The speaker says that God has supported him since birth and will keep being his source of praise. Even though many see him as a wonder, God is his strong refuge. He asks not to be abandoned in old age or when his strength fails, because enemies are plotting against him.

The speaker says his enemies claim God has abandoned him and that no one will rescue him. He asks God to come quickly, wishes shame and ruin on those who want to harm him, and says he will keep hoping and keep praising God all day.

The speaker trusts in the Lord's strength and will proclaim God's righteousness. He says God has taught him since youth and has shown his wonders so far. Now, in old age, he asks God not to abandon him, so he can declare God's strength to the coming generations. He ends by praising God as incomparable.

The speaker says that God, who sent great troubles, will bring them back to life and lift them up from deep distress. He promises to praise God with instruments and song, and says his soul rejoices because God has rescued it.
The speaker says his tongue will speak of God's righteousness, meaning God's justice and faithfulness, all day long. He also says that those who seek to harm him will be put to confusion and shame.

A prayer asking God to give the king the ability to rule justly, so that he will defend the poor and needy and crush the oppressor. It hopes the people will fear God for as long as the sun and moon last.

The passage describes a king whose reign will bring blessing and lasting peace. Under him the righteous will prosper, his rule will reach across the whole earth, distant peoples will bow to him, and foreign kings will bring him gifts.

The psalm describes a king who will rule over all kings and nations. He will rescue the poor and needy when they cry out, protect their lives from fraud and violence, and be honored for it. Gold will be brought to him, and people will pray for him and praise him continually.

Psalm 72 closes with a prayer for a rich, fruitful land under a king whose name will last as long as the sun. It ends by blessing the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things, and asking that the whole earth be filled with his glory.
This line marks the end of a collection of prayers attributed to David, the son of Jesse. It says that the set of David's prayers is now complete. It is a closing note, not a prayer itself.

The writer says God is good to Israel, to those with a pure heart. But he admits his own faith nearly failed when he envied the proud and wicked. They seem to have an easy life, free of trouble and illness, with wealth and arrogance around them.

The speaker describes wicked people who boast arrogantly, speak against heaven, and mock whether God knows anything. They seem to prosper and grow rich. The speaker then says that keeping a clean heart and innocent hands has been pointless.

The speaker says he has suffered all day and every morning, and he found it too hard to understand why until he entered God's sanctuary. There he saw that the wicked will be brought down suddenly into ruin and terror.

The speaker says that when God acts, the enemies' empty show will vanish like a dream on waking. He admits he had been bitter and foolish, but says he remains close to God, who guides him and will take him to glory. He wants nothing on earth or in heaven apart from God.

The speaker's body and heart are failing, but God is his strength and his lasting portion. Those who turn far from God will perish, while being close to God is good, and the speaker trusts the Lord and plans to tell of his works.

The writer asks God why he seems to have rejected his people for good, and why his anger burns against them. He reminds God of the people he once bought and freed, and of Mount Zion where God lived. He describes enemies roaring in the Temple and setting up their own battle flags there.

The psalm describes enemies who have smashed the carved woodwork of the temple with axes and hammers, burned the holy place, and destroyed the places of worship across the land. The writer mourns that no signs from God remain, no prophets speak, and no one knows how long this will last.

The writer asks God how long enemies will be allowed to mock him and his name, and why God holds back his powerful hand. The writer then recalls God's past victories: dividing the sea, crushing sea monsters called dragons and Leviathan, and giving Leviathan's body as food to people in the wilderness.

The psalmist first recalls how God split the sea and rivers, and made day, night, the sun, the seasons and the borders of the earth. He then asks God to remember the enemies who mock him, not to hand over his people to the wicked, and never to forget the poor who gather before him.

The speaker asks God to keep his promise (the covenant) because the land is full of violence. He asks that the oppressed and poor not be shamed, but instead praise God. He urges God to act for himself against the foolish mocker and enemies who keep insulting him.

God is thanked because his name is near and his wonders are told. He says he will judge fairly, and that though the earth shakes, he holds up its pillars. He warns the foolish and wicked to stop their arrogance, because lifting up one's power and status comes from God alone, not from any direction on earth.

God is the judge who raises up some and brings down others. He holds a cup of mixed wine, and the wicked of the earth must drink its dregs to the last. The speaker, however, will praise God, and God will cut off the wicked's power while lifting up the righteous.

God is known in Judah and honored in Israel, with his dwelling in Salem and Zion. There he broke the weapons of war. The strong warriors are made helpless, and at God's rebuke, even chariots and horses fall into a deep sleep.

God is to be feared, and no one can stand before him when he is angry. At his judgment he saves the humble of the earth, and the earth falls silent. Even human anger serves his purpose, and people are urged to make vows and bring gifts to him.
God will take away the courage or life of rulers, and he is feared by the kings of the earth. The verse says this of God, who is the one spoken of as "he" in the psalm.
The speaker cries out to God in distress and says God listened. Through a night of pain he could not be comforted, and he was too troubled to speak. He ends by thinking back on the days of old.

The speaker wonders at night whether God has permanently rejected them, whether his mercy has ended and his promises failed. The speaker then decides that this doubt is a weakness and resolves to remember God's past deeds instead.

The speaker resolves to think about and speak of God's works. He praises God as unmatched, the one who performed wonders and rescued his people. The passage then describes God's power over the waters, the clouds, and the sky, which respond to him with fear and noise.

God's thunder and lightning shake the earth, and his way runs through the sea and great waters, though his footsteps cannot be traced. The psalm says he led his people like a flock, through Moses and Aaron.

The speaker asks the people to listen closely, promising to speak in riddles and sayings from the past. These stories were handed down from their fathers, and they will not be hidden from the children. They will be told to coming generations so that the LORD's power and wonderful deeds are remembered.

God set up a law for Israel and told the parents to teach it to their children. Each new generation would pass it on in turn, so that they would trust God, remember his works, and keep his commandments.

The psalm describes the people of Ephraim as stubborn and unfaithful. Though armed, they turned back in battle, broke God's covenant, refused his law, and forgot the wonders God had done for their fathers in Egypt.

The passage recounts how God made a way for the people through the sea, led them by cloud and fire, and gave them water from rocks in the wilderness. Despite these acts, the people kept sinning by provoking God and testing him by demanding food out of their desire.

The people doubted God's power in the desert. They asked whether he could set a table there, and whether he could give bread and meat, even though he had already struck a rock so water flowed. Because they did not believe or trust him, God grew angry and fire burned against them, even though he had sent food from the sky.
God sent food to the Israelites in the wilderness: manna from heaven, and quail that fell around their camp. They ate until they were full, because God gave them what they wanted.

The passage describes Israel in the wilderness. They kept craving what they wanted, and God punished them, killing some of the strongest. Their sin continued, and they did not trust his wonders. Only after they were struck down did they turn back to God and remember him as their rock and redeemer.

Despite their false words toward God, the people were not loyal to his covenant. Yet God, full of compassion, often held back his anger and did not destroy them. He remembered that they were only mortal flesh, like a wind that passes and does not return.

The psalm says the people turned away from God and put limits on him, forgetting what he had done for them. It recalls the plagues on Egypt: rivers turned to blood, swarms of flies and frogs, and crops and labour destroyed by caterpillars and locusts.

The verses list plagues that God sent on Egypt. He destroyed their vines and trees with hail and frost, killed their cattle and flocks, and sent evil angels, pestilence and death. The last line says he struck down the firstborn in Egypt.

God led the people of Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness like a shepherd leads a flock. He protected them, drowned their enemies in the sea, brought them to his holy mountain, and gave them the land by lot. Yet the people tested God and disobeyed his commands.

The psalm says that Israel turned away from God, as their ancestors had, and worshipped at local shrines and idols. God became angry and gave up his dwelling at Shiloh. He let his people be captured and killed by enemies.

The passage describes disaster falling on Israel: young men die in fire, priests die by the sword, and no one mourns the widows. It then says the LORD woke up like a warrior and drove off his enemies. He rejected the tribe of Ephraim and the tent of Joseph, and chose Judah and Mount Zion instead.
God built his sanctuary to last as long as the earth, and chose David, a shepherd taken from the sheepfolds, to lead his people Israel. David led them with an honest heart and skilful hands.

Foreign nations have invaded God's land, defiled the Temple, and destroyed Jerusalem. They have left the dead of God's people unburied for birds and beasts to eat, and the survivors are mocked by their neighbours.

The speaker asks God how long his anger will last and calls for it to fall on the nations that do not know him, because they have devoured Jacob and destroyed his homeland. The speaker begs God not to hold past sins against the people, to act quickly with mercy, and to save and forgive them for the sake of God's own name.

The psalmist asks why the surrounding nations should mock, saying "Where is their God?" He asks God to show himself by avenging the blood of his servants. He also asks God to hear the prisoners' groans, spare those condemned to die, and repay the neighbouring nations sevenfold for their insults against the Lord.
The speakers, calling themselves God's people and the flock he tends, promise to thank him forever. They will also tell his praise to every future generation.

A prayer to God, addressed as the shepherd of Israel, asking him to appear and save his people, who are named by their tribes (Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin, Manasseh). The speaker asks how long God will stay angry at their prayers, and says that he has fed them tears instead of bread.

The psalmist speaks to God, complaining that neighbouring nations mock Israel. He asks God to restore them, and recalls how God brought Israel out of Egypt like a vine, planting it, clearing land for it, and letting it spread across the country and far beyond.

The speaker asks God why he has broken down the walls protecting a vine, which stands for the nation of Israel. Passersby strip it, wild animals destroy it, and it has been burned and cut down. The speaker begs God to turn back, look down, and restore it, saying the people perish when God shows his anger.

A people asks God to support the man he has chosen, a figure called "the son of man," and to revive them. In return they promise never to turn away from him and to call on his name. They ask him to restore them and show his favour so that they will be saved.

The psalm calls the people to sing, play instruments and blow trumpets at the new moon and on the appointed feast days. It says this is a law given to Israel and ordained in Joseph as a testimony. It then recalls God freeing Joseph's people from heavy burden-work in Egypt, where they heard a language they did not understand.

God speaks to Israel. He recalls how he rescued them in their trouble and tested them at Meribah. He tells them to worship no other god, since he brought them out of Egypt. Yet the people refused to listen to him.

God let Israel follow its own desires and plans. He wished they had obeyed him, for then he would have defeated their enemies, and they would have been fed with the finest wheat and honey from the rock.

God stands in a heavenly assembly and judges the gods gathered there. He asks how long they will rule unjustly and favor the wicked, and orders them to defend the poor and needy. They do not understand and walk in darkness, so the earth's foundations are unstable. God has called them gods and children of the Most High.
The divine beings addressed here will die like ordinary humans and fall like any ruler. The psalm then calls on God to rise up and judge the earth, because all nations belong to him.
The psalmist begs God not to stay silent or inactive. He describes enemies who are plotting together to destroy Israel so that its name is forgotten. He asks God to act against this united plot.

The psalm lists nations allied against Israel and asks God to defeat them as he defeated earlier enemies: the Midianites, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna. It asks that they be destroyed and that their leaders be struck down like those past enemies. "Selah" is a musical or liturgical marker.

The psalmist asks God to scatter and shame enemies who plan to seize the houses of God for themselves. He compares them to chaff blown by wind and to wood and mountains burning, and asks God to pursue them with storm and terror until they seek God's name and are put to shame and perish.

The psalm says that people should come to know that God, whose name is Jehovah alone, is the highest ruler over the whole earth. "Jehovah" is an English form of the Hebrew divine name, and the verse stresses that God is supreme over all the earth.

The speaker longs deeply for the courts of the LORD, the place of God's presence. Even small birds find a home near God's altars, and the poem calls blessed those who live in God's house and keep praising him.

The passage describes pilgrims travelling to Zion, the holy city, where they gather before God, and turning even dry valleys into places of water on the way. It then prays for God's favour and states that one day in God's courts is worth more than a thousand elsewhere. The speaker would rather serve as a doorkeeper in God's house than live among the wicked.
The writer says God is like a sun and a shield. God gives grace and honour, and withholds no good thing from those who live honestly. The closing line calls blessed the person who trusts in God.

The speaker praises God for past mercy: God has restored the people, forgiven their sins and turned away his anger. The speaker then asks God to turn back to them again and to revive them, so that the people may rejoice in him.

God asks for mercy and salvation, and promises peace to his people and faithful ones, as long as they do not return to foolishness. His saving help is near to those who fear him, so that glory will dwell in the land. Mercy, truth, righteousness and peace are described as meeting and joining together, with truth rising from the earth and righteousness looking down from heaven.

The writer says that the LORD will give what is good, and the land will produce its crops. Righteousness, meaning right living or justice, will go ahead of the LORD and guide people onto the path of his steps.

The speaker asks God to listen and help. He calls himself poor and needy, trusts God to save him, and asks for mercy because he prays every day. He praises God as good, ready to forgive, and full of mercy toward all who call on him.

The speaker says that in trouble he will call on the Lord, who will answer him. No other god is like the Lord, and all nations will come to worship him. The speaker asks to be taught the Lord's way and to have a heart united in reverence for God's name.

The speaker promises to praise God with a whole heart and forever. He thanks God for great mercy that rescued him from death. Proud and violent people attack him, yet he trusts that the Lord is merciful, patient, and faithful.

The speaker asks God to turn toward him, show mercy, and give strength, calling himself God's servant and the son of God's handmaid. He asks for a sign of good so that his enemies will see it and be ashamed. He ends by saying God has already helped and comforted him.

The psalm praises Zion, the city of God, as the holy place the LORD loves most. It says that people from other nations, including Egypt (called Rahab), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia, will be counted as born in Zion. When the LORD records the peoples, each one is registered as having been born there.

Singers and instrument players will be there, and the speaker says all their sources of life and joy are in Zion, the city of God. "Springs" here means fountains or sources, so the line says that everything the speaker depends on is found in that city.

The speaker prays to God day and night, asking to be heard. He feels close to death, as if he already belongs with the dead in the grave and is cut off from God's care. He describes himself as lying in the deepest darkness.

The speaker feels crushed by God's anger and abandoned by friends, shut in and close to death. He has prayed every day with raised hands, and he asks whether God's wonders, praise and faithfulness can be shown to the dead, who cannot praise him.

The speaker asks whether God's wonders and righteousness can be known in the grave, a place of darkness and forgetting. Still, he has cried out to God each morning, and he asks why God has turned away and hidden his face. He says he has suffered terror and near death since youth, and that God's anger and fears surround him constantly.
The speaker says that God has taken away his loved ones and close friends, leaving his companions in darkness. He feels completely alone, with no one near him and no one who knows him.

The writer promises to sing forever about the LORD's mercy and faithfulness. He says God's mercy will stand firm forever and his faithfulness is set even in the heavens. God made a covenant, a binding promise, with David, his chosen servant, that David's line and throne will last for all generations. The heavens and the holy assembly are called on to praise God's wonders.

No one in heaven or among the heavenly beings can be compared to the LORD. God is to be feared in the assembly of the holy ones, and no one is as strong or as faithful as he is. He rules the raging sea and calms its waves when they rise.

The psalmist praises God as the powerful creator and ruler of the world. He has defeated his enemies, and he made heaven, earth, north and south. His throne rests on justice and judgment, and mercy and truth go before him.

Happy are the people who know the sound of the festival shout and walk in the light of the LORD's face. They rejoice in his name and are lifted up by his righteousness and strength, because the LORD is their protector and king. The passage then recalls God speaking in a vision, saying he has raised up a mighty helper from among the people.

God says he has chosen David, his servant, and anointed him with holy oil. He promises to support David, protect him from enemies, defeat his foes, and keep his faithfulness and mercy with him. He also promises David power over the sea and the rivers.

God speaks of a chosen king, promising him a special father-son bond, lasting mercy, and a line that will endure forever. He also warns that if the king's children break God's law, they will be punished, though the promise itself is not withdrawn.

God says he will never withdraw his steadfast love or break his covenant with David. He swore by his holiness that David's line will last forever, with a throne as enduring as the sun and moon. The final line turns to complaint: God has rejected and become angry with his anointed king.

The speaker complains to God that God has turned against God's anointed king. God has broken the covenant, humiliated the king's crown and throne, left his defences in ruins, and let his enemies win in battle.

The speaker complains that God has cut short the life of the king and covered him with shame, and asks how long God will stay hidden and angry. He pleads that human life is brief, asks who can escape death, and calls on God to keep the promise of loyal love made to David.

The speaker asks the Lord to remember the scorn that enemies have poured on his people and on the Lord's anointed king. He says he carries that insult himself, then closes with a blessing on the Lord forever.

God has always been a home for his people, existing before the mountains and the earth and forever. Humans return to dust at his command, and a thousand years mean no more to him than a day or a single night watch. People are swept away like a flood, fading like grass that sprouts in the morning.

Human life is compared to fast-fading grass that grows in the morning and is cut down by evening. The speaker says people are destroyed by God's anger, because God has placed their sins openly before him. Their days pass away under his wrath, and their years end quickly, like a story told and finished.

Human life is short and full of trouble, even when it lasts eighty years. The speaker says that God's anger is great and that people should learn to count their days so they can gain wisdom. He then asks God to return, show mercy early, and bring lasting joy.

The speaker asks God to give joy in proportion to the years of suffering and evil the people have known. He asks that God's work and glory be shown to his servants and their children, and that God's beauty rest on them and make their own work lasting.

Whoever lives in the shelter of God, the Most High, stays safe under his protection. The speaker says the LORD is his refuge, fortress and God, and trusts in him. God will rescue him from hidden traps and deadly disease, guard him like a bird covering its young, and keep him from fear of night dangers and daytime arrows.

The passage says that harm will not reach the person who trusts the LORD, who is called a refuge and a dwelling place. Plague and destruction may fall all around, but they will not come near. That person will only see the punishment of the wicked, and God's angels will guard them on every path.

God promises protection and rescue to the person who loves him and knows his name. He says he will keep such a person from harm, even from lions and snakes, answer when they call, stay with them in trouble, honour them, and give them long life and salvation.

It is good to give thanks to God and sing praises to him, especially his love and faithfulness shown morning and night, with stringed instruments. The speaker says God's works make him glad, and God's plans are deep. Foolish people do not understand this.

The wicked may grow quickly, like grass, but the psalm says they will be destroyed forever. The LORD alone remains highest forever. The speaker trusts that God will scatter the wicked, raise up the speaker, and let the speaker see defeat of enemies.
The righteous will thrive like palm trees and grow tall like cedars. Those planted in God's house will keep bearing fruit even in old age, showing that the LORD is upright and has no wrong in him.

The LORD rules as king, clothed in majesty and strength, and the world is fixed so it cannot be moved. His throne has existed since long ago and forever. Even when floods roar and waves rise, the LORD on high is greater, and his decrees are sure and holy forever.

The psalmist calls on God to act as judge and punish the proud and wicked. He asks how long the wicked will keep winning, boasting and speaking harshly. He describes them crushing God's people and killing the widow, the stranger and the fatherless.

Some people say that the LORD does not see what happens and does not care. The psalm answers that the one who gave people ears and eyes must himself hear and see, and that he knows human thoughts. It then calls blessed the person whom the LORD corrects and teaches by his law.

The psalmist says God gives rest from hard times and will not abandon his people. Justice will return to what is right, and the upright will follow it. Without the LORD's help, he would have died, but when he felt he was slipping, God's mercy held him up.

The writer says that when many worries fill his mind, God's comfort brings him joy. He asks whether corrupt rulers, who make harmful laws, can have any part with God. He states that God is his protector and will punish those who attack the innocent, destroying them through their own wickedness.

The psalm calls the people to come together, sing, and worship the LORD with thanks and joy. It praises him as a great God and King over all other gods, who rules the depths of the earth, the hills, and the sea, and who made the dry land. It ends by urging them to bow down before him as their maker.

The speaker claims God as the people's shepherd, and they are his flock. He warns them not to harden their hearts against his voice, as their ancestors did in the wilderness. Because that generation tested him and did not know his ways, God swore they would not enter his rest.

Everyone is urged to sing a new song to the LORD and to tell of his greatness among all nations. The writer says the LORD is great and worthy of praise, and that the gods of other nations are idols, while the LORD made the heavens. Honour and strength belong to him.

Peoples across the earth are called to honor the LORD, bringing offerings and worshiping him. They are told to proclaim among the nations that the LORD reigns and will judge the people with righteousness. Heaven, earth and sea are invited to rejoice.

Let the fields and everything in them be glad, and let the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD. He is coming to judge the earth, to rule the world fairly and the peoples with his faithfulness.

The LORD is king, and the earth and distant coastlands are called to rejoice. Storm imagery shows his power: clouds, fire, lightning, and mountains melting before him. His justice is the foundation of his rule, and all people can see his glory.

The psalm says that those who worship idols will be put to shame, while the LORD alone is high above all gods. Zion and Judah rejoice at God's judgments. Those who love the LORD are told to hate evil, and he protects them from the wicked, bringing light and gladness to the righteous.

Those who are righteous, meaning those who do what is right, are told to be glad in the LORD (the Hebrew name for God). They should also give thanks when they call to mind God's holiness, his separateness and purity.

Everyone on earth is called to sing a new song of praise to the LORD. God has won a victory with his own strength, shown his saving power and justice to the nations, and remembered his faithful love for Israel.

The psalm calls on people to sing and play instruments before the LORD, who is king. It asks the sea, the land, the rivers and the hills to join in, because the LORD is coming to judge the earth fairly and with justice.

The LORD is king, and the people and the earth should tremble before him, since he sits enthroned above the winged cherubim. He is great in Zion, holy, and the one who sets up fairness and justice in Jacob. So people are urged to praise his name and worship him.

Moses, Aaron and Samuel are named as leaders who called on the LORD, and he answered them, speaking to them from a cloud pillar. He forgave them, though he punished their wrongdoing, and the psalm closes by urging people to worship at his holy hill because the LORD is holy.

All the earth is called to worship the LORD with joy, singing and thanks. The psalm says God made the people and they belong to him, like sheep to a shepherd. It ends by saying the LORD is good, and his mercy and faithfulness last forever.

The speaker, who is probably a king, vows to sing of mercy and justice to God. He promises to live blamelessly at home, to avoid wicked deeds and people, and to remove anyone who secretly slanders others or is arrogant.

The speaker says he will look favorably on faithful people in the land and let them serve and live near him. He will keep out those who deceive or tell lies, and he will destroy the wicked in the land so that they are removed from the city of the LORD.

A person in great distress begs God to hear and answer quickly, and not to turn away. They describe their suffering: their days are fading like smoke, their body is wasting away, and they have lost their appetite. They compare themselves to lonely desert birds.
The speaker feels lonely, mocked by enemies, and worn down by suffering, which he blames on God's anger. His life is passing quickly, like a shadow or dying grass. In contrast, God will last forever.

The psalmist prays that God will rise and show mercy to Zion, the city of Jerusalem, because the appointed time has come. Then he says that God will rebuild Zion, nations and kings will honour God, and this will be recorded for future generations to praise the LORD.

The LORD looks down from heaven to hear prisoners groaning and to free those condemned to die. This is so his name may be praised in Zion and Jerusalem, when peoples and kingdoms gather to serve him. The speaker, weakened and with shortened days, asks God not to take him in the middle of his life, since God's years last through all generations.

The speaker says God laid the earth's foundations long ago and made the heavens. The heavens and earth will wear out and be changed like old clothes, but God stays the same and lasts forever. The servants' children will also continue before him.

The speaker urges the soul to praise the LORD and not forget his gifts. These include forgiveness of sins, healing, rescue from death, kindness and mercy, and good things that renew strength. The last line says the LORD brings justice to all who are oppressed.

God is described as merciful, patient and slow to anger. He does not punish people as their sins deserve, and he does not stay angry forever. His mercy toward those who fear him is as great as the height of the heavens, and he removes their sins as far away as the east is from the west.

The Lord shows pity to those who fear him, as a father does to his children. He knows that people are made of dust and that their lives are brief, like grass or a flower that the wind blows away. Yet his mercy and righteousness last forever, passing from generation to generation.
God's mercy reaches those who keep his covenant and obey his commandments. God rules from heaven over all things, and the speaker calls on his angels, his hosts, and all his works to bless the LORD.

The speaker calls on the soul to praise the LORD, who is very great and dressed in light. The verses describe God as the builder of the sky, the clouds, the wind, and the earth, with his angels and servants being like wind and fire. The point is that God is powerful and rules over all creation.

God covers the earth with deep waters, then commands the waters to retreat to fixed places in the valleys and mountains. He sets a boundary they cannot cross, so they never flood the land again, and he sends springs that give water to wild animals.

Birds nest in the trees and sing among the branches. God waters the hills and makes grass grow for animals and plants for people, so that food, wine, oil and bread come from the earth. The trees of the LORD, such as the cedars of Lebanon, are full of sap.

The verses describe how each creature has its place and rhythm in creation. Birds nest in trees, wild goats and rock badgers live in the hills and rocks, and God set the moon for seasons and made night, when forest animals come out. Young lions hunt for their food from God, and at sunrise all the animals return to their dens.

Humans go out to work until evening. The verses praise God for the many creatures on land and sea, all made wisely and all depending on him for food. He provides it, and they gather it and are filled with good things.

God controls the life and death of all living things. When he hides his face, creatures die and return to dust; when he sends his spirit, they are created and the earth is renewed. The writer vows to sing praise to God for as long as he lives.
The writer asks that sinners and wicked people be destroyed and removed from the earth. The psalm then turns to praise, calling the speaker's own soul to bless the LORD, the Hebrew name for God.

Give thanks to the LORD, make his deeds known among the nations, and sing and speak of his wonders. Seek him and remember what he has done, addressing the descendants of Abraham and Jacob, whom he chose. He is the LORD our God, and his judgments reach all the earth.

God remembers his promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that their descendants would receive the land of Canaan. He kept this promise for ever, even though the family was small and lived as strangers, moving from nation to nation.

God protected Abraham's family from harm and rebuked kings on their behalf, telling them not to touch his anointed ones or harm his prophets. He sent a famine on the land, then sent Joseph ahead as a slave. Joseph was chained until God's word proved true, and then the king freed him.

Joseph was sent ahead into Egypt, where he gained power over the Egyptian leaders. Jacob's family then settled there, grew strong, and was treated with hostility by the Egyptians. God then sent Moses and Aaron, who performed signs and wonders in Egypt.

The passage recounts a series of plagues God sent on Egypt: darkness, water turned to blood, frogs, flies, lice, hail, fire, and locusts. Each one came at God's command, and the land and its people suffered under them.

The passage recalls how God acted for Israel during the Exodus from Egypt. It describes the plagues that destroyed Egypt's crops and firstborn sons, the Israelites leaving with silver and gold and none weak among them, and Egypt's fear as they went. God then guided them with a cloud by day, fire by night, and fed them with quails and bread from heaven.
God made water flow from a rock and led his people out with joy, because he remembered his holy promise to Abraham his servant. He gave them the lands of other nations so they would keep his laws.

The psalm calls people to thank the LORD, because he is good and his mercy lasts forever. It says no one can fully describe his mighty acts, and it blesses those who keep justice and do right at all times. The writer then asks the LORD to remember him, save him, and let him share in the joy of the LORD's chosen people.

The speaker confesses that he and his ancestors sinned. The ancestors failed to remember or understand God's wonders in Egypt, and they rebelled at the Red Sea. Even so, God saved them for his own name's sake, to show his power, drying up the sea so they could cross on foot.

God saved Israel from their enemies, and the sea covered the Egyptians so none were left. The people believed and praised him, but soon forgot his deeds. In the desert they craved food and tested God. He gave them what they asked, but it left them weak in spirit. They also envied Moses and Aaron.

The passage recalls episodes of rebellion against God. The earth swallows Dathan and Abiram's followers, fire consumes others, and the people make a golden calf to worship at Horeb (Sinai). They forget God, who had done great works in Egypt and at the Red Sea.

God had said he would destroy the Israelites, but Moses, his chosen one, stood in the gap and turned away his anger. The people had rejected the good land, disbelieved God's word, complained in their tents and refused his voice, so God vowed to overthrow them in the wilderness and scatter their descendants among the nations.

The passage recalls Israel's sins in the wilderness: joining in the worship of Baal-peor and eating sacrifices offered to the dead. God sent a plague, which stopped when Phinehas acted with judgment, and this was counted to him as righteousness. It also says Moses suffered at the waters of strife because the people provoked God's spirit, so Moses spoke rashly.

Israel failed to drive out the nations living in the land, as the LORD had commanded. Instead they mixed with those peoples, copied their ways, and worshiped their idols, which became a trap for them.
