They even sacrificed their own sons and daughters to these idols, and the land was made unclean by the blood shed. The writer says this defiled them, as if they had been unfaithful to God.

God grew angry with his people and let their enemies rule over them. He rescued them many times, but they kept rebelling and were humbled for their wrongdoing. Still, he took notice of their suffering and answered when they cried out to him.

God remembers his promise to Israel and shows pity, even to those who held them captive. The people then ask him to save them and gather them back from the nations, so they can give thanks and praise his name. The psalm closes with a blessing and a call to say "Amen."

The passage calls people to thank the LORD, because his mercy lasts forever. It describes people he rescued from an enemy and gathered back from every direction. They had wandered lost in the desert, hungry and thirsty, and when they cried out to him in their trouble, he saved them.

God led his people by a straight road to a city where they could live. The passage then praises God's goodness and says he satisfies hungry people. It also describes people who sat in darkness and chains because they had rebelled against God's words.

People who were worn down and trapped, with no one to help them, cried out to the LORD, and he freed them from darkness, death and their chains. The psalm calls on people to praise him for this, breaking even gates of brass and bars of iron.

Foolish people suffer illness because of their sins and wrongdoing. They lose their appetite and nearly die, but when they cry out to the LORD in their trouble, he saves them, sending his word to heal them. The psalm ends by urging people to praise God for this goodness.

Sailors who travel the sea see the LORD's works and wonders there. When he commands a storm, the waves rise high and then fall, and the sailors are terrified, swaying like drunken men and at their wits' end.

When people in danger cry out to the LORD, he rescues them from their trouble and calms the storm so the waves go still. They are glad for the quiet and reach the harbor they wanted. The psalm then calls people to praise him publicly, in the gathering and before the elders.

God reverses the land's fortunes: he turns rivers and springs into dry wilderness, and fertile land into barren ground, because of the wickedness of its people. He then turns wilderness back into water and dry ground into springs, letting the hungry settle, build a city, farm, and grow in number.

God brings down the proud and powerful, and lifts up the poor from suffering, giving them large families like a flock. The upright will see this and be glad, and wrongdoers will be silenced. Whoever is wise will notice these things and understand the Lord's steadfast love.

The speaker says his heart is steady and he will sing praise to God, waking early with harp and lute to do so. He will praise God among all peoples and nations, because God's mercy and truth reach very high. He asks God to be raised up above the heavens and to save him with God's right hand so that God's loved ones are rescued.

God promises, from his holy place, to claim the lands of Israel's neighbors and tribes as his own, with Judah as his ruler. The speaker then asks who will lead him into the fortified cities of Edom, and pleads that God, who had rejected them, go out with their armies and give help, since human help is worthless.
With God's help, the speaker expects to act bravely and win, because God is the one who will trample the enemies underfoot.

The speaker asks God not to stay silent, because wicked and deceitful people have attacked him with lies and hatred without cause. He says he repays their hostility with prayer. He ends by calling for an accuser to be set against his enemy, with Satan standing at his right hand.

The speaker calls down curses on an enemy. He asks that the man be found guilty when judged, that his prayers count as sin, and that his life, family, property and any future kindness toward him all be taken away.

The speaker calls for a wicked man's family line to end and his name to be erased, and for his ancestors' and mother's sins to be kept in view before the LORD. The reason given is that he showed no mercy and persecuted the poor, needy, and broken-hearted.

The speaker asks that the curses his enemies gave out, and the cursing they loved, come back on them. He wants them to lose all blessing and to wear cursing like a garment that soaks into their body and bones. He asks the LORD to give this as their reward.

The speaker asks God to rescue him for the sake of God's name and mercy. He describes himself as poor, weak from fasting, wounded in heart, and fading like a shadow. He says others mock him by shaking their heads, and he pleads for help.

The speaker asks that his enemies, who curse him, be put to shame, while he himself will rejoice and praise the LORD. He trusts that God will stand beside the poor man and save him from those who condemn him.

The LORD (God) tells "my Lord," a king, to sit at God's right hand until his enemies are beaten. God will give him power from Zion, and his people will support him. God has sworn that he is a priest forever in the line of Melchizedek, and God will strike down kings in his anger.
He will judge the nations and fill their lands with the dead, wounding leaders across many countries. He will drink from a stream along the way, and so he will lift up his head in victory.

The writer praises the LORD wholeheartedly before the gathered faithful. The LORD's works are great, glorious and fair, and his righteousness lasts forever. He is gracious and compassionate, provides food for those who fear him, and always remembers his covenant, or agreement, with them.

God has shown his people his mighty works and given them an inheritance among the nations. His commands are true, just and lasting, and his covenant stands forever. His name is holy and awe-inspiring. Fearing the LORD is the start of wisdom, and those who keep his commandments gain good understanding.

Psalm 112 says that a man who respects the LORD and takes great pleasure in his commands is blessed. His descendants will be strong, his household will have wealth, and his goodness lasts forever. Such a good person is generous, lends to others, and manages his affairs wisely.

The righteous person will not be shaken and will be long remembered. He is not afraid of bad news because his heart is steady in trust in the LORD. He gives freely to the poor, and his honour rises. The wicked will see this with grief and anger, and their hopes will come to nothing.

The psalm calls on God's servants to praise the LORD's name, now and always, from sunrise to sunset. It says the LORD is higher than all nations and the heavens, and asks who is like him. It ends by describing him as one who stoops down to look at heaven and earth.

God lifts the poor out of dust and the needy out of the ash heap, seating them with princes of their people. He also gives the childless woman a home and makes her a joyful mother. The psalm ends by calling for praise to the LORD.

The psalm recalls Israel leaving Egypt, when the sea and the river Jordan retreated and the mountains and hills leapt like animals. It asks why nature fled, then calls the earth to tremble before the Lord, the God of Jacob.

It describes God changing solid rock into a pool of standing water, and hard flint into a spring of flowing water. The verse refers to water flowing from stone in the desert, as the wilderness journey is recalled.

The psalm asks that glory go to God, not to the people, for his mercy and faithfulness. It says the God of Israel is in heaven and does as he pleases, while the idols of other nations are made of silver and gold and cannot speak, see, hear or smell.

Idols are described as having hands, feet and mouths but unable to act, speak or move. Those who make them and those who trust in them become like them. Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD are urged to trust in the LORD instead, who is their help and shield.

The psalm first says that the LORD remembers his people and will bless Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear him, great and small. It then says the heavens belong to the LORD, while the earth was given to human beings. The dead cannot praise the LORD, because they have gone down into silence.
The speaker says that they will bless the LORD (God) now and always. The verse ends with a call to praise the LORD.

The speaker loves the LORD because God heard his cries for help. Near death and in great distress, he called on God, who saved him. He now says God is gracious, righteous and merciful, and that he will keep calling on God for as long as he lives.

The speaker tells his soul to relax, because the LORD has been good to him by saving him from death, tears, and falling. He says he will live faithfully before God. He admits he once spoke rashly in distress, saying everyone is a liar, and he now asks how he can repay God. He answers that he will take the cup of salvation and call on God's name.

The speaker promises to keep his vows to the LORD openly, before all the people, and to offer a sacrifice of thanks. He says he is God's servant, freed from his bonds, and he calls on Jerusalem's temple courts to praise the LORD. The line "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints" is a statement that the death of God's faithful people is valued by him.
All nations and peoples are called to praise the LORD. The reason given is that his steadfast kindness toward Israel is great, and his faithfulness lasts forever.

The speaker calls on everyone to thank the LORD, because his mercy lasts forever. Israel, the priestly house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD are each urged to say so. The speaker then tells how a cry for help in distress was answered with freedom, and so fears no human threat.

The speaker says the LORD is on his side, so he will see his enemies defeated. He states that trusting the LORD is better than trusting people or rulers. Surrounded by many nations, he says he will destroy them in the LORD's name.

Enemies surround the speaker like bees and die out quickly like burning thorns. The speaker, pushed hard to the point of falling, is helped by the LORD, who is now strength, song and salvation. The speaker expects to live and to tell of the LORD's works.

The speaker says the LORD punished him severely but did not let him die. He asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened so he can enter and give thanks, because God has answered him and saved him. The stone the builders rejected has become the main cornerstone, and the speaker says this is the LORD's work and a day to rejoice.

A prayer for help and success, followed by joyful thanks. The worshippers bless the one who comes in the LORD's name, and they call on him to bring the sacrifice to the altar. The psalm ends by praising God, whose mercy lasts forever.

Those who live blameless lives and follow the LORD's law are called blessed. The speaker wishes his own ways were guided to keep God's commands, so he would not be ashamed. He promises to praise God sincerely once he has learned God's righteous judgments.

The speaker vows to keep God's laws and asks not to be abandoned or led astray from them. He says a young person can stay on a clean path by following God's word, which he has stored in his heart so he will not sin. He praises God, speaks God's judgments aloud, and says he takes more joy in God's commands than in wealth.

The speaker vows to study and delight in God's laws and asks God for life, understanding, and help. He describes himself as a stranger on earth who longs constantly for God's judgments. He ends by noting that God rebukes the proud who wander from his commandments.

The speaker asks God to remove shame and scorn, because he has kept God's laws. Even though powerful men speak against him, he meditates on those laws and finds them his delight. He is deeply weighed down and asks God to revive and strengthen him, and to teach him God's ways.

The speaker asks God to keep him away from lying and to give him His law. He says he has chosen the way of truth, holds to God's commands, and asks for understanding and guidance so he can keep them fully. He says he delights in God's commandments.

The speaker asks God to turn his heart toward God's laws and away from greed and worthless things. He asks for life, mercy and rescue from insults, so that he can answer those who mock him, because he trusts God's word.

The speaker asks God never to take the true word out of his mouth, because he has hoped in God's judgments. He promises to keep God's law always, to speak of God's commands before kings without shame, and to delight in and meditate on them.

The speaker finds comfort in God's word, which has kept him alive in hard times. Proud people mock him, but he does not turn away from God's law. He remembers God's old judgments, feels horror at those who abandon the law, and keeps God's name and law even at night.

The speaker says the LORD is his portion, meaning his chief possession and support. He promises to keep God's words, asks for mercy, and turns his steps to God's commands. Despite robbery by the wicked, he stays faithful and joins those who fear God.

The speaker praises God's mercy and goodness and asks to be taught God's laws. He says that before his suffering he went astray, but now he keeps God's word. Proud enemies have invented lies against him, yet he says he will stay faithful and finds joy in God's law, while they have dull, fat hearts.

The speaker says that suffering was good for him, because it taught him God's laws. He values God's teaching more than any amount of gold or silver, asks God for understanding, and states that God's judgments are right, even though God has allowed him to be afflicted.

The speaker asks God to show his mercy and comfort him, as God promised. He says God's law brings him delight. He asks that the proud, who wronged him without cause, be shamed, while he keeps meditating on God's commands. He hopes in God's word even while his soul feels weak with longing for rescue.

The speaker is worn out, waiting for God's word to bring comfort and relief from enemies who persecute him and set traps for him. Even so, he says he has not forgotten God's laws and has not turned away from God's teachings.

The speaker asks God to give him new life, out of God's kindness, so he can keep God's commands. He says God's word lasts forever, God's faithfulness lasts for all generations, and all things continue by God's rules. He says he would have died in his trouble without God's law, and he begs to be saved because he has sought God's precepts.

The speaker says wicked people are waiting to destroy him, but he will keep thinking about God's laws. He claims that God's commandments have made him wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the elders, because he loves and keeps them.

The speaker says they have kept their feet from every evil path so they can keep God's word. They find God's words sweeter than honey, and his teaching gives understanding and guidance. Suffering greatly, they ask God to give them life again according to his word.

The speaker asks God to accept his spoken praise and to teach him God's laws. Though his life is in danger and enemies have set a trap, he says he has not turned from God's commands. He loves God's law, hates empty thoughts, and trusts God as his refuge and shield.

The speaker tells evildoers to leave him, because he will keep his God's commandments. He asks God to support him so he can live and not be shamed in his hope. He says God destroys the wicked like worthless waste, and he trembles in fear of God's judgments.

The speaker says he has lived by justice and asks God not to leave him to his oppressors or to the proud. He asks for mercy and for understanding of God's laws, which he says others have broken. He loves God's commandments more than gold.

The speaker says he values all of God's commands and hates every false way. He keeps God's laws because they are wonderful, and he asks God to look kindly on him, guide his steps by God's word, and keep sin from ruling him.

The speaker asks God to rescue him from harassment by other people, promising to keep God's commands in return. He weeps because others ignore God's law, praises God's laws as just and pure, and says that although he is small and despised, he does not forget them.

The speaker says God's justice and law last forever and are true. Although trouble and distress have overtaken him, he still finds joy in God's commands. He asks God to hear and save him, promising to keep God's laws, and he prays early each morning, placing his hope in God's word.

The speaker stays awake through the night to think about God's word and asks God to hear and save him. He says his enemies, who follow evil, are far from God's law, while God is near and his commands are true. He asks God to see his suffering, defend him, and give him life again, because he has not forgotten the law.

The speaker says that salvation is far from the wicked, because they do not follow God's laws. Asking God to give him life again, he says that many enemies pursue him, yet he does not turn from God's commands. He ends by affirming that God's word is true and his judgments last forever.

The speaker says that powerful men persecute him for no reason, yet his heart stays in awe of God's word, which he loves and rejoices in. He hates lying, praises God seven times a day, and says those who love God's law have great peace and nothing can make them stumble.

The speaker says he has kept God's commands and that God sees all his ways. He asks God to hear his cry, give him understanding, and rescue him according to God's word. He promises to praise God and speak of God's word, and says he longs for God's saving help and delights in God's law.

The speaker asks to be kept alive so that he can praise God, and asks that God's laws help him. He admits he has wandered off like a lost sheep and asks God to search for him, saying he has not forgotten God's commandments.
The speaker cries to God in trouble and asks to be saved from liars and deceitful tongues. He feels he lives among people who hate peace. He wants peace, but when he speaks, they push for war.

The speaker looks up to the hills and says that help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. The LORD is described as a guard who never sleeps, a shade at the speaker's right hand, and one who protects from harm, day and night.
The LORD will keep you safe in everything you do, whether leaving or returning, now and always. "Going out and coming in" means all of a person's daily movements, from this time on and forever.

The speaker is glad to be invited to go up to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. He describes the city as tightly built, where the tribes of Israel gather to give thanks and where judges' seats of the house of David stand. He asks for peace and prosperity for the city and for those who love it.
The speaker says he will wish peace on Jerusalem, the city, for the sake of his brothers and friends. He will also seek its good because of the house of the LORD, the temple, which stands there.

The speaker raises his eyes to God, who dwells in heaven, and compares this to servants watching their master's hand for a sign. He asks God for mercy because his people have been overwhelmed with scorn from the comfortable and the proud.

Israel gives thanks that the LORD was on their side when enemies attacked. Without that help, they would have been destroyed, as if swallowed by a flood or caught in a trap. Their survival is credited to God alone.
Help comes from the LORD, the name used for God, who made heaven and earth.

Those who trust in the LORD are compared to Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, and the LORD surrounds his people as mountains surround Jerusalem. The wicked will not hold power over the righteous, so the righteous will not be pushed into doing evil. The writer asks the LORD to do good to those who are good and upright.
Those who turn away to their crooked paths will be led off by the LORD along with evildoers. Israel, however, will have peace.

The psalm celebrates a time when the LORD brought back the exiled people of Zion, so that they felt as if they were dreaming. It asks God to restore them again, as streams return in the dry south. It promises that those who sow in tears will reap in joy.

Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders work for nothing, and unless the LORD guards the city, the guards watch in vain. Rising early and staying up late is useless, because the LORD gives sleep to those he loves. Children are a gift from the LORD, like arrows in a warrior's hand.

A man whose quiver (a case for arrows) is full of sons is called blessed. Such sons will not be shamed, and they will speak for their father against his enemies at the city gate, where legal matters were settled.

Those who fear the LORD and walk in his ways are blessed. They will enjoy the fruit of their own work, with a fruitful wife and children gathered around their table. The LORD will bless them from Zion, and they will see Jerusalem prosper all their lives.
The speaker says that a person who fears the Lord will live to see their grandchildren. The verse also hopes for peace across Israel, the Israelite nation.

The speaker says enemies have harmed him for a long time, beating him like a field is plowed, but they never defeated him. He trusts that the LORD, who is righteous, will cut the wicked loose from their power. He asks that those who hate Zion be shamed and turned back, becoming like grass on a roof that dies before it grows and is never gathered.
Passers-by will not greet the people described with the usual blessing in the LORD's name. The verse is part of a psalm that describes enemies being cut off from such blessing.

The speaker cries to God from deep distress and asks to be heard. He admits that if God counted every wrong, no one could stand, but he says forgiveness is with God. So he waits for the Lord eagerly, more than night watchmen wait for morning.
Israel is urged to put its hope in the LORD, because the LORD offers mercy and full redemption. The psalm says he will free Israel from all its sins, or iniquities.

The speaker says they are not proud and do not chase great or lofty matters beyond their reach. They describe their soul as calm and content, like a weaned child resting with its mother. The psalm ends by urging Israel to put its hope in the LORD always.

The psalm asks the Lord to remember King David and his hardships. It recalls David's oath that he would not rest until he found a fitting place for the Lord's dwelling. The writer then says they have found that place and will go there to worship.

The psalm asks God to come to his resting place with the ark, and to bless his priests and people. It also says that God swore to David that a descendant of David would sit on his throne forever, as long as David's children keep God's covenant.

The LORD has chosen Zion, the city of Jerusalem, as his home forever. He promises to bless its people with food, to clothe its priests with salvation and its holy people with joy, and to make a descendant of King David flourish, while his enemies are put to shame.

It says that it is good when brothers live together in harmony. The writer compares this unity to precious oil poured on Aaron's head, which runs down his beard and robes, and to the dew on the mountains Hermon and Zion. Blessing and life are said to come from there.

Temple servants who stand in the house of the LORD at night are urged to bless the LORD and lift their hands in the sanctuary. The closing line says that the LORD, the maker of heaven and earth, will bless them from Zion, the holy hill of Jerusalem.

Praise the LORD, the servants of God are urged to sing to him in his house, because he is good and has chosen Israel, his special people. The writer says the LORD is greater than all other gods and does whatever he wishes in heaven, on earth and in the seas.

The psalm praises God as the one who controls the weather, such as clouds, lightning and wind. It then lists his acts against Egypt, including the death of the firstborn and the signs sent to Pharaoh. It ends by saying he defeated great kings and gave their land to Israel.

The LORD's name and memory last forever, and he will judge and show compassion to his servants. The idols of other nations are only silver and gold made by human hands. They cannot speak, see, hear or breathe, and those who trust in them become as lifeless as they are.
The verses call on the houses of Israel, Aaron and Levi, and all who fear the LORD, to bless God. They end by saying the LORD is blessed from Zion, the city of Jerusalem, where God is said to dwell.

Give thanks to the LORD, who is good, because his mercy lasts forever. The verses then praise God as the God of gods and Lord of lords, who alone does great wonders and made the heavens, the earth and the great lights. Each line repeats the same reason: his mercy endures forever.

The psalm praises God for his enduring mercy, repeating the phrase after each act. It names his works: setting the sun, moon and stars to rule the day and night, striking down Egypt's firstborn, bringing Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand, and dividing the Red Sea so Israel could cross.

The verses list things God did for Israel: he drowned Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, led his people through the wilderness, defeated great kings including Sihon and Og, and gave their land to Israel. Each act is followed by the refrain "his mercy endureth for ever."

God gave Israel its land as an inheritance, and he remembered his people in their low state and freed them from their enemies. He also feeds all living things. So the psalm calls on people to thank God, because his steadfast love lasts forever.

Exiles in Babylon sit by the rivers and weep as they remember Zion, which is Jerusalem. They hang their harps on the willows and refuse to sing for their captors, who ask for a song of Zion. They say they cannot sing the Lord's song in a foreign land, and they vow never to forget Jerusalem.

The speaker vows never to forget Jerusalem, then asks the LORD to remember what Edom did when the city fell, urging it to tear the city down to its base. He calls happy anyone who repays Babylon for its cruelty, even by dashing its infants against stones.

The speaker promises to praise God with a whole heart, even before other gods. He says God answered his cry and gave him strength. He ends by saying the kings of the earth will also praise God and sing of his glory.

God is high above all, yet he looks kindly on the humble, while the proud he knows only from a distance. The speaker, though in trouble, trusts that God will revive him, defend him against enemies, and complete what concerns him, because God's mercy lasts forever.

The speaker says that God knows everything about him: when he sits and rises, his thoughts, his path, his resting, and every word before he speaks it. This knowledge is too wonderful for him to grasp. He asks where he could go to escape God's spirit or presence.

Wherever the speaker goes, God is already there: to the heavens, to the grave, to the farthest sea, or into darkness. God's hand guides and holds him in every place. To God, darkness and light are the same, because nothing is hidden from him.

The speaker says God knew and shaped them before birth, while they were hidden in the mother's womb. Nothing about their body was hidden from God, and every part was written down in God's book before it took form. So the speaker praises God for this careful making.

The speaker praises God's thoughts as too many to count and says he stays close to God. He then asks God to destroy the wicked and says he hates those who oppose God, counting them as his own enemies.
The speaker asks God to examine his heart and thoughts, to check whether he has any evil way in him. He then asks God to guide him along the everlasting way.

The speaker asks the LORD to protect him from wicked, violent men. He says they plot harm, stir up quarrels, and speak venomously like snakes. He claims they have laid traps and nets along his path to catch him.

The speaker prays to the LORD for protection against enemies. He asks God not to grant the wicked their plans, and he asks that the harm they plan for others fall back on their own heads. He wants them destroyed, cast into fire and deep pits so they never rise again.

Let a slanderer not be secure in the land. Evil will hunt down the violent man and bring him down. The LORD will defend the cause of the poor and needy, and the righteous will give thanks and live in God's presence.

The speaker calls on the LORD to hear and answer quickly. He asks that his prayer rise to God like incense and his raised hands be like an evening offering. He then asks for help to guard his speech and his heart, so that he does not join wicked people or share in their pleasures.

The speaker says that even a rebuke from the righteous, though it may hurt, is a kindness he will accept, and that he will still pray for them in their trouble. He says the wicked judges will be overthrown and his words will then be heard as sweet. He ends by trusting only in God and asking not to be left helpless.
The speaker asks to be protected from the traps that evil people have set for him. He prays that the wicked will be caught in their own nets while he himself gets away.

The speaker cries out to the LORD in distress, pouring out his troubles before him. He feels overwhelmed, has been trapped by hidden enemies, and finds no human help or friend. He ends by declaring that God is his only refuge and his share in life.

The speaker is in deep distress and asks God to hear his cry and rescue him from enemies who are stronger. He asks to be freed from his trouble so he can praise God, and he expects righteous people to gather around him because God will treat him generously.

The speaker asks God to hear his prayer and answer him in faithfulness and righteousness. He begs God not to put him on trial, because no living person can be declared righteous before God. He says an enemy has crushed him and left him in darkness, so his spirit and heart are overwhelmed.

The speaker recalls God's past deeds and reflects on them, then reaches out to God with a deep thirst for him. He asks for a quick answer, for God not to turn away, and for God's love and guidance to be shown to him in the morning.

The speaker asks the LORD to rescue him from his enemies and to teach him to do God's will. He asks for life and relief from trouble for the sake of God's name and justice, and asks that his enemies who trouble him be destroyed, because he is God's servant.

The speaker praises the LORD as his strength, protector and shield, the one who trains him for battle and gives him victory over his people's enemies. He then asks why God cares about humans, who are as brief as a shadow. He ends by asking God to come down and act with visible power.

The speaker asks God to strike his enemies with lightning and arrows and to rescue him from them. He describes these enemies as liars whose words and right hands are false. He then promises to sing new songs of praise to God, who saves kings and rescues David his servant from the sword.

The speaker asks to be rescued from foreign people whose words are empty and whose oaths are false. He then prays for a settled life: strong sons, graceful daughters, full granaries, and flocks that multiply in the streets.

The psalmist describes a blessed nation as one where cattle are strong for work, there is no breaking into homes or going out to war, and no complaints in the streets. He calls that people happy, and says the happiest people are those whose God is the LORD.
The speaker promises to praise God, called king, every day and forever. He says God is great and beyond understanding, and that each generation will tell others about God's works and mighty deeds.

The passage praises God. It says people will speak and sing of God's goodness, mercy and power, and that God's works and faithful people will praise him. It also says they will make known God's mighty acts and the glory of his kingdom to all people.
God's rule lasts forever, and he supports the fallen and lifts up the bowed down. He feeds every living thing at the right time, and he is just, holy, and near to all who call on him sincerely.

God grants the wishes of those who fear him, hears their cries, and saves them. He protects all who love him but destroys the wicked. The speaker vows to praise the LORD, and calls on all living creatures to bless his holy name forever.

The psalmist vows to praise God for as long as he lives. He warns against trusting human rulers, since a person dies and his plans end with him. Happy is the one whose help and hope rest in the LORD, the God of Jacob, who made heaven, earth and sea and keeps faith forever.

God is described as the one who acts for those in need: he judges fairly for the oppressed, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, heals the blind, lifts up the bowed down, protects strangers, and cares for orphans and widows. He also overturns the way of the wicked, and his reign is said to last forever.

Praise to the LORD is good, pleasant and fitting. God rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers the scattered people of Israel, heals the broken-hearted, counts and names the stars, and has infinite understanding. He lifts up the humble and brings the wicked low.

Praise God, who sends clouds and rain, makes grass grow on the hills, and feeds the animals, including the young ravens. God does not value military strength, such as horses or strong legs. Instead, God takes pleasure in those who reverence him and hope in his mercy. Jerusalem and Zion are called to praise their God.

God is described as protecting and blessing the city of Jerusalem, giving it peace and good harvests. He also controls the weather: his word sends snow, frost and ice, and his word or wind melts them so the waters flow again.

God has made his word, laws and judgments known to Jacob, meaning Israel. He has not done this for any other nation, and other nations do not know his judgments. The psalm ends by calling on people to praise the LORD.

The psalm calls on all of creation to praise the LORD: the heavens, the angels, the sun, moon and stars, and the waters above the sky. It says they praise him because he commanded them into being and fixed them in place for ever. The call then turns to the earth, including the sea creatures and deeps.

Everything in creation is called on to praise the LORD: the weather, mountains and trees, animals, rulers and common people, young and old alike. The reason given is that God's name alone is excellent, and his glory is higher than earth and heaven.

God raises up the strength of his people, who are praised by all his faithful ones, especially the people of Israel, who are close to him. The psalm ends by calling on everyone to praise the LORD. "Horn" here means power or strength.

Believers are called to praise the LORD with new songs, dancing, and musical instruments. The passage says God takes pleasure in his people, and that he gives salvation to the humble. Even the faithful in bed are told to sing with joy.

Praise to God should be in the mouths of God's faithful people, and weapons in their hands. They are to carry out God's judgment on the nations, binding their kings and nobles, and this is described as an honour given to all his saints.

Everything that breathes is called to praise the LORD. The psalm names the places and the many instruments to use: the sanctuary, the sky, trumpets, harps, drums, dancing and cymbals. It ends by calling again for praise.

Jesus, seeing the crowds, goes up a mountain and teaches his disciples. He says that certain groups are "blessed" (fortunate or favoured): the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, and the merciful. Each is promised a reward, such as the kingdom of heaven, comfort, the earth, being filled, or receiving mercy.

The passage says that certain kinds of people are fortunate, or "blessed," in a religious sense. These include the pure in heart, who will see God, and peacemakers, who will be called God's children. It also promises a great reward in heaven to those who are persecuted, insulted, or lied about for following Jesus, as the prophets of old were.

Followers are told they are the salt and the light of the world. Salt that has lost its taste is useless and gets thrown away, and a lit lamp is not hidden under a basket but set where it can light the whole house. The point is that people should let their good works be seen, so that others will praise God in heaven.

Jesus says he has not come to abolish the law and the prophets (the Jewish scriptures) but to complete them. Until heaven and earth pass away, not even the smallest letter or stroke of the law will disappear. Whoever breaks even the least commandment and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, while whoever keeps and teaches them will be called great.

Jesus says that unless people's righteousness goes beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees (religious teachers of the Jewish law), they will not enter the kingdom of heaven. He points to the commandment "Thou shalt not kill," which was taught long ago, and says that whoever breaks it will face judgment.

Anger at a brother without cause, or insulting him, is treated as serious enough to bring judgment. If you remember that your brother has something against you while bringing a gift to the altar, leave the gift there, make peace with him first, and then offer it.

Settle matters with your opponent quickly while you are still on the way to court, or you may be handed to the judge and jailed until every debt is paid. The passage then says that lusting after a woman in one's heart is already adultery, even without the act.

It says that if a body part causes a person to sin, it is better to lose that part than to have the whole body thrown into hell. The last sentence, which starts a new topic, repeats an older law: a man who divorces his wife must give her a written notice of divorce.

Jesus says a man who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and a man who marries a divorced woman also commits adultery. He then says people should not swear oaths at all, not even by heaven, earth, or Jerusalem, because each belongs to God.

Do not swear oaths by your head or anything else, since you cannot change even one hair. Let your speech be a plain yes or no, because anything more comes from evil. Do not resist someone who wrongs you; if struck, offer the other cheek, and if sued for your coat, give your cloak as well.

Whoever forces you to walk one mile should go two miles with him. Give to whoever asks, and do not turn away someone who wants to borrow. He contrasts the old teaching to love your neighbour and hate your enemy with his own command to love your enemies, bless and do good to those who hate or curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.

God gives sun and rain to good and bad alike, so his followers should act the same way. Loving only those who love you earns no special reward, since tax collectors do that too. Greeting only your own brothers is no more than others do. Be perfect, as your Father is perfect.

Giving to the poor should be done privately, not to be noticed by others. Those who give publicly to win people's praise have already received their reward, while a private giver is promised a reward from God.

Give to the poor and pray privately, not to be seen by others. A person who prays in public to be admired has already received that admiration as their reward. God, who sees what is done in secret, will reward the private giver and the private prayer openly.

Do not pile up empty repeated words when praying, as the pagans do, because they think they will be heard for their many words. God already knows what people need before they ask. The passage then gives a model prayer, starting with praise of God's name and asking for his kingdom, daily food and forgiveness of debts.

Asking God not to lead us into temptation and to rescue us from evil is followed by a condition: God forgives people only if they forgive others. The passage then warns against fasting to be seen by others, saying such people already have their reward in full.

Fasting should be done privately, so that God, who sees in secret, is the one who rewards it, not other people. Likewise, do not store up wealth on earth, where moths, rust and thieves destroy it, but store it up in heaven, where those things cannot reach it.

Where a person's treasure is, that is where their heart will be. A "single" eye, meaning a clear or generous one, lets light into the whole body, while an evil eye fills it with darkness. A person cannot serve two masters, and cannot serve both God and wealth (mammon).

Do not worry about food, drink or clothing, because life is worth more than food and the body more than clothes. The birds do not sow or store grain, yet God feeds them. Worry also cannot add a single cubit, about eighteen inches, to a person's height.

The speaker asks why people worry about clothes. He points to the lilies of the field, which do not work or spin yet are dressed more finely than Solomon, and says God clothes the grass, which lasts only a day. If God cares for plants in this way, he will care much more for people, so one should not worry about food, drink, or clothing.

Your heavenly Father already knows what you need, so the passage tells the hearer to put seeking God's kingdom and righteousness first, trusting that other needs will be provided. It says not to worry about tomorrow, since each day has enough trouble of its own.

Do not judge others, or you will be judged by the same standard. Why look at a small speck in your brother's eye while ignoring the large beam in your own? Fix your own fault first before pointing out someone else's.

Remove the large fault in your own eye before pointing out a small speck in another person's eye. Do not give sacred things to those who will mock or harm them. Keep asking, seeking and knocking, because whoever does so will receive, find and have the door opened.

A father would not give his child a stone when the child asks for bread, or a snake when the child asks for fish. If people, though flawed, know how to give good gifts, God in heaven will give good things to those who ask him. So treat others as you would want to be treated, which the passage calls the law and the prophets.

The passage contrasts two roads: a wide road to destruction that many take, and a narrow road to life that few find. It then warns against false prophets who look harmless but are dangerous, and says they can be known by their fruits, meaning their actions and results.

A good tree produces good fruit and a bad tree produces bad fruit, so people can be known by what they produce. Calling on Jesus as Lord does not by itself bring entry into heaven; only doing the will of God the Father does.

On the day of judgment, many people will claim they did great works in Jesus's name, such as prophesying and casting out demons. He will reject them, saying he never knew them and telling them to leave. Whoever hears his words and acts on them is compared to a wise man who built his house on rock.

Two houses face the same storm. The house built on rock stands, while the house built on sand falls. The point is that a person who hears these teachings and acts on them is like the wise builder, and a person who hears but does not act is like the foolish one. The crowd was amazed at the teaching.
Jesus taught the crowd in a way that carried personal authority. He did not teach the way the scribes, the Jewish experts in the law, did, who relied on the opinions of earlier teachers.

Christ says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness. The passage concludes that people who want true spiritual insight, and freedom from blindness of heart, should closely study and imitate the life of Jesus.

Christ's teaching is said to go beyond that of all other holy men, and only those with his Spirit find its hidden value. Many people hear the Gospel often but feel little desire for it, because they lack Christ's mind. So anyone who wants to understand Christ's words fully must try to shape their whole life to that mind.

Knowing hard theology, or even the whole Bible and the philosophers, gains nothing without humility and God's love. Being holy means living a good life, not speaking cleverly about God. The highest wisdom is to put the world aside, love God, and serve Him alone.

It is vanity to chase wealth that will perish, seek honour, follow bodily desires, or care only for a long life in this world rather than a good life. It is vanity to love what fades quickly and not to aim for lasting joy.

The passage urges the reader to turn their attention away from visible things and toward unseen things, since seeing and hearing never fully satisfy. It warns that those who follow bodily desires stain their conscience and lose God's grace.

Knowledge is worth little without the fear of God, the author says. A humble peasant who serves God is better than a proud scholar who studies the stars but ignores knowing himself. Even knowing everything counts for nothing without love, since God judges a person by their deeds.

Stop wanting knowledge too eagerly, because it brings distraction and deception. Learned people want to look wise and be called wise, and much of what can be known does little or nothing for the soul. A good life and a clear conscience give the mind more peace and trust in God than many words do.

The more a person knows, the more strictly they will be judged unless they live a holy life. So a person should not feel proud of their learning, but should admit how much they still do not know. The passage advises that to gain real benefit from learning, one should be content to be unknown and regarded as nothing.

The passage teaches that the best lesson is to judge yourself humbly and to think well of others. It says you should not count yourself better than a neighbor, even one who sins openly, because you cannot know how long you will stay good. Everyone is weak, so you should not consider anyone more frail than yourself.

Blessed is the person whom Truth teaches directly, without symbols or fleeting words. Our own judgment and feelings often mislead us. It is foolish to debate hidden matters we will not be blamed for not knowing, and to ignore what is useful and necessary.

The speaker says that debates over genus and species, the classes used in old logic, do not matter. Truth comes from God, the Eternal Word, and a person who sees all things as one in Him finds rest. The speaker wants God alone to speak, not the scholars or the world.

A person who is single-minded and sincere understands more, and more deeply, without great effort, because understanding comes to them from God. Such a mind is not pulled apart by many tasks, since it does everything for God's honour and is free of selfish aims. The last line asks what hinders a person most, and answers: one's own undisciplined heart.

A good and devout person plans his outward actions in his own heart first. So he is not pulled along by his evil desires, but puts everything under sound reason. The passage says the hardest fight is the struggle to master oneself, and that this struggle should be pursued daily toward spiritual perfection.

Even the best things in this life have some imperfection, and human sight always has some darkness. Knowing oneself humbly leads to God more surely than deep academic learning does. Learning is not condemned, but a good conscience and holy living matter more, and those who chase knowledge instead of goodness often go wrong.

The author says that people who spend their effort on useless debates should instead work to root out vice and grow virtue, since many wrongs would then disappear. He adds that at the Day of Judgment people will be asked what they did and how they lived, not what they read or how well they spoke. Famous teachers are soon forgotten after death.

Learning and fame do not make a person truly great, wise or learned, according to this passage. Greatness comes from love, humility, and doing God's will rather than one's own. The passage warns that people who value empty learning and honour, and care little for serving God, are lost.

We should not believe every word we hear or every feeling we have, but test them carefully and patiently to see whether they come from God. People find it easier to believe and repeat bad things about others than good, and those who are spiritually mature do not accept every report, knowing that people are weak and quick to speak evil.

Wisdom, the passage says, means not acting in haste and not clinging stubbornly to your own opinions. It also means not believing everything you hear, nor repeating all of it, and seeking advice from a wise, good person who may know more than you. A good life and humility before God bring wisdom and inner peace.

Scripture should be read for its truth, not for clever wording, and in the spirit in which it was written. Simple devotional books are worth reading alongside difficult ones. A writer's learning or fame should not put a reader off, and the reader should judge the content, not who said it.

Holy writings teach truth that lasts, and God speaks to people in many ways. The passage advises reading them humbly and simply, without wanting to appear learned, and listening patiently to holy men, even when their words are hard, because those words have a reason behind them.

Wanting something beyond what is right leaves a person restless. Proud and greedy people never find rest, while humble people find peace. Someone not yet free of self-centred desires is easily tempted and beaten by small matters. When such a person tries to give up earthly desires, he often becomes sad and quick to anger if anyone blocks his will.

If a person gives in to a desire, his conscience immediately weighs him down, and he does not find the peace he hoped for. Real peace of heart comes from resisting passion, and it is found only in someone who is devoted to God and lives by the Spirit.

Trusting in people or in any created thing is empty and useless. Instead, a person should be willing to serve others and accept poverty for Christ's sake, put hope in God rather than self, and trust God's favour rather than their own learning or cleverness, since God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

Do not take pride in wealth, powerful friends, bodily strength or beauty, or skill. Boast instead in God, who gives all good things and wishes to give himself as well. Such gifts can be lost quickly, and God is the source of every good gift.

Do not think yourself better than others, because God sees the heart and may judge you worse. Count others as having more good than you, and place yourself below them, since the proud person is troubled by envy and anger while the humble person has peace.

Keep your heart closed to most people and share it only with a wise person who fears God. Avoid long time with the young, with strangers, and with the rich and powerful. Choose humble, devout, gentle companions, and keep close company with God and the angels alone.

We should love everyone, but we should not make close friends with everyone. A person we have never met may be well spoken of, yet look unpleasing in person. Also, trying to please others by getting close to them can backfire, because they see our faults more clearly.

Living under obedience and authority, not being one's own master, is described as a great and safer thing than holding authority. People who obey only out of necessity resent it, and they gain inner freedom only when they submit willingly for love of God. Peace comes from humble submission to one's superior, not from moving to new places.

People naturally prefer their own view and favour those who agree with them. The passage says that, when Christ is among us, we should sometimes set our own opinion aside for the sake of peace, since no one knows everything. Giving up your own good opinion for love of God brings greater benefit.
It is safer to listen and take advice than to give it. Even when each person's opinion may be good, refusing to listen to others when reason or circumstances call for it shows pride or stubbornness.

Stay away from crowds where possible, because idle talk about worldly things easily pulls the mind away and stains it. The writer wishes he had kept silent, since talking rarely ends without harm to the conscience. People talk to gain comfort and refresh tired minds, and they most readily talk about what they love or hate.

Talk that only brings outward comfort can get in the way of the inner comfort that comes from God, so the writer urges us to watch our time and our speech. Speak only what builds up others, when speaking is right at all. Still, talk about spiritual things helps spiritual growth, especially among people who share the same mind and faith in God.

Peace of mind comes most fully when a person stops concerning himself with what other people say and do, and with matters that do not belong to him. Someone who spends his attention on outside affairs and rarely attends to his inner self cannot stay peaceful for long. The single-hearted, meaning those focused on one thing, will have much peace.

The Saints were so devoted to God because they worked to put aside worldly desires, which left them free to focus fully on God. The writer says we are instead caught up in our own feelings and in temporary things, rarely overcome even one fault, and so stay half-hearted and without spiritual life.

If we watched ourselves closely and were not tied in spirit to outward things, we could gain wisdom for salvation and grow in contemplation of God. Our main failing is that we do not free ourselves from our feelings and desires, so we do not follow the perfect way of the saints. When small troubles come, we quickly lose heart and turn to the world for comfort.

If we truly commit ourselves to the spiritual struggle, God will help us, and He even sets up occasions for struggle so we can win. Real spiritual progress is not just outward rituals, which soon fade; it means cutting out the root of our desires so the soul can be at peace.

If we removed one fault each year, we would quickly become perfect. Yet people often find they were better and more devout at the start of their faith than after many years in it. The writer says that keeping even some of the first fervour now seems a great achievement, and that a little effort at the beginning would make later efforts easy and joyful.

It is hard to break a habit and harder still to act against your own will. The passage argues that small struggles should be faced early, because giving in to a bad habit leads to bigger problems, and it says a holy life would bring peace to oneself and joy to others.

Hardships and sorrows are presented as useful to a person. They remind him that he is only a passing guest in this world and should not trust in worldly things. Being unfairly criticized, even when doing good, helps keep him humble and guards against vanity, and makes him look more earnestly to God for approval.

When trouble, fear or dark thoughts come, a believer sees more clearly that he needs God, since nothing good can be done without him. Such trials make him long to be with Christ, and they teach that the world can never offer full security or lasting peace.

While we live in this world, we will always face trouble and temptation. No one is so holy that he is free from temptation, so we should stay alert and pray so the devil cannot trick us. The devil is described as always watching for a chance to harm.

Temptations are useful to a believer, even when they are severe, because they humble, purify and teach. Saints have all gone through them and gained from them, while those who could not endure them fell away. No place or position is free from temptation.

People are never fully free from temptation while they live, because the cause lies within them from birth. One trial ends and another follows. Running away from temptation often leads to deeper falls. Victory comes through patient endurance and humility, not through flight.

Merely pushing back temptation from the outside, without pulling out its root, gains little and brings it back stronger. Temptation is overcome slowly, through patience and with God's help, not by force of will alone. When others are tempted, they should be given advice and support, not harshness.

Temptation to evil, the passage says, starts when a person's mind is unsteady and does not trust God. Like a ship without a helm, such a person is pushed back and forth by temptation. Temptation also shows a person what they really are, and the best time to resist it is at its first approach, before it gets inside the mind.

A temptation grows in stages: first a simple thought, then a strong image, then pleasure, then desire, and finally agreement. The enemy gets in fully because it was not resisted at the start. The longer a person waits to resist, the weaker they become and the stronger the temptation grows.

Temptations come to people in different ways. Some face their hardest trials at the start of their turn to God, some at the end, and some struggle all their lives while others are only lightly tested. The writer says God arranges this wisely and justly, knowing each person and working everything for the good of his chosen people.

When we are tempted, we should not lose hope. We should pray harder to God for help, trusting that He will give a way out so we can bear it. Being humble under God's power is the right response, because God saves and raises up those who are humble in spirit.

Trials show how far a person has really advanced in the spiritual life, and they bring a greater reward. Being devout while nothing hard happens is not much; patience in hardship is the real sign of progress. Some people are spared great temptations but fall to small, everyday ones, so they learn not to trust themselves.

Judging other people is wasted effort and often leads to error and sin. It is more useful to examine oneself. We tend to judge things according to our own feelings and likes, and this makes our judgment unreliable. If God were our only desire, such mistaken judgment would trouble us less.

Hidden motives, such as seeking our own ends without realizing it, can turn a person from what is right. People feel calm only while things go their way, and become upset when their wishes are blocked. Differences in feeling and opinion often cause quarrels even among friends and devout believers.

People rarely give up old habits easily, and nobody readily sees things the way someone else does. The passage says that if a person trusts their own reason and experience more than the power of Christ, understanding will come slowly. God wants people to submit fully to him, with their reason lifted up through love of him.

Nothing wrong may be done for any worldly gain or out of love for a person. A good work may sometimes be put off or replaced by a better one to help someone in need. Works done with love count for good, however small, because God looks at what a person is able to do rather than the size of the deed.

Doing much good depends on love, and doing good for the common welfare counts for more than doing good for oneself. The author warns that what looks like charity can really be self-interest, if it comes from natural preference, self-will, or hope of return or gain.

Someone with true charity, meaning selfless love, does not seek their own good. They want God alone to be glorified, do not envy others, and find their highest good in God. Such a person also sees that worldly things are empty.

Faults that you cannot correct, in yourself or in others, should be borne patiently until God decides otherwise. The passage suggests this may be better for testing and building patience, which it treats as valuable. When such burdens appear, one should ask God for the strength to bear them willingly.

If someone ignores advice given once or twice, do not argue with them; leave the matter to God, who can turn evil into good. We should be patient with others' faults, since we have our own faults that others must bear. We are quick to want others made perfect but slow to correct ourselves.

We want others to be strictly corrected while we ourselves avoid correction. We resent others' freedom and want rules for them but not for us. So we seldom judge our neighbour by the same standard we use for ourselves. If everyone were perfect, there would be nothing to bear from others for God's sake.

God has arranged things so that people learn to carry each other's burdens, since everyone has faults, burdens, and limits. We should bear with one another, comfort, help, teach, and advise each other. Hard times show a person's true strength, because they reveal character rather than create weakness.

A person who wants to live peacefully among others in a religious community must learn to deny his own wishes in many things. Living faithfully in such a community until death is hard, and whoever does it well is called blessed. The one who lives this life must also regard himself as a stranger on earth, and may be thought a fool for Christ's sake.

Outward dress and appearance count for little. What makes a religious person is a changed character and the giving up of strong desires. Someone who seeks anything other than God and the health of their soul will find only trouble, and no one can stand firm without humbling themselves for God's sake.

Look at the lives of the holy fathers, the early saints who showed true devotion. Compared with them, the author says, our own efforts seem almost nothing. They endured hunger, cold, labour, fasting, prayer and persecution in serving the Lord.

The passage says that the apostles, martyrs, and other faithful followers of Christ suffered many hardships, because they gave up their lives in this world to keep them for eternal life. It then describes the early desert fathers, who lived strict, withdrawn lives, faced long temptations and attacks from the devil, and prayed often and fervently.

The passage praises the early holy men (the "Fathers" of the Christian Church, monks and hermits of the desert) for their hard discipline. They fasted strictly, fought their sinful habits, worked by day, prayed at night, and kept up silent prayer even while they worked.

The passage describes early Christian monks, the Holy Fathers, who spent all their time in prayer and quiet thought with God. They gave up wealth, status, friends and family, and lived on the bare minimum, so they were poor outwardly but rich in grace and virtue inwardly.

The holy men of earlier times were looked down on by the world and seemed worthless to themselves, yet God regarded them as dear friends. They lived in humility, obedience, love and patience, and so became strong in spirit. The writer says their example should inspire believers to a better life more than the poor example of lukewarm, half-hearted people encourages carelessness.

The author looks back at the first monks and religious communities and praises their deep love, prayer, strict discipline and obedience to their rule. He says their remaining traces show they were truly holy men who overcame the world. Today, he says, a person is considered great merely for not doing wrong and for patiently keeping a commitment.

The writer laments that people in his time quickly lose the earlier love for holiness, and that living a devoted life has become tiresome because of laziness and lack of zeal. He then urges the reader, who has seen many examples of devout men, not to let their own spiritual progress stop completely.

A Christian should have virtue inside as well as outside, so that his inner heart matches how he appears to others. Since God sees the heart, he should live purely before God, and renew his commitments every day as if it were his first day, asking God for help to make a good start.

Progress in the spiritual life depends on how firmly a person resolves to make it, and so it needs steady effort. Even a small neglect of holy practices usually costs something. Still, the author holds that a good person's resolve rests more on God's grace than on their own wisdom, since man plans but God decides.

A religious practice may be skipped for a good reason, such as an act of kindness to others, and picked up again later. Skipping it out of dislike or laziness is a sin with real harm. The writer adds that we should set clear resolutions, resist our strongest faults, and examine both outer and inner conduct, since both affect spiritual growth.

A monk is advised to examine himself at least twice a day, in the morning and evening. In the morning he should set his resolves, and in the evening review how he has done in word, deed and thought. He should also keep busy with reading, writing, prayer, meditation or useful work for the community, and take physical exercise carefully, since it does not suit everyone equally.

Private devotions that are not expected of everyone should be kept secret. A person must first do their common duties faithfully, and only then give time to their own devotions. Different people, seasons and moods call for different spiritual exercises.

Before the great feasts, a person should renew spiritual practices and ask holy men for prayers more earnestly. Each feast should be treated as if it were the last before death and entry into eternal life, so that preparation and careful observance are kept as if the reward for one's labours were about to come from God.

If the reward is delayed, the reader should think of himself as not yet ready and not yet worthy of the glory promised for the appointed time, and should work to prepare better for his death. He cites Luke's teaching that the servant found watching when the Lord comes will be given authority over all his master's goods.

Set aside time for quiet thought on God's kindness, and avoid idle questions and chatter. Focus on matters that lead to sorrow for sin rather than entertainment. The greatest saints, the passage says, kept away from crowds where they could and chose to live privately with God.

Being among people tends to make a person less self-controlled, so it is easier to stay quiet and at home than to guard one's words and conduct outside. The writer holds that anyone seeking inner, spiritual things should withdraw from the crowd, and that only those who like rest, silence, obedience, and being ruled can safely go out, speak, or lead.

Real joy is safe only for someone with a clear conscience. Holy people stayed humble and fearful of God even when they were very virtuous, while the confidence of wicked people comes from pride and ends in their own downfall. So no one should count on being safe in this life, however devout they seem.

Inner temptation is often good for people, because those who are highly respected can grow overconfident and proud, or rely too much on worldly comforts. The passage then praises the person who avoids fleeting worldly joys and cares, and who places all hope in God, saying such a person has a good conscience and deep peace.

Real spiritual comfort comes only to those who have sincerely practised inner repentance. To feel that repentance, a person should withdraw from worldly noise into private quiet, as the verse "commune with your own heart... and be still" advises. Solitude feels tiresome if abandoned early, but if kept up faithfully it becomes a dear and pleasant companion.

Quiet and silence help a devout person learn the hidden meaning of Scripture and bring tears of repentance that cleanse the soul. Staying away from worldly distractions, and from people, is held to bring a person closer to God. Being unknown and watching over one's own soul is called better than seeking attention through showy deeds.

Going out to look at worldly things brings no lasting good, only distraction and regret, since the pleasures of the senses fade and leave the heart burdened. The writer asks what can be seen outside that cannot be seen at home, pointing to heaven, earth and the elements, which are all around the reader already.

The passage tells the reader that lasting satisfaction cannot be found in the things of the world, even by seeing everything at once. It advises turning to God in prayer, staying quietly alone with Jesus, and avoiding idle talk. Hearing new things, it says, brings trouble of heart.

If you want to grow spiritually, keep the fear of God, hold your senses under discipline, and avoid empty amusement. Heartfelt sorrow for sin brings devotion and opens the way to many good things. A person who thinks about how far away they are from home, and the dangers to the soul, will find it hard to rejoice in this life.

Being careless about our faults makes us laugh when we should grieve over our soul's state. Real freedom and joy come only from fearing God with a clear conscience. The passage urges clearing away distractions and whatever burdens the conscience, and says that if we leave others alone, they will leave us alone to do our own work.

Do not interfere in other people's affairs, and first watch over your own conduct. If people do not favour you, do not be discouraged; instead, be concerned that you are not living as well as a servant of God should. Lacking spiritual comfort is our own fault, because we do not seek heartfelt repentance or give up worldly pleasures.

A person who truly feels sorrow for sin should see himself as unworthy of God's comfort and deserving of trouble. Such a person finds the world heavy and bitter, and the more he examines himself, the more he grieves. Our sins keep us so tangled that we rarely think about heavenly things.

If you thought about your death more often than about how long your life might last, you would surely work harder to improve. Because such thoughts do not move the heart, and people still love pleasures, they stay cold and careless.

The writer says that complaining often comes from a poor spirit, a lack of inner strength or devotion. He advises asking God for a heartfelt sorrow for sin, quoting a psalm that asks God to feed the speaker with tears.

Nobody is free from trouble, not even a king or a pope, and wherever a person goes he remains unhappy unless he turns to God. Nobody gets everything they want. The happiest person is the one who is able to bear some suffering for God's sake.

Foolish people envy the wealth, rank and power of others. The writer says these worldly things are uncertain and bring worry and fear, so they are nothing next to heavenly good. Human happiness comes from a modest amount, not abundance, and earthly life is full of misery.

The more a person wants to live in the spirit, the harder ordinary life feels, because they see more clearly how flawed human nature is. Basic bodily needs such as eating, sleeping and working are a real burden to a devout person who longs to be free of all sin.

The body's needs weigh heavily on the inner self, so the prophet prays to be freed from them. Kempis says it is a great misfortune not to see one's own misery, and a greater one to love this short, decaying life so much that people would stop caring about God's Kingdom if they could live here forever.

Those who are absorbed in worldly things and care only for bodily pleasures will eventually see how worthless their loved things were. The saints and true followers of Christ, by contrast, set their hope and desire on eternal, unseen things so they would not be pulled down by what is visible.

The speaker urges a brother not to give up his wish to grow spiritually, and to begin change now rather than delay. He says hardship is part of the way: trouble can bring a person closer to blessing, and faults are overcome only through self-discipline.

While we live in this weak body, we cannot avoid sin, weariness and trouble. We want rest from all suffering, but because sin has cost us innocence and true happiness, we must be patient and wait for God's mercy until this life of troubles ends and mortality gives way to life.

Human weakness is constant: a person confesses sins today and repeats them tomorrow, and resolutions to avoid faults soon fail. So people should be humble and not think highly of themselves. Gains won with great effort and grace can be lost quickly through carelessness.

The passage warns that someone who is lukewarm and idle at the start of the spiritual life will end badly. It says that resting in false security, before any real holiness shows in one's life, is dangerous. It advises beginning again, like a new novice, so that improvement and growth might still come.

Life here is short, so a person should think about what comes after death. People soon forget the dead and live only for the present. The passage urges living each day as if it were the last, since tomorrow is not certain, and it says that avoiding sin matters more than fearing death.

Living a long time does not help unless a person improves; long life often adds to guilt instead. Those who keep the thought of death before them each day, and prepare for it, are called happy. The passage urges the reader to see death as something that will come to him too.

Live each day as if it could be your last, because death can come without warning. When that final hour arrives, a person will see their past life differently and regret having been careless and lazy about preparing for it.

A person who lives now in the way they hope to be found at death is called happy and wise. Such habits as scorning the world, eagerly seeking virtue, and accepting hardship for Christ give confidence at death. While healthy, one can do much good, but during illness little may be possible, and few people become better through sickness.

Do not count on friends and family, and do not postpone spiritual preparation. People will forget you sooner than you expect, so it is better to act now and send good works ahead of you. Time is precious, and a day may come when you wish for even one hour to change your life, but that hour may not be granted.

The speaker urges the reader to keep death in mind and live so that dying brings joy rather than fear. The way to do this is to give up worldly things, to stop caring about the world, and to discipline the body through penance. Doing so, the speaker says, leads to a life with Christ and to a secure confidence.

The speaker scolds a foolish person for expecting a long life, since no one can be sure of even one day. He lists many people who died suddenly and in different ways, such as by sword, drowning, fire, or plague. He concludes that death comes to everyone and that human life passes quickly, like a shadow.

Who will remember you after death, and who will pray for you? The passage urges the reader to act now, while still alive, to secure lasting reward. It says to focus on salvation and God, and to make friends among the saints by following their example, so that they will be welcomed into everlasting dwellings.

Live on earth as a stranger and traveler, not bound to its goods. Keep your heart free and turned toward God, since this world is not a lasting home. Pray to him constantly, in tears, so that after death your soul may be found ready to go to its Lord.

A reminder to keep in mind the end of one's actions and the coming judgment before God, who sees everything and cannot be bribed or persuaded by excuses. Each person must answer for himself, so the speaker urges preparation now, while present labour, weeping and sorrow still bear fruit before God.

Patience helps a person cleanse the soul even in this life. This means grieving more over another's wrong than over one's own, praying for and forgiving enemies, asking pardon, showing pity before anger, and denying the self and bringing the body under the spirit. It is better to cleanse sin now than to face purging later, and people deceive themselves through too much love of the body.

The passage says that the fire of judgment will burn away nothing but a person's sins. The more someone indulges the body and its desires, the heavier the punishment will be, since each sin is punished in the same area where it was committed. Slothful people are goaded, gluttons starve and thirst, the lustful are plunged into burning pitch, and the envious howl in grief.

Every sin will be punished in its own way after death. The proud will be overwhelmed with shame, and the greedy will suffer hard poverty. The pain there will be far worse than any hard penance in this life, and the lost will have no rest or comfort, unlike here, where pain sometimes pauses and friends bring relief.

Be anxious now about your sins so that you will have confidence before the blessed on judgment day. Then the righteous person, who was humbled and mistreated by others, will stand boldly before them and judge, while the proud will be overcome with fear.

Here the passage says that on the day of judgment things will be reversed. Those who looked wise in this world, but were willing to be called fools for Christ, will be shown to be wise. Patient suffering, humility, poverty and simple obedience will be valued above worldly power, riches and wisdom, while the ungodly fall silent.

A good conscience, prayer, silence, holy deeds and a strict, penitent life are said to bring more joy and worth than learning, wealth, feasting, talk and worldly pleasure. The point is that inner goodness outweighs outward things. The judgment day is the setting: the reader is told that these values will matter most then.

Endure small sufferings now, the passage says, so you can avoid greater ones later. If you cannot bear a little hardship now, you will not bear eternal punishment in hell. You cannot have both comfort in this world and a place with Christ afterward.

Only love of God and service to Him truly matter, since worldly honours and pleasures gain nothing when death comes suddenly. Someone who loves God fully does not fear death or judgment, while someone who still enjoys sin has good reason to fear them. Fear of hell is a lesser but useful restraint for those whose love is not yet strong enough, and without any fear of God a person soon falls into the devil's traps.

The passage urges the reader to keep working hard at spiritual growth, remembering that they left the world in order to live for God. It promises that faithful effort will bring lasting rest and joy, and that God will reward it. It also warns against becoming complacent, which would lead to laziness or pride.

A man, worried and torn between hope and fear about whether he would keep going in his spiritual life, prayed and wished he knew he would persevere. He then seemed to hear a divine voice answer: if he knew, what would he do? He should do that now, and he would be safe.

Once he was comforted and strengthened, he gave himself up to God's will and his inner turmoil stopped. He no longer wanted to pry into what would happen to him, but sought to learn what God's good and pleasing will was, the source and completion of every good work.
