Many people hold back from real spiritual progress because they fear difficulty or the struggle involved. The passage says those who bravely fight against what is hardest and most opposed to their nature advance furthest in virtue, gaining more grace by overcoming themselves.

A person with stronger faults can still gain more spiritual progress by working hard at it than a calmer person who is less eager to pursue virtue. The passage names two keys to growing in holiness: resisting the sin one is most naturally drawn to, and zealously pursuing the good one lacks most. It also urges working against the faults that bother one most in others.

Learn from good examples wherever you find them, and avoid copying what is blameworthy. If you do wrong, correct yourself quickly, because others are watching you too. The passage also says it is harmful for members of a religious community to neglect their calling and take up matters that are not their concern.

The writer urges a devout person to keep the suffering of Christ in mind and to study his life and death closely. Such a person, he says, will find there everything useful and needed, so there is no need to look for anything better than Jesus. He adds that if Jesus crucified were truly within us, we would quickly learn all we need to know.

A person who is earnest bears well whatever is laid on him. A careless or lukewarm person suffers trouble after trouble, lacks inner comfort, and cannot find outward comfort either. Whoever looks for an easier discipline will always be unhappy, since something will always displease him.

The author wishes that people had no duty except to praise God wholeheartedly, and no bodily needs such as eating, drinking, or sleeping. Then they could devote themselves only to spiritual exercises, which would make them happier. As things are, the body's needs take much of their time, and the soul's spiritual comfort is tasted too rarely.

When a person no longer looks to any created thing for comfort, he can truly begin to enjoy God. He then accepts whatever happens, feels neither great joy nor great sorrow over small things, and trusts himself fully to God, for whom nothing perishes and all things obey.

Keep your final goal in mind and remember that lost time never comes back. Virtue is gained only through care and effort, and if your devotion cools, things go badly. Eager effort brings inner peace and makes the work lighter, with God's grace helping, and an eager person is ready for anything.

Resisting sins and strong desires is harder than physical work. A person who ignores small faults gradually falls into greater ones. The passage says that the more a person forces himself to change, the more he gains from it.

The passage says that God's kingdom is found inside a person, not in outward things. It urges turning away from the world and focusing on the inner life, where Christ comes, brings peace and joy, and stays. Peace and joy are not given to the wicked.

The speaker urges the faithful soul to prepare its heart so Christ, the bridegroom, will come and live within it, and to leave no room for others. With Christ, the soul has enough and needs no human help, since people change and pass away while Christ remains constant.

Do not rely too much on people, however useful or dear they are, since they may turn against you, and do not grieve greatly when they disagree with you. Place your full trust in God, who will act for your good. Life here is temporary, so rest is found only in being closely united to Christ within.

The speaker tells the reader not to look around restlessly, because earth is not the place of rest. Heaven should be the true home, and worldly things should be seen only as passing. Since everything fades, one should not cling to it, but keep thinking on God and keep praying to Christ.

If you cannot reach high, heavenly thoughts, the passage says, rest in Christ's suffering and turn devotedly to His wounds. Doing so brings comfort in hardship, and insults and unkind words from others will not trouble you greatly.

Christ was despised, rejected and left by his friends, and he accepted suffering. The passage asks why the reader should expect to escape hardship when Christ did not, and says that patience is tested only through adversity. It ends by saying that sharing Christ's reign requires bearing suffering for him.

If a person truly tastes Jesus's tender love, they stop caring about their own comfort or discomfort and even welcome trouble. Such love makes a person think little of himself. A person who loves Jesus and is free from disordered desires can turn to God easily, rise above himself in spirit, and find lasting peace.

A person who sees things as they really are, not as others say or appear, is wise and taught more by God than by people. Such a person does not need special places or times to be close to God, because the inward person is not wholly given over to outward things. He adapts to events and is not disturbed by others' conduct, while a person is distracted only to the degree he is moved by outward things.

Things that bother you are said to come from not yet being fully detached from yourself and from earthly things. Impure love of created things is named as the greatest tangle for the heart. Letting go of outward comfort is said to allow contemplation of heavenly things and inward joy.

Do not worry much about who supports or opposes you. Focus on your present duty and keep your conscience good, trusting that God will protect you and will choose the time and way to help. It can also be useful when others point out your faults, because it keeps you humble.

A person who admits his own faults calms others who are angry with him. God protects, loves and comforts the humble, raises them up, and reveals His secrets to them. The humble person stays at peace even when criticised, because he rests on God rather than the world. Progress is measured by feeling oneself lower than everyone else.

Be at peace within yourself first, and only then can you bring peace to others. A calm person does more good than a learned one, because an angry person twists good things into bad and readily believes the worst. A person at peace sees the best in others, while a restless person suspects everyone, says and omits the wrong things, and watches what others owe while neglecting his own duties. Put your own house in order before judging others.

You readily excuse your own faults but refuse to excuse others, when it would be fairer to blame yourself and excuse your neighbour. Getting along with people who are easy to like is simple; living peaceably with the hard, the disorderly, or those who oppose you is the real test, and a rare virtue.

Some people keep peace within themselves and with others, while others disturb both others and themselves. The passage says real peace in this life comes from patiently enduring hardship, not from avoiding it. The one who suffers best has the most peace.

Simplicity and purity are two wings that lift a person above earthly things. Simplicity aims the intention at God and the good of one's neighbour, while purity keeps the desires free from disordered attachment. With a right heart, even the smallest creature shows the goodness of God.

A pure heart sees things clearly and judges the world by what it is inside. Joy is found most by the pure-hearted, while a guilty conscience feels trouble most. A person who turns fully to God is freed from laziness and made new, as iron becomes glowing and loses its rust in fire.

When a person grows lukewarm, meaning less eager in faith, he fears even small hard work and gladly takes comfort from outside things. But once he truly masters himself and steadily follows God, he regards as nothing the troubles that once seemed heavy to him.

We should not trust ourselves much, since we often lack grace and understanding and fail to see our own faults. We are quick to notice wrongs done to us and slow to notice the wrongs we do to others. Someone who judged his own actions honestly would not judge others harshly.

A person who is truly spiritual puts attention on his own inner state before anything else, and does not dwell on other people's affairs. Peace and unity, the passage says, come from turning away from outside concerns and looking closely at oneself.

The passage teaches that a person makes spiritual progress by keeping free of worldly concerns and not valuing anything of the world above God. Comfort that comes from created things should be regarded as empty. Only God, who is eternal and fills all things, gives the soul true rest and joy.

A good conscience brings lasting joy and inner peace, even in hard times, while a guilty conscience brings fear and unrest. The passage says the wicked cannot have true peace, even if they claim they are safe, because God's judgment will come on them.

Glorying in suffering is not hard for someone who loves Christ, because it is a glorying in the Cross. Worldly glory is brief and brings sadness with it. The real glory of a good person lies in their own conscience, not in what others say, and it comes from God. Someone who cares for neither praise nor blame has great inner peace.

A person with a clear conscience stays calm and at peace. Praise does not make them holier, and blame does not make them worse, because what counts is what they are before God. God judges the heart and the intent, not outward appearance or deeds, so a humble person does good and thinks little of themselves.

A person who does not look for outside approval of himself shows that he has fully given himself to God. Quoting Paul, the passage says that approval comes not from self-praise but from being commended by the Lord. Such a person walks inwardly with God and is not held by outward attachments.

Loving Jesus above everything else is presented as the only lasting love. Love for created things is unreliable and will fail, while Jesus stays faithful, and one must in the end give up everything else anyway.

Hold fast to Jesus in life and death, and rely on his faithfulness, since he alone can help when others fail. He wants the heart to himself and will not share it with rivals. Trust placed in people rather than in Jesus is nearly wasted, because human help is as weak and short-lived as grass.

Looking only at how people appear on the outside leads to being fooled, and seeking comfort or gain from others often brings loss. Whoever seeks Jesus in everything will find him, while whoever seeks only himself will find himself, to his own harm.

When Jesus is felt to be present, everything seems easy; when he is absent, everything seems hard and comfort means nothing. Even a single word from him brings great comfort. The writer says that to lose him, or to want anything more than him, is a greater loss than losing the whole world.

Without Jesus, the world offers nothing of real value, and life without him is the worst state. Being close to Jesus brings the greatest good, so the one who has him is rich and the one who lacks him is poor.

The passage says that keeping Jesus close depends on humility, peace and a godly, quiet life, and that turning to worldly things drives him away. Without Jesus as a friend, a person is sad and alone, so Jesus should be loved above all others.

Everyone should be loved for Jesus' sake, but Jesus should be loved for his own sake, since he alone is good and faithful above all friends. The writer adds that a person should not seek special praise or love, because that belongs to God alone, and should let Jesus live in them and in every good person.

A person must keep the heart pure and free from attachment to created things, and can reach union with God only through God's grace. When that grace is present a person can do all things, and when it leaves, the person feels weak and troubled. In those times the person should not despair but rest calmly in God's will, knowing that hard times pass, as winter gives way to summer.

It is easy to be content when God's comfort is felt. The real achievement is to bear the loss of both human and divine comfort, and to serve God without seeking one's own reward. Feeling joy when grace comes is nothing remarkable, since anyone would be glad then.

People tend to want comfort, and it is hard to free oneself from self-interest. The martyr Laurence gave up his love of the world and of his priest Sixtus, whom he was then made to lose, choosing God's will over human comfort. The passage urges the reader to give up a dear friend for God's sake, and not to resent being left by a friend, since all people must part in the end.

A person must struggle for a long time to rise above self-interest and turn all their love toward God. When someone relies on themselves, they easily fall back on worldly comforts. A true follower of Christ, however, does not seek such pleasant comforts but prefers hard tasks and difficult labours for Christ.

When God gives spiritual comfort, the believer should accept it thankfully, as a gift and not something earned, and stay humble and careful. When comfort is taken away, the believer should not despair but wait patiently, since God can restore it, as happened to earlier saints and prophets.

When God's favour was present, the speaker felt secure and said he would never be moved. When that favour withdrew, he felt troubled, yet he did not despair. Instead he prayed more earnestly and found that he was heard and helped.

Even the great saints knew times of joy and times of dryness, so people who are poor and needy should not despair when their feeling of warmth comes and goes. The Spirit comes and goes as God wills, and Job speaks of God testing him suddenly after a morning visit.

When the speaker feels abandoned by God, nothing else gives real hope or help. Not good friends, holy books, or hymns, however pleasant they are. He concludes that the best remedy is patience, giving up self-will, and remaining in God's will.

Even the most devout people, the author says, sometimes lose God's favour and feel cold in their devotion, and no saint has been spared temptation. Temptation comes before the comfort of God, and those who are tested this way are promised heavenly comfort, as a biblical verse about the tree of life is quoted to show.

Spiritual comfort from God is given to make a person stronger against hardship. Temptation follows so that the person does not become proud over the gift. The devil never rests and the body is not yet dead, so the person must keep preparing for struggle, since enemies are always close.

Human beings are born to work and suffer, so one should prepare for patience and the cross rather than seek rest. Spiritual comfort is the greatest joy, far above worldly pleasures, but it cannot be had at will, because temptation returns after a while.

Spiritual comfort from God is very different from a false sense of freedom or self-confidence. God gives this grace freely, but people fail when they do not thank him for it at once. Gifts of grace stop flowing to those who are ungrateful. Grace stays with the grateful and is taken from the proud, who would otherwise receive it as the humble do.

The speaker does not want comfort that removes his sense of guilt, or spiritual insight that leads to pride, since not everything high, sweet, or dear is holy or pleasing to God. He welcomes grace that makes him humbler and more ready to give up self-will. When grace is withdrawn, he should credit God with any good and accept blame for his own faults.

The highest holy people see themselves as the least, and the greater they are, the humbler they become. Resting on God, they are not proud, and they give all their good to God, seeking only the glory that comes from God and wanting God praised above all.

Be grateful for even the smallest gift, because it comes from God, and gifts from God are never truly small. Even punishment should be accepted with thanks, since God allows it for our good. Whoever wants to keep God's favour should give thanks for what he has, accept its loss patiently, pray for its return, and stay humble and careful not to lose it.

Many people love Jesus and his heavenly kingdom, but few are willing to suffer for him. They want his comforts and his gifts, but they turn away from hardship. When he seems distant or withdraws, they complain or sink into deep discouragement.

Those who love Jesus for his own sake, not for the comfort they get from him, praise him in suffering and distress as if it were the greatest comfort. Even if he never gave them comfort, they would still praise and thank him.

Pure love of Jesus, free of any wish for personal gain, is described as very powerful. The writer asks why those who always look for comfort or advantage are not called paid workers, since they seem to love themselves more than Christ. He asks who can be found who will serve God with nothing expected in return.

Very few people are free enough of self-interest to be truly spiritual. The author asks who can be truly poor in spirit and free of all created things, and says such a person is rare, hard to find. Giving away goods, doing penance, or having great knowledge are each described as small or distant by comparison.

The passage says that even a person with great virtue and devotion still lacks the most necessary thing. That thing is to give up oneself completely, keeping no self-love, and to feel after doing all one's duty that one has done nothing.

A person should not think much of his own good deeds, even if others might praise them. He should see himself as an unworthy servant, as Christ taught, and so be poor and empty in spirit. Yet such a person is, in fact, richer, stronger and freer than anyone else.

Many find Christ's call to deny oneself and take up the Cross hard to hear. The author argues that it is far harder to hear the words of final judgment, sending the wicked away to eternal fire. Those who accept the Cross now will not fear that judgment, and they will approach Christ the Judge with confidence.

The passage urges the reader not to fear taking up the cross, meaning hardship and suffering for Christ, because it leads to God's kingdom. It says that health, life, strength, joy and holiness of the soul are found only in the cross. Following Jesus, who bore his own cross and died on it, the reader will share in his life and glory.

Everything depends on the cross and on dying to self, and there is no other route to life or true inner peace than the daily discipline of the cross. Whatever path a person chooses, they will still find something to suffer, whether in body or in spirit, so they will always find their cross.

Sometimes God seems to abandon the reader, other people trouble them, and they grow weary of themselves, with no comfort or relief available. They must endure this for as long as God wills, learning to suffer without consolation and to become more humble. Only someone who has suffered in a similar way truly understands Christ's Passion.

The cross of suffering is always close by and cannot be escaped by moving somewhere else, since a person carries himself wherever he goes. Whether one looks up, down, outward or inward, it is found there. To keep inner peace and gain the eternal crown, one must be patient everywhere.

Accepting one's suffering willingly makes it easier to carry, and it leads to an end of suffering, though not in this life. Bearing it unwillingly makes the load heavier, yet it must still be carried. Rejecting one hardship only brings another, possibly harder.

No person in history has avoided suffering and hardship, and Christ himself suffered throughout his life. The passage asks why anyone would look for another path than the way of the cross, which it calls the royal way.

Christ's whole life was marked by the cross and suffering, so the speaker says it is wrong to look for rest and joy in this life instead of expecting trouble. Human life on earth is full of hardship, and the more spiritually advanced a person becomes, the heavier their crosses tend to be, because their longing for God grows stronger.

A person who suffers in many ways still finds comfort, because he sees good growing in him from carrying his cross. When he accepts his suffering willingly, it becomes a sign of God's comfort, and as the body weakens, the spirit grows stronger through inner grace.

A devout person can come to desire suffering and hardship, out of love for the Cross of Christ. He believes he will be more pleasing to God the heavier the burdens he bears for Him. The author says this is not human strength but the grace of Christ, which makes the weak flesh love what it would naturally avoid.

Humans cannot manage the hard demands of the Christian life, such as bearing the cross, accepting insults, and wanting no worldly success, by their own strength. The passage says that if a person trusts in the Lord, God gives the needed endurance, and with faith and the sign of the cross, even the devil need not be feared.

Christians should be ready to bravely carry the cross of Christ, who was crucified for them out of love. The passage says that hardship and sorrow will come in this life wherever a person goes, and the only way to face them is to bear them patiently.

Accept suffering willingly as the cup of Christ if you want to share his lot. Leave comfort to God to give as he sees fit, and treat hardships as the best comfort. The present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come, even if they were endured in full.

When a person finds suffering for Christ's sake sweet and pleasant, the passage says, that person may count himself well off, since he has found a kind of paradise on earth. While suffering still feels hard and the person wants to escape it, things are not well, and troubles will keep following him wherever he goes.

Suffering and dying are what the reader should accept, and doing so will bring peace. Even a person who experienced great spiritual visions, like Paul, is not free from suffering. Anyone who wants to love and serve Jesus must expect to suffer.

The speaker wishes the reader were worthy to suffer something for the name of Jesus, since such suffering would bring great glory, joy among the saints, and a good example to others. He notes that many people praise patience but few practise it. He argues that a little suffering for Christ is fitting, given that many endure heavier hardships for worldly reasons.

The passage says that a Christian should live as if dying to self, and that the more a person gives up their own will, the more they turn toward God. Accepting hardships willingly for Christ is presented as more pleasing to God and more useful than seeking comfort, because spiritual growth comes through suffering rather than pleasure.

Christ would have shown any better path to human good than suffering, and He told His followers to take up their cross. The passage concludes that entering God's kingdom requires much tribulation, or hardship.

The speaker resolves to listen for what God says inwardly, and calls blessed the soul that hears God's inner voice and turns away from the noise of the world. It is the inner teaching of truth, not outward sounds or sights, that matters here.

Those who look inward and train themselves daily to receive spiritual truths are called blessed, as are those who want time for God and free themselves from worldly distractions. The speaker urges the soul to close the door on physical desires so that it can hear what God says inside it.

Christ, speaking to the faithful soul, says that He is salvation, peace and life, and that peace is found by staying close to Him. The soul is told to set aside passing things, since they are deceptive, and to devote itself to the Creator so it can reach true blessedness.

The speaker asks God to speak to him directly, not through Moses or the prophets. He recalls how the Israelites asked Moses to speak for God because they feared God's own voice would kill them. The speaker rejects that request and copies the young Samuel's words, "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." He says God alone can fill him with knowledge, and the prophets are of no use without God.

Human teachers can speak, explain and give outward instruction, but only God gives the inner spirit, understanding, strength and growth. Words alone do not change the heart; God does that work within the listener.

The speaker asks God, not Moses, to speak to him directly. He fears that hearing good words from outside, without being moved inwardly, will leave him fruitless and will count against him at judgment. He asks God to speak so that his soul may be comforted and his life changed.

Christ speaks to the reader, saying that his words are sweeter and worth more than human learning. They give life and cannot be measured by human understanding, so they should be received quietly, humbly and with love, not used to win praise. The speaker then calls blessed the person taught by the Lord, who finds rest in hard times.

The Lord says He has always spoken to people, but many refuse to hear Him. They prefer the world and their own desires. The world offers small, short-lived rewards and people serve it eagerly, while God offers great, eternal rewards and people respond slowly. He asks who serves Him as carefully as people serve the world and its rulers.

People will travel far and work hard for small rewards, such as a coin or a worthless promise. Yet for eternal life, many will hardly make the effort of lifting a foot. The passage points out this contrast in what people are willing to work for.

Christians who seek worldly pleasure, though they find it empty, are shown to work harder for it than the reader does for eternal good, and they are rebuked for this. The speaker promises that God never fails those who trust him and remain faithful to the end, and that he rewards all who are godly.

Christ, speaking in this passage, tells the reader to keep his words in mind, because they will be needed during temptation. He says he tests his chosen people through both temptation and comfort, and teaches them through rebuke and encouragement. Whoever has his words and rejects them will be judged by them on the last day.

The speaker addresses God, calling himself nothing, with nothing, and able to do nothing, and far lower than he can say. He asks God to remember his weakness, to fill his heart with grace, since God alone is good and fills all things.

The speaker asks how they can bear this hard life without God's mercy and grace to strengthen them. They beg God not to turn away or delay his help, and ask to be taught to do God's will and walk humbly before him, since God knows them completely, even from before their birth.

God tells the speaker to walk before him in truth and to seek him with a simple heart. Those who live in truth are protected from evil attacks and from the schemes and lies of wicked people, and they need not care about empty talk. The speaker asks that truth teach, keep and free him from wrong desires, so he can live with great freedom of heart.

Here, Truth (a name for God in the passage) teaches that a person should feel deep regret for their sins and never take pride in their good deeds. The person is a sinner, weak and easily overcome, so they have nothing to boast about and should see themselves as lowly.

Only what is eternal, such as God's truth, should be counted great or desirable. A person should dislike their own faults and sins more than any material loss. Those who pursue curiosity and pride, trying to learn God's hidden matters while neglecting their own salvation, often fall into serious sin, and God opposes them.

Stop trying to probe God's hidden works and instead examine your own sins and the good you have neglected. The passage adds that some people show devotion only through books, pictures or outward signs, or speak of God with their mouths while their hearts are far from him.

Some people, whose minds are enlightened and whose desires are purified, constantly long for eternal things. They dislike hearing about earthly matters and meet bodily needs only with reluctance. They understand that the Spirit of truth is teaching them to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones.

The speaker praises God the Father for remembering him despite his unworthiness, and for giving comfort when he does not deserve it. He says that when God enters his heart he rejoices, and he calls God his glory, his joy, his hope and his refuge in trouble.

The speaker admits that his love and virtue are still weak and incomplete. He asks God to visit him often, teach him, free him from harmful passions, and cleanse his heart, so that he can love, suffer, and endure with steadiness.

Love is presented as the greatest good, one that makes heavy burdens light and smooths out unevenness. It makes hard things sweet, moves a person to great deeds and to seeking greater perfection, and refuses to be held down by anything lowly.

Love should stay free of worldly attachments, so that good times and hard times cannot cloud its sight or hold it back. Love is described as the sweetest, strongest and highest thing, born of God, and it finds rest only in God above all created things.

Love is described as free, swift and joyful. A person who loves gives everything, rests in God, who is the source of all good, and asks for no reward. Love does not count its burdens or admit impossibility, so it achieves what someone without love fails to do.

Love, the passage says, stays alert even when asleep, and it does not tire, give way to force, or panic. Like a flame, it rises up and prevails. A loving person understands this inner cry, which is a strong appeal to God: "My God, my Beloved! Thou art all mine, and I am all Thine."

The speaker prays to be filled with love for God. He asks to feel love deeply, to be lifted above himself, and to love God more than himself. He also asks to love other people through their love for God.

Love is described as a list of qualities: quick, sincere, gentle, patient, humble, and obedient to authority. It is also said never to seek its own advantage, since a person who seeks their own gain falls away from love. The passage ends by saying that love cannot be lived without sorrow, even when God seems hidden.

A person who is not willing to bear all things and to accept the Beloved's will (meaning God's will) cannot rightly be called a lover of God. A true lover should willingly take on hard and bitter things for God's sake, and should not turn away from God because of troubles that come along.

The passage describes the true lover of God as one who stays firm under hardship and does not give up or seek easy comfort. Such a lover values the giver above the gifts, and wants God Himself rather than His rewards. Whether times are good or bad, the lover keeps the same devotion.

Even when your thoughts of God and the saints are weaker than they should be, nothing is lost. Warm feelings of devotion are gifts of grace that come and go, so one should not rely on them too much. Resisting bad thoughts and the devil's temptations is what shows real virtue and earns great merit.

Do not let strange thoughts disturb you, wherever they come from. Keep your purpose and good intentions toward God steady. Sudden moments of rapture followed by a return to ordinary vain thoughts are not a deception. Since you resist them and they displease you, they count as merit, not loss.

The old enemy, meaning the devil, tries to stop the reader from seeking good and from every religious practice. These include thinking on the saints, remembering Christ's suffering, recalling sin, guarding the heart, and growing in virtue. He sends evil thoughts to cause weariness and fear, so that the reader turns away from prayer and reading the Scriptures.

The passage advises a believer to resist the inner voice that discourages confession and Communion and that puts evil or impure thoughts into the mind. Such thoughts are to be counted as coming from the tempter, and the believer is to reject them with firm words, ordering the spirit to leave.

The speaker says that Jesus will stand with him like a strong warrior, so the enemy will be put to shame. He refuses to give in to the tempter, even if it means death, and tells the tempter to be silent. He ends by saying that the Lord is his light, salvation, strength and Redeemer, so he has no fear.

Keep fighting bravely even when you fail through weakness, trusting in greater grace. Beware of vain confidence and pride, because many who lift themselves up foolishly are led into error and fall into a nearly irreversible blindness. Let their ruin remind you to stay humble.

The passage advises keeping a sense of spiritual closeness to God private, not boasting about it or trusting it too much, and staying humble, as if one did not deserve it. It warns that such feelings can quickly fade, so one should remember how poor one is when that grace is absent.

Spiritual growth does not depend only on receiving comfort from God. It also means accepting, humbly and patiently, when that comfort is taken away. The person should keep praying, keep doing their regular duties with more effort, and not neglect themselves while feeling dry and anxious.

People who meet hardship often become impatient or lazy, yet a person cannot control his own spiritual comfort. God gives and withholds comfort as He chooses. Others who felt too confident in their inner devotion ruined themselves by attempting more than they could do, following feeling rather than sound judgment.

Those who overreached and claimed more than pleased God quickly lost his favor, and were brought low so they would stop relying on their own strength and trust in God instead. Beginners in the Christian way, the passage adds, can easily be misled unless they follow the advice of wise people.

If people insist on their own ideas instead of trusting others' experience, it will harm them. Those who think themselves wise rarely accept being guided by others. Modest, limited wisdom is better than great learning joined with vanity.

It is better to have little of what could make you proud than a lot. Someone who gives himself fully to joy, forgetting his weakness and his reverent fear of losing God's grace, does not act wisely. Likewise, someone who despairs in hardship and trusts God less than he should is not acting with proper strength.

The passage warns that someone who feels too safe in good times will be anxious and weak when trouble comes. It advises staying humble and self-controlled, and remembering that when spiritual warmth fades, it may return. The loss of comfort can be useful, even more so than constant good fortune.

A person's worth before God is not measured by visions, comforts, scriptural learning, or high rank. It is measured by true humility, by love of God, by seeking God's honour alone, and by being glad to be looked down on rather than praised.

The speaker addresses God as someone who is only dust and ashes. If he thinks well of himself, God stands against him, and his sins prove the case so he cannot deny it. If he humbles himself completely and gives up all pride, God's grace and light will draw near to him, and any remaining self-esteem will be swallowed up and destroyed.

The speaker says that when left to himself he is nothing and weak, but when God looks upon him he becomes strong and joyful. He wonders at being lifted up and embraced by God, since his own weight always drags him down toward the depths.

The speaker thanks God for love that comes first, helps in many needs and saves from many dangers. By loving himself wrongly he lost himself, but by loving God alone he found both himself and God. Through this love he has come to feel himself even more worthless, because God treats him far better than he deserves.

The speaker praises God for continuing to give good things even to people who are unthankful or have turned away from him. He then asks God to turn people back to him, so that they become grateful, humble and devout, since God is their salvation, courage and strength.

God, speaking to the reader as "my Son," says that He must be the highest and final aim of a person who wants true happiness. A person's love is purified when it is directed toward God rather than toward oneself or created things. Every blessing should be seen as coming from God, the source of all good.

God is the source of all good, and anyone can receive it from him whatever their rank or wealth. A person who takes pride in their own goodness, apart from God, will not find lasting joy but will be troubled. So a person should credit all good to God, who gave it and will ask for thanks in return.

Where truth and divine love fill a person, boasting, envy, self-love and a narrowed heart fall away. Such a person, if wise, finds joy and hope in God alone, who alone is good and is to be praised above all things.

The speaker addresses God directly and praises his goodness, especially toward those who love and serve him. He says that the sweetness of contemplating God is beyond words. He notes that God created him when he did not exist, brought him back after he had wandered away, and commanded him to love God.

The speaker addresses God with thanks. God has shown mercy and grace to someone who had fallen into ruin and does not deserve it. The speaker says serving God is no great thing, since every creature owes that service. What seems wonderful is that God accepts such an unworthy person among his chosen servants.

The speaker says that everything they have belongs to God and is offered back to him. Yet God is the one who truly serves people: he made heaven, earth and the angels for their use. Greater still, God promised to give himself to them.

The speaker asks how to repay God for his many mercies. He wishes he could serve God all his life, or even one day, in a way worthy of God. He calls himself God's poor servant, bound to serve with all his strength, and asks God to supply whatever he lacks.

Serving God and giving up everything for his sake is described as a great honour. Those who choose this willingly, leaving behind worldly pleasures and cares, will receive great grace, comfort from the Holy Spirit, and freedom of spirit.

Serving God is praised here as a pleasant and freeing way of life. The writer says it makes a person free and holy, puts a religious servant on the level of the angels, and leads to a lasting joy and the highest good.

Here the speaker, in the voice of God, tells the reader to bring their desires under God's will rather than their own. The reader should look at whether their urges serve their own ends more than God's honour. If they seek God alone, they will accept whatever God decides, but any hidden personal aim becomes a burden that holds them back.

Do not rush after a desire you have formed without seeking guidance. A desire that seems good may later bring regret, so not every good-seeming wish should be followed at once. Even good desires sometimes need to be held back, to avoid restlessness, bad example, or confusion when others resist.

Sometimes a person must use force against physical desires and not ask what the body wants. The body should be made to obey the spirit, even against its will, until it accepts little, enjoys simple things, and complains about no hardship.

The speaker prays to God, saying that patience is badly needed, because many things in life go against what they want. However carefully they plan for peace, their life cannot go on without conflict and trouble.

Christ tells the reader that true peace does not mean being free from trouble. A person finds peace by enduring many trials and hardships with courage. Since present suffering is less than eternal punishment, one should bear it bravely for God's sake. Even the most prosperous people of the world suffer too.

Even if people get what they want, it does not last. Worldly riches fade like smoke, and their past joys leave no trace. Even while alive, the rich find no rest, only bitterness, weariness and fear, because the very things that please them bring sorrow. Their pursuit of pleasure without limit leads to confusion and bitterness.

Worldly pleasures are short, false and wicked, the passage says. People, blind and foolish, chase them like beasts and so bring death to their souls. The reader is told to resist their desires and to find delight in the Lord, who will grant the heart's desire.

Christ tells the reader that real comfort comes from rejecting worldly things and empty pleasures, and from turning away from creature comforts. The first steps are hard, because old habits resist, the body complains, and the tempter attacks. These are overcome by better habits, inner zeal, prayer, and useful work.

The passage says that a person who refuses to obey those set over him loses God's grace and the shared good that others enjoy. Refusing to submit freely shows that the self's desires are not yet under control, so the person should learn quickly to obey, if he wants to bring his own nature under control.

The main point is that a person's worst enemy is their own self-love, not an outside foe. Outward enemies are easily beaten once the inner self is humbled. The reader must not fully despise themselves, yet they resist giving way to others because they love themselves too much.

Speaking as Christ, this passage asks why a humble person should find it hard to submit to others, since Christ, the all-powerful God, humbled himself for human sake. It tells the human, called dust and clay, to learn obedience, humility and the control of his passions.

Be fiercely against your own pride and accept being looked down on, even being trampled like mud in the street. The speaker says the reader has sinned often and deserves hell, yet God has spared him out of love, so he should be humble and patiently bear the contempt he deserves.

The speaker feels great fear before God's judgment. He reasons that if God did not spare the angels, and even fallen stars, then he, who is only dust, has no grounds for confidence. He notes that people once thought highly of their deeds later fell into deep disgrace.

Holiness, wisdom, strength and purity count for nothing unless God keeps them in place. Left on their own, people fall and perish, but when God visits them they are lifted up and live. Without God's help, they are unsteady and grow cold, and only His help makes them strong and warm again.

The speaker feels that, before God, he has no real worth of his own and is nothing at all. He asks where any pride or confidence from his virtues could remain, since all empty glory is swallowed up by God's judgments against him.
A person whose heart is truly humbled before God cannot be lifted up by empty talk or by the praise of others. Human speakers are nothing, since their words fade, but the Lord's truth lasts forever.

The passage advises the reader to pray in every matter, leaving the outcome to God. Each request should end with a willingness to have it denied if God sees it as harmful to the soul. It also warns that a strong desire may come from a good spirit, an evil spirit, or one's own mind, and that it is hard to tell which, so some who began well were later misled.

Whatever a person wants, they should seek it with reverence and humility, and leave the outcome to God. The speaker asks God to decide what is best, to place them wherever God wills, and says they wish to live for God rather than for themselves.

The speaker asks Jesus for grace so that his own desires, choices and refusals match God's will. He wants his will to follow God's will so closely that he could not choose or reject anything except as God wills.

The speaker asks God for two things: to be free of worldly desires, even accepting being despised and unknown for God's sake, and to rest in God alone, since only God brings true peace of heart. Everything else is described as hard and restless without God.

The speaker says that real comfort is not found in worldly things but in God and in the future life. Even all the pleasures of this world would not last. Worldly things should be used, while eternal things should be desired. The soul was made for more than temporary goods, so it cannot be satisfied by them.

Even with every good thing that has been created, a person cannot be truly happy. Real blessedness is found only in God, the creator of all things. Human comfort is empty and short-lived, while the true comfort is felt inwardly and comes from truth.

A devout person carries Jesus with him everywhere as his source of comfort. He prays that Jesus will stay with him, and that he can accept losing human comfort. If divine comfort is withheld, he asks that God's will remain his highest comfort, trusting that God will not rebuke or stay angry forever.
God tells the reader to let him act as he wishes, because God knows what is good for them. The reader is said to judge by human feelings and ordinary human reasoning, which can mislead them.

The speaker tells God that God cares for him more than he can care for himself. He says that a person who does not hand all his worries over to God stands on unsafe ground. Whatever God does, whether it brings darkness, light, comfort or trouble, the speaker accepts it as good, so long as his will stays firm in God.
To walk with God, the speaker says, one must be ready equally for suffering or joy, and willing to be poor as readily as rich.

The speaker says they will willingly accept whatever God sends, good or bad, and thank God for it. They ask only to be kept from sin and not cast off from God's book of life. With that, no trouble can harm them.

Speaking as Christ, this passage says he came down from heaven to save people and chose to share their troubles out of love. It says he endured sorrow, poverty, insults, ingratitude and rejection from birth to his death, so that people might learn patience in hardship.

The speaker prays to Christ. Because Christ was patient during his life, following his Father's command, the speaker says it is right for a sinner to bear patiently the burden of this mortal life, for as long as God wills, as a means to salvation.

Although life still feels heavy, the speaker says it is now full of merit through God's grace, and easier to bear through Christ's example and the lives of the saints. Life is also more comforting than it was under the Old Testament, when heaven's gate was shut and few sought it.

Even people who lived justly and were on the path to salvation could not enter the kingdom of heaven before Christ's suffering and death. The passage says that his Passion and death made that entry possible.

The speaker thanks Christ for showing the faithful the right road to God's eternal kingdom. Christ's way is the path the believer walks, with patience, toward him. The speaker admits that, even having heard Christ's teaching and seen his signs, they are still lukewarm, and asks how they could follow without his example to guide them.

Christ tells the reader to stop complaining and think of his own suffering and that of the saints, who endured far more. Because others suffered more, the reader should bear smaller troubles more easily. Whether the troubles seem small or great, they should be borne patiently.

Patience is worth more the more you work at it, and it becomes easier with practice. The passage rejects the idea of bearing hurt from some people but not from others, since that judges by who the offender is and what was done to you, rather than by the value of patience itself and the one who rewards it.

The passage says that a person is not truly patient if they will only endure hurts that seem right to them or that come from people they choose. A truly patient person accepts suffering from anyone, whether superior, equal, inferior, good, or wicked, as coming from God, and counts it a gain, since nothing borne for God's sake goes unrewarded.
To gain the reward of patience, a person must be ready to struggle and endure hardship. Refusing to suffer means refusing the crown, and rest and victory come only through labour and fighting.

The speaker asks God to make possible, by grace, what seems impossible by nature: to bear hardship well. He admits he is weak and quickly discouraged when trouble comes. He prays that any trial may become welcome to him, since suffering for God's sake is very good for the soul.

The speaker confesses to God that small things often knock him down and make him sad. He resolves to stand firm, but even a slight temptation throws him into great difficulty. Sometimes a minor matter starts a serious temptation, and he is nearly overcome by something as slight as a puff of wind.

The speaker prays to God, admitting his weakness and his frailty. He says he is easily pulled into sin and struggles daily against his passions. Unwanted, hateful thoughts come to him far more easily than they leave.

The speaker asks God to look on his struggle and give him strength. He wants heavenly strength so that the weak, sinful human body does not gain control over him, and he must keep fighting this as long as he lives. He then complains that life is full of troubles and enemies, and one trial is followed quickly by another.

Human life is full of bitterness, suffering and death, so it is hard to see why it should be loved or even called life. The world is often blamed for being deceitful and empty, yet people hold on to it because fleshly desires rule them. Some things draw a person toward the world, while the punishments and miseries that follow from those same things produce hatred and weariness of it.

A mind that is attached to the world takes its misery for happiness, because it cannot taste God's sweetness or the inner beauty of virtue. Those who fully reject the world and live for God know that divine sweetness is promised to them, and they see how badly the world errs.

The speaker asks to find their rest in God, placing him above everything else. The list names health, beauty, honour, power, knowledge, riches, joy, praise, hope, and even the gifts and joys the mind can feel, and says God is greater than all of them.
The passage says that God is greater than all created beings: angels, archangels, the heavenly host, and everything seen or unseen. In short, God is above anything that is not God.

The speaker says God alone is supreme, complete and lovely above all things. Any gift from God, or any promise about God, falls short while God is not seen or fully possessed. The heart can rest only in God, going beyond all gifts and creatures.

The speaker asks Christ when he will be free enough to rest fully in God. He longs to be completely absorbed in God's love, to lose awareness of himself, and to know God beyond the ordinary limits of the senses.

The speaker says he often groans and suffers in sorrow because many troubles in this world weigh on him. These troubles keep him from freely approaching God and from the close fellowship that blessed spirits enjoy. He asks God to hear his deep sighs and his loneliness on earth.
The speaker prays to Jesus, feeling lost, empty and trapped without him. He asks Jesus to come, bring joy, free him, and show his loving face, since only Jesus can give him relief and happiness.

The speaker says that other people may seek other things, but for him only God pleases. He will keep asking until God's grace returns and God speaks to him inwardly. He then imagines God's answer: God has come to him because of his tears, longing, humility and contrition.

The speaker says he has called on God and longs to enjoy him, ready to give up everything for him. He thanks God for first drawing him to seek God, and then humbles himself, remembering his own sin. He ends by praising God's works, judgments and govern of all things.

The speaker asks God to open his heart to God's law and to teach him to follow God's commands. He wants to understand God's will and remember God's gifts so he can thank God properly. He admits he cannot give enough thanks even for the smallest of God's mercies, and feels overwhelmed when he considers God's greatness.

Every gift a person has, of body, soul, or fortune, comes from God, so nothing is owed to one's own merit. Whoever has received more should not boast or look down on others. The one who credits himself least, gives thanks most humbly, and sees himself as least worthy is the one best prepared to receive greater gifts.

Someone who has received fewer gifts should not feel discouraged, resentful, or envious of those who have more. Instead, they should look to God and praise his goodness, since God gives freely and impartially and knows what each person deserves.

The writer says it is a benefit to lack the possessions that bring outward praise and worldly regard. A poor and humble person should feel comfort, not grief, because God chose the poor and humble as friends. The apostles, he notes, lived humbly and gladly bore insults for God's sake.

The lover of God should find more joy in God's will and his eternal plan than in any gift given to himself. Such a person should be as content to be the least honoured as to be the greatest, and should value God's will and honour above all benefits.

Doing someone else's will instead of your own, wanting less rather than more, taking the lowest place, and praying that God's will be done are said to bring a person into peace and quiet. The speaker is addressing a son, as in a teacher speaking to a student.

The speaker says that Christ's short teaching holds much in few words and would bring peace if fully kept. Whenever he feels troubled, he finds he has strayed from it. So he asks God for more grace to follow it and reach salvation.

The speaker prays to God for help against troubling thoughts and great fears that weigh on the soul. He asks how to get through them, and recalls God's promise to go ahead of him, straighten the crooked paths and open locked doors. His only comfort is to turn to God in trouble and wait patiently for God's mercy.

The speaker asks Jesus to bring light into his heart, drive out dark thoughts and temptations, and calm his inner conflict. He hopes that, as Jesus once calmed the wind and sea, his heart will be given peace.

The speaker asks God to send light, truth and grace, because without God he feels empty and formless, like barren earth. He asks that his mind, weighed down by sin, be lifted up so that it turns toward heavenly things and no longer takes pleasure in earthly ones.

The speaker asks to be freed from comforts that come from created things, since none of them can fully satisfy the heart. He asks instead to be bound to God by love, because God alone is enough for those who love him, and everything else is empty.

Christ tells the reader not to be nosy about other people or worry over their affairs. The reader is only answerable for their own conduct, while Christ knows everyone's thoughts and intentions. So the reader should leave others to God and keep their own life in peaceful devotion.

Do not worry about having a great reputation, many friends, or people's affection, because these bring distraction and deep sorrow. Instead, look eagerly for the divine presence, open your heart, stay alert in prayer, and be humble in all things.

Christ tells the speaker that his peace is not the peace the world gives. Many people want peace, but not the things that bring true peace. That peace is found with the humble, in patience, and in listening to and following Christ's voice. The speaker then asks what to do.

Be careful about your own words and actions, and aim to please God alone, seeking nothing apart from Him. Do not judge others harshly or interfere in matters that are not yours. Still, never being troubled in heart or body is not possible in this life; it belongs only to eternal rest.

True peace is not proved by feeling no sorrow, having no enemies, or getting everything you want. Strong spiritual warmth and sweetness do not show that a person is specially loved or perfect either. Those things do not show real virtue or spiritual progress.

Giving yourself wholly to God's will, without seeking your own gain in anything, large or small, earthly or heavenly. The aim is to stay calm and thankful alike in good times and bad, treating both as equal.

If a person keeps hope and patience when inner comfort is taken away, accepts the hardship without claiming they do not deserve it, and praises God's will and name, they walk the true path of peace. Such a person can be sure of seeing God's face again with joy.

Coming to a complete contempt of oneself brings great peace of heart, as much as is possible while one is still a wayfaring man, a pilgrim on earth. The verse cited is John 14:27, about Christ's peace.

It is a prayer saying that a perfect person keeps their mind on heavenly things and does not let it drop. Among many worries, they move through life without being anxious, not because they do not care, but because their mind is free and they are not attached to any created thing in an excessive way.

The speaker asks God to keep him from the worries of ordinary life, from bodily needs that could take control of him through pleasure, and from inner troubles that could crush his spirit. He is not asking to be spared worldly vanities, but the burdens that all mortal people carry, which hold his soul back from the freedom of spirit it longs for.

The writer asks God to make worldly comforts bitter to him, because they pull him away from love of eternal things. He prays for strength to resist the flesh, the world and the devil, and asks God to replace earthly pleasure with the Spirit's comfort and love of God's name.

Food, drink, clothing and other bodily needs weigh down a devout spirit. The writer asks for moderation and freedom from strong attachment to them. Giving up necessities is not allowed, since the body must be sustained, but seeking luxuries and mere pleasures is forbidden, lest the flesh overpower the spirit. The writer asks God to guide him so he does not go beyond this.

Give everything up and hold nothing as your own, because self-love does more harm than anything else. Love that is pure and well-ordered will not make you a prisoner of things. Desire only what you can rightly have, and give yourself fully to God.

The speaker, God in this dialogue, asks why the reader wastes energy on worry and needless cares. He says that staying within God's will keeps a person from loss. Seeking one's own advantage or pleasure, in any place, brings no peace, because something will always be missing and someone will always stand in the way.

Real advancement comes not from gaining more of things that help you but from giving them up inwardly, including money, riches, and the desire for honour and praise. A change of place or outward peace does not last without a true inner foundation, which the author says is God, and a person who changes only outwardly will meet the same problems again, even worse.

The speaker asks God for strength, so that the heart is freed from useless worry and is not pulled after desires for things, great or small. He wants to see all things, including himself, as passing away, since everything under the sun is vanity. He calls the person who thinks this way wise.

A prayer for heavenly wisdom, so the writer can seek, find and love God above all else, and understand other things in their right order. He asks for the wisdom to avoid flatterers calmly, and to bear opposition patiently, so he is not swept along by every word and can keep safely on his chosen path.

Do not be upset when others speak badly of you or say things you would rather not hear. You should think even less of yourself than they do, and not weigh passing words too heavily. Keep quiet in hard times, turn inwardly to God, and do not let other people's judgment disturb you.

Your peace should not depend on what other people say about you. Whether they praise or criticize you, you remain the same person. True peace comes from God, and whoever does not try to please others, nor fear displeasing them, finds deep peace. Restless hearts and scattered thoughts come from too much love of approval and empty fear.

The speaker blesses God for sending this trial and asks for rescue from it. He admits he is troubled and cannot escape on his own, so he turns to God for help, patience, and deliverance, trusting that God will bring good out of the suffering.

The speaker accepts that his trouble may be deserved and asks that God's will be done. He hopes to bear it patiently until the storm passes. He trusts that God can take the trouble away or reduce its power, as God has helped him before, and that such relief is easy for God though hard for him.

The main obstacle to heavenly comfort, the passage says, is coming to prayer too slowly. The speaker says people first look for comfort in outward things, and these help little until they learn that only God delivers those who trust in him. Then, after the storm, they are told to take courage, because God will restore all things, and more abundantly.

God speaks to the reader, asking where their faith is and urging them to stand firm, endure patiently, and wait, because relief will come in its time. He says fear and worry about the future only add sorrow, since the day has enough trouble of its own, and fretting over things that may never happen is useless.

Humans are easily fooled by such fancies, and a mind that is still weak is quick to be led astray by the enemy (the devil, in Christian belief). The enemy does not care whether he deceives with true or false means, or whether he pulls a person down through present pleasure or future fear. So the reader should not be troubled or afraid, but trust in God's mercy.

Even when you feel far from God, he may be close, and when things seem almost lost, a chance of gain may be near. A setback does not mean everything is lost. Feelings in the moment should not decide how you judge your situation.

Do not think yourself wholly forsaken when hardship comes or comforts are taken away, because this is the way to the Kingdom of Heaven. Trials are better for God's servants than always having what they want, since they keep a person from pride and from seeking self-pleasure. God gives and takes away as He chooses.

God speaks here as the giver of all good things. Whatever he gives belongs to him, and whatever he takes away is not really the person's own. When he sends grief or trouble, the believer should not be angry or despairing, because God can quickly turn the burden into joy and acts justly.

When hardship comes, a person should not be deeply discouraged but should rejoice and give thanks, even counting it a great joy that God allows suffering. The speaker recalls that Christ sent his disciples not to worldly pleasure, honour or rest, but to struggle, contempt and labour, so that they would bear fruit patiently.

The speaker asks God for more grace so that nothing, neither people nor any other creature, will stop him from coming to God. Anything that holds him back keeps him from flying freely to God. He quotes the psalmist's wish for dove's wings to find rest, and says the freest person is one who wants nothing on earth.

To reach God, a person must rise above all created things and even above self. Only someone freed from all creatures can freely seek divine things. Few manage this, because few can fully separate themselves from things that pass away.

Unless a person is lifted up in spirit, freed from all created things, and fully united to God, any knowledge or possessions count for little. Only God is truly great, and everything else is nothing. Wisdom that comes from God is worth more than learning gained through human study.

Many people want to reach deep prayer and inner stillness, yet they do not do the hard work of self-discipline that leads there. The author faults them for focusing on outward signs and rituals instead of mortifying (denying) their desires. He says they spend great effort on fleeting, worthless things and rarely examine their own inner state.

The author says we act without first examining ourselves, and we do not grieve over how corrupt our inner desires are. Since those desires are corrupt, our actions are corrupt too, because they show a weak inner strength. Good living comes only from a pure heart.

People judge others by outward things, such as deeds, strength, wealth, talent, or skill. They seldom ask about the inner spirit, such as humility, patience, gentleness, or devotion. Nature looks at outward appearance, while grace looks at the heart, and trusts God not to be deceived.

Real freedom, the passage says, comes only when a person fully denies self. Those ruled by wealth, self-love, curiosity, restlessness, or comfort are called slaves. Giving up one's desires, it says, brings rest and understanding.

The speaker, in the voice of Christ addressing a disciple, tells the disciple not to be discouraged or turned aside when hearing about the way of the perfect. Instead, the disciple should be stirred to aim higher, or at least desire that way. He expresses the wish that the disciple would stop loving himself and be ready to obey God and the person set over him as a father.

Speaking as Christ, the passage says that if the reader gives up everything they still hold onto, their life will be joyful and peaceful and they will please God. It urges them to seek heavenly wisdom, which looks down on worldly things, and to set aside earthly wisdom and all pleasures, whether shared or personal.

True heavenly wisdom looks small and ordinary in the eyes of the world. It does not boast or seek fame, and many people praise it only with their words while their hearts stay far from it. Few find it, like a hidden pearl.

Do not trust your feelings, because they keep changing: a person moves between joy and sadness, peace and unrest, devotion and coldness. A wise person stays above these shifts and keeps the aim of the mind fixed on God, so he remains steady.

A person who aims at God with a pure motive keeps steady through hard times. But the aim often gets distracted by pleasant things, and few people are free of seeking their own gain. The example given is the crowd who came to Bethany to see Lazarus rather than Jesus. So the aim must be cleaned and kept fixed on God alone.

The speaker says that God is everything to them and that nothing more is needed. To love the Word (God) rather than the world makes the world sweet, while being without God makes everything wearisome. Anything that pleases, the speaker says, does so only through God's grace and wisdom.

The passage contrasts two kinds of enjoyment. Those who taste God find nothing bitter, while those who seek only worldly pleasure fail to find true wisdom. Enjoying the Creator is said to be very different from enjoying created things, which are only a reflection of God's goodness.

The speaker asks God, the "Light everlasting," to shine into the heart and bring purity, joy and life to the soul, so that it can cling to God. He longs for the time when God will fill him completely. Until then his joy is incomplete, because his old, sinful nature is not yet fully dead and still fights against the spirit.
The speaker asks God, who calms the stormy sea, to rise up and help him. He asks God to scatter those who love war and to show His power, because he has no hope or refuge except in God.

Life offers no lasting safety from temptation. The speaker, presented as God addressing a disciple, says the believer is attacked from every side and must always stay armed with patience and steady devotion to God. Those who keep struggling will be rewarded, while the lazy will face misery.

If you seek rest in this life, you will not gain the eternal rest. Seek patience instead, and find true peace in God alone, not in the world or in people. Accept hardships, sorrows and insults for God's sake, because they build virtue and lead to a heavenly reward.

Spiritual comfort does not come whenever a person wants it. The saints had many griefs, temptations and hard times, and they endured them by trusting in God rather than themselves. The speaker urges the reader to wait, stay firm, and keep faith, promising reward and God's presence in trouble.

Trust firmly in God, and do not be troubled by other people's judgment when your conscience says you are good and innocent. People hold many different opinions, so their opinions cannot be relied on, and it is impossible to please everyone. Even Paul, who tried to please all people in the Lord, cared little about being judged by men.

The passage describes a person who worked hard to help and save others, yet was still judged and despised by some. He left the matter to God and answered his critics with patience and humility. Now and then he did reply, so that his silence would not cause the weak to stumble.

Do not fear a mortal man, who dies and is soon gone. Fear God instead, and trust that men cannot truly harm you. Their words and deeds hurt themselves more, and God will judge them. If you are wronged and humiliated, do not answer in anger; leave justice to God, who can deliver you.

Christ tells the speaker that by giving up their own self-will and self-concern, they will find him and gain more grace. The speaker then asks how often they must give themselves up and in what things they must let go of themselves.

Christ speaks here and asks for complete surrender in every matter, large or small. He says that the person cannot belong to him fully unless they are free, inside and out, from their own will. The sooner and more completely this is done, the better it will be for them.

Some people give themselves up to God only partly, keeping something back because they do not fully trust him. Others start out giving everything, but return to their own ways when tempted. The passage says such people cannot reach true freedom of heart or close fellowship with God unless they fully give themselves up each day.

Christ speaks to the reader, urging them to give themselves fully to him, asking nothing back. Doing so, they will gain inner peace, freedom of heart, and freedom from vain worries, excessive fear, and disordered love.

The main point is that a person should stay inwardly free in every place and task, keeping control over themselves rather than being controlled by outside things. Such a person uses worldly things for good purposes, not clinging to them, because God gave them a purpose.

If you do not judge by outward appearances or by what the senses report, but take each matter to God in prayer, as Moses went into the tabernacle to ask counsel, you will receive a divine answer. Moses always went there to settle his doubts.

When people threaten harm, the passage says one should turn to prayer in the inner heart for help. It points to Joshua, who was tricked by the Gibeonites because he did not ask the Lord for counsel and was too quick to trust their flattering words and false show of piety.

In this passage, God tells the reader to leave his affairs to God, who will arrange them at the right time for his good. The speaker replies that his own planning helps little, and he wishes he did not dwell so much on the future, so he could give himself fully to God's will at once.

A person often works hard for something they want, but once they get it their feelings change, because their desires move quickly from one thing to the next. So resisting the self in small matters is said to be important.

Real spiritual progress comes from denying oneself, and a person who does so is free and safe. The old enemy, the opponent of all good, never stops tempting people and sets traps day and night for the careless. Therefore one must watch and pray, as Christ taught.

Man is nothing and has nothing good of his own. He asks what he has deserved from God, and he admits he has no grounds to complain if God withholds help or refuses to hear him. Without God's inward support, he says, he becomes lukewarm and careless.

God stays the same, always good and wise in all he does. The speaker, by contrast, keeps changing and cannot hold steady. Only God can help him, and if God gives aid, his heart will turn to God and rest in him alone.

If I could truly learn to set aside all human comfort, whether I seek it for devotion or because I am forced to look for help, and no person could console me, then I could rightly trust in God's grace and be glad in new comfort from him.

The speaker thanks God for any good that comes to him, since all good comes from God. He admits that he himself is weak and empty before God, so he has nothing to be proud of. Seeking praise from others is a harmful vanity, because it pulls a person away from true glory, which is God's, and from divine grace.

True glory and joy, the passage says, come from praising God rather than oneself. The speaker asks that God's name and work be honored, not their own, and wants no human praise. Only in weakness will they boast about themselves.

The writer says he wants only the honour that comes from God, not the praise people give one another. Human glory and worldly honour are empty and foolish when set against God's eternal glory, so all praise belongs to the Holy Trinity alone.

If others are honoured and you are looked down on, the speaker advises not to make it your concern. Instead, the reader should turn their heart toward God, and then the scorn of people will not cause sadness.

The speaker admits that people are quick to be deceived by empty pride. He says no creature has ever really wronged him, so he has nothing to complain about before God. Because he has sinned often, he feels that others rightly turn against him. He concludes that he must be willing to be despised, forgotten and counted as nothing if he is to find inner peace and be united to God.

Christ tells the reader that if peace is placed in a person, because that person is admired and close, the reader will become unsteady and tangled up. Peace is found instead in the eternal Truth, so a friend's leaving or death will not cause sadness. Friends should be loved for Christ's sake.

Friendship lasts and is true only when God is part of it, so the speaker says. He advises the reader to be detached from loving human friends, even to prefer being without human company. The closer a person comes to God, the less he relies on earthly comfort, and the lower he sees himself, the higher he rises toward God.

Whoever claims any goodness as his own blocks God's grace, which comes to humble hearts. Emptying oneself of love for creatures lets God pour grace in, and fixing one's eyes on created things hides the Creator. Even small things, loved too much, hold a person back from the highest good.

The speaker, presented as God, tells the reader not to be moved by clever human speech, because God's kingdom lies in power rather than words. His words stir the heart, bring sorrow for sin, and give comfort. Reading should aim at overcoming one's sins, not at looking learned, since that helps more than knowing hard questions.

Learning many things is not the main goal; the reader should keep returning to one basic truth. God teaches people directly and gives plain understanding to the humble, so those who focus on clever questions and neglect serving God are warned. At the coming of Christ as judge, every person's conscience will be examined, hidden things revealed, and empty debate will end.

In this passage, Christ speaks in the first person. He says he can instantly teach a humble person more about eternal truth than years of school study could. He teaches without noise, arguments, or a quest for honour, and he teaches people to value heaven over earthly things and to love him above all.

Christ, speaking in the first person, says that one man learned divine things through love of him and gained more by giving up worldly things than by studying clever arguments. He teaches some people plainly and others through signs or deeper mysteries. Books say the same thing to everyone, but he alone teaches each person inwardly, as he judges fitting.

Ignore many things, and treat yourself as dead to the world. Let go of matters that upset you, and do not argue about other people's opinions. If you are right with God and keep His judgment in mind, you will easily accept being defeated.

The writer complains that people grieve over material losses and work hard for small gains, while losses to the soul are quickly forgotten and seldom repaired. People chase worthless things and neglect what matters most, and unless they quickly pull themselves back, they let themselves settle into outward concerns.

The speaker asks God for help in trouble, because human help is empty. People have often proved unfaithful when trusted, and faithful when least expected. So hope placed in people is vain, and salvation comes from God. The speaker admits that humans are weak and easily changed.

No one can always avoid being caught in trouble, however careful they are. But a person who trusts God and seeks Him sincerely does not fall so easily, and if he is caught, God delivers or comforts him. Human friends who stay faithful in hardship are rare, while God alone is completely faithful.

The speaker admires a holy soul that said its mind was firmly fixed on Christ, and wishes it were so with him. If it were, he says, fear of people and hurtful words would not move him so easily. He then faults himself for not preparing better and for paying too much attention to others.

We are only frail humans, even if others call us angels, so the speaker asks whom to trust and answers that only God is truthful and cannot be deceived. People, by contrast, are liars and unstable, especially in what they say, so even apparently sound words should rarely be believed.

The speaker recalls warnings to beware of people, including those in one's own household, and not to trust claims that the Christ is "here" or "there." Having suffered a loss, the speaker hopes to be more careful and less foolish. Someone's advice to be cautious and keep private what is shared is then quoted.

The speaker says that when he keeps a secret, another person cannot stay quiet and passes it on, betraying both the speaker and himself. He asks the Lord to keep him from such careless talkers, and from becoming one himself. He adds that he must avoid doing to others what he would not want done to him.

It praises keeping quiet about other people, not believing every report or repeating it, and opening one's heart to only a few. It also says a person should seek God as the one who sees the heart, and want everything, inward and outward, to follow God's will rather than being swayed by every word people say.

Keeping away from public praise is a safer way to keep God's grace. It is better to pursue what improves one's life and inner warmth of faith than to seek admiration from others. The writer notes that many people have been harmed when their virtue was publicly known and praised too quickly, and that grace kept quietly hidden in this hard life has proved more valuable.

Harsh words cannot really hurt a person, the speaker says, just as words cannot break a stone. If the listener is guilty, he should want to improve; if not, he should bear the insult for God's sake. Being hurt by such small matters shows that a person still cares too much about what others think.
