The speaker tells the reader that if they flinch from being shamed for their faults, they still care about the world and about pleasing people. He then says that if every cruel word were spoken against them, none of it could really harm them, since it could not even take a single hair from their head.

A person with no inner faith in God is easily hurt by insults, but one who trusts God and does not rely on his own judgment is free from fear of people. God says he knows every secret and every motive. He allows the insult so that hidden thoughts come to light, and he will judge both the guilty and the innocent in the end.

People's opinions about us can be wrong, but God's judgment is always true, even when it is hidden or looks wrong to foolish people. So people should turn to God for judgment rather than rely on others' views. The just person will suffer no real evil, whatever God allows to happen.

A person who is wrongly accused will not worry much about it. Likewise, if others clear his name, he will not become overly proud. He trusts that God judges hearts and inner motives, not outward appearances, and that what people praise may be faulted by God, and the reverse.

The speaker prays to God as judge and asks for strength and trust, because his own conscience is not enough to rely on. He admits he may fail to bear criticism patiently, and asks for forgiveness. Even if he knows of no wrong in himself, he says he is not thereby made right before God, since no one living would be justified without God's mercy.

Christ speaks to the reader, telling them not to be crushed by the hard work or troubles they face for his sake. He promises a reward greater than any measure, and says the hardship will not last long and will soon end. Everything that passes with time is small and brief.

Do your work faithfully, whatever it is, and trust that God will reward it. Hardships such as writing, prayer, silence and suffering are worth bearing for eternal life. The passage promises a future peace with no night, no death and no anxiety, so the believer should not lament or complain about the length of this life.

The passage says that if a person could see the rewards of the saints in heaven, they would humble themselves, prefer serving others to ruling them, and welcome suffering for God's sake. Saints who were despised by the world now rejoice in great glory, so being looked down on by people would seem a gain.

Those who suffer hard things in this life should bear them, since eternal life and the Kingdom of God are worth far more. The speaker tells the listener to look up to heaven, where the saints who endured conflict on earth now rest in peace with Christ.

The writer longs for the heavenly city and its eternal day, which never ends or grows dark, and wishes that this earthly life would end. He says that the saints in heaven enjoy this light fully, while people still on earth see it only faintly, from a distance and as if through glass.

Those in heaven know how glorious the day of eternity is, while people still living on earth, described as exiles, groan under the hardship of this life. The author says this life is short and evil, full of sins, fears, cares, errors, labours and temptations.

The speaker longs for an end to sin, suffering and conflict, and for true freedom and lasting peace. He wants to see Jesus and to be with him in his kingdom. Meanwhile he feels left alone, an exile in a hostile land full of daily wars and misfortunes.

The speaker asks for relief from life on earth, which feels like exile, because his deepest desire is for God. He wants to rest in heavenly things, but his body and worldly desires pull him down. He feels torn between his spirit, which reaches upward, and his flesh, which keeps him low.

The speaker is distracted during prayer: while thinking about heavenly things, worldly and sinful thoughts rush in. He asks God not to turn away, to drive these thoughts off, to free his mind from them, and to bring him back to heaven's sweetness and truth.

The speaker asks to be forgiven when his mind wanders from God during prayer. He admits that his thoughts often carry him away, so that he is not where his body is. His mind goes where he loves, and it readily returns to what he naturally enjoys or is used to.

A person's thoughts follow what they love. If someone loves heaven, they gladly think about heavenly things. If they love the world or the body, they dwell on worldly or bodily things, and what they love shapes what they talk about, hear, and carry in their minds.

Blessed is the person who, for God's sake, gives up all worldly things. He denies his bodily desires with a fervent spirit, so that with a clear conscience he can offer God pure prayer and become worthy to join the angels.

When a person feels a strong longing for eternal happiness, sent from above, and wants to leave this earthly body to see God's glory directly, the voice urges them to open their heart fully and welcome that inspiration with all their desire.

The reader is told to thank God for how kindly God deals with them, visits them, stirs them up and lifts them, so they do not sink into earthly things. The speaker says this gift does not come from their own thinking or effort, but only from God's grace.

The passage gives the purpose of the trials it describes: to help the reader grow in virtue and humility, get ready for further struggles, hold firmly to God with the whole heart, and serve him eagerly. In the book, God is the speaker, addressing the reader as "thee."

Some people's longing for heavenly things is mixed with worldly, selfish desire, so their prayers are not purely for God's glory. The passage says that a desire tainted by one's own self-seeking is not pure or perfect.

Do not seek what pleases or benefits you, but what is pleasing and honourable to God, and accept God's appointment over your own wishes. The speaker knows the listener longs for heaven, but says that time has not yet come. Until God's kingdom arrives, the listener must endure a time of struggle and wait for God, who is the highest good.

The speaker tells the reader that life on earth brings trials and training. Comfort comes only now and then, and full satisfaction is not given. So the reader must be strong and bear what goes against their nature, becoming a new person. They must often do what they do not want, and leave undone what they want to do.

Others succeed, are listened to, and are given honor and responsibility, while the speaker is ignored, gets nothing he asks for, and is judged useless. The speaker is describing a life where others gain what he is denied.

Human nature will sometimes feel sad, and it is good to bear that sadness quietly. The true servant of God is tested most by how far he can deny himself and submit, especially when he must obey orders he thinks useless or unwise, and give up his own opinion.

Christ tells the reader to think about the result of their hardships: a quick end and a very great reward. Bearing these burdens will then feel easy, and will comfort their patience. Giving up a small desire on earth will be repaid with having their will fulfilled in Heaven, where all good is held without fear of loss and nothing is wanted for oneself.

In the life to come, nothing will oppose or hinder the faithful person, and all they desire will be given to them in full. Suffering and scorn borne on earth will be repaid with honour and a throne in the Kingdom, and obedience, repentance and humility will be rewarded.

Accept requests from anyone, whether superior, inferior, or equal, and try willingly to meet them, without worrying about who gave the order. Let others seek praise for their own achievements, but find joy only in humbling yourself and in pleasing God, so that God is glorified through your life or death.

The speaker prays to God, praising him and giving him all credit. He says that his joy, hope and worth come from God alone, not from himself or others. He admits that he is poor, sorrowful and sometimes troubled by coming suffering.

The speaker longs for the peace and comfort that come from God, and says that when God gives joy, his soul sings praise. When God withdraws, he cannot easily keep God's commands. Instead he grieves and kneels, because his earlier sense of God's light and protection is gone.

The speaker prays to God, accepting that the hour of testing has come. He says it is right that he suffers for God's sake for a short time. He will be humbled and seem to fail in others' eyes, but he will rise again and be glorified. He accepts that God has ordained this.

The speaker says that suffering for God's sake is a sign of favour, and that nothing happens on earth without God's will or purpose. Trouble has taught him humility, so he turns to God for comfort rather than to people. He accepts that God's judgment is hidden from him, but he trusts that it is always just.

The speaker thanks God for not sparing him from sin but punishing him with loving blows, painful trials, and troubles both outside and inside him. He says only God can comfort him, and he accepts God's discipline as his teacher.
The speaker gives himself completely to God, asking God to correct him and bend his stubborn will. He accepts punishment now rather than later, and trusts that God knows everything in his heart.

The speaker tells God that God already knows the future and what is good for him. He accepts that trouble can cleanse his sin, asks God to act as God pleases, and asks not to be rejected, since God alone fully knows his sinful life.

The speaker asks God for good judgment. He wants to know, love, praise and value what God considers right, and to blame what God considers wrong. He asks not to judge by appearances or by what ignorant people say, but to tell clearly between outward and spiritual things, and always to seek God's will.

People often judge wrongly, and lovers of the world are fooled by looking only at outward things. Praise from other people makes no one truly greater. When people flatter each other, they are only deceiving or shaming one another, because what a person truly is depends on how God sees him.

The speaker tells the reader that he cannot always keep up strong desire for virtue or stay in deep prayerful thought. Because of his fallen human nature and his mortal body, he must sometimes return to ordinary, lower concerns, and he feels this as a weary burden.

When a person feels spiritually dry and distant from God, the passage advises turning to humble outward works and good deeds, and waiting patiently for God to return. It promises that God will bring relief from worry and open the Scriptures to them.

The speaker tells God that he does not deserve comfort or spiritual visits. He says that when God leaves him poor and lonely, God is acting fairly, because he has sinned often and deserves punishment.

The speaker admits he deserves none of God's comfort. Yet God, who does not want His works lost, gives him comfort beyond what he has earned, more than people usually receive. This comfort, the speaker says, is not like the comfort that people offer one another in words.

The speaker asks what he has done to deserve any heavenly comfort from God. He admits he has done little good and often sinned, and says he deserves hell. He chooses to confess his sins openly, hoping this will make him more worthy of God's mercy.

A guilty speaker, overwhelmed with shame, can say only that he has sinned and asks for mercy, and asks to be left alone briefly before death. He argues that God asks nothing more of a sinner than true sorrow and humility for his sins. Such contrition brings hope of forgiveness, a troubled conscience is calmed, lost grace is restored, and God and the repentant soul come together.

Sorrow for sin, when it is humble and sincere, is described as a sacrifice pleasing to God, more sweet to him than incense. A heart that is broken and contrite is never rejected by God. Such sorrow offers shelter from the enemy's anger and washes away the wrongs a person has committed.

Grace, here meaning God's gift of inner blessing, is said to be unwilling to mix with outward things or worldly comforts. So the reader is told to give up whatever blocks grace, to seek solitude, and to pray for a humble heart and a clear conscience, counting the world as worthless.

To be alone with God, one must give up delight in passing things. The passage advises separating oneself from friends and worldly comfort, and it cites the apostle Peter's view that believers should live in this world as strangers and pilgrims.

A dying person has great confidence if nothing in the world holds his heart. Such detachment is hard to reach, because a weak soul and a worldly person do not understand it. To attain it, a person must let go of both distant and close attachments and guard most against himself. Conquering oneself is the true victory, and whoever keeps his desires under reason, and reason under God, is master of himself and of the world.

To reach this height, a person must boldly uproot the hidden tendency to love oneself too much and to seek selfish and worldly gain. Most other faults come from this self-love. Once it is overcome, lasting peace and calm will follow.

Few people seriously try to die to their own self-interest and leave themselves behind. Because of this, they stay caught up in themselves and cannot rise above themselves in spirit. Whoever wants to walk freely with Christ must put to death his sinful and disordered desires and attach himself to no created thing out of selfish love.

The passage warns that the urges of ordinary human nature and the pull of divine grace work in opposite and subtle ways. Only a person who is spiritual and inwardly enlightened can tell them apart. Many people appear to do good, and so are fooled by what looks good.
Human nature, left to itself, is described as deceitful, always seeking its own gain. Grace, by contrast, is simple and honest, avoids every appearance of wrong, and acts entirely for God's sake.

Human nature resists dying to self, being pressed down, and submitting to a yoke, or burden. Grace, the help God gives, willingly accepts discipline, self-denial, and submission to others for God's sake, and does not seek power over anyone.
Nature seeks its own gain, honour and ease, and avoids shame. Grace looks instead to the good of many, gives glory to God, accepts shame for Jesus' name, and gladly takes on work.

Nature wants things that are showy and appealing, and turns away from things that are coarse and cheap. Grace, by contrast, takes pleasure in what is plain and humble, does not scorn what is rough, and is willing to wear old clothes.

Nature cares about worldly things. It is glad when it gains money, sad when it loses it, and upset by a small insult. Grace, by contrast, looks toward eternal things. It does not cling to earthly goods, and it is not shaken by loss or harsh words, because its treasure and joy are placed in heaven.

Nature, meaning our natural self, is greedy. It prefers to receive rather than give, and it cares mostly for what belongs to itself. Grace, meaning God's gift to the soul, is generous, avoids selfishness, is content with little, and finds more joy in giving than in receiving.

Nature pulls a person toward created things, bodily pleasures, empty amusements and being seen by others. Grace pulls toward God, virtue and inner comfort in God alone, away from the world and its outward pleasures.

Nature acts only for its own gain. It gives nothing freely and expects good, praise or honour in return. Grace, by contrast, seeks no worldly reward, only God, and wants no more material goods than are needed to reach eternal life.

Nature, meaning ordinary human inclination, favours friends, family, status, the powerful and the rich, and those who are like itself. Grace, meaning God's gift of help to the soul, instead loves enemies, values virtue over rank, favours the poor and innocent, and urges the good toward holiness.

Nature sees everything in relation to itself and argues for its own interests. Grace, by contrast, turns everything back to God, claims no credit for itself, and submits its own judgment to God's wisdom.

Human nature, left to itself, wants to learn secrets, hear new things, be seen, experience much through the senses, and be praised. Grace, which comes from God, does not seek such novelties, because these desires come from the old corruption of human nature, and nothing on earth is truly new or lasting.

Grace, here called "she," teaches a person to control the senses and avoid showy pride and display. It asks that good qualities be kept modest and that all knowledge serve a useful purpose and the honour of God, not the person's own praise.

Grace is described as a special light from God that marks the chosen and guarantees eternal salvation. It lifts a person's love from earthly things to heavenly ones and turns the worldly self into a spiritual one. The more a person's natural inclinations are subdued, the more grace is given, and the inner self is renewed day by day in God's image.

The speaker prays to God for grace, which he says is needed to overcome his sinful nature. He feels a conflict in his body between what his mind wants and what his fleshly desires push him toward, and he says he cannot resist those desires without God's grace poured into his heart.

Human nature has been prone to evil since youth, and the speaker says it needs God's grace, a large amount of it, to be overcome. The passage explains that through Adam's fall, sin corrupted nature, and its punishment came on all people. Left to itself, nature pulls people toward evil and lower things.

Human reason is compared to a spark hidden in ashes. It is still covered by thick clouds, but it can still tell good from evil and true from false. It cannot carry out everything it approves of, and it lacks full light and healthy desires.

The speaker says that inwardly he delights in God's law, knowing it is holy, just and good. Yet in his flesh he obeys his desires rather than reason, so he wants to do good but cannot carry it out. He sees the right path clearly, but his own weakness keeps him from following it without God's help, or grace.

The speaker tells God that his grace is absolutely necessary for every stage of a good life, from the start to its completion. Without it, human effort and natural gifts such as talent, wealth, beauty, or strength count for nothing, because such gifts are shared by good and bad people alike.

Grace, which the passage equates with love, is the special gift given to the chosen, and it brings everlasting life. Without grace and love, even prophecy, miracles, deep thought, faith, hope and other virtues count for nothing before God.

Grace, meaning God's free help, is praised here as the thing that makes the poor in spirit rich in virtue and keeps the proud humble. The speaker asks for grace to come, saying it is enough for them even when they lack what they naturally desire, and that it gives strength against trials and enemies.

The speaker says that grace, meaning God's help given freely to people, is the thing that teaches truth, brings comfort, removes sorrow and fear, and stirs devotion and tears. Without it, the speaker says, he is like a dry, useless branch fit only to be thrown away. He then asks God for grace to guide him always toward good works.

Christ speaks to the reader as "My Son." The more a person sets aside self, the closer that person can come to God. Desiring nothing outward brings inner peace, and following Christ, "the way, the truth, and the life," is the only way to go, know, and live.
In this passage Christ speaks of himself as the Way, the Truth and the Life. He says that whoever stays on his way will know the truth, be made free by it, and receive eternal life.

Each line gives a condition with a reward: keep the commandments to enter life, believe to know the truth, give up possessions to be perfect, deny yourself to be a disciple, and so on. The final line says that only those who carry the cross find the way to blessedness and true light.

The speaker asks Jesus for the grace to follow his example by rejecting the world, since a servant is not greater than his master. He says that living by Christ's life is his salvation and true holiness, and that other reading or hearing gives him no comfort or pleasure.

Knowing these teachings and reading them all is not enough by itself. The speaker, who is Christ, says a person is blessed only if they put the teachings into practice. Those who keep his commandments are the ones who love him, and he promises to love them, show himself to them, and give them a place with him in his Father's Kingdom.

The speaker prays to Jesus and accepts the hardships of a devoted life as a cross given by God. He promises to carry it until death, because he believes such a life leads to paradise. Having started, he says he cannot turn back.

Let us go forward together, the speaker urges, carrying the cross for Jesus' sake and bearing it steadily. Jesus, described as the leader who goes ahead of his followers, will help and fight for them, so they should face fear bravely and not turn away from the cross.

Patience and humility under hardship please God more than comfort and devotion in good times. When someone speaks against you, you should not be upset by it, since such things happen often and will keep happening. The speaker notes that people can give good advice and seem strong until trouble comes to them personally, and then their strength fails.

Put troubling thoughts out of your heart as far as you can, and bear hardship patiently even if you cannot bear it gladly. Hold back angry words so that others are not hurt, and trust that the Lord will return with comfort and help for those who call on him.

Be calmer and prepare yourself to endure more, because failing and being tempted does not undo everything. A human being is not God or an angel, so he cannot stay in perfect virtue at all times, as even an angel and the first man fell. God lifts up those who mourn and those who recognize their own weakness.

The speaker praises God's word as sweeter than honey and says it is his only comfort in great troubles. He accepts any suffering, as long as he reaches salvation, and asks God for a good death and a safe way into God's Kingdom.

God tells the reader not to argue about why some people are favored or suffer while others do not, because God's judgments are beyond human understanding. When such doubts arise, the reader should answer with words affirming that God's judgments are just and true.

Do not spend time asking which saint is holier or greater in heaven. Such questions cause quarrels and feed pride, and they do not please the saints. True peace comes from humility rather than from trying to raise oneself up.

Some people feel a strong love for particular saints, but the passage says this is more human feeling than divine. The speaker, presented as God, claims that he made all the saints, chose them, guided them through trials, and rewarded their patience, so the saints' love for him is not the source of their holiness.

God speaks in this passage and says he is the first and last, and that he is to be praised and honoured in all his saints, whom he chose and raised up without any merit of their own. Whoever despises the least of his people is also despising him, since he made both small and great. Speaking against any saint is speaking against God.

Those who are lifted above their own self-love love God for his own sake, resting in him with full joy and nothing able to turn them away. The passage says that unspiritual people, who care only for their own pleasure, should keep silent about this state, since they judge it by their own inclinations rather than by divine truth.

Many people, especially those with little spiritual understanding, love others mainly through natural affection and human friendship. They picture heavenly things in the same limited way they think about earthly ones. This is far below what enlightened people see through divine revelation.

Do not spend effort on questions beyond your understanding, such as who is holiest in heaven. Aim instead to be found least in God's Kingdom. Knowing who is greatest gains nothing unless it leads to humility and praise. Someone who sees his own sins and falls short of the saints pleases God more than someone who argues about rank among them.

The saints are fully content, as long as people would learn to be content and stop empty talk. They take no pride in their own merits, since they credit all good to God, who gave them everything. The higher they rise in glory, the humbler they are in themselves, and the closer they stand to God.

Many people ask who will be greatest in heaven, though they do not know if they will even be counted among the least. The passage says that being least in heaven is a great thing, since everyone there is great. Jesus answered the disciples' question by saying that one must become humble, like a little child, to be greatest.

Those who refuse to humble themselves like little children, and the rich who find their comfort in this life, are warned of trouble. The humble and the poor are told to rejoice, because the kingdom of God belongs to them if they walk in the truth. The list of Bible references at the end points to the sources of these sayings.

The speaker asks God whether anything in this life, or anything visible in the world, could be a greater source of trust or comfort than God himself. He says he would rather be poor with God than rich without him, and would rather wander on earth with God than enjoy heaven without him.

The speaker says that being close to God means heaven, and being without God means death and hell. He says he longs for God and can trust no one else to help him in need. God alone is his hope, trust, and comfort.

God is said to seek only the speaker's salvation and good, and to turn all things toward that good. Even when God allows temptations and hardships, the speaker says they are meant for his benefit, so God should be loved and praised just as much as when he gives heavenly comfort.

The speaker places all hope, refuge and trouble in God alone, because everything else seen apart from God seems weak and unreliable. Friends, helpers, wise advisers, books, wealth and safe places cannot help unless God himself gives support, strength, comfort, guidance and protection.

The writer says that everything that seems to bring peace and happiness means nothing without God, and gives no real happiness. God is the end of all good and the source of full life, so placing hope in him above all else is the greatest comfort for his servants. The writer ends by turning to God as the one he trusts.

The speaker prays that God will bless and purify his soul so it becomes a fit dwelling for God, free of anything that offends him. He asks God to hear him, as a poor servant living far from God in a dangerous world, and to guide him safely to eternal light.

The passage is Christ speaking in the Gospels, offering rest to the weary and promising that the bread he gives is his flesh, given for the life of the world. It says that eating his flesh and drinking his blood means living in him, and that his words are spirit and life.

The speaker says Christ's words are true and must be received gladly, since they were spoken for the speaker's salvation. Yet the speaker feels held back: the sweetness of these words draws him on, but his own sins and an impure conscience make him feel unworthy to receive such great mysteries.

The speaker says God calls them to come close and receive Communion, the bread and wine said to be Christ's body and blood, which gives eternal life. He invites the weary and burdened, and the speaker finds this welcome sweet. Yet the speaker asks who he is to approach God, since heaven itself cannot contain him.

The speaker is amazed that God invites him to come close. He feels he has no merit of his own and has often sinned, while angels and saints stand in awe of God. He says he would never have believed the invitation, or dared to approach, unless God himself had said it.

Noah spent a hundred years building the ark to be saved, and Moses covered his ark with pure gold to hold the law. The speaker asks how he, a weak human, can prepare himself in one hour to receive Christ, and whether he can dare to receive him so easily.

The speaker compares King Solomon's long and lavish dedication of the temple with his own weak devotion. Solomon spent seven years building and celebrated with great feasting, while the speaker can hardly manage half an hour of prayer. He wishes that even that half hour were spent well.

The speaker prays to God and compares his own preparation for Holy Communion with that of earlier holy men. He admits his preparation is small and brief, and often full of distractions. He says no unworthy thought should enter his mind, since he is about to receive the Lord of the Angels as his guest.

The passage says that the Ark of the Covenant and the old Jewish sacrifices were only signs or foreshadowings. Christ's body and his sacrifice are far greater, because they are the real thing that the old rites pointed to and fulfilled.

The speaker asks why he does not long more eagerly for Christ's holy presence and prepare more carefully to receive the sacred elements. He points out that the Patriarchs, Prophets, kings, princes and the whole people of old showed great devotion in worshipping God.

King David danced and played music with great devotion before the Ark of God, praising God with the whole heart. The author argues that Christians should show even greater reverence when receiving the Sacrament, the Body and Blood of Christ.

Many people travel to visit the tombs and shrines of dead saints, enjoying the stories of their deeds and the fine buildings. The speaker says that God is present right here with him, and that this presence is greater than any saint's shrine.

Many people look at religious relics and similar objects out of curiosity, and few come away improved, especially when they are careless and not truly sorry for their sins. In the Sacrament of the Altar (the Eucharist, or Communion), Christ is fully present, and anyone who receives him worthily and devoutly receives abundant eternal life.

The speaker praises God for the way he deals with his chosen people by offering himself to be received in this sacrament (the Eucharist, or Communion). This is beyond human understanding, and it stirs devout hearts. Faithful people who live to improve their lives often receive great devotion and love of virtue from it.

Only faithful Christians can know the hidden grace of the Sacrament, while unbelievers and those who serve sin cannot experience it. The Sacrament gives spiritual grace, restores lost virtue to the soul, and brings back beauty that sin had spoiled. Sometimes its devotion strengthens both mind and body.

The author laments that people are lukewarm and careless about Christ, in whom all hope of salvation rests. He says Christ is the believers' sanctification, redemption, and comfort, yet many people pay little attention to this gift. Through daily familiarity they grow careless about it.

If the Eucharist were celebrated in only one place and by only one priest in the world, people would feel a very strong longing to go there and see the holy rite. The point is that its rarity would make it seem far more precious than it is when it is available everywhere.

Many men are now ordained as priests, and the Sacrament is celebrated in many places. The author says this is so that God's grace and love toward people may be seen more clearly, as Holy Communion spreads across the world.

The speaker thanks Jesus for giving believers his body and blood, which feed them while they are poor and in exile on earth. He also thanks him for inviting them to share in this sacred meal, using his own words: "Come unto Me, ye who labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you."

The speaker approaches God in the sacrament, going to him as the sick go to a healer and the needy to a king. Yet he asks how a sinner could deserve that God should come to him, since he has nothing good in himself to earn such a gift.

The speaker admits his own unworthiness and thanks God for coming to him in this sacrament. He says God does this for God's own sake, not because of anything the speaker deserves, so that God's goodness, love and humility may be shown more fully. The speaker is glad this pleases God and asks that his own sin not get in the way.

The speaker feels that no one can fully honour Christ's body and blood in Communion, yet still longs to receive them. So the best thing to think about is their own unworthiness, humbling themselves before God and praising God's great goodness. They say they despise themselves and cast themselves down before God.

The speaker, a humble believer, addresses God as the holiest of beings while calling himself a sinner unworthy of him. He marvels that God comes down to him and invites him to a meal, offering himself as the heavenly bread that gives life to the world.

The speaker marvels at God's love and humility in giving himself as food in the sacrament. He praises God's wisdom and power, noting that God spoke and all things were made, and that what God commands is done.

The speaker marvels that God, though needing nothing, gives himself fully to people in the small forms of bread and wine in the sacrament of Communion. The speaker asks to keep heart and body pure so that he can receive this often, for lasting spiritual health.

The speaker is told to rejoice and thank God for the Sacrament, which is given as a comfort in this life of sorrow. Each time one remembers it and receives Christ's body, one takes part in the work of redemption and shares in Christ's merits. Christ's love and the power of his atonement never diminish.

The reader is told to prepare for Communion by constantly renewing their spirit and thinking carefully about the mystery of salvation. Communion should feel as fresh and joyful as if Christ were being born or dying on the cross that very day.

The speaker comes to receive communion, the Christian rite of sharing bread and wine as the body and blood of Christ. He asks to be blessed and made joyful by this gift, calls Christ his salvation, hope and strength, and says his soul longs to be united with Christ's body. The speaker compares himself to Zacchaeus, a tax collector in the Gospels who welcomed Jesus into his house.

The speaker asks for God himself, saying nothing else brings comfort and that he cannot live without God's visiting. So he needs to come to God often and receive him, as spiritual food, so he does not fail on the journey. He points to Jesus, who once said he would not send the hungry crowd home fasting, lest they faint on the way.

The speaker asks Christ to deal with him kindly, since Christ left himself in the Sacrament for the comfort of believers. Because the speaker often sins and grows cold in faith, he says he needs to renew himself through frequent prayer, penance, and receiving the Body and Blood of Christ, so that long periods without it do not make him fall short of his resolutions.

Human desires are naturally bad from youth, and without God's help a person keeps sliding toward worse things. Receiving Holy Communion pulls a person back from evil and gives strength to do good. Communion is also the main comfort of a faithful soul while it is still in the body and away from God.

Thomas à Kempis marvels that God, the creator of all spirits, humbly comes to a poor and weak soul to satisfy its hunger with his full divine and human nature. He calls blessed the soul that is allowed to receive God devoutly and so is filled with spiritual joy.

The speaker praises Christ, who is received in the Eucharist, as the greatest Lord, dearest guest, best companion, faithful friend, and most beautiful spouse, the one to be loved above all things. Everything else in heaven and earth is asked to fall silent before him, since all its beauty and praise come from his goodness.

The speaker prays to God before taking the Sacrament (Communion). He asks God to bless him first with sweetness, so he can approach worthily and with devotion. He asks to be woken from spiritual sleepiness and to taste God's sweetness, which he believes is hidden in the Sacrament like water in a spring.

The speaker asks God to open his eyes and strengthen his faith so he can accept the Eucharist, a great mystery. He says it rests on God's word and institution, not human invention, and that no person is fit to understand it by his own power. He, a sinner made of dust, asks how he could ever grasp such a deep sacrament.

The speaker approaches God in the Sacrament (the Communion rite) with simple, sincere faith, hope and reverence. They believe Christ is truly present there, both God and man. They understand that God wants them to receive him and be united with him in love.
The speaker asks God for special grace, so that he may be completely melted into love for God. He wants no other comfort to enter him at all.

The passage says that the Sacrament (the Christian rite of Communion) heals both soul and body. In the speaker's view, it cures sin, calms the passions, weakens temptation, and strengthens faith, hope, and love.

The passage says that God gives many good things, and keeps giving them, to his chosen people who receive the Sacrament with devotion. He comforts them in trouble, lifts them out of their misery, and renews and enlightens them with fresh grace.

Those who feel anxious and cold before receiving Communion often feel changed for the better afterward, once they have been refreshed by the heavenly food and drink. God deals this way with his chosen people so that they will recognize that they have nothing of their own, and that all goodness and grace come from him.

People who are cold, hard-hearted and without devotion become warm, eager and devout through God. The author compares God to a fountain that never runs dry and a fire that never goes out, and says that whoever comes to it takes away at least some of its sweetness or heat.

Even if the speaker cannot drink fully from the fountain of grace, they will still put their lips to the heavenly source. They hope to receive at least a small drop, enough so that their heart does not run dry.

The speaker admits he cannot yet be as heavenly and fiery as the angels called Cherubim and Seraphim. Still, he will try to devote himself and prepare his heart, so that he may receive at least a small flame of divine fire by humbly taking the Sacrament, the Christian rite of Communion.

The speaker asks Jesus, the merciful Saviour, to supply whatever he lacks, out of his kindness and grace. He bases this request on Jesus's invitation to all who are weary and burdened to come to him and find rest.

The speaker describes his own hardships: hard work, sorrow, sin, temptation and strong passions, with no one to help except God. He entrusts himself to God, asks to be led to eternal life, and prays that frequent receiving of the Eucharist (the bread and wine taken as Christ's body and blood) will increase his devotion.

Even a person of great purity could not deserve to consecrate the Sacrament of Christ, because no human merit earns it. Only priests properly ordained in the church have this power, which is not given even to angels. Yet the priest is only God's minister; God is the true author and worker.

The passage tells a newly ordained priest to trust God in the Eucharist more than his own senses or any visible sign. It says the work of celebrating the sacrament must be approached with fear and reverence, and that he has been made a priest and consecrated to celebrate it.

A priest is told to serve God faithfully and be blameless. Being ordained does not make his load lighter; it binds him to stricter discipline and a higher standard of holiness. He should be full of virtue, set a good example, and keep company with angels or the most perfect people, not with ordinary worldly folk.

A priest in holy vestments stands in Christ's place to pray to God for himself and for all the people. He should keep Christ's Passion in mind, follow Christ's example, patiently bear the wrongs done to him, and mourn his own sins and those of others. When he celebrates Mass, the passage says, he honours God and benefits the Church, the living, the dead, and himself.

The speaker feels deep fear when he thinks about God's greatness and his own unworthiness. He sees two dangers: staying away from communion means losing life, while coming unworthily brings God's anger. He turns to God, asking what he should do.

The speaker asks God to show him a short practice for getting his heart ready before taking Holy Communion. He wants to know how to prepare devoutly and reverently, so that receiving the sacrament will be good for his soul.

Before a priest celebrates, gives, or receives the Sacrament, he should approach with deep humility and faith. He should examine his conscience carefully, confess and cleanse it of sin, and feel sorrow for his sins, especially his daily faults.

The speaker is urging himself to grieve over his own faults. He lists them: he is still worldly and ruled by his desires, his senses wander, his mind fills with empty thoughts, and he cares more for outward things than inner ones. He laughs easily but weeps rarely, loves comfort and the body's pleasures, and lacks eagerness and warmth in devotion.

The passage lists faults of a careless soul, each set against its opposite. It names a person who is eager for novelties, beauty, food, rest, and gossip, but reluctant toward humility, giving, silence, labour, God's word, and holy watchfulness.

This is a list of faults a person finds in himself when he looks honestly at his own life. He is careless about set times of prayer, cold in worship, and gains little from spiritual sharing. He is easily distracted and easily angry, quick to judge others, joyful in good times but weak in hard ones, and often makes good resolutions that come to little.

After confessing and grieving over his faults, the reader should firmly resolve to live better and keep improving. He should then give himself fully to God, offering body and soul as a whole burnt offering, so that he may be worthy to receive the Sacrament of Christ's Body and Blood.

The passage says that offering oneself to God through the Body and Blood of Christ in Holy Communion is the most worthy offering and the greatest way to destroy sin. It adds that if a person truly repents and turns to God for pardon, however often, God will not hold past sins against him, citing Ezekiel 18.

Christ speaks here and says he gave himself fully on the Cross for human sins, and he asks the reader to offer himself to God in the same way, every day, with all his strength and feeling. He wants the person himself, not gifts or possessions.

Gifts alone do not please God; the giver must offer himself completely. Christ, speaking here, says he gave himself wholly to the Father for the reader and his own body and blood as food, so the reader would belong fully to him. If a person keeps himself back and does not freely submit to God's will, his offering is incomplete and the union with Christ is not complete either.

The main point is that a person must first give themselves completely to God before doing anything else, if they want freedom and grace. Few achieve this inner freedom because they do not fully deny themselves. The passage quotes Jesus saying that whoever does not forsake all cannot be his disciple, and calls on the reader to offer themselves wholeheartedly.

The speaker offers himself to God as a willing gift, to serve God for ever. He asks God to accept him through the Communion he celebrates that day, so that it may bring salvation to himself and to all God's people.

The speaker lays all his sins before God at this act of worship, from the time he first became capable of sin until now. He asks God to burn them away with love, cleanse his conscience, restore his favour, forgive him fully, and welcome him back with the kiss of peace.

The speaker can do nothing about his sins except confess and mourn them and keep asking God for forgiveness. He says he hates his sins, will not commit them again, and will keep grieving over them. He asks God to forgive him and deal with him by mercy, not by his wickedness.

The speaker offers God his own goodness, though he calls it very small and flawed. He asks God to improve it, make it acceptable, and move it toward perfection. He also asks God to bring him safely to a happy and blessed end, despite describing himself as slothful and useless.

The speaker offers up to God the good wishes of devout people and the needs of family, friends, and others, including those who helped him or asked for his prayers. He asks that they receive God's grace, comfort, protection from danger, and relief from pain, so they may thank God gladly.

The speaker prays for people who have hurt, upset, or wronged them, and for anyone they have ever hurt themselves, knowingly or not. They ask God to forgive everyone's sins and offences alike, remove anger and rivalry from their hearts, and show mercy so that they may reach eternal life.

The passage urges the reader to go often to the fountain of grace, meaning Holy Communion, so that faults and sins are healed and temptations are resisted more easily. It adds that the devil, knowing how strong this help is, works in every way to keep believers from it.

Some people who prepare to take Holy Communion are troubled by evil thoughts sent by Satan. The evil spirit, as the Book of Job says, comes among the sons of God to disturb them or make them overly fearful and confused.

The passage says that the devil tries to weaken people's love and faith so they will stop taking Holy Communion or take it with a cold heart. Believers should not give in to these tricks, however wicked they seem, but should turn them back on the devil himself.

The passage says that a person who stirs up trouble and insults others should be despised and mocked. Even so, a believer should not skip Holy Communion because of that person's insults or the inner turmoil he causes.

Excessive worry, including worry about confession, can block devotion, so the reader is told to set aside anxiety and scruples. Small troubles should not stop someone from taking Holy Communion; instead they should confess quickly, forgive others, and ask forgiveness from anyone they have wronged.

Putting off confessing your sins or delaying Holy Communion does no good. The writer urges that you clean yourself at once, like removing poison quickly, because waiting today can lead to bigger obstacles tomorrow and leave you further from receiving Communion.

Do not let heaviness and laziness keep you from God for long, because putting off Holy Communion for a long time makes the spiritual dullness worse. The author criticises lukewarm people who make excuses to delay repentance and Communion so they will not have to watch themselves more strictly.

Those who take Holy Communion lightly, or put it off, are described as lacking love and devotion. Someone who lives so purely that he could receive it on any day is praised, and a person who sometimes abstains out of humility or a good reason is commended. But if he abstains from laziness, he should rouse himself, and God will help his good desire.

If a person is kept from receiving communion for a good reason, a sincere wish to receive it still brings them its benefit. A devout person can always take part in Christ spiritually. Still, on set days a believer should receive the Body and Blood with reverence, seeking God's honour more than personal comfort, and thinking devoutly on Christ's incarnation and Passion.

Someone who prepares for Communion only when a feast day comes or when custom requires it will often be unprepared. The writer praises those who offer themselves fully to God each time they receive or celebrate it. He also advises following the accepted customs of one's community and not burdening others, putting others' benefit ahead of one's own feelings.

The speaker prays to Jesus, praising the joy of the devout soul that feeds on him in the sacrament, the Eucharist. He wishes he could weep for devotion, as Mary Magdalene did at Jesus' feet. He asks where that devotion and those tears are, and says his heart should burn with joy, since Jesus is present there, though hidden under bread and wine.

The speaker says that God's full brightness is too strong for human eyes, so God hides himself under the Sacrament, the consecrated bread of the Mass, out of kindness to human weakness. The speaker holds and worships by faith the one whom angels see directly in heaven without any veil.

It is good to be satisfied with the light of true faith and to live by it until eternal brightness comes and the symbols fade. Then, when the perfect state arrives, the use of the sacraments will end, because the blessed in heaven need no sacramental help.

Those who are in heaven rejoice without end in God's presence. They see his glory directly and are changed from one degree of glory to another. They also experience the Word of God, who became flesh, as he was from the beginning and remains forever.

The speaker says that when he thinks on God's glory, all spiritual comfort feels like a burden, and the things of the world seem worth nothing to him. Only God can give him rest, but he cannot see God openly while still living in this mortal life. So he must be patient and submit to God in every desire.

The speaker says that the saints of God, who now rejoice with him in heaven, lived by faith while they waited for God's glory. The speaker shares their beliefs and hopes, and expects to reach the same heaven by God's grace. Meanwhile he will live by faith, using the saints' examples, holy books, and above all the Eucharist, the bread and wine taken as Christ's body and blood.

The speaker says that two things are necessary for life while trapped in the body: food and light. He names these as the sacrament of Christ's body and blood, which feeds soul and body, and God's Word, which guides his steps and lights his soul.

The passage says the Church has two tables, one on each side. One holds the altar bread, which is the body and blood of Christ. The other holds the divine law, which teaches the true faith and leads toward the innermost part of the temple, the Holy of Holies.

The speaker thanks Jesus for the teaching handed down by the prophets, apostles and other teachers. He also thanks him for the Holy Supper, in which Jesus gives his own body and blood in place of the old lamb sacrifice. This meal brings joy to believers, and the speaker says it holds all the delights of Paradise.

Priests have a very high and honourable role: they consecrate the Sacrament with holy words, bless it, hold it, receive it, and give it to others. For this reason, the passage says, a priest's hands, mouth, body and heart should be clean, pure and holy, and his speech should be only holy, honest and useful.

Priests should keep their eyes and hands pure, because their eyes look upon the Body of Christ and their hands hold the Creator in the sacrament of Communion. For this reason the Law says to priests, "Be ye holy, for I the Lord your God am holy."

A prayer asking God for help to live purely and devoutly as a priest. If the priest cannot live as blamelessly as he should, he asks God to let him truly grieve over his sins and then serve God more earnestly in humility and good will.

Christ speaks here as the one who loves purity and wants to rest in a pure heart. He asks the reader to clear out sin and the world, make the heart ready like a furnished room, and grieve over past wrongs. He notes that a lover always prepares the best place for the beloved.

A person cannot earn the right to take part in Communion, however well they prepare. They come to the Lord's table only by his mercy and grace, like a beggar invited to a rich man's dinner who can offer only humility and thanks. So they should prepare as well as they can, and then receive the Body of Christ, because Christ has called them and will supply what they lack.

Christ speaks to the reader. When he gives the feeling of devotion, the reader should give thanks, because it is a gift of mercy, not a reward. When devotion is missing, the reader should keep praying until some grace comes. Christ needs the reader less than the reader needs him, and the reader should prepare the heart to receive it.

After receiving Communion, the reader should stay just as careful as before it. Going straight back to outward pleasures leaves a person unready for good. Instead, the passage advises quiet, few words, and inward prayer with God, who is the one the reader should give himself to completely.

The speaker prays for a time when they can be alone with God, open their heart fully to him, and enjoy him as much as they long to. They wish no other person or creature to draw their attention, so that God alone speaks with them and they with him, as lovers or close friends do.

The speaker prays to be fully united with God, to turn their heart away from all created things, and to come to enjoy heavenly things more through Holy Communion. They long to be lost in God and to forget themselves, asking that they and God remain joined as one.

The speaker calls God his beloved and his peacemaker, the one source of perfect peace and true rest, and says that life apart from God brings only labour, sorrow and misery. He also says God hides himself, and that God's counsel is not with the wicked but with the humble and simple.

The speaker praises God for feeding his faithful people with the sweet "bread from heaven," meaning the Eucharist, or communion. He says no other nation has gods so close to it as God is to his believers. God gives himself as their daily food and delight, comforting them and lifting their hearts toward heaven.

The passage praises the Christian people as especially honored, and says the devout soul is the most beloved creature under heaven because God comes into it to feed it with his body. The writer marvels at this grace and asks what he can give back to the Lord in return.

The speaker says the most pleasing offering he can make is to give his whole heart to God and join it inwardly to Him. He imagines God replying that if the speaker stays with Him, God will stay with him, and the speaker answers that his whole desire is for his heart to be united with God.

The speaker feels ashamed. He approaches the Lord's altar and Holy Communion coldly and without much feeling, and compares himself with devout people who weep and long for the sacrament so strongly that only receiving the Lord's Body can satisfy them.

The speaker admires people whose faith is so strong and warm that they clearly feel Christ's presence. He admits such deep love is rare in his own life. He then asks Jesus to let him feel a little of that love during Holy Communion, so his faith, hope and love may grow.

The speaker asks God for the grace of fervent devotion, which he says he does not yet feel as strongly as others who love God deeply. Even so, he admits he desires that intense love and wishes to share in the company of those who have it.

Devotion, meaning a warm sense of closeness to God, is a gift that must be sought, asked for, waited for, and used carefully, with the timing left to God. When a person feels little or no devotion, they should humble themselves without becoming overly discouraged, since God sometimes grants long-denied gifts suddenly or at the end of prayer.

Grace, meaning a sense of God's gift or closeness, is not always given on demand, and that is for the good of weak people. The reader should wait patiently and hopefully. When grace is withheld, the author says to blame one's own sins, and even a small obstacle that blocks grace matters. If that obstacle is removed and fully overcome, the person will receive what was asked for.
If you give yourself fully to God and stop seeking your own wishes, you will find inner unity and peace. Nothing will then bring you more sweetness and delight than doing what God wills.

Someone who turns their will fully toward God, and is free of any excessive love or dislike for created things, is best prepared to receive grace and the gift of devotion. The passage compares such a person to an empty vessel, which God fills with his blessing.
The more fully a person gives up things that do no good and puts self aside, the sooner grace comes, the more of it comes in, and the higher it raises a free heart.

Someone who trusts fully in God's hand will feel their heart widen with wonder. Such a person, who seeks God wholeheartedly, gains a deep closeness to God when receiving Communion. This happens because they care more for God's glory than for their own feelings of devotion or comfort.

The speaker prays to God before receiving communion. He admits his weakness, sins, and temptations, and says that God alone knows his secrets and needs. He asks God for comfort, support, and the virtues he lacks.

The speaker stands before God as poor and in need, asking for grace, mercy and warmth of love. He asks God to make earthly things seem bitter and worthless, to lift his heart toward heaven, and to be his only true delight and good from now on.

The speaker prays to God to fill him completely with God's presence, so that he becomes one spirit with God through inward union and burning love. He asks not to be left empty, and says it would be no surprise if he were set on fire by God and lost his own self, since God is a fire that never fails and purifies the heart.
The speaker says they long to receive God in Communion with the deepest love and devotion. They say this desire is as strong as, or stronger than, that of any saint who ever lived.

The speaker says that, though unworthy of such devout feelings, he offers God his whole heart and every devout longing he can imagine, as if he alone had them. He keeps nothing back and gives himself and all he has to God as a sacrifice.

The speaker wants to receive Christ in Communion this day with the same love, faith, humility and purity that the Virgin Mary showed when she accepted the angel's news that she would bear Christ. He quotes her reply, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word."

The speaker prays to feel the same burning joy and longing for Christ that John the Baptist showed. He recalls how John leapt for joy in the womb and later rejoiced at Christ's coming, like a friend who is glad at the bridegroom's voice. The speaker wants to be filled with holy desire and to offer himself to Christ wholeheartedly.

The speaker offers to God, on behalf of himself and those he prays for, the joy, deep feelings, spiritual raptures, inner enlightenments and heavenly visions of all devout hearts. He also offers every virtue and praise sung by creatures in heaven and earth, so that God may be honored forever.

The speaker asks God to accept his prayers and his wish to praise God endlessly, every day and every moment. He also calls on the heavenly spirits and all faithful people to join him in giving thanks and praise to God.

The speaker asks that all peoples praise God and honour the Sacrament, the Communion meal. He asks that those who receive it with faith and devotion pray for him, a sinner, and remember him after they leave the table.

The passage warns against prying into the Eucharist, the sacrament of communion, with idle curiosity, since this can lead into doubt and overwhelm the searcher. It says God can do more than human minds grasp. Honest inquiry is allowed, but only if it stays willing to be taught and follows the teachings of the early Church fathers.

Simple faith and an honest life are blessed, and it is better to follow God's clear commandments than to chase hard questions. Many have lost their devotion by digging into deep mysteries. Submit to God and accept faith, and the knowledge you need will be given to you.

Doubts about faith and the Sacrament that trouble a believer are said to come from the devil, not from the believer's own fault. The believer should not argue with these thoughts but simply trust God, the saints and the prophets, and the devil will leave. The passage adds that the devil bothers faithful people, not unbelievers and sinners, whom he already holds.

Approach the Sacrament with simple, trusting faith, and leave what you cannot understand to God without worry. God does not deceive; a person is deceived only by trusting too much in himself. God gives his understanding to the humble and simple, while human reason is weak and can be misled, but true faith cannot.

Human reasoning and investigation should come after faith, not before it or against it. In the Sacrament of the Eucharist, faith and love work in hidden ways, and God's works are too great for human reason to fully grasp. If they could easily be understood, they would not be called wonderful.
The speaker, once a writer of happy verse, now writes sad poetry in tears. His Muses, the goddesses of the arts, have stayed loyal to him as he is exiled and grows old, and they are his only comfort.

The speaker says that sorrow has aged him early, leaving him grey and wrinkled. He observes that death is a release for the broken-hearted when they call for it, yet it ignores the wretched and does not come to them.

The speaker says that while Fortune, the goddess of changing luck, showered him with gifts, he was close to a dark death. Now that bad luck has clouded that false smile, he is weary of life yet still lives. He asks his friends why they once called him happy, since a man who falls so easily was never firmly grounded.

The narrator, sitting in silent grief and writing down his complaints, sees a woman standing above him. She is very dignified and looks ageless. Her eyes are bright and piercing, and her height seems to change, sometimes ordinary and sometimes reaching the sky.

The passage describes a woman of great stature whose head reaches into the heavens. Her robe is finely woven, though faded by age and neglect. Its hem bears the Greek letter Pi, its top the letter Theta, and steps run between them, standing for the move from practical life to contemplation.

Lady Philosophy, a figure who appears to the narrator, is angry to see the Muses of poetry at his bedside writing down his laments. She says these poetic muses feed his illness rather than cure it, and that they harm reason by stirring up emotion. Her robe is torn, and she carries a notebook and a staff.

Philosophy speaks here, scolding the Muses of poetry, whom she calls sirens, for trying to lure a man away from her. Because he has been trained in serious philosophy, she tells them to leave him to her, and they leave in shame.

The narrator, whose eyes are blurred from weeping, cannot tell who the commanding woman is. He stares at the ground in silence while she comes close, sits on his couch, and looks at his grief-stricken face. Then she begins to lament the troubled state of his mind.

The speaker is lamenting a man whose mind has fallen into darkness and confusion, tossed by worldly troubles. The second half recalls how this same mind once explored the heavens, studying the sun, moon, stars, winds, sea and the turning of the sky. The contrast is between his past knowledge and his present state.

The poem asks who controls the seasons, making spring bloom with roses and autumn heavy with grapes. It says the one who knew these things once studied nature closely. Now, having lost his reason, he lies bound by chains and is weighed down, with his eyes fixed on the dull earth.

Philosophy, personified as a woman, speaks to the narrator, who is overcome and silent. She says that this is a time for healing rather than weeping. She reminds him that he was once strong, raised on her teaching and armed for defence, but he threw that protection away. She asks whether he recognises her, and says his silence looks more like stupor than shame.

Philosophy, a figure who appears to the narrator, finds him speechless and dazed. She says this is a common sickness of confused minds, that he has forgotten himself, and that he must first recognise her to recover. She then wipes away the tears that blur his eyes.

The narrator's sight comes back after the darkness lifts, and he compares this to weather. When a rainy south-west wind brings storm clouds, the sun and sky go dark. When the north wind blows the clouds away, the sun suddenly bursts out and dazzles the eyes.

In this passage, the narrator's gloom lifts and he can see clearly again. He recognises Philosophy, whom he has known since youth, and asks why she has come to his place of exile. He wonders whether she too has been falsely accused, as he has.

Philosophy, speaking to Boethius, asks whether she could abandon him after he has suffered for her sake. She says that sharing his trouble is her duty, and that it is no surprise that wisdom is attacked in a bad age.

Philosophy speaks of her past struggles against foolish rashness, and of how she aided Socrates in his unjust death. After Plato and Socrates died, rival schools such as the Epicureans and Stoics each claimed her as their own. They tore her apart, taking only fragments and believing they had possessed the whole.

Some philosophers were killed because people wrongly thought they were followers of Philosophy, simply because her robe had left marks on them. The speaker notes that the reader may not know of older cases, such as Anaxagoras, Socrates and Zeno, but may know of Arrius, Seneca and Soranus, whose deaths were recent and well known.

Men who followed Boethius's principles were destroyed simply because their good lives set them against the wicked. So it is no surprise that those who refuse to go along with evil-doers are tossed by storms in this life. Although the wicked are many, they are worth nothing, since they have no leader and are driven about by blind error.

Philosophy speaks of her followers as besieged by worldly troubles. When these troubles attack with great force, Philosophy withdraws her forces into a safe fortress, leaving the attackers to seize only worthless goods. The wise, sheltered there, can watch them with amusement, because the fortress is beyond their reach.

A person who stays calm and steady, whatever happens, cannot be frightened by storms, volcanoes, lightning or the threats of rulers. The poem tells the reader that fear of a tyrant has no real power over such a person. Whoever gives way to hope or fear, though, loses self-control and makes his own chains.

Philosophy, speaking to the narrator, asks whether he is following her words or has gone dull to them. She asks why he is weeping and tells him to speak openly, since a physician can only help someone who reveals the wound.

Boethius, in prison and in despair, speaks to Philosophy, who has come to him. He asks whether his suffering from fate's cruelty is not already obvious, and recalls how she once guided his studies of nature, the stars and his own conduct. He asks whether this is the reward for his devotion to her.

Philosophy speaks, and the narrator, Boethius, reports that he has followed her teaching. Plato held that states are happy only if philosophers rule them or rulers become philosophers, and that philosophers should take up public office so good people are not harmed by corrupt governors. The narrator says he has tried to put into public administration what he learned from philosophy in private study.

The speaker says he served public office only for the common good, and that he defended the weak against powerful men. Because of this he made bitter enemies, and he names Conigastus and Trigguilla, officials he opposed when they tried to harm others.

The speaker says he often risked his position to defend poor people against false charges brought by greedy and lawless barbarians. He claims he never let anyone turn him from justice toward wrongdoing. When provincials were ruined by private theft and public taxes, he grieved as much as they did.

Boethius describes three occasions when he stood up for others against powerful opponents. He opposed a forced sale that would have starved Campania, defended the nobleman Paulinus from greedy court officials, and risked hatred to protect Albinus from a rigged charge.

Boethius is speaking in his own defence. He says that his strict sense of justice made enemies of many, yet he expected safety among his fellow countrymen. Instead, his accusers are men with debts or past convictions, such as Basil, Opilio and Gaudentius.

Men who refused to leave Ravenna and took sanctuary were ordered branded and expelled. The same men then brought a charge against the speaker, and it was accepted. He protests that he has done nothing to deserve this and asks how such accusers could be trusted, or why fortune does not feel shame at such a wrong.

Boethius, imprisoned and facing charges, imagines Philosophy asking what he is accused of. He says he tried to save the senate from a false treason charge brought by an informer. He asks whether he should deny his wish or admit it, and he says he will not stop wishing to protect the senate, which the senate itself has now made a crime.

Blind folly may call things by false names, but it cannot change what things really are. The speaker, following the teaching of Socrates, will neither hide the truth nor let falsehood go unchallenged. He leaves the judgment to his listener and has written down an account of events so later generations will know the facts.

Boethius says that the forged letters meant to prove he hoped for Rome's freedom are false, and the truth would show this if his accusers' confessions were heard. He asks what hope of freedom remains, and says that if he had known of a plot, he would have kept it from his accuser, as Canius did against Caligula.

Boethius says he is not surprised that wicked people plot against good people, since evil plans come from human weakness. What troubles him is that such villains succeed in harming the innocent while God sees it. He quotes a disciple's question: if God exists, why is there evil, and if He does not, why is there good?

Boethius says that his enemies may also want to destroy him, since they see him as a defender of the senate and of honest men. He argues he has not earned such a fate from the senators. He recalls that at Verona he defended the innocence of all the senators, even though the king wanted to charge the whole senate with treason against Albinus, and he risked his own safety to do so.

Boethius says he has never boasted of his good deeds, because public praise takes away the inner reward of a good conscience. Now, though he is innocent, he is punished for a crime he did not commit instead of receiving the rewards of virtue.

Boethius says that in his case the judges showed no mercy, unlike past trials where some judges softened their verdicts. He argues that even someone accused of the worst crimes, such as arson or murder of priests, would have been brought to court and allowed to confess or be proven guilty. Instead, he was condemned to exile and death without a hearing or defense, while he was about 500 miles away. He was punished for his loyalty to the senate.

Boethius says his accusers knew his real charge was honourable, so they falsely claimed he had committed religious crimes to cover it up. He answers that his inner conscience, guided by philosophy, had removed any desire for worldly success, so he could not have committed such acts.

The speaker argues that he would never have sought help from evil spirits, since he had been shaped by God toward goodness. He adds that his home, his friends and his respected father-in-law protect him from any suspicion of sacrilege. Yet, shockingly, his accusers claim support for the charge from God himself.

The speaker says that his devotion to philosophy now brings him blame, as if he were guilty of wrongdoing. He adds that people judge by outcomes rather than by real merit, so wise foresight is recognised only when good fortune rewards it.

Boethius says that a person's good name is the first thing to desert someone in misfortune. Once a charge is made against an unhappy person, people assume they deserved their suffering. He adds that he himself has been punished for doing good.

Boethius imagines the wicked celebrating and the good terrified. Criminals feel free to make false accusations, and innocent people have lost both their peace of mind and any means of defending themselves.

The poem praises God as the maker who turns the heavens and steers the stars by fixed laws. It then uses the moon as an example: when she is full and bright she outshines the stars, but when she moves close to the sun she loses her light.

This is a hymn to a power that governs the heavens and the seasons. It says that the evening star and the morning star, the length of day and night, and the turning of the year all follow this power's will, and that every thing keeps its place under a fixed law.

The speaker asks God whether he has turned away from humans alone, since Fortune, the goddess of chance and changing luck, treats people so harshly. Wicked people are raised up and do harm, while the innocent suffer the punishment that the guilty should receive.

Wrongdoers seem to prevail, and good people suffer, so the speaker appeals to God to bring order to the world. The first verse says virtue hides while crime and deceit succeed, and the second asks God to calm the troubles of "fortune's tide" and guide earthly affairs by his heavenly order.
The narrator has finished a long outburst of grief. The figure who has come to him, Philosophy, is calm and not upset by his complaints, and she is about to speak.

Philosophy speaks to the narrator, who is sorrowful and weeping. She says she knew at once he was wretched and exiled, but she did not know how far he had been sent away until he told her. She then says he has not really been banished but has wandered off, and that if he insists on calling it banishment, he banished himself, since no one else could lawfully have that power over him.

Philosophy reminds the speaker that their homeland is not ruled by the mob, as Athens once was, but by one king who wants his citizens to stay, not be exiled. Serving this king is true freedom. Ancient law there forbids sending anyone who has settled there into exile.

Philosophy's words to Boethius, who is in exile. A person who stays loyal to the place of learning cannot be exiled from it, but one who stops wanting to stay there loses that claim. Boethius says he misses not the physical room and its books but the mind of his teacher, which holds the ideas that give the books their worth.

Philosophy is speaking to Boethius, who has complained of his treatment. She agrees his services to the state are true but too small for what he deserves. She says the charges against him, true or false, are public knowledge, and that the informers' crimes have already been condemned by public opinion, so he was right to pass over them lightly. She notes that he has bitterly complained about the senate's injustice.

Philosophy speaks to the narrator, who is upset. He has grieved over false accusations against him, the loss of his good name, and the unfair reward for his good deeds, and he has even prayed that heavenly peace might rule the earth. Because his mind is crowded with anger, pain and grief, Philosophy says that strong remedies would not suit him yet.
Philosophy says she will first use gentle methods. Her aim is to soften the swollen hardness that strong emotions have caused, so that the mind can later bear stronger treatment.

Each thing has its proper season, set by God, and acting out of season brings bad results. Sowing grain in the heat of summer, gathering violets in winter, or pressing grapes in spring all lead to loss. Whoever breaks this fixed order will suffer for it.

Philosophy asks the narrator a few questions so she can judge his state of mind and decide how to help him. The narrator agrees to answer. She first asks whether the world is run by chance or by some rational guiding order.

The speaker refuses to believe that the orderly movements of the heavens could be produced by chance. He holds firmly that God, the Creator, governs His work, and says nothing will ever make him give up this belief.

Philosophy speaks to the narrator, who is unwell and in despair. She points out that he has just said in verse that God cares for men, and that he has always believed the world is ruled by reason. She finds it strange that he has fallen ill despite holding these beliefs, and asks him how God actually governs the world. He admits he does not understand her question.

Philosophy asks the speaker whether he remembers the ultimate purpose toward which all nature aims. He says he once heard it but has forgotten it through sorrow. She then reminds him that he knows all things came from God, and he agrees.

Philosophy asks the speaker whether he knows the source of his existence and what a man is. He answers that he is a being with reason who will die. When she asks if he knows anything else about himself, he says no.

Philosophy tells Boethius that his illness has two causes. The main one is that he has forgotten his own true nature. This forgetting leads him to think of himself as an exile, and to believe that wicked men are happy and powerful, because he does not know what the purpose of existence is.

Philosophy tells the sick speaker that his illness comes from forgetting how the world is governed. He thinks fortune's changes happen by chance, with no guiding hand. Yet he still holds that the world is ruled by divine reason, and this belief gives hope of recovery.

Philosophy says that the time for strong treatment has not yet come. The mind, once it drops true beliefs, takes up false ones, and this confusion clouds its sight. So she will first use gentle methods to clear away the mists of misleading feeling, so the speaker can see the true light.

This is a chapter summary rather than the argument itself. It lists the topics of the next chapters: Philosophy scolds Boethius for complaining about Fortune, and Fortune is said to be by nature changeable. Fortune then argues that the goods she gives are hers to take back. Finally, Boethius feels miserable, and Philosophy reminds him how bright his past good fortune was.

Boethius complains that remembering past happiness makes present misery worse. Philosophy replies that he still has many blessings to be grateful for, that no one's lot is wholly satisfying, and that true happiness lies within a person, not in gifts from Fortune, which are external and can never truly belong to us.

Wealth brings worry and trouble, and high rank without virtue is an evil rather than a good. Power and fame are also shown to be worth little. The only real service Fortune performs is to reveal her true nature and separate true friends from false ones.

Philosophy falls silent for a moment, then speaks again. She says she has understood the cause of the narrator's distress: he longs for his former good fortune, and he believes the loss of that fortune has disturbed his mind.
