Fortune is described as a siren: she charms people with false friendship, then suddenly abandons them to grief. The speaker urges the listener to consider her true nature, and then he will see that she never gave anything of real worth and took nothing of real worth away.

Philosophy speaks to Boethius, who is in distress. She reminds him that he used to argue back against her teachings even when she was gentle with him, and she says that sudden misfortune naturally disturbs the mind. She now offers a mild remedy first, to prepare him for stronger ones.

Philosophy says she now calls on Rhetoric, the art of persuasive speaking, to help her. She asks it to stay true to her teaching. She also asks Music, her servant, to join in with singing, sometimes light and sometimes serious.

Philosophy speaks to a grieving man and says his sorrow comes from a mistake. Fortune has not changed toward him; she has always behaved this way. Her changeability is her steady nature, and she showed it earlier too, when she flattered him with false happiness.

Fortune, the goddess of changing luck, is speaking here to a man who has lost her favour. She says she has shown her true nature, so he should accept her as she is or reject her. Her unreliability should bring him peace, since no one can trust that good fortune will last.

Fortune's favours cannot be kept, and when they leave they bring suffering, so her visits are really signs of trouble to come. Wisdom looks beyond what is in front of us to the outcome of things. Seen this way, Fortune's threats lose their fear and her rewards lose their appeal.

Once you accept Fortune's rule, you must put up with whatever she sends you. Trying to set terms on how she stays or leaves only makes you bitter over what you cannot change. Like a ship with its sails set to the wind, you go where the wind drives you, not where you intended.

Philosophy tells the speaker that Fortune's changes must be accepted, just as a farmer accepts good years and bad years when he sows seed. Fortune is always turning like a wheel, and if it stopped, it would no longer be Fortune. Trying to hold it still is foolish.

Fortune, personified as a wild and unpredictable force, raises some people to power and throws down others without warning. She ignores their suffering and mocks it. Her favourites can go from great happiness to deep misery within a single hour.

Boethius has Lady Fortune, the goddess of luck and changing fortune, speak to a complaining man. She asks what wrong she has done him and what goods she has taken from him. She offers to let a judge settle whether wealth and rank truly belong to a human being.

Lady Philosophy speaks here as Fortune, who says she once raised a man from birth and gave him many goods. Now she is taking them back. She says he should thank her for what was never his, and has no right to complain about losing it.

Lady Philosophy, speaking as Fortune, says that wealth and honour are under her control and come and go as she pleases. She argues that if things were truly the speaker's own, they could never be lost. She asks why she alone should be stopped from doing what she wishes with what is hers, and points to the changing seasons as an example of nature doing the same.

Fortune speaks here, describing herself as unpredictable. Like the sea, she is calm one day and stormy the next, and she will not stay fixed to anyone. She enjoys raising people up and bringing them down, and she tells the listener that rising comes with the risk of falling.

Philosophy reminds the speaker of familiar stories about reversals of fortune. Croesus, a powerful king, was nearly burned on a pyre but was saved by rain sent from heaven. Paullus pitied Perseus, the king he had captured. Tragedies, too, mourn kingdoms toppled by Fortune's blind blows, and the myth of Zeus's two jars shows good and bad fortune given out to all.

Fortune, speaking to the narrator, suggests that his own turns of fate may be a reason to hope for better things, and that he should stop wearing himself out with worry. She reminds him that he cannot expect to live by his own rules in a world shared by everyone.

Human greed never ends, the passage says. Even if wealth, honours and fame are poured out without limit, people still complain and crave more. Wanting more keeps growing with each gift, so the person who fears poverty is never truly rich.

Lady Philosophy is speaking here as if Fortune were giving her side of the argument. She says that if Fortune could make such a case, Boethius would have no answer. If he thinks he has a valid complaint, he must state it, and she will let him speak.

Boethius, speaking as the prisoner, says that Philosophy's arguments are pleasing, like sweet music or fine speech, but they only work while they are being heard. Once the words stop, his deep sorrow returns and hurts even more.

Philosophy tells Boethius that she has only started with gentle remedies, since his grief is stubborn, and deeper cures will come later. To talk him out of thinking himself wretched, she asks whether he has forgotten how fortunate he once was, and she begins by reminding him of his good fortune in being taken in by distinguished men after he was orphaned.

Philosophy is reminding Boethius of the good fortune he once had. He was chosen as an ally of the most powerful men in the state, was loved by their family before marrying into it, and was praised for his wife's virtues, her father's honours, and his sons. The speaker sets aside other honours and turns to the greatest of his blessings.

Boethius asks whether a past moment of worldly success, if it counts toward happiness, can be wiped out by later troubles. He recalls the day his two sons were made joint consuls, honoured by the Senate and the people, and when he himself won fame for a speech praising the king.

Boethius is speaking to himself through Lady Philosophy, reminding him of his past honours. He was once a consul, giving public shows in the Circus, and Fortune seemed to favour him. Now that she has turned against him, he should compare his losses with his earlier blessings, and he still has more good fortune than bad.

Philosophy is speaking to Boethius, who has lost his good fortune. If you do not count yourself favoured by Fortune now that your prosperity is gone, do not count yourself miserable either, because what seems bad now will also pass. Nothing in human life is stable, since people themselves pass away, and death ends whatever luck remains.

Each image in the poem shows something that is overcome by a stronger force: the stars fade in sunrise, the rose grove loses its blossom to the wind, and the calm sea is roused by storms. The point is that human fortune and happiness are as short-lived as these changes, because only one law lasts, namely that created things do not last.

Boethius, speaking to Philosophy, admits her words are true and that his past good fortune changed quickly. What hurts him most, he says, is remembering that he was happy, because that memory makes his present misery sharper.

Philosophy tells Boethius that if he is suffering because of a wrong belief, he cannot blame his circumstances. She suggests he count up the many good things he still has, since they are the true source of happiness that Fortune gives, even if that happiness is only a name.

Boethius is told that if he still has what he valued most, he has no right to complain about bad luck while keeping Fortune's better gifts. He is also reminded that his father-in-law Symmachus, a man of great character, is safe and unharmed.

Philosophy speaks to Boethius, who is in prison and grieving. She points out that his friend Symmachus, a man of wisdom and virtue, is safe from danger, and that his wife is alive but grieving for him and only wishes to keep living because of him. Philosophy says this absence is the one thing that might spoil his happiness.

Boethius, speaking as Philosophy, tells his grieving narrator that his sons have reached the consulship, an honour that shows the character of their father and grandfather. He says that since keeping one's life is the chief human concern, the narrator is fortunate to still have what he values more than life, so he should stop weeping because Fortune has not taken everyone dear to him.

Philosophy tells Boethius that his distress is not unbearable, because some anchors still hold: he still has comfort now and hope for the future. Boethius replies that while these hold, he can ride out the storm, though he admits much of his former good fortune has been stripped away.

Philosophy tells the speaker that his complaint is too strong. Nobody has perfect happiness, she says, because people either lack some part of it or lose it. Someone rich may still be unhappy about his low birth.

Each person has some lack or trouble in their situation. The noble man is poor, the rich man has no spouse, the married man has no children, and the parent has a troubled child. So no one is fully content with their lot, and each hidden burden hurts only the one who carries it.

People who have had the most good fortune are the most easily upset, since they are not used to hardship, so small setbacks can overwhelm them. Many others would count themselves blessed to have even a little of what the speaker has lost. Nothing is miserable in itself; it is made so by how we think about it, and any condition can be happy if borne calmly.

Worldly good fortune never brings complete happiness. Its pleasures are always mixed with bitterness, they cannot be kept once they choose to leave, and they do not last even for people who stay calm. So the happiness it offers is plainly unreliable and cannot fully satisfy an anxious mind.
Happiness is not found in outside things but within a person. Philosophy says that if you are master of yourself, you hold something you would never give up and that Fortune cannot take away.

Happiness cannot come from the things chance controls, such as wealth and status. The reasoning is that the highest good cannot be taken away, while anything Fortune gives can be, so Fortune cannot give true happiness. The passage adds that a person enjoying such fleeting happiness either knows it is unstable or does not.

Philosophy is arguing with a man who thinks his happiness is secure. She says there are only two cases. If he does not know his happiness can be lost, it is a poor happiness that rests on ignorance. If he does know, he must live in fear of losing it. Either way, he cannot be truly happy. The passage then turns to his firm belief that human souls do not die with the body.

Worldly good fortune ends at death, so if happiness came from it, everyone would fall into misery at death. Yet many people have sought happiness through death and suffering, so life cannot make people happy just by being present when its loss does not make them unhappy.

A builder who wants a secure home should avoid sand and mountain peaks, which are open to shifting ground and fierce winds. Instead, the house should be set on a low rock, where it can stand firm through storms and waves and keep its occupant calm.

Philosophy is arguing that worldly goods are not truly one's own and have no lasting value in themselves. She asks whether riches are precious by nature, and answers that they are only gold and piles of money, which show their worth when spent rather than when hoarded.

Money is valuable only when it is given away, because what is passed to someone else stops being one's own. If all the wealth were held by one person, everyone else would be poor. Greed makes people hated, while generosity wins fame.

Riches are shown to be a poor kind of good. Sound can reach many listeners at once without being divided, but money or property passed to one person is lost to others, so wealth cannot be shared whole and every gain for one means a loss for the rest. The author asks whether the attraction of wealth comes only from the shine of jewels.

The shine of jewels belongs to the stones, not to the person who owns them. The speaker wonders why people admire gems, since a living, thinking being should be moved only by what has life and movement. Even though gems gain some beauty from their maker and their own brightness, they do not deserve admiration, because they rank below the human being who admires them.

Philosophy asks Boethius whether the beauty of fields, sea, sky and stars belongs to him at all. He did not make these things, so he has no reason to claim their beauty as his own or to feel proud of it.

Fortune cannot make your own what nature has ruled out of your ownership, so there is no need to chase what is not yours. Nature needs only a few things, and only a little of them, to supply life's wants.

Nature needs only a little, and extra things given to a person who is already satisfied become unpleasant or harmful. Showing off in clothes of many colours is also questioned: if such sights give pleasure at all, the speaker would admire the weaving or the craftsman's skill, not the showiness itself.

Good behaviour in servants does not make a master's wealth his own, since their virtue belongs to them. Bad servants bring danger and burden. So a long train of servants cannot truly make a person happy, and none of these possessions is really his.

Worldly goods are either worthless, in which case losing them or keeping them should not matter, or they are valuable in themselves. Either way, their worth does not depend on being owned. You count them as yours only because they seemed precious to you.

Philosophy asks why people chase wealth to escape poverty, when more possessions only bring more to guard and more need. Those who need little, measuring by nature rather than showy display, want less. She asks whether people have no good within themselves that they look for outside.

Boethius asks whether humans, who are divine in their reason, can only feel splendid by owning lifeless possessions. Other creatures are content with what they have, but humans seek their glory in the lowest things. He says this wrongs their Maker, who meant humans to surpass everything on earth, so they lower their own worth beneath the lowest things.

Man is above other things only when he knows himself. If he loses that self-knowledge, he falls below the beasts. Other creatures not knowing themselves is natural, but in a man it is a failing. The passage also says that when people value lesser things as their good, they put themselves beneath those lesser things.

Things cannot be made better by borrowed decorations. Any shine they add is credited to the decorations, while the thing itself stays as ugly as before. Something that harms its owner is also not good.

Wealth often harms its owners, because wicked people want all the riches for themselves and will attack to get them. A poor traveller has nothing to fear from robbers, so wealth ends up costing the owner his safety.

Boethius describes an early age when people needed no luxuries. They lived simply, on grass, water and the shade of trees, without trade, sea voyages or war. He wishes people would return to that way of life, and he blames greed for their having left it.

The speaker laments the person who first discovered gold and precious gems hidden in the earth. By digging them up, that person brought out treasures that were better left concealed, and so brought danger.

Rank and power do not give true dignity, and they often end up in the hands of the worst men, who cause great harm. Romans once abolished the kings and then the consulship because of the arrogance of those who held them. Power is only welcome when good men hold it, and then it is their virtue that pleases, not the office itself.

Honour comes to a person from their virtue, not from their rank; rank gets its worth from virtue. Boethius then asks people to see how absurd their pride in power is: a mouse claiming authority over other mice would seem laughable, and yet a human body is weaker than many small creatures, such as a fly or an insect.

Power over a person reaches only the body and outward fortune, not the free mind, which reason keeps calm. The story of a prisoner who bit off his tongue rather than betray his friends shows this. Also, whatever harm one person does to another may come back on him in turn.

Busiris used to kill his guests, yet he was killed by his own guest, Hercules. Regulus bound many Carthaginian prisoners, and later he was himself bound by the Carthaginians. The point is that a man does not have real power if he cannot stop others from doing to him what he does to them.

Boethius argues that rank and power cannot be good in their own nature. Good things would never be found with utterly bad people, because opposites do not normally join together. Yet wicked men often hold high positions, so these things must not be good in themselves.

Boethius argues that a quality is known by what it produces. A brave spirit makes a man brave, speed makes a man swift-footed, and music, medicine and rhetoric each make people musicians, physicians or public speakers. Each thing has its own natural work, which shows what it is.

Wealth does not satisfy greed, and power does not free a person whose vices hold him in chains. Honours given to wicked people do not make them worthy but instead expose how unworthy they are. The passage asks why this happens.

Boethius says that people wrongly call things like wealth, power and high rank by names they do not deserve, since their effects show they are not what the names claim. He concludes that nothing within the realm of Fortune (luck or chance) is truly worth desiring or good in itself.
The speaker says that worldly success has not greatly moved him. He still wanted the chance to act, because he feared that his virtue would fade if it were never put into practice.

Philosophy says that the love of glory, meaning fame for serving the public, is the last weakness that can still tempt minds of good nature that have not yet been fully refined by virtue. She then asks the listener to consider how small and empty this glory really is.

Compared with the vast sphere of heaven, the whole earth is so small it counts as almost nothing. Only about a quarter of this tiny earth, according to Ptolemy's calculations, is inhabited by the living beings we know of.

Boethius's Philosopher tells his listener that most of the earth's surface is covered by seas, marshes and deserts, leaving only a tiny area for people to live in. He asks why anyone would seek fame across such a small space, since glory confined to so small a place cannot be wide or great.

Fame does not travel far. Many nations on earth do not speak the same language or share trade, and travel is hard, so even the names of famous men and great cities do not reach them. Cicero noted that Rome's fame had not crossed the Caucasus, so people hoping to spread their glory are working within very small limits.

Fame cannot spread far. Even Rome's glory does not reach everywhere, and different peoples praise and blame different things, so a person's name cannot be famous among many nations. A person who wants fame must accept that it stays within his own people.

Even written records fade with their authors over time, so many famous people are forgotten. Philosophy asks why anyone would take pride in a name lasting a few years, when eternity is so vast that such fame counts for almost nothing.

Any finite span of time, however long, has some size when measured against another finite span. Compared with endless eternity, though, even the longest fame lasts for so little that it amounts to nothing at all.

Boethius scolds people who act only to win crowd approval and popular praise, instead of valuing conscience and virtue. He says they seek reward in other people's empty words. He then promises to tell a witty story that mocks this kind of vanity.

A man insulted someone who called himself a philosopher, claiming the title only as a show of pride, and said that a true philosopher would bear insults calmly. The philosopher kept quiet for a while, then mockingly asked whether he had shown patience. The critic replied that he would have believed him had he simply stayed silent.

Boethius asks why outstanding people who seek fame through virtue should care about being remembered after death. If people die completely, he argues, there is no glory at all, because the person who would receive it no longer exists.

The passage says that a mind that knows it is good, once freed from the body, which it calls an earthly prison, flies up toward heaven. In doing so it looks down on worldly things and takes joy in its freedom and in heaven's pleasures.

Glory seekers should look at how vast the heavens are and how small the earth is, and see that human fame cannot fill even that small space. Death ignores all pride and titles, and it brings every person, high or low, to the same level.

Fame cannot keep the great dead alive. The famous Romans Fabricius, Brutus and Cato are gone, and only a few carved letters still record their names. Fame is short-lived, so people who hope it will extend their life are mistaken, since death comes a second time when their name is forgotten.

Boethius says that bad fortune is more useful to people than good fortune. Good fortune often seems pleasant but is deceptive, while bad fortune is honest because its changing nature shows it cannot be relied on.

Good Fortune is a false guide: she seduces people with the look of good things and keeps them from the true good, while they do not notice they are deceived. Ill Fortune is a teacher: hardship makes people wiser and sober, and often pulls them back toward the true good.

Philosophy is speaking to Boethius, who has lost his wealth and status. She says that Fortune, though cruel, has shown him who his true friends are, and has left them with him when she took everything else. He should therefore stop mourning his lost wealth, because true friends are worth more.

Boethius asks what keeps the natural world in its regular order: the cycle of seasons, the sun and moon, and the sea kept within bounds. His answer is Love, which rules heaven and earth. If Love withdrew its care, the peace that holds things together would turn into conflict and the world would fall apart.

Love joins tribes and nations through fair treaties, and it makes marriage holy through tender affection. It also binds true friends by fitting laws. The poem closes by saying people are blessed if the love that rules the heavens rules their own hearts.

Boethius says that Philosophy's song and words have comforted him. He now feels strong enough to face the blows of Fortune, the goddess of changing luck. He no longer fears the stronger remedies she mentioned earlier and eagerly asks to hear them.

Philosophy tells the narrator that she has been quietly guiding his thinking, and that what comes next will taste bitter at first but become sweet once understood. She says she will lead him to true happiness, which he glimpses in dreams but cannot yet see clearly, because his eyes are still fixed on appearances.

Philosophy agrees to help, but first she will describe, in words, a more familiar matter. Once the reader has examined it closely, the reader can turn toward the true happiness that is the real subject.

All people, however different their pursuits, aim at one goal: happiness. The supreme good is whatever leaves a person lacking nothing, and it contains all lesser goods. So happiness is a state made complete by gathering all good things together.

All people seek the same goal, the true good, but they take different roads. Some look for it in wealth, believing that having nothing lacking is the highest good. Others seek respect through public office, and some seek it in supreme power.

Boethius describes several kinds of people who mistake what makes life good. Some seek power or attach themselves to those who hold it, some chase fame in war or peace, and some think pleasure is the highest happiness. The passage then turns to others who confuse means with ends.

Human wishes and actions tend to aim at a few goals: riches, power, fame, noble birth, popularity, family, and friendship. Most of these are sought for pleasure, power, or renown. Only the most sacred friendship belongs to virtue rather than to luck or fortune.

Bodily gifts such as strength, beauty, speed and health are treated the same way as the earlier goods. Each of them is valued for what it brings: power, fame or pleasure. The argument concludes that all these things are sought for the sake of happiness, since whatever a person wants most is, to him, the highest good, and happiness is that highest good.

Philosophy here asks Boethius to consider common goals of human life: wealth, rank, power, glory and pleasure. Epicurus concluded that pleasure is the highest good, since all these other things seem to bring the soul some delight. The passage then says the human mind seeks its true good but, like a drunk man, cannot find the way back to it.

Happiness is a state full of all good things and needing nothing outside itself. The passage argues that what is best must also deserve respect, since people everywhere strive for it. It then asks whether power should count as a good too.

Philosopher Lady Philosophy is arguing that power, fame and a life free of worry are the things people want and count as good. She asks whether power can be called weak, whether fame means nothing, and says that happiness must be free from care and trouble, as even small pleasures are expected to be.

People pursue wealth, status, power, fame and pleasure because they think these will bring them independence, respect, influence, renown and happiness. Though their methods differ widely, all of them are really seeking the good as their goal.

Boethius's poem opens by saying that Nature's power guides the whole world in an orderly way, and that unbreakable laws govern even its smallest parts. The speaker says he wants to sing about this in verse, accompanying himself on his lyre.
The lion, though tamed and fed by hand, is still dangerous. If it tastes blood again, its wild nature wakes, it breaks its chains, and it kills the trainer who once controlled it.

The passage uses three images to show that things return to their natural state. A caged songbird ignores food and longs for the woods it can see. A bent sapling springs back when the pressure is released. The sun sets in the west but returns to the east by a hidden path.
All things seem to long for their proper return at the right time. No fixed order can last unless it runs in its set way, joining the end to the beginning in a steady, repeating circle.

Humans, though only dimly aware of where they came from, still sense what true happiness is, and nature points them toward the true good. Many mistaken beliefs, however, lead them away from it. The speaker asks whether people can really reach happiness by the means they think will get them there.

Wealth, rank and similar things may seem to supply everything good, and so bring happiness. But if they fail to keep their promises and lack many goods, the happiness people seek in them is shown to be false. The speaker then asks whether a rich man's mind was ever troubled by some wrong done to him, and he agrees it was.

Wealth cannot make its owner independent or free of all need, as it seems to promise. Money can also be taken from its owner against his will, and lawsuits show this, since the stronger often take it from the weaker by force or fraud.

Wealth, which was supposed to make a person self-sufficient, actually makes them need more protection. The speaker asks how riches can drive away want, since the rich still feel hunger, thirst and cold. A reply is then raised: the rich can buy food, drink and warmth to meet these needs.
Riches can ease want, but they cannot remove it. Wealth only satisfies a craving that is still there, and it creates new wants of its own. So wealth cannot give true independence.
Even if a greedy man grows rich, piling up gold, jewels and vast herds, he will never be free of anxious worry while he lives. At death, his wealth stays behind and goes with him nowhere.

Public office does not make a man good. Offices of state tend to make wicked men more visible rather than removing their vice, which is why it is shocking when the worst men hold high office. The poet Catullus mocks Nonius, a corrupt man, for sitting in a high seat, and the point is that high position only brings more disgrace on the bad.

Office and rank do not make a man worthy of respect. Philosophy argues that if a person is unworthy, the office he holds does not make him worthy either. By contrast, a man who has wisdom deserves respect because of that wisdom itself.

Virtue has its own dignity, and it passes that dignity on to the people who possess it. Public honours cannot do this, so they do not give true dignity. High position also does not win respect for wicked people; it only draws more attention to them, which makes their contempt greater.

Titles of office do not bring real respect, the passage argues. A man who was consul many times would not be honoured by barbarians in a foreign land, yet fire gives off heat everywhere. So if offices truly produced respect, they would work everywhere in the same way.

Boethius argues that honours and offices have no power of their own. Their importance comes only from people's mistaken opinion, so they lose their value when people stop respecting them. He gives examples: the prefecture was once powerful but is now an empty title that costs a senator money, and the office of grain supply, once distinguished, is now looked down on.

Worldly honours have no real beauty of their own. Their shine comes and goes with the judgments of those who hold them, so they cannot earn respect, are stained by wicked holders, fade over time, and fall into contempt when people stop esteeming them. Having none of this worth themselves, they cannot give it to others.

Here the speaker says that a certain ruler gave high public offices to dignified men, but those offices brought them no real honour. He then asks whether people who are raised to power in this way should really be called happy.

Boethius's Philosophy asks whether royal power and close friendship with kings can really make a person happy. Her point is that kings often lose their happiness, so power cannot even protect itself. If power is the source of happiness, then any shortfall in that power must bring unhappiness instead.

Even the widest kingly power leaves some peoples outside the king's rule. Wherever a person's power ends, helplessness begins, and so a king must also carry a share of misery. Dionysius, a tyrant, showed this fear with a sword hanging over a man's head.

Power that cannot calm a tormented mind or escape fear is not real power, the speaker argues. A ruler who wants safety but cannot get it, who needs bodyguards, and who fears the people he frightens more than they fear him, does not truly have power. He depends on the slaves he seems to command.

Royal power is weak, and it often destroys the friends of kings. Nero forced his tutor Seneca to choose how he would die, and Antoninus gave Papinianus to his soldiers to be killed. Both men had tried to give up their power, but neither got his wish.

Power and wealth make people afraid: while they hold it they feel unsafe, and they cannot easily give it up. Friends won by good fortune are not reliable, since bad fortune turns them into enemies, and a former friend can do more harm than an open enemy.
Whoever wants power must first master his own desires, since being ruled by lust is a kind of slavery. Even if he rules distant lands, he is powerless unless he can drive away anxiety and sorrow.

Many people have gained fame through the mistaken opinions of the crowd, which is a shameful thing. Praise that is false should make the praised person blush. Even deserved praise adds little to the wise person, who judges their own worth by inner truth rather than popular reputation.

Fame is shown to be worth little. If a person's name cannot reach many peoples across the world, then someone celebrated in one place is unknown and unremarkable in another. Popular approval is dismissed as not worth mentioning, since it does not come from sound judgment and does not last.

Noble birth brings no real fame, because any renown belongs to the ancestors who earned it, not to their descendants. If nobility has any value, it is only that the well-born should try not to fall below the virtue of their forebears.

All people share one origin, since God is the Father of all and gave every person a soul from heaven. So boasting about noble birth or ancestry makes little sense. Only sin and vice can make a person base, by staining that heavenly origin.

Bodily pleasures, Boethius argues, bring unrest while desired and regret once satisfied, and they often cause illness and pain. He adds that if such pleasures made a person happy, animals would be happy too, since they live only to satisfy bodily needs.

Children can be a source of great pain as well as joy. Philosophy points out that the speaker has never suffered such trouble, so he cannot know how painful it is. She agrees with the poet Euripides that a man without children is fortunate in the misfortune of having none.
Pleasure is compared to a bee. If someone robs her of her honey, she stings them and flies away, leaving a painful wound that stays in the heart.

Boethius argues that the usual goals of wealth, office, power and fame do not bring happiness. Each one costs something: wealth must be taken from its holder, high office means begging for favour, power brings danger from plotting subjects, and fame is pursued at a similar price.

Boethius argues that bodily pleasure and physical strength are poor things to value. People who enslave themselves to the body are looked down on, and animals such as the elephant, bull and tiger are stronger or faster than we are. He asks the reader to stop admiring such trivial things and look instead at the vast, steady movement of the heavens.

Beauty does not come from the thing itself but from the viewer's weak sight. Beauty also fades quickly, faster than spring flowers. Even Alcibiades, a famously handsome man, would look repulsive if his inner parts could be seen, so his looks depend on the eyes that see him.

Bodily beauty and similar goods can be destroyed by a short illness, so they are not lasting. Things that cannot deliver what they promise, and that do not bring together all good things, neither lead to happiness nor make a person fully happy.

Ignorance leads people away from the truth, the poem says, by making them look for things in the wrong places. Gold is not found on leaf stems, gems not on vines, and fish not on hilltops. Instead, people know where things are really found: pearls and shells in the sea's depths.

Boethius says that people who do not know where true good lies, and keep their eyes on earthly things, are blind to what lies far above the stars. He wishes them to chase wealth and fame until they grasp a false good, and only then, too late, recognise the true one.

Philosophy has shown what false happiness looks like, and now turns to what true happiness is. The speaker agrees that wealth, power, high office, fame and pleasure do not bring lasting independence, authority, respect, renown or real joy. He admits he only partly sees why, and asks to be taught more fully.

Philosophy argues in a question-and-answer exchange that what is complete and lacks nothing must also have power. Something weak needs outside protection, so self-sufficiency and power are one and the same. Then she asks whether such a thing deserves contempt or the greatest respect.

Philosophy is arguing that fame or renown is not something separate from the other three qualities the passage has been discussing: power, self-sufficiency and worthiness of honour. The reasoning is that these qualities together already make a thing famous, so renown adds nothing new and is the same as them.

Philosophy leads the speaker to agree that a being which needs nothing else, has full power, fame, and respect must also be full of joy. The speaker adds that these qualities, though given different names, are really one and the same thing.

Human error splits what is one and simple in nature, so people try to grab a part of something that has no parts. They fail to get any part, since there are none, and they also miss the whole, which they never aim for.

Those who seek wealth give up power and often pleasure, and still do not gain security. Those who seek power spend their wealth and scorn pleasure, yet their position is also flawed in many ways. Each pursuit, on this view, leaves something important out.

Philosophy is describing how a person who seeks power, rank, glory or pleasure can lose the very thing he wants. Power may fail when a man lacks necessities or is troubled by worries, and the same reasoning applies to rank, glory and pleasure. Each of these goods is the same as the others, so seeking one apart from the rest means not even getting that one.

Philosophy argues that a person who wants true happiness, meaning all the goods together, will not find it in the separate things people usually chase, since those cannot give what they promise. Having shown the false kind, she points the mind toward the true happiness she has promised.

Philosophy has the speaker agree that true happiness must bring together independence, power, reverence, renown and joy. The speaker adds that whatever gives any one of these gives complete happiness, since all are the same. Philosophy approves of this view but says one thing must be added, and the speaker asks what that is.

Worldly goods like wealth and power give only shadows or partial forms of the good, never the true and perfect good. Having learned this, the speaker asks where true happiness can be found, and Philosophy asks what must be done to deserve finding it, suggesting that one should first call on God's help.

This is a hymn to God as the creator. It says God rules the world by reason and set time going from eternity. God is unmoved yet causes all movement. No outside cause forced God to shape the world; instead, God shaped it from the perfect good within God's own nature, and the world reflects that perfect pattern.

This is a hymn of praise to God as the maker of the world. It says God arranged the elements so that they stay in balance: hot and cold, wet and dry do not fight, fire does not escape upward, and water does not flood the earth.

This is a hymn addressed to God, who is said to bind the whole universe together and to move it. It describes the world soul, which travels in circles around the limits of mind, and the lesser souls and lives that God sends out into the stars and the earth. God is asked to bring them back to himself at last.

The speaker prays to God, asking to be lifted by reason to see the source of goodness and the true light. The prayer asks God to clear away earthly confusion so the soul can rest in him, described as its beginning, end, guide, and destination.

Philosophy says that now that the nature of imperfect and perfect good has been shown, it will explain how complete happiness is formed. First, it asks whether the kind of excellence just defined really exists in reality, or whether it is only an empty idea in the mind.

Boethius argues that the highest good must exist, because the idea of imperfection depends on the idea of perfection. Something is called imperfect only because it lacks some perfection. So wherever an imperfection is found, a corresponding perfection must also exist.

Imperfection could not exist unless perfection existed first, because nature begins with what is whole and perfect and only later produces weaker things. So since a frail, imperfect happiness exists, a complete and perfect happiness must also exist.
Boethius argues that God is good, since nothing better can be imagined than God. Reason shows that God's goodness is perfect, because otherwise God would not be the highest of all things.

Something more excellent than the highest good would have to exist if the highest good were not God, and that would lead to an endless chain of higher goods. So the supreme God must hold all perfect good. Since true happiness is the perfect good, true happiness must exist within God.
Philosophy invites the speaker to see how firmly one can prove that God possesses the highest good most fully. The speaker asks how this proof can be made.

God is not given his highest good from outside, nor does he have it as something separate from his own nature. If it came from outside, then whatever gave it would be greater than God, which is unthinkable.

Boethius argues that God is the highest good and that God's goodness cannot be something separate from God's nature. If goodness were really in God by nature yet distinct from God, that would be impossible, because God is the supreme being. Two things that are truly different cannot also be the same thing.

Whatever is distinct by its own nature from the highest good cannot itself be the highest good. Since nothing can be better than its source, and God is the source of all things, God must be the highest good. Happiness has already been accepted as the highest good, so God must be happiness itself.

Philosophy argues that there cannot be two different supreme goods, because each would lack what the other has, so neither would be perfect. Since happiness and God have both been shown to be the supreme good, it follows that God must itself be supreme happiness.

Philosophy argues that happiness is the same as being God, so anyone who gains happiness becomes a god, in the same way that gaining justice makes a person just. God is one by nature, but many people can become gods by sharing in that nature.

Boethius asks whether happiness is a whole made of many separate parts, or whether one single element is its true essence and the others depend on it. His companion asks him to explain fully. The reply is that happiness is judged to be the highest good, and it is taken to include independence, power, reverence, renown and pleasure.

Philosophy asks whether goods such as independence and power are parts that make up happiness, or whether they are all directed toward good as their highest point. The speaker replies that he understands the question and wants to hear how the other person would answer it.

The argument here is that the things people look to for happiness, such as wealth, power, fame and pleasure, cannot be separate parts of happiness. Parts of a whole must differ from one another, but these have already been shown to be the same. So they cannot be parts, since happiness would then be made of one part only, which is impossible.

Everything people seek, such as independence, power, reverence, renown and pleasure, is sought only because it seems good. Good is therefore the source of all desirable things. Nothing that has no good in it, real or apparent, can be wanted at all.

Even things that are not good in nature are wanted as if they were truly good, whenever they seem good. So goodness is the root and cause of everything people desire. A person who rides a horse for his health wants the health, not the riding itself.

Everything people seek, they seek for the sake of the good. So the good itself, not the other things, is what all people really want. Happiness is what all other wishes aim at, so happiness is the one thing sought. The passage concludes that the highest good and happiness are the same, and so God and true happiness are the same.
Those whose minds are held by desire, which binds people to base, earthly things, are invited to come to a single refuge. There they will find an end to their toil and rest from their troubles.

Gold, silver sands and jewels from distant rivers cannot brighten the mind; they leave it in its own darkness. The true light, which gives strength to the heavens and governs the universe, is not found in them. Once a person has seen that light, even the sunbeam seems dim.

Worldly goods such as wealth, power, fame and pleasure are not true good on their own, because each lacks what the others offer. They become true good only when all of them are joined into one thing, so that a single good has all these qualities. Otherwise they cannot be counted as worth desiring.

Boethius argues that things become good only when they are unified, since being good means sharing in goodness. From this he concludes that unity and goodness are the same thing, because things with the same natural effects have the same essence.
Everything that exists lasts only as long as it stays one whole thing. When it stops being one, it falls apart and perishes.

Each thing exists as long as it stays one unified whole. Living creatures and bodies are given as examples: when soul and body are joined, or the parts of a body are joined, the thing is alive or recognizably itself. When that unity breaks apart, the thing dies or stops being what it was, and the same holds for all other things.

Philosophy asks whether anything that acts in keeping with its nature ever gives up the wish to live and seeks death and decay instead. The question implies that no such thing exists, since every natural thing wants to keep living.

Living creatures, even those with some flaws in their choices, never give up the will to live on their own. Without outside force, every creature works to preserve itself and avoids death. The speaker is unsure whether the same holds for plants and inanimate things.

Plants grow best in the places their own nature suits, whether plains, mountains, marshes, rocks or sand. Moved elsewhere, they wither. Nature gives each plant the ground it needs and works to keep it alive for as long as it can live.

Boethius's passage asks why plants are built as they are: roots draw food from the soil, bark protects the softer inner parts from weather, and seeds let each kind of plant reproduce. The implied answer is that these features are designed to keep each species alive now and for all future generations.

Even things without life, the passage says, act according to their own natures. Fire rises and earth falls because those movements suit each one. Things are kept whole by what suits their nature and harmed by what opposes it, and stones hold together because their parts cling tightly.

Fluids like air and water give way when cut but close up again, and fire cannot be cut at all. Boethius says he is speaking of nature's unthinking movements, not of deliberate choices of the mind. Breathing, digesting and the love of life work this way, though the will can sometimes choose death over the life that nature clings to.

Living things naturally want to keep existing and avoid destruction. Even creatures that must die still have this drive, and it is built into nature by providence, the divine ordering of the world. So, the speaker says, this desire for continued life is not doubtful but clear.

Philosophy and her student agree on a dilemma: either all things aim at no single end, or they all aim at one end, which must be the highest good. Since everything desires the good, they conclude that the end of the whole universe is the good itself.

Truth is found by looking inward, not outward, through deep thought. The soul already holds the seeds of truth, so learning is really remembering what it once knew. Boethius presents this as Plato's teaching, which he says is correct.

Boethius's narrator says he agrees with Plato and that he has forgotten these truths twice: first through the body's weight on the mind, then through deep grief. Philosophy replies that he will soon remember more, namely how the world is governed, which he had earlier admitted he did not know.

Boethius's speaker, Lady Philosophy's pupil, admits that he earlier held as certain that God governs the world. Philosophy reminds him of this earlier admission, which he now must defend. The speaker says he expects her next point but wants her to lay out the argument clearly.

The speaker is sure that the world holds together as one whole. Its parts are very different and opposed, so something must join them, and that joining power must also keep them joined. Without such a power, the differences would tear the world apart.

The regular order of nature, with its fixed positions, times, ranges, powers and kinds of motion, could not continue unless something remained unchanging and arranged all the changes. Boethius calls this power, which keeps things in their created state and in motion, God.

Philosophy argues step by step. If independence is part of happiness, and God is perfect happiness, then God needs no outside help to govern the world. So God must rule all things by his own power alone.

Philosophy says that God arranges all things for good, ruling the world as a helm steers a ship and keeps it steady. The speaker agrees and says he had guessed where she was heading. Philosophy replies that he now sees truth more quickly, and that her next point is just as plain, and asks what it is.

Philosophy argues that if God rules all things with goodness, and all things naturally move toward good, then everything willingly accepts His rule. A rule would not be a good one if it forced unwilling subjects, and nothing that follows its nature resists good. Such resistance would be powerless.
The speaker says he is glad of the arguments and their conclusion, and especially of the other person's wording. He now feels ashamed of the foolish worry that had troubled him.

Philosophy argues that God is all-powerful, yet God cannot do evil. From this she concludes that evil is nothing, since nothing is impossible for God except what would be evil. The argument sets up a puzzle about how evil can exist if God is all-powerful.

The speaker accuses Philosophy of confusing him with twisted arguments that seem to loop back on themselves. He points out that she first said happiness is the highest good, seated in God, and then concluded that anyone who is happy must also be God.

Philosophy is recalling for Boethius things he has already taught him. She says that the highest good is God and is also true happiness, that God rules everything through goodness, and that evil has no real existence in nature. He stresses that these points were proved from within the argument itself, not from outside assumptions.

Philosophy tells Boethius that she is not mocking him, and that their prayer to God has reached its goal. She then describes God's nature: God cannot move outward into external things, nor take external things into himself. She supports this with a line from the ancient Greek thinker Parmenides, who describes the divine as a perfectly round sphere.

Philosophy says that the highest good, like the still centre of the universe, moves the spinning heavens while staying itself unmoved. She adds that her arguments come from within the subject itself, not from outside, because Plato taught that words should match their subject.

Orpheus, the legendary singer from Thrace, grieves for his dead wife. His music moves woods, rivers and animals, yet it cannot ease his own pain. In anger at the gods, he goes down to the gates of Hell.

This verse tells the myth of Orpheus, the singer. His songs, taught by his mother, the goddess, carry his grief and love. He plays so movingly in the underworld that its king is moved to pity, and the three-headed guard dog, Cerberus, lies down at his feet.

The verse says that the music of the song brings a brief rest to the figures of Greek myth who suffer endless punishment. The Furies, who chase guilty minds, melt into tears. Ixion's wheel stops, Tantalus forgets his thirst and hunger, and the vulture pauses in tearing at Tityus.

The shadowy king of the underworld, moved by pity, agrees to give Orpheus back his wife Eurydice on one condition: he must not look back at her until they have left Hell. Orpheus breaks the condition, looks back just before reaching the upper world, and loses her for good.

Those who seek the light, and want to find their way to a clearer day, are addressed here. The warning is that if they look back at the darkness they have left behind, their weak, wandering eyes will lose the greatest prize.

Boethius describes Philosophy finishing her song of verses calmly and seriously. Still grieving, he interrupts her before she can speak again, praising everything she has said so far as divine and as too strong to be refuted.

The speaker says he already knew these truths, but anger over his wrongs had made him forget them. What troubles him most is that evil exists at all, and goes unpunished, even though a good ruler governs the universe.

Evil people prosper while good people go unrewarded, are pushed down and trampled, and are punished in place of wrongdoers. The speaker finds it hard to believe this could happen under a God who knows all, can do all, and wills only good.

Philosophy tells Boethius that it would be monstrous if, in a well-ordered world, worthless things were honoured and precious things neglected. She says this is not so: the good are always strong and the bad weak, vices are always punished and virtues always rewarded.

Philosophy tells the speaker that good people receive good fortune and bad people receive bad, and that this will quiet his complaints and give him firm confidence. Having shown him where happiness is found, she now promises to show him the way back home and to give his mind the means to rise up and return safely.
The speaker says the soul has wings and rises above the earth. It passes the clouds, the sun, the planets and the stars, then goes beyond the outermost sphere to the source of all light.

The verse describes a heavenly place where the Sovereign of the world rules calmly and guides the universe like a charioteer. It says that a wandering soul who reaches this place will recognise it as its true home, the land it came from. It also warns that anyone who returns to the gloom of earth will find tyrants, feared by nations, living there in miserable exile.
The speaker tells Philosophy that her promises are very great. He says he has no doubt she can keep them, and asks her not to leave him waiting after raising his hopes.

Philosophy says that good has real power, while evil is weak and has no true strength. Each truth proves the other, because good and evil are opposites. She will argue both sides to make her case more convincing.
Any human action needs both will and power; without either, nothing gets done. If someone wants something and fails, he lacked the power. If someone succeeds, he had the power to do it.

Philosophy and her student agree that all people, good and bad alike, seek the good, since happiness is the good that everyone wants. The student then refuses to accept that reaching the good makes people good, which sets up the next argument.

Since good people achieve the good they seek and bad people do not, Philosophy asks whether the good are not clearly powerful and the bad weak. Anyone who doubts this, she says, cannot understand how things work or follow an argument.

Philosophy asks which is stronger: something that performs its natural function naturally, or something unable to do so that only feigns it by an unnatural means. Walking is her example of natural human motion. The final lines are unclear, but they seem to turn on whether the speaker walks naturally.

Philosophy asks a simple question. Of two men, one who can walk on his feet and one who lacks the use of his feet and walks on his hands, which is the stronger? The answer given is the one with the natural ability, since he has more strength than the one who lacks it.

Everyone aims at the supreme good, but good people reach it through natural virtue, while bad people chase it through desire, which does not lead to it. From this, the speaker concludes that the good have real power and the bad are powerless.

Philosophy tells Boethius that his quick insight is a good sign, like a doctor seeing the body begin to heal itself. She then argues that wicked people are very weak: they cannot reach the good that nature itself pushes everyone toward, and they cannot win or keep the great prizes they chase.

Boethius argues that the good are truly strong because they reach their highest aim, the good itself, so nothing more remains to be desired. By the same reasoning, the wicked are weak: they fail to reach what they seek, and they turn from virtue to vice.

Boethius asks why people do wrong. If they do not know the good, they are weak, blinded by ignorance. If they know the good but lust pulls them away, they are still weak, because they cannot resist vice. If they knowingly turn from the good, they do not even have real power, and in the end they cease to exist, since the good is the common end of all things.

Boethius argues that bad people are bad in a limited sense, but do not truly exist in the full sense. He compares them to a corpse, which is called a dead man but is not simply a man. Only what keeps its own nature truly exists, and whatever falls away from its nature loses that existence.

Evil people can do harm only because they lack real power, since doing evil is a weakness rather than a strength. Evil itself is nothing, so the wicked cannot achieve anything, and only the supreme good has true power.

Boethius argues that the power to do evil is not real power. Only the power to do good counts as omnipotence, so those who can do evil are less powerful. Since all power is desirable and all desirable things aim at good, the ability to do wrong cannot be desirable, and so it cannot be power.

Only the wise can do what they want, while the wicked, though they chase what they desire, never reach it, because shameful deeds do not lead to happiness. Boethius presents this as proof that good has power and evil is weak, in line with Plato's view.

A king may look powerful, with his robes and guards and fearsome presence. But strip away his outward state, and he is shown to be bound by inner troubles: lust, rage, sorrow and false hopes. He is no freer than any other captive, since he cannot always do what he wants.

Good always receives its reward, and wrongdoing its punishment. Just as a wreath is the prize for which a race is run, the reward of an action is the thing it is done for. Happiness has already been shown to be the good that all things aim at, so it is the true reward of goodness.

Good is the reward that comes with good actions, and a good person cannot be separated from it, since someone without good cannot be called good. So the wicked cannot take away the wise person's reward or honour, however fiercely they rage against them.

The reward of a righteous person is not something given from outside, which could be taken away by another. It comes from the person's own goodness, so it is lost only if that goodness is lost. Since good is what every prize is valued for, the good person already has the greatest reward.

Good people are happy simply because they are good, and happiness is the same as being divine. So the reward of goodness cannot be lost to time, power, or wrongdoing. From this, the wise person can have no doubt that the wicked are punished.

Good and bad are opposites, so reward and punishment are opposites too. Each reward for the good has a matching penalty for the bad. Being righteous is itself the reward of the righteous, and being wicked is itself the punishment of the wicked. No one who suffers punishment doubts that it is an evil.

Boethius is asking a rhetorical question: people whom wickedness has not only touched but deeply stained cannot really think they escape punishment, if they would only consider their own situation. The point is that wicked people are already punished by their own corruption.

Boethius argues that goodness is what makes a thing fully what it is, so evil things lose their real existence. Wicked people, he says, stop being what they were and keep only their outward human form. By turning to evil, they lose their true human nature.

Righteousness raises people above the human level, and vice drags them below it. So a person changed by vice is no longer really human. A greedy robber is like a wolf, a quarrelsome litigant like a snarling dog, and a sly schemer like a fox.

A person who gives up virtue stops being fully human, and cannot rise to a godlike state. Instead, each vice turns them into an animal: rage makes a lion, cowardice a deer, ignorance an ass, fickleness a bird, and lust a hog.

Odysseus and his crew are blown by storms to the island of Circe, the sorceress who is the daughter of the Sun. She mixes a magic cup, and anyone who drinks it is turned into a beast. The verses describe the animals some of the men become, such as a boar, a lion, a wolf, and a tiger.

Odysseus is saved from the sorceress Circe by Hermes, the god with the staff. His men drink her potion and are turned into pigs, losing human speech and shape. Only their minds stay human, and they mourn the change.

Evil arts and poisons can change a person's outward body, but they cannot reach the inner self. The spirit stays safe in its true home. The poisons that do real harm are those that leave the body unharmed while corrupting the soul, which removes a person from his high place.

The speaker agrees that wicked people, though they look like humans, are rightly said to be turned into beasts in their spiritual nature. He wishes they were not allowed to use their cruel, corrupt minds to harm good people.

Philosophy argues that evil people would suffer less if they could not carry out their wicked desires. Wanting evil is already wretched, and having the power to act on it makes things worse. So those who will, can, and do commit crime suffer a threefold misery.

Philosophy is saying that wicked men will lose their power sooner than expected, since even the longest human life is short. Their grand plans and crimes are often brought down by a sudden, unforeseen end, and that end at least brings their misery to a close.

If wickedness makes people wretched, then the longer someone stays wicked, the more wretched they are. Death is the only thing that ends a wicked person's evil deeds, so a wicked person who lives forever would be infinitely wretched.

Philosophy tells Boethius that if someone doubts a conclusion, they must either show a flaw in the starting premises or show that the premises do not force the conclusion. If the premises are accepted, the conclusion cannot be rejected. She then introduces another point that seems surprising but follows just as necessarily from the same premises.

Boethius's speaker argues that wicked people are worse off when they escape punishment than when they are punished. He sets aside the usual reasons for punishment, such as reforming the offender or deterring others. The reason he gives is that a wicked person who goes unpunished is more unhappy, since the wicked are already agreed to be wretched.

Philosophy asks Boethius two questions. Is a miserable person happier when some good is mixed in with the misery than when there is no good at all? And is someone who is wretched and has no good at all even more unhappy if an extra evil is added? Boethius agrees to both points.

Boethius argues that the wicked are made worse off when they escape punishment than when they are punished. Punishment is a good, because it is just, while escaping it is an evil, because it is unjust. So unpunished wrongdoers suffer more than those who are justly punished.
The speaker agrees that the conclusions just reached follow logically. He then asks his companion whether she takes no account of the soul being punished after the body dies.

Philosophy says that the power of wicked people is not real power, and that the wicked are never without fitting punishment for their wrongdoing. She notes that some punishments are meant as justice and others as purification, but she will not discuss those now.

Philosophy tells the speaker that the freedom he asked for will not last long, and that a longer or endless freedom would make his state worse. It also argues that wicked people suffer most when they seem to escape punishment, since unpunished wrongdoing is worse for them than receiving a just penalty.
The speaker says that while he follows Philosophy's arguments and finds them convincing, most people will not even listen to such arguments, let alone accept them as believable.

Those who judge by their own inclinations, not by the order of the universe, wrongly think crime and escaping punishment are good fortune. Philosophy says a person who shapes their soul toward the better needs no judge to reward them, since their own conduct has already raised them.

Boethius says that a person who turns their desires toward lower things brings their own downfall, so no outside punisher is needed. He compares this to sight: looking at the earth or the sky makes a person seem to sink or to rise, though nothing outside has moved. Most people ignore this, and he asks whether we should then follow them, since they are like beasts.

Boethius argues that a blind man who forgets he was ever able to see would wrongly think he lacks nothing, and that people who see would not agree he is blind. The speaker then turns to a claim his listener doubts: that wrongdoers are more wretched than those they wrong. He begins to prove it by asking whether every wicked man deserves punishment, which the listener grants.

The passage argues that the person who commits a wrong is more miserable than the person who suffers it. The speaker gets the other to agree that a judge would punish the wrongdoer, and so the wrongdoer is the one who is worse off. Since wickedness itself makes people wretched, the harm of a wrong falls on the doer, not the victim.

Philosophy says that courtroom practice works the wrong way round. Lawyers try to make judges pity the wronged, when pity is really owed to the wrongdoer. A criminal should be brought to judgment kindly, like a sick man to a doctor, so that his fault is cut out through punishment.

Boethius argues that if lawyers were used only to bring about justice, they would mostly have no need to defend anyone and would only accuse. He adds that wicked people who saw that punishment would cleanse them of their vices and earn them righteousness would no longer feel that suffering as pain.

Wicked people are compared to the sick. Just as we pity someone who is ill rather than hate them, the wise feel no hatred toward the wicked. Hating the bad is unreasonable, because wickedness is a disease of the soul that deserves pity.

Why do men rashly seek death and wage cruel wars against their own kind? Wild beasts do not harm their own kind this way, and men fight only because their lands and laws differ. The closing lines say that justice requires love for the good and pity for the wicked.

Boethius's speaker accepts that the righteous and the wicked get happiness or misery that matches what they deserve. He still asks whether fortune, meaning worldly success as ordinary people see it, is really good or bad, since no sensible person would prefer exile and poverty to wealth and honour at home.

Boethius says that wisdom works most clearly when the happiness of rulers spreads to the people around them. He wonders why the opposite happens: good people suffer punishments meant for criminals, while bad people receive the rewards of virtue.

The speaker asks why the world seems so unjust, with good people sometimes suffering and bad people often prospering. He says that if events were only random he would be less puzzled, but because he believes God governs the world, the unfairness is harder to accept. Unless a reason can be found, he sees no real difference between God's rule and chance.

Things can look random and confused when the order behind them is not understood. Even without knowing the causes of the whole system, one can trust that a good ruler governs the world and that everything is done rightly.

The passage says that people wonder at strange-seeming sights in the sky, such as the Bear constellation seeming slow and sinking late, or stars appearing when the moon is full. Yet nobody wonders at familiar events like waves breaking on shore or glaciers melting in summer. The reason given is that we fear what is hidden and unexplained, and we do not fear what we understand.

Weak minds make rare and strange things seem greater than they are, and ordinary people are overwhelmed with awe when things change unexpectedly. Wonder goes away from wise minds once ignorance no longer clouds them.

Boethius's speaker, who is troubled, asks Philosophy to explain the hidden causes behind a puzzle they have just discussed. He asks her to share her own answer, because the strangeness of the matter bothers him more than anything else.

Philosophy replies that the subject she has been asked to discuss is the greatest of all. Each doubt raised about it breeds many more, like the heads of the Hydra, a many-headed monster from Greek myth, so they must be stopped by the mind's own fire. The subject covers providence, fate, chance, God's foreknowledge, and free will.

Philosophy tells Boethius that she will examine the weight of his troubles, since understanding them is part of curing his distress, though time is short. She asks him to set aside music and song for a while so she can lay out her arguments in order. He agrees.

Everything that happens, changes, or moves gets its cause, order, and form from the unchanging mind of God. That mind plans how it governs the world in more than one way. Seen from God's own view, this plan is called providence; seen from the side of the things it governs, the ancients called it fate.

Providence is the divine reason itself, held in the highest being, and it arranges everything as a whole. Fate is the order built into moving things that carries out that arrangement, giving each thing its place, form and time.
Providence is the whole order of events seen as one in the mind of God. Fate is that same order unfolded in time. The two differ, but fate comes from providence's simple unity.

Just as a craftsman first sees the whole of what he will make in his mind and then makes it step by step, God sees all things together in one unchanging plan. God then carries out that plan over time through fate, which unfolds the plan in a sequence of events.

Whatever agency carries out fate, whether spirits, stars, angels, demons, or nature, one thing is clear. Providence is the single, unchanging plan of events held in God's mind. Fate is that plan unfolding over time as a changing sequence of events.

Everything under fate is also under providence, the divine foresight that fate itself depends on. Some things under providence, however, stand above fate's chain of cause and effect. These are the things placed so close to the highest God that they stay fixed and sit outside fate's changing order.

The passage uses the image of concentric circles around a centre. Things closer to the centre are simpler and more unified, while things farther out spread wider and are more tied up in fate. So the closer something draws to the primal mind, the freer it is from fate.

Whatever stays fixed close to the supreme mind is free from change, so it stands above fate's necessity. Fate's changing sequence relates to providence's unchanging simplicity as reasoning relates to pure intelligence, time to eternity, or a circle's edge to its centre.

The passage says that a chain of causes moves the heavens and stars, mixes the elements, and drives the cycle of birth and death. Because this chain starts from unchanging providence, the fates of people are bound to it and cannot be changed.

The world is run for the best because God's unified mind sets an unchanging chain of causes. This fixed order keeps changeable things from moving at random. Things may look confused to humans, who cannot fully grasp it, but every event is limited so that it leads to good.

Nothing is done for the sake of evil, even by evil people, because they really seek good but are led astray by wrong thinking. Much less can the order that comes from the highest good turn away from its starting point.

Philosophy answers an objection: it seems wrong that good people sometimes suffer and bad people sometimes prosper. The reply is that people do not agree on what is right or wrong, so their verdicts about who deserves reward or punishment often conflict. Human judgment is therefore not a reliable measure of how fortune should be distributed.

Boethius asks whether someone who can tell good from bad could also see into the inner nature of the soul, much as a doctor reads the body's make-up. He compares this to a puzzle: why sweet foods suit some healthy people and bitter ones others, and why some sick people respond to gentle treatment while others need harsh treatment.

The passage compares the soul to the body. Just as a doctor knows what makes a body healthy or sick, God knows what the soul needs. Righteousness is the soul's health and vice is its sickness. God, seen as the guide and healer of the mind, keeps good and removes evil, and from His watchtower of providence He assigns to each what suits them.

Boethius says that human reason cannot fully understand God's plans. A man who seems perfectly just may still suffer, because divine providence sees matters differently. When events seem to go wrong, the fault lies in our judgment, not in the order of the world.

Some people are spared hardship by God's wise plan. One who is weak in mind might be ruined by suffering, so he is not allowed to suffer. Another who is perfectly virtuous and close to God is protected from misfortune, even from bodily illness.

Providence, the divine order that governs the world, gives each person a fitting mix of good and hard things. Some are tested by hardship so their virtue grows stronger, and some are troubled so they do not become proud from long good fortune. Some people fear what they could actually bear, and others scorn what is beyond their strength.

Misfortune tests people and shows what they really are. Some earn lasting fame by dying gloriously, and others show by their steady endurance of suffering that hardship cannot defeat virtue. The author holds that all this happens justly and for the good of those involved.

Boethius says that the wicked suffering punishment is not surprising, since everyone thinks they deserve it. Punishment warns others away from crime and corrects the wrongdoers themselves. The good fortune of the wicked, he adds, teaches good people how to judge such prosperity, which often comes to bad people.

Some people, Boethius says, are so reckless that poverty would push them toward crime, so providence lets them gather wealth instead. Such a person may then feel uneasy about his guilty conscience and fear losing the riches he now enjoys.

Boethius here argues that hardship and power both serve a purpose. Fear of losing wealth can make a wicked person change his ways. Some people who bear good fortune badly are brought to ruin. Rulers with the sword are allowed to test the good and punish the bad. Wicked people cannot even agree with each other.

Even wicked people often feel their own guilt, because their vices trouble their conscience. Providence, the divine order that governs all things, uses this to make some bad people lead others to virtue. When people are wronged by evildoers, they come to hate those wrongs and try to be unlike the wrongdoers, so they return to virtue.

Only divine power can turn evil to good, by using evil things for a suitable purpose that leads to some good end. Everything falls within some order, even what departs from the established laws, so nothing in divine providence is left to chance.

God, who created all things, arranges them and leads them toward good. He keeps his creation like himself and removes evil from his order through a chain of fate. So if one looks at this divine ordering, the evils people think are common on earth cannot be found in it.

Philosophy tells Boethius that she sees he is tired from the long argument and wants a break in the form of poetry. She offers him a verse, hoping it will refresh him so he can focus harder on the rest of the discussion.

The poem says that the heavenly bodies follow fixed laws set by God, and that they keep to their courses without getting in each other's way. The sun never blocks the moon, and the Great Bear, which never sets, does not wish to sink into the sea like the other stars.

Love governs the natural world in this poem. It keeps day and night, morning and evening, in their fixed order, and it keeps the opposing elements (hot and cold, wet and dry) in harmony. Each element also has its natural place: fire rises and earth sinks.

The poem describes the seasons, each bringing its gifts in turn: flowers in spring, grain in summer, fruit in autumn, rain and snow in winter. This steady cycle gives life to all living things, but after a short time, everything it brought is taken away again.
One ruler steers the universe, keeping the heavenly spheres in their orbits. If that controlling power were withdrawn, the orderly world would collapse into total ruin.

Everything in the connected universe moves toward one goal, which is the Good. Many paths lead there, but all end in the same place. Nothing endures unless it turns back and returns to the source it first came from.
Every kind of fortune, pleasant or painful, serves either to reward or test good people or to punish or correct bad people. Since each one is either fair or useful, every fortune is good.

Boethius, speaking through Lady Philosophy, has just argued that bad fortune is not truly bad. The speaker agrees the argument is sound but wants to keep a claim that seemed paradoxical, since everyday speech often calls some people's fortune bad. Philosophy agrees to speak more like ordinary people, and asks whether the speaker calls what is advantageous "good."

Lady Philosophy and Boethius reason about punishment. Popular opinion holds that punishment, though harsh, is good for the wicked, yet it also counts as the most miserable thing. Following this through, they conclude that virtuous people have good fortune and wicked people have utterly bad fortune. Boethius admits this is true, though few would dare to say so.

Philosophy says that a wise person should not be upset when hard times come, just as a brave soldier is not upset when the battle trumpet sounds. Hard times give the wise person a chance to show courage and to grow in wisdom. Virtue is named for its strength to withstand adversity, so those who have climbed toward virtue must not be weakened by pleasure.

Stay firm against the ups and downs of fortune, so that neither bad luck crushes you nor good luck spoils you. Keep to the middle way, since going too far either way loses the reward of your effort. Hard fortune is only punishment unless it teaches you or improves you.

Boethius uses three stories from Greek myth to show how people who gave way to anger, cruelty or greed were later punished. Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter to win favourable winds. Odysseus wept when his men were eaten by the Cyclops, and Polyphemus was later blinded and paid for his feast.

This verse lists the twelve labours of Hercules, the Greek hero famous for his superhuman feats.
