It names several of his tasks, such as killing the birds, taking the golden apples, and bringing up Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld. The final labour was holding up the sky, and it earned him a place among the gods.
Brave people are urged to keep going and not run away from the struggle. If they win their fight on earth, their reward will be the stars, meaning a place in heaven.

Philosophy has finished one line of argument and is about to move on. The speaker interrupts with a difficulty about providence, meaning God's foresight and govern of the world, and asks whether chance exists at all and, if it does, what it is.

Philosophy tells Boethius she will return to the main subject, which is how he can get back to his homeland. She says the side topics she has been discussing are useful but may tire him and pull him away from the goal. Boethius replies that he is not tired, since learning gives him great pleasure, and her reasoning has been so sure that he has no doubts.

Philosophy replies that chance does not really exist. If chance means an event with no cause, then the word means nothing, except as a name for the idea itself. Since God orders all things, there is no room for events happening at random.

Boethius's speaker recalls the old principle that nothing comes from nothing. The ancients applied it to physical matter, not to the cause that makes things happen. If something arose without any cause, it would seem to come from nothing, and so chance, as just defined, would be impossible. The speaker then asks whether chance or accident is therefore a mere name, or whether it names something real that ordinary people do not understand.

Chance is defined here as what happens when an action aimed at one goal produces a different result for unplanned reasons. Its example is a farmer digging a field who finds buried gold. Such a find only looks accidental, because it still has causes that come together unexpectedly.

Gold is found by chance because two separate causes happened to come together: a farmer digging in the field and a man burying money in that exact spot. Neither person intended the discovery, so it is called chance.

Chance is defined here as an unexpected result that comes from several causes coming together, when each of those causes was aimed at its own purpose. The example given is a man who buried gold and a farmer who dug in the same spot, and neither meant for the gold to be found.
Events come together through a fixed chain of cause and effect. This chain comes from Providence, meaning divine foresight or care, and it puts every thing in its proper time and place.

Boethius uses the image of two rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates, which meet and then separate, carrying driftwood that seems to move by chance. The channel's shape and the water's force actually steer every piece. So even what looks random is controlled by fixed law.

The speaker agrees that events follow one from another in a necessary way. He then asks whether anything is left of human free will, or whether this chain of fate also controls the movements of the mind.

Philosophy says that every rational being has free will, because reason lets a being judge what to seek and what to avoid, and choice follows from that judgment. She adds that this freedom is not the same in every being.

Higher divine beings have perfect judgment, a will that cannot be corrupted, and full power to carry out their wishes. Human souls are freer when they contemplate the divine mind, less free when they enter the body, and least free when they are bound to earthly matter. When they give themselves to vice and lose their proper reason, they are in complete slavery.

When people turn their eyes from the highest truth to the lower world, ignorance soon blinds them. Their harmful desires then bind them more tightly, even though they seem free. Still, God sees everything from eternity and gives each person what their merits deserve.

Homer praised the sun, but his light cannot reach the depths of the sea or the dark centre of the earth. God, who built the universe, is not limited in this way: earth and night cannot hide anything from his eye. So God, not the physical sun, is the true sun.

The speaker finds it hard to believe that God knows everything and yet people still have free will. His reasoning is that if God foresees an event and cannot be wrong, then the event must happen. So foreknowledge seems to remove free choice.

If God knows eternally not only what people will do but also what they intend, then human free will seems impossible. Nothing can be done or intended except what God's unerring foreknowledge has already seen.

If events could be diverted from the outcome that providence (God's foreseeing care) has foreseen, then God would not have sure knowledge of the future, only guesswork. Boethius calls it impious to think this of God.

Boethius rejects one way of solving the puzzle of divine foreknowledge and free will. Some people say that events do not happen because God foresees them. Instead, God foresees them because they are going to happen, so the necessity lies in the foreseeing rather than in the event.

Boethius is saying that it does not matter which comes first, foreknowledge or necessity. Even if foreknowledge does not itself force future events to happen, those events are still necessary once they are foreseen. His example: if a man is seated, the statement that he is seated must be true.

Boethius is working through an example: if someone is sitting, then the belief that he is sitting is true, and that belief must be true while he sits. The necessity runs both ways, but the cause runs one way. The man is not sitting because the belief is true; the belief is true because he is sitting.

Even if God foresees future events only because they will happen, the foreseeing still makes them necessary, and that necessity is enough to remove free will. Yet it is absurd to say that events happening in time cause God's eternal foreknowledge.

Boethius argues that if God foresees events because they will happen, then the events would be the cause of God's foreknowledge, which seems wrong. He also argues that anything known in advance must necessarily happen, so foreknown events come about inevitably.

Knowledge is never a belief that something could be otherwise than it is, so a future event that is not certain and necessary cannot be known in advance. Whatever knowledge grasps must be exactly as it is known, so an uncertain future cannot be foreknown.

God's knowledge is always true, because each thing must match the knowledge that grasps it. So the question is how God can foreknow events that are uncertain. If God took an event that might never happen to be certain to happen, God would be mistaken.

God's foresight, if it only saw future events as possible and not fixed, would be no real knowledge at all. Boethius compares such uncertain prediction to the empty prophecies of Teiresias, a seer from Greek myth who always said something that could turn out either way.

Boethius argues that if God's foreknowledge is perfect, it cannot be uncertain, so the events God foresees must certainly happen. On this view, human choices cannot be free, because God's certain knowledge fixes each one to a single outcome.

If people do not freely choose their actions, but are forced by what must happen, then rewards and punishments make no sense. Punishing the wicked and rewarding the righteous would then be the greatest injustice, not justice.

Boethius's opponent argues here that if everything is decided by divine providence and humans have no free choice, then virtue and vice make no real difference. Vices would also have to be traced back to God, which the speaker finds a deeply shocking idea.

If everything is fixed by an unbreakable chain of cause and effect, then hope and prayer have no purpose. Boethius argues that this would cut off the only link between God and people, since people earn God's favour through humble prayer and hope.

Prayer is presented as the way people can commune with God and draw near to him, even before their requests are granted. But if the future is fixed by necessity, it is hard to believe prayer has any real effect, so the question arises how people can then reach God at all.
Because humans have been separated from their Source, which is God, they are bound to fall into ruin. Philosophy says this, recalling a line of poetry she sang earlier.

The poem asks why truths that each seem plain can appear to contradict one another, and whether the fault lies in truth itself, which is always consistent. It suggests that the human mind, held in the body, is too dim to see how the truths link together. It then asks why people search for truth at all, since they either already know it or do not know what they are looking for.

Boethius asks how anyone can long for a good they do not know, or search for an end they cannot recognise. His answer is that the soul once knew the whole truth. Though clouded by the body, it still keeps some memory of that knowledge, so a person who seeks the truth is neither fully blind nor fully able to see.

The verse describes a person who knows only part of a thing and has lost the rest. He still holds on to what remains, feels his way in dim light, and works to recover the whole by means of that remaining part.

Philosophy tells Boethius that the question of providence (God's foreknowledge of events) is old and hard, and that many thinkers, including Cicero, have failed to settle it. The difficulty, she says, is that human reasoning cannot grasp God's simple, unified foreknowledge. If we could form a clear idea of its nature, no uncertainty would be left.

Philosophy says she will first look at why the reader is unhappy with an earlier answer. That answer said that foreknowledge, knowing in advance what will happen, does not cause future events to be necessary, so it does not limit free will.

Philosophy argues that foreknowledge does not force future events to happen. If foreknowledge imposes no necessity, then there is no reason to think freely chosen actions are fixed in advance. Assume there is no foreknowledge at all, and Philosophy asks whether willed actions are then bound by necessity. Boethius's interlocutor answers that they are not.

Boethius suggests that foreknowledge does not force events to happen, so free will remains intact. Someone may object that foreknowledge still signals that events are necessary. He answers that a sign only reveals what is already certain; it does not cause it, so events would be certain even without foreknowledge.

Boethius argues that foreknowledge can only prove something if everything happens by necessity. If nothing is necessary, a foreseen event could not be a sign of anything fixed. He also holds that a sound proof must rest on necessary causes, not on mere signs, and asks how foreseen events could ever fail to happen.

Boethius argues that foreseeing an event does not mean the event is forced to happen. He compares this to a charioteer steering his chariot: his movements are not compelled by necessity, since if everything were forced, skill would have no effect.

Things that happen without necessity in the present must also have been going to happen without necessity beforehand. So some future events are not bound by necessity, and they stay free even when they are known in advance.

Knowing something as it happens does not make it necessary, and knowing the future does not make future events necessary either. The objection is that if future events can be foreseen, they must be necessary, and if they are not necessary, they cannot be foreseen.

Boethius's speaker says that if something is known as certain while it is actually uncertain to happen, that is mere opinion, not real knowledge. Knowledge means thinking of things as they really are, so a false picture of them cannot count as knowing.

Things are not grasped in the way their own nature would suggest, but in the way the knower is able to grasp them. Boethius uses sight and touch to show this: sight takes in a round body all at once from a distance, while touch feels its roundness part by part.

Man can be known in different ways, depending on the faculty that perceives him. Sense perceives him as a bodily form in matter, and Imagination as a form without matter. Thought grasps the general type found in the individual, and pure Intelligence grasps the form itself, beyond all universals.

A higher power of knowing contains and understands the lower ones, but the lower cannot reach up to the higher. Senses only grasp matter, imagination cannot see universal ideas, and reason cannot grasp pure form. Intelligence looks down on all of these and understands them through its own higher grasp of form.

Boethius says that the highest kind of knowing grasps universal forms directly, in one act of insight, without using the senses or the imagination. Reason, too, can think about universals, such as the definition "man is a two-legged animal endowed with reason," while still dealing with images and sense impressions.

Boethius says that a universal idea can be pictured by the senses, yet thought grasps it through reason, not through sense or imagination. Imagination also works on sense-impressions, but with its own power. So every knower uses its own faculty rather than the faculty of the thing it knows.

The verse describes the Stoic view (from the Porch, the Stoa) that the mind starts as a blank page, and all knowledge is written onto it by the senses through experience. Boethius then argues that if the mind is wholly passive, merely reflecting outside things like a mirror, it cannot be trusted to show what is true.

Boethius asks what gives the mind its power to perceive, know and order the world. He suggests that this power comes from the mind itself rather than from impressions left by outside things. Still, he notes that the body's senses do stir the mind's understanding.
When light strikes the eye or sound reaches the ear, the mind, stirred to respond, takes in the message. It joins these outside signs to the forms it already holds inside.

Boethius argues that if the mind in living bodies does more than passively receive impressions from the senses, and actively sorts them, then purely mental beings, free of bodies, must know even more through their own mental activity rather than by taking in outside objects.

Boethius sorts living things by the kind of knowing each has. Creatures that cannot move, like shellfish, have only sense perception. Moving animals also have imagination. Humans alone have reason, and God alone has pure intelligence. So the highest kind of knowing is the one that can grasp the objects of all the lower kinds too.

Boethius asks what happens if the senses and imagination deny that the universal, which reason claims to grasp, is anything at all. Sense and imagination only deal with particular things, so either reason's grasp of universals is true and no particular objects exist, or reason's idea of the universal is empty, since the senses clearly show many particular objects.

Reason replies that it grasps the same objects as Sense and Imagination, but in their general, universal form. Sense and Imagination can only know bodily shapes, so Reason, the stronger faculty, should be trusted about what is real. The passage then asks whether, since humans have reason as well as imagination and perception, they should side with Reason in this dispute.

Human reason assumes that God can only foresee the future the way humans know things. The argument runs: if events do not seem certain and necessary, they cannot be known in advance as certain to happen. So either there is no foreknowledge of such events, or else everything must happen by necessity.

Boethius says that if humans could share in the judgment of the divine mind, human reason should accept it, just as reason rightly rules over imagination and sense. He invites us to rise toward that highest intelligence, where reason can see how uncertain future events can still be known with certainty by God.

The passage lists the many kinds of living creatures on earth, grouped by how they move. Some crawl on their bellies, some fly through the air, and some walk over the ground. The speaker finds this variety remarkable.

Boethius says that animals, with their heads bent toward the ground, have dull souls and senses, while humans alone stand upright and can look up at the sky. He urges the reader to lift the soul toward heaven as well as the eyes, so the mind does not stay stuck in earthly things.

Things are known according to the nature of the mind that knows them, not according to their own nature. So the passage proposes to consider God's nature, as far as it is permitted, in order to understand how God knows.

Eternity, the passage says, is endless life held completely and perfectly in one single moment. Temporal things cannot do this: anything that lives in time moves from past to future and never has its whole life present at once.

Mortal life, even if it had no beginning or end, as Aristotle thought of the world, is still not eternal. It lives only one moment at a time, having lost yesterday and not yet reached tomorrow, so it cannot hold its whole endless life together at once.

Eternity is the complete, unending life that holds all of time at once, with nothing future or past missing from it. Boethius adds that people are wrong to think Plato's view makes the created world equal in age to its Creator, just because Plato held that the world had no beginning and will have no end.

God's eternity is not the same as a world that lasts forever. An endless life is held all at once in the present, which belongs only to the divine mind. God is earlier than created things not by passing time but by the unique simplicity of his nature.

Things that unfold endlessly in time try to copy the unchanging life of God, which exists wholly in an eternal present. Since they cannot match that fullness, they move away from stillness into change and stretch out into an endless past and future.

Boethius is describing how temporal things, which can never hold their whole life at once, try to imitate eternity. They do this by attaching themselves to any passing moment, however brief. Because this resembles the eternal present, it gives everything it belongs to a kind of existence.

Because the world cannot stay still, it moves on through endless time, and so it keeps going by constant change the full life it could not hold all at once. For that reason, Plato's view is followed: God is eternal, but the world is everlasting.
God's knowledge works differently from ours. Since God exists in an eternal present with no past or future, His knowledge sees all of time at once, as if every event were happening now.

God's knowledge is not a foreseeing of future events but a single, timeless grasp of everything at once, like seeing from a high place. It is called providence for this reason. Just as people seeing something do not make it happen, God's seeing does not make events necessary.

God sees all things at once, in one eternal present, just as people see things in their own present time. Because of this, God's foreknowledge does not change the nature of things: it sees what will happen as it will actually happen, and it still tells apart what happens by necessity from what does not.

God sees all things at once, yet he does not mix up what is free with what is necessary. Just as a viewer can see a man walking and the sun rising in one glance and still know that one act is chosen and the other is not, God's vision keeps each thing's nature distinct, even though events that are future in time are all present to him.

God's knowledge of a future event is not mere opinion but true knowledge, even when the event is not forced to happen. Someone who says that what God foresees must necessarily happen is stating a solid truth, but few people can grasp it without deep study of the divine.

Boethius says a future event is necessary when seen from God's knowledge, yet in itself it can still be free. He separates two kinds of necessity: a plain one, such as all men being mortal, and a conditional one, such as a walking man having to be walking because someone knows it. Knowing something does not make it necessary in the plain sense.

Boethius argues that God's foreknowledge does not force events to happen. A man walking freely must go forward while he walks, but nothing in his nature compels him to walk. Likewise, God sees freely chosen future events as present, so they are necessary only because God knows them, not because of their own nature.

Things that God foreknows will happen will indeed happen. Some of them happen by free will, and even after they happen they keep their own nature, which means that before they happened they could really have failed to happen.

Boethius asks what difference it makes that future events are not necessary in themselves, if God's foreknowledge makes them happen as if they were necessary. He answers with two examples: the sun's rising is necessarily going to happen before it happens, while a man's walking is not necessary beforehand, though both cannot fail to happen once they are occurring.

Boethius says that things present to God definitely exist. Some happen by necessity and others by the free choice of their agent. Seen from God's knowledge, they are all necessary, but considered in themselves, many are free from necessity, just as sensible objects are universal when viewed by thought yet particular in their own nature.

Boethius imagines an objection: if a person can change their mind, they could make God's foreknowledge wrong. He replies that a person can change their purpose, but God sees in advance whatever choice is made. Foreknowledge still holds, just as a person standing in front of a watcher cannot escape being seen.
God's knowledge does not change to match what a person decides to do. Philosophy asks Boethius whether he would say that divine foreknowledge shifts depending on his own choices, and he answers no.

God sees all of time in one present moment, not one event after another. So God's knowledge of the future does not depend on what happens in the future, and our future actions do not cause what God knows.

Human will is free, so laws that reward and punish are just, because people act without being forced. God sees all things at once from an eternal present, and that sight matches what people will freely do, so He rewards the good and punishes the bad.

Prayers and hopes aimed at God, if rightly directed, will have an effect. For this reason, the passage urges resisting wrongdoing, practising goodness, and praying humbly, because every action is seen by a Judge who sees all things.

The passage says the guardians of hell-fire are angels, and their number is set as nineteen only as a test. It is meant to unsettle unbelievers, to confirm the faith of believers and of People of the Book, and to leave the doubters without certainty. God guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills, and only God knows the full number of His hosts.

God knows that the Prophet and some of his followers pray for about two-thirds, half, or a third of the night. Since people cannot measure the hours of the night exactly, God shows mercy and allows them to recite as much of the Qur'an as they can easily manage.

The passage tells believers to recite as much of the Qur'an as they easily can, to keep the daily prayers, and to give charity. It promises that good deeds sent ahead will be repaid by God, and urges asking God for forgiveness, since God is merciful.

The opening prayer of the Qur'an. It praises God as Lord of all worlds, merciful and ruler of the Day of Judgment. It asks God to be worshipped and helped, to guide the reader to the straight path, and to keep them from the path of those who earned anger or who went astray.

God describes the fate of those who refuse to bow in worship and who call the revelation a fraud. He says he will lead them step by step to ruin, and he will wait patiently. The Prophet is told to be patient and not to act like the man in the fish, who cried out in distress.
Unbelievers look at the Prophet so fiercely that they nearly strike him down, and they call him possessed. The verse insists that the Quran is nothing less than a warning for all creatures.

Those who believe and do good will have gardens with flowing rivers, which is great happiness. God is powerful, forgiving, and loving, and he creates and restores all things. The unbelievers, like Pharaoh's people and Thamud, are surrounded by God, and the Qur'an is written on a preserved tablet.

On the Day of Judgment, the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows and will not speak, except for those whom the Merciful God allows, and who will say what is right. The passage warns of a punishment close at hand, when people will see the deeds they have done, and the unbeliever will wish he were dust.

The passage describes God's punishment of past peoples: a violent wind lasting seven nights and eight days, the drowning of Pharaoh's people and earlier cities, and the Flood, from which believers were saved in the Ark. These events are meant as a warning, and it ends by pointing forward to the blast of the trumpet.

Believers will be reunited with their children who also followed the faith, and they will receive their full reward for their deeds. They will be given plenty of fruit and meat, and a cup that brings no idle talk or sin. They will speak with one another and give thanks to God for saving them from torment.

Names given to beings, including angels called female, have no divine proof behind them. People follow guesses and desires, although guidance has reached them. Angels cannot intercede unless God permits it. Those who deny the afterlife are the ones who give angels female names.

God alone knows who has gone astray and who has been guided, and everything in heaven and earth belongs to Him. He will repay evil-doers according to their deeds and reward those who do good with good things.

God forgives minor faults in those who avoid great sins, and people should not claim their own purity, since God alone knows who truly fears him. It then rebukes a man who turns away and withholds, and recalls that no soul bears another's burden.

The passage is a note by the translator about a verse episode. It says Muhammad first accepted some words that pleased the idolaters, then within a few days rejected them as a Satanic suggestion and replaced them with the current text. The translator thinks he was under pressure and tried a compromise, which he later regretted.

The passage speaks to humans and jinn, beings made of fire in Islamic belief, and says they cannot escape the limits of heaven and earth without God's permission. It then describes a Day of Judgment, when fire and molten brass will be sent down, the sky will split open, and sinners will be seized and shown Hell.

The people of Noah rejected him as a liar and called him mad, and he appealed to God for help. God then sent a great flood, with rain from the sky and water from the ground, and saved Noah in a ship. The ship was left behind as a sign, and the passage asks whether anyone will take the warning.

On the Day of Judgment, after one blast of the trumpet, people look around in fear and realise the day of reckoning has come, the day they had denied. The wrongdoers and their false gods are gathered and sent toward Hell. They are questioned, then turn on one another with blame, each saying the others led them astray.

Those condemned blame each other: the followers say the leaders were the ones who refused belief and misled them, and both will share the punishment. The passage then says that when people were told there is no God but God, they grew proud and mocked the messenger as a crazed poet, though he brought the truth and confirmed earlier messengers.

God speaks here of blessings given to Abraham's son Isaac, to Moses and Aaron, and to the prophet Elias. He says he rescued Moses and Aaron and their people from great distress, gave them a clear book and guided them, and rewards those who do good.

Noah tells God that he has preached to his people day and night, but the more he calls them, the more they turn away, stop their ears and refuse to listen. He tries calling them openly and also in private. The passage also carries God's promise that forgiveness and a delay until a fixed time will be given, and that heavy rain will follow if they turn back.
Noah prays to God for forgiveness for himself, his parents, believers who enter his house, and all believing men and women. He asks that the wicked receive only destruction.

Those who are rewarded wear green silk and brocade, wear silver bracelets, and drink a pure drink from their Lord. The passage tells the Prophet to be patient, to refuse the wicked and unbelievers, to remember God morning, evening and night, and warns that people who love this fleeting life ignore the coming Day of Judgment.

God invites people to look at the sky and the earth as signs of his power. He made the heavens flawless, spread the earth out, set mountains on it, and grew plants and palm trees. He also sends rain that brings gardens and crops, all as a lesson for those who turn to him.

Earlier peoples such as Ad, Pharaoh and Thamud's neighbours rejected their prophets and were punished. The passage then asks whether God is tired from creating the first time, and so doubts a second creation (resurrection) are misplaced. It says God knows a person's inner thoughts, and two recording angels, one on each side, write down every word.

This part of Sura 50 describes a scene at judgment. A person is told he was heedless in life, but now his sight is sharp. God orders every unbeliever, one who set up other gods, into Hell. The accused person blames the companion assigned to him, who replies that he did not lead him astray and tells them not to argue, since warnings were given earlier.

The passage warns that many earlier peoples, stronger than the Meccans, were destroyed, and asks whether any of them could escape. It says God created the heavens and earth in six days without tiring. It tells the listener to bear the Meccans' words patiently, to glorify God at dawn, dusk and night, and to wait for the day when a crier will call everyone.

God owns everything in the heavens, on the earth, between them, and under the soil, and He knows even whispered and hidden speech. The passage then begins the story of Moses, who sees a fire, goes toward it, and is called by God and told to take off his shoes because he stands in a holy valley.

A mother is told to place her infant in a chest and set it on the river, where the waters will carry it to the shore. An enemy will find the child, but God says He has made the child loved and has kept him under His watch.

God tells Moses of the events of his early life: his sister led him back to his mother, he was rescued after killing a man, and he spent years in Midian. God then sends him and his brother Aaron to Pharaoh, who has gone beyond all limits, and orders them to speak to him gently, in the hope that he will reflect or fear.

Moses and his brother are sent to Pharaoh with a message from their Lord. They ask that the Israelites be released and not harmed, and they warn that punishment falls on whoever denies the message and turns away. When Pharaoh asks who their Lord is, Moses answers that He gives every thing its form and then guides it. Pharaoh then asks about the fate of earlier generations.

God is described as having made the earth a resting place, with paths, rain, and plants for people and animals, and as the one who will bring people back to life. Pharaoh is then shown to reject these signs, and he accuses Moses of coming to drive the people out of their land through magic.

Pharaoh challenges Moses to a contest of magic on a feast day, in daylight before the assembled people. Moses warns the magicians not to lie against God, since liars will be destroyed. The magicians then confer together in secret about their plan.

Pharaoh's magicians accuse Moses and Aaron of sorcery and challenge Moses to a contest of magic, letting him throw first or going first themselves. When their cords and rods seem to Moses to move like snakes, he feels afraid, and God tells him he will prevail.

God tells Moses to throw down the staff in his right hand, which will swallow the magicians' tricks. Their illusions are only the deceit of a magician, and no magician succeeds wherever he goes. The magicians then bow down and declare their belief in the Lord of Aaron and Moses.

Pharaoh speaks to his court or to the magicians who have come to believe in Moses. He accuses them of following Moses, whom he calls their teacher of magic. He threatens to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and to crucify them on palm trunks, and he says they will learn whose punishment is harsher and lasts longer.

Speaking to Pharaoh, the sorcerers say they will not put him above God, who has shown them clear signs. They tell him to decide as he wishes, since he can only rule this present life. They have believed in their Lord so that he will forgive their sins and the sorcery they were forced into. Those who come before God guilty face Hell, where they neither die nor live. Those who come as believers who do good deeds receive the highest ranks.

Pharaoh chased the Israelites with his army, but the sea swept over him and his men, because he had led his people astray instead of guiding them. God then reminds the children of Israel that he saved them from their enemies, gave them manna and quail, and told them to eat without excess. He promises forgiveness to anyone who turns to God, believes, does good, and follows guidance.

Moses speaks to his people after his absence. He asks whether God had not promised them a good promise, and whether his time away felt too long. He asks if they wanted God's anger to fall on them, since they broke their promise to him.

The people say they broke their promise to Moses only because they were made to carry the people's jewelry. They threw it into the fire, and Samiri cast it in too, producing a golden calf that lowed. They called it their god and the god of Moses, who had forgotten it. The passage asks why they did not see that it could neither answer nor help them. Aaron had warned them that the calf was only a test, and that their Lord is merciful.

Moses asks the Samiri why he did what he did. The Samiri answers that he saw something others did not. He took a handful of dust from the messenger's path and threw it into the golden calf, because his soul urged him to.

Moses (or a speaker in the story) tells a man to go away, saying he will be shunned in this life and punished later. He says the man's idol will be burned and its ashes scattered in the sea, and that only God, who knows all things, is God. The final lines say the story is a warning, and whoever turns from it will bear a burden on Judgment Day.

On the Day of Judgment, people will follow the summoner without speaking above a whisper before God. No one can plead for another unless God allows it. Those who carry the burden of wrongdoing will be lost, while believers who do right will fear neither injustice nor loss.

The passage says God sent down an Arabic Qur'an with warnings in many forms, so people might fear God or think carefully. It tells the prophet not to rush its recitation before the revelation is complete, and to pray for more knowledge. It also recalls that God made a covenant with Adam, but Adam forgot it and did not hold firm to it.

God tells the angels to bow to Adam, and all do except Eblis (Satan), who refuses. God warns Adam and his wife that Satan is their enemy and should not drive them from the garden. Satan then tempts them with the tree of eternity and an everlasting kingdom. They eat from it, become aware of their nakedness, cover themselves with leaves, and Adam disobeys his Lord and goes astray.

God punishes those who transgress and reject his signs, and the punishment of the next world will be harsher and longer-lasting. People who walk through the ruins of past nations should see how many generations were destroyed before them. Punishment has been delayed by a decree, and its appointed time is still to come.

Bear patiently what the opponents say, and keep praising God at dawn, at sunset and during the night. Do not long for the worldly goods given to others, since God's reward is better and lasting. Tell your family to pray, and God will provide for you and reward piety.

The speakers demand a visible sign from God before they will believe. The passage replies that clear proof has already come in the earlier scriptures, and that if punishment had come first they would have asked for a messenger. It ends by telling the believer to wait, since each side will see in time which of them followed the right path.

Moses admits he killed a man earlier and fled from Pharaoh in fear, but says God then gave him wisdom and made him a messenger. He asks whether Pharaoh's favour, raising him in Pharaoh's house, is worth much when Pharaoh has enslaved the Israelites. Pharaoh asks who the Lord of the worlds is, Moses says it is the Lord of heaven, earth and all between, and Pharaoh calls Moses's messenger mad.

Pharaoh threatens the sorcerers who believed in Moses before he gave permission, promising to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them. They answer that the threat cannot harm them, since they will return to their Lord and trust he will forgive their sins. God then orders Moses to leave by night with the Israelites, because Pharaoh will pursue them.

God sends rain and winds, gives life and death, and holds all things, and He knows every person from first to last. He created man from dried clay and the djinn from subtle fire. When God told the angels He was creating man from clay, He ordered one being, Iblis, away as "a stoned one," meaning cast out.

Iblis, the devil, says he will lead humans astray, except God's sincere servants, and God replies that only those who follow the devil will have power over them. Hell is their destination, with seven gates. The pious will instead dwell in gardens and fountains, in peace and without weariness, and will never be expelled.

Lot is told to take his family out of the city by night, without looking back, because the town's people will be destroyed at dawn. When the townspeople come to his house wanting his guests, Lot offers his daughters instead, and they are described as blinded by their desire.

God made the heavens and earth for a purpose, and the Last Hour will surely come. The Prophet is told to forgive kindly, not to envy unbelievers their worldly goods, and to be gentle with believers. He is only a plain warner, and those who split the Quran into pieces will be punished.

Zechariah asks God for an heir who will continue his family line and be pleasing to God. God answers that he will have a son named John, which Zechariah questions because his wife is barren and he is old. God replies that this is easy for him, since he created Zechariah before when he was nothing.

Zechariah asks God for a sign that his wife will conceive, and God answers that he will be unable to speak to people for three nights while otherwise healthy. Then God tells John to hold the Book firmly. John is given wisdom as a child, is kind, pure, dutiful to his parents, and not proud, and peace is upon him at birth, death, and resurrection.

In this passage, a messenger says that a son will be born as a sign and mercy from God, and that this is already decided. Mary gives birth far away, under a palm tree, and wishes she had died before. A voice tells her that God has provided water and fresh dates, so she should eat, drink, and be calm.

The passage says that religious groups disagree about Jesus, and it warns unbelievers of a coming day of judgment, when all people will return to God, who will inherit the earth. It then tells the reader to recall Abraham, described as a truthful prophet.

Abraham says he will leave his people and the gods they worship besides God, and will pray to his Lord instead. After he leaves them, God gives him Isaac and Jacob, makes each of them a prophet, and then turns to Moses, a pure man and prophet whom God called from a mountain for private conversation.

The passage names a line of prophets, from Adam through Noah, Abraham and Israel, who were chosen and guided by God. They wept and bowed in worship when God's signs were recited to them. Later generations abandoned prayer and followed their desires, and they will face harm, except those who repent, believe and do right, who will enter the Garden.

The speaker says that angels come down only by God's command, and that God is Lord of everything in heaven, on earth, and between them, so He should be worshipped steadily. It then answers a man who doubts he will be raised after death: God created him from nothing before, and God will gather all people and the Satans and set them on their knees around Hell.

Unbelievers mock believers by asking which side has the better position and company. The reply is that many earlier generations, richer and grander than them, were destroyed. God lets those in error live on for a time, until they face their threatened punishment or the Hour, and then they will see who is worse off.

Everything in heaven and earth will come before God as a servant, and each will come to him alone on the Day of Resurrection. God will show love to believers who do right. The Quran is made easy in Arabic so it can bring good news to the God-fearing and warn the quarrelsome. Past generations were destroyed, and no trace or sound of them remains.

The speaker asks whether the critics own God's mercy or rule heaven and earth, and says they should climb up by ropes if they do. He warns that these opponents, like earlier peoples who rejected their prophets, will be defeated. He names Noah's people, Ad, Pharaoh, Thamud and Lot's people as examples of those who came to ruin.

Two men come to David with a dispute. One has ninety-nine ewes, and the other has only one, which he asks to keep. The speaker says the richer man talked him into giving it up, so David is asked to judge fairly between them.

David is told a story about a rich man who takes a poor man's only ewe, and David sees that he has been tested. He asks his Lord for forgiveness, bows down and repents. God forgives him and promises him a high rank and a good place in Paradise.

God addresses David, made a ruler on earth, and tells him to judge fairly and not follow his desires, since straying from God leads to punishment. The passage says creation has a purpose, not being empty, and that the faithful who do right cannot be treated the same as those who spread evil.

Solomon says he loved worldly possessions more than remembering his Lord, until the horses were out of sight, and orders them brought back so he can deal with them. He then asks God for forgiveness and for a kingdom no one else could have. God gives him power over the wind and over spirits and others bound in chains.

Followers and leaders in hell blame one another. The leaders are told that the group will join them in the fire, and each side says the other brought this fate on them. They also wonder where the people they once mocked as wicked have gone. The passage calls this quarrel among the people of the fire a truth.

This note explains a Quranic phrase usually read as "Lord of stakes", meaning forces. The translator cites Sprenger's suggestion that a Jewish source described Pharaoh as rich in fortresses, while the Arabic word may originally have meant a pillar, later replaced by the word for tent stakes.

Only those who accept the warning and fear God in private are the ones the speaker should warn and give good news to, promising forgiveness and a generous reward. God says he will raise the dead and record everything people have done and left behind. Then a story about a city's people and messengers follows.

Messengers sent to a town are rejected by its people, who call them mere men and accuse them of lying. The messengers answer that their only duty is to deliver a clear message, and the people threaten them with stoning. The messengers reply that the bad omen they fear comes from the people themselves, and that the people are going astray.

A man speaks to his people, refusing to worship other gods and saying he trusts his Lord. He is told to enter Paradise, and he wishes his people knew of God's favour to him. The people are then destroyed by a single shout, and all will be gathered before God.
God created all paired things, including humans and things unknown to them. The night and day, the sun and moon each follow their set course, and none can overtake the other.

Unbelievers refuse to give charity, mocking believers who say God can feed the poor. They ask when the promised Judgment will come, and the passage answers that it will come suddenly, with a blast of the trumpet. Then the dead will rise from their graves and go to their Lord.

The dead are raised at the Last Day by a single blast, and they gather before God. Nobody is wronged that day, and each person is repaid only for what they did. The people of Paradise are happy, resting with their spouses in shade, receiving whatever they want, and hearing "Peace" from the merciful Lord.

On the Day of Judgment, God will seal people's mouths so their hands and feet testify to what they did. God says He could also blind them or freeze them in place, and He can shorten or lengthen life as He chooses. The passage then says the Prophet was not taught poetry, and that this Book is only a warning and a clear message.

The passage has two parts. First, it tells believers to remember God's favour when they ride on animals and to thank Him for making them usable. Then it attacks those who claim God has daughters, noting that people themselves would be unhappy to have a daughter announced to them.

The passage criticises people who call the angels, servants of God, female, and who claim that worshipping them is God's will. It says they have no real knowledge of this, since they did not see the angels created and have no scripture backing their view. They simply follow the beliefs of their fathers.

Whenever a warner was sent to a city, its wealthy people replied that they would keep the religion of their fathers. Even when a better religion was offered, they rejected it, and they were punished for denying the messengers. The passage then turns to Abraham, who told his father and people that he rejected what they worshipped.

God says he let the idolatrous Arabians and their fathers enjoy their comforts until the truth and a clearly sent messenger came to them. Now that the truth has come, they call it sorcery and refuse to believe it. They also say the Koran should have been sent to a great man of one of the two cities instead.

God asks whether people who reject him control his mercy, and says he alone divides their livelihood and raises some above others in rank. God's mercy is better than all their wealth. He would have given unbelievers silver houses and furnishings, but would not do so because everyone might then turn to disbelief.

Worldly wealth, such as gold ornaments, is only the enjoyment of this life, while God keeps the next life for those who fear Him. Those who turn away from God's warning are given a Satan as a constant companion, who leads them astray while they think they are guided. On the Day of Judgment, such a person will wish he were far from that companion. The passage ends by asking whether the speaker can make the deaf hear or guide the blind.

Pharaoh is shown here as a ruler who, after God sends punishments and then removes them, breaks his promise and boasts of his power. He points to Egypt's kingdom and rivers and calls Moses a lowly man who can hardly speak clearly.

Some people argued that their own gods were better than Jesus, and the passage says this was only a dispute, not a sincere question. It states that Jesus is only a servant whom God favoured and showed as a sign to the Children of Israel. It says he is a sign of the Last Hour, so there should be no doubt about it, and it warns against Satan turning people away.

Jesus comes with clear proofs and wisdom, to settle some of the disputes among his people. He tells them to fear God, obey him, and worship God as his Lord and theirs. The groups still divide and argue, and the passage warns that they face punishment on a coming day of judgment, when friends will turn into enemies except the God-fearing.

Believers in Paradise will be served with gold dishes and bowls, and will have whatever they desire and whatever pleases their eyes, forever. The wicked in Hell will have no relief, will be silent in despair, and are told they brought this on themselves. The final line warns the opponents of the speaker that God will match their schemes.

God alone owns the heavens and the earth and knows when the Hour (the end of the world) will come. The false gods people call on cannot intercede for anyone, though people admit God created everything. The passage tells the speaker to turn away from the unbelievers and say "Peace," and says they will learn their folly in the end.

Some speakers say they submit to God and follow the right way, while others have gone astray and will be punished in Hell. The passage tells those who keep to this path that God will give them abundant water as a test, and warns that turning away from God brings severe punishment. It ends by stating that worship belongs to God alone, and that the speaker has no power to harm or help anyone.

The speaker says his only task is to deliver God's message. Those who rebel against God and His messenger will face the fire of Hell forever. He does not know when the threatened punishment will come, because God alone knows the timing and reveals His secrets only to chosen messengers, who are guarded as they carry the message.
God is described as knowing whether his messengers have truly passed on the messages from their Lord. He knows everything they do and keeps a full account of all matters concerning them.

The passage says that God made seven heavens stacked one above another, and that no flaw can be found in His creation, even after repeated looking. It adds that the lowest heaven is decked with lights, which also serve to drive off the Satans, and that unbelievers face the torment of Hell.

The speakers admit that a warner came to them but called him a liar and rejected God's message. Now they wish they had listened, and they are told to go to the fire. God rewards those who fear Him in private, and He knows all hidden thoughts, since He is the Creator.

God made the earth level for people to walk on and eat from its provisions, and all will return to Him. The passage warns that God, who is in Heaven, could split the earth or send a stone-carrying storm against them, as He punished earlier peoples who rejected their prophets.

The passage argues that God alone keeps the birds in the air, and that God alone gives people protection and provision. It asks whether someone who stumbles blindly is better guided than someone who walks upright on a straight path. It then reminds people that God gave them hearing, sight and heart, and says few are thankful for this.

When the punishment comes close, the unbelievers will look grieved, and they will be told that this is what they had been demanding. The speaker asks whether God destroys him and his followers or shows them mercy, no one can save the unbelievers from painful punishment. He says his trust is in the Merciful God. He then asks who could bring them clear water if their wells sank away.

The passage describes human development in stages: a drop of fluid becomes a clot of blood, then flesh, then bones covered with flesh, and finally a new kind of creature. It then says God is the best of creators, that people will die and be raised on the day of resurrection, and that God made the heavens, sends rain, and can take it away.

God points to cattle and ships as signs of His care for people, then recalls Noah. Noah urged his people to worship God alone, but the unbelieving leaders dismissed him as an ordinary man seeking status, and said they had never heard of such a message from their forefathers.

God tells Noah to build an ark under God's watch and to carry in a pair of every kind, along with his family, except those already condemned. The wicked are to be drowned, and Noah is not to plead for them. Once aboard, he is to thank God for the rescue and pray for a safe landing.

God sent a messenger from among the people, telling them to worship God alone and fear Him. The unbelieving chiefs, who were rich and who denied the meeting with God after death, rejected him. They said he was only a man who ate and drank as they did, and that they would be lost if they followed him. They also mocked his claim that they would be raised from dust and bones.

The passage says that God destroyed earlier peoples who rejected Him, sweeping them away like leaves, and then raised up new generations in their place. Each nation had its set time and was not destroyed early or late. Messengers were sent one after another, and most nations called them liars. The passage then introduces Moses and his brother Aaron, sent with God's signs and clear power.

The passage says God made Jesus, son of Mary, and his mother a sign, and gave them a safe, peaceful home with springs. It then tells the prophets to eat good food and do right, and says all people share one religion under one Lord. But people have split this faith into rival sects, each proud of its own, so God tells the Prophet to leave them in their error for now.

Those who reject this Book have hearts lost in error and act differently from Muslims. When punishment seizes their wealthy leaders, they cry for help, but are told they will not be saved. The passage asks whether they reject their messenger because something new has come to them, which never came to their ancestors.

Had the truth followed what people want, the heavens and earth would have been ruined. Instead, the messenger brings them a warning, which they turn away from. He asks them for no payment, since his reward comes from God, and those who do not believe in the afterlife wander from the right path, even if they are relieved of their troubles.

God has no children and no partner gods; if there were other gods, each would take away what he created and they would fight for power. The passage declares God far above what people claim about Him. It then has the Prophet ask God not to place him among wrongdoers, while affirming God can show the punishment promised to them.

In this part of Sura 23, God speaks of believers who prayed for forgiveness and mercy. Those who mocked them are told that the believers will be rewarded for their patience. God then asks the mockers how long they stayed on earth, and tells them the time was short.

God asks whether people thought they were created for nothing and would never return to him. The passage then praises God as the true King and the only god, and warns that anyone who calls on another god without proof will be held to account. It ends with a prayer for forgiveness and mercy.

Those who have done wrong, with their hearts set on desires, mock the messenger. They ask whether he is anything more than a man, call his message sorcery, dreams, forgery or poetry, and demand a sign like the earlier prophets. The passage answers that no earlier city believed when destroyed, so these people will not believe either.

The passage says that God sent only human messengers before Muhammad, and that they were mortal, needing food and not living forever. It tells listeners to ask people of earlier Scriptures if they doubt this. It then says God saved the believers, destroyed wrongdoing cities, and now sent the Book as a warning.

The passage describes a group of wrongdoers who, when punishment comes, cry out that they have done evil, and are then destroyed. It then says God did not create the heavens and earth as a game, and that God's truth will overcome falsehood. It ends with a warning to those who speak falsely about God.

The passage argues that if there were other gods besides God, heaven and earth would have been destroyed, so there is only one God. It says God is not questioned about what he does, while people are. It also says every messenger was told that there is no God but God and was commanded to worship him alone.

God describes the sky and the earth as once joined together, then separated, with water giving life to all things. He set mountains on the earth to keep it steady, made wide paths across it, and raised the sky as a protected roof. He also made night and day, the sun and the moon, each moving in its own orbit. The unbelievers are asked why they do not see these signs and believe.

Unbelievers mock the prophet when he speaks of their gods, and they refuse to believe when he speaks of the merciful God. They demand to know when the threatened punishment will come. The passage warns that they would not mock if they knew the time of hellfire, when they cannot keep the fire off their faces or backs and no one will help them.

God asks whether the idols people worship can protect them, and says they cannot. He notes that God has given these people and their ancestors comfort for a time, and that God can reduce their land. The people are warned, but they do not listen. Only when punishment touches them will they admit their wrongdoing.

On the Day of Judgment, God will weigh every deed exactly, and no one will be wronged, even a deed as small as a mustard seed's weight. The passage then points to earlier revelations given to Moses, Aaron and Abraham, and to the Quran as a blessed warning, which some people reject.

Abraham asks his people why they worship idols that can neither help nor harm them. They respond by ordering him burned to defend their gods. God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, so the plot fails, and God then blesses Abraham and Lot, and gives him Isaac and Jacob.

God made certain prophets leaders who guided others, and gave them good deeds, prayer and charity. He rescued Lot from a wicked city and Noah from a great disaster, and drowned the people who rejected God's signs.

David and Solomon judged a dispute over a field damaged by someone's sheep, and God gave both of them wisdom and knowledge. God made the mountains and birds praise along with David, taught David to make armour to protect people, and made the strong wind obey Solomon.

God answers the prayers of several prophets who were in distress, including Job, whose suffering is eased and whose family is restored. He also rescues Dhoulnoun, usually identified as Jonah, who had left his people in anger and prayed from the darkness, admitting his wrongdoing. God rescues such faithful servants.

God answered the prayer of Zechariah, gave him John, and made his wife able to bear a child. He also made Mary and her son a sign to all people. God says his religion is one, so people should serve him, but they split into sects. All will return to God.

Those who do good and believe will have their deeds recorded and not lost. Cities that God destroys will not rise again until Gog and Magog break out and the promise is fulfilled. Unbelievers will be shocked and admit their error, and they and their false gods will be fuel for hell.

On the day of judgment, God will roll up the sky like a scroll and bring creation back as He first made it, a promise He will keep. The righteous will inherit the earth, as written in the Psalms. The Prophet is sent as mercy to all creatures, and God is one.

The speaker says he has warned everyone equally, but does not know whether the threatened punishment is near or far. God knows both what people say openly and what they hide. The speaker also does not know whether the delay is a test for them or a time for their enjoyment. He asks God to judge with truth and to be the help against what they say.

God alone rules heaven and earth, has no son or partner, and created all things and set their destinies. The passage says the gods others worship created nothing and have no power over themselves, life, death or resurrection. It ends with unbelievers calling the Qur'an a fabrication made with outside help.

Some opponents of the prophet object that he eats food and walks in the streets like an ordinary man. They ask why an angel or a treasure or a garden has not been given to him. The passage replies that God can give him better things than these, namely gardens with rivers and pavilions.

Those who deny the Hour (the coming of Judgment Day) are promised a blazing fire. When it sees them from far off, they hear its roar, and when they are thrown into its narrow confines, they cry out for destruction. They are told to call for many destructions, not one. Then the question is asked whether this fire or the eternal Paradise promised to the God-fearing is better, and Paradise is named as their reward and resting place.

On the day of judgment, God asks those who were worshipped beside him whether they led people astray. They deny it, saying the people chose their own path after being given many good things. God then tells the idolaters that these false gods have proved them liars and cannot help them.

God tells the Prophet that earlier messengers were also ordinary men who ate and walked in the streets, and that people are tested through one another. Those who deny meeting God demand angels or a direct sight of God. God says that on the day they see the angels, they will get no good news, and their deeds will be scattered like dust.

The unbelievers object that the Qur'an was not sent down all at once. The passage replies that it came in parts so as to strengthen the Prophet's heart, and that God will answer their challenges with the truth. Those who reject it will be punished in hell. The passage then recalls that Moses was sent with Aaron, and that earlier people who called God's signs lies were destroyed.

The passage says that earlier peoples who rejected their messengers were destroyed, such as Noah's people, Ad, Thamud and others, and were left as warnings. It adds that the unbelieving Meccans have passed the ruined city where a deadly rain fell, yet they still doubt there will be a resurrection.

The speakers here say they nearly turned away from their gods, but the passage says that those who worship their own desires, and those who do not hear or understand, have strayed furthest from the right path. It then points to God's control over the shadow, which the sun guides and God gradually draws in.

God made the fresh and salt seas and keeps them apart with a barrier. He made man from water and linked people by family and marriage. Yet people worship beings that can neither help nor harm them. The messenger is sent only to warn and asks no payment, except that people follow the way to God.

The passage tells the believer to trust in God, who lives forever, and to praise Him. It describes God as the creator of heaven and earth in six days, and says that when people are told to bow to "the God of Mercy," they ask who that is and turn away. It ends by praising God for placing the sun, moon and zodiac in the sky.

Those who worship no other god beside God, do not kill anyone God has forbidden to be killed unless there is a just cause, and do not commit fornication, are described here. Whoever does these things faces doubled punishment on Resurrection Day, except those who repent, believe and do good deeds, whose evil deeds God changes into good ones.

Those who endure steadfastly will receive high places in Paradise, where they will be greeted with welcome and peace, and remain forever. The passage then tells the unbelievers that God does not care about them if they do not call on Him, since they have called His messenger a liar, and punishment will come upon them.

Praise belongs to God, who took his servant by night from the sacred temple in Mecca to a more distant temple, to show him signs. The passage then recalls that Moses was given the Book as guidance for the Israelites, and warns them that they will twice commit crimes on earth in proud arrogance.

The passage says that when a warning about a first wrongdoing was carried out, God sent powerful servants who entered the innermost parts of the people's homes and fulfilled the threat. Afterward, God gave the people power over those enemies again and increased their wealth, children and numbers.

Good and bad actions fall back on the people who do them. The passage recalls that God sent an enemy to punish the Israelites for a later wrongdoing, and warns that if they return to evil, God will return to punishment. It ends by saying the Quran guides to the straightest path and promises a great reward to believers who do right.

God made night and day as two signs, so people can seek provision, count the years and keep track of time. Each person's deeds are fastened to their neck, and on the Day of Resurrection they will receive a open book of their record and be told to read it and judge themselves.

Each person's guidance or going astray affects only himself, and no one carries another's burden. God does not punish before sending a messenger. When a city's wealthy people act wickedly after being warned, it is destroyed, and God knows His servants' sins fully.

Those who seek this fleeting life may be given worldly gifts, but they will end in hell, disgraced. Those who seek the next life with true belief will have their effort accepted by God. God gives worldly gifts to both kinds, and some people receive more than others, but the next life has greater ranks and greater excellence.

God commands people to worship no one but Him and to be kind to their parents, especially when they grow old. Children should speak to them respectfully, act with humility and tenderness, and pray that God have mercy on them as they once cared for the child. The passage also tells people to give what is due to relatives, the poor and travellers, and not to waste wastefully.

The passage tells the believer to speak kindly to people who ask for help when he cannot give, and not to be stingy or wastefully generous. It says God gives generously or sparingly as he wills, and it forbids killing children for fear of poverty and committing adultery.

Do not kill anyone God has forbidden, except for a just cause. If someone is killed unjustly, the heir may seek retribution, but must not go beyond proper limits. The passage also covers guarding orphans' property, keeping promises, and honest measuring and weighing.

Do not associate any other god with God, and do not claim that God has sons or that angels are His daughters. The passage says such claims are a dreadful saying. If other gods existed alongside God, they would compete against the one on the throne, but God is far above what they claim.

Everything in the heavens and on earth praises God, though people do not grasp how they praise him. The passage then says that when the Prophet recites the Quran, God places a veil between him and those who do not believe in the afterlife, so they cannot understand it and turn away when God is named.

God knows why the unbelievers listen to the Prophet and whisper among themselves. They call him a man under a spell, and they make comparisons for him that lead them astray. They also doubt that the dead, reduced to bones and dust, can be raised again as a new creation.

Even if people were stones or iron, or anything harder, God could raise them up again, since he first created them. When people ask when this will happen, the reply is that it may be near. The passage ends by telling believers to speak kindly to one another, because Satan stirs up quarrels between them.

God alone knows people fully and decides whether to show them mercy or punishment, and the Prophet is not sent to force them. God also gave some prophets greater gifts than others, and gave David the Psalms. The Prophet is told to say that the false gods people call on cannot remove their troubles.

Those that people call upon instead of God are themselves seeking to draw near to their Lord and hope for his mercy and fear his punishment. Every city will be destroyed or severely punished before the Resurrection, and this is recorded in the Book.

Miracles were not sent to the Prophet because earlier peoples called such signs lies. Thamud, for example, was given a she-camel as a sign, yet they harmed it. The passage says miracles are sent only as a warning.

God tells the Prophet that he has set up a vision and the cursed tree of the Qur'an as tests, so people would argue over them, and that this will only increase their wickedness. The passage then recalls how God ordered the angels to bow before Adam, and Iblis (Eblis) refused, saying he would not bow to one made of clay. He vows to lead Adam's descendants astray, except a few.

Satan, speaking in this passage, says he will lure people with his voice, his troops and promises, but his promises will be empty. He has no power over God's servants, who are protected by their Lord. The passage then turns to God, who moves ships across the sea so people can seek His provision, out of mercy.

When people are in danger at sea, they call on their false gods, who cannot be found, and only God answers. Once they reach dry land, they turn away from him. The passage warns that God could still destroy them on land or at sea, and then no one would help them.

God has honoured the children of Adam, giving them land, sea travel, good food and many gifts. On a future day all people will be called with their leaders, and those given their record in the right hand will read it and not be wronged at all. Whoever is blind here will be blind in the afterlife and stray even further from the path.

The passage says that opponents nearly tempted the speaker away from the revelation and nearly forced him out of his land. It adds that God kept him steady, so he did not lean toward them, and warns that if he had, he would have faced hardship and found no helper. It also says the opponents would not have stayed long after him.

The passage has the speaker pray for a good entry and exit and for help from God. It then says truth has come and falsehood will vanish, that the Quran heals and brings mercy to believers but only adds to the ruin of wrongdoers, and that people act in their own way while God knows who is best guided.

Human beings and spirits together could not produce anything like this Quran, even by helping each other. Many people refuse to accept it and instead make demands, such as a spring from the ground, a garden with rivers, the sky falling in pieces, or God and the angels appearing as witnesses.

Opponents demand signs before they will believe: a house of gold, or a climb into Heaven, or a written book they can read. The speaker answers that he is only a man sent as a messenger, and asks why a human messenger should seem strange to them. He adds that if angels lived on earth, a angel messenger would have been sent, and that God is the witness between him and his critics.

Whoever God guides is truly guided, and whoever God leads astray will find no helper besides Him. On the Day of Resurrection, such people will be gathered blind, mute and deaf, and Hell will be their home, its fire renewed whenever it dies down. This is their punishment for rejecting God's signs and doubting that they would be raised again after becoming bones and dust.

God, who made the heavens and earth, could create people like them again, and he has set a fixed time for this. The wicked reject everything but disbelief. The passage then says people would hold back even God's mercy from fear of giving it away, and it recalls that Moses was given nine signs, which Pharaoh dismissed as enchantment.

Moses tells Pharaoh that the clear signs came from the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and that he considers Pharaoh lost. Pharaoh then tries to drive the Israelites out of the land, but God drowns him and his followers.

The passage says that God will gather the people of Israel together for judgment when the promised next life comes. It then says the Quran was sent down truthfully, that the prophet was sent only to announce and warn, and that the Quran was revealed in parts over time so he could recite it gradually.

Those who were given knowledge earlier fall on their faces in worship and weeping when the revelation is recited to them, saying that God's promise has been fulfilled. The passage then tells the believer to call upon God by either name, God or the Merciful, since God has excellent names. It also says prayer should be neither too loud nor too quiet, but in a middle way.
God is praised for having no son, no partner in His rule, and no helper needing His protection because of weakness. The believer is told to glorify Him by declaring His greatness.

Moses comes to a fire and is called by a voice from within it, which declares God to be mighty and wise. God tells him to throw down his staff, and it turns into a moving serpent, so Moses runs back without returning. God reassures him that messengers need not fear in God's presence, except one who has done wrong but then turns to good, because God forgives and shows mercy.

Moses is told to show his hand, which comes out white without harm, as one of nine signs sent to Pharaoh and his people. They call the signs plain magic and deny them, though inwardly they know they are true. The passage then notes the fate of these wrongdoers and says David and Solomon were given knowledge and thanked God for their favor.

Solomon, heir to David's knowledge, says he has been taught the speech of birds and given many gifts from God. His gathered armies of jinn, men and birds march until they reach a valley of ants. An ant warns the other ants to hide in their homes so that Solomon's army does not crush them without noticing.

Solomon smiles at the ant's words and prays to God to help him be thankful, do good, and be counted among the righteous. He then notices the hoopoe, here called the lapwing, is missing and threatens to punish it unless it gives a clear excuse.

A hoopoe bird reports to Solomon that it has found a queen of Saba (Sheba) and her people, who worship the sun instead of God. The bird says Satan has made their deeds look good to them, so they have been turned from the right path. It ends by naming God as the one who knows all hidden things and the only god.

The passage describes a queen who answers the nobles' boast of strength by sending a gift to Solomon instead of fighting. When her messenger arrives, Solomon rejects the gift, saying God has given him more than they have, and that they take pride in their wealth.

Solomon sends a message to the Queen of Sheba's people, warning that his armies will drive them out if they do not submit. He asks the nobles who will bring her throne to him first. A powerful Djinn offers to bring it before he rises from his seat.

A man with knowledge from the Scripture offers to bring the Queen of Sheba's throne to Solomon in an instant. When it appears before him, Solomon says this is a gift from his Lord, meant to test whether he will be thankful. Thankfulness benefits only the thankful person, and Solomon orders the throne disguised so that the Queen will not recognise it, to see whether she is guided.

Solomon asks whether the Queen of Sheba's throne is like her own, and she answers that it seems the same. Solomon says he had knowledge before her and has submitted to God. When she enters a glassy floor and mistakes it for water, she admits she has wronged herself and submits to God with Solomon.

Saleh was sent to the people of Thamud with a command to worship God alone. They split into quarrelling groups, and he urged them to seek God's forgiveness rather than hurry toward evil. They blamed him and his followers for bringing bad omens, and he replied that any ill fortune comes from God, and that they were being tested. The city also had nine men who spread corruption and did what was wrong.

A group plots in secret to kill a man and his family at night, planning to deny any guilt afterward. God turns their scheme against them, destroys them and their people, and leaves their houses empty. The passage then says those who believed and feared God were saved, and it moves on to Lot, who rebukes his people for their open wickedness.

The passage asks rhetorical questions about God's power in creation: he made the heavens and earth, sends rain that makes gardens grow, set the earth firm, placed rivers and mountains, and separated two seas. It then asks whether there could be another god beside God, and says most people lack knowledge for thinking so.

The passage is a series of rhetorical questions asking who is more worthy of worship than God, since God answers the distressed, guides people on land and sea, sends winds as signs of His mercy, and creates and renews life. Each time it asks, "What! a god with God?", meaning that no other god stands beside Him. It ends by challenging the listeners to bring their proofs if they speak the truth.

The passage says that the prophet cannot make the blind see or make the deaf hear; only those who believe God's signs will listen, and they are Muslims. On the Day of Judgment, a creature from the earth will speak to unbelievers, and they will be gathered before God and questioned about why they rejected His signs.

Night and day are given as signs for believers. Then a trumpet blast will come on the Day of Judgment, and everything in heaven and earth will be terrified, except those God chooses to save. All will come to God humbly, and mountains will pass away like clouds. God orders all things and knows what people do.

Those who come with good deeds receive a reward greater than they deserve and are safe from terror that day, while those who come with evil deeds are thrown face-first into the fire and are repaid only for what they did. The speaker is commanded to worship the Lord of this land, to submit to God, and to recite the Qur'an, and guidance benefits only the one who is guided.

The speaker is told to say that, for one who goes astray, he is only a warner. He is then told to say "Praise be to God," adding that God will show His signs and that people will recognise them, and that God is not unaware of what people do.

The passage says the revelation warns of severe punishment for those who say God has a son, and promises a lasting reward to believers who do right. It calls their claim a lie with no knowledge behind it. It also tells the Prophet not to wear himself out with grief if they refuse, and says earthly things are a test of who excels in good works.

Young men who refused to worship other gods alongside God stood up and declared that their Lord alone is the Lord of heaven and earth. They told each other to leave their people and their false gods and go to the cave, trusting that God would show them mercy and arrange their affairs well.
