The sun passes to the right of the cave when it rises and leaves it on the left when it sets, so the sleepers inside stay in shade. The passage calls this a sign from God. It then says that God guides whom He chooses, and that anyone He leads astray will find no guide.

The passage describes the Sleepers of the Cave, young men who sleep for a very long time. They look awake, they are turned from side to side, and their dog lies at the entrance with its paws stretched out. Anyone who came upon them suddenly would run away in fear.

The sleepers wake and ask each other how long they have stayed in the cave. They guess a day or part of a day, leave the answer to God, and send one of them into the city with silver to buy food. He must be careful and discreet, because if the townspeople discover them they will stone them or force them back to their old faith.

The people of the town learned of the sleepers' story so they would know that God's promise is true and that the Hour, the Day of Judgment, will certainly come. Afterward, when they argued about what to do, some wanted to build a structure over the sleepers' tomb, while the stronger group decided to build a place of worship there.

The passage concerns the Companions of the Cave, sleepers who hid in a cave. People differ on how many there were, with guesses of three, five or seven plus a dog, but God alone knows the exact number. It tells the reader not to argue too much about it, and not to promise a future action without adding "If God will."

The passage says that God alone knows the hidden matters of heaven and earth, including how long the Companions of the Cave stayed asleep. People should turn to God alone, since no one else can protect them or share in his judgments. The speaker is told to recite the revealed Book, which no one can alter, and there is no shelter apart from God.

The Prophet is told to stay patient with those who pray to their Lord morning and evening, seeking God's favor. He should not turn away from them to chase the wealth and show of this world. He should also not follow a person whose heart has become careless of God and who acts on his own desires without restraint.
Truth comes from God, so each person is free to believe or refuse. Those who wrong others will face a fire, with scalding water to drink. Those who believe and do right will not lose their reward.

The passage describes the rewards promised to believers in the gardens of Eden: rivers flowing beneath, gold bracelets, green silk and brocade robes, and reclining on thrones. It then begins a parable about two men, one of whom was given two fruitful gardens of vines and palms with fields between them.

A rich man boasts about his wealth and his garden to a poorer companion. He says the garden will never perish, doubts the Last Hour, and claims he would find something better even if returned to his Lord. His companion rebukes him, asking whether he disbelieves in the God who created him from dust and then shaped him as a man.

A man with a rich garden is rebuked by a poorer companion for not saying that everything depends on God's will. The speaker says God may give him something better, or may destroy the garden with a heavenly bolt or dry up its water.

A man's garden and its fruit are destroyed, and he wrings his hands over the money he spent on it. He regrets having associated other gods with his Lord, and he has no helpers besides God. The passage concludes that protection comes only from God, who gives the best reward and the best outcome.

Worldly life is compared to rain that makes plants grow, which then dry up and blow away. Wealth and children are its adornments, but lasting good works are better in God's sight, both as reward and as a source of hope. The passage ends by pointing to a day when mountains vanish and all people are gathered together.
On the Day of Judgment, people will be brought before God in rows. God will tell them they have returned to Him just as He first created them, and that they had doubted He would keep His promise.

On the day of judgment, each person receives a book recording his deeds. The wicked are alarmed at what it contains, saying it leaves out nothing, and they find all their actions present before them. God treats no one unjustly.

God tells the angels to bow before Adam. All obey except Iblis (called Eblis here), a jinn, who refuses. God asks why people would take Iblis and his offspring as protectors instead of God, when they are enemies. God says he did not make them witnesses of creation and did not use misleaders as helpers.

On a day of judgment, God will tell those who set up false gods beside him to call on them. They will get no answer, and the wicked will see the fire with no way out. The closing line says humans argue about most things, even though the Quran gives them many examples.

People now have received guidance, yet they refuse to believe or ask their Lord for forgiveness, unless they wait for the fate that struck earlier peoples or a punishment in plain view. The messengers are sent only to announce and warn. Unbelievers argue with empty words to disprove the truth and mock God's signs and the warnings.

The passage describes people who turn away from God's signs and forget their own past wrongs. It says God has veiled their hearts and deafened their ears so they cannot understand the Koran, so they will not be guided even if called. God is merciful and could punish them at once, but has set a fixed time, and they cannot escape it.

Moses and his young companion realise they have lost the fish they had with them, which had swum off into the sea. They go back the way they came and find a servant of God, who has been given mercy and knowledge. Moses asks to follow him and learn from him, but the servant tells Moses that he will not be able to be patient with him.

Moses travels with a companion, whom the passage calls "the unknown" (later identified in the wider story as a servant of God). The companion damages a ship, and then kills a young man. Moses objects both times, saying the acts are wrong. Each time the companion reminds him that he said Moses would not have patience with him.

Moses travels with a companion who refuses to explain his actions at first. Here the companion repairs a wall in a town whose people refused them food, and Moses asks for payment. The companion then promises to explain, starting with why he damaged a boat: its poor owners would otherwise lose it to a king who seized every ship.

This passage ends the story of the wall and gives the reason for the repairs: the wall protected a hidden treasure belonging to two orphan boys, and their dead father had been a good man, so God wanted them to reach adulthood and recover it. The speaker says he did not act on his own will. Then it introduces Dhul-Qarnayn, a ruler whom God gave power and a way to everything, and who followed a route.

The speaker says that the wicked will be punished severely by their Lord, while those who believe and do right will be rewarded. He then travels east to where the sun rises over a people with no shelter from it, and later to a place between two mountains, where he finds a people who barely understand speech.

Dhoulkarnain, a ruler, is asked by a people to build a wall against Gog and Magog, who are attacking their land. He refuses payment, saying his strength comes from God, but accepts their help. He builds an iron-and-brass barrier that the attackers can neither climb nor break through.

On the Day of Judgment, people will be gathered and Hell will be shown to those who rejected God's warning. The passage asks who has lost the most effort, and answers that it is those whose aim in life went wrong while they believed their actions were right.

Those who reject God's signs and do not expect to meet him will have their deeds count for nothing on the Day of Resurrection, and they will go to Hell. Those who believe and do right will live forever in the gardens of Paradise, never wishing to leave.

The passage says that the words of God are so many that even a sea of ink, with more sea added, would run out before they did. It then says the speaker is only a man, and that God is one. Whoever hopes to meet God should do good deeds and should not worship anyone else alongside him.

Some people claim the Prophet made up this message. The passage answers that it is the truth from God, sent to warn a people who had received no warner before. It then describes God as the creator of heaven and earth, who rules all things and knows the unseen and the seen.

The guilty are shown begging their Lord to send them back to life so they can do right and believe. The reply is that God could have guided every soul, but his word stands that hell will be filled with jinn and humans together. They are told to taste punishment for having forgotten their meeting with this day.

Those who truly believe in God's signs fall down in prostration when they hear them, praise their Lord, and stay humble. They pray with fear and hope and give charity. Believers and evildoers are not equal, and the faithful who do good will receive gardens as their reward.

Those who commit serious sins will have the fire as their home. Whenever they try to escape it, they will be pushed back in, and told to taste the punishment they once called a lie. God also sends a lesser punishment first, so that they may turn back to him, and He will punish the guilty.

God gave the Book of the law to Moses and made it a guide for the Children of Israel. He appointed leaders from among them who guided people by God's command, because they had been steadfast and had believed God's signs. God will judge their disputes on the Day of Resurrection, and past destroyed generations are offered as signs that people should heed.

God points to rain that brings crops to dry land as a sign that people should see. When the unbelievers ask when the final judgment will come, the reply is that on that day their faith will not help them and they will get no more delay. The prophet is told to turn away and wait, since they are waiting too.

The speakers say their hearts are closed to the message, their ears are deaf, and a veil stands between them and the speaker, so they will do as they please. The reply tells them the speaker is only a man, that God is one, and that they should turn to Him and seek forgiveness. It condemns those who give partners to God, who withhold required alms, and who deny the afterlife, while promising a full reward to believers who do good.

God set firm mountains on the earth, blessed it, and gave it food for all who need it, all within four days. He then turned to the heaven, which was then smoke, and to the earth, and they agreed to come obedient. He made seven heavens in two days, filled the lowest with lights and guardian angels.

The passage says that messengers called people to worship only God, but the people refused to believe them, saying God would have sent angels instead. It then describes the people of Ad, who acted proudly and boasted of their strength, even though God, their creator, was stronger than they were. They also rejected God's signs.

The passage describes God sending a violent wind as punishment on a people who rejected warnings, and says their punishment in this world was less than what awaits them after death. The people of Thamud are named as having been shown guidance but choosing blindness. Believers and God-fearing people were saved, and the enemies of God will be gathered into the fire.

On the Day of Judgment, the guilty ask their own skins why they gave evidence against them. The skins answer that God gave them speech, and that the sinners wrongly believed God did not see their deeds. Their false belief has ruined them, and the fire will be their home, whether they endure patiently or beg for mercy.

Unbelievers are given evil companions, the Satans, who made their wrong lives look good to them, so they share the fate that earlier peoples of jinn and men received. The unbelievers also tell others to talk loudly so the Qur'an reader cannot be heard. God says He will punish them severely for their worst deeds.

Unbelievers, on the Day of Judgment, will ask God to show them the jinn and humans who misled them, so they can put them beneath their feet. Those who said "Our Lord is God" and stayed on the straight path will be met by angels who tell them not to fear or grieve, and promise them paradise, with whatever they desire.

Good and evil should not be met in the same way. Answer evil with something better, and an enemy can become like a close friend. Only the patient and the highly favoured manage this. Those tempted by Satan should seek refuge in God. Worship God, not the sun or moon, which are among His signs.

The passage uses the rain reviving dry earth as a sign that God can raise the dead. It then warns that those who reject God's signs are not hidden from Him, and that those thrown into the fire are worse off than those who come out safe on resurrection day. It ends by praising the Qur'an as a glorious book.
The message given to the prophet Muhammad is the same kind of message that earlier messengers received. God offers forgiveness, but He also punishes severely.

The passage says that if the scripture were in a foreign language, unbelievers would object that it should be clear and in Arabic. It claims the revelation guides and heals believers, while for those who refuse it, it is like deafness and blindness. It also notes that earlier disputes over the Book given to Moses were settled only by a delay decreed by God.

The passage says that only God knows when the Hour (the end of the world) will come, just as only He controls the growth of fruit and the bearing of children. On the Day of Judgment God will ask people where the partners they worshipped besides Him are. They will have no answer, and those false gods will vanish. The passage also notes that people pray eagerly for good things but lose hope when evil comes.

The passage describes people who, when blessed, claim the good fortune is theirs by right and doubt any future judgment, yet they pray at length when troubled. It warns that such people will face punishment. It then asks whether anyone is more lost than someone who rejects this revelation as coming from God.

God says he will show people his signs in the wider world and within themselves, until they see that the message is true. He asks whether it is not enough that God witnesses all things, and whether God does not surround everything, even though some doubt they will meet their Lord.

The passage points to natural signs, such as the alternation of night and day, rain that brings dead land back to life, and changing winds, as proof of God for thoughtful people. It then warns that those who reject God's signs, and stay proudly deaf to them, will face painful punishment.

God has put the sea at people's service so ships can cross it, and so they can seek his provision and give thanks. He has also placed everything in the heavens and on earth under them, all coming from him. Those who reflect will find signs in this, while those who reject God's signs face a painful punishment.

Good and evil each benefit or harm only the person who does them, and all people will be brought back to their Lord. God gave the Children of Israel scripture, wisdom and prophecy, but they disagreed out of envy after they had received knowledge. God will judge their disputes on the Day of Resurrection.

God is the protector of those who fear Him, while evildoers protect only one another. The passage says it is wrong to think that people who do evil will share the same fate as believers who do right. God created the heavens and earth so that each person is repaid for their deeds, and no one is treated unjustly.

Those who make their own desires their god are described as lost, cut off from guidance by God, with their hearing, heart and sight closed off. The passage then says some deny an afterlife, claiming only time destroys us, and answer the recited signs only by demanding their dead fathers be brought back.

God gives life, causes death, and then will gather everyone for judgment on the Day of Resurrection. Every nation will be called to its own record, and each will be repaid for what it did, because that record states everything they have done.

The passage describes people who doubted that the Last Hour, the day of judgment, would come. When it is said that God's promise is true and the Hour is certain, they answer that they know nothing of it. On that day their evil deeds and mockery will surround them, and they will be told they are forgotten and will face the fire with no one to help.

People who mocked God's signs and were taken in by worldly life will not be able to leave Hell on that day, and they will not be asked to seek God's favour. The passage then praises God as Lord of the heavens, the earth and all worlds, the Mighty and the Wise.

God sends angels with revelation to warn people that there is no god but him, and so they should fear him. The passage also says God created the heavens, the earth, humans and cattle, and it calls humans open disputers, though it does not say what they dispute.

God provides animals that carry loads and travel to places that would otherwise be hard to reach, and rides and ornament besides. He also shows the right path, though some turn away from it, and sends rain that gives drink and pasture for animals.

The passage lists things God has provided for people: grain, olives, dates, grapes and other fruits, the cycle of night and day, the sun, moon and stars, and the many colours of the earth. It says these are signs for people who reflect, understand and remember.

God is said to have made the sea, mountains, rivers, paths and stars for human benefit: food, ornaments, travel, trade, and guidance. The passage asks whether the Creator is the same as what creates nothing, and says the favours of God cannot be counted. It ends by calling the false gods dead and unaware.

On the day of judgment, people will carry their own sins and also the sins of those they misled through ignorance. Earlier peoples who plotted against God were struck down when their buildings collapsed on them. God will then shame the unbelievers and ask where the false gods they worshipped are.
Wrongdoers, at the moment the angels take their souls, will claim they did no evil. God replies that He knows what they did, and they are told to enter Hell to stay forever.

Those who feared God are asked what their Lord has given them, and they answer that it is the best. They are promised a good reward in this world and a better one in the next, in gardens of Eden with flowing rivers, where they will have all they wish. At death, angels greet them with peace and invite them into Paradise as the reward for their deeds.

The passage warns that unbelievers face only two outcomes: the angels of death coming for them, or God's decree being carried out. Earlier peoples met the same fate. God did not wrong them; their own wrongdoing brought the evil they had mocked back on them.

Those who worship other gods alongside God argue that, if God had wished, neither they nor their fathers would have worshipped anything but Him, nor forbidden anything on their own authority. Earlier peoples acted the same way. The passage then asks whether the messengers' task is anything more than clearly announcing the message.

God has sent a messenger to every people, telling them to worship God alone and reject Taghout, a word for false gods. Some were guided and others were left to go astray. Those who called the messengers liars are shown as an example, and those whom God leads astray cannot be helped. The passage ends by saying God has bound himself to a promise, though most people do not know it, and this is set against the claim that the dead will never be raised.

God promises a good home in this world to those who flee their country after being oppressed for God's sake, and a greater reward in the next life. He also says that earlier messengers were only men sent with inspiration, and that the Prophet has been sent this Book to make its message clear.

The passage warns those who plot evil that God could punish them in ways they do not expect, such as an earthquake, a sudden disaster, or a slow wasting illness. It then says God is good and merciful, and points to the shadows of all created things bowing down to God.

Everything in the heavens and on earth, including the angels, bows down before God and is humble before Him. God says there must be no two gods, only Him, so people should fear and serve Him alone. Yet when trouble ends, some people still give Him partners.

The passage describes people who hide their faces in shame when they hear of a daughter's birth, and asks whether they should keep the child in disgrace or bury her alive. It says such judgments are wrong, and that God is above these evil comparisons. God would destroy everything if He punished people at once, but He gives them an appointed time, which they cannot delay or hasten.

The passage says that some people attribute to God what they themselves dislike, and claim a good fate for themselves, but they will face the fire. It adds that earlier messengers were also sent to nations, whose work Satan had corrupted. The Book was sent so the Prophet could settle their disputes and guide believers.

God sends rain that brings dead land back to life, and this is a sign for listeners. He also says that livestock give milk, and that palm and vine fruits give drink and food, all signs for thoughtful people. The passage then begins to speak of the bee, which God taught to make its home in mountains, trees and hives.

The passage describes the bee: it feeds on many kinds of flowers and fruit, and from its body comes a honey of varying colours that is medicine for people. It then turns to human life: God created people, will take them back to himself, and some will live until old age, when they forget what they once knew.

God gives some people more provision than others, yet the wealthy do not share it equally with the slaves they own. The passage asks whether people who deny that these gifts come from God will then turn to false idols, calling them ungrateful for God's blessings.

People are described as worshipping beings beside God that cannot provide them any food from heaven or earth and have no power of their own. The passage tells them not to make comparisons with God, because God has knowledge and they do not.

God compares a slave, who owns nothing and has no power over anything, with a free man who has been given provision by God and gives charity openly and in secret. The answer is that they are not equal, but most people do not recognise this.

God uses two men as an example: one is mute from birth, powerless, and a burden to his master, while the other commands justice and walks the straight path. The passage asks whether these two can be considered equal, and then affirms God's power over the heavens, the earth, and the coming Hour.

God brought people into the world knowing nothing, then gave them hearing, sight and heart so they might be thankful. The passage then points to birds in the sky, which no one holds up but God, as a sign for believers.
God says He has given people tents to live in, made from animal skins that are light to carry when they move or stop. From wool, fur and hair He also provides furnishings and goods for temporary use.

God lists the shade, mountains and clothing he has given people as signs of his care, so that they will submit to him. If people turn away, the prophet's duty is only to deliver the message clearly. Many of them recognize God's goodness and then deny it.

On a day of judgment, a witness will be raised from every nation, and those who rejected God will be given no chance to make excuses or find favour. When they see their punishment, it will not be eased, and when they see the false gods they worshipped, those gods will be called liars by the worshippers themselves.
Those who rejected faith and also led others away from God's path will receive extra punishment, added to the penalty for the corrupt things they did.

God will raise a witness from every nation on the Day of Judgment, and Muhammad will be a witness against the Meccans. The Book sent to him explains everything and guides believers. God commands justice, good deeds, kindness to relatives, and forbids wickedness, wrong and oppression.
Keep your promises made to God, and do not break your oaths once you have sworn them. Having sworn, you have made God your guarantor, and God knows what you do.

Believers are warned not to break their oaths, as a woman breaks a thread she has spun, just because another group is larger or stronger. God is testing them, and will settle their disputes on the Day of Judgment. God could have made them one people, but He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and all will be held accountable for their deeds.

Do not use oaths to deceive others, because a person who breaks faith may fall after being secure and suffer for misleading others from God's way. Trading God's covenant for a small worldly gain is a mistake, since what God holds is better and lasts, while worldly things pass away. God will reward those who endure patiently.

Those who do right, male or female and believing, will be given a good life and rewards for their deeds. Believers who seek God's help against Satan are safe from his power, which reaches only those who turn from God. When God changes one verse for another, critics call the speaker a fabricator, but the passage says they simply lack knowledge.

The passage answers the claim that a human teacher gives Muhammad the Qur'an. It says the Holy Spirit brought the revelation down from God, and that the man they point to speaks a foreign language, while the Qur'an is in clear Arabic. Those who reject God's signs are called liars.

Someone who rejects God after believing in him is condemned, unless they were forced to deny their faith while their heart stayed firm. Those who freely choose unbelief face God's anger and severe punishment, because they love this worldly life more than the next one.

Those who fled their homeland after suffering, then fought and endured, are promised forgiveness and mercy from God. On the Day of Judgment, each soul will answer for itself and be repaid for its deeds, without injustice. As an example, a city that was safe and well supplied but ungrateful for God's gifts was made to suffer hunger and fear.

God sent a messenger to a people who rejected him, and they were punished for their wrongdoing. The passage then says to eat what God has provided that is lawful and good, and to be thankful. It forbids carrion, blood, pork, and meat sacrificed to anyone other than God, but excuses a person who is forced to eat them without desire or deliberate wrongdoing, since God is forgiving.

The passage warns against falsely declaring things lawful or forbidden on one's own authority, since that invents a lie about God. It says the Jews were forbidden certain things as a result of their own wrongdoing, not as an injustice to them. It ends by pointing to forgiveness for those who repent, and praising Abraham as devoted to God alone.

The passage says that God will settle disputes about the Sabbath on the Day of Resurrection, and that believers should call others to God's way with wisdom and kind words. It allows retaliation only in proportion to the injury, but says patient endurance is better.
Be patient, and look for the strength to endure only from God. Do not grieve over the unbelievers or be troubled by their plots, because God is with those who fear him and do good deeds.
God created the heavens and the earth and everything between them for a serious purpose and for a set period of time. The passage adds that most people do not believe they will meet their Lord.

Earlier peoples were stronger and more numerous, yet their messengers came with proofs and they rejected them, so they met a bad end. The passage says God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves. It ends by saying God creates, brings back, and all will return to Him.

Those who reject God's signs and the meeting in the next life will face punishment. Believers are told to glorify God morning, evening, and at other times of day. The passage then points to God's power over life and death, such as bringing life from the dead and reviving dead earth, and says people will likewise be brought forth again.

The passage says that God's "signs" (evidence of his power) include the creation of spouses so people can live together with love and tenderness, the making of the heavens and earth, the variety of human languages and skin colours, and the cycle of sleep by night and activity by day. These signs are presented as meaningful to thinking, observant, and listening people.

The passage lists signs of God's power: lightning that brings both fear and hope, rain that revives dead land, and the heavens and earth standing firm by his command. It says that God will one day call people out of the earth, and that everything in heaven and earth obeys him.
God creates a living being, then brings it back again, and this is easy for Him. He is like the highest thing in heaven and earth, and He is mighty and wise.

The passage uses a comparison from everyday life. It asks whether people would share their property equally with the slaves they own, and answers that they would not. It then argues that people who follow their own desires, without knowledge, are led astray by God, and no one can guide them.

Turn your face to the true faith that God made for people, and do not change God's creation. Keep to prayer and fear God, and do not join other gods with Him. The passage criticises people who split their religion into rival sects, and people who turn to God in trouble but then give Him partners once they are blessed.

People rejoice when God grants them mercy but despair when misfortune comes as a result of their own deeds. God gives abundance and scarcity as He chooses, and this is a sign for believers. The passage then urges giving what is due to relatives, the poor and travellers, saying this is best for those who seek God's face.

Money lent at interest does not grow in God's sight, but charity given to seek God's favour is repaid many times over. God alone creates, sustains, causes death and brings back to life, and no false gods share in this. Human wrongdoing has brought ruin on land and sea, so that people may taste the results and turn back to God.

Travel and look at how earlier peoples ended, since most of them associated other gods with God. Turn sincerely to the true faith before a day comes that no one can prevent. On that day believers who did good will be rewarded from God's bounty, while unbelievers will carry their unbelief with them.

Winds are described as signs from God that bring rain, which shows his mercy, and that carry ships so people can trade and give thanks. The passage adds that God sent messengers to earlier peoples with clear proofs, and that he helped the believers while punishing the wrongdoers.

God sends the winds, which lift and scatter the clouds so rain falls on whomever He chooses, and people rejoice even though they had despaired before. The dying earth then comes back to life, which is a sign that God can also raise the dead. Yet if He sends a blast that turns the crops yellow, people become ungrateful.

God alone guides people, and a messenger cannot make the blind see or the deaf hear unless they already believe. The passage then says God made people weak, then strong, then weak and old again, and that on the Day of Judgment the wicked will swear they waited only an hour.

On the Day of Resurrection, those who were given knowledge and faith will say that the unbelievers were told the day would come but did not recognise it. The wicked will then be unable to plead for mercy. Meanwhile, unbelievers who hear the Quran's verses call them empty talk, and God has sealed their hearts so they do not understand.

God calls people to ask His forgiveness and turn back to Him, promising good provision for a set time and a warning of judgment for those who turn away. The passage then says people cannot hide their hearts from God, since He knows both what they conceal and what they show.

God provides food for every creature on earth and knows where each one lives and rests, all of it recorded in a clear Book. He also created the heavens and earth in six days, with his throne over the waters, to test who among people does the best deeds. When the prophet speaks of being raised again after death, unbelievers call it plain sorcery.

The passage describes two reactions to God's dealings with people. Those who mock the promised punishment are warned that it will come on a day when no one can stop it, and it will surround them. People who receive mercy and then lose it become despairing and ungrateful, while people who are relieved after hardship become proud and boastful.

The passage tells the Prophet not to hide any part of the revelation, even though people ask for a treasure or an angel to accompany him as proof. He is only a warner, and God controls all things. If critics claim the Qur'an is his own invention, they are challenged to produce ten similar suras with the help of their gods. If they cannot, it is said to be sent down by God alone, and there is no god but Him.

Those who want only this present life and its finery will be paid for their deeds here, with nothing held back. But they will have nothing in the next world except the Fire, and everything they did in this life will count for nothing.

The passage contrasts two groups: those who rest on clear proof from their Lord, who accept the Qur'an as a guide and mercy, and idolaters who reject it and face the fire. It tells the listener to have no doubt that the Qur'an is true, though most people will not believe.

Those who invent lies about God are called the greatest wrongdoers. On the day of judgment they will be brought before their Lord, and witnesses will declare that they called their Lord a liar. The passage says God's curse falls on these wrongdoers.

Those who turn others away from God's path and deny the afterlife will not escape God's power, and their punishment will be doubled. Their false gods will fail them and they will be lost. Those who believe, do good, and humble themselves before their Lord will enter Paradise forever.

The passage contrasts two kinds of people with the blind and deaf versus the seeing and hearing, and asks whether they can be seen as alike. It then recounts Noah warning his people to worship only God, and the unbelieving chiefs dismissing him as an ordinary man, followed only by lowly people, and calling him a liar.

A prophet speaks to his people. He says he has a clear message from God and cannot force it on people who refuse it. He asks for no money, says his reward comes from God alone, and refuses to send away believers, even though the people call them lowly. He asks what help he would have against God if he did so.

Noah tells his people that he does not claim divine treasures, knowledge of the unseen, or angelic status. He also says he will not declare that God withholds good from those they despise, since God alone knows their hearts. His opponents then challenge him to bring the punishment he has threatened, and he replies that God will send it when God chooses.

Noah's people cannot be helped if God means to lead them astray, and all will return to God. When people accuse the Prophet of inventing the Koran, he says any guilt is his own, and he is innocent of their wrongdoing. God tells him that only those who already believe will believe, so he should not grieve. He is told to build the Ark and not plead for the wrongdoers, who will be drowned.
Noah builds the ark while the leaders of his people mock him. He answers that they will be laughed at in turn, and that they will learn who faces a shaming punishment and who faces a lasting one.

Noah is told to load the ark with a pair of every kind of animal, along with his family and the believers, while the flood rises. Only a few people believe with him. He calls on God as the ark sets out, and then urges his son, who stands apart, to board with them and not stay with the unbelievers.

Noah's son says he will climb a mountain to escape the flood, but Noah replies that only those God shows mercy to can be saved. A wave sweeps the son away. The water then drops, the ark settles on Al-Judi, and Noah asks God about his son, saying God's promise is true and he is the most just judge.

God tells Noah that his son is not really of his family, so Noah was wrong to ask for him to be saved. God warns Noah not to ask about things he does not know. Noah replies that he turns to God and asks for forgiveness and mercy, or he will be among the lost.

God tells Noah to leave the ark in peace, with blessings for him and for the peoples who will come from his companions. Unbelieving peoples will have worldly goods but a painful punishment later. Noah is told to be patient, since the God-fearing will prosper. Then Houd is sent to the people of Ad to call them to worship God alone.

Speaking to his people, the prophet says he rejects their other gods and places his trust in God alone, his Lord and theirs. He tells them to plot against him if they wish, since God controls every creature. If they turn away, God will replace them with another people, and they cannot harm God.

God rescued the prophet Hud and his believers when punishment came, but the people of Ad rejected God's signs, disobeyed His messengers, and followed arrogant leaders. They were cursed in this life, and on the Day of Resurrection they are reminded of their disbelief and called far-removed from God's mercy.

Saleh tells his people of Thamud to worship God alone, since He created them from the earth and settled them on it, and to ask His forgiveness and turn back to Him. The people reply that they had hoped well of Saleh, but they doubt his call and refuse to give up the gods their fathers worshipped.

Salih, a prophet sent to his people, asks them to leave God's she-camel, given as a sign, alone and warns that harm to her will bring punishment. They hamstring the camel anyway, and he tells them they have three days left before the threat comes true.

Saleh and the believers with him were saved from disgrace, while the wicked were destroyed by a violent storm and found dead in their homes. The passage then mentions Themoud (the people of Saleh) who rejected their Lord, and it ends with Abraham receiving visitors who bring good news and serving them a roasted calf.

Abraham offers food to visitors, but they do not eat it, and he becomes afraid. They tell him they are messengers sent to the people of Lot. His wife laughs, and they announce that she will have a son, Isaac, and then a grandson, Jacob. She doubts this because she and her husband are old. They reply that she should not wonder at God's command, and they bless the household.

Abraham, now free of fear after receiving good news, pleads with God for the people of Lot. God tells him to stop, because a punishment has already been decreed for them. When the messengers come to Lot, he is distressed and feels unable to protect them.

Lot's people rush to his house wanting to abuse his guests, who are angels. Lot offers them his daughters instead and urges them to fear God and not shame him. They refuse, and Lot says he wishes he had the strength to resist them or a powerful protector to turn to.

Angels tell Lot, a messenger, to leave his city with his family at night and not look back. His wife will be destroyed with the others. The angels then overturn the cities and rain down stones on their people, and the passage warns that these people are not far from the wicked of Mecca.

Shoaib, sent to the people of Madian, tells them to worship God alone and to deal honestly in weights and measures. He warns them of a day of punishment and says that what God leaves them lawfully is better than cheating. He then says he is not their keeper, meaning he cannot force them to believe.

The people speak to Shu'ayb (called Shoaib here) in mockery. They ask whether his prayers require them to abandon the gods their fathers worshipped and to stop spending their wealth as they wish. They call him gentle and rightly guided, which is said ironically.

The speaker, a prophet, asks his people to consider whether he has a clear message from God and whether he is acting only for their good. He says he will not do what he forbids them, and he trusts only in God. He warns that their opposition could bring the same punishment that fell on earlier peoples who rejected their prophets.

Shoaib's people mock him. They say he is weak among them and would have been stoned if not for his family. Shoaib replies that they honor his family more than God, and tells them to act against him as they can. He says they will learn who is punished and who is the liar, and he waits with them.

Shoaib and the believers with him are saved by God's mercy, while the wicked are destroyed by a violent storm and found dead in their homes. The passage then recalls the fate of Madian and Themoud, and says Pharaoh led his people wrongly, so he will lead them into the fire on Judgment Day.

God did not wrong these peoples; they wronged themselves. Their gods could not help them when God's punishment came, and it only made their ruin worse. The same punishment is a warning about the Last Day, when all people will be gathered together, and it will come at an appointed time.

The passage says that the blessed will stay in the Garden (Paradise) for as long as the heavens and earth last, unless God wills otherwise, and God may add further gifts. It then tells the listener not to doubt what these others worship, since they only follow what their fathers worshipped, and God will give them their full share.

The passage says that Moses' people argued over the Book given to him, and that only a delay set by God stopped them from being judged. It tells the Prophet to keep straight on as commanded, along with those who turned to God with him, and not to lean on wrongdoers. God sees all deeds and repays each person by them.

Prayer at dawn, evening and night is urged, because good deeds drive away evil ones. The passage then says that God does not let the reward of the righteous be lost, and that God does not destroy righteous cities unjustly. Earlier generations who opposed corruption were saved, while evildoers who followed their desires were destroyed.

God could have made all people share one religion, but only those he shows mercy to stop disagreeing. The passage says God has said he will fill hell with jinn and humans. Stories of earlier prophets are told to strengthen the Prophet's heart, and believers are warned. Unbelievers are told to act as they can while the Prophet waits.
God alone knows the hidden things of heaven and earth, and all things return to him. The passage tells the reader to worship him and trust in him, because God is aware of what people do.

The Qur'an says it was sent down so that the prophet can lead people from darkness into light, onto the path of God. It warns that those who disbelieve, who prefer this present life to the next, and who block others from God's way, are far astray.

God sent each messenger in the language of his own people, so that he could speak clearly to them. God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. Moses was sent with signs to bring his people out of darkness into light.

Moses reminds his people that God rescued them from Pharaoh, who had cruelly oppressed them and killed their sons. God warns that gratitude brings more blessings, while ingratitude brings severe punishment. Moses adds that even if everyone on earth is ungrateful, God needs nothing and deserves all praise.

Earlier peoples, whom only God knows, received prophets with clear proofs. They covered their mouths, refused the message, and doubted it. The prophets asked whether there could be doubt about God, who calls people to forgiveness. The people replied that the prophets were only men who wanted to turn them from their fathers' worship, and demanded a clear proof.

Messengers say to their opponents that they are only men like them, but God gives favours to whomever He chooses. They cannot show any proof except by God's permission. So believers should trust God, who has already guided them, and they will patiently endure the harm their opponents may do.

Unbelievers told their messengers they would be driven out of the land or forced back to their old religion. God answered that he would destroy the wicked and give the land to the messengers instead. Proud rebels who opposed them would perish and face Hell.

The passage describes the fate of those who reject God. They will suffer torment and gain nothing from their deeds, which are compared to ashes blown away by the wind. It then says God created the heavens and earth and could replace people with a new creation, which would be easy for him.

On the Day of Judgment, the weak ask the powerful to take some of God's punishment off them. The powerful answer that it is too late, since God's guidance was not theirs to give, and Satan says he only deceived them and had no real power over them.

Speaking after the judgment, the passage says that the speaker only called people to belief and they answered. He cannot help them, and they cannot help him, so they should not blame him. Those who do wrong face painful punishment, while believers who do right enter gardens with rivers, greeted with "Peace." A good word is compared to a good tree with firm roots and branches reaching heaven.

God keeps believers firm, in this life and the next, through his steady word, while he lets the wicked go astray. Those who reject God's goodness and mislead others with false gods will be burned in Hell. They are told to enjoy their pleasures for a while, since their end is the fire.
God tells the messenger to instruct believers to keep up their prayers and give charity, both in secret and in public, before a day comes when there will be no buying and selling and no friendship.

God created the heavens and earth, and provides for people through rain, crops, ships, rivers, the sun, moon, day and night. His gifts are too many to count, yet people are described as unjust and ungrateful.

Abraham speaks to God, saying that many people have been led astray by idols. He says that whoever follows him belongs to him, and he leaves the fate of those who disobey to God, whom he calls merciful and forgiving.

Abraham prays that God will care for his descendants, whom he has settled in a barren valley near the holy house (the Kaaba). He asks that people be drawn to them and that they be given fruit, so they will give thanks and keep up prayer. He affirms that God knows all things, and he thanks God for giving him Ishmael and Isaac in his old age.

Abraham prays that he, his descendants and believers will keep up prayer and be forgiven on the day of judgment. The passage then says God does not ignore the wicked; He only delays their punishment until a day of terror, when they will beg for a little more time.

The passage warns that earlier peoples who did wrong were destroyed, and that their schemes against God's messengers failed because God is stronger. It says God will keep his promise to his messengers. On the Day of Judgment, the earth and heavens will be changed, and wrongdoers will be shown bound together in chains.
The message is addressed to all people, to warn them and to teach them that there is only one God. It also invites thoughtful people to reflect on it.

Muhammad is told that he is being given a story of Joseph, one of the most beautiful narratives. Joseph tells his father he dreamed of eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. The father warns him not to tell his brothers, who might plot against him.

Joseph's father is told that God will choose Joseph and bless his family, as God blessed Abraham and Isaac. Joseph's brothers then grow jealous, because their father loves Joseph and his younger brother more than them. They plan to kill Joseph or send him far away so that their father will turn his attention to them.

Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and God tells Joseph that he will one day remind them of this deed. They return to their father in tears, claiming a wolf ate Joseph and showing a shirt stained with false blood. The father doubts their story, says patience is best, and asks God for help.

Travellers stopped at a well and sent their water-drawer down, and a boy was pulled up in the bucket. They hid his discovery and treated him as goods to sell. They sold him cheaply, for a few silver coins, though God knew what they had done.

An Egyptian man buys Joseph and asks his wife to treat him well, perhaps as a useful servant or an adopted son. Joseph is given wisdom and knowledge. When the wife of the household tries to seduce him, he refuses, saying God protects him and that wrongdoers do not prosper.

The woman wanted Joseph, and he would have yielded had he not seen a sign from his Lord, so he was kept from wrongdoing. At the door, she accused him of trying to harm her household, and he said she had tried to seduce him. A witness from her own family proposed a test: a shirt torn at the front showed she was lying, and one torn at the back showed he was lying.
In the city, women gossip that the governor's wife has tried to seduce her servant, and that his love for her has inflamed her. They say she is clearly in the wrong.

The wife of Potiphar, the Egyptian official's wife, hears that other women are gossiping about her. She invites them to a banquet, gives each a knife, and has Joseph brought in. The women are so struck by his beauty that they cut their hands. She then tells them he is the man she wanted, who refused her, and that he will be jailed if he does not obey her.

Joseph prays to God, saying he would rather go to prison than give in to the women who are trying to tempt him. He asks God to protect him from their schemes. God hears him and turns the schemes away. Even so, the people involved decide to imprison him for a time, despite seeing signs of his innocence.

Two young men who are in prison with Joseph each tell him a dream. One dreams he is pressing grapes, and the other dreams he carries bread on his head that birds eat. They ask him to explain what the dreams mean, because they consider him a good person.

Joseph, imprisoned with two fellow prisoners, offers to interpret their dreams before they are told them, and says this knowledge comes from his Lord. He explains that he rejects the beliefs of people who deny God and the afterlife, and follows the faith of his forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He then asks whether many lords are better than the one God.

Joseph tells his two fellow prisoners that worshipping other beings besides God is worshipping mere names that people and their fathers invented, with no authority from God. Judgment belongs to God alone, and he has commanded that only he be worshipped. He then tells the prisoners that one will be freed to serve wine to his lord, and the other will be crucified.

A prisoner who is about to be freed asks a fellow prisoner to remember him to his lord, but he forgets, and Joseph stays in prison for years. Later the king dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones and seven green ears of grain beside seven withered ones. His nobles cannot explain the dream, so the freed prisoner offers to find the meaning.

Joseph interprets a dream for the king's servant. Seven fat cows and seven green ears of corn are followed by seven lean cows and seven withered ears. Joseph says there will be seven years of good harvests, with most grain kept in its ear, then seven years of famine that will eat the stored food, then a year of rain and grapes.

The king orders that Joseph be brought to him, but Joseph first sends the messenger back. He asks that the king look into the case of the women who cut their hands, since Joseph's lord knows the trap they set for him.

The women say they know no wrong in Joseph, and the Prince's wife admits she tried to lead him into sin and that he is innocent. Joseph says this shows he did not betray his master, and he adds that he does not claim to be free of fault, since the heart tends toward evil unless God shows mercy.

The king brings Joseph into his service and gives him authority over the storehouses of grain. Joseph asks for this role, and God establishes him in the land. The passage adds that the reward of the life to come is better for those who believe and fear God.

Joseph gives his brothers grain and tells them that to get more, they must bring back their younger brother from their father. He refuses them any more grain if they do not. The brothers agree. Joseph then secretly has their money put back into their sacks, so they will notice it and return.

Joseph's brothers return to their father and say that grain is being withheld from them unless their youngest brother goes with them. They promise to look after him. The father refuses to trust them as he did before, and says God is the best protector.

Joseph's brothers find their money returned in their sacks and say it makes the trip worth making. They promise their father they will bring back their younger brother, and their father agrees only after they swear an oath before God to do so, with the exception of being prevented by force. They make the pledge, and the father calls God a witness to it.

Jacob tells his sons not to enter the city through one gate but through different gates. He says he cannot protect them from anything God has decided, since judgment belongs to God alone. He places his trust in God, and he tells others who trust to trust in God too.

Jacob's sons entered Egypt as their father told them, but this could not change what God had decreed; it only fulfilled a wish Jacob had. Joseph then privately revealed himself to his brother Benjamin, comforting him, and hid a drinking cup in Benjamin's luggage. A crier then accused the brothers of theft.

Joseph searches his brothers' sacks and finds the stolen cup in his own brother's sack, though the king's law would not have let him keep that brother without God's permission. His brothers say that his brother has stolen before, meaning Joseph himself. Joseph hides his reaction and tells them, in private, that they are in the worse position, since God knows what they have done.

Joseph's brothers ask the ruler to take one of them as a slave in place of Benjamin, their younger brother, because their old father needs him. The ruler refuses. He says it would be wrong to take anyone except the man in whose bag the stolen property was found.

The brothers, unable to bring Benjamin back, hold a private meeting. The eldest refuses to leave Egypt until their father allows it or God decides, and he sends the rest home with a claim that Benjamin has stolen, saying they only report what they saw.

Jacob, grieving for his sons' missing brother Joseph, says his sons have plotted something, but he will bear it patiently and hopes God will bring all of them back to him. When they tell him he will grieve until he dies, he replies that he brings his grief to God alone, and that he knows things from God that they do not.

Jacob tells his sons to go and look for Joseph and his brother, and not to lose hope in God's mercy, since only unbelievers lose that hope. When the sons come before Joseph, poor and short of money, asking for full measure as charity, he asks whether they remember how they treated Joseph and his brother in their ignorance.

Joseph's brothers, who did not recognise him at first, now realise who he is. He reveals himself and says God has been kind to them, and he forgives them. He sends his shirt to restore his father's sight and asks for the whole family. The brothers still treat his claim as an old error on his part.

Joseph honors his parents by seating them on the throne with him, and they bow before him. He says this fulfills the dream he had long before. He thanks God for freeing him from prison, bringing his family out of the desert, and resolving the quarrel Satan had stirred up with his brothers.

Joseph prays to God as his guardian, asking to die as a Muslim and to be joined with the righteous. The passage then tells Muhammad that this account is revealed to him, that he was not present when Joseph's brothers plotted, and that most people will not believe, though he wishes they would. He is asked for no payment; the message is for all mankind.

The passage warns that people who feel safe may be caught off guard by God's punishment or by the Hour, the end of the world. It then tells the speaker to declare his way: he calls people to God on the basis of clear proof, together with his followers, and he rejects associating any other gods with God.

God sent only men, chosen from towns, as messengers with revelations. Those who doubt are urged to look at how earlier peoples ended, since the next life is better for the God-fearing. When the messengers despaired of being believed, God rescued whom He chose, but punished the wicked.

The story of Joseph, told in these verses, is presented as a lesson for thinking people. It is not invented fiction. It confirms earlier scriptures, explains all things, and offers guidance and mercy to believers.

The passage says that earlier peoples, such as the people of Noah, called their messengers liars and argued against the truth with empty words. God punished them severely for this. The same fate, it says, has been decreed for the unbelievers, who will be people of the fire.

The angels who carry God's throne and those who surround it praise their Lord, believe in Him, and pray for forgiveness for the believers. They ask God to forgive those who turn to Him and follow His path, to save them from hell, and to bring them into the Gardens of Eden, along with their righteous parents, wives, and children.

Unbelievers will be told that God's hatred of them is greater than their own self-hatred, because they refused the faith when called to it. They will ask for a way out, and they are told their fate comes from rejecting the one God and accepting partners with him. The judgment belongs to God, so the believers should worship him alone, even though the unbelievers dislike this.

God, exalted and enthroned, sends the Spirit to whichever of His servants He chooses, so that they warn people of the coming Day of Meeting. On that day the dead rise from their graves, nothing is hidden from God, and every soul is repaid according to what it has earned.
God will judge everything with truth. The gods that people call upon besides God cannot judge anything at all. God hears and sees all things.

Past peoples who were stronger than the Meccans were destroyed by God for their sins and for rejecting their messengers. Moses was also sent with clear signs to Pharaoh, Haman and Karun, and they called him a sorcerer and an impostor. Karun is a rich man in the Qur'an's stories.

Pharaoh orders that the sons of Moses's followers be killed and the daughters spared, but his plot fails. Pharaoh then says he wants to kill Moses, fearing Moses will change the people's religion or bring disorder to the land. Moses answers that he seeks protection from God against every proud man who does not believe in the Day of Judgment.

A man from Pharaoh's own family, who secretly believed, argues against killing Moses for claiming God as his Lord. He says that if Moses is lying, the lie will hurt only Moses, but if he speaks truly, some of his threats may strike the people. Pharaoh rejects this and says he will guide them only in the way he sees fit.
On the Day of Judgment, people will be driven back from the court of God into hell. They will have no one to protect them from God, and anyone whom God leads astray will have no guide.

Joseph came earlier with clear proofs, but his hearers kept doubting his message, and after he died they said God would never send another messenger. The passage says God leaves such doubters and proud rejecters of God's signs to their own error. It then tells how Pharaoh ordered a tower built so he could reach God, whom he called a liar.

A believing man urges Pharaoh's people to follow him, saying this present life is only a fleeting pleasure while the life to come lasts forever. He teaches that evil deeds are repaid only with their like, and that those who do right and believe will enter paradise, where they receive good things without measure.

A believer warns his people that the idols they call on cannot help them now or later, that all return is to God, and that wrongdoers will end in the fire. He commits his own affair to God, and God protects him from the plots of Pharaoh's people, whose punishment is the fire morning and evening and then the severest torment on Judgment Day.

In hell, the weak blame the proud, who had led them astray. The proud answer that everyone is in the same fire, because God has judged. The damned then ask the guards to plead for one day's relief, and they are told to call for help themselves, though their cries will do no good.

God promises to help his messengers and believers in this life, and on Judgment Day the wrongdoers will get no help from their excuses and will face curse and Hell. He gave Moses guidance and the Book to the Israelites, and tells the Prophet to be patient, trust God's promise, ask forgiveness, and praise God morning and evening.

Those who dispute God's signs without any authority behind them are, the passage says, driven only by pride, and they will not succeed. Creating the heavens and earth is greater than creating man, though most people do not realise it. The blind and the seeing, or the evil doer and the righteous believer, are not equal, and the Hour of judgment will surely come.
God made the night for rest and the day for light, and He made the earth a firm base and the sky over it. He shaped people and gave them good things, so He alone is their Lord and should be praised.

The speaker says he is forbidden to worship the beings people call upon besides God. He says this is because clear signs have come to him from his Lord, and he is commanded to submit himself to the Lord of all worlds.

God created people from dust, then through stages of life to infancy, strength, old age, and death, all set by his decree. He gives life and death, and when he decides something, it happens. Those who reject his signs and his messages will learn the truth later.

Unbelievers are asked where the false gods they worshipped alongside God are now. They answer that these gods have vanished and were nothing. They are then told to enter Hell for their arrogance and their excessive pleasure in earthly life.

God tells the Prophet to be patient, because God's promise is true. Whether God shows him some of the punishments promised to the deniers during his life, or lets him die first, all of them will in the end return to God.

Earlier messengers of God were sent to people, some named to Muhammad and some not. No messenger could perform a miracle except by God's permission. When God's command comes, judgment will be made in truth, and those who mocked the message will be lost. God also gave people animals to ride and eat, and ships to carry them.

Past peoples who were more numerous and powerful than the listeners still perished, and their achievements did not save them. When their messengers brought clear signs, they mocked them and relied on their own learning. Only when God's punishment came did they say they now believed in God alone and rejected the other gods they had worshipped.
Faith that people express only after they have seen God's punishment does them no good. This is God's usual way with those who lived before, and the unbelievers were then destroyed.

Pharaoh, a powerful ruler, split his people into groups and oppressed one group by killing their sons and sparing their daughters. God decided to favour the oppressed: to make them leaders, to make them Pharaoh's heirs, and to settle them in the land. Pharaoh, Haman and their armies would see the very thing they feared.

The mother of Moses is told to nurse him and, if she fears for his safety, to set him adrift on the river. She is promised that he will be returned to her and made a prophet. Pharaoh's household takes the baby in, though it will later become a source of enemy and grief for them. Pharaoh's wife asks that he not be killed, hoping he will be useful or be adopted as a son, but the passage notes that they did not understand what they were doing.

Moses' mother, afraid for her baby, is steadied by God so she can keep faith. Her daughter follows the baby and offers to find a nurse, and the baby is returned to his mother, so she is comforted and knows God's promise is true. Most people do not understand this.
When Moses reached full manhood, God gave him wisdom and knowledge. The verse says this is how God rewards those who do right.

Moses enters a city unseen and finds a man of his own people fighting a man of the enemy's people. The Israelite asks for his help, and Moses strikes the enemy with his fist and kills him. Moses calls it the work of Satan, asks God for forgiveness, and vows never to help wrongdoers again.

Moses walks into the city at midday, afraid, and meets a man from his own people who is fighting another man. When Moses tries to stop the attack, the man he is trying to protect accuses him of wanting to kill him as he killed someone the day before. A messenger then warns Moses that the city's nobles plan to kill him, and urges him to leave.

Moses arrives at a well and finds two women who are holding back their flock because they cannot water it until the male shepherds leave. He waters their animals for them, then prays for help. One woman comes back and invites him to meet their father, who will pay him for the work. When Moses tells the old man his story, he is told he has escaped from a wrongdoing people.

A man offers to marry one of his two daughters to another man, on condition that the suitor works for him as a hired servant for eight years, or ten if the suitor chooses. The suitor agrees, and whichever term he completes, neither side will be wronged. They call God as witness to the agreement.

Moses, travelling with his family, sees a fire on a mountain and goes to it. A voice from a bush tells him that it is God and orders him to throw down his staff. The staff turns into a snake, Moses runs away, and the voice tells him to come back and not be afraid.

Moses is told to put his hand into his coat and draw it out white but unharmed, as two signs to Pharaoh and his nobles. Moses says he has killed a man and fears being killed in return, and asks God to send his brother Aaron with him, since Aaron speaks more clearly and can support his case.

Moses responds to Pharaoh's people, who call his signs mere magic and say they never heard of such things from their ancestors. Moses leaves the outcome to God, who knows who is rightly guided and who will receive the heavenly home. He adds that wrongdoers will not succeed.

Pharaoh tells his nobles that he knows of no god but himself, and asks Haman to build him a tower so he can climb up to the God of Moses, whom he calls a liar. God then drowns Pharaoh and his armies in the sea. The passage says they are leaders who call people to the fire, and they will get no help on the Day of Resurrection.

God gave Moses the Law as light, guidance and mercy after earlier peoples were destroyed. The passage then tells Muhammad that he was not present at these events, at Sinai or among the people of Madian, so the stories came to him by revelation. Later generations were sent prophets too.

Muhammad was not present at Mount Sinai when God called to Moses. God sent him as a warner to a people who had received no warner before, so that they would reflect and not later claim they had no messenger to follow when disaster struck for their deeds.

People rejected the truth brought by Muhammad, demanding he have the same miraculous powers as Moses. The passage points out that they had already rejected Moses' books and called both sorcery. It then tells Muhammad to challenge them to produce a better guiding book from God, if they are sincere.

The passage says that people who do not answer the message are only following their own desires, and that such people are far astray without God's guidance. It then describes earlier recipients of Scripture who accept the recited message, saying it is the truth from their Lord and that they were already submitters to God before it came.

Those who are patient in hardship, answer evil with good, and give charity will be rewarded twice. When they hear empty talk, they turn away, saying they will answer for their own deeds and the others for theirs. The passage then says that the Prophet cannot guide whomever he wishes; God guides whom He wills.

The passage says that some people objected that following the guidance would cost them their land. God answers that he has already given them a safe sacred sanctuary with abundant produce. It also says that many earlier cities were destroyed for their prosperous ease, and God then inherited what remained.

God does not destroy a city until He has first sent it a messenger to warn its people, and cities are destroyed only for their wrongdoing. The worldly goods people receive are temporary, while what is with God is better and lasts longer. The passage then asks whether someone promised a good reward is the same as someone given only worldly pleasures and later brought up for punishment.

Those who are condemned will tell God that they led others astray, just as they themselves had been led astray, and that they did not worship God's rivals. They will call on the false gods they had worshipped, but these will not answer. Then God will ask them how they responded to His messengers.

God alone creates and chooses as He wills, while the false gods have no such power. God is far above the partners people give Him, and He knows all hidden thoughts. The passage ends by asking who else could bring light if God brought endless night.

God alone gives night for rest and day for work, so only God can do this. On the day of judgment, people will be asked for their proofs, will see that the truth belongs to God alone, and the gods they invented will abandon them.

Korah, a man from the people of Moses, grew proud over his great wealth, so much so that its keys would have been a heavy load for a group of strong men. When his own people warned him not to exult, because God does not love those who exult, he did not stop.

Seek the future home with what God has given you, without neglecting your share in this world. Be generous to others as God has been generous to you, and do not cause corruption on earth, because God does not love those who do such harm.

Korah claims his wealth comes from his own knowledge. The passage answers that God destroyed earlier, stronger and richer peoples, and that the wicked are not questioned about their sins. Korah goes out in display, and some who love worldly life wish they had his fortune.

The passage tells how a wealthy man, who was proud of his riches, was swallowed up by the earth along with his home, and had no power to save himself. People who had earlier envied his wealth then admitted that God gives plenty or withholds it as He chooses, and that God's reward is better than worldly riches.

The passage says that the future home of peace is given to those who do not seek to rise up over others on earth or do wrong, and that good deeds bring a reward beyond what they deserve. Evil deeds bring only the punishment they earn. It ends by telling the prophet that the Book was sent as a mercy from God, and not to help those who reject it.

The passage tells the believer not to turn away from God's revealed signs and not to worship any other god alongside God. It states that God alone is God, that all things will perish except God, and that all return to Him for judgment.

Those who take other beings as lords, claiming they serve them only to be brought near to God, will be judged by God on their disagreements. God does not guide the liar and unbeliever. The passage adds that if God wanted a son, He could choose one from His creation, and it declares God free of such a need, the One and Almighty.

The verse says God created the heavens and the earth for a true purpose. It describes how night follows day and day follows night, and how God controls the sun and moon so that each moves toward a set end. It closes by calling God mighty and gracious.

God made all people from one man and formed his wife from him, and He sent down four pairs of livestock. He shaped human beings in their mothers' wombs through three layers of darkness. He alone is Lord and King, so the question is asked why people turn away from Him.

God does not need human thanks, but He is pleased when His servants are thankful and displeased by ingratitude. Each soul carries only its own deeds, and people will return to God, who will tell them of all they did and knows their hidden thoughts.

When a person is in trouble, he turns to God, but once God grants him a blessing, he forgets God and sets up rivals to God to lead others astray. The passage tells him to enjoy his ingratitude briefly, for he will end up in the Fire.

The passage contrasts the devoted night-worshipper with those who lack knowledge, asking whether they can be treated alike, and says only people of understanding heed the warning. It then urges believers to fear God, promises good to those who do good and endure patiently, and says that reward will be unmeasured. The speaker also says he fears punishment if he rebels against his Lord.

Those who serve other beings besides God will lose their own souls and families on the Day of Resurrection, and fire will surround them. God warns His servants to fear Him. Good news is promised to those who turn away from false gods such as Thagout and turn to God, and who listen to His word and follow it.
Those who fear their Lord will be given mansions with rivers flowing beneath them. This is a promise from God, and God does not break his promise.

God sends rain that feeds springs and grows crops, which then wither and crumble, and this is a lesson for thoughtful people. The passage contrasts this with someone whose heart God has opened to Islam, who has light from his Lord, and says those whose hearts are closed to remembering God are clearly misguided.

God has sent down a scripture that is consistent with itself and teaches through repetition. Those who fear God are moved by it, and their hearts soften when they remember Him. God guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills. The evildoers, facing punishment on the Day of Resurrection, will be told to taste the results of what they earned.

God humbles those who deny him in this life, and their punishment in the next will be greater. The Quran is presented as a clear Arabic warning, and God compares a man serving many quarrelling masters with a man devoted wholly to one master, asking whether they are alike. Muhammad is told that he and his opponents will both die.

The passage contrasts two groups. Those who lie about God and reject the truth when it comes to them will end up in Hell. Those who bring the truth and believe in it are God-fearing, and God will forgive their worst deeds and reward their best ones. It ends by saying that God is enough for his servant, and that whoever God leads astray has no guide.

People who worship other beings alongside God are asked whether those beings could stop God's punishment or withhold His mercy if He chose to send either. The speaker answers that God is enough for him and tells his people to act as they can, while he does the same, and that they will learn who faces shame and lasting punishment.

God has sent the Book (the Qur'an) to people as a guide. Those who follow it gain for themselves, and those who go astray lose only themselves, since the Prophet is not responsible for keeping them. God takes souls at death and also during sleep, and the passage asks whether people have taken other beings as intercessors, though those beings have no power.

When the One God is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the afterlife tighten with distress, but when other gods worshipped alongside Him are mentioned, they rejoice. The verse then has the speaker address God directly, asking Him to judge between His servants in their disputes.

On the day of resurrection, the wicked would pay any amount to escape punishment, but they will face things they never expected and see their own bad deeds clearly. The passage then criticises people who call on God only in trouble and claim credit for good fortune as their due. It says such good fortune is a test, though most people do not understand this.

Wrongdoers will be punished by their own evil deeds, and they cannot escape God. God gives provision generously or withholds it as He wills. The passage then tells people who have sinned not to despair, because God forgives all sins, and urges them to turn back to their Lord before punishment comes.

The passage warns people to follow the best teaching sent from God before a sudden punishment arrives. It imagines a soul in that moment regretting its neglect and mockery, wishing for another chance to be righteous. The reply is that God's signs had already come, and the person had rejected them out of arrogance.

On the day of resurrection, those who lied about God will be shown with black faces, and the arrogant will be sent to Hell. God will save those who fear Him, and He is the creator and guardian of all things. The Prophet is told to reject worship of any god but God.

The passage tells the Prophet, and earlier prophets before him, that associating partners with God would make all their works worthless and lead to ruin. It urges worship of God alone and gratitude. It then says that people have not understood God's greatness: on the Day of Resurrection the whole earth will be in His handful and the heavens folded in His right hand. God is far above the partners people give Him.

At the end of time, a trumpet blast will cause all beings in heaven and earth to die, except those God chooses to spare. A second blast will raise everyone to stand and look around. Then God judges all people fairly, and each soul receives what its deeds have earned.

Unbelievers are driven into Hell in groups. At the gates, its keepers ask whether messengers had come to warn them of their Lord and of the coming meeting with Him. They admit that messengers had come. They are then told to enter and stay forever.

The passage describes the reward of those who feared God. They are led in groups to Paradise, where its keepers welcome them and tell them they may enter and stay forever. They then thank God for keeping His promise and giving them the earth to live in Paradise as they wish.
Angels are shown circling the divine Throne, praising their Lord. Judgment is then given fairly between people, and the closing words are a declaration of praise to God, Lord of all worlds.
