God tests earlier peoples to know who is sincere and who is lying, and He will judge those who do evil and think they will escape. Those who believe and do right will have their evil deeds erased and be rewarded for their best actions. Striving for the faith benefits only the one who strives, since God needs nothing from anyone.

People should be kind to their parents. But if parents try to make a person associate others with God, whom the person has no knowledge of, the person must not obey them. All people will return to God, who will tell them what they did, and those who believe and do right will enter among the righteous.

Some people claim to believe in God, but when they suffer for their faith they treat hostility from other people as if it were punishment from God. When success comes, they claim they were on the believers' side. God knows what is in people's hearts. Unbelievers also promise to carry the believers' sins if they follow them, but they will not bear any of those sins.

Those who lead others astray will carry their own burdens and some of the burdens of those they misled, and will be questioned about their lies on Judgment Day. The passage then tells how Noah preached for many years, was saved from the flood with those in his ship, and how Abraham told his people to worship God and fear Him.

Worshipping idols beside God is called a lie, and idols cannot provide anything. People should seek their needs from God alone, since everyone will return to Him. The messenger's only duty is to preach openly. God created life and will bring it back again, which is easy for Him.

Abraham tells his people that those who reject God's signs and the meeting with him will lose God's mercy and face punishment. When his people respond by calling for him to be killed or burned, God saves him from the fire. Abraham then warns that the idols they have taken as their bond in this life will turn them against one another on Judgment Day, and that the fire will be their home with no one to help.

Abraham's line is blessed with Isaac and Jacob, and prophecy and scripture are given to his descendants. Lot then warns his people against sexual wrongdoing, including attacks on travelers and public wrongdoing. They reject his warning and challenge him to bring God's punishment, so Lot asks God for help against them.

Angels bring Abraham news of a son, then say they will destroy the city's people for their evil. Abraham asks about Lot, who lives there, and the angels say they will save Lot and his family except his wife, who will be left behind to perish. They then say the same to Lot when they reach him, telling him not to fear.

Shoaib was sent to the people of Madian with a message to worship God, expect the Last Day, and stop causing harm in the land. They rejected him, so an earthquake destroyed them, and Ad and Themoud were destroyed in the same way. The passage says Satan made their wrong deeds look good to them and led them away from the right path.
Korah, Pharaoh and Haman are named as people to whom Moses came with clear signs from God. They acted proudly on earth, but they could not escape God's power.

God punished each people for their sin, sending a stone-laden wind, a cry, an earthquake or a flood. God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves. Those who take guardians besides God are compared to a spider's web, the frailest of houses.

Believers are told to recite the scripture revealed to the prophet and to keep the prayer ritual. Prayer keeps a person from shameful and blameworthy acts. The greatest duty is remembering God, who sees all that people do.

Believers should argue with the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) only in a courteous way, except with those who have wronged them. They should say that they believe in the revelation given to both sides, that their God and the Jews' and Christians' God is one, and that they submit to him. The Qur'an is presented as sent down in the same way, and some Arabians also believe in it, while only unbelievers reject these signs.

The Prophet had never read or written any scripture before, so critics could not say he copied it from earlier books. The Qur'an itself is presented as a clear sign to those who have knowledge, while deniers reject it. Critics ask for a miraculous sign, but the reply is that signs belong to God alone, and the Prophet is only a warner. The Book is itself a mercy and warning for believers.

Those who believe in false things and reject God will be among the lost. They ask that punishment be hastened, but it is held back until a fixed time, and when it comes it will be sudden and surround them. God then tells them to taste the results of their own actions.

Those who believe and do good will be given gardens with palaces and flowing rivers, to remain forever. The passage then notes that many animals do not store their own food, yet God feeds them and people. It ends by saying that people who admit God created the heavens and earth should not invent lies.

People agree that God sends rain, yet they do not fully grasp it. Present life is only play, while the life to come is the real life. When they are in danger at sea they pray sincerely to God, but once saved they associate others with Him. They reject the revelation but enjoy worldly good things, and they will later learn their error.

The passage contrasts God's protection of a sacred enclosure with people turning to false idols and denying God's goodness. It says that lying about God or rejecting the truth is the worst wrong, and that those who reject it will face Hell. It ends by promising that God guides those who strive for him and do good.

A man who buys an idle tale to lead others away from God, and mocks God's signs, will face a shameful punishment. Those who believe and do good deeds will enter gardens of delight forever, as God has promised.

God made the heavens without visible pillars, set mountains on the earth to keep it steady, and sends rain to grow plants. No other being can show such creation, so the unbelievers are plainly mistaken. The passage then says that Lokman was taught to be thankful to God, since gratitude benefits the thankful person, while God needs nothing and deserves all praise.

Lokman warns his son not to associate other gods with God, calling this the great impiety. The passage then tells people to be grateful to God and to their parents, recalling how a mother carries and nurses a child, and says all will return to God.

If others press you to associate something with God, of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but treat them kindly in this life and keep to the way of those who turn to God. Nothing is hidden from God, even a tiny seed, and a son is told to pray, do good, forbid wrong, and endure hardship.

God has given people everything in the heavens and on earth, and has been generous to them in body and soul. Yet some argue about God without knowledge or guidance, and refuse to follow what God has sent down, saying they will keep the religion of their fathers. The last line asks whether they would still do so even if Satan were calling them to the fire.

Whoever submits fully to God and does good holds on to a firm support, since all things return to God. Do not be troubled by others' disbelief: God will judge them for their deeds and knows every hidden thought. When asked who created the heavens and earth, they admit it is God, yet most of them do not understand this.

God's words are so vast that they could not be used up even if every tree became a pen and the sea became seven seas of ink. The passage adds that creating and raising people from the dead is as easy for God as creating and raising one person.

God controls the cycle of night and day and the movement of the sun and moon, each moving toward a set end. The passage says God knows what people do, that God is the truth, and that anything people call on besides God is worthless. Ships sailing the sea are also presented as signs of God's favour.

When storms threaten at sea, people pray to God sincerely, but once they reach land safely, some go back to doubting. The passage warns people to fear God and to remember a day when no one can atone for another, and not to be fooled by worldly life.

God alone knows when the Hour (the end of the world) will come, when rain will fall, and what is in the womb. No person knows what they will earn tomorrow or where they will die. God knows all things.

The heavens are so awed by God that they nearly split apart from above, and the angels praise their Lord and pray for forgiveness for people on earth. God is merciful. Those who take other beings as lords are watched by God, and the speaker is not responsible for them.

God has sent this Arabic revelation to warn the central city (Mecca) and the people around it about the coming Day of Gathering, when some will be in Paradise and some in the fire. God could have made all people one nation with one faith, but He admits whom He wills to His mercy. Evildoers will have no protector, and God alone is their Lord, who raises the dead.

God is the final judge of any disagreement, and the speaker trusts in Him and turns to Him. God created the heavens, the earth, human pairs and animals, and He gives provision generously or sparingly as He wills. He knows all things.

God says the same faith was given to Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and to Muhammad. He tells them to keep it and not split into sects. Those who worship other gods besides God reject it, but God chooses whom He pleases and guides those who turn back to Him.

People split into sects only out of jealousy, and only after knowledge had reached them. Had God not already set a fixed time for delay, the matter would have been settled at once. Those who inherited the Book later remain uncertain about it.

The speaker is told to call people to faith and to hold to the path he was commanded to follow, not their wishes. He says he believes in all the scriptures God has sent, and that each side will answer for its own deeds, with no conflict between them. Those who argue about God after pledging obedience face condemnation and severe punishment.

Those who do not believe in the Hour (the coming of the Last Day) mock its speed, while believers fear it and know it is true. God gives to His servants as He wills. Whoever seeks reward in the next life will receive increase there, while whoever seeks only this world's harvest gets a share of this world and nothing in the next.

The verse asks whether these people have gods who have approved for them religious practices that God has not permitted. It adds that God has delayed judgment until a set appointed day, and that the wicked will then face severe punishment.

On the Day of Judgment, wrongdoers will be afraid of what their own deeds have brought on them. Believers who do right will live in gardens of paradise and receive whatever they wish from their Lord, which the passage calls the greatest reward.

God promises good things to believers who do right. The speaker says he asks no payment for this message except love for his own family. God forgives and accepts repentance, and God will expose falsehood and confirm the truth.

God answers believers who do right by increasing their blessings, while unbelievers face a terrible punishment. He gives out provision in measured amounts, because if people had abundance they might act wantonly on earth. God knows his servants fully, and he sends rain and mercy after people have given up hope, showing he is the Protector and Praiseworthy.

God's signs include the creation of the heavens and earth and the living things spread across them, and his power to gather all creatures together when he wills. Misfortune comes to people because of their own deeds, though he forgives much. He also controls the seas, stilling the wind so that ships lie motionless on the waves.

Worldly goods are only temporary enjoyment, while what God gives is better and lasts longer. This is promised to those who believe and trust their Lord, avoid serious sins and indecency, forgive when angry, pray, decide their affairs by mutual consultation, give charity, and defend themselves when wronged.

Wrongs may be repaid with an equal wrong, but forgiving and making peace earns a reward from God. Those who wrong others unjustly and spread injustice on earth will face punishment, while patient forgiveness is described as a firm duty.

On the Day of Resurrection, wrongdoers will stand ashamed before the Fire and look at it in secret. Believers will say they are the true losers, and the wrongdoers will have no protector but God. The passage urges listeners to heed their Lord before that Day comes, since no one can delay it or escape their deeds.

God tells the Prophet that he is not responsible for making people accept the message; his task is only to preach. The passage then says that people are thankful when given blessings but ungrateful when trouble comes. God owns the heavens and earth and gives children, daughters, sons, both, or none, as He wills.

God says he sent a revelation to the Prophet through the Spirit (the angel Gabriel), though the Prophet did not know the Book or the faith before. God made it a light to guide whomever he chooses, and the Prophet will guide people to God's way. All things belong to God and will return to him.

The passage says that people of Mecca find it strange that a man from among them has been sent with a message. He is to warn others and bring good news to believers. Those who reject him call him a sorcerer, and the passage then declares that God created the heavens and earth and rules over all, and that no one can intercede without his permission.

God will bring all people back to Himself, and this promise is certain. He will reward believers who do right with justice, while unbelievers will receive boiling drink and painful punishment because they did not believe.

God made the sun and moon with purpose, and the day and night show signs to those who understand and fear Him. Those who do not expect to meet God, who are content with worldly life and ignore these signs, will have the fire as their home, as payment for what they did.

Believers who do good will be guided by their Lord because of their faith, and they will dwell in gardens with rivers, where they will praise God and greet each other with peace. If God hurried evil upon people as eagerly as they ask for good, their end would already be decided. Those who do not hope to meet God are left in their confusion.

People call out to God in trouble, but once the trouble is lifted they carry on as if they had never called. Earlier generations were destroyed for wickedness after rejecting their messengers, and later peoples were placed on the earth in their place to see how they would act.

Those who do not expect to meet God ask for a different Quran or for changes to it. The speaker answers that he cannot change it on his own will, since he only follows what is revealed to him. He adds that God could have prevented him from reciting it, and that he has lived among them for years before the revelation came.

People worship beings that can neither harm nor help them, calling them intercessors with God. The reply is that God knows everything, so such claims are false. Men once shared one religion but split apart, and God has delayed the judgment. The unbelievers ask for a sign, and the answer is to wait, since only God knows the unseen.

When people who had suffered hardship are given relief, some of them then plot against God's signs. The passage answers that God is quicker at planning than they are, and that his messengers record their schemes.

God lets people travel by land and sea, and ships sail happily on fair winds. When a violent storm surrounds them and they feel lost, they pray to God sincerely, promising to be thankful if he saves them.

When people are saved from danger, they go back to doing wrong on earth. The passage says that this wrongdoing only brings short-lived enjoyment in this life, and that everyone will return to God and be told what they did.

Life on earth is like rain that makes crops grow until the land is green and full. Then a sudden command from God destroys the harvest as if it had never grown, reminding people that their power over the earth does not last. God calls people to a home of peace and guides whom He chooses.
Those who do good will receive the best reward and even more besides. Their faces will not be darkened or covered with shame. They will live forever in Paradise.

Those who did evil will receive matching punishment, with shame and no protector against God, and will stay in the fire forever. On the day of gathering, God will separate those who worshipped other gods from the gods they served, and those gods will deny that they were worshipped.
Every soul will face the results of what it did before, and all people will return to God, their true Lord. The gods they invented will disappear from them.

The speaker asks who provides for people from heaven and earth, who controls hearing and sight, who brings life out of death, and who rules all things. People will answer "God." The speaker then asks why they do not fear him, says this God is their true Lord, and asks what remains once the truth is gone except error.

The passage asks whether any of the other gods that people associate with God can create a living being and then bring it back to God. It answers that only God does this, and so it asks why people turn away from him.

The passage argues that God alone guides people to the truth, so He is more worthy to be followed than any false god people set beside Him. It says most people follow only guesswork, which cannot reach the truth. It also claims the Qur'an is from God and confirms earlier revelations.

People reject a message they do not yet understand, as earlier peoples rejected their prophets, and the wrongdoers came to a bad end. Some believe and some do not. If they call the speaker a liar, he should say that each side answers for its own deeds, and he cannot force listeners who will not hear.

On the day of judgment, God will gather everyone together, and they will seem to have stayed only an hour. Those who denied meeting God will be lost, and God will witness their deeds. Each people had a messenger, and each was judged fairly. Still, the unbelievers ask when the threatened punishment will come.

Muhammad is told to say that he has no power over his own good or harm, except as God wills. Each people has an appointed time that cannot be delayed or brought forward. When God's punishment comes, the wrongdoers will believe, though they once mocked its coming and asked for it quickly. They will then be told to taste eternal punishment, paid according to their deeds.

Every sinner, even if they owned everything on earth, would offer it all to escape punishment. On the Day of Judgment, people will admit their wrongdoing, and they will be judged fairly. God owns everything in heaven and earth, He gives life and death, and He sends a warning, healing, guidance and mercy to believers.

The passage asks whether people have declared some foods lawful and others unlawful by God's permission or by making it up themselves. It warns that those who invent lies about God will face judgment on the Day of Resurrection. It adds that God gives many blessings, though most people do not thank him.

God is watching over every act and knows even the smallest thing, and all of it is recorded in a clear Book. Those who believe and fear God, the passage says, will have good news in this life and the next, and God's words do not change.

Everything in heaven and earth belongs to God, so the idols or deities that people worship beside Him are only a fancy, and those who make them are liars. The passage also rejects the claim that God has children, and says that those who invent such claims about God will come to harm.

Noah tells his people that his preaching of God's signs troubles them, but he trusts in God. He tells them to gather their plans and their false gods and act on them openly, without hiding them, and to decide what they will do about him. He asks no payment from them, since his reward is with God alone.

God sent messengers to many peoples, and each time the people rejected them. The passage says God saved the messenger and his followers, and drowned those who called God's signs false. It then says God sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his nobles, who acted proudly and refused them.

Pharaoh's people refuse to leave the faith of their fathers and do not believe Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh calls his skilled magicians, and Moses tells them to throw down their magic. Moses says God will make their sorcery come to nothing and will prove the truth, even though the wicked resist it.

Few of Moses' people believed in him, and only out of fear of Pharaoh and his leaders, who might persecute them. Moses urged them to trust God, and they prayed to be spared from the unjust people and saved by God's mercy.

God tells Moses and his brother to set aside houses in Egypt for their people, to make a place of prayer facing the qibla (the direction of prayer) inside them, to keep up prayer, and to bring good news to the believers.

Moses prays that God will ruin Pharaoh's wealth and harden his heart, so that Pharaoh will not believe until he faces painful punishment. God answers that the prayer is heard, and tells Moses and his brother Aaron to keep to the straight path and not follow those who lack knowledge.

Pharaoh and his army chase the Children of Israel into the sea and drown. As the water closes over him, Pharaoh says he now believes in the God of Israel. God replies that his belief comes too late, since he rebelled before. God says his body will be saved so that it becomes a sign for later people, and notes that most people ignore such signs.

God gave the Children of Israel a settled land and good things, and they only split into disagreement after the Law reached them. God will judge their disputes on the Day of Resurrection. The Prophet is told not to doubt the revelation sent to him and not to deny God's signs.

Only the people of Jonah, among earlier cities, believed in time and so escaped shame in this world. God could have made everyone believe, but belief comes only by God's permission, so the Prophet cannot force people to believe. Signs and warners do nothing for those who refuse.

The speaker tells people that he will not worship what they worship besides God, but will worship God, who causes death. He is ordered to be a believer and to turn toward pure faith. He warns against worshipping other gods or calling on anything that can neither help nor harm, since doing so would make a person a wrongdoer.

God alone can remove hardship or grant good, and He gives His favours to whom He chooses. The message is that the truth has now come, and each person is guided or misled only for himself. The speaker is not a guardian over people, so he should follow the revelation and be patient until God judges.

God is praised, since everything in heaven and on earth belongs to Him, and praise is due to Him in the next world too. The passage says He knows everything that goes into the earth, comes out of it, comes down from heaven, or rises up to it, and that He is merciful and forgiving.

The unbelievers say the Hour (the end of the world and Judgment) will never come. The reply is that it will surely come, because God knows all things, even the smallest, and everything is recorded in a clear Book. God will reward believers who do good with forgiveness and provision, and those who try to undermine God's signs will face painful punishment.

Those who have been given knowledge recognize that the revelation sent to the Prophet is the truth and leads to God. Unbelievers mock the Prophet's warning of resurrection, calling him a liar or a jinn-possessed man, and say that those who deny the afterlife will be punished and lost.

The passage asks whether people have not considered the heavens and the earth, which God could cause to swallow them or fall on them, and calls this a sign for those who turn back to God. It then recounts that God gave David special favour: mountains and birds sang his praises, and iron was softened so he could make armour, with a command to work righteousness.

God gives Solomon power over the wind, which carries him a month's journey in a single morning or evening, and a fountain of molten brass. Jinn (unseen beings) work for him by God's will, and those who disobey are punished with fire. They build halls, statues, large basins and cooking pots. God tells David's family to work in thankfulness, but few of God's servants are thankful.

Solomon's death was hidden from the jinn, who kept working for him. Only a worm eating his supporting staff revealed it, after which the jinn saw that they would not have stayed in their hard labour had they known the unseen. The passage then points to the people of Saba, who lived in a fertile land with two gardens and were told to eat God's provision and give thanks.

The people who turned away were punished with a flood, and their fertile gardens were turned into a barren place of bitter fruit and a few thorny trees. The passage says this punishment was for their ingratitude. It also describes how travel routes between towns were made safe and easy.

Sura 34 describes the people of Saba, who asked God to lengthen the distances between their towns and so wronged themselves. God scattered them and made them a story. Eblis (Satan) was proven right about them, and only a few believers escaped his influence. God's purpose is to tell those who believe in the afterlife from those who doubt it.

The passage says that the beings people treat as gods have no real power in heaven or earth, and cannot intercede with God except as God permits. It ends by asking who provides for people from heaven and earth, and answers that it is God, while the speaker and listeners cannot both be right.

The unbelievers refuse to accept the Qur'an or earlier scriptures. The passage then describes them before their Lord on Judgment Day, blaming one another: the weak say the powerful led them astray, and the powerful reply that they themselves chose to do wrong.

The weak tell the powerful that they were led into disbelief by their plotting, day and night. Both groups face punishment, and the rich people of every town who rejected a warner claimed their wealth and children would keep them safe.

Wealth and children do not bring a person closer to God. Those who believe and do right will receive a double reward and live safely in Paradise, while those who work against God's signs will be punished. God gives generously or sparingly as he chooses, and whatever is given in charity will be repaid.

On the Day of Judgment, the worshippers will deny that they served their own gods, saying those they followed were jinn, unseen beings, and that these people believed in them. No one will be able to help or harm anyone else. The evil doers will be told to taste the fire they had called a lie.

Those who reject the message dismiss the recited verses as the words of a man trying to turn people away from their ancestors' worship, as forgery, and as sorcery. The passage adds that these people were given no earlier scriptures to study and that no warner had come to them before.

Earlier peoples also rejected their messengers, and God punished them harshly. The speaker tells his listeners to consider, alone or in pairs before God, that their fellow citizen is no madman but only a warner of severe punishment. He asks no payment, since his reward is from God, who knows the unseen and sends the Truth.

The speaker says that any error will harm only himself, and any guidance comes from God, who hears all and is near. The passage then describes unbelievers who, when punished, will say they now believe, but it will be too late. A barrier will separate them from what they want, as happened to earlier unbelievers lost in doubt.

God is the creator of heaven and earth, who sends angels with wings as messengers and gives what he wills. No one can block his mercy or withhold what he releases. He asks people to remember his favour, since no other creator feeds them from heaven and earth, and warns that unbelievers face a terrible punishment.

Those who think their evil deeds are good are not the same as those who see the truth, and God leads astray or guides whom He wills. The Prophet should not grieve over them, since God knows what they do. God's sending of winds and rain to revive dead land is given as a sign that the resurrection will happen the same way.

Greatness belongs entirely to God, so anyone who seeks it should look to Him. Good words rise up to Him and He raises up righteous deeds, while those who plot evil face severe punishment and their schemes will come to nothing.

God formed people first from dust, then from small living seeds, and then made them male and female. Nothing in pregnancy or in a person's lifespan happens outside God's knowledge and the recorded decree, and this is easy for God.

The verse says that the two bodies of water are not alike. One is fresh and sweet enough to drink, and the other is salty and bitter. Yet people get fresh fish from both, take out ornaments to wear, and sail ships through the waters so they can seek God's bounty and be thankful.

God controls the cycle of night and day and the courses of the sun and moon. He alone has power, while the other gods people call upon have none, cannot hear them, and will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. People depend on God, who needs nothing.

No one can carry another person's burden, even a close relative who asks for help. Each person answers for their own actions, and purity benefits only the one who keeps themselves pure, since all people will finally be gathered before God.

The passage says that the living and the dead are not alike, and that God alone guides whom He wills. The Prophet's task is only to warn, not to make the dead hear. He was sent with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner, as earlier warners were. Those who called earlier messengers liars were punished.

God sends rain that makes fruits of many colours grow, and the mountains and living things also come in varied colours. Only those among his servants who have knowledge truly fear God. Those who recite God's Book, pray, and give alms openly and secretly may hope for a gain that will never perish.
God says that the Book He has revealed to Muhammad is the true message and confirms the Scriptures that came before it. The verse ends by saying that God knows and sees His servants.

God has given the Book to chosen servants, and they fall into three groups: some wrong themselves by evil deeds, some stay in the middle, and some go ahead in good deeds by God's permission. The last group enters the gardens of Eden, wearing gold, pearls and silk, and thanks God for taking away their sorrow.

The passage contrasts two fates. Those who enter the everlasting home are free from toil and weariness, while unbelievers face the fire of Hell, where they cannot die and their torment is not eased. In Hell they beg to be sent back to do good, but are told they had their chance to be warned, and that the unjust have no protector.

God has made people his deputies on earth. Whoever does not believe will bear the cost of his own disbelief, and for those who disbelieve, their denial only adds to their hatred from their Lord and to their own ruin.

The speaker asks what the gods that people call on besides God have created, and whether they had any part in making the heavens or have any scripture backing their claim. The answer is no, and God alone holds up the heavens and the earth so they do not fall away.

The people who once swore they would follow a preacher sent to them have instead grown more distant from the message. Their pride and scheming will only trap them, and God will treat them as he treated earlier peoples, since his way never changes.

God is described as all-knowing and all-powerful, so nothing can thwart Him. People who were stronger than the listeners have been destroyed, and if God punished people fully for their wrongs, none would be left. He gives them a set time, and when it comes, He watches over His servants.

The Book sent to the Prophet is meant to warn and to remind believers, so he should not be troubled about it. People are told to follow only God and not other masters. Past cities were destroyed by God's anger, and their only cry was an admission that they had done wrong.

God will call every people to account, including those sent messengers, and judge their deeds with full knowledge and justice. Those whose good deeds outweigh their bad will be happy, while those whose scales are light have lost themselves for rejecting God's signs. The passage ends by noting that God has settled people on earth and given them the means of life, and that few are thankful.

God created humans, then ordered the angels to bow down to Adam. All obeyed except Iblis (called Eblis here), who refused, saying he was nobler because he was made of fire and Adam of clay. God cast him out as one of the despised, and he asked for respite until the Resurrection, which was granted.

Iblis (Satan) speaks here. He says he will attack people from every side and that most of them will not be thankful. God tells him to leave Paradise in disgrace, and warns that he will fill hell with those who follow him. God then tells Adam and his wife to live in Paradise and eat freely, except from one tree, which they must not approach.

Satan tempts Adam and his wife to see their nakedness, which had been hidden from them. He tells them God forbade the tree only so they would not become angels or immortals, and swears that he is giving them honest advice.

Satan tricks Adam and his wife into eating from the forbidden tree, and they become aware of their nakedness and cover themselves with leaves. God reproaches them, and they admit their wrong and ask for mercy. God then tells them to go down to earth, where they will be enemies to one another and live for a set time.

God has given people clothing to cover their bodies and fine garments, but the clothing of piety, meaning devotion to God, is said to be the best. This is presented as a sign from God so that people may think about it.

Satan is warned not to lead people into trouble, as he once led Adam and Eve out of the Garden by stripping them of their clothes. The passage says that unbelievers follow Satan, and that when they defend wrongdoing by claiming God commanded it, the reply is that God does not command filthy deeds.

The passage tells believers to face God in worship and to pray sincerely to him, and says people will return to him. It says God guides some people and leaves others in error because they took the Satans as protectors beside God. It ends by telling people to wear good clothes at the mosque and to eat and drink without excess.

The passage first asks who has forbidden the good clothing and wholesome food that God gave his servants, and answers that these are meant for believers in this life and especially in the resurrection. It then lists what God really forbids: shameful deeds, wrongdoing, unjust violence, associating others with God, and speaking about God without knowledge. It ends by saying every nation has an appointed time that cannot be delayed or hastened.

God says that messengers will come to humankind from among their own people to recite his signs. Those who fear God and do good deeds will have nothing to fear or grieve over. Those who deny the signs and turn away from them in pride will remain in the fire forever.

Those who invent lies about God or reject God's signs will receive a share of worldly life as decreed. When their messengers come to take their souls and ask where the false gods they called upon are, the wrongdoers will answer that those gods have left them, and they will admit their own unbelief.

Those who are sent into the Fire, both jinn and humans from earlier generations, are shown blaming one another. Each new group curses the one before it, and the latest group asks that those who misled them receive a double punishment. God answers that all will have double, and the earlier group tells the later one that they have no advantage and must suffer for their deeds.

Those who reject God's signs (verses) and turn away from them with pride will not enter Heaven, and will instead have Hell as their bed. Those who believe and do what is right will enter Paradise and stay there forever.

In this passage, people in Paradise are freed from any hatred they held in their hearts, and rivers flow at their feet. They thank God for guiding them there, and a voice tells them that Paradise is their reward for what they did.

The dwellers of Paradise call out to the people in the fire, saying they have found God's promise true, and the people in the fire admit the same about their own warning. A herald then declares God's curse on wrongdoers who block others from God's way, try to bend it, and deny the life to come.

Between Paradise and Hell there is a barrier, and on it stand men called the people of Al Araf. They can recognise both groups by their marks. They greet the people of Paradise but cannot yet enter, and they pray not to be placed with the wrongdoers in the Fire. They tell the proud and wealthy that their riches and pride have done them no good.

People in Paradise are told to enter, and they are spared fear and grief. The dwellers of Hell beg for water or food, but are refused because God has forbidden these things to unbelievers. Those who treated their faith as a game, and were fooled by worldly life, will be forgotten by God, just as they ignored God's signs and the Day of Meeting.

People who ignored the warnings now have only to wait for the event they were warned about. When it arrives, they will admit the prophets told the truth and ask whether they can get an intercessor or be sent back to act differently. Their false gods will have abandoned them, and they will have ruined themselves.

God created the heavens and earth in six days, then took His throne. He made night and day, the sun, moon and stars, all following His laws. Believers should pray to Him humbly and with fear and hope, and not cause corruption on the earth, because God's mercy is near to the righteous.

God sends winds that carry clouds to dry land, where they bring rain and make plants grow. The writer says this is like how the dead will be brought back to life, and that good soil yields much while poor soil yields little, so that people may reflect and give thanks.

Noah tells his people to worship God alone and warns them of a coming day of punishment. The leaders reply that he is clearly in error. Noah answers that he is a messenger from the Lord, bringing God's warnings and advice, and asks why it is strange that a warning should come through one of their own people.

Those who called Noah a liar were saved with him in the ark, while the people who denied God's signs were drowned. Then God sent Hud to the people of Ad, telling them to worship God alone. Their leaders mocked him as mad and a fraud, but he replied that he was a messenger sent by the Lord of the worlds.

This passage is a speech from a prophet to his people, followed by their reply. He reminds them that God sent them a warning through one of their own, and asks them to remember God's favours. They answer by asking him to leave the worship of their fathers and to bring on the punishment he threatens.

Prophet Hud (in the Qur'an, the prophet sent to the people of 'Ad) warns his people that God's punishment is coming. He asks why they argue with him over names they have given to their idols, names God never authorised. He says he will wait with them. God then saves Hud and his followers, and destroys those who called God's signs lies.

Saleh tells the people of Thamud to worship God alone, since he has come to them with a clear sign from God, a she-camel that they must leave free to graze and must not harm. He reminds them that God made them heirs after the Adites and gave them homes and castles, so they should remember God's gifts and not spoil the land by acting wickedly.

The proud leaders of Saleh's people mock the weak believers who accept that Saleh was sent by God, and they reject his message. They kill the she-camel, which was a sign from God, and defy him. An earthquake then destroys them, and they are found dead in their homes.

Shuaib (Shu'ayb) has just warned his people, and here the passage shifts to Lot (Lut). Lot warns his people against sexual acts with men instead of women, and calls them excessive. They answer by ordering him and his followers out of the city. Lot and his family are saved, but his wife, who stayed behind, is not.

Shoaib, sent to the people of Madian, tells them to worship God alone and to be honest in trade, giving full measure and weight and not taking what belongs to others. He also warns them not to spread corruption on the earth, not to block travellers or lead believers away from God's way, and to remember how God once made them numerous and how the corrupt before them came to ruin.

Shoaib tells his people that if some of them believe his message and some do not, they should wait patiently for God to judge between them. The proud chiefs of his people threaten to drive him and his followers out of their cities unless they return to the old religion. Shoaib replies that they will not return, even though they hate that religion.

Speakers say that returning to their former religion would be a lie against God, and that they can only return if God wills it. They ask God to judge between them and their people. The unbelieving chiefs warn that following Shoaib will bring ruin, and then an earthquake kills the people in their homes.

Those who called the prophet Shoaib a liar were destroyed, as if they had never lived in their homes. Shoaib then turned away and said he had delivered his Lord's message faithfully, so he would not grieve for people who refused to believe. The passage adds that God sent hardship to every city a prophet came to, so that its people might become humble.

The passage says that God replaced hardship with prosperity, but the people grew rich and claimed that hardship and blessing had always come to their ancestors as a matter of course. God then punished them suddenly while they were unaware. Had they believed and feared God, blessings from heaven and earth would have been given to them. Because they rejected the signs, they were punished.

God asks whether people who feel safe from His plan are right to do so, since only those who are ruined feel that way. He warns that He could punish later inhabitants of the land for their sins and seal their hearts so they refuse to listen. The past cities are given as examples: their messengers brought clear proof, yet the people rejected what they had already called lies, and God sealed their hearts in the same way.

Moses is sent to Pharaoh and his nobles with signs from God. He tells Pharaoh he speaks only the truth and asks him to free the children of Israel. When Pharaoh asks for proof, Moses turns his rod into a serpent and makes his hand shine white.

Moses' staff turns into a snake and swallows the magicians' illusions, which had frightened the crowd. The magicians are defeated, and they fall down in worship, declaring their belief in the Lord of Moses and Aaron.

Pharaoh accuses his court magicians of conspiring against him after they believed in Moses, and threatens them with having their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides and then crucifixion. The magicians answer that they will return to their Lord, that Pharaoh punishes them only for believing in the signs of God, and they pray for patience and for death as Muslims.

Pharaoh's chiefs fear that Moses and his people will stir up trouble and abandon Pharaoh's gods. Pharaoh answers that he will kill the newborn boys and keep the girls alive, so he stays in control. Moses tells his people to seek God's help and be patient, because the earth belongs to God, who gives it to whomever He chooses, and good ends await those who fear Him.

Moses tells his people that God may destroy their enemy, Pharaoh's people, and make them rulers of the land. God had sent hardships on Pharaoh's people as a warning, but when good things came they claimed them as their due. When hardship came, they blamed Moses and his followers. The passage says the true cause of their misfortune was from God, though most did not understand this.
God sent a series of plagues on these people: a flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood. The passage says these were clear signs, but the people acted proudly and continued in sin.

When plagues struck them, the people asked Moses to pray to God to lift them, promising to believe and let the Israelites go. After God removed the plague, they broke their promise, so God drowned them in the sea for rejecting his signs.

After Pharaoh's people were overthrown, the Israelites were given the lands of the east and west, and they were brought across the sea. When they came to a people who worshipped idols and asked Moses for a god like theirs, Moses replied that they were ignorant and that those people's worship and works would come to nothing.

God reminds the Israelites how he rescued them from Pharaoh's people, who had inflicted cruel suffering on them. Pharaoh's people killed the sons and spared only the daughters, and the passage calls this a great trial sent by the Lord.
God set a meeting with Moses lasting forty nights in total. Before going, Moses told his brother Aaron to take his place among the people, to act rightly, and not to follow those who do wrong.

Moses asks God to let him see Him. God says he cannot, but tells him to look at a mountain. When God shows Himself to the mountain, it crumbles to dust, and Moses faints. Waking, Moses praises God and repents, saying he is the first to believe.

God speaks to Moses, saying he has chosen him above all people and given him a message directly. Moses is told to accept the tablets of commandments firmly, to teach his people to keep their best rules, and God promises to show the wicked their final place.

God says he will turn away from his signs those who are proudly unjust, so that even when they see every sign they will not believe, and they choose the path of error over the path of right. Their deeds will come to nothing, and they will be repaid only for what they have done.

While Moses was away, his people made a golden calf from their jewelry and worshipped it as a god. The passage asks why they did not see that it could neither speak nor lead them. When they regretted this and saw their error, they prayed that God would show mercy and forgive them, or they would be lost.

Moses returns angry to find his people have turned to idol worship in his absence. He throws down the stone tablets and grabs his brother Aaron by the head. Aaron pleads that the people had treated him as weak and nearly killed him, and asks not to be counted among the wrongdoers. Moses then prays for forgiveness for himself and his brother.

Those who worshipped the golden calf will face their Lord's anger and shame in this life, because they told lies. But those who did wrong, then repented and believed, will be forgiven. When Moses' anger calmed, he picked up the tablets, which contained guidance and mercy for those who fear God.

Moses, after an earthquake strikes the seventy men he had chosen, prays to God. He asks whether God will destroy them and him for what foolish people among them did. He says the event is a trial from God, by which God leads some astray and guides others, and he asks God for forgiveness and mercy.

Moses asks God to decree good for his people in this world and the next. God answers that his punishment falls on whom he wills, while his mercy reaches all things, and he will write mercy for those who fear him, give alms, and believe in his signs.

Those who follow this unlettered Prophet, whom they already find described in the Law and the Gospel, will be shown what is right and wrong, allowed good food, relieved of their burdens and yokes, and will prosper. The passage then has the Prophet declare he is God's messenger to all people.

The passage calls people to believe in God, who rules heaven and earth and gives life and death. It urges them to believe in God's messenger, the unlettered Prophet, and follow him. It ends by saying that some of Moses' people also guide others rightly by truth and right action.

God divided the Israelites into twelve tribes. When they asked Moses for water, God had him strike a rock, and twelve springs came out, one for each tribe. God also sent clouds for shade, manna and quails for food. The passage ends by saying the people harmed only themselves, not God.

God told the people of an unnamed city to enter its gate bowing low and say "Hittat," meaning forgiveness, in exchange for their sins being pardoned. Some of them changed the word to something else, so God sent punishment on them for their wrong-doing.

The passage tells of a seaside town whose people broke the Sabbath rest. Fish came openly on their Sabbath, but not on other days, and God tested them this way because they did wrong. When some townspeople asked why others still warned those God planned to destroy, the warners replied that they gave the warning to clear themselves before their Lord and so that the people might fear Him.
When a group forgot the warnings they had been given, God saved those who had spoken against evil, and punished severely those who had done wrong. The punishment was because they were evildoers.

The passage says that some people who kept defying what was forbidden were turned into apes, and that God would send others to punish their descendants until the Day of Resurrection. It also says God has divided the people into good and bad groups and tested them with both good and bad things, so that they would turn back to God.

Later generations inherited the Scripture but took the fleeting goods of this world and still claimed they would be forgiven, though they had been bound by covenant to speak only the truth about God. The passage contrasts them with those who fear God, hold fast to the Book and pray, whose reward in the next world will not be lost.

God lifts a mountain over the people of Israel so that it looms above them like a shadow, and they fear it will fall on them. God then tells them to take hold of the scripture firmly and to remember what it contains, so that they may be mindful of God.

God took the descendants of Adam's children out of their backs, asked them whether he was their Lord, and they agreed. The passage says this was done so people could not later claim they had not known, or blame their ancestors for false gods. God makes his signs clear so that people may turn back to him.

The verse tells the listener to recount the story of a man who was given God's signs (revelations) but turned away from them. As a result, Satan led him astray, and he became one of those who were deceived.

The passage compares a person who rejects God's signs, meaning revelations, to a dog that pants with its tongue hanging out whether it is chased or left alone. Such people, it says, harm only themselves. Only God guides, so those he leads astray are lost.

Many people and spirits are said to be destined for Hell, because they have hearts, eyes and ears but do not use them to understand or perceive God's signs. The passage contrasts them with a people who guide others rightly and act justly.

The passage says that people should look at the heavens, the earth and all of creation and consider whether their end is near. It adds that those who reject the Koran have no other book to turn to, and that God alone knows when the Hour (the end of the world) will come. That moment will arrive suddenly.

The speaker says he has no power over what helps or harms him; that lies with God alone. If he knew God's hidden things, he would gain all the good he wanted and harm would not reach him. He says his only role is to warn and to bring good news to believers.

God created humans from one person and gave that person a wife. When the wife became pregnant and the child was healthy, the couple gave thanks to God, yet they then attributed partners to Him. The passage asks how anyone can join with God beings that create nothing and cannot even help themselves.

The speaker says that the beings people call on besides God cannot help them. They are servants like the people themselves, and they have no feet, hands, eyes or ears. The speaker says his protector is God, who sent down the Book.

Some people mock the Prophet, asking whether he has invented the verses of the Quran. He replies that he only follows what his Lord reveals to him, and that the revelation is a proof, guidance and mercy for believers. Listeners should be silent and attentive while it is read, and the speaker should remember God quietly and humbly. The angels around God never refuse to worship Him.
God made the heavens, the earth, and everything between them with a true purpose and for a set period of time. Those who do not believe, however, turn away from the warning they are given.

The passage argues that the gods people call on besides God have created nothing on earth or in the heavens, and have no written revelation or knowledge to show for themselves. It says anyone who prays to such beings is misguided, since they cannot answer. On the Day of Resurrection, these beings will turn against their worshippers and reject their worship.

Critics claim the Prophet made up the Qur'an. He replies that if he had, God would not help him, and that God is the witness between him and them. He says he is not teaching anything new and only follows what is revealed to him, and his task is to warn plainly.

The passage argues that the Qur'an must be from God if a witness from the Children of Israel confirms that it agrees with their Law, yet some people reject it anyway. It says that God does not guide those who do such wrong. The unbelievers say that if the Book were good, believers would not have come to it first. Since they refuse guidance, they call it an old lie.

Before the Koran, the Book of Moses was given as a rule and a mercy, and this Koran confirms it in Arabic. Its purpose is to warn wrongdoers and bring good news to those who do good. Those who say "Our Lord is God" and keep to the straight path will have no fear or grief, and will live forever in Paradise as their reward.

People are commanded to be kind to their parents, since a mother bears and nurses a child with great pain over thirty months. When a person reaches full strength at forty, he prays that God will help him be thankful, do good deeds, and bless his children, and he says he turns to God in submission.
God says that He will accept the best deeds of certain people and overlook their bad deeds, placing them among the people of Paradise. He calls this a true promise made to them.

A man rejects his parents' appeal to believe in resurrection, calling the promise of being raised from the grave an old fable. His parents urge him to trust God's promise, but he refuses. The passage says such people will perish like earlier nations, while everyone is rewarded or judged by their deeds, and no one is treated unjustly.

Those who reject belief will one day be brought before the fire. They will be told that they wasted their good things on earth, enjoyed their pleasures, and acted proudly and unjustly, so they will be punished with shame. The passage also recalls the brother of Ad, a prophet, who warned his people to worship only God and feared for them a great day of punishment.

The speaker says that only God knows when the punishment will come, and that he only delivers the message he was sent with. When a cloud approaches the people's valleys, they take it for rain. He corrects them: it is the punishment they asked for, a violent wind that destroys everything. By morning their homes are empty, and the narrator says this is how God punishes wrongdoers.

The passage says that God gave earlier peoples strength, senses and understanding, but these did not help them when they rejected God's signs, and the punishment they had mocked came upon them. Their gods, whom they had taken as partners of God, did not help them either and abandoned them.

A group of djinn, spirits in Islamic belief, listened to the Qur'an being recited. They then went back to their own people and urged them to follow the one they called the Summoner of God, that is, the Prophet Muhammad, and to believe in him, so that their sins would be forgiven.

The passage says that people who refuse to answer God's messenger cannot escape God's power, and have no protectors besides Him. It argues that the God who created heaven and earth can also raise the dead. On a coming day, unbelievers will be shown the fire and told to taste the punishment for their refusal to believe.

Be patient, as earlier messengers were, and do not ask for the punishment to come sooner. When the threatened day arrives, it will seem to the unbelievers as short as an hour. Only those who wrong others, the passage says, are destroyed.

God is praised as creator of the heavens, the earth, darkness and light. Yet unbelievers set up other beings as equals to Him. The passage says God created people from clay, set the term of their lives, and knows all they hide and show, but people still doubt and turn away from His signs.
People have now called the truth itself a lie, even though it has already come to them. But they will eventually learn the consequences of the things they have mocked.

The passage reminds listeners that earlier generations were given much comfort and power, yet God destroyed them for their sins and replaced them with others. It then says that even if a written book were sent down on parchment and touched by hand, the unbelievers would still call it plain sorcery.

The passage answers people who demand that an angel be sent down to the prophet as proof. It argues that if an angel came, judgment would follow at once with no delay, and that an angel sent to humans would have to appear as a man. It notes that earlier messengers were mocked, and the mockers were overtaken by what they scorned.

God is the owner of everything that exists, day and night, and He has made mercy a fixed law for Himself. He will certainly gather all people on the Day of Resurrection, and those who refuse to believe have harmed only themselves.

The speaker says he will not take any lord other than God, who created the heavens and earth and feeds all creatures without needing food himself. He says he is commanded to be the first to submit to God, and he fears punishment on the Day of Judgment. God alone can remove hardship or grant good, since His power is over all things.

God is named as the true witness between Muhammad and those who deny him. Muhammad says that the Quran was revealed to warn them and everyone it reaches, and he rejects any claim that other gods exist beside God, who is one. People who were given earlier scripture know him as they know their own children, but those who refuse to believe bring their own ruin.

God will judge those who invent lies about Him or reject His signs, and they will not succeed. On the Day of Judgment, the people who had set up other gods beside God will be asked where those gods are. They will deny having worshipped partners with God, and the gods they made up will abandon them.

Some listeners hear the message but cannot take it in, because God has placed veils over their hearts and a weight in their ears. Even when they see signs, they refuse to believe, and they dismiss the Quran as old fables. The passage says they bring their own ruin without realizing it.

The people described are shown at the fire of hell, wishing they could be sent back so they would believe. The passage says they would not really change: even if returned, they would go back to what was forbidden, and they deny any life after this one.
On the Day of Judgment, the people are brought before their Lord, who asks whether this reckoning is true. They admit it is, and God tells them to suffer the punishment because they did not believe.

Those who deny meeting God are lost, and they will regret their neglect when the Hour suddenly arrives, carrying their burdens on their backs. Worldly life is only play and amusement, while the future home is better for the God-fearing. The passage also says that the opponents' rejection is aimed at the Prophet, but really they reject God's signs.

Earlier messengers of God were also called liars, but they endured the accusations patiently until God helped them. No one can alter God's words, and the account of these messengers has already come to the listener.

God says the unbelievers' refusal is not something the Prophet must fix by any means. Even if he sought a sign from earth or sky, God could send one, but He alone decides who is guided. Only those who listen will be answered, and the dead will be raised and return to God.

Every animal and bird is a community like humans, and all will be gathered before their Lord. Those who reject the signs are described as deaf, dumb and in darkness. The passage then asks whether, when punishment or the Hour comes, people will call on anyone other than God.

People call on God in hardship, and He can free them from it, yet they forget the partners they set beside Him. Earlier messengers were sent to nations, who were tested with troubles so they would humble themselves. They did not humble themselves; their hearts hardened, and Satan made their behaviour seem right to them.

When people ignore their warnings, God gives them plenty, then suddenly seizes them so they fall into despair and are destroyed. The passage then asks who besides God could restore hearing and sight if God took them away, and notes that people still turn away from God's signs.
Messengers are sent only to bring good news and to warn. Those who believe and do good will have no fear or sorrow. Those who call God's signs false will be punished for their wrongdoing.

The Prophet says he does not claim divine treasures, secret knowledge, or angelic status; he only follows what is revealed to him. He asks whether the blind and the seeing are equal, and urges warning those who fear being brought before God, since they have no patron or intercessor besides Him.

The Prophet is told not to send away those who pray to God morning and evening, seeking his favour. He is not to judge their inner motives, and they are not to judge him. Sending them away would be wrong. God alone knows who is truly grateful.

God tells the prophet to greet believers with peace and says that God has made mercy a rule for himself, so those who sin out of ignorance and then repent are forgiven. The prophet is also told to refuse to worship the beings others call on besides God, and to refuse to follow their wishes.

The speaker says he acts on clear signs from his Lord, while his listeners reject them as lies. He says the punishment they ask to be brought quickly is not in his power, since judgment belongs to God alone, who will decide the matter.

God alone holds the hidden knowledge and knows everything, from the leaves that fall to the seeds in the dark earth. He also takes people's souls at night and returns them in the morning, and in the end all people return to Him to be told what they did.

God is above his servants and sends guardians who watch over people and take their souls at death, and these messengers never fail. The passage then says God rescues people from dangers on land and sea when they pray to him, yet afterwards they give him partners.

God alone has the power to send punishment on people from above or below, or to split them into factions and make them fight one another. The speaker says his people have called the revelation false, though it is true, and that he is not their guardian. Every message has its own appointed time, and they will learn the truth in due course.

Believers are told to leave a gathering when people mock or argue against God's signs (revelations), and to stay away until the talk turns to something else. If they forget and sit with such people, they should leave as soon as they remember. Their duty is not to judge these people, but to keep themselves mindful of God.

People who treat their religion as a game and are taken in by worldly life are to be warned. Every soul will be held to account for its own deeds, with no protector or intercessor beside God, and no ransom accepted. Those who are condemned for their deeds will receive boiling water and severe punishment, because they did not believe.

Calling on anything besides God is pointless, since such things can neither help nor harm. Turning back after being guided is compared to a lost traveller who is misled by Satans and ignores his companions calling him to the right path. True guidance comes from God, and people are told to submit to the Lord of the Worlds, pray, and fear God, since all will return to Him, the Creator who speaks and things come into being.

God alone holds the kingdom and knows all things, seen and unseen. Abraham tells his father that carving idols and calling them gods is error. When he sees a star, he calls it his Lord, but drops that claim when the star sets, saying he does not love gods that set.

Abraham looks at the moon, then the sun, and calls each one his Lord. Each time, the object sets, and he rejects it. He concludes that he will follow the Creator of the heavens and the earth and will not associate other gods with God.

Abraham argues with his people, who oppose his belief in one God. He says he does not fear their false deities, since only God has power, and asks which side deserves safety. Those who believe without mixing their faith with wrongdoing, he says, are safe and rightly guided.

The passage says God gave Abraham a argument against his people and raised to high wisdom whomever he chooses. It then lists prophets God guided or favoured, including Noah, Isaac, Jacob, David, Solomon, Moses, Jesus and others, calling them righteous people.

God guides whom he chooses through this revelation. Those who associate others with God will have their deeds count for nothing. The earlier prophets were given scripture, wisdom and prophecy, and if their descendants reject these, God will give them to a people who will not reject them. The prophet is told to ask no payment, since this message is for all creatures.

Some people claim God has sent down nothing to humans. The passage replies that Moses' Book, a light and guidance, was sent by God. It accuses those who copy parts of it onto paper while hiding most of it, and tells the Prophet to leave them to their arguments.

The passage says that this Book, the Qur'an, is blessed and confirms earlier scripture. It is sent so that the speaker can warn the mother-city (Mecca) and the towns around it. Those who believe in the afterlife will accept it and keep their prayers carefully.

The passage condemns people who invent lies about God, such as claiming a revelation they never received or boasting they can produce a book like God's. It describes the punishment awaiting such people at death: angels tell them they will be humiliated for their false claims and for rejecting God's signs.

Sura 6 says that people will return to God alone, as they were created, leaving behind their possessions and the false partners they had worshipped alongside him. It then points to God's power over life: he brings grain and date seeds to sprout, and brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living. It asks why people turn away from him.

God makes the dawn appear, sets the night for rest, and sets the sun and moon to measure time. He also gives the stars so people can find their way on land and sea, and created humans from one man, giving them a home and a resting place.

God sends rain from heaven, and by it brings forth plants of many kinds, including grain, date palms, grapes, olives and pomegranates, some alike and some different. The passage says that people who believe can see signs in their fruit as it ripens.

God is said to have no partners, no children, and no equal. The passage says that the jinn, though God created them, are wrongly given a share in worship, and that God alone is the creator to be worshipped. It also says God sees everything, while no human sight can take Him in.

The passage says that clear proofs have come from God, and each person chooses whether to see them and benefit or to stay blind and lose. The speaker is not a guardian over the people. He is told to follow what has been revealed to him, turn away from those who associate other gods with God, and accept that God could have prevented their polytheism if He had wished.

Believers are told not to insult the gods others worship, since that could lead people to insult God in return. Signs and miracles are up to God alone, and people who demand one will not believe even when it comes. God will judge everyone's deeds at the end.

God says he will turn the hearts and eyes of those who first refused to believe away from the truth, leaving them lost in their wrongdoing. Even if angels came to them, the dead spoke, or all things were gathered before them, they still would not believe unless God willed it.

God has given every prophet an enemy: evil beings, both human and jinn, who whisper false, showy words to mislead others. God could have prevented this, but the prophet is told to leave them to their empty talk. Those who do not believe in the afterlife are left to be drawn to it and to take their pleasure in it.

God alone is the true judge, since he sent down the Book that makes things clear. The Book's words are perfect and cannot be changed. Following most people in the land would lead away from God's path, because they follow mere guesswork and lies. God knows best who strays and who is guided.

Eat freely of meat over which God's name has been spoken, since God has already made clear what is forbidden, except under compulsion. Many people mislead others through their desires and lack of knowledge. Give up open and hidden sin, and those whose only gain is wrongdoing will be repaid for it.

Do not eat meat over which God's name has not been spoken, because that is a sin. Those who follow the Satans, or evil whisperers, and obey them in this are counted with those who give God partners. The passage then compares the believer, given a light to walk by, with the unbeliever, who stays in darkness.
In this verse, God says that in every city he has set up leaders among the wicked to plot there. Yet their schemes harm only themselves, and they do not realize it.

People who reject a sign from God say they will only believe if they receive the same kind of message given to God's earlier messengers. The passage answers that God alone knows where to place his mission. It warns that disgrace and severe punishment will fall on these wrongdoers for their deceitful schemes.

God opens the heart of those He guides to Islam, and makes the heart tight and constricted for those He leads astray. Those who believe are promised a peaceful dwelling with their Lord and His protection as a reward for their deeds.

God will gather jinn and humans together and tell the jinn they exploited people. Their human followers reply that both sides served each other and have now reached the term God set. God answers that their home is the fire, to stay there forever unless God wills otherwise, and that He places some wrongdoers over others as repayment for their deeds.

God addresses humans and spirits (djinn), saying messengers came to them, warned them of the coming day of judgment, and they will admit their guilt. Worldly life deceived them, so they will confess they rejected faith. God does not destroy cities without first sending warning, and everyone receives reward or punishment according to their deeds.

God is self-sufficient and merciful, and could destroy the listeners and replace them with others, just as He raised them up from other peoples. What He has promised will certainly happen, and they cannot stop it. The speaker tells his people to act as they can, while he does his part, and says the wrongdoers will not succeed.

The passage criticizes people who set aside part of their crops and livestock for God and part for the "companions" they associate with him, meaning the idols or partner gods they worship alongside him. They claim that the share for God goes to these partners. The passage says their judgment is wrong, because the share given to the partners never reaches God, while the share meant for God goes to the partners.

The passage says that false "companion-gods," meaning the idols that some people set beside God, have led many believers to kill their own children. This ruins them and confuses their religion. It adds that God could have stopped this if he had wished, so the speaker tells the listener to leave these people and their schemes alone.

Some people declare certain cattle and crops sacred, so that only people they choose may eat them, and they forbid some animals to be worked or to be named over in God's name at slaughter. They also make rules about unborn young, allowing males to eat them but not females. The passage says these rules are invented lies about God, and that God will repay them for these distinctions.

People who, in their ignorance, killed their children and banned foods that God had given them are described as lost. They have invented a falsehood about God and have gone astray without being guided.

God made gardens of vines, palms, grain, olives and pomegranates, and cattle for carrying loads and travel. People may eat the fruit and must give its due share at harvest, without wasting it. They should eat what God gave them and not follow Satan, whom the text calls an open enemy.

God asks the speaker to say whether He has forbidden the two males or the two females of the sheep and goats, or what their wombs carry. The point is a challenge: the listeners must give real knowledge if they claim God forbade these animals.

The passage challenges claims that God has forbidden certain animals or their young. It asks whether the speaker witnessed God giving such a command, and calls someone who invents a lie about God against Him wicked. It ends by saying God does not guide the wicked.

The passage lists the only foods it says are forbidden: meat from an animal that died on its own, blood poured out, and pork, which is called unclean, and any animal slain in the name of someone other than God. Anyone who is forced to eat these, without wanting to and without going beyond need, is forgiven.

God forbade the Jews certain foods: animals with undivided hooves and the fat of cattle and sheep, except fat on the back, in the entrails, or on the bones. He says this was a punishment for their wrongdoing, and that he is just. If they call the Prophet a liar, he should say that God is merciful, but his punishment will fall on the wicked.

Those who worship other gods alongside God claim that God would have stopped them if He had wanted, so their practices must be what He wills. The passage rejects this: they have no real knowledge, only guesses and lies. It says God's proof is decisive, and that He could have guided everyone.

Believers are told to say to those who claim God forbade certain animals: bring your witnesses to prove it. Even if they produce witnesses, the speaker must not join them, nor support those who deny God's signs, deny the afterlife, or give God equals.

God tells the believer to set up no partner beside Him, to be good to parents, and not to kill children out of poverty, since God provides for both them and you. It also forbids gross sins, public and private, and killing anyone God has forbidden, except for a just cause.

God tells believers to protect an orphan's property until he comes of age, to use honest weights and measures, and to judge fairly even when a relative is involved. They are to keep God's covenant and follow His straight path, not other paths, so that they stay faithful to Him.

The passage says God gave the Book to Moses as a complete guide, a decision on all matters, and a mercy, so people would believe in meeting their Lord. It then says this Qur'an is also blessed and sent down, so people should follow it and fear God, so they cannot claim earlier scriptures were only for two earlier peoples.

People who turn away from God's signs (revelations) are told that a clear book has now come to them as guidance and mercy, so they cannot claim they would have followed it better if it had been sent to them. Those who reject these signs will be punished for turning away.

Those who refuse to believe are shown to be waiting for something: the angels, the Lord Himself, or certain signs to appear. Once those signs come, faith will no longer help a soul that did not believe earlier or do good works through faith. Those who split their religion into sects are left to God, who will judge them later.

Whoever brings good deeds receives ten times the reward, and whoever brings evil deeds is repaid only with an equal punishment. The speaker then says his own path is the true religion of Abraham, a faith in one God with no partners, and that his life and death belong to God alone.

God is Lord of all things, so no other lord should be sought. Each person is responsible only for their own deeds and not for another's, and all will return to God, who will settle their disagreements. God has placed people in different ranks to test them with His gifts, and He is both swift to punish and merciful.

The passage opens with a set of letters, which are a code-like marking found at the start of some Qur'anic chapters. It then says that the revelation sent to the Prophet from God is the truth, though most people will not believe it.

God made the heavens without visible pillars, set the sun and moon on fixed courses, and spread out the earth with mountains, rivers and fruits. These signs are meant for those who think carefully about them.

The passage points to varied plants growing side by side on the same land and watered by the same water, yet producing different fruit, as signs for thoughtful people. It then describes those who doubt that they will be raised again after turning to dust. They are said to disbelieve in their Lord and to face punishment in the fire.

God is merciful to people despite their sins, but also severe in punishment. Unbelievers demand a sign, and the reply is that the messenger is only a warner, since every people has its guide. God alone knows everything, including what each pregnancy carries and how the womb changes, and He measures all things.
God knows equally whether a person keeps his words secret or speaks them openly, and whether he hides at night or goes out in the day. Nothing is hidden from Him.

God does not take away his gifts from people until they change what is within themselves. Angels guard each person, and nothing can turn back what God wills. The passage then describes lightning, clouds and thunder, which praise God and are part of his power.
