The passage says that true prayer belongs to God alone. Prayers offered to other deities get no answer, like a man who stretches his hands toward water that can never reach his mouth. Everything in heaven and earth, even shadows, bows down to God, willingly or not.

The passage asks who rules the heavens and the earth, and answers that it is God. It then asks why people have taken other protectors that have no power to help or harm, and says God alone is the Creator of all things and is the One, the Conquering.

God compares truth and falsehood to rain and metal. Floodwater carries a foam that quickly vanishes, while what is useful stays on the earth. Those who answer their Lord receive a good reward, but those who refuse face Hell, even if they offered everything on earth to buy their way out.

Shall someone who knows that the revelation is true act like a blind man? Only people with understanding take this to heart. They keep their promises to God, join what God commands to be joined, fear their Lord, and act with patience and prayer, giving alms openly and in secret. They also answer evil with good, and they will receive a reward in the next life.

The passage contrasts two groups. The righteous enter gardens of Eden with their ancestors, spouses and descendants, and angels greet them with peace for their endurance. Those who break their covenant with God, sever what God commanded to be joined, and spread corruption on earth face a curse and a bad dwelling.

God gives or withholds provision as he chooses. Worldly life is only a brief good compared with the life to come. Those who believe, and whose hearts rest in remembrance of God, are guided to him, and they will receive blessedness and a good home.

The passage says that God has sent a messenger to a people who, like earlier nations, will not believe in the God of Mercy. The messenger is told to declare that God is his Lord and the only God, and that he trusts and returns to Him. Even a miracle such as moving mountains would not change them, since all power belongs to God, who could guide everyone if He chose.

Disasters will keep falling on the unbelievers for their deeds, until God's threatened punishment arrives. God keeps his promises. Earlier messengers were also mocked, and God delayed for a time before seizing the unbelievers, whose punishment was severe.

The passage argues that God watches over every soul and records its deeds, and that the idols or partners people set up beside God are empty names with no real power. It says those who follow them are led astray, will be punished in this life, and will be punished more severely afterward, with no one able to shield them from God.

The passage describes a Paradise promised to those who fear God, with flowing rivers, lasting food and shade, while unbelievers face the Fire. It then says some People of the Book rejoice in the revelation, though others reject part of it. The Prophet is told to worship God alone and call on Him.

God sent the Qur'an in Arabic and warns the Prophet that following the desires of others, after receiving this knowledge, would leave him without help from God. It says earlier messengers also had wives and children, that no messenger brought miracles except by God's permission, and that God may cancel or keep whatever He wills, since all revelation comes from Him.

The Prophet's job is only to deliver the message; God is the one who judges and holds people to account. God controls the outcome of all plots against the believers, knows what each person does, and the unbelievers will learn who receives the final reward.
Unbelievers say the messenger has not been sent by God. The reply is that God is enough as a witness between him and them, and so is anyone who has knowledge of the Book (the scripture).

The passage contrasts three groups. Believers, who accept the revelations sent to Muhammad and earlier prophets and trust in the afterlife, are said to be guided by God and to have a good future. Those who refuse belief are described as unable to respond to warning, and some who claim belief while not truly believing are said to deceive only themselves.

Those who reject the prophet are described as having diseased hearts, and God is said to increase that disease. When told not to cause disorder on earth, they insist they are setting things right, yet the passage says they are the real source of disorder without knowing it. When told to believe as others have, they call believers fools, but the passage says they themselves are the fools without realizing it.

The passage describes people who claim to believe when they are with believers, but mock the faith when they are with their own leaders. It says they have traded guidance for error, and God leaves them lost in darkness, unable to see, hear or find their way back.
The passage compares people to those caught in a storm who cover their ears against the thunder, afraid of dying. It adds that God surrounds the unbelievers, meaning they cannot escape him.

The passage uses the image of lightning to describe people who see the truth only briefly and then stop when darkness returns, and it says God could take away their hearing and sight. It then calls people to worship their Lord, the Creator who made the earth, sky, water and fruits, and not to set up equals with God.

If you doubt the revelation sent to the Prophet, then produce a chapter like it, calling on your witnesses apart from God. If you cannot, and never will, then beware the fire prepared for unbelievers, whose fuel is people and stones.

Those who believe and do good are promised gardens with flowing rivers. Whenever they are given fruit there, they will say it is what they had before, and they will receive something similar. They will have pure wives there and will live in those gardens forever.

God uses even small things like a gnat as examples, and believers accept them as true. Unbelievers ask what the comparison means. God leads many astray by these examples, but only those who break their covenant with God, cut what He ordered joined, and cause corruption on earth. Those people will suffer loss.

The passage asks why people would deny God, since God gave them life after they were dead, will cause them to die, will raise them again, and they will return to Him. It adds that God created everything on earth, moved on to the heavens, shaped seven heavens, and knows all things.

God announces to the angels that he will place a successor on earth. The angels question this, fearing it will bring evil and bloodshed. God then teaches Adam the names of all things and shows them to the angels, who admit they have only the knowledge God gives them.

God tells Adam to name the creatures, then shows that He knows all hidden things. The angels are ordered to bow down to Adam, and all do except Eblis (Iblis), who refuses out of pride. God then tells Adam and his wife to live in the Garden and eat freely, but not to approach one particular tree.

Satan caused Adam and his wife to slip from the garden, and they were sent down to earth. God told them they would live on earth for a time, and Adam learned words of prayer from his Lord, and God turned to him with mercy. God then promised that those who follow His guidance will have no fear and no grief.

God addresses the Children of Israel, urging them to remember his favours and keep their covenant with him, and to believe in the revelation that confirms their own Scriptures. They are told not to hide or distort the truth, to pray and give alms, and not to urge others to do right while neglecting it themselves.

God addresses the Children of Israel, reminding them of the favours he gave them and of his rescue from Pharaoh's people, who had enslaved them and killed their sons. He warns them to fear a day when no soul can pay for another, no intercession will be accepted, and no ransom taken. He also recalls how the sea was parted, they were saved, and Pharaoh's people drowned.

Moses tells his people that they sinned by worshipping a calf, and that they must turn back to their creator and kill the guilty among them. God then accepts their repentance. Later, when they demand to see God plainly, a thunderbolt strikes them, but God brings them back to life afterward.

God gave the Israelites manna and quails in the wilderness and told them to enter a city, bow down at its gate, and ask for forgiveness. The wrongdoers changed the words they had been told to say, so God sent punishment on them. The passage says they harmed only themselves.

Moses asked God for water for his people, and God told him to strike a rock with his staff. Twelve springs then flowed out, and each tribe had its own place to drink. God told them to eat and drink what he had provided and not to cause harm on earth through wrongdoing.

The Israelites complained to Moses that they were tired of having only one kind of food, and asked for earthly foods like herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions. Moses asked why they would trade what is better for what is worse. They were told to go down into Egypt, and were then struck with humiliation and poverty and returned under God's anger, because they rejected God's signs, killed prophets unjustly, and rebelled.

Anyone who believes in God and the Last Day and does what is right will receive their reward from their Lord and need not fear or grieve, whether they are Muslims, Jews, Christians or Sabeans. The passage then recalls the covenant God made with the Israelites, when the mountain was lifted over them, and tells them to hold firmly to the revelation given to them.

God spared the listeners after they turned away, showing grace and mercy, or they would have been lost. The passage then recalls people who broke the Sabbath and were changed into apes, a warning to their own time, later generations, and those who fear God.

Moses tells his people that God orders them to sacrifice a cow. They doubt him and ask for details. First they ask its age, and he says it should be neither old nor young. Then they ask its colour, and he says it should be bright fawn-coloured.

The Israelites ask Moses to have God specify which cow to sacrifice, and God describes an unblemished, unused cow. After they sacrifice it, they are told to strike a murdered man's body with part of it, and the dead man comes back to life and names his killer. The story shows God bringing hidden truth to light and giving life to the dead.

The passage says that some hearts have become harder than rocks, though rocks can still give forth water or split open out of fear of God. It then asks whether the believers really hope the Jews will believe, and notes that some Jews heard God's word, understood it, and deliberately distorted it.

This passage describes a group who claim to believe when they meet the faithful, but who, when alone together, question whether the faithful should share God's revelation with them, since it could be used against them before their Lord. It says God knows what they hide and what they show.

Some of the people described here cannot read the Scripture and rely on lies and guesses. Others write out the Book falsely, claim their writing comes from God, and do it for cheap profit. They also say the fire of Hell will touch them only for a few days. The reply is that God does not break His promises, so they must be speaking about God without knowledge.
People whose only gains are evil deeds, and whose sins surround them, will live in the fire forever. Those who believe and do what is right will live in Paradise forever.

God made a covenant (solemn agreement) with the Children of Israel. They promised to worship only God, to care for parents, relatives, orphans and the poor, to speak what is right, to pray and to give alms. Most of them broke this promise, and the passage also recalls a later pact not to kill or drive out their own people, which they agreed to and witnessed.

The passage rebukes people who slew and expelled a part of their own community, and fought against them with injustice, yet ransomed captives when they were taken. It asks whether they believe in some parts of their scripture and reject others, and says such people will face shame in this life and severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

Those who trade the afterlife for the pleasures of this present life will have their punishment neither reduced nor eased, and no one will come to their aid. The passage describes this as the result of choosing the present world over the world to come.

God sent Moses the Book and later prophets, and gave Jesus clear signs and the Holy Spirit's support. The passage then asks why, whenever a messenger came with teachings the people did not want, they grew proud, called some liars and killed others. It says their hearts are "uncircumcised," meaning closed, and that God has cursed their unbelief, so few believe.

Some people who had earlier received scripture, and who had asked God for victory over unbelievers, refused to recognise the new Book (the Qur'an) when it came to them, even though it confirmed what they already had. The verse ends by calling down God's curse on those who reject it.

The passage says that some people have traded away their own souls for a low price. They reject what God has sent down, out of jealousy that God gives his grace to whichever servants he chooses. As a result, they bring wrath upon themselves, and those who disbelieve face a shameful punishment.

The passage describes people who accept only the revelation given to them earlier and reject newer revelation, even though it confirms their own scriptures. It then points to their history: they killed earlier prophets and, while Moses was away, worshipped a golden calf.

The passage recalls how the Israelites, after God gave them a covenant and lifted the mountain over them, rebelled and were punished with the calf worship. It then tells them to wish for death if they really believe they alone will enter God's future dwelling, and says they never will, because of their own past deeds.

The passage says that the people it describes cling to life more than even the polytheists do, and that a long life will not save them from punishment. It then states that Gabriel brought the Qur'an by God's leave, and that anyone who opposes God, his angels, Gabriel or Michael is an enemy of God, who is an enemy to unbelievers.

Some people who had already been given scripture rejected God's Book when a messenger from God came to them. That messenger confirmed the earlier revelations they had received, yet they turned away from the Book as if they did not know it.

The passage says that people followed what evil spirits taught in Solomon's time, namely sorcery. Solomon himself did not disbelieve; the spirits did. Two angels, Harut and Marut, warned learners that they were a test, yet people still used their teaching to cause marital discord. The passage adds that such practice brings loss and no share in the next life.

The passage tells believers not to use the word "Raina" when speaking to the Prophet, but to say "Ondhorna" instead, since both mean roughly "look at us" or "regard us." It also says unbelievers do not want good to come down to believers, that God gives His mercy to whom He chooses, and that God can replace any verse He cancels with a better one.
Believers are warned not to question their prophet in the way Moses was questioned in the past. Whoever trades faith for disbelief has already strayed from the right path.

Many People of the Book (Jews and Christians) want to turn the believers back to disbelief, out of envy, even after the truth is plain to them. The believers are told to forgive them and wait for God's action, while keeping prayer and giving alms. The passage also says Jews and Christians alone will enter Paradise, and asks them to produce proof.
Those who submit themselves wholly to God and do what is right will receive their reward from their Lord. They will have no fear and no grief.

The passage says that Jews and Christians each deny the other has any valid ground, though both read the same Book, and that God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. It also condemns those who block God's name from being remembered in His places of worship, and states that God creates by simply saying "Be."

Those who lack knowledge demand that God speak to them or show them a sign. Earlier peoples made the same demand, and their hearts were alike. God says he has already shown clear signs to believers, and that Muhammad was sent with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, not answerable for those who reject it.

Jews and Christians will not be satisfied with the prophet until he follows their religion. God's guidance alone is the true guidance, and following their desires after receiving this knowledge leaves a person without any protection from God. Those given the Book who read it properly believe in it, and whoever rejects it faces ruin.

The passage warns that on the day of judgment no soul can repay for another, pay a ransom, or gain help through intercession. It then tells how God tested Abraham with commands he fulfilled and made him a leader (imam) for mankind. When Abraham asked that this honor extend to his descendants, God replied that the covenant does not include those who do wrong.

God tells the people that the Holy House (the Kaaba) is a place of refuge and gathering. He orders that the station of Abraham be used for prayer. He also commands Abraham and Ismael to keep the house clean for those who circle it, stay there in worship, and bow and prostrate themselves.

Abraham prays that the land of Mecca be made safe and that its people be fed, especially those who believe in God and the Last Day. God replies that unbelievers will enjoy good things briefly but then be sent to the Fire. Abraham and Ismael then build the House (the Kaaba), asking God to accept it and to make them and their descendants Muslims.

Abraham prays for a messenger to be sent to his descendants, to recite God's signs, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify them. The passage says that only a foolish person would reject Abraham's faith. When God told Abraham to submit, he did, and he passed this submission on to his children and to Jacob, urging them to remain Muslims until death.

Jacob's sons promise to worship the one God of their fathers Abraham, Ismael and Isaac, and say they submit to Him. The passage then tells the listeners that the earlier generation will be judged only by its own deeds. When people urge them to become Jews or Christians to be rightly guided, the reply is that the true path is the faith of Abraham, who worshipped no other gods alongside God.

The passage tells believers to affirm faith in God and in the revelations given to Abraham, Ismael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Moses, Jesus and the other prophets, making no difference between them. If others believe in the same way, they are rightly guided; if they turn away, God will protect the believers against them.
The speaker asks whether his opponents want to argue with him about God, since God is his Lord and theirs too. He says each side has its own deeds, and that he is devoted to God alone.

The passage asks whether Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes were Jews or Christians, and answers that God knows best. It says the people of the past have their own reward for their deeds, and the listeners have theirs. It ends by saying that the East and the West belong to God, who guides whom he chooses, in reply to critics who ask why the prayer direction (kebla) was changed.
God has made the believers a "middle" or balanced community, so that they will be witnesses over other people, and the Prophet will be a witness over them.

The passage says that the earlier direction of prayer, the kibla, was set so that God could tell true followers of the messenger from those who turn back. The change of direction is hard for some, but not for those God has guided. God will not let the faith of believers be wasted, because He is merciful.

God tells the prophet that he will have him face a new direction for prayer, the sacred Mosque in Mecca, and all believers are to turn to it wherever they are. People who have received earlier scripture ("the Book") know this is true, and God watches what everyone does.

Even if the People of the Book saw every sign, they would not accept Muhammad's direction of prayer (the qibla), and they would not accept each other's either. Muhammad is told not to follow their wishes, since they know the truth about him as they know their own children, though some hide it. The truth comes from God, so he must not doubt it.

Each community faces its own direction in prayer, but believers should compete to do good wherever they are, since God will gather everyone together. Wherever a person travels from, they should turn their face toward the sacred Mosque in Mecca, because this direction comes from God, who sees all that people do.

Believers should turn their faces toward the sacred Mosque (the Kaaba in Mecca) in prayer, wherever they are, so that others have no reason to argue. God tells them not to fear the wrongdoers among them but to fear God, and says he sent a messenger to teach them, purify them, and guide them. They are asked to remember God and give thanks.

God will test believers with fear, hunger, and losses of goods, lives and crops. Those who are patient, and say "We belong to God and to Him we return" when trouble comes, receive blessings and mercy from their Lord. The passage also says that Safa and Marwah, two hills, are sacred sites, so walking between them during pilgrimage is not a sin.

People who hide the clear proofs and guidance that God has sent down, after making them plain in the Book, are cursed by God and by all who curse. Those who repent, mend their ways and make the truth known are forgiven. Those who reject faith and die in unbelief remain under God's curse, angels' and people's curse forever.

The passage lists natural things: the creation of heaven and earth, day and night, ships on the sea, rain that brings life to dead earth, the spread of animals, the winds, and clouds moving between sky and earth. It says these are signs for people who understand.

Some people set up idols beside God and love them as they should love God. But believers love God more strongly. The wrongdoers will see, when punishment comes, that all power belongs to God. Then leaders and followers will disown each other and the bonds between them will break.

The passage describes followers who wish they could return to life so they could cut ties with their leaders, who in turn have cut ties with them. God shows them the results of their deeds, and they cannot escape the fire. It then tells people to eat what is lawful and good, and not to follow Satan, who urges evil and urges them to speak about God what they do not know.

When people are told to follow what God has sent down, they refuse and say they will keep the customs of their fathers. The passage says those fathers had no knowledge or guidance, so following them leads nowhere. It then tells believers to eat the good things God has provided and to thank Him.

Carrion, blood, pork, and meat over which a name other than God's has been invoked are forbidden to believers. However, a person who eats them under compulsion, without desire or deliberate defiance, commits no sin, because God is forgiving and merciful.

Those who conceal the revealed Scripture and trade it for a small worldly price will receive only fire. God will not speak to them or purify them on Judgment Day, because they have exchanged guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment. The passage adds that those who argue over the Book, which God sent down with the truth, are far removed from it.

Piety does not lie in the direction you face in prayer, east or west. It lies in believing in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Scriptures and the prophets, and in giving money to relatives, orphans, the poor, travellers and captives, and in praying, giving the required alms, keeping promises, and staying patient in hardship.

Retaliation for killing is set as a rule for believers: free for free, slave for slave, woman for woman. If the victim's family forgives the killer and accepts a fine, the case is to be handled fairly and the fine paid generously. Those who kill again after this face severe punishment. The rule is presented as a safeguard for life, so that people may fear God.

When a dying man leaves property, he is told to leave a fair share to his parents and close relatives. Anyone who changes the bequest after hearing it bears the blame, while someone who fixes an unfair will to settle a dispute between the heirs does no wrong.

Fasting is set for a fixed number of days. A person who is sick or travelling makes up the same number of days later. Those who can fast but break the fast must feed a poor man as atonement. Doing good freely brings its own reward, and fasting is said to be good for believers who understand it.

The verse says the month of Ramadan is when the Quran was sent down as guidance. When a person sees the new moon, they should begin fasting. Someone who is sick or travelling may fast the same number of days later, because God wants ease for people, not hardship.

God says that when his servants ask about him, he is close to them and answers the prayer of anyone who calls on him. He asks them to listen to him and believe in him so that they may be guided rightly.

During the fast, the passage permits believers to be intimate with their wives at night, and to eat and drink until dawn, when the fast begins again until nightfall. Believers should stay away from their wives while in the mosques, and God is said to forgive them for having broken this rule before.
Do not waste your wealth on worthless things, and do not bribe judges to take part of another person's property unfairly. The passage stresses that the wrongdoer knows the act is sinful.

The passage says the new moons are fixed times for worship and for the pilgrimage. It then states that piety is not about entering houses from the back, but about fearing God, and that people should use the proper doors. Finally, it allows fighting against those who fight you, but forbids starting the attack.

Believers are told to fight those who have attacked them and driven them out, and to continue until worship is only of God. Fighting at the sacred Mosque is allowed only if the enemy attacks there first. If the enemies stop, fighting must stop, except against wrongdoers.

The passage says that the sacred month and the sacred places are protected by the rule of equal retaliation: if someone attacks you, you may answer with the same kind of violence. It also urges believers to give generously for God's cause, not to bring ruin on themselves, and to do good.

The passage gives rules for the pilgrimage to Mecca. If enemies block a pilgrim, he must send an offering and not shave his head until it reaches the sacrifice site. A sick pilgrim, or one with a head ailment, may instead fast, give alms, or make an offering. Those who cannot afford an offering must fast ten days.

The passage gives rules for the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, held in set months. Pilgrims should avoid sexual relations, quarrelling and wrongdoing while on it. They should bring provisions but are told the best provision is fear of God. Trade during the pilgrimage is allowed, and after leaving Arafat they are to remember God at the holy monument.

After completing the holy rites, believers are told to remember God as they remember their fathers, or with even more devotion. Some people ask God only for worldly goods and will have no share in the next life. Others ask for good in both this world and the next, and protection from the fire, and they will receive what they have earned.

The passage first gives a rule about the days of pilgrimage: a person may leave after two days or stay longer, with no blame either way, provided they fear God. It then warns about a man whose fine words hide hostility, who secretly works to cause disorder, harm crops and livestock. God does not love such disorder.

The passage contrasts two groups. Those who reject God and mock believers are shown to be in a worldly state, with a sealed fate, while those who fear God will be raised above them on the day of resurrection. It also warns that anyone who changes God's gift after receiving it will be severely punished.

Humankind once formed a single community. God then sent prophets to bring good news and warnings, along with a Book of Truth to settle people's disagreements. The disputes arose only among those who had received the Book, out of envy toward one another, and God guided believers to the truth on which they had differed.

The passage tells believers that entering Paradise does not come without hardship, since earlier believers were tested by troubles until they cried out for God's help, and that help is near. It then says that good deeds should go first to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor and travelers, and that God knows all good done. Last, it says fighting has been ordered, though some are unwilling.
People may dislike something that is good for them, and love something that is bad for them. God knows what is truly good or bad, but people do not.

Fighting during the Sacred Month is called bad, but the passage says that blocking people from God's path, rejecting God, and driving believers out of the Sacred Temple are worse, and that civil strife is worse than killing. It also warns that anyone among the believers who turns away from the faith and dies rejecting it will lose the value of his deeds and face the fire.

People ask the prophet about wine, games of chance, charity and orphans. The answer is that wine and gambling bring both harm and benefit, but the harm is greater. Give what you can spare to charity, and deal fairly with orphans, since they are your brothers in faith. God knows who deals fairly and who does not.

Believers should not marry idolaters until those idolaters believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even if the idolater seems more attractive. The passage adds that idolaters invite people to the Fire, while God invites them to Paradise and forgiveness.

The passage says that menstruation makes women a source of pollution, so husbands should keep away from their wives until the wives are clean again. After that, intercourse is allowed as God has ordained. It also tells believers to act for their souls' good, to fear God, and to remember they will meet Him.

The passage deals with oaths and marriage. It says God will not punish a mistake made in an oath, but will judge what the heart intends. It also sets a waiting period of four months for a husband who swears to stay away from his wife, after which he either returns to her or divorces her.

Divorced women must wait three menstrual cycles before remarrying, and they must not hide whether they are pregnant. Husbands may take them back during this time if they want to reconcile. Women have the same rights as men in fairness, but men have a higher position.

A husband may divorce his wife twice, and then he must either keep her with honour or let her go kindly. He may not take back any of the gifts he gave her, unless both fear they cannot keep God's limits. If they fear this, the wife may give something to buy her freedom without blame. These limits must not be crossed.

A man who has divorced his wife three times may not take her back until she has married another husband and that marriage has ended. If the second husband also divorces her, the couple may then remarry, provided they believe they can keep within the limits God has set.

When a divorce is due, a man must either keep his wife kindly or let her go kindly, and must not hold her by force to wrong her. Doing so harms only himself. He is also told not to treat God's revelations as a joke, and to remember God's favour and fear Him, since God knows all things.

When a divorced woman has finished her waiting period, her former husband must not stop her from remarrying the man she has agreed to marry, if they agree honourably. The passage says this is the better and purer course for those who believe in God and the Last Day.

After divorce, mothers nurse their children for two full years if the father wants the nursing completed, and the father must provide fair food and clothing for them. Neither parent may be pressed unfairly over the child. Weaning early or hiring a nurse is allowed if agreed and paid fairly.

When a man dies, his widow must wait four months and ten days before she may remarry, and after that she may decide for herself. Men may propose marriage to such women, or keep the intention private, without blame. They should not make secret promises, unless they speak in honourable terms.
Do not commit to a marriage until the set waiting period is over. God knows what is in people's hearts, so they should be mindful of Him. God is also forgiving and gentle.

A man divorcing a wife before the marriage is consummated and before any dowry is set does not commit a wrong. Even so, he must give her a provision, with the wealthier man giving according to his means and the poorer man according to his. This duty is owed by those who act rightly.

If a husband divorces his wife before the marriage is consummated but after a dowry has been agreed, he must give her half the dowry, unless she or the man who holds the marriage tie waives it. Waiving it is said to be closer to piety. The passage also urges generosity, regular prayer, and prayer even under threat, on foot or mounted.

Men who die leave a will providing their widows a year's support without forcing them out of their homes. If the widows leave on their own, no blame falls on the heirs for what they then do with themselves in a fair way. Divorced women are also to receive a fair provision.

God tells of a group who fled their homes in fear of death, and God caused them to die and then brought them back to life. The passage then urges fighting for God's cause and asks who will make a generous loan to God, promising to repay it many times over.

The Israelites, after Moses died, asked a prophet to appoint a king so they could fight for God's cause. When the prophet asked if they would really fight if ordered to, they said they would, since they had been driven from their homes. But when fighting was commanded, most of them turned back, and God knew who had done wrong.

God has appointed Saul (called Talout here) as king over the Israelites. When they object that he is not wealthy and that they have a better claim to the throne, the prophet replies that God chose Saul, gave him greater knowledge and size, and gives kingdom as God wills.

The people are told by their prophet that a sign of Saul's kingship will be the return of the Ark, a chest that holds a pledge of security from God and relics of the families of Moses and Aaron. Angels will carry it to them, and this will be a clear sign for those who believe.

Saul tells his army that God will test them at a river: whoever drinks from it is not his true follower, while whoever only takes a handful is. Nearly all drink, and only a small group keeps faith. Those who believe that they will meet God answer that a small army can defeat a large one by God's will.
When the group went out to fight Goliath and his army, they prayed to God for patience, firm footing, and help against the unbelievers.

God allowed one side to defeat the other, and David killed Goliath, then was given kingship and wisdom. The passage says that God's restraint of some people by others keeps the earth from being corrupted, and that these events are signs from God that Muhammad recounts truthfully.

Some prophets were given higher rank than others. Jesus, son of Mary, received clear signs and was strengthened by the Holy Spirit. The later communities still argued and split into believers and unbelievers, and the passage says that God could have prevented this, since God does what He wills.

Believers are urged to give charity from what God has provided them, before a Day comes when no buying and selling, friendship, or intercession will help. The passage calls those who reject faith wrongdoers.

God alone is divine, living and eternal, and never sleeps or tires. Everything in heaven and earth belongs to Him, and no one can intercede with Him except by His permission. He knows all things, and people understand only what He allows. His power over heaven and earth requires no effort.

There is to be no forcing anyone to accept the faith, because the right way is now clearly separated from error. Those who reject Taghut (an idol or false power) and believe in God hold a firm grip that cannot break. God protects believers and brings them into light, while those who do not believe are led by Taghut into darkness and fire.

A king argues with Abraham about God. Abraham says his Lord gives life and causes death. The king claims he can do the same. Abraham then says God brings the sun from the East, so the king should bring it from the West. The king is left speechless, and the passage says God does not guide wrongdoers.

A man passes a ruined city and doubts that God can bring it back to life. God causes him to die for a hundred years, then raises him. When asked how long he waited, he says a day or part of a day. God shows him his unspoiled food and drink and his ass's bones being rebuilt with flesh, and he admits God has power over all things.

Abraham asks God to show him how the dead are brought back to life, so that his heart may be fully at peace. God tells him to take four birds, cut them up, scatter the pieces on hills, and call them back. The passage then compares those who spend their wealth for God to a grain of corn that grows seven ears, each with a hundred grains, and God multiplies the reward as he wills.

People who spend their money for God's cause and do not follow the giving with reproaches or harm will be rewarded by their Lord, with no fear or grief. A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. God is self-sufficient and forgiving.

Believers are told that reproaches and injury make their charity worthless, just as giving to be seen by others does. Such giving is compared to rain falling on bare rock with thin soil: it washes away and leaves nothing that can be gained from it.

People who spend their wealth seeking God's approval and to strengthen their own souls are compared to a garden on a hill. Heavy rain makes it bear double fruit, and even light dew keeps it fruitful. God sees all their deeds.

The passage uses the picture of a garden of palms and vines, watered by rivers, that is destroyed by a fiery wind just when its owner is old and his children are weak, to show how a loss can come when it is least expected. It then urges believers to give charity from the good things they have earned and from what the earth produces, not from poor or bad goods they would not accept themselves.

Satan tries to frighten people with the fear of poverty and pushes them toward shameful deeds. God instead offers forgiveness and plenty, and He gives wisdom to whom He chooses. Only people with a thoughtful heart truly keep this in mind.

God knows every charity and vow people make, and those who do wrong will have no helpers. Giving alms openly is good, and giving them secretly to the poor is also said to be of advantage, wiping away sins.

Guidance belongs to God alone, not to the prophet, who cannot make people follow the right path. Charity benefits the giver and is done for God's sake, and it will be repaid. The passage then describes the poor who are confined to fighting for God and cannot travel to seek wealth. They look rich because they are modest and do not beg, so they are known by that trait.
Those who give money to charity, whether at night or during the day, secretly or openly, will receive their reward from their Lord. They will have nothing to fear and will not be sad.

Those who take usury (lending money at interest) will rise on Judgment Day like someone driven mad by Satan. They claim trade is no different from usury, but God allows trade and forbids usury. Whoever stops after this warning is forgiven for the past, but those who return to usury go to the fire forever.

God says he will remove the gains from usury, while rewarding charity. Believers are told to stop taking the interest still owed to them. Those who refuse face war from God and his messenger, but those who repent may keep their original capital, without loss to anyone.

If a debtor cannot pay, the creditor should wait until he is able to. Forgiving the debt is said to be better, and the passage ends by urging awareness of a future day of return to God, when each soul will be repaid justly.

When a debt is taken on for a set date, the believers are told to have it written down by a scribe who writes it fairly. The person who owes the debt dictates the terms. If he is foolish, weak, or unable to dictate, his friend may dictate on his behalf, fairly.

This verse is about testimony in a financial dispute. It asks for two witnesses from among the believers, or, if two men cannot be found, one man and two women. If one woman forgets, the other can remind her. Witnesses must come when called.

Record debts in writing, large or small, with the date of repayment, and have witnesses when you sell. Writing and witnesses are said to be fairer and to prevent doubt. If goods are exchanged on the spot, no record is required. Writers and witnesses must not be harmed, and doing so is a wrong.

If no written record is available on a journey, pledges may be taken instead. A person trusted with something must return it and fear God. Refusing to give evidence is called wicked at heart. God knows all deeds and thoughts, and He judges and forgives as He chooses.

The Prophet and the believers both accept the revelation sent from their Lord. They believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, and make no difference between any of the messengers. They say they hear and obey, and ask for God's mercy, since they will return to Him.

God gives no soul a burden beyond its ability, and each person gets the reward or bears the consequence of their own deeds. The believers then pray that God will not punish them for forgetting or sinning, will not lay on them heavy burdens like those given to earlier peoples, and will forgive and help them against unbelieving nations.

Those who were commanded to worship God sincerely, to pray and to give the stated alms, are described as following the true religion. Unbelievers, both among the People of the Book and the Polytheists, are said to face the fire of Gehenna forever. Believers who do right are promised gardens of Eden with flowing rivers, to remain forever.

Everything in heaven and earth gives praise to God, who has all power and rules over all things. God created all people, some of whom believe and some of whom do not, and He sees everything they do. He knows what people hide and what they reveal, including the secrets of their hearts.

Those who rejected earlier messengers suffered for it, and a harsh punishment awaits them. They refused to accept human guides, turned away, and denied that the dead will be raised. The passage answers that they will be raised and told of their deeds, and that God can easily do this.

On the day of gathering, believers who did right will have their bad deeds cancelled and enter gardens with rivers, while unbelievers who rejected the signs will go to the fire. People are told to obey God and the messenger; if they turn away, the messenger is not blamed, since his only duty is to preach clearly.

Believers are warned that their wives and children may sometimes distract or lead them away from God. If they forgive and show patience, God will forgive them too. Wealth and children are described as a test, while the greater reward is with God, so believers are urged to fear God, obey, give charity, and lend to God.

God sent an Apostle (messenger) to the Arabs, one of their own people, to recite God's signs to them, purify them, and teach them the Book and wisdom. Before this they had been in clear error. God also gives this goodness to others not yet among the earlier believers, to whom He chooses.

Those given the Torah but who refuse to live by it are compared to a donkey carrying books it cannot understand. The passage then challenges Jews who claim special closeness to God to wish for death, and says they will not, because of their past deeds.

Death cannot be escaped, and after it people will be brought back to God, who knows all their actions. Believers are told that when called to Friday prayer they should leave their trade and hurry to remember God, and afterwards they may go out and seek God's provision.

People who see trade goods or entertainment rush off after them and leave the Prophet standing alone. He is told to say that God has something better in store than amusement or goods, and that God is the best provider.

The passage first says that the spoils of battle belong to God and his messenger, and that believers should settle disputes over them by fearing God and obeying him. It then describes true believers as those whose hearts tremble when God is named, whose faith grows as they hear his revelations, who trust in their Lord, pray, and give charity. They will receive a high rank, forgiveness, and generous provision from God.

God reminds the believers of his promise that one of the two armies would fall to them, and that he would send a thousand angels to help them. He made this promise to encourage their hearts, since help comes from God alone.

The passage recalls a time when God sent sleep as a sign of safety, and rain to cleanse the believers and steady them. It then says God told the angels to strengthen the faithful and to put fear into the unbelievers, so the angels should strike off their heads and fingertips. The reason given is that these people opposed God and his messenger, and God is severe in punishing such opposition.

Believers who flee from battle on that day face God's anger and Hell, unless they turn back to fight or join another group. The passage says the victory was God's doing, not the believers' or the Prophet's alone, and it was a test for the faithful and a way to defeat the unbelievers' schemes.

Addressed to the Meccans, the passage says that a decision has already come, so they should stop fighting, since their larger forces will not help them against believers who have God on their side. It then urges the believers to obey God and his messenger and not to be like those who pretend to listen but do not truly hear.

God says that if He had seen any good in certain people, He would have let them hear His message, and even then they would have turned away. He calls on believers to answer God and His messenger, because that call gives life. They are warned that God stands between a person and his heart, that all will return to Him, and that temptation can strike the wicked and others alike.

The passage reminds believers that God once rescued them when they were few and weak, and gave them strength and provision. It warns them not to betray God and his messenger, and says wealth and children are a test. If they fear God, He will deliver them, forgive their sins, and show great generosity.

The passage describes unbelievers who plotted against the Prophet, to imprison, kill, or banish him, and who mocked the revelations as old tales. They asked God to send a punishment on them if the message was true. God did not punish them while the Prophet was among them, and would not punish them when they asked for forgiveness.

The passage says that some unbelievers blocked believers from the Sacred House (the temple at Mecca), though they had no right to guard it. It claims only the God-fearing are its true guardians, and that the unbelievers' worship there is only whistling and clapping. It warns that their spending to turn people from God will end in regret and defeat, and that they will be gathered into Hell.

God will separate the bad from the good and gather the bad into Hell. The unbelievers are told that if they stop disbelieving, their past will be forgiven, but if they return to it, they face the fate of earlier peoples. Believers are told to fight until opposition ends and religion belongs wholly to God, and that God protects them if the unbelievers turn away.

A fifth of any war booty belongs to God and the Prophet, to relatives, orphans, the poor, and travellers in need. The verse ties this rule to belief in God and to the revelation sent down on the day of the battle between the two armies, and it ends by affirming God's power over all things.

The verse looks back at the battle of Badr. The Muslims met the enemy though they had not planned that fight, because God meant the event to happen. The clear sign of this outcome was meant to decide who would die and who would live.

God reminds the believers that he showed them the enemy in a dream as few in number, and later made them look few to each other in battle. Had the enemy seemed large, the believers would have lost heart and argued. God did this so that his plan would be carried out, and he tells believers to stand firm and remember him when facing an enemy force.

Believers are told to obey God and his messenger, not to argue among themselves, and to stay firm, since God is with those who endure. They are also warned not to act like certain Meccans who left their homes boastfully, wanting to be seen, and who blocked others from God's way. God knows all their deeds.

Satan encourages the unbelievers before a battle, promising to help them. When the armies meet, he withdraws, saying he fears God. The passage then says that hypocrites claim the believers have been misled, and that God is mighty and wise, and describes angels striking the unbelievers at death.

Those who rejected God's signs are compared to Pharaoh's people and earlier nations, who were seized and destroyed for their sins. God does not change the favour he gives a people while they do not change what is in their hearts. Pharaoh's people were drowned because they were all wrongdoers.

Prepare as much military strength as you can, so that you can frighten God's enemies and your enemies, along with others you may not know. Whatever is spent for God's cause will be repaid in full. If the enemy inclines to peace, accept peace too and trust in God.

God is presented as sufficient protection for the prophet against those who plan to betray him. God has united the believers' hearts, something no amount of wealth could do. The believers are urged to fight, with twenty steadfast men said to defeat two hundred opponents.

God lightens the burden on the believers, saying that a steadfast group of one hundred can defeat two hundred, and a group of a thousand can defeat two thousand, with God's permission. The passage then rebukes them for taking ransom from captives, saying they wanted worldly gain when God wanted the next life for them.

Speaking to the prophet about captives taken in battle, the passage says that if God sees goodness in their hearts, He will give them more than they lost and forgive them. If the captives instead act treacherously, they are told that they have already betrayed God before, so God has given the believers power over them.

Believers who left their homes for God's cause and those who sheltered the Prophet are bound closely to one another. Believers who have not yet emigrated get no such kinship rights, though they may ask for help in matters of faith, which must be given unless a treaty exists with the people they are fighting.

Those who believed, left their homes, fought for God, and sheltered and supported the Prophet are described as true believers who will receive mercy and honour. Later believers who emigrated and fought alongside them are counted as part of the same community. Blood relatives are the closest to one another under God's Book.

Those who believe and do good, and accept the revelation to Muhammad as true, will have their sins removed and their hearts guided. Unbelievers are described as following falsehood. The passage then orders believers to strike the unbelievers' necks in battle and to take the rest as captives.

After a war, captives may be freed or ransomed. God could punish the unbelievers himself, but he lets believers fight so that some are tested by others. Those who fight for God will be guided and rewarded with Paradise, while God will defeat the unbelievers' deeds.

God destroyed earlier peoples who did not believe, and the same fate waits for unbelievers. God protects those who believe and brings them into gardens with flowing rivers. Those who do not believe feed only on worldly pleasures, like animals, and end in the fire.

The passage contrasts two groups. It says the believer who follows the clear guidance of God is not the same as the one whose wrongdoing seems good to him or who follows his own desires. It then describes Paradise, promised to the God-fearing, with rivers of water, milk and wine.

The passage contrasts two groups. The righteous enjoy rivers of honey and fruit from their Lord, while those in the fire drink boiling water. Some listeners mock the speaker and ask what he means, but God has sealed their hearts. Those who are guided, by contrast, receive more guidance.

The unbelievers are only waiting for the Hour, the day of judgment, to arrive suddenly. Its signs have already appeared, and once it comes, it will be too late to be warned. The passage tells the prophet to affirm that there is no god but God, to ask forgiveness for his sin and for believers, and notes that God knows all of people's activities and their final resting places.

Some believers ask for a new revelation, but when a chapter ordering war arrives, those with weak faith look at the Prophet in fear, as if facing death. The passage says obedience would be better for them, and that those who turn away from God would spread disorder and break family ties. It calls such people cursed and spiritually blind.

Those who turn back to error after the truth has been made clear are led astray by Satan. They secretly promise those who reject God's revelation that they will partly comply with them. God knows their hidden intentions, and their deeds will come to nothing. Their malice will be exposed.

God will test the believers to show who is brave and steadfast, and He knows their deeds. Those who reject faith, block others from the path, or turn away from the Prophet after guidance has been made clear will not harm God, and their works will be made worthless. Believers are told to obey God and the Prophet and not let their deeds be wasted.

The passage tells believers not to lose heart or offer peace to unbelievers when they have the upper hand, since God is on their side and will reward their deeds. It says worldly life is mere play and urges belief and fear of God, adding that God does not demand all of their wealth, and that if He did, they would show themselves stingy.

God calls on believers to give money for His cause. Some are stingy, but their stinginess harms only themselves, since God is rich and they are poor. If they refuse and turn away, God will replace them with another people who will not be like them.

God has sent down the Book (the Quran) to confirm the earlier scriptures, the Law and the Gospel, which were given as guidance. Those who reject God's signs face severe punishment. God knows everything on earth and in heaven and shapes human beings in the womb; there is no god but Him.

The passage says that the Book (the Qur'an) has some verses that are clear in meaning, which form its foundation, and others that are figurative. People whose hearts lean toward error chase the figurative verses to stir up conflict, but only God knows their true meaning. Those firm in knowledge simply affirm that all of it comes from their Lord, and they pray not to be led astray.

Believers pray to God about the coming Day of Judgment, when all people will be gathered, and God will keep His promise. Unbelievers will not be saved by their wealth or children, and they will be punished in Hell, as earlier peoples like Pharaoh's were for rejecting God's signs.

The passage recalls the battle where a small Muslim force faced a larger enemy, and God gave the believers victory, which is taken as a lesson for thoughtful people. It then says that worldly desires such as wealth, women, children, horses and land are attractive but only a passing enjoyment, while the reward with God is better.

Those who fear God are promised better things than worldly goods: gardens with flowing rivers, where they will live forever, along with pure spouses and God's approval. The passage describes them as patient, truthful, humble, charitable, and people who ask forgiveness every morning.
God testifies that there is no god except Him, and the angels and people of knowledge who uphold justice say the same. They declare that there is no god but God, the Mighty and the Wise.

The passage says that the true religion before God is Islam, meaning submission to God. People who were given earlier Scriptures split apart only after knowledge had reached them, out of jealousy. If others dispute, they are told to submit to God, and if they turn away, the messenger's only duty is to preach.

Those who reject God's signs and kill prophets and people who call for justice are warned of painful punishment, and their deeds will count for nothing. Some who were given earlier scriptures turn away when called to God's Book to settle their disputes. They do so because they claim the fire will touch them only for a few days, and their own inventions have misled them.

The passage speaks of a coming Day of Judgment, when everyone will be paid fully for what they have done and no one will be treated unjustly. It then addresses God directly as the one who holds all power: he gives power and takes it away, raises up and humbles whom he chooses, and all good is in his hand.

The passage praises God as the one who controls the cycle of night and day and who brings life out of death and death out of life. It also says he gives provision to whomever he chooses, in abundance.

Believers should not take unbelievers as close friends in place of other believers, and anyone who does so gets nothing from God. The exception is when they must guard themselves against real danger from them. God warns believers to fear Him, since He knows everything hidden in their hearts, whether they hide it or reveal it.

On the Day of Judgment, each soul will find its good and evil deeds present before it, and will wish its evil deeds were far away. God warns people to be careful of Him, and says that those who love God should follow the Prophet, and that God will then love and forgive them. Those who turn away are not loved by God.
God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran over all other people. These families are descended from one another. The verse ends by saying God hears and knows all things.
The wife of Imran makes a vow to dedicate the child in her womb to God's service. When she gives birth to a girl, she names her Mary and asks God to protect her and her descendants from Satan.

Mary is taken into the care of Zacharias, and God makes her grow well. Each time he visits her in the sanctuary, he finds food with her, and she says it comes from God, who gives without limit. Moved by this, Zacharias prays to God for good descendants, and angels then speak to him while he is praying.

God tells of the birth of John (Yahya), who will confirm a word from God and be a prophet among the righteous. Zachariah asks how he can have a son when he and his wife are old and she is barren. God answers that it will happen, and gives him a sign: he will not speak to anyone for three days except by signs. Angels then speak to Mary, saying God has chosen and purified her above all women.

The passage tells Muhammad about events he did not witness: people casting lots with reeds to decide who would care for Mary, and arguing over it. It then reports an angel's announcement to Mary that she will bear a son named Messiah Jesus, honored in this world and the next, who will speak in the cradle and be one of the righteous.

In this passage, a messenger to the children of Israel says he comes with a sign from God. He will shape a bird from clay, breathe into it so it comes alive by God's leave, heal the blind and the lepers, raise the dead, and tell people what they eat and store at home.

Jesus says he has come to confirm the earlier law and to allow some things that had been forbidden, and he tells his hearers to fear God and obey him, since God is his Lord and theirs. When he sees disbelief, he asks who will help him for God's sake. His apostles answer that they will be God's helpers, believe in God, and ask to be counted among the witnesses.

God tells Jesus that He will take him up to Himself and protect him from those who reject him. He says his followers will be placed above the unbelievers until the Day of Resurrection, when all will return to God for judgment. Unbelievers will be punished in this world and the next, while believers who do right will be rewarded.

Some people argue with the Prophet about God, even after he has received the knowledge. He is told to invite them to a mutual curse: each side calls down God's curse on the liars, with families gathered. He says the message is the truth and there is no god but God. If they refuse, God knows who the wrongdoers are.

Muhammad is told to invite the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) to agree that they will worship only God and take no partners or human lords beside Him. He also asks them why they argue about Abraham, since the Law and the Gospel came only after him. They are told they argue about things they do not know, while God alone has true knowledge.

Those closest to Abraham are said to be those who follow him, along with Muhammad and his believers. The passage then rebukes some People of the Book (Jews and Christians) for trying to mislead believers, for hiding or distorting the truth they know, and for pretending to believe in the morning and rejecting it by evening.

This passage is spoken as a reply to people who would trust only their own community. It says that true guidance comes from God alone, and that God gives His gifts and mercy to whomever He chooses. Nobody can claim these gifts as their own right.

Some people of the Book (Jews and Christians) can be trusted with large sums, while others will not return even a small amount unless pressed constantly. They excuse this by saying they owe no honesty to non-Jews or non-Christians, whom they call "ignorant," and they claim this lie about God knowingly. Those who keep their word and fear God are loved by God.

People who trade away their covenant with God and their oaths for a small price will get no share in the next life. On the day of resurrection God will neither speak to them nor look on them, and they will face a severe punishment.

Some people among the Scripture-holders twist the sacred text with their tongues, so that listeners think their words come from the Scripture. They claim what they say is from God, but it is not, and they knowingly tell a lie against God.

A prophet, given scripture and wisdom by God, would not tell people to worship him alongside God. Instead, he would tell them to be devoted to God, since they already know the scriptures. God does not order people to take angels or prophets as lords, and would not order them to turn unbeliever after becoming Muslims.

God makes a covenant with the prophets. They must accept a future prophet who will confirm the earlier scriptures, believe in him, and help him. The prophets agree, and God calls them witnesses. Anyone who turns away afterwards is called perverse.
Do they want any religion other than God's? Everything in the heavens and on earth submits to Him, whether willingly or by force, and all of them return to Him.

The speaker says that he believes in God and in the revelations given to Abraham, Ismael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Moses, Jesus and the prophets, and makes no difference between them. He states that anyone who seeks a religion other than Islam will not have it accepted and will be lost in the next world.

God will not guide people who, after believing and having clear proof, turn away from faith and wrong others. Their punishment is God's curse, the curse of angels and of all people, and it lasts forever. The exception is those who repent and reform, because God is merciful.

Those who turn from faith after believing, and keep growing in unbelief, will not have their repentance accepted, and they are described as astray. Those who die as unbelievers will not be saved even by offering all the gold the earth could hold. The passage ends by saying that goodness comes only through giving from what one loves, and God knows whatever is given.

Before the Torah was revealed, all foods were lawful to the Children of Israel except what Jacob had forbidden himself. The passage tells the Prophet to challenge them to bring the Torah and read it, and it calls those who invent lies about God evil. It then urges following the faith of Abraham, who worshipped no other gods besides God, and names the first temple built for mankind, at Becca (Mecca).

The passage says that the pilgrimage to the sacred house (the temple at Mecca) is a duty owed to God by those able to make the journey. It then rebukes the People of the Book, meaning Jews and Christians, for rejecting God's signs and turning believers away from His path. God, it says, sees all that they do.

The passage urges believers to stay faithful to God, since God's signs and his prophet are present among them. It says they should fear God properly, remain Muslims, and hold together firmly as a community. It reminds them that God united their hearts after they had been enemies and saved them from the fire.

The passage tells believers to be a group that calls people to good, urges what is right, and warns against wrong. It warns them not to split into factions after clear proof has come to them. Those who divide and then turn back from belief will face a severe punishment on the Day of Judgment, when some faces are white and others black.

The passage praises the community of believers as the best people raised up for humanity, because they command what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in God. It says the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) would have done better to believe, though some among them do. It adds that most of them are rebellious, and that if they fight the believers they will be defeated and receive no help.

Those who reject God's signs and kill the prophets will be marked with shame and poverty, unless they find protection with God and people. But not all of the People of the Book are the same. Some are upright: they recite God's signs at night, believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin justice, forbid evil, and hasten to good works.

Those who reject God will gain nothing from their wealth or children when facing God. Their charity in this life is compared to a freezing wind that destroys a field, and the passage says they harm only themselves.

Believers are warned not to take outsiders as close friends or confidants. The passage says such people will try to harm them, wish for their downfall, and hide hostility that is worse than what they show openly.

The passage describes a group who pretend to believe when they meet the believers, but in private they are full of anger toward them and are glad when harm comes to them. God knows their hidden feelings. It promises that if the believers stay firm and fear God, their schemes will not hurt them.

God reminds the believers of their help at the battle of Badr, when two groups of them were afraid and God protected them. He had already aided them when they were weaker. He promises that if they stay steadfast and fear God, He will send five thousand angels to help them against the enemy.

God says he gave this news of victory to comfort the believers, and that victory comes only from him. He may destroy the unbelievers or defeat them, and it is not for the prophet to decide whether God turns to them in mercy or punishes them. Everything belongs to God, who forgives whom he wills and punishes whom he wills.

Those who sin, then remember God, ask for forgiveness, and do not keep on in the wrong they knew they did, will receive pardon and gardens with flowing rivers. The passage then tells listeners to look at what happened to those who called the prophets liars.

The passage speaks to believers after a setback in battle. It says reverses and successes are shared among people, so God can test who truly believes and who endures. It rebukes those who wanted death and martyrdom but then fled when they faced it.

Muhammad is only a messenger, and earlier messengers have died before him. The passage asks whether the believers will turn back if he dies or is killed. It says that turning back harms no one but the person who does it, and that God rewards those who stay thankful.

Death happens only when God permits it, and the timing is already written in a fixed record. People who want the rewards of this world receive some of them, and people who want the rewards of the next life receive those, with thankful people rewarded. Earlier prophets fought large enemy armies without losing courage, weakening, or giving in, and God loves such steadfast people.

Believers are asked to pray for forgiveness, firmness, and help against those who reject God, and God rewards them in this world and the next. The passage then warns believers not to obey unbelievers, since this would turn them back into ruin, because God alone is their protector and the best helper.

God will cast fear into the hearts of unbelievers, because they worship other gods alongside God without any authority sent down to them, and their dwelling will be the fire. The passage then recalls that God had kept His promise to the believers at a battle, but they lost heart, argued over orders, and disobeyed the Prophet after he had shown them the victory they wanted.

Some of the believers wanted worldly gain and others wanted the reward of the next life. God then tested them by making them flee from the enemy. He has now forgiven them, because He is generous to those who believe.

God rebukes believers who climbed a hill during a battle and ignored the Prophet, who was calling them back to the fight. He says he sent them trouble after trouble so they would not grieve over lost spoils or their misfortunes. God knows everything they do.

After a defeat, God gave calm to some of the believers, while others, driven by their own fears, doubted God and asked what they had gained from the fight. The passage answers that the outcome belongs to God alone. It adds that the dead would have died anyway, and that God tests what people hold in their hearts.

Some believers turned back when the two armies met in battle. The verse says Satan alone caused them to fail in their duty, because of some of their actions. God has now forgiven them, since he is forgiving and merciful.

Believers are told not to speak like unbelievers, who said that their relatives would not have died if they had stayed home from travel or war. God makes people live and die, so such deaths come from Him, and forgiveness and mercy from God are better than any wealth gained in this life. All people will be gathered back to God in the end.

Gentleness toward the believers is presented as the reason they stayed close: harshness would have driven them away. The passage tells the speaker to forgive them, seek pardon for them, consult them on war, and then trust God once a decision is made. Victory comes only if God helps, and believers should place their trust in Him.

The Prophet will not cheat his followers. Anyone who cheats will carry those thefts on the Day of Resurrection, and each soul will receive what it has earned, without unfairness. Those who please God and those who bring God's anger upon themselves are not equal; God sees everything people do.

God first sent the believers a prophet from among their own people, to recite his revelations, purify them, and teach them the Book and wisdom. When they suffer a setback after having inflicted one, they ask where it came from, and they are told it comes from themselves, since God has power over all things.

The passage describes a battle that God allowed to happen so that true believers and hypocrites could be told apart. Some men who stayed home, when called to fight, said that if they had known how to fight they would have joined in. They are said to be close to unbelief and to say one thing while hiding another. Their claim that the dead would have lived had they stayed home is answered with a challenge to avoid death themselves.

The passage says that believers who have died in God's cause, and those still to follow them, will feel joy and will have no fear or grief. God will not let the reward of the faithful be lost. Those who answer God and the Prophet after a setback, and who do good and fear God, will receive a great reward.

Believers were warned that a large enemy force was gathering against them. Instead of growing afraid, their faith grew stronger, and they trusted God alone. They returned from the encounter unharmed and blessed, and the passage says that the warning came from Satan, who wants his followers to fear people, so believers should fear God instead.

Those who rush into unbelief should not be a worry to the believer, because they cannot harm God at all. God will deny them any share in the next life and will punish them severely. The long life God gives them is not a blessing, but a means for them to increase their sins.

God does not reveal hidden matters to everyone, but chooses certain messengers to know them. People are urged to believe in God and his messengers. Those who withhold the wealth God has given them will find it becomes a burden around their necks on Judgment Day, since God inherits the heavens and earth.

God has heard those who mocked, saying that God is poor and they are rich, and says their words will be written down along with their killing of the prophets. They will suffer the fire for what they have done, since God does not wrong his servants. The passage then turns to people who claim God ordered them not to believe any messenger unless he brings a sacrifice that fire from heaven consumes.

Earlier messengers of God also came with miracles, clear proofs and holy books, and they were rejected before. Everyone dies, and people receive their reward only on the Day of Resurrection. Those who escape the fire and enter Paradise succeed, while worldly life is only a deceptive pleasure.

Believers will be tested through their wealth and their own selves. They will hear much hurtful talk from earlier People of the Book (Jews and Christians) and from those who associate other gods with God. If they stay patient and conscious of God, that is counted as a matter of firm resolve.

God once bound the earlier scripture-holders to make his message known and not hide it, but they ignored this and traded it for a small gain. The passage warns that those who enjoy claiming credit for deeds they did not do will not escape punishment, because God rules heaven and earth.

People who understand are described as remembering God at all times, whether standing, sitting or lying down, and reflecting on the creation of the heavens and earth. They conclude that God did not create this in vain and pray to be protected from the fire. They also say that those sent into the fire will be shamed and that wrongdoers will have no helper.

The believers pray to be given what God promised through his messengers and not be shamed on Judgment Day. God answers that he will not lose the deeds of anyone, male or female, and that those who left their homes, suffered, and fought or died for his cause will have their sins erased and enter gardens with flowing rivers. This reward comes from God, who gives it perfectly.

The passage tells believers not to be fooled by the wealth of unbelievers, since their success is short-lived and ends in Hell. Those who fear God get gardens with rivers and an everlasting reward. It also praises some People of the Book, meaning Jews and Christians, who believe in God and humbly refuse to trade God's signs for a small price.

This is a note from the translator, not Qur'anic text itself. It explains that the phrase "my helpers unto God" means helpers of God's religion, following an earlier commentator. It also suggests that the Arabic word for "helper" (ansar) may match an Ethiopic word meaning helper or disciple.

Moses asks his people why they hurt him, since they know he is God's messenger to them. When they turn away, God lets their hearts go astray, because God does not guide people who keep refusing the truth.

Jesus is quoted as telling the children of Israel that he confirms the earlier law and announces a coming messenger named Ahmad. When that messenger arrives with clear proofs, people call him a sorcerer. The passage says God will complete his light despite their opposition.

God sent his messenger with guidance and the true religion, so that it will win out over all other religions, even though those who join other gods with God dislike this. Believers are urged to trust God and his messenger and to fight for God's cause with their money and their lives. In return, they are promised forgiveness of sins and entry into gardens with flowing rivers.

Believers are urged to be helpers of God, as Jesus' disciples were when he asked who would help God. Some of the Israelites believed and some did not. God gave the believers victory over their enemies.

God created the heavens and the earth in six days and then took His seat of rule. He knows everything that goes into or comes out of the earth and everything that descends from or rises to heaven. He is with people wherever they are, owns all of creation, and controls the alternation of night and day.

Believers are urged to have faith in God and His messenger and to give to charity from the wealth God has given them, since those who do so will receive a great reward. The passage asks why they would not believe, given that the messenger calls them to faith and God has made a covenant with them. It also says God sends clear signs to lead people from darkness into light.

Believers are urged to spend their wealth for God's cause, since all inheritance of the heavens and earth belongs to God. Those who gave and fought before the victory at Mecca are ranked higher than those who did so later, though God promises a good reward to all. Giving to God is described as a loan that God will repay many times over.

On the day of judgment, believing men and women will have light going before them and at their right hand. Angels will welcome them with good news of gardens with flowing rivers, where they will live forever.

On the Day of Judgment, the hypocrites ask believers to wait so they can take some of their light. They are told to go back and look for light elsewhere. A wall with a gate separates them, and they admit they led themselves into doubt and temptation.
