On that day, no ransom will be accepted from unbelievers or from those who believed but did not act on it. Their dwelling will be the fire, which is their proper place, and the journey there is a terrible one.

The passage urges believers to soften their hearts toward God's warning and the revelation he has sent. It warns them not to become like earlier communities that had Scripture but grew hard-hearted over time. It ends by promising a large reward to those who give to charity and lend generously to God.

Those who believe in God and his messenger are described as truthful witnesses before their Lord, and they will receive their reward and their light. Those who disbelieve and deny God's signs will be people of the Fire, meaning Hell.

The passage says that worldly life is only play, distraction, show and empty pride. Wealth and children are like crops that grow after rain, look lively, then dry up and turn to straw. What matters more is the next life, which brings either severe punishment or forgiveness and God's approval.

Believers are urged to race for forgiveness from God and for Paradise, which is promised to those who believe in God and His messengers. Nothing bad happens, on earth or to people, unless it was already written in the Book before creation. This is so that people do not grieve over losses or become overly proud of gains. God does not love the arrogant and boastful.

The passage condemns people who are greedy and also push others toward greed. It then says that anyone who turns away from giving alms (charity) is still in God's hands, since God needs nothing and is worthy of praise.

God sent messengers with clear signs, along with the Book and the balance (a symbol of justice), so that people would act fairly. He also sent down iron, which can bring both harm and benefit. Earlier, Noah and Abraham received prophecy and scripture, though many of their descendants did wrong.

God sent Jesus after earlier messengers and gave him the Gospel, along with kindness and compassion in the hearts of his followers. The passage says the monastic life was an invention of the people themselves, not something God commanded. They were asked only to seek God's pleasure, and they did not keep this as they should. Those who believed were rewarded, though many were disobedient.

Believers are told to fear God and trust His messenger, and they will receive a double share of His mercy, light to walk by, and forgiveness. The passage adds that the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) have no control over God's favours, which are given to whomever God chooses.

People are told to be mindful of God, who created all humans from one soul and one pair, a man and his wife. They are also told to respect family ties and to give orphans their property, without swapping good goods for worthless ones or consuming their wealth. Taking an orphan's property is called a great crime.

The passage says that if a man fears he cannot treat orphan girls fairly, he may marry other women, up to two, three, or four. If he still fears he cannot be fair to several wives, he should marry only one. It also gives rules on the bride-gift (dowry), on not giving property to people unable to manage it, and on providing for and speaking kindly to dependants.

Guardians of orphans are told to test the orphans until they reach marriageable age, and only return their property once they show good judgment. Guardians must not waste the property or hand it over hastily. A rich guardian must not touch it, while a poor guardian may take a reasonable amount for his support. When the property is handed back, witnesses should be present.

Men and women each have a set share of what their parents and relatives leave, whether the amount is small or large. When relatives, orphans and the poor are present at the division, they should also be given something and spoken to kindly. Those who handle orphans' property should be careful not to wrong them, and should keep God in mind.
Those who wrongfully take and consume an orphan's property are, in this verse, said to be eating fire. They will swallow only fire into their bellies and will burn in the flame.

This passage sets out how a dead person's property is divided among heirs. A son receives twice the share of a daughter, and a daughter alone receives half. Parents and a surviving spouse or children each receive fixed shares, and the division is made after debts and bequests are paid. The passage closes by saying the arrangement comes from God and that people cannot be sure which relative will benefit them most.

Husbands and wives inherit from each other's estates. A husband gets half of his wife's estate if she has no children, or a quarter if she has children. A wife gets a quarter of her husband's estate if he has no children, or an eighth if he has children. In both cases, debts and bequests are paid first.

This verse sets out how an estate is shared when a person without children leaves it to a distant relative, and that relative has a brother or sister. Each sibling receives a sixth, or, if there are more than two, they share a third, after bequests and debts are paid. The verse ends by promising that obeying God and his prophet brings paradise.

The passage sets out consequences for rebellion against God and his messenger, which it says lead to eternal fire. It then describes punishment for sexual sin: women guilty of it, once four witnesses confirm the charge, are to be confined to their homes until death or until God provides a way out. Two men guilty of the same sin are to be punished, but if they repent and change their ways, they are to be left alone, since God is merciful.

God accepts repentance from those who do wrong out of ignorance and turn back to him soon after. Repentance is not accepted from those who keep doing evil until death is near, or from those who die as unbelievers; for them a painful punishment is prepared.

Believers are told not to inherit wives against their will, nor to keep them from remarrying just to take back the dowry, unless they have been openly immoral. They should treat wives kindly, even when disliked, and must not take back a dowry given to a wife when they divorce her to marry another, especially by slandering her.

It lists the close relatives a man may not marry: mothers, daughters, sisters, aunts, nieces, foster relatives, wives' mothers, stepdaughters from wives he has been with, sons' wives, and two sisters at once. It ends by saying God is forgiving and merciful, and it makes an exception for marriages already made before this ruling.

Married women are forbidden to men, except those held as slaves. Men may otherwise take wives using their wealth, in modest conduct and not in fornication, and must give the women their dowry. Agreements beyond this rule are not a sin.

If a man cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, he may marry a believing slave woman, with her masters' permission and with a fair dowry given to her. If such a wife commits adultery, her punishment is half that of a free married woman. Abstaining is said to be better.

God wants to guide believers toward the ways of earlier peoples and to show them mercy, while those who follow their own desires want them to stray far off course. He wants to lighten their burden, since people were made weak. Believers are told not to consume one another's property in empty dealings, except through trade by mutual consent, and not to kill themselves.

If you avoid the major sins, God will forgive your lesser faults and admit you to Paradise. Do not envy what God has given others; men and women each receive a share according to what they earn, and you should ask God for His gifts. Heirs are assigned to each person, and inheritance is to be given to each of them.

Men are said to have a higher standing than women, because of the qualities God gave them and because they support women with their wealth. Good wives are obedient and guard what is left in their husband's absence. Where a wife is defiant, the passage allows the husband to admonish her, separate from her in bed, and beat her, but to stop if she obeys.
If a husband and wife are in serious conflict, the passage says each side should choose a judge from its own family. If both judges want to make peace, God will bring the couple together again.

Worship God alone and do good to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbours, travellers and one's slaves. God does not love the proud, the boastful, or those who are stingy and tell others to be stingy too, hiding what God has given them. Those who reject faith are promised a shameful punishment.

God condemns those who give charity only to be seen by people and do not truly believe in God and the Last Day. Such people have Satan as a companion. Believers who give out of what God has given them will be rewarded, since God knows their deeds, does no wrong, and doubles any good deed.

On the Day of Judgment, God will bring a witness from every nation and will bring Muhammad as a witness against those who disbelieved and rejected him. These people will wish the earth would swallow them, yet they cannot hide anything from God.

Believers are told not to pray while drunk, until they can understand what they say, or while in a state of ritual impurity, unless travelling, until they have washed. If water is unavailable, due to sickness, travel, or other impurity, they may cleanse their face and hands with clean sand instead.

The passage warns believers about people who have received earlier scriptures and who, it says, want the believers to go astray. It accuses some Jews of twisting the words of their scriptures and of mocking the message with insulting, double-meaning speech. It also says God is enough protection and help against them.

Some people are told to say "We have heard and we obey" and to ask the speaker to "regard us," meaning to look kindly on them. The passage says this would be better and more right for them. It adds that God has cursed them for their unbelief, and only a few of them believe.

The passage tells People of the Scripture (Jews and Christians) to believe in the revelation sent down to confirm their own scripture, warning of punishment if they refuse. It says God will not forgive associating other gods with Him, though He forgives other sins to whom He wills. It also says God alone declares people righteous, and no one will be wronged at all.

The passage criticizes people who were given earlier scripture for believing in Djibt and Thagout, idols or false powers, and for saying that unbelievers are better guided than believers. It says they are cursed by God. It asks whether such stingy, envious people can share in God's kingdom, and recalls that God gave earlier scripture, wisdom and a great kingdom to Abraham's family.

Those who reject God's signs will eventually be thrown into the fire. Whenever their skins are burnt through, they will be given new skins, so that they continue to feel the punishment. The passage ends by saying God is mighty and wise.

Those who believe and do good deeds are promised gardens with flowing rivers, where they will live forever, with pure wives and endless shade. The passage then orders people to return what they hold in trust to its rightful owners and to judge between people fairly.

Believers are told to obey God, the messenger (the apostle, Muhammad), and those in authority among them. If they disagree about something, they should refer it to God and the messenger, which the passage calls the best and fairest way to settle disputes.

Some people claim to believe in the revelations sent to Muhammad and earlier prophets, yet they want their disputes judged by Thagout, a false authority they were told to reject. When told to accept God's message and the messenger, they turn away. Later, after misfortune strikes because of their own deeds, they come swearing they only meant good and harmony.

The passage says that messengers are sent to be obeyed, by God's will. Those who have sinned through unbelief are told that if they come to the messenger and ask God's forgiveness, with the messenger asking it for them, they will find God merciful. It also says that people will not truly believe until they accept the messenger as judge in their disputes and accept his rulings fully.

Had God commanded hardship such as self-killing or leaving homes, few would have obeyed. Those who did obey would have gained stronger faith, a great reward, and guidance. Whoever obeys God and the Prophet will be counted among the Prophets, the sincere, the martyrs, and the righteous, a fine company.

Some believers hold back from fighting. When a defeat comes, they are glad they stayed out, but when victory comes, they wish they had joined to share the spoils. The passage tells those who fight for God to fight, since whether they die or win, God will reward them greatly.

Believers are urged to fight for the weak men, women and children who pray to God to rescue them from an oppressive city and send them a protector. Those who believe fight for God's cause, while unbelievers fight for Taghut, a false power. The believers are told to fight Satan's allies, since Satan's schemes will fail.

Some people were told to hold back from fighting and to keep prayer and give alms. When fighting was later ordered, some of them feared the people around them as much as God, or even more, and asked why they had been commanded to fight. The reply is that worldly gain is small, and the next life is better for those who fear God, and no one will be wronged at all.

Death comes to everyone, even those in strong towers. When people have good fortune they credit God, but when they have bad fortune they blame Muhammad. The reply is that all things come from God, and the prophet is only a messenger, not a guardian over those who turn away.

The passage describes people who promise obedience to the Prophet in his presence but plot against his words in private. It says God records their secret plotting, tells the Prophet to turn away from them and trust God, and argues that the Qur'an would contain many contradictions if it were not from God.

The passage says that some people spread news, whether good or alarming, before checking it. It urges that such news be taken first to the Prophet and to the leaders, who can judge it properly. It then tells believers to fight for God's cause, to carry their own load only, and to encourage the faithful, trusting that God will restrain the unbelievers, who are weaker than He is.

Whoever acts as a go-between for a good cause shares in the good it brings, and whoever mediates for an evil cause bears its harm. God watches over all things, and He will certainly gather everyone on the day of resurrection.

The verses ask why the believers are divided over the hypocrites, whom God has rejected because of their deeds. They ask whether people want to guide those God has left astray, and state that no path can be found for anyone God leads astray.

The passage tells believers not to take those who reject their faith as friends, unless those people leave their homes for the sake of God. If such people turn back to their old ways, the believers are told to seize and kill them wherever they are found, and still not to take them as friends or helpers.

Some groups are exempt from attack: those who take refuge with your allies, or who come to you because they are unwilling to fight you or their own people. God could have let them fight you, but did not. If such people stay away from fighting and offer peace, God gives you no reason to act against them.

Some people seek peace with the Muslims while also keeping the trust of their own people. If they keep returning to rebellion, they will be defeated by it. If they do not leave the Muslims alone, offer terms of peace, or hold back their hands from fighting, the Muslims are told to seize and kill them wherever they are found.

The passage sets out the penalty for killing a believer by accident. The killer must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim's family, unless they waive it. If the victim belongs to a hostile people, only the slave's freedom is required. If the victim's people are allied with the Muslims, blood-money and freedom are both required. A person who cannot afford a slave must fast for two months in a row.
Whoever deliberately kills a believer will receive hell as punishment, remaining there forever. God will be angry with that person, curse them, and prepare a great punishment for them.

Believers going out to fight are told to check carefully before judging others. They should not tell someone who greets them with peace that he is not a believer, just to seize the goods of this life. God has far greater spoils to give, and God knows what they do.

Believers who stay at home without risk and believers who strive in God's cause with their wealth and their lives are not treated the same. God gives those who strive a higher rank, a greater reward, forgiveness and mercy, though He promises good things to all.

Angels ask people who wronged themselves at death why they did not leave the land where they were oppressed. The people answer that they were too weak to act. The angels reply that God's earth was wide enough to flee. Those who could have escaped go to Hell, but the truly helpless men, women and children may be forgiven by God.

Anyone who leaves home to follow God and his messenger will find many other places and resources on earth, and God promises a sure reward even if death comes during the journey. The passage also says that soldiers at war may shorten their prayers if they fear an attack by unbelievers.

Muslims in battle are told how to pray in two groups, so that one group stands guard while the other prays. Each group keeps its weapons ready, because the unbelievers would like to catch them unarmed. Laying weapons down is allowed only in rain or sickness.

Believers are told to remember God at all times, keep up prayer at set hours, and not give up the pursuit of enemies, since they hope for God's reward where their enemies do not. The Book is sent down to judge fairly, and believers should not argue for the deceitful and should ask God for forgiveness.

God sees what people do even when they hide it from others, and He is present in their secret night talks. Those who plead for wrongdoers in this life cannot plead for them before God. Anyone who does wrong harms only himself, but God forgives those who repent and ask pardon.
Whoever commits a fault or crime, whether by accident or on purpose, and then blames an innocent person for it, takes on the guilt of slander and a clear wrong.

The passage tells the prophet Muhammad that God's grace protected him from a group who plotted to deceive him, though their scheme would only harm themselves. It says God gave him the Book and wisdom. It then states that most secret talk among these people is worthless, except talk that urges charity, what is right, or peace among people, and promises a great reward to whoever does this to please God.

Whoever turns away from the Prophet after the guidance has been made clear to him, and follows a path other than that of the believers, will be left to his own choice and sent to Hell. God will not forgive associating other gods with Him, though He forgives other sins to whomever He wills. Those who call on goddesses or on Satan have gone far astray.

Those who follow Satan instead of God are cursed and will be ruined. Satan says he will lead people astray, stir up their desires, and make them change God's creation, but his promises are only deceit. Such people will end up in Hell with no escape.

Believers who do right will enter gardens with flowing rivers and remain there forever, as God has promised. Wishes do not decide this, whether those of the believers or of the People of the Book (Jews and Christians). Those who do evil will be repaid for it and will find no protector besides God. Men and women alike who do right and believe will enter Paradise and will not be wronged at all.

The passage says that the best religion belongs to the person who submits fully to God, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham sincerely. It adds that God took Abraham as his friend, and that everything in heaven and earth belongs to God.

God answers questions about women and orphans, and the passage says that this instruction is already written in the Book. It tells believers to give orphan girls their proper legal share, not to refuse to marry them, to protect weak children, and to treat orphans fairly.

If a wife fears her husband will mistreat her or turn away from her, the two may settle things by mutual agreement, and that is best. Human souls tend toward greed, but acting kindly and fearing God is noticed by God.

A husband cannot treat all his wives exactly equally, however much he wishes to. He should not turn fully away from one wife so that she is left as if hanging. If the couple make peace and fear God, God forgives. If they separate, God will provide for both from His abundance.

Everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, who needs nothing and deserves praise. God told earlier peoples who received scripture, and the believers, to fear him, and says that even if people refuse belief, he remains rich and self-sufficient. He could replace humanity with others if he chose. Whoever wants worldly reward should know that God holds both this world's reward and the next.

Believers are told to stand firm for justice when giving testimony, even against themselves, their parents or relatives, and whether the person is rich or poor. They should not follow their desires, since that could make them turn from the truth. Twisting testimony or refusing to give it is known to God.

Believers are told to keep faith in God, his messenger, the scriptures, the angels and the Last Day. Anyone who rejects these has strayed far from the right path. People who repeatedly switch between belief and unbelief, growing ever more faithless, will not be forgiven or guided, and the hypocrites are warned of painful punishment.

God's revelation has already warned that when people mock His signs, believers should not sit with them until they change the subject, since otherwise the believers would become like them. God will gather such hypocrites and unbelievers together in Hell.

The passage describes hypocrites who act loyal to the believers when the believers win, and claim they were on the side of the unbelievers when the unbelievers succeed. It says God will judge them on the Day of Resurrection, and that they pray carelessly, only to be seen by people.

The passage warns believers not to take unbelievers as close friends, and says that hypocrites, people who waver between faith and unbelief, will be in the lowest part of hell. It makes an exception for those who repent, hold firmly to God, and are sincere in their faith; they will be counted among the faithful and receive a great reward.

Those who accept God but reject some of his messengers, believing in some and not others, are described as unbelievers who will face a shameful punishment. Those who believe in God and all his messengers equally will receive their reward.

The people of the Book ask for a written scripture to be sent down from heaven. The passage says they earlier asked Moses to show them God plainly, and it recalls that they then worshipped a calf after clear signs had come to them. It says God forgave them and gave Moses clear authority.

God made a covenant with the Israelites, lifting Mount Sinai over them and telling them to enter the gate humbly and not break the Sabbath. The passage says they broke this covenant, rejected God's signs, killed prophets, and spoke against Mary, so God sealed their hearts against belief.

The passage says that the people who claimed to have killed Jesus, son of Mary, did not in fact kill or crucify him. Someone only resembled him, and those who argued about it had no real knowledge, only guesses. God instead took Jesus up to Himself, and before death everyone of the People of the Book will believe in him.

God punishes certain Jews, as the passage describes it, for their wrongdoing. They turned many people away from God, and they took usury (lending money at interest), which they had been forbidden. Because of these sins, some good foods that had been allowed to them are now forbidden, and a painful punishment is prepared for the unbelievers among them.

The passage says that people of deep knowledge among the Jews and Christians, along with believers who accept both the revelation to Muhammad and earlier revelations, will receive a great reward. It then states that God revealed the message to Muhammad just as he revealed it to earlier prophets, including Noah, Abraham, Moses's brother Aaron, Jesus, and David.

God says he is the witness to the revelation sent to Muhammad, and the angels witness it too. Those who reject faith, turn others from God's way, or act wrongly will not be forgiven or guided, and will go to Hell forever.

A messenger has come to people with the truth from their Lord. The passage tells them to believe, since this is better for them. If they refuse, it says that everything in the heavens and earth still belongs to God, who knows all and is wise.

Addressing People of the Book (Jews and Christians), the passage tells them not to go beyond proper limits in their religion and to speak only the truth about God. It states that Jesus, son of Mary, is only God's messenger and servant, not God's son, and that God alone is one. It rejects the belief in a Trinity.

God will fully reward those who believe and do right, adding extra from His generosity. Those who are arrogant and proud will be severely punished, and they will find no one other than God to protect or help them.
God has sent people a clear proof and a clear light. Those who believe in God and hold firmly to Him will be brought into His mercy and grace and guided along a straight path to Himself.

The passage gives rules for inheritance when a person dies without children. A sister inherits half of the estate, and if there are two or more sisters, they share two-thirds. When there are both brothers and sisters, a brother receives the share of two sisters. God is said to make these rules clear so people do not go astray.

Divorce should happen at the wife's fixed waiting period, with the time counted exactly, and women should not be sent out of their homes or allowed to leave, except for proven adultery. Breaking these rules harms the person who breaks them. The passage also notes that God may bring the couple back together after this.

When a divorced woman's waiting period ends, a husband should either take her back kindly or let her go kindly, with witnesses called to confirm it. Those who fear God and trust in Him are promised a good outcome and provision, and God's purpose is fixed in time.

The passage sets the waiting period, called the 'idda, that a woman must observe after divorce. If she is past monthly bleeding, or has not yet had it, the period is three months, and a pregnant woman waits until she gives birth. It ends by promising God's ease and reward to those who fear Him.

Divorced women should be housed according to the husband's means and not treated harshly. If they are pregnant, he must support them until the birth, and if they nurse his children, he must pay them fairly. Each man should give according to what he has, since God asks only what He has provided.
Many cities rejected God's command and his messengers, so God judged them harshly and they suffered ruin for their own conduct. The passage closes by urging people of understanding to fear God.

God has sent a prophet to recite clear signs to believers, to lead those who believe and act rightly from darkness into light. Those who do so will enter gardens with flowing rivers and remain there forever. God created seven heavens and as many earths, and his command passes through them all, showing that he has power over all things and knows all things.

God forced the unbelieving People of the Book out of their homes, as he had done to those who came before. They had trusted their fortresses to protect them, but God brought fear into their hearts, and they tore down their own houses along with the believers. The passage ends by calling on people with understanding to take a lesson from this.

The passage describes God's punishment of a Jewish group who opposed God and his messenger. Their exile in this life spared them harsher punishment there, but they face the fire in the next world. It also says that cutting down some of their palm trees was permitted by God, and that the spoils taken from them went to the messenger without a battle.

Spoils taken from the people of the towns belong to God, his messenger, his relatives, orphans, the poor and travellers, so that wealth does not stay only with the rich. Poor refugees who were driven from their homes also have a share, and these are described as the truly virtuous.

The passage praises two groups of early Muslims. The people of Medina welcomed the refugees who came to them from Mecca, preferring them to themselves even when they were poor. Later believers pray that God will forgive them and their earlier brothers in faith, and keep hatred out of their hearts.

The passage describes hypocrites who promise their unbelieving allies among the Jews of Medina that they will stand by them if they are expelled or attacked. God says they are lying. If the allies were expelled or attacked, these hypocrites would not really help them, and if they did help, they would soon turn and flee, leaving them without support.

The passage says that the Jewish groups it describes will not fight openly, only from fortified towns or behind walls, and that their inner divisions make them weak. It compares their fate to that of earlier peoples who suffered for their deeds. It ends with an image of Satan who tempts a man to disbelieve, then disowns him, saying he fears God.

Believers are told to fear God and to consider what they are storing up for the future, since God knows all their deeds. Those who forget God are described as wrongdoers, and the people of Hell and the people of Paradise are not equal. The passage adds that if the Quran were sent down on a mountain, the mountain would humble itself out of fear of God.

The passage declares that God is the only god, and it lists His titles, such as King, Holy, Peaceful, Creator and Fashioner. It states that God is far above any partners people attribute to Him, and that everything in heaven and earth praises Him.

God says a person does not have two hearts, and that wives you divorce are not your mothers, and adopted sons are not your own sons. These are only things said with the mouth, while God speaks the truth and guides people rightly.

Adopted children should be called by their fathers' names, which the passage says is more right before God. If their fathers are unknown, they should be called brothers in the faith and companions. Mistakes made in this matter are not a sin unless made deliberately.

The passage says the Prophet stands closer to believers than they are to themselves, and that his wives are their mothers. It then says blood relatives are nearer to one another than other believers or those who fled their homeland for God's cause, and that God records every kindness shown to kin. It ends by recalling the covenant God made with earlier prophets.

The passage describes the siege of Medina, when enemy armies attacked from outside and the believers were badly shaken. It says God helped them, though they could not see his forces. It also says the faithful were tested, and that some people with weak faith or hidden doubt claimed that God and his messenger had only made false promises.

Some men in Medina told others to go home during the siege, saying their houses were unprotected and the city was not safe. The passage says this was only an excuse, since they simply wanted to run away. It adds that they had earlier promised God they would not turn their backs, and such a promise must be answered for.

Fleeing from battle will not save people, and any enjoyment they gain afterward will be brief. No one can shield them from God's will, whether it brings harm or mercy. God knows those who hinder others, who urge their brothers to join them, and who take little part in the fighting.

The passage describes hypocrites who were unwilling to fight. In danger they look anxiously at the believers, but once the threat passes they attack them with harsh words, eager for a share of the spoils. They would rather be far away among the desert Arabs, asking news of the believers, and they fought only a little even while present.

When the believers saw the enemy armies, they said this was what God and His Messenger had promised, and it made their faith and devotion stronger. Some believers kept their word to God, some died for it, and others are still waiting, without having changed. God will reward the faithful and may punish the hypocrites, or turn to them in mercy.

God brings the Jewish tribe that had helped the attackers down from their forts, frightens them, and gives their land and goods to the Muslims. The Prophet is then told to offer his wives a choice: if they want this worldly life and its finery, he will provide for them and release them honourably.

If the wives of the Prophet choose God, His Apostle and the next life, God promises them a great reward. Any of them who commits a proven lewdness will be punished twice as severely, while any who obeys God and the Apostle and does right will receive a double reward.

The passage tells the wives of the Prophet that they are not like other women. It advises them, if they fear God, not to speak in a overly soft or flattering way, so that a man with a corrupt heart does not desire them, and to speak in a modest, careful manner instead.

The passage tells the women of the Prophet's household to stay at home and not dress up and show themselves in public as women did in the time before Islam. It asks them to pray, give the required alms, and obey God and the Prophet. It says God wants to remove impurity from them and purify them, and it asks them to remember the revelations recited in their homes.

God promises forgiveness and a great reward to men and women who have these qualities: they submit to God, believe, are devout, truthful, patient, humble, give alms, fast, stay chaste, and often remember God.
A believer, whether man or woman, has no free choice once God and His Apostle (the Prophet Muhammad) have settled a matter. Anyone who disobeys God and the Apostle is clearly going astray.

This verse explains why the Prophet Muhammad married Zaynab, the former wife of his adopted son Zaid. It says the marriage was arranged so that believers would not be blamed for marrying the former wives of their adopted sons once those sons had divorced them. The Prophet had hidden his inner concern about this, though God was about to make it public.

The passage says that a prophet is not blamed for acting under a permission from God, as earlier prophets were not. It states that Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but is God's messenger and the last of the prophets. It ends by urging believers to remember God often, morning and evening.

God blesses believers and His angels pray for them, bringing them from darkness into light, and their greeting on the day they meet Him will be "Peace." The Prophet is sent as a witness, bringer of good news, warner, and a light calling people to God, so he is to announce great rewards to believers.
If a man divorces a believing woman before the marriage has been consummated, he owes her no waiting period. He should provide for her and let her go honourably.

The passage says that God has allowed the Prophet Muhammad certain marriages and women beyond the limits set for other believers. These include his existing wives who received a dowry, enslaved women from war booty, close female relatives who migrated with him to Medina, and any believing woman who offered herself to him. The text adds that these rules are a special privilege for him, and that God has set limits for other believers so that the Prophet is not blamed.

This verse gives the Prophet Muhammad permission to set aside or take to his bed whichever of his wives he chooses, including one he had earlier neglected. It says this will not be a wrong on his part, and that it will help the wives feel content. It ends by saying God knows what is in people's hearts.

It forbids the Prophet from taking any more wives from now on, or swapping his current wives for other women, even if those women are attractive. The only exception is slaves he owns. The verse ends by saying God sees everything.

Believers are told not to enter the Prophet's houses without permission, and not to stay for idle talk after a meal, since this troubles him. If they ask his wives for anything, they should speak from behind a veil. They must not marry the Prophet's wives after his death, which would be a serious wrong before God.

The passage says the Prophet's wives may speak without a veil to their close male relatives and to their women and enslaved men. It then tells believers to honor the Prophet with blessings and greetings, and says that those who insult God or His Messenger are cursed in this life and the next, and face a painful punishment.

Those who insult believing men and women without cause bear the guilt of slander and open wrong. The Prophet is told to bid his wives, daughters and the wives of believers to let their veils fall low, so they will be recognised and not insulted. If the hypocrites and troublemakers in Medina do not stop, they will be driven out and allowed to stay only a little while.

People ask when the Hour (the end of the world, the Day of Judgment) will come. The answer given is that only God knows. The passage then describes the punishment of unbelievers in the fire. They regret not obeying God and the messenger, and blame their leaders for leading them astray. They ask God to punish those leaders doubly.

God offered the Faith to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused it out of fear. Humans accepted the burden but acted unjustly and foolishly. Therefore God will punish hypocrites and those who associate other gods with God, while turning mercifully to believing men and women.

The hypocrites tell the Prophet that they bear witness he is God's messenger. God says He knows the truth, and that these people are liars. They use faith as a cover, turn others from God's way, and their hearts have been sealed so they cannot understand.

The passage describes hypocrites who look impressive and speak well, but are really enemies of the believers. They turn away when invited to seek the Prophet's forgiveness, so asking for forgiveness for them makes no difference, because God will not forgive them.

The passage describes a group called the Hypocrites, who say that money should not be spent on Muhammad's followers in Medina, because those followers will then leave him. It answers that all wealth belongs to God, that real power belongs to God, his messenger and the believers, and it warns believers not to let wealth and children make them forget God.

Believers are urged to give from what they have before death comes. The passage describes a dying person asking for a little more time to give charity and live righteously, and it says God will not delay a soul once its appointed hour has arrived.

The passage sets punishments for sexual sin and for false accusations of it. An unmarried man or woman who commits fornication is to receive a hundred lashes, and believers should not show pity in carrying this out. Such people may marry only others of the same kind, and anyone who accuses a virtuous woman without four witnesses gets eighty lashes and is never again accepted as a witness.

If a husband accuses his wife of adultery but has no witnesses, the procedure is that he swears four times that he speaks the truth, then calls God's curse on himself if he lies. The wife can avoid punishment by swearing four times that he lies, then calling God's wrath on herself if he is telling the truth.

This passage deals with the accusation of adultery made against a woman of the Prophet's household, known as the "lie" of Sura 24. It tells believers not to see the slander as harmful to them, and says the accusers must bring four witnesses. Without witnesses, the accusers are liars before God.

This passage rebukes believers for spreading an unverified accusation with their tongues, treating it as minor when it was serious in God's eyes. It says they should have rejected such talk at once, calling it a gross slander, and warns them never to repeat it.

Believers are warned not to follow Satan, since he urges what is shameful and wrong. The passage says that God's goodness and mercy are the reason anyone is cleansed, and that God grants purity to whom He chooses.

Wealthy believers should not swear to stop giving to relatives, the poor, and those who fled their homes for God's cause. They should forgive instead, and hope God forgives them. Those who falsely accuse virtuous women of carelessness will be cursed and punished, and their own tongues, hands, and feet will testify against them.

Bad women are matched with bad men, and good women with good men. Believers are also told not to enter other people's houses without first asking permission and greeting the occupants. If no one answers, or they are told to go back, they must leave.

It is permitted to enter uninhabited houses when you have a need for them, because God knows both open and hidden actions. Believers are told to lower their gaze and keep their chastity, which the passage says will make them more pure.

Believing women are told to lower their gaze, keep modest, and not show their adornments, except to close male relatives, other women, their slaves, certain male servants without sexual desire, and children who are not yet aware of women's bodies. They should also not stamp their feet so that hidden ornaments are heard or seen.
God urges believers to marry those among them who are single, along with their good male and female servants. If these people are poor, God will make them rich out of his generosity.

People who cannot marry should keep chaste until God enriches them. Masters who are asked for a deed of freedom for their slaves should grant it if they see good in them, and should give them some of their wealth. Masters must not force slave women into prostitution for profit, if the women want to stay modest. If someone is forced, God forgives them.

God has sent down clear signs, along with an example from earlier peoples and a warning for those who fear God. The verse says these are given as guidance and a lesson for believers who are mindful of God.

God is described as the light of heaven and earth, and His light is compared to a lamp in a niche, glowing through glass and fed by olive oil. The passage says God guides whom He wills to this light, and that people praise Him in the temples where His name is remembered.

Men who are not distracted by trade or business from remembering God, from prayer, and from giving the set alms, because they fear the Day of Judgment. God will reward them for their best deeds and give them more from His generosity, since He provides without limit to whom He wills.

Unbelievers' deeds are compared to two images. First, a mirage that a thirsty traveler mistakes for water, and finds to be nothing when he reaches it. Second, darkness on a deep sea under layered waves and clouds, where a man cannot see his own hand. The point is that those without God's light have none at all.

Everything in heaven and on earth praises God, even birds in flight. Each creature knows its own way of prayer and praise, and God knows what they do. God rules the heavens and the earth, and all things will finally return to him.

God drives clouds along, gathers them, and piles them up until rain falls from within them. He sends down hail-laden clouds like mountains, striking whom He wills and turning it away from whom He wills. His lightning is so bright it nearly blinds.

God alternates day and night and created all moving animals, showing His power, and He sends clear signs. He guides whom He wills. Some who claim belief and obedience then turn away; the passage says they are not truly faithful, and that if the truth were on their side they would come to God willingly.

Those who refuse to accept God's and the Prophet's judgment are described as diseased in heart, doubting, or unjust toward themselves. True believers answer a call to judgment by saying, "We have heard, and we obey," and such obedience and fear of God bring success and happiness.

Some people swear strong oaths that they will go out to fight when the Prophet calls them. The reply is that obedience is worth more than such oaths. The Prophet's duty is only to deliver the message clearly. Those who obey will be guided, and those who turn away carry their own responsibility.

God promises believers who do right that they will inherit the land as earlier peoples did, that their faith will be firmly established, and that their fear will turn to safety. They are told to worship God alone, keep prayer and charity, and obey the Prophet, so that they may receive mercy.
Unbelievers should not think they can get the better of God on earth. Their home will be the Fire, which is a very bad destination.

Believers are told that household slaves and children who have not yet reached adulthood must ask permission before entering a room at three set times: before the dawn prayer, at midday when people take off their outer clothes, and after the evening prayer. These are times of privacy. Outside those times, entering without asking is allowed, since people move around the house attending to one another.

Once children reach puberty, they should ask permission before entering a room where their parents are, just as older people have had to do. The verse adds that God makes his commands clear in this way.

Older women who are past having children and have no prospect of marriage are not blamed for taking off their outer garments, provided they do not display their adornments. It is still better for them to keep the garments on, and God hears and knows all things.

It says that people are not blamed for eating at certain homes without special permission. These include the homes of the blind, lame or sick, one's own house, close relatives, and the house of a friend. People may eat together or separately without fault.
When people enter a house, they should greet one another with a good and blessed greeting, presented as coming from God. God makes His signs clear in this way so that people may understand them.

True believers are those who believe in God and His Messenger, and who do not leave a shared community matter until they have his permission. When they ask leave for their own private affairs, the Prophet may grant it as he sees fit, and he is asked to pray for their forgiveness.

God tells believers not to call the Prophet by everyday names, as they call one another. He knows who quietly slips away from gatherings, hiding behind others. Those who disobey his command are warned of trouble, and everyone will one day be brought before God to account for their deeds.

A woman brings her complaint against her husband to the Prophet, and God hears it. The passage then says that a man who divorces his wife by saying she is to him like his mother's back is not making her his mother. Only the women who gave birth to them are their mothers. Such words are called blameworthy and false, though God forgives.

Men who divorce their wives by the formula of zihar (declaring the wife to be like their mother) and then wish to take back their words must first free a slave before they may resume marriage. God says this is a warning they must follow, and he knows what they do.

This passage sets out a penalty for those who cannot free a slave: they must fast two months in a row before the couple come together again, or, if they cannot fast, feed sixty poor men. It then warns that those who reject God and His messenger will be humbled and punished.
God will raise all people to life on a day of judgment and tell them what they did. God has already recorded all their deeds, even those they have forgotten, and God sees everything.

God knows everything in heaven and on earth. Whenever a few people speak together in private, God is present with them as well, and on the Day of Resurrection He will tell them what they did, because He knows all things.

Some people secretly plot together in wickedness and hostility toward the Prophet, even after being told to stop. When they meet him they greet him in a way that God does not, and they wonder among themselves why God does not punish them for their words. The passage says their reward is Hell.

Believers should keep their private conversations free from wickedness, hatred and disobedience to the Prophet, and speak with justice and fear of God. Secret talk of that kind comes from Satan, who wants to cause believers grief, but he can harm them only with God's permission, so believers should trust in God.

The passage tells believers to make room for others in their gatherings and to rise when asked, with the promise that God will raise up those who believe and those given knowledge. Before a private meeting with the Prophet, they should give charity first, which is better and purer for them; if they cannot afford it, God is forgiving.

The passage first tells believers to give alms before private talks with the Prophet, or else to keep prayer, charity and obedience to God and His Apostle, since God knows their actions. It then condemns hypocrites who befriend people God is angry with, swear falsely, and use their faith as a cover while leading others away from God. They are promised a severe punishment.

Wealth and children will not help these people against God, and they will end up in the fire. On the Day of Resurrection they will swear falsely to God, as they swear to people now, thinking it will help them. Satan has taken control of them and made them forget God, so they belong to his party, which is lost forever.
Those who oppose God and His messenger will be among the most humiliated. God has decreed that He and His messengers will surely win. God is strong and mighty.

Believers do not love anyone who opposes God and His Messenger, even close family members. God marks such believers in their hearts, strengthens them with His Spirit, and promises them gardens with flowing rivers. They are called God's party, and they are described as pleased with God and God pleased with them.

On the day of judgment, mothers will abandon their nursing babies and pregnant women will miscarry, and people will look drunk though they are not, because God's punishment is so severe. The passage also warns that a man who argues about God without knowledge, following a rebellious Satan, will be led by him into the fire of Hell.

Humans are told that God created them in stages, from dust to a fully formed body, and controls each stage, from birth through old age to death. The passage says this shows God's power, and it compares this to dry land that springs to life after rain. The argument is aimed at people who doubt that the dead will be raised.

The passage describes two kinds of people who turn away from God. The first mislead others and will face disgrace now and burning torment later, because God is not unjust. The second serve God only when things go well, and when trouble comes they turn to unbelief, losing both worlds. Such people call on things that can neither help nor harm them.

God will bring believers who do right into gardens with flowing rivers. The passage then says that anyone who thinks God will not help His messenger in this world or the next should try to reach the sky by a rope and cut it, to see whether his schemes can undo what angers him. It ends by saying God sends the Quran with clear signs and guides whom He wills.

God will judge between all the religious groups named here, believers, Jews, Sabeans, Christians, Magians and those who associate other gods with God, on the Day of Resurrection. The passage adds that all things in heaven and earth bow to God, though many people still deserve punishment, and God does as He wills.

Believers and unbelievers are described as two sides arguing about their Lord. For the unbelievers, the passage describes fiery garments, boiling water poured on their heads, and iron maces. They will try to escape the anguish of the fire, but they will be forced back into it and told to taste the burning.
God rewards believers who do right with gardens, rivers, gold, pearls and silk. Those who reject faith, lead others away from God, or try to desecrate the Holy Mosque will face a severe punishment.

God told Abraham to set apart the House (the Kaba, a shrine) for worship of God alone, for people who walk around it and pray there. He then calls all peoples to make a pilgrimage to it, so they can see its benefits, name God over sacrificed animals, and share the meat with the poor.

Believers should honor God's sacred rules and avoid idols and false speech, staying true to God alone. Eating cattle is permitted, except for the animals already named. Anyone who joins other gods with God is compared to something falling from the sky and snatched away by birds or blown far off, meaning they are utterly lost.

God gave every community its own rites, including naming God over the animals sacrificed. He is the one God, so people should submit to Him. Those who are humble, who tremble when God is mentioned, who endure hardships, pray, and give charity are the ones to receive good news.

Camels are given as offerings to God, and God's name is to be spoken over them when they are slaughtered. The meat is to be eaten and shared with the poor and with those who ask. God's gift is for thanks, and what reaches God is not the meat or blood but piety.

God permits fighting in defense of those who were driven from their homes only for saying "Our Lord is God." He says that without this defense, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques, where God's name is remembered, would be destroyed. God promises to help those who help Him, and those He establishes in the land will pray, give alms, and promote good and forbid evil.

God tells the listener that earlier peoples also called their prophets liars, naming Noah, Ad, Thamud, Abraham, Lot, Midian and Moses. God says He was patient with the unbelievers for a long time, then punished them, destroying cities, wells and castles.

God asks whether the doubters have not travelled the land and seen what happened to past peoples, and whether they lack hearts and ears to understand. The problem, it says, is blind hearts, not blind eyes. God will not fail His threat of punishment, and those who work against His signs will end up in Hell.

Every messenger sent before Muhammad was, in the same way, subject to Satan putting wrong desires into his mind. God then cancels what Satan suggested and makes it firm that His revelations stand. The wrong suggestions become a test for people whose hearts are diseased or hardened, who are wicked and far from the truth.

Those who have been given knowledge will recognise the Qur'an as the truth from God and will believe in it. Unbelievers will keep doubting until the Hour arrives suddenly or a day of punishment comes. On that day God alone rules and judges, and believers who do right will enter gardens of delight.

Those who left their homes for God's cause and were then killed or died will be given a good provision and admitted to a place that pleases them. The passage then says that anyone who takes exact revenge for a wrong done to them, and is wronged again, will be helped by God.

God controls the cycle of night and day, and He is the truth, while the false gods people call upon besides Him are empty. The passage gives as proof God's power over nature, such as sending rain that makes the earth green, and His ownership of everything in heaven and earth.

God made the earth, the sea and the sky work for people, and holds up the heaven so it does not fall. He gives life and death, yet people are ungrateful. Each community has its own rituals. If they argue, the speaker should call them to God and leave the judgment to God.

God knows everything in heaven and on earth, and this is written in the Book and is easy for Him. The passage then condemns those who worship others beside God, things for which God has given no authority and about which they have no knowledge, saying such wrongdoers will have no helper.

When God's clear verses are recited to unbelievers, they show scorn and nearly attack those reciting them. The speaker asks if he should name something worse: the fire God has promised to those who do not believe, a grim destination.

The passage argues that the beings people pray to besides God have no power at all. They cannot even create a fly, and cannot get back what a fly takes from them. It says God alone is powerful, hears and sees everything, and chooses messengers from angels and men.
God calls believers to strive for His cause as they should. He has chosen them, placed no hardship on them in their religion, which is the faith of their father Abraham, and named them Muslims.

The passage says that the Apostles will act as witnesses against the believers, and the believers will be witnesses to the rest of mankind. So the believers should keep up prayer, pay the required alms, and hold firmly to God, who is described as their lord and helper.

God sends a feeling of calm into the believers' hearts so that their faith grows stronger. He then promises believing men and women gardens with flowing rivers where they will live forever, and forgiveness of their wrongs. The passage calls this the greatest reward from God.

God will punish hypocrites and those who join other gods with Him, and who think evil of Him, and He has prepared Hell for them. The passage then says the Prophet was sent as a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner, so that people will believe in God and His Apostle and honour and praise Him.

Those who pledge loyalty to the Prophet are, in fact, pledging it to God, and God's hand is over their hands. Anyone who breaks the pledge harms only himself, while anyone who keeps it will receive a great reward from God.

Some Arabs who stayed behind from the military expedition ask the Prophet to pray for their forgiveness, though their words do not match their hearts. The passage answers that no one can protect them from God's will, and that God knows what they really did. It says they had secretly expected the Prophet and the believers never to return, and were pleased by that.
God owns the heavens and the earth. He forgives whom He chooses and punishes whom He chooses, and He is gracious and merciful.

Some who stayed behind from the expedition now ask to join the group when spoils of war are to be taken. The Prophet is told to answer that they may not follow, because God has already decided this. The passage says they are foolish to claim the others are simply jealous.

God tells the desert Arabs who stayed behind from earlier campaigns that they will be called to fight a very strong people. They must either fight or accept Islam. Obedience brings a good reward, while turning back again brings severe punishment.

The blind, the lame and the sick are excused from going to battle. Those who obey God and His messenger are promised gardens with rivers, while those who turn back face severe punishment. God is described as pleased with the believers who pledged loyalty under the tree, and He rewards them with calm, a quick victory and plunder.

God promises the believers rich plunder, some already given and more still to come. He says that if unbelievers fight them, they will be defeated and get no help. This is God's unchanging way of acting.
God stopped both sides from fighting each other in the valley of Mecca, after giving the believers victory over their opponents. The verse adds that God sees everything people do.

God kept the believers from fighting the unbelievers at Mecca, because some believing men and women lived among the enemy and could have been harmed by mistake. Had the two groups been fully separated, God would have punished the unbelievers severely. God chose to hold back, so He could bring whomever He wills into His mercy.

God sent His peace down on the Prophet and the believers after the unbelievers had filled their hearts with angry, ignorant fury. He also made the word of piety firm in them, because they deserved it. The passage adds that God knows all things.

God confirms that the Prophet's dream, in which his followers entered the sacred Mosque in safety, will come true, and that a quick victory is also promised. God sent him with guidance and the true religion so that it would rise above all others.

Muhammad is God's messenger, and his followers are firm against those who reject faith but kind to one another. They are shown bowing and praying to God, and they are compared to a seed that grows strong and stands tall, which pleases the farmer and angers the unbelievers. God promises forgiveness and a great reward to those among them who believe and do good.
The Prophet is asked why he has forbidden himself something God has made lawful, done only to please his wives. The verse says God is merciful and has allowed him to release himself from his oaths.

The Prophet told one of his wives a secret, and she passed it on. God revealed this to him, and he confronted her about part of it. He then warns the two wives that if they turn back to God in repentance their hearts can be forgiven, but if they plot against him, God, Gabriel, faithful believers and angels will protect the Prophet.

The passage first warns that if the Prophet divorced his wives, God would give him better replacements, described as devout, obedient believers. It then calls believers to protect themselves and their families from a fire fueled by men and stones, guarded by strong angels who obey God exactly. It ends by telling unbelievers that they will be repaid for their deeds.

Believers are urged to turn sincerely to God, so that their wrongs may be forgiven and they may enter gardens with rivers. On that day God will not shame the Prophet or his followers, and their light will go before them as they pray for perfection and pardon. The passage ends by ordering the Prophet to fight unbelievers and hypocrites, whose end is Hell.

God offers two examples. Noah's wife and Lot's wife betrayed their righteous husbands, so their husbands could not save them from God. Pharaoh's wife is a model for believers: she asked God for a house in Paradise and for rescue from Pharaoh and the wicked.
Mary, daughter of Imran, is praised here for keeping her virginity. God breathed of His spirit into her womb, and she believed in her Lord's words and scriptures and was among the devout.

Believers are told not to make friends with those who oppose their faith and have driven them out, and not to show them secret kindness. Such people are their enemies, who would harm them with hands and tongues and want them to return to unbelief. Anyone who does this has strayed from the right path.
On the day of resurrection, family ties will not help a person. That day will separate people from one another, and God sees what each one has done.

Abraham and his followers told their people that they cut ties with them and with the false gods they worshipped, and that enmity would last until the people believed in God alone. Believers are told not to copy Abraham's promise to pray for his unbelieving father, since he could not win God's forgiveness for him. The closing prayer asks God for trust, forgiveness, and protection from being tested by unbelievers.

Believers are told that Abraham and those with him were a good example for anyone who hopes in God and the last day. Whoever turns away does not harm God, who needs nothing. God may create friendship between the believers and those they count as enemies, since God is powerful and merciful.

God does not forbid kindness and fairness toward people who have not fought against you over your religion or forced you from your homes. But God forbids making friends with those who fought you for your religion, drove you out, and helped others do so.

Believing women who flee to the Muslims must be tested on their faith. If their belief is confirmed, they must not be returned to the unbelievers, and the marriage ties with unbelieving husbands end. The husbands are repaid the dowers they paid, and the Muslim men who marry these women must pay their dowers.

If a wife leaves her husband and goes over to the unbelievers, and the Muslims later capture goods from them, the husband is to be repaid from that spoil the amount he paid as her dowry. The verse ends by telling believers to keep their duty to God.

When believing women come to the Prophet and promise not to worship other gods, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, or make false accusations, or to disobey him in what is right, he is told to accept their pledge and ask God to forgive them. Believers are also told not to make friends with people God is angry with, who have lost hope in the afterlife.

Believers are told not to raise their voices above the Prophet's voice or speak loudly to him as they do to one another, or their deeds may be wasted without their knowing. Those who speak quietly before him are promised forgiveness and a great reward. Those who shout at him from outside his private rooms are said to lack understanding, and waiting patiently for him to come out would be better for them.
Believers are told that if a wrongdoer brings them news, they should check it immediately. Otherwise they might harm others out of ignorance and later regret what they have done.

The passage tells believers that the Prophet is among them, and that if he gave in to them on many matters they would fall into sin. It says God made faith dear to them and made unbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful, and that this right course comes from God's grace.

If two groups of believers fight each other, others should make peace between them. If one side keeps wronging the other, fight that side until it returns to God's commands, then make a fair peace. Believers are brothers, so keep peace among them and fear God.

Believers are told not to mock one another, men or women, since the person mocked may be better than the mocker. They must also not slander each other or use insulting nicknames. Calling someone wicked after they have accepted the faith is wrong, and those who do not stop are wrongdoers.

Believers are told to avoid much suspicion, since some suspicion is sinful, and not to spy on one another or speak badly of someone who is absent. The passage compares backbiting to eating the flesh of a dead brother, something people would hate, and ends by urging fear of God, who is forgiving and merciful.

People were created from one male and one female, and divided into nations and tribes so that they would come to know one another. In God's sight, the most honoured person is the one who is most conscious of Him.

Some desert Arabs claim to believe, but the passage says they have only submitted to Islam, since faith has not yet entered their hearts. Real believers are those who trust God and His Messenger without doubt and give their wealth and selves in God's cause. God, who knows all things, does not need to be taught about religion.

Some people mock the Prophet for having become Muslims. He tells them not to count their conversion as a favour to him. Instead, God has guided them to the faith, and that is the real favour, if they are sincere. God knows all hidden things and sees what they do.
Travel freely through the land for four months, the verse says, but know that you cannot escape God's power. It adds that God will bring shame on those who do not believe.

God and His Apostle announce on the day of the greater pilgrimage that God is free of any bond with those who worship other gods. Those who turn to God gain by it, while those who turn away cannot weaken God, and unbelievers are promised a severe punishment.

Polytheists who have kept their treaty with the Muslims and have not helped anyone against them are to be honoured in the agreement until its term ends. The passage says God loves those who fear Him, meaning those who keep their word.

After the sacred months end, the passage tells believers to fight polytheists wherever they find them, but to spare those who convert, pray and pay alms. A polytheist who asks for protection is to be granted it so he can hear God's word, then sent safely to his home.

The passage asks how idolaters can keep a treaty with God and his messenger, except those who made a pact at the Sacred Mosque. It says Muslims should keep faith with such people as long as those people keep faith with them. It warns that the idolaters would not respect ties of kinship or faith if they gained power over the Muslims, and that they speak fairly but mean otherwise.

If the enemies repent, pray, and pay the tax, they become fellow believers. But if they break their oaths and attack the faith, the believers should fight their leaders, because such people keep no binding oath. The verse asks why the believers would fear these enemies when God deserves more fear.

The passage tells believers to fight those who oppose them, saying God will punish them, grant victory, and heal the hearts of believers. It then says God knows who among the believers strive bravely and take no allies apart from God, His Apostle, and the faithful.

Only those who believe in God and the Last Day, pray, give the required alms, and fear God alone should visit God's temples, according to this passage. People who worship other gods alongside God, and so mark themselves as unbelievers, are not to visit them. Their works are called vain, and they will remain in the fire forever.

Those who give drink to pilgrims and care for the sacred temple are not equal, in God's eyes, to those who believe in God and the last day and fight in God's way. Those who believed, left their homes, and struggled with their wealth and persons for God's path hold the highest rank with God, and their Lord promises them mercy, pleasure, and lasting gardens.

Believers are told not to take their fathers or brothers as close friends if those relatives prefer unbelief to faith. Anyone who does take such relatives as friends in that case is said to be doing wrong.

The passage tells believers that if family, wealth, trade and homes mean more to them than God, His messenger and striving in God's cause, they should wait for God's judgment. It then recalls past battles where God helped them, and the defeat at Honein, where their numbers did not save them and they fled.

After a battle, God sent calm to the Prophet and the believers and punished the unbelievers. God may still forgive whom He wills. Believers are told that those who join other gods to God are unclean and must not approach the sacred Temple after this year. If they fear poverty, God can provide for them from His abundance.

Believers are told to fight people of earlier scriptures (Jews and Christians) who do not believe in God and the last day, and who do not follow what God and his messenger forbade, until they pay a tax and submit. The passage also condemns the claims that Ezra and the Messiah are sons of God.

The passage says that people have taken their religious teachers, monks and the Messiah (Jesus, son of Mary) as gods alongside God, though they were told to worship one God only. It then states that God alone is worthy of glory, that God will complete His light and make His guidance and true religion prevail over all others, even though those who associate partners with God dislike this.

Many religious teachers and monks take people's money in vain and lead them away from God's way. Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it for God's cause will be punished in hell: their treasure will be heated and used to brand their foreheads, sides and backs.

The passage sets the year at twelve months, counted by God's book from the time of creation, and says four of them are sacred. It then tells believers not to wrong themselves in those months, and to fight those who join other gods with God, as those enemies fight them.

The passage condemns a practice of moving a sacred month to a different time of the year. It says this shifting is a form of unbelief, that it leads people into error, and that they adjust the calendar to keep the number of sacred months while breaking the ones God set apart.

Believers are rebuked for being reluctant to march out "on the Way of God," that is, to join the fighting. They are told that worldly life is small compared with the next life. If they refuse, God will punish them and replace them with another people, and God needs nothing from them.

The passage recalls how God helped the Prophet Muhammad when his enemies forced him to leave Mecca, and he hid in a cave with one companion, who was afraid. God calmed the Prophet and sent unseen help, so the unbelievers' cause was brought low. It then urges believers to go out to fight and to give their money and their lives for God's cause.

Some people stayed behind when the Muslims were called to go on a military campaign, claiming they could not go. The passage says God knows they were lying, and it rebukes the Prophet for excusing them before the truth was clear. True believers, it says, do not ask to be excused from fighting with their wealth and their lives.

The passage says that people who do not truly believe in God and the Last Day ask leave to stay home from fighting. It adds that, had they gone to war, they would only have caused trouble and stirred up discord among the believers. God, it says, held them back and knows those who do wrong.

Some people who opposed the community tried to cause trouble and disrupt its affairs, but the truth prevailed and God's command became clear. Some of them ask to stay home to avoid being tested. When good things happen to the believers, these people are upset; when harm comes, they say they had prepared beforehand and walk away pleased. The reply is that only what God has decreed can happen, so believers should trust Him alone.

The passage is a message told to the Prophet to say to opponents. Believers wait for one of two good outcomes, victory or martyrdom, while the opponents wait for God's punishment. It also says that offerings made by these people are not accepted, because they do not truly believe in God and His Messenger and give offerings and prayer only unwillingly.

The passage says that the wealth and children of certain people should not impress the Prophet, because God lets these things be a means of punishing them in this life. It says they swear they belong to the believers but are really people who fear them and would flee to hide if they could. It adds that some of them criticise the Prophet over the distribution of charity, being pleased when they receive a share and angry when they do not.

It expresses a wish that people would be content with what God and His Messenger have given them. It says they should trust that God will grant them more from His favour, and turn their requests to God alone.

Alms (charity) are to go to specific groups: the poor, the needy, those who collect the alms, new converts, captives being ransomed, debtors, the cause of God, and travelers. Some people mock the Prophet by calling him "all ear," and the reply is that he listens to good and is a mercy to believers, while those who insult him will be punished.

Those who oppose God and His messenger face the fire of Hell forever. The hypocrites fear that a revelation will expose their secret thoughts. When questioned, they claim they were only joking. The passage answers that mocking God, His signs and His messenger is unbelief, and that some will be punished for their wrongdoing.

Hypocritical men and women are alike in their conduct. They command wrong, forbid right, and withhold their hands from giving. Because they have forgotten God, God has forgotten them, and they are promised the fire of Hell and a lasting curse.

The passage tells listeners that they are repeating the behaviour of earlier peoples, who were stronger and richer but enjoyed their share of worldly life and talked in the same way. It says that the works of such people are worthless both in this world and in the next, and that they are lost.

Earlier peoples were sent messengers with clear proof, and God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves. Believing men and women, by contrast, support one another, call for what is right, forbid what is wrong, pray, give the required alms, and obey God and His Messenger. God will show them mercy.

God promises believers, men and women, gardens with flowing rivers where they will live forever, and God's approval will be the greatest reward. The passage then tells the Prophet to struggle against unbelievers and hypocrites, and says Hell will be their home.

The passage describes people who swore they had not said something against Islam, though it says they did speak words of unbelief. It says they plotted and resented the wealth God and His messenger gave them. It warns that if they repent it will be better for them, but if they return to their sin they will be punished. It also mentions some who promised to give alms if God made them rich.

God punishes certain hypocrites for breaking their promise to Him and for lying. He knows their secret thoughts and private talk. He also punishes those who mock believers who give to charity, even the poor who can give only a little, with a painful punishment.
Muhammad is told that asking God to forgive certain people makes no difference. Even seventy prayers for forgiveness would not win them pardon, because they do not believe in God and His Messenger.

Some people stayed home instead of joining the fight for God's cause, and told others not to march in the heat. The reply is that the fire of Hell will be hotter, and that they will laugh little and weep much for what they have done.

Muhammad is told to refuse permission to those who stayed behind from the fighting and now ask to join later. They are to be left behind, and Muhammad must not pray over them when they die or stand at their graves, because they did not believe in God and His messenger. Their wealth and children are not to impress him, since God uses these only to punish them in this life.

Some wealthy men asked to be excused from fighting and to stay at home with those who stayed behind. The passage says those men have hearts sealed so they do not understand. It contrasts them with the Apostle and believers, who fight with their wealth and their persons, and it promises them good things, including gardens with rivers.

Some desert Arabs came to ask to be excused from going to war, and others who had opposed God and His Messenger stayed home. The passage warns that a severe punishment awaits those among them who do not believe.
