The weak, the sick, and those with no means to give money or supplies do not sin by staying home from a campaign, as long as they are sincere toward God and his messenger. Those who came asking for a mount and were turned away, weeping because they had nothing to contribute, are also not to be blamed.

Those who are wealthy but still ask to be excused from going to war are the ones open to blame. They prefer to stay behind with those who remain, and the text says God has sealed their hearts so they have no understanding.

Some people who stayed behind from a military campaign will make excuses when the believers return. The reply is that their excuses will not be believed, because God has already told the believers about them. God and His Apostle will see their actions, and they will be judged. The believers are told to keep away from them, since they are unclean and will end up in Hell.

Bedouin Arabs of the desert are described as especially firm in disbelief and hypocrisy, probably because they do not know the laws God sent to his Messenger. Some of them treat their contributions to God's cause as a forced tax and wait for a turn of fortune against the believers, but a bad change will fall on them instead.

Some of the desert Arabs believe in God and the Last Day, and they count the alms they give as a way to draw near to God and to the Prophet's prayers for them. The passage says these alms do bring them close, and that God will admit them to His mercy.

God is pleased with the first believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and with those who follow them in good conduct, and they are pleased with God. He promises them gardens with flowing rivers, where they will remain forever.

Some desert Arabs and people of Medina are described as hypocrites, though God knows them even if Muhammad does not. Others who have admitted their wrongs, mixing good deeds with bad, may be forgiven. Muhammad is told to take alms from them to purify them and to pray for them, and his prayers will settle their minds.

God accepts repentance from those who turn back to Him and accepts charity. People are told to keep working, since God, His messenger and the believers will see their deeds, and all will be brought before God to be told of them. Others must wait for God's decision, whether He punishes them or turns to them in mercy.

The passage contrasts two mosques. One was built to cause division among believers and to support an enemy of God and His messenger, and its builders falsely claim good intentions, so the Prophet is told never to enter it. The other, founded on piety from its first day, is the better place for him to pray, because its people seek purity.

The passage compares two kinds of building. One is set on the fear of God and the wish to please Him, and it stands firm. The other is set on the edge of a bank that floods wash away, so it falls into the fire. It says the wrongdoers' structure will keep causing them unease until their hearts are broken.

God says he has bought the lives and property of believers in exchange for Paradise. They will fight and be killed for his cause, a promise recorded in earlier scriptures and in the Qur'an. Believers are told to rejoice in this agreement, which they call the great bliss.

The passage first praises believers who turn to God, worship, fast, pray, do good and avoid evil, and then tells the faithful to announce good news to them. It also forbids the prophet and believers from asking God to forgive people who associate other beings with God, even relatives, once it is clear those people are destined for Hell.

Abraham asked forgiveness for his father only because he had promised to do so. When he learned that his father was God's enemy, he cut himself off from him. The passage then says God does not lead people astray after guiding them, and that God alone has power over life and death.

God turns back in mercy to the Prophet, to the Muslims who fled with him (the refugees), and to the Medinan helpers (the Ansars) who stood by him in a hard time, even though some of them had nearly lost heart.

God turns back toward three believers who had stayed behind and were left in deep distress, until they turned back to God, having no refuge except Him. The passage then urges believers to fear God and stay with the sincere.

Believers who go out for God's cause, enduring thirst, hunger, hardship, or any step that angers the unbelievers, are credited with a good deed for each one. Their alms and crossings of rivers are also recorded, and God will reward them with more than they have done.

The passage says two things. Not every believer must join a campaign, because some should stay behind to learn their religion and teach their people. It also tells believers to fight nearby unbelievers firmly, and says that new revelations strengthen the faith of believers while some others mock them.

Some people glance at each other when a new chapter is revealed and slip away, as if they do not want to be seen. The passage says God will turn their hearts away because they lack understanding. It then says the messenger cares deeply for believers, and tells him to rely on God if they refuse.

Believers are told to keep their promises and to respect certain sacred things. Cattle meat is allowed, except game animals while on pilgrimage. Neither the rites of God, the sacred month, the offerings, nor those travelling to the sacred house may be violated.

After the pilgrimage rites are finished, believers may hunt again. They are told not to act out of hatred toward those who blocked them from the sacred mosque, and to help one another in goodness and piety rather than in evil and malice. They should fear God, who punishes severely.

The passage lists kinds of meat that are forbidden to believers: animals that died on their own, blood, pork, animals offered to any name other than God's, animals strangled, struck, fallen, gored, or mauled by beasts (unless slaughtered in time), and animals sacrificed on stone altars. Dividing meat by arrow lots is also called impiety. It ends by warning against those who abandon the religion and saying to fear God alone.

God declares that he has completed the religion for believers and that Islam is his chosen faith for them. He also allows a person who is forced by hunger to break food rules, provided he does not do so out of deliberate wrongdoing, and promises forgiveness and mercy.

The passage says that good things are permitted to believers, including game caught by trained hunting animals such as dogs. The hunter may eat what these animals catch, provided he speaks God's name over it, and he is told to fear God, who is swift to call people to account.

The passage says that good foods are now allowed, including the food of Jews and Christians, and that Muslim men may marry believing women and virtuous women from earlier scriptural communities. The marriage must be done properly, with a dowry paid and without immorality. It ends by saying that the deeds of anyone who rejects the faith will come to nothing, and that such a person will be lost in the next life.
Believers are told that before they pray they must wash their faces, hands up to the elbows, and feet up to the ankles, and wipe their heads. This is the ritual washing required before prayer.

If a person is ritually unclean and cannot find water, they may wash with clean sand instead, rubbing the face and hands. God does not want to burden people, but wants to purify them, so that they will be grateful. The passage ends by urging fear of God, who knows the innermost thoughts. Word count: about 50.

Believers are told to stand firmly for justice toward God, even when they feel hostility toward someone, since acting fairly is closer to piety. God knows their actions. Those who believe and do right receive forgiveness and a great reward, while those who reject God's signs are destined for Hell.
Believers are told to remember that God protected them when some people tried to attack them, and God stopped their hands. Because of this, they should fear God and put their trust in him.

God made a covenant, or agreement, with the Israelites and chose twelve leaders from among them. God promised to stay with them and forgive their wrongs, and to bring them into gardens with rivers, if they prayed, gave charity, believed in God's messengers and helped them, and gave generously to God. Whoever did not believe after this, the passage says, had lost the right path.

The passage says that some people broke their covenant with God, so God cursed them and hardened their hearts. They change the meanings of Scripture and have forgotten part of their teaching. The speaker is told to forgive them, except for the few who are not deceitful, because God loves those who act generously.

Those who call themselves Christians also made a covenant with God, but they forgot part of their teaching. As a result, enmity and hatred were stirred up among them, to last until the Resurrection, and God will finally judge what they did.

The passage addresses the People of the Scriptures (Jews and Christians) and says a messenger has come to make clear much they had hidden from their Scriptures. It calls the new Book a light that guides people to peace. It then declares that those who say God is the Messiah, son of Mary, are unbelievers, since God could destroy the Messiah, his mother, and everyone on earth if he chose.
God holds supreme rule over the heavens, the earth, and everything between them. He creates whatever He wills, and He has power over all things.

Jews and Christians claim to be God's sons and beloved. The reply asks why God would then punish them for their sins. It says they are only some of the people God created, and that God forgives and punishes whom he wills, since he rules heaven, earth, and everything between them.

The Prophet Muhammad has come to make clear that there were gaps between prophets, so that people cannot say no messenger ever came to them. Then the passage recalls Moses telling his people to remember God's favours, including the prophets and kings given to them, and to enter the Holy Land God had promised them without turning back.

The Israelites refuse to enter a land because powerful people live there. Two men who fear God urge them to go in through the gate and trust God for victory. The people still refuse, and tell Moses to go and fight with his Lord while they stay seated.

Moses prays to be separated from a disobedient people, and God replies that they will wander forty years in the wilderness. The passage then tells the story of Adam's two sons: one offering is accepted and the other is not, and the rejected son threatens to kill the other, who answers that God accepts only from the God-fearing.

This is a speech by one brother, who says he will not raise his hand against the other even if attacked, because he fears God. He says he would rather the other bear the guilt of both, and then the other kills him anyway. The passage ends by saying that the attacker's passion drove him to murder and he was lost.

God sends a raven that scratches the ground, showing a man how to bury his dead brother's body. Seeing this, the man says he is too weak to act like the bird and hide his brother's shame, and he then becomes one of the repentant.

God's command to the Children of Israel is that killing a person is like killing all mankind, unless the killing is punishment for murder or for spreading corruption in the land. Saving one life is likewise like saving all mankind. The verse adds that, despite the messengers sent to them, many of them still did wrong in the land.

Those who make war on God and his Messenger and spread corruption in the land face severe punishment: death, crucifixion, cutting off of hands and feet on opposite sides, or banishment. This is their disgrace in this life, and a great torment awaits them in the next. Those who repent before they are captured are forgiven. The passage then urges believers to fear God and strive earnestly for his cause.

The passage says that unbelievers will not be spared punishment on Judgment Day, even if they offered twice the earth's riches as a ransom, and they will never leave the Fire. It then orders that a thief, man or woman, have a hand cut off as punishment. A thief who repents and mends his ways, however, can turn back to God and be forgiven.
God owns the heavens and the earth, and He decides who is punished and who is forgiven. He has power over everything.

The passage tells the Prophet not to be troubled by people who rush toward unbelief. These include men who claim to believe but do not, and Jews who listen to lies and do not come to him. They twist the meaning of God's law and accept only the rulings they like. The passage says that God cannot be overruled, and that those whose hearts God does not purify will face disgrace and punishment.

The speaker is told that when people who listen to lies and take forbidden gains come to him for judgment, he may either judge them fairly or refuse to judge them, and he is not harmed by refusing. The point is that these people already have God's Law, yet they do not follow it, so asking him to judge is not sincere.

The passage says that God sent down the Torah, which gives guidance and light, and that earlier prophets and scholars used it to judge the Jews. It tells the Jews not to fear people more than God, not to trade away God's signs for a small gain, and it calls those who refuse to judge by God's revelation unbelievers.

The passage sets out a rule of equal retaliation: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, and so on for other injuries. It adds that someone who gives up his right to retaliation, as a kind of charity, gains forgiveness for his own sin. Those who do not judge by what God has sent down are called wrongdoers.

God sent Jesus after earlier prophets, confirming the earlier law, and gave him the Gospel as guidance and light. The people of the Gospel are told to judge by what God revealed in it, and those who do not judge by God's revelation are called perverse.

The passage says the Quran confirms earlier scriptures and guards them, so the prophet should judge between people by what God has sent down, not by their desires. God gave each community its own law and path, and chose not to make everyone one people, so that people would be tested by what they were given. Believers should compete in good deeds, since all will return to God, who will settle their disputes.

The Prophet is told to judge between the people by what God has revealed, and not to follow their desires or let them lead him away from God's commands. If they turn away, God will punish them for some of their sins. Believers should accept God as the best judge, not the old pagan customs.

Believers are told not to take Jews or Christians as close friends or allies. Those who do so are described as belonging to them, and are said to be people whose hearts are sick. When a victory or misfortune comes, these people will regret their secret dealings and find their earlier oaths of loyalty shown to be false, and their deeds will come to nothing.

God warns believers that if any of them turn away from His religion, He will bring up another people who love Him and whom He loves. These people will be humble toward fellow believers and firm against unbelievers, and they will not fear criticism. The passage then names God, His Messenger and the believers as the true protectors, and says that those who take them as friends are God's people and will prevail.

Believers are told not to take as close friends those from earlier scriptures, or unbelievers, who mock their religion and its call to prayer. The passage then asks the People of the Book why they reject the believers, who simply believe in God and in the revelations sent down to them and before them. The answer it implies is that these critics are themselves mostly wrongdoers.

Believers are warned that some people, cursed and angered by God, have been turned into apes and swine, and worshippers of Taghut are in a bad state. The passage says some who claimed faith came in and left as unbelievers, that God knew their hidden thoughts, and that many of them rush toward wrongdoing and forbidden food.

Their religious leaders and teachers are blamed for not stopping people from speaking evil and eating forbidden food. The verse says that without such restraint, their conduct would have been very bad.

The passage answers a Jewish claim that God's hand is chained up, meaning God is restricted or inactive. It says the opposite: God's hands are outstretched and He gives freely as He wills. It also says that the Jews' own hands will be chained, and that God will extinguish their attempts to stir up war and disorder.

If the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) believe and fear God, God will forgive their sins and reward them with gardens and good things. They must keep their own scripture, the Torah and the Gospel. Some of them do right, but many do evil.

The Prophet is told to announce everything revealed to him from his Lord, since holding anything back would mean he has not delivered the message at all. God promises to protect him from hostile people, and says God does not guide those who reject faith.

People of earlier scriptures (Jews and Christians) are told they have no firm standing unless they follow their own Law and Gospel along with the revelation sent to Muhammad. The revelation will increase rebellion in many of them, so the prophet should not grieve over the unbelievers. Anyone who believes in God and the last day and does good, whatever group they belong to, will have no fear or grief.

The passage says that God made a covenant with the Israelites and sent them prophets. Whenever a prophet brought a message they did not want to hear, some were called liars and some were killed. They thought no harm would follow, yet they became spiritually blind and deaf, and God saw all they did.

The passage rejects the Christian beliefs that Jesus is God and that God is one of three persons. It says there is only one God, and that the Messiah told the Children of Israel to worship God, his Lord and theirs. It urges those who hold these beliefs to turn back to God and ask forgiveness, since God forgives and is merciful.

The passage says that the Messiah, son of Mary, is only a messenger of God, like earlier messengers, and that he and his mother were human and ate food. It warns people not to worship anything besides God, and not to go beyond the truth in their religion or follow those who have already strayed.

Those among the Israelites who refused to believe were cursed by David and by Jesus. The passage says this was because they rebelled, did not stop each other from wrong, and made friends with unbelievers. It adds that if they had believed in God, the Prophet and the Qur'an, they would not have taken such friends.

The passage says that Jews and polytheists (those who join other gods with God) are the most hostile to believers, while Christians are the closest in friendship. It gives the reason as Christian priests and monks being humble. It also says that when Christians hear the revelation given to the Prophet, they weep and declare their belief.

The passage promises a reward of gardens with flowing rivers to believers who ask God to bring them to Paradise, and warns that those who reject God's signs will go to Hell-fire. It then tells believers not to forbid the good food God has allowed, and not to go beyond that limit.

God does not hold people to account for careless words in their oaths, but does hold them to oaths sworn in earnest. For breaking one, the penalty is feeding ten poor people, clothing them, or freeing a captive, or fasting three days if none of these is possible. The passage then calls wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows an abomination of Satan's work, to be avoided.

Satan wants to cause hatred and quarrels among believers through wine and gambling, and to draw them away from remembering God and from prayer. The passage asks whether they will therefore stay away from these things. It tells them to obey God and the Apostle, and says the Apostle's duty is only to deliver a clear message.

Believers who fear God and do good are not blamed for food they have already eaten, even if it was forbidden before. God then tests them with game they can catch by hand or with spears, to see who fears him in secret. Anyone who breaks this rule afterward will face severe punishment.

Believers on pilgrimage must not hunt or kill game animals. If someone kills one on purpose, he must make amends: offer an equal domestic animal at the Ka'ba, feed the poor, or fast. Repeating the offence brings God's punishment.

Sea fishing and eating fish are permitted to believers, both at home and for travelers. Hunting on land is forbidden while they are on pilgrimage, and the passage ends by telling them to fear God, before whom all will be gathered.

God made the Kaaba, the sacred house, along with the sacred month and the offerings, as a support for people, so they would know that God knows everything in heaven and on earth. The messenger's only duty is to preach. Good and evil are not equal, so people should fear God and understand this.

Believers are told not to ask about matters that could only cause them distress, though answers will be given if such questions are asked while the Qur'an is being revealed, and God will forgive them for asking. Earlier peoples who asked similar questions then rejected what they were told. The passage also says God did not command the practices of Bahira, Saiba, Wasila and Hami, which are animal customs, and that unbelievers invented them.

People were told to follow what God had sent down and the Messenger. They replied that their fathers' faith was enough for them, even though the fathers knew nothing and had no guidance. The believers are told to look to their own conduct, since others who go astray cannot harm them once they are rightly guided, and all will return to God for judgment.

When a believer is dying and writing a will, the passage says two trustworthy men must act as witnesses. If the witnesses are travelling far from home, two men from another tribe may serve. If there is doubt about them, they must swear by God that they have taken no bribe and will not hide the truth.

If two witnesses are shown to have lied, two relatives of the dead man may take their place and swear an oath that their own testimony is true. The passage says this makes honest witness more likely, since false witnesses fear being countered by a second oath. It ends by urging people to fear God and obey.

God will gather the messengers and ask what answer their peoples gave them. They will say they have no knowledge, because God alone knows what is hidden. God then speaks to Jesus, son of Mary, reminding him of the favours given to him and his mother, including the Holy Spirit's support that let him speak as a baby and as an adult.

God speaks to Jesus here, listing the miracles he performed by God's permission: teaching the Scripture and wisdom, shaping a bird from clay that came alive, healing the blind and lepers, and raising the dead. It also says that some of the Israelites who did not believe called these signs plain sorcery.

The passage describes disciples asking Jesus whether God could send down a set table from heaven. Jesus tells them to fear God if they believe. They say they want to eat from it, to have their hearts reassured, and to know that he has spoken truth and to be witnesses of it.

Jesus asks God to send down a table of food from heaven, so that its arrival can be a festival for his followers and a sign from God, and so that God will provide for them. God agrees to send it, but warns that anyone who disbelieves after that will receive a punishment unlike any given to other creatures.

In this verse God asks Jesus whether he told people to worship him and his mother Mary as gods beside God. Jesus replies that he would never say what is not true, and that God knows everything hidden, including what is in Jesus himself.

Jesus, speaking at the end of time, says he told his people only what God commanded: to worship God, his Lord and theirs. He says he watched over them only while he lived among them, and that God now watches them and judges them. God then declares that the truthful will gain reward: gardens with rivers, and lasting pleasure with God.

Wake up! The night is ending and dawn has come, chasing the stars away like stones thrown into a bowl. The sun, pictured as a hunter, rises in the east and catches the top of a sultan's tower in a net of light.
In a dream at dawn, the speaker hears a voice in a tavern calling on his companions to wake up and fill their cups before the wine of life runs out. The message is to drink while there is still time.
As the rooster crows at dawn, people waiting outside a tavern call for the door to be opened. They say that life is short and that once gone, we cannot come back.

At the New Year, the thoughtful soul withdraws into solitude. There, a tree in bloom and the ground's breath, which are compared to the white hand of Moses and the breath of Jesus, show that spring has come back to life.

Iram, a legendary garden city, and Jamshyd's seven-ringed cup have vanished, and no one knows where they are. Yet the vine still gives its red wine, and a garden still blooms by the water. The lost wonders of the past are gone, but ordinary things of nature continue.

The quatrain says that David's lips are sealed, meaning the psalms of the prophet David are silent. Instead, the nightingale sings loudly in Pahlavi, the old Persian language, calling for red wine. It sings this to the rose so that the rose's yellow cheek will turn red.
Fill the cup and throw off the heavy winter coat of regret, since life is short. Time is like a bird that has only a little distance left to fly and is already leaving.

Flowers open at dawn, and a thousand of them fall to dust by evening. The coming of the rose in early summer will likewise end the lives of Jamshyd and Kaikobad, two legendary Persian kings. Even great rulers of the past will pass away, as the blossoms do.

The speaker invites the reader to stop caring about famous kings and heroes of old, such as Kaikobad, Kaikhosru, Rustum and Hatim Tai, and to join him instead. Whatever these figures do or say, he says, they should be ignored.

The speaker wants to sit with a loved one on a strip of grass between the desert and the farmland. There, the difference between slave and sultan is hardly known, and he pities Sultan Mahmud sitting on his throne.
A speaker sits outdoors under a tree with bread, wine, a book of poems, and a companion who sings beside him. He says that this simple setting in the wilderness is enough to be paradise.
Some people praise earthly power, others praise the joys of heaven. The speaker says to take the ready money now and let the rest go, since distant promises are only like the far-off sound of a drum.

The rose speaks, saying it blows into the world laughing. It tears open its silken purse, scattering its treasure, which is its petals and scent, across the garden. The image suggests that beauty is given freely and spent without holding anything back.
Worldly hopes, the things people set their hearts on, either turn to ashes or succeed. Even success is brief, like snow on a desert that melts after an hour or two.

Those who saved the golden grain and those who scattered it like rain have both become earth, and that earth is not turned back into gold. Once people are buried, they are not dug up again, so the wealthy and the wasteful end up the same.
Picture this worn-out inn, where the doorways are night and day. Many kings, one after another, with all their grandeur, stayed there for an hour or two and then left.

Famous kings of the past, Jamshyd and Bahram, are now gone. The lion and the lizard now occupy the halls where Jamshyd feasted, and a wild ass stamps over the grave of Bahram, the great hunter, who sleeps on. Jamshyd and Bahram are legendary Persian kings; the poem says their power has passed away.

The speaker imagines that roses bloom redder where dead rulers, such as a Caesar, once bled. He also imagines that each hyacinth in the garden grew from the fallen head of someone who was once lovely. The flowers are seen as made from the dead.

The grass growing on the riverbank is green and pleasant, and we lean on it as we sit there. The speaker urges that we lean on it gently, because no one knows whose beautiful lip, meaning a buried person, it may have grown from.

The speaker asks his beloved to fill the cup that wipes away regrets about the past and fears about the future, so he can live today. He reasons that tomorrow he may be dead, joining the vast stretch of time that has already gone by.

The speaker says that some people they loved, the best of them, have died. Time and Fate have taken them like wine pressed from grapes. They drank their cup before the speaker and quietly went to rest, one by one.

We who now enjoy life will one day go down beneath the earth and make our own grave. Those who came before have already gone, while summer keeps blooming without them. The verse asks, in effect, who that grave is ultimately made for.

The speaker urges us to enjoy life while we still can, because soon we will die and turn to dust, lying under the dust with no wine, no song, no singer, and no end. "Sans" is an old word meaning "without." The last line adds that even the end of life brings no release, since the speaker imagines a death with nothing left at all.

A caller from the tower of a mosque (a muezzin) tells two kinds of people alike: those who plan for today and those who gaze toward tomorrow. He calls them fools, since neither the present nor the future will bring them any reward.

The saints and wise men who debated learnedly about this world and the next are cast out like foolish prophets. Their words are scorned and scattered, and their mouths are stopped with dust, meaning they are dead and forgotten.
Come drink and enjoy life with Khayyam rather than listen to the wise. Life passes quickly, and that is the only certain thing; everything else is false. Once a flower has bloomed, it dies for good.
When young, the speaker often visited learned teachers and holy men and listened to long debates. Yet he always left the same way he had entered, learning nothing new about life's deeper questions.

The speaker says he planted the seeds of wisdom and worked hard to make them grow. The only harvest he gained was the knowledge that he came into life like water and will leave it like wind, passing without lasting trace.

Human beings come into this world without knowing why or where they come from, flowing like water. They leave it again without knowing where they go, carried like wind across a desert, with no choice in either case.

The speaker says that we are brought into the world and taken out of it without being asked where we come from or where we go. Since this is such an insult, he wants more cups of wine to drown the memory of it.

The speaker says he climbed up from the centre of the earth, through seven gates, and sat on the throne of Saturn. Along the way he untangled many puzzles, but he could not solve the riddle of why humans die and what their fate is.

A door with no key and a veil that cannot be seen past stand for limits on what a person can understand. The speaker says that for a short time there seemed to be talk of "me" and "thee," meaning a self and another, and then that talk ended.

The speaker asks the sky what light Fate had to guide humans, who he calls its little children stumbling in the dark. The sky answers that the guide is a blind understanding, meaning human reason cannot see the way clearly.
In this verse, the speaker goes to a clay bowl to learn the secret of life from its edge. The bowl whispers to him, "While you live, drink, because once dead you will never come back."

The speaker imagines that a clay jar, which once spoke with a brief, fleeting voice, was once alive and cheerful. He then thinks of the cold lips of such a jar, which he has kissed, and wonders how many kisses it could have taken and given back when it was alive.
A potter is seen beating wet clay in the marketplace at dusk. The clay, though its voice has been worn away, seems to speak and asks the potter to be gentle with it, calling him "Brother."

Fill the cup and enjoy the present. There is no point in repeatedly complaining that time is slipping away. Tomorrow has not yet come and yesterday is gone, so there is no reason to worry about them while today is pleasant.

The speaker says that life is only a brief moment between two voids, the emptiness before birth and the nothing after death. He urges that this short moment be used quickly, because the stars are fading and the caravan of time is already moving toward nothingness.

The speaker asks how long people will keep chasing this and that through endless effort and argument. He says it is better to enjoy wine, the "fruitful Grape," than to be left with sorrow or bitter regret afterward.
The speaker tells his friends how long it has been since he held a wedding feast at home. He says he sent reason away from his bed and married wine, which he calls "the Daughter of the Vine."
The speaker says he could define exact, logical ideas such as "is" and "is not" and measure things with a ruler and line. Yet the only thing he ever truly cared about or went deep into was wine.
In this verse, the speaker sees a figure like an angel at a tavern door at dusk, carrying a jug. The figure offers him a drink, and it turns out to be wine made from grapes.

The grape is praised as a clever kind of reasoning that can settle the arguments of the seventy-two quarrelling sects. It is also called a skilled alchemist that turns the dull metal of life into gold. In the poem, wine is the grape's juice and stands for this power.
The speaker praises Mahmud, a victorious lord, who scatters and kills the dark army of fears and sorrows that attack the soul, using his magic sword.

The speaker tells the reader to let the wise argue about the universe's big questions and to stay out of it. He suggests sitting quietly in a corner of the noise and mocking the very thing that treats you as important. The phrase "makes as much of Thee" means something that values you highly.
Everything, inside and outside, above and below, is only a shadow show. It is played in a box lit by the sun, and we are the phantom figures who move around the light, appearing and disappearing.

If the wine drunk and the lips kissed end in nothing, as all things do, then while a person lives they are only what they will become, which is nothing. Death brings no loss beyond that, since they will be no less than nothing.
Drink wine while the rose is blooming by the river, in the company of the poet himself. When the Angel comes to you with his darker cup, which stands for death, accept it without flinching.

Life is compared to a chessboard made of nights and days, on which Fate plays with people as its pieces. Fate moves them about, captures them, and then puts each one back in its box, one at a time, when the game is over.

The speaker compares human life to a ball in a game. The ball does not choose which way it goes; it moves right or left as the player strikes it. The one who threw the ball onto the field knows everything about what happens to it.
Once something is written, it cannot be changed. The Moving Finger, a figure for fate or destiny, has written the lines of life, and neither piety, cleverness, nor tears can undo any part of them.

The speaker says the sky is like an upturned bowl under which people live and die, like creatures crawling in a cage. Do not pray to the sky for help, because it moves on without power to help, just as we do.

The poem says that the first man was made from earth, and that the end of the world was planned at the same time as the beginning. Creation's first morning already wrote down what the final day of judgment will reveal.

The speaker says that when the stars Parwin (the Pleiades) and Mushtari (Jupiter) were flung over the shoulders of the flaming Foal of Heaven, starting from the Goal, they set the course of his fate, which was fixed in advance as a plot of dust and soul. In plain terms, he claims that his life, made of dust and soul, was already decided by the movement of the stars.

The speaker says that wine has touched something deep in him, so that his whole being clings to it. Let the Sufi (a Muslim mystic) mock him if he likes. His crude nature can be filed into a key that opens the door the mystic is howling outside, meaning the speaker has found a way into the wine-induced ecstasy that the mystic lacks.

The speaker says that whether the one True Light burns him with love or destroys him with wrath, he knows one brief glimpse of it found in a tavern is better than losing it completely in a temple. He values a moment of the divine found in a wine house over being lost to it in a place of worship.
The speaker addresses God. He says God set traps along the road he had to travel. He asks God not to trap him again through predestination and then blame him for falling into sin.

The speaker addresses God, saying that God made man from base earth and also created the snake in Eden. Because of the sin that stains humanity, the speaker asks God to forgive man, and to accept forgiveness in return.

The speaker stands alone one evening at the end of Ramadan, the Muslim month of fasting, just before the new moon rises. In an old potter's workshop, he sees rows of unfinished clay vessels around him, which he treats as a crowd of people.

Some of the clay vessels in a potter's workshop could speak and others could not. Then one impatient vessel suddenly asked who the potter was, and who the pot was, meaning who made whom. The question suggests that humans, like pots, may not know who or what shaped them.

A speaker reasons that his body was taken from common earth for a purpose, and that the maker who shaped him so carefully would not simply return him to the same earth. He cannot believe his life ends in nothing, so he expects a different fate than dust.

A speaker argues that no boy would smash a bowl he had enjoyed drinking from, so the maker of the vessel would not destroy it in anger after shaping it out of love and fancy. The image is of a potter and his pot, used to ask whether a creator would discard what he made with such care.

After a silence, a clay pot with a crooked shape speaks up. It mocks the pot-maker's skill: it asks whether the potter's hand was shaking when he made it, since the pot leans badly and others sneer at it.

One speaker says that people describe the tavern keeper as a grim figure, blackened with the smoke of hell. They talk of a strict test of us after death, but he dismisses this and says the keeper is a good fellow and all will be well.
A speaker sighs and says that his body, which has been dead a long time, has dried out. He asks to be filled with his old favourite wine, and he thinks that with it he might come back to life soon.

Wine jars are talking among themselves when one of them sees the new moon, the crescent everyone has been looking for. The jars nudge each other and say they hear the porter's shoulder-knot creaking, meaning the wine seller's helper is coming with the wine. The jars are the vessels, and they respond to the crescent by signalling that the drinking is about to begin.

The speaker asks to be prepared for burial with wine: his body washed in grape wine after death, wrapped in a shroud of vine leaves, and buried beside a garden. He wants his fading life to be renewed with wine before he dies.

The speaker imagines that even after he is buried, his ashes will send up a scent so strong that any passing true believer will be caught off guard by it. The image suggests the scent will tempt or ensnare devout people who walk by the grave.
The speaker says that the "idols" he has loved for so long have damaged his good name in other people's eyes. He has let his honour drown in a small cup of wine and traded his reputation for a song.
The speaker says he has often promised to repent, but doubts he was sober when he made those promises. When spring came with a rose in hand, his worn-out repentance fell apart.
The speaker says wine has led him astray and taken away his honour. Even so, he wonders what wine-sellers pay for anything worth as much as the wine they sell.
Spring ends with the rose, and youth's fragrant book closes, like a page turned shut. The nightingale sang in the branches, but no one knows where it came from or where it has gone.

The speaker imagines that he and his beloved, working together with Fate, could seize this unsatisfactory world as a whole. They would break it apart and rebuild it closer to what the heart wants. "Thou" is an old word for "you," used here for the beloved.

The speaker addresses a beloved, whose beauty never fades, and watches the moon rise over the garden. He imagines the moon rising again in future years and looking through the same garden, but he will no longer be there to see it.

The speaker imagines the beloved, or the dawn, arriving at the garden where he used to drink with friends, and asks that an empty glass be turned down. Turning the glass over signals that he is dead and no longer drinking there.

Wake up! The rising sun chases the stars out of the night sky, pushes the darkness away with them, and shines its first light on the top of a sultan's tower. The speaker calls the sleeper to get up at dawn.

A voice from inside a tavern (a wine-house) calls out before dawn's false light fades. It asks why the sleepy worshiper outside still nods, when the temple within is already ready. The speaker invites people to come in and drink rather than stay outside in sleep.
As dawn comes and the cock crows, people waiting outside a tavern call for the door to be opened. They say their time on earth is short, and once they are gone they cannot come back.

Iram, a legendary garden, and Jamshyd's seven-ringed cup have vanished, and no one knows where they are. Yet wine still glows red in the vine, and gardens still bloom beside the water. The point is that lost splendors are gone, while ordinary beauty continues.

The poet says that King David's lips are closed, meaning he no longer speaks. Instead, the nightingale sings to the rose in a heavenly language, calling for red wine, so that the rose's pale cheek turns red.
Fill the cup and cast off your winter coat of regret in the warmth of spring. Time is short, the poem says, like a bird that has only a little distance to fly and is already in the air.

Wherever a person lives, in a famous city or a distant one, and whether life brings sweetness or bitterness, life keeps passing away slowly and steadily. The speaker describes time running out, one moment at a time, for everyone.

Each morning brings a thousand new roses, you say, but the speaker asks where yesterday's roses have gone. The coming summer month, which brings roses, will also take away two legendary Persian kings, Jamshyd and Kaikobad, showing that even the greatest pass away.

Let the famous kings and heroes of Persian legend go, the speaker says, since they have nothing to do with us. Kaikobad, Kaikhosru, Zal, Rustum and Hatim are names from that legend, and the speaker tells the reader not to worry about any of them.

Sitting with the speaker on a strip of grass between desert and farmland, a place where the names of slave and sultan are forgotten, the speaker wishes peace to Mahmud, who sits on his golden throne. Mahmud was a sultan, so the wish is said with the throne still in view.
A speaker imagines a simple shared life: poetry under a tree, wine, bread, and a loved one singing beside him. He says that even a wilderness would be paradise enough with that company.

Some people chase the pleasures of this world, while others long for the paradise promised by the Prophet. The speaker urges taking what is present and certain now, and not worrying about the distant reward or its promised noise.

The rose speaks: it blows open laughingly into the world, and it tears open its silken purse so that its treasure, the petals or scent, is scattered over the garden. The image suggests giving freely and spending everything at once.

Those who saved the golden grain and those who scattered it like rain have both become earth, and the earth gives no sign of which is which. Once buried, the dead are not dug up again, so the wise and the wasteful end up the same.
Worldly hopes, the things people set their hearts on, either turn to ashes or succeed. Either way, success is brief, like snow falling on a desert: it lasts an hour or two and then is gone.

Consider how many rulers, each with their grand show, stayed in this worn-out inn for their appointed time and then left. The inn is the world, whose doors open alternately to night and day. A caravanserai is a roadside inn for travelers.

The lion and the lizard are now said to guard the palaces where the old kings Jamshyd and Bahram once feasted and rejoiced. Bahram, the great hunter, is now asleep under the earth, and even the wild ass that tramples over his grave cannot wake him.

The speaker imagines that roses bloom redder where emperors or other great men were buried and died, and that hyacinths in a garden grew from the heads of people who were once beautiful. The point is that the flowers are made from the dead.

The grass growing on the riverbank is fresh and green, and we lean on it. The speaker asks us to lean on it gently, because no one knows whose body it may have grown from, perhaps that of a beautiful person who has died.

The speaker asks his beloved to fill the cup so that today is free of regret about the past and fear of the future. He reasons that tomorrow he may be gone, lost in the long stretch of time that has already passed.

Some people we loved, the finest and best that time has pressed from its vintage, have already drunk their cup and quietly died, one by one. The poem uses the image of wine and a drinking round to describe death.

We who now enjoy life in the room left by those who have died, while summer flowers bloom again, must ourselves go down beneath the earth. There we will make a bed for ourselves, but for whom? The question is left unanswered, since no one is left to lie there after us.

Spend the time we still have while we can, because we will soon die and turn to dust, lying there with no wine, no song, no singer, and no end to it. "Sans" means "without." The last line says death will bring nothing after it.

A muezzin, the official who calls Muslims to prayer, cries out from a tower that both those who plan for today and those who look ahead to tomorrow will get no reward, either in this life or the next. He calls them fools.

The saints and wise men who debated the two worlds, this life and the next, have been cast out like foolish prophets. Their words are scorned and scattered, and their mouths are now filled with dust, meaning they are dead and forgotten.
When young, the speaker went often to scholars and holy men and listened to long debates. Each time he left as wise as he had entered, learning nothing new.

The speaker says he planted wisdom and worked hard to make it grow. His only harvest was the feeling that he came into the world like water and leaves it like wind, passing through without lasting trace.

Human beings come into this world without knowing where they came from, flowing like water that has no choice in its path. They leave it again without knowing where they go, carried like wind across a empty desert. Neither arrival nor departure is chosen.

The speaker says that we are brought into the world and taken out of it without being asked, coming from an unknown "whence" and going to an unknown "whither." He suggests that only many cups of forbidden wine can drown the memory of this unfair treatment.

The speaker says he climbed up from the earth, through the seventh gate, and sat on the throne of Saturn. Along the way he untied many knots, meaning he solved many problems, but he could not untie the biggest knot, the one that controls human fate.

The speaker describes life as a closed door he cannot open and a veil he cannot see through. For a short time there is talk of "me" and "you," meaning two separate people, and then that talk ends and the distinction is gone.

Earth, the seas, and the heavens could not answer the speaker's question. The seas are said to mourn their lost lord, and the heavens, with their signs shown and then hidden by night and morning, also stay silent.
The speaker leans down to a clay jar and asks it the secret of life. The jar answers in a whisper: while you are alive, drink, because once you die you will never come back.

The speaker imagines a clay jar, which once spoke and drank like a living person. He thinks of the lips he once kissed, and how many kisses those lips could have taken and given. The jar's shape may be the old lover's body, so the image links the dead to the living.

The speaker remembers stopping on the road to watch a potter pounding wet clay. The clay, though it can no longer speak, seems to murmur, "Gently, brother, gently, please." The image suggests that the clay is a human being, perhaps once alive, asking to be treated with care.

The speaker asks whether this same story has not been passed down through the generations of mankind: that a lump of wet earth was shaped by the Maker into human form. The line refers to the old idea that God made people from clay.
The speaker says that no drop of wine spilled from our cups is wasted on the earth. Each drop soaks down to someone buried long ago, where it eases their grief.

The tulip looks up from the soil for its morning drink of wine from heaven, and the speaker tells the reader to do the same. Keep looking up in devotion until heaven turns the reader over, as Earth is turned over, like an empty cup.
Stop worrying about questions of humans or gods, or about what tomorrow will bring. Let it all go, and spend your time with the wine-server, a slender youth who pours wine.

The speaker says that wine and the lips that drink it end in the same fate as everything else, which is death. He asks the reader to think that today you are what you were yesterday, and tomorrow you will be no less, so you are just as much a part of that fate.

An "Angel of the darker Drink" (a figure of death, offering a cup) will one day find the speaker by a river. He will invite the soul to drink from his cup, and the speaker will not hesitate or draw back.

The speaker asks why the soul should stay trapped in a weak, crippled body of clay if it could throw off the dust and ride free through the air of heaven. He suggests it would be a shame to remain in such a body.

A sultan, a ruler, stops for one day's rest in a tent on his way to death. He rises and leaves, and the tent's servant, the dark Ferrash (a tent-keeper), takes it down to make ready for the next guest. Life is a temporary stay, and death is the next lodging.

The speaker tells the reader not to fear that, when life ends, their own existence and his will never be repeated. The Eternal Saki, a cupbearer figure for the divine or fate, has poured countless bubbles like us from his bowl in the past and will keep pouring them in the future.

The speaker says that after he and his listener die, the world will go on for a very long time. The world will not notice their coming or going, just as the sea does not notice a pebble thrown into it.
A brief stop at a well in the desert gives a moment of life. Then the caravan, which is like a ghost, arrives back at the nothing it left, so the speaker urges the reader to hurry.

The speaker asks a friend whether they want to spend their short life trying to uncover the hidden secret of existence, and urges them to be quick about it. He says the line between truth and falsehood is as thin as a hair, so he asks what life could really depend on.

The poem says that the line between what is false and what is true may be as thin as a hair. A single letter, the Arabic alif, could be the clue that opens the treasure-house, and perhaps leads to the Master, meaning God.

A hidden presence runs through all of creation like quicksilver, slipping away from every attempt to grasp it. It takes every shape, from the moon to the fish, and all those forms change and die, but this presence stays the same.
A brief moment of life is glimpsed, and then it vanishes behind a fold of darkness. The whole drama of existence unfolds this way, and God plans, performs and watches it as a pastime for eternity.

Searching for answers in vain, both on the earth and toward the closed gate of heaven, leaves the speaker unprepared for the day when he no longer exists. The question is how anyone can face that day with nothing found.

Do not waste your time chasing this and that through endless effort and argument. It is better to be cheerful with the fruit of the grape, wine, than to be left sad, with only bitter regret afterward.

The speaker tells his friends that he has taken wine as his new partner. He has put aside reason, which he calls old and barren, and "the Daughter of the Vine" (wine) has taken its place in his house.

The speaker says that he has used logic, with its rules of "is" and "is not" and its up-and-down reasoning, to define things. Of all the subjects worth deep study, he claims he has gone deep into only one: wine.

The speaker says people claim his calculations have improved the calendar. He denies this. He says his work only removed "Unborn To-morrow" and "dead Yesterday" from the calendar, meaning that the future and the past were never really part of the time we live in.
A recent memory: at the open door of a tavern, at dusk, a bright, angel-like figure came carrying a jug on his shoulder. He offered the speaker a taste, and the drink was wine made from grapes.

The grape is praised as a power that can, by pure reasoning, prove wrong the seventy-two quarrelling sects. It is also called a supreme alchemist that turns the heavy metal of life into gold in an instant. Here "grape" stands for wine.

Mahmud, a powerful ruler praised as breathing with God's spirit, drives away the "misbelieving" horde of fears and sorrows that trouble the soul. He scatters them with his whirlwind sword, as a conqueror scatters an enemy army.

The speaker asks why anyone would curse the wine vine's twisting tendril as a trap, since the juice comes from God. If wine is a blessing, we should enjoy it. If it is a curse, the question is who put it there, meaning God.

The speaker says he must give up the "Balm of Life," the wine of this world, either because he fears a reckoning after death, which he accepts only on trust, or because he hopes for a better drink in the afterlife. Either way, he will fill his cup only after he has turned to dust.
Whatever is said about hell and heaven, the only certain thing is that life passes quickly. Everything else is lies, and a flower that has bloomed dies for good.
Countless people have died before us, and none has come back to describe what lies beyond death. We must all make that same journey ourselves to find out.

The visions of learned and devout men, the prophets who came before us, are now only tales. They are like stories told by people who woke from sleep, passed them on to their friends, and then went back to sleep.

The speaker sends his soul out to learn what the afterlife is like. When the soul returns, it answers that it is itself heaven and hell. The point is that heaven and hell are states of the self, not places one goes to after death.

Heaven is described as only the vision of a desire that has been fulfilled, and Hell as the shadow cast by a soul on fire. Both are images thrown onto the darkness we came out of, and we will soon pass back into it again.

We are like a line of shadow puppets moving across a wall. They come and go as a lantern is turned around, and the one holding it is the Master of the Show. The figures are not free; they are moved by the lantern's light, held by a hidden operator.

The speaker says that people are like helpless pieces in a board game. A player, here God or fate, moves them across the board of days and nights, capturing them one by one and then putting them back into a box.

The poem compares human life to a polo or ball game. The ball does not ask questions; it goes here or there depending on how the player strikes it. The one who threw the ball onto the field, meaning God or fate, knows everything about what happens.

The moving finger, a image of fate or time, writes down what happens and then moves on. Neither your piety, nor your cleverness, nor your tears can bring it back to erase any part of what it has written.

The speaker says the sky, which he calls an upturned bowl, is a place where people live and die like trapped creatures. He tells the reader not to raise their hands to the sky for help, because it has no more power to act than people do.

The poem says that the first human was shaped from the earth's first clay, and that the seeds of the final harvest were planted at the same time. The first morning of creation wrote down what the last day of judgment will read out.

Yesterday's events led to today's foolishness, and tomorrow will bring silence, triumph, or despair. The speaker urges drinking because no one knows where they came from, why they are here, or where they are going.

The speaker says that when the stars were set moving from their starting point across the sky, they were flung over the heavens, and that this movement was already fixed in the plot of dust and soul that made him. In plain terms, he believes his life and nature were decided by the motion of the stars at the start of creation. Parwin (the Pleiades) and Mushtari (Jupiter) are star names.

The wine has touched a nerve, so that my whole being clings to it, and let the dervish (a Sufi holy man) mock me. Even my base metal can be filed into a key that opens the door he is howling outside of, meaning the mystery of the divine he cannot reach.

The speaker says he knows that, whether the one True Light sets him on fire with love or burns him up in anger, a single flash of it found in a tavern is better than being lost completely in a temple. The tavern stands for drinking and worldly pleasure, the temple for formal religion.

The speaker asks how a senseless Nothing could create a conscious Something, and then make that being feel bound by a yoke of forbidden pleasures. He adds that breaking this rule brings everlasting punishment. He is questioning whether such a creation and such a penalty make sense.

The speaker finds it unfair that God would demand repayment of pure gold from a helpless creature who was given only base metal, and would sue him for a debt he never agreed to and cannot pay. He calls this a sorry bargain.

The speaker addresses God. He says God set traps along the road he had to travel, and that God surrounded him with evil that was already fated. He argues that God will not then blame him for falling into sin.

The speaker addresses God. He says God made man from baser earth and placed the serpent in Paradise, and so the sins that darken man's face are partly God's doing. He asks God to forgive man, and to accept forgiveness in return.

The speaker says that, as the day ended, the hungry month of Ramadan slipped quietly away. He then stands alone again in the potter's house, surrounded by clay figures. Ramadan is the Muslim month of fasting, and the potter's house is a workshop where pots are made.
The speaker describes a room full of pots and vessels of every size, standing along the floor and walls. Some of them seem to chatter, while others may have listened but never spoke at all.

A speaker says that his body was made from common earth and shaped into a human form. He asks whether this was for nothing, and whether the shape will only be broken and the earth trampled back into formless dust.
A second speaker argues that no spoiled child would smash a cup he had happily drunk from, so the maker of the cup, who shaped it by hand, would not destroy it later out of anger.
A clay pot that is badly shaped speaks up after a short silence. It complains that others mock it for leaning crooked, and asks whether the potter's hand must have shaken while making it.

A talkative listener, whom the speaker jokingly calls a "Sufi pipkin" (a small clay pot, a mystic's vessel), grows heated and asks who the potter is and who the pot is, if the talk is all about pots and potters. The question challenges the metaphor of a maker and his made things.

Another speaker asks why anyone would believe a story about a maker who threatens to throw his badly made pots into Hell. He dismisses the idea with "Pish!" and says the maker is a good fellow, so everything will turn out well.
A speaker, who has been dead for a long time and is now only dry clay, asks for someone to fill a cup with wine. He thinks that wine might bring him back to life.

The jars and pots, as they talk among themselves, are shown as a group of clay vessels. The moon looks in on them, and they nudge each other, joking that it is time for the porter to hoist them onto his shoulders and carry them away. The verse plays on the idea that the vessels are made of clay, like the potter's work that a porter carries to market.

The speaker asks that, while his life is fading, he be given wine. After he dies, he wants his body washed, wrapped in a leaf, and buried beside a garden that people sometimes visit. The grape and the leaf stand for wine and the living green of a garden.

The poem says that even dead ashes, once turned into wine, will send up such a strong vapour that any believer walking past will be caught off guard and overcome by it. The "snare" is the intoxicating pull of wine, and the "True-believer" is a devout Muslim who would normally avoid it.

The speaker says that the "idols" he has loved for so long have harmed his good name in the world. He has let his glory drown in a small cup of wine and traded his reputation for a song. Here "idols" most likely means the pleasures he has pursued, such as wine and poetry.
The speaker has often sworn to repent, but he doubts he was sober when he made those vows. Then spring arrives with a rose in hand, and his worn-out repentance falls apart.
The speaker says wine has led him astray and taken away his honor. Still, he often wonders what wine sellers could buy that is worth as much as the wine they sell.

The speaker grieves that spring ends with the roses fading, and that youth, like a sweet-scented book, comes to an end. He asks where the nightingale that sang in the branches came from and where it has gone, and no one knows the answer.

If the desert of the fountain (the place where the water of life is found) would show even one dim but real glimpse of itself, the weary traveler would leap toward it, the way trampled grass springs back up.
The speaker wishes that a winged angel could stop the scroll of fate before it is fully written. He wants the recorder to write something different, or to erase what has been written altogether.

The speaker imagines that if he and his beloved could join with God to take hold of this unsatisfactory world as a whole, they would break it apart and rebuild it closer to what the heart truly wants.

The Moon will rise again and again, waxing and waning over the years, and will keep looking for the speaker in this same garden. But the speaker will not be there to see it. The one who is gone is the speaker, who will never return to look back.

Addressing his cupbearer (the Saki), the speaker imagines that after his death the cupbearer will go out to the place where the speaker once sat with friends, among the scattered stars and grass. When he reaches that spot, he should turn down an empty glass in memory of the speaker, who once drank there.

Socrates says his accusers nearly made him forget who he is, because they spoke so persuasively, yet they told almost no truth. He is most surprised by their claim that the Athenians should beware of being fooled by his own skill in speaking.

Socrates says his accusers spoke falsely and were shameless to claim eloquence, because they would be exposed as poor speakers once he began. He says he is eloquent only in the sense of speaking the truth, and he will tell the whole truth, though not in a polished, ornamented speech.

Socrates says he will speak with the words that come to him in the moment, because he is sure his cause is just. He says he is too old to address the Athenian court as a polished young speaker, and he asks that no one expect that from him.

Socrates asks the jury not to be surprised or interrupt if he speaks in his usual way, the way he talks in public places like the marketplace. He explains that he is over seventy and this is his first time in a court, so he is unfamiliar with the court's way of speaking.

Socrates asks the jury to treat him like a foreigner who speaks in his own way and accent, and to ignore his style of speaking. They should focus on whether what he says is true, and the judge should decide fairly.

Socrates says his oldest accusers worry him more than the men now charging him. These earlier accusers spread a story since childhood about a wise man named Socrates who studied the sky and the earth and made the weaker argument seem stronger. He fears these people most.

Socrates says his accusers are many, and their charges are old, made when the jurors were young and no one answered them. He cannot name most of these accusers, except perhaps a comic poet. He finds people who slander him out of envy or malice hard to deal with.

Socrates says he cannot bring his accusers before the court to question them, so he must defend himself against shadows, arguing with no one to answer him. He asks the jury to treat his opponents as two groups, old and new, and to let him answer the older accusers first, since those charges were heard earlier and more often.

Socrates says he must now answer a slander that has circulated for a long time, and he hopes to clear it up quickly. He admits the task is hard, so he leaves the outcome to God and will make his defence as the law requires.

Socrates describes the charges against him, as his accusers have framed them. He is said to be a wrongdoer who pries into things under the earth and in the heavens, makes the weaker argument seem stronger, and teaches these same ideas to others.

Socrates says the charge against him is like the mockery in Aristophanes' comedy Clouds, where a character called Socrates claims to walk on air and talks nonsense about things he does not claim to understand. He adds that he has nothing against students of natural philosophy, meaning the study of the natural world, and says he would be sorry if Meletus, his accuser, could bring so serious a charge.

Socrates says he has never studied physical speculation, the theories about nature that some thinkers pursued. He calls on those present, who have heard him, to say whether they ever heard him discuss such matters, and he claims their answer will show whether the rest of the charge against him is true.

Socrates denies that he is a teacher who takes money for lessons. He says that taking pay would be an honour for a man who could really teach. He points to Gorgias, Prodicus and Hippias, who travel between cities, take fees, and draw young men away from their own teachers, who taught them for nothing.

Socrates asks Callias, a rich man who has paid large sums to the Sophists (paid teachers of wisdom and speaking), who should be put in charge of his sons. He argues that young horses or calves would have a trainer or farmer to improve them, so human sons need a suitable teacher too.

Socrates asks a man whether anyone teaches human and political virtue, and the man names Evenus of Paros, who charges five minae. Socrates says that if Evenus really has this wisdom and teaches it so cheaply, he is fortunate. Socrates adds that he himself would be proud if he had such knowledge, but he admits he has none.

Socrates imagines an Athenian asking why he has such a bad reputation and why he is called wise, if he is not doing something unusual. He says this is a fair question and promises to explain the reason.

Socrates says he will speak the whole truth, and that his good name comes from a wisdom he has. It is only human wisdom, the kind a person can reach. He says he does not have the superhuman wisdom that others claim, and that anyone who says he does is lying and harming his reputation.

Socrates asks the Athenian jury not to interrupt, because what he is about to say may sound strange. He says the claim about his wisdom does not come from him but from the god at Delphi, and he names Chaerephon, a friend known to the jurors, as the one who brought it.

Chaerephon, a friend of Socrates, asked the Delphic oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The priestess answered that no one was. Socrates says Chaerephon's brother can confirm this, since Chaerephon himself has died.

Socrates explains that he has a bad reputation because of a message from a god, which he found puzzling. He says he knows he has no wisdom, so he cannot see why the god called him the wisest of men. He decides to test the claim by finding someone wiser than himself, so he could prove the god wrong.

Socrates describes testing a man who had a reputation for wisdom. In talking with him, Socrates concluded that the man only thought himself wise and was not really wise. Pointing this out made the man hate him, and others who heard it shared his hostility.

Socrates describes questioning a man who claimed wisdom. He concludes that he is better off than the man, because the man wrongly thinks he knows, while Socrates admits he does not know. He then questions another man with the same result, and both men become his enemies.

Socrates says he went to one man after another who seemed wise, though he knew this made enemies, because he felt bound to test what the oracle (a divine message) had said. His conclusion was that the men with the highest reputation were, in fact, the most foolish.

Socrates says he tested others he thought were wiser than himself, to prove the oracle wrong, but found the oracle true. After visiting the politicians, he expected to find poets wiser than he was, and expected to learn that he knew less than they did.

Socrates says he asked poets about the hard lines in their own work, hoping to learn from them. He found that almost anyone present could explain the poetry better than the poets could. So he concluded that poets write not from wisdom but from a kind of natural gift and inspiration.

Socrates says that poets, like seers, speak many fine things without understanding them. He found that poets wrongly thought their skill made them wise in other matters too, so he judged himself wiser than them, as he had judged himself wiser than the politicians.

Socrates says he went to skilled craftsmen and found they knew many useful things he did not. But he noticed they, like the poets, wrongly thought their skill made them wise in all high matters. He concluded he was better off as he was: neither knowing their knowledge nor sharing their mistaken belief in their own wisdom.

Socrates says that his enemies and false accusations have come from his questioning of people. People call him wise, but he says only God is truly wise. He claims the god's answer means human wisdom is worth little or nothing, and that Socrates is named only as an example of someone who knows his own wisdom is worthless.

Socrates says that, obeying the god, he goes around questioning anyone who seems wise, and when he finds they are not, he shows them so. This work takes up all his time, so he has no leisure for public affairs or his own affairs, and he lives in poverty as a result.

Young wealthy men with spare time follow Socrates on their own, enjoy watching self-proclaimed experts being questioned, and copy him by questioning others. When those people are shown to know little, they blame Socrates instead of themselves, calling him a corrupter of the young.

Socrates says that when people are asked what wrong Socrates actually does or teaches, they cannot say. Instead they repeat the stock accusations made against all philosophers: studying things in the sky and under the earth, denying the gods, and making the weaker argument seem stronger. They do this because they would rather not admit that their claim to knowledge has been exposed.

Socrates says that many people have spoken against him for a long time, and their slander has turned the jury's ears against him. He names three accusers, each acting for a different group: Meletus for the poets, Anytus for the craftsmen and politicians, and Lycon for the public speakers. He admits he cannot clear away so much slander quickly.

Socrates says he has held nothing back and hidden nothing from the Athenians. He claims that people hate him for his blunt speech, and that this hatred is itself proof he is telling the truth. This, he says, is the source of the prejudice against him.

Socrates says he has answered the first group of accusers and now turns to the second, led by Meletus. He reads out their formal charge: that Socrates corrupts the young, does not believe in the state's gods, and worships new divinities of his own.

Socrates turns to the charges against him. He says it is Meletus, his accuser, who does evil, because Meletus pretends to be serious about the youth when he has never really cared about the matter. Socrates says he will prove this by questioning Meletus, and the first answer Meletus gives is that he does care about improving the young.

Socrates presses Meletus, his accuser, to name the person who improves the young men he is said to corrupt. When Meletus answers "the laws," Socrates says he means a person who first knows the laws, and asks who that is.

Socrates argues that it is absurd to think one man corrupts the young while everyone else improves them. He points out that with horses, one trainer does good while many others harm them, so the usual pattern is the reverse. He concludes that Meletus, his accuser, has shown no real concern for young people.

Socrates questions Meletus, his accuser, about whether people prefer living among good or bad neighbours. Meletus agrees that good people do good to those around them and bad people do harm, and that no one wants to be harmed. Socrates then asks whether Meletus accuses him of corrupting the youth on purpose, and Meletus says yes.

Socrates is questioning his accuser, Meletus. He points out that the accuser has admitted that good people benefit those around them and bad people harm them. Socrates argues that no sensible person would knowingly corrupt those they live with, since that would bring them harm, so either he does not corrupt others or he does so only by accident.

Socrates argues that if he harmed the city unintentionally, the law should not punish him. Instead, his accusers should have privately warned him so he could change. Court, he says, is for punishment, not for teaching.

Socrates asks the accuser Meletus exactly how he is supposed to corrupt the young. Meletus replies, as the charge reads, that Socrates teaches them to reject the state's gods and to worship new divinities or spirits instead.

Socrates asks the accuser Meletus to state the charge more plainly. He wants to know whether Meletus means that he teaches people to believe in other gods than the city's gods, or that he is a plain atheist who teaches atheism. Meletus answers that Socrates is a complete atheist.

Socrates is answering the charge of his accuser Meletus. He asks whether Meletus means that he does not believe the sun and moon are gods, as other people do. Socrates says Meletus is wrong, since Meletus claims the sun is a stone and the moon is earth.

Socrates tells his accuser Meletus that the views he is blamed for are already in the books of Anaxagoras, a well-known earlier thinker, so the judges would know them. He adds that such ideas are also mocked openly in the theatre, where audiences can laugh at them. He then asks Meletus whether he really thinks Socrates believes in no god at all.

Socrates says Meletus, his accuser, does not believe his own charge. He thinks the indictment is a careless trick, a riddle meant to test whether Socrates can spot its contradiction. The charge says Socrates both refuses to believe in the gods and believes in them, which Socrates says no serious person would write.

Socrates asks the Athenians to look closely at what he thinks is a contradiction in Meletus's charge, and he asks Meletus to answer his questions. He also asks the audience not to interrupt him while he speaks in his usual way.

Socrates argues that no one can believe in human activities without believing in the people who perform them, such as horsemanship without horses. From this he concludes that a person cannot believe in divine activities without believing in the spirits or demigods who carry them out.

Socrates argues that he cannot believe in gods without also believing in spirits or demigods, since spirits are either gods or the sons of gods. So, he says, the charge that he believes in spiritual beings means he must believe in gods, and the court's silence agrees with this reasoning.

Socrates is answering a charge that he denies the gods but believes in spirits. He argues this is a contradiction: spirits called demigods are the children of gods, so anyone who accepts them must accept gods too.

Socrates says that Meletus's charge is absurd: it is like saying a man believes in mules but not in horses and donkeys. He claims Meletus invented the charge only to test him, since he had no real accusation. He adds that no sensible person could believe a man can accept divine beings yet deny that gods, demigods and heroes exist.

Socrates says he has already answered the charge brought by Meletus, so a long defence is not needed. He believes his real danger is the many people who have turned against him, not Meletus or Anytus. He notes that this kind of hostility has killed many good men before him and will likely kill more.

Socrates answers a critic who asks whether he is ashamed of a way of life that may lead to an early death. He says a good man should not weigh the chance of living or dying. He should only ask whether an action is right or wrong, and whether it is the act of a good man or a bad one.

Achilles, a hero of the Trojan War, cared more about avoiding disgrace than about danger. When he was eager to kill Hector, his mother Thetis, a sea goddess, warned him that he would die soon after Hector.

Socrates recalls Achilles, who chose to avenge his dear friend Patroclus and die rather than live in disgrace. Achilles faced death without fear, and the passage says a man should stay at his post in danger, whether he chose that post or was given it by a commander.

Socrates says it would be strange of him to abandon his post out of fear of death now. He stood firm in battle when his generals ordered him to, and he believes God has now ordered him to examine himself and others as a philosopher.
