Socrates argues that fearing death is a false sort of wisdom, because it claims to know something no one can know. No one knows whether death might be the greatest good rather than the greatest evil. Thinking you know what you do not know is, he says, a shameful kind of ignorance.

Socrates says his only claim to wisdom is that he does not pretend to know what lies beyond death, while he does know that wronging or disobeying a better being, god or man, is evil. So he will not fear an uncertain good more than a known evil. He then begins to address the jury, saying they might let him go if they are not persuaded by Anytus.

Socrates imagines the Athenians offering to free him on one condition: that he stop questioning and examining people as he has been doing, on pain of death. He says that if this were the offer, he would answer that he honours and loves them, but would still obey the god rather than them.

Socrates says he will obey God rather than the court, and will keep practicing and teaching philosophy for as long as he lives. He will question anyone he meets, asking why they care so much about money, honour and reputation and so little about wisdom, truth and the health of the soul. If the person says they do care, he will not leave them alone.

Socrates says he questions and tests anyone he meets who claims to have virtue but seems to lack it, and he rebukes them for valuing the lesser things above the greater. He says he does this with everyone, especially fellow citizens, because God has commanded it, and he believes this service to God has done the city more good than anything else.

Socrates says his whole activity is urging people, young and old, to care first about the improvement of their soul rather than their money or property. He argues that virtue does not come from money; instead, money and every other good come from virtue. He adds that if this teaching corrupts the young, he is guilty, and he tells the Athenian jurors to acquit him or not as they choose.
Socrates asks the Athenian jury to let him finish speaking without interruption, promising it will benefit them. He warns that killing a man like him would harm the Athenians more than it harms him.

Socrates says his accusers cannot really harm him, because a bad man cannot injure a better one. Anytus may kill him, exile him, or take away his civil rights, and others may think this is a great harm. Socrates disagrees: the greater evil lies in Anytus's own unjust act of taking a life.

Socrates says he is not defending himself for his own sake but for the Athenians', so they do not wrong God by condemning him. He compares himself to a gadfly, a biting insect sent by God to wake up a large, slow horse, which stands for the state. His job, he says, is to keep stirring, urging, and criticising the Athenians.

Socrates tells the Athenian jury that he is like a gadfly sent by God to wake up a sluggish horse, meaning the city. He warns that if they kill him, as Anytus urges, they will go back to sleep and not easily find anyone like him.

Socrates argues that his mission from God is shown by his behavior. He has neglected his own affairs for years to advise people one by one on virtue, which he says no ordinary person would do. He adds that he never took payment for this, and his accusers have no proof that he did.

Socrates explains why he does not take part in public politics. He has a private inner sign, a kind of voice from a divine source, which has come to him since childhood. It never tells him to act, only warns him off doing something, and it has kept him out of politics.

Socrates says that if he had taken part in politics, he would have been killed long ago without helping anyone, himself included. He adds that a person who opposes a crowd to stop its unjust acts will not survive, so anyone who wants to live must stay a private citizen.

Socrates says he will prove his point with his actions, not just words. He will tell a true story from his own life, about a court case, to show that he would never give in to injustice out of fear of death.

Socrates says that his only public office was as a senator, when his tribe presided over the trial of generals who had failed to recover the dead after the battle of Arginusae. The Athenians wanted to try them all together, which was against the law. Socrates alone among the presiding officers opposed this and voted against it.

Socrates says that during the democracy he refused to join an unjust act demanded by the crowd, even though he risked punishment for refusing. Later, under the rule of the Thirty, he was ordered with four others to bring Leon of Salamis in to be executed, and he again defied an unjust order.

Socrates says that when the authorities ordered him to take part in an unjust arrest, he refused. He was not afraid of death; his only concern was not to do wrong. So he went home while the other four men went to fetch Leon, the man they were ordered to seize.

Socrates tells the Athenian jury that he could not have lived so long in public life if he had always stood for justice as he should. He says he has acted the same way in public and in private, never giving in to improper demands, including from people who call themselves his followers, though he has no formal students.

Socrates says that anyone, young or old, rich or poor, may come and listen to him and talk with him, and he charges no one for it. He says he never taught anyone anything in secret, so nobody can rightly blame him for how any listener turns out. Anyone claiming a private lesson from him is lying.

Socrates says people enjoy hearing him question those who claim to be wise, because it is entertaining. He says a god has given him this task, shown through oracles, visions and other signs. If this were not true, he adds, it would soon be disproved.

Socrates says that if he has corrupted young men, those who grew up and now see that his advice harmed them should step forward as accusers. Their fathers, brothers or other relatives could also speak up about any harm done to their families. He notes that some of them, including Crito and his son Critobulus, are present in the court.

Socrates names several men in the court who have relatives who spent time with him. He notes which of them are present and which are dead, and says the dead man's brother can no longer be expected to stop him from speaking.

Socrates says that several men, including Aeantodorus, brother of Apollodorus, are present and could testify. He invites Meletus to call any witnesses he has forgotten or has. He then claims that these men are ready to speak in his favour, though Meletus and Anytus call him a corrupter of the young.

Socrates says that the older relatives of the young men might also speak for him. He asks why they would do so, and answers that it would be for the sake of truth and justice, because they know he is telling the truth and that Meletus, his accuser, is lying.

Socrates says that some listeners may be offended that he will not do what others did in court. Those others, facing lesser charges, wept, begged the judges, and brought their children and friends to plead for them. Socrates says he will not do these things, even though his life is in danger.

Socrates imagines a juror who might vote against him out of anger at his refusal to beg for mercy. He answers that he is an ordinary man with a family, including young sons, but he will not bring them to court to plead for his acquittal.

Socrates says he is not refusing to beg for mercy out of pride or disrespect toward the jury. He will not discuss whether he fears death. He says that acting in a humble, pleading way would bring shame on himself, on the jury, and on the city, because he is known as a wise man and the public already regards him as superior to others.

Socrates says that men thought to be wise, brave, or good behave shamefully when they are condemned to death. He has seen them act strangely, as if death were a terrible fate and as if they could live forever if only they were spared.

Socrates says that men of reputation who weep and wail in court shame the city, as if the most respected Athenians were no better than women. He says such men should not do this, and that the jurors should punish the man who makes a sorrowful scene more than the man who stays quiet.

Socrates argues that it is wrong to ask a judge for a favour to win an acquittal, rather than trying to inform and convince him. A judge's job is to give a true judgment under the law, not to hand out justice as a gift, and he has sworn to judge by the laws rather than by his own wishes. Begging for favour would encourage the judge to break that oath, which Socrates says is not pious.

Socrates refuses to ask the jury to break their oaths by acquitting him through pleading, since that would mean teaching them there are no gods, which would prove the charge against him. He says he does believe in the gods, more deeply than his accusers do, and leaves his case to the jury and to God.

Socrates says he is not upset by the guilty verdict. He expected it, and he is surprised the vote was so close, since he thought the majority against him would be much larger. He adds that Meletus, his accuser, would have failed to win a fifth of the votes, which would have fined him heavily, had Anytus and Lycon not helped him.

Socrates says that, since the accuser has proposed death, he must ask what he himself deserves. He says he has lived without seeking wealth, family advantage, public office, or political influence. He judged that he was too honest to be a politician and survive, so he avoided public life where he could do no good to the city or to himself.

Socrates says he went to each Athenian in private to urge them to care first for their own virtue and wisdom, and only then for their personal interests and the good of the city. He then asks what reward would fit a poor man who does this kind of good for them and wants free time to teach.

Socrates says that the fitting reward for him is free meals in the Prytaneum, the city's public hall, which he argues he deserves more than an Olympic victor. He claims the victor only seems happy, while Socrates is truly in need and gives the city something real. So he proposes this as the just penalty he should receive.

Socrates says he is not speaking defiantly. He says he is sure he never knowingly wronged anyone, but he cannot make the jury believe this, because the trial has been too short. He adds that if Athenian law required a death case to last more than one day, he thinks he could have convinced them.

Socrates says he will not claim he deserves any punishment, because he knows he has never wronged anyone. He asks why he should propose a penalty at all. He does not know whether death is good or bad, so he will not propose death as his penalty, since that might be an evil. He also rejects imprisonment as a penalty he would be unwilling to accept.

Socrates is on trial and is being asked to propose his own penalty. He says he cannot pay a fine, so jail until payment would not work for him. He also says exile is unlikely to be accepted by others, since his own fellow citizens cannot bear his talk.

Socrates says he is too old to spend his life wandering from city to city, always being exiled. He expects that young men will follow him wherever he goes, and that either the young men's elders or their families will then drive him out, whether he sends the young men away or lets them come.

Socrates imagines a critic asking why he cannot simply stay silent and leave the city to live elsewhere. He says he cannot stop speaking, because that would disobey the god, and he expects that his listeners will find this hard to believe.

Socrates says that talking every day about virtue and examining himself and others is the greatest good for a person, and that a life without such examination is not worth living. He admits the jury will find this hard to believe, but insists it is true. He also says he has never thought he deserved any harm.

Socrates, on trial, says he has no money, so he cannot pay a large fine. He offers a fine of one mina, and his friends, Plato, Crito, Critobulus and Apollodorus, propose thirty minas instead, promising to stand as guarantors for that sum.

Socrates tells the jurors that they will gain little by executing him. Critics of Athens will say they killed a wise man, and they will call him wise even though he is not. He also says he is old and would soon have died naturally, so they could have waited.

Socrates says he was not convicted for lack of persuasive words. He was convicted because he would not beg for mercy, weep, and wail before the jury as they expected, since he thought such behaviour beneath him.

Socrates says he will not act in a cowardly or dishonourable way to save himself from danger, and he does not regret the way he defended himself. He would rather die speaking in his own manner than live by speaking as others wish. Escaping death is easy in many cases; the real difficulty is avoiding wrongdoing.

Socrates says that death is coming to him slowly, as an old man, while his accusers are swift to be overtaken by wrongdoing, which he calls a faster runner. He has been condemned to death and accepts his sentence, as his accusers accept theirs, which he thinks is fated and good.

Socrates, sentenced to death, says that as he is about to die he can foretell the future. He tells his judges that they will face a heavier punishment after his death, because they killed him to avoid being called to account for their lives. He says more accusers will come against them than had accused him.

Socrates warns the judges who condemned him that if they kill people to stop them criticising their bad lives, they are mistaken. Silencing critics is neither possible nor honourable. The better course is to improve oneself rather than to silence others.

Socrates, after being condemned, speaks to the jurors who voted to acquit him, and to those who judged him. He asks them to stay a little longer so he can tell them what has just happened to him before he goes to his death.

Socrates says his inner divine sign has always warned him off, even about small matters, when he was about to go wrong. Now he faces what is generally thought to be the worst evil, yet the sign has given no warning about anything he did today, whether leaving home, going to court, or speaking.

Socrates says his divine sign, which usually stops him when he is about to do wrong, has not stopped him this time. He takes this silence as a sign that what has happened to him is good, and that death is not an evil, as his opponents think.
Death is presented as possibly good, because it is one of two things. Either it is a total lack of feeling, like a dreamless sleep, which would be a great gain, or the soul moves to another world.

Socrates argues that death may be a good thing. If death is like a deep, dreamless sleep, then it would be better than most of a person's waking days and nights, even a king's. On that view, death is a gain, and eternity would be just one such night.

Socrates suggests that if death is a journey to another place where the dead gather, it would be a great good. There he could meet the judges of the underworld and famous poets such as Orpheus, Homer and Hesiod, and he says such a meeting would be worth any price.

Socrates says that if death is a kind of sleep or a move to another place, he would gladly die many times over. In the afterlife he expects to talk with heroes who were wrongly condemned, and to keep questioning people about true and false wisdom.

Socrates imagines meeting famous figures from Greek myth, such as the Trojan leader Agamemnon and the cunning Odysseus, and questioning them. He says the afterlife would be a pleasure, since the dead there do not execute people for asking questions, and they are also happier and immortal.

Socrates tells the judges not to fear death, because no harm can come to a good man in life or after death. He believes the gods have not neglected him, and that his death came at the right time. He bears no anger toward his accusers and judges, since they did him no real harm, though they did not intend to help him.

Socrates asks the jurors to rebuke his sons if they care more about money or other things than about virtue, or if they think they are important when they are not. He wants them corrected in the same way he has corrected the jurors. If they do this, he says, he and his sons will have been treated justly.

Every skill, every systematic field of knowledge, and every action or deliberate choice is thought to aim at some good. For this reason, a widely accepted definition of the highest good is that it is what all things aim at.

Some aims are simply the activity itself, while others are a product that exists apart from the activity. Where the aim is a product, that product is better than the activity that produces it. Since there are many activities and skills, there are also many aims: health for medicine, a ship for shipbuilding, victory for war, and wealth for household management.

The main point is that when several arts or sciences fall under one master art, the aim of the master art is more worth choosing than the aims of the arts beneath it. The lesser arts are pursued for the sake of the greater. Horse-bridle making, for example, serves horsemanship, and horsemanship's aim is more valued.

In this sentence Aristotle says it does not matter whether the activity itself is the goal of an action or whether the goal is something beyond the activity. Both cases occur in the arts and sciences he has just discussed.

Every action aims at some end. Some end is wanted for its own sake, and all other things are wanted for its sake. If we chose everything for the sake of a further end, desire would have no stopping point and would never be satisfied, so there must be one highest good, the Chief Good.

Knowing the highest good matters a great deal for how we actually live. Like archers aiming at a target, we are more likely to hit what is right if we know what we are aiming at. So we should try to outline what this good is and which science or skill it belongs to as its end.

Aristotle says that the end of the most commanding and far-reaching kind of knowledge is the good that all other pursuits aim at. He names politics as this kind of knowledge, because it decides which sciences a city should teach, who should learn them, and to what level. Military skill, household management and rhetoric fall under it too.

Aristotle argues that the science of politics (the highest practical science) governs all the others, so its aim must include their aims and be the good of human beings. He adds that the good of a whole community is greater and more complete to achieve and keep than the good of one person, and so more noble.

Aristotle says his study of politics can only be as exact as its subject allows, since ideas of nobleness and justice vary so much that some think they exist only by convention. Goods such as wealth and courage can also cause harm, as some people have been ruined by them.

Aristotle says that in ethics it is enough to give the truth roughly and in general outline, because the subject itself is general and its data are general. Each subject should be treated with only as much exactness as its nature allows. Demanding strict proof from a speaker on such matters is as unreasonable as accepting mere persuasion from a mathematician.

A person judges well in matters they know about. So on a particular subject, the person who has been taught in it is a good judge, and in general, the person with broad education is a good judge across many subjects.

A young man is not suited to study moral philosophy, Aristotle says, for two reasons. He lacks experience of real life, which the subject assumes, and he tends to follow his emotions, so he will gain nothing from lessons meant to shape conduct rather than just to inform.

Aristotle means that age alone does not make a person unfit to learn ethics; the real problem is being ruled by passion and chasing whatever desire comes up. Such people gain nothing from this knowledge, just as those lacking self-control do not. Those who shape their desires by reason, however, benefit greatly from it.

The author says he has said enough at the start about three things: who the student is, the attitude in which his remarks should be taken, and the goal he has in mind. He is finishing his introduction and moving on to the main subject.

Aristotle returns to his starting question: since every kind of knowledge and every choice aims at some good, what good does politics (the science of the city-state, here called politikē) aim at? He asks which of all the goods that can be acted for is the highest.

Most people agree on the word "happiness," and on the idea that living well and doing well mean the same as being happy. They disagree, however, about what happiness actually is. Some say it is something obvious, such as pleasure, wealth or honour, and different people name different things.

Aristotle says that people often give different answers about what the good is: a sick man calls health the good, and a poor man calls wealth the good. Some think the good is a separate thing that causes all particular goods. He decides to examine only the views that are most widely held or have some reason behind them.

Aristotle notes that there is a difference between reasoning from first principles and reasoning towards them. Plato, he says, asked whether the right path runs from principles or towards them, much as a race can be run from the judges' post to the far end or the other way round.

Aristotle says that a person who wants to study ethics needs a good upbringing in good habits first. For a starting principle is a fact that is clear to the person, so no further reason is needed. Someone who can neither hold such principles nor learn them is beyond help.

A person is best if he works things out for himself. He is good if he accepts a sound suggestion from someone else. He is useless if he does neither, ignoring both his own judgment and the advice of others.

People's ideas of the highest good, or happiness, follow from the kind of life they lead. Most people, who are of low character, think happiness is pleasure and so settle for a life of physical enjoyment. Aristotle names two other main ways of life: public life and the life of contemplation.

Aristotle says that most people choose a brutish, pleasure-seeking life, and that the active and refined people aim at honour instead. He rejects honour as the highest good, because it depends on others giving it and so is not truly one's own. The highest good, he argues, must belong to a person and be hard to take away.

People seek honour in order to be thought good, and so virtue seems higher than honour. Yet virtue alone is not enough for happiness, since a virtuous man could sleep through life or suffer great misfortune, and no one would call such a man happy.

Aristotle says that the life devoted to making money is forced on a person, and that wealth is not the good we are looking for. Wealth is wanted only for the sake of something else. The honours and pleasures he has just discussed are likely to be the right ends, since people value them for their own sake, though he says they are not the final aim either.

Aristotle says we should examine whether there is one Universal Good shared by all things, even though this means criticising Plato's Forms, which were introduced by friends. He holds that truth must come first, even if it means giving up our own theories, since we love wisdom.

Aristotle argues that the Platonists' doctrine of Forms cannot apply to good in its different senses. Good is said of substance, quality and relation, and substance comes first because relations depend on it. So, by their own principle, there cannot be one common Form of good covering all these cases.

Good is said in as many senses as there are kinds of being, such as substance, quality, quantity, relation, time and place. So good cannot be one single universal thing shared by all of them. If it were, it would be said in only one category, not in all of them.

Aristotle argues that if all good things shared one Form, one science would study them all. In fact, even goods in the same category have different sciences. For example, the right moment in war belongs to generalship, while the right moment in disease belongs to medicine.

Aristotle is questioning Plato's idea of a "very-good," a single Good that exists apart from particular good things. He argues that if the Form of Man and any individual man are both fully man, they do not differ in being man, so the Good itself would not differ from any particular good. He adds that lasting forever does not make the Good better, just as something white that lasts a long time is no whiter than something white that lasts a day.

Aristotle says that the Pythagoreans give a more believable view on this question. They list "One" among the goods in their table that sets goods against bads. Speusippus seems to have followed them in this.

Aristotle says that some objectors might argue that the theory he has criticized, which claims all goods share one form, does not apply to all goods. Only goods pursued for their own sakes, such as those wanted simply in themselves, would fit under one form. Other things are called good because they produce, preserve, or prevent the opposite of those goods. So goods are good in two ways: in themselves, or because of something else.

Aristotle asks which goods are worth pursuing for their own sake, apart from anything else they bring. He suggests examples such as wisdom, sight, certain pleasures and honours. He then wonders whether only the Form of the Good, a single ideal standard, could count as such a good.

Aristotle argues that if goods such as honour, wisdom and pleasure were each good in their own separate way, then their goodness would have to be defined in the same way, as whiteness is the same in snow and white lead. But the definitions of honour, wisdom and pleasure, as goods, are different. So the highest good is not one common thing with a single shared form.

Aristotle asks whether the word "good" is applied to many things in one shared sense, such as having one source, aiming at one end, or being alike by analogy. He sets this aside as a matter for another field of study. He also says that even a single good existing apart from particular things could not be something humans can act on or reach, and so that is not what he is looking for now.

Someone might think it would be better to study the Good so that it serves as a model for practical goods that can actually be reached. With that model in mind, a person would know more clearly which things are good for them personally, and once known, could obtain them.

Aristotle is answering an argument that the highest good must be known to everyone who wants it. His reply is that the crafts and sciences all aim at some good yet do not study that highest good itself. It is unlikely that every craftsman would ignore such a great help and never look for it.

Aristotle is saying that knowing the general "good" in the abstract would not help a craftsman like a weaver, carpenter, or doctor in his work. A physician studies the health of a particular person, not health in general, because he has to heal individuals.

Aristotle asks what the good is that people aim at in their actions. Different activities have different goods: health in medicine, victory in war, a house in building. He concludes that the good is the end that each action aims at, and if there is one end for all actions, that is the good; if there are several, those are the goods.
The discussion has wandered around and returned to where it began. The speaker says this point needs to be made even clearer.

Aristotle argues that not every end we pursue is final. We pick some goals only for the sake of others, such as wealth or instruments. The highest good must be something pursued for its own sake, so if only one such thing exists, it is what we seek; if several exist, the most final of them is.

Aristotle ranks ends by how far they are pursued for their own sake. Something pursued only for itself is more final than something pursued for the sake of another thing. The "absolutely final" end is the one always chosen for itself and never for anything else.

Happiness is the one thing we always choose for its own sake and never for the sake of something else. We do choose honour, pleasure, intellect and other excellences for their own sakes too, but we also choose them because we think they will make us happy. Nobody chooses happiness in order to get any of these.

Aristotle says that self-sufficiency, which he treats as a feature of the highest good, does not mean a person living alone. It includes parents, children, wife, friends and fellow citizens, because humans are naturally social. He adds that some limit must be set, since extending it to every relative and friend of a friend would have no end.

Aristotle says that happiness is self-sufficient: on its own it makes life worth choosing and lacks nothing. Happiness is also the most choice-worthy of all things, and it should not be counted alongside other goods. If it were added to something else, even a tiny extra good would make the whole more choice-worthy, which shows happiness cannot be ranked as one good among many.

Calling happiness the highest good may sound like an empty statement, so a clearer account of what happiness really is would be useful. The way to get it is to first find out what a human's special work is. Just as a flute-player, sculptor or any craftsman has their highest good in their work, a person may too, if they have a work of their own.

Aristotle asks whether a human being, unlike a carpenter or a cobbler, has no particular job that nature assigns. He suggests that just as each part of the body, such as the eye or hand, has its own function, the whole person likely has a function of his own too.

Aristotle is looking for what is distinctive about human life. He rules out mere living, which plants share, and sensation, which animals share. What remains is a life of the rational nature that acts, and this rational part has two sides: one that obeys reason and one that has reason and uses it.

Aristotle says that the good life is best understood as active living, since that is what the name most properly refers to. He argues that the human work (function) is an activity of the soul in line with reason, and that a good person does this work well, as a good harp-player plays the harp well.

Aristotle argues by analogy: just as a good harp-player is one who plays the harp well, a human being's good is doing the work proper to a human, which he takes to be active life of the soul guided by reason. Done well and in the way of excellence (virtue), that activity is the human good. If excellence comes in degrees, it is the best and most complete excellence.

Aristotle says his account of the highest good is only a rough outline, to be filled in later. He thinks anyone can improve and complete it over time, just as skills have improved through the work of many people adding what was missing.

Each subject should be studied only to the degree of precision that suits it. A carpenter needs a straight line only as far as his work requires, while a geometrician studies its nature and properties for their own sake. Side questions should not outweigh the central ones.

For some things, you should not ask for a reason at all. It is enough that the fact has been clearly shown. This is true of first principles, which are the starting points of knowledge, so the fact itself is the basic starting point.

Aristotle says that the starting points of a subject are reached in different ways, such as by induction, by perception, or by habit. We should work out what each one is and define it carefully, since the starting point shapes everything that follows and is, in his view, more than half of the whole matter.

Aristotle says that the inquiry into happiness should use not only his own conclusions and starting facts, but also what people commonly say about it. His reason is that what is true fits together with everything that really exists, while what is false soon clashes with the truth.

Goods are commonly divided into three kinds: external goods, goods of the body, and goods of the soul. Goods of the soul are called the most truly good. Since happiness is defined as the activities of the soul, it belongs to the soul.

Aristotle says his account of the good is sound, at least by the view of ancient thinkers and philosophers. He adds that treating certain actions and activities as the end is correct, because it places the good among goods of the soul rather than external goods.

Aristotle says that the common view, that a happy man lives and acts well, fits with his own account of happiness. He adds that the views people hold about what happiness consists of (virtue, practical wisdom, philosophical understanding, pleasure, or outside success, alone or combined) all fall within that account.

Aristotle says that views held by many people, or by old tradition, or by a few respected thinkers, are unlikely to be wrong entirely and are probably right in at least some points. He adds that those who call the good a kind of virtue or excellence agree with his own account, since acting well belongs to excellence.

Aristotle says it matters whether the highest good is a state a person possesses or an activity a person performs. A state can exist while a person sleeps or is otherwise inactive, so it does no good then. Activity, however, always acts and acts well. He compares this to the Olympic games, where the crown goes to those who compete, not to the strongest men who merely exist.

Aristotle says that a life of virtue is pleasant in itself, because each person takes pleasure in what they love, such as a horse for a horse lover. Most people's pleasures conflict, since those pleasures are not natural. For lovers of what is noble, the actions of virtue are naturally pleasant, both to them and in themselves.

Aristotle argues that a good person takes pleasure in virtuous actions. A man who feels no pleasure in noble, just, or generous acts is not truly good. So virtuous actions must be pleasant in themselves, and they are also good and noble, as a good person's judgment confirms.

Happiness is the highest, noblest and most pleasant good, and these qualities are not split apart as they are in a famous Delian inscription that gives each one to a different thing. Instead, they all come together in the best kinds of activity, and happiness is those qualities together, or the best of them.

Aristotle says that a happy life needs outside goods as well as virtue. Without tools like friends, money, and political influence, noble actions are hard or impossible to do. Lacking some of these outside goods also spoils happiness.

Aristotle says that outward goods such as good birth, good children, good friends and beauty seem necessary for happiness. A person who is ugly, badly born, alone, or childless is hardly able to be happy. For this reason some people count good fortune as part of happiness, and others count virtue.

The question being raised is whether happiness can be learned, gained through habit or some other training, or whether it comes from God's gift or simply from chance. The passage only asks the question and does not answer it.

Aristotle says that happiness may be a gift from the gods, but he leaves that question for another inquiry. Whether or not it comes directly from the gods, he argues that happiness, reached through virtue and learning, is among the most godlike things, since the goal of virtue is excellent, divine and blessed.
Aristotle is saying that happiness, on this view, is open to many people. It can come through learning and a certain kind of effort, to anyone who has not been crippled in their capacity for virtue.

It is better for happiness to come from a cause than from chance, and this supports the view that it does. Things that follow nature, art, or any cause, especially the best cause, are arranged in the best possible way. So leaving the greatest and noblest things to chance would clash with all of this.

Happiness is defined as the activity of the soul in accordance with excellence, or virtue, of a certain kind. Some other goods must be present from the start, and helpful goods are given by nature as tools for achieving it.
Politics, the art of running a community, is said to aim at the highest good. Its main work, then, is to make the citizens good people who are inclined to do what is honourable.

Animals are not called happy because they cannot do the activities that make up a happy life. A child is not happy for the same reason, since its young age keeps it from such actions. If we call a child happy, we do so only by anticipation, meaning we speak of what it may later become.

Happiness needs complete virtue and a complete life, because many changes and chances come during a life. A man who was prosperous may still fall into great misfortune in old age, as Priam did in the Greek epic poems, and someone who dies in wretchedness is not called happy.

Aristotle asks whether anyone can be called happy while still alive, as the saying of Solon suggests, that one must wait to see the end of a life. He then asks whether a man can be happy after he is dead, which he calls absurd, since happiness is an activity.

Aristotle is considering a view that a dead man can be called happy because he is now beyond harm. He says this is still open to doubt, since the dead may still share in some good or bad things, such as honour or dishonour, and the fortunes of their children and descendants.

Aristotle is raising a problem for the view that a man who has lived happily to old age stays happy after death. His descendants may later have good or bad fortune, so the dead man's happiness seems open to change. Yet it seems absurd that the dead man should swing between happy and miserable with them, and also absurd that their affairs should not affect him at all.

Aristotle argues that if we judge a man's happiness only by how his life ends, then we cannot call a living man happy. Yet happiness seems stable, while fortune keeps changing. So a man could be called happy one moment and miserable the next, which he finds absurd.

Aristotle is saying that a person's happiness should not be judged by good or bad luck. Outside events are helpful extras to a human life, but what makes a life happy or unhappy is how a person acts in accordance with virtue.

Aristotle says that happiness lasts longer when it rests on actions done in line with virtue, because these are more lasting than even the sciences. The most valued of these activities last longest, since the happy person lives in them most and most continuously, which is why people do not forget them.

The passage says that the stability people look for will be found in the happy man. He stays steady through life, always or nearly always acting and thinking in line with virtue. He handles life's changes with dignity and balance, because he is truly good, a "faultless cube," a Greek saying for something perfectly balanced.

Small strokes of good or bad luck hardly change a life. Large and frequent ones do: good fortune makes a life happier, while bad fortune harms its happiness by causing pain and blocking action. Even so, a noble person shows his character by bearing great misfortunes calmly, not because he feels no pain but because he is high-minded.

A good person, Aristotle argues, can never become wretched, because he always acts well whatever his circumstances. Like a skilled general or shoemaker who makes the best of what he is given, he does the noblest thing possible in each situation. Still, he is not called blessed if he suffers the misfortunes of Priam, the king of Troy.

The happy person does not change easily. Ordinary bad luck will not shake his happiness, only great and repeated misfortunes will. And if he does lose it, he cannot get it back quickly, only over a long time in which he achieves great and noble things.
Aristotle asks why we should not call happy a person who acts with complete virtue and has enough outside goods to play his part in life. This holds over a full lifetime, not just a short stretch.

Aristotle says that a person must also die in a way that fits a happy life, because the future is unknown to us. He calls living people blessed if they have these goods, though only in the human sense of blessedness, and then he ends the discussion.

Aristotle is saying that the good or bad fortunes of a dead person's descendants and friends do not really affect how that person fares after death. He admits this sounds heartless and goes against common opinion. He adds that the details of how different events touch the dead are too many to sort out, so he will only give a general outline.

Aristotle is asking whether the happiness of a person is affected by misfortunes that befall their friends. He says some troubles weigh heavily on a life and others weigh less, just as with one's own misfortunes. He adds that it matters whether the friend is alive or dead, and he doubts whether the dead can still share in good or evil.

Aristotle is saying that the dead may be touched by the good or bad fortunes of their friends, but only slightly. Such events cannot make a happy dead person unhappy, or take away the blessedness of one who has it.

Aristotle is saying that, having settled some earlier points, the next question is whether happiness is something to be praised or something to be valued. He adds that happiness clearly is not a mere ability or capacity.

Praise is given to things because of their kind and their relation to something else. Just or brave people and virtue are praised for their actions and results. Strong or fast people are praised for their nature and for how they relate to something good and excellent.

Aristotle says that praise is for things measured against a standard, so it cannot fully fit the very best things. Those are honoured with something higher, which he illustrates by calling the gods blessed and calling humans blessed in so far as they are most like the gods.
Aristotle says that people do not praise happiness the way they praise justice. Instead they call happiness blessed, because it is more like a god and more excellent.

Eudoxus argued that pleasure is the highest good. His reason was that pleasure is not praised, which he took to show that it ranks above the things that are praised. He applied the same ranking to God and the Chief Good, since they are the standard by which everything else is measured. Praise goes to virtue and to particular deeds, so pleasure, not being praised, is placed higher.

Happiness is a thing of great worth and is an end in itself, the final goal we aim at. Aristotle also calls it a starting-point, since everything we do is done for its sake, and he says that the cause of good things must be something precious and divine.

Happiness is a kind of active working of the soul in line with excellence, or virtue. So to understand happiness, we must first study excellence. Aristotle adds that the statesman, who wants citizens to be good and law-abiding, has usually concerned himself most with this subject. If the study of excellence belongs to politics, the inquiry fits the original plan of the book.

Aristotle is saying that the topic now is human excellence, meaning virtue, and specifically excellence of the soul rather than of the body. His reason is that happiness, which he has just described as the chief good of man, is an activity of the soul.

The passage argues that a statesman needs some knowledge of the soul, just as an eye doctor needs knowledge of the whole body. The point is stronger because politics is higher and more valuable than medicine. Good doctors also study the body in depth.
The statesman should study the soul only as far as his own purpose needs. Going into greater detail would be more work than his field requires.

Aristotle says that the soul has two parts, one non-rational and one rational. He adds that whether these parts are physically separate, like parts of the body, or only separable in thought, like the two sides of a curve, does not matter for his present purpose.

Aristotle says that the non-rational part of the soul includes a part shared with other living things, the power that causes nourishment and growth. He notes that this power must be present even in embryos, and that it is probably the same in them as in fully grown creatures.

Aristotle says that the part of the soul that handles growth and nourishment does not share in the excellence special to humans, so he sets it aside. The point he makes on the way is that good and bad people look much alike while asleep, since sleep is a kind of inactivity of the soul, though good people may have somewhat better dreams.

The passage says the soul has a non-rational part that still shares in reason. We praise reason in people who control their appetites, and also in those who try to control them and fail. In such people, some other natural force pushes against reason.

Aristotle compares the soul to a paralysed body. When a paralysed limb is moved one way, it swings the other way, and we can see this. In the soul, people who cannot control their appetites are pulled in opposite directions, though we cannot see it. He suggests that the soul still has a part besides reason that opposes reason.

The passage says that the non-rational part of the soul also shares in reason. In a self-controlled person it obeys reason, and in a fully self-mastered or brave person it obeys even more fully, agreeing completely with reason.

The passage divides the non-rational part of the soul into two. The plant-like part, which handles growth and nourishment, has no share in reason at all. The part that desires does share in reason to some degree, because it can obey reason and be ruled by it.

The irrational part of the soul can be persuaded by reason, as shown by advice, rebuke and encouragement. So if this part is said to have reason too, then reason has two parts: one that rules by its own nature, and another that listens to reason the way a child respects a parent.

Aristotle divides human excellence into two kinds. Intellectual excellences include science, intelligence and practical wisdom, which belong to the mind. Moral excellences include qualities of character such as gentleness and self-control. Praised mental states are the ones called excellences.

Aristotle says human excellence comes in two kinds. Intellectual excellence grows mainly through teaching and needs experience and time. Moral excellence comes from habit or custom, and its Greek name is only slightly changed from the Greek word for custom.

Aristotle argues that the moral virtues are not part of our nature, since nothing that is natural can be changed by habit. A stone always falls and cannot be trained to rise. Instead, we are born with the capacity for virtue, and we develop the virtues through habit and practice.

Some abilities come to us by nature, and we have them before we use them. Our senses are an example: we did not first see and hear many times and so gain our senses; we had the senses already and so used them.

Virtues are acquired by doing the actions they describe, much as craftsmen learn a trade by practising it. Builders become builders by building, and harp-players by playing. In the same way, people become just by doing just acts, self-controlled by doing acts of self-control, and brave by doing brave acts.

Lawmakers make citizens good by training them through repeated habit, and this is what every lawmaker aims at. Those who do this well succeed, and those who do not fail. This is what separates a good constitution, or system of government, from a bad one.

Aristotle says that virtues are formed and destroyed by the same kind of actions that form and ruin a skill. People become good harp-players or good builders by practising well, and bad ones by practising badly. If this were not so, no teachers would be needed.

We become just or unjust, and brave or cowardly, by repeatedly acting in certain ways. Dealing with other people makes some people just and others unjust, and facing danger while getting used to fear or confidence makes some brave and others cowards.

Some people become self-controlled and gentle when faced with desire or anger, while others become undisciplined and quick-tempered. The difference comes from how they act in these moments. Habits are formed by repeating acts of the same kind, so the way we act shapes the character we build.
Being trained in one way or another from childhood matters a great deal. The speaker says it is not a small difference but in fact the whole difference.

Aristotle says this inquiry aims at making people good, not just at knowing what virtue is. So we must consider how to perform particular actions, since the habits we form depend on them. That we should act according to Right Reason is a general rule he will take as given for now and explain later.
Aristotle says that talk about moral action can only be rough and general, not exact. The subject does not have fixed rules, just as matters of health do not.

Ethics cannot be made exact, least of all in particular cases. No set of rules covers them, so each person must judge the specific situation, as a doctor or ship's navigator does. Even so, the subject should still be treated as well as possible.

Things of this kind are harmed by too much or too little. Too much or too little training weakens strength, and too much or too little food and drink harms health, while the right amount builds up and keeps both.

Virtues like courage and self-control are damaged by going too far or not far enough. Someone who fears everything becomes a coward, and someone who fears nothing becomes rash. Someone who indulges in every pleasure loses self-control, while someone who avoids all pleasure loses the ability to perceive properly. Only the middle course keeps these qualities intact.

Habits are formed by the same kinds of actions that later put them to use. Just as strength grows from eating well and working hard, and then lets a person do more of that work, so a person becomes self-controlled by abstaining from pleasures and becomes brave by facing fears.

A person's habits are tested by the feelings that follow their actions. Someone has self-control only if he refuses bodily pleasures and is glad to refuse them, not merely if he refuses while feeling sorry. Likewise, someone is brave only if he faces danger with pleasure or without pain.

Moral virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains. People do wrong because of pleasure and hold back from right action because of pain. So, as Plato said, children should be trained from the start to feel pleasure and pain at the right things. Virtues also involve feelings and actions, and both bring pleasure or pain.

Aristotle argues that habits of the soul are formed and spoiled by pleasures and pains. People become bad when they pursue or avoid pleasures and pains wrongly, in the wrong way, at the wrong time, or in excess. He also says that defining virtue as freedom from feeling is wrong, because it leaves out the need to feel and act rightly.
Virtue is a settled character trait that, in dealing with pleasures and pains, produces the best outcomes. Vice is the opposite trait, one that produces the worst.

Aristotle says that people are moved to choose or avoid things by three kinds of consideration: what is honourable or dishonourable, what is useful or harmful, and what is pleasant or painful. A good person judges rightly about all three, and a bad person judges wrongly, especially about pleasure, since pleasure comes along with every other thing that attracts us.
The passage says that a certain feeling or habit begins in us from infancy and grows along with us. Because it becomes part of our very life, it is hard to get rid of.

Aristotle says that people judge actions by how much pleasure and pain they bring, so good conduct depends on handling these feelings correctly. He adds that resisting pleasure is harder than resisting anger, and hard tasks show what skill and virtue are. A person who uses pleasure and pain well becomes good, and one who uses them badly becomes bad.

Virtue deals with pleasures and pains. The same things that create a virtue, used in different ways, can also strengthen it or damage it, and a virtue acts on the same kinds of things that produced it.

A reader might object that doing just or self-controlled actions already makes a person just or self-controlled, just as doing grammatical or musical acts makes someone a grammarian or musician. Aristotle replies that this is not so even in the arts. Someone may produce something grammatical by luck or by another's prompting. He becomes a grammarian only when he produces it knowing the grammar himself.

Unlike craft products, which are good simply by being made in the right way, virtuous actions count only if the doer is also in the right state. The agent must know what he is doing, choose it deliberately, and choose it for its own sake.

Aristotle is saying that knowing about something is enough to have a skill or craft, but knowing about the virtues counts for little. What matters for the virtues is the other conditions, which come from often doing just and self-controlled actions.

A person does not have a virtue just by performing actions that a just or self-controlled person would perform. He has the virtue only if he also does those actions the way a just or self-controlled person does them, that is, with the right inner disposition.

Virtues are built by doing the right actions, not by merely talking about them. People who only discuss ethics and do not act on it are like patients who listen closely to their doctor but ignore his instructions: they will not get better, in body or in mind.
Aristotle begins his inquiry into what virtue is by noting that mental states fall into three kinds: feelings, capacities, and states of character. Virtue must belong to one of these three kinds.

Aristotle sorts the mind's states into three kinds: feelings such as anger, fear and joy; capacities, which are our ability to have those feelings; and states, which are how well or badly we stand toward them. Anger, for example, is right when it is neither too strong nor too weak.

Aristotle argues that feelings such as anger and fear are not virtues or vices. We are not called good or bad for having them, nor praised or blamed for them alone. Also, we feel them without choosing to, while virtues involve deliberate choice.

Aristotle argues that virtues are neither feelings nor abilities. We are moved by feelings, but virtues are a settled way of being disposed. We are not called good or bad merely for being able to feel, and we are born with abilities, not with goodness or badness. So virtues must be states of character.
Virtue has been described as a general kind of thing, namely a state of mind or character. Aristotle says that this is not enough: one must also say what sort of state it is.

Aristotle argues that every excellence makes a thing both good in itself and good at its job. A good eye sees well, and a good horse is fast and carries its rider well. So human excellence, which is virtue, must be a state that makes a person good and lets them do their proper work well.

Aristotle says that any quantity, whether it can be divided into continuous parts or separate units, can be judged as more, less, or exactly equal. The exact equal sits between too much and too little. He is about to explain what he calls the mean of the thing itself, as opposed to the mean relative to us.

Aristotle separates two kinds of middle. The absolute mean is the point exactly halfway between two extremes, the same for everyone. The mean relative to us is what is neither too much nor too little for a particular person, so it can differ from one person to another. His example: if ten is too much and two too little, six is the absolute mean.

Aristotle is describing the mean, or middle point, between two extremes. The middle is the same distance above the smaller amount as it is below the larger. This kind of middle is set by arithmetical proportion, meaning equal differences, as in 2, 4, 6.

Aristotle says the right amount is not a fixed number that fits everyone. Ten minae is too much food and two is too little, but six is not automatically right, because the right amount depends on the person. A strong athlete like Milo needs more than a beginner. So a skilled person avoids excess and deficiency by choosing the mean relative to the individual.

Aristotle argues that just as a skilled craftsman aims at the mean, avoiding too much and too little, and produces work that cannot be improved by adding or removing anything, excellence of character works the same way. Since excellence is more exact than any craft, it must be naturally suited to aim at the mean.

Moral excellence, or virtue, is the topic. Feelings and actions can go too far or fall short, and both extremes are wrong. Virtue is the middle point: feeling and acting at the right time, toward the right people, for the right reasons, and in the right way.

Virtue deals with feelings and actions, and each can go too far, fall short, or hit the middle. Going too far is wrong, falling short is blamed, and the middle is praised and right. So virtue is, in a way, a middle state, because it aims at that middle.

Aristotle argues that there are many ways to fail at being good but only one way to succeed. Wrong action can take many forms, like too much or too little, while right action hits a single target, the mean. So going astray is easy and hitting the mean is hard, which is why vice includes both excess and deficiency and virtue is the mean.

Virtue is a settled character trait that leads a person to make deliberate choices. It lies at a middle point between extremes, is set by reason, and is fixed the way a person of practical wisdom would fix it.

Virtue is a middle state between two faults, one of too much and one of too little. Faults on either side miss what is right, in feelings and in actions, while virtue finds and keeps the mean. So virtue is a mean by its nature, but in terms of the highest good and excellence, it is the highest state possible.

Not every action or feeling can be found in a mean. Some, such as malice, shamelessness, envy, adultery, theft and murder, are bad in themselves. People blame them for being bad, not for having too much or too little of them.

Some actions are wrong in themselves, so a person can never do them rightly. For such acts, being right or wrong does not depend on choosing the right person, time, or manner. Adultery is the example given: committing it is simply wrong.

Aristotle is saying that some things have no mean, excess, or deficiency. Acting unjustly, cowardice, and giving up all self-control are bad in themselves, so it makes no sense to look for a middle point between them. Trying to do so would only make a middle of too much and a middle of too little.

Aristotle is saying that virtues like perfect self-control and courage have no excess or deficiency, since they are themselves the mean, the best possible state. Vices such as spite or shamelessness, by contrast, have no mean at all: whatever way they are done, they are wrong.

Aristotle says that general rules about moral conduct are not enough on their own. They must be applied to particular cases, since actions happen in specific situations. He will therefore take his examples from a known list, beginning with fear and confidence.

Aristotle says that courage is the middle state between two extremes. Too much confidence in the face of danger is called rash, and too little confidence, with too much fear, is called cowardice. The excess of fearlessness has no common name.

Aristotle says the middle state here is full self-control, and its opposite extreme is a complete lack of self-control. He notes that few, if any, people actually lack feeling for pleasure, so there is hardly a name for them. He calls such a person "insensible" for the sake of discussion.

Aristotle says that the right state about money is generosity, with wastefulness as too much and meanness as too little. The wasteful person gives out too much and takes in too little, while the mean person takes in too much and gives out too little. He adds that this is only a rough summary, to be made more exact later.

Aristotle lists more virtues that sit between an excess and a defect. Munificence is the mean for large spending on great wealth, unlike liberality, which deals with smaller sums. Greatness of Soul is the mean in matters of honour, with excess and defect on either side.

Aristotle says there is a further quality related to greatness of soul, just as liberality is related to munificence, except that it concerns small rather than great honour. A person can reach for honour either too much or too little.

Aristotle says that a person who wants honour too much is called ambitious, and one who wants it too little is called unambitious. The person who has the right amount has no name of their own. So the middle state is often called by either extreme's name, and people praise it sometimes as one and sometimes as the other.

Aristotle says that the state between too much and too little anger has no ordinary name, so he gives it one: "meekness." He then names the extreme states too: "passionate" for the person who feels too much anger, and "angerless" for the person who feels too little.

Aristotle says there are three more mean states, all concerned with how people speak and act toward others. One is about being truthful in speech and conduct, and the other two are about what is pleasant, one in play and amusement, the other in everyday life. He adds that the mean in every case is praiseworthy, while the extremes deserve blame.

Aristotle says that most of the states of character he is discussing have no proper names. He still thinks new names should be invented for them, so that they can be clearly understood. The passage then begins with the first case, truthfulness.

Aristotle names the character traits that sit at the middle point between two extremes in each area of life. For truthfulness, the middle is Truthfulness, exaggeration is Braggadocia, and understatement is Reserve. For amusement, the middle is Easy-pleasantry, too much is Buffoonery, and too little is Clownishness.

Aristotle's three kinds of social behavior are described here. A person who behaves as he should is called friendly, and the middle state is friendliness. Someone who goes too far is complaisant if he has no selfish reason, or a flatterer if he does. Someone who falls short and is unpleasant in every case is quarrelsome and cross.

Aristotle says that feelings also have a mean between too much and too little. Shamefacedness is not a virtue, yet people are praised for it, because it sits in the middle. Someone who is overwhelmed by shame on every occasion has too much, and someone with no shame at all has too little.

Indignation at undeserved success is the right middle feeling between envy and malevolence. All three concern pleasure or pain at what happens to others. The envious person is annoyed at every success of others, while the malevolent person feels no annoyance at all and even takes pleasure in others' misfortune.

Aristotle says that he will treat certain other virtues later, in their own place, just as he will do for justice, since the word "justice" has more than one meaning. He plans to examine each one closely and show how each is a mean state, and he will do the same for the intellectual virtues.

Every quality of character has three states: two faulty, one of excess and one of deficiency, and one right, the mean. Each extreme is opposed to the mean and also to the other extreme. The mean is greater than the deficient state and less than the excessive one, just as half is larger than a smaller part and smaller than a larger part.

A virtue can look like a vice when it is compared with the vice on the opposite side. The brave man seems rash next to the coward, and cowardly next to the rash man. The generous man seems wasteful next to the stingy, and stingy next to the wasteful.

The people at the two extremes each label the person in the middle as being like the other extreme. The coward calls the brave man rash, and the rash man calls him a coward. Because the two extremes are further apart from each other than either is from the middle, they are more opposed to each other than either is to the mean.

Sometimes an extreme looks like the middle point it sits beside. Rashness, for example, can look like courage, and wastefulness like generosity. But the two extremes are most unlike each other, and things that are furthest apart count as opposites.

In some cases the mean is opposed more to one extreme than the other. Courage is opposed more to cowardice, the deficiency, than to rashness, the excess. Self-mastery is opposed more to total lack of self-control, the excess, than to insensibility, the deficiency.

Aristotle explains why we set one extreme against the mean more than the other. Rashness is closer to courage and looks more like it, so we oppose cowardice to courage instead. The extreme further from the mean is treated as the more opposite one.

Aristotle says that we judge some extremes as worse because of our own natural tendencies. People naturally lean toward pleasure, so they find lack of self-control (an excess) more opposed to the right middle than self-discipline (a deficiency) is.

Moral virtue is a middle state between two faults: one of too much and one of too little. It lies in the middle because it is able to aim at the mean in both feelings and actions. Aristotle says this has now been fully explained.

Being good is hard because hitting the right middle point in each action takes skill, like finding the exact centre of a circle. Anyone can get angry, give money, or spend freely, but doing these things toward the right person, in the right amount, at the right time, for the right reason, and in the right way is difficult. That is why goodness is rare and admirable.

When aiming for the middle course, a person should first avoid the extreme that is further from the mean. Since hitting the exact middle is hard, the safest approach is to accept the lesser of the two errors.

Aristotle says we should notice our own natural tendency to go wrong, which we can detect by the pleasure and pain we feel. To correct it, we should pull ourselves hard in the opposite direction, as one straightens bent wood, and so reach the mean. Above all, we must be wary of pleasure, since we cannot judge it fairly.

Aristotle says we should treat pleasure the way the old counsellors treated Helen, the figure from the Trojan War story, and reject it. Doing so, he claims, makes it less likely we will go wrong, and these measures help us reach the mean, the balanced middle course between extremes.

Aristotle is saying that it is hard to judge exactly when, toward whom, for what reason, and for how long anger is right. People sometimes praise those who feel little anger and call them meek, and at other times they praise the quick-tempered as manly and spirited.

Small departures from what is right, either too much or too little, do not draw blame; only a considerable one does. Exactly where the line falls cannot be fixed in words. That judgment is a matter of detail and is left to moral perception.

Aristotle says that the middle state, between too much and too little, is always good. In practice, we should sometimes lean toward excess and sometimes toward deficiency, since this is the easiest way to reach the middle, which is what is right.

Aristotle argues that friendship should be studied next because it is either a virtue or closely tied to one, and because life is hard to bear without friends. He says that even rich and powerful people need friends, since wealth and power are unsafe without them, and that in poverty or misfortune friends are people's main refuge.

Friendship helps people at every age avoid mistakes. It helps the young stay on course, helps the old make up for weakness in attention and action, and helps those in their prime do noble deeds and carry out plans. Aristotle supports the last point with a line from Homer about two people going together.

Aristotle says that affection seems to be natural to living things. Parents feel it for their young and the young for their parents, and this is found in birds and most animals too. People also feel it toward others of their own tribe or nation, and travelers notice how people feel close to one another.

Aristotle says that friendship holds communities together, and that lawmakers care about securing it even more than justice. Where people are friends, justice is not needed, though just people still need friendship too. The most truly just relationship is thought to have something of friendship in it.

Friendship is not only necessary but also admirable. People praise those who love their friends, and having many friends is seen as a credit to a person. Some even say that a good man and a friend mean the same thing.

Aristotle notes that people disagree about what friendship is. Some say friends are alike, as the proverbs "Like will to like" and "Birds of a feather" suggest. Others say the opposite, that people in the same trade do not get along. Some explain it through nature, as Euripides does, with rain and earth pulling toward each other.
Heraclitus held that opposites are useful, that the best harmony comes from things that differ, and that everything arises through conflict. Empedocles, in direct contrast, held that like seeks like.

Aristotle sets aside questions about the natural world and turns to questions about human character and feelings. He asks whether friendship exists among everyone or only among good people, and whether there is one kind of friendship or several. He also argues that the claim there is only one kind, because friendship comes in degrees, is not well supported, since things of different kinds can also differ in degree.

Aristotle says that friendship does not have just anything as its object. It is directed at something specific: the good, the pleasant, or the useful. Since what is useful is useful because it brings some good or pleasure, he concludes that the good and the pleasant are the true objects of friendship.

Aristotle asks whether friendship is directed at what is good in itself or at what seems good to each person, since these can differ. He suggests each person loves what seems good to him, but concludes that this makes no real difference, because what is truly good will also seem good to the mind.

Friendship needs mutual goodwill, so we do not call love of inanimate things friendship. Nobody really wishes good to wine; a man who loves wine only wants it kept safe for his own enjoyment. A true friend, by contrast, is wished every good for the friend's own sake.

Aristotle says that wishing good to someone who does not return the feeling is called kindliness, not friendship. Friendship needs the feeling to be mutual and known to both sides. He notes that people often feel kindly toward others they have never met, because they judge them lovable or useful.

Aristotle says that people who merely feel goodwill toward each other cannot yet be called friends if neither knows the other's feelings. For friendship to be complete, each must wish the other well for one of the reasons he has named, and both must know that the goodwill is mutual.

Friendships differ in kind because the reasons for loving someone differ, so there are three kinds of friendship. Each kind matches one of the three things people can be loved for, and in each kind the love is mutual and both sides know it.

People who are friends wish good for each other, and they do so because of the friendship itself. Those whose reason for friendship is usefulness are not truly friends. They are only connected to the extent that each gets some benefit from the other.

Friendships based on usefulness or pleasure love the other person only for what they provide, not for who they are. A useful friend is valued for the advantage gained, and a pleasant friend for the enjoyment given. Such friendships last only as long as that benefit or enjoyment lasts.

Friendships based on usefulness or pleasure tend to end when the two people stop being pleasant or useful to each other. Usefulness keeps changing, so once the reason for the friendship is gone, the friendship ends too, since it only existed because of those circumstances.

Aristotle says that friendships based on usefulness are found mostly among older people, and among younger men who chase profit. Such friends do not spend much time together, because they enjoy each other only when they expect some gain. Hospitality is also counted among these friendships.

Young people's friendships, Aristotle says, are based on pleasure. Because they follow their passions and chase whatever pleases them at the moment, their pleasures shift as they grow older. So their friendships form and end quickly, changing with the pleasure they bring.

Young people are strongly drawn to love, which comes largely from impulse and the pursuit of pleasure. Because of this they form friendships quickly and drop them just as fast, sometimes changing within a single day. They do, however, want close company with their friends, since that is how they reach the goal of their friendship.

Perfect friendship is the bond between good people who are alike in their goodness. They wish good to each other for each other's own sake, not for what they gain, so the friendship lasts as long as they stay good, and goodness itself tends to last.

Good friends, Aristotle says, are good in themselves and also good for each other, since they help one another. They are also pleasant to each other, because each person enjoys actions that fit his own nature and similar actions. When people are good, these actions stay the same, or nearly the same.

Friendship lasts when it joins all the qualities that make friends good. Every kind of friendship rests on something good or pleasant, and on some likeness between the friends. Friendship is strongest and best between people who are good in themselves and alike in that goodness.

Friendship of the perfect kind is probably rare, because good men are rare. It also takes time and close acquaintance for two people to really know each other and prove they are worthy of friendship. A quick wish to be friends can arise fast, but real friendship cannot.
This kind of friendship is complete, lasting over time and in every other way. Each friend gets the same kind of good from the other, as friends should.

Friendship based on pleasure is a lesser copy of true friendship, because good people give each other pleasure. Friendship based on usefulness works the same way, since good people are useful to each other. Such friendships last longest when both people get the same kind of benefit from each other, and especially when it comes from the same source, such as two people who both enjoy good humour.

Aristotle says that a friendship between a lover and his beloved is based on pleasure that each gets from the other: the lover enjoys seeing the beloved, and the beloved enjoys the lover's attention. When youth fades, this friendship often ends, though it can last if the two have grown to like each other's character.

Friendships based on gain rather than shared pleasure are weaker and shorter-lasting. Such friends usually separate once the advantage ends, because they were really attached to the advantage, not to each other.

Friendships based on pleasure or profit can form between any kinds of people, good or bad. Only good people can be friends for the sake of each other alone, because bad people take no pleasure in themselves unless they gain something from it.

Only friendship between good people is safe from slander, because people do not easily believe a third party's accusations against someone they have long tested and found trustworthy. Such friends trust each other and never expect wrong from one another. In other kinds of friendship, nothing stops these suspicions.

Aristotle says that people are often called friends when they are linked by profit or by pleasure, and that such bonds can be called friendships too. The main kind, though, is friendship between good people, because they are good. Other friendships are friends only by resemblance, since they offer some good or shared likeness.

Friendships based on usefulness or pleasure rarely go together in the same people. Bad people are friends for pleasure or profit, since that is what they share. Good people are friends for each other's own sake, because they are good, and only these are friendship in the full sense.

Aristotle says friendship can be held in two ways: as a lasting inner state, or as active deeds done together. Friends who are asleep or far apart are not acting as friends, but they still have the friendship in them. Long absence, however, can make people forget the friendship.

Aristotle says that old or gloomy people are not well suited to friendship, because they give little pleasure, and people do not want to spend time with someone who is painful or dull to them. He also says that people who get on well but are not close are more like well-wishers than friends.

Friends are above all people who live together, since those in need want help and those who are doing well want company. People can only spend time together if they enjoy each other and share the same interests, and this is thought to be the mark of friendship based on companionship.

Aristotle says that friendship is strongest between good people. Two reasons support this: good things in general are thought to be lovable and worth choosing, and each person loves what is good or pleasant to him. A good man therefore loves another good man for both reasons.

Liking someone is a passing feeling, like an emotion, while friendship itself is a settled character trait. Feeling can attach even to lifeless things, but returning friendship involves a deliberate choice that comes from that settled trait. Friends also wish good for each other for the other's own sake, which marks it as a lasting disposition rather than a mere feeling.

In good friendship, each person loves the other as a good to himself, so each loves his own good in loving his friend. Each pays the other back equally, both in wishing well and in giving pleasure. Equality is said to bind friendship, and these features belong most to friendship between good men.

Friendship is less likely between sour-tempered or elderly men, because they enjoy each other's company less. Such men can still wish each other well and help one another in need, but they are not true friends, since they do not spend time together or take pleasure in each other.

Aristotle says that true, complete friendship can only be held with a few people, not many, much as one cannot be deeply in love with many at once.
