Such friendship needs time, shared experience and close intimacy, and few people are truly good enough for it. Friendships based on usefulness or pleasure are easier, since many people fit those and such favours can be given quickly.

Aristotle says that of the two imperfect kinds of friendship, the one based on pleasure is closest to perfect friendship. In it both friends gain the same things and enjoy each other or the same activities, as young people often do. Friendship based on advantage is the kind that ties together shopkeepers, who deal in gain.

Very happy people do not need useful friends, but they want pleasant company to live closely with. Since no one can bear constant pain, not even the highest good if it hurt them personally, they seek pleasant friends. Ideally those friends are also good and good to them, so the friendship has everything it should.

Powerful men often keep several kinds of friends. Some are useful to them and others are pleasant company, but rarely the same person is both. They look for amusing companions for enjoyment and for capable workers for business, and these qualities seldom appear together in one man.

A good man can be a friend to someone above him in rank only if he is also better than that person in goodness. Otherwise he is behind in one respect and cannot balance the friendship on equal terms. Men who are both higher in rank and better in character are rare.

Aristotle says the friendships already discussed are based on equality. In some, both partners gain the same thing and want the same for each other. In others, they exchange one benefit for another, such as pleasure for profit, and these last kinds are weaker and do not last as long.

Some friendships seem real only because they resemble true friendship, which is based on virtue. Those based on pleasure or usefulness share something with it, but they differ from it in being unstable: they quickly change, while true friendship lasts and is not open to slander.

Aristotle says there is another kind of friendship, where one person is above the other, such as father and son, elder and younger, husband and wife, or ruler and ruled. Each of these relationships is different, because each person has a different role and virtue, so the feelings of friendship differ too.

Friendship between parents and children lasts and is fair when each gives what they owe. Children repay their parents for giving them life, and parents give their children what is owed to offspring. The two sides do not need to get the same return from each other.

In friendships between unequals, the feeling should be proportionate: the better or more useful person should be loved more strongly than he loves in return. Once the feelings reach that balance, a kind of equality is created, and this equality is thought necessary for friendship.

In justice, the proportionate equal (equal according to a ratio, where each gets what fits their worth) comes first, and strict numerical equality comes second. In friendship the order is reversed, with numerical equality ranking first.

Aristotle says that friendship needs equality. When one person is far better, or richer, or more fortunate than the other, they stop being friends, and they do not even feel they should be. He gives the gods and kings as examples: people far below them do not think they can be their friends.

Very unequal people cannot easily stay friends with those far above them in excellence or wisdom. Aristotle says it is impossible to fix exactly how far the difference can go before a friendship ends. Friendship can survive many lost points of agreement, but it cannot survive when one side is as far apart as a god is from man.

Aristotle raises a doubt: if friends wish their friends the highest goods, such as becoming gods, the friendship would end, since the friend would no longer be a friend in the same way. So a friend wishes good things for the friend as the friend is now, meaning the greatest good a human being can have, though perhaps not every good, since each person wants good most for himself.

Many people, driven by a love of honour, would rather be loved by others than love others. That is why they like flatterers, who act as friends while being inferior to them or only pretending. Being loved is seen as nearly the same as being honoured, which most people want.
Ordinary people seem to value honour not for its own sake but for what it may bring. They enjoy being honoured by powerful people because they hope to receive help or benefits from them later.

Aristotle says that people who seek honour from good men want their own good opinion of themselves confirmed, and they enjoy that confirmation. But being loved in friendship is enjoyed for its own sake. So friendship is higher than honour and is better worth choosing in itself.

Aristotle argues that friendship lies in the feeling of loving rather than in being the one loved. He points to mothers, some of whom give up their children to be raised by others and still feel affection for them, without asking for that love back.

Aristotle is describing a kind of love that stays content just to see loved ones doing well, even when those loved ones, through ignorance, give no filial respect or affection in return. The passage concerns how parents may feel toward children who do not return their love.

Friendship lies more in feeling affection than in being the object of it. Since people are praised for loving their friends, feeling affection is treated as the true virtue of friends. Where this affection exists in the right measure, friendships last, and unequal people can become friends by being made equal in this way.

Friendship is held together by equality and similarity, especially similarity in goodness. Good people are steady in their own conduct, so they neither ask for degrading service from friends nor give it, and they stop friends from doing wrong.

Bad people have no lasting basis for friendship. Their bond lasts only briefly, based on enjoying each other's wrongdoing. Friendships based on profit or pleasure last a little longer, but only while each can keep giving the other something useful or enjoyable.

Friendships based on profit, Aristotle says, are usually between opposites: the poor man befriends the rich, the ignorant man the knowledgeable, and the lover the beloved, or the beautiful the ill-favoured. Each gives something he lacks in exchange for what he wants. Lovers who insist their feelings are returned look foolish unless they are truly worthy of such friendship.

Aristotle suggests that opposites do not really aim at their opposite for its own sake. Instead, what they seek is the middle point. For example, dry things do not want to become wet, but to reach a balance between the two. He then sets this question aside as not central to his topic.

Aristotle says that friendship and justice cover the same ground and apply to the same people. Wherever people share something in common, there is some justice and some friendship, so friendship extends as far as shared community does. This explains the proverb that friends' goods are common, since friendship rests on sharing.

Brothers and close companions share everything, while other friends share less, since friendships differ in degree. For the same reason, the principles of justice also differ: they are not the same between parents and children, brothers, companions, or fellow citizens, and so on for every other kind of friendship.

Wrongs get worse when they are done against friends, so the wrong is greater the closer the relationship. For example, robbing a companion is worse than robbing a fellow citizen, and striking one's father is worse than striking a stranger. Justice follows the same pattern: it grows with the strength of friendship between the same people.

Every smaller association, such as a partnership, is a part of the larger society. People join together for some advantage or to get what life needs. The larger society also seems to have arisen and continued for advantage, which is why lawmakers judge as just whatever is generally useful.

Other kinds of friendship or partnership are formed for a particular gain. Sailors on a ship share a voyage aimed at profit, soldiers share a war aimed at wealth, victory or political power, and members of the same tribe or deme share a common group interest.

Some associations, such as those for drinking parties or dining clubs, are said to exist for pleasure or simply for company. Still, these fall under the larger social association, whose aim is a lasting shared life. Its members hold sacrifices and assemblies to honour the gods and to rest from work in pleasant company. Long ago, such gatherings were held after harvest, when people had the most free time.

Aristotle concludes that every kind of partnership or community is part of one large social community, and that each kind of community brings with it a matching kind of friendship. "Communion" here means a shared association between people, and "Social" refers to the whole political community.

Aristotle names three good forms of government: kingship, aristocracy, and the rule of those who count wealth as the basis of rule, which he calls timocracy. Of these three, kingship is the best and timocracy the worst.

Despotism is the corrupt form of monarchy. A despot rules for his own advantage, while a true king rules for the good of his subjects. Aristotle says a true king must be self-sufficient and lack nothing, so he has no need to seek his own gain.

Despotism is the opposite of kingship, because the despot rules for his own good rather than for the good of his subjects. This makes it the worse form, and it arises when a bad king turns into a despot.

Aristocracy turns into oligarchy when the rulers share out public property unfairly. They give themselves the best goods or the largest share, keep offices for the same people, and value wealth above all. So a few rule, and they are bad men instead of the best.

Aristotle says that a timocracy (rule by those with a set amount of property) changes most easily into a democracy, because the two are close neighbours. Democracy is the least bad form of rule, since it changes least from the original constitution, and these are the simplest and smallest changes between constitutions.

Aristotle says that family life shows a small version of kingly rule: a father cares for his children as a king cares for his people. The Persians rule their sons like masters rule slaves, which he thinks is wrong, because different people should be ruled in different ways.

Aristotle says that marriage can take three forms, each matching a kind of government. When the husband rules only in matters that properly belong to him and leaves the wife her due share, the marriage is like an aristocracy. When the husband rules over everything without right, it becomes like an oligarchy, and when wives rule because they inherit wealth, that too is like an oligarchy.

Aristotle compares types of government to kinds of family friendship. Timocracy resembles a friendship between brothers who are equal, except that age makes some difference; if they differ greatly in age, the bond stops being brotherly. Democracy resembles a household with no head, or with a weak head, where everyone does what they think is right.

Friendship goes with every form of government, just as justice does. In a kingdom, the friendship between king and subjects is one where the king gives more benefit, since he cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his flock.

Paternal friendship is the same kind of friendship as the kind just described, but greater, because a father gives his children their existence, which is the greatest benefit, along with food and upbringing. For the same reason, a father has natural authority over his sons, ancestors over their descendants, and a king over his subjects.

Aristotle says that friendships between unequals, such as parents and children, involve honour as well as love. Justice between such people is proportional rather than identical. Likewise, friendship between husband and wife resembles the friendship of aristocracy: each gets what suits them, and the better partner receives the greater share.

Brotherly friendship resembles friendship between companions, because brothers are equal in standing, close in age, and usually share feelings and character. Friendship in a timocracy, a state ruled by property-holding citizens, is similar, since its citizens are meant to be equal and fair, taking turns in ruling.

In the corrupt forms of government, friendship shrinks along with justice, and under despotism there is little or none. Where ruler and ruled share nothing, there is no friendship, because there is no justice. The relation is like that of a craftsman to his tool, or of soul to body, or of master to slave.

Friendship and justice do not apply to inanimate things, or to animals like horses and oxen, because they share nothing with them. A slave is treated as a living tool, so there is no friendship with him as a slave, but there is some friendship with him as a man, since every man can share in law and agreements.
In despotisms, friendship and a sense of justice reach only a little way. In democracies they reach furthest, because citizens who are equal have much in common.

Aristotle says all friendship rests on sharing something in common. Friendship between relatives or companions might seem to be set apart, but friendship between people of the same city, tribe, or crew is more clearly based on this sharing. Such ties exist because of some agreement, stated or unstated. Friendship of hospitality also belongs in this group.

Parents love their children because the children are, in a sense, part of themselves. Children love their parents because they came from them. Parents also know their children as their own more fully than children know that they came from their parents. The passage compares this to a tooth or hair, which belongs to the person who has it, while the source of a thing does not belong to it in the same way.

Parents love their children from the moment they are born, but children love their parents only later, once they have gained understanding or instinct. This is also given as the reason mothers feel a stronger love than fathers.

Parents love their children as a kind of second self, since the children come from them and are separate from them. Children love their parents because they come from them. Brothers love each other because they share the same origin, which makes them alike in a sense even though they are separate people.

Growing up together and being close in age help friendship, since people like those their own age and those they are used to. This is why brothers resemble close companions. Cousins and other relatives are bound by shared descent, and the closeness of the bond depends on how far each is from the common ancestor.

Children feel friendship towards their parents, and people towards the gods, because these beings are seen as good and superior to them. The reason given is that they gave the greatest benefits: bringing them into being, feeding them, and educating them.

Aristotle says that friendship between family members, such as brothers, has more of the pleasant and useful qualities than friendship between unrelated people, because they share more of their lives. Brothers also start with affection, are often alike in character, and have had more time to test each other, so they can rely on one another more firmly.

Aristotle says that husband and wife have a friendship that comes from nature. Humans pair up naturally, and the family comes before the wider community in time and need. Unlike other animals, humans live together not only to have children but for the whole of life, dividing tasks and each adding their own work to the shared household.

Friendship can combine usefulness and pleasure, and it can also rest on virtue if the friends are good people, since each admires the goodness of the other. Children are also thought to bind a couple together, because a shared good creates a tie, so childless couples more often part.

Aristotle asks how a man should live with his wife, or one friend with another, and says this comes down to asking what is just between them. Justice between friends is not the same as justice between strangers, companions, or chance travellers.

Aristotle says friendship can be between equals or between unequals, whether the bond is goodness, pleasure, or advantage. Equals should match each other in the degree of their friendship, and unequals should give friendship in proportion to the other person's superiority.

Quarrels and blame arise most naturally in friendships based on usefulness. Friends who are bound by goodness do kindnesses for each other freely, so no blame or strife comes up. Even if one friend gives more, the other does not complain, because each is aiming at the good.

Friends who are together only for pleasure rarely quarrel. If one tires of the other, he can simply stop seeing him, so complaints would seem foolish. Friendships based on advantage breed more complaints. Each side keeps asking for more, feels shortchanged, and the giver can never give enough to satisfy the receiver.

Aristotle says that friendship based on advantage comes in two kinds, just as justice does: an unwritten, moral kind and a legal kind with set terms. Most quarrels arise when two people take on obligations and repay them in different kinds of friendship. The legal kind is an exchange of goods or services, either immediate or deferred, agreed in advance.

In this kind of friendship, based on law, the debt is clear and cannot be disputed, so the friendly part is the willingness to wait before demanding payment. For this reason, in some places people cannot sue to recover such debts; those who lend on credit must accept the outcome.

Aristotle is describing a kind of giving that comes with no fixed terms, such as giving to a friend. Even so, the giver expects something back, as much or more, as if it were a loan, and complains if the return does not match what was given.

People generally want to do what is honourable, but in practice they choose what benefits them. Giving kindness freely is honourable, while receiving benefits is profitable. So when someone has done you a kindness, you should repay it in proportion and willingly, since you should not have accepted help from someone who was not a true friend acting without self-interest.

A person who receives a favour should repay it if able, on the terms under which it was given, and should first find out from whom it comes and on what understanding. The passage then asks whether a favour should be valued by the benefit it brought the receiver or by the giver's good intention, and it leaves this question open.

Recipients of kindnesses often downplay them, saying the gift was small or could have been obtained elsewhere. Givers, by contrast, say they gave their best, something unavailable from anyone else, perhaps at personal risk.

In a friendship based on usefulness, the amount a person repays should match the benefit they received. The one who got help should give back as much as they gained, or even more, since that is considered more admirable.

In friendships based on goodness, people never ask whether the friend is useful or pleasant, so the reason behind a person's action is what counts. This is because virtue and moral character depend mainly on the motive.
Quarrels also happen in friendships where the two people are not equal. Each one thinks he deserves the bigger share, so when this happens the friendship ends.

In a friendship, people who are better or who do more for the other often think they should get a bigger share. They argue that a useless partner should not get an equal share, since that would be a tax rather than friendship. They compare it to a money partnership, where those who put in more take out more.

In this part of the discussion of friendship, poor people and those with less virtue make the opposite argument. They say a good friend should help those in need, since otherwise having a good or powerful friend would bring no benefit at all.

In a friendship between unequal people, each side can rightly claim a fair return, but not the same kind of return. The better person should receive more honour, because honour rewards goodness and kindness. The person in need should receive more material help, because that is what meets need.

In cities, honour goes to those who benefit the community, because public property is given to them and honour is itself a public good. A person cannot both profit from the public and receive honour as well. So those who take less money are given honour, and those who are rewarded with money receive it in return for gifts, since fair proportion keeps friendship in balance.

In friendships between unequal people, the one who receives more in money or goodness should repay with honour as far as he is able. Friendship asks for what is possible, not for an exact payment, since some debts, such as those owed to the gods and parents, can never be fully repaid.

A son may never disown his father, because a debtor must pay what he owes, and a son can never fully repay the benefits his father gave him. A father, as the creditor, may disown his son, since those owed something may release their debtors.

Aristotle says that a father will hardly ever cut off a son completely, unless the son is extremely wicked, because people naturally do not want to lose help a son could give. A depraved son, by contrast, is unlikely to want to help his father.

In friendships between people who are unlike each other, fairness in proportion keeps the friendship equal and steady. As an example, a cobbler gets a fair return in value for his shoes, and a weaver and others do the same.

Aristotle notes that in money dealings a common measure, money, lets people compare and settle what each side owes. In love, though, no such measure exists. So complaints arise on both sides: lovers feel their love goes unrewarded, and those loved feel the lover's promises are not kept.

Friendships based on pleasure or usefulness break up when the pleasure or usefulness ends, because the people loved only those qualities, which do not last. Friendship based on good moral character lasts, because it does not depend on gain.

Quarrels can start when each side gets a different result from the one it wanted. Aristotle's example is a man who promised a musician payment for a performance, then paid him only with the pleasure of hearing it. The deal is unfair when each party wanted something different and only one got what he wanted.

The passage asks who should set the price in a paid exchange, the giver or the receiver. Protagoras, a teacher, let each pupil name the value of what he had learned and then charged that amount. Some people say a friend should accept whatever reward has been set.

People who take payment in advance and then fail to do what they promised deserve blame, especially when their promises went beyond what they could actually deliver. Aristotle says the Sophists, paid teachers of his day, may have to act this way because nobody would pay much for their knowledge.

When no terms are set for who gives what, the person who freely does the first service will not raise the matter of repayment. Friendship based on mutual goodness is about the other person's intention, and that intention is what marks a true friend and goodness.

Aristotle says the same rule about repayment applies to teachers and students of philosophy. Philosophy cannot be paid for with money, since no exact price can be set on it. Instead, it is enough to give what one can, as one does with the gods or one's parents.

Where a gift is made expecting something back, the return should ideally be agreed by both sides as fair. If they cannot agree, the person who received the gift should set the value, because the giver then gets back what equals the benefit received. Aristotle notes that this is how buying and selling works, and some places do not allow lawsuits over voluntary dealings.

When someone has trusted another with a debt or favour, the one who was trusted should accept repaying it in the same spirit it was given. Fairness, it says, lets the trusted person set the value of what is owed, not the person who trusted.

People who give something and people who want to receive it value the thing differently. Aristotle suggests that a receiver should judge the gift by the value he put on it before getting it, not by how much he values it once he has it.

Aristotle lists several hard questions about duties that can conflict. Should a son always obey his father? Should a sick man obey his doctor? Should a general be chosen only for fighting skill? Should a favour go to a friend or to a good person, and should a benefactor be repaid or a companion given something when both cannot be done?

Working out exactly what each person owes is hard, because such questions involve many differences in amount, honour and necessity. No one can satisfy every claim at once. Still, repaying a kindness is generally a higher duty than offering an unrequested favour to a companion.

Aristotle is saying that paying back a debt is usually a stronger duty than giving something to a friend. He then notes that this rule has exceptions and asks which duty is higher in some hard cases. For example, if someone was ransomed from robbers, should he repay his ransomer, or ransom his own father? He suggests a son should ransom his father even before himself.

Generally a debt should be repaid. But if giving back is clearly the more honourable or necessary course, that consideration should decide the matter. Sometimes a return cannot be equal. For example, a benefactor may have helped a good man knowing his worth, while the good man must repay a man he believed to be a scoundrel.

Aristotle says that a man need not repay a loan made to him by someone he took to be a good man, when that person was really bad and so could not be expected to repay in return. Such a case is either a real unequal exchange or only seems so, and in either case the man who refuses is not to be thought to act wrongly.

Statements about feelings and actions can only be exact as far as their subject allows. People have different claims on us, so each person should get what is owed to them, and a father's claims are not unlimited. Just as Jupiter does not want every kind of sacrifice, the claims of parents, brothers, friends and benefactors differ.
People commonly invite their relatives to weddings and funerals, and Aristotle gives the reason: relatives share a common stock, so the events that concern them are shared as well.

Children should help their parents first, when support is needed, because they owe them and because parents gave them life. Honour is owed to parents as to the gods, but it must fit each parent: a father receives the honour that belongs to a father, and a mother the honour that belongs to a mother, not the honour due to a scientist or a general.

Aristotle says we owe respect and fair treatment to different people in different ways. Elders get honour such as rising in their presence, friends and brothers get frankness and sharing, and family, tribe or city members get what is due to each according to closeness, goodness or intimacy. Sorting these claims is harder when people belong to different classes, but the effort should still be made as far as possible.

Aristotle asks whether it is right to end a friendship when the two people have changed from what they were when the friendship began. The question is whether such friendships should be dissolved or kept.

When friends are linked only by usefulness or pleasure, it is reasonable to end the friendship once those qualities are gone. They were never really friends of each other, only of what each gave the other, so when that stops, the friendship stops too.

A person has grounds for complaint when a friend who really valued him for profit or pleasure pretended to value him for his good character. Quarrels between friends most often arise because each is not friends on the grounds the other assumes.

If someone thinks a friend loves him because of his good character, and the other has given no sign of that, the mistake is his own fault. But if he was deceived by the other's pretence, he has good reason to blame that person, even more than someone who passes counterfeit money, since friendship is the more valuable thing to be cheated of.

If someone has taken another person to be good but finds him to be a scoundrel, Aristotle asks whether the friendship must still continue. He concludes that it does not: friendship is only for what is good, no one should love evil, and like tends to become like.

Should a friend be dropped at once when he goes wrong? Not always. If his character can still be improved, one should help repair it, even more than help with his money or property. Yet someone who ends the friendship when the other is beyond repair does nothing wrong, since he was never a friend to the person the other has become.

Aristotle asks what happens when one friend stays the same while the other becomes much better morally. He is asking whether the friend who improved should still treat the unchanged friend as a friend.

Aristotle asks whether friendship can last when two friends grow far apart in character. He gives the example of a boy who stays childish while his friend becomes a man of high character. Such friends no longer enjoy the same things or share likes and dislikes, and without that shared life they cannot remain friends.

Aristotle is asking whether a friend who has become better should treat a former friend in exactly the way he would have if the friendship had never existed. The question expects a reply, and the passage itself does not give one.
When a friendship has ended, one should still make some allowance for the past closeness. The exception is when the friend's wrongdoing was extremely bad.
Aristotle says that the warm feelings we show to our friends, which make up friendship, seem to grow out of the feelings we have toward ourselves.

People offer several definitions of a friend. One says a friend wishes good to another for that other's sake. Another says a friend shares the other's choices, or shares in their sorrows and joys. Aristotle notes that mothers toward their children fit these definitions best.

Aristotle says that the marks people use to describe friendship are all found in the good man toward himself. Other people have these marks only to the extent that they think of themselves as good, since the good man is the standard for everyone else.

The good man is at peace with himself: all parts of his soul want the same things. He wants what is truly good and what he believes to be good, and he acts for his own sake, meaning for the sake of his intellect, which is taken to be the true self. He also wants that intellect to stay alive, because being alive is good for him.

Aristotle argues that people wish good things for themselves, not for some other self they might become. Nobody would want a changed self to have everything indiscriminately; a god has the highest good because of what he already is. The mind or reasoning part is what each person most truly is, though other parts also make up the person.
A good man wants to keep living with himself, because he can enjoy his own company. His memories of what he has done are pleasant, and he looks forward to the future with pleasure too.

The good man, Aristotle says, has plenty of material for his thinking mind to reflect on. He feels his own joys and sorrows most deeply, because what gives him pain or pleasure stays the same over time. So he has no reason to change his mind or regret his choices.

Aristotle means that people think friendship is one of the feelings a good man has toward himself, and that a good man feels toward a friend as he does toward himself, since a friend is another self. So those who have these feelings toward each other count as friends.

Aristotle sets aside, for now, whether a person can really be a friend to himself. He says that a kind of friendship may still be seen in a person to the degree that the usual requirements for friendship are present. He also notes that these requirements seem to appear even in ordinary people of low character.

Aristotle is answering an objection: perhaps bad people share in friendship only because they enjoy themselves and think they are good. He replies that such qualities are not found, in reality or even in appearance, in anyone who is deeply corrupt.

Bad people, Aristotle says, are not really friends even to themselves. They are divided within, often wanting things their own reason rejects, and they avoid being alone with their memories of wrongs. Because they feel no real goodwill toward themselves, they cannot feel friendship toward themselves.

Wicked people cannot feel at peace with themselves, because their soul is divided against itself. One part of them is pained by giving up certain pleasures, while the better part is glad to give them up, so they are pulled in two directions. Afterwards they regret the pleasures they enjoyed, since the wicked are full of remorse.

A wicked man cannot be a friend even to himself, because he has nothing in himself that can produce friendship. Since such a state is deeply miserable, a person should avoid wickedness and try to become good, so that he can be a friend to himself and then to others.

Kindly Feeling (goodwill) looks like friendship but is different. It can be felt toward strangers, without them knowing, which friendship cannot. It also lacks the intensity and longing of affection, and it can arise suddenly, so it is only a shallow liking that does not lead people to act together.

Aristotle says that first liking someone's appearance can be the starting point of friendship, just as pleasure in sight starts love. Being pleased by how someone looks does not yet mean you love them. Love begins when you miss the person when they are absent and long for them to be near.

Kindly feeling is the first stage toward friendship, but it is not yet friendship. People who feel kindly toward someone wish them well, yet will not act together with them or make sacrifices for them. Aristotle calls this feeling dormant friendship, which becomes real friendship once it lasts and grows into close intimacy.

Aristotle says that kindly feeling is the return owed to someone who has done you a kindness, and it is the right response. Wishing a person well only because you hope to gain from them is really self-interest, not goodness toward them. Kindly feeling comes from admiring another person's goodness or qualities.
Aristotle says that agreement in feeling is closely tied to friendship. So it is not the same as agreeing in opinion, since people who do not know each other could share an opinion.

People do not call a group "united in sentiment" just because its members hold the same opinion on a matter of theory, such as astronomy. Such unity is said to exist in communities that agree on practical matters, act together, and carry out what they have decided in common.

Aristotle says that real agreement, or "unity of sentiment," means people agreeing about the same thing in action, especially important matters of shared interest. Mere agreement in thought is not enough. When people each want power for themselves, they split into factions. When both the common people and the wise want the best men in office, they all reach the same goal.
Unity of sentiment, meaning agreement of feeling between people, is a kind of friendship that rests on community. Its subject is what is useful and bears on everyday life.

Good people share a kind of unity: they stand the same way toward themselves and toward each other. Their wishes stay steady rather than shifting like the tides of the Euripus, a narrow strait known for its changing currents, and they aim together at what is just and useful.

Bad people cannot share a common mind or be true friends, except to a very small degree. Each one wants more than his fair share of profits, avoids work for the common good, and resents and obstructs others, so the common good is lost and they end up quarrelling.
People who do good to others are commonly thought to love those they help more than those helpers love them back. This is debated and examined, because it seems to go against what we would expect.

Many people think that a benefactor and the person helped stand like creditor and debtor. Just as a debtor wants his creditor gone and a creditor wants his debtor to survive, a benefactor wants the person he helped to live, hoping for a return, while the one helped is less concerned about repaying.

Aristotle says that people who answer a certain question this way are judging by their own bad character, as Epicharmus would probably say. Still, he adds, the view fits human nature, since most people forget what they have given and prefer to receive favours rather than grant them.

People who have done a kindness feel friendship for the person they helped, even when that person can never repay them. Aristotle says this is not like a creditor's concern for a debtor, which is only a wish to get the money back. The cause seems to lie in human nature.

People tend to love what they have made more than what they have made loves them back. Aristotle gives craftsmen, poets, and benefactors as examples. A poet loves a poem like his own child, and a benefactor loves the person he helped more than that person loves him.

People love their own work because they love existing. We exist through our activity, living and acting, so a maker who has produced something is, in a sense, existing through that act. The work therefore makes visible in action what the maker was before only in potential.

The giver of a benefit feels a kind of honour in what he has done, so he can take pleasure in the person who has this feeling. The receiver, however, sees nothing honourable in his benefactor, only something useful to him. That is less pleasant and less likely to produce friendship.

Aristotle says the greatest pleasure comes from doing a good action while it is happening, not from looking forward to it or remembering it. He adds that a benefactor keeps the value of his kind deed, because honourable things last, while the person helped gains only a benefit that fades. Remembering a noble deed brings pleasure, but remembering a useful gain brings little or none.

In this passage, Aristotle says that feeling friendship toward someone is like doing something to them, while being the object of that feeling is like having something done to you. So the feelings of friendship belong to the person who gives the benefit, the one in the stronger position.

People tend to value most what cost them effort to create. Those who earned their money love it more than those who inherited it, and mothers love their children most because bearing them took the most labour and they are surer the children are theirs. Benefactors, the passage suggests, feel the same way about those they have helped.

Aristotle asks whether a person should love himself more than others. He notes that people criticize those who love themselves most, calling them selfish. Bad people act only for their own gain, and good people act for honour and their friends, not for their own interest.

Aristotle says that this view clashes with the facts. People commonly hold that the best friend is the one who wishes good to another for that other person's own sake, even when no one else knows about it.

Aristotle says that the qualities that make someone a good friend belong first to a person's relation to himself. Friendly feelings toward others come from the feelings a person has toward himself. Common sayings such as "one soul" and "the knee is nearer than the shin" are offered as support.
Aristotle says that the qualities that make someone a good friend apply first to a person's own self. Because a person is his own closest friend, he should love himself most.

The passage says that the debate between two opposing views about self-love has good arguments on both sides, so neither can simply be followed. Instead, each view should be examined to see how far it is true and in what sense. Clearing up what each side means by "self-loving" would help settle the matter.

Aristotle says that "self-lover" is a term of insult used for people who grab the largest share of wealth, honour and bodily pleasures. Most people chase these things and treat them as the best goods, so they become the object of rivalry. Such people indulge their desires, which Aristotle links to the unreasoning part of the soul, and he holds that they deserve blame.

Aristotle says that ordinary people use the word "self-lover" for those who give themselves the most selfish goods, such as wealth or pleasure. A man who strives to do more than others in justice, self-mastery, or other virtues, and so gets what is noble for himself, would not be called self-loving or blamed for it.

The passage argues that the truest form of self-love belongs to the person who gives himself the best things and serves the part of his nature that rules. Just as the ruling element defines a state or any system, the ruling part defines a person, so the one who loves and serves that part is the most truly self-loving.

Aristotle says that people are called self-controlled, or lacking self-control, depending on whether their intellect, or reason, governs them. He takes this to mean that reason is what makes up each person. Actions done through reason are seen as most fully a person's own and voluntary.

A person's rational part, or reason, is what most fully makes them who they are, so a good person loves this part of themselves most. Such self-love is different from the selfishness people usually criticise. It is better because it means living by reason and aiming at what is truly noble, not following passion or chasing apparent gain.

Aristotle says that people praise those who are serious about doing honourable deeds. If everyone competed to do what is truly noble, society would get what it needs, and each person would gain the greatest good, which is virtue.

A good person should love himself, because by doing what is noble he benefits himself and others. A bad person should not, because following base desires harms both himself and his neighbours. The good person does what he ought to do, since he lets reason guide him and reason chooses what is best for itself.

The good man will give up money, honours and other goods that others fight for, in order to win what is noble (kalon). He will choose a short, great joy over a calm, lasting one, and one noble deed over many small ones, even dying for friends or country if needed.

Aristotle says that men who die for their country or friends choose great glory for themselves. Likewise, they spend their own money so that friends get more, since the friend gets the money while the man himself gets the noble (kalon) reward of honour. In this way he gives himself the greater good. The same holds for honours and offices.

A good man gives up things he could keep, such as wealth or chances to act, so that his friend gets them. He does this because he prefers the honourable to everything else. In this sense, he is self-loving in a way that is right, though not in the ordinary, common sense of the word.

Some hold that a happy, self-sufficient person needs no friends, since a friend's role is to supply what one cannot get alone, and such a person already has everything. Others find it odd to give the happy person every other good but deny him friends, which are thought to be the greatest external goods.

Aristotle argues that a good man needs people to be kind to, since giving kindness is more typical of a friend and more noble than receiving it. This raises the question of whether friends are needed more in good times or bad: the unfortunate need others to help them, while the fortunate need others to give kindness to.

Aristotle argues that the happy person cannot be alone. No one would choose all the good things in the world if they had to live in solitude, because people are social by nature. So the happy person needs friends, and good friends are better company than strangers or ordinary people.

Aristotle asks whether the common idea of friendship, which is friends who are useful, fits the claim that the happy man needs no friends. He answers that the happy man has all good things already, so he does not need useful friends, nor friends for pleasure, since his life is pleasant already. So people think he needs no friends at all.

Aristotle is pointing out that happiness was earlier described as a kind of activity. An activity is something that happens and comes into being over time, unlike a possession that is simply held and already there.

Happiness, on this view, is living and working well, and a good person's actions are pleasant to them. We see our friends' actions more clearly than our own, so a good man's good friends are pleasant to him too. The most happy person therefore needs such friends, to contemplate good actions that are like his own.

Common opinion holds that a happy man needs company, because living alone makes continuous activity hard. With others, good activity is easier and more continuous, since a good man takes pleasure in virtuous actions. Virtue is also improved by living with good people.

Aristotle argues that a good friend is naturally worth choosing for a good man. He bases this on the idea that living, for animals, means having the power to perceive, and for humans, means perceiving or reasoning. The main thing is the actual use of these powers.

Aristotle argues that living is mainly the activity of perceiving or reasoning, and that being alive is itself good and pleasant. What is naturally good is good to the good person, so living seems pleasant to everyone. He adds that a corrupted life or one full of pain does not count, since such a life has no fixed nature.

Living is good and pleasant in itself, Aristotle argues, because everyone desires it, especially the good and truly happy. Just as a person who sees knows that he sees, and one who hears knows that he hears, so a living person perceives that he lives.

Aristotle says that in every activity there is a faculty that notices we are doing it. So we can perceive that we perceive, and know that we know. To perceive that we perceive or know is to perceive that we exist, because existence was defined as perceiving or knowing.

Being aware that one is alive is pleasant in itself, because life is naturally good. So living is worth choosing, especially for good people, since they take pleasure in being aware of what is good within themselves.

A good man regards his friend as a second self. Since living is good to a person who knows himself to be good, the good man wants to be aware of his friend's existence. This awareness comes from living together and sharing words and thoughts, which for humans is what living together means, not merely eating together as animals do.

A happy person finds his own existence worth choosing, and so he also finds his friend's existence worth choosing. Whatever is worth choosing, he must have, or he lacks something. So a truly happy person needs good friends.

Should a person try to have as many friends as possible? Aristotle suggests a middle course, borrowing an old saying about acquaintances: have some, but not too many. He applies the same rule to friendship: have friends, but not an excessive number.

Friends who are useful to us are a burden if there are too many. Returning their services takes so much effort that a whole life would not be enough, so more than enough such friends get in the way of living well. Friends for pleasure are needed only in small numbers, like a little sweetening in food.

Aristotle asks whether a person should make as many good friends as possible, or whether there is a limit on how many friends one can have. He compares this to a city: a state cannot be made from ten people, and a hundred thousand no longer forms one community. So the number is probably not one fixed figure but falls somewhere between a lower and an upper limit.

Aristotle says there is a limit to how many friends a person can be truly intimate with, and that this is one mark of friendship. He adds that for many people to live together, they must also be friends with one another, which is hard to achieve among a large group.
It is hard to feel the joys and sorrows of many people as your own. You would probably have to share, at the same moment, one person's happiness and another's grief.

Aristotle suggests it is best not to have very many friends, but only as many as allow real closeness. His reason is that a person cannot be a very close friend to many people at once, just as strong feelings such as love can be directed at only a few objects.

Aristotle observes that true close friendships are usually between two people, since few people can be close friends at the same time. Those who claim many intimate friends and treat everyone as a close friend are, in fact, friends only in a general, social sense. He gives the over-complaisant, people who try too hard to please everyone, as an example.

A man can have many friends in the ordinary social sense without being overly eager to please them. But he cannot have many friends who are truly good and whom he loves for their virtue and for their own sake. Finding even a few such friends is enough to be content.
Friends are needed both in good times and in bad. The unfortunate need help, and the prosperous want companions to live with and to be kind to.

Friends are most needed in hard times, so in that case people want friends who can actually help them. Having friends when things go well is more honourable, which is why prosperous people want good men as friends, since it is better to do good to them and spend time with them. Even in trouble, a friend's presence brings comfort, because sympathy eases grief.

Friends seem to lighten our grief, but Aristotle asks how this happens. Either they actually share the weight of the suffering, or their presence is pleasant and their sympathy eases the pain. He sets the exact cause aside and says only that the relief itself is a plain fact.

A friend's presence in misfortune has mixed effects. Seeing a friend is pleasant and helps ease grief, since a tactful friend knows what comforts the sufferer. But seeing the friend grieve also causes pain, because people do not want to hurt their friends.

A man of strong character avoids burdening his friends with his grief and does not invite them to mourn with him. Women, and men like women, prefer to have others grieve alongside them. Aristotle concludes that we should copy the best kind of character in everything.
Friends make good times better in two ways. Spending time with them is enjoyable, and knowing they are glad about our good fortune adds to that enjoyment.

Friends should be called on readily in good times, since it is noble to be ready to help others. In bad times, one should call on them reluctantly, so as not to burden them with one's troubles. The best time to ask for help is when a friend can give great aid at little cost to themselves.

A friend should go to the other in trouble without being asked and eagerly, since helping is a friend's duty, especially for those who need help and do not claim it as their right. When a friend is doing well, one should readily help too if possible, while holding back from sharing in the friend's good fortune, or being too eager to gain from it, is not praiseworthy.

Aristotle is saying that a person should be careful not to seem sulky when turning down a friend's sympathy or help, since this sometimes happens. From this he concludes that having friends around is always something worth choosing.
Aristotle is saying that lovers value seeing the beloved above all the other senses. He supports this with a line of poetry, which says love is born in the eyes and fed by gazing.

Aristotle argues that close companionship is the most desirable part of friendship, since friendship is a sharing of life. He reasons that a person values his own awareness of existing, and because a friend is like oneself, the friend's shared existence is valued in the same way.

Friends want to be together because they want to share closeness, so they do the things they enjoy most with one another. Aristotle gives examples such as drinking, gambling, sport, hunting, and studying philosophy together.

Friendships between bad people turn bad, because such people are unstable and make each other worse. Friendships between good people grow better over time, as they correct each other and shape one another in what they enjoy. The chapter then ends the discussion of friendship and moves on to pleasure.

Aristotle says that pleasure and pain are closely tied to human nature, so teachers use them to steer young people. Liking and disliking the right things matters most for building good character, because these feelings last a whole life and push a person toward virtue and happiness.

Aristotle says we should not skip the question of pleasure, since people disagree sharply about it. Some call pleasure the highest good, others call it very bad. Some of the critics believe this, while others call pleasure bad even when they do not think so, because they want to pull the common run of people, who are ruled by their pleasures, toward the middle course.

Aristotle is saying that theories about how people feel and act are less trustworthy than real experience. When a theory clashes with what people actually observe, it is rejected, and the truth it contained is lost with it. For example, someone who condemns pleasure but is seen pursuing it is judged to have fallen back into it, because most people cannot make fine distinctions.

Accounts that match the facts are most useful not just for knowing, but for how people live and act. Because they agree with what actually happens, wise people are persuaded to live by them. Aristotle then sets this aside and turns to popular sayings about pleasure.

Eudoxus held that pleasure is the highest good. His reasoning was that all living things, both reasoning and non-reasoning, seek pleasure. Since whatever all seek must be good, and what all seek most must be best, he concluded that pleasure is the best for everyone. He compared this to how each creature finds the food that nourishes it.

Aristotle is describing Eudoxus, a thinker who held that pleasure is the highest good. His views were respected mainly because his character was seen as self-controlled, so people did not think he praised pleasure out of greed but sincerely believed it. Eudoxus also argued that since pain is naturally avoided, its opposite, pleasure, must be naturally chosen.

Pleasure is the good that is chosen for its own sake, since no one asks what purpose being pleased serves. The passage also says that adding pleasure to another good, such as justice or self-control, makes that good more choice-worthy.

Aristotle says that an argument showing a thing is a good does not show it is the best good, since every good becomes more desirable when combined with something else. He notes that Plato used this same kind of argument to show that pleasure alone cannot be the highest good, because pleasure with wisdom is more desirable than pleasure on its own.

Aristotle answers those who say that what everyone aims at is not necessarily good. He argues that the common view of all people counts for something, and that the objection fails, since rational people also desire pleasure. He adds that even animals may aim at a natural good suited to their own kind.

Aristotle rejects an objection to the argument that pleasure is good because pain is bad. The objection says opposites need not be one good and one bad, since two evils can be opposed. He replies that this does not fit here: if pleasure and pain were both bad, people would avoid both, or neither, but they avoid pain and choose pleasure, so they are truly opposed.

Pleasure is not ruled out as a good just because it is not a quality. Virtuous acts are not qualities either, and happiness is not one, yet both are goods. Some critics also say pleasure cannot be the highest good because it has no fixed limit and can increase in degrees.

Aristotle is arguing that if pleasure can be judged by how strongly people feel it, the same standard must apply to justice and the other virtues. We already say that people are more or less just, more or less brave, or practise self-control to a greater or lesser degree.

Aristotle suggests that people may be missing the real reason why some pleasures seem better or worse. Some pleasures are pure and others mixed. He compares this to health: health has limits yet still varies in degree, and pleasure may work the same way.

Some thinkers argue this: the highest good must be perfect, but every movement and every process is imperfect. So they try to prove that pleasure is a movement or process, which would mean it cannot be the highest good.

Aristotle argues that pleasure is not a movement. Movements can be fast or slow, but pleasure cannot be. A person can quickly enter a state of pleasure, as with anger, but cannot be in that state quickly or slowly. By contrast, walking or growing can be done quickly or slowly.

Aristotle says that a person can come to feel pleasure quickly or slowly, but cannot quickly be aware of feeling pleasure while acting. In Greek, the word for "state" here means a settled condition of the mind or body.

Aristotle is questioning the view that pleasure is a process of coming into being. He argues that nothing comes from something that is its opposite, and that pain is the destruction of what pleasure generates. He also notes that pain is seen as a lack of what suits our nature, and pleasure as its replenishment.

Aristotle argues that pleasure is not simply the filling of a need. If it were, the body would feel it, yet pleasure is not thought to be a bodily sensation of that kind. The idea seems to come from the pleasure of eating and drinking, where a person first feels a lack and is then pleased when it is filled.

Aristotle is pointing out that not all pleasures come from filling a lack. Pleasures of mathematics, of certain smells, sounds, sights, memories and hopes involve no pain beforehand, so they cannot be "generations," that is, processes that restore something missing.

Aristotle argues that pleasures which are disgraceful are not truly pleasant. Just because bad people enjoy them does not mean they are pleasant in fact, any more than food that tastes good to the sick is truly wholesome or things that look white to someone with sore eyes are truly white.

Pleasures are worth choosing, but not when they come from bad sources. The comparison is to wealth, which is good, yet not when it is gained by betrayal, and to health, which is good, yet not when it is gained by eating anything at all, however disgusting.

Pleasures differ in kind, Aristotle suggests. Pleasures from noble things are different from those from shameful things. You cannot enjoy the pleasure of a just person unless you are just yourself, or the pleasure of a musical person unless you are musical.

Aristotle says that the usual difference between a friend and a flatterer points to one of two conclusions. Either pleasure is not a good, or there are different kinds of pleasure. The friend is thought to seek the good in his dealings with others, while the flatterer seeks only pleasure, and the flatterer is blamed while the friend is praised.

Nobody would choose to live with a child's mind for their whole life, even if they got the greatest pleasure a child gets. Nor would anyone choose to enjoy the most shameful acts, even if they were sure never to feel pain from them.

Some things are worth pursuing even if they bring no pleasure, such as seeing, remembering, knowing, and having the virtues. The fact that pleasure naturally follows from them does not change this, since we would choose them anyway.
Pleasure is not the highest good, and not every kind of pleasure is worth choosing. Some pleasures are worth choosing for their own sake, and they differ in kind according to where they come from.
An act of seeing is complete at every moment. It needs nothing added later to make it whole, so it is not a process still heading toward an end.

Aristotle argues that pleasure is not a movement. A movement takes time and aims at an end, like house-building, which is complete only when the builder finishes what he intended. Pleasure is complete at any moment, so it cannot be a movement.

Aristotle is saying that the smaller activities that make up a larger process are incomplete while under way, and each differs in kind from the others and from the whole. Fitting stones together, fluting a column, and building the whole temple are different activities. Only the finished temple is complete, because it lacks nothing of its intended result, while the basement or a single triglyph (a grooved block in a Doric frieze) is only a part of the work.
Aristotle says that different kinds of movement are not all alike. A movement cannot be complete at any moment you pick; it is complete only over the full time it needs.

Aristotle says that motion has many kinds, such as flying, walking and leaping. Even walking differs in kind, because each part of a walk has its own starting point, end point and place, so no two stretches of the same walk are exactly alike.

Aristotle says that a movement does not seem to be complete at any single moment, and that most movements are incomplete. Different movements are different kinds because they have different starting points and end points.

Aristotle argues that pleasure is not a movement. A movement takes time and is never complete at any single instant, but pleasure is complete at every moment it is felt. So pleasure belongs to the class of things that are whole and complete at each moment.

Aristotle argues that pleasure cannot be a movement or a generation (a coming-to-be). These terms apply only to things that have parts and are not complete wholes. Seeing, a point, and a unit are not movements or comings-to-be, so pleasure, being a whole, is not one either.

Aristotle is saying that each faculty of perception acts on its own kind of object. When it is in good condition, it works best on the most excellent object within its range. He calls this perfect working, which he treats as the best kind of activity.

Aristotle says that each faculty (a power or capacity, such as sight or thought) works best when it is in its best condition and works on its best object. This activity is the most complete and the most pleasant, because pleasure goes along with every power of perception and every act of thinking.

Pleasure is strongest where an activity is most complete, meaning the best faculty working on the finest object it can reach. Pleasure completes such activity, but not in the same way the faculty and its object do. Compare health and the physician: both matter to a healthy state, yet they cause it in different ways.

Pleasure comes with the use of every sense. We say sights and sounds are pleasant, and the pleasure is greatest when the sense is at its best and meets a suitable object. Whenever the object and the sense are both like this, pleasure follows, provided there is something that acts and something that is acted on.

Pleasure completes an activity not as a permanent state within it but as an added finishing touch, like the bloom of health in a person in their prime. So when the thing perceived is as it should be and the faculty perceiving it is also sound, pleasure naturally follows the activity.

People cannot enjoy something continuously because their faculties tire and cannot keep up steady activity, and pleasure comes from that activity. Things that please when new often stop pleasing for the same reason: at first the mind works on them with full attention, but later the attention becomes careless, and the pleasure fades.

Aristotle's argument here is that people seek pleasure because they seek life, and life is a kind of activity. Each person works hardest at what he most enjoys, such as a musician using his hearing for music. Pleasure completes these activities, so it is part of the life people want.

Aristotle says that people aim at pleasure because pleasure completes life, and life itself is worth choosing. He sets aside whether we choose life for the sake of pleasure or pleasure for the sake of life, since the two are closely linked: pleasure arises from activity, and every activity is completed by pleasure.

Aristotle argues that pleasures differ in kind because the activities they complete differ in kind. Just as different natural things and made things need different completing features, intellectual activities differ from sense activities, and sense activities differ from each other, so the pleasures that perfect them also differ.
Pleasure that belongs to an activity makes that activity better. People who do something with pleasure examine each detail more closely and carry the work out with more precision.

People who enjoy an activity, such as geometry, music or architecture, get better at it, because the enjoyment leads them to understand its details more fully. Each person improves in whatever pursuit gives them pleasure.

Pleasures help activities to grow stronger, and whatever helps an activity in this way belongs specially to that activity. Since different kinds of beings have different proper activities, their proper pleasures also differ in kind.

A pleasure from one activity can crowd out another. Aristotle's example is people who love flute-music: when they hear a flute, they cannot keep up a conversation, because the pleasure of the music is stronger than the talk they are already doing, and so it ends the talk.
When someone is doing two activities at once, the more pleasant one pushes the other out. If the difference in pleasure is large enough, the person may stop the less pleasant activity altogether.
When we enjoy something greatly, we do nothing else. We switch to another activity only when we enjoy the first one moderately. People eat sweets in the theatre most when the play is dull.

Aristotle says that the pleasure belonging to an activity sharpens it and makes it last longer, while pleasures from outside the activity damage it. Foreign pleasures work much like the pains proper to an activity, which ruin it. If a man dislikes writing or calculating, he simply stops doing it.

Pleasures and pains affect an activity in opposite ways. The pleasure or pain that belongs to an activity itself makes that activity stronger or weaker, depending on its kind. Pleasures from outside the activity also harm it, though in a different way.

Just as actions differ in goodness: some are worth choosing, some worth avoiding, and some neither. Pleasures follow the same pattern, since each action has its own pleasure. A pleasure that goes with a good action is good, and one that goes with a bad action is bad. Desires for noble things are praised, and desires for base things are blamed.

Pleasures that go with an activity are closer to it than the desires for it are, because they arise together with it and cannot be separated from it. This closeness makes some people think pleasure and the activity are the same thing. Aristotle says pleasure is neither an act of thought nor an act of perception, though it is hard to tell them apart.

Pleasures differ in the same way their activities differ. Sight is purer than touch, and hearing and smell are purer than taste, so their pleasures differ in purity too. Intellectual pleasures differ from sensual ones, and each kind differs within itself.

Each kind of animal has its own pleasure, just as it has its own proper work or function, and the pleasure belongs to doing that work. Horses, dogs and humans enjoy different things, so animals of different kinds have different pleasures, while animals of the same kind likely share the same ones. Heraclitus is quoted: an ass prefers hay to gold.

Among human beings, people differ widely in what they find pleasant. The same thing may please one person and pain another. Taste and feeling also change with a person's condition: sweet things seem different to someone with a fever than to someone healthy.

Aristotle holds that the good person's judgment sets the standard for what is truly pleasant. Things that seem pleasant to him are real pleasures, while things that seem pleasant to corrupted people are only pleasant to them, because their nature is damaged.

Aristotle is raising a question about which pleasures count as good. Pleasures that are openly disgraceful are real pleasures, he says, unless one has corrupt tastes. For the pleasures people think of as good, the answer should come from the activities they accompany, since pleasures follow from those activities.

If a perfect and happy person has certain activities, then the pleasures that complete those activities are the pleasures properly called human. Other pleasures count as human only in a lesser sense, and they rank higher or lower depending on how closely they relate to the best activities.

Having covered the two kinds of excellence, friendship, and pleasures, Aristotle now turns to describing happiness. He treats happiness as the one goal of all human activity, and he plans to restate briefly what he has already said rather than start from scratch.

Happiness is not just a state a person is in, since someone asleep or suffering great misfortune would then count as happy. So it must be a kind of activity. Activities are either wanted only for something else or wanted for their own sake, and happiness belongs to the second group because it lacks nothing and is self-sufficient.

Things that are choice-worthy in themselves are those that people want only for the activity itself, with nothing more sought beyond it. Actions done according to virtue are of this kind, because doing what is noble and excellent is wanted for its own sake alone.

Aristotle says that people pursue amusements for their own sake, not for any further goal, and these often cost them more than they gain, since they neglect their health and money. Still, many people judged happy turn to such pastimes. Those skilled at them win favour with tyrants, because they please the tyrants in the very things the tyrants want.

Aristotle argues that we cannot judge what is truly good by looking at powerful men and how they spend their free time. Power itself does not bring virtue or intellect, which are the real sources of good activity. Men who have never known pure pleasure turn to bodily pleasures, but that does not make those pleasures better. Children likewise value what seems precious to them.

Aristotle says that just as children and adults value different things, bad and good people do too. So the things that are truly valuable and pleasant are those that seem so to the good person. For each person, the activity most worth choosing is the one that fits their own nature, and for the good person, that is the activity that fits virtue.

Happiness is not amusement. It would be absurd to work hard all one's life just to be amused, because we choose everything else for the sake of something further, while happiness is the final end that includes all others. Amusement is valid only as rest, so that one can return to serious work afterwards.

The passage argues that a happy life must be an active life of excellence, carried on seriously rather than through amusement. Activity of the better part of a person, or of the better person, is more serious and so also better and more able to bring happiness.

Bodily pleasures can be enjoyed by anyone, even a slave, as much as the best man. Happiness, however, is not found in such pleasures. A slave can share in happiness only in so far as he is alive. Happiness consists in activity that expresses excellence of character.

If happiness is activity in accordance with excellence, then it must be the excellence of the highest part of us. That highest part is intellect, or whatever else rules and leads and grasps noble and divine things. Its activity in its own proper excellence is complete happiness.

Aristotle argues that the best human activity is contemplation, meaning thinking about the highest things. He gives two reasons: the intellect is the highest part of us, and we can keep contemplating for longer than we can keep doing anything else.

Aristotle argues that pleasure must be part of happiness. He says the activity of scientific study, which is one way of living well, is the most pleasant of such activities. He adds that people who have already mastered a subject enjoy it more than those still learning it.

Aristotle says that self-sufficiency belongs most of all to a life of contemplation, meaning thinking and study. Everyone needs the basic necessities, but the just or brave person also needs other people to act with, while the scientist can contemplate alone. The scientist may do better with fellow workers, yet is still the most self-sufficient.

Aristotle says that contemplation, the act of thinking about truth, is valued for its own sake, because nothing comes from it except the act itself. Actions of moral conduct, by contrast, are done for some further result beyond the act.

Aristotle argues that happiness cannot be perfect rest, since the practical virtues, such as public life and war, involve activity rather than rest. Nobody goes to war just for the sake of fighting, and a statesman seeks power and honour for himself and his fellow citizens, which is a goal beyond the work of government itself.

Aristotle argues that the activity of the intellect, meaning contemplation or study, is the highest kind of happiness. Political and military actions are honoured, but they aim at something beyond themselves, while contemplation is valued for its own sake, is self-sufficient, and can be sustained. If a person lives a full lifetime in this activity, that would be perfect happiness.

A life of pure thought goes beyond ordinary human life, because the person living it is acting through the divine part within them, not simply as a human being. Since pure intellect is divine compared with human nature, the life lived by it is divine compared with ordinary human life.

Aristotle says we should not accept the advice to think only about human matters because we are human, or only about mortal matters because we are mortal. We should instead try to live like immortals, guided by the highest part of ourselves, the mind. Since this part is the true self and the most valuable thing in us, it would be foolish to choose someone else's life over our own.

Each thing's own proper activity is naturally its best and most pleasant. For a human being, that activity is the life of pure intellect, since the intellect is what most truly makes us human. So that life is also the happiest.

Aristotle says that the second-best kind of happiness comes from living by the other kind of excellence, the moral virtues such as justice and courage. These are proper to human beings, since we practise them in dealings with each other and in our feelings. He adds that moral character partly depends on physical conditions and is closely tied to the passions.

Practical wisdom and good moral character are closely linked, each depending on the other. The basic principles of practical wisdom match the moral virtues, and the virtues are right only when they agree with practical wisdom.

Aristotle says that the virtues tied to the emotions belong to the mixed human nature of body and soul, so the happiness that comes from them is also human. The life of pure intellect is separate from this, and he will not go into more detail.

Aristotle is comparing the contemplative life with the life of moral virtue. He says the contemplative person needs fewer external goods than the moral person. Both need the same basic necessities, though the socially active person spends a little more on appearance. The real difference lies in what each person actually does.

Virtues need the means to show themselves in action. The generous person needs money to give, the just person needs resources to keep promises, the brave person needs power to act bravely, and the self-controlled person needs temptation to resist. Without these, a person's real character cannot be shown.

Aristotle says that a person who devotes himself to contemplation needs few outside resources for that work, and that such things can even get in the way of it. As a human living among others, though, he still needs them to live virtuously and maintain his character.

Aristotle argues that perfect happiness must be a kind of contemplation, using the gods as the example. The gods are thought to be supremely blessed, but moral actions such as justice, bravery or keeping contracts would look absurd if attributed to them. So their happiness cannot rest on such actions.

Aristotle is asking what the gods could do that would count as generous or self-controlled acts. Giving needs someone to receive, and gods have no money to give. Praising a god for lacking bad desires would be demeaning. So, he concludes, looking at the details of moral action makes it seem too trivial for the gods.

Aristotle argues that if life is mainly action, and action is taken away, what is left is contemplation, or thoughtful study. So the gods' activity must be contemplation, and human activity closest to it brings the most happiness. Animals get no share of happiness because they have no such activity.

Gods live blessed lives at all times. Humans are blessed only to the extent that they have some copy of this activity, which is contemplation. Other animals are not happy at all, because they take no part in contemplation.

Happiness, on this view, goes exactly as far as contemplation does. People are happy to the degree they actually engage in contemplation, not by chance, but because contemplation is valuable in itself.

Happiness is mainly a kind of contemplation, meaning quiet thinking about truth. Because human beings are involved, though, a person also needs outside goods such as good health, food, and care, since human nature alone cannot manage contemplation.

Aristotle is warning against a mistake: even though a happy life needs some outside goods, it does not follow that a person needs a great many of them. Self-sufficiency and action do not require excess, and a man with modest means can still act virtuously and nobly.

Private citizens are thought to act justly at least as much as rulers, and even more so. A person needs only enough possessions to live on, because a life lived in accordance with virtue is already happy.

Solon, an early Greek lawgiver, is said to have described the happy person as someone with moderate material wealth, who has done noble deeds and lived with self-control. The reason given is that people of modest means can still act rightly.
