Anaxagoras held that the happy man is not defined by wealth or power. He said such a man would not be surprised to seem strange to the crowd, because the crowd judges only by outward circumstances, which is all they can see.

Aristotle says that the views of wise men agree with his account, but such views count for only so much. In matters of moral action, truth is tested against facts and real life. Earlier claims should be accepted if they match experience and treated as mere theory if they do not.

The person who lives by pure intellect and cultivates it is, Aristotle says, likely to be in the best state of mind and dearest to the gods. The gods are thought to care for humans, and they would favour what is best and most like themselves, which is intellect. Such a person, the man of science, therefore is probably also the happiest.
Knowing about virtue is not enough for living well, Aristotle says. Good action is the real goal, so we must also practise virtue and use every other means of becoming good.
Aristotle says that talk and writing alone cannot make people good. They can encourage well-born young people who are already inclined to virtue. But they cannot lead ordinary people to goodness.

Aristotle says that some people avoid wrongdoing only from fear of punishment, not from shame. They chase their own pleasures and avoid pains, and they have no idea what is noble or truly pleasant, because they have never experienced it.

Mere words can hardly change people who have long had bad habits built into their character. Aristotle says this is either impossible or very hard. Still, if we have every means to goodness available, reaching virtue is reason enough to be satisfied.

Some people think good character comes from nature, some from habit or custom, and some from teaching. Aristotle says that nature's part is not up to us. It depends on a kind of divine gift given to the truly fortunate.

Words and lessons alone may not reach everyone. A student's mind must first be shaped to like and dislike the right things, as soil must be ready before seed will grow. Someone ruled by passion cannot take in advice or be reformed by argument, since passion gives way to force rather than reason. So a person must first have some natural inclination toward virtue.

Aristotle says that good habits in virtue are hard to build in young people unless they are raised under suitable laws. Self-control and endurance are not pleasant to most people, especially the young. So diet and daily living should be regulated by law, because habits become no longer unpleasant once they are established.

Aristotle says that good upbringing in childhood is not enough. People must also be guided by laws in their adult lives, because most people obey force and punishment rather than reason or a sense of honour.

Some thinkers hold that lawgivers should use honour to encourage people toward virtue, since well-trained people will obey. Those who resist should be punished, with penalties opposed to the pleasures they desire, and the incurable should be expelled. Good people obey reason, while the base are held back by pain, as beasts of burden are.

To be good, a person must be raised and trained well, live under good laws and customs, and never do what is base, whether willingly or not. Aristotle says these things can happen only when people are guided by reason and good order, backed by authority to enforce them.

Aristotle says that a father's authority has no real force to compel, and neither does any single person's rule, unless that person is a king or in a similar position. Law can compel because it is a statement that comes from practical wisdom and reason. People resent others who oppose their wishes, even when those others are right, but they do not hate the law, even though it enforces what is right.

Aristotle observes that Sparta is almost the only city whose lawgiver set rules for what people eat and how they live. In most cities, he says, these matters are ignored, and each man lives as he pleases, ruling his household harshly.

Aristotle says that since public systems of training in virtue are neglected, each person should try to improve his own children and friends, and should act as a lawgiver for himself. Good laws make good public systems, whether written or unwritten, just as practice builds skill in music or gymnastics.

Just as a city is governed by laws and customs, a household is governed by the head's commands and by custom. Family rule works even better, the passage says, because family members are related by blood, owe each other benefits, and naturally feel affection and obedience toward the one in authority.

Private training can serve people better than general rules, because a rule that suits most cases may fail in a particular one. A fever patient is usually told to rest and fast, yet a single case may differ, and a boxer must change his style for each opponent.

Aristotle argues that individual people are best looked after through private care, since each person is then more likely to get what suits him. He adds that in medicine, gymnastics and other arts, a practitioner treats each case better when he knows the general rules.

Aristotle is answering the objection that general rules cannot guide action well. He says that a person can still care well for a single case through experience alone, without scientific knowledge of general principles. He compares this to people who treat themselves well but could not treat others.

Aristotle is saying that someone who wants to be a true expert in a craft, and know its theory well, must learn its general principles and understand everything they can do. He recalls that such principles are what the sciences deal with.

If people can become good through laws, then anyone who wants to make others better through a system of care and training must try to become a lawgiver himself. Only someone with real knowledge can treat any person skilfully, just as only a trained doctor can heal, not an ordinary person.

Aristotle asks how a person could acquire the skill of making laws. He suggests that statesmen might be the ones to learn it from, since lawmaking was thought to belong to political science. He then says that political science does not stand in the same position as other sciences and skills.

Aristotle says that in other skills, such as medicine and painting, the teachers also practise what they teach. The Sophists, who claim to teach statesmanship, do not practise it. Statesmen seem to succeed through practical knack rather than theory, and they do not write about politics or train their own sons to be statesmen.

The earlier thinkers would surely have passed on the greatest gift they could to their communities, which is the ability to contemplate, or think deeply about truth. They would have valued this ability above any other, for themselves and their closest friends.

Practice seems to play a large part in learning statesmanship. Simply being around political life would never have made people statesmen, so anyone who wants to gain this knowledge must also practise it.

Aristotle says the Sophists, who claim to teach lawmaking, do not really understand it. If they did, they would not treat it as on a par with rhetoric, nor think that lawmaking is easy because one can simply pick the best existing laws. Choosing well is a skill, just as judging music is. Only people with practical knowledge can judge performances properly. Others can only tell whether the result is good or bad, as with painting.

Aristotle asks whether laws, which are the practical results of political science, can teach a person how to make good laws. He points out that reading medical handbooks does not make someone a physician, though such books describe diseases and treatments. He suggests such guides help trained practitioners but are of little use to people without training.

Collections of laws and constitutions are useful to people who can think about them and judge what is good, what is bad, and which things fit together. People without that ability cannot judge them well, unless they have a natural feel for it, though studying them can still make them more informed.

Aristotle says that earlier thinkers did not study lawmaking, so he will study it himself, along with the whole subject of the state. This is so that the study of human affairs can be finished as far as he is able.

Aristotle proposes a plan of study. He will first gather whatever useful points earlier thinkers have made about the good life, then study the constitutions (the forms of government) he has collected. He wants to learn what keeps cities stable or destroys them, and why some are well run and others badly run. This will help him decide which constitution is best, and which laws and customs suit each.

Cicero says that the priest Quintus Mucius Scaevola often told stories about his father-in-law Gaius Laelius, always calling him "the wise." Cicero, as a young man, was introduced to Scaevola and stayed close to him for as long as he could.

Cicero says that after his teacher died, he became a follower of Scaevola the Pontifex, a man he considers the most distinguished Roman of his time for ability and integrity. He promises to speak of Scaevola's uprightness later, and returns to Scaevola the augur, whom he recalls from one particular occasion.

Cicero describes a conversation in a garden, where a speaker turned to a subject that many people were talking about. The subject was the bitter public quarrel between Publius Sulpicius, a tribune, and the consul Quintus Pompeius, two men who had once been very close friends.

Cicero says that Scaevola told him about a talk on friendship that Laelius gave shortly after Africanus died. Cicero wrote down the main points from memory and arranged them his own way. He made the speakers appear directly in the dialogue, so it reads as spoken aloud rather than as a report.

A friend has repeatedly asked the writer to write about friendship. The writer agrees that the topic is worth everyone's study and suits the close bond between the two of them, so he is willing to write it for the public at his friend's request.

Cicero explains why he chose Cato as the main speaker in his earlier work on old age. In his view, Cato was the right choice because he had been old for longer than anyone else and had stayed vigorous in his old age.

Cicero explains why he chose Laelius to lead a discussion of friendship. Tradition held that the friendship between Laelius and Scipio was the most famous, and Scaevola remembered Laelius actually taking part in such a talk. Cicero adds that discussions gain weight when they are attributed to famous men of the past.
Cicero says that when he rereads his own writing, it sometimes seems to him that Cato is the one speaking, not himself. Cato is the older speaker in the dialogue, so the words feel like his.

Cicero says he is sending this essay on friendship to a friend, as he earlier sent his essay on old age. This time the main speaker is Laelius, a famous wise man known for his friendship, not Cato. Cicero asks his friend to imagine Laelius talking.
Gaius Fannius and Quintus Mucius visit their father-in-law, Laelius, after Africanus has died. They raise the topic of friendship, and Laelius gives the answer that makes up the whole essay.

Fannius tells Laelius that Africanus was a remarkable man, but that people now look to Laelius and call him "the wise." He notes that Cato and Lucius Atilius were also called "the wise," though the title meant something different in each case. Atilius was called wise for his knowledge of law.

Cato was called "Wise" as an honorary title, late in life, for his political experience, foresight, firmness and sound counsel. The speaker says the addressee is wise in a different sense: through natural gifts, character, hard work and learning, the sense scholars use rather than the common one.

Cicero says that only one man in Greece, at Athens, was really called wise, and even he was named so by an oracle of Apollo. Strict critics do not count the Seven Sages as wise. In their view, true wisdom means thinking you are self-sufficient and that life's changes cannot touch your virtue.

People keep asking the speaker, and Scaevola too, how Laelius is coping with the death of Africanus. Their curiosity grew because Laelius missed the augurs' meeting on the Nones, which he had never missed before.

Scaevola is answering a question about why Laelius missed a meeting. He says Laelius is bearing his grief well for a dear friend who has died, and that he missed the meeting because he was ill, not because he was sunk in sadness.

Laelius thanks Scaevola and agrees with him. He says a man of principle should not drop a duty he has regularly performed, even because of personal misfortune. He rejects the honourable title Fannius gave him, and says Fannius, out of affection, does not give Cato his due.

Cicero's speaker says that Cato, who lost a grown son, bore grief better than men who lost young sons, so Cato should not be ranked below Socrates, whom the oracle called the wisest. Cato's fame rests on what he did, while Socrates' rests on what he said.

Cicero says he grieves for his friend Scipio, but he does not need outside comfort, because he has let go of a common mistake. He argues that Scipio has suffered no harm, so any loss is Cicero's own. Deep sorrow over one's own loss, he says, shows self-love rather than true love for the friend.

The speaker says that Cato (the Elder, who is spoken of here) had nothing left to wish for, except perhaps immortality. He won great honour early in life, and was elected consul twice without ever having sought the office, once before he was old enough by law.

Cicero is praising Scipio Aemilianus, a Roman general who died young. He ended two enemy cities, Carthage and Numantia, and was loved by his family and fellow citizens. The speaker asks what more years could have added to such a man.

Old age need not be a burden, but it does take away strength and freshness. Scipio died suddenly, so he was spared the experience of dying, and his life had been as fortunate and glorious as it could be. The manner of his death is hard to describe, and people have their suspicions about it.

Scipio's last day was his greatest. The senators, the people of Rome, the allies and the Latins all walked him home. Cicero says that after such public honour, a man's next move seems to be upward to the gods rather than down to the underworld.

Cicero rejects the modern view that the soul dies with the body and death ends everything. He sides instead with older belief, citing the funeral rites of his ancestors, which would make no sense if the dead were wholly gone, and the teaching of early Greek philosophers in southern Italy.

Cicero describes Socrates, the man the Delphic oracle called "most wise," who taught that human souls are divine and return to heaven after death, most easily for the most virtuous and just. Cicero says Scipio shared this belief, and that Scipio spent three days discussing the state shortly before he died.

The speaker, Laelius, reports a talk about the soul's immortality that Scipio gave, which Scipio said came from the elder Africanus in a dream. The main claim is that the better a person is, the easier it is for the soul to leave the body, which is called a prison. On that reasoning, Scipio would have had the easiest journey to the gods.

Cicero argues that if the soul dies with the body and feels nothing afterward, death is neither good nor bad, since a dead person is like one never born. He adds that he is still glad that this friend was born, and that the state will rejoice in him until its end.

Cicero says his friend Scipio is now at peace after death, while he himself has outlived him, which he thinks was the wrong order. Still, he counts his life happy because he shared public and private life with Scipio, and the two agreed closely in tastes, aims and feelings.

Laelius says his happiness does not come from the reputation for wisdom Fannius mentioned, which he calls groundless. It comes instead from hoping that people will remember his friendship with Scipio. He values this because history records only a few famous pairs of friends, and he hopes theirs will be counted among them.

Fannius and Scaevola ask Laelius to share his views on friendship: what it is and how one should behave within it. Scaevola adds that he too would be glad to hear them, since he had been about to make the same request.

Laelius declines to give a formal speech on friendship. He says he is not skilled enough, and that such a talk should come from professional philosophers. He will only urge that friendship is the greatest thing in the world, since it suits human nature and helps in both good and bad times.

Friendship, Cicero says, can exist only between good men, but he does not insist on a strict definition of "good." Philosophers who say only the perfectly wise count as good may be correct, but no real person reaches that wisdom. Friendship should be judged by how people actually live.

Cicero says that the old Romans Fannius, Curius and Coruncanius were not wise by the strict standard of the philosophers. He mocks the rigid label "wise," which he says few understand, and notes that critics will not even call these men good. So he drops the debate and speaks in ordinary common sense.

Cicero says that "good" people are those whose lives show honour, purity, fairness, and generosity, who are free from greed, lust, and violence, and who stand by their convictions. Because such people do their best to follow nature as a guide to a good life, they are called good.

Nature, Cicero says, links all people together, and that link grows stronger the closer people are. So we feel more affection for fellow citizens than for foreigners, and for relatives than for strangers. Such ties are a kind of friendship, though they lack some of its lasting quality.

Friendship differs from family ties in that affection can be removed from a family relationship and the relationship still exists in name, but friendship without affection does not exist at all. Friendship is also narrower than the general natural bonds among people: its affection is shared by only two people, or at most a few.

Friendship is defined as complete agreement on all matters, human and divine, together with mutual goodwill and affection. Cicero says that, apart from wisdom, nothing better has been given to people by the gods. Other goods like wealth, health, power, or pleasure are weak and uncertain, and virtue is what creates and keeps friendship alive.

Cicero says we should use "virtue" in its everyday sense and not define it in lofty terms. Good people are those commonly regarded as good, such as Paulus, Cato, Gallus, Scipio and Philus. These people are good enough for ordinary life, so there is no need to worry about perfect ideal figures who do not exist.

Friendship gives life its calm and comfort, because a friend offers goodwill and a person to share everything with. Good fortune is worth much less, the speaker suggests, if there is no friend to share one's joy.

Cicero says that other goals each serve one purpose: wealth for use, power for respect, pleasure for enjoyment, health for freedom from pain. Friendship, he argues, offers many benefits at once. It is always available, and it is never out of place or unwelcome. It also shares misfortunes, which would be hard to bear alone.

Cicero says friendship is as useful to people as fire and water. He is not talking about ordinary friendship, but the true, complete kind found among a few famous people. Such friendship makes good times better and shares out bad times, so that the burden is cut in half.

Friendship is described as the greatest of its blessings: it gives hope for the future and keeps a person from weakness and despair. A true friend feels like a second self, sharing in the friend's wealth and strength. Even after death, a person is said to live on in the respect and remembrance of friends.

Cicero argues that friendship holds families, cities and farming together, while quarrels and factions can destroy even well-established households and states. Friendship therefore brings great benefit, and its opposite shows this clearly.

Cicero reports a Greek philosopher's teaching that friendship holds unchanging things together, while discord breaks changeable things apart. He adds that people recognise this from experience, since they applaud any clear case of loyal friendship in danger, as audiences did for a scene in a play.

The passage describes the story of Orestes and Pylades, where each claims to be Orestes so the other will not be killed. The audience in a play applauds this loyalty. Cicero argues that people admire such self-sacrifice in others even when they would not do it themselves.

The speaker says he has nothing more to add about friendship, though he thinks more could be said. He suggests that others, who claim expertise in such matters, can be asked. Fannius replies that they would rather ask him, and the speaker admits he has heard those experts with some pleasure but finds the present talk different.

Scaevola tells Fannius that Scipio would be the best person to talk about friendship. Scipio's friendships were known for loyalty, steadiness and honesty. Fannius agrees that Scipio easily defended justice in an earlier debate, since he was a just man.

Laelius is replying to a request that he is being pressed to accept. He says that whatever form the pressure takes, it amounts to force, and that it is neither easy nor right to refuse his sons-in-law when their wish is good in itself.

Cicero asks whether friendship arises mainly from human weakness and need, so that friends can help each other with what they lack. He suggests instead that its true origin is something earlier, nobler, and more closely rooted in human nature, with mutual help only a secondary benefit.

Cicero says that the Latin word for friendship comes from the word for love, and that love is what mainly draws people into mutual affection. He adds that people can gain material benefits through a show of friendship, but true friendship cannot be feigned: where it exists, it is genuine and spontaneous.

Friendship, Cicero says, comes from a natural impulse and affection of the heart, not from hoping for help or gain. He points to animals, which show a similar instinctive love for their young and are loved by them in return.

Cicero says that natural love between parents and children is strong and only extreme wickedness can break it. He adds that love between people grows when one person shows what he calls the "beacon-light of virtue," because virtue alone wins love and affection.

Cicero says we can feel affection for men we have never met, simply because of their honesty and virtue. He gives Roman examples: we admire Fabricius and Curius and hate Tarquinius Superbus, a Roman king remembered as a tyrant, along with Spurius Cassius and Spurius Maelius. Pyrrhus and Hannibal, enemies of Rome, are mentioned as great generals.
The passage contrasts two men. One is not greatly hated because he was honest. The other is hated, and will always be hated, by the speaker's country because he was cruel.

Cicero argues that if people can admire goodness even in an enemy, it is no surprise that affection arises when they think they see virtue in someone they could know closely. Affection grows further when real favours are given, when a wish to help is shown, and when people spend more time together. Added to the first impulse, these produce a strong warmth of feeling.

Cicero is answering the view that friendship arises from weakness, from needing help. He says that if this were true, friendship would have a low origin, and that people would seek friends in proportion to how poor they think their own resources are. He holds the opposite: the truth is the reverse.

Cicero says that a man who is strong in virtue and wisdom, and needs nothing from others, is the one most inclined to seek and keep friends. He gives his own friendship with Scipio Africanus as an example: neither needed anything from the other. Their bond grew from mutual admiration of character, and closer contact deepened it.

Friendship is not valued for the material benefits it brings, though such benefits often follow. Just as kindness is given freely without expecting thanks or return, friendship is sought for its own sake, because its whole reward lies in the affection itself.

Those who treat everything as a matter of physical pleasure, like animals, are the opposite in their view of friendship. Cicero says that people who have made their thinking serve such a low aim cannot look up to anything noble or divine, so he sets them aside from the discussion.

Love and affection, Cicero says, begin in a spontaneous feeling that arises as soon as a person's honesty and goodness become apparent. Once people feel this inclination, they naturally try to draw closer to the one they admire.

Friends should be equals in affection, more eager to do favours than to be repaid, and competitive in generosity. Cicero says this makes two things true: friendship brings great practical benefits, and it comes from a natural impulse rather than from need, which is both nobler and closer to the facts.

Cicero argues that if friendship were built on material benefits, it would end whenever those benefits changed. Since true friendship is based on nature, which does not change, genuine friendships last forever. The speakers then ask Laelius to continue.

Laelius introduces talks he often had with Scipio about friendship. Scipio used to say that keeping a friendship intact until death is the hardest thing in the world, since many things can come between friends, such as clashing interests and differing political views.

Friendships often change, sometimes because of misfortune and sometimes as people age. The speaker compared this to boyhood, when close bonds between boys often end as they grow up, or break apart over rivalry in love or some other advantage.

Friendships that lasted for years often broke down when two friends competed for public office. Greed for money was the most common cause of ruin, but among good men the rivalry for office and reputation often turned close friends into bitter enemies.

Friends sometimes ask each other to help with wrongdoing, such as indulging improper desires or harming someone. When a friend refuses, which is the right thing to do, the one asking often accuses them of breaking the duties of friendship. Such accusations often end friendships and create lasting hostility.

Cicero asks how far loyalty to a friend should go. He gives examples: should Coriolanus's friends have helped him invade Rome, or should the friends of Maelius and Vecellinus have helped them seek tyranny? He also notes that Tiberius Gracchus was deserted by his friends when he pursued radical reforms.

Blossius, a friend of Tiberius Gracchus, was questioned about his part in the conspiracy. He said he would have obeyed Gracchus even if Gracchus had ordered him to burn the Capitol, the temple in Rome. Cicero, who was questioning him, reports this as his own words and treats the statement as a clear sign of wrongdoing.

Cicero is describing a man who went beyond what his friend Tiberius Gracchus asked, leading his radical actions rather than just supporting them. When that man was put on trial, he fled to Asia and joined the enemies of Rome. The speaker concludes that claiming to have acted for a friend does not excuse a wrong deed.

Friendship starts from believing in a person's virtue, so it cannot last if that virtue is lost. Cicero also argues that friends should not grant every wish or make every demand, since that would need perfect wisdom on both sides, and ordinary friends do not have it.

Cicero gives examples of close friends from early Rome, such as Papus Aemilius and Gaius Luscinus, who were consuls and censors together. He argues that none of these men ever asked a friend to do anything that went against his honour, his oath, or the good of the state.

Cicero is saying that the men he has in mind were very devout, so they would not have agreed to such a request, since granting it would have broken their religious duty. He adds that Gaius Carbo and Gaius Cato did side with Tiberius Gracchus, and that Gracchus's brother Gaius, who did not at first, is now the most eager of all.

Friendship does not justify doing wrong, and a friend should neither ask for nor agree to wrongdoing "for friendship's sake." This rule matters most when the wrong would betray the republic, the state. Cicero adds that things have reached a point where his friends must look ahead to what may happen to the state.

Cicero says that Rome's constitution had already begun to drift from its proper course. Tiberius Gracchus tried to gain kingly power and held it for a few months, something the Roman people had never seen before. He also says that the followers of Gracchus, even after his death, did something to Publius Scipio that he finds too painful to describe.

Cicero, speaking through Laelius in this dialogue, worries that political reforms are leading to a steady decline. He points to the secret ballot laws (the lex Gabinia and lex Cassia) as a blow that has already turned the people against the Senate, and fears that the most important decisions will soon be left to the crowd.

Cicero says it is easier to start a revolution than to stop one, and that no one tries to stir up such trouble without friends to help. So good men who find themselves bound in friendship with such people owe no duty to stand by friends who are disloyal to the state.

Cicero argues that bad men should fear punishment, since those who take part in wrongdoing are punished as severely as those who lead others into it. He gives two examples: Themistocles, the Greek leader who was exiled and turned against his country, and Coriolanus, a Roman who did the same. Neither found anyone to help him, and both killed themselves.

Friendship cannot excuse a group of wicked men who plot together. Such conspirators should be severely punished, so that no one believes loyalty to a friend can justify waging war on one's own country. Cicero adds that he cares about the state's future after his death as much as about its present condition.

In friendship, the first rule is that friends should ask only for good things and do only good things for each other. Friends should offer help without waiting to be asked, speak their advice frankly, and, when needed, firmly. A friend's good advice should carry great weight and be followed.

Cicero reports that some Greek thinkers advise against very close friendships. Their reason is that a person should not have to bear the worries of several people, since each man already has enough of his own troubles.

Cicero advises keeping friendships loose, so they can be tightened or loosened as one wishes. He argues that a happy life needs freedom from worry, which is lost if one must carry the troubles of others. He then mentions a rival school that values friends only for the help they give, not for affection.

Those who are weakest in power or wealth seek friendship most, which is why women, the poor and the unfortunate look for it more than men, the rich and the prosperous. The speaker calls this a noble view and says friendship is the greatest gift the gods have given to human life.

Cicero questions the value of "freedom from care," the Epicurean ideal of avoiding anxiety. He says it is tempting at first, but in practice it must often be set aside, because duties of honour cannot be refused or dropped just to avoid worry.

Virtue brings anxiety with it, so avoiding anxiety would mean avoiding virtue. Good people are most troubled by the opposites of their virtues: the kind by cruelty, the brave by cowardice, the self-controlled by vice.
A well-ordered mind is pleased by what is good and pained by its opposite. Since even wise people feel heartache, Cicero asks why we should give up friendship just to avoid the distress it may bring.

If you remove emotion from a person, Cicero asks, what is left to tell a man apart from a beast, or even from a stone or a log? The question suggests that emotion is what separates a human being from inanimate things.

Friendship is not a hard, unbending thing; it grows with a friend's joy and shrinks with his sorrow. The pain that friends sometimes cause us is not enough reason to give up friendship, just as the main virtues are not dropped because they bring worry and grief.

Friendship begins when one person sees virtue in another and is drawn to it, and so affection follows naturally. Cicero argues it would be unreasonable to enjoy lifeless things such as office, fame, fine buildings and decoration, yet care little for a living person who has virtue and can love in return.

Friendship is most delightful when affection is returned and both sides show kindness. Like is drawn to like, so good people love other good people and bind themselves to them as if by family ties. Nature itself seeks what is similar to it.

Good men naturally feel goodwill toward one another, and this is the root of friendship. That same goodwill also reaches ordinary people and even whole nations, since it looks after their interests. If it looked down on everyone outside a small circle, it could not do this.

Cicero argues that those who say friendship is valued for what it brings us spoil its best quality. What delights us in a friend is mainly his warm affection, and we value his help only when it comes from that affection.

Cicero argues that poverty is not the reason people seek friendship. Often the richest and most virtuous need others least, yet they are the most generous. He adds that friends should sometimes need each other, as Scipio's need for his help gave Cicero a chance to show affection.

Cicero says that people who dismiss friendship are wrong to do so. He argues that even a life of great wealth and power would be bad without love, since tyrants have no loyalty or affection and live in suspicion, and fear rules out friendship.

Men who are powerful or prosperous get friendship only while their fortunes last, and that friendship disappears when they fall. Tarquin, the exiled king, is said to have found out which friends were false only once he could no longer reward anyone.
Very rich people often cannot keep true friends, because their wealth blinds them. Good luck makes them proud and self-willed, and once they gain power they drop their old friends for new ones.

Cicero says it is foolish for rich people to buy horses, servants, fine furniture and expensive dishes, yet not gain friends. He calls friends the most valuable and beautiful possessions a person can have in life.

Wealth and property may pass to whoever is strongest, and the owner cannot know who will enjoy them later. A friendship, by contrast, is a lasting possession that belongs securely to the person who has it. Even if material goods last, life without friends is joyless.

Cicero asks how far friendship should go and where affection should stop. He lists three views on this and says he agrees with none of them. The two given here are that we should love a friend only as much as ourselves, and that our affection should exactly match the friend's affection for us.

Cicero rejects the view that the way we care for a friend should match the way we care for ourselves. He points out that people often do things for a friend that they would never do for their own sake, such as begging favours from unworthy people.

Good men will give up advantages for themselves, even accept losing them, so that their friends can have them. The passage also says that harsh personal attacks, such as sharper insults, are not admirable when done for one's own sake but are admirable when done for a friend.

Cicero rejects the view that friendship must be a strict balance of favours and affection between two people. He says true friendship is more generous than keeping exact accounts, and that friends should not worry about giving more than they receive.

A friend should not judge a person by that person's own low opinion of himself. When someone is too humble or too hopeless about his prospects, his friend should instead encourage him and help him feel more hopeful.
Scipio criticized the saying "Love your friend knowing you may one day hate him" as the opposite of true friendship. He doubted it really came from Bias, one of the Seven Sages of Greece.

Cicero is answering the view that friendship is a matter of self-interest. His argument is that a person who expects a friend might one day become an enemy would want that friend to make mistakes, so he could use them against him. He would also resent the friend's successes.

Cicero rejects the saying that a friend might one day become an enemy, because it would destroy friendship. He says we should choose friends carefully, so that we never befriend someone we could come to hate. If a choice turns out badly, we should accept it rather than plan for a future break.

Friends should be men of good character, and their aims should match completely. If a friend asks for help with something that is not quite right, but that concerns his life or reputation, one may bend a little from the straight path. This holds only as long as it does not bring great disgrace.

Friendship deserves some consideration, but a person should still care about their reputation and the good opinion of fellow citizens. Winning that approval by flattery is beneath a person, yet virtue, which earns genuine affection, must never be given up.

Scipio complains that people take more care counting their livestock than choosing their friends, and have no clear way of judging who would make a good friend. He says the qualities to look for in a friend are firmness, stability and constancy.

Good men with the right qualities are rare, and their worth is hard to judge without testing them. But friendship often starts before any judgment can be made, so a test first is not possible. Cicero therefore advises testing friends gradually, the way horses are tried before they are driven hard, and holding back one's rush of affection until then.

Cicero argues that few people put friendship above money, public office, military rank or political power. When a real choice comes up, most people prefer these rewards to their friends. He adds that wanting political power is part of human nature.

Men in politics and the race for office often think that gaining power will outweigh the loss of a friend. For this reason, true friendship is rare among them: few will put a friend's advancement above their own, or share a friend's political ruin.

Most people show they are unreliable as friends in two ways: they look down on friends when they prosper, or they abandon them when they suffer. A person who stays steady as a friend in both situations is, Cicero says, extremely rare and almost more than human.

Loyalty is the quality that keeps friendship stable and lasting, and nothing without it can last. When choosing friends, one should also look for simplicity, sociability, and a sympathetic nature that shares our feelings, since these support loyalty. A twisted or complicated character cannot be trusted.

A true friend must be steady and reliable, which a person cannot be if he is cold by nature or indifferent to what happens to his friend. He also must not enjoy accusing his friend or readily believe accusations against him. Cicero concludes that only good men can be friends.

In Cicero's view, a good man who is also wise shows two traits toward his friends. The first is that he is never false or pretending in his feelings. He would rather openly show dislike than hide his real feelings behind a show.

A good friend does not accept accusations against his friend from others, and he does not suspect the friend himself or assume the friend has done wrong. He should also be pleasant in speech and manner, since this adds much to friendship. Constant seriousness and a gloomy mood may impress people, but they do not make friendship warm.
Friendship, the passage says, should be somewhat less rigid and more lenient and kind. It should be more open to companionship and good humour.

Cicero asks whether new friends should ever be preferred to old ones, as we prefer young horses to old. He answers that friendship should not wear out like other things, and that older friendships grow sweeter, like well-kept wine. A long shared history is needed for true friendship, though new friendships still have value because they promise future good.

Friendship lasts well when people keep old friends, much as we prefer a horse we are used to or a place we have lived in for years. Cicero's point is that a friend should also be made equal to oneself, so that neither looks down on the other.

Scipio, though clearly superior to his friends, never acted as if he were. He deferred to his older brother Quintus Maximus, even though Quintus was not his equal in ability, and he wanted all his friends to benefit from his help.

If a person has advantages in character, intelligence, or wealth, they should share them with their friends. If a friend's parents or relatives lack status or ability, the better-placed person should make up for those lacks and help raise the friend's standing.

The point is that people who discover they are the children of gods or kings should still love the shepherds who raised them, and this should hold even more for their true parents. Good qualities and talents only reach their full worth when they are shared with those closest to us.

Those who are less fortunate in friendship should not resent being outdone in talent, wealth, or status by their friend. Yet many of them complain constantly or keep pressing their own claims, especially when they think they have done loyal service at some cost to themselves.

People who keep reminding others of favours they have done are tiresome, and the person who did the favour should never mention it. Among friends, the more important person should stoop to the lesser one, and should help the lesser person feel valued. Those who think they are undervalued, and feel they deserve it, should be shown otherwise by actions as well as words.

Cicero says that the favors you give a friend should fit two things: what you are able to give, and what the friend is able to handle. Even a powerful man cannot raise every friend to high office. Scipio could make Publius Rupilius consul but not his brother Lucius. Even when you can give something, it should not be more than the friend can bear.

Friendships should not be judged firm just because people shared a youthful interest such as hunting or sport. Time alone does not make a bond, or else nurses and slave-tutors would hold the strongest claims on our affection. They still deserve care, but on a different footing.

Only friendships between mature people can last, because differences in character lead to differences in aims, and those differences pull friends apart. Good men and bad men cannot be friends for this reason: their characters and aims are as far apart as they can be.

Cicero says that too much affection for a friend should not stop you from serving that friend's highest interests. He gives the myth of Neoptolemus, who could not have taken Troy if he had listened to Lycomedes, the man who raised him and wept to keep him from going.

Sometimes important business forces friends to be apart, and a man who resists this because he cannot bear the separation is weak and makes a poor friend. Still, there are limits to what friends should expect from each other and what they may demand, and these limits must be judged case by case.

Sometimes a friendship has to end, and it cannot always be avoided. If a friend's bad conduct brings shame on us, or hurts us, the friendship should fade away slowly by seeing less of each other, rather than ending in a sudden break.

According to Cato, a friendship should be allowed to loosen gradually rather than be ripped apart suddenly. The exception is when a friend's wrongdoing is so severe that an immediate break is the only course that honour allows.

Cicero says that when friends change in character or aim, or split over politics, they should be careful not to turn a quiet end of the friendship into open hostility. He notes that open war with a former close friend is very disgraceful. He adds that Scipio once dropped his friendship with Quintus Pompeius because of Cicero.

Someone (Cicero's friend, the subject of the discussion) grew apart from Cicero's fellow consul Metellus because they disagreed about politics. In both quarrels he showed he was hurt, but he did not hold a grudge or act bitterly.

Cicero's point is that when friends part, the aim is first to avoid a break. If one happens anyway, the friendship should fade away gently rather than end in violence. Friends should also keep affection from turning into open hostility, which brings quarrels, insults and bitter accusations.

In Cicero's view, a friend's faults of this kind should be borne patiently, as long as they do not go beyond reasonable limits. Out of respect for an old friendship, the one who does the wrong, not the one who suffers it, is to be counted as at fault.
The passage says the only real protection against the faults and troubles of friendship is to be slow to give your affection and not to give it to people who do not deserve it.

Cicero says that people worthy of friendship are those who have qualities that naturally win affection, and such people are rare, as all excellent things are. He adds that most people value only what is useful, and treat friends as investments, valuing them for the profit they expect.

Those who seek friendship only for what it brings never find the truest kind, which is valued for its own sake. We know what friendship is by how we love ourselves, for that love needs no reward. A real friend is only revealed when this same feeling is directed toward another person, who becomes a second self.

Cicero argues that friendship has natural roots. Animals show two instincts: love of themselves and a drive to seek out and join others of their own kind. If animals feel something like love in this, humans must feel it even more, because they not only love themselves but seek another person whose spirit can merge with their own.

Most people wrongly want a friend who has qualities they lack themselves, and they expect from others what they do not give. The right approach is to be good yourself first, then seek a friend of similar character, since only between such people can lasting friendship be found.

Friends, according to this passage, learn to control the passions that enslave others, to delight in fair conduct, and to help each other without asking for anything wrong. They must also respect one another, since losing respect costs friendship its finest quality. Friendship, the passage says, does not excuse wrongdoing.

Nature gave us friendship to help virtue reach its highest goals, which a person alone cannot reach. Those who have such a friendship, or will have one, have found the best way to reach nature's highest good.

Real friendship, according to this passage, brings together moral goodness, honour, peace of mind and calm, and these are what make life happy. Because friendship depends on virtue, people who neglect virtue cannot have it, and they only discover that they lack true friends when a serious misfortune tests them.

Choose friends by judging their character first, and only then give them your affection. People often do this backwards, so a friendship built on long closeness or shared obligations can end suddenly over a single offence.

Cicero says that carelessness about friendship deserves blame because friendship is the one thing everyone agrees is useful. Other goods are disputed: some people look down on virtue, riches, or public office as empty or unimportant.

Cicero says that people disagree about most things people value, but all agree about friendship. Whatever their way of life, whether public, scholarly, private or pleasure-seeking, they hold that life without friendship is no life, at least if any part of it is to be worthwhile.

Friendship reaches into everyone's life in some form, and no way of living escapes it. Even a person who hates society, like the legendary Timon of Athens, still looks for someone to whom he can pour out his bitterness.

Cicero says that if a god placed a person alone far from other people, with every physical need met but no chance to see another human being, that person could not bear such a life. Without other people, he would lose all enjoyment of pleasures.

Even if a person could climb to heaven and see the order of the universe and the beauty of the stars, the sight would give little pleasure without someone to share it with. Cicero concludes that human nature cannot bear to be alone and needs support, which is found most pleasantly in a close friend.

Friends sometimes cause offence, and a wise person handles this in different ways: avoiding it, removing it, or overlooking it. The one offence that must be faced is when a friend's interests or your honesty are at stake, since friends sometimes need correction. Such correction, given kindly, should be accepted well.

Frank criticism can harm a friendship if it breeds resentment. Going along with a friend's faults is worse, because it lets him ruin himself. The most to blame is the person who resents honest speech and listens to flattery. So rebukes must be given carefully and without bitterness or insult.

Cicero says that a friend should not go along with a man's wrongdoing just to please him, since that kind of compliance is unworthy of a free man. A true friend is not a tyrant's servant, and someone who refuses to hear the truth from a friend cannot be helped.

Cato said that some people owe more to bitter enemies than to pleasant friends, because enemies often tell the truth while friends never do. Cicero adds that people are often angry when they are corrected for a fault, when they should instead feel sorry for the wrong and be glad to be set right.

Cicero says that friends should give and receive honest advice, and that flattery is the greatest threat to friendship. Flattery is praise given only to please, with no regard for truth. Pretence of any kind, he adds, clouds our ability to see what is true.

Cicero says that flattery is the greatest enemy of friendship, because it destroys the honest openness friendship needs. Friends can only become as one if each keeps a steady, independent mind. A person who agrees with everything another says, and changes with every look or nod, cannot truly join with a friend.

Cicero says that flatterers like Gnatho, a character from a Terence comedy, are dangerous when they are powerful or respected, because their position gives their flattery weight. Still, with reasonable care, a true friend can be told apart from a false one as easily as real things can be told apart from fake ones.

Cicero says that even an unlearned crowd can tell a flatterer from a man of principle. He gives the example of Gaius Papirius, whose speech to the assembly he calls flattery, and contrasts it with Scipio's speech, which he praises as dignified and impressive.

Cicero recalls two cases where a popular proposal failed or was not pursued. In the first, a speaker he praises was seen as a true leader, not a tool of the Roman people, yet the people rejected a law meant to please them. In the second, Crassus proposed letting the people, rather than the priestly colleges, fill their own vacancies.

Cicero recalls that a rival speaker, who had first begun turning toward the forum when addressing the people, argued against a conservative position. Cicero spoke for the traditional side during his praetorship, five years before his consulship, and won. He says the victory came from the strength of the case, not from the prestige of his office.

Cicero argues that truth wins out even in a public assembly, where lies and half-truths are common, if it is clearly shown. Friendship depends wholly on honesty, he says. Without open-hearted candour between friends, you cannot trust them or be sure even of their affection.

Those who flatter themselves most are the ones most open to flattery from others. Virtue does love itself, because it knows its own worth, but the passage is concerned with people who only believe they have virtue. Few people actually have it, yet many want to be seen as having it, and these are the people who enjoy flattery.

Flattery is not true friendship. When one person refuses to hear the truth and the other is willing to lie, the bond is false. Cicero points to comic parasites and boastful captains, whose excessive praise is funny only because such people exist.

Flatterers tell their targets what they want to hear, and they stretch the truth to do it. The danger is greatest with people who welcome praise, but even steady, brave men can be fooled by hidden flattery. Obvious flattery is easy to spot; the sly, indirect kind is the one to guard against.

The flatterer is hard to spot, because he often disguises his fawning as argument. He pretends to dispute with you, then gives way and lets himself be beaten, so that you think you have seen through him. Being fooled in this way is shameful.

Cicero says that old men who are short-sighted and easily fooled are a common picture of foolishness on stage. He admits he has moved away from his topic, the friendship of wise people, to ordinary and weak friendships. He proposes to go back to his main subject and finish it.

Cicero says that virtue, meaning moral goodness, both produces friendship and keeps it going. When a virtuous person recognises the same goodness in another, they are drawn to each other, and this produces a warm bond that he calls love or friendship.

Love, Cicero says, means clinging to someone for their own sake, not because you need them or hope to gain. Such affection can also bring advantage, though that was not the goal. He gives examples of older friends and friends of the same age, including Scipio.

Cicero says that in old age he enjoys the friendship of younger men. Because each generation replaces the one before, it is best to share your life with people your own age and also to guide younger ones toward your goal. Since mortal things do not last, he says we should always look for people to love and to be loved by.

Cicero says that even though his friend Scipio died suddenly, he still feels Scipio alive. What he loved was Scipio's virtue, which death cannot destroy. Scipio's glory will last for future generations, and anyone seeking noble goals will look to Scipio's memory as an example.

Cicero says that, of all the good things fortune or nature gave him, none equals his friendship with Scipio. The friend gave him support in public and advice in private, and they shared a home, meals, daily life, military service and travel.

Cicero says that the memory of the shared studies and talks he had with his dead friend has not disappeared, but grows stronger through thought and remembrance. Even if he had none of that, his old age would ease his grief, since he has little time left to bear it.

Cicero ends his discussion of friendship with a final piece of advice. He says that virtue comes first and is needed for friendship. After virtue, he says, friendship is the greatest thing, and nothing else ranks beside it.

Cicero opens by quoting verses that offer help to a grieving friend and ask what reward the helper might expect. He then applies them to Atticus, saying Atticus is not, like Flamininus, tormented by constant worry.

Cicero tells his friend that he admires his calm, sensible character, the qualities he brought back from Athens. He suspects the friend is sometimes deeply troubled by the same events that trouble him. Consoling him over these will have to wait, so for now he dedicates a essay on old age to him.

Cicero says he wants to ease the burden of growing old, which he shares with his friend. He knows the friend already bears it calmly and with philosophy, but he chose the friend as the right person to receive this work on old age.

Cicero says that writing this book on old age has been so pleasant to him that it has removed the unpleasant parts of growing old and made that time of life enjoyable. He concludes that philosophy deserves high praise, since its followers can live every stage of life calmly. He then sends the book to a friend.

Cicero explains why he gave his essay on old age to the character Cato rather than to a mythical figure like Tithonus. A made-up story would not be convincing, so he sets the talk at Cato's house, with Laelius and Scipio as listeners. He adds that Cato's learning here may seem greater than in his own writings, because Cato took up Greek studies late in life.

Scipio admires Cato for his wisdom in every respect, and especially because Cato never seemed to find old age a burden. Scipio notes that most old men find it so hateful that they feel crushed under a weight heavier than Mount Etna.

Cato says that people who rely on outside things for a good life find every age hard to bear. Those who find happiness within themselves do not complain about what nature makes unavoidable, such as old age. He mocks people who long for old age yet complain when it comes, and asks who forced them to believe in a false hope.

Cicero argues that old age does not come on faster than youth did, and that living longer would not make old age easier to bear, since past years offer no comfort to a foolish old man. He says his own wisdom lies in following nature as a guide and obeying her commands.

Life, like a well-written play, has a natural ending, as fruit ripens and then falls. A wise person accepts this end without complaint, since rebelling against nature is as futile as the giants' war against the gods.

Laelius asks Cato to explain how a person can get the strength to bear the burdens of old age, so they can prepare before they reach it. Cato agrees to do so, provided Scipio and Laelius are willing to hear it.
Laelius asks Cato to describe what old age is like, since Cato has reached it after a long life, and Laelius expects to follow the same path one day.

Cato says he will answer as best he can. He recalls that men of his own generation often complained, and first among their complaints was the loss of the pleasures of the senses, which they felt made life not worth living.

Cicero says that some old men blame old age for being neglected by people who used to serve them. He argues that this is the wrong cause. If old age were really to blame, every old man would suffer the same neglect, but he has known many old men who never complained about old age.

Cato argues that the unhappiness people feel in old age comes from their character, not from their age. Reasonable old men, who are not bad-tempered or surly, find old age bearable, while unreasonable and surly people are uneasy at any age. Laelius then notes that Cato's wealth and high position may be why he finds old age bearable, and few people have such good fortune.

Cato says that old age is not easy or hard for everyone in the same way; it depends on the person. He gives an example: a famous man's success owes something to his country, but not all of it, and so old age is also shaped by more than age itself. A wise man poor in old age still finds it hard, and a foolish rich man finds it a burden too.

Cicero says that the best support for old age is a cultivated mind and a life of active virtue. If these have been kept up throughout life, they bring a rich reward. They last into old age, and the memory of a well-spent life gives great pleasure.

Cicero describes his close friendship with Quintus Fabius Maximus, a much older Roman statesman. Even though Fabius was old, Cicero felt as attached to him as if they had been of the same age. He says Fabius kept his serious dignity, softened by courtesy, and that old age did not change his character.

Cicero recalls serving under Cato the Elder as a young soldier, and then as a quaestor, a junior public office. He says Cato, though very old, fought with the energy of youth. By his steady persistence, Cato wore down Hannibal, who was still full of youthful confidence.

Cicero's verse praises Quintus Fabius Maximus, a Roman general. He saved Rome, when it was struck by disaster, by delaying rather than fighting. He stayed committed to his aim whatever people said of him, and his fame will last.

Cicero recalls Quintus Fabius Maximus, a Roman general, who took back Tarentum from the enemy. When the man who had lost the town, Salinator, boasted that Fabius owed his success to him, Fabius replied with a joke: had Salinator not lost it, Fabius could not have won it back. The speaker adds that Fabius was as skilled in public affairs as in war.

Cicero describes an earlier statesman, Gaius Flaminius, a tribune. Flaminius proposed dividing public land among citizens against the Senate's ruling. This man opposed the plan as long as he could, even without his fellow consul's support. As an augur, a priest who read omens, he also argued that any law harming the state went against the omens.

Cato the Elder, Cicero's model of an old man, is praised here for how he faced the death of his son, a man of great character who had been consul. Cicero says his funeral speech for the son is so famous that, next to it, the speeches of philosophers seem poor. Cato was also admired at home, for his rich conversation and wise sayings.

The speaker praises an older man for his wide knowledge of ancient history, Roman religious signs called augury, literature, and military history. He says he enjoyed talking with him eagerly, sensing that once the man died, he would have no one left to learn from.

Cicero says that a happy old age does not need a famous military career like Scipio's or Maximus's. Not everyone can have such a life. But a quiet, thoughtful life can also bring a calm, gentle old age, as Plato is said to have had when he died at his desk at eighty-one.

Cicero tells of Gorgias, who lived to 107 and kept working, and of Isocrates, who wrote a famous book at 94 and lived five years more. When asked why he stayed alive so long, Gorgias said he had no complaint against old age. Cicero says foolish people blame old age for faults that really belong to themselves.
A horse that once won the Olympic wreath is now too old to race and rests instead. The image compares an aging person who has stopped taking part in active life to this retired champion.

Cicero recalls an old man, Cato the Elder, who died in a year that can be dated by two consuls, Caepio and Philippus. He notes that Cato, though seventy, bore poverty and old age, usually seen as the heaviest burdens, almost cheerfully, while Cicero himself, at sixty-six, still had a strong voice.

Cicero says that people think old age is unhappy for four reasons: it takes us away from active work, it weakens the body, it removes most physical pleasures, and it leads toward death. He proposes to examine each reason in turn.

Cicero argues that old age does not stop people from doing useful work. He points to older Roman statesmen, such as Quintus Maximus, who gave the State good counsel and influence. He also cites Appius Claudius, who was blind yet opposed a peace treaty with Pyrrhus.

Cicero is describing Appius Claudius Caecus, who gave a speech against making peace with Pyrrhus, the king of Epirus. He argues that Appius must have been very old at that time, because the dates of his offices do not fit a younger man. The story of the speech is still passed down anyway.

Old age still matters in public affairs, Cicero argues, because its value lies in judgment, character and the ability to speak wisely, not in physical strength or speed. He compares the old man to a ship's steersman, who sits quietly at the tiller while the young crew do the physical work, yet steers the ship and holds the most important role.

Cicero argues that old age does not take away a man's active powers, and he points to himself. Though he is old, he still gives the Senate advice on war, urging that Carthage be destroyed and that he will not rest until it is levelled with the ground.

Cicero prays that the gods will grant Scipio the glory of finishing what his grandfather began. The grandfather died over thirty years earlier, but his memory will last. Cicero then asks whether this man, had he lived to a hundred, would have regretted growing old.

Cicero's speaker argues that older men contribute counsel, reason and skill in debate, not physical fighting. He points to the Roman Senate, named for its elders, and to Sparta, where top officials were called elders. He adds that great states have been endangered by young men and saved by old ones.

Cicero argues that memory does not necessarily fade with age. It weakens only if it is not used, or if a person is naturally slow-witted. He points to Themistocles, a famous Athenian statesman who knew all his fellow citizens by name, and to himself, who remembers people and their families, and even refreshes his memory of the dead by reading tombstones.

Old men usually keep their memory well, as long as they keep their minds active and busy. Cicero says this holds for ordinary people in quiet lives as well as for those in high office. He gives Sophocles, who wrote tragedies into extreme old age, as an example.

Sophocles' sons asked a court to take control of his property, claiming he was too old and mentally weak to manage it. To show his mind was sound, the old poet read the court a play he had just written, the Oedipus at Colonus, and asked whether a weak-minded man could have written it. The jury then acquitted him.
Cicero asks whether old age stopped famous writers and philosophers from working. He suggests it did not: for these men, active study continued until they died.

Cicero says that old Sabine farmers keep working on crops and planting, even though they may not live to see the results. He quotes a line about a man planting trees for a future generation. The point is that old people still invest in things they may never enjoy.

Cicero quotes a farmer who plants trees for future generations, saying he works for the gods who let him inherit land and pass it on. He prefers this view of old age to a verse by Caecilius, which says long life brings much to dread and weep over.

Wise old men enjoy the company of promising young men, and old age feels less dull to those whom young people seek out and like. In the same way, young men enjoy the advice of older men, which leads them toward striving for excellence. The speaker adds that he thinks the young listeners enjoy his company as much as he enjoys theirs.

Old age, the passage says, is not idle or dull but busy, with people continuing the activities they loved earlier in life. It gives Solon, the Athenian lawgiver and poet, as an example of an old man who keeps learning new things.

Cicero says that he only began studying Greek literature in old age, and he studied it eagerly, as if quenching a long thirst. He notes that Socrates learned the lyre in his old age, and says he would have liked to do the same, but instead he worked hard at literature.

Cicero says that in old age he does not miss the physical strength of youth, just as in youth he did not miss the strength of a bull or an elephant. He argues that a person should use whatever strength they have and give full effort to what they are doing. He mocks the story of Milo of Croton, a famous athlete who wept over his old arms, saying that Milo was no more finished than anyone else.

Cicero is answering a claim that old men lose their mental powers. He says orators do lose some strength with age, since speaking depends on lungs and body as well as the mind. Yet he adds that his own voice has not weakened, and he is still in good voice himself.

Old men should speak quietly and calmly, and their measured speech often wins a hearing. Even if an old man cannot speak eloquently himself, he can still teach young men such as the Scipios and Laelius. Cicero argues that old age keeps the strength to teach and prepare the young for life's duties, which he calls a noble task.

Cicero argues that old age does not by itself weaken the body; a wasted youth is often the real cause. He points to Xenophon's Cyrus, who on his deathbed in old age said he felt no weaker than in his youth.

Cicero recalls Lucius Metellus, who held the high priesthood for twenty-two years and stayed physically strong until the end of his life. He then says that old men commonly talk about their own merits, as Nestor does in Homer, and that such talk is allowed at his age.

Cicero says that Nestor's wise speech was worth more than physical strength. He notes that Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks, wanted ten men like the wise old Nestor rather than ten strong warriors like Ajax, because Nestor's counsel would bring about the fall of Troy.

Cicero, speaking in his eighty-fourth year, says he is not as strong as he once was in his younger military and public years. Still, old age has not destroyed his physical strength or ruined his public and social life. He says he has never accepted the famous old saying that the passage is about to quote.

Cicero says he would rather grow old at the natural time than age too early. He answers the objection that he is weaker than younger men: strength is not what makes a man eminent, as the example of an old centurion shows. What matters is using one's strength wisely, in proportion to what one has.

Cicero says that an old person will not grieve much over losing physical strength. He compares the strength of the athlete Milo with the mind of the philosopher Pythagoras, and he asks which would be preferred. His point is that a good thing should be enjoyed while it lasts, and not wished back once it is gone, just as children and young men should not wish to return to their earlier years.

Life follows a fixed course that can be run only once, and each stage has its own natural strengths to be enjoyed in its proper time. Cicero then mentions Masinissa, a foreign king and friend of Scipio's grandfather, who still does such things at ninety years old.

Cicero describes an old man who still walks everywhere on foot once he starts, rides without dismounting, and goes out in rain and cold bareheaded. Because his body stays free of harmful humours and he keeps up his royal duties, Cicero concludes that exercise and self-control can keep some of a person's former strength even in old age.

Old men are not required to do what needs physical strength, by law or custom, and they are not even bound to do all they could. Feebleness, the speaker says, is not special to old age but also belongs to people in poor health. He gives the weak health of Scipio's adopted son as an example.

Old age brings weakness, but Cicero says it can be resisted through effort, like an illness. People should keep their bodies healthy with moderate exercise, food and drink, and should care for their minds and souls even more.

Cicero argues that old age does not by itself make people foolish or forgetful. Those faults belong to a lazy, dull old age, just as wildness belongs to only some young men. Mental effort keeps the mind sharp, much as oil keeps a lamp burning.

Cicero uses the example of Appius, an old, blind man who still ran his large household with full authority, and whom his children, slaves and clients respected and loved. His point is that old age deserves respect as long as it keeps its strength, its rights and its independence, and does not become a slave to others.

Cicero says he admires an old man who keeps a young man's spirit, just as he admires a young man with an old man's wisdom. Someone who aims at this may grow old in body but never in mind. To show his own vigour, he lists his current work: a history of Rome, collected speeches from famous cases, and books on religious and civil law.

Cicero says that he keeps his mind sharp through study, Greek, and a nightly review of his day, as the Pythagoreans did. Because of this work he feels little loss of physical strength, and he still pleads cases for friends and proposes motions in the Senate, relying on his mind rather than his body.

A man who has spent his life busy with study and hard work does not notice old age arriving. Life then ends slowly and gradually, not with any sudden break. Even if he can no longer do such things, he can still enjoy them in his mind, because of the life he has already lived.

Cicero begins his case that old age lacks sensual pleasures and treats this as a benefit, since it removes what he calls the greatest fault of youth. He introduces a saying by Archytas, a Greek thinker, which calls physical pleasure the most deadly curse nature has given humans.

Cicero says that the desire for physical pleasures leads people to treason, revolt, crime and sexual wrongdoing. He calls the mind the finest gift of nature or God, and argues that pleasure cannot coexist with self-control or virtue.

Cicero asks the reader to picture someone at the peak of sensual pleasure. Such a person cannot use reason or thought while under that excitement. So pleasure, when it is very strong and lasting, is described as harmful, because it clouds the mind.

This is a framing note, not the argument itself. Cicero says he heard the words of the Pythagorean Archytas, spoken to the Samnite Caius Pontius, from his friend Nearchus of Tarentum, who had heard them from old men. He adds that the philosopher Plato was present at the time.

Cicero argues that if reason and philosophy cannot keep a person from wanting pleasure, then old age is a kind of help, since it takes away the desire for things a person should not do. Pleasure, he says, clouds thinking and has nothing to do with virtue.

Cicero says he felt it was necessary to publicly condemn a man's shameful act of indulgence. While the man was consul in Gaul, he had a prisoner beheaded at the request of his lover during a dinner party. Cicero and his colleague Flaccus, as censors, would not allow such conduct, since it also disgraced the government.

Cicero reports that the Roman Gaius Fabricius was amazed when he heard, while serving as envoy to King Pyrrhus, that an Athenian philosopher taught that all human actions aim at pleasure. The story comes to Cicero through older men who had heard it in their youth.

Manius Curius and Publius Decius said they wished the Samnites and Pyrrhus, the enemies of Rome, held the same view that pleasure is the highest good, because Rome would then find them easier to defeat. Decius had earlier given his life in battle for the Republic, and Curius was his close friend.

Fabricius and Coruncanius, Roman figures Cicero names, held that something is noble and great in itself, sought for its own sake, and that the best men aim at it while ignoring pleasure. Cicero then asks why he spends so much time on pleasure.

Cicero admits that old age lacks the pleasures of rich feasts and heavy drinking, but says it also avoids their pains, such as headaches, indigestion and broken sleep. He adds that old age can still enjoy modest social gatherings. He also quotes Plato's view that pleasure is a bait that lures people into vice.

Cicero recalls seeing the old Gaius Duilius come home from dinner with a torch and flute-player leading him, a honour he had been granted for his military glory. He then says he will turn to his own case, starting with his long membership of a club.

Cicero's speaker says he used to attend his club's feasts, drinking with moderation. He says he enjoyed these dinners more for the company and conversation of friends than for the physical pleasures they offered.

Cicero says the Latin word "convivium," meaning "a living together," is better than the Greek words for "a drinking together" or "an eating together." The Latin word names the shared enjoyment of company, while the Greek words focus on the least important part of the meal.

Cicero says he enjoys long afternoon dinners, especially for the talk they bring. Few of his own age are left, but he still enjoys the company of younger men. He is grateful that old age has increased his love of conversation while reducing his appetite for food and drink.

Cicero says that old men can still enjoy the pleasures of life, and he does not think old age removes the ability to appreciate them. He admits that some may think he is rejecting all pleasure, and he says that feeling is perhaps natural. He himself still enjoys even the old custom of being the host who runs a dinner party.

Cicero is listing things in Roman country life that show old people still enjoy simple pleasures. Here he names customs at dinner: the conversation starts from the lowest-ranked couch, the small cups filled a little at a time, and ways of keeping cool in summer and warm in winter.
The speaker says that, even in the countryside among his Sabine neighbours, he keeps up these habits. Each day he hosts a large dinner with neighbours and talks with them late into the night.

Old men may feel less sexual pleasure, but they also miss it less, because nothing that gives no uneasiness is missed. Cicero repeats Sophocles' reply that he was glad to be free of desire, which he likened to a harsh master. He argues that not wanting something is more pleasant than lacking it while still desiring it.

Cicero argues that even if young people enjoy physical pleasures more keenly, those pleasures are trivial. Old people still have some of them, though not in abundance. He compares this to theatre seats: a front-row viewer enjoys a play more than someone in the back row, but the back-row viewer still enjoys it.

Cicero argues that old age can be enjoyable, though in a different way from youth. Once a person has finished with the strong desires, ambitions and quarrels of life, the mind can live with its own thoughts. If it has learned from study and philosophy, a peaceful old age can be very pleasant.

Cicero recalls old men who kept working on their interests until they died. Gallus worked on astronomy, mapping the sky and land and predicting eclipses, often from dawn to night. Naevius and Plautus, both Roman writers of plays and poems, found similar pleasure in their literary work.

Cicero points out that men stayed active in their work even in old age. He names Livius Andronicus, who was still alive when Cicero was young and had staged a play long before, and Publius Licinius Crassus, an expert in religious and civil law. He says all of them were eagerly devoted to their fields when they were old.

Cicero says that old men can still take pleasure in learning and public speaking. He names Marcus Cethegus, who kept working at oratory even in old age, and says no feast, game or love affair gives greater pleasure. He adds that Solon, the Athenian lawmaker, said he kept learning new things every day as he grew old.

Cicero says that farming gives him great pleasure, and that old age does not reduce this pleasure. He thinks farming comes closest to the life of the ideal wise man. He values the earth's own power to produce crops as much as the crops themselves.
