The passage describes how a crop grows from a seed sown in soil. The earth first hides the softened seed, then, warmed and pressed, splits it open so a shoot appears. The shoot's roots support it as it rises, and the grain forms an ear protected by spiky awns against small birds.

Cicero's speaker, an old man, says that planting and growing vines gives him great pleasure and comfort in his old age. He marvels at how a tiny seed or grape-stone grows into a huge tree or vine, and at the many ways plants are propagated, such as cuttings and layers.

The passage describes how a vine grows and how it is pruned. Left alone, the vine sprawls and falls to the ground, so it clings to supports with its tendrils. A gardener cuts it back so it does not grow wild, and from the buds left on the shoots in spring the grapes appear.

This describes a grape, which is bitter when young but turns sweet as it ripens. The vine's leaves keep it warm enough, yet shade it from the sun's heat. The speaker asks whether anything could be more fruitful or more lovely to look at.

Cicero says he enjoys farming not only for its profit but also for the way crops are grown and how plants naturally develop. He lists practices such as supporting vines, pruning, irrigation, and digging the soil. He adds that he has already written about manure in his book on agriculture.

Cicero says that the poet Hesiod, who wrote about farming, never mentioned old age, while Homer shows the old man Laertes easing his grief for his son by working his farm. He adds that farm life is pleasant in many ways, including gardens, orchards, sheep, bees and flowers.

Cicero says he could go on listing the pleasures of country life, but he thinks he has already said too much. He asks to be forgiven, admitting that he loves farming and that old age tends to be talkative, though he does not want to claim old age is free of faults.

Manius Curius, a Roman general who won many victories, spent his last years on a simple farm. When Samnite envoys offered him a large amount of gold, he refused it, saying he would rather rule those who had gold than own it himself. Cicero says such a spirit made his old age pleasant.

Cicero points out that in early Rome, senators were older men who lived on their farms. Cincinnatus was ploughing when he learned he had been made Dictator, and senators were summoned to the Senate at their farmhouses.

Cicero argues that farmers' old age is not a sad thing to pity. He says farming is very useful to all people, gives simple pleasure, and provides plenty of food and what is needed for worship. Since some people desire these things, he concludes we should accept pleasure.

Cicero describes a well-run farm as richly supplied, with full storerooms, many animals, dairy and honey, a garden, and hunting for extra pleasure. He concludes that nothing gives more necessities or a finer sight than land that is well cultivated.

Old age does not stop a person from enjoying simple pleasures. It actually encourages them, such as warming in the sun or by a fire, and cooling in shade or water. Young people may keep their active sports, while old men can keep only light games like dice, or give those up, since old age is happy without them.

Cicero recommends Xenophon's books and praises his writing on farming in the work on household management. He says Xenophon thought farming the best occupation for a ruler, and he plans to quote Socrates saying this to Critobulus.
Cicero tells how Lysander, a Spartan commander, visited the Persian prince Cyrus at Sardis bringing gifts from Sparta's allies. Cyrus welcomed him warmly and showed him a carefully planted park.

Lysander admires the tall trees, their neat rows, the well-kept soil and the sweet-smelling flowers in a garden. He says he admires the skill of the person who designed it, not only the hard work. Cyrus replies that he planned the whole garden himself and planted many of the trees with his own hands.

Lysander, a Spartan commander, looks at Cyrus, the Persian prince, in his purple robe and gold jewelry. He tells Cyrus that people rightly call him happy, because his high fortune matches his personal excellence.

Old men can still enjoy this kind of good fortune, the passage says. Age does not stop them from keeping up many activities, farming especially, until the very end of old age. The passage then breaks off just as it begins an example.

Valerius Corvus stayed active on his farm until he was a hundred, even after his public career ended. His public career spanned from his first to his sixth consulship, with a gap of forty-six years between them. Those years matched the span that the ancestors counted from birth to the start of old age.

Cicero says that the last years of an old man's life can be happier than his middle years, because he has more influence and less hard work. In his view, the best thing about old age is this influence.

Cicero lists famous Romans who held great influence, even in their old age, and says their authority came from their reputation for wisdom and respect. He concludes that old age, especially when honoured, carries more influence than all the pleasures of youth combined.

Cicero's point is that old age earns respect only if it rests on a good life lived earlier. A person cannot demand influence just because they are old, with grey hair or wrinkles. Authority comes at the end from honourable conduct in the years before.

Cicero says that small courtesies, such as being greeted, given way to, and asked for advice, are signs of respect for old people. He adds that these honours are strongest where morals are highest, and that the Spartan Lysander called Sparta the most respectful place for old age.

Cicero says that the Athenians once gave great respect to old age. An elderly Athenian found no seat among his own people at the games, but the Spartan ambassadors rose and gave him a place. The whole audience then applauded them.

In Cicero's view, a respected old man's influence is worth more than physical pleasures. He points to the augurs, Roman priests who read omens, where older members speak first, a rule he calls one of the best. Those who use their influence well, he says, finish life's drama well, like actors who do not falter at the end.

Cicero's speaker admits old men can be fretful, irritable and disagreeable, but argues these faults come from character, not from age itself. He adds that the faults have some excuse, since old men feel neglected and mocked and bodily weakness makes every slight painful. Good character and good upbringing soften these faults.

Cicero says that old age does not have to turn sour. Some people become harsh as they age, while others stay gracious, just as not every wine goes bad with keeping. He accepts serious dignity in the old, but not bitterness, and he finds greed in old age senseless, since the less of life's journey remains, the less sense it makes to collect money for it.

Cicero says that an old man who has lived long enough should have learned not to fear death. Death either ends the soul completely, so it need not be feared, or it leads the soul to eternal existence, so it may even be welcomed. He sees no third possibility.

Cicero argues that there is no reason to fear death. Whether death brings no misery or even happiness, fear is pointless. He also says that young people die more easily than old people, since they catch diseases more often and suffer more serious illnesses, so few reach old age.

Cicero argues that old men bring wisdom and sound judgment, and that states could not have existed without them. He then turns back to the fear of death in old age, pointing out that young people die too. He recalls that his own excellent son, and Scipio's brothers, died young, showing death comes at every age. A young man may expect a long life, but that expectation is not certain.

Cicero argues that an old man is wrong to think he has nothing left to hope for. Hope is for things not yet certain, and an old man is already in a better position than a young one. The young person hopes to live long, while the old person has already lived long.

Cicero says that no span of life seems long once it has an end, because when the end comes, only the good deeds and virtue a person has achieved remain. Time that has passed does not return, and the future cannot be known.

A person should be content with whatever length of life is given to them. Like an actor who need not perform the whole play, or a wise man who need not wait for the final applause, a short life can be lived well and honourably. Living longer is no reason to complain, just as farmers do not complain that spring has passed.

Spring stands for youth, which points ahead to a harvest, just as the other seasons are for gathering and storing crops. Cicero says old age is the harvest: the memories and good things stored up from earlier life. He also argues that death in old age fits nature, while the early death of young men goes against it, like a great fire put out by a flood.

Old men die naturally, like a fire that burns down until it goes out, or ripe fruit that falls from the tree. Young men are cut off early by force, like unripe apples torn from a branch. The speaker finds this natural ripeness pleasing and feels he is nearing harbour after a long voyage.

Old age has no fixed starting point, and a person uses it well as long as they can still do their duty and are not afraid of death. Because of this, old age can be more confident and brave than youth. Solon, the Athenian lawmaker, showed this when he told the tyrant Pisistratus that he relied on his old age to speak boldly against him.

Cicero says that the best way to die is when the mind and senses are still sound, and nature simply takes the body apart, as it once put it together. He compares this to a builder who can take apart what he built more easily than anyone else, and to old glue that comes apart more easily than new.

Old men should neither greedily cling to the little life left to them nor give it up without reason. Cicero cites Pythagoras, who forbids leaving life without God's order, and Solon, who wanted to be mourned by friends. Cicero prefers Ennius, who wants no tears at his funeral.

Death may bring a brief feeling of dying, but after death there is either no feeling or a feeling one would want. The main point is that a person must learn early not to fear death, since it can come at any time and fear prevents a calm mind.

Cicero lists Roman heroes who gave their lives for their country or for their word. He names Lucius Brutus, the two Decii, Regulus, the two Scipios, and Lucius Paulus. The list is cut off before it ends.
Cicero argues that death should not frighten older men, since young soldiers marched cheerfully toward likely death. He adds that weariness of life comes from growing tired of all activities.

Each stage of life has its own activities, suited to childhood, youth, middle age and old age. Just as the activities of earlier years fade away in their time, so do those of old age. When they fade, a weariness with life brings the right time to die.

Cicero says that he believes the dead fathers of his listeners, Scipio and Laelius, are still alive, in a true life. While we are shut inside the body, he says, we carry out a hard task given to us by fate.

Cicero says the soul comes from heaven and has been pushed down into the earthly body, which is foreign to its divine nature and immortality. He believes the gods placed souls in human bodies so that people could observe the heavens and copy their orderly movement. He holds this view because of reasoning and the authority of leading philosophers.

Cicero says he was told that Pythagoras and his followers believed human souls come from the universal divine mind. He also says he was shown Socrates' speech on the last day of his life about the soul being immortal. Socrates was the man the Delphic oracle called the wisest.

Cicero argues that the soul cannot be mortal, because its many abilities (memory, foresight, knowledge, discovery) show a nature too rich to die. He also reasons that the soul moves itself, with no outside source of motion, so its motion will never end.

Cicero argues that the soul is not made of parts, so it cannot be divided and therefore cannot die. He adds that children learn things so quickly that they seem to be remembering them from before birth, which he presents as support for the same view.

Cicero's speaker, addressing his sons, tells them not to think that he will be nowhere after death. He argues that the soul is real even though it cannot be seen, since people know a person's soul by his actions. He also says that the lasting honour paid to great men shows that their souls continue to affect us after they die.

Cicero's speaker argues that the soul does not lose its understanding when it leaves the body. Instead, once freed from the body it becomes pure and wise. He adds that at death the body's elements return to where they came from, while the soul cannot be seen either coming or going, and that sleep resembles death.

Cicero's speaker, a dying man, argues that the soul shows its godlike nature in sleep, when it foresees events and is free of the body. So if the soul survives death, his listeners should treat him as a god. If it does not, they should still keep his memory alive by living loyal and pious lives out of reverence for the gods.

Cicero's speaker says he cannot believe that great Roman leaders, such as Scipio's father and grandfathers, would have done famous deeds that lasting fame would remember unless they had believed that later generations would care about them. Their greatness, in other words, depended on their thought of the future.

Cicero, speaking as an old man, says he worked hard day and night because he wanted glory that would last beyond his own life. He could have chosen a life of ease, but his soul always looked toward future generations, as if it would only truly live after leaving the body.

Cicero argues that the best men strive for lasting fame because they believe their souls are immortal. If souls were not immortal, the noblest people would not have worked so hard to be remembered after death.

Cicero argues that wiser people die more cheerfully than foolish ones, because a wise mind sees further and understands that it is heading toward something better. He says he himself longs to meet the great men he admired, including those he knew, those he only read about, and those he wrote about in his histories.

Cicero's speaker says he would not want to be brought back to life or made young again, even by a god. He compares his life to a race he has nearly finished, and asks whether life offers any real blessing or only toil.

Cicero says that life has an end, either in its pleasures or in existence itself. He does not look down on life, and he is glad to have lived well. Still, he leaves life the way a traveler leaves an inn, not the way a person leaves their own home, because nature gave us life as a temporary stay.

Cicero's speaker, an old man, looks forward to dying and joining the souls of the dead, including his son Cato. He says his son died before him, and that he was thought to bear the loss well, though he was in fact distressed. He comforts himself with the belief that their separation will not last long.

Cicero says that his old age is light and even pleasant for him, and he credits this to the beliefs he has described. He adds that even if his belief in the soul's immortality is mistaken, he is glad to hold it and will not give it up while he lives.

Cicero's speaker says that if the dead feel nothing, he is not worried about being mocked by dead philosophers. Even if people are not immortal, a man should still want his life to end at its natural time, since nature sets a limit on all things. Old age is like the final act of a play, and its exhaustion should be avoided once one has had enough of it.

Montaigne says he is not troubled by sorrow at all, and he does not like it in himself or admire it in others. Still, the world has agreed to honour sorrow and treats it as a sign of wisdom, virtue and conscience. He calls this a foolish and shabby way of dressing up sorrow.

Montaigne says that the Italians rightly call sadness (tristezza) by a word meaning malignity, because it is always harmful and useless. He adds that it is cowardly and base, so the Stoics, a school of ancient Greek philosophers, forbade their wise men to feel it.

Psammenitus, king of Egypt, was defeated and captured by the Persian king Cambyses. He stayed silent and still as he watched his daughter and then his son pass by under guard. He only broke down in grief when he saw one of his close servants being led away as a captive.

This is the opening of a story about a prince who, while at Trent, received news of the deaths of his elder brother and then a younger brother. He bore both blows with great firmness. The passage is incomplete, so its full point is not yet given.

A man who had kept calm through earlier losses broke down when a servant died a few days later. Some people concluded that this last loss was the only thing that had truly hurt him. In fact, he was already full of grief, so this small extra blow overflowed his patience.

Psammenitus, an Egyptian king, was asked why he wept for the misfortune of his friend but not for the deaths of his son and daughter. He answered that his grief for his children was too great for tears, and tears were only fit for the smaller sorrow.

Montaigne describes an ancient painter who painted Iphigenia's father with his face veiled, because no face could show grief that deep. He adds that poets likewise turned the grieving mother Niobe into stone, as a sign that her sorrow had gone beyond expression.

Great grief can strike the mind so hard that it becomes numb and unable to function, as when bad news leaves a person stunned and unable to move. Tears and cries then seem to release the soul from this shock, giving it room to breathe and act again.

In a war over Buda, a common soldier fought with notable bravery and was praised by everyone, though no one knew his name. After he was killed, the German lord Raisciac mourned him more than anyone, having become deeply admiring of his courage.

A count sees his dead son, still wearing armour, and recognizes him only when the armour is removed. He says nothing and keeps staring at the body until grief overwhelms him and he falls dead. The Italian quotation means "Who can say how he burns with a small fire," a saying used to describe unbearable passion.

It is a Latin poem by Catullus, quoted by Montaigne, in which the speaker describes what happens to his body when he sees Lesbia. His senses are taken from him, his tongue goes numb, a thin fire runs under his skin, his ears ring, and his eyes are covered by darkness.

Montaigne says that a person in the peak of a strong feeling cannot speak well of his grief or persuade a lover. His mind is overloaded and his body is weak with desire. This is why sudden failures in love can happen, even at the moment of union. Only feelings that can be taken in and digested stay moderate.

This is a Latin quotation from Virgil's Aeneid, where Creusa's ghost is seen by Aeneas. The lines describe a person so overwhelmed by sudden fear and grief that she freezes, loses her strength, and can barely speak. Montaigne uses it to show how terror can strike the body and voice at once.

Montaigne lists several people who died from joy: a Roman woman whose son came home alive after the defeat at Cannae, the poet Sophocles, and the tyrant Dionysius. The bracketed note adds that Dionysius, by one account, drank so much at his feast that he fell seriously ill.

Montaigne gives two examples of people who died from sudden joy. Thalna, in Corsica, died on hearing that the Roman Senate had honoured him. Pope Leo X died of a fever after hearing that Milan had been taken, something he had longed for.

Montaigne recounts that the logician Diodorus died on the spot from shame. He had failed, before a large audience in his own school, to escape from a difficult argument put to him. Montaigne says he himself is not much prone to such violent passions.

Just as unused land fills with weeds unless it is planted with useful seed, and women can bring forth only shapeless lumps without a man's seed, Montaigne says an idle mind does not stay still. Without a fixed subject of study to hold it, the mind wanders into many wild fancies in the open field of imagination.

Montaigne quotes Latin verses to show a restless mind. Like light reflected off water and dancing across a ceiling, the mind darts everywhere and catches every foolish fancy, like a sick man's dreams. His point is that a soul without a fixed aim loses itself, since someone who lives everywhere lives nowhere.

Montaigne had retired to his house to rest his mind and let it wander freely, expecting it would now settle down. He finds instead that idleness keeps producing restless, changing thoughts, as the Latin quotation says: "Leisure always gives a restless mind."

My mind, left to itself, is like a runaway horse. It produces a stream of disordered fantasies, and Montaigne has begun writing them down to study their oddness and hope they will shame him into stopping.

Constancy does not mean refusing to protect yourself from danger or harm. Avoiding harm by any honest means is allowed and even praiseworthy. Constancy is mainly about bravely enduring the harms that cannot be avoided. So any awkward movement that blocks a blow is acceptable.

Montaigne notes that some warlike peoples treated retreat and flight as a useful tactic, so that their backs were more dangerous to enemies than their faces. He points out that Socrates, in Plato, mocked the idea that standing firm is the only form of courage, asking whether winning by giving ground could be called cowardice.

Montaigne describes how the Spartan foot soldiers, unable to break the Persian line at Plataea, pretended to flee. The Persians chased them, which split their large army apart, and the Spartans won the battle this way. Laches is the speaker who first admits this kind of retreat is acceptable for cavalry, then uses the Spartan example against him.

The Scythian king Idanthyrses answered Darius's taunt that he kept retreating and avoided battle. He said he was not afraid of Darius or anyone. His people had no fields, cities or houses to protect, so retreating was their normal way of fighting. If Darius wanted a fight, he could visit their ancient burial grounds.

Soldiers standing in line before enemy cannon should not leave their post to dodge the fire. Cannonballs move too fast to avoid, and men who ducks or sidestep out of fear are mocked by their comrades. The passage then turns to an example from the Emperor Charles V's campaign, which is not yet given.

In this episode from a siege, enemy commander the Marquis de Guast approaches Arles from behind a windmill. Men on a walkway spot him, and an artillery officer aims a cannon at him so accurately that he would have been hit if he had not stepped aside when the gun fired.

Montaigne tells of Lorenzo de' Medici, who ducked a cannon shot aimed at him during a siege, so the ball only grazed his head. He then says he does not think such dodging is done by careful thought or reasoning.

Montaigne is answering the idea that some soldiers in a sudden attack showed great skill in aiming. He says no one can judge their aim in such a moment, and that luck may have decided the outcome. He admits he himself flinches when a gunshot goes off unexpectedly, as do braver men he has seen.

The Stoics, a school of ancient Greek philosophy, did not claim their wise man would be untouched by sudden fears. He may tremble at thunder or a falling ruin and even turn pale, as a natural reaction. What matters is that his judgment stays sound and he does not agree to the fear.

Montaigne says that a frightened person who is not a philosopher is affected deeply. Fear reaches the mind itself, so the person judges and acts according to the fear. A Stoic wise man keeps his mind unmoved even while tears fall, as the Latin verse puts it. A Peripatetic sage still feels passions but controls them.

Montaigne says he does not know the hidden causes that make fear work in us. Still, he states that fear is a strange feeling, one that physicians say removes reason from its proper place faster than any other passion. He has seen many people go mad from fear, and even calm people are thrown into terrible confusion while it lasts.

Montaigne says that fear makes ordinary people see ghosts, werewolves and monsters. Even soldiers, who should be the least affected, often mistake sheep for armed troops, reeds for weapons, friends for enemies, and French white crosses for Spanish red ones.

An ensign on guard at Borgo San Pietro, during the sack of Rome by Bourbon's army, panicked at the first alarm. He ran out through a breach in the wall, straight toward the enemy, believing he was going back into the city. Only when Bourbon's men prepared to meet him did he come to his senses and see his mistake.

Montaigne describes two soldiers overcome by fear during a battle. One ran blindly out into the open field and then fled back through the same gap in the wall. The other, Captain Giulio's ensign (the flag-bearer), jumped out of a window with his flag and was at once cut down by the enemy.

Montaigne gives two examples of how fear can overwhelm people. In one siege, a gentleman was so frightened that his heart seemed to stop, and he fell dead in a gap in the wall without any wound. In another battle, two large groups panicked and ran in opposite directions, with one group running back to the place the other had just fled.

Fear sometimes gives speed, so that a person runs away quickly, and sometimes it holds a person in place so they cannot move. Montaigne gives the example of the Emperor Theophilus, who was so frozen with terror in a battle he lost that he could not flee. The Latin quote says fear is afraid even of the help that might save it.

Montaigne describes a ruler so frozen by fear that he does not respond until a commander shakes him awake and threatens to kill him, arguing that losing his life is better than losing his empire. He then says that fear is at its strongest when it drives a person into a desperate kind of bravery, after first stripping away any sense of duty or honour.

Ten thousand Roman foot soldiers, frightened and seeing no way to escape, charged straight into the main body of the Carthaginian army. They broke through and routed it with heavy slaughter. Their panic thus won them a way out at the cost that a glorious victory would have cost.

Fear, Montaigne says, is the thing he dreads most, because it overwhelms everything else. After Pompey was murdered before their eyes, his friends on the ship felt no grief at first. Their fear of pursuing ships made them think only of rowing away. Only once they were safe at Tyre did grief come out.

Fear can be worse than the thing feared. Soldiers who have only been beaten in a fight will go back into battle, but those who are truly afraid of the enemy will not even face him. People who dread losing their property, exile or freedom suffer constant anguish, while people who already suffer those losses often live cheerfully. Some who could not bear constant dread have killed themselves, showing that fear can be harder to endure than death.

Montaigne describes a kind of fear the Greeks called "panic." It comes without any visible cause, as if sent from heaven, and can strike whole nations or armies. He gives the example of Carthage, where the people attacked one another in a frenzy until they had calmed their gods with prayers and sacrifices.

Studying philosophy, Cicero said, means preparing to die. Montaigne gives two reasons. Study turns the mind away from the body, which is a kind of practice for death. Also, all wisdom and reasoning finally aim at teaching us not to fear death.

Montaigne argues that reason either serves only our contentment or is useless to us. He says every school of thought aims at pleasure, though they differ on the means, and that their arguments over this are only about words.

Montaigne says that the people he has in mind show more opposition and stubbornness than fits so holy a calling as philosophy. Still, whatever role a person takes on, he always adds some of himself to it.

Montaigne argues that even virtue aims at pleasure, though he means a deeper, sturdier kind than the word usually suggests. He says that if virtue brings the highest contentment, it does so because of virtue's help. This pleasure is more manly and serious, so he thinks it deserves the name pleasure more than the lesser pleasures that the word normally names.

Montaigne is comparing bodily pleasure with virtue. He says that bodily pleasure, if it deserves the name at all, should only be measured against virtue as an equal rival, not given first place. He argues that it brings more trouble than virtue does: it is shorter-lived and weaker, it demands sleeplessness, fasting and toil, and it brings painful feelings and a dull weariness afterward, so that it is as hard to bear as the strictest penance.

Montaigne says that the hardships of virtue do not make it less pleasant, nor do they make it harsh or out of reach. They give it more worth and make its divine pleasure keener. Someone who weighs the cost of virtue against its reward does not understand its value and cannot use it.

Those who say that philosophy is hard to reach but pleasant once reached are, in effect, saying it is never enjoyable. People can only strive toward it and never fully possess it. Montaigne argues they are wrong: the pursuit itself is pleasant, because the striving shares in the nature of what is sought.

Montaigne says that the happiness and blessedness found in virtue shine through everything connected to it, all the way to its outer edges and its very entrance. In other words, virtue's joy is present in every part of it, including the first steps toward it.

Contempt of death, which Montaigne counts among virtue's greatest benefits, makes life calm and easy. It gives a clean and pleasant enjoyment of living, without which no other pleasure would last. For this reason, all the moral rules come together on this one point.

Montaigne says that philosophers all teach people to despise pain, poverty and other hardships. But they do not stress these lessons as much, because most people never face extreme poverty, and some never suffer illness at all. As an example he names Xenophilus the musician, who lived 106 years in good health.

Death cannot be avoided, so a person who fears it has no relief from that fear. Montaigne says death can end other troubles whenever we choose, but it always stays close, like the rock hanging over Tantalus in the old myth, and no escape from it exists.

Montaigne describes condemned criminals being taken back to the place of their crime, with fine food and music along the way. He asks whether they could enjoy any of it, since the death waiting at the end of the journey would spoil their taste for every pleasure.

Death is the end toward which all human life moves, so fear of it would stop us from taking any step forward. Ordinary people try to avoid the thought of death, which Montaigne calls a brutish blindness. He says this is like trying to bridle a donkey by its tail, and he quotes a Latin line about someone who walks backward.

People are so afraid of the word death that many avoid even saying it. As a result, they do not make their wills until the doctor has given up on them, and then they make them in fear, so their judgment is poor.

The Romans avoided the harsh word "death" by using softer phrases, such as "he has lived" or "he has ceased to live." Even past tense mention of life seemed comforting to them. The French phrase "the late" comes from this habit, and the author suggests that the time we have lived is worth what we paid for it.

Montaigne says he was born in February 1533 and is now nearly thirty-nine, and he expects to live about as many more years. He calls it foolish to worry about something so far off. He adds that young and old die on the same terms, so death can come at any age.

Everyone who dies seems to have been just starting out, and even very old people think they have many good years left. Montaigne tells the reader that no one can be sure how long life will last. By the usual course of things, a person who has reached an old age has already lived longer than most people do.

Montaigne argues that many famous people died young, not in old age. He points to Jesus and Alexander the Great, who both died at about thirty-three, and says death can come at any time. The closing Latin line says that no one can ever be fully careful against what each person might fear, hour by hour.

Montaigne lists deaths that no one could have expected. A duke of Brittany was crushed in a crowd at a papal entry into Lyons, one French king was killed in a jousting contest, and an earlier ancestor died after being knocked over by a hog. Death can come from ordinary or unlikely causes.

Montaigne lists men who died from small, chance accidents: a tortoise dropped by an eagle, a grape stone, a comb scratch, a stumble at a doorstep, and a bump against a door. The point is that death can come from trifles that no one could guard against.

Montaigne lists men who died in the middle of their own work or pleasures. Gallus, a Roman lawyer, died between a woman's thighs; the judge Bebius died while postponing a case for eight days; the physician Caius Julius died while treating a patient's eyes. The point is that death can come at any moment, even during ordinary activity.

A young man named Martin was hit on the head by a tennis ball, just above the ear. He showed no sign of injury, so he carried on without resting, but he died within five or six hours from bleeding in the brain caused by the blow.

Montaigne asks how anyone can avoid thinking about death, since examples of it appear every day. He says he would gladly hide from death by any means, even crawling under a calf's skin, and simply wants to spend his time comfortably, choosing whatever pleasures help with that, however unimpressive they look.

Montaigne says it is foolish to live as if death were never thought about. People go on with ordinary pleasures and never mention death. But when death strikes themselves or those they love, unready, they are overcome with torment and despair. So a person must prepare for death early.

Montaigne argues that ignoring death is a bad bargain, because death cannot be avoided by running away or by hiding. Even a coward who flees will be caught, and a man in full armour will be dragged out by death. The Latin lines are quotations from classical poets making this same point.

Montaigne advises that we should get used to the idea of death so it no longer seems strange or frightening. We should think about it often, imagining it in many forms, such as a fall or a small injury, and tell ourselves, "What if this were death itself?" Doing so builds our courage.

Montaigne says that even while enjoying parties and feasts, people should keep their own mortality in mind and notice how such pleasures lead toward death. He gives the example of the Egyptians, who brought a dried skeleton into their feasts as a reminder to guests. The Latin quotation adds that each day may be your last, and the hour you do not expect may arrive.

Learning to face death frees a person from being controlled by others, because someone who is not afraid of losing life has nothing to fear from those who hold power over him. Montaigne illustrates this with the Roman general Paulus Aemilius, who refused a captured king's plea to spare him from being paraded in a triumph, telling him to make that request to himself.

Montaigne says that good results need natural ability, since effort alone rarely achieves much. He describes himself as naturally thoughtful rather than gloomy, and says he has often dwelt on thoughts of death, even in the carefree years of his youth.

Montaigne describes being at a social gathering with ladies and games while thinking about a friend who died of a sudden fever soon after leaving such a party, his mind full of light pleasures. He realizes that the same fate could await him, and the Latin quotation says that what is past cannot be recalled.

Montaigne says that thoughts of death did not trouble him much. At first such thoughts sting, but repeated thinking makes them familiar. He adds that he has always doubted how long his life will last, and that his good health does not make him expect a long life, nor does illness make him expect a short one.

Montaigne says that death can come at any moment, so doing a task today rather than tomorrow makes sense. Dangers do little to bring death closer, since many other threats always hang over us. Healthy people, sailors, soldiers and those sitting safely at home are all about equally close to death. The Latin quotation means no one is more fragile than another, and no one can be sure of tomorrow.

Montaigne says that a friend found a note in his notebook about something he planned to do after his death. He explains that he wrote it down at once, even though he was only a league from home and in good spirits, because he was not sure he would live to get back.

Montaigne says that because he constantly thinks about his own thoughts and keeps to his own concerns, he is always as ready for death as he can be. Death can bring nothing he has not already expected. He adds that people should always be ready to leave, and above all should have no business left with anyone but themselves.

Some people, facing death, grieve over specific losses: a victory they will miss, a daughter not yet married, children not yet raised, a wife or a son whose company they will lose. Each man regrets the thing that matters most to him.

Montaigne says he is ready to die whenever God wishes, without regret. He has cut his ties with worldly affairs and expects to leave life completely, letting go of every concern. He adds two Latin quotations about people whose lives end suddenly, leaving their work and rewards unfinished.

Do not plan projects that take so long to finish, or at least do not feel such eager longing to see them completed. Humans are born to act, and Montaigne quotes a Latin line meaning "When I die, I want to be released in the middle of my work."

Montaigne says he wants a person to keep busy and make the most of life's tasks for as long as possible, so that death finds him still working on ordinary things like planting cabbages. He describes a dying man who regretted only that he could not finish his history book, which had reached only the fifteenth or sixteenth king. The Latin quotation says that the dying do not add this, that no single desire for such things remains.

Montaigne says that people first placed burial grounds next to churches and in busy parts of town. The aim was to make ordinary people, women and children used to the sight of dead bodies, so they would not be frightened by them. Constant sight of graves was also meant to remind people how fragile human life is.

The Latin is a quotation from the Roman poet Lucan, and it describes a past custom: men used to enliven their feasts with killing, mixing grim sights of gladiators fighting with swords into the meal. Often the dying fell over the cups, and the tables were splashed with plenty of blood.

Montaigne says he keeps the thought of death constantly in his mind and often on his lips. He is especially curious about how other people die, including their words, looks and behaviour, and he reads more eagerly about those moments in history than anything else.

Montaigne says that if he wrote books, he would make a collection of accounts of how various men died, with commentary. Such a collection would teach people how to die and, in the same way, how to live. He notes that Dicarchus made a similar work, but for a different and less useful purpose.

Someone may argue that the pain and terror of dying are so great that even the best fighter would be lost when the moment comes. Montaigne replies that thinking about death in advance is still a great help, since it lets a person reach the end calmly. He also says nature helps: a sudden death leaves no time to fear, and a slow illness gradually brings a loss of interest in life.

Montaigne says he finds it harder to accept the idea of dying when he is healthy than when he is sick with fever. The less he enjoys the good things of life, the less frightening death seems to him. He hopes that as he moves away from health and nearer to death, he will more easily give up one for the other.

Montaigne says that when he is well, he imagines illness as far worse than it feels when he actually has it. Healthy, he magnifies its troubles by about half. He hopes death will turn out the same way: less frightening up close than it looks from a distance.

Montaigne points out that we rarely notice our bodies getting weaker day by day, because nature hides the loss from us. He asks what strength an old man keeps from his youth, and quotes a Latin line lamenting how little of life is left to the aged.

Caesar, asked by an old, worn-out soldier for leave to kill himself, replied with a joke: the soldier must think he is still alive. The point is that a man so frail is already close to death, so he has no need to end his own life.

Montaigne says that if old age came suddenly, people could not bear it. Instead, nature brings it on slowly, step by step, so we barely notice. Our youth dies within us this way without our feeling the blow, and he calls this a harder death than the final decline of an old, worn-out body.

The fall from a troubled life into no life at all is less hard than the fall from a lively, flourishing life into a painful one. So the soul must be kept upright and firm against death, since it can never be at rest while it fears death.

The passage says that a soul which has reached a settled state can claim it is free from unrest, anxiety, fear and any other disturbance. The writer calls this boast almost beyond human nature. He supports the claim with a Latin verse from the Roman poet Horace, which says that a tyrant's threatening stare, the storm wind over the Adriatic, and Jupiter's thunderbolt cannot shake such a mind.

Philosophy, in Montaigne's view, frees a person from fear and desire. Once a person has learned to face death, they become master of their lusts, passions, shame, poverty and the other blows of fortune. This inner freedom, he says, lets them defy violence and injustice and scorn prison and chains. The Latin quotation, from Horace, has a speaker who says that death will free him when he chooses, and that death is the final limit of all things.

Montaigne says that religion rests on contempt for life, and that reason supports this. Fearing death is pointless, since a lost life cannot be mourned, and it is worse to fear every kind of death than to face one death once. He adds that death is inevitable, so it hardly matters when it comes. He ends with Socrates' reply to the news of his sentence: nature has sentenced them too.

Worrying about death is foolish, Montaigne argues, since death ends all troubles. Just as we did not exist before birth and feel no loss over that, we will not exist after death and should not mourn the time we will miss. He concludes that death is only the start of another life.

Death is a single event that cannot be suffered twice, so it is not reasonable to fear for a long time something that will be over quickly. Once a person is dead, a long life and a short one are the same, because time means nothing to someone who no longer exists.

Aristotle reports tiny creatures on the river Hypanis that live only a day, so a life that is short to us can seem enormous or tiny depending on the measure. Montaigne says that our own lives, compared with eternity or with long-lived mountains, rivers, stars and trees, are just as laughably brief.

Death is part of human life from the start, so trying to avoid it means avoiding yourself. Life and death are mixed together in the very being you have, and each day of life moves you one step closer to the grave.

Every moment of life uses up time and moves us toward death, so living is itself a slow dying. Death is not only the final end but a process that runs through the whole of life. If you have gained what life offers, you should be content and leave.

If you have not used your life well, and it has done you little good, then there is little reason to mind losing it or to want more of it. The Latin quotation, from the poet Lucretius, asks why one would seek to add more time that will only be wasted and lost. Word count: about 50.

Life itself is neither good nor bad; it becomes good or bad depending on how a person lives it. Any single day holds everything life offers, since all days are alike, with the same sun, moon and stars that earlier generations saw and later ones will see.

Montaigne says that even if his life ends soon, nothing new will happen in it. The year, like his life, only runs through the same stages again and again. He has no fresh entertainments to offer, because all things are always the same.

Everyone shares the same fate, so no one has cause to complain of being included in it. Living longer does not change the total time a person spends dead, since that time is the same whether one dies young or old. The Latin quotation says the same: however many ages a person lives, eternal death remains.

Death is nothing to us, the passage says, whether we are alive or dead. While we live, we still exist; once dead, we no longer do. The time before we were born was no concern of ours either, and the time after our death will be no concern of ours.

Life is complete wherever it ends, because what matters is how time is used, not how long one lives. A person can live many years and still have lived little. The passage also says that every journey has an end, and that everyone walks the same road toward death. The Latin line at the end, "Omnia te, vita perfuncta, sequentur," means "All things will follow you once life is finished."

Death comes to everyone and everything at the same time. Montaigne asks whether the whole world is not doing the same dance of life and ageing that the reader is doing, and notes that thousands of people and creatures die at the very moment the reader dies. The Latin quotation says that no night or dawn passes without wailing of the newborn mixed with mourning for the dead.

Since death cannot be avoided, there is no sense in trying to escape it. Many people have been glad to die, freed from great suffering, and no one has been known to regret dying. So it is foolish to fear or condemn something no one has experienced. The speaker also asks whether we have wronged the person complaining, or whether that person has any right to govern us.

A short life is still a whole life, just as a small man is still a full man. Montaigne says that a life is not judged by its length. He also argues that endless life would be harder to bear than the life people have, and that without death, people would blame the one who gave it to them.

The speaker, a voice presented as Nature addressing humans, says he mixed bitterness into life so that people would not chase it greedily, and would not come to hate life or fear death. He tells how he taught the sage Thales that living and dying are equally matched. When asked why he did not then die, Thales answered that it made no difference to him.

Death is not a special force that works against life. The elements that sustain life are no more the cause of death than of life, and the last day adds no more to dying than any earlier day. Every day moves a person toward death, and the final day only reaches it.

Montaigne asks why death seems less frightening on the battlefield, whether in oneself or in others, than at home. He also notes that ordinary people often face death more calmly than those of higher rank, even though death is the same everywhere.

Montaigne says that the frightening part of dying is mostly the show around it, not death itself. The sickroom fills with mourning family, tearful servants, doctors and priests, and dim candlelit surroundings, so that a dying person seems already buried.

Montaigne says that fear of death comes from the disguise we put on it, much as children fear a familiar person wearing a mask. Remove the mask, and underneath is the same death that a servant or chambermaid faced recently, without any fear. He adds that a sudden death is fortunate, because it leaves no time for preparing such show.

Montaigne compares his writing to a painter's work. The painter puts his best effort into a carefully made picture in the centre of a wall, and fills the empty space around it with grotesques, which are odd, fantastic shapes. Montaigne asks whether his own scribbled essays are anything more than such grotesques: bodies made of mixed parts, with no fixed shape or order.

Montaigne says he cannot match the painter's skill in the main part of his work, so he will instead include a discourse by his friend Étienne de La Boétie. He calls it "Voluntary Servitude," which others have named "Le contr'un" (Against One), and says La Boétie wrote it when he was not yet eighteen.

This is a note about a short essay written by a friend of Montaigne, La Boétie, which was meant as an attack on tyrants. The note says the essay has been much praised by learned readers for its fine writing, but that its author could have done much better.

Montaigne says that if his dear friend Étienne de La Boétie had written down his thoughts in his mature years, as Montaigne was now doing, the result would have been remarkable and close to the finest works of ancient times. He adds that no one he knew matched La Boétie in natural talent.

Montaigne is speaking of his friend Étienne de La Boétie, who left behind only one finished work, a treatise, and some notes on the January edict of 1562. That edict allowed the Huguenots, French Protestants, to practise their religion in public. Montaigne says the notes may appear elsewhere.

Montaigne says that his dying friend, La Boétie, left him his library and papers, and that he published only one small book of the friend's writings. He owes that book a personal debt, because it first introduced him to the friend, long before they met.

Montaigne describes his friendship with Étienne de La Boétie, which began the moment they first heard of each other's names and lasted as long as God allowed. He says such a perfect friendship is rare in history and absent in his own age, and that it takes so many conditions to form that fortune may produce one only once in three centuries.

Montaigne says that true friendship is at its most perfect when it is not mixed with any other motive. Friendships based on pleasure, profit or personal interest are less noble and less true, the more such motives they include. The four traditional kinds of friendship, natural, social, hospitable and sexual, do not make a true friendship on their own or together.

Montaigne says that the bond between children and parents is mainly respect, not friendship. The great difference in age and rank blocks the open sharing that friendship needs. He adds that parents cannot fully share their private thoughts with children, and children cannot properly advise or rebuke their parents. He then starts an example of countries where children killed their fathers, which he uses to show the limits of such a bond.

Montaigne describes cases where fathers killed their children, or where people's hopes depended on others dying, so that family ties gave way to self-interest. He also tells of the philosopher Aristippus, who, when asked about his duty of love to his children, spat and said they came from him just as spit and lice do.

Montaigne says that calling someone "brother" sounds fine, but real brothers often lose the bond. Shared money, divided inheritances, and pursuing the same career make them compete and get in each other's way.

Montaigne asks why family ties should always produce true friendship, since a father, son or brother may have a very different character and may even be foolish or bad-tempered. He adds that bonds set by law and nature leave less room for our own free choice, which is the source of real friendship. The passage breaks off before finishing this thought.

Montaigne says that friendship and family affection are a different thing from love between a man and a woman. He gives his own father as an example of close family love, and he says that the love for women is his own choice and not to be ranked with the others. He then begins to speak of its fire, quoting Latin lines about love that mixes bitterness with cares.

Montaigne contrasts love with friendship. Love is a sharp, eager feeling that seizes only one part of a person, and it swings between fits and calms. Friendship is a steady, even warmth felt through the whole self. He adds that love is a desire for what runs away, like a hunter chasing a hare, who stops caring once he catches it.

Montaigne contrasts two kinds of love. Desire that aims only at physical possession ends once it is satisfied, because it is fleshly and wears out. True friendship works the other way: it grows stronger the more it is shared, since it is spiritual and refines the soul through practice.

Montaigne says that, in his younger years, he also felt other, shorter-lived affections besides his great friendship. He always knew the two apart and never set them side by side as equals. The true friendship stayed high above, while the lesser feelings flew far lower.

Montaigne says marriage is a contract where entering is free but staying is forced, and it is often made for other purposes. This brings many complications that can break a lively affection. Friendship, by contrast, has no dealings with anything except itself.

Montaigne claims that women generally lack the ability to hold up the conversation and sharing of thought that a close friendship needs. He also says they do not seem to have the steadiness of mind to endure the strains of such a lasting bond.

Montaigne says that a friendship would be fuller and more perfect if it joined the body as well as the soul, but he adds that no example of women reaching this kind of perfection exists. He also notes that the ancient schools of thought agreed in excluding women from such friendship altogether.

Montaigne rejects the Greek custom of love between an older man and a younger male. He says that its unequal ages and roles could never produce the perfect union of friendship he is describing. He quotes Cicero to ask why no one loves an ugly youth or a handsome old man, which shows that true friendship is not about looks or age.

Montaigne says that the Academy (Plato's school) describes early passionate love as based on outward beauty, a false image of physical generation. Such love cannot rest on the soul, because a young person's soul has not yet developed or matured.

In Montaigne's account, a lover's passion takes different forms depending on the person. A lowly man tries to win the beloved with expensive gifts and favours. A nobler man instead offers lessons in virtue, such as duty to religion, law and country, and shows courage, wisdom and justice, hoping to win love through the beauty of his soul rather than his fading body.

In Montaigne's account of Greek-style love between men, the lover pursues the beloved in the hope of a meeting of minds. The beloved, who must judge the inner beauty, then desires a spiritual union, with spiritual beauty as the main thing and physical beauty as secondary. For the lover it is the other way round.

Montaigne reports that the Greeks who wrote on this subject held that the beloved, not the lover, was the more honoured partner, since the gods also favoured him. They criticise the poet Aeschylus for making Achilles the lover in his story of Achilles and Patroclus. Good results were said to come from a friendship in which the worthier partner led.

Montaigne says that the love between men, as the Greeks understood it, was seen as a source of strength for states and a guard of liberty and justice, with the loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton as examples. Such love was thought sacred, and only tyrants and the common people opposed it. Its best outcome was friendship, which fits the Stoic definition of love as an attempt to make friends through beauty.

Montaigne says that ordinary friendships are just acquaintances or convenient connections that let some small contact pass between two minds. True friendship, by contrast, merges two people so completely that no join can be seen. Asked why he loved his friend, he can only answer: because it was he, because it was I.

The writer says that a friendship between him and another man began through a force he cannot fully explain, which he thinks was arranged by heaven. They had heard of each other before meeting, and those reports drew them together more than reason would suggest. When they first met at a city banquet, they quickly became close and stayed that way.

Montaigne says his friend, in a Latin satire, excused how quickly their friendship became close. Since they were already grown men and expected to have only a short time together, they had no time to waste on the slow, cautious steps of ordinary friendships. He adds that this friendship is unlike others: it refers only to itself, with no single reason behind it.

Montaigne describes a bond of friendship so complete that his will and his friend's will merged. Each drew the other's will into itself, so that nothing was kept back as either his own or the other's. He is speaking of Étienne de La Boétie.

Laelius asks Blosius, a close friend of the rebel Tiberius Gracchus, how far he would go for him. Blosius says he would do anything, even burn the temples if asked. Montaigne uses this exchange to show how far a friend's loyalty could go.

Montaigne is saying that even if Blossius was a perfect friend to Gracchus, he did not need to admit so boldly to the consuls that he would have obeyed Gracchus's wishes. He could have kept his confidence in Gracchus's character without giving that answer. He adds that those who call the answer seditious have misunderstood its meaning.

Blosius, a friend of Tiberius Gracchus, is asked how far he would have gone for him. The passage says the two men were bound more by friendship than by loyalty to Rome, and that each held the other's will. Blosius's answer, given on the assumption that their bond was guided by virtue and reason, was fitting.

Montaigne says that if a friend's action went wrong, the two were no true friends, to each other or to themselves. He compares this to a hypothetical question about killing one's daughter: saying "I would" does not mean consent, because he trusts his own will and his friend's will completely.

Montaigne says that no speech could make him doubt his friend's intentions, and that he could always see the reason behind any of his friend's actions at once. The two men had bonded so closely, and had opened their hearts so fully to each other, that he knew his friend's mind as well as his own.

Montaigne warns that ordinary friendships are not as firm as the close bond he has just described, so they must be handled carefully. He quotes the saying of Chilo: love a friend as if he might one day become an enemy, and treat an enemy as if he might one day become a friend.

Montaigne says that the advice he has just mentioned is bad for perfect friendship but sound for ordinary friendships. He adds that in perfect friendship, gifts, favours and benefits, which hold other friendships together, are not even worth mentioning, because the friends' wills agree.

Montaigne says that true friends feel no sense of owing each other anything, just as a person does not feel indebted to himself for help he gives himself. Because the friendship is complete, they drop words that suggest division, such as benefits, obligation, thanks and entreaty.

In true friendship, two people share everything, so neither can lend or give anything to the other. Montaigne cites Aristotle's idea that such friends are one soul in two bodies. Lawgivers use the same logic to forbid gifts between husband and wife, since all their goods already belong to both.

In true friendship, the one who lets the other help him is the generous one, since he gives his friend the pleasure of doing what that friend most wants. Diogenes said he was asking his friends for money back, not begging for it.

Eudamidas, a poor Corinthian, left his two rich friends the task of supporting his mother and marrying off his daughter. If one friend died, the other would take his place. People who heard the will laughed at it, but the two friends were happy to accept it.

Areteus, one of three friends, was left alone to care for the mother of his friend Eudamidas, who had died, and for the family of another friend, Charixenus, who died within five days. He looked after the old woman with great care. He then split his five talents of wealth between the two dead men's daughters, giving each two and a half, and married both girls on the same day.

Montaigne argues that perfect friendship cannot be shared among many people. A person gives himself so completely to one friend that nothing is left over for others, and he wishes he had several souls to give. Ordinary friendships, however, can be divided among several people.

Montaigne says that one person can love another for many different reasons, such as beauty, kindness or family feeling. True friendship, however, takes over the whole soul and rules it completely, so it cannot share that place with a second friend. He asks, as an example, which of two friends calling for help you would go to, and how you could serve both if they needed opposite things.

Montaigne asks what a person should do if a friend asks him to keep a secret that the friend needs to know. His answer is that a close friendship cancels other promises. He can share a secret with his friend without breaking his oath, because the friend is treated as part of himself, not as an outsider. He adds that doubling oneself is already miraculous, and that talk of tripling is nonsense.

Montaigne says that a friend cannot be loved equally by two people, since true friendship is single and one of a kind, and it is very hard to find even one such friend. He then notes that Eudamidas, in his will, left his friends the favour of helping him in his need.

Montaigne says that a generous friend lets the other person do him a favour, which shows friendship more clearly than the gift itself. He admires a young soldier who, when Cyrus asked if he would trade his prize-winning horse for a kingdom, refused.

A man says he would give a great deal to have a true friend, if he could find someone worthy of such a bond. The author agrees that the wording "could I find" is apt. Many people are fit for casual acquaintance, but a true friend must be trusted completely, so that person's character must be thoroughly sound.

In relationships based on only one purpose, we need to consider only the flaws that affect that purpose. Montaigne says a doctor's or lawyer's religion does not matter to him, because it has nothing to do with the services they provide, and he feels the same about his servants.

Montaigne says he judges servants by their skill, not their private morals. He hires a footman for diligence rather than chastity, and a muleteer or cook for strength or cooking, not for gambling or swearing. He does not claim to tell others how to run their households; he only describes his own way, with a Latin saying meaning "this is my custom; you do as the job requires."

Montaigne says he prefers different qualities for different settings: wit over learning at the dinner table, beauty over goodness in bed, and skill in speaking in conversation, whether or not the speaker is sincere. He adds the story of a man caught playing on a hobby-horse with his children, who asked the observer to keep quiet until he became a father himself, since fatherly feeling would make him a fairer judge.

Montaigne says he wishes he could talk with people who have known the kind of friendship he describes, but he doubts he will find any, since such friendship is rare. He also finds the ancient writings on friendship dull next to what he feels, and he thinks real friendship achieves more than the teachings of philosophy.

Montaigne says that a man who had even a small share of friendship, as Menander put it, was lucky. He compares his own calm life with the four years he spent with a dear friend, and finds the rest of his life worth little. Since losing that friend, his days have felt like a dark, dull night.

The speaker has lived in grief since his friend died. Even the pleasures that come to him make his sorrow worse, because the two were so close that he feels only half of himself now. He feels he is cheating his dead friend by still going on living.

Montaigne says that he misses his dead friend in everything he does or imagines, and he believes the friend would have missed him too. He adds that the friend was far better than him in virtue and in the duties of friendship. The Latin lines, quoted from Horace, express the same grief: if half of his soul has gone early, why should the other half stay behind?

Montaigne quotes a Latin lament, written by a grieving friend about his dead brother. The speaker says that with his brother's death all his joy has died, and that he will never see him again, but he will always love him.
Montaigne does not report what the boy said. Editions differ on his age: eighteen, the age at which La Boetie wrote "Servitude Volontaire", or sixteen, which the editor judges correct.

Montaigne says he has left out a certain work from this chapter. Others have published it with bad intent, trying to overturn the government, and have mixed it with their own writing. He does not say the work itself is bad; his objection is to how it has been used.

Montaigne says that the essay he is discussing (by Étienne de La Boétie) was written when its author was a boy, as a school exercise on a familiar topic. He adds that the author truly believed what he wrote, since he was too honest to lie even in jest. He also notes that the author would have preferred to be born in Venice rather than in Sarlat, his small French hometown.

The passage describes a man, Étienne de La Boétie, whose main principle was to obey the laws of the country he was born in. He loved his homeland and opposed uprisings and political upheaval in his time. He would rather calm civil unrest than stir it up, and his outlook belonged to an earlier, better age.
Montaigne is saying that, after a serious piece, he will offer a second one in a lighter, more cheerful mood. He adds that it was written by the same author and at the same age.

Montaigne says that people can spoil good things by holding them too tightly or wanting them too intensely, so that virtue itself can turn into a vice. He rejects the claim that virtue can never be excessive, calling it a mere play on words. The Latin quotation says that a wise man would be called mad, and a just man unjust, if they sought virtue itself beyond what is enough.
Montaigne says a person can love virtue too much and be excessive even in doing something right. He supports this with a line from the Bible: do not be wiser than you should, but be wisely moderate.

This is an editor's note, not Montaigne's own words. It explains that Montaigne probably meant King Henry III of France. It then gives a joke by Pope Sixtus V: the king did everything possible to act like a monk, and the pope did everything possible not to be one.

Montaigne says he prefers calm, moderate characters. Zeal that goes beyond measure, even when it is aimed at something good and causes no harm, surprises him so much that he struggles to find a name for it.

Pausanias, a Spartan leader, fled into Minerva's temple to escape arrest, and the temple's sanctuary protected him from being dragged out. His mother came, said nothing, and left a brick on the threshold before going home. Montaigne presents this silent act as a hint of the punishment to come.

The Spartans walled up the gate of a temple, which left Pausanias to starve inside. Montaigne cites this as an example of a story he has been told, one that reports the Spartans took the hint from Pausanias's mother. Pausanias was a Spartan commander who died this way.

This is a footnote-style note from Montaigne's essay, which names Pausanias's mother and reports a story that she laid the first stone when the gates of a chapel were walled up. Pausanias had taken refuge there. The note cites a commentator on the historian Thucydides and a later editor, Coste, as its sources.

Montaigne says that two examples of harsh justice, a mother who helped bring about her son's death and a Roman dictator who had his own son executed for fighting bravely but without orders, seem to him strange rather than fair. He would not advise or choose to follow such a severe virtue, because it costs too much.

Montaigne reports a Roman story about a commander who may have had his son killed for disobeying orders in battle. Livy doubts it is true, since the Roman writers did not record that this commander was branded with the shame that Titus Manlius later received for the same kind of act. Manlius's name became a byword for harsh orders, which Livy says were both terrible at the time and a bad example for later generations.

This is a note, not Montaigne's own argument. It is an editor's remark, quoted from Coste, that questions an earlier claim about Posthumius. The note says that Livy suggests a harsh command might have been named after Posthumius, and that Valerius Maximus and Diodorus of Sicily report that Posthumius had his own son put to death.

Shooting too high and shooting too low both miss the target, and looking up at a bright light troubles the eyes as much as looking down into a deep pit. Montaigne adds that Callicles, in Plato, warns that philosophy becomes harmful when pursued too far, and that it is only useful and pleasant when kept within limits.

Montaigne says that excess of a certain kind (here, excessive subtlety or cleverness, which he calls "impertinent") makes a man brutish, scornful of religion and law, unfit for society, pleasure and public duties, and open to insult. In excess it takes away natural freedom and pulls us off the plain path nature laid out.

Montaigne notes that the love between husband and wife is lawful, yet theology still limits it. He recalls that Thomas Aquinas forbade marriages within the banned degrees of kinship, partly because a husband's love could become excessive if it were doubled by family affection. Such extra love, Aquinas reasoned, could carry the husband beyond reason.

Montaigne says that moral philosophy and religious teaching claim authority over every part of human life, even the most private. He adds a sharp remark: women show their bodies freely for pleasure but are shy about medical examination. The passage breaks off before he finishes his point.

Montaigne says that husbands who are too eager in marital relations should learn that excessive pleasure in marriage is blameworthy, just as improper behaviour outside it is. He argues that the wild positions and tricks that passion suggests are both shameful and harmful when used on wives. He adds that wives can learn such boldness from others, since they are willing enough already, and that he himself kept to plain, simple ways.

Montaigne says marriage is a sacred bond, so the pleasure in it should be calm, serious and restrained. He notes that since the main purpose of marriage is having children, some ask whether it is lawful to be intimate with a wife who can no longer conceive or is already pregnant. Plato, he reports, called such intimacy murder.

Montaigne notes that some peoples avoid sexual relations with pregnant women, and some also avoid them during menstruation. He cites Zenobia, a queen who received her husband only once and then waited until after the birth before taking him again, which he admires as a sign of self-restraint.

Montaigne retells a story Plato borrowed: Jupiter is so eager for his wife that he throws her to the floor before they reach the couch. In the heat of the moment he forgets the important decisions he had just made with the other gods, and he boasts afterward that the encounter was as good as the first time he took her virginity, unknown to their parents.

Persian kings sent their wives away once heavy drinking and pleasure began, and brought in other women instead, because they did not owe their wives that kind of respect. The passage then states the general point that not every pleasure is fitting for every kind of person.

Montaigne gives two examples of public men held to a stricter standard than ordinary people. Epaminondas refused a favour to Pelopidas's request but granted it at once to a servant girl, saying it suited her, not a captain. Pericles rebuked the poet Sophocles, his fellow praetor, for admiring a handsome boy, saying a magistrate must keep his eyes chaste as well as his hands.

Aelius Verus, the emperor, defended his affairs with other women by saying that marriage is a dignified bond, not a means of indulging lust. Montaigne also praises a wife who left her husband rather than submit to his excessive demands. His closing point is that even lawful pleasures become wrong when taken to excess.

Montaigne says that people are naturally unable to enjoy any pleasure fully and without mixture. Yet they still invent rules and teachings that cut down even the little enjoyment they have. He adds a Latin line saying people make their own misfortunes worse by art, meaning by skill and learning.

Human wisdom misuses its skill when it takes away the pleasures that are naturally ours, just as it uses that skill well when it disguises the troubles of life to ease them. Montaigne says he would have chosen a more natural way, one that is both convenient and good.

Montaigne says that doctors of the body and of the soul seem to agree that the only cure for illness of either kind is suffering. For this reason, practices such as fasting, sleepless nights, hair shirts, exile, lifelong imprisonment and whipping have been adopted, and they are meant to hurt.

The story is about Gallio, who was exiled to the island of Lesbos as a punishment. Word reached Rome that he was enjoying himself there, so the punishment was not working. The Senate therefore called him back and ordered him to stay confined in his own house, so the punishment would match how he actually felt.

Montaigne says that a medicine or a fasting rule works only when it is unpleasant to the person taking it. If a man enjoys fasting or prefers fish, the rule does him no good. Likewise, a person who eats rhubarb as if it were buttered turnips gets no cure from it.

Montaigne compares a belief he has just described to the ancient idea that killing people can please the gods and nature. He notes that this idea was once common in all religions. As an example from his own fathers' time, he cites Sultan Amurath, who sacrificed six hundred young Greeks at the taking of the Isthmus to atone for his father's sins.

In the newly discovered lands of Montaigne's time, the people practise cruel rites as a common custom. Their idols are stained with human blood, and their victims are burned alive, have their hearts torn out, or are flayed, with the skins used as clothing.

Montaigne is describing people who were to be sacrificed. Before their deaths, the victims, including old people, women and children, went around begging for alms for the offering, then gave themselves up to be killed while singing and dancing with onlookers.

The Mexican king's envoys told Cortez how powerful their ruler was: thirty vassals, each able to raise a hundred thousand fighting men, and a capital that was the finest under the sun. They ended by saying that he had to sacrifice fifty thousand men to the gods every year.

Montaigne reports that a ruler kept up a constant war with strong neighbouring peoples. The aim was partly to train his young men and partly to get prisoners to sacrifice. In one town, fifty men were sacrificed at once to welcome Cortez, the Spanish conquistador.

Some people defeated by a conqueror sent messengers to ask for peace. They offered him three kinds of gifts, each matched to a possible nature: human victims if he was a fierce god who eats flesh, incense if he was a kindly god, and fruit and fowl if he was merely a man.

Montaigne sets aside the old debate between the active and the solitary life. He challenges men in public office to admit honestly that they seek titles, posts and the bustle of public life for their own gain, not for the public good, despite claiming otherwise.

Montaigne argues that ambitious people, who pursue power and success by corrupt means, show that their goals cannot be good. He says ambition itself gives us a taste of solitude, since it avoids company and seeks room to move alone. He adds that most people are bad, quoting the Preacher that good people are few, as rare as the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the Nile.

Being among many people is risky, because bad company spreads bad behavior. A person is left with two poor choices: copy the wrong-doers, or turn against them. Sailors are right to avoid taking on dissolute or blasphemous shipmates, since such company brings misfortune.

Bias, a wise man of ancient Greece, told people praying to the gods during a storm to speak quietly so the gods would not learn they were there with him. Albuquerque, a Portuguese governor in India, carried a young boy on his shoulders during a shipwreck danger, hoping the child's innocence would protect them both and win divine favour.

A wise man can be content even in a crowded palace, but if he may choose, he would rather avoid the crowd and be alone. He wants to be rid of vice altogether, not fight it in other people. Charondas, an ancient law-giver, punished people who knowingly kept bad company.

Montaigne says people are both unsociable and sociable: unsociable through their vice, sociable by their nature. He thinks Antisthenes gave a weak reply to the charge of keeping bad company. Antisthenes compared this to physicians who live among the sick, but Montaigne says constant exposure to disease harms the physicians too.

Montaigne says that people who withdraw from public affairs often just swap one kind of busy work for another. Running a household can be as troublesome as running a kingdom, and a worried mind stays in disorder wherever it is. Leaving the court or the market does not remove life's main troubles.

Even monks in their cloisters, philosophers in their schools, and hermits in deserts and caves cannot escape their troubles of mind. Montaigne illustrates this with Socrates' remark that a man gained nothing from travel because he took himself along with him.
