Moving away from others does not cure a troubled mind by itself. Motion only makes the burden sit heavier, as moving a sick man or a stake only fixes the trouble more deeply. A person must first free his own mind from the common attitudes that have taken hold of it, and so return to himself.
Even after we leave our burdens behind, we are not truly free. We still look back at what we left, and our minds keep dwelling on it.

Montaigne says the real problem is the mind, which can never escape itself. So the mind must be brought back home and kept within itself. This inward solitude can be had even in crowded cities and royal courts, though it is easier to find apart from them.

Montaigne proposes that, if a person wants to live alone and avoid all company, he should arrange his life so that his contentment depends only on himself. He should cut the ties that bind him to other people, and live alone fully and comfortably.

Stilpo, a Greek philosopher, lost his wife, children and goods when his city burned. Asked by the enemy king whether he had lost anything, he said no, because nothing that was truly his had been lost. Antisthenes said the same idea: carry only what can float, so it escapes the storm with you.

A wise man loses nothing as long as he keeps himself. When the barbarians destroyed the city of Nola, its bishop Paulinus lost all his property and was taken prisoner. He prayed that he would not feel the loss, because the enemy had not touched what was truly his: his inner riches and goodness.

Montaigne says that a person should keep a private inner space that cannot be taken away or spoiled by others. Family, possessions and health are worth having, but he warns against tying one's happiness to them, so that a part of the self stays wholly one's own.

Montaigne says we should spend much of our time alone with our own thoughts, shutting out outside knowledge and company. Doing so prepares us to live without family, possessions and servants if we lose them. He adds that the mind can keep itself company, so we need not fear emptiness in solitude. The Latin quotation means "Be a crowd to yourself in lonely places."

Montaigne says that virtue needs no outside witness or reward, since it is satisfied in itself. He points to soldiers storming a wall under fire, or defenders starving rather than surrender, and asks whether they act for their own sake. His answer is no: they act for the common cause, not for themselves.

Montaigne is mocking scholars who spend their lives on books. He asks whether such a man, coming out of his study after midnight, has studied to become better, wiser, or happier. He answers no: the scholar only passes on technical details, such as the meter of a Latin playwright's verses or the correct spelling of a Latin word.

Montaigne says people willingly trade their health, peace and even their lives for reputation and fame, which he calls worthless, empty coin. Not satisfied with the troubles of their own death, they also take on worries about their families, their friends and their neighbours' affairs. The Latin quotation asks why anyone would set his mind on anything more precious than himself.

Montaigne argues that people who have spent their strongest years serving others should now withdraw and attend to themselves, their own peace and rest. He says that preparing this withdrawal takes care, and that it helps to stop taking on new business. He urges leaving society while there is still time, and freeing oneself from demands that pull one away from oneself.

Montaigne says we should loosen our ties to others, keeping only enough attachment that we can be separated without serious harm to ourselves. Knowing that we belong to ourselves is the greatest thing. When we can no longer give anything to others, we should stop depending on them, and gather our strength for ourselves.

If a person can no longer keep up friendships and social ties, he should at least avoid being a burden to himself. He should treat himself kindly and govern himself so closely by his reason and conscience that he would be ashamed to do wrong in their sight. The Latin quote says few people respect themselves enough to do this.

Montaigne reports Socrates' view that each stage of life has its own duty: boys should learn, men should work at doing good, and old men should step back from public and military duties and live freely. He adds that some temperaments suit this kind of withdrawal better than others.

Montaigne says that people who are slow to take things in and not easily moved or led are more inclined to seek solitude than busy, eager people who throw themselves into everything. He adds that outside comforts should be enjoyed only as far as they please us, and should not be used as the main foundation of our lives, since neither nature nor reason allows that.

Montaigne asks why people should hand their happiness over to someone else's power. He lists self-chosen hardships, such as denying oneself comforts, living in poverty, or seeking grief, that some religious people and philosophers have practised. He calls these acts of excessive virtue.

When a person has little, he praises a safe, modest life and says ordinary people can be brave in poverty. Once richer things come, he claims that only those whose money is spent on fine, polished country houses live wisely and well.

Montaigne says he needs little to be content. When times are good, he imagines the troubles that could come, as men practise war in peace at tournaments. He argues that Arcesilaus, a Greek philosopher, was no less self-controlled for owning gold and silver cups while his wealth allowed it.

Montaigne says he thinks more highly of a man who uses what he has with generosity and moderation than of one who refuses himself all comforts. He also imagines himself in the place of a beggar at his door, who is often happier and healthier than he is, and tries to shape his own mind to that poor man's way of living.

Montaigne says that when he imagines death, poverty, contempt and sickness closing in on him, he can easily decide not to be frightened. He reasons that people with less wit or learning bear these things calmly, and he does not believe that a duller mind can do more than a finer one, or that learned teaching cannot match what habit achieves.

Montaigne says that, knowing how short-lived his pleasures are, he always prays that God will make him content with himself and his own situation. He compares this to young men who feel bold about catching cold because they carry pills ready to take.
Everyone should prepare in the same way. If someone suffers from a more violent illness, they should keep remedies on hand that numb and dull the affected part.

The passage says that the work a person chooses for a retired life should be neither hard nor unpleasant, or retiring gains nothing. Which work fits depends on each person's taste. Montaigne himself has no liking for farming, though those who enjoy it should take it up in moderation.

Montaigne says farming is generally a low, slavish job, though some parts, such as tending gardens, are more respectable. The best course lies between two extremes: the anxious worry of those who make farming their whole life, and the careless neglect of those who let everything go to ruin. He ends with a Latin line about Democritus's cattle eating the crops while his mind wandered far away.

Pliny advises his friend to leave the farm work to others and devote his retirement to study, so that he gains something truly his own. Montaigne says Pliny means reputation, and he compares Cicero, who wanted writing to win him lasting fame. The Latin line asks whether knowledge is worth anything unless someone else knows you have it.

Montaigne says that a man who retires from the world should fully leave worldly concerns behind. Those who retire only partly still plan for their life after they leave, yet expect to gain the rewards of that plan from the world they have left, which he calls a foolish contradiction.

Those who seek solitude for religious reasons have a better foundation for their hope. They trust in God's promises of a future life, which fill them with courage. In that view, suffering helps them gain eternal joy, and death is welcomed as the way to it.

Montaigne says that strict self-discipline becomes easier with habit, and that bodily desires weaken when they are not indulged. The hope of an immortal life after death, he says, is the only reason worth giving up worldly pleasures. Someone who holds this hope with real fervour finds solitude more pleasant than any other way of living.

Montaigne rejects a suggested way of living that is devoted to books. He says it can be as tiring and harmful to health as any other occupation. He also warns against being drawn into it by its pleasure, the same pull that ruins people who are greedy, stingy, self-indulgent, or ambitious.

Many of our pleasures look attractive at first but lead to harm, the way a drinker might ignore a headache that only comes later. The wise, the passage says, warn us to tell pure pleasures apart from those that carry greater pain, because pleasure hides the pain that follows it.

Montaigne says that books are enjoyable, but if studying too hard harms your health and spirits, it is better to stop. He thinks no benefit from reading can make up for such a loss. He compares this to sick people who finally accept medical rules and keep to them.

Someone who withdraws from ordinary life, tired of it, should shape the new life by reason and careful planning. He should give up all work, whatever it might gain him, and drop the emotions that upset calm of body and mind. Then he should pick the path that fits his own temperament, since each person must know his own way (the Latin quotation).

Enjoy activities like farming, study or hunting only up to the point where they stop being pleasant and start causing trouble. Keep only enough work to stay active and avoid dull laziness. Obscure, knotty learning is for those who serve the world; the speaker reads only light books that amuse him or that teach him how to live and die.

Montaigne says that wiser people may seek a purely spiritual rest, but he, with a more ordinary soul, needs physical comforts. As old age takes away his favourite pleasures, he trains his appetite for the ones left. He holds that we should cling to life's pleasures while they last, since death will come, quoting a Latin line that says we shall become ash, ghosts and a story.

Montaigne says that the desire for fame is the opposite of wanting to be alone. Men who chase glory may leave the crowd in body, but their minds stay tied to it, always looking for others' approval. The Latin line he quotes, from Plautus, mocks an old man who seeks food by catching at other people's ears.

Montaigne is saying that people who withdraw from public life often do so only to return with more force, like a jumper who steps back to leap further. He then offers two philosophers' advice, given to friends, to retire from worldly honours and affairs for good. Their message is to spend the rest of life in quiet, after a life spent in public.

To leave public business, you must also give up the rewards it brings, especially fame and praise. Your past achievements will shine on you even in private retreat, so drop the wish for others' approval. Your learning and talents will still work for you if they make you better, so you need not worry about them.

Montaigne quotes a man who worked at a hard art known to only a few people and said that a few were enough for him, even none at all. He says a person alone, or with one friend, can be a full audience to himself. Seeking fame from hiding is unworthy, so one should hide one's tracks like hunted animals do.

Montaigne tells the reader to care less about what others say and more about how he speaks to himself. Before withdrawing into oneself, one must first become someone one can trust, since a person who cannot govern himself will go wrong even when alone. The Latin phrase at the end means that a noble image should appear before the mind.

Imagine great men of the past, such as Cato, Phocion and Aristides, as if they were watching you. Then your own conduct will stay on course, and you will be content with yourself, needing nothing from others. Montaigne calls this true, natural philosophy, unlike the showy kind he has just described.

Montaigne says he disagrees with how people fix the length of a life for themselves. Wise men, he notes, count a life as shorter than ordinary opinion does. He gives Cato the Younger, who killed himself at forty-eight, as an example: Cato thought that age was already mature, since few people reach it.

Montaigne says that people who count on living until old age, and expect to die only from simple weakness of the body, are foolish. Death from extreme old age is the rarest kind of death, and most people are exposed to many other accidents that can end their lives earlier.

Montaigne argues that calling only a death from old age "natural" is a misleading phrase. Deaths from falls, shipwreck, or disease are just as much part of ordinary human life, so the word "natural" should apply to what is common to all, which includes these deaths.
Dying of old age is rare and unusual, so it is less natural than other kinds of death. It is the furthest point nature sets for human life, a limit we cannot pass, but nature seldom lets us reach it.

Montaigne says that living past forty is a rare favour, granted to few people across generations, almost like a special permit to get through life's hazards. He therefore suggests we should treat forty as an age few reach. Since most people do not live that long, reaching it shows we have already come a good distance.

Having already lived past the usual span of life, and having escaped many deaths that others did not, the speaker should not expect to live much longer. Such unusual luck, he says, is unlikely to last.

Montaigne argues that the law's set age for managing one's own affairs, twenty-five, is wrong, since a person often struggles to manage their own life at that age. He gives examples of Roman rulers who lowered age limits for judges and soldiers, showing that such limits have been set and changed before.

Montaigne argues that people are kept out of public work too long, often until their mid-fifties or sixties, when they could be useful sooner. He points to a Roman emperor who ruled the world at nineteen, yet men were judged unfit to settle even a minor dispute about a gutter until they were thirty.

Montaigne argues that a person's mind is fully formed by about twenty. If a soul has not shown its strength and goodness by then, it will probably never show them later. He backs this with an old French proverb: a thorn that does not prick when young will hardly ever prick.

Montaigne observes that many great deeds, in past and present times, were done before the age of thirty, often by the same men. He gives Hannibal and Scipio as examples: they lived much of their later lives on the fame won in youth, and though still notable, were not as great as they had once been.

Montaigne says that, in his own case, his understanding and his physical health have declined since his earlier years rather than improved. He admits that knowledge and experience may grow with age, but he believes quick wit, readiness, steadiness and other more important qualities weaken. He ends with a Latin quotation describing an aging body, dulled limbs, a faltering mind and tongue.

Sometimes the mind declines before the body, and a failing mind can be the hardest decline to notice. Montaigne therefore says the law errs by starting men on their work too late, not by keeping them at it too long. Since life is fragile, he thinks too large a share of it should not go to childhood, idleness and training.

People who study human behavior find it hard to make a person's actions fit together, because the same man often seems to act in ways so contradictory that they could not come from one person. Montaigne gives examples: the younger Marius was sometimes brave like Mars and sometimes soft like Venus, and Pope Boniface VIII began as a fox, ruled as a lion, and died like a dog.

Montaigne notes that Nero, the cruel emperor, once cried out that he wished he had never learned to write, because signing a death sentence troubled him. He says such examples are common and that irresolution, or inability to stay firm, seems to him the most common human weakness.

Montaigne says that biographers and writers are wrong to look for a fixed, solid character in people. They pick one general image of a man and read all his actions through it. When some actions do not fit that image, they call them pretence.

Augustus escaped judgment because his life showed so many sudden and changing actions that critics could not pin him down. Montaigne says he finds steadiness of character harder to believe than other virtues, and he would rather believe the opposite. Judging a person piece by piece, he says, is more likely to get at the truth.

Montaigne says it is rare to find people who have kept one steady course in life, which he calls the main aim of wisdom. An ancient writer defined the whole of life's rules as always wanting, and not wanting, the same thing. Montaigne notes that this only holds if the will is just, since an unjust will cannot stay the same.

Montaigne says that vice is simply lack of order and measure, so it cannot be made steady or constant. He quotes Demosthenes that good conduct begins with careful thought and ends with constancy. He then notes that people do not choose their course by reason, so they drop what they seek, go back to what they gave up, and live out of step with their whole life.

People act on whatever impulse their desire or the moment pushes them toward, going one way and then another. We decide what we want only when we suddenly feel the wish, and we change our minds just as quickly, so our conduct is shifting and inconsistent. The Latin quote says we are pulled like a puppet moved by strings that are not its own.

Montaigne says people are not in control of their own movement. They are carried along, like floating objects pushed by a current that is sometimes slow and sometimes strong. Their moods change with the time, and they keep wanting to change place as if that would relieve a burden. The Latin lines, quoted from Roman poets, say the same thing: human minds are as changeable as the weather.

Montaigne says that people shift between different desires and never fully commit to anything. A person who had set firm rules for their conduct would show consistent behavior throughout life. He points to the Agrigentines, who indulged as if each day were their last yet built as if they would live forever, showing the same inconsistency.

Montaigne says that people should judge each action on its own, using the circumstances closest to it, rather than building a long chain of reasoning. He follows this with an example: a maid who jumped from a window to escape a soldier who meant to force her during a civil war.

A woman who had been pressed by a soldier, but not forced, wounded herself with a blade after a fall, and confessed that he had only courted her with pleading and gifts, fearing he would later turn to violence. Her manner and her blood-stained state made her seem to Montaigne like the Roman Lucretia, who killed herself after being raped.

Montaigne says that a woman who refused a man once may not have been so unwilling at other times, and that a refusal does not prove she is chaste. He supports this with a tale from Ariosto, in which a lady's refusal of a worthy gentleman is followed by her taking a muleteer, a common carter, as lover.

Antigonus cured a soldier he valued, and afterward the soldier fought less eagerly. When asked why, the soldier said the cure had removed the suffering that had made him weary of life, so he no longer cared to risk it. A second story, about Lucullus's soldier, is cut off here.

Montaigne says that when Mahomet angrily scolded the commander Chasan, Chasan threw himself alone into the enemy and was killed. Montaigne suggests this was not a proof of courage or a rescue of honour, but a sudden rage born of insult.

A man who acts brave one day may act cowardly the next, because his courage came from passing circumstances such as anger, need, company, wine or a trumpet call, not from settled reason. Changed circumstances therefore change how he behaves.

Some people have explained the changeable and contradictory behaviour of humans by saying that each person has two souls. These two powers pull us toward good and toward evil, and such sudden shifts could not come from a single source.

Montaigne says that he is changed by every chance event and cannot keep one steady state. He finds that he is not the same person for long, so he presents his self differently depending on which side he looks at. He calls himself a mix of opposites: shy and bold, chaste and lustful, talkative and quiet.

Montaigne says he finds opposite traits in himself, such as being melancholic and cheerful, or honest and deceitful, depending on his mood. He concludes that he cannot describe himself as simply one thing, and that his favorite method of reasoning is to distinguish between cases ("distinguo").

Montaigne says that people often do good things for bad reasons, so a good act should not be judged by the intention alone. One brave deed does not prove a man is brave. A truly brave man would show courage in every situation, not just now and then.

Montaigne argues that a man's courage is not the same in every situation. A person may face battle bravely yet grieve like a woman over a lost lawsuit or a dead child, or flinch at a barber's razor. So a brave act reflects on the act itself, not on the man as a whole.

Cicero reports that many Greeks cannot face an enemy in battle but show courage when they are sick, while the Cimbrians and Celtiberians are the opposite. His Latin quotation means that nothing can be even and consistent unless it comes from a fixed principle.

Montaigne says Alexander was extremely brave, but only in one way, and not in every part of his character. Even so, his bravery had flaws. One clear example was how he reacted to slight suspicions that his officers were plotting against him, acting with so much anger and unfair harshness that fear clouded his judgment.

Montaigne says that a ruler's excessive superstition and his deep regret over killing his friend Clytus both show weakness and uneven courage. He concludes that everything people do is like a patchwork of different parts, so they claim honour they have not fully earned.

Virtue can only be practised for its own sake. If someone uses it as a disguise for some other aim, it soon slips off. Once virtue has truly soaked into the soul, like a deep dye, it stays. So to judge a person, we must watch their conduct over a long time, to see whether steadiness rests on its own foundation.

Montaigne says that if a person changes his course because of events, changing speed is allowed too. Such a person, he says, is like a ship running before the wind, and he quotes the motto of the Talbot family, "Avant le dent," meaning "Forward, the tooth" (a phrase about moving ahead as the situation requires).

Montaigne quotes an ancient writer who says it is no surprise that chance rules us, since we live by chance. A person who has not set a clear aim for life cannot arrange its parts, just as a painter without a plan cannot use colours. Most people never fix a whole plan for their lives and decide only piece by piece.

Montaigne says that people's plans go astray when they have no fixed goal, just as an archer misses without a target and a sailor gets no help from the wind without a port. He also rejects a judge's ruling that Sophocles could manage his household, based only on the quality of one of his tragedies.

Montaigne rejects the idea that a man who manages his own farm well will also govern the state well, which is how the Parians reasoned about the Milesians. He then says that each person is so changeable and mixed that one part of him acts on its own, and a person differs from himself as much as from other people.

Montaigne argues that strong passions can produce good qualities in people. Ambition can teach courage, self-control, generosity and even justice. Greed can make a poor shop-boy brave enough to sail the sea, and love can make boys and girls bold. He ends with a Latin line from Ovid about a girl who sneaks past guards to reach her lover.

Judging a person only by their outward actions is not enough, Montaigne says. Understanding must reach into the soul and find the inner causes that move a person. He adds that this is a difficult and risky task, and he wishes fewer people would try it.

Montaigne and his brother once met a well-bred gentleman on the road during a civil war. He belonged to the opposing side, though Montaigne did not know it at first, because the man hid it. He adds that in such wars enemies look and speak just like their neighbours, so it is hard to tell friend from foe.

Montaigne says that after a past mistake, he feared meeting soldiers from his own side in a place where no one knew him, since he might have to give his name and be harmed. He recalls that such a mistake once cost him men, horses, and a young Italian page he had raised with great care, who was killed.

Montaigne describes a gentleman he met who was terrified whenever he saw a horse or passed towns loyal to the King, and he realised the fear came from his conscience. The man felt as if anyone could see his guilty secrets through his helmet and clerical-style crosses. Montaigne concludes that conscience makes people betray and accuse themselves, even without other witnesses.

Bessus the Paeonian killed his father in secret, but his guilty conscience drove him to confess it. When scolded for killing sparrows, he said the birds kept accusing him of the murder. The passage claims that punishment is born at the same time as the sin, so the wicked suffer it even before it comes.

Just as cantharides (Spanish fly, a beetle used as poison) carry a natural antidote to their own poison, the conscience sends its own pain alongside the pleasure of sin. This pain troubles a person in sleep and waking, and the Latin quotation says that people in fever or dreams have often revealed sins they had hidden for a long time.

Apollodorus dreamed that his own heart accused him of causing his suffering. Epicurus taught that wicked people cannot hide from themselves, because their conscience reveals their guilt to them. The Latin line says the first punishment is that no guilty person is acquitted when he is his own judge.

A guilty conscience makes us afraid, while a clear one gives confidence. Montaigne says that because he knew his own intentions were innocent, he faced several dangers with a steadier step. The Latin quotation says that each mind, aware of its own deeds, feels hope and fear in its heart according to them.

Scipio, on trial before the Roman people for serious crimes, did not defend himself or flatter his judges. He reminded them that they owed their power over the whole world to him, so it was fitting for them to judge him.

Faced with charges brought by a tribune of the people, this Roman leader did not defend himself. Instead he told the citizens to go and thank the gods for his victory over the Carthaginians that day. He walked toward the temple, and the whole assembly, including his accuser, followed him.

Scipio, accused in the Roman senate of misusing money from his province, pulled out an account book that he said recorded all his spending and income. When asked to hand it over for checking, he refused, saying that would insult him, and tore it to pieces in front of the senators.

Montaigne argues that a guilty man would not have been able to fake such confidence, since he was too proud to stoop to defending his innocence. He also says torture is an unreliable way to find the truth. It tests endurance, so the brave may hide the truth and the weak may confess falsely.

Montaigne is describing the logic behind judicial torture. An innocent person may endure the rack and stay silent, while a guilty person may be pushed to confess because conscience weakens their resistance. He suggests the method rests on the power of conscience: it aids the torture against the guilty and strengthens the innocent against it.

Montaigne is talking about torture used to get confessions. He says it is an uncertain and dangerous way to find the truth, because under such unbearable pain a man will say or do almost anything to make it stop. The Latin quotation adds that pain forces even innocent people to lie.

Torture is used on an accused person so that he will not die innocent. But the result is that he dies both innocent and tortured. Many people have falsely confessed under torture, and Montaigne counts Philotas among them. He calls torture a very inhuman method that does little good.

Many peoples regard it as cruel to torture a man over a crime he may not have committed. Montaigne asks how the accused can cure the judges' ignorance, and says that torturing an innocent or doubtful man is worse than killing him. He notes that many prefer to die rather than face this torture.

Montaigne tells a story about a soldier accused of taking the last scraps of soup meat from a poor woman's children. The woman had no proof, so the accusation could not be settled, and Montaigne uses the tale to illustrate how justice can act too quickly on suspicion.

The general warned the woman that she would be guilty of false accusation if she lied, but she insisted on her story. To settle the matter, he had the soldier's belly cut open, and the woman proved to be right.

Good intentions, when pursued without restraint, often lead people to very bad actions. Montaigne grants that in the French civil war the side defending the old religion and government probably has the better cause.

Montaigne says that even among sincere men on one side of the religious conflict, many are carried away by passion. Passion sometimes drives them to advice that is unjust, violent and rash. He sets aside those who only pretend to a cause for revenge, greed or favour with princes.

Montaigne says that zealous early Christians, once their religion had legal power, destroyed many non-Christian (pagan) books. He thinks this loss did more harm to learning than the fires set by invading barbarians. As proof, he notes that the emperor Tacitus had ordered copies of the historian Cornelius Tacitus placed in every library, yet one complete copy was still destroyed, because of a few sentences that conflicted with Christian belief.

Montaigne says that certain historians readily praised every emperor who favoured their own side and condemned everything done by those who opposed them. He gives the Emperor Julian, called "the Apostate", as a clear example.

Montaigne praises a man, probably Lucius Cornelius Pompeius... no, the passage names no one directly here, so the safest reading is that he describes a man who lived by philosophy and showed every virtue. As an example of chastity, he refused to look at beautiful captives, as Alexander and Scipio were said to have done. He was killed by the Parthians at thirty-one.

The ruler heard both sides in lawsuits. Although he asked what religion people belonged to, his dislike of the writer's own Christian faith never tipped his judgments. He also made good laws and cancelled many taxes set by earlier rulers.

Montaigne says that two eyewitness historians describe the Roman emperor Julian's actions against Christians. Marcellinus criticised Julian's decree banning Christian teachers of rhetoric and grammar from running schools, and wished it had gone unrecorded. Montaigne argues that a harsher act would not have been left out, so Julian was hostile to Christians but not cruel to them.

Montaigne tells a story about the Roman emperor Julian, whom Christians called "the Apostate." Julian mocked a bishop, Maris, who had called him an enemy of Christ. Maris answered that he thanked Christ for blinding him, so he would not have to see the emperor's shameless face. Montaigne says this act still does not match the cruelty Julian is said to have shown toward Christians.

Montaigne quotes the historian Eutropius, who describes the Roman emperor Julian as hostile to Christianity but never a killer. Eutropius says Julian was just, apart from harsh punishments early in his reign of those who had backed his predecessor Constantius. The passage also describes Julian as austere, living like a soldier, and sleeping only briefly at night.

The passage describes two habits of rulers. One is that the ruler spent his time checking on his army and guards, or studying, since he was very learned. The other is that Alexander the Great kept a copper ball in his raised hand over a basin, so that when he began to fall asleep and dropped the ball, the noise would wake him and he could keep thinking and studying.

The passage praises a commander for two things. His mind was so fixed on his goals, and his life so sober, that he did not need stimulants to keep his judgment clear. He was also an excellent military leader, having spent most of his life at war, much of it against the Germans and Franks, and few men have faced more danger or shown more personal bravery.

Montaigne is describing the death of an unnamed commander in battle. Wounded by an arrow, he tried to pull it out, but its edge cut his hand and disabled him. He kept asking to be carried back into the fighting to encourage his men, and he ended up with a firm belief in the immortality of the soul and a deep disregard for his own life.

Montaigne says that the emperor (Julian, who gave up Christianity) was wrong about religion throughout, and was called the Apostate for it. He thinks Julian probably never truly accepted Christianity, but pretended to, to obey the laws until he became emperor. Julian was also so devoted to pagan sacrifice that people of his own pagan faith mocked him, joking he would have wiped out the world's oxen for his sacrifices.

Montaigne describes a ruler who believed in omens and predictions. As he died, he thanked the gods for warning him of the time and place of his death. He felt honored to die in the middle of his victories and at the height of his fame, rather than by a slow or shameful death.

Montaigne is saying that the words some people attribute to the dying emperor Julian, "Thou hast overcome, Nazarene," would not have been left out by his eyewitnesses if they were true. He treats them, and other reported miracles about Julian's death, as doubtful because the eyewitnesses who recorded his last moments do not mention them.

The Roman emperor Julian, according to the historian Marcellinus, kept his pagan (non-Christian) beliefs hidden for a long time because most of his army was Christian. Once he felt strong enough, he openly reopened the pagan temples and worked to revive the worship of the old gods.

Montaigne is describing a ruler at Constantinople who found the people and the church leaders divided. He urged them to end their quarrels and let everyone follow their own religion freely. He pushed this because he hoped that such freedom would deepen their splits and stop them from uniting against him.

Having seen how cruelly some Christians behaved, the speaker concludes that no wild animal is as dangerous to a person as another person is. He says these are nearly his exact words, meaning he is quoting another writer.

Montaigne notes that the Roman Emperor Julian used freedom of conscience to stir up conflict among his subjects, just as kings today use it to end conflict. He adds that letting people hold any opinion they like can spread division, since nothing legal holds them back.

Letting people hold any opinion they like, the speaker argues, calms them and blunts the edge that novelty and opposition sharpen. He also thinks it reflects better on the devotion of kings that, unable to do what they wanted (suppress dissent), they at least appeared willing to do what they could.

Even while dying of an illness, the Emperor Vespasian kept handling government business from his bed. When his doctor warned that this harmed his health, he replied that an emperor must die standing, meaning he should keep working to the end.

Kings are reminded that ruling is not a job of ease. A subject is discouraged from risking labour and danger for a prince who spends his time on comfort and pleasures and cares about his own safety while neglecting that of his people.

Montaigne argues that a prince should lead his own wars rather than leave them to his generals. He says that examples can be found on both sides, since some generals' successes and some princes' presence have each done harm. Still, a brave prince would not patiently accept advice that keeps him from the field.

Montaigne says a ruler should not claim the honour of a victory he did not help win in person. Soliman I (Suleiman the Magnificent, Ottoman sultan) is cited as holding that victories won without the ruler present are never complete. Real command, Montaigne argues, is the orders given on the spot during the fighting, not orders sent from a distance.

Montaigne argues that rulers who stay active in war and government keep their power, while those who withdraw to scholarly or leisure pursuits lose ground. He gives the Ottoman sultans Bajazet II and Amurath III as examples. He also cites Edward III of England, who admired how little Charles V fought yet still troubled him greatly, though Edward thought this came more from luck than from good judgment.

Montaigne doubts that the Kings of Castile and Portugal deserve praise as brave conquerors. They ruled distant lands from their comfortable homes, using captains to win the Americas and Asia. He asks whether they would have had the courage to go there themselves.

The Roman emperor Julian held that a philosopher and a brave man should need as little bodily care as possible, allowing the body only what cannot be refused. He wanted body and mind kept busy with worthy tasks, and he was embarrassed to be seen spitting or sweating. Seneca adds that the ancient Romans trained their young people to stand and learned them nothing that had to be learned sitting.

The passage says that wanting to die bravely in battle is a noble wish, but whether it comes true depends on luck, not just on resolve. Many soldiers who vowed to win or die were wounded or captured and forced to live. Illness can also defeat our plans and our knowledge, so Fortune should not support the Roman legions' oath.

Montaigne reports that Portuguese soldiers in the Indies met men who had sworn, with terrible curses, to accept no outcome except death or victory. To show this vow, they had shaved their heads and beards.

It is pointless to risk ourselves and to be stubborn. Blows seem to miss those who rush eagerly to meet them, and they fall less often on those who seek them too eagerly, so the attackers fail to get what they want.
Some soldiers, unable to get killed by the enemy despite trying every way, had resolved either to bring home victory or die. Unable to do either, they killed themselves in the middle of battle.

Philistus, commanding a navy in battle against the Syracusans, was winning at first through his own bravery. When his ship was surrounded and he could see no hope of rescue, he killed himself, after having risked his life for nothing.

Moloch, the sick king of Fez, was dying while Portugal invaded his lands. Even so, he used his remaining strength with great energy and courage. He was too weak to take part in the usual ceremony of entering his capital.

This passage describes a commander who, though ill and lying on a couch, kept full control of his army's strategy. He handed only the ceremonial duties of his camp to his brother. He could have defeated an enemy who had carelessly pushed into his lands without fighting a battle.

This is about a general, who was sick and needed a quick win to end a war and settle troubled affairs at home. He could have won another way that was safer and surer, but he chose a risky, bloody battle. Before that, he used his illness to wear down the enemy and draw them away from their naval support and African ports, saving the battle for the last day of his life.

The attacking army surrounded the Portuguese with a ring of battalions. The ring stopped them from fighting on every side and blocked their escape after defeat, so they were pressed together and piled up by both slaughter and flight.

Though dying, a commander has himself carried to where the fighting is hardest and encourages his men. When his line breaks, he tries to ride into the thickest of the battle, but his men hold him back by his bridle, robe and stirrups.

The dying man, after a final effort, comes to himself long enough to order his people to hide his death so his soldiers would not lose heart. He dies with a finger on his lips, the usual sign for silence. Montaigne asks who ever died so composed and so much like a man.

The strongest and most natural way to face death, the passage says, is to meet it without fear or worry and to keep living as usual right up to the end. Cato, the Roman who chose to kill himself, is the example: he studied and went to sleep while he was ready to die by his own sword that night.

Montaigne praises Plutarch for his judgments on human conduct, especially his remark that states foolishly leave children to their fathers' care. He quotes Aristotle saying that most governments, like the Cyclopes, let each man raise his wives and children by his own foolish and careless whim.

Only the Spartan and Cretan states, the passage says, left the raising of children to the law. Everywhere else, children are left to their parents, however foolish or badly behaved those parents may be. The author argues that a state depends on how its children are brought up, so this leaves the most important matter to chance.

Montaigne says he has often wanted to stage a mock performance in the street to take revenge on the children he has seen beaten by angry parents. He describes the parents coming out with fire in their eyes, driven on by rage. A Latin quotation follows, comparing such rage to rocks falling from a cliff.

Montaigne says that parents who beat and maim small children are not punished, though the children are members of the community and will later serve it. He quotes a Latin verse saying that a child is a gift to the state only if it is made fit to serve the country in farming, war and peace.

Anger, Montaigne argues, pulls people away from sound judgment more than any other feeling. A judge who condemned a criminal out of his own rage would be punished, so fathers and teachers should not beat children in anger either. Punishment given in anger becomes revenge, not correction.

Montaigne advises that we should not punish our servants while we are still angry. We should wait until we are calm, because anger makes faults look much worse than they are, like objects seen through mist. The passage then breaks off in the middle of a comparison about hunger.

Punishment works best when the person giving it is calm and measured. If the punisher is furious, the one punished will not feel justly condemned. Instead, he will point to the angry face, the oaths and the rash haste as his excuse. The Latin quotation describes such a raging face, with swollen veins and eyes blazing like the Gorgon's.

Suetonius reports that Caius Rabirius was condemned by Caesar, but the people, to whom he had appealed, were moved to acquit him mainly by the anger and harshness Caesar had shown in passing that sentence.

Montaigne says that what a person says and what a person does can be judged separately. Those who attacked the truth of the Church by pointing to the bad behaviour of its clergy argue foolishly, since the Church's truth rests on other grounds. A good man may hold false beliefs, and a wicked man may preach true things.

Montaigne says that words carry more weight when actions follow them. He gives two examples: Eudamidas dismisses a philosopher who talks about war but has never heard a trumpet, and Cleomenes laughs at an orator on courage, saying he would listen to an eagle but not to a swallow.

Montaigne says that a writer who truly believes what he writes has much more force than one who only pretends to. He gives Cicero and Brutus on liberty as an example of real conviction. Cicero, writing on death, sounds weak and unsure, so he fails to move the reader, while Seneca's words stir the reader to courage.

Montaigne says he always wants to know what kind of man an author was, because a writer's character can be judged from his work. He gives the example of Sparta's overseers, who silenced a corrupt man who gave good advice and had a virtuous man present it instead. He says Plutarch's writings reveal Plutarch so well that he feels he knows him deeply, though he wishes more were known of his life.

Montaigne says he has wandered from his topic because of a story Aulus Gellius wrote about his own conduct, which brings him back to anger. The story concerns a slave who, while being whipped on the orders of Plutarch, first protested that he had done nothing to deserve it.

A servant, angry at his master Plutarch, accuses him of breaking his own teaching that anger is shameful, since he had him beaten in a rage. Plutarch replies calmly that his face, colour and voice show no anger, so the servant has no proof that he is angry.

The speaker is saying that he does not show the usual outward signs of anger: his eyes, face and voice are calm, and he does not redden, foam or tremble. He tells his listener that these are the true signs of anger, and he then calmly orders the man whipping him to carry on while they talk.

Three examples show men who held back from punishing someone because they were angry. Archytas said he would have beaten his steward, Plato left the punishment of a slave to Speusippus, and Carillus said he would have had a servant killed. In each case the speaker judged that his anger made him unfit to punish.

Anger is a feeling that takes pleasure in itself and feeds on its own sense of being right. Even when the person who wronged us offers a good defence, we can stay angry, even at innocence and truth. Montaigne says he recalls a striking example from ancient times.

Piso, a commander of great virtue, angry at a soldier who could not say where his companion was, assumed the companion was dead and sentenced the soldier to hang. Just as the soldier stood on the gallows, the missing companion returned alive.

Out of shame and spite, the angry ruler's rage grew stronger instead of calming down. Following a sudden idea from his passion, he had three men killed for one innocent man's sake: the soldier already sentenced, the soldier who had lost his way and caused his companion's death, and the hangman who had refused to carry out the order.

Angry people need opposition to keep their anger going. Montaigne notes that a calm, agreeing listener starves a hot temper, as the orator Celius showed when he asked a dinner companion to disagree with him so that there would be two of them arguing.

Montaigne says that women get angry only so that others will get angry back, copying the way lovers behave. He gives the example of Phocion, an Athenian statesman, who answered a heckler's insults with silence, let him finish, and then carried on his speech as if nothing had happened. Montaigne concludes that nothing stings a man more than this kind of contempt.

Montaigne says a certain very quick-tempered Frenchman, a soldier, is nonetheless the most patient man he knows, and the most careful in controlling his passions. Those passions rise in him with great violence, and the Latin verses below compare them to boiling water in a pot.

Montaigne says that a person who holds back anger must force himself hard, and he does not admire such restraint as wisdom. He judges a man less by what he does than by how much effort it takes him to avoid doing worse.

Montaigne tells a man who prides himself on his calm, gentle manners that a calm outside is good, especially for a person of high rank, but the more important thing is to look after one's inner self. He fears the man is wearing a mask of calm that chafes and hurts him inside.

Montaigne says that hiding anger makes it grow inside a person. He would rather let anger out, even at a servant, than keep a calm face and brood on it, because bottled-up feelings harm the person who holds them more than they harm others.

Montaigne advises those with authority in his household to control their anger and not spend it on every small matter. Constant, hasty scolding loses its force and becomes ignored. He also says that anger should be aimed at the person at fault, not vented before they arrive or long after they have left.

Montaigne is criticising people who rage loudly during an argument when their target is not present, attacking a shadow instead of the person who offended them. He says such loud threats should be saved for the one who actually wronged them. He compares this to a bull that bellows and paws at a tree before a real fight.

When Montaigne is angry, his anger is sharp and quick but also brief and kept as private as he can manage. He becomes hasty and violent without being confused. He throws out insulting words at random, without aiming them at the spots that would hurt most, and he uses only his tongue as a weapon.

Montaigne says his servants wrong him more often in small matters, where he is caught off guard and his anger rises at once. In serious matters, he expects a fair reason for anger, so he prepares himself and keeps calm, which he takes as a kind of victory.

Montaigne says he can hold back anger when he sees it coming, but once it takes hold of him, even a small cause sweeps him away. So he makes an agreement with people who argue with him: when one of them is angry, the other leaves him alone, and each does the same in turn. He believes quarrels grow when anger passes from one person to another, so letting each person have his way keeps peace, though he admits this is hard to do.

Montaigne says that he sometimes pretends to be angry to keep his household in order, though he does not really feel it. He also says that as he grows older his moods become sharper, so he works against them. He wants to become less irritable in the future, even though he has always been known for patience.

Aristotle said that anger can sometimes act as a weapon for virtue and courage. Montaigne notes that others answer this with a joke: anger is an odd weapon, because we normally move our arms, but here anger moves us, and it holds us rather than being held by us.

Montaigne says he does not shape people as an ideal; he only describes the one he knows, himself, who is imperfect. Even though that self-portrait keeps changing, it stays true to life, because everything in the world is always moving, even the mountains and pyramids.

Montaigne says that even steadiness is only a slower kind of change, because he cannot hold still the thing he is describing. He says he does not portray a person's fixed being but the moment-to-moment passing of it, so his account of himself must shift with each hour, and his views may change through chance or through his own will.

Montaigne says his views shift with changing moods and circumstances, so he may contradict himself. He claims he never contradicts the truth as he sees it at the time. If his mind could settle, he would stop testing ideas and firmly decide, but it is always still learning.

Montaigne says that a plain, private life is as fit a subject for moral thought as a grand one, because every person shows the whole of human condition. He writes about himself not as a scholar, poet or lawyer but as a man in general. He adds that if critics blame him for talking about himself, he blames them for never thinking about themselves, and he asks whether it is sensible for someone with such an ordinary life to seek public attention.

Montaigne asks whether it is right to show the world simple, natural writing, weak as it is, in an age that values skill and learning. He compares it to building a wall without stone or brick. His writing comes from chance, while music is shaped by art.

Montaigne claims he knows his subject better than anyone, that he has examined it more thoroughly, and that he has reached his goal fully. He says the only thing needed to complete the work is honesty, which he says he has in full. He admits, though, that he tells the truth only as far as he dares.

Montaigne says that as he gets older he feels freer to talk about himself. He adds that a writer's book and his everyday talk should match. If a man speaks plainly but writes brilliantly, his learning is borrowed, not his own. A truly capable man is capable in everything, even in admitting what he does not know.

Montaigne says that his book and himself cannot be separated: whoever judges the book judges the author too. Anyone who judges it without knowing him wrongs himself more than Montaigne. He would be content if readers of good sense saw that he could have learned much, had he had the knowledge, and that he deserved a better memory.

Montaigne says he rarely repents, and that his conscience is content with itself, though it is the conscience of a man, not of an angel or a horse. He adds that he speaks by questioning and doubting, and leaves final judgments to common and accepted beliefs. He says he is reporting his views, not teaching them.

Montaigne argues that every real vice is plainly harmful and ugly, so a sound judgment condemns it. Some people say vice comes mainly from foolishness and ignorance, since it seems hard to think a person could truly know the harm of vice and still embrace it. Malice, he adds, harms the malicious person most of all.

Wrongdoing leaves regret inside a person, like a sore that keeps itching and tearing at the flesh. Other pains can be eased by reason, but regret cuts deeper because it comes from within, as a fever's chills hurt more than cold felt only on the skin.

Montaigne says that he counts as vices not only the wrongs that reason and nature condemn. He also counts as vices those that people wrongly regard as wrong, when law and custom have approved that view. Each is judged by its own degree of seriousness.
Good actions bring an inner joy and a bold confidence that come from a clear conscience. A bad person may feel safe from punishment, but cannot get this same inner satisfaction.

Montaigne describes a private sense of being clear of wrongdoing in a corrupt time. He says that if anyone could look into his soul, they would find him innocent of harming others, breaking laws, or breaking his word. Even though the times allowed such conduct, he says he took no one's goods, lived on his own means, and paid his workers.
A good conscience gives us a natural inner satisfaction. This pleasure is useful to us, and it is the one reward we can always be sure to receive.

Montaigne argues that a person should not base the reward for good deeds on other people's praise, since the crowd is ignorant and its opinions are unreliable. He notes that what people now call honour is often vice dressed up as virtue, and the Latin quotation says that what were once vices have become customs.

Montaigne says that some friends have sometimes criticised him honestly and directly, either on their own or at his request. He says that a well-balanced mind values such frankness above other kinds of friendly help, and he has always welcomed it warmly and gratefully.

Montaigne says that other people often judge us unfairly, both in blame and praise, so he has sometimes felt he did no wrong by doing what they called wrong, and no good by doing what they called good. Since private people are seen only by themselves, he argues that each person should set his own standard for judging his actions, and use it to encourage or correct himself.

Montaigne says he judges himself by his own laws and reason, and holds himself to those more than to any outside rule. Others see only his outward behaviour and can merely guess at what he is inside. So he trusts his own judgment of his character, not theirs, because the weight of a person's virtues and vices lies in their own conscience.

Montaigne says that the saying "repentance follows sin at once" does not fit sins that have become deeply settled in a person. Quick impulses can be taken back, but vices built up over a long time, held by a strong will, are not open to reversal. Repentance, he says, is a change of will that turns against one's own whims.

Montaigne says that living well in private matters more than appearing good in public. Anyone can play the part of an honest man on stage, but the real test is how a person behaves in secret and at home, where no one checks. He cites Bias, who praised a household whose master behaves the same inside as outside, not from fear of laws or public opinion but from his own character.

Drusus paid masons to make his house so that neighbours could see into every room, rather than pay to hide his private life from them. Agesilaus, a Spartan king, chose to lodge in temples so that people and the gods could observe his private conduct.

People who know someone well often fail to see his greatness, and those closest to a great man rarely admire him. Montaigne applies this to himself: people in his home region of Gascony find it funny that he is in print, and he is valued more by readers far away.

Montaigne says that some people build their reputation by hiding their real selves while alive, so they will be remembered after death. He would rather have less public fame and show himself only as he really is. He compares a public official, who is cheered through the streets and then removes his robe, to a man who falls lower the higher he was raised, with turmoil inside him.

Montaigne says that ordinary private life is as hard as public life, though less noticed. Keeping order in everyday matters takes sharp judgment, and it is a dull virtue. Public deeds such as leading armies or governing people win fame, but being fair and honest in daily dealings with family and oneself is rarer and harder.

Montaigne says that ordinary people often practise virtue more seriously than rulers, because they act for honour in public moments rather than from inner conscience. He thinks that doing good from conscience, as one would do it for fame, is the quickest path to glory. He judges Socrates's quiet, humble life to show more virtue than Alexander's grand public career, since he can imagine Socrates in Alexander's place but not the reverse.

Montaigne contrasts two answers to the question of what a person can do. One answer is to conquer the world. The other is to live a human life in line with its natural condition, which he calls the broader, more important, and more lawful skill.

Real virtue, Montaigne says, lies not in grand deeds but in steady, orderly living. People who judge us from the inside see our public achievements as mere surface shine, like clear streaks of water rising from muddy ground. Those who judge us only by that outward show are wrong to conclude the same about our inner character.

People cannot picture things they do not know, so they give those things strange forms. Demons get savage shapes, and Tamerlane, the conqueror, is imagined with huge eyebrows and a dreadful face, based only on his name. Montaigne adds that he would have expected Erasmus to speak only in proverbs, not in ordinary talk.

Montaigne says we find it easier to picture a respected judge doing ordinary bodily things, like an craftsman on the toilet, than we find it to picture him living like a normal person. We imagine such high figures would never humble themselves that far. He adds that good people can act badly and bad people can act well under outside pressure, so a person should be judged by their settled character, when they are at rest and in their natural condition.

Natural tendencies are strengthened by upbringing, but they rarely change the training a person received. Many people in Montaigne's time, he says, turned toward virtue or vice even though they were raised in the opposite way.

The lines are Latin verse, quoted by Montaigne, describing wild beasts. Once tamed in captivity, away from the forests, they lose their fierceness and learn to endure human company. But when a little warm blood touches their mouths, their rage and fury return, and their throats swell with hunger for more, so that they can hardly be held back from attacking their trainer.

Montaigne says that a person's basic nature cannot be removed, only hidden. Although he has hardly used Latin for forty years, he finds that in moments of strong emotion his first words still come out in Latin, which he says is common in others too.

Montaigne says that people who try to fix the world's bad habits by promoting new beliefs change only the visible faults. The deep, inner faults stay the same, or may even grow. People then feel they have made up for their sins by these easy outward reforms, instead of dealing with their real inner failings.

Everyone, Montaigne says, has a personal core that governs them and pushes back against their upbringing and their strong passions. He describes himself as usually steady: he is rarely taken by surprise, his distractions do not carry him far, and he returns easily to his own center.

Montaigne says that people who withdraw from the world are often no cleaner inside, and that their plans to reform and their regret for sin are as flawed as the sin itself. Some men cannot see how ugly their vice is, because they are tied to it by nature or long habit. Others feel its weight but offset it with pleasure or other reasons.

Montaigne suggests that a wrong act might be excused if the pleasure it brings is far greater than the harm, much as we excuse a theft that is done for gain. He applies this even to giving in to sexual temptation, which he says can sometimes be too strong to resist.

A peasant nicknamed "the thief" tells Montaigne how his life went. Born poor, he found he could not earn enough by honest labour, so he chose to steal. Using his physical strength, he did this safely through his youth.

The passage describes a thief who stole crops from fields far from his own, taking so much that no one man could have carried it in one night. He spread his thefts thinly so each victim lost little. He has grown old and rich, and he openly admits his trade to everyone.

A man says he wants to make peace with God. He will keep returning stolen goods to the people he robbed, and leave the rest to his heirs. He regrets theft but fears poverty more, and he does not regret the part he has already repaid. Montaigne says this is not the deep, habit-driven kind of wrongdoing that corrupts a person's judgment.

It says that repentance does not come from a sudden storm of passion that clouds the soul and, for a while, pushes a person's judgment along with everything else into the hands of vice. The sentence is part of a longer statement, so its full point depends on what comes before it.

Montaigne says that when he acts, he acts wholeheartedly, in one movement, without hidden impulses or inner conflict. His judgment, he says, is fully responsible for both praise and blame, and it has stayed the same since childhood in its direction, its tendencies and its strength.

Montaigne says that sudden, impulsive sins are one matter, and he sets them aside. For sins that are repeated, planned, and built into a person's nature or job, he finds it hard to believe they last so long unless the person's reason and conscience keep choosing them.

Montaigne doubts that a sudden change of heart, or repentance, can really happen. He rejects the Pythagorean idea that people get a new soul when they consult the gods' images for oracles. He would accept it only if the new soul were borrowed for a short time, since our own souls seem too impure to be made new.

Montaigne says that some Stoics told people to fix their faults but not to trouble their inner calm, so they show great inner grief yet change nothing. Repentance that does not end in real change, he argues, is no cure and would not outweigh the sin. Devotion is easy to fake, since its inner truth is hidden while its outward show is easy.

Montaigne says that wishing he were a different person is not true repentance. He cannot be an angel or a model of virtue like Cato, and repentance applies only to things within our power. His own actions match his nature and situation, so he has nothing to repent of, though he can imagine many better natures.

Admiring a better way of acting does not make a person's own abilities any stronger, just as an arm does not grow stronger by imagining another's arm is stronger. If merely imagining a nobler way of acting were reason to repent, people would have to repent even their most innocent actions, since a finer nature might have done them with more dignity.

Montaigne says that his character is the same in his youth and his old age, so he finds nothing in himself to regret in a shallow way. He calls his faults a whole-body stain, not a patch. For him, real repentance must hurt him completely, as deeply as God sees into him.

Montaigne says that in business he has sometimes missed good chances through poor management, though his decisions were sound given the facts before him. He always chose the easiest and safest course. He believes he acted wisely by his own rules, and would act the same way again in similar cases.

Montaigne says that a choice should be judged by the circumstances when it was made, not by how things look now. Good advice depends on timing, since situations keep changing. He admits his serious mistakes came from bad luck rather than poor judgment, because some hidden factors, especially in human nature, cannot be foreseen.

Montaigne says that when a hidden circumstance, which even the person involved could not foresee, causes a bad outcome, he does not blame his judgment, because it was only responsible for what it could know. If things turn out against the choice he rejected, he blames his luck rather than his own decision. So this is not regret.

Phocion once advised the Athenians to do something, and they did not follow his advice. The outcome turned out well anyway, against what he had expected. When asked if he was pleased, he said he was glad the result was good, but he did not regret giving his own advice.

Montaigne says that when friends ask him for advice, he gives it openly and directly. He does not hold back, even though the advice might turn out badly and he might be blamed for it. He does not mind that, since the fault would lie with those who asked him, and he could not refuse them.

Montaigne says he usually blames only himself for his mistakes and bad luck, because he rarely takes advice. He asks others only for courtesy or when he needs facts or specialist knowledge. On matters of judgment, he listens politely to others, and their reasons may strengthen his own view, but he says he has never let them change his decision.

Montaigne says that his own opinions do not weigh much with him, and he gives others' opinions little weight too. In return, he receives little advice and is rarely consulted or believed, and he cannot name any affair that his advice has improved.

Even people placed under Montaigne's guidance have preferred to follow other advice. He is glad of this, since he wants peace and wants to keep himself to himself. He enjoys not being responsible for other people's affairs or answerable for what they do.

Montaigne says that past events bring him little regret, because he believes everything happened as it had to within the vast course of the world and its chain of causes. No wish or imagination can change a single detail, since the great flow of events cannot be reversed, neither in the past nor in the future.

Montaigne rejects the regret that comes with old age. He says he cannot be grateful to weakness for taking away his pleasures, since a loss of strength is not a good thing. The Latin quotation says that nature would never be so opposed to its own work as to count weakness among its best gifts.

Montaigne argues that old age weakens our desires, but that should not change our judgment of right and wrong. Losing appetite does not make vice look good or pleasure look bad to him. He claims he judges these things as clearly now as he did in his youth.

Montaigne says that his reason is no better now than when he was young, and perhaps weaker from age. He notes that he would not give up the pleasures he is now denied for the sake of his soul any more than he did before. His desires have faded so much that he resists them easily, but if they returned in full force, he thinks he would resist them less well than before.

The writer says that illness or hardship has not made his judgment any wiser or given him new insight. If he seems to recover from trouble, that recovery is a kind of magic, not real improvement. He adds that he sees more clearly when times are good than when they are hard.

Montaigne says that good health teaches him better than illness does. He tried to curb his pleasures while he was still healthy and able to enjoy them. He would be ashamed if people judged him by his weak old age rather than by his earlier strong years.

Montaigne holds that a good life lies in living well, not in dying well, as the Greek Antisthenes had claimed. He does not want his final years to contradict the healthy, happy years before them, so he presents himself as consistent throughout. He would live his life again exactly as he has lived it, with no regret for the past and no fear of the future.

Montaigne says he is the same inside as he appears outside. He is grateful that his body has aged in the natural order, from youth to decline, so his illnesses come when he expects them. This makes him bear them more easily and remember his earlier good years with more pleasure.

Montaigne argues that giving up vices only because old age weakens our desires is not real reform. True change must come from God or from our own reason, not from the loss of appetite. He adds that pleasure itself does not look faded; only dim, worn-out eyes see it that way.

Montaigne argues that abstaining from pleasure because illness forces you to is not real temperance or chastity. Someone can only claim to resist pleasure if they know what it is and feel its appeal. He adds that the soul often suffers more troubles in old age than in youth.

Montaigne says that growing old does not make people truly better. What looks like wisdom, such as being hard to please with present things, is really a change of vices, and for the worse. He finds older people more proud, prating, superstitious, greedy, envious, unjust and malicious, and he adds that age wrinkles the mind more than the face.

Old age slowly spoils the mind as well as the body, so that people often grow sour and dull without noticing it. Montaigne suggests Socrates may have chosen his own death at seventy, fearing his sharp thinking would decline.

Montaigne says that avoiding the faults that human nature brings takes great study and care, and even then his own faults keep gaining ground on him. He does not know how far they will bring him down. Whatever happens, he wants the world to know the height from which he falls.

Opposing someone's grief head-on usually backfires, because argument only makes the person hold on to it more stubbornly. Montaigne compares this to a doctor, who should first approach the patient kindly and pleasantly rather than rush in roughly.

Montaigne says a doctor who looks grim and gloomy never helps a patient. Instead, one should first agree with the patient's grief, which earns trust, and then gradually move to firmer advice that can cure. He admits that he himself only tried to ease the illness, since his real aim was to fool the people watching him.

Montaigne says he is poor at persuading people. When he tried to comfort a grieving woman, he did not use strong arguments, and he did not use the usual philosophical consolations, such as the view of Cleanthes that what we complain about is not an evil.

Montaigne lists several ancient ways of coping with grief and rejects none of them outright. He mentions the Peripatetics, who held that sorrow is a light evil; Chrysippus, who held that lamenting is neither fitting nor right; Epicurus, who advised turning the mind from painful things to pleasant ones; and Cicero, who suggested gathering these views together for use when needed.

The speaker kept a woman calm and cheerful by gently steering their talk, bit by bit, away from her sad thoughts, toward other subjects. He calls this diversion. Others who took over his task did not improve her state, because he had not dealt with the cause of her sorrow.

Montaigne notes that generals have often used diversions to draw enemy forces away from their own lands, citing Pericles in the Peloponnesian War. He then gives an example: Monseigneur d'Hempricourt, sent into the besieged city of Liège to carry out surrender terms, saved himself and others by a clever trick.

A crowd gathered at night, angry about an agreement and ready to attack the officials they held. The leader sent two townspeople out with new, softer terms, which turned the crowd aside and led them to the town hall to hear the proposal.

This describes a crowd stirred up against a group of men meeting in a conclave. Each time the crowd grew angry again, the leader sent new messengers with fresh promises, keeping them busy with talks until morning came. His aim was to calm them down until the day broke.

Atalanta, a beautiful virgin, set a condition to end the many offers of marriage from her suitors: she would marry only the man who could beat her in a footrace, and any man who lost would die. Many men accepted the risk and paid with their lives.

Hippomenes races the maiden Atalanta, who will marry only the man who beats her. Goddess Venus gave him three golden apples. He drops one during the race, and Atalanta stops to pick it up, which lets him pull ahead.

Sometimes the mind must be turned aside to other pursuits, cares or affairs, and a change of place can help, just as doctors move a sick body's illness to a less dangerous part when they cannot stop it. The quoted Latin says much the same: a mind that does not recover is often treated by such a change.
Attacking a person's weaknesses head-on does little good. The person neither bears the attack nor pushes it back; they simply turn away from it and avoid it.

Montaigne says that facing death calmly, even playfully, is too hard a lesson for most people. Only Socrates managed it: he treated dying as a natural, neutral event and looked at it directly, without seeking comfort from anything outside it.

Followers of the philosopher Hegesias starved themselves to death after hearing his lectures, so many that King Ptolemy banned him from teaching such ideas. Montaigne says they were not thinking about death itself or judging it. Their minds were fixed on reaching a new state of being.

Condemned prisoners on the scaffold pray with great intensity, using their ears, eyes, hands and voices. Montaigne says this deserves praise for their devotion, but not for their constancy, meaning their firmness of mind in facing death.

People who face death often avoid thinking about it, much as a child is distracted with a toy before a surgeon's needle. Some, seeing the instruments of death around them, turn their minds away in panic. Like someone crossing a steep drop, they are told to shut their eyes or look elsewhere.

Subrius Flavius, about to be executed by Niger, a fellow officer, criticised the badly dug grave as not up to military standards. When Niger urged him to keep his head steady, Flavius told him to strike just as firmly. Niger's hand shook, and he needed several blows to finish the job.

A man dying in battle, or in a duel, is usually too caught up in the fight to think about death. Montaigne's example is a man mortally wounded in a duel who ignored those urging him to think of his soul, focusing instead on fighting back and killing his opponent.

Silanus, condemned to death, said he was ready to die but would not be killed by base hands. The soldiers rushed at him, and in the struggle he was killed. His sudden fury took his mind off the slow death he had been sentenced to face.

We are always thinking of something other than the present. Hopes for a better life, for our children's worth, for lasting fame, for escape from life's evils, or for revenge on those who cause our death bring us comfort. Montaigne ends with a Latin line from Virgil's Dido, who hopes her enemy will suffer and be remembered.

Xenophon dropped his garland when he heard his son Gryllus had been killed in battle. When he learned how bravely Gryllus had died, he picked it up and put it back on. Epicurus, dying, comforted himself with the lasting value of his writings. Both examples show grief being eased by something else.

Xenophon says a wound or hardship hurts a general less than it hurts a common soldier. Epaminondas, a Theban commander, faced his own death more calmly once he learned his side had won. His Latin words mean that such things are the comfort and relief of great pain.

Montaigne says that even philosophers' arguments often circle around their subject without really touching it. As an example, he gives Zeno's two syllogisms: one arguing death is no evil, and one arguing a wise man is no drunkard. He sees these as weak hits on the target, showing that great thinkers are still ordinary humans.

Montaigne says revenge is a strong and natural feeling, though he has never felt it himself. To distract a young prince from wanting revenge, he did not preach forgiveness or describe the tragic results of revenge. Instead, he pointed out the honour and goodwill that mercy would bring, and so turned the prince toward ambition.

Montaigne advises that a strong love can be weakened by splitting it into several smaller desires, so that none of them can dominate. He says it is best to deal with such feelings early, before they take hold and become hard to control. The Latin quotations, from the Roman poets, support the same idea of spreading out and releasing the built-up urge.

Montaigne says that when a strong feeling, such as grief or displeasure, took hold of him, he found it easier to escape it by setting another strong feeling in its place, as he once did with love, than to overcome it directly. Change of any kind, he concludes, relieves and scatters such feelings.
When Montaigne cannot fight off a troubling thought, he gets away from it. He changes place, work and company, so his mind fills with other thoughts and the worry loses track of him.

Time eases grief mainly because it fills the mind with new concerns, which gradually wear down the first sharp feeling of loss. Montaigne adds that a wise man still feels the loss of a friend after twenty-five years about as keenly as in the first year. Epicurus, he notes, held that neither foreseeing a misfortune nor its age eases it.
