Alcibiades cut off his beautiful dog's ears and tail and let it run into the street, so that people would gossip about the dog and leave his other actions alone. The writer adds that he has seen some women fake minor love affairs for the same purpose: to distract gossip from their real ones.

Some men pretend to love a woman, and in the act they are caught by real feeling and drop the pretence. Montaigne says the sensible view is that a man who sincerely loves should not take on such a disguise. A pretender who fails to swap places with the woman he courts is a dull fool, and such a courtship amounts to making a shoe for someone else to wear.

Small things distract us because small things hold our attention. We rarely look at whole subjects at once. Instead we are caught by minor details, passing images, and the outer surface that comes off the subjects themselves, like the empty shells cicadas leave behind in summer, which the quoted Latin line describes.

Small, everyday things often hurt more than the loss itself. A parent's childish antics, a last farewell, or a loved one's words or name can bring grief back sharply. Caesar's bloodstained robe, shown to Rome, moved the crowd more than his death did.

Montaigne says that when repeated words or phrases annoy him, the irritation is only about the wording and tone, not the real substance of the matter. He compares this to preachers whose outcries move listeners more than their arguments do, and to the pitiful look of an animal being killed. The Latin quote says that pain itself is provoked by these goads, so these small things are the basis of our grief.

Montaigne describes how his kidney stone sometimes blocked his urine for three or four days, bringing him near death. He says that death would have been a welcome escape from the pain of these fits. He then mocks an emperor who had criminals tied up so they died from being unable to urinate, calling him a skilled master of executioners.

Montaigne, facing his own death, notices how small things cling to him: a dog, a horse, a book, a glass. He sees that others cling to equally trivial things such as ambition, money and learning, and he thinks these are no less foolish than his own attachments.

Montaigne says that he can face death calmly as an idea in general, but not when it comes close. Small things, like a servant's tears, his clothes being handed out, or a friend's touch, weaken him. Even fictional grief, such as the laments of Dido and Ariadne in poems, moves him and others.

Feeling no emotion at all is a sign of a stubborn, hard nature, Montaigne says, even though Polemon was praised for not reacting when a mad dog bit his leg. Even the wisest person cannot fully feel a sorrow through reason alone when the eyes and ears, which are moved only by trivial things, still take part in it.

Montaigne asks whether the arts should take advantage of people's natural foolishness and weakness. He gives an example: a speaker in court, using rhetoric, is moved by his own voice and by emotions he pretends to feel, and so is fooled by the feeling he is acting out.

Montaigne describes actors who work themselves into real grief in order to move their audience, even though the audience cares less than they do. He compares them to paid mourners at funerals, who sell their tears by weight, yet who often end up truly sorrowful after settling their faces into mourning.

Montaigne describes escorting the body of a dead nobleman, Monsieur de Grammont, from a siege. Along the route, people who did not even know the dead man's name were moved to weep, simply by the solemn procession.

Quintilian reports that some stage actors, playing mourners, became so caught up in their roles that they kept crying after leaving the stage. They had set out to move their audience, but they were moved themselves, showing tears and pale faces like real grief-stricken people.

In some country near the mountains, widows mourn their dead husbands by praising his good qualities and also listing his faults. In doing so they move from grief to scorn, as if to settle the account between themselves and him.

When we lose a friend, we often praise them falsely and imagine them as something other than they were, as if grief made us wiser. Montaigne says he will refuse the kind things people say about him after his death, not because he deserves them but because he will be dead.

A soldier is asked why he is at a siege. He answers that he has no personal gain, glory or quarrel, only duty to his prince. Yet the next day he is furious and eager to attack, stirred up by the sight of weapons and the noise of cannon and drums.

The mind can be stirred up by no real cause at all. A passing fancy, with no physical object behind it, is enough. Daydreams of imagined pleasures can make us feel real joy, and imagined anger or grief can wear down both soul and body.

Montaigne asks whether a person who is restless amid other people is being haunted by false visions or an inner demon. He suggests the cause lies within us, not in outside things. He gives Cambyses as an example: after a dream that his brother would become king, Cambyses had his trusted brother killed.

Montaigne tells of two kings who killed themselves over a bad omen and a dream, and says that giving up life for a dream means not valuing life properly. He then turns to the body's weakness and the soul's suffering, quoting a Latin verse that blames Prometheus for shaping the body without giving the mind its proper path.

Montaigne says few things move or take hold of him, far fewer than move other people. He thinks it is reasonable to be affected by things only so long as they do not take full possession of a man. He works hard to increase this natural calm. He sees clearly and feels keenly, but he fixes his attention on very few things.

Montaigne says he avoids getting emotionally tied to things, even to his own affairs. He would rather hold back his feelings than let them run away with him, because he cannot fully control such things. Health is one example: he values it, yet he thinks he should not care for it so eagerly, since illness would then be harder to bear.

Montaigne says a person should keep a balance between avoiding pain and seeking pleasure, following Plato's middle path. He resists any strong attachment that would pull him away from himself. He would lend himself to others but give himself fully only to himself. He admits his own will is too delicate to be easily swayed, and he prefers a quiet, unhurried life.

Montaigne says that if a heated argument ends with his opponent winning, the loss would upset him badly, since his own heat and stubbornness would look shameful. He adds that if he argued as fiercely as others do, the inner turmoil would throw his mind into disorder.

When Montaigne has handled other people's business, he says he took it on as a duty but did not let it take over his body or feelings. He will work at it and care about it, but not be consumed by it, because he already has enough of his own inner concerns to manage.

A person who knows how much they owe to themselves and what duties are their own will find enough natural work to do. Such a person has no time to be idle or to interfere in other people's affairs. The quoted line tells the reader to attend to matters at home first.

Montaigne says people hire out their own minds and time to others, so their abilities end up serving other people rather than themselves. He argues that a person should guard the freedom of the soul and give it away only on rare, worthwhile occasions. People who answer every call, for big or small matters alike, are described as lifeless unless they are busy.

Some people cannot stay still, and keep busy even when it does them no good. Montaigne says they seek calm through restless activity, like a child soothed in a cradle. He adds that we waste our time and life far more freely than our money, though time and life are what we should guard most carefully.

Montaigne says he is the opposite: he holds back, wants things with little intensity, and works at a measured pace. Others put their full force into whatever they do. Since the world has many dangers, he thinks one should skim over it lightly rather than plunge in. Even pleasure becomes painful when taken too deeply.

Montaigne was chosen mayor of Bordeaux while he was far away in Italy and had no thought of such a post. He asked to be excused, but his friends told him that refusing was a mistake, and an even bigger one because the king had also ordered him to accept.

Montaigne describes his term as mayor of Bordeaux. The post pays nothing and offers only honour, lasts two years, and is rarely renewed. He notes that a few men before him held it twice, and he is proud to be among them. He ends with a Latin line praising each as a good servant of both peace and war.

Montaigne says that Alexander the Great turned down an offer of citizenship from Corinth. He accepted it gladly only when the Corinthians pointed out that the gods Bacchus and Hercules were already listed as citizens there. Montaigne uses this to describe how an honour he received came about by chance.

Montaigne describes himself honestly to those he is entering service with, so they know what to expect from him. He admits he lacks memory, alertness, experience and energy, but says he is free of hatred, ambition, greed and violence.

Montaigne is turning down an office offered to him by a town's leaders, because of his late father's record in that role. He tells them he would be sorry if the city's affairs weighed on him as heavily as they had weighed on his father while he held the same office.

The author recalls an older man he knew as a boy who, despite his age and poor health, kept taking on public business. He neglected his own comfort, household, and affairs, and risked his life on long, hard journeys for public causes. The writer says this came from a very kind nature.

The speaker praises someone for being very kind and well liked. He admires this way of behaving in others, but he says he does not like to act that way himself, and he claims he has a reason for this.

Many moral teachings urge people to forget themselves and serve others, because they assume people are already too focused on themselves. Montaigne adds that wise teachers often preach what is useful rather than what is true, and that people sometimes must deceive themselves, or shut their eyes, to live with the truth.

Montaigne says that when people are told to love things far above themselves, they are like archers who aim higher than the target to hit it. Likewise, a bent stick is straightened by bending it the other way. The idea is that demanding more than is wanted is a way to get the amount actually wanted.

Montaigne suggests that, as in ancient temples with public and secret rites, the true friendship a person owes to himself lies in a hidden, higher teaching. He rejects two false kinds: attachment to glory, knowledge or riches as if they were parts of oneself, and a weak friendship that harms what it clings to, as ivy destroys the walls it covers.

A true friendship, useful and pleasant at once, is described here. A person who knows his duties in it, and knows what he owes himself, must also take part in the world and serve society. Someone who does not live partly for others, Montaigne says, does not really live for himself either.

Each person's first duty is to manage his own conduct and live well, and that is the reason we are here. Someone who neglects his own virtuous life in order to teach others is foolish, and someone who gives up his own healthy, pleasant way of living to serve others is on a wrong, unnatural path. Still, he does not want people to hold back effort or even their blood when a task demands it.

Montaigne says that a calm mind can act without strain, almost as if acting costs it nothing. The body takes on its tasks as they really are, but the mind often makes them heavier than they need to be, and at its own cost. So people do similar things with very different amounts of effort and will.
Soldiers often risk their lives in battle without caring much how it ends. A man safe at home may care far more about the outcome of the war than the soldier who is fighting it.

Montaigne says he could have taken on public duties without neglecting his own affairs, and served others without losing himself. Strong, violent desires, he argues, slow down what we set out to do. They make us impatient with delays, angry at obstacles, and suspicious of the people we deal with, and things done under such pressure are rarely done well.

Someone who pursues a goal using only judgment and skill stays flexible. He adapts, yields, and waits as circumstances require, and when he fails he recovers easily and is ready to try again. By contrast, a person driven by a violent, overwhelming desire acts unwisely and unjustly, and without good luck his rash efforts bring little result.

Philosophy advises that when avenging a wrong, we should first remove anger. The aim is not to punish less but to punish more effectively, since anger both clouds judgment and drains the strength of the person doing the punishing. Haste, like anger, works against itself.
Greed is its own worst obstacle, Montaigne observes. The more intensely a greedy person pursues wealth, the less he gathers, and greedy people often get rich sooner when they pretend to be generous.

A friend of Montaigne's was in danger of harming his own mind by caring too intensely about a prince's affairs. The prince described himself as able to see troubles coming as clearly as anyone, but once a trouble could not be fixed, he at once decided to accept it and endure it.

A man takes every precaution he can for a difficult matter, then calmly waits for the outcome. Montaigne says he stays composed in great affairs and is greater in misfortune than in good fortune, with his defeats more glorious to him than his victories.

Even in trivial games like chess or tennis, eager and intense desire to win throws a person's mind and body into confusion and poor judgment. Whoever keeps calmer about winning or losing keeps his wits about him and plays better and more safely.

Montaigne says that the mind is weakened when it is given too many things to hold on to. It can perceive everything, but it should draw its nourishment only from itself and learn what belongs to its own nature. Natural law, he adds, shows what a person truly needs.

Nature needs little, so a person is poor only in opinion. Some wants come from nature and have a limit we can see; others come from our own imagination and have no end. Lack of goods can be fixed, but a poverty of the soul cannot. The Latin quotation says that if enough were enough, wealth would satisfy the mind, but it never does.

Socrates said he was glad of how many things he did not want, when he saw wealth paraded through Athens. The examples that follow show people living on very little: Metrodorus and Epicurus ate almost nothing, and Cleanthes earned his own living by manual work.

Montaigne argues that what nature strictly requires to keep us alive is very little, so little that misfortune cannot reach it. He then suggests we allow ourselves more, counting our acquired habits and living conditions as a second nature. He adds that custom is as powerful as nature itself.

Montaigne says that losing his usual way of living would almost be as bad as losing his life. He is now too set in his ways to change or start anything new, even something that would improve him. Good fortune arriving now would come too late to enjoy, so he quotes a line asking what use riches are if one cannot use them.

Montaigne says it would be almost better never to gain inner wisdom than to gain it too late, when there is no time left to use it. He compares it to mustard served after the meal, and says that help arriving when one can no longer act only brings resentment.

Montaigne says that patience is the most useful quality of all, since it lets a person bear what cannot be changed. He compares this to giving a singer a fine voice when his lungs are weak, or a skill in speech to a hermit cut off from people. He also says that a fall or an ending needs no art to help it along, because every affair ends by itself.

Montaigne says he cannot easily accept a new calendar. He was raised under the old way of counting years, and that habit is hard to give up. His mind keeps pulling him ten days off, and he feels that the new rule suits only those who are just starting out. Even his returning health brings him more regret than joy, since he has no time left to enjoy it.

Montaigne says that he values high public offices little, because they are often given to men near the end of their lives, and the choice looks at how soon they will leave office rather than how well they will serve. He ends by saying that after long habit, his own form and luck have become part of his nature.

Montaigne says that people may reasonably call their own only what falls within a modest limit of need. Claiming more than that is confusion. The more we enlarge our needs and possessions, the more we expose ourselves to misfortune. Our desires should stay within a small range of things close at hand.

Montaigne says our actions should loop back to ourselves, like a circle, rather than run straight ahead toward some outside goal. Actions done without this inward turning, such as those of greedy or ambitious people, are unhealthy. He adds that most human business is a kind of play-acting, quoting the Latin saying that the whole world acts out a stage play.

Montaigne says a person should play a public role properly but remember it is only borrowed, like a costume. He criticises people who take their official status for their real selves, so that they act grand even in private and mistake respect shown to their office, their attendants or their horse for respect shown to themselves.

Montaigne says that men in high office puff up their minds and their natural manner of speaking to match their rank. He keeps his own self apart from the role of Mayor of Bordeaux, which he held. He adds that a lawyer or a financier cannot ignore the dishonesty in those jobs.

An honest man is not to blame for the wrongs of the job he holds, so he may take it up even if the work is corrupt or foolish. Everyone must live by the world as it is. An emperor, though, should judge his power from above it, seeing his empire as something outside himself.

Montaigne says he does not let his commitments cloud his judgment. He praises good qualities in his opponents and criticises faults in his own side, and he is fair to a good deed even when it is done against him. Apart from the core of the dispute, he keeps himself even-minded and impartial.

Montaigne says he is pleased with himself for keeping his anger within the matter in dispute. He notes that most people let anger spread beyond the issue, which shows it comes from some private cause. Such people are angry because the quarrel touches their own interests, not the common good.

Montaigne says he wants to be on the side he thinks is right, but he does not want to be treated as a personal enemy of the other side beyond the general conflict. He rejects the habit of judging a man's loyalty from small things he admires or says, such as praising a leader's charm, and so concluding he belongs to the opposing party.

Montaigne argues that a magistrate was wrong to condemn a book simply because its author, a heretic, was counted among the best poets of the time. He compares this to saying a thief has a handsome leg, or a bad woman must smell foul. A person's faults do not decide the worth of what they make.

Montaigne asks whether wise societies ever took back honours given to Marcus Manlius, a Roman hero, because he later sought to become king and broke the laws. He suggests that such a fall erased his earlier services from memory. He adds that if people dislike a lawyer, they will not then call him eloquent.

Montaigne says that men of good character often let their zeal push them into errors. He can judge one person's action as bad and another's as good, and he thinks partisans wrongly expect their side to see only what suits it. He says he fears his own desires could bias him, so he leans the other way.

Montaigne says he has often seen people let their hopes and beliefs be guided by their leaders, even when those beliefs rest on repeated mistakes and mere dreams. He is not surprised that people have been fooled by the tricks of Apollonius and Mahomet, because their passion has taken away their judgment.

Montaigne says that people's judgment only follows whatever flatters their side and helps their cause. He had seen this at the start of the civil troubles in France, and he thinks later factions copied it and went even further. For him, this is a trait that always goes along with popular errors.

Once opinions start to spread, they push each other along like waves in the wind. A man who wants to stay with a cause should not rely on tricks to defend it. Such tricks, Montaigne says, only work on weak minds, while sound minds can be kept firm by honest means.

Montaigne says that Caesar and Pompey, though bitter rivals, showed restraint toward each other. Their quarrel was over honour and power, not personal hatred, and each would have preferred to win without destroying the other. He contrasts this with the far more vicious hatred between Marius and Sylla.

Montaigne says we should not throw ourselves too eagerly into our desires and interests. When young, he resisted love that was growing too quickly, so it would not take complete control of him. He does the same whenever his will rushes forward too keenly, leaning against it to hold it back.

Montaigne says that people who see only part of things, through their own dullness, suffer less from painful events. He compares this to a kind of spiritual leprosy that looks like health. He grants that philosophy does not wholly despise it, but he says it should not be called wisdom, though people often call it that.

Diogenes embraced a snowman in winter to test his endurance. A bystander asked whether he felt cold, and Diogenes said no, so the bystander asked what was hard about it. Montaigne concludes that to judge real steadiness, you must first know how much the suffering actually hurts.

Montaigne says that people who face hard blows from fortune should try to avoid their causes and turn aside the blow, so that they do not feel its full weight. He then asks what King Cotys did, pointing to a story he goes on to tell.

Montaigne describes a man who broke a fragile gift at once, so that it could not later cause anger at his servants. He says he has likewise avoided owning land next to relatives and close friends, because shared borders often lead to quarrels.

Montaigne says he gave up gambling because, although he hid his losses well, he felt inwardly upset by them. He adds that a man of honour should avoid situations likely to start a quarrel, and he keeps away from gloomy, bad-tempered people. The best way to handle such moments, he concludes, is to prepare for them in advance.

Some wise men have chosen a different way: they face hard subjects head on, trusting their own strength. They hold firm against every misfortune, as a rock stands unmoved against wind and waves. The Latin quotation is the image they rely on.

Montaigne says we should not try to copy the great examples of people who faced their country's ruin calmly. Such calm is too hard for ordinary people. Instead, lesser minds should avoid the blows they cannot bear, as far as they can, rather than try to endure them.

Zeno jumped up when a young man he loved came to sit beside him, saying doctors order rest and avoid agitation in any swelling. Socrates advised not to resist beauty but to run from it, like a poison that harms from a distance.

Montaigne says that Xenophon, in his account of Cyrus, shows Cyrus fearing he could not resist the beauty of his captive Panthea, so he left her guard to another man. He adds that the Lord's Prayer's plea "lead us not into temptation" makes the same point: people should avoid putting themselves in danger of temptation.

The writer says that people should not pray merely to win a fight against their desires, but to never be tempted at all. They ask God to keep their consciences free from any contact with evil, so that even its approaches are never felt.

People who defend their anger or other disturbing feelings may be right about the situation as it is now, but not about how it began. Trace the cause back to its start, and their case falls apart, since a long-lasting wrong does not become right. Montaigne adds that he cares for his country, yet without letting worry overwhelm him.

The main point is that a person who does not depend too much on princes' favour, children, honours, or other people's praise can bear losing them calmly. A little patience, he says, protects against such troubles, and he finds relief in this method of dealing with them.

Montaigne says that he avoids much trouble by stopping his feelings at the very start, before they carry him away. His reasoning is that someone who cannot stop a feeling at its first movement will not be able to stop it once it has taken hold, and so will not bear its full force either.

Montaigne says that once a person has drifted from reason, weakness feeds itself and carries him further out without finding a place to stop. He compares the first faint stirrings of his own anxiety to the early breezes that warn sailors of a coming storm. He admits he has often wronged himself to avoid a worse harm from the courts.
Avoid lawsuits as far as possible, perhaps even somewhat more than the law allows. Giving up a small part of one's legal right now and then is not only generous but sometimes profitable too.

Montaigne says that a wise person would be glad, even proud, if a relative lost a lawsuit, as if losing it were a burden to be rid of. He adds that he has always refused to use his own family or social connections to gain an advantage over others or to push his claims beyond what is rightfully his.

Montaigne says that through his own efforts he has avoided lawsuits and quarrels, even when he had fair offers and a just claim to pursue them. He has lived a long life with no serious offence given or received, and has never heard anything worse than his own name, which he calls a rare gift from Heaven.

Some of the biggest upheavals in history had trivial beginnings. Montaigne gives examples: a dispute over a cartload of sheepskins, and the cutting of a seal that started a civil war between Marius and Sylla. He adds that important state treaties were sometimes really decided by the whims of women.

Montaigne means that people often fight over trivial causes. He points to the old story of the Trojan War, which began over a golden apple, and says a man who risks his life for a quarrel would blush to explain how small its cause really was.
It is easier to avoid getting involved in something than to get out once you are in. A small matter can draw you in, and once you are caught, every tie pulls harder and far more is needed to escape.

Montaigne says we should do the opposite of the reed. The reed shoots up straight at first but then grows weak, with knots that show it has lost its early strength. It is better to start slowly and save our full effort for the most demanding part of a task.
We control affairs at the start, when they are still in our hands. Once they are underway, though, they control us, and we have to follow where they go.

Montaigne admits that following this advice has not freed him from difficulty. He often had to work hard to control his passions, which do not always match the situation and can arrive suddenly and strongly. Still, he says good results can come from it, though not for those who want public praise for their good deeds, since such results matter only to the person who does them.

Montaigne says that a man who avoids a quarrel before it starts is calmer, though not more respected. He adds that people seeking honour behave differently from those who act by reason and order. Some rush into a fight in anger and then lose heart. Plutarch is cited for the idea that people who give in out of false shame are just as quick to break their promises.

Someone who starts a quarrel easily is likely to drop it just as easily. Montaigne says he himself would be hard to talk into a quarrel, but once he is in one, he would defend it stubbornly, because custom makes a man feel he must see it through. He quotes Bias, an ancient Greek sage, who advised starting things calmly but carrying them out with passion.

Montaigne says that most patched-up settlements of quarrels are shameful and false. People only save appearances while privately knowing what they really meant, and they disown their true views. Doing so costs them their frankness and their courage.

Once someone has said or done something, that person must stand by what they really meant, even at cost, rather than inventing a new reading to escape blame. Honesty is owed to one's conscience and virtue, and such evasions are left to lawyers.

Montaigne argues that apologising for a rash insult can look worse than the insult itself. It would be better to insult the other person again than to grovel to him, because by apologising you show yourself lower than the man you had claimed to stand above.

Montaigne says it is more shameful for a gentleman to take back what he has said when someone forces him to, than to hold firm out of stubbornness. He adds that he finds it easier to avoid strong emotions altogether than to control them once they arise. The Latin quotation means that passions are cut off more easily than they are tempered.

Montaigne says that people who cannot reach the hard calm of the Stoic philosophers can rest in his own plain, dull temperament, which gives him the same result naturally. The middle ground between philosophers and peasants is full of troubles, while both extremes find calm and happiness. He backs this with two Latin verses by Virgil about the happy man who understands the causes of things and the happy man who knows the country gods.

Things are weakest at the start, so one should watch beginnings closely, since a danger missed while young is hard to cure once it has grown. The writer says he met many setbacks in ambition that were harder to bear than the effort it took to restrain his own natural inclination toward it. The Latin quotation means he rightly shrank from raising his head where it could be seen.

Montaigne says that people read public actions in many different ways, and some call his own public service lazy and slack. He admits they have some reason for saying so, because he tried to keep his mind calm and quiet.

Montaigne says that his slowness in some matters should not be taken as proof that he is incapable, since carelessness and lack of judgment are different things. He also says he is not ungrateful to the body that honoured him, which tried hard to win him over and later chose him again.

Montaigne says he wishes a people well and would have helped them at any cost if the chance had come. He notes that they call his rule unremarkable and blame him for holding back when others were doing too much. He says he is eager to act wherever his own will drives him.

Montaigne says he works well in tasks that call for energy, freedom, and quick, bold action, even risky ones. If a job needs long, subtle, painstaking, or tangled handling, he says someone else should be chosen. He adds that important work is not always hard, and that he would have been ready for rougher labour if it had been needed.

Montaigne says he has done what his duty really required, and he readily let go of the showy duties that ambition dresses up as duty. Such displays impress onlookers, who judge by appearance rather than substance. He adds that he dislikes noise and commotion.

Montaigne says he can calm a disturbance without getting worked up himself, and punish wrongdoing without losing his temper. When he needs anger, he puts it on as a pose. He prefers a calm, quiet, unhurried way of life, neither humble and downcast nor showy.
Montaigne says that, by chance, his family has always lived quietly, without fame or disorder, and for a long time has cared mainly about being known as honest and upright.

Montaigne says people today are trained to value noise and display, so quiet, gentle qualities like kindness, moderation and steadiness are no longer noticed. He compares this to the body: rough, harsh things are felt, while smooth, mild things pass unnoticed, just as we feel sickness much more than the health or the soothing oils that treat it.

Montaigne says it is done for personal fame and profit, not for the public good, when someone does in a public square what could be done quietly in a council chamber, or does at noon what could have been done the night before. He compares this to Greek surgeons who operated in public to attract more patients. Such people, he says, think good advice only gets heard when it is announced loudly.

Montaigne says ambition is not limited to humble people like himself. He gives two examples: Alexander, who wanted his father's wars and justice rather than an easy, peaceful empire, and Alcibiades, who preferred a short, brilliant life to a quiet one. He suggests such ambition may be forgivable in a strong, full soul.

Small-minded people flatter themselves that they have won fame for some minor act, such as a sound judgment in a case or keeping watch at a city gate. Their pride only exposes their faults. Such little deeds, Montaigne says, do not last and spread no further than the next street.

Montaigne says that if a man wants to praise his own worth, he may do it even to a servant or to himself. He gives two examples: an old man bragging to his maid, and a lawyer who, after a noisy speech, quietly thanked God for his glory while relieving himself.

Fame should not be handed out cheaply. Only rare and unusual deeds deserve it, not ordinary good acts, which are too many to count. Even praise is not owed to every virtuous act, according to the Stoics, who say a man who refuses an ugly old woman out of self-control does not even deserve thanks.

Montaigne says we should not claim the pleasures of high rank, since our own simpler pleasures are more natural, solid and secure. He argues that even out of ambition alone we should reject the craving for honour and fame, which is so humble that it makes us beg for it from everyone. The Latin quote asks what praise can be sought from a meat market.

Montaigne says that a good deed loses value when it is done for show. The more loudly an action is praised, the less he trusts that it was done for its own sake. He prefers good actions done quietly, which are only noticed later by others and admired for themselves.

Montaigne says that his task was only to keep things going and maintain what already existed, which goes unnoticed. He notes that new ideas are admired but are unwelcome in his age, and that holding back from action can be as admirable as acting. He is grateful that circumstances suited his temperament.

Montaigne says that no one would wish for illness just so a doctor could show his skill, and a doctor who wished for a plague to practise his art would deserve punishment. He adds that he has never wanted public troubles to raise his own standing as a ruler, and has always worked for peace and calm in the city.

Montaigne says that even if others do not credit him for the calm and order of his administration, he still wants his share of the good luck behind it. He would rather his successes come from God's favour than from his own skill. He admits he is unfit for public office and does not much mind, or try to fix, that unfitness, given the life he has chosen.

Montaigne says he has done about as well as he expected in his work, and better than he promised the people he dealt with, since he usually promises less than he can deliver. He believes he has left no offence or hatred behind, and he never aimed to leave regret or longing in them. The Latin quotation is Virgil's line from the Aeneid, where Aeneas, trusting a calm sea, is warned that the sea can turn treacherous.

People naturally want to know things. When reason cannot reach knowledge, they turn to experience instead. The Latin quotation says that experience, through many trials, makes an art and shows the way by example.

Montaigne argues that experience and reason are unreliable guides to truth, because no two things are ever truly alike. Even eggs, the usual example of sameness, differ enough that one man at Delphi could tell each egg apart and identify which hen laid it.

Things made by people never come out exactly alike, because differences creep in on their own. Even the best craftsman cannot make cards so identical that gamblers cannot tell them apart by how they are shuffled. Nature, Montaigne says, never makes two things that are not unlike each other.

Montaigne rejects the idea that many laws can limit judges, since laws can be interpreted as freely as they are written. He adds that trying to end disputes by returning to the exact words of the Bible fails too, because people argue over the meaning of a text as fiercely as they argue over their own ideas. He notes that France already has more laws than the rest of the world combined.

Montaigne argues that laws cannot keep up with human behavior. Lawmakers have written a huge number of specific rules, yet these rules are still far fewer than the endless variety of things people actually do. So judges are left to decide many cases on their own.

Even if one collected a huge number of past events, no new event would match an old one exactly; some difference would always need a different judgment. Human actions keep changing, so they fit fixed rules poorly, and the best rules are the rare, simple, general ones.

Montaigne says that nature gives simple peoples better and happier lives than the ones people build for themselves. He points to the Golden Age of the poets, a legendary time of innocence, and to nations that still live without civilised ways. Some such peoples, he adds, settle disputes by asking the first traveller who passes by, or by choosing a judge on the spot on market day.

Montaigne argues that the wisest judges should decide each case on its own facts, without being bound by past examples or their results, since each situation needs its own fitting answer. As a supporting example, he notes that King Ferdinand banned law students from going to the new American colonies, fearing lawsuits would spread there, a view he says Plato shared.

Why does ordinary language, clear in everyday use, become confused in wills and contracts? Montaigne suggests it is because legal experts pick out unusual words and build complicated sentences, weighing every syllable and every fine distinction, until their texts are so tangled that no clear rule or certain meaning can be drawn from them.

Montaigne compares fine-spun argument to quicksilver: the harder children press it, the more it splits into tiny beads that cannot be counted. In the same way, subtle hair-splitting in learning multiplies doubts and disputes, just as digging the soil makes it more fertile.

Montaigne says that endless commentary on old legal and philosophical texts causes more confusion than clarity. Each new interpretation of a writer such as Ulpian, Aristotle or Bartolus breaks up the truth further. Writers should aim to be understood, and later commentators who cannot make the originals clear only add to the problem.

Montaigne says that when people discuss one subject they split it into endless parts, so it never settles into a single view. No two people, and not even the same person at different times, hold exactly the same opinion. He also finds doubts most often in plain matters that others have passed over, just as some horses stumble most on smooth ground.

Montaigne says that commentaries make doubts and confusion greater, not smaller. Each commentator leaves a text harder to understand than before, and people never agree that a book needs no more explanation. The law shows this most clearly, since endless interpretations still never end the need for more.

Montaigne asks whether all the laws and lawyers have brought any real progress toward peace, or whether they are still as needed as when the law was new. He argues they only cloud understanding and trap the mind. He says the mind, left to itself, keeps twisting and tangling itself until it suffocates, like a silkworm in its own silk.

Human reason, the passage says, seems to see some faint light or truth from far away. But as it hurries toward it, so many difficulties and new questions get in the way that it loses its direction and grows dizzy. Montaigne compares this to Aesop's dogs, which tried to drink the sea to reach a floating body and choked.

Crates said Heraclitus's writings needed a strong swimmer, or the depth of their learning would drown the reader. Montaigne's point is that being satisfied with what others or we have discovered is due to weakness. A sharper mind always finds more to pursue, and the search never ends. Being content means either the mind has grown short-sighted or it has tired.

A noble mind never settles within its own limits. It keeps reaching past what it can do, moving restlessly and without fixed aim, and it is fed by wonder and by puzzles. Apollo, the god of oracles, was said to speak in riddles on purpose, to stir the mind rather than satisfy it.

The lines compare life to a running stream. Each wave follows the one before and is pushed on by the next, so the water is always changing. The stream stays the same brook, yet the water in it is always new.

Montaigne says that people spend more effort explaining earlier explanations than studying the things themselves. Scholars mostly comment on one another, and each new opinion is built on the one before it. So someone at the top of this chain may get more credit than he deserves, since he stands only a little higher than the person just below him.

Montaigne admits he has often talked about himself in his book, and he may have been foolish to do so. He says he criticises others who do the same, since their praise and harsh self-criticism both show self-love. His only excuse is that he writes about himself and his own works, so his subject turns back on itself, though he is unsure others will accept this.

Montaigne says that Luther's teaching caused more arguments over doubts about his views than Luther's own disputes over Scripture did. He adds that many debates are only about words: asked to define a term, one answers with another term, which can be pushed on endlessly. "Calepin" was a famous Latin dictionary of the time.

Montaigne says that explaining one word with another often adds confusion rather than clearing it up. Answering one doubt brings up several more, like the many heads of the Hydra. He gives Socrates and Menon as an example: when asked what virtue is, Menon listed many kinds of virtue, so Socrates said he had brought a swarm instead of one answer.

Things are never exactly the same, and never exactly different, because nature mixes likeness and unlikeness. We could not tell people from animals, or one person from another, without both. So comparisons from past experience are always imperfect, and laws only fit our affairs by being bent to them.

Montaigne argues that if it is hard to set down the moral rules for a single person's own duties, it is even harder to make laws that govern many people. He points to the justice that governs us as proof of human weakness, since it is full of mistakes and inconsistencies.

Montaigne says that mercy and severity are both found so often in justice, and so often faulty, that a fair middle course is rarely seen. He then describes villagers finding a badly wounded man in his forest, still alive and begging for water.

Some people who came upon a murdered man ran away instead of helping him. They feared that if they were found near the body, they would be accused of the crime and ruined, since they had no money or friends to defend them. The speaker says that even a simple act of help would have got them into trouble.

Montaigne notes that many innocent people have been punished without any fault of the judge, and many more cases are never known. He gives an example from his own time: men were condemned to death for a murder, and then the court learned that other men in custody had confessed to it in full detail.

The judges debated whether to stop the execution of a sentence already passed on the first accused men. They worried that reversing a judgment would set a new precedent, and that judges should not be left without the chance to change their minds. In the end, these men were put to death, sacrificed to the rules of legal procedure. A king named Philip then avoided such a problem in another way.

Montaigne describes a judge who discovered, later, that he had passed an unjust sentence. He left the sentence standing to respect legal procedure and paid the condemned man compensation from his own money. Montaigne notes this could repair the harm, unlike his own men who were executed irreparably, and he asks how many sentences have been more wrongful than the crimes they punished.

Montaigne lists old philosophical views that clash with ordinary ideas of right and wrong. Some say small wrongs are needed before a person can do great right, or that justice is only what is useful. Others say nature itself works against justice, that nothing is just by nature but only by custom and law, and that a wise person may commit theft if it benefits him.

Montaigne says he would not willingly place his life and reputation in the hands of a court where his fate depends more on his lawyer's skill than on his own innocence. He would rather face judges who would weigh his good deeds as well as his faults, giving him reason to hope as well as fear. Simply being cleared of blame is not enough reward for a man who has done good.

In China, officials sent by the ruler to inspect the provinces punish those who do their jobs badly. They also reward generously those who do better than ordinary duty requires, giving them gifts as well as pay.

Montaigne says he has never been brought before a judge, in any kind of case, and has never been held in a prison, not even as a visitor. He loves liberty so much that the thought of a jail is unpleasant to him, and he would hate being barred even from a distant land. As long as he can go somewhere openly, he will not hide away.

Montaigne says it would be hard to bear being confined to one corner of the kingdom and barred from its main cities, courts and public roads for opposing the laws. If the laws threatened him, he would leave for somewhere else. In the civil wars, he says, his only care is to keep his freedom to travel.

Laws are obeyed not because they are just but simply because they are laws, and that is the hidden source of their authority. Montaigne says they are made by foolish or vain people, often biased, and that no thing is more often or more clearly faulty than the laws.

Montaigne says that people who obey laws only because the laws are just do not really obey them as they should. He adds that French laws are so irregular and confused that they partly encourage disorder, since their confusion seems to excuse both disobedience and careless interpretation and enforcement.

Montaigne argues that however much we learn from other people's examples, it counts for little if we ignore the lessons of our own experience, which is closer to us and enough to teach us what we need. He says he studies himself more than any other subject, and that this is his metaphysics and his physics. The Latin lines that follow are a quotation from the Roman poet Lucretius, asking about the workings of the universe.

Montaigne says he lets himself be led, without much knowledge or care, by the general law of the world. He will understand it when he experiences it. His learning cannot change nature's course, so hoping for an exception is foolish, and worrying about it is an even greater folly, since the law applies to everyone equally.

Montaigne says that a good and capable ruler should free us from worrying about government. He argues that philosophers, though they rightly point us back to nature's rules, distort nature by painting it too grandly and falsely, so they give many different pictures of one unchanging subject.

Just as nature gives us feet to walk, it gives us a plain, calm good sense to guide our lives. This sense is less clever and showy than the kind people invent for themselves, but it does what that kind promises, if a person uses it honestly and in line with nature. Trusting nature in the simplest way is the wisest course.

Montaigne says he would rather understand himself through his own experience than through the books of Cicero. He claims that remembering how far he was carried away by past anger teaches him more about that passion's ugliness than Aristotle's writing does, and gives him a stronger hatred of it.

Remembering past troubles and the small events that moved us from one state to another prepares a person for future changes and helps them understand their own situation. Even Caesar's life, though powerful, was subject to all the same chances of human life, so it serves us as an example. We take from such examples whatever we most need.

When Montaigne is shown that one of his opinions is false, he says he learns less about the particular mistake than about his own weakness and the unreliability of his understanding in general. He uses this lesson to correct his whole way of judging, and he finds that this habit helps him in daily life.

Montaigne says he does not treat a single mistake as one stone to trip over and then forget. He learns to doubt his own steps in general and to watch where he puts them. He also says that his memory, though it confidently insists it is right, has often failed him, and he takes those failures seriously.

Montaigne says that when anyone challenges his memory, he hesitates and will not stake anything important on it, or vouch for it in someone else's affairs. He would rather take the facts from another person than from himself. He adds that others are often unreliable not from forgetfulness but from dishonesty.

Montaigne says that if a person examines how his strong emotions work, he can see them coming and weaken them before they grow. Passions do not strike suddenly; they build up in stages, like a sea that rises slowly before a storm. The Latin quotation, from the Roman poet Virgil, makes the same comparison.

Montaigne says his judgment tries to rule his mind as a judge would. It lets his desires, likes, dislikes, and even his feelings about himself run their own course without changing them. If it cannot shape those other parts, it at least keeps itself from being corrupted by them.

Montaigne says that the old advice "know yourself," carved on the temple at Delphi, is a very important instruction, since he takes it to hold everything the god had to teach. He adds that Plato saw prudence (good judgment) as simply carrying out this command, and that Socrates shows the same idea in Xenophon. He also notes that the difficulties of a subject are only seen by those who have entered it.

Knowing that you do not know takes some intelligence, just as you must push a door to learn whether it is locked. Montaigne cites Plato's puzzle that neither the knower nor the non-knower needs to inquire. He adds that when everyone feels satisfied with their own wisdom, this shows that no one truly knows, as Socrates showed Euthydemus.

Montaigne says that the more he studies, the more he sees how much there is still to learn. He credits his own admitted weakness with making him modest, willing to accept what he was taught to believe, and cautious in his opinions. He dislikes people who are arrogant and sure of themselves, and he says their first statements sound like the language used to set up religions and laws.

Montaigne says that people who insist on their opinions with great confidence show that they lack good sense. He describes a man who keeps arguing firmly even after being proven wrong again and again, as if each defeat only gave him new strength, like the giant Antaeus who grew stronger when he fell to the earth.

Montaigne says that his own experience shows how little humans know, and that this lesson is the most reliable one the world teaches. If readers doubt his example, he points to Socrates, whose ignorance-based wisdom was the model. He adds that Antisthenes, a student of Socrates, said virtue alone makes life happy, except that it needs Socrates' strength.

Montaigne says that his long habit of examining himself has also made him good at judging other people. He claims he can often see his friends' qualities more clearly than they can, and that he has sometimes told them things about themselves they had not noticed.

Montaigne says that when he has taken an interest in a subject, he notices almost everything about him that relates to it, including faces, moods and talk, and he learns from both good and bad examples. He reads his friends by what they do, but he does not sort their many different actions into fixed categories. He quotes a line from Lucretius saying there is no set number of kinds or names for things.

Montaigne says that wise people state their views carefully and in order, piece by piece. He presents his own opinions loosely and by trial, one separate point at a time, because he sees things only as far as his everyday experience shows him. He thinks ordinary minds like his cannot hold a connected whole, while true wisdom is a solid, complete structure where every part fits together.

Montaigne says that he leaves to painters the task of sorting out the endless variety of human faces and of fixing our changeable nature. He finds it hard enough to connect one of our actions with another, and even harder to describe any single action by one main quality, because each action looks different from different sides.

Montaigne says that a remark about Perseus, king of Macedon, who could not be known even to himself because his mind never settled on one way of life, seems to describe almost everyone. He has also seen a man like this, whose behavior swung between extremes without any steady course or single clear quality.

Montaigne says that few people can take honest criticism without resentment, so those who offer it show real friendship, since it means risking offence for our good. He also thinks it is harsh to judge someone by their faults when those outweigh their virtues. He notes that Plato required knowledge, goodwill and boldness in anyone who would examine another person's soul.

Montaigne says he would rather not know things that would bind him to others. He claims he could have guided his master's behaviour, had he wished, through plain honest speech rather than through school-taught lessons, which he says he does not understand and which he has never seen truly reform anyone.

A ruler should judge the people around him honestly, one by one, and tell him what ordinary people really think of him, against his flatterers. Even Alexander, a great king and philosopher, could not defend himself against such flatterers, whom the passage calls the court's rabble.

Montaigne says that telling the truth is not always right. Speaking it to a prince can do harm and achieve nothing, even when the speaker means well. He holds that a good reproof can still be badly timed, and that the substance of a matter often matters less than the manner of saying it.

Montaigne describes the ideal personal companion of a great man. He should be of modest rank, so he can speak frankly without fear of losing favour, and mix easily with all kinds of people. Only one such person should hold the post, since more would make the master too familiar and disrespected, and that one must above all keep secrets.

A king should not be trusted when he boasts of his firmness in facing enemy attacks for the sake of his glory, if he cannot bear a friend's frank advice for his own good and improvement. That advice can only sting his ear, and the rest of its effect depends on the king himself.

Kings and other rulers need honest, frank advice more than anyone, because they live in public view. Those around them often hide anything that might turn them from their chosen course. As a result, rulers can end up hated by their people over matters that could have been avoided if they had been warned in time. Their favourites, he adds, care more for themselves than for their master.
Montaigne is saying that when real friendship is offered to a ruler, its duties carry rude and dangerous risks. Doing them well therefore needs strong affection, frankness, and courage.

Montaigne says his essays record his own life, and that his experience of bodily health is the most useful kind he can offer, since it is untouched by learned rules or opinion. He adds that experience counts most in medicine, where reason gives way to it. He cites Tiberius, who held that a man of twenty should know by himself what harms or helps him and manage without doctors.
Socrates told his followers to take care of their health above all. He added that a sensible man who watches his exercise and diet should know better than any doctor what is good or bad for him.

Montaigne notes that medicine relies on experience, and he recalls Plato's view that a good doctor must have suffered every disease he treats. He adds, with irony, that doctors should catch the pox if they want to cure it, and says he would only trust a doctor who had been through it.

Montaigne says that some teachers can describe a skill or illness well, like a painter drawing a ship from a safe table, yet they fail when faced with the real task. He compares them to a town crier who lists a lost animal's features but would not recognize the animal if it were brought to him.

Montaigne says that the arts meant to keep body and soul healthy promise much but deliver least. In his time, the people who practise them show fewer results than anyone else. At most, they sell medicines; they cannot truly be called physicians.

Montaigne says he has lived long enough to describe the habits that have shaped his life. He offers them as a trial for anyone who wants to test them, and he lists only the habits he knows best and that have held the strongest hold on him. He adds that none of his habits has stayed the same under changing conditions.

Montaigne says he keeps the same routine, food, bed and drink whether he is sick or well, changing only the amounts to suit his strength and appetite. For him, health means staying undisturbed in his usual way of life. Illness pulls him away from it, and following doctors' rules would pull him away in another direction.

Montaigne says that habit shapes a person's life in whatever way it likes, and that people who are used to something are not harmed by it. He gives an example: people a few steps away think the night air, which seems harmful to us, is a silly idea, and even our own boatmen and farmers laugh at the fear.

Montaigne notes that people are used to different customs. A German falls ill on a mattress, an Italian on a feather bed, and a Frenchman without curtains or fire. A German once criticised French hearths, using the same arguments the French use against German stoves, because the smothered heat and smell bother those not used to them.

Montaigne says that the people he is writing about heat their homes evenly, without flame, smoke or drafts from chimneys, so their method compares well with ours. He asks why we do not copy the Roman method, where fires were lit outside the building and heat ran through pipes in the walls.

A German praises his city to Montaigne, then worries that the stoves and fires of other places will give Montaigne a heavy head. The German says he heard this complaint elsewhere and blames it on those places, since he cannot notice it at home. Montaigne says that fire's heat weakens and dulls him, so he prefers other ways to keep warm.

Montaigne says that customs differ widely between nations, and what seems strange to one people can be ordinary or even prized by another. He then asks what to make of people who accept only what is printed in books, and who trust nothing that is not written down or old enough.

Montaigne says that writing gives foolish ideas more weight than they deserve, since people write as carelessly as they speak. So he trusts a friend's spoken account as much as a book by an ancient author, and treats what he has personally seen as equal to what others have written.

Montaigne argues that truth does not become better because it is old, just as virtue is not greater for lasting longer. He criticises people who rely on borrowed examples from ancient or scholarly sources, saying such examples are no more fruitful now than in Homer's or Plato's time. He asks whether people seek more credit from quoting authorities than from the truth itself, and suggests that proofs taken from everyday local experience would serve better.

Montaigne says that people fail not because of a lack of authority to be believed, but because they cannot see what is in front of them and use it. He argues that ordinary, familiar things, if their meaning were understood, could give the greatest examples, especially about human actions.

Montaigne describes a gentleman he met who says he once rode from Madrid to Lisbon in summer heat without drinking anything. The man is healthy, and he sometimes goes a month or a year without drinking. When he feels thirst, he waits for it to pass, and he drinks more from whim than from need or pleasure.

A learned Frenchman, wealthy and surrounded by noisy servants, said the din helped him. Being driven by the noise, he withdrew further into himself and concentrated more on his thinking. Seneca, the Roman writer, said something similar about himself.

Montaigne says that a man who studied at Padua worked so long beside street noise that he grew used to it and even found it useful for his work. He gives Socrates' reply to a complaint about a noisy wife: he was used to it, like people used to the creak of water wheels. Montaigne says he himself is the opposite: easily disturbed, so a fly's buzz can ruin his concentration.

Seneca gave up eating meat for a year, and dropped the habit so he would not seem to follow a new religion's rules. He also slept only on hard beds that did not sink under weight, a habit he kept into old age. Montaigne notes that his own age would call such hardness weakness, though Seneca's time saw it as toughness.

Montaigne compares his own way of life with that of his labourers, and says the gap is as wide as between himself and the Scythians and Indians. He took in poor boys as servants, but they soon left his household to go back to their old life. One of them preferred picking mussels from a sewer to the comforts he was offered.

Custom, meaning habit or long-established practice, shapes people strongly. Even beggars have their own pleasures and order, and custom can mould us into whatever form it chooses. Its most valuable lesson, Montaigne says, is that it teaches us to change and vary.

Montaigne says that he is flexible and not stubborn, and that he changes his habits easily. He holds that a young man should sometimes go against his own rules to keep his energy alive, since a life run strictly by rule is dull and weak. The Latin quotation mocks people who consult a book or their star chart before every small act.

Montaigne says a man who is too fussy, or stuck to one fixed way of doing things, is hard to be with and a poor companion. He should be able to do what others around him do, and a soldier especially must be ready for every kind of life. Someone who cannot or will not join in should stay at home.

Montaigne says that although he was raised to be free and independent, age has made him set in certain habits. Custom has fixed them in him without his noticing, so that giving them up now feels excessive. He cannot sleep in the daytime, eat between meals, skip breakfast, or go to bed without a long gap after eating unless he forces himself.

Montaigne lists his personal habits and fussy preferences, things he feels he cannot do without. These include eating and drinking at set times, keeping his head covered, and having clean gloves, a shirt, a napkin and bed curtains. He says he could manage without a tablecloth but not without a clean napkin.

Montaigne says he dislikes eating with a spoon or fork and prefers his own napkin and cup. He compares himself to the soldier Marius, who grew particular about his drink. He would rather not drink from shared glasses or metal ones, preferring clear glass, and he wants his eyes to enjoy it too.

Montaigne says that some of his habits come from custom, and others from his own nature. His body cannot take more than two full meals a day, and skipping a meal makes him bloated and dulls his appetite. He also finds night air harmful, and on long night travel he becomes sick before dawn.

Montaigne says he sleeps while others eat breakfast and wakes refreshed. He had heard that night dew falls only early in the night, but a lord he knew, who avoided the dew of late afternoon and scorned the night dew, persuaded him more by his experience than by argument. He wonders whether mere doubt and questioning can really change a person's mind.

Those who give in completely to their ailments ruin themselves. Montaigne feels sorry for young, healthy men who, on their doctors' advice, shut themselves away from ordinary social life. He argues it is better to put up with a cough than to lose such useful company for good, and that keeping one's habits as long as possible often strengthens the body.
A person should follow good rules closely but should not become a slave to them. The only exception is a rule where being bound to it does real good, if any such rule exists.

Montaigne says that kings, philosophers and ladies all relieve themselves like anyone else, and that his own private life is free of the formal ceremony public figures must keep. He advises himself to keep to set hours, as he has done by habit, but not to tie himself to one particular place or seat, which makes it tiresome to sit so long. He adds that cleanliness is a reasonable concern in such matters.

Montaigne says he dislikes being interrupted when his body does its natural business. Many soldiers, he notes, have trouble with their bowels, but he and his body keep to a regular schedule: he goes at once on getting out of bed, unless urgent business or illness gets in the way.

Montaigne argues that sick people are safest if they keep to the way of life they grew up with. Any sudden change harms them, even a change that would seem healthy. He gives examples: people used to chestnuts, milk, or walking would be harmed by a new diet or confinement that suits others.

The Latin verses say that people are forced to hang their minds on everyday things, and in order to keep living they stop really living. Montaigne's point in the English line is that these cares, or the treatments he is speaking of, at least prepare sick people for death by slowly wearing down their hold on life.

Montaigne says that, in sickness and in health, he has usually followed his own appetites and desires. He would rather not treat one illness with a cure that causes its own trouble, since a cure worse than the disease just adds a second evil.

Montaigne argues that since we always risk being wrong, we may as well take the pleasure first and accept the risk of error afterward. He notes that most people think only what is painful is worthwhile. He gives his own case: when his stomach stopped liking spicy sauces, his taste changed to match.

Montaigne says that wine, which he dislikes, always harms him when he is sick, and that food he eats with enjoyment never hurts him. So he has let his pleasure outweigh medical rules. As a young man he also indulged his strongest desires without restraint.

Montaigne says he fell in love very young, before he could choose or understand what he was doing, so he cannot remember a time before it. He compares his case to Quartilla, a woman in an old Latin poem who could not remember when she stopped being a girl.

Doctors often change their treatment to match the strong cravings of sick people, and this usually works well. Montaigne says that the imagination is the strongest part of us and that it causes most of our worst troubles. He ends with a Spanish saying, "God defend me from myself," meaning that we are our own worst enemy.

Montaigne says that when he is sick he wishes he had some desire to satisfy, and no medical rules would easily stop him from pursuing it. When he is well, he finds little left to hope for or want. He thinks it would be a pity for a person to become so weak that he has no wishes left at all.

Medicine, Montaigne says, is not a fixed science, so there is always another authority to turn to. Physicians disagree with each other and change their advice with place and season, so if one doctor forbids sleep, wine or certain foods, another can be found who allows them.

Montaigne describes two cases where doctors disagreed about treatment. A sick man suffered terrible thirst on a doctor's advice, and another doctor mocked that advice as harmful. A physician who starved himself to fight kidney stone died, and his colleagues argued the starvation had made the disease worse.

Montaigne says that talking hurts him when he is ill or wounded, as much as any careless act of his own would. His voice is loud and strained, so it tires him, and when he lowered it to a whisper for important men, they often asked him to speak more quietly.

A man in a Greek school was asked to speak more quietly. He replied that the other should tell him what tone to use, and the answer given was that he should take his tone from the listener's ears. Montaigne says this is a good saying if it means to fit your speech to the subject and the listener, but not if it means only that the listener should be satisfied.

Montaigne says that the tone and manner of his voice carry much of his meaning, and that he must control it so he is understood. He wants his voice to do more than reach a listener; he wants it to strike him. He adds that a servant could fairly tell him to speak more quietly, since he hears well enough.

Speech is shared between the speaker and the listener, so the listener must get ready for what is said, much as a tennis player readies himself by watching the striker. The writer also says that impatience causes our own ruin, and that troubles have a natural course, from onset to end.

Diseases have a natural course with a set length, like the lives of animals. Forcing them to stop early only makes them last longer and grow worse. So, following Crantor, we should neither fight illness stubbornly nor give in without courage, but yield to it as its nature and ours allow.

Montaigne says that his illnesses got better when he left them alone, and some serious ones went away by themselves, without doctors or medicine. He thinks Nature understands her own affairs better than people do. He adds that people die whether or not they are treated, and that examples from others can be read in many different ways.

Montaigne says he will take any pleasant remedy, since pleasure is a real benefit. He also says that his illnesses, like colds and heart palpitations, have worn away over time, and that such ailments yield better to gentle treatment than to force. We must accept the natural limits of our state in life.

Human beings are born to age, weaken, and fall ill, whatever medicine can do. The writer says the Mexicans teach their children to endure this without complaint, and he calls it unjust to grieve over what everyone must suffer. An old man who prays to stay healthy, as if to be young again, is asking for something foolish.

Montaigne argues that for a body worn down by age and illness, medicine cannot restore health. Doctors can only patch it up and delay death for a short time. He adds that Plato did not think a god of healing would bother to prolong such a weak life.

The lines are Latin verse, quoted by Montaigne from Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (a Roman poem). They say that a man propping up a falling wall leans it against many supports. But the day comes when the whole structure gives way, and the props fall down with everything else. The point is that outside aid cannot save a thing from its fate.

Life is made of opposites, like the tones of music, so we must accept both good and bad, since neither can be removed without harming the whole. Trying to fight what nature makes necessary is as foolish as Ctesiphon kicking at his mule, a story Montaigne takes from Plutarch.

Montaigne says he seldom asks doctors about the changes he feels in his body. When he was sick, doctors frightened him with grim predictions and bossy pronouncements, threatening pain and death. These threats shook him and disturbed his thinking, but they did not overturn his judgment.

Montaigne says he would like his imagination to be calm and free of worry, and that he should help it along with comforting untruths if he can. His mind is suited to this job. He gives an example: his imagination tells him that having kidney stone is good for him, and that the wear of old age is natural and that his body is now starting to break down.

This is Montaigne speaking of his kidney stone, a painful illness of old age. He says it is a common burden that comes with age and nothing unusual. He takes comfort in the fact that many men of high rank suffer from it too, and he calls it a noble disease.

Montaigne writes that others suffer strict diets and bad-tasting medicines, paying doctors and making vows to the healing god Aesculapius just to pass a little gravel (kidney stones). He says his own better health is simply good luck. He passes stones naturally and keeps his composure in company.

Montaigne describes his bladder stone and his ability to hold urine for hours. He imagines his own mind speaking to him: the disease once frightened him only because it was unknown, and the groans of others made it seem worse. It is a punishment, his mind says, aimed at the body parts he has sinned with most. The Latin quoted at the end means roughly "A punishment that comes undeserved is painful to bear."

Montaigne is writing about his kidney stone disease as a kind of punishment that is milder than it could be. He says it came late, after the wild years of youth, and hit only a part of life that was already empty. He adds that people's fear of the illness gives him a reputation, and that even if his reason has cured his vanity, his friends still notice some trace of it.

Montaigne describes a sick man who is praised for his strength and patience. Though he sweats, turns pale, vomits blood and passes black urine because of a stone in the bladder, he keeps a calm face and chats with the people around him.

Montaigne is writing to a sick friend or reader who is in pain. He suggests that illness is a kind of school that nature sets us in, something we would never choose, and asks what disease is not dangerous or fatal.

Death does not need illness to happen. A person dies simply because they are alive, and sickness is only one of the roads that lead there. Sometimes illness even delays death, and some diseases do good, just as some wounds do. A stone, Montaigne notes, may last as long as a living person.

Montaigne is speaking to someone who is ill, possibly with a long illness. He says that the illness is more likely to be killed off by the sick person than to kill him, and that the approach of death is a useful reminder. He adds that the sick person no longer has a reason to want to be cured, and that death will soon take him, gently loosening his hold on life.

Here, the speaker says that the illness of old age does not press down on a person all the time, as other sicknesses do in old men. Instead, it gives warnings and lessons now and then, with long rests in between, so the person can think them over at their own pace. This lets the person judge their whole condition, good and bad, and face it with courage.

Our lives swing between good and bad days, sometimes within one day. Because we often come close to death and step back, we may one day be taken by it without warning. Illness is fair, since it shares our time with health, so no one can reasonably complain of it.

Montaigne says that misfortune has repeatedly struck him with the same kinds of blows, and this repetition has trained him to bear them. Since his natural memory is weak, he keeps a written record instead, noting what he has learned from experience.

Montaigne records each new symptom of his illness in writing. Over time he has seen almost every kind of case, so when something alarming happens, he looks back through these notes, like the Sibylline leaves (prophecy books of ancient Rome), and always finds a past sign that gives him comfort. Habit also makes him expect better times ahead.

Montaigne reasons that his illness, a kidney complaint with stone, will probably continue as it has, since it has run for so long. He notes that its attacks are either mild and long, or sharp and short, which suits his quick temperament. His kidneys went a long time without change, and he has lived a long while since they altered.

Montaigne suggests that his illnesses may ease with time, just as good things pass. He reasons that as his aging body digests less well and changes how it handles waste, his kidneys may stop turning that waste into stones, and nature may find another way to clear it.

Montaigne says that the relief after a sudden, severe kidney-stone attack is the sweetest feeling he knows. When the stone passes and pain ends, health returns at once, and he finds it more pleasant because the sickness was so close that he can feel the contrast between the two.

Montaigne says that pain seems to exist mainly to serve pleasure and rest, much as the Stoics claimed vices exist to make virtue stand out. He gives Socrates as an example: once his chains were removed, Socrates enjoyed the itch the chains had caused and saw how closely pain and pleasure are linked.
Montaigne says that certain things are so linked by a necessary connection that each one brings about the next. He suggests that the writer Aesop should have turned this observation into a fable.

Montaigne says that the real trouble with many illnesses is not how bad they feel while they last, but how slowly a person recovers. Recovery takes a long time, with weakness and fear throughout, and many small steps must be passed before a person is allowed normal activities again. Even then, a relapse into another illness is likely.

Montaigne says that kidney stone is unusual because it leaves the body completely once it passes. Other illnesses leave damage behind that makes the body open to new ones. Since his stone attacks, he feels free of all other ailments and has had no fever.
