Montaigne argues that his frequent vomiting, his dislikes of certain foods, and the strict fasts he is forced to keep all clear the body of harmful humours, and that his kidney stones do the same. He says that the cost of this cure is not too high, since many harsh medical treatments can kill a patient. So he regards the stone as a kind of medicine.

Montaigne says his illness, kidney stone, leaves him free to live as he likes if he has the nerve to endure it. He says he rode horseback for ten hours during its worst attacks. He suggests that someone with this complaint needs no strict diet and can play, run, and dine freely, even with indulgence doing more good than harm. Other diseases, such as the pox, gout, or hernia, impose stricter rules.

Montaigne is describing the difference between minor pain and serious illness. A sharp pain in the skin, he says, leaves the mind, the will, and the body's limbs under our own control and even wakes us up. Fevers, epilepsy, and severe headaches, however, do not reach the soul at all.

Montaigne says that when a body fails, the fault lies with the body itself. He argues that a hard kidney stone cannot be dissolved by drinks, so once it moves, the only option is to let it pass, and it will come out on its own.

Montaigne is describing the disease of kidney stone, which he has suffered from. Unlike other illnesses, its cause, course and location are obvious, so there is no need for doctors to puzzle over it. The senses reveal what it is and where it is.

Montaigne says that he uses arguments, weak and strong, to calm his mind about his illness, as Cicero did about old age, and he will try new ones if these fail. He describes passing pure blood from his kidneys with little movement, yet he still rides hunting with energy. He counts this as acceptable because it brings only a dull heaviness and discomfort.

Montaigne describes his kidney stone as something slowly wearing away his body, which he accepts with some quiet satisfaction. He says he will not keep checking his pulse or urine for signs of new trouble, since the pain will come soon enough. Fearing pain, he adds, is already a kind of suffering.

Nature's ways are hidden, and people who claim to predict her course, including through their own skills, are often wrong. The only sure sign of coming death is old age. For other events, the author says he judges only by what he feels, not by reasoning, and he will wait with patience.

Montaigne says that people who follow many doctors' opinions and remedies often suffer from fear alone, even with no bodily pain. He once described symptoms to doctors while he was perfectly well, heard their grim verdicts calmly, and so felt more grateful to God and more convinced that medicine is worthless.

Montaigne says that young people should be encouraged above all to be active and alert, since life is movement. He describes himself as slow to rise, eat and go to bed, and he blames long morning sleep for past illnesses. He notes that Plato was angrier at too much sleep than at too much drinking.

Montaigne says he likes to sleep alone and rather heavily covered, like kings, and that as he has aged he uses cloths laid on his feet and stomach for warmth. He notes that people criticised Scipio for sleeping too much, suggesting they simply resented that he had no fault to find. He admits he is fussy only about his bed; otherwise he adapts to circumstances.

Montaigne says he sleeps eight or nine hours at a stretch, even now in middle age. He is trying to cut down on this love of sleep by force of habit, and he finds that it works. He can go without much sleep when needed, handles long journeys well, and has grown to prefer gentle exercise over sweaty, strenuous activity.

Montaigne says he can walk all day without tiring, but he has always preferred riding on paved roads, since walking in dirt muddies him and crowds in the streets push him around because he is short. He also likes to rest with his feet raised as high as or higher than his seat.

Montaigne lists what makes the military life attractive. He names two sources of honour: the courage the profession requires and the protection of one's country. He also praises its company, its frank and informal way of living, and its variety of activities.

Montaigne says that the sound of martial music, the honour of soldiering, and even its hardships are pleasing to the soldier. He adds that Plato thought such hardships so slight that he let women and children share them. A man who volunteers for risky exploits, judging them by their glory and worth, finds that even dying in battle is a fitting use of his life. The Latin quoted means "it is fine to die in arms."

Montaigne argues that it is weak to fear dangers that many people face together, since courage grows in company, even among children. He adds that death from illness in bed is no easier than death in battle, so someone who has trained himself to bear everyday hardships does not need extra courage to become a soldier.

Montaigne says he cannot recall ever having an itch, though scratching is a pleasant act that is always within reach. The pleasure, he adds, is soon followed by regret. He scratches mostly his ears, which sometimes itch.

Montaigne describes his good health. His senses, stomach, head and breathing have stayed sound, even during high fevers. He has some short spells of health almost as good as in his youth, but he does not claim the same energy and liveliness, which he says it is not reasonable to expect at his age.
Montaigne says that his face and eyes show his health before he himself notices any change. His friends often feel sorry for him before he feels ill, and his mirror does not alarm him.

Montaigne describes times in his youth when his complexion looked unhealthy and seemed to foretell trouble, though nothing serious followed. Doctors found no bodily cause and blamed his mind or a hidden worry, but they were wrong. He wishes his body would obey his mind's discipline as well as his mind obeys him.

Montaigne says that at that time his mind was not only free of worry but also full of joy and contentment. He explains this as coming partly from his natural temperament and partly from his own plan for living. The Latin quotation means that the diseases of a sick mind do not infect the body.

Montaigne says that his mind has often kept his body from sinking when he is ill. Even during a long fever, his mind stayed calm or cheerful. He would rather bear physical weakness than the agitated passions he sees in others, and he accepts that he can no longer run, only crawl.

Montaigne says his imagination does not trouble him. His dreams are rare, and they tend to be silly rather than sad, arising from pleasant thoughts. He believes dreams reveal our inclinations, but only someone with skill can interpret them. The Latin quotation says it is no surprise that what people think about and do while awake appears in their sleep.

Montaigne reports several views and observations about dreams. Plato said that wise people can read the future from dreams, and Montaigne names Socrates, Xenophon and Aristotle as reliable witnesses to such cases, though he does not know whether it is true. He notes that some people are said never to dream, that Pythagoras used diet to shape dreams, and that his own dreams are calm, while some he knew were badly disturbed, one even walking in his sleep on rooftops.

The writer rarely chooses his food at a meal. He takes whatever dish is closest and dislikes swapping it for another. He prefers a few dishes to a mixed jumble, and he rejects the view of Favorinus, an ancient Greek writer, that the best food should be taken away and replaced with something else.

Montaigne describes his own food tastes. He says a supper is poor unless it serves many kinds of fowl, and he likes salt meat but prefers unsalted bread, which his baker makes for him against local custom. As a child, he refused sweets, which adults tried to correct.

Montaigne's tutor saw his dislike of rich, delicate food as mere fussiness about taste. He argues that curing a child of picky tastes in simple food also cures the habit of spoiling one's palate. People who claim simplicity while secretly wanting fancy dishes are, he says, showing a refined kind of luxury, and refusing to enjoy what others enjoy and being fussy about food is the core of that vice.

Montaigne says it is better to train your appetites toward things that are easy to get, and that binding yourself to need is always a fault. He gives an example: a kinsman who had lived on the galleys (rowing ships) lost the habit of using a bed and undressing to sleep, and Montaigne calls him overnice, meaning fussy or overly particular.

Montaigne says that if he had sons, he would wish them the upbringing he had. His father sent him as a baby to a poor village and raised him in very simple, ordinary ways. He quotes a Latin saying that a well-disciplined stomach is a large part of freedom.

Montaigne advises fathers not to shape their children's upbringing themselves, but to let chance and natural custom train them toward plainness and hardship. He also explains that his own father chose poor people as his godparents, so that Montaigne would feel bound to those who most needed help.

Montaigne says he feels more kindly toward ordinary people, either because it is more honourable to stoop to them or from a natural pity he feels strongly. He also says he would blame a faction in the wars more harshly if it were winning, and that seeing it defeated and ruined would make him more sympathetic to it.

Montaigne admires Cheilonis, a Spartan princess who was daughter and wife to kings. When her husband Cleombrotus gained power and her father Leonidas was driven into exile, she stayed with her father in his misfortune rather than side with the victor.
A woman, whose side in a war was losing, changed her loyalty to match her husband's cause. She stayed with him to the end, as he fell, because she felt she had to stand with whoever needed her most.

Montaigne says he is more inclined to copy Flaminius, who helped those who most needed help rather than those who could repay him. He is less inclined to copy Pyrrhus, who fawned on the powerful and bullied the weak.

Montaigne says that long meals trouble him, and that he eats steadily while seated, so he likes to sit on after the others finish. He enjoys listening to conversation there, as long as he does not have to talk himself. He finds talking after a full meal tiring and harmful, while arguing and speaking aloud before dinner suits him well.

The ancient Greeks and Romans gave long hours, often most of the night, to meals. They ate and drank slowly and used the time for talk worth having. Modern people, Montaigne says, rush through everything, including eating.

Montaigne says that he does not want food he cannot see, so others can easily keep him from harmful dishes. Once food is in front of him, though, he gives in, so when he plans to fast he must be kept away from supper and given only a small set portion. When his stomach is upset, he orders his cook to change how a dish is prepared, and his household knows this means he will not eat it.

Montaigne says he likes meat cooked lightly and kept until it is well aged, even nearly spoiled for some kinds. Hardness is the only quality that bothers him; he is otherwise easygoing about food. He finds fish too fresh and too firm, and he says this is not because of bad teeth.

Montaigne says that dying in stages is a kindness of God, and that old age is the one advantage of this. Parts of his body have already died, some are half dead, and a tooth fell out painlessly when its natural life ended.

Montaigne says he is slowly fading away, and he refuses to picture his decline as a sudden drop from a great height. He finds comfort in thinking that his death will be just and natural, so he would be asking for an unfair favour from fate to hope for more. He also says that people wrongly believe men once lived longer and were taller.

Montaigne says Solon set the normal span of life at seventy years. He prefers moderate measures and so does not expect an unusually long old age. He adds that whatever follows nature's course should be welcomed, citing a Latin saying that all things done according to nature are to be counted as good.

Montaigne says that death caused by wounds or disease is violent. Death that comes with old age, he says, following Plato, is the easiest of all and somewhat pleasant. He adds a Latin line: force takes life from the young, but ripeness takes it from the old.

Death is present in life from the start, as decay runs alongside us as we age. Montaigne compares portraits of himself at different ages and finds his present self less like his earlier self than he would be like himself at death. He says it is too much to let nature wear us out so far that we must hand our bodies over to artificial help.

Montaigne describes his own eating habits and how they shift over time. He likes most sauces though his father disliked them, and he cannot say for sure which meats upset him. He notes that his tastes change without a clear cause, such as with radishes or wine, and that moon phases and seasons seem to make no difference to him.

Montaigne says he loves fish so much that he eats it on fast days and meat on feast days, reversing the usual rule. He also believes fish is easier to digest than meat. He will not eat meat and fish together at one meal, because the two seem too different from each other to mix.

Montaigne sometimes skipped meals for two reasons. One was to make his appetite sharper for the next day, so he could enjoy plenty more fully. The other was to keep his body and mind clear for some task, since a full stomach dulls both.

Montaigne dislikes pairing the goddess Venus with the god Bacchus, who he sees as a belching drunkard. He agrees with Epicurus that company matters more than food. He also praises Chilo for asking who the other guests would be before accepting an invitation.

Montaigne says he enjoys meals most when they are shared with company, and he prefers to eat somewhat less often but to eat when he is hungry. He refuses to starve himself on small, strict meals to follow a medical routine. Older men, he adds, should eat whenever a good chance comes, rather than wait on predictions about the future.

Montaigne says that keeping to one fixed routine, such as a set fasting diet, makes the body grow used to it. After about six months, the only result is that a person loses the freedom to live another way without harm.

Montaigne says he does not dress warmer in winter than in summer, wearing only thin silk stockings on his legs. He admits he has added extra warmth to his head and belly when colds or colic troubled him. But his illnesses soon get used to these measures and ignore his usual remedies, so he must keep adding more layers.

Montaigne is describing how people who follow strict medical diets end up adding ever more rules to their daily routine. Each new precaution, like wearing animal skins or an extra cap, leads to another, and he says this only wears a person down. He refuses to start such a course himself, and he warns that once someone has taken on one new habit, changing it again is wasted effort.

Montaigne says that the ancients were right to skip dinner and eat in the evening, since it kept the day free for work. He has found, from his own experience, that eating at midday is better for digestion, and that he rarely feels thirsty, though his mouth is often dry.

Montaigne says he drinks only when thirsty after eating, and well into the meal. In summer, at a tasty meal, he goes beyond the three glasses Augustus allowed himself, and when needed drinks a fifth glass, about three half-pints.

Montaigne says he likes to drink wine from small glasses and to drink it all at once, which others avoid. He usually waters his wine, using half or a third water. At home the water is mixed in hours before serving, following an old custom his father's doctor had prescribed. He notes that the custom is said to have started with Cranabs, a king of Attica.

Montaigne says children should drink no wine until about sixteen or eighteen. He holds that the most common way of living is the most fitting, and that people should avoid being peculiar in their habits. He would dislike a German who waters his wine as much as a Frenchman who drinks it undiluted, since common custom decides such matters.

Montaigne says he dislikes mist and smoke and avoids them. He had the chimneys and privies in his house repaired first, because they were the usual faults of old buildings. He also names dust as a trouble of war, and says his own breathing is easy and his colds rarely reach his lungs.

Montaigne says he dislikes summer heat more than winter cold. Heat is harder to escape than cold, the sun beats on his head, and bright light hurts his eyes so much that he cannot sit at dinner facing a blazing fire.

Montaigne says that when he read a lot, he laid a piece of glass on the page to cut down the glare of the white paper, and it helped his eyes. At fifty-four he still does not use spectacles and sees as well as ever. He notes, though, that reading by evening now strains his sight a little, which he calls a clear step backward.

Montaigne says that aging comes so slowly that he will go nearly blind before he notices his sight failing, and he may lose his hearing while blaming others' voices. Only by tightening the mind to a high pitch can a person feel how their life is slipping away.

Montaigne says his body and mind are both restless. He cannot sit still during a formal service, even when a sermon holds his attention, and his limbs keep moving while others sit stiff and fixed. He always carries a small stick when walking or riding.

Montaigne tells a joke about the philosopher Chrysippus, whose maid said he was drunk only in his legs, because he always kicked them about. He applies it to himself: he has always been restless on his feet, wherever he sits or stands.
Montaigne admits he eats too fast. He often bites his tongue and fingers, and this harms his health and spoils the pleasure of eating. He also loses the chance to talk at the table, which he values.

Pleasures can get in each other's way. Alcibiades, a skilled host, removed music from dinners so that it would not spoil good conversation. Plato reports his reason: people call musicians only when they lack good talk, which thoughtful men can provide for one another.

Montaigne says that eating well is a real art and a real pleasure, one that great generals and great thinkers have not looked down on. He recalls three meals he enjoyed in his younger years, but he can no longer have such meals now. Each meal's pleasure depends on the mood and health of the person eating it at the time.

Montaigne rejects both extremes: hating bodily pleasures is as unfair as loving them too much. He says a person should neither seek out nor avoid the pleasures nature gives, but accept them. He admits he accepts them rather warmly and readily follow his natural inclinations.

Montaigne says we need not mock the vanity of human opinions, because the mind does this itself. Our restless mind dislikes whatever it considers, and it judges both itself and what it receives in changing ways. The Latin quotation means that whatever you pour into an unclean vessel turns sour.

Montaigne says that even the comforts of life he takes such care over seem to him mostly empty, like wind. He then adds that people are all wind too, while wind is wiser: it bluster and moves about, and is content with its own work without wanting firmness or solidity, which do not belong to it.

Montaigne says that some people think pleasures and pains that exist only in the imagination are the greatest, citing the scale of Critolaus, an ancient Greek philosopher. He admits such imagined pleasures can be striking, but says he is too mixed and heavy by nature to fix on one such object. He prefers to enjoy the ordinary pleasures shared by all people, which engage both mind and senses.

Montaigne is mocking people who claim to refuse bodily pleasures. He asks why such people do not also refuse breathing or daylight, which cost them no effort. He suggests their pretended contentment is only a show put on out of pride or ambition.

Montaigne says that people should not let their minds drift off into abstract thought while their bodies are busy with ordinary things like eating or sharing a bed. The mind should be present and engaged, but not lost in other matters. He criticises philosophers who focused only on the body (Aristippus) or only on the soul (Zeno), and praises the middle path of Plato over Pythagoras's pure contemplation and Socrates's pure action.

Montaigne says that the right balance of mind is found in Socrates, not in the more showy ways of Pythagoras, and that Plato follows Socrates more than Pythagoras. He then gives an example: when he dances, he dances; when he walks alone in a garden, he brings his wandering thoughts back to the walk and to himself.
Nature has made the actions we need to survive also pleasant, so that we are drawn to them both by reason and by desire. The writer says it is wrong to break these natural laws.

Montaigne argues that Caesar and Alexander, even while busy with great affairs, took ordinary bodily pleasures without weakening their minds; he says this strengthened them. He adds that they would have been wiser to treat their ordinary daily life as the main task and their great undertakings as the exception. He mocks people who call a day idle unless it was spent on visible achievements, asking whether such people have not lived at all.

Montaigne says that managing one's own life well is the most important work a person can do, more than any public or great task. He also holds that nature shows itself equally in every station, whether in plain view or hidden, so greatness in a big office is not needed to display one's worth.
Managing your own conduct well is worth more than writing books. Knowing how to rest calmly is worth more than conquering empires and cities.

Montaigne says that the finest thing a person can do is to live well and with purpose, while power, wealth and building are only minor extras. He admires leaders who can set their cares aside, such as a general who dines and jokes before an assault, or Brutus who reads history during the night of his defeat. Only small minds, he says, are so crushed by their duties that they cannot put them down and pick them up again.

Montaigne says that the Sorbonne theologians, known for their wine and feasts, have good reason to enjoy their dinners. They spend the morning on serious study, and that gives them a clear conscience. He says this conscience makes the meal taste better, as the wise have always lived.

Montaigne says that the two Catos, famous for their strict virtue, still accepted the natural pleasures of life such as wine and love. He cites the Stoic view that a wise man should enjoy such pleasures as skillfully as he performs his other duties, quoting the Latin saying that a wise man should have a wise palate too.

Montaigne argues that a strong, noble person looks even better when relaxed and easygoing. He gives two examples: the general Epaminondas joined in songs, sports and dances with young men, and Scipio the elder played childish games like collecting shells and throwing quoits, and these did not lessen their honour.

Montaigne gives examples of great men who kept up pursuits outside their main work. Scipio enjoyed writing comedies about ordinary people even while planning his campaign against Hannibal, and he attended philosophy lectures, which fed his enemies' jealousy in Rome. Socrates, though old, learned dancing and music and thought the time well spent.

Montaigne is describing Socrates, the Greek philosopher, through a set of examples of his courage and endurance. The passage says he once stood still for a whole day and night in deep thought, and that in battle he rescued Alcibiades and Xenophon, his fellow Athenians, when they were in danger.

Montaigne describes Socrates, the Athenian philosopher, through a list of his deeds. He bravely tried to rescue Theramenes from the Thirty Tyrants who were leading him to execution. He resisted a beautiful woman he loved, went barefoot even on ice, and wore the same robe in every season.

Montaigne describes Socrates, who could bear hardship better than anyone, and who ate at a feast no more than at home. He endured poverty, a difficult family, and finally false accusation, imprisonment and poison with the same calm face. Yet he did not feel bound to drink heavily at parties, though he could drink more than any soldier. He happily played childish games and rode a toy horse with children.

Philosophy says a wise man is equally fitting and honourable in every kind of action. Montaigne argues that we should keep before us the image of the great, perfect man, since few examples of full, pure life exist. Copying weak, imperfect models does more harm than good. He adds that it is easier to follow a clear extreme as a guide than the wide middle road.

Greatness of soul, for Montaigne, lies less in striving upward than in managing and limiting oneself. He counts as great whatever is enough, and prefers moderate things to lofty ones. He also holds that living one's own life well is the hardest skill, and that looking down on being alive is the worst of human failings.

If a person's body is unwell, the mind may be kept apart from it if that is possible; otherwise the mind should join in the body's natural pleasures, with moderation. Too much indulgence spoils pleasure, while moderation makes it sweeter. Eudoxus and his followers, who held pleasure to be the highest good, enjoyed it most through their own strict moderation.
Montaigne says that knowing good well also means knowing evil well. Pain is hard to avoid at its start, while pleasure can be avoided at its excessive end.

Plato says that bravery should resist both pain and the tempting pull of pleasure. Both are like two springs of water. A person may drink from them when needed: the first sparingly, as medicine, and the second to quench thirst but never to the point of drunkenness.

Pain, pleasure, love and hatred are the first feelings a child notices. When reason develops later, if a person uses it to direct these feelings toward themselves, that is what Montaigne calls virtue.

Montaigne uses his own words for time. When time is bad or uneasy, he says he "passes it away," getting through it quickly. When time is good, he does not pass it away but lingers over it, savoring it again. In short, he hurries past the bad and dwells on the good.

Montaigne says that people who speak of "passing the time" or "killing time" treat their lives as something to get through and ignore, seeing time as troublesome and worthless. He disagrees: he finds time valuable and useful, even in his old age, when he is now enjoying it.

Nature has given us life in such favourable conditions that, if it becomes troublesome or is wasted, we have only ourselves to blame. The Latin quotation says the fool's life is ungrateful and anxious, always rushing toward the future.

Montaigne says he accepts that his life will end and does not mind losing it, since death is part of life's nature. Because his time is short, he wants to make each part of it count for more by using it fully and intensely.

Montaigne says that other people enjoy good times without really noticing them, while he tries to notice and savour each pleasure as it happens. He even had himself woken during sleep so that he would not miss the feeling of rest. He examines contentment closely rather than passing over it.

Montaigne describes how, when he feels calm or pleasure, he does not let his body enjoy it alone. He also brings his mind in, not to be absorbed in the pleasure, but to take delight in it while staying aware of it. His mind then considers how fortunate it is and gives thanks to God for its inner peace.

A person in good health, whose body works well and feels comfortable, is aware of how fortunate this is. Their mind is calm, free of desire, fear and doubt, and they can look back or ahead without distress. They appreciate this most when they compare it with other people's troubles.

Montaigne is saying that some people, through bad luck or their own mistakes, suffer, and others, like himself, take their good fortune for granted. The second group lets the present go by and waits for hopes and empty images, like the ghosts said to wander after death or dreams that fool a sleeping mind.

Life is like something people chase: it speeds up and lengthens as they pursue it, and the pursuit itself is its own end. Montaigne says he loves life as God gave it, with its needs for food and drink, and would not wish it longer than it is.

Montaigne rejects complaints that the body should be different: that it should need less food, that children should come from some other part of the body, or that it should lack desire and pleasure. He calls such complaints ungrateful and wrong. He accepts nature's gifts gladly, since God, the giver, made everything good.

Montaigne says he prefers the philosophical views that are most down to earth and most true to human nature. He thinks it is childish for philosophy to insist, as a grand argument, that the divine should not be joined with the earthly, or reason with unreasonableness, or strictness with kindness, or honesty with dishonesty.

Montaigne mocks a school of thought that says a wise man should take no real pleasure in sex, even with his own wife. Its only satisfaction, he says, is the sense of having done a proper duty, like putting on boots before a journey. He adds that its followers show no more strength or vigour in that act than in their own teaching.

Montaigne says that Socrates valued bodily pleasure but ranked pleasure of the mind higher, because it is stronger, steadier, easier to get, more varied and more worthy. Pleasure does not go alone: temperance guides it and does not oppose it, and nature is gentle but also wise and just.

Montaigne is searching for nature's true path, which he says has been mixed up with artificial rules by philosophers. He argues that necessary bodily actions are no less worthy than others. Body and mind should support each other rather than be split apart.

Someone who calls the soul's nature the highest good and blames the body's nature as evil still seeks the soul in a fleshly way and shuns the body in a fleshly way. He judges this by human vanity, not by divine truth.

Montaigne argues that nothing in the life God gave us is too small to deserve our attention, and that God has plainly commanded people to live in a way that suits their human condition. He adds that authority, such as the opinions of others, only counts for ordinary, shared judgments, and carries more weight when it is in a foreign language, so he will attack that authority directly here.

Folly is shown by doing necessary things lazily and stubbornly, with the body pulling one way and the mind another, so that a person is torn between opposed urges. Almost anyone, the passage suggests, would call this foolish.

Montaigne suggests that if you asked someone what thoughts had pulled him away from a good meal, you would find them dull. His idle musings are less tasty than the dishes on the table, and most people would do better to sleep than to think so foolishly.

Montaigne says that people whose minds are fixed on God and eternal life, driven by strong religious hope, do not bother with everyday needs and pleasures. They leave the care of the body and its earthly comforts to the body itself.

Montaigne tells the story of Aesop, who saw his master urinating while walking and asked whether a person must also stop to relieve himself while running. The point is that people should use their time well, and that the mind needs little time apart from the body for its basic needs. Trying to leave the body behind and stop being human is, he says, foolish.

Montaigne criticizes people who, when they try to rise above ordinary life, end up sinking into beastly behavior. He finds lofty, otherworldly ideas hard to accept. He says Socrates' trances and talk with spirits are the hardest part of his life to take in, and that Plato seems most down-to-earth where he is called divine. He also suggests the highest branches of learning can be the most earthly.

Montaigne finds nothing so humble and mortal in Alexander's life as his wish to be made immortal. Philotas, one of Alexander's officers, mocked this in a letter after Alexander was declared a god by an oracle. He said he was glad for Alexander's sake, but pitied the men who must live under a ruler who wants more than a human's share.

The Athenian inscription says a person is a god to the degree that he accepts he is a man. Montaigne means that the greatest skill is to enjoy one's own human condition fully. People look for other states because they do not know how to use what they have, and going beyond themselves is as useless as walking on stilts, since you still have to use your own legs.

Even on the highest throne, a person is only sitting on their backside. Montaigne says the best lives are ordinary ones that follow the normal human pattern, without miracles or excess. Old age needs gentler handling, and he asks God for health and wisdom, along with a cheerful, sociable old age.

An editor's note, not Montaigne's own words, says the many classical quotations in the Essays were added over time, mostly in the edition published after his death in 1595. The quotations become fewer in the third book.

Bacon opens with Pilate's question "What is truth?" and notes that some people enjoy restlessness in thought and see fixing a belief as a kind of bondage. He says that even if the ancient schools of this kind have gone, similar thinkers remain, though with less vigor. He then begins to say that finding truth is hard and that truth, once found, can constrain thought, but he has not yet stated his full point.

Bacon notes that some people love lies for their own sake, not for profit or pleasure, and he cannot explain why. He then says that truth is like plain daylight, which does not flatter the world's show as well as candlelight does, though truth is still valuable, like a pearl that shows its worth by day.

Bacon says that a little falsehood mixed into life makes it more pleasant, as a diamond shows its brilliance in varied light. He claims that if people lost their vain opinions, flattering hopes and false valuations, many would be left gloomy, shrunken and dissatisfied with themselves.

Bacon says that a church father once called poetry "the wine of demons," because it stirs the imagination. A lie that merely passes through the mind does little harm; the harm comes when a lie sinks in and takes hold. He then argues that seeking truth, knowing it, and believing it together make up the highest good of human nature.

Bacon describes God's creation of light in three stages: first the light of the senses, then the light of reason, and afterwards the light of God's Spirit, which he keeps giving to his chosen people. He then quotes a poet who says it is pleasant to watch ships tossed on the sea from the safety of the shore.

Bacon compares standing on the high ground of truth to watching a battle from a castle window, and says that viewing other people's errors from there is the greatest pleasure. He adds that this view should be held with pity, not pride. A mind that acts in charity, rests in providence and turns on the poles of truth he calls heaven on earth.

Bacon says that honest, straightforward dealing is the true honor of human nature, even for those who do not practise it. Falsehood in business is like cheap metal mixed into gold or silver coin: it may make the metal easier to work, but it lowers its value. He adds that being found false and treacherous brings more shame than any other vice.

Bacon quotes Montaigne's view that lying is a kind of cowardice: a liar is bold toward God, who sees the lie, yet fearful before men, from whom he hides it. He then says falsehood and broken faith are the worst sins, as shown by the prophecy that Christ will find no faith on earth when he returns.

Men fear death the way children fear the dark, and stories make that fear grow in both cases. Thinking about death as the price of sin and a passage to another world is holy, but fearing it as a natural debt is weak. Religious thoughts about death can also mix in vanity and superstition.

Bacon notes that friars' books advise imagining death by thinking of pain in a fingertip, but he argues that death itself often causes less pain than a hurt limb, since the vital organs feel little. He then quotes a saying that the show of death frightens more than death itself.

Bacon says that the signs of death, such as groaning, pale faces, mourning and funeral rites, make death look terrible. But every strong feeling in a person can overcome the fear of death. So death is not as frightening as it seems, since many other feelings can defeat it. He gives examples: revenge, love, honor, grief and fear each face death in their own way.

Bacon notes that people have died out of pity for a ruler who had killed himself, and that others have chosen death from simple weariness with repeating the same things, even without hardship. He then observes that cheerful people often stay cheerful as death comes near.

Bacon says that many famous Roman emperors faced death as if it were an ordinary part of life, behaving much as they did before. Each man is remembered for a last word or act: a compliment, a joke, a sharp order, or a plain request to get on with business. He ends by saying the Stoics, a school of philosophers who trained people to face death calmly, spent so much effort preparing for it that they made it seem more frightening.

Death is a natural part of life, as natural as birth, and may be no more painful to the dying. A person who dies while deeply committed to a worthy cause feels little of the pain, much as a wounded man in the heat of battle does. Death also brings good fame and ends envy.

Religion holds society together, so it is good when it stays united. Bacon says the ancient pagans had few religious quarrels because their religion was mainly rituals rather than fixed belief. The true God, being jealous, will accept no rivals or partners in worship.

Bacon argues that unity among believers has two benefits, and the first is toward outsiders. Splits and heresies cause more harm to outsiders than bad behavior does. Such divisions keep people from joining the church and push people out of it.

Bacon warns that people who look for Christ in heretical meetings, or only in the outward form of a church, need to hear the call "Go not out" (stay within the church). He cites Paul's point that outsiders who hear many conflicting religious voices will think the believers mad or be turned away, and become scorners.

Bacon says that a mocking writer once listed a made-up book called "The Morris-Dance of Heretics," and he thinks the title fits. Each heretical sect has its own odd bodily posture or bow, which, he claims, makes worldly and corrupt politicians laugh and look down on holy things.

Unity in religion, in Bacon's view, brings peace inside the church and in people's hearts. That peace strengthens faith, increases love, and turns time spent arguing over disputes into time spent on prayer and self-discipline.

Bacon says that getting the limits of religious unity right matters greatly, and that there are two mistaken extremes. Some zealous people reject any talk of peace, caring only about their own side. Others, lukewarm people, try to blend doctrines through clever compromises, as if they could judge between God and man. Both should be avoided.

Bacon says that two sayings of Jesus, "He that is not with us is against us" and "He that is not against us is with us," would settle religious disputes if they were properly explained. The key is to separate the basic points of faith from matters of opinion, order, or good intention. He admits many think this is already done, but says it would gain wider agreement if done more fairly.

Bacon says Christians should avoid splitting the church in two ways. The first is over trivial matters that are not worth the anger and conflict they cause. He points to the idea that the church may have varied colors but no tears, meaning variety is allowed but division is not, since unity and uniformity are different things.

Bacon describes a kind of religious dispute where the real question has been pushed into such fine distinctions and vagueness that it becomes clever wordplay rather than a matter of substance. He notes that a wise person can sometimes see that people who argue fiercely actually mean the same thing, yet those people would never agree with each other.

Bacon suggests that God, who knows the heart, may see that people who seem to disagree often mean the same thing and accepts both. He adds that such quarrels follow the warning of St. Paul to avoid empty word-battles and "falsely named knowledge," because people create oppositions that do not really exist.

Bacon says there are two false kinds of religious unity. One rests on people not knowing the truth, so they seem to agree, as colors look alike in the dark. The other joins people by accepting directly opposite beliefs on core matters, like iron and clay that stick together but never truly blend.

Bacon warns that in seeking religious unity, people must not destroy the laws of charity and human society. He says Christians have two proper powers, the spiritual and the temporal, which may both support religion. He rejects using war or bloody persecution to force belief, which he compares to Mahomet's sword (the sword of Muhammad, that is, the spread of Islam by force), except in cases of open scandal, blasphemy, or religious practice that threatens the state.

Bacon argues that religious zeal should not be used to stir up rebellion, plot against rulers, or arm the people, since this overturns all government, which he says God ordained. Treating men only as Christians while forgetting they are human is, he says, a mistake. He ends by quoting Lucretius: religion has been able to persuade people to do great evil.

Bacon argues that religious violence is wrong. Rulers should use the sword in religious matters only with great care, and it is monstrous to hand it to ordinary people. He calls it greater blasphemy to claim that God would act in cruelty than for the devil to claim power above God.

Bacon asks what good it does to lower the cause of religion to the level of cruel acts: murdering princes, slaughtering people, and overthrowing states. He says this turns the Holy Ghost from a dove into a vulture or raven, and turns a Christian church into a pirate ship flying a flag of murderers.

Bacon says that the church, through its teaching and rulings, and rulers, through force, should condemn to hell forever those beliefs and acts that support the opposing side in religious quarrels. He then warns that anger does not produce God's righteousness, quoting the apostle James.

Revenge is a wild, lawless kind of justice, and the law should work harder to remove it the more natural it is to people. Bacon says that forgiving an injury is nobler than taking revenge, since revenge only makes a person equal to the enemy, while pardon shows superiority. He adds that dwelling on past wrongs wastes time that wise people need for the present and future.

Bacon argues that people who wrong others usually do so to gain profit, pleasure, or honor, or simply out of ill-nature, so anger at them makes little sense. He says revenge is most acceptable only where no law can give redress, and then the revenge should be something the law cannot punish, or the avenger becomes the offender.

Bacon says that the pleasure of revenge lies more in making the other person feel regret than in the harm itself, and that cowardly, sneaky people strike like an arrow shot in the dark. He sets against this Cosmus of Florence, who said we must forgive enemies but never friends, and Job, who accepted evil as well as good from God.

Bacon says that someone who dwells on revenge keeps his own wounds open, so they never heal. He claims that revenge against rulers or public enemies often succeeds, but private revenge does not, and that vengeful people end unhappily, as witches do.

Seneca, a Roman Stoic, said that good things in prosperity should be wished for, but good things in adversity should be admired, since adversity shows what is wonderful. Bacon adds that Seneca's further saying, that true greatness is to have a man's frailty and a God's security together, is too lofty for a pagan and would suit poetry better.

Bacon says that poets have written about adversity, using the myth of Hercules crossing the ocean in an earthen pot to free Prometheus. He reads this as a picture of Christian courage sailing through the world in the frail body. He ends with the claim that prosperity is tested by temperance, and adversity by fortitude.

Bacon says that adversity may be the greater virtue, and that it is the blessing of the New Testament, while prosperity belongs to the Old. He then argues the difference is smaller than it seems: David's psalms are full of sorrow, the Bible describes Job's troubles in more detail than Solomon's wealth, and prosperity has its fears while adversity has its comforts.

Bacon compares the heart to embroidery: a bright design looks best on a dark background, so a cheerful heart shows its true quality best against hardship. Just as crushed spices give off their best scent, virtue shows its strength most under adversity, while good times mainly reveal vice.

Hiding the truth is a weak form of wisdom, Bacon says, because it takes a strong mind and a brave heart to know when to tell the truth and then to tell it. So people who hide the truth most often are the weaker kind of political operators.

Bacon notes that Tacitus describes two different qualities. Augustus is praised for skilled statecraft, while Tiberius is described as secretive and guarded, and Bacon says these are separate traits that should be told apart.

A man with a sharp enough judgment can tell what to reveal, what to hide, and what to show only partly, and to whom and when. For such a man, a habit of pretending is a drawback. If he lacks that judgment, he should generally keep quiet and be secretive, since choosing case by case is not possible for him, so the safest general course is best.
The ablest men have usually been known for openness and honesty. Because of that reputation, when they chose to hide their intentions, people did not notice it, so the hiding went unseen.

Bacon describes three levels of hiding what a person really is. The first is simply keeping oneself private, giving others nothing to observe. The second is dropping hints that suggest one is not what one is. The third is actively claiming to be something one is not.

A person known for keeping secrets is like a priest hearing confession. People tell their secrets only to those they trust not to talk, so a discreet man learns many things. Others feel drawn to open up to him, just as air rushes into a closed space that is less open.

Bacon says that keeping some things secret is wise, since mysteries depend on secrecy. People who are not somewhat reserved in their conduct and speech lose dignity, and talkers are usually vain and gullible, because someone who repeats what he knows will also repeat what he does not know.

Bacon says that keeping secrets is both wise and right. He adds that a man's face should let his tongue do the talking, because a face often reveals what a man feels. People tend to believe facial expressions more than words, so showing one's inner self through the face is a serious weakness.

Keeping a secret often forces a person into some pretence, because others will press with questions and read meaning into silence. Vague or riddling answers do not hold up for long either. So a person who wants to keep secrets must allow himself a little dissimulation, which Bacon calls the train or skirts of secrecy.

Bacon says that pretending, or falsely claiming to hold views you do not hold, is worse than other forms of concealment and is usually unwise. It is acceptable only in great and rare matters. A habit of pretending comes from a natural untruthfulness or timidity, or from hidden faults that must be disguised, and the person then pretends in other things too to keep the skill in practice.

Bacon lists three advantages of hiding one's real aims or pretending. Hiding plans keeps opponents calm and allows a surprise. It leaves a way to back out without losing face. And it helps a person learn what others really think, since people who are open about themselves rarely show opposition in return.

Bacon is saying that people who hide the truth or pretend should be careful, since a lie can be found out by its own clumsiness. He adds that such pretence has a cost: it looks like fear, and fear spoils a person's chances of reaching a goal in any business.

Bacon argues that too much pretending harms a person in two ways: it confuses others who might otherwise help him, and it takes away trust, a key tool for getting things done. The best balance, he says, is to be open in reputation and opinion, private in habit, and to pretend only when the moment calls for it, and to be able to feign if there is no other way out.

Parents keep their joys, griefs and fears to themselves. Children make hard work easier but make misfortunes worse, and they add to life's worries while easing the thought of death. Having children lets a line continue, as it does for animals, but lasting fame and great deeds belong to humans. Bacon notes that many of the greatest works were made by men without children.

People who have no children often take the most care for later generations, and they try to leave behind works of the mind in place of heirs. Founders of families are also very fond of their children, since they see them as carrying on both their line and their achievements.

Parents often love their children unequally, and sometimes in ways that are not deserved, especially mothers. Bacon notes that the eldest are often favoured and the youngest spoiled, while middle children are overlooked, though they often turn out best. He calls stinginess towards children a harmful mistake.

Bacon is describing harms of spoiling children with money: it makes them base, teaches them to get by with tricks, puts them in low company, and makes them overindulge when they become rich. He says the best method is for parents to keep authority over children while withholding money. He also warns that setting brothers against each other in childhood often leads to lasting discord in adult families.

Bacon says that children can be as close in nature to a nephew or kinsman as to their own parent, since blood ties vary. He advises parents to choose their children's careers early, while the children are still flexible, and not to shape those choices around what the parents themselves want.

Bacon says that if a child has a strong, unusual talent or inclination, it is good not to go against it. In general, though, he advises choosing the best course of life, since habit will make it pleasant and easy. He adds that younger brothers often do well in life, but rarely when the elder brothers have been disinherited.

A man with a wife and children has, in Bacon's words, given hostages to fortune, because his family can hold him back from large undertakings, whether good or bad. He says the greatest public works have usually come from men without wives or children, who give their love and resources to the public instead. Still, he notes that fathers have good reason to care about the future, since they must pass on their dearest ones to it.

Some men who never marry think only of themselves and see the future as none of their concern. Others treat wife and children as mere expenses. Some rich, greedy men even take pride in having no children, believing that makes them seem wealthier.

Bacon says the most common reason people stay unmarried is love of freedom, especially in self-centred, moody people who feel every limit as a chain. He adds that single men make good friends, masters and servants, but poor subjects, since they are quick to run away. He also says a single life suits churchmen, because their charity would otherwise be used up on a wife and family.

Bacon argues that wives and children make men more humane. Generals appeal to soldiers' families to rally them, and single men may give more to charity but are harder and crueller, since their tenderness is rarely called on.

Bacon lists what wives tend to be for men at different ages and character types. Serious, steady men often make loving husbands, and virtuous wives can be proud of their virtue. A wife stays faithful and obedient if she respects her husband's wisdom, which she cannot do if he is jealous. The last line says a man has reason enough to marry whenever he wishes.

Bacon notes that bad husbands often have good wives, perhaps because the wives value their husbands' kindness more or take pride in their patience. He adds that men who marry against their families' wishes always end up proving their own folly, which is his claim about marriages made by choice.

Bacon says that only love and envy are strong enough to "fascinate" or bewitch, meaning to harm others by a look or influence. Both feel intense desire, easily form images in the mind, and show themselves strongly when the object is present. He notes that Scripture calls envy an "evil eye," as astrologers call harmful star influences "evil aspects."

Bacon reports an old belief that envy works through the eye, sending out a harmful force that strikes the person envied. He adds that this harm is worst when that person is seen in glory or triumph, because envy is then sharpened and the envied person's spirits come out to meet the blow.

Bacon says he will set aside some side matters, then discuss three things: which kinds of people tend to envy others, which kinds of people are most often envied, and how public envy differs from private envy.

A person with no virtue of his own tends to envy the virtue of others. Minds feed either on their own good or on others' harm, and someone who lacks the first turns to the second. Unable to reach another's merit, he tries to pull that person down to his own level.

A busy, nosy person is usually envious, because someone who knows much about other people's affairs must take pleasure in watching their fortunes. Someone who minds only his own business has little to envy. Envy, Bacon says, wanders about and does not stay at home. The Latin tag means: a meddler is always also a spiteful person.

People born into high rank tend to resent newcomers who rise in status. Bacon says the gap seems to shrink as others advance, like an optical illusion, so the nobles feel they are the ones moving backward.

Bacon says that people with deformities, eunuchs, old men and illegitimate children tend to envy others, because someone who cannot improve his own situation tries to harm someone else's. The exception is a very brave person who turns his disadvantage into a source of honor, wanting to be admired for great deeds done despite it. Narses, Agesilaus and Tamerlane are given as examples.
Men who rise to power after disasters or misfortunes are, in Bacon's view, people who feel at odds with their times. They see other people's harm as a kind of payment for their own suffering.

People who want to be good at too many things, out of light-mindedness and vanity, are always envious. They cannot avoid envy, because someone will always beat them at one of those things. Bacon gives the Emperor Hadrian as an example: he envied poets, painters and craftsmen in the arts he himself wished to excel in.

People who are close to us, such as relatives, colleagues, and those raised together, are more likely to envy us when we rise in the world. Their own fortunes are a constant reminder, and others notice the comparison, which makes envy grow. Cain envied Abel more bitterly because no one else was there to see Abel's sacrifice accepted.

People of great virtue are envied less when they rise, since their good fortune seems like something owed to them, as a debt paid is not envied. Envy comes from comparing oneself with others, so kings are envied only by other kings. Unworthy people are envied most when they first rise and less later, while worthy people are envied most after their success has lasted a long time, because newer rising people then make their virtue seem less bright.

People of noble birth are envied less when they rise in rank, because their rise seems only fair given their birth and adds little to their fortune. Likewise, those who climb step by step are envied less than those who jump up suddenly.

People who gain high honor through hard work, danger or hardship draw less envy, because others pity them for the struggle. Wise, serious statesmen often complain about the burdens of their high position, not because they truly feel them, but to soften the envy of others.

Burdens that are given to a man by others do not stir envy as much as work he takes on himself out of ambition. Envy is reduced when a powerful person leaves lesser officials their full rights and honours, since they then stand between him and envy like screens.

People who hold great fortune and show it off proudly attract the most envy, since they always need to display their status or defeat rivals. Wise people would rather give up small matters to others. Still, greatness shown plainly and openly, without arrogance, draws less envy than greatness shown in a sly, crafty way.

Bacon says that envy works like witchcraft, so its only cure is the cure for witchcraft: passing the curse onto someone else. Wise great men therefore put forward others, such as servants, ministers or colleagues, to take the envy that would otherwise fall on themselves. Bold, ambitious people are always ready to accept this role for the power and work it brings.

Bacon says that public envy, unlike private envy, does some good. It works like an ostracism, the Athenian practice of banishing a man, which pulls down people who have grown too powerful. So it also acts as a check that keeps great men within limits.

Envy in a state is like an infection: once it takes hold, it spreads and turns even good actions into something bad in people's eyes. Trying to avoid it by doing popular deeds gains little, because that only shows weakness and fear, and fear of envy invites it more.

Public envy seems to fall mostly on chief officers and ministers rather than on kings or the state itself. But Bacon gives a rule: when envy against a minister is far larger than his fault justifies, or spreads across all the ministers, the envy is really aimed at the state.

Envy, Bacon says, is the most constant of all feelings, because it is always at work, while other feelings arise only now and then. He calls it the vilest and most corrupt feeling, and says it works secretly and harms good things, like the devil sowing weeds among wheat at night.

Bacon says love gives more material to plays than to real life, where it mostly causes harm. He claims that no great and worthy person in history has been driven to mad love, because great minds and great work keep this weak passion out. He names two exceptions: Mark Antony and Appius Claudius.

Bacon says that love can enter even a wise, strong-minded heart if a man is careless about guarding it. He calls Epicurus's saying that we are a big enough audience for each other a poor one. He argues that people, made to contemplate heaven and noble things, should not make themselves slaves to a small idol seen with the eye, which was given for higher purposes.

Bacon says it is strange how love goes beyond the true worth of things. Lovers speak in extravagant exaggeration, and this is acceptable only in love. A lover thinks more highly of the loved one than a proud man thinks of himself, so love and wisdom cannot go together.

Bacon warns that love for someone who does not love back is always answered with secret scorn, and that love can cost a person more than anything else, including himself. He adds that people who value love too highly give up wealth and wisdom, as the poet's story of Helen shows.

Bacon argues that love is foolish, since the times that stir it up make it stronger. People who cannot avoid love should keep it in its own place, separate from serious work and life, because when love interferes with affairs it ruins a man's fortunes and stops him reaching his goals. He suggests soldiers are prone to love because danger is repaid with pleasure, much as they are prone to wine.

People have a natural pull toward loving others. If that love is not focused on one person or a few, it spreads out to many and makes people kind and charitable. Marriage love creates humankind, friendship love improves it, and loose, lustful love corrupts and lowers it.

Men in high office, Bacon says, serve three masters at once: the sovereign or state, their reputation, and their daily business, so they have no freedom of person, action or time. He adds that seeking power means giving up liberty and power over oneself, and that climbing up is hard, while falling from high place is a downfall or eclipse.

Great people cannot easily step back from public life, even when they should, and they dislike being out of the spotlight, even in old age or sickness. Bacon says they feel happy only when they think others envy them, while their own feelings may tell them otherwise.

Powerful people learn of their troubles before anyone else, but they are often the last to see their own faults, and they are strangers to themselves. Busy with affairs, they have no time to look after their health. Bacon says that a position of power allows good and evil alike, and that the only proper goal of seeking power is the power to do good.

Good thoughts are of little use toward other people unless they are acted on, and acting needs power and a high position as a firm base. A person's rest comes from knowing that his merit and good works are done, and he shares God's rest when he has done them. Bacon also advises taking the best examples as models, since imitation teaches more than rules.

Bacon advises a person in high office to test their own record against their first performance, and to study how earlier holders of the post acted, so as to avoid their mistakes. Reforms should be made quietly, without boasting or attacking past officials. The officer should restore old practices, while asking both old and recent sources what is best and what is most suitable now.

A person in high office should run their work in a steady, predictable way, and should not be rigid when they must depart from that routine. They should keep their own authority without arguing over its limits, respect the rights of those under them, and welcome advice and information instead of treating those who offer it as meddlers.

Bacon lists four faults of people in power: delay, corruption, harshness, and too easy agreement. On corruption, he says an official must not only refuse bribes himself but also stop those seeking favours from offering them. Even the appearance of corruption should be avoided, since sudden changes of mind without clear reason invite suspicion.

Bacon advises a person in high office to announce any change of opinion or course openly, with reasons, rather than slip it in unnoticed. He warns against favorites with no clear merit, against harshness that breeds hatred, and against being too easily swayed, which he calls worse than bribery.

Bacon says that a high position reveals a man's character, and that it can make some men better and others worse. He notes that a noble spirit is shown when honor improves a person, because honor should be the place where virtue is found.

Bacon compares a man's ambition to a thing moving quickly toward its place, while power once held should be steady and calm. He advises a new official to join a faction while rising and to stay neutral once in office, to treat his predecessor with fairness, and to include fellow officers rather than shut them out.

An official should not be too aware of his rank in ordinary talk or in private replies to people who ask him favors. Instead, people should say that once he takes his office, he becomes a different man.

Bacon recounts that Demosthenes, the Greek orator, was asked what mattered most in public speaking and answered "action," meaning delivery, repeated three times. Bacon finds it strange that this surface skill, more like an actor's craft, should outrank invention and style. He says the reason is plain but does not state it here.

Bacon says most people have more foolishness than wisdom, so the tricks that catch the foolish side of people's minds work best. Boldness is the quality that matters most in public affairs, yet it comes from ignorance and lack of worth. It still holds those who have weak judgment or courage, and even wise men at weak moments.

Bold people tend to do best at the start of an action, not long after, because boldness does not keep its promises well. Bacon compares bold men to quacks: they may have a lucky success or two but lack real knowledge, so they cannot last. He adds that a bold man can also pull off a trick like Mahomet's, who promised to make a hill come to him, to impress his followers.

Bacon uses the story of Mahomet and the hill: when the hill would not come to him, Mahomet simply went to it, showing no shame. He says bold men who make big promises and fail badly will brush it off and move on without fuss. Wise people find such boldness entertaining, and even ordinary people find it a little ridiculous.

Bacon says that bold behaviour is often a little absurd, and it is funny to watch a bold person lose composure. When such a man is embarrassed, his face freezes, because bold people do not let their spirits move as shy people do. He adds that boldness is always blind, meaning it does not see its own faults.

Bold people do not see danger and its drawbacks, so they are poor at giving advice but good at carrying out plans. Their best use is as subordinates under others' direction, since good advice needs a sight of dangers, while good action needs them not to be seen unless they are very great.

Bacon defines goodness as a real concern for other people's welfare, which he says the Greeks called philanthropia. He calls it the greatest of virtues and says that without it a person is restless, harmful and miserable. Goodness can be excessive only in the sense of going wrong.

Bacon argues that love or charity can never be taken too far, unlike the desire for knowledge, which caused man's fall. He says the urge to be good is so deep in human nature that, if it is not shown to other people, it turns to other living creatures. Even cruel people, he notes, are kind to animals.

Bacon notes an Italian saying that a person who is too good is good for nothing. He says Machiavelli claimed Christianity leaves good men easy prey for tyrants and unjust people. Bacon then advises that a good person should help others but not be controlled by what others think or want.

Bacon warns against being too soft or indulgent: giving everyone the same favours is weakness that can trap a good mind. He says God gives rain and sunshine to all alike, but gives wealth and honour unequally, so common benefits should go to everyone while special ones should be chosen carefully. Finally, self-love is the model and love of neighbour is only a copy of it.

Bacon says that giving away all your wealth is only right if it lets you do more good, such as through a calling or vocation; otherwise you dry up the source of your help. He adds that goodness can come from a natural disposition as well as from reasoned habit, just as some people are naturally inclined to harm others.

Bacon describes people who take pleasure in others' misfortunes. The milder kind only make trouble through stubbornness or a habit of opposing others. The deeper kind feel envy and enjoy harming people, hovering over anyone in trouble like flies on raw flesh. He adds that such dispositions, though faults of human nature, make good material for skilled political leaders.

Bacon says that goodness shows itself in several ways. A good man is kind to strangers, which shows his heart is open to the wider world rather than cut off like an island. He pities others in their troubles, like a tree that gives balm even when wounded. He forgives easily, which shows his mind is too high to be hurt by insults.

Someone who is grateful for small favors shows that he values people's minds rather than their material gifts. Greater still, if he is willing to be cut off from Christ for the sake of his fellow believers, as St. Paul was, this shows a godlike nature and likeness to Christ.

Bacon argues that a monarchy without a nobility becomes pure tyranny, because nobles temper the king's power and turn people's attention away from the ruler alone. Democracies do not need nobles and tend to be calmer and less prone to revolt when they have none, since people focus on the issues rather than on particular persons.

Bacon argues that states last and govern well when offices go to people chosen for their usefulness to the work at hand, not for their rank or ancestry. He gives the Swiss cantons and the Dutch provinces as examples of states that hold together through shared usefulness and equality rather than privilege. A powerful nobility adds dignity to a monarch but weakens his power, while lifting the people's spirit and pressing on their wealth.

Bacon says it is good for nobles to be powerful enough to stand against the king's authority and the law, but not so powerful that they overwhelm it. Their strength should be kept high enough to check the pride of lower people before that pride threatens the king. He adds that a large number of nobles makes a state poor and costly, and that many of them will lose their wealth, leaving their rank out of step with their money.

Bacon says that an old noble family deserves respect in the way an old castle or sound tree does, having lasted through the changes of time. New nobility comes from someone's power, while old nobility comes from the passing of time.

People newly raised to noble rank are usually more virtuous but less innocent than their children, since rising usually mixes good and bad methods. Their virtues are remembered by their descendants, while their faults end with them. Noble birth tends to weaken effort, and a man who is not hard-working resents one who is.

Bacon says that a noble who stays in place while others rise is likely to feel envy. Nobility, on the other hand, protects nobles from others' envy, since they already hold honor. Kings who have capable nobles find them easy to employ, because people naturally accept nobles as born to lead.

Leaders of people need to know when political storms are likely. Such storms are usually worst when groups in a state become roughly equal in power. Like natural storms, they are preceded by warning signs, such as hidden unrest and secret stirrings.

Frequent, open attacks on the government in writings and speech, and rumours spread quickly and eagerly, are signs that trouble is coming. Bacon adds a comparison: Virgil describes Rumour (Fame) as the sister of the giants, born of the earth in anger at the gods.

Bacon says that rumours are not only left over from past uprisings but also warn of uprisings to come. Rumours and riots are closely related, like brother and sister. The sign of real danger is when a government's best and most popular actions are twisted and spoken of badly, which shows how strong envy is.

Rumours that spread against those in power are not always a sign that trouble is coming, and harsh efforts to silence them do not necessarily prevent unrest. Ignoring such rumours often calms them best, while trying to stop them only keeps them alive.

Bacon warns that officials who argue about, explain away, or quibble over orders, instead of simply carrying them out, are showing a kind of disobedience. Such arguing is a way of shaking off authority. It is worse when those who support the order speak timidly and those who oppose it speak boldly.

Rulers who take sides in a conflict, instead of standing above it as a common parent to all, become unstable, like a boat tipped by weight on one side. Bacon gives the example of Henry III of France, who joined a league against the Protestants, only to see that same league turn against him. When a ruler's power serves only one cause, and other loyalties bind people more strongly than loyalty to the crown, kings lose their power.

When open quarrels and factions among the powerful become bold, it shows that respect for authority has been lost. Bacon compares the great men of a state to planets that move gently under the outermost sphere, so when they act violently, the whole order is out of balance. He adds that respect is what God grants to rulers, and God threatens to loosen it.

When any of the four pillars of government (religion, justice, counsel, and treasure) are badly shaken or weakened, people need to hope for good luck. The author then says he will move on from these predictions and discuss the causes of rebellion, its motives, and its remedies.

Bacon says the surest way to stop uprisings is to remove their causes before they start, because fuel left lying around will catch from any spark. He names two causes: great poverty and great discontent. He adds that ruined estates often bring rebellion, and quotes the Roman poet Lucan on Rome before its civil war.

A state is in danger of revolt when its wealthier people are ruined and the common people are also in need. Bacon says that hungry people are the most dangerous rebels. Discontent in a state works like harmful bodily humours, which gather heat and become inflamed.

Rulers should not judge the danger of a revolt by whether the people's complaints are fair or whether the grievances are real or serious. Revolts are most dangerous when fear is greater than the actual suffering, because fear pushes people further than pain does. Great oppression can wear down patience, but it also weakens courage, which fear does not.

A ruler should not feel safe just because discontent has existed for a long time without causing harm. Such unrest may pass many times without disaster, but it can still break out eventually, just as a rope snaps under the final small pull.

Bacon lists the things that cause rebellion or unrest, such as changes in religion, new taxes, changed laws, general oppression, and unworthy people being promoted. He adds that any cause that unites an offended people in a common purpose also works this way. A true cure depends on the specific problem, so it should be decided by advisers rather than fixed by a general rule.

The main point is that the first way to prevent rebellion is to remove its root cause, which is poverty among the people. This means encouraging trade and manufacturing, stopping idleness and waste, managing land and prices, and keeping taxes moderate. The population should also not grow beyond what the country's resources can support.

A country's strength is not measured by headcount alone. A small group that spends heavily and earns little can ruin a nation's wealth faster than a larger group that lives frugally and saves. So too many nobles, too many clergy who produce nothing, or too many educated people with no jobs to fill will quickly drive a state into poverty.

Bacon says a nation gains wealth from foreigners, since any gain in one place is a loss somewhere else. Nations sell three things: raw goods from nature, manufactured goods, and transport or carrying of goods. When all three work well, wealth flows freely. Often the making and carrying are worth more than the raw material itself, as the Low Countries show, having the best "mines" above ground.

Good government should prevent wealth from collecting in a few hands, because a state can hold much money and still starve. Money, like muck (manure), does good only when spread around. The method is to restrain harmful trades such as usury (lending money at interest) and buying up large grazing lands.

Bacon says a state is safest when only one group is discontented. Ordinary people rarely rise on their own, so danger comes when the nobles, waiting for unrest among the common people, use it to reveal their own opposition.

Rulers stay safe by winning the goodwill of ordinary people, and by allowing their complaints to be voiced in moderation, so that discontent escapes harmlessly. Pallas and Briareus are figures from Greek myth; Bacon uses the tale of Briareus, the hundred-handed giant, as a symbol of the common people's support. Suppressing complaints lets them fester inside and grow more dangerous.

Bacon says that the role of Epimetheus, the figure who kept hope inside Pandora's jar when all the evils flew out, would suit Prometheus better when it comes to discontent. Keeping men supplied with hopes, and moving them from one hope to the next, is among the best cures for the poison of discontent.

A government shows wisdom when it can keep people loyal through hope, even when it cannot satisfy them. It should handle matters so that no trouble seems completely hopeless. This is easier because people and groups tend to fool themselves or pretend to be confident.

Bacon says that a wise government should prevent any likely leader from appearing for discontented people to gather around. He defines a "fit head" as a person of rank and standing, trusted by the malcontents, and who is himself discontented. Such a person should be won over and truly reconciled to the state.

The passage advises that factions opposed to the state should be divided and set against each other, or at least made to distrust one another. It argues that the situation is desperate if supporters of the state are split by discord while its opponents stand united.

Clever or cutting remarks by rulers have sometimes started rebellions. Caesar harmed himself by saying Sylla could not write, since it ended hope that he would give up his dictatorship. Galba ruined himself by saying he chose his soldiers rather than bought them, which removed their expectation of a gift of money.

Bacon warns that rulers must be careful with what they say in tense times, especially short remarks. Such sayings spread quickly and are taken as signs of the ruler's secret intentions, unlike long speeches, which are dull and draw little notice. He gives Probus's remark about needing no more Roman soldiers as an example of a short saying that caused despair.

Bacon advises rulers to keep a powerful, skilled soldier close by, so that uprisings can be put down at once. Without one, the court panics when trouble first breaks out. Such a soldier must be loyal and well regarded, not a popular troublemaker, and must get along with the other leading men, or the cure will be worse than the illness.
