Bacon says he would sooner believe any of the legends, the Talmud, or the Koran than believe that the universe has no mind behind it. He argues that shallow learning can push a person toward atheism, but deep study of how causes link together leads the mind to God.

Bacon argues that even the ancient atoms-based schools, often accused of denying God, actually make a stronger case for a divine order. He says it is far easier to believe that a fixed, eternal arrangement of elements needs no God than that random, unplaced particles could produce the order of the world without a divine arranger. He adds that the Bible calls the fool one who says in his heart there is no God, not one who merely thinks it.

Bacon argues that atheists do not truly believe what they say. They repeat their denial of God like a lesson learned by heart, and they seek agreement from others, as if they doubt it themselves. He adds that they even try to win followers, as other sects do.

Bacon says that men who die for atheism rather than take back their views show that they truly believe there is no God, since a real atheist would have no reason to suffer. He defends Epicurus, who was accused of pretending to believe in gods for reputation's sake, and quotes his saying that it is wrong to deny the gods of the common people but wrong to attach the common people's opinions to the gods.

Bacon argues that even people who deny God's governing of the world cannot easily deny the basic idea of nature's God. He says that "savages" in the West name many particular gods but have no word for God in general, so they still hold the notion. He adds that thinkers who truly reason their way to atheism are rare.

Bacon says that people who attack an accepted religion or superstition are often labelled atheists by their opponents. He argues that real atheists are hypocrites who handle holy things without feeling, so they become hardened. He then lists causes of atheism: many divisions within religion, scandal among priests, and the habit of mocking holy matters.

Bacon lists reasons why atheism is harmful. Denying God, he says, removes man's dignity: man is like the beasts in his body, and if he is not akin to God in his spirit, he is base. Atheism also weakens courage and greatness of mind, which he illustrates with a dog that gains boldness when a man looks after it.

Bacon argues that trust in divine protection gives people a courage and strength they could not reach on their own, so atheism removes the means by which human nature can rise above its weakness. He adds that this holds for nations as well as individuals, and cites Rome as a state marked by greatness of spirit.

Bacon quotes Cicero, who says that Rome is greater than other nations not in numbers, strength, cunning, or arts, but in piety, religion, and the one wisdom of knowing that the immortal gods rule and govern all things.

Bacon argues that a wrong idea of God is worse than having no idea of God at all. Denying God is unbelief, but a false picture of him is an insult, and superstition insults God. He adds that atheism leaves people some guides, such as their senses, reason, natural goodness, laws and reputation, while superstition is more dangerous to people.

Bacon argues that superstition is more dangerous to society than atheism. Superstition takes over people's minds the way an absolute ruler would, and it has often thrown states into disorder. Atheism, he says, has not caused such upheaval; in times when it was common, as under Augustus Caesar, society was peaceful. Superstition also makes wise men follow fools, and people's reasoning is bent to fit what they already do.

Some churchmen at the Council of Trent said that the scholastic thinkers were like astronomers who invented circles and wheels to explain the planets' movements, though those things did not really exist. In the same way, they said, the scholastics built complicated rules to defend church practice. The passage then lists causes of superstition: pleasing ceremonies, outward show of holiness, and too much respect for tradition.

Bacon names causes of superstition: greedy church leaders, too much zeal for good ideas, human attempts to grasp divine matters, and hard times. He says superstition without disguise is ugly, and that it looks more ugly because it resembles true religion. Good rules and forms of worship, he adds, decay into many small trivial observances.

Bacon warns that people can become superstitious about avoiding superstition. They think they do best by going as far as possible from the old beliefs. He adds that when ordinary people carry out the reform, the good is often thrown out with the bad, as happens with a harsh medicine.

Bacon says travel suits young people as a form of schooling and older people as a way of gaining experience. Someone who does not yet know the language is still at school, not travelling. He approves of young men going abroad with a tutor or older servant who knows the language and the country, so that he can point out what is worth seeing, who to meet, and what training the place offers. Without such a guide, young men will see little.

Bacon finds it odd that travelers keep diaries at sea, where there is little to see, but skip them on land, where there is much to observe. He says travelers should keep diaries of what they actually observe, such as royal courts, law courts, churches and monasteries.

Bacon lists the sights a traveler should look at in each place visited. These include city walls, harbors, ruins, libraries, schools, ships, gardens, armories, markets, theatres, treasuries, collections of rare objects, and anything else worth remembering.

Bacon advises that a young traveller should use a tutor or servant who knows the country and make careful enquiries, and should learn some of the language before leaving. He also suggests carrying a map or guidebook of the place. The aim is to gain as much as possible from a short trip.

Bacon gives advice to a young man travelling abroad. He should keep a diary, avoid staying too long in one town, and move his lodging around within a city to meet more people. He should also live apart from fellow countrymen and seek letters of introduction to important people in each new place.

Bacon advises a traveller to use the favour of important people to see what he wants to see, which saves time. The most useful contacts abroad are the secretaries and officials of ambassadors, since they gather knowledge from many places. He should also meet famous people so he can judge whether their real lives match their reputations, and he should avoid quarrels.

Bacon gives practical advice to travellers. He warns them to avoid quarrelsome companions, to keep up letters with their best friends abroad after returning, and to show their travels through what they say rather than through their clothes or manners. He also advises them to answer carefully rather than rush to tell stories.
A traveller should not give up the customs of his own country for those of foreign lands. He should only add a few good things he has learned abroad to the customs of home.

Kings often have few things left to want but many dangers to fear. Having nothing strong to desire makes them listless, and endless suspicions cloud their judgment. So, Bacon says, a king's heart is hard to read, as the Scripture also says.

Rulers often become fixated on trivial things, such as buildings, honours for others, or skill in an art or sport, and Bacon gives emperors like Nero and Commodus as examples. He says this seems strange to those who do not understand that the human mind gains more pleasure from progress in small matters than from being stuck in big ones.

Conquerors who succeed for a time, Bacon says, cannot keep advancing forever. When they meet a setback, they often turn superstitious and melancholy in their later years, as Alexander the Great, Diocletian and Charles V did. A ruler used to constant advance who is stopped loses his former confidence and is no longer himself.

Bacon says that governing well is hard because good government mixes opposite qualities, such as firmness and softness. Mixing them is acceptable, but switching between them at the wrong times is not. He uses Apollonius's answer to Vespasian: Nero, a skilled harpist, ruined his rule by tightening the strings too far at one moment and loosening them too far at another. Authority is most damaged by power applied too harshly, then relaxed too much, at unfitting times.

Bacon says that rulers today usually deal with danger only by cleverly putting off problems once they arrive, not by solid plans that keep them away. He warns that this is a gamble with luck, and that trouble should not be allowed to build up, since no one can stop a spark or tell where it will come from. He adds that a ruler's greatest difficulty is often his own divided will: he wants two opposite things, and wants the goal without accepting the means to reach it.

Kings must manage many groups of people: neighboring rulers, their wives and children, the clergy, nobles, gentry, merchants, common people, and soldiers. Danger can come from each of these groups unless the king takes careful thought and caution.

Princes should always watch their neighbors closely. No neighbor should grow so much, through new land, trade, or other gains, that it becomes able to harm them more than before. Standing councils exist to foresee and prevent this.

In this passage, Bacon describes three rival rulers of his time: Henry VIII of England, Francis I of France, and Charles V. Each kept a close watch on the others, so that none could gain even a small piece of land without the other two acting against him, either by forming an alliance or by going to war. They would not accept peace on terms that gave one of them an advantage.

Bacon gives two points. The league between three Italian rulers, which Guicciardini called the guarantee of Italy's security, is an example of the same kind of action. He also rejects the view of some medieval scholars that war is only just in response to a prior wrong or attack. A real fear of imminent danger, even with no blow yet struck, is a lawful reason for war.

Bacon says that rulers are in danger from their wives in certain cases. He gives examples of wives who poisoned or helped depose and kill their husbands. He says the danger is greatest when a wife plots to advance her own children or when she is unfaithful.

Bacon says that rulers who come to suspect their own children have often met disaster. He gives two examples. Solyman's destruction of his son Mustapha was followed, he says, by doubts about the later Turkish sultans' descent. Constantine the Great's killing of his son Crispus was followed by the violent deaths of his house.

Bacon gives examples of rulers who harmed their sons out of distrust, and the harm turned back on the fathers. Constantius and Demetrius suffered for it, and the father of Demetrius died of regret. Fathers gained good from such distrust only when the sons rebelled openly against them, as with Selymus and Henry II's sons.

Bacon says that powerful bishops can threaten a ruler, as Anselm and Thomas Becket did against English kings. The real danger, he says, comes when the church depends on a foreign authority, or when churchmen are chosen by the people rather than by the king or local patrons.

Keeping nobles at a distance is acceptable, but pushing them down makes a king more absolute yet less safe and less able to get things done. Bacon gives Henry VII of England as an example: his nobles stayed loyal but did not help him, so he had to do everything himself.

Bacon is saying that a monarch need not fear the lesser nobles, whose scattered position makes them weak. They may speak boldly, but this does little harm. They also balance the greater nobles so that those do not become too powerful, and because they deal directly with ordinary people, they are well placed to calm popular unrest.

Bacon is giving advice on keeping a kingdom healthy, using the body as a comparison. Merchants are like the main vein that carries blood, so if trade does not thrive, the state gets little nourishment. High taxes on trade usually bring the king less money, because the trade itself shrinks. Ordinary people are a danger only when they have powerful leaders, or when the ruler interferes with their religion, customs or livelihood.

Bacon is saying that soldiers who live together as one large body and expect gifts of money from their rulers are dangerous to the state. He gives the Turkish janissaries and the Roman praetorian guard as examples. Training and arming men in separate places, under different commanders, and without such payments, he says, protects the state and poses no danger.

Rulers are compared to the stars: they bring good or bad times to others, they are highly respected, yet they never rest. Bacon says all advice for kings rests on two reminders: that a king is a man, which limits his power, and that he is God's deputy, which limits his will.

The deepest trust between people is the trust placed in a counsellor, someone asked for advice. Other trusts cover only parts of a person's life, such as property, children or a single matter. A counsellor is trusted with the whole of it, so he must be especially faithful and honest.

Even the wisest rulers should not think it lowers their power or ability to seek advice. The passage says that God is called "The Counsellor," and that Solomon taught that stability comes from counsel. Without advice, matters are driven by chance instead.

Bacon says that a king who takes bad advice acts unsteadily, undoing what he has done, like a drunk man staggering. Solomon's son Rehoboam took such advice, and the kingdom of God was split apart because of it. The Bible marks bad advice by two signs: it comes from young advisers and it proposes violent measures.

Bacon reads an old myth as a lesson about kings and advisers. Jupiter's marriage to Metis, whose name means counsel, stands for the bond between sovereignty and counsel. The next part of the myth, where Jupiter swallows Metis before her child is born, stands for a king's wise use of counsel, which he takes in and keeps as his own.

Bacon reads the myth of Jupiter giving birth to Pallas Athena from his head as a lesson for rulers. Kings should bring matters to their counsellors first, to be worked out. But when the plan is ready, the king should not let the counsellors finish it as if the decision were theirs; the king must keep the final say.

Leaders should take back control of decisions so the public believes the final orders came from the leaders' own wisdom and plan, not only from their authority. Pallas is the Greek goddess of wisdom, shown in armour.

Bacon lists three problems with seeking advice: secrets get out, rulers look less like their own masters, and advisers may serve their own interests instead of the ruler's. He says the cabinet councils that Italy and France used to avoid these problems are a cure worse than the disease.

Rulers need not share every matter with every adviser, and a man asking advice need not reveal his own plans. The bigger danger is that rulers let their secrets leak through their own carelessness. A single talkative person who boasts of telling secrets can do more harm than many people who know it is their duty to keep quiet.

Some matters need such strict secrecy that only one or two people, besides the king, should know them. Such private counsel can still succeed, since it stays consistent and undistracted. But this works only if the king is capable of doing much work himself, and the inner advisers are wise and loyal to his aims, as Henry VII of England was with Morton and Fox.

Bacon says that a king's authority is not weakened by taking advice; it is raised when he sits in the council chair. Kings have lost power through counsel only in two cases: when one adviser grows too powerful, or when several advisers band together too tightly. Both problems can be noticed and corrected.

Bacon says the problem of counsellors who advise for their own gain is a fault of the times, not of every person; some men are naturally faithful, sincere and straightforward, and princes should choose such men. Counsellors also watch one another, so self-serving advice usually reaches the king. The best remedy is for princes to know their counsellors as well as the counsellors know them.

Counsellors should know their master's affairs well rather than study his personality too closely. Then they can give real advice instead of flattering his moods. The passage also says rulers should hear their advisers both one by one and all together, since private opinions are freer and opinions given before others are more respectful.

Bacon says that a ruler should seek advice both privately and in groups. Private advice keeps freedom for lesser people, while group advice gives weight to greater people. Most importantly, a prince must also choose the right people to advise him, because plans are lifeless without good people to carry them out.

Bacon says that describing the ideal kind of counsellor in general terms is not enough, because the worst mistakes come when choosing specific people. He quotes the saying that the best counsellors are dead, since books speak plainly when living advisers hold back the truth. So he advises reading books, especially those written by men who took part in public affairs themselves.

Bacon says that councils today often just chat about matters rather than debate them, and they move too quickly to decisions. He thinks important questions should be put forward one day and discussed only the next, using the Latin saying "in nocte consilium" (counsel in the night). He points to the commission on the union of England and Scotland as an example of this done well.

Fixed committees are a good idea, Bacon says, because they give petitioners more certainty and leave meetings free for state business ("hoc agere", to do this one thing). When forming committees to prepare matters for council, he advises choosing neutral people rather than those strongly partisan on both sides.

Bacon argues that separate advisory boards for particular fields are of little use when there is only one main council of state, since they act as standing committees with more authority. He also says that experts should first be heard by smaller committees and then by the full council when needed, and not come in large crowds or in a noisy, rebellious manner, because that shouts at councils rather than informing them.

Seating matters more than it seems: at a long table, a few people near the head control the discussion, while a square table lets more of the lower-seated advisers speak. A king should also avoid revealing his own preference too early, or advisers will just echo him with flattery instead of giving honest counsel.

Bacon says that chances and opportunities behave like a market or a seller: waiting can lower the price, but opportunity must be seized at the right moment, since it is hard to grasp once it has passed. He concludes that the best wisdom is to choose the right time to begin things, and that dangers do not shrink just because they first look small.

Bacon says that people are more often fooled by dangers than overcome by them. Meeting a danger early, even one that is still far off, is better than watching it too long, because a long watch leads to falling asleep. Acting too early is also a mistake, as is mistaking a long shadow for a real threat. The right moment for action must always be judged carefully.

Bacon says that great actions should be planned with great watchfulness, like Argus with his hundred eyes, and carried out with great speed, like Briareus with his hundred hands. Secrecy in planning and speed in acting are what keep a wise man hidden, like the helmet of Pluto, the god of the underworld, that made its wearer invisible. Once an action is underway, speed hides it better than anything else.

Bacon says that cunning is a crooked kind of wisdom, and a cunning man is not the same as a wise one, either in honesty or in skill. Some people manage schemes and political struggles well yet are weak in general, and some understand people's moods well without being able to handle real business.

Bacon says that men who have learned mostly from watching people, rather than from books, are good at handling practical matters but not at giving advice. They are skilled only in familiar situations and fail with strangers. The Latin saying he quotes, about sending two naked men to strangers to tell fools from wise men, barely applies to them.

Watching the face of the person you are talking to is a clever tactic, which the Jesuits teach as a rule. Bacon notes that many wise men hide their thoughts in their hearts but show them in their faces, so you can read them that way. He adds that you should sometimes lower your eyes modestly, as the Jesuits also do.

A useful trick is to keep the other person busy with a different topic while you get what you want quickly, so they do not stop to raise objections. Bacon gives an example of a secretary who talked to Queen Elizabeth about state affairs before presenting documents for her to sign, so she would pay less attention to them. He adds that the same method works when the other person is in a hurry and has no time to think carefully.

If you want to block a plan that someone else would push through well, pretend to support it, then propose it yourself in a way that ruins it. Stopping mid-sentence, as if you had caught yourself, makes the listener more eager to learn the rest.

A person who wants another to ask about something should first change his usual look or manner, so the other will wonder why. This works better than offering the information directly, because people trust what they seem to have drawn out of someone. Bacon gives Nehemiah, who looked sad before the king and so was asked the reason, as an example.

Bacon describes tactics for delivering hard or sensitive news indirectly. One is to have a less important person raise the subject first, so the key figure can answer as if asked by chance. Another is to attribute your own opinion to "the world" or rumour, so you are not seen to say it yourself. A third is to hide the most important point in a postscript, as if it were a minor matter.
A man Bacon knew would skip over the main thing he wanted to say when he got the chance to speak. He would leave the room, come back, and mention that matter as if he had almost forgotten about it.

Some people arrange to be caught unawares, at moments when the person they are working on is likely to walk in on them. They pretend to be found with a letter or doing something unusual, so that they will be questioned about things they themselves want to reveal.

It is a clever trick to put forward words under one's own name in the hope that another person will learn them, repeat them and then be exploited. Bacon mentions two rivals for a royal secretary's post who stayed on good terms and discussed their business together.

Two men discuss the job of secretary to a failing monarchy. One says it is a risky post and that he does not want it. The other repeats these words to friends, and the first man then has them reported to the Queen, so the remark is used against the second man.

Bacon describes a trick called "the turning of the cat in the pan": a man repeats a remark to someone as if that person had said it first, so it is hard to tell who started it. He also notes that some people hint at things against others by denying them outright, such as saying "This I do not" intend. The Latin quotation is Tigellinus claiming he sought only the emperor's safety, not other hopes.

Bacon describes several tricks of clever speakers. Some wrap what they want to suggest inside a story, which keeps them guarded and makes listeners accept it more willingly. Others phrase an answer in their own words so the other person finds it harder to object, and some wait patiently, circling around a subject before they reach the point they want to make.

A sudden, unexpected question can catch a person off guard and reveal what he is. Bacon compares this to a man who, under a changed name, turns round at once when someone calls his real name. He adds that tricks of cunning are endless and that clever schemers do great harm when people mistake them for wise men.

Some people know the small workings and turns of business but cannot grasp its substance. They can spot minor flaws in a plan but cannot examine or argue the real matters, and they often pass off this weakness as clever judgment. Others rely on tricking people rather than on sound conduct. The closing Latin quotes Solomon: the prudent man watches his steps, the fool turns aside to deceits.

Bacon compares the ant to a self-centred person: wise only for itself, and harmful to a garden or orchard. He says people who love themselves too much harm the public, and that a person should balance self-love with duty to society, especially to the king and country. A life centred only on oneself is like earth, which stays fixed, while heavenly things move around the centre they benefit. Such self-centredness is more tolerable in a sovereign prince.

Bacon warns that a servant who puts his own interests first is dangerous to a prince or state, since he bends every task toward his own ends, which often differ from those of his master. He advises rulers to avoid such servants unless they want to be served only in a minor way.

Bacon says it is bad enough to put a servant's good above a master's, but worse when a servant's small gain outweighs the master's great interests. Corrupt officers, treasurers, ambassadors and generals do this, steering affairs toward their own petty aims and grudges, which ruins their master's business. Such servants usually gain only in line with their own fortunes.

Bacon says that servants who harm their masters for their own gain behave like extreme self-lovers. Such men will burn down a house just to cook an egg. Yet they often keep their masters' trust, because they aim only to please them and benefit themselves, and for either reason they will give up their masters' real interests.

Bacon says that self-serving wisdom is a corrupt kind of wisdom, and gives animal examples: rats leaving a house before it falls, foxes pushing out badgers, crocodiles weeping as they devour. His main point is that people who love only themselves, with no rival, often come to ruin. They sacrifice everything to themselves, and in the end fortune, which they thought they had tamed, turns against them.

Bacon says that new things, like new living creatures, start out imperfect. Still, the first person to do something good is usually better than those who follow, and a good first example is rarely matched by copying it. He adds that bad habits persist naturally, while good change needs force and fades over time. Time itself is the greatest innovator, so refusing new remedies means accepting new harms.

Bacon argues that old customs, though not always good, are at least suitable, because things that have long existed together fit together well. New things fit less smoothly. They may be useful, but they cause trouble because they do not match what is already there, and people admire them more than they like them. He adds that all this would hold only if time stood still.

Stubborn clinging to old customs causes as much disorder as sudden change does, and those who revere old times too much are mocked by the new. Bacon advises that reformers copy time itself, which changes things greatly but quietly and gradually. Sudden innovations help some and harm others, and the harmed blame the one who introduced them.

Bacon advises that changes to a state's laws or government should be tried only when there is urgent need or clear benefit. Reform should be the reason for change, not a wish for change dressed up as reform. New ideas may be allowed, but they should be treated with suspicion, and one should first stand on the old way, then look around to find the right path.

Hurrying to finish business is harmful, Bacon says, like rushing a meal that the body cannot digest properly. Judge speed by how far the work has moved, not by how long you sit at it. Real speed comes from staying close to the matter and not trying to take on too much at once.

Some people only want to finish quickly, or pretend to finish business early so they look efficient. Bacon says that shortening work by condensing it differs from cutting parts off, and that business rushed this way usually moves back and forth unsteadily. He recalls a wise man who answered hasty conclusions with "Stay a little," since haste slows the finish.

Quick action is valuable, because time is the measure of business the way money is the measure of goods. Slow dispatch makes business costly to get done. Bacon points to the Spartans and Spaniards as slow in this, and quotes an Italian saying that a death from Spain would surely be slow in coming.

Listen patiently to people who first report a matter of business, and guide them at the start rather than cut in while they speak. Someone pulled off their own track will wander back and forth and take longer. Yet the person who keeps interrupting can sometimes be a bigger nuisance than the speaker.

Bacon says that repeating the main question over and over wastes time, though restating it at the start can cut off many empty remarks. Long, elaborate speeches slow down getting business done, and prefaces, apologies and remarks about oneself are wasted time. The exception is when listeners are unwilling, because a prepared mind needs a lead-in, as a warm cloth helps an ointment soak in.

Good order, dividing a task into clear parts, and choosing the right moment are what make business move quickly. The division must not be overly fine, since dividing too little makes a person slow to start and dividing too much makes them slow to finish. Business has three stages: preparation, discussion or examination, and completion.

To get business done quickly, Bacon says the middle stages should be handled by many people, while the beginning and end should be handled by few. Working from a written draft also helps speed, because even a draft that is rejected gives clearer direction than a vague plan, just as ashes are more fertile than dust.

Some people look wiser than they are, and others look less wise than they are; this holds between nations and between individuals. Bacon's point is that some men appear very capable while doing little or nothing of value. He quotes the Latin phrase "magno conatu nugas," meaning "great effort spent on trifles."

Bacon mocks people who pretend to be wise by looking deep without really being so. He says they make a thin surface look solid, hide their knowledge behind a dim light, and act as if they know more than they do. Some even pass for wise through facial expressions and gestures.

Bacon describes ways people pretend to know more than they do. Some raise an eyebrow or speak boldly and insist on points they cannot prove. Others brush off what they cannot understand as trivial or pointless, so that their ignorance looks like good judgment.

Some people always find a distinction to make, using small verbal points to muddy the issue. Such men, in any debate, prefer to take the negative side and enjoy raising objections, since once a proposal is denied, it is finished.

Bacon says that people who only seem wise must work hard to keep up their reputation, much as a failing merchant hides his losses. He advises against giving such men important work, since a plain, slightly foolish man is a better choice than one who is overly formal and pretends to wisdom.

Bacon says it would be hard to pack more truth and falsehood into so few words than the saying "Whatsoever is delighted in solitude, is either a wild beast or a god." He agrees that a natural, hidden dislike of company is somewhat like a savage beast. He denies that such dislike shows anything of the divine nature.

Bacon says a person may rightly seek solitude only from a wish to withdraw for a higher kind of company, not from simply liking to be alone. He adds that most people do not understand how much solitude involves, since a crowd is not real company and faces around us are like paintings on a wall.

Talk without love is empty noise. The Latin saying "a great city is a great solitude" fits this, since in a big city friends are spread apart and seldom meet. Bacon adds that lacking true friends is a plain and wretched loneliness, and without them the world is like a wilderness.

A person whose nature and feelings make him unable to have friends, Bacon says, has this from the beasts and not from being human. The point is that the lack of friendship belongs to animals, not to people.

A main benefit of friendship, Bacon says, is that it relieves the heart when it is overfull with feelings. He compares this to the body, where blocked passages are most dangerous. Medicines can open the liver, spleen, lungs or brain, but only a true friend can open the heart, by sharing every burden with him.

Great kings often value friendship so highly that they risk their own safety and power to get it. Because they stand so far above their subjects and servants, they can only enjoy friendship by raising some people to near-equal status, which often causes trouble. Modern languages call these people favorites, as if the role were only a matter of favor or social company.

The Romans called such a friend "participes curarum," meaning sharers of cares, and Bacon says this name gets at the real purpose of friendship: it ties the bond. He adds that even the wisest rulers have chosen servants as friends, and let others use the ordinary word "friend" for them.

Sulla raised Pompey to great power, and Pompey later boasted that he now outshone Sulla. When Sulla objected to Pompey backing a candidate for consul, Pompey told him to be quiet, saying more people honour the rising sun than the setting one. Decimus Brutus similarly gained such favour with Julius Caesar that Caesar named him heir after his nephew.

Bacon describes a man who had great influence over Julius Caesar. On the day Caesar wanted to dismiss the senate because of bad omens, including his wife Calpurnia's dream, this man persuaded him to stay. Bacon adds that Antony called him a witch, as if he had put a spell on Caesar.

Augustus raised Agrippa, a man of low birth, so high that Maecenas warned him he had only two choices: marry his daughter to Agrippa or kill him, since no lesser option remained. Bacon gives this as an example of how a friend's power can grow dangerous. Tiberius and Sejanus were another such pair, called friends, and Tiberius wrote to Sejanus that he had kept nothing hidden from him out of their friendship.

Bacon describes two Roman emperors and their close bonds with favourites. The senate honoured one pair's friendship with an altar, and Severus wrote that he loved his favourite so much he hoped the man would outlive him. Bacon adds that such feelings would seem like natural goodness only in better rulers.

Bacon says that even very wise, strong-minded men, who loved themselves greatly and were highly fortunate, found their happiness incomplete without a friend. Such men had wives, sons and nephews, yet these family ties could not replace the comfort of friendship.

Bacon notes that Comines (Commines) reported that Duke Charles the Hardy kept his secrets to himself, especially his worries, and that this secrecy weakened his mind in his later years. Bacon says the same could be said of Louis XI, whose secrecy tormented him. He ends with Pythagoras's saying "Eat not the heart," which means do not consume your own heart with worry.

Bacon says that people who have no friend to confide in are, in a harsh phrase, "cannibals of their own hearts," meaning they consume themselves. He adds that sharing one's feelings with a friend has two opposite effects: it doubles joy and halves grief.

Bacon says that friendship acts on the mind like the alchemists' philosopher's stone acts on the body: it produces opposite effects, always for good. He adds that nature shows the same pattern in bodies, where union strengthens natural action and weakens harmful force, and minds work the same way.

Bacon says that friendship benefits the mind as it benefits the feelings. It calms the emotions the way a clear day follows a storm, and it brings clarity to thinking that is dark and confused. He adds that this benefit is not only the good advice a friend gives.

A person with many thoughts gains clarity by talking them over with someone else. Speaking lets him arrange his thoughts more easily and see them in words, so he becomes wiser than he was alone, and an hour of talk does more for him than a day of thinking by himself. Bacon adds that Themistocles compared speech to a richly woven tapestry, which shows its pattern only when it is spread out.

Bacon says that talking with a friend helps a man think clearly, even when the friend cannot give advice. Speaking his thoughts aloud brings them into the open and sharpens his mind, as a blade is sharpened on a stone. A man would do better to speak to a statue or painting than to keep his thoughts shut up inside him.

Bacon says that honest advice from a friend is the second great benefit of friendship. He quotes the ancient Greek thinker Heraclitus, "Dry light is ever the best," and argues that advice from another person is clearer and less biased than a person's own judgment, which is coloured by their feelings and habits.

Bacon says a friend's advice is worth more than advice a man gives himself, because a person flatters himself more than anyone else does. Advice from a friend is the best check against this self-flattery. He also says that a friend's advice about personal conduct keeps the mind healthy, while judging oneself strictly can sometimes be too harsh.

Bacon says that books of moral teaching are dull and lifeless, and that watching others' faults does not always fit our own situation. The best remedy, he argues, is a friend who points out our faults. Without such a friend, even powerful people make serious mistakes that harm their reputation and fortune, like someone who looks in a mirror and then forgets his own face.

Bacon warns that people often overrate their own judgment in business, believing they see more alone than others do, or that they can manage without help. He says that good counsel is what really puts business right. He adds that seeking advice in small separate pieces, from different people on different matters, is not enough.

Bacon says that a man who asks for advice runs two risks. First, he may not get honest advice, since advice from anyone but a true, complete friend is usually bent toward the giver's own aims. Second, he may get advice that harms him, even when well meant, because it mixes some harm with some help, like a doctor who knows the cure but not the patient's body.

A cure that fixes one problem can harm a person's health in another way, so it cures the disease and kills the patient. A true friend knows a person's whole situation and avoids helping with one task in a way that causes a different trouble. So do not rely on scattered pieces of advice, because they confuse more than they guide.

Bacon says friendship's last benefit is practical help: a friend joins in our actions and helps with many tasks. To see how much friendship offers, he suggests listing everything a man cannot do alone. By that measure, he argues, the old saying that a friend is "another himself" understates the case.

A friend is worth more than oneself, Bacon says, because a man's deepest wishes, such as seeing his child settled or his work finished, can outlive him. If he has a true friend, he can feel fairly sure that someone will carry on caring for those things after he dies. In this way, his desires give him a second life.

A friend can do for a man the things he cannot do decently himself. Praising your own merits, or begging for something, sounds awkward coming from you, but the same words sound fitting when a friend says them for you.

A man is always bound by his roles: he speaks to his son as a father, to his wife as a husband, and to an enemy only on set terms. A friend can speak freely as the situation requires. So if a man cannot play his own part well without one, he may leave the stage.

Wealth is meant to be spent, on honor and good deeds. Large, one-off spending should be measured by how worthy the cause is, even if it ruins the spender, since such ruin can serve a country as well as heaven. Everyday spending should fit a man's income, be kept under his control, and be arranged so that it looks grander than the bills show. A man who wants to stay balanced should spend only half of what he takes in.

Bacon argues that a man should regularly examine his own finances, even though this may be unpleasant, because problems cannot be fixed without looking at them. Those who cannot check their affairs themselves should choose their agents carefully and change them often. Those who check only rarely should stick to certain, secure dealings.

A man who spends freely in one area should be thrifty in another, such as saving on clothes if he is generous with food. Someone who spends lavishly on everything will likely be ruined. Selling property in a hurry can cost as much as letting debts grow, and a man who pays everything off at once tends to fall back into debt.

A man who is in money trouble and clears his debts slowly builds a habit of thrift that changes his mind as well as his finances. Cutting small expenses is less shameful than hunting for small profits. He should be careful with spending that keeps going once started, but can be lavish with one-time costs.

Themistocles, an Athenian leader, said he could not play the lute but could make a small town into a great city. Bacon says that the saying, though boastful when Themistocles applied it to himself, is a wise remark that could apply to others. It shows two different skills that men in public affairs may have.

Bacon says that few counsellors and statesmen can make a small state great, yet many are skilled at trivial pursuits like playing the fiddle, which is a figure for frivolous accomplishment. Other men are so far from building a state that their talent works the other way, bringing a great and prosperous nation to ruin.

Bacon says that some counsellors and governors win favor from their masters and popularity with the common people through showy tricks, which he calls "fiddling." These tricks please for a moment but do not help the state they serve. He adds that other officials are competent, able to manage affairs and keep the state from danger and obvious harm.

Bacon says that, whoever does the work, the real subject is what makes kingdoms and states truly great and how to achieve it. This matters to powerful rulers, so they judge their strength correctly: overestimating it leads to failed ventures, and underestimating it leads to timid decisions.
A country's land area, its wealth, and its population can all be measured or counted. But judging a state's true strength is the hardest part of public affairs, and the easiest to get wrong.

Bacon uses the parable of the mustard seed to make a point about states. Some states are large in land but do not grow or gain power. Others are small in size yet have the energy to become the base of great empires.

Fortifications, weapons, and horses mean little on their own, unless the people themselves are brave and warlike. Large numbers of soldiers also count for little when their courage is weak, as the wolf and the sheep saying shows. Bacon gives the Persian army at Arbela as an example of a huge force that still frightened Alexander's commanders.

Bacon gives examples showing that numbers do not decide battles; courage matters far more. A commander refuses a night attack because it would take the victory unfairly, and the Armenian king Tigranes mocks a small Roman army as too many for a messenger and too few for a fight. Before sunset, though, that small army routs his huge force.

A state's greatness depends mainly on having a race of soldiers, not on money. Money is not what really wins wars; men's arms are. Bacon uses Solon's reply to Croesus to make the point: whoever has better iron (weapons) will control the gold. So a ruler should rely on his fighting forces above all, unless his native army is made of brave, good soldiers.

Princes with warlike subjects should recognise their own strength, unless they fail themselves. Relying on hired soldiers, according to Bacon, lets a ruler grow proud for a while, but he soon loses his power, as a bird moults its feathers.

A people weighed down by heavy taxes will not become brave or warlike, and so is not fit to rule an empire. Bacon adds that taxes agreed to by the people's own assembly hurt courage less than taxes forced on them, even though both drain the purse the same amount.

Bacon warns that if a state has too many nobles and gentlemen, the common people will sink into low, spiritless laborers who serve the gentry. He compares this to a coppice wood: if too many tall trunks are left standing, the wood grows only weak shrubs instead of good underwood. Too few fit men would then be left for soldiering.

Bacon argues that a large population does not guarantee military strength, especially in the infantry. He points to England and France: England, with less land and fewer people, beat France because its middle-class people made good soldiers, while French peasants did not. He calls Henry VII's policy toward this end clever and wise.

Bacon argues that farms should be kept at a set size, with enough land to support a family in comfortable plenty rather than servitude, and worked by the owners themselves, not by hired labourers. He says this produces the kind of land Virgil praised: strong in arms and rich in its soil.

Bacon says that free servants and attendants of lords and gentlemen, a group he thinks is found mostly in England, are as useful in war as the common yeomen. He concludes that lavish display and large households of the nobility help build military strength, while a frugal, private way of living leaves a country short of soldiers.

A state must have enough native-born subjects to outnumber the foreigners it governs. So states that grant citizenship freely to outsiders are fit for empire. A small people, however brave and wise, may hold a large empire for a time, but will suddenly fail. Sparta was strict about citizenship.

Bacon says that a state which grows too big for its own base falls suddenly, like a tree whose branches are too heavy for its trunk. He points to Rome as the opposite case: it admitted outsiders freely and granted them full citizenship, rights of trade, marriage, inheritance, voting and public office, and so it became the greatest power.

Bacon says that Rome grew great because it spread outward, and the world flowed into it, rather than Rome spreading over the world. He points to its practice of founding colonies, which moved Roman settlers into other lands. He then notes that Spain holds vast lands with few native Spaniards, and suggests this is because Spain's whole territory forms a large, strong body.

Bacon is praising a state, apparently Rome, for admitting outsiders into its citizenship and army. He says that even where the state did not grant full citizenship to foreigners, it used people of all nations as ordinary soldiers and sometimes as commanders. He adds that the ruler's recent decree shows he now feels the lack of native-born people.

Bacon argues that indoor crafts and fine handwork do not suit a warlike spirit. Warlike peoples tend to be somewhat idle and prefer danger to hard work, and they must not be fully trained out of this if they are to stay strong. So ancient Sparta, Athens and Rome used slaves to do such work.

The "that" refers to an earlier idea in the essay, which this passage does not state. Bacon says Christian law has mostly done away with it. The next best course is to leave the crafts and trades mainly to foreigners, who can be more easily admitted for that work. The native common people should be kept in three groups: farm workers, free servants, and skilled manual workers such as smiths, masons and carpenters. Professional soldiers are not counted in these groups.

For a nation to become great and rule others, Bacon says, it must make war its main honor, study and business. Other qualities only prepare a people for arms, and preparation means nothing without actually taking up arms. He adds a legend that Romulus told the Romans to focus on arms, and they would then become the greatest empire.

Bacon says that several peoples have held the kind of state Sparta had, built around one aim, for shorter or longer periods, and that Spain is the main example in Christian Europe. He thinks the point is so obvious that it needs no argument, only a hint.

Nations do not become great by chance; greatness comes to those that train for war and keep it up. States that stayed committed to military life for a long time, such as the Romans and Turks, achieved remarkable things. Even nations that practiced arms only briefly often gained a greatness that lasted long after their military activity faded.

A state should have laws or customs that give it reasons for war that look just, since people rarely go to war without some apparent justification. The Turks always have a ready reason in spreading their religion, while the Romans, though they valued expanding their empire, did not rely on that alone to start a war.

Bacon says that a nation seeking greatness should, first, feel and answer wrongs done to its neighbors, traders, or diplomats, and not delay long in responding to an insult. Second, it should be quick to help its allies, as the Romans always did, even taking the lead so that no one else gets the credit.

Bacon says that ancient wars fought to back a political faction, or to spread or end a form of government such as democracy or oligarchy, cannot easily be justified. Wars fought in the name of freeing others from tyranny are also in this category. He concludes that a state cannot expect to be great unless it is ready to arm itself for a just cause.

A nation, like a body, stays healthy only through exercise, and a just and honorable foreign war is that exercise. A civil war is more like a fever, harming the body. Without outside conflict, a peaceful nation grows weak in courage and its morals decay.

A standing army, though expensive, is what usually lets a state set the law or at least gain respect among its neighbors. Bacon gives Spain as an example, since it kept a veteran army almost continually for about 120 years.

Whoever rules the sea holds a large share of power, almost like a king's. Bacon cites Cicero, who says Pompey's plan against Caesar was based on the idea that controlling the sea means controlling affairs. Bacon adds that Pompey would have worn Caesar out had he not abandoned that strategy, and that the battle of Actium decided who ruled the empire.

Bacon says that sea battles often decide wars, but this is only when rulers stake everything on one battle. He argues that whoever controls the sea has great freedom to fight as much or as little as he wants. Those strong on land, by contrast, often face serious difficulties.

Naval power is a great advantage for Europe, and especially for Britain, for two reasons. Most European kingdoms border the sea, and the wealth of the East and West Indies depends largely on controlling the seas.

Bacon says that wars in his own time seem to bring less glory and honor to soldiers than wars did in ancient times. Today's honors, such as knighthoods given to soldiers and non-soldiers alike, are weaker than the old public tributes, such as victory monuments and funeral praises for the dead.

Bacon lists honors that once stirred men's spirit: personal crowns, the emperor's style, generals' triumphs, and gifts to soldiers. He says the Roman triumph was not mere show but a wise institution. It gave the general honor, filled the treasury with spoils, and rewarded the army.

Bacon says that the honor of a triumph, a public victory parade, may not suit monarchies unless the monarch or his sons won the war in person. Roman emperors kept the full triumph for themselves and their sons, leaving generals who were subjects only triumphal robes and insignia.

A person cannot add height to his body by worrying over it, but rulers can make their kingdoms larger and greater by setting up the right laws and customs, which will pass greatness on to later generations. Bacon notes that rulers usually neglect this and leave such matters to chance.

Bacon says a person's own experience of what suits or harms them is the best guide to staying healthy, even beyond medical rules. He advises that it is safer to stop a habit that seems to disagree with you than to keep it because you feel no harm yet. Strong youth hides excesses that will be paid for later, so a person must notice aging and change habits, since age cannot be resisted.

Do not change one big habit of eating suddenly. If you must, change the other habits to match. Change several things gradually rather than one thing at once. Try giving up a harmful habit slowly, and go back to it if it causes trouble, since what is generally healthy may not suit your own body.

Keeping a cheerful mind and regular times for eating, sleeping and exercise is one of the best ways to live long. Bacon also lists mental habits to avoid, such as envy, anxious fear, bottled-up anger, and too much joy or sadness that is kept hidden. He recommends hope, gentle mirth, varied pleasures, and studies that fill the mind with wonder, such as history, stories and the study of nature.

Bacon advises against taking medicine too often when you are well, since the body then reacts strangely when you really need it, and medicine has little effect. He prefers occasional special diets, which change the body gently. He also says to take notice of any new symptom and ask a doctor about it. When ill, keep health as the main aim, and when well, stay active, so that most mild illnesses can be treated by diet and careful nursing.

Celsus, an ancient physician, advised that a person should alternate between opposites, such as fasting and eating or waking and sleeping, but lean toward the gentler side of each. This keeps the body healthy while still training it. Bacon adds that some doctors are too agreeable to their patients and so fail to treat the real illness.

Some doctors follow medical rules so strictly for the disease that they pay too little attention to the patient's own condition. Bacon advises choosing a doctor of moderate temperament, or two doctors combining the two kinds, and calling both the one who knows your body best and the one with the best reputation.

Suspicions are compared to bats: they come out in the half-light of the mind and are harmful. Bacon says they should be held back or closely guarded, since they cloud judgment, lose friends, and disrupt work. They are faults of the brain rather than the heart, and even brave men such as Henry VII of England were prone to them.

Suspicions do little harm when they are checked before being accepted, but they spread quickly in fearful people. Bacon says the best cure is to learn more rather than keep suspicions hidden. He also asks whether people expect those they deal with to be saints, when everyone naturally pursues their own ends.

Bacon advises treating suspicions as possibly true, so you can guard against them, while not letting them control you. Suspicions that arise in the mind alone are harmless, but those planted by other people's gossip sting. The best way to clear them, he says, is to speak openly about them with the person you suspect.

Bacon says that when you suspect someone, you should speak to them directly, since this shows you the truth and makes them more careful. Men of base character are the exception: once suspected, they will not be trustworthy. He quotes an Italian saying that suspicion gives a license to faith (breaks trust), and argues instead that suspicion should stir up faith to clear itself.

Some people in conversation want to be praised for cleverness, meaning the ability to argue either side, rather than for judgment, meaning the ability to tell what is true. They treat it as admirable to know what can be said, not what should be believed. Others rely on set topics they handle well but never vary, and this sameness soon becomes tiresome and, once noticed, faintly absurd.

The most honourable part of conversation is to start a topic and then steer it along, moving on to something new, so that the speaker leads the dance. Good talk mixes many kinds of speech, such as argument and story, questions and opinions, and jest and seriousness, because staying on one thing too long wears people out.

Some subjects should be left out of jokes: religion, affairs of state, important people, a person's serious current business, and anything that deserves pity. Bacon also says some people think they are dull unless they make cutting, personal jibes, and that this habit should be restrained. The Latin quotation means "Spare the goad, boy, and use the reins more firmly."

Bacon advises that a person with a sharp, mocking wit should beware, since people who fear his wit will also be wary of remembering what he says against them. A good questioner learns much and pleases others by asking questions suited to their skills, but should not pester them, and should let others have their turn to speak.

Bacon gives advice on conversation. If someone wants to dominate the talk, others should be drawn in to take over, as musicians stop dancers who go on too long. Talking about yourself should be rare and careful. The only good way to praise yourself is by praising virtue in someone else.

Bacon says that personal remarks aimed at others should be used rarely, because conversation should range widely without landing on any one person. He gives two lords as examples: one mocked guests yet ran a pleasant house, while the other asked guests whether any insult had been made at dinner. He concludes that knowing what to say and what to leave unsaid matters more than eloquence.

Good conversation means answering the other person well, not just speaking in fine words or good order. A long speech with no quick give-and-take shows slowness, while quick replies without a solid main speech show shallowness. Too many preliminaries before reaching the point are tiring, and none at all is blunt.

Bacon says that founding new colonies is an old, heroic kind of work, and that new colonies are like children of older kingdoms. He prefers a colony set up on empty land, where no people are driven out, since moving people out is destruction rather than settlement. Like planting a forest, a colony loses money for many years before it pays back.

Bacon argues that the main cause of failed colonies is greed for quick profit in their first years. Profit may be sought only so far as it does not harm the colony. He also says it is shameful and harmful to settle a colony with criminals and the worst of the population, since they will be lazy, cause trouble, and send bad reports home.

Bacon advises that a new colony should be settled with working people such as farmers, craftsmen and fishermen, plus a few specialists. He says settlers should first use the food the land already gives, then grow quick-harvest crops, because grain like wheat, barley and oats takes too much labor.

Bacon advises colonists on which food to bring and grow first. Peas, beans and rice are good because they need little work and can serve as both meat and bread. Hardy, fast-breeding animals such as pigs, goats and poultry are recommended, and stored food should be rationed carefully, as in a besieged town.

Bacon advises that most of a new colony's land for gardens or grain should be held in common and handed out in fair shares, with a few plots kept for individuals to farm privately. He also suggests choosing crops or goods the land naturally produces to help pay the colony's costs, as tobacco did in Virginia, and notes that timber is a likely choice because wood is usually plentiful.

Bacon lists natural goods a colony could produce and sell, such as iron, salt, silk, pitch, tar and sweet woods, where the local land or climate suits them. He warns settlers not to spend too much effort digging for mines, since that hope is uncertain and tends to make them idle at other work. He ends by saying that government should rest with one leader, helped by advisers.

Bacon advises how a new colony should be run. Settlers should be allowed to use martial law, within some limits, and should keep God and worship in view above all. Government should rest on a modest number of leaders, preferably gentlemen rather than merchants, since merchants focus on immediate profit. Colonists should also be free from customs duties until the colony is strong.

Settlers should be free to sell their goods where they earn the most, unless there is a special reason for caution. Colonists should not be sent in large, rapid groups; numbers should be matched to what the settlement can support so people do not become poor. Settlements should also be built on higher ground, away from the shore and rivers, because marshy coastal sites have harmed health.

Bacon gives advice to colonists. They should bring enough salt for food, treat native peoples fairly and kindly while keeping guards, and avoid helping them attack their enemies, though defending them is acceptable. He also suggests sending some natives to see the colony's better way of life, and bringing women only once the colony is strong.

A colony should keep growing from its own people, not be kept alive by new settlers sent from outside. Bacon says that abandoning a colony once it is well under way is the worst of sins, bringing dishonor and the blame for the deaths of many people who would suffer.

Bacon says riches are to virtue what baggage is to an army: they cannot be dropped, but they slow the march and can even cost the victory. Great riches have little real use, he argues, except in how they are given out, since an owner can enjoy only the sight of them.

Bacon argues that great riches often have little real use to their owner. Expensive jewels and grand building projects are valued mainly for show. Riches may seem to protect a man from danger, as Solomon said, but that protection exists only in the rich man's mind. In fact, Bacon says, great wealth has more often led men into ruin than rescued them.

Bacon advises that wealth should be sought honestly, used with moderation, given away generously, and left behind without regret, and that it should not be despised or rejected outright. He adds that riches gained in haste are dangerous, and he notes the old saying that wealth from Jupiter comes slowly but wealth from Pluto, god of the underworld, comes quickly.

Bacon says that wealth gained honestly through hard work grows slowly, while wealth that comes from another person's death, such as inheritance or wills, arrives suddenly. He adds that wealth gained by fraud or oppression comes even faster, and that most ways of getting rich are dishonest.

Bacon says farming is the earth's blessing, though it is slow to pay. Yet when very rich men take up farming themselves, it multiplies their wealth greatly. He describes an English nobleman with many kinds of land-based income, so that the earth seemed like a sea of constant returns to him. One observer noted that small wealth comes hard, but great wealth comes easily.

Once a man has enough wealth, he can buy goods at the best prices, take part in large deals, and invest in younger men's ventures, so his fortune grows fast. Gains from ordinary trade are honest and come mainly from hard work and a good reputation for fair dealing. Gains from large bargains are more doubtful, since they often rely on exploiting others' needs and using tricks.

Bacon lists ways of making money and how each one works or fails. Buying goods only to resell them usually hurts both buyer and seller. Shared profits can enrich people if they are trusted well. Usury (lending money at interest) is the surest way to gain, but one of the worst. Being first with an invention or a legal monopoly can bring very large wealth.

Bacon says that a person who combines sound judgment with new ideas can achieve great things, especially in the right times. Relying only on safe gains rarely brings great wealth, while risking everything often leads to ruin, so risks should be balanced with safeguards. He also notes that monopolies and buying goods to resell make people rich, especially when they know in advance what will be in demand.

Wealth won by serving well ranks high, but wealth won by flattery, pleasing people's moods, or other servile ways ranks among the lowest. Chasing inheritances and executorships is worse still, since it means submitting to lesser people than a servant would. Bacon also warns not to be stingy, because riches can fly away, so sometimes they must be sent out to bring in more.

Men who leave wealth do best with moderate amounts, whether to family or to the public. A large fortune left to an heir attracts danger unless he is mature in age and judgment. Grand gifts and endowments made after death are empty, like sacrifices without salt, and rot inwardly. Give in measured amounts during life, not only at death.

Bacon sets aside divine prophecies, pagan oracles, and predictions based on nature. He will discuss only prophecies that are well remembered and that come from hidden causes. He gives examples: a witch's words to Saul, a line in Homer that seems to foresee Rome's rule, and lines by Seneca foretelling distant lands being discovered.

Bacon gives examples of dreams and omens that seemed to predict later events, and of the interpretations people gave them. Polycrates' daughter dreamed her father would be bathed and anointed, and he was later crucified in the open air. Philip of Macedon read a dream of a sealed womb as a sign of barrenness, while his soothsayer read it as pregnancy.

Bacon gives examples of prophecies and omens that seemed to come true. A rumor in the East said that someone from Judea would rule the world, and Tacitus applied it to Vespasian, though Bacon notes it may have meant Christ. Domitian dreamed of a golden head before his death, and a long, prosperous succession followed him.

Bacon gives two examples of prophecies that seemed to come true or to mean something. First, a astrologer told the French queen mother that her husband, King Henry, would die in a duel, and he was killed in a tilting accident when a splinter from a lance entered his visor. Second, a childhood saying warned that England would fall when hemp was spun, which Bacon notes as a trivial rhyme.

People once believed that England would fall into ruin after rulers whose first names formed the word HEMPE: Henry, Edward, Mary, Philip and Elizabeth. The only change that came was the name, since the king's title is now Britain rather than England. Bacon also mentions another prophecy about the year 1588, which he says he does not understand.

A supposed prophecy says that a black fleet from Norway will appear between Bough and May, and that after it passes, England will build houses of stone and lime because there will be no more wars. Bacon notes that people took this to mean the Spanish Armada of 1588, since the Spanish king's surname was said to be Norway.

Bacon says the stories of a great fleet, Cleon's dream, and similar dreams and astrological predictions are not worth believing. He thinks they are only fit for idle talk by the fireside. He adds that he means "despised" only as a judgment about belief.

Bacon says that prophecies, though they are not to be taken lightly, have caused much harm, and many severe laws have been passed to stop them. He gives two reasons they gain belief: people remember the hits and forget the misses, and vague guesses or old stories are later read as predictions.

Bacon says that some predictions were reasonable guesses, since geography then suggested land beyond the Atlantic, and an old story about Atlantis could encourage such a guess. His main point is that most prophecies are frauds, invented by clever people after the event had already happened.

Ambition works like the bodily fluid of choler (anger or bile). When an ambitious man can keep rising, he is merely busy. When he is blocked, he turns secretly bitter, resents others, and wants things to go badly, which Bacon calls the worst trait in a servant of a prince or state.

Bacon says rulers should avoid using ambitious men unless they must. If they do use them, the rulers should keep those men moving forward rather than backward, since a man who is not promoted for his service may work to pull his masters down. The exception is good military commanders, who must be used whatever their ambition, because their service outweighs their faults.

Bacon says ambitious men are useful to rulers in three ways: they can take on dangerous tasks that others refuse, they can shield princes from danger and envy, and they can be used to pull down a subject who has grown too powerful. Because rulers must use them this way, he turns to how such men can be controlled so they are less dangerous, starting with the point that low-born men are less risky than noble ones.

Bacon says that a ruler can limit ambitious powerful men in two ways. One is to keep a favorite, since whoever controls the rewards and punishments through that favorite leaves no one else able to grow too great. The other is to set other proud men against them, with moderate counsellors in between to keep things steady.

A ruler can use lesser men as whips against ambitious nobles. Keeping such men in danger of ruin works only if they are timid; bold men may rush into action and become dangerous. The safest way to bring a powerful man down, when needed, is to alternate rewards and disgraces so he cannot tell what to expect.

Bacon says that ambition to excel in great matters does less harm than ambition to show off in everything, which causes confusion. A man who wants to be the only important person among mediocre people harms a whole age, while a man who wants to stand out among capable people does good for the public. Honor, he adds, gives a chance to do good, access to kings, and a way to raise one's own fortunes.

A man who seeks power with the best of motives is honest, and a prince who can tell such motives apart in others is wise. Princes and states should therefore pick ministers who feel duty more than personal gain, and who work from conscience rather than show. They should also tell a restless, busy nature apart from a truly willing mind.

Bacon says these entertainments are minor matters, but since princes want them, they should be elegant rather than overloaded with expense. He praises song-based dancing and acting, with singers placed high and music suited to the show. He wants dialogue sung by strong, manly voices, not high treble voices, and says plain dancing is vulgar.

Bacon gives advice on staging court masques. He says music should be lively and not delicate, with several choirs singing in turn. He calls turning dances into patterns a childish display. Changes of scenery are pleasing if done quietly, and the stage should be bright with varied colored light.

Bacon gives stage advice for masques, the court entertainments of his day. Performers should move on the stage before they step down among the audience, since partial sight draws the eye and creates desire. Songs and music should be loud and bright, and by candlelight white, flesh-pink and sea-green colors show best, while cheap spangles shine more than costly embroidery.

Bacon gives advice on court entertainments. Masquers should wear graceful costumes that suit their own character once their masks are removed, not copies of familiar foreign or trade outfits. Anti-masques, the comic interludes, should be short and may use figures like fools or witches, but not angels or frightening monsters like devils and giants. The music should be lively and full of unexpected changes.

Sweet scents that rise up suddenly, with no liquid dripping, are very pleasant in a crowded, hot room. Paired masques, one of men and one of ladies, add dignity and variety. Yet none of this matters unless the room itself is kept clear and tidy.

Bacon says that the splendor of jousts, tournaments and similar contests lies mainly in the showy parts. These include the chariots the challengers ride in, especially chariots pulled by exotic animals, the entrance displays, the fine costumes of attendants, and the rich decoration of horses and armor. He then dismisses these as trifles.

Human nature can be hidden or held back, but rarely destroyed. Only habit truly changes and tames it; force makes it spring back harder, and teaching only softens it. To master your nature, set tasks that are neither too hard nor too easy, and train with aids first, then with handicaps.

Bacon says that when a person's natural habit is strong, giving it up is hard, so it is best to go about it in steps. He lists the steps: first slow the habit down, then reduce it, then stop it completely. He adds that the best way is to break free all at once, if one has the courage to do so.

Bacon says the old rule of bending your nature like a stick, to the opposite extreme so it straightens, is fine, as long as the opposite extreme is not a vice. A person should not force a habit with constant practice but with breaks, since rest strengthens the next effort. Constant practice also fixes mistakes along with skills.

A person's true nature stays hidden for a long time but comes out when tempted. Bacon's advice is either to avoid such temptations or to face them often until they no longer stir you. Nature shows most clearly when a person is alone, angry, or facing something new. Those whose nature fits their work are fortunate.

Bacon says that a man should set fixed hours for studies he has to force himself to do. Studies that suit his nature need no set times, because his thoughts return to them on their own. Like a gardener, he should nurture his natural bent and remove the rest.

People's thoughts follow their natural inclinations, their talk follows what they have learned, but their actions follow their habits. So neither natural temperament nor fine words can be trusted unless habit supports them. Bacon illustrates this with Machiavelli's example: for a dangerous conspiracy, choose a man who has already committed violence before.

Bacon says that Machiavelli did not know of the religious assassins named here, yet Machiavelli's rule still holds: custom is stronger than nature or solemn promises. He adds that religious devotion now makes men as ready to kill as butchers, and that in general people keep doing what they have always done, whatever they vow.

Bacon uses examples to show how strong custom is: people accept extreme and painful things because they are used to them. He gives cases of Indian wise men who lie on wood to be burned, widows who want to die on their husbands' funeral fires, Spartan boys who bore beatings without crying out, and an Irish rebel who asked for a particular kind of rope for his hanging.

Custom, meaning habit, has a strong hold on both mind and body, and it governs much of human life. So people should work to build good habits, and these are best formed when young. Education, in this view, is just early habit.

Bacon says that young people learn languages and physical skills more easily than adults, because their minds and bodies are more flexible. Late learners find it hard to adapt, except for rare people who stay open to improvement. He adds that custom acting on people in groups is even stronger than custom acting on one person alone.

Bacon says that good communities help people grow in virtue, because example, company, rivalry and honour all encourage it. Well-run states and governments nourish virtue that already exists, but they do little to improve people's actions. He laments that the most effective means are used for the least worthy ends.

Bacon says that outside chance plays a part in fortune, but a person mainly shapes his own luck. He adds that many people rise because others make mistakes, and that hidden personal qualities, which have no name, bring success more than visible virtues do.

Bacon says that a person whose mind moves in step with his luck, with no stubbornness or resistance in his nature, is said to have good fortune. He points to Livy's praise of Cato the Elder, who seemed able to make his own luck wherever he was born, and to Livy's remark that Cato had a flexible mind. Fortune is blind, but a careful observer can still see her at work.

Bacon says that good fortune comes from many small qualities working together, like a cluster of stars that gives light as one. He gives an example from Italian speech: a man who never makes mistakes is said to have "a little of the madman" (poco di matto). He adds that a touch of foolishness and not too much honesty are two of the most useful traits for success.

Bacon says that people who are too devoted to their country or to their masters are never lucky, because they put their thoughts outside themselves and do not follow their own path. A sudden stroke of luck makes a restless, bold go-getter, while experienced good fortune makes a capable person. Fortune deserves respect, he adds, because it brings two daughters: self-confidence, which is felt inside a person, and reputation, which is held by others.

Wise men often credit their success to Providence (God's guiding care) and Fortune (luck). This makes their virtues easier to claim without envy, and it suggests they are under higher protection. Those who openly credit their own wisdom and planning too much are said to end unlucky.

Timotheus, an Athenian general, was said to have often told the state that luck had no part in his successes. After that, he never succeeded in anything he attempted. Bacon adds that some people's luck flows easily, like Homer's verses, and that this depends largely on the person himself.

Bacon notes that many people have made clever attacks on usury, the lending of money at interest. These attacks say that the usurer takes what belongs to God, claim he breaks the Sabbath because his money works even on Sundays, and compare him to a drone bee that lives off others' labour.

Bacon lists common arguments against usury, such as that it breaks the curse-era rule that man earns bread by his own sweat, not by another's. He ends by saying usury is allowed only because people are too hard-hearted to lend freely, and lending is still needed.

Bacon says that others have offered sly schemes about banks and other money ideas, but few have discussed usury (lending money for interest) in a useful way. He argues that we should set out both the harms and benefits of usury, so we can keep the good and pick out the bad, and take care not to end up with something worse.
