Bacon argues that usury, lending money at interest, harms trade in two ways. It keeps money idle instead of invested in trade, so fewer merchants exist. It also makes the merchants who borrow poorer, because high interest limits what they can do, just as a high rent limits a farmer.

Bacon lists harms of usury, and this part gives two. Usury tends to gather a country's wealth into a few hands, since the lender collects sure gains while others risk losses, so the money ends up with the usurer. A state does best when wealth is spread more evenly.

Usury, the lending of money at interest, is harmful in three ways here. It blocks trade and buying of property, it discourages all business, improvement and invention that money would otherwise fund, and it ruins many men's fortunes, which over time leads to poverty for the whole public.

Bacon lists two benefits of lending money at interest. First, he says that although usury sometimes slows trade, it often helps it, because most merchants start out by borrowing at interest, and if lenders call in or hold back their money, trade quickly stalls. Second, without easy loans at interest, people in need would be quickly ruined.

Bacon argues that if usury were banned, borrowers would be forced to sell their land or goods at very low prices in a poor market, which would ruin them more completely than interest does. He adds that pawning or mortgaging would not help, because lenders either refuse pawns without interest or insist on seizing them when the debt is not repaid.

Bacon argues that lending without interest is unrealistic, since every state has always had some form of usury (interest on loans) in one kind or another. He adds that restricting borrowing would cause many problems. So the idea of abolishing usury belongs only in Utopia, an imaginary perfect country.

Bacon argues that usury (lending money at interest) should be regulated in two ways. Interest must be kept low enough that it does not bite too hard on ordinary borrowers, yet high enough that lenders still want to lend to merchants, since trade needs that money. He proposes two rates: a lower one for ordinary borrowing and a higher one for trade, which can afford it.

Bacon proposes a two-tier system for interest on loans. Ordinary lending would be capped at five percent and allowed openly, with the state taking no penalty for it, which he says keeps borrowing flowing and eases country borrowers. A higher rate would be permitted only to certain people and in certain trading places.

Bacon argues that lowering the legal interest rate would push up land prices, since land bought at sixteen years' purchase yields about six percent, more than the new five percent rate. He adds that people would then invest in productive improvements rather than accept low interest. He then proposes that licensed lenders be allowed to lend to known merchants at a higher rate, under certain safeguards.

Bacon proposes lowering the interest rate that merchants pay, so that all borrowers gain some relief. He wants lending to stay in private hands rather than through a bank or shared fund, though he does not entirely oppose banks. The state would take a small fee for granting the license, and the rest of the interest would go to the lender.

Bacon argues that if interest is set at a legal rate, moneylenders who charged higher rates will still prefer to lend at the lower legal rate than give up lending. He proposes that licensed lenders be limited to certain trading cities, so they cannot draw in money from the countryside and push interest rates up.

Bacon answers an objection that setting a legal interest rate would seem to approve of usury (lending money at interest), which had only been tolerated before. He replies that it is better to limit usury by a public rule than to let it grow unchecked by quietly ignoring it.

A young man can be old in wisdom if he has wasted no time, but this rarely happens. Young people's first thoughts are less wise than later ones, though their ideas flow more vividly and freely than those of older people.

People with strong heat, violent desires and great emotional upheavals are not ready for action until they are past middle age, as Julius Caesar and Septimius Severus show. Severus spent his youth in errors and even madness, yet he was nearly the ablest emperor of all. Calm natures, however, can do well when young.

Bacon says that young men are better at inventing new ideas and carrying out plans than at judging or advising. Older men are better at settled business, since their experience guides them in familiar matters, but in new matters that same experience can mislead them. He also gives examples of men who did well with the energy of age.

Bacon says the mistakes of young men can wreck a project, while the mistakes of older men only mean that something could have been done more, or sooner. He lists young men's faults: they take on more than they can manage, rush toward goals without planning how to reach them, and refuse to admit or undo their errors.

Bacon says older men tend to hesitate, deliberate too long, take few risks, and regret decisions too quickly, so they often settle for partial success. He argues that mixing young and old in the same work is good, since each age corrects the other's faults. He adds that youth tends to be better in moral matters, and age in political ones.

A rabbi reads a verse about young men seeing visions and old men dreaming dreams, and concludes that the young are closer to God, since a vision is clearer than a dream. Bacon adds that age mainly improves understanding, not the will or emotions. Some people ripen early and then fade, usually because their minds are dull or quickly worn out.

Bacon describes two kinds of people whose strengths suit youth but not old age. One kind has a flowing, showy way of speaking that looks fitting in the young but not in the old. The other kind starts out with a bold, lofty spirit that the years cannot sustain.

Virtue, like a gem, looks best in a plain setting, so it shows best in a person who is well-proportioned but not strikingly beautiful. Bacon observes that very beautiful people rarely have great virtue. He suggests nature spends its effort on looks and not on greatness, so such people tend to be polished in manners but lack deep character.

Bacon says that great and bold men can also be beautiful, citing several famous rulers and leaders as examples. He ranks beauty: grace of face matters more than skin colour, and graceful movement matters most of all. The finest beauty cannot be captured in a painting or seen at first glance, and every excellent beauty has some unusual element in its proportions.

Bacon says it is hard to say whether Apelles or Albert Dürer was the bigger fool. One built a figure from geometric measurements, the other combined the best features of many faces. Such figures would please only their makers. A painter can still make a beautiful face, but by a kind of natural talent, not by rules. Some faces look good as a whole even though no single part is good.

Bacon says that beauty lies mostly in graceful movement, so older people can sometimes seem more pleasing than the young. Beauty is like summer fruit: it spoils easily and does not last. It often makes young people careless and leaves older people feeling awkward. But when beauty is well placed, it makes virtue look brighter and vice ashamed.

Bacon says deformed people are often treated unfairly by nature, and they respond by lacking natural affection for others, which he calls nature's revenge. He believes body and mind are linked, so a flaw in one tends to bring a risk to the other. Still, he holds that a person can choose how to shape the mind, and that discipline and virtue can overcome natural tendencies.

Bacon says a physical deformity is better judged as a cause than as a sign of a person's character, since a sign can mislead while a cause usually produces its effect. A permanent flaw that invites contempt gives the person a constant urge to escape scorn. So deformed people tend to become bold, first to defend themselves and later out of habit. They also work hard and watch others' weaknesses, so they can pay back scorn.

Bacon argues that a physical deformity can help a clever person rise in the world. Rivals do not see the deformed man as a threat, so they relax and do not expect him to gain power until it is already his. He compares this to kings who trusted eunuchs, since a man whom others do not fear is more loyal and eager to serve one master.

Deformed people, Bacon says, often try to escape the scorn of others. They do this either through virtue or through malice, so some of them turn out to be excellent people. He gives Agesilaus, Socrates and others as examples.

Bacon says a house exists to be lived in, not just looked at, so function should come before uniform design when both cannot be had. Beautiful houses are for poets' imagined palaces, which cost little to build. A fine house on a bad site is like a prison. A site is bad not only when the air is unhealthy but also when the air is uneven, as with houses set in a hollow surrounded by higher hills.

Bacon lists the faults that make a house site bad. Enclosed sun and wind trap can cause sudden swings between heat and cold. Other faults include poor roads, poor markets, unpleasant neighbors (Momus was the Greek god of mockery), lack of water, wood, shade, shelter, fertile soil, a view, or flat ground.

Bacon lists the factors to weigh when choosing a site for a house. These include nearness to hunting grounds, the sea, rivers, and cities, and whether the land yields plenty or is scarce. He admits they are unlikely to all be found together, so a builder should know them and take as many as he can.

Bacon says a man with several homes should arrange them so that each makes up for what the others lack. He gives the example of Lucullus, a wealthy Roman, who answered Pompey that he moved between houses with the seasons, as migrating birds do.

Bacon says that, having discussed the setting of a house, he will now describe the house itself. He will describe an ideal princely palace in brief, as Cicero wrote about oratory in two books. He finds it odd that Europe has huge buildings such as the Vatican and the Escorial, yet hardly a single fine room among them.

Bacon says a perfect palace needs two separate sides. One side is for banquets and celebrations, and the other is for everyday living. Both sides should look alike from outside but be divided differently inside, with a tall central tower joining them.

Bacon describes how he would lay out a house. On one side, facing the banquet area, he would put a single fine upper room about forty feet high, with a dressing room below it for use during festivities. On the household side he would have a hall and a chapel, divided by a partition, and at the far end a winter parlor and a summer parlor, with a large cellar dug beneath.

Bacon describes parts of an ideal house: small service rooms such as pantries, a two-storey tower above the two wings with a flat leaded roof edged by statues, and a main staircase with an open central post, railed with wooden figures painted to look like brass, ending in a fine landing.

Bacon advises that the lower rooms should not be used as a dining room for servants, because the smell of their cooking would rise through the house like up a chimney and reach the family's meal. He also gives the height of the first stairs as sixteen feet, matching the lower room.

Bacon describes the design of a building's inner court. Three sides are lower than the front, and staircases stand in turrets at the four corners, set outside the main walls. The turrets are kept lower than the front. The court is not paved, because stone holds heat and cold; it has side paths and grass instead.

Bacon describes how to plan a large house. One wing holds stately galleries with windows and cupolas (domed roof sections), while the other side has rooms for receiving guests and everyday use. The rooms should face different directions so they get sun or shade, suiting both summer and winter.

Bacon says some fine houses have so much glass that you cannot find a spot free from sun or cold. He likes bay windows, which stick out from the wall, because they make good places for talking and block wind and sun. He wants only a few of them, placed on the sides of the courtyard.

Bacon describes an inner court inside the outer one, square and the same height, surrounded by a garden. Its sides are lined with arches, and the ground floor facing the garden is a shaded grotto or summer room. The court has a level floor, not sunk below ground to avoid damp, and a fountain or statues at its center.

Bacon describes the layout of a palace courtyard's side buildings. One wing should hold a sickroom for the prince or another important person, with connected chambers, placed on the upper floor. The ground and top floors should have open galleries on pillars, giving views and fresh air over the garden.

Bacon describes the fine rooms and features he wants in a grand house: two decorated side cabinets at the far corners, a dome in the middle, and fountains in the upper gallery. He then says that before reaching the front of the palace there should be three courts, starting with a plain green courtyard walled around.

Bacon describes how a grand house should be laid out. Behind the front, there is a second courtyard decorated with small towers, and a third courtyard that closes a square. The third court has no solid walls on its sides. Instead it has roofed terraces, and its inner side has pillars without arches. Service buildings stand apart, linked to the palace by low galleries.
Bacon says gardens are the purest human pleasure and a great refreshment to the mind, more so than buildings. He thinks a royal garden should have something in bloom in every month of the year.

Bacon lists plants to grow for each season so a garden has flowers or green leaves all year. For December to November's end, he names evergreens and shrubs such as holly, ivy, rosemary, and lemon trees. For late January and February, he names early bloomers such as crocuses, primroses, and hyacinths.

Bacon lists flowers and trees in the order they bloom through the spring months. March brings violets, daffodils, daisies and blossoming fruit trees, April brings more violets, lilies, tulips and other flowers, and May and June bring pinks.

Bacon lists plants in the order they flower or bear fruit through the year, from spring roses and honeysuckles, through summer gilliflowers and plums, to August melons and monkshood, and September grapes and apples. The point is a garden planned so that something is always in bloom or fruit.

Bacon lists fruits and flowers that ripen or bloom in each season, such as late-autumn medlars and services. He says these examples suit London's climate, but his real aim is that a garden should have flowers and fruit all year round, as far as the local climate allows.

Flowers give their scent best to the air, not when held in the hand, so the best garden plants are those that send out fragrance into the air. Bacon notes that damask and red roses, bay, and rosemary give off little or no smell as they grow, even when you walk past a whole row of them.

Bacon ranks garden plants by how sweet their scent is in the air. The white double violet is first, blooming twice a year. Next come the musk-rose, dying strawberry leaves, vine flowers, sweet-briar, and wall-flowers, which he says are pleasant under a window.

Bacon lists flowers that give off the sweetest scent, especially when their leaves are crushed underfoot. He names burnet, wild thyme and watermint as the three best for this. So he advises planting whole paths of them, so that walking on them releases their fragrance.

A princely garden should cover at least thirty acres, split into three main parts: a green lawn at the entrance, a heath or wild area on the way out, and the main garden in the middle, with walkways along both sides. Bacon suggests a layout of four acres for the green, six for the heath, four on each side, and twelve for the main garden.

Bacon says the lawn, or "green," gives two pleasures. Short, neatly cut grass is pleasing to look at. A lawn also leaves a clear path down the middle, so you can walk along a fine hedge that encloses the garden.

Bacon advises building a covered walkway, about twelve feet high, along each side of the lawn, so that people can walk to the garden in shade rather than in the hot sun. He dismisses patterned flower beds of colored earth under the windows as mere toys, saying one can see as good sights in pastries.

Bacon describes the layout of an ideal garden: a square plot enclosed on all four sides by a tall hedge shaped into arches. The arches stand on wooden pillars about ten feet high and six feet wide, with a further hedge of four feet on top.

Bacon describes the planned garden's hedge: on top of it, above each arch, a small turret large enough to hold a cage of birds, and between the arches small gilded figures with round coloured glass plates for the sun to shine on. The hedge will sit on a gently sloping bank about six feet high, planted with flowers. The square garden will not fill the whole plot, leaving room on each side for side alleys.

Bacon says that the long enclosed walk in a garden should have no hedged side-alleys at either end. A hedged alley at the near end would block the view of the fine hedge from the lawn, and one at the far end would block the view from the hedge out through the arches onto the heath.

Bacon says the layout of the garden inside the outer hedge is up to the gardener, but it should not be too busy or full of work. He dislikes figures cut from juniper and similar plants, calling them fit only for children. He prefers low, round hedges, some pyramids, and columns on wooden frames, with wide, fair walkways.

Bacon says that narrow paths may be placed along the sides of the garden, but not in the main garden. In the middle he wants a high mound with three ways up it, wide enough for four people to walk side by side, and a fine banqueting house on top.

Bacon says fountains are beautiful and refreshing, but pools spoil a garden by breeding flies and frogs. He wants two kinds of fountain: one that sprays water, and one that holds a clear, still basin of water with no fish, slime or mud. The water in the spraying fountains must keep moving so it never stands and turns coloured or green.

Bacon says a fountain must be kept clean: free of moss and rot, and cleaned by hand every day. He adds that a bathing pool may be decorated with fine paving, images, colored glass and statues, but the main concern is the same cleanliness as for the first kind of fountain.

Bacon says a garden pool should have water constantly flowing in from a higher source and draining away underground, so it does not stand still. He calls fancy water tricks, such as arches and fountains shaped like feathers or glasses, pleasant to look at but of no use for health or freshness.

The third part of the garden, the heath, should look as wild as possible, with no trees. It should have thickets of sweet-briar and honeysuckle, wild vine, and violets, strawberries and primroses scattered here and there with no fixed arrangement, since these plants are sweet and grow well in shade.

Bacon says he likes small raised mounds, like mole-hills found on wild heaths, planted with low flowers. He lists many kinds, such as thyme, pinks, violets, strawberries, daisies and roses, all chosen for being sweet-smelling and pleasing to look at.

Some garden beds are to have small shrubs planted on top of them, and some are to have none. The shrubs named are roses, juniper, holly, barberries, red currants, gooseberries, rosemary, bay, sweetbriar and similar plants. These are to be clipped so they do not grow out of shape.

Bacon describes how to lay out the side areas of a garden. He advises many paths, some fully shaded, some sheltered from the wind so they can be walked in bad weather, and some with gravel rather than grass so they stay dry. Fruit trees should also line many of these paths.

Bacon advises how to lay out a garden. Fruit-tree borders should be wide, low and gently sloping, with flowers planted thinly so they do not draw nourishment from the trees. At the ends of the side grounds he wants a raised mound, and the enclosing wall kept chest-high so that people can look out over the fields.

Bacon says the main garden should have open air, not dense planting. It should have fruit-tree alleys and arbors, but the trees must not be packed closely together. Shade is to be found in the side alleys, and the main garden is for mild seasons, or for summer mornings, evenings and cloudy days.

Bacon says he dislikes aviaries unless they are large enough to be turfed and planted with living bushes, so the birds have room and can nest naturally, and the floor stays clean. He says great princes often build gardens with statues for show, but these add nothing to the true pleasure of a garden.

Bacon says that talking face to face is usually better than writing, and that using a go-between is usually better than dealing directly yourself. Letters are useful when you want a written reply, when you may need your own letter later as proof, or when a message could be interrupted or read in pieces. Meeting in person helps when your presence earns respect, as it often does with people of lower rank, or when delicate matters let you judge from the other person's face how far to go.

Bacon advises that when choosing people to carry out negotiations, it is better to pick plain, straightforward men who will do what they are asked and report results honestly. He warns against clever men who twist other people's work to make themselves look good. He also suggests choosing people who care about the task and are suited to it.

Bacon advises choosing negotiators by their strengths: bold men to protest, smooth-talking men to persuade, sly men to probe and watch, and even awkward or foolish men for tasks that cannot survive on their own merits. He also says to feel out the other side gently before stating your main point, and to deal with people who still want something rather than those already satisfied.

When two people make a deal with conditions, the first act of doing one's part is the key point. A person cannot fairly expect the other to go first unless the nature of the deal requires it, or he can convince the other that he will still need him for something else, or that he is seen as the more honest of the two. Bacon adds that people reveal their true selves when they trust, feel strong emotion, act unaware, or are forced to act.

Bacon says that in dealing with someone, you can move them by appealing to their own goals, by using their weaknesses to make them fear you, or by working through people who have influence over them. With clever people, watch their aims, say little, and prepare matters slowly rather than expecting quick results.

Bacon warns against followers who cost a great man too much, whether by draining his money or by wearing him out with constant demands for favours. Ordinary followers should only expect support, recommendation and protection from harm. Factious followers, who join a patron out of resentment toward a rival rather than real loyalty, are worse, and often cause bad feeling between powerful men.

Bacon warns that two kinds of followers do harm. Showy followers who loudly praise their master spoil business by being indiscreet and draw envy toward him. Spies who pass on the household's secrets are dangerous, though they often gain favor because they are eager to help and trade gossip.

Having a following of men who share the same work or calling, such as soldiers loyal to a former commander, has long been accepted, even under kings, provided it is not showy or aimed at winning popular favour. The most honourable following is that of a person who promotes virtue and merit in all kinds of people. Where two candidates are equally capable, it is better to choose the more agreeable one. In corrupt times, however, active men are more useful than virtuous ones.

Bacon says that in government, treating men of the same rank equally avoids resentment, since favoring a few makes them proud and the rest bitter. In personal favor, uneven treatment works better, making the favored grateful and others more eager. He also advises not to give too much at first, and warns that being ruled by one man is unsafe and invites scandal.

Bacon says that being pulled in many directions by many friends is worse than having only a few. Taking advice from a few friends is always honorable, since outsiders often see more than players do. Real friendship is rare, and the friendship that does exist is mostly between a superior and an inferior, not between equals.

Bacon says that some projects are bad, and private requests can harm the public good. Some people take up good causes with bad motives, such as seeking favour, using a suitor's hopes for their own gain, or using a case to block another person.

Bacon warns against taking on other people's legal suits carelessly, or only to use them for one's own ends, or even to drop them on purpose to help the other side. He says every suit has some right in it, either the right of fairness in a dispute or the right of merit in a request. If personal feeling pushes a man toward the unjust side, he should try to settle the matter rather than press it.

If a man favors a less worthy applicant out of personal liking, he may do so, but he must not harm or shut out the more deserving one. When he does not understand a request, he should pass it to a trusted friend with sound judgment, and choose that friend carefully. Plain, honest dealing, saying no at once and claiming no more credit than is due, is now seen as both honorable and pleasing.

Bacon advises on asking for favours. A suitor who first brings useful information should be given some consideration and reward, and not have that information used against him. Timing matters most, and keeping a request secret helps, because talk of it can spur rivals.

Bacon advises that a person seeking a favour should pick the right timing and the right go-between, choosing someone well suited to the task rather than someone merely powerful or important. He adds that a refused request can still be won later if the asker does not appear hurt or angry. The Latin saying means "ask for something unfair so you can get what is fair," which he says works only when the asker has strong favour; otherwise, it is better to back down from the request.

Bacon warns that a man who refuses a suitor at first may keep his own favor, while one who goes along and later refuses loses both. A letter of recommendation seems an easy favor, but if the cause is bad, it damages the great person's reputation. Middlemen who handle many requests for others do harm to public business.

Studies are useful in three ways: for private pleasure, for polish in conversation, and for good judgment in running affairs. Experienced practical men can handle single matters, but broad plans and strategy are best left to the learned. Excess is a fault: too much study is laziness, using it only to show off is pretension, and deciding everything by book rules is a scholar's foolishness.

Bacon says that studies and natural talent need each other and need experience. Study trims natural ability as pruning shapes a plant, while experience keeps study from giving advice that is too broad. He adds that studies do not teach their own use, and that reading should be done to weigh and consider, not to argue, accept without question, or make conversation.

Bacon says that books should be read in different ways. Some should only be sampled, some read in parts, and only a few read fully and carefully. Summaries by others are acceptable only for minor works, and he adds that reading makes a full man, talking a ready man, and writing an exact man.

Bacon says that studies shape the mind in different ways: history makes people wise, poetry makes them witty, mathematics sharpens them, and logic and rhetoric train them to argue. He adds that any weakness of the wit can be cured by the right studies, just as bodily illness is treated with the right exercise.

Bacon says that each weakness of the mind has a matching study that can cure it. A wandering mind should study mathematics, where a lapse of attention forces a fresh start. A mind weak at making fine distinctions should study the Schoolmen, medieval scholastic philosophers known for hair-splitting. A mind poor at comparing and linking ideas should study legal cases.

Bacon says many people wrongly think a ruler should govern by favouring one faction over another. He argues the wiser course is to act on matters all factions share, or to deal with people one by one. He does not say faction should be ignored, and notes that men of low rank must attach themselves to a faction while they rise.

Strong men do better to stay neutral and not take sides. Newcomers should lean moderately toward one party, the one most acceptable to the other side. A small, unbending faction often wears down a larger, more moderate one, and when one party is destroyed, the survivors split apart.

Factions that unite against a common rival tend to split apart once that rival is gone. The Roman senate's party held out against Pompey and Caesar until its power was destroyed, and then those two broke apart. Antonius and Octavianus did the same after defeating Brutus and Cassius. Bacon says the same holds for private factions.

Men who are second-in-command in a faction sometimes rise to lead when the faction splits, but often they lose their place, because their strength lay in opposing others. Men who gain a position often switch to the opposing side, hoping to win a new advantage. Bacon adds that a traitor in a faction usually gets away with it.

When two sides are deadlocked, one man's victory often tips the balance and he gets all the credit. Someone who seems neutral between two factions may really be keeping both for his own use, not acting from moderation. Bacon notes that Italians suspect popes who call themselves "common father" of this, and he warns that kings should not take sides as a party.

Leagues or factions formed within a state are always harmful to a monarchy, because they create loyalties stronger than loyalty to the sovereign, so the king is treated as just one of the group ("tanquam unus ex nobis", as one of us). When factions grow too strong and violent, Bacon says, this shows weakness in the ruler. Factions under a king should move like the inner planetary spheres, following their own motions but kept steady by the outer sphere.

A man who is entirely sincere, with no pretence, needs very great virtue, as a jewel set without a backing needs to be very fine. Bacon adds that small, everyday courtesies win more praise than rare great virtues, because they come up constantly, just as small gains often add up more than occasional large ones.

Good manners and polite forms add to a man's reputation, but they should come easily rather than be forced. Trying too hard to perform them makes a man lose their natural grace, and a mind busy with small courtesies cannot take on great matters. Dropping ceremonies altogether also sets a bad example for others.

Bacon says that ceremonies should not be skipped with strangers and formal people, but dwelling on them or praising them too highly is tiresome and weakens a speaker's trust. He adds that a skilled speaker can make a point stick through polite phrases. Among equals, a man keeps some distance to hold his standing; among inferiors, he is a little familiar to be liked.

A person who is too present or too eager in anything tires others and makes himself seem worthless. Going along with others is good, but only when it is clearly shown to come from respect, not from an easy willingness to agree. In supporting someone, add something of your own, such as a qualification, a condition, or a further reason. Excessive politeness should be avoided.

Bacon warns that being overly concerned with formal courtesies and waiting for the perfect moment both hurt a person's chances. Rivals will label a man of ceremony as only a formalist, which hides his real merits. A wise person creates opportunities rather than watching for them, and good behavior should be relaxed enough to allow free movement.

Praise is a reflection of virtue, but it depends on who gives it. Praise from ordinary people is usually false and worthless, and tends to go to showy people rather than good ones. Ordinary people notice only lesser virtues, admire middle ones, and cannot perceive the highest at all.

Praise from ordinary people is like a river that carries light, swollen things and sinks heavy, solid ones, so it is not a sure guide to a person's worth. Praise from people of rank and sound judgment is different: it lasts, like the scent of perfume, which holds longer than the smell of flowers. Still, much praise is false, and some is only flattery made of general phrases that could fit anyone.

A flatterer who is subtle will praise whatever a man already thinks best of himself. A flatterer who is bold will praise the very thing a man secretly knows is his weakness, pushing it on him even though his own conscience rejects it.

Some praise is a polite courtesy paid to kings and great people, and it also shows them what they ought to be. Other praise is meant to harm the person praised, by stirring envy and jealousy against them. The old Greek proverb says such a person will get a pimple on the nose, much like a blister on a liar's tongue.

Praise helps only when it is moderate, fitting to the moment, and not crude. Excessive praise of a person or thing invites argument, envy and mockery. Praising yourself is seldom proper, but praising your job or profession can be done gracefully.

Bacon says that Roman churchmen, such as cardinals, theologians and friars, look down on worldly public work like war, diplomacy and law. They call it "sbirrerie," a term for minor officials' work. He adds that this work often does more good than their abstract learning, and that St. Paul praised his own office, not himself, when he spoke of it.

Bacon uses Aesop's fable of a fly on a chariot wheel that claims to raise the dust, to make a point about vain people. They think they cause results that others produce, and they boast and cannot keep quiet, so they achieve little.

Bacon says that praising others can be useful in public affairs, where people are used to build a reputation for virtue or greatness. He gives an example from the historian Livy: a go-between who flatters each side to the other, or who claims more influence than he has, gains credit with both.

Bacon says that praise and show often create real results. Lies can start a rumor, and the rumor then becomes a real reputation. Glory spurs soldiers on, as iron sharpens iron. Men of solid, sober nature give steady weight to a venture, but a showy, glorious spirit gives it momentum. A scholar's fame, he adds, rises slowly without some display.

Even those who write books against seeking fame put their own names on them, and famous philosophers and writers such as Socrates, Aristotle, Galen, Cicero and Seneca were full of self-display. Bacon claims that vanity helps keep a person's memory alive, much as varnish keeps a ceiling shining and lasting. He then sets aside a different kind of vanity from the one he means here.

Skilled display is not always vanity; it can come from a generous spirit and good judgment. Even excuses, yielding, and well-managed modesty count as display. The best such method, Pliny says, is to praise others in the skill where you excel, since praising another does you credit.

Bacon argues that praise is a dilemma: if the person you praise is lesser than you, the praise should go to you instead; if he is greater, your praise adds little. He ends by saying that glorious, showy men are mocked by the wise, admired by fools, flattered by hangers-on, and enslaved by their own boasting.

Honor, Bacon says, is simply the public showing of a man's real virtue and worth, with no harm to him. Some men chase honor through their actions and are much talked about but little respected inside. Others hide their virtue in how they present it, so people think less of them. The passage then begins to list what makes an act honorable: doing something never tried before, or abandoned, or done with better circumstances.

Bacon says a man gains more honor by a task that is less hard or noble, where he leads, than by a harder one where he only follows. He also says that taking on an action whose failure would disgrace him is poor management of one's honor, since success adds less than failure would take away.

Bacon advises that a man should try to outdo rivals at their own skill, that good servants help build reputation, and that envy is best defused by showing that one seeks merit rather than fame. He also suggests crediting success to providence and good fortune rather than to one's own virtue or cleverness.

Bacon ranks the highest kinds of honor for rulers. The first rank goes to founders of states and nations, such as Romulus and Cyrus. The second goes to lawgivers, who keep ruling through their laws after they die, such as Lycurgus and Solon.

Bacon lists kinds of honor a ruler can earn, in rising order. The third kind is "liberators or saviors": men who end long civil wars or free their countries from foreign or tyrannical rule. The fourth is "extenders or defenders of the empire": men who win territory in honorable wars or defend against invaders. The last is "fathers of the country."

Bacon lists kinds of honor a subject can win from a ruler. The first are the ruler's chief helpers, who carry the heaviest share of state business. The second are great war leaders who serve the ruler well in battle. The third are favorites.

Bacon describes kinds of honor. One is for people who serve in great offices under rulers and carry out their duties well. The rarest and greatest is for those who give up their lives or face death for their country, such as Regulus and the two Decii.

Judges should only declare what the law already says, not create new law or lay down rules of their own. Bacon compares a judge who goes beyond this to the Church of Rome, which he says adds to and changes Scripture while claiming to explain it. He adds that judges should be learned, reverent, and careful rather than clever or showy, and above all honest.

A corrupt judge who gives a wrong ruling about land or property does more harm than many bad examples set by others. Bad examples only spoil the stream, but a corrupt judge spoils the source it flows from. The Latin quote from Solomon says a just man who falls in his own cause before an opponent is like a troubled spring and a polluted well.

Bacon says that a judge's main duty is to stop force and fraud in lawsuits. Open force is the worse of the two, while fraud is worse when it is hidden. He also says that unjust decisions and long delays spoil justice, and that quarrelsome lawsuits should be rejected.

A judge should level the field when one side is much stronger, with more power, skill or lawyers, so that the case is decided on even ground. He should also avoid forcing laws into harsh readings, because twisted interpretation of the law does as much harm as torture.

Penal laws, which set punishments, should not be applied so harshly that their purpose of frightening people becomes cruelty. Old or outdated laws should be softened by wise judges. In cases of death, judges should be strict about the example set for others but merciful toward the accused person.

Bacon says a judge should be patient and calm when listening to lawyers, because listening fully is part of justice. A judge who talks too much, cuts counsel short, or asks questions before hearing the case is criticised. He lists the judge's duties in hearing a case, starting with directing the evidence and limiting long or irrelevant speech.

A judge's job, the passage says, is to sum up the main points of what was argued and then state the rule or verdict. Anything beyond that comes from vanity, a wish to talk, impatience, poor memory, or a failure to listen steadily. Bacon finds it odd that bold advocates sway judges, when judges should copy God, who humbles the proud and favors the modest.

Bacon says it is strange when judges have favorite lawyers, because this drives up legal fees and makes people suspect secret dealings. He also says a judge should praise good advocates, even those on the losing side, since this keeps the client's trust in his lawyer and weakens the client's false confidence in his own case.

Lawyers should be openly criticised when they act badly, for example by using clever tricks, being careless, or pressing or defending their case too boldly. Lawyers must not argue with the judge or reopen the case after the judge has given a decision. Judges, in turn, must not favour one side early, and must hear both sides fully.

Bacon says that courts of justice must be kept free of corruption, including the lower officials around the bench. He argues that justice cannot bear fruit while it is surrounded by greedy clerks and officers, just as grapes do not grow on thorns. He then begins listing four kinds of bad influence on court attendance.

Bacon lists types of court officials who harm justice. The first makes the court grow proud while the countryside suffers. The second are false friends of the court who stir up disputes over jurisdiction, inflating the court's power for their own gain. The third use sly tricks to twist straight justice into crooked paths. The fourth extorts excessive fees.

Bacon says that a court can be like a bush: a sheep runs to it for shelter from the weather but loses some of its wool there. He adds that a skilled old clerk, who knows past cases and the court's business, is an excellent guide and often shows the judge the way.

Judges should keep in mind the Roman maxim that the welfare of the people is the highest law. Laws that do not serve that end are mere tricks, and Bacon says it is good when kings and judges often consult each other on matters of law and of state.

Bacon says that a case may look like an ordinary dispute over property, yet its outcome can affect the state. He counts as "matters of state" any case that brings a big change, sets a dangerous precedent, or affects many people. He adds that just laws and good government are not opposed; they work together, as spirits and sinews do in the body.

Judges should be strong and bold in their role, like the lions that held up Solomon's throne, but they must stay under the king's authority and not oppose any royal power. They should also know that applying the law wisely is a main part of their job. Bacon ends by quoting Paul: "we know the law is good, if a man use it lawfully."

Bacon says that trying to remove anger completely is only a show of bravery, as the Stoics attempted. Instead, he follows the Bible: anger may be felt but not allowed to become sin, and it should end by sunset. He then announces that he will limit anger in time and degree, and explain how to calm a person's natural tendency toward anger, control its outbursts, and stir up or soothe anger in others.

The main advice in this passage is to reflect on anger after the fit has passed, and to see how it harms a person's life. Bacon supports this with a saying from Seneca that anger falls back on the person who feels it, and with a line from Scripture about keeping one's soul through patience. The closing Latin phrase, about bees that die after stinging, is a warning that anger can cost a person his own life.

Anger is a low quality, seen in people who are weak, such as children, women, the old and the sick. Men should show their anger through scorn rather than fear, so they seem above an insult rather than beneath it. This is easy to do if a man controls himself.

Bacon names two main causes of anger. The first is being too sensitive to hurt, since a person must feel hurt before becoming angry, so easily wounded people get angry often. The second is taking an injury as contempt, which sharpens anger more than the hurt itself.

Anger grows when people pick out insults and feel their reputation is under attack. The cure for this is a thicker skin about one's honour, and the best way to hold back anger is to delay: tell yourself the moment for revenge has not yet come, so the anger can wait.

Bacon gives two warnings for keeping anger from doing harm. First, avoid harsh, cutting words, especially sharp personal insults, and do not reveal secrets while angry. Second, do not abruptly end any business in anger, and do not take any step that cannot be undone.

Bacon describes how to stir up anger in someone else: pick moments when they are most irritable, and collect every slight you can find to make them feel scorned. The remedies are the opposite. Choose a good moment to raise an angry matter, since first impressions count for a lot, and explain the injury as coming from misunderstanding, fear, or passion rather than from contempt.

Solomon says there is nothing new under the sun, so what seems new is really forgotten old things returning. Bacon compares this to Plato's idea that all knowledge is remembering, and to the river Lethe, whose waters cause forgetting.

Bacon says that everything in the world is constantly changing and never stays still. He names two great forces that wipe out whole histories and memories: floods and earthquakes. Fires and long droughts destroy too, but they do not erase everything as completely.

Bacon argues that after floods and earthquakes, the survivors are usually isolated mountain people who keep no record of earlier times, so the past is lost as if no one had lived through the disaster. From this he suggests that the peoples of the West Indies are probably newer, or younger, than those of the Old World.

Bacon argues that the lost lands of the Americas were more likely destroyed by a great flood than by earthquakes, which are rare there. He notes that the region has huge rivers and very high mountains.

Bacon says that religious rivalry between sects does not usually destroy the memory of older things, as Machiavelli claimed. He points to Gregory the Great, who was said to have tried to wipe out pagan antiquities, and notes that such zeal did not last. Sabinian, Gregory's successor, revived the old works.

Bacon sets aside changes in the heavens as not suitable for his topic. He says a "great year" (a long cycle of the stars, from Plato) might affect things in general, but not repeat the same individual events. He adds that comets influence the whole mass of things, yet people only stare at them rather than carefully study what specific effects each kind produces.

Bacon reports a folk belief, heard about the Low Countries, that weather patterns repeat in a cycle of thirty-five years, a cycle they call the "Prime." He says he mentions it because his own backward calculation seemed to match it.

Bacon says that changes among religions and sects are the greatest changes among people, because religion rules men's minds most. He holds that the true religion stands firm like a rock, while others are carried away by the waves of time. He then turns to the causes of new sects and what can be done about them, as far as human judgment can help.

Bacon says a new religious sect is likely to arise when religious leaders have lost their holiness and are corrupt, when the times are ignorant and uncivilized, and when a strange, bold figure claims to found it. He gives Muhammad as an example of these conditions. He adds that a new sect is dangerous mainly if it attacks established authority, since that appeals most to people.

Bacon says that abstract religious disputes, such as the old Arian and modern Arminian heresies, stir people's minds but rarely change governments unless political events give them a push. He then lists three ways new religious sects spread: by miracles, by persuasive speech, and by the sword.

The best way to stop new religious sects and splits, Bacon says, is to correct abuses, settle minor disagreements, and act gently rather than through bloody persecution. He advises winning over the leading figures of a movement rather than angering them with force.

Bacon says that wars have changed in three ways: where they happen, what weapons are used, and how they are fought. Ancient wars seemed to move mostly from east to west, since the invaders were usually eastern peoples. He then argues that east and west are not fixed points, so this pattern is not a reliable rule, while north and south are fixed.

Invasions have almost always gone from north to south, never the reverse. Bacon concludes that the northern regions are by nature more warlike. He gives three reasons: the stars of the northern sky, the large northern landmasses, and the cold, which hardens bodies and warms courage even without training.

When a great state or empire breaks apart, wars usually follow. Big empires weaken the peoples they conquered by relying on their own armies to hold them, so when the empire fails, those peoples fall into ruin and become easy prey. Bacon gives Rome and Charles the Great's empire as examples, and says the same could happen to Spain. He adds that joining kingdoms together also stirs up wars.

When a state grows too powerful, Bacon says, it is like a great flood that is bound to overflow, as Rome, Turkey and Spain showed. Floods of people are unlikely now, because most peoples marry only when they can support a family, except in Tartary.

Bacon says that when a population grows too large for its food and living, it must send part of its people to settle in other lands, as the old northern peoples did by drawing lots. He also says a warlike nation that turns soft and weak invites war, because it has grown rich, which tempts attackers, and has lost its courage to defend itself.

Bacon says that weapons also change over time, as their use and design rise and fall. He points to early gunpowder weapons: the Oxidrakes in India had them, the Macedonians took them for thunder and magic, and China is said to have used them for over two thousand years. He then lists what makes a weapon better: reaching a target from far away, stronger impact than older devices such as battering rams, and easy use in all weather and transport.

Early armies relied mainly on sheer numbers, strength and courage, fighting open battles on set days with even forces. Later commanders used smaller but capable forces, relied on good ground, tricks of deception, and better battle formations.

Bacon says states go through stages like people: arms flourish in a young state, learning in its middle age, and trade and crafts in its decline. Learning also passes through infancy, youth, maturity and old age. He adds that staring too long at these cycles makes one dizzy, and he sets aside their deeper explanation as mere stories.
Poets describe Fame as a monster covered with feathers, with an eye, tongue, voice and ear for each one. The image shows Fame as something that sees, speaks and hears everywhere at once.

Bacon says that the lines before this are a rhetorical flourish, followed by fine parables about Fame. The best of them tells how Earth, angry that her giant sons were destroyed by Jupiter, gave birth to Fame.

Bacon compares rebels and false rumours to giants and their monstrous sisters, both children of the same kind of trouble. If a ruler can tame this monster and use it against other threats, that is worth something. He then says that the subject of fame is neglected in politics, and promises to examine what false and true fame are and how to tell them apart.

Bacon says that fame, meaning rumour or reputation, can be started, spread and stopped, and that it matters greatly in great affairs, especially war. As an example, Mucianus defeated Vitellius by spreading a false rumour that Vitellius meant to swap the legions of Syria and Germany, which angered the Syrian legions.

Bacon gives three examples of rulers who used false rumours to gain an advantage. Caesar spread a report that made Pompey relax his guard, and Livia kept it secret that Augustus had died so her son Tiberius could take the throne. Turkish pashas hid the death of the sultan from their soldiers so the troops would not loot cities.

Themistocles tricked the Persian king Xerxes into leaving Greece by spreading a rumour that the Greeks meant to destroy his bridge of ships. Bacon says such examples are common, and so wise rulers should watch and guard their reputations, or public rumours, as closely as they watch their actual deeds and plans.
It is a glossary of old English words, each paired with a plainer modern meaning. For example, "abridgment" means miniature, and "fame" means rumor.

Pascal contrasts two kinds of thinking. In the mathematical mind, the basic principles are clear but unfamiliar, so it takes effort to turn toward them; once one does, they are easily seen. In the intuitive mind, the principles are everyday and in plain view, so no special effort is needed to see them.

Pascal says that understanding mathematics takes clear sight to see every basic principle, since missing just one leads to error. It also takes an accurate mind to avoid wrong conclusions from known principles. If mathematicians had clear sight, he says, they would all be intuitive, meaning they would grasp things directly.

Pascal is saying that intuitive thinkers could be good at mathematics if they looked at its basic principles, which they are not used to doing. Some intuitive thinkers fail at mathematics because they cannot direct their attention to those principles at all.

Pascal says mathematicians often fail at intuition because they are used to clear principles that they arrange carefully before reasoning. In matters of intuition, the principles cannot be laid out that way, so mathematicians struggle. Such principles are felt rather than seen, and they are hard to get across to people who do not already sense them.

Pascal is saying that the basic principles we reason from are too subtle and too many to prove one by one, as mathematics proves its results. They must be grasped directly, in a single view, rather than worked out step by step.

Mathematicians are rarely intuitive, and intuitive people rarely become mathematicians, because mathematicians try to apply their rigid method of definitions and axioms to matters that are grasped by intuition. Pascal says the mind does reason this way, but silently and naturally, without formal rules, and only a few can perceive it.

Pascal says that intuitive minds, which judge things at a single glance, are put off when shown mathematical proofs that start from definitions and axioms, because those proofs seem dry and are unfamiliar to them. Dull minds, he adds, are neither intuitive nor mathematical. Pure mathematicians think exactly, but only when everything is explained to them through definitions and axioms.

Pascal says that thinkers who rely only on intuition, meaning quick gut judgment, are often wrong or hard to deal with, since their reasoning works only when the starting principles are perfectly clear. Such people also lack the patience to reach first principles of abstract, theoretical matters, because they have never encountered them in everyday life.

People can reason well in some areas and badly in others. Some reach sound conclusions from a few starting points, which shows sharp judgment, while others handle many starting points well. Hydrostatics, the study of fluids at rest, is given as an example of a field with few premises but very subtle conclusions.

Pascal says some people may be sharp thinkers yet still fail at mathematics, because mathematics relies on many premises at once. He sees two kinds of mind: the precise mind, which reasons deeply and accurately from a given set of premises, and another kind that can handle a few premises but cannot grasp matters with many.

Pascal distinguishes two kinds of intellect. The mathematical intellect can hold many premises together without losing track of them, while the other kind has force and exactness. He says these two qualities can exist apart, so an intellect may be strong but narrow, or broad but weak.

People who are used to judging by feeling do not follow step-by-step reasoning, because they expect to see everything at once and never look for underlying principles. People used to reasoning from principles, in turn, cannot grasp matters of feeling, because they look for principles and cannot see things at a glance.

Pascal says that true eloquence and true morality do not care about their own rules or formal forms. He separates two kinds of judgment: intuition, which belongs to judgment and perceives things directly, and mathematics, which belongs to the intellect and reasons step by step. So, he concludes, to scorn philosophy is to be a true philosopher.

Pascal compares judging a work by fixed rules to checking a watch. Those who measure by rules are like people who each look at a watch and still disagree about the time. He says that the rule-based judge is right and others who say he judges by feeling are simply mistaken.

Our understanding and feelings are shaped by the company we keep: good company improves them, bad company corrupts them. Choosing good company requires that our judgment is already sound, which is the trap. Those who manage to escape this loop are lucky.

The more intelligent a person is, the more differences they notice between people, so each person seems original to them. Ordinary people, by contrast, see little difference between one man and another.

When you want to correct someone, Pascal says, first find the side from which they see the matter, since that side is usually true. Admit that part to them, then show the side where they are wrong. They accept this because they see they were not wholly mistaken, only that they missed other sides. People dislike being wrong, he adds, because we naturally cannot see everything, while what we perceive from our own side is always true.
People tend to believe reasons more when they have worked them out for themselves than when they hear them from someone else.

Pascal says that the theatre is the most dangerous of all worldly amusements for a Christian. Its lifelike show of strong feelings, especially love, stirs those same feelings in the audience. The more innocent and virtuous the love on stage looks, the more easily innocent viewers are moved by it.

Pascal says that the violence shown in such portrayals flatters our self-love, making us want to produce the same effects. It also gives us a feeling that the emotions shown are proper, so pure-minded people lose their fear that such love could harm their purity.

After watching a play about love, people leave the theatre feeling full of love's beauty and tenderness and convinced of their own innocence. They are then ready to feel love themselves, or even to look for someone to awaken it in, so they can have the same pleasures and sacrifices they saw on stage.

Pascal gives two examples of people ruled by a single trait. Scaramouch, a stock comic character, thinks only of one thing. The doctor keeps talking long after he has said everything, because he is so eager to speak.

Pascal says that people enjoy seeing Cleobuline's error and passion because she does not know she has them. If she knew her own faults, she would be unpleasant to others, so she is only pleasing while she is deceived about herself.

When a writing describes a feeling or event naturally, the reader recognizes its truth as something already within them. So they come to love the writer, because the writer has shown them their own inner riches rather than his own.

Eloquence is the skill of speaking so that listeners hear us without discomfort and enjoy it. It also makes them feel they have a stake in what is said, so their own self-regard moves them to think about it.

Good speech, in this view, matches the head and heart of the listeners with the thoughts and words we use. This requires first studying the human heart closely, so that we know its powers and can shape the discourse to fit them.

Speakers should test their own words on their own hearts, imagining how a listener will receive them. They should keep to what is simple and natural, neither inflating small things nor shrinking great ones.
A thing being beautiful is not enough by itself. It must also fit its subject, and it must have nothing too much or too little in it.

Pascal says that when people cannot know the truth about something, it is useful for them to hold a shared mistaken belief that settles their minds. His example is the moon, credited with causing seasonal change and the spread of disease. He argues that wanting to know what we cannot understand is a greater harm than being wrong.

Pascal says that the style used by Epictetus, Montaigne and "Salomon de Tultie" (his own pen name) is the most common and most remembered. It works because it grows out of everyday talk. He gives an example: people often repeat a saying that the moon causes everything, and then attach it to Tultie's remark that a common error is useful when we cannot know the truth.

Pascal asks why virtues should be counted as four, six, or one, and why one maxim should be preferred over another. He argues that a single summary maxim hides the virtues inside it, and they only become clear when unpacked, where they appear jumbled together again. So each virtue exists separately in nature, not folded inside another.

Nature's truths stand apart, each independent of the others. Human art, or skill and reasoning, links one truth to another so that one depends on the other. Pascal says this linking is not natural, and that each truth should keep its own place.

Pascal answers a charge that he has said nothing new. He argues that the newness lies in how the material is arranged, just as two tennis players hit the same ball but one places it better. Words and thoughts, he says, make a new whole only when their order changes.
The same words put in a different order can change their meaning, and the same meanings put in a different order can change their effect on the reader or listener.

Pascal says we should only shift our attention from one thing to another for rest, and only when it is needed and the timing is right. Someone who gives rest at the wrong moment wears us out, and someone who wears us out at the wrong moment makes us weary and we turn away. Our stubborn nature likes to do the opposite of what others want from us, unless they offer us some pleasure in return.
Good speaking needs two things: it must be pleasing to hear and it must be about what is real. The pleasing part, though, has to come from what is true.

Eloquence is compared to a painting of thought. Someone who adds extra detail beyond the thought itself makes a picture rather than a true portrait, meaning the result no longer shows the thought as it really is.

Writers who build antitheses, pairs of contrasting phrases, by bending words to fit are compared to builders who put fake windows on a wall just to make it look balanced. Their aim is neat-sounding figures of speech, not accurate speech.

Symmetry is something we notice at once. It rests on there being no reason for one side to differ from the other, and on the human face, which is balanced left to right. So symmetry is wanted side to side, but not from top to bottom or front to back.

Pascal says that a natural style surprises readers, because they expect to meet a writer and instead find a plain human being. People with good taste expect to find a person behind a book and are surprised to find a skilled author instead. The Latin phrase, "You have spoken more like a poet than a man," is a remark to a writer who sounds too artful. He concludes that Nature is honoured when she is shown able to speak even on theology.
Pascal says that people judge by how a thing sounds only because they lack a feeling heart. The true standard is honesty of character, and real beauty lies in what is left out and in good judgment.

Pascal says that beauty comes from a fit between human nature, weak or strong as it is, and the thing that pleases us. Anything made to match this fit pleases people with good taste, whether it is a house, a song, or a tree. Things that match the same good model are related to each other, though each is of its own kind.

A badly made work can still follow a bad pattern perfectly, just as a bad sonnet copies its false model. The clearest way to see how absurd a false sonnet is, Pascal says, is to picture a woman or a house built to the same faulty standard.

Pascal says we easily speak of mathematical and medical beauty because we know what those arts aim at: proofs and healing. We do not know what poetry aims at, which he calls grace, or what natural model it should copy. So we invent showy phrases like "The golden age" and call them poetical beauty.

Pascal compares bad poetry to a showy village girl. A poet who writes big words about small things is like a girl dressed in mirrors and chains, which only the unsophisticated would admire as a queen. Such sonnets are therefore called "Village Queens."

Pascal says that skilled people who are truly educated do not show their skills through labels like "poet" or "mathematician," unlike those who want to be recognised for a trade. Such educated people are in fact skilled in many fields and judge them all, yet nobody can tell what they are. In company they simply join in whatever is being discussed, and their particular talents only show when they are needed.

Pascal says that people are called fine speakers only when the subject is speaking or oratory itself, not in ordinary talk. So praising someone as a clever poet as soon as he walks in is empty praise, and being left out of a request for your opinion on verses is a sign of low regard.

Pascal says a person should be known as a whole human being, not for one skill. He prefers that a man be called "a gentleman" rather than a mathematician, preacher, or speaker. Seeing one striking talent first is a bad sign, because that talent would then define the man.

Pascal says people only value others who meet their particular needs, such as a skilled mathematician or a good soldier. Such a person is useless to someone who needs something else. So, he concludes, a person needs an upright man who can suit all his needs in general.

Pascal says that if lightning struck only low places, poets and those who reason only about such matters would have no proofs. The point is that such thinkers rely on examples like this to support their arguments.

Pascal says that we tend to find the thing we want to prove obscure, and the examples used to prove it clear. So when proving a general rule, we should start with a particular case, and when proving a particular case, we should start with the general rule. Our sense of which is clearer shapes how we argue.

Pascal says people do not enjoy malice toward the unlucky, such as one-eyed men, but toward the fortunate and proud. He claims this is the real source of our actions. He also says a joke aimed at the one-eyed is worthless, because it brings them no comfort and only makes its author look clever.

Authors who call their work "my book" or "my history" are compared to homeowners who always say "my house." Pascal says they would be more accurate to say "our book," since most of what such works contain comes from other people.

Languages work like codes in which whole words stand for other words, not single letters for single letters. Because of this, a language nobody knows can still be worked out, or deciphered, by someone who studies it.
Some people speak well but write poorly. The setting and the listeners stir them up, so they bring out more from their minds than they would manage when writing alone.

When a repeated word fits so well that changing it would harm the writing, it should be kept. Trying to remove such a repetition comes from envy, which cannot see that repeating a word is not a fault in that place, since no general rule forbids it.

Pascal says that people often hide plain facts behind grand titles, so that "king" becomes "august monarch" and "Paris" becomes "the capital of the kingdom." He adds that the right name depends on the place and occasion: in some settings we should say Paris, and in others the grander title.

The same idea can seem more or less impressive depending on the words used to express it. In Pascal's view, words give ideas their weight, rather than ideas giving weight to words. He adds that examples should be looked for to show this.

Pascal says that people only call others by a label such as "Cartesian," "pedant," or "provincial" when they share that quality themselves. He jokes that the word "Provincial" in the title of his Letters was probably added by the printer, not by him.

This is a fragment with unclear meaning. It seems to be a note on two senses of a word, "overturned" or "upset," with a reference to an argument by M. le Maître against a friar. The note does not say more.

Pascal is making a point about wording. He says that "the part that I take in your trouble" is a phrase meant to be guessed at, not said plainly, and that a Cardinal did not want to be guessed at. He prefers the plain "I am disquieted" to "my mind is disquieted."

Pascal says he always feels uncomfortable when people offer polite apologies such as "I have given you a great deal of trouble" or "I fear this is too long." His point is that a speaker either keeps the listeners engaged or annoys them, so such apologies do not change that.

Pascal is saying that an apology or polite excuse for a rude remark makes the rudeness more noticeable, not less. Without the excuse, the speaker would not have realised anything was wrong. The only fault left is the excuse itself.

Pascal is criticizing two phrases in a speech about a historical figure. He says "to extinguish the torch of sedition" is too ornate, and that "the restlessness of his genius" uses two grand words that add nothing. He is judging the writing style, not the ideas behind it.

Pascal is laying out the plan of a larger work. The first part shows that human nature is corrupt, and that without God people are miserable. The second part shows that a Redeemer exists, that is, a savior, and that this is proved from Scripture, the Bible.

Pascal says he could have arranged his argument in a set order, moving from the emptiness of ordinary lives to that of philosophers. He admits he could not keep that order, and that few people understand what order means. He adds that no human learning keeps it, though mathematics does, but mathematics is too deep to be of use.

Pascal criticises Montaigne's way of writing about the self. He says Montaigne jumped from topic to topic on purpose, to appear fashionable, and that his plan to describe himself was foolish. Pascal adds that this was done by design, not by accident, which he calls worse than an occasional slip.

Pascal says Montaigne's book has serious faults. He finds its coarse language, its credulity and its ignorance poor, but his main objection is to its views on death and salvation. Pascal says a Christian must at least wish to die as a Christian, and that Montaigne's view of death is cowardly and unworthy.

Pascal says that Montaigne's good qualities were hard for him to gain. His faults, apart from his morals, could have been fixed quickly, if someone had pointed out that he gave too much weight to small matters and talked too much about himself.
Pascal says that a person should know himself. Even if self-knowledge does not lead to finding the truth, he claims it still gives a guide for how to live, and nothing is better for that purpose.

Knowledge of nature cannot comfort a person in suffering, because it does not answer questions about how to live well. Knowledge of morality, by contrast, can comfort a person even when they know nothing about the physical sciences.

People are taught almost everything, but never taught how to be gentlemen, meaning how to behave well among others. Yet they are proud of their knowledge of manners, which is the one thing they have not actually learned.

Pascal says that human nature is placed so exactly in the middle that a change on one side brings a change on the other. He takes this as a sign that the springs of the brain are set so that touching one spring also touches its opposite.
Too much wine and too little wine both stop a man from finding the truth. If he drinks none, he cannot find it; if he drinks too much, he cannot find it either.

Pascal says that man's innate knowledge of his own situation leads to humiliation, since man has to lower himself in some way if that knowledge is true. Before studying nature in depth, he urges man to look at nature in her full greatness and to turn away from the small things around him.

Pascal asks the reader to picture the sun, earth and stars as ever smaller points against ever larger circles. He says the visible universe is only a tiny atom within nature, and that the imagination will run out before nature runs out of room to be imagined.

Pascal says that even our largest mental images of space are tiny next to what really exists. The idea of an infinite sphere, with its centre everywhere and its edge nowhere, shows God's power, because the imagination cannot grasp it. He asks people to see themselves as lost in a small corner of nature and to judge the earth, kingdoms, cities and themselves by their true small size.

Pascal asks the reader to imagine dividing a tiny mite into ever smaller parts, from body to blood to drops and vapours. Even when the reader reaches what seems the smallest point, Pascal says it is really another endless depth, a new abyss.

Pascal invites the reader to imagine that a tiny atom holds whole universes, each with its own sky, planets, earth and living creatures, down to mites that contain the same pattern again. The smallest things are as wonderful and endless as the vastness of the visible world.

Pascal says that a human body is tiny next to the vast universe, yet large compared with the nothingness below it, so it sits between two abysses: the infinite and the nothing. A person who sees this will feel awe and fear, and will be more inclined to quietly admire these wonders than to study them with arrogance.

Man stands between two extremes: he is nothing when compared with the Infinite, and everything when compared with nothing. He cannot know where things begin or end, so he can only see the middle of things. Everything comes from nothing and moves toward the Infinite.

Pascal says that only the Author of nature's wonders can fully understand their workings. Men who ignore the infinite in nature still rush to study it, as if they were equal to it. Trying to grasp the beginnings of things and the whole from there would take either arrogance as large as its object or a mind as vast as nature.

Pascal argues that nature, which he says bears the mark of its Creator, shows an endless quality in almost everything. Each science, such as geometry, has endlessly many problems to study. Its starting principles also rest on other principles, so no basic principle is ever final.

Pascal says that reason, like the senses, has a limit it treats as final, even though the thing is really endlessly divisible. Of the two kinds of the infinite, the infinitely large is easier to see, so some have claimed to know everything. The infinitely small is harder to grasp, and philosophers who tried to reach it have all failed.

Pascal says that people think they can understand small things, the "centre" of things, more easily than the vast whole, the "circumference." He adds that reaching the Nothing takes as much capacity as reaching the All, so both extremes are beyond us in a similar way.

Pascal says that understanding the basic principles of existence and knowing the Infinite need the same capacity, and that each leads to the other. Both meet in God alone. Because we are something but not everything, our existence hides from us the first beginnings, which come from nothing, and our smallness hides the Infinite from us.

Our minds sit in the middle of the world of thought, much as our bodies sit in the middle of nature, and we are weak in both. The passage says our senses and reason fail at both extremes: too much of anything, too little, or too close or too far, leaves us unable to grasp it.

Pascal says that things taken to an extreme do not sit well with us. Too much harmony in music grates, and great favours turn into resentment once we cannot repay them. Extremes of heat, cold, youth, age, or learning escape our notice or go unfelt, so we live without properly registering them.

Humans cannot reach certain knowledge or complete ignorance. We are like sailors on a vast, shifting sphere, always drifting. Every point we try to hold on to slips away, and we long for a firm foundation that never gives way.

Human reason cannot reach certainty or stability, because it is always misled and stays fixed between two infinities that surround it and escape it. Given this, people should accept the place nature has given them. Knowing a little more about the universe changes little, since we remain far from either extreme.

Pascal argues that any finite span of human life, even one ten years longer, is infinitely far from eternity, so all finite things are equal when set against the infinite. Since people cannot grasp the whole, he suggests they might at least hope to understand the parts that relate to them.

Everything in the world is so closely connected that Pascal thinks one thing cannot be fully known without knowing the others and the whole. Man depends on many things, such as air, food, warmth and light, so to understand man one must understand those things too, and they in turn depend on man.

Everything in nature is linked in a chain of causes and effects, so we cannot fully know any part without knowing the whole, or the whole without its parts. Pascal adds that we are also unable to know things fully because they are simple, and because we are made of two opposite natures, soul and body.

Pascal argues that the thinking part of us cannot be purely material, because matter cannot know itself. If we were only matter, we could know nothing at all. If we are a mix of mind and matter, we still cannot fully know things that are simple, whether spiritual or material.

Many philosophers mix up the two kinds of thing. They describe physical objects in the language of minds, saying bodies fear, seek or feel sympathy. They describe minds in the language of bodies, saying they occupy a place and move from one place to another.

We tend to colour simple ideas with our own mixed nature, made of mind and body. Yet we understand this mixture least of all. Pascal says man cannot grasp what the body is, what the mind is, or how the two are joined, and this joining is his very being.

The first sentence says that humans cannot grasp how spirit is joined to the body, yet this joining is what a human being is. The fragment then says the author will end his proof of human weakness with two final points.
