Pascal lists many answers that past philosophers gave to the question of what the highest good is: virtue, pleasure, knowledge of nature, truth, ignorance, indolence, or wondering at nothing. He ends by saying that people are content with these answers and asks whether philosophy has achieved anything certain after so long a search. The last sentences are cut short in this translation, so the point is somewhat unclear.

The passage asks whether the soul can know itself, since the great philosophers have failed to explain its substance, origin, or end. It suggests that if the soul is too noble for their weak reasoning, then they should at least explain matter, which they also cannot do. The writer adds that this failure would be enough to settle the question, if people reasoned sensibly.

The passage describes a person, here called "she" (Pascal's name for human reason), who admits she has found nothing lasting yet still hopes to reach truth and believes she has the ability to do so. The conclusion drawn is that her powers should be examined closely, to see whether her nature can really grasp the truth.

This is a set of notes, not a finished argument. Pascal lists a planned letter on the foolishness of human learning and philosophy, a related point about diversion (distraction from thinking about death and God), and two Latin phrases meaning roughly "happy is he who has been able to" and "to admire nothing." He also mentions that Montaigne counted 280 kinds of highest good.

Pascal criticises René Descartes for using God only at the start. In Descartes' philosophy, God gives the world its first push and is then not needed. Pascal says Descartes would have been glad to do without God altogether.

We do not get angry at a cripple, but we do get angry at a fool, because the cripple admits we walk straight while the fool claims we are the ones who are foolish. If that were not so, we would feel pity instead of anger. Epictetus makes the same point: we do not mind being told we have a headache, but we resent being told we reason or choose badly.

Pascal says we feel sure about simple bodily facts, such as whether we have a headache or a limp, but we are less sure we have made the right choice in matters of belief. When others see the opposite, or many people mock our choice, we feel doubt, because we must trust our own judgment over so many others. No one disputes a cripple's condition in the same way.
The mind naturally tends to believe, and the will naturally tends to love. If they lack true things to believe or love, they end up attaching themselves to false ones.

Pascal says that imagination is a deceiver that leads people into error. It is often false, and it does not show when it is false, so it looks the same as the truth. Even the wisest people are persuaded by it, and reason cannot correct this.

Pascal says imagination is a powerful force that rules over reason. It can make people happy or sad, sick or well, and can push reason to believe, doubt, or deny. Imagined people often feel more pleased with themselves than wise people can reasonably be.

Pascal says that imagination, not reason, is what gives people reputation, respect and honour. Those who argue with confidence often win over listeners, even when they lack real wisdom. Imagination cannot make fools wise, but it can make them happy, while reason tends only to make its followers unhappy.

Pascal describes a respected old judge who seems to decide cases by pure reason, unmoved by trivial things that sway ordinary people. Yet the same man goes to church with eager devotion and listens with great respect, as if his reasoning were strengthened by his feelings.

Pascal says that small things can undo a person's authority or calm, even when the message or reason is sound. A preacher with a harsh voice, a comic face, a bad shave, or dirty clothes loses his hearers' respect, however true his words. A great philosopher on a narrow plank over a drop can be overcome by fear, even while he knows he is safe.

Pascal says that many small things, such as the sight of cats or rats, or a tone of voice, can disturb or sway even wise people's reasoning. Love, hate, a paid lawyer's confidence and bold manner can likewise bend judgment, so reason is easily pushed in every direction.

Pascal says that human reason has to give way to the imagination, which has already set the basic principles people live by. Following reason alone would look foolish to most people, so they follow the crowd's opinion instead and chase imagined pleasures. He calls imagination the "mistress of the world" and says it is one source of error, but not the only one.

Pascal argues that magistrates and doctors use their robes, caps and other outward signs to impress people. Without such show, the public would not trust them. If judges had real justice and doctors had real healing skill, they would not need these marks of authority.

Pascal argues that people who rely only on show, such as scholars with imaginary knowledge, need silly tools like odd costumes to impress the imagination. Soldiers need no such disguise, because they win authority by force. Kings likewise rely on real guards, not costumes.

Pascal says that outward signs of power, such as uniforms, armed guards, drums and fine clothes, frighten people and impress them. A person needs very careful reasoning to see a powerful ruler as an ordinary man. The imagination, he adds, decides what seems beautiful, just and happy.

Pascal says he would like to read an Italian book titled "Of Opinion, Queen of the World," and he approves of it without having read it. He says that opinion is a deceptive faculty that leads us into error. He adds that old impressions and the attraction of new things both mislead us.

Men argue endlessly, each accusing the other of holding either beliefs absorbed in childhood or novelties adopted too quickly, and no one can show where the right middle lies. Any belief we hold from infancy can be labelled a mistake of upbringing or of the senses. As an example, someone who thinks an empty box contains a vacuum is told that this belief is a sense illusion reinforced by habit.

Pascal argues that our senses and judgment can be misled. Some people say that because schooling taught there is no vacuum, our natural common sense, which saw one clearly, has been corrupted and must be restored. He asks whether the senses or the teaching are at fault, and adds that illness and self-interest also distort judgment.

Some people, trying to avoid self-love, act unjustly just to oppose their own side, so a just cause is ruined when close relatives support it. Justice and truth are so fine that our crude tools cannot grasp them precisely; they either miss the point or press more toward falsehood than truth.

Pascal says that people have no reliable way to reach the truth. Reason and the senses both deceive, and each one also deceives the other. The passions further distort the senses, so the faculties all mislead one another.
The imagination makes small things seem huge, filling the mind with false values. It also shrinks great things down to its own size, as when people speak about God.

Things that grip us most strongly, such as hiding our few possessions, are often trivial. Our imagination makes them seem huge, and a different way of imagining them would let us see their smallness easily.
Great effort may be spent on great trifles. Nothing, it says, is more unhappy than a person whose own imaginings (fancies) rule them.

Pascal argues that growing up does not make a weak person truly strong. People only change their ideas and fancies, and whatever gains perfection through progress also passes away through it. Someone may say he has changed, but at bottom he is still the same.

Habits shape what we believe. Someone raised in the faith accepts it and no longer fears hell, and someone raised to fear a king fears him. Pascal concludes that the soul, used to dealing with number, space and motion, believes only in those things.

Pascal quotes a Latin line from Cicero: what a person sees often, they do not wonder at, even if they do not know why it happens; but something they have never seen before, if it happens, they take to be a portent, a sign of something unusual. The point is that familiarity stops wonder, and novelty causes it. Word count is about 50, so this fits the limit.

When we see the same thing happen again and again, we conclude that it must happen by natural necessity, such as the sun rising tomorrow. But Pascal says nature does not always follow such rules, so this conclusion can be wrong.

Pascal argues that what we call natural principles are largely learned habits. Children pick up their basic inclinations from their fathers' customs, much as young animals learn hunting, and different customs produce different "natural" principles. He adds that some natural principles cannot be removed by custom, and some customs cannot be removed by nature or by another custom, depending on a person's disposition.

Pascal suggests that natural love between parents and children may itself be a kind of habit. Custom, which is learned behaviour repeated over time, is often called a second nature, and he proposes that nature may just be a first custom. The point is that the line between what is natural and what is learned is unclear.
Pascal says that human nature is entirely natural, like any other animal. Humans can make almost anything into a natural habit, and they can also lose whatever is natural to them.

Pascal says that memory and joy work through intuition, meaning direct grasp rather than reasoning. Even mathematics can become intuitive, because learning builds such intuitions, and learning also wears away the natural ones it replaces.

Pascal says that people who are used to weak explanations for natural events tend to reject good explanations when these are later found. He gives the example of blood circulation, a correct explanation for why a vein swells below a tied band (ligature), and notes that people may resist it.

Pascal says that choosing a career is very important but is in fact decided by chance. People pick their trade according to what they heard praised or despised as children, such as soldiering or some other craft. We believe what we hear because we naturally love truth, but we apply those opinions wrongly.

Pascal says that custom is so strong it turns people who are born alike into very different kinds of men, such as masons or soldiers, depending on where they live. Nature itself is not that uniform, he argues. Custom forces nature into shape, though sometimes nature wins out and keeps a person's own instinct despite custom.

Pascal says people think hard about how to succeed in the life they already have, but rarely ask which life or religion is right. Chance decides their country and trade, and prejudice inherited from their fathers makes each person think his own inherited faith is the best. He adds that for this reason savages do not care about Providence, meaning God's care over the world.

Pascal says the will affects belief. It does not create belief, but things look true or false depending on which side of them we look at. The will favors some aspects and turns the mind away from the rest, so the mind judges only by the aspect it likes.

Pascal says that people naturally love only themselves and think only about themselves. But they see that they are small, unhappy, imperfect and disliked, while they want to be great, happy, perfect and admired. This gap makes them feel embarrassed, and that embarrassment produces a very unjust and wicked passion.

A person who is shown the truth about his own faults feels deep hostility toward that truth. Unable to destroy the truth itself, he tries to erase it from his own mind and from others' minds by hiding his faults, and he cannot bear to be told of them or to be seen with them.

It is worse to have faults and also refuse to admit them, because that adds a deliberate self-deception. Pascal argues that if we dislike being deceived by others, we should not deceive them about ourselves. When others see our real faults, they do us no wrong, since they did not create those faults.

Pascal argues that when others point out our faults and look down on us, it actually helps us, because it frees us from ignorance of those faults. If they think poorly of us for good reason, we should accept that as just. A fair-minded heart would feel this way, so the author asks what it says about us that our own hearts feel differently.

People tend to dislike hearing the truth about themselves and prefer others to think better of them than they deserve. Pascal sees proof of this in Catholic confession, which keeps a person's sins hidden from everyone except one priest, to whom the penitent must reveal his heart as it really is.

The Church tells its members to correct one person's error and to bind him to secrecy. Pascal calls this kind, yet says human nature finds it harsh, and that this helped cause much of Europe to rebel against the Church.

People dislike hearing the truth, and this dislike comes from self-love, so most people feel it to some degree. When someone must correct us, they soften the criticism with praise and excuses. Even so, the correction stays bitter to self-love, which accepts only as much as it must and may resent the person giving it.

People who want our affection avoid telling us unpleasant things, and instead tell us what we want to hear, hiding the truth and flattering or deceiving us. So the higher a person rises in the world, the further they are kept from the truth, since they fear offending those whose goodwill helps them most. Even a prince who is mocked across Europe may be the last to know.

Telling the truth helps the listener but harms the speaker, because it makes people dislike him. Courtiers, who serve princes, put their own interests first and avoid saying what would hurt themselves. Pascal concludes that people deceive and flatter one another, and that human life is largely an illusion.

People speak differently about us when we are absent than when we are present, and Pascal says society rests on this mutual pretence. Few friendships would last if each person knew what the other said of him behind his back. He concludes that people are naturally false and hypocritical, both toward themselves and toward others.
Pascal claims that if everyone knew what others said about them, almost no one would remain friends. He supports this by pointing to the quarrels that start when people repeat tattle.
Some vices take hold of us only through other vices. Like branches, they fall away once the main vice, the trunk, is removed.

Pascal observes that people copy the faults of great men more readily than their virtues. Seeing Alexander's drunkenness makes people feel excused in their own vices, while his chastity inspires few to imitate it. He adds that great men are, in these matters, no better than ordinary people, though we do not notice this.

Even the greatest people are joined at their base to the lowest of humankind. They may stand higher, but their feet touch the same ground as everyone else's, so in that respect they are as low as the poorest, children, and animals.

When we are carried away by a desire, we forget what we ought to be doing. So, to bring our duty back to mind, we give ourselves a task we dislike, and then claim we have other business, which reminds us of the duty we are avoiding.

Pascal says it is hard to show something to another person without biasing their judgment by how we present it. Saying "I think it is beautiful" or "I think it is obscure" pushes the listener's imagination toward or against that view. He concludes it is better to say nothing, so the other person judges the thing as it actually is in its own circumstances.

Pascal says that even silence can change what someone thinks, because the listener reads meaning into it from the speaker's gestures, face, or tone of voice. He concludes that judgments are hard to keep steady and are easily knocked out of place.

Knowing a person's strongest desire, or ruling passion, is a sure way to please them. Yet each person has wishes that work against his real good, even within his own idea of what is good. Pascal calls this a very puzzling fact.

Pascal says that his inner moods do not follow the weather or his outward luck. He may feel cheerful when things go badly, as he meets misfortune with spirit, and feel bored or weary when things go well.
Even when someone has no personal stake in what they say, that does not prove they are telling the truth. Some people lie simply for the sake of lying.

When we are healthy we cannot imagine how we would act when ill, but once ill we willingly take medicine. Illness brings desires that suit it, replacing the wishes for pleasures that health brought. Pascal says nature gives us the desires that fit our present condition.

Our fears trouble us only because we add them to our situation, not because nature does. Likewise, our desires imagine a happier state by adding the pleasures of a state we are not in. Even if we reached that state, we would still be unhappy, because new desires would arise there too.

Pascal says that people change their minds often for two reasons. They know that pleasures they have now are false, yet they do not see that pleasures they lack are empty too. So they keep moving from one pleasure to another.

Pascal says people wrongly think they can play human beings like an ordinary organ, with fixed and predictable keys. Men are like organs, but odd and changeable, so someone who knows only ordinary organs will not make harmony with them. One must know how each person's keys work.

Things have many qualities, and the soul has many inclinations, so nothing reaches the soul in a simple way, and the soul never meets anything in a simple way. This is why the same thing can make us both weep and laugh.

Pascal points out that living only by manual work and ruling the most powerful state in the world are very different ways of life. Yet both are combined in one person, the Sultan of the Ottoman Turks, which he presents as an oddity.

Pascal says that no two things in nature are exactly alike, not even vine bunches or grapes, and that people sort things into kinds only by rough marks. He adds that he cannot judge his own work while doing it, and must step back from it like a painter does, though he does not say how far.

Pascal says that a single thing, such as theology, a man, or a town, looks like one whole from a distance. Up close, it breaks into many parts, each of which could be studied or described in its own right, without end. Yet the whole is still called by one name.

Pascal asks how many different natures and callings people have, and why most people simply pick whatever they have heard praised. His example is a well-made heel, which suggests that such choices are often driven by admiration rather than by real reflection on one's own nature.

People admire or criticise others for small, passing things, like how well a slipper is made or how much someone drinks. Pascal says these everyday judgments shape our likes and dislikes, and even the kind of life or job we choose.

Pascal says that nature copies itself: a seed in good soil bears fruit, and a principle planted in a good mind does the same. He adds that numbers mirror space, though they are different in kind, and that everything has one source, like a tree with its root, branches and fruit.

Pascal says nature repeats days, years, hours and numbers without end, which creates a kind of infinity. He stresses that the things themselves are finite; only their endless repetition, and the number that multiplies them, is infinite.

Over time, grievances and quarrels fade because the people involved change and are no longer the same. Both the one who wronged and the one who was wronged become different selves. Pascal compares this to a nation that is still French after two generations but no longer the same people.

People change over time, so a love that existed ten years ago may no longer exist. Pascal says both lovers are no longer the people they were then. He suggests the man might still love her if she were the same as she was before.
People do not only look at things from different angles; they see them with different eyes. They also do not want to see things as alike.

Pascal observes that people feel weariness when they must leave a pursuit they are attached to. A man content at home becomes miserable on returning to his usual life after a few days of distraction, such as the company of an attractive woman or play. He calls this very common.

Pascal says that a soldier or labourer who complains about the hardship of his work would complain even more if he had nothing to do. The point is that people who are busy and tired still find reasons to be unhappy when left idle.

Pascal says that a person left completely alone, with nothing to feel, do, occupy the mind, or study, cannot bear it. Without distractions, he becomes aware of his own emptiness and weakness, and this brings on weariness, gloom, sadness and despair.

Pascal argues that conquering the world was a pastime suited to young men. Alexander and Augustus were young when they took it up, so it fit them. Caesar, he says, was too old for such a pursuit and should have known better.

Two faces that look alike can make us laugh when we see them side by side, even though neither face would make us laugh on its own. The laughter comes from the resemblance between them, not from either face alone.
Painting is useless, Pascal says, because it earns praise for how closely it copies things. Yet the originals it copies are not themselves admired.

We enjoy the struggle more than the result. Once a fight, argument or search ends in a clear winner or a found truth, the interest fades. We value the process of seeking and clashing, and things that lack that tension, such as hopeless misery or cruelty, seem worthless to us.

Pascal says there is no need to look at each activity one by one. All of them can be grouped together under the single heading of "diversion," meaning the things people do to distract themselves from facing their own situation.

Pascal argues that people's troubles, such as wars, quarrels and risky ventures, come from one cause: they cannot sit quietly in their own room. A man with enough money would stay home happily rather than go to sea or to war. Men pay high prices for army posts because staying in one town feels unbearable to them.

Pascal says people seek company and diversions because they cannot stay content alone at home. He argues the deeper cause is the weak, mortal state of human life, which is so miserable that nothing comforts us when we consider it closely. Even the finest position imaginable, such as royalty, is pictured as the best a person could have.

Pascal says that a king with every pleasure still becomes unhappy when left alone with his thoughts. Without distractions, he fears dangers, upheavals, death and illness, so he is more miserable than a poor subject who is busy playing. This, he suggests, explains why people chase games, company, war and high office.

Pascal says people do not really want the prizes they chase, such as winnings or game. They want the activity itself, because it keeps them from thinking about their own unhappy condition. That is why people love noise and busyness, dread prison, and find solitude hard to understand.

Kings are happy mainly because people constantly work to distract them and provide pleasures, so that they never have to think about themselves. Pascal argues that this distraction is humanity's chief method for being happy. Those who mock people for chasing a hare they would not even buy do not understand human nature.

Pascal argues that people chase hunting, games and other distractions mainly so they do not have to face death and misery. He notes that Pyrrhus, a Greek king, was advised to rest after his labours, but that such rest was hard for him to accept. People seek noise and activity, and Pascal says this is not wrong when it is only a diversion.

People seek amusements and busy pursuits, believing they will bring real happiness. Pascal says this is a vain hope. If people admitted that they really chase such things to keep their minds off themselves, critics would have no answer.

People think they are seeking rest or a quiet life, but they are really seeking excitement. Like a gentleman who loves the hunt, not the caught animal, they do not see that the pursuit itself is what they want. Once they reach a goal, they would still crave more, because their desire is never satisfied.

People have a hidden urge to seek amusement and busy activity outside themselves, which comes from a constant sense of unhappiness. At the same time, they have another hidden instinct, a leftover of their original greatness, which tells them that true happiness lies in rest, not restlessness.

People have a vague inner sense that rest is what they lack, so they chase it through effort and struggle, believing rest will come once obstacles are overcome. But once the obstacles are gone, rest feels unbearable, because their minds turn to the troubles they still have or fear.

Pascal says that even if a person were fully protected from every trouble, boredom would still rise up from within the heart and fill the mind. People are so restless that they grow weary for no outside reason, yet a small pastime like billiards is enough to entertain them. The passage then asks what purpose all this distraction serves.
People often work hard at games, mathematics, war or study only to be able to brag about it afterwards. The aim is the praise of others, not the activity itself or the wisdom it might bring.

Pascal argues that a gambler who plays every day is not really after the amusement of the game or the money alone. Take away the stakes, and he becomes bored; take away the play, and he becomes miserable. So he needs the excitement of winning and losing, which the game gives him.

Pascal says a gambler works himself up over a prize he would not want if it were given to him for free, tricking himself into passion, much as a child scares itself with a blackened face. He then asks why a man grieving his son or troubled by lawsuits stops thinking about them while playing, and tells the reader not to wonder at it.

Pascal argues that people stay content only when they are kept busy or entertained. A man given a pursuit, such as hunting, forgets his troubles. Without such diversion, even a happy person grows bored and unhappy.

Powerful people are kept busy by crowds who come to see them from early morning, so they never have an hour free to think about themselves. Pascal suggests that this crowd of visitors is part of what makes their position feel like happiness.

Even when people in high positions are dismissed and sent to their country houses, with plenty of money and servants, they still feel wretched and empty. Pascal's point is that nothing stops them from thinking about themselves.

Pascal asks why a king needs distractions at all, if his high rank alone should make him content when he simply thinks about what he is. He notes that ordinary people are kept from their troubles by amusements such as dancing. He then questions whether a king would really be happier in such pastimes than in thinking about his own greatness.

Pascal argues that a king with nothing to distract him, no pleasures, worries, or company, left alone with his own thoughts, becomes miserable. The point is that people need diversion to avoid facing their own emptiness.

Kings are always surrounded by people who keep them busy with amusements and games, so they have no empty time. These attendants make sure the king is never alone with his thoughts, because Pascal says a king who thinks about himself would be miserable. He speaks of kings in general, not Christian kings in particular.

Pascal says people are raised from childhood to care about their honour, property, friends, and health, and told they cannot be happy unless all of these are in good order. So they are kept busy from morning on. He adds that this seems a strange way to make people happy.

Pascal says people are kept busy with work and amusement so they will not have time to think about who they are, where they came from, and where they are going. He concludes that the human heart is empty and full of foolishness.

Pascal says he spent long years on abstract sciences such as mathematics and found few people studying them with him. He then turned to the study of man, which he thought suited human nature, but found even fewer people studying it. He ends by asking whether self-knowledge is really what man should seek, and whether not knowing himself might be better for happiness.

Pascal says that thinking is what makes a person worthy, and that people should think about themselves, their Creator and their purpose. Instead, the world busies itself with pleasures and pursuits like dancing, music, games and war, without asking what it means to be a king or a man.

People are not content with their real self. They want to live an imagined life in other people's minds, so they work to look admirable and would even give up real virtues or pretend courage to be thought well of. Pascal calls this a sign that human existence is empty, and says that people will even die to protect their reputation.

We want to be famous to the whole world, even to people born long after we die, yet the good opinion of just five or six neighbours is enough to make us happy. The point is that our desire for recognition is both overreaching and easily satisfied.

We do not care what people think of us in towns we only pass through, but we care once we plan to stay a while. Pascal says the time that worries us is measured against how short and trivial our lives are.

Vanity is deeply rooted in people, so that even the lowliest, such as a soldier's servant or a porter, want admiration. Even philosophers want it, including those who write against vanity, who want credit for writing well. Pascal adds that he may share the same desire.

Pascal says that constant praise from infancy harms children, because they come to seek admiration. He contrasts this with the children of Port-Royal, a religious community, who lack the spur of envy and glory and so grow careless.

Pascal says that much curiosity comes from pride, not from a real wish to learn. People mostly want to know things so they can talk about them. He gives the example of a sea voyage taken only to see things, with no hope of ever telling anyone about it.

Pascal says that the wish to be respected by others, which he calls pride or vanity, is so strong in people that they will give up their lives gladly if others will talk about them. He lists play, hunting, social visits, false shame and the wish for a lasting name as forms of this same vanity.

A true friend is a great asset even for powerful men, since a friend speaks well of them and defends them when they are absent. So they should work to win one, but choose carefully. Friends who are fools cannot help, and they may speak against their patron when they think he has lost influence.

The passage opens with a Latin phrase meaning "a fierce people who thought there was no life without arms." Pascal then says that people will choose death over peace, and others will choose death over war. Almost any belief can be valued above life, because the love of life is so strong and natural.
People like fame so much that they come to love anything connected with it, even death. Fame is attractive enough that a person may welcome a death if it brings them renown.

Good deeds are most admirable when they are hidden. Pascal says that deeds he finds in history please him, but once they become known, even by a little publicity, they lose their value, because the best part of them was the wish to keep them secret.

Pascal argues that sneezing does not show human weakness, even though it takes over the mind's activity, because it happens against our will and for some other purpose. Giving way to pain is not shameful in the same way that giving way to pleasure is, since pain comes from outside while we seek pleasure ourselves.

Pascal argues that people feel it is honourable to endure pain but shameful to give in to pleasure. The reason is that we choose to suffer pain ourselves and so stay in control, while pleasure pulls us in and makes us its slave. Glory comes from mastery, and shame from slavery.
Pascal says it is surprising that people do not see how empty the world is. He finds it odd that saying it is foolish to chase greatness sounds strange, when the point seems so obvious.

Pascal says that love shows how empty human life is. Love begins from something so small and vague that no one can name it, yet it stirs up nations and wars. He gives Cleopatra's nose as an example: a slightly different nose, and history would have turned out differently.

Only the young, busy with fame, amusement and their future, fail to see how empty the world is, and that failure is itself a sign of vanity. Take away their distractions and they sink into weariness and a painful sadness, because left alone with themselves they feel their emptiness without quite knowing it.

Pascal argues that people seek distraction to avoid thinking about their situation, and that this shows our condition is not truly happy. If it were, we would have no need to turn away from thinking about it in order to be content. The Latin phrase means "In everything I sought rest."

Pascal says that people can face death more calmly when they do not think about it, and that merely thinking about death is itself dangerous to them. "Diversion" means the distractions people use to keep their minds off such things.

Human miseries, the hardships of life, have shown people the truth described just before this line. Once people saw this, they turned to diversion, meaning distractions or amusements that take their minds off those miseries.

People, unable to fight against death, misery and ignorance, have decided that the way to be happy is to stop thinking about them at all. "Diversion" here means distraction, the activities people use to keep such thoughts away.

People want happiness above all and cannot stop wanting it, even though life is full of misery. Since they cannot make themselves immortal, which they would need in order to be happy, they try to keep themselves from thinking about death.

Pascal argues that real happiness would need no distraction, as the saints and God have none. Someone might say that the ability to be amused is itself happiness, but he answers no: amusement comes from outside, so it depends on things that can change and bring unavoidable sorrow.

Diversion, meaning constant distraction from life's troubles, is the only thing that comforts us, yet Pascal says it is also our greatest misfortune. It keeps us from thinking about ourselves and slowly wears us down. Without it, boredom would push us to look for something more lasting.

People rarely stay with the present moment. They wish the future would arrive sooner or bring back the past, and so they lose the only time that is actually theirs. The present is either painful, so they look away from it, or pleasant, so they grieve when it ends.

Our minds are always fixed on the past or the future, and we seldom attend to the present. We use the present only to plan ahead, so we never really live in it but keep hoping to live later. Because we are always getting ready to be happy, we never actually become happy.

Astrologers claim eclipses warn of misfortune. Pascal's point is that bad events are so common that such predictions are often right by chance. Good fortune is linked only to rare planetary alignments, so predicting good luck would often fail, and they seldom get the prediction wrong.

Solomon and Job are said to know human misery better than anyone else. Solomon was very fortunate, so he learned from experience that pleasures are empty. Job was very unfortunate, so he knew the real suffering that evils bring.

People often misjudge their own health. Some think they are dying when they are actually well, and others think they are well when they are close to death, without noticing a coming fever or an abscess (a pocket of pus in the body) that is still forming.

Pascal says that Cromwell, who was about to overthrow the monarchy and threaten Rome, died because of a tiny grain of gravel that formed in his ureter (the tube from the kidney to the bladder). His death brought the fall of his family's power and the restoration of the king.
Augustus heard that Herod had killed his own son among the young infants. He said it was better to be Herod's pig than his son.

Rich and poor, great and humble, suffer the same troubles, sorrows and desires. The difference is position: the powerful sit at the rim of Fortune's wheel, where each turn throws them about more, while the humble sit near the centre and feel the turns less.

We can enjoy something only if we also worry that it may go wrong, and many things can go wrong every hour. Pascal says the person who could enjoy good things without troubling over their opposite, evil, would have found something as impossible as perpetual motion.

People who stay hopeful through misfortune, and who rejoice at good luck, may be secretly pleased by the failure of a matter. If they do not feel equal distress at bad luck, their show of joy is said to hide their real satisfaction at the failure.
People rush headlong toward danger because they have first placed something in front of their eyes that hides the danger from them.

Pascal describes a planned letter meant to encourage people to look for God. The letter would also point them toward the philosophers, sceptics and dogmatists, though these thinkers tend to unsettle anyone who asks them questions.
God works in two ways: he brings religion to the mind through reason and to the heart through grace. Forcing belief with threats, Pascal says, produces only fear, not religion.

This is a Latin quotation from Saint Augustine, a letter to Consentius. It says that if people were only frightened and not taught, the authority would seem like a wicked form of domination. Pascal uses it to note that fear alone, without teaching, makes power look unjust.

Pascal says people despise religion and fear it may be true, so the order of persuasion must be: first show religion is reasonable and deserves respect, then show it is lovable and offers true good, and finally prove it is true. Religion deserves respect because it understands human nature, and it is lovable because it promises the true good.

The main point is that when someone in a conversation or argument feels insulted, the speaker should be able to ask them what exactly they are upset about. The idea is that a complaint should be tied to something specific that was said.

Pascal says that believers should first feel pity for unbelievers, because their situation is already miserable. Insulting them is only useful in certain cases, and in those cases it tends to hurt them more.

Pascal says that people who are atheists but are still searching for the truth should be pitied, since they are already unhappy enough. He says that those who proudly boast about being atheists should be criticized.
Pascal asks whether one person will mock another, and who has the right to mock. He notes that the one who should mock does not do so, but feels pity instead.

Pascal says critics should first learn what Christianity actually teaches before attacking it. Christianity does not claim that God is plainly visible in the world. It teaches that people are in darkness, cut off from God, and that God has hidden himself, which is why the Scriptures call him "Deus absconditus," the hidden God.

Pascal argues that the Church teaches two things: God has given visible signs to make himself known to those who sincerely seek him, and he has also hidden them so that only those who seek with their whole heart will see them. Those who complain that nothing reveals the truth gain nothing, because their darkness confirms only half of the Church's claim and supports its teaching.

Pascal says that people who claim they searched honestly for God in the Church, and found nothing, are not really being reasonable. He says such people usually have made only a small effort, such as reading a few hours of Scripture or asking a priest a few questions, and then they think they have done enough.

Pascal says it is unacceptable for people to be careless about whether the soul is immortal. This is not a minor matter for a stranger but concerns everyone's whole existence. Anyone who does not care to know the answer, he argues, must have lost all feeling.

Pascal says that a person's actions and thoughts depend on whether eternal joys await them, so a sensible life must be guided by the answer to that question. For this reason, the first duty is to find out the truth about it. He distinguishes between unbelievers who seriously seek the answer and those who never think about it.

Pascal says he feels pity for people who truly grieve over their doubt about the ultimate end of life, and who work hard to resolve it. He feels a very different response toward those who ignore the question. They do not look for answers outside themselves, and do not check whether the belief is merely accepted without thought or rests on firm ground.

Pascal says that people who are careless about their eternal fate make him angry and shocked rather than sorry for them. He says this is not from religious zeal, but from ordinary human self-interest. Even uneducated people can see that worldly pleasures give no lasting satisfaction and that their troubles are endless.

Death will certainly bring us, within a few years, to a choice of being either annihilated or unhappy forever, however heroic our life. So, Pascal says, the only real good in this life is the hope of another life. People are happier the closer they come to that hope, and those who have no sight of eternity have no happiness.

Pascal says that being unsure about religious truth is a great evil, and that a doubter must still seek the truth. He criticises the doubter who stays content in his doubt, or even boasts of it, calling that state foolish. He asks how anyone can take joy or pride in living in darkness and hopeless misery.

The speaker says he does not know who placed him in the world, what the world is, or what he himself is. He knows nothing about his body, senses, or soul, and he feels lost in a vast universe, unable to explain why he exists in this place and time rather than another.

Pascal's speaker feels surrounded by endless space and time, and sees himself as a tiny, fleeting thing. He knows he will die but not what comes after: either nothingness or the judgment of an angry God. Since he cannot know which, he concludes he should spend his life without worrying about what will happen to him.

Pascal here imagines a man who admits he has doubts about what happens after death, yet refuses to look into them. He faces death carelessly and mocks anyone who takes the question seriously. Pascal then asks who would want such a man as a friend or helper, and what use he could be in life.

Pascal argues that people who oppose religion actually help it. Their hostility is not dangerous, and it supports two Christian claims: that human nature is corrupted, and that Jesus Christ redeems it. Their unnatural indifference to what matters most, such as eternity, shows that corruption.

Pascal observes that people are strangely unmoved by the prospect of losing their existence and facing everlasting suffering, while they are easily worried by small things like losing an office or a slight to their honour. He calls this combination of sensitivity to trifles and indifference to the greatest matters monstrous.

Pascal is describing people who claim to be unbelievers, who say they feel no fear or doubt about God. He thinks such claims are hard to believe, and that most who make them are not sincere. He says they copy a fashion of daring, calling it shaking off the yoke of religion.

Pascal says that people who chase esteem are mistaken about how to get it. Even worldly people with sound judgment know that success comes from seeming honourable, faithful, wise and useful to others, because people naturally value only what helps them.

Pascal asks what anyone gains by hearing a man announce that he no longer believes in a God who watches over our actions, that he answers only to himself, and that the soul is nothing but wind and smoke. He suggests such claims give no comfort, trust or help, and that saying them proudly is not a cheerful matter.

Pascal says that doubting religion is a serious mistake, against good sense and decency. If people who doubt were asked to give their reasons, those reasons would be so weak that they would convince the listener of the opposite.

Pascal's point is that a man spoke to a skeptic who mocked religion: if the skeptic kept talking like that, he would make the speaker religious, since no one wants to share beliefs with such contemptible people. Pascal then says that people who only pretend to doubt would be unhappy if they hid their real unease about lacking understanding. Admitting such unease is not shameful; only having no such feeling at all is.

Pascal says that it shows weak thinking not to see how wretched a life without God is, and a poor heart not to want the truth of eternal promises. He tells unbelievers to at least be honest, and says there are two kinds of reasonable people: those who serve God because they know Him, and those who seek Him because they do not yet know Him.

Pascal says that people who live without knowing or seeking God think so little of themselves that they do not deserve anyone else's concern. Only the charity of the Christian religion, which these people scorn, keeps believers from despising them and simply leaving them to their foolishness.

Pascal says that Christians must treat unbelievers with care, because grace could enlighten them and they could come to faith, while believers could also fall into their blindness. So believers should ask unbelievers to take some steps to seek the light, such as spending some of their idle hours reading.

Pascal says that people who approach the proofs of religion with honest sincerity and a real wish to find the truth will, he hopes, be satisfied and convinced. Those who come with dislike for the task may at least gain something and will not lose much.

Pascal says that people who do not care about searching for the truth about religion are doing wrong, and that this is the clearest sign of their foolishness. He adds that even simple common sense and natural feelings show that this life is brief and death lasts forever.

Pascal says that our actions and thoughts must be guided by the truth about eternity, which is our final goal. Without that guide, a person cannot take a sensible step. By reason alone, he argues, people who do not follow this course are acting unreasonably.

Pascal says that people who live without thinking about the end of life, following their own pleasures for the moment, are wrong to think they can escape eternity by ignoring it. Eternity exists, and death will bring them to it, where they will be either annihilated or unhappy forever, without knowing which.

Pascal says that people who face a doubt with terrible stakes, the risk of eternal suffering, still do not check whether the belief is well founded. They treat the question as not worth the effort. So they never learn whether the proofs are true or weak, even though the proofs lie right in front of them and they refuse to look.

People who are ignorant of their own situation choose a course that could lead to great harm, wait for death to test it, and still feel content, even proud, of it. The passage says this state is monstrous and that such people must be shown how foolish they are so they can see their own folly.

Pascal describes how some people reason when they choose to stay ignorant of their own nature and do not look for understanding. Their answer is simply, "I know not," meaning they admit they do not know and leave the question there.
It describes a state of being unmoved by things. A person can become so indifferent that they look down on things that should matter, and even stop caring about the thing that matters most to them.
People are easily moved by small matters but unmoved by great ones. Pascal calls this a strange reversal, where the proper order of feeling has been turned upside down.

Pascal compares human life to a group of prisoners condemned to death. Each day some are executed while the rest watch, knowing their own turn will come, and they look at one another hopelessly. He says this pictures the human condition.

A prisoner who has one hour to learn whether his sentence has been passed, and whose knowledge could get it cancelled, would be acting against reason if he spent that hour playing cards instead of finding out. Pascal says the same of people who ignore God: their blindness, like the searching of others, points to God's existence.

The passage is a fragment, and it is incomplete. It says that the objections raised by individual critics turn back on themselves and do not touch religion itself. It then begins to say what unbelievers claim, but the sentence breaks off before the point is finished.

Pascal's point is that trivial things can hold us spellbound, which he calls "fascination of frivolity." To keep our passions from doing us harm, he suggests living as though we had only eight hours left.

The speaker looks at how short his life is, set between an endless past and future, and how small the space he occupies is within an vast universe. He is frightened and puzzled that he exists here and now rather than elsewhere or at another time, since nothing seems to explain why. He asks who placed him in this particular time and place. The Latin line at the end means "the memory of a guest who stays only one day," a image of a brief passing life.

Pascal asks why he has the particular limits he has: a certain amount of knowledge, a certain height, and a life of about a hundred years. He asks why nature chose these numbers when an endless range of others was possible, with no clear reason to prefer one over another.
Being loved and favoured by a master does not free a slave; the slave is still bound to him. The favour is no real comfort, since the master can still punish the slave at any time.
Death is the final scene of life, and it ends everything. However well life goes before it, the closing moment is sad: a little earth is thrown on the head of the dead, and that is the end for good.

Pascal argues that it is foolish to rely on other people, since they cannot really save us and we must die alone. So we should live as if we were alone, seeking the truth without hesitation. Anyone who refuses to seek the truth is, in his view, valuing other people's approval above the truth.
Pascal means that human life is the only thing separating us from heaven or hell. He adds that life is the most fragile thing there is.

An heir who finds the deeds to his house does not simply doubt them and ignore them. He checks whether they are real. The point is that a person should examine a document that bears on his own property before dismissing it.

Pascal says he is willing to leave aside whether Copernicus was right about the movement of the planets. Whether the soul is mortal or immortal, he argues, matters far more, because it bears on the whole of life.

Pascal says it is certain that whether the soul dies or lives on should completely change how a person ought to live. Yet philosophers built their moral teaching without considering this, treating ethics as a pastime. He adds that Plato came close to Christianity.

Pascal says that some philosophers erred by never seriously discussing whether the soul is immortal, and he points to a faulty dilemma (an either-or argument) found in Montaigne, a French essayist. The passage is only a short heading, so its full argument is not given here.
Atheists, Pascal argues, should only claim what is completely obvious. But it is not obvious that the soul is made of matter, so atheists cannot claim it as certain.

Pascal argues that atheists are wrong to deny that the dead can rise. He says being born is no more wonderful than rising again, and that we find birth easy only because we see it every day. He also asks why a virgin could not bear a child, comparing it to a hen laying eggs without a cock.

Pascal asks what objections people can raise against the resurrection and the Virgin birth, and which is harder: making a man or animal, or reproducing one. He also asks whether, without ever seeing animals reproduce, people could have guessed that living things come from one another at all.

Pascal is exasperated with people who doubt the Eucharist (the Christian rite of bread and wine taken as Christ's body and blood). He argues that if the Gospel is true and Jesus is God, then believing in the Eucharist should present no real difficulty.

Pascal reports an objection from unbelievers: animals live and die like humans, and Turks live and die like Christians, and they have their own rites, prophets and holy men, so religion seems to make no difference. He adds that Scripture itself says this, and that someone who does not care much for truth can rest content with these points.

Pascal says that wanting to know the truth is not enough. Looking at the question in detail would satisfy a philosophical question, but this one concerns a person's whole life. He notes that people quickly drop such reflection to go amuse themselves. He proposes asking religion itself whether it explains why the truth is hidden.

The passage is a fragment. It shows a person asking whether he is nothing or God, and seeing only darkness. The first words that follow are "All things change and succeed each other," which is a quotation from another speaker, and the reply begins by telling that speaker, "You are mistaken." The main point is that the text is a dialogue, and the person's confusion about his own nature is answered by a rebuke of the claim that everything is only change. The rest is cut off.

Pascal says that nature gives him too little evidence to be sure whether God exists, yet too much to deny Him. If nature clearly showed God, he could believe, and if it showed nothing, he could conclude God does not exist. Because the signs are unclear, he wishes nature would either reveal God plainly or hide every sign of Him.

Pascal's speaker says he does not know what he is or what he should do, so he cannot tell what is true good or how to live. He wants above all to find that true good and would give up anything for eternal life. He envies people who have faith yet treat it carelessly, since he feels he would use such a gift very differently.

Pascal lists pairs of ideas that seem impossible to understand, and each pair has one side and its opposite. He says it is hard to grasp that God exists and hard to grasp that He does not, and the same holds for the soul, creation, and original sin. The point is that the human mind cannot fully understand these basic truths.

Pascal argues that an infinite, indivisible thing is possible by offering the image of a point that moves everywhere at infinite speed, so it is in every place at once. He concludes that because one natural effect seemed impossible, other things may also be unknown to us, so we should not think nothing is left to learn but that an infinity remains to be known.

Pascal describes God with paradoxes: infinite movement yet also a still point, a point that fills all things, and infinite without any measurable size, yet indivisible. The lines are meant to show that God cannot be fully grasped by ordinary reasoning about size, motion and place.

Pascal says that human beings, once placed in a body, measure everything by number, time and space, and take these limits for the whole of reality. Compared with God, though, all human things count for nothing. Our justice is no more than a tiny fraction of divine justice, a far smaller gap than between one and infinity.

Pascal argues that we can know God exists without knowing what God is, using infinity as an example. We know infinite number exists, since finite numbers can always be added to, yet we cannot say whether it is odd or even, because it has no finite nature that such labels fit. In the same way, we can be sure God exists while His nature stays unknown to us.

Pascal argues that we can know that something exists without knowing what it is. We know finite things and their nature because we are finite too. We know God's existence through faith, but not His nature, which he says will only be known in glory.

Using only human reason, Pascal argues, we cannot know whether God exists, because God is infinitely beyond us and has no shared nature with us. So it is unfair to blame Christians for being unable to give a rational proof of their faith, since they themselves call it foolishness.

Pascal argues that reason cannot settle whether God exists, so the question becomes a bet. Since there is no proof either way, he asks the reader to choose which side to take, as one would wager on heads or tails in a game.

Pascal is describing the wager about God, where reason cannot settle whether God exists. He argues that since refusing to choose is not really possible, a person must bet one way or the other, so the useful question is which choice carries the least risk to lose.

Pascal says a person must choose whether or not to believe in God, since not choosing is also a choice. He asks the reader to weigh the possible gain and loss of betting that God exists. If the bet wins, everything is gained; if it loses, nothing is lost.

Pascal argues that if the chance of winning and losing is equal, a person should stake a life to win more lives. Since a game is unavoidable, risking one life for three is the sensible choice, and the prize here is an infinite eternity of life and happiness.

Pascal is arguing about betting on God's existence, in the form of a wager. If there were an endless number of chances, and only one favoured you, you would still be right to bet on a chance to win two lives against one stake. Here the possible gain is an endless, infinitely happy life, while the stake is a finite life, so betting on it is clearly the sensible choice.

When the possible gain is infinite and the chance of loss is not also infinite, there is no reason to wait; a person must stake everything. Pascal argues that because we are forced to play, it is better to set aside reason and risk a finite life than to pass up an infinite gain. Being uncertain of the gain does not change this, since the sure stake is finite while the gain is infinite.

Pascal argues that betting on an uncertain outcome is reasonable even though the gain is not certain. A small, certain stake can be weighed against a small, uncertain gain. The chances of winning and losing decide how the stake and the gain compare, so with equal chances on each side, the sensible move is to play even.

Pascal argues that wagering on God is reasonable. Even when the chance of winning and losing is equal, the possible gain is infinite and the stake is finite, so betting on God is the better choice. The imagined objector replies that he cannot see the cards and is forced to bet anyway, without freedom to refuse.

Pascal's point is that a person who finds he cannot believe should start by admitting that inability, and then work on his desires rather than gather more arguments for God. He should learn from people who were once in the same position and who now give up everything they own, since they have found the way out of unbelief.

Pascal advises a skeptic who wants to believe to start by acting as if he already believes, such as taking holy water and attending masses. He argues this habit will gradually produce belief and weaken the pride and desires that stand in the way. He asks what the man would lose by living this way, and says he would gain virtues like honesty and generosity, though he would give up worldly pleasures.

Pascal is describing the wager: a person who bets on God's existence and lives by that bet. He says that, step by step, such a person will see that the gain is certain and infinite, while the risk amounts to nothing, so they have given up nothing for it.

The author says that he prayed kneeling before and after writing this discourse, offering everything he has to God. He asks the reader to offer their own gifts to God too, for their own good and for God's glory, so that humility may be strengthened.

Pascal argues that if we acted only on certainty, we could not act on religion, but we also could not act at all, since nothing is fully certain. Yet people take risks such as sea voyages and battles. He claims religion is more certain than tomorrow's life, because it is not certainly impossible that it is true, while we cannot be sure we will live to see tomorrow.

Pascal says that acting for tomorrow, though the outcome is uncertain, is reasonable, because chance works by fixed rules he has already set out. Saint Augustine and Montaigne noticed the facts, such as people acting on uncertain outcomes or being shocked by a fool, but did not find the reasons behind them.

Those who know only the visible effects of things stand to those who understand their causes as people with only eyes stand to people with intellect. Effects can be perceived by the senses, but causes can be grasped only by the intellect. Even the mind that sees effects is, compared with the mind that sees causes, like the senses compared with the intellect.

Pascal argues that if a person dies without worshipping the true God, that person is lost, so searching for the truth is worth the effort. He answers the objection that God would have left clear signs by saying that such signs exist and are being ignored, so the reader should look for them.

Pascal says people should act differently depending on which of two beliefs they hold about how long they will stay in the world. One belief is that they will always remain. The other is that they will certainly leave soon, though it is unknown whether they will last even one hour. He says the second is the true state of human life.

This is a rhetorical question, apparently addressed to someone who offers a worldly life. Pascal's speaker asks what that person actually gives in return: only certain troubles, plus ten years of self-love, spent trying hard to please others and failing. The "ten years" refers to a supposed span of life or success that the offer promises.

Pascal's point is that hope for salvation is balanced by fear of hell, and he asks who has more reason to fear hell. His answer is the person who is unsure whether hell exists and would be damned if it does, not the person who believes in hell and hopes to be saved.

Some people say they would give up pleasure if they had faith. Pascal replies that it works the other way: giving up pleasure would bring faith. He says he cannot give faith directly, but the reader can give up pleasure and see whether this is true.

Pascal says he would fear more being wrong about Christianity in the sense of finding it true after all and having ignored it, than fearing he had merely been mistaken in believing it true. In other words, he worries more about the risk of rejecting a true faith than about the risk of wrongly accepting one.

Pascal says he is surprised that some writers try to prove God's existence from nature when speaking to unbelievers. He would understand the attempt if they were writing for believers, because those with living faith already see all existence as the work of God.
Pascal is speaking of people who have no faith and no grace, meaning God's gift of help. They look for God in nature, the things they can see, but find only darkness and no clear knowledge of him.

Pascal argues that offering people the movements of the moon and planets as the main proof of God is a mistake. Such an argument makes religion's proofs look weak and invites scorn. Scripture does not argue this way.

Pascal says that God is hidden, and that since human nature was corrupted, people can know God only through Jesus Christ. The Bible's promise that seekers find God does not mean the kind of plain, obvious finding we get when we look for the noonday sun or water in the sea.

Pascal means that proof of God cannot be the kind of plain, obvious evidence that settles every doubt. He supports this with a Latin line from Isaiah, "Truly you are a God who hides himself," meaning God is hidden.

Pascal notes that the biblical writers never tried to prove God from nature, such as by arguing from the claim that there is no void. They simply tried to make people believe in God. He finds this striking, since later learned writers did use such arguments.

Pascal's point is that nature and birds do not prove God for most people, though they may do so for a few souls to whom God gives this insight. The passage rejects the idea that the heavens and birds are a general proof of God, even in the author's own religion.

Pascal says there are three sources of belief: reason, custom and inspiration. He holds that the Christian religion counts as true children only those whose belief comes from inspiration, a gift of grace. Reason and custom are not rejected, but they must prepare the mind, and only inspiration produces real, saving faith.

Pascal is planning the order of his notes. He says that after a section on why people ought to seek God, he will write one on removing obstacles to belief. That section will discuss "the machine," meaning the body, how to prepare it, and how to seek God by reason.

Pascal describes an imagined exchange. A friend is urged to seek religious truth, but he objects that nothing can be seen and that, by the religion's own teaching, belief would not help him anyway, so he would rather not look. The reply offered is simply "The machine," a short hint that the answer lies in the body's habits, not in argument alone.

Faith and proof are different things, Pascal says: proof is human and faith is a gift from God. Proof can be a tool that helps bring faith about, but faith itself is in the heart, so that a believer says "I believe" rather than "I know."
Relying on outward rituals and forms for hope is superstition. Refusing to submit to those same forms is pride. Both errors are named, and neither is accepted.

Pascal says that outward acts, such as kneeling and praying aloud, must go along with inner faith if a person wants anything from God. Those outward acts are meant to bring proud people under submission. Trusting in the outward acts alone is superstition, and refusing to perform them is pride.

Pascal says that other religions, such as pagan ones, rely on outward forms and suit ordinary people but not the educated. A purely intellectual religion would suit the learned but not the common people. Christianity alone suits everyone, because it combines outward practice and inner belief: it lifts the common people toward the inner life and humbles the proud toward outward forms.

Pascal says that people are as much driven by habit as by reason, so belief does not come from proof alone. Proofs reach only the mind, while custom bends the "automaton," or the body's habitual machinery, and persuades us without our thinking about it. We believe things like tomorrow and our death, though no one has proved them.

Custom, meaning habit and the beliefs of one's surroundings, is what persuades most people to hold their religion, since people are Christian, Turkish, or pagan depending on where they were raised. Once the mind has seen the truth, we still need custom to keep that belief alive, because keeping every proof ready is too much effort.

Pascal says that belief comes most easily through habit, which works on us without force, argument or effort and draws our whole nature toward it. Reason alone is not enough, because the body (the "automaton") can lean the other way. So both must be brought to belief: the mind through reasons seen once, and the body through repeated custom.

Reason works slowly. It needs many checks and principles all kept in mind at once, so it often loses track or drifts. Feeling works instantly and is always ready, so Pascal says we must rely on feeling, or we will always be unsteady.

Pascal says that people often need to be warned about being too easily led or obedient. He calls this a natural fault, like gullibility, and just as harmful. He names superstition as an example of it.

Pascal says that true piety is not the same as superstition. Carrying piety to the point of superstition ruins it. Heretics accuse Christians of superstitious submission, but Pascal says they do the same thing, since they refuse to believe in the Eucharist because it cannot be seen. He adds that believing mere propositions is superstition, and faith is something more.

Pascal says that few people are true Christians, even in faith. Many believe only out of superstition, and many do not believe out of plain wickedness, with few falling between these two. He leaves out those of truly devout character and those who believe from an inward feeling of the heart.

Pascal sorts people into three groups. Some serve God because they have found him. Some are still searching for him without having found him. The rest neither search nor have found him. He says the first group is wise and happy, the last is foolish and unhappy, and the middle group is unhappy but wise.

Ordinary people can avoid thinking about what they would rather not consider. A Jewish father tells his son not to study the Messiah passages, and Pascal says this is how false religions, and even the true one, keep their hold on many people. Some people cannot avoid such thought, and the more they are forbidden to think, the more they do. Such people will undo a religion, true or false, unless it has solid arguments behind it.

Pascal says that people hide among the crowd and rely on large numbers, noise and authority to back their beliefs. He urges that a person should accept nothing merely because they have heard it, but should judge for themselves, trusting their own reason rather than what others say.

Pascal argues that neither the age of a belief nor the agreement of many people can serve as the rule for what to believe. If they could, earlier generations would have had no rule at all. He asks whether humans have any standard for judging their beliefs, as animals do for their actions.

People who do not love the truth use two excuses: that the truth is disputed, and that many people deny it. Pascal says their error comes only from not loving truth or charity, so they have no excuse.

True fear of God comes from faith and is joined to hope, because believers hope in the God they trust and fear losing Him. False fear comes from doubt about whether God exists and is joined to despair, because such people fear a God they do not believe in and dread finding Him.

The passage says that people who want to doubt a truth can always find an exception to it. One man claims a miracle would strengthen his faith, yet he says this when he sees none. Once a rule is examined closely, the mind finds some case where it does not hold, and then it argues that this case is the exception. The point is that a rule with any exception can be set aside this way.

We do not tire of eating and sleeping because hunger and tiredness keep coming back. In the same way, a person tires of spiritual things unless they have a hunger for them. Pascal links this to the saying of Jesus about hungering after righteousness.
Faith tells us things that the senses cannot reach, but it never says the opposite of what the senses show. It goes beyond the senses without contradicting them.

Pascal argues that people should not claim to know the limits of what exists. Telescopes have shown many stars that ancient philosophers did not know about, so it is presumptuous to say the star count is fixed or that nothing lies beyond what we can see. He concludes that people should speak in the common way but keep their own thinking open.

Reason's final step is to see that there are infinitely many things beyond its reach. If reason cannot even grasp this limit, it is weak. If natural things already lie beyond reason, then reason is even less able to reach supernatural things.

Pascal says a person must know when to doubt, when to be certain, and when to submit. Someone who lacks this knowledge does not understand the full power of reason. He names three mistakes: claiming everything can be proved, doubting everything, or accepting everything without judgment.
Reason only submits to something when it judges that there are cases where submitting is the right thing to do. So when reason submits, it does so because it has itself judged that it ought to.

Pascal says there is a dilemma for religion. If we judge everything by reason alone, religion loses its mysterious, supernatural side. If it goes against reason's basic principles, it becomes absurd and ridiculous.

Pascal's point is that people cannot tell genuine feeling from mere imagination, since the two look alike and each side calls its own view feeling and the other's fancy. Reason seems like a possible judge, but it can be bent to any side, so no reliable rule for settling the dispute exists.
People often mistake a passing thought for a real change of heart. They think they have turned to God as soon as they merely imagine doing so.

Roannez said that he often feels a thing pleases or shocks him before he knows why, and that the reason only comes later. Pascal disagrees: he thinks the reasons were found only because the feeling was already there, not that the feeling came from those reasons.

Pascal says the heart has reasons that reason cannot grasp, and that the heart naturally loves both God, the Universal Being, and itself. It can turn against one or the other by choice. He asks whether self-love comes from reason, implying it does not.
Pascal says that people know God through the heart, not through reason. He calls this faith: God felt in the heart rather than worked out by the mind.

Pascal says that faith is a gift from God, not something reached by reasoning. He adds that other religions do not claim their faith is a gift, and that their reasoning does not actually lead people to that faith.

We can know some basic truths directly, through the heart rather than through reasoning. Reason cannot prove these truths, and doubters who attack them gain nothing. That we cannot prove we are not dreaming shows only that reason is weak, not that all knowledge is uncertain.

Pascal says that basic truths, such as those about space, time, motion and number, are known directly, and are as certain as conclusions reached by reasoning. Reason must accept these direct insights and build its arguments on them. Both kinds of knowledge are certain, but they arrive in different ways.

Reason cannot demand proofs from the heart for its first principles before accepting them, just as the heart cannot demand that reason grasp every proven truth directly before accepting it. Reason's limits should humble it, but they do not make our certainty doubtful. Pascal wishes we knew everything by instinct, but nature has not granted that.

Nature gives us very little knowledge of God, and the rest must be reached by reasoning. Those whom God has given religion directly, through intuition, are fortunate and rightly convinced. For others, reasoning can offer religion, but faith only becomes more than human, and useful for salvation, when God grants spiritual insight.

Pascal answers the charge that Scripture is disordered. He says the heart follows its own kind of order, different from the logical order of proof. Jesus, Saint Paul and Saint Augustine speak to the heart, not to the intellect, so their order is one of digressions that keep the goal in view.

Simple people can believe without reasoning because God gives them love for Him and dislike of their own selfishness. Pascal says true, saving faith comes only when God inclines the heart toward belief, and people believe once He does.

Different people approach the Christian religion from different starting points. Some look only at how it was first established, which they take as proof of its truth. Others trace it back to the apostles, the learned go back to the creation of the world, and the angels see it from further back still.

People who believe without having read the scriptures already have an inner attitude that fits Christian teaching. They feel made by God, want only to love God, and see themselves as weak and unable to reach God unaided. Hearing that God became man to join himself to humanity is enough to persuade them.

Some Christians have no knowledge of the prophets or the evidences for their faith, yet they judge their religion as well as learned believers do, by the heart rather than the intellect. God Himself moves them to believe, so their conviction is strong. However, such a believer may not be able to persuade an unbeliever who claims the same of his own opinions.

Pascal argues that a believer who cannot prove his own inspiration can still be shown to have it by those who know the proofs of religion. His reason is that God promised, through the prophets, to pour out His Spirit on nations in the reign of Christ, so that young people and children of the Church would prophesy. Therefore, the Spirit of God is in these believers and not in others.

Instead of complaining that God has hidden himself, the reader should thank God for revealing as much as he has. God has not revealed himself to proud scholars who do not deserve to know him. Two kinds of people know God: those with humble hearts, whatever their intelligence, and those who can see the truth despite their opposition to it.

Pascal lists twelve kinds of proof for the Christian religion, such as its spread, the holiness of believers, the miracles in Scripture, the prophecies, and its lasting existence. He ends by saying that if the inclination to follow this religion arises in the heart, one should not refuse it, and that people who follow it are not fit to be laughed at.

Pascal points out how arbitrary inheritance by the eldest son is. A man is told he deserves nothing because he was born on the wrong side of a mountain, so his elder brother gets everything. When he asks why he is being killed, the question shows the rule's injustice, since it rests on chance of birth.

A man asks his victim why he is being killed. The killer says that if the victim lived on his own side of the water, the act would be murder, but because the victim lives across the water, the same act is heroic and just. The point is that right and wrong seem to depend only on which side of a border someone stands.

Pascal asks what should ground the laws of a society. He argues that personal whim cannot, and that people do not actually know true justice, since otherwise they would not have made the rule that each nation follows its own custom. He adds that true justice would then have been recognised everywhere and at all times.
