Pascal notes that justice and injustice seem to shift with geography and time: a change of latitude, a river, or a few years can alter what counts as law or truth. Yet people generally agree that true justice does not lie in these local customs but in natural laws shared by every country.

Pascal argues that human laws vary so widely that no law is shared by every society. Practices like theft and killing a parent have been counted as virtues somewhere. He notes that a war between rulers can make one man kill another who has done him no wrong. He concludes that natural laws exist but have been corrupted, so that nothing is left that is truly ours.

Pascal says that justice has no fixed basis in reason. People base it on different things: the lawmaker's authority, the ruler's interest, or custom. Custom is what people accept as fair, and tracing it back to first principles would undermine its authority. Laws that correct other laws are themselves faulty.

Pascal says that people who obey laws only because they seem just are obeying an imagined justice, not the real basis of law. Law is simply law, and its supposed reasons are weak. He adds that questioning established customs back to their roots, to show they lack real authority, is the method of those who oppose or overturn the existing order.

Pascal argues that two mistakes about custom and law are both harmful. One mistake is to demand a return to supposed natural laws that older custom has covered over, which Pascal says ends in ruin for everyone. The other is to think anything is justified simply because no earlier example of it exists. He adds that the wisest lawgivers therefore said men must sometimes be deceived for their own good.

Pascal quotes a Latin saying: when a person does not know the truth that would set him free, it is useful for him to be deceived. He adds that laws often began through force without good reason, but are now treated as reasonable. To keep them respected as eternal, their origin must be hidden, or they will not last.
Children claim a dog and a patch of sunlit ground as "mine." Pascal says this small act is the start and a picture of how people seize the whole earth for themselves.

When a nation asks whether it should go to war and kill many people, the only judge is one of the two parties involved, and that party has a stake in the answer. Pascal says a third judge is needed, one with no personal interest in the outcome.

Pascal says that people no longer have true justice. If they did, they would treat the customs of their own country as the standard of what is right. Since they cannot find real justice, they have settled for force instead.

Justice needs force to be obeyed, and force without justice is tyranny. Since justice is disputed while force is plainly recognised, people could not join justice to force. So, unable to make justice strong, they have made the strong party seem just.

Pascal argues that laws are obeyed because of the power behind them, not because they are fair. Since people cannot make the strong obey justice, they have made justice obey the strong, so that might and right are joined and peace is kept.

We follow the majority not because they are more right but because they have more power. We follow old laws and opinions not because they are sounder but because they are the only ones, so they remove the source of disagreement.

Pascal says that people who come up with new ideas are few, while most people simply follow. Most will refuse glory to inventors who seek it, and if inventors insist on it and look down on others, the rest will mock them and may even beat them. So no one should boast of cleverness or keep self-satisfaction to himself.

Pascal says that force, not public opinion, rules the world. Opinion only uses force, and force is what creates opinion. He gives an example: someone who dances on a rope is alone, while a larger crowd can be gathered to say such behaviour is unbecoming, so opinion follows whoever has the greater numbers.

Pascal argues that the ranks people hold over one another come from necessity, since everyone wants to rule but only some can. He imagines society forming: men fight until the stronger side wins and a ruling party is set up.

Once a struggle for power is settled, the rulers decide how that power will pass on, whether by election or by inheritance. Pascal says imagination then takes over: power that began as a matter of fact is kept going by belief in certain groups, such as the nobility in France or the citizens in Switzerland.

Pascal is saying that the bonds tying people's respect to a particular person are not based on real merit. They come from imagination, the mind's habit of forming impressions and fancies about others.
The Swiss dislike being called gentlemen, so they act like common people. They do this so that they will be seen as fit for high positions.

Pascal says that duchies, kingdoms and offices of rule are real and needed, and because force governs the world, they exist everywhere and always. But the choice of which particular person rules comes only from chance or whim, so the basis for who rules is not fixed and can change.

Pascal says that a chancellor's grave manner and fine robes are a show, because his authority is not real. The king's power is real and does not depend on imagination. Judges and doctors, by contrast, rely only on people's imagination to carry their authority.

Kings appear awe-inspiring because people always see them surrounded by guards, drums and officers. Those trappings produce respect, and people then link that respect to the king himself, even when he appears alone. Ordinary people do not realise that habit causes this and think the awe comes from a natural power in the king's face.

This is a set of short, loose notes on how power and wealth should be used and what they are for. Pascal says that the great find pleasure in making others happy, that riches should be given away freely, and that power exists to protect. He ends with an image of ordinary force overturning official show, such as a soldier throwing a judge's cap out of a window.
Rule based on opinion and imagination lasts only for a time, but it is pleasant and freely accepted. Rule based on force lasts forever. So opinion is the queen of the world, and force is its tyrant.
Pascal says that justice is simply whatever has been established. Because of this, all our established laws must be accepted as just without anyone checking them, since they have been set up.

Pascal argues that civil war is a great evil, and that rewarding merit inevitably leads to it, because every candidate will claim to deserve reward. By contrast, the harm from a foolish ruler who gains power by birth is smaller and less certain.

Pascal says that God made everything for himself and holds the power of pain and pleasure. A person can direct this power toward God, guided by the Gospel, or toward himself, which makes him a rival to God. Pascal warns that someone who seeks his own pleasure is only a king of lust.

Pascal observes that people show respect to a man dressed in fine clothes and followed by servants, and will even punish someone who fails to bow to him. He says this is only custom, a kind of force, just as a finely harnessed horse is treated differently from a plain one. He criticises Montaigne for wondering why people react this way.

Being well-groomed is not simply foolish, Pascal argues, because it shows that many people serve you. Fine hair, lace and linen signal the servants and workers behind them. Having many people at your command is a real form of power, so dressing well displays that power.

Deference, Pascal says, is really a willingness to be put to trouble, and it is the trouble that makes it meaningful. Someone who takes trouble for another is saying they would do so if needed. Because only real inconvenience counts, deference also marks out who is great, since a mere gesture like sitting in a chair would be shown to everyone and would distinguish no one.

Pascal says that people are ranked by outward signs, such as the number of servants a man has, rather than by inner worth. When two men meet, the one with fewer servants gives way, since a visible count settles precedence without any argument. Giving way keeps the peace, which the author calls the greatest of boons.

Pascal argues that choosing a king by birth, specifically the eldest son, is not reasonable in itself. It is accepted because people are quarrelsome and would each claim to be the most fit to rule. Birth gives a clear answer that no one can dispute, and avoiding civil war is the strongest reason for it.

Being born into a noble family gives a person a head start. It places them among the respected elite at eighteen, a position someone without that birth would need fifty years to reach. Pascal calls this a gain of thirty years with no effort.

Pascal asks what the "self" really is. He argues that it cannot be the body's looks, a person's mental abilities, or the person who happens to be watched or passed by, since each of these can change or be lost while the self remains. He concludes that he cannot find where the self is located, whether in the body or in the soul.

We love a person only for qualities, such as looks, mind or status, and not for the self underneath them. Since those qualities pass away or are borrowed, it is unjust to mock people for being honoured for rank or office.

Pascal argues that common people's opinions often look foolish to clever critics but are sound for reasons the critics miss. Examples include preferring hunting to poetry, valuing rank by birth or wealth, and resenting a blow or seeking glory, since honour brings other goods and an insult to a man who ignores it brings contempt.

Pascal says that custom ought to be followed only because it is custom, yet people actually follow it because they think it is just. Without that belief, they would stop following it, since they submit only to reason and justice. He adds that reason and justice are natural to humans, so obeying laws simply because they are laws would be right.

Pascal says that people should admit that no true justice exists in laws and customs, and simply follow what is accepted. People refuse this, because they believe truth can be found in laws and customs, and they treat their age as proof of their truth rather than only of their authority. So they obey laws but rebel when those laws are shown to be worthless, which can be shown of all laws from some point of view.

People obey laws because they think the laws are just, so telling them the laws are unjust is dangerous. Pascal says people should be taught to obey laws because they are laws, as they obey superiors because they are superiors. This, he says, prevents rebellion, provided people understand what justice really is.

Pascal says that people start out in natural ignorance, and that great thinkers who study everything can end up in the same ignorance again. The difference is that the scholar's ignorance knows it is ignorance. The two ends of learning therefore look alike, but one is unaware and the other is aware.

Pascal describes three groups. The common people are ignorant, and the truly wise see the limits of knowledge. In between are those with a little learning who pretend to be wise; they cause trouble and judge everything badly. The wise and the people make up the world, and the world judges the half-learned correctly.

Pascal argues in a back-and-forth way about whether ordinary people are foolish. He first says their judgments of minor things are foolish, then that those same judgments are sound, so the people are not foolish. He then aims to show that people remain foolish even when their opinions are sound, because they look for truth in the wrong place.

Pascal says that people admire certain skills, such as playing the lute well, only because human beings are weak. The admiration comes from that weakness, and the skill would be a fault only because of our weakness.

Royal power, Pascal says, rests on people's folly as much as on their reason, and especially on their folly. Its base is weakness, which is a very secure base because people can be counted on to stay weak. Power built on sound reason, by contrast, is a poor foundation.

Pascal says that Plato and Aristotle should not be pictured as grave scholars in robes. In private they were ordinary men who joked with friends, and their writing on laws and politics was a pastime. Their political writing was like rules for an asylum: they spoke to people they regarded as mad, so they could make that madness less harmful.

Tyranny is wanting power over everything, beyond the area where one's own kind of strength or merit applies. Pascal says strength, beauty, wisdom and piety each rule only in their own domain, so when they clash, the claim to rule everywhere is false. Might, he adds, has no say in matters of wisdom.

Tyranny, Pascal says, is wanting to get by one kind of claim what can only be earned by another. Each kind of worth should get its own response: love for the pleasant, fear for the strong, belief for the learned. It is unjust to withhold these responses, and unjust to demand them where they are not due.

Some people complain that others do not give them enough attention, and they point to great men who respect them. Pascal's reply is that he will respect them too, once they show him the quality that won those great men's regard.

Pascal says that two things drive everything we do. Desire ("lust" here means strong wanting) produces the actions we choose freely, and force, meaning compulsion or outside pressure, produces the actions we do without choosing them.

Pascal says that people are mostly right in their opinions but wrong about why. They think the truth lies where it does not, though it is present in their views. For example, we should honour noblemen, but not because noble birth is true greatness.
Thinking should be kept private and used to judge everything, while speech follows the ordinary manner of ordinary people. The point is that inner judgment and outward talk can differ.

Pascal says people judge men of high birth differently depending on how much they understand. Ordinary people honour them. The half-educated despise them, calling birth mere luck. The learned honour them for hidden reasons. Zealous but less learned believers despise them, while true Christians honour them by a higher light.

True Christians go along with worldly foolishness, not because they honor it, but because God commands it, having made people subject to these follies as a punishment. The writer adds that Saint Thomas read a passage in Saint James about showing respect to the rich the same way: it is done as a religious duty, not as a sign of approval.

Pascal says he can imagine a person without hands, feet or even a head, since only experience shows the head matters more than the feet. He cannot imagine a human being without thought, because such a thing would be no better than a stone or an animal.
Pascal says that his calculating machine produces results closer to thought than anything animals do. Still, the machine does nothing that would let us say it has a will, as we say animals do.

This is a short note on a story about a pike and a frog, which Pascal names by its place, Liancourt. He says the animals always act in the same fixed way and never differently, and that nothing they do shows thought or mind.
If an animal reasoned instead of acting by instinct, it would speak of its own pain as it now speaks of hunting, asking another animal to gnaw a cord that hurts it and that it cannot reach.
Reason gives orders more strongly than a master does. Disobeying a master brings misfortune, but disobeying reason makes a person foolish.

Human beings are physically weak, as easily killed as a drop of water, yet they are greater than the universe that could destroy them, because they can think and know they die. So human dignity rests on thought, and thinking well is the basis of morality.

Human dignity, Pascal says, does not come from physical size or from owning a vast universe. It comes from how well we govern our thinking. Space would crush a person like a speck of dust, but through thought a person can grasp the whole world.
The passage argues that the soul is not material. It points to philosophers who controlled their passions, and asks what matter, which is physical stuff, could do such a thing.

Pascal says that the Stoics reason too quickly from one example to all people. They argue that because someone did a hard thing once, anyone can do it, just because a strong desire for glory once gave some people power. He answers that a fever can produce movements that good health cannot copy. He then mocks Epictetus, who concluded from the existence of consistent Christians that anyone could easily be one.
The soul sometimes makes great spiritual efforts, but it does not hold on to them. It only jumps to such heights for a moment, and does not stay there permanently, as if seated on a throne.
A person's virtue is judged by how they live day to day, not by the special efforts they make. Hard, occasional acts of goodness do not show how strong that virtue really is.

Pascal says that a virtue taken to an extreme impresses him only when the opposite virtue is also present at its extreme, as with Epaminondas, who had both great courage and great kindness. Going to one extreme alone is a fall, not a rise. Greatness lies in holding both extremes and everything between them. He allows that a quick swing between extremes, like a spark moving across a firebrand, shows only agility of soul, not breadth.

Human nature does not always move forward; it goes back and forth, like a fever with its cold and hot fits. The cold fit shows the fever's strength just as the hot one does. Human progress and human kindness or malice stay much the same over the ages. The Latin line at the end says that changes of fortune are usually welcome to rulers.

Continuous things grow tiresome, so rest and change are needed. Pascal says nature works the same way, moving forward and back in turns, like the tides and the sun's course, rather than in a straight line.

Pascal's point is that the body is fed slowly, bit by bit, so that a full meal is built from very small amounts taken in over time. The passage is a short, cryptic note, and its wider meaning is not stated here.

Pascal says that when people push a virtue to either extreme, they slide into vices. Going toward the very small, vices creep in unnoticed. Going toward the very large, vices crowd in so thickly that the virtue disappears from view, and people end up criticizing perfection itself.
People are neither pure spirits nor mere animals. The trouble is that someone who tries to behave like an angel ends up behaving like a beast.

We stay virtuous, Pascal says, not through our own strength but by two opposite vices holding each other in balance. He compares this to a ship or person staying upright between two opposing winds. Take away one vice, and we fall into the other.

The Stoics, an ancient school of philosophy, held that anyone short of complete wisdom is equally foolish and wicked. Pascal says this is too hard to reach and unreasonable, comparing it to someone two inches under water, who is no more drowned than one who is only a little below the surface.

Pascal is quoting a Latin saying, "that you may be content with yourself and with the goods that come from yourself," and he says it contradicts itself. Its advice, followed to the end, would lead to suicide, which he calls a happy life one should escape "as from the plague."

A string of Latin sayings from ancient Roman writers, with no comment added. Their shared thread is that crowds, decrees and fixed opinions do not make wrong things right, and that people often defend views they cannot prove.

The passage is a string of Latin sayings. They criticise people who claim to know things before they have really understood them, and they praise openly admitting what one does not know. Some sayings also warn against self-deception and quarrelling over many competing beliefs.

Pascal says that human dignity lies in thought, which makes thought wonderful by nature. Yet thought also has defects so serious that it can seem contemptible and ridiculous, and he asks what thought is that it can be so foolish.

Pascal argues that the human mind, even though it seems to rule the world, is easily upset by small noises such as a creaking weathercock or a buzzing fly. Such trifles make it unable to judge well. He mocks this powerful mind as a ridiculous hero.

Pascal says that when scientists describe heat as the motion of tiny particles, or light as a feeling of pushing away, these claims seem strange to us. Sensations such as warmth, sound and light feel unlike physical blows, yet he argues they are material in the same way a stone's blow is.
The writer had a thought and meant to write it down, but it slipped away. So instead he writes that the thought has escaped him.

When Pascal writes down a thought and it slips away from him, the lapse reminds him of his own weakness, which is that he forgets. That reminder teaches him as much as the lost thought would have, because his real aim is to know how little he is.

Pascal says he will write his thoughts on scepticism without order, and that this disorder is itself a deliberate way of showing his point. He adds that giving the subject an orderly treatment would give it too much honour, because the subject cannot be put in order.

Pascal is amazed that people do not wonder at how weak they are. They live seriously by their customs, as if they already knew for sure what is reasonable and just. When they are repeatedly proved wrong, they blame themselves instead of the supposed skill they trust in.

Pascal says it is fortunate that most people are not sceptics for the sake of scepticism itself, since such people would show that humans can hold extreme beliefs, such as thinking they have natural wisdom rather than natural weakness. He adds that the fact that some people are not sceptics is what strengthens scepticism, because if everyone were sceptical, they would be mistaken.

The sect, meaning the Christian faith here, gains more strength from its opponents than from its supporters. The reason given is that human weakness is more obvious to people who do not recognize it than to those who do.

Talk about humility can make a proud person prouder and a humble person humbler. Likewise, talk about doubt makes believers more certain. Few people speak about these virtues in a humble, pure, or doubting way. Pascal's point is that humans are full of falsehood and contradiction, and they hide this from themselves.

Pascal says that people who go beyond the average, whether far above or far below it, are often called mad, and that the majority holds that only the middle is good. He accepts this middle position, not because it is low, but because it is a limit he will not cross in either direction. For him, greatness of soul lies in staying in the middle, not in leaving it.

Pascal says that good principles already exist and only need to be applied, but people apply them unevenly. Each principle, taken too far, can open the way to abuse, such as tyranny or debauchery. So people want firm limits, yet he holds that things themselves have no limits, and the mind resists having laws set them.

Judgment is only reliable from one right distance or time, just as a painting is seen best from one exact spot. Too young, too old, too close, or too far, we judge badly. Perspective fixes that spot for painting, but Pascal asks who can fix it for truth and morality.

When everyone is moving in the same disorder, the movement is not noticed, just as a ship's passengers do not feel the ship moving. Only the person who stands still shows how far the others have gone, as a fixed point shows motion.

Pascal says that people who live loosely accuse orderly people of leaving nature's path, while they themselves are the ones who keep to it. It is like people on a ship thinking the shore is moving. To judge, we need a fixed point, as a ship's crew uses a harbour, but he asks where such a fixed point can be found in morals.

Being contradicted is not a reliable test of whether something is true. Some certain things are contradicted, and some false things go unchallenged. So a contradiction proves nothing either way: its presence does not show falsehood, and its absence does not show truth.

Pascal argues that no human truth or goodness is pure. Every idea we have is partly true and partly false, mixed together. He tests this with examples: killing is wrong, yet not killing would let the wicked harm the good, and killing destroys nature. So we hold truth and goodness only in part, mixed with error and evil.

If we dreamed the same dream every night, it would affect us as much as the things we see every day. Pascal suggests that an artisan who dreamed nightly of being a king would be almost as happy as a king who dreamed nightly of being an artisan.

Pascal argues that dreams affect us less than waking life because each dream is different and separate. If we dreamed the same troubling events every night, we would suffer almost as much as if they were real. Waking life is more continuous, so it weighs on us more, though even it is not perfectly steady.

Pascal says that ordinary life changes gradually, unlike dreams, which shift abruptly. Only rarely, such as when travelling somewhere new, does life seem so strange that we feel we are dreaming. So life is a dream, but a less unstable one.

Pascal says that people who question someone's sincerity are forced to say, "You are not being honest; we are not asleep." He is pleased to see this proud reason made humble and pleading. A man with a true right does not need to argue for it; he simply uses force against those who act in bad faith.

Pascal says that a person without God is completely ignorant and cannot avoid misery. He wants to be happy and sure of some truth, but he can neither know the truth, nor stop wanting to know it, nor even doubt.

Pascal is rejecting objections of the kind "Would God make the world only to condemn it, or demand so much from weak people?" He says such talk is foolish and that a proper doubt about one's own reasoning will remove this pride.

Pascal's note, in short form, says that in ordinary talk, people speak of religion as a grand thing, and then deny it. He also says that doubt, or scepticism, works in favour of religion. The note is brief and does not explain its reasoning.

Pascal says it is odd that we cannot define certain basic things without making them unclear, yet we talk about them with complete confidence. We assume everyone understands them in the same way, but we have no proof of this and assume it without reason.

Pascal observes that people use the same words in the same situations. When two men see a body move, both call it "moved." From this agreement in how words are used, we feel sure that they also share the same ideas.

Pascal says that the arguments he has just given are not fully convincing, though they are strong enough to justify betting that God exists. Such doubt clouds the matter but does not wipe out the natural light that tells us these things. Without that light, the skeptics (the Academicians) would have won the argument.

Pascal says that uncertainty and vagueness trouble the dogmatists, who claim to know things for sure, and this gives glory to the skeptics. He means that neither doubt nor human reason can fully clear up the dimness of our knowledge.

Pascal observes that some people reject God's and nature's laws yet strictly follow rules of their own, such as soldiers, robbers and heretics. He says logicians are similar: having broken so many just and sacred limits, their freedom to reason seems to have no limits at all.
Pascal says that the basic ideas of sceptics, stoics and atheists are correct. Their conclusions are wrong, he argues, because the opposite ideas are also true.
Pascal says we cannot prove everything by argument, and no confident claim to certainty can overcome that limit. Yet we still have a sense of what truth is, and no doubt can wipe that sense out.
Man is great because he knows he is miserable, something a tree cannot know. Knowing one's misery is therefore a form of misery, yet it is also a form of greatness.

The miseries of human life, the author says, are evidence of human greatness. He compares them to the troubles of a lord who has lost his position or a king who has been removed from the throne. The misery is felt because the person once had something higher.

Pascal says that misery needs a mind that can feel it. A ruined house is not miserable because it has no awareness, but a human being is. The Latin phrase means "I, a man, seeing" and is his way of stressing that humans alone can see and know their own misery.

People think very highly of the human soul, so much so that they cannot bear being looked down on or going unrespected by any other person. In this view, most of human happiness comes from being respected by others.

Animals do not admire one another, Pascal says. Horses may compete in a race, but that does not matter to them, and in the stable they do not expect others to give way to them as people do. Their merit is enough for themselves.

Pascal says that people's greatness shows even in their lust, because they have been able to draw from it a fine set of rules and a picture of goodwill. The idea is that humans can turn even their weakest desires into something admirable.
Pascal says that the causes people find for things they do show how great humans are. Out of desire, which he calls lust, people have built a fine and orderly system of reasons and explanations.

Pascal says that the desire for glory, or the esteem of others, is both man's lowest fault and a sign of his greatness. People are not satisfied with health, comfort or possessions alone, because they want to be highly thought of by other people. Their wish for good standing in others' judgment is the thing he calls the finest position in the world.

Even people who claim to despise humanity and treat it as no better than animals still want to be admired and believed by others. Pascal says their own nature shows them the greatness of man more strongly than reason shows them his baseness.
Pride balances out human misery. People either hide their troubles, or, if they admit them, they take pride in being aware of them.

Pascal says that pride makes up for all of human misery, so people do not feel their suffering fully. He describes man as a fallen creature who has left his proper place and keeps searching anxiously to get back to it, as everyone does.

Pascal says that when wickedness can point to some reason, it grows proud and shows that reason off. Likewise, when strict self-denial has not reached the true good and so goes back to following nature, it becomes proud of having gone back.

Evil is easy to find and takes countless forms, while good is nearly one of a kind. A certain special kind of evil, though, is as hard to find as good is, so it is often mistaken for good. Reaching it, like reaching good, takes great strength of character.

Pascal argues that man's misery itself shows his greatness. Man feels wretched because he is now like an animal, though he once had a better nature. Only a deposed king feels unhappy at no longer being king, which suggests man once held a higher place.

People judge a loss by what they expected to have. A man who held an office only for a set time is not counted unhappy when it ends, but Perseus, who lost a kingship he was meant to hold for life, is pitied. Nobody mourns having one mouth or two eyes, yet everyone grieves having none.
Even though we can see all our troubles clearly and they weigh heavily on us, we still have a built-in urge that we cannot hold back, and that urge raises us up above them.

Man is always at war within himself, because he has both reason and passions. With reason alone, or passions alone, he would have no conflict. But since he has both, he cannot be at peace with one without being at odds with the other, so he stays divided against himself.

Some people try to end the inner conflict between reason and the passions by giving up one side. One group would give up the passions and try to become like gods, while the other would give up reason and become like beasts. Pascal says neither can succeed: reason keeps condemning the passions, and the passions stay alive in those who want to renounce them.

Pascal says there are two ways to judge human nature. Looked at by its purpose, or end, a person is great and unmatched. Looked at by the common crowd of people and their behaviour, the same person seems low and worthless, as a horse or dog is judged by its everyday qualities. Philosophers argue because each side denies the other's premise.
Pascal observes that people have reasoned in two opposite ways about human nature. Some take man's greatness as proof of his misery, while others take his misery as proof of his greatness.

Pascal says that every proof of human greatness also shows human misery, and the reverse. The more a person knows of his fall from a higher state, the more wretched he is. So people keep moving between the two views, and the more light a person has, the more he sees both his greatness and his wretchedness. Man knows he is wretched, and so he is wretched.

Some people have believed that humans have two souls, because one mind seemed unable to swing so suddenly between extreme pride and deep despair. Pascal is describing the two sides of human nature that he sees as clear to everyone.

Pascal says that a person should see both sides of his nature: his likeness to animals and his greatness. Seeing only one side is dangerous, and being ignorant of both is more dangerous still. He must understand that he is neither simply a beast nor an angel, and know both sides together.

The passage is cut off, so its full meaning is unclear. It most probably says that man should not rely on himself or on other people, so that he is left without a firm footing or rest. The rest of the sentence, which would give the purpose, is missing.

In this line, God speaks of how he deals with a human being. If the person proud, God brings him low; if he humbles himself, God raises him up. God keeps opposing him until the person sees that he is an incomprehensible monster.

Pascal says he faults three kinds of people equally: those who praise man, those who blame man, and those who simply amuse themselves. He approves only of those who search for truth while grieving over their condition.

Pascal says it is good to become worn out by searching fruitlessly for the true good in worldly things. Such weariness leads a person to reach out to the Redeemer, meaning Christ, who saves people from sin.

Man should both value and reject himself, at the same time. He should love himself because he has a nature able to do good, but not love the faults in him. He should despise himself because that ability is currently unused, but not despise the ability itself.

Man can know truth and find happiness, but he has no truth that is lasting or satisfying. The passage says the aim is to lead him to want truth, and to be free of passions, since passions cloud his knowledge. It also says he should reject the desire that drives his will alone, so that it neither blinds his choice nor hinders him once he has chosen.

The apparent contradictions that seemed most likely to keep the writer from understanding religion are the very things that led him most quickly to the true religion. He says the puzzles pushed him toward the truth rather than away from it.

Pascal argues that everyone seeks happiness, and every action aims at it, even going to war or hanging oneself. Yet people without faith have never reached this goal, so they cannot truly know the good.

People of every rank, age and country complain about their lives. Such a long and uniform record should show that people cannot reach the good by their own efforts. Yet each time we hope things will go better, and experience keeps deceiving us, leading us from misfortune to death.

Pascal argues that human longing and inability to be satisfied point to a lost true happiness once known by man. People try to fill the gap with things around them, but only God, an infinite and unchanging being, can fill it. Since people have turned away from God, nothing in nature has been left unused as a stand-in for Him.

Pascal says that people who have lost the true good can take anything for good, even things that harm them and go against God, reason and nature. Some look for it in power, some in learning, and some in pleasure.

Some thinkers held that the good all people seek cannot be a thing only one person can own, since sharing such things causes more pain than pleasure. The true good, they argued, must be something everyone can have fully at once, without loss or envy, and that no one can lose against their will.
When people lose their true nature, each thing takes its own nature as the standard. In the same way, when the true good is lost, each person treats whatever they happen to want as their true good.

Pascal says that people do not know where they belong in the order of things. They believe they have wandered away from their proper place and cannot find their way back, so they search for it anxiously and without success.

If people think proving God through nature shows weakness, they should not despise Scripture (the Bible). If knowing the contradictions in human nature shows strength, they should value Scripture for that reason.

Pascal says that a true religion must explain two facts about humans: they have great dignity and they have great misery. It must give a reason for this contradiction. It must also show that God exists, that people should love him, and that happiness lies in him, while being cut off from him is the only real evil.

Pascal argues that a true religion must explain why people turn away from God and the good, and must offer a cure. He proposes to test the world's religions against this standard, starting with the philosophers, who taught that the chief good lies within ourselves. He asks whether that teaching is the true good and whether it cures our faults.

Pascal asks which religion can cure human pride and lust. He argues that other religions fail, because some make man equal to God and others make earthly pleasure the highest good. He then says he will look to the wisdom of God, which tells people to expect neither truth nor comfort from other men.

In this speech, God describes how he made man holy, innocent and perfect, full of light and able to see God's glory. Man could not keep that glory, fell into pride, wanted to be his own centre, and turned away from God's rule.

This is God speaking of what followed when man wanted to be equal to God and find his happiness in himself. God left man to himself, and the creatures that had served man turned against him. Man became like the animals, losing almost all knowledge of his Creator. His senses, not guided by reason, have led him to chase pleasure.

Pascal says that all creatures either hurt or lure a human being, ruling him either by force or by their charms. Humans still have a faint memory of their former happiness, but they are sunk in blindness and desire, which have become second nature. This, he says, explains the contradictions that have divided people into opposing camps.

Pascal argues that people cannot find their own cure for their troubles by looking inside themselves. Human reason can show that truth and the good are not found within us. The philosophers promised a remedy but could not give one, because they did not know what our true good or true condition is.

Pascal says that human beings have two main illnesses: pride, which pulls them away from God, and lust, which ties them to earth. Teachers who offered God only to feed pride made people think they were like God, while others who saw that claim as absurd pushed them toward thinking they were like animals and should seek pleasures animals share. Neither approach cures the underlying wrongdoing.

Pascal argues that human beings are split between two conditions: their original created nature, linked to Adam, and a state of union with God and humility, which comes through Jesus Christ and grace rather than from nature. He says people can see these two states in themselves, and that their contradictions do not prove the matter is unreal, even if it is hard to understand.

Pascal argues that doubting God could unite Himself with humans comes from seeing how low we are. He says that if we admit we are too weak to know whether God's mercy could make us fit for Him, we have no right to limit that mercy by our own imagination.

Pascal argues that a person who doubts God can be united with Him is ignorant of both God and himself. The author asks why such a person thinks God cannot make Himself known and loved, since humans are capable of knowing and loving. He points out that everyone at least knows they exist and loves something.

Pascal argues that if a person can see some truth in the darkness of human life, or find love for something on earth, then God could likewise give him some glimmer of His nature. So it is presumptuous to say that God cannot be known or loved in the way God chooses to reveal Himself. Such an argument only looks humble. Real humility, he says, means accepting that we can learn what we are only from God.

Pascal's speaker says he will not force belief on anyone or claim to explain everything. Instead, he plans to show clear proofs and signs of his divine authority, so that people can accept his teachings. Their only reason to reject them would be that they cannot tell for themselves whether the teachings are true.

God wants to save people who seek salvation, but people make themselves so unworthy that God is right to refuse some of them the mercy He gives to others. God could have overcome the most hardened hearts by showing Himself plainly, as He will at the last day with thunder and great upheaval.

Pascal says God did not come in a way that would plainly prove His divinity to everyone. Many people had made themselves unworthy of His mercy, so He left them without the good they did not want. Yet He also did not come so hidden that those who sincerely seek Him could not recognise Him.

God shows himself openly to those who seek him wholeheartedly and stays hidden from those who turn away from him. He gives visible signs to seekers, so there is enough light for those who want to see and enough darkness for those inclined the other way.

Pascal says that no other religion has correctly seen both sides of human nature. Some religions stress human greatness and call people's low opinions of themselves mean and ungrateful. Others stress human worthlessness and mock feelings of greatness. The first kind tells people to look up to God, whom they resemble, and to become like him through wisdom.

Two opposite voices urge man either to lift his head as a free being or to look down at himself as a worm, close to the animals. Pascal asks what man is then, between God and the beasts, and concludes that man has lost his true place, cannot find it again, and that even the greatest men have failed to lead him back.

Pascal says that scepticism, the view that certain knowledge is impossible, is true about people before Christ. Those earlier people did not know their place in the world or whether humans were great or small. Any claim either way was only a guess, and each side wrongly ruled out the other. The Latin at the end means "what you seek in ignorance, religion announces to you."
A religion can only be true if it understands human nature: both how great and how small people are, and why. Pascal claims that only Christianity has shown this understanding.

The sceptics argue that our basic principles can only be known as true through faith and revelation, or through the natural sense we have of them. But that natural sense proves nothing, because we cannot know whether we were made by a good God, an evil demon, or chance. So the principles may be true, false, or uncertain.

Pascal argues that without faith, no one can be sure whether they are awake or asleep. Dreams feel just as real as waking life, with space, motion and time all seeming present. Since we spend about half our lives asleep, he concludes that we cannot claim to know the truth from our own experience.

Pascal suggests that if our perceptions can all be false, we cannot be sure that waking life is not also a kind of sleep, like the dreams we take for reality. He sets aside weaker doubts drawn from custom, upbringing and country, saying ordinary people hold their beliefs on shallow grounds that collapse under mild skeptical challenge.

Pascal says that dogmatists (who claim we can know basic truths) have one strong point: when we speak sincerely, we cannot really doubt natural principles. Sceptics reply that we cannot be sure where we came from, and so cannot be sure of our nature. Because of this, people must take a side, and anyone who claims to stay neutral is in fact a sceptic.

Pascal describes a group he calls the sect, whose members stay neutral and undecided about everything, even themselves. He asks whether a person in that state could doubt everything, even his own existence, and answers that no one truly can. He claims there has never been a complete sceptic.

Pascal says human reason is weak and needs nature to keep it from going wild. He argues that a person who cannot defend a claim to truth when questioned has no right to claim certainty. He calls man a contradiction: a judge of all things yet a weak worm, a holder of truth yet full of error. He says nature answers the sceptics and reason answers the dogmatists.

Pascal argues that human reason alone cannot show us our true condition, so people must humble themselves and listen to God. He says that if humans had never been corrupt, they would know truth and happiness with certainty, and if they had always been corrupt, they would have no idea of either.

Pascal says that people are wretched, yet they still have an idea of happiness they cannot reach and a sense of truth they only partly hold. He suggests we once stood higher and have fallen. He adds that the doctrine of original sin, the mystery of how sin passes to humankind, is the key to understanding ourselves.

Pascal says that the idea of original sin shocks human reason. It seems unjust that infants, who could not have chosen anything, should be condemned eternally for a sin of the first man committed long before they were born.

Pascal says that human nature cannot be understood without the mystery of God, and that humans are harder to explain without it than the mystery is to explain to humans. He adds that religion shows two equally certain truths: people, whether in their created state or under grace, are raised above nature and share in God's divinity.

Pascal says that humans have two states that are both true. By grace, a person is made like God and shares in his divinity. Without grace, after falling into sin, a person is like the beasts. He supports this with Bible verses that speak of both.

Without knowledge of God, people can only swing between two errors. Either they feel proud of the greatness they still sense in themselves, or they despair at their present weakness. Seeing only half the truth, they fall into either pride or laziness, and cannot reach true virtue.

Pascal says that people who saw human weakness but not human greatness fell into despair, while those who saw greatness but not weakness fell into pride. Various philosophical schools arose from these two errors. Only Christianity, he says, cures both, by teaching humility and dignity together, with the righteous raised to share in God's own nature.

Religion, the passage says, tells people that even their highest state still carries the root of sin, which leaves them open to error, suffering, death and wrongdoing. It also tells the most ungodly that they can receive their Redeemer's grace. So it humbles people more than reason can, yet without despair, and lifts them up more than natural pride does, yet without arrogance.

Pascal argues that only one source is free from error and able to teach and correct people, so people should believe it. He says we see both our own greatness and our miserable condition, and this mix of order and confusion proves the truth of both.
Men chase wealth, but they have no fair claim to it beyond human whim, and they cannot keep it safe. Knowledge is lost to illness too. So people are unable to reach either truth or goodness.

Humans long for truth and happiness, yet within themselves they find only doubt, misery and death. They cannot stop wanting these things, and they cannot reach them. Pascal says this longing is left in us partly as a punishment and partly to show us how far we have fallen.
Pascal asks two questions. If people were not made for God, why do they find happiness only in God? If they were made for God, why do they resist him so strongly?

Pascal says that the many strange and differing customs among people show that human reason has been damaged. He adds that truth had to come so that people would stop living only inside themselves, turned in on their own ideas.

Pascal says that once Christianity teaches that human nature is corrupt and has fallen away from God, he can see signs of this everywhere. He claims that nature, both inside people and in the world around them, points to a lost God and a corrupted human nature.

Pascal says that knowing what a human being really is, what really counts as good, what real virtue is, and what true religion is, cannot be separated. You cannot know one of these without knowing the others.

The more knowledge a person has, the more they see both greatness and baseness in human beings. Religion, Pascal says, does not add anything new; it only shows more deeply what we already know, in line with how much light we have.

The religion, here the Christian faith, teaches its followers something that people could reach only through their highest learning. The passage contrasts simple religious teaching with the hard-won results of human scholarship. Pascal's point, in this line, is that the faith gives in a simple form what reason alone found only with great effort.

Pascal says original sin looks like foolishness to people, and he admits it has no reason behind it. Yet he calls this foolishness wiser than all human wisdom, because human beings cannot understand their own state without it. He adds that reason cannot discover this doctrine by itself and resists it when it is put forward.

Pascal cites Jewish writings to show that the idea of original sin, an evil inborn in people from the start, is found in Jewish tradition. He quotes Genesis, which says the human heart's imagination is evil from youth, and rabbinic sources that call this inner evil a "leaven" placed in people when they are formed. They also say God will free people's good nature from it.

The passage says that an inner evil impulse, which Pascal calls "malignity," is always working against people. Scripture says the wicked watch the righteous to kill them, but God does not abandon them. The impulse tests people in this life and will accuse them before God later. Rabbinic writings are cited to support this view.

Pascal quotes Jewish commentaries (midrash) that read an old saying about a poor wise child and a foolish old king as a picture of the human heart. The child stands for virtue, and the old king for the evil in human nature, which rules every part of a person from youth to age and leads people toward ruin without their seeing it. He adds other verses that he reads as pointing to the same inner tyrant.

Pascal quotes Jewish commentaries (midrash) that read Scripture as saying that the "evil leaven," meaning the evil inclination in a person, should be fed with wisdom and water instead of being fought directly. Another commentary calls it a great king besieging a small city, and says a poor wise man, meaning virtue, saves the city.

Pascal's note reads a line from Psalm 78 as referring to an "evil leaven" that leaves at death and does not return at the resurrection, not to the soul itself. He says some people wrongly used the line to deny that the soul is immortal. The note ends with a reference to a Jewish teaching about two Messiahs.

Pascal asks whether people who said that righteousness had left the earth were therefore aware of original sin, the Christian doctrine that humanity is born corrupted by Adam's fall. He also quotes the Latin saying "No one is happy before death," and asks whether they understood death as the start of true, lasting happiness.

Pascal says that people in the state of corruption, meaning sin, should all know they are in it, whether they accept that state or not. But he says it is not right for everyone to see Redemption, the saving of humans from sin.

If we do not see our own faults, such as pride, ambition, lust, weakness, misery and injustice, we are blind. Pascal says that a religion which understands these faults so well deserves respect, and that its promised cures make its truth worth wanting.
Pascal says that people naturally hate each other. They use lust to serve the common good, but this is only a false show of love, because underneath it is still hate.
Pity for the unfortunate does not conflict with self-indulgent desire. Indeed, a person can show friendship and earn a reputation for kindness while giving nothing away.

Pascal says that people have drawn good rules of government, ethics and justice from their own desire, yet that desire is still there underneath. The rules only hide it; they do not remove it. He calls this desire the "vile root" of man, the evil inclination in human nature.

Pascal says that people have found no way to satisfy their desires without harming others. Injustice, he suggests, comes from this: the only available means of gratifying lust involve hurting someone else.

Pascal argues that the Self is hateful in itself, not only because it causes trouble for others. Hiding it or being polite does not remove the hatred. Even if a person is careful not to annoy others, the Self remains unjust, since it makes itself the centre of everything, so it stays hateful.

The Self, meaning a person's selfish nature, wants to rule over others. Removing only its annoying behaviour does not remove its unfairness. So it can be made pleasing only to unjust people, who no longer see it as a threat, and never to those who hate injustice.

Pascal says it is a warped way of thinking for people to place themselves above everyone else. It is wrong to value one's own good and continued fortune and life more than the good of the rest of the world.

Each person treats himself as the centre of everything, because for him the world ends when he dies. So each one wrongly assumes everyone else sees him the same way. Pascal says we should judge nature by nature itself, not by our own view of it.

Everything in the world, the passage says, comes from three desires: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. Pascal names these in Latin as the desire to feel, the desire to know, and the desire to dominate. He calls them rivers of fire that burn the land instead of watering it, so the world is wretched.

Those who are not swept away by the rivers of worldly life are called happy. They sit firmly on a secure base and wait for God to lift them up. Then they stand firm in the holy city, where pride can no longer bring them down.

Pascal describes people who weep not over earthly things being carried away by floods, but over longing for their true homeland, the heavenly Jerusalem. They keep this homeland in mind constantly while they remain far from it in exile.

Pascal uses the rivers of Babylon as a picture of worldly pleasures, which rush past and vanish, while Jerusalem stands for what is firm and lasting. He says we should sit on these waters, not sink under them, staying humble and secure. Pleasures that pass away are rivers of Babylon.

Pascal sorts people into three kinds, each ruled by a different weakness. The rich and kings are concerned with the body, where lust rules. Scholars are concerned with the mind, where curiosity rules. The wise are concerned with righteousness, where pride rules. He adds that God must rule over all of them.

Pascal argues that pride is out of place in wealth or learning, because a learned man can easily be shown that he has no reason to be proud of it. Pride fits only wisdom, since a man cannot be told he is wrong to be proud of wisdom he made himself. Wisdom comes from God alone, so the one who boasts should boast in the Lord (a Latin quotation from St Paul).

Pascal says that the three lusts (desires) have produced three schools of thought, and that the philosophers did nothing more than follow one of these three desires. The "three lusts" refer to a list of desires the wider work discusses, which this fragment does not spell out.
Ordinary people look for the good in luck, possessions, or at least entertainment. Philosophers have shown that these things are empty, and they have tried to locate the good elsewhere.

Pascal says that philosophers knew God deserves love and admiration, yet they wanted people to love and admire them instead. If they did not want to be loved for their own sake, that is the horrible part: they wanted men to stop at them rather than turn to God, and wanted men to take pleasure in them freely.

Pascal says that our instincts, passions and the outside world all pull us away from ourselves and toward things outside us. So the philosophers' advice to look within for our good does not work, and those who accept it are, in his view, the emptiest and most foolish.

Pascal rejects two common answers to where happiness is found. One says to look inside yourself, the other says to look outside in amusement. Neither works, since illness can come at any time. He concludes that happiness is found in God, both outside and inside a person.

Pascal says that the Stoic thinker Epictetus pointed to a true way of life, the way of willing what God wills, but could not lead people onto it. Only Jesus Christ, whom he calls the way and the truth, can lead there.

Pascal criticises Epictetus, a Stoic philosopher, for claiming that everything is either within our power or not. Pascal says the claim is wrong because we cannot govern our own hearts, and he says Epictetus drew a mistaken conclusion from the existence of some Christians.

Pascal says that Christianity alone asks people to hate themselves. Only a religion like that could appeal to people who already hate themselves and want a truly lovable being. Such people, he adds, would accept a God who was humbled, even without having heard of him.

Pascal reasons that he is not a necessary being, since he could have never existed had his mother died before his birth. Because his self depends on his thoughts, which began at a point, he is neither eternal nor infinite. He concludes that there must be a necessary, eternal, infinite Being in nature.

People say they would become believers if they saw a miracle, but they cannot know how they would act. They picture conversion as a kind of trade with God, or a friendly fellowship. True religion, the passage says, means giving up pride before God, admitting that we deserve only his anger, and accepting that a mediator is needed to reach him.

Pascal's point is that it would be wrong for people to attach themselves to him, even willingly. He cannot be their final goal, and he cannot give them what they seek. Since he is mortal, the one they cling to will die.

Pascal argues that it is wrong to make people believe a falsehood, even by pleasant means or when they enjoy it. By the same reasoning, it is wrong for him to make people love him or attach themselves to him. He says he should warn such people not to accept the lie, or to attach themselves to him, whatever benefit he gains.

Pascal says that a person who insists on getting their own way will never be satisfied, even if they gain everything they want. Peace comes only when that self-will is given up. Without self-will a person cannot be discontented, and with it a person cannot be content.

Pascal says that to know how much we should love ourselves, we should picture a body made of thinking parts. Each part is part of the whole, so each should love itself in a way that fits its place in the body.

Pascal's point is that the parts of the body, such as the hands and feet, are only in order when they submit their own wills to the will that governs the whole body. Without that submission they fall into disorder, but when they serve the good of the whole body, they also achieve their own good.

The main point is that people should love God alone and reject love of self. Pascal compares this to a foot that learns it belongs to a body. The foot would feel regret for having lived only for itself, since the body gives it life and it depends on the body for its existence.

Pascal uses the picture of a body and its limbs. A limb should accept being cut off if the body needs it, because the limb exists only for the sake of the whole body. Its life counts for nothing apart from the body it belongs to.

We do not deserve other people's love, and it is wrong to want it. Pascal argues that people are born with a self-centred bias, which he sees as the root of all disorder, so we are born unjust and our will is corrupted.
When we try to think about God, we are pulled away by other thoughts. Pascal says these distractions are bad and arise naturally within us.

If God exists, people should love God alone and not temporary created things. The ungodly reasoning in the Book of Wisdom starts from the denial that God exists, and so it concludes that people should enjoy creatures. Pascal says that if God were real and worth loving, that reasoning would have pointed the other way.

Pascal argues that anything that pulls us toward created things and away from God is harmful, because it keeps us from serving or seeking God. Since people are full of desire, they are full of evil, so they should hate themselves and whatever draws them to anything other than God.

Pascal says that the deaths of ancient Greek and other non-Christian heroes move us little, because we have no connection to them. The deaths of Christian martyrs move us more, since they are fellow members of the faith, and their example may even earn our own resolve. He compares this to how a stranger's wealth does not make us rich, but a father's or husband's does.

God made the heavens and the earth, which cannot feel their own existence, and then made thinking beings who could know that happiness. Pascal compares people to limbs of one body: they do not notice the care and unity that sustain them, and they would be happy if they did.

The passage says that members of a body are meant to share what they have with the rest, rather than keep it for themselves. Someone who hoards for their own sake would, in fact, hate themselves more than love themselves. Their happiness and their duty both lie in accepting the guidance of the whole, which cares for them more than they care for themselves.

A part of a body has life and movement only through the whole body that it belongs to. Cut off from that body, the part decays, yet it wrongly thinks it is complete and tries to become its own centre. Having no life of its own, it wanders lost and feels unsure of its own existence.

The soul, having recognised that it is not a body, still does not see itself as part of one, and so it loves itself only through the body, since it exists in it and for it. Pascal adds that a body part, such as the hand, loves the whole body in the same way.

Pascal compares people to parts of one body. Just as a hand should love itself only as much as the whole body loves it, people should love themselves in right measure. Our love for ourselves and for Jesus Christ belongs to one unity, as we are members of his body, and the Latin phrase means that whoever clings to God becomes one spirit with him.
Pascal says that two laws are enough to govern the whole Christian community. He claims they work better than all the laws that rulers make for the state.

The passage argues that true virtue is to hate the self, which Pascal sees as ruled by lust, and to love something lovable beyond it. Since we cannot love what is wholly outside us, the passage says we must love a being within us that is not ourselves, which it identifies as the Universal Being, or God's kingdom within us.
Before the fall, people had worth because they ruled over the other creatures. Now they have cut themselves off from those creatures and placed themselves under them.
Pascal says that a religion is false unless it does two things. It must worship one God as the source of all things, and it must love that one God as the goal of all things.

Pascal says that God cannot be the goal of a person's life unless God is also where that life begins. People may look up toward heaven while resting on unstable ground, so they will fall while looking up.

Pascal argues that if God is the single source and goal of all things, a true religion must teach people to worship and love God alone. Since people cannot do this on their own, such a religion must also explain why and offer a remedy. It says humans were cut off from God through one man, Adam, and are restored through one man, and that people are born guilty because they are born turned away from God.

People are used to rewarding merit only where it already exists, so they judge God by their own habits. In other words, they expect God to reward people only for goodness they already have, rather than creating that goodness in them first.

The passage argues that the true religion should have three marks: it commands people to love God, it recognises human desire and weakness, and it offers a remedy for them, which is prayer. Pascal says only Christianity has all three, and that no other religion asks God for the grace to love and follow him.

Pascal says that people who do not hate their own self-love, and the urge that makes them want to be like God, are blind. Self-love is unjust, since no one can truly deserve the place it claims and everyone wants the same thing. He notes that this injustice is innate, yet no religion has called it a sin or offered a cure.

The true religion, according to this passage, does three things. It names what people must do, the weaknesses they have (pride and lust), and the cures for those weaknesses, which are humility and mortification, meaning the discipline of denying the body and its desires.
The true religion, Pascal says, must show people both their greatness and their misery. It must make them value and despise themselves, and love and hate, in the right measure.
It is a great blindness to live without examining what we are, but a worse one to live an evil life while believing in God.

Pascal argues against people who rely on God's mercy and so neglect good works. He says that pride and laziness are the two sources of sin, and God shows two matching qualities to cure them: mercy, which answers laziness, and justice, which humbles pride even when a person's works are good.

Pascal says that mercy works against laziness about doing good. Mercy urges people to do good works, citing Scripture: God's goodness leads to repentance, and the people of Nineveh did penance, hoping God would pity them. So mercy does not excuse idleness; it is the quality that directly opposes it.
Pascal says we should not reason that, if God had no mercy, we would have to work hard at virtue. Instead, the reason we must strive toward virtue is that God does show mercy.

Pascal says that the difficulty of turning to a holy life comes from the sinful nature still inside us, not from the new faith that is starting to grow there. The pain we feel is caused by our natural faults fighting against God's grace. That inner struggle should be blamed on the pull of the world, not on God who is calling us.

Pascal says that God's harshest act toward people in this life is to leave them alone in a false peace. He compares this to a child who should be glad of a mother's forceful rescue from kidnappers. Christ's coming brought conflict, which he calls a sword and fire, and the world before him lived without it.

Some outward actions or conditions please both God and people, and that is dangerous. A holy state can please God through one quality, such as humility, and please people through another, such as the brilliance of its teaching. Pascal says people then copy the visible words of such a person instead of the inner state God values.

Pascal says it is better to skip fasting and stay humble than to fast and feel proud of it, using the Pharisee and the Publican (tax collector) from the Gospel as an example. He then asks what good memory is if it can harm as easily as help. His answer is that everything depends on God's blessing, which comes only to acts done for God and in God's way, since God can bring good out of evil but people turn good into evil without him.

Pascal describes two stages in how a person may regard the opinions of others. The first stage is to be blamed when doing wrong and praised when doing right. The second is to receive neither praise nor blame at all.

Pascal says a righteous person keeps the passions under control, as a master keeps servants. Used this way, the passions count as virtues, but when they rule the person they become vices that poison the soul. The Latin phrase means "your desire shall be subject to you."
Pascal says that philosophers made vices holy by claiming them as qualities of God. Christians, by contrast, made virtues holy. The point is that each group sanctified something different.

The just man, in small matters as well as large, relies on God. When he corrects his servants, he hopes God will change their hearts and asks God to make his correction work. He acts in everything by the Spirit of God, though his actions can sometimes look wrong when that guidance is absent or hidden in him.

Everyday things like walls and stairs can cause harm if we are careless, and small movements in nature have large effects, such as a rock changing the whole sea. In the same way, in matters of grace, every small action has consequences, so each action must be considered with regard to our past, present and future, and to others it affects.

Pascal asks God not to hold our sins against us. He means not only the sins themselves but all their results, which can be terrible, even those that come from small faults, if those results are traced out without mercy.
Grace, meaning God's free help given to people, is needed to make someone a saint. Anyone who doubts this, the passage says, does not understand what a saint or a human being is.
Pascal says it is pointless to tell a person to come to God on their own. A man who does not know himself cannot do it, and a man who does know himself would not find the advice useful either.

Pascal says that people do not deserve God, but they are able to be made worthy of him. He argues that it would be beneath God to join himself to miserable people, yet it is not beneath him to rescue them from their misery.

Pascal argues that if someone claims a person is too unimportant to be united with God, that person would have to be very great in order to make such a judgment. The point is that the claim itself requires a standard of greatness that humans do not have.

Pascal argues that the Eucharistic bread can be called the whole body of Christ only in a loose sense, not in the full sense. Mere union of two things without change does not make one become the other, as a soul joined to a body or fire joined to wood does not change them. Real change is needed for one thing's form to become another's, as when the Word is united to man.

Pascal is arguing that being in the same place or the same body is not enough to make two things one and the same. Identity of a single thing at one time needs more than that, namely identity of matter. He uses the example of a river: two stretches of water running at the same moment in different places are not the same river.

Pascal lists three reasons God set up prayer: to let people share in the power of causing things, to show them that virtue comes from God, and to let them earn other virtues through effort. He answers an objection that people pray by their own power, arguing that if faith cannot come from ourselves, neither can the virtues that follow it. Prayer itself is granted by God as he chooses.

Pascal's point is that God is bound only by what He has promised. God promised to answer prayers, but He never promised that prayer would be granted only to those already chosen. He also notes that Saint Augustine's statement that strength would be taken from the righteous was made by chance, not as a settled rule.

The passage says that, given a person's principles, it was certain he would say a particular thing when the occasion came, and could not have said the opposite. So his speaking was less a matter of free choice than of necessity. Pascal says the two possibilities are that he was forced to say it or that he happened to say it, and that these two are all we can ask.

The chosen people will not know their own good deeds, and the rejected will not know how serious their sins are. Pascal supports this with the words of the righteous and the condemned in Matthew 25, who ask the Lord when they saw him hungry or thirsty.

Pascal cites Romans 3:27, where Paul says boasting is shut out. The reason he gives is faith, not the works of the law. So Pascal concludes that faith is not something we produce by our own effort, like good deeds, but is given to us from outside ourselves.
Do not look to yourselves for God's grace, which is his free gift of help. You receive it by expecting nothing from your own efforts and placing your hope in God instead.

Pascal says that everyone, even the martyrs who died for their faith, should fear, as Scripture teaches. He adds that the worst suffering in purgatory, the place where souls are cleansed after death in Catholic belief, is not knowing how God will judge them. The Latin phrase "Deus absconditus" means "hidden God."

Pascal is discussing John 8, where Jesus says that the truth will make people free. He says there is a difference between followers in general and true followers. The test is how someone answers the claim that the truth will set them free: those who insist they are already free from sin's power are followers, but not true ones.

Pascal says that the Jewish law did not destroy human nature but taught it, and that grace (God's free help) did not cancel the law but made it work in people. He adds that faith received at baptism is the source of the whole Christian life.

Pascal says that grace, the free help of God, is always present in the world, just as nature is, so grace is in a way natural too. For this reason, two opposing camps will always exist: Pelagians, who stress human nature and our own power, and Catholics, who stress grace. Their conflict will never end, because birth into nature produces one side and the second birth, through grace, produces the other.
Pascal says that the doctrine most suited to human beings is the one teaching that people can both receive grace and lose it. He gives the reason: humans face two dangers, despair and pride.

The philosophers taught only pure pride or pure humility, yet human beings are in neither state alone. Pascal says people need humility that comes from repentance and leads onward to greatness, and a sense of greatness that comes from grace, reached only after humility.

Human misery leads to despair, and human pride leads to presumption, which means overconfidence. The Incarnation, God becoming human in Jesus, shows how great human misery is, because the cure needed was so great.

Knowing God without also knowing human misery leads to pride. Knowing human misery without also knowing God leads to despair. Knowing Jesus Christ gives a balance between the two, because in him a person finds both God and their own misery.
Jesus Christ is presented as a God that people can come near to without arrogance, and before whom they can bow down without losing hope. Both attitudes are held together: humility without despair.

Humans are neither so corrupted that they cannot do good, nor so holy that they are free from evil. The fragment is a partial sentence, so this is its most likely meaning: it describes a middle state between total ruin and perfect goodness.

Two people described their feelings after confession. One felt joy and confidence, the other stayed afraid. The speaker thought that each lacked what the other had, and that together they would make one good person.

Pascal says that greater knowledge, greater justice, and greater help all bring greater responsibility. Each is tied to a saying from the Gospels or the Bible: the servant who knows his master's will is beaten more, the righteous should still be made righteous, and much given means much asked back. The point is that the more a person has been given, the more is expected of them.

Scripture offers words of comfort and warning for every kind of person. Pascal says nature does the same through the contrasts it always contains, such as higher and lower, cleverer and less clever. These are meant to lower human pride and raise humility.

Pascal sets two quotations side by side. The first, "a broken heart," comes from Saint Paul and stands for the Christian character. The second, from Corneille's play, where a character disowns a former friend, stands for a cold, inhuman character. He says the human character is the opposite of the inhuman one.
Pascal says people fall into two groups. One group is made up of good people who see themselves as sinners. The other group is made up of sinners who see themselves as good.

We should be grateful to people who point out our faults, because they hurt our pride and show us we have been looked down on. They do not stop others from despising us later, since we have other faults. Still, they give us the chance to correct ourselves and become free of those faults.

Pascal says that people come to believe whatever they are repeatedly told, including that they are fools, and that they do the same to themselves through their own inner talk. So a person should guard that inner talk, speaking to himself mainly of God, who is true, and so come to know the truth.

Christianity asks people to see themselves as wretched, even detestable, and also to long to be like God. Pascal says that each idea needs the other as a balance: without the dignity, humility would make a person utterly hopeless, and without the humility, the sense of dignity would make a person proud.

A Christian, in Pascal's view, believes he is united with God yet feels little pride about it. He also places himself beside the lowly worms of the earth without feeling much humiliation. Because of this, he meets both life and death, good and evil, in a noble way.
