The passage compares a soldier with a Carthusian monk, a member of a strict religious order. Both are under obedience and bound to hard work. The difference is that the soldier hopes to become a commander, which he never reaches, while the monk has taken a vow to remain dependent and has no such hope.

Christians hope for an infinite good, and this hope is mixed with both present enjoyment and fear. Their hope is not like that of a subject who hopes for a kingdom he would never share in. They hope for holiness and freedom from injustice, and they already have some of these things.
Only the Christian religion makes a person both lovable and happy. Speaking honestly, the passage suggests that people without it may not be able to be both.

Pascal says that abstract proofs of God are too complicated to move most people, and that even those who are convinced by them soon doubt. He argues that knowing God without Jesus Christ as a go-between leads to pride, while those who know God through Christ also recognize their own weakness and sin.

The passage says that the Christian God makes the soul feel that God alone is its good and its rest, and that it finds delight in loving Him. At the same time, God makes the soul hate the things that block that love, such as self-love and lust. God also shows the soul that self-love is a root that destroys it, and that only God can cure it.

Jesus taught that people love themselves too much, and that they are enslaved, blind, sick, miserable and sinful. He said he would free, enlighten, bless and heal them. This would happen through hating the self and following him through suffering and death on the cross.

Pascal says that without Jesus Christ, people are left with sin and suffering. With Jesus Christ, they are free from both and have goodness and happiness. Apart from him there is only vice, misery, darkness, death and despair.

We can know God only through Jesus Christ, who is the mediator between God and people. Without him there is no real connection with God. Those who tried to prove God without Jesus had only weak proofs. The prophecies about Jesus, which came true, are solid proof that Jesus is divine.

Pascal says that people know God only through Jesus Christ. Without Jesus, Scripture, the doctrine of original sin, and the promised Mediator, he holds that God cannot be fully proven and right teaching and morality cannot be found. Through Jesus, both become possible, and so Jesus is the true God of men, while people also recognise their own wretchedness.

The passage says that God is known as the saviour from human misery, so people know God well only when they know their own sins. Those who knew God without recognising their misery did not honour God but honoured themselves. The Latin at the end comes from the New Testament (1 Corinthians 1:21): God chose to save believers through the foolishness of preaching.

Pascal says that we know God, ourselves, life and death only through Jesus Christ. Without Jesus Christ, and the Scripture that centres on him, people know nothing clearly and see only darkness and confusion about God and about their own nature.

Knowing God without Jesus Christ is both impossible and useless. The fragment breaks off, but it adds a Latin saying that the better a person is, the worse he becomes if he claims that goodness as his own.

The speaker says he loves poverty because Christ loved it, and he loves riches because they let him help the poor. He keeps faith with everyone, does not repay wrong with evil, and wants those who wrong him to have a life like his, free of harm or favour from others. He tries to be just, honest and faithful, with special tenderness toward those God has bound him to closely.

Pascal says that whether or not anyone is watching, he does everything as if before God, to whom he has dedicated his actions. He thanks his Redeemer for changing him from a weak, sinful man into one free of those faults, through God's grace, and he credits himself only with misery and error.

Pascal's point is that Jesus's burial was a hidden event, cared for only by the saints, and that his tomb, not the cross, is where he begins a new life. The tomb is the final mystery of the Passion and Redemption. It is also the only place where his enemies stopped persecuting him.

Pascal describes Jesus in his agony in the garden before his arrest. He suffers not only from other people's cruelty but from a distress he brings on himself, which Pascal says only an all-powerful being could bear. Jesus asks his three closest friends to stay awake with him, but they fall asleep, so he is left alone to face God's wrath.

Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, suffers alone. No human knows of his suffering, only Heaven does. Pascal says Jesus complained only once, and then said his soul was sorrowful to the point of death, seeking human companionship and comfort.

Jesus, in the garden, finds his disciples asleep when they should be watching with him. He is troubled not for his own sake but because they are in danger. He warns them for their own good, gently, even though they have failed him, and reminds them that the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.

Pascal presents Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane as acting with care for others even when they fail him. Jesus lets his sleeping disciples rest, prays with submission to his Father's will, and goes willingly toward death. The passage says that his actions during their sleep brought about their salvation.

Pascal reflects on Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane, before his arrest. Jesus accepts God's will calmly, even toward Judas, and separates himself from his disciples to face his suffering. Believers are urged to copy this, praying longer and asking God to free them from their sins, not to leave them undisturbed in them.

God is presented as directing events and setting masters over people, so obeying them willingly is necessary. Guessing in advance how one would act is treated as testing God, because God will act in a person when the moment comes.

God speaks to the reader in this passage. He says that the reader's conversion, or turning to God, is his own work, so the reader should pray with trust. God is present through Scripture, the Church, inspiration, priests and prayer. He heals the soul now, while bodily sickness and chains remain for a time.

Pascal's passage is a dialogue in which God speaks to a sinner. God says he has suffered and died for the person more than any friend would, and that his love continues now. When God says that knowing one's sins would make a person despair, the speaker agrees he will despair. God replies that he can heal those sins, and that his words are a sign he will do so.

This is a prayer-like dialogue in which God speaks and the speaker answers. God tells the speaker that knowing one's sins brings forgiveness, and that repentance is needed for hidden sins too. The speaker gives himself to God, admits his own pride, curiosity and lust, and says he has no relation to God on his own, but that Christ was made sin for him.

Pascal's passage says that Christ has already suffered the blows meant for humans, and that a believer should join his own suffering to Christ's, trusting that Christ will save him by saving himself. It adds that people make their own gods by calling things good or bad, and urges treating small acts as great because Christ lives within them.
God is all-powerful, so for him the greatest works are as easy as small ones. Pascal's point is that God does great things as though they were little and easy, because of his omnipotence.

Pascal says that Jesus let people touch his wounds only after the resurrection, citing the words "Noli me tangere" ("Do not touch me"). He adds that we should join ourselves only to his sufferings. Jesus gave himself in the Last Supper as one about to die, to the disciples at Emmaus as risen, and to the Church as ascended into heaven.

God speaks to the reader here and says: do not measure yourself against other people, but against God. If you compare yourself to someone who lacks God, you compare yourself to something wrong; if you compare yourself to God in you, you compare God to himself. God says he guides the reader directly, even through a spiritual director's prayers.

What we call virtue is often just a collection of different actions and interests, arranged by luck or by our own effort. Men are not always brave because of courage, nor women chaste because of purity.
Self-love, meaning a person's love of himself, is the strongest flatterer there is. It praises a person more than any outside voice could.
Despite all that has been discovered about self-love, much of it is still unknown. The maxim says that people have not yet mapped the full extent of this hidden part of human nature.
Self-love is cleverer than even the shrewdest person. The saying means that a person's love of themselves can deceive them more skillfully than any other trickster could deceive them.
Our passions last as long as they last, and we cannot control how long they continue, just as we cannot control how long we live.
Strong emotion often makes a clever person act foolishly, and it can sometimes make a foolish person act wisely.

Politicians often explain dazzling public deeds as the result of grand plans, but these deeds usually come from temperament and passion instead. As an example, the war between Augustus and Antony, usually blamed on a wish to rule the world, was probably caused by jealousy.

Strong feelings are the only lawyers that always win people over. They work like a natural skill with fixed rules that never fail. So a plain person who feels strongly will persuade more than a gifted speaker who feels nothing.
The passions are unfair and self-serving, so following them is risky. We should not trust them, even when they seem most reliable.
The heart is always producing new passions, so when one passion is destroyed, it usually becomes the starting point for another.

Strong feelings often turn into their opposites. A greedy person may become wasteful, and a wasteful person may become greedy. Likewise, people are sometimes stubborn out of weakness and bold out of fear.
People may try hard to hide their desires behind a show of religious devotion or good reputation. Even so, those desires can still be seen through the cover.

People take criticism of their tastes harder than criticism of their opinions. Self-love, meaning vanity or pride in oneself, resists being told that what one likes is poor more than being told that what one thinks is wrong.

People tend to forget both kind acts and wrongs. They often come to resent those who helped them and stop resenting those who harmed them. Feeling bound to repay a favour or take revenge seems to them like a kind of slavery they refuse to accept.
Rulers' mercy is often not true kindness. It is usually a calculated move to win the people's loyalty.
Mercy that people present as a virtue, the maxim says, usually comes from vanity, sometimes from laziness, often from fear, and most often from all three together.
People who are happy tend to be moderate because good fortune gives them a calm temper. Their restraint comes from their luck, not from any effort of their own.

Moderation in success, according to this maxim, comes from fear of arousing envy and scorn in people who would judge the successful as proud or foolish. It is really a show of mental strength, meant to make a person look greater than his good fortune alone makes him.
We all have enough strength to bear the misfortunes of others. The maxim states this as a general truth about human ability.
Wise people who seem steady and unmoved are, in this view, not free of strong feelings. Their calm is a skill at hiding the turmoil inside them.
Condemned prisoners sometimes pretend to be brave and to scorn death. This pretence is really a cover for their fear of facing it, just as a blindfold hides their eyes from what is about to happen.
Philosophy can easily overcome troubles that are past or still to come. It fails when the trouble is happening now.
Few people truly understand death; most simply endure it, out of resolve, thoughtlessness, or habit. Most men die only because they do not know how to avoid dying.
Great men who are crushed by long misfortune show that their strength came from ambition rather than from their own mind. Once that ambition fails, they are no different from ordinary people.
It takes more strength of character to cope with good luck than with bad. Good fortune tests a person's virtues in a way that misfortune does not.
It is hard to look straight at the sun or at death. Just as the eyes close or blink when faced with bright sunlight, people turn away from thoughts of death.
People can be proud even of their worst passions, but envy is so timid and ashamed that nobody admits to having it.
Jealousy is a kind of fair feeling, because it tries to keep hold of something good that we have or think we have. Envy, by contrast, is a rage that cannot bear to see other people happy.
Our good qualities bring more persecution and hatred upon us than our wrongdoing does. People tend to be harsher toward those who stand out for their virtues than toward those who do wrong.

We often claim something cannot be done when the real problem is that we do not really want to do it. The maxim says we have more ability than desire, and that calling things impossible is often just a way of giving ourselves an excuse.
People enjoy pointing out other people's faults because they have faults of their own. The maxim suggests that if we were free of flaws, we would find less pleasure in criticising others.
Jealousy depends on uncertainty. Once a jealous person becomes sure that the suspected betrayal is real, the jealousy either ends or turns into rage.
Pride does not lose anything when a person gives up vanity. It gets something back in return, so it stays whole even after vanity is dropped.
If we were not proud ourselves, we would not resent the pride of other people. The complaint about others' pride comes from our own pride.
Everyone has the same amount of pride, according to this maxim. People differ only in how they show it.

Nature, the passage suggests, has given us pride so that we are spared the pain of seeing our own flaws. The idea is that pride protects us from knowing our imperfections, much as the body's organs are arranged for our well-being.
When we scold people for their faults, pride plays a bigger role than kindness. We rebuke them less to fix their behaviour than to show that we ourselves have none of those faults.

We make promises based on what we hope will happen, but we keep them based on what we fear will happen if we don't. Hope makes us eager to commit, while fear is what actually drives us to follow through.
Self-interest can imitate any manner of speaking and any role, including the appearance of being unselfish. What looks like generosity may be a disguise for seeking one's own advantage.
Self-interest affects people in two opposite ways. For some it blinds them, so they cannot see clearly, while for others it sharpens their sight and helps them see what they want to see.
People who concentrate too hard on small matters often lose the ability to handle big ones.
Our power to act is weaker than our power to reason. We can see what is sensible, but we often lack the strength to carry it out.
A person often thinks he is in control of his actions when his feelings are actually steering him. While his reason aims at one goal, his heart secretly pulls him toward another.

La Rochefoucauld says that "strength of mind" and "weakness of mind" are the wrong names for these qualities. In his view, they are really just the way our physical bodily organs happen to be arranged, whether well or badly.
Our moods change even more unpredictably than luck does. The saying claims that a person's own temper is less steady than fortune, which is itself thought of as random.
Philosophers' love of life or their calm indifference to it is just a way their self-love expresses itself. Such tastes cannot be argued about, any more than a preference in food or colours.
Our moods and disposition determine how much we value whatever good luck brings us. In other words, the same gift is worth more or less depending on the person's temperament.
Happiness comes from what a person enjoys, not from the objects themselves. We are happy when we have what we ourselves like, not when we have what other people like.
We tend to think our happiness or misery is greater than it really is. The maxim says that our feelings are usually not as extreme as we imagine them to be.
People who believe they deserve praise convince themselves that suffering brings them honour. They do this to show others, and themselves, that they are worthy to be targets of bad luck.
Nothing lowers our satisfaction with ourselves more than noticing that we reject at one time what we approve of at another.
Although people's fortunes may seem very different, the passage says that good and bad things balance out, so that in the end they are equal.
Even when nature gives a person great gifts, those gifts alone do not make a hero. Luck, or fortune, also has to play its part.

Philosophers who scorned wealth, the passage says, did so secretly out of resentment. Unable to win respect through riches, they despised riches as a way of protecting their pride and gaining standing by another route.

Hatred of those who are favoured by a powerful person is really a wish to be favoured oneself. Those who lack the favour comfort themselves by looking down on the favourites and withholding their respect, since they cannot take away the admiration others give them.
People try to look secure and settled in the world in order to become so. Their outward show of stability is meant to bring about the real thing.
People like to credit their great achievements to careful planning, but such actions usually come from chance rather than from a grand plan.
Many of our actions seem to owe much of the praise or blame they receive to lucky or unlucky stars. Astrology is the old belief behind this idea.

Clever people can gain something from even the worst accidents, while foolish people can make harm out of even the luckiest ones. Good fortune and bad fortune, in this view, depend less on events themselves than on the person who meets them.
Luck makes everything work out in favor of the people she favors. Those who are lucky find that even events which might seem harmful end up helping them.
Whether people are happy or unhappy depends just as much on their temperament, or character, as on their circumstances or wealth. The passage gives equal weight to the two.
Sincerity means being open and honest in one's heart. The writer says few people really have it. What is usually seen instead is a clever pretence, meant to gain other people's trust.
Refusing to lie often hides a wish to make our words seem believable and important, and to give our talk a kind of sacred dignity.
Fake truths, or false imitations of truth, cause more harm in the world than real truth does good. The saying claims that the harm done by counterfeit truth outweighs the good done by truth itself.
Prudence, or careful good sense, is praised more than almost anything else. Yet it cannot guarantee even the smallest outcome. The point is that careful planning does not make results certain.

A clever person should arrange his interests so that each one is handled in its proper order. Greed often pushes us to chase many things at once, so that while we eagerly pursue the smallest, we lose the largest.

Good sense, or sound judgment, stands to the mind as grace, or natural ease and charm, stands to the body. The comparison suggests that good sense gives the mind the same kind of pleasing, effortless quality that grace gives a person's bodily movements.

Love is hard to define. La Rochefoucauld says it is a wish to rule in the soul, a sympathy in the mind, and a hidden, gentle wish to possess the loved one in the body, with many further mysteries beyond these.
Pure love, free of our other passions, may exist, according to this maxim. If it does, it is hidden deep in the heart, so that even the person who has it does not know it is there.
Love cannot be hidden for long when it is really there, and it cannot be faked when it is absent. Pretending to love does not work, and hiding real love does not last.

Most people, once they have stopped loving someone, feel embarrassed that the other person still loves them. The passage suggests that being loved after one's own love has ended is something few people would want to admit to.
Judged by most of its results, love looks more like hatred than like friendship. The point is that love's usual effects are closer to those of hatred than to those of friendship.
It is easy to find women who have never had a love affair, but hard to find one who has had only one. The point is that once a woman has begun an affair, she usually has several.

Love is one thing in its true form, but it appears in countless imitations that look like it. The maxim says that the many different kinds of love people experience are only copies of a single real love.
Love and fire both need constant movement to keep going, the maxim says. Once love stops hoping or fearing, and fire stops moving, each dies out.
Real love is as rare as real ghosts: everyone talks about it, but few have actually seen it.

Many dealings and relationships are called love, yet love has no more to do with them than the Doge, the ruler of Venice, has to do with every small matter that happens in the city. The maxim says that love is blamed or credited for much that it does not actually cause.

Most people's love of justice is really just a fear of being treated unjustly themselves. In other words, they want fair treatment mainly to protect themselves, not out of concern for justice as such.
A person who does not trust their own judgment should keep quiet. Speaking without care can lead them to reveal or commit things they might regret, so silence is the safest choice.

Our friendships often change because we can easily judge a person's intelligence, but it is hard to know the true character of their soul. We form opinions from what we see of their wit and mind, and those opinions may not hold once their deeper qualities show.
We can only love what suits us, and we only follow our own taste when we put our friends before ourselves. Yet this preference is the only thing that makes friendship genuine and complete.
Making peace with enemies, according to this maxim, is not really about forgiveness or goodwill. It comes from wanting to improve one's situation, being tired of fighting, or fearing some bad event.
Friendship, as people call it, is really just a business arrangement. Two people share interests and trade favours, and each one's self-interest hopes to gain something from the deal.
The maxim says that it is more shameful to mistrust a friend than to be deceived by one.

We often convince ourselves that we love powerful people, but self-interest is what really creates the friendship. We give our affection not for the good we do others, but for the good we hope to get back.
When we distrust someone, we excuse their lying to us. The maxim suggests that our suspicion gives the other person a reason to deceive, so we share the blame for the deceit.
People could not stay together in society for long if they did not fool one another. The saying claims that social life depends on each person being deceived by others.
Self-love makes us value our friends' good qualities more or less, depending on how pleased we are with them. We judge their worth by how they treat us.

People are quick to say their memory is poor when they forget something, but almost no one admits their judgment is weak. The saying suggests that people accept blame for forgetting more easily than for making bad decisions.

In everyday dealings with others, people tend to be liked more for their flaws than for their virtues. The saying claims that our faults often make us more agreeable to others than our good qualities do.
Very great ambition looks least like ambition when its goal is completely out of reach. Because the goal cannot be won, the ambitious person seems to give up wanting it.

Waking a person who wrongly thinks highly of his own worth does him harm. The author compares this to the Athenian madman who was content believing every ship in the harbour was his, and who was made unhappy by learning the truth.
Old people like to give good advice because they can no longer set bad examples themselves. Giving advice makes up for lost chances to misbehave.
A famous name does not raise people who lack the ability to live up to it. Instead, it lowers them.
Real excellence is shown when even those who envy it most are forced to praise it. Their praise, given against their will, is the proof of its worth.

A person who fails to show thanks may be ungrateful, but the blame often lies less with him than with the one who did the favour. The benefactor, the giver of help, is sometimes the one more at fault.

Judgment and mind are not two separate things, the passage says. Judgment is simply how far the mind's light reaches. Whatever we credit to good judgment is really the mind's light reaching deeper and seeing more.

People are happy to be praised for their kindness or feeling, but almost no one dares to claim that they are clever or have good judgment. The saying suggests that people are more confident about their good hearts than about their minds.
Good manners of the mind, according to this maxim, mean having thoughts that are pure and delicate. The saying links politeness with what a person thinks, not only with how they speak or act.
Being charming in conversation means saying empty or meaningless things in a pleasant way. The maxim says that this skill is what "gallantry of mind" consists of.
Thoughts often come to us in a finished form, more complete than we could later produce with a great deal of effort.

A person may understand their own thoughts well and still not understand their own feelings. Clear reasoning about oneself does not automatically bring knowledge of one's heart, meaning one's emotions and desires.
Some people and things can only be judged fairly when seen up close, while others can only be judged fairly from far away. Each has its own proper distance for clear judgment.
A person who gains understanding only by chance is not truly rational, according to this maxim. Real reason belongs to someone who understands, separates ideas, and tests them.
To understand something properly, we would need to know all its details. Since those details are almost endless, our knowledge always stays shallow and incomplete.
Claiming that one never flirts is itself a form of flirtation. The passage says this is one way people flirt.
A person's reason cannot keep up a pretence of feeling for long. In other words, a show of emotion that comes from thinking rather than from the heart will not last.
Young people often change what they like because their blood runs hot, while older people keep their likes out of habit.
People give advice very freely. The maxim says that advice is handed out more lavishly than anything else. "Profusely" means in great abundance.
The more intensely a person loves a woman, the more likely they are to come to hate her. The maxim states this as a general truth about love.

Faults of character, like wrinkles or marks on the face, become more noticeable as a person gets older. The comparison is between flaws of the mind and flaws of the face, both of which grow stronger with age.
Marriages can be good, in the sense of sound or worthy, but none of them is pleasant. The maxim says that a marriage may be good without being enjoyable.
We are upset when enemies deceive us or friends betray us, but we often accept being deceived and misled by ourselves in the same way.
A person can fool themselves without meaning to just as easily as they can fool other people. The maxim treats self-deception as being as simple as deceiving others.

Asking for advice is rarely sincere. The person asking appears to respect his friend's opinion, but really wants the friend to agree with him and share the blame for what he does. The person giving advice seems eager and unselfish, but usually acts for his own gain or reputation.
The subtlest move is to pretend not to see a trap we know has been laid for us. People are most easily fooled when they are themselves trying to fool others.
Deciding never to deceive others can leave a person open to being deceived by them. The maxim suggests that an honest person, trusting others and not expecting lies, is easier to fool.
People who keep pretending to others end up losing track of who they really are. After so much habitual disguise, they no longer see their own true selves.
People often betray others because they are weak, not because they have planned to do so for a set purpose. The betrayal comes from lack of firmness rather than from a settled intention.
People sometimes do good deeds so that they can then do wrong without being punished or blamed. The good act works as cover, buying freedom to behave badly later.

When we overcome our passions, the reason is usually that the passions have grown weak, not that we have become strong. The credit for self-control belongs more to the passions' weakness than to our own power.

We would enjoy ourselves very little if we never deceived ourselves with flattering beliefs about who we are. Much of our pleasure, the maxim suggests, comes from the good opinion we form of ourselves.
Those who are most deceitful often spend their time condemning deceit. They do this so that, when a big chance comes, they can use deception to advance some important aim of their own.
Using cunning every day shows a small mind, the maxim says. People who use it to guard themselves in one way usually leave themselves exposed to attack in another.
Cleverness and betrayal come from a lack of ability. People who cannot succeed openly or by their own strength turn to trickery and deceit.
You are most easily fooled when you believe you know more than other people. The passage says that thinking yourself wiser than others is the surest way to be misled.

Excessive cleverness is only a false kind of refinement, while true refinement is the most solid form of cleverness. The maxim sets a showy, over-subtle wit against a genuine, sound sense of what is fitting.
Sometimes a person has to pretend to be foolish in order to avoid being tricked by clever, crafty people. Acting unaware can protect a person from those who want to deceive them.
Weakness of character, in this maxim, is the one flaw a person cannot get rid of. Every other fault can be corrected, but weakness cannot.

In this maxim, the writer says that the smallest mistake a woman can make, when she gives herself completely to love, is the act of loving itself. The point is that loving is seen as the least of her failings, while the other faults are thought to be larger.
It is easier to be wise for other people than for oneself. Judging others' affairs is simpler than managing one's own.
Good examples are only useful when they show how foolish bad models are. In other words, a good example works by exposing the folly of the bad one it is set against, not by simply being copied.
People look most foolish not because of the habits they really have, but because of the habits they pretend to have.
People can change their opinions or behaviour so much that they become more unlike themselves than they are unlike other people.
Some people would never have fallen in love at all if they had never heard the idea of love talked about. The thought of love, learned from others, is what started their feelings.
People tend to talk a lot when they are driven by vanity, the wish to be admired. Without that motive, they say little.
People would rather speak badly of themselves than not speak at all. Even self-criticism is preferred to silence, because a person wants to be talking.

Few people talk well because they care more about what they want to say than about answering what others say. Even polite people often seem to listen while their minds have already moved on to their own remarks. The passage holds that listening well and answering well are among the greatest charms in conversation.
A clever person would often be stuck for something to do or say without the company of fools. The maxim suggests that wit needs foolish people around it to show itself.
People often claim they are never bored, yet they are so full of themselves that they do not notice how often they bore other people.
Great thinkers say much in few words, while small minds use many words and still say nothing. The saying compares brevity with real meaning, and wordiness with emptiness.
We often praise others more for how we feel about ourselves than for what they actually deserve. When we praise them, we usually hope they will praise us in return.

We rarely praise others without a hidden reason, and praise is a subtle kind of flattery. It pleases both sides in different ways: the person praised feels it is earned, while the person praising shows off his fairness and judgment.
Sometimes people choose praise that is meant to hurt. The praise seems kind, but it makes the person praised look bad, so it reveals faults that the speaker could not have pointed out directly.
Few people are wise enough to prefer criticism that helps them over praise that does them harm. Praise can hide a danger, while honest blame can do good.
Some criticisms are really a form of praise, and some compliments are really a form of criticism. The meaning of a remark can be the opposite of what its words seem to say.
Someone who says they do not want praise is really hoping to be praised for that modesty. Turning down praise is thus a second wish for praise, not a true lack of desire for it.
Wanting to be praised makes people improve their good qualities. Praise for cleverness, bravery, or good looks also makes those qualities grow stronger.
It is easier to rule other people than to avoid being ruled yourself. The saying suggests that people who want to control others often do so because they cannot refuse control from someone else.

If we were honest with ourselves, we would not be hurt by other people's praise. Flattery works only because we already believe the good things said about us, so it has no power over a person who does not deceive himself.
Talent and ability come from birth, but luck decides whether they are put to use. A person may have real worth, yet success depends on chance opportunities to show it.
Sometimes luck, or chance, changes a person for the better where careful thinking has failed. The idea is that good or bad fortune can free us from flaws that our own reason could not correct.
Some people displease others even when they are skilled, while others charm them even though they have faults. The maxim contrasts talent that repels with flaws that attract.
Some people succeed only because they say and do foolish things at the right moment. If they change their behaviour, they spoil everything they have achieved.
A famous person's reputation should be judged by the methods they used to win it. How a person became famous matters more than the fame itself.
Flattery is like counterfeit money: it is worthless, and it is accepted only because we are vain. Our own pride is what makes us take praise that is false and treat it as valuable.
Having great qualities is not sufficient on its own. A person must also know how to use them well.
An action can look brilliant, but it counts as great only if it comes from a great motive. The reason behind the act matters more than how impressive the act looks.
To judge what effects our actions will have, our deeds and our thoughts should fit together. Action and thought must agree if we want to be able to predict the results of what we do.
Skill in making the most of ordinary talents earns praise, and it often brings more fame than true brilliance does.
Many activities that look foolish from outside have hidden reasons that are very sensible and important. The maxim says appearances can hide good sense behind them.

It is easier to look qualified for a job we do not have than for one we already hold. Once someone holds a post, others can see how well they actually do it, while a post not yet held lets people only imagine what they could do.

Skill earns respect from people of real worth, while luck earns respect from the crowd. The saying contrasts the two sources of success: talent is recognised by the wise, and good fortune impresses the masses.
People are more often rewarded for seeming to have merit than for actually having it. The saying claims that public recognition goes more to appearance than to real worth.
Greed is the opposite of generosity more than it is of thrift. The maxim says a miser is further from careful saving than from giving freely, since "economy" here means careful management of money.
Hope is often false, yet it still leads people pleasantly through their whole life. Even though it deceives us, it keeps us moving forward with good feeling until death.

Laziness and fear are what usually keep people doing their duty, yet it is their virtue that gets the credit. The saying suggests that people are praised for goodness when the real causes are idleness and fear.

When someone behaves well and honestly, it is hard to tell whether this comes from real moral character or from cleverness at seeming good. The saying suggests that good conduct can look the same whatever its cause.

Virtues lose their identity when they are absorbed into self-interest, just as rivers disappear into the sea. The maxim says that good qualities end up serving the self and cease to be what they were.
Looking closely at the many results of indifference shows that people fail more often in their duties than in their own interests.
Curiosity can come from two sources. One is self-interest, which makes us want to learn anything that could benefit us. The other is pride, which makes us want to know what other people do not know.
It is better to train the mind to endure the troubles we already have than to worry about troubles that might come later.
Constancy in love, the passage says, is really a kind of inconstancy. The heart keeps moving from one quality of the loved person to another. Constancy is just this movement held within one person.

Love can stay faithful for two reasons, according to this maxim. One is that the lover keeps finding new things in the beloved to love. The other is that the lover considers constancy a matter of personal honour.
Steadfastness is neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy, because it is simply the continuing of likes and feelings that a person cannot make or end by choice.
We take up new studies less from boredom with old ones or a wish for change than from wanting admiration from those who know more than we do. We also hope to gain an edge over those who know less.
People sometimes blame their friends for being careless or unserious, so that they can excuse their own carelessness ahead of time.
People often feel sorry for their wrongdoing less because they regret the harm they caused than because they fear what might now happen to them as a result.

Inconstancy, or changing one's mind, has two sources. One comes from lightness or weakness of mind, which makes a person accept whatever opinion they hear. The other, which is more forgivable, comes from having too much material to weigh at once.
Vices are mixed into virtues the way poison is mixed into medicine. Prudence, or good judgment, combines the two so that they become useful for dealing with life's troubles.
La Rochefoucauld says that the worst troubles people suffer are the ones they bring on themselves through their own wrongdoing. He admits this, he says, to make virtue look good.
We confess our faults so that our honesty will make up for the harm our wrongs have done to how others see us. The admission is meant to win back their good opinion.
People can be admired as heroes for doing evil as well as for doing good. The maxim treats both kinds of hero as real, placing bad and good deeds side by side under the same name.
We do not look down on everyone with faults, but we do look down on everyone who lacks good qualities. In other words, having vices does not make people despised, while simply lacking virtue does.

The maxim says that the word "virtue" helps our self-interest just as much as the word "vice" does. People can use a good reputation, claimed through the language of virtue, to gain advantage, in the same way that a bad label can be used to hide or serve selfish ends.
The mind can be ill just as the body can, and it is no safer. Even when the passions seem to be far away, a person is still at risk of catching them, just as a healthy person can still fall sick.
According to this maxim, a person's basic virtues and vices seem to be set by nature from the moment of birth. The idea is that each person's moral limits are already fixed, not chosen.
Our vices are like innkeepers we stay with one after another during life. The writer doubts that, if we could live the same road again, our experience would lead us to avoid them.
We often believe we have overcome a fault when it is really the fault that has left us. We then take credit for a change we did not make.
Mental illnesses can return after seeming to be over, just as bodily illnesses do. So what looks like a cure is often only a pause in the illness, or the illness changing into another form.
Faults of the mind are compared to wounds of the body. However hard a person works to cure them, they leave marks behind, and they can open again.
We often fail to give up a vice because we have so many of them. Having many faults makes it hard to drop any single one.
People tend to forget their own faults when no one else knows about them. A fault that is hidden from others is easily let go of in our own memory.
Some people are so good that we would never think them capable of wrongdoing unless we saw it ourselves. Few people, though, are so good that we would be surprised to find them doing wrong.

People often inflate the reputation of one man so that they can belittle another. The praise given to Prince Condé and Marshal Turenne, the maxim says, would be much smaller if people were not also trying to criticise them both.
Wanting to seem clever often stops a person from actually being clever. The effort to impress gets in the way of real understanding.
Good qualities would not get very far without pride helping them along. The maxim says that vanity, or the wish to be seen and admired, often accompanies virtue and pushes it forward.
A person who believes he can please everyone is badly mistaken. A person who believes everyone can be pleased with him is more mistaken still.
Men who only seem honest hide their faults, both from themselves and from others. Truly honest men know their faults fully and admit them openly.
A person is truly wise when nothing irritates or annoys them. The maxim says that real wisdom means staying calm and not being bothered by things that would upset others.
A woman's coldness, or lack of warmth toward others, is described as something that adds weight to her beauty. It both balances her looks and acts as a burden alongside them.
Many women who seem virtuous are really driven by a wish for a good reputation and a quiet, untroubled life. The maxim suggests that their virtue comes from these motives rather than from principle.
A truly good man, in this view, is one who always wants his conduct to be open to the judgment of good people. He is not troubled by their scrutiny but welcomes it.
Folly stays with a person through every stage of life. Someone who seems wise has only a folly that suits his age and wealth.
Some foolish people are clever enough to know they are foolish, and they use that knowledge to their advantage. The maxim suggests that folly can be put to use as a skill.
A person who never does foolish things may still be less wise than he believes. Living without folly does not prove that someone has wisdom.
As people age, they gain wisdom but also grow more foolish. The maxim presents both changes as happening together, not as one replacing the other.
Some people are compared to farces: they are praised only for a short time, even though they are foolish and unpleasant. The praise does not last.
Many people judge others only by whether they succeed or by their luck. The meaning is that outcomes, rather than a person's true worth, are what usually count in such judgments.

La Rochefoucauld says that the bravery people praise is often driven by other motives. These include love of glory, fear of shame, greed for wealth, the wish for a comfortable life, and the wish to belittle others.
Bravery in ordinary soldiers is described as a risky way of making a living. The point is that a common soldier's courage is less a noble choice than a dangerous job he has to do to get paid.

Perfect bravery and complete cowardice are both rare. Most people lie somewhere between them, and their courage varies: some are brave at the start of a fight but tire later, some act only to keep their reputation, and some freeze or charge out of fear of being seen to run.

Different people are brave in different ways: some can take a sword cut but not a bullet, and others the reverse. The passage says that night hides brave or cowardly acts, so men often hold back. It concludes that fear of death always reduces courage to some degree.
Real courage means doing without an audience the same brave acts one would perform in front of everyone. The person acts the same whether or not others are watching.

Intrepidity, or fearlessness, is a great inner strength. It lifts a person above the disturbance that great danger would otherwise cause. Because of it, heroes stay calm and keep their judgment and freedom even in the most shocking and frightening events.
Vice pretends to be virtuous. Hypocrisy is the way bad behaviour shows respect for goodness, by putting on a show of being good.
Most men risk their lives in battle only as much as needed to keep their reputation for courage. Few go further, and only do so when it is needed to help their plan succeed.
Pride, shame, and above all natural temperament often make men brave and women chaste. The maxim says these motives, not virtue as such, often produce such behaviour.
Brave men want glory more than they want to keep their lives. Because of this, they are more skilful at avoiding death than thieves and cheats are at keeping hold of their money.

Few people, when old age first begins to approach, fail to show where their body or their mind is starting to decline. The maxim says that almost everyone reveals their physical or mental weakening as they grow older.

Gratitude is compared to a merchant's good faith, which keeps trade running. The point is that people repay kindness not because it is right to do so, but because doing so makes it easier to get help again later.

Paying back a debt of gratitude does not prove that a person is truly grateful. Someone can repay what they owe while still feeling no real thankfulness. The maxim warns against believing that repayment alone shows gratitude.

People often fail to reckon gratitude correctly because the giver and the receiver each judge the value of the favour differently. Each one's pride makes the benefit seem larger or smaller than the other sees it.
Rushing to repay a debt or obligation, too eagerly, is a form of ingratitude. The eagerness to be free of the obligation shows that the favour is no longer wanted or valued.
People who have good luck are poor at fixing their own mistakes. Because things go well for them even when they act badly or foolishly, they assume they must be right.

Pride will not admit a debt to anyone, and self-love will not pay one off. The saying means that people who think highly of themselves refuse to feel they owe others anything, and so they do not repay what they owe.
A kindness someone has done for us should make us forgive the harm they later do us. In other words, past good deeds are a reason to overlook present wrongs.

Example spreads more easily than anything else, and every great good or evil act tends to be copied. We copy good acts out of rivalry, and bad acts out of our hidden inclination to wrong, which shame keeps locked up until someone else's example frees it.
It is foolish to want only to be wise. The maxim suggests that a person who seeks wisdom alone, and nothing else, has made a serious mistake.

Whatever reason we give for our sorrows, the real cause is always self-interest or vanity. We may claim to grieve for one thing, but according to this maxim, our own gain or pride is what truly stirs the pain.

In grief, people often claim to mourn a loved one while really pitying themselves. They regret losing the dead person's good opinion, comfort, or standing. So the tears seem to be for the dead, but they are really for the mourner's own losses.

Some people keep up a show of grief long after their real sorrow has faded with time. They want to be seen as having a noble, lasting mourning. They keep weeping, sighing and wearing a solemn face, and act as if their grief will last their whole life.

Ambitious women, the passage says, show deep grief to win fame, since other paths to glory are closed to them. Other tears come from small causes and stop just as quickly. People weep to seem tender, to be pitied, or to avoid looking unfeeling for not weeping.

People who strongly reject popular opinions usually do so out of pride rather than lack of knowledge. Such people see that the best positions are already taken by others, and they refuse to come after them, to be last.
We feel comfort over a friend's misfortune when it gives us a chance to show how much we care for them. The friend's trouble is, in a sense, the occasion for our kindness being seen.

Self-love can seem to forget itself when it helps others, as if goodness had fooled it. But the passage says this is only a shorter route to self-love's own goal. Helping others is a way of gaining everyone's favour, like lending at interest while pretending to give.
La Rochefoucauld says that a person deserves praise for being good only if he could have done evil and chose not to. Most goodness, he claims, is really laziness or a lack of will to do wrong.
Doing harm to most people carries less risk than doing them too much good. Great kindnesses can leave people feeling burdened or resentful toward the one who gave them.

Nothing pleases our pride more than being trusted by important people, because we take it as proof of our own merit. We forget that such trust often comes from the other person's vanity or from an inability to keep a secret.

Conformity, or good proportion of looks, is different from beauty. It is a kind of balance that follows no fixed rules. It comes from a hidden agreement between a person's features and between those features and the person's colouring and general appearance.
Flirtation, the maxim claims, is a basic part of women's nature. Not every woman acts on it, because some are held back by fear and others by good sense.
People often bore others while believing they are not boring them at all. The speaker's confidence that they are interesting does not match how the listener feels.
Few things are truly impossible in themselves. People more often fail because they do not put in the steady effort needed to succeed than because they lack the means.
Real skill at governing or leading lies in understanding how much things are really worth. The maxim suggests that a capable person is one who judges correctly what matters and what does not.
Skill is greatest when it is hidden. Someone who can hide how clever or capable they are shows a real talent of its own.
Some acts that look generous are really ambition in disguise. The person gives up small gains only to pursue bigger rewards.
Most men's loyalty, according to this maxim, is not real devotion. Self-love invents it to gain trust, which lifts a man above others and makes him the keeper of important secrets.
A speaker's voice, eyes and manner can be as persuasive as the words he chooses. In other words, how something is delivered counts for as much as what is said.
Good speaking means saying what is needed, and leaving out the rest of what could be said. The point is about choosing what to say, not about saying as much as possible.
Some people look better because of their faults, while others look worse because of their virtues. The same trait can suit one person and spoil another.
People change what they like or enjoy far more often than they change their basic drives or leanings. Tastes shift easily, but deep inclinations rarely do.
Self-interest is the motive behind many different virtues and vices. A person's pursuit of their own advantage can produce both good and bad conduct.
Humility is often a pretended submission, used to push others aside and take their place. Pride lowers itself in order to rise, and it disguises itself best when it appears as humility.

Every feeling shows itself through a certain tone of voice, gestures and expression. The quality of this combined display, whether good or bad, pleasant or unpleasant, is what makes a person likeable or off-putting to others.
People in every walk of life put on a role and an outward manner so that they appear to be what they want to be. For this reason, the author says, the whole world is made up of actors.
Seriousness of bearing is a deliberate outward manner of the body, used to hide a lack of intelligence. The maxim suggests that a grave, dignified look may stand in for real understanding.
Good taste comes more from sound judgment than from cleverness or quick wit. The maxim sets the two against each other and gives judgment the larger share.
Love's pleasure lies mainly in the act of loving itself. People feel happier from the passion they have for someone than from the passion that person feels for them.
Politeness, according to this maxim, is not really kindness toward others. It is a wish to be treated politely in return and to be thought well-mannered.
Ordinary schooling, according to this maxim, teaches young people to love themselves in a new way. The "second self-love" is a second layer of self-regard, not a replacement for the first.
In this maxim, love is described as the passion in which a person's self-love is strongest. People are more willing to disturb the peace of the person they love than to give up their own peace.
Generosity is often just pride in giving. The giver enjoys the sense of their own generosity more than they care about the gift itself.
Pity, according to this maxim, is really self-interest. We feel for others because we see our own possible misfortunes in theirs. Helping them is a way of securing help for ourselves later.
A person with a limited outlook tends to be stubborn, and people find it hard to believe things they have not seen for themselves.

Idleness, or laziness, is said to be stronger than even the fiercest passions such as ambition and love. Without much noise it takes control of our plans and actions, slowly wearing away both our passions and our virtues.

Quickly believing something bad about someone, without checking the facts, comes from pride and laziness. People want to name a guilty person, but they do not want the effort of looking closely at what actually happened.

We assume judges act from the worst motives, yet we still want our reputation to depend on the verdicts of people who, because of jealousy, distraction or poor judgment, are against us. We risk our peace and our lives just to win their approval.
A person cannot know the full extent of the harm he causes. Nobody is clever enough to see all the wrong he does.

Young age is like being constantly drunk, and it is a fever of the mind. The saying means that the strong feelings of youth cloud judgment and reason, much as intoxication or fever disturbs a person's thinking.

Men who have earned great praise should feel most ashamed when they recall how hard they worked to get it, even by petty means. The shame comes from seeing that their efforts to win applause were small and calculated.
Some people win the world's approval, yet their only real qualities are the vices they use to get ahead in life. Without those vices, they would have no merit at all.
The maxim compares the newness of love to a flower, and love itself to fruit. The shine that new love brings is easily lost, and once gone it does not come back.
Goodness that comes naturally, though it claims to be obvious, is easily overwhelmed by even the slightest self-interest.
Being away from someone weakens minor feelings but strengthens strong ones. The writer compares this to wind, which puts out a candle but makes a fire burn higher.

Women often mistake their feelings: they believe they are in love when they are only flirting. The busy pursuit of an affair, the emotions it stirs, the wish to be loved, and the difficulty of saying no all convince them that flirtation is real passion.

We are often unhappy with people who handle our affairs for us because they usually put the success of the task ahead of our interests. They care more about succeeding at what they have taken on than about the people they act for.
When we claim that our friends care for us more than they really do, we are often less motivated by thankfulness than by wanting to show off our own worth.

We praise newcomers to a field or society, the maxim says, because we resent the people who are already well established there. The praise is driven by envy of those already in place, not by real admiration for the newcomers.
Pride sometimes acts as a check on envy. Although pride can drive a person to great deeds, it can also keep them from feeling jealous of others.
Some lies are disguised so well that they look like the truth. If we were not fooled by them, we would be wrong to trust our own judgment.

Sometimes knowing how to use a good idea or a skill takes as much ability as having come up with it. Giving good advice is one kind of skill, and making use of advice or talent well is another, which can be just as hard.
Some wicked people would do less harm if they had no goodness at all. Their partial goodness makes them more dangerous than they would be if they were fully wicked.
Magnanimity, or greatness of spirit, needs little definition, since its name already explains it. Still, the author says it is pride used wisely, and the noblest way a proud person can accept praise.
Once a person has truly stopped being loved, a person cannot love them again. The feeling does not come back once it has ended.
Having many ideas about one matter does not make a person act more easily. Too many possibilities make us hesitate over each one and stop us from quickly seeing which is best.
Some problems and illnesses get worse when treated at certain times. Real skill lies in knowing when a cure would do harm.
Pretending to be simple and natural is a more subtle kind of deception. Someone who acts artless is, in fact, carefully putting on an act to fool others.
Mistakes come from a person's character as often as from their thinking. A bad mood or a flaw of temperament can lead people to wrong conclusions just as poor reasoning can.
A person's worth or reputation for good qualities, like a harvest, comes and goes at certain times. It is not always present but appears only in its proper season.
A person's temper, like a building, can be viewed from many sides. Some of these views are pleasing and others are not.
Moderation cannot take credit for holding back ambition, because the two never exist together. Moderation is a kind of laziness of the soul, while ambition is the soul's energy and fire.
People like those who admire them, but they do not always like the people they admire themselves.
Some of our wishes stay hidden even from ourselves, and the maxim says this is a good thing. If we knew every wish we had, we would see desires we would rather not admit to.
It is hard to love people we do not respect. It is just as hard to love people we respect far more than we respect ourselves.

Physical moods, or temperaments of the body, follow a shared pattern and quietly shape our choices. They act together, one after another, and without our noticing, they come to drive much of what we do.
Most people's thanks, according to this saying, hides a wish to be given still larger favours in the future. Gratitude is thus described as a hope for more, not as a return for what was received.

Most people willingly repay small debts and thank others for minor kindnesses, but almost no one stays grateful for large favours. The saying claims that great benefits are the ones people most often forget to acknowledge.
Some foolish behaviour spreads from person to person in the same way that illness does. The idea is that people can catch folly from others, just as they catch an infection.
Many people look down on wealth, but only a few know how to give it away well. The point is that scorn for money is common, while the skill of using it generously is rare.
We tend to dare to look past appearances only when the matter is unimportant. When something is trivial, we are willing to question how it seems. When it matters, we accept what looks true.

Any good quality others credit us with is nothing we have not already known about ourselves. In other words, we are not surprised when others praise us, because we already believe we have those qualities.

People can forgive those who bore them, but they cannot forgive those they themselves have bored. The point is that we resent being the cause of another's boredom more than we resent being bored ourselves.

Self-interest is blamed for many of our bad actions, but it often deserves credit for our good ones too. The maxim suggests that the motive we praise in ourselves is sometimes the same selfish motive we condemn.

People seldom seem ungrateful when we are in a position to do them favours. The point is that a person who can give help or gifts is rarely met with ingratitude, because those who receive benefit from them tend to thank them.

Boasting is acceptable when you are alone, but it looks foolish when other people are present. The saying contrasts private self-praise, which it treats as fitting, with the same behaviour in company, which it treats as absurd.
Moderation is praised as a virtue for two reasons. It keeps powerful people from wanting too much, and it helps people with little money or talent accept their lot.
Some people are destined to be foolish. They act foolishly not only because they choose to, but because circumstances force them into it.
Sometimes a person gets into a difficult situation, and the only way out of it needs a bit of foolishness. Getting clear of some troubles requires acting unwisely.
Some people may seem wise only because nobody has examined them closely. Their foolishness stays hidden simply because no one has looked for it carefully.
Lovers never grow bored with each other because they only talk about themselves. The point is that each lover's favourite subject is his or her own self, so conversation between them never runs out.
Our memory keeps even the smallest trivial event, yet fails to keep track of how many times we have told that same story to the same listener.

We enjoy talking about ourselves very much, and this enjoyment is not shared by the people listening to us. The strong pleasure we feel when speaking of ourselves should therefore make us aware that our listeners do not feel it too.
We often fail to open our hearts to friends not because we doubt them, but because we doubt ourselves. We are unsure of what we would reveal about our own feelings and character.
Doing a favour for an ungrateful person is a small misfortune. Accepting a favour from a scoundrel, a dishonest and disreputable man, is much harder to bear.
A fool's foolishness can be cured, but there is no way to correct a stubborn, contrary temper. The saying contrasts ignorance, which can be fixed, with a difficult disposition, which cannot.

If we allow ourselves to keep dwelling on the faults of those who have helped us or whom we love, we will not be able to keep feeling toward them as we should. Constant criticism of our friends and benefactors wears away the proper feelings we owe them.

Praising rulers for virtues they lack is a way of criticizing them while escaping punishment. The praise points out their faults in a form they cannot object to. "With impunity" means without being punished.
People feel nearer to those who hate them than to those who love them more than they wish to be loved. Excessive affection seems to create distance.
Only people who are afraid of being looked down on are truly contemptible. The maxim says that the fear of contempt is itself what makes a person despicable. "Despicable" means deserving scorn.
Our wisdom depends on luck just as much as our wealth and possessions do. Fortune here means chance or fate, the uncontrolled forces that bring good or bad outcomes.

Jealousy, according to this maxim, is driven more by a person's concern for themselves than by real love for the other person. The jealous person mainly cares about their own pride and feelings, not the one they love.

We often find comfort in how small our troubles are, since our reason is not strong enough to console us. In other words, we turn to the feebleness of our misfortunes because reasoning itself cannot calm us.
Being mocked does more harm to a person's reputation than being openly disgraced. Ridicule, in this view, stings more than the dishonour it follows.
We admit small faults so that others will believe we have no serious ones. Confessing minor flaws is a way of hiding larger ones.
Envy cannot be reconciled as easily as hatred. The maxim states that a person who envies is harder to make at peace with than one who hates.
We sometimes think we dislike flattery, when we really dislike only the way it is done. In other words, the objection is to the manner of the praise, not to the praise itself.
Being faithful to a lover is harder when she treats you well than when she treats you badly. The maxim claims that a man finds it easier to stay loyal while he is unhappy in love.
Women are not fully aware of how much they can attract or charm others. The maxim suggests they have more skill at flirting than they realise.

A woman can only be fully strict or harsh with someone if she hates them. The maxim suggests that severity, in the sense of refusing all warmth or indulgence, comes from dislike rather than from any other feeling.
People find it harder to give up flirting than to give up love. The saying applies to women in particular.
In love, people deceive others more often than they feel doubt. Deceit usually goes further than any suspicion the lover has.
Some love is so intense that it leaves no room for jealousy. The maxim says that the very strength of this kind of love rules jealousy out.

Some good qualities can only be recognized by someone who has them, just as a person born without a sense cannot perceive what that sense shows. Those who lack these qualities cannot see or understand them in others.
When we hate someone too intensely, that hatred puts us in a lower position than the person we hate.
We judge how good or bad something is for us only by how much it touches our self-love. In other words, we value our own gains and losses according to how much we care about ourselves.
Most women's cleverness makes their foolishness stronger, not their good sense. In other words, their wit tends to support their unwise opinions more than it helps them reason well.
Passionate youth is as much a danger to a person's safety as the lack of feeling that comes with old age. Both extremes can lead to harm, so neither one is the safer state.

A person's native accent stays with them for life, not only in how they speak but also in their deeper feelings and thoughts. Where a person comes from shapes who they are inside, not just the sound of their voice.
To be great, a person must know how to use every change in their luck to their advantage.
Most people have qualities they keep hidden, and these only come to light by accident, much as some plants reveal properties that were unknown until chance uncovers them.
Circumstances reveal a person to other people, but they reveal even more to the person himself. Only when tested by events do we learn what we are really like.

If a woman cannot control her temper, the saying implies she also cannot control her mind or her heart. Her feelings and thoughts are as unruly as her outbursts. The point is that uncontrolled temper and uncontrolled inner life go together.
People tend to see only those with good sense as the ones who agree with them. In other words, we judge others to be wise mainly when they share our views.
In love, a person doubts even the things they feel most sure of. Being in love makes certainty about other things unsteady.
The maxim says that the greatest wonder love can work is to end flirting. Flirting is light, playful attention to someone, and love is presented as the force that would bring that to an end.
We hate those who deceive us bitterly because they think they are cleverer than we are. The deceiver's assumed superiority in cunning is what makes the hatred so strong.
It is hard to end a relationship with someone after the love has already faded. The maxim says that the difficulty of breaking off remains even when the feeling that held the two together is gone.
We often feel bored with people we ought not to be bored with. The maxim suggests that boredom is frequent even where it should not arise.
A gentleman may be wildly or foolishly in love, the saying goes, but he must not love in a crude, purely physical way like an animal. Madness of passion is allowed to a gentleman; brutishness is not.
Some faults look like virtues when they are set off well, so they seem to shine as virtue does. The point is that a fault can be shown in a way that makes it appear admirable.
Some friends we lose cause us more regret than grief, and others cause us more grief than regret. The saying notes that the two feelings do not always match the friend we have lost.
We usually give sincere praise only to people who admire us first. In other words, we tend to praise those who already think well of us.
Small-minded people are hurt by small things, while great-minded people notice everything and are not hurt at all. The saying contrasts how minor and major characters react to the same slights.
Humility is what truly shows whether a person has Christian virtues. Without it, a person keeps all their faults, and pride only covers them, hiding them from others and often from the person too.
Unfaithfulness ought to end love, and a person should not feel jealous when there is a real reason for it. Anyone who deserves to cause jealousy will always do so.
We feel more hurt by even a small betrayal committed against us than we feel shame over a much bigger betrayal we commit against others.
Jealousy starts together with love, but it does not always end when love ends. The feeling can last after the love itself has gone.
Many women, the maxim says, mourn a dead lover less out of real love than to prove that they were worthy of being loved.
The harm we cause to other people hurts us less than the harm we cause to ourselves. People feel their own self-inflicted damage more keenly than the damage they do to others.
It is considered bad manners to talk about one's wife in public. The maxim says that talking about oneself is just as bad, though people are less aware of this.

Some virtues turn into vices when they come from natural temperament alone, while others acquired by effort are never fully perfect. Reason has to teach us to manage our money and our trust, whereas goodness and courage are things Nature should give us.
We may doubt that the people we speak with are honest, yet we still think they are more honest with us than they are with other people.
Many women who are considered virtuous, meaning faithful and chaste, grow weary of living by those strict standards. Few of them are content with the role their virtue requires.
Most virtuous women, the maxim suggests, are like hidden treasure: they remain unharmed only because no one has tried to find them. Their goodness is not tested, so it is not proven.
The hard efforts people make to stop loving someone can hurt them more than the cruelty of the person they love does.
Most cowards do not fully understand how afraid they are. Few people see the full extent of their own fear. The maxim suggests that fear often hides even from the person who feels it.
The passage claims that when love ends, the person who is loved is usually the one who fails to notice it. The lover's feelings have faded, but the beloved does not see the change.
Many young people believe they are being natural, when in fact they are only rude and ill-mannered. The maxim suggests that what looks like honest behaviour is often just a lack of good manners.
Some people cry after they have fooled others, and their tears deceive the one crying. The maxim says that a show of sorrow can convince the person who sheds the tears that they are truly sorry.
It is a mistake to think we love a woman for her own sake. The maxim suggests that our love is really for something else, not for the woman herself.

People of average ability tend to criticize whatever lies beyond their understanding or skill. The statement says that when something is too difficult for them to grasp, they tend to speak against it.
Envy is overcome by true friendship, and flirtation is overcome by true love. In each case, the real feeling takes the place of the lesser one.
The worst error of insight is not failing to see far enough, but seeing too far. A person who looks past what is really there, and reads in more than the facts support, makes the greater mistake.
We can give someone advice, but we cannot make them act on it. Advice can be offered freely, yet it cannot produce the behaviour it recommends.
As a person's worth or ability goes down, their judgment of what is good also goes down. The saying links how good we are with how well we can tell good from bad.

Good luck or bad luck brings our virtues or vices into view, much as light makes objects visible. The point is that circumstances reveal what a person is already like, rather than creating those qualities.

The maxim says that the effort it takes to stay faithful to someone we love is almost as bad as being unfaithful. In other words, having to struggle against temptation already shows that the feeling of loyalty is weak.

Bouts-rimés is a game in which players must fill in lines that end with given rhyme words. The point is that people can give our actions any meaning they like, just as each player makes his own sense of the given line endings. Our actions do not carry one fixed meaning; others read them as they choose.

Talking about ourselves and showing our faults in the way we want them seen is, he says, a large part of why we seem sincere. In other words, what looks like honesty about our flaws is often a way of controlling how others see us.

The main point is that a person should be surprised only that they can still be surprised. In other words, after long experience of human behaviour, nothing should seem shocking, and being shocked at all is what needs explaining.
Being too loved and being too little loved are equally hard to bear, since neither state leaves a person satisfied. Too much love and too little love both make it difficult to feel content.
People who refuse to admit they could be wrong are, the saying claims, the people who are wrong most often. Their refusal to admit error is what leads them to make it again and again.
Vanity may not destroy every virtue, but it at least makes them unsteady. The saying treats vanity as a force that weakens good qualities even when it fails to topple them completely.
Other people's vanity is hard to bear because it hurts our own vanity. When someone else's pride is shown, it offends the pride we already have.
People will more readily give up what is good for them than what they enjoy. Pleasure in a thing holds on more strongly than advantage gained from it.
Fortune seems most blind to those she has never favoured. Those who have received no good from luck are the ones who see it as unseeing.

Good fortune should be enjoyed, bad fortune endured patiently, and drastic measures used only when there is no other option. The comparison is to caring for one's health: gentle care in ordinary times, and strong medicine only in a real emergency.

Awkwardness can sometimes vanish among soldiers on campaign, but it never vanishes at court, where people must always keep up appearances. The saying contrasts the rough, plain life of the army with the formal, watchful world of the royal court.
One person may be cleverer than any single other person, yet not cleverer than everyone else put together. The point is that a person can beat one rival in wit but still be outmatched by the many.
People often feel less hurt when a person they loved deceives them than when they are deceived by someone else.
People tend to stay attached to their first love for a long time, but only if they do not find another. The maxim suggests that a second love can end the hold of the first.
People do not dare to say outright that they are free of faults and that their enemies have no good points. Yet in practice they come close to believing exactly that.
Of all our faults, we most willingly confess to idleness. We think it cancels out our other virtues, or at least stops them from working, even if it does not destroy them completely.

Greatness, in this view, does not come from luck or fortune. It is a personal manner that sets a person apart and seems to mark them for great things, which is a sense of worth a person gradually places on themselves. This quality wins other people's respect and raises a person above them more than birth, rank, or even merit does.
A person can have talent and still hold no official post. But no one can hold a post without having some kind of talent. Talent is needed for any position, while a position is not needed for talent.
Rank stands to merit as clothing stands to a beautiful woman. Just as fine dress adds to her appearance without making her more beautiful, rank adds visible status but does not create real worth.
In flirtation, people show the least love of all. The maxim says that love is the thing that is found in flirtation to the smallest degree.
Sometimes our faults bring us success by chance. Some annoying people would get less reward than they deserve if others did not want to pay them to stay away.

Hidden in every person, according to this maxim, are talents we do not know we have. Only the passions can bring them out, and they sometimes produce insights more accurate and complete than skill or training could.
We arrive at each stage of life without knowing how to handle it. Even when we are old, we often still lack experience.
Coquettes take pride in showing jealousy of their lovers, while hiding their envy of other women. Their display of jealousy is a show, and the envy they actually feel stays concealed.
