When someone deceives us, we tend to see them as less foolish than we see ourselves for having been fooled. The deceiver may not look clever to us, even though we feel foolish about being tricked.

It is most dangerous for older people who were once attractive to forget that they no longer are. The maxim says that this forgetting is the worst kind of foolishness. The word "loveable" means charming or pleasing to others.
Our best actions can sometimes cause shame, if other people could see the real reasons behind them. The point is that the motives behind good deeds are often less admirable than the deeds seem.

The hardest thing a friend can do is not to reveal his own faults to someone else, but to point out the other person's faults to him. The idea is that true friendship means being willing to show a friend his own flaws.
However badly a person has been disgraced, he can almost always win back his good name.
A person cannot stay pleasing for long if his wit, or cleverness, comes in only one form. Others soon tire of him when he has nothing else to offer.
People who lack good sense, or who are mad, are only able to see their own cleverness. The saying means they cannot notice or value the wit of others.
Being witty can sometimes let a person behave rudely without being punished for it. Clever remarks may make rude behaviour go unchallenged.
Liveliness that grows stronger as a person gets older is close to being foolish. The saying suggests that late-life high spirits can look more like silliness than wisdom.
In love, the fastest way to be cured is the best way. The maxim suggests that a quick end to a love affair, or to the feelings behind it, is better than a slow one.

Young women who want to avoid seeming flirtatious, and old men who want to avoid seeming foolish, should not speak about love as if they had any personal stake in it. The point is that talking about love draws suspicion on people who are no longer, or not yet, expected to take part in it.
A person may look impressive in a job that is below their ability, but more often they look small in a job that is above it.

We often think we bear misfortune with courage when we are really just feeling low and defeated. We accept our troubles in the way a coward accepts being killed because he is too afraid to fight back.
People talk more about someone's vanity than about their cleverness. Conceit, or excessive pride in oneself, gets more people talking than wit does.
Every strong passion can lead a person into wrongdoing, the saying claims. Only love, however, makes a person look foolish in the eyes of others.
We often claim faults that are the opposite of the ones we really have. For example, a weak person may boast of being stubborn, as if firmness were a strength.
Seeing into people's hidden motives feels like a kind of fortune-telling, and this gives our pride more pleasure than any other mental skill does.

Being attracted by something new and being used to something old work in opposite ways, yet both stop us from seeing the faults of our friends. Each one hides those faults from us just as well as the other.

Many people who are friends, or who are devoted to a cause, end up making us tired of friendship or devotion itself. The bad experience with the people involved turns us against the feeling they were meant to show.
We are willing to overlook a friend's faults when we do not notice them. The point is that we excuse in friends only the flaws we are unaware of.

A woman in love will more easily forgive a big indiscretion than a small act of unfaithfulness. The maxim says that love makes a person more willing to excuse a lover's large mistakes than minor betrayals.
In love's old age, as in life, people keep living on for its pains, even after its pleasures are gone.
Wanting to appear unaffected by feelings is the thing that stops a person from really being unaffected. The wish to look calm gets in the way of actually being calm.
Praising good actions warmly means sharing in them to some degree. The person who praises sincerely is, in a sense, partly a participant in the good deed.
Not feeling envy is the surest sign that a person was born with great qualities. Envy here means wanting what others have and resenting their success.
When friends have betrayed us, we owe them no warmth for their shows of friendship. Even so, we still owe them pity when they suffer misfortune.
It is easier to understand individual people than to understand human nature in general. The saying contrasts knowing particular people with knowing "man" as a whole, meaning humankind.
A person's worth should be measured not by how talented he is, but by what he does with his talents.
Some gratitude is so quick and lively that it does two things. It cancels the debt we owe for a favour, and by repaying a friend it leaves that friend owing us in turn.
Most of the things we want, we would not want so strongly if we understood exactly what we were wanting. Clear knowledge of our own desires would make us want far fewer things.
Most women, according to this maxim, do not care much for friendship because, once they have felt romantic love, friendship seems dull to them.
People in friendship and in love are often happier when they do not know everything about the other person than when they do. Not knowing the full truth often brings more contentment than knowing it.
People often present the faults they do not want to give up as if they were good qualities. Instead of changing a bad habit, they dress it up as a virtue.
The strongest passions, such as love or anger, sometimes leave a person a break from their pain. Vanity, or the desire to be admired, never gives any rest and keeps troubling a person.
People who act foolishly in old age are, in the author's view, even more foolish than foolish young people. Age does not make a fool wiser.
Weakness of character does more damage to virtue than vice does. In other words, a person who is simply weak tends to work against goodness more than a person who openly does wrong.
Shame and jealousy hurt so badly because vanity, our pride in ourselves, cannot help us bear them.

Good manners are the weakest kind of rule, yet people follow them more faithfully than any other. The saying notes that social correctness is not enforced by law, but is still obeyed more than laws are.
A mind that has been well trained finds it easier to follow others than to lead a poorly trained mind. The saying points out that guiding someone less capable is harder than being guided.
When a great office comes to us by surprise, with no gradual build-up and no raised hopes beforehand, it is almost impossible to hold it well and seem worthy of it.
We often feel prouder when we give up or cut back on some of our faults. Admitting that we have cured one bad habit can make us feel more pleased with ourselves.
People who are foolish but have some cleverness are the most tiresome kind of fool. Their small amount of wit makes their foolishness harder to bear than that of a plain fool.
People tend to think they are at least somewhat better than the person they regard as the most capable in the world. In other words, nobody believes they are inferior to that person in every way.
In important matters, a person should not try so hard to make chances for themselves. Instead, they should make good use of the chances that come along on their own.

Few times would we lose by giving up a good thing if, in return, no one spoke ill of us. The maxim says that people seldom mind giving up a real advantage just to escape criticism, since that is usually a fair trade.
People often judge wrongly, but the mistake usually goes one way: the world praises false merit much more often than it fails to honour true merit.
Clever fools exist, but people who are foolish and also sensible do not. The saying claims that wit can sit with foolishness, while good judgment never does.
It is better to be seen as we really are than to pretend to be something we are not, because pretending gains us less.
Our enemies judge us more accurately than we judge ourselves. The saying claims that the views hostile people form about us are closer to the truth than our own view of ourselves.
There are many ways to get over love, but none of them always works. The saying admits that cures for love exist and that each one can fail.
It would be good for us to know everything our passions drive us to do. The idea is that we often do not know the full reach of what our strong feelings make us do, and that knowing it would help us.
Growing old is described as a harsh ruler who bans all the pleasures of youth, and the ban is enforced with death. In other words, a person cannot keep the enjoyments of youth as they age.
Pride makes us criticize faults that we think we do not have. For the same reason, it makes us look down on good qualities that we lack.
Our sorrow over the misfortunes of our enemies is often driven more by pride than by kindness. We show them pity mainly to display our own superiority over them.
Some good and some evil are greater than we can understand. Their size goes beyond what human minds can grasp.

It is lucky for an innocent person to be shielded in the same way that a guilty person is. The saying implies that innocence seldom gets such protection on its own, so it is only well off when it receives the same help that crime gets.
Of all the strong passions, the author says, love suits a woman best. The saying is a claim about which passion is most fitting for women.

Vanity leads us to do wrong more often against our good taste than against our sense of reason. In other words, pride pushes us into bad choices in matters of style and judgment, where we know better, more than into errors of logic.
People rarely want something with real passion when they want it for good reasons. The point is that strong desire tends to come from feeling, not from reasoned judgment.
Our qualities, good and bad alike, are uncertain and unclear. Most of them depend on circumstances: they appear or show themselves only when the situation gives them a chance.
A woman's first love is for the man himself. Her later love affairs are different: in them she loves being in love, not any particular man.
Pride, like other passions, can be foolish. People feel shame at admitting they are jealous, yet they take pride in having been jealous, and in being able to be jealous.
True love is uncommon, but true friendship is even less common than that. The saying compares the two and ranks friendship as the rarer of the pair.
Few women keep their charm once their beauty is gone. The saying suggests that charm usually fades along with good looks.
Much of what we feel as self-confidence, according to this saying, comes from wanting others to pity us or to admire us.
Our envy outlasts the good fortune of the people we envy. Even after they stop being happy, we keep resenting them.
Strength of character that lets a person resist love also lets them keep up that resistance over time. Weak people, who are constantly stirred by passions, seldom truly have any passion at all.

The main point is that people's inner nature holds more contradictions than the imagination could ever make up. Each person's heart already contains a wide range of opposing qualities, and no amount of invention could produce as many.
True gentleness, according to this maxim, belongs only to people who are firm. What looks like gentleness in others is usually weakness, and weakness can easily turn into harshness.
It is risky to criticise someone for being timid if you want to help them overcome it. The criticism can make the timidity worse.
True good nature is very rare. People who think they have it are usually just easygoing, or weak and willing to give way.
The mind clings to what is easy or pleasant, through laziness and habit. That habit limits what we can know, and no one has ever made the effort to stretch the mind to its full ability.
People often mock others more out of a wish to seem clever or superior than out of real ill will. The main point is that vanity, not malice, is usually what drives their sharp remarks.
A heart that is still stirred up by traces of an old passion is more likely to fall into a new one than a heart that has been fully healed of the first.

People who have had strong passions often find that, once they are cured of them, the rest of their lives becomes unhappy. The maxim suggests that losing a great passion can leave a lasting emptiness.
Many more people are free of self-love than are free of envy. The saying claims that envy is an even more common feeling than a lack of self-regard, so envy is found in nearly everyone.
The mind gets tired of doing nothing more often than the body does. In other words, people are more likely to be lazy in their thinking than in their physical activity.

Our peace of mind depends less on the big matters we think important than on how well we handle the small everyday things. Whether we arrange these wisely or badly decides whether we are calm or troubled.
Wicked people do not openly oppose virtue. When they want to attack it, they either claim that virtue is not real or they accuse it of crimes.
People often move from being in love to wanting power or success, but they never move back from ambition to love.
Extreme greed is very often wrong about what it wants. Of all the passions, none misses its goal more often, and none gives the present so much power to harm the future.
Greed does not always work in the way one would expect. Some greedy people give up what they own for uncertain and far-off hopes, while others choose small gains now over much larger ones later.

People seem to think they have too few faults, so they add some on purpose. They pretend to have certain odd traits and practise them so often that the traits become real, and they can no longer change them.

People seem to know their own faults better than we think, because when they talk about their own behaviour they are never wrong. The same self-love that usually blinds them also gives them clear sight here, so they hide or soften even the smallest fault that others could criticise.
Young men starting out in the world should be either modest or confident. A serious, dignified manner, he says, tends to turn into rudeness.
A quarrel keeps going because both people are at fault. If only one person were to blame, the dispute would soon end.
A woman's youth is worth little to her unless she is also pretty, and her beauty is worth little unless she is also young. Each quality needs the other to count for anything.
Some people are so light and changeable that they have neither real faults nor real good qualities. Their character is too empty to be called bad or good.
A woman's first flirtation is usually not counted as one. People only treat it as a flirtation once she has had a second.
Some people are so focused on themselves that, even when they are in love, they manage to be absorbed in the feeling of love without being absorbed in the person they love.

Love is pleasant, the maxim says, but the pleasure it gives comes mostly from the way it behaves, not from what it is in itself. The attractions of love lie in its manner and habits more than in its essence.
A small amount of wit combined with good sense becomes less tiresome over time than a large amount of wit combined with a mean or unkind nature. Wit here means quick, clever talk.
Jealousy is the worst of all evils. Yet people who make others feel jealous feel little pity for the one who suffers it.

Pagans claimed that their own reason let them scorn death without any hope of an afterlife. The author argues that facing death bravely is common, but truly despising it is, in his view, always pretended.

Writers have tried hard to prove that death is not an evil, yet the author doubts any sensible person has really believed it. The effort itself shows how hard the belief is to hold. People may grow tired of life, but they never think it worthless, and even those who kill themselves are alarmed when death comes in a way they did not choose.

Brave men often face death differently than they expected. Those who scorned death while it seemed far away often fear it once it comes near. The passage says that the wisest avoid thinking about death, since seeing it clearly makes it seem terrible, and that philosophers' calm about death came only from having no choice but to die.

The passage says that since people cannot avoid death, they should accept it gracefully and leave a lasting reputation. It also advises not to say everything one privately thinks, and to trust one's natural feelings rather than reason, which might wrongly suggest that death can be faced with indifference.

La Rochefoucauld says that comforts facing death, such as courage, being missed, leaving a good name, and escaping life's troubles, are worth using. But they cannot be fully trusted. They help only a little, like a single shelter that looks safe from far off but gives little cover to soldiers storming a fortress up close.

People often assume that death will feel no closer when it arrives than it does from afar, or that their feelings are strong enough to withstand the harshest trials. Pride will not help either, since it cannot make us ignore what will destroy it. The mind we rely on to face death is too weak, and it tends to show us only what is frightening about it.

La Rochefoucauld argues that people facing death often keep their composure for different reasons. Cato and Brutus looked to noble causes, a servant danced on the scaffold, and all of them show the same outward calm. The difference lies in motive: a nobleman's scorn for death is really a love of fame that keeps death out of his sight.
Some kind of calm or courage in a peasant facing trouble is said to come from his narrow outlook. He cannot see how bad the evil really is, so his mind is free to think about other things.

Schopenhauer takes Aristotle's three-part division of life's blessings and keeps only the number three. He proposes instead three basic kinds of human lot: what a person is (health, character, intelligence and similar qualities), what a person has (property and possessions), and what a person represents to others (their standing in the eyes of other people).
A person's standing is how others regard him, meaning the view they hold of him. That view shows up in the honor he receives, and in his rank and reputation.

Differences that nature itself creates between people affect happiness more deeply than differences created by human arrangements. Real personal qualities, such as a great mind or a great heart, matter far more than rank or birth, even royal birth, just as actors playing kings differ from real kings.

Schopenhauer says that a person's well-being depends most of all on what kind of person he is inside. His inner nature produces the inward satisfaction or dissatisfaction that comes from his feelings, desires and thoughts. He adds that the old Epicurean Metrodorus made the same point.

Schopenhauer says that a person's own inner states, such as thoughts, feelings and wishes, are what he experiences directly. Outside events affect him only indirectly, so the same events affect people differently. Each person therefore lives in a world shaped by how he sees it.

Many people envy the interesting events in someone else's life and wish the same had happened to them. Schopenhauer suggests they should instead envy the mind that made those events meaningful. For a man of genius they were interesting, but for an ordinary mind they would have been dull and routine.

Many poems by Goethe and Byron are clearly based on real events. A foolish reader may envy the poet for the delightful things that happened to him, when he should instead envy his imagination, which could turn an ordinary experience into something great and beautiful.

Different temperaments respond to the same event in different ways: a melancholy person sees a tragedy, a sanguine person sees an interesting conflict, and a phlegmatic person sees nothing meaningful. Schopenhauer's point is that every event needs both a subject (the person perceiving) and an object (the thing perceived) to be experienced, and these two are as inseparably joined as oxygen and hydrogen in water.

Two people can face the same outside event and still have different experiences of it, because each person's inner response differs. For someone with a dull mind, even the finest object is only poorly grasped, much as a fine landscape looks dull in bad weather.

Each person is shut inside their own consciousness and cannot step outside it, so help from outside does little good. Like actors on a stage, people differ only in outward roles, such as prince or servant, while the inner self is the same: a player facing the same worries.

Differences in rank and wealth change the role a person plays, but not how happy or unhappy they feel inside. Everyone shares the same basic lot of hardships and troubles. Their causes may differ, and their intensity varies, but that intensity does not follow social position or wealth.

Everything a person experiences exists only within his consciousness, so the nature of that consciousness matters more than the outside circumstances that fill it. The wealth and glory of the world look poor when seen through a foolish mind, while a great imagination can create great work even in a miserable prison.

Life has two halves. The outer half, the events and circumstances we meet, is controlled by fate and varies from case to case. The inner half is the self, which stays essentially the same in everyone.

Each person's life keeps the same basic character whatever happens to them, like variations on one theme. Nobody can step outside their own nature. The passage compares this to animals, which stay within the limits nature has set for them, so a pet can only be made happy in ways that fit what it can feel.

Schopenhauer says that a person's inborn mental abilities set the limit on how much happiness he can reach. If those abilities are small, outside help such as other people or good luck cannot lift him above ordinary, largely animal pleasures like appetite, family comfort, and crude amusements.

Schopenhauer argues that happiness depends mainly on what a person is, meaning their inner abilities and character, rather than on what they have or how others see them. Mental pleasures are the highest and most lasting, and they rest on the powers of the mind. Education can do little to widen that inner horizon.

A person's own inner qualities matter more to happiness than outside circumstances. A rich inner life makes outside goods matter less, while a fool stays a fool even in paradise. Goethe's verse says that people of every station agree that personality is the highest happiness on earth.

Our happiness depends more on how we experience life inside ourselves than on external circumstances. Schopenhauer offers proverbs and examples to show this, such as health being worth more than wealth or rank: a healthy beggar can be happier than a sick king.

A calm, cheerful temperament, good health, a clear mind, a gentle will and a good conscience are said to be worth more than rank or wealth. The reason given is that what a person is in himself matters more to him than his possessions or his reputation with others.

A person with a rich inner mind can enjoy solitude, while a dull person is bored even amid crowds and entertainment. Likewise, a good-natured person can be happy with little, but a greedy, envious, or spiteful person is unhappy even when very rich. For someone with strong intellect, many common pleasures are unnecessary and even burdensome.

Horace and Socrates both show that a person can do without luxury goods. Horace says some people lack such things, and he is one who does not care to have them. Socrates, seeing goods for sale, remarks how many things in the world he does not want.

The first and most important part of happiness, Schopenhauer says, is what a person is: his character and inner self. Unlike possessions or reputation, this cannot be taken away by fate, so it has absolute worth, while the other two have only relative worth. For this reason, others find it harder than expected to influence or control a person from outside.

Time wears away physical and mental advantages, but it cannot touch moral character. So the blessings of the other two kinds, which time cannot directly take from us, may seem better than the first kind. They also seem open to anyone, since they are external and can, in principle, be acquired.

Schopenhauer says that a person's subjective nature, meaning character and temperament, cannot be acquired or changed. It comes to us as a fixed gift and stays with us for life. He supports this by quoting Goethe, who describes a fate set at birth that no person and no passage of time can escape.

At birth, a person's nature is fixed by the position of the sun and planets, and it develops by a law that cannot be escaped. Neither time nor any power can break up this living, shaped form. Prophets and sibyls, the ancient seers, already foretold it.

The only thing we can really control, according to this passage, is how best to use the personal qualities we have. So we should choose pursuits, work and a way of life that bring those qualities into play and let them develop as far as they can.

A man with great physical strength who is forced into delicate handwork or demanding mental study, which needs abilities he lacks, cannot use his greatest strength. Such a man, the passage says, will never be happy in his whole life.

A man with very high intellectual gifts may be even more unhappy if he must leave those gifts unused in a job that does not need them, such as hard physical labour he is too weak for. Still, especially when young, he should take care not to overrate his powers and think he has more ability than he really has.

Schopenhauer argues that health and mental ability matter more for a good life than money, so it is wiser to cultivate them than to pile up wealth. He adds that this does not mean ignoring the basic necessities. Great surplus wealth, he says, does little for happiness.

Many rich people are unhappy because they lack real mental culture or knowledge, so they have no genuine interests to occupy their minds. Wealth adds little to happiness beyond meeting basic needs, and it can even disturb happiness, since guarding property brings constant worries.

People try much harder to get rich than to improve their minds, even though what a person is matters more for happiness than what he owns. Many work endlessly to pile up money, and beyond that single goal their minds stay empty and closed to anything else.

Schopenhauer describes a person who cannot enjoy the highest pleasures of the mind and instead chases brief physical pleasures at great cost. Even if he gains a large fortune, he leaves it to an heir to grow or waste. Such a life, though it looks serious and important, is as foolish as any other.

Schopenhauer says that a person's inner qualities matter most for happiness. Since most people have very little of these, many who are free from money worries still feel as unhappy as those who are struggling to get by.

People with empty minds, dull imaginations and poor spirits, Schopenhauer says, seek out others like themselves. Together they chase pastimes such as physical pleasure, amusement, and finally excess and loose living. "Similis simili gaudet" is Latin for "like delights in like."
A young man who inherits a large fortune often spends it quickly on wild extravagance. The passage says the reason is that his mind is empty, so he is bored with life.
A person who has little inside himself tries to make up for it by gathering wealth and possessions from outside. This never works, so in the end he becomes poor in outward things too.

Schopenhauer says that the first two kinds of blessings, which make up happiness, need no praise, since everyone already values them. The third kind, reputation, is made only of other people's opinions and so seems less solid, yet everyone should still seek a good name. Rank is for those who serve the state, and fame for very few.

Schopenhauer says people value reputation and fame above almost everything, and value rank above wealth only if they are foolish. He adds that reputation and wealth cause each other: having something brings more of it, and other people's favor often helps us get what we want.

Schopenhauer's point is that a person's own nature matters more to their happiness than their possessions or other people's opinions of them. Whatever a man is shapes every experience he has, and the pleasure he gets from any enjoyment depends mainly on himself, especially for mental pleasures.

Schopenhauer says that enjoyment depends mostly on the person, not the place. The English phrase "enjoy oneself" shows this, since we say "he enjoys himself in Paris," not "he enjoys Paris." A man with a poor character finds that pleasure tastes sour to him, and in good and bad events alike, what matters most is how a person responds to them.

A person's own inner qualities, what he is in himself, decide his happiness more directly than anything he owns or that happens to him. Outside things can be blocked or cancelled, but personal qualities always keep their effect. For this reason, envy aimed at personal qualities is the most lasting kind, and it is the most carefully hidden.

Our basic character, the way our consciousness is made, is present in everything we do or undergo and lasts throughout life. Other influences, such as circumstances and luck, come and go, which is why Aristotle said that character lasts while wealth does not.

Misfortune that comes from outside hurts less than misfortune we bring on ourselves, because outside luck can change but our character stays the same. So inner qualities such as a noble nature, a clear mind, a cheerful temper and good health matter most for happiness. Schopenhauer says we should work to keep these more than to gain wealth and honor. "Mens sana in corpore sano" is a Latin saying meaning a healthy mind in a healthy body.

Good spirits, in Schopenhauer's view, bring happiness directly, because being cheerful is already its own reward. A cheerful person has no further reason needed for being cheerful. Cheerfulness can make up for the lack of other advantages such as youth, looks, wealth or status. So the test of whether someone is happy is whether they are cheerful and good-humoured.

Schopenhauer recalls an old saying that laughing a lot means happiness and crying a lot means unhappiness. He says it is a simple truth, but he remembers it. He adds that when cheerfulness comes, people should welcome it, yet they often hesitate and wait until they feel fully justified in being cheerful.

Cheerfulness is presented as an immediate form of happiness, felt directly in the present moment, unlike other goods that only pay off later. Because our lives are very short, this present feeling matters most, so securing cheerfulness should be the main goal of seeking happiness.

Schopenhauer argues that money does little to make a person cheerful, while good health does a great deal. He points out that cheerful faces are more often found among poorer country workers than among the rich, and so he concludes that health should be kept as high as possible, since cheerfulness grows from it.

Good health depends on avoiding excess, violent emotions and mental overstrain, and on daily exercise in the open air, cold baths and similar habits. Schopenhauer argues this because life itself is movement, so the whole body needs regular exercise to work properly.

The body's organs are described as working constantly and without rest. The heart beats, the lungs pump, the intestines move, the glands absorb and release, and even the brain moves with each pulse and breath.

People who get no bodily exercise, such as those who sit all day, have a restless inner life that has no outlet in outward movement. This inner agitation needs some physical release, and without it the feelings build up and must be held down. Schopenhauer compares this to trees, which must be shaken by wind to grow well.

Our happiness depends largely on our spirits, and our spirits depend on our health. The same events affect us differently when we are well than when we are ill. What makes us happy or unhappy is not how things are in themselves, but how we experience and view them.

Our happiness depends mostly on how we think about things, not on the things themselves. Above all, health decides most of our happiness: with good health everything gives pleasure, while without it even great abilities or a good temperament lose their value.

Good health matters more than anything else for happiness, so people rightly ask about each other's health when they meet. Giving up health for money, status, learning, fame, or brief sensual pleasures is therefore the greatest folly. All other goals should be put after health.

Good spirits do not depend entirely on health. A person can be physically healthy and still be melancholy by temperament. Schopenhauer traces this to a fixed bodily makeup, mainly how sensitive a person is compared with their physical energy. Too much sensitivity causes uneven moods: long gloom broken by bursts of liveliness.

Schopenhauer says a genius is a person whose nerves are unusually sensitive or powerful. He notes that Aristotle observed that people outstanding in philosophy, politics, poetry or art tend to have a melancholy temperament, meaning a gloomy or brooding disposition.

Schopenhauer quotes lines from Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost. The point is that people differ by nature: some laugh easily and at anything, while others look so sour that they will not smile even when a wise old man swears a joke is funny.

Plato distinguished people of easy disposition from those of difficult disposition, and people differ in how strongly they feel pleasure and pain. One person may laugh at what drives another to despair. Generally, the more sensitive someone is to unpleasant things, the less sensitive they are to pleasant ones, and the reverse.

Schopenhauer contrasts two kinds of temperament, using the Greek words for "ill-humoured" (dyskolos) and "good-humoured" (eukolos). The ill-humoured man is upset by failure and gains no joy from success, even when most of his efforts succeed. The good-humoured man keeps his cheer, taking pleasure in whatever goes well.

Gloomy, anxious people suffer less in the end, Schopenhauer says, because their troubles are mostly imagined rather than real. Someone who always expects the worst and prepares for it is less often disappointed than someone who always expects good outcomes. The Greek word "auskoloi" here means people of gloomy, anxious temperament.

Schopenhauer says that when bodily illness, such as nerve trouble or poor digestion, feeds a person's natural gloominess, the gloom can grow so strong that life feels wearying. At its worst, a person may decide to end his life simply because he is always unhappy, even without any particular cause, and carry out that decision calmly.

Schopenhauer says that a person suffering badly will look for a chance to end his own life, and will do it without fear once the chance comes. Even a healthy, cheerful man may choose death if his pain or his dread of a coming disaster becomes greater than his fear of dying.

The passage says that the amount of suffering needed to drive someone to suicide depends on their temperament. A gloomy person needs only a little suffering, and in the extreme case almost none. A cheerful, healthy person needs a great deal of suffering before they would take their own life.

Suicide comes in many degrees, lying between two extremes. At one end is suicide that comes from a diseased increase of a person's natural gloom. At the other is suicide by a healthy, cheerful person who has clear outside reasons for ending his life.

Beauty is partly a matter of health and counts as a personal advantage. It does not directly make a person happy, but it helps indirectly by making a good impression on others, which the author calls an open letter of recommendation.

Schopenhauer says that pain and boredom are the two main enemies of happiness. Life swings back and forth between them: escaping one tends to bring us closer to the other. Hardship causes pain, while having more than enough leads to boredom.

Schopenhauer says the poor are always fighting hunger and pain, while the rich fight boredom. Inside a person, he claims, sensitivity to pain and sensitivity to boredom move in opposite directions, because both grow with mental power.

A dull mind usually goes with dull feelings: the person is not much hurt by pain or worry, however severe. Schopenhauer adds that this mental dullness lies behind the empty look seen on many faces, shown by close attention to small, trivial things around them.

Boredom comes from a constant craving for excitement, just to give the mind something to do. The things people pick for this, such as idle pastimes, gossip and staring out of windows, show how little they demand from their amusements.

People look for company, entertainment and luxury mainly because their own inner life is empty. Rich inner life, the wealth of the mind, protects best against this, since the more of it a person has, the less room there is for boredom.

A mind that keeps finding new material in the many things it observes, both in itself and in nature, and can form new combinations from them, is strengthened. Apart from times of rest, such a mind stays well away from boredom.

Greater intelligence, Schopenhauer says, comes with greater sensitivity, will, and passion. These bring a stronger capacity for emotion, more pain from both mind and body, less patience with obstacles, and more resentment of interruption. Imagination makes all of this stronger. The pattern holds at every level, from the dullest person to the greatest genius.

Schopenhauer says that a person tends to shape the outside world to fit their own inner nature, guarding most against the kind of suffering they are most prone to. A wise person, he adds, aims above all to avoid pain and annoyance, seeking quiet, leisure and a modest life with few encounters.

A man with a lot of inner resources needs little from other people, so he tends to prefer retirement or even solitude, and high intellect makes him unsocial. Crowds do not help: a hundred fools together do not add up to one wise man.

Once a person is no longer driven by need, he quickly looks for amusement and company at any price, joining whoever he meets. He avoids being alone with himself, because in solitude a person's inner worth shows itself.

A foolish person, however well dressed, is weighed down by his own dull self, and cannot escape it. A clever person fills even empty places with lively thoughts. Seneca and Ben Sira are cited as agreeing that foolishness is its own burden.

Schopenhauer argues that people tend to be sociable to the degree that they are intellectually limited and common. In his view, a person's real choice is between being alone and being vulgar. As an example of the link, he reports the claim that the most sociable people are Black Africans, whom he places at the bottom of the scale of intellect.

A French newspaper, as the writer recalls it, claimed that Black people in North America, whether free or enslaved, like to pack into very small spaces because they cannot get enough of each other's "snub-nosed" company.

Schopenhauer says the brain is like a parasite living off the body, and that leisure is what the rest of life produces. Yet for most people, leisure brings only boredom and dullness, unless they fill it with sensual pleasure or foolishness. He adds a line from Ariosto: the idle hours of ignorant men are miserable.

People with limited intellect get bored because their minds only serve their will, so they need an outside stimulus to get going. When nothing moves the will, the intellect rests too, leaving their mental power idle. Schopenhauer calls this idleness boredom.

People who feel empty or bored turn to small pleasures such as card games, fidgeting or smoking. These keep the will busy for a moment and set the mind moving. Schopenhauer says such pastimes are like paper money: their worth is arbitrary, not real and natural like true motives.

Schopenhauer argues that card-playing is what society mostly does because its people have no real ideas, so they play for each other's money instead. He then admits one defence: cards teach people to make the best of chances they cannot change, and to hide their feelings and look calm when things go badly.

Schopenhauer argues that card-playing is harmful because its aim is to use tricks to take what belongs to someone else. This habit, he says, carries over into everyday business, where people treat property as they treat cards. They use any advantage they have, as long as they stay within the law.

Leisure is valuable because it lets a person be in possession of himself. Those who have something real within themselves are truly fortunate. Most people, however, use their free time poorly and end up bored and a burden to themselves. The closing line draws on the Bible's image of the free children versus the children of the slave woman, Hagar, to suggest that those who have inner worth are of the free kind.

The happiest person is the one who has enough inner resources and needs little or nothing from outside. Just as a country does best when it imports little, a person should depend as little as possible on others or on the outside world. Outside goods are costly, create dependence and danger, and are a poor substitute for what one produces oneself.

Other people can give us only a little, since in the end each person stands alone. What matters most is what kind of person that lone self is. Each of us must therefore rely on ourselves for what we need, as Goethe and Goldsmith both say.

Schopenhauer says that a person's greatest source of good and happiness lies within themselves. He agrees with Aristotle that happiness means being self-sufficient. Other sources of joy are uncertain and depend on chance, so they can run out and are not always available.

In old age the things that bring happiness fade away: love, wit, travel, social life, and friends through death. What remains is what a person has within himself, which is the only lasting source of happiness. Outside of that, the world offers little, being full of misery, pain, and boredom.

Schopenhauer says that evil and foolishness usually win out in the world, and that a person with a rich inner life is like a warm, lit room in a cold winter night. He concludes that the happiest fate is to have a rich character and a good mind, even if this does not bring outward success.

Queen Christina of Sweden said that Descartes, who had lived alone in Holland for twenty years, was the happiest of men and a man to be envied. Schopenhauer presents this as a wise remark, since she judged his life from his solitude, not from fame or company.

Outside conditions must be good enough for a person to control his own life and happiness, and wisdom is worth most when it comes with money and sunlight, as the Bible book Ecclesiastes says. A wise person, given these, will work hard to keep his inner sources of happiness flowing, and that needs independence and free time.

A person with a rich inner life will not give up his own standards to chase office, money, or public praise. He will keep his desires modest and his resources in reserve. Schopenhauer supports this with a line from the Roman poet Horace: he would not trade his free leisure for the wealth of the Arabs.

It is foolish to give up your inner life, with its peace, free time and independence, for outward things such as display, social rank, ceremony, titles and public honor. The author says Goethe, the German writer, did exactly this, while his own good fortune pulled him the opposite way.

Schopenhauer uses Aristotle to support his claim that happiness comes mainly from within a person. Aristotle observed that every pleasure needs some activity or use of a power to exist. Stobaeus, a later writer who summarized Aristotle's school, said happiness means vigorous and successful activity in one's undertakings.

Schopenhauer says that people's natural strengths are meant for struggling against the difficulties of life. When there is no longer any struggle, these strengths become a burden, and people use them for nothing in particular just to escape boredom. He adds that wealthy upper-class people suffer most from boredom.

Rich people, Schopenhauer says, are restless. They are bored at home in town, so they leave for their country houses, but they are bored there too. They go back and forth between the two, never finding peace in either place.

Schopenhauer quotes Lucretius here, a Latin poem about a man who cannot bear being at home. He leaves his great house, then rushes back, as if to save a burning building, yawns as soon as he crosses the threshold, and either falls asleep or hurries off to the city again. The point is that a restless man finds no relief by changing places, because he carries his discontent with him.

Schopenhauer is describing people who, when young, had plenty of physical energy but little mind. That physical energy fades, and their mental powers either never developed or are unused, leaving them in a poor state. Their will, however, remains, because it is the one power that never runs out.

Schopenhauer says that people with nothing to do try to stir up their will through strong excitement, such as high-stakes gambling, which he calls a very degrading vice. He adds that an idle person usually picks a pastime that fits the kind of ability they are best at, such as chess, hunting, music, or cards.

Schopenhauer suggests that a person's interests could be sorted by tracing them to three basic powers that make up human physical nature. These powers can be viewed on their own, apart from any particular goal, as three sources of pleasure. Each person then picks the one that suits them best, depending on where they excel.

Schopenhauer lists two kinds of pleasure. The first comes from the body's basic energy: eating, drinking, digesting, resting and sleeping. The second comes from physical activity such as walking, running, dancing, riding and fighting, whether as sport or as war.

Schopenhauer says that pleasures of the mind, such as thinking, feeling, art, learning and philosophy, come in different degrees of value. The nobler the mental power being used, the greater the pleasure it gives. This is because pleasure always comes from using one's own powers, and happiness is the frequent repetition of such pleasure.

Schopenhauer argues that the pleasures of sensibility, meaning the senses and feeling, rank higher than the other basic kinds of pleasure, which animals share just as much. Because human mental powers are a form of sensibility, a larger share of sensibility gives people intellectual pleasure, and the more it dominates, the greater that pleasure becomes.

Schopenhauer says that ordinary people only care about things that touch their personal wants. Since stirring the will always brings some pain, he calls card-playing a small, harmless way of stirring it, a "mere tickling of the will," that causes only brief and slight pain.

A man with a powerful intellect can take a lively interest in things purely for the sake of knowing them, without any personal desire driving it. For him this interest is almost a necessity. It lifts him into a realm where pain cannot reach him, a clearer higher air where the gods live untroubled.
Most people spend their lives struggling for small personal gains and suffering through hardship. When those aims are met, they fall into boredom and can only be stirred to action by strong passion.

A man with strong mental powers has a rich inner life full of thought and meaning. He finds his interests in his own mind, and draws his outside stimulation from nature, from human affairs, and from the achievements of great people of all ages. Only a man of this kind can fully appreciate these things, because only he can truly understand them.

Only the intellectual man truly takes in the great thinkers, while others hear them only in part. Because of this, he has one extra need: time free from work for reading, observing, studying and thinking. Schopenhauer adds that real pleasures come only from real needs.

A person with a rich inner nature can enjoy things, such as nature, art and literature, that others cannot appreciate. Such a person lives two lives, a personal one and an intellectual one, and the intellectual one comes to count as the real life, with the personal life serving only as a means to it. Most people treat their own shallow, empty existence as the goal itself.

A person of this kind puts the life of the mind above all other pursuits. Over time, steady gaining of insight and knowledge gives such a life lasting depth and unity, like a slowly built work of art. Schopenhauer says that a life aimed only at personal comfort, which can widen but never deepen, is far inferior, yet many people treat it as the goal itself.

Everyday life, when it is not stirred by strong feeling, is dull and flat, and when it is stirred, it soon turns painful. Only people with more intellect than they need to pursue their desires can be happy, because that extra mind lets them live an intellectual life, free of pain and full of lively interests.

Free time alone does not make a mind active, Schopenhauer says. A person needs a surplus of mental energy, not used to serve the will, to put toward thinking. Seneca's saying that idle leisure without learning is a living tomb is quoted to support this.

Schopenhauer says that a mental interest, whether collecting specimens or studying great poetry and philosophy, protects a person from boredom and its harmful results. Such interests keep a person from bad company, dangers, losses and wasteful spending that befall someone who puts all his happiness in external things. He jokes that his philosophy never earned him any money, yet it saved him many costs.

Schopenhauer says that ordinary people look for happiness in outside things such as money, status, family, friends and social life. Because these can be lost or disappoint, their happiness is never secure. Their sense of well-being keeps shifting with every wish, so they chase one pleasure after another.

Schopenhauer compares a person who tries to make up for lost health or strength with jellies and drugs, rather than rebuilding his own vital power, to a common type of man. He then turns to a middle type: someone with somewhat more than ordinary intellect, though not exceptional.

Schopenhauer describes a person who, when outside pleasures run out, turns to hobbies such as art or science for enjoyment, so his happiness is partly within himself. He adds that an amateur interest in art is not the same as creating art, and that amateur science tends to stay on the surface.

Schopenhauer says that a person cannot fully give himself over to a single pursuit and lose interest in everything else. Only the highest intellectual power, which he calls genius, reaches that intensity, taking all of time and existence as its subject. Such a man therefore needs to be left undisturbed with his own thoughts and works.

Schopenhauer says that a rare kind of man has his centre of gravity entirely within himself. Because he needs only himself, he does not show the warm, unlimited concern for friends, family and community that others often show. Losing everything else does not leave him inconsolable.

People with a strong sense of their own distinct character often feel that others are not quite like them, so they come to see themselves as outsiders among humanity. They even refer to people in general as "they" rather than "we."

Schopenhauer concludes that a person with rich inner intellectual gifts is the happiest. His reason is that what goes on inside us matters more than outside things, because outside things can affect us only indirectly, through our inner experience of them.

Inner wealth, meaning the richness of the mind and character, is the only true wealth, since outward riches bring their own harm. A person with inner wealth asks from the outside world only to be left alone, with time to develop and enjoy the mind, and to be free to be himself at all times.

If a person is meant to shape the thinking of a whole people, the only real measure of his happiness or unhappiness is whether he perfects his abilities and finishes his work. Other things matter little. For this reason, the greatest thinkers have valued quiet, undisturbed time as highly as they valued themselves.

Several thinkers are cited to show that leisure and the free use of one's abilities bring the greatest happiness. Socrates is said to call leisure the finest possession, Aristotle is said to hold that a philosophical life is happiest, and Goethe is said to hold that using one's given talent brings the most happiness.

Schopenhauer says that having free, undisturbed leisure is not the usual situation for people. Most ordinary people spend their lives earning what they need to survive, so they soon grow tired of leisure. Without invented aims, such as games, hobbies, or pastimes, free time becomes a burden.

Schopenhauer means that people with unusually high intelligence need quiet, unoccupied time to be happy, while ordinary people find such idle time hard to bear or harmful. Without that leisure, a person of great intellect is like a winged horse forced to pull a cart, and so is unhappy.

Schopenhauer says that when a person has both undisturbed leisure and great intellect, which he calls two unnatural circumstances, that is a great stroke of luck. Such a person can live a higher life, protected from both pain (the struggle to make a living) and boredom (being unable to handle free time). These two troubles cancel each other out, so a person can avoid both.

Great mental gifts, Schopenhauer says, come with a highly nervous kind of activity. This makes a person far more sensitive to pain of every kind. The passage gives this as an objection to a view stated just before it.

Great intellectual gifts, Schopenhauer says, bring a strong temperament with vivid ideas. These make the emotions far more intense than those of an ordinary person. Since more things in the world cause pain than pleasure, this intensity tends to bring more suffering. He adds that great intellect also tends to separate a person from other people and their concerns.

A man with much inner richness will find little to enjoy in what most people enjoy, and will find those pleasures dull. Schopenhauer suggests this is another case of compensation: people often say the narrow-minded are happiest, even when their lives are poor.

Schopenhauer notes that Sophocles, the Greek playwright, gave two opposite opinions: once that wisdom is the greatest part of happiness, and once that the thoughtless life is the most pleasant. The Old Testament writers also contradict themselves, saying a fool's life is worse than death and that more wisdom brings more sorrow.

Schopenhauer says a man with no mental needs, whose intellect is only ordinary, is a "philistine" in the strict sense. The word began as German university slang for someone who is not a lover of learning or the arts. He would rather use it for people who are always busy with things that are not truly real.

Schopenhauer says that one definition of a "philistine" (a person who is narrow-minded and uninterested in culture) is too abstract for a popular book, so he prefers a simpler one. That definition is that a philistine is a man without mental needs, which means he takes no pleasure in intellectual things.

The philistine, Schopenhauer says, has no real interest in learning or in art for their own sake. When such pleasures are fashionable, he pays attention to them only because he feels he must, and he cares little for them. His true enjoyment is in physical pleasures, which he thinks make up for the rest. Good food and drink are, to him, the peak of life.

Schopenhauer says that a person whose life is aimed only at physical comfort will be bored once luxuries are given to him. Such people try many distractions, such as parties, gambling, drinking and travel, but none of these cures boredom. Without intellectual needs, there can be no intellectual pleasure, and this makes the "philistine" (a narrow, materialistic type) dull and serious like an animal.

A man with little inner resource, Schopenhauer says, finds nothing truly satisfying: sensual pleasures wear out fast, dull company becomes a burden, and even card games lose their appeal. What remains for him is the pleasure of vanity, gained by feeling superior in wealth, rank or power, or by basking in the status of richer, more important people, which the English call being a snob.

Because the philistine has only physical needs and no intellectual ones, he looks for companions who can meet those physical needs, not intellectual ones. He does not expect his friends to have any intellectual ability, and if he meets someone who does, that person arouses his dislike and even hatred.

A man who lacks inner worth feels inferior, and this quietly turns into envy he hides even from himself, sometimes growing into resentment. Still, he does not judge people by their inner qualities. He keeps valuing rank, wealth, power and influence, which he sees as the only real advantages in the world.

Schopenhauer says that people with no interest in ideas, whom he calls philistines (narrow-minded, unthinking people), must constantly seek out real-world things to avoid boredom. Real things, though, either disappoint or harm, and once they stop interesting, they wear a person out. The world of ideas is endless and calm, and it lies far from life's sorrows.

Schopenhauer says that his remarks on the qualities that make for happiness have dealt mostly with a person's physical and intellectual nature. He points readers to his essay The Foundation of Morals for the direct effect of morality on happiness.

Epicurus sorted human needs into groups. The first group is natural and necessary needs, such as food and clothing, which cause pain when unmet and are easy to meet. The second group is natural but not necessary, such as pleasures of the senses.

Schopenhauer is saying that Epicurus's list of needs is unclear on one point, and that his own version is more precise. He then describes a third kind of need: needs that are neither natural nor necessary, such as luxury, show and splendor. These never end and are very hard to satisfy.

Reason cannot set a fixed limit on how much wealth a person should want, because no set amount satisfies everyone. What counts is the balance between what a person wants and what he gets. Judging happiness by possessions alone, ignoring expectations, is like a fraction with no denominator: it cannot be properly measured.

A person does not feel the lack of things he never thinks of wanting, and is content without them. Someone with far more can still be unhappy if he lacks the one thing he wants. Each person's happiness depends on what he expects to be able to get: when it seems within reach he is content, and when obstacles appear he is miserable.

Schopenhauer's point is that wealth and fame do not satisfy a person in the way one might expect. A poor man is not troubled by what he cannot see, and a rich man is not comforted by his riches when his hopes fail. Like sea-water, more wealth only increases the craving for it. After a loss, a person soon returns to his usual mood.

When our possessions shrink, we quickly lower our expectations, which is painful at first but then stops hurting, like a healed wound. When good fortune comes, our demands keep rising, because nothing holds them in check.

Wealth brings pleasure only while it is growing, because that growing feeling of expansion is the delight. Once the increase is complete, the pleasure stops, since we get used to our larger demands and no longer care about the amount that meets them.

Discontent comes from constantly trying to raise our demands, even though we cannot raise what would satisfy them. The opening image compares a person's thoughts on earth to a day given by the father of gods and men, meaning Zeus, the Greek chief god.

Schopenhauer says that because people depend so much on their needs, it is not surprising that wealth is respected above all else. He adds that money-making becomes the only goal in life, pushing aside things like philosophy, even among those who claim to practise it. People who are criticised for wanting money above everything are the subject of the passage's next point.

Money is loved because it can be turned into whatever a person wants at the moment. Other goods only meet one particular need, such as food when hungry or fur in winter, so they are good only in relation to that need. Money, by contrast, satisfies every need in the abstract, which Schopenhauer calls absolutely good.

Someone with inherited wealth should treat it as a protection against life's misfortunes, not as permission to spend freely on pleasure. People who make their own fortune often think of their talents as the real capital and their savings as mere interest, so they spend what they earn instead of keeping a lasting reserve.

People whose earnings come from a special talent or a passing set of circumstances can fall into poverty, because that talent may become old-fashioned or those circumstances may end. Manual workers are different: their skill rarely disappears, and fellow workers can replace them, so their work stays in demand.

Schopenhauer contrasts earned income with inherited money. Artists and professionals, he says, spend their earnings as if they were income, when they should save part of them as capital, so they often end in ruin. People who inherit money usually keep their capital safe, set aside part of the yearly interest, and so keep their position.

Schopenhauer says that his earlier remarks about capital and interest do not apply to merchants. For merchants treat money as a tool for making more money, like a workman with his tools, so they keep and grow their capital by using it. For this reason, he adds, wealth is most firmly established among merchants.

People who have actually experienced need tend to fear it less, and so spend more freely, than people who only know poverty from hearsay. Those born into comfort are usually more careful with money than those who suddenly became rich after being poor. From this, Schopenhauer suggests that poverty may be less dreadful than it looks from a distance.

The passage contrasts two kinds of people. Those born rich treat their wealth as essential, like air, so they guard it carefully and tend to be orderly and thrifty. Those born poor see poverty as their normal state, so if they suddenly gain a fortune, they treat it as extra, to be enjoyed or spent freely.

People who have risen from poverty trust, both in their minds and their hearts, that fate and the methods that lifted them before will work again. So they do not see poverty as a bottomless pit. They comfort themselves that if they fall back, they can rise again.

Schopenhauer argues that women who were poor before marriage often demand more and spend more freely than women who brought a large dowry. He says rich brides usually come with a stronger instinct to keep their wealth. He notes that someone who disagrees can cite Ariosto, a poet, for support.

Johnson, as Schopenhauer quotes him, says a woman used to handling money spends it carefully, while one who gets money only through marriage spends it recklessly. So Schopenhauer advises that a husband who marries a poor woman should leave her only the interest from his fortune, not the capital, and keep control of the children's money away from her.

Schopenhauer says it is worth taking care to keep what one has earned or inherited. Starting life with enough to live without working is a great advantage, even if it only covers oneself, because it frees a person from the constant threat of poverty.

Being free from the forced work that every person normally must do is what counts most. Such a person is master of their own time and can say each morning that the day is their own. So the gap between having a little money and having more is much smaller than the gap between having a little and having nothing.

Inherited wealth is worth most to a person of great mental gifts who chooses a path that does not aim at making money. Such a person is favored twice by fate, so he can devote his life to his genius and produce work that benefits humanity.

A rich man can use his wealth to support good causes and help others. A man who does none of this, and does not even try to learn something useful, is judged to be a waste of time and a worthless person, however he was born into his riches.

Schopenhauer means that a man with no money worries, who has nothing he must do, does not become happy. Freedom from need brings him boredom, which is torment to him, so he might have been better off poor and busy. Bored, he spends freely, and often ends up in want.

In political life, success depends on favor, friends and connections, so Schopenhauer argues that a poor man is better placed than a wealthy one. A talented man without noble birth gains more by having no money, because people in ordinary dealings mainly want to show that others are beneath them.

Schopenhauer argues that only a complete pauper, someone who is convinced of his own worthlessness, can calmly fit into the political system. Such a person can bow to anything without resentment, and he alone sees that merit counts for nothing.

Schopenhauer says that the man who is mean-spirited and lacks real merit is the one who flatters those in power and praises their weak work. He is skilled at seeking favour, and he gets ahead. The closing German verse, quoted from Goethe, means that base aims cannot be complained about, because it is the powerful who rule the world.

A man born with enough money to live on tends to be independent and proud. He does not learn to flatter or beg, and he resents being insulted by those above him, so he becomes stubborn or withdrawn. Schopenhauer says this is not the way to succeed in the world.

Schopenhauer says that a man of limited means may at least agree with Voltaire that life is too short to spend fawning over contemptible people. He adds that such people are very common. He then quotes Juvenal: people whose narrow circumstances at home hold back their talent rarely rise. In his view, this applies more to art and literature than to politics and social climbing.

Schopenhauer says a man's wife and children should not be counted as his property. Instead, he belongs to them. Friends could be counted as possessions more easily, but a man belongs to his friends no more than they belong to him.

People tend to care too much about what others think of them, even though others' opinions do not really decide whether a person is happy. Still, people visibly brighten when praised or flattered, much as a cat purrs when stroked.

A man is pleased by praise even when it is false, if it concerns something he is proud of. Praise from others can make up for real misfortune or for having little else. In contrast, he is hurt by any slight to his sense of self-importance, however small.

Schopenhauer says that a sense of honor can help people behave well in public, serving in place of morality. But it does more harm than good to their happiness, since it disturbs their peace of mind and their independence.

The passage says we are very sensitive to what other people think of us, whether their opinion praises us or hurts us. It recommends limiting this sensitivity by judging the real worth of advantages more carefully. Praise and criticism both touch the same feeling, so the same limit applies to each.

A person who depends on the opinions of others becomes their slave. A mind that craves praise can be upset or calmed by very small things, as the Latin quotation says: it is so light and so small a thing that it can undermine or restore such a mind.

Schopenhauer says that our happiness is better served by comparing two things: what we are in ourselves, and what we are in other people's eyes. What we are in ourselves includes our personal qualities and possessions, and it exists in our own consciousness. What we are to others exists only in their minds, as the impression we make on them.

Other people's opinions of us do not reach us directly. They affect us only through how those people treat us, and only if that treatment should lead us to change what we really are. Otherwise, what others think of us in their own minds does not matter to us.

Over time we stop caring much about other people's opinions. We come to see that most people have shallow, foolish, mean, and mistaken thoughts, and that they speak slightly of others when they feel safe from fear or believe their words will not be heard.

Schopenhauer means that when even the greatest people are treated lightly by a few foolish critics, we see that caring much about public opinion gives other people far too much importance. Respect for what others say is therefore misplaced.

A person is in poor shape if he finds no happiness in what he has in himself, and must look instead to what others think of him. Happiness rests first on physical health, and second on being able to support oneself free from worry.

Schopenhauer says that the basic things that make life good, such as health and inner well-being, cannot be weighed against honor, rank and reputation. A person would give up the second group for the first if forced to choose. He adds that people would be happier if they accepted that a man's real life lies within himself, not in what others think of him.

Our own living conditions, such as health, character, ability, money, spouse, children, friends and home, matter far more to happiness than what others think of us. If we care too much about others' opinions, we will be unhappy. When people say honor is worth more than life, they mean that their own existence and well-being count for nothing next to others' opinions.

Schopenhauer suggests that the view he has just described may be an exaggeration of a plain fact: a person's reputation, meaning what others think of them, is needed to get on in the world. He returns to this point later. He then notes that people spend their lives, through great effort and danger, to gain standing in others' eyes.

Schopenhauer says that people seek offices, titles, wealth, knowledge and art mainly to earn the respect of others. He calls this a sad sign of how foolish people can be. He adds that overvaluing other people's opinion is a common mistake, perhaps rooted in human nature or in society.

Schopenhauer says that concern for what others think, whatever its cause, has too strong a hold on how people act and harms their happiness. He gives extreme examples: fear of others' opinion, a father killing his own daughter to avoid shame (Virginius, a figure from Roman legend), and men giving up life itself for fame after death. He adds that this concern is useful to those who control others.

Schopenhauer says that while keeping alive a sense of honor is central to moral training, it does not help a person's happiness. He advises against putting too much weight on what other people think, but notes that people commonly make exactly this mistake.

Most people value what others think of them more than their own inner experience, which is what is closest to them. In effect, they treat other people's opinions as real and their own consciousness as unreal, and they care more about the image they show the world than about themselves.

People who try to get a direct reward from things that have no real direct existence fall into vanity. Vanity is the right name for what has no solid or intrinsic worth. Like a miser, they lose sight of the goal while chasing the means.

Schopenhauer says that people care about others' opinions far more than any real gain could justify. He calls this a common craze that everyone inherits. He adds that much of life's trouble comes from worrying about what others will say.

Schopenhauer says that the root of vanity, pride and show is anxiety about what other people will say. He claims that most luxury and displays of honour would disappear without this worry, and that people will make large sacrifices to avoid it. He adds that the same anxiety can be seen even in a child.

Vanity and pride last longest in old age, because when the body can no longer enjoy pleasures, they are left as the main passions alongside greed. Schopenhauer uses the French as an example: he says their national vanity and boasting are so common they amount to an epidemic. Other people mock them for it, calling France "la grande nation" (the great nation), so their boasting defeats its own purpose.

Schopenhauer introduces an example of people placing too much weight on what others think of them. He plans to use a newspaper report of a 1846 execution of an apprentice who murdered his master out of revenge. The passage is only the opening of that example.

The passage describes a condemned man, Wix, who on the morning of his execution showed little interest in the clergyman attending him. His only concern was to face the watching crowd with courage. Schopenhauer uses this to show how far people will go in caring about the opinion of others.
A condemned man, Wix, walks to the gallows eagerly, quotes a saying about learning a "grand secret" at death, and bows twice on the scaffold. The crowd below responds with loud cheers.

Schopenhauer says that even a man facing execution and the afterlife may care only about how he appears to the watching crowd and what they will think of him. He gives the case of Lecompte, who was annoyed at not being allowed to appear in proper clothes before the court.

Even on the day of execution, some men cared more about how they appeared to others than about their own situation. One condemned man grieved that he could not shave, and Schopenhauer says Mateo Aleman, in his Spanish novel, reported criminals who spent their last hours memorizing speeches for the scaffold instead of preparing their souls.
Most of our anxieties, worries and efforts, Schopenhauer says, come from concern about what other people will say about us. He adds that envy and hatred often have the same root.

Schopenhauer says that people would be happier if their desire for the good opinion of others were cut down a great deal, since this desire causes constant pain. He calls it a natural flaw that is hard to overcome. The only cure he names is to see clearly that the desire is foolish.

Schopenhauer says that most people's opinions are false, foolish or worthless, so they deserve little attention. Other people's opinions also rarely affect our lives much, and hearing all the unkind things said about us would be harmful. Honor, he adds, is valuable only indirectly, not for its own sake.

If people gave up this general foolishness of caring about others' opinions, they would be far more peaceful and cheerful, and they would act with more confidence and less awkwardness. A quiet, withdrawn life helps peace of mind mainly because it spares us constant concern for what others casually think of us, so we can turn inward.

Schopenhauer says that much real suffering would be avoided if people stopped chasing empty appearances, which he calls a foolish habit. Then we would have more time for solid realities. He adds a Greek proverb: good things are hard to do.

Pride is a settled belief that you are worth more than others in some respect, held from within. Vanity is wanting others to share that belief about you, often in the hope that you will come to believe it yourself. In short, pride judges yourself directly, while vanity seeks the same judgment indirectly, through other people.

Vain people talk too much, but they would win others' good opinion more easily by staying silent, even when they have worthwhile things to say. Someone who only pretends to be proud is not truly proud, and the pretense will not last.

Pride, in Schopenhauer's sense, is a firm belief that one has special worth, whether or not that belief is correct. Like other beliefs, it is not something a person can choose at will. Vanity is different: it seeks the approval of others to create a high opinion of oneself, while true pride already has that opinion in place.

Pride is usually criticized by people who have nothing to be proud of. Schopenhauer's point is that a person with some real superiority or merit should keep it in view, because if he acts as though he were equal to everyone, others will treat him as their equal and forget what sets him apart.

People with a truly personal kind of superiority, which cannot be seen or heard at every moment as rank or titles can, should keep some distance. Otherwise familiarity breeds contempt, as the Romans said, and as the Arabian proverb about the slave who runs off after being joked with also shows.

Schopenhauer suggests that the rule of modesty benefits fools, since everyone is expected to speak of themselves as if they were foolish. He calls this "leveling down," because it makes it seem that the world holds nothing but fools.

National pride is the cheapest kind of pride, Schopenhauer says, because a person who takes pride in his nation has no real personal qualities to be proud of. Such a person turns to qualities he shares with millions of others. A man with real personal worth, by contrast, tends to notice the faults of his own nation.

Schopenhauer says that a foolish person with nothing to be proud of personally falls back on pride in his nation. He defends its faults and follies eagerly, to make up for his own lack of worth. As an example, he claims that almost no Englishman would agree that English bigotry deserves contempt, and the rare one who did would probably be an intelligent man.

Schopenhauer mocks German national pride. He says Germans have none, and that those who claim to be proud of Germany are pretending, often to mislead the crowd. He adds a joke that gunpowder's German origin is doubtful, and he quotes Lichtenberg noting that non-Germans rarely pretend to be German, preferring to pose as French or English.

Individual character matters far more than national character, Schopenhauer argues, and praising a whole nation means speaking dishonestly about the people in it. He says national traits are just the ways human faults show up in each country. Every nation mocks the others, and he thinks each is right to do so.

Rank, meaning social position, is treated briefly here. Schopenhauer says it has only a conventional value, a value created by agreement rather than by nature. Strictly speaking, he calls it a sham that demands an artificial respect, though he admits it is useful to the State.

Orders, such as medals or decorations, are described as promises of credit from the public, worth only as much as the trust placed in whoever grants them. They work like cheap substitutes for pensions and are useful when handed out carefully. Ordinary people, the author says, have little judgment or memory, so many services go unrecognized or are soon forgotten.
