Schopenhauer argues that a cross or star works as a public sign that its wearer has done something exceptional, so it sets him apart from ordinary people. Such honors lose their meaning when handed out unfairly, carelessly, or in large numbers. A medal for distinguished service, he says, already implies distinguished service, so adding those words is redundant.

Honor, Schopenhauer says, has two sides. Outwardly, it is what other people think we are worth. Inwardly, it is the respect we give to that opinion. Being a man of honor, on this view, is not purely a matter of morality, though it can be good for others.

Schopenhauer's point is that people value honor because a person alone can achieve little. Only in society, where others are present, can a man's abilities be fully used. Robinson Crusoe, the castaway on a desert island, stands for a man cut off from others.

A person, as his awareness grows, comes to want to be seen as a useful member of society, someone who does his share as a man and so earns a right to the benefits of social life. The passage then begins to say what being useful requires, starting with a first requirement that applies everywhere.

A person quickly learns that his worth depends on being useful in the eyes of others, not in his own view. So he works to make a good impression on the world. Schopenhauer calls this innate tendency the feeling of honor, or, seen another way, the feeling of shame.

A person feels shame at the idea of losing other people's good opinion, even when he is innocent or has only failed a duty he took on himself. In contrast, believing that others think well of him gives him great courage.

Schopenhauer means that a person's good standing with others brings help and protection from many others together. He says this shields a person from life's troubles far better than anything the person could do alone.

Schopenhauer says that people's trust and good opinion of a man can rest on three kinds of honor. Civic honor concerns how a man treats other people's property and rights. Official honor concerns whether he keeps his promises and duties. Sexual honor concerns his conduct in relation to the sexes.

Civic honor is the reputation that a person will fully respect the rights of others and never use unjust or illegal means to get what they want. It is what makes peaceful dealings between people possible. Anything that openly breaks this peace, and that the law would fairly punish, destroys it.

Honor rests on the belief that a person's moral character cannot change, so one bad action shows that similar bad actions will follow. Once honor is lost, it cannot be regained, unless the loss was based on a mistake, such as slander or a false view of the person's actions.

Schopenhauer says that when someone insults another person, it shows the insulter has no real grounds for complaint. A proper complaint would give its reasons, but the abuser only states the conclusion, hoping listeners will assume the reasons were left out just to be brief.

Civic honor, or the good name a person has in the eyes of society, applies to everyone, even the highest ranks. Once a person breaks someone's trust, that trust is lost for good, whoever that person is, and the harm that follows cannot be undone.

Honor, according to this passage, means being thought to have the ordinary qualities a person is expected to have, and not failing in them. Fame means standing out from others. Honor can only be lost, while fame must be won, and having no fame is simply obscurity, whereas losing honor brings shame.

Honor, in this passage, is something a person creates through his own conduct, not something others can give or take away. It depends only on what he himself does or fails to do, not on other people's actions or the obstacles they put in his way. The Greek phrase means "things within our own power."
Slander is the only way someone can damage a person's honor from outside. The only defense is to disprove the slander openly and to expose the person who spread it.

Respect for age exists because older people have had a long life in which to show whether they kept their honor intact. Young people are given the same respect, but their honor has not yet been tested.

Schopenhauer argues that age alone does not deserve the respect young people are expected to give the old. Years and experience are not enough reason, since the frailty of old age would call for pity rather than respect. Still, he notes that white hair naturally earns reverence.

Wrinkles, though they are a surer sign of old age, do not earn respect. People speak of venerable white hair, but never of venerable wrinkles. Respect is given to grey hair, not to the lines of the face.

Honor matters only for what it brings in practice. What others think of us affects us only through how they treat us, and only while we deal with them. Society, the author says, is what keeps our safety and possessions secure.

Other people's opinion of us matters mainly because we need their help and their trust to get things done. Schopenhauer sees no direct value in reputation itself. He agrees with Cicero, who said a good name is worth little effort except for its usefulness.

Schopenhauer says that Helvetius argued we value esteem only for the benefits it brings, not for its own sake. Since a means can never be worth more than the end it serves, the saying that honor is dearer than life is exaggerated.

Official honor is the general belief that a man holding an office is truly capable of carrying out its duties. The more important the office and its duties to the State, the stronger the belief must be about the man's moral and mental qualities for the job.

Schopenhauer says that a person's official rank sets how much honor is due to him, shown through titles, decorations and deference from others. Someone with special duties is honored more than an ordinary citizen, whose honor mainly means not being disgraced.

An official must defend the respect due to his office, both for his colleagues and for future holders of it. He does this by doing his duties properly and by answering any attack on the office or its holder. He should not let claims pass that the office is badly run or useless, and should use the legal penalties against such attacks.

Schopenhauer says that people who serve the State in other roles, such as doctors, lawyers and teachers, are held in honor second only to government officials. This applies to anyone who has qualified in a subject or publicly declared a skill and so claims the right to practise it.

Military honor, in the true sense, is the public belief that soldiers who have sworn to defend their country have the qualities needed for that task. These qualities are courage, personal bravery and strength. It also means they are ready to die for their country and never desert the flag they have sworn to.

Schopenhauer says that he is using the word "official honor" more broadly than usual. Normally it means the respect citizens owe to a public office itself, and he is extending it to cover more than that.

Schopenhauer says that the idea of sexual honor rests on practical, useful grounds, and he sets out to show this. He splits the subject into the honor of women and the honor of men, each with its own shared sense of group loyalty. He judges women's honor to be the more important, because a woman's life centres on her relationship to men.

Schopenhauer argues that "female honor" means a girl being seen as pure and a wife as faithful. He says this matters because women depend on men in almost every part of life, while men depend on women in only one. Men therefore take on responsibility for women's needs and their children, and this arrangement supports the welfare of women as a whole.

Schopenhauer argues that women, in his view, unite as a group to win men and the goods men control. Their shared aim is to make men marry them, by insisting that women give themselves only within marriage.

Schopenhauer describes a rule that women keep: a woman must not have sexual relations outside marriage. He says that by keeping it, women secure marriage for the whole female group. A woman who breaks the rule is cast out by other women, as is a woman who breaks her marriage.

Schopenhauer argues that a wife who is unfaithful breaks the terms of her marriage, and this harms all women, because it makes men wary of marrying. He says such a breach is a crime that costs a woman her civic honor as well as her personal honor. That is why a girl's loss of honor can be repaired by marriage, but a wife's cannot.

Schopenhauer says that the shared sense of honor among women, which he calls esprit de corps, is a useful and necessary matter of prudence and self-interest, and so important for women's welfare. Still, it is only valuable for what it serves. It is not an ultimate goal that stands above all else, even life itself.

Schopenhauer says that extreme, showy acts of honor, such as those of the Roman figures Lucretia and Virginius, deserve no praise. Such acts can turn into absurdity and leave the viewer uneasy. He gives the endings of two plays as examples of this unease.

Schopenhauer says that taking the idea of a woman's honor too far means losing sight of its purpose and treating the means as the goal. Such excess treats sexual honor as absolute, when he holds it is more relative than any other kind of honor.

Schopenhauer suggests that the value placed on female honor is only a matter of custom. He points to Thomasius, who reports that in many times and places, up to the Reformation, sexual irregularities were allowed by law without harming a woman's honor. He also mentions the temple of Mylitta in Babylon, where such practices were part of religious life.

Schopenhauer argues that where marriage is legally impossible, as in Catholic countries without divorce, a ruling prince would do better to live without a formal marriage than to enter a morganatic one. A morganatic marriage is a union in which the spouse and children have no claim to the rank or throne, and the children could still claim the throne if the legitimate line died out.

Schopenhauer argues that a marriage made without the usual public ceremony gives too much freedom to women and priests, so such marriages should be avoided. He then notes that a prince is the one man who cannot freely choose his wife, since his marriage must serve the state, though he still wants to follow his heart like any other man.

It says it would be wrong to forbid a prince from having a love affair of this kind, provided the lady has no say in running the government. The author argues that such a woman stands outside the usual rules of sexual honor, because she has given herself to a man she loves but cannot marry.

Schopenhauer argues that the importance placed on female honor is not natural, since it has led people to kill children and to take their own lives. He adds that a girl who breaks the code wrongs her sex only in a secret, unspoken way, and that she mainly harms her own future, so her mistake is worse than her offence.

Schopenhauer says that men have a shared sense of loyalty, a kind of group code, that requires a married man to keep the marriage terms. He argues that this keeps the agreement strong and gives men at least one thing in return for giving up so much: exclusive possession of their wife.

According to Schopenhauer, a man is expected to resent his wife's adultery and at least separate from her. If he forgives it, others will shame him, but his shame is far less serious than the shame a woman suffers, because a man's marriage is only one of many important matters in his life.

Schopenhauer notes that Shakespeare and Calderón each wrote two plays about a man's honor. He says honor only requires punishing the wife, and punishing her lover goes beyond what honor demands. He takes this as support for his view that honor comes from loyalty to one's group.

Schopenhauer says that the kind of honor he has been discussing has existed in many forms among all peoples and times, though its rules on women's honor have changed in some places and periods. He adds a second kind of honor, which the Greeks and Romans did not know and which, he says, is unknown to Chinese, Hindus and Muslims.

Schopenhauer says that knightly honor, or point d'honneur, arose only in the Middle Ages and belongs to Christian Europe, and only to the upper classes and those who imitate them. Its principles differ from, and in some ways oppose, the honor he has discussed so far. He plans to set out its principles as a kind of code.

Honor, as Schopenhauer defines it here, does not depend on what people privately think of us. It depends only on whether they say their opinion out loud. If no one openly voices a low opinion, our honor stays intact, even if others despise us in secret.

If our conduct wins other people's full respect, then any slighting remark, even from a wicked or foolish person, is taken as an injury to our honor. Schopenhauer adds that the honor is lost for good unless we can win it back.

In Schopenhauer's view, knightly honor rests on what a person says publicly, not on what others privately think. Proof of this is that an insult can be withdrawn or apologized for, which makes it as if it was never spoken, whatever the speaker actually believed.

Schopenhauer's point is that this kind of honor depends not on what a man does himself but on how others treat him. Anyone who insults him can take it away with a few words, and the only way to win it back is a dangerous process, one that can cost his life, health, freedom, property or peace of mind.

A man can be good, wise and noble, yet still lose his honor the moment any person insults him, even a worthless person who has no standing himself. Schopenhauer adds that such worthless people are usually the ones who like to insult others.

Schopenhauer says that the more worthless and ridiculous a man is, the more ready he is to insult others. Such insults usually aim at people of real merit, because people with different tastes cannot be friends, and a worthless man resents a person who stands out. Goethe is cited to say that complaining about enemies is pointless, since a person whose whole being reproaches them will never win them over.

Schopenhauer says that people of low worth benefit from the code of honor, since it places them level with far better people. A insult, such as calling someone bad, is taken at first as a true, well-founded judgment, and unless it is answered in blood, it stands for good.

Schopenhauer says that a man who is insulted and does not fight back is, in the view of "honorable" people, whatever the insulter called him, even if the insulter is a worthless person. Because he has accepted the insult, decent people keep away from him, as if he were a leper, and may refuse to join any gathering he attends.

In medieval courts the accused, not the accuser, had to prove innocence. He could swear to his innocence and find people to swear that he was not a liar. If he had no such supporters, or the accuser rejected them, the matter was settled by trial by combat, usually a duel.

Schopenhauer traces the modern idea of honor and disgrace back to older legal practice, where an accused person had to clear his name, perhaps by oath. He says the code of honorable people today keeps this idea but drops the oath. Being called a liar must be answered in blood, that is, by a duel, though this rarely happens, and he calls the belief especially strong in England.

Schopenhauer's point is that a man who threatens to kill someone for lying should not have lied himself, since the threat only makes sense if the accusation is true. He compares this to the old medieval trial, where a denial of the charge was settled by trial by combat, and to the knightly code, where an accusation of lying led to a duel. The passage mocks the idea that such violence proves who is right.

In this passage, the worst insult of all is being struck with a slap or a blow, which Schopenhauer treats as worse than death. Other insults can be answered with a duel, but a blow can only be wiped out by killing the opponent.

Schopenhauer says that this kind of honor has nothing to do with a person's real inner worth or moral character. If a man's honor is attacked or seems lost, he can get it back at once by fighting a duel.

If the attacker is not from a class that follows the code of knightly honor, or has broken that code himself, the passage says a safer answer exists. If you are armed, you may strike him down right away or later, and this, it claims, restores your honor.

If you do not want to fight a duel, Schopenhauer says there is another way to defend your standing: the "Avantage." It means answering rudeness with greater rudeness, and, if insults fail, striking a blow.

Schopenhauer describes a chain of escalating responses to insult: a slap is answered with a stick, a stick with a horsewhip, and the horsewhip with spitting. If none of these works, a man must be ready to draw blood. The passage ends before it gives the reason for these methods.

Schopenhauer's point is that in matters of honor, insulting someone gains honor for the insulter and takes it from the one insulted, whatever the truth or reason in the dispute. The insulted person can only win honor back by violence, such as fighting a duel, not by proving he is right. So rudeness outweighs every other claim, and the rudest person is always, in this sense, right.

Rudeness, Schopenhauer says, can excuse any fault, however bad a man is. When someone else is cleverer or wiser in a discussion, a person can wipe out that advantage by insulting him. Insults, he claims, work better than any argument.

Schopenhauer says that when someone meets an attack with rudeness, the contest turns into a fight over who can be ruder. Whoever wins that fight is seen as having honor, while truth, knowledge and wit are pushed aside.

Schopenhauer says that people who feel honor is at stake, when their opinion is challenged or someone is cleverer than they are, quickly turn to insult when they have no answer. They then claim victory. He adds, with irony, that people praise this "honor" as improving society, and that it comes from a deeper principle at the core of the code of honor.

Schopenhauer says that the code of honor treats physical force as the final judge of a quarrel. Every insult is, in effect, a call to settle things by brutality rather than by reason or moral insight, and the outcome of such a fight is final. He calls this the principle of "right of might," and says the honor of a knight is really the glory of might.

Schopenhauer contrasts two codes of conduct. Civic honor, the respectability of ordinary citizens, keeps strictly to property rights and to promises. The code of honor he is discussing is more relaxed about promises: only a pledge given on one's honor must never be broken, and all other promises are assumed to be breakable.

Schopenhauer's point is that the code of honor makes some obligations absolute and others optional. A broken promise can be defended by a duel, and gambling debts must always be paid, but other debts may be left unpaid, even to Jews and Christians, without harming one's honor.

Schopenhauer argues that the European code of honor, with its duels and sensitivity to insult, has no basis in human nature or in sound common sense. He notes that it has applied only to a small group, the upper classes, officers, soldiers and those who copy them, and only in Europe since the Middle Ages. The ancient Greeks and Romans knew nothing of it.

Schopenhauer says that the civilized peoples of Asia, past and present, recognized only one kind of honor: a person's worth lies in what he actually does, not in what others say about him. Their view was that words could not damage another person's honor, and a blow was just a physical hit, one that a horse or donkey could also give.

Schopenhauer says that ancient Greeks and Romans had no concept of honor in the modern sense. They did not track insults or blows or demand satisfaction for them. He adds that the ancients were just as brave and unafraid of death as Christian Europeans, but they had no "point d'honneur," a French term for the code of honor that governed dueling among nobles.

Schopenhauer says that Roman gladiator fights were deadly contests between slaves, criminals and captives, staged for public entertainment. When Christianity ended them, the duel took their place as a way of settling disputes, supposedly by God's judgment. He calls dueling a sacrifice to social prejudice, but one that claims free and noble men rather than the condemned.

The passage says the ancient Greeks and Romans were free of certain social prejudices about honour and insult. Its examples are Marius, who answered a German chief's challenge to a duel with scorn, and Themistocles, who was threatened with a stick by the Greek admiral Eurybiades and did not treat it as a matter of honour.

Themistocles, an Athenian general, is struck or threatened by a fellow officer but answers only, "Strike, but hear me," without drawing his sword. Schopenhauer mocks the idea that such a man would be seen as dishonorable, and notes that a French writer called Demosthenes and Cicero dishonorable too.

Schopenhauer notes that ancient Greeks did not treat physical assault as a matter of personal honor. Socrates, often beaten after his debates, accepted such blows calmly. When a friend was surprised that someone had kicked him, Socrates asked whether he would be offended if an ass had kicked him.

Ancient wise men did not take insults personally. One man answered that an abuser's words were not really aimed at him. The ancients had only one legal way to get satisfaction for an insult, such as a slap, and wise people looked down on even that.

Schopenhauer tells of Lucius Veratius, a Roman who struck passing citizens for no reason. To avoid serious consequences, he had a slave bring small coins and paid the minor legal fine on the spot. The point is that he treated the insult as a cheap price he could afford to pay.

Schopenhauer uses two stories about ancient Greek philosophers who were beaten. Crates was struck by the musician Nicodromus, and he wore a label on his forehead naming his attacker, which shamed Nicodromus. Diogenes was beaten by drunken young Athenians.

Schopenhauer notes that Seneca, in his discussion of insult, holds that a wise man ignores it. Seneca offers Cato as the model: when someone struck Cato in the face, Cato neither reacted angrily nor struck back, but simply let it pass. When it is objected that Cato was a philosopher, Schopenhauer ironically replies that the objectors must then be fools.

Schopenhauer says the ancients did not treat a slap in the face as a serious insult. To them it was just a minor physical hurt. Modern people, he claims, turn such a blow into a major disaster, as in the play The Cid or a German comedy he mentions.

Schopenhauer says that a blow to a French legislator's ear would be widely reported across Europe. He then points to a story in Diderot's novel Jacques le fataliste as an example of modern knightly honor, which he expects readers to find amusing and instructive. The remark is ironic, since the story is presented as a model of how such insults are handled.

Schopenhauer argues that the code of knightly honor is not a natural part of human nature but an artificial invention. He ties its origin to the Middle Ages, when force settled disputes more than reason, the Church controlled thinking, and trials were decided by ordeals believed to be God's judgment.

Schopenhauer says that in the past a challenge to a duel, usually to the death, could be used to answer almost any judgment, for nobles and ordinary citizens alike. He argues that this put physical strength in place of reason. Right and wrong were decided by who could fight better, not by what a person had actually done.

Some people who still defend dueling believe that the winner of a duel shows which side is right, as if God had judged the dispute. Schopenhauer suggests this belief comes from old tradition rather than careful thought, and he says its supporters are usually not the most educated or thoughtful people.

Schopenhauer says that the idea of knightly honor mainly uses physical threat to force an appearance of respect that people cannot or will not earn in reality. Civic honor, by contrast, rests on others trusting that we respect their rights, while knightly honor wants us to be feared because we will defend ourselves at any cost.

Schopenhauer says that since people cannot be fully trusted, it might once have made sense to rely on inspiring fear rather than trust. That was true in a state of nature, where each person had to defend his own rights. In civilized life, where the state protects person and property, the idea no longer applies, like an old castle left standing in a peaceful countryside.

Knightly honor, the old code of gentlemen, still responds to insults in this way, but only for small personal attacks. The law either punishes these lightly or not at all, since the law ignores trivial wrongs, and such wrongs are sometimes committed just as a joke.

Schopenhauer is describing the code of honour, where people treat even small insults as serious matters. He says this comes from excessive pride. Because the state punishes such slights too lightly, people take revenge themselves, sometimes by attacking the offender's life or body. Such people expect to be free from any attack or criticism at all.

Schopenhauer says that people who try to enforce the rule "whoever insults or strikes me shall die" by brute force, making it their way of acting, deserve to be banished from their country. The "principle" refers to the earlier point about defending one's honour against insult.

Schopenhauer says people usually avoid this kind of quarrel by giving way on everything. He argues that when two proud men refuse to yield, a small disagreement can escalate from insults to blows and even death, so it would be more proper to skip straight to a duel, which has its own set formal rules.

Schopenhauer is describing the code of honor, the rules that govern duels. He says these rules are an absurd ceremony. When two bold men quarrel over something trivial, the wiser one will back down, and they agree to disagree.

Schopenhauer means that people who do not live by the code of knightly honor let disputes end on their own, and so they rarely kill or even strike one another. The few who follow that code account for far more killings, even though they are a tiny share of the population.

Schopenhauer argues that good manners do not depend on the code of honor and duelling. He points out that ancient Athens, Corinth and Rome had refined society without it. He also says that women played a smaller public role then, and that conversation was more serious.

Schopenhauer argues that personal courage is a minor virtue, the mark of a junior officer, and that animals such as lions surpass people in it. He adds that "knightly honor," the code of gentlemen's honor, protects dishonesty, wickedness and rudeness, because people avoid confronting rude behavior for fear of being challenged to a duel.

Schopenhauer suggests that the nation with the most fierce devotion to duelling is also one whose political and financial dealings are not very honourable. He adds that its private manners are a matter for people who know it well, and says its politeness and social refinement have long been missing.

People tend to answer hostility with hostility, just as a dog snarls when snarled at and fawns when petted. Insults and contempt hurt and provoke anger in almost everyone, even wise and worthy people. Only a few religious groups, the author says, take an insult or a blow calmly.

Schopenhauer argues that a fitting reply to an insult should match the offence, and that death is never a fair penalty for calling someone a liar, a fool, or a coward. He calls the old German idea of "blood for a blow" a shameful superstition from the age of chivalry. He adds that answering an insult comes from anger, not from any real duty of honor.

Schopenhauer says that people react more strongly to a small charge that is true than to a severe charge that is false. A man who knows an accusation is baseless can ignore it safely. The code of honor, however, expects him to feel offence he does not feel and to fight over insults. Fighting to stop someone's opinion, he suggests, shows a low opinion of oneself.

Schopenhauer says that a man who truly knows his own worth will not be bothered by an insult. If he still feels angry, he can hide it, and he would do better to drop the belief that insults take away honor and that answering an insult with another insult restores it.

Schopenhauer says that if people stopped believing that a willingness to duel can make wrongs, bullying and insults acceptable, everyone would come to see that an insult is a battle the loser wins. He adds, quoting the Italian poet Vincenzo Monti, that abuse is like a church procession: it always ends up back where it started.

Schopenhauer says that if people did not take insults so personally, no one would need to be rude to prove a point. In reality, a serious view often offends a dull person, who reacts with alarm and anger to any sign of intelligence. So a clever mind may end up in conflict with an empty-headed one.

If the usual social distinctions were removed, intellectual ability would take the top place in society that it deserves. At present, Schopenhauer says, physical strength and plain courage hold that place, though people rarely admit it. Then the best people would have less reason to keep away from society, and real courtesy and good company could develop, as he says they did in ancient Athens, Corinth and Rome.

Schopenhauer answers the claim that knightly honor keeps the world from becoming a brawl. He argues that people who do not follow the code often exchange blows without deadly results, while those who follow it usually see a blow end in death for one side.

Schopenhauer says he has tried, without success, to find good reasons for the widespread belief that being struck is a very dreadful thing. He calls a blow a trivial physical injury that one person can do to another, not a serious harm in itself.

Schopenhauer says that a blow from a person's hand is felt as a deep insult, while a much harder blow from a horse is shrugged off. He concludes that the human hand is the real source of the offence, not the pain itself.

Schopenhauer notes that a knight in battle may be wounded yet dismiss the injuries as trivial. He points out that a blow from the flat of a sword counts as less shameful than a blow from a stick, and that the accolade, a knighting tap with a sword, is the highest honor. He says these distinctions are all the basis he can find for such attitudes.

Schopenhauer says that a certain belief, which he has been discussing, is an old superstition that spread only because of tradition. He supports this by noting that in China, beating with a bamboo stick is a common punishment for ordinary people and officials alike, so human nature there differs from European habits.

Schopenhauer argues that hitting is as natural to humans as biting is to wild animals or butting to horned animals. So man is, in his view, the animal that strikes. A man being bitten by another man offends our sense of what is fitting, while being struck, or striking, is an ordinary event.

The passage argues that the idea of a blow as a disgrace needing blood to wash it away is a harmful superstition. Schopenhauer says it causes real deaths and murders, adding to the genuine evils of the world with imaginary ones. He calls this belief both foolish and harmful.

Schopenhauer argues that governments are unwise to abolish flogging as a punishment. They think they are helping humanity, but he says that ending it will only strengthen a cruel and harmful belief that honour can be restored or protected by such punishment.

Schopenhauer argues that, for most offences except the very worst, beating is the natural punishment, since a person who will not accept reason will give in to blows. He thinks corporal punishment is fitting for a poor man who cannot pay a fine, or who cannot be jailed without harming his employer's interests.

Schopenhauer argues that the objection to flogging rests on a vague belief in human dignity, not on clear reasoning. He offers an example: militaries once swapped the cat-o'-nine-tails for a stick, though both aimed at causing physical pain.

The passage argues that the state encourages the idea of knightly honor, which leads to dueling, while claiming to ban duels by law. It says this idea, that might is right, survives from the Middle Ages and should be removed entirely.

Schopenhauer argues that the code of dueling forces men into deadly fights over trivial matters, which he calls ridiculous and superstitious. He suggests that the word "duel" be replaced by "baiting," since it may come from the Spanish word for suffering or annoyance, not from the Latin for war.

Schopenhauer says that the code of honour, which he calls a foolish system, has grown absurdly strict. He describes it as a power inside the state, a state within a state, that recognises only force. It acts like an inquisition, hauling people in on flimsy grounds to settle matters of life and death in a duel.

Schopenhauer says that people of low character, if they belong to certain social classes, can use their position to attack and even destroy good people, whom they hate for being good. He then notes that modern justice and police now stop a street robber from demanding money or life.

Schopenhauer says that people of high social rank should not have to risk their lives and bodies at the whim of any rude or foolish person. He calls it outrageous that two hot-headed young men can be wounded or killed over a few angry words, meaning duels.

Schopenhauer says that the rule of honor is so strong that some men, unable to restore their honor because the other man is higher or lower in rank, kill themselves in despair. He points to an absurdity: an officer may not fight a duel, yet if he refuses a challenge he is dismissed from the service.

Schopenhauer argues that the difference people draw between a fair duel and an ambush is based on the idea that might makes right. A fair fight proves only that one man is stronger or more skilled, so calling it justified means accepting that the stronger has the right.

Being able to kill an opponent who cannot defend himself only gives the chance to do it, not the right. Whether the act is justified depends on the killer's motives. Once a motive exists, the way the killing is done, such as skill with a weapon or attacking from the front or behind, makes no difference.

Schopenhauer argues that being stronger is no more morally right than being more skilled. Both are simply ways of getting an advantage, and a trick in a duel is just a form of treachery. So if you think you are justified in killing someone, it is foolish to first check whether he is the better shot or swordsman.

Rousseau held that the right way to avenge an insult is not a duel but murder of the insulter. Schopenhauer says this shows Rousseau still bound by the old knightly idea of honor, which would justify killing a man who calls you a liar. He adds that Rousseau must have known everyone deserves that charge at times.

Schopenhauer says the custom of dueling treats might as right and sees a duel as God's judgment. An Italian who kills his attacker on the spot in anger, without ceremony, acts more openly and naturally. He is no worse than the duelist.

Schopenhauer answers a defence of dueling: the claim that killing an opponent is self-defence. He replies that the challenger caused the danger, so the fight is really a pretext for murder. He prefers a different justification: both sides freely agree to risk their lives, so no wrong is done to either.

The argument is answered by saying the injured man did not consent to the harm (volens, Latin for "willing"). Schopenhauer says the real cause is the rule of knightly honour, with its absurd code, which forces at least one of the fighters into a bloody duel.

Schopenhauer says he spent a long time on the idea of knightly honor because he thinks the great mass of moral and intellectual wrong in the world can only be swept away by philosophy. The "Augean stable" is an allusion to a filthy stable in Greek myth that took heroic effort to clean, and the "besom" is a broom.

Schopenhauer says that two things make modern social life look worse than ancient life: modern honor and modern disease. He calls them a pair of brothers, and he says they have together spoiled every part of life, public and private.

Sexual love, probably the second of two things named earlier, does more harm than it seems: it is a moral as well as a bodily sickness. Because its arrows are poisoned, fear and mistrust, even something devilish, enter relations between men and women like a dark thread woven through them.

The passage says that a certain thing indirectly weakens the basis of human society and so affects the whole course of a person's life. The author then says he will not explore the subject further, because it lies outside his present aim.

Schopenhauer argues that the code of knightly honor is a foolish custom that makes European society stiff and wary, so that people watch every word they say. He calls it a Minotaur, a monster that demands a yearly tribute of young men from noble families across Europe. He wishes this and similar harmful customs would end soon.

The passage hopes that medicine can prevent one evil and that philosophy can end the other by clarifying people's ideals. Schopenhauer argues that the evil can only be removed by clearing up ideas, and notes that governments tried to fix it through laws and failed. The "one" and "other" refer to evils named just before this passage, which the excerpt does not state.

Schopenhauer proposes a law against dueling that uses no death penalty, scaffold or long imprisonment. Anyone who sends or accepts a challenge would be publicly beaten with a stick, twelve strokes for an officer and six for a common soldier. If a duel actually happens, normal criminal proceedings would follow.

Schopenhauer is arguing against dueling. He says a man with old-fashioned ideas of honor might claim that a harsh punishment would drive honorable men to suicide, and he answers that such men would be better off killing themselves than killing others. He then claims governments do not seriously want to stop dueling, pointing out that officers and officials are poorly paid.

Honor, shown through titles, orders and rank, is said to make up for what officers lack in pay. Schopenhauer's point is that the duel is a useful extra for people of rank, which is why they learn about it at university. The risks of dueling, he says, pay in blood what the salary does not.

A nation's honor, in Schopenhauer's view, is its standing among other nations. Since there is no higher court to settle disputes, a nation must be seen as both trustworthy and able to defend its rights, so that no attack goes unanswered.

Honor and fame are compared to twins, like Castor and Pollux, one of whom was mortal and one immortal. Honor lasts only as long as the person lives, while true fame lasts forever. Honor is given for qualities that anyone in the same situation might be expected to show, but fame is given only for qualities that no one can be required to show.

Honor is what a person may claim for himself, based on his own qualities, and it reaches only as far as people actually know him. Fame is different: it is granted by others, spreads beyond those who know a person, and is open only to those with exceptional achievements.

Fame can be won in two ways: by deeds or by works. Deeds depend on a great heart, works on a great mind. The main difference is that deeds pass away quickly, while works of genius keep their influence for many ages.

Actions fade from memory over time, and only history keeps a faint record of them. Works of the mind last much longer, since writings such as those of Plato, Homer and the Vedas remain alive and still act on people today, while the deeds of Alexander survive mainly as a name and a record.

Schopenhauer contrasts two kinds of fame. A great deed becomes famous quickly with a loud burst of attention, but that attention fades, and the deed ends up as a faint mention in history. A great work starts quietly and grows over time, and because the work survives, its fame can last for thousands of years.

Actions depend on chance to happen at all, and their fame comes partly from the circumstances that made them important, not only from their own worth. Also, fame for personal deeds, such as in war, rests on fewer witnesses, who may be absent or unfair.

Actions are easy for ordinary people to understand, so once the facts are reported correctly, people judge them fairly right away. The exception is when the reason behind the action is missed at first. An action cannot be properly understood without knowing the motive that prompted it.

Unlike a person's position in others' eyes, which can depend on chance, a work of art or thought depends entirely on its author, and it stays what it is for as long as it exists. Judging such works is hard, since few people are qualified or fair, but their fame can be appealed to other judges over time.

Schopenhauer is saying that deeds reach later generations only as remembered stories, which can be distorted, while written works usually survive in their original form. Any bias that surrounded a work when it first appeared fades over time, so later readers judge it on its own merits.

Schopenhauer says that great works are often judged correctly only after a long time, when rare, competent critics arrive and give their verdicts one after another. Once these judgments build up, they form a fair assessment that later time cannot overturn, even when it has taken centuries to form.

Whether an author lives to see his fame begin depends on chance, and the greater the work, the less likely he is to see it. Schopenhauer quotes Seneca's saying that fame follows merit as a shadow follows a body, sometimes ahead of it and sometimes behind.

Schopenhauer notes that Seneca said envy can keep good work unnoticed through silence, though later judges will assess it fairly. He takes this to show that people have long deliberately ignored merit and hidden good work to favor poor work, a tactic he says is still used today.

Generally, the longer a person's fame is likely to last, the later it arrives, because good work takes time to develop. Lasting fame grows slowly like an oak, short-lived fame springs up quickly like a yearly plant, and false fame appears overnight like a mushroom and dies just as fast.

Writers whose work speaks to all of humanity across time tend to seem strange to their own contemporaries, because their work lacks the local familiarity that would make it appeal to them. People usually value those who respond to their own time and its passing mood.

The greatest works of the human mind, the passage says, are usually not welcomed when they first appear. They stay unknown until people of high intelligence notice them and bring them into public view. After that, their standing rests on the authority that those people gave them.

People can only truly understand and appreciate things that are like themselves. Dull people enjoy what is dull, ordinary people enjoy what is ordinary, and muddled thinkers enjoy confusion. Most of all, a person likes his own work, because it matches his own nature.
It means that people who are pleased with themselves should not surprise us. Each creature finds its own kind the best thing in the world: a dog thinks a dog is best, an ox an ox, and so on.

A very strong arm cannot drive a feather far, because the feather is too light. It soon drops to the ground, having used up the little force it was given, since it has no weight of its own to carry that force forward.

Great thoughts and masterpieces are wasted on small, weak, or perverse minds, which cannot understand or value them. Schopenhauer supports this with a saying from Ecclesiasticus, a fool hears a tale as if asleep, and a line from Hamlet. The German verse adds that a stone dropped into a swamp makes no ripples.

Schopenhauer quotes Lichtenberg and Gellert to make one point: many people cannot recognise good work. When a book seems empty, the fault may lie with the reader, not the book. Most people praise the trivial and overlook the best, and they cannot change this, since the foolish would have to become wise first, which they never do.

Schopenhauer says that people's failure to recognize real merit is joined by envy. When someone wins new fame, others feel lowered by comparison, so every outstanding achievement seems to cost those who have none. He quotes Goethe: when we give honour to others, we lower ourselves.

Ordinary people, who make up most of humanity, tend to band together against anyone who is truly excellent, trying to hold them back. Even established figures dislike new rivals, and people often ignore others simply to seem important themselves.
If I had waited to be born until others gave me permission to live, I would never have come into the world. The verse mocks people who want to look important and would gladly deny others their place.

Honor is usually granted to everyone unless proven otherwise, and envy does not stand in its way. Fame, by contrast, must be won against envy, and it shrinks as more people share in it. Honor can be shared freely, but fame cannot.

Schopenhauer says that fame is harder to win the fewer readers a work is likely to have. So a learned book is harder to make famous than a book meant only to entertain. Philosophical works are the hardest of all, because their aim is vague, brings no material use, and they mainly reach readers already working on the same questions.

Schopenhauer argues that people who work mainly for personal ambition rarely produce lasting works. Those who truly seek the good must resist popular opinion, and fame tends to avoid those who chase it and find those who ignore it, because the first adapt to their contemporaries' taste while the second work against it.

Fame, once won, is easy to keep, because the deed that earned it can never be undone and it stays with its author even if he does nothing more. Honor works the other way: it is given to everyone by default and needs only to be kept, but one unworthy act can destroy it for good.

Fame that fades, or is later surpassed, shows that it was never deserved and rested on a brief over-rating of someone's work. Schopenhauer adds that fame built by admiring students, like Hegel's, will seem empty to future generations, who will find no real thought behind the grand, word-filled reputation.

Fame only means how a man stands compared with others, so it is not valuable in itself. It disappears once others reach the same level. What has real worth is what a person is in himself, such as a great heart or a great mind, and that is what a man should value more than fame.

Fame is not the real thing a person has. It is only an outside sign that confirms what he already thinks of himself. Fame does not prove merit, since some people have fame without deserving it, and others deserve it without having fame.

Schopenhauer says it would be a poor kind of life if a person's worth depended on what others thought of them. Even a hero or genius would be living such a life if his value rested only on public praise. Each person lives mainly for himself, and what he is matters to him more than it matters to anyone else.

Schopenhauer argues that a person's worth is not measured by what others think of them. Other people's opinions are secondary and depend on chance, so they affect a person only indirectly. Placing happiness in others' minds gives only an imagined happiness, not a real one.

Schopenhauer says that fame's temple holds a mixed crowd of generals, ministers, performers, millionaires and Jews. People there receive real respect for their various talents, while great intellectual ability gets only empty words of praise from most people.

Schopenhauer says fame adds little to real happiness. It is only a rare treat for pride and vanity, which exist in everyone, and are strongest in those who most want to be famous. Such people often wait uncertainly for a chance to prove their worth, and meanwhile feel they are being treated unfairly.

Schopenhauer says people give other people's opinions far more value than they deserve. He agrees with Hobbes that we feel joy when we compare ourselves with others and conclude we can think well of ourselves. That is why people will make any sacrifice for fame, even with only a slight chance of getting it.

Vain people talk a lot about glory, trusting it to inspire great deeds. But fame, the passage says, is secondary: it is only an echo or shadow of real merit. Whatever earns admiration must be worth more than the admiration itself.

A person is made happy not by fame itself but by the qualities that earn it, whether moral or intellectual. A man's own best qualities matter far more to him than anyone else's view of them, which affects him only slightly.

A person who deserves fame but never receives it still has the more important source of happiness. Being truly great matters more than being admired by the crowd, and his happiness lies in having produced thoughts worth keeping and studying for centuries, not in being remembered by later generations.

Schopenhauer says that what a man has in himself cannot be taken away, unlike fame, which depends on what others think. Fame that is not earned is empty, because the person holds the outward sign of fame without the real substance behind it. Such a person may even come to feel dissatisfied with himself.

A person who has risen above his real worth may one day feel exposed, like counterfeit coin or a man who holds his property under a forged will. He will then see how the wise judge him. Yet the fame that comes after death is never known to the one who receives it, though he is still called happy.

Schopenhauer says that a great man's happiness came from two things: his outstanding qualities, which brought him fame, and the free time to use them and follow what he loved. He adds that only work done with real passion earns lasting honor.

Schopenhauer says that a great mind makes its owner happy, and that its best thoughts give that happiness at once. Fame after death matters only because it shows the work deserved it, and the deserving is itself the reward. Whether the work is praised during the author's life is a matter of chance and of little importance.

Most people cannot judge a difficult work for themselves, so they accept whatever authorities praise. Widespread fame therefore rests mostly on borrowed belief. A famous man should not place much value on it, since it often comes from a few voices favored by chance.
The point is that applause from a crowd means little if the applauders cannot really hear, or are paid to clap. The musician would have no reason to feel flattered by praise that is faked or bought.

Praise from one's own time rarely lasts into fame after death, according to the author. He cites d'Alembert's image of a temple of literary fame, where the great dead dwell and only a few living people hold a place, most of whom are later removed. He adds that a monument raised during a man's lifetime implies that posterity cannot be trusted to judge him fairly.

Schopenhauer says that people usually gain true fame only late in life, rarely while young. Philosophers are the least likely of all to see it early. Portraits of famous people, especially philosophers, usually show them old and grey, and he calls this arrangement proper, since a person cannot have fame and youth together.

Life offers few pleasures, so they must be used sparingly. In old age, when youthful joys are gone, fame can take their place. The greatest comfort in old age, the passage says, is knowing that one's best youthful efforts still survive as living works.
Schopenhauer is about to look more closely at the different kinds of fame that go with various intellectual work. He says this is the kind of fame his remarks mainly concern.

Intellectual superiority, on this view, lies in building theories, meaning new ways of combining known facts. The more familiar the facts are to everyday experience, the wider the fame that theorizing about them can bring.

Fame won from working with narrow, technical facts, such as numbers, scientific branches, or obscure texts and inscriptions, reaches only a small circle of specialists. Those few are mostly quiet scholars, and they are often jealous of others who gain renown in the same field.

This is an incomplete sentence: it sets out a condition, that the facts in question are ones everyone already knows. Its examples are basic traits of the human mind and heart, the large natural forces seen every day, and the general laws of nature. The sentence is cut off before it says what follows from this.

Fame gained by explaining a new theory that is clearly true will eventually spread across most of the civilized world, provided the facts behind it are ones everyone can understand. How far the fame reaches, though, depends on how hard the difficulties were that the theorist had to overcome.

The more widely known a set of facts is, the harder it becomes to build a theory about them that is both new and true. Many thinkers have already worked on those facts, so little is left that has not been said before.

Facts that few people can reach, and that take much work to uncover, can still be arranged in new ways to form fresh theories. Sound judgment is enough to find one that is true. But the fame such a discovery brings reaches only the people who already know those facts.

Solving hard problems takes great study and labor, just to learn the facts. The path to the widest fame needs little labor, because its facts are easy to grasp, but it demands more talent or genius. Such talent cannot be compared with the drudgery of research, either in its worth or in how people esteem it.

People with sound judgment but not the highest mental gifts need not fear hard study. Through study they can rise above the ordinary crowd, who see only what lies before them, and reach insights that only careful scholarship can give.

In a field with few competitors, even a man of modest ability can soon put forward a new and true theory, and its value partly lies in how hard the facts were to reach. Still, praise from fellow specialists, the only people who understand the subject, means little to the wider public who are far removed from it.

Fame can rest on hard-to-reach facts alone, without any theory behind them. Travel to remote, little-known places is one example: a man becomes famous for what he has seen, not for what he has thought.

Fame won by travel is easier to earn than fame won by thought, because people find it simpler to follow a story about what someone saw than to grasp that person's ideas. Schopenhauer adds that meeting famous travelers often shows that seeing new places does not bring new thoughts. He quotes Horace: those who run across the sea change their sky, not their minds.

A man with great intellect, who could tackle the hardest questions about nature and humanity, should keep his view wide in all directions. He should not get lost in narrow specialist fields or small details of particular subjects.

Schopenhauer says a scholar need not choose obscure subjects to avoid rivals, since everyday matters can give rise to serious and true new theories. He adds that the public values such work most when it concerns facts they already know. He then contrasts natural sciences and scholarship with poets and philosophers, who deal with the great facts of human life.

Schopenhauer says the first rule for living wisely comes from Aristotle, who noted in passing that the wise person aims not at pleasure but at freedom from pain. The Greek phrase he quotes says this, and Schopenhauer offers it as a fitting translation.

Pleasure, on this view, is just the absence of pain, while pain is what we actually feel as a real presence in life. A single painful spot in an otherwise healthy body takes over our attention, so that we stop noticing our general well-being and our comfort is spoiled.
Schopenhauer says that one failed aim worries us more than many successes, even when the failure is trivial. He concludes that the will is satisfied only when it meets no resistance at all.

Pleasure, for Schopenhauer, is not a thing in itself but the removal of something that blocks the will. Pain is the blocking force, which makes itself felt directly, while pleasure is only noticed when we look back on our state. Because pleasure is just the ending of that block, it cannot last long.

Schopenhauer says that life should be aimed at avoiding its many evils rather than at seeking pleasure. He adds that this is why Voltaire's saying, that happiness is a dream and sorrow is real, is true.

Schopenhauer says that to judge whether a life has been happy, you should count the evils you avoided, not the pleasures you had. "Happiness" really just means living less unhappily, and life is meant to be endured and gotten through, not enjoyed.

The passage says that people often describe getting through life in phrases like "getting by" or "making it through." In old age, it is a comfort to feel that life's work is finished. The happiest lot, it argues, is not the greatest pleasures but reaching the end without great pain, whether bodily or mental.

Schopenhauer argues that happiness should not be measured by pleasure, since pleasure is only the absence of pain and not a positive thing in itself. He holds that freedom from pain and from boredom are the real basis of happiness, and that anything beyond these is illusory.

Pleasure is treated as something positive and pain as something negative. So a person should not buy pleasure at the cost of pain, or even risk pain for it. Giving up a pleasure to avoid pain is a gain, and the order in which pain and pleasure come does not matter.

Schopenhauer argues that it goes against nature to aim at pleasure and joy in a world full of suffering. He says it is wiser to expect the worst, treat the world as a kind of hell, and aim mainly to avoid pain. Fools chase pleasures and are fooled by them, while the wise avoid life's evils.

Someone who takes precautions against misfortune is not deceived, because the evils he avoids are real. If misfortune still comes, blame fate rather than his own folly. Giving up some pleasure to avoid harm costs him nothing, since pleasures are illusory and mourning them is pointless.

Our restless wishes, even in calm moments, show us an imagined happiness that does not exist in real life. We chase it, and the chase brings real pain. Afterwards we regret the painless state we lost and cannot get it back.
Dreams of wishes coming true can seem like the work of an evil spirit. Their purpose, one might think, is to lure us away from a painless calm, which Schopenhauer treats as our highest happiness.

A young person without much thought assumes the world is a place built for enjoyment, where real happiness can be found by anyone clever enough to get past the obstacles. Reading poetry and novels, and being fooled by appearances, makes this belief stronger, so he spends his life chasing positive happiness.

Someone who believes happiness is just a string of specific pleasures chases them and runs into danger. He hunts for something that is not really there, and ends up suffering real troubles such as pain, loss, and poverty. Only then does he see how he was deceived.

A life planned around avoiding pain, by guarding against want, sickness and distress, has a real and reachable aim. Its success grows the more it is not spoiled by chasing positive happiness, which Schopenhauer calls a chimera, or illusion.

Wanting to escape a specific evil is a clear goal, but wanting a better lot than you already have is pointless. The French proverb "le mieux est l'ennemi du bien" says the same: the best can be the enemy of the good, so leave well enough alone.

The Cynics rejected pleasure altogether because they held that pain is always mixed into pleasure to some degree. They found it easier to avoid pain than to gain pleasure, so they focused all their effort on avoiding pain.

The passage describes a group of people who believed that the first step toward their goal was to completely and deliberately reject pleasure. In their view, pleasure was a trap that drew a person in so that pain could follow.

Schopenhauer says that people start life expecting happiness and pleasure, since Schiller called us all born in Arcadia, a mythical land of contentment. Life soon teaches them that they own nothing, not even their own body, because fate can take any of it away.

Over time, we learn from experience that happiness and pleasure are like a mirage: they look real from a distance but disappear as we get close. Pain and suffering, by contrast, are real and felt directly, needing no illusion or false hope to have their effect.

Experience teaches that the best life can offer is freedom from pain, a quiet and bearable existence. So instead of chasing pleasure and happiness, we should aim for that more modest goal, because avoiding great misery is more likely than achieving great happiness. Expecting little is the surest way to avoid being very unhappy.

Schopenhauer quotes Merck, a friend of Goethe's youth, who says that people ruin their lives by demanding happiness in proportion to their desires. The remedy given is to drop that demand, want only what is in front of them, and keep expectations of pleasure, wealth, rank and honor low.

Schopenhauer argues that striving hard for happiness, fame and a life of pleasure tends to bring great misfortune. So it is wiser to lower one's demands, because great unhappiness is easy to suffer while great happiness is almost impossible to reach. He supports this with a Latin verse from the Roman poet Horace, which praises the moderate, middle way of life.

The main point is that the middle way is safest: a modest home that is neither squalid nor so grand that it draws envy. The passage compares this to tall pines, high summits and lofty towers, which are the things the wind and storms strike hardest.

Schopenhauer says that a person who accepts his philosophy will judge life as something better not having existed, and will see disowning it as the highest wisdom. Such a person will expect little from life, will not care deeply about anything, and will not grieve much over failure. He backs this with Plato's saying that human affairs are not worth great concern.

Even if worldly things slip away from you, do not grieve, since they are worth nothing. Even if you possess a whole world, do not rejoice, since earthly things are worthless. Because you are destined to pass into a better world, move on quickly, since this world is worth nothing.

The main obstacle to seeing things this way is the world's hypocrisy, which, the passage says, should be shown to young people early. Most of the world's glories, it says, are only outward show, like scenery on a stage, with nothing real behind them.

Festive displays such as flags, cannon fire, lights, drums and cheering are only outward signs meant to stand for joy. Real joy is often absent from such occasions. It tends to arrive unannounced, quietly and without fuss.

Joy shows up unexpectedly, often in ordinary places and company, and never in the grand, fashionable settings people aim for. It is like gold found by chance in Australian mines: rare, small in amount, and following no rule. The lavish display at festivals is only an attempt to make people believe that real joy has arrived.

Schopenhauer describes a long funeral procession that looks sad and impressive, but the carriages are all empty. Only the hired coachmen follow the dead man to his grave. He sees this as a sign that the world's friendship and respect are false.

Schopenhauer says that a crowded formal gathering only looks noble. In fact, its real guests are compulsion, pain and boredom. Large gatherings are a crowd, however grand they look, and truly good company is always small. Even lively parties leave an underlying feeling of emptiness.

Social gatherings give a false impression of cheerfulness, which only makes our miserable and empty lives look worse by contrast. Still, they look impressive from outside, and that is their purpose. Chamfort compared society to a poor play or opera that has no real interest of its own and is kept going only by costumes and scenery.

Schopenhauer says that universities and philosophy chairs only show where wisdom is supposed to live, but real wisdom is found somewhere else. Religious display is likewise a false show of piety. Real worth is rare and usually hidden, like a small kernel inside an empty nut.

To judge how happy a person is, look at what annoys them rather than what pleases them. The smaller the things that annoy them, the happier they are. Only someone who is basically comfortable gets upset by small troubles, since small troubles go unnoticed when real misfortune strikes.

Schopenhauer says that happiness should not rest on many needs. The more things a person needs in order to be happy, the easier happiness is to break, because more things can go wrong. Keeping your demands low compared with what you have is the surest way to avoid great misfortune.

Making large plans for life is foolish, Schopenhauer says, because it assumes a long life that few people reach. Even those who do live long enough usually find their plans take more time than expected, and many obstacles get in the way, so goals are seldom reached.

We often work hard for a goal, but forget that time changes us. Our ability to achieve or enjoy things does not last our whole life. So we may reach a goal when it no longer suits us, or spend so long preparing that we lose the strength to act on it.

Many people gain wealth or success only when they can no longer enjoy it, or when the world has moved on and no longer wants what they offer. Schopenhauer says these are the hard facts of life that made the Roman poet Horace lament that all advice is useless.

The illusion Schopenhauer describes is that life seems very long when we are young and very short when we look back at its end. This false sense of time is the cause of a common foolishness, such as putting off living. He adds that the illusion has one benefit: without it, people would not undertake great works.

Our wishes often turn out differently than we planned. Looking for pleasure or happiness, we often find something else instead, such as experience or knowledge, which the passage calls a lasting good rather than a passing one.

Schopenhauer says that Goethe's novel Wilhelm Meister has one central idea running through it, like a bass line in music. He claims it is a novel of the intellect, which he ranks above other novels, including Walter Scott's, because those focus only on the will, or moral character.

Schopenhauer says that Mozart's opera The Magic Flute shows an idea in a symbolic way, though in crude, broad strokes. He adds that the symbol would be complete if the hero Tamino gave up his desire for Pamina and were instead initiated into the Temple of Wisdom.

People of real worth come to accept that life shapes them through hard lessons, and they gladly let it. They judge that life's value lies in experience rather than happiness, and they trade hope for understanding. Their only remaining pleasure is learning, as the poet Petrarch put it.

Schopenhauer suggests that some people pursue their old goals only in outward show, while in truth they are seeking knowledge. This gives them a look of genius. He compares this to alchemists, who searched for gold but found other things, such as gunpowder and china. In that sense, he says, everyone is an alchemist: we all find things while looking for something else.
A stonemason on a house may not know, or keep in mind, the plan of the whole building. In the same way, a person living day to day often pays little attention to the overall shape of his life.

If a person has a serious career or work, Schopenhauer says he should now and then step back and look at its overall plan. To do this well, he must first know himself, the old Greek advice "Know yourself." That means knowing what he most wants in life in order to be happy.

Once a person has settled what matters most to him, he should next work out his calling, meaning the role he means to play and his general place in the world. A clear outline of this kind, kept in view, will inspire him, drive him to act, and keep him from going wrong.
Just as a traveler sees the whole road only from a height, we see how our past actions connect, and what they achieved, only when a period of our life is over or our life is nearly ending.

While we are living our lives, we act according to our character, our motives and our abilities, so our actions follow from necessity. At each moment we do what seems right to us. Only when we look back over our whole life do we understand why things happened as they did.

When we do great things, we do not see them as great at the time. We only think about the task in front of us. Looking back over a whole life, we see that a kind of inspiration, which Schopenhauer calls our genius, guided us to the right path and away from ruin.

A wise life needs a fair balance between caring for the present and caring for the future. Some people, the frivolous, live too much in the present. Others, anxious and full of care, live too much in the future. Few manage to keep the right balance.

People who live only for the future, always waiting for some coming thing to make them happy, are compared to donkeys chasing a bit of hay tied in front of them on a stick. Schopenhauer says such people are always deceived about their whole existence, living only in the meantime until they die.

The passage advises focusing on the present, which is the only thing we can be sure of. It notes that the future rarely matches our expectations, the past was not what we remember, and both matter less than we usually think.

Distance makes things seem larger in memory and hope, while the present is the only real time, where our existence actually lies. So we should value each present hour that is free of pain and annoyance and enjoy it fully.

Schopenhauer says it is foolish to spoil the present with regret about the past or worry about the future. Repentance and forethought have their proper times, but once they are over, we should treat the past as finished and the future as outside our control.

Live each day as though it were your whole life, making it as pleasant as you can, because the present is the only time we actually have. The Latin phrase is from the Roman philosopher Seneca, meaning "consider each single day a single life."

Only evils that are certain to come at a fixed time should really disturb us, and few evils meet that test. Evils are either merely possible or probable, or else certain, and even certain ones have an uncertain timing. To keep our peace, we should treat the first kind as unlikely to happen and the second as not coming soon.

Schopenhauer argues that peace of mind is lost in two ways: through fear, and through desire and expectation. He says a person finds peace only after giving up all pretension and accepting plain, unadorned existence. Peace of mind is the basis of happiness and of enjoying the present moment.
Each day comes only once and never returns, so each day is a necessary part of life. We tend to forget this and treat life as a general idea that would be unharmed if one day were lost.

We tend to overlook good days while we have them and only value them once they are gone. Schopenhauer suggests we should notice our well-being while we are well, because hours of health later look like a lost paradise. Many pleasant hours are wasted in bad temper and are longed for only when trouble comes.

Schopenhauer says that ordinary moments that are bearable are often ignored or pushed aside, yet they are the ones we should value. Time carries them into the past, where memory keeps them glowing, so that in hard times we look back on them with longing.

Narrower limits make a person happier, and wider ones make worry and anxiety more likely, because they multiply our cares, desires and fears. Schopenhauer offers the blind as an example: they are less unhappy than one might expect, which he takes to be shown by their calm, peaceful faces.

As life goes on, the range of what a person aims at and deals with grows wider. A child's world is very small, a young person's is larger, an adult's may cover a whole state or nation, and an old person's reaches to future generations.

Schopenhauer says that limiting our mental work, as well as our outward activity, helps us be happy, because it calms the will. Suffering is a positive thing, while happiness is only the absence of pain, so fewer stirrings of the will mean less suffering.

Boredom is a direct cause of much suffering, because people who want to escape it turn to distractions such as society, gambling, drinking and extravagance. These distractions in turn bring harm, ruin and misery. The Latin saying means that it is hard to stay calm when you have nothing to do.

Schopenhauer argues that a limited outward life helps make people happy, or is even needed for it. He points to idyllic poetry, which shows happy people in very simple, narrow circumstances, and to genre paintings, which give the same kind of pleasure.

A simple, even dull, way of life tends to make us happier, as long as it does not leave us bored. Life's burdens are then felt least, and our existence flows calmly, like a stream without waves or whirlpools.

Whether a person feels good or bad depends mainly on what fills their mind. Schopenhauer says that for a mind able to do it, purely intellectual work usually brings more happiness than practical life, with its ups and downs and troubles. He adds that this kind of work needs a high level of intellectual ability.

Outward activity pulls a person away from study and takes away the calm focus that thinking needs. In the same way, long periods of thought make a person less suited to the busy demands of practical life. So when practical affairs require energy, the passage advises setting mental work aside for a time.

To live sensibly and learn from experience, a person should often look back on their past. They should review what they did and felt, compare old judgments with new ones, and check their goals against what they actually got. This repeated review is how the lessons of experience are learned, and these lessons come to everyone.

Schopenhauer compares life to a book. Experience is the main text, and reflection and knowledge are the commentary that explains it. Too much commentary with little experience is like a book with a few lines of text and many pages of notes. Much experience with little thought is like a text with no notes, hard to understand.

Schopenhauer says that, like the rule of Pythagoras to review the day each night, we should look back on what we have done. Living without reflection on the past, caught up in busy work or pleasure, leaves a person with no clear idea of what they are doing.

A person who lives in this state has disordered feelings and muddled thoughts, which show in choppy, broken speech. This happens most to someone who leads a restless life full of outside impressions while doing little active thinking of his own.

We cannot bring back the feelings we once had about past events, but we can recall what we thought, said and did about them. Those records show what the events meant to us, so keeping a written record of our thoughts at key moments is valuable, and a journal serves this purpose.

Being self-sufficient, needing nothing from outside, is the main requirement for happiness. Schopenhauer supports this with Aristotle's saying that happiness means self-sufficiency, and with a remark by Chamfort: happiness is hard to find within oneself and impossible to find anywhere else.
Schopenhauer says that a person can only be sure of himself. Dealing with other people brings burdens, dangers and annoyances that are endless and cannot be avoided.

Worldliness, partying and high society are described as the least reliable route to happiness. Their aim is to turn a miserable life into a run of pleasures, and that aim, the passage says, always ends in disappointment and self-deception, much like the lying that goes along with it.

Society cannot exist without members adjusting to one another and holding back their own wishes. The bigger the group, the blander its tone. Schopenhauer argues that a person can only be truly himself and free when alone, so someone who does not enjoy solitude will not really value freedom.

The more a person's individuality stands out, the harder it is for them to put up with the sacrifices that dealing with others requires. So solitude is welcomed, endured, or avoided depending on how much a person is worth in himself: a wretch feels his misery alone, while a great mind enjoys its own greatness.

A person of unusual gifts naturally feels alone. He is better off if his surroundings do not make this feeling worse, because spending much time with people unlike himself disturbs his peace of mind. Such company takes away his sense of who he is and gives nothing back in return.

Schopenhauer says that nature makes large differences between people in character and intelligence, but society ignores them and sets up its own ranks instead, which often run against nature's order. As a result, people nature made low are raised, and the few nature made high are pushed down. Those few often withdraw from society, where vulgarity rules once a crowd forms.

Schopenhauer argues that in society, great intellect is resented because everyone has equal rights and so claims equal standing, while real differences in ability bring differences in influence. Polite society accepts every kind of claim except the claim of intellect, so clever people must tolerate foolishness and hide their merit. Superior intellect offends just by existing.

Schopenhauer says the worst part of polite high society is not just that its members are dull or unworthy of respect. Its real harm is that it forces people to hide their true selves and conform, shrinking or changing who they are to keep social harmony.

Ordinary people find it distasteful to be pleased by anyone unusual, and to please them one must be commonplace and dull. Doing so means giving up much of oneself to be like others. The gain of their company does not make up for this loss, and the more valuable a person is, the more the loss outweighs the gain.

Most people have little to offer in company, so their society gives nothing back that outweighs its boredom, irritation and the self-restraint it demands. For that reason, Schopenhauer argues, being alone is usually the better bargain.

Society often uses a false, artificial kind of superiority in place of real intellectual superiority, which is rare.
