This "bon-ton" superiority rests on arbitrary rules passed down in high society, like a changeable password. When it meets real superiority, it is shown to be weak, and good manners imply a lack of good sense.

Schopenhauer says that no one fully agrees with anyone else, not even a close friend or spouse, because people differ in character and temperament. He claims that lasting inner calm comes only from solitude, and that a person with something great in himself lives the happiest life available.

Schopenhauer argues that even close bonds like friendship, love and marriage leave a person mainly concerned with his own welfare, and perhaps his child's. He holds that the less one must deal with people in business or personal life, the better off one is. Solitude has its hardships, but society harms more, and the young should learn early to bear being alone.

Schopenhauer says that a person is best off when he depends on himself and can be everything to himself. He quotes Cicero, who said that such a person cannot fail to be very happy. The more a man has within himself, the less he needs from others.

People with great inner worth are held back from the sacrifices that dealing with society demands, and so they seldom go out of their way to seek company. Ordinary people are sociable for the opposite reason: being with others is easier for them than being alone with themselves. The passage adds that the world does not reward real merit with respect.

Retirement from society is both a sign and a result of having real inner worth. So a person of worth would be wise to need as little as possible and to let others close to him as rarely as he can, in order to keep his freedom.

Schopenhauer says that people who cannot bear their own company seek out others, travel, or drink to escape it. Their minds feel empty and lifeless, so they look for stimulation, including the excitement of being with people like themselves.

Schopenhauer says that people who cannot keep their minds occupied sink into dullness. Such people have only a small part of full humanity in them, so many of them together are needed to make even a modest amount. A complete man, by contrast, is a whole unit in himself, not a fraction of one.
Schopenhauer compares ordinary people to Russian horns, each of which plays only one note. Most people, he says, seem to have just one thought at a time, with no room for another.

Schopenhauer says people are bored because they are dull within themselves, and that this is why they seek company and find being alone unbearable. The Latin quote means that all foolishness is weighed down by its own dissatisfaction with itself. Gathering many such people together only produces a noisy result.

A man of intellect is compared to a solo performer playing a piano, which can sound like a whole orchestra by itself. Such a man produces alone, within his own mind, the effect that many instruments produce together. Like a piano, he does not fit into a symphony; he works best by himself or as the leading voice.

Schopenhauer's point is that people who enjoy company can make up for weak quality with quantity. A single clever companion may be enough, but when the people available are ordinary, it is better to have many of them, since together they can offer some benefit, as a group of horns does.

Schopenhauer says that when people of good character form a society for a noble aim, crowds of dull, restless people join too, mainly to escape boredom. These newcomers often wreck the society or change it until it serves the opposite of its original purpose.

People seek each other's company for warmth, as crowds keep cold bodies warm, and minds warm one another in the same way. Schopenhauer says a man with much intellectual warmth of his own needs this less, so sociability tends to fall as intellectual worth rises. A very unsociable person is, in his view, usually a person of great ability.

Solitude has two benefits for a person like this: it lets him be with himself, and it keeps him away from other people. Schopenhauer argues that dealing with others is often troublesome and even risky, since most people are morally bad, dull, or perverse. Being unsociable, in this view, simply means not caring about such people.

Schopenhauer argues that having enough inner resources to do without other people's company is very fortunate, because most suffering comes from dealings with others. Peace of mind needs a good deal of solitude. He compares this to the Cynics, who gave up property to avoid worries, and says that giving up society for the same goal is the wisest course.

Schopenhauer quotes Bernardin de Saint-Pierre, a French writer, who said that eating sparingly keeps the body healthy and avoiding too much company keeps the mind calm. He adds that enjoying solitude is valuable but not easy for everyone. People seek each other out mainly from need, and when that need is met, boredom brings them together again.

Solitude lets a person keep the feeling that he is especially important, as if he were the only person in the world. In crowds and daily life, that feeling quickly fails, since every step contradicts it. So solitude is, for Schopenhauer, man's natural state, where he is as happy as his nature allows.

Schopenhauer argues that people are not born wanting to be alone. Every person starts life among parents and siblings, so society comes first. A love of solitude instead grows out of experience and reflection, which develop with intellectual power and increase with age.

Schopenhauer says that the older a person gets, the less they need other people's company. Small children cry when left alone, young people enjoy each other's company, and only a few young people with a noble mind like being alone sometimes. A grown man can spend time alone without difficulty.

A person with great mental ability finds solitude easier as he grows older, and the more capable a person is, the more he tends to withdraw from company. An old man who has lost his friends and no longer enjoys life's pleasures is, Schopenhauer says, naturally suited to being alone.
The tendency being discussed is not something people are born with. It comes from reflection on what we really need, and from seeing how poor most people are, both in character and in intellect.

Moral and intellectual faults in a person tend to feed each other, which makes dealing with most people not just unpleasant but intolerable. So, although the world holds many bad things, Schopenhauer says that society is the worst of them.

Voltaire admitted that the earth is full of people not worth talking to. Petrarch said he sought a solitary life to escape crooked, dim-witted people who have lost the road to heaven. Both give this as their reason for wanting to be alone.

Schopenhauer says the love of solitude is a secondary, indirect feeling. He quotes Chamfort, who mocks the idea that a man living alone must dislike society. Chamfort compares this to saying a man dislikes walking because he avoids walking at night in a particular forest.

Schopenhauer notes that the Persian poet Sadi and the German mystic Angelus Silesius express the same feeling: people should withdraw from society into solitude, because solitude offers safety. Silesius uses the Christian story of Herod and the flight to Egypt to make this point, comparing the world to a dangerous ruler from whom one must escape.

Herod, the biblical king, is an enemy. Reason, like Joseph in the Bible story, is warned of danger in a dream. The world is Bethlehem and solitude is Egypt, so the soul must flee there or die of grief.

Giordano Bruno, quoting others, says that people who wanted a taste of divine life have all said the same thing: they would flee far away and live alone in the wilderness. The quoted Latin means "Lo, I have fled far off and stayed in the desert." Seclusion is presented as the way to that kind of life.

Schopenhauer says that people of better nature avoid company because they have little in common with others except what is base in themselves. Sadi, a Persian poet, withdrew from his friends into the desert for the same reason. Such people, he claims, want to pull others down to their own level, and this urge to be alone comes from an aristocratic feeling.

Schopenhauer claims that people of low character enjoy company, while a noble person needs it less and prefers solitude. He says that, apart from a few exceptions, the only real choice is between being alone and being common. He notes that the Christian poet Angelus Silesius agreed, advising that a person should avoid vulgarity even if solitude is painful.

Great thinkers, Schopenhauer says, do not much want the constant company of other people. He compares them to a schoolmaster who does not join in the games of the boys around him. Their task is to lead people away from error and crude ignorance toward truth and culture, and so they live in the world without really belonging to it.

People of unusual intellect, Schopenhauer says, sense from childhood that they differ from others, and only slowly, over the years, understand why. Their mental isolation then becomes physical, as they avoid anyone who has not risen above common thinking.

Schopenhauer says that love of solitude is not a natural first instinct in people. It is a later development, found mainly in finer minds, and it often needs them to overcome their natural desires. He adds that the tempter Mephistopheles, a devil figure from Goethe's Faust, pushes people away from solitude toward company, saying even bad company gives a sense of human fellowship.
Stop indulging your sorrow, which gnaws at your life like a vulture. Even the worst company reminds you that you are simply a human being among other humans.

Schopenhauer says that being alone is the lot of great minds. They sometimes regret it, but they still choose it as the lesser of two evils. With age, solitude becomes a natural instinct, because after sixty even the strongest urge, the desire for female company, has little effect.

Schopenhauer says that in old age, the loss of sexual desire brings a kind of self-sufficiency that slowly removes the wish for other people's company. Illusions fade, active life is over, and the man's generation has died out, so younger people see him as no longer part of their world.

As we grow older, time seems to pass faster, and we prefer to spend what is left on learning and thinking rather than on practical affairs. If the mind stays sharp, our knowledge and skill make study easier and more rewarding, and many things once unclear become understood.

After long experience, a person stops expecting much from others, since closer acquaintance usually brings little gain. Apart from a few rare exceptions, people seem flawed and best left alone, so we rarely want to get close to anyone.

Over time, being alone stops feeling like a burden and becomes a habit, almost a second nature. Where solitude once meant giving up company, it becomes the natural setting of a person's life, as water is to a fish. So a person who is unlike others finds, as they age, that isolation weighs less than it did in youth.

Old age brings a particular privilege, which the passage says depends on intellect: it is felt most by people with real mental power and to some degree by everyone. Only people of dull, coarse nature stay as sociable in old age as they were in youth. They then become a burden to company they no longer fit, and are at most put up with, when before they were much sought after.

Young people learn most from simply mixing with others, because nature gives them a kind of mutual schooling in their early years. Schopenhauer compares human society to a large school run on the Bell and Lancaster method, where pupils teach each other, and he sees this as more natural than learning from books and formal schools. So a young person is well suited to be an eager student of life among others.

Nothing in life is free of drawbacks, and solitude is no exception. It has small annoyances, but these are minor compared with the troubles of living among other people. Because of this, a person of real worth usually does better alone than in company. The passage then says solitude has one further disadvantage, which is harder to notice.

Just as people who stay indoors all day catch cold from the smallest draught, a long stretch of solitude makes a person's temper so easily upset that tiny things, such as a word or a look, can irritate or offend them. People who live amid the bustle of life do not notice these small things.

Schopenhauer suggests that if you find company tiring and cannot stand long periods of loneliness, especially when young, you should learn to keep some solitude inside you while among other people. In other words, you should be partly alone even in a crowd.

Do not say everything you think at once, and do not read too much exact meaning into what others say. Expect little from people, morally or intellectually, and become indifferent to their opinions. Schopenhauer says this is the surest way to stay patient and tolerant toward them.

Keep a distance from other people so that you do not get too close to society. If you stay at a proper distance, you will not be harmed or disgraced by it. Society is compared to a fire, which a wise person warms himself beside but does not stand too near.

The passage uses the image of a fool who gets burned by a fire, then runs off to shiver alone and complains that the fire burns. The point is that people who are hurt by being too close to others often blame the others, rather than their own closeness.

Envy is a natural human feeling, but Schopenhauer says it is both a fault and a cause of unhappiness, so it should be crushed like a bad thought. Quoting the Roman writer Seneca, he says we will be content with what we have if we stop comparing our lot with happier people, since someone tormented by a happier person is never happy.

When others seem better off, think of the many who are worse off. The passage says that in real misfortune, the best comfort is thinking of greater misfortunes than our own, and the next best is the company of others suffering the same thing.

Envy that others feel toward us is dangerous, because the hatred it produces is the fiercest kind. So we should take care never to provoke envy, and even give up any enjoyment we might get from causing it, since the results can be serious.

Schopenhauer divides aristocracy into three kinds: birth and rank, wealth, and intellect. He says intellect is the most distinguished, and that its claim to first place is recognized over time. As an example, King Frederick the Great agreed, saying gifted people stand level with monarchs, when he seated the writer Voltaire among kings and princes.

Those who are not part of an elite group, which the passage calls an aristocracy, are described as envious. They resent members in secret and, unless afraid, try to show them they are no better than anyone else. The passage adds that this eagerness to say so shows they know the opposite is true.

Keep envious people at a distance, and if you cannot, meet their attacks calmly. Schopenhauer says the thing that draws envy also protects you from it. Members of one aristocracy get along with another because each has its own privileges, so no one envies the rest.

Think carefully about any plan, and even then allow for the limits of human judgment. Unforeseen circumstances may overturn all your calculations, so it is wise to hold back from unnecessary action in important matters. Schopenhauer ends with the Latin saying "quieta non movere," meaning "do not disturb what is quiet."

Once you have decided and started a task, let it run its course without reopening the decision or fretting over possible dangers. Schopenhauer compares this to an Italian proverb, which Goethe rendered as: tighten your girths well, then ride on boldly.

Human affairs are often controlled by luck and mistakes, so even careful effort can fail. Schopenhauer points to Socrates, who needed an inner warning voice, his daimonion, to act rightly in his own affairs. From this he concludes that human reason alone is not capable of guiding us in such matters.
Misfortune is often our own fault, at least in part. The passage admits this saying is not true in every case, but says it holds in most cases.
People try hard to hide their misfortunes and look cheerful about them. The passage suggests they do this because they fear their troubles would show how much fault lies with themselves.

Once a misfortune has happened and cannot be undone, the passage advises against telling yourself it could have gone differently or been prevented. Such thoughts only add to the pain and make it unbearable. The Greek phrase at the end means "self-tormentor," and the passage points to King David as a better model.

A man prayed to God for his sick son's recovery, then after the son died, he shrugged and stopped thinking about it. Those who cannot be so carefree can instead accept fatalism, the view that everything happens by necessity and so cannot be prevented.

Schopenhauer says that the advice being discussed is one-sided. It may ease our pain for a moment, but when our misfortunes come from our own carelessness or folly, it is good to think about how they could have been avoided, even though this is painful. Doing so teaches us to become wiser and better.

When we make plain mistakes, Schopenhauer says we should not hide them or make excuses. We should admit our faults fully and face how serious they are, so we can resolve to avoid them later. He accepts that this brings self-inflicted discontent, and he compares it to the saying that sparing the rod spoils the child.

Schopenhauer advises against letting the imagination run wild about matters that affect our happiness or unhappiness. Imagining castles in the air is costly, because they must be torn down, which causes grief. Picturing possible misfortunes is worse, since such fears are often illusions that we would see through on waking.

Imagination is said to work in two ways. Pleasant daydreams, or castles in the air, come in idle hours and are always agreeable. Gloomy dreams are built from real dangers that are distant, but imagination makes them seem larger, closer and more frightening than they really are.

Gloomy imaginings are harder to shake off than pleasant dreams, because a bad vision always might come true. We cannot judge exactly how likely it is, so a mere possibility can seem like a probability, and we torment ourselves over it.

We should not let worry about our own good or bad fortune grow beyond what is reasonable. Instead we should weigh the matter calmly, as if it were a general question that did not concern us personally, and not let imagination add painful pictures, since imagination only creates images rather than sound judgment.

Schopenhauer compares evening to darkness: just as the dark makes people fearful and inclined to see threats everywhere, unclear thinking brings a sense of danger. In the evening, when the mind is tired, it becomes confused and cannot get to the bottom of things.

When we think about our own concerns while lying in bed at night, those thoughts soon seem dangerous and frightening. The mind is then too tired to judge well, while the imagination is still active, so our thoughts become distorted, much like dreams.

Our thoughts at night, especially about our own troubles, tend to look far darker than they really are. Mornings clear them away, so the morning is the best time for serious thinking, especially about unpleasant matters, and for hard work of any kind.

Schopenhauer says the morning is the freshest, strongest part of the day, so it should not be wasted by rising late or spent on idle things. He compares each day to a whole life: waking is a birth, morning is youth, evening is old age, and sleep is a small death.

Our mood depends on many outside things, such as health, sleep, food, weather and surroundings. Because of this, how we see a matter and how well we can work change with time and place. So it is best to make use of a good mood when it comes, since such moods are rare.

We cannot always produce new ideas or original thoughts when we want them, because they come only when they choose. Likewise, we cannot always think about a personal matter at the time we planned, since a useful train of thought may arise on its own at another moment, and then reflection follows its own timing.
Schopenhauer says we should not bring back in our minds past wrongs, losses, insults and slights, because doing so wakes up old anger and resentment that were lying quiet and spoils our inner peace.

Schopenhauer compares a person to a town with a rich, respectable part and a low, unruly crowd living alongside it. Every person, however noble, has a crowd of base desires deep within, and these make him an animal. The crowd must be kept from rising up or even showing itself, because its leaders are the wild flights of imagination.

Small annoyances can grow in our minds into something terrible, because we keep brooding over them and make them look far worse than they are. Viewing unpleasant things calmly and plainly is the easier way to bear them.

Small things held close to the eye block out the wider view. In the same way, people and matters nearest to us, however unimportant, tend to take up more of our attention than they deserve, crowding out serious thoughts and important affairs.

Looking at things we do not own tends to make us wish they were ours, and so feel lacking. Schopenhauer suggests the reverse exercise: picture our own possessions as already lost, so we see their value more clearly.

We usually only notice how much we valued things such as property, health, friends, or pets after we lose them. Schopenhauer says that if we look at these things in his suggested way, we will enjoy them more now and work harder to keep them.

The passage is a list of examples of things a person should avoid doing: risking their money, angering friends, putting their wives in danger of temptation, and neglecting their children's health. It is a fragment, so the list is cut off from the sentence it completes.
When we feel low in the present, we often imagine future success to cheer ourselves up. This habit creates unreal hopes, which are bound to fail when real life proves them wrong.

Thinking about possible misfortunes as a subject to reason through does less harm than simply worrying about them. Doing so lets us prepare against them, and we are pleasantly surprised when they do not happen. The writer also notes that our spirits lift once a period of anxiety begins to pass.

Imagining serious misfortunes that might happen to us, as if they had already happened, can make smaller setbacks that do happen easier to bear. Looking back on great misfortunes that never occurred is also a comfort. The author adds that this should not cause us to neglect the point made in the previous section.

Things that hold our attention, whether work matters or everyday events, are so varied that, taken one by one with no order, they form a jumble of sharp contrasts. Their only shared feature is that each one touches us personally.

Our thoughts and worries should be kept separate, each one belonging to its own matter and time. So when we start something, we first set aside everything else, so that we can give that one thing full attention and deal with it without being pulled by our other concerns.

Worrying about one matter should not spoil small present pleasures or take away rest, and it should not crowd out other business. Anyone capable of higher thoughts should not let private troubles absorb all their attention, because that loses sight of life's true purpose. The Latin phrase means "for the sake of living, to lose the reasons for living."
Self-control is needed for managing oneself well, but it may not be as hard as it seems. Everyone already accepts strict limits from their surroundings, and no kind of life is possible without them.

Self-control at the right moment can prevent much later forced restraint by others. Schopenhauer compares this to a small arc near a circle's centre matching a far larger arc at the edge. Self-control is said to be the best protection against outside compulsion.

Submitting yourself to reason, as Seneca put it, is a way of bringing everything else under your control. Self-control is also in our own power, and we can ease its strictness when it hurts us most. Other people, however, will not spare our feelings when they must use force, and will treat us without pity.

Limit your wants, control your desires and anger, and remember that you can only get a small part of what is worth having and must suffer many of life's troubles. Wealth or power will not stop you from being unhappy if you fail to do this. Horace said the same: seek a calm life and avoid being driven by useless desires, fears and hopes.

The lines say that a person should read widely and ask wise people how to get through life calmly. They want life not to be constantly troubled by need, craving, fear, or hope for merely modest gains.

Life, Schopenhauer argues, depends on constant motion in the body and on steady activity of the mind, whether practical work or thinking. People with nothing to do or think about soon start drumming their fingers or tapping with a stick, which he presents as evidence of this need.

People are naturally restless and quickly become bored when they have nothing to do. This urge to act should be guided by some method, which will make the satisfaction they get from it greater. The passage says it is fortunate that people cannot live without activity, such as making, learning, or testing their strength.

Making something gives a direct pleasure, the pleasure of watching work take shape day by day until it is finished. This holds for art, writing, or plain manual labor, and the higher the work, the greater the pleasure it brings.

Those who feel they have the ability to produce great works with a meaningful purpose are, on this view, the happiest. Such a purpose gives their whole life a richer interest, which ordinary people lack and which makes ordinary life seem dull by comparison.

People with rich natural gifts look at life and the world with an interest beyond their own personal concerns, a formal interest in it. They see life as the source of material for their work, and once they are free of pressing personal needs, they spend their whole lives gathering that material.

Schopenhauer says that a person of genius has an intellect split into two parts. One part handles everyday practical affairs, as ordinary people do. The other part is given to calm, objective observation of existence. Most people only play their small role in life, while the genius acts in the world and also watches it.

Everyone should have some work suited to their abilities, because having no regular activity is wretched. Even long pleasure trips can leave a person unhappy, since without occupation they are out of their natural element. Striving against difficulties is as natural to people as digging is to a mole.

Having every want met feels unbearable, because pleasures that go on too long produce a sense of stagnation. Real enjoyment of life comes from overcoming difficulties, whether in business, daily affairs, or intellectual work, and there is always some pleasure in the struggle and in winning.

People who have nothing to do and no outside stimulation, Schopenhauer says, will make their own excitement. They hunt, play games, start quarrels, make plots, or even turn to swindling, just to escape a restless calm they cannot bear. The Latin phrase he quotes means that quiet is hard to keep when there is nothing to do.

Schopenhauer warns against being led by fanciful images in the mind rather than by ideas that are clearly thought out. He observes that in most decisions, the choice is usually tipped by a vivid picture of one option, not by a clear, reasoned judgment.

In this story, a young man at a turning point can only picture Virtue as his old tutor, who takes snuff and lectures, while Vice appears as a pretty chambermaid. Virtue looks dull and Vice looks attractive.

In youth we often form a vivid picture of future happiness and chase it for years. When we reach what we imagined, the picture vanishes and we find none of its promises have come true. Schopenhauer gives the image of a home life as one example.

People often picture an imagined future in great detail, such as a life in society, a country home, or the respect they will receive. Each person has a favourite fantasy, as the French saying "chaque fou a sa marotte" puts it. Such imagined pictures affect us as if they were real.

Schopenhauer says that concrete examples, such as vivid pictures or cases, affect our will more directly than abstract ideas, which are general and lack detail. Abstract ideas affect us only indirectly, yet they are the ones that deliver what they promise, so education should teach us to trust them. Still, abstract ideas sometimes need to be explained through pictures.

Schopenhauer says a person should not let fleeting impressions and outward appearances control them. These affect us more strongly than abstract thoughts do, not because they carry more real content, but because they are physical, immediate, and forceful. They break into the mind, disturb calm, and undo our resolutions.

Immediate things, like a pleasure or an insult right in front of us, act on us at once. Thought and reasoning need time, so we cannot weigh them calmly in the moment. That is why we give in to pleasure despite our resolve, and why we feel stung by a criticism even when we know its author is not qualified to judge.

The passage says that people are often moved more by what they feel right now than by good reasons. Ten sound reasons against danger can be outweighed by one false belief that danger is close, and a person can be deeply upset by an insult from someone they despise. Schopenhauer calls this the unreason of human nature, and says few men are free of it.

If you cannot overcome an outside influence by thinking alone, the best course is to counter it with an opposite influence. For example, an insult can be eased by seeking the company of people who think well of you, and fear of coming danger can be eased by focusing on how to prevent it.

An Italian under torture kept his mind fixed on the gallows that would have awaited him if he had given away his secret. He cried out "I see it!" to keep the thought in front of him, and later said this had been his plan. The story is told by Leibniz. Word count: about 50.

People find it hard to hold a view alone when everyone else disagrees, even when they are sure the others are wrong. Schopenhauer compares this to a fugitive king who is hidden: a single loyal follower, secretly showing respect, gives him comfort and keeps him from doubting who he is.
Schopenhauer says that health is the most important part of happiness. He says he has already argued this earlier in the work, and here he will add a few general rules for keeping health.

To harden the body, you must work it hard and expose it to harmful influences while it is healthy. When illness strikes, the opposite applies: rest and nurse the body or the sick part, because a weak body cannot be hardened.

Muscles grow stronger with hard use, but nerves grow weaker. So while the muscles should be exercised as much as suitable, the nerves should be spared as far as possible. In practice this means protecting the eyes from strong or reflected light, from straining in the dark, and from long close work, and protecting the ears from loud sounds.

Schopenhauer says the brain should not be overworked, and should be rested at the wrong times. It should rest while the stomach is digesting food, because the body's energy is then needed for digestion. It should also not be used during or just after hard physical exercise, since the nerves that move the muscles work in a similar way to those that carry sensation.

Pain from a wounded limb and tiredness in the arms and legs are both felt in the brain, not in the limbs themselves. The brain also moves the limbs, sending signals through the spine to the nerves that set them in motion.

Fatigue is felt only in the muscles that move by conscious will, since those depend on the brain. Muscles that work on their own, such as the heart, do not produce it. So forcing the brain to do hard physical exercise and mental work at the same time, or in quick succession, harms it.

Schopenhauer is saying that a short walk can make the mind feel sharper at first. He gives two physical reasons: the brain parts being used have not yet tired, and light exercise gets the breathing going, sending more oxygen-rich blood to the brain.

Sleep should last as long as the brain needs to recover, and that amount depends on how much the brain is developed and used. Sleeping longer than this is wasted time, because the extra hours are not deep sleep, so the sleep gets no more restorative.

Thinking is a physical process of the brain, like digesting is for the stomach. So the brain follows the same rules of work and rest as other bodily organs, and overstraining it can damage it, just as it can damage the eyes.

Schopenhauer argues that the idea of the soul as a separate thinking thing, needing nothing from the body, has led people to harmful habits that dull their minds. He gives Frederick the Great as an example, who tried to live without sleep. He says philosophy professors should stop spreading this idea.

Schopenhauer says that university philosophers try too hard to agree with Christian teaching. He advises treating the mind's abilities as bodily functions, to be rested or exercised as needed, since any bodily illness affects the mind.

Schopenhauer says that many gifted thinkers and scholars became weak-minded, childish, or even mad in old age because they neglected a certain rule. He names the English poets Scott, Wordsworth and Southey as examples, who grew dull and incapable soon after sixty.

Schopenhauer argues that writers who wrote for money, pushed by the promise of high pay, misused their minds and paid for it with weakness of thought in old age. He suspects Kant's decline in his last years came from overwork after he had become famous.
Each month of the year affects a person's health and general bodily condition, and even their state of mind. This effect depends on the weather.

Getting through life well, according to this passage, requires two skills. One is looking ahead, which guards a person against loss and harm. The other is overlooking, meaning letting small offences pass, which guards against quarrels.

A person should not be cut off completely, even if he is wicked, contemptible or ridiculous, because he has a fixed place in nature. Such people must be accepted as a fact that cannot be changed. In bad cases, one can recall Mephistopheles' line that there must be fools and rogues in the world.

Schopenhauer argues that if someone is rejected or condemned in every respect, he is left with only one option: a fight to the death. People cannot change their basic nature, such as character, intellect, or temperament. So condemning a person entirely amounts to allowing him to live only if he becomes someone else, which is impossible.

Accept that other people have the character they have, whatever it is. Instead of hoping they will change or condemning them outright, work with their nature as it is. Schopenhauer calls this the true meaning of "live and let live," and admits it is hard to do, so he counts it fortunate to need contact with few people at all.

Patience with people can be trained by practicing on objects that resist us, such as a stone in the road or a stubborn machine. We should then see people's opposition as the natural result of their nature, just as a stone's resistance is, and not take it personally. Since some people cannot be changed, the passage suggests it is often wiser to work with them as they are.

When two people talk, their likeness or difference of mind shows almost at once, even in small remarks. People of very different natures tend to annoy each other whatever the subject, while people of similar nature quickly feel in agreement and can be in complete harmony.

Ordinary people feel at home in any company, while people of unusual mind are unsociable and seek out others only when they find some small point of shared nature. Each person can relate to another only as far as that other matches him, and great minds, like eagles, live apart in lofty solitude.

People of similar character quickly feel drawn to one another, as if by a magnetic pull. This is seen most often among people with coarse tastes and limited intellect, simply because there are so many of them. People of finer and rarer nature are seldom met, which is why they are called rare.

Bad people in a group tend to recognize one another quickly and plot together, as if they wore a visible sign. Likewise, if a group is mostly clever, the only two fools in it will find each other and feel glad to have one companion.

Schopenhauer observes that two people of lesser moral and intellectual quality often seem to recognize each other at once and become friendly quickly, as if they were old friends. He says this is so striking that one might be tempted to believe the Buddhist idea of rebirth, that they knew each other in an earlier life.

People who would otherwise get along are sometimes kept apart, or fall out for a while, because their moods differ. Mood depends on each person's circumstances, work, surroundings, health, and current thoughts. Such differences cause conflict even between people who are naturally very compatible.

Keeping one's mood steady, like keeping a room at an even temperature, takes a high level of inner cultivation. Schopenhauer says that how well a steady mood builds friendliness can be seen in how it works on a large group of people.

When many people share an interest that affects them all in the same way, such as a common danger, good news, a play or a piece of music, they become eager to talk to one another and show real interest. Their shared feeling makes them pleasant to one another.
When people lack a shared interest in some outside subject, they usually turn to something personal, such as drinking wine, to create a sense of companionship. Tea and coffee serve the same purpose.

Memory tends to make our past attitudes look better than they were. The reason, the passage says, is that we forget the passing moods and small annoyances that disturbed us at the time, and so we remember those moments as calmer and finer.

Memory works like the lens of a camera obscura: it narrows what it holds and makes the picture better than the real scene. So, the passage says, time apart from a person makes them look better in memory, and it is wise to see friends only now and then.

A person can only recognize in others what he can recognize in himself. If your own intelligence is low, you will notice only another person's weaknesses and miss his higher qualities, just as a colorblind person cannot see colors.

A person without intelligence cannot see intelligence in others. When someone judges another's work, the critic's own range of knowledge counts as much in that judgement as the qualities of the work itself.

When people mix, the result is a lowering to a common level. Qualities one person has but the other lacks cannot be used when they meet. The one who gives up something for the sake of the other gets no thanks for it.

Schopenhauer says that most people are so coarse and foolish that talking with them makes you coarse too, at least for a while. He compares vulgarity to electricity, something that spreads easily from one person to another. This is why the phrase "to make yourself cheap" fits: lowering yourself to their level costs you your standing.
The main point is that people who connect with you only through your weakest side are best avoided. In dealing with fools, the only way to show intelligence is to keep away from them.

The point is that going into society can feel frustrating. A skilled person arrives expecting to enjoy the company of others, but finds that no one else has the same ability, so there is no one to share it with.

Schopenhauer says he admires the rare person who, while waiting or sitting idle, does not drum or tap on things nearby, such as a stick or cutlery. Such a person, he suggests, is probably thinking about something.

Many people seem aware of their own existence only when they are making noise or smoking, and they constantly watch and listen to what happens around them. Separately, La Rochefoucauld observes that deep veneration and great affection are hard to feel for the same person, so Schopenhauer concludes that we must choose which of the two we want from others.

Others tend to love us for selfish reasons. They love us most when we ask little of their goodwill and understanding, and our restraint must be sincere, not a mask for scorn. Helvetius added that the intellect we need in others to be pleased shows how much we have ourselves.

Schopenhauer says that respect or admiration is given grudgingly and is often kept hidden, unlike love. Still, he holds that respect gives more real satisfaction, because it rests on a person's real worth, while love is more personal and subjective. He adds that being loved is more useful in practice.

Most people are so self-centred that they only care about themselves. Any remark that touches their own interests or situation takes over their attention, so they cannot form an objective view of the subject. They also reject any argument that goes against their interest or vanity.

Many people are quickly hurt or irritated, so when talking about any general subject you must take great care not to let your words seem to refer to the people present, since they may take offence. Such people care only about what touches them personally, and they cannot grasp clever or subtle remarks.

People are very sensitive to anything that touches their small vanity or lowers their opinion of themselves, even in a remote or indirect way. The author compares them to a small dog that yelps when stepped on, or a sick man covered in sores who must be handled with great care.

Some people feel so threatened that if someone they are talking to shows intelligence or good judgment, or does not hide it well enough, they take it as a personal insult. They may hide their anger at the time, but the other person is left puzzled, trying to work out what he did to cause their hostility.

People of this kind are easy to flatter and win over, so their judgment is often corrupt. They take their opinions from the favor of their own party or class rather than from what is true and right. The cause, the passage says, is that their will is much stronger than their knowledge, so their weak intellect serves the will and never gets free of it.

Astrology is presented as proof that people tend to see everything as being about themselves. It tries to link the movements of the stars and planets to individual lives, so that a comet in the sky seems tied to quarrels and wrongdoing on earth.

A false statement that is widely accepted, or simply not challenged, does not mean the error will last. Over time the question will be examined and discussed, and the correct view will usually win out, though it may take a long time depending on how hard the subject is.

A person who sees the truth while everyone around is deluded is like a man with a correct watch in a town where all the clocks are wrong. He knows the right time, but it does not help him, because people still follow the false clocks. The passage then adds that people, like children, become worse when they are indulged.

Being too generous or obliging with people tends to backfire, according to this passage. Refusing a loan rarely costs you a friend, but granting one often does. Likewise, a little pride or carelessness seldom drives people away, while great kindness can make them presumptuous, and that can end in a falling-out.

Schopenhauer says that the feeling that someone depends on you is what most easily makes people lose their composure. When they believe they hold power over you, they tend to become arrogant and bossy. Some people also grow rude once they are in a close or frequent dealing with you, and begin to treat you with disrespect.

Schopenhauer's point is that people who find you depending on them will feel that you have taken something from them, and they will want to get it back. So to be superior in dealing with others, you must show that you do not need them. The passage also says that this is why few people are worth becoming close to, and why familiarity with coarse people should be avoided.

Keep your distance from acquaintances, and show now and then that you could do without them. Schopenhauer argues this makes friendships stronger and makes people value you more. He adds that a high opinion of someone should be hidden from them, because excessive kindness is unwelcome, even to a dog.

People of noble character and great intellect often lack practical worldliness and knowledge of people, especially when young, so they are easily deceived. People of more ordinary temperament tend to get on better in the world.

Without much experience, a person judges by ideas formed in advance. For ordinary people, those ideas simply reflect their own self-interest. People of higher mind and character are unselfish, so they judge others by their own high standard, and their predictions about others often turn out wrong.

A person of good character may come to learn, from experience or from others, that most people are morally and intellectually poor company, and that one should keep clear of them unless circumstances force contact. Even so, he will never fully grasp how mean they are, and will keep revising his low opinion of them, making mistakes and harming himself along the way.
When a person has truly learned life's lessons, he is sometimes surprised to find strangers seem reasonable, honest, sincere, virtuous and trustworthy, while also shrewd and clever.

Schopenhauer says that nature does not label its people as fools or villains the way clumsy writers do, with a narrator warning the audience. Instead, nature presents each person so that they seem right in the moment, as Shakespeare and Goethe do with their characters, even the devil.

Well-drawn characters in fiction seem real because their words and deeds follow a hidden inner logic, much as in nature. Likewise, dangerous and foolish people do not show their nature openly, so anyone who expects obvious signs of them, such as horns or bells, will be easily fooled.

People, when they deal with others, show only one side of themselves, as the moon shows only one face or a hunchback turns only one side toward you. Each person also has a natural gift for putting on a face, so that they can look like whatever they want to seem.

Schopenhauer says that a person's outward appearance fits them well, because it is built on their own nature, so it is very deceptive. Such a person puts on this mask whenever they want to win someone's good opinion of themselves.

The point is that even the worst dog wags its tail, so every person has some good in them and may show some kindness. The passage uses this Italian proverb to suggest that a person's friendly signs should not be taken too seriously, since even a bad character can show them.

Do not hold a high opinion of someone you have just met, because you are likely to be disappointed and may feel ashamed or be harmed. Also, a person's character shows most clearly in small matters, when he is not guarding himself.

Small signs in a person's ordinary behaviour show his deep self-centredness and lack of concern for others. The same faults also tend to shape his important actions, even when he hides them. Such moments should not be missed.

If a man is careless about small everyday matters and takes what suits him at others' expense, Schopenhauer says he has no real justice in him. Such a man would behave like a large-scale criminal if the law did not stop him. So he should not be trusted.

Schopenhauer's point is that if most people were mostly good, it would be wiser to appeal to their sense of justice, gratitude, love and similar virtues. Since most people are mostly bad, it is wiser to appeal to their fears instead.

If someone we deal with has annoying traits, we should ask whether that person is valuable enough to us to tolerate those traits, even when they show up again and again in a worse form. If the answer is yes, complaining does little good, so we should let it pass, with or without a brief remark.

If someone has wronged you and the answer to whether you should trust them again is no, you should end the friendship for good, or dismiss a servant. Schopenhauer's reason is that the person will repeat the offence when the chance comes, even if they sincerely promise otherwise now.

A person can forget almost anything except his own character, because character does not change. Schopenhauer means that everything a man does comes from an inner principle, so under the same circumstances he must act the same way and cannot act otherwise.

Taking back a friend, or a servant, after a quarrel or dismissal is described as a sign of weakness. The person then tends to repeat the same offence, and bolder, because they sense you cannot do without them.

Do not expect people to keep acting the same way when circumstances change. People change their behavior and feelings as quickly as their interests change. Anyone who trusts their past conduct, as if it were a promise, is being foolish. (The "bill" image: their agreement is a debt that will not be fully paid.)

To judge how a man will act in a job, do not rely on his promises or assurances, even if he means them sincerely, because he cannot know how he will act before he faces the situation. Instead, look at the circumstances he will face and how much they will clash with his character.
Reading how people act in books and comparing it with how they act in real life can show what most people are really like. This helps you avoid false ideas about yourself and about others.

When you meet an example of meanness or stupidity, the passage says not to be annoyed or upset by it. Instead, treat it as a new fact about human nature, the way a mineralogist treats a clear sample of a mineral he has found.

Schopenhauer says that people are generally bad: in primitive places they eat each other, and in civilized places they cheat each other. He argues that states, laws and the use of force exist only to hold back this unlimited wickedness of humankind.

Schopenhauer argues that wars are usually fought to seize goods, not for any higher reason. He says that conquered peoples were once made slaves who worked for their conquerors, and that war taxes amount to the same thing: people handing over the fruits of their own labor.

People need some general plan and rules to guide them. But if a person takes on a character that is not natural to him, built only by reasoning, it will not last. His true nature will return, as the Latin proverb says: you may drive out nature with a pitchfork, but it will always come back.

Knowing a rule of conduct in theory is easy, and you can still break it in practice soon after. That does not mean rules are useless or that you should simply live as you please. First you understand the rule, then you slowly learn to practise it.

Learning a skill like music or fencing takes many small mistakes before it is mastered. A learner who errs may wrongly think the rules cannot be followed, but steady practice, through repeated slips and new attempts, gradually makes him skilled. The same, the passage says, holds for other things.

Learning a skill like Latin, or a social manner, works like forgetting grammar rules: over time the habit takes over. Schopenhauer says that a person who has trained themselves to act against their natural temperament, such as a passionate man made calm or a frank person made reserved, is still held in that role by outside pressure. Their natural character keeps pushing back and sometimes breaks through unexpectedly.

Acting on abstract principles is like a watch: a shape and motion are imposed on dead, shapeless material from outside. Acting from one's innate nature is like a living organism, where form and matter cannot be separated and grow together.

Anything unnatural is imperfect, the passage says, and this holds in both the physical and moral worlds. The one exception the author can think of is aventurine, a mineral that is better when man-made than in its natural form.

Affectation, meaning pretending to have a quality you lack, is always despised. Schopenhauer says it is a kind of deception rooted in fear, and that it shows a person knows they fall short. Showing off a quality is, in effect, admitting you do not have it.

When someone boasts about a quality, such as courage, learning, wit or wealth, the boasting suggests he is weak in that very area. A man who truly has a strength does not feel the need to show it off and is content simply to know he has it.

Schopenhauer says that a person should not let all their faults show, because many bad sides of human nature must be kept hidden. Hiding them is allowed, but pretending to have virtues one does not have is not. The Spanish proverb he quotes means that a clattering hoof means a missing nail.

Pretence is noticed quickly, even before people know what it is meant to hide. It cannot be kept up for long, because sooner or later the false front drops. Schopenhauer supports this with a saying of Seneca: nobody can keep up a fake character for long, since real nature soon returns.

Schopenhauer says we notice the faults of others easily but not our own, much as we feel the weight of an object we lift but not the weight of our own body. Other people therefore work like a mirror, showing us our own vices. Yet we usually fail to see this and treat the reflected faults as belonging to someone else, like a dog barking at its own reflection and thinking it is another dog.

Someone who often criticises other people's conduct, Schopenhauer says, thereby improves himself. Harsh judgment of others gives him enough sense of justice or pride to avoid doing the same things himself.

Schopenhauer says that the eye sees other things, not itself, so noticing faults in others is a useful way to become aware of our own. He treats other people as a mirror for our own character. He also says the Bible's image of the mote and the beam does not really fit this idea.

Schopenhauer says that writers copy the literary fashions they applaud, so praising a new style leads to imitating it. He says this is why silly literary trends are so popular in Germany: Germans are very tolerant, and their motto is "we grant this pardon and ask it in return" (a Latin line from Horace), meaning they excuse each other's follies.

A young man of noble character tends to believe that the bonds between people, and the friendships they form, are based at heart on shared ideals. He thinks these bonds rest on matching temperament, feeling, taste, or mental ability.

Schopenhauer means that friendships or alliances that look sincere often turn out to rest on a shared material interest, such as money or advantage. He adds that most people cannot imagine an alliance built on any other basis.

People are judged by their job, rank, nationality or family, which society gives them, rather than by who they are as individuals. Schopenhauer says they are labelled and treated like goods on a shelf, with a fixed price tag.

Schopenhauer says that people are seldom judged by their real personal worth, except when it is convenient. Such a judgment is dropped as soon as it becomes unpleasant, which usually happens. A man of greater worth enjoys these social conventions less and tends to withdraw from them.

Schopenhauer says that life is mainly full of suffering and want, so people's central task is to find ways to ease them. He also compares social esteem and friendship to paper money: most of what passes for them is only an outward imitation of the real thing.

Schopenhauer suggests that few people truly deserve sincere, genuine regard, "the true coin" meaning real esteem or honest feeling. He says he values a faithful dog's wagging tail more than a hundred shows of human respect.

True friendship, as the passage defines it, means caring about another person's joy and sorrow for its own sake, so completely that one's own self is in a sense identified with the friend. The writer argues that human selfishness works so strongly against this that real friendship is as rare as the sea-serpent, a creature whose existence people doubt.

Schopenhauer says that most human friendships rest on some hidden self-interest, yet a small genuine feeling of friendship often still exists in them. That small feeling is valuable enough to justify calling these relations friendship. Ordinary friendships, he adds, are so weak that if you heard what your friends said about you behind your back, you would stop speaking to them.

A good test of a friend's real feelings is how he reacts when you suffer a misfortune, unless you would need some great personal sacrifice from him. His face at that moment will show whether his first thought is honest sympathy for you.

Schopenhauer says that even when a friend is in trouble, a person's face may show a small trace of pleasure rather than pure sympathy. He quotes La Rochefoucauld's saying that in the misfortune of our best friends we always find something that does not displease us.
People tend to become cheerful when you tell them about a recent misfortune of yours or openly admit a personal weakness. Schopenhauer sees this as typical of human nature.

People we rarely see slowly lose their hold on us, even if they were once our closest friends. They become mere ideas, and our interest in them turns into habit or memory. Schopenhauer says this shows how much we depend on what our senses show us in the present.

Schopenhauer's point is that people who seem to be friends often value the household more than the person in it, so they stay close only while things go well, like cats rather than loyal dogs. He adds that enemies are more honest about your faults, so their criticism can teach you about yourself. He also says that friends in need are not rare; instead, a new friend soon asks for a loan.

Showing intelligence and good judgment will not make a person popular in company, Schopenhauer claims. Most people feel hatred and resentment toward the clever, and they hide the real cause of that anger even from themselves. The passage ends just as it begins to say why: people sense that the other person is far more intelligent than they are.

Schopenhauer says that when someone shows they are clever, the listener quietly concludes that the clever person must think poorly of the listener's own abilities. This resentment makes people dislike the clever person. So, he agrees with Gracian that to be liked, one should appear as simple as an animal.

Showing off your intelligence is really a hidden way of saying others are dull. People who feel superior are also quick to get angry when someone disagrees with them, and their hostility often comes from envy. Vanity needs comparison with others to be satisfied.

People take most pride in their intellect, so showing that you are clearly smarter than someone is risky. The person will want revenge and will likely look for a chance to insult you, since insults move the conflict from the mind to the will, where everyone is equally able to feel hostility.

Social rank and wealth usually earn respect from others, but intellectual ability rarely does. People tend to ignore clever people, and when they do notice them, they often see it as presumption, and quietly try to humble them.

Schopenhauer says that people who feel inferior to a clever person will wait for a chance to hurt them, even if that person behaves modestly. Their resentment is over being outshone in intelligence. He supports this with a saying from the Persian poet Sadi: foolish people avoid wise people far more than wise people avoid fools.

Schopenhauer says people enjoy feeling superior to others, so they seek out company that lets them feel this. A person who is clearly more intelligent is therefore disliked, and to be liked one must actually be less intelligent than others. He adds that showing real, genuine inferiority to some people is very hard to do.

Schopenhauer says that a moderately pretty woman is friendly and warm toward a plain one, because she feels no rivalry. He claims that in men, dull and ignorant people, and in women, plain ones, tend to be the most welcomed by others, since they threaten no one's standing.

People who are liked by others are said to be good-natured, but people mainly look for a reason to care about them and hide the true reason they like them. Likewise, people with unusual mental ability tend to be left alone, because others dislike them and then invent criticisms to justify keeping away.

Very pretty girls struggle to find female friends, and a beautiful woman seeking a job as a companion will be rejected, since her employer sees her looks as a threat to herself and her daughter. The situation changes, though, when the young woman has high social rank.

Rank affects how others see a person indirectly, by reflection, much as skin colour looks different depending on the colours around it. Personal qualities, by contrast, work directly, through the force of contrast with others.

Competition for honor, office, reputation, and recognition in science, literature and art works the same way as political advancement. In learned societies, mediocre people are usually promoted first, while real merit is recognized late or not at all.

Much of the trust we give other people, Schopenhauer says, comes from our own laziness, selfishness and vanity. We trust others to avoid checking for ourselves, because we are busy, or because we are proud of the matter. Even so, we expect those we trust to be faithful to that trust.

When people do not trust us, we should not be angry, because their distrust means they see honesty as so rare that they doubt it exists at all. In this view, their doubt is a kind of compliment to honesty.
Politeness is an unspoken agreement between people not to point out each other's faults, whether of character or of mind. Because those faults are made less noticeable, both sides benefit.

Politeness is useful, so rudeness is foolish. Making enemies through needless rudeness is as senseless as setting your own house on fire. Politeness is like a counter, a coin everyone knows is false, so it costs little to spend it freely. But being polite to the point of harming your own interests is like paying with real money where only counters are expected.

Politeness and friendliness work on people the way warmth works on wax. A little of it makes people who are normally harsh or ill-natured soft and willing to be guided. So politeness is, for human nature, what heat is for wax.

Being polite is hard, Schopenhauer says, because it asks us to show respect to people who mostly do not deserve it, and to pretend an interest in people we would rather avoid. Keeping up courtesy while still holding onto one's own dignity is, he suggests, a very wise achievement.

We would get angry less often at an insult if we did not think too highly of ourselves, and if we understood what people really think of each other inside. An insult, in the strict sense, means being treated without respect.

Most people resent even a slight hint of blame, and would be far more upset if they overheard what others really think of them. Ordinary politeness is only a thin mask, so one should not complain when it slips. Rudeness is like a man stripped naked: not a pleasant sight.

Do not copy other people when deciding what to do, because each person's position and character differ. Even the same action can mean something different when done by different people. Act according to your own character, after careful thought, or your actions will not match who you are.

Do not argue against other people's opinions, since you could never correct all their mistakes. Correcting someone in conversation is also likely to offend them and hard to undo. If you overhear foolish remarks, treat them as the lines of foolish characters in a comedy.

A person who arrives in the world expecting to teach people about the most important matters should count himself lucky if he is not harmed for it. The sentence is a joke: such a person is likely to be met with hostility.
If you want others to accept your view, state it calmly. Schopenhauer argues that strong emotion makes people think your opinion comes from your will, not from reason, so they doubt it.

Even when someone really deserves praise, he should not praise himself. People assume that anyone who does so is driven by vanity and is foolish enough not to notice how he looks. Vanity is common and real merit is rare, so such self-praise is read as vanity almost every time.

Schopenhauer says that, as with slander, repeated self-praise can leave a mark, so small amounts of it may be worth using. He then advises that if you suspect someone of lying, you should appear to believe them. This encourages the liar to keep talking more forcefully, and so he eventually gives himself away.
If someone is hiding something from you and only partly succeeds, act as if you do not believe them. Your doubt will push them to bring out the rest of the truth to convince you.

Keep your private affairs to yourself, even from friends. Share only what others can already see for themselves. Over time and as circumstances change, even harmless facts that people know about you may turn out to be a disadvantage.

Keeping quiet usually shows your intelligence better than speaking up. Silence comes from good judgment, while talking often comes from wanting to show off. People still choose the brief pleasure of speaking over the lasting benefit of staying silent.

Talking aloud to yourself when nobody is listening is a relief to lively people, but it should not become a habit. If it does, speech and thought grow so close that a conversation turns into thinking out loud. Good sense requires a clear gap between what we think and what we say.

People often feel that others cannot doubt a fact about us, when they in fact never thought to doubt it. Yet once given a chance to doubt it, they find it impossible to believe. We then give ourselves away, much as a person on a height throws himself down to end the dizzy strain of feeling he cannot keep his footing.

People are often very clever about other people's affairs, even when they show little sharpness elsewhere. Given just one fact, they can work out the most complicated problems about someone else's business, much as a skilled mathematician solves equations from a few known values.
If you tell an old story without names, you must avoid any detail that could point to the real event or people. That includes places, dates, or even minor figures connected to it.

Schopenhauer says that when people are given a concrete starting point, they can work out the rest, much as they would with algebra. Their interest in such details becomes eager, and their desire drives their thinking toward distant conclusions. People who care little for general truths are often very keen on particular facts.

Keeping silence is the main advice here, and the passage adds three short Arabian proverbs to support it. The first warns against telling a friend what you would hide from an enemy. The second says a kept secret is under your control, while a secret that gets out leaves you as its prisoner. The third says silence brings peace.
Money is said to be best spent when you have been cheated out of it, because in one stroke you buy wisdom. The loss teaches you to be more careful, so the cost gives you prudence in return.

Feel no hostility toward anyone if you can. But watch how a person behaves and remember it, so you can judge what he is worth to you and treat him accordingly. Do not forget his faults, since character does not change, and doing so would waste what you have learned about him.

Do not let love or hate move you, and do not say or believe everything you hear; Schopenhauer calls these two halves of worldly wisdom. He adds that a world needing such rules is one a wise man may well turn away from. He also says that showing anger or hatred to another person in words or looks is unnecessary, dangerous, foolish and vulgar.

Schopenhauer says that anger and hatred should show only in what a person actually does, not in words or displays of emotion. Feelings work best in action when they are not shown in other ways. He adds that only cold-blooded animals have poisonous bites, meaning that the most dangerous attacks come from those who do not show their anger openly.

Speaking "without accent" means stating your words flatly, without stressing them, so listeners must work out the meaning for themselves, which slows them down. Stressing your meaning appeals to their feelings and backfires. Courteous manner can even let you insult some people without them taking offence.

Human lives look very different from one another, but Schopenhauer says they are made of the same basic elements. Whether a person lives in a cottage or a palace, or succeeds or fails, the difference is smaller than it seems. Like a kaleidoscope, the world shows new patterns, yet the pieces are always the same.
Schopenhauer quotes an ancient writer who named three great powers in the world: good sense, strength, and luck. He adds that he thinks luck is the most effective of the three.

Schopenhauer compares a human life to a ship at sea. Luck is the wind that drives the ship, and a person's own efforts are like a rudder, which helps only a little. A Spanish proverb, quoted to show how strong luck is, says to give your son luck and throw him into the sea.

Schopenhauer says that chance is the only giver who hands out gifts while making clear they are not earned. Those who receive from chance cannot claim them as their merit, and yet they may still hope for more. In this way chance shows that merit counts for nothing, like a king's grace.

Looking back, a person often sees moments where bad luck or misfortune hit him, and it is easy to blame himself too harshly for them. His life is not entirely his own doing. It results from both external events and his own choices, and each keeps shaping the other.

A person can see only a short way ahead, both in the plans he makes and in what will happen. He knows only his present plans and present events. Because his goal is far away, he cannot head straight for it. He must roughly keep to a course and often change direction, as a sailor tacks against the wind.

A person can only make decisions that fit his circumstances at each moment, hoping to move a little closer to his final goal. Our actual path is shaped by two unequal pulls: where we stand and what we aim for. It ends up as their combined result, like the diagonal of a force diagram.

Life is compared to games of chance and skill. Dice and cards are dealt by luck, so you make the best of what comes up. Chess is better, because our plans are shaped by an opponent, here fate, and we often have to change them until little of the original plan remains.

Schopenhauer says we are often more foolish than we think, and sometimes wiser than we believe. Only those who are truly wise in this way discover it, and it takes them a long time. Our intellect, he adds, is not the best part of us.

At life's major turning points, a person usually acts from an inner impulse, almost an instinct, that comes from the deepest part of who he is, rather than from clear knowledge of what is right. If he later judges that action by fixed general rules of right and wrong, which he has memorised or taken from others, those rules are not much use to him.

If someone applies general rules that worked for others to his own life, without properly considering that what suits one person may harm another, he risks being unfair to himself. Only with mature wisdom can a person judge fairly either his own actions or those of others.

Schopenhauer suggests that a particular impulse or instinct in our lives may come from a kind of dream we forget on waking. This hidden dream would give our life a steady tone and a unified shape. Ordinary waking thought, he says, is too changeable and error-prone to produce such unity.

A person who feels called to great work in some field often seems to have a kind of inner, prophetic dream guiding him. From youth he pursues that path by a secret inner sense, much as a bee instinctively builds its cells in the honeycomb.

Schopenhauer is describing an impulse that Balthazar Gracián (a Spanish writer) called "la gran sindéresis," meaning "the great power of moral discernment." He says a person feels this impulse instinctively as their salvation, and that without it they would be lost.

Acting on general rules is hard, and they often do not fit a particular case. Every person, however, has innate concrete principles, formed from all their thoughts, feelings and wishes. They usually do not know these principles in abstract form, but they see in hindsight that these principles have guided their life all along.

Things change and nothing lasts, so Schopenhauer advises picturing the opposite of your present situation. In good times, imagine misfortune; in trust, imagine betrayal; in hardship, recall happier times. Doing this keeps you from being easily deceived, because you expect the changes that years bring.

Experience teaches that everything in this world is unstable and temporary, and only change lasts. Each situation seems fixed because it has its reasons, yet none of them lasts forever. The wise person is not fooled by apparent stability and can foresee the direction in which things will shift.

People tend to assume that the present state of things will continue unchanged. They make mistakes because they do not grasp the causes behind what they see. Those causes, unlike the visible effects, carry within them the seeds of future change.

People see only the results of things, and they assume the hidden causes behind those results will keep them the same. This is a common mistake, but because everyone makes it together, the harm it causes is shared by all and so easier to bear.

Schopenhauer means that we should predict what time will bring, not try to force it to pay early. Someone who demands that time fulfill its promises now will find Time a harsher lender than any moneylender, charging a heavier price than even the most ruinous interest.

Forcing a tree to leaf and blossom early with lime and heat makes it wither soon after. Likewise, a young man who tries at nineteen to do what he could manage at thirty may gain a short advantage, but he pays for it later. The cost is taken from his strength in his later years, which is part of his life itself.

Some illnesses clear up fully only when they are allowed to run their course, leaving no trace. If an impatient sufferer insists on being well before the illness has really passed, the illness may still go, but it leaves lasting weakness and harm as a cost.

In a war or general crisis, a person may need cash at once and sell land or government bonds (consols) for a third or less of their real value. If he could have waited for the market to recover, he would have got much more. His loss is the price he pays for not waiting.

A man who wants money for a journey cannot wait to save it from his income, so he borrows or takes it from his capital. Schopenhauer says this means he has effectively borrowed from Time, and the interest is a growing shortfall in his accounts that he never repays. Everyone who cannot wait becomes a victim of this, since trying to speed up Time's steady pace is wasteful.

Ordinary people judge the danger of an undertaking only by the risks that have occurred before. A prudent person looks at everything that could happen in the future. The Spanish saying behind this idea is that what does not happen in a year may happen in two minutes.
Seeing what has already happened takes only ordinary alertness. Working out what might happen takes real judgment. So the gap between people in this matter is only to be expected.

Schopenhauer advises that a person should willingly pay the cost of avoiding possible misfortune, even in time, money, comfort, or ambitions. He points out that the worst disasters are the least likely to happen, and he compares this to buying insurance, which he calls a public sacrifice made to anxiety.
Do not let good or bad luck make you overly joyful or overly sad. Fortune can change at any time, and people often misjudge what is really good or bad for them.

People often cry over events that later prove to be the best thing that could have happened to them, and they celebrate events that bring their greatest suffering. Schopenhauer cites Shakespeare's lines to show the right attitude: a person should not be carried away by the first face of joy or grief, since neither shows what it will bring.

A person who bears misfortune calmly does so because he keeps in mind how many dreadful things can happen in life, so the present trouble looks small by comparison. This is the Stoic attitude: never to forget the sad condition of human beings, and to see how full life is of suffering. Looking around, one sees people struggling in pain for a poor, empty existence.

If a person keeps in mind that life is relative and no perfect state exists, he should expect little from life. He should adapt to this kind of world, face misfortune directly, and meet unavoidable misfortune with courage.

Misfortune, large or small, is always part of life, so we should not complain about it constantly or pray at every minor annoyance. Instead, we should watch carefully and avoid troubles as cleverly as a fox, since most mishaps are really caused by our own clumsiness.

Thinking in advance that a misfortune might happen makes it hit less hard when it comes. Once we have calmly considered its possible size and reach, we know how much it can affect us. So when it actually arrives, it weighs no more than it really does.

A misfortune that comes without warning frightens the mind and makes its harm seem greater than it really is, because the mind cannot see its full size. If we have already thought about the possibility of misfortune, we have also thought about where help and comfort might come from, or at least we have got used to the idea.

Schopenhauer says that knowing everything happens by necessity helps a person bear misfortune calmly. Once a person accepts that events must happen as they do, and that even strange chances follow necessity, he settles into what cannot be changed.

Small daily annoyances, such as quarrels, gossip and rude behaviour, are seen as practice for enduring great misfortunes, so that a comfortable life does not make a person weak. The advice is to ignore these irritations, push them aside like stones in the road, and not dwell on them.
