Schopenhauer argues that what people call fate is usually the result of their own foolish behaviour. He says stupidity is punished in this life, while wickedness may only be punished in the next, and that cunning frightens people more than brute strength does.

Courage and prudence (good judgment) both matter greatly for happiness. A person cannot give himself these qualities, since they are inherited, but someone who has them can strengthen them through determined practice.

Life is a constant struggle, and success comes only through effort and force, not ease. Schopenhauer says a person needs a tough temper and must not lose heart at the first sign of trouble. He argues that one should meet misfortune with more courage, not give in to it.

While a dangerous matter is still open and some hope of a good outcome remains, a person should not panic and should keep resisting. He should not give up, just as one does not despair of the weather while a patch of blue sky is visible. The passage ends with a Latin line meaning that even if the world broke apart, the ruins would strike a man who stays fearless.

Life as a whole is not worth fearful trembling over its troubles, so we should meet life bravely and stand firm against every misfortune. The Latin line at the end, from the Roman poet Horace, says the same: live bravely and oppose brave hearts to adverse fortune.

Courage can go too far and turn into recklessness. Schopenhauer adds that some fear is needed to live in the world at all, and cowardice is just an extreme form of that fear. He points to Bacon's view of "panic" terror, which he links to Pan, the figure of Nature.

Fear is natural to every living thing and helps keep it alive, but it often arises without a real cause, and people are especially prone to it. Its main feature is that it has no clear idea of any specific danger. It assumes danger exists and, when pressed, gives its own fright as the reason for being afraid.

Schopenhauer quotes Voltaire's saying that each age of life brings its own kind of mind, and that a person whose mind does not match his years is unhappy. He says that looking at what each stage of life brings will close his discussion of happiness.

Throughout life we only ever have the present. What changes is how we see it: young people look ahead to a long future, and older people look back on a long past. Our mood shifts with age, but our basic character stays the same.

Schopenhauer says that in childhood the intellect is more active than the will, because a child has few needs and few dealings with others. Children therefore spend their energy learning about the world, and everything feels new and delightful. This is why early life seems like a lost paradise when looked back on.

Childhood is compared to a long poem because poetry, like all art, aims to grasp the "Idea" in Plato's sense. That means seeing a single thing's essential nature, the qualities it shares with its whole kind, so one example stands for many and one experience applies to a thousand.
Someone might object that children only attend to single objects or events as they come up, and only when those things stir their desires at the moment. The author says this objection is mistaken.

In early childhood, everything feels new and vivid, so a child, without knowing it, is constantly working out what life is like. It learns the basic nature of life from individual scenes and experiences.

Spinoza's phrase "sub specie aeternitatis" means seeing things from the viewpoint of eternity. Here the child is said to learn to see the people and things around it as particular examples of general laws.

Young people tend to see each single thing as a sample of its whole kind, and this fades with age. Because of this, the few things learned early on become the basic headings under which all later experience is sorted, often without our noticing.
The earliest years of life set the basic way a person sees the world, whether that view is shallow or deep. Later experience can add to and refine this view, but it does not really change its core.

In childhood, people focus more on gaining knowledge for its own sake than on using their will to act and get things. Schopenhauer says this comes from a purely objective, poetic way of seeing the world, and from the will not yet being fully developed.

Children often have a grave, serious look, which Raphael painted in his cherubs, as in the Sistine Madonna. Schopenhauer says this look comes from childhood being so full of happiness that people later remember it with longing and regret.

Education tries to give us ideas, which are learned from outside, but ideas do not tell us the real nature of things. That deeper knowledge comes only through intuition, a direct grasp of things, and no one can be given it from outside; each person must reach it alone.

A person's mind and character come from within his own nature, not from outside influences. So no teaching method, not even Pestalozzi's (a famous Swiss educator), can make a born simpleton sensible. Such a person stays a simpleton all his life.

Childhood memories stay firm, Schopenhauer says, because as children we give our full attention to what is right around us. We treat each thing as if it were the only thing of its kind. Once we learn how many things exist, that total absorption fades, and our patience goes with it.

Seen from outside, as something presented to our senses, the world looks pleasing. Looked at from within, as will, it is mostly full of pain and trouble. In short, it is beautiful to see but terrible in what it actually is.

In childhood, we know the world mainly by its outward appearance, which looks pleasing. We do not yet know its inner side, which Schopenhauer calls will, a force of striving. So the young person believes the beautiful things they see must be even more beautiful inside, and the world seems like a paradise.

Schopenhauer says that a desire to act and suffer leads a young man into the world, where his will is blocked at every turn. Disillusion then grows slowly. A man often thinks he has already outgrown his illusions, but the process is still beginning and reaches more and more of his life.

Life seen in childhood is like theatre scenery viewed from far away, looking attractive and full of promise. In old age, the same life is like that scenery seen up close, where the painted effect is no longer convincing.

In childhood people are alike and get along well, as young leaves in spring look much the same. At puberty people begin to differ, and they move further apart, like the lines of a circle spreading from its centre.

Young people spend their early years chasing happiness, assuming it is waiting for them somewhere in life. This hope always fails and brings discontent. They are pulled by a vague picture of future bliss, made from dreams and imagination, and they look for it in vain.

Young people are usually unhappy with their situation and blame it on the particular circumstances they meet when they first enter life. In fact, they are only now discovering that life is empty and miserable everywhere.

Schopenhauer says it would help a young man if his early training removed the belief that the world has much to give him. Instead, education usually strengthens this false belief, and young people often form their first ideas of life from stories rather than real experience.

Young people picture life as a gorgeous, romantic vision and long to make it real, which is like trying to grab a rainbow. The visions charm us because they stay unreal, and we enjoy them as pure contemplation, free from life's struggle. Trying to make them real turns them into objects of desire, and that always brings pain.

Youth is driven by a longing for happiness that is never satisfied, while later life is ruled by fear of misfortune. As people age, they come to see that happiness is illusory and only pain is real. So older people, especially the wiser ones, focus more on avoiding pain and securing their lives than on chasing pleasure. Old age is better at preventing misfortune, while youth is better at enduring it.

As a young man, the author welcomed a ring at the door, hoping for something pleasant. Later, the same sound filled him with dismay. He says people of talent or distinction often feel this same change toward other people, so they do not really belong to the world.

People of great superiority feel alone at first, as young people who sense the world has left them behind. Later they feel they have escaped the world instead. The first feeling comes from ignorance and is unpleasant; the second is pleasant because they have by then come to understand the world.

In youth, people think great happiness and pleasure exist in the world but are hard to reach, so they long for them. In old age, a person realises there is no such happiness, so the mind becomes calm, and they enjoy the present and small things.

Life experience, according to this passage, gives a clearer view of the world. A young person sees a distorted world made of personal whims, inherited prejudice and false beliefs. Experience first frees us from these false notions picked up in youth.

Schopenhauer says the best education would keep false ideas out of a child's mind from the start. That is hard to do. A child should first see only a small, limited world, learn it clearly and correctly, and only then have that world slowly widened, with nothing left vague or misunderstood.

Schopenhauer suggests that a child's early ideas about people and things should be simple but accurate, so they only need to be expanded later rather than corrected. The same approach would continue into youth. Novels would be banned, and biographies such as the life of Franklin would take their place.

Young people expect that the big events of their lives, and the people who will matter most, will arrive with great fanfare. Looking back in old age, though, they see that these things arrived quietly, almost without notice.

Schopenhauer compares a human life to embroidery. In the first half, we see the neat front side, which looks attractive. In the second half, we see the back, which is less attractive but shows how the threads were actually joined together.

In conversation, a clever young man will not dominate until he is past forty. Age and experience can outweigh even great intellect, and can balance it even against a person of little ability. This refers to personal standing, not to fame from published work.
After about forty, a man with a good mind will probably show some dislike of people. He has, as is natural, judged other people's character by studying his own.

Someone who has come to see that other people fall short, in mind or in heart, tends to keep away from them. Schopenhauer's general claim is that a person's liking for solitude depends on his own worth: the more he is worth in himself, the more he enjoys being alone with himself.

Schopenhauer says that a young man who quickly learns how the world works and easily fits into its ways is a bad sign, showing a common nature. A young man who is surprised by how people behave and is awkward with them shows a nobler character.

Young people feel lively partly because they cannot see death, which seems far off on the far side of life's hill. Once past the top, death comes into view, and people become less cheerful and more serious as they sense their strength fading.

The young see life as endless and spend their time freely, while older people become more careful with time. Near the end of life, each day feels to the old man like the steps a condemned criminal takes on the way to his trial.

Young people look forward and see life stretching on for a very long time. Old people look back and see how little time has passed. Life seems long at the start and short at the end, and only a person who has lived a long time sees how short it is.

As people grow older, everything seems smaller, and life, which once seemed firmly grounded, now looks like a quick series of moments with no lasting worth. The older person concludes that the whole world is empty and not worth much.

Schopenhauer says that time seems to pass more slowly when we are young. Because of this, early youth feels longer and leaves more memories than later years. He compares youth to spring, when days feel tiresomely long, and later life to autumn, when days are shorter but more pleasant and even.

Old people feel their lives were short because their memory has lost much of the past, including small details and unpleasant events. Schopenhauer adds that a person must regularly think back over what they have learned and lived through, or these will gradually be forgotten.

We tend not to think about trivial matters or unpleasant experiences, yet we need to think about them if we want to remember them. Also, things that seem important at first can become trivial through repetition, so that in the end we forget how often they happened.

We remember early years better than later ones because, as we get older, fewer events seem important enough to keep in memory. Events not felt to be significant are forgotten once they have passed, so the years leave fewer marks as they go by.

People prefer not to dwell on unpleasant things that have happened to them, especially when those things wound their pride, since few misfortunes are entirely their own fault. For this reason, they readily forget both unpleasant and trivial matters.

Our memory of the past gets shorter as life fills up with more experiences. Old events grow faint and hard to make out, much as the coastline looks to a sailor leaving shore, shrinking and blurring with every minute.

Sometimes a long-past event comes back to memory as vividly as if it were yesterday, so it seems close to the present. Schopenhauer's explanation is that the years in between cannot be recalled with the same clarity. No single image runs through that stretch of time that could be taken in at once, so it leaves no sharp mark to measure the distance by.

Most details of a long past period are forgotten, leaving only the general sense that we lived through it. Because of this, a single old event can seem recent, the years between seem to vanish, and the whole of life seems very short.

Sometimes in old age a person can hardly believe how many years they have lived, or that their long past was real. Schopenhauer says this feeling comes mainly from the fact that the present always seems fixed and unchanging when we look at it.

Schopenhauer says that certain states of mind come from a basic fact: our true nature is not in time, only its outward appearance is. The present moment is where the inner self, as subject, meets the outside world, as object.

In youth, the years seem endless because we fill them with so many hoped-for goals. So many plans are packed into them that, if all were carried out, we would die early even if we lived as long as Methuselah, a very long-lived figure in the Bible.

When we are young, life seems long because we judge its length by the few years we have lived so far. Early experiences are new, so they feel important, and we often recall them. Youth therefore seems full of events, and so it seems to last long.

Sometimes we think we want to be far away, but what we really want is to get back the time we spent there, when we were younger. Time seems to be a place, but it is only the past. Travelling there shows that we were mistaken.

Long life can come in two ways, once a person has a sound constitution, which is a necessary condition. Schopenhauer compares this to two lamps: one burns long on little oil because its wick is thin, and the other burns as long because it has plenty of oil and a thick wick. The oil stands for vital energy, and the wick for how that energy is spent.

Schopenhauer compares human life to money. Until about age thirty-six, a person spends only what comes in each day, like someone living on interest. After that, the person starts using up their store of vital energy, like an investor who begins to spend the capital itself. At first the loss is hardly noticed, since most spending is still covered.

Schopenhauer says that as a person ages, a sense of losing their resources grows stronger, like a falling body that speeds up. When both their vital energy and their wealth start running out at the same time, the situation becomes desperate. He argues that this fear of loss is why the desire to possess things grows with age.

Young people, like someone who saves part of their yearly interest and adds it to their capital, have a steady surplus of vital energy. Their health and strength grow, often under careful protection, while old age has nothing left to build on.

Schopenhauer says a person should save his strength even while young. He points to Aristotle's remark that very few Olympic victors won a prize both as boys and as men. The reason, he says, is that the hard training used up their powers too early, so they could not last into adulthood.

Child prodigies, who seem clever early on, often grow into ordinary adults, because their intelligence was pushed too hard in childhood. Schopenhauer suggests that forcing boys to learn the ancient languages early may be part of the cause of the dullness he sees in many scholars.

Each person's character tends to suit one stage of life, and they are at their best during that stage. Some are charming only when young, some are active only in middle age, and others improve in old age, when they become gentler. The author notes that this last pattern is often true of the French.
A person's character may contain traits that match one stage of life, such as youth, manhood or old age. Or these traits may balance the faults that belong to that stage.
A sailor tells he is moving forward by watching the coastline shrink into the distance. Likewise, a person knows he is growing older when those who were older than him start to seem young.

Schopenhauer's point is that people seem to be fully conscious only in youth, and that old people are only half alive. With age, experiences leave fewer marks on the mind. Life passes without much impression, and an old person often acts without remembering whether he has acted at all.

The passage says that time seems to speed up as life goes on, and to slow down when things are new. Childhood feels long because everything is novel and wakes us to full awareness. A trip also feels longer than the same stretch spent at home, for the same reason.

Time seems longer when we are young or travelling, because everything is new and makes a strong impression. As the mind grows used to things, impressions weaken, time seems less important, and so it feels shorter. Schopenhauer's point is that a boy's hours feel longer than an old man's days.

Time seems to speed up as we get older. Schopenhauer compares this to a ball rolling faster down a hill and to a point moving faster the farther it is from the centre of a turning disc. A year feels shorter in proportion to how much of life it already makes up: at fifty, a year seems one-tenth as long as it did at five.

Time seems to pass at different speeds at different ages, and this affects how we experience life. Childhood, though only about fifteen years long, seems the longest stretch of life, so it holds the most memories. Also, the younger a person is, the more often they tend to feel bored.

Children need constant activity, work or play, and feel terrible boredom when they have neither. Boredom is still a dread in youth, but it fades as adulthood arrives, and old men feel their remaining time pass far too quickly.

Schopenhauer says that as people get older, time seems to speed up and boredom fades. The passions and their pain quiet down, so life feels lighter than in youth, as long as health lasts. That is why the years just before old age are called a person's best years.

Schopenhauer says that youth, when the mind is open and receptive, is the time when basic ideas take root, like seeds sown in spring. He adds that deep truths come to us first as sudden insights, triggered by a passing impression, not worked out by reasoning. Such insight needs strong, vivid and lasting impressions.

Youth is the time for taking in deep truths and forming basic ideas, which shape the rest of thinking. Later in life people are more able to act on the world, because their characters are set and they are less open to new views. The world, in turn, has less effect on them.

Young people are mainly moved by what they see and experience around them, so youth suits poetry. Older people are more guided by reflection, so age suits philosophy. The same holds in action: the young decide by outside impressions, while the old decide by thought.

Old age brings more experience of the outside world, which is enough to sort observations into the ideas they show. This lets a person understand those ideas fully and judge how far they can be trusted. Old people also become used to life's events, so those events no longer affect them as strongly as before.

In youth, the impressions of outward life are so strong, especially for lively, imaginative people, that they see the world as a kind of picture. Their main concern is the figure they cut in it, and they often do not realise this. Personal vanity and love of fine clothes show this.

Schopenhauer says that mental strength is greatest in youth, up to about age thirty-five, and then slowly declines. He adds that later life still brings a benefit: only in later years can a person be truly rich in experience and learning, because there has been time to see life from all sides.

Old age, according to this passage, brings a deeper and wider knowledge than youth. Ideas learned early are better understood later, with more examples to support them. The old person's knowledge also forms a connected whole, while a young person's knowledge is incomplete and in pieces.

Only someone who reaches old age, Schopenhauer says, can fully understand life. An old man sees its whole course, including its end, and so grasps how empty it is. Younger people keep believing that things will work out in the end.

Young people are better at forming new ideas from little knowledge, while older people are stronger in judgment and care. Youth is the time for gathering the raw material that later becomes a person's own view of life. Great writers usually produce their best work around fifty, though the foundations are laid in youth.

Each generation tends to think it is wiser than the ones before it, and a person often thinks the same of his younger self. Schopenhauer says this is often a mistaken view. A habit of looking down on the past forms while we are growing, and it stays even after our mental powers start to fail, when we should instead look back with respect.

Schopenhauer says that a person's basic character is fixed from birth, but the intellect, or mind, can change much more. He gives two reasons: the intellect rests on the body, and it works with material that comes from experience.

Schopenhauer says a person's natural powers rise to a peak and then slowly decline into weakness. But the knowledge, experience and insight a person gathers keep growing over time, until old age brings a sudden failure of those powers.

The passage says that a person has two parts: one that never changes, and one that changes in two opposite directions. How these two parts mix in one person explains why his mental outlook and his worth differ at different stages of life.

Life's first forty years are like the main text, and the next thirty are like the commentary that explains it. Without that later commentary, a person cannot fully grasp what the early years meant, their overall sense, or the lessons they hold.

Near the end of life, people's true characters become clear, much as masks come off at the end of a masked ball. Actions show their results, achievements get their proper value, and false pretences collapse. Only time can bring this about.

Only near the end of life does a person truly understand who he has been, including the goals he chased and how he related to others and the world. Usually this lowers his opinion of himself, though sometimes it raises it, because he had set himself a higher aim than most people and had underestimated how base the world is.

Schopenhauer argues that old age, not youth, is the happier part of life. Youth is ruled by the passions, which cause much pain and little pleasure. In age the passions fade, the mind turns to quiet thought, and a person feels happy to the extent that the intellect rules over the rest of the self.

Pleasure, on this view, is only the ending of a need or craving, and pain is the real feeling. So passions cannot bring lasting happiness, and old age should not be pitied for losing pleasures. When a pleasure stops once its need is met, that is no more a cause for complaint than being unable to keep eating after dinner.

Schopenhauer argues that youth is not the happiest time of life. He says old age deserves the prize, because by then a person is free of sexual desire, which otherwise keeps troubling them. While that desire rules, he says, a person is in a kind of mild madness and is not truly reasonable.

Schopenhauer says young people are usually sad and melancholy because they are still ruled by desire, which he calls an "evil spirit," and it rarely leaves them alone. Old people are cheerful because, after long being bound by their passions, they are finally free to move about.

When the passion of love (the sexual drive, which the passage is about) fades, life loses its real core and is left as an empty shell. Life then resembles a play that real actors begin but that puppet-like machines finish, wearing the actors' costumes.

Youth is a time of restlessness and age a time of calm, and this difference shows how much pleasure each stage tends to bring. Children reach eagerly for everything they see, delighted by the world because their senses are fresh. Young people do the same, and pursue their goals with even more energy.

Young people, in this passage, are caught up by the attractive things around them. Their imagination pictures pleasures that the world cannot actually give, so they feel a restless longing for things they cannot name and cannot rest. In old age this longing fades, partly because the blood cools and the senses are less easily drawn in.

With age, experience shows that things are less valuable than they seemed and that pleasure is empty. Old illusions and biased ideas fade, so a person sees the world more clearly and begins to understand that everything on earth is worthless.

Old age brings a calm peace of mind, which Schopenhauer treats as the core of happiness. The young believe life holds many good things they could reach if given the chance. The old man, like the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, sees that all things are empty, much as a gilded shell can hide a hollow nut.

In later life, a man finally understands Horace's saying "Nil admirari" (wonder at nothing). He sees that everything is empty and that the world's glories mean little. He no longer believes that happiness is more available in a palace than in a cottage, and worldly ranks of great and small no longer matter to him.

An old man in this calm state sees through all false ideas about life. He knows that however much people decorate life with show and luxury, it stays shabby underneath. Human existence has value only when it is free from pain, not when it has pleasure, and certainly not when it has display.

Old age brings disillusion, because the illusions that made life attractive and drove people on have faded. A person comes to see that most desired pleasures and worldly splendors are worth very little, and that life seems empty. This is why old men are sometimes irritable and gloomy.

Schopenhauer argues that illness is not a necessary part of old age, since health and sickness both tend to grow as life goes on. He also says old age is less prone to boredom than youth, for reasons he gave earlier in the work.

Boredom is not a necessary result of the loneliness that comes with old age. It mainly strikes people who have only enjoyed sensual pleasures and social life, and who have never developed their minds. Those who had strong minds in youth still keep enough mental power to resist boredom, even though their intellect declines.

An old man gains, through experience, knowledge, reflection and dealing with people, a sharper understanding of how the world works and a more unified view of life. He keeps learning by finding new uses for what he knows, and this ongoing self-education keeps his mind occupied and satisfied.

Old age brings less mental and physical strength, but this is partly made up for, and time seems to pass faster, which keeps boredom away. Losing bodily strength matters little unless a person must work to earn a living. Being poor in old age is a great misfortune, while good health and money together can make old age quite tolerable. Money becomes more valued then, since it stands in for lost strength.

In old age, desire for pleasure fades. The old man turns to wine and to talking and teaching, not to seeing and learning. It is lucky if he still keeps some interest in study, music or theatre. At that stage, what a man has inside himself matters more than ever.

Schopenhauer says that people who were dull and unthinking when young tend to become like machines in old age. They keep their old habits, and new experiences hardly change them. Talking to them leaves no lasting mark, so old age is only a dead remnant of life.

Schopenhauer says that losing mental and physical strength in old age is sad but useful, because it prepares a person for death, which would otherwise be too hard to bear. The best outcome of very old age is a gentle death, without disease or pain. He adds that in later years the mind forgets more each day than it learns.

Youth looks forward to a long life, while old age looks toward death. Schopenhauer asks whether life is better behind a person or ahead of them, and quotes the Preacher, who said the day of death is better than the day of birth. He also quotes a Spanish proverb: to live long is to see much evil.

Schopenhauer says that a natural human life lasts about one hundred years, as an old Indian text states. He claims that only people who live past ninety die peacefully, without disease or pain, simply ceasing to live. Anyone who dies before ninety, he says, dies early from illness.

Schopenhauer argues that the biblical and Herodotean view that human life lasts about seventy to eighty years is mistaken. He says people who die around that age do not die of old age but of disease, which he calls abnormal, so the natural length of life must be longer.

Death from old age, without disease or struggle, comes naturally only between ninety and a hundred. Schopenhauer holds that a hundred years is the natural length of human life, a view he credits to the ancient Hindu Upanishads.

A single person's life cannot be predicted from the planets, as astrology claims. Still, the stages of human life in general can be compared to the planets in turn, each stage coming under the influence of one planet after another.

Schopenhauer uses the planets as a way of describing stages of life. At ten, a boy is quick and restless over small things but learns fast. At twenty, a young man is mostly ruled by love of women. At thirty, a man becomes energetic, bold, quarrelsome and proud.

Schopenhauer says that at forty a man is ruled by the four asteroids, which are named after classical goddesses. His life has grown wider, and he has become thrifty, keeping to useful things. He has a home of his own, has learned what he needs to know, and his wife manages the household.

At fifty, Schopenhauer says, a man is at his peak: he has outlived most of his peers, has strength, experience and knowledge, and wants to lead rather than take orders. The work that suits him now is guiding and ruling within his own area. Jupiter, the planet, is used here as a symbol of this stage of life.
In old age, people often seem already dead: slow, clumsy, heavy and pale. The final stage is death, which the saying calls going to heaven, here expressed through Uranus, the Greek god of the sky.

Schopenhauer says that Eros (love, the drive to produce life) is closely tied to Death, and that Death is the source from which all life comes. He calls the Greek god of the underworld, Orcus, both the receiver and the giver of all things. Everything alive once existed there, he says, but he claims the way this happens is hidden.

Emerson says that original verses, unlike conventional ones, always carry a message to the reader's soul, whatever the subject. The feeling they give matters more than the ideas in them. To trust your own private conviction, believing it holds for everyone, is genius, and once spoken it becomes shared truth.

Emerson says that a person's own inner thought, which comes first, eventually becomes outward truth, as if announced by the trumpets of the Last Judgment. He praises Moses, Plato and Milton for ignoring books and tradition and speaking their own thoughts. Yet people often ignore their own thought simply because it is their own.

Great works of art show us our own earlier thoughts, returned to us in a grander, strange form. Their lesson is to hold to our first honest impression, most of all when everyone else disagrees. Otherwise, we later hear a stranger say what we already thought, and we feel ashamed to take our own view back from them.

A person eventually comes to see that envy is a kind of ignorance and copying others is self-destroying. He must accept himself as he is, and good things come to him only through working on his own assigned ground.

Each person has a power that is new in the world, and only that person can know what it is, and this is found only by trying. What strikes a person deeply is not random: a person's memory is shaped to take in certain faces and facts, just as the eye is made to receive one particular ray of light.

Emerson says people only partly express themselves because they are ashamed of the divine idea each person carries. That idea can be trusted to turn out well if it is honestly shared. A person feels relief and happiness only after putting full heart into their work, while doing otherwise brings no peace.

Trust your own inner self, because it is a reliable guide. Emerson says great people have always accepted their place in the world and their own age, trusting the inner force they felt within them. He urges people to act as leaders and helpers, not to hide or flee, moving forward against disorder and darkness.

Emerson says that children, babies and even animals are admirable examples because their minds are whole and undivided. They do not doubt their own feelings by calculating whether they can succeed, so adults feel uneasy when they look at them. Babies conform to no one, yet adults all adjust to them.

Emerson says that youth has its own appeal and strength, and that young people do not need older people's approval to matter. A young person may not speak to adults, yet he speaks clearly to his own generation, and he will soon make older people seem unnecessary.

Emerson says that boys who are sure of their dinner feel no need to win favor from anyone, not even a lord, and this carefree attitude is natural and healthy. Sitting apart in the parlor like spectators, boys quickly judge the adults and events around them as good, bad, silly, or interesting.

Emerson says that a person who speaks or acts boldly becomes bound by it. Once he has done so, others watch him with sympathy or hatred, and their feelings become part of his obligations. He cannot forget this, and he wishes he could return to being neutral.

A person who makes no promises or commitments, and who observes things again and again with a clear, unbiased mind that cannot be bought or frightened, will be feared. His opinions on current events will seem to come from necessity, not personal interest, so they strike people deeply and make them afraid.

Emerson says that the inner voices we hear when alone fade once we join society. He claims society works against each person's independence, asking members to give up their freedom and growth in exchange for security. Society prizes conformity and dislikes self-reliance, valuing names and customs over real things and creative people.

Emerson says a person who wants to be truly themselves must refuse to simply conform. Even goodness should be examined rather than accepted just because of its name. The only thing finally sacred is the honesty of one's own mind; if you trust that inner judgment, the world will accept you.

Emerson says that if his impulses came from the Devil, he would still follow them, because only his own nature can set the law for him. He holds that good and bad are just labels that can shift, so right means what suits his nature and wrong means what goes against it. He adds that a person should act as if only his own self lasts and everything else is passing.

Emerson admits he too readily gives in to respectable labels, big organizations and established institutions, and to well-spoken people, when he should stand upright and speak plainly. He argues that a cruel or vain person should not be excused just because he uses the language of a good cause, such as the campaign against slavery. Instead, that person should first do simple good in his own home and daily life.

Emerson argues that real goodness should be honest and sharp rather than soft and sentimental. He says that caring for distant people while being harsh to those nearby is false, and that a truthful rebuke is better than polite affection. He also says he will follow his own inner calling even above family ties, and he jokingly calls that impulse "Whim."

Emerson rejects demands to justify his choice of company or to give money to poor people who are not his own. He says he owes his devotion only to those bound to him by spiritual affinity, and for them he would even accept prison.

Emerson lists kinds of giving he doubts are worth it: general charity, college education for fools, church buildings, money to drunks, and many relief societies. He admits he sometimes gives anyway, out of shame, but says he will one day have the courage to refuse.

Emerson says that most people treat their good deeds as payment for the bad or as a way of excusing how they live, much like a fine or a fee paid to avoid trouble. He rejects this approach. He wants to live honestly and steadily for its own sake, not to put on a display, even if that life seems plainer.

Emerson says he wants a sound, healthy self, and he asks for proof that a person is a true man in the person's own being, not in deeds. He says his worth does not depend on doing praised actions, because he already has the right to be himself and needs no outside proof to be sure of it.

A person should care most about doing what they themselves believe is right, not about what others think. Emerson says this is hard, because others often claim to know your duty better than you do. Living by the crowd's opinion is easy, and so is living by your own opinion alone, but the great person stays independent while surrounded by others.

Emerson argues that following customs you no longer believe in wastes your energy and hides who you really are. Joining dead churches, dead societies or party habits makes your true self hard to see. He says that doing your own work reveals your character and strengthens you, and that conformity is a kind of blindman's buff, a game of being blind to what is real.

Emerson says that if you know a speaker's religious group, you can predict his argument. A preacher praising his church's institutions will not offer anything new, because he has already bound himself to defend only the approved view. He is like a hired lawyer pretending to be an impartial judge.

Emerson says most people blindfold themselves and join some group of shared opinions. Because of this, they are not just wrong about a few things but untrue in everything they say, so their words never quite match reality. Over time, he adds, such people even take on the look of their group.
Emerson describes a forced smile put on in company where we feel uneasy and bored by the talk. The smile is not natural but is held by a sort of willful pressure, and it feels very unpleasant.

Emerson says that people who refuse to conform are punished by the disapproval of others. But the sour looks of the crowd have no deep cause; they change with fashion and the press. Still, the crowd's disapproval is more powerful than that of lawmakers or scholars.

It is easy for a firm man to withstand the anger of educated, upper-class people, because their anger is restrained and careful, as they feel vulnerable themselves. It takes greater inner strength, which Emerson ties to generosity of spirit and religious faith, to remain calm when the anger of ordinary, uneducated people joins in.

Emerson says that we fear being inconsistent, so we stick to what we said or did before. Others judge us only by our past actions, and we do not want to let them down. This keeps us from trusting ourselves.

Emerson says you should not worry about looking back at what you said before or being caught contradicting yourself. Judge the past by your present view instead of clinging to old memories or theories. When a moment of real devotion comes, follow it, even if your earlier beliefs about God don't fit.

Emerson says that sticking to a fixed set of opinions is a foolish habit of small minds, and that a great person does not worry about it. He says a person should speak what they think at each moment, even if it contradicts earlier views. Being misunderstood for this is not a bad thing, since great thinkers have always been misunderstood.

Emerson says a person cannot act against their own nature. Even their strongest impulses stay within the limits of what they are, much as tall mountains look flat on the curve of the earth. However a person is tested or examined, their character shows the same pattern, like a word puzzle that reads the same in any direction.

The speaker is living simply in the woods and wants to write down his honest thoughts each day, without planning ahead or looking back. He trusts that his writing will still have a good shape, even without intending it. He ends by saying that a person is judged by what he really is, and that character shows itself beyond what he chooses to show.
People think they show their goodness or badness only through what they openly do. They fail to see that virtue or vice spreads from a person at every moment, like a breath.

Emerson says that honest, natural actions can look very different from one another, yet they come from one will and so fit together. Seen from close up, they seem scattered, like a ship's zigzag course, but from far away they form one direction. Real action explains itself, while mere conformity to others explains nothing.

Past acts of integrity give a person the standing to act rightly now, without worrying about what others think. Character builds up over time, so each good day of virtue supports the next. Heroes seem majestic because their earlier victories stand behind them and light their present actions.

Emerson says that a person of real self-reliance seems to have an unseen escort of angels, giving them force and dignity. Honor earns our respect because it is ancient virtue, not something new or fashionable. It is worthy of love because it depends on itself and so has a pure, old lineage, even in a young person.

Emerson hopes that people will stop valuing conformity (fitting in) and consistency (sticking to past positions), and will treat such words as outdated. He says he will not flatter a great man to please him. He wants the visitor to want to please him, and he will stand for humanity, making it kind but above all true.

Emerson says that a truly independent person is not tied to one era or place. Such a person is the centre of things, and wherever he stands, nature is present. He judges other people and events, while most people only remind us of someone else.

Emerson says that a person of real character stands out so strongly that he makes outside circumstances seem unimportant. Such a person is a cause, a country and an age in himself, and later generations follow him. He gives the example of Caesar, after whom the Roman Empire came.

Emerson says that great individuals become so admired that their influence spreads widely. Movements and institutions, he argues, are like long shadows cast by a single person, such as Christ, Luther or Wesley. In his view, most of history is really the story of a few determined people.

Emerson says a person should know his own worth and stand firm, not sneak around as if he does not belong in a world that is his. The ordinary man feels poor before great buildings, statues and books, as if they ask who he is. Yet he says these works are really his, waiting for his notice and his judgment.

The passage uses a folk tale about a drunk man who is taken to a duke's house and made to believe he is the duke. Emerson says the tale fits human life: people are like drunkards who forget their true nature, but sometimes wake up, use their reason, and see that they are truly princes.

Emerson argues that we admire famous rulers too much and undervalue ordinary people. A private man's everyday work matters as much as the deeds of kings, and when ordinary people act with their own original thinking, the admiration will shift from kings to them.

Emerson says that kings, nobles and great landowners have taught people to respect one another. Men have willingly accepted these rulers living by their own rules, and in doing so they were, without knowing it, expressing their own worth and the right that belongs to every man.

Emerson argues that the force behind original action, and the reason we can trust ourselves, comes from an inner source he calls spontaneity or instinct. He describes this source as the root of genius, virtue, and life, and as something that brings beauty even to small actions when they show independence.

Emerson says that the deepest knowing, which he calls intuition, is direct and comes first, while everything learned later from teaching is only "tuition." The sense of being that comes to the soul in quiet moments is not separate from things, space, light, time or people. All share one source, and we first live that shared life before we see things as outside objects and forget our common origin.

Emerson says that the source of human thought and right action lies in a vast intelligence that we rest within. When we see what is just or true, we are not producing it ourselves; we are letting its light pass through us. We cannot explain where this source comes from, so all we can say is whether it is present or absent.

Emerson says that people can tell their deliberate thoughts apart from their involuntary perceptions, and that the perceptions deserve complete trust. A person may describe them badly, but the perceptions are still true. His own chosen actions and acquisitions, by contrast, seem to him like aimless wandering, while faint, natural feelings and idle daydreams are what hold his interest. Careless people often dispute such perceptions even more readily than they dispute opinions.

Emerson argues that seeing something is not a matter of personal choice. Once he perceives a trait, it is a fact, as real as the sun, and others will come to see it too, even if no one saw it before him.

When the soul is pure, it is wrong to seek outside help to reach God. A mind that is simple and receives divine wisdom no longer needs teachers, texts or temples. It lives fully in the present, and past and future are taken up into that moment.

Everything gains its holiness from its connection to the divine source, and so all things are equally sacred. Emerson says that a person who claims to speak of God through the old language of some distant past and foreign nation should not be believed. He compares this to the acorn and the oak: the later, fuller form is no less worthy than what came before.

Emerson asks why people honor the past. He says the centuries work against the soul's own good sense and power. He holds that history matters only as a story that illustrates the individual's own life and growth.

Emerson says people have become timid and rely on the words of great thinkers instead of stating their own views. He contrasts this with a rose, which does not compare itself to other roses but simply exists fully in each moment.

Emerson says a plant with no leaves is still complete, because it fully lives in the present moment. People, by contrast, dwell on the past or strain toward the future, missing what is around them. He concludes that people can be happy and strong only when they live in the present, outside the flow of time.

Emerson says that even strong thinkers hesitate to hear God unless he speaks in the words of biblical figures such as David, Jeremiah, or Paul. He predicts that people will not always value a few texts and lives so highly. He compares them to children who memorize the words of elders and admired people instead of thinking for themselves.

Once people reach the same insight as the sages who first spoke these sayings, they no longer need to hold onto the words. Emerson says that living truly brings true seeing, and that a person who lives with God speaks as naturally and sweetly as a brook or the wind in the corn.

Emerson says the highest truth cannot really be put into words, because everything we say only recalls a deeper inner intuition. He suggests that when good is near, and a person has life within, it does not come by any known or familiar route, and no outside sign or human face or name marks it.

The passage says that true insight, the "way" or "good," must be entirely new and must not rely on examples from others or on past experience. It treats earlier people as forgotten helpers, and it says that even hope is a lower feeling. In the moment of vision, the writer claims, there is no room for gratitude or ordinary joy.

A soul that rises above strong feelings sees that cause and effect are eternal and that truth and right exist by themselves, and so it stays calm. Distance in space and time means nothing to it. The thinking self, it says, has underlain every earlier state of life and every present one, and also what we call death.

Emerson argues that living only counts when a person is still changing and acting, not because of what they have already done. Power exists in the moment of moving from one state to another, not in rest. The world dislikes the idea that the soul is always becoming, since that makes past achievements count for little. Real self-reliance, he says, is power that acts, not a claim to confidence.

Emerson says that a person who acts from real inner strength, without needing to show it, commands more obedience from others than any master could. Such a person draws others toward them naturally. He claims that true virtue is a kind of height, and that people open to right principles will, by nature, rise above cities, kings, the rich and poets who lack that inner strength.

Emerson says that all things are ultimately one divine source, and that self-existence belongs to this highest cause. The more a thing shares in this self-existence, the more good it has. Ordinary activities like trade, farming, war and speech matter to him only as partial, imperfect signs of it.

In nature, strength is the measure of what is right, and nothing survives that cannot support itself. Emerson gives examples such as planets keeping their orbits and bent trees springing back. He presents these as proof that a self-sufficient soul should rely on itself.

Emerson urges the reader to stay focused on their own inner source instead of wandering off to follow others. He says that by simply stating the divine truth within, they can make outside people, books and institutions seem like unwelcome intruders, and that their own inner law shows how poor outside wealth and luck really are.

Emerson says people now act as a crowd, no longer respecting themselves or looking within. Instead, each person's talent goes to others for what it needs. He concludes that a person must act alone, and he prefers a quiet church before the service to any sermon.

Emerson argues that family ties or shared blood do not oblige a person to take on the faults of relatives or friends. Although he sees himself as connected to all people, he will not copy their irritability or foolishness, or feel shame for it. He adds that true independence must be a matter of the spirit, a raising of oneself, rather than a mere withdrawal from others.

Friends, clients, children, illness, fear, need and requests for charity all call the writer out of his private room, but he says he will stay in his own calm state and not join their disorder. People can bother him only because he gives them the chance through his own curiosity. The closing quotation adds that we keep what we love only while we do not crave it.

Emerson urges that, if people cannot yet reach obedience and faith, they should at least resist their temptations and act with courage. In everyday life this means speaking the truth, dropping false politeness and pretended affection, and telling family and friends that from now on one will live by the truth rather than by appearances.

The speaker says he will follow only the eternal, or universal, moral law, not a formal agreement. He will still care for his parents, family and wife, but in his own new way rather than by social custom. He will be himself, will not hide his likes and dislikes, and will not change his nature to please others.

Emerson says he will trust what is deep and holy within him, and act boldly on what his inner feeling and conscience tell him. He will not pretend to affection for people he does not respect, and those who share a different truth should keep to their own company. He claims this is good for everyone, and asks whether it sounds harsh today.

The speaker says that following one's own true nature will lead to a good outcome, even though it may hurt friends. He refuses to give up his freedom and power just to spare their feelings. He adds that people, in their moments of clear reason, will agree with him.

Emerson argues that rejecting popular standards does not mean rejecting all moral standards. He says an inner "law of consciousness" still holds, and that a person must answer to it either directly or indirectly, by checking whether they have fulfilled their duties to family, neighbors, and others.

Emerson says that he can set aside outside standards of judgment and answer to his own inner law instead. This inner law, which he calls a "perfect circle," rejects many duties that society calls duties. If he fully meets its demands, he is free from the common moral code. Anyone who thinks this law is easy should try to keep it for just one day.

It takes something almost divine to drop the usual human motives and trust yourself as your own master. Emerson hopes such a person will have a noble heart, a faithful will and clear sight, so that he becomes his own teaching, community and law, and his simple purpose binds him as strongly as necessity binds others.

Emerson says that modern society has drained people of strength and courage. People have become timid and hopeless, afraid of truth, fortune, death and one another. In his view, the present age produces no great or complete individuals.

Emerson says society needs people who can renew life, but most people cannot support themselves. Their ambitions far exceed their abilities, so they depend on others. He claims that even their housekeeping, work, marriages and religion are chosen for them by society rather than by themselves, so they are only "parlor soldiers," playing at being brave without facing real struggle.

Young men who fail at their first ventures often lose heart and treat themselves as ruined. A gifted graduate who does not get a city office within a year is likewise expected to feel disheartened and complain for life.

A hardy young man from rural New England, who tries many jobs one after another and always lands on his feet, is described as worth more than a hundred pampered city men. He does not wait to settle on one profession before living; he lives each day as it comes and has many opportunities.

A teacher who opens up a person's inner strength and tells them to stand on their own, not bend like willows, would restore human life to its full worth. Such a person, acting from themselves and dropping old laws, customs and idols, would earn thanks and respect instead of pity, and would be remembered by history.

Emerson says that if people rely more on themselves, this will change every part of their lives. The change would reach their religion, schooling, work, way of living, social ties, property, and their beliefs about ideas.

Emerson says that prayer which asks for some outside gift or particular thing is weak and even wrong. True prayer is instead a calm, joyful view of life from the highest standpoint, a soul looking at existence and finding it good.

Emerson says that asking God for a private gain is selfish and dishonest, because it assumes God and the person are separate. A person truly at one with God would not beg, and would see prayer in all honest work, such as a farmer weeding or a rower at the oar, even when those tasks serve small ends.

Emerson says that regret and discontent are a weakness of the will, a lack of self-reliance, and so are a kind of false prayer. Regret for misfortune is useful only if it actually helps the sufferer; otherwise, it is better to get on with your own work. Joining others in weeping is also poor sympathy, since it does not restore their own reason.

Emerson says that people admire and welcome the self-reliant man most when he has not asked for their approval. Men love him because he did not need their love, and they praise him because he ignored their criticism. The gods favor him for the same reason: he persisted despite men's hatred. Zoroaster, an ancient Persian prophet, is quoted to say that the gods come quickly to the persistent person.

Emerson says that just as prayer can be a weakness of the will, creeds are a weakness of the mind. People ask other humans to speak for God instead of hearing God directly. He also says a strong, original thinker tends to force his own system of ideas on others, creating a new system each time.

Emerson says that a student feels more pleasure the deeper and wider the thought is. This is most visible in religious creeds and churches, which are systems that a powerful mind builds on basic ideas of duty and humanity's relation to God. Calvinism, Quakerism and Swedenborgism are his examples. Followers enjoy fitting everything into the new terms, much as a girl new to botany enjoys seeing the world through it.

Emerson says a student may first gain mind-power from a teacher's thinking. But people with narrow minds treat their teacher's system as the final goal rather than a tool that can be used up. They think the system covers the whole universe, and they cannot believe others can see truth without having taken it from their teacher.

Emerson says that a higher, untamed light will break into any small, enclosed life, even the cramped and comfortable ones people build for themselves. Those small structures may seem secure, but they will eventually crack and fall apart, while the light keeps shining over the whole universe as it always has.

Emerson argues that people who travel to famous places like Italy or England do so because they lack self-development. The great figures of those places became admired by staying put, and a wise person stays at home in spirit. If duty takes such a person abroad, they still carry their home with them and go as a teacher of wisdom, not as a servant or intruder.

Emerson says travel is fine for art, study or kindness, but only if the traveler is already settled in himself and does not expect to find something better abroad. Someone who travels to be entertained, or to find what he lacks, only escapes himself. He grows old in spirit, like the ancient ruins he visits, and carries his own decay with him.

The main point is that travel does not free a person from themselves. The speaker hopes that a famous place will lift his sadness, but when he arrives he finds the same unchanging self he was trying to escape. Wherever he goes, this self goes with him.

Emerson says that restless travel is a sign of a deeper weakness in thinking. He argues that people copy foreign and past models in houses, décor, opinions and tastes, when true art comes from the soul and the artist's own mind.

Emerson argues that American builders and artists need not copy old European styles like the Doric or Gothic. Instead, they should study their own climate, land, daily life and government, and design something that fits those conditions while still satisfying taste and feeling.

Emerson says a person should rely on their own gifts and not copy others. A talent you were born with can be used with the full force of a lifetime's development, while a borrowed one is only partly yours. No one can teach a person what they do best; that can only be shown by the person doing it, as Shakespeare shows with no teacher behind him.

Emerson argues that great men cannot be taught or copied, because each one is unique. Scipio's greatness lay in what he could not take from others, and Shakespeare cannot be produced by studying Shakespeare. He ends by saying that a person should do the task given to them and aim high without limit.

The main point is that the soul always has a fresh, powerful way of speaking, different from the great works of the past. Because hearing and speaking come from the same nature, a person who can understand these older voices can also answer them in their own voice.

Emerson says that our religion, education and art all look outward, toward others, and so does our sense of community. People take pride in improving society, yet none of them actually improves himself.

Emerson argues that society does not really move forward. Each gain is paid for with a loss: people gain new skills and knowledge but lose older instincts. Its changes, whether toward civilization or wealth or science, are not true improvement.

Emerson contrasts a well-dressed American, carrying a watch, pencil and bill of exchange, with a New Zealander who owns only a club, spear, mat and a small share of a shed. Yet when he compares their health, he says the American has lost the natural strength of his origins.

Emerson is saying that a traveller's reports show that a blow which heals quickly in a "savage" would kill a white man. The point is that people from different places are not made the same way, and he uses this example to argue that rules and customs are not fixed for all people alike.

Emerson says that modern people have many tools that do their work for them, so they have lost the natural skills those tools replaced. People can travel by coach, check time by a watch, and find dates in an almanac, yet they no longer walk well, tell time by the sun, or know the stars and seasons.

Emerson argues that many modern tools and institutions weaken people: notebooks dull memory, libraries clutter the mind, and machines and refinement may drain energy. He also says that Christianity, built into churches and set forms, has lost its strong, wild virtue, and he asks where a true Christian now is, just as every Stoic once was one.

Emerson argues that people do not grow greater over time. Moral greatness is as fixed as height, and the great men of today equal those of ancient times, such as Plutarch's heroes. Great men do not form a lasting class; each true great man stands alone and starts his own path.

Emerson argues that each era's tools and inventions are just surface decoration and do not truly strengthen people, and that new machinery can do as much harm as good. He gives examples: explorers in simple boats did as much as later expeditions with elaborate equipment, and Galileo's small telescope revealed more than later instruments. Old machines are often dropped after being praised. A great person, he says, returns to basic human nature.

Emerson says that Napoleon won Europe by stripping his armies down to bare courage, without supply wagons, stores or other aids. Napoleon believed an army could only be perfect if it dropped its arms, supplies and carriages, and let each soldier grind his own corn and bake his own bread, as Roman soldiers did.

Society is compared to a wave: the shape keeps moving forward, but the water in it does not. Emerson means that a nation looks like one unchanging whole, yet its people are constantly replaced, and each generation's experience dies with them.

Emerson says that relying on property, and on governments that protect it, shows a lack of self-reliance. People have come to value religion, learning and government mainly as protectors of their possessions, and they judge one another by what they own rather than by what they are. A truly cultivated person, he says, becomes ashamed of property because they respect their own nature more.

Emerson says that possessions a person did not earn, such as inherited goods, gifts, or stolen wealth, do not truly belong to him and can be taken away at any time. What a person becomes through his own character, by contrast, is real property that no ruler, mob, disaster, or bankruptcy can take, and it keeps growing wherever he lives.

Emerson quotes the Caliph Ali, who said that a person's share of life will come to them on its own, so there is no need to chase it. He then argues that people depend on outside goods, such as the support of large crowds, and so respect numbers too much. A young party supporter feels stronger when more delegations join the cause.

Emerson argues that reformers gather crowds, hold votes and pass resolutions, but that God enters a person by the opposite route. A man is strong only when he drops outside support and stands alone, and every new follower weakens him. He urges self-reliance: a single firm person can hold up everything around him.

A person who believes his strength is within him, and who sees that he has been weak because he looked for good outside himself, will rely on his own thought. That reliance sets him upright and gives him power, as a man standing on his feet is stronger than one standing on his head.

Emerson says that people who depend on luck, which he calls Fortune, gain and lose with its turns. He urges instead that one work and act within the order of Cause and Effect, so that chance no longer controls you. Good events may lift your spirits, but he warns not to trust them. Only yourself and firm principles bring real peace.

The poem says that opposites keep the universe in balance. Time's black and white wings, mountains and oceans, and the moon and tides all hold things even. The lonely Earth is pictured as a counterweight, a small body that offsets the others as it moves through empty space.

The passage says that a person's true strength comes from within, like an elm tree that holds up a vine. Wealth and power come to those who use their own strength, and whatever belongs to a person by nature will come to them, even across hills and seas, like a shadow that follows them.

Emerson says that as a boy he wanted to write about compensation, the idea that things balance out. He felt that everyday life, such as tools, bread, trade, greetings, debts, and character, showed this idea more clearly than churches did.

The speaker hopes that a certain teaching could show people a glimpse of the divine, the soul of the world acting now, free from old traditions. Such a teaching would give comfort like a flood of love, and would guide people through dark times as a star guides a traveler.

The narrator heard a preacher say that justice is not carried out in this life: the wicked prosper and the good suffer, so balance must come in the next life. The congregation accepted this without objection and left without comment.

The speaker asks what it means to say that good people suffer in this life and will be repaid later. He suggests the usual reading is that the saints, who are poor and despised, will one day get the same worldly pleasures that wicked people enjoy now, such as money, food and wine.

Emerson is saying that a promised reward cannot be a true prize if it only means doing things people can already do, such as praying or serving others. He claims that if a believer's real hope is to enjoy the sinners' pleasures now or to take revenge later, then the reward being sought is just worldly satisfaction.

The main point is that it is a mistake to accept that wicked people succeed and that justice is not done in this world. The preacher was wrong to measure success by the market's crude standards, when he should have declared that the soul and the will decide what is good, bad, and successful.

Emerson says that popular religious writings and the literary men who touch on religion share the same low, basic assumptions. He claims that today's popular theology has become more polite but has kept the same core beliefs as the superstitions it replaced. Still, ordinary people act better than the theology they profess, and their daily conduct contradicts it.

Every sincere, striving person eventually outgrows the doctrines they were taught, and everyone sometimes senses a falsehood they cannot prove. People know more than they realize. Teachings accepted without thought in school or church would likely be doubted if spoken casually in conversation.

When someone states firm views about divine law in mixed company, listeners answer with silence. Emerson says this silence shows they are unhappy with the claim but cannot put their own view into words. He then says he will record some facts about the law of Compensation, and he hopes to manage even a small part of it.

Emerson says that polarity, meaning action and reaction, appears everywhere in nature. He gives many examples, such as light and dark, heat and cold, tides, male and female, and the beating of the heart.

Emerson says that in nature every force comes with an opposite. When one end of a magnet is charged, the other end takes the opposite charge, and to empty one place you must fill another. Each thing is half of a pair, such as spirit and matter, or man and woman, and it points to its partner to be whole.

Every part of the world has the same two-sided pattern as the whole. Each small thing, from a pine needle to an animal, shows this balance. In animals, a gain in one body part is paid for by a loss in another, so that a larger head means a shorter trunk and limbs.

Emerson gives several examples of one idea: a gain in one area is paid for by a loss in another. In machines, what is gained in force is lost in time. Climate and soil work the same way, since cold weather strengthens people while barren land produces no fevers or dangerous animals.

Emerson says that every gain in human life comes with a matching loss, and every loss with a gain. Each excess leads to a lack, and each pleasure carries a penalty when it is abused. Wealth, for example, is said to increase those who use it, not simply the holder.

Nature balances out unequal fortune. If a person gathers too much, the wealth that swells his estate costs him his life, and differences in people's conditions always tend to even out. Some leveling circumstance eventually brings the powerful, rich, and fortunate down to the same level as everyone else.

Emerson suggests that nature softens even a fierce, rough man through his love and fear for his children. A violent, scowling man becomes gentle and polite because of his young sons and daughters, so nature keeps the balance between people.

The passage argues that high position has a price. A President gives up peace and much of his manly strength to keep a brief public image, and he must bow to the hidden powers behind him. Genius, too, is not free of cost: the great person who stands above thousands bears the burdens that greatness brings.

A person who receives new insight must stay true to it, even when it means moving past the approval that once pleased him. Emerson says he must even turn away from family and from what the world admires, and accept being scorned for it.

Emerson says that a natural law of balance shapes human laws, so that schemes against it fail. Things do not stay badly managed for long. When rulers act unjustly, the harm returns to them: cruel governments endanger their leaders, high taxes bring in no money, harsh punishments stop juries convicting, and overly mild laws invite private revenge.

Emerson argues that a person's real inner life does not depend on the kind of government or conditions they live under. Strict or harsh systems, and mild or free ones, lead to much the same character, whether in Turkey or New England, and even under ancient Egyptian despots people were as free as their culture allowed.

Emerson says that the whole universe is present in each of its parts, and that everything in nature holds all of nature's powers. Everything is made of one hidden substance. A naturalist sees one basic form behind different creatures, so a horse is like a running man, a bird like a flying man, and a tree like a rooted man.

Every form of work or activity, from a trade to an art, is said to contain the whole pattern of the world and of every other activity. Each one mirrors human life in full, including its good and bad, its struggles, and its end, so each one must hold the whole person and their fate.

Emerson says that the whole world is present in each small thing, such as a drop of dew or a tiny creature. Each small being has all the parts and powers of life, and God appears complete in every moss and cobweb. Every good in the universe is matched in each point by its opposite, such as evil, repulsion, or limitation.

Emerson says the universe is alive and moral, and the same moral force that lives inside a person as a feeling works outside us as a law. Justice is never delayed, and the world always balances out, like a mathematical equation. He sums this up with the Greek saying that God's dice always fall favorably, meaning they are loaded.

Whatever you put into the world comes back to you in exact measure. Every secret, crime, virtue and wrong is answered quietly and surely. Emerson calls this retribution a universal law: as smoke shows fire, a visible part shows the whole it belongs to.

Every act brings its reward in two ways. The first is within the act itself, which the soul perceives. The second is in its outward consequences, which people call retribution, and which the understanding sees, often only years later.

Punishment is not separate from wrongdoing; it grows out of it. Like a fruit hidden in a flower, the punishment is already present in the pleasure of the wrong, so cause and effect, means and ends, cannot be split apart.

Emerson says the world is whole and cannot be split apart, yet people keep trying to separate things. For example, they try to enjoy physical pleasures while cutting them off from moral character. He claims humans have always tried to separate sensual qualities, such as sweetness and brightness, from moral ones.

The passage says that the body wants only the surface of things, cut off from their deeper part, so that it gets an end without any other end. The soul sets its aims as eating for nourishment, union of man and woman in spirit, and power used for virtue. The body takes each of these aims and turns it toward mere appetite, flesh, or self-interest.

Emerson says the soul wants to live and act through everything, and that all good things would follow from it. Ordinary people instead chase private gain, such as riding, dressing, or governing merely to be seen. They think greatness means having only the pleasant side of life, without its bitterness.

Emerson says that attempts to split things into separate parts always fail. Pleasure, profit and power vanish when pulled away from the whole they belong to. Nature, he adds, always returns, however hard one tries to push it out.

Life comes with unavoidable conditions that foolish people try to escape, and some boast they are not affected by them. But such conditions are real inside a person, and if he avoids them in one area, they strike him in a deeper one. Escaping them only in appearance means he has run from himself, and the penalty is a kind of death.

Emerson says that every attempt to separate the good from its cost always fails so clearly that no one would try it, except that the mind goes wrong once the will has turned toward rebellion and separation. Then the person sees the pleasure of a thing but not the harm it brings.

Emerson means that a person who wants only the good part of something, like the mermaid's head, cannot separate it from the harm that comes with it, the dragon's tail. He then quotes a prayer saying that God quietly sends blindness on those who have uncontrolled desires, so they fail to see this.

Emerson says that stories and sayings show the soul's sense that moral right prevails, even when the storytellers do not intend it. The Greeks gave Jupiter, the supreme god, many bad deeds, so they unknowingly limited his power. In their myths he depends on other gods, such as Prometheus and Minerva, who hold secrets and keys he needs.

Emerson says that myths from many cultures, including Indian mythology, all teach moral lessons, since a story that lacked a moral would not survive. He gives examples: Aurora forgot to ask youth for Tithonus, so he became immortal but old, and Achilles was not fully invulnerable because the heel his mother held was not washed in the sacred waters.

Emerson says that even the legend of Siegfried, a hero who bathed in dragon's blood to become invulnerable, has a flaw: a leaf fell on his back, leaving one spot mortal. He argues that every created thing has such a crack, and that even myths meant to escape natural law carry a reminder that the law still applies.

Emerson describes the old Greek idea of Nemesis, a force that watches the world and punishes every wrong. He notes that the Furies, spirits of vengeance, serve justice, and that poets said even objects like stone walls and swords were linked to the wrongs done by their owners.

Emerson gives two stories from ancient Greek legend to show that gifts and deeds come back on their makers. Ajax's belt drags Hector behind Achilles's chariot, and Hector's sword is the one that kills Ajax. A rival who attacks a statue of the athlete Theagenes at night is crushed when it falls on him.

Emerson says that the best part of a writer is the part that is not personal or deliberate. It comes from deeper within than the writer's conscious will or clever invention. Such qualities are seen only when many writers are compared, where they appear as a shared spirit.

Emerson says he cares less about the famous artist Phidias himself than about what humanity as a whole was trying to make in that early Greek period. He sees individual geniuses like Phidias, Dante and Shakespeare as the tools through which that collective aim was carried out, and as sometimes shaping or limiting it.
