Proverbs of every nation state a basic truth without exceptions, and they say it more freely than formal speakers do. Emerson claims that the law he calls the highest one, which churches, lawmakers and universities deny, is repeated every day in markets and workshops through proverbs.

Every action brings back a matching result, for good or for harm. The passage gathers old sayings from many places to show this idea: what you give, you get back, and what you do to others returns to you.
Our actions are shaped by a natural law beyond our control. Even when we aim at a small, selfish goal, what we do ends up lining up with the larger order of the world, as if pulled by a magnet.

Whatever a person says also reveals and judges that person, whether he means it to or not. Like a ball of thread thrown out with one end still in the thrower's hand, or a harpoon whose line can pull back and harm the boat, each opinion comes back on the one who states it.

Harming others harms the one who does it. Emerson argues that people who exclude others, treat them as mere objects, or grab what they want from them lose something themselves, such as enjoyment, heaven, or their own heart. He says the old saying about getting what you want from someone's purse or skin is sound.

Wrongs done in close relationships, such as selfishness or dishonesty, are punished by fear and mistrust between the people involved. When two people deal with each other simply and honestly, they meet without any unease. Once one seeks an advantage at the other's expense, the other pulls away, and hatred and fear take hold on both sides.

Emerson says that old social wrongs, such as unjust hoarding of property and power, bring their own punishment. Fear is a sign of this: wherever fear shows up, something is rotten, much like a carrion crow circling over a dead body. Fear hangs over property and government, so the great wrongs it points to need to be corrected.

The passage says that when we stop acting by choice, we quickly expect something to change. Fears of sudden reversal, such as the fear of a bright, calm noon, and the unease that comes with good fortune, are signs of a built-in sense of balance. Emerson treats this sense as justice working inside people. Polycrates was a Greek ruler whose lucky run ended in disaster.

Emerson says it is best to pay as you go, because putting off a cost often ends up costing more. A borrower falls into debt to others. Taking favors without giving any back gains a person nothing, and each favor creates a debt of gratitude on one side and a recognized obligation on the other.

Every favor or deal leaves a lasting mark on the relationship between the two people involved, fixing who seems higher and who lower. A man may come to see that accepting help from a neighbor costs him more than suffering would have, and that asking for something is the most costly way to get it.

Emerson argues that a wise person should meet every fair claim on their time, talents, or heart, because every debt is eventually paid. Delay by people or events only postpones the reckoning. Even good fortune carries a cost: every benefit brings a tax with it.

Emerson says that the greatest person is the one who gives the most benefits, and that receiving favors without returning them is the only truly base act. Since we often cannot repay the very people who helped us, he says each benefit must be passed on to someone else. Good kept hoarded decays, so it should be given away quickly.

The main point is that cheap labor costs more in the end. What you pay for in any tool or service is really skill, or good sense, applied to a common need. So it is wiser to pay for skilled workers, such as a good gardener, sailor, cook, or agent, than to save money on them.

Cheating cannot succeed, because a thief or swindler only harms himself. Wealth and reputation are like paper money: they stand for something real, namely knowledge and virtue, and only those signs can be faked or stolen, while the real thing cannot.

Real results in work come only from honest mental effort and pure motives. Cheats and gamblers cannot gain the knowledge that careful, sincere work brings. In Emerson's view, nature gives power to those who do the thing, and no power to those who do not.

Emerson says that all human work, from sharpening a stake to building a city or writing an epic, shows the universe's perfect balance of give and take. Every thing has a price, and nothing can be gained without paying it. He says this rule is as grand in a ledger of accounts as in national budgets or in the laws of light, darkness, and nature.

Emerson says a worker sees deep moral laws at work in the tasks he knows well. These laws show up in his tools and measures, and in a small bill as much as in a nation's history. So they make his trade appealing and raise his work in his own imagination, even if he rarely speaks of it that way.

Emerson says that nature is set against wrongdoing. Every crime leaves a trace, like footprints in fresh snow, and nothing can hide it. Even ordinary forces such as water, wind and gravity work as punishment for the thief.

Good action brings its own reward with the same certainty: love returns as love, and the good person is so fixed in goodness that harm turns into good for him. Hardships such as sickness, insult and poverty end up helping him, as enemy armies once turned into friends for Napoleon.

Good people are helped even by their weaknesses, because every fault turns out to be useful to them somewhere. Emerson uses the fable of the stag: its horns, which it admired, got it caught in the thicket, while its feet, which it blamed, let it escape the hunter.

A person only truly knows a truth after arguing against it, and only truly knows people's obstacles and gifts after suffering from some obstacle and seeing others overcome what he lacks. If a flaw of temper makes someone unfit for company, he is pushed to rely on himself and build self-reliance, as an oyster covers an irritant with pearl.

Emerson says that strength comes from weakness. A person is roused to real effort only when hurt or attacked, and a great person is willing to feel small. Comfort and advantage make a person complacent, while defeat teaches him facts, his own ignorance, and cures him of vanity.

The wise man does not resist attacks. He accepts them, and this makes him stronger, since the wound heals and falls away. Blame, he says, is safer than praise, because praise brings defenders who weaken him, while criticism leaves him feeling secure.

Praise makes Emerson feel exposed, like someone left open to his enemies. He argues that any evil we refuse to give in to does us good, and that we gain the strength of the temptation we resist, much as a Sandwich Islander (a Hawaiian) believes he takes the courage of an enemy he kills.

Emerson says the same protections that guard us from harm can also guard us from greed and dishonesty. He claims no one can really cheat a person except that person themselves. Every deal, he says, has a silent third party, which is probably a moral or natural order that holds people to account.

Honest work is always rewarded by the nature of things, so it never truly loses out. Even if a master is ungrateful, the advice is to serve him more, because the debt owed for each effort will be repaid, and waiting only increases the return, like compound interest.

Persecution is presented as a failed attempt to go against nature, like making water flow uphill. Whether one tyrant or a crowd carries it out makes no difference. A mob, Emerson says, gives up its reason and sinks to the level of a beast, and its violence is aimed at principles and justice themselves.

Emerson says that attempts to punish or silence a person who stands for the truth backfire. Whipping, imprisonment, burning books, or erasing words only spread the truth further, and communities eventually see that the martyrs were right.

Emerson says that circumstances do not matter in themselves, since every gain has a cost and every loss brings some other gain. He warns that this idea of balance is not the same as saying nothing matters. Careless people draw that wrong conclusion and decide that no action is better than another.

Emerson says the soul is more basic than the idea of balance or payback that he has just been discussing. The soul simply exists as a life, and beneath all changing events lies a deep reality of Being, which he calls God. This Being is whole and complete, containing all relations, parts and times within itself.

Emerson says that nature, truth and virtue flow from a single source, and vice is their absence. Falsehood is "nothing": it creates no real fact and does no good or harm of its own. Its only harm is that it is worse to be nothing than to exist.

Emerson argues that a wrongdoer who never faces a visible reckoning in this life has not escaped justice. By holding on to his evil and lies, he separates himself from nature, and that loss is itself a penalty. Even if we never see it, the account is settled in the end.

Virtue and wisdom cost the person nothing. They add to what a person is and to the world. Love, knowledge and beauty have no excess when taken in their purest form, because the soul accepts no limits.

Emerson says that a good life is a moving forward, not a fixed position, and that trust comes naturally to us. When we call one person "more" or "less" a man, we measure how much soul is present, not how much is missing. So the brave, true and wise are more fully human than the coward, the fool or the knave, and virtue carries no hidden cost, because it is the presence of God himself.

Material goods come with a cost, and goods gained without effort or merit do not last, since they can be lost as easily as they came. Real good belongs to the soul and is earned through labor that the heart and head approve. The speaker therefore does not want unearned gains, such as buried gold, or more outside goods like wealth, honor, power, or people.

The speaker says that while every wrong brings its price, knowing this brings peace. Because of it, he can limit the harm others might do to him. He quotes St. Bernard: nothing can harm him except himself, and he only truly suffers through his own fault.

Emerson says that the soul itself holds a balance for the unequal conditions of people. He admits that the gap between those with more and those with less seems deeply unfair, causing pain, resentment, and sadness toward people who have less ability.

Emerson says that large differences between people seem to disappear when looked at closely, because love dissolves them, as the sun melts an iceberg. Since all people share one heart and soul, my neighbor's gain can become mine, and whoever loves a greatness makes it their own.

Emerson argues that what we admire in others already belongs to us, because the soul takes in everything it loves. By love, a person makes great figures like Jesus and Shakespeare part of their own inner life. Qualities such as virtue or wit count as ours only if we can make them our own.

Hardship, in this view, is a sign that nature is always growing. A person must sometimes leave behind everything familiar, such as friends, home, customs and beliefs, just as a shellfish leaves a shell that has become too small and builds a new one.

In a strong person, outward circumstances change often and hang loosely, like a thin membrane through which the living self shows. In most people, by contrast, their circumstances form a hard, mixed shell that traps them. Emerson says a person's outer life should keep shedding dead circumstances, as one changes clothes each day.

We grieve for lost friends and old comforts, and we will not believe that the soul can provide new ones. Emerson says we cling to the past, though the divine voice calls us forward, and we cannot stay in the ruins. We also do not trust the new, so we keep looking backward.

Hard losses, such as illness, injury, disappointment, or the death of a loved one, seem at first to be permanent losses with nothing given back. Over time, Emerson says, the hidden good in them becomes clear, and a lost friend can later seem like a guide.

Emerson says that a loss or hardship often brings big changes to our lives. It ends a stage of youth that was ready to end, breaks old routines, households, or ways of living, and makes room for new ones that help a person grow. It also brings new friends and influences that matter greatly in later years.

A person who might have stayed a delicate garden flower, with too little room for roots and too much sun for the head, becomes instead a banyan tree, a large tree whose branches give shade and fruit to many people. This happens when the walls that protected them fall and the gardener neglects them.

The verse says that a living heaven, which your prayers look toward, is both the house and its builder. It uses the leftover hours of human life to build lasting towers. It grows through its own decay, and through the force of reaction, it turns flame to ice and ice to boil, forging innocence out of the dark arms of wrongdoing.
When we think back on our lives, we find they are surrounded by beauty. Looking behind us, even ordinary things seem pleasing, and painful or terrible events look fair once they are remembered.

Ordinary things, even neglected or foolish ones, seem graceful once they belong to the past. Death in a house adds dignity to it. The soul is never harmed by ugliness or pain. Looking clearly, Emerson says, we would admit we have never really made a sacrifice.

In moments of great inner clarity, Emerson says, any single loss or pain feels small, because the whole universe still seems whole to the heart. Only the limited, finite part of us suffers, while the infinite stays calm and untouched.

Emerson says a person's thinking stays healthy if they live simply by nature and do only what truly belongs to them, without taking on puzzles that are not theirs. He claims that hard theological questions, such as original sin and predestination, were never real problems for anyone who did not go looking for them.

Emerson says that people who have never had the soul's childhood-like troubles cannot describe them or cure them. A simple person may not even know these troubles exist. Being able to explain one's faith and inner freedom takes rare gifts, but a person without such self-knowledge can still have natural strength and honesty, guided by a few instincts and simple rules.

Emerson says that the thoughts that really shape him did not come from formal schooling or a set course of study. Books he read on his own as a boy, outside lessons, taught him more. He argues that learning outside formal education is often worth more, and that schooling can work against the mind's natural way of choosing what fits it.

Emerson argues that moral goodness is harmed when a person's will tries to force it. People often treat virtue as a hard fight and take pride in it, but he says true goodness is not a struggle. It is either present in a person or not, and we admire characters most when their goodness is spontaneous and natural.

The best virtue is unconscious: a good person who does not think about his own goodness is the most admired. Such graceful, effortless acts should be welcomed and celebrated, not resented by comparing them with someone who struggles against his faults.

Emerson says that in history, nature counts for more than human will. People like Caesar and Napoleon seem to have had far-sighted plans, but their power came mostly from natural forces rather than from their own intentions. Successful men, when honest, admit this and credit Fortune, Destiny, or a saint instead of themselves.

Emerson says that the success of certain great men came from how well they matched the flow of thought of their time, so that ideas passed through them freely. They looked like the source of their achievements, but they were only channels, like wires carrying electricity or a smooth, hollow pipe. What looked like strong will was really giving themselves up.

Emerson asks whether a great genius like Shakespeare could explain his own genius, or whether a gifted mathematician could explain his methods to others. He suggests that if such a secret could be passed on, it would lose its special value and become ordinary, like daylight.

Life could be much simpler and happier than we make it, with no need for constant struggle and despair. Emerson says we create our own troubles, and that the natural order of things is good. When we look back or see more wisely, we notice that we are surrounded by laws that carry themselves out.

Emerson says that nature does not want people to worry or get angry. He claims nature values their good works and learning no more than their frauds and wars. When people leave their meetings and causes for the fields and woods, nature mocks their heated zeal with a teasing remark: "So hot, my little Sir?"

Emerson argues that many charitable works, such as church programs and relief societies, have become forced duties that make people unhappy and resentful. He says good ends can be reached naturally, without everyone giving money in the same organized way, and that giving should be left to those who have money, such as merchants.

Emerson argues against forcing religious instruction on people. He says children should ask questions and adults should answer them when asked, not lock young people in church pews to hear lessons they did not choose. Each person should contribute what they naturally can, like farmers giving corn or children bringing flowers.

Emerson says that when we look at the bigger picture, laws, creeds and ways of living all seem like a mockery of the truth. He gives examples of society's large structures, such as Roman aqueducts, the Great Wall of China and standing armies, which he calls outdated or unnecessary compared with simpler arrangements, such as town meetings.

Emerson argues that nature works by short, direct means, and that movement everywhere is a kind of falling. Ripe fruit and leaves fall, waters circle by falling, people walk by falling forward, and even planets and stars keep falling.

Nature's simplicity is not like a machine's, which can be fully understood. Nature is inexhaustible, so no final analysis of it is possible. Emerson says that someone who claims to know moral nature completely is a pedant, and that a person's wisdom shows in their hope, since seeing nature as endless keeps the mind young.

Our fixed labels and reputations, such as belonging to a school or being known as learned or pious, do not match how changeable our inner experience is. Inside, we feel like beginners. Emerson says this inner uncertainty explains how skepticism arose: a person can be described in opposite ways, each with equal reason.

Emerson says that no one stays wise all the time, and that the Stoics' idea of a permanent wise man is only imaginary. We admire heroes over cowards and robbers, yet we have each been like those cowards and robbers ourselves, and may be again, measured against what the soul could reach.

Events are governed by a higher law than our own will, so our hard struggling is unneeded and useless. We are strongest when we act simply and naturally, and by obeying this law we become divine. Belief and loving trust remove much of our worry, because God exists and a soul lies at the centre of nature and over every person's will.

Emerson says that the moral law, which he calls a kind of enchantment in nature, guides people who follow it: they prosper when they heed it and are stopped when they try to harm others. He argues that each person has a right path and duties, and that by listening humbly they can find it without painful choosing.

Emerson says that if a person lets go of the self and joins the flow of a larger power and wisdom, they will act rightly without strain and be content. In that case, people would not need to interfere, and human work and society would improve on their own, as nature does.

Emerson says that ordinary "choice" is only a partial act, made by the hands, eyes or appetites, not by the whole person. Real goodness is choosing what fits one's own nature, and a person must answer to reason for their daily work. Doing something merely because it is the custom of one's trade is no excuse, and a person's character itself calls them to a worthy calling.

Each person has one calling, shown by his natural talent. Only in that one direction are his path and abilities open, so he moves freely toward it, as a ship in a river meets resistance everywhere except along its channel, which leads out to the open sea.

Each person has a particular talent, shaped by his own make-up, which pulls him toward work that is easy for him and useful once done, and that no one else can do in the same way. The more he relies on his own powers, the more unlike anyone else's work his will be, and his ambition matches what he can do.

Emerson says a person's greatness depends on how broad their foundation is. Each person has only one calling: to do something unique. Claiming a special, personal summons marked by outward signs is fanaticism. It shows a failure to see that all people share one mind and no one is favored above others.

A person who does his own work shows others the need he can meet and builds the taste that will enjoy what he offers. By doing his own work, he also reveals who he is. Emerson says the fault of public speaking is that it lacks full openness, and that every person should freely express the strength and meaning within him.

A typical person fits himself to whatever job he falls into and works at it mechanically, like a dog turning a spit, until he becomes just a part of the machine and is lost as a person. Only when he can express his whole character through his work, so others see its worth, has he truly found his calling.

If the work seems humble, the worker should make it noble through his thinking and character. He should also share what he knows and values, or others will not recognize his worth. It is foolish to focus on the work's dullness and routine rather than letting it express his character and aims.

We tend to admire only actions that society has long approved, and we miss that any human act can be done in a noble way. Greatness, we think, belongs only to certain roles or occasions. Yet a skilled musician can make beauty from a cheap string, and a hero can rise from humble surroundings.

Emerson says that what seems ordinary or low in society has poetry not yet written, and it can be made as admired as anything else. He suggests we judge things as kings do, giving our own values to hospitality, family, and death. Making such new judgments often is what he calls elevation.

A person has only what he does, and his strength lies within himself, so hope and fear have no real hold on him. He should count as lasting only the good that is part of his own nature and grows from him. Wealth and luck are fleeting, like summer leaves, and he may let them go as signs of his own power to produce.

A person's own particular nature, or genius, decides which influences he takes in and which he rejects, and so shapes the world as he experiences it. Like a boom catching driftwood or a magnet picking out steel, he gathers only what matches him from the many things around him.

Facts, words, and people that stay in our memory without our knowing why still matter to us, because they connect to parts of our inner life that we cannot put into words. We give our attention to whatever speaks to us, as a man at the door gets our answer while many others pass unnoticed.

Some small stories, habits, or faces stay in your memory far more strongly than their ordinary importance would justify. Emerson says these memories relate to your own particular gift, so you should give them weight instead of dismissing them for more conventional examples. What your heart judges great is great, and the soul's sense of emphasis is always correct.

A person has a natural right to whatever suits his own nature and gifts, and he can take only what belongs to his spiritual inheritance, even if everything else is open to him. A secret cannot be kept from someone who has a right to it, because it will reveal itself. A friend who brings us into a certain mood gains power over the thoughts and secrets of that mood.

Napoleon could not win over Austria's diplomats by fear alone, so he sent Narbonne, an old French noble, to Vienna. Narbonne shared the manners and social ties of the Austrian aristocracy, and within two weeks he had learned the secrets of the Austrian imperial cabinet.

Speaking and being understood seem easy, but being understood can turn out to be a strong defence and bond. Holding an opinion that others have accepted can also become a heavy burden that is hard to escape.

A teacher's hidden opinions spread to his students just as openly stated ones do, because ideas flow through everything he teaches. Like water poured into a bent vessel, they reach every part. Students feel the effects of a belief even when they cannot trace its logic, and a single part of a teaching reveals the whole.

Wise people across centuries understand each other because we reason from what we can see to what we cannot. No author can hide his meaning so well that later thinkers who share his outlook will not find it. So no secret teaching of Plato could stay hidden from later great minds such as Bacon, Montaigne and Kant.

A person can only learn what they are prepared to learn, even if the thing is right in front of them. A chemist could explain his secrets to a carpenter, and the carpenter would understand nothing. Emerson says that until the mind has matured, we cannot see what is plainly before us, and later the earlier blindness seems like a dream.

Emerson says that the beauty and worth we see in nature come from within us, not from nature itself. Places like Tempe, Tivoli and Rome are, in plain terms, only earth, water, rocks and sky, and many other places are just as good yet move no one.

Simply being near beautiful things, such as sunsets, landscapes, art, or books, does not make people nobler or wiser. Refined qualities in a noble person are also missed by a coarse man, just as starlight that has not yet reached us is unseen.

Our dreams grow out of what we know while awake, and they keep the same scale as our daytime thoughts. Frightening dreams are exaggerated versions of the day's faults, much as a traveller on the Alps sees his own shadow enlarged into a giant.

The main point is that people tend to see their own qualities, good and bad, magnified in the people and events around them, without realizing it is themselves they are seeing. An old man's warning to frightened boys makes the point: the scary figure in the dark is only the boys' own fears, and nothing worse than themselves.

A quincunx is five objects arranged in a square, with four at the corners and one in the middle. Emerson says a person who is truly himself shows the same pattern in every direction. He chooses friends who are like him, and in the end every part of his life, from his work to his habits, reflects who he is.

Emerson says a reader gets from a book only what he already is. Two readers of the same book, even in translation, will find different things, and no reader can keep a book's wisdom to himself. Like a base person in good company, an unfit reader cannot truly share in the book, even though he is present with it.

Emerson argues that the inner laws of the mind match people to each other by what they really have and are, so fighting them is useless. Gertrude loves Guy for his grand manners, but he cares only for politics and leisure, and she has no interests of her own to hold him. Having him does not give her what she wanted.

Emerson says people are drawn only to what is close to their own nature. Talent, skill and fame do little to win us over, even when people give their best effort. Nearness or likeness of nature wins easily, while admiration for gifted people is something we give only as a polite duty.

When a person of similar mind and nature finally arrives, they come so easily and closely that it feels like their presence is natural, not like a stranger entering. We feel relieved and refreshed, a kind of joyful solitude. Emerson adds that we wrongly think we must win friends by following society's fashions, manners and judgments.

A true friend is a soul that meets you on your own path and shares your inner experience, not one who bends toward you or you toward them. Emerson also says a scholar who imitates fashionable society to win admiration chases shallow attraction, and that real love follows greatness of character.
Ignoring the natural bonds of likeness between people, which alone should form true society, brings serious harm. So does picking friends only to please what others will see.

The world, Emerson says, lets each person set his own worth. Whatever place a man claims for himself, others accept it, and the world does not interfere whether he is a hero or a fool. It takes a person at his own valuation, whether he hides his name or his work is seen across the sky.

Emerson says that real teaching is not done by words alone but by one person passing on his own state of mind or principle to another. When that transfer happens, the pupil becomes like the teacher and keeps the benefit. Words spoken without this transfer, he says, are quickly forgotten.

Emerson says he would not attend the public orations of these speakers because they will not share their own character and experience with the audience. If they promised such honest sharing, he would gladly endure any trouble to hear them. A public oration, he argues, is an evasion or empty display rather than a true expression of the speaker as a person.

Saying something aloud does not make it true. A statement must prove itself through its own content, and no argument or oath can give it proof. A good sentence must also justify itself by its own wording.

Emerson says a piece of writing affects people in proportion to how deep its thinking is. Writing that makes readers think, or moves them strongly, lasts a long time, while writing that teaches nothing is quickly forgotten. To keep writing from going out of fashion, the writer must be sincere, and an argument that does not change the writer's own life is unlikely to change anyone else's.

Emerson quotes the advice "Look in thy heart, and write," meaning a writer should take subjects from his own inner experience, not from what he hears. Such writing reaches a lasting audience, while empty work gathers praise but has no real life, and only what is genuinely alive can give life to others.

Literary fame cannot be bought or arranged. Only a book's own worth decides whether it survives, judged by an impartial final court, not by the noisy readers of its first season. Fine bindings and free copies to libraries cannot keep a weak book in print.

Only lasting books survive. Minor works by writers like Walpole, Blackmore, Kotzebue, or Pollok fade quickly, while Moses, Homer and Plato are kept alive. Plato has only a few readers at any time, yet his works are still copied and passed on to each generation. Bentley's saying supports this: a book's worth shows in the book itself.

Books last because of their own inner weight, the lasting value of what they say to the human mind, not because of anyone's praise or attack. Michael Angelo makes the same point with a sculptor: a statue is judged by the open public square, not by how it is lit in the studio.

A great person's actions matter in proportion to the deep feeling behind them. Such a person does not know he is great, and his deeds seem natural to him. Only later, over a century or two, do people see their greatness, and then even small acts are treated as lasting institutions.

Emerson says that natural laws show a single direction, like a stream, and that every part of nature is alive and serves the truth. Even errors, lies and disease fit into this pattern. Just as a shadow points to the sun, negative facts point toward the truth.

Everything a person does, says, or even fails to do shows their character, and that cannot be hidden. Someone who stays silent on public questions is not holding back a secret wisdom; their silence tells others that they have nothing to offer.
Nature makes it hard to hide the truth in the face and body. A careful observer can read a person's expression. An honest speaker's eyes look clear, while a liar's eyes look muddy or crooked.

A lawyer who does not sincerely believe his client deserves a verdict will fail to persuade a jury, because his doubt shows through whatever he says. Emerson uses this to show a general rule: a work of art passes on to its audience the state of mind its maker had while creating it.

We cannot say adequately what we do not believe, however often we repeat the words. Emerson gives the example of Swedenborg's account of spirits who tried and failed to speak a statement they did not believe, twisting their lips in frustration.

A person is recognized for what he is really worth, so worrying about how others rate us, or fearing we will go unnoticed, is pointless. A man who knows he can do something better than anyone else already has proof that others will see it. Every time he enters a group or acts, he is judged and assessed.

Among a group of boys, a newcomer is quickly judged and given his true rank, as if tested formally. A stranger who arrives with fine clothes and showy airs is dismissed by an older boy, who expects the group to see through him soon and asks what he has actually done.

Emerson says that a divine question tests people and strips away false reputations. A vain pretender may sit among great people, but his pretense cannot produce real achievements. Such pretense has never written a great epic, defeated a great invader, spread a faith, or ended slavery.

Emerson says that a person's real virtue and goodness show openly and earn respect, even from wicked people. Sincere words and generous acts are never wasted, and people eventually recognize them. A person is judged by what he truly is, which shows in his face, conduct and fortunes, while hiding it or boasting about it does no good.

Emerson says that a person's wrongdoing shows itself without words, in glances, smiles, greetings and handshakes. People sense something wrong in such a man and distrust him, even when they cannot say why. The wrongdoing marks the face and head, and even a king who does wrong is shown to be a fool.

Emerson says that a person cannot hide their true nature. If you do something, it will be seen, even in an empty desert, and a man's face, manners and deeds reveal what he is. Confucius is quoted to make the same point: no one can be concealed.

A brave man does not need others to see or praise his good act. He knows it himself, and that knowledge keeps him at peace and aimed at noble goals, which speak better for his deed than telling the story would. Virtue, in this view, means acting in line with how things really are, replacing appearance with reality.
Emerson urges people to be genuinely good rather than merely appear so. He asks them to stop relying on worldly wisdom, to accept a higher power, and to trust that truth alone brings real worth.

Emerson says that a person should not apologize for past neglect or wrap a visit in excuses. Instead, he should simply visit now and give himself as a gift, shining with his own light rather than borrowed gifts or appearances. Common people, he says, make apologies for themselves because they lack real substance.

Emerson says we wrongly judge by outward size and visible show. We call the poet idle because he holds no public office, and we honor institutions without seeing the thought behind them. He claims that real action and the turning points of life happen in quiet private thought, not in visible events like a career or marriage.

A single moment of insight can overturn the way we have lived, telling us we should have acted differently. All the years that follow serve that insight, carrying out what it asks, and this inner correction keeps working throughout our lives.

The writer says a person should let a higher moral law pass through their whole life without blocking it. Then any part of their conduct, such as diet, home, religion, friends, fun, or voting, would show their true character. But most people are mixed and divided inside, so the light does not pass cleanly through them.

Emerson says there is no need to belittle the self we are or the life we have been given. A good person is content with that. He admires the Theban general Epaminondas but does not wish to be him, and he prefers to love his own present time. Taunts that others acted while he sat still do not trouble him, since he sees both action and stillness as good when each is needed.

Emerson says that a man like Epaminondas, a Theban general, would have been content even with a quiet life, because there is room in the world for every kind of love and courage. Action and inaction are equal to a person who is truly good, just as a tree's wood serves well whether it becomes a weathervane or a bridge support.

Emerson says he will not shame his soul by hiding from his place in the world. Since he is here, he reasons, the soul must need him here, so he should take up his post rather than doubt his own worth. He is content, and he refuses to turn down the good he has been given just because others received good in a different form.

A person may feel that they must prove their worth through visible deeds, such as a special diet, a dress, a religious practice, a charity, or a public office. Emerson argues this is only a sense-based illusion. Every action begins as a thought, so thinking is itself a kind of acting.

Emerson urges people to make ordinary actions great, since any small act can be expanded to become significant. He argues that peace comes from faithfully doing one's own duties first. Reading about distant history or famous generals is wrong while one's own obligations remain unmet, because it abandons one's own work to watch others.

Emerson says people often read out of boredom when they have nothing better to do, as when he picks up a biography of Brant because he cannot think what else to fill his time with. He thinks reading a famous man's life is too great a compliment to pay such men. He would rather do his own work so well that it matches theirs.

Emerson argues that we undervalue ourselves and overvalue great figures like Paul and Pericles because we forget that all people share the same nature. Famous names are only borrowed material for artists. A poet who writes a true drama is not playing Caesar; he is, in that moment, Caesar himself.

A person with pure emotion, subtle wit, quick and lofty thought, and a great, self-reliant heart can lift up worldly things like palaces, money and kingdoms. Such a person looks down on these as trifles, and by this power stirs nations. Emerson's closing line says a man should believe in God, not in names, places and persons.

A great soul, even when it appears in a poor and humble woman doing menial housework, shines out so clearly that the work itself seems noble and admirable, and people copy it. Once the same soul moves on to some other form and deed, that new deed is then seen as the highest thing in life.

We humans are like instruments that detect a subtle, invisible force, the way a photometer or gold leaf registers light or electric charge. We can recognize the real effects of a hidden, inner fire even when it appears in many forms.

Every hope of the soul is fulfilled in countless ways, and each joy grows into a new desire. Nature, which cannot be contained, is said to foresee in the first feeling of kindness a wider goodwill that will go beyond single attachments. This wider joy begins with a private bond between two people, which Emerson calls the enchantment of human life.

Emerson is describing a powerful feeling of love that suddenly takes hold of a person and changes both mind and body. In his account, this love connects a person to other people, to family and community, to nature, and to the senses and imagination. He says it also makes people more heroic and sacred, leads to marriage, and keeps human society lasting.

Emerson says that love is naturally linked with youth, so to describe it vividly one must be young. Young people reject any mature philosophy, which they feel would chill love's bright colors. He expects to be called cold and hard by young lovers, but he appeals to older readers instead.

Love does not leave people when they grow old. It stays with the aged, though in a nobler form than in the young. It starts as a small fire between two people and spreads outward until it warms all people and the whole world.

Whatever age a writer chooses to describe love from, something is lost: a portrait of love at twenty misses its later features, and one at eighty misses its earlier ones. Emerson hopes that, through patience and inspiration, a writer can grasp the underlying law of love, a truth that stays young and beautiful from any viewpoint.

The passage says we should stop clinging closely to the actual facts of past love and instead consider the feeling as it appeared in hope, not as it turned out in history. Each person sees his own experience as stained by error, while other people's lives look fair. Even remembering the best moments of his own life, a person shrinks back with regret.

Emerson says that seen as a whole, through reason or ideas, life is beautiful and joyful. Seen as lived experience, with its particular people, places and daily concerns, it is sour and full of sorrow, because grief attaches to specific names and persons.

Emerson says that people are strongly drawn to stories and glimpses of love between others. We want to know how a worthy person has fared in love, we enjoy novels about passion, and a small sign of affection between strangers makes us feel close to them.

Emerson says that people feel warmly toward lovers, and that the first signs of kindness and courtesy in rough people are very appealing. He gives the example of a village boy who, once he falls for a girl, treats her as special and distant, where before he had been rude to all the girls.

Two young neighbors who were once close have come to respect each other as individuals. Emerson also describes schoolgirls chatting idly with a good-natured shop boy in a village shop. He says they meet as equals there, and their warm, open nature shows in this harmless talk.

Emerson says that a good boy who spends his youth in easy, friendly talk with girls about parties, dances and small social matters will later know where to find a sincere and sweet wife. He adds that such a choice carries none of the risks that Milton saw in the marriages of scholars and great men.

Emerson says that people have accused him of being too cold toward personal relationships because of his respect for the intellect. He now regrets such remarks. He argues that love is the world of persons, and that even the most detached thinker owes a debt to love and should not speak against our social feelings.

Emerson says that the intense rapture of first love comes mostly to the young, and that the beauty that overwhelms us is rarely seen after about thirty. Still, the memory of these visions lasts longer than any other memory, staying with a person even in old age.

Looking back on love, many people remember warm moments that seemed magical, even though the magic came from ordinary, trivial details rather than from the love itself. Still, Emerson says, no one forgets the times when love's power seized their heart and mind and made everything new.

This describes how falling in love changes a young man. He sees everything as beautiful, hears a single voice as moving, and keeps small things linked to the beloved in his memory. He watches windows and studies small belongings such as a glove or a ribbon.

In love, a lover feels that solitude is never lonely, because the beloved's image stays so vividly in his mind that it is better company than any friend. The beloved's gestures and words are not fleeting; they are fixed deeply, like marks burned into enamel by fire. The quoted lines say the beloved, though absent, remains present in the lover's watching eyes and loving heart.

Even in middle and later life, people still feel the pull of memories of youthful love, when happiness seemed too mild unless it was mixed with pain and fear. The writer quotes someone who said that love's pains are worth more than all other pleasures.

In love, the lover's mind is so full of the beloved that days feel too short and nights are spent thinking. Moonlight seems like a fever, stars like letters, and ordinary work and passing people seem unimportant or unreal.

In young love, the youth feels that the whole world has come alive. Birds seem to sing to his heart, clouds seem to have faces, and plants seem aware, so that he almost fears to share his secret with them. He finds more comfort in nature, in the quiet green places, than among people.

Emerson's lines list the things that feed romantic passion: secluded springs and wooded paths, moonlit walks at night, and eerie sounds like a midnight bell or a groan. The point is that lovers are nourished by such lonely, melancholy settings and sensations rather than by ordinary daily life.

A man in love, shown as a "fine madman" in the woods, feels intensely alive. He feels close to nature, and passion sharpens his love of music and poetry. The passage notes that people often write their best verse only when moved by passion.

Being in love, Emerson says, transforms a person completely. It makes the dull gentle and the timid brave enough to face the world, as long as the beloved looks on. The lover becomes a new person, with deeper feelings and goals, and so belongs to no family or society but to himself, becoming a true individual.

Beauty is shown as complete in itself and enough on its own. A lover cannot picture his beloved as poor or alone; she seems rich in her own company, like a flowering tree. Her presence, the passage says, makes the whole world richer.

In love, the lover sees the beloved as a representative of all that is fine and rare, not as an individual. Her family and friends see her resemblance to particular people, but he sees only likenesses to nature's beauty, such as summer evenings, rainbows and birdsong.

Beauty is an charm that cannot be pinned down or explained. The ancients saw it as virtue in bloom, but the feeling of tenderness it stirs has no clear object. Trying to trace it to the body's structure ruins it for the imagination.

Emerson says that the kind of love he means is not the friendship or romance people know in society. It belongs to a finer, unreachable realm, like the hint of roses and violets. Beauty cannot be grasped, and the best things, like beauty, slip away from any attempt to own or use them.

Emerson suggests that great music and art move us in ways words cannot capture. Jean Paul Richter's remark that music speaks of things he has never found shows this. A statue is most beautiful when it cannot be fully measured or defined, and so calls on the viewer's imagination to say what it expresses.

Great sculpture, painting and poetry succeed when they point beyond what the senses can grasp. A statue of a god, for example, is shown moving from the visible toward the invisible, and a poem works best when it stirs us to strive for what we cannot reach.

Emerson says that personal beauty is at its most charming when it does not satisfy us completely. It points beyond earthly pleasure to something higher, and it makes the viewer feel unworthy. Even a powerful man like Caesar could not claim it as his own, any more than he could claim the sky or a sunset.

When we love someone, we feel the love is not under that person's control, but comes from something above their will. What we love is not the person as such, but a radiance in them that they do not know about in themselves and never can.

According to the ancient writers, the human soul came from another world and wanders on earth searching for it. The light of the natural sun dazes it, so it can see only the things of this world, which are mere shadows of real things.

Emerson says that divine power gives youth its beauty so that the soul can be reminded of heavenly goodness and beauty. A man who sees such beauty in a woman takes great delight in her form, movement and intelligence, because these point to the higher good that lies within the beauty and causes it.

If the soul focuses only on the body, it finds only sorrow, since the body cannot keep the promise that beauty seems to make. If instead the soul looks past the body to admire good character in lovers, it rises to a truer beauty and, loving that, leaves base desire behind and becomes pure.

Through close contact with what is truly excellent, generous, humble and just, a lover comes to love these virtues more warmly and to recognize them more quickly. He then moves from loving them in one person to loving them in all people. The one beautiful soul is thus only a doorway into the company of all true and pure souls.

In a close partnership, each partner can see the other's faults more clearly and point them out without offence, helping to cure them. The lover also sees the divine beauty in many people, separates it from the stains the world has put on them, and so climbs toward love of God.

Emerson says the true view of love has been taught by wise people in every age, and it still needs to be brought out more fully. He criticizes a worldly, money-minded attitude to marriage. He says this attitude is wrong to teach young women that marriage is only about household thrift and that a woman's life has no other purpose.

The idea is that love is only one stage in the growth of the soul. The soul's influence spreads outward in widening circles, like ripples from a thrown pebble, reaching first familiar things and then larger ones such as politics and history. Yet all these things are later arranged by deeper, higher laws.

As people grow, things like closeness, numbers, habits and particular people gradually lose their hold on us. Deeper bonds and the wish for the soul to match its surroundings take over, and we cannot go back to the lower ties. So even love, which Emerson calls the making of a god out of a person, must become less focused on the individual over time, though it does not show this at first.

Emerson says that young people exchanging glances across a room do not realize where that small beginning may lead. He compares it to plants: growth starts in the buds, and the attraction then grows into courtesy, passion, and marriage. In passion, each person sees the other as a complete whole, with soul and body fully joined.

In Emerson's view, for two lovers nothing else matters: they want only each other. Even death would be worth it if it made the heavens finer, and all other things, such as work, religion and duties, are seen as contained in the beloved. Apart, they comfort themselves by picturing each other.

Lovers ask whether the other person shares their inner world: the same sights, books and feelings. They find that they would give up everything they own to save the beloved from harm. But human life brings danger, sorrow and pain to everyone, lovers included, so love can do nothing but pray.

Romantic love, Emerson says, makes a bond with eternal power and seems to give every part of the world new worth. But this state does not last. Neither flowers, poetry, vows, nor a home in another person's heart can always satisfy the human soul.

In Emerson's view, love first seems like a playful attachment, but later the deeper soul wants complete happiness. So partners notice flaws in each other, which brings surprise, complaint and hurt. Still, the virtues that first drew them together remain, even when hidden, and keep attracting them.

In love, the attachment moves from the outward sign to the inner substance, which heals hurt feelings. Over time, lovers come to know each other's strengths and weaknesses, and the relation stands for the whole human race. The quoted lines say the beloved holds a taste of everything, as manna did.

In this passage, love between two people is described as changing over time. Strong early passion, which is violent and fiery, cools into a calm, lasting mutual understanding. The "angels" and "gnomes" are the good and bad qualities a person shows, and virtue makes the vices known for what they are.

Partners in a long marriage stop demanding passion from each other and instead support each other's plans, calmly, whether together or apart. They come to see that the qualities that first attracted them were temporary, like scaffolding that is taken down once a house is built.

Emerson says that the growing purity of mind and heart over the years is the true marriage, planned from the start and beyond the couple's full awareness. He suggests that the heart expects this from early childhood, and that instinct, nature, intellect and art all join in celebrating it.

Emerson says that love, in its fullest form, looks for goodness and wisdom wherever they are, not for one person or sex. Our feelings for particular people are temporary, like tents set up for a single night, and they change over time. Still, at certain moments, our affections take over and make our happiness depend on specific people.

When the mind is well again, its bright, starry vault returns, and our warm loves and fears, like clouds, must lose their limits and merge with God to reach their full beauty. Nothing is lost as the soul grows. Each attachment is replaced only by something more beautiful, and so on forever.

The speaker says a friend's love outweighs the restless world and its changes. He thought this friend had gone away, but after years found the friend's kindness still there, like a daily sunrise. Through the friend, the speaker feels the sky, the rose, and his own life have become nobler and brighter.

Emerson says there is more kindness among people than anyone speaks aloud. Even though selfishness often chills the world, he claims that all people are surrounded by a kind of love. We silently honor and enjoy the company of many people we barely talk to, and our glances show it. "The heart knoweth" means the heart understands this without words.

Friendly feeling toward others, from strong love down to mild goodwill, brings a warm, lively glow to the mind. Emerson says that people often compare these feelings to fire, though they are swifter and more cheering than fire. Together they make life sweet.

Emerson says that our thinking and our actions grow stronger when we feel affection. A scholar may struggle for hours to write anything worthwhile, yet when he writes to a friend, good thoughts and fitting words come easily.

When a praised stranger is expected, a household feels both pleasure and anxiety. They rush to tidy the house and prepare a dinner, and they hear only good things about him. To them he seems to stand for all of humanity and embodies what they wish for.

When we imagine a great friend and then meet such a person, we feel uneasy and afraid of how to act with him. Yet the same ideal also lifts our talk: we speak better than usual, think more quickly, and share deep, sincere experience, surprising those who know us well.

Once a stranger starts bringing in his own biases, flawed definitions and shortcomings, the real conversation ends. He may still be given courtesies like a meal and proper manners, but genuine warmth and open exchange of the inner self are no longer offered to him.

Emerson says that the feeling of friendship makes the world seem new and bright, and that all sorrows and even duties seem to disappear when a person gives way to affection. He adds that a soul sure of meeting its friend again would be content to wait alone for a thousand years.

The speaker wakes up grateful for his friends, old and new. He calls God "the Beautiful," who shows himself in these gifts. He says he dislikes society yet values solitude, but still appreciates good people who pass by. Anyone who truly understands him becomes lasting companionship, and such bonds form a new web of relationships.

Emerson says that as his thoughts build on one another, he will stand in a new world of his own making instead of an old inherited one. He says his friends came to him without his seeking, given by God. Through the divine spirit shared in them and in him, the usual barriers of character, age, sex and circumstance are broken down, so that many people become one.

The speaker thanks his close friends for opening up the world to him and deepening his thoughts, calling their companionship a kind of endless poetry. He is not afraid they will drift away, because their bond rests on natural attraction, which will reach any equally noble person wherever he goes.

The speaker says he is very sensitive about feelings for others. A new person affects him so strongly that he cannot sleep. His fancies about people give pleasure but produce no lasting results in his thinking or actions. He takes pride in a friend's achievements and virtues as if they were his own.

When a friend is praised, the speaker feels as warmly as a lover hearing praise of his betrothed. We tend to think our friend is more good and more finely made than we are, and to see everything of his as finer. Our own ideas sound greater when he says them.

Emerson says love and friendship rise and fall like a heartbeat. Friendship seems almost too good to be true, so even in its best moments we doubt it. We also doubt that the friend really has the virtues we credit him with, and later we admire the person we had given those qualities to.

Emerson says the soul does not honor other people as it honors itself, because in strict thought every person stands at the same vast distance from the ultimate truth. He asks whether probing this foundation will cool our love. He answers no: if we are real, we should not fear to know things as they really are, since their hidden essence is as beautiful as their appearance, though it needs finer perception to grasp.

Emerson says he must state a hard truth even at a pleasant gathering, like a skull at a banquet. A man who is at one with his own thought sees himself as great and feels success overall, even though he fails in many small ways. Such a man needs no outside wealth or power to match him. Emerson would rather trust his own modest resources than another's riches, and he says he cannot make another's inner awareness equal his own.

The speaker says he cannot fully trust a friend who seems admirable and steady. He admits that this friend, like everything in the changing world of appearances, is only a shadow. The friend is not true being, like truth or justice, but only a picture of the speaker's soul. The friend has also come and is already preparing to leave.

The soul gains friends the way a tree grows leaves, and as new ones form, the old ones fall away. Nature moves in constant alternation: the soul takes up friendship for a while, then withdraws alone to know itself better, and later returns to friends with a richer understanding.

Emerson says that the urge to love revives our hope of joining with others, and the feeling of being cut off pulls us back from the pursuit. So every person spends life looking for friendship. If he wrote down his true feelings, he would address each new possible friend in the way the letter below does.

The speaker says that if he could be certain his friend would understand his moods and match them, he would stop worrying about small matters of the friend's coming and going. He admits he cannot be sure of this, so the friendship troubles him in a pleasing way.

Emerson says that the pleasant, emotional feelings we chase in friendship are only for curiosity, not for real life, and should not be indulged. We treat friendship as a thin, dreamy thing, so our friendships end quickly and poorly. True friendship is strong and lasting, governed by laws as fixed as those of nature and morals, but we seek quick personal gain instead.

People try to make friendship happen too quickly, like picking fruit that needs many seasons to ripen. They want to possess a friend for themselves, and that wish fails. Hidden rivalries then spoil the meeting, and most people only come down to one another's level.

Every close connection, Emerson says, forces some compromise. When gifted people meet, the finest quality of each one fades, and real company keeps disappointing even good and talented people. Even after careful planning, meetings are spoiled by sudden dullness and lapses of wit and spirits, just when friendship and thought should be at their best.

Emerson says he should be equal to every friend. If he fails one friend, the pleasure he takes in his other friendships feels cheap and cowardly, and he would hate himself for hiding among them. He quotes a verse: a warrior who loses one battle is erased from the book of honor, whatever his past victories.

Emerson says that slowness and reserve in friendship protect something delicate, which would be lost if it were exposed too early. Good things, like the ruby that takes a million years to form, need time. Friendship should not be casual or hasty. It should rest on the full worth of a person, with bold trust in the truth of a friend's heart.

Emerson sets aside the smaller social advantages of friendship to write about a special, sacred bond that he calls almost absolute. He says this bond is so much purer than ordinary love that the word "love" seems worn out and inadequate for it.

Emerson says true friendship is not fragile but the most solid thing we know. Human knowledge of nature and of our own destiny has made little progress, but the joy and peace he finds in friendship are, for him, the real core of things, with all nature and thought as mere outer covering.

Emerson says friendship could be built like a party arch meant for one day, but it is better if people understand its serious nature and keep its rules. A person who seeks friendship enters a hard contest against time, need and danger, and only one whose character is true enough keeps the bloom of the friendship intact.
Good friendship, Emerson says, rests on two equal parts, and the first is truth. A friend is someone before whom he can be completely sincere and think out loud.

Emerson says that when he meets a friend who is truly his equal, he can drop all the small pretenses of politeness and second thoughts that people normally keep up. He can meet that friend as openly as one chemical atom meets another. He also claims that sincerity is a privilege, like a crown or power, reserved for the highest rank, and that only a person alone is fully sincere.

People keep others at a distance with politeness, gossip, entertainment and business, hiding what they really think. Emerson describes a man who, in a religious fervor, dropped this pretence and spoke frankly to everyone's conscience. People first thought him mad, but his persistence brought every acquaintance into a true relationship with him.

Emerson describes a friend whose honesty made others speak to him just as honestly, sharing their real thoughts instead of small talk. He contrasts this with ordinary society, where people show only their outward side. He suggests that real honest relations are rare in a false age and cost something, and that most people we meet need to be flattered or humored.

A true friend is a sane, sensible person who challenges and engages your whole self, not just your cleverness, and asks nothing in return for the pleasure of his company. Emerson calls this a paradox: a friend is another self, a being outside you who reflects your own nature in a different form, so a friend may be seen as nature's finest work.

Emerson says people are bound to one another by many things, such as blood, pride, fear, hope, money and hate. But he finds it hard to believe that another person could have enough real character to draw us by love alone, or that we could be pure enough to offer them tenderness. For him, a man becoming dear to him is the highest success in life.

Emerson quotes a saying that people offer themselves most weakly to those they truly belong to, and hold back most from the person they love most. He wishes friendship to be grounded in everyday practical life, like a good citizen, before it aims at something heavenly. He notes that ordinary citizens are criticized for treating love as a trade, though such give-and-take is still good neighborliness.

Emerson says that ordinary helpfulness, like nursing the sick or carrying the coffin, can seem far from the high ideal of friendship. Still, he insists that a friendship with only lofty feeling and no practical loyalty, justice and kindness is not enough. He rejects using the word "friendship" for fashionable social ties.

Emerson says he would rather spend time with plain working people, such as farm boys and travelling sellers, than with fashionable friends who show off with carriage rides and expensive dinners. For him, friendship is a strict, plain bond of mutual help through all of life and death.

Friendship, in this passage, suits every kind of life: calm days and hard times alike, and both wit and religious feeling. Friends should lift the everyday tasks of life, make them finer through courage, wisdom and unity, and never let the bond become routine. It should stay lively and inventive, turning dull work into something with meaning.

Emerson says true friendship needs people who are rare, well matched, and well placed, so it is seldom achieved. Some hold that it can only exist between two people. He is less strict and prefers the idea of a circle of noble people linked to one another by a high understanding.

Emerson says that the best conversation happens between two people only. Groups of three hurt it: each of two men may be useful company alone, but when all three meet, the talk becomes flat. Two can talk while one listens, but three cannot share the most honest and probing kind of conversation.

In good company, people set aside their private feelings and join a shared group mind. Personal bonds like friendship or family love do not count there. Good sense requires this social rule, but it blocks the free meeting of two souls that real deep conversation needs.

Good conversation depends on the pair of people, not on a fixed gift in one person. Two people who share an affinity bring out each other's powers, while unrelated people may never discover them. A man who seems silent with his relatives may speak well with those who value his thought, just as a dial shows the hour only in the sun.

Emerson says a true friendship needs a balance: friends must be alike enough to connect, yet different enough that each keeps his own power and will. He would rather be alone than have a friend bend his real feelings, and he dislikes both opposition and easy agreement. A friend should stay fully himself, and Emerson values the friend's separateness most.

True friendship, the passage says, needs two strong and independent people. Each should be able to challenge the other rather than simply repeat him, and they should first see each other's differences before they find the deeper bond between them.

Real friendship cannot be hurried or arranged. It grows slowly, like a diamond, and it is chosen by the people themselves rather than picked by a person's will. It calls for reverence, so a friend should be regarded with a kind of awe.

Emerson says a true friend should let the other person grow in his own merits, even those you do not share, instead of holding him close. A friend is valued for his thought, not his small details. Treating a friend as property is a childish habit that gives brief pleasure rather than the greater good of friendship.

Emerson argues that friendship should be earned slowly and kept at a distance from everyday contact. He asks why a friend's home, family, and daily visits should matter. He wants his friend to be a spirit: a thought, a sincere look, not gossip or ordinary favors, which cheaper companions can supply. Friendship should be as pure and great as nature.

The speaker asks whether a friendship should seem small next to nature, such as a cloud or a clump of grass. He says the friend should not be belittled or reduced. Instead, the friend's strengths should be admired and kept, and the friend should stay a respected, untamed equal, not a convenience to be dropped later.

Friendship is best valued from a little distance, like an opal seen across the room. Emerson says a letter exchanged with a friend may seem a small thing to others, but to him it is enough, a spiritual gift. In such letters the heart speaks more freely than it can aloud, hinting at a higher way of living than heroes have yet achieved.

Friendship needs each person to be whole in himself before he can truly share himself with another, and waiting for that wholeness is necessary. Emerson adds that a lack of self-possession spoils the whole relationship. Real peace and respect come only when each person stands on his own as a complete world.

Friendship is treated as something too great to force with clever words. Emerson says to stay silent and wait, so that the deeper truth can speak through you, rather than trying to say something pleasing to a select few. Any speech of your own, however skilled, would be empty chatter.

Virtue is its own reward, and the only way to gain a friend is to become one yourself. Visiting someone's home does not bring you closer to them. If their character is different from yours, they will pull away from you, and you will never truly see them. Noble people keep others at a distance, so we should not force our way in.

Eventually we see that social arrangements, introductions and habits cannot create the close bonds we want. Only when our own inner nature rises to the same level as the other person's can we truly meet them, and then we are already one with them. In the end, love just mirrors a person's own worth as seen in others.

The higher our standard for friendship, the harder it is to find in real people, so we often feel alone. Still, Emerson hopes that somewhere in the universe there are souls who could truly love us and whom we could love. He expects that, once we are fully grown, we will meet such friends as equals.

Don't hurry into friendships with shallow people, since no true friendship can grow there; impatience leads to foolish bonds that have no higher blessing. Stay true to your own path, even if you lose small gains, and you will attract rare, deep companions. Ordinary important people will seem like shadows beside them.

Emerson argues that we cannot truly depend on other people, travel, or books to show us who we are, because each of them is only as limited as we are. He calls this dependence idolatry and asks us to give it up, since everything we need is already within us.

The speaker argues that we should stop relying on our closest friends and be independent of them. Yet this separation only leads to a higher kind of meeting, because people become truer friends when each stands on their own. A friend, he says, looks back to our past and forward to our future, and points toward an even greater friend.

Emerson says he treats friends like books: he likes to have them nearby but rarely uses them. He says he cannot talk much with a friend, because a great friend raises him so high that ordinary conversation feels beneath him. His real concern is inner insights, which come to him as fleeting visions he must pursue alone and fears losing.

Emerson says he values his friends but cannot afford to talk with them too much, because their visions might cause him to lose his own lofty thinking. Being close to them would bring comfort, yet he would mourn his "mighty gods," his high ideals. Even when he misses them, a visit might only fill his mind with new visions.

The speaker says he will take from his friends not their possessions but their character, the qualities that flow out of them. He wants bonds with them that are subtle and pure, not based on ordinary ties. Their meetings and partings will be so light they seem not to happen at all.

Emerson argues that a person can give deep friendship even when the other person does not return it fully, and that this need not cause regret. Like the sun, which keeps shining though most of its light is wasted, the giver's own generosity lifts and enlarges him. The unequal friend will eventually drop away, while the giver rises above him.

True love, Emerson says, cannot be wasted, because it rises above an unworthy loved one and stays fixed on the eternal. Yet real friendship asks for complete trust and generosity, never doubting or planning for the other's weakness, and treats the friend almost as a god.

This is a short verse from Emerson's poem "Friendship." It says that the love of small things and details should not be scorned, because the whole perfect shape is made up of the tiny parts that hold together.

Emerson says he has little prudence, and only the negative kind: he avoids spending and goes without, rather than planning or managing well. He argues that he has as much right to write on prudence as on poetry or holiness, because writers write from wishes and opposition as well as from experience.

People tend to praise and display the qualities they lack. A poet admires energy and skill, a merchant wants his son in a respectable profession, and a man who is not vain will be found praising vanity in others. The writer also admits he must balance lofty words about love and friendship with plainer talk about his debt to the senses.

Prudence, in Emerson's view, is the outer, practical side of good conduct, dealing with the senses and visible facts. It works within the physical world by its rules, keeping the body healthy by following physical conditions and the mind healthy by following the laws of thought. "God taking thought for oxen" means that prudence looks after ordinary, material matters.

Emerson says the physical world is a set of appearances that point beyond themselves. Practical wisdom about appearances is only valid when it knows it serves higher laws and works on the surface, not the center. When cut off from those laws, it is false; when joined to them, it shows the soul's laws at work within the senses.

Emerson sorts people by how far they see past the outward "symbol," meaning the visible world of things. The first group values the symbol only for its usefulness, such as health and wealth. The second values its beauty, as artists and scientists do. The third looks through the symbol to the truth it stands for, and these are the wise.

Rarely, a person moves through all the levels of perception. He sees nature as a symbol of spiritual truth, admires its beauty, and then, while living in nature, does not try to build on it or claim it. He honors the divine glory that shines through every crack in it.

Emerson criticizes a narrow, base kind of prudence that cares only for material gain and asks only whether a project will "bake bread." He compares this to a disease that destroys the vital organs. Real culture, he says, treats bodily life and health as mere means to the higher goal of human perfection.

Emerson says prudence is not a separate power of the mind but wisdom and virtue applied to the needs of the body. Cultivated people treat wealth, social success and personal influence as signs of a strong spirit. A person who loses that balance and pursues work or pleasure only for its own sake is useful at most as a small part of a machine, not truly cultivated.

Emerson says that false prudence treats the senses as the final guide, which he calls the god of drunkards and cowards and the source of comedy. True prudence limits this by recognizing an inner, real world beyond the senses. Once that is accepted, studying the order of the world rewards close attention, because human life, tied to nature's cycles, learns its basic lessons from that order.

Prudence, or practical good sense, does not question why the world works as it does. It accepts the natural laws that limit human life, such as time, climate, need, sleep, growth and death, and follows them to gain what is good for people. The passage also notes that civil property and rules add more limits on each new person.

We depend on the food and air around us, and the air can harm us when it is too hot, cold, dry or wet. Time, which seems whole and sacred when it arrives, gets cut into small, worthless pieces by everyday needs, such as a door to paint, a lock to fix, or wood, food and a smoking house.

Small irritations, such as taxes, tiresome dealings with dull people, and hurtful remarks we keep replaying, use up our time. The writer adds that nature brings its own annoyances, like flies, mosquitoes and rain, and that people who want to be idle find the weather hard to ignore even when they try.

Emerson says that hard lessons from everyday life, the small struggles that fill our hours and years, teach us. He contrasts the cold northerner, who must store food and fuel and so grows wiser and more capable, with the islander of warm lands, whose food and shelter nature provides without effort.

Emerson argues that every bit of work done with the hands teaches something about nature, and that nature always has more to reveal. So people in colder climates have shown more strength than southerners. He urges a person to sharpen careful observation and to gather facts from chemistry, natural history and economics.

The more a person owns, the less willing he is to give any of it away. Time keeps bringing chances that show what things are worth. Simple, harmless daily life teaches something, and a man who enjoys home life finds comforts others never notice. Using the right means to reach an aim brings success, whether on a farm, in a shop, or in politics or war.

A good husband, meaning a careful householder, brings the same orderly method to small chores like stacking firewood or storing fruit as to large affairs such as military campaigns or government files. On a rainy day he sets up a workbench and a tool-box, and in doing so enjoys the pleasure he had as a child in attics and storerooms.

A man who keeps to his duties and to whatever rules govern his life, Emerson says, will find his path full of small pleasures. He adds that people differ more in the kind of pleasure they get than in how much they get.

Nature punishes carelessness about prudence, so people who treat the senses as the final guide, or who grab pleasure before it is ready, suffer for it. Emerson says that dealing with people who see and report things loosely is unpleasant, and he notes that Americans take special pleasure in accurate perception.

Being late, muddled about facts, or careless of what the future will need is a failing common to all peoples. Once people break the natural order of time and space through carelessness, they get ruin instead of benefit, as a disturbed hive yields bees, not honey. Words and deeds are only good when they come at the right time, just as mowing sounds cheerful in June but sad after the hay season has passed.
