Emerson says that scattered, careless people spoil the mood of those who deal with them, not only their own affairs. He then quotes the Grand Duke of Weimar, who says that in great paintings, the figures seem alive and true because the artist places them at the right centre of gravity.

Emerson says that figures in a painting must look firmly balanced, with hands and eyes placed where they belong, or they lose their effect, even objects like stools. He points to a quiet Raphael painting of two saints as more moving than a scene full of writhing martyrs.

Emerson wants the people in life's "picture" to be solid and reliable, not vague or drifting. He asks them to keep memory separate from dreams, speak plainly, deal in facts, and trust what their own senses tell them.

Emerson asks who can rightly call another person imprudent, since the greatest people are the least prudent by worldly standards. He argues that humans have fallen out of harmony with nature, so that health, beauty and genius have become rare, and that this has prompted people to seek reform.

Emerson says that knowing plants, animals and natural laws does not come from feeling kinship with them, though poets have dreamed it might. He argues that poetry and practical wisdom should go together, with poets guiding everyday law and work. Right now, he says, the two seem completely separated.

Emerson says that people have broken natural laws so often that they now live among ruins. When reason and nature happen to agree, people are surprised. He adds that beauty, health and genius should be common to all, but they are rare, and what we call genius is often only partial insight.

Emerson contrasts clever people who use their talents to earn money and comfort with truly good or inspired people. He says the clever ones make luxury more refined instead of removing it. Real genius, he claims, tends toward self-discipline, faith and love, and finer souls see appetite as a sickness and find beauty in limits that check it.

Emerson says that talented people often call their indulgences in the senses minor, as if they did not matter next to their art. He argues that art never taught them greed for pleasure, drink, or gain, and that every such lapse reduces their art's worth and their own good sense.

Those who look down on the world are punished by it, and small neglects grow into ruin over time. Emerson also holds that the most painful tragedy is not a tyrant's cruelty but a clash between two people who are both partly right and so wrong each other.

Emerson describes a split between two kinds of people. One follows worldly rules and stays consistent. The other has noble ideals but also wants physical pleasures and ignores the laws that govern them, and so becomes unhappy and troublesome to himself and others. He calls this a painful knot we cannot untie, and he names the poet Tasso as a common example.

The passage says that a scholar lives two lives. When he is moved by high ideas, he seems great, even greater than Caesar, but when he needs practical good sense, he becomes a burden. He can fall from greatness to misery within a day, and his troubles are blamed on himself.

Emerson compares two kinds of people to men who waste themselves. Some are like wretched idlers in Constantinople who sneak to the opium shop each evening and feel briefly calm and inspired. Others are gifted people who, worn down by small money troubles, end up exhausted and achieving nothing.

A person should treat the early hardships that nature sends as signs that he can expect only the reward of his own work and self-restraint. He should value health, food, climate and social standing for what they are worth, and let nature's order measure how far he has strayed. He should keep regular habits and control spending.

Emerson says a person can learn as much wisdom from managing a household's money as a ruler can from running a nation. Even ordinary coins show the basic rules of the world, and any practical knowledge helps, such as the thrift of Poor Richard (a folk almanac saver) or the shrewd buying and selling of Wall Street-style dealers.

Emerson argues that prudence means constant watchfulness over small things, because almost everything left alone loses value. Iron rusts, beer sours, ships' timber rots, and money either earns nothing or can be lost or devalued. The smith's saying "Strike, while the iron is white" makes the same point: act at the right moment.

Emerson describes Yankee traders as prudent in a quick way: they pass goods and money on so fast that nothing spoils or loses value while they hold it. He compares this to skating on thin ice, where safety depends on moving quickly.

Emerson urges a deeper kind of common sense: believe that everything follows natural law rather than chance, so each person reaps what he sows. He advises self-reliance through hard work and self-control, so that a person need not depend on others. He also asks for keeping small duties, such as not keeping others waiting and keeping one's word.

A sealed letter can cross the world on a ship and still reach the person it was written for, even among crowds. The passage says a person should likewise hold their own being together against scattered distractions, and keep their word intact through storms, distance and chance, so that a promise is kept years later in faraway places.

Emerson says we should not study one virtue alone, because human nature is balanced and has no real contradictions. Practical wisdom about everyday affairs, such as property and social forms, cannot be separated from heroism and holiness. Good management of outward things depends on understanding their inner source in the soul.

Honesty is presented as the wiser and more useful course. Lies harm the liar and the wider society, and events eventually punish them. Frankness, by contrast, builds trust and friendship. People tend to live up to the trust and respect shown to them.

Prudence, or wise caution, does not mean running away from frightening or difficult things. It means facing them with courage. Someone who wants a calm life must make up their mind to face what they fear most, and this usually shows the fear to be groundless.

Full calm and composure can make a battle hardly more dangerous than a fencing bout or a game of football. Soldiers report men who watched the cannon fire and stepped out of the ball's path. Fear of storms belongs mostly to people indoors, while drovers and sailors work in bad weather and stay healthy.

Fear makes us think our neighbors are more dangerous than they are, but fear is a poor guide. Emerson says everyone seems strong to others and weak to himself, and the bully who threatens from a distance is usually timid when confronted. Peace among people often rests on each side being afraid of the other.

Emerson says that kindness helps us see clearly, so love is not blindness but a way of seeing. When you meet someone who disagrees with you, he advises not to dwell on the dividing lines but to find the common ground that remains, such as the shared sun and rain. Doing so makes the differences seem to fade, while arguing would bring out the worst in people.

Arguments about religion turn even good people into petty, dishonest players who bluff, hide and boast, so no one gains a thought or real feeling. Therefore, Emerson says, you should not put yourself in a false position with others by giving way to hostility and bitterness.

Emerson advises that when your views clash with those of others, you should speak as if your listeners already agree with you, and state your ideas boldly without doubt. He says that arguing in a forced, defensive way makes your thought come out weak and distorted, so it does not show its true shape.

Emerson means that if people are willing to agree on something, they will soon agree, because all people share the same basic heart and mind beneath their surface differences. The "assume a consent" phrase means to act as if agreement already exists.

Wisdom tells us not to hold back from people or treat them coldly while waiting for better companions. Life runs out while we wait, and new friends are unlikely to arrive, so we should enjoy the warm bonds we already have near us.

Emerson says that old friends, though plain and comfortable like old shoes, are the ones we should keep. We may like the more glamorous people our imagination invents, but those relationships are worth having only on fair, mutual terms. If we build new relationships out of ambition rather than something higher, their real value disappears, like strawberries losing their flavor when grown in a garden bed.

Emerson argues that virtues such as truth, courage, love and humility all serve prudence, which he defines as the skill of securing present well-being. He adds that human conduct is made of one basic stuff, so whatever moral question we start from quickly leads back to the basic moral rules.

Good things often come to bad or lowly people, while hardship and danger belong to the noble. Wine, sugar and roses go to knaves, slaves and fools, while the hero feeds on his own heart and great men's rooms become prisons. Storms, the poem suggests, are what bring a ship toward its royal destination.
In old English plays by Beaumont and Fletcher, a character recognizes at once whether a newcomer is a gentleman, and treats him with great courtesy. Everyone else is treated as worthless.

Emerson says that in certain English plays, the characters are so earnest and strong in their character that their speech turns into poetry when even a small new event happens in the plot. He gives an example: a Roman conqueror of Athens is moved by the beauty of a duke's wife and tries to save her husband.

This is not from Emerson's Heroism as written; the lines are from a play, a dialogue in which Dorigen, about to die, asks Sophocles to blindfold her so she will not see her husband bleed, and says she will teach the Romans how to die. Martius then asks whether she knows what dying is. The main point is a willing death, and the question that follows.

Sophocles, facing death, says that dying is the start of real life. It ends a tired, deceitful world and brings him to the gods and to those he loved best. He feels no grief, and his last act is to kneel and offer a final act of worship to the gods.
Martius is torn between his love for a married woman and his sense of duty. He vows to crush his own heart rather than break a sacred bond. Others then praise him for this self-control.

Martius says that Valerius, though taken prisoner, has won Martius over by his fearlessness toward fortune and death. Because Valerius's spirit cannot be chained, Martius concludes that his captor won nothing. Valerius is the free one, and Martius is the one held captive.

Emerson says that recent American poems, plays, sermons and speeches rarely have a bold, heroic tone. Their writers make many soft, pleasant sounds but few strong ones. He names a few exceptions: Wordsworth's poems "Laodamia" and "Dion," some sonnets, and a passage by Walter Scott.

Emerson says that Thomas Carlyle, who likes bold and manly character, keeps every heroic trait in the people he writes about. He adds two further examples worth reading: a few songs by Robert Burns, and an account of the battle of Lutzen in the Harleian Miscellanies.

Emerson says that Simon Ockley's history of the Saracens (Arab armies of the early Islamic period) praises the bravery of their individual fighters, even though the author, a Christian at Oxford, feels he must claim to disapprove. He then names Plutarch, the ancient Greek writer of biographies, as the chief source of stories about heroes, and he thinks Plutarch is more valuable than all other ancient writers.

Each story in Plutarch's "Lives" answers the gloom and timidity of religious and political thinkers. Its wild courage, a Stoicism lived in the blood rather than taught in schools, appears in every anecdote and explains the book's great fame.

Emerson says that books which sting and purify the reader are more needed than books on politics or household management. Life looks joyful only to the wise; to the cautious, it looks rough and risky. Disease and suffering, he argues, show that natural, mental, and moral laws have been broken, by earlier and present generations alike.

Emerson says that diseases such as lockjaw, rabies, madness, war, plague and famine show a violent side of nature. He argues that since evil entered nature through human wrongdoing, nature releases it through human suffering. No one is free of this, because everyone shares in the sin and so must share in the suffering that pays for it.

Emerson says a person should be trained from youth to expect conflict, not to live carelessly in peace. A prepared person stays calm, neither fears nor defies danger, and risks reputation and life to speak the truth and act rightly, even against hanging or a hostile crowd.

Heroism is the soul's readiness to face outside harm alone, trusting its own strength to meet any enemy. In its rudest form it shows as scorn for safety and comfort, the reason people find war appealing. It is a self-trust that ignores caution, because it believes it can repair whatever harm it suffers.

The hero is a man whose balance nothing can shake, so he moves calmly toward his own goal in danger or in general chaos. Emerson admits heroism is proud and not fully philosophical or holy, yet says we must still deeply respect it, because great deeds cannot be questioned. Heroism acts from feeling rather than reasoning, so it is always right.

A hero's act may be one that a different upbringing, religion, or learning would have judged differently. Still, for the hero it is his highest deed, beyond the criticism of philosophers and clergy. It is the plain claim of an untrained man who feels within himself a will that scorns cost, danger, and reproach, and that he believes is greater than any opponent.

Heroic action goes against what most people think and, for a while, against what respected good people think. It comes from a private inner impulse, which only the person feeling it can fully see. Wise people first object, but later agree once the act's worth shows itself.

Emerson says that self-trust is the core of heroism, a soul at war against falsehood, wrong and harm. A hero speaks truth, stays fair and generous, and does not give up. Heroism mocks small everyday concerns and the false caution that cares only about health and money.

Emerson asks what to make of trivial pastimes such as games, dressing, gossip and sweets that occupy ordinary society. He suggests that people easily slide from great things to petty ones. When the spirit does not rule the world, the world fools it instead.

Emerson says that ordinary people take the great "hoax" of life very seriously, busying themselves with small comforts, pleasures and praise. A great soul, seeing this, can only laugh at such earnest nonsense. The quoted lines, from Shakespeare's Henry IV, add that a person of greatness would be ashamed to count trivial possessions like silk stockings.

Ordinary people weigh the trouble and cost of hosting strangers and hold back. A nobler spirit sets such calculation aside and trusts that God will provide. To illustrate, Emerson cites a geographer's account of a palace in Sogd whose gates are always open, nailed back to the wall.

The passage describes a household that keeps its doors open day and night to any stranger, and the master is glad when guests stay long. It then says that generous people, who help strangers out of love rather than show, earn a kind of return from the universe, which Emerson puts as God being in their debt.

Emerson says that generous people, though they seem to lose time and effort, are repaid by it, since they spread love and civic virtue. Hospitality should serve others, not display wealth, because showiness weakens the host. A brave person gives freely and sees no need for fine furnishings, since plain food and water, given with dignity, carry more grace than a grand city feast.

A hero is temperate because he does not want to disgrace his own worth, but he values restraint for its grace rather than its severity. He does not bother to preach against meat, wine, tobacco, or luxuries like silk and gold. His way of living is natural and graceful without fuss.

Two examples of choosing water over wine or other comforts. John Eliot, a missionary, said wine was a good gift to be thankful for but that water came first. King David poured out water his men had risked their lives to bring him, offering it to God instead of drinking it.

Emerson doubts that Brutus really despaired of virtue before his death, as a famous story claims. He argues that a truly heroic person does not trade away justice or nobility for comfort. For such a person, virtue alone is enough, and even poverty or loss does not diminish it.

Emerson admires heroes most for their good humor and cheerfulness. Ordinary duty can reach the point of facing suffering and danger with seriousness, but heroic people value opinion, success and even life so little that they do not beg enemies for mercy or display grief. They keep their usual dignity instead.

Emerson gives examples of people who meet disgrace or death with pride rather than submission. Scipio tears up his own accounts instead of waiting to be cleared, Socrates accepts honor instead of punishment, and More jokes on the scaffold. In the play, a captain answers his captors that they can hang him, and he can still scorn them.

Emerson says that truly great or simple-hearted people treat even the largest human works, such as building cities or tearing down old churches and nations, lightly, as play. They ignore the world's customs and rules. Seen from above, all of humanity would look like children playing, though to ordinary people it looks serious and solemn.

Our enjoyment of heroic stories, even as schoolboys reading forbidden romances, shows that the qualities in those heroes already belong to us. When we admire Greek energy or Roman pride, we are already taking that same spirit into ourselves. Emerson urges us to make room for this heroic spirit in our ordinary lives.

Emerson says we should drop the habit of thinking some places and times are more special than others. Famous names like Athens or Rome sound grand only because we are used to them, while local places like Massachusetts seem humble. He argues that the best things can be found right where we are, if we stay long enough to see it.

The main point is that a person needs only to be fully present in their own life, because great things come with them wherever they are. Epaminondas did not need a famous place like Olympus to die in, and Washington and Milton were great in ordinary places like New Jersey and London. A great person makes any place seem special in people's minds.

The best country is the one where the greatest minds live. Reading about the deeds of famous heroes shows Emerson how small our own lives are. He says we should live deeply enough to give our lives more splendor than kings or nations have, guided by principles that matter to people and nature for as long as we live.

Many young men seem remarkable at first, speaking boldly about society, books and religion as if they will overturn everything. Once they take up an ordinary working career, however, their apparent greatness shrinks to the size of any other person.

Emerson says that people who follow high ideals often look foolish next to everyday reality. When they try to act on those ideals in the real world, they find no models or fellow believers and lose heart. Still, he holds that their first hopes were true and will one day be put into practice by a better courage and truer belief.

A woman should not assume she cannot match the great women of history, such as Sappho or Madame de Staël, just because they did not fully satisfy the ideal of wisdom and beauty. Emerson asks why she should think this, since she may have a new problem to solve and a nature as happy as any that has existed.

A young woman is urged to walk confidently through life, open to each new experience and to the things that catch her attention. She should choose her influences firmly and proudly, without worrying about pleasing others. Such independence lifts the people who see her, and the inner conviction of her own heart supports her, so she should never give in to fear.

Heroism means staying firm once you have chosen your course, rather than drifting with occasional bursts of generosity. A hero should not water down the choice to win the world's approval. Heroic acts often go beyond what others can sympathize with, so the hero should not withdraw a good act just because sensible people do not praise it.

Stand by what you have done, even if it was unusual, and do not feel sorry for it. Emerson recalls advice to always do what you frighten you, and says a plain, upright person has no need to apologize for past actions. Phocion, an ancient Athenian general, is his example: he was glad the battle turned out well but did not regret having argued against fighting it.

Emerson says that a person can always find comfort in accepting their own weakness, since nature has promised no one that they will never look foolish. He urges being as free with one's dignity as with money. Real greatness no longer cares what others think. Telling others about one's good deeds is a mistake, because it is only done to justify oneself.

Emerson says that people who are comfortable should voluntarily take on hardships, such as telling hard truths, living strictly, or being generous to an extreme, as a sign of solidarity with those who suffer. He adds that a wise person should also face debt, loneliness, unpopularity, disease, public hatred and the sight of violent death, so the soul is tested and strengthened.

Emerson says that heroic times are usually frightening, but a brave person can always find chances to test their courage. Although life today is easier and freer than before, virtue still needs champions and martyrs. He points to Lovejoy, who was shot by a mob while defending free speech.

Emerson says the only path to real peace is to follow one's own inner judgment. He advises a person to spend less time with others, stay close to home, and keep to the ways they approve of. Steady high feelings kept up in ordinary duties build a character that can act with honor even in violent crowds or at execution.

In a republic, a young man who holds unpopular opinions may face slander, mob violence, and even hanging, if society turns against those opinions. Still, the author says that Nature limits how far such malice can go, and that people will soon reach a point beyond which no enemy can follow them.

Emerson says that when we feel unsure about the future and cannot hear our higher ideals, we may envy people who finished their hard work. He suggests that seeing the meanness of current politics makes him glad Washington is dead, so that Washington's hope for humanity was never crushed.

Many people sometimes wish they could already be free of the troubles of this world, waiting calmly for their own death. But the kind of love that would rather be destroyed than betray someone has already made death impossible for it. Such love shows that it belongs to a deep, endless being rather than to mortal life.

Emerson quotes a poem by Henry More, which says that God loves souls that share in his good life as he loves himself. God will never abandon them, and they live forever in blessed eternity, even though God himself would have to die for them to die.

Emerson's lines say there is plenty of room in the world, yet two people cannot walk side by side or share one path. A cuckoo pushes every other egg out of the nest, and a strong force works on all of nature, bending time and things to its will.

Some hours of life carry more weight than others. Moments of faith are brief, while our faults are repeated, yet those moments feel more real than everything else. So the argument from past experience, used to deny that people can hope for much, fails. Even when we grant the past to critics, we still hope, and they must explain that hope.

Emerson argues that the feeling that human life is small and that we lack knowledge is itself a sign of the soul's vast claims. He says people always outgrow what has been written about them, so no account of human nature is complete, and six thousand years of philosophy have not explored the soul's inner depths.

Emerson says that no matter how carefully people test and measure things, something always remains that cannot be explained. Human life comes from a source we cannot see, and even the most precise calculation cannot foresee every next moment. He concludes that events come from a higher origin than his own will.

Emerson compares thoughts to a river that flows into him from a source he cannot see. He says he does not create his thoughts. He only receives them, like a watcher who is surprised by what comes, and they arrive from a power outside himself.

Emerson describes the Over-soul as a great, unified nature that judges past and present errors and alone foretells what must come. Every person's individual being is held within it and joined with all others. Sincere talk is its worship, and right action is submission to it.

Emerson says a deeper reality exposes pretense, so that each person shows what they truly are, and this reality keeps flowing into human thought and action as wisdom, virtue, power and beauty. Our ordinary life is split into fragments, but within each person lies the soul of the whole, one unified source that connects every part.

Emerson says that the deep power we exist within is complete at every moment, and that seeing and the thing seen are one and the same. We perceive the world in separate pieces, such as the sun, the moon, and trees, but these are parts of a whole, which he calls the soul.

Emerson says that the deepest wisdom can only be understood by someone who has the same inner vision. He admits he cannot speak for it, since his own words fall short. Only that wisdom itself can inspire a person, and then their speech becomes full and universal.

Emerson says he wants to describe the "heaven" of this higher power and the hints he has gathered about its simple, powerful highest law. He admits he may have to use ordinary, non-sacred words to do so, since sacred language is not available to him.

Emerson says that by looking at everyday experiences such as conversation, daydreams, regret, strong feeling, surprises and dreams, we can learn something about the deeper nature of things. He argues that the soul is not a body part or a single mental power like memory or reasoning. Instead, it works through all the organs and powers, using them as tools, and it is a kind of light.

Emerson says there is a deeper source behind our minds and wills, which controls them and cannot be owned or fully grasped. A light from this source shines through us, so that we see ourselves as nothing and the light as everything. The ordinary person, who eats, works and counts, does not show his true self but hides it.

Emerson says a person deserves no special respect in himself. But when the universal soul works through a person, it shows up as genius in the mind, virtue in the will, and love in the feelings. Trouble starts when a person tries to act on his own account, apart from that soul. Reform, he adds, is an effort to let the soul work through people so they obey it.

Emerson says that a pure spiritual nature is present in every person and cannot be fully described in words. He argues there is no barrier between the human soul and God, so people are open to the deeper spiritual qualities such as justice, love, freedom and power. These qualities stand above us, and they are most noticeable when our self-interest tempts us to betray them.

Emerson says the soul is not held back by the limits that bind ordinary life. He claims it goes beyond experience and even overrides time and space. Most people, he says, are so shaped by the senses that time and space seem fixed, and mocking them looks like madness. In his view, time and space are simply ways of measuring the soul's power.

Emerson says that a person's real age is not only the number of years since birth. Some thoughts keep a person feeling young, such as contemplating universal, eternal beauty, which seems to belong to all ages rather than to a short human life. Even small use of the mind, like reading a poem or a deep sentence, lifts a person out of the limits of time and refreshes them, even when they are sick or weak.

Reading a book by Plato or Shakespeare, or simply hearing their names, makes us feel that their thought is timeless and still alive across the centuries. Emerson suggests that the soul measures things on a different scale from the senses and understanding, so that time, space and nature seem to shrink before its insights.

Ordinary speech treats everything as happening in time, saying that judgment or reform is near or far. Emerson means that some things we see are passing and outside us, while others last and belong to the soul. The things we now think fixed will drop away from our experience like fruit.

Emerson says that places, people, institutions and society are as temporary as mist or smoke. The soul, by contrast, keeps moving forward, making a new world ahead of itself and leaving old ones behind. Events are only the changing robe the soul wears.

The soul does not progress in steady, measurable steps like a line moving forward. Its growth comes in sudden shifts of condition, as an insect changes from egg to worm to fly. Its pace follows its own law, not a calculation.

Genius does not grow by raising one special person above others one at a time. Instead, each stage of growth widens the person in the place where he works, so he moves beyond whole groups of people. Each divine impulse breaks through the limits of the visible world and carries the mind into eternity.

The mind, when it takes in truths that people have always known, feels closer to the ancient Stoic thinkers Zeno and Arrian than to the people living around it. Zeno founded Stoicism, and Arrian recorded the teachings of Epictetus.

Emerson says that moral and mental growth comes from rising into the spirit that holds all the virtues, not from aiming at one virtue at a time. Purity, justice and kindness are each less than the soul itself, so naming a single virtue feels like coming down from the whole. A well-born child has these virtues naturally, and speaking to his heart makes a person good at once.

Emerson says that a person who has humility, justice, love and aspiration already stands on a level that gives access to learning, art, speech and poetry. Such a person already has the powers that people value most. He compares this to a lover, whose beloved values his small talents above all else, even when she has little skill of her own.

When the heart gives itself fully to the Supreme Mind (the divine, universal spirit), it feels connected to everything and gains knowledge and power easily. Rising to this basic feeling, the person moves from the edge of the world to its centre, where they see the causes of things and foresee the universe, which is only a slow result.

Emerson says that one way the divine speaks to us is through the spirit appearing in other people. When we meet others who share our thoughts and instincts, we feel a shared nature, and they stir strong feelings in us. These feelings lead to social life, conflict and politics. Other people, he concludes, add to the lessons the soul teaches directly.

In youth, people are drawn to individual persons, but later experience shows one shared nature behind them all. When two people talk, they implicitly refer to this common nature as a third party, which Emerson calls impersonal and identifies with God.

When people argue earnestly about deep questions, the whole group feels that the thought belongs equally to everyone present, not only to the speaker. Everyone becomes wiser, feeling a shared power, duty and calm self-control that lifts them together.

Emerson says that a kind of human wisdom is shared by great and humble people alike, and that schooling often works against it. Truth belongs to no one person, so the best thinkers do not claim it as their own. Scholars do not hold wisdom exclusively, and their narrow focus can make it harder for them to think clearly.

Some of our best insights come from plain speakers who say, without effort, what we have been searching for. The soul's real work often lies in what people feel but do not say. We know more than we act on, and we have not yet fully grasped ourselves, though we sense we are greater than we are.

Emerson says that even in small talk with neighbors he senses a truth. He means that a higher part within each person watches these ordinary exchanges, and that the divine in each person quietly recognizes the divine in the other. "Jove" is the Roman name for the god Jupiter, used here for the divine spirit.

People lower themselves to meet the world's demands, giving up their higher nature for ordinary, petty work. Emerson compares them to Arab sheiks who live in plain houses and seem poor to avoid the greed of a ruler, keeping their wealth hidden in private rooms.

Emerson says the soul is fully present even in a small child, so the same soul can meet the child's soul directly. Learning and wealth do not help a parent with a child. Only soul helps. If the parent sets aside personal will and lets the soul judge between them, the child responds with respect and love. If the parent insists on his own will, the child simply opposes it, and the parent is left only with force.

Emerson says that the soul is what recognizes truth, and that people know truth directly when they see it. He argues that doubters who ask how you can be sure are wrong to demand proof, just as you know you are awake without having to prove it.

Swedenborg's point, quoted here, is that proving whatever one wants shows nothing about understanding. The real sign of intelligence is being able to tell true from false. Emerson adds that a good thought he finds in a book comes back to him as a reflection of the whole soul.

When a person's own mind takes in a bad thought, the same deeper soul acts like a sword that cuts it away. If a person does not interfere with their thinking and sees things as they stand in God, they know each thing and each person. Emerson says God stands behind us and sees all things through us.

When the soul communicates truth, it does not hand over something separate from itself. It gives itself, so that the person it enlightens is taken into it, in proportion to the truth he receives. Emerson calls this the highest event in nature.

Emerson says that when the soul shows its own nature, this is called revelation, and it always brings a feeling of awe and delight. He describes it as the divine mind flowing into the human mind, and a new truth or great deed stirs people in the same way.

Emerson says that when a person receives this higher wisdom, seeing and doing are not separate. Understanding comes through obeying, and obeying comes from a glad sense of truth. Each time a person feels this inflow, it stays in memory, and an excitement naturally comes with awareness of the divine presence.

Emerson says that the spiritual feeling he is describing comes in many strengths. At its strongest it is ecstasy, trance, or prophetic inspiration, and at its faintest it is a quiet glow of goodness that holds families and communities together. He also notes that people who first feel this religious sense often seem close to madness, as if dazzled by too much light.

Emerson lists famous religious figures, such as Socrates, Paul and George Fox, whose intense spiritual experiences he calls "of this kind." He adds that similar experiences occur in ordinary life in milder form, and that religious history shows a steady tendency toward enthusiasm, or ecstatic feeling.

Religious experiences such as those of the Methodists are different forms of one feeling. In that feeling, a single person's soul joins with the universal soul in a mix of awe and delight. Methodists are a Christian group, and "over-soul" refers to a shared spiritual reality beyond each person.

Revelations, or moments of insight, all work the same way: they show the soul the absolute law. They answer the soul's own questions, not the questions that the reasoning mind asks. The soul does not reply in words but gives the thing being sought itself.

Revelation, Emerson says, is the soul opening itself up, not a way of predicting the future. People who ask God for personal details, such as how long they will live, who they will meet, or what they will do, are chasing idle curiosity. Answers given in words to such questions do not really answer them.

People want detailed descriptions of the afterlife, such as the soul's immortality and what heaven is like. Emerson says such descriptions cannot be given in advance, and that we know these places only by living in them. He adds that Jesus never answered such questions in that way.

Emerson says that truth, justice and love are linked with unchanging existence. Jesus focused on these moral qualities and never separated them from lasting duration, nor spoke about the soul's duration. His disciples were the ones who separated the two and taught the soul's immortality as a doctrine backed by proof.

Emerson says that teaching immortality as a separate doctrine is already a sign of decline. A truly inspired person, moved by love and humility, does not ask whether the soul continues, because such a person lives in the present, which he sees as infinite, and does not look toward a finite future.

Emerson says that asking what the future holds is a kind of sin, because no words can answer such questions. The future is hidden by a veil, and this is part of human nature, so that people learn to live in the present. The only way to get an answer is to stop prying and simply work and live, and then the question answers itself.

Emerson says people know one another through a deep, shared spiritual insight, even when they cannot explain how. We sense who can be trusted without knowing why. We also know whether each person has been honest with himself, and whether his teaching is just an aspiration or a real effort he makes too.

People are always judging each other's character, in daily dealings of every kind. Yet the judging is not done by reason or learning. The wise person does not pass judgment himself. He lets people reveal their own character, and simply records what they show.

A person's private will cannot stop their true nature from showing. What we are teaches others without our choosing to teach, and thoughts enter and leave our minds in ways we do not control. Character influences people more than deliberate instruction does, and a person's real progress shows in their tone.

A person cannot escape being shaped by a higher spiritual reality, whatever his background or circumstances. If he has not found his home in God, his speech and opinions will reveal it, however boldly he hides it. If he has found his centre in God, the divine will shine through him despite ignorance or hardship. Seeking and possessing sound different.

Emerson says the main difference between teachers is whether they speak from inside their own experience or not. One kind speaks as people who actually possess the truth they describe. The other kind speaks from outside it, as observers.

Emerson says that a teacher who only speaks from outside, as a mere observer or from what others report, is of little use. He holds that Jesus spoke from within, in a way beyond all others, and that a true teacher must speak from within the inner truth, where the word and the truth are one. Otherwise, the speaker should humbly admit it.

Emerson says the same universal spirit that gives wisdom also gives genius to the mind. Many learned writers, he claims, lack true wisdom and seem to have only a clever skill, not inspiration. Their gifts feel less like virtue and more like a flaw.

Emerson argues that great genius is not set apart from ordinary people. It is a fuller share in what all people hold in common, and great poets show a human wisdom that matters more than their skill. They care for truth itself and do not put on airs, such as being a clever writer or a fine gentleman.

Emerson says that great poets seem cold to readers used to showy, emotional writing, because their poetry comes from a soul that is free to express itself. The soul knows more than it has made, so a great poet makes us feel our own richness, and we then value his works less. Shakespeare, he adds, suggests a wealth greater than anything he actually wrote.

Great works of art, such as Shakespeare's plays, seem to be lasting, but they touch the true nature of things no more deeply than a passing shadow touches a rock. The same inspiration that produced Hamlet and Lear could produce equally good works continually. So the author asks why such works should be valued above the source they came from, the soul.

Emerson says this higher spiritual force enters a person only when that person gives themselves over to it completely. It reaches the humble and simple who drop their pride, and it shows up as insight, calm, and dignity. Once a person is filled with it, they stop caring what others think and test people by their own standard, and this demands honesty and plainness.

Emerson here criticizes people who try to make their lives seem grand by pointing to their connections and possessions. Vain travellers name the lords and countesses they met, ambitious people show off jewellery and calling cards, and the more refined pick out impressive episodes such as trips to Rome or famous friends.

The soul that truly worships God is plain and honest. It does not seek romance, fine friends, adventure, or admiration. It lives fully in the present, ordinary day, where even small things open up to a deeper spiritual insight.

When someone with a very simple, great mind speaks, writing down their words seems like trying to catch words in a net. Their simplest sayings are the most worth recording, yet they seem so ordinary that recording them is like bottling air. Entry into this kind of closeness requires dropping pretense and speaking plainly, honestly, and with full confidence.

Such souls treat others as equals and do not praise them, even for good deeds, because they see those deeds as their own kind of nature. Their plain, brotherly manner shows up the empty flattery that writers give and take from one another.

Emerson says he is not surprised that certain men visit famous rulers such as Cromwell, Queen Christina, and the kings Charles II and James I. Because these men are as elevated as kings, they speak to rulers as equals, without flattery or giving way. That frank meeting refreshes the rulers, who otherwise hear only servile talk.

Emerson says that people of great soul leave others wiser and better, and that their honesty shows that sincerity is worth more than flattery. Dealing plainly with others draws out honesty and rules out trifling. He quotes Milton to say that even plain advice from such people is a form of praise.

Emerson says that when a person worships God with a sincere heart, the person and God become united in that act, and this union is always new and beyond full understanding. The idea of God comforts people, filling lonely places and easing the pain of mistakes. He adds that God can only fill the heart after people have given up inherited beliefs and empty speech about God.

The passage describes a trust that comes from a heart opened to something larger than itself. This trust gives a person a settled certainty that the best is also the true. So he can set aside his personal doubts and fears, trusting that time will answer his questions, and he is sure that his well-being matters to the basic power of existence.

Emerson says that a person who sees the moral law as supreme trusts it so completely that such trust overrides even their dearest plans. He holds that what is truly meant for a person will come to them, so the seeker may run after a friend while the mind stays calm. If the friend is not found, the person should accept that not finding them is for the best.

Emerson says that a power within each person also works in others, so it can bring people together if that is best. He asks whether a person who sets out to serve others, driven by talent, love and hope of fame, is also ready to accept being stopped. He adds that whatever words should reach a person will reach them.

Emerson says that whatever help or comfort a person truly needs will come back to them, by direct or roundabout ways. The friends a person's deepest heart longs for will also come to them. He gives the reason: the heart in each person is the same heart shared by all, so people are connected like one blood or one sea.

Emerson says a person should learn from nature and thought that the highest power lives within them, and that to hear God clearly they must go into private quiet, as Jesus advised, and listen to their own inner voice. He adds that even other people's prayers can get in the way until one has formed a prayer of one's own.

Emerson says that true religion does not depend on how many people believe. Whenever someone appeals to numbers, he claims that religion is absent. A person who truly feels God's presence does not count other believers, and in that experience no human authority, such as the theologians Calvin or Swedenborg, has any say.

Emerson argues that true faith cannot rest on authority, whether that means a crowd or a single leader. Relying on outside authority shows a weak religious life, and the reverence given to Jesus as an authority says more about the people who give it than about any eternal truth. The soul is self-reliant and trusts itself, and compared with its possibilities, even the holiest past lives count for little.

Emerson says that, measured against the heaven our inner feelings point toward, no real person or way of life seen or read about seems truly admirable. Even the saints and heroes that history honors are accepted only with reservations. They help us in private moments, but when crowds and routine keep them in view, they wear us out.

When the soul gives itself wholly to the divine, the divine works through it, and the soul feels free, lively and clear-sighted. It sees that nature follows laws below the soul's own nature, and it believes it belongs to a universal mind it calls its Perfect.

When the writer opens himself to the great soul, the sun and stars seem like passing effects. He feels that he becomes more public and human, acting with immortal energies. Seeing the world as one lasting miracle of the soul, he will be less amazed by single wonders and will learn that no history is ordinary or unholy.

A person who sees that all history is sacred and that the whole universe appears in a single atom or moment will stop living a broken, patchwork life. Instead, he lives with a sense of divine unity, accepts any place or task, and faces the future calmly, trusting that God already holds it.

Nature gathers itself into round forms, and its short-lived creatures stay on the surface, looking only at the outline of the sphere. The poem says that if they understood what this shape meant, it would mark the start of a new creation.

Emerson says the eye makes the first circle, and the horizon it sees is a second. The circle shape repeats everywhere in nature and is the highest symbol of the world's hidden meaning. He adds that St. Augustine described God as a circle with its centre everywhere and its edge nowhere.

Every action can be surpassed by another, so nothing is final. Emerson says that around every circle another circle can be drawn, every end is a new beginning, and every depth has a lower depth beneath it. Life, he suggests, is a training in accepting this.

Emerson says that a certain natural fact stands for a moral truth: there is a perfection that people can never fully reach. This ideal both inspires every success and shows its limits. He suggests the idea can link many examples of human power in different fields.

Nothing in nature stays fixed; everything is changing. Human culture, cities and institutions last only as long as the idea behind them, and when a new idea arrives they fade away. Greek sculpture is an example: it has melted like ice, leaving only scattered pieces, because the creative power that made it now works in other forms.

Old ideas and old things eventually give way to new ones, just as the Greek letters are slowly fading. Emerson argues that new creations are built from the remains of what came before, and that new arts replace old ones, with examples such as railways replacing canals and electricity replacing steam.

Behind every solid-looking thing is a finer cause, such as a thought or a hand, that made it and could undo it. A granite tower seems lasting, but a small hand built it and could topple it faster. Things seem permanent only until their hidden source is understood.

Things that look fixed, like orchards, fields and the natural world, only seem permanent. Emerson argues that nature has a cause, like everything else, so once that cause is understood, its apparent solidity loses force. Permanence is a matter of degree, and nothing is final; even the moon does not limit spiritual power.

A person's basic beliefs guide how he sorts all his experience, and he can only change if shown a new idea that is stronger than his own. Human life grows outward like expanding circles, and how far it reaches depends on the strength or truth of the individual soul.

Emerson says that every settled idea or institution, such as an empire, an art, a custom or a religious rite, forms a wave that piles up and tries to fix and confine life. A strong soul breaks through that limit and forms a larger wave, and the heart always pushes outward past any boundary.

Every final truth or law is only a step toward a wider one, so no view is ever the last word. When one speaker declares his account complete, another draws a bigger circle around it, and the first speaker can only answer by drawing a still larger circle outside his rival.

Emerson says that today's ideas, however firmly held, will later be reduced to a single word or folded into a broader idea. Tomorrow's thought can overturn every existing belief and lead people toward something no dream has yet pictured. Each person is less a worker in the world than a hint of what they could become, and people live as forecasts of the coming age.

Each new step of understanding, or new action, opens a wider view. Every truth seems to cancel the one before it, but it only limits that older truth. The new idea first looks like a threat to those used to the old one, yet they soon accept it. Then it too fades before the next new insight.

Do not be afraid of a new broad idea that seems to conflict with your view of the spirit. If a fact looks crude and physical, do not resist it, because it will improve your understanding of matter just as much.

Emerson says that no person is ever fixed or fully known, at least from the inside. Each man feels that he is not fully understood, and that some part of him can never be opened or explained. For this reason, every man believes he has a greater possibility within him.

Emerson says that his moods do not agree with one another. When he is full of ideas he feels sure of his writing, but he knows that yesterday he felt empty, and he expects that in a month he will not recognize the writer of today's pages. He swings between feeling like God in nature and feeling like a weed by the wall.

Emerson says a person always wants to rise above his present self, and this shows in his friendships. We want praise but resent the one who gives it, and a friend's love makes us feel our own faults. A person grows as he loses friends who cannot follow him and gains better ones.

The speaker, walking alone in the woods, reflects that he should stop treating his friends as objects of worship. Even people called great have short, limited powers, and no personal attachment is worth giving up the spiritual state we could have. Such attachments trade away something far greater for brief, restless pleasure.

Emerson says that people stop interesting us once we see their limits. In his view, limitation is the only fault, and once we find a person's limits, we lose interest, however talented or knowledgeable they are. A person who seemed like a great hope yesterday can seem ordinary today.

Each deeper step of thought shows that seemingly conflicting facts or opinions are really two ends of one underlying principle. For example, Aristotle, usually seen as Plato's rival, is shown to share Plato's outlook. There is always a still higher view to reach.

A new thinker, or a new general idea, can upset everything people trust, including science, fame, hopes, religion and morals. Emerson says such a broad idea is a fresh flow of the divine into the mind, which is why it brings a thrill.

Real courage is the ability to recover from challenge, so that no one can outflank or outmaneuver a person wherever he stands. This rests on preferring truth to one's past understanding of it, and accepting new truth from any source, even though one's laws, society, religion and world may be replaced and fall away.

Emerson describes stages in how a person comes to accept idealism, the view that the mind and spirit are the basic reality. At first it is a game of ideas, then something that seems partly true, and finally something that must be true and guides how one lives. The last stage holds that God exists, dwells in the self, and that everything else is a shadow of him.

Emerson argues that the world as we see it comes from ideas in people's minds. Berkeley's view that reality depends on the mind is, in his eyes, a rough form of a deeper truth: that nature is the continuing outflow of goodness. History and the state of the world, he says, follow from the ideas people hold at a given time, much as a tree bears apples.

In conversation, people briefly break out of ordinary silence and reach a higher mood, like a sudden burst of inspiration. The speaker says they will soon slip back to their old habits, but the moment is worth enjoying while it lasts.

Each new speaker seems to free us from the last one, only to dominate us with his own ideas, and then a further speaker frees us in turn. Each time, we feel we regain our rights and become fully human. Emerson also says that every truth announced seems to carry far-reaching meaning, while ordinary hours feel dull and lifeless.
We are all waiting and empty, though we could be full. Things around us seem to be just ordinary objects, but a sudden insight, which the passage calls a god, makes their meaning clear to us.

Things that once seemed solid and important, such as wealth, climate, and inherited traits, now look different and unstable, as if all settled certainties were shaking. Yet the speaker adds that silence is better than talk, and that long speech shows how far apart the speaker's thought is from the listener's.

Emerson means that when people fully understand each other, words are not needed. If they agreed completely on everything, speech would not even be allowed to happen. The point is that words are only a stand-in for understanding that is missing.

Literature works like a vantage point outside our own time and place. Studying old works, such as Greek or Roman ones, lets us see our present world more clearly, just as an astronomer needs a distant base line to measure a star's position. A thing is hard to judge from inside it.

Emerson says that poetry holds more truth and wisdom than encyclopaedias or theology books. A poet's bold work wakes him from his routine habits and makes him see new possibilities. He then believes again that he can choose a clear course in thought and action.

Emerson says we cannot understand Christianity by studying the catechism, a book of set questions and answers. We may see it more clearly when we are outdoors, in nature, and have stepped away from formal teaching. Only then might we look back at its history with a clearer eye.

Emerson says that young thinkers raised in the Christian church have often valued Paul's line that God will be "all in all." He argues that people naturally move beyond individual persons toward something impersonal and boundless, and they use this verse against narrow-minded dogmatists.

Emerson says nature is made of rings within rings, and its solid-seeming surface is actually shifting. The chemistry, plants, metals and animals that look like they exist for themselves are only means and methods, like words of God, and they pass away as words do.

Emerson says that the familiar rule "like draws to like," which scientists see in atoms and chemical attraction, is only a partial version of a deeper law. He holds that friends and facts come to a person not through hidden channels but from the soul itself.

Emerson says that every virtue is overtaken by a higher one, the way a lesser light is outshone by a brighter one. A great person will not be prudent in the ordinary sense, since worldly caution takes away from greatness. Prudence may be given up only for a higher purpose; if it is given up for comfort, it is better to remain prudent.

Geoffrey wears boots in the woods to protect his feet from snakes, while Aaron never worries about such danger, and neither is harmed in many years. Emerson suggests that every precaution against an evil places you under its power. So the highest wisdom may be the same as the lowest.

Emerson says we often slip back into small, narrow calculations before we settle into a larger, higher feeling. He adds that even the boldest such feeling is known to ordinary people, who express it in sayings like "Blessed be nothing" and "The worse things are, the better they are."

Emerson argues that each person judges justice, beauty and wisdom from their own viewpoint, so one person's justice can look like another's injustice. He gives the example of a man who thinks paying debts is the highest duty, while another man sees larger debts, such as those owed to the poor, to thought and to nature.

Emerson argues that his duties are many, including love, faith, and the striving of the soul, so he will not devote all his energy to paying money debts. He trusts that his growing character will settle those debts in time, without wronging his higher obligations.

No virtue is ever the last word; every virtue is only a starting point. Emerson means that the good habits society praises can be as much in the way of growth as vices are, so that real reform may mean giving up even what we have always thought of as virtues.

In moments of strong spiritual feeling, Emerson says, the sense of guilt over wasted days disappears. In such moments he stops measuring his life by the time left, because the mind feels able to do whatever work is needed, regardless of how much time there is.

An imagined reader accuses the writer of having reached a Pyrrhonism, a doctrine that all actions are equal and nothing can be known for sure. The reader says the writer thinks that even crimes, if done honestly, can become parts of a true temple.

Emerson says he is glad to see sweetness spread through plants, and also glad to see goodness flood into every gap that selfishness leaves, even into selfishness and sin. So no evil is entirely pure, and even hell has some pleasures.

Emerson says he is only trying things out, not declaring what is true or false. He does not treat any fact as sacred or as unholy, and he questions everything. He presents himself as a seeker who has no fixed tradition behind him.

Movement and change can only be noticed against something that stays fixed in the soul. While creation keeps producing new circles, the source of them stays unchanged. That central life is greater than creation, knowledge and thought, and it keeps trying to make something as large as itself, but each thing made only shows how to make a better one.

Nature is always renewing itself, and the old is something to be thrown off. Emerson says that many human failings, such as fever, crime and stupidity, are really forms of old age, meaning rest, clinging to habit and inertia. He adds that by staying in contact with what is higher, a person does not grow old but grows young.

Emerson contrasts the open, eager mind of childhood with the closed, settled mind of old age. He says older people often stop hoping, claim to know everything, and accept things as they are. He argues that they can regain hope and power by becoming receptive again, through love and seeing truth, and that this decline need not happen.

Emerson says that nature is always new, the past fades, and only what is coming is sacred. Nothing lasts except life and change, so no vow or truth can be held fixed forever. He adds that people want to feel settled, yet they can only hope for growth while they remain unsettled.

Emerson says we cannot predict the moods, pleasures, or powers we will have tomorrow, because the deepest growth of the soul is hidden and unpredictable. Routine and sensory matters can be roughly known, but we can know truth is divine and helpful without knowing how it will help us. Knowing it comes only through becoming it.

A person who moves forward into a new stage keeps the strength of the old, but feels it as fresh. He says he drops all the knowledge he had gathered before, because it now seems empty. Real understanding of simple words, he suggests, comes only through love and aspiration.

Emerson says talent is skill at working within familiar routines, while character is the power and courage to open new paths toward better aims. A person of strong character makes others see that more is possible than they thought, and makes single events seem less important, since such a person finds hard things easy.

A great person is not easily shaken, and events pass over without much effect. Boasting about having overcome misfortune does not count if the misfortune is still remembered. True victory is when the disaster fades into a small, unimportant cloud in a much larger history.

We most want to forget ourselves, to be startled out of our usual manners and habits, and to act without knowing how or why. Emerson calls this drawing a new circle. He says great achievements come from enthusiasm and from giving oneself up.

Emerson quotes Cromwell saying that a man rises highest when he does not know where he is going. He argues that dreams, drink, opium, gambling and war imitate this inspired state without real insight, which is why people are drawn to them. The poem that follows, "Intellect," asks thought to reach its goals and scatter seed that becomes souls.

Thoreau says he wrote most of this book while living alone in a house he built himself, in the woods near Walden Pond, supporting himself only by his own manual work. He lived there for two years and two months, and he is now back in ordinary town life.

Thoreau explains that his townsmen have asked him very personal questions about how he lives at Walden. They ask what he eats, whether he feels lonely or afraid, how much of his income he gives to charity, and how many poor children he supports. He says these questions seem natural to him, given his circumstances.

Thoreau asks readers who are not interested in him to excuse his use of "I" throughout the book. Most books leave out the first person, but this one keeps it. He says he talks about himself only because he knows no one else as well, and his experience is narrow.

Thoreau says he wants every writer to give a plain, honest account of his own life, not just repeat what he has heard about others. He adds that readers should take only the parts that fit them, as a coat fits one person and not another.

Thoreau says he wants to talk less about distant peoples and more about the people of New England, especially their outward living conditions. He asks whether those conditions must be as bad as they are, and whether they could be improved. He says that in Concord he sees people in shops, offices and fields suffering in many odd ways, as if doing penance.

Thoreau lists extreme penances that he has heard Brahmins, members of the Hindu priestly class, perform. These include sitting between fires, hanging upside down over flames, twisting the neck until only liquid can be swallowed, chaining oneself to a tree, and crawling the length of large empires with the body.

Thoreau says his neighbors work harder and more endlessly than the legendary tasks of Hercules, or the self-punishing feats of ascetics who stand on pillars. Hercules' twelve labors had an end, but his neighbors finish nothing. Like the hydra, every problem they defeat is replaced by two more.

Thoreau says that young men who inherit farms and property are burdened by them, since such things are harder to shed than to acquire. He wishes they had been raised outside society so they could see clearly what work they should do. He asks why they should be tied to the land and consume it, and why they should start their own ruin from birth.

Thoreau says many people struggle through life weighed down by their possessions, such as a large barn and a farm they inherited. He notes that people with nothing to inherit have enough work just taking care of their own bodies.

Thoreau says people work under a mistake: their best part gets worn down by labor, driven by what they call necessity. He compares their lives to hoarding treasure that decay and thieves can destroy, and calls such a life foolish. He adds that men born from stones, as in the old Greek myth, are hard and used to toil.

Thoreau says most people, through ignorance and mistake, spend their lives on needless cares and heavy work, so they cannot gather life's finer rewards. Laborers in particular have no time for steady honesty or real relations with others, and they become little more than machines.

Thoreau argues that people who constantly rely on what they already know cannot easily keep the humility that growth needs. He says we should sometimes give others care freely, as a gift, before judging them. He compares our finest qualities to fruit bloom, which needs gentle handling, and notes that we do not treat ourselves or each other that gently.

Thoreau tells his readers that many of them are poor and struggling to pay for food and clothes. He claims that some are reading his book while putting off debts, using time they have not paid for. He says he can see this clearly from his own experience of how people live.

Thoreau describes people who are always close to ruin, forever trying to start business and escape debt. He says they live and die under debts owed to others, always promising payment tomorrow and dying insolvent, while chasing customers and favor by any means short of crime. The Latin phrase "æs alienum," meaning "another's brass," is the old name for debt.

Thoreau lists ways people work to earn money: lying, flattering, voting, putting on forced politeness or false generosity, and making themselves ill with overwork. They do this to win customers and to save money for a future sickness, hiding it in a chest, a stocking, or a bank.

Thoreau says it is odd that people focus on slavery in the South, which he calls a foreign and gross form of servitude, when many subtle masters enslave people in both North and South. The worst master, he says, is the one who drives himself. He then asks whether the ordinary teamster on the road shows any divine spark within him.

Thoreau mocks the idea that a man's highest duty is ordinary work, like caring for horses, or that his fate matters less than business interests. He says people act as if they were small and fearful, slaves to their own opinion of themselves and their reputation. In his view, a person's own private opinion of himself binds him more than public opinion does.

A person's fate is shown by what he believes about himself, and freeing the mind is something a man must do for himself, as no outside reformer can do it for him. Thoreau also mocks people who fill their time with trivial work, saying that wasting time harms the soul.

Most people live with a quiet, hidden despair. Thoreau says that accepting this situation only confirms the despair, and that even games and amusements hide it, since they come after work and are not true play. Wisdom, he adds, means not doing desperate things.

Thoreau argues that people seem to have chosen their ordinary way of life on purpose, yet they honestly believe they have no other option. Healthy, alert minds can still see that new possibilities exist, and no old way of thinking should be trusted without testing it first.

Thoreau argues that what people accept as true today may later prove false, like smoke mistaken for a rain cloud. He says that what older people claim cannot be done often can be done, and that each generation needs its own deeds. He notes that old people once lacked knowledge that new people now have.

Thoreau argues that old age does not make a person a better teacher than youth. Life has taken more from the old than it has given them, so even the wisest may have learned little of lasting value. Older people, he says, have little useful advice for the young, since their own experience was narrow and their lives feel like failures to them. Any faith they still keep may contradict that experience, so they are only less young than before.

The speaker says that after thirty years he has never received useful advice from his elders. He feels they cannot teach him anything relevant, because their own experience of life does not help him. Whatever he has learned that he values, his elders never mentioned it.

A farmer argues that a diet of plants cannot build bones, so he eats animal food to get what bones need. Thoreau points out that his own oxen, fed only on plants, have strong bones and pull the plough. He concludes that what counts as a necessity depends on a person's circumstances: what is essential for the weak and sick may be a luxury for others, or unknown to them.

Some people feel that earlier generations have already covered every part of human life, down to the smallest details. Thoreau gives examples: Solomon's rules about how far apart trees should be planted, Roman judges' rulings on gathering fallen acorns from a neighbor's land, and Hippocrates' advice on cutting nails.

Thoreau argues that boredom and weariness are old human complaints, but no one has yet measured what people can do. Past experience is no guide, because so little has been tried. He ends by quoting a saying that tells a person not to grieve over past failures, since no one can say what they have left undone.

Thoreau suggests that his life could be measured against simple tests, such as the fact that the same sun that ripens his beans also lights other worlds like Earth. He admits that remembering this would have saved him some mistakes, since he did not see his work in that wider light. He ends by wondering how different beings across the universe may be looking at the same star at the same moment.

Every person's nature and life differ, so no one can say what life looks like to another. Thoreau says it would be a miracle to see through another person's eyes for a moment, and that doing so would teach us more than history, poetry or myth.

Thoreau says that most of what his neighbors call good seems bad to him, and that he regrets his own good behavior more than anything. He hears an inner voice pulling him away from conventional life, even against the advice of older, respected people. He adds that each generation drops the projects of the one before, like abandoned ships.

Thoreau argues that we can trust the world more than we do and need not guard ourselves so anxiously. He notes that we overrate our own work, that nature suits our weakness as well as our strength, and that we are constantly on guard, yet at night we reluctantly pray and place ourselves in uncertain hands.

Thoreau says people feel forced to live in one fixed way and treat that way as the only one, yet many other ways are possible. Change looks miraculous, but it happens constantly. When someone turns an idea of the imagination into a settled fact of understanding, Thoreau expects others eventually to base their lives on it too.

Thoreau suggests that it would help to see what people truly need to survive, such as by living a simple frontier life or by checking old merchants' records of what they bought. He argues that human existence has changed little over the ages, since people's basic nature and needs remain the same.

Thoreau defines "necessary of life" as anything people obtain by their own effort that has become so important that almost no one, whether savage, poor, or philosophical, goes without it. Animals need only food, and some also need shelter, such as the bison seeking forest or mountain shade.

Thoreau says that food, shelter, clothing and fuel are the basic needs of life in a cold climate. Only after these are secured can a person turn to the deeper questions of life. He suggests that the need to sit by a fire began as a luxury from the discovery of warmth and became a necessity, as it has for cats and dogs.

Thoreau argues that shelter, clothing and fire only keep in the body's own warmth when they are used in the right amount. Once the outside heat is greater than the body's own heat, he suggests, the process has become cooking, not keeping warm. He backs this with Darwin's report that naked people in Tierra del Fuego sweated while sitting farther from a fire than Darwin's well-clothed party, who were not too warm.

Thoreau asks whether the toughness of people who go naked in the cold could be joined with the mental skill of civilized people. He describes a scientist's view that the body works like a stove, with food as fuel that keeps the inner burning going.

Thoreau argues that "animal life" and "animal heat" mean nearly the same thing. Food acts as fuel that keeps the body's inner fire going, while fuel, shelter and clothing only prepare food or keep in the heat the body makes.

Thoreau says the basic need of the body is to keep warm and hold on to its inner heat. People go to great lengths for this, even stuffing their beds with feathers and down taken from birds, much as a mole lines its burrow with grass and leaves. He notes that the poor complain about a cold world, and that much of our suffering is traced to cold, both physical and social.

In warm climates, summer makes a kind of paradise-like life possible. Little fuel is needed, since the sun cooks some food, and food is easier to get and more varied, while clothing and shelter are needed far less. The sentence breaks off before saying what Thoreau finds sufficient in his own country.

Thoreau says that books, lamps and paper are cheap and count as basic needs for a student. He criticises people who travel to distant, dangerous lands to trade for decades just to stay warm, and then die at home in New England. The very rich, he adds, are not merely warm but overheated, as if cooked.

Most luxuries and many so-called comforts are not needed, and can even hold people back from rising to a higher life. The wisest people have lived more simply than the poor, and the ancient philosophers were poor in possessions but rich in inner life.

Thoreau says that only a person living in voluntary poverty can judge human life fairly, since a luxurious life produces luxurious results in farming, trade, writing and art. He adds that today there are teachers of philosophy but few real philosophers, though teaching it is admirable because philosophy was once a way of life.

To be a philosopher, for Thoreau, means living by wisdom in daily life: simply, independently, generously and with trust. Clever thinking or founding a school is not enough. He says most famous scholars only succeed by fitting in with society, and so they do not produce a better kind of person.

Thoreau asks why people and families decline, and whether luxury, which weakens nations, is present in his own life too. He argues that a philosopher, living ahead of his time, cannot live as others do, and must keep his body strong by better means than ordinary people use.

Once a man has the basic necessities of warmth, food and shelter, Thoreau says he should not keep chasing luxuries. Instead he should begin to live in earnest, since the hard work of getting by is done. He compares this to a seed whose roots have taken hold, so it can now safely grow upward.

Thoreau argues that people put down roots in the earth so they can grow upward toward heaven, much as nobler plants bear their fruit high in air and light. Humbler vegetables are grown only for their roots and are cut down before they flower, so their flowers are hardly ever seen.

Thoreau says he is not trying to set rules for two groups. The first is people with strong, brave natures who manage their own affairs and spend freely without ruin. The second is people who find encouragement in the present state of things and love it, and he counts himself among them.

Thoreau says he is not addressing people who are well employed, since they already know it. He is speaking to discontented people who complain about their lot or the times instead of improving them. He also means wealthy people who have piled up possessions they do not know how to use, and so have bound themselves with their own chains.

Thoreau says that if he tried to describe the way he had wished to spend his life, his readers would be surprised, and people who know nothing about his life would be astonished. He will only hint at a few of the projects he had cherished.

Thoreau says he has always wanted to make good use of each present moment, marking it as if on a notched stick. He describes the present as the point where past and future meet. He admits his work has secrets that are hard to share, but he would gladly tell all he knows.

Thoreau says he lost a hound, a horse and a turtle-dove long ago and is still searching for them. He has told many travellers about them, and a few who claim to have heard or seen them seem as eager to help find them as if the animals were their own.

The narrator describes getting up before dawn, often before his neighbors, to be out early and see the sunrise. He admits he did not help the sun rise, but he thinks it mattered a great deal simply to be there to witness it.

Thoreau describes spending many autumn and winter days outdoors, trying to catch news or meaning carried on the wind. He says the effort cost him a great deal and gained him little. If the news had concerned politics, it would have appeared in the newspaper first. He compares his catches to manna, the bread said to fall from heaven, which melted in the sun.

Thoreau says he worked for a long time as a reporter for a small-circulation journal. The editor rarely printed most of what he wrote, so he received only the labor itself as pay, though he felt the effort was rewarding in its own right.
