Thoreau says that for years he took on jobs no one had asked him for. He watched the weather, and he kept forest paths and shortcuts clear and bridged the ravines, but only where people had already been walking.

Thoreau describes his work as a kind of caretaker of wild things. He watched over stray cattle and the quiet corners of a farm, and he watered wild plants that might have dried up in dry weather. He did not concern himself with the farm's human workers, saying who worked where was not his business.

Thoreau is joking that his neighbors never gave him a town job, even though he did his own affairs faithfully. He says he never got his accounts audited, accepted, or paid, but he does not mind, since he never wanted that reward.

A Native American basket seller offers his wares to a lawyer, who declines. The seller is shocked and asks whether the lawyer means to starve them. He had seen that the lawyer earned wealth and standing by mere words, so he decided to make his living by weaving baskets, as if that were a similar kind of trade.

The speaker describes an Indigenous basket-maker who thought that making the baskets was his whole share of the work, leaving the buyer to decide to purchase them. He had not realized that he had to give the buyer a reason to buy, such as making the baskets worth the buyer's while. The speaker admits that his own baskets had the same flaw: he had never given anyone a reason to buy them.

Thoreau says that although he still thought basket-weaving worth doing, he focused on finding ways to avoid having to sell the baskets, rather than on how to make people want to buy them. He adds that the kind of life society praises as successful is only one kind, and it should not be overvalued at the cost of others.

Thoreau says that since his neighbors offered him no paid position, he had to make his own way. He went to the woods, where he was better known, and decided to start his own project without waiting for money. He went to Walden Pond not to save or spend money, but to carry out his own private work with as few obstacles as possible.

Thoreau says he has always tried to build strict business habits, because every person needs them. He describes a small trading office on the coast, sending out local goods like ice, pine timber and granite, and doing every job himself, from steering the ship to keeping the accounts.

Thoreau is listing the endless duties of a merchant who runs a shipping business. He must read and answer every letter, watch over cargo unloaded day and night, and track ships along the coast, all while keeping goods flowing to a far-off, demanding market. The sentences pile up tasks to show how busy and scattered such a life is.

Thoreau lists the constant tasks a modern person supposedly must keep up with: following market prices, war and peace news, trade trends, and new navigation charts. He warns that even small calculation errors can wreck a ship on a rock, and he mentions the lost explorer La Pérouse as an example of a fate that remains unknown.

Thoreau describes the kind of learning a careful man of business would need: keeping up with all branches of knowledge, studying the lives of explorers and merchants, and regularly checking his accounts to see where he stands. He says that handling profit, loss, interest and measures such as tare and tret takes a broad, general knowledge.

Thoreau jokes that Walden Pond would make a good site for business, since it has a sound foundation and needs no filling of marshes. He adds that building there means driving your own piles, and he compares the risk to St. Petersburg, which is said to be built on unstable Neva marshes that a flood could wipe away.

Thoreau is saying that a person starting this project without ordinary money would still need some means to pay for basic needs, and it is unclear where those would come from. On clothing, he suggests that people often buy it because they like new styles and want approval from others, rather than because it is actually useful.

Clothes exist to keep the body warm and, in society, to cover the body. Thoreau says a person who keeps this in mind can see how much necessary work can be done without buying more clothes. He adds that kings and queens, who wear each suit only once, never know the comfort of clothes that fit, and are no better than wooden horses that hold clean clothes.

Our clothes gradually take on the shape and character of the person who wears them, so that we become reluctant to take them off. Thoreau says a patch does not lower a man in his esteem. He thinks people worry more about clothes looking fashionable and clean than about having a clear conscience. He also names carelessness with money as the worst fault shown in a torn garment.

Thoreau says people fear wearing mended clothes more than they fear real injury. A torn pair of trousers is treated as worse than a broken leg, because people care about looking respectable rather than being truly respectable. He adds that people respond to clothes, not to the person inside them, as a scarecrow dressed in fine clothes would be saluted over a man in shabby ones.

Thoreau notes that a scarecrow-like hat and coat on a stake made him think of the farm's owner, who looked only slightly more weathered than before. He then asks whether people would keep their social rank if they had no clothes, suggesting that clothing may be what signals status.

Thoreau says that people in New England, even in towns that call themselves democratic, respect others mainly for their money and the clothes and carriages that show it. He adds that this respect is so widespread that these people are, in his view, heathen and need a missionary. Madam Pfeiffer's remark about being judged by clothes is his example.

A person who has real work to do does not need new clothes for it; old clothes and even bare feet will do. Only people who attend parties and sit in legislatures need new coats often, because they must keep changing their appearance to suit the company.

Thoreau asks whether old clothes are good enough for worship, and whether worn-out clothes are ever really thrown away or are passed on to poorer people. His point is that before starting any project that needs new clothes, a person should first become a different kind of person, not just buy new things.

Thoreau argues that a person should not buy new clothes until he has changed inwardly, so that he feels like a new man in his old ones. New clothes only suit someone who is already new. Men want not just tasks to do but a way of being, and a new suit should come after that change, not before it.

Thoreau compares a person's periods of change to the moulting of birds and the shedding of skin by snakes and caterpillars. Such change comes from within, through inner growth, and not from outward dress or appearance. Without it, a person pretends to be something he is not and will eventually be judged so by himself and by others.

Thoreau compares clothes to the layers of a plant. Outer clothes are like a thin false skin that can be removed without serious harm. Shirts are like the inner bark, and removing them would kill the person, as stripping a tree's bark around its trunk kills it.

Thoreau says people should dress simply, with few clothes, so they could find their way in the dark. He also says a person should live so lightly that they could leave a besieged town with nothing in hand, as an old philosopher did. He adds that one thick coat does the work of three thin ones.

Thoreau argues that clothing can be bought cheaply, or made at home for little cost, and that a man dressed in such plain clothes, which he earned himself, need not be poor in the eyes of wise people. In his view, such a man would still be respected.

Thoreau describes a tailor who refuses his request for a garment in an unusual form, saying "They do not make them so now," as if an unquestionable authority decided the matter. He wonders who these "They" are and what right they have to decide how he dresses.

Thoreau is mocking the way a seamstress or tailor measures him. She cares only about his shoulders, as if he were a peg for a coat, not about his character. He says people follow fashion blindly, like monkeys copying a leader, and so he doubts that anything simple and honest can be done with other people's help.

Thoreau is saying that people's old, fixed ideas are so hard to remove that even a strong effort to crush them would fail, since some foolish notion always survives and hatches again. He ends with a joke: seeds of wheat kept in an Egyptian mummy still sprouted, so old things can sometimes prove useful.

Thoreau argues that clothing has never become a true art. People simply wear whatever is available, like shipwrecked sailors dressing from the beach. Each generation mocks the fashions of the past while eagerly following its own.

A person's clothing matters less than the sincere, serious character behind it. Without that inner seriousness, any costume looks silly or pitiful, whether it is royal or not. Real feeling gives even plain rags dignity, as when a soldier is wounded.

Thoreau says people chase new fashions in cloth patterns with childish eagerness. Makers know the taste is arbitrary: a pattern differing only by a few threads of color may sell well or sit unsold, and the unsold one may later become fashionable. He adds that tattooing is no more barbarous than this, since fashion too leaves its mark permanently on the wearer.

Thoreau doubts that factories are the best way to make clothing. He says factory workers are increasingly treated as the English workers were, because the real goal is to make companies rich rather than to clothe people well. He adds that people usually achieve what they aim at, so they should aim high even if they fail at first.

Thoreau grants that a shelter is now a necessity, though some people in cold places have gone without one for long periods. He cites a traveler's report that Laplanders (a northern people) sleep on snow in skin clothing and skin bags, and that they are no hardier than other people.

People probably learned early on how useful a house is, and the phrase "domestic comforts" may first have meant the benefits of the house itself rather than of the family. Thoreau adds that in warm climates, where rain and winter are rare, a house is needed only part of the year.

In summer, Thoreau says, a shelter was used mainly as a cover at night. Among Native peoples, a wigwam stood for a day's journey, and a row of them marked how many nights had been spent camping. He argues that people, not being large and strong enough to live openly in the world, shaped their own smaller space and enclosed it with walls.

Thoreau argues that people needed shelter before clothing. Heat, rain and winter would have harmed early humans without a house, so they built one first. He compares this to the Adam and Eve story, where a bower (a leafy shelter) came before clothes, and says a home gave first physical warmth, then emotional comfort.

Thoreau suggests that people first sheltered in rock hollows, and that children still feel the same pull toward caves, rocky overhangs and outdoor play. He presents this childhood urge as an inherited instinct, a leftover from our earliest ancestors.

Thoreau traces how people have moved from caves to houses built of many materials, and he suggests we have lost touch with living in the open air. He argues that people would do well to spend more time outdoors, under the stars, rather than under roofs. He compares this to birds that do not sing in caves and doves that do not keep their innocence in dovecots.

Thoreau warns that anyone building a house should be careful, or the house may become a trap, a tomb, or a prison. He suggests first asking how little shelter is really needed, and points to Penobscot Indians who lived in thin cotton tents in deep snow and would have welcomed more snow to block the wind.

Thoreau recalls that when he worried about earning an honest living while keeping time for his own pursuits, he noticed a large tool box by the railroad. He imagined that a poor man could buy such a box for a dollar, bore air holes in it, and live inside it, free in his personal life and soul.

Thoreau argues that a small, simple dwelling is better than a large, costly one. Many people work themselves to exhaustion paying rent on a bigger house than they need, when a plain shelter like his would keep them warm. He adds that economy, or careful management of resources, is a serious matter and cannot be dismissed as a joke.

Gookin, a colonial official who oversaw the Native peoples of the Massachusetts Colony, reports that their houses were well built, tight and warm. He says the best were covered with bark and the cheaper ones with woven bulrush mats, and that he found the wigwams as warm as the best English houses.

Thoreau describes Native American lodges, which were lined with embroidered mats and fitted with tools and household items. A mat hung over the roof opening could be moved by a string to control the wind. Such a lodge could be built in a day or two and taken down and set up again in a few hours, and each family had one or a part of one.
In Thoreau's view, people in simple societies nearly all have a decent shelter, while in modern civilized society at most half of families own one. In big cities, owning a shelter is rare.

Thoreau argues that a house costs so much to rent or buy in civilized society that people cannot afford to own one and must rent instead, and renting does not get them ahead in the long run. He contrasts this with the "savage," who owns a simple shelter because it costs very little. Renting here means paying a yearly sum for housing.

Thoreau is recording an objection: a poor civilized man pays rent, but in return gets a house far better than a savage's. For that rent he receives the accumulated improvements of centuries, such as spacious rooms, paint, fireplaces, blinds and a pump.

Thoreau asks why people called civilized are often poor, while people without civilization's comforts seem rich in their own way. He argues that civilization only counts as progress if better homes can be had without costing more. He defines cost as the amount of life a person must trade for a thing, now or later.

Thoreau argues that buying a house costs so much labor that a worker would spend more than half his life earning it, and renting is no better, since both are a poor choice. He asks whether a savage would be wise to trade his simple wigwam for such a costly palace.

Thoreau suggests that, for a single person, the main use of spare possessions saved for the future is paying for a funeral. He adds, with some irony, that a man is not really required to bury himself, and he treats this as a key difference between civilized people and savages.

Thoreau says that in a civilized society the individual's life is largely taken up by the institution, so that the race as a whole can be preserved and improved. He claims this benefit comes at a high cost, and suggests people might gain the benefit without that cost.

Thoreau quotes Bible verses that reject two sayings: that the poor will always be with us, and that children suffer for their fathers' sins. He cites God's words that no one will use the sour-grapes proverb again, and that every soul belongs to God, so each person answers for his own sin.

Thoreau observes that Concord farmers, though as well off as anyone, usually spend decades working to own their farms outright. Many inherited their farms with debts or bought them with borrowed money, and they still have not finished paying for their houses.

Farms often carry so much debt that they become a burden, yet heirs still take them on. Thoreau says that almost no one in town owns a farm outright, and that a farm's real history can be learned from the bank holding its mortgage. He adds that a man who has paid for his farm through his own labor is so rare that everyone knows him.

Thoreau says that very few farmers in Concord succeed, just as most merchants fail. He quotes a merchant who argues that many business failures are not really about money. They happen when men break their promises because keeping them is inconvenient, which means their moral character gives way.

Thoreau is saying that the "three" people he has just mentioned, presumably those who can pay their debts, may be in worse financial and moral trouble than honest bankrupts. He adds that failure and debt drive much of civilization forward, while the poor savage is held back by hunger. Yet the county fair goes on cheerfully each year, as if farming were running smoothly.

The farmer tries to earn a living through schemes more complicated than the problem they solve. He gets a little money, such as for shoestrings, by trading in cattle, and the trap he sets for comfort and independence catches him instead. In the same way, people stay poor in basic comforts even while surrounded by luxuries.

Thoreau argues that a house can end up owning its owner. He says a house is so hard to move that people are trapped in it, and the neighborhood they most need to escape is themselves. He notes families who have wanted to sell and move for a generation but cannot, until death frees them.

Thoreau argues that although civilization has made houses better, it has not made people better in the same way. It has built palaces but not noble men. So if civilized people spend their lives on basic needs, as savages do, he asks why they should have a better home.

Thoreau argues that gains in comfort for some people come at the cost of others. The rich live in palaces while the poor end up in almshouses, and workers who built grand monuments lived on garlic and were not properly buried. Their own homes were sometimes worse than a Native American's wigwam.

Thoreau says that a country with the usual signs of civilization can still have many poor people who live as badly as savages. He points to the shanties beside the railroads as evidence, and he is speaking of the poor, not the rich.

Thoreau describes poor people he sees on his walks who live in pig-pen-like shelters with open doors for light and no visible woodpile, so their bodies and abilities are stunted by constant shrinking from cold and hardship. He says this is true of the workers in England, which he calls the world's great workhouse, the people whose labor makes the age's achievements possible.

Thoreau argues that Irish poverty shows that a nation can be called civilized and still live in great squalor. He says the Irish are worse off than people he calls savages, such as Native Americans, and he doubts their rulers are less wise than others. He also points to enslaved laborers in the Southern States, whom he describes as a product of the South like its exports.

Many people never stop to think about what a house really is, and so they stay poor all their lives trying to own the kind of house their neighbors have. Thoreau compares this to buying a crown when a simple hat would do. He adds that even a more luxurious house than any now built is one no one could afford.

Thoreau asks whether people should always strive for more possessions instead of sometimes being satisfied with less. He mocks respected citizens who teach young men to collect useless things such as extra shoes, umbrellas and empty guest rooms. He asks why our furniture should not be as plain as that of Arabs or Native Americans.

Thoreau says that the great teachers humanity honours as gifts from heaven did not travel with piles of fashionable furniture. He then mocks the idea that people who are morally and intellectually superior should need more elaborate furniture than others, such as the Arab he mentions.

Thoreau says that houses fill up with clutter that must be swept out every morning, and he asks what a person's real morning work should be. He describes dusting three stones on his desk, then throwing them out because his mind was still full of dust and needed more attention. He asks how he could ever have a furnished house, meaning a mind that is properly furnished.

Thoreau says that the rich and self-indulgent set the fashions that ordinary people copy. A traveller who stays at the grand hotels finds this out, because the innkeepers assume he is a pleasure-seeker like the legendary Assyrian king Sardanapalus, and would weaken him if he accepted their service.

Thoreau says that railroad travelers spend too much on luxury and too little on safety and comfort, so their cars end up no better than fancy parlors full of cushions and ornaments. He would prefer a simple seat to be alone than a soft cushion among a crowd.

Thoreau says he would prefer to travel slowly on earth in a simple ox cart, where the air moves freely, than to reach heaven in a fancy train car while breathing bad, poisonous air. He values a free and healthy way of living over a fashionable or easy route to a better place.

Thoreau says that in early times people lived simply and stayed free to move on, like travelers camping in nature. Now, he claims, people have become slaves to their tools: the man who once picked fruit when hungry is now a farmer, and the man who sheltered under a tree is now a householder.

Thoreau says people have stopped living as temporary travelers and have settled down on earth, forgetting heaven. Religion has become a tool for improving worldly life, and houses are built for this world while graves serve the next. Great art, he says, tries to free people from this state, but in practice it only makes earthly life more comfortable and the higher life easier to forget.

Thoreau says the village has no room for fine art, because its houses and streets have no fitting place to display it, with no nail for a picture or shelf for a bust. He suggests the houses are so shakily built and financed that the floor might collapse under a visitor admiring cheap ornaments, dropping him toward the cellar and a more solid base.

Thoreau says that the so-called rich and refined life is a kind of leap that people make, and that he cannot enjoy the fine arts that decorate it because he keeps watching the leap. Even the best human jump lands back on the ground after about twenty-five feet, so he asks the owner of such a life what is holding him up.

Thoreau argues that people should first secure a simple, solid way of living before filling their homes with decorative things. Ornaments placed before that foundation are like a cart before a horse. He adds that a love of beauty grows best outdoors, away from houses and their furnishings.

Thoreau quotes an early settler's account of Concord's first colonists. They lived first in holes dug into hillsides, roofed with earth and timber, and kept smoky fires. They did not build proper houses until the land produced enough food, and the first harvest was so poor that they had to make their bread very thin for a long time.

The passage describes how early settlers in New Netherland and New England, lacking money for proper farmhouses, first lived in a dug-out pit. They dug a square hole several feet deep, lined its walls with wood, and covered the wood with bark so the earth would not collapse.

Thoreau describes how early New England settlers, including wealthy and leading men, first built their homes. They dug a cellar, floored it with planks, lined it, and roofed it with spars covered in bark or sod, so families could live dry and warm there for several years. The passage breaks off before giving the two reasons for this practice.

Thoreau is describing how early settlers in a new country first built plain, simple shelters so they would not waste time or go hungry. Later, once the land was farmed, they built fine houses, and the passage notes that they spent several thousand on them.

Thoreau argues that people should first meet their basic, pressing needs before spending on luxury. He says the country is not yet ready for refined living, so he hesitates to buy a fine house. He wants a house's beauty to be inside, near daily life, like a shell, not piled on as decoration, and he finds that most fine houses fall short of this.

Although people could still live in caves, wigwams or animal skins, Thoreau says it is better to use the benefits that human invention and labor have produced, even though they cost a great deal. In his local area, boards, bricks and similar building materials are cheaper and easier to get than caves, logs, bark or clay.

Thoreau says he knows his subject both from study and from practice. He argues that with more cleverness, people could use the materials of the world to become richer than today's rich and make civilization a blessing. He calls the civilized man a wiser, more experienced savage, then turns to his own experiment.

Thoreau describes starting to build his house by borrowing an axe and cutting young pine trees near Walden Pond in March 1845. He says borrowing is a generous way to let others share in his project. He returned the axe sharper than he received it.

Thoreau describes a spring day while he works on a wooded hillside above Walden Pond. The ice on the pond is breaking up, and a few snow flurries fall now and then. On his walk home, the sand heap and railroad rails shine in the sun, and he hears birds returning for the new year.

Thoreau describes spring thawing both the earth and people's stiff, dormant lives. He watches a striped snake lie still on a pond bottom, apparently unharmed, and suggests it stays there because it has not fully woken from its winter sleep. He then says men, for the same reason, remain in their low, primitive state.

Thoreau says that if people felt the force of spring, they would be moved to a higher, more refined way of living. He describes snakes stiff with cold, waiting for the sun, and a lost goose calling through the fog after an April rain.

Thoreau is working alone in the woods, cutting timber with a small axe, and his mind is not busy with learned ideas. He sings a verse saying that people claim to know much, but their arts, sciences and tools have flown away, and the only thing anyone truly knows is the wind.

Thoreau describes how he shaped the timbers for his cabin by hand. He squared the main beams, trimmed some sides and left the bark on others, which he says kept them straight and made them stronger than sawn wood. He also cut the joints himself with borrowed tools.

The narrator eats his lunch at noon among the pine branches he has cut down, and his bread takes on their smell while his hands get covered in sticky pitch. By working with the trees he comes to feel friendlier toward them, even though he has cut some down.

Thoreau describes buying an old shanty from James Collins, an Irish railroad worker, to use its boards for his own house, which is now framed and ready to be raised. He walks around Collins's shanty, which is small, low, and has a peaked roof, with its walls banked by earth.

The narrator is being shown around a run-down house. The roof is sound but worn, there is no door sill, hens walk in under the door, and the floor is mostly dirt, damp and unhealthy. The woman of the house lights a lamp to show him the roof, walls, and a hole under the floor that he must not step into.

Thoreau describes a small, poor house he is buying from a man named James. The house has few furnishings, including a stove, a bed, a silk parasol and a coffee mill nailed to a sapling. Thoreau agrees to pay four dollars and twenty-five cents, and James will move out the next morning.

A man advises the narrator to arrive early at a place, to get ahead of vague but unfair claims over ground rent and fuel, which he calls the only burden. Later the narrator sees him leaving with his family and all their belongings. Their cat runs off to the woods, becomes wild, and is later found dead in a trap.

Thoreau describes taking apart his cabin and carting the boards to the pond to dry in the sun. An Irish neighbor, Seeley, pocketed the usable nails while watching, and Thoreau jokingly casts him as a idle onlooker who makes the moving of the house seem as grand as the carrying off of the gods of Troy.

Thoreau describes digging a small cellar into a south-facing hillside, down to dry sand where potatoes would not freeze. He left the walls unlined, and the sand has held its shape because the sun never reached it. The whole job took two hours.

Thoreau enjoyed digging the ground because people everywhere dig into the earth to keep a steady temperature. Even under the grandest city house, the old root cellar remains, and long after the house is gone its hollow stays in the ground. He suggests that a house is little more than a porch at the entrance to a burrow.

In early May, Thoreau put up the frame of his house with help from friends. He says he did it mainly to enjoy their neighborly company, not because he needed the help. He honors them and hopes they will help raise bigger buildings someday.

Thoreau moved into his house on July 4th, as soon as its walls and roof were up, since the carefully fitted boards kept out rain. Before the boards went on, he began a chimney foundation at one end, carrying stones up from the pond by hand.

Before cold weather made a indoor fire necessary, Thoreau cooked outdoors on the ground in the early morning, a method he still thinks is in some ways better than the usual one. When a storm came, he propped boards over the fire and sat beneath them, enjoying the time while his bread baked.

When Thoreau's hands were busy with work, he read little, but even small scraps of paper lying around, such as the wrapping of his pen-holder or his tablecloth, gave him as much pleasure and served the same purpose for him as Homer's Iliad, a long epic poem.

Thoreau suggests that people should build more carefully, asking what each part of a house, such as a door or cellar, really means for human nature, and not raising walls merely to meet immediate needs. He compares a man building his own house to a bird building its own nest, as something fitting and natural.

Thoreau suggests that if people built their own homes and grew or earned their own simple food, creative skill would be widespread, as birds sing naturally when they build their own nests. He says people instead act like cowbirds and cuckoos, which leave their eggs in other birds' nests, and he asks whether we must leave the joy of building entirely to carpenters.

Thoreau says that most people never build their own homes, which he finds odd, since building a house is a simple and natural task. He argues that people have become too divided into specialized jobs, so that each person does only a small part of life, like the tailor, preacher, merchant, or farmer. He asks what this division is for. He also holds that others may think for him, but that this does not mean he should stop thinking for himself.

Thoreau says an American architect wanted decorations to rest on real need and truth, so that their beauty would come from that. Thoreau thinks this is only slightly better than shallow amateur taste, because the architect started with the decoration at the top rather than the structure underneath.

Thoreau says that people have focused on decorating the outside of their lives, like putting a seed inside a sugar coating, instead of building the inner self truly and letting outward decoration follow. He argues that real ornament grows from within, as a tortoise's shell or a shell's pearly colors do, not from a deal like the one behind Broadway's church.

A person's house style should matter no more to him than a tortoise's shell does to the tortoise, and a soldier need not paint his virtue on his flag, because the enemy will test it in battle. Thoreau says that a man who hides a half truth in fine words is whispering to people who already know better.

Thoreau says that real architectural beauty grows from the inside out, shaped by the needs and character of the people who live in a building, not by a wish to look fine. Beauty of this kind follows an unplanned beauty of life. He adds that the most interesting homes are the plain log huts and cottages of poor people.

Thoreau says a building is interesting because of the simple, real lives of the people inside it, not because of its surface decoration. A plain suburban house can be just as appealing if its owner's life is simple and honest and the house is not showy. Most ornaments are hollow and would blow away in a storm without harming the solid structure. People who lack fine luxuries need no fancy architecture.

Thoreau asks what would happen if writers fussed over the decoration of their books as much as church builders fuss over cornices. He says that scholars of fine writing and art make such a fuss over ornament. He mocks the idea that it matters how a man's house of sticks is slanted or painted, unless he builds and paints it with real earnestness.

Thoreau is mocking the idea that a man's house should be painted to match the color of the soil, as if he were choosing his own grave. The "tenant" is the body, and the house is a stand-in for the body, which he says has lost its spirit. He suggests that such a choice is idle, and that a man should simply let his house show his own face.

Before winter, Thoreau built a chimney and covered the sides of his house with shingles. The shingles were rough, sappy boards cut from the outer slice of a log, and he had to plane their edges straight. The walls were already rainproof.

Thoreau describes the small house he built: a shingled and plastered room about ten by fifteen feet, with a loft, a closet, windows, doors and a brick fireplace. He says he will list its exact cost, excluding his own labor, because few people know what their houses cost.

Thoreau lists the materials he has used for his cabin. Apart from timber, stones and sand, which he took by squatter's right (occupying unclaimed land), he says he built a small woodshed from leftover scraps. He also says he plans a future house more splendid than any on Concord's main street, at no greater cost than his present one.

Thoreau claims that a student could get a lifetime shelter for no more than the yearly rent he already pays. He says he boasts for the sake of others, not himself, and admits he may be imperfect, but he will speak freely rather than let false modesty help the devil's case.

Thoreau argues that students at Cambridge pay a high rent for small, noisy rooms, even though the college built many rooms together under one roof. He thinks that with more real wisdom, less schooling would be needed, and the cost of getting an education would largely disappear.

The main point is that the things a student pays for, such as comforts and tuition, cost far more in human effort than they should. The things he most values, like learning from his cultivated peers, are free and are not the things that cost the most money.

Thoreau says colleges are usually built by raising money, then hiring a contractor who uses paid workers to lay the foundations, while the students are supposed to be preparing for the work. He thinks it would be better if the students who wish to benefit from the college built its foundations themselves.

Thoreau argues that a student who avoids all necessary manual work to gain free time gets a worthless kind of leisure, missing the experience that would make it valuable. He does not mean students should swap books for manual labor. He means they should stop playing at life or merely studying it, and live it fully.

Thoreau asks why young people should not learn how to live by actually trying to live, which he thinks would train their minds as well as mathematics does. He criticizes schooling that teaches science and crafts but not the art of living, such as how bread is made or earned.

Thoreau mocks people who study distant things, such as new moons of Neptune or tiny creatures in a drop of vinegar, while ignoring what is near them, like their own faults. He then asks which boy learns more: the one who made his own knife by digging and smelting ore, or the one who attended lectures and was given a ready-made knife. The implied answer is that the boy who did the work himself gains more.

Thoreau says that college teaches subjects like navigation and political economy, but not the practical "economy of living," which he equates with philosophy. As a result, a student can read famous economists while running his family into debt.

Thoreau argues that modern improvements, like new colleges and inventions, do not always bring real progress. He says inventions are often pretty toys that distract people from serious matters. They improve the means of getting somewhere, but not the goal itself, just as railroads only take people to Boston or New York faster.

Thoreau criticizes the rush to build fast communication links, such as a telegraph between Maine and Texas or a tunnel under the Atlantic. He suggests that speed matters more to people than whether they have anything worth saying. He compares this to a man who has nothing to say to a deaf woman once they are introduced.

Thoreau is mocking the idea that speed of communication means important news. Fast news, like a royal illness reported across the country, is trivial, and the fastest horse, Flying Childers, never did ordinary useful work such as carrying grain to the mill.

Thoreau argues that walking is faster than taking the train. A train ticket to Fitchburg costs about a day's wages, while he can walk the thirty miles in a day and arrive first. He says he has often travelled this way for whole weeks.

Thoreau is describing a traveler who takes the train to get somewhere, and he says that by staying put and working locally he would get ahead of that traveler. Even if the railroad circled the globe, he claims he would arrive first, and the traveler would gain no real experience of the country.

Thoreau says that building railroads everywhere would be like levelling the whole earth, and that no one can escape the cost of such work. He suggests that people wrongly hope that enough shareholders and labourers will eventually let everyone travel for free, quickly. The sentence breaks off before it says what happens to that hope.

Thoreau is describing the building of a railroad. Once the smoke clears, only a few will be riding while the rest are crushed, and the deaths will be called a melancholy accident. He adds that people who can pay their fare may ride eventually, but by then they will likely have lost the energy and wish to travel.

Thoreau says it is foolish to spend most of one's life earning money so as to enjoy freedom only in the last, least valuable part of it. He compares this to an Englishman who went to India to get rich before living as a poet, when he could have started living that way at once. He also answers Irish railroad workers who ask whether the railroad is good: yes, but only relatively good.

Thoreau planted about two and a half acres of his land with beans and some other vegetables, to earn a little money to pay his extra building costs. He notes the land was poor, and one farmer joked it was good only for raising squirrels.

Thoreau says he did not fertilize his field, since he was only a squatter on the land and did not expect to farm it for long. He cleared tree stumps while ploughing, which gave him firewood, and he burned other dead wood and driftwood from the pond for the rest of his fuel.

Thoreau says that, after counting the crops he grew and the value of what he had left over, he judges his small experiment to have done better than any farmer in Concord that year. He weighs this against the worth of a man's soul and of the present day, and he counts the short, temporary nature of the experiment in its favor.

Thoreau says that after two years of growing his own food, he found that a person who lives simply needs only a few rods of ground. Spading the soil by hand is cheaper than using oxen to plough, and moving to fresh ground is cheaper than manuring old ground. Such work could be done in summer at spare hours.

Thoreau says he is free of the ties that bind a farmer to animals, land and a house. He claims to judge the farming and social arrangements of his day fairly, having no stake in their success or failure. He says he could follow his own unusual inclinations at any moment.
If his house had burned or his crops had failed, he says he would still be nearly as well off as before. He means that his possessions had not made him dependent, so losing them would change little.

Thoreau argues that people who keep herds are not really in control. The herds take a great deal of human labor, so the animals gain more from the arrangement than the owners do. He adds that a nation of true philosophers, living simply, would not use animals for labor, though he doubts such a nation will ever exist.

Thoreau says he would never use a horse or ox to do his work, because he would then become only a horseman or herdsman. He asks whether society's gain from such animal labor is really everyone's gain, since the stable-boy may not share his master's benefit. He also questions whether people could have achieved greater things without that help.

Thoreau argues that when people use their labor for luxury rather than necessity, a few end up serving the strongest, and people end up working for their animal appetites and for the symbols of wealth. As evidence, he notes that a farmer's prosperity is judged by how large his barn is compared with his house.

Thoreau argues that a nation should remember itself through its thinking, not through grand buildings. He says a book like the Bhagavad-Gita matters more than the ruined temples of the East, which were built for rulers. Real genius, he says, does not serve kings or need costly stone.

Nations spend great effort on stone monuments to be remembered, but Thoreau says it would be wiser to polish their manners. One sensible act outlasts a huge monument. He prefers a simple stone wall marking an honest man's field to famous cities like Thebes, which he calls vulgar and misdirected.

Thoreau argues that nations waste their labor on monuments and tombs, which bury the people who build them. He says the Egyptian pyramids show only how many men were made to serve a vain ruler, and that such building, whether a temple or a bank, costs more than it is worth.

Thoreau is mocking the building of grand monuments. He says they are driven by vanity and appetite, not by any higher purpose. He compares them to a foolish digger who tried to tunnel to China and admired nothing in his result, so the speaker sees no reason to admire such monuments either.

Thoreau says many people want to know who built the famous monuments of the East and West. He would rather know who in those days did not build them, since he thinks only those who were above such trivial work were left out.

Thoreau reports what he earned from odd jobs in the village, such as surveying and carpentry, which came to $13.34. He then starts to compare this with what he spent on food over eight months, from July 4 to March 1, though the passage breaks off before giving the total.

Thoreau admits he spent $8.74 on food and says most readers have spent money the same way, so he is not ashamed to print it. The next year he sometimes caught fish and once killed and ate a woodchuck that had raided his beans. He found the meat briefly enjoyable, but decided that eating it regularly would not be a good habit, even though buying meat from the butcher seemed no different.

This sentence is the start of Thoreau's list of his yearly costs at Walden Pond. It lists the money he spent on food, clothes, and similar needs. It ends before giving the total, so the sum itself is not in this fragment.

Thoreau's bookkeeping shows that, after subtracting all his spending from his earnings, he has $25.21¾ left, nearly the same sum he began with. On the other side of the ledger he has gained leisure, independence and health, plus a house he can live in as long as he likes.

Thoreau says that, though his spending figures may seem trivial, they are complete and so worth recording. His food cost about twenty-seven cents a week. For nearly two years it was mostly rye and corn meal, potatoes, rice, a little salt pork, molasses, salt, and water to drink.

Thoreau says it made sense that he lived mostly on rice, since he admired Indian philosophy. He adds that he sometimes ate at other people's houses, which sometimes upset his own household plans, but this does not change the general comparison he has made.

Thoreau reports that from his two years at Walden he learned that getting necessary food takes very little effort, even in this northern climate, and that a person can live on a diet as plain as an animal's and stay healthy and strong. As proof, he describes a satisfying meal of boiled, salted purslane, a wild green he gathered in his cornfield.

A reasonable man, Thoreau asks, needs little more than plain food, such as boiled sweet corn with salt, to be content. He admits that even his small extras were given in to appetite, not to health. He notes that people often go without luxuries rather than necessities, and that one woman blamed her son's death on drinking only water.

Thoreau is discussing food as a matter of cost and household management, not as a matter of health or diet. He adds that a reader would not dare to copy his plain eating unless he had a well-stocked food supply.

Thoreau describes how he made his own bread at his cabin. He first baked plain corn-meal cakes on a board or timber end by the fire, but they tasted smoky and piney. After trying flour, he settled on a mix of rye and corn meal, and he enjoyed tending the small loaves carefully in cold weather.

Thoreau describes making his own bread from grain he grew himself, which he kept fragrant by wrapping it in cloth. He studied the history of bread-making, from early unleavened bread up through the accidental souring of dough that led to leavening, until he arrived at plain, sweet, wholesome bread.

Thoreau describes yeast, the leaven that makes bread rise, which he says some people treat as sacred and which, he jokes, arrived in America on the Mayflower. He got his yeast regularly from the village until one morning he forgot the method and ruined it by scalding it.

Thoreau found that yeast, the leaven used to make bread rise, was not necessary. He stopped using it, despite warnings from housewives and older people, and he was still healthy after a year. He was also glad to avoid carrying a bottle of it, which sometimes burst in his pocket.

Thoreau says it is simpler and more respectable to leave out an ingredient, and that people can adapt to any climate or circumstance. He made his bread without chemical leavening such as sal soda, following an ancient Roman recipe by Cato, which he begins to quote in Latin.

The passage gives a simple recipe for bread: mix meal with water, knead it, shape it, and bake it covered in a kettle, with no yeast added. Thoreau adds that he once went more than a month without any bread at all, because he had no money to buy it.

Thoreau says New Englanders could grow their own grain, yet people in Concord rarely use it for food. Farmers feed their own corn to animals and buy store-bought flour, which is no more healthy and costs more.

Thoreau says he could grow his own grain, grind it by hand, and make sweetener from pumpkins, beets, or maple trees he might plant. Rice, pork, and store-bought sugar would not be needed. He adds a line from an old hymn, the Forefathers' song, to support the point.

Thoreau says that getting salt could be a reason to visit the seashore, or he could go without it and perhaps drink less water. He adds that, as far as he knows, Native Americans never bothered to go and get it.

Thoreau says he could avoid buying food by growing it, and he already had a shelter. He still needed clothing and fuel. His trousers were woven by a farmer's family, which he values more than factory-made cloth. He also notes he could buy an acre of land for about what he paid for the plot he farmed, and he thinks his squatting there added value to the land.

Thoreau says that people who doubt him and ask whether he can live on plain vegetables are really asking about faith, and he would answer that he could live on nails. He welcomes such experiments, like a young man who tried living on raw corn, and thinks the human race has a stake in them.

Thoreau lists the few household items he owned and says all of them were either made by him or paid for in a way he can account for. He mocks the idea that anyone is so poor they must sit on a pumpkin, and says good chairs can be had free from village attics.

Thoreau says he is glad he needs no furniture warehouse to sit or stand. He thinks it shameful to have furniture hauled openly on a cart, since the loads look the same whether the owner is rich or poor. In his view, the more furniture a person owns, the poorer that person is.

Thoreau says that people move house or change their lives only to shed the possessions they have piled up, and that these possessions hold them back like traps. He compares this to a fox or muskrat that gnaws off a leg to escape, and he says that because of such burdens people have lost their flexibility and are often stuck.

Thoreau says that a seer, someone who sees clearly, would notice that a person's possessions drag behind them, even the things they claim to have given up. A man weighed down this way is stuck, unable to get through a narrow gap where his heavy load cannot follow.

Thoreau says that people who seem free of possessions still have some somewhere, like things stored in a barn, so they are caught up in them. He compares England to an old gentleman weighed down by useless baggage he cannot bring himself to get rid of. He concludes that a person burdened this way cannot easily move, so he would advise a sick man to drop his bed and run.

Thoreau pities a poor immigrant carrying all his belongings, not because he owns so little, but because he has so much to carry. He compares possessions to a heavy trap that can injure its holder. The safest course, he suggests, is never to get caught in it at all.

Thoreau says he needs no curtains, since only the sun and moon look in, and he is happy for them to do so. He would rather use shade from nature than add household items, and he declines a mat so he has less to care for. He concludes that it is best to avoid the start of trouble.

Thoreau describes the household junk of a dead man, including an old dried tapeworm, which was not destroyed but sold at an auction. The neighbors bought it all and stored it in their own attics, where it will sit until their own estates are settled. The point is that people keep accumulating possessions and passing them on rather than getting rid of them.

Thoreau suggests that some so-called savage nations do something worth copying: they hold a yearly renewal ceremony, which he compares to a snake shedding its skin. He asks whether modern people should hold a similar feast of first fruits, as the Mucclasse Indians did according to the naturalist William Bartram.

The passage describes a ceremony in which a town gets rid of its old clothes, goods and food by burning them, cleans itself, puts out all its fires, and fasts for three days. During the fast, people give up every appetite and desire. The speaker presents this as a custom of a people he is reporting on.

Thoreau describes a ceremony in which people put out old fires and kindle new ones from a single fire made by a priest rubbing dry wood. The celebration follows with feasting, dancing, and visits from neighboring towns. He notes that the Mexicans held a similar purification every fifty-two years, believing the world might end then.

Thoreau says he has hardly heard of a truer sacrament, meaning an outward sign of an inward spiritual grace, than the custom he has just described. He believes it was first inspired directly by Heaven, though the Bible does not record that revelation.

Thoreau says that by working about six weeks a year with his hands, he could pay for his living costs and keep his winters and most summers free for study. He tried teaching school instead, but found its costs rose faster than its pay, and that it forced him to dress, act and even think in set ways while costing him time.

Thoreau says his teaching was a failure because he did it only to earn a living, not to help others. He also tried business, but judged that it would take ten years to succeed and would likely lead him to ruin. He feared that by then he would be doing well in business, which he saw as a bad outcome.

Thoreau, while looking for a way to earn a living, considered picking huckleberries. He thought it could bring in enough money, since he needed very little, and it required little money and would not disturb his usual moods. He now calls this thinking foolish.

Thoreau says that while his friends chose business or professional careers, he thought of working as a picker of wild berries or herbs, or as a seller of evergreens to villagers. Later he decided that trade corrupts whatever it touches.

Thoreau says he chose not to spend his time earning fine carpets, furniture, rich food, or a grand house, because he valued his freedom more and could live simply. He leaves those pursuits to people who enjoy them and can use such things well. He has nothing to say to those who work hard for its own sake.

Thoreau says that people with too much free time should work harder until they earn their freedom. He himself found day-labor the most independent work, since a few weeks of it per year paid his living costs. A day-laborer is free once the sun sets, while an employer who speculates has no rest all year.

Supporting oneself on earth is, Thoreau believes, a pleasure rather than a burden, if a person lives simply and wisely. He compares the work of simpler peoples to the games of more artificial societies, and says hard labor to earn a living is unnecessary unless a man sweats more than he does.

Thoreau says he does not want anyone to copy his way of living. He would rather that people each find and follow their own path, not one inherited from parents or neighbors, and he hopes the world has as many different kinds of people as possible.

Thoreau says that a young person should be free to pursue what he wants to do. He claims that our wisdom is only a tiny point, like the North Star that a sailor or a fugitive slave follows, yet that point is enough to guide a whole life. We may not reach our goal on any set schedule, but we should keep to the right direction.

Thoreau argues that a shared house saves money, since one roof, cellar and wall can serve several households. He still prefers a house of his own. Building alone is easier than persuading a neighbor to share a wall, and a shared wall may be thin, and the neighbor may be careless about repairs.

Thoreau says that real cooperation between people is rare and mostly shallow, and that true harmony between them cannot be heard. A person of faith cooperates well with anyone, while a person without faith lives like everyone else, whoever they join. In the fullest sense, cooperating simply means making a living together.

Thoreau imagines two young men setting out to travel the world, one working his way with no money and the other carrying a bank draft. He concludes they would soon split up, since they could not share the same way of doing things. A solo traveler, he says, can leave at once, while a companion must wait until the other is ready.

Thoreau answers townsmen who call his way of life selfish. He admits he has done little charity, though he has given up some pleasures out of duty. He says that if he had nothing to do, he might take up charity as a pastime, since idle people are easily led into trouble.

Thoreau says he once offered to support some poor people as comfortably as he supported himself, but they all refused and chose to stay poor. He says he will leave charity work to others, since many of his neighbors already devote themselves to helping people, and he adds that doing good is a crowded profession.

Thoreau says he has tested a certain way of life and found it does not suit him, so he will not give up his own calling to do what society asks. He tells anyone whose true work is different from his to keep going, even if the world calls it wrong.

Thoreau says he does not assume his way of living is unusual, since many readers would defend themselves the same way. He claims he would be good at any job he took on, but he leaves it to the employer to decide what that job is. Any good he does, in the ordinary sense, comes from outside his main purpose and is mostly not intended.

Thoreau says that instead of trying to do small good deeds here and there, a person should work at becoming good in full. He compares this to the sun, which grows steadily brighter and warmer rather than wasting its light on minor, meddling tasks. Once it is fully bright, it does good simply by keeping its own course.

Phaeton, a son of the sun god, tried to prove his divine birth by driving the sun's chariot for a single day. He lost control, scorched the earth, and was struck down by Jupiter with a thunderbolt. The sun then mourned and gave no light for a year.

Thoreau says that goodness that has gone bad smells worse than anything, and that kindness done on purpose is harmful. He would flee a person who came to help him deliberately, as he would flee a dust-filled desert wind, for fear of catching that help like a poison in his blood.

Thoreau says he would rather bear hardship naturally than be helped by someone who merely rescues him from danger. A man who feeds, warms, or saves him is not, for that reason, a good man to him, since a Newfoundland dog could do the same. He adds that philanthropy, or helping others out of duty, is not true love for one's fellow man.

Thoreau is saying that charity work, however large, means little if it does not help people when they are at their best and most deserving of help. He adds that he has never seen a charitable gathering that sincerely aimed to help people like him. Howard refers to the English prison reformer John Howard, whose good works are the comparison.

Some Native American captives, burned at the stake, were so unafraid of pain that they invented new ways to torture their captors. Because they did not fear suffering, the missionaries' comfort and the Christian rule of treating others as you wish to be treated had little effect on them. They seemed to forgive their enemies almost completely.

Thoreau says that the most useful help to the poor may be to set an example, even if it leaves them far behind. Giving money is not enough; the giver should put themselves into it. He adds that the poor are often less cold and hungry than they are dirty and ragged, partly by their own taste, so money may just buy more rags.

Thoreau once pitied the Irish laborers who cut ice on the pond for their ragged clothes, thinking himself better dressed. Then a worker who fell into the water came to warm up at his house, and Thoreau saw that the man wore three pairs of pants and two pairs of stockings under his rags. The man had so many layers that he could refuse the spare clothes Thoreau offered.

Thoreau suggests that giving money or goods to the poor treats only the symptoms of poverty. Those who spend the most on charity may, through their own way of living, be helping to cause the very suffering they try to relieve. Real good would require attacking the root cause instead.

Thoreau argues that giving a small share of one's wealth to charity does not make up for how that wealth was gained. He points to a slave-owner who frees one slave in ten while keeping the rest. He suggests that people who help the poor should instead stop the harm they cause themselves, and he asks whether a man keeps his property out of generosity or because the law fails to recover it.

Thoreau says that people praise charity more than it deserves, and that this praise comes from self-interest. He gives an example: a poor man praised a neighbor for being kind to the poor, but he meant himself, since he was the one who benefited. Kind relatives, he adds, are valued more than the people who do deeper spiritual good.

Thoreau says a clergyman lecturing on England listed its great scientists, writers and statesmen, then placed three Christian figures, Penn, Howard and Mrs. Fry, above them all. Thoreau calls this false and insincere. In his view, these three were good philanthropists, but not England's greatest people.

Thoreau says he does not doubt that kindness and honesty deserve praise, but he cares less about them than about something finer in a person. Good conduct is like a plant's stem and leaves, useful in a humble way. He wants the flower and fruit: a personal quality that gives pleasure and warmth in dealing with others.

Thoreau argues that real goodness should be a steady overflow that costs the giver nothing and is not even noticed by him. Much so-called charity, he says, is really a giver spreading his own old sorrows over others and calling it sympathy. We should share our courage and health rather than our despair and illness, and he ends by asking where the suffering and the "heathen" really are that we claim to help.

Thoreau is mocking reformers who want to fix the world. He says such a man, when his own body is sick, decides the whole world must be sick too, as if the globe were an unripe apple that people are eating too early.

Thoreau mocks the reformer who rushes off to help distant peoples, such as Eskimos, Patagonians, Indians and Chinese, mainly to cure his own indigestion, while powers use him for their own ends. He then says he has never known a worse man than himself. The irony is that the reformer's cure for his own discomfort makes the world seem sweeter to him.

Thoreau argues that a reformer's troubles often come from his own private discomforts, not from real concern for others, and that such a reformer would abandon his cause once his own situation improved. He says he does not lecture against tobacco because he never chewed it. He ends by advising quiet, unhurried, self-chosen work over show of charity.

Thoreau says that religious hymns and holy writings express gloom and complaint rather than joy. He claims that no recorded text shows a simple, lasting delight in being alive or real praise of God. He adds that any sign of health or success, however distant, pleases him.

Thoreau says that sickness and failure in others make him sad and harm him, even though he sympathizes with them. So if people want to heal the world, they should first become healthy and simple like nature, clear their own gloom, and live fully. He urges them not to stay merely as helpers of the poor, but to aim to be admirable people.

Thoreau quotes a story from the Persian poet Sadi. People asked a wise man why the cypress alone is called "free" among tall shade trees. He answered that every tree has its own fruit and season, and the cypress is not tied to one, since it is always green.

The passage compares two kinds of living things. The date tree gives its fruit freely when it has plenty, while the cypress, which gives nothing away, stays green and is never harmed by lack. Azads, or religious independents, are said to be like the cypress, free of worldly attachments. The advice is not to fix the heart on what passes away, such as rulers and their dynasties.

This is a speech in verse, spoken by a character, that mocks a poor man for claiming a high spiritual rank because of his simple living. The speaker says such self-denial numbs feeling and dulls the mind. He prefers active, emotional life over a forced, passive endurance.

Mediocre, servile people are told to return to their hated cell and study only what the old heroes were. The speaker holds that true virtue shows only in excess: bold, generous, grand deeds like those of Hercules, Achilles and Theseus.

Thoreau describes how, at a certain time in life, he looked at every piece of land nearby as a possible place to build a house. In his imagination he went round the farms within about twelve miles, learned their prices, and "bought" them, even though he had no money to pay.

Thoreau describes how he bought a farm, took the owner's word on the deed instead of a formal document, and later left the farm to the man to work. Because of this, his friends joked that he was a kind of real-estate agent. He adds that wherever he sat he could live, and that a house is just a seat, better still a country seat.

Thoreau says he found many building sites that people would likely not develop soon, and that to him the village seemed too far from these sites, not the sites too far from the village. He imagined living there through summer and winter, and says that future settlers of the area will find he has already been there first.

Thoreau spent one afternoon planning how his land would be divided into orchard, woodlot and pasture, and which trees to keep. After that he left the land untouched, and he says a man is richer the more things he can afford to leave alone.

Thoreau says he enjoyed imagining owning farms and was content just to be offered them, never really taking possession. The closest he came was buying the Hollowell place, where he began sorting seeds and gathering materials for a wheelbarrow to move things with.

Thoreau describes buying a farm, but the owner's wife changed her mind and wanted to keep it. The owner offered him ten dollars to give up the purchase. Thoreau had only ten cents himself, so he could not work out which of them owned what. He let the owner keep both the farm and the ten dollars and withdrew from the deal.

Thoreau says he sold his bean field back to the farmer for what he paid, and gave him ten dollars as a gift. He kept his profit, so he felt rich without losing his poverty. He still keeps the view of the land, which he says is his, quoting a line from a poem about being master of all he sees.

A poet can take the best value from a farm while the farmer thinks he has only gained a few wild apples. The farmer may not realize for years that the poet has written about the land, taken its real worth, and left him with the least valuable part.

Thoreau lists what drew him to the Hollowell farm: it was very secluded, far from the village and the nearest neighbor, and set back from the road. He also liked its run-down house, barn and fences, because they put a clear distance between him and the previous occupant.

Thoreau describes why he wanted to buy a certain farm. Its old, damaged apple trees hinted at the neighbors he might have, and he remembered it from boat trips up the river, when the house was hidden by red maples. He hurried to buy it before the owner cleared rocks, cut down trees, and made other changes to the land.

Thoreau says he was ready to take on heavy work, like Atlas carrying the world, in order to pay for a piece of land and keep it. He knew the land would yield its best crop if he could simply leave it alone, but things turned out otherwise.

Thoreau says that, though he has kept seeds ready for a large farm, he has not yet planted them, and he may wait until they age well. His main advice to others is to stay free and uncommitted for as long as possible. He adds that being tied to a farm is no better than being tied to a jail.

Thoreau quotes the Roman writer Cato's advice on buying a farm: do not buy in greed, look at the land carefully, and visit it often, since a good farm pleases more the more it is seen. He says he will not buy greedily and will keep walking over his land for the rest of his life, until he is buried in it.

Thoreau says he will describe his next experiment in living, which he has condensed into the story of two years. He says he will not write a gloomy poem about sadness. Instead, he will boast loudly, like a rooster crowing at dawn, to wake his neighbors.

When Thoreau first moved into the woods on July 4, 1845, his house was not finished for winter. It was only a shelter from rain, with no plaster or chimney, and its rough boards left gaps that let in cold air at night.

Thoreau describes his newly built cabin in the morning. Its freshly cut wood looks clean and bright, and he imagines the damp timbers will give off sweet sap by noon. In his mind the house keeps this fresh, dawn-like feel all day, much like a house he once saw on a mountain.

The speaker describes his cabin as open to the wind, which carries bits of music from the earth and the heavens. He says the morning wind always blows and creation's song never stops, but few people hear it. Olympus, the home of the Greek gods, is not far away; it is everywhere on earth.

Thoreau says his earlier shelters were a tent and a boat, both now gone or stored away. His new, more solid house made him feel he had moved toward settling down in the world. He adds that the house, though lightly built, shaped him in return, as a crystal forms around a core and then affects the one who built it.

Thoreau says his cabin felt open and fresh, almost like being outdoors, even in rain. He quotes an old Indian text saying a home without birds lacks something, and he notes that his home was not like that. He lived close to the birds, not by trapping one, but by building his own small home near them.

Thoreau says that at his cabin he was closer to wild forest birds than most villagers ever are. These birds, such as the wood-thrush and the whippoorwill, rarely sing near town, but they were near him.
Thoreau describes where he sat: by a small pond, in the woods a mile and a half south of Concord, and low enough that the far shore, half a mile away, was the furthest thing he could see.

Thoreau describes how Walden Pond looked to him in his first week there. It seemed as high and clear as a mountain lake, and at sunrise the morning mist lifted off it slowly, like ghosts slipping back into the woods.

On a still, cloudy August afternoon during light rain, Thoreau's small lake is at its calmest and most valuable. The water reflects the grey sky so fully that it seems like a second heaven below the real one.

From a hilltop where the trees had been cut, Thoreau looks south over the pond. Between two hills the slopes seem to suggest a valley with a stream, but no stream is there. Beyond the nearer green hills he sees higher blue hills on the horizon.

Thoreau says that from a hill he can see distant mountains and part of the village, but the woods block his view in other directions. He then argues that water nearby is useful because it makes the earth seem to float. Looking into even a small well shows that the earth is surrounded by water, like an island, rather than being one large continent.

Thoreau says that the pond's water is as useful as a cooler for butter. Looking from a hill across the pond, the land beyond looks like a thin crust floating on water, which reminds him that where he lives is only dry land.

Thoreau says that his small view from his cabin door did not make him feel cramped, because his imagination had plenty of room. He supports this with a saying from Damodara, a herdsman, that only those who freely enjoy a wide horizon are happy.

Thoreau says his new home at the pond felt as remote as the distant places astronomers study, and that it was in the same kind of quiet, far-off spot people often picture when they imagine an ideal place. The imagined place is somewhere far beyond the stars, away from noise.

Thoreau says his house stood in a remote, untouched part of the universe, as far from ordinary life as the distant stars. Life he had left behind looked tiny and faint to him, visible only on moonless nights. He ends with a line from an old poem about a shepherd whose thoughts were as lofty as the mountains where his flock grazed.

Thoreau says that each morning invited him to live as simply and innocently as nature does. He rose early and bathed in the pond, which he calls a religious act. He links this to a saying about renewing oneself every day, and he feels that morning brings back the heroic ages.

Thoreau says that the faint hum of a mosquito in his room at dawn moved him as much as any loud, famous music or poem could. He compares its buzzing to an epic song about its own struggles and travels. To him it stands for the endless energy and fertility of nature, and he says morning is the hour when people are least sleepy.

Thoreau says that a day is worth little if we are woken by a routine signal, such as a factory bell or a servant's nudge, rather than by our own inner drive toward a higher life. He hopes to wake to something better than we went to sleep from, so that night, like day, proves good.

Thoreau argues that every day has an earlier, purer hour, the morning, when a person can start over and try again to live well. Someone who denies this has given up on life and is moving toward darkness. He adds that the best deeds, poetry and art all come from the morning.

Thoreau says that morning is not a matter of the clock. For a person whose mind is alert, every day feels like a fresh dawn. Moral reform means shaking off sleep, and people would accomplish more if they were not drowsy.

Thoreau says that most people are awake enough to do physical work, but very few are awake enough for hard thinking, and far fewer for a poetic or spiritual life. To him, being awake means being fully alive, and he has never met anyone who was fully awake.

We need to learn to wake ourselves and stay awake, not with alarms or machines, but through a constant hope for the new day that stays with us even in deep sleep. Thoreau finds it encouraging that people can raise their lives through deliberate effort, such as making art that adds beauty to the world.

The main idea is that the best art is to shape the mood and quality of ordinary life itself, not just make objects. Each person should live so that even small daily details are worth reflecting on in their most serious moments. If people stopped wasting the minor facts they receive, they would clearly learn how to do this.

Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately, facing only the basic facts of life, so he could learn what life had to teach and not find at death that he had never really lived. He did not want to live a false, empty life, and he did not want to accept things passively unless it was truly necessary.

Thoreau says he wanted to live fully and simply, stripping life down to its basic essentials. He would then either find out what life really is, whether it is mean or sublime, and report the truth of it.

Thoreau says most people are unsure whether their restless, striving nature comes from the devil or from God. Still, they have quickly accepted that the main purpose of human life is to "glorify God and enjoy him forever," a line from the Westminster Shorter Catechism.

Thoreau says people live in a small, mean way, like ants, and waste their lives on needless troubles and petty details. He urges simplicity: keep one's affairs to two or three, not hundreds or thousands.

Thoreau says that modern life is so full of hazards and details that a person can barely keep track of them, like a ship steering by rough estimate rather than sure navigation. His remedy is to simplify: fewer meals, fewer dishes, and less of everything else.

Thoreau compares modern life to the German Confederacy, a loose group of small states whose borders keep shifting. He says the nation is similarly bloated and cluttered, weighed down by luxury, careless spending, and a lack of purpose, much like ordinary households.

Thoreau argues that people live too fast, chasing trade, ice exports, telegraphs and fast trains without asking whether these things improve life. He doubts that such progress makes people better than baboons. He asks who would build railroads if everyone stopped working to improve their own lives.

Thoreau argues that people do not really ride the railroad; the railroad rides over them. The wooden ties under the tracks are, he says, men, Irish or Yankee workers, who are buried under sand while others travel smoothly on top. Some get to ride on the rails, and others are run over.

Thoreau compares people living routine lives to sleepers lying on railway track. When a train runs over a man who is walking in his sleep and wakes him, the railway stops and makes a fuss, as if it were unusual. He is glad that crews are needed to keep the sleepers down in their beds, since this suggests they may one day wake up.

People rush through life and waste it, even though they could slow down. They work hard now to prevent trouble later, which only keeps them busy. Thoreau says their real problem is restlessness: they cannot keep still.

Thoreau says that if a fire bell were rung, almost everyone in Concord would drop their work and run to the scene. People would go less to save property than to watch the fire burn, or to help put it out, even if the burning building were the parish church.

Thoreau mocks people who are eager for the news. He says they wake from a short nap and ask what is new, and they read the latest reports with their breakfast as if they cannot start the day without them. The example he gives is a grim item about a man blinded on a river, read calmly over coffee.

Thoreau says he could easily live without the post office, since few important messages pass through it. He has received only one or two letters worth the postage, and he has never read important news in a newspaper. He adds that a letter mostly pays for a thought that people often offer only as a joke.

Thoreau says that one example of any kind of event, such as a robbery or a fire, is enough to show the general principle behind it, so there is no need to read about every similar case. To a philosopher, he argues, the daily news is just gossip, yet many people eagerly consume it.

People pushed so hard to get the latest foreign news at a newspaper office that they broke several large glass windows. Thoreau adds that a clever person could write such news in advance, years ahead, and be quite accurate.

Thoreau says that newspaper reports on Spain could be written from a set of stock names and events, such as a king, an infanta, cities, and a bull-fight, and they would still seem accurate. He adds that for England, the last news worth reporting was the revolution of 1649.

Thoreau is saying that if you know how a farm's crops usually turn out in a normal year, you need not keep checking on them again, unless you are only interested in money. He adds that, judging by someone who rarely reads the newspapers, nothing new happens abroad, not even a revolution in France.

Thoreau contrasts fleeting news with eternal truth. He tells a story from the Chinese sage Confucius: a messenger says his master is trying to reduce his faults but cannot finish. Confucius praises the messenger as worthy, showing that the honest reply to a question about someone's news is an account of ongoing self-improvement.

Thoreau says a preacher should not bore tired farmers on their day of rest with another dull sermon. Instead he should shout a sharp warning: stop, because people look busy but are really moving slowly toward a dead end. He adds that Sunday ends a wasted week rather than starting a fresh one.
