Thoreau says that people treat illusions as the surest truths and see real things as strange, like fiction. If people looked only at what is real and necessary, life would seem like a fairy tale, and music and poetry would fill the streets.

Thoreau says that when people think clearly, they see that only great and worthy things truly last, while small fears and pleasures are just shadows of what is real. Men who close their eyes and accept appearances keep their everyday routines standing, though those routines rest on false foundations.

Thoreau says that children, who play at living, understand the real rules of life better than adults, who have failed to live well yet claim wisdom from their failures. He then starts a tale from a Hindu book about a king's son raised by a forester who came to think he belonged to the wild people around him.

Thoreau tells a story from a Hindu text: a prince who did not know his rank until a minister told him, and a soul that mistakes its true nature until a holy teacher reveals it as Brahman, the ultimate reality. He then says New Englanders live small lives because they take surface appearances for what is real.

Thoreau argues that ordinary things, like a mill-dam, a church or a jail, would not look the same if a person saw what they really are. Their familiar meaning would fall apart under a true look. People place truth far away, in distant stars or in the far past and future, instead of in everyday things.

Thoreau says that eternity holds something true and grand, but all that matters happens in the present moment. God is fully present now and would be no more divine in any future age. We grasp what is noble only through the constant soaking in of the reality around us, and the universe follows our thoughts, so he urges that we spend our lives forming those thoughts.

Thoreau urges that a person should live each day with the same steady purpose as nature, without being pulled off course by small interruptions. He says to face the day calmly, whatever visitors, noise or routine come, and not simply drift along with others. The midday meal is named as the hardest test, and once it is passed, the rest of the day is easy.

The narrator describes ignoring the distractions of modern life, like a train whistle or a bell, by staying alert and focused, as Ulysses tied himself to the mast to resist the Sirens. He will not rush to answer them, but will instead listen to them as music and think about what kind of sound they make.

Thoreau urges the reader to dig down past surface layers of opinion, prejudice, tradition and illusion, the mud that covers everything, until reaching firm ground. Once there, he says, one can find what is real and be certain of it.

Thoreau says that if a person could find a firm footing beneath floods of false beliefs, cold, and passion, it would be a base for building something lasting, like a gauge that shows how high pretense has risen. He adds that facing a fact directly is painful and sharp, like a sword's edge, and that it ends one's worldly life.
We want only what is real, whether we are living or dying. If we are dying, we should feel the death as it happens; if we are alive, we should simply get on with our living.

Thoreau says that time is like a shallow stream where he fishes, and he can see its bottom clearly. He wants to go deeper, into eternity, which he compares to a sky full of stars that he cannot count. He regrets that he is not as wise as he was on the day he was born, and he describes the intellect as a tool that cuts into the secrets of things.

Thoreau says he wants to use his hands as little as possible, because his head does the real work. He compares his head to a burrowing animal's snout, and he says he will dig with it, starting where he believes a rich vein of ore lies.

If people chose their work more carefully, they would all become students and observers, since human nature and destiny interest everyone. Property, family, state and fame all end with our mortal lives. Truth, however, lasts forever and cannot be changed or lost by chance.

Thoreau says that an ancient Egyptian or Hindu thinker lifted a corner of the veil hiding the divine, and the view he saw is still there for Thoreau to see with the same wonder. He treats the past and present as one, since the same mind is at work in both. The time that truly matters to him is not measured as past, present, or future.

Thoreau says that living alone by the pond gave him more time and focus for serious reading than a university would. Though he had no access to a lending library, he felt closer than ever to the old books that have been read around the world. He then quotes a Persian poet, saying that books let him travel the spiritual world, as wine intoxicates.

Thoreau describes how, while building his cabin and hoeing his beans, he had little time to study. He kept Homer's Iliad on his table and hoped for later reading, but he found the light travel books he read in his breaks so shallow that he felt ashamed and asked himself where he was living.

Thoreau says that reading Homer or Aeschylus in Greek is a worthy study, because it means matching the heroes' virtues and giving morning hours to their works. Even in English translation, these heroic books stay like a dead language to a degenerate age. Readers must work hard to find each word's meaning, and printed translations have not made the ancient writers much closer to us.

Thoreau argues that studying the classics, the great works of ancient literature, is worth the time and effort even if you learn only a few words of an old language. Such words lift a reader above everyday triviality and keep giving new thoughts. He adds that serious students will keep studying the classics whatever their age or language, despite claims that modern, practical subjects should replace them.

Thoreau argues that the great books of the past are worth reading because they hold the finest human thoughts, and they still answer modern questions better than ancient oracles did. Reading them well is hard work, needing discipline like an athlete's training, and it should be done as slowly and carefully as the books were written.

Knowing a language as it is spoken is not enough to read the great books written in it. Spoken language is a loose, everyday tongue we pick up as children, like animals do. Written language is a more refined and deliberate form, which a reader must work to master, and the author says this takes a kind of rebirth.

Many medieval people could speak Greek and Latin, but that did not give them access to the great works written in those languages. Those works used a finer literary language that they had never learned, so the classics meant little to them and they preferred cheap, contemporary writing.

Once the nations of Europe had their own written languages, learning revived and scholars could again see the value of ancient works. Books that the ordinary Roman and Greek public could not appreciate are now read only by a small number of scholars.

Thoreau says that the best written words are far more lasting than spoken speech, even the speech of a skilled orator. Spoken words are like clouds or breath that pass quickly, while written words are like stars that stay fixed and can be studied by anyone able to read them.

Speeches that move a crowd in public are often just rhetoric when read in private. A speaker responds to the moment and the people in front of him, while a writer, who lives a steadier life and is not pulled by the crowd, addresses people in every age who can understand him.

Thoreau says a written work is the most precious kind of relic, because it is closer to life than other art. It can be translated into any language and spoken aloud by people, not just shown in paint or stone.

Old ideas, once written down, stay alive and become understandable in new language. Ancient Greek books have aged well, like marble that gains color over time, and they are the shared wealth of the world. So the oldest and best books belong in every ordinary home.

Great books have no cause of their own to argue for, yet they enlighten readers, and sound common sense will accept them. Their authors form a natural aristocracy in every society, and they shape humanity more than kings or emperors do.

A merchant who has become rich and fashionable finds that money cannot give him learning or genius. He feels how poor his own education is, and so he works to give his children the intellectual training he lacks.

Thoreau argues that people who cannot read ancient classics in their original languages know little about human history. He says no translation has ever fully captured these works, so Homer, Aeschylus and Virgil remain untranslated in the sense that matters, apart from modern civilization itself.

Later writers, however gifted, have rarely matched the polished beauty and lifelong labor of the ancient classics. Thoreau argues that people who talk of forgetting the ancients have never really known them. We should only set them aside once we have the learning and talent to understand them fully.

Thoreau imagines a future in which the world's great books, including ancient scriptures and classics, keep piling up, filling even the Vatican with them. He suggests that such a huge collection of writings might eventually let people reach heaven.

Thoreau says that great books are not really read by most people, because only great minds can read them fully. Most people read only for practical gain, like keeping accounts. True reading, he argues, is demanding work that needs our most alert hours, not the easy kind of reading that lulls us to sleep.

Thoreau argues that once people have learned to read, they should move on to the best works of literature instead of staying at the simplest level. He says most people stop at one good book, the Bible, or at easy reading, and so waste their mental abilities.

Thoreau jokes that a multi-volume book called "Little Reading" made him think of a town. He says some people read any kind of trivial material eagerly, as cormorants and ostriches eat anything, and that they waste nothing. Others produce such material, and these readers consume it.

Thoreau mocks cheap popular novels. He describes a love story about Zebulon and Sephronia full of obstacles, where a minor character is needlessly put in danger on a steeple, and the author then rings a bell to gather everyone and dramatize the hero's difficult descent. The stories are shown as contrived and trivial.

Thoreau says that novelists who write grand adventure stories should be made into weathervanes, spinning in the sky like constellations, so they stop bothering honest readers. He will not answer the novelist's bell even if a building burns. He mocks a fake advertisement for a silly romance as a crowd-pulling trick.

Thoreau says that people who read cheap, popular books with wide-eyed eagerness gain no real skill. Like a small child reading a storybook, they do not improve their reading or understanding of meaning. The result, he claims, is dulled sight and a loss of mental ability.
Thoreau says that this kind of gingerbread, a sweet cake, is baked every day and with more care than plain bread made of wheat or of rye and corn meal. It also sells more easily and reliably.

Thoreau says that even the best books go unread, including by people who think of themselves as good readers. In his town of Concord, few people care for the finest books, English or ancient. Even educated men rarely know the English classics, and hardly anyone makes a real effort to learn the old wisdom of humankind.

Thoreau describes a woodchopper who reads a French newspaper to keep up his French, and who values keeping up and improving his English. He says college-educated people do about the same with English papers. He asks how few people one could talk with about a good English book after reading it.

Even a reader who can read a Greek or Latin classic in its original language will find no one to talk with about it. Few professors who know the language also grasp the wit and poetry of the text, and most people do not know that any nation besides the Hebrews has had sacred scriptures.

Thoreau says people will go out of their way for a silver dollar, yet they ignore the great books of the wisest thinkers. Instead, they stop at simple school primers and children's stories, so their reading and thinking stay at a very low level.

Thoreau says he wants to know wiser people than his own small town has produced, even ones whose names are hardly known there. He points out that Plato's books sit on a nearby shelf, yet he has never read them, and he concludes that people in general are poorly educated and unread.

Thoreau sees little difference between a neighbor who cannot read at all and one who reads only simple children's books. He says people should aim to match the great thinkers of the past, which means first understanding how great they were. Today, he claims, our minds rise no higher than the newspaper.

Thoreau says that some books are not dull, and that the right book could speak exactly to a reader's situation. Such a book could change how a person sees the world and could mark the start of a new stage in life. He hopes to find, in some book, words for experiences he cannot yet put into speech.

Thoreau says that the hard questions that trouble people have troubled every wise person before them, and each answered them in his words and way of living. He adds that wisdom teaches openness to others. He then points to a solitary farm worker who, with his own religious experience, may believe otherwise.

Thoreau says that Zoroaster, an ancient Persian prophet, had the same inner experience as he did, and understood it as something shared by all people. Thoreau therefore suggests that he should seek fellowship with great teachers like Zoroaster and Jesus, and set aside his own church.

Thoreau says his village does little for its own learning and culture, despite its boasts of progress. He wants neither flattery nor to flatter, and says people need to be pushed to improve. The town has schools only for small children, a weak lecture series, and a new library, yet spends more on food and medicine than on the mind.

Thoreau says people should not stop learning when they become adults. He wants villages to act like universities, with older residents free to study for their whole lives, and asks why learning must stay in famous places like Paris or Oxford. He laments that daily farm and shop work keeps people out of school too long.

Thoreau argues that towns in America should do what European noblemen once did and pay for the fine arts. He says towns have the money but lack generosity and taste, spending it on practical things instead. He points to a town hall costing seventeen thousand dollars, while true intellectual life, which he calls "living wit," is unlikely to be funded.

Thoreau argues that a town should spend its money on a winter lecture series (a Lyceum) rather than on other things, because it gives access to the wider world. He asks why people in the nineteenth century should not use its advantages, such as the best newspapers and the reports of learned societies, instead of local gossip and cheap family papers.

Thoreau argues that a village should choose its reading as a rich nobleman does, surrounding itself with the best culture: genius, learning, books, art and music. It should not settle for the few basic resources that the early Pilgrims made do with. He adds that a village, acting together, has more means than a nobleman.

Thoreau says New England does not become narrow or backward just by hiring wise teachers from elsewhere. He wants a better kind of school: one where the whole community is educated, not a privileged few. He would even give up a bridge to build a bridge over ignorance.

Thoreau describes a cool, cloudy evening by a pond, when he feels fully at home in nature and his whole body seems to take in pleasure. Sounds of frogs and a whippoorwill, and moving leaves, stir him deeply, yet his inner calm stays steady, like the lake's surface.

Even at night the pond and woods are never fully still. Wind still stirs the water and trees, some creatures make sounds, and wild animals such as the fox, skunk and rabbit go out to hunt or roam. Thoreau calls these night animals Nature's watchmen, linking one day of living things to the next.

Thoreau comes home to find that visitors have left small marks of their presence: flowers, evergreen wreaths, names written on leaves or wood chips, and a willow ring. People who rarely go into the woods pick up a piece of nature to play with as they walk, then leave it behind, on purpose or by accident.

Thoreau says he could tell when visitors had come to his cabin while he was away. He read signs such as bent twigs, crushed grass, shoe prints, dropped flowers, and the smell of tobacco smoke. He could even sense a passing traveller on the road from the scent of a pipe.

Thoreau says that people usually have open space around them, and that their surroundings are already cleared and claimed from nature. He has a large area of forest to himself, with no neighbor within a mile and no house in sight from most places, so his view is bounded only by woods.

Although a railroad and a fence are close by, Thoreau says his place is mostly as lonely as the open prairie. He feels it is as far off as Asia or Africa, with its own sun, moon and stars, and at night no traveller came to his door, as if he were the only person in the world.

Thoreau says that the few villagers who came to Walden Pond in spring to fish seemed to be fishing more in the pond of their own inner nature, using darkness as bait. They left quickly, so the night stayed undisturbed by people. He adds that people still fear the dark, even though witchcraft beliefs and superstitions are gone.

Thoreau says that even a person who dislikes people or feels deeply sad can find warm company in nature. For someone who lives close to nature and keeps their senses, gloom cannot become very dark, and even a storm sounds like music to a healthy, innocent mind. He trusts that nothing can make life a burden while he enjoys nature's company.

Thoreau finds the steady rain good even though it stops him hoeing his beans. He says it helps the grass and so helps him, even if it spoils some crops. He judges the rain by its wider good, not by how it suits his own work.
Sometimes Thoreau feels that the gods favor him more than other people, even more than he thinks he deserves. He says he does not flatter himself, but suggests that the gods may be flattering him.

Thoreau says he has almost never felt lonely in the woods. He had one exception, a few weeks after he arrived, when for an hour he wondered whether living near other people was necessary for a calm, healthy life. He saw that this mood was a kind of temporary madness and expected to get over it.

During a gentle rain, Thoreau felt that nature around his cabin was company enough. The sounds, sights and even the pine needles seemed friendly to him, so that the idea of human neighbors no longer mattered.

Thoreau says that when he sensed something related to himself even in wild, bleak places, he felt that no place could feel strange to him again. He adds that his closest kin was not a person or a villager but nature itself. The quoted line, from an old poem, is about sorrow and the brevity of life.

Thoreau says some of his happiest hours came during long spring and autumn rainstorms, which kept him indoors through the afternoon and evening. While village maids struggled to keep water out of their front halls, he sat safe behind his door in his small house and enjoyed being sheltered.

Thoreau describes a pine tree that lightning struck eight years earlier, leaving a deep spiral groove that he still finds striking. He then notes that people often ask whether he feels lonely living alone by the pond, especially on rainy and snowy days.

Thoreau answers someone who thinks he must feel lonely living apart from others. He argues that the earth is only a tiny point in space, so distance on the map means little. He says the real question is not physical distance but what kind of space keeps one person from another. Walking closer does not bring minds together.

Thoreau says that the places where most men gather, such as the depot, the bar-room, or the meeting-house, are not where a person's true life comes from. He says the real source is a deeper, constant spring, like water that feeds a willow's roots. A wise man, he claims, builds his foundation there.

Thoreau meets a neighbor driving cattle to market at night. The neighbor asks how he can give up so many comforts. Thoreau replies that he is quite sure he likes his way of living well enough, and then goes home to bed.

Thoreau says that if a person could truly awaken to life, every time and place would be the same to them, and all places would be equally pleasing. Outside events and passing circumstances are what distract us. The deepest powers that shape existence, and the grandest laws, are always close at hand. The real maker of our lives is not the hired worker we chat with, but the one whose work we ourselves are.

The passage says that we try to perceive and hear certain things but fail, because these things are part of the substance of the world itself. They cannot be separated from that substance, so they cannot be picked out and seen or heard apart from it.

This passage is Thoreau quoting an older Chinese source, the Doctrine of the Mean, about spirits. It says these spirits make people across the world purify their hearts and dress in holiday clothes to make offerings to their ancestors. The spirits are described as an ocean of subtle intelligences, surrounding people on every side.

Thoreau asks whether people can go without the company of their gossips for a while and rely on their own thoughts for comfort. He then quotes Confucius, who says that virtue cannot be left alone and will always have neighbors.

By thinking hard, a person can step back from their own actions and what happens to them, and watch events pass like a river. Thoreau says we are not fully caught up in nature: we can be the floating wood carried by the stream, or the god Indra looking down on it from the sky. He also notes that we can be moved by a play yet remain untouched by a real event, and that he knows himself only as a human being, a place of thoughts and feelings.

Thoreau says that he can step outside himself and watch his own experiences like a spectator. This watching part of him takes no part in what happens and treats it as a play. It can make a person a poor neighbor or friend.

Thoreau says he finds being alone healthy and prefers it to company, even good company, which he finds tiring. He claims people are often lonelier among crowds than at home, and that solitude depends on the mind, not on distance from other people.

Thoreau says a hard-working student at Cambridge College is as alone as a dervish (a Muslim mystic) in the desert, even among crowds. A farmer can be alone all day at work without feeling lonely, but in the evening he wants company and cannot bear to sit alone with his thoughts.

A farmer wonders how a student can sit alone indoors all day without boredom. The writer answers that the student is also working, in his own mind and field, and seeks the same kind of company and recreation as the farmer, only in a more concentrated form.

Thoreau says people see each other so often that they have no time to gain fresh value for one another, so their meetings feel stale and worn. Rules of etiquette and politeness exist mainly to keep these constant meetings bearable and to prevent open conflict.

Thoreau argues that crowding makes people lose respect for one another, and that meeting less often would still allow for all important and sincere contact. He says a person's worth lies in who they are, not in physical closeness, so being near others is not what matters.

Thoreau describes a starving man lost in the woods who, in his weakness, imagines strange visions and takes them for real company, so his loneliness is eased. He argues that a healthy mind and body can find a similar but more natural company, so that a person never feels truly alone.

Thoreau says he is not lonely, though he has no visitors in the morning. He compares himself to the loon, to Walden Pond, and to the sun, each of which is alone yet has its own company, such as the pond's blue reflected light. He says a lake is never truly lonely.
Thoreau says that God is truly alone, while the devil has many companions. He claims he is never lonely, since he is no more alone than small plants, animals, brooks, weather, and stars around him.

Thoreau describes winter evenings spent with an old settler, a wise and humorous friend who is said to have dug and shaped Walden Pond. Together they talk of old times and the eternal, and pass a cheerful evening without food or drink. The friend hides himself more carefully than the regicides Goffe and Whalley did, and is thought dead, though no one knows his grave.

Thoreau describes Nature as an old woman who lives nearby, though most people cannot see her. He likes to walk through her herb garden, gather medicinal plants, and listen to her stories, which she can trace back to their true origins. She is healthy, enjoys every season, and will probably outlive all her children.

Thoreau says that nature is innocent and kind, and that it feels with people. If anyone grieved for a good reason, the sun would dim, the wind would sigh, and the woods would turn to mourning. He asks whether he himself is not part of the earth, made of leaves and soil.

Thoreau asks what remedy will keep people healthy and calm. He answers that he prefers Nature's own plant-based medicines, and for his own cure he wants only fresh, unmixed morning air rather than the patent medicines sold from traveling wagons.

Thoreau says that if people will not take in fresh morning air at its source, it could be bottled and sold to those who have missed it. But the bottled air will not stay fresh until noon, even in a cool cellar, and will escape well before then.

Thoreau says he does not honor Hygeia, the goddess of health, daughter of the old healer Asclepius. He prefers Hebe, the cupbearer of the gods, who could restore youth and vigor, and wherever she went it was spring.

Walking home in the dark with his fish, Thoreau saw a woodchuck and felt a sudden wild urge to catch and eat it raw. He was not hungry for food but for the wildness the animal stood for. A few times while living by the pond, he felt the same urge and would have eaten anything savage.

Thoreau says he feels two pulls within himself: one toward a higher, spiritual life, and one toward a wild, primitive way of living. He respects both and loves the wild as much as the good. Fishing and hunting, he suggests, gave him his closest knowledge of nature.

Fishermen, hunters and woodcutters, who live outdoors and are in a way part of nature themselves, often notice nature more easily than philosophers or poets. Those who approach nature expecting to find something tend to miss it, while nature shows itself freely to those who are simply there.

Thoreau says that people who live by a place's resources know it best: a prairie traveller becomes a hunter, a trapper on the western rivers, and a fisherman at the falls. A mere passing traveller learns only secondhand and partially. He values science most when it records what such people already know from practical experience.

Some people say New Englanders have few amusements because they have fewer public holidays and fewer team games than the English. Thoreau replies that they are wrong: the older, solitary pastimes of hunting and fishing are still common here, and most boys of his time owned a shotgun by their early teens.

Thoreau says that hunters once had hunting grounds larger than those of an English nobleman or of any native people. Now hunting is changing, not because people have become kinder, but because game has become scarce. He jokingly claims hunters are the animals' greatest friends, even more than animal protection societies.

Thoreau says that while at the pond he sometimes fished for variety and for food, just as the first fishers did. Any objection he might raise on grounds of compassion was only a matter of his philosophy, not his real feelings. He had given up hunting birds before going to the woods, but he felt no real pity for fish or worms, and he calls that a matter of habit.

Thoreau says he once hunted birds with a gun, claiming he was studying them, but now thinks watching their habits closely is a better way to study them. He gave up the gun partly for that reason. He still doubts that any other pastime is as valuable as hunting.

Thoreau says that when friends ask whether to let their boys hunt, he tells them yes, because hunting was one of the best parts of his own education. He wants the boys to become skilled hunters who go after bigger game, even spiritual game, which he compares to fishing for people. He agrees with Chaucer's nun, who said hunters are not holy men.

Thoreau says that many people go through a stage, both as individuals and as a whole society, of admiring hunters. He argues that a boy who has never hunted is not less kind, and that a grown person with a conscience will not kill animals for sport, since animals hold their lives as we do.

Young men first come to the forest as hunters and fishers, the most basic part of their nature. Those with a finer nature later move on to higher pursuits, such as poetry or natural science, and leave the gun behind. Most men stay at the hunting stage. A hunting clergyman might be a useful sheepdog, but he is not the Good Shepherd, the spiritual leader.

Thoreau notes that few townspeople spent a half day at Walden Pond except to chop wood, cut ice, or fish, and fishing was the most common. Even when they fished, they felt rewarded only with a large catch, and they could go to the pond many times before the wish to fish would settle and leave their reason for going pure.

Thoreau says that the governor and his council have grown too dignified to fish in the pond they once knew as boys, so they no longer know it at all. Even so, they expect heaven, and the legislature's concern with the pond only covers fishing rules. He concludes that even civilized people still pass through a stage like the early hunter.

Thoreau says that fishing, though he is skilled at it and still feels an old urge toward it, always leaves him feeling he should not have gone. Over the years he has come to fish less and less, and now he no longer fishes at all. He admits this change has not made him more humane or wiser.

Thoreau says that if he lived in the wilds he would again be drawn to hunting and fishing. He finds meat-eating unclean, and says that this uncleanness, along with the work of keeping a house tidy, was his practical reason for rejecting animal food.

Thoreau says that fish he caught, cleaned and cooked did not really nourish him, and that bread or potatoes would have done as well with less work. He had long avoided meat, tea and coffee, not because they had harmed him, but because they did not appeal to him. He felt this dislike of meat was an instinct rather than something learned from experience, and he found plain, simple living more beautiful.

Thoreau says that people who want to keep their higher, poetic powers at their best tend to avoid meat and eat little food in general. He supports this with an entomology book, which notes that many insects eat much less as adults than as larvae, such as a caterpillar that becomes a butterfly.

Thoreau argues that people who eat greedily are like insects still in their larva stage, even after they have grown. He says that some whole nations are in this state, lacking imagination, and that their large appetites show it.

Thoreau argues that food should be simple and clean, because the body and the imagination are both fed at the same meal. Plain fruit, eaten in moderation, does not shame the appetite or get in the way of worthy work. Rich, heavily seasoned cooking is harmful and not worth living for.

Thoreau argues that people would be ashamed to cook the meals others prepare for them, and that until they are, they are not truly civilized. He questions whether humans should be meat eaters at all, noting that people can live by preying on other animals but are not made for it.

Thoreau says that hunting and killing animals is a miserable way to live, and that anyone who teaches people to eat a more innocent, healthy diet would be seen as a benefactor. He adds that he expects the human race, as it improves, will stop eating animals, just as savage tribes stopped eating each other once they met more civilized people.

Thoreau argues that a person should follow the quiet inner promptings of their own genius, meaning their deepest nature, even if it seems to lead to strange or extreme places. He claims that a faint but sure objection felt by a healthy person will outweigh the common arguments and customs of society, and that nobody who truly followed their genius was ever led astray by it.

If a life lived by higher principles brings physical weakness, that cost should not be seen as a loss. If your days feel joyful and your life seems fragrant, lively and more lasting, that counts as success, and nature itself seems to congratulate you.

The most valuable experiences are the ones people least recognize, soon forget, and rarely manage to share with others. Thoreau says the real harvest of his daily life is as hard to put into words as the colours of morning or evening, like a bit of star-dust or a piece of rainbow he has caught.

Thoreau says he has long preferred water to other drinks, and he wants to stay sober, since drunkenness comes in many degrees. He thinks water is the only drink for a wise man. He admits that coffee and tea tempt him and make him feel he has fallen low, and that even music can intoxicate.

Thoreau says that small habits, like what a person eats and drinks, can ruin a nation as surely as they ruin an individual. He admits that hard manual labor made him eat and drink coarsely, and that he now cares less about table manners and blessings. He says this is not because he is wiser, but because he has grown coarser and more indifferent with age.

Thoreau says that his practice falls short of his opinion, so he does not claim the freedom from dietary questions that a Hindu scripture grants to those with true faith. He adds that a Hindu commentator limits that freedom to times of distress.

Thoreau describes getting a deep, lasting pleasure from food even when he is not hungry, and feeling that eating berries on a hillside even stirred his mind. He then quotes an old Chinese saying: when the mind is not in control of itself, a person looks without seeing, listens without hearing, and eats without tasting.

Gluttony depends on the eater, not on the food. A person who tastes food well is never a glutton, and one who does not taste it cannot be otherwise. A plain-living Puritan can eat brown bread as greedily as a rich city official eats turtle soup. What makes eating wrong is the appetite behind it, not how much or what kind of food it is.

Thoreau argues that the hunter and the fine lady are equally coarse in their appetites. He eats wild turtles and muskrats, while she eats calf's-foot jelly and imported sardines, so neither is better. He finds it strange that people live such a crude life of eating and drinking.

Thoreau says that every moment of life involves a choice between good and evil, with no pause between them. Goodness is the only reliable investment. The "harp" is a figure for the world's constant pull toward virtue, and each small act of goodness is the premium we pay for that protection.

Even if a young person grows indifferent to moral feeling, the laws of the universe stay on the side of those who are most sensitive. For such people, the wind carries a rebuke, and even harsh noises heard from far away sound like music that mocks the small-mindedness of ordinary life.

Thoreau says that a lower, animal part of people wakes up as the higher, spiritual part sleeps. This animal part is sensual and may never be fully removed, though a person can pull away from it. He fears it can have its own health and strength, so a person may be physically well without being pure. A hog's jaw with sound teeth shows him that animal vigor exists apart from the spirit.

Thoreau says that the creature in question got ahead by means other than self-control and moral purity. He quotes Mencius, who says the human quality that sets people apart from animals is small and easily lost, though wise people keep it. Thoreau adds that he would seek out anyone who could teach him purity, and he cites Hindu scripture saying that control of the passions and senses, together with good deeds, is necessary for the mind to draw near to God.

Thoreau argues that the body's sexual energy, when restrained, becomes a source of spiritual strength, while indulgence makes a person impure and weakens them. He calls chastity the highest growth of a person, from which genius, heroism and holiness follow. Purity opens the way to God, and impurity pulls a person down.

The passage says that a person is fortunate when they feel the animal side of their nature fading and the divine side growing stronger. Most people, though, have reason to feel ashamed of their lower, beast-like nature. Thoreau fears that humans are only minor gods, like fauns and satyrs (half-goat woodland creatures of Greek myth), mixing the divine with appetite, so that their life is partly a disgrace.

Happy is the person who puts his animal desires in their proper place and clears his mind of them. He can use these lower urges, like a horse or a wolf, without becoming a beast himself. Otherwise he is like swine, or like the devils that drive the swine into a frenzy.

Thoreau argues that all forms of sensual indulgence come from one appetite, so that eating, drinking, sex and sleep are the same vice in different forms. Someone who indulges in one shows how far he indulges in all. Purity works the same way: to be chaste, a person must first be temperate, and chastity cannot be known by the person who has it.

Thoreau says that people speak of virtue without really knowing what it is. He argues that hard work brings wisdom and purity, while laziness brings ignorance and indulgence of the senses. Even humble labor, such as cleaning a stable, guards against moral failings.

Thoreau says that natural human appetites are hard to master but must be mastered. He asks what good it does to call yourself a Christian if you are no purer or more self-denying than people of other faiths. He adds that some non-Christian religious teachings shame readers into trying harder, even if only at outward rituals.

Thoreau says he hesitates to write these things because he is ashamed of his own impurity, not because the subject is shameful. He notes that people speak freely about one kind of physical desire but stay silent about another. He contrasts this with the Hindoo lawgiver, who treated even basic bodily functions with respect and taught how to perform them properly.

Every person builds a body as a temple to the god they worship, in a style that is entirely their own, and cannot escape this by making temples of stone instead. Our own flesh is the material we shape, so good qualities refine our features and bad ones coarsen them.

John Farmer, tired from his day's work, sits at his door on a cool September evening, his mind still on his labor. He hears someone playing a flute, and the music suits his mood, yet his thoughts keep returning to his work.

Even when his worries about work kept returning, he felt they mattered little, like skin flakes that are constantly shed. The sound of a flute reached him from a different world than his daily labor, awakening dormant abilities and making the street, village, and society around him seem to fall away.

A voice asks a man why he stays in this poor, toiling life when a better existence is open to him, since the same stars shine over other places. He cannot see how to leave his condition, so he decides to practise some new self-discipline and to treat his body with growing respect.

Doctors advise sick people to travel to new places. Thoreau says the world is larger than one region, pointing out that some plants and birds are found only elsewhere. The wild goose moves across many regions in a single day, more widely than people do.

Thoreau says that animals like the bison move freely to find better grass, while people think that fences and walls, or a town office, fix their lives and limit where they can go. He suggests these limits are only apparent, since a person can still go to a far, even harsh, place, such as the land of infernal fire, which is a figure for hell.

Thoreau says we should look around our journey more often, as curious passengers do, instead of working through it dully like sailors. Travel to distant places, such as hunting giraffes in Africa, misses the real aim. He suggests the nobler hunt is to pursue one's own self.

Look inward, the lines say, and you will find many parts of your mind that no one has explored yet. Explore them, and you will come to know your inner world as well as a map-maker knows the land. "Home-cosmography" means the mapping of one's own inner territory.

Thoreau asks what Africa and the American West really mean to us, and whether finding the sources of great rivers or a northwest sea route matters most. He suggests that people should instead explore their own inner lands, streams and seas, as famous explorers did elsewhere.

Thoreau urges the reader to explore the inner life rather than only material gain, calling each person the ruler of an inner realm greater than any empire. He says some people claim patriotism for their country while lacking self-respect and neglecting their own spirit. He calls such patriotism a maggot in the head, meaning a corrupting obsession.

Thoreau argues that the large government expeditions to explore distant seas are a sign that people know there are unexplored regions within themselves. Each person is like a narrow strip of land or a bay leading into an unknown inner sea. He says it is easier to sail the real oceans with a crew of hundreds than to explore one's own inner self alone.

Thoreau says that travelling far to study trivial things is not worthwhile. He suggests that a person should keep searching, and may find a way into the inner truth of things. He notes that European and African coastal nations face this inner sea, yet none of their ships has dared to sail out of sight of land, even though that route is the direct way to India.

Thoreau says that the real journey is inward. Learning every language, travelling everywhere, and mastering all customs are less demanding than exploring yourself, which needs courage and sharp perception. He mocks people who seek adventure abroad as cowards running from the harder task.

Thoreau urges the reader to set out on a westward path that does not stop at the Mississippi or the Pacific, nor lead to old Asian lands like China or Japan. Instead it runs straight off the edge of this world, past sun, moon, and finally the earth itself.

Thoreau reports that Mirabeau, a French revolutionary, once turned to highway robbery to test how much resolve it took to break openly with society's most sacred laws. Thoreau calls this bold by worldly standards but says it was also pointless, even desperate.

A wiser person, Thoreau says, would often find himself at odds with society's laws only by obeying higher laws, and would not seek out conflict. A person should not deliberately place himself against society, but should stay true to the laws of his own nature, which will not oppose a just government.

Thoreau says he left the woods for the same reason he went there: he felt he had other lives to live and could not spend more time on this one. He notes how easily people fall into habits, as his own feet wore a path to the pond within a week, and the path is still visible years later.

Thoreau says that people's minds wear down well-used paths, as feet wear down the ground, and these paths are the worn ruts of custom and conformity. He preferred to work at the front of the ship, on the open deck, rather than in the comfortable cabin below, because from there he could see the world most clearly.

Thoreau says that if a person moves confidently toward their dreams and tries to live the life they have imagined, they will find success they would not expect in ordinary times. As they leave some things behind and cross an unseen boundary, new and freer laws begin to take hold around and within them.

Thoreau says that as a person simplifies life, the laws of the universe seem less complicated, and loneliness, poverty and weakness no longer feel like hardships. Dreams are not wasted; they belong in the air, so the next step is to build a foundation under them.

Thoreau argues that it is silly to demand that every writer be understood by England and America alike. Nature has room for many kinds of understanding, just as it has room for many kinds of creatures, and clear speech is not the only good. He adds that dullness is not a safe thing to hope for.

Thoreau worries that his writing may not be bold enough to match the truth he has come to believe. He says "extravagant" depends on one's limits: a wild buffalo roaming far is free, while a cow kicking over its pail is merely confined and running loose. He wants to speak without limits, as a fully awake man speaks to others who are awake, because he thinks he cannot overstate enough to lay a true foundation.

Thoreau says that we should stay open and loose about the future, not fixed in our outlines, the way shadows show a faint sweating toward the sun. Words capture truth only briefly, leaving a fixed statement that is always inadequate. Words of faith are vague, yet they still mean something and are fragrant to finer minds.

Thoreau asks why people always lower their thinking to their dullest understanding and call that common sense. He says true common sense is the sleepy state of men who snore, and that people often judge others as dull because they grasp only part of what those others mean. He adds that critics of the morning sunrise would change their minds if they woke early enough.

Thoreau reports that the verses of Kabir, a Hindu poet, are said to carry four levels of meaning. He notes that in America a writer is blamed if his work can be read in more than one way. He then asks why people fight the potato disease in England but do not try to cure what he calls "brain-rot," which he sees as more widespread and deadly.

Thoreau says that his writing may not be obscure, but if it is faulted, he hopes the fault is no worse than the complaint about Walden ice. Southern buyers disliked its blue colour, which shows it is pure, and preferred white Cambridge ice, which tastes of weeds. He concludes that people love a purity like misty air near the ground, not the clear blue sky above.

Some say modern Americans are intellectual dwarfs next to the ancients and the Elizabethans. Thoreau replies that this does not matter: a living dog is better than a dead lion, so a person should not give up, but should be as good as he can be and become what he was made to be.

Thoreau argues that people should not rush to succeed or chase goals that are empty. If someone falls behind others, he may be following a different beat, and he should move at his own pace, as a tree grows at its own rate. Settling for a false substitute for the true good is pointless, since we would still look toward the real thing.

An artist in Kouroo decided to make a perfect staff, and he would not let time limit the work. He searched the forest for the right wood, rejecting stick after stick, while his friends aged and died. He himself never grew older.

Because the man kept single-minded and devout, time seemed to pass him by: he never gave in to it, so it could not overtake him. While he worked, whole cities fell and dynasties ended, but he simply wrote the last ruler's name in the sand and kept carving his stick.

Thoreau tells a tale from Hindu myth: an artist carves a staff so long that the stars have shifted and the god Brahma has gone through many ages while he works. When he finishes, the staff unfolds into a whole new world, more splendid than any earlier one.

The speaker, looking at fresh wood shavings at his feet, realizes that the long time he thought had passed was only an illusion for him and his work. Only a moment has gone by, like a single spark from the mind of Brahma (the supreme god in Hindu belief) lighting a human mind. Because the material and the craft are both pure, he sees the result as wonderful.

Thoreau says that the truth is the only way of seeing a matter that holds up over time, and that people often live in a false position by imagining a situation and then placing themselves inside it. He urges speaking what is actually the case rather than what one should say, and gives Tom Hyde's gallows remark as an example: his practical advice is remembered, while his companion's prayer is forgotten.

Thoreau says that however poor or dull your life seems, you should face it and live it fully rather than despise it. Life is not as bad as a complaining person makes it out to be, and even a poor-house can bring bright moments, since the sun and spring shine on it as they do on a rich man's home.

Thoreau argues that a calm mind can be as content in a simple cabin as in a palace. He suggests that the town's poor often live more independently than others, and that people who refuse town support may still rely on dishonest means, which he calls worse. He recommends keeping life simple, without chasing new possessions or friends.

Thoreau says that outward things stay the same and people are the ones who change, so he urges a return to older ways of living. He claims that a person's own thoughts make the world large, even if the person is shut in a small room. He adds a saying that no one can take away a person's thought, even from the lowliest man.

Thoreau advises against anxiously trying to be shaped by many outside influences, which he calls mere scattering of the self. He argues that humility and poverty, like darkness, make a larger world visible. He adds that great wealth would not change our real goals or our basic means of reaching them.
If you are too poor to buy books and newspapers, you are forced to focus on the most important and essential experiences of life. Money can only buy extra things, not the things the soul truly needs.

Thoreau says that the talk of his neighbors, about meeting famous people and fashionable dinner-table society, holds no interest for him. He compares it to newspaper news, and says such society is only surface: costume and manners, and underneath it is still the same, as a goose is a goose however it is dressed.

Thoreau says he is tired of hearing news of distant places and public figures, which he finds fleeting and unimportant. He would rather stay grounded, reflect quietly, and watch his restless age pass by than join the crowds celebrating it. He sees people as busy with organizing events and waiting for speeches.

Thoreau says he wants to follow what truly and rightfully draws him, rather than weighing options or imagining cases. He wants a solid foundation before building anything, and he holds that there is a solid bottom everywhere, as the boy told the traveller about the swamp.

Thoreau uses a story about a traveller whose horse sinks into a bog that seemed firm, to say that society has hidden traps that look solid. Only rare, well-timed thoughts, words or deeds are sound. He would rather test for solid support, like a hammer striking the wooden strips behind a wall, than trust surface finish like putty.

Do each small task, like driving a nail, so well that you can think back on it with pride even at night. Thoreau says this is the only way to receive God's help, and that each finished task becomes a part of the universe's work.

Thoreau says he would choose truth over love, money, or fame. At a lavish dinner, he found the food and service plentiful but sincerity missing, so he left still hungry. The host's kindness felt as cold as the ice served.

Thoreau says that the fine things rich people offer, such as their house, grounds and entertainment, mean nothing to him. He had visited a king, who kept him waiting and treated him poorly. A man living in a hollow tree near him showed truly royal manners, so Thoreau would have done better to visit him.

Thoreau asks how long people will sit idly practising old virtues like patience and kindness, which real work would make unnecessary. He compares this to someone who practises patience at breakfast and then hires a man to hoe his potatoes. He then urges the reader to notice mankind's smug, stagnant self-satisfaction.

Thoreau mocks modern civilization for taking pride in its art, science and famous men, as if these were lasting achievements. He compares this to Adam admiring his own virtue, and he points out that the learned societies of ancient Assyria are now forgotten, so our own may be too.

Thoreau says that his readers have not yet lived a full human life, and that people know very little of the world they live on. They have barely scratched its surface and do not understand where they are. Still, they think themselves wise and have settled their affairs on the surface.

Thoreau watches an insect hide from him among the pine needles and wonders why it fears him, though he could help it. He then realizes that a greater intelligence may look down on humans in the same way, as humans look down on insects.

Thoreau says that the world constantly brings new things, yet people still put up with deadly dullness. Even joy and sorrow have become empty words, like a hymn sung without feeling. People believe only in what is ordinary and petty, and think that a change of clothes is all the change they need.

Thoreau is saying that great powers like Britain and the United States are not as permanent or important as they seem. He suggests that a single person with a strong idea could shake them, and that the government he lives under was not shaped by the casual dinner-table talk that shaped Britain's.

Thoreau compares the life in a person to a river that can rise far above its usual level, flooding dry ground and even drowning the muskrats. He notes that the land where people now live was once under water, as shown by old riverbanks far inland, long before anyone recorded floods.

A story told across New England says a live beetle came out of an old wooden table. The table was made of apple wood and had stood in a farmer's kitchen for sixty years. The beetle's egg had been laid in the tree long before the table was built, and the insect was heard chewing its way out for weeks.

Thoreau uses the image of a beetle's egg laid inside a living tree. The egg is slowly sealed in dead wood and furniture, and then, after years, the insect hatches out. He suggests that a hidden, living life can come out unexpectedly from ordinary, lifeless society, and he says this makes him feel more sure of resurrection and immortality.

Thoreau says that time alone will not bring the coming day of awakening; only people who are awake to it will see it. He suggests that the light we take for truth can blind us, and that the true day is still ahead, so the sun we know is only a morning star.
Love calls people to follow it, accept its embrace, and trust its words, even though it may hurt them. The speaker says love gives and takes away alike: it crowns a person and also crucifies them.

Love both nurtures and cuts a person back. It lifts the branches toward the sun and also shakes the roots loose from the soil. Like grain, the person is gathered, threshed, sifted, ground and kneaded, then given to a sacred fire to become bread for God's feast.

Love works on a person in ways that reveal the hidden truths of their heart and connect them to life as a whole. Anyone who fears this and wants only love's comfort and pleasure should leave love's process and live a life without its full joys and sorrows. Love gives only itself and asks for nothing but itself, and it does not own or want to be owned.

Love is enough for itself and needs nothing else. Lovers should not claim God lives in their hearts; instead they should see themselves as living within God. Love, not the lover, decides its path, and if love has any wish at all, it is to fulfil itself. Even so, the wishes it names are to melt like a brook, to feel tenderness as pain, to be wounded by one's own understanding of love, and to bleed willingly and joyfully.

Living with love means giving thanks at dawn, feeling its joy at noon, returning home grateful at evening, and sleeping with prayer for the beloved. On marriage, the speaker says the two were born together and will stay together forever, even after death and in God's memory.

Lovers should stay separate individuals even while they are close. They should share love, joy and daily life without merging into one another or holding each other's hearts in a way that takes away their own selves. The image is of two shores with a moving sea between them, and of lute strings that sound together but are not fixed to each other.

Lovers should keep their own space while they are together. Only life itself can hold their hearts, so they should stand side by side without crowding each other. Pillars of a temple stand apart, and an oak and a cypress do not grow in each other's shadow.
Children belong to life itself, not to their parents. Parents can give love and shelter, but not control their children's thoughts or souls, which belong to a future the parents cannot enter.

Parents are told not to make their children copy them, because life moves forward and does not wait for the past. Parents are compared to bows, and children to arrows sent out by an unseen Archer, who bends the parents to launch the children far. The parents should accept this bending gladly, since the Archer values the steady bow as much as the flying arrow.
Giving your possessions is only a small gift, the speaker says; the true gift is giving yourself. Possessions are often kept out of fear of future need, and that fear is itself a kind of need.

Giving is judged by the spirit behind it. Those who give a little for praise have gifts spoiled by hidden motives. Those who give everything, or give with joy or with pain, each receive something in return: a full coffer, the joy itself, or a kind of baptism.

Some people give without feeling pain, without seeking joy, and without thinking about being virtuous. Their giving is as natural as a myrtle sending out its scent. The author says that God speaks through such givers. He also says it is better to give before being asked, out of understanding, and that for generous people, looking for someone to receive is a greater joy than giving itself.

Give now, while you still control what you have, rather than leaving it to your heirs. Trees and flocks give freely and do not ask who deserves it, since holding back means death. If someone is worthy of life itself, they are worthy of your smaller gifts too.

Giving is not the only hard part; receiving well takes courage and humility too. The speaker warns against expecting others to expose their pride so that the giver can see their worth. A person should first ask whether they truly deserve to give. Life is the real giver, and the person who thinks they give is only a witness to that process.

Receivers should not feel heavy with gratitude or debt, since that burdens both themselves and the giver. Instead they should rise up together with the giver, as if lifted on wings. To keep worrying about what you owe is to doubt the giver's generosity, which comes from the earth and God.

Gibran says that people would ideally live on air and light alone, like air plants. Since humans must kill animals to eat and take milk meant for the young, he says eating should be treated as a sacred act. The table becomes an altar where the innocent creatures of forest and field are offered up for the more innocent part of human beings.

When you kill an animal or eat fruit, the passage asks you to think of the creature as sharing your fate. The beast's death is tied to your own, since you too will be consumed by a greater power. The apple's seeds, buds and fragrance will live on in you, so eating becomes a shared life.

The passage compares a person's life to the grape harvest: as grapes are pressed into wine, a person is gathered and kept in something lasting, and the wine is later drunk with song and memory. The final line says work is a way to keep pace with the earth and its soul.

Idleness, the passage says, cuts you off from the seasons and from life's steady march forward. Work is like a flute: through it, the passing hours become music. The passage rejects the common view that work is a curse.

Work is presented as a way of fulfilling the earth's dream and of loving life, and being close to life's deepest secret. If someone treats birth and earning a living as a burden or curse, the answer given is that only honest labour, the sweat of the brow, can wash that curse away.

Life is dark unless there is urge, and urge is blind unless there is knowledge. Knowledge is empty unless it leads to work, and work is empty unless it is done with love. Working with love, the speaker says, binds a person to themselves, to others and to God, like weaving cloth for someone one loves.

Work done with love, as if for someone you care about, is the point here. The speaker says to build, sow and make things with affection and a breath of your own spirit, aware that the dead are watching. The last line claims that a sculptor who finds his soul in stone is nobler than a farmer who ploughs the soil.

The passage says that no kind of work is greater or lesser in itself. The wind speaks as sweetly to small grass as to great oaks, and a person becomes great by turning what they receive into a song made sweeter by their love. Work, it ends, is love made visible.

If you do work without love, only with dislike, the passage says it is better to stop and beg from those who work gladly. Bread baked with indifference is bitter and only half satisfies hunger, grudging wine turns poisonous, and singing without love shuts out the sounds of life.

Joy and sorrow come from the same source, so your joy is really sorrow in another form. The deeper sorrow cuts into a person, the more joy that person can hold, just as a cup must be fired in an oven and a lute must be carved out to be useful.

Joy and sorrow come from the same source in a person. The joy you feel is tied to what once caused you pain, and the sorrow you feel is tied to what once gave you delight. The speaker says the two cannot be separated.

Joy and sorrow always come together, so when one is near you, the other is close by too. Your life is like a scale, held between the two. It only rests level when you are empty, and when someone weighs you, one side must rise and the other fall.

The speaker tells a builder to first imagine a retreat in the wild, before building a house in town. He says a house is like a larger body that grows, sleeps, and even dreams, and may long to leave the city for a grove or hilltop.

The speaker wishes people could spread their houses out across forests, meadows and valleys, so they could meet among vineyards and carry the smell of the earth with them. He says this is not yet possible: their ancestors built close together out of fear, and city walls will keep homes apart from fields a little longer.

The speaker asks the people of Orphalise what their houses hold behind their locked doors. He asks whether they have inner peace, lasting memories, and beauty that lifts the heart above wood and stone toward something holy. The question is left open, with no answer given.

The passage warns that the wish for comfort can slowly take control of a household and of a person. It starts as a welcome guest, becomes a master, and then works like a tamer, forcing your larger desires to obey it. It soothes you, but then mocks your body and weakens your senses.

The passage says that a love of comfort kills the soul's desire to live fully, and it tells the people it addresses not to be confined by their homes. A house should be a mast, something that lifts and supports, not an anchor that holds them down. It should guard them like an eyelid guards the eye, not hide problems like a thin shine over a wound.

Your house, however grand, cannot contain your inner self or hold your deepest desires. What is limitless in you lives instead in the sky, which has morning mist for a door and the sounds and stillness of night for windows.

Clothes hide some of a person's beauty but do not hide what is ugly. Although clothes can seem to give privacy, they can also become a restraint. The speaker wishes people would expose more skin to sun and wind, since life itself comes through them.

Modesty is described as a shield against the unclean, and the speaker asks what it would be once the unclean are gone, suggesting it would then only bind and dirty the mind. The passage ends by urging a closer contact with earth and wind, with bare feet and loose hair.

The earth gives enough, and people will have plenty if they know how to gather and take what it offers. Trading those gifts brings abundance and contentment, but only if it is done with love and fair dealing. Without that, trade leads some to greed and others to hunger.

In the marketplace, workers should call on a spirit of the earth to bless the scales and the fair weighing of value against value. They should not let people who produce nothing but empty words take part in their trade, and should send such people to work in the fields or at sea.

Buyers are told to also buy from singers, dancers and flute players, because their art, though made of dreams, feeds the soul. Before leaving the market, no one should go away empty-handed, since the spirit of the earth will not rest until everyone's needs are met.

The speaker says that a wrong done when your spirit is wandering, and you are alone and unguarded, harms others and therefore yourself. For such a wrong, you must knock and wait unheeded at the gate of the blessed. He compares your true self, your "god-self," to the ocean, the sky and the sun, which stay pure and lift up only the winged.

The speaker says a person has three parts: a divine "god-self," a part that is still only partly human, and the human self. He claims that the human self, not the god-self or the sleeping part, is the one that commits crimes and receives punishment for them.

Gibran says that a wrongdoer is not a stranger to the community but one of its own. Just as the best people can rise only to the highest that lies within everyone, the worst can fall only to the lowest that lies within everyone too. Like a leaf that yellows only with the whole tree, the wrongdoer acts only with the hidden will of all.

Everyone is part of a shared path, so a person who stumbles harms or warns those who follow, and those ahead who did not remove the stone are also at fault. The passage claims that victims share responsibility for their harm, and that good people share responsibility for the wrongs of the wicked.

The passage says that guilt and innocence are tangled together, so the guilty may be victims of the wronged, and the condemned may carry the burden of the innocent. Good and bad cannot be fully separated, just as black and white threads are woven into one cloth. If one thread breaks, the weaver must examine the whole cloth and the loom, not just the broken thread.

Gibran says that whoever wants to judge or punish a wrong must look at the whole picture. The person who judged must also weigh the husband's heart and the spirit of the one wronged. A tree's roots show that good and bad grow together, so a wrongdoer cannot be cut off from the rest.

Gibran asks judges how they would punish people whose inner wrongs don't match their outer deeds, such as an honest-looking thief or a killer who is himself spiritually slain. He also suggests that remorse is already a form of justice, the same law judges claim to serve.

Remorse cannot be forced onto the innocent or removed from the guilty; it comes on its own, often at night, so people face themselves. To understand justice, one must view all deeds in full light. Then one sees that the upright and the fallen are the same person, caught between his smaller self and his divine self, and that the top stone of a temple is no more important than the lowest stone in its base.

Laws are the subject here. The speaker says people enjoy making laws but enjoy breaking them even more. He compares this to children who build sand towers and then knock them down, while the ocean keeps bringing more sand and laughs with the innocent.

The passage asks about people who see life as solid rock, not as the shifting sand the speaker describes, and who use man-made laws as tools to shape others to their own image. It offers examples: a cripple who hates dancers, an ox who thinks wild deer are lost, and a serpent that cannot shed its skin and calls others shameless. Each shows people judging others by their own limits.

Those who come to life's feasts early, then leave tired and call all feasts wrongdoing, are like people standing with their backs to the sun. They see only shadows and treat those shadows as laws. The speaker asks the reader to face the sun, so that no shadow drawn on the ground can hold them.

The speaker asks who can judge or bind a person who is free in spirit and harms no one else. Such a person breaks no human law, because the only chains and doors are those men make. The closing image says that, as no one can stop a skylark from singing, no one can stop a free spirit from its natural expression.

The speaker says people bow down to their own freedom, much as slaves praise a tyrant who kills them. Even the freest among them, he says, wear their freedom like a yoke and handcuffs, which hurts him deeply.

Real freedom comes when you stop treating freedom as a goal to chase, since even that wish can become a burden. It does not mean having no cares, wants or griefs. It means rising above them while they still surround your life, by breaking the chains you made for yourself earlier in your understanding.

The speaker says that what people call freedom can be the strongest chain, because it hides its bonds behind bright appearances. A law you want to abolish is one you wrote yourself, so burning law books or washing the judges' foreheads cannot remove it.

To free yourself from a despot, the passage says, first remove the tyrant's throne inside you, since a ruler can only hold power through your own lack of freedom and pride. Cares and fears are likewise chosen or kept by the inner self, not forced on it from outside.

Everything inside a person exists in pairs that cling together, such as desire and fear, or pursuit and escape. When one side fades, the other becomes a shadow to something newer. In the same way, freedom that breaks its chains becomes a chain to a greater freedom.

The speaker says that a person's soul is often a battlefield where reason and judgment fight against passion and desire. He wishes he could bring peace and harmony between these forces, but he says this can only happen if people make peace with, and love, all parts of themselves.

Reason and passion are compared to the rudder and sails of a ship. If either one fails, the soul either drifts aimlessly or stops dead. Reason alone confines, and passion alone burns itself out, so the soul should raise reason up to the level of passion.

Reason should guide passion so that passion is renewed each day, like the phoenix rising from its ashes. Judgment and appetite should be treated like two welcome guests in a house, with neither honored above the other.

In calm moments, the heart should say that God rests in reason. In storms, when nature shows its power, the heart should say in awe that God moves in passion. The first clause, about losing the love and faith of both, is cut off from its context.

Pain, in this passage, is compared to the breaking of a fruit's stone so that its inner heart can reach the sun. Pain breaks open your understanding. If you keep wonder at everyday life, pain can seem as marvellous as joy, and you can accept grief's winters calmly, as you accept the seasons in your fields.

Much of a person's pain, the passage says, is chosen by the person. It is like a bitter medicine that an inner healer gives to cure the sick self. So the reader should accept the healer's cure quietly, because the healer is guided by a hidden higher power and the cup was shaped by a divine maker.

Your heart already knows the secrets of life, but you want to hear that knowledge put into words. The passage says this is good, because your inner depths should be brought out and shown. It warns only that you should not try to measure that hidden treasure with scales.

Self-knowledge cannot be measured or mapped. The speaker should not claim to have found the one truth or the one path of the soul, but only a truth and a soul that walks many paths. The soul does not move in a straight line or grow like a reed; it opens outward, like a lotus with many petals.

A good teacher cannot hand over his own understanding. He can only point to what the student already half knows and lead the student to the edge of their own mind. The teacher gives faith and love rather than finished wisdom, and the student must reach knowledge personally.

A musician can describe rhythm, and a scholar of numbers can describe measure, but neither can give you the ability to perceive it yourself. Each person must reach knowledge of God and of the world alone, since one person's vision cannot be passed to another.

A friend is someone who meets your needs, a place where you give love and receive gratitude, and a source of rest and comfort. With a friend you can speak freely, saying yes or no without fear, and in silence your heart still listens to theirs.

In friendship, thoughts and feelings are shared without needing words, and the joy goes unannounced. Being apart does not bring grief, because a friend's best qualities can seem clearer from a distance. The only true purpose of friendship is to deepen the spirit; love that aims at anything else is like a trap that catches only what is worthless.

A good friend should be given your best, and shown both your low and high moods. Friendship should be sought for its fullness, not to pass idle time or to fill your emptiness. Laughter, shared pleasures and small everyday joys refresh the heart.

You talk when you are no longer at peace with your own thoughts. Talk then becomes a way of passing time, and much of it kills thinking. Thought is like a bird that can spread its wings inside a cage of words but cannot fly.

Some people talk a lot because they fear being alone, since silence would show them their true selves. Others speak truths they do not understand. Some people hold the truth within but do not express it in words, and in them the spirit lives in quiet rhythm.

When you meet a friend, the passage says, let your inner spirit speak through your words. Your friend's soul will take in the truth of your heart, much as the taste of wine lasts after its colour and its container are gone.

The prophet tells an astronomer that people try to measure what cannot be measured. They shape their behavior and inner life by hours and seasons, turning time into a stream they sit beside and watch flow past.

The timeless part of a person knows that life has no real time limits. Yesterday is only today's memory, and tomorrow is only today's dream. The part that sings and reflects still belongs to the first moment that scattered the stars, and the speaker asks who does not feel their power to love is endless.
Love, though endless, sits at the center of a person and does not move from one loving thought or deed to another. The speaker asks whether time is the same way: undivided and without a set pace.
If you divide time into seasons in your mind, each season should contain all the others. Today should hold the past as memory and the future as longing.

In this passage, the speaker says evil is really good driven by its own hunger and thirst, so that it seeks food and drink even in bad places. You are good when you are at one with yourself, and being divided within yourself is not the same as being evil.

Giving of yourself is good, but seeking gain for yourself is not evil. Gain-seeking is like a root that feeds on the earth, and a fruit cannot fairly ask the root to be as full and giving as itself. The point is that people who seek gain should not be judged by the standard of those who give freely.

Being good is described as acting with full awareness and firm purpose, like speaking clearly or walking boldly toward a goal. But failing to do so is not called evil. Even clumsy speech or a limping walk still moves forward and does not go backward.

Gibran tells the strong and quick not to pretend to be weak in front of the lame, as if that were kindness. He says that people who are not good in a given moment are not evil; they are only idle and lazy. Your deepest goodness lies in your longing for a greater self, and everyone has that longing. Word count: about 50.

Some people's longing for something is strong and fast, like a rushing river, while others' is slow and winding. The passage says the person with strong longing should not scold the person with weak longing for being slow. The truly good do not ask the poor or homeless why they lack clothes or a home.

Prayer is not only for hard times. The speaker says people should also pray in joy and plenty, since prayer lets the self spread out into the air around it, bringing comfort in sorrow and delight in happiness. Even when weeping, one should keep praying until joy returns.

Prayer, the passage says, is a meeting with others who are praying at the same hour, and it should be entered only for ecstasy and sweet communion. Praying to ask, to humble yourself, or to beg for others will not bring what you seek. Simply entering the invisible temple is enough, and words cannot teach prayer.

God does not hear your words unless God speaks them through you. The speaker cannot teach the prayer of nature, but people born of mountains, forests and seas can find that prayer in their hearts. In the still night they can hear nature praying that God's will, desire and urge within it turn its nights into days.
Pleasure is a song of freedom, but it is not freedom itself. It is desires in bloom, not their fruit. It is a caged creature beginning to fly, but not open space.

Gibran's speaker says he will not condemn young people who chase pleasure, since they may find something greater. Pleasure is only one of seven sisters, and the least of those is more beautiful than pleasure itself. Older people who regret their past pleasures are described as regretting them like wrongs done while drunk.
