Regret, the passage says, clouds the mind rather than punishing it, so people should recall past pleasures with gratitude, like a summer harvest. Those who are neither young nor old, and who avoid all pleasure out of fear, still find a kind of pleasure in giving them up.

The main point is that nothing we do can really harm or disturb the spirit, just as a nightingale or a firefly cannot disturb the night or the stars. Denying yourself pleasure does not remove the desire; it only stores it inside, and the body keeps its natural needs and cannot be fooled about them.

The body is like a harp that the soul plays, and a person can make it sound sweet or harsh. When asked how to tell good pleasure from bad, the speaker points to nature: the bee takes honey from the flower, and the flower gives it freely, so both find pleasure in the exchange.

A bee and a flower each give the other something they need: the flower gives life, the bee carries love, and both find giving and receiving pleasure essential. The people of Orphalese are told to take their own pleasures in the same way, as the flowers and bees do.

Beauty cannot be found or described except through beauty itself, which guides the seeker and shapes the words used to speak of it. The passage then shows that different people describe beauty in different ways: the wounded see it as gentle, the passionate as powerful and frightening, and the weary as a quiet whisper.

Different groups of people describe Beauty in different ways, each according to their own situation. Those who are restless hear her shouting in the mountains, watchmen expect her to rise at dawn, workers see her at sunset, and the snowbound expect her with spring. Her voice is faint, like light trembling in fear of shadow.

Beauty is not something we want because we lack it, the way a thirsty mouth wants water. Instead, it is an intense joy that fills the heart and soul. We perceive it as an inner image or sound, even with eyes and ears closed.

Beauty is not the sap in a tree's bark or a wing on a claw. It is life showing its holy face, and eternity looking at itself in a mirror. The speaker says the listeners are both the life and the veil, and both the eternity and the mirror.

Religion, in this passage, is not kept apart from ordinary life. Deeds, thoughts, and daily work all belong to it, and a sense of wonder can arise in the soul even while a person is working. The speaker asks who could split their time into parts, one for God and one for themselves.

Gibran says that morality worn as a show, or conduct bound by rigid ethics, is like clothes or a cage that hinders what is true and free. A person whose worship is only a window that opens and shuts has not reached the inner self, which is open at all times. Daily life itself is the place of worship, so one should bring all of oneself into it.

Bring your tools and your music, the things you have made for work or pleasure, and bring everyone else too. In quiet thought you cannot rise above what you have made or sink below your failures, and in worship you cannot rise above others' hopes or sink below their despair. To know God, do not try to solve riddles; look around and see Him playing with children.

To learn the secret of death, one must look for it within life itself. The owl, blind in daylight, cannot understand light, and in the same way the spirit of death can only be seen by opening the heart fully to life.

Life and death are one, like a river and the sea. Your deepest hopes hold a quiet sense of what lies beyond, and your fear of death is like a shepherd's trembling before a king who is about to honour him. The shepherd trembles even while he is joyful about the honour.

Death is described as standing naked in the wind and melting into the sun, and ceasing to breathe as freeing the breath to rise toward God. The passage then says that true singing, climbing and dancing come only after these things, once one has drunk from silence, reached the mountain top and been claimed by the earth.

Almeitra... no, this is the prophet Almustafa speaking to the people of Orphalese as he prepares to leave. He says he must go, even though he is less hasty than the wind that calls him. He explains that wanderers always move on, starting each day somewhere new, and that they keep travelling even while others sleep.

The speaker compares people to seeds that are scattered by the wind when they are ripe. He says his time with them was brief and his words few. Even if his voice fades from their ears and his love from their memory, he promises to return with a richer heart and to seek their understanding again, even after death.

The speaker, who is leaving his listeners, says that if his words were true, the truth will show itself later in clearer words. He will return from a deeper silence, as mist rises and falls again as rain.

The speaker says he has been like mist and a lake among the people he describes. Unseen, he moved through their streets and homes, felt their hearts and breath, and shared their joys, pains and dreams. Among them, he reflected their inner lives like a lake mirrors mountains.

The speaker says that what came to him from people's laughter and longing was something greater: the "boundless" or "vast man" in whom all people are like cells and sinews. People are vast only through this shared whole, and the speaker loved people by seeing them within it.

Gibran says a person is like a great oak in blossom: grounded in earth yet lifted toward heaven, and enduring. He rejects the saying that you are only as strong as your weakest link, calling it half the truth, since you are also as strong as your strongest link. Judging someone by their smallest deed is like judging the ocean by its foam.

Judging people by their failures is like blaming the seasons for changing. People are like the ocean: they cannot hurry their own tides, and their spring stays inside them even in their winter. The speaker asks listeners not to take these words as simple praise.

The speaker says his words only remind people of what they already know in thought. Words are just a shadow of a deeper, wordless knowing, which is like waves from a sealed memory holding the past of humanity and the earth. He came to learn from others, and he found something greater than wisdom.

Your spirit is a flame that keeps growing, and life keeps seeking life through bodies that fear death. There are no graves here: the land is a cradle and a stepping-stone. Where your ancestors are buried, you will see yourselves and your children dancing together.

The speaker says that others gave their followers worldly promises, while he gave only a small promise. Yet his listeners gave him more: they awakened in him a deeper desire for life. He finds his reward in the fact that, each time he comes to drink, the living water itself seems thirsty, and it drinks him as he drinks it.

The speaker says he will accept gifts but not wages. He has often gone without comfort, eating berries and sleeping in a temple porch, yet he feels that people's care for him made his food sweet and his sleep full of visions. He blesses them because they give generously without realizing they are giving.

The speaker answers critics who call him aloof. Kindness that admires itself and good deeds that praise themselves lose their value, becoming hard or harmful. He admits he goes to the hills and remote places, and asks how one can truly see people without distance, suggesting that closeness requires some separation.

Some people called out to the speaker without using words, asking why he lives on the high peaks and chases what cannot be reached. They invite him to come down, eat their bread and drink their wine. They say these things silently, in the privacy of their own souls.

The speaker says he searched only for the hidden meaning of the other person's joy and pain, and for their greater selves. Along the way he found that each of his own roles held its opposite: the hunter was also hunted, the flier also crawled, and the believer also doubted. He doubted so that his belief in the other could grow stronger.

The speaker says that a person is not limited to the body, a house, or a field. The true self is free, like a spirit that spreads over the earth and moves through the air. He admits these words are vague and asks readers not to try to make them clear, since vagueness is where all things begin.

Life begins in something vague and misty, not in something clear and fixed, and even a crystal may be mist that is slowly breaking down. The passage also says that the weakest-seeming part of a person is the strongest, and that human works, such as a city, come from a dream no one remembers having had.

The speaker says that if people could perceive the "breath" (a spiritual life force) and hear the "dream" behind all things, they would notice nothing else. People cannot yet see or hear this, and that is acceptable. The veil and clay blocking them will be removed by the same hands that made them, and then people will see and hear. They will not regret their earlier blindness or deafness.

The speaker says that in a future day people will see the hidden purpose behind everything and will bless darkness as they bless light. He then looks at his ship's pilot, who waits calmly while the wind and sails strain, and says the crew has listened to him patiently, as the pilot waits for his silence.

The speaker, about to die, says he is ready and that his life has ended, like a stream reaching the sea. He asks the people of Orphalese to keep what they were given and, if it is not enough, to gather together and ask the giver for more. He promises to return in another body.

The speaker is leaving, and the time they spent together is compared to a dream that has ended. Now it is full daylight and they must part. If they meet again in memory, they will speak again, and the other will sing a deeper song.

The speaker says that if their hands meet in another dream, they will build another tower in the sky. He then signals the sailors, who sail east while the people cry out together. Only Almitra stays silent, watching the ship disappear into the mist.

After the crowd has scattered, a woman stands alone on the sea-wall, keeping in her heart a saying of the prophet. He had said that his time with people would be only a short moment, and that another woman would bear him, meaning he would be born again in another life.

God, addressed as "thou," is said to have made the speaker endless. He keeps emptying and refilling the speaker like a vessel, and shapes the speaker like a reed flute to play new melodies. The speaker's small heart opens in joy, and God's endless gifts keep coming, with room always left to fill.

The speaker says that when God asks him to sing, his heart swells with pride and tears come to his eyes. Singing turns the harsh parts of his life into harmony. He knows God enjoys his singing, and that is the only way he comes before him. Caught up in the joy of song, he forgets himself and calls God friend, though God is his lord.

The speaker cannot understand how God, called "my master," sings, but listens in awe. God's music lights the world, flows across the sky, and breaks through every obstacle. The speaker's heart wants to join this song but cannot find a voice, so the speaker feels held captive by it.

The speaker vows to keep the body pure, the thoughts free of falsehood, and the heart free of evil and full of love. The reason given is that the divine "Life of my life" is present in each part of the self: in the body, in the mind as the light of reason, in the heart, and as the power behind action.

The speaker asks for a short pause from his work to sit with God, whom he addresses as "thee." Without that closeness, his heart finds no peace, and his work feels like endless, pointless labour. Now that summer has come, he wants to sit quietly in that presence and offer his life in song.

A speaker asks to be picked and offered up before the flower fades and the day ends. The flower is humble, with little colour or scent and no place in the garland, yet the speaker still asks to be used in service and plucked while there is time.

The speaker says the song has dropped all decoration, because ornaments would block closeness to God, whom the speaker calls "master poet." The speaker gives up personal vanity and asks only to be simple and open, like a reed flute that God can fill with music.

The speaker tells a mother that fine clothes can be a burden. A child dressed in princely finery cannot play freely and keeps away from the world for fear of spoiling them. So such finery is no real gain if it cuts a person off from ordinary human life.

The speaker tells the reader to stop carrying their own burdens and to leave them with God, who can bear everything, without looking back in regret. Desire is described as spoiling what it touches, so gifts should be accepted only when they come from sacred love.

The speaker says that God rests His feet among the poorest, lowliest and lost, and so the speaker's bowing, pride and heart cannot reach Him there. Pride in particular can never come close to where God walks among the humble. God is found with the poor and the lonely, not with the proud.

God is not found only in a shut temple, in chanting or in rituals. The poem places him with labourers who till the ground and break stones, sharing their dust and toil. Freedom from the world is not sought apart from this, because God has joined creation and is bound to it.

The speaker says the long journey through many worlds leads back to the self, or to God, which is nearest. The search ends when the seeker shuts the eyes and finds the divine presence, so the question "Where?" becomes the certainty "I am!"

The speaker has been preparing to sing a song, to welcome a visitor, but nothing is ready yet. The song is unfinished, the flower unopened, and the lamp unlit. The speaker has heard the visitor's footsteps but has not yet met him, and is still waiting.

The speaker says that God keeps refusing his many desires, and that these refusals are a kind of mercy that protects him from wanting too much or wanting weakly. He also says God gave him basic gifts, such as sky, light, body, life and mind, without being asked.

The speaker says he has been given a place in God's hall, and his only role is to sing to him. He has no real work in God's world, so his life can only pour out as songs without purpose. He asks to be called to sing at night in worship and in the morning.

The speaker says his life has been blessed by being invited to the world's festival. He has seen, heard, and played his part as fully as he could. Now he asks whether the time has come to enter and see God's face and greet him in silence.

The speaker says they are only waiting to give themselves over to love. Because of this, they have neglected their duties and ignored the laws and codes others set for them. People call them careless, and the speaker agrees they may be right. Others who came for them have given up and left.

A speaker waits alone at a door on a dark, rainy day, longing for a beloved who has not appeared. In the busy daytime he is among the crowd, but on this gloomy day he can hope only for the beloved, and he fears being left out entirely.

The speaker says that even if God stays silent, they will wait patiently, like the night before dawn. They believe the silence will end, and God's voice will then come as morning light, filling the speaker's life with song and flowers.

The speaker missed a lotus blooming because their mind was wandering, so their basket stayed empty. Stirred by a faint fragrance on the south wind, they longed for something they felt was incomplete. Only later did they realize that this sweetness was already theirs, blossoming inside their own heart.

The speaker feels they must set out on a journey now, but they are still waiting on the shore while spring has passed and the flowers have faded. They watch the restless waves and falling leaves, and they hear a distant song calling from the other shore, which stirs them to go.

The speaker addresses God as a figure walking unseen through a dark, silent rainy July day, when everything has shut itself away. The speaker has opened the gates of the house and begs this visitor not to pass by without stopping, like a dream.

The speaker stays awake on a stormy night, waiting for a friend who may be travelling through the dark to reach them. They open the door again and again, cannot see the path, and wonder where the friend is making their way.

The speaker asks God to cover him in night, as he covers the earth in sleep and closes the evening lotus. He asks that the tired traveller, whose supplies, clothes and strength are spent, be freed from shame and poverty and given new life through the night.

The speaker asks to rest in sleep at the end of a tiring day, without forcing a tired spirit into a weak attempt at worship. He trusts that God draws the night over the day's tired eyes so that they wake refreshed.
The speaker says that someone came and sat beside them at night, playing a harp, but they were asleep and did not wake. Their dreams were filled with the music, and they lament missing his visit.

The speaker feels lost in darkness and asks for light, which they can only find by lighting a lamp with desire and love. The heart is called toward a meeting with its lord through the dark night, and the speaker urges it not to let the hours pass unlit.

The speaker feels trapped by his own limits and wants to be free, yet he cannot bring himself to give up the worthless things that fill his life. He knows he has great wealth in God, who is his closest friend, but he clings to the dust and debts that hold him. He even fears that his prayer for good will be answered.
The speaker builds a wall of their own name and keeps adding to it, proud of it and careful to seal every gap. The wall grows so high that it hides their true self, which is trapped inside it.
The speaker goes out alone to meet God, but a loud, shameless self follows and cannot be escaped. The speaker feels ashamed to arrive at God's door with this lesser self in tow.
A prisoner explains that he was bound by his own greed and pride. He hoarded the wealth due to his king and forged a chain to hold the world, only to find that the chain held him instead.

The speaker says that people who love him try to hold him close, but God's love is greater and leaves him free. Even so, God's love keeps waiting for the speaker's love, even when he does not pray or think of God.

The speaker describes visitors who, by day, claim they want only a small corner and will modestly share in worship. At night, the speaker finds them breaking into the sacred place and greedily taking the offerings meant for God.

The speaker asks that very little of the self be kept: just enough to name God as his or her all, to sense God everywhere, to love God at every moment, and never to hide God. Even the remaining bond is wanted only as the bond of God's love, through which God's purpose is carried out.

The speaker prays that his country may wake up into a state of freedom, a heaven of freedom, addressed to God as "my Father." He describes that state as one where minds are fearless, knowledge is free, people are not divided by narrow walls, and thought and action keep growing.

The speaker asks God for strength: to bear joys and sorrows lightly, to use love in service, to not reject the poor or bow to arrogant power, to rise above small daily matters, and to give that strength back to God's will with love. The prayer also asks God to remove the deep poverty of spirit in the speaker's heart.

The speaker once thought their journey was over, with no strength, path or supplies left, and that only silence lay ahead. Yet they find that God's will has no limit in them: when old words fail, new songs rise from the heart, and when old paths vanish, new lands appear.

The speaker's heart keeps repeating one wish: to want only God. Every other desire that fills their days is false and empty. Even in their deepest unawareness, and even while they rebel against divine love, that same cry remains.

The speaker asks God to come to him in different ways whenever his life falls apart. When his heart is dry, he asks for a shower of mercy. When work or noise shuts God out, he asks for peace. When desire clouds his mind, he asks for light and thunder.

The speaker prays to God from a dry, suffering heart. He would rather receive a violent storm than the silent, burning heat he feels now. He asks for grace to come gently, like a mother's tearful look.

A woman waits by a dusty road for her lover, who she believes will come, though he has passed unnoticed among the crowds. She offers her flowers to passers-by, feels ashamed when they mock or smile at her, and will not explain why she waits. She keeps her hope and pride private.

The speaker sits waiting and imagines a grand arrival, in which a god-like "thou" would step down from a royal chariot to lift up a ragged beggar girl and honour her. But the chariot never comes. Many other processions pass instead, and the speaker asks whether only she is left waiting and weeping.

The speaker imagines a private voyage with a beloved, far from the world, where songs would flow freely like waves. But the boat has not yet set out. Evening has come, and the speaker asks whether the time has come yet, or whether there is still work to do, wondering when the chains will fall away.

The speaker says that in the past, without preparing for it, God (addressed as "my king") entered his heart and left his mark on many ordinary moments. Now he finds those moments in the dust of forgotten days, and sees God's mark on them. He adds that God did not scorn his childish play, and the footsteps he heard then are the same ones sounding across the stars.

The speaker is happy to sit and wait at the roadside, watching light, shadow and rain, while messengers from unknown places pass by. He expects that a happy moment of seeing will come suddenly. Until then he smiles and sings, and he feels that the air already holds the sweet scent of what is promised.

The speaker says that a presence, which they call "he," is always coming. This coming happens in every season, in joy and in sorrow. Whatever song the speaker sings, its notes always announce that he is coming.

The speaker feels that a divine presence, which they call "thee," has been drawing closer to them for a long time, through signs felt in the heart. Today this brings a trembling joy, and the speaker senses that the time has come to finish their life's work.

The speaker has waited all night for her lord, who has not come. She fears he will arrive while she sleeps, and asks her friends not to wake her. When she does wake, she wants the first sight to be his face and the first joy to come from him, so that returning to herself means returning to him.

The speaker describes a journey in which others rush ahead, ignoring the morning's beauty and never stopping. The speaker stops to rest by the water, and the companions laugh and go on until they disappear into the distance.

The speaker set out on a long journey with a group of travelers, but gave up the effort. Lulled by the shade and music of a quiet green place, they forgot their purpose and drifted off to sleep. On waking, they found the one they sought standing beside them, smiling, and realized the hard road had been unnecessary to fear.

A god or lord leaves his high place to stand at the humble door of a singer. He is drawn by one simple song, though his great hall is full of other music. He comes for that small voice, as if it were a gift worth a flower.

A beggar sees a king's golden chariot stop beside him, and hopes his luck has changed. Instead, the king holds out a hand and asks what he has to give. The beggar gives one grain of corn. Later he finds a tiny piece of gold among his grain, and regrets that he did not give everything.

The people in a village go to sleep at night, dismissing every sign that the king is coming: knocks, a messenger, wheels, a drum. Some warn them, but they laugh and explain the signs away. Then a voice calls them to wake, and they fear.

The speaker describes a king arriving at night, during a storm, to a poor and dark house. Some want to prepare lights, wreaths and a throne, but others say to greet him with empty hands and bare rooms. The speaker tells the house to open its doors and spread its tattered mat in the courtyard to receive him.

A woman wakes after her beloved has left and looks for a small keepsake, such as a petal from the rose wreath he wore. Instead she finds his heavy, flashing sword, a gift she cannot hide or understand.

The speaker receives a painful gift from God, which they accept as an honour. Pain and death are now their companions, and they no longer fear the world. They give up small, decorative ways of behaving, such as waiting and weeping, and take up God's sword as their adornment.

The speaker finds the god's sword more beautiful than his jeweled wristlet. The sword is curved like lightning, glows red in the sunset, and seems to burn away earthly feelings. Its beauty is terrible, both frightening to see and hard to think about.

A woman at a well, alone after the others have gone home, is lost in daydreams and does not notice a weary traveller approach. He says he is thirsty, and she wakes from her thoughts and pours water into his cupped hands. She asked him for nothing and he asked her for nothing; she simply gives what he needs.

A speaker is asked by someone for his name and feels ashamed, because he has done nothing worth being remembered. Still, he holds onto the memory of having given water to a thirsty traveler, and that memory comforts him. He sits alone in the late morning, thinking.

The speaker calls a sleepy, lazy heart to wake up and not waste its time. A friend, presumably the divine, waits alone at the end of a hard road, so the heart should not fail or mislead him. Even through heat and thirst, the speaker asks whether joy and music can still be found along the way.

The speaker says that God's joy and love depend on the speaker. God came down to the speaker, made him a partner in all of God's wealth, and took on beauty to win his heart. In the union of the two, God's love is seen fully.

The speaker addresses light as a beloved "darling" and describes it filling the world with joy. Light dances at the centre of the speaker's life, and everything around it, from butterflies and flowers to clouds and leaves, seems to overflow with gladness.

The speaker asks that every kind of joy be mixed into his final song. He names several: joy in the overflowing grass, joy that holds life and death together, joy that comes with storms, joy that sits with tears in pain, and joy that gives everything away without speaking.

The speaker says that the everyday sights and feelings of a morning, such as the light on the leaves, the drifting clouds and the cool breeze, are all the love of a beloved god. The morning light is a message to the speaker's heart, and the speaker feels close to this divine presence, as if God were looking down and the heart had reached His feet.

Children play on an endless seashore, building sand houses, floating leaf boats and gathering pebbles. They do not swim, fish or look for treasure as pearl divers and merchants do. The passage describes this carefree play as the children's way of being there.

Children play on a seashore where the sea rises and waves crash, even though storms wreck ships and death is near. The poem presents the sea's violence and the children's play side by side, as if both belong to the same endless world.

Tagore asks where a baby's sleep, smile and soft freshness come from, and answers with folk-like rumours. The sleep comes from a fairy village in the forest, the smile was born from a crescent moon touching an autumn cloud, and the freshness was hidden in the mother's heart when she was a young girl.

The speaker says that when he gives a child toys, sings, offers sweets, or kisses the child, he understands why the world holds colour, music, sweetness and pleasure. The child's simple joys reveal the same things found in nature.

The speaker says that God has brought him to new friends, new homes and strangers who feel like family. When he is uneasy about leaving a familiar place, he remembers that God is present in the new as well as the old. Once one knows God, nobody is a stranger and no door is closed. He asks never to lose the joy of feeling God in the many forms of life.

A speaker in a dark, lonely house asks a maiden on a river bank to lend him her lamp. She answers that she is carrying her lamp to float it on the stream at dusk, and she does not give him any light. He watches her small flame drift uselessly on the water, then asks again, now that her own lights are all lit.

A woman carries a lamp out into the dark, and the speaker asks her to light his own dark house. She answers that she is lighting her lamp for the sky, or for a festival of lamps, so she cannot give it away. Her light is lost among the others, and the speaker watches it fade without helping him.

The speaker asks God what drink he would like from the cup of the speaker's life. The speaker then suggests that God enjoys seeing the world through the speaker's eyes and hearing his own harmony through the speaker's ears. God gives himself in love and finds his own sweetness within the speaker.

The speaker has kept a hidden, veiled presence within himself all his life, never fully seen by anyone. He plans to offer her to God as his final gift, and she has waited alone for God to recognise her.

The poem sets two places side by side. Here, the beloved is a nest of love, full of colours, sounds and scents, where morning and evening bring beauty and peace. Beyond this, in the open infinite sky, there is only pure white light, with no day, night, form, colour, or words.

The speaker's life is pictured as a process that feeds God. Sunlight, which stands for God's love, reaches the speaker's door and carries back to God the speaker's tears, sighs and songs, which form clouds. God loves these clouds because they are soft, fleeting and sad, and they can shade God's bright light.

The speaker feels that the same life flowing through his own body also flows through the whole world, in the grass, the flowers, the sea, and in birth and death. Because of this shared life, he feels his body glorified and his pride comes from life across all ages.

Tagore asks whether we can share the joy of this endless movement and be swept along by it, even though it is wild and frightening. He describes all things rushing forward without looking back, with seasons, colours, sounds and scents passing away as quickly as they arrive.

Tagore's speaker says that the self's sense of being separate from God is God's own doing, a illusion called maya. God divides himself into many selves, and this division takes form in the speaker. The world of colours, songs, and changing ages is the play of God and the self hiding and seeking each other.

The speaker says that one inner presence, closest to the self, wakes the heart and stirs its feelings of joy and sorrow. This presence also weaves maya, the world of changing appearances, and the speaker feels it through that world. Across days and ages, it keeps moving the heart under many names and forms.

The speaker says freedom does not come through giving up the world. Instead, freedom is found within the pleasures of life, which are seen as expressions of the divine. Senses, desires and even illusions are imagined as turning into joy and love.

The speaker goes out at dusk to fetch water from a stream. The evening feels restless and the way is empty, and the speaker does not know if they will return or whom they will meet. At the river crossing, a stranger in a small boat is playing a lute.

Everything given to people by God meets their needs, yet it all returns to God whole. A river serves villages on its way, but its flow still ends at God's feet. A flower's scent serves the air, but it is finally offered to God. Each use of the world is said to lead back to God.

The speaker says that every day, and at the end of his life, he will stand face to face with God, the lord of his life and of all worlds. He will do this in solitude, in the busy world of work and crowds, and finally alone and without words.

The speaker says they know God only from a distance, as a master or father to be honoured, and will not come close to God as a friend or as one who is one's own. They also refuse to share with other people, stand beside them in joy or sorrow, or risk their life, and so they do not truly reach God.

The gods sing of a perfect creation until one of them notices that a star is missing, and the song breaks off. They mourn the lost star as the best of all, and they keep searching for her. The stars alone, in the silence of night, whisper that the search is pointless and that perfection is already complete.

The speaker asks that, if he cannot meet God in this life, he will never stop feeling the loss of that meeting. He wants this sense of missing God to stay with him in dreams and while awake, even in busy work, when resting, and in times of joy.

The speaker feels like a leftover autumn cloud drifting aimlessly, still apart from the sun, which is God in this poem. The speaker accepts whatever the sun wishes: to let the cloud be coloured and scattered by the wind, or to dissolve into night or morning light.

Time spent in idleness is not really lost, because God is working in every moment of a person's life. While the speaker slept, believing all work had stopped, hidden growth went on, and in the morning the garden was full of flowers.

God has unlimited time and can wait patiently, even for something as small as a wild flower to be perfected. The speaker, by contrast, is always short of time and gives it away to demanding people, so the altar is left empty. Yet at day's end the speaker finds that there is still time.

The speaker offers the Mother (God) a chain of pearls made from their own tears of sorrow. Stars are like jewelled ornaments for her feet, but the speaker's offering hangs on her breast. Wealth and fame belong to her to give or withhold, while the sorrow is the speaker's own gift, and she rewards it with grace.

Separation, or the ache of being apart, is presented as the force behind everything. It shows up as the shapes of the universe, the silent gaze of stars, the sound of rain-soaked leaves, human love, desire, suffering and joy, and the songs the speaker writes.

The poem asks where the warriors' power was hidden, since they came out of their master's hall looking weak and unarmed. On their return they had put down sword and bow, and they had left the results of their life behind. Their peace is what stands out.

Death is pictured as a servant sent by God to call the speaker home. Although the speaker feels fear, they will welcome Death at the door, offer their heart's treasure, and give their lonely self as a final offering.

The speaker has lost someone dear and cannot find her in his small home. He goes instead to God, whose dwelling is infinite, and asks to have his empty life plunged into the vast fullness of the universe, so that he may feel that lost touch again.

The speaker addresses a god whose temple has fallen into ruin and is no longer worshipped. Spring breezes and festival days pass without any worship, and the old worshipper still returns in hunger, unanswered. Other new idols are made and then forgotten, but this forgotten deity alone remains neglected for good.

The speaker says he will stop speaking loudly and will speak only in quiet, sung murmurs, as his master wishes. He leaves the busy world of buying, selling and daily strife, and turns to a playful, idle pleasure with God, though he does not know why he is called to it.
When death comes to the door, the speaker says they will offer it their whole life as a gift. They will give all their days, their harvests and their work, so death leaves with nothing empty-handed.

The speaker addresses death as the final fulfilment of life and asks it to come to them. They say everything they have lived for and loved has been directed toward death, and that after death their life will belong entirely to it. The speaker compares this to a bride who leaves home to meet her husband alone at night.

The speaker knows that one day his life will end and the world will go on without him. Thinking of this end makes him see the world as precious, even its humblest parts. He lets go of what he wanted and got, and asks to truly possess what he once ignored.

The speaker says he has been released and is leaving. He bids farewell to his companions, returns the keys to his house, and gives up his claims to it. He thanks them for what he received, and says he is ready, because a call has come to him.

The speaker is leaving on a journey and asks friends to wish them well. They go with nothing to carry, but with a hopeful heart, dressed for a wedding rather than for travel. They are not afraid of the dangers ahead, and expect to be met at the end by music from the King's gateway.

Tagore says that birth felt to him like entering a vast mystery, and that the unknown force behind it came to him in the form of his mother. Just as the unknown will appear familiar at life's start, he expects death to seem known too. Since he loves life, he says he will love death as well, much as a child cries when one breast is taken away and then finds comfort at the other.

The speaker is leaving this life and says his final message: what he has seen is beyond compare. He feels he has tasted a hidden sweetness and has seen the formless divine present in the world of many forms. He accepts whatever end comes next.

In the speaker's childhood, playing with God felt easy and carefree, and they never asked who God was or what his songs meant. Now that this time has ended, the speaker sees the whole world bowed in awe before God's feet.

The speaker says that they will offer God their own defeat as a garland. They know their pride will break, their life will burst its limits, and their heart will pour out in music. In the end, they will lose everything and die at God's feet.

The speaker gives up control and steers no more, trusting that the divine "lord" will take over. They stop struggling, accept their failure, and wait quietly in the dark, ready for the lord to come whenever he chooses.

The speaker gives up searching among the visible, changing things of life. He wants to dive into the unseen and the eternal, and he is ready to die into it. He will offer his life, like a harp, to the silent source of all things.

The speaker has always searched for God, called "thee," through songs. The songs led the speaker from place to place, taught life's lessons, and showed hidden paths. At the end of the journey, the speaker asks which palace gate the songs have finally brought them to.

The speaker once boasted that he knew God, and his works show God's image. When people ask who God is, or what his songs mean, he cannot explain, so they mock him and leave, while God sits there smiling.

The speaker asks that all of his senses, thoughts, songs and whole life be brought together in one act of respect toward God. He compares this to a low rain-cloud about to release its rain, to scattered songs flowing into one stream, and to homesick cranes flying back to their nests.

Tea, the passage says, moved from medicine to drink, then to a polite pastime in China, and in Japan became "Teaism": a way of life that finds beauty in ordinary, messy daily existence. It values purity, harmony, and social order, and it honors imperfection as an honest attempt to do something good within a flawed life.

Okakura says the Philosophy of Tea is more than love of beauty. It combines beauty with ethics and religion to show a whole view of humanity and nature. In his words, tea teaches cleanliness, simplicity over costly show, and a sense of proportion to the universe, and it makes everyone who practises it a judge of taste.

Okakura says that Japan's long isolation from the rest of the world encouraged inward reflection, and this helped Teaism, his name for the tea tradition, grow strongly. Teaism shaped many parts of Japanese life, from homes and clothing to food, art, and literature, and it reached both the nobility and ordinary people.

Even ordinary Japanese people, such as peasants and labourers, are said to share a sensitivity to beauty, shown in flower arranging and in respect for nature. People are called "with no tea" if they feel nothing for life's dramas, and "with too much tea" if they are wild aesthetes who ignore its tragedies.

The passage defends the fuss people make over tea. Critics may call it a storm in a teacup, but the writer says human pleasure is small and easily used up, so people have always devoted themselves to something. Other peoples have given themselves to wine or war, and tea is no worse. In tea, he says, one can taste the qualities of Confucius, Laotse and the Buddha.

People who cannot see the smallness of great things in themselves tend to miss the value of small things in others. The author says that a typical Westerner sees the tea ceremony as just another odd custom of the East. He notes that such a person called Japan barbaric while it practised peaceful arts, but calls it civilised now that it wages war in Manchuria.

Okakura says that people have written much about the samurai warrior code, which he calls the art of death, but have paid little attention to tea culture, which he calls the art of life. He would rather remain seen as barbarians than have Japan's claim to civilisation rest on the glory of war, and he hopes his nation's art and ideals will one day get proper respect.

Western writers have built a distorted picture of Asian peoples. Asians are shown as either fanatical or sensual, and their traits are mocked: Indian spirituality as ignorance, Chinese calm as stupidity, Japanese patriotism as fatalism. The author finds this picture strange and wrong.

Asia teases Europeans and Americans in return for their own mockery. Asian writers once imagined Westerners as strange and absurd, with hidden tails and a taste for eating babies, and as people who preached what they did not practice.

Asian nations are losing old misunderstandings about the West, as trade brings European languages to Eastern ports and young Asians study at Western colleges. The author admits his countrymen do not yet understand Western culture well, but says they are willing to learn. He notes that some copy Western manners and dress, wrongly thinking that stiff collars and silk hats are what make a civilisation, and he calls this a sign of eagerness to approach the West humbly.

Okakura says that Western people often fail to understand the East. Christian missionaries come to teach and not to learn. Western knowledge of Eastern culture rests on poor translations or on careless stories from travellers, with only a few writers, such as Lafcadio Hearn, explaining it with real sympathy.

The author says he may be showing his lack of knowledge of the tea ceremony by speaking so frankly. Politeness would normally require saying only what is expected, but he will not follow that custom. He believes misunderstanding between East and West has caused much harm, so he feels free to add his own part toward better mutual understanding.

The author argues that the Russo-Japanese War could have been avoided if Russia had understood Japan better. He says Western powers wrongly mock Asia's concerns and fail to see that Asia could also turn against them. He ends by joking that Westerners lack the calm, refined spirit that tea stands for.

Okakura proposes that East and West stop trading clever sayings and instead learn from each other, since each has developed differently. He says the West has gained expansion at the cost of restlessness, while the East has a harmony that is weak against aggression, and he claims the East is better off in some ways.

Okakura says tea is the one Asian ceremony that people everywhere respect. Western people have mocked Eastern religion and morals, yet they readily drink tea and have made afternoon tea an important social custom. He claims this shows the Eastern spirit winning out in at least this one case.

Tea first appears in European accounts through a few early references. An Arab traveller noted that tea and salt duties were major income in Canton after 879, and Marco Polo recorded a Chinese finance minister removed in 1285 for raising tea taxes unfairly. Only in the late 1500s did the Dutch bring Europe word of a drink made from a bush's leaves.

The passage traces how tea spread to Europe. Several early European travellers wrote about it, and Dutch ships brought it in 1610. It then reached France, Russia and England over the next few decades, and England's early name for it came from the Chinese word "Tcha."

Early critics of tea in England called it a filthy custom and said it harmed people's looks and health. Its high price also kept it for the rich and for gifts to nobles. Even so, tea drinking spread quickly.

Tea spread quickly in eighteenth-century Britain and its colonies, where it became a common drink and a source of tax revenue. The passage points to tea's role in history: heavy taxes on it provoked American colonists, and the protest against them, the Boston Tea Party, is said to mark the start of American independence.

Okakura says tea has a subtle charm that makes it easy to idealise, and Western writers liked to link their thoughts to its scent. He contrasts tea with wine, coffee and cocoa, which he describes as arrogant, self-conscious and simpering. He then quotes an early 1700s English periodical that recommends its essays to families who set aside a morning hour for tea.

Okakura quotes two writers who praised tea in a playful way. One asks that a newspaper be served with tea and treated as part of the tea things. Samuel Johnson describes himself as a devoted tea drinker who used tea for meals, evenings, nights and mornings.

Okakura says that Teaism, his name for the way of tea, is the art of hiding beauty so that others must find it themselves, and of hinting at things without stating them. He calls it a calm, thorough way of laughing at oneself, which he treats as a kind of humour and a "smile of philosophy." He supports this by quoting Charles Lamb's pleasure in doing good quietly and being discovered by chance.

Okakura says that writers who find humour in life, such as Thackeray and Shakespeare, are a kind of "tea-philosopher." He also suggests that poets who rejected materialism opened a path toward Teaism, and that today East and West might meet by quietly accepting imperfection.

In this Taoist story, the Yellow Emperor, who represents heaven's sun, defeats Shuhyung, a demon of darkness and earth. As Shuhyung dies, he breaks the sky, and the Emperor searches for someone to mend the heavens and succeeds.

In the myth, the goddess Niuka repairs the sky with a rainbow but leaves two small gaps. Because of these gaps, love begins as two souls moving through space, restless until they join and complete the world. The passage ends by saying that each person must rebuild their own sky of hope and peace.

Modern people, the author says, are caught up in a fierce struggle for wealth and power, driven by selfishness and vulgarity, and East and West are both failing to recover what matters in life. He calls for a great repairer to arrive, and in the meantime invites the reader to enjoy a cup of tea and the quiet beauty of the moment.

Tea, like painting, is an art that needs a skilled hand to show its best qualities. No fixed recipe makes perfect tea, just as no rules produce a great painting. Each brewing has its own character and way of relating to water and heat, and true beauty must be present in it.

A Sung-dynasty poet named Lichilai is quoted as saying there are three sad wastes in the world: young people spoiled by false education, fine art cheapened by vulgar admiration, and good tea ruined by clumsy preparation. The writer says people constantly fail to notice the basic rule of art and life behind these losses.

Tea has changed over time in three main stages: boiled, whipped, and steeped. Okakura says the way people prepare tea reflects the spirit of their age, because our unconscious habits show our deepest thoughts. He adds that Confucius said people do not hide themselves.

Okakura argues that people show their true character in small everyday habits, since they have little of greatness to hide. Small routines reveal a culture's ideals as much as great philosophy or poetry does. He compares this to how different European countries and periods have different favorite wines, and says the ideals of tea reflect the different moods of Eastern culture.

Okakura says that three ways of preparing tea mark three periods of Chinese history. Boiled cake-tea, whipped powdered tea, and steeped leaf-tea reflect the Tang, Sung, and Ming dynasties. He suggests calling them the Classic, Romantic, and Naturalistic schools of tea, borrowing terms from art.

The passage describes how the tea plant, native to southern China, was known and valued in early Chinese plant lore and medicine. People believed it relieved tiredness, refreshed the mind, strengthened the will and improved eyesight. Taoists saw it as part of an elixir of immortality, and Buddhists used it to stay awake during long meditation.

By the fourth and fifth centuries, tea had become popular in the Yangtse valley in China. Poets praised it, and emperors gave special tea leaves as rewards. But the way people drank it was still very simple.

Tea was once prepared by steaming and pounding the leaves into a cake, then boiling them with other foods and spices such as rice, salt, ginger, and milk. Okakura says this method still survives in some places, including Tibet, parts of Mongolia, and the Russian habit of adding lemon to tea.

Luwuh, an 8th-century Chinese poet, is presented as the first great teacher of tea, who turned it from a rough drink into a refined art. He saw in the tea ceremony the same harmony and order found throughout the universe. He wrote the "Chaking," which set out the rules of tea, and later Chinese tea merchants honored him as their protecting spirit.

Luwuh, author of the Chaking (the classic tea book), describes the best tea leaves through a series of images. He says they should have creases like a Tartar horseman's leather boot, curl like an ox's dewlap, unfold like mist from a ravine, gleam like a breeze-touched lake, and feel wet and soft like freshly rained-on earth.

This passage is a short note on a later chapter of the book. It says the chapter lists and describes twenty-four pieces of tea equipment, from the tripod brazier to the bamboo cabinet that holds them all. It also points out two things: the author's fondness for Taoist symbols, and the effect of tea on Chinese pottery.

Early Chinese potters tried to copy the colour of jade, which led to blue and white glazes. Luwuh, an early tea expert, preferred blue cups because they made the tea look greener, while white cups made it look pinkish. Later, Sung tea masters, who used powdered tea, chose heavy dark bowls instead.

Luwuh, a Chinese writer on tea, sets out how to make tea. He says to use no ingredients except salt, and he ranks water: mountain spring water is best, then river water, then spring water. He also names three stages of boiling, marked by the size and movement of the bubbles.

The passage describes how a compressed tea cake was prepared in old Chinese-style tea drinking. The tea is roasted soft, ground to powder, and added to boiling water in stages, with salt in the first boil and a splash of cold water at the third to settle it. The tea is then poured and drunk, and the writer praises its appearance, with its floating leaves compared to clouds and lilies.

Lotung, a Tang poet, describes how each cup of tea affects him, moving from wetting his throat to easing his loneliness, cleansing his body, and finally lifting him toward the immortals' realm of Horaisan. By the seventh cup he feels only a cool breeze and imagines riding it away to that land.

The remaining chapters of the Chaking, an old Chinese book on tea, are described as covering several subjects. These are the poor manners of ordinary tea-drinking, notable tea-drinkers of the past, famous tea farms in China, ways to arrange the tea service, and pictures of tea equipment. The last chapter has been lost.

Lu Yu, the author of the Chaking (a famous book on tea), became a favourite of Emperor Taisung and gained many followers. Some refined connoisseurs were said to tell his tea apart from that of his students. One official is remembered mainly because he failed to recognise the tea of this master.

In the Sung dynasty of China, tea was prepared by grinding the leaves into fine powder and whisking it into hot water with a bamboo whisk. This replaced the older way, and salt was no longer added. People of the time were very keen on tea.

Tea lovers competed to find new kinds of tea, and held contests to judge which was best. Emperor Kiasung spent his wealth collecting rare teas and wrote about twenty varieties, ranking "white tea" as the finest.

The Sung-dynasty tea ideal differed from the earlier Tang one, just as their view of life differed. Where the Tang had tried to suggest ideas through tea, the Sung tried to put them into practice. For Sung thinkers, the everyday world was itself the cosmic law, and the process of constant change mattered more than any single act.

Tea came to be seen as more than a pleasant pastime. It became a way for a person to come to know and become their true self, facing nature directly. Two early writers praise tea: one likens its bitterness to good advice, the other to a virtuous man who resists corruption.

Zen Buddhist monks developed a formal tea ritual. They gathered before a statue of Bodhidharma, the founder of Zen, and shared tea from one bowl in a very solemn way, like a sacred rite. This ritual later grew into Japan's tea ceremony in the 1400s.

Mongol invaders in the thirteenth century conquered China and destroyed the culture of the Sung dynasty. Later the native Ming dynasty tried to restore Chinese rule but faced internal troubles, and the Manchus took power in the seventeenth century. Over these changes, old customs disappeared completely.

Powdered tea, once the usual way of drinking tea, has been forgotten in China. A later Chinese writer could not recall the shape of a whisk named in an older classic. Tea is now made by steeping leaves in hot water. Europe learned tea only late, so it never knew the older method.

In this passage, Okakura says that the modern Chinese drink tea as a pleasure but no longer treat it as something ideal. He claims that long national hardship has left them without enthusiasm for life's meaning, so they accept things calmly rather than conquer or worship nature. The grand ceremonial spirit of the earlier Tang and Song dynasties is missing from their tea.

Japan adopted tea from China and used it in three stages. The passage gives early records: Emperor Shomu served tea to monks in 729, a monk named Saicho planted tea seeds in 801, and later tea gardens and a taste for tea among nobles and priests are mentioned.

Tea of the Sung dynasty in China reached Japan in 1191, brought back by the monk Yeisai, who had studied Zen there. He planted the seeds in three places, and as the Zen school spread quickly, so did the Chinese tea ceremony and its ideals.

By the fifteenth century the tea ceremony had become a separate, non-religious practice under a Shogun's patronage, and Japanese tea culture was firmly established. Steeped tea, common in China, reached Japan only in the mid-1600s. It has since replaced powdered tea for everyday drinking, though powdered tea remains the most prized kind.

Japanese tea ceremony is presented as the highest form of the tea ideals. Tea in Japan became more than a way of drinking: it became a way of living, and a ritual in which host and guest worship purity and refinement and reach a high happiness within ordinary life.

The passage describes the tea-room as a calm refuge from everyday life, where guests share art and the tea ceremony. Its aims were harmony and simplicity: no clashing colour, sound, gesture or word, and every movement natural. The author says this approach was often achieved, and that Teaism was a form of Taoism in disguise.
Zen and tea are closely linked, as is widely known. The tea ceremony grew out of Zen ritual. The name of Laotse, the founder of Taoism, is also closely tied to the history of tea.

According to a Chinese manual, the custom of serving tea to a guest began with Kwanyin, a disciple of Laotse, who offered a cup of tea to Laotse at a mountain pass. The author does not vouch for the story, but says it shows that Taoists drank tea early. He also regrets that no good English account of Taoist and Zen teaching yet exists.

Translation can never fully capture the original, much as the back of a brocade shows the threads but not the fine colours and design. The author adds that great teachings are hard to explain, so the ancient sages spoke in paradoxes rather than systematic statements, to avoid half-truths. Laozi adds that people of low understanding laugh at the Tao, and that this laughter is itself a sign it is the Tao.

Tao means "path" or "way," and it has been translated in many ways, such as the Absolute, the Law, or Nature. Laotse, the founder of Taoism, describes it as an all-containing thing that existed before Heaven and Earth, which he calls the Path because he does not know its real name.

The Tao, the Taoist idea of the ultimate way of things, is described here as constant change rather than a fixed road. Infinity passes into fleeting things, which vanish and return, so the Tao is an endless cycle of new forms, like clouds that fold and unfold. Its unchanging reality is the changing world itself.

Okakura says Taoism and Zen belong to an individualist way of thinking found in southern China, while Confucianism reflects the more communal north. He compares the two regions to Europe's north and south, noting that the southern and northern Chinese still differ in thought after centuries of unity.

Okakura says that in the old days, when travel and communication were hard, the thinking of northern and southern China differed sharply. The southern art and poetry, he says, had a different feel from the northern, which was more practical and moral. Laotse, who lived five centuries before the Christian Era, is named as an early example of the southern idealism.

Taoist thought, according to this passage, has roots earlier than Laotse, the teacher also called Long-Eared. Ancient Chinese records, such as the Book of Changes, already hint at his ideas. The passage then turns to the strong respect for the laws and customs of China's early classical age, which ended with the Chow dynasty.

Okakura says that individualism, the value of the self, was held back for a long time in early China. It flowered freely only after the Chow dynasty fell and many small kingdoms formed. Laotse and Chuangtse, both from the south, led this new free-thinking school, while Confucius worked to keep old traditions in place.

Taoists held that right and wrong are only relative, so fixed moral rules are not absolute. Okakura says that society's moral codes came from past needs and that keeping them means the individual gives way to the state. He adds that education keeps people in a kind of ignorance that props up this arrangement.

Okakura argues that people learn to act properly rather than to be truly good, and that we behave well mainly because we fear being seen as we really are. He sees the world as full of trade, where virtues like honour and religion are sold as goods, and religion amounts to ordinary morality dressed up with ritual.

The passage says that people sell themselves cheaply, such as trading a prayer for a ticket to heaven. It warns that anyone whose real worth became known would be sold to the highest bidder, and asks whether the urge to advertise oneself comes from the days of slavery.

Okakura says that Taoism was a strong force in its own time, in the Qin dynasty, the period that unified China and gave the country its name. He suggests it also shaped later thinkers, such as mathematicians, writers on law and war, mystics, alchemists and nature poets, but he has no space to discuss this in detail.

Okakura says that Chinese thinkers who argued about abstract matters, including a famous question about whether a white horse is real, deserve notice. He especially credits Taoism with shaping the Chinese character toward reserve and refinement, and notes that Taoist believers, both rulers and hermits, acted on its teachings in many ways.

Okakura says that Taoist tales offer both teaching and entertainment, full of stories, parables and short sayings. He mentions figures such as an emperor who never died because he never lived, and Liehtse, who rides the wind and finds it still because he is the wind. He adds that even modern Chinese Taoism, which he calls a grotesque version, is rich in images found nowhere else.

Okakura says that Taoism's greatest influence in Asia lies in aesthetics, which he describes as the "art of being in the world." Taoism focuses on the present moment, where life is lived. He argues that life's art is constantly adjusting oneself to one's surroundings.

Taoism accepts everyday life as it is and looks for beauty in it, while Confucianism and Buddhism do not. A Sung-dynasty story shows this: Confucius tastes life's vinegar and finds it sour, the Buddha finds it bitter, and Laotse finds it sweet.

The Taoists taught that life goes better when each person keeps a sense of the whole and makes room for others without giving up their own place. Laotse, the founder of Taoism, used the image of emptiness, or vacuum, to show that what matters most is found in that empty space.

A room is useful because of the empty space inside it, not because of its roof and walls. Likewise, a water pitcher works through the empty space that holds the water. The passage says that emptiness is what makes things useful and able to contain and move, and that a person who becomes empty, open to others, can master any situation.

Jiu-jitsu takes its name from a Taoist text, and it works by not resisting an attack. The fighter lets the enemy use up his own strength, then wins with the strength he has kept. In art, the same idea appears as suggestion: what is left unsaid lets the viewer complete the work and feel it fully.

The passage describes the ideal "Real man" of Taoist thought, who has mastered how to live. He stays modest and gentle, hides his own brilliance to blend in with ordinary people, and is cautious and humble in how he acts. His three main values are pity, thrift, and modesty.

Zen says it follows the teachings of Taoism. Its name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning meditation, and it holds that deep, focused meditation leads to full self-realisation. Zen followers also claim that the Buddha stressed this method in his later teaching and passed it on to his chief disciple, Kashyapa.

According to Zen tradition, the secret teaching passed down through a line of early teachers, from Kashiapa to Ananda and onward, until it reached Bodhi-Dharma, who brought Zen to China. The author admits the history of these teachers is uncertain. Early Zen, he says, resembles two Indian philosophies: Nagarjuna's Negativism and Sancharacharya's Gnan.

Zen teaching as it is known today is traced mainly to three Chinese teachers. Huineng (Yeno), the sixth patriarch, founded Southern Zen. Mazu (Baso) made Zen a living influence in China, and his pupil Baizhang (Hiakujo) set up the first Zen monastery with its rules.

After the time of Baso, Zen discussions took on a more Chinese way of thinking, moving away from earlier Indian idealism. The author sees a strong resemblance between Southern Zen and the Taoist teachings of Laotse, whose book, the Tao-te-ching, already mentions self-concentration and control of the breath, both key parts of Zen meditation.

Zen, like Taoism, is presented as the understanding of relativity: truth is reached by grasping opposites. It also stresses individualism, holding that only what concerns the working of one's own mind is real.

Two short Zen stories make one point: the real movement is in the mind, not in the wind, the flag, or the outside world. A hare runs from a monk because of the monk's own inner state, not because of what the monk is thinking or doing.

Zhuangzi (Soshi) is walking by a river with a friend and says the fish are enjoying themselves. The friend asks how he could know that, since he is not a fish. Zhuangzi replies that the friend is not him, so the friend cannot know whether he knows the fish are happy.

Zen Buddhists valued direct insight into the inner nature of things over words, scriptures and outward forms, which they saw as obstacles to truth. This preference is why they favoured simple black and white sketches over the coloured paintings of older Buddhist schools.

Tankawosho, a Zen monk, burned a wooden Buddha statue to warm himself on a cold day. When a bystander called this sacrilege, he said he was looking for sacred relics, called shali, in the ashes. When told he would find none in a wooden image, he replied that if he found none, the statue was not a Buddha, so he had committed no sacrilege.

Zen holds that ordinary, everyday matters are as important as spiritual ones. Every small thing, like an atom, has the same possibilities as the whole universe. A seeker should find the inner light in his own daily life, and the layout of Zen monasteries reflected this view.

In a Zen monastery, the senior monks were given the hardest chores, such as weeding, peeling vegetables and serving tea, while novices had lighter work. Every small task had to be done perfectly, and serious philosophical debates often happened during these jobs. The author says the whole ideal of tea comes from this idea that small everyday actions matter greatly.

European architects, used to stone and brick, have tended to think Japanese wood and bamboo building hardly counts as architecture. Only recently has one Western scholar praised the great Japanese temples. So an outsider could not be expected to appreciate the tea-room, which follows entirely different building and decoration principles.

The tea-room, called the Sukiya, presents itself as nothing more than a simple straw hut. Its name has been written in different ways over time, and the meaning shifts with the characters chosen. The writer says it is an "Abode of Fancy" because it is a temporary building made to hold a poetic feeling.

The tea-room is described as empty of decoration, holding only what suits the mood of the moment, and as unsymmetrical, leaving something unfinished so the viewer's imagination can complete it. Since the sixteenth century these tea ideals have shaped Japanese houses so strongly that ordinary interiors look bare to foreigners.

Rikiu, a sixteenth-century tea master, is credited with building the first tea-room that stood on its own, apart from other rooms. He also helped set the formal rules of the tea ceremony. The size of the room had earlier been fixed by Jowo, a fifteenth-century tea master.

Early tea-rooms were just a part of an ordinary room, cut off from the rest with screens. This section was called the Kakoi, or "enclosure," a name still used for tea-rooms built inside a house rather than as separate buildings.

The passage describes the parts of a Japanese tea house, called a sukiya. These are the small tea-room itself, built for no more than five people, a washing room for the tea utensils, a waiting porch for guests, and a garden path linking the porch to the tea-room. The tea-room itself looks plain.

A tea-room is very small, and its plain materials are chosen to look like modest poverty. But this look is the result of careful artistic planning. Building one costs more than an ordinary house because its materials and craftsmanship need great care.
Carpenters who built for tea-masters formed their own respected group among craftsmen. Their work was as fine and careful as that of makers of lacquer cabinets.

The tea-room is unlike Western buildings, and also unlike Japan's older grand buildings. Those older temples and palaces were impressive in size, and the few that survived fires still awe viewers with their grandeur and rich decoration.

Japanese wooden buildings were built with huge pillars and a network of supporting brackets. This design was weak against fire but strong against earthquakes and suited to the local climate. Two old temples, the Golden Hall of Horyuji and the Pagoda of Yakushiji, have stood almost intact for nearly twelve centuries.

Early Japanese temples and palaces were richly decorated inside, with canopies, gilded hangings, mirrors, mother-of-pearl and painted walls. Later buildings such as Nikko and Nijo castle put even more ornament into their surfaces, at the cost of the structure's own beauty.

The tea-room copied the bare simplicity of the Zen monastery. Zen monasteries exist only as places for monks to live, study and meditate, not as places of worship or pilgrimage. Their main room is empty apart from a central alcove holding a statue of the sect's founder, or of Sakyamuni, the Buddha, with two early patriarchs.

Zen monks once drank tea from a bowl in front of an image of Bodhidharma, and this ritual became the basis of the tea ceremony. The author adds that the Zen chapel's altar was the model for the tokonoma, the honored alcove in a Japanese room where paintings and flowers are displayed for guests.

The tea-room is kept at four and a half mats, about ten feet square, because of a story in a Buddhist sutra. In that story a king welcomes a great saint and eighty-four thousand disciples into a room of this size. The story is a picture of the idea that, for a truly enlightened person, space does not really exist.

The garden path (roji) leading to the tea-room is meant to be the first step of meditation. Walking along it cuts the visitor off from the outside world and prepares the mind to enjoy the tea-room. The walk, past stepping stones, pine needles and moss-covered stone lanterns, lifts the walker's spirit above everyday thoughts.

Some tea-masters designed the garden path (roji) leading to the tea-room to create a feeling of being far from the city, as if in a forest. Rikiu, one such master, aimed for utter loneliness and quoted an old poem about a lone cottage on a beach at autumn dusk.

The passage describes the mood a tea-room was built to create: a soul just waking up, still caught in dim memories of the past, but calm in a soft spiritual light and longing for the freedom of the open space beyond. "He" refers to the builder of the tea-room, the tea master Sen no Rikyu.

Guests in a tea-room must leave their swords outside, since the room is meant as a place of peace. They then crawl through a very low door, a custom meant to make everyone, high or low, humble. Once inside, they take their seats quietly, after bowing to the picture or flower arrangement in the alcove.

The host waits to enter until every guest is seated and the room is silent. The only sound is water boiling in an iron kettle, which is built so that it makes a melody like distant waterfalls, surf, rain, or wind in pines.

The room is kept dim, with muted colors and old-looking furnishings, so that nothing looks newly bought. The only exceptions are the white bamboo dipper and linen napkin, which are new. Even though the room and its utensils look worn, they are spotlessly clean.

In a tea-room, the host must keep it free of dust, since a tea-master is judged by his cleanliness. Yet cleaning is an art, not a matter of scrubbing everything hard. Old metal should not be scrubbed harshly, and a few drops of water on a flower vase can be left, since they suggest dew and coolness.

Rikiu, a famous tea master, made his son Shoan sweep and water the garden path again and again, calling it not clean enough each time. The story shows how tea masters understood cleanliness: it was a matter of a very thorough standard, not just tidying up.

A young attendant has swept the garden path until it is spotless, leaving not a single leaf. The tea-master Rikiu corrects him by shaking a tree himself, so that gold and crimson autumn leaves fall across the garden. The point is that a natural scene looks better with some fallen leaves than with perfect bareness.

The tea-room is built to suit one particular person, the tea master, and not the other way round. It is not meant to last for later generations, so it is temporary. The author links this to an old Japanese belief that a home should be abandoned when its main occupant dies.

Okakura notes that ancient Japanese customs often involved building new things. A newly married couple was given a new house, and the Imperial capital was often moved to a new site. The Ise shrine, dedicated to the Sun-Goddess, is still rebuilt every twenty years.

Okakura says the tea customs needed light wooden buildings that could be taken down and put up again easily. Brick or stone buildings would have made moving them impossible. Later, heavier Chinese-style wooden building was adopted, and that made such moving impractical.

In the fifteenth century, Zen individualism gave the old idea of the tea-room a deeper meaning. Zen, following the Buddhist teaching that all things pass away, and stressing that spirit should rule over matter, saw the house only as a temporary shelter for the body.

The body is compared to a hut in the wilderness, a flimsy shelter of tied-together grasses that falls back into wasteland when the binding comes apart. The tea-room expresses the same idea through its thatched roof, slender pillars, bamboo supports and plain materials, which suggest impermanence and fragility.
The passage says that the eternal, or the lasting and true, is found only in spirit. When that spirit is present in simple surroundings, it makes them beautiful through its refined, subtle light.

The main point is that a tea-room should be built to fit one person's taste, because art must be alive and connected to the present. Old styles should be absorbed into today's thinking, not copied slavishly. Strict following of traditions and formulas blocks personal expression in architecture.

Okakura laments that modern Japanese buildings copy European styles without originality. He suggests that art may be in a period of democratisation, waiting for a great master to start a new line, and he wishes people copied older models less and valued them more.

The tea-room is kept almost empty. Only a single art object is brought in for a particular occasion, and everything else in the room is chosen to support it. Okakura ties this emptiness to the Taoist idea that the empty space contains everything, and to the need for decoration to keep changing.

Real appreciation of beauty, the passage says, comes only from focusing on one central idea, just as we can only follow one piece of music at a time. For this reason, Japanese tea-room decoration is the opposite of Western houses, which are often filled with many objects like a museum.

A Japanese viewer, used to plain decoration that changes often, sees a Western room crowded with pictures, statues and ornaments all the time as simply showing off wealth. The passage is describing how that room looks to a Japanese eye.

It takes great appreciation of art to enjoy even a masterpiece when it is always in view. Living every day among the jumbled colors and shapes often found in Western homes would require an even greater capacity for artistic feeling.

Japanese art often avoids perfect symmetry, a trait Western critics have often noted. The author says this comes from Zen's development of Taoist ideas. Older Chinese and Buddhist art, by contrast, often strove for symmetry.

Classical Japanese rooms were arranged in a fixed, orderly way. The Taoist and Zen view of beauty instead values the process of seeking perfection over perfection itself. In the tea-room, each guest is meant to complete the scene in his own imagination.

Under the influence of Zen, Far Eastern art avoided symmetry, since it suggested repetition and dulled the imagination. So artists preferred landscapes, birds and flowers to human figures, leaving the viewer to supply the human presence. The author adds that people already stand out too much, and even self-interest becomes dull.

In the tea-room, objects are chosen so that no colour, design or shape is repeated. A flower and a painting of flowers should not appear together, and the room's parts should differ from one another. The aim is to avoid any sense of sameness.

Japanese room decoration works differently from Western decoration, which often places objects in matched, symmetrical rows on mantelpieces and elsewhere. The writer finds such repetition pointless, and says that talking with someone while their full-length portrait stares at you from behind them is awkward.

The passage asks why people hang pictures of hunted animals, carved fish and fruit, or display old family plates in a dining room. Such displays of abundance seem out of place at a meal, and they can even make the diner uneasy.

The tea-room is a quiet place, free from coarseness, where a person can give full attention to beauty and escape the troubles of the outside world. The author says it served warriors and rulers in the past, let people of every rank meet as equals before art, and that modern industry makes refinement harder, so the tea-room is needed even more now.

A legendary harp, made from a great Kiri tree, would sound only for a true master. The Emperor of China owned it, but everyone who tried to play it got harsh, discordant notes instead of the music they wanted. The harp would not accept any player as its master.
Peiwoh, a legendary master harpist, plays so that a tree he has made from wood remembers its life in nature. Spring returns in its branches, and the waterfalls seem to laugh with the flowers.

Each sentence describes a season through sounds and sights: summer with insects, rain and a cuckoo's call; autumn with a roaring tiger and a moon over frost; winter with snow, swans and hailstones. The lines show nature changing through the year, each season given its own vivid scene.

Peiwoh, a legendary harpist, plays love, then war, and the emperor asks how he won. He explains that others failed because they played only themselves. He let the harp choose its own theme, so he no longer knew whether he was playing the harp or the harp was playing him.

A great artwork works like music played on our deepest feelings. Peiwoh was a legendary musician, and the harp of Lungmen is the instrument he played; the passage says true art is his playing and we are the instrument. When art touches us, it wakes feelings we did not know we had, and the work and the viewer become part of each other.
