Art appreciation needs a shared understanding between viewer and artist, and the viewer must prepare to receive the artwork's message. The tea-master Kobori-Enshiu compared approaching a great painting to approaching a great prince: humbly and attentively, ready to hear even its quietest words.

A man says that as his judgement grew, he stopped praising the masters for pictures he liked and began praising himself for liking what the masters had selected for him to admire. The author adds that many people fail to study the masters' moods, so they miss the beauty offered to them. The fault, he says, lies with the viewer, not with the masters.

For a viewer who is open to a masterpiece, the work feels like a living thing that creates a bond between them and its maker. The artist's feelings still live on in each new viewer, and we respond most to the person behind the work rather than its skill, just as readers share the feelings of characters in stories.

Chikamatsu, a Japanese playwright, judged one student's play best because the audience knows more than the characters. In the play, twin brothers are mistaken for each other, and the viewers see the confusion the actors do not. Chikamatsu saw this shared knowledge as the true spirit of drama.

Great artists of East and West, Okakura says, used suggestion to draw the viewer in, so that a masterpiece opens onto a wide range of thought. He contrasts these works, which feel like a person's heartfelt expression, with modern work that gives only a formal greeting, because modern artists are absorbed in technique and rarely go beyond themselves.

Vanity blocks real feeling in art. An artist who only sings of himself makes work that is more like science and less human. The old Japanese saying gives the same idea: a truly vain man leaves no gap in his heart for love, and in art vanity shuts out sympathy in both the artist and the audience.

When people who share a feel for art meet in front of a work, the viewer goes beyond his ordinary self and glimpses something infinite, beyond words. Art then becomes like religion and raises people up, which is why a masterpiece is sacred.

In the past, Japanese tea-masters kept their finest art objects hidden and treated them as sacred. Each was wrapped in several nested boxes and silk, and only rarely shown, and then only to people who had been admitted into the tradition.

In Okakura's account, during the period when tea culture was rising, Japanese generals valued a rare artwork more than a large gift of land. He adds that many popular plays turn on the loss or recovery of a famous masterpiece, such as a painting that is destroyed in a fire.

A samurai, a warrior, goes into a burning building to save a painting by the artist Sesson. Trapped by the fire, he cuts open his own body and hides the painting inside the wound, dying there. The story shows how highly the painting was valued and how loyal the samurai was.

Art only has value for us to the extent that it speaks to us. It could be a universal language, but our limited nature, our traditions, our inherited instincts and our individuality narrow how much of it we can enjoy. We tend to seek out works that match our own taste.

Training in art makes us able to enjoy more kinds of beauty. Yet, the passage says, we ultimately see only ourselves in the world, since our personal tastes shape how we perceive things. So the tea masters collected only the objects that matched their own personal taste.

Kobori Enshiu's disciples praised his collection as more widely appealing than Rikiu's, which only one person in a thousand could appreciate. Enshiu took this as a criticism of himself. He said Rikiu chose only objects that personally moved him, while he himself had catered to what most people would like.

Much of today's enthusiasm for art, the passage says, does not come from genuine feeling. People demand whatever is generally seen as best, without regard for their own response. They prefer what is expensive or fashionable over what is refined or truly beautiful.

Ordinary people, the passage says, find cheap magazine pictures easier to enjoy than old masterpieces, which they only claim to admire. For them the artist's famous name counts for more than the quality of the work. A Chinese critic long ago made the same complaint: people judge a painting by what they hear about it, not by what they see.

Okakura says that people often confuse art with antiquity, valuing old works just because they are old. He grants that respect for the old masters is good and that they opened the way for later artists. But he argues that a work should be judged on its artistic merit, not its age, and that people praise artists mainly after they are dead.

Okakura says that people now tend to focus on whole categories instead of single works. A collector may gather examples to represent a period or school, yet one masterpiece can teach more than many ordinary pieces from that group. He concludes that we sort too much and enjoy too little, and that museums suffer when a scientific display method takes priority over beauty.

Modern art cannot be dismissed in any worthwhile way of living, because it is the true reflection of our own time. Blaming today's art is really blaming ourselves. We praise old art but neglect what we ourselves could create, leaving present artists to struggle unrecognized.

Okakura argues that his age offers little inspiration and that its art is barren, so later times will judge it poor. He says modern life is destroying beauty. He wishes someone could build a society that responds to real artistic genius, like a harp that sounds when touched.

Flowers are a sign of love and of the human step beyond animal life. Okakura suggests that the first person to give a flower to a loved one rose above basic need and so entered the world of art, by valuing something that is useless for practical purposes.
Flowers have been part of nearly every human activity: celebrations, weddings, worship, meditation, war, and even attempts at communication. The writer finds it hard to imagine life without them.

Flowers are described as a comfort to people. They bring relief to the sick, lift weary spirits, and restore trust in the world, much as a child's gaze revives lost hopes. Even after people die, flowers are said to remain at their graves in sorrow.

Despite our closeness to flowers, the author says, people remain little better than animals. Beneath a civilized surface, selfish appetites drive us. He suggests that people who never stop being animals may end up as criminals, and that for most people only hunger feels real and only their own desires feel sacred.

Old shrines and temples have fallen, but the altar of self-worship lasts forever. People now treat money as their god and damage nature to serve it. They think they have mastered matter, yet matter has actually enslaved them, and they commit cruelties in the name of culture.

The speaker addresses garden flowers and warns them that they will soon be cut and taken from their home by a cruel hand. He tells them to enjoy the summer while they can. The last line suggests the person who cuts them may be beautiful, though she is still a cruel "wretch."

The passage describes the fate of a flower that is picked and given to people who may not treat it well. It may be worn by a cruel woman, pinned to a man who would not dare to face others, or kept in a small vase with little water, so it slowly dies.

The speaker jokes that a flower arranger in Japan would treat flowers like a doctor treating a patient. He cuts, bends and twists them into forced shapes, then uses fire and wires to keep them alive, which is the mock-medical harm he describes.

Okakura is describing a torturer who kept prisoners alive for weeks with harsh treatment, such as salt and vinegar diets and scalding water on the feet. He then asks the reader, in a mocking way, whether death would have been kinder, and what past sins could deserve such punishment.

Okakura says that Western people waste flowers far more than Eastern flower arrangers do. Huge numbers of flowers are cut each day for ballrooms and banquets and then thrown away the next morning. Compared with this, the fault of the Eastern flower arranger seems small.

Okakura contrasts how a certain creature treats flowers with how Westerners treat them. He says Westerners use flowers as a show of wealth for a passing moment, then throw them away when faded, which he finds sad.

Flowers are beautiful but cannot defend themselves. Insects, beasts and birds have ways to fight or flee from those who hunt them, but flowers have no wings or means of escape, except the butterfly, and so they are left helpless before anyone who would destroy them.

Flowers are said to suffer when cut, but people do not hear their cries. The author suggests that people, who treat the flowers that serve them cruelly, may lose them. He notes that wild flowers are growing scarcer and imagines they may have left the earth until people become kinder.

Okakura argues that a person who grows plants in pots is kinder than one who cuts flowers for display. The grower cares for each plant over time, worrying about water, pests and frost and taking joy as it blooms. He notes that in the East such care for plants has a long history and is often the subject of poetry.

In Tang and Sung China, flowers were kept in fine ceramic containers and given personal care. Attendants washed their leaves with soft rabbit-hair brushes, and one writer suggested a peony should be bathed by a beautiful maiden, and a winter plum watered by a slender monk.

The Hachinoki is a No-dance about a poor knight who, on a freezing night with no fuel, burns his prized plants to warm a traveling friar. The friar turns out to be a powerful ruler in disguise, who rewards the knight for the sacrifice. The play still moves audiences in Tokyo today.

People once took great care to protect delicate flowers. A Tang Dynasty emperor hung golden bells on his garden branches to keep birds away, and he played music to the blossoms in spring. The passage also mentions an old tablet said to be by Yoshitsune, still kept in a Japanese monastery.

A notice protects a beautiful plum tree by threatening that anyone who cuts a branch will lose a finger. The author wishes that people today who destroy flowers and damage works of art could be punished as strictly.

The author questions whether it is right to take potted plants out of their natural homes and make them bloom in unfamiliar places. He compares this to keeping birds in cages. He suggests that orchids may feel trapped in heated greenhouses and long for their native southern lands.

The ideal lover of flowers, the passage says, sees them where they grow naturally, not cut or indoors. It gives examples of Chinese poets who sat with or dreamed among flowers, and a Japanese empress who would not pick a flower, offering it to the Buddhas instead.

Change and death are seen as unavoidable parts of life. The passage says that since destruction surrounds us everywhere, death should be accepted as readily as life. It adds that death and life are counterparts, like night and day, and that new creation becomes possible only when the old breaks down.

Okakura says that people have honored Death under many names, as a goddess who frees them. Fire and the sword are two examples: fire burns away weakness, and the sword cuts the chains of desire. From this destruction, he says, comes a new hope and a higher form of human nature.

Tea-masters, who founded the Cult of Flowers, argued that cutting flowers was acceptable if it created new forms that honored beauty. They saw the flowers as offering themselves to beauty, and believed the masters would make up for the act by devoting themselves to purity and simplicity.

Tea and flower masters in Japan treat flowers with great care. They cut only what they need, choosing each branch for the arrangement they have in mind, and they keep the leaves with the flower to show the whole plant. Western arrangements, by contrast, often show bare flower heads stuck into a vase.

In a tea room, the master places a well-arranged flower in the place of honour and keeps other objects away from it. Guests bow to the flower before greeting the host. When the flower fades, it is respectfully returned to the river or the ground.

Flower arranging is said to have begun around the same time as the tea ceremony, in the 1400s. Legend gives the first arrangements to early Buddhist monks who gathered flowers blown down by a storm and placed them in water. Soami, a court painter, is said to have been one of its first skilled practitioners.

Flower arrangement grew to its full development alongside the tea ceremony, which was perfected by the tea master Rikiu in the late 1500s. Rikiu and later tea masters competed to create new styles of arranging flowers. Juko and Senno, founder of the Ikenobo school, are named as earlier figures in this art.

Flower arrangement was one part of the tea master's overall aesthetic ritual, not a religion of its own. Flowers had to fit the whole look of the tea room. For example, white plum blossoms were not used when snow covered the garden, and showy, "noisy" flowers were left out of the room.

A flower arrangement made by a tea-master only has its full meaning in the place it was made for. Its lines and proportions were planned around that particular setting, so moving it elsewhere takes away its significance.

From the mid-seventeenth century, flower arranging became a separate art, no longer tied to the tea room, and only the vase limited it. It developed many schools, which fall into two main branches: the Formalistic and the Naturalesque.

Two schools of flower arranging are compared. The Formalistic school, led by the Ikenobo family, followed a classic ideal, and its early arrangements look much like painted flower pictures. The Naturalesque school took nature as its model, changing forms only to make the whole arrangement feel unified.
The author says he would like to explain in more detail the rules for arranging flowers that the flower masters of the Tokugawa period set out. He says there is not enough time to do so here.

Flower arrangers, as the passage describes them, built each arrangement around three principles: a leading one called Heaven, a subordinate one called Earth, and a reconciling one called Man. An arrangement that lacked these three was judged lifeless. They also treated each flower in three styles: formal, semi-formal, and informal.

Three kinds of flower arrangement are compared to women's clothing: a formal ballroom gown, an easy afternoon dress, and a relaxed, informal outfit worn in a private room. The first arrangement suits a grand setting, the second a casual one, and the third an intimate one.

The writer prefers the flower arrangements of the tea-master to those of the flower-master. He sees the tea-master's work as true art, fitted to its setting and close to life. The tea-master chooses the flowers and then lets them speak for themselves.

In a tea-room, flowers are arranged to suit the season. A spray of wild cherry with a budding camellia in late winter suggests winter leaving and spring coming. In summer, a single dew-covered lily in a hanging vase in the dim alcove seems to smile at the foolishness of life.

Okakura describes tea-room displays where flowers are arranged together with other art, such as a painting, a poem, or a bronze object, so that the whole scene works as one unit. In each example the arrangement evokes a natural mood, such as marshes, wild ducks, a seaside, or late autumn.

Rikiu, a tea master, had a garden of rare morning-glories. When the ruler Taiko asked to see them, Rikiu cleared the garden of every flower and invited him to tea instead. Inside, Taiko found one perfect morning-glory in a bronze vase, and his anger gave way to delight.

Okakura suggests that flowers may understand the meaning of their own sacrifice, since they are not cowards like men. He points to cherry blossoms, which seem to welcome their death as they drift away on the wind and water, as if saying goodbye to spring and heading toward eternity.

Okakura says that in religion the past is the source of authority, while in art only the present matters. Tea-masters believed art must be lived, not just admired, so they tried to shape everyday conduct by the refined standards of the tea-room. Calm mind, careful speech, dress, posture and walking were all treated as ways to express an artistic self.

Okakura says a tea master must first make himself beautiful before he can approach beauty, so he tries to become art itself. Perfection is present everywhere, if a person chooses to see it. He illustrates this with an old poem about spring hidden in the unopened buds of snowy hills.

The tea-masters changed Japanese building and interior design. Their new style, set out in the earlier chapter on the tea-room, shaped later palaces and monasteries built after the sixteenth century. Kobori-Enshiu, a tea-master, left notable work in several famous buildings, and the tea-masters also designed Japan's celebrated gardens.

Japanese pottery and other crafts, the author says, owe much of their quality to the tea-masters. The tea ceremony needed finely made utensils, which pushed potters to great skill. Tea-masters also shaped textile colors and designs and left their mark on nearly every kind of art.

Okakura says that tea masters made large contributions to painting and lacquer work. He names Honnami Koyetsu, a tea master who founded a painting school, and says the later Korin school, which grew from tea culture, reflects the spirit of Teaism.

The tea-masters shaped Japanese daily life far more than they shaped art. Their influence reaches polite manners, household arrangements, food and its serving, clothing in plain colors, the way people treat flowers, and a love of simplicity and humility. Through them, tea became part of ordinary people's lives.

People who do not know how to live steadily in life's stormy troubles stay unhappy while pretending to be calm. They fear a storm in every cloud. The passage suggests instead accepting life's constant motion, as the waves do, or even riding the storm itself as the philosopher Liehtse did.

The passage says that a person who has lived surrounded by beauty will die in a beautiful way. The great tea-masters met their deaths with the same refinement they showed in their lives. They tried always to stay in step with the universe's rhythm, so they were ready to face the unknown. The "Last Tea of Rikiu," a famous tea ceremony held before the death of the master Rikyu, is described as the highest example of tragic greatness.

Rikiu, a tea master, was close to the warlord Hideyoshi and highly respected by him. But the passage says that being close to a ruler like this is dangerous, since the age was full of betrayal and people did not trust even their own family. Rikiu also often argued openly with Hideyoshi instead of simply agreeing with him.

Rikiu, a tea master, was falsely accused by his rivals of plotting to poison the ruler Hideyoshi. They claimed the poison was to be served in a cup of tea he had prepared. Hideyoshi acted on mere suspicion and ordered Rikiu's execution, and there was no way to appeal.

Sen no Rikyu, the tea master, invites his chief disciples to a farewell tea ceremony on the day he is to take his own life. The guests arrive somberly, and the garden around them feels eerie, with shuddering trees and stone lanterns that seem like guards at the gate of the underworld. Incense drifts from the tea room, calling them inside.

Guests enter a tea room one by one and sit down. A scroll on the wall shows an old monk's writing about how everything in the world passes away. The boiling kettle sounds like a cicada mourning the end of summer. The host serves tea to each guest in turn, and the chief guest then asks to look over the tea utensils, as custom requires.

Sen no Rikyu, the tea master, gives his guests the tea utensils as keepsakes after they admire them. He keeps only the bowl, declares that no one may use it again because misfortune has touched it, and smashes it.
Rikiu, a tea master, ends his life on the order of his ruler. After the guests leave, he folds his tea robe to show a white death robe underneath. He greets his dagger in a poem, then dies calmly.

In Dakota belief, there was no church or priest to take charge of a person's soul. That duty belonged to the parent, who was allowed a kind of priestly role because a parent's power to create and protect is closest to the sacred power of God.

In Dakota belief, a mother's spiritual state during pregnancy and nursing shapes the child's religious nature. Her inner thoughts should instill love of the "Great Mystery" and a sense of kinship with all creation, so she lives in silence and quiet withdrawal.

Before birth, a Dakota mother walks alone in quiet woods or open prairie. In her imagination, the coming child stands for a future great man or hero, or the mother of heroes. She pictures this in the wild, quiet land, where the only sounds are pine trees sighing and a distant waterfall.

Eastman describes a Dakota woman giving birth. She does not seek human help, because she has been prepared for this duty since childhood. She meets the ordeal alone in nature, and when her child is born she feels joy at having done her part in creation.

A mother returns to the camp carrying her newborn baby. She feels its warmth and hears its breathing, and she regards the child as still part of herself, since both are fed from the same milk. The baby's trusting gaze is described as the sweetest look possible.

In this passage a mother teaches a child about the sacred through nature, first by pointing and then through soft songs sung at morning and evening. To them, birds are living beings close to the "Great Mystery" (the Dakota name for the sacred power), trees show His presence, and falling water sings His praise.

A Dakota mother teaches her young child to be quiet and to listen to nature, such as the rustling of aspen and birch trees, and at night she points to the stars as a sign of the Creator. Silence, love and reverence are the first lessons, and later generosity, courage and chastity are added.

According to a Dakota chief quoted here, warfare can kill men, but it cannot defeat women, because children are raised in their care. Each new child is a gift from the Great Good, and men only play a secondary part in bringing life into the world.

Among the Dakota, a mother teaches her child by following her own mother's customs and by learning from animals such as ants, bees, and birds. The child then comes to pray on his own, sees himself as kin to all living things, and regards the storm wind as a messenger of the "Great Mystery."

After about age eight, a boy goes to his father for stricter training, while a girl comes under her grandmother's care. Grandparents mainly pass on the people's traditions, beliefs and stories to the young. The old teach and advise the young, who in return respect them.

In Dakota life, old age was in many ways the happiest time. Older people were freed from hard and dangerous work and from the strict social rules that everyone else had to follow. The author adds that the Dakota are a polite people, as anyone who knows them at home would agree.

In this passage, the fiercest warriors, the ones who frightened their enemies most, were usually very gentle and refined at home with their families and friends. A soft, quiet voice was valued in men as well as in women.

Living in a small tent with the same family would quickly become unbearable without the natural restraint and courtesy the passage describes. These include respect for each person's place and belongings, along with calm, order, and good manners at all times.

Among Dakota families, adults did not show strong affection openly, especially before guests. Elderly people were the exception: they could joke with children and speak bluntly, even harshly, without being contradicted, and others cared for their hardships and frailty.

Among the author's people, marriage had no religious ceremony, but the bond between a man and a woman was seen as mysterious and sacred. He contrasts this with church weddings, which he says can come with frivolous or indecent customs. He holds that lovers should first be united privately, alone with nature, before their union is made public.

In this Dakota custom, a young couple could marry whether or not their parents had approved. They first went off alone into the wilderness for days or weeks, then returned to the village as husband and wife. Their marriage blessing came from Nature itself.

In this passage, the family is described as the basic unit of both society and government. A clan is a larger family led by a chief, and several clans joined together form a tribe. Close relatives, including cousins, were treated as brothers and sisters, so marriage within the clan was forbidden.

Households were usually a man with one or more wives and their children, often living together under one roof. Multiple wives were mostly held by older, prominent men and were often sisters. Marriages could be honorably ended for good reason, and unfaithfulness was rare.

Among the Dakota, women held a secure and respected place. Wives kept their own family name, children belonged to the mother's clan, and property and family descent passed through the mother. Older women of wisdom or proven courage could sometimes sit in the council.

Before outside traders and soldiers arrived, the woman ruled her own household and was a source of moral and spiritual strength to the people. Once these newcomers brought alcohol and used it to corrupt husbands and buy the virtue of wives and daughters, the decline of women meant the decline of the whole people.

Before the disruption of their way of life, Eastman says, Native American women created very happy homes. He describes them as natural and sincere, and says their training, clear role, and deep religious outlook gave them a strength that ordinary hardship could not break.

Dakota names were of several kinds: playful nicknames, names earned through deeds, birth names, and names with religious or symbolic meaning. A child's name was not always set by a chance event at birth. Names often reflected a person's character, such as a strong warrior being given a name of a powerful animal or force, and a gentler person being given a name like Swift Bird.

Women's names often described the home and used words like "pretty" or "good." Names of high standing or spiritual meaning were given by elders, and one such name could pass through three generations, though each bearer had to prove worthy of it.

Daily prayer was the one duty a Dakota man could not skip, and he treated it as more necessary than food. Each morning he bathed in cold water at the river's edge, then faced the rising sun and prayed silently. His wife might pray before or after him, but never with him; each person met the dawn alone.

The Dakota hunter, when he sees a scene of great beauty, such as a storm cloud with a rainbow or a sunset over a prairie, stops briefly to worship. He does not need a special set-apart day of worship, because for him every day belongs to God.

In this passage, the Dakota hunter treats every part of life as religious. He believes all creation has spirit, and he honors the spirit of an animal he kills. He lays out the body, decorates its head, and holds up a filled pipe in prayer to free that spirit with honor.

In Dakota custom, meals begin with quiet prayers. The woman softly says "Spirit, partake!" as she lowers the kettle, and the husband murmurs his own prayer when he receives his food. An older man shows his thanks by throwing the best piece of meat into the fire.

In Dakota custom, a guest's safety in the camp is guaranteed by the host's honor, even if the guest is an enemy. Hospitality is limited only by war, but a visiting enemy can trust that he will be treated generously while he stays there.

Loyalty to family comes easily, since their blood is shared. Love between a man and a woman is tied to instinct and desire. The passage holds that true friendship, staying loyal through every trial, is the hardest test of a man's character.

A "brother-friend" is the closest kind of friendship, formed between two men in early youth and lasting until death. The two give each other moral support and encouragement, not pleasure or profit. Each vows to die for the other if needed, and each asks only what fits the highest ideals of the Dakota mind.

The passage is only a list of section headings from the chapter. It names topics it covers: changes to older religious rites, the Sun Dance, the Great Medicine Lodge, totems and charms, the vapor-bath, and the ceremonial pipe. The list itself gives no argument or claim.

The Plains peoples had only a few public religious ceremonies, and most of these were recent. The author says they belong to a "transition period," which he dates from when outside contact first began to change their customs, often well before they gave up their nomadic way of life.

The passage claims that fur traders, Catholic priests, soldiers and Protestant missionaries began breaking apart Native nations and their religions long before those nations were moved onto reservations. It adds that by the time anyone studied these peoples accurately, alcohol and trade had already corrupted their traditional values.

Over time, these communities changed their customs and beliefs, mixing Christian and traditional elements. Their folk stories came to include Bible stories in Indian form, and their music shows Catholic chant influence. So much of the material that modern observers have gathered is mixed in this way.

Eastman says that after contact with white settlers, cruelty and brutality among Native peoples grew worse. As an example, he says the Plains peoples' Sun Dance, their most important public ceremony, was corrupted into a brutal spectacle and was finally banned by the government.

A Dakota warrior in mortal danger might pray to the Sun for his life. If he was saved, he had to fulfill the vow made in that prayer by performing a Sun Dance, which included physical ordeal. The ordeal thanked the Great Mystery and atoned for any appearance of weakness, and it did not ask for future favors.

Ceremonies were held six months to a year after a vow was made, to allow time for preparation. They took place in midsummer before a large gathering, and usually included a feast and the giving away of goods. These gifts were not a required part of the religious rite itself.

A tree was chosen and cut down for a sacred dance, with a ceremony that included the filled pipe. It was carried back like a litter, standing for the body of the man who was to lead the dance. It was then raised outside the village, inside a ring of cut branches, beside a single tent.

Carved figures of a man and a buffalo, sometimes a bird for the Thunder, were hung from a crossbar near the top of the Sun Dance pole. The man was painted red and the animal black. The author says he could never find any meaning in the crossbar itself, and thinks its resemblance to the Christian cross was probably just a coincidence.

A man who is about to give public thanks in a Dakota ceremony is shown as one who was nearly dead and has been spared by the Giver of Life. His painted body, a hanging buffalo, and a buffalo skull he drags behind him each stand for this escape from death, the buffalo being the support of life.

In this part of a Dakota ceremony, a dancer cuts his chest so that he bleeds and feels pain, which stands for his figurative death. He then dances for a day and a night or longer, dragging a skull tied to his shoulders, or pulled on skewers fixed in his flesh, while he gazes at the sun.

The passage says that a Dakota rite, once a simple act of atonement or thanksgiving, became in later times a cruel display of endurance. Dancers were hung from a pole by cuts in their flesh and had to tear free. It was also turned into a prayer for success in war or in raids, which the author saw as a loss of its original meaning after contact with white settlers.

The Grand Medicine Lodge, a notable Native American society, probably grew out of contact with early Jesuit missionaries. Its features show European ideas, and its founders likely wanted an organization strong enough to resist the Jesuits, whom they called the "Black Robes."

Eastman says that the two best-known Native religious leaders after white settlers arrived, the Shawnee Prophet and the Ghost Dance prophet, both based their claims on Christian scripture. So the religious movements they started, though they worried the settlers, came from outside Native tradition.

The Medicine Lodge, a religious society, spread from the Algonquin people to other tribes, including the Sioux, and resisted early Christian missionaries. Few Sioux converted until after 1862, when defeat, hunger, and imprisonment led many to turn to Christianity as their only apparent hope.

The passage describes a secret society of Dakota healers, made up of several lodges with their own songs and medicines. Members advanced by merit, women could join on equal terms, and candidates had to show good moral conduct and serve a probation of one or two years. The society's rules were much like the Ten Commandments, and it taught the secrets of proper medicine.

In this Dakota society, members learned the healing uses of all the medicinal roots and herbs they knew, and the older members taught and practiced this while the young were trained to replace them. The author's grandmother was a skilled healer, and his parents belonged to the society but did not practice.

A medicine feast was a closed gathering open only to members. Members showed their sacred bags and totems and sang their medicine songs. The hosts did not eat the food; only invited guests did. The Grand Medicine Dance initiated candidates who had completed their probation, enough to replace members who had died since the last meeting.

Invitations to a ceremonial dance were sent as small bundles of tobacco. Two large tents faced each other across a space roofed only by cut branches. One tent belonged to the society holding the dance and its new members, and the other to warriors chosen for their courage, who served refreshments and kept order.

Before the dances and songs begin, each society's members enter the hall in single file behind their oldest man, the "Great Chief." They face the setting sun, then the rising sun, addressing the "Great Mystery" and singing a short invocation with raised right arms.

Novices in a Dakota ceremony are placed kneeling on robes and furs for their final initiation. Men sit on the right, stripped and painted black with a red spot over the heart, and women on the left in their best clothes, all with loose hair as in mourning. Medicine-men, one assigned to each novice, stand facing them at a distance.

Each medicine man, a spiritual leader, spoke to the person he was training. He urged that person to keep the order's rules and to behave well toward other people and toward the Ruler of Life. Then all stood in a strong, dignified crouch, holding their medicine bags tightly.

The men, holding sacred bags, step toward a row of kneeling initiates and swing the bags forward while shouting in unison. The bags seem to send their spiritual power into the initiates, who then fall forward as if dead.

In this ceremony, new members lie on the ground while dancers circle them and cover them with robes and gifts. They then rise and join the final dance. The author says the whole ritual represents death and rebirth.

The author doubts that this elaborate ritual, with public prayers and sermons, is very old. He says its members sincerely believed in it and the people respected it for a time. Later, it became corrupt and was suspected of witchcraft.

The passage says that outsiders have misread the Indian idea of "medicine." Things held sacred were loosely called "medicine," meaning mystery or magic. As a healer, the Indian used bark, roots and leaves he knew well, usually as a tea, and one plant at a time.

The medicine-man, a Dakota healer, used some practical treatments such as an internal cleansing, steam baths and setting broken bones, though he did not perform surgery. He also tried to restore a patient's balance through mental and spiritual influence, using his personal authority.

In Dakota, the word for healing means "readjusting" or "making anew." The word for medicine literally means "root," and the word for spirit or mystery is "wakan." The three ideas were often linked but were kept separate in meaning.

In the old days, medicine men did not take payment for their healing, which was seen as an honorable duty. Once payment and fees came in, greed and rivalry spread, and the healer became a fraud, a "conjurer." The author says that this kind of healer's time is practically over.

Many Native groups chose an animal as their "totem," a symbol for a family, clan, or society, to build a spiritual bond with the animal world. The author thinks the chosen animal was probably the group's traditional ancestress, since stories say the First Man had animal wives.

Sacred animals, shown by a stuffed skin or a rough painting, were honored and taken into battle to bring protection from the spirits. People who wore an animal's badge were believed to receive its qualities, such as wisdom, cunning, or courage.
A healer's totem or charm usually came from the medicine lodge, or society, that he belonged to. A few highly regarded healers claimed their charm came from a special personal revelation instead.

Two ceremonies are described as the most important and widespread among American Indians: the vapor-bath, called "eneepee," and the pipe ceremony. The author says these appear in Siouan (Dakota) legends as the most ancient customs, and as lasting until recent times.

In the Dakota creation story, the First Man brings his dead younger brother back to life with a vapor bath. He gathers the brother's bones inside a small lodge of cedar branches and heats stones in a nearby fire pit. He then rolls the hot stones into the lodge to make the steam.

Here a man closes a sweat lodge, a small enclosed structure, except for one opening. He chants, then sprinkles water with sage onto heated stones. Each time he does, something happens: steam rises, bones rattle, singing is heard, and finally a voice asks to be let out.

The sweat lodge, called the "eneepee," is a small enclosed structure used for purification. Both healers and the sick use it. Anyone preparing for a spiritual crisis, possible death, or immediate danger must take a steam bath and then a cold plunge.

Many things used in a sacred ceremony, such as the lodge, cedar and sage, water, and especially smooth river stones, are treated as holy or fit for spiritual use. The stone is called "Tunkan," a shortened Sioux word meaning Grandfather.

Natural boulders play a part in some important Dakota ceremonies, such as the Rain Dance. A lone hunter or warrior may also lift a filled pipe to Tunkan, a sacred stone, to honor what he sees as a miracle. To him it is as true and holy as the raising of Lazarus is to a devout Christian.

According to a legend, the First Man was taught by his Elder Brother to use the pipe in prayer for healing. The passage says the pipe ceremony is an everyday way of giving thanks, a vow of loyalty before a dangerous undertaking, and part of private prayer, with its smoke rising to the Father of Spirits.

The passage describes how a pipe is used in worship. Warriors use a special pipe for war ceremonies and healing, and their own pipe at home or on the hunt. The worshiper lights it, takes a few puffs, then holds it up silently toward the Sun and the Earth. Some people also hold it toward the Four Winds, Fire, Water, and other sacred things.

The passage says that while many local festivals ask for hunting, war, rain, or good harvests, two rites serve as the main sacraments. The sweat-lodge purification (called "eneepee") takes the place of baptism, and smoking tobacco takes the place of bread and wine in communion.

The passage is only a list of section headings from a chapter. It names topics the chapter covers: silence as the base of character, basic moral ideas, the saying "Give All or Nothing," rules for honorable warfare, and a Native view of courage.

The author says that, before he ever learned of Christ or met a white man, a Native woman taught him the basics of morality. With help from nature, she taught him to know God, to recognize goodness, and to love what is truly beautiful. He adds that civilization has taught him nothing better.

The narrator says that as a child he gave freely and valued simple things like pebbles and trees. Since growing up in white society, he has lost that way of living and now values things by their money worth. He compares this change to natural rock being ground into blocks for building walls.

Eastman says that the early Native American people were proud but not arrogant. They did not treat speech as proof of being better than other living things, and they saw it as a risky gift. They valued silence as a sign of inner balance, a calm body, mind and spirit that storms cannot disturb.

In this passage, silence is described as a sacred mystery, and the way it is spoken of as a holy voice of the Great Mystery. Its fruits are self-control, courage, patience, dignity and reverence, and silence is called the base on which character is built. The old chief Wabashaw advises guarding the tongue when young so that wise thoughts can be offered to the people later.

Once people imagined a strong, graceful, healthy body, they had started a moral life. To keep such a body past youth, a man must control his appetites for physical pleasure. Based on this idea, the Indian built a strict system of physical training and a moral code that guided his whole life.

A Dakota boy is taught from childhood to aim for a high standard of strength and beauty in men. To reach it, he must eat moderately, control his sexual life, and exercise hard. He does this so he will not weaken the strong, pure blood that his ancestors built through their own hard self-control.

Young Dakota men were trained to fast briefly and to use up extra energy through running, swimming and sweat baths. The author says that this physical tiredness, together with eating less, reliably curbs strong sexual desire.

Children were taught modesty and self-respect, partly by being watched by the whole community from birth. Their births, first steps, ear-piercing and first kills were announced publicly, so the clan knew of each stage. This gave young people a sense of reputation to live up to as adults.

Among the Dakota, a young man was urged to take public service early and to seek the honors of leader and feast-giver. He could earn these only by being truthful, generous, brave, and personally chaste and honorable. Certain ceremonies also taught moral discipline, such as seclusion of women and bans on husbands approaching their wives before war or religious events.

In this passage, a person's standing in the tribe depends on his personal virtue, and he is always reminded that he lives for his tribe and clan, not only for himself. Because of this, self-control developed early, and he faced no unnatural conditions or complex temptations until a stronger people defeated him.

Among the Dakota, a "Feast of Virgins" was a semi-religious ceremony held to keep young people true to their honor. When a girl held it for the first time, it publicly announced that she had reached marriageable age. A herald called out the feast through the village.

Eastman describes a Dakota ceremony in which a young woman lights her first maidens' fire. Only girls who have never been with a man are invited to come forward and publicly affirm their chastity before the Sun, the Earth, their companions and the Great Mystery.

The village became excited about an upcoming event. People ranked it just below the Sun Dance and the Grand Medicine Dance in importance. It was held every midsummer, in the middle of the large circular camp where several clans gathered for summer festivities.

Eastman describes a Dakota gathering with a set arrangement: a rock marked with red paint, a knife and two arrows, and two rings of seats, one for young women and one for older chaperones. Warriors of high standing kept order. Any man could publicly challenge a young woman he judged unworthy, but if he could not prove the charge, the warriors punished him severely.
Each girl touched a sacred rock as a solemn vow to stay a virgin until marriage. If she broke this oath, she would accept being killed with a knife or arrows.

Among the Dakota, girls might give a feast before marriage to answer gossip about their conduct, a way of daring rumor-spreaders to prove their claims. Young men held similar feasts, but only if they had never spoken of love to a girl. Honor came from success in war, hunting, and a seat on the council before any courtship.

Among the Dakota, love of possessions was seen as a weakness that could throw a person's spiritual balance off course. Children were therefore taught generosity early: they gave away what they valued most, were made the family's almoner (the one who distributes gifts to others), and heard stories about the scorn that falls on stingy people.

Giving is a set part of major ceremonies such as births, marriages, and deaths, or any time honor is shown. People often give until they have nothing left, especially to relatives, guests, and the poor and elderly, who cannot repay them. A religious offering to the "Great Mystery" may be small in value, but the giver should feel it as true sacrifice.

Among the Dakota, orphans and the elderly were cared for by the whole clan, not just by their close relatives. Parents took pride in raising daughters who visited and helped the needy, and the name "Wenonah," given to the eldest daughter, carried the expectation of such charity. A girl who neglected these duties was considered unworthy of the name.

A successful hunter gives feasts and invites the older men of his clan, who enjoy eating together and talking about the past. In return they make speeches praising his ancestors and him, which brings him a good reputation. Such a man becomes nearly as famous as a warrior, or as a respected "man of peace."

In this passage, Eastman says the true Indian puts no price on his goods or his work, and gives as much as he is able. He sees being chosen for a hard or dangerous task as an honor, and would feel shame asking for payment. He leaves thanks up to the person served.

Among his own people, a man respects property rights, and stealing brings a lasting shame, marked by the name "Thief." The one exception is food, which a hungry person may take if no one is present to offer it. With no locks or doors, the moral law was the only protection.

Enemy property may be taken as spoil of war when possible. The author says there was little of this in the old days, because there was little to take before white people arrived. In modern times, though, stealing horses from enemy tribes has become common and is not seen as dishonorable.

Eastman says that, in the old days, his people saw war as a formal contest of courage and skill, held to build manliness, with honor (the eagle feather) as the prize. It was not fought to win land or to destroy another nation. Battles could last all day yet cause few deaths.

Among the Dakota, a man who killed an enemy in battle did not count it as sin, but he still mourned the dead for thirty days, blackening his face and loosening his hair. The text says the killing of women and children in war was partly explained by a belief that the dead warrior's spirit would be happier if no widow or orphan were left in want.

Originally, a war leader took only a small scalp lock, carried it for thirty days of victory celebration, and then gave it a religious burial. Cruel war customs grew much worse after white men arrived, bringing liquor and guns that stirred revenge and greed, and even paid bounties for the scalps of women and children.

A murderer within the tribe was expected to face punishment, often death, as the council decided. He did not try to escape, because he believed the "Great Mystery" sees everything, even crimes done unseen in the forest or at night. So he gave himself up for trial.

Under this Dakota custom, a killer was judged by the known facts. If he acted in self-defense or was severely provoked, he could go free after thirty days of solitary mourning. Otherwise, the dead man's closest relatives could take his life, and if they chose not to, the killer was cast out from the clan.

Crow Dog, a Sioux man, killed the Sioux chief Spotted Tail in 1881. He gave himself up calmly, was tried and convicted in a South Dakota court, and was then allowed unusual freedom in prison, more than a white man under a death sentence is usually given.

Crow Dog killed the chief Spotted Tail because his people had long before given him a sworn duty to do so if the chief ever disgraced the Brule Sioux name. The author says the chief had committed public and private wrongs, so the killing was justice, not a personal revenge.

Crow Dog, a condemned Dakota man, was allowed to go home to say goodbye to his family before his execution. He did not come back on the set day, and his wife said he had gone alone to the prison. A telegram then reported that he had arrived there on his own.

Public attention to the case led to the case being reopened, and Crow Dog, a Dakota man accused of killing another man, was acquitted. He is still alive, now about seventy-five, and remains respected by his own people.

In the old days, lying was punished by death among this people. They believed a deliberate liar could commit any crime while hiding behind deceit, so such a person was killed at once to stop the harm from spreading.

Eastman says that critics of Native people admit their courage but think it is reckless and wild. He argues that in Native belief, true bravery is mainly self-control: not yielding to fear, anger, desire, or pain. On this view, such courage is a high moral virtue.

An old chief tells a scout that nothing, not cold, hunger, pain, danger, or death itself, should stop him from doing a good deed. The scout is going to find buffalo in midwinter to feed starving people. The author calls this the chief's simple idea of courage.

A missionary, a Christian teacher trying to convert people, told a group of Native listeners the Biblical story of creation and the fall. One listener then shared an old tradition about the origin of corn. The missionary rejected it as false, while the listeners had politely accepted his own stories.

A Native American man, offended, tells a visitor that he lacks good manners. He points out that the Native listeners believed the visitor's stories, so he asks why the visitor will not believe theirs in return.

Eastman says that the Dakota people had no written holy book like the Bible. Their sacred literature was a living body of history, poetry, proverbs, fables and legends. It was passed on by memory from elders to children, and their customs and beliefs rested largely on it.

The author says that Native American thinkers believe God's spirit is not given to humans alone, but is shared by the whole universe. They see spirits, like the Greeks did, in mountains, trees, and springs, some kind and some harmful. They also give personality and will to the sun, stars, and other natural things.

In this Dakota creation story, the great Mysterious One stays in the background and is not pictured as a person. The Sun and the Earth, seen as male and female, do the work of creating. The Sun's warmth enters the Earth, and she brings forth plants and animals.

In Dakota tradition, Ish-na-e-cha-ge, the "First-Born," is a being who looks like a man but is greater than one. He lives alone among the animals, understands their language, and knows everything they do. He can go anywhere in the land.

In this Dakota origin story, the first being, called the First-Born, makes a companion for himself out of a splinter from his toe, not from a rib. This companion, the Little Boy Man, is created as a helpless child. The First-Born then teaches him through every stage of life, and his rules are the source of many Dakota beliefs and customs.

Spider, the animal who causes trouble, warns the other animals that the growing Little Boy will one day rule them all, and urges them to kill him. Most animals like the boy and refuse, but the sea monsters kill him and hide his body. Through the magic of the First-Born, his body is recovered and brought back to life in a sacred vapor-bath.

In this Dakota story, the first man lives happily among the animal people, learning their ways and languages. Even though he is their friend and harms none of them, the trickster Unk-to-mee stirs up quarrels among the animals. They then send word to every part of the world, calling all the tribes to unite in war against him.

After the young man learns that his animal friends are plotting against him, he is saddened. His Elder Brother then gives him weapons and raises rock walls around the lodge, telling him to fight, since the animals started the trouble.

Animals of many kinds, from buffalo and elk to bears, wolves, badgers and climbing creatures, gather around the Little Boy Man, who keeps watch from the top of his rocky fortress. The Thunder joins them with a war cry, and the burrowers dig beneath the walls while the climbers try to scale them.
In this part of the story, people first learn to use the bow and arrow. Arrows bring down many animals, and a stone war-club, swung by the Boy Man, defeats his enemies in great numbers.

In this story, insects attack a man and make him despair. His Elder Brother tells him to strike rocks with his stone club. Sparks light the dry prairie grass, and the smoke and flames drive the insects away.

In this Dakota story, animals and humans have made a peace treaty that divides their world. Animals agree to provide humans with meat and skins, though hunting remains hard and dangerous. Insects refuse to agree, so they still trouble people, and the birds punish them for it.

Dakota people say that the stone arrowheads found across the land were used by the first man when he fought the animals. Their own traditions do not record making such points, and the old men do not remember anyone making them. The points also do not work well with the bow used when Europeans arrived.

Eastman suggests that the old stone tools and arrow-heads found today may have been made by an earlier people, not by his own ancestors, who did not work stone in this way. He adds that many of the arrow-heads in museums were found lying on the ground or in fields, and some were faked and sold.

The author says that his people had no idea of a devil or hell before white settlers brought them. He compares Unk-to-mee, the Spider, a trickster figure in Dakota stories, to the serpent who tempted Eve in Genesis. Both are tempters in animal form who bring sorrow and death into the world.

Among Dakota families, the story of Unk-to-mee served as a warning that parents and grandparents often used to teach children. Ish-na-e-cha-ge, by contrast, was a demigod, a mysterious teacher who showed the first man how to do his work and find joy on earth.

After the battle with the animals, a second battle with the elements (wind, water and the like) follows. Its purpose, the passage says, was to destroy the wicked animal people, who were too many and too strong for the lone man.

In this Dakota legend, the First-Born tells his younger brother, the Little Boy Man, to prepare a warm shelter and store food before winter. The brother does so, and when heavy snow falls for many months, he makes snowshoes and hunts easily. Fiercer animals die of cold and hunger, while the wolves, foxes and ravens that beg from him are helped.

In a story of deep winter, snow has buried the family's shelter, but the Little Boy Man's fire keeps a hole open to the air. Hungry visitors look down through it and see the boy and his Elder Brother lying still, their faces covered in ashes, as the Elder Brother had advised.

In this Dakota story, enemies of the young man and his Teacher believe they have died in the snow. Then the sun melts the snow and floods the land. The two survive in a birch-bark canoe, and only a few animals survive on the highest peaks.

In this Dakota story, the young first man has overcome the animals and the elements, but he is still alone. His Elder Brother tells him to find a woman to love so they can have children. The young man replies that he does not know where to find one.

A young man, told by the Great Teacher to go and find a wife, sets out to look for one. Since he does not know how to court, the first courtship is carried out by lively young women from the Bird, Beaver and Bear peoples. The passage says these are part of a legend of many tender and playful love stories.

A young man, alone in a forest lodge, hears a sweet voice from the wilderness during his quiet thought. The voice stirs him deeply, and the passage identifies it as the voice of the eternal woman, that is, a figure of feminine allure.

A young wanderer is won over when a shy girl brings him wild cherries at his shelter. When she leaves, he looks after her and sees only a robin flying off through the trees. The story shows love as a force that can both build up and destroy.

A wanderer marries a woman who is at work by a stream, and they live happily with their son. When he goes away for a short visit to his Elder Brother, he comes back to find the stream dried up, the home empty, and his wife and child gone for good.

A husband left alone grieves until a young woman, a bear in human form, comforts him. They later part again after a mishap. Their children who look like their father become the ancestors of humans, while those who look like their mother go back to the bear clan.

According to these traditions, people who were deformed or monstrous were not allowed to have children, and any love or mating between humans and animals was strictly forbidden. Some young people who broke this law without knowing it, tricked by an animal such as a deer, were put to death.

Eastman says that many tribes traced their animal totems to a shared ancestor, a belief that supported their close bond with animals. He wonders why the scientific idea that humans descended from earlier forms of life has not similarly made white people respect animals more.

Eastman describes several later heroes in Dakota oral tradition, each marking a new period in human history. He gives three examples: a boy born from a blood clot who avenges the innocent, a poor boy who wins fame and a wife by killing a bird of bad omen, and the Star Boy, whose mother was human and whose father was a star.

In this story, Star Boy fights the North-Wind, the cold god, and the two wear each other out. Star Boy then fans himself with a fan of eagle feathers, which melts the snow so fast that North-Wind agrees to rule only half the year. This is how the seasons came to follow their order, with spring brought by Star Boy's warm winds.

This is only a list of topics from the chapter's table of contents: death and funeral customs, a sacred lock of hair, reincarnation, communication with spirits, psychic powers, and prophecy. The passage itself does not explain any of these topics.

Death does not frighten the Dakota man, who faces it calmly and seeks an honorable end, especially in battle. Dying in a private quarrel would be seen as shameful. When someone is dying at home, the bed is carried outside so the spirit can leave under the open sky.

Next to the fear of death, the Dakota man is most troubled by leaving his loved ones, especially small children who would be left in need. His family bonds are strong, and he grieves deeply for those he has lost, even though he firmly believes they remain spiritually present with him.

In Dakota mourning, people show grief through outward acts that look more heartfelt than Western black clothing does. Men and women loosen or cut their hair, with the amount depending on how close they were to the dead. They also strip their clothes of fringes and ornaments, or cut them short, as a way of giving up personal beauty.

Mourners show their grief in several ways. Men blacken their faces, and widows or bereaved parents may cut their arms and legs until they bleed. They give away their belongings, even their beds and homes, and wail for the dead day and night until they lose their voice.

Plains peoples once buried their dead on raised platforms of poles or in tree branches. They did this because they had no tools to dig graves, and the platform kept the body away from wild animals. The body was dressed in fine clothes, wrapped in robes, and sealed in rawhide.

Some dead young women and warriors were laid out in a new tepee with household goods and food beside them. The food and tools were not meant for the spirit to use but as a final honor. The whole camp then moved away, leaving the body alone.

Burials had no fixed ritual. Bodies were carried out by chosen young men, and the dead were usually laid on a high hill with a wide view. A warrior killed in battle was propped sitting against a tree or rock, facing the enemy, to show he remained brave and defiant even in death.

Among the author's people, a lock of hair from a dead person was wrapped in clothing and hung in a place of honor in the family lodge. Food was set beneath it at each meal, and a person of the same sex and age was invited to eat it. After a year, the family held a feast, gave away the clothing, and buried the hair.

The passage says that the Dakota did not doubt that the human soul lives on, but they did not try to guess what it is like after death. The soul came from the Great Mystery and returns to it, spreads through all nature, and sometimes stays near the grave to comfort friends and hear prayers. Because of this respect, the dead were not named aloud.

Eastman says that American Indians were widely believed to have had some hidden spiritual power. He admits that later frauds existed and that some may have existed in earlier times too. He still holds that well-documented cases of accurate prophecy and other mystical practices exist.

Eastman says that some Dakota prophets foretold the arrival of white people and their steamboats, and that the old word used for "steamboat" shows the prophecy was made early. He also admits that many predictions were changed later and that false prophets appeared during the transition, but that some true prophets of the old type were still trusted to the end.

Ta-chank-pee Ho-tank-a, also called His War Club Speaks Loud, is said to have foretold a Dakota war party against the Ojibways a year ahead. He predicted seven battles, with the last one a crushing defeat. The events happened exactly as he said, and this was only one of his predictions.

The passage tells of a famous Dakota medicine man born during a fierce battle with the Ojibways, when his people seemed about to be wiped out. His grandmother wanted him placed under fire so he could die a warrior's death, but an old man ordered the women to care for him, saying one warrior's strength might someday be precious to the nation.

A holy man of the Dakota people was believed to have been marked for greatness even at birth. Twice in his old age he warned his band of attacks by enemies, through dreams, and they prepared in time to defend themselves. Unlike other medicine-men, his readings of omens were said to be consistently accurate.

Little Crow's father, a Dakota prophet, once said that three enemies would be killed in an upcoming battle and that he would lose two of his own men. Three enemies were killed as he foretold, and in that battle he lost both of his sons.

The author says that trustworthy witnesses, including Christians, confirm events that happened as foretold, and he cannot explain them. He suggests that his people's strong focus and closeness to nature keep the spirit open to subtle impressions and in contact with unseen powers.

Some people in the author's community were said to sense where a grave lay, which they explained as messages from the dead. The author's grandmother was one of them, and as a child he and his brother would find human bones at the spots she named, even though no visible marks of the burials remained.

A woman, the author's relative, is described as having a bodily feeling in her chest that warned her when something important happened to her absent children. The author notes that other Native women have reported similar warnings, but none he knew read them as accurately as she did.

Eastman's family once heard that his uncle and the uncle's family had been murdered weeks earlier. His grandmother told the mourners to stop, saying her son was coming and they would soon see him. Two days later, the uncle arrived alive at their camp.

Eastman's grandmother refused to camp at a spot the family had chosen, so they moved on after dark. The next day they learned that a family who had stopped at that spot behind them had been attacked in the night by a war party and killed, which deeply affected the people.

Many Dakota people believed a person could be born more than once, and some claimed to remember a past life. Others said they had a "twin spirit" born into another people. One Sioux war-prophet said his twin spirit was an Ojibway war-prophet, even though the Ojibways were traditional enemies of the Sioux.

A Sioux leader tells his warriors that on their next hunt they will meet a band of Ojibway hunters led by his spirit twin, who will look like him, share his totem and sing his war songs. He asks the young men not to fight them, since the two men were born as strangers to each other.

Scouts report that a group is approaching, and the leaders go out carrying a peace-pipe. Both sides fire three volleys to show they want a peaceful meeting. A prophet from the visiting party meets a prophet from the camp, and the people notice how alike the two men look, and the two embrace warmly.

Two Sioux and Ojibway groups camped together, and at a feast a Sioux prophet asked his twin brother to sing one of his sacred songs. The brother sang the very song the prophet himself used to sing, which convinced the warriors that the prophet's claims to special sight were true.

The passage presents the Buddha as a source of comfort and help for people who are suffering, tired, or without hope. It promises healing, food, water, hope, light, and blessing to all who struggle and seek truth.

The passage is an encouraging call to people who are suffering, tired or lost. It says that truth, which the Buddha has revealed, heals, nourishes and guides people, and that it alone overcomes error in life and in death.

The passage describes life as restless: people chase pleasure, flee pain and death, and are driven by burning desires, with everything in constant change (Samsāra, the cycle of rebirth). It asks whether anything lasting or peaceful exists, and wishes for an end to anxiety and desire, and for a calm mind.
The Buddha was saddened by the troubles of life. He saw that worldly happiness is empty and so sought a lasting good that never decays or ends.

Real life and lasting wealth are found in truth, not in the body or possessions. Bodies and compounds decay, but the truths behind natural laws, and the truth of the mind, do not die. Truth has no birth or end, and it is the immortal part of mind.

Hold the Buddha's teaching of truth firmly in the mind, since truth reflects the eternal and grants immortality. Desires that oppose the Buddha should be extinguished, and whatever in the heart cannot grow into Buddhahood is described as illusion, the source of error and suffering.

Immortality comes from filling the mind with truth, and that requires purifying oneself of evil. The passage says the self is the source of selfishness and evil, and it is not eternal. Truth, by contrast, belongs to no self, is universal, and leads to justice and righteousness. So one should seek truth, not the self.

If a person frees the soul from self-centred concerns, wishes harm to no one, and becomes clear like a crystal, the passage says, they will reflect things as they truly are. Such a mind is free of burning desire, false illusion, and restless clinging.

The passage tells people who love themselves to separate two kinds of self. The false self is the ego and its selfishness, which is an unreal illusion that does not last. Those who identify with truth reach Nirvana, and the Buddha's teaching alone lasts forever.

Liberation means letting go of the self, which the passage calls salvation, enlightenment and Nirvana. A person who stops living for pleasure and rests in truth is happy, and a calm, untroubled mind is the highest happiness.

Followers say they take refuge in four things: the Buddha, who has found what lasts within what changes; that unchanging reality amid the changes of life; the truth shown through the Buddha's enlightenment; and the community of those who seek and live by that truth.

Everything in the world changes and is built from earlier elements, and every living being is shaped by its past actions, because cause and effect follow fixed law. Beneath this change lies a constant law, and seeing that law is seeing truth. Truth, hidden within the cycle of rebirth (Samsāra), seeks to become known.

Things in nature have different degrees of truth. A stone exists and cannot be destroyed, but it has no awareness. A plant grows, but also lacks awareness. An animal perceives, chooses and learns, so it has awareness, but only of itself, not yet the awareness of Truth.

The passage says that the sense of self clouds the mind and hides the truth, and that it is the root of all error, illusion and evil. Every wrong, from hatred and theft to bloodshed, is said to come from asserting the self. The self is called Māra, the tempter of Buddhist tradition.

The passage says that the self tempts people with pleasures that are unreal and lead to misery, and that its desires can never be satisfied. It asks how one can be freed from this, and answers that truth brings peace, overcomes error, quiets desire, and leads to Nirvāna, the Buddhist state of liberation from suffering.

A person who has reached Nirvana, the state of peace in Buddhist teaching, is called blessed. Such a person stays calm amid life's struggles, is not moved by change, and is not affected by birth, death, or the hardships of life.

He who has reached enlightenment is called blessed, and he remains so even when he is hurt, suffers, weakens, or dies. His true nature is purity and goodness, whatever happens to his body or circumstances.

A person who has reached Buddhahood, the enlightened state, is praised as able to bring salvation to other beings. In him, truth dwells, wisdom gives him clear understanding, and righteousness guides all his actions.

Truth is presented as a force for good that cannot be destroyed or defeated. It says that people should work it out in their own minds and share it with others, because truth alone rescues them from evil and suffering. The Buddha is said to have found this truth and to have announced it.

King Suddhodana, a ruler of the Sakya people in Kapilavastu, is introduced along with his wife Māyā-devī, who is described as pure and free from desire. The passage then says a holy spirit, shown as a white elephant, came to her, which in the tradition marks the start of the Buddha's birth.
Queen Maya, close to giving birth, asks King Suddhodana to let her go to her parents' home. He agrees gladly, because he is worried about her and the child she is carrying.

Queen Māyā-devī gives birth to a child under a large sāla tree in the grove at Lumbinī. Her attendants step back behind a curtain, and four angels catch the baby in a golden net as he comes forth from her right side, shining like the rising sun.

At the birth of the Buddha, the passage describes a world transformed by light and good signs. The blind see, the deaf and mute speak, the crooked and lame are made whole, prisoners are freed, and the fires of the hells go out.
Nature and the heavens grow calm and joyful at the birth of the Buddha, whose coming brings release to all suffering beings. Only Māra, the evil one, the tempter who opposes the Buddha, is saddened.

Serpent-like Nāga kings come to honor the newborn Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, by scattering flowers, as they did for earlier Buddhas. The king is both joyful and troubled as he thinks about these signs, and the queen mother is anxious and doubtful about the commotion caused by the birth.

A holy man named Asita, a hermit skilled in reading signs, visits the newborn prince. He weeps at the sight of the child, and the worried king asks why. Asita then speaks, though the passage stops before giving his words.

An old seer weeps because he is near death and will not live to see the infant's greatness. He says the child will either rule the world as a universal king or become a Buddha. His teaching will save people, as a shore saves the shipwrecked and a cool lake gives water to the thirsty.

The passage is a prophecy, spoken by the seer Asita, that the child will bring relief to suffering beings. He will quench greed with the rain of his teaching, free people trapped by folly and ignorance, and rescue the poor and helpless. The parents then name the baby Siddhattha, meaning "he who has accomplished his purpose."

The queen tells her sister Pajāpatī that she is about to die and asks her to raise the child Siddhattha as a mother. After the queen dies, Pajāpatī takes the boy and raises him, and he grows in body and mind, with truthfulness and love in his heart.

The prince's father wanted him to marry, so he asked the relatives to bring their princesses for the prince to choose from. The relatives refused, saying the prince was too young and frail, had no training in the sciences, and could not support a wife or lead in war. The prince himself was quiet and thoughtful, preferring to sit under a tree in the garden and reflect on the world.
A young prince asks his father to invite their relatives so they can see him and test his strength. The father agrees and does as his son requests.

Prince Siddhattha, when tested by his kinsfolk and the people of Kapilavatthu, excelled in all bodily and mental exercises and outmatched the wise men in questioning and answering. He then chose his cousin Yasodharā, daughter of the king of Koli, as his wife, and she was betrothed to him.

A son is born to Siddhattha and his wife, and he is named Rāhula, meaning "fetter" or "tie". King Suddhodana, the boy's grandfather, hopes the child will bind Siddhattha to worldly life and keep the Sakya kingdom under his line.

Prince Siddhattha (the Buddha before his enlightenment) performs his religious duties without any personal motive, out of care for his child and for everyone. He wants to bring peace to the world, as a parent wants happiness for their children.

The king kept his son Siddhattha in a luxurious palace and shielded him from all suffering and knowledge of evil. Yet the prince longed to see the world beyond, as a chained elephant longs for the jungle, so he asked his father for permission to go out.
Suddhodana, the father of the prince who later became the Buddha, prepares a chariot with four horses and has the roads decorated along the route his son will take.
The prince Siddhattha rides through his city with his charioteer Channa and sees an old man, bent and frail, leaning on a staff. He asks Channa who the man is and what has happened to him.

The charioteer reluctantly explains that an old man is someone who was once a child and then a lively youth, but whose beauty and strength have faded with the years. Prince Siddhattha is deeply moved by this and sighs. He wonders what joy anyone can find when they know they must wither and decline.

A sick man appears beside the road while the travellers are walking on. He is struggling to breathe, his body is twisted and shaking, and he is groaning in pain. The scene shows sickness as one of the sufferings the travellers meet on their journey.

The prince asks his driver about a sick man he sees. The driver explains that sickness comes to everyone, rich or poor, wise or ignorant. The prince is deeply troubled, finds all pleasures dull, and the driver tries to hurry the horses away from the scene.

A prince sees a funeral procession for the first time and asks his charioteer what it is. The charioteer explains that the man is dead, and the prince, shaken, asks whether this is the only death or whether such things happen elsewhere in the world.

The charioteer says that everyone who is born must die, and there is no escape from death. The prince, deeply shaken, says that people foolishly live on carelessly, though their bodies will turn to dust. The charioteer then turns the horses back toward the city.

Kisā Gotamī, a young princess, praises the prince Siddhattha for his looks and calls happy the people close to him. He replies that those who have found deliverance are the happy ones, and that he will seek peace of mind and Nirvāna, a state of release from suffering.

Asked how Nirvana is reached, the prince gives an answer: it comes when the fires of lust, hatred and delusion have gone out, and when mental troubles and other evils have ceased. Pleased with the answer, he gives the woman his pearl necklace, and afterward he looks down on his palace riches.
The prince tells his wife that he is troubled because he sees change everywhere: people grow old, fall ill and die. This loss of joy in life distresses his father, the king, deeply.

The prince cannot sleep, so he goes out into the garden at night. He cries out that the world is full of darkness and ignorance, and that no one knows how to cure the troubles of life. He groans in pain.
Siddhattha sits under a large jambu tree and reflects on life, death and the suffering of decay. By focusing his mind, he becomes free of confusion, loses all base desires and reaches complete calm.

The prince, later known as the Buddha, sees in a meditative trance the suffering of the world, the pain hidden in pleasure, and the certainty of death. People do not wake up to this truth, and he feels deep compassion. He then sees a calm, majestic figure under a jambu tree and asks where it comes from and who it is.

A figure who appears in a vision explains that he is a samana, a wandering religious seeker. He left home because he was troubled by old age, sickness and death, and he wants a lasting happiness and a life without beginning or end. He has given up worldly concerns, lives alone in a quiet valley, and begs for food while pursuing that one goal.

Siddhattha, the future Buddha, asks whether peace can be found in a world full of unrest. He says that pleasure seems empty to him, that he is disgusted with desire, and that life itself feels unbearable.
