The passage says that suffering and happiness go together, so where there is much pain, there can be much bliss, if one looks for it. It compares this to a man in filth who can find a clean lotus pond nearby. The pond is there whether or not he goes to it.

If a person does not walk the road to Nirvana, or does not seek the healer, the fault lies with that person, not with the road or the physician. The same holds for the spiritual guide: when someone does not seek enlightenment from him, the guide is not to blame.

The prince tells a visitor that his father wants him to enjoy worldly life and duties because he is too young for a religious life. The visitor shakes his head and answers that no time is wrong for seeking a religious life.

Siddhattha, the future Buddha, decides that the time has come to leave worldly life, cut his ties, and live as a homeless wandering monk in search of enlightenment. A heavenly messenger approves of this decision and tells him that he is destined to enlighten the world.

A prophet or seer tells the young prince (the Bodhisatta) that he is a great spiritual master, called the Tathāgata, who will complete all duty and become a king of truth, the Dharmarāja. He is also called the Blessed One, because he is destined to save and redeem the world.

Keep to the truth even when it brings great danger, and do not give in to temptations that pull you off the right path. As the sun always keeps its own course, staying on the straight path of righteousness will lead to becoming a Buddha.

A vision tells Siddhattha, the man who will become the Buddha, to keep up his search, pursue his goal without wavering, and struggle hard. It promises that he will reach enlightenment and save the world. After the vision vanishes, he feels peace.

The speaker says he has awakened to the truth and has decided to leave his home and cut his worldly ties in order to seek salvation. He also states that the Buddhas always speak the truth and never say anything false.

The Bodhisattva, the future Buddha, uses several everyday certainties as comparisons: a stone falling when thrown, death coming to mortals, dawn following night, a lion's roar, and childbirth. He says that the word of the Buddhas is just as sure and cannot fail, and he declares that he will become a Buddha.

The prince goes back to his wife's room to say a last goodbye to the people he loves most. He wants to hold his baby son once more, but the child is asleep in the mother's arms, and lifting him would wake them both, so he cannot.

Prince Siddhattha looks at his sleeping wife and son and feels deep grief at leaving them. Though his resolve is firm and tears run down his face, he forces himself to leave, holding back his feelings without forgetting them.

Māra, a tempter figure, tries to stop the Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) from leaving his palace. He promises him worldly rule over the continents if he stays. The Bodhisatta refuses, saying he wants to become a Buddha instead.

Prince Siddhattha gives up his power, wealth and kingdom, and cuts his ties to family and home to become a homeless wanderer. At night he rides away from the palace with only his loyal charioteer, Channa.

Siddhattha, the prince, has cut his hair, put on plain clothes in earth colour, and left his royal life. He sent his charioteer Channa and his horse Kanthaka back to King Suddhodana, his father, with word that he had left the world. He now walks the road carrying a beggar's bowl.

The passage describes a young man in poor clothes whose noble bearing, royal birth and holy, glowing look make everyone who sees him stop and honour him. It is a portrait of a figure who appears humble on the outside but is clearly great within.

The prince, who later becomes the Buddha, walks silently through the city of Rājagaha and receives food from the people as they offer it. People bow to him and feel grateful that he visits their homes. The local king, Bimbisāra, hears of the stir and sends a servant to see the stranger.

The king of Magadha hears that a holy man, a muni, has sat down by a river in the woods to eat his meal. Moved by this, he dresses in royal robes and goes out with his wise counselors to meet him. He finds the muni under a tree and greets him respectfully, struck by his calm face and gentle manner.

A king speaks to a wandering holy man, urging him to take up power over the kingdom instead of begging. He argues that power and wealth are fitting, and that the best person keeps religion alongside them, using all three wisely. The Buddha is about to reply, but the reply is not given here.

A king is praised for being generous and devout, and his words are called wise. The passage says that a kind person who uses wealth well has a true treasure, while a miser who hoards riches gains nothing. Giving is called the greatest wealth, because it brings no regret even though it spends what one has.

The speaker has left all worldly ties because he seeks liberation, and he says a seeker of religious truth must drop every distraction and aim at that one goal. He must free the mind from greed, lust and the desire for power, since small indulgences grow and power brings burdens. Holiness is worth more than earthly rule, heaven, or lordship over all worlds.

The passage uses a series of everyday examples to make one point: a person who has escaped harm would not go back into it. A rescued rabbit does not return to the snake, a burnt man does not pick up the hot torch again, and a sick man does not seek out what makes his fever worse.

A speaker asks not to be pitied. He says rulers and the very rich live in fear of losing their wealth, and cannot take gold or a crown with them at death. He has therefore given up his royal inheritance, and asks not to be pulled back into new ties or duties that would stop him finishing his chosen work.

A king blesses the Bodhisatta (the future Buddha, here called Sakyamuni) with peace, wisdom and righteous rule. He asks that, once the Bodhisatta has reached his goal, he return and accept the king as a disciple. The Bodhisatta leaves in friendship and resolves to grant the request.
Alāra and Uddaka were well-known teachers among the Brahmans, the priestly class of India. At that time, no one was considered more learned or skilled in philosophy than they were.

The Bodhisatta (the future Buddha, before his awakening) studied the teachings of the Brahmans, the priestly class of Hindu tradition. He learned their views on the self, rebirth, and karma, and their rituals, which were said to lead to a higher rebirth or to freedom from material existence.

Alāra, a teacher, asks what the "self" is that perceives through the senses and moves the body. He says the soul is not the body or any sense organ, and that the "I" is whatever feels touch in the body.

It says the self, or soul, is what smells, tastes, sees, hears, and thinks, and what moves the body. Believing in the soul is necessary for salvation, and deep speculation leads to confusion. Deliverance comes by purifying the soul and living as a hermit who relies on alms for food.

The teacher says that by letting go of all desire and seeing that matter does not really exist, a person reaches an empty, immaterial state and is set free like a bird from a cage. The Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) rejects this teaching, saying people stay bound because they still hold on to the idea of a self.

In our minds a thing and its quality can be separated, but in reality they cannot. Heat can be thought of apart from fire, yet heat cannot actually be taken away from fire. Anyone who follows this idea to its end will see that a quality cannot be removed while the thing itself stays.

Man is made of several parts: body, sensation, thought, dispositions and understanding. The "I" is not a separate soul behind these parts but arises from how they work together. Looking for a permanent self (ātman) is therefore a mistaken starting point.

Self-centred thinking clouds the mind. Thoughts about one's own greatness or deeds block a person from seeing things as they are. Once the idea of "I" is set aside, a clear thinker gets rid of ignorance and gains wisdom.

The speaker argues that as long as the self (ego) continues, liberation cannot be reached. A self reborn in hell, on earth, or in heaven would still face sorrow, rebirth, and death, so the speaker questions whether this is a true escape.
Uddaka argues that a whole is more than its parts. The self, he says, is not the body's parts, yet it possesses them, just as the Ganges river is not its sand, water, or banks, yet has all of them.

The Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) answers that the Ganges is nothing apart from its parts, such as the water, the sand and the banks. In the same way, human activities working together do not show any separate self beyond those parts.

A Brahman sage argues that a permanent self, or ego, must exist. His reason is that karma, the moral results of deeds, needs someone to perform the deeds and carry their effects. He points to differences between people in character, status, wealth and fate as proof that each person's past deeds carry over into later lives.

Human life follows cause and effect, so the present comes from the past and the future from the present. There is no fixed, unchanging self that moves from one body to another. Rebirth happens, but no self passes from body to body.

The speaker asks whether his self is just a mix of body and mind that developed gradually over time. He says his senses, his ideas, and even his thoughts come from earlier people and from his own mind. He treats those earlier beings as his ancestors, and says the deeds of his past shape his present life.

The passage argues against the idea of a permanent self (ātman) that acts through the senses. If such a self existed, it would see, hear, smell, taste and feel better after the eye, ears, nose, tongue and body were destroyed. Since that is absurd, the self cannot be what the senses depend on.

The speaker accepts that actions have consequences and that rebirth happens, but denies that there is a permanent self (ātman) who does the deeds or passes between lives. The self felt in "I say" and "I will" is an illusion. If a real self existed, there could be no escape from it, and suffering would be part of our nature rather than the result of ignorance and wrongdoing.

The Bodhisatta (the future Buddha, here called Sakyamuni) goes to the temple priests and is troubled by the cruel animal sacrifices made at the altars. He says such sacrifices come from ignorance, and that it is better to honor the truth than to calm the gods with blood.

The passage argues that killing living beings cannot make up for wrongs, and that new wrongs cannot cancel old ones. True religion, it says, means purifying the heart, ceasing to kill, and giving up greed, lust, hatred and ill-will. Rituals, prayers and incantations do not save.

The Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, left home to look for a better way and joined five monks living in a forest. He admired their strict discipline and joined them. He practised even harsher self-denial than they did, and so they treated him as their master, though he was younger.

For six years the Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) practiced extreme self-denial, starving his body and training his mind in harsh discipline. At last he ate only a single hemp grain a day, hoping to reach liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

Māra, the Evil One, tells the Bodhisatta (the future Buddha) that he is weak from fasting and should eat so he can do good works. The Bodhisatta refuses. He says he would rather let his body waste away than lose calm and focus, and that defeat is worse to him than death.

The Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, had starved his body into extreme thinness, and people far away came to honor him. He was still not satisfied. He concluded that such self-punishment could neither end desire nor bring enlightenment through deep meditation.

Sitting under a jambu tree, the seeker reflected on his mind and on the results of his self-punishment. His body had grown weaker, and his fasting had not brought him closer to salvation. Seeing that this was not the right path, he decided to give it up.
He had grown so weak that he could barely leave the river, pulling himself out with a tree branch. On his way back to his dwelling he collapsed, and the five monks with him believed he had died.

Nandā, the eldest daughter of a chief herdsman living near the grove, came upon the Buddha-to-be where he had fainted. She bowed and offered him rice-milk, which he accepted. After eating it, his body was restored and his mind cleared, so he was ready to attain full enlightenment.
After Siddhattha (the Bodhisatta, a future Buddha) eats again, his five disciples grow suspicious. They believe his devotion to his goal has weakened and that he has forgotten his purpose.

The Bodhisatta (the future Buddha, here still called Siddhattha) leaves his former companions, who turned away from him and thought he was simply seeking a more pleasant place to live. He walks alone to the Bodhi-tree, where he will reach his goal, and as he sits down, the earth shakes, light fills the world, and all beings rejoice.

Māra, the evil lord who tempts people away from the truth, comes with his daughters and an army of demons to disturb Sakyamuni, the Buddha, as he sits under the Bodhi tree. He tries threats and a storm, but the Buddha stays calm and unafraid, knowing no harm can reach him.

Māra, the tempter, sends his daughters and then his evil spirits to distract and frighten the Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, while he is seeking enlightenment. The Bodhisatta pays them no attention and watches calmly, and their attacks have no effect. Their hellish flames and thunderbolts turn into perfume and lotus flowers.

Māra, a figure who tempts and opposes the Buddha, retreats from the Bodhi-tree, the tree under which the Buddha sat. Heavenly voices then praise the sage, whose heart is not moved by hatred, and say that anyone who keeps searching will find the truth.

The Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, reflects on suffering. He thinks people would give up evil deeds if they saw their results, but self-centred desire blinds them. They seek pleasure, cause pain to others, find no peace at death, and are reborn because their craving for existence continues.

People who cling to desire keep going round in the same cycle and cannot escape the hell they have made for themselves. Their pleasures and efforts are empty, like the plantain tree, which has no inner core, and like a bubble, which has no substance.

The world suffers evil and sorrow, the passage says, because it is full of lust, and people follow error because they prefer delusion to truth. The Bodhisatta, a being on the path to Buddhahood, then teaches the Dharma, which the passage calls the truth, the sacred law and religion, as the only way out of error, wrong and sorrow.

Reflecting on how birth and death arise, the Buddha realized that ignorance is the root of all evil. He then describes a chain of twelve linked steps in the development of life, called nidānas (causes or links of dependent origination).

The passage lays out a chain of causes, often called dependent origination, by which ignorance leads step by step to rebirth, suffering, old age, death and despair. Each stage arises from the one before it. It describes how existence unfolds from ignorance through senses, desire and clinging.

Sorrow, according to this passage, starts with ignorance, the root from which life grows. Remove ignorance and the desires that come from it disappear, then the false perceptions built on those desires, then the errors of separate selves and the illusions of the six senses.

Removing illusions, then misconception, then thirst (craving), then clinging, ends the selfishness of the self. Without that, a person is free of birth, old age, disease, and death. The passage then introduces the Four Noble Truths, beginning with the existence of suffering and its cause.

The speaker says that after many lives spent searching, he has finally seen the builder of the house of suffering, meaning the cause of pain. With that cause destroyed, the roof beams and frame of the house are broken, so his heart is at peace and all desire ends.

The passage says that self and truth cannot exist together: where one is, the other is not. Self is described as an illusion, the source of separateness, envy, hatred and desire, while truth is the correct understanding of reality. All wrong and evil, it claims, comes from asserting the self.
Truth can be reached only when the self is seen as an illusion. Right conduct needs a mind freed from selfish passions, and lasting peace is possible only when vanity is gone.

Those who understand the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching) are called blessed, as are those who do no harm, overcome wrong, and are free from passion. The one who has conquered all selfishness and vanity reaches the highest bliss and becomes the Buddha, meaning "the Awakened One."

Two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, meet the Buddha just after his enlightenment and offer him rice cakes and honey, the first food he eats as a Buddha. He then teaches them the way to liberation, and they take refuge in him and in the Dharma, the Buddha's teaching.

The passage says that the Buddha, here called "the Blessed One," reached Buddhahood, which means full enlightenment, while sitting under a Nigrodha tree, a type of fig tree, by the river Nerañjarā. It then says he spoke a solemn statement, though the statement itself is not given here.

The passage praises the blessings of solitude, kindness, self-restraint and freedom from desire. Its highest bliss is to give up the pride of "I am I." It then says the deepest truth is peaceful but hard to grasp, because most people are absorbed in worldly desires.

An ordinary person, who finds happiness only in the self, cannot grasp the teaching. He takes what the enlightened see as pure joy, immortality, and everlasting life to be loss, nothingness, and death.

Buddha says that the truth stays hidden from people ruled by hate and desire, and that Nirvana is a mystery to those whose minds are clouded by worldly concerns. He doubts that teaching would help people who cannot understand it. Māra, the Evil One, then urges him to enter final Nirvana, and Brahmā appears to honor him.

Show mercy and pity to those who struggle and suffer, since they are caught in sorrow. Some beings are nearly free of worldly attachment; if they hear the teaching they will be saved, but if they never hear it they will be lost.

The Buddha, moved by compassion, looks over all living beings and sees some whose minds are only lightly clouded by worldly concerns and who are ready to learn. He tells the god Brahmā that the door to immortality is open to everyone willing to listen, and asks that they accept the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching) with faith.

The Buddha tells Māra, the tempter, that he will not enter final Nirvana until his teaching is fully carried on. That means monks, nuns and lay followers who know the scriptures, live by the precepts, can teach the doctrine, and can answer false teachings.
The Buddha says he will not die until his teaching has spread widely among people. Brahmā Sahampati, a god in Indian belief, then understands that the Buddha has agreed to teach the doctrine.
The Buddha asks himself who should hear his teaching first. His former teachers have died, so he decides to go to his five former companions, who are still alive, and teach them first.

The Buddha goes to visit the five monks who had earlier left him. He does not hold their desertion against them. He remembers the help they once gave him and feels pity for their hard practices, which he sees as bringing them no result.

Upaka, a young Jain and former acquaintance of the Buddha (then called Siddhattha), meets him on the road to Benares. Struck by his calm, joyful look and bright eyes, Upaka remarks that he seems pure and blessed.

The Buddha says he has reached liberation by ending the self, so his body is disciplined, his mind is free of craving, and he has attained Nirvana. He says he wants to spread the truth and bring light to people in darkness. Upaka answers that this claim makes him a conqueror, the absolute and holy one.

Jina means one who has conquered the self and its desires. The Buddha says he is a Jina for this reason, but Upaka does not accept the claim. He shakes his head, says the Buddha's way lies elsewhere, and walks off on another road.

Five former companions of Gotama, the Buddha, had agreed to ignore him and use only his name, because they thought he had given up his holy life and become worldly. When he approached with dignity, however, they stood and greeted him anyway, though they still called him by name.

The Buddha tells his listeners not to address him by name or as "friend," since he is the Holy One who regards all living beings with equal kindness, so they call him "Father." He says he has avoided both severe self-denial and worldly indulgence, and has found the middle path.

The Buddha tells his monks that a person who has left worldly life should avoid two extremes: indulging in pleasure, and punishing the body with pain. He adds that outward practices such as fasting, nakedness, shaved heads, rough clothing, or fire offerings cannot purify someone who is still bound by delusion.

The passage says that Vedic reading, offerings to priests and gods, and harsh bodily penances do not purify a person who is still under delusion. Real uncleanness comes from inner faults such as anger, envy, deception, self-praise and evil intent. Eating meat is not what makes a person unclean.

The Buddha says he has found a "middle path" that avoids two extremes. This path leads to understanding, peace of mind, higher wisdom, and Nirvana, which is the final liberation from suffering. The passage then asks what this middle path is.

The Buddha tells his monks that the right way lies between two extremes. He says that harsh self-torture, or mortification, clouds the mind and does not even help with ordinary knowledge, let alone with mastering the senses.

The passage says that freedom from self cannot come from a miserable life of harsh self-denial. Freedom comes when the desire for pleasure, worldly or heavenly, has died out. A person in this state can meet the body's ordinary needs in moderation without being defiled by them.

Meeting basic bodily needs is not wrong, and keeping the body healthy is a duty, because it supports clear thinking and wisdom. The Buddha calls this the middle path, which avoids both extremes, and he gently corrects his disciples until their resentment fades.

The Buddha begins teaching five fellow monks, and he describes his teaching as a wheel. Its spokes are rules of good conduct, its tire is wisdom, and its hub is modesty and thoughtfulness, which hold the axle of truth. He says that whoever understands the four noble truths (suffering, its cause, its end, and the way to end it) will walk the right path.

The passage uses the image of a traveler on a road to describe the Eightfold Path, the Buddhist way of practice. Right views, aspirations, speech, conduct, livelihood, effort, thought and contemplation each serve the traveler, and the path leads to peace. It then turns to the first noble truth, that suffering exists.

Life's common experiences, such as birth, aging, sickness, death, losing what is loved, and meeting what is disliked, are all painful. Unsatisfied craving is painful too, and the passage calls this the first noble truth about suffering. It then introduces the second truth, on where suffering comes from.

Craving, or thirst, causes rebirth and suffering. It comes in three forms: desire for pleasures, for a future life, and for happiness in this life. The noble truth on ending suffering is the complete destruction of this craving, so that no passion remains and the mind is free of it.

The passage gives the Buddha's teaching on the path that ends suffering: the noble eightfold path, made up of right views, aspirations, speech, behavior, livelihood, effort, thoughts and contemplation. It ends with the Buddha saying that through lovingkindness he has reached liberation, will not be reborn, and has already attained Nirvana, a state of release from suffering.

Gods, saints and even animals gathered to hear the teaching of the Buddha (called the Tathāgata here, a title meaning "one who has thus come"). Every kind of being heard the message of release and understood it in its own language.
Kondañña, the oldest of the five monks, understood the teaching as soon as it was explained. He declared that the Buddha had found the truth, and the other monks agreed with him.

Beings in the spirit realms hear the Buddha's sermon and rejoice. They proclaim that he has set the wheel of Truth turning, so that no being can stop it. They expect his teaching to spread across the earth and bring righteousness, goodwill and peace among people.

A person alone who has chosen to follow the truth may weaken and return to old habits, so followers should stand together, help one another, and share the same love, holiness, and zeal. They should also spread the teaching widely so that all living beings may come to live under a kingdom of righteousness.

The Sangha is the community of Buddhists. The passage says it is a holy brotherhood, like a church, made up of the Buddha's followers, and that it brings together all who have taken refuge in the Buddha.

Kondañña becomes the first disciple to fully grasp the Buddha's teaching, and the Buddha confirms it by reading his mind. Kondañña then asks to be ordained, and the Buddha accepts him, telling him to live a holy life to end suffering. Kondañña and the other monks then take the vows.

The speaker declares faith in the Buddha, whom he calls holy, supreme, and the Perfect One. The Buddha is described as a teacher who gives instruction, wisdom, and salvation, and who knows the law of existence. The refrain repeats the speaker's commitment to look to him in faith.

The speaker says he will trust the teaching because the Buddha taught it well. He describes the teaching as open to sight, timeless, based on direct seeing rather than rumor, leading to well-being, and understood by wise people within themselves.

The speaker says he puts his trust in the sangha, the community of the Buddha's disciples. He says this community teaches a righteous life, honesty, justice and truth, and it is a brotherhood bound together by kindness and to doing good.

The Buddha's teaching grew steadily, and more people came to hear it and take ordination to live a holy life aimed at ending suffering. Because he could not personally attend to everyone, he sent out some of his disciples to teach the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching).

The Buddha's teaching and monastic rules are meant to be shared openly, not hidden. But they should not be given to people who are unworthy of them and would mock or disrespect them. The monks are now allowed to ordain new members in different countries, but only those who are eager and found worthy.

The speaker tells the monks to go out and teach the doctrine for the good of many people and out of compassion for the world. He says some people are only slightly clouded by worldly dust, and they can only be saved if someone teaches them. They will understand and accept the teaching.
Monks, called bhikkhus, went out to preach when the weather was fine. During the rainy season they gathered again with their teacher, the Tathāgata (an epithet of the Buddha), to hear his teachings.

A young nobleman named Yasa, troubled by the world's sorrows, slips away at night to the Buddha. When Yasa cries out about distress, the Buddha answers that there is no distress here and offers to teach him the truth that will remove his sorrow.

Yasa, a young nobleman, was comforted on hearing that there was no distress or sorrow in the teaching. He sat near the Buddha, who taught about giving, good conduct, the emptiness of the idea "I am," the dangers of desire, and avoiding life's evils to walk the path to liberation.

Yasa, a young man wealthy with jewels, feels ashamed of his finery after hearing the Buddha's teaching. The Buddha then says that outward appearance does not make someone religious: a person can wear jewels with a conquered heart, or wear ascetic robes while the mind is still caught up in worldly things.

A man who lives alone in the forest but still wants worldly vanities is a worldling, while a man in ordinary clothes can have his heart rise to heavenly thoughts. Monks and laymen are alike if both have given up the idea of self. Yasa then joins the Buddha's community as a monk.
Yasa's father, who is searching for his son, walks past while the Buddha and Yasa are talking about the teaching. He stops and asks the Buddha whether he has seen Yasa.

Yasa's father comes to the Buddha looking for his son. The Buddha invites him in, and the father sits beside Yasa without recognizing him. The Buddha then begins to teach, and the father understands the teaching.

Yasa, a young man, praises the Buddha for restoring what was overturned, revealing what was hidden, and guiding those who have lost their way. He declares that he takes refuge in the Buddha, his teaching, and the monastic community, and asks to be accepted as a lay follower from that day on.

A wealthy merchant, now a follower of the Buddha, sees his son Yasa dressed as a monk. He asks Yasa to go home to comfort his grieving mother. The Buddha asks whether Yasa should return to worldly pleasures, and the father answers that if Yasa finds it good to stay with the Buddha, he should stay, since he is freed from worldly bondage.
Yasa's father invites the Buddha to a meal at his house, with Yasa attending him. The Buddha goes there with Yasa, and Yasa's mother and former wife greet him and sit near him.

The Buddha teaches, and two women, the mother and the wife of a young man named Yasa, understand his teaching. They declare that they take refuge in the Buddha, his teaching, and the community of his followers, and they become the first women lay disciples.

Yasa's friends hear that he has shaved his head, put on monk's robes and left worldly life to live without a home. They conclude that this cannot be an ordinary teaching but must be a noble way of giving up the world, since Yasa is known to be good and wise.

Yasa, a young man from Benares, asks the Buddha to teach his four friends. The Buddha teaches them, and they accept his teaching and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching), and the Sangha (the monastic community).

Kassapa was the leader of a group of Brahman hermits in Uruvelā. They wore matted hair and kept a sacred fire, and he was widely honored as a wise man. The Buddha goes to him and asks to spend a night in the room where the fire is kept.

Kassapa, a fire-worshipping ascetic, warns the Buddha that a serpent lives in the room where the sacred fire is kept and may kill him. The Buddha insists on staying there anyway. Kassapa lets him in, and the Buddha sits upright and fully alert.

The Buddha spends a night facing a fire-breathing dragon. The fire cannot harm him, and the dragon dies in its own rage. Kassapa, a fire-worshipping ascetic, fears for the Buddha, but in the morning the Buddha shows him the dead dragon and says his fire has been overcome by the Buddha's fire.

Kassapa feared that people would leave him to follow the Buddha, and he grew envious. The Buddha stayed away from the festival. When Kassapa asked why, the Buddha answered by pointing out Kassapa's own thought: that it was better for the Buddha not to attend.

The Buddha tells Kassapa that he sees the truth but refuses to accept it because of envy in his heart. Kassapa admits this, his envy fades, and he asks to be ordained. The Buddha tells him first to inform his followers, the Jatilas, whom he leads.

Kassapa tells the Jatilas, a group of matted-hair ascetics who practise fire-worship, that he wants to follow the Buddha. They agree to join the Buddha's community too, and they throw their fire-worship equipment into the river and go to him.

Two brothers of the fire-worshipping ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa see their fire-worship tools floating down the river and assume something has happened to him. They go to the Buddha, who then preaches a sermon on fire to them.

Everything is compared to a fire that keeps burning as long as it has fuel, and the fuel here is the senses, thoughts, lust, anger, ignorance and hatred. While this fire burns, there is birth, death, grief and suffering. A disciple who understands this follows the Buddhist path, becomes wary of the senses and thoughts, and so is freed from passion and reaches Nirvana, a state of liberation.

The Buddha left Uruvelā and travelled to Rājagaha with many monks. Some of them had once been Jatilas, a group of matted-hair ascetics. The senior Kassapa, their leader and formerly a fire-worshipper, went along too.

King Bimbisara, ruler of Magadha, heard that Gotama, the Buddha, had arrived. People praised him as a teacher who guides men as a driver steers oxen, and who teaches both high and low. The king then went out with his advisers and generals to the grove where Gotama was staying.

Some people see the Buddha with Kassapa, a leader of the Jatila ascetics, and wonder which of the two is the teacher. The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, asks Kassapa what knowledge he has gained that led him to give up his sacred fire rituals and harsh penances.

Kassapa, a fire-worshipper, says he has given up fire worship and penances because they only kept him bound to rebirth, with its suffering. He now seeks Nirvana, the highest liberation, having seen the truth. The Buddha then sees the assembly is ready to hear his teaching and speaks to King Bimbisara.

The passage teaches that understanding the nature of the self ends selfishness and brings lasting peace. It rejects two views: that the self lasts forever after death, and that it perishes. Both are called wrong, because if the self perished, good and evil and any hope of an afterlife would have no meaning.

The passage argues against the view that a self is permanent and unchanging. If the self were already perfect and could never change, good deeds would add nothing, and moral effort and salvation would serve no purpose.

The speaker sees joy and sorrow changing and asks where anything lasts. He argues that if there is no permanent self, then there is no doer behind actions, no perceiver behind perception, and no lord behind deeds.

Senses meeting their objects produce sensation, then memory, then a mind and a sense of self. The passage compares this to a seed and shoot: they are not the same thing, yet they form one continuous growth. This is how living beings come to be.

The speaker says that the self is an illusion, like a dream or a rope mistaken for a snake. Those who wake up and see things as they are will no longer be afraid, and will give up the desires that come from clinging to a self.

The passage says that clinging to things, greed, and desire for pleasure cause suffering and emptiness in the world. Giving up selfish grasping leads to calm, peace, goodness, and wisdom. It ends with a call to avoid deceit, contempt, anger, and hidden resentment, and to love all beings as a mother loves her child.

The passage tells the reader to hold goodwill toward everyone, at all times and in all places, without limits, envy or hatred. It says that whatever a person is doing or thinking, being loving and kind is the best rule for living.

Gifts, building monasteries, meditation and understanding the truth all have value, but the passage says lovingkindness (goodwill toward others) is greater than all of them. It compares this to moonlight outshining starlight, saying it frees the heart sixteen times more than all other practices together. It urges a person to stay in this state at all times, whatever they are doing.

A king speaks to the Buddha and lists five wishes he had as a prince. Each one has come true: becoming king, the Buddha coming to his kingdom, paying respect to him, hearing the teaching, and understanding it. He treats the last wish as the greatest.

The speaker praises the Buddha's teaching and says the Buddha restores what was overturned, reveals what was hidden, and guides those who have gone astray. He is said to have brought minds to accept the truth, so that the seeds of virtue were sown across the kingdom.

King Bimbisara invites the Buddha, called the Tathagata, and his monks to a meal at the palace. The next morning the king leads them into the city of Rajagaha. Sakka, king of the gods, walks ahead disguised as a young Brahmin, a member of the Hindu priestly class.

Visitors greet the Buddha as he enters the city of Rājagaha, praising him as a teacher and savior who helps those he has taught and given peace. Sakka, a heavenly king, then praises the blessings of an age when Buddhas appear, the teaching is spoken, and the monastic community and its followers flourish.

King Bimbisara asks where the Buddha could live: a spot near the town but not too near, easy to reach, quiet at night, and suitable for a retired life. He offers his pleasure-garden, the Veluvana bamboo grove, to the monks, and the gift is accepted.
The Buddha, without speaking, agreed to a request. He then left his seat after cheering and teaching the king of Magadha, and went away.
Sāriputta and Moggallāna, two Brahmans who led the followers of a teacher named Sañjaya, made a pact. Whoever first reached Nirvāna, the state of liberation, would tell the other.

Sāriputta sees the monk Assaji walking humbly for alms and asks which teacher he follows and what he teaches. Assaji says he follows the Buddha but, being new to the order, can give only the essence of the teaching. Sāriputta asks for that essence, and Assaji recites a verse.
The Buddha explains how everything that arises does so from causes. He also teaches how, in the end, all desire and craving come to an end.

Sāriputta, after hearing a verse, understands that everything that arises also ceases, and he feels he has reached the path to Nirvana. He and Moggallāna then decide to go to the Buddha as their teacher, and the Buddha sees them coming and calls them highly auspicious.

The Buddha tells his other disciples that Sāriputta is well able to help him as his chief follower, comparing him to the eldest son of a world-ruling king who supports his father. The image is of spreading the teaching, which is called setting the wheel of the law rolling.

People of Magadha were angry that many young men of good families had joined the Buddha's religious community. They accused him of persuading fathers to abandon their wives and families, and they insulted the monks, asking who would be led astray next.

The Buddha tells his monks that the complaints against them will fade within seven days. If people insult them, they should reply that teaching the truth is how Buddhas lead people, and ask who would blame the wise or the virtuous. He ends with a verse urging good deeds and a pure heart.

Anāthapindika, a very rich man in Rājagaha, was known for his generosity and was called a helper of orphans and the poor. When he heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in a nearby bamboo grove, he set out that same night to meet him.

The Buddha tells Anāthapindika, a devoted lay follower, that restless busyness is the root of suffering. He urges him to reach a calm mind that rests in peace, and says the self is only a collection of changing parts and the world is empty, like an illusion.

The passage argues against the idea that a personal creator god, Iśvara, shapes human lives. If Iśvara made everything, people would have no free choice to practise virtue, and sorrow and evil could not exist. If other causes exist, Iśvara would not be self-existent, so the idea fails.

The passage rejects two claims that the world was made by an Absolute or by a Self. It argues that an Absolute cannot be a cause, since a cause must come before what it produces, and that if the Absolute fills all things, it cannot have made them. It also argues that a Self cannot be the maker, because the pleasant and painful things in the world would then have been made pleasant.

The passage argues that things are not without cause, since otherwise there would be no point in shaping one's life or choosing means to reach goals. It holds that no god (Iśvara), absolute, self, or chance makes things happen. Instead, a person's deeds bring good or bad results by the law of cause and effect.

Anāthapindika, a wealthy follower, is urged to drop belief in worshipping and praying to Iśvara, a god, and to stop wasting time on empty, useless debates. Instead he should give up selfishness and do good, since all things follow cause and effect. He then tells the Buddha he is ready to speak openly and asks for advice.

A speaker says his life is busy with work and that he has gained great wealth, which brings him worries. He still enjoys his work and gives it full effort, and many people working for him depend on how well his businesses do.

A man tells the Buddha that he has heard his disciples praise the peaceful life of a hermit and criticize worldly unrest. He asks whether he must give up his wealth, home and business to reach the bliss of a religious life.

Enlightenment-style religious life is open to anyone who follows the eightfold path. Wealth and power harm people only when they cling to them; using riches rightly is fine. A monk who withdraws from the world to live in idleness gains nothing, because laziness is wrong.

The teaching does not force anyone to leave home and give up the world. Anyone who feels called to do so may. Everyone, however, must free themselves from the illusion of self, purify their heart, give up craving for pleasure, and live righteously.

Whether a person stays in ordinary work or leaves the world for meditation, they should give full effort to their task. They should stay free of envy and hatred, like the lotus that grows in water without being wet, and live for truth rather than self. Then joy, peace, and bliss will be in their minds.

Anāthapindika, a wealthy supporter of the Buddha, offers to build a monastery (vihāra) for the Buddha's community at Sāvatthi, the capital of Kosala. The Buddha accepts the gift, seeing that Anāthapindika's motive is selfless generosity.

A generous person is loved by others, and at death feels peace and joy without regret, receiving the reward that grows from giving. The passage says giving brings strength, beauty and treasure, and that giving works best at the right time and in the right way, like a skilled warrior going to battle.

Giving to others is compared to planting a young tree: it brings future shade, flowers and fruit. The passage says charity, joy in helping the needy, and Nirvana (the Buddhist state of liberation) all come from this kind of giving, and that the soul is perfected through kindness and compassion. The closing note tells how the merchant Anathapindika asked the monk Sariputta to help him find a site for a monastery.

Anāthapindika, a wealthy supporter of Buddhist monks, wants to buy a garden owned by Prince Jeta as a monastery for the Buddha's community. Jeta refuses to sell at a normal price and says he will sell only if the garden is covered with gold.

Anāthapindika, a rich merchant, offers gold to cover a piece of land, and Prince Jeta refuses to sell it. Anāthapindika keeps insisting, so the two quarrel until they take the matter to a magistrate, a local official who judges disputes.

Prince Jeta learns that the merchant Anāthapindika is wealthy and honest, and asks about his plans. When he hears the Buddha's name, Jeta wants to share in the gift. He takes only half the gold, saying the trees on the land are his contribution. The two men then give the land and the trees to the Buddha, placed in the care of Sāriputta.

A wealthy supporter of the Buddha had a monastery built at Sāvatthi, following the Buddha's own instructions for the design. It was named Jetavana, and the supporter then invited the Buddha to come and accept it as a gift. The Buddha left Kapilavatthu and travelled to Sāvatthi.

Anāthapindika, a donor, gives the Jetavana monastery grounds to the Buddhist monastic community, pouring water as a sign of the gift. The Buddha accepts it and blesses the gift, hoping it will bring benefit to people, the land of Kosala, and the giver himself.

King Pasenadi, a ruler, arrives at the Jetavana monastery to greet the Buddha, whom he calls the Lord of the world and King of Truth. He says his kingdom is blessed by the Buddha's presence and asks to receive the Buddha's teachings.

Worldly gain does not last, but spiritual gain does. A worldly person, even a king, has much trouble, while a holy person, even a common one, has inner peace. The Buddha, seeing the king's greed and love of pleasure, uses this moment to speak.

Even people born low, because of bad karma (deeds carrying over from earlier lives), show respect to a virtuous man. A king, who has merit from past lives, should respect a Buddha even more. The Buddha then says that good and bad deeds follow a person like shadows, and that a loving heart is what matters most.

Addressed to a ruler, this passage advises him to treat his people with care, avoid oppression and pride, and not be swayed by flattery or self-punishment. Instead, he should meditate on the Buddha and follow his teaching.

Life is surrounded by birth, old age, sickness and death, which make up a mountain of suffering. Escape comes only through practising the true law, and wise people reject bodily pleasures and lust. Truth cannot live where passion rules, and a person who does not see this stays in ignorance, however learned or praised they may be.

Whoever has this true knowledge gains real wisdom and avoids craving pleasure. Wisdom is presented as the one essential thing for reaching this mind-state, and neglecting it leads to failure. All religious teachings, the passage says, should focus on wisdom, since without it there is no sound reason.

The main point is that this truth applies to everyone, whether a monk who has taken vows or a layman living with his family. Being a hermit does not guarantee salvation, and an ordinary householder can reach a high spiritual rank. Religious status alone does not decide a person's fate.

Craving for pleasure is a danger that affects everyone and sweeps people away, and those caught in it cannot escape. Wisdom is presented as the boat that carries a person across, with careful reflection as its rudder. The passage urges people to resist Māra, the tempter, by doing good and guarding their thoughts, since deeds bring their results.

The passage says that people can move from light to darkness or from darkness to light, and that a wise person uses the light he has to gain more. He keeps growing in knowledge of truth, through good conduct, reason, and deep thought on how empty worldly things are and how quickly life passes.

A teacher advises a king to raise his mind, hold to sincere faith, keep to the duties of a ruler, and find his happiness within himself rather than in outside things. The king listens respectfully and keeps the Buddha's words in mind. ("Tathāgata" is an epithet of the Buddha, meaning one who has "thus come" or "thus gone.")

Buddhas may or may not appear in the world, but the fact that all conformations (all made or compounded things) are transitory, meaning impermanent, stays true regardless. A Buddha discovers this truth, understands it fully, and then teaches it to others.

Whether or not Buddhas appear in the world, it is a permanent fact that all conformations (the compounded things that make up experience) are suffering. A Buddha discovers this truth, understands it fully, and then teaches it to others.

Whether or not Buddhas appear in the world, it is always true that all conformations (the compounded things that make up experience) have no self. A Buddha discovers this truth, understands it fully, and teaches it to others.

The Buddha gave a talk on Nirvana, the state of liberation from suffering, and the monks listened closely and understood it. One monk still had a doubt, so he stood up and asked for permission to ask a question.

The passage gives a challenge: if all conformations (all made or conditioned things) are impermanent, painful, and without a self, how can Nirvana, a state of eternal bliss, exist? The Buddha is then said to answer with a solemn utterance, which the passage does not yet quote.

The passage describes the "uncreate," a state that has none of the things we know in this world, such as earth, water, heat, air, space, consciousness, sun or moon. It has no coming, going, birth or death, and no change. It is called the end of sorrow.

The passage says that the truth is hard to see, and that a person who knows and sees clearly masters desire and sees all things as empty of lasting substance. It then says there is an unborn, unoriginated, uncreated, unformed reality, and that escape from the world of birth, origin, creation and form depends on it.
King Suddhodana, the Buddha's father, sends a message asking his son to visit him. He says he is growing old, wants to see him before he dies, and feels left out while others have heard the teaching.

King Suddhodana goes out to meet his son Siddhattha, the Buddha, who is returning home after gaining enlightenment. Seeing his son from a distance, the king is moved by his beauty and dignity and is so full of joy that he cannot speak.

King Suddhodana, the father, meets his son Siddhattha, who has now become the Buddha, the enlightened teacher. The father feels the son is close to his heart, yet the son is no longer simply his son but a religious teacher. The king gets down from his chariot, greets him, and says he has longed for this moment for seven years.

A king sits across from his son, who has become the Buddha, and longs to call him back by his old name and be his son again. Seeing his son's firm resolve, the king keeps silent, and he feels both joy and sorrow. His pride is shaken by the thought that his son will never become his heir.

The Buddha tells the grieving king that his love for his lost son could instead be spread with equal kindness to all living beings. If he does this, he will gain something greater than the son he lost: the Buddha, the teacher of truth, and the peace of Nirvana.

Suddhodana, the Buddha's father, is overjoyed at his son's words. He says his grief has ended, and he praises his son for giving up royal power to seek enlightenment. Now, he says, the Buddha can teach the path of deliverance to the world.

The king is upset that his son, Prince Siddhattha (the Buddha), is going from door to door begging for food in the city where he once rode in a chariot. The Buddha answers that begging is the custom of his family. The king replies that none of his royal ancestors ever begged.
The Buddha tells a king that the king's family may trace its line back to kings, but his own line goes back to earlier Buddhas. He notes that those earlier Buddhas lived by begging for their food.

The Buddha responds to a king who has not answered by offering him a teaching, which he calls a treasure. He compares it to a precious jewel given to a father who has found a hidden treasure. He then recites a verse urging the king to wake from dreams, open his mind to truth, practise righteousness, and so reach lasting bliss.

Yasodharā, the wife of the Buddha (called Siddhattha here) and mother of Rāhula, stays away when the king brings him to the palace. She says that if she deserves any regard, he should come to her. The Buddha then goes to her apartments himself.

The Buddha tells his two disciples that he is free of worldly ties, but his former wife, Princess Yasodharā, is not yet free of grief after long separation. He allows her to touch him and tells the disciples not to stop her. When he enters her room, she is overwhelmed with love, and cannot contain it.

Yasodhara, forgetting for a moment who he was, held the Buddha by his feet and wept. When she remembered that King Suddhodana, his father, was present, she felt ashamed, rose, and sat respectfully a short distance away.

The king pleads on behalf of the princess, Siddhattha's wife, who has been left behind. He explains that for seven years she has copied her husband's way of life: shaving her head, giving up perfume and ornaments, eating from a plain bowl, and refusing other suitors. He asks that she be forgiven.

The Buddha speaks kindly to Yasodharā, the wife he left behind when he sought enlightenment. He tells her that her past good deeds, her purity, gentleness and devotion, helped him on his path and earned her a place of honour. He says her grief will be eased by the glory of her spiritual inheritance.

Many people in Kapilavatthu, the Buddha's home town, became followers of his teaching. Among them were his half-brother Nanda, his cousin Devadatta, and others. Later, his cousin Ānanda joined the community and stayed close to him until the Buddha died.
Yasodharā, the Buddha's former wife, dresses their son Rāhula, who is seven, in princely finery and speaks to him. The passage is only the opening of the scene, so its full meaning is not yet clear.

Yasodhara tells her young son Rāhula that the holy man he sees, the Buddha, is his father and that he should ask him for the family's wealth. Rāhula answers that he knows only the king as his father. When the boy sees the Buddha eating near the palace, he goes to him and calls him "My father," without fear and with affection.

Rāhula, the son of the Buddha, follows him after a meal and asks for his inheritance. The Buddha says he cannot give worldly wealth, which decays and brings worry, but he can give the inheritance of a holy life, which never decays.

The Buddha tells Rāhula that he has no gold, silver or jewels to give, but offers spiritual teachings instead: the four truths and the eightfold path. He asks whether Rāhula wants to join the community of monks, and Rāhula agrees.

The king grieved when his grandson Rāhula joined the Buddhist monks, since the king had already lost other close family to the path. He asked the Buddha about it, and the Buddha agreed from then on not to admit any young boy into the order without his parents' or guardians' consent.

Before the Buddha reached enlightenment, seekers of salvation practiced self-mortification. They aimed to free the soul from life's necessities and from the body itself, so they avoided every comfort in food, shelter and clothing. They lived like wild animals, some going naked or wearing discarded rags.

After leaving home, the Buddha first rejected the bare-bodied ascetics' practice and wore rags from graves and rubbish heaps. Later, when the monks fell ill, he allowed and ordered medicines, including ointments when needed.
Jīvaka, a devoted follower of the Buddha, cared for him with medicines and baths until his body had fully recovered. The passage describes this healing as the result of Jīvaka's service.

King Pajjota of Ujjenī fell ill, and the physician Jīvaka cured him. In thanks, Pajjota sent Jīvaka a fine cloth. Jīvaka decided that only the Buddha or King Bimbisāra was worthy to receive such a gift.

Jīvaka, a physician, approaches the Buddha and asks for a favour. The Buddha says he does not grant requests before knowing what they are. Jīvaka replies that the request is proper and harmless, and the Buddha tells him to speak.

A man speaks to the Buddha and offers him a fine suit sent by King Pajjota, asking that the Buddha and his monks be allowed to wear such lay robes instead of the rags they normally wear. The Buddha accepts the suit, gives a teaching, and then speaks to the monks.

The Buddha lets his monks choose between wearing rags picked from the discarded cloth they once used, or wearing robes given by lay people, and says he accepts either choice. When the people of Rājagaha hear that lay robes are now allowed, many of them happily give robes to the monks, so thousands are offered in a single day.

Suddhodana, the father of the Buddha, fell ill in old age and asked to see his son before he died. The Buddha came to his bedside, and Suddhodana died in his son's arms after reaching perfect enlightenment.

According to this account, the Buddha went up to heaven to teach his mother, Queen Māyā, who was living among the gods. After finishing this teaching, he came back to earth and resumed teaching people who were willing to listen.

Yasodharā had asked the Buddha three times to let her join the Sangha, the community of monks and nuns, and he had refused. Now Pajāpatī, the Buddha's foster-mother, goes to him with Yasodharā and many other women, begging to be ordained.

The Buddha warns that letting women join the Sangha (the monastic community) will shorten the life of the true teaching, from a thousand years to about five hundred. He gives in anyway, because Pajāpatī and Yasodharā are so keen to live a religious life. Pajāpatī was the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, and Yasodharā was his former wife.

This is a question put to the Buddha by a speaker who asks whether women can, after leaving household life to become homeless (that is, monastic), reach the stages of spiritual attainment: the fruit of conversion, release from endless rebirths, and saintship.

The Buddha says that women are able to reach the goals of his teaching. If they leave household life to become homeless monks, they can attain the fruit of conversion (the first stage of awakening), freedom from endless rebirth, and sainthood.

Buddha tells his disciple Ānanda to remember how much Pajāpatī did for him, since she raised him after his mother died. He says that because of this, women may also leave household life and become homeless monks under his teaching. Pajāpatī was the first woman to take that step.

Monks who must speak with a woman should do so with a pure heart, seeing themselves as a lotus leaf that stays clean in muddy water. They should treat older women as mothers, younger ones as sisters, and very young ones as children. A monk who regards or touches a woman as a woman has broken his vow, and strong desire must be resisted with steady effort and wisdom.

Monks are told that it is better to suffer terrible harm than to feed lustful thoughts about women, even to the point of gouging out their own eyes or facing death. The passage says women naturally display their forms and charms, even in pictures, and so can lead men away from steady hearts. It ends by asking how the monks should protect themselves.
Monks are told to see a woman's tears, smiles, stooping posture, hanging arms and loose hair as traps set to catch the heart. For that reason, the heart must be held in check and not given free rein.

Visākhā, a rich woman of Sāvatthi, invited the Buddha to a meal at her house, and he accepted. That night and the next morning heavy rain fell, and the monks took off their robes so that the rain would fall on their bodies and keep the robes dry.

Visākhā, a lay follower, asks the Buddha for eight boons after his meal. He replies that a Tathāgata (a title for the Buddha) grants no boon until he knows what it is. She answers that the boons she asks are proper and unobjectionable.

Visākhā asks the Buddha for permission to give many kinds of support to the Buddhist monastic community for the rest of her life. These gifts include robes, food, medicine, and rice-milk for monks and nuns, and the Buddha asks her why she wants these eight gifts.

A woman who served a wealthy householder explains why she wanted to give monks special rain-season robes. Her maid went to call the monks to a meal and found them standing unclothed in the rain. She thought they were naked ascetics, not monks, so she came back and had to be sent a second time. She felt nakedness was impure and offensive, so she wanted to supply proper garments.

This passage gives reasons for a wish to supply monks (bhikkhus) with food for their whole lives. A monk arriving on the road may be tired from looking for alms, a monk leaving may arrive too late or be left behind, and a sick monk may not get suitable food and may die.

A speaker says he has heard that the Buddha praised rice-milk, because it calms the mind, relieves hunger and thirst, nourishes the healthy, and heals the sick. So he offers to supply rice-milk to the monastic community (the Sangha) for the rest of his life.

Visākhā is raising complaints about nuns (bhikkhunīs) who bathe naked in the river at the same place as courtesans. The courtesans mock the nuns and tell them to keep chastity only when they are old, so they can enjoy worldly pleasure while young. Visākhā says that nakedness is impure and disgusting for a woman.

Monks who have spent the rainy season in other places will come to the Buddha at Sāvatthi and ask about a fellow monk who has died. The Buddha will tell them what state that monk has reached, such as the first stage of enlightenment, arahatship, or Nirvana.

The speaker imagines asking fellow monks whether a certain monk once lived at Sāvatthi, a town where the Buddha taught. If they say yes, the speaker concludes that this monk must have received various gifts there, such as robes, food, and medicine for the sick.

This is a speaker describing the inner results he expects from having asked the Buddha for eight boons. He expects gladness, joy, peace of mind, and a blissful contentment that brings rest to the heart. He sees these as a training of his moral sense, moral powers, and the seven kinds of wisdom.

The Buddha praises Visākhā for her request and says that gifts to people who are free of their passions bear great fruit, like good seed in good soil. Gifts to people still ruled by their passions do little good, because those passions choke the growth of merit, like seed planted in bad soil.

King Bimbisara of Magadha, now old, gave up worldly life and took up a religious life. He noticed that Brahmin sects in Rajagaha kept certain days as holy, and that people gathered in their meeting-houses to hear their teachings.

The king asked the Buddha whether his monks should also meet on set days, since rival wanderers who kept such days were gaining followers. The Buddha ordered the monks to gather on the eighth and on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of each half-month for religious practice.

A monk is supposed to preach the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching) to the gathered people on the Uposatha, a holy day. The monks follow this rule and gather, but they stay silent and give no talk, so the people who came to listen are disappointed.

The Buddha orders the monks (bhikkhus) to recite the Pātimokkha, a ceremony for clearing the conscience. Each monk who remembers a fault should confess it so he can be cleansed, since a confessed fault weighs less on him.

A senior monk announces to the monastic community that it is the Uposatha, a fortnightly observance day, and asks whether the community is ready to hold the service and recite the Pātimokkha, the list of monastic rules. The monks reply that they are listening and attentive.

In this part of the ritual, the presiding monk asks any monk who has broken a rule to confess it. If no one has a fault to confess, the monks should stay silent, and their silence will be taken to mean they are free of offences.

In this monastic rule, a monk who is asked a question three times in a formal assembly must answer it. If he remembers a fault he has committed and does not confess it after the third asking, he is deliberately lying.

Deliberate lying is said by the Buddha to block spiritual progress. So a monk who remembers a fault he has committed, and wants to be pure again, should confess it. Once confessed, the fault is dealt with properly.
A monk living at Kosambī was accused of a wrongdoing. Because he would not admit it, the other monks voted to expel him from the community.

A learned monk, known for knowing the teaching and the monastic rules, is told he was expelled from the order. He says the act is not a real offence, the verdict is invalid, and he still counts himself a member. He asks his fellow monks to help him keep that right.

Monks who supported a monk who had been expelled argued that his act was not an offence. The monks who had expelled him said it was an offence. The dispute split the monastic community into two hostile groups, and news of it reached the Buddha.

The Buddha tells monks not to expel a fellow monk just because they feel he is at fault. Expulsion must not be based on guesswork or personal feeling, and a monk who is learned, disciplined and willing to submit must not be expelled merely for refusing to admit an offence.

The Buddha tells the monks who support the expelled monk not to refuse to admit a fault just because they feel innocent. If the community judges them guilty, they should trust its judgment, since it is wise and fair, and accept their offence rather than cause a split.

The Buddha ruled that both groups of monks could keep their own separate ceremonies, called Uposatha (a regular day of confession and observance) and carry out their official acts on their own. Each group was treated as valid, since they had split and could not agree.

Hatred is never ended by more hatred, only by non-hatred, and this is presented as a lasting law. Those who understand should live in harmony, even when others quarrel. A wise, righteous friend is worth keeping close, even through danger.

If no good and steady friend can be found, the passage advises going alone, like a king giving up his realm or a lone elephant in the forest. It says there is no real companionship with fools, and the Buddha, finding his listeners stubborn and foolish, leaves them.
The Buddha left the city of Kosambī while a quarrel among its monks was still unresolved. He travelled from place to place and finally reached Sāvatthi.

Lay supporters of the monks in Kosambī grew angry because the quarrels among the monks got worse after the Buddha had left. They decided to stop greeting and supporting the monks, and said the monks must either make peace with the Buddha or give up the monastic life.
The monks of Kosambī, who had lost the respect and support of the lay followers, began to feel regret. They decided to go to the Buddha so that he could settle their dispute.

Two groups of monks, both quarrelling, have arrived at Savatthi to see the Buddha. Sariputta, a senior monk, asks the Buddha how he should treat these monks from Kosambi, whom he calls the cause of the disputes.

The Buddha tells Sāriputta not to scold the quarrelling monks, since harsh words heal nothing. He advises keeping the two sides apart, hearing both fairly and patiently, and having the monastic community (Sangha) reach an agreement to restore harmony.

Pājapatī, a senior nun, asks the Buddha for advice. He answers that both sides of the dispute may accept gifts from lay supporters, such as robes or food, as they need them, and that no one should be given special treatment over the other.

Upāli asks whether the monastic community (Sangha) may declare its quarrel settled without first examining what the dispute was about. The Buddha answers that such a declaration is neither right nor lawful. He adds that there are two ways to restore harmony: one only in the formal wording, and one in both the spirit and the wording.

A reconciliation counts as real only when the community first looks carefully into the dispute and settles it at its root. If it simply announces peace without that inquiry, the peace exists only on paper. A peace that is both genuine in spirit and formally declared is the only proper kind.
King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, ruler of Benares, goes to war against King Dīghīti of Kosala. He attacks because he thinks Kosala is small and its king cannot resist his armies.

Dīghīti, unable to resist the large army of the king of Kāsi, fled and left his small kingdom to Brahmadatta. He wandered until he reached Benares, where he lived with his wife in a potter's house outside the city, and their son Dīghāvu was born there.

The king sends his son Dīghāvu away to keep him safe from King Brahmadatta, who might seek revenge. Dīghāvu grows up well educated and skilled. Later, a barber who once served King Dīghīti sees him in Benares and, out of greed, betrays him to Brahmadatta.
King Brahmadatta of Kāsi learns that a fugitive king of Kosala and his queen are hiding in a potter's house. He orders them bound and killed, and his officer leads King Dīghīti away to be executed.

A captive king, about to be executed, tells his son Dīghāvu not to hold on to grudges or plan far ahead, because hatred is never ended by hatred, only by letting it go. Dīghāvu later does not take revenge. He gets the guards drunk and gives his parents a proper funeral.

King Brahmadatta grows afraid that Dīghāvu, the son of a king he had wronged, will seek revenge and kill him. Dīghāvu, grieving his parents, goes to the forest to weep, then returns to the capital and takes a job as an assistant in the royal elephant stables.

The king hears a beautiful singing voice at night, accompanied by a lute, and it pleases him. His attendants tell him the singer is probably a young man who serves the master of the elephants, a man well liked by his fellow servants and skilled in many things.

The king takes a young man, Dīghāvu, into his service because he is impressed by how wisely and carefully the youth works, and soon gives him a position of trust. On a hunt, when the king is separated from his attendants and falls asleep tired, he rests his head in Dīghāvu's lap.

Dīghāvu has the king who killed his parents in his power and draws his sword to take revenge. He remembers his father's last words, that hatred is never ended by hatred but only by not-hatred, and so he puts the sword back.

A king wakes in fear from a recurring dream in which the young man Dīghāvu comes at him with a sword. He tells the youth who asked that the dream came to him again while he rested with his head in the youth's lap.

Dīghāvu, a young man, has captured the king who killed his father and mother. He says he has a chance for revenge. He adds that people find it easier to forgive wrongs done to them than wrongs they have done, so he does not expect mercy.

King Brahmadatta, who had been captured by young Dīghāvu, begged for his life. Dīghāvu replied that he never meant to kill the king, so the king should spare him instead. They agreed to spare each other's lives and swore never to harm one another.
King Brahmadatta asks young Dīghāvu what his dying father meant. The father's words say that hatred is not ended by hatred, but only by not-hatred.

A young man explains his dying father's advice. The father's words meant that hatred should not be carried far or started quickly against friends, and that hatred ends only through not-hatred. The young man spared the king, who had killed his parents, and the king spared him, so the hatred between them ended.

The king Brahmadatta praises young Dīghāvu for fully understanding his father's brief words, and returns the kingdom to him. The Buddha then tells the monks to follow his teaching, and the monks settle their disputes in goodwill, restoring unity in the monastic community (the Sangha).
Senior monks saw the Buddha walking barefoot, so they took off their shoes and did the same. The younger novices ignored this example and kept their feet covered.
The Buddha scolds some novice monks for disrespect toward their fellow monks. He asks what will happen to the monks' conduct after he dies, and he worries about the future of his teaching.

Even lay people who earn a living by a trade show respect, affection and hospitality to their teachers. The speaker tells the monks to do the same toward their teachers and superiors. He says their current behavior drives outsiders away from the faith instead of winning them over, and asks them to be more considerate, thoughtful and respectful.

Devadatta, a cousin of the Buddha (Gotama Siddhattha) who had joined his community, became jealous when he did not gain the same status. He criticized the Buddha's rules as too lenient, won the support of King Ajātasattu, and founded his own sect with strict rules and self-denial.

Devadatta asks the Buddha to approve stricter monastic rules, so that greater holiness can be gained. He argues that the body is impure, impermanent and a source of suffering and disease, so monks should treat it as a corpse and wear only rags taken from cemeteries or dung-heaps.

The Buddha says the body is impure and impermanent, and it will decay into its basic elements. Because the body carries the results of past actions, people can choose whether it serves truth or evil. Indulging its pleasures is wrong, but so is neglecting its needs or making it dirtier.

Neglecting the body through harsh self-denial does not help a person receive the light of truth. The body should be cared for in a practical way, and strict rules should not be forced on others, though anyone may choose to keep them on his own.

Devadatta, a rival of the Buddha, rejected the Buddha's teaching and spoke against it as too easy and inadequate. When the Buddha heard this, he said that everyone is blamed, whether they stay silent, speak, or teach the middle path.
Devadatta persuaded the prince Ajātasattu to plot against his father, King Bimbisāra. The son imprisoned the king in a tower, where he died, and Ajātasattu inherited the kingdom of Magadha.

A new king, following the advice of Devadatta, ordered the Buddha killed, but every attempt failed. Murderers became converted on seeing him, a thrown rock split and missed him, and a wild elephant turned gentle. The king himself, troubled by guilt, came to the Buddha for peace.
The Buddha welcomed the king Ajatasattu and taught him how to be saved. Devadatta, however, kept trying to start his own religious group.

Devadatta, who had plotted against the Buddha and lost many followers, fell ill and asked to be carried to the Buddha, hoping to be saved because they were related by marriage. As he rose from his litter to go to him, his feet burned, he collapsed, and he died after chanting a hymn in the Buddha's honour.

Some people greet a teacher with folded hands and sit down, calm themselves, and the Blessed One (the Buddha) asks what they were discussing. He notices they seem very excited about something and wants to know the subject of their conversation.

Sāriputta asks the Buddha how a human being, made of Name (the non-physical parts: sensation, perception, dispositions, and consciousness) and Form (the four bodily elements of earth, water, fire and air), can endure and stay alive.

Life, in this teaching, exists only for a single moment of thought. Like a chariot wheel that touches the ground at just one point at any instant, a living being lasts only as long as one thought, and it is said to end once that thought stops.

Past moments of thought have lived but no longer live, and future moments will live but have not yet lived. Only the present moment of thought is living now, having not lived before and not going to live again. The point is that each moment of thought exists only in its own time.

Name and Form (the two parts of a person, mental and bodily) have no power to act on their own. Each moves only when supported by the other. When Name wants to eat, drink, speak or move, Form carries out the action.

The blind man can walk but cannot see the road, and the cripple can see but cannot walk. Each one has a need that the other can meet. The point is that each man needs the other's ability to make the journey.

A blind man carries a lame man on his shoulders, and the lame man gives him directions. The lame man can see the way and the blind man can walk, so together they can travel. The image is one of two people combining their different abilities to move forward.

The passage describes a blind man and a cripple. Neither can move by his own strength, but when each supports the other, they can travel together. The point is that two weak parties, working together, can do what neither can do alone.
Neither Name (the mind or mental side of a being) nor Form (the physical body) has power on its own to arise or act. Only when the two support each other can they come into being and continue.

Name and form do not come from any stored material before they arise, and when they cease they do not go off somewhere or remain stored up. The lute example makes the same point: a sound has no prior store, and when it stops it is not kept anywhere.

Like a musical sound made by a lute, things come into being from non-existence and then pass away again. The passage says the same holds for all elements of being, physical and non-physical. It adds that no permanent self lies within Name and Form; what is called a person is produced by the combined workings of these parts.
Just as "chariot" names only the parts put together, a living being is only the groups of the four elements joined as one. No self exists apart from these parts, either in a chariot or in a person.

Everything happens through causes, with no separate person behind the action. A path is walked, deeds are done, and wind blows, yet there is no traveler, doer, or wind apart from the activity itself. The idea of a permanent self is therefore a mistake, and all things are empty and without lasting substance.

There is no fixed self that passes from one life to the next. What continues is karma, the effects of deeds, which carry on through rebirth by cause and effect. Like a seal pressing its shape into wax, a person's thoughts and character leave their mark on others, and good or bad deeds bring blessings or curses in turn.

Rebirth is compared to an echo or a repeated stanza: nothing moves from one life to the next as a self, yet something passes on, as a teaching is repeated by a listener. The second part says the body decays, so it should be cared for like a wound, without attachment or love.

The passage says the body works like a machine or cart, moved by "windy elements" (breath or vital forces) and mental pulls, not by any independent self. A self that acts on its own is denied. The verses compare this to ships driven by wind and arrows sent from a bowstring.

The Buddha tells monks to let go of the idea of a permanent self and of attachment to possessions, since these pass away. Deeds, however, last, and a person's karma continues through them, so they should take care with their actions. Karma shapes each being's lot, whether low or high.

Only your deeds, good and bad, go with you after death; nothing else can be taken beyond it. Because of this, the passage urges that good deeds be done now, storing up future well-being and a bliss that keeps growing.

It is because they did not understand the four noble truths that the monks, and the speaker too, had to wander for so long in samsara, the cycle of rebirth. The idea is that this lack of understanding kept them going round that cycle.

The passage says that thoughts arise from sensation and take shape from it. It also says a mind's state depends on its deeds, and that a Bodhisatta (a being aiming at Buddhahood) follows a straight path of wisdom until reaching full enlightenment. Each creature's condition comes from deeds done in past and present lives.
