Human reason is a small spark of true light and the first step upward. Reaching the summit of existence requires further rebirths, until the mind and heart are enlightened. The speaker says he has attained this higher birth, found the truth, and shown others the path to peace and the lake that washes away evil desire.

The passage says that whoever drinks in the perception of truth is freed from excitement, passion and wrongdoing. Such a person has crossed the floods of passion and reached Nirvana, and his heart stays clean. Like a lotus in water that stays dry, he lives in the world without being stained by worldly desires.

Someone who has not seen the four noble truths or understood the three characteristics is still far from the goal, stuck in repeated rebirths and error. Once a listener has gained understanding, the cause of further rebirth is removed, craving is destroyed, and liberation, called salvation or immortal bliss, is reached.

A rich householder in Rajagaha put a valuable sandalwood bowl on top of a tall pole and offered a reward to any holy man (samana) who could take it down by magical power alone, without using a ladder, a hooked stick, or climbing.

The people praise the Buddha and his disciple Kassapa, who took down a bowl that had been placed on a high pole to show off his powers. The Buddha breaks the bowl and forbids all his disciples from performing miracles.

During a famine, some monks falsely praised each other to village households as saints with visions and miracle powers. The villagers gave generously because of this, and the monks were spared hunger.

In this passage, the Buddha asks his monks when a monk stops being a monk. Sāriputta answers that a monk who commits any unchaste act, or takes anything not freely given, even something worth a penny, is no longer a disciple of the Buddha.

A monk must never knowingly and maliciously kill any harmless living creature, even a worm or an ant. Anyone who does so is no longer a follower of the Buddha. The passage then introduces this as one of three great prohibitions and announces a further one.

Monks must not claim superhuman powers, such as visions or miracles, especially out of greed or bad intent; anyone who does so is no longer a disciple. The Buddha forbids spells and prayers for such ends, since all things are governed by karma, and a person who tries to perform miracles has not understood his teaching.
A poet who had gained a clear, true understanding came to believe in the Buddha. The Buddha's teaching gave him inner calm and comfort when he was suffering.

During an epidemic, some people were so frightened that they felt the horror of death before dying. Others pretended to be cheerful, saying they should enjoy today since tomorrow is uncertain, but their laughter was not real happiness.
A Buddhist poet stayed calm during a plague, caring for the sick. A man came to him, shaken by the deaths he saw, and asked for help overcoming his own fear.
A poet tells a self-absorbed man that he can find help only by caring for others. He asks whether he can see others suffering and still be ruled by his own selfish desires.

Unless a person takes refuge in the Buddha and finds rest in Nirvana, life is empty and without substance. Worldly life, including people themselves, is like an illusion, and the hope of heaven is like a mirage.

Worldly people chase pleasures and are like a caged bird that is fed well but will end up in the pot. A Buddhist saint is like a wild crane: he has no stored food, yet the whole world is open to him. The poem adds that hard times should teach people, and that the poet will keep his own mind calm and free of worry.

People chase pleasure and wealth without ever being satisfied, and they fall hard when their hold on these things fails, like puppets whose strings snap. Death treats everyone alike, rich or poor, high or low. Life passes quickly, so change one's ways now rather than later.

Reforming oneself, urging others to reform, living righteously, and trusting in the Buddha are all good. Yet talents, wealth, and worldly success count for nothing unless one reaches Nirvana, the peace that ends suffering.
Three things, the Buddha says, are marked by secrecy: love affairs, priestly wisdom, and any departure from the path of truth. The passage lists these three and says nothing more.

Those who have something to hide, such as women in love, priests claiming secret revelations, and people who have strayed from the truth, prefer secrecy and avoid being seen. The passage then turns to three things that shine openly before the world and cannot be hidden.

The Buddha says that the moon, the sun and the truth he teaches all shine light on the world and cannot be hidden. "Tathāgata" is an old title the Buddha used for himself. So his teaching is open to all and is not kept secret.

Killing, stealing, sexual passion, lying, slander, abuse, gossip, envy, hatred and clinging to false doctrine are all evil. The root of this evil is desire, hatred and illusion. The passage then turns to ask what is good.

The passage lists several good things: refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, slander, and envy, along with other virtues like truthfulness. It then says that the root of all these goods is freedom from desire, from hatred, and from illusion.

Birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, despair, being joined to hateful things, and losing or failing to get what one loves or wants are all called suffering. The passage then names the cause of suffering as craving: lust, passion, desire for existence and pleasure, which keeps leading to rebirth.

The passage says that ending suffering means completely destroying craving and freeing oneself from passion. The path that leads to this end is the eightfold path: right views, right decision, right speech, right action, right living, right struggling, right thoughts, and right meditation.

If a noble youth understands suffering, its cause, its ending, and the path that leads to its ending, and gives up desire, anger, pride of self, and ignorance to reach enlightenment, he will end all suffering in this present life.

The Buddha teaches that people's actions become bad through ten evils and good when they avoid them. The evils are three of the body (murder, theft, adultery), four of speech (lying, slander, abuse, idle talk), and three of the mind (covetousness, hatred, error).

Do not make up or spread bad stories about others, and do not find fault with them. Instead, look for their good qualities and defend them honestly. The passage also advises avoiding oaths, idle talk, envy and hatred, and treating all living beings with kindness.

Clear your mind of ignorance and seek the truth, especially the one truth that matters most. Otherwise you may fall into doubt that leads to indifference, or into false beliefs that lead you off the noble path to eternal life.

Before he dies, the teacher tells his followers to choose capable men to preach in his place. Those men are to take on his inner qualities: patience and forbearance as their robe, charity and love for all beings as their dwelling, and a full understanding of the teaching as their pulpit.
A teacher of the Buddhist truth should state it boldly, without fear or hesitation. His ability to convince others should come from good conduct and from keeping faithfully to his sacred promises.

A preacher should stay within his proper role and keep steady. He should avoid seeking the company of the powerful or of frivolous and immoral people, and when tempted he should think of the Buddha. He should receive all listeners kindly, and he should not criticize or slander other preachers or name them in reproach.

A Buddhist preacher should go to his teaching seat clean and dressed properly, with a mind free of blame and at peace with everyone. He should not enjoy arguing to show off his skill, but stay calm. He should hold no hatred, keep kindness toward all beings, and aim for all beings to become Buddhas.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata here, promises that a preacher who works hard at teaching will be shown the Buddha's teaching in its full, glorious form. The preacher will be honored, and the Buddha blesses both the preacher and those who listen respectfully and gladly accept the teaching.

Anyone who accepts the truth will reach full enlightenment. The teaching is so powerful that even reading one verse, or reciting, copying, or remembering one sentence of it, can turn a person to the truth and onto the path that leads away from evil.

Beings ruled by impure desires are purified when they listen to the teaching. The ignorant gain wisdom by reflecting on its depth, and those driven by hatred become filled with goodwill and love by taking refuge in the Buddha. A preacher should stay energetic, hopeful, and persistent, never giving up on success.
A preacher is compared to someone digging a well in dry land. When the sand is still dry, the water is far off, so he should keep digging rather than give up. Damp sand is a sign that water is close.

The passage describes the preacher's task. When people do not yet listen to the truth, the preacher must work harder to reach their hearts, but when they start to listen, he expects them to reach enlightenment soon. The Buddha hands the teaching of truth to those who have vowed to preach it, telling them to receive it, study it, and teach it to all beings everywhere.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata here, is not greedy or narrow-minded and freely shares his full awakening with anyone ready to receive it. Followers are urged to copy him by generously giving out the truth.

The Buddha tells his followers to gather listeners, comfort them with the teaching, and lead the unbelievers toward the truth until they see it clearly. The disciples respond by praising him as a great cloud that puts out suffering and pours down the rain of the law.
The disciples make a vow, and it spreads through the whole universe. It is answered by all the future Bodhisattas, the enlightened beings who will teach the true law to later generations.

The Buddha compares himself to a king who rewards soldiers who fight his enemies. His followers are the soldiers, and Māra, the Evil One (the tempter who opposes the Buddha), is the enemy to be defeated. The reward for victory is Nirvana, a state of perfect peace and enlightenment.

Each person is responsible for their own evil, suffering, and purification, and no one can purify another. Teachers only point the way, so each person must make the effort themselves. Lazy and idle people will not reach enlightenment, while those who watch and guard themselves are protected by the truth.

A person can only truly guide others if he first trains himself to live as he teaches. Controlling one's own self is harder than controlling others, and the man who conquers himself is greater than one who wins a thousand battles.

Fools, whether lay people or clergy, act for their own pride. They want others under their control and want to be the one who matters in every task. They care nothing for the duty or the goal, only for themselves. The passage ends by urging that whatever is to be done should be done with energy.

The body will decay and be left like a useless log, but thoughts continue. Thoughts lead to actions: good thoughts bring good actions and bad thoughts bring bad ones. Being earnest, or careful and attentive, leads to immortality, while thoughtlessness leads to death.

Those who mistake falsehood for truth, and truth for falsehood, never reach truth and chase empty desires. Those who see clearly what is true and what is false reach truth. Passion gets into an unthinking mind as rain gets into a badly roofed house, and it cannot get into a mind that reflects carefully.

Wise people shape themselves, much as craftsmen shape water, arrows and wood, and they stay calm under praise or blame. Evil words or deeds bring pain that follows the doer, while good deeds bring no later regret.

Wrongdoing brings pain and good brings happiness, so a person should avoid repeating wrong and repeat good. Evil should not be dismissed as harmless, because small wrongs add up over time, as drops of water slowly fill a pot.
Do not think that good deeds are unimportant or will never reach you. A wise person fills up with goodness gradually, one small act at a time, just as a water pot fills drop by drop.

A person who lives only for pleasure, without self-control, lazy and weak, will be easily overthrown by Māra, the tempter, as a weak tree falls in the wind. A self-controlled, moderate, faithful and strong person cannot be overthrown, like a rocky mountain. Those who know their own foolishness are wise in that respect, but those who think themselves wise are true fools.

Wrongdoing seems sweet while it has no consequences, but its bad results come later. Good conduct can seem a burden at first, yet its good results appear in time. A misdirected mind harms its owner more than any enemy can, and a well-directed mind helps its owner more than any relative can.

The main point is that a person's own wrongdoing and desires harm them most. A wicked person is his own worst enemy, as a creeper kills the tree it climbs. Passions such as hatred, vanity and lust damage people just as hurricanes and weeds damage crops.

Attachment to pleasure brings grief, and fear of pain brings fear, so a person free from both knows neither. Someone who chases pleasure and neglects meditation, forgetting life's true aim, will in time envy the one who has devoted himself to meditation.

It is easy to see other people's faults but hard to see our own. The passage says a wise person should worry only about his own wrongs and failings, not those of others, because judging others lets one's own passions grow. Good people are seen from far away, like snowy mountains, while bad people are hidden, like arrows shot in the dark.

Hatred is not ended by more hatred but by its opposite, not-hatred. The passage urges overcoming anger with love, evil with good, greed with giving, and lies with truth. It also says a wise person removes his own faults slowly, one at a time, as a smith removes impurities from silver.

If no companion is as good as you or better, the traveller should keep walking alone, since fools make poor company. The passage then contrasts the foolish, for whom life drags, with a single day spent seeing the highest truth, which it calls worth more than a hundred years without it.

Some people make up their own teachings and build complicated theories, claiming good results come only from accepting those theories. The speaker says the truth is one, not many. Having weighed these theories, the speaker has joined with a person who has shed all sin, and asks whether they can keep walking that path together.

The passage says the eightfold path is the best way and the only route to a purified mind. Everything else is a trap set by Māra, the tempter (a figure who works against spiritual progress). Following this path ends suffering, and the Buddha (called Tathāgata here) taught it after he understood how to remove the "thorn in the flesh," a image for suffering.

The passage says that discipline, vows and much learning are not enough on their own to reach release. A monk should not feel secure until he has ended craving, which the text calls the highest religion. Few people cross the river to the goal, while most stay on the shore, but whoever finishes the journey is free from suffering.

The main point is that a follower of the Buddha stays pure and good even among people who are corrupt, unhappy or greedy. Like a lily blooming on a heap of rubbish, he keeps his wisdom and calm, and does not return hatred, sickness of mind or greed for what surrounds him.

Each thing shines in its own way: the sun by day, the moon by night, a warrior in his armor, a thinker in meditation. The passage says that the Buddha, the Awakened one, shines brighter than all of them, both day and night.

Two young Brahmans, Vāsettha and Bhāradvāja, who belong to different schools of Brahman (Hindu priestly) learning, come to the Buddha in a mango grove in a village called Manasākata. The passage stops just as Vāsettha begins to speak to him.

Two Brahmans, men of the Brahmin priestly class, disagree about which teaching shows the true way to union with Brahmā, the Hindu creator god. Each names a different teacher as the authority: one says Pokkharasāti, the other says Tārukkha.

Two Brahmans (priests of the Hindu tradition) ask the Buddha whether all religious paths lead to salvation and to union with Brahmā, their chief god. The Buddha asks them whether all paths are right. They first answer yes, then change their answer to no.

Two Brahmans (priests of the Hindu tradition) say that no one can see or understand Brahmā, their creator god, because a mortal cannot grasp something immortal. The Buddha then offers an illustration to answer them.

A man builds a staircase at a crossroads, but cannot say where the mansion it leads to is, or even what direction or size it is. He admits he does not know. The image shows someone working toward a goal without knowing what the goal is.

The Buddha asks the two Brahmans (Hindu priests) about a man who builds a staircase toward a mansion he has never seen, while admitting he cannot know it. The Brahmans agree that such a man's talk would be foolish.

The Buddha argues that Brahmans claim to show the way to union with something they neither know nor have seen. If that is the core of their teaching, he asks, then their work is pointless. Bhāradvāja, a Brahman in the dialogue, agrees that it follows.

The Buddha says that Brahmans, the priests who know the three Vedas (ancient sacred texts), cannot lead others toward union with something they have never known or seen. He compares them to a line of blind men holding each other, none of whom can see the way, so their teaching is blind talk, empty words.

The Buddha asks a simple question: if a man wants to cross a river, will praying to the far bank make it come to him? The answer given is no. The point is that a goal must be reached by action, not by calling on something to come to you.

The Buddha says that Brahmans call on gods such as Indra, Soma, Varuna and Brahmā, but neglect the good qualities that make a person a true Brahman. So, he says, their prayers will not lead them to be united with Brahmā after death. He then asks whether Brahmā has lust, malice, sloth or pride, and the Brahmans say no.

The Buddha says that Brahmans, the Hindu priestly class, are held back by worldly attachments, sensory temptations, and five hindrances: lust, malice, sloth, pride, and doubt. So their threefold wisdom, the Vedas, is like a dry desert, a trackless jungle, and hopeless ruin. A Brahman replies that he has heard the Buddha knows the way to union with Brahmā, the creator god.

The Buddha asks two young Brahmans whether a man raised in the town of Manasākata would doubt the direct way back there. They say no. He then says a Tathāgata (his term for an enlightened teacher) knows the straight path to union with Brahmā, the creator god of Brahmanism, as if he had already lived in Brahmā's world. The two Brahmans ask him to show them the way.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata here, is said to see the world as it really is and to teach the truth fully, both in its words and its meaning. He shows the way to a pure higher life. He also fills the whole world with boundless love, and that love is said to continue to spread everywhere.

The Buddha, called here the Tathāgata, is compared to a trumpeter whose sound reaches all four directions with ease. In the same way, he does not pass over any living being. He looks on every one with a free mind and deep love.

A person on the right path is upright, careful about small wrongs, moral in word and deed, and self-controlled. Whoever follows the eightfold noble path steadily will reach Nirvana, and the Tathagata (the Buddha) lovingly guides his followers toward that light.

A hen sits on her eggs and wishes her chicks will hatch safely, and they surely do as they break out of their shells. In the same way, a monk who keeps firmly to the noble path will surely reach enlightenment.

Sigāla, a householder (a lay man with a family and home), was seen bowing toward all directions, up and down, as a traditional ritual to ward off evil. The Buddha, knowing this was done out of superstition, asked him why he performed these strange ceremonies.

Sigāla answers the Buddha's (called Gotama, the Tathāgata) apparent objection by saying he guards his home against demons because he is honoring his father's words. He does not claim that the rite itself has saving power.

The Buddha tells the young man Sigāla that honoring his father's words and protecting his family is good, and he finds no fault with the father's ritual. But Sigāla does not understand the ceremony's meaning, so the Buddha offers to explain the six directions.

The passage says that protecting one's home is not done by magic rites but by good conduct. Each direction stands for a group of people to be cared for: parents in the East, teachers in the South, wife and children in the West, friends in the North, religious duties above, and servants below. The ceremony is only a reminder of these duties.

Sigāla, a young man, praises Gotama as the Buddha and admits he did not know what he was doing before. Gotama has shown him the hidden truth, like a lamp brought into darkness. Sigāla then takes refuge in the Buddha, the teaching, and the community of monks.

Simha, a army general who follows the Niggantha teacher Nātaputta, hears citizens praise the Buddha at a town meeting. Persuaded that the Buddha is holy, he goes to his own teacher to say he wants to visit the monk Gotama.

Nātaputta, a leader of the Jain Niggantha group, tells Simha, a general, not to visit the Buddha. He claims the Buddha denies that actions have results and teaches non-action. Simha's wish to visit fades, and Nātaputta twice talks him out of going.

A general, after hearing respected men praise the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching) and the Sangha (his community of monks), decides he will visit the Buddha. He resolves to go without first asking permission from the Nigganthas, a rival religious group that he follows or serves.

Simha, a military commander, reports that others say the Buddha (called "Gotama" here) teaches that actions have no reward, that everything is annihilated and worthless, and that he teaches the destruction of the soul. He asks whether these accusations are true or are false claims that twist the Buddha's teaching.
The Buddha tells Simha that both a claim and its opposite can be true of him, depending on how the claim is understood. He says he will explain which sense is meant.

The Buddha tells Simha what he teaches: avoiding wrong actions, words and thoughts, and not allowing evil states of mind to arise. He also teaches doing right actions, words and thoughts, and cultivating good states of mind.

The Buddha tells Simha that what must be destroyed is evil in the heart and in action, such as egotism, lust, ill-will and delusion. Once these are rooted out, the self is said to be eradicated. Forbearance, love, charity and truth are not to be destroyed.

The Buddha tells Simha that he considers wrong actions, whether done by body, speech, or mind, to be contemptible, and right conduct to be praiseworthy. Simha then says he still has a doubt about the teaching and asks the Buddha to clear it up.

A soldier named Simha asks the Buddha whether his teaching allows punishing criminals and fighting wars to protect home and family. He also asks whether the teaching requires a person to give up all resistance, even against violence and theft, or forbids all fighting, including wars fought for a just cause.

Punishment and kindness do not conflict, the Buddha says. A wrongdoer suffers because of his own deeds, not because the judge hates him. So a judge should punish without hatred, and a condemned murderer should see the punishment as the result of his own act, which will purify his soul.

The Buddha says that war in which one person tries to kill another is regrettable. He does not blame those who fight in a just cause after every effort to keep the peace has failed. The one to blame is the person who starts the war.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata here, teaches giving up the self completely. He does not teach giving in to evil powers, whether human, divine, or natural. Struggle is part of life, but a struggle for personal gain brings no reward, while one for truth and righteousness brings reward even in defeat.

The passage contrasts the small, fragile self with a larger truth. A self is like a brittle vessel that spills its contents, while truth can hold all selves' desires, so that when a self breaks its contents are kept and live on in truth. It ends by saying a warrior must accept that he may be killed in battle, even for a just cause.
The main point is that a winner should keep in mind how unstable worldly things are. However great his success, fortune can turn and bring him down to nothing.

The passage says that the true victory is over one's own anger and hatred, not over an enemy in battle. A person who puts down hatred and offers peace to a defeated opponent gains a lasting success. Self-conquest is taught to preserve people, not destroy them, and such a person is better fit to live and succeed than someone enslaved by self.

A person whose intentions are right and just will not fail and will keep his success. Whoever holds love of truth in his heart will not die, because he has drunk the water of immortality. The speaker urges a general to fight hard but as a soldier of truth, promising him the Buddha's blessing.

Simha, a general, praises the Buddha as the teacher who shows the way to salvation and true deliverance. He then declares that he takes refuge in the Buddha, his teaching, and the monastic community, and asks to be accepted as a lifelong disciple from that day on.
The Buddha tells Simha to think carefully before he acts. He says that people of high standing, as Simha is, should never act without due thought.

Simha, a general, becomes more devoted to the Buddha. He says that if other teachers had won him as a follower, they would have paraded through Vesālī announcing it. Instead, he takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community) again, asking to be accepted as a lifelong disciple.

The Buddha tells Simha that his household has long given offerings to the Nigganthas, a name for Jain monks. He asks Simha to keep giving them food when they come to his house on their begging rounds.

Simha reports a claim he heard: that the Buddha said gifts should go only to him and his pupils. He notes that the Buddha instead urged him to give to the Nigganthas, rival wanderers. Simha says he will consider what is fitting, and he again takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the community of monks.

A military officer asks the Buddha whether it is true that he denies the existence of the soul. The Buddha answers that critics are right in one sense and wrong in another. He does not give a flat yes or no.

The Buddha teaches that there is no permanent self, meaning no soul that thinks thoughts and performs deeds. Yet he also teaches that mind exists, and calls that understanding true. When an officer asks whether this means two things exist, the question is about whether the senses and the mind are two separate realities.

The Buddha says that the mind has a spiritual nature, and that the world perceived by the senses is not empty of spirit either. Bodhi, or enlightenment, is eternal and guides all beings toward truth. It can turn even crude nature into mind, so every being can become a vessel of truth.

Kūtadanta, a Brahmin (a member of the priestly class in India), challenges the Buddha to prove his claim by appearing with royal glory. The Buddha replies that Kūtadanta's mind is dim and that truth's glory can only be seen with a clear mind. Kūtadanta then asks to be shown the truth, but says the Buddha's teaching is inconsistent and so will not last.

Kūtadanta, a Brahmin (a member of the priestly class), tells the Buddha that he is accused of tearing down religion. His followers reject rituals and animal sacrifice, and he argues that honoring the gods is possible only through sacrifice.

The Buddha says that giving up one's own evil desires is worth more than sacrificing bulls. Killing animals on the altar cannot cleanse anyone; only ending greed and lust makes the heart pure. Following the laws of righteousness matters more than worshiping gods.

Kūtadanta, who had made many blood sacrifices to secure his fate after death, now doubts the Buddha's teaching. He accepts rebirth and karma but asks how they can hold if there is no soul. If a person is only a mix of mental and physical parts, he asks, what could move on after death?

The Buddha tells a Brahman that his efforts are wasted because he lacks the one essential understanding. Rebirth passes on character and thought-patterns, but no permanent self moves from one life to the next. He says people believe in separate, lasting souls only through ignorance and delusion.

The Buddha tells a Brahman that his mind is still attached to the self. He wants heaven, but only for his own pleasure, so he cannot see the truth. The Buddha says he came to teach life, not death, and the Brahman does not understand what living and dying really are.
The body will decay whatever is offered for it, so one should seek the life of the mind. Self leads to death and truth to life, and Nirvana is found wherever the precepts are kept.

Asked whether wisdom, enlightenment and salvation exist just because Nirvana is not a place, the Buddha answers with an image. The Tathagata (a title for the Buddha) is like a cool wind on a hot day, bringing relief to people suffering from fever, which is the way his love affects human minds.

Kūtadanta asks how there can be immortality if there is no ātman, a lasting self or soul, since thoughts end when thinking ends. The Buddha answers that thinking stops but thoughts continue, and reasoning ends while knowledge remains. Kūtadanta then asks whether reasoning and knowledge are not the same.

The Buddha uses a comparison: a man writes a letter by lamplight, then puts the lamp out, but the letter remains. In the same way, reasoning and mental activity stop, while knowledge, wisdom and the results of past actions continue.

Kūtadanta asks how his self can keep its identity if its thoughts and soul pass on and the parts that make up a person are dissolved. The Buddha answers with an image: a lamp burning through the night. He asks whether the flame of the first watch is the same flame as that of the second.

Kūtadanta is asked whether a flame burning through the night is the same flame at different hours. He first says no, to be careful, then admits it is the same in one sense and not in another. It is the same kind of oil, light and purpose, though the flame itself changes.

The Buddha asks whether a lamp's flames are the same flame across a day, even if they were put out in between. Kūtadanta answers that in one sense the flame is different and in another it is not. The question is about whether one thing stays the same through change.

The Brahman, a Hindu priest, is answering a question about whether something has stayed the same over time. He says it has not stayed fully the same, yet it is also the same, whether a long time or one second has passed, and whether the lamp was put out in between or not.

The Buddha uses the example of a flame to show that a thing can be the same in one sense and different in another. He then asks Kūtadanta whether a man who thinks and acts exactly like Kūtadanta is the same man, and Kūtadanta says no. The Buddha asks why the same reasoning would not apply to Kūtadanta himself.

Kūtadanta, a speaker in the dialogue, says that he does not accept the general rule that applies to all things. He claims his own self is unique: even a person who thinks, feels, acts, and shares his name and possessions would still not be him.

Buddha asks whether a pupil who grows up, or a criminal who is later punished, is the same person as before. Kūtadanta agrees they are the same, and says sameness comes from continuity together with, mainly, identity of character.

The Buddha argues that two people can be called "the same" in the way two flames of the same kind are called the same. A Brahman (a member of the Hindu priestly class) agrees. So another person with the same character and karma (the results of past actions) counts as the same as you, in this sense only.

The Buddha says a person stays the same only in a limited sense. A person is not the body's matter but the combined sankhāras (the forms of body, sensation and thought), so where these go, the person goes. Anyone who denies all identity would have to say the questioner is not the same person a minute later. He then asks whether the continuing person, kept in karma (the results of past actions), should be called death or continued life.

Kūtadanta, a speaker in the dialogue, says that ordinary continued life is just the going on of his own existence, and he does not care about that. He cares only about a different kind of continuation, one in which every person is an altogether different self, whether or not they are the same as him.

Buddha tells his listener that clinging to a self is the error behind his desire. He says all compound things, meaning anything made of parts, are impermanent, painful, and without a self or ego. The listener then asks how this can be so.

The Buddha asks a man named Kūtadanta where his self is, and then argues that the self keeps changing. A person was once a baby, then a boy, then a man, so there is only a limited sense in which they stay the same. He compares this to a lamp's flame, which is more alike across the watches than the man is across his life, and asks which of these selves the man wants to protect.

The Buddha tells Kūtadanta that his mental formations (sankhāras, the habits and tendencies shaped by past deeds) carry his self forward into later lives, so he will reap in future lives what he has sown now and in the past. Kūtadanta objects that it is unjust for others after him to reap what he sows now.

The Buddha asks whether his teaching is wasted, and says the others someone is blaming are really the listener's own self. He adds that each person will receive the results of their own actions, not someone else's.

The passage argues that a person's present misery comes from their own past actions, even though the grown man is not the same as the lazy boy he once was. It adds that no hiding place escapes the results of evil deeds, and that good deeds bring their rewards in the same way.

A traveler who comes home safely is welcomed by family and friends. In the same way, a person who has lived by the right path is welcomed by the fruits of his good deeds when he passes from this life to the next.

Kūtadanta, a Brahmin (a member of the priestly class), tells the Buddha that he now sees there is no self and that sacrifices and prayers cannot save him. He asks how to reach eternal life, since knowing the Vedas (ancient sacred texts) has not given him the truth.

The Buddha says that learning alone is not enough; true wisdom comes only through practice. He urges practising the truth that one's brother is the same as oneself, and following the noble path of righteousness. Kūtadanta then asks to take refuge in the Buddha, the teaching, and the monastic community, and to become a disciple.

Only those who do not believe call him Gotama; his followers call him the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Teacher. He says this is right, because he has entered Nirvana in this life, and the life of Gotama, the man, has been extinguished.

The speaker says his sense of self is gone and the truth now dwells in him. His physical body, called Gotama's, will decay, and no one will see him again after that. But the truth remains, so the Buddha will live on in the body of the law, meaning his teaching.

The Buddha's passing into extinction (nirvana) leaves nothing that could create another self, so he cannot be located here or there. He is like a flame that has gone out. He can still be found in the Dharma, the teaching he preached.

The speaker says that, having crossed to the far shore and found release himself, he now helps others cross and find release too. He promises to bring joy and relief to suffering beings, and says he was born into the world to save it.

The speaker says that truth is what he thinks about, practises, talks about and keeps in mind, and that he has become the truth itself. The passage adds that whoever understands the truth will see the Buddha, because the Buddha taught the truth.
All things come from one essence, but they differ in the forms they take under different impressions. Each thing acts according to the form it has taken, and it is what it does.

Different pots are made from one clay, and their different uses come only from the potter's shaping. In the same way, all things come from one essence, develop under one law, and aim at one goal, Nirvana (the Buddhist state of liberation from suffering).

Nirvana, the state of liberation, is one, because all things share one essence and follow one law, just as there is only one truth. The Buddha (called Tathagata here) treats all beings alike, like a cloud that waters everything without distinction, though he responds to each according to how they differ.

The passage uses the image of a rain cloud that spreads over the whole world and falls on every kind of plant, on hills, mountains and valleys alike. It is a picture of teaching reaching all beings equally, though the passage itself only describes the rain falling on all plants.

Plants of many kinds, such as grasses, shrubs, herbs and trees, take in water from one great cloud. Because the water is all of the same kind, each plant grows according to its own nature. All of them grow from the same soil and are given life by the same water.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata, knows the truth that leads to Nirvana, the state of peace. He teaches everyone the same truth but gives each person only what they are ready to receive. As an example, he sent his son Rāhula away to a distant monastery to train his mind and speech, because Rāhula's conduct had not always been truthful.

The Buddha teaches his son Rāhula by comparing him to a water vessel. Once the water is poured out, the vessel is still stained and unclean, so it cannot hold drinking water. The Buddha says Rāhula is the same: though he is a monk, his lying has made his mind unclean and unfit for any high purpose.

The Buddha speaks to his son Rāhula after Rāhula has told a lie. He says the body is made of the same material as other things that break down, so breaking it is no great loss. He adds that a person who often tells lies is looked down on by the wise, and then promises a parable.

A king's war elephant, trained to keep its trunk coiled to protect it from arrows, stretched its trunk out in battle to grab a sword. Because of this, the master and king decided it could no longer be used in war.

The Buddha tells his son Rāhula that guarding one's speech would make everything well. He compares this to a fighting elephant that protects its trunk, and to a well-trained elephant that lets the king mount it, showing that a person who values truth and righteousness stays steady throughout life. Rāhula takes this to heart and, from then on, gives no cause for complaint.
The Buddha watched how people lived together and saw that much suffering came from spite and foolish wrongs. These wrongs were done only to feed vanity and self-centred pride.

The Buddha says that when someone wrongs him, he answers with unlimited kindness, so that the more harm comes from that person, the more good comes from him. A foolish man then insulted the Buddha, and the Buddha stayed silent, feeling pity for the man's foolishness.

The Buddha asks an insulting man a question: if someone refuses a gift, who keeps it? The man answers that it still belongs to the person who offered it. The question is meant to show that the insult, like an unaccepted gift, returns to the one who gave it.

The Buddha says that he refuses to take an insult, so the abuser must keep it for himself. Harm from evil words, he says, comes back to the one who speaks them, just as spit thrown upward falls back on the thrower and never touches heaven.

The one who slanders others is compared to a man who throws dust against the wind, so the dust falls back on him. A virtuous person cannot be harmed, and the harm the abuser meant returns to the abuser. Ashamed, the abuser later comes back and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (the teaching), and the Sangha (the community of monks).

A celestial being, appearing as a bright-faced Brahman (a member of the Indian priestly class), asks the Buddha four questions. The Buddha answers that anger in speech is the sharpest sword, greed the deadliest poison, passion the fiercest fire, and ignorance the darkest night.

The Buddha answers a deva, a heavenly being, with a set of contrasts. The greatest gain comes from giving, and the greatest loss from taking without thanks. The most dangerous thief is an evil thought, the most precious treasure is virtue, and the safest store of wealth is immortality.

The Buddha answers a heavenly being's questions in a short series of contrasts. He says good attracts and evil repels, and that a bad conscience hurts most while freedom from suffering brings the greatest joy. He names ignorance as the cause of ruin, envy and selfishness as what breaks friendships, hatred as the worst fever, and himself as the best physician.

A deva (a heavenly being) asks what cannot be burned, rusted, or blown away, yet can reform the whole world. The Buddha answers that blessings, meaning the results of good deeds, cannot be destroyed by fire, water, or wind, and they can reform the world. The deva is pleased, bows, and vanishes.

Disciples address the Buddha as a teacher they trust, asking him to remove their doubts. They ask how a bhikkhu, a Buddhist monk who has left home and given up desire, should live rightly in the world. The Buddha's answer follows.

A monk who overcomes his desire for earthly and heavenly pleasures, who has ended his lusts and pride, and who has a steady, calm mind will "wander rightly in the world." The passage describes such a monk as faithful, knowing the way to Nirvana, impartial, pure, and virtuous.

The monks agree that a monk who lives subdued, free of all bonds, will walk rightly in the world. The Blessed One (the Buddha) then says that whoever seeks the peace of Nirvana should be able and upright, careful and gentle, and not proud.

A person should find his delight in the Dharma, the Buddhist teaching. He should stand firm in it, learn how to examine it, avoid arguments that spoil it, and spend his time thinking over its true sayings.

True wealth is the store of good deeds, such as charity, piety, temperance, self-control and merit. Unlike money or goods, it cannot be stolen or lost, and it goes with a person after death. Ordinary possessions must be left behind when one dies.
The speakers praise the Buddha, calling him enlightened, free from pain and passion, and wise. They thank him for lifting them past their doubts and clearing away the uncertainty they had before.

A speaker addresses the Buddha in praise. He is called the Master and a muni (a sage) who defeats Māra, the figure who stands for temptation and death in Buddhist texts. The speaker says the Buddha has cut off desire, crossed over to the far shore (liberation), and is carrying others there too.

A disciple, troubled and doubting, asks the Buddha why they should give up worldly pleasures if he forbids them to perform miracles or seek supernatural powers. He points out that Amitābha, a figure of infinite light, is said to be the source of countless miracles.

The Buddha tells a disciple, who is anxious and seeking the truth, that he has not yet understood. He says the law of karma (the principle that actions bring their own results) cannot be overturned, and that prayers and pleas do nothing. The disciple asks whether this means there are no miraculous things at all.

The passage says that the true miracle is a person turning from wrongdoing and selfishness to the truth and to holiness. A monk who gives up worldly pleasures for lasting spiritual bliss performs this miracle. Wanting to perform visible wonders, the passage says, comes from greed or pride.

A monk does right if he does not expect to be honored and bears no ill-will toward a world that despises him. He also does right if he pays no attention to omens, dreams and signs, which are set aside for him. The passage then praises Amitābha, the "unbounded light," as the true source of wisdom and virtue, above all magic and miracles. A disciple then asks whether the promised happy realm is empty talk.
The passage describes a paradise in the west, called the Pure Land, filled with gold, silver and jewels. It has clear waters, lotus flowers, sweet music and flowers that fall three times a day.

Birds in this place sing notes that praise the religion. Listeners who hear them are reminded of the Buddha, the law (his teaching), and the monastic community. In this place there is no rebirth into a bad state, and even the word "hell" is not known.

Whoever repeats the name "Amitābha Buddha" with devotion and a sincere heart will be carried to the happy realm of the pure land. When death is near, the Buddha will appear before them with a company of holy followers, and they will find perfect peace.

The Buddha says the happy paradise is spiritual and open only to spiritual people, so the western direction is a symbol rather than a place. Sunset looks like darkness and death, but it is not extinction; where we see an ending, there is light and endless life. The listener, a disciple, concludes that the Western Paradise story is not literally true.

The Buddha says that a listener's description of paradise is lovely but falls short. Worldly people can only describe it in worldly terms, using everyday comparisons and words. The pure land, where the pure live, is more beautiful than anyone can say or imagine.

Chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha has merit only when it is done with a devout mind that purifies the heart and turns the will toward righteous deeds. Only a person who is filled with the light of truth, or who has reached enlightenment, can enter the Western Paradise.

The Buddha tells a disciple that the Tathāgata (a title for the Buddha) dwells in a pure land of endless bliss even while still in the body, and that he teaches the law so others may share that peace. When the disciple asks how to enter this paradise in the mind, the Buddha begins to name five meditations.

The passage describes the first three of a set of meditations. The first is love, wishing well for all beings, even one's enemies. The second is pity, imagining others' suffering so as to feel compassion for them. The third is joy, rejoicing in the good fortune of others.

The passage describes two meditations. The fourth is on impurity, where one thinks about the bad results of wrongdoing and how a pleasure of the moment can have serious consequences. The fifth is on serenity, where one rises above love and hate, power and servitude, wealth and poverty, and accepts one's own fate with calm.

A true follower of the Tathāgata (a title for the Buddha) does not place trust in harsh self-denial or ritual. Instead, letting go of the idea of a separate self, he relies wholeheartedly on Amitābha, the Buddha of unbounded light.

The Buddha has just taught about Amitābha, a boundless light that makes a person who receives it into a Buddha. He sees that a disciple still has doubts and worries, so he invites the disciple to ask his questions.

A disciple asks whether a humble monk can gain supernatural wisdom and powers through self-sanctification, and asks to be shown the paths and meditative states that lead to them. The Buddha replies by asking the disciple to name what these supernatural wisdoms are.

The disciple lists six "Abhiññas," which are supernatural powers or higher knowledge. They are: seeing from afar, hearing from afar, changing or controlling the body, recalling former lives, reading other people's thoughts, and understanding the end of the stream of life.

The Buddha says that these abilities are not rare, since every person can reach them. He points to the mind's own power: a man can think himself back to his birthplace and recall his father's home, even when far away. He also asks whether the mind can see the roots of a tree that stays standing in the wind.

The Buddha compares his own knowledge to skills a person can use at will: a herb-gatherer who recalls every detail of a plant, or a language expert who recalls any word's meaning. He says the Buddha understands the nature of things even more fully, reading minds and foreseeing outcomes. A disciple then concludes that people can reach such knowledge through the Jhānas, which are states of deep meditative absorption, and that this brings the bliss of Abhiñña, or supernatural knowledge.

The disciple lists the four Jhānas, which are stages of meditative absorption. They run from freeing the mind of sensual desire, through joy and gladness, to delight in spiritual things, and finally to a state of pure peace beyond both joy and sorrow. The teacher approves and tells him to stay clear-minded and drop practices that dull the mind.

A student asks the teacher to be patient with him, because he has faith but does not yet understand, and he is searching for the truth. He then asks the teacher to explain the Iddhipāda, a term meaning the "bases of spiritual power" in Buddhist teaching.

Iddhi, a Buddhist term for spiritual power or attainment, is said to come through four efforts: stopping unwanted qualities from arising, removing those already present, bringing about goodness not yet there, and strengthening goodness already present. The passage adds that one should search sincerely and keep searching until finding the truth.

The Buddha says that when he entered any gathering, such as of nobles, Brahmans, householders, or monks, he took on the look and speech of that audience before sitting down. He then taught them in their own language. He compares his teaching to the ocean, which has the same eight wonderful qualities.

The Buddha compares his teaching to the ocean. Like the ocean, it grows deeper over time and stays the same through all changes. Just as rivers lose their names when they reach the sea, people of every caste lose their old family ties when they join the Sangha (the monastic community) and become brothers, sons of Sakyamuni.

The Buddha compares his teaching (the Dharma) to the ocean. Like the ocean, it receives many streams yet neither grows nor shrinks, it has one taste, which is freedom (emancipation), and it holds treasures and room for great beings. It also treats all people alike, noble or low, rich or poor.

The speaker says his teaching is as roomy as the sky, open to everyone: men and women, boys and girls, the powerful and the humble. Yet people did not recognize him, even after he taught them and then disappeared.

The Buddha reasons that his teaching is clear in itself, but people find it hard to grasp. So he will explain it through stories, since they are like children who enjoy tales. Parables can make the truth understandable even when abstract arguments fail.
A poor widow, seeing holy men gathered on a mountain, had nothing valuable to give them. She remembered two coins she had once found in a dungheap, and she gave those instead.

A senior priest, who can see into people's hearts, praises a poor widow's small gift of coppers. He says her gift is worth more than all the rich people's treasures, because it was given in pure devotion and without selfish greed, and so she has reached salvation.

The Teacher tells a woman that good deeds are like storing up treasure. He gives a parable of three merchants: one gains much, one keeps his capital, and one loses it. He says the same holds true in religion as in ordinary trade.

Capital here means the state a person has reached in life, and gain means rising to heaven. Losing that capital means being reborn in a lower state, such as a hell-dweller or an animal. These are the paths open to a sinner.

People who keep only their original capital are reborn as humans, and those who make good use of their virtues in this life are also reborn as humans. Those who grow their capital, meaning practise greater virtue, are reborn in heaven among the gods.
A blind man says he does not believe in light, colors, the sun, the moon or the stars. He claims no one has ever seen these things, so he rejects them as real.

The blind man insists that colors are illusions, since he cannot touch them or feel any weight. A physician then cures his blindness with four medicines. The passage says that the physician is the Buddha, the cataract is the false belief "I am," and the four medicines are the four noble truths.

A rich man's son has gone off to a far country and become very poor. He wanders back near his father's home and is seen by his father, who sends servants to call him. Frightened, thinking he will be imprisoned, the son runs away before he meets his father.
A rich father has his runaway son caught and brought home. Instead of punishing him, he gives him work on the estate under a supervisor. The son does well, and the father gradually promotes him.

The father calls his son and his servants together and tells them the secret of their relation, and the poor son is glad to be reunited with him. The closing line states the lesson: people must be guided toward higher truths step by step.
A monk (bhikkhu) found it very hard to control his senses and desires. He decided to leave the monastic order and went to the Buddha to ask to be released from his vows.

The Buddha warns a young man not to let his misguided heart and sensual desire ruin him, since he has suffered from lust in past lives and will be undone in this one unless he conquers it. He then starts to tell a story about one of those earlier lives, as a fish.

A fish swims with his mate and, blinded by desire, follows her into a fisherman's net while she escapes. The fish is about to die, but the Bodhisatta (a future Buddha in Buddhist belief) buys him, saves him, and warns him to give up lust.
Use the time you have in this life well, and be wary of desire, which can wound like a dart. If you do not guard your senses, it will lead you to ruin.

A tailor who cheated his customers met a stranger who cheated him in a business deal, and he lost heavily. The Buddha says this is not a one-time event: in earlier lives the tailor also suffered losses and ruined himself by trying to trick others.

In this old story, a crane who lives by a pond in the dry season pretends to care about the fish. He asks them what they will do when the pond dries up, and the fish, trusting him, ask him what they should do.

A crane tells the fish in a pond that he can carry them to a lake that never dries up. After one fish is taken and returned safely, the others trust him. The crane then carries them away one by one and eats them on a tree.

A crane tells a lobster that it will carry it to a large lake, where the crane has already taken the fish. The lobster doubts the crane can hold on, and the crane promises to hold tight. The lobster's wary question sets up the trick the crane is planning.

A lobster plans to trick a crane that wants to eat it. He says he will go along willingly if the crane lets him grip the crane's neck with his claws. The lobster's real aim is to cut the crane's throat, so the crane is outwitted.

The crane agrees to carry a lobster to a lake. The lobster grips his neck like a pair of pincers, then warns that the crane is flying toward a tree instead of the lake, so the crane's plan is turning against him.

The crane answers a monkey who has flattered it and asked for a ride. The crane says it is no kinsman or servant, and it threatens to eat the monkey, pointing to fish bones under a tree as proof of how it has eaten its previous meals.
The lobster refuses to be eaten. He says the crane will die too if he is killed, and he grips the crane's neck. The frightened crane then begs for his life, saying he never meant to eat the lobster.
A crane that tries to trick a lobster is killed by it. The Teacher then says the crane was outwitted in the same way in earlier lives too, because of his own schemes.

The Buddha says that a rich man's yearly rounds of gifts and sacrifices to the gods count for less than one moment of a mind fixed on righteousness. Even a thousand monthly sacrifices, given without ceasing, do not equal that single moment.

The Buddha lists four kinds of offering, based on how large the gift is and how much merit it brings. He gives the first kind as an example: a deluded man kills animals to sacrifice to the gods, with feasting, so the gift is large but the merit is small.

Gifts given while keeping back part of the offering out of greed or an evil heart carry little merit, even if the gift is large. A small gift given out of love, and with the wish to grow in wisdom and kindness, carries great merit.

A wealthy person who gives gifts and sets up institutions in an unselfish spirit, with Buddhist wisdom, earns great merit. The gifts aim to enlighten others and meet their needs. This is the last of the four kinds of merit listed.

A Brahman, a priest of the Hindu caste of learned men, in the town of Kosambī, was a skilled arguer who had beaten everyone he met in debate. He carried a lit torch and said he did so because the world is dark and he wanted to light it as far as he could.

A wandering ascetic, called a samana, tells a man who claims to bring light to others that his effort is pointless. If the man cannot see the daylight, he should not say the world is dark, since his torch adds nothing to the sun's brightness.

A Brahman asks where the sun is, and a samana (a Buddhist monk or ascetic) answers that the sun is the wisdom of the Tathagata (a name for the Buddha). This wisdom shines in the mind, and a person with strong faith will not lack light on the way to Nirvana, the state of final release.
A wealthy man who was very ill comes to the Buddha and apologizes for not bowing to him properly. He explains that his obesity, heavy drowsiness and other complaints make it painful for him to move.

The Buddha asks a wealthy man, who is unwell, whether he wants to know the cause of his illness. He names five causes: large meals, too much sleep, seeking pleasure, carelessness, and having nothing useful to do. He advises self-control at meals and taking on useful work, and says this will lengthen his life.

A wealthy man, who had grown weak from a life of luxury, recovered his health and energy after remembering the Buddha's teaching. He then came to the Buddha on foot, without his horses or servants, and asked for help with his mind rather than his body.

A worldly person looks after the body, while a wise person looks after the mind. Those who give in to their appetites bring about their own ruin, but those who follow the path gain freedom from evil and a longer life.

A slave named Annabhāra, working in a meadow, saw a holy beggar asking for food. He ran to the house and brought back his own rice to give him. The beggar ate it and comforted him with religious words, and Sumana's daughter, watching from a window, praised Annabhāra.

Sumana, a woman, offers money to Annabhāra, a slave, to share in the merit (the "bliss") of his gift of rice to a holy man. Annabhāra first asks the holy man whether it is right to share it with his master.

A man who has received a gift is told by a wise teacher, through a parable, that good things can be passed on without losing anything. Just as one lamp can light many houses without dimming, the blessing of an offering can be shared. The man then gives a share of his own blessing to his master.

Annabhāra refuses his master Sumana's money, saying that taking payment would make it look as if he had sold his share of bliss, and bliss cannot be sold. He asks for it as a gift instead. Sumana then frees him and asks him to live as a friend.

A rich, elderly Brahman (a member of the Hindu priestly class) built a large house as if he expected to live a long time, forgetting that worldly things do not last. The Buddha sent his disciple Ānanda to teach him the core Buddhist teachings, but the Brahman paid no attention and only showed Ānanda his rooms.

Ānanda says that fools claim to own their children and wealth. But a person cannot even control himself, so he cannot truly possess children, riches, or servants. Worldly people have many worries and do not know what the future will bring.

A fool cannot grasp the true teaching, even when living among wise people, just as a spoon cannot taste the soup. Such a person thinks only of himself, ignores good advice, and so cannot save himself.

A disciple under a vow to meditate alone in the forest loses heart in a weak moment. He decides he belongs to the lowest kind of person, so he will gain no path or fruit in this life, and he gives up the solitude and goes back to Jetavana, the monastery.

Some monks confront a fellow monk who has given up his vows and stopped trying to reach the goal of the monastic life, and they bring him to the Buddha. The Buddha asks what he did, and the monk admits that he has indeed given up the effort.

The Buddha tells a discouraged monk that this life is a chance to reach a happy state, and that he once showed great determination. He reminds the monk of a past life when his effort saved five hundred wagons of men and oxen in the desert. Hearing this, the monk's resolve returns, and the other monks ask the Buddha to explain the story.

The Buddha calls his monks to listen, then tells them a story from an earlier life. In it, he was born into a merchant's family in the kingdom of Kāsi, and as an adult he travelled to trade with five hundred carts. ("Bodhisatta" means the Buddha before he became enlightened.)

Travelers crossing this vast sandy desert could not move by day, because the sand grew hot enough to burn. They traveled at night, rested in the shade by day, and relied on a guide who steered by the stars.

The merchant's caravan had nearly crossed the desert and planned to leave the sand that night. The pilot, who was guiding them by the stars, fell asleep from exhaustion. The oxen then turned around and took the same road they had come by, so the travelers were going back the way they had come.

The travellers have wandered back to the camp they left the day before, with little wood and no water, and they lie down in despair. The Bodhisatta, the future Buddha, refuses to give up, walks out in the cool morning, and notices a tuft of grass that must be growing on water hidden beneath the ground.

Diggers dig a well sixty cubits deep, then hit rock and give up. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be, a title for a future Buddha) believes water lies beneath. He listens at the rock, hears water flowing, and tells his page to strike it with an iron hammer.

A young man strikes a blocking rock in a desert well with a single blow, and the rock splits and falls away. Water fills the well, and the travelers and their animals drink, cook, sell goods at a profit, and go home. The story ends with each of them dying according to their deeds, the Bodhisatta included.

The Buddha ends a story by naming who each character really was in an earlier life. The caravan leader was the Buddha himself, before he became Buddha. The page who did not despair, but broke the stone and gave water to the crowd, was a monk who had lacked perseverance. The other men were the Buddha's followers.
A wealthy Brahman (a member of the Hindu priestly class) farmer was holding a harvest thanksgiving feast when the Buddha arrived with his begging bowl, asking for food.

A Brahman (a member of the Hindu priestly class) scolds the Buddha, here called the Tathāgata, for begging instead of working. The Buddha replies that he also ploughs, sows and eats. The Brahman doubts him and asks where his oxen, seed and plough are.

The Buddha compares his spiritual work to farming. Faith is the seed, good works the rain, and wisdom and mindfulness the tools used to plough away illusion. The harvest is Nirvana, the end of suffering. A Brahman then offers him rice-milk, saying his ploughing bears the fruit of immortality.

When a Brahman priest calls the Buddha an outcast, the Buddha answers by saying who really is one. In his view, an outcast is a person who is angry, holds hatred, is wicked, hypocritical, clings to error, and is full of deceit, not someone born into a low caste.

A person who stirs up quarrels, is greedy, envious, wicked, shameless and fearless in doing wrong is an outcast. The passage says that birth does not make someone an outcast or a Brahman (a member of the highest Hindu priestly caste). Actions do.

Ānanda, a close follower of the Buddha, asks a girl of the low Mātanga caste for water at a well. She protests that touching her would make his holiness impure. He replies that he is asking for water, not caste, and she gives him a drink, then follows him at a distance.

A girl who has heard that Ānanda, a disciple of the Buddha (called Gotama Sakyamuni here), goes to the Buddha. She asks to be allowed to live where Ānanda lives, so she can see him and serve him, because she loves him.

The Buddha tells the woman Pakati that she loves Ānanda's kindness rather than Ānanda himself, though she does not yet understand her own feelings. He urges her to take up that kindness and show it to others in her humble position.

A king who gives land to a slave earns merit, but the slave earns more by ignoring the wrongs done to him. Instead of hating his oppressors, he feels goodwill and pity toward them, even when he cannot resist their abuse of power.

Pakati, a woman of low birth (a Mātanga, outcast caste), is praised by the Buddha. He says that despite her low caste she will be an example even to nobles and Brahmans, and that if she stays on the path of justice and righteousness she will outshine queens.

The Buddha asks two kings and their armies why they are fighting over an embankment, a dam or wall used for water. He gets them to admit that the embankment has no value in itself, and that the battle will likely cost many lives, including their own.
A cruel king, hated by his people, wants to see the Buddha and asks him for a teaching that will both entertain and benefit him. The Buddha agrees to tell him a parable about a hungry dog.

A wicked king is visited by the god Indra, disguised as a hunter, and the demon Mātali, disguised as a huge dog. The dog's howl shakes the palace, and the king asks the hunter what causes the terrible noise.

A hungry dog is brought to a king, and no amount of food from the royal stores satisfies it. The hunter says only the flesh of the king's enemies would do. The dog stands for a greed that cannot be fed, and the king's fear and tyranny are the cause of his trouble.

The tyrant asks who the dog's enemies are. The hunter answers that the dog will howl while people in the kingdom go hungry, and that its enemies are those who do injustice and oppress the poor. Hearing this, the oppressor feels remorse for his evil deeds and starts to follow teachings of righteousness, which are ethical teachings.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata, can wake the spiritual hearing of powerful people. The speaker tells a great king that when he hears the dog bark, he should remember the Buddha's teachings, and so he may still learn to calm the wild creature.

King Brahmadatta wanted a merchant's beautiful wife. He secretly had a jewel put in the merchant's carriage, then had the merchant arrested for theft. The king pretended to weigh the defence, had the merchant executed, and sent the wife to his harem.

King Brahmadatta watches an execution he enjoys. The condemned man looks at him with deep compassion, and the king suddenly sees himself on the block. He shouts for the executioner to stop, but it is too late, and the man is already killed.

A cruel king faints, and when he wakes he is changed. From then on he lives a good and upright life. The people believe the character of a Brahman, a member of the priestly class, has been fixed in his mind.

The speaker tells murderers and robbers that they are blinded by self-deception. If they saw things as they really are, they would stop harming themselves. He warns that they will pay for their evil deeds, since people reap what they sow.

Vāsavadattā, a courtesan (a woman paid for companionship), falls in love with the young monk Upagutta and invites him to visit her. He refuses both times, saying that the time for his visit has not yet come, and he does not go.

Vāsavadattā, a woman in the city of Mathurā, takes a rich merchant as a new lover and has her existing lover, the chief of the artisans, killed and hidden under a dunghill. When his body is found, she is tried, sentenced to have her ears, nose, hands and feet cut off, and left in a graveyard.

Vāsavadattā was a passionate woman but kind to her servants. When she was dying in pain, one of her maids stayed with her out of loyalty and kept the crows away. The passage then says that Upagutta, a Buddhist monk, chose that time to visit her.

A woman whose limbs have been cut off speaks bitterly to a young man who comes to her. She recalls her former beauty and says her body is now ruined. He replies that he has not come for pleasure, but to give her a higher kind of beauty than the one she has lost.

The speaker tells someone that, while they were caught up in temptation, desire and worldly pleasure, they could not have listened to the Buddha's teaching. Their heart was unsteady, and they trusted in the false, fleeting appeal of their own beauty.

Vāsavadattā, a woman punished for a crime, is told that lovely appearances lead to temptation, while a lasting beauty and peace come from listening to the Buddha's teaching. She becomes calm, takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community), and accepts her punishment as she dies.

The Buddha visits a man who is about to be married, because the man silently wished for him to attend the wedding. The host has little money, but he welcomes the Buddha and his many monks as well as he can and invites them to eat.

The host's food never runs out while the holy men eat. When he wishes he had invited all his relatives and friends, they arrive, the small hall holds them all, and everyone has more than enough to eat.
The Buddha was happy to see the many guests in good spirits. He encouraged and cheered them with true teachings, speaking about the happiness that comes from living righteously.
Marriage is described as a great happiness, but embracing truth is said to be greater. Death ends a marriage, while a person who has committed to truth is not affected by death in the same way.

Spouses should be faithful to each other in the way truth is faithful, and remain bonded to truth itself. Such a union, lasting and faithful on both sides, makes the children like their parents and shows their happiness.

Each person should be bound in devotion to truth, so that when Māra (the Buddhist figure of death and destruction) separates the body from life, one still lives on in truth, which is eternal. The guests took this teaching to heart and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (the teaching), and the Sangha (the community of monks).

A group of thirty young men, who had been enjoying time with their wives in a grove, found their belongings stolen and went looking for the thief. The Buddha asked whether it would be better to search for the thief or for themselves, and they answered that they should search for themselves.
The group sat down and listened closely to the Buddha. After they understood his teaching, they praised it and took refuge in him, meaning they committed themselves to the Buddha as their guide.

A Brahman, a religious man who loved his family but lacked deep wisdom, loses his seven-year-old son to a fatal disease. He is so overcome with grief that he throws himself onto the body and lies there as if dead.
After his child is buried, a grieving father loses control and wanders around, asking where Yamarāja, the king of death, lives. He wants to beg the king to bring the child back to life.

A grieving father, in a dream, asks some wise holy men where to find Yama, the king of death. They tell him no living person can reach Yama's realm, but that Yama visits a city four hundred miles west every eighth day of the month, where the father may meet him and ask a favour.

A Brahman (a Hindu priest) goes to the realm of Yama, the god of death, after hearing news from wandering ascetics (samanas). Yama tells him that his son is alive in the eastern garden and asks him to bring the son back with him.

A father asks how his son, who did no good works, now lives in paradise. Yamarāja, the lord of death, answers that the son gained heaven through faith and love for the Buddha, not through good deeds. The answer is presented as the Buddha's own words, which are compared to a king's seal on a decree.

A father finds his dead son playing happily with other children in a heavenly place and begs him to come home. The boy refuses to recognise him, saying that in his present state he knows no such words as father and son, because he is free from delusion.

A Brahman, a member of the Hindu priestly class, wakes from a dream and decides to visit the Buddha for comfort. At the Jetavana, the monastery where the Buddha stayed, he tells how his son refused to recognize him or come home with him.

The Buddha tells a grieving person that the body breaks back into its basic elements at death. The spirit is not sealed in a tomb but moves on to a higher way of life, where family ties such as father, son, wife and mother no longer apply. He adds that people worry most about what fades away.

Life ends quickly, like a fast flood carrying away everything temporary. A wise person who understands that worldly ties are impermanent removes the cause of grief and escapes the whirlpool of sorrow. A Brahman then asks the Buddha for permission to join the monks, seeking the wisdom that alone can comfort a troubled heart.

A rich man's gold turns to ashes and he falls ill with grief. A friend tells him that his wealth was worth no more than ashes even when he hoarded it unused. He is told to sit in the market and sell the ashes as if they were goods, which he does.

A poor orphan girl, Kisā Gotamī, tells a rich merchant that he is piling up gold for sale. When he asks her to hand him the gold, she takes a handful of ashes, and they turn into gold. The rich man then marries her to his son, saying that for most people gold is no better than ashes, but for her ashes become gold.

Kisā Gotamī's only son has died, and she carries his body from neighbor to neighbor asking for medicine. People think she has lost her mind. A man sends her to the Buddha, whom she asks for medicine to cure her son.

The Buddha asks for a handful of mustard seed, but sets one condition: it must come from a house where no one has died. The point is that the seed is to be gathered only from a home untouched by loss.

Kisā Gotamī, a grieving mother, went from house to house asking for mustard seed, the cure she had been told to find, but only if no one had ever died in the home. Every household had lost someone, so she could not get the seed. The people told her the dead outnumbered the living, and that she should not bring up their grief.

Kisā Gotamī, grieving and without hope, sits in the dark and reflects that all lives flicker out like lights, and death comes to everyone. She then sees that her grief is selfish, and that a path to immortality exists for anyone who gives up selfishness.

Kisā Gotamī buries her child in the forest and goes back to the Buddha, where she finds comfort in the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching). The Buddha then says that human life is brief and full of pain, that no one born can escape death, and that people are always at risk of dying, like ripe fruit always at risk of falling.

Things often turn out differently than people expect, and this brings disappointment. Grief does not bring peace of mind or save the dead; it only adds to pain. People die, their fate follows their deeds, and everyone is eventually parted from their relatives and this life.
Someone who has pulled out the "arrow" (a image for a painful inner wound or craving) and become calm will gain peace of mind. Someone who has overcome all sorrow will be free from it and blessed.

The Buddha goes to a riverside village of five hundred houses, wishing to save its people. He sits under a tree, and the villagers respect him, but they do not believe his teaching when he begins to preach.

Sāriputta, a disciple of the Buddha, wanted to go to the Buddha and hear him teach. He crossed a deep, fast river by walking on its surface, as if on solid rock. When his heart failed in the middle and he began to sink, he regained his faith and effort, went on, and reached the far bank.
The villagers were amazed that Sāriputta, a disciple of the Buddha, had crossed a stream with no bridge or ferry. They asked him how he had managed it.

Sāriputta, a disciple of the Buddha, says he was ignorant until he heard the Buddha teach. Eager for the teaching, he crossed a river and walked over its rough water, which he credits only to his faith. The Buddha approves, saying such faith alone can carry people across the endless cycle of rebirth to the far shore.

The Buddha urged the villagers to keep working to overcome suffering and to free themselves from worldly attachments, so they could cross to liberation from death. Hearing this, the villagers were glad, accepted his teaching, took the five rules of conduct, and placed their trust in him.

The Buddha, called here the World-honored One, hears of an old monk with a repulsive illness whom no one will go near. He goes to the sick room himself, prepares warm water, and cleans the man's sores with his own hands.

The Buddha, called the Tathāgata, came into the world to help people in need, including the poor, the unprotected, the sick, the blind, the confused and the old, whether or not they followed his teaching. Doing this is said to complete his work and bring him to the goal of life, as rivers reach the ocean.

The Buddha looked after a sick monk every day while he stayed in that place. The city's governor then came to honor the Buddha, heard about this care, and asked him about the monk's past life. The Buddha is about to answer that question.

An officer was ordered by a greedy king to whip a respected man. He obeyed without thinking about the pain it caused. When the man begged for mercy, the officer pitied him and struck him only lightly.

In a past life, a king became Devadatta, who was deserted by his followers for his harshness and died miserable and regretful.
