The officer became the sick monk, who was left unhelped by his brethren after often offending them. The wronged man who begged for mercy was the Bodhisatta, now reborn as the Buddha.

A sick monk is rebuked for his harsh temper. The Buddha says that whoever harms the gentle or falsely accuses the innocent will suffer great calamities, while whoever learns to bear suffering patiently will be purified. The monk then confesses his bad temper, repents, and honors the Buddha.

A householder in Sāvatthi, known as patient and kind, was robbed of much of his property by his own wicked relatives, who used threats to get it. He did not take them to court or complain, but bore the wrongs with great patience.

The monks at Jetavana hear about a matter the neighbors are gossiping over and discuss it in their assembly hall. The Buddha asks what they were talking about, and then says that wicked relatives will one day be punished. He adds that this has happened before and tells them an old story.

In an old tale, the Bodhisatta (a being who is on the path to becoming a Buddha) is born as a strong, large elephant in the Himalayan hills. The passage describes him roaming the hills and valleys and then eating beneath a pleasant tree.

In this tale, monkeys jump on a patient elephant, pull his tusks and tail, and bother him over and over. He ignores them. A spirit living in the tree asks the elephant why he puts up with these rude monkeys.

The Bodhisatta, a future Buddha here shown as an elephant, refuses to answer the monkeys' mistreatment with insults about their birth or family. He reasons that the monkeys will mistreat others, and that a rogue elephant would punish them, freeing him from their annoyance and from guilt over harming others.

A new, savage elephant took the place of the Bodhisatta, the wise elephant who had been there before. Monkeys, expecting the old elephant to behave as before, climbed on his back, but this elephant seized them, threw them down, and killed them.

In this closing part of a Buddhist story, the Master ends his teaching and names who each character was in an earlier life. The wicked monkeys were the bad relatives of a good man, the rogue elephant was the one who will punish them, and the virtuous noble elephant was the Buddha himself in a previous birth.

A monk asks the Buddha whether wrong should be answered with wrong, and whether an evil doer should be made to suffer so that evil does not grow and good does not vanish. He asks what should be done in that case.

The Buddha tells his followers not to repay evil with evil or hate with hate. He says that wrong cannot be undone by more wrong. Wrongdoers should be left to face the results of their own deeds, which will bring punishment sooner or later.
King Ajātasattu of Magadha plans to attack the Vajjīs, a rival people. He sends his minister Vassakāra to the Buddha to ask for his health and to report back what the Buddha says about the plan.
The Buddha asks his attendant Ānanda whether he has heard that the Vajjis, a people or clan of ancient India, hold full and frequent public assemblies. Ānanda confirms that he has heard this.

The Buddha tells Ānanda that the Vajjis, a people who governed themselves through assemblies, will keep growing stronger as long as they meet often and in harmony, honor their elders, respect women, keep up their religious duties, and protect holy people. As long as these things continue, they will not decline.

The Buddha tells the king's messenger, Vassakāra, that the Vajjis of Vesālī will keep prospering as long as they stay well instructed, keep to the right path, and follow the precepts of righteousness. Then he gathers the monks near Rājagaha to teach them the conditions for a community's welfare.

The Buddha tells his monks that the community will prosper as long as they meet often and act together in harmony. It will also thrive while they keep tested practices, respect their senior members, and listen to them.

The monks of the Sangha (the Buddhist community of monks) will keep growing rather than decline, as long as they stay free of craving, enjoy religious blessings, welcome holy men, avoid laziness, and practise seven qualities such as energy, self-control and calm contemplation.
The Buddha is speaking to his monks (bhikkhus) and listing the qualities they should have: faith, humility, a fear of doing wrong, eagerness to learn, energy, an active mind, and wisdom.

Sāriputta, a leading disciple of the Buddha, says that no one before or after the Buddha, or now, is greater or wiser than him in higher wisdom. The Buddha answers that this is a bold claim, and asks whether Sāriputta knew all the earlier Buddhas. Sāriputta replies that he did not.
Sāriputta is told that he cannot know the inner minds of the Buddhas of the past or future. The speaker then asks why he speaks so boldly and joyfully about them anyway.

The speaker says he cannot know the inner hearts of all Buddhas, past, future, and present. He only knows the line of transmission of the faith. He compares this to a city with one gate, guarded by a wise watchman who admits only friends.

A man cannot check every small gap in a city wall, so he might miss where a cat could slip out. But every larger living being must pass through the main gate. The speaker says this is how he knows the lineage of the faith: by the gate, not by checking every crevice.

Sāriputta says he knows that the Buddhas of the past, present and future all reached full Enlightenment by putting away lust, ill-will, sloth, pride and doubt, and by training their minds. The Buddha praises his faith but tells him to make sure it has a firm foundation.

The Buddha arrives at a rest-house in Pātaliputta, a town on the edge of Magadha, and sits in the hall facing east. His monks sit around him along the western wall, and the lay followers of the town sit across from him along the eastern wall, facing west.

The Buddha says that a person who lacks rectitude, meaning moral uprightness, suffers five losses. He becomes poor through laziness, gets a bad reputation, feels shy and confused among respected people, is anxious at death, and after death his mind stays unhappy while his karma, the results of his actions, continues to bring suffering.

The Buddha says that a person who does good and acts rightly gains five things. He gets wealth through hard work, good reputation, confidence in any company, a peaceful death, and a happy mind after death.

After the Buddha taught late into the night and sent the listeners home, the disciples of Pātaliputta bowed and left. Meanwhile, the king of Magadha ordered the town's governor to build fortifications to protect the town.

The Buddha, watching workers build a fortress, predicts that the city of Pātaliputta will become a busy center of trade. He also warns that it faces three dangers: fire, water, and internal conflict. The governor, pleased by this prophecy, names the gate the Buddha passed through "The Gotama Gate."

The Buddha crosses the Ganges on foot, without a boat, so that he does not favor any one of the many people who offered their boats. He does this to show that rituals and ascetic practices are not strong enough to carry a person across the storms of worldly life (Samsāra), while the enlightened teacher (Tathāgata) can cross without them.

Ānanda, a close disciple of the Buddha, asks about the fate after death of monks and nuns who have died. He wants to know whether they were reborn as animals, in hell, as ghosts, or in some other place of suffering. The Buddha is about to answer him.

Those who have fully destroyed three bonds, lust, greed, and the self-centred clinging to existence, have no reason to fear what comes after death. They will not be reborn into suffering, and their minds will not carry on the results of evil deeds, since their final liberation is certain.

After death, only a person's good thoughts, right actions and the happiness that comes from truth remain. Like rivers flowing to the sea, their minds are reborn into higher states and keep moving toward Nirvana, the eternal peace.

The Buddha tells Ānanda that death is not strange, and that being anxious about the dead after hearing the truth wearies him. Instead, he gives a set formula for a disciple to recite, stating that the speaker is free from rebirth in hell, as an animal, a ghost, or any state of woe, and is assured of final salvation.

The Buddha, speaking to his disciple Ānanda, names the "mirror of truth" as a disciple's inner conviction. It is faith that the Buddha is holy, fully enlightened, wise, and the teacher of gods and humans.

The passage describes a disciple who has faith that the truth was taught by the Buddha for the good of the world. This truth does not fade away, welcomes everyone, and leads to salvation. Wise people reach it through their own efforts.

The passage describes the disciple's faith in the Buddhist community of monks and nuns, the "order," which follows the noble eightfold path. The disciple sees this community as worthy of honor, gifts and respect, and as a fertile field for merit in the world. Its virtues are seen as pure, free from selfish aims, and leading to holy thought.

The passage says that the "mirror of truth" shows the most direct path to enlightenment, the goal shared by all living beings. Whoever has this mirror is free from fear, finds comfort in life's hardships, and is a blessing to others.

The Buddha tells the monks to stay mindful and thoughtful at all times. He says they should overcome grief that comes from physical craving, from desire for sensory pleasures, and from wrong reasoning. Whatever they do, they should act with full awareness, whether eating, walking, sleeping, or speaking.

Ambapālī, a courtesan (a woman paid for companionship), hears that the Buddha is staying in her mango grove. She rides in a carriage as far as it can go, then walks to him and sits respectfully at his feet. She comes dressed plainly, without jewelry, yet still looks beautiful.

The Buddha observes a woman who is wealthy, young, and admired by kings, yet calm and wise. He notes that such wisdom is unusual, and then he sits with her and teaches her, filling her with understanding and joy.
A woman listens to the Buddha's teaching and is pleased. She then invites him and the monks to a meal at her home the next day. The Buddha accepts by remaining silent.

The Licchavi princes are on their way to see the Buddha, who has arrived at Vesālī. Ambapālī, a courtesan, drives her carriage right up against theirs, and the princes ask her to give up a meal she has arranged with the Buddha in exchange for a hundred thousand.

The Buddha sees a group of Licchavi (a noble clan) approaching and tells the monks who have never seen gods to look at them. He says the visitors are dressed so splendidly that they look like immortal beings.

The Licchavi, a group of noblemen, arrive on foot and sit respectfully near the Buddha, who teaches them. They then invite him and his monks to a meal at their palace the next day. He refuses, saying he has already promised to dine with Ambapālī, a courtesan (a woman who worked as a companion to wealthy men).

The Licchavi nobles had asked the Buddha to dine with them, but he had already accepted an invitation from Ambapālī, a courtesan. They groaned that a woman had beaten them to it. Ambapālī then prepared a meal and sent word that it was ready.

Early in the morning the Buddha and his monks went to the house of Ambapālī, a courtesan (a woman who was paid for her company). She served them food until they had enough. Afterward she offered her house to the community of monks, with the Buddha as its head.
The Buddha accepted a gift from a woman. He then taught her, moved her spirit, and gave her joy through his religious teaching. After that he stood up from his seat and left the place.

The Buddha tells his monks to spend the rainy season in places near their friends, while he stays at Beluva. There he falls seriously ill with sharp pains, but he endures them calmly and without complaint.

The Buddha decides that he must not die before speaking to his disciples and saying farewell to the monastic community. By a strong act of will he overcomes his illness and stays alive until the time he has set. The sickness then eases.

Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, tells the Buddha that he was deeply distressed by his illness. He found some comfort in believing the Buddha would not die until he had left instructions for the monastic community.

The Buddha asks Ānanda what the community of monks expects from him. He says he has taught the full truth openly, with no secret teaching held back for an inner circle. He compares this to a teacher who keeps something hidden in a closed fist.

The Buddha tells Ānanda that a teacher who thinks he alone leads the community should give it instructions. He himself does not think this, so he sees no need to leave instructions about the order. He then says he is old, near the end of his life, and about eighty.

The Buddha says his aging body is hard to keep going and only rests when he withdraws into deep meditation. He then tells his disciple Ānanda to rely on himself and the truth, not on outside help. Tathāgata is a title the Buddha used for himself.

A brother (a monk) is asked how he can be a lamp to himself and rely only on himself, holding to the truth as his guide. The answer given is that he should see his body clearly, staying earnest, thoughtful and mindful, so he can overcome the grief that comes from bodily desires.

The Buddha tells his followers to watch their sensations, thoughts and feelings closely and calmly, as they arise. By doing this, while still living in the world, they can overcome the grief that comes from clinging to sensations, ideas and reasoning.
Those who, now or after the Buddha's death, rely only on themselves and on the truth, not on any outside help, will reach the highest state among his monks. They must also be eager to learn.

Māra, the Evil One (a tempter figure in Buddhist stories), comes to the Buddha and urges him to enter final Nirvāna, the state beyond death. The Buddha replies that his final passing will happen soon.
Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, three times begs the Buddha to stay alive for the good of many people. The Buddha first tells him to stop, then asks whether Ānanda has faith, and Ānanda says he does.
The Buddha notices that his disciple Ānanda is deeply grieved, and asks him whether he has faith. Ānanda answers that he does.

The Buddha tells his disciple Ānanda that he should not keep pressing him to stay alive. Everything made up of parts must break apart, so the Buddha's body must also dissolve. He has already let go of his mortal life.
The Buddha asks his attendant Ānanda to gather the monks living near Vesālī in the Service Hall. When they are assembled, the Buddha sits on a prepared mat and speaks to them.

The Buddha tells his followers to master the teaching, practise it, and spread it so it lasts and benefits many beings. He then says that star-gazing, astrology, and predicting good or bad fortune from omens are forbidden.

The passage says that a mind left unchecked cannot reach Nirvana, so one should restrain the heart and withdraw from worldly excitement. It advises moderate eating and drinking, like a butterfly taking nectar without harming the flower. It adds that wandering through rebirths happened because the four truths were not understood.

The Buddha, near the end of his life, urges his followers to keep practising meditation and moral discipline. He tells them his death is near, and that everything made of parts ages and dissolves, so they should seek what is permanent and work for their liberation with diligence.

Chunda, a metalworker, invites the Buddha and his monks to a meal and serves them rice-cakes and dried boar's meat. After the Buddha eats, he falls gravely ill with sharp pain, yet bears it calmly. He then tells his companion Ānanda that they will travel on to Kusinārā.
Tired on his journey, the Buddha stops to rest under a tree. He asks his attendant Ānanda to spread out his robe for him to sit on, and then asks for water because he is thirsty.

Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, tells the Buddha that the brook is muddy because carts just crossed it, and that a clear river is nearby. The Buddha asks Ānanda twice to bring him water. Ānanda twice suggests they go to the river instead.
The Buddha asks his attendant Ānanda three times for water, saying he is thirsty. The request is repeated, so the Buddha is shown making it again and again.

Ānanda, a disciple of the Buddha, is asked to fetch water from a stream that has been muddied by passing wheels. When he reaches it, the water has already become clear. He takes it to the Buddha, who drinks. Ānanda takes this as a sign of the Buddha's great power.

A young man named Pukkusa, of low caste and a disciple of the teacher Alāra Kālāma, is walking along the main road between the towns of Kusinārā and Pāvā. The passage simply sets the scene and introduces him.
Pukkusa, a young nobleman, meets the Buddha sitting under a tree and listens to his teaching. Moved by what he hears, he asks a passing man to bring him two robes of gold cloth, ready to wear.

Pukkusa, a young nobleman, offers the Buddha two golden robes. The Buddha asks him to dress himself in one and Ananda, his attendant, in the other. Then the Buddha's body shines like a flame, beyond description in its beauty.
Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, marvels that the Buddha's skin is so clear and bright. When he laid a robe of gold-colored cloth on the Buddha's body, the robe seemed to lose its shine by comparison.

The Buddha tells Ānanda that a Tathāgata (a title for the Buddha) looks especially clear and bright on two nights. One is the night he reaches full enlightenment. The other is the night he dies and passes completely away, leaving nothing of his earthly life behind.

The Buddha tells Ānanda how to answer if someone makes Chunda, the smith, feel guilty. The guilt-stirring words say that Chunda's gift was bad for him, because the Buddha died after eating his last meal from Chunda's food. Ānanda should reply that the death after that meal was good for Chunda and a gain to him.

Buddha says that two meals offered to him are the most valuable of all. One is the meal given just before he attains full enlightenment, and the other is the meal given just before his final death, when nothing of his earthly existence remains. Both bring equal and very great benefit.

The Buddha tells Ānanda that Chunda the smith has built up good karma that leads to a long life, a good birth, good fortune, good fame, and a share in heaven and great power. So Chunda should not be troubled by regret over the meal he gave the Buddha.

Just before his death, the Buddha speaks a short teaching. He says that giving brings true gain, and that self-control frees a person from being ruled by desires. He adds that a righteous person casts off evil, and that removing lust, bitterness and illusion leads to Nirvana, the state of liberation.
The Buddha, tired, asks his attendant Ānanda to prepare a couch between two sāla trees in the grove of the Mallas at Kusinārā. Ānanda does so, and the Buddha lies down, calm and aware of himself.

The Buddha tells his follower Ānanda that flowers blooming out of season and heavenly music do not truly honor him. Such signs are not the right way to show respect for a Tathāgata, the title the Buddha used for himself.

The main point is that the best way to honor the Buddha is to keep steadily to all the greater and lesser duties and to live by the precepts (the moral rules). Ānanda is told to do this, since such conduct is the highest form of respect for the Teacher, the Tathāgata.

Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, goes into a dwelling and weeps, sad that he is still a learner who has not yet perfected himself and that the Master, who has been so kind to him, is about to die. The Buddha then calls the other monks and asks where Ānanda is.

Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, is grieving because the Buddha is about to die, which he feels will leave the world in darkness. The Buddha tells him not to weep and reminds him that all things we love must eventually be separated from us and left behind.

The foolish person believes in a fixed "self," while the wise person sees that no such self can be found. The speaker holds that bodies and all made things pass away, but the truth lasts. He is resolved to let go of his body and rest once his work is done.

The Buddha praises Ānanda, his close attendant, for his long devotion and tells him to work hard so he too can be freed from desire, selfishness, delusion and ignorance. Ānanda, holding back tears, asks who will teach them once the Buddha has died.

The Buddha says he is neither the first nor the last Buddha to appear in the world. A future Buddha will come, teach the same eternal truths, and proclaim a religious life that is perfect and pure, just as he himself does.

The Mallas, a people grieving the Buddha's approaching death, come to see him. He tells them that seeing him is not enough. They must make effort on the path he has taught and free themselves from sorrow by following it.

Seeing the Buddha in person does no good if a person does not follow his teaching. Someone who lives far away but follows the Dharma (the Buddha's teaching) is close to him. Obedience to the Dharma brings the Tathāgata's presence (another name for the Buddha) into a person's life.
Subhadda, a wandering monk, comes to Ānanda, the Buddha's attendant, on the night the Buddha is about to die. He says he has doubts and trusts the Buddha can resolve them, and he asks to see him.
Ānanda, a close disciple of the Buddha, tells the monk Subhadda to stop. He asks him not to disturb the Buddha, because the Buddha is tired.

The Buddha overhears Ānanda turning away a mendicant named Subhadda, and tells Ānanda to let him in. The Buddha says Subhadda asks out of a wish to learn, not to cause trouble, and will quickly understand the answers. Ānanda then invites Subhadda in.

Subhadda was the last person the Buddha taught before his death. This short passage says that the Buddha instructed him, roused and gladdened him with wise and comforting words, and then Subhadda began to speak to the Buddha.

A speaker praises the Buddha's words, saying they restore what was overturned, reveal what was hidden, guide a lost traveler, and bring light to the dark. He then declares that he takes refuge in the Buddha, the Truth (Dharma), and the Order (Sangha), and asks to be accepted as a lifelong disciple.
Subhadda, a fellow monk, tells the monk Ānanda that he is very fortunate. Ānanda has spent many years as a follower in the community under the Buddha himself.

The Buddha tells his disciple Ānanda not to think that they have lost their teacher when he dies. He says his teaching and the monastic rules he laid down will guide them after his death. He also allows the community to drop the minor rules if it wishes.

The Buddha invites the monks to ask any doubts they have about him, the teaching, or the path, so they will not later regret not asking. The monks stay silent, and Ānanda replies that he believes none of them has any doubt.

The Buddha tells Ānanda, his close disciple, that he knows no monk in the gathering doubts the Buddha, the truth, or the path. Even the least advanced monk has already converted and is certain to reach final liberation.

The Buddha asks his monks whether, if they truly understand the Dharma (his teaching) on the cause of suffering and the path to liberation, they would still claim to speak only out of respect for him. The monks answer that they would not. The point is that real understanding should speak for itself, not rest on reverence for the teacher.

The Buddha says that he alone broke through the shell of ignorance that traps other beings, and so reached the highest Buddhahood, which makes him the eldest and noblest of beings. He then asks his disciples whether they have not themselves known and seen the same truth, and they agree.

The Buddha's last words to his monks were that all compound things decay, but the truth lasts forever, so they should work for their liberation with diligence. He then entered deep meditation and passed into Nirvana, the state beyond suffering and rebirth.

When the Buddha died, a great earthquake and thunder came, and some of his followers who had not yet overcome their desires wept, stretched out their arms, or fell to the ground in grief. They cried that he had died too soon and that the light of the world had gone out.

Anuruddha tells the monks to stop weeping. He says that everything born or made must come apart, so the Buddha's body, which is also subject to this, cannot escape dissolution. Those free from passion should bear the loss calmly, remembering the Buddha's teaching.
Anuruddha tells Ānanda to go to the Mallas of Kusinārā and announce that the Buddha has died, leaving them to act as they think best. When the Mallas hear this, they are filled with grief and sorrow.

The Mallas of Kusinārā, a local people, honored the body of the Buddha after his death. They spent a day offering music, flowers, perfumes and cloth, and then cremated the body with the honor given to a great king.

After the Buddha's cremation, Devaputta tells the crowd that his body has been dissolved, but his teaching remains alive in their minds and cleanses them of error. Nature is shown reacting to the death: the sun and moon dim, the earth shakes, and flowers fall from heaven.

Disciples are urged to go out into the world with the same compassion as their master, the Buddha, and to teach others the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. The goal is that all people may reach final salvation by taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching), and the Sangha (the community of monks).

After the Buddha entered Nirvana and was cremated, envoys from kingdoms that followed his teaching asked for shares of his relics. The relics were split into eight parts, and eight dāgobas (memorial mounds, or stupas) were built to keep them, one by the Mallas, the people who had cremated him, and seven by other kings.
After the Buddha died and entered Nirvana, his disciples gathered to decide how to keep the Dharma, his teaching, free from false views. Upali then stood up to speak.

The Buddha tells his followers that after his death they should respect and obey the Dharma, his teaching. He compares it to a light in darkness that shows the way and to a precious jewel worth any effort or sacrifice. He asks them to treat the teaching as no different from himself.

The speaker argues that the Buddha's teaching is now the true presence of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, and so should be honored above building shrines for relics. Anuruddha adds that the Buddha was holy and perfect because eternal truth dwelt in him.

The main point is that the truth existed before the Buddha was born and will last after his death into Nirvana, which is the state of release from suffering. The Buddha is not any single law or teaching, but the whole truth itself, which is eternal and present everywhere.

Some monastic rules were made for particular situations and may change. The truth itself is not temporary. It can be investigated and found by those who seek it earnestly, and it remains the standard for judging true and false teachings.

Kassapa agrees with Anuruddha that the truth, which is Buddha, should be revered, studied, stated and obeyed. He then says the Buddha has three personalities, all equally important: the Dharma Kāya, the Nirmāna Kāya and the Sambhoga Kāya. The Dharma Kāya is the eternal, unchanging truth, and the Sambhoga Kāya is the Buddha in perfect bliss.

In this passage, the Buddha is described as the blessed teaching of the religion itself. He is the spirit of the Sangha, the community of monks, and the meaning of the commands in his sacred word, the Dharma. This whole body of teaching is called the Dharma Kāya, the body of the most excellent law.

The passage argues that the teachings of Buddha depend on his appearance as Gotama Sakyamuni, a historical teacher. Without him, his doctrine could not be handed down, and the eternal truth behind it would remain unknown.

After the Buddha's death, the monks agree to honor the teachings and the memory of Gotama Sakyamuni so that people can find the truth. They decide to hold a council at Rājagaha to fix the pure doctrines, gather the sacred writings, and set up an official collection to teach future generations.

Eternal truths shape the universe and its natural laws from the start. But when the universe first burned with fire, no being existed to see, hear, or understand it. Truth had no place to exist in that early cosmos.

Once sentient beings and sense-perception came into being, the world divided into pairs of opposites: pleasure and pain, self and not-self, friend and foe, hatred and love. The truth was present throughout this world of feeling, yet nowhere in it could the truth remain in its full glory.

Reason first helped people in their struggle to survive, letting them rule over animals and nature. But it also fed hatred and conflicting desires, so that people killed their own brothers for short-lived pleasures. Truth went to reason looking for a home, but could not find a place within it where it could stay in its full glory.

Reason, serving the self, drew all living beings deeper into lust, hatred, and envy, and these three gave rise to wrongdoing. People were crushed by the weight of life until the Buddha, the holy teacher of humans and gods, appeared to save them.

The Buddha taught people to use their feelings and reason rightly, to see things as they are without illusions, and to act according to truth. Through this teaching, people became just, kind, and faithful, and truth came to live in human hearts.
Feeling alone does not contain truth, whether the feeling is pleasant or painful. Feeling is the first step toward truth, but it is not the truth itself, even when it seems bright and full of life.

Reason alone does not give truth, though truth cannot be reached without it. Reason can serve love or hatred equally, so it is only the base on which truth rests. Truth itself is grounded in righteousness, with love, justice and good-will as its adornments.

Righteousness is the place where truth lives, and people who seek righteousness leave room for truth to be revealed more and more. The passage then presents itself as the teaching of the Buddha, and says that those who believe in the truth take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community of monks), asking to be accepted as his disciples for life.

Truth is said to be the purpose of all existence, and the world exists so that truth may come to dwell in it. Those who do not seek truth miss the purpose of life. Things pass away, but truth lasts forever. Wrong patterns of thought distort reality and produce error.

Errors and lies can be shaped to suit those who love them, so they look attractive but are unstable and carry the seeds of their own collapse. Truth cannot be shaped; it is one, unchanging, beyond death, and lasting. Illusions and lies are described as daughters of Māra, the tempter, who leads people toward evil and ruin.

Errors and lies are compared to gaudy ships with rotten timbers, so anyone who sails in them is doomed to be wrecked. Those who follow error end up caught in selfish desires and suffering. Only truth can heal and bring peace, and it lasts beyond death and beyond the end of heaven and earth.
Truth shows the way of the eightfold path, the Buddhist route to right living. It is described as a straight path that people who love truth can easily find, and those who follow it are called happy.

All the Buddhas are praised as wonderful, equal to none on earth, and teaching the same truth. The passage says they show people the path of life and help those who have gone astray. It ends by describing the Buddhas as one in essence, present in all beings, and the place where the speaker finds final rest.

Lucilius has asked why good men suffer many evils if the world is governed by divine providence, meaning a divine plan that guides events. Seneca replies that a full answer belongs later, after proving that providence rules the universe, so he will first defend the gods on this single question.

The passage argues that the universe is not run by chance. The orderly movement of the stars, and of the things on sea and land, shows that a guiding power or law governs it. Things moved by chance, it says, soon fall into disorder.

Seneca argues that the order of the world cannot come from matter moving at random. Chance-driven particles could not arrange themselves so skillfully that the earth stays still at the center, the heavens turn around it, and the seas fill the valleys without rising from the rivers that flow into them. Nor could tiny seeds grow into huge plants by chance.

Seneca says that even events that look chaotic, such as rain, clouds, lightning, volcanic fire, earthquakes, hot springs in the sea and new islands, have causes. They happen suddenly, but not without reason.

The sea's tides rise and fall on a regular schedule, not at random. Seneca says they follow a hidden law of change, and that the moon's pull decides how high and how low the water goes at each set time.

Seneca says he will set aside some questions for later, because his correspondent does not doubt that providence (the belief that the gods guide the world) exists but complains about it. He argues that good men and the gods are bound together by a friendship that virtue creates, since the nature of things never lets good harm good.

Seneca says the good man is like a god, differing only in time, and is a god's student, rival and true child. The gods train good people harshly, as strict fathers train sons. So when good people struggle while bad people enjoy pleasures, we should remember that we like restraint in our sons but boldness in slaves born in the house.
God treats a good man the way a strict teacher treats a promising student. He does not indulge him but tests and toughens him so that he becomes fit for God's purposes.

Seneca argues that bad things cannot really harm a good person, because good and bad cannot mix. He compares this to the sea, which stays salty however many rivers, rains or springs flow into it. In the same way, hardship does not change a brave mind, which stays steady and colours events with its own character.

The speaker says a wise person does feel hardships, but overcomes them and stays calm, treating every misfortune as a test of his own strength. He then argues that any man with honourable ambition wants meaningful work and wants to do his duty despite danger, and that idleness is a punishment to a hard-working man.

Seneca says that athletes who train only their bodies want the strongest possible sparring partners, and will even fight several opponents at once. Their strength only shows itself when they face resistance and can endure hardship.

Good people should meet troubles without fear or complaint, accept whatever happens, and turn it into something good. The key point is that what matters is not what a person endures but the way they endure it. The passage then compares this to how parents treat their children differently.

Seneca compares strict fathers, who push their sons to work hard and even to sweat or weep, with mothers who want to shield their children from all hardship. He says God treats good people like a strict father, testing them with labour, suffering and loss so they grow strong. People who have been spoiled by ease fall apart even under light effort.

Those who have faced many hardships grow stronger and do not give way to disaster, even when they fall. Seneca suggests that God sets misfortune against good people so they can reach the highest goodness, much as people enjoy watching a brave youth face a wild beast.

Seneca says that a brave man facing a lion, or any danger, is only entertainment for people. Such sights do not catch the gods' attention. A worthy sight for a god is a brave man struggling against bad luck, especially one who chose that challenge himself.

Seneca says that if the god Jupiter looked down on earth, he would find no nobler sight than Cato. Cato stays firm amid the ruin of the Roman republic, even though Caesar now holds power. Cato still has a way out, his own death by sword, which lets him keep his freedom.

Cato, about to die by his own hand, speaks to his soul and urges it to leave the world of men. He notes that Petreius and Juba have already killed each other, a brave end. He rejects that way for himself, holding that asking anyone for death would be as shameful as asking for life.

Seneca describes a man who, facing death, is his own harsh judge. Even as he kills himself, he keeps working to save others, arranges their escape, and keeps studying until his last night. The gods, he says, watched his death with great joy.

Seneca suggests that the gods did not let Cato die on his first attempt, because they wanted his courage to face a harder test. He adds that a noble death can raise a man to the level of the gods, admired even by those who fear the gods.

Seneca argues that what seem like evils, such as hardship and misfortune, actually benefit the people who suffer them and mankind as a whole. He adds that good people are not really unhappy, so they should not be pitied.

Seneca says that the things people fear most, such as exile, poverty, the loss of loved ones, disgrace and illness, can still benefit those who suffer them. He compares this to surgery and hunger, which seem harmful but do good in the end.

Seneca argues that some misfortunes help the people who suffer them, just as surgery hurts the body to cure it. He also notes that some pleasant things, such as overeating and drunkenness, harm those who enjoy them.

Seneca quotes Demetrius, who said that a man who has never met misfortune is the most unhappy of all. Such a man never gets the chance to test himself. Hard fortune avoids cowards, so the gods do not count him worthy to face it.

Fortune, or luck and misfortune, is compared to a fighter who will not bother with an opponent who gives up at once. Like a gladiator who is ashamed to face an weaker man, Fortune picks out the bravest and most upright people to test her strength against.

Seneca argues that misfortune is what reveals great men's virtue, and that these heroes were not unhappy because of their hardships. Mucius, who burned his own hand in front of an enemy king, and Fabricius, who farmed his own land when poor, are asked whether hardship made them wretched, implying it did not.

This passage praises the old Roman general Curius Dentatus for his plain meal of roots and herbs from his own field. Seneca asks whether he would have been happier with rich, exotic food from distant lands, and implies that he would not.

Seneca asks whether Rutilius was really unhappy. He points to three things: his accusers will be judged by posterity, he bore exile calmly, and when Sulla recalled him, he refused and stayed away. The implied answer is no.

The speaker tells a listener to look at the terrible events in Rome under the Sulla-era killings: blood in the Forum, senators' heads displayed, assassins roaming the city, and thousands of citizens slaughtered after being promised safety. He says this to those who cannot escape into exile.

Seneca asks whether Sulla can be called happy, since he had men killed and profited from their deaths. He then contrasts Regulus, who was tortured for keeping his word, and argues that fortune did him no real harm, because his suffering only increased his glory.

Seneca says that a man who sacrifices his honour and is then made whole will still give the same advice, so he does not regret the cost. He then argues that Maecenas, a wealthy man troubled by love and by his wife, is no happier. Music, wine and luxury cannot bring him sleep, just as Regulus, tortured on the rack, could not rest.

Seneca compares two kinds of men. A man who suffers for honour finds comfort in the cause of his pain, while a man worn out by pleasure is hurt more by what caused his suffering. He claims that most people, if they could choose, would pick Regulus, who endured hardship for duty, over Maecenas, who lived in luxury.

Seneca asks whether Socrates was mistreated when he drank the state's poison and died calmly, talking about death to the end. He says Socrates is more to be envied than a rich man who is served cold drinks in gold cups by a servant from a corrupt class.

Seneca contrasts men who vomit up what they drank, sick at their own bitterness, with Socrates, who drank his poison cheerfully. He then says Cato reached the highest happiness, because Nature chose him to face her hardest trials, such as being opposed by powerful rivals and defeated by lesser men.
The speaker says that Cato should face defeat, fight in civil wars, and even take his own life, since these are hard things. His aim is to show that such hardships are not real evils.

Prosperity is shared by the crowd and by lesser men, but only great men are tested by hardship and fear. Someone who is never troubled has not seen half of nature. Seneca says that his friend has not yet shown real greatness, since he has had no chance to show courage. He is like a man who has the crown but not the victory, so he is congratulated only for his rank.

Seneca says that a person who has never faced hardship has never shown the strength of his mind, so he cannot know what he is capable of. A man learns his own powers only by being tested. The point is that one must meet difficulty to know oneself.

Many brave people have chosen hardship on purpose, because without trouble their courage would go unseen. Seneca gives the example of a gladiator who regretted that fewer dangers and rewards came along in his day. In his view, courage wants danger, and even the suffering it meets counts toward its glory.

Seneca says that soldiers are proud of their wounds, and a wounded man who returns from battle is admired more than one who came back unhurt, even if both were equally brave. He argues that God gives hard trials to those He wants to honour, since only trials show true courage, as a storm shows a pilot's skill. Wealth hides a person's strength, so it cannot show how well they would bear poverty.

Seneca is saying that a person cannot really know how strong they are while life is going smoothly. Hardships, such as public hatred, losing children, or grief, are the test of inner firmness. He urges Lucilius not to fear these trials, since the gods use them to push the mind toward virtue.

Seneca says that people who live in constant ease and pleasure are unhappy, because misfortune catches them unprepared and hits them hardest. Someone used to hardship, like an experienced soldier, can face injury calmly because he has already endured it.

Seneca says that God tests and toughens those he loves, while sparing others only delays their misfortunes. No one escapes trouble; those who seem to have been spared have only had it postponed. The passage then asks why God lets good people suffer illness and sorrow.

Seneca compares hardship to dangerous army duty. The bravest soldiers get the riskiest tasks, and they take it as a mark of trust rather than a grievance. He says people asked to suffer should see their trials the same way: as a sign that God thinks them strong enough to bear them.

Seneca warns against luxury and soft living. He says that someone kept always warm and sheltered becomes too weak to bear even a light breeze, and that too much comfort is the most harmful kind of excess, dulling the mind and filling it with empty fancies.

Seneca says that too many good things can do more harm than hardship, since an overloaded stomach bursts while starvation is gentler than death. He compares the gods to teachers who push their best pupils hardest, and he notes that the Spartans flog their children out of love. Hardship, then, is a sign of care.

Seneca says that hardship is a kind of training. Just as fathers have their children bear beatings to make them brave, God tests good people, and misfortune strengthens them. The more often we face it, the stronger we become, until we can stand up to misfortune itself.

Repeated exposure to danger makes people fear it less, as sailors, farmers and soldiers grow tough through their work. Seneca argues that the mind, trained by hardship, can likewise learn to look down on misfortune. He points to tribes beyond Rome's borders, such as the Germans, who live rough lives and are hardened by them.

Seneca describes people living in a harsh, frozen land with little food, shelter or clothing. He asks whether they are unhappy, and answers that hardship does not make them unhappy. Over time, he says, people come to enjoy what necessity first forced them to do.
Good people benefit from hardship, just as trees grow stronger when the wind shakes them. Trees in sheltered valleys stay brittle, and hardship is only harmful to those who bear it badly.

Seneca argues that good men should face hardships, because God and the wise man both aim to show that what ordinary people desire or fear, such as wealth, health or pain, is not good or bad in itself. If such things came only to good men, people would think they were good; if only to bad men, they would think they were bad. Blindness would be terrible if only the deserving lost their sight, so the wicked should be the ones punished.

Seneca argues that wealth is not really good. He points out that rich men are often bad, like the pander Elius, and that God gives riches to the worst people while withholding them from the best. He is answering an objection that it is unfair for good men to suffer while bad men prosper.

Seneca asks whether it is unfair that brave soldiers guard the walls while eunuchs and idle men live at ease, that noble maidens wake for worship while fallen women sleep soundly, and that senators work all day while worthless men enjoy themselves. The point is that hard work falls on the best people while the worthless enjoy comfort.

Good people willingly work hard and give themselves up for the common good, moving with fortune rather than being pulled by it. Seneca illustrates this with Demetrius, who told the gods that he wished they had revealed their will sooner so he could have accepted it readily, even the loss of his children.

Seneca says that he will give up anything his opponent asks, even his life, since it all came from that person. He adds that nothing can really be taken from a man who does not resist, so a robber cannot take what he has not defended.

Seneca says he is forced to nothing and bears nothing against his will, because he accepts God's order willingly. He holds that everything happens by a fixed, unending law, with each event caused by an earlier one, so that all things, public or private, follow one chain of fate.

Events do not happen by chance or to suit us. They follow a fixed natural order that was settled long ago. Though individual lives look very different, all of them end the same way: people die and the gifts they receive are lost. So there is no reason to be angry or to grieve.

A good person accepts fate and cheerfully meets whatever happens, since death and loss come to all things. Seneca says the same law of living and dying binds the gods too, so being swept away with the whole universe is a comfort. Even the creator of the universe follows fate; he gave its laws once and has obeyed them ever since.

The passage answers the question of why God lets good men suffer poverty, wounds and early death. The answer is that good men are made of stronger material, and some qualities cannot be separated from others. A man worth noting must have a hard course, so such hardships come with his nature.

Seneca says a person of virtue must face storms and hardship, steering through rough waters and overcoming difficulties that fortune brings. Just as fire tests gold, misfortune tests brave people. Virtue, he says, is a hard climb with no easy or safe road.

The passage is a verse image of a journey across the sky, described as the sun's daily course. It starts with a steep climb, moves through the high sky where the speaker looks down on earth and sea and feels fear, and ends with a steep descent that needs careful control. Tethys, the sea goddess, fears being struck when the speaker sinks into the sea.

Phaethon, a young man, says he will take the risky road anyway, even if he falls. His father keeps warning him about the dangers on the way: the Bull, the Lion and the Archer, the star signs he must pass through. Phaethon then asks his father for the chariot.

Seneca is saying that the things meant to frighten him actually give him courage. He wants to go where even the Sun seems to hesitate, since only cowards and grovellers stick to safe, low roads, while bravery seeks the high path.

Seneca answers the question of why God lets evil befall good men by saying that God does not allow it. God keeps good men from real evils such as crime, wicked desires and greed. Outward things like possessions are not the concern of God, and good men themselves do not care about them.

Seneca argues that misfortunes which befall good people are not unreasonable, because good people sometimes choose similar hardships for themselves. Losing children, exile and death are compared to voluntary acts such as giving up wealth or leaving one's country. The misfortunes, he says, serve to teach others how to endure them.

In this passage, God speaks to a person who has chosen virtue and says he has no reason to complain. God explains that he gave other people false goods, such as gold, silver and ivory, which look valuable but contain no real good.

Seneca says that people who look fortunate are often unhappy and worthless inside, like a house with a fine front and rotten walls behind. Their good fortune is only a thin surface layer. It holds up while they appear secure, but when trouble strikes, their inner decay shows.

Seneca tells Lucilius that the lasting goods he has given him are inner ones: freedom from fear and from strong emotion. Like the world, which is turned inward and finds its joy in itself, Lucilius's virtues lie within him. He needs no outside good fortune. The last quoted line raises the objection that many hard things still happen to him.

Seneca tells his friend that he cannot remove hardships from his path, so he has given him the inner strength to face them. The friend should meet them bravely. Poverty, pain, death and fortune can each be despised, because none of them can truly harm the mind. God is beyond suffering evil, but the person can rise above it.

Seneca tells Lucilius that he has made sure no one can hold him against his will, since death is always open as a way out. He says life is like standing on a steep slope that soon slips away, and that death is a short, easy path to freedom.

Seneca says that leaving life is not made as slow as entering it, since a person who died as slowly as he is born would be at the mercy of chance for a long time. He urges that dying is simple and can be learned anywhere, even at the altar during prayers for life, and he compares this to animals that fall dead from a tiny wound.

Death can come from a small wound in many places in the body. Seneca says that a thin blade cutting the joint between head and neck can bring down a large animal, and that life is not deep inside the body. Death lies near the surface, so the body can be pierced almost anywhere.

Death itself is so quick that no one can measure how fast it comes, whether by strangling, drowning, a fall, or fire. The speaker asks why anyone should spend a long time fearing something that happens so briefly.

Seneca says the Stoics differ from other schools of philosophy as much as men differ from women. Both groups are equal in society, but the Stoics are born to command and the others to obey. The other schools treat people gently, as family doctors do, using the methods patients accept rather than the best and quickest cure.

The Stoics, Seneca says, do not try to make their path look easy or inviting. They aim to lift people quickly out of ordinary life to a height that Fortune, or bad luck, cannot reach. He admits the climb is hard, but argues that high places cannot be reached by a flat road, and that the slope is less sheer than some believe.

Seneca compares a hard undertaking to hills seen from far away. From a distance they look steep and joined into one wall, but as one comes nearer they separate and their slopes prove gentle. The first stage only seems blocked and without a way out.

Seneca says that Cato's contemporaries failed to recognize his worth. Although Cato was greater than Caesar and Pompey, the people ranked him below Vatinius, a lesser figure. Cato was once mobbed in the Forum while speaking against a law: his toga was torn off, and he was pushed through the crowd and insulted.

Seneca is saying that a friend had good reason to worry about the state, which powerful men such as Clodius and Vatinius were selling off for their own gain. These men were so blinded by greed that they did not see they would be sold along with it.

Seneca tells his friend not to worry about Cato, because a wise man cannot be harmed or insulted. He says the gods have set Cato before us as a model of wisdom, more surely than they gave earlier ages Ulysses or Hercules. The Stoics, he adds, held those two to be wise men who overcame hardship, rejected pleasure, and feared nothing.

Cato did not hunt wild animals, a task for hunters and farmers, and did not destroy mythical monsters with fire and sword. He also did not live in an age when people could believe one man could hold up the sky.

The passage praises a man who lived in a time of growing material knowledge and fierce ambition. Ambition is called a many-headed monster, and the lust for power was so great that the whole world shared among three men could not satisfy it. Alone, he resisted the corruption of a Roman state collapsing under its own size.

Cato tried to hold up the falling Roman republic as long as one man could. When the republic finally collapsed, he died with it. Seneca says the people could not really harm a man like Cato by stripping him of his office and insulting him, because his worth was not in those honours.

Seneca imagines a critic who says Stoic teaching makes big promises and then fails them. The critic points out that the wise man, though said never to be poor, can lack servants, shelter and food, and though said never to be mad, can still lose his reason.

Seneca is arguing against a Stoic claim that the wise man cannot be a slave. He says that a wise man who is sold and forced to obey still lives as a slave, so the claim only changes the name of the condition. He suspects the same kind of word-trick hides behind the saying that the wise man cannot be harmed or insulted.

Seneca distinguishes two claims about the wise man. Saying he bears wrongs calmly is not special, since ordinary people can learn that through patience. Saying he can never be injured, because no one would try to harm him, would be a remarkable claim, and one he says would make him join the Stoics.

Seneca says he has not aimed to praise the wise man with empty words, but to place him where no harm can reach him. Someone may object that people will still tease or wrong him. He answers that even sacred things on earth can be attacked, yet the holy stays holy, because those who attack it cannot reach its greatness.

Being invulnerable means not being hurt, even when attacked, rather than never being attacked. The author argues that the wise man is best shown this way: strength proven in challenge is more reliable than strength that has never been tested.

A wise person is better than one who is never harmed only because he is not harmed. He is brave because war and enemy violence do not overcome him, not because he lives in comfort among people who are lazy. Such a person cannot be hurt by any injury, however many attacks come at him.

Seneca gives three examples of things that cannot be damaged. Very hard stones and adamant (a legendary hard substance) resist steel and fire, and cliffs stand firm against waves for centuries. The point is that such things stay unchanged under force.

The passage says that the mind of a wise person is steady and grows so strong that it cannot be harmed, just as the things Seneca has listed before this line cannot be harmed. "Wise man" here means a person who has reached the Stoic ideal of wisdom.
Someone may try to harm the wise man, but the harm will never reach him. He stands so far above lesser people that any harmful intent loses its force before it can touch him.

Seneca says that a wise man is out of reach of harm, even from powerful people. Their attacks fall short of him, like arrows shot upward that never reach the heavens. He gives two examples: a king who shot arrows at the sun and threw chains into the sea, neither of which could touch the sun or the sea god Neptune.

Just as attacks on temples and statues do not harm a god, insults aimed at the wise man cannot harm him. The speaker answers a wish that nobody would insult him: that wish is hard to fulfil, and such wrongs would be stopped mainly for the sake of those who would commit them, not for the wise man, who cannot be hurt by them.
Wisdom is best shown by staying calm when things annoy us. Seneca compares this to a general who shows his skill by remaining quiet and confident while deep inside enemy territory.

Seneca separates injury, which does real harm, from insult, which only offends. He says insult is less serious and only hurts people who are overly sensitive. Still, many people feel insults more keenly than blows, as some slaves would rather be whipped than be insulted with words.

People suffer not only from pain itself but from the idea of pain, much as children are frightened by shadows or masks. Harm aims to do evil to someone, but a wise person has no room for evil, since the only real evil is baseness, which cannot enter a mind already filled with virtue and honour.

Seneca argues that a wise man cannot be harmed. Injury means some evil, evil means baseness, and a wise man is already full of honour, so baseness cannot reach him. Injury also makes a person lose dignity, body, or possessions, and the wise man loses none of these.

Virtue, the Stoic ideal of moral excellence, cannot be added to or taken away, because fortune, meaning luck or outward circumstances, never gave it in the first place. So nothing outside a person can remove it. Virtue is therefore secure and cannot be broken or bent by misfortune.

The wise man, in this view, belongs only to virtue, and virtue cannot be taken from him. Other things, such as wealth or status, are held only at fortune's pleasure, so their loss does not grieve him. Since he cannot lose what matters to him, no injury can truly harm him.

Demetrius captured the city of Megara, and asked the philosopher Stilbo if he had lost anything. Stilbo replied that he had lost nothing, since he carried all his possessions with him. Even though his city, daughters and property had been taken, Stilbo gave this answer to the conqueror.

The passage describes a man whose city was captured, yet who remained unharmed because his real possessions were inner goods that no enemy can seize. He never regarded his plundered property as truly his, since outside possessions come and go by chance and cannot be held securely.

Seneca says that a wise man cannot be harmed by thieves, false accusers, quarrelsome neighbours, or greedy heirs. He gives the example of a man who stayed calm while a city was sacked and burned around him. So Seneca asks the reader to accept this claim as serious, not as empty boasting.

A man of ordinary human birth can rise above human troubles. He can stay calm amid pain, loss, illness and disaster, bear hardship and good fortune without being broken or spoiled by either, and keep his inner self steady, regarding nothing as his own except his better, inner part.

A speaker says that, though cities, walls and towers can be broken by siege machines and mines, no siege weapon can break a settled mind. He has just escaped his burning house through bloodshed and does not know what has happened to his daughters.

Seneca says that even when he is old and has lost everything outside himself, his true possessions are still whole. He claims that only what is within his own mind belongs to him and cannot be taken. Wealth and pleasures pass from one owner to another, so they were never really his to keep.

The speaker says that people who lose office, lawsuits, debt records, or money suffer real loss, while he has nothing taken from him. He claims the wise person keeps all his true goods, because they are protected from outside harm. Those goods are his own virtues.

The passage compares the wise man's inner defenses to famous city walls that were taken by enemies, such as Babylon, Carthage, Numantia and Rome's Capitol. Those walls fell, but the defenses of the wise man cannot be burned, invaded or breached, and so they are described as lofty, impregnable and divine.

Seneca says the wise man he describes is not imaginary. Such a person is rare, appearing only at long intervals, as great things usually do. He adds that Cato, the man they were discussing, came close to or even surpassed that ideal.

Seneca argues that the wise man cannot be harmed. Wickedness is weaker than virtue, and only bad people try to hurt good ones. Since the only people who can hurt the good are unlike them, and only the wise are truly good, no injury reaches the wise man.

Someone can wrong another person without that person being harmed by it. The example given is a thief who takes goods from a country house: he commits theft, but the owner loses nothing, since the goods were not really lost to him. The point is applied to Socrates, who was unjustly condemned: the wrong was done by others, but Socrates himself was not injured.

A person can be guilty of a wrong even when the harm does not happen. A man who intends adultery or poisoning is still an adulterer or poisoner if his plan fails, and a robber is still a robber if his sword misses. The act and the intent make the wrong, not the result.

Some crimes are already complete in their wrongness before the deed itself is done, because one part can happen without the rest, while the rest cannot happen without it. The author illustrates this with running and swimming: moving the feet does not mean running, but running requires moving the feet.

Being wronged and receiving an injury are not the same thing. Someone may do harm to us, yet we need not actually be harmed, because chance can intervene. A thrown weapon may be knocked off course before it hits.

Some wrongs can be stopped partway, through particular circumstances, so that the wrong is done but the person it was aimed at does not suffer it. The idea is that an injury can be done without being received.

Seneca argues that a wise man cannot be wronged, because justice and injury cannot exist together, and an injury is always done unjustly. In the same way, a bad man cannot do the wise man any good, since the wise man lacks nothing and the bad man has nothing worth giving him.

The main point is that nothing done to the wise man can really harm or help him, just as the gods are not hurt or helped by anything. The wise man is close to the gods, like a god except that he is mortal. Such a person aims at a calm, orderly, fearless life that benefits himself and others, and so does not long for or mourn lowly things.

A person who relies on reason and goes through life with a godlike mind cannot be harmed from any side. That includes harm from other people and from fortune, or chance, which always gives way when it struggles against virtue.

If we calmly accept death, the greatest fear of all, we will more easily bear lesser troubles such as loss, pain, disgrace, exile, and bereavement. Death is not an evil, so it cannot harm us, and the wise person is not overwhelmed by these troubles even when they all come together.

The wise man bears insults and harms just as he bears winter cold or illness, as chance events. He does not think other people act on deliberate plans, since only the wise man plans on purpose. Other people's conduct is mere impulse and scheming, which he treats as accident, and accident cannot be aimed at him on purpose.

The passage lists the greatest harms a person can suffer. These are dangers arranged against him, such as a bribed accuser, a false charge, or the anger of powerful men. It also names losing a gain he has worked for, such as an inheritance or the favour of a noble household.

The wise man, in this view, is not troubled by hopes or fears, and an injury does not stir him up. He is calm and master of himself. Because he knows no one can really harm him, he is free from anger.

The wise man, in this view, is so steady and cheerful because he does not fear hardship or other people. He even uses injury as a test of his own virtue. The author asks the reader to hear the claim that the wise man cannot be harmed, and says this claim takes nothing away from the reader's own faults.

The main point is that the wise person does not aim to stop others from harming him. He aims to rise above injuries through his own strength of mind, much as an athlete in the sacred games wins by enduring blows until his opponent tires out.

Seneca argues that a wise person cannot be insulted. He says there is a minor kind of injury that should be complained about rather than punished, and that the law also does not treat it as needing special punishment. This feeling comes from a small-minded spirit that shrinks from any act showing it disrespect.

Seneca describes small slights, such as being left out of a host's house, laughed at, or given a lowly seat at dinner, and calls them the complaints of an oversensitive mind. He adds that only people with comfortable, easy lives notice such things, since those facing greater troubles have no time for them.

Seneca says that people who are easily upset by small slights are usually idle, with weak minds that feed on imagined wrongs. Most such hurts, he claims, come from misreading what others did. Someone who feels insulted shows a lack of judgment, because he assumes he is being scorned and so lowers his own standing.

The wise man cannot be made to feel scorn, because he knows his own worth and does not let anyone have power over him. He does not even feel the small worries of the mind. Some blows still reach him, such as pain, illness, the loss of friends and children, and war's ruin of his country, but these do not shake his principles.
The wise man still feels hurts, since he is not made of stone or iron. He takes hard blows, rises above them, and heals them. Small annoyances he does not even notice, or he treats them as laughable.

Insults usually come from proud people who cannot handle their own success. The best reply is greatness of spirit, which treats such insults as empty, like dream images with no real substance. A person should also remember that everyone is too low to look down on someone far above them. The Latin word for insult, contumelia, comes from the word for contempt, since no one insults another without looking down on him.

Seneca says that children and infants who insult or handle their parents are not really acting with contempt, because they lack the ability to show it. In the same way, a slave's mocking of his master is only amusing, since such rudeness is tolerated when it is aimed at the master himself.

Some people buy young slaves, train them to mock others, and then call the insults clever jokes. Seneca calls this foolish: the same words count as an outrage from a friend but as wit from a slave-boy.

The wise man treats many grown adults as the way we treat children, because their childish mindset has lasted into old age. Seneca asks what age is worth if people keep a child's faults, such as instability, indiscriminate desire and fear, and only their bodies have grown.

Seneca says that grown men who chase gold, silver and power are no different from children. Children play at being magistrates with toy robes and axes, while these men do the same things seriously in public places.

Seneca compares grown men to children who build houses of sand on the beach. He says adults make the same mistake, but with more serious things: they pile up walls and roofs for their supposed safety until those structures become a danger to them.

A wise person can treat insults from foolish people as jokes. Sometimes such a person still corrects them with pain or punishment, not out of personal hurt, but so they will not repeat the wrong. The writer compares this to breaking in an animal with blows, which is done without anger.
The question was why a wise man, who cannot be harmed or insulted, still punishes wrongdoers. The answer is that he does not punish out of revenge but to correct them.

Seneca argues that calm strength of mind is possible for the wise person, since we already see similar calm in others, even if their reasons differ. He gives two examples: a doctor does not get angry at a mad patient, and a doctor does not take to heart the curses of a feverish patient who is refused cold water.

The wise man treats people as a doctor treats patients. He puts up with their embarrassing conditions and their angry outbursts without disgust. He sees the proud, healthy-looking men in showy robes as sick in mind and full of folly.

The wise person does not get angry when sick patients are rude to their doctor, or when ordinary people fail to greet him. He values neither the honours nor the disrespect of others, so he is not lifted up by praise from the rich, nor hurt by slights from the low.

The wise man, Seneca says, does not envy the rich. Rich men are no better off than beggars, and in some ways worse, since they always want more. A king who ignores him with contempt does not move him either, because such a king is no more enviable than a keeper of sick and mad servants.

A wise person does not care if a dealer in cheap, bad slaves fails to greet him. Such a man has nothing good in him, so his courtesy is worth nothing. The wise person feels the same about the greeting of a king.

The passage describes a ruler who holds distant peoples only by fear, so that he can never relax his guard. From this it concludes that the wise man, who is not moved by insults, sees all people as alike in their shared foolishness, whatever their differences.

The main point is that a wise man who let an insult or injury disturb him would never again feel secure. Being upset by someone's scorn would also mean that he values that person's approval. So the wise man does not admit he was hurt, since that would give the offender respect he does not deserve.

Seneca says some people foolishly think they can be insulted by a woman, but the woman's rank or wealth makes no difference, since she is still shallow and driven by desire unless she is educated. He adds that some men take offense at small slights from servants, such as being bumped by a hairdresser or a doorman's slowness to open the door.

Seneca says a wise person can enjoy seeing how foolish others are, because his own mind is at peace. If he must visit a house with a rude doorkeeper, he will win the man over, as one calms a fierce dog with food. He will not be angry about paying a fee to enter, just as tolls are paid on some bridges.

Seneca says a wise man should not be proud of insulting or fighting with a doorkeeper who blocks his way, since such a fight makes him the servant's equal. Instead, when he is struck, he should respond as Cato did when Cato was hit in the face.

The wise man, in this view, does not answer an insult with anger, revenge or even formal forgiveness; he simply ignores it, which the writer calls a greater greatness of mind. More broadly, he does not judge things as good or bad, or as low or wretched, the way ordinary people do. He moves against common opinion, as the stars move against the earth's motion.

Seneca imagines someone objecting that a wise man would still be hurt by being beaten, insulted, or made to serve humiliating food. He answers that all such troubles are of one kind, so if small ones do not affect the wise man, larger ones will not either.

The wise man, in Seneca's view, is not limited by the same weakness as ordinary people. We judge his endurance by how much we could bear and then set his limit a little higher, but his virtue places him in a different position altogether. Even when many hardships are piled together, he bears them just as he bears each one alone.

Seneca argues that a wise person must be fully free from Fortune, meaning chance and misfortune. Saying the wise can bear some hardships but not others lets Fortune win, so the wise person should be unconquered in every case. He adds that even Epicurus, usually seen as a teacher of pleasure, nearly reached this view.
The wise man's house is small and plain, with no servants demanding bribes at the door. Fortune cannot enter it, because she has nothing there that belongs to her.

Seneca says that even Epicurus, who allowed much to physical comfort, takes a firm line on injuries, so Stoics should not find it hard to accept. The Stoic view is that injuries do not exist for the wise person, though being beaten or losing a limb is unpleasant.

Seneca says that Stoics do not deny that an insult causes real pain. What they deny is that the pain counts as an "injury" to a person whose virtue stays intact. He compares two gladiators: one hides his wound and stands firm, the other shows it lightly. Both despise the harm, so the dispute is small.

Seneca says the main concern is to ignore insults and small injuries, which both schools of philosophy advise. This does not need a wise man, only a sensible person who reasons that a deserved rebuke is a fair judgment and an undeserved one shames the person who gave it.

Seneca says that a joke about a fault everyone can already see should not hurt. People laugh at such things in private but get angry when they hear them in public. They also expect to joke about themselves while disliking when others do the same.

People are often hurt most by small, silly insults. Seneca gives two examples: a man angry at being called a "sea-sheep," and Fidus Cornelius, who wept in the Senate over being called a "plucked ostrich," though he had kept calm under far worse charges. His point is that when reason stops guiding people, they lose control over their feelings.

Seneca observes that people get upset when others mock their habits, speech, or physical flaws, even though those flaws are already obvious from their own behaviour. He also notes that some dislike being reminded of their age or grey hair, and that poverty causes distress, with those who hide it making it a source of shame for themselves.

If you mock your own flaws first, others have nothing left to sneer at, since no one laughs at a man who laughs at himself. Seneca gives the example of Vatinius, an unpopular man who joked about his own feet and short neck and so escaped the mockery of his enemies, Cicero above all.

Seneca says that a person who has improved in good manners and philosophy should not be easily shamed, since shameless people can insult without feeling it. The best revenge on an insulter is to deny him the satisfaction he wants. An insult works only if the victim shows hurt or anger, so calm indifference spoils the insulter's enjoyment.

Seneca describes the Roman emperor Caligula as a man who loved to mock others, even though he himself was the easiest target. He lists his own physical features as laughable: his pale face, fierce eyes, bald and misshapen head, bristly neck, thin legs, and huge feet.

Seneca describes how the emperor Gaius (Caligula) insulted many people, and he picks out the insults that led to his downfall. The main example is an insult Gaius shouted at his close friend Asiaticus Valerius, mocking the conduct of Asiaticus's wife, at a drinking party in front of others.

The passage describes how the emperor Gaius (Caligula) humiliated men in his court. He told a consular, a close friend, about his own affair with the man's wife. He also mocked Chaerea, a military tribune, for his high, weak voice and effeminate manner, though Chaerea was brave, by giving him insulting watchwords and calling him effeminate.

Gaius Caligula, the Roman emperor, was killed by conspirators. Chaerea struck first, and many others then stabbed him, some to avenge personal wrongs. Seneca notes that Gaius took every slight as an insult, since those who most like to insult others can least bear insults themselves.

Caligula was angry when people called him Gaius, and when a senior centurion called him Caligula. That name was a childhood nickname from his years in the army camps, where the soldiers knew him by it. By then he took it as an insult.

Those who have been hurt should comfort themselves that, even if they do not take revenge, someone will punish the arrogant and insulting man, since such a man does not limit his insults to one victim. The passage then points to Socrates, who bore mockery in comedy and ridicule from his wife with good humour.
Antisthenes was mocked for having a foreign, Thracian mother. He replied that the mother of the gods also came from Mount Ida, so his answer turned the insult back on the critics.

We should not get drawn into quarrels or petty disputes, and should treat the praise and blame of ordinary people as equally unimportant. If we let insults hurt us or let praise please us, we neglect our duties to the state and to private life, and even miss what would benefit us.

Real freedom, the passage says, is not being free from all hurt or insult. It is a state of mind that rises above injuries and finds pleasure within oneself, so that a person is not shaken by what others say or think. Since anyone can insult anyone, the wise and the less wise deal with this in different ways.

Seneca says that only people with an unfinished philosophical education, who still follow public opinion, think they must live surrounded by insults and injuries. Everything is easier to bear for those who are prepared for it. The more noble a person is, the more bravely he should face such troubles, just as the tallest soldiers stand in the front line.

Insults and verbal abuse should be treated like shouts and missiles that hit a soldier's helmet without wounding him. Real injuries are wounds, but a person should endure them without retreating from his place. Giving way under attack is shameful, because the place assigned by nature is simply being a human being.

The passage says that the wise man has a different kind of help from the one just described. He has already won the struggle, while the reader is still working toward it. Until the reader reaches the truth, the reader should keep hope alive, welcome news of a better life, and support it with admiration and prayer. A person who cannot be defeated by bad luck benefits humanity as a whole.
