Seneca says that anger is the most frightening of the passions, because it is wild and inhuman. Unlike other passions, it is made entirely of action and rage. It seeks harm to others, even at the cost of the angry person's own ruin.

Anger is described as a short madness. It makes a person lose self-control, ignore good manners and family ties, refuse reason and advice, and act over trivial things. The passage adds that such people are not sane, and that this can be seen from how they look.
Seneca says that angry men show the same outward signs as madmen. Their eyes blaze, their faces turn deep red, their lips and hands tremble, and their breathing becomes hard and hissing.

Seneca describes the outward signs of anger: twisting joints, groaning, shouting, clapping, stamping, and a body that looks wild. He says the vice is hard to say whether it is more hateful or more disgusting, and that other vices can be hidden in secret, unlike this one.

Anger shows itself openly on the face, and the stronger it is, the more visibly it rises up. The writer compares this to animals, which show clear signs before they attack, as their calm appearance changes into fierceness.

Seneca says that angry animals show extra fierceness: boars sharpen their teeth, bulls toss their horns, lions growl, snakes swell, and dogs look sullen. Every animal, even one that is naturally hateful and venomous, becomes more savage when anger takes hold of it.

Seneca says that other strong feelings, such as lust, fear and boldness, show on the face and can be seen coming. Anger differs in that it is not just visible but openly conspicuous, standing out far more clearly.

Seneca says anger has caused more harm to humankind than any plague. He lists its results: killings, poisonings, lawsuits, cities sacked, peoples destroyed, and whole regions burned. He claims that ruined cities and empty deserts were made so by anger.

Seneca lists famous rulers and leaders from tradition whose misfortunes came from anger. Anger stabbed one in his bed, killed a guest under protection of hospitality, and tore another apart in public. It also led to a father's death at his son's hand, a king's murder by a slave, and a crucifixion. These are only single cases.

Seneca asks whether anger is really about single people who wrong us. He points to mass killings, such as crowds slaughtered by soldiers or whole nations destroyed, and to crowds in the arena who grow angry when gladiators do not die bravely. The crowd feels scorned and turns from watchers into enemies.

Seneca says that some outbursts that look like anger are only a copy of it. He compares them to small boys who strike the ground after a fall, angry for no real reason. Such anger is calmed by fake apologies, so a pretend hurt is soothed by a pretend revenge.

Seneca reports an opponent's two arguments against the idea that anger comes from a wrong done to us. People are sometimes angry at those who have not yet hurt them, and weak people are angry at the powerful, even though they cannot hope to punish them. Seneca replies that someone who intends harm is already doing harm.

Seneca argues that anger is a desire to punish, not just the power to punish, and that people desire things they cannot get. He adds that even the lowest person can wish to punish the greatest, since everyone can cause harm. He notes that Aristotle's definition, a desire to repay suffering, is close to his own.
Seneca argues that wild animals do not really feel anger, even though they may seem to. Anger is opposed to reason, so it only arises where reason can exist, which means in humans alone.

Seneca says that wild animals have urges, rage-like impulses, cruelty and a fighting spirit, but not true anger, just as they have no luxury in the human sense. He adds that animals often lack self-control in their pleasures more than people do, so the poet's claim that beasts forget their wrath is wrong.

Animals may seem angry, but they only have rough impulses that look like human feelings. They cannot truly be angry, just as they cannot truly forgive. Real feelings such as love, hate, friendship and enmity belong to humans alone, along with wisdom, foresight and reason.

Animals cannot have human virtues or human vices, because their whole nature is different from ours. Seneca compares their faculties to ours: their voice is unclear, their tongue cannot form words, and their reason is crude and imprecise.

Seneca is describing animals. He says they perceive only vague images that move them to act, so they do not truly feel fear, grief, or anger, only something like these feelings. That is why they quickly swing to the opposite state, moving from furious rage to calm sleep.

Seneca separates anger from irascibility, which is a habit of being quick to anger. Anger is a passing state, like being drunk, while irascibility is a lasting trait, like being a drunkard. So a person can be angry without being irascible, and the reverse.

Seneca lists several kinds of anger. Some are loud and quick to pass, some are fierce in action but quiet in speech, some burst out in bitter words, some show only as complaining or turning away, and some are deep and lasting. He says there are countless other forms of this one evil.

Having finished asking what anger is, Seneca now asks whether anger fits with nature, and whether it is useful and worth keeping to some degree. The passage only sets out this next question; it does not yet give an answer.

Seneca argues that anger is not natural to humans. Human nature is gentle and social, made for helping one another, while anger is cruel and destructive, aiming at ruin and separation, even against close friends.

Seneca argues that anger is not part of human nature. He says human life rests on kindness and cooperation, and people are joined together by love rather than by fear. So it is wrong to think the urge to punish belongs to nature's best work.

Correction can be necessary, but it should be done calmly, not in anger. Its purpose is to heal, not to harm. Seneca compares this to straightening a bent spearshaft by heating it and forcing wedges in, not to break it but to remove the bend. In the same way, pain can be used to correct a character bent by vice.

The passage compares a doctor's treatment with how a wise person deals with anger. The doctor starts with the mildest measures, such as changing the order of meals, and only moves to harsher ones like fasting or bleeding when gentler methods fail.

Seneca compares punishment to medical treatment: a doctor may cut off an injured limb, and this is not harsh if it restores health. In the same way, a ruler should first correct wrongdoers with words, gently if possible, to make them act rightly and value honour, justice and virtue.

A person correcting others should first advise and rebuke, and only later use punishment, and then mild and short-lived punishment. Death is reserved for the gravest crimes, and only when dying would truly benefit the criminal.

A wise ruler, Seneca says, punishes criminals not out of pleasure in cruelty but to deter others and to make some use of those who cannot be reformed. Because of this, he concludes, human nature does not naturally want to inflict punishment.

Seneca argues that anger does not fit human nature, since anger wants to punish. He then gives Plato's argument: a good man does no harm, but punishment is a kind of harm, so a good man does not punish. Anger goes with punishment, so anger does not fit a good man either.
A good person does not enjoy punishing others, so he also does not enjoy the anger that finds pleasure in punishment. From this, Seneca concludes that anger is not part of human nature.

Some people ask whether anger, though not natural, might be worth keeping because it often helps. They say it stirs the spirit and gives courage its fire in war. So some hold that anger should be controlled and trimmed rather than fully removed, keeping the useful part that drives action.

It is easier to stop anger from getting into the mind than to control it once it is there. Once passions take hold, they become stronger than reason and will not weaken. Reason can only hold control while it stays separate from the passions.

Once the mind is stirred up by emotion, it goes wherever the passions push it and can no longer hold back what it could once have dealt with. Some things start within our control, but once they grow they carry us along by their own force and leave no way back.

Once a person has fallen over a cliff, they cannot control their motion or slow down. Their reckless speed leaves no time to think or regret, so they go further than they could otherwise have stopped. The comparison is to anger, which carries a person past limits they might have avoided.
Once the mind gives itself over to anger, love, or another passion, it cannot hold itself back. Its own weight and the pull of vices drag the person down into the deepest ruin.

The best course is to refuse anger from the very start, before it takes hold. Once anger carries us away, reason loses its power, and anger, once let in by our own choice, will then do as it likes rather than only what we permit.

Seneca says anger must be stopped at the start, before it gets inside the mind, because once it takes over, the mind cannot limit it. The mind does not stand outside its passions and control them; it becomes the passion itself. Reason and passion are not separate parts but two states of the same mind, good or bad.

Seneca asks how reason can recover once anger has overpowered it and mixed it with lower passions. He then answers an opponent who says some angry men still control themselves. He argues that if such men do nothing anger dictates, then anger is not needed to get things done, even though his opponents claimed it is stronger than reason.

Seneca asks whether anger is stronger or weaker than reason. If anger is stronger, reason could not control it, since only the weaker side obeys. If anger is weaker, reason can act well without it. He adds that angry people seem to keep control only when their anger is already fading, not when it is at its peak.

Seneca says that people sometimes spare an enemy even when angry, but only when another passion, such as fear or greed, takes over for a while. In that case, anger does not stop because of reason. It stops because the passions have made a fragile, temporary truce.

Seneca argues that anger gives nothing useful to the mind and is not needed for brave action. A virtue is self-sufficient, so it can raise or lower its own energy as needed, much as a catapult's tension is adjusted. He then quotes Aristotle's claim that anger is necessary to win a fight, which he is setting up to dispute.

Seneca is answering the idea that anger can be used as a soldier serves a general, under orders. He says this is wrong. Once anger obeys reason, it is no longer anger, and when it runs wild it is as useless to the mind as a soldier who ignores the retreat call.

Seneca argues that anger leaves us with a dilemma. If anger accepts limits, it is no longer what anger really is, which is wild and unmanageable. If it refuses limits, it is harmful and cannot be useful. A person who punishes because punishment is right, not out of a wish to hurt, is not angry at all. Such a person is like a soldier who follows orders. Passions cannot obey, just as they cannot command.

Reason should never call on blind, fierce impulses to control other impulses, because reason has no power over them. Reason can only hold them back by setting other strong passions against them, such as fear against anger. Seneca says reason must never need to turn to vices for help.

Seneca argues that a mind ruled by passion has no peace. If bravery needs anger, diligence needs greed, or calm needs fear, then virtues depend on vices. In that case reason loses its power and becomes like the passions it should control.

Seneca argues that passion without reason is as reckless as reason without passion is weak, so neither is better than the other. He asks how anyone could accept passion being treated as equal to reason. His opponent replies that passion is useful if it stays moderate, which Seneca is about to answer.
Anger is useful only if it is naturally useful. If it refuses to obey reason, then keeping it mild only means it causes less harm. So a mild anger is still just a smaller evil.

Seneca answers the view that anger is needed against enemies. He argues that attacks should be controlled and reasoned, not disorderly. He points out that anger harms the angry person, and that skilled fighters such as gladiators and hunters succeed by skill and reason rather than rage.

Seneca says that a wise person meets attackers and pursues fleeing enemies calmly, guided by reason rather than anger. He cites the Cimbri and Teutones, who were destroyed so completely that no messenger reached their homes. In his view, anger took the place of courage in them, and anger often ruins the one who feels it.

Seneca says that the Germans are fierce fighters, bred for war and hardened against cold and hardship. Yet Spaniards, Gauls and even weaker peoples of Asia and Syria defeat them before the main Roman legion arrives. Their own quick temper, he says, is what leads them to die.

Seneca says that if people had sense and self-discipline, free of luxury and greed, Rome could return to its old simple way of life. He points to Fabius, a Roman general who saved the state by patiently delaying, something angry men cannot do.

Fabius, a Roman commander, did not act on his anger when the empire was in danger. He counted his forces, saw that losing any part would mean losing all, and set aside grief and revenge to focus on what was useful. He controlled his anger before he defeated Hannibal.

Seneca is giving examples of Roman generals who did not act in anger. Scipio Africanus left Hannibal and Carthage alone and waited, so his enemies thought him slow and lazy. Scipio Aemilianus stayed at Numantia for a long time, accepting criticism, and his siege starved the town until its people killed themselves.

Anger is not useful even in war, the passage says. It is quick and reckless, so it puts others in danger without protecting itself. The more reliable quality is one that thinks carefully, controls itself, and acts slowly and deliberately.

A good man, Seneca argues, does not need anger to act when his father or mother is harmed. He will still avenge or protect them, doing his duty calmly and without fear. Weeping and fainting, which the passage links to women reacting to rumours of danger, are not what a good man does.

Seneca argues that a wise man acts against an attack on his father because it is his duty, not because he feels grief or anger. He rejects the view of Theophrastus that good men are angered by harm to their friends. He says that view appeals to the crowd, since people usually think their own anger is justified.

The speaker is describing a person who gets angry over small things: lukewarm water, a broken glass, or mud on a shoe. Such anger is not a sign of virtue but of a weak mind, much as a child cries as much over a lost toy as over a lost parent.

Seneca says that getting angry on behalf of friends shows a weak mind, not a loving one. Standing up for parents, children, friends and fellow citizens is worthy, but only when duty calls, and when it is chosen freely and judged calmly, not done in a rush of passion.

Anger wants revenge more eagerly than any other feeling, but this haste defeats it. Like most desires, it is too rash and frenzied to reach its goal. So anger has never helped in peace or in war: it turns peace into war, and in battle it loses control and falls into the enemy's hands.

Seneca argues that vices should not be accepted as useful just because they sometimes produce good results. He compares anger to a fever or a poison: occasionally helpful by accident, but still not good to have. It is better to be free of them altogether.

Seneca argues that anger cannot be good. Virtues like justice and bravery become better as they grow, but anger becomes worse as it grows. So, he reasons, anger is not useful and should not exist at all. He then answers an opponent who claims anger makes men readier to fight.

Seneca is arguing against the view that anger is useful because it gives courage. He points out that drunkenness and madness also sometimes make men bold or strong, so by that same reasoning they would count as good. He adds that fear and the terror of death can also make cowards fight, which shows that such effects do not prove a thing is good.

Seneca argues that anger, fear and drunkenness are poor and short-lived motives for action, and cannot supply real strength to virtue. Anger does not make a brave man braver; it only stands in for courage in those who lack it. He adds that the most angry creatures are infants, the old and the sick, which he takes to show that anger belongs to weakness.

Theophrastus claimed that a good man must be angry at bad men. Seneca argues this is backwards: a better man should be calmer and hate no one, since wrongdoers act out of error, so there is no reason to hate them.

A sensible person should not hate those who do wrong, because a person who looks honestly at his own faults would then have to hate himself. Everyone has things to be forgiven for, and no one can truly declare himself innocent. People who claim innocence rely on what others say rather than on their own conscience.
It is kinder to correct people who go wrong gently, like a father, than to chase them away. Someone who has lost his way in our fields should be shown the right path, not driven off.

A wrongdoer should be corrected through warning, force, gentleness or harshness, but not through anger. Seneca compares this to a doctor who does not get angry at the patient whose wounds he treats. The quoted objection, that some people cannot be corrected at all, is raised and left in the passage as a challenge.

Seneca says that dangerous people who corrupt others may be removed from society, but this should be done without hatred. He compares it to a surgeon cutting off a limb: it is a painful way of healing, not an act of anger.

Seneca argues that punishing people is best done calmly, not in anger. He compares it to killing diseased animals or unhealthy newborns, which is done to protect the rest, and says that separating the harmful from the sound is a matter of reason. A punishment carefully judged works better to reform, and so Socrates said he would strike a slave only if he were not angry.

A man who was angry at his slave delayed punishing him until he was calmer, and in the meantime he first checked himself. The passage then asks who can claim to control his passions, since Socrates, a famous Greek philosopher, did not trust himself to act while angry.

Punishing wrongdoers does not require anger, because anger is itself a fault of the mind, and it is wrong to punish sin with sin. Seneca compares punishment to a doctor's treatment: a wrongdoer is corrected as a remedy, the way a patient is bled, with reproof in private or public for slight faults and disgrace for those who have gone too far.

Seneca describes how punishment should be matched to the offender. Milder faults call for a brand of shame, such as exile. Worse villainy calls for chains and public imprisonment. The worst case is a mind so corrupted that it sins for sin's own sake, and it cannot be cured without destroying the person.

The speaker says he is not angry at the person he is harming, because he is acting for that person's good. He compares himself to a doctor who gives different treatments to different patients, and he suggests that for some, death is the kindest cure.

Seneca says he sees many kinds of faults in many people, and he must treat them all like a doctor healing a whole city. Each fault needs its own cure: one person may be moved by honour, another by travel, pain, need, or even death. If he must act as a magistrate, he will go to judge calmly, not in anger or hatred.

Seneca says a judge can order even severe punishments, such as execution, without feeling anger. He compares this to killing venomous snakes: a calm act, not a rage. He argues that the law itself is not angry with the criminals it punishes, since it does not know them personally.

Seneca says a good person should judge wrongdoing the way a law court does: condemning the offence without becoming angry. He argues that if anger at wicked crimes were allowed, envy of wicked men's success would be allowed too. A good man should see both their crimes and their wealth without anger or envy.

Even the wise man, in the Stoic view, may feel slight traces of emotion when dealing with such matters. These are like a scar left after a healed wound. He feels the first stirrings, but he is not ruled by the full passions themselves.

Seneca disagrees with Aristotle's view that passions can be used like weapons. A weapon can be picked up and put down at will, but passions act on their own and take control of a person. Seneca says reason is the only weapon we need, since it obeys us and cannot turn against us.

Seneca argues that reason is enough on its own, even for acting well and getting things done. It would be foolish, he says, for reason to ask anger for help, since anger is unreliable and unhealthy. Once reason has decided on a course, it keeps to it, because it has nothing better to replace it with.

Seneca says that anger is weak and short-lived, unlike a settled purpose, which holds once it is formed. Anger rises quickly like an empty bladder or a gust of wind, then fades. Angry people who planned harsh punishments often become gentle when the moment to punish arrives.

Anger burns hot at first and then fades, so its punishments are not fair. Two people equally guilty may get different punishments, and the one who did less may be punished more, simply because he met anger while it was still fresh.

Anger is described here as a judge who goes wrong in two ways: sometimes it punishes too harshly, sometimes too little. It follows its own moods, ignores evidence and the defence, and refuses to give up a mistaken opinion.

Reason takes its time, lets both sides speak, and asks for delay so it can find the truth. Anger is in a hurry, wants its verdict to look fair, and is provoked by side issues such as a confident manner, a loud voice, showy clothes, or public popularity.

Anger, Seneca says, clings to its own mistakes and refuses to admit being wrong, even when the truth is plain. He gives the example of Gnaeus Piso, who had a stiff, stubborn nature. In his rage, Piso had a soldier executed for coming back from leave without his comrade, as if the soldier must have killed him.

A condemned soldier was led out to be executed after a man he was thought to have killed in a mutiny. Then the supposed victim returned alive. The centurion stopped the execution and took the condemned man back to Piso, the commander who had ordered it, so that the innocence could be restored to him.

Piso, in a rage, orders the execution of two men: one who was supposed to have murdered and one who was supposed to have been killed, who is still alive. He then adds a third death, that of the centurion who brought the condemned man back. The point is that three men are put to death because one man was found innocent.
Anger is shown to be very good at finding excuses for its wild behavior. The speaker gives three charges against people he orders killed, yet the point is that he had no real fault to name in them.

Seneca contrasts anger with reason. Anger refuses correction, rages at the truth when it is revealed, and attacks its targets with noise, gestures and curses. Reason, by contrast, acts silently and calmly, even when it must punish, carrying out harsh measures without any display of emotion.

Seneca says a judge should stay calm when passing sentence, without grinding his teeth, shaking his head, or acting in any way unfitting for a judge. He quotes Hieronymus asking why a man should bite his own lips when he wants to strike someone. The point is that visible anger is improper in a judge, and the writer mocks an official who leaps down, seizes the lictor's fasces (the rods of office), and tears his own clothes in rage.

Seneca describes a furious man who smashes things and hurts himself because he cannot immediately strike the person he is angry with. Such a man must be held back by others. A man who is calm, by contrast, judges fairly and gives each person the punishment they deserve without these outbursts.

The wise judge, in Seneca's view, often pardons a wrongdoer who is truly sorry and whose wrongdoing is not deep in his character. He may also punish a great crime more lightly than a small one if the great crime came from sudden passion, while the small one was planned, sly and long practised.

Two men who commit the same fault may deserve different punishments, depending on whether the act was careless or planned. Punishment should aim at reforming the wrongdoer or removing him from society, and should look forward rather than back, since the past cannot be undone and the future can be prevented from going wrong.

Seneca says that a ruler who executes criminals in public does so to frighten others, and that someone who holds the power of life and death must be calm while weighing such decisions. An angry person should not hold the power to punish.

Anger does not add to true greatness of mind; it only produces empty pride. Like a swollen body full of disease, it looks bigger but is not healthy. People driven by such anger feel lofty, yet their ideas have no firm base and will fall apart.

Anger is not a firm or solid thing. It is empty and unstable, and it only looks like nobility or courage. Constant irritation, Seneca says, shows a weak and unhappy mind, like a sore body that cries out at the lightest touch.

Seneca argues that anger is mainly a fault of women and children, and that angry men show the same weak minds. He says that angry words only seem great to people who do not know true greatness. As an example he cites the saying "Let them hate me, provided they fear me," which he links to the Roman dictator Sulla, and he says he cannot tell which of the two wishes, to be hated or to be feared, is worse.

Seneca describes a ruler who wants people to hate him, and who only asks that they fear him, not obey or approve of him. Seneca rejects this as no greatness at all but a monstrous attitude. He says even being loved on those terms would be unwanted.

Seneca argues that loud, threatening anger is not a sign of real strength, since angry men are often inwardly timid. He also rejects the idea that a person can be great without being good. In his view, greatness of mind means being steady and sound throughout, which an evil character cannot have.

Seneca says that true greatness rests on goodness and gets its strength from it. Showy speech and action can make people look great, as Gaius Caesar did when he raged at the sky over thunder and challenged Jove, king of the gods, to a fight to the death.

Seneca is describing a man who boasted he could hurt Jupiter or could not be hurt by him. He says this boast encouraged the conspirators, since it seemed they were bearing a man who could not bear Jupiter, which seemed an extreme endurance.

Anger is not a sign of greatness or nobility, even when it looks powerful and defies gods and men. Seneca compares this to a mistaken belief that luxury makes a person great. Such a person wants luxury: ivory couches, purple clothes, gold roofs, and vast building projects that reshape land and sea.

Seneca says that someone who thought vices showed greatness of mind would see greed and lust that way. The greedy man hoards wealth and treats whole provinces like his own estates, while the lustful man risks his life for pleasure without fear of death.
Seneca says that ambition, though it may look like greatness of mind, is really narrow and low, however far it reaches. Only virtue is lofty, and nothing is truly great unless it is also calm.

Public executions in Rome were announced by trumpet so that the people would gather to watch and learn from the punishment. The passage cites Tacitus on the astrologer P. Marcius, who was put to death outside the Esquiline gate before a crowd summoned this way.

Seneca says his first book had an easier subject, and this one is drier. The question is whether anger comes from a deliberate choice or from a sudden impulse, like many other feelings that arise in us without our knowing. He must first deal with this plain question before he can move on to higher topics.

Seneca compares the body to a well-made thing: the bones, sinews and joints come first. They are not attractive to look at, but they hold the body together and keep it alive. Then come the features that make up the face and shape, and last of all the colour, which is added once the rest is complete.

Anger is agreed to be stirred up when a harm seems to be done. The open question is whether anger follows that appearance straight away on its own, or whether it only arises when the mind goes along with it.

Seneca, writing as a Stoic, holds that anger cannot act on its own without the mind's agreement. Anger needs a judgment: that a wrong was done, that we should not have been harmed, and that we must take revenge. Such a judgment is a complex act, unlike a bare impulse that arises without our consent.

Anger, in this view, is a chain of steps: a person judges that something wrong has happened, feels indignant, condemns the act, and seeks revenge. None of these steps can happen unless the person's mind first agrees to the judgment that the event touched him.

Anger is being examined in this way: if anger rose up against our will, reason could never control it. Other bodily reactions, such as shivering, blushing or feeling dizzy, happen without our choice and cannot be stopped by reasoning. Anger, however, can be driven off by wise sayings, so it is not that kind of reaction.

Seneca says anger is a mistake the mind makes by choice, not a feeling that comes from ordinary human conditions and so might strike even the wisest people. He gives the first example of this kind of anger: the sudden rush of feeling when we think of a wrong. People feel it even at stage plays or when reading about old events, such as the banishment of Cicero or the wars of Marius.

Seneca says that people easily catch feelings from what they see and hear. Anger rises at the murderers of Pompey, Theodotus and Achillas, and at the boy king who allowed it. Music, trumpets, cruel sights, laughter, mourning and other people's battles all stir our minds in the same way.

Seneca says that some feelings are not yet full emotions. They are quick, involuntary reactions, like a frown at a stage shipwreck, or a soldier's start at a trumpet. These reactions are not passions, but early signs that could grow into passions.

A passion, in this view, is not the same as a sudden feeling or bodily reaction. Things like paling, tears, or a quick glance happen to the mind and body without being passions. A passion only arises when a person gives in to these first impulses and follows them.

Even the bravest soldiers and generals, and the most skilled speakers, feel fear or nerves before battle or a speech. Their pale faces, shaking knees, racing hearts and cold hands show that strong people are not free of these bodily reactions.

Seneca argues that anger is not just a feeling that stirs us but an impulse that goes beyond proper limits, and every impulse needs the mind's agreement. A person who thinks they were wronged, wants revenge, but is talked out of it and calms down is not, in his view, angry. That state is a mental response still controlled by reason.

Anger is not the first jolt a person feels when they seem to be wronged. That jolt is only an impression. Anger is the step after it, when the mind accepts the impression as true and deliberately moves to seek revenge.

Seneca describes three stages of anger. First comes a sudden feeling that is not chosen and only warns of anger. Next, the mind agrees with a wish to take revenge, believing it is right. Last, the feeling overrides reason and wants revenge whether or not it is justified.

Reason cannot stop our first immediate reaction to something, just as we cannot stop yawning when others yawn or blinking when a finger comes at our eyes. Such reflexes might be weakened by practice and attention. Anger, by contrast, is a feeling that starts and stops through a conscious decision of the mind.

Seneca argues that cruelty of the kind shown by tyrants like Apollodorus and Phalaris is not anger at all. Such people hurt others even when they have not been harmed, and even welcome harm to themselves if they can inflict pain. They do it for their own pleasure, not to get revenge, so he calls it ferocity.

Seneca says that anger, when it is repeatedly indulged, wears away a person's mercy and sense of human fellowship, and finally turns into cruelty. Cruel people then feel relaxed and happy, not angry. He gives Hannibal, who admired a trench full of blood, as an example.

Seneca mocks a cruel man who enjoys seeing blood. He says the man would admire rivers or lakes filled with blood, and that he was raised among killing. Fortune will keep favouring him, showing him slaughter at Trasimene, Cannae and finally Carthage.

Volesus, a Roman governor, had three hundred people beheaded and then strutted among the bodies, calling the deed a kingly action. Seneca says this was not anger but a worse, incurable sickness of the mind, since he would have done worse if he had been a king.

Seneca's opponent argues that virtue should feel anger at wrongdoing, just as it approves of what is good. Seneca replies that this makes virtue both petty and grand at once. He holds that anger at another's sin is base and suits a narrow mind, while joy at a good deed is noble, so virtue would copy vice by being angry.

Seneca says that anger is often worse than the wrongs that cause it, so it deserves punishment itself. Virtue's natural state is joy, and anger is as unworthy of it as grief is. Anger always ends in sorrow, either from regret or from failing to get what it wanted.

Seneca is stating an argument his opponents would make. If the wise man should be angry at wrongs, then the greater and more frequent the wrongs, the angrier and more often angry he would be, so he would be prone to anger. Yet if great and frequent anger cannot exist in the wise man, why not free him from anger altogether?

If anger is set to match each wrong a person commits, there is no stopping point. The angry person must either treat small and great wrongs as equal, which is unjust, or be angry so often that he is the most easily angered of men.

Seneca argues that a wise person should not have feelings that depend on other people's wrongdoing. If anger and grief at crimes were a duty of the wise, such a person would live in constant anger and sorrow, which he calls unhappy. He uses Socrates as an example of someone who stayed calm.

The main point is that a person who judges every wrong they see would be angry all the time. Everywhere they go they meet criminals, misers and spendthrifts, and every corner of life gives them something to be shocked by. Such a person would wear themselves out with anger.

People often attack others for faults they share or worse. A son challenges a will he has not earned, a man accuses his mother, and an informer charges someone with a crime he commits himself. Judges condemn others for what they have done, and crowds side with whoever speaks most persuasively.

Seneca says that crowds in public places hold as many vices as there are people in them. Men who look peaceful are not at peace, since each will harm another for a small gain, and no one profits except at someone else's cost.

Seneca describes people who envy the lucky, scorn the unfortunate, and harm one another for small gains or pleasures. He says human society is worse than a pack of wild animals, because animals at least do not attack their own kind, while people tear each other apart.
Seneca says that people differ from animals in one way: wild animals stay gentle toward those who feed them, but human anger turns against the very people who raised and cared for the angry person.

Seneca argues that a wise man who once gives way to anger will never stop being angry, because wrongdoing is everywhere. He says that more wrong is done than punishment can cure, that sin grows more eager and less modest each day, and that crimes now happen openly. People break the law together, as if following a common signal, to erase the difference between right and wrong.

Nobody can trust family or guests. Hosts may turn on guests, fathers-in-law on sons, and brothers rarely love each other. Wives plot against husbands, husbands against wives, stepmothers poison, and children wait for their fathers to die.

Seneca says that the poet's list of human crimes is far too small. He names many worse horrors that the poet left out: civil war, parents against children, burning cities, poisoned wells, and tyranny. He also mentions men who now boast of shameful acts that were once hidden as crimes.

Seneca lists many wrongs: broken treaties, theft, fraud, and unpaid debts that courts could not handle. He then argues that if a wise man were to feel anger as strongly as such crimes deserve, that anger would have to become madness.

Seneca argues that anger at people's faults is pointless. We would not be angry at someone who stumbles in the dark, a deaf person who cannot hear, a child who forgets his duty, or a sick, old or tired person. Human minds are confused, so people cannot help going wrong, and some even love to do so.

To stop being angry at single people, Seneca says, you must forgive all of humankind. Anger at grown men for their wrongs would also mean anger at children, who will soon do wrong too. Yet we do not get angry at children, who cannot yet understand right and wrong, and being human is a better excuse than being a child, since we are born prone to faults of mind as well as body.

Seneca says that people who go wrong mostly do so because they copy others who have already gone astray, much as a traveler may stray when a crowd takes the wrong road. When nearly everyone shares a fault, the wise person does not get angry at it, because it would be unjust and dangerous to be angry at a failing that all people share.

Heraclitus wept at the sight of people living, or rather dying, miserably, while Democritus laughed at their serious affairs. Seneca says that since such folly can be met with tears or laughter, there is no room for anger.

The wise man does not get angry at wrongdoers, because he knows that nobody is born wise and that very few people become wise. Seneca compares this to anger at nature: no sane person is angry that a thorn bush bears no fruit, so there is no reason to be angry at human faults.

The wise man, staying calm, expects to meet people who are drunk, greedy, ungrateful and driven by ambition. He looks at them kindly, as a doctor looks at patients, and does not treat their faults as personal enemies. He is compared to a sailor who blames neither crew nor ship for a leak.

The passage compares a sailor bailing out a leaking ship to a person facing lasting faults in their own character. The sailor keeps working, stopping leaks and pumping out water even though more keeps coming in. The point is that such evils cannot be fully ended, only kept from overwhelming us through steady, ongoing effort.

Seneca's opponent claims anger is useful because it prevents contempt and frightens wicked people. Seneca replies with a dilemma: if anger is strong, it makes people hate us, which is more dangerous than being despised; if it is weak, it invites scorn and ridicule.

Something can be frightening without being good. Seneca says a wise person does not want to be feared the way a wild beast is feared, as if fear were a useful weapon. Fevers and gout cause fear, yet they are not good. Anger, he says, is ugly in itself and should not be feared.

A tyrant or powerful man is feared by many, much as children fear a frightening mask. Seneca argues that fear comes back on the one who causes it, so a man who is himself at peace is not feared. He then quotes a line by Laberius: "He must fear many, whom so many fear."

Those who cause fear in others are not free from fear themselves. Even lions, the fiercest beasts, are easily startled by faint noises, strange shadows, voices or smells. Whatever terrifies others is afraid for itself.

A wise person has no reason to want to be feared. Anger should not be admired just because it frightens people, since even small, harmful creatures cause fear. Seneca gives the example of a feathered string that scares wild animals into traps, so fear alone proves nothing about worth.

Seneca says that people fear anger for the same silly reasons animals fear trivial things, like lions fleeing moving chariots or elephants fleeing pig squeals. Anger has nothing real or brave behind it, and it only frightens weak minds.

The objection says that anger cannot be removed unless wickedness is first removed from nature. Seneca answers that a person can avoid feeling cold or heat even when the season is winter or summer, either by living in a sheltered place or by training the body to endure them.

Seneca is setting up an argument he then answers. The opening claim is that anger must be removed before virtue can enter the mind, since a person cannot be both angry and good, just as no one can be sick and well at once. The objection he raises in reply is that anger cannot be fully removed from the mind, because human nature does not allow it.

The main point is that no task is too hard for the human mind, and no strong feeling is beyond training. The mind can give itself orders and keep them. Seneca gives examples: some people never smiled, some gave up wine or sex, and some learned to stay awake for long stretches.

Seneca points out that people have learned hard feats such as walking tightropes, carrying heavy loads, and diving deep under water. He says that steady effort can overcome almost any obstacle. Yet those who do these things gain little or nothing worth their long labour.

Seneca argues that people will endure hard, pointless labours such as tightrope walking or deep diving for small rewards, so we should be willing to practise patience for a far greater prize: a calm, happy life free from anger. He calls anger the worst of evils, bringing with it frenzy, cruelty and madness.

Seneca argues that anger should not be defended as useful or unavoidable, even though many vices have defenders. He holds that the faults we suffer from can be cured, that human nature leans toward good and will help us improve, and that the road to virtue is not as hard as some believe.

Seneca says that the way to happiness is easy, while vice is hard work. A peaceful mind rests, but anger is toilsome. Mercy has leisure, while cruelty is full of business. Virtues cost little effort to practise, but vices cost a great deal.

Seneca argues that anger should be removed from the mind completely, not just kept under control. He says that without anger, people can deal with wrongdoing more fairly and effectively, and that a wise person can do his duty without any harmful emotion, which could otherwise get out of hand.

Anger should never become a habit. A teacher may sometimes pretend to be angry to stir up dull listeners, much as a driver uses goads to start a slow horse. Yet anger is no more useful than grief or fear, and when provoked, a person should hold their anger back.
Controlling anger is not hard, Seneca says, because boxers train their bodies to take blows and pain. They strike when a chance arises, not when rage pushes them to.

Pyrrhus, a famous trainer of athletes, told his pupils never to lose their temper. Anger ruins their skill because it only thinks about hurting the opponent. Reason advises patience, but anger pushes for revenge, and so people who could have survived their first misfortunes end up facing worse ones.

People have been exiled over a single insulting word, have fallen into great misery because they would not bear a small wrong quietly, and have become slaves because they would not give up even a little of their freedom. The point is that anger over small slights leads to serious harm.

Seneca's opponent argues that anger shows something noble, since free peoples like the Germans and Scythians are quick to anger. Seneca replies that anger strikes strong, bold minds before discipline tames them, much as fertile land grows tall weeds when left untended.

Natural boldness, left untrained, can turn into irritability and rashness instead of courage. Seneca's point is that people who rise only on their natural strengths, without discipline, let their energy go in the wrong direction. The question at the end suggests that gentler natures carry their own weaknesses, such as tenderness, love and shyness.

Seneca says that fierce, untamed peoples, like wild animals, cannot rule because they cannot be ruled either. Only people who can accept discipline are able to govern, which is why world power has mostly belonged to nations living in milder climates.

Seneca's opponent argues that animals with a strong capacity for anger are the most noble, and holds them up as models for people. Seneca replies that people should follow reason, not impulse. He adds that each animal has its own natural strength: anger suits lions, fear suits stags, boldness suits hawks, and flight suits doves.

Seneca argues that anger does not make an animal better. Wild beasts that hunt for food may seem fiercer and so better, but he prefers the patient oxen and horses that obey the reins. He says humans should model themselves on the universe and God, the only creatures able to understand Him, not on wild animals.

Seneca is saying that short-tempered men seem honest only because they are compared with cheats and tricksters. He argues they are not really simple but careless, and that "simple" is a word we use for fools, gluttons, spendthrifts and anyone whose faults are easy to see.

Seneca's opponent claims an orator speaks better when truly angry. He replies no: speakers do better when they only pretend anger, as actors move audiences by acting anger rather than feeling it. To sway a crowd, a speaker must first display the emotion, and a show of passion can work better than real passion.

Seneca says that a mind without anger is weak only if it has nothing stronger to rely on. A person should be neither too soft nor too harsh. The wise person stays moderate and, when firm action is needed, uses calm force rather than anger.

Seneca says there are two kinds of remedy for anger. One keeps us from becoming angry in the first place, and the other keeps us from doing wrong once we are angry. He compares this to the body: we keep healthy by a routine, and we cure illness by other rules.
Teaching should be pursued with great care and constant effort. Young minds are easy to shape, but bad habits that have grown up with a person are hard to remove.

Seneca says that a hot temperament is most likely to become angry. He explains that the four elements (fire, air, earth, water) carry qualities of hot, cold, dry and moist, and their mix shapes regions, animals, bodies and character. So a person's disposition depends on which quality is strongest in them.

Seneca, reporting Stoic views, says a person's temper follows whichever bodily element is strongest in them. Warm, fiery people are quick to anger, while cold people tend toward cowardice. Some Stoics thought anger was caused by blood boiling around the heart, and people with more moisture grow angry slowly, because they must build up heat.

Seneca explains that anger depends on the body's heat and moisture. Women and children get angry quickly but weakly, while people in dry, hot states of life get angry strongly. The old, the sick, the hungry, the thirsty and those low in blood are irritable, and wine stirs anger by adding heat.

People differ in how easily they lose their temper, and drink can bring it on in some at small doses and in others only at heavy ones. Seneca says fair, ruddy people are prone to anger because their blood runs hot and is quick to stir, much like the flushed look others get when angry.

Seneca says that anger has many causes beyond a person's natural temper, such as illness, injury, exhaustion, worry, strong desire, and love. These things make a troubled mind quicker to find fault. He adds that a person's habitual way of thinking, if harsh, makes the problem worse.

Seneca says a person's basic temperament cannot be changed, but knowledge can limit its effects. Hot-tempered people should avoid wine and rich food, which feed their fire, and should take exercise that tires them only enough to calm their natural heat.

Moderate amusements, such as games, help clear the mind and keep it balanced. People who are naturally dull or gloomy are not much prone to anger but are open to worse faults like cowardice and despair, so they need comfort and cheering up. Since anger and gloominess need opposite treatments, one should fight whichever fault is currently taking control.

Bringing up boys well matters greatly, but it is hard to do. Parents must avoid fostering anger while not dulling their spirit, and both qualities grow from the same sources, so even a careful guardian can be fooled by how alike they look.

A child's spirit grows with freedom and is crushed by slavish treatment. Praise lifts it, but it can also become arrogant and quick-tempered, so a child must be guided between these, sometimes restrained and sometimes encouraged. He should not be made to beg or be rewarded for begging; gifts should be given for his own sake, for past good conduct, or for promised good behaviour.

Seneca advises how to raise a boy so he does not grow angry. The boy should play games without sulking or rage, learn to want to win rather than to hurt, and enjoy success without wild elation. He should have rest but not idleness, and be kept away from luxury, since soft, indulgent upbringing makes children more prone to anger.

Seneca says that anger grows in people who are spoiled and powerful. Someone who never hears "no", whose mother always comforts him, or who is rich, noble or high in rank, becomes more easily angry. Flatterers who tell such a person that accepting any slight lowers his dignity make this worse.

Seneca says children must be kept away from flattery and taught to respect the truth, even when it frightens them. He lists rules: respect elders, never get what they want by throwing a tantrum, receive things only when calm, and accept blame for wrongdoing.

Seneca says that boys should have calm teachers and attendants, because young people copy the habits of those around them. He gives the example of a boy from Plato's household who, seeing his own father angry, said he had never seen anyone act that way at Plato's house. Seneca thinks the boy copied his father's anger more readily than he had learned Plato's calm.

Seneca advises that a person's food and clothing should be plain and the same as those of the people around him. If he is treated as equal to many others from the start, he will not become angry when someone else is compared with him.

Adults can no longer be corrected from childhood, so they must deal with their habits as they are. The root of anger is the belief that one has been wronged, so that belief should not be accepted easily.

Do not get angry right away, even when a wrong seems obvious, because false things can look true. Give it time, since time brings out the truth. Be slow to accept slander, and remember that people tend to believe what they dislike and become angry before they have judged the matter.

We can be angered not only by slander but also by mere suspicion, even by someone's look or smile, and so turn against innocent people. The passage advises holding back anger and defending absent people against our own first judgments, because a punishment can be delayed but never undone once carried out.

Under torture, a would-be assassin of a tyrant named the tyrant's closest friends, and the tyrant had each one killed. When asked if anyone was left, the man replied that the tyrant was the last, because no one else was left alive whom the tyrant loved.

Seneca says anger once led a tyrant to help kill another tyrant, and cut down guards himself. He contrasts this with Alexander, who, though quick to anger, trusted his physician Philip and drank the medicine Philip gave him despite a warning of poison.

Caesar, a merciful victor in the civil war, burned letters that named people who had supported or seemed to support his rival Pompey. He did this so he could not be angry at them. He believed the kindest way to pardon them was never to learn what they had done.

Quick belief in what we hear does great harm, and it is often better not to listen at all, since being fooled is sometimes less bad than suspecting deceit. We should clear our minds of suspicion and mistrust, which Seneca calls untrustworthy causes of anger, and he gives small slights such as a cold greeting or a missed invitation as examples.

Suspicion can always find reasons, so we should not be quick to suspect. We should accept nothing as true unless the evidence is plain to see. When our suspicions turn out to be baseless, we should blame ourselves for having been too ready to believe, since this habit will make us slow to believe what we hear.

Seneca says it is madness to get angry over tiny annoyances, such as a slow slave, lukewarm water, a messy couch, or a badly laid table. He compares this to a sick person who cannot bear a light breeze or sensitive eyes that are hurt by white clothing. The point is that such anger shows a weakness in the person, not a fault in the thing that annoys them.

The point is an anecdote about a wealthy man from Sybaris, a town known for luxury, who was so soft that he could not bear to watch someone else working. He even complained that rose petals under him were uncomfortable because they were folded double.

Seneca says that when pleasures have weakened a person's body and mind, even small annoyances seem unbearable. The cause is not that the annoyances are hard to bear, but that the person has become soft. He gives small examples: coughing, sneezing, a fly, a dog, or a dropped key.

The passage asks whether a person who is easily irritated by small things can stay calm under bigger troubles. Someone who cannot bear a scraping bench or a badly cooled drink, it suggests, will not be able to bear insults in public debate, hunger, or a hard march in the heat.
Excessive and discontented luxury feeds anger more than anything else, according to this line. Seneca says the mind should be toughened by hardship, so that only a severe blow hurts it.

We get angry at people who can harm us, or at things that cannot harm us at all. Objects such as a book with tiny print or clothes we dislike are examples. Seneca calls being angry at such things foolish, since they cannot deserve or feel anger.

Seneca argues that people often get angry before they have thought clearly about the matter. He says makers of goods may have done poor work through lack of skill, not to insult the owner. He also calls it foolish to take out anger meant for people on inanimate things.

Being angry at dumb animals is as mad as being angry at objects, because animals cannot intend harm. A wrong needs a deliberate act, so animals can hurt us as a sword or stone can, but they cannot wrong us.

Seneca argues that it is foolish to take offence when a horse behaves differently with different riders, as if the horse chose to misbehave. Being angry with children, and with people who think like children, is equally foolish. Before a fair judge, ignorance would excuse wrongdoing just as innocence does.
Some things cannot harm us and only do us good. Seneca gives the immortal gods as an example: they neither want nor are able to do harm, because their nature is gentle and calm.

Foolish people blame or credit us for weather such as storms, heavy rain and hard winters, as if these happened for our sake. In fact natural events follow their own laws and have nothing to do with human concerns.

Seneca says that people overrate their own importance if they think the world is disturbed for their sake, and that events do not really work to harm us. Some things cannot hurt us, and some that seem harmful are meant for our good, like a good ruler's or teacher's correction, which we should accept as we accept a surgeon's knife.

When we feel we are being punished, Seneca suggests we should look at our own past wrongs rather than only at our suffering. If we judge ourselves honestly, we will find that we deserve worse than we get.

If we want to judge fairly, we must first accept that none of us is free of fault, since much of our anger comes from denying our own wrongs. Even someone who has broken no law is only innocent in a narrow, technical sense.

Seneca says that moral duty asks far more than the law does, since things like kindness and honour are not written in any statute. He adds that we cannot even meet the narrowest idea of innocence: we have done, thought, wished for, and encouraged wrong, and sometimes we stayed innocent only because we failed to act.

Seneca argues that when we are wronged or harmed we should judge others more fairly and not blame ourselves or the gods. Our sufferings come from the common law that governs all mortal life, not from divine decree. He adds that if someone insults us, we should first remember how often we have spoken ill of others ourselves.

Seneca advises that when someone seems to wrong us, we should not assume it is a deliberate injury, even when they act knowingly. He suggests others may have acted from good intentions, compulsion, ignorance, a wish to be witty, or a need to get ahead, rather than from a desire to harm us.

Seneca says that a person can avoid sudden anger by remembering his own past mistakes. He has himself been wrongly suspected, has been misjudged, and has once hated people he later loved. If he silently tells himself "I have done this very thing myself" when someone offends him, his anger is less likely. He then asks who would be fair enough to judge this way.

Seneca points out a pattern of hypocrisy: people who do wrong themselves often demand strict loyalty from others. A man who chases other men's wives will not tolerate anyone looking at his own wife. Traitors, liars and cheating lawyers likewise punish others for the same faults.

People tend to see faults in others while ignoring their own. A father who is worse than his son scolds him for lavish feasts, and tyrants rage at murderers. Seneca says most people are angry at the sinner rather than the sin, and that asking oneself whether one has done the same wrong should make us milder.

The main advice in this passage is to wait before acting on anger. Delay lets anger cool, and it lets you judge the offence clearly. Seneca also says not to try to stop anger all at once, but to weaken it bit by bit. Finally, he warns that gossip and reports are often false, so they should be believed slowly.

Some people invent wrongs or tell lies to stir up anger, either to win favour, to set friends against each other, or just to watch the trouble. Seneca says a judge would not accept any claim about even a small sum of money without a witness, and that the witness must be sworn.

The speaker says a case should be heard from both sides, over more than one sitting, because the truth becomes clearer the more it is examined. He asks why someone would condemn a friend before hearing his side or knowing the charge. He points out that an accuser says less once he has to prove what he claims.

A person who spreads a story but refuses to stand behind it in public is criticised. He urges you on, yet withdraws from the quarrel and will only speak in secret. Seneca calls it unjust to believe such secret reports while openly showing anger.

Seneca advises looking at the offender's reasons before getting angry. A child may not know he is doing wrong, a father may have earned the right to wrong us, and a woman may simply have made a mistake. Someone who acts under orders should not be blamed, and only an unjust person would be angry at such an act.

Seneca gives a series of cases for when someone has wronged you and you feel anger. If the offender is a judge, defer to his judgment. If he is a king, yield to him whether he punishes fairly or unfairly. If he is an animal or as dull as one, anger would make you like it. If it is a disease or misfortune, the same reasoning applies.

Seneca says that anger is pointless in several cases. If a wrong comes from a god, anger is as wasteful as praying for a god to be angry at someone else. If the wrongdoer is a good man, you should not believe he meant harm; if he is bad, you should not be surprised, since he will be punished by others and his sin already punishes him.

Seneca says that anger comes from feeling wrongly treated, and that people call something unjust for two reasons. Either they think they should never have had to suffer it, or they did not expect it, and so feel it is beneath what they deserve.

Anger comes most strongly from events we did not expect. That is why small slips at home, or a friend's carelessness, can seem like deliberate harm. Asked why enemies' injuries anger us, the answer given is that we did not expect those particular harms, or not so many of them.

Anger, Seneca says, comes from too much self-love or from ignorance. We expect to go unhurt even by our enemies, and we are surprised when bad people do evil, enemies hurt us, friends quarrel, or children and servants err, though all of this is common. He adds that "I did not think" is the most shameful excuse a general can give.

Seneca says it is a shameful excuse to be caught off guard by human faults. He advises expecting the worst: people can be treacherous, ungrateful, greedy, or impious, even good ones. Assume trouble is always near and that you will be offended at some point.

Seneca says a wise person should keep control even when things seem safe, as a pilot keeps tackle ready to shorten sail. He argues that harming others is shameful and unnatural for humans, since even wild animals can be tamed by kindness. He concludes that people should be ashamed to have taken on the cruel habits of beasts.

Because all people belong to one larger community, as parts of one body do, harming anyone is wrong, just as harming one's own country is. Humans should spare each other because they are born for society, and society can only last if it protects and cares for all its members.

Punishment should be aimed at stopping future harm, not at paying back a past wrong. Seneca compares it to killing a dangerous snake only when it cannot be tamed or kept from harming us. If everyone with a bad nature were punished, no one would be spared.

Seneca rejects the idea that anger brings a sweet satisfaction in paying back pain. He argues that returning injury for injury is not honourable, while repaying kindness with kindness is. In the first case, it is shameful to win; in the second, it is shameful to lose.

Seneca argues that revenge is little better than the wrong it answers; the only difference is that the avenger wrongs someone second. To show a better way, he tells how Cato, struck by a stranger in a public bath, said he did not remember being struck when the man apologized.

It is better to ignore an insult than to take revenge for it. Seneca's point is that a great mind despises wrongs done to it, and the strongest way to answer an enemy is to think them not worth punishing. He adds that the insulting man was in fact lucky, since the insult brought him into contact with Cato, a famous Roman model of virtue.
Many people take small insults far too seriously and try to pay them back. The great man, Seneca says, is like a large wild animal that stays calm while small dogs bark at it.

Seneca argues that if revenge is used at all, it should be a practical tool, not something driven by anger. Often it is wiser to pretend an injury was never received. Wrongs from the powerful should be endured calmly, because the powerful tend to repeat a wrong they see it has hurt, and they hate those they have injured.

The passage says that a courtier survived long at court by putting up with insults and thanking the offender, and that it is often wiser not even to admit a wrong than to take revenge for it. As an example, the emperor Gaius Caesar (Caligula) jailed a young Roman knight simply for his fine clothes and hair.

Caligula (called Caius here) had a young man executed after his father begged for mercy. He then invited the grieving father to dinner the same day. The father hid his grief and acted cheerfully, while the emperor watched him closely.

Seneca describes a man who, on the day of his son's death and before the burial, dined with a large party, drank heavily, and showed no grief. Asked why, Seneca answers that he still had another son. He compares this to Priam in Homer's Iliad, who hid his anger and begged Achilles for his dead son's body.

This refers to Atreus, who unknowingly ate a meal made from his own son, and afterward dined with Thyestes, the man who had killed his son. Seneca points out that the meal was plain, without luxuries, and that the host spoke kindly and urged him to eat, while a guard stood by to make sure he did.

A father whose son has been killed by a tyrant would have ignored the tyrant if only his own safety were at stake. Because he loved his son, though, his anger gave way, and he had to ask leave to go and collect his son's remains. The tyrant refused that leave and kept pressing him to drink instead, as a way of easing his grief.

This describes a father who seemed cheerful and as if he had forgotten the terrible events of that day. The reason given is that he would have lost his second son if he had been an unwelcome guest to the man who had killed his eldest son.

We should avoid anger toward anyone, whether they are equal, superior, or inferior to us. Fighting an equal is risky, fighting a superior is foolish, and fighting an inferior is shameful. Lashing back at one who hurts us is the act of a weak, base person, as even mice and ants bite when touched.

Seneca advises that when we are angry, we should remember the good turns the other person has done us, so that these weigh against the wrong. He adds that forgiving someone can win us credit and turn enemies into valuable friends. He also warns against Sulla's example of punishing the children of enemies, since it is unjust for anyone to inherit their father's quarrels.

Before refusing to forgive someone, we should ask whether we would want everyone to be unforgiving toward us. Seneca points out that people who refuse mercy have often needed it themselves, and that forgiveness turns enemies into faithful friends, as Rome's former enemies became its loyal allies.

When someone is angry with you, answer with kindness rather than anger, because a quarrel needs two people to continue. Even in a mutual fight, the one who backs down first is the better man, since striking back only gives the other person a reason to strike again.

Anger is compared to a heavy weapon that is hard to control. A blow struck in anger can leave the striker's own hand caught in the wound, and anger is hard to pull back once it starts. Seneca argues that people should avoid such impulses, and that a good movement is one that can be stopped or slowed when wanted.

Seneca says the strongest and healthiest mental acts are those we control ourselves, not those that rush us along. He advises first considering how ugly anger is, since it spoils a calm face and turns a pleasant look fierce.

Seneca describes how anger shows in the body: the hair bristles, veins swell, breathing quickens, and the limbs shake. He argues that the inner state must be worse than the outward signs, with greater pride and fiercer rage that will burst a person unless it is released.

Seneca asks us to picture anger as a bloody, savage figure, like a killer dripping with blood or a fearsome monster from the underworld. Such monsters, in the poet's story, come up from hell to start wars and destroy peace between nations.

Seneca asks the reader to picture Anger as a wild, self-destroying figure: burning-eyed, bloodied, scarred, and hateful to everyone, herself included. She would even overturn earth, sea, and heaven to hurt an enemy. He then suggests that if we must see her, we should imagine her as the poets have described her.

Some angry people have calmed down when they saw their own face in a mirror, because the change in their looks shocked them and they did not recognize themselves. Seneca's point is that the mirror shows only a small part of how ugly anger really is.

Seneca says that if the mind could be seen directly, it would look black, disturbed and ugly, especially when angry. He argues that a mirror cannot calm an angry person, because angry people already see a fierce face as fine and even want to look that way.

Seneca argues that anger harms the body and mind. He lists physical damage it causes, such as burst veins, vomiting blood and eye injury. He says it can lead to permanent madness, and gives Ajax, who went mad with anger and then killed himself, as an example.

Enraged people pray for disaster on their own children and homes, yet insist they are not angry or mad. They turn on their closest friends, ignore laws, overreact to small things, refuse advice, and act by force, even ready to fight or kill themselves. Seneca says anger is the worst of all evils, worse than any vice.

Anger takes over the mind all at once, unlike other passions that grow slowly. Once it arrives, it overrules every other passion. It can overcome even deep love, and it can drive a greedy person to throw away the wealth he has hoarded.

The passage claims that anger rules over every other passion, and it gives examples of people who gave up rank or refused office, which ambition might seem to forbid. The quoted lines from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar praise a man whose temper was so balanced that nature itself could point to him as a true man.

Seneca says that anger can be driven out of the mind, or at least curbed and held back. Sometimes this can be done openly, when anger is only mild. When anger is very strong, it has to be handled in secret, because opposition only makes it flare up more.

Seneca says that anger is strong and sudden, so we must know how strong it is before choosing how to deal with it. The right method depends on the person: some respond to pleading, others to fear, reproach, admitting fault, shame, or delay. Delay is a last resort, since other passions can wait and be treated later.

Anger does not build up slowly the way other vices do. It reaches full force at once, takes control of a person's mind, and makes them lash out at anything in their path, not just the person they are angry with. Other vices merely disturb the mind, but anger throws it into violent disorder.

Seneca says that anger is the most dangerous passion. Unlike other vices, which creep up slowly, anger rushes on at once, like a lightning strike or storm, and it harms the mind's sanity. It destroys itself: it is arrogant when it wins and frantic when it fails.

Anger, even after it has lost, does not tire. If it cannot reach the person it is against, it turns on itself. Its strength has no link to its cause, so it can grow very large from a very small start.

Anger affects every age and every people, the passage says. Some peoples are spared luxury, idleness, or lawsuits and fraud, but none is spared anger. It is as harmful among law-abiding people as among those ruled only by force.
Seneca says that anger differs from other passions. Love, greed and ambition affect single people, but anger can seize a whole state or nation, and people can become angry together in crowds.

Seneca describes how anger spreads through a crowd. Men, women, old, young, rulers and common people all behave alike once roused. A few words can stir a mob to violence, so that it goes further than the person who stirred it. Speakers praised earlier are then hated, and soldiers turn on their commander.

Seneca describes a state ruled by anger. Its senate picks leaders in haste, without raising troops or naming a general, and the mob kills nobles in their homes. Ambassadors are mistreated, and fleets are sent out at once with hastily gathered soldiers, before the excitement has cooled.

Seneca describes how an untrained crowd, driven only by anger, charges into battle without order, omens, or weapons worth the name, and is then crushed. He says this is typical of savage peoples, who rush at Roman legions without discipline, fear, or caution, seeking danger.

The passage describes people who seem to enjoy being hit. They move toward the blow, twist their bodies onto the weapon, and die from a wound they bring on themselves. In the context of Seneca's essay on anger, this image refers to people ruled by their own rage and violence.

Seneca's friend Novatus asks how anger can be cured, since it is so powerful and harmful. Seneca says that Aristotle defended anger as a spur to virtue, but Seneca argues that anger must be shown to be shameful and savage. He says a man who rages destroys both himself and his enemy.

Seneca argues that anger is a kind of madness that drives a man, rather than something he controls. An angry man takes revenge himself, acts blindly, and may harm even those he loves. Anger cannot help virtue, because it disturbs the calm reason virtue needs. Its strength is like a fever's: short-lived and destructive.
Seneca answers a critic who thinks arguing against anger is pointless. He says some philosopher still argues that anger is useful, helping in battle, in business, and in any task that needs spirit.

Seneca says that anger must be shown for what it really is, so no one thinks it can ever be useful. He pictures it surrounded by its tools of cruelty, such as torture, executions and beasts, and says anger itself is more frightening than any of them.
Seneca says that anger looks uglier than any other passion. He describes the angry man's face: pale or flushed, and eyes that either dart about or stare fixed in one place.

Seneca lists the bodily signs of a man in anger: grinding teeth like a wild boar sharpening its tusks, cracking joints, wringing hands, slapping his own chest, fast breathing, sighs, staggering, broken speech, and trembling lips that hiss curses.

Seneca says that an angry man looks more shocking than any wild beast, even a dying or wounded one. He points out that anger harms the angry person first, so he asks why anyone would not want to give it up.

Seneca argues that people who treat anger as a sign of power, and quick revenge as a great good, are mistaken. A person ruled by anger is not powerful or free. He also says anger can take hold even of learned and sensible people, who are usually safe from other vices.
Some people say that anger is a sign of straightforwardness. It is also commonly believed that people with the kindest natures are the most prone to it.

Seneca argues that no one can count on being safe from anger. Even calm, good-tempered people can be overcome by it, just as a plague strikes strong and weak alike. For such people, anger is more shameful and more dangerous, because it changes their usual character more.

Seneca lists three goals for his discussion of anger: first, not to become angry; second, to get rid of anger once it has arisen; third, to calm an angry person and bring him back to reason. He says he will take these up in that order.

Seneca says that anger can be avoided by repeatedly examining it and judging its true cost, much as a court would try and condemn a wrongdoer. He compares anger with greed: greed hoards wealth for others to enjoy, while anger wastes money, and an angry master may drive slaves to flee or kill themselves.

Seneca argues that anger costs the angry person more than the thing that angered him is worth. He lists the harm anger does to fathers, husbands, officials and candidates. He says anger is worse than luxury, spite or envy, because anger wants to cause another's suffering and does not wait for chance to do it.

Seneca says anger wants to hurt its victim personally, not just see him harmed. He argues that anger causes jealousy and war, even among ordinary people, and that it harms the angry person too, since it gives up human feeling.

Anger pushes people toward hatred and harm, while kindness pushes them toward love and good deeds. Anger may look like high spirit, but Seneca argues it is really mean. A truly great mind knows its own worth, so it does not feel an insult and does not seek revenge.

A great mind is not harmed by insults, just as hard objects throw back weapons. Taking revenge would admit that one has been hurt, so the wise person ignores injury. If the wrongdoer is weaker, forgive him; if stronger, protect yourself by not reacting.

The passage says that the clearest sign of greatness of mind is not being moved to anger by anything that happens to you. It compares this to the heavens: the higher part of the sky, closer to the stars, never has clouds, storms or whirlwinds, while the lightning happens lower down.

A calm, lofty mind keeps its feelings under control, so it stays modest, respected and composed. Seneca says an angry person loses all of these qualities: they drop their shame, ignore their duties, speak harshly and cannot keep their body still.

Seneca says that peace of mind comes from not working too hard, beyond one's strength, in public or private affairs, as the philosopher Democritus taught. A busy day with many tasks rarely goes so smoothly that something does not cause offence and make the mind ready to become angry.

Seneca compares a life of scattered, restless activity to hurrying through a crowded city. Such a life, he says, brings many troubles: people deceive, delay, or ruin our hopes, and our plans do not turn out as we intended.

Fortune does not always favour a person, even one who keeps taking risks. When many plans fail, a man grows angry at people, events, places, and himself. To keep the mind calm, one should not rush from one task to another or tire it with huge aims or goals beyond its strength.

It is easy to carry a small load, but hard to bear burdens that others place on us. When we cannot manage them, we pass them on to other people. Even when we stay upright, we stagger under weights greater than we can handle.
Small, simple tasks, whether public or private, go smoothly and as the person in charge wishes. Very large tasks that exceed his ability to handle are not easily started.

Seneca describes a man who gets others to help him with his affairs, only for them to obstruct him and drag him down just as success seems near. His point is that wishes are often defeated when a person takes on hard tasks, yet he still wants the tasks he chooses to be easy.
