Before starting any task, judge your own abilities, the size of the task, and the means you will need to finish it. If you must quit halfway because you misjudged, the disappointment will make you bad-tempered.

Seneca says that people react to failure differently depending on temperament: a spirited person gets angry, while a sluggish one feels sorrow. He advises that we should set goals that are neither trivial nor reckless, keep our hopes modest, and avoid attempts whose success would surprise us.

Since we cannot bear injury well, Seneca advises avoiding it by keeping company with calm, easygoing people rather than anxious or sullen ones. He argues that we pick up the habits of those around us, just as diseases spread by touch, so bad traits pass from person to person. Drunkards, wild company and greed all corrupt those close to them.

Good character spreads to the people around it, just as vice does in the opposite direction. A person with unsteady principles benefits from keeping company with better people, much as a sick person benefits from living in a warm, healthy climate.

Seneca says that wild animals become tame when they live for a long time among people. However fierce an animal is, its savageness softens and is gradually forgotten in peaceful surroundings. The point is that living calmly with others can change even the wildest nature.

Living among calm people helps a person in two ways: they set a good example, and he is given no cause to become angry, so his fault is not exercised. For this reason, he should avoid people he knows will provoke his anger.

Seneca lists kinds of people who each stir anger: the proud, talkative, impudent, spiteful, quarrelsome, boastful, suspicious, obstinate and overly refined. He advises choosing companions who are straightforward, good-natured and steady, since they will not provoke anger and will put up with it.

Seneca says that gentle, agreeable people can help hot-tempered men, but only if they do not flatter them, since too much flattery annoys such men. He notes that a friend of his who was quick to anger was dangerous to flatter or to curse, and that the orator Caelius was so bad-tempered that even a very patient client found it hard to dine with him without quarrelling.
Caelius was annoyed that the other man kept agreeing with everything he said. He wanted an argument, and said so. Yet even Caelius calmed down soon after, because there was no one to quarrel with.

Seneca advises that a person who knows they are quick to anger should choose friends who agree with them, so their anger gets rest. He adds that even fierce animals calm down when stroked, and that disputes should be stopped early, before they grow strong.
A quarrel grows stronger the longer it goes on, and it traps anyone who gets too deeply involved. Staying out of it at the start is easier than getting free once you are caught up in it.

People prone to anger should avoid hard, serious work, or at least stop before they become tired. Instead, they should turn to pleasant arts such as poetry and stories, since gentle music calms the mind as harsh trumpets stir it up. Pythagoras, he notes, calmed himself by playing the lyre.

Just as green soothes tired eyes and certain colours hurt weak sight, cheerful activities calm an unhealthy mind. Seneca says we should avoid lawsuits, trials and anything that feeds our anger, and also physical exhaustion, since it wears down our calm nature and stirs up bitterness.

People who do not trust their digestion eat before important business, to calm their bile. Tiredness irritates bile, and a worn or weak body affects the mind, which is why the sick and the old are more easily angered.

Hunger and thirst should be avoided because they make people irritable and quick to anger. A weak or sick mind takes offence at small things, just as a sore hurts at the slightest touch. Even a greeting, a letter or a question can anger such a person.

The main point is that anger, like sickness, gives warning signs before it takes hold. A person should treat the first signs early, keep speech in check, and hold back their impulsiveness. Those early signs are easy to spot, just as clouds come before a storm.

Epilepsy sufferers can tell when a fit is coming from signs like cold limbs, failing sight and trembling. They try to stop it with remedies such as strong smells, tastes or warm treatments. If these fail, they go away alone so that no one sees them collapse.

Seneca says it helps to know which of our own weaknesses makes us angry, and to weaken it early. He lists different triggers: insults, actions, slights to one's family, appearance, fashion, learning, pride, or stubbornness in others.

People get angry in different ways and over different things. One man thinks it is beneath him to be angry with his slaves, while another is harsh at home but mild in public. So each person should know which offences hit him hardest, so he can watch that spot closely.

Seneca advises not to seek out everything said about you, since many insults can simply be ignored. Someone who digs up gossip, even secret gossip, ruins his own peace of mind. Some remarks can be read as insults, so it is best to let some pass, laugh at others, and forgive the rest.

Anger can be controlled, and many things can be treated as a joke. Socrates, when struck on the ear, joked that a man should know when to wear his helmet. The main idea is that how a person bears an insult matters more than how it was done, and that even tyrants sometimes hold back their rage.

Pisistratus, ruler of Athens, was insulted by a drunk guest who accused him of cruelty. When others urged him to punish the man, he stayed calm. He said he was no more angry with the guest than with someone who bumped into him while blindfolded.

Many people create their own grievances, through groundless suspicion or by blowing small matters out of proportion. Anger should not be invited or chased; if it comes, it should be pushed away. People also rarely admit that they have done, or could have done, the same thing they blame others for.

We should judge a wrong by the doer's intention, not just by the act itself. We should ask whether the person acted by accident or by force, out of hatred or self-interest, or to help a friend. Sometimes the wrongdoer's age or circumstances make it kind or sensible to overlook what was done.

Seneca advises us to imagine ourselves in the position of the person we are angry with, since we would not want to be treated that way. He also says that waiting is the best cure for anger, because the first heat fades and many wrongs seem smaller, or disappear, after a short time.

Delaying a decision lets it look like careful thought rather than anger. Seneca says that clear judgment is impossible while one is upset, so hard questions should be left until the mind is calm. He gives Plato as an example: angry with a slave, Plato stopped himself from striking, and stood with his hand raised.

Seneca describes a philosopher, Plato, who held back from punishing a servant while angry. He said he was making an angry man pay for his fault, and he gave the job of whipping the servant to another man because he himself was too angry to do it fairly.

Seneca describes a man who refuses to punish his slave while he is angry, since he knows that anger would make him punish too harshly and enjoy it too much. Seneca argues that an angry person should not be allowed to act, because an angry person wants to be allowed to do anything.

Seneca advises that when a person cannot fully stop feeling anger, they should at least keep it from showing. Anger should be hidden inside, so that the person controls it rather than being controlled by it. Outward signs of anger should be replaced by their opposites.

Seneca says that calming your outward behaviour, such as your face, voice and walk, can gradually calm your inner feelings. He gives Socrates as an example: when Socrates lowered his voice and spoke little, his friends could tell he was angry, and he was glad they noticed it but did not feel it himself.

Seneca says that people should ask their closest friends to speak frankly about their faults, and especially when they are angry, since that is when anger is hardest to bear and friends should not simply agree with them. He urges asking for this help while a person is calm and in control, because anger is a powerful evil that people treat too kindly.

People who know they will act badly when drunk tell their slaves to remove them from the feast. Likewise, people who know they become unreasonable when ill order that no one obey them while they are sick. Both take precautions against their own anger-driven or unreasonable commands in advance.

Seneca says it is best to prepare in advance for known weaknesses and to train the mind so that it can take sudden shocks without anger. If anger does rise after an unexpected wrong, the mind should hide it and not show the wound. He adds that examples will show this can be done.

King Cambyses drank heavily, and his friend Praexaspes warned him that drunkenness was shameful in a king. Cambyses replied by boasting that he could still see and act well after drinking, so he would prove he had not lost control.

A tyrant, after drinking heavily, forced the son of a man who had criticized him to stand still while he shot an arrow at the boy's heart. He then showed the father the arrow in the dead boy's chest and asked if his hand had been steady. The father replied that even Apollo could not have aimed better. Seneca calls the tyrant a slave in mind, whatever his rank.

Seneca is describing a king who praised an archer for shooting a man's son, when the father was forced to watch. Seneca says the king should instead have ordered another shot aimed at the father, to show the archer's skill was even greater. He calls the king savage and says the father was a fitting target for the king's followers' arrows.

Seneca is saying that cursing the king is one thing, but praising the king's cruel act is worse. He then points to a father who, though he had caused and witnessed his son's murder, did not curse the king or speak a single bitter word. Seneca presents this self-control as proof that anger can be held back.

This refers to a ruler who ignored a friend's good advice and suffered for it. Seneca says the friend would have been wiser to hold back, since he was not speaking as a father, and that the ruler, who was more interested in wine than in bloodshed, was a poor judge of how to be told what to do.

Seneca tells the story of Harpagus, a man whom the Persian king punished by serving him his own children at a meal. Harpagus showed no distress and calmly replied that every dinner was pleasant at the king's table. The story illustrates the anger of the king and the composure of the victim.

The passage describes a courtier who hid his anger at a king's cruel act and flattered him instead. Seneca argues that a person can conceal even strong anger and speak words that mean the opposite, and that this is necessary for anyone who dines at a king's table.
Seneca says that a person under a cruel master, however enslaved, can always escape by ending his own life, unless his mind is sick. If he suffers, the fault is his own, since death ends his misery.

Seneca tells a man suffering under a cruel king or master that he need not wait for rescue. Freedom is always within reach, since he can end his own life. The precipice, sea, river, well and tree are all named as ways to escape.

Seneca says that even a stunted, withered tree still bears the fruit of freedom, meaning death is always available as a way out of slavery. He points to the throat, neck, heart and any vein as ways to escape, saying no great strength is needed to reach liberty.

Seneca says that anger harms the person who is ruled by it, because its rage only adds to their own suffering. He compares this to an animal that tightens its own noose when it struggles, and to birds that cover themselves in birdlime while trying to free themselves.

Seneca says that a burden hurts more when a person fights against it than when they accept it, so it is better to bear hard things calmly. He adds that controlling anger helps subjects, and helps kings even more, since a ruler who acts on every angry impulse can ruin everything.

Power cannot last long if it harms many people, because shared fear unites those who were each suffering alone. Kings have therefore been overthrown, sometimes by one person and sometimes by whole peoples, whose shared outrage made a single man the means of their revenge.

Seneca cites King Darius of Persia as an example of rulers who indulged their anger as if it were a privilege of royalty. When Darius went to war, the aged noble Oeobazus asked that one of his three sons be left at home, and Darius's anger was the focus of the story.

Seneca uses two Persian kings as examples of cruelty. Darius, after promising a father to spare his three sons from war, killed them and threw their bodies before him. Xerxes was even crueler: when a father asked to keep one of his five sons, the king let him choose, then had that son cut in two and placed on either side of the road as the army marched between.

The passage describes a defeated commander whose army has been scattered in complete rout. He walks among the dead bodies of his soldiers and sees everywhere the signs of his own defeat. Seneca presents this as the end he deserved.

Seneca uses the example of Alexander the Great to show that learning does not stop a king's anger. Even though Alexander had been taught by Aristotle, he killed his close friend Clitus at the dinner table for not flattering him enough. He also shut his friend Lysimachus in a cage with a lion.

Seneca points out that Lysimachus, a king who had once narrowly escaped a lion, did not become gentler when he gained power. He mutilated his friend Telesphorus, cutting off his nose and ears, and kept him for a long time in a den, where he was starved and left in filth until he no longer looked human.

The passage describes a man confined in a space too narrow to stand in, so that his hands and knees became hardened and his sides sore from rubbing the walls. He became so changed that he was no longer pitied. The closing point is that the man who imposed this cruelty was even less human than the one who suffered it.

Seneca says that cruelty in anger and punishment should have stayed in foreign lands and not come into Roman ways. He gives the example of Marcus Marius, a man the people honored with statues and offerings, whom Sulla had brutally tortured and killed. He then asks who carried out Sulla's orders.

Seneca describes how Catiline killed Marius Gratidianus, a supporter of Marius, by tearing him apart at the tomb of Quintus Catulus. Seneca says Marius deserved punishment, but the cruel order came from Sulla and the cruel execution from Catiline.
Seneca points out that Gaius Caesar (the emperor Caligula) had senators and knights flogged and tortured on a single day. He did this not to hold any legal inquiry but only for his own entertainment.

Caligula, the Roman emperor, was so eager to act on his cruelty that he had some senators and ladies beheaded at night in his mother's garden, by lamplight. Seneca asks what he feared, since no danger threatened him that night, and points out that waiting until morning would have cost him little.

Seneca is describing how a cruel ruler treated senators. He had them beaten with rods so often that people came to treat it as normal. He also tortured them with cords, boots, the rack, fire, and even the sight of his own face.

The speaker argues that punishing three senators by whipping and burning them was not a great crime, since the emperor in question wished to kill the whole Senate and wished the Roman people had one neck so he could destroy them all in one blow. The point is that his cruelty was already far worse, so a night execution seems hardly unusual.

Robbers hide in the dark, but a public execution teaches more because everyone sees it. Seneca imagines a reply that a cruel ruler made this his daily habit, then notes that no one else gagged the condemned with a sponge so they could not even groan.

Seneca describes a ruler who had dying men gagged with torn-up clothing, so they could not speak their final words, since he feared what they might say against him. He condemns this cruelty and says a dying man should be allowed to breathe his last and let his soul leave freely, not be forced out through a wound.

Seneca says he will not dwell on the cruelty of Gaius (the emperor Caligula) in particular. His real subject is anger itself, which lashes out not only at people but at whole nations, cities, and even rivers and other things that cannot feel pain.

Seneca gives examples of cruel rulers. The Persian king cut off the noses of a whole nation in Syria, which is why the place was named Rhinocolura (a name meaning "nose-cut"). Seneca says this was not mercy, since the king was simply pleased to have invented a new punishment.

Cambyses, a Persian king, was enraged when certain people did not submit to him gladly and sent a blunt reply. In his anger he marched his army into a barren desert without supplies or knowledge of the route.

Seneca describes an army starving in the desert under a king driven by rage. The soldiers first eat leaves, then scorched hides, and finally draw lots to kill and eat every tenth man. Only when the king fears he himself might be chosen does he order a retreat.

Seneca describes a ruler who spares his fine hawks and carries his feasting supplies on camels, while his soldiers draw lots to decide who will die and who will live on in misery. The point is that he cares for his luxuries while his men suffer, and the contrast shows how anger and cruelty can lead to such indifference.

Seneca tells how Cyrus, the Persian king, was angry at the river Gyndes. While rushing to attack Babylon, he tried to cross the river, which is dangerous to ford even when it is at its lowest in summer.

A king was so angry when a river swept away one of his white horses that he vowed to make the river so shallow that even women could walk across it. He had his army dig 180 channels, splitting the river into 360 small streams and leaving its bed dry.

Seneca gives two examples of anger's folly. A king wasted time and his soldiers' strength by making war on a river that had hurt him, so his army was not ready for the real enemy. Caligula, a Roman emperor, destroyed a fine villa because his mother had once been held there, which only made the place known for bad luck.
Seneca gives Antigonus, a king, as an example to follow. Two common soldiers spoke badly of him while leaning against his tent, and he could easily have had them executed, but he did not.

Antigonus, a king, once overheard soldiers cursing him, and he kindly lifted the cloth between them to tell them to move away so he would not be heard. Another night, he pulled stranded soldiers out of the mud without revealing who he was, and told them to curse Antigonus but bless the one who saved them.

Antigonus, besieging a small fort, was mocked by the people inside for being short and having a broken nose. He took the insults calmly and said he was glad, because he had a Silenus (a figure from Greek myth, a snub-nosed, short companion of Dionysus) in his camp, which he took as a sign of good luck.

Seneca is describing a conqueror who starved a group of clever, sharp-tongued people into surrender. He then enlisted the fit ones as soldiers and sold the rest as slaves at auction, saying that people with such dangerous speech were better off under a master.

Seneca says that Alexander, grandson of Philip, had a cruel habit of hurling his lance at guests and of letting people be killed for his anger. He did not inherit this from his grandfather or father. Philip, by contrast, was known for patiently enduring insults, which protected his kingdom.

Athens sent envoys to King Philip, who asked what would please the Athenians. Demochares replied rudely, telling him to hang himself. Philip did not punish him. He said the man who insulted him was more arrogant than the king who let the insult pass unanswered.

Augustus, the Roman emperor, did not let anger rule him. When the historian Timagenes mocked him and his family, Augustus only warned him and then banned him from his house. Other homes stayed open to Timagenes, and he was welcomed across the city.

The passage describes a historian who read aloud his later history but burned his books about Augustus, the Roman emperor, with whom he was at odds. Even so, people were not afraid to befriend him, and when he fell from high favour, someone was still there to catch him.

Caesar tolerated a historian, Cremutius Cordus, who had written critically of him, and did not punish him. When Asinius Pollio offered to banish the man from his house, Caesar refused, saying he had just made the two friends again and would not undo it.

When someone angers you, Seneca suggests reminding yourself of powerful rulers who tolerated insults: Philip let a man curse him, and Augustus left a critic's company without punishment. Why, then, should a person beat a slave for a rude answer, a sullen look, or a mutter? The main point is that anger over small slights is unjustified, since even the mighty showed restraint.

Seneca says that we should excuse people's faults in the way we already excuse others. Children are excused for their age, women for their sex, strangers for being unfamiliar with our ways, and household servants for their habits. If a wrong is first offence, or a long-standing habit, we should keep putting up with it, and a friend should be taken to have meant no harm.

The main point is that we should excuse a foolish person, because even the wisest people make mistakes. Nobody is so careful or so sensible that they never slip, and even someone who tries hard not to offend will sometimes do so anyway.

Seneca says that a person hurt or insulted can bear it more calmly by remembering that even the most powerful can be harmed. Like a poor man who grieves more easily when he sees a rich family's funeral, the thought that everyone is exposed to misfortune makes injury easier to take. He adds that if even the wisest people do wrong, others should not be surprised by faults.

Seneca advises looking back at our own youth, when we were often lazy, rude, and drunk. If someone is angry, we should give him time to think about what he did, and he will correct himself. Even if he deserves punishment, that does not give us a reason to act as he does.

A person who looks down on the one who hurts them stands above the hurt. True greatness of mind does not feel the blows it receives. Like a cliff that waves break against without moving, the man who is not angry stays unshaken, while the angry man has already been moved by the injury.

The man described here is so secure that no harm can reach his inner calm. He tells fortune, meaning bad luck, that she cannot disturb him, because reason, which guides his life, forbids him to be angry. For him, getting angry would do more damage than any outside violence.

Seneca argues that people who cannot bear injury are wrong, since bearing injury is the same as bearing anger. He compares an insult from a grown person to the actions of a sick man, a madman or a child, who do not really know what they are doing and so are not fully responsible for it.

Wrongdoers suffer most from knowing they did wrong, since remorse is the heaviest punishment. We should also judge a person's faults against the common faults of all people, because it is unfair to blame someone for something everyone shares. Seneca gives examples: dark skin is ordinary among Ethiopians, and red hair is ordinary in Germany.

Seneca argues that a fault shared by a whole nation cannot be counted as shameful in one person, and that faults common to all of humanity are even more forgivable. He concludes that everyone is hasty, untrustworthy, discontented and ambitious, so each person has the faults he criticises in others.

Everyone is flawed, so people should forgive one another, since that is the only way to have peace. Someone who feels wronged should remember that they have probably wronged others too, or will, and should judge a person by their whole character rather than one moment.

Seneca argues that it is better to heal an injury than to take revenge for it, since revenge takes time and tends to bring new harms. He asks whether a sensible person would kick back at a mule or bite a dog, and notes that those animals do not know they are doing wrong.

Seneca argues that anger is unfair when it is aimed at people. Animals are excused from blame because they lack reason, so a foolish person, who also lacks wisdom, should be excused in the same way. He asks whether a wrong is a first offence or a repeated one, implying that this matters little to the case.

Seneca says that a person who is angry should not be trusted to stop, even if he promises to. Anger keeps returning, so the best response is gentleness. He suggests asking the angry man whether he will ever stop, and pointing out that it is better to give up anger himself than to have anger give him up.

Seneca argues that living in constant anger makes life restless and miserable. He adds that anger fades on its own over time, so it is better for a person to master it than to wait until it wears itself out.
Seneca warns that anger keeps finding new targets: slaves, freedmen, family, friends, strangers. Unless reason steps in to restrain it, anger never stops, and so it leaves no time for love.

Seneca says it would be far better to make friends, calm enemies, serve the state, or attend to one's own affairs. Instead, people look for ways to harm others in their standing, wealth, or body, even though this costs them effort and risk, even against a weaker opponent.

Even if an enemy were bound and fully at your mercy, anger would still harm you. In the heat of striking, a person can dislocate a joint or tear a sinew, and anger often leaves the angry person crippled. Even the weakest victim can sometimes harm his attacker, since grief or chance can make the weak equal to the strong.

Seneca says that many things that make us angry are only insults, not real injuries, and that the difference is large. Yet we treat all these cases alike: being robbed or merely denied a gift, having hope cut off or only delayed, and whether the other person meant harm or acted for some other reason.

Some people must oppose us out of duty to their father, brother, country or friend, and we often blame them anyway, even when we admire what they did. A great and just man, though, respects the bravest enemy who defends his freedom and wishes such a man were on his own side.

Seneca argues that people often get angry at others, including slaves, when they should first ask whether the person truly can't do something or simply won't. He says we should forgive many slaves if we judged them calmly before getting angry. Instead, we act on first impulse and then keep our anger going so we don't look unjustified.
Anger is unjust, and the fact that it is unjust makes us hold on to it even more. We feed it and stir it up, as if how fiercely we feel it proved that we were right to feel it.

Seneca says it is worth watching how small and harmless anger's first beginnings are. He notes that people are upset by trivial things, just as animals are: bulls react to red colour, and bears and lions to a shaken rag. Anger rises from such trifles in both restless and sluggish people.

People who feel slighted often think small favours are injuries, and they get angry with close friends for giving them less than they expected or less than others got. Seneca's remedy is to enjoy what one has and stop comparing, since a person who is pained to see others doing better can never feel well off.

Seneca says that anger often comes from hoping for more than we deserve or than we are given. Julius Caesar was killed not by his enemies but by friends whose greedy hopes he had not met, even though he was generous and kept little of his victories for himself.

Seneca is describing Julius Caesar's assassination. Caesar's followers were so greedy for power and rewards that no one could satisfy them, so even former supporters, such as Tillius Cimber, turned on him with drawn swords. Kings' most trusted followers, he says, can likewise come to plot the death of the man they once served gladly.

People are unhappy with what they have when they compare themselves to someone who has more. This makes them angry even at the gods, since they forget how many people are behind them. Even after receiving much, they feel wronged if they do not get still more, as with a man who wanted the consulship after receiving the praetorship.

The speaker lists the honours he received from a ruler and points out what was missing each time. He got the twelve axes of office, a name for the year, and a priesthood seat, but never the full consulship, the priesthood itself, or private wealth. He stresses that the ruler gave only what the state already offered to someone, and gave nothing from his own resources.

Seneca advises that when you are given less than you hoped, you should still be grateful and keep hoping for more. If others are favoured over you, remember how many are below you. His main charge is that you value what you give too highly and what you receive too little, which he calls keeping your accounts wrongly.

Seneca says we should hold back from anger. Some people we should fear to be angry with, others we should be ashamed to be angry with, and others we should scorn to be angry with. He mocks the habit of punishing a slave at once, saying that we lose none of our power by waiting before we act.

Seneca says we should wait until anger has passed before giving orders, since angry people speak under its pressure. Once calm, we will see the harm done. He warns that angry people often punish too harshly, using death, chains or starvation for faults that deserve only a light whipping.

Seneca urges the reader to take on a high, noble mind and then look at the things that seem to wrong us. Seen from that height, these everyday quarrels appear small and base, not worth a second thought.

Seneca says that money causes more conflict than anything else. It fills the courts with lawsuits, turns fathers and sons against each other, drives poisoning and murder, and leads kings to plunder and destroy cities. He ends by asking whether a person enjoys looking at their stacked money-bags.

Seneca is describing how people shout and fight in court over money, with jurors coming from far away to judge whose greed is fairer. He then asks what should be said when an old man, about to die with no heir, rages over only a few coins or a small debt owed by a slave.

Seneca asks whether a wise man should be troubled by a sick, greedy moneylender who demands his interest even in the middle of his pain. He says that even a huge pile of money, including all the gold and silver buried in hoards, would not be worth a frown from a good man.

Seneca lists everyday things that can provoke anger: food, drink, showy display, insults, rude gestures, suspicion, stubborn animals, lazy slaves, and reading malice into other people's words. He even says that the human gift of speech gets counted as one of nature's wrongs.

Seneca says that the things that make us angry are trifles, like the quarrels of children. Anger and madness come from placing great value on such small things, such as an inheritance, a legal charge, or a lover being taken.

Two people who want the same thing can end up fighting, even though shared wishes could have bound them together. The reason is that the things they want are small and limited: one person cannot have them without someone else losing them. Large, plentiful goods, by contrast, let many people share without colliding.

Seneca says that a man who is angry when his slaves, freedmen, wife or clients talk back, or who calls their silence stubbornness, is destroying freedom at home. He should let them speak, stay silent, or laugh, and not shout or rage at them.

Seneca criticises a master who orders a slave whipped during dinner just because the servants are talking or making noise. He argues that a person with ears must expect ordinary noise, such as laughter, arguments, and the sounds of animals, and cannot avoid harsh sounds like thunder.
The eyes can be as easily upset as the ears, if they have not been trained well. They are bothered by stains, dirt, dull silver, and pools that are not clear to the bottom.

Seneca says that a person who is very fussy about fine things at home can still calmly accept ugliness outside. Outdoors, the same eyes tolerate muddy roads, shabby people and cracked, crumbling walls without being bothered.

Seneca asks why people are not upset by things outside the home that would shock them at home. He suggests the answer is their mood: they are calm and patient when away from home, but irritable and quick to find fault at home.

The main point is that a person should examine their own mind every day, as Sextius did at nightfall, asking which bad habit they cured and which fault they checked. Seneca says that anger will soften if it knows it must face this daily judgment.

Looking back over the whole day and judging one's own conduct is praised here as admirable. The author says the sleep that follows such self-examination is sweet and calm, especially after the mind has been praised or rebuked by its own inner judge.

Each night, when the lamp is put out and his wife has stopped talking, the speaker goes over his whole day in his mind. He admits nothing to himself and leaves nothing out. He then forgives his faults on the condition that he does not repeat them.

Seneca advises a friend to be careful when correcting others. Do not argue with people who will not learn, since you spoke too harshly and offended the man instead of improving him. Before speaking a hard truth, consider whether the listener can bear to hear it.

Seneca warns against dinner companions who mock you, since people become more shameless when drinking. He points out that we often get angry at trivial people, such as a doorkeeper or a slave, and asks whether anyone would be angry with a chained dog.

Seneca advises that when an angry person barks at you, you should step back and smile, since a porter who guards a busy door only feels important for the moment. The man inside thinks a hard-to-enter door shows his power, but the hardest door to open is that of a prison. So one should expect to put up with a great deal.

The main point is that a strong mind can accept discomforts it expects, such as cold, seasickness or crowding. Anger over seating at a dinner is pointless, since a place on a couch cannot really give or take away honour.

Seneca asks whether you would apply to yourself the rule of getting angry at anyone who criticises your abilities. He points out that if you did, famous poets and orators such as Ennius, Hortensius and Cicero would each have been your enemy for disliking or mocking their work, and a candidate who resents voters who reject him would be doing the same.

Seneca gives two examples of people who stayed calm when insulted. The philosopher Diogenes was spat on during a lecture about anger, and he replied that he was not angry, though he was not sure he ought not to be. Cato was spat on by Lentulus during a court speech, and he wiped his face and answered with a joke about Lentulus's lack of shame.
Having learned to keep our own minds free of anger, Seneca now turns to how we can calm other people's anger. He wants not only to stay well himself but also to help others get well.

Seneca says that you cannot calm the first rush of anger by arguing with it, because in that state it will not listen. Like a swollen eye or a disease at its peak, it must be left alone until it eases. Then reasoning can work, ending anger sooner and preventing it from returning.

The passage describes how a wise friend deals with an angry person. He cannot calm the rage directly, so he removes weapons, pretends to share the anger so his advice is heard, and stalls for time. The aim is to give the angry man a pause from his frenzy.

Seneca says that anger can be calmed in two ways. A strong anger can be checked by fear or shame, while a weak one can be dropped by distracting the person with amusing or new topics. He illustrates this with a doctor who hid his lancet under a sponge so the princess would not shrink from the cut, and concludes that some illnesses need trickery to cure.

Seneca describes how to talk to two kinds of angry people. To the first kind, he says to avoid letting anger please their enemies. To the second, he says to avoid damaging their reputation for strength, and then promises that the wrongdoer will be repaid at the right time.

Scolding an angry person only makes his anger worse, because you become angry too. Better to approach him gently and agreeably, unless you are so powerful that your word alone can calm him, as Emperor Augustus once did at a dinner.

Vedius, a wealthy man, ordered a slave to be thrown to his giant eels as punishment for breaking a crystal goblet. Others might assume this was mere showiness, but the passage says it came from cruelty. The slave begged Caesar only to be killed some other way, so he would not be eaten.

Caesar was appalled that a host had ordered a slave thrown to fish in a tank because a cup had broken. Caesar had the slave freed and the crystal smashed and the tank filled in instead. Seneca praises this as the right way to rebuke a friend. He then asks whether a man's life should be torn apart just because a dish was broken.

If a person is powerful enough to deal with anger from a position of authority, he may crush it, but only the fierce, cruel kind that yields to nothing except a stronger force. For everyone else, Seneca suggests calming the mind through steady reflection on sound principles, good deeds, and a focus on honour alone.

Seneca says a person should keep a clear conscience and not chase praise, accepting criticism if they have acted well. Crowds often admire bold deeds and think calm people are lazy, but over time a steady life shows that calmness comes from inner peace, and people then come to respect it.
Anger, the passage says, brings no benefit at all, only harm of every kind. It destroys self-control, drives people to murder and crime, and once it hardens into hatred, it cannot be reversed.
Seneca says we should remove anger completely rather than just control it. He argues that moderating a bad habit makes no sense, and that anger returns if even a small part of it is left behind.

The main point is that remembering we will die is the best way to stop anger. Since our life is short, we should not waste its days on angry feelings or on hurting others, and we should not look for quarrels.

Seneca asks why people wage bitter feuds against others when they are weak and will soon die. Illness or death will end these fights, and fate is steadily approaching. He suggests that our short lives are being wasted on hatred and conflict.

Seneca asks why people spend their short lives fighting and seeking revenge, when they could instead live peacefully and be loved while alive and missed when dead. He points out that anger is pointless in every case, whether the angry person is a master or a slave.

Death will level everyone, so quarrels between a client and his patron are pointless. Seneca compares such fights to a bull and a bear tied together in the arena: the winner is killed too. People hurt those close to them even though both sides are soon to die.

Seneca says that we should spend the short time we have left in peace, not in quarrels, so that no one hates us after we die. He notes that fear of a larger danger, such as a fire or a wild beast, makes people stop their small fights. Since death will come to everyone anyway, there is no need to add to it through anger.

Seneca argues that a person who wants to harm an enemy with lesser punishments, such as exile, public shame or loss of property, is not better than one who wants to kill. Such a person is petty, and the pleasure of seeing the enemy suffer lasts only a short time.

Life is short, so while we are alive we should treat other people kindly and not frighten or harm them. We should keep our temper when we suffer losses, wrongs, insults or mockery, and bear our brief troubles calmly. Otherwise, we spend our time worrying about our own rights until death comes.

Seneca says he would not have dared to console Marcia in her grief, a grief many men also cling to, if he did not know she has a strong mind and a virtuous life. He is confident because her strength has already been tested by a hard loss.

Seneca tells Marcia that everyone knows how devoted she was to her father, Aulus Cremutius Cordus, and that she loved him deeply, perhaps even wishing he would outlive her. She tried hard to prevent his death. When it was clear he could not escape the agents of Sejanus, a powerful official, except by slavery, she accepted his decision to die, though she did not approve of it.

Marcia is praised for grieving openly for her father, the historian Cordus, and for not hiding her tears. She also rescued his books, which had been burned, and published them again, so that his work survives and he is remembered.

Seneca is praising Cremutius Cordus, a Roman historian who was put to death under Sejanus, the powerful official of Emperor Tiberius. He says the historian did two things: he left an honest record for future readers, and he kept his fame alive. He also remained free in thought, feeling, and action while others submitted to Sejanus.

Seneca praises Cremutius Cordus, a historian whose book was once banned and destroyed. He says Cordus's work is now read and loved again, while the men who had him killed are remembered only for their crime. Seneca adds that Marcia's strength of mind has led him to set aside her sex and her grief.

Seneca tells Marcia he will not use gentle comfort or hide her sorrow. He will argue against her grief directly, and he says her tears now come more from habit than from real sorrow. He asks her to accept the cure, or else keep clinging to her grief over her dead son.

Seneca is asking how the grief of Marcia can ever end. Everything that usually helps has failed: friends who have grown tired of comforting her, powerful relatives, books she once loved, and even time, which normally eases sorrow. Only in her case does none of it work.

Seneca tells Marcia that her grief has lasted three years without weakening, and has settled into her mind as if it belonged there. He says that, like any vice, such feelings grow stronger the longer they are left alone, until the mind takes a kind of unhealthy pleasure in sorrow.

Seneca says he would have liked to treat this grief early, when it was still mild and could be eased with gentle remedies. Now that it has lasted a long time, it is like an old wound or ulcer, and only strong, forceful measures will work.

Seneca says that advice usually starts with general rules and ends with examples, but he will change this order. Some people respond better to famous names than to reasoning, so he will show Marcia two great examples from her own sex and time. The first is a woman who gave herself completely over to grief.

Seneca is pointing to a woman who, though she suffered a similar or greater loss, did not let grief rule her for long and soon returned her mind to its usual state. He gives Octavia and Livia as examples: both lost sons who were young men about to become emperor.

Octavia lost her son Marcellus, a young man whom Augustus and his own uncle had begun to rely on to carry the empire's burden. Seneca praises his strength, self-control and ability to endure heavy work, and says Augustus rightly chose him as a foundation that would bear any weight.

Seneca describes a mother who, after her son's death, kept mourning for the rest of her life. She refused comfort and good advice, would not let her grief be distracted, believed that giving up her tears would be a second loss, and did not want his portrait or any mention of him.

Octavia, sister of Augustus, grieved for her son Marcellus, who had died young. She resented Livia, whose son was now set to receive the honours and prospects Marcellus had been expected to have. She shut herself away, refused comfort and tributes to him, and neglected her usual duties.

Even with her children and grandchildren around her, the woman would not take off her mourning clothes. Keeping them on seemed to dismiss her living relatives, as if she counted herself bereaved even though they were alive.

Livia's son Drusus died while on campaign in Germany. Seneca says he had already done great deeds as a general, and that even his enemies respected him so much that they kept a truce and would not wish for his survival in a way that would help them.

The passage describes the public mourning for a man who died while serving his country. Citizens, provinces and towns across Italy came out to honor his body as it was carried to Rome, in a procession like a triumph.

Drusus, a young man, died far from home, and his mother could not be with him at his death. She followed his body on the long journey back, and her grief was renewed at every funeral pyre along the way. When she finally buried him, she set her grief aside and mourned only as much as was fitting for her rank and her son.

Seneca describes Livia, who kept her dead son Drusus constantly in mind, speaking of him and displaying his portrait, and says that anyone who makes memory of the dead painful to themselves cannot live with that memory at all. He then tells Marcia to choose between this example and another, warning that following Livia's way would cut her off from the living.

Seneca warns Marcia that if she goes on grieving, she will avoid other children and even her own, refuse ordinary pleasures, and resent living on. He says he is charitably assuming she will not really act this way, since it would be unworthy of her character.

Seneca is telling Marcia that grieving without limit shows she does not want to live, yet she is also unable to die. He urges her to follow the calmer example of a lady he praises, so she will neither be miserable nor wear out her life. He calls it madness to punish oneself for misfortune and so make one's troubles worse.

Seneca tells Marcia that she should show restraint in her grief, as she has in the rest of her life. He says the best way to honour her dead son is to think of him with gladness, and to speak of him cheerfully, as he was when alive.

Seneca says he will not ask Marcia to follow harsh maxims or bear her loss with superhuman calm, and he will not try to stop her tears on the day of her son's burial. Instead, he frames the question as a dispute to be judged: whether grief should be deep or endless.

Seneca points to Julia Augusta as a model for grieving. In her first and sharpest grief, she turned to Areus, the philosopher who had taught her husband, and said his comfort helped her more than the thought of the Roman people, whom she did not want to upset with her mourning.

Seneca is saying that Marcia's grief should not be greater than that of others who lost important people. He points to the emperor Augustus, who had lost one of his two main supporters, and to Marcia's own son Tiberius, who buried a man mourned by whole nations.

Seneca is speaking to Julia, a woman who has kept her own opinions firmly. He says that as far as he can tell, she has always been careful that no one could find fault with her conduct, and he claims close knowledge of her husband's life and her private thoughts.

Seneca praises Marcia for conducting herself so that nothing she does, even in small matters, would need to be hidden or regretted, since public opinion watches rulers closely. He adds that she should follow the same rule in her mourning, doing nothing she would later wish undone or done differently.

Seneca asks Marcia not to be stubborn and to let her friends guide her. He says her friends do not know whether to mention her dead son Drusus in her presence. They do not want to forget him, and they do not want to hurt her by speaking of him.

Seneca tells the grieving mother that her son's friends speak of him openly and with respect when she is not present, but fall silent when she is. He urges her to allow talk about her son and to welcome hearing his name and memory.

Seneca tells Marcia that she should not treat consolation as a source of pain, which some grieving people do. He says she has fixed only on the worst part of her loss, her son's death, and forgotten the happy years she had with him.

Seneca tells Marcia not to take pride in looking like the most miserable of women. He says bravery is easy in good times, just as a pilot is only tested in storms. He urges her to stay firm under whatever hardship comes, because giving up would be the way to let Fortune win.

Seneca tells Marcia that her grief is the same kind of grief that Areus, a philosopher, once comforted in someone else. He then says that even if her loss were greater than any mother has suffered, mourning would still do no good. He asks whether tears could overcome fate. He concludes that they cannot.

If the dead cannot be brought back, and fate cannot be changed by grief, then endless mourning is pointless. We should stop grieving and steer our own course rather than be blown off it by our misfortune.

A bad pilot lets the storm take the rudder, the sails and the ship. A brave pilot holds the helm to the end, and deserves praise even if the ship sinks. The point is that how one meets disaster matters, even when it cannot be avoided.

Grief for a dead child is natural, and Seneca does not deny it, as long as it stays reasonable. Even the strongest people feel a pang when loved ones leave, even on a journey. But the mourning that society expects goes beyond what nature requires.

Animals grieve intensely but briefly. A cow lows for a day or two, mares stop their wild gallops quickly, and beasts and birds soon stop mourning their lost young or empty nests and return to their normal lives.

Only humans keep grieving the loss of their children for long, and the depth of that grief depends on the person's own choice rather than on the suffering itself. Seneca argues that excessive grief is not natural, because it varies with sex, culture and learning, while natural feelings are equally strong in everyone.

Natural forces like fire and steel affect everyone alike, because nature does not favor anyone. Poverty, grief and ambition hit people differently, depending on their habits. Fear of these things, which are not really to be feared, is what makes a person weak and unable to bear them.

Natural feelings are not hurt by waiting, but grief fades as time passes. Even stubborn grief that returns daily gets weaker over time. Marcia's grief is still strong but already less sharp, and the years will gradually take it away.

Seneca tells Marcia that her mind will feel lighter once she turns to other activities, and that she is now holding onto her grief by watching herself. He argues that it is much better to choose to end her mourning than to wait until the sorrow fades on its own against her will.

People keep grieving for their friends, Seneca says, because they never expect misfortune to reach them. They see other people's deaths but assume their own path is safe. So they think only of ordinary hopes for their children, not of death.

Seneca says that people are shocked when rich men suddenly lose everything, yet rarely think their own wealth could be lost the same way. Misfortune hits hardest when it comes unexpected, so we should see that any of us can be struck by fate at any time.

Seneca asks the reader to imagine going into battle without armour, expecting to be hit, and to treat every blow that lands near him as aimed at himself. He then notes that people rarely think of their own lives as always at risk, or of exile, poverty, or grief as things they might face.

Seneca says that people who are told to think about misfortune reject the idea as bad luck. He argues that nothing should be thought impossible, since such things have happened to many people. He adds that a line from a stage play, "What one hath suffered may befall us all," is a truth worthy of a better source.

Seneca says that we are fooled and weakened when misfortune strikes us unexpectedly, because we never imagined it could happen. If we picture our possible sorrows in advance, they lose much of their force when they really arrive.

Seneca says that the things that seem to make life fine, such as children, public office, wealth, a noble name, and a good marriage, are not really ours. They are like borrowed furniture, given for a time and bound to be taken back, some sooner and some later.

Our possessions are not really ours but loaned to us, for a time set by the lender. We should be ready to give them back whenever they are asked for, without complaint, since complaining about the return is like a debtor abusing his creditor.

Seneca says we should love our relatives and the things of this life knowing we cannot keep them forever, or even for long. We should treat them as things that may leave us at any moment. Any gift from Fortune, which is the goddess of chance, should be enjoyed with the understanding that it can be taken away as easily as it was given.

Enjoy your children and your company now, and do not put off pleasure, because you cannot count on today or tonight. Death is coming like an enemy that will break up every gathering, and life is only a brief flight from it.
Death was fixed for the son from the moment of his birth, so grief over it is misplaced. Human life is ruled by Fortune, a harsh power that brings suffering on people whether or not they deserve it.

Seneca describes Fortune as cruel and unpredictable toward people's bodies. She burns some, imprisons others, drowns or buries them at sea, and wastes others away with disease. Her rewards and punishments are as arbitrary as those of a careless master toward his slaves.

Seneca argues that there is no reason to weep over single parts of life, since the whole of life brings trouble. New miseries arrive before the old ones are over. He says the reader should hold back from excessive grief and use all their inner strength against fear and pain, and that forgetting one's own situation and that of all humans is a mistake.

Seneca tells Marcia that her son's death is simply the end every mortal reaches. Mortals are weak and fragile, so children born of them cannot be strong or lasting. Everyone, including those thought luckier, is moving toward the same end, just at different speeds.

Everyone, loved or despised, ends up equal in death as ashes. Seneca says the command "Know thyself," carved at the Pythian oracle at Delphi, means recognizing how weak humans are. A person is like a clay pot that breaks easily, with a fragile body, no natural defenses, and dependence on others.

Seneca describes the human body as weak and easily harmed. A person can be attacked by any wild animal, cannot stand cold, heat or hard work, and suffers if idle, starved without food, or harmed by too much. Life is held only briefly, and every sudden noise or danger startles him.

Seneca says that humans are fragile and constantly under threat, so it should not be surprising that they die. A single hiccup can kill a person, and even ordinary things like smells, tastes, tiredness, lack of sleep, food and drink can cause death.

Seneca describes how a human being, wherever he goes, soon finds his own weakness: he cannot tolerate every climate, falls ill from unfamiliar water or air, and is fragile from birth. Yet this frail creature still stirs great fuss and holds grand ideas, forgetting how humble his condition really is.

The passage describes a person whose mind is busy with things that last forever and with plans for distant descendants. Death then comes while these long plans are still unfinished. It adds that what we call old age is only a few years at the end of life.

Seneca asks a grieving mother why she mourns her son. If she says he gave her no pleasure, her loss is easier to bear, since people miss little what never brought them joy. If he did give her joy, she should give thanks for that joy rather than complain about the part she has lost.

The speaker argues that raising a child is rewarding in itself, even if the child gives nothing back. People enjoy raising pet animals for the pleasure of their company, so a parent should likewise count the pleasure of having and loving a son as enough reward, whatever he achieves or provides.

Seneca answers a mourner who says the son's life should have lasted longer. He argues that a short time with a good son is better than never having him, and that a son of noble character is better than a disgraceful one who only bears the name.

Seneca says that the young man quickly became discreet, dutiful, a husband, a father, eager for public honours, and a priest. Great prosperity seldom lasts long, and the gods, not intending to keep the son long, gave him a life that others would take far longer to reach.

Seneca tells Marcia that her grief is not a sign that the gods have singled her out for misfortune. Many people, including famous generals and princes, have suffered similar losses. Even myths say the gods lose children too, which is meant to ease grief over death.

Seneca says that finding others who are worse off is a spiteful kind of comfort, and he does not think Marcia would be comforted by a crowd of mourners. He will instead give examples of people who bore their misfortunes calmly, to show that such endurance has been done before.

Seneca says that Sulla, despite losing his son, remained as cruel and proud as ever. Sulla's grief did not stop him from keeping the title "The Fortunate," which he took after his son died, even though his prosperity came at the cost of other people's suffering.

Whether Sulla was really a good man is still open to debate. Even his enemies admit he took up and laid down arms honourably. So, Seneca argues, a misfortune that strikes even a very fortunate man cannot be among the greatest evils.

Seneca says that a Greek father is not the only example of calm grief. A Roman, Pulvillus the high priest, did the same: when told his son had died while he was dedicating the Capitol, he finished the ceremony properly.

The speaker is describing a father who, on hearing that his son had died, pretended not to hear. He went on reciting the prayer a high priest would say on such an occasion, without a single groan, asking Jupiter for favour at that very moment.

Seneca is describing a man who grieved for his son but still did his public religious duties. Even after the first shock, his grief did not stop him from attending the state altar or from speaking words of ill omen during a dedication ceremony. Seneca says such a man deserved high priestly office because he kept honoring the gods even when they seemed angry.
A man went home, wept, spoke a few words of mourning, and carried out the customary funeral rites. Then he put back the calm expression he had worn in public at the Capitol.

Paulus, after his great triumph over Perses, gave two sons away for adoption and buried two others who had been kept at home. Seneca uses this to ask what those kept at home must have been like, since Scipio, one of those given away, was so remarkable.

Seneca describes Lucius Aemilius Paulus, a Roman general, after he lost his two sons within a few days of each other. Paulus gave thanks to the gods, saying he had prayed that any punishment for his great victory would fall on him rather than on Rome. He even counted it a blessing to be left without children.

Seneca says it would be easier to list the unhappy great men than the happy ones, because few families have kept all their members to the end, and nearly everyone has suffered some loss. As an example, he points to the consuls of one year, Bibulus and Caesar: rivals and bitter enemies, yet their misfortunes were the same.
Lucius Bibulus lost both his sons, who were killed together. Their killers also insulted them, so the manner of their deaths caused as much grief as the deaths themselves.

Bibulus, a Roman consul, stayed indoors for a whole year after his office was overshadowed by his colleague Caesar. When both his sons died, he came out the next day to do his official duties. Seneca's point is that he grieved for one day over two sons but for a whole year over his lost consulship.

Seneca uses the example of Julius Caesar. When news came that his daughter had died, he was already facing a rival, Pompey, who was likely to block his rise to power. Caesar returned to his duties as general within three days and overcame his grief as quickly as he overcame everything else.

Seneca says that some Roman emperors (Caesars) met violent or cruel deaths, and that fortune allowed this so their fate would show others something. Even men called sons of gods could not control their own fortunes as they controlled the lives of others.

Augustus outlived his children and grandchildren and had to adopt an heir to keep his household going. Even so, he bore these losses calmly, as if he were himself one of the gods and it were his duty to make sure no one blamed Heaven for being unfair.

Tiberius lost both his natural son and his adopted son. He still gave a public speech praising his dead son and stood in view of the body without changing his expression, while the Romans wept. Seneca uses this to show how well Tiberius could bear the loss of family. Word count: about 50.

Seneca says that even the most admirable and distinguished people have not escaped this misfortune, which strikes everyone alike regardless of rank or merit. Every person, he says, has suffered some hardship simply for being born.

Seneca anticipates an objection: that he is offering examples from men to a woman. He replies that women have the same intellectual power and capacity for honourable action as men, and can endure sorrow and hardship when trained to. He points to Lucretia and Brutus, Roman heroes, as proof.

Seneca says Roman liberty came from Brutus, and Brutus owed his deed to Lucretia, a woman who killed herself after being wronged. He praises Cloelia, a woman who escaped Porsenna's camp by swimming the Tiber, and says her horse statue in Rome shames young men who ride only in comfortable carriages.

Seneca gives the example of Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, who lost twelve children, most of them early and privately, and then saw her two sons Tiberius and Gaius killed and left unburied. Even people who do not call the Gracchi good admit they were great men.

Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, was consoled after her son Drusus was murdered before his laws passed. She refused to see herself as unfortunate, saying she would always count herself happy to be the mother of the Gracchi. She bore her son's death as calmly and proudly as he had carried out his public work.

Seneca tells Marcia that misfortune is part of ordinary life and that no one escapes it for long. He compares her losses to a volley of arrows: in a crowded group of soldiers, some arrow is bound to hit someone. Her children's deaths, he suggests, should not surprise her, since she has had four children and Fortune strikes everyone.

Marcia is said to think Fortune has been unfair, since she lost her son and also her favourite child. Seneca replies that she still has two daughters and their children, and that she should look to them rather than dwell on her grief for the son.

Seneca compares a farmer whose trees are destroyed by storms to a grieving mother. Just as the farmer replaces the lost trees with new plantings that soon grow, Marcia should take her two grandchildren in place of her lost son Metilius and let their comfort ease her single grief.

Human nature tends to value what has been lost and to undervalue what remains. Seneca says Marcia should count the blessings she still has, such as her grandchildren and two daughters. He also suggests she accept that fortune strikes good and bad people alike.

Seneca admits that losing a young son is painful, but he says such loss is part of ordinary human life. He lists other things that mortals must endure, such as losing others, fearing, hoping, and not knowing their true situation.

Seneca compares life to a sea voyage. He says that a traveller to Syracuse who was told every discomfort and pleasure in advance would gain little from the trip itself. The passage is the start of that comparison, describing what the traveller would be told about the island.
Seneca describes the whirlpool Charybdis, a famous danger from old Greek poetry. It looks calm when no south wind blows, but when a gale comes from the south it pulls ships down into the deep.

Seneca describes sights the reader will see during a journey: the spring of Arethusa in Sicily, whose water is clear to the bottom and flows cold, and a harbour sheltered more than any other, whether made by nature or by human building.

This part of the letter describes Syracuse, a Sicilian city. It mentions its ruined Athenian prison, its mild winters, and its hot, unhealthy summers. It ends by naming the tyrant Dionysius, who ruled there, as a man who kept seeking power and life even after he had met Plato and been exiled.

Seneca compares life to a voyage to Syracuse, a city ruled by a cruel tyrant. Nature has told everyone the dangers in advance, so anyone who goes there cannot blame anyone but himself for what happens. Nature, he says, deceives no one.

Having children is uncertain: they may be handsome or deformed, and they may turn out to be either a country's saviour or its betrayer. They may bring you great honour, or they may disgrace you so badly that they become a source of misery to you.

Seneca tells Marcia to expect that any child she has may die at any age, from boyhood to old age, and that every such death is untimely. If she still chooses to have children knowing this, she cannot blame the gods, because they never promised her that her children would live.

Seneca compares a person's birth to arriving in a city. He imagines advising someone just before they are born, describing the world as a city ruled by eternal laws. It is filled with stars and the sun, which mark day, night, and the seasons.

Seneca describes the heavens as a place of wonder. He lists the moon's changing phases, the five planets moving against the general sweep of the sky, and the storms of cloud, rain, and lightning. He adds that the planets' movements are said to shape the fortunes of nations.

Seneca describes the sights of the earth that a person sees after looking at the heavens. He lists wide plains, high snowy mountains, rivers, forests, birds, cities, nations cut off by natural barriers, farmland, meadows, bays, harbours and islands.

The passage lists natural wonders: shining stones and gems, gold carried by streams, fires that burst from the earth and the sea, and the ocean that joins and divides lands. It is a catalogue of the world's marvels, not an argument on its own.

Seneca describes the sea: huge animals swim in it, some clumsy, some very fast, some that spout water and endanger ships. Ships sail toward unknown lands, and human daring tries everything. The reader will see these great efforts and take part in them.

Seneca is listing the two sides of human life on earth. Men can learn skills that support, decorate, and govern their lives, but the same world brings plagues, wars, robbery, shipwreck, illness, the early loss of loved ones, and a death that may be painful. He asks the reader to weigh which of these they would choose.

Life comes with pains as well as blessings, and you cannot have the good without the bad. Seneca argues that since we chose to live, we accepted these terms. Nobody asked our opinion before birth, but our parents chose for us, knowing what life would bring.

Seneca says that the pain of grief comes mainly from an idea in our minds, not from the loved one's absence alone, since we accept absences during life without great suffering. Because an evil is as great as we judge it to be, the cure lies with us.

The passage suggests we imagine our dead loved ones are simply travelling ahead, and that we will follow them later. It also names a common grief: the fear that, with them gone, no one will defend us or take revenge when we are mocked.

Seneca says that in Rome, losing children can bring an old man more influence, not less, and childlessness can make the elderly powerful. Some old men even pretend to quarrel with their sons or disown them to gain that standing. He adds that a man who grieves his son only as he would grieve a slave does not deserve consolation.

Seneca asks Marcia whether her grief is that her son died or that he died young. If it is his death, she should have grieved all along, since she always knew he would die. He argues that the dead feel no harm, and the frightening stories about the underworld, such as darkness, prison, fire, and the river Lethe, are only myths made up by poets.

Death ends all pain, and it returns us to the same peaceful state we were in before birth. Since death is nothing, it is neither good nor bad, because only something that exists can be good or bad. So nothing that happens after death can make a dead person unhappy.

Marcia's son has died, and the passage says he is now free of worldly troubles. He no longer fears poverty, worries about wealth, suffers from desire, envies others, or hears coarse talk. He is also safe from harm to his country or himself.

The person described does not stay anxious about how events turn out, since that only brings more uncertainty. Instead he has reached a settled position that nothing can shake, so nothing can make him afraid.

Seneca says people fail to see how wretched they are, because they do not welcome death as the best thing Nature has provided. Death ends happiness, but it also ends suffering: it stops old age from wearing people out, takes the young before their hopes fail, and spares children the hard parts of life. Death comes to everyone, and it treats best those who meet it before they ask for it.

Death is presented as a release from every kind of human bondage. It frees slaves and captives, ends exile, and levels the unequal divisions that Fortune has made between people. After death, no one is subject to another's commands or to the shame of a low station.

Seneca says that the way out of life is always open, and knowing this is what keeps him from fearing misfortune and lets him stay calm and in control of his mind. Even when he looks at the many cruel methods of execution and torture used by different peoples, he sees that death is still there as a release.

Seneca says that even under cruel enemies or harsh rulers, death is always near as an escape. Slavery is bearable because a person can end it at any time by dying. He concludes that a timely death is a blessing, since many people have been harmed by living longer than they should.

Seneca says that Pompey would have died at the height of his fame if illness had killed him at Naples. Instead, he lived a little longer, lost his army in battle, and survived as a sad remnant of his own defeat.

Seneca gives two examples of men who would have been better off dying earlier. Pompey, after his defeat, offered his body to an Egyptian king's soldier, and Seneca says he would have regretted staying alive, since he would then owe his life to a king's mercy. Cicero, he says, should have died when he escaped Catiline's assassins, as a saviour of the Republic, or at least soon after his daughter's death.

Seneca is saying that Marcus Cato was spared from seeing the worst of Rome's civil wars: murders of citizens, property of the dead sold off, and public chaos. He suggests Cato would have been better off if the sea had drowned him on his voyage home with money from Cyprus, even if that money had been lost too.

Seneca says that Cato's early death spared him from further harm. Had he lived longer, he would have been forced to flee from Caesar and side with Pompey, despite being born for freedom. So dying young did him no wrong, since it ended any power evil men had to hurt him.

Seneca argues that a life, even a long one, is very short when set against time as a whole. He compares our life to a stay at an inn, and notes that even the oldest cities have existed only briefly. Human works, he says, take up no part of infinite time.
Measured against the whole universe, the earth is a mere point, and a human life is even smaller next to all of time. Since life is so small, adding more years to it cannot make much difference.

Seneca says a life becomes long only by being content with its length. Measured against eternity, the longest life is no different from the shortest, and a person who dies has lived as long as he needed to, with nothing left to accomplish.

Each person's lifespan is fixed in advance, and no one dies before the time set for them. Effort and favour cannot change that limit. So the speaker tells Marcia that her son died only because his allotted time had come, and he reached the end his life was given.

Seneca says that a person's lifespan is fixed from the start and cannot be shortened by chance or lengthened by prayer or effort. Each man gets exactly the life that was set for him. Every year that is added to youth is also a step closer to death.

Seneca says that people wrongly think only the old are close to death. Death is present from infancy onward, but we do not notice it. Each stage of life we name, such as boyhood or manhood, is really a loss of the stage before it.

Marcia is grieving her son, who died young. Seneca asks whether a longer life would really have been better for him, since no one can be sure of their future. He adds that all human affairs pass away and that the things we value most are the most fragile.

Seneca argues that since life is so uncertain, we can only be sure of what has already happened, so it is wise to hope for death while things are going well. He points to Marcia's son, whose good looks she had kept safe in a dangerous city, and asks who could have promised that his body would stay free of disease into old age.
Good natural qualities in young people do not always last. Some men fall into extravagance late in life and end in disgrace, while others give all their attention to eating and drinking.

Seneca lists the harsh things that happen to people: fires, collapsing houses, shipwrecks, and painful surgery. He adds exile, imprisonment, and suicide, and says that the person he is consoling, whose son was lost in such a way, was no more innocent, wise, or holy than famous men who suffered the same fate.

Seneca argues that people who die young are fortunate, because nature spares them the troubles of life. Human life is deceptive and treacherous, and no one would choose it if they could judge before being born. Not being born is the happiest state, and the next best is to die soon and return to the rest we had before birth.

Seneca reminds Marcia of a painful time when her father was handed over by Sejanus, the powerful minister under Tiberius, to Satrius Secundus, a man who served Sejanus. Her father had spoken too freely, and was punished. Later, he was honoured with a statue in a theatre, and the jest of Cordus is that the theatre was now truly destroyed, since honours had been given to a man of such character.

Seneca describes Cordus, a historian who has been prosecuted for his writings. Sejanus, the powerful minister under Emperor Tiberius, had a statue or inscription set up over the tomb of Pompey, the famous Roman general, and the people who were loyal to Sejanus turned on Cordus. Cordus then faced a choice: live only with Sejanus's approval, or die with his daughter's approval.

This is a story of a father who starves himself in secret. He pretends to eat, throwing food out of the window and saying he has already eaten, so that his family will think he is fine. On the fourth day his weakness shows what he has been doing.

The speaker, speaking to his daughter, announces that he has decided to die and has already begun the journey toward death. He tells her she cannot and should not stop him. He then has the light shut out of the room and shuts himself into the darkness, and people who hear of it feel relieved, as though he has escaped his persecutors.

Cordus was accused before the consuls, the chief Roman magistrates, at the urging of Sejanus, a powerful official under the emperor Tiberius. His accusers asked that he be stopped from dying by his own hand, since they had driven him to it. While the debate went on, Cordus killed himself first, escaping them.

Seneca is pointing out that death was always going to come to a person in the family, so grieving over it is strange. He adds that the person was already close to being spared death altogether, meaning that death was never something they could escape.

Seneca says that the future is uncertain and most likely to bring trouble. He adds that a soul released early from life, before it has taken on earthly corruption, rises more easily to the gods and is cleansed more easily.

Great minds dislike staying in the body. They want to break free of it, and they look down on human affairs from above. Plato says the wise mind is devoted to death and always reaches toward what lies beyond this life.

Seneca is telling Marcia that she should not have expected her young son to stay with her for long. His early maturity and flawless character were signs that he was ready to be taken away, since anything that reaches perfection is ready to break apart.

Brilliant and perfect qualities in people tend to be short-lived, just as a bright fire burns out quickly while a dim, badly fed one lasts longer. Once a mind has reached its full growth, it has little time left.
Seneca's point is that a boy who grows too large too fast is a sign he will die young. Once growth is complete, the end is near, so early maturity warns of an early death.

Seneca says that his son's life should be measured by his virtues rather than his years, and that he lived long enough by that measure. The son stayed under his mother's care and roof, even when he had his own household, and he turned down a military career that would have taken him away from her.

Seneca tells Marcia that the years her son spent away from her were not really lost time, since she was able to watch him closely during his youth. He was clever, though shy, and he resisted the advances of women who tried to seduce him, blushing when they showed interest in him.

Seneca is praising a dead young man, who became a priest while still a boy because of his holy life, not just his mother's influence. He urges the grieving mother to dwell on those virtues and to treat her memory of her son as a comfort, since he now has no duties to pull him away from her and cannot cause her trouble.

Seneca tells Marcia that her grief is over the only loss that could truly hurt her, the death of her son.
