He argues that everything else is beyond fortune's power and can still give pleasure, if she knows how to value what her son was. What died was only his outward appearance, which he says was not even a very good likeness.

Seneca says the dead person's soul is immortal and now free of the body. He calls the body (bones, skin, face, hands) chains and darkness that weigh down the soul, deceive it, and keep it from its true home.

The passage describes the soul, which is said to long to return to the place it came from before being sent down to earth. There it will find eternal rest and see what is pure and clear, instead of the dirt and confusion of this world.

Seneca tells Marcia she need not rush to her son's grave, because the grave holds only his bones and ashes, which he calls no more part of him than clothes are. He says the son's soul has left the earth, been purified of earthly faults, and gone up to join the blessed dead.

Seneca tells Marcia that her dead father, now free of life's burdens through death, is with the souls of the dead and will welcome her newborn grandson. He will teach the boy about the stars and the secrets of nature through real knowledge, just as a guide shows a stranger around an unfamiliar city.

The dead son and father are pictured as now living in a higher place, looking down on the earth. Marcia is told to act as if they are watching her, but as the better, more exalted beings they now are. So she should be ashamed to act meanly or to grieve for relatives who have been improved by death.

Seneca is describing the souls of the dead, who are free to move across the whole universe. Nothing blocks them: not seas, mountains, valleys, or the dangerous Syrtes, which were sandbanks on the North African coast. They travel easily and share the company of the stars.

Seneca imagines Marcia's dead father speaking to her from heaven. He is no longer troubled by the civil wars or by old political enemies, and he is in a happier state than before. He asks her why her grief has lasted so long.

Seneca argues that a son who died young, in his prime and with his family prospering, has not been treated unfairly. Fortune, or chance, brings storms to everyone and is kind only to those who deal with her least. Many kings would have been happier had they died before their downfall.

This passage is a list of examples to show that a short or hard life can still be complete. It names Roman generals who died young, men of high birth who faced the sword calmly, and Seneca's own father and grandfather. The last example describes a grandfather who refused to let anyone take liberties with him and starved himself, showing that his spirit matched what he had written.

Seneca asks why a family member who died most happily should still be mourned for so long. He says that the dead now gather in a bright light, while life on earth is poor, sad and anxious, with little of that light.

Seneca is describing a happy, peaceful place, likely the afterlife or the state of the dead, where there is no war, no murder, no lawsuits, and no secrecy. Everyone's mind is open, and people can see all of time, past and future.

The writer says he once liked studying the events of one century in one small corner of the world. Now he enjoys looking at the whole course of history across all the centuries, including the rise and fall of kingdoms, the ruin of cities, and changes in the coastline made by the sea.

Seneca tells Marcia that if it comforts her to know that loss is shared by everyone, then she should know that nothing stays where it is. Time will bring down everything and carry it away, and it will treat people, and even the things of the world, in the same way. Human beings are only a small part of what Fortune, or chance, controls.

Seneca describes a vast catastrophe that would hit whole regions and the world at large. It would flatten mountains, raise new ones, dry up seas, divert rivers, cut off nations from one another, swallow cities in chasms, bring plague, flood the land, or burn all mortals alive.

Seneca describes a future end of the world, when the heavenly bodies collide and burn together. He says that afterward the world will be remade, and that even the souls of the blessed will be dissolved back into the basic elements of nature.

Everyone wants a happy life, but people often fail to see what actually makes life happy. Happiness is hard to reach, and if a person takes the wrong road, working harder only takes them further away from it.

First, we must define clearly the goal we are aiming at. Then we must find the quickest way to reach it. Along the way, if we move in the right direction, we can see each day how far we have advanced toward the goal that our natural desires push us toward.

Seneca says that a person who follows the many voices around them, going in every direction, wastes a short life even when working hard. He advises choosing one's course only with the guidance of someone experienced who has already travelled that path, because this journey is unlike others.

Seneca says that in some places a clear path and local guides keep travelers from getting lost, but in life the most worn and crowded paths often lead people furthest wrong. So the most important thing is not to follow the crowd like sheep, going wherever the others go.

Seneca says that following popular opinion and copying what others do leads people into serious trouble. Like a crowd pressing together, one person's fall pulls down the people behind, and those in front cause the ruin of those who follow.

Seneca says that people rarely judge life for themselves. They follow the crowd and accepted beliefs, which leads them to ruin. He suggests that they would be helped by separating themselves from the herd.

Seneca says that crowds will defend their own mistakes even against reason. He compares this to elections, where voters later admire the officials they just chose, once public opinion shifts. He concludes that decisions made by majority vote simply make everyone approve or reject the same things, whether or not they are right.

In a debate about the happy life, the fact that many people hold a view does not show it is right. Seneca says the opinion of the majority is more likely to be the worse one, because most people do not choose the better course.

The main point is that we should ask what is truly best to do, and what leads to lasting happiness, rather than follow what most people do or approve of. Seneca says "the vulgar" means common people, whether poor or rich, since both can be wrong about what is true.

The speaker judges people by inner reason, not by outward appearance or wealth. He says the mind can find out what is good for it. When a person gives his mind quiet time to examine himself, he will admit hard truths to himself.

The speaker regrets much of what he has done and said, and envies people who cannot speak. He finds that what he once wanted turned out to be what his enemies would have wished on him, and what he feared was easier to bear than what he desired. Though he has made peace with many people, he is still not at peace with himself.

Seneca says that trying to stand out from ordinary people, by gaining some talent or reputation, only makes a person a target. Those who praise, desire, or flatter a successful man are either enemies already or could become them. Admirers and envious people are about equally numerous.

Seneca asks why a person should not look for a good that can be used and personally felt, rather than one that merely looks impressive to others. He says the goods people stare at and admire from outside seem bright, but they bring misery to those who own them.

Seneca says the good life is not far away but close at hand, something sound and good through and through, and that people miss it by reaching for things beyond what is nearest. He sets aside rival schools of thought and gives only the Stoic view.

Seneca says he does not feel bound to follow any one Stoic leader. He will respect some of their views, ask others to clarify theirs, and may add his own ideas. The point all Stoics agree on, he says, is that wisdom means living in line with nature and shaping conduct by nature's laws.

A happy life, in this view, is one that fits the nature of the one living it. It needs a sound, steady mind that meets hardship with courage, cares for the body without anxiety, values the good things of life without overvaluing any of them, and enjoys good fortune without being ruled by it.

Once we drive away the things that excite or frighten us, such as sensual pleasures and trivial, short-lived concerns, we gain lasting joy, peace, calm, greatness of mind, and kindness. Cruelty, he says, shows weakness.

Seneca says the highest good can be described in different words, just as an army can be arranged in different shapes. The shape changes, but its strength and loyalty stay the same. The same idea stays the same even when it is worded differently.

Seneca says that the highest good can be described either briefly or at length, and the meaning stays the same. He gives two versions: a mind that ignores the chances of fortune and delights in virtue, and a mind that is strong, understands the world, and treats others gently and considerately.

A happy person, in this definition, is one who judges good and bad only by the state of the mind. Such a person values virtue and honour above all, is not lifted up by good luck or crushed by bad luck, and finds pleasure in scorning pleasures.

A happy life, Seneca suggests, is a free and steady mind. Such a mind is not moved by fear or desire, counts only honour as good and only shame as bad, and treats everything else as trivial details that cannot change the highest good.

A person who lives by these principles is always cheerful and content, because he enjoys what he already has and wants no pleasures beyond those of his own home. Such a person can let these lasting inner pleasures outweigh the brief bodily pleasures. Once he has become immune to pleasure, he is also immune to pain.

Seneca says that a person ruled by pleasure and pain is a slave to them. Freedom from that slavery comes only through contempt for Fortune, meaning indifference to luck and chance. Once a person reaches that, calm, clear thinking, cheerfulness and similar qualities follow, and they come from the true good of a human being.

Seneca defines a happy person as one who, through reason, no longer hopes or fears. He then objects that rocks and cattle also feel neither fear nor sadness, yet nobody calls them happy, because they cannot understand what happiness is.

Some people have so little understanding and self-knowledge that they are no better than animals. Their reason is only twisted and used for harm. A happy life, the passage says, cannot be lived by someone who is cut off from truth; it rests on sound and reliable judgment.

The mind is truly free only when it can withstand not just serious harm but even minor irritations, and keep its position against the hard blows of bad luck. Pleasures of the body are also dismissed: no human would want to be constantly indulged while neglecting the mind.

Seneca argues that a mind which seeks pleasure, even pleasure of its own, is still in a poor state. Looking back on past indulgences and planning for more, it chooses harm over good. Since no insane person can be happy, and choosing what harms as the highest good is a kind of madness, such a mind cannot be happy.
A person is happy when they judge rightly about everything. Such a person is content with whatever their present circumstances are. Their reason approves of the whole state of their affairs.

Seneca is criticising people who call pleasure the highest good, which he compares to placing it "in the belly." He argues that these thinkers link pleasure and virtue together, saying one cannot live well without the other. He does not see how the two are connected, and asks what would stop virtue from existing without pleasure.

Seneca argues that pleasure and virtue are not the same thing. All good things come from virtue, but some pleasures are not honourable, and some honourable things are hard to reach. Pleasure also reaches bad lives, while virtue cannot exist alongside an evil life.
Seneca argues that pleasure and virtue cannot be joined. Virtue can exist without pleasure and does not need it, while pleasure is base and weak, and belongs to places like brothels and taverns.

Virtue is found in public and active life: temples, the marketplace, the senate, and the city walls, where people work hard and get dirty. Pleasure, by contrast, hides in private, indulgent places such as bathhouses and it is shown as soft and made up.

The highest good, Seneca says, lasts forever and never wears out or brings regret, because a sound mind does not change and turn against itself. Pleasure is different: it fades at the moment it is most enjoyed, soon bores us, and cannot be relied on because it changes.

Seneca is saying that a thing which passes so quickly cannot have any lasting, solid substance. It wears itself out by the very act of living, reaching the point where it stops existing even as it begins, so its end is always present from the start.

Pleasure is found in good and bad people alike, so it cannot be the guide to a good life. The old teachers said to choose the highest life rather than the most pleasant, letting pleasure follow reason. Living happily, Seneca says, means living according to Nature, with reason watching and following her.

Bodily gifts, health, and pleasures are worth having only when we hold them loosely. We should treat them as temporary and never let them rule us, using them as servants rather than masters. Used that way, they can be of value to the mind.
A wise person should not be controlled by outside events. He should rely on his own mind, keep his judgments firm and consistent, and stay calm and composed whether his luck is good or bad.

Reason should use the senses to find truth and take its starting points from them, but it must then return to itself. The passage compares this to God, who spreads out into the world and still returns to himself. The mind should likewise go out through the senses to outward things while staying in control of them and of itself.

A mind that has put all its parts in order and made them work together reaches the highest good. Nothing can shake it or make it stumble, so whatever it does turns out well and easily. Hesitation and slow action, by contrast, show inner conflict and a lack of settled purpose.
The highest good, according to this passage, is a single, unified mind. Where agreement and unity exist, the virtues must be present too, while the vices are the ones that fight among themselves.

Seneca answers an objection that people practise virtue only for the pleasure it brings. He says pleasure is not the reason we pursue virtue. Virtue does bring pleasure, but that is an extra gift, not the goal virtue works toward.

Pleasure is not the goal or cause of virtue. It comes along with virtue, like flowers that grow in a field sown for corn: they please the eye, but they were not the reason for the work. We do not choose virtue for the pleasure it gives; virtue gives pleasure to those who choose it.

Seneca says the highest good is virtue itself, found in choosing it and in a mind that has fulfilled its proper function. Nothing lies beyond it, just as nothing lies beyond the whole or the end. So asking what virtue is sought for is a mistake, because that would mean looking for something higher than the highest good.

The passage argues that virtue is the highest good and needs no reward beyond itself. Strength of mind, wisdom, and related qualities are the true good, so pleasure of the body is not what the search is about. Animals, the writer says, have greater bodily pleasures than people do.

Seneca's opponent says a pleasant life must also be honorable, and that animals, which seek only food, do not live pleasantly in this sense. Seneca replies that fools enjoy pleasures most deeply, and that vice is full of enjoyments, so pleasure alone does not show a life is virtuous.

Seneca lists faults that a person can have: arrogance, self-centred blindness to others, luxury, childish excitement, idle talk, cruelty in insults, laziness, and a dull mind. He says virtue removes all of these, checking pleasures before allowing them.

Seneca is contrasting two ways of living. The wise person uses pleasures only in moderation and does not regard pleasure as the highest good, or even as good at all. The opposing view treats pleasure as the highest good and lives to pursue it.

Seneca argues that a wise man cannot be ruled by pleasure. If pleasure overcomes him, he would have no strength left to face hardship, danger, poverty, pain, death, or the troubles of the world. Being beaten by something so weak would make him unfit for those struggles.

Seneca argues against the view that pleasure can be the highest good if it is joined with virtue. He says that if virtue must guard pleasure to keep it good, pleasure cannot be the highest good. He adds that virtue would then follow pleasure, when it should rule it, and so serve only as a taster of pleasures.

Seneca argues that people who are given pleasure and good fortune can still be bad, so pleasure does not show a person is good. He points to Nomentanus and Apicius, two rich men who ate the finest food from sea and land. Nomentanus and Apicius were notorious glutton-spendthrifts of Rome, and Seneca treats them as examples of bad men.

Seneca describes people who indulge in every kind of luxury: music, food, perfume and soft comforts. He says they seem to be surrounded by pleasure, yet they are uneasy, because the pleasures they seek are not good.

Seneca says that people who are troubled and divided in their minds still take real pleasure in their lives. He admits they are foolish and will feel regret, yet they are not free of trouble. They are like madmen who laugh while they rave.

Seneca says that the pleasures of wise men are mild and quiet, kept under control and hardly noticed. They are not welcomed eagerly, and they are not used to fill empty time like a comic show between serious work. He concludes that pleasure should not be joined to virtue, since doing so attracts the worst kind of people.

Seneca says that a reckless drunkard believes he lives virtuously because he enjoys pleasure, and he takes his vices for wisdom. Epicurus does not encourage such excess. Instead, vicious people hide their indulgence behind philosophy and gather in the schools where pleasure is praised.

Seneca says that people who hide behind Epicurus's name for "pleasure" are wrong about what he meant. Epicurus's pleasure, he claims, is sober and temperate. These people use his name to excuse their vices, and so they lose their sense of shame, which was the one good thing left in their lives.

Seneca says that his rivals' praise of pleasure does harm because people overlook its noble teaching and see only its shameful side. The degrading part is obvious to everyone, so the good part is lost.

Seneca says that he thinks Epicurus' teaching was upright and even strict, though Stoics would not like to hear it. Epicurus limited pleasure and required it to follow nature, just as Stoics require virtue to do. Luxury, by contrast, wants more than nature needs.

Seneca says that a person who already believes happiness means lazy idleness and cycles of overindulgence can join the Epicurean school for its appealing name. Such a person keeps his old pleasures, not the ones the school teaches. Thinking his vices match its teaching, he now indulges them openly rather than in secret.

Seneca says he will not call Epicurus's school a teacher of crime, as many Stoics do. He admits the school has a bad reputation that it does not deserve, because its outward appearance invites scandal. He compares it to a brave man in a woman's gown, who is in fact respectable but looks disgraceful.

Seneca tells his correspondent to put a better motto over the door of his school, one that stirs the mind toward virtue. The motto now there, he says, was made up by the vices. He contrasts the person who chooses virtue, which shows a noble character, with the person who follows pleasure, who is weak and worn out and needs guidance to tell harmless desires from endless, growing ones.

Seneca is saying that virtue should guide a person's life, because it keeps every step safe. Pleasure is harmful when taken in excess, but virtue already contains moderation, so virtue prevents excess. Something that is damaged by its own size cannot be good, and reason is the best guide for humans.

Seneca says that virtue should lead the way in a happy life, with pleasure only following behind like a shadow. Making virtue a servant to pleasure, he argues, is the mark of a mind that cannot aim at great things.

Seneca says that virtue should lead, and pleasure may follow as her servant, so we stay in control of it. If pleasure leads instead, a person loses virtue and is ruled by pleasure. Such a person suffers when pleasure is absent and is overwhelmed when it is too strong, like a ship caught in the shifting sandbanks of the Syrtes.

Great pleasures are dangerous, the passage says. Like wild beasts that are hard to catch and can turn on their keepers, great pleasures turn out to be great evils and take their owners prisoner. Seeking evil instead of good is what makes this danger possible.

Seneca says that the more things a person owns and the bigger those things are, the more that person becomes a slave to many masters. The passage then turns to a comparison with a hunter who tracks wild animals, though the comparison is cut off here.

The main point is that a person who chases pleasure puts it above everything else. He gives up more valuable things and his duties, and he gives up freedom, which the Stoics regarded as the most essential good. In this view, he does not get pleasure by paying for it; he becomes its slave.

The imagined opponent asks why virtue and pleasure could not be joined so that the highest good includes both and honour and pleasure are the same. Seneca's reply is no: only what is honourable can be part of honour, and the highest good would lose its purity if it held anything unlike its better part.

Joy that comes from virtue is good, but it is not the highest good itself. Like cheerfulness and peace of mind, it follows from the highest good and does not add to its completeness, even though virtue is what produces it.

Seneca warns that someone who mixes virtue with pleasure, leaning toward pleasure, weakens virtue. Freedom then becomes enslaved, because the person depends on luck and lives in constant fear and anxiety about what may go wrong.

Virtue needs a firm foundation, and a person who depends on luck, the body, or the things that affect the body has none. Someone ruled by small pleasures and pains cannot calmly accept what happens, serve God, or protect his country and friends.

Seneca says the highest good is a height that pain, hope, fear, and other outside forces cannot reach. Only virtue can climb there, and it faces hardship calmly and even willingly, knowing that all hard events follow natural law. Like a soldier, it accepts its wounds and remains loyal to God.

Seneca says that a person who complains while being forced to do something gains nothing. He is still dragged along, so it is foolish to resist rather than go willingly. Likewise, it is foolish to grieve over lacking things or to be surprised by illness and death, which come to good and bad people alike.

We should bear calmly whatever the order of the universe requires us to bear, since everyone has sworn to endure life's troubles and accept what cannot be avoided. Our freedom, he says, lies in obeying God, who rules us as a king rules a kingdom.

True happiness, in this view, comes from virtue. Virtue tells a person to regard as neither good nor bad anything unconnected with virtue or vice, to stand firm against misfortune, and to make the good as close to divine as is right. Its reward is a freedom from restraint, want and harm, and success in all one attempts.
Seneca argues that virtue alone is enough for happiness. A person who is beyond all desire lacks nothing, and if everything he needs is within himself, he has no need of anything outside himself.

A person who is only on the road to virtue, even a far advanced one, still needs some help from luck while freeing himself from human concerns and the ties of mortal life. The difference between people lies in how tightly they are bound. The one who has advanced far is held by a looser chain and is almost free, though not yet fully so.

Seneca imagines a critic of philosophy attacking a philosopher for inconsistency. The critic asks why he talks more boldly than he lives: he is careful with powerful people, values money, grieves over losses and deaths, cares about gossip, and keeps a costly estate and furniture.

Seneca lists questions that a critic might ask about a wealthy man's luxuries: old wine, large estates, useless trees, costly jewels and clothes, trained servants, and property overseas. The point is that such possessions go beyond what is needed, and the questions challenge their purpose.

Seneca's speaker first says it is shameful not to know one's slaves by sight, since that shows either carelessness or an excess of slaves. He then admits he is not a wise man and does not claim to be. He only asks to be better than the worst people, and is content to lose a little of his faults each day.

Seneca says he has not reached a sound mind and never will. He treats his faults the way one treats gout, easing the pain rather than curing it, and he compares himself to a runner beside someone who is lame. He speaks for a friend who has made some progress, not for himself.

An opponent accuses the speaker of saying one thing and doing another. The speaker replies that this same charge was made against Plato, Epicurus and Zeno, who taught how people ought to live, not how they actually lived.

Seneca says he praises virtue and blames vices, starting with his own. He admits he does not yet live as he should, but he knows the right way and follows it, though far behind. Others' spite will not stop him from doing so.

Seneca asks why anyone should expect slander to spare them, since it did not spare the blameless Rutilius or Cato. He then notes that critics faulted Diogenes the Cynic, a man who gave up nearly everything, for not being poor enough. Their complaint, he says, missed the point: Diogenes taught virtue, not poverty.

Diodorus, an Epicurean philosopher, took his own life by cutting his throat, which some judged to be madness or recklessness. Seneca says that in dying he showed himself content, having lived as far as Fortune allowed.

People who gossip about others' lives and deaths, and attack anyone admired for a rare virtue, are compared to small dogs barking at strangers. Seneca says they do this because they want no one to seem good, since another person's virtue makes their own wrongs look worse.

Seneca is rebuking someone who envies others' good reputations while living badly himself. He argues that if even people who pursue virtue show greed, lust and love of power, then the envious person, who openly despises virtue, must be far worse.

Seneca says that people's words about virtue are bold and strong enough to face any hardship, yet in practice they are caught up in their own troubles and struggle to free themselves from them. He suggests they are, in effect, nailing themselves to these troubles.

Seneca says that people who punish themselves for their desires suffer worse than crucified men, since they are torn across as many crosses as they have lusts. Yet these same people speak ill of others and scorn others' faults so loudly that one would think they had none of their own.

Seneca answers the charge that philosophers do not live up to what they teach. He grants the charge, but says their good teaching and noble thoughts still do real good. People who try worthwhile study deserve praise even if they do not fully succeed, just as a climber who does not reach the top has still made progress.

Seneca says that a noble mind should admire people who aim high, even if they fail. Such a mind sets its goals beyond ordinary human strength, and he gives example rules: face death or a comedy calmly, bear hard work with a strong mind, and treat wealth the same whether one has it or not.

Seneca describes an attitude of calm independence from circumstances. He says that his mood will not rise or fall with his surroundings or with luck, that he sees the world as shared, and that he was born to serve others and is grateful to Nature for this. He will use his possessions neither greedily nor wastefully.

Seneca says that gifts given to worthy people are the only wealth he truly counts as his own. He judges a gift by how much the receiver values it, not by its size or number. He also says he acts from conscience rather than public opinion, and behaves as if watched even when alone.

Seneca describes how he wants to live: eating and drinking only to satisfy natural needs, treating friends kindly and enemies gently, and forgiving before being asked. He says the world is his home city, ruled by the gods, who watch and judge all his actions.

A person who is ready to die when nature or reason calls should live by a clear rule: keep a good conscience, pursue good aims, and never take away anyone's freedom, including his own. Such a person aims high, reaching toward the gods, and even if he falls short, the effort is still worthwhile.

Seneca says that people who hate virtue and good men act like sick eyes or night creatures, which cannot bear bright light and hide from it. He tells such critics to keep attacking good men, but says they will only wear out their own teeth without harming anyone.

The passage asks why a man who studies philosophy still lives as a rich man. He says wealth, life and health should be despised, yet he keeps them and cares for them, and he calls exile an empty word but would rather stay in his own country. The questions point out this gap between what he says and how he lives.

The speaker says that a wise person may treat a long life, or a long old age, as something to be despised, yet still be glad to have it. He does not push such things away. He simply holds them without fear, and if they leave him, he goes after them without worry.

Seneca says that the best place to keep wealth is in a place where it can always be recovered without dispute. He notes that Cato the Censor praised old heroes who owned little, yet Cato himself owned four million sesterces, a fortune smaller than Crassus's but larger than Cato's own earlier wealth.

The wise man does not think he is too good for wealth that comes to him by chance, and he does not reject it. He does not love riches or let them into his mind. He keeps them, and he sees them as more material for his virtue to work with.

A wise man who is rich has more chances to show his virtues than one who is poor. A poor wise man can show only one virtue: not being corrupted or broken by poverty. Wealth allows him to show temperance, generosity, hard work, orderliness, and dignity.

The wise man does not look down on himself because of a small body or a bad eye. He still prefers good health and strength, and he accepts illness while hoping for recovery. These things are minor next to virtue, but they add a little to the steady cheerfulness that virtue brings.

Seneca says that wealth is like a favourable wind or sunny weather: it brings comfort and pleasure. Even a wise Stoic, who holds that only virtue is good, must admit that such "indifferent" things have some value and are preferable to others. So wealth counts among things worth wanting.

Seneca is contrasting two ways of holding wealth. For the speaker, riches are an add-on that can leave without changing him. For his opponent, riches have taken over his whole self, so losing them would leave him feeling empty. In short, the speaker owns his riches, while the opponent belongs to his.

Philosophers may own a lot of money, as long as it was honestly earned and honestly spent. Wealth is acceptable if it was not taken from others or gained by wrongdoing. The key test is that nothing he owns should be something another person can claim as their own.

A wealthy man who has gained his wealth honestly need not be ashamed of it or proud of it. He would be admirable, though, if he opened his house to his fellow citizens and let them take back anything that was theirs, and still kept as much as before.

Seneca says a wise man may keep wealth openly, provided he could show his accounts to anyone and find nothing dishonestly gained. He will not let stolen money into his house, but he will welcome riches that come by good fortune and fit with virtue. He should neither boast of them nor hide them.

The wise man does not throw his wealth out of his house, because he has no reason to reject it. He owns riches but does not depend on them, knowing they may leave him one day. He does not let them weigh on him or others, and he gives them to good people, or to those who may become good.

The wise giver chooses carefully who receives his gifts, and gives only for good reasons, since a badly placed gift is a shameful loss. His purse opens easily but has no hole, so money leaves it on purpose and nothing is lost by accident.

Giving is not easy, Seneca says, if it is done with careful reason rather than on impulse or at random. He then lists sample motives: repaying a kindness, helping out of pity, and making someone less open to being held down by poverty.

Seneca says he gives selectively, not to those who will stay poor anyway. He believes giving puts others in his debt, so nothing he gives is wasted. He hopes his gifts will be returned to him, though he cannot demand it.

Seneca says a kindness should be kept back, like buried treasure, and given only when truly required. He then argues that a rich man's home offers many chances to help people, since nature tells us to do good to all humans, whether they are slaves or free, and however they gained their freedom.

Generosity, Seneca says, can be practised anywhere people are, even at home. It is named for coming from a free, generous mind, not for duties owed to free men. A wise person never gives to unworthy people, yet his giving never runs out whenever he finds someone deserving.

A student of wisdom is not yet a wise person. Such a student may speak admirable principles while still struggling with many faults, and so should not be held to the standard of his words. He is still working to improve his character.

The speaker says that his critics cannot judge him until he has fully lived up to his own ideals, and that he has already drawn hatred from bad men, which he takes as a sign he is doing right. He then starts to explain his values, beginning with the claim that wealth is not a good thing.

Seneca says that things like health, wealth and comfort cannot be called good, because bad people also have them and they do not make anyone good. He still grants that such things are desirable, useful, and bring real comfort to life.

Seneca says he would not think more of himself if he owned great wealth, such as gold and silver plate used for everyday things. Possessions in his house are not part of who he is, so they do not make him better.

Seneca says that being put among beggars would not make him feel lowered, since lacking bread cannot matter to someone who is free to die when he chooses. He adds that a luxurious house would not make him happier, though he would still prefer it to the bridge.

Seneca says that a hard bed or shabby clothes would not make him miserable, and that he would not feel he had earned good luck by being fortunate. Even if losses, grief and quarrels came to him, he would not call himself wretched or curse any day, because he has trained himself to treat no day as unlucky.

Seneca says he would rather control his joys than suppress his sorrows. He gives Socrates as an example: even if Socrates won great conquests and was honored as a god, he would still remember that he is only a man.

Seneca imagines being led in a conqueror's triumph after a fall from high rank, and says he would bear it with no more humility than he showed in his own success. Even so, he would still prefer to be the conqueror than the captive. He claims to scorn Fortune's power, yet would still choose its better side if he could.

Seneca says that a good person turns whatever happens into something good, yet he would still prefer that events be easy and pleasant. Some virtues need a push to get going, while others need holding back, just as the body must be restrained going downhill and urged on going uphill.

The passage says that some virtues, such as patience and courage, are hard. They must push against difficulty and misfortune, like climbing a steep hill. Other virtues, such as generosity, moderation and gentleness, come easily, like going downhill, so the mind must hold them back to keep from going too far.

Seneca says that hardship calls for tough, fighting virtues, while wealth calls for quieter, thriftier ones that carry their own weight. He prefers the quieter virtues, which can be practised calmly, to those tested only through pain and effort. He then has the wise man reply that his words are not empty talk but must be understood, not just heard.

A wise man and a fool may both own wealth, but the difference lies in how they hold it. For the wise man, riches are servants that he can lose without much harm, so he stays ready for poverty even while rich. The fool treats wealth as his master and clings to it as if it were guaranteed to last.

Seneca warns that people who feel secure in their big houses and wealth ignore the dangers around them, just as besieged savages watch enemy siege machines without understanding them. The wise man, by contrast, keeps everything that is truly his even if he loses his riches, because he lives happily in the present and does not fear the future.

Socrates, or anyone with the same firmness against the troubles of life, would say he will not change how he lives to please other people's opinions. If they criticise him, he will not take it as abuse but as the complaining of small children.

A wise man, free from faults, may criticize others, but only to help them improve, not out of hatred. If others dislike him, he says it hurts them more than him, since hating what is good means giving up on doing well. Their attacks do him no harm, just as men do not harm the gods by knocking down their altars. Such people, he says, mean harm and would do it if they could.

Seneca says he puts up with his friend's chatter the way Jupiter puts up with the poets' silly stories about him. Those stories show Jupiter with wings, horns, adulteries, violence and crimes against his own father. Such tales only make people feel less ashamed of sinning, since they assume the gods did the same.

Seneca urges his friend Gallio to respect virtue, trusting those who have long pursued it and found it ever more powerful. He compares virtue to the gods and its followers to priests. He also explains that the Latin phrase "favete linguis" means "keep silent," not "show favour," so that sacred rites are not spoiled by unlucky words.

Seneca says that people follow self-proclaimed prophets who act out divine messages. Some beat a sistrum (a rattling instrument), some cut their own skin, some crawl through the streets, and some cry out that a god is angry. Crowds listen and call these men inspired.

Socrates, speaking from his prison cell, scolds people who slander virtue and insult the gods with malicious accusations. He tells them to praise good men or else stay silent. If they want to attack someone, they should attack each other, since cursing Heaven is not even sacrilege, just a waste of time.

Seneca says that comic writers have mocked him since he once gave Aristophanes a joke to use. Instead of harming his virtue, their attacks have made it look brighter, because people come to know its strength by testing it. He compares this to flint, which is best known by those who strike it.

Seneca says he stands firm against every attack, like a rock in the sea that waves beat on but cannot move or wear down. Attacks only harm the attacker, so he says they should aim at something softer instead.
Seneca says that people who have many faults of their own should not spend their time judging others' small failings. He compares them to a man covered in mange who mocks the moles on handsome men.

Seneca answers critics who attack him by pointing to famous philosophers' faults, such as Plato's pursuit of money or Alcibiades' bad conduct. He says his critics enjoy copying vices and should look instead at the troubles inside and around themselves.

Seneca tells his listener that, though he may not know his own place, people have not yet reached a state where they are free to spend time slandering those above them. The "pass" means a point or state, and "betters" means social superiors.

Seneca tells his friend Gallio that he fails to see his own situation. Like people who sit at the games while their home is already in mourning, Gallio looks cheerful while troubles are coming, or are already upon him. The author, seeing from a higher viewpoint, says a storm of confused desires is stirring his mind.
In Roman Senate debates, a senator who liked only part of a proposal could ask that the acceptable part be separated from the rest. He would then vote for that part alone.

Seneca asks why people so readily recommend vices. He says that withdrawing from others alone would do us good, since we would be better men when taken singly. Retiring to the company of the best people, and choosing one of them as a model for life, would be a greater gain still.

Seneca says that leisure, meaning freedom from outside demands, is needed to carry out the best decision a person has made. Without it, crowds can distort a judgment that is still weak, and life is split between conflicting aims instead of flowing in one calm course.

The worst part of our troubles, the passage says, is that we keep swapping one vice for another, so we never settle into one known fault. We enjoy one thing and then another, our opinions are wrong and quickly formed, and we drift like waves, grabbing one thing and dropping it for the next.

We judge our lives by what other people do and praise, not by what is actually good. We follow the crowd's path just because many have walked it, even though none of them have come back to tell us where it leads.

Seneca says that Stoics must stay active until the end of life. They should keep working for the common good, help individuals, and even help enemies in old age. Stoics are never released from service, however long they have served, and he quotes a poet saying a man still wears the helmet when his hair is grey.

Seneca says that Stoics work so hard that they do not rest even while dying. When someone asks why he praises Epicurus's teaching among Stoics, he answers that he follows his own leaders, the Stoic founders, and goes where they lead, not where others send him.

Seneca says he will show that he is not abandoning Stoic teaching, since the Stoics themselves did not abandon it. He will argue two points: a person may devote life to studying truth from the start, and a person who has finished public service may turn to study after failing health. He compares this to Vestal virgins, who learn sacred duties first and then teach others.

Seneca says he may follow other Stoic thinkers, not just Zeno and Chrysippus, because he is not bound to one master. A thinker who always follows one teacher becomes a partisan rather than a debater. He also wishes truth were already fully known, but says it must still be sought, even among the teachers who share it.

Epicurus and Zeno, founders of two rival schools, both recommend leisure, that is, withdrawal from public life, though they reach it differently. Epicurus says the wise man avoids politics except on special occasions. Zeno says he takes part unless something prevents him. Seneca notes that Zeno's "reasons" for withdrawing can cover a lot.

The wise man should not spend his effort on public life when the state is too corrupt to be saved or when he lacks the influence or strength to guide it. Just as a sensible person would not sail in a worn-out ship or join the army while sick, he stays out of affairs he cannot manage.

Someone who has not yet faced illness or misfortune may, before trouble comes, settle into a secure life and turn to honest work and undisturbed leisure. The main duty, he says, is to be useful to other people: to as many as possible, or failing that, to a few.

A person who cannot serve others should still do good to himself, since that helps mankind too. Becoming a worse person harms others as well as oneself, so improving oneself benefits others by preparing what will later be useful to them.

Seneca says that a person belongs to two communities. One is the vast community of gods and humans, which has no fixed borders and reaches as far as the sun shines. The other is the city of one's birth, such as Athens or Carthage. Some people serve both, and some serve only one.

Seneca argues that a person at leisure can still serve the wider community, and may serve it better, by studying big questions. He lists such questions: what virtue is, whether nature or training makes people good, whether God rules the world or simply watches it, and whether the world will last forever.

Seneca argues that nature made people for both thinking and doing, and that the urge to discover the unknown proves it. People are so eager to learn hidden things that some sail far and endure hardship just to find something remote, with no other reward.

Seneca says people are drawn to shows, to prying into secrets, to ancient history and to tales of foreign customs because nature gave humans a curious mind. Nature made her works so grand and beautiful that they would be wasted if seen by no one, so she made people to watch them.

Nature has placed humans at the centre of the world with a wide view around them, and has made them upright with necks that turn. This lets them follow the stars across the sky from rising to setting, which shows she meant them to look up and watch the heavens.

Seneca says that nature shows only a little of itself, so that what we see makes us want to study the rest. Our observations should lead us to ask about the origin of the universe, how its elements were separated and ordered, whether a higher power governs them, and whether human souls are sparks of the stars.

The passage describes the mind reaching beyond what it can see, asking questions about what lies outside the world. It lists open questions: whether the universe has an end, what shape it has, whether it is joined to or separate from our world, whether matter is made of tiny separate particles or is continuous, and whether the basic elements fight each other or work toward one goal.
Even if a person kept every hour of a long life safe from waste and loss, his time would still be too short to understand immortality. Human life is simply too brief to grasp what lasts forever.

Seneca says he lives according to Nature by giving himself fully to her and by admiring her. Nature, he argues, meant people to do two things, contemplation (quiet thought) and action, and he does both, since contemplation itself involves some action.

Seneca's objector says that choosing a contemplative life for its own pleasure, with no aim beyond quiet thought, makes a difference. Seneca replies that the same difference applies to a public man who never rests and never sets aside time to turn his mind from earthly things to heavenly ones.

Seneca argues that wealth-seeking and hard work should be joined with love of virtue and study, and that virtue kept only in leisure is incomplete. Virtue must be tested in action, putting thoughts into practice.

The passage argues that a wise man may withdraw from public affairs and live for himself, if the right work for him is not available. Even in leisure, he still knows he can do something useful for future generations.

Seneca says that his school holds that Zeno and Chrysippus did more by their writing than they could have done as army generals, office holders or lawmakers for one city. Their teaching gives guidance to later generations and to all peoples, so a good man's leisure for such work cannot be improper.

Seneca asks whether the Stoic teachers Cleanthes, Chrysippus and Zeno lived by their own teaching. He says they did, yet none of them held public office, and the reply given is that they lacked the wealth or rank that usually allows people to take part in public affairs.

Even though these men did not live idle lives, they made their withdrawal from public life more useful to people than the busy efforts of others. So they are thought to have achieved great things, though they took no public office or action.

Seneca says there are three ways of life: pleasure, contemplation (thoughtful study), and action. He suggests that these may amount to the same thing under different names. Each way includes elements of the others, so no one is wholly without contemplation or pleasure.

Seneca grants that there is a real difference between making something your main aim in life and treating it as a side part of another aim. But he argues that the two cannot be fully separated. Thinking without acting, or acting without thinking, does not work, and even the Epicureans, who seek pleasure, act through reason.

Seneca notes that Epicurus himself would sometimes give up pleasure and accept pain, either to avoid being overfull of pleasure or to escape a greater pain. He uses this to argue that all people are drawn to contemplation. Some make it the whole aim of their lives, while for Seneca it is only a place of rest, not the final destination.

According to Chrysippus, a wise person may live in leisure, and should choose it rather than merely put up with it. Stoics hold that the wise person would not take part in running any state. Seneca asks whether it matters if this leisure comes because the state has no use for the wise person or because the wise person withdraws from the state.

Seneca argues that if every state falls short for wise thinkers, then no state suits them. He asks where a wise man could go, pointing to Athens, which condemned Socrates to death and drove Aristotle into exile. He notes that a wise man would not want to join such a state.

Seneca asks whether the wise man should take part in public life in Carthage, a state full of factional fighting, cruelty, and disregard for justice. He answers that the wise man would flee it too. He adds that no existing state would suit the wise man, or let him live in it.

Seneca argues that since the ideal state he has described cannot be found on earth, leisure is necessary for everyone, because nothing better than leisure is available. He compares this to praising sailing while warning that the sea is too dangerous to sail on, which in effect forbids the sailing he praised.

The lines are a quotation of verse about an old warrior. Even in old age he refused rest, kept his helmet on his head, and his hair was white as snow. Seneca uses the image to show a man who keeps working hard late in life.

Seneca describes three kinds of faults he finds in himself. Some are obvious and easy to catch, some are hidden and hard to reach, and some come and go at intervals. He says the last kind is the most troublesome, like a raiding enemy who attacks when he finds an opening and gives no time for either readiness or rest.

Seneca describes his own state: he is not fully free of the faults he fears and hates, yet not fully enslaved to them, so he feels discontented and neither ill nor well. He rejects the idea that virtues grow strong over time, because he knows that even outward qualities such as grandeur and eloquence also grow with time.

Seneca says that habit slowly wears down his ability to tell good people from bad. Long familiarity with both makes him treat them all alike. He admits his mind hangs between two views, leaning toward neither good nor evil, and he will describe this state bit by bit and describe his own case.
The speaker says he loves thrift very much. He prefers plain, cheap bed covers and clothes to fine, showy ones that need careful storage, pressing and cleaning.

The speaker wants simple food. He does not want dishes that need many servants, long preparation, or expensive, far-off ingredients. He wants food that is easy to get, cheap, and easy on both wealth and body.

Seneca says he prefers plain, practical things in his household: a home-raised servant, old silver with no maker's mark, and a table chosen only for use. He wants nothing that is showy, famous, or likely to make guests admire it or envy him.

Seneca describes the luxury of wealthy people: a schoolboy dressed with great show, slaves covered in gold, floors of precious stones, painted ceilings, clear pools around dining guests, and lavish feasts. He suggests that such display is excessive and wasteful, leading an inheritance toward ruin.

Seneca describes visiting a life of showy luxury after long years of plain, frugal living. He says the sight dazzles him and leaves him somewhat sad and unsettled, and he doubts whether the rich life might be better. His principles stay the same, but they are shaken by the experience.

Seneca describes a past intention: he once followed his school's teaching and entered public life to seek high office, including becoming consul. He did not want the honor's trappings for their own sake. His aim was to help his friends, family, fellow citizens, and all people.

Seneca says he follows the Stoic teachers who urged people to take part in public affairs, even though they did not do so themselves. Whenever public business upsets him, or proves disgraceful, difficult, or trivial yet time-consuming, he gladly goes back to a quiet private life at home.

The speaker says that no one will take a day from him unless they give something of equal worth in return. He wants his mind to stay within itself and improve itself, to stay out of other people's affairs, to avoid depending on others' approval, and to keep calm despite public or private troubles.

Seneca says that when reading brave words or noble examples stirs him to act, he feels like rushing into public life, such as helping people in court. But he thinks it is better in philosophy to look at things as they really are, and let the words follow from the things themselves rather than from style.

Seneca advises writing simply, just to pass the time and for oneself, not for fame after death, since everyone is born to die and a quiet death is the least miserable. He also notes that a mind full of lofty ideas tends to reach for grand, showy words that match the importance of its subject.

Seneca admits that when he is moved to speak with more force than usual, he slips into a style that is not his own. He fears he may never fully rise above his normal calm, or that he is in a worse state than he realises, since people tend to judge their own affairs too kindly.

Many people would become wise if they did not think they already were, and if they did not deceive themselves about parts of their character or ignore others on purpose. Seneca says our own flattery of ourselves does more harm than other people's, and few people dare to tell themselves the truth.

The speaker asks a friend for a cure for his constant wavering of mind. He says it is not a serious danger, like a storm, but more like seasickness: unpleasant and unsettling, yet not life-threatening. He asks to be helped while he is still close to land, meaning before the trouble becomes worse.

Seneca compares a troubled state of mind to people who have recovered from a serious illness but still fear a relapse. They keep checking their pulse and worry at every warm feeling. They are no longer ill, but they have not yet grown used to being well.

Seneca tells the reader that the best remedy for a troubled mind is not harsh self-control, anger at oneself, or stern self-reproach. Instead, one should trust oneself and keep to the right path, without being drawn off by the many confused tracks that cross it.

Seneca says that being undisturbed in mind is the greatest good, nearly godlike. He calls this state euthymia in Greek and peace of mind in Latin, and he says a translation need only give the same meaning, not copy the Greek word exactly.

Seneca says the goal of this discussion is a mind that stays steady, content with itself and its surroundings, never lifted up or cast down. He calls this state "peace of mind" and proposes to look at how it can be reached.

Seneca says that people must first bring the whole problem into the open so each person can see his own share of it. He adds that someone who puts himself down suffers less than people trapped by a grand claim or title they have made, who keep up the act out of shame rather than choice.

Seneca describes several kinds of restless or unsettled people. Some keep changing their plans, some drift, and some keep their habits only because they grew old in them. Others stay put not from firm purpose but from dullness, so they keep living the way they already began rather than the way they want.

People who are torn by unfulfilled desires end up dissatisfied with themselves. They either fear to act or fail after trying, so they stay unsettled and will use dishonourable means to reach their goals. When they fail, they feel shame, and their regret is that they failed to get what they wanted, not that they wanted something wrong.

People who regret their past actions and fear to start again slowly fall into constant wavering. They cannot control their passions or follow them, their lives stall, and their minds grow dull from repeated disappointment.

People who have given up public life for idleness and private study find that minds used to action cannot bear it. Lacking inner resources, such a mind, once cut off from business, cannot stand being at home or alone and comes to dislike its own company.

Restlessness, self-dissatisfaction and unwilling idleness come from keeping one's troubles hidden. When a person is ashamed to admit what is wrong and holds the feelings inside, the pent-up desires have no outlet and end up crowding and choking each other.

Restlessness and low spirits come from a mind that is kept waiting by hopes, and hurt when they fail. The same state shows in people who hate having nothing to do and resent others' progress. Idleness breeds envy, so those who cannot succeed themselves want everyone else to fail.

Envy of others' success and despair over one's own leads a person to resent fortune, complain about the times, and brood in seclusion until they sicken of themselves. Seneca says the restless mind seeks busy activity to escape itself, the way a sore longs to be touched or an itch to be scratched.

People ruled by desires enjoy restless discomforts, such as tossing and turning in bed or cooling off in one position after another. Seneca compares them to a sick man who changes posture constantly, never staying in one for long, and treats each change as a cure.

People set out on aimless travels, by sea and by land, trying to ease a restless mind that is never content with where it is. Each new place is chosen, then dropped, as they look for the next one to satisfy them.

Seneca is describing people who keep changing their surroundings, going back to the city's noise or to violent shows, and then moving on to another sight. He says this restlessness is a way of running away from oneself, quoting the poet Lucretius to support the point.

Seneca's point is that the trouble lies in the person, not in the place they travel to, since escaping yourself is impossible. People who cannot bear work, pleasure or any task for long grow weary of everything, and some have even been driven to suicide.

Seneca is quoting the philosopher Athenodorus, who says the best cure for restless boredom is to take up public business and the duties of a citizen. He compares this to athletes who spend most of their time building up the strength their training depends on.

A person who trains the mind for public life is better off working than sitting idle. Someone who aims to serve his fellow citizens and all people does good and improves himself while busy with affairs, working for both the public and private individuals.

Seneca reports an argument that a good person should leave public life, since innocence is rarely safe among ambitious rivals and gets more harm than help there. A great mind can grow just as well in private life. He answers that caged animals are restrained, but people often do their greatest work in retirement.

A man who steps back from public life can still serve the state. He does so by using his mind, voice and advice to benefit others, such as by teaching young men virtue or restraining those chasing wealth and luxury. Such a person serves the public even while holding no official post.

Seneca asks which is more useful: a magistrate who settles legal cases between citizens and foreigners, or a teacher who shows people virtues such as justice, courage and a good conscience. He concludes that if a man moves his time from public office to philosophy, he is not abandoning his duty.

Being a soldier is not only about fighting in the front line. Guarding the gates, keeping watch, and looking after the arsenal are less dangerous jobs with no bloodshed, but they still count as military service.

Seneca says that once a person commits to philosophy, they will lose their disgust with life and gain friends, since good people are drawn to virtue wherever it is found. Withdrawing from society and living alone, he warns, leads to restless idleness, where time is wasted on pointless projects.

Some people spend their lives so that they have a clear record of gains and losses, and others so that nothing is left of their time. The writer calls the second case very shameful. Often an old man has only his years to show that he has lived long.

Seneca disagrees with Athenodorus, who withdrew from public life too quickly. He grants that a person sometimes must withdraw, but says it should be done slowly and with dignity, like a soldier who keeps his standards and honour. Such a person earns more respect from enemies and stays safer.

When Fortune (bad luck or outside circumstances) blocks a virtuous person from acting, he should not simply give up and hide. He should be more careful about taking public office and find another way to serve the state. If he cannot serve in the army, he can seek civic honours instead.

If a man cannot speak in court, he can still help others quietly with advice. If he is not free to take part in public life, he can still be a loyal friend and a moderate guest. The point is that a person can keep doing good even when public life is closed to him.

Seneca says that a person who is shut out of public life at home, such as judging in the courts or speaking to the people, should look beyond Rome to the wide world. The Stoic idea of being a citizen of the world is presented as a way to find a larger field for showing virtue.

Seneca tells his friend that his frustration with public life comes from his own choice. He will only take the top offices, like consul, so he is blocked from many other roles. He asks whether a soldier who would serve only as general would be seen as reasonable.

Even if you cannot take the front line in a struggle, you should still play your part through voice, encouragement, example and spirit. Even if you are cut off from action, staying firm and cheering others on still helps. If silenced, you can still help in quiet.

Even when a good person is unseen, unheard, or unable to act openly, their virtue still does good. Seneca compares it to a remedy that helps by its smell as well as by its taste, so goodness spreads its benefit whatever its circumstances.

Seneca says it is best to mix rest with work when chance events or public affairs stop a person from living a fully active life. Even a person who has withdrawn from most activity still has room for honourable action.

Seneca describes Athens under the Thirty Tyrants, who killed about thirteen hundred of the city's best citizens and grew more cruel as they went on. He says that even though Athens had its famous court, Senate and assembly, these institutions were overrun by the tyrants and their killers.

Seneca describes a city ruled by so many tyrants that they could have formed one ruler's bodyguard. People there could not even imagine winning back their freedom, because they had no one to kill so many tyrants, the way Harmodius once killed a tyrant in Athens.

Socrates stayed in the city even under the Thirty Tyrants, the oligarchy that ruled Athens. He comforted grieving citizens, encouraged those who had lost hope in the state, and rebuked wealthy men into regretting their greed. He remained free in spirit while the Thirty ruled over him.

Seneca points to Socrates, whom Athens put to death in prison, to argue that a wise man can still show his worth under oppression. He adds that a prosperous, free state can be ruled by arrogance, envy and other cowardly vices.

We should adjust how far we go to fit the circumstances and the chances life offers, but never freeze in fear. The best person keeps their virtue visible even when danger surrounds them, because staying safe does not mean hiding away.

Seneca says that when public life is hard to serve in, a person should take more time for leisure and literary study. He compares this to a sailor putting into harbour during a dangerous voyage, withdrawing from public business on his own terms rather than waiting to be forced out.
Before acting, a person should first examine himself, then the task he plans to carry out, and then the people for whose benefit he does it or with whom he works.

We tend to overestimate what we can do, so we need an honest view of our own abilities. Examples given are a man who trusts his speaking skill too far, one who expects more from his property than it can yield, and one who gives a frail body a hard task.

Seneca says that people whose temperament does not suit public life are better off in private leisure. Those who are too shy, too proud, too quick to anger, or too fond of risky jokes should avoid public office and court work, since their outspoken nature could bring them to ruin.

Before taking on a task, judge it against your own strength, since a load heavier than its bearer will crush him. Some matters should also be turned down because they are not very important in themselves but breed many more tasks.

Do not take on work you cannot leave whenever you choose. Choose tasks you can finish, or at least hope to finish. Avoid undertakings that grow larger as they proceed and will not stop where you meant them to.

Choose companions carefully, Seneca says, so that your time is not wasted on people who do not deserve it, and some people feel they are owed favours by you. He quotes Athenodorus, who would not even dine with someone who was ungrateful for the invitation. The point is that he would avoid those who repay friends with meals, treating food as a gift that earns thanks.

Seneca says that people who enjoy good food only when watched will not enjoy eating alone. A person should choose between active public life and quiet study, depending on natural talent. As an example, Isocrates steered Ephorus away from public speaking toward writing histories, because forcing a mind into work it does not suit achieves nothing.

Good friendship brings the mind great delight. A good friend is someone you can trust with your secrets, whose advice helps and whose company lifts your mood. Friends should therefore be chosen from men with few strong desires, because vices spread from person to person like a contagion.

Seneca compares choosing friends to avoiding infected people during a plague: pick companions who are as untainted by worldly corruption as possible, since mixing healthy with rotten spreads the disease. He adds that one need not insist on a wise man alone, because such a person is very hard to find.

Seneca says that when good men are rare, you should accept someone who is less than ideal. He notes that in better times you could choose from famous philosophers or from the age of Cato, which had both good and very bad men, and that Cato's virtue showed up against that contrast. Today, with so few good men, the choice must be less strict.
Avoid gloomy people who complain about everything that happens. Even if such a person stays loyal and friendly, a companion with a bitter, complaining mind still wrecks your peace of mind.

Seneca says that property causes more human suffering than anything else. He compares money's troubles with deaths, illnesses, fears, regrets and hardships, and claims that the troubles caused by money outweigh all of these.

Never having had money hurts less than losing it, because a poor person has less to lose and so less to grieve over. Seneca also says the rich do not bear losses better than the poor, since a wound hurts a large body and a small one equally.

Bion's joke is that losing hair hurts bald and hairy men alike, so rich and poor suffer equally when they lose money. Still, it is easier never to gain wealth than to lose it, so those who never had fortune are happier than those who lost it. Diogenes avoided this by owning nothing that could be taken from him.

Seneca argues that a person who cannot lose anything is happy, even if others call that state poverty or need. He says few people can claim such security, since most are misers, cheats or robbers who face loss. Doubting the happiness of Diogenes, a famous poor philosopher, is like doubting the gods, who own no property and so cannot lose any.
Seneca asks why people admire wealth. He says the gods own no property yet give everything, so a person who has stripped away outside possessions should not be called poor but seen as godlike.

Seneca contrasts two men. Demetrius, a freed slave who grew very rich, needed a long list to keep track of his many slaves. Diogenes, the Cynic philosopher, had only one slave, who ran away, and he refused to chase him, saying it would be shameful if he could not live without his slave.

Seneca describes Diogenes, a Stoic-school figure, who said that Fortune has no claim on him, since his runaway slave had left as a free man. The point is that a person with many slaves must feed, clothe, and guard them, and deal with their tears and curses. Someone who depends on nothing except what he can easily give up is happier.

Since most people cannot bear loss as calmly as a wise person would, Seneca says they should keep their wealth small so that fortune's blows hit them less. He compares this to a soldier whose body fits inside his armour, while a very large man is more exposed to wounds. The best amount of property is just enough to avoid poverty and no more.

Seneca says that a person will be content with a modest amount of wealth if they have first learned to value thrift, since no riches are enough without it and any amount is enough with it. He urges us to judge things by their use rather than their decoration, and to satisfy hunger, thirst and desire only as far as need requires.

The passage urges a simple, disciplined way of life. It asks readers to follow the customs of their ancestors rather than new fashions, to restrain desire, anger and pride, to accept poverty calmly, and to find their wealth within themselves rather than in luck or fortune.

Seneca says that we cannot fully protect ourselves from misfortune, so it is better to keep our affairs small and simple. He adds that a minor setback can sometimes cure a worse problem, and that when a person ignores gentler advice, loss or disgrace may do them good. One harm can thus balance another.

Seneca says we should live simply: eat without showing off, have fewer servants, wear practical clothes, and keep a modest house. He adds that even books are only worthwhile within limits, since owning huge libraries that no one can read through in a lifetime serves no purpose.

Seneca says that a student buried under huge numbers of books learns nothing, so it is better to study a few writers closely than to read many quickly. He adds that the great library at Alexandria, with its forty thousand burned books, was praised by some as a royal monument, such as the historian Livy did.

Seneca criticises owning books only to show off, like expensive dining-room decorations, rather than to study them. He says a person may collect as many books as they need, but not for display. Even spending on books is wrong if it goes too far.

Seneca criticizes people who collect large libraries of books they never read. They buy fine bookcases and rare or worthless works, yawn among them, and admire the look of the book spines. He says a library has become a status item, like a bath, and he would excuse such owners only if they truly loved learning.
Costly books of learned writing, with their decorative illustrations, are bought only to be displayed and to decorate the walls. Their owners do not use them for learning.

If your life is caught in trouble you cannot escape, Seneca says, it helps to remember how prisoners in chains feel. At first the chains hurt, but once they stop fighting them, they learn to bear them, and in time they bear them easily. He adds that every situation still offers some pleasures.

Seneca says that habit helps people bear misfortune, because it soon makes us used to even the hardest evils. Nobody could endure trouble if it kept its full force from the start. He adds that everyone is bound to Fortune, or luck, whether the chain is loose and gold or tight and cheap.

Everyone is held in some kind of bondage, and even those who seem to control others are bound too. People differ only in their chains: public office, wealth, birth, or obligations to others. So, Seneca says, each person should accept his own situation, complain as little as possible, and make the most of whatever good is available to him.

No situation is so miserable that a calm, fair-minded person cannot find some advantages in it. Good sense can make hard circumstances easier to bear, and desires are best kept within what is close at hand, since they cannot be shut in completely.

Seneca advises setting aside goals that are impossible or very hard to reach, and pursuing those that are close and within hope. He says all things are equally unimportant, though they look different on the outside, and that people in high positions should not be envied, since their position is steeper and harder than it appears.

Seneca says that people in powerful, risky positions are safer if they are modest about their status and bring their fortunes closer to those of ordinary people. Those who cannot step down without a dangerous fall should be just, merciful and generous, so that others will help break their fall.

The main idea is that the way to escape swinging between hope and fear is to set a limit on your successes and stop on your own before fortune forces you to. Stopping early keeps your desires within bounds, so they do not drive you toward huge, uncertain undertakings.

The wise man is not timid about fortune, the changing events of life. He feels sure of himself and faces misfortune directly. He treats even his own body and self as things he may lose, so he does not depend on them.

The wise person treats his possessions, and even his life, as things lent to him for a time. He looks after them carefully, like a trustee caring for property that belongs to someone else. When they are taken back, he gives them up without complaint, thanking the lender for what he had.

Seneca imagines giving back to Nature everything she lent him, including his life, and says he does so willingly. He asks what hardship there is in returning to the place one came from, meaning death is simply a return to where we began.

Seneca says a person cannot live well unless they know how to die well, so life should be valued as something cheap. He notes that people admire gladiators who face death without fear and despise those who clutch at their lives. He adds that we often die because we fear death, and Fortune treats our lives as entertainment, asking why she should spare a coward.

Someone who fears death cannot live as a living person should. Whoever accepts from birth that death is fixed for them and expects every misfortune can meet it calmly, so nothing comes as a shock. Those who never think about misfortune are the ones it hits hardest.

Seneca says that illness, captivity, disaster and fire are things he always expected, because he knew what kind of world he was born into. He has seen many deaths and disasters around him, so he asks why he should be surprised when danger finally reaches him.

Seneca says that many people never consider the dangers they might face before they start a journey. He defends quoting a line from Publilius, a playwright he thinks is poor overall but sometimes writes well: "What one hath suffered may befall us all."

Seneca says that a person who keeps in mind that other people's misfortunes could happen to him too will be prepared before trouble arrives. Once a disaster has struck, it is too late to train the mind to endure it. He points out that wealth is never safe from poverty, hunger and beggary.
Every high office or royal power can quickly turn into disgrace, exile, or death, sometimes within an hour. So no position in life lasts, and whatever has happened to others can happen to anyone.

Seneca uses the examples of Pompey and Sejanus to show that wealth and high office do not guarantee security. Pompey, though he owned many rivers, died of hunger and thirst in the house of a relative, and Sejanus held power that was as great as any could be.

Seneca gives examples of rulers who fell from great power. Sejanus, a favourite of the emperor Tiberius, was torn apart by the mob after the Senate condemned him, and nothing large enough was left to drag to the river. Croesus saw his own funeral fire lit and put out while he lived, and Jugurtha was led captive in Rome within a year of being feared there.

Seneca points out that kings have been seized, exiled, or forced into exile by the emperor Gaius's guards, so sudden reversals are common. He says that if you do not expect that anything at all may happen to you, misfortune gains power over you, and a person who foresees it can take that power away.

Seneca says we should avoid working for things that are empty or pointless, and avoid wanting what we cannot get. Sadness, he says, usually comes from one of two things: failing to get what we worked for, or being ashamed after we have got it.

Seneca says people should cut down on the aimless wandering most men do, going from house to house, theatre to market, poking into others' affairs. Such people go out with no real plan and end up doing whatever happens to come their way, not what they had decided to do.
