Seneca says that many people move about with no real aim, like ants that climb a bush only to come back down with nothing gained. He calls this way of living restless idleness.

Seneca describes people who rush about busily without purpose. They push past others and drag them along, going to greetings, funerals, trials and weddings of people they barely know. When they get home they cannot say why they went out, and the next day they repeat the same round.

Seneca says that restless people are not restless because of hard work. They are driven by false ideas. They chase things that look attractive, without seeing that those things are worthless, so they wander the city for empty reasons.

A busy man goes out at dawn with no real business, paying calls on important people and being turned away by many. He finds that the hardest person to find at home is himself. This restless habit leads to gossip and prying into secrets that are dangerous to share or hear.

Democritus taught that a person who wants peace should not take on much business, public or private. He meant unnecessary business only. When business is truly necessary, a person should take it on, even if it is large and endless.

Unless a clear duty calls us, it is better to stay still. Acting often leaves us at the mercy of chance, so we should not count on any plan succeeding. Seneca's examples, such as sailing or holding office, show plans that are always made with the proviso "unless something prevents it."

The wise man is not protected from the ordinary chances of life, only from its errors of judgment. Things do not go as he wishes, but he expects that they may not go his way, so disappointment hurts him less.

We should not cling too tightly to our assigned place in life. We can accept other conditions that chance brings, as long as we do not become fickle, since fickleness most disturbs peace of mind. Stubbornness is also unhappy, because fate often forces it to give way, but fickleness is worse because it never holds back.

The passage says that the mind should turn away from outside things and look to itself, relying on and taking pleasure in its own resources. It should not dwell on losses but read even misfortunes in a good light. To show this, it recalls Zeno, who, after losing all his property in a shipwreck, said that fortune was pushing him to follow philosophy with less baggage.

Two men facing death at the hands of tyrants stay calm and defy them. Theodorus tells his threatener that he does not care whether his body is buried or left to rot. Julius Kanus thanks Gaius for ordering his execution, since it ends any false hope he might have had.

The passage describes a man, Canus, who was condemned by the emperor Gaius and answered him in a daring way. Seneca cannot be sure what Canus meant: he might have been mocking Gaius's cruelty, mocking his madness, or calmly welcoming death as freedom. Whatever the meaning, Canus's reply was brave, and he expected no mercy, since Gaius always carried out such orders.

The passage describes a man awaiting execution who stayed calm. Shortly before being called to die, he was playing a board game, and when summoned he joked about the score and asked the officer to witness that he was ahead. Seneca's point is that the man treated even his death with lightness, playing the game with full attention rather than despair.

Seneca's passage describes a great man facing death, who, even as he is about to die, keeps searching for the truth about whether the soul lives on. His friends grieve, but he says he will soon know the answer himself. Walking with his teacher, he is asked what he is thinking, which shows he keeps his mind on philosophical questions to the end.

Kanus, a Stoic facing death, resolves to watch whether his spirit is aware of leaving his body. He promises to report back to his friends what he finds. Seneca praises him for staying calm and learning even at the moment of dying.

Seneca praises a man who lived as a true philosopher, and says he will not quickly drop the subject. He promises to hand this man's memory down to future generations. The man is named as one of the many victims of Gaius, the emperor Caligula.

Even after personal worries are removed, a person can still fall into hatred of humanity. Seeing how rare honesty, innocence and faithfulness are, and how often crime, greed and ambition succeed, the mind feels as if all virtue has collapsed and that good qualities can no longer be hoped for.

Seneca says we should treat the faults of ordinary people as ridiculous rather than hateful. He recommends the attitude of Democritus, who laughed at human folly, over that of Heraclitus, who wept at it. Life is better met with mockery than with grief.

Laughing at human folly is better than mourning it, Seneca says, because laughter still hopes people can improve, while weeping treats their faults as hopeless. A person who laughs at the whole world shows a greater mind, since they are only slightly affected and see none of it as truly important, serious, or sad.

Human life is no better than its beginnings, the saying of Bion goes, so each person should see for themselves what makes them happy or sad. The passage advises meeting people's wrongs and vices calmly, neither laughing at them nor weeping over them. Feeling others' pain endlessly is misery, and enjoying it is cruel.

Seneca says that a person should feel grief for their own misfortunes only as much as reason justifies, not as much as social custom expects. Many people weep only when others are watching, and they feel shamed if they do not weep when everyone else does. He adds that people have become so used to following others' opinions that even grief is now faked.

Seneca says that it is natural to feel sad when good men meet bad ends. He lists Socrates forced to die in prison, Rutilius exiled, Pompey and Cicero killed by their own followers, and Cato killing himself. Seeing this, one may wonder what a good man can hope for.

Seneca says that if great men faced death bravely, we should admire and copy their courage. If they died weakly, we should not copy that weakness, since nothing is lost by it. He ends by praising the brave, saying that the braver a person is, the happier they are.

Seneca says that a man who has escaped misfortune in life should not fear death. If someone shrinks back at death and clings to life, Seneca says he must be pushed toward it. Seneca will not mourn a man who dies cheerfully, and a man who dies weeping makes himself unworthy of tears.

Seneca asks whether anyone should grieve for Hercules, Regulus or Cato, who died in painful ways. His answer is implied: these men spent only a short time suffering and in exchange gained lasting fame and eternal life.

Hiding your true feelings and keeping up a false front causes constant trouble. The effort of watching yourself is a torment, and you are always afraid of being caught. Even when the pretence works, life is neither happy nor safe while you wear a mask.

Living openly, without hiding one's character, is good in itself, even though some people may look down on those who live this way. Seneca says it is better to be scorned for simplicity than to live with constant pretence. He adds that simplicity must still be moderate, since simple living is not the same as careless living.

Seneca says we should often withdraw into ourselves, because being with people unlike us disturbs our calm and reopens old wounds in the mind. He advises alternating between solitude and company, so that each cures the discomfort of the other: solitude restores us when crowds weary us, and crowds restore us when we tire of being alone.

The mind should not stay under constant strain. It needs relaxing through amusement. Seneca gives examples: Socrates played with boys, Cato drank wine to rest after public work, and Scipio danced in a manly way at festivals, which he saw no shame in even before his enemies.

Minds need rest in order to work well, just as fertile fields need fallow periods to stay productive. Constant labour wears the mind down into numbness and sluggishness, while a short break restores its strength and liveliness.

Play and amusement appeal to people for a natural reason, but too much of them drains the mind of seriousness and strength. Sleep is the comparison: it refreshes us, yet stretched over days it becomes death. Relaxing your grip on something is not the same as dropping it altogether.

Seneca says that lawmakers set up festivals so people would be encouraged to be cheerful, and that busy men should mix work with relaxation. As an example, he describes the orator Asinius Pollio, who stopped all business after the tenth hour and used that time to recover from the day's tiredness.

Seneca argues that the mind needs periodic rest, just as the body does. He gives examples: people who nap at midday, Roman senators who could not start new business late in the day, and soldiers who share night watches or are excused after returning from duty. Rest, he says, feeds the mind and restores its strength.

Seneca says that walks in the open air, rides, travel, change of scenery, social meals and some wine can lift the spirits and ease the mind. He adds that wine, taken in moderation short of drunkenness, can wash away troubles, much as it cures some illnesses.

Wine is called Liber, the name of a god, because it frees the mind from worries and makes a person bolder in what they try. The passage adds that moderation is healthy both with freedom and with wine, and notes that Solon and Arcesilaus drank heavily.

Seneca defends Cato, who was accused of drunkenness, by saying that critics would have a hard time showing Cato did wrong, and that the charge could even be turned into praise. He adds that the mind should not drink often, but that it sometimes needs a break from strict seriousness. He supports this with a Greek poet, Plato, and Aristotle.

Seneca says that the mind cannot speak in lofty, elevated language while it stays calm and within its ordinary habits. It needs to be stirred up, like a horse driven into frenzy, before it can rise to heights it would never reach on its own.

Seneca says he has described what keeps peace of mind, what restores it, and what stops the faults that secretly wear it down. But none of these methods is strong enough to keep such a fleeting good unless the wavering mind is guarded with constant, close attention.
Most people complain that nature gave us only a short life, and that it passes so fast we die just as we are ready to enjoy it. Even great men have voiced this complaint, not only ordinary people.

Seneca recalls the saying that art (skill or learning) takes a long time while life is short. He also mentions Aristotle's complaint that Nature gave some animals very long lives but gave humans shorter ones, even though people are born for great deeds.

Life is not too short by nature; people waste most of the time they are given through luxury, carelessness, and pursuits with no good purpose. Only at the end do they realise it is gone. So we do not receive a short life, we make it short.
Great wealth given to a careless owner is soon wasted, while modest wealth in the hands of a wise keeper grows. Life works the same way: it offers much to the person who knows how to use it well.

Seneca argues that people wrongly blame Nature for short lives, since life is long enough if used well. Instead, most people waste their time on greed, pointless work, drink, idleness, ambition, war, or aimless wandering. The passage ends by saying he believes a line of Virgil's, which speaks of life passing too fast for those who do not use it well.

Seneca says that people held down by vices do not really live; they only pass time. Vices keep them from standing up, looking at the truth, or finding peace. Even when they rest for a moment, their desires keep them restless, like the sea that keeps rolling after a storm. He adds that this is true not only of openly bad people.

Seneca says that the people others envy for their success are often harmed by it. Wealth weighs them down, talent for speaking and showing off can cost them their lives, indulgence wears them out, and crowds of dependent followers take away their freedom.

Seneca says that people in every rank of society spend their lives serving others, whether as defenders, defendants, jurors or supporters. Even the famous are caught in the same pattern, with each person tied to someone else. As a result, nobody truly belongs to himself or spends time on his own life.

Some people angrily complain that powerful patrons refuse to see them. Seneca says this is unreasonable, since those same people never take time to examine their own conscience. The patron may eventually grant an audience, but a person who ignores himself never hears his own complaints.

Seneca is saying that a person should not ask others to do favours for him. He points out that the one who asks is often too busy even to spend time alone with himself, so he cannot even claim to have spent time with other people by choice.

People will fiercely defend their land and property against small claims, yet they let others take over their time and lives, even inviting them in. Nobody wants to give away money, but people freely hand out their lives to many others.

People guard their money carefully, yet they waste time freely, even though time is what they should be most careful with. Seneca then imagines speaking to an old man of about a hundred, pointing out how near the end of his life he is.

Seneca tells the reader to list how their time was really spent: on debts, on a lover, on superiors, on clients, on quarrels, on servants, on errands, on illness they caused themselves, and on idle hours. He says that when this is added up, the person will find they have not lived as many years as they think.

Seneca asks the reader to recall how little of their time was spent on what they intended. Much of life has been taken by others, by grief, desire, idle talk, and so little remains that the reader will see they are dying before their time.

People act as if they will live forever. They forget they are mortal, do not notice how much of their time has already passed, and spend their days carelessly. They fear everything, as mortals do, yet want everything, as if they were immortal.

Many people plan to enjoy leisure only after their working years, such as at fifty or sixty. Seneca asks what guarantee they have that they will live that long, and he suggests it is shameful to leave only the leftover time for themselves. Starting a real life at the very end is too late.
It is foolish to forget that we will die, and to delay sensible advice until middle or old age. People choose to start living properly at an age that very few people actually reach.

Powerful men often say they long for leisure and would prefer it to all their privileges, and some would give up their high position if they safely could. Even Emperor Augustus, who was given more blessings than anyone, prayed for rest from the burdens of rule and comforted himself with the hope of one day living for himself alone.

Augustus, the Roman emperor, wrote to the Senate that he would rather act on his promises about retirement than talk about them. Yet he took pleasure in speaking of his longed-for rest, even though it was still far off, so he enjoyed it in imagination.

Seneca describes Augustus, the first Roman emperor, who held power over men and nations yet wished his happiest day would be the day he gave up that greatness. He had learned that his fame came with heavy labour and hidden anxiety, and that it was won through civil wars, bloodshed and campaigns across many lands.

The passage describes how Augustus, while busy with wars and expanding Rome's borders, faced plots at home. Several nobles were plotting to kill him, and after he escaped them, his own daughter Julia and young men bound to her by adultery alarmed him in his old age.

Seneca describes a ruler who kept removing threats to the state, such as the figures Paulus and Antonius's mistress, yet new troubles always appeared in their place. Because of this, he longed for leisure, and all his work aimed at reaching it, even though he could grant almost any wish others had.

Seneca describes how Cicero, buffeted by rival politicians and enemies during the crisis of the Roman republic, was eventually exiled. Cicero could bear neither good fortune nor bad with calm. Seneca suggests he must have cursed the consulship he had always praised, and he quotes Cicero's despairing letter to Atticus after Pompey's defeat.

Seneca quotes Cicero, who called himself "half a prisoner" at his country villa and complained about his life. Seneca says a wise man would never describe himself that way. The wise man is always fully free, and is greater than all others because he is greater than Fortune, or chance.

Drusus, a Roman politician, pushed hard reforms and gathered a large crowd of supporters. He could not carry his plans through, and he could not drop them once he had begun. He then complained that his whole life, from childhood on, had been restless, with no time off.

The speaker argues that a man who was bold and ambitious in the courts while still a boy was bound to become a serious nuisance in public and private life as an adult. So he cannot now complain that he never had a childhood free of work.

Seneca notes that some doubted whether a certain man, who died from a sudden groin wound, had killed himself, though all agreed his death came at a fitting time. He adds that many people, admired by others, have confessed they hated their own lives, yet their complaints changed nothing, and they soon returned to their usual ways.

Seneca says that even a very long human life seems short, because vices (bad habits and faults) waste any amount of time. Our ordinary span can be made longer by sensible living, but people let it slip away. They neither grasp time nor hold on to it, and treat it as worthless, as if they could always get more.

Seneca ranks people who spend their lives on drinking and sexual indulgence as the most disgraceful of those wasting their time. He argues that others, such as misers, angry men, and warmongers, at least chase something like glory or make mistakes that are human, while the gluttons and lustful sin in a shameful way.

Seneca says that people fill every hour of their lives with busy or troubling affairs, such as scheming, fearing, flattering, making financial promises, and feasting. Even their pleasures and pains leave them no rest. He adds that no one can do anything well, such as speaking or writing, while busy with other things.

Seneca says that a mind busy with other things cannot take in lessons about life. Business people know little about living, because it is harder to learn than any craft. Other skills can be picked up quickly, but learning to live, and even to die, takes a whole lifetime.

Many people give up wealth, work and pleasure to learn how to live, yet most die admitting they still do not know how. Only a rare person, free from ordinary weakness, guards his time so closely that none of it is taken by others. Such a person, Seneca says, has a long life, because all of his time is spent on himself.

Seneca says that busy public men, who give most of their time to others, do not have enough time for themselves. Even they sometimes complain, "I am not allowed to live my own life," because the people who need their help keep pulling them away from themselves.

Seneca asks how many of our days are taken up by other people's demands, such as lawsuits, political ambition, feigned illness for inheritance, and empty friendships. He says that if we add up our days, only a very few remain that we have not given away for such purposes.

People who have reached high public positions, such as the consulship (the fasces were the rods carried before a magistrate), often wish them over as soon as they have them. A man who gives public games wants them ended, and a busy lawyer longs for the court holidays. The point is that people keep wishing away the very things they once desired.

Most people rush through life, wanting the future and tired of the present. A person who plans all his time for his own purposes, as if laying out his whole life, feels neither hope nor fear about tomorrow. He has already known and enjoyed every pleasure life offers, so nothing new is left to gain.

Seneca says that a wise man's life is already secure from chance, so he can gain nothing essential and lose nothing essential. Having many years, marked by wrinkles or grey hair, does not mean a person has lived long. Such a person has only been alive for a long time.

Seneca asks whether a sailor caught by a storm right after leaving port, and blown in circles by shifting winds, could be said to have travelled far. His answer is no: he has only been tossed about. The point is that constant movement is not the same as making progress.

Seneca says people readily ask others for their time and readily give it, yet neither side thinks about the time itself. Because time is invisible and has no physical form, people treat it as worth very little, even though it is the most precious thing we have.

People pay high prices for gifts, money and services, but they treat time as if it were free and give it away carelessly. Yet when they are sick or facing death, they will beg their doctor and give up everything they own to stay alive, which shows how inconsistent they are.

If a person could see how many years were left to them, as they can see the years already lived, they would use those few years with care. Since no one knows when their time will end, the time they have is what they should guard most closely.

People often tell those they love most that they will give them some of their own years. They do give them, without realizing it, but in a way that costs the giver the time while the receiver gains nothing from it.

Some people do not notice where their time comes from, so they put up with losing it without seeing the loss. But no one can give back lost years. Once life begins, it runs on without restarting or undoing what it has already done.

Time passes steadily and cannot be slowed or stopped, not by a king or a nation. Whatever you are busy with, life keeps moving on, and death will arrive at some point, whether one is ready for it or not.

Seneca says it is foolish for people to work hard now so they can enjoy life later, because they put off living. Waiting for tomorrow takes away today, and so it is the greatest waste of life and the biggest barrier to really living.

Seneca says that people give away the time they control and hold on to what they cannot control, so they should live in the present, since the future is uncertain. He supports this with a line from a poet, which says that the best days of unhappy people are the first to pass.

Time slips away quickly, so one should seize it at once rather than hesitate, and use it as eagerly as one would drink from a fast-flowing stream. The poet is said to mock our endless plans by speaking of "the first day" rather than "the first age."

Seneca says people waste time as if life were long, though each day passes quickly. He argues that the people who suffer most are busy ones whose minds stay childish, so old age finds them unprepared to face it.

Busy people do not notice how fast their lives pass. Old age comes on them suddenly, just as travellers absorbed in talk or reading reach their destination without realising they are close. Life moves at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake.

Seneca says he could list many proofs that busy people have the shortest lives. He then quotes Fabianus, a teacher he admired, who said that passions must be attacked head-on and defeated, and that clever arguments must be crushed, not just scratched.

Life has three parts: past, present and future. The present is brief and the future uncertain, but the past is certain and cannot be taken away by chance. Busy people neglect it, because they will not look back at wasted time, which shows their faults only when they review it.

Only a person whose past deeds would stand up to his own conscience looks back on them willingly. Someone who has been ambitious, arrogant, cruel, dishonest, greedy or wasteful has reason to fear his memories. Yet the past is also a sacred possession that no misfortune can take away.

Only the present is ours, and even it comes one hour at a time. Past days, by contrast, can be recalled and studied at will, but only a calm mind has the leisure to look back over its life. Busy people, Seneca says, are like oxen under a yoke, unable to turn aside or look behind them.

Time given to people is wasted if their minds cannot hold it, just as water poured into a leaking vessel is lost. Present time is so brief that it seems to hardly exist, since it is always moving on and cannot be delayed, like the heavens that never stop moving.
Busy people have only the present moment, and it is so brief they cannot hold onto it. When their attention is spread over many tasks, they lose even that.

People want to live long, so they pray for extra years, lie about their age, and fool themselves as if they could trick fate. When illness reminds them they are mortal, they die in fear, seeming to be dragged out of life rather than leaving it calmly.

People who are seriously ill often promise that, if they recover, they will finally live for themselves and rest. They then see that their hard work was wasted on things they never enjoyed. By contrast, a person whose life is not taken up by demanding business has enough time, because none of it is given away to others.

The wise man's time is not left to chance, wasted through carelessness, spent on showy giving, or left unused. Every part of it is put to good use, so a small amount is enough. Therefore, when his last day comes, he faces death calmly and without delay.

Seneca is answering a question about who he means by "busy men." He says he does not mean only the lawyers and office-seekers of Rome, who are crowded, pushed about and kept running to their patrons' doors, or who chase profit from public auctions.

Seneca argues that some people who have withdrawn from public life are not truly at leisure. Their retirement is still filled with anxious busywork, such as fussing over rare bronzes or rusty metal, or watching wrestlers. He calls this kind of occupation idleness in disguise.

Seneca mocks people who spend their time on pointless concerns. He describes wealthy men who sort their slaves by age and colour, keep fashionable athletes, and spend hours at the barber's, growing furious if a hair is out of place.

Seneca mocks people who become furious when their hair is cut or badly arranged. He asks whether they would rather see the state ruined than their hair disturbed, and whether they care more for looks than for health or honour. He then asks if such people, who spend their lives on combs and mirrors, can really be called idle.

Seneca describes people who spend their lives on music: composing, listening, learning songs, and bending their voices into elaborate tunes. Even when asked to attend to serious matters, they hum to themselves. He says such people are not truly at leisure but are busy with trifles.

Seneca describes how busy people are at dinner parties. Hosts anxiously arrange their silverware, servants are trained to move quickly, and food is carved with great skill, all with close attention. He says these banquet preparations cannot count as free or unoccupied time.

Seneca criticizes wealthy people who do everything for show, even eating and drinking, and who let their daily routine be set by others. He says they have become so weak and dependent that they cannot tell for themselves when they are hungry.

A wealthy idler, carried out of the bath and set in his chair, asks whether he is seated. Seneca argues that someone who cannot even tell he is sitting down has lost track of his own life, and he is unsure whether to pity the man more if the ignorance is real or feigned.

Seneca says that some people are so lost in their vices that they enjoy their faults, seeing them as signs of a good life, and they hate to be thought aware of what they do. He adds that comic writers who mock luxury leave out more vices than they invent, because the vices of his age are so many and so strange.

Seneca says that a man who needs someone else to tell him whether he is sitting or standing has lost his senses through luxury. Such a man is not truly at leisure; he is only half alive. Only the person who knows for himself that he is at leisure really has it, so this man cannot make use of his time.

Seneca says that many people waste their lives on games such as draughts, ball games, and sunbathing. He adds that people are not truly at leisure if their pleasures are as busy as work. He also says that scholars who spend their time on pointless literary questions are busy triflers, and that there are many of them in Rome.

Seneca says that the Greeks had a habit of asking pointless scholarly questions, such as how many rowers Ulysses had or which of Homer's two epics came first. Such questions do not benefit a person privately, and sharing them only makes the asker seem tiresome rather than learned.

Seneca says that Romans have become eager to learn useless facts, such as which general first won a sea battle or first used elephants in a triumph. He admits these stories concern great deeds but adds nothing real to glory, so the knowledge is not useful, though it holds people's interest as a kind of folly.
Claudius got the nickname Caudex. In early Rome, caudex meant a block of wood made of many planks, and the word was also used for public record books and for a kind of cargo boat on the Tiber.

Seneca mocks trivial historical facts that people think worth knowing. He gives two examples: how a Valerius got a family name from conquering Messana, and how Sulla was first to release lions in the circus, a show that had only been done with chained animals before. The point is that such details add nothing to a good life.

Seneca says that learning which Pompey was the first to stage a show with eighteen elephants fighting convicts serves no useful purpose. He criticises Pompey, a man remembered for his goodness, for thinking such cruel killings a fine spectacle, with the victims crushed by huge animals.

Seneca says a cruel ruler's great success made him blind to his own faults. While he sent crowds of people to be torn apart by wild animals and staged bloody fights, he still believed he ruled the whole world. He would soon be killed in the same bloodshed he had caused.

Seneca is pointing out that Alexander the Great, despite his title, was betrayed by the Alexandrians and killed by a lowly slave, so his greatness proved empty. He then says he will return to his main topic and show that some people waste effort even on that subject.

Seneca is listing examples of Roman achievements that were rare. Metellus was the only Roman to parade a hundred and twenty captured elephants after a Sicilian victory over Carthage. Sulla was the last to extend the pomerium, the sacred boundary of Rome, and that honour was normally given only for conquests in Italy, not in distant provinces.

Seneca asks whether it helps to know trivial facts about Rome, such as why the Aventine Hill lies outside the sacred boundary. He says such stories are mostly false or as good as false, and that learning them does not reduce anyone's errors or calm their emotions.

Seneca quotes his friend Fabianus, who doubted that studying the liberal arts was better than not studying at all. The question before this is whom such studies make braver, more just, or more gentlemanly. The point is that these studies do not clearly improve character.

Only those who devote themselves to philosophy truly have leisure and truly live, because they gain access to all past ages through the thinkers of those ages. Seneca says we should see the great philosophers as having prepared life for us, and that we owe them for bringing beautiful truths out of darkness into light.

Through reading and thought, a person can reach any age and any philosopher, since the mind is not limited to its own time. Seneca asks why we do not give our full attention to these lasting, greater minds instead of to our own short lives.

Seneca describes busy men who spend their days paying social calls on powerful patrons, going from door to door. He points out that in a huge city, few of these callers will actually be received. Many patrons will refuse them out of laziness, self-indulgence or rudeness, or will rush past them pretending to be busy.

Many powerful men avoid the crowd of clients waiting in their entrance hall by slipping out through a hidden back door. Others, still half asleep after a night of drinking, greet their waiting callers only with a huge yawn. Seneca mocks the rudeness of such men toward those who have come to see them.

Seneca says that people who spend each day studying the great philosophers, such as Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, Aristotle and Theophrastus, are following the true path of duty. These thinkers are always available, send each visitor away better in mind, and can be consulted at any hour, day or night.

Seneca says that the wise men of the past will not harm the reader in any way. They will not force him to die or waste his time, and they will not cost him money. Instead, they teach him how to live well and how to die, and he may take as much of their wisdom as he wants.

The passage describes the kind of friend a wise person would have: someone to talk with about everything, who speaks the truth without insulting and gives praise without flattery, and whose character serves as a model. It then notes that people say they cannot choose their parents, who were given to them by chance.

Seneca says a person may choose which great thinkers to follow, as if adopting into their family. Their wisdom is shared freely and grows as more people receive it, and it leads to eternity. Through it, a short mortal life can be made to last and even become immortal.

Public honours and monuments of power do not last, because time wears them down. Works that philosophy has stamped with its seal survive untouched, and each later age respects them more, since people judge what is distant more fairly than what is near.

The wise man's life is long, Seneca says, because he gathers all of time into it. He is not bound by the usual limits of life. He uses past time through memory, present time by acting in it, and future time by looking ahead to it.

Seneca says that people who forget the past, neglect the present and fear the future have short and unhappy lives. They realise too late that they were busy all along while achieving nothing. Their fear drives them to wish for death, even though their lives seem long to them.

People who say their days drag are not proving that their lives are long. When they have no regular work, they feel restless and do not know how to fill the time. So they seek some task, and any time between tasks feels tedious to them.
People want to skip over the time that lies ahead, much as they would skip the days before a gladiator fight or a planned show or pleasure. Any delay of something they desire feels painful to them.

Even the time people enjoy is short, and they make it shorter by jumping from one pleasure to another without settling on any one. Their days feel long and unpleasant to them, while their nights of drinking and sex seem brief. Seneca says poets distorted this by inventing a myth in which Jupiter made a night longer for his own pleasure.

Seneca asks two questions. First, is it harmful to blame our vices on the gods, since that gives our bad habits an excuse set by divine example? Second, he says people who spend heavily on night pleasures find those nights seem short, because they wait all day for night and then fear the dawn.

Even the pleasures of powerful men are unsettled, because at their happiest they worry about how long it will last. Kings have wept over their power, frightened less by its grandeur than by the fact that it must one day end.

Seneca points to Xerxes, the Persian king, who wept as he looked at his huge army and thought that none of them would be alive in a hundred years. He notes that Xerxes himself would soon cause many of their deaths in sea battles, land battles and flight. The closing point is that people's joys are mixed with fear because those joys rest on nothing firm.

Even the greatest pleasures people enjoy are mixed with fear, because they depend on luck. Success needs more luck to keep it, and every answered prayer leads to another prayer. The higher something rises by chance, the more ways it has to fall.

Seneca says that people who work hard to gain things, and then work even harder to keep them, have short and miserable lives. They never end their unhappiness; they only switch its object, moving from one goal or ambition to the next. He ends by asking whether their own rises in rank trouble them.

Seneca says that men who finish one public task or office soon take up another. Once they stop canvassing for votes, they start voting or judging, and retirement from one job leads straight to the next. He gives Marius, Quintius and Scipio as examples of men who never rested from public duties.

Even a man who won great victories and could have been honoured like a god was troubled by political quarrels and chose exile. From this the author concludes that life always brings worries, so people are pushed from one task to another and never really enjoy the leisure they want.

Seneca urges his friend Paulinus to withdraw from public affairs and the busy crowd. Paulinus has already faced many hardships in his public and private life, and should now give some of his remaining time to himself and to a quieter life.

Seneca tells Paulinus not to retire into idle comfort or ordinary pleasures, which he calls mere sloth and not true rest. He says Paulinus can take up greater work than his past labours, and he praises how Paulinus runs the empire's revenues: fairly, diligently, and with public spirit, earning love in a post where people usually earn hatred.

Seneca tells Paulinus that knowing his own mind matters more than managing the grain supply. He says Paulinus should leave a post that is honorable but does not make life happy, since his education was meant for something greater than overseeing corn.

Seneca says that people who are good at strict, careful management and hard work are easy to find, much as slow beasts of burden suit heavy loads better than fast horses. He warns that the task of feeding people is risky, because a hungry crowd will not listen to reason, justice, or prayers. The passage breaks off mid-sentence.

Seneca describes Julius Caesar's reckless ambition. While Caesar was building bridges of ships and spending the empire's resources, Rome nearly ran out of grain, enough for only a week or so. The passage says this came close to causing famine and civil upheaval, and that Caesar was copying an arrogant foreign king.

Those in charge of Rome's grain supply, facing death at the hands of Emperor Gaius, hid the serious danger facing the state from the public. Seneca says they were right to do so, comparing it to illnesses that must be treated without the patient knowing, since some people have died after learning their diagnosis.

Seneca urges the reader to turn to a calmer, safer and wider kind of activity: the study of sacred and divine knowledge. He asks whether checking that grain is stored properly in the public granary can compare with learning what the gods are made of, how they live, and what the soul will go through.

Seneca urges the reader to turn their thoughts from earthly concerns toward questions about the nature of the universe and where the soul goes after death. He says this should be done while still young and strong, by taking the "better path."

Seneca says that a life spent in quiet study of virtue brings many goods, while busy people are unhappy. The worst case is people who must live by others' wishes, even in sleep, walking, and feelings of love and hate. Such people, he says, should see how little of their life is really their own.

Seneca says that when you see a man often wearing official robes and hearing his name called in the public square, you should not envy him, because he got those honours by spending much of his life to win them. Some men waste all their years chasing a single consulship, some die before reaching it, and some who reach it find that their only reward is a name carved on a tombstone.

Seneca criticises people who are old but still start grand projects or chase ambitions, and then die in the middle of them. He calls it shameful to die while still working in a law court, or while busy with money matters, when one is worn out with living rather than with work, or while an heir waits to inherit.

Turannius, an old man devoted to his work, was dismissed from his post as revenue collector when he was about ninety. He had himself laid on his bed and mourned as if dead, and his household mourned with him until his duties were returned to him. The writer asks how anyone can take pleasure in dying while still working.

Many people keep wanting to work long after their strength has gone, and they count old age a misfortune only because it sets them aside. Yet the law releases soldiers after fifty and senators after sixty, while people find it harder to grant themselves leisure than the law does.

People spend their lives robbing one another, disturbing each other's peace, and making each other miserable. In doing so, their lives gain nothing: no pleasure, no growth in wisdom. They also forget that they will die and keep hoping for things far ahead.

Some people plan monuments, public works and grand funerals that will outlast their own lives. Seneca says such men should instead have funerals as modest as if they had lived only a few days. The closing verse calls it foolish to judge others proud while denying oneself the same pride.

Important people have sometimes invited a busy man to hear them, but he never gave them even a moment of his time. He should not blame others for ignoring him, since he does the same, and he cannot even stay with himself.

This is a verse quotation, not Seneca's own prose, and it is cut off partway. It says that words are easy to find, but deeds should be done rather than spoken. The speaker has thought so hard about a longed-for time that he feels its effect, though he has not yet gained what he wants.

Seneca writes to his mother, Helvia, who is grieving. He says he often wanted to comfort her but held back. He had hoped that comforting her would ease his own sorrow, and that he would speak with more authority once he had freed himself from his own grief. He also feared that Fortune, the Roman idea of luck or chance, might hurt another member of the family.

Seneca says he did not try to comfort his mother Helvia at first, because it would only make her grief worse. He waited until the grief wore itself out and she was ready to accept comfort, just as medicine applied too early can harm a disease.

Seneca says he searched the works of great writers for a model of consoling grief, and found none where someone comforted his relatives while those relatives were mourning him. Because this was new ground, he worried that his words might deepen his reader's sorrow instead of easing it.

Seneca says that a grieving person who wants to comfort friends may not find new words, since deep grief can even take away the voice. Still, he will try, not because he trusts his own skill, but because he has been through such a loss himself and so his comfort will carry weight.
Seneca is asking his mother Helvia to let him limit her grief. He says she has never refused him before and hopes she will not refuse this request, even though grief is usually stubborn.

Seneca begins by admitting that he is going to stir up Helvia's old sorrow before he tries to comfort her. He plans to let grief speak first, so that it does not hit her all at once. He expects a critic to ask how reopening buried pain can console someone who can hardly bear to look at it.

Some grief is so severe that gentle comfort only makes it worse, so Seneca says he will instead lay out all of Helvia's sorrows in full, as a harsh cure. His hope is that she will feel ashamed to mourn one more wound when she has already survived many.

People who have lived a long time in comfort, Seneca says, break down over even small losses. Those who have lived through constant disasters should bear great losses with steady courage, since repeated misfortune makes a person hardened to pain.

Misfortune has struck Helvia from the start: her mother died at her birth, and she was raised by a stepmother. Seneca says Helvia treated that stepmother with the devotion of a true daughter, and that even a good stepmother is costly to anyone who has one.

Seneca describes the losses that struck Helvia in quick succession: first her uncle, whom she had been expecting to return, then her husband within a month. The news came while she was already grieving and while her children were away, so she had no time or place to rest from sorrow.

Seneca is consoling his mother Helvia for a run of losses. In a few days she buried a grandchild, received the remains of three other grandchildren, and then learned that Seneca himself had been exiled. He says this was one more blow on top of all the rest.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that her latest grief is the worst she has suffered, but she should bear it like a seasoned soldier. Recruits cry out at small wounds, while veterans endure even serious ones quietly. He asks her to stop wailing, since her many misfortunes gain her nothing unless she learns to endure them, and he admits he has listed all her sorrows openly.

Seneca is writing to his mother Helvia, who is grieving over his exile. He says he will fully overcome her grief, not just reduce it. He plans to show first that he himself does not suffer enough to be called unhappy, and second that her own misfortune, caused by him, is not serious.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that he is not suffering, despite the hardships she has heard about. He says he is not miserable and that he cannot be made miserable, and he asks her not to rely on what others say about him.

Nature gave us enough to live well without elaborate means, and each person can make himself happy by himself. Outside circumstances matter little, good or bad. The wise man is not lifted up by good fortune or crushed by bad, because he relies mainly on himself for his joys.

Seneca says he is not wise enough to claim he is free from unhappiness, so he relies on the company of wise people instead. Their example, he says, has taught him to stay alert and watch for the blows of Fortune, or bad luck, before they arrive.

Fortune, or bad luck, is frightening only to people who are caught off guard. Someone who always expects her attack can bear it easily, just as a prepared army holds its ground against a surprise invasion. The speaker says he never trusted Fortune, even when she seemed calm.
Seneca says he received wealth, high office and influence from Fortune, but he always held them at a distance. So when Fortune took them back, it did not tear them from him or cause him pain.

Only people who were fooled by good fortune lose heart when bad fortune comes. Those who believed their prosperity was permanent, and felt superior because of it, fall into deep grief when it leaves them. A person who was not puffed up by success does not collapse in failure, because his mind stays steady in either state.

Seneca says that the things people usually desire have no real good inside them, like painted surfaces with nothing behind. He also says that adversity, which ordinary people fear as dreadful, is not as harsh as common opinion makes it seem. Wise people reject many of these common judgments.

Seneca proposes to examine exile by setting aside popular opinion. At its core, exile is simply moving from one place to another. He will deal with the added poverty, disgrace and contempt later, and for now asks what is harmful in the bare act of changing one's home.

Seneca's point is that losing one's homeland is not as unusual as people think. He asks the reader to look at Rome's crowds, most of whom came to the city from other towns, colonies and parts of the world, and so have already lost their native land.

People come to Rome for many different reasons, such as ambition, public office, pleasure, study, friendship, work, or selling their beauty or eloquence. Rome, the passage says, rewards both good qualities and bad ones alike.
Most people in a great city were not born there; they came from somewhere else. Even the grandest city is not really any one person's home, and every other town also holds many outsiders.

Seneca says that even the most barren and harsh islands, places used for exile, are not empty. People choose to live there for their own pleasure. He names Gyarus, a rocky island, as an example, and notes that it has more outsiders than native inhabitants.

Seneca says that moving to a new place can be pleasant, so some people have even left their homeland for the sake of it. He reports that some writers claim people naturally crave change, because the human mind is restless, never still, and loves novelty.

Seneca says that the soul is not made of heavy earthly matter but of heavenly spirit. Because heavenly things are always moving swiftly, the soul is naturally restless, as the stars show by never standing still.

The passage says the sun never stays still. It moves across the sky from one point to another, against the turning of the whole heavens, passing through every constellation without resting in any. It then concludes that all things keep turning and changing.

Seneca says the heavenly bodies move in fixed, unchanging cycles, returning to the paths they had already travelled. Because the human mind comes from the same source as these bodies, it is natural for it to enjoy change and movement. He adds that the divine nature may itself enjoy swift motion, or even keep its existence through it.

Seneca points out that whole peoples have moved from their homelands over time. Greek cities stand among non-Greek peoples, Macedonian speech is found in India and Persia, and Greek cities lie on the shores of the Black Sea in cold, savage Scythia. Harsh climates and fierce peoples did not stop such migrations.

Seneca lists how peoples have spread across the world. Greeks settled in Italy, Phoenicians in Africa, Carthaginians in Spain, and Germans crossed the Pyrenees. He says human restlessness carries whole families, including the old, far from home.

Some people, tired of wandering, simply settled wherever they happened to be. Others conquered foreign lands by force, some nations were lost at sea while seeking new places, and some stayed where poverty had first left them stranded.

Seneca lists the many reasons people have left their homeland. Some fled after enemy armies destroyed their cities, some were driven out by civil strife, some by overpopulation, some by plague, earthquakes, or poor soil, and some by the lure of fertile lands praised too highly.

Nothing stays in the place where it began. Peoples move, cities are founded, and old nations vanish or are absorbed by stronger ones. Seneca says these large migrations are really the exile of whole peoples, and that the examples of ancient founders like Antenor and Evander make the point clear.

The passage argues that exile is nothing new or shameful. It points to Diomedes and other Trojan War heroes who were scattered from their homes, and to Aeneas, founder of Rome, who fled his conquered country. Since then, Rome has sent colonies across its provinces, so exile has long been part of its history.

People kept leaving their homes to join settlers overseas, even old soldiers. Seneca says no more examples are needed, but he adds one he can see for himself: the island he lives on has often changed its inhabitants.

The passage says the Greeks who founded Marseilles were not driven from their home city by hostile locals, since they settled among fierce Gallic tribes. The reasons for their departure from Phocaea are unclear; the writer lists possibilities such as the harsh climate, the nearby power of Italy, or a lack of harbours.

Seneca describes how the population of the island of Corsica has changed many times. Ligurians and Spaniards settled there, shown by shared clothing and some shared words, and Greeks and Ligurians made the Spaniards lose their own language. Later, Romans founded two colonies there under Marius and Sulla.

Peoples have never stayed in their own lands for long. Each group has mixed with others, taken land from someone else, or been driven out in turn. The point is that fate lets nothing keep an unbroken run of good fortune.

Seneca reports two comforts offered to exiles. Varro held that the same Nature surrounds us wherever we go, so a change of place matters little. Brutus held that exiles can take their virtues with them. Seneca says that together these comforts are strong, since so little is really lost.

Whatever happens, we keep two things: the common nature shared by all, and our own particular virtue. The Creator, whatever he is, has so arranged things that no one can take hold of the best things in life, which lie beyond human power. The world and our minds for seeing and admiring it stay ours as long as we live.
Seneca says that a person should go wherever circumstances send them, without fear. Exile cannot take away a home, because a person can look up at the same sky from any place.

Seneca says that the heavens are equally close to everyone, wherever they live. As long as he can watch the sun, moon and stars and study their movements, he asks, what does it matter what ground he stands on?

Seneca is listing what a place lacks: fine trees, large rivers, goods other nations would want, marble, gold and silver. The quoted list is a claim about a country, and the closing words "What of that!" show that the lack is treated as unimportant.

Seneca says that a narrow mind takes pleasure in earthly things, and should turn instead to the heavenly things that can be seen everywhere. He adds that people, by mistaken values, build so much (porticos, towers, roofs) that they block their own view of heaven.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that a humble cottage need not be a source of shame or comfort through old stories about Romulus's hut. He says a poor dwelling becomes finer than any temple once virtues such as justice, self-control and wisdom fill it, so no place is too small when it holds them.

Seneca says that exile cannot be wretched for someone who has the company of virtue and learning. He recalls Brutus saying that Marcellus, while in exile at Mytilene, was happy and devoted to his studies, and that Brutus felt he himself was the one in exile when he had to leave him. Seneca concludes that Marcellus was happier then than when Rome honoured him as consul.

Seneca is describing Marcus Brutus, who praised Gaius Caesar for sailing past Mytilene without landing. Brutus said Caesar would not look on a fallen man, that is, the exiled Marcus Brutus or his friend Cicero's circle. Seneca calls Caesar's refusal to visit a sign of his admiration for the man he left behind.

The Senate got Marcellus recalled from exile, anxious and sorrowful as if they feared losing him themselves. But Marcellus earned more honour when Brutus could not bear to leave him in exile and Caesar could not bear to see him there. Each of them showed, by grieving or blushing, how highly they valued him.

Seneca quotes Marcellus, a Roman exiled from his homeland, consoling himself. His point is that the loss of his country is no real misery, since a wise person regards the whole world as home. He adds that the man who exiled him was himself away from Rome for ten years while expanding the empire.

This passage describes threats across the empire: a renewed war in Africa, a revived rebel faction in Spain, and plotting in Egypt. It asks which problem a leader should face first, and notes that each victory will send him to another country. Seneca's sarcastic close says the leader may have nations worship him, while the person addressed should be content with Brutus's admiration.

Marcellus bore his exile calmly, and moving away did not change his mind, even though he became poor. Seneca says that a person of real virtue does not lack much, since the body needs only protection from cold and enough food and drink. Wants beyond these are vices, not needs.

Seneca criticizes extreme luxury. He says there is no need to dive into the deepest seas, to eat huge amounts of slaughtered animals, or to gather shellfish from far-off shores. He wishes ruin on people whose luxury goes beyond what the already very large empire can bear.

Seneca describes wealthy Romans who gather rare foods from distant lands, even from beyond the Phasis river and from the Parthians' territory, and who vomit so they can keep eating. He then asks what harm poverty can do to a man who does not care for such luxuries.

Seneca makes two points. A man who wants things is helped by poverty, because being unable to get what he desires is like not having those desires at all. He then gives the example of Gaius Caesar (the emperor Caligula), who spent enormous sums on a single dinner and still struggled to spend the tribute of three provinces on one meal.

People who can only enjoy food when it is expensive are unhappy. Its price comes from rarity and difficulty of getting it, not from taste. If they returned to sound judgment, they would not need so many trades, long-distance trade, and resource-stripping efforts to feed their appetite.

Food is available everywhere, but people overlook it and travel the world at great expense to satisfy hunger that could be met cheaply nearby. Seneca asks why people build ships, fight, and gather wealth, when their bodies are so small and can hold so little. He calls such desire madness.

Even if you gain more money and land, your body cannot grow to match it. Once you have collected far more than you need, you will have nowhere to store it all. The passage asks why people keep striving for so much.

Seneca asks whether the ancestors were unhappy, despite living simply: they cooked their own food, slept on the ground, and had no gold or jewelled temples. They swore oaths by clay gods and kept their word so strictly that they would return to the enemy to face certain death rather than break a promise.

Seneca asks whether the old Roman general Curius Dentatus, who roasted his own simple food, enjoyed life less than Apicius, a famous glutton of his own day. He implies the frugal general lived better, and says Apicius's end is worth knowing.

Seneca describes a rich spender, Apicius, who ran through his large fortune on lavish food and feasts. When he finally checked his accounts and found he had ten million sesterces left, he judged that too little to live on and poisoned himself. Seneca's point is that his luxury had made even that large sum seem like poverty.

Wealth, Seneca suggests, is not measured by how much a person actually owns but by the owner's own mind. He gives the example of a man who dreaded a fortune of ten million sesterces, a sum other men pray for, and so ended his life with poison.

Seneca says that for a man with a diseased mind, his final drink of poison was actually the most helpful thing, since he had been poisoning himself all along with lavish feasting and vice. He adds that people who spend their wealth by fashion rather than by reason are in the same position, because fashion's demands have no limit.
Greedy desire is never satisfied, but nature needs only a small amount to be content. So an exile's poverty does no real harm, because even a barren place yields enough to support a person.

An exile need not miss his old clothes or house if he values them only for what they are useful for. Little is needed to cover the body, just as little is needed to feed it, because nature does not make the basic needs of life difficult.

If a man grieves over losing luxury goods, such as a dyed purple robe with gold thread, then his poverty is his own doing, not the fault of fortune. Giving him back his property would not help, because his unmet desires would only grow larger than they were while he was in exile.

A man who wants luxury goods of every kind will never be satisfied by collecting them. His craving is not a real need that could be met, like thirst met by drink. It is an inner sickness, so no amount of possessions can cure it.

Wants that come from vice, not from real need, cannot be satisfied: the more you give them, the stronger they grow. A person who keeps to what nature requires never feels poor, while one who goes beyond it stays poor however rich he is. Even a place of exile can supply what is necessary, but whole kingdoms cannot supply luxuries.

The mind is what makes a person rich, not money. The mind goes with a person even into exile or the wildest places, where it finds its own resources once the body has enough to live on. Money has no more to do with the mind than the gods have with the things that ignorant people, tied to their bodily desires, value so highly.

Wealth such as gems, gold, silver and fine tables is worthless earth-matter to a pure mind. Such a mind comes from heaven, stays free of sin, and while in the body it thinks about divine things as far as its bodily limits allow. After death it rises to the highest heaven.

A free mind cannot really be exiled, because it is not tied to one place or one time. The body is only a prison that can be moved, hurt or sickened, but the spirit is holy and eternal, and no one can touch it.

Seneca argues that poverty is not really terrible unless a person believes it is. He notes that poor people are not generally sadder or more anxious than rich people, and may even be happier because they have fewer distractions. He adds that rich people often find themselves in the same situation as the poor.

Wealthy people often give up their comforts. On journeys, in the army, or on chosen days, they cut back their baggage, servants, silver and gold, and eat from earthenware on the ground. Seneca calls them mad, because they fear the poverty they sometimes want.

Seneca mocks people who run from poverty yet still enjoy luxuries. He says that when he looks at the great men of the past, he is ashamed to seek comfort for his own poverty, since an exile now gets a bigger allowance than the old princes ever inherited.

Seneca points out that great thinkers had different numbers of slaves, from one to none, yet none of them was pitied for a poor life. Menenius Agrippa, a Roman who helped reconcile the classes, was given a public funeral paid for by subscription. The point is that owning few or no slaves did not make these men miserable.

Seneca gives two examples of famous Romans who were poor because they served the state. Regulus lost his hired worker while away at war, so the Senate ordered his farm worked at public expense. Scipio left no money for his daughters, so the state paid their dowries. The point is that such men gained more from the state's care than they would have gained from wealth of their own.

Seneca argues that great Roman men of the past were poor, yet their families were honoured. Scipio's daughters received a dowry from the state in old bronze coins, Regulus could not pay for a hired worker, and Menenius needed public money for his funeral. So, he says, poverty should not be seen as shameful, and no exile should complain about lacking things.
Seneca argues that poverty is not harmful when men of good character defend it. Their lives make it look appealing rather than shameful.
Seneca answers an objection that misfortunes are bearable one at a time but crushing together. His reply is that anyone who can withstand a single misfortune has the strength to withstand them all.

If your mind is hardened by virtue, outside blows cannot reach it. Once greed is gone, ambition no longer troubles you, and a mind free of the fear of death lets in no other fear. Likewise, seeing sexual desire as meant for raising children, not for pleasure, makes other desires harmless.

Reason defeats vices all together, not one at a time, so if reason is beaten, it is beaten completely. A wise man who depends on himself and is free of common opinions cannot be shaken by disgrace. Socrates kept his calm when he went into prison, so the prison did not seem a prison to him.

Seneca says that Cato's two election defeats did not shame Cato. The shame belonged to the offices he sought and failed to win. Only a person who already despises himself can be looked down on by others, while a brave person who endures hardship turns his misfortunes into honour.

Aristides was led to execution at Athens, and people mourned him as if justice itself were dying. One man spat in his face, but Aristides was not upset. He wiped his face calmly, smiled, and asked that the man be told not to be so rude again, showing that he treated insult with contempt.

Some people think disgrace is worse than anything, even death. Seneca replies that exile need not bring disgrace. A great man stays great after his fall, just as a ruined temple keeps its dignity and is still treated with respect.

Seneca tells his mother that if she weeps without end over him, the tears must be for her own sake. He names two possible reasons: she has lost his support, or she cannot bear being apart from him. He sets the first reason aside briefly, saying her love is for her children themselves, not for what they provide.

Seneca praises his mother Helvia for never using her sons' success for her own gain. She rejoiced in their honours, never sought profit from them, and managed their money carefully and honestly. So her grief at his exile cannot rest on any selfish reason, since such a reason never mattered to her before.

Helvia is grieving because her son is gone. She laments that she can no longer embrace him, see him, talk with him, or share his studies and meetings, and Seneca takes up this loss as the real cause of her sorrow.

Seneca is writing to his mother Helvia, who is grieving. He says the things that keep her thinking of him, such as places they shared and their recent time together, are painful. He adds that she was spared worry because she left three days before his disaster, and so did not expect it.

Seneca is consoling his mother Helvia over the death of his son, though the passage speaks to her as if she had been away from him. He says that her long absence from him should have prepared her for loss, but it did not, since she was not with him during his good fortune and yet never grew used to being apart from him.

Seneca tells Helvia that the harder her troubles are to bear, the more courage she must call on, fighting them as an old enemy she has beaten before. He adds that her grief comes from an old wound, not a fresh one, so the pain touches a sore that was already there.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that being a woman gives her no excuse for unlimited grief. Women may weep, but not without limit, so the ancestors set a ten-month mourning period for widows to control their grief by public rule.

Seneca says that grief after a loss should be limited, not endless, but also not absent. Feeling regret while holding it in check is the best middle course, and he contrasts this with women who never stopped mourning. He adds that Helvia is stronger than them, so more is expected of her.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that she cannot excuse her faults by saying she is a woman, because she does not have the usual female vices. He lists them: immorality, love of jewels and pearls, desire for wealth, and copying the fashions of others. She was raised strictly and has avoided all of these.

Seneca praises his mother Helvia for her virtue. He says she never hid her pregnancies, never ended a pregnancy, never used cosmetics or revealing clothes, and that her modesty was her greatest glory.

Seneca tells Helvia that she cannot use being a woman as an excuse for grief, since her virtues should lift her above it. He says that even women admired for their virtue would not waste away in mourning but would mourn briefly, then rise and move on.

Cornelia had twelve children but only two survived. She told her weeping friends not to blame fortune for taking her sons, the Gracchi, because she counted their worth above their number. Seneca says her attitude was greater than her son's pride in his birth.

Seneca praises Rutilia, a mother who stayed with her exiled son and later bore his death without visible tears. She showed courage in his exile and wisdom at his death, and let neither her love nor her grief turn into a long, pointless mourning.

Seneca tells his reader, Helvia, that she should be counted among certain women who held back their grief. He says she has strong reasons to do the same, since she has always followed the example of those women's lives.

Grief is not something we can simply command away. Trying to suppress it fails, because tears still come and the mind stays troubled even while we distract ourselves with shows. So Seneca concludes that it is better to overcome grief directly than to trick it.

Grief that is only pushed away by pleasure or busy activity comes back later, and stronger. Grief that reason has overcome stays gone for good. So Seneca will not recommend the common cures of a long trip or a pleasant view to distract the mind.

Seneca advises his mother Helvia, grieving over his exile, that busy tasks like managing accounts and estates only distract from sorrow rather than cure it. He would rather she face her grief fully than hide from it, and urges her to turn to philosophy, which he calls a refuge from misfortune that heals sadness.

Seneca regrets that his aunt Helvia's father, following old Roman custom, kept her education shallow. He wishes she had studied philosophy thoroughly, so that she could now help him face misfortune. He says her father limited her studies because some women used learning for luxury rather than wisdom.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that the learning she already gained in philosophy can protect her. Once it is fully part of her mind, grief and anxiety will not enter, and philosophy alone can guard her against the blows of Fortune, meaning bad luck and misfortune.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that she has comfort while she waits for philosophy to bring her peace. Her sons and brothers are still alive, so she has no reason to blame Fortune. She can take pleasure in each of them: one has risen to high office through public work, the other has chosen a quiet life and turned away from such posts, and both show her affection.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that her two surviving sons are each doing something that benefits her. One holds high public office to bring her honour, and the other has retired to a quiet life of study so he can spend time with her. Their devotion will make up for the son she has lost.
Seneca tells Helvia that her grandson Marcus is so charming that no sorrow can resist him. His presence lifts any grief, and his liveliness and playfulness cheer up everyone who sees him.

Seneca's grieving mother Helvia is asked to see her son's charm and chatter as a comfort, and the speaker prays that the gods let him outlive them. He asks that all the misfortune fate has in store for his mother and grandmother fall on him alone, so his family suffers nothing more. He accepts his childlessness and exile if that is enough to satisfy the gods.

Seneca asks his mother Helvia to care for her granddaughter Novatilla, who has lost her own mother and now feels fatherless toward Seneca, whom she had loved as a parent. He suggests Helvia's affection can ease the grief, and that teaching a child in early years shapes her character deeply.

Seneca advises that Helvia's mind, which is full of grief for her absence from her son, be turned to something else. Her son's character can be shaped by her example and by listening to philosophy, and the duty of doing this will itself help her. Only philosophical reasoning or worthwhile work can pull a grieving mind away from its sorrow.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that her father would be one of her greatest comforts if he were not far away. He says her love for him shows how much her father loves her, so she should live for him rather than grieve for Seneca. He also reminds her that she has many grandchildren, so she is no longer her father's only daughter.
Seneca is comforting Helvia, and he names her sister as her main source of comfort. The sister shares all her sorrows, has wept with her, and feels for the whole family like a mother.

Seneca is describing how his aunt Helvia cared for him. She nursed him back to health, used her influence to get him the post of quaestor, and overcame her normally shy, quiet nature to act on his behalf. Even though she lived modestly and privately, she became ambitious for his sake.

Seneca tells his mother that the best comfort for grief is to turn to a particular person, the one he is about to name as the source of consolation. He says that people in sorrow often shun those they love most, but she should let that person share her every thought. Whether she wants to keep grieving or put grief aside, this person will go along with her.

Seneca says that Helvia, a woman of great wisdom, would not want her son or reader to waste life in pointless grieving. He gives her own case as proof: when her husband died at sea, she grieved and feared for herself, yet after a shipwreck she saved his body.

Seneca is saying that if Helvia had lived in simpler, earlier times, writers would have competed to praise her. He describes a wife who braved the sea and risked death to bury her husband, caring little whether she was buried with him.

Seneca praises his aunt, who risked her life to bury her husband. He says this shows more love than the famous wives of poetry who died with their husbands. He adds that for sixteen years, while her husband governed Egypt, she stayed out of public view and asked no favours from him.

The province, though quick to gossip about its governors and often slandering even innocent officials, never spoke ill of this woman. It treated her as a rare model of virtue and still hopes for another governor's wife like her, though it does not expect to find one.

Seneca praises his mother-in-law Helvia's conduct, though this is not the passage's stated context. Hmm, careful: the passage is about Seneca's mother Helvia, who lived quietly abroad for sixteen years, and was praised for not seeking power or wealth. Her courage in shipwreck is shown by her saving her dead husband's body rather than herself.
Helvia is told to show a strength equal to another person's, to stop her mind from dwelling on grief, and to make sure no one thinks she regrets having had a son.

Seneca tells his mother Helvia that, whatever she does, her thoughts will often turn to him, more than to her other children. This is not because she loves them less, but because people naturally touch most often the place that hurts.

Seneca, writing from exile, tells his mother Helvia that he is as cheerful as ever. He says his days are now his best, since he is free of public business and can spend his time on study, including questions about the nature of the world and the sea.

The passage describes the mind (the soul) rising above the world. It looks past the storms and weather between heaven and earth, then rises to the highest heaven, where it sees divine things. Knowing it is eternal, it considers all of past and future time.

Seneca says that human achievements seem firm and lasting only when measured against human lives. Measured against nature, which destroys everything and returns it to its origin, they are temporary. Even the famous wonders of the world, he says, will one day be levelled to the ground.

Nothing lasts forever, and everything that has a beginning will end, though in many different ways. Some thinkers hold that the whole universe, gods, people and all they have made, will one day be destroyed and return to its original darkness and chaos.

Seneca argues that grieving a single person's death is pointless, since even great cities such as Carthage and Corinth have fallen, and the whole world is destined to perish. Fate, he says, will one day bring a worse harm, so there is no reason to weep over any one loss.

Nothing is exempt from the natural law that everything comes to an end, so no one can expect his own household to escape loss. Seeing that others have suffered the same and others will too is presented as a source of comfort.
Nature has made its harshest blows fall on everyone equally. Because the misfortune is shared by all, people may find some comfort in it.

Grief does no good, either for the person who has died or for the mourner, so there is no point in prolonging it. Seneca says that if sorrow could gain anything, he would weep for his friend's losses too, even with his own eyes already worn out from crying.

Seneca speaks as if he shares a grief with his friend Polybius, addressing Fortune (chance or luck) as an unjust enemy. He says Fortune had spared Polybius so far, since his success had brought him respect without envy. Now she has struck him at the one point where he was vulnerable: the death of a close relative while Caesar (the emperor) still lives.

The speaker asks what harm could still be done to a certain man. He was never a slave to his wealth, and he has even put much of it away, so losing it would change little. The question then turns to his friends.

Seneca tells Polybius that his friend was so pleasant to be around that he could easily win new friends to replace any he lost. Seneca says this man was the only powerful Imperial official whom everyone wanted as a friend, not for any personal gain. He adds that even Polybius could not damage this man's reputation, which is firmly established.

Seneca says that the dead man's mind was trained in philosophy, so bodily suffering, including the loss of breath, could not really harm him. His lasting part lives on through his eloquent writings, which will keep him alive as long as Latin and Greek literature are valued.

Seneca is speaking to Polybius, a powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, who has harmed someone. He says the better a man is, the more often he suffers from Polybius's wild anger, and that Polybius's gifts seem scattered at random rather than given by any plan.

Seneca is consoling Polybius over the death of his young brother. He says the brother was worthy of such a relation, so Polybius should not be hurt by his loss. Everyone praises the brother for his own merits, and Polybius loved him more freely because he was so deserving.

Seneca praises a dead brother of Polybius. He never hurt anyone or used his family position to threaten people, and he modelled himself on Polybius's modesty. Seneca says Fate was cruel to take him before he could enjoy his success, and he admits he cannot fully express his grief.
