Seneca addresses Fortune in grief over a young man's death, asking why she has been so cruel. He points out that she struck a family of fine brothers, each as admirable as the others, and took one of them away without reason.

Seneca says that Polybius's good qualities did not protect him: his innocence, thrift, wealth, love of learning and clean conscience all failed. Polybius grieves for a brother who died, fears for his remaining family, and still mourns despite Caesar's favour. Fortune, he suggests, wanted to show that even Caesar cannot shield a person from her blows.

Fate cannot be changed by blame, tears, or appeals to justice, and it treats no one with special mercy. Since grief cannot bring the dead person back, Seneca urges that tears be stopped by reason, because otherwise only fortune, not reason, will end them.

Seneca says that people everywhere have plenty of reasons to weep. Some are worn down by poverty or work, some by ambition or fear of the wealth they wanted, some by loneliness or crowds, and some by having children or by losing them. There are always more causes for tears than tears to shed.

Seneca says that life starts with crying, and the years that follow match that start, full of sorrow. Since we must weep so often, we should hold back our tears and save them, because they are needed so often.

Seneca tells Polybius that his grief would not please the dead man it is meant to honour. The dead man either does not want Polybius to suffer or does not know that he is suffering. So mourning does no good to the dead, and if the dead could feel it, it would only displease them.

Seneca asks the grieving reader whether his dead brother could really hold a grudge, wish him harm, or want him kept from his work in philosophy and from Caesar. The brother was always kind and respectful, and he would not want his memory to cause pain. So the grief should end if the dead can feel anything at all.

Seneca says that if the brother in question were anyone else, he would argue that a good brother would not want to be mourned with endless grief. But this brother has clearly shown his love, so Seneca is sure that nothing would hurt him more than seeing his surviving brother suffer and weep without end.

Seneca tells Polybius that the best way to stop his useless weeping is to remember that he should set an example for his brothers by facing this blow from fortune with courage. He compares this to great generals who keep a cheerful face in defeat so their soldiers do not lose heart.

Seneca tells the reader to keep a calm face and hide personal grief, so that grieving relatives can copy this and take heart. He adds that a person who indulges their own sorrow cannot ease the grief of others.

Seneca tells a grieving man that everyone is watching how he handles his loss. Visitors offering comfort are studying him to see whether he can bear hardship with courage, or only enjoy good fortune. Even his facial expression is being observed.

Because your high position makes everything you do visible, others will see how you bear this loss, whether you give way at once or hold firm. Seneca says that a person of your rank should not sink into grief, since that would be weak and unworthy of you.

Seneca tells Polybius that, although his grief is as great as his brothers', he cannot show it as openly. His reputation for philosophy and good character means people expect more from him. Having drawn everyone's attention, he must now live up to what he has promised.

Those who praise Polybius's writings, copy them, and rely on his talent rather than his good fortune are, in effect, guards over his mind. Because of them, he cannot act unworthily of a true philosopher without many people regretting that they ever admired him.

Seneca tells Polybius that a high position takes away many ordinary freedoms. He cannot weep without limit, sleep late, retreat to the country, take a holiday, or arrange his own day. Even the poorest beggars have such freedoms, so great fortune is a form of slavery.

Polybius, to whom this letter is addressed, is told that he cannot do as he pleases. He must receive crowds of petitioners and handle their requests, and keep his spirits up, so that the emperor's business from across the world can be properly presented to him.

Seneca tells Polybius that he must not weep himself, so that he can hear many people begging for help. His own tears must stop, so that the tears of those in danger, who seek Caesar's pardon, can be dried.

Seneca tells Polybius that thinking about Caesar can fully end his grief. Caesar is so busy that his work keeps everyone else safe, free and at rest, so Polybius should feel he can bear his own burden as Atlas bore the world. Even Caesar's power has limits, because he must work for others' peace.

Seneca says that Caesar, having given himself wholly to the public work of ruling the world, no longer has any time of his own, like a planet that never stops moving. He tells the addressee that the same restriction now applies to him: his own interests, studies, joy and grief must all give way to Caesar.

Seneca tells Polybius that, since he has always said Caesar meant more to him than his own life, he has no reason to grieve while Caesar is alive. Because Caesar's safety means his friends are still alive and nothing is lost, Polybius should not weep but rejoice.

Seneca is advising Polybius, a freedman who had lost his brother, and the "remedy" he offers concerns time spent alone. Here "divinity" means the emperor Claudius, and "Caesar" is the same person; while Polybius is in the emperor's presence, he is occupied by him. Once alone, grief creeps in and attacks him when his mind rests.

Seneca urges Polybius to fill every free moment with reading and writing about literature. He says Homer and Virgil deserve his time, since Polybius has made them known to more people than they first reached, and time spent with them is never wasted.

Seneca urges Polybius to write a history of the emperor Claudius's deeds, a praise-writing that future readers will study. He says Claudius himself gives the finest subject for such a work. He adds that he would not dare to advise Polybius to turn Aesop's fables into Latin verse, a task no Roman has yet tried.

Seneca says that a mind hit by a hard blow finds it difficult to turn quickly to light, cheerful subjects. If it can move from serious study to lighter topics, that shows it has recovered. A mind not yet healed will still manage serious subjects, but cannot bear cheerful ones.

Seneca suggests asking whether your grief is for yourself or for the dead person. If it is for yourself, it is not true tenderness, and it is not fitting for a good man to measure his grief for a brother by his own losses.

If the dead feel nothing, Seneca argues, the brother has escaped all the troubles of life and is back in the state he was in before birth. So grieving for him, who will never grieve again, would be foolish.

If the dead still feel anything, the speaker's brother is now free, like a prisoner released, and is looking at nature and divine matters from a closer view. So grieving is pointless: if he is happy, weeping would be envy, and if he does not exist, it would be madness.

Seneca tells Polybius that a dead man, though he lost great blessings just as they were arriving, has also escaped many troubles. These include anger, disease, suspicion, envy, terror and the unpredictable turns of fortune. Counted fairly, he has been spared more than he has lost.

Seneca says that a person who does not need wealth, office, or influence is happier than one who has them. He argues that these things only seem pleasant, while in fact they demand hard work to keep, arouse envy in others, and bring more trouble than benefit to their holders.

Seneca says that worldly goods are unstable, so even great wealth is hard to enjoy calmly. Some thinkers hold that life as a whole is full of suffering, like being thrown into a rough sea where fortune constantly lifts people up and drops them down. People are always tossed about, colliding, wrecked, and afraid.

Death is presented as a harbour from life's stormy sea, a place of rest and freedom. The speaker urges the reader not to begrudge the dead brother this rest, saying he has escaped Fortune, the goddess of chance, while she still favoured him, and now moves freely through the heavens.

Seneca tells a grieving man that his brother has not really been lost. The brother has been freed from the body and has gone to a better place, which everyone will reach in the end. So there is no reason to mourn, because he has only gone ahead.
Nothing can be known for certain, even for a single day, because the truth is hidden and hard to reach. So no one can say whether the death of your brother was sent in anger or in mercy.

Seneca tells Polybius that a just person should see the death of his brother not as a wrong but as a gift, since he had the brother's love for a long time. He then lists faults: refusing a benefactor's gift is unjust, counting only losses is greedy, calling a loss a wrong is ungrateful, and thinking good things give nothing beyond the present is foolish, because past joys remain securely one's own.

Pleasures pass quickly, so a person who counts only present pleasures, what they can touch and see, limits their enjoyment too much. Seneca says we should recall past pleasures in the mind, since memory of them is more lasting and dependable than the pleasures themselves.

Seneca tells Polybius to count his brother's life as a great blessing, measured by the time he actually had him, not by the time he might have had. Nature lent the brother, as it lends brothers to others, and has now taken him back. Being angry at this is like being angry at repaying a loan.

Nature lent your brother his life, just as she lent you yours, and now she has asked for his back first. Nature cannot be blamed, since life was given on those terms. Human hopes are at fault for forgetting this. The writer tells the reader to be glad of such a brother and grateful for the time they had with him.

Think of your brother's company as something delightful you enjoyed, and of its ending as a loss that happens to everyone. It is inconsistent to grieve that he was not with you longer while failing to be glad that he was with you at all.

Seneca says that people wrongly treat a death as sudden. Everyone knows their loved ones are mortal, but they prefer to forget it. Nature shows daily, through funerals, that death follows its own laws for everyone, so when it comes, it should not surprise anyone.

Seneca says that people are wrong to be angry when they must leave life, since life was only lent to them. A father who heard of his son's death calmly replied that he had known the son would die, and Seneca argues that death is no surprise, because life itself is a journey toward death.

A father says he knew his son would die one day, and that this was why he raised him. Seneca argues that everyone is born to die, so we should enjoy what we are given and give it up when it is taken. Death can come at any time, so the mind should not fear what is certain but stay ready for it.

Seneca says that great men, generals and whole nations have all died, and that every person and thing must eventually come to an end. People die at different ages, but all go to the same place. He ends by asking whether it is more foolish not to know that all must die, or more arrogant to refuse to accept it.

Seneca tells Polybius that the poets Polybius has translated, with the verse form removed but its charm kept, are full of examples. Their works show the changes of human life, the uncertainty of events, and tears shed for many reasons.

Reading aloud the grand phrases should be done with energy, so the delivery does not seem weaker than the words. Otherwise listeners may wonder how a weak mind could produce such firm, well-connected ideas.

Seneca urges a grieving man to turn his mind away from his sorrow and toward the family he still has: his brothers, wife and son. He says Fortune has taken one loss so that the others may be kept safe. He warns that it would be shameful to let one grief outweigh all these comforts.

Seneca tells Polybius that others share his grief, and so they cannot give him much help. Since they look to him for encouragement, he should resist the trouble more firmly, the less learning and wisdom they have. He also says that shared grief is easier to bear, because each person's part is smaller.

Seneca tells Polybius that Emperor Claudius, who rules the world and governs by kindness rather than force, is a source of comfort. When Polybius weeps, he should look up at Caesar, whose brilliance will dry his tears and hold his gaze.

The passage tells a grieving man that Caesar, the emperor, should be his main comfort against misfortune. It says Caesar has already offered many remedies for the grief, and that simply seeing and thinking about him would console the man even if he had done nothing else.

Seneca wishes a long life for a powerful man, Polybius's patron, the emperor Claudius. He hopes Claudius will outlive Augustus, never face the death of his family, see his son trained to rule, and die only when grandchildren are grown.

Seneca is praying that Fortune, the goddess of chance, will stop harming the emperor Claudius and instead bring him good. He asks that Claudius heal the long suffering of Rome, repair the damage done by the previous ruler Caligula, and bring peace, conquest, and triumphs to the city.

Seneca is praising the emperor Claudius, hoping he will show mercy and bring him back from exile. He says Claudius has not fully ruined him, but has held him up when he was falling, and has even pleaded for his life before the Senate. He trusts Claudius to judge his case fairly.

Seneca is speaking to Polybius, a powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, who could grant pardons. He says Polybius's kindness will be the same whether the emperor judges him innocent or simply chooses to treat him as innocent. He takes comfort in seeing the emperor's pardons spread, since they have already brought many exiles back, and he hopes he will not be left out.

Seneca praises the emperor Claudius for showing mercy to exiles. Under his rule, exiles no longer live in constant fear of execution or of ships arriving with bad news, as they did under the cruel rule of Gaius (Caligula). Claudius has limited the harm Fortune, or chance, can do to them, and they now have peace and hope for the future.

Seneca tells Polybius that the emperor Claudius, the "universal consoler," has already comforted him better than Seneca could. Claudius has supplied examples, arguments and wise sayings, and his words carry the weight of an oracle, so they will overcome Polybius's grief.

The speaker tells the listener that misfortune is not special to him. Every family in the world has suffered some loss, and the listener should look at the famous Roman examples in the Caesars' hall, whose images are displayed there.

Seneca says that every great man he has in mind suffered deeply over family losses, either through grief for a relative or through the grief of those he left behind. As an example he gives Scipio Africanus, a Roman general, who learned of his brother's death while in exile and could not save his brother from that fate, though he had saved him from prison.

Seneca gives examples of strong family feeling among Roman leaders. Scipio Africanus freed his brother from an officer's custody and protested against a tribune's action, even though he held no office. Later he mourned his brother as bravely as he had defended him. Scipio Aemilianus saw his father's triumph and the funerals of two brothers at nearly the same time.
Though still a boy, Scipio bore a sudden family bereavement, which came during Paulus's triumph, with great courage. Seneca says he was born so Rome would keep a Scipio and be rid of Carthage.

Seneca lists famous brothers and sisters from Roman history who were close until death. He notes that the Pompeys were not even allowed to die together. Sextus Pompeius outlived both his sister and his brother, yet he still endured his grief and went on to make war.

Seneca notes that many brothers have died apart, and few have grown old together, and he will give examples from his own family. His point is that no reasonable person should complain about losing someone to death, since Fortune has also taken grief from the emperors themselves. Fortune here means chance or fate, the force that the Stoics held was beyond human control.

Augustus, the Roman emperor, suffered many deaths in his family: his sister, her son who was meant to succeed him, his son-in-law, children and grandchildren. Seneca says that, though Augustus was destined for heaven, nature did not spare him grief while he lived, and he was reminded often that he was mortal.

Seneca says that Augustus, who could bear anything, bore the heavy losses of his life and overcame his own sorrows. He then gives the example of Gaius Caesar, who lost his younger brother Lucius and grieved for him more in his mind than in his body, and bore both with great calm and courage.

Tiberius Caesar, Seneca's uncle, lost his brother Drusus while Drusus was campaigning in Germany. Tiberius held back his own grief and the army's, and he told them to mourn with the restraint expected of Romans, just as they kept discipline in battle.

Mark Antony, Seneca's grandfather, heard that his brother had been executed at the moment when he held great power. He was one of three rulers and nearly everyone else was under him. Seneca cries out that Fortune, or luck, mocks human grief in this way.

Marcus Antonius, a powerful Roman ruler, was in charge of life and death at the very moment his brother was being executed. He bore this blow with the same strength of mind he showed in his other troubles. He honoured his brother's death by sacrificing the blood of twenty legions to his spirit, and the speaker then sets aside such examples to mention deaths in his own family.

Seneca says that Fortune, or chance, has twice struck him by taking a brother, but has not overthrown him. He loved his brother Germanicus deeply. Still, he held back his grief so that he neither failed in his duty as a brother nor did anything a ruler could be blamed for.

Fortune, the goddess of chance, is shown to be cruel even to the royal family, sending funerals from the very house where people would seek gods' help. So no one should be surprised when she is unjust to ordinary families, since she has so often brought mourning to the throne itself.

Seneca says that Fortune, the goddess of chance and luck, will not change her ways even when the whole nation begs her to. She has always struck at anything and anyone, and she will keep bringing misfortune, even into homes that are sacred to the gods.

Seneca hopes that Fortune, if she has not decided to destroy the Romans, will spare the emperor Claudius. He asks her to learn mercy from him, since Claudius is the gentlest of rulers and was sent by the gods to bring rest after the nation's troubles.

Seneca urges Polybius to bear misfortune calmly, following the example of famous people who were deified or closely related to gods, and who endured suffering with steady courage. He adds that rank and birth separate people in other matters, but virtue is open to anyone who believes himself worthy of it.

Seneca advises that people should accept the death of a loved one as part of mortal nature rather than as a personal wrong. They should bear grief without excessive anger or bitterness, yet without weakness. Feeling sorrow is human, but refusing to bear it is unmanly.

Seneca is listing emperors who lost a brother or sister, and he refuses to include one particular Caesar. This man, he says, was born to ruin and disgrace the human race, and he wrecked the state. The state is now recovering under a gentle, kind ruler.

Seneca describes how the emperor Gaius Caesar (Caligula) responded to his sister Drusilla's death. He avoided her funeral and the usual mourning, and instead played dice and carried on his normal official duties. Seneca calls this shameful for a Roman emperor.

Gaius (the emperor Caligula) is described as acting wildly after his sister Drusilla died. He did not decide whether people should mourn her or worship her, and he punished those who did not show enough grief. Seneca says his mind was unstable: he was as crushed by hard times as he was overly proud in good times.

Seneca says that no Roman should copy a certain example of grief. He lists three wrong ways to handle mourning: distracting oneself with foolish pleasures, making the grief worse through dirt and neglect, or finding comfort in enjoying other people's suffering.

Seneca tells Polybius that he does not need to change his usual habits, because he already loves the studies that make life happier and help a person bear misfortune more easily. He urges him to study even more deeply, building a wall of learning around his mind so that grief cannot get in.

Seneca urges Polybius to keep his dead brother's memory alive by writing about him in his own works. He says written works last longer than stone monuments, which decay, and that this is a better way to honour the brother than useless grief.

Seneca speaks to Polybius, who is grieving the death of his brother. He says he will defend Fortune later, once Polybius is calmer and can judge fairly. Fortune has already given Polybius many good things to make up for the loss, and she gave him this brother in the first place.

Seneca tells Polybius to stop using his skill with words against himself, either to make his grief seem bigger or to shrink great things into trifles. Instead, his eloquence should be used to console him. He adds that consolation may not even be needed, since nature brings a certain amount of grief and imagination adds more. He says he will never forbid mourning altogether.

Some philosophers claim the wise person never mourns. Seneca replies that such people have probably never grieved themselves, since real loss would force them to admit sorrow. Reason should only trim grief of what is excessive and useless, not remove grief altogether.

Seneca urges the grieving person to keep sorrow within limits: neither cold indifference nor wild frenzy. Tears and groans should eventually stop, while the mourner still behaves so that philosophers and family can approve, and keeps the dead brother warmly in mind.

The speaker advises the grieving person to think about the dead brother in a way that brings pleasure rather than pain, because thoughts that only bring sadness are hard to keep hold of. He suggests recalling the brother's modest nature, business skill, diligence and loyalty, and imagining what a great future he could have had.

Seneca apologises for the consolation he has written. He says his mind is dulled by long exile, that a grieving man cannot easily comfort others, and that writing Latin is hard when he hears only a foreign tongue around him.

Seneca says he is writing a book on mercy to show the young emperor Nero how much pleasure comes from doing good. He holds that good deeds are their own reward, but he still wants Nero to examine a clear conscience and then look at the large, quarrelsome, angry mass of humankind.

The passage imagines a ruler speaking to himself and taking pride in his power. He claims he decides who lives or dies, who gets what fortune, which peoples are destroyed or moved, which kings are enslaved or crowned, and which cities are built or razed. The speech shows absolute power over others.

The speaker, who holds great power, says he does not punish people unjustly out of anger, impulse, or a wish to frighten others. He spares even the lowest subjects, and values any man simply for being human.

The speaker, a ruler, says he keeps his harshness hidden and shows mercy when he can. He weighs his decisions carefully, as if he must answer to the laws he has restored. He pardons people for youth, age, rank or lowliness, and when no reason can be found he pardons himself. He says he is ready to answer to the gods for mankind.

Seneca tells the emperor Claudius that he can say with confidence that he has kept everything in his care safe and has harmed the state in no way, openly or secretly. He has gained the rare reputation of innocence, and the people of Rome are grateful to him and value him highly.

Seneca tells the emperor that his reign is now a model in its own right, so no one looks back to earlier rulers for an example. He adds that a goodness which is only put on, like a mask, cannot last, while genuine goodness grows stronger over time.

Seneca tells Polybius that the Roman people were anxious while it was unclear whether Claudius would stay merciful. Now they can be sure of his mercy, since he is unlikely to change his character. He adds that great success tends to make people greedy, so their desires grow beyond what they already have.

The passage says that Romans now admit they are happy, and that their blessings could only be improved by lasting forever. It gives reasons: a deep and prosperous peace, a law that is openly respected and protected from violence, and a government that has nearly all the features of liberty except the ability to destroy itself.

Seneca praises the emperor's clemency, or mercy. Other blessings of his rule reach people only as far as their own luck allows, but everyone can hope for mercy. Even the innocent are glad that such mercy exists, since everyone makes mistakes.

Some people think clemency (mercy) only rescues guilty criminals, since it has no use before a conviction and no role for the innocent. The passage answers that, as a physician is honoured even by the healthy, clemency is respected by innocent people too.

Clemency, or mercy, can help people who are innocent, because bad luck sometimes takes the place of crime. It can also help good people who are punished for right actions over time. Many others could return to virtue if they were offered pardon, but mercy should not be given to everyone without judgment.

Good and bad people must be told apart, because treating everyone alike lets disorder and vice spread. Pardoning everyone is as cruel as pardoning no one, so the right course lies between the two. Since that middle is hard to find, any error should lean toward mercy.

Seneca announces how he will divide his discussion of clemency (mercy). He will cover three things: gentleness of temper, the true nature of clemency, which must be told apart from vices that look like it, and how the mind can practise and strengthen this virtue until it becomes habit.

Seneca says that clemency, or mercy, is the most humane virtue and the one most fitting for a man. He claims this is accepted even by rival schools: Stoics, who see man as made for the community, and Epicureans, who seek pleasure, since clemency promotes peace and restrains violence. He adds that mercy suits a king or prince most of all.

Great power is admirable only when it does good; power used only to harm is like a plague. A ruler's greatness is secure when his people know he cares for them and is on their side, so they come to him gladly, as to warm sunshine, rather than fleeing from him in fear.

Seneca says that a ruler's bodyguards will gladly die to protect him, even clearing a path to safety with their own corpses, and will stand watch over his sleep. He adds that peoples and cities willingly give their lives and property to defend a king they love when his safety is at stake.

Seneca argues that it is not foolish for a ruler to have many people die to protect one man. He compares this to the body, which serves the mind even though the mind is hidden and the body is larger. The one man stands for the mind, and the many are like the limbs that obey it.

A ruler's will directs a huge crowd the way a master directs his servants. If the ruler is greedy, people hunt for profit, and if he is ambitious, they risk themselves for glory, as Mucius and Curtius did. Without the ruler's wisdom, the crowd would destroy itself by its own strength.

Soldiers fight hard to protect their leader, because the leader holds the whole army together. Without him, the thousands of men would be only a burden and easy prey. The writer compares this to bees, which scatter when their king dies.

Seneca warns that Rome will stay peaceful and prosperous only while its people accept being controlled, like a horse that accepts its reins. If they cast off that control, or refuse to take it up again, the empire will break into pieces, and it will end on the day Rome forgets how to obey.

Good citizens value the state's interests above their own, so a ruler who carries the state's burden is dearer to them than their friends. Seneca adds that the emperor has become so bound up with the state that neither can be separated from the other without harm to both: the state needs power, and the emperor is its head.

Seneca argues that mercy toward citizens is necessary because a ruler and the state are like soul and body. Sparing others is really sparing oneself, so even guilty citizens should be spared, as weak limbs are, and punishment should stop before it goes too far.

Clemency, or mercy, suits all people but especially rulers, since they have more power to spare or harm and their cruelty causes wider damage. Each virtue fits some people better than others, though all virtues are linked and none is greater than another. Magnanimity, or greatness of spirit, suits even the humblest person, since resisting bad fortune is a great achievement.

Seneca says that magnanimity, or greatness of spirit, shows itself more clearly when a person holds power and sits in judgment than when merely standing in a court. Clemency, or mercy, brings peace to any home it enters, and because it is rarer, it is even more admirable in a royal palace.

The passage praises a ruler who could act on his anger without fear of consequences, yet holds himself back and uses his power more gently. He reasons that anyone can break the law to kill a man, but only he can break it to save one.

A high position needs a high mind, because a mind that does not rise above its station will drag the station down. A great mind stays calm and looks down on insults, while biting and attacking a fallen enemy belongs to base animals, not noble ones like lions and elephants, which pass by those they have beaten.

A king should not give way to fierce anger, because raging brings him down to the level of the man he is angry with. Instead, by sparing the lives of those who deserve death, he shows a power that belongs only to a supreme ruler, since life can be taken from anyone but given only to those below.
A ruler, copying the mind of a god, should be glad that some of his people are useful and good. Others he should simply tolerate, letting them stay to fill out the population.

Seneca asks the reader to picture Rome, crowded with people and goods, and imagine how empty it would be if only those a strict judge would find innocent were left. The point is that almost everyone in the city would count as guilty by such a standard.

Seneca says that few judges would deserve to be punished under the very laws they enforce, and few accusers are free of fault. He adds that people who have often needed pardown themselves are often the least willing to forgive others, since everyone has sinned in some way.

Some people have not kept their good resolutions firmly, so they have lost their innocence, even if reluctantly and after a fight, and they will keep sinning for the rest of their lives. Even a person who has fully purified his mind reached that innocence only by first sinning.

The gods are offered as the model a ruler should copy: he should treat his subjects the way he hopes the gods will treat him. The author then asks whether anyone would want the gods to punish every fault harshly, since no king would be safe under such a standard.

The passage argues that if the gods are merciful and do not punish the powerful right away with thunderbolts, then a ruler should be even more merciful toward others. It compares the world on a calm, fine day with the world during a storm, suggesting that a calm, gentle world is the better picture to follow.

A calm, lawful rule is compared to a clear, bright sky, while a cruel rule is like a dark storm that frightens everyone, including the ruler himself. Private people who stubbornly press their claims are easier to excuse, since they may have been wronged and their anger may come from that.

Rulers worry that being looked down on will make them seem weak if they do not strike back at those who wrong them. Yet a powerful man who holds back from revenge is praised for his kindness. Ordinary people can rage, sue, and fight without much notice, but a king's every outburst is judged harshly.

Seneca tells Polybius that a ruler should be careful of his conduct. Kings are not allowed the free speech that ordinary people enjoy, and this is the price of their position. Ordinary people can hide their faults, but a ruler's words and deeds are widely reported, so his reputation is always at stake.

Seneca tells Polybius that the emperor cannot move about freely as ordinary people do. He has no safe solitary walks, must always be guarded, and is bound to his high rank. This burden is shared with the gods, who likewise cannot come down from heaven.

A ruler is being told that his position makes him impossible to hide. Ordinary people can come and go unnoticed, but a person in power is watched by everyone, so his every move, word and anger affects the wider world.

Harsh punishment by powerful rulers frightens far more people than it actually harms, much as lightning kills few but scares everyone. People fear what an absolute ruler might do next, not just what he has done. Kings are therefore safer through kindness, since many punishments turn everyone against them, and a ruler should pardon while he still has cause to be severe.

A cruel king who kills his enemies does not reduce them. Like cut trees that sprout new branches, each execution brings forth new enemies, because the victim's parents, children, relatives and friends take the victim's place.

Seneca uses the example of Augustus to argue a point about human nature. Augustus was gentle later in his reign, but as a young man, while Rome was ruled by the triumvirate, he took part in plots, assassination and proscription. Seneca is writing to Polybius, whose family Augustus belonged to.

Augustus learns that Lucius Cinna plans to kill him. After a sleepless night, he is troubled because punishing Cinna means executing a young noble, a grandson of Pompey, whose only crime is this plot.

Antonius has signed a list of men to be put to death, but now he cannot bear to kill any of them. He groans and argues with himself. He asks why a man who plotted to kill him at an altar should go unpunished, now that peace has come and his life has survived many wars.

Augustus, lying awake, asks himself why he should keep living when so many men want him dead and killings never end. His wife Livia then urges him to try the opposite of his usual approach, as doctors do when normal remedies fail.

Augustus, the emperor, has been advised by his wife Livia to pardon Lucius Cinna, a man who plotted against him. Harsh punishments had not stopped earlier plots, so she argues that mercy would serve him better. Pleased to hear support for his own view, Augustus dismisses his other advisers and calls Cinna in alone.

Augustus speaks to Cinna, a man who plotted against him. He asks Cinna to hear him out without interruption, then reminds him that he once spared Cinna's life when Cinna was in the enemy's camp and gave back his father's estate.

Augustus accuses Cinna of plotting to kill him, reminding him of favours given: he was made a priest although others were passed over, and Augustus had treated him well. When Cinna denies it, Augustus says Cinna broke their agreement not to interrupt, and repeats the charge.

Augustus has just heard the full details of a plot against him from Cinna, one of the conspirators. Seeing Cinna silent and guilty, Augustus asks whether Cinna wants to become emperor himself, and mocks that the Roman people would be in a sorry state if only Augustus's life stood in Cinna's way.

Seneca is scolding a man who cannot even protect his own household. He lost a lawsuit to a freedman, a former slave, and now wants his powerful friends to join him against Caesar. The speaker asks whether the great old noble families would accept his rule.

Augustus, speaking to the conspirator Cinna, pardons him after a long speech and offers friendship. He says he forgives Cinna's life a second time, since Cinna had been an open enemy before and is now a secret plotter. He invites Cinna to prove who is more sincere: the one who grants the life, or the one who owes it.

Augustus, after forgiving Cinna, gave him the consulship even though Cinna had not asked for it, and Cinna became loyal to him from then on. Cinna also named the emperor his sole heir, and no one plotted against the emperor again.
Seneca is pointing to Julius Caesar's mercy toward defeated enemies. He argues that sparing them was useful to Caesar: it let him gain loyal men, including Sallust and Cicero, from the opposing side.

Augustus waited many years for Lepidus to die before taking the office of chief priest (pontifex maximus). He wanted the office to look like an honour he received, not a prize taken from a defeated rival.

Seneca says that the ruler's mercy kept him safe and well loved, even though he had seized power over Romans who were not yet used to being ruled. That mercy has made him famous since his death, and people believe him to be a god, not just because they were told to.

Seneca says Augustus is called a good emperor, and worthy of his adoptive father's name (Julius Caesar), for one main reason: he did not act cruelly even when personally insulted. Many rulers take personal insults more badly than real harms.

This is a list of reasons why a ruler was known for mercy. He smiled at insulting jokes about himself, he visibly suffered when he had to punish people, and he did not execute men convicted of plotting with his daughter. Instead, he sent them into exile with travel papers so they could leave safely.

The passage says that when a ruler knows many people will take up his quarrels and try to win his favour by killing his enemies, he really pardons them only if he does more than spare their lives. He must also make sure they do not lose their own lives.

Seneca says that Augustus was harsh when young and only became mild in old age, after many bloody acts such as the battles at Actium and Sicily and the killings at Perusia and the proscriptions. He adds that stopping cruelty only after tiring of it is not what he calls mercy.

Seneca praises Caesar's clemency, meaning mercy. It is genuine because it does not come from regret over past cruelty and because Caesar has never shed Roman blood. With absolute power, this mercy shows self-control and love for all humankind. It is free from base desires and from the example of earlier emperors who tested how far they could tyrannize their own people. Instead, Caesar chooses to blunt the sword of empire.

Seneca praises the emperor for sparing bloodshed, noting he had power over the sword at a young age. He argues that mercy makes rulers safer and more respected, and that it is the surest way to keep an empire intact.

Seneca asks why rightful kings keep their thrones for long and pass them to their heirs, while cruel usurpers are hated and short-lived. He answers that the difference lies in the ruler's attitude: tyrants enjoy cruelty, while kings use harshness only when they have good reason and have no other choice.

Kings may execute people, but only when the public good calls for it. A tyrant is cruel for its own enjoyment. Seneca says a tyrant differs from a king in actions, not in name, and he cites Sulla, who stopped killing only when he ran out of enemies.

Seneca is pointing to Sulla, the Roman dictator, who gave up his dictatorship and went back to being an ordinary citizen. Yet he had seven thousand Roman citizens killed. While thousands were being slaughtered nearby, he told the shocked senators to get on with their business, calling the victims mere troublemakers.

Seneca says that a ruler's mercy, or clemency, is what separates a true king from a tyrant. He notes that he will return to Sulla, a Roman dictator, and to how anger should be felt toward enemies, especially fellow citizens who have turned against the state.

Two rulers can both be guarded by soldiers, but their reasons differ. One uses his troops to keep his kingdom at peace, while the other uses fear to hold down widespread hatred, and even he cannot fully trust the men who guard him.

A tyrant is pulled two ways at once. He is hated because he is feared, so he wants to be feared even more, since that is the only thing keeping him hated. He lives by a line of verse, "Let them hate me, if they fear me too," which the passage says has brought many rulers down from their thrones.

Excessive fear makes people desperate, so they may act with reckless courage. Seneca compares this to beasts caught by a feathered rope: when frightened from another side, they break past the very thing that held them and trample it.

Seneca argues that people who see no hope and no safety, whatever they do, become fearless. A ruler who wants to keep people under control by fear must therefore leave them some security and some hope, because otherwise they may risk their lives recklessly.

A calm, fair king is trusted by his guards and soldiers, who see that their work keeps the whole people safe, so they serve willingly. A cruel tyrant is disliked even by his own guards, because he uses them as tools of torture and execution. Such a ruler cannot expect loyal service.

A tyrant is always in fear, because he dreads gods and men who will punish his crimes. Yet he cannot turn back, since each crime must be protected by another. So cruelty traps him, and he is forced to keep being cruel.

A tyrant who has used his power to kill and plunder is, in Seneca's view, to be pitied, but only by himself, since others pitying him would be wrong. He is distrusted by all, fears even his own soldiers, and cannot trust friends or children. Haunted by his crimes, he fears death yet also wishes for it, hating himself more than his subjects hate him.

Seneca describes a ruler who cares about the whole state and watches over all its affairs as carefully as if they were his own. He prefers gentle measures and is reluctant to use harsh punishment, even when punishing would benefit him.
A ruler who is calm, fair and gentle, who wants his people to prosper, and who is easy to approach and hears reasonable requests kindly, is loved, protected and honoured by his whole empire.

People speak of such a ruler the same way in private as in public. They are glad to raise children under his rule, and they feel their children should thank him for being born into so happy a time. Because people are loyal to him, he needs no bodyguards; his soldiers' weapons are only for show.

A ruler's duty, in this passage, is compared to that of a good parent. Such a parent scolds, threatens, and sometimes flogs a child, and disinherits him only after many repeated wrongs and a real fear of worse to come. Before that, the parent tries to guide the child toward what is right.

A ruler should use execution only when a person cannot be reformed. Seneca compares this to a parent, who also corrects a child before any harsher step, and says a prince should act the same way as the "Father of our Country."

Titles like "The Great" or "The August" only flatter a ruler's love of grandeur. A title like "Father of his Country" means something more: the ruler is given a father's power, which is meant to be gentle, since a father puts his children's interests before his own.

A father is slow to cut off one of his own limbs, and even then he grieves and hesitates. The same care should apply to judging others: someone who condemns quickly is close to condemning gladly, and someone who punishes too harshly comes close to punishing unjustly.

Seneca contrasts two fathers. Tricho, who flogged his son to death, was attacked in public, even though Augustus could hardly protect him. Tarius, whose son plotted to kill him, had him tried and only exiled him, still paying him the same yearly allowance, and was praised for it. Everyone agreed the son deserved his sentence.

Seneca tells of Tarius, who asked Augustus to help judge his own son. Augustus came to Tarius's house and sat beside him, letting the father keep control of the trial. Had Augustus insisted on hearing it at his own house, Caesar, not the father, would have run it.

Emperor Augustus asked the judges to write their verdicts in secret instead of speaking them aloud, so they would not simply copy him. Before the votes were opened, he said he would refuse any inheritance from Tarius, a rich man, so no one could suspect he wanted the estate by condemning the young man.

Seneca argues that a private person can rely on his own clear conscience to answer slander, but a ruler must also avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing. As an example, Caesar swore he would not take the dead man's property, so he could judge a case without self-interest. He then sentenced the son to exile wherever the father chose.

The judge did not give the harshest sentence, such as being sewn into a sack with snakes or imprisonment. He chose a mild penalty because he considered the relationship between himself and the accused, not only the crime. He held that the young man, who had tried the crime half-heartedly, should simply be sent away from Rome and out of his father's sight.

The passage praises a ruler who is merciful to others, so that people trust him enough to ask him to join family councils or make him heir alongside innocent children. It says a prince should make everyone more generous, and that even the lowest person counts as part of the empire and deserves the ruler's notice. It ends by urging that great kingdoms learn from the examples of smaller ones.

Seneca argues that a ruler of any kind, whether a prince, father, teacher or officer, should lead by gentle correction rather than harsh punishment. He asks which kind of father or teacher is better, the one who beats for small faults or the one who instructs kindly.

Harsh officers drive their men to desert, and the men cannot be blamed for it. People should not be ruled more cruelly than animals are handled. A good horse-breaker avoids frequent beating, since that makes a horse fearful and vicious, and uses gentle handling instead.

A huntsman does not often threaten his dogs with beating, because fear would break their spirit and make them dull and cowardly. He also does not let them run wild, so he trains them with control but without constant harsh punishment.
Seneca compares this to oxen and other slow draught animals. Even though they are treated harshly and live miserably from birth, excessive cruelty can still make them refuse to pull.

Seneca says people are hard to manage and deserve gentle handling. It is foolish to feel ashamed of anger toward animals yet want a person harshly punished. Anger is a sickness of the mind, so it should be cured with patient, calm care, the way a doctor treats a patient.

A good ruler, like a good doctor, should not give up on people who have faults. He should treat their vices with a suited method, sometimes blunt and sometimes gentle, even hiding the treatment if that works better. The ruler's aim is that people heal well, leaving no shameful marks.

A king gains no credit from cruel punishments, since anyone can see he has the power to inflict them. He earns real honour by holding back that power, protecting many from others' anger, and punishing no one out of his own anger.

Seneca says a decent man should treat his slaves within reasonable limits, not by asking how much cruelty he can get away with. Natural goodness and justice call for kindness even to slaves and prisoners, who should be seen as people placed under one's protection rather than as mere property.

Even though the law let masters treat slaves very harshly, some acts are still forbidden by the common rules of human life. The writer uses Vedius Pollio, a rich man who fed his lampreys (eels) with human blood and threw offenders into his fish-pond, to show that such cruelty deserves more hatred than even his slaves felt.

Seneca condemns a rich man who threw his slaves to lampreys, eels he kept to eat, and says such a man deserves many deaths. He adds that cruel masters are hated by everyone, and that kings' wrongs are remembered for ages, so it would have been better never to have been born than to harm one's country.

A ruler is most fitting when merciful, and the more power he has, the more his mercy stands out. Power does no harm when it follows the laws of nature. Nature itself shows the idea of a king, as in bees, whose king sits in the safest, central place of the hive.

The passage describes bees as a model for rule. The king bee does no work himself but keeps the others working. When the king dies, the whole swarm scatters, and they allow only one king at a time, testing which of rival bees is the better by setting them to fight. The king is also set apart by being larger and more brightly coloured.

Bees fight fiercely and die when they sting, but the king bee has no sting. Seneca says nature gave him none so that he would not be savage or seek revenge, and so his anger is disarmed. The king is offered as a model for great rulers.

Seneca says people should learn restraint from small creatures, since humans can do far more harm and so should control themselves more. He wishes human anger were like a sting that destroys itself when used, so that anger would fade quickly if each act of harm cost the angry person his own life.

A ruler who rules by fear cannot act safely. He must always feel as much fear as he causes, watch everyone, and suspect plots even when none are happening. The passage asks who would choose such a life when a ruler could hold his high position with general joy and without harming anyone, and so have nothing to fear.

A ruler cannot be safe in a state where no one is safe from him. He keeps his own life free of fear only by making sure his subjects are safe too. Mercy protects a king better than walls or fortresses, because people's love for him cannot be overcome.

Seneca says that a good ruler's illness should cause people fear, not hope. Men would gladly give up their most precious possessions to save the emperor's health. They would say he must live for the state's sake, since his goodness has made him belong to the state. Such a ruler, he asks, would no one dare to plot against.

Seneca says that people would wish a good ruler to be spared misfortune, since under him justice, peace and security flourish and the state prospers. He claims such a ruler comes close to the gods by acting kindly and generously, and he urges the ruler to aim at being thought the best as well as the greatest of men.

A ruler usually punishes for one of two reasons: to defend his own rights or the rights of someone else. The writer says he will first take the case where the ruler is personally hurt, because it is harder to stay moderate when anger comes from real pain than when punishment is only meant as a lesson.

Seneca says that a ruler shows clemency not by judging other people's wrongs fairly, but by controlling his own anger when he is personally wronged. He should forgive an injury to himself if he safely can, and otherwise soften the punishment. Just as true generosity means giving up what is one's own, a merciful prince is one who bears his own injuries calmly.

Seneca argues that revenge has only two uses: it pays the injured person back, or it prevents future harm. A ruler needs neither. He is too rich to need payment, and his power is already plain, so he does not need to prove it by punishing anyone. Seeing former equals placed below him is enough revenge.

A king can be killed by anyone, even a slave, a snake, or an arrow, but he can only be saved by someone greater than himself. So a ruler who holds the power to give or take life should use that power carefully and with restraint, as a gift from heaven.

A ruler who once had a former equal completely under his power has already gained his revenge. Such a man owes his life to his conqueror, so in a sense he is already dead. Sparing him brings the conqueror more glory than killing him would.

The passage argues that a defeated king is best left alive and in power. A conqueror who restores him to his throne gains more lasting fame than one who displays him in a triumph, where he would soon be forgotten. The conqueror gains the most by asking nothing from the king except the victory itself.

Showing mercy to the defeated is a victory over one's own anger, and it shows that the conqueror found nothing among the beaten worth taking. The ruler should be all the more gentle toward his own people, foreigners and the lowly, because they are far easier to overcome.

Some people you would gladly spare, and others are so beneath you that you would not bother to punish them, like insects you would not want to touch. But when many eyes are on a man, whether you spare or condemn him, you should use the chance to make your mercy widely known.

Seneca says that laws punishing wrongs against others aim at three things: correcting the wrongdoer, deterring others, or removing dangerous men so others can live safely. He adds that a light punishment corrects the offender more easily, since a man who keeps part of his property will act less recklessly.

Once a person has lost their good name, they no longer care about it, so punishment has nothing left to take away. Seneca argues that punishment should be used rarely in a state. When many people are guilty, wrongdoing becomes familiar, shame weakens, and frequent harsh sentences lose the force that makes them useful as a cure.

A good king sets a good moral standard for his people and drives out vices by being patient with wrongdoers. He is not meant to appear to approve of them, but to be reluctant and distressed when he must punish. A merciful ruler also makes people ashamed of wrongdoing, since punishment from such a man seems harder to bear.

Seneca argues that punishment does not stop crime. Severe punishments for a crime seem to go with more of that crime, since under a time when parricide had no special law, children were more fearful of committing it.

Seneca says that the early Romans did not name parricide, the killing of a parent, as a crime, because naming it might teach people to commit it. Once a law and penalty were set, the crime appeared, and later men were punished more often for killing relatives than for other crimes. He argues that when punishment is rare, innocence becomes the normal state.

A state that believes it is innocent will stay innocent, and it will be angrier at the few people who spoil its general good manners. Seneca warns that showing a state how many bad men it has is dangerous.

Seneca argues that harsh punishment is counterproductive for a ruler. He recalls that a plan to mark slaves by their dress was dropped, since it would have revealed how many slaves there were. Similarly, if no offence is ever pardoned, people will discover how many wrongdoers there are. A ruler who governs more mildly is better obeyed.

The human mind resists being forced, so it responds better to gentleness than to harshness. Just as spirited horses are steered with a loose rein, mercy inclines people toward goodness of their own accord, and so it does more good than severity.

Cruelty is not a human trait and does not fit a gentle human mind. Taking pleasure in blood and wounds is simply animal madness. Seneca tells Alexander that ordering Lysimachus thrown to a lion is no different from tearing him apart himself, since Alexander then has the lion's jaws and fierceness.

Seneca is speaking to Nero's freedman Polybius; the passage says that a person who harms others with a cruel and bloodthirsty nature is not expected to heal or be kind. He claims cruelty is the most hateful vice because it goes past ordinary limits and then past what is human.

A cruel ruler, the passage says, invents new punishments and enjoys men's suffering. This cruelty becomes a kind of madness when killing itself gives him pleasure. Such a ruler, it adds, is soon overthrown and faces repeated attempts on his life.

A cruel ruler, the passage says, faces as many dangers as there are people he harms, and can be killed either by individual plots or by a general uprising. Small wrongs against single people do not stir whole communities, but cruelty that reaches everyone turns all men against the ruler. The comparison is with small snakes, which go unnoticed and are not hunted by the whole country.

Seneca says that people act strongly only against great evils. A huge snake is attacked with siege weapons, and a deadly plague causes panic and even anger at the gods. Small troubles, or one sick person, are hardly noticed.
A small fire in one house is put out by the household and neighbours with water. A large fire that has already spread to many houses can only be stopped by pulling down a whole district of the city.

Cruel masters have often been killed by their own slaves, even though the slaves knew they would be crucified for it. Guards have turned on the rulers who trained them in deceit and violence. Seneca's point is that a cruel master teaches wickedness, so he cannot expect obedience from those he has corrupted.

Seneca says that even if a tyrant can be cruel without fear of consequence, his kingdom is wretched. Its people live in constant fear: they cannot speak freely at dinner, cannot enjoy public shows without risk, and find no pleasure in entertainment while living under threat.
Seneca says it is a wretched life to kill, to enjoy chains and bloodshed, and to make people flee in fear. He compares such rule to being governed by bears, lions, or poisonous snakes.

Even animals, which lack reason, usually spare their own kind, but tyrants do not stop at their own relatives. They harm friends and strangers alike, and their cruelty grows the more they give in to their passions.

Seneca describes a ruler whose cruelty grows step by step, from killing individuals to destroying whole nations and cities, and who sees this as a sign of power. He argues that true happiness lies instead in saving many lives and showing mercy.

A ruler's highest honour is the crown given for saving citizens' lives, not the trophies, chariots or spoils of war. Saving many lives is godlike, while mass killing is the power of ruin and destruction.

Seneca says he was moved to write on clemency (mercy) by a remark of the young emperor Nero. He admired the remark, which he thinks showed both a great mind and gentleness, and which slipped out unplanned. It revealed a struggle between Nero's natural goodness and the demands of being emperor.
Burrus, the prefect, asks Nero to sign the death orders for two robbers. Nero is unwilling to sign and cries out that he wishes he had never learned to write.

Seneca praises a speech, presumably one given by the emperor Nero, as something everyone should hear, including foreign peoples and enemies. He says it deserves to be obeyed by kings and rulers and could restore a golden age. He ends by saying all people should agree to love righteousness and goodness.

Seneca says that greed, which he calls the root of all evil, should be removed. He hopes that piety, virtue, good faith and modesty will return to rule, and that the long-dominant vices will give way to a happier and purer age.

The passage says that the emperor's own kindness will spread through the whole empire, and people will take on his character. It compares this to the head guiding the body: the limbs are lively or weak depending on the head's condition.

Seneca says he will speak at some length about a remark Polybius made, though he admits the subject will not please him. He prefers to give offence through truth rather than win favour with flattery, and he begins by asking what his reason is.

Seneca says he wants Polybius to know his own good deeds and words well, so that his current untrained impulses can grow into settled judgment. He also notes that harsh sayings, such as "Let them hate me, provided that they fear me," and a Greek line wishing the earth to burn after one's death, have become common in people's speech.

Forceful, striking language comes more easily to people when they express cruel or cynical views than when they express kind ones. The writer says he has never heard a spirited saying from a good, gentle person. So when he must write on such harsh matters, he does so rarely, reluctantly and after delay.

Seneca says that the word "mercy" may sound appealing and mislead people into going too far in the other direction. So he proposes to examine what mercy is, what qualities it has, and where its limits lie.

Mercy is defined here in two ways: as holding back from revenge when one has the power to take it, and as gentleness shown by a powerful person when setting punishment for a weaker one. The author adds that giving more than one definition is safer, since a single one may miss part of the subject, so mercy can also be described as a tendency to be mild in punishing.

Seneca says that a common definition of mercy has a flaw. The definition calls mercy holding back part of a penalty that is deserved. But a virtue should never give a person less than what is due, and everyone understands mercy as doing less than the punishment that could justly be imposed.

Seneca says that the opposite of mercy is not strictness, since no virtue is the opposite of another virtue. Mercy's opposite is cruelty, which he defines as stubbornness in demanding punishment. An objection follows: some people are cruel without punishing anyone, such as killers of strangers and torturers.

Cruelty is usually defined as excessive punishment for a wrong, so this case does not fit that definition. Seneca says it is not cruelty in that sense but ferocity, a delight in savagery, or else a form of madness: killing and mutilating people for no offence.

Seneca defines cruelty as a tendency of the mind toward harsh punishment, even when the person punished is guilty. Phalaris, a tyrant, is his example: he tortured criminals with extreme brutality. Mercy is opposed to cruelty, but it can exist alongside strictness.

Seneca argues that pity is not a virtue but a disease of the mind, even though many people praise it. Pity sits close to mercy, and excessive strictness can slide into cruelty. Both extremes should be avoided. Pity is the less dangerous error, but both lead equally far from the truth.

Seneca says good men should show mercy and mildness but avoid pity. Pity is a weakness of mind that cannot bear to see others suffer, so it is found most often in bad people. Mercy, by contrast, is guided by reason and asks why a person is suffering, not only how much.

Seneca reports that Stoic teaching is disliked because it says the wise man cannot feel pity or grant pardon, which seems to leave no hope of correcting mistakes. He then asks how true wisdom can tell people to give up human feeling and shut out mutual help, which he calls the safest refuge against misfortune.

Stoic philosophy teaches kindness and service to all, yet it holds that pity is a disorder of the mind, a sadness caused by seeing others suffer. The wise man, therefore, does not feel pity, because his mind stays calm and nothing can disturb it.

The passage argues that greatness of spirit cannot exist alongside sorrow. Sorrow weighs down and shrinks the mind, but the wise man, a Stoic ideal, stays calm and steady even in great misfortune, keeping the same composed face.

The wise man, Seneca argues, plans ahead and needs a clear mind, but sorrow clouds judgment. So he does not feel pity. He still helps others as those who pity do, comforting them without weeping with them.

The passage describes the ideal merciful person, who helps people in need such as shipwrecked sailors, exiles, captives and criminals. He gives help as an equal sharing what is common to all, not with the proud pity of those who want to be seen as kind and pull away from the people they help. He does all this with a calm mind and steady face.

The wise man, in this view, does not feel pity for people but still helps them and serves them, since he is born to be useful to all. He gives a fair share of his help even to those who deserve blame, though he gladly helps more those whose troubles come from bad luck.

The passage describes the ideal of a merciful person who steps in to help people hit by bad luck. Such a person does not feel disgust at the weak, the old or the crippled, but helps those who deserve it and looks kindly on all who suffer. The last sentence adds that pity is close to misery, partly made from it and partly coming from it.

Seneca argues that pity is a weakness of the mind. He compares it to tearing up at another's sore eyes or yawning when others yawn, both involuntary reactions. A wise man, he implies, should not feel or show pity for other people's suffering.

Seneca argues that a wise man should not pardon. Pardon means letting go of a punishment that is deserved. The wise man never does what he ought not to do, and never skips what he ought to do. So he never cancels a punishment he should impose.

The wise man gives you what a pardon would give, but in a more honourable way. He makes allowances, looks after your interests, and corrects your faults. He does not pardon you, because a pardon admits that the pardoner has failed in his duty.

The wise ruler, in this view, may reprimand young offenders who can still change, and excuse people who were tricked or drunk when they did wrong. He may also let enemies go free if they fought for honour, promises, or freedom. Such acts, the passage says, belong to mercy, not to pardon.

Mercy is not bound by fixed law. It decides according to fairness and goodness, and may acquit or set a penalty as it sees fit, without acting as if it were falling short of justice. Pardon, by contrast, means letting go of a punishment that was rightly due.
Mercy, in this view, has an advantage over pardon: it does not tell the person it spares that they deserved to be punished. Mercy is therefore the fuller and more honourable of the two.

Seneca says the disagreement with his opponent is mostly about wording, since both agree on the substance. A wise person will pardon many wrongdoers whose faults can still be corrected, treating each case as a gardener treats trees: straightening the bent, pruning the overgrown, and freeing the shaded.

Plutarch writes to his wife after hearing that their little daughter has died. He assumes the funeral is already over and hopes it was handled so as to cause her the least sorrow. If she has held anything back while waiting for his view, he tells her to go ahead without ceremony or superstition, which he says do not suit her character.

Plutarch asks his wife to bear their loss with patience. He says he understands how serious it is, and that her excessive grief would trouble him more than the loss itself. He adds that he is not hard-hearted, since they raised their many children together at home.

Plutarch is writing to his wife after the death of their young daughter, who was the first girl after four sons and was named after her mother. He says the mother, who loves children, must feel the loss sharply when she remembers the girl's cheerful nature, which had no trace of irritability or ill temper.

Plutarch describes his late wife's gentle, kind nature from childhood. Even as a little girl, she had her nurse give the breast-feed to her favourite toys, as if inviting them to share her table and her good things.

Plutarch says that the good qualities of his dead wife, which once gave him joy, should not now bring him grief when he remembers them. He fears, however, that if he stops grieving he may also stop remembering her, and gives the example of Clymene, who in a play rejects the things that once reminded her of her son.

The bereaved mother avoided anything that reminded her of her dead son, because it brought grief. The speaker argues that the memory of the dead child should now bring more joy than grief, as the joy of his company once did. He also says they should not sit and blame fortune, but use the arguments they have often given to others.

Plutarch tells his wife that people at the funeral were surprised she wore no mourning clothes, spent nothing showy, and kept everything quiet and orderly. He says he is not surprised, because she never liked display, even at festivals, and was thrifty in grief as in pleasure.

A chaste wife should stay pure amid wild festivity, and she should be just as firmly self-controlled in grief. Her task in mourning is not to fight natural feeling, as most people suppose, but to resist the excessive desires of the mind.

Natural grief and remembrance of the dead are acceptable. But an excessive show of mourning, with loud wailing and beating the breast, is as improper as overindulgence in pleasure. People excuse it only because it involves pain instead of enjoyment.

Plutarch argues that it is inconsistent to restrain joyful laughter while letting grief run free, since both come from the same feeling. He points to husbands who scold their wives for wearing perfume and fine clothes, yet let them shave their heads, dress in black and sink into mourning.

Plutarch criticizes husbands who step in when their wives punish servants too harshly, yet let their wives harm themselves severely at times when rest and gentle care are needed. The point is that the husbands are inconsistent in what they allow.

Plutarch tells his wife that they have never competed over such things, and he does not think they ever will. He praises her plain dress and simple way of life, which philosophers and citizens have noticed, and her courage after the deaths of their eldest son and of Chaeron.

Plutarch is recalling how, when news of their son's death reached his house, the household stayed so calm that visiting guests from overseas assumed the report was false. He praises his wife for keeping order at that painful time, and for nursing the boy even though her breast was injured.

Plutarch says that many mothers treat their children as playthings while they live, and then grieve wildly when they die. He argues that this grief comes less from true affection than from a desire for vain glory mixed with a little natural feeling. He adds that Aesop told a story in which Grief also received a share of honours from Zeus.

Grief, once it has settled into a household, is hard to drive out, so one should refuse it entry from the start. The passage advises keeping grief outside the home by not showing it through mourning clothes or cutting the hair.

Daily troubles, if they keep pressing, shrink the mind and make it harsh, timid and withdrawn. Grief then makes a person stop laughing, avoid light and company, and neglect the body. Plutarch argues the opposite is needed: a troubled mind especially needs the body kept healthy.

Grief is eased when the body is calm, as the sea calms in fine weather. But if the body is worn down by poor diet and the soul is fed only sorrow, the soul cannot easily recover, however much people wish it would.

Plutarch warns that visits from certain women, with their chatter and group weeping, make grief worse and keep it from fading. He recalls his wife's struggle with such visitors while comforting Theon's sister, who was grieving.

Plutarch says that people in grief make their pain worse, much as one would fan a fire or irritate an injured eye. A grieving person lets anyone talk to them about their sorrow, so a small hurt grows into a serious disease. He adds that he trusts his wife will guard against this.

Plutarch advises his wife to remember a time before their daughter was born, when they had nothing to complain of from Fortune (chance or luck). He says that if they treat that earlier time as better than their present situation, they will seem unhappy about the child's birth.

Plutarch urges his wife not to erase the two years they had their daughter from memory, but to treat them as a source of joy. He says they should not count the short time as a great evil, nor resent Fortune (luck or fate) for not giving more. Staying grateful and cheerful, and careful in speech about the gods, brings good results.

When trouble comes, a person who recalls his past blessings and turns his mind toward the bright things in life can either remove his grief or make it seem smaller. Remembering past happiness works like perfume against a bad smell, giving relief to those who do not dwell only on their misfortune.
Plutarch's point is that a person should not condemn their whole past because of one flaw. He compares a life to a book with one erasure among otherwise clean pages.

Happiness, the passage says, comes from sound reasoning and a settled mind, so that changes brought by chance need not disturb it. Yet if a person does measure life by outward events and by what others think, then Plutarch's wife should note that visitors still count her happy because of her family, home and life, despite their tears.

Plutarch tells his wife that it would be shameful if others would gladly trade their fortunes for hers. He says she should not rage against their situation or grow impatient with it, and that in their grief they should still remember the comfort they have left.

Plutarch tells his wife that listing life's hardships while ignoring its blessings is like quoting only the weak lines of Homer or like a miser who hoards wealth but mourns when it is lost. He adds that if she grieves over their daughter dying unmarried and childless, she can remember that the girl had both of those blessings while she lived.

Plutarch argues that a dead person who is free from pain has no reason for us to grieve on her account. He adds that the things she lost were small ones, which she knew and enjoyed only in small ways, so her loss is not a great one.

Plutarch tells his wife that she should not accept the view that the dead feel no pain, because their family tradition and the rites of Dionysus teach otherwise. He then says the soul cannot decay, and after death it is like a bird that has been caught and is still alive and held.

Plutarch is saying that a soul which has stayed a long time in the body, and has grown tame through the many affairs and habits of mortal life, may swoop down and enter a body a second time. Once in a body again, it is caught up once more in the changes and chances that come with being born.

Plutarch says old age is not criticized only for wrinkles, grey hair and weak bodies. Its worst effect, he argues, is that it weakens the soul's memory of the world beyond death and strengthens its attachment to this world, bending the soul down if it keeps the shape it took from bodily life.

Plutarch's point is that a soul that stays in the body only briefly is freed quickly and regains its earlier clarity and vigor, much as a fire relit soon after going out flares up again. A soul that stays in the body a long time, or has not been released early, becomes attached to earthly life and weakened, like a fire that is hard to relight after being out for long.

Plutarch says that Greek custom and law give no funeral rites or mourning to infants who die, because they have gone to a better, more divine place and so have no share in earthly things. He admits some people doubt this, but he advises outward obedience to the laws while keeping one's inner life pure.

Plutarch says people debate whether virtue can be taught, yet they are not surprised that good men are rare, almost as mythical as centaurs. He adds that no virtuous act is free of base motives, and that natural goodness is spoiled by faults, like fruit choked by weeds.

Plutarch points out that people are taught many everyday skills, such as playing the harp, dancing, farming, and cooking. Yet the art of living well, which all these other skills serve, is left untaught and is assumed to come naturally.

Plutarch argues that if virtue can be taught, then it is not unreal, since lack of teaching would prevent it. He contrasts this with Plato's point that disagreements about music or weaving, such as a wrong note on the lyre, never cause wars or quarrels between families or cities.

Plutarch argues that people will not practise a craft like weaving or lyre-playing without training, because they fear looking foolish. Yet they assume they can run a household, a state, or a public office without any learning. Diogenes shows the same point: he blamed a boy's bad table manners on the tutor who failed to teach him.

Plutarch argues that if a person can learn simple table manners as a boy, surely the larger skills of running a household, a city and public office can also be learned. He then gives the joke of Aristippus, a Greek philosopher, who said that if he were everywhere he would lose his fare money, and asks whether the fees paid to teachers are wasted if learning does not improve people.

Plutarch argues that teachers shape a child's character from infancy, much as nurses shape the body, by training habits. He gives a Spartan's reply that good conduct is made pleasant to boys, and lists small rules of manners that tutors teach, such as how to walk, eat and dress.

Plutarch argues that saying a doctor's skill is needed for minor complaints but not serious illnesses is like saying teaching matters only for small tasks while great matters are left to chance. He calls such a view absurd, as it would be to learn rowing but not steering, and says it is the opposite of what the Scythians did.

Plutarch argues that the skills of war, such as archery, riding and fighting with weapons, can be taught, so the higher skill of command must be taught too. He says it is absurd to claim that generalship comes naturally while lesser military skills must be learned. He also says that a free person's mind should be trained in virtue, not kept in servile crafts.

Plutarch argues that good sense, the faculty that directs all other skills and makes them useful, must also be taught, and it is ridiculous to say otherwise. He compares it to a banquet: even well-trained servants cannot make the feast pleasant without good order among them.

Clothes do not make a man warm by giving off heat of their own; they keep in the heat the body produces. In the same way, a happy life does not come from outside things like big houses, slaves and money. A person brings pleasure to what surrounds him, and his own temperament is the real source of his feelings.
Wealth, fame and power are more enjoyable when a person is joyful inside. A calm and gentle character lets a person bear poverty, exile and old age easily and quietly.

Plutarch says that virtue makes any kind of life painless and pleasant, even a poor one, as perfume makes worn rags smell sweet.
