Vice does the reverse: it makes wealth and splendour painful and unwelcome to their owners. He supports this with a line about a man who seems happy in public but is miserable at home.

A man cannot simply divorce his vice the way he could divorce a bad wife. The vice stays inside him day and night, troubling his meals, his travels and his sleep, so that even when his body rests, his mind is full of fear, dreams and anxiety.
Vice, here, is described as acting in two ways. In daylight it is careful: it copies what others do, hides its bad desires, and sometimes even fights against them instead of giving in fully.

In sleep, the unruly part of the soul escapes notice and the law's restraint. Freed from fear and shame, it indulges desires and lawlessness in dreams, which give no real satisfaction but only stir up the passions.

Plutarch asks where the pleasure of vice can be found, since vice offers no freedom from anxiety, pain, or lasting calm. He argues that bodily pleasures are not enough, because the soul only finds lasting joy through cheerfulness, fearlessness, and courage. Without these, any brief pleasure is soon overturned by worry, like a calm that covers a hidden rock.

Piling up wealth, slaves and property does no good while the soul is ruled by desire, fear and anxiety. Such possessions only feed a sick person who cannot digest them, making him worse. Riches cannot cure an inner disorder.

Just as sick people reject rich food but enjoy plain bread and cheese once they are well, the mind is similar: when reason is healthy, a person is content with simple things once they have learned what is good and honourable.

Philosophy, the passage says, lets a person find something good in any situation. Wealth helps by letting one do good for others, poverty brings fewer worries, fame brings honour, and obscurity brings safety from envy. The quoted lines add that the mind makes its own heaven or hell, and that a life of pleasure brings pain.

Plutarch says he will examine moral virtue, the kind of goodness that deals with emotions and is shaped by reason. He will ask what it is, how it exists, and whether the part of the soul that receives it has its own reason or borrows reason from something else.

Plutarch argues that virtue can exist and last without being mixed with matter. Before giving his own view, he will briefly review what others have said, so that his own ideas will be clearer and better grounded.

Menedemus held that there is only one virtue, which has many names. Temperance, bravery and justice are, to him, the same thing, just as "mortal" and "man" refer to the same being. Aristo also taught that virtue is one in substance, which he called soundness of mind. Its different forms, he said, come only from its relations to different things, as sight is called white-sight or black-sight depending on what it sees.

Virtue is one thing that shows itself in different forms. When it judges right and wrong action, it is called prudence; when it restrains the passions and keeps pleasure within proper limits, it is called self-control; when it governs dealings between people, it is called justice. Plutarch compares this to a single knife that cuts different things, or a fire that acts on different materials.

Zeno of Citium, the founder of the Stoics, is said to have treated prudence as the root of other virtues: justice in sharing out, self-control in choosing, and courage in enduring. Chrysippus, by contrast, gave each virtue its own separate quality, which Plutarch says multiplied virtues into a large, strange crowd.

Plutarch is criticising a thinker who formed new abstract nouns like "acceptableness" and "honourableness" from ordinary adjectives, as "brave" gives "bravery". He says this added many odd names to philosophy, which did not need them.

Plutarch here reports the view of the Stoics, a Greek school. They held that virtue is reason itself, made steady and unchanging, and that the emotional part of the soul is not a separate part but the same reasoning part, which becomes vice or virtue depending on how the passions and habits have changed it. It is called "unreasoning" only when appetite overpowers reason and drives it to excess.

Plutarch says that some philosophers wrongly held passion to be nothing more than reason gone bad, driven by faulty judgement. In his view, they missed that a person is made of two parts, and saw only the obvious mixing of soul and body.

Plutarch says the soul has a second, unreasoning part mixed with reason, and that Pythagoras knew this. That is why Pythagoras used music to calm and soften the soul. Reason alone, he thought, could not fully discipline it, so the soul needed another influence working alongside reason.

Plato held that the soul of the universe is not simple but made of two kinds of motion. One kind keeps a fixed order and circles in a single path. The other kind moves in opposing, changing orbits, and so produces the differences among things.

Plutarch says the human soul is a part of the soul of the universe and is built on the same pattern. It is not one simple thing. One part reasons and is meant by nature to rule, while the other part is unreasoning, driven by feeling and whim, and needs guidance.

The passage describes the non-rational part of the soul as split in two. Desire is the part closest to the body. Anger is the part that sometimes sides with the body and sometimes with reason, and it can push against the body. Reason and sense are opposed to anger and desire, so these parts often disagree about what is best.

Plutarch says that Aristotle first treated anger as a kind of desire, then later as part of the emotional side of the soul. Aristotle held that this emotional part is separate from reason, but not wholly without reason. It can listen to reason, unlike the plant-like and sense-based parts of the soul, which are deaf to reason and tied to the body.

The emotional part of the soul has no reason of its own, but it is naturally able to listen to reason and to shape itself to it. It can do this unless it has been fully ruined by animal-like pleasure and self-indulgence.

Plutarch says that reason can guide the body and the lower parts of the mind without force. It works through gentle persuasion, which he holds is more effective than compulsion. Just as reins guide a horse, reason directs the spirit, nerves, and bones, and the body moves when reason gives the signal.

Plutarch quotes Homer to show Odysseus pretending to feel nothing. His wife Penelope weeps, and Odysseus pities her inwardly, but he keeps his eyes hard and holds back his tears on purpose, out of cunning.

Reason can calm strong feelings at once. The passage gives two cases: a person's passions fade when handsome people are present whom reason and law forbid touching, and lovers lose their passion on learning that the one they loved is a sister or daughter. Then the body follows reason's lead.

People who enjoy a rich food may, on learning afterwards that it was unclean or forbidden, feel distress in their minds. Their bodies can also react, with violent retching and vomiting, just from the thought of it.

Plutarch says that musical instruments such as lyres, harps and flutes seem to share in people's feelings. They sound joyful when their players are joyful, sorrowful when they are sorrowful, and wild when they are wild, matching the mood and character of whoever plays them. He is comparing this to something he worries will sound like a strange new argument.

Plutarch asks why people doubt that our passions and feelings can obey reason. He notes that animals such as dogs and horses are trained to understand commands and act usefully, and that Achilles urges on his horses in battle. Yet our passions are part of us from birth and grow within us, so he wonders whether they can really be guided by reason.

Moral character gets its name in Greek (ethos) from habit (also ethos). It is a quality of the non-rational part of the mind, shaped by reason through habit. Reason does not aim to remove passion completely, but to keep it within limits and turn it into a good habit.

Plutarch divides the soul into three parts: power, passion, and habit. A power is the capacity to feel something, such as anger. A passion is that capacity actually acting, and habit is a settled state formed by repeated use. Habit is vice when reason trains the passions badly, and virtue when reason trains them well.

Plutarch separates two kinds of things. Some things simply exist, such as the earth, sky, stars and sea, and reason studies them in a detached, theoretical way. Other things concern us, such as good, evil, pleasure and pain, and reason deals with these by weighing choices and acting. Prudence is the virtue for the second kind, as knowledge is for the first.
Prudence, the practical skill of applying reason to action and feeling, often needs luck to succeed. Knowledge, which deals only with things that never change, needs neither luck nor deliberation.

Deliberation, or weighing choices, is only needed for things that change over time. A geometer does not weigh whether a triangle's angles add up to two right angles, because that is a fixed truth. Likewise, the contemplative mind, which deals with unchanging first principles, has no need to deliberate.

Practical wisdom often has to act in unclear situations and on uncertain matters. In carrying out its decisions, it needs the non-rational part of the mind, which supplies the drive to act. Reason must then control that drive, so that it helps in the right amount and at the right time, since the emotions can be too fast or too slow.

Reason's job, according to this passage, is to keep our passions at the right strength. A right action is like hitting a target: there is only one correct aim, but people can miss it by falling short or overshooting. When passion weakens out of fear or hesitation, reason spurs it on; when passion rushes ahead recklessly, reason holds it back.

Reason sets limits on the emotions, and this produces moral virtues in the non-rational part of the soul. These virtues are a middle point between too much and too little. Wisdom and prudence, however, do not depend on that part and are the complete perfection of reason, which brings the highest kind of understanding.

Plutarch says that the virtue needed because of the body uses the passions as tools for practical action. It does not remove the passions but orders and regulates the non-rational part of the soul. In strength it is complete, but in amount it sits at a middle point, avoiding both too much and too little.

Plutarch says that "mean" has three senses. A mean can be a blend of two opposites, like grey between white and black. It can be a number that sits between a larger and smaller number, like eight between twelve and four. Or it can be a neutral middle that belongs to neither extreme, like the indifferent between good and bad. He concludes that virtue is not a mean in any of these senses.

Moral virtue is not a blend of vices, nor is it a state that either lacks something or has too much. It is also not free of passions altogether. Instead, it is a mean, like the middle note in music that is in tune, avoiding both the sharpness of the highest note and the flatness of the lowest.

Moral virtue, the passage says, is a power in the non-reasoning part of the soul that brings the desires and feelings to a middle point between two faults, one of too little and one of too much. Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between meanness and wastefulness, and gentleness between numbness and savagery. Justice gives litigants neither too much nor too little.

Plutarch argues that reason and passion belong to separate parts of the soul. He says this is shown by the difference between temperance and mere continence: temperance is when reason controls the desires, which then obey it like a well-trained animal.

Continence, or self-control, is not a smooth obedience to reason. It is a state full of struggle, like a horse that resists the bit and whip. Plato's image of a charioteer with two horses, one unruly, shows the same thing: the driver must hold the reins tightly to keep control.

Plutarch's point is that continence, meaning self-control, is not a full virtue but something lesser. In it the better and worse parts of the soul do not truly agree. Desire still fights against reason, so the mind is like a town divided by factions, with one side celebrating and the other mourning.

Plutarch distinguishes two faults. Incontinence (lack of self-control) is less serious than intemperance, a full vice, because the incontinent person still knows what is right and is overpowered by strong feeling against that judgement. The intemperate person has both appetite and reason corrupted, so he consents to wrong desires and no longer sees that they are wrong.

Plutarch contrasts two kinds of people: one whose reason is overpowered by passion and fights against it, and one whose reason gives no resistance and even leads the desires. The second is worse, since it takes part in wrongdoing willingly. He adds that the two groups also speak differently, and quotes the self-indulgent man's line about life being empty without Aphrodite, goddess of love.

Plutarch contrasts two kinds of bad speech. Some people openly say they give themselves wholly to pleasure or ruin, which shows their judgement itself is corrupted by desire. Others, who lack self-control, admit their nature pulls them against what they know is right, which is a different condition.

A soul that has no firm reasoning is like a sandy anchor that does not hold. Such a soul gives up its judgment out of weakness. Plutarch supports this with a line about a ship whose cables cannot hold it when the wind blows.

Plutarch uses a ship image. Judgement is the cable that holds back from what is shameful, though it can be pulled loose by a strong storm of passion. The self-indulgent man, by contrast, is carried toward pleasure with full sail, letting his desires steer the ship.

The incontinent man is pulled toward wrongdoing against his will. He wants to resist his desires but is overpowered by them. Plutarch uses a quotation from Timon, mocking Anaxarchus, to show this struggle. He then says the wise man is temperate, not merely continent, and the fool is intemperate, not merely incontinent.

Plutarch says that a self-controlled person enjoys what is good and is not upset by what is bad. Incontinence, or lack of self-control, shows a clever-but-deceptive mind that has reason yet fails to hold to what it knows is right.

Plutarch contrasts the continent person, who still feels remorse and inner struggle, with the temperate person, whose soul is calm and orderly. In the temperate person, reason calms the wild desires and brings the natural appetites into line, so they follow reason willingly, like a foal walking beside its mother.

Plutarch says that true philosophers alone do willingly what others do only under compulsion, as a dog is pulled away from its pleasures by a blow. From this he concludes that the soul can tell the difference between its desires and something that opposes them.

Some thinkers hold that reason and passion are not truly different. They say one and the same reason simply shifts from one state to the other so quickly that we fail to notice. On this view, desire, repentance, anger, fear, and recovery from them are all one natural power of the soul.

Plutarch reports a view that desire, fear, anger and similar feelings are nothing but mistaken opinions and judgements. He rejects this view first because it contradicts what people observe in themselves: no one notices his feelings turning into judgement and back again.

A person in love can still see that the affair is harmful and try to end it, and even when desire wins, he still knows he is at fault. Reason never fully removes passion, and passion never fully removes reason. Instead, a person is pulled back and forth between the two.

Plutarch says that people who think the soul's leading part is desire at one moment and reason at another are making a mistake. It is like saying a hunter and his prey are one person who keeps swapping roles. In fact, he argues, the soul contains two opposing elements in conflict, not one thing that changes.

Plutarch's objector asks whether the reasoning part of a person can change its mind about what is useful and still remain one thing. The answer given is yes, but this is not a case of inner conflict. The rational part has one power, and it reasons about different subjects, as one mind works on different matters.

Plutarch says that inner conflict is usually not a clash between two reasons. Instead, a passion such as ambition, jealousy or fear secretly tips the balance, and we only seem to be weighing two reasons against each other.

Passions, such as anger or pity, cause the greatest delay in judging contracts and disputes. Reasoning without passion leads straight to justice. Once passion enters, pleasure and pain compete with judgement and justice.

Philosophers can drop old opinions easily, without the distress people feel in other matters. Plutarch's point is that in the part of the mind that deals with knowledge and reasoning, the emotions do not get in the way. So reason willingly accepts the truth once it is clear and gives up error.

Plutarch says that a willingness to hear good reasons and change one's mind comes from reason, not from emotion. Most people, though, mix their judgements with emotion, so reason cannot get a clear hearing. Pleasure, fear, pain or desire hold reason back. When one side wins, the other is not destroyed but only forced along against its will.

When a man is ashamed of falling in love, reason fights his passion and pushes it down. But when a question is weighed calmly, with no passion involved, and the arguments are equal, the mind makes no choice and simply stays in doubt.

When two parts of the mind agree or differ only in reasoning, one view wins quietly, without pain. But when reason clashes with unreasoning desire, the struggle is painful and splits the soul into two visibly opposed parts.

Plutarch argues that the passions come from a source separate from reason. He notes that people can love a bad child, or be unreasonably angry at their own family, yet feel rightful anger toward enemies or tyrants. Passion and reason can therefore agree or conflict, and they do not share one origin.

Plutarch compares two states of the mind. In one, passion and reason struggle against each other; in the other, they agree and work together. He gives the example of a good man whose marriage, begun in a lawful and sober way, grows into strong affection that reason also supports.

Young men who first come under kind teachers submit to them out of necessity and a wish to learn, but in the end they come to love them, so that they become known as their lovers rather than their pupils. Plutarch says the same happens in cities with good magistrates, neighbours and relatives by marriage.

People who first join together out of need and good manners gradually come to love one another, almost without noticing, as reason guides and wins over the emotions. The passage then cites a line about two kinds of shame and asks whether that shame often works against reason and causes hesitation that costs people their chances.

Some people give pleasant names to unruly feelings: they call shame modesty, pleasure joy, and timidity caution. Plutarch says this would be acceptable if such names were kept only for feelings that agree with reason, and other names used for feelings that go against reason.

Plutarch is criticizing certain philosophers who, though their tears, trembling and pale faces show fear and pain, refuse to call these feelings by their names. They prefer softer words such as "bitings" or "inclinations," which he regards as clever evasions rather than honest philosophy. He grants that they are right to call joy, wishing and caution good states of the mind rather than apathies, meaning freedom from passion.

In temperate people, reason does not destroy the emotions but sets them in order. The question then asks about worthless and weak-willed people, who love someone they judge they should not, and cannot love their parents as they judge they should.

Plutarch argues that passion and judgement are not the same thing. If they were, we would always feel love or hate as soon as we judged something worth loving or hating, but passion sometimes follows a judgement and sometimes does not. So passion is only the judgement that drives strong, excessive impulse, and the two are distinct, like a mover and what is moved.

Plutarch argues that Chrysippus, a Stoic philosopher, is forced by his own definitions to admit a division within the mind. One part follows reason without resistance, while another part follows reason only when persuaded and resists when not persuaded.

Plutarch is criticising people who say all wrongs are equally bad. On the subject of emotions, he says their view goes against reason and plain evidence. He argues that passions such as grief, fear and desire differ greatly in how strongly a person feels them, so they cannot all count as sin.

Plutarch argues that emotions of the same name are not all alike. He asks who would say that Dolon's cowardly fear equals Ajax's fear, or that Plato's grief at Socrates' death equals Alexander's grief at the death of Clitus.

Grief becomes much worse when bad news comes unexpectedly, because it hits harder than a misfortune we already feared. Plutarch gives two examples: a father who hears his friend has been tortured after expecting him to be prosperous, and a comparison of two angry rulers whose reactions were not equal.

Two rulers reacted differently to insults. Nicocreon had the philosopher Anaxarchus pounded to death, while Magas only threatened Philemon with a sword and then released him. Plato's saying follows: anger is like the mind's nerves, tightened by bitterness and loosened by gentleness.

Plutarch argues against a view that strong feelings are only bodily urges, not matters of judgement. He replies that people clearly judge things differently: some think poverty is no evil, others think it a great evil, and some think it the worst evil, so much so that they throw themselves off cliffs or into the sea because of it.

Plutarch says people disagree about what is truly bad or good. Some see death as bad only because it takes away good things, while others fear punishment and torment after death. Some value health so highly that they rank it above wealth, children and power, even above virtue. He concludes that people differ in how far they go wrong in such judgements.

The author argues that his opponents admit the unreasoning part of the soul is different from judgement, since they agree that it makes passions grow stronger. They may dispute the name, but in substance they concede the point to those who say the emotional part is separate from the reasoning part.

Chrysippus argues that anger is blind: it stops people seeing what is obvious and distorts what they do see. He says the passions drive reason out and force people into unreasonable acts. He supports this with a line from the poet Menander, where a man asks where his wits were when he made a bad choice.

Chrysippus, a Stoic thinker, is quoted as admitting that people, though naturally inclined to follow reason, often reject it when a stronger impulse carries them away. Plutarch adds that without this admission it would be absurd to say a person is sometimes better or worse than himself, or sometimes in control of himself and sometimes not.

Plutarch argues that every person has two parts, a better part and a worse part. A person who lets the reason rule the lower part has self-control and is a good person. A person who lets the lower, unreasoning part rule the higher part is lesser than he could be and is called incontinent.

By nature, reason, which is divine, should rule over the unreasoning part of the soul. That part comes from the body, is like the body, and is mixed up with it. Bodily desires show this, since they grow fierce or weak as the body changes.

Plutarch argues that desire is strongest in young men, whose blood and body heat run high, and weakest in old men, whose bodies have dried up, so that reason gains the upper hand. He adds that the same holds for animals' sexual appetite, and that differences in bravery among animals come from bodily nature, not from their beliefs.

Plutarch says that differences in emotion come from the blood, spirit and body, with emotion growing out of the flesh like a root. He points to blushing, paling, trembling and a racing heart as signs that the body responds to feelings, and joy at expected pleasures as a sign that it can be lifted by them.

When the mind works alone, without strong feeling, the body stays still and takes no part in its thinking, unless the emotional or unreasoning part of the soul gets involved. So, Plutarch concludes, the soul has two separate parts with different functions.

Plutarch says that all things are governed in different ways: by nature, by habit, by an unreasoning soul, or by a reasoning soul. Man shares in all of these, including an unreasoning element and passion. Passion is a natural part of him, so it should not be wholly removed but must be managed with care.

Reason should not destroy every feeling, as the harsh Thracian or Lycurgan way would do. Instead it should trim the wild parts, correct excess, and train the useful parts. Just as people mix wine with water rather than pour it away, reason should moderate passion rather than uproot it.

Plutarch says reason should tame the passions, not destroy them, much as a trainer curbs a horse's wild leaps but keeps its strength for work. Passions that obey reason and follow virtue are useful, even more so than tame animals used for plowing, riding or hunting.

Moderate anger helps courage, and hatred of evil helps uprightness. Righteous indignation is appropriate toward people who have good fortune they do not deserve and who are swollen with folly and pride. Natural affection, pity, and shared joy and grief cannot be removed from friendship, humanity, and true goodwill.

Those who want to get rid of love because it can become sexual madness are wrong, and so are those who condemn all desire because of greed for money. Such people are like someone who refuses to run for fear of falling, or to sing for fear of a wrong note: they reject a whole activity because it can go badly.

Plutarch says that virtue in the soul does not come from removing the emotions, just as music does not come from removing sharp and flat notes, or medicine from removing heat and cold. Instead, reason brings the passions into balance. Excessive grief, fear or joy is like a swollen or inflamed body.

Virtue does not require removing all feelings, only the excess of them. Fear, pleasure and anger should be kept within bounds, so that courage does not become recklessness and justice does not become cruelty. Without the passions entirely, reason would be dulled, as a pilot is idle when there is no storm.

Lawgivers use trumpets and flutes to stir ambition, emulation and courage in citizens before battle. Plutarch argues that strong feeling, like the inspiration Plato describes in poets, makes soldiers irresistible in war, as Homer shows gods filling Hector with might.

Plutarch argues that teachers use both praise and blame to guide the young, since praise brings pleasure and rebuke brings pain. Rebuke causes shame and fear, which are used to correct behavior. He ends with Diogenes' remark that a philosopher who has never caused anyone pain has nothing to boast of.

Plutarch says that the emotions of young men, such as shame, desire and ambition, are the handles by which reason and the law can take hold of them and guide them to the right path. He agrees with a Spartan tutor who said his aim was to make his pupil pleased by what is good and displeased by what is bad, since no higher aim suits the education of a free-born boy.

Plutarch argues that a person cannot tell they are becoming virtuous unless their folly is actually shrinking. Vice still weighs down every good intention, like lead on a fishing net. He compares this to music and grammar: no one could claim to improve there without losing some of their earlier ignorance.

A sick person does not feel that treatment is working while the illness is only slightly easing. The person notices improvement only when the body has fully recovered its strength and health has been completely restored.

Progress only shows when a person actually sheds some of their faults, as a scale rises only when the weight on it is reduced. Plutarch means that someone studying philosophy cannot be seen to improve while the soul stays fully flawed, and improvement requires getting rid of some imperfection.

Virtue cannot arrive in an instant, because a person cannot drop all their faults at once after a long time of holding them. Those who hold this view find it puzzling that a wise person might not notice they have become wise. Progress happens slowly, through small removals and additions, so it is hidden and quiet.

Plutarch imagines a change so sudden that a bad man could become good overnight, going to bed vicious and waking up wise. Such a man would then dismiss his past faults as meaningless dreams. The point is that Plutarch treats this kind of instant transformation as unlikely.

Plutarch argues that no one could fail to notice a sudden, complete change from cowardice and self-indulgence to bravery and self-control. He compares this to Caeneus, a figure in myth who was changed from a woman into a man, and says such a person would sooner fail to notice that transformation than fail to notice his own moral change.

Plutarch criticises the Stoics for bending facts to fit their own theories instead of testing theories against facts. Their claim that everyone except the perfect person is equally vicious leads to a confusing idea of "progress," which he calls close to foolish. It treats a person who is still ruled by passions as no better off than one who has not improved at all.

Some philosophers teach in their schools that good men like Aristides, Brasidas and Plato were as bad as notorious wrongdoers such as Phalaris, Dolon and Meletus. Yet in daily life they avoid those who are truly harsh and trust others with important matters as if those others were upright. Their own conduct contradicts their teaching.

Plutarch argues that evil in the mind comes in degrees, so people can improve by different amounts. As reason clears the soul, like light driving out a shadow, the change should be noticeable, just as a person climbing out of a ravine can see how far they have risen.

A person can judge how far they have advanced in philosophy in the same way a sailor judges his course: by steady, unbroken progress guided by reason. Progress shown by frequent stops or sudden bursts does not count as the same kind of measure.

Small, repeated gains add up to large ones, and Plutarch says this holds for virtue as well as for money, because habit strengthens reason's progress. Lapses and inconsistencies in some philosophers do more than slow moral progress: they can halt it altogether, since vice presses on steadily and drives back whatever gives way to it.

Philosophy never rests in one place; it keeps moving, tipping toward good or bad. So if a person fights vice day and night, without often lowering guard or accepting pleasure, idleness or busy affairs as truce-makers, that person can move forward into the future with courage and confidence.

If you have breaks in your study of philosophy, but your later work is steadier and more continuous than your earlier work, this is a good sign: your laziness has been driven out by effort and practice. The opposite is a bad sign, when lapses in your zeal soon become frequent and steady, as if your zeal were fading away.
Plutarch compares a young student of philosophy to a reed. Like a reed, the beginner first grows quickly but then is held back and shaken by small setbacks. When he feels no progress, he gives up.

A person who is eager and single-minded moves toward their goal and brushes past obstacles as if they were just bumps on the road. Plutarch compares this to strong love: real devotion shows in grief at being apart from the loved one, not just in joy at being together. Many people say they love philosophy, but they drop it as soon as other business distracts them.

A lover of philosophy who is strongly attached to a beloved companion is calm and easygoing when they study wisdom together. When he is away from that person, he becomes restless, irritable, and neglectful of his friends, driven entirely by his passion for philosophy.

Plutarch says that people should not enjoy philosophy only while they are hearing it, like a perfume that is enjoyed only while it is smelled. They should keep pursuing real progress in it, as hungry people miss food, even when marriage, wealth, friendship or military service pull them away. The more a person gains from philosophy, the more it hurts to lose it.

Progress in virtue, in this view, is the point where the road of philosophy stops feeling steep and hard. Practice smooths out the difficulty, and philosophy's light clears away the doubts, mistakes and regrets that trouble beginners. Beginners feel like sailors who have left home but cannot yet see the shore they are heading for.

People who give up familiar ways of life before they understand something better often get lost halfway and want to go back. Plutarch gives the example of Sextius, a Roman who left his public offices for philosophy, then grew so discouraged by its early difficulties that he nearly threw himself from a window.

Diogenes of Sinope, when he first became a philosopher, sat alone in a corner of the marketplace during an Athenian festival of feasting and revelry. There he began to doubt his chosen way of life, thinking that he had taken up a hard, unusual life for no necessary reason and was shutting himself out of its pleasures through his own choice.

A man, Diogenes, is sitting alone, and a mouse nibbles his barley-cake crumbs. He scolds himself, asking whether he, a gentleman, should be grieving that he is not drunk on soft couches, while a mouse feasts on his leftovers.
When these low moods of the mind are rare, and the mind soon recovers from them and shakes off the annoyance and distraction easily, then a person can be sure they are making progress in virtue.

Plutarch says that a sign of progress in virtue is staying calm when others shake a person's commitment to philosophy. This includes serious advice from friends, mockery from opponents, and reports that former companions have gained wealth, royal favour, marriage money, or public office.

Someone who feels no envy toward what most people admire has, by this sign, already been taken hold of by philosophy. Such indifference is possible only if a real love of virtue has been firmly planted in the mind. Mere overconfidence, which can come from anger or foolishness, does not produce it.

People who have reached this state of mind compare themselves with others and take pride in it. Solon said virtue is not worth exchanging for wealth, since wealth passes from one owner to another while virtue stays. Diogenes likened his moving between cities to the Persian king's seasonal residences. Agesilaus asked what advantage the great king had over him if the king was not more upright.

Aristotle told Alexander that having many subjects was no reason for pride, since anyone with correct ideas about the gods had as much reason to be proud. Zeno, hearing Theophrastus praised for his many students, said his own group was smaller but more harmonious. Both sayings measure worth by quality, not by numbers.

Plutarch says that one sign of progress in virtue is losing envy and jealousy, which trouble beginners in philosophy, once you compare virtue with outside things. A second sign is a change in how you talk: beginners tend to speak in ways that make themselves look good, and some are drawn to lofty talk about the heavens and nature.

Plutarch says that many people who study philosophy use it badly. Some turn to arguing and word-games like quarrelsome puppies, some train in debate for its own sake, and others collect quotations and stories without using them in their lives.

Antiphanes joked that in one city words froze as soon as they were spoken in winter and only thawed out in summer, so people heard them then. He applied this to Plato's teaching: most young men only understood it when they had grown old.

Plutarch says that people stay in this state with regard to philosophy until their judgement becomes sound and healthy. Once it does, it starts to favour teachings that build character and greatness of mind, and it looks for discourses that lead inward rather than outward.

Plutarch compares philosophy to the poet Sophocles, who said he improved on Aeschylus by dropping showy language, then harsh artificial method, then changing his diction. Likewise, students of philosophy show real progress in virtue once they move from flattering, artificial speech to speech that deals with character and feelings.

Read philosophy and poetry for their substance, not their verbal cleverness or puzzling detail. Pay closest attention to whatever in them is useful, that can improve one's character or calm strong emotions.

Plutarch says a reader should be like a bee that gathers the valuable substance from poems, not just the pleasing surface. People who read Plato and Xenophon only for their polished style are like those who love drugs for their smell and colour but ignore what they actually do to the body.

Advanced learners can learn from what they see and do, not only from spoken lessons. Aeschylus, the Greek playwright, shows this at a boxing contest: while the crowd shouted at a boxer who was losing, he nudged a friend and remarked that the beaten man stays silent because of his training, while the spectators cry out.

Two stories show how a person who practises self-discipline learns from ordinary events. Brasidas, bitten by a mouse he had caught, let it go, reflecting that even the smallest creature will fight for its life. Diogenes threw away his cup after seeing a boy drink from his hands. The point is that close attention and steady practice make a person quick to take lessons in virtue from any source.

Plutarch says that people who test their philosophy in real life, in dangers, pleasures, quarrels, lawsuits and public office, show their beliefs through what they do. He compares those who simply talk about philosophy in public, at parties or among young men, to sellers of drugs who are not really doctors.

A teacher of this kind is said to be little different from the bird in Homer's poem, which feeds its young from its own mouth even though it suffers for it. In the same way, the sophist (a paid teacher of rhetoric and argument) hands his pupils whatever knowledge he has, and gains nothing for himself.

Talk should help the speaker improve, not seem like showing off or ambition. A person should be as ready to listen as to teach, and should drop arguing for its own sake, enjoying winning fights more than learning and teaching.

Plutarch says that a sign of moral progress is staying calm in an argument: starting and finishing without anger, not gloating when winning, and not sulking when losing. Aristippus, a Greek philosopher, is his example. He lost a debate to a clever talker who was otherwise foolish, and he took it calmly.

A man who lost an argument said he would sleep better than the winner, who was puffed up with pride. Plutarch then suggests a test for progress: whether you are unafraid when speaking to a large crowd, not discouraged by a small one, and prepared when you must address the people or a magistrate.

Plutarch says that Alcibiades, a gifted Athenian, often failed when speaking in public because he lacked confidence. He compares this to Homer, whose first line was faulty yet who went on writing confidently. Therefore, people seeking virtue should speak in public whenever they can and not care much about crowd noise or praise.

A person should judge his actions as well as his words, asking whether they serve a real purpose or only make a show. The passage compares this to private love, which seeks no onlookers. A true philosopher, it says, should take pride in quiet virtue and need no audience's praise.

Plutarch compares a man who announces his own good behaviour to a householder who shouts to his maid that he is no longer angry. Such a person, he says, wants public praise and is vain. He has only a dream-like idea of virtue, not the real thing, and shows off his deeds the way a painter shows off a picture.

Plutarch says that real progress in virtue shows in quiet acts of integrity, not only in good deeds that are talked about. Examples include casting an honest vote, refusing bribes or improper requests from the powerful, going without a drink when thirsty, and resisting temptation and keeping it private. Agesilaus, a Spartan king, is cited as an example of the last.

Being content with your own good opinion, and trusting your own judgment about what is honourable, shows that your reason is firmly established within you. Plutarch says, borrowing a phrase from Democritus, that such a person takes their pleasures from themselves.

Plutarch compares young would-be philosophers to ears of grain. Full, fruitful ears bend low, while empty ones stand upright and proud. So the students who look most confident and scornful of others are often the emptiest, and real learning makes them humble and drop that arrogant manner.

Just as a full vessel of water leaves no room for air, a man full of real virtue loses his pride. He thinks less of himself, stops showing off with outward signs of philosophy like a long beard and shabby cloak, and works on his mind instead. He is strict with himself but gentle with others.

Advanced students of philosophy, the passage says, no longer eagerly claim the name "philosopher" or list themselves as one. If someone calls them that, a modest young man would smile, blush, and say he is no god. The passage then adds a quotation from Aeschylus about recognizing a woman who has known a man, a comparison that ties the image of recognition to the point.

A young man who has truly begun to make progress in philosophy is described with two lines of the poet Sappho about burning desire, a dry tongue and fire in the body. Plutarch says such a man shows a gentle, mild look and is pleasant to hear speak.

Plutarch compares the start of philosophy to a religious initiation. Newcomers at first crowd and push, seeking fame. Once someone truly enters and sees the inner truth, they become quiet, reverent, and humble, and follow reason as if it were a god.

Menedemus joked that students at Athens began by thinking themselves wise, then fancied themselves philosophers, then orators. As they studied more, they became ordinary people and gave up their pride and high opinion of themselves.

People who need a doctor react in different ways. Some call for help at once for a small pain, some send for one only when they are ill, and some, too sick in mind to see they are ill, refuse the doctor altogether. In the same way, wrongdoers differ: some get angry at anyone who corrects them, while others accept rebuke.

When someone has done wrong, offering oneself for blame and confessing the fault, instead of hoping it stays hidden, is a clear sign of moral improvement. Diogenes, a Greek philosopher, said a person wanting to do right should seek a friend or a fierce enemy who will correct them.

Someone who shows off small faults, such as dirty clothes or a torn shoe, or who jokes about his own physical flaws, while hiding serious faults of character like envy, spite, pettiness and love of pleasure, has made little or no progress in virtue. Those inner faults are the ones that count.

A person who takes on his own faults, and feels more pain over the faults themselves than anyone else would, shows real progress in virtue. Even if he cannot do that, he still shows progress by listening calmly to criticism and changing his behaviour. Such a person cares more about the vice than about how others see it, so he does not mind criticism that helps him improve.

Diogenes once told a young man who hid in the kitchen when seen leaving a tavern that the more he hid, the more he was still in the tavern. Plutarch uses this to say that the more a bad person denies his vice, the more it takes hold of him, just as poor people who pretend to be rich only grow poorer.

Someone who is truly advancing in virtue, Plutarch says, admits mistakes openly, as the physician Hippocrates did when he publicly acknowledged an error about the skull's sutures. Such a person cannot accept being shown wrong about his own faults. Bion's and Pyrrho's sayings show a more settled virtue rather than progress.

Bion said a friend has made progress when he can hear insults as calmly as praise. Pyrrho, caught in a storm at sea, pointed to a pig eating grain calmly and said a wise person should keep the same calm mind through reason and philosophy, untroubled by life's changes.

Zeno held that a person can judge how far they have progressed in virtue by their dreams. If in dreams they take pleasure in nothing shameful, wish to do nothing wrong or unjust, and their imagination and passions stay under the control of reason, they are making progress.

Plato had already noted that in sleep, the part of the soul that is naturally tyrannical, meaning the one ruled by desire rather than reason, shows its wild wishes. It dreams of incest with its mother, eating forbidden food, and acting on the worst desires that law and shame keep in check by day.

Plutarch compares a well-trained pack animal that keeps to the road even when the reins are loose to a person whose unruly desires have been brought under reason. Such a person, he says, does not easily act badly in dreams or illness, but keeps to habits that have grown strong through careful attention.
If the body can be trained to hold back tears, fear and desire, Plutarch argues, then the soul's passions can be trained too, even to the point of shaping what they do in dreams.

In this story, the philosopher Stilpo dreams that the god Poseidon is angry because he did not sacrifice an ox, as the people of Megara usually did. Stilpo is not afraid. He replies that he gave what he had at home, rather than borrowing money for a lavish offering.

Plutarch says that dreams can show how far a person has advanced in virtue. A person whose dreams are pleasant, clear and free of fear, harshness or harm may be said to have such signs of progress. The dream about Poseidon, a sea god, is given as an example of a pleasant dream.

Plutarch says that fear, panic, childish pleasures, and grief over bad dreams are like waves on a shore. They show that the soul is not yet settled, since it is still being shaped by opinions and laws and escapes them in dreams. The reader is then asked to check whether such signs show real progress in virtue or only a habit that reason has not yet made firm.

Complete freedom from the emotions is described as a great and godlike thing, and getting better at virtue is said to mean the emotions have become somewhat weaker and gentler. To measure this, one should check whether desire, fear, and anger are now weaker than before, because reason puts out their force and heat quickly.

Plutarch suggests that people should check their own character by asking a series of questions. Are they more moved by modesty or fear, emulation or envy, love of glory or love of riches? Are they plainer or more luxurious in living, slower or quicker in acting, too admiring or too scornful of others? The "Dorian" and "Lydian" are Greek musical modes, used here as a comparison for going too far or not far enough.

Plutarch says that when a person improves in virtue, bad feelings first move toward milder forms, and this is a sign they will soon fade away. Like a disease that shifts away from vital organs, vice is weakening. Progress first reduces the excess and sharpness of the passions, aiming at a balanced middle.

Plutarch says that a clear sign of moral progress is when a person turns the praise they give to virtue into actual deeds. Admiring a good quality is not enough; one should want to copy it and refuse to do what one condemns. He begins an example about the Athenians admiring Miltiades' courage.

Themistocles, the Athenian general, was kept awake by the victory of Miltiades and went on to copy his deeds, not just admire them. Plutarch concludes that we have made little progress if our admiration for noble people does not move us to imitate them.

Real praise of virtue stirs a person up rather than leaving them jealous of others. It makes them want to match what is noble, and it makes a true learner compare his own conduct with that of a good man. He feels grief at his own shortcomings, but also hope and a restless drive to improve.

A person who is really progressing in virtue loves and admires good people, copies them gladly, and gives them honour and praise. Someone full of envy and rivalry toward better people may be driven by a wish for glory or power, but does not truly respect virtue.

A reader knows they are making real progress in virtue when they come to love good people so much that they count them happy. They admire such a person's words, looks and manner, and want to copy him and stay close to him.

Good people should be admired not only when they are prosperous but also in hardship. Like lovers who find beauty even in a loved one's weakness or sorrow, we should love virtue even when it brings exile, imprisonment, poverty or condemnation. The passage supports this with a line from Euripides: "Unto the noble everything is good."

People with strong enthusiasm for what is good do not give up when trouble is certain, and no one can turn them from what is noble. In any task, office or crisis, they picture how great men such as Plato, Epaminondas, Lycurgus or Agesilaus would have acted and follow that example.

Those who are advancing in virtue keep the memory of good men in mind, as a way of checking their own bad speech and passions. Just as people who learn the names of the Idaean Dactyli repeat them to drive away fear, remembering good men steadies them in hard moments so they do not fall. Plutarch offers this as a sign of moral progress.

Plutarch says that a person with a good conscience does not become flustered, blush, or hide when a respected and virtuous man suddenly appears. Instead, they calmly go to meet him. He illustrates this with Alexander the Great, who stayed composed when a joyful messenger ran up to him.

Plutarch describes a man who asks whether Homer has come back to life, meaning he is so impressed by someone that he compares him to the great poet. He then says a young man of good character naturally enjoys the company of good and noble people and likes to show them his home, his life, and his work.

A person who has made real moral progress grieves that a dead father or guardian never saw him in his improved state. He would wish above all that the dead could return to watch his conduct. By contrast, those who have wasted their lives dread even seeing their relatives in dreams.

A sign of growth in virtue, Plutarch says, is to treat no wrong as small and to guard against every one. He compares this to money: people who think they will never get rich ignore small expenses, while those who see wealth coming care more for each coin. The passage breaks off before finishing its point about people who ask "Why trouble about hereafter?"

A person who notices every fault, and is troubled when even a small wrong is excused, shows that he has already become fairly pure. He refuses to be stained by anything. Thinking that nothing we do really matters makes people careless about small things.

Plutarch compares a person who has made progress in virtue to a skilled builder. Such a person builds their life carefully, using reason as a measuring tool, as a good builder uses a line and level. Bad workers, by contrast, pile up any material they find. Polycletus, a sculptor, is quoted as saying the best work is the one where the model passes the test of the nail.

Plutarch compares wealth gained by marriage or trade with wealth that brings no real enjoyment. A man who marries for a dowry sells himself and gains little, and a man who chases great riches through hard, risky sea trade has great wealth but no time to enjoy it. Tantalus was a figure of Greek myth who was punished with unreachable food and water.

Plutarch says a wise man gave Agamemnon a swift mare as a gift so that Agamemnon would stay home and not go to war at Troy. He contrasts this with people today who push themselves into royal courts and hard campaigns uninvited, just to win a horse, a brooch, or some similar reward.

Plutarch describes a man who chases ambitions far from home, leaving his wife and house behind. He is pushed around by fortune, wastes time on empty hopes, and suffers insults. Even when he gets what he wants, he grows restless and wishes for a quiet life, while people who live obscurely envy him.

Vice, or wrongdoing, causes unhappiness all by itself. Tyrants need executioners and torture tools to make their victims miserable, but vice works on the soul directly, without any such tools, and fills a person with sorrow, grief, and remorse.

Some people can stay silent under torture, because reason eases their pain and holds them back. But anger, grief, fear and remorse cannot be held back in the same way. Plutarch concludes that vice is therefore stronger than fire and sword.

Plutarch uses a comparison with a city hiring builders. He imagines a contest to make human life miserable, with Fortune and Vice as the rival contractors bidding for the job. Fortune arrives with many tools and costly equipment for producing misery.

Plutarch imagines Fortune listing the disasters she can bring on people: wars, tyranny, storms, poison, prisons. He admits most of these come from Vice, or wrongdoing, not from luck. Even so, he grants that they come from Fortune, and then says that Vice alone, with no outside troubles, is what must be asked how to make a person unhappy.

Fortune is challenged with three threats: poverty, slavery and poison. The passage answers each with a philosopher who did not fear it: Metrocles, who was content with poverty; Diogenes, who joked when he was sold as a slave; and Socrates, who drank the poison.

The passage gives two examples of brave death. The first is a man who calmly drank a poison and was thought by survivors to be blessed in the afterlife. The second is Decius, a Roman general who threw himself onto a funeral pyre between the armies to save his country.

Plutarch describes two customs he attributes to Indians: wives competing to be burned on their husbands' funeral fires, with the winner praised as happy, and wise men being honored only if they deliberately burn themselves alive while healthy, freeing the soul from the body.

Plutarch lists hardships that some people have treated as good things. Losing wealth and living in poverty was, for Diogenes and Crates, the start of happiness and freedom. Death by crucifixion or impalement, or having one's body left to animals, was for some peoples and for Theodorus a matter of no concern or even a happy custom.

Only people without manliness or reason, who are soft, untrained, and still hold the opinions they had as children, are made unhappy by such misfortunes. Bad luck alone does not bring complete misery; that happens only when vice joins it.

Plutarch compares two things: a thread cutting bone softened in ashes and vinegar, and ivory shaped only after it is softened in beer. Likewise, Fortune (chance or luck) harms a person who is already weak and soft through vice, cutting into them easily.

Plutarch compares a poison from Parthia, which harms only a person who already has a wound, to a person who is upset by bad luck. Just as the poison kills only the wounded, a person is shaken by outside events only if they already carry some hidden inner weakness.

Vice does not need bad luck to make a person unhappy. Plutarch says she needs no storms, robbers, hail or false accusers. Instead she works inside people, stirring up lust, anger, superstitious fear and envy, even among the rich and fortunate.

Socrates asks Menon what virtue is. Menon answers quickly that virtue differs for boys and old men, men and women, rulers and private citizens, masters and servants. Socrates replies that Menon has given many virtues instead of the one he was asked about, and suspects Menon names many because he does not know the single one.

Plutarch is mocking the idea that someone with no firm friends should worry about ending up with too many. That is like a maimed, blind man fearing he will grow a hundred hands or many eyes. He also praises a young man in Menander who thought anyone with even a shadow of a friend was admirable.

Plutarch says that wanting many friends is the chief obstacle to gaining a true friend. People who chase every new acquaintance, like a woman who gives herself to everyone, lose the old ones and end up with none. Like a child picking flower after flower, we are drawn to what is new and neglect what we already have.

Plutarch says that, going by old traditions about lasting friendship, friends usually come in pairs. He gives famous pairs from myth and history as examples, such as Achilles and Patroclus and Orestes and Pylades.
Friendship, Plutarch says, is a bond between two people, not a flock like crows. Good will and kindness joined with virtue are rare and costly, so a person can only love or be loved deeply by a few.

Just as a river split into many channels runs thin and weak, so love in the soul is weakened when it is spread among many people. For this reason, parents with only one child love that child most strongly.

Plutarch does not say a person should have only one friend. He says there should be one friend who stands above the others, a close bond like that of a child born late in life, built over long shared experience, as the proverb about eating a bushel of salt together suggests. He contrasts this with the shallow friendships people make over drinking, games, or chance meetings.

Wealthy and powerful men are praised for having many friends, because crowds of visitors and followers come to their houses. Plutarch says these crowds are like flies that gather only for food, since they come only for what they can gain. He then begins to list what true friendship needs: virtue, familiarity, and usefulness.

Plutarch argues that having many friends is hard, mainly because good judgement is needed to choose them. He compares this to testing dancers, rowers or stewards, which takes time and care. True friends are rare: people who will help you in good times and bad.

Plutarch says that ships face many storms and cities build walls against many dangers, yet a well-tested friend offers protection and refuge that is worth even more. If friends are not tested and turn out to be worthless, like bad money, then losing them is a relief, and the quoted verse says those who have such friends should pray to lose them.
It is hard to end an unpleasant friendship. Like harmful food, a bad friend hurts you if kept, and if you force him out, the break is bitter, full of hostility and hatred.

Do not make friends quickly with just anyone who approaches you, or love whoever clings to you. Test people first, and bond only with those who deserve friendship and can be useful to you. Plutarch compares easy friends to brambles that catch on your clothes while you walk past them toward the olive and vine.

Plutarch says that friendship should be tested slowly over a long time before it is kept, as the painter Zeuxis said he painted slowly so his work would last. He then asks whether it is easy to test and keep many friends at once, since close companionship is the full pleasure of friendship.

Menelaus says that nothing divided him and Odysseus while they lived, since they loved each other. Plutarch claims that a large number of friends has the opposite effect. A close friendship between two people joins them tightly, as fig juice curdles milk, while many friends weaken that bond.

Having many friends, Plutarch argues, divides people and pulls them apart, because friendship is spread across too many people to blend into real closeness. Kindness then becomes uneven and weak, since its benefits are scattered too thinly to be useful.

People do not all share the same natural inclinations, and their circumstances in life differ. Chances to act come to some people and not to others, much as winds blow fair for one ship and against another.

Plutarch argues that having many friends causes problems. If all of them want your help at once, with the same tasks or with different ones, you cannot satisfy everyone. Each friend asks you to join a different activity at the same time, such as a voyage, a lawsuit, a business deal, a wedding, or a funeral.

People accept it when a friend neglects them and says he forgot or did it by accident. But a friend who excuses his neglect by saying he was busy helping someone else does more harm, because it also makes the person feel jealous.

Most people value friendship only for what they can get from it, forgetting that friends also expect favours in return. Plutarch compares this to Briareus, the many-handed giant, who had to feed fifty stomachs and so was no better off than a person with two hands feeding one. Having many friends means doing many services for them and sharing their worries and hard work.

Plutarch rejects a line from Euripides that advises moderate friendship, so that a friendship can be easily ended or tightened as needed. He says instead that this advice should apply to enmities: people should hold their hatreds in moderation, so that their anger and suspicions can be easily dropped.

Plutarch quotes Pythagoras, who said not to give many people your right hand, meaning not to make many friends. Many casual friendships bring trouble, since you must share others' worries, griefs and dangers. Chilo adds that a man with no enemies seems to have no friends either, because enmities come along with friendships.

A friend cannot avoid sharing in a friend's troubles, injuries and quarrels. Enemies of one's friend come to hate him too, and even other friends may turn envious. So those who gather many friends may end up with enemies as well, as an oracle warned Timesias that bees would be followed by wasps.

Plutarch says that a friend's kindness and an enemy's wrongs are not remembered with equal weight. He points to rulers who turned on the friends of men they had destroyed, such as Alexander, Dionysius, Nero and Tiberius, and had them tortured and killed.

Some friends share in their friends' misfortunes even though they gained nothing from their friends' good fortune. Plutarch compares this to Creon, who ran to rescue his daughter from the poisoned gifts and was burned too. He adds that Theseus was bound in prison with his friend Pirithous, and that this happens most of all to philosophers and kind people.
Thucydides reports that during the plague at Athens, the people who showed the most virtue died, because they cared so little for their own lives that they went to visit their sick friends.

Plutarch advises against spreading one's goodwill across too many people. Friendship should be kept for those who deserve it and can return it. He adds that friendship arises from similarity, which is the strongest reason against having many friends.

Animals will not willingly mix with creatures unlike themselves, but gladly join their own kind. So the question is how friendship could arise between people who differ in character, temperament and outlook on life.

Friendship, the passage says, is unlike music. A harp or lyre sounds well through a mix of high and low notes, but true friendship needs no difference at all. Friends should agree in opinion, wish and feeling, as if one soul lived in several bodies.

Plutarch asks who is so busy and changeable that he can fit himself to many different kinds of people, and not laugh at the saying of Theognis, an old Greek poet. That saying tells a man to copy the octopus, which takes on the colour of whatever stone it clings to.

The polypus (an octopus-like sea creature) changes colour only on its surface, taking the look of whatever touches it. Real friends, by contrast, try to become alike in character, feelings, speech, interests and temperament.

Plutarch says that only a man with no fixed character of his own, a kind of shape-shifter like the sea god Proteus, could try to be a scholar with scholars, a wrestler with wrestlers, a hunter with hunters, a drinker with drinkers, and a politician with politicians at the same time.

Plutarch compares the soul that makes many friends to formless matter, which takes whatever shape outside forces give it, becoming fire, water, air or earth in turn. Such a soul is easily changed, but true friendship needs a steady, unchanging character. So a lasting friend is rare.

Self-love makes a person unable to judge himself fairly, because love is blind toward whatever it loves. The only exception, the passage says, is someone who has trained himself to value what is noble over his own private interests.

Flatterers find an easy way in through our self-love. Each person already flatters himself, so he readily welcomes outside flattery that seems to confirm his good opinion of himself. Someone who is fond of flatterers is really very fond of himself, and wants to have every good quality and believes he already has them.

Plutarch argues that the flatterer is an enemy of the gods, especially Apollo. Truth is divine and the start of all good things, but the flatterer works against the saying "Know thyself." He fills people with self-deception, so their good qualities stay flawed and their bad ones cannot be corrected.

Flattery does not target poor or obscure people. It preys on good, honourable, and powerful people, ruining great households and even kingdoms. Because of this, it is important to learn how to detect flattery so that it cannot harm true friendship.

Flatterers cling to rich and powerful people and leave when their fortune fails, much as lice leave a dying body. Plutarch says we should test friends in good times, as money is tested before it is needed, rather than discover they are worthless in hard times.

We should guard against a flatterer before any harm is done, not only after, just as testing a deadly poison by tasting it can kill the taster. Plutarch also rejects the view that every pleasant companion can be judged a flatterer on sight.

A friend should not be unpleasant or harsh, and friendship should not be proud or stern. Even its proper behaviour should be pleasing and attractive, since the Graces and Desire are said to dwell in it. The Graces are minor goddesses of charm and grace in Greek myth.

Friendship brings pleasure in good times as well as in bad, not only comforting people in trouble. Plutarch compares it to fire, which Evenus called the best sauce, and says the deity mixed friendship into life so that everything becomes bright, sweet and pleasant.

A flatterer wins people over by giving pleasure, much as fake gold copies the shine of real gold. He seems pleasant and cheerful and never argues, as a real friend might. Still, Plutarch says, not everyone who praises you is a flatterer.

Real friendship includes both praise and criticism, each at the right time. A friend who praises freely and gladly is trusted when he criticises, because people see his blame as coming only from need. Fretful complaining has no place in friendship.
Someone objects that it is hard to tell a flatterer from a friend, since both can please and praise in the same way. Flatterers can even outdo friends in services and attentions.

Plutarch means that a true flatterer is a clever, skilled schemer, not the crude sort most people call flatterers. Those crude ones are the hangers-on who start fawning as soon as dinner begins, and whose servility and rudeness show at the first course and drink. "Oil-flask-carriers" were servants who attended a man at the baths, and "table-men" were dinner companions kept for amusement.

Plutarch gives three examples of obvious flatterers. Melanthius, a hanger-on of the tyrant Alexander of Pherae, joked that Alexander was killed through his side and into Melanthius's belly, meaning he ate at the tyrant's table. Other flatterers would run to a feast whatever danger stood in the way, and female flatterers in Cyprus let kings' wives step on them to climb into carriages.

The main point is a warning about a kind of flatterer who does not look like one. He is not a hanger-around at dinnertime or a drunk. He is sober, meddles in your affairs, wants your secrets, and plays the part of a serious friend rather than a joker.

Plutarch argues that the most dangerous flattery is the hidden, serious kind rather than the open, playful kind. Such flattery can make even a real friendship look suspicious, so people may mistake one for the other. He illustrates this with the story of Gobryas, who tells Darius to strike through both men wrestling together.

The main point is that flattery is hard to tell apart from true friendship, because the two look alike and share feelings and habits. Plutarch compares this to wild grains mixed with wheat: a sieve with small holes keeps out the good grain too, and one with large holes lets the bad through. So we must be careful not to reject a real friend along with a flatterer.

A flatterer wins people over in the two ways that friendship does. Friendship is very pleasant and brings favours and services, so the flatterer offers pleasure and eagerly volunteers help, appearing zealous and obliging at every turn.

A flatterer wins a person over by copying that person's tastes and habits. Since friends are usually brought together by shared likes and dislikes, the flatterer shapes himself to match whoever he wants to win, changing easily and imitating so closely that he seems to be the person himself.

Flatterers copy the sign of true friends, who speak frankly. But they do not speak genuinely or usefully. Like cooks who add bitter or sharp flavours so that sweet food does not cloy, they add a show of teasing, sly hints that only seem frank.

A flatterer is hard to spot because he copies the people around him, much as some animals take on the colour of their surroundings. Since he hides his true nature behind these imitations, the task is to expose him by comparing him with a true friend. Plato's saying is that he wears other people's colours and shapes because he has none of his own.

Friendship, the passage says, usually arises between people who are alike in character, habits and interests. It supports this with a quotation: old men prefer the voice of old men, boys of boys, women of women, the sick of the sick, and someone in trouble finds comfort in one who has suffered the same misfortune.

A flatterer wins someone's trust by first copying that person's interests, habits and way of life, as a hunter lures an animal. Once the victim feels close and at ease, the flatterer can easily take hold of him.

The flatterer criticises whatever he knows his target dislikes and praises whatever the target likes, often with exaggerated surprise and admiration. This makes the target more sure that his tastes come from sound judgement rather than whim.

The writer says the first test of a true friend, as opposed to a flatterer, is consistency. A real friend keeps the same likes, praises the same things, and lives by one steady pattern. Someone who does this is a friend.

A flatterer has no settled character of his own. Instead of living by his own standards, he copies whoever he is with, changing shape like water poured from one vessel into another. He always adapts himself to the tastes of the people who host him.

The passage compares a flatterer to an ape. An ape copies a man's movements and gets caught for it. The flatterer, though, copies each man in a different way, singing and dancing with one, wrestling with another, and joining a third in hunting, so he can win them over.

The passage describes a flatterer who adapts his manner to whoever he wants to win over. With a young scholar he poses as a serious philosopher, with books and a shabby cloak, but with a rich, drinking man he strips him of his money, as Odysseus stripped the beggar of his rags.

Plutarch describes a flatterer who drops the trappings of a philosopher and mocks philosophers. He compares this to Dionysius of Syracuse: when he was keen on philosophy, his court crowded in to study geometry, but when he lost interest and returned to wine, women and pleasure, the whole court became foolish and ignorant.

Plutarch says that the great flatterers and demagogues (popular political leaders) win favour by copying the habits of whoever they are with. He gives Alcibiades as the chief example: at Sparta he lived plainly, in Thrace he drank and fought, and at the Persian court he lived in luxury.

Epaminondas, Agesilaus and Plato kept the same character and habits wherever they went. They did not change their dress, diet, speech or conduct to suit different companions, so Plato was the same man at Syracuse with the tyrant Dionysius as he was at his school in Athens and with his friend Dion.

A flatterer changes his views to match whoever he is with, like a polypus changing colour. Plutarch says a man can test this by pretending to switch opinions himself and watching whether the flatterer copies him. The flatterer never loves, hates or feels anything on his own; he only reflects other people's feelings, like a mirror.

A flatterer agrees with whatever his target says. If you criticise a friend to him, he says he never liked that friend. If you praise the friend, he swears he is glad and trusts him. If you talk of leaving public life for a quiet, private life, he says they should have done so long ago.

A flatterer praises every plan you have, even when you change your mind. Plutarch says a true friend should instead tell you the truth and help you judge well. Someone who simply agrees with everything you say is no better than your own shadow.

A true friend does not copy everything you do or rush to praise you. He praises only what deserves praise, and he is loyal in love rather than in hate, as the quoted line from the playwright Sophocles puts it.

A true friend is born to share in doing right and loving what is noble, not in wrongdoing. Still, close companionship can pass on a bad habit without the friend meaning it, much as eye irritation spreads. Plutarch gives examples: Plato's followers copied his stoop, and Alexander's companions copied his tilted head.

A flatterer, Plutarch says, is like a chameleon: he copies everything except what is good, so he copies the faults of his friend. He is like a weak painter who paints every wrinkle and scar because he cannot paint a fine likeness. He copies bad habits because he thinks imitating faults is the safest way to avoid blame.

A flatterer, Plutarch says, is one who pretends to enjoy his friend's faults. People who truly dislike their friends' failings are distrusted, and this has harmed men such as Dion, Samius and Cleomenes. So the flatterer acts as if he shares his friend's vices, passing for a loyal companion.

Flatterers pretend to share their friend's bodily faults or misfortunes, such as poor eyesight or deafness, so they seem alike. One example is the flatterers of Dionysius, who was short-sighted: they bumped into each other and knocked dishes off the table, as if they too could not see. Some even dig into family secrets to find more matches.

Flatterers, seeing a friend troubled over a marriage or a son, pretend to share the trouble. They reveal their own family troubles in return. Feeling equal in misfortune, the friend then trusts them with his own secrets, and so is bound to keep silent.

A man once sent away his own wife because his friend had sent away his, yet he secretly kept visiting her. His friend's wife noticed, which exposed him. Plutarch uses this to show that the man did not understand what a flatterer is, since he thought a crab-like image of a greedy parasite described a flatterer.

A flatterer copies the good qualities of the person he flatters, but always makes sure that person comes out ahead. Real friends have no rivalry. They are content whether they are equal or one of them is better.

The flatterer always makes himself seem a little lesser than his friend, admitting he is outdone in everything except faults. In those, he claims to go further: a friend who is peevish is called bad-tempered, a friend who is superstitious is called a fanatic, and a friend who is in love is called madly in love.

Plutarch describes how a flatterer behaves toward someone he wants to please. He praises every small thing his friend does, even laughter, and claims to match or exceed him in skills like running, riding, and poetry, while still giving his friend the higher place. The flatterer and the true friend can look alike in this way, and the passage ends by saying that their differences lie in these details.

A friend and a flatterer both give pleasure, but they differ in purpose. Plutarch compares this to perfume, which exists only to please, and medicine, which works to heal and treats its pleasant smell as a side matter.

Plutarch says that painters use bright colours, and some drugs look pleasant too, but the two are told apart by their purpose. In the same way, friends use cheerful talk, good food, wine and teasing to make serious and worthy matters more pleasant.

Plutarch contrasts a flatterer with a true friend. The flatterer aims only to please, so he shapes his words and actions to give pleasure. The true friend does what is right, which sometimes pleases and sometimes causes pain, and he accepts the pain when it is best. He compares this to a doctor who uses pleasant remedies or harsh ones as the patient needs.

A true friend is compared to a doctor. Sometimes he praises and encourages a man toward what is noble, as with the quoted lines from Homer, and sometimes he rebukes him sharply when correction is needed. In both cases he aims only at the good of the one he helps.

A true friend sometimes corrects a friend with harsh action, not just words. Menedemus shut out a wayward young man, and Arcesilaus cut off a student who mocked a rival, both only until the offender changed. Plutarch says a friend may cause pain for the friend's good, but not so much that the friendship ends, much as a biting medicine heals.

A friend is compared to a musician who sometimes loosens and sometimes tightens the strings. He is pleasant but always helpful, and will oppose or cause pain when needed. A flatterer plays one note over and over, only to please, agreeing with every wish of his patron.
