A friend is someone who can also disagree with us and cause us pain, not only someone who pleases us. Plutarch says we should distrust a relationship that only pleases and never stings. He adds a Spartan's saying: a king who is not stern even with bad people cannot be good.

Flatterers are compared to a gadfly or a tick that attacks the ears of people who love praise and clings there. The passage says we must check whether praise is for what someone did or for the person himself. Praise is for the deed when it comes from people who praise absent people as well as present ones, and who praise others of like mind, not only us.

A good test of whether praise is deserved is to check your own conscience. If you do not regret the act, feel no shame about it, and would not have acted differently, then your inner judgement agrees with the praise. If your inner judgement disagrees and refuses the praise, it cannot be swayed by flattery.

People in trouble usually prefer sympathy to advice. When they have done wrong, they see the person who blames them and stirs up regret as an enemy, and they welcome the one who praises their actions as a friend.

People who praise a bad word or deed, even in fun, do only small, passing harm. Worse harm comes from flatterers who praise vice under the names of virtue. They spoil a person's character at its root, like thieves who steal the seed corn instead of food from the bin.

In times of political conflict and war, people change the meanings of words to suit themselves. Reckless daring is called loyalty to one's side, careful delay is called cowardice, and caution is called a cover for cowardice.

Flatterers give bad qualities good-sounding names. Waste is called generosity, cowardice is called caution, and madness is called wit. Meanness is called thrift, and a passionate, vain man is called manly.

Plutarch recalls Plato saying that a lover flatters the beloved. The lover calls a snub nose graceful, a hooked nose royal, and dark skin manly, and praises pale skin as divine. Even an olive complexion is just a lover's way of hiding excessive paleness.

A man who wrongly thinks he is handsome or tall soon finds out his mistake and suffers little harm. Praise that calls vices virtues is far more dangerous, because it removes shame and led the Sicilians to admire the cruelty of tyrants like Dionysius and Phalaris as hatred of wickedness.

Flatterers have done great harm by calling bad behavior admirable. They called Ptolemy's weakness, superstition and noisy rites religion, and they excused Antony's luxury and excess as good humor. The passage asks whether flattery's praise was also what led Ptolemy to music and Nero to acting.

Kings are often flattered with the names of gods, such as Apollo for singing, Dionysus for drinking, and Heracles for wrestling. They enjoy these titles, and flattery then drags them into all kinds of shame.

A flatterer is careful about praise, since he knows people will suspect him if he praises too freely. He does not flatter everyone. When he meets a foppish man or a plain country man in a thick leather coat, he mocks him instead, as Struthias did to Bias by pretending to praise his stupidity.

A flatterer who meets a refined, cautious person does not praise him openly. Instead he approaches slowly, as a hunter would a wild animal. Sometimes he reports praise that supposedly came from strangers or respected men, so the compliment seems to come from someone else.

The flatterer invents small false accusations against his target, claiming other people told him of them. When the target denies saying or doing them, the flatterer praises him with mock-logical compliments, such as saying he would never speak ill of enemies or steal, so the praise looks like proof of his good character.

Flatterers sometimes praise vices by running down the opposite virtues. They call modesty rustic and out of place among corrupt people, and they call contentment and honesty a lack of spirit. Plutarch's point is that such criticism secretly flatters the faults of the person they want to please. Word count: about 50.

Flatterers tell each man what he wants to hear. They join idle people and call public duty meddling and the wish for office empty vanity. They run down a philosopher to please an orator, and mock faithful wives to win favour with loose women. Their trickery is so complete that they sometimes mock themselves too.

Flatterers often pretend to criticise themselves so they can praise others more smoothly, just as wrestlers bend low to throw an opponent more easily. A flatterer may call himself a coward or a bad-tempered man, only to make his friend look brave and patient. The passage then turns to a different kind of person, one who thinks well of his own judgment and wants to appear strict and proud of his moral rectitude.

A flatterer who wants to win over a man who is hard to flatter pretends to seek his advice on private matters. He asks, as if the man were wiser than everyone else, whom the flatterer should trust. After hearing the answer, he leaves, saying he has received an oracle, not just an opinion.

Plutarch describes how flatterers pretend to admire a person's abilities. King Mithridates liked to act as a surgeon, so his friends offered to let him operate on them, though they did not say so openly. They acted this way because being believed would seem to prove his skill. The quotation at the end means that fortune or fate takes many different forms.

To test a flatterer, a person can give strange or absurd advice on purpose. If the listener agrees with everything and keeps praising it, he is not a true friend. He is seeking some other gain and only wants to make the speaker feel proud.

Flattery works best when it does not look like praise. Just as hunters catch their prey more easily when they seem to be doing ordinary work, flatterers succeed most when they seem to be busy with something else while they praise.

A man who gives up his seat to a great man, or stops his speech in the middle to let a rich man speak, shows by his silence that he thinks the other man is better and wiser. Such yielding says more than any loud praise would.

Flatterers, according to this passage, take the best seats at theatres and meetings but give them up to rich people, not because they think they deserve them but to win favour. At meetings they speak first, then yield to supposed better men, and quickly drop their own view when a wealthy, powerful or famous person disagrees.

Flatterers, Plutarch says, lower their sails before the rich and famous, not before real skill, virtue or age. Apelles, the painter, did not do this. When the wealthy Megabyzus tried to talk about painting, Apelles let his assistants mock him, since they knew he was speaking of things he did not understand.

Solon told the rich king Croesus that ordinary people like Tellus, Bito and Cleobis were happier than he was. Flatterers, by contrast, call kings and rich men happy and also wise and virtuous in every way.

Some people reject the Stoic claim that the wise man is rich, handsome, noble and a king all at once. Flatterers, by contrast, say a rich man is also a fine orator, poet, painter and athlete, even letting others win races to please him. Plutarch uses this to show how flatterers praise people with false claims.

Carneades said that rich men's sons and kings learn nothing well except riding. Their teachers flatter them and let them win at wrestling, but a horse throws any rider who cannot ride well, whatever his rank.

Plutarch mocks a saying of Bion, which claimed that praising people is useful as praising a field makes it fruitful. He replies that a field does not get worse from praise, but people who are praised falsely and beyond what they deserve become conceited and are harmed.

A flatterer can copy a friend in many outward ways, like Patroclus wearing Achilles' armour. But he cannot copy the friend's outspokenness, the frank speech that is the heavy burden of true friendship. Like Patroclus, who could not lift Achilles' spear, the flatterer leaves that part alone.

Plutarch says that flatterers sometimes avoid blame by using stern looks and mild criticism instead of jokes and drink. He compares this to a fake Hercules on stage carrying a hollow cane instead of a club, and to cushions that look firm but give way under pressure. So a flatterer's criticism seems strong but is actually soft and yielding.

Plutarch contrasts false frankness with true friendly frankness. Fake outspokenness is all show, so it collapses and drags down the person who depends on it. Real frankness rebukes wrongdoers with a painful sting that helps them improve, like honey that bites a sore but cleanses it. The flatterer, by contrast, first appears harsh and unforgiving toward others.

Plutarch describes a certain kind of man who is harsh to his servants and eager to expose the faults of his relatives and friends. He looks down on strangers, stirs up quarrels between people, and seeks a reputation for hating vice, so that he will not appear to be soft on wrongdoers.

The flatterer pretends not to notice serious wrongdoing. Instead, he loudly attacks small matters, such as a pot out of place, a poorly housed man, untidy grooming, or careless care of a horse or dog.

Plutarch says a flatterer will ignore serious faults in a man, such as cruelty to parents, neglect of children, bad treatment of his wife, arrogance toward friends, and wasting money. The flatterer stays silent about these but still complains about small matters. He compares this to a trainer who lets his athlete drink and live badly while scolding him over a dirty oil flask, or a teacher who fixes a boy's writing tools but ignores grammar errors.

A flatterer, Plutarch says, avoids the real faults of a poor speech or writing. Instead he criticizes small, unimportant things, such as the speaker's voice or the quality of the paper, so he never has to judge the content.

Flatterers pleased King Ptolemy by arguing with him about words and history late into the night, but none of them ever objected to his cruelty. Plutarch compares this to a surgeon trimming hair and nails while ignoring serious wounds: flatterers speak frankly only about harmless matters that cause no pain.

Agis of Argos, seeing Alexander give large gifts to a jester, cried out "What a piece of absurdity!" Alexander turned angrily and asked what he meant. The point is that some flatterers pretend to speak frankly and criticise, but do so to amuse the person they are trying to please.

Plutarch's speaker says he is annoyed that the sons of Zeus, such as Hercules and Dionysus, enjoy flatterers and jesters. He notes that Hercules had his Cercopes (mischievous imps) and Dionysus his Sileni (wild woodland spirits), and that such companions are also well thought of among the speaker's own circle.

A flatterer addresses the Emperor Tiberius in the senate. He first says that free men should speak openly, which gets everyone's attention. Then he announces that he will tell Tiberius what everyone secretly blames him for.

A speaker tells a man that he neglects his own health and wears himself out with worry and work for others, never resting by night or day. When the speaker goes on at length in this vein, the orator Cassius Severus remarks that such frankness will be the man's ruin.

Flatterers sometimes praise people for the opposite of their real faults. They may accuse a stingy man of being a wasteful spender, or accuse a spendthrift of being mean. Plutarch gives two examples: Himerius and a rich miser, and Titus Petronius and the extravagant emperor Nero.

Plutarch describes flatterers who turn good advice into its opposite: they urge rulers to drop mercy and be cruel, and they pretend to fear a fool as if he were clever. He also describes a person who, when a slanderer praises someone, attacks the slanderer for being too fond of praise.

Flatterers, Plutarch says, mostly attack the people their targets love. When they see someone quarrelling with his brothers, scorning his parents, or treating his wife with contempt, they do not rebuke him. Instead they stir up his anger further.

A flatterer tells a man that he is too humble and is letting others take advantage of him. When a quarrel breaks out over a mistress, the flatterer takes her side, fans the anger, and blames the man for treating her cruelly.

Antony's friends told him that the Egyptian queen loved him, and they blamed him for being cold toward her. They said she had given up her kingdom and her comfortable life to follow him on campaign, while he remained unmoved by her charms. The friends were flattering him, pretending to take his side while encouraging his vanity.

A person who enjoys being scolded for his faults, and likes critics more than he ever liked those who praised him, does not see that such blame is corrupting him too. Harsh-seeming frankness works like the playful bites of loose women: it looks like harm but actually stirs pleasure.

Plutarch says that flatterers take frankness, which is a good cure for flattery, and use it as a tool for flattering, just as someone might mix pure wine with hemlock poison to make it deadlier. He also suggests that Bias's answer, naming the flatterer as the most dangerous tame animal, was not a good one.

Flatterers who hang around baths and dinner tables are tame, Plutarch says. The worse kind is the one who gets into the inner rooms of the house, including the women's quarters, spreading gossip and spite. Like the arms of an octopus, he is wild and cannot be controlled.

A friend, like a doctor, appeals to the better, reasonable side of the soul and helps keep it healthy. A flatterer works on the emotional and unreasoning side, pleasing it with indulgence and drawing it away from reason.

Plutarch compares the flatterer's words to foods that do no good to the body but harm it, stirring up desires and making it weak. In the same way, flattery adds nothing sound to a person's thinking. It feeds love, anger, envy, pride, and suspicion, and people who watch closely will see through it.

The flatterer does not calm our strong feelings but feeds them. Whatever we feel, he urges us to act on it: anger leads to revenge, desire to getting, fear to running away, suspicion to believing it. He is hard to spot this way, since strong passions often overpower reason. He can still be caught in smaller matters, because he acts the same way there too.

A friend tries to restrain a person who overindulges, telling him to be careful, while a flatterer encourages whatever the person wants: pushing him to bathe and eat after a binge, and telling him not to delay a trip or business.

If you have promised a friend money but now regret it, a flatterer will side with your wish to keep your purse closed. He will press your reluctance and urge caution, so the flatterer is easy to spot once you know your own desires. He always supports those desires and speaks out against resisting them.

A flatterer is hard to tell apart from a friend when it comes to helpful and kind acts, because he always seems eager and never backs out. Plutarch says a true friend acts plainly and simply, while a flatterer's conduct is unsound and needs much careful management to keep it going.

A real friend, when they meet by chance, may only look and smile, and pass on, and that silent warmth is enough. A flatterer rushes over, follows you, and if you speak first he swears he never saw you.

Plutarch contrasts friends and flatterers in business. A true friend does not push into every task or fuss over small matters. A flatterer, by contrast, keeps offering help without rest, leaves no room for others to help, and becomes distressed and loudly miserable if given nothing to do.

Plutarch says that a true friend promises help only within what he can actually do, as in "if I can do it, and it is to be done." A flatterer promises anything at all, as in "Tell me whatever you want." The passage contrasts the two kinds of promise, and says that the flatterer's warm embraces go beyond what the situation calls for.

A true friend joins in a matter only after being asked for advice and after testing whether the plan is sound and useful. A flatterer, once given the chance to judge, agrees with the wealthy man's wishes and even pushes him on. He does this to please him and to avoid seeming unwilling to take part.

Plutarch says that flatterers, like tragic actors, need a chorus of agreeing companions or an audience's applause. He then quotes Merope, a character in a tragedy, advising that a person should choose friends who speak their mind and keep out those who speak only to please.

Those being discussed do the opposite of what a wise person should do. They reject people who speak frankly and disagree with them about what is useful, yet they welcome flatterers, who only say what pleases them, into their homes, their affections and their private confidence.

Plutarch describes two kinds of flatterers. The simpler sort does not offer advice on important matters and only helps carry out decisions already made. The more cunning sort stays silent during a discussion, nodding and frowning, then claims he was about to say whatever his friend has just said.

Plutarch compares the flatterer to a geometric line or surface. Just as a line or surface changes only when the body it belongs to changes, the flatterer simply copies the moods and opinions of the person he is with, agreeing and feeling as they do. This makes flatterers easy to tell apart from true friends.

A true friend's help does not need to be seen or praised. Like a doctor who cures a patient without the patient noticing, a friend may act for another's benefit, such as paying his debts or managing his affairs, even when the one helped is unaware of it.

Arcesilaus secretly put twenty drachmae under the pillow of the sick painter Apelles, who was poor. When the housekeeper found the money, Apelles guessed it was Arcesilaus's doing. The story ends with a saying that children are like their parents.

Cephisocrates was on trial, and the prosecutor wanted his ring, the main evidence against him. Cephisocrates dropped it on the ground, and his friend Lacydes secretly covered it with his foot, hiding it. Cephisocrates won, and a juror told him to thank Lacydes, who had said nothing about it to anyone.

The gods often do good quietly, out of pleasure in giving. A flatterer's help is different: it is not honest, sincere, or generous. It is loud and strained, meant only to look hard-working, like an overdone painting that adds harsh colours and wrinkles to seem more lifelike.

A flatterer keeps telling you about the favours he has done for you, complaining about the trouble they cost him, even while he is doing them. A true friend, if he must mention a favour, does so briefly and says little about himself.

The Spartans sent grain to Smyrna, a city in need, and said it cost them little: they had only skipped a day's dinner, along with their pack animals. Plutarch notes that such a gift is more welcome to the receiver, because it seems to have cost the giver little.

A flatterer can be told apart from a friend less by how eagerly he offers help or makes promises than by the kind of help he gives. A friend aims at what is honourable and truly useful, not at pleasing. Plutarch rejects Gorgias's definition of a friend, which allowed a friend to do wrong for another, since a friend should share only in good actions.

A friend should help and support you but never join you in doing wrong. Plutarch gives the example of Phocion, who told Antipater that he could not have him as both a friend and a flatterer, since a flatterer is no true friend. The friend should stand by him in hardship, but not in wrongdoing.

A true friend will accept any burden for a friend, such as expense, danger or trouble, and will do so willingly. But he refuses anything dishonourable. Plutarch compares this to the Spartans, who after defeat asked Antipater to impose any burden except a shameful one.

The flatterer avoids hard or risky work, and when tested he gives a hollow answer and makes excuses. But he will put up with any degrading or humiliating treatment, however bad, if it serves his interest. The closing question compares him to an ape, a creature that imitates and cringes.

Plutarch says a flatterer is like a jester or a performer kept for laughs: he is useless for real work, such as defending you, giving sound advice, or sharing your struggles. Instead, he will help with shameful deeds, from secret dealings and affairs to cruel orders against your family.
A flatterer is easy to spot in this way: if you ask him to do something shameful or dishonourable, he will go to any trouble to please you.

A true friend is glad when his friend is loved and honoured by many others, and he tries to bring this about. He follows the saying that friends share everything, and he thinks this applies most of all to friends.

A false friend, like debased coin, is envious by nature and shows it even toward people like himself, trying to outdo them in insults and gossip. He trembles before anyone better than himself, and is far below them, as the quoted image of lead beside gold suggests.

A flatterer, who is false and weak, cannot survive close comparison with a true friend, so he is quickly exposed. He tries to keep real friends away. If they come near anyway, he praises them to their faces while secretly slandering them. Plutarch compares him to a painter who had his servant chase away live cocks so they could not be compared with his bad painting of cocks.

Medius, a flatterer at Alexander's court, taught that slander should be spread boldly, because even if the victim healed the wound, the scar would stay. Plutarch says Alexander, poisoned by such scars, went on to have Callisthenes, Parmenio and Philotas put to death.

Plutarch says that even a powerful ruler let himself be fooled by flatterers, who praised him as a god and dressed him up as one. He adds that flattery works best on the greatest people, because they already think well of themselves and so believe the flatterer.

Just as high mountains are hard to climb, a proud person who has become unbalanced by good luck or natural talent is easy for petty, low people to reach and influence. Their arrogance makes them open to flattery from small-minded people.

Plutarch says we should drop self-love and an inflated view of ourselves, because these make us easy targets for flatterers. He urges people to heed the saying "Know thyself" by honestly seeing their own faults. Then they will not be so easily flattered.

Alexander said he did not believe those who called him a god, because he was most weak and driven by desire in sleep and sex. Plutarch's point is that when we see our own faults, we need a friend who criticises us, not one who praises us.

Few people dare to tell their friends the plain truth instead of simply pleasing them, and fewer still do it well. Many think they are being frank when they only insult and scold. Like medicine, frankness given at the wrong time just causes pain, and so it becomes the same kind of error as flattery, which also aims at causing a feeling rather than helping.

Blaming people at the wrong time harms them, just as praising them at the wrong time does. Constant harsh criticism drives people to flatterers, who offer easy comfort. So frankness should be softened with kindness and guided by reason, so people do not run to flatterers to escape constant rebuke.

Plutarch says that vices should be removed by virtue, not by swapping one vice for its opposite. For example, a person should not trade modesty for shamelessness, or fear for reckless daring. He also says some people move from superstition into atheism, or from foolishness into dishonesty, as a bent stick is bent the other way.

Plutarch says that being rude and disagreeable for no good reason is as shameful as flattery. Someone who avoids flattery by being harsh destroys friendship, just as a flatterer does by pleasing too much. Honest speech should be moderate so that it stays pleasant to the friend.

Frank criticism helps only when the speaker is not acting from personal grievance. Speech that comes from private anger looks like selfish reproach and is resented, while open speech that seems friendly is respected. Plutarch gives the example of Agamemnon, who would not accept Achilles' mild frankness but accepted the harsh words of Odysseus.

Plutarch notes that Odysseus spoke to Achilles calmly and with no personal anger, only for the sake of the Greek army, while Achilles seemed angry on his own account. Achilles himself, though harsh-tempered, let his friend Patroclus insult him at length, calling him pitiless and flinty-hearted, and listened in silence.

A true friend's rebuke is trusted when it is free of personal motive. If a friend ignores wrongs done to himself, blames only faults that harm others, and speaks harshly anyway, his frankness is hard to resist, and his gentle manner makes the criticism hit harder.

Plutarch says that when a friend is angry with us, we should act for the friend's own good or honour. It is also a friendly act to speak up for others who have been neglected, as Plato did. Plato, who had fallen out of favour with the tyrant Dionysius, raised the case of a neglected man instead of his own grievance.

Plato tells the tyrant Dionysius that Aeschines, a follower of Socrates, has come to help him, and asks whether it is right to ignore him without thanks. Dionysius replies that Aeschines is being neglected, even though he made a long journey to discuss philosophy with him.
Dionysius, the ruler, was so moved by this speech that he embraced Plato at once, praising his goodwill and high-mindedness. He then treated Aeschines kindly and generously.

Plutarch says that frank speech, especially rebuke, should be free of insolence, jeering, mocking and coarseness. Like a surgeon's careful cut, it may be tactful and polite, but only as long as the polish does not weaken the rebuke itself. Rudeness spoils the effect entirely.

Plutarch gives three examples of replies to rulers. A harper flatters King Philip by saying he would be unlucky to understand harping better than the king. Epicharmus rebukes Hiero, who had killed some friends, by saying he was not invited to the sacrifice of those friends. Plutarch calls the last two replies bad: Epicharmus's is blunt, and Antiphon's bronze answer is a dangerous hint about tyrannicide.

Harsh, bitter, and mocking speech does not help the person who uses it. Such talk shows a tongue that cannot control itself and is driven by hatred and spite, and it ruins the speaker, like a person dancing carelessly at the edge of a well.

Plutarch says that Antiphon was executed by the tyrant Dionysius, and Timagenes lost Augustus's friendship, not through speaking too boldly but by always joking and avoiding serious talk. Their lives show that a friend who only wants to amuse and mock is no real friend.

Plutarch says that serious moral advice on the stage is spoiled when jokes and crude humour are mixed in with it, so the audience gets no benefit. He concludes that a friend may joke at other times, but frank speech on important matters should be serious, sincere and delivered with feeling.

Frank speech should be held back when people are drinking. A serious or unpleasant topic at a merry party spoils the mood, and wine makes people quick to anger, so blunt words spoken then often turn people into enemies.
Hiding your real opinions while sober and then voicing them freely over wine is, he says, a cowardly habit, like a dog snarling only when it is safe. He considers the point settled.

Plutarch says that many people will not criticise a friend while he is prosperous, treating that time as beyond reproach. Instead they attack him when he makes a mistake or falls into misfortune, and they enjoy his downfall, especially if they once looked down on him when they were poor themselves. He proposes to discuss this and answer a line by the poet Euripides.

People who are doing well need honest friends to speak frankly and check their excessive pride, because few are wise enough to keep themselves humble in good fortune. When misfortune humbles them, their own circumstances correct them without any help.

In times of misfortune, a friend should not speak harshly or bluntly. A calm, kind face comforts a person, as Xenophon said of Clearchus encouraging his soldiers. Harsh criticism is like a strong medicine on an inflamed eye: it does not heal the hurt but makes the distress worse.

A healthy man does not get angry when a friend criticises his excesses, such as drinking, women, idleness and overeating. A sick man, however, finds such criticism unbearable, even worse than his illness. He protests that it is the wrong time for a lecture, since he is making his will and taking medicine.

People in misfortune need kindness and help before any blunt criticism, just as a nurse first lifts and cleans a fallen child before scolding it. The example given is Demetrius, an exile, who dreaded the approach of Crates because he expected harsh, cynical rebuke rather than support.

Crates comforted the exiled Demetrius by saying his exile brought no real harm, since it freed him from the risks of public life, and by urging him to trust his own state of mind. Demetrius cheered up and regretted that his earlier busy life had left him no time to know such a man.

Flatterers stick close to a rich or successful man, but desert him in hard times, and they even seem to enjoy his misfortunes. A true friend, by contrast, reminds a man of his mistakes only gently, by saying he had warned him against the course he took.

A true friend should speak forcefully and frankly when he needs to stop someone from acting on pleasure, anger, arrogance, greed or careless folly. The passage gives two examples: Solon warned the rich king Croesus to think about how things would end, and Socrates reproved Alcibiades until he wept and changed his ways.

Plutarch gives examples of frank, honest advice from friends. Plato warned Dion that if he only pleased himself, he would lose all his friends. Speusippus urged Dion not to take pride in being admired only by young men and women, but to bring piety, justice and good laws to Sicily instead.

Euctus and Eulaeus were companions of Perseus, the king of Macedon. While he was prosperous they flattered him and agreed with everything he said. After his defeat by the Romans at Pydna, they turned on him and harshly blamed him for his past mistakes. In anger and grief, Perseus drew his sword and killed both of them.

A friend who truly cares will also use specific openings that the friend's own actions provide to speak frankly. A question, a story, or praise or blame of someone else can serve as a signal for honest speech.

Demaratus, a Corinthian visitor, was asked by King Philip of Macedon whether the Greeks were getting along. He replied that Philip should first look at the quarrels in his own household, where he was at odds with his wife and son. Demaratus said this as a friend, pointing out the king's own problems in a blunt way.

Diogenes was caught sneaking into King Philip's camp and asked if he was a spy. He replied that he had come to observe Philip's foolishness in risking his kingdom and life for a single throw of the dice. The writer adds that this remark was perhaps a little too harsh.

A good time to rebuke a friend is when others have criticized his faults and he has become humble as a result. The wise friend should quietly tell him to take more care, so that his enemies lose their power to mock him. He should ask: if you stop doing the things you are criticized for, what can they say against you?

A friend can correct another person more gently by blaming someone else for the same fault. Plutarch's teacher Ammonius shows this: he had a freedman whip his own son for eating with vinegar, but the real aim was to rebuke the pupils who had overeaten and were the ones who needed to hear it.

Do not criticise a friend harshly in front of other people. Plato told Socrates that his rebuke should have been given in private, and Socrates answered that Plato's own remark should also have been made in private. Pythagoras once scolded a pupil in public, and the pupil killed himself, so Pythagoras never rebuked anyone in front of others again.

A true friend should point out another's wrongdoing privately, as one would treat a shameful disease, not in front of witnesses. Showing it off to gain reputation is the mark of a sophist, like a public doctor who performs cures on stage to attract customers. Public insult also hardens the wrongdoer, since vice is stubborn and quarrelsome.

A friend who points out a fault should do it gently and in private, not harshly in front of others. Public scolding makes faults worse, while a mild, careful rebuke weakens the fault and encourages the friend to be modest too.

It is improper to criticize a man in front of his wife, his children, his beloved, or his students, because people are hurt and angry when shamed before those whose respect they want. Plutarch suggests that Alexander's anger at Clitus came less from wine than from being humiliated in front of many people.

Aristomenes woke King Ptolemy during an audience with foreign envoys. Flatterers used this to say he had insulted the king, and they argued he should have rebuked him in private. Ptolemy then ordered him to drink poison. Plutarch also cites Aristophanes' report that Cleon faulted a critic for attacking the state in front of foreigners.

Frank criticism should aim at helping others, not at showing off or winning applause. Plutarch adds that speakers should remember the Corinthians' claim, as Thucydides reports it, that they had the right to blame their neighbours.

Lysander once told a Megarian that his bold words needed a state behind them to carry weight. The same holds for anyone who criticises others: their right to speak frankly depends on their own good character. A man of poor character who rebukes others is likely to be answered with a sharp retort.

When people who are faulty themselves must rebuke others with the same faults, the best way is to include the speaker among those blamed. Plutarch gives two lines from Homer as examples, where the speakers blame their companions and themselves together.

Socrates corrected young men gently, presenting himself as someone who also lacked knowledge and needed to pursue virtue and truth alongside them. People gain goodwill and influence when they seem to share their friends' faults and try to improve themselves along with them.

Someone who lectures others from a position of superiority, as if he had no faults himself, does no good and is seen only as a tiresome bore. The exception is an elderly man or someone widely known for virtue and worth.

Phoenix tells Achilles about his own past mistakes, including nearly killing his father in anger. He does this so he does not seem to scold Achilles from a position of never having been angry himself. People are more willing to be persuaded by someone who seems sympathetic than by someone who looks proud and superior.

Plutarch says that a person ruled by strong feelings cannot take plain blame and scolding, just as an inflamed eye cannot take strong light. A small amount of praise mixed in works better as a remedy. He gives Homeric lines as examples, where a leader's praise of warriors encourages them.

When rebuking someone, the passage advises reminding him of his own past good deeds rather than comparing him with others. Such comparisons make a faulty person angry and defensive. The exception is praising the parents of the person being rebuked.

When a friend rebukes you, you should not answer back with rebuke or plain speech, since that starts quarrels and shows an inability to accept frank criticism. Instead, listen patiently, because a friend who has been frankly criticized will later be willing to accept correction, seeing it as kindness rather than anger.

A true friend should save harsh criticism for serious matters. If he scolds people constantly, like a schoolmaster, his rebuke will have no force when it really matters. He is like a doctor who wastes a strong medicine on minor complaints and so has none left for the times it is needed.

A friend who constantly nitpicks over small faults should be handled carefully, because this habit gives the friend a way to criticise him on bigger failings. Plutarch illustrates this with a doctor who, seeing a patient fixated on a sore finger while his liver was badly diseased, told him that the finger was not what mattered.

A friend who is willing to accept a gentle rebuke over small faults will also take criticism on weightier matters. By contrast, someone who constantly finds fault and pries into everything is hard to bear even for his family and servants.

Plutarch advises that we should notice and praise a friend's good points first, and only then criticise his faults. He compares this to tempering iron: heat softens it, and cold water hardens it. Praise softens a friend, so that gentle criticism can then take hold.

A true friend corrects a person by praising what is good rather than by blaming what is bad. The passage says that a friend should point to virtuous actions and their results and ask for more of them, rejecting the bad conduct. It compares this to a wise doctor who prefers gentle cures like sleep and diet over harsh purgatives like castor oil or scammony.

Rebuking someone works best when it is gentle and calm, not angry. Even when a person refuses to admit a fault, the rebuker should not press hard or stop them from speaking. Instead, the rebuker should offer a kinder reason for the wrong, as Hector did for Paris, saying his hiding from battle came from anger rather than cowardice.

Plutarch says that gentler wording is better when correcting someone. "You forgot" is preferred to "You acted unfairly," and "Avoid the woman who is your ruin" to "Stop ruining the woman." Such phrasing aims to reform the person rather than hurt them.

Sometimes a friend must stop someone who is about to do wrong, calm a rash impulse, or spur on someone who is slacking in virtue, even by giving them false or unflattering motives. Plutarch illustrates this with Odysseus, who pretends Achilles is only afraid of Troy's walls, which pushes Achilles to act.

A true friend steers people toward good conduct by warning them of the opposite fault. Brave people are told they will look cowardly, orderly people that they will look licentious, and generous people that they will look mean. The friend also holds back where a fault cannot be fixed, and speaks with more sorrow and sympathy than blame.

Friends, when trying to stop wrongdoing or to fight the passions, should be fierce, firm and persistent and speak with blunt honesty. Plutarch adds that enemies openly criticise each other's faults, and he quotes Diogenes: a person who wants a good life needs either good friends, who say what is right, or fiercely hostile enemies, who blame what is wrong.

It is better to avoid doing wrong by heeding good advice than to regret wrongdoing later because enemies criticise us. So frank speech between friends should be used with care, at the right time, and in moderation, since it is the strongest remedy in friendship.

When a friend has to speak frankly and hurt someone, he should then soothe the hurt, as a surgeon bathes and warms a wound after an operation. Like a sculptor smoothing a chipped statue, he should follow the rebuke with gentle, kind words.

When a person is hurt by criticism and stays angry and upset, he becomes hard to win back or reason with. So those who rebuke others should take care not to leave them too soon, or cut off contact while the person is still angry and in pain.

Plutarch tells his friend Pulcher that he knows Pulcher prefers gentle conduct in public life, since that makes a man useful to the community and pleasant to those he deals with. He then adds that no community is free of envy, rivalry and strife, which breed enmity, so enemies are hard to avoid.

Friendships can bring enmities too, as the sage Chilo noticed when he asked a man who claimed to have no enemies whether he had any friends. So a public man should study the whole question of enemies and take seriously Xenophon's view that a sensible man profits even from his enemies.

The writer says he has written down ideas he recently wanted to share and is sending them to the reader. He has kept nearly the same wording, except for a few points taken from "Political Precepts," a work he has seen the reader often holding.

Early people were content just to avoid being harmed by wild beasts. Later people learned to use animals for food, clothing, medicine and shields. Plutarch suggests that without animals, human life would become crude and lack resources.

Most people are content just to avoid harm from their enemies. The wise, however, also gain something from them, so we should not doubt this and should look for a way to get that benefit, since a life with no enemies is impossible.

Plutarch's point is that useful things can come from things that seem useless or harmful. A farmer gets value from barren trees, a hunter from wild animals, and sea water still feeds fish and carries ships. A satyr, a wild creature of Greek myth, wanted to embrace fire, and Prometheus warned him that he would lose his beard.

Fire harms anyone who touches it, but it also gives light, warmth and use to people who know how to handle it. Likewise, an enemy may be harmful and hard to deal with, yet he still gives us some way to make use of him.

Some people turn hardships into gains. Illness can give the body rest, hard labour can make it stronger, and exile or loss of money can open the way to leisure and philosophy, as it did for the philosophers Diogenes and Crates.
Zeno heard that a ship carrying all his belongings had sunk. He said that Fortune had done well to leave him only his worn cloak, meaning that he was now left with very little.

Wise people can gain something useful even from their enemies, just as strong animals digest things that would harm weaker ones. Foolish people, by contrast, ruin even their friendships, much as sick people reject ordinary food.

Plutarch says that an enemy can be useful, because a hostile person watches your every move closely. The enemy studies your whole life, looks for weak points, and tries to uncover your plans, even through your friends and family.

Our enemies watch us more closely than our friends do. They notice our illnesses, debts and quarrels at home, and they focus on our faults, much as vultures are drawn to rotting carcasses and ignore healthy bodies. Our flaws are what attract them.

An enemy's watchfulness is useful to us because it makes us careful. We learn to live with caution, to think before we speak or act, and to give an enemy no opening. Such caution keeps the passions under control and leads a person to live well and without blame.

Plutarch says that a people sobered by constant wars come to love order and peace. In the same way, people forced by enemies to live carefully, watching against carelessness and acting for practical ends, slowly become well-behaved and calmer in character, even without much moral instruction. The passage then breaks off mid-sentence, so its full point is unclear.
Enemies can push a person to improve. People avoid the things their enemies would mock, and actors and singers work harder when they have rivals than when they perform alone.

A person who knows his enemy dislikes his character and way of life pays closer attention to himself and corrects his behaviour. Bad people fear enemies more than friends when it comes to their faults. Nasica, a Roman, argued that Rome was in danger once Carthage and Achaia were defeated, because no rival was left to make Romans careful.

The main point is that the best revenge on an enemy is to become a good and honest person, as Diogenes said. Plutarch also observes that people who are jealous of their enemies get upset when those enemies' horses, dogs, farms or gardens are well kept or praised.

Plutarch says that a good person who lives justly and well leaves enemies with nothing to say against them. Only those who see that the good person surpasses them in virtue fall silent. The passage closes with the advice to be better than the bad, which is within your power.

If you want to hurt an enemy, do not insult him with words like "effeminate" or "intemperate." Instead, be decent, honest, and fair yourself. If you feel tempted to insult him anyway, check your own character first, since you may have the same faults you accuse him of.

If you accuse your enemy of ignorance, cowardice or lust, work harder to fix the same fault in yourself. Slander is most shameful when it turns back on the one who makes it, because the faults you name in others then show up in you.

Plato, when he saw people behaving badly, asked himself whether he was like them. Plutarch's point is that someone who criticizes another's conduct gains something only if he examines and corrects his own life; otherwise the criticism is wasted.

Mocking others for a flaw you share is foolish, because the other person can easily hit back at you. Plutarch gives examples: a hunchback who jeers at a man with weak eyes is answered that he carries his own deformity on his back, and a man should not call another an adulterer or a spendthrift while guilty of the same faults.

Plutarch's point is that anyone who wants to insult others should avoid giving openings for insults in return. Each man in the exchange answers an insult with a sharper one about a painful fact in the other's life. The passage ends by saying that the advice "Know thyself" applies most to the person who criticises others, so that he does not hear things he dislikes.

Antisthenes said that a good life needs either true friends or fierce enemies. Friends correct you through reproof, and enemies through insults. Because friends now tend to flatter and hold back criticism, the truth often comes only from enemies.

Plutarch says that people without friends willing to correct them can still benefit from an enemy's criticism. Even if the enemy means harm, the criticism can expose and cure a fault. He compares this to Telephus being healed by the spear that wounded him, and to a surgeon who cuts a tumour while trying to kill someone.

Most people, when insulted, do not check whether the insult is true. Instead they throw insults back at the abuser, like wrestlers who cover themselves and their opponents in arena dust. Plutarch says that a person who is slandered by an enemy should clear that charge off himself, even more carefully than he would brush off a stain on his clothes.

If a charge is false, a person should still look into where it came from. He should check that he has not, without knowing it, done something close to what he is accused of. Plutarch gives two cases: Lacydes was called effeminate because of his hair and walk, and Pompey because he scratched his head with one finger, though neither man was in fact like that.

Crassus was accused of an affair with a Vestal Virgin, a priestess of Rome, because he visited her often to try to buy a pleasant estate from her. Postumia, who joked and talked freely with men, was tried for incest and acquitted, but the chief priest told her to be no freer in her words than she was in her conduct.
Themistocles was not guilty of treason, but his close friendship with Pausanias and their frequent letters and messages made people suspect him.

When someone makes a false accusation against us, Plutarch says we should not just dismiss it. We should look for whatever word or deed made the charge seem believable, and take care to avoid it in future.

Plutarch argues that enemies can teach us useful things for free, because they watch us closely and speak openly. Friends and loved ones tend to overlook our faults. As an example, Hiero learned of his bad breath from a foe, not from his wife, who had assumed everyone's breath smelled the same.

Controlling the tongue, which Plutarch calls an important part of moral goodness, is possible only after a person has trained himself through practice and effort to master his strongest passions, such as anger. Speech follows reason only when those passions are first brought under control.

Plutarch says that careless words, the ones that slip out without thought, show a poorly controlled character, one that is unstable and badly trained. He adds that, according to Plato, a word may seem trivial, yet it brings the heaviest punishment from gods and men.

Silence cannot be held to account for anything said. Plutarch says it is not "thirsty" for argument, and that when insulted it stays calm, like Socrates, or like Hercules, who (as the saying goes) ignored sharp words as he would flies.

Plutarch says that staying silent when an enemy insults you is admirable, and that doing it in practice is even better. Practising patience with an enemy's abuse, he argues, makes it easier to bear abuse from a wife, friend, brother, or parents without being upset.

Plutarch says that Socrates' patience with his difficult wife, Xanthippe, made him easier to get along with others. He argues that it is better to train your temper to bear insults and mockery from enemies and estranged people calmly, without being upset by them.

Plutarch says that in disputes we should show gentleness and patience toward enemies, and generosity and kindness toward friends. Not taking revenge on an enemy is called generous. Helping an enemy in trouble, including his children and family, is praised as humane and kind, and the passage ends before stating what is concluded about such a man.

Plutarch recalls that when Caesar restored statues of his enemy Pompey, Cicero joked that Caesar had thereby set up statues to himself. From this he argues that we should freely praise a deserving enemy. Praising an enemy brings the praiser more credit, and makes his later criticism more believable, since it shows he is criticising only the act, not the person.

A person who is used to praising his enemies, and not resenting their success, is also far from envying the good luck of his friends. The writer asks which habit could do more good for the mind than one that drives out jealousy and envy.

Enmity brings bad habits with it, such as hatred, envy, jealousy and revenge, and these become part of a person's character. Tricks like deceit and villainy seem acceptable against an enemy, but once learned they are hard to drop and may be used against friends too, unless a person is on guard against them.

Plutarch argues that if Pythagoras taught his followers to avoid cruelty even to animals, then it is much nobler to treat human enemies fairly and honestly. He says a person should also control bad and mean impulses, so that he keeps the peace with friends and does no harm.

Scaurus, an enemy of Domitius, refused to hear a slave who wanted to reveal useful information and sent him back to his master. Cato, prosecuting Murena, told people who asked that he was not gathering witnesses that day, and they believed him and left.

Plutarch says that the trust people placed in Cato is a great sign of his good name, but a more important habit is to treat even enemies fairly. Someone who does this will not be likely to betray friends.

Plutarch says that every person has a natural tendency toward fighting, jealousy and envy. Because of this, a person can gain a lot by getting rid of these feelings toward enemies and redirecting them away from friends, the way a sewer carries waste away from a house.

Onomademus, a Chios statesman, advised his victorious party not to drive out every member of the opposing faction. His reason was that once the enemies were gone, his own side might turn on its friends. Plutarch applies this to anger: if our angry feelings are spent wholly on enemies, they will cause less trouble for friends.

Plutarch says people should not envy one another, even though Hesiod observed that craftsmen, neighbours and relatives often do when they chase wealth. If envy and quarrels cannot be avoided any other way, he suggests training yourself to feel annoyance at an enemy's success.

Just as gardeners plant garlic and onions beside roses and violets so that the strong or bitter qualities pass to the onions, a man's enemy can draw off his envy and spite. This leaves him gentler and more pleasant toward friends who are doing well.

Plutarch urges that we should compete with our enemies for glory, office or honest gain. We should not only resent it when they get ahead, but study how they succeed and try to match or beat them in effort, diligence, self-control and good judgment. He illustrates this with Themistocles, who said that Miltiades' victory at Marathon kept him awake.

If a rival gets ahead in office, influence, or favour, a man can either sink into envy and give up action, or look closely and see that such success usually comes from hard work, good sense, and good deeds. Seeing this, he can copy those qualities and so overcome his own vanity and laziness.

If our enemies gain power or position through flattery, fraud, bribery or paid favours, we should not be troubled. We should instead take comfort in our own freedom and integrity, since virtue is worth more than all gold, as Plato and Solon are quoted as saying.

Plutarch says we should not give up virtue for public applause, honours, or favour from rulers, since nothing good comes from what is bad. Because we tend to notice our enemies' faults more than our own, he advises that when they fail or succeed, we should ask how we can become better than them, avoiding their mistakes and copying their good qualities.

Plutarch says that talkativeness is hard to cure, because a cure needs listeners and talkative people do not listen. Their habit of never being silent leads to an inability to listen, which he calls a chosen deafness. He links this to a line of Euripides about pouring wise words into a person who cannot hold them.

Plutarch compares a talkative person to the sea that rushes away and then returns with more force, and to a echoing colonnade at Olympia that multiplies one sound many times. The point is that a talker does not really take in what others say but repeats it back, enlarged. The talker's own words are then the ones that keep coming back.

Plutarch says that talkative people do not keep what they hear, because their ears seem to lead only to the tongue, not to the mind. They are like empty vessels that make noise. So the advice offered to them is simply to be silent, since silence has great benefits.

Talkative people cannot enjoy the two best things in conversation, hearing and being heard, because nobody wants to listen to them. Other faults, such as greed for money, fame or pleasure, at least get what they want. Talkers want listeners but never find them, since people avoid them and move away when they approach.

Talkers who cannot stop talking find that people avoid them. When such a person joins a drinking party or gathering, everyone falls silent and quietly slips away, expecting the chatter and discomfort to follow. As a result, these talkers are left with only companions who have no choice, such as those forced to share a table or journey with them.

The passage describes a tiresome talker who keeps grabbing at people and pestering them. Aristotle is shown answering such a man with a joke: it is remarkable that anyone with legs stays to listen to him, meaning that the listener would rather walk away. Another such talker asks Aristotle if he has wearied him, and the passage gives Aristotle's reply, which is not quoted here.

A listener says he did not hear the speaker, because he was busy with his own thoughts. Even when talkative people force us to listen, the mind only lets their words reach the outer ear and keeps working on other matters. So their chatter has no real effect and gets no belief.

Nature has guarded the tongue more than anything else, placing the teeth in front of it as a barrier. If the tongue will not obey reason, a person can bite it to control its excess. Euripides says trouble comes from an unrestrained mouth.

Plutarch compares talkers to houses without doors and purses left open: people who speak constantly treat speech as worthless. Because of this, they are not believed, even when they tell the truth, though belief is the proper purpose of speech.
Just as stored grain grows in bulk but loses in quality, a talkative man's speech swells with a lot of falsehood, and this ruins his reputation for honesty.

Drunkenness is described as a kind of madness that a person chooses for himself, and it is criticized most for causing endless, foolish talk. Singing, laughing and dancing are not harmful in themselves. The real danger is that wine makes a man say things better left unspoken.

The speaker says that a drunk man shows what is really in his mind, because the proverb says what is in a sober man's heart comes out on a drunk man's tongue. He gives an example: Bias, a wise man, stayed silent at a drinking party and was mocked as stupid. He answered that only a fool could keep quiet while drunk.

Zeno, a Greek philosopher, sat silent at a dinner in Athens where the king's envoys were present and philosophers were talking. When the envoys asked what they should report to the king about him, he said they should tell the king only that an old man in Athens could keep quiet while drinking.

Silence is described as deep and sober, while talkativeness is linked to drunkenness, which the philosophers define as foolish talk over wine. Drinking itself is not blamed if it is accompanied by silence; the fault lies in foolish chatter. A drunk man chatters only over his drink, but a talkative man chatters everywhere, at all times.

Plutarch says that a man who is tactless with his words is harder to bear than a man who is unpleasant in other ways. A doctor, shipmate or flatterer who talks clumsily annoys more than the illness, the seasickness or the blame would. Good deeds are spoiled by bad speech, so a clumsy talker is worse company than a tactful person with bad morals.

A client shows Lysias, a speechwriter, a defence speech he has been given. At first it seems impressive, but on rereading it seems dull. Lysias replies that the speech was never meant to be read repeatedly, only heard once by the jury.

Homer is praised as the one poet who has never grown dull, because he moves from subject to subject and so keeps listeners from getting bored. He is said to avoid repeating a plain story. Talkative people, by contrast, wear out their listeners by repeating the same things, like writing over old pages.

Plutarch compares speech to wine: meant for pleasure, it spoils when used badly, just as wine forced on people in large amounts makes them sick with drunkenness. A speaker who uses words badly bores and offends his listeners, and so makes himself unpleasant company.

Plutarch says that talkativeness combines the faults of other passions: it makes people a joke, makes them hated when they carry bad news, and puts them in danger when they reveal secrets. He praises Anacharsis, who held his mouth shut more tightly than his private parts, because he thought the tongue needed the stronger restraint.

Plutarch says that many more cities and leading states have been destroyed by a leaked secret than men have been ruined by sexual excess. He gives an example: during Sulla's siege of Athens, old men chatting in a barber's shop noted a weak point in the city's defences, and spies overheard them and told Sulla.

Sulla's army broke into Athens at midnight and killed huge numbers of people, so much that the Ceramicus, a district of the city, ran with blood. Plutarch says Sulla was this cruel because of the Athenians' insults about him and his wife Metella, not because of anything they had done. The insults mocked him as a mulberry covered in barley meal.

Plutarch gives two examples of how careless talk brought harm. Some people were punished heavily for words that Plato calls very small matters. In Rome, a man's chatter ruined a plan to kill the tyrant Nero: the night before the murder, the would-be killer told a prisoner, who was about to be taken before Nero, to wait for tomorrow.

A man who guessed the meaning of a riddle chose a sure, honourable safety over a risky hope. He told Nero what the man had said, so the man was arrested and tortured. Under torture he denied what he had earlier admitted freely.

Zeno the philosopher bit off his own tongue so that he could not reveal secrets under torture, and spat it at the tyrant. Leaena, the mistress of the conspirators Harmodius and Aristogiton, is also praised for keeping silent about the plot against the tyrants, even though she knew it.

A woman was caught in a plot against a tyrant and died rather than name her fellow conspirators. The Athenians honored her with a bronze lioness without a tongue, which stood for her courage and her silence. The passage ends by saying that unspoken deeds can do more good than words.

Once a word is spoken it cannot be taken back, while what is left unsaid can still be said later. So people teach us to speak, but the gods teach us silence, which is required in the mysteries and religious rites. Homer shows even the most eloquent characters, such as Odysseus, as keeping quiet.

Plutarch quotes a line of Homer describing a man who keeps his eyes dry and his face still while he privately feels pity. He says this shows how fully the man's body obeyed reason, so that his eyes, tongue and heart did what reason ordered.

Reason should control even the body's instincts, so that spirit and blood obey it. Plutarch gives two examples of self-control: Odysseus's men, who kept silent under torture from the Cyclops rather than reveal secrets, and Pittacus, who sent the king of Egypt a sheep's tongue, because the tongue can bring both the greatest blessings and the greatest harms.

Plutarch says that a well-educated person learns to keep silent before learning to speak. He gives the example of King Antigonus, who rebuked his son's question about moving camp by saying the son would hear the trumpet when it was time. The king was not distrusting his son but training him to be discreet about military plans.

Metellus said he would throw his coat into the fire if he thought it knew his plans, so tightly did he guard secrets. Eumenes hid the fact that Craterus was coming against him, and let his soldiers believe the enemy was the less respected Neoptolemus. Eumenes's men fought and won, killing Craterus without knowing it.

Eumenes kept the name of the enemy's general secret before the battle. His friends wondered at this more than they blamed him for not telling them. The passage adds that it is better to be criticised for keeping a plan secret and acting well than to blame others after being harmed by trusting them.

Plutarch argues that a person who tells a secret has only himself to blame if it gets out. If you trusted someone with it, you placed more faith in them than in yourself. Whether that person proves weak or trustworthy, the outcome depends on the choice you made when you shared it.

A secret is only safe while one person keeps it. Once it is shared with a second person, it spreads further, because each person tells another. Plutarch compares this to numbers: one stays one, but two opens the way to many.

Spoken words cannot be taken back once they leave the mouth. Plutarch compares them to a bird let go from the hand and to a ship that leaves harbour, which cannot be stopped or anchored. Such a word can spread and harm the speaker.

A Roman senator's wife begs her husband to reveal a secret the Senate has been debating, promising she will keep it. He agrees, not because he wants to share it, but to show her how foolish her curiosity is. He then tells her he is about to reveal a dreadful matter.

Priests have reported a portent, a lark seen flying with a golden helmet and spear, and a man asks his wife to keep it secret. Instead, she loudly mourns in front of her maid and coaches the maid to ask what is wrong, so the news gets out anyway.

The passage shows how quickly a secret spreads. A woman tells her maid to keep something quiet, but the maid tells a fellow servant and her lover, and the news reaches the public square before the man who first started it. He hears of it from a friend, and he has not yet heard the news himself.

A man hears his wife repeating a rumour that a lark carrying a golden helmet and spear has been seen, and that the Senate is meeting about the omen. He smiles at how fast the news travelled, calms the senators he meets, and then tells his wife, as a punishment, that her gossip means he must now be exiled.

A husband pretends to have heard a state secret, then tests whether his wife will pass it on. When she tries to deny the leak by pointing to the three hundred senators who also knew, he admits the story was invented to catch her. Plutarch compares his careful testing to pouring water into a leaky jar, a way of finding out what is kept inside.

Augustus, growing old, grieved that his family line was dying out. Two of his grandsons were dead, and his last remaining grandson, Agrippa, had been exiled on false charges. Augustus was also forced to name his stepson Tiberius as heir, though he pitied Agrippa and nearly brought him back. A friend, Fabius, repeated these private words to his wife, who passed them on to Livia, Augustus's wife.

Livia angrily told Augustus that if he meant to recall his grandson, he should have done it long ago rather than make her an enemy of the heir. Fabius, a friend of the Emperor, learned from a cold farewell that Augustus knew he had not kept a secret, so he decided to kill himself.

A wife tells her husband he has brought his fate on himself, because after so many years of marriage he did not guard against her habit of speaking carelessly. She then takes his sword and kills herself before him.

Philippides the comic poet told King Lysimachus that he would accept any gift except the king's secrets. Plutarch uses this to show that talkative people are also curious. They chase after secrets to have something to chatter about, and holding onto them causes them trouble, like holding ice or a snake.

Secrets, like the young of garfish and vipers, destroy those who cannot keep them when they come out. To show this, the passage tells how King Seleucus Callinicus, defeated by the Galatians, fled alone with a few men and, faint with hunger, asked a farmer for bread and water.

A farm owner gave a traveler, who turned out to be King Seleucus, everything he needed and more. He recognized the king and could not hide his joy, so he walked with him to the road and said goodbye using the king's name, though the king had wanted to travel unknown.
A man is lured close with a pretended kiss, and at a signal from the speaker one of his guards cuts off his head. The quoted line describes the head falling into the dust at that command.

The speaker says that if a man had stayed silent for a while, he would have earned more favour from the king later than he got for his hospitality. He admits the man had some excuse for speaking out, namely hope and joy.

Talkative people often bring ruin on themselves without need. Plutarch's example is a barber who joked, in the shop, that he held his razor at the throat of Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, and the tyrant had him crucified for it.

Plutarch tells two short stories about barbers who talk too much. King Archelaus tells a talkative barber to shave him in silence. Another barber hurries into Athens with news of an Athenian defeat in Sicily, so that he, not someone else, will be first to report it.
A barber spread a rumour in Athens, and when the people demanded to know its source, he could not name the man who had told him. The crowd, angry, ordered him tortured on the rack as a liar.

The crowd left to mourn their own losses after news of the defeat in Sicily arrived. They forgot a barber who had been tied to a wheel as punishment. When he was finally freed in the evening, he asked his executioner whether he had heard how the general Nicias had been killed. Plutarch uses this to show that a habit of talking is very hard to break.

People dislike those who bring bad news, just as people dislike the cup of bitter medicine they must drink from. Plutarch illustrates this with a scene from Sophocles, where a guard brings bad news to Creon and says that he only pains Creon's ears, while the act itself pains his mind.

Plutarch says that gossip hurts people as much as the deed itself, and that nobody can stop people from talking. He then gives an example: a temple at Sparta was broken into, and a bystander, eager to comment, offers his own theory about a lone empty flagon lying there.

Plutarch suggests that these temple robbers drank hemlock before their crime. If they were not caught, they would take wine to counter the poison and escape. If they were caught, the hemlock would kill them quickly and painlessly before they could be tortured.

A man spoke a clever remark that seemed too well informed to be a guess. The crowd pressed him with questions, and he confessed he was one of those who had committed a sacrilege. The passage then recalls that the murderers of the poet Ibycus were caught in a similar way.

Two men who had killed the poet Ibycus were caught when they joked, in a theatre, that cranes flying overhead were the avengers of Ibycus. Nearby listeners heard them, reported it to the magistrates, and the men were convicted. The passage says they were undone not by the cranes but by their own loose talk.

Plutarch compares a talkative person's tongue to an inflamed body part that draws in whatever is nearby. Such a tongue pulls secret matters out of others, so it must be restrained by reason, like a wall that stops it from slipping. The passage breaks off mid-sentence before finishing its comparison with geese.
Cranes crossing the Taurus mountains, which are full of eagles, carry a large stone in their beaks. The stone keeps them from screaming, so they can fly over at night without being seen.

Traitors are the most despised of men, the passage says. It gives examples of men who were paid for betraying others: one roofed his house with Macedonian timber, another spent his reward on women and fish, and two received an estate from King Philip for handing over Eretria.

Plutarch says a talkative man is like an uninvited traitor who spills secrets in courts and political quarrels, and nobody thanks him for it. He still thinks he is doing a favour. He compares this to a man who gives away everything he owns, and says that both acts come from a sickness, not from kindness.

Plutarch says that criticism of talkativeness is meant to cure the habit, not just to condemn it. Passions are overcome first by understanding and then by practice. People only turn away from a fault once reason shows them the harm and shame it brings.

Talkative people end up with the opposite of what they want: they are hated when they seek love, mocked when they think they are admired, and they harm their friends while helping their enemies. The first step toward curing this fault is to count up the shame and trouble it brings.

Plutarch argues that people should practise the opposite of talkativeness: they should value restraint and silence. Brief, concise speakers are admired and seen as wiser than people who talk without control. He cites Plato, who compared concise speakers to skilled javelin-throwers, and Lycurgus, the Spartan lawgiver, who trained his citizens in silence from boyhood.

Plutarch compares Spartan speech to steel, which is refined from iron ore by removing everything unneeded. Spartan speech is short and sharp because its speakers practice silence. He adds that such sayings suit talkative people, and gives a Spartan retort to King Philip as an example.

Plutarch's point is that the Spartans (Lacedaemonians) were admired for short, sharp replies. When Philip threatened to destroy them, they answered only "If." When Demetrius complained that Sparta sent just one envoy, the envoy replied that one man was enough for one man. The passage adds that the Delphic temple carried short sayings rather than long poems.

The passage praises short, precise speech over long speeches. It says the god Apollo's oracles are brief, and that his name Loxias is linked to ambiguity, which the passage treats as a preference over wordiness. It also notes that people who communicate by signs alone are admired.

Heraclitus, asked by citizens for his view on harmony in the city, drank a simple mix of cold water, barley-meal and herb. He showed by this that being content with simple things, not wanting expensive luxuries, is what keeps a city at peace.

Scilurus, a king of the Scythians, had eighty sons. On his deathbed he had them try to break a tied bundle of sticks, which they could not do. He then broke the sticks one at a time, showing that sons who stay united are strong, while sons who quarrel are weak.

Plutarch says that repeating short, pointed sayings would likely make a person lose interest in idle talk. He admits that a slave of the orator Pupius Piso embarrasses him, because Piso ordered his slaves to answer only his questions and say nothing more, so he would not be annoyed by their chatter.

A host invites Clodius, a powerful man, to a grand dinner. Clodius never comes, and when the host asks his slave whether the invitation was really sent, the slave insists it was. The host's question, "Why then has he not come?", is left hanging, so the story points to the slight of being ignored by a powerful man.

The passage is a short anecdote about slaves who answer only what they are asked. A Roman slave reports a refusal only after his master asks, and an Athenian slave will tell his master the terms of a peace while he digs. The point is that habit controls behavior in all matters, and the author will go on to discuss this.

Plutarch advises a talkative person to train the habit by waiting. When people are asked questions in company, the talker should let others answer first. Answering quickly is not a contest to be won. If someone has already given a good answer, agreeing with them is enough to be seen as pleasant company.

Plutarch advises that when someone else has been asked a question or a favour, we should not jump in and answer or grant it ourselves. Doing so would seem to criticise both the person asked, as unable to help, and the person who asked, as not knowing whom to approach.

Interrupting someone to answer a question meant for them is insulting, because it suggests the other person is not worth asking. Questions are often asked not to get information but to draw a person into conversation and friendship, as Socrates did with Theaetetus and Charmides.

Plutarch says that pushing in to take someone else's place, such as stealing their kiss or drawing away the attention they are getting, is the same as cutting in on another person's answers to get people to listen to you instead. Instead, a person should wait for their own turn to speak, then answer modestly, as if the questioner had asked them directly.

People who are asked a question and cannot answer it are rightly excused. But someone who answers before being asked, or who jumps ahead to another question, annoys others even when correct. If his answer is weak, the whole company mocks him and enjoys his failure.

Plutarch advises talkative people not to treat every question seriously. Some people ask questions only for fun or to pass the time, and they are not asking for real information. The talkative person should learn to notice this and not answer such questions in earnest.
Do not answer questions in a hurry, as if you owed the questioner a reply. First consider what kind of person is asking and why. If he truly wants information, pause briefly before answering.

The passage advises a listener to take time before answering, so that the answer is clear and fits the question actually asked. It notes that the Pythian Priestess at Delphi sometimes spoke her oracles before a question was put, since the god she served could hear even unspoken thoughts.
A good answer depends on understanding both the question and the mind of the person asking it. Otherwise the reply misses the point, as in the proverb about asking for shovels and being given pails.

Plutarch says we should restrain our eagerness to talk, so that we do not rush to speak whenever a question is asked. He gives Socrates as an example: Socrates would not drink after exercise until he had first poured out a bucket of water, training his unreasoning desires to wait for reason.

Plutarch sorts answers into three kinds: necessary, polite, and superfluous. He gives the example of answering "Is Socrates at home?" with a bare "No" to be brief, as the Spartans (Lacedaemonians) did when Philip asked to enter their city and they replied with just "No."

A polite servant answers a caller briefly: the master is out with the bankers and expects some visitors. A talkative servant, by contrast, gives a long and detailed answer, citing a poet and a chain of political news about Alcibiades and a Persian official. The point is that the talker says far more than he needs to.

Plutarch describes a talkative critic who buries his opponent in long recitals of history, such as the whole Eighth Book of Thucydides, until the listener loses track of the question. He says that in such a case we should keep our speech short, answer the question closely, and fit our reply to what the questioner needs.

The gymnasium supervisor once told the philosopher Carneades to lower his voice, which was very loud. When Carneades asked how loud, the supervisor said the right level was set by the person he was speaking with. The point is that a reply should be measured against what the questioner means.

Just as Socrates told his students to avoid foods and drinks that tempt them when they are not hungry or thirsty, a talkative person should beware of the topics he enjoys most and keeps repeating. Soldiers, for example, love stories about war, as Homer shows with Nestor boasting of his own brave deeds.

People who have won lawsuits or unexpectedly gained the favour of kings and princes cannot stop retelling their successes, including their struggles, their clever speeches, and the praise they received. Joy, the author says, talks even more than sleeplessness does, so such people bring up these stories at any chance.

Pleasure, Plutarch says, makes people keep talking about what they enjoy, so that they remember it. Lovers, for example, talk constantly about their love, and when no person will listen, they speak to objects such as a bed or a lamp.

A person who likes to talk should watch his words most carefully about the subjects he enjoys, since those subjects can lead him into long, dull speeches. People also tend to talk and study most in the areas where they feel they excel, because they like to be admired and well known.

Plutarch says we should be careful about talking too much on our favourite subjects, since they tempt us to chatter, much as a familiar place draws an animal back.
