He praises Cyrus for challenging his companions in contests where he was weaker, so as not to hurt them by winning and so that he could learn from them.

The talkative person does the opposite of listening: when a subject comes up that he could learn from, he refuses it and keeps repeating stale, ordinary talk. Plutarch gives an example: a man who had read a few books by Ephorus kept telling everyone about the battle of Leuctra, so people nicknamed him Epaminondas.

Talkative people are a nuisance, but the harm is smaller when their talk is turned into writing on some subject. Plutarch gives an example: the Stoic philosopher Antipater, unable or unwilling to argue face to face with Carneades, wrote many books against him and so earned the nickname "Noisy-with-the-pen."

Plutarch's advice here is aimed at people who talk too much. He suggests they might take up writing, so their urge to speak is spent on paper, much as dogs turn their anger on sticks and stones. He also suggests spending time with people who are older and more respected, so they learn silence out of respect, and pausing to ask whether a word is worth saying before speaking it.

Plutarch argues that speech should have a purpose. People talk to get something, to help the listener, or to please each other, much as salt is added to food. If words serve none of these ends, they are as idle as useless deeds and should not be spoken.

Simonides said he had often regretted speaking but never regretted staying silent. The passage adds that silence never causes thirst or pain, and that a habit of keeping quiet can be built with practice, much as a person can cure a cough or hiccup with effort.

If a house is dark, airless, exposed, or unhealthy, the simplest course is usually to move out. If a person is too attached to the house to leave, they can instead improve it by changing the windows and stairs and by adding and blocking doors.

Plutarch gives two examples of places made better by a change in their surroundings. His home town was said to have been turned to face east by a man named Chaeron, and the philosopher Empedocles is said to have ended a plague by blocking a mountain gap that let in the south wind.

Harmful faults of the soul, which bring storm and darkness, are best driven out by bringing them into open air and light. If that is not possible, they should at least be changed and made better in some way.

Plutarch calls curiosity, the wish to learn about other people's troubles, a mental disease. He says it seems linked to envy and malice, and he quotes a line asking why a person looks for a neighbour's faults while ignoring his own.

Stop looking outward at other people's faults and look inward instead. If you enjoy collecting stories of wrongdoing, you will find plenty in your own life, in your passions and in the duties you have failed to perform. The Alizon is a river in Greek poetry, so the image means "as many as there are".

Faults come from different sources, such as envy, jealousy, cowardice and meanness, just as a careful household keeps its tools in separate places. The advice is to examine one's own failings rather than prying into the lives of neighbours.
Curiosity is turned inward here, away from gossip and spite. Each person is to ask himself what wrong he has done and what good he has failed to do.

People look hard at other people's faults with a sharp, nosy eye, but stay blind to their own. Plutarch compares this to Lamia, a mythical monster who supposedly keeps her eyes off at home and puts them in only when she goes out.

The curious man, who busies himself with other people's faults, ends up helping his enemies more than himself. He points out their failings and neglects his own affairs at home. The passage then turns to Odysseus, who would not speak to his mother until he had first asked the seer Tiresias what he came to learn.

Plutarch says that people who ask about other people's family histories and debts often neglect their own faults. The passage contrasts a curious questioner, who wants gossip about other women, with ordinary people who know their neighbours' ancestry and money problems but are careless about themselves. Tyro, Chloris and Epicaste are figures from old Greek stories.

Instead of gossiping about trivial matters, Socrates studied how Pythagoras persuaded people. Aristippus heard a few samples of Socrates' conversation from Ischomachus, became so eager to learn more that he wasted away, and sailed to Athens to hear Socrates himself. Socrates' aim was to help men see their faults and rid themselves of them.

Some people cannot bear to examine their own lives, because they find them ugly. Like a burdened soul fleeing its own inner state, they wander outward to feed their malice elsewhere, much as a hen ignores its food to scratch for scraps on a dunghill.

Plutarch says that nosy people skip ordinary matters and dig into the hidden troubles of other families. He gives an Egyptian's reply to someone who asked what he was carrying wrapped up: it was wrapped so the other man would not know. The point is that a hidden thing is probably something bad, so the curious should leave it alone.

In old times, houses had door knockers so visitors could announce themselves. This let the household know someone had come, so a stranger would not catch the women in undress, a slave being punished, or the maids shouting.

The main point is that a nosy person pokes into other people's affairs, even though he would not want to be a guest at a well-run household. Yet he spreads openly the very things that ought to be kept behind locked doors and bolts, meaning private faults and troubles.

The passage says that the most troublesome people are like harsh winds that blow off clothes. A curious person does worse: he strips his neighbours bare, breaks into their homes, and spies on and slanders their parties and gatherings, much as a wind pushes into a young woman's private rooms.

Plutarch says that the nosy man is always mentally elsewhere, poking into the private affairs of the rich, the poor, kings and newlyweds, even foreign and royal matters. He compares this to tasting poison to learn its effects: the meddler may be harmed or destroyed before he learns what he wants to know.

Kings' private affairs are best left alone, just as the sun's full light is easy to enjoy but its bright disc is too dazzling to stare at. When King Lysimachus offered the poet Philippides anything he wanted, Philippides asked for anything except the king's secrets. The pleasant gifts of kings are open ones, such as feasts, wealth and favours, so one should not try to learn their hidden matters.

A powerful ruler hides his dark moods, such as anger, a wish for revenge, and suspicion of those close to him, while his joy and goodwill are openly shown. The writer warns that these hidden feelings are dangerous and will break out, so one should keep away from such a ruler.

Plutarch suggests that when a person is tempted to dwell on something harmful, they should turn their attention to larger, better things instead. He recommends studying the sky, earth, air and sea, especially the sun and moon. The moon's waxing and waning is compared to the rise and fall of mortal life.

Plutarch suggests that if a reader will not study great questions about nature, they can still look closely at small things, such as how plants differ in their growth, seasons and shapes. He adds that such study may not seem worth the effort, since it will reveal nothing harmful.

Plutarch suggests that if a person must spend time on bad things, they should read history, which is full of human suffering: murders, betrayals, abuse, and downfalls of rulers. Reading such accounts, he says, will not upset or anger anyone close to them. The "serpent" image means the reader lives on bad material the way a snake lives in deadly matter.

Curious people, the passage says, are not interested in old bad news, but love fresh scandal. They grow bored when told of weddings or festivals and ask the speaker to get to the point. But when told of a seduction, an adultery, or a family quarrel, they stay alert and make time to listen.

Curious people's ears, like cupping-glasses or the gloomy city gates used for criminals and waste, take in only the worst gossip. Nothing good or pure reaches them, only tales of murder and obscene stories, as the closing quotation about constant wailing in the house suggests.

Curious people, Plutarch says, love hearing bad news most, because curiosity seeks what is hidden, and people do not hide their good fortune. Such a listener is driven by malignity, a pleasure in others' misfortunes. Malignity, he argues, is related to envy, the pain at others' blessings, and both come from ill-nature.

People hide their private illnesses so much that some would rather die than tell their doctors. Plutarch says that even famous physicians, if they went from house to house uninvited asking about people's hidden ailments, would be thrown out. Doctors must wait to be sent for.

Nosy people search out other people's faults, not to help cure them but to show them to others, and so are rightly disliked. Customs officers are not resented for collecting duty on honest goods, only when they search bags for smuggled items. Such busybodies also neglect their own affairs.

Plutarch contrasts two kinds of people. Town-dwellers rarely visit the countryside, and when they do, they only look at their neighbours' misfortunes, such as dead cows or spoiled wine, before hurrying back to town. A true countryman, by contrast, avoids gossip coming from the town.
Plutarch describes people who dislike quiet country life and rush to markets and harbours to hear news. They welcome anyone with news, but grow annoyed when someone reports that nothing has happened.

The Locrians, an ancient Greek people, fined travelers who asked for news from abroad, because such questions stirred up gossip. The passage compares curious people to cooks and fishmongers: just as those trades hope for plenty of meat and fish, curious people hope for trouble and change to talk about.

Charondas, a lawmaker of Thurii, allowed only adulterers and nosy people to be mocked on stage. The passage argues that adultery grows out of curiosity about other people's private pleasures, and that curiosity is a prying into hidden matters.

Curiosity about other people's affairs tends to lead to slander. People like to hear gossip and then eagerly pass it on to others. Plutarch also says the harm of curiosity works against what people actually want.

People avoid those who are known to be hostile to them. They hide their plans, hold back discussions, and fall silent when such a person arrives, like someone hiding fish from a cat. As a result, those people often miss matters that everyone else knows about.

People do not trust a nosy person with private things, such as letters, papers and seals. Bellerophon is given as an example: he carried a letter that called for his death, yet he did not open it, showing self-control. Plutarch ties prying to the same weakness that leads to adultery, which he calls madness.

Plutarch says that people who are overly curious waste their time on petty, risky spying instead of enjoying open pleasures. He compares this to choosing a married woman over common ones, which he calls the height of madness. Such spying is described as low and often dangerous.

Simonides said he had two chests: one held the rewards he had been given, and the other, meant for thanks, was always empty. The idea is that people who pry into others' affairs should remember their past experience, which shows that gratitude is rare.
If a person opened the stores that curiosity had piled up, they would find many useless, idle and ugly things. Seeing all this worthless material might fill them with disgust.

Plutarch asks what would happen if someone collected only the worst lines of the ancient writers, such as Homer's flawed verses and Archilochus' insults against women. He suggests such a collector would deserve a curse, the one a tragedy gives to someone who gathers up other people's faults.

Plutarch says that collecting and dwelling on other people's wrongs is shameful and pointless. He compares it to founding a town full of wicked people, and to people who ignore fine art and beauty to seek out deformed freaks at a market.

People who are fascinated by other people's faults, family scandals and private troubles soon tire of such sights and feel disgust. Plutarch says they should first recall how little good their prying has ever brought them before.

Plutarch says that a habit of curiosity can be stopped by training oneself early, starting with small things. He asks what harm there is in not reading gravestone epitaphs or wall inscriptions while walking in public places.

Plutarch says that inscriptions on tombs, such as "Here lies the best of friends," are of no real use or pleasure to us. He adds that they do little harm, except that they encourage readers to be curious about unimportant things.

Just as hunters keep hounds on a leash so they stay focused on the scent of their quarry, a person should hold back his curiosity. He should not chase every thing he sees or hears, but keep it to what is useful.

Just as eagles and lions keep their claws sheathed so they stay sharp, the passage says we should not use up our eagerness to learn on minor matters. We should save it for worthwhile subjects so it does not become dull.

We should not look into other people's houses as we walk past, or stare inside as if planning to steal. Looking in is as improper as trespassing with one's feet, and it is never pleasant. The quoted line warns that a prier will see unpleasant things.

Plutarch says that idle, messy household scenes and stray glances distort the mind and are a harmful habit. He gives an example: Diogenes, a Greek philosopher, mocked the Olympic victor Dioxippus for turning his head to stare at a pretty woman while driving his chariot.

Plutarch says the senses should not wander about freely. They should carry out their task for the mind, report back quickly, and then stay within reason and obey it. He compares unrestrained senses to runaway horses, quoting a line from Sophocles.

The senses, if not trained and disciplined, can pull reason along and push it into bad excesses. Plutarch says the story that Democritus blinded himself to think better is false. Still, he holds that people who use their minds most are least swayed by the senses.

Philosophers set up their places of study far from cities. They saw night as the best time for thinking, and held that quiet, away from worldly distractions, helped them reflect on and solve life's problems.

Plutarch says it is easy to stay away when people insult each other in public, or to leave a noisy crowd. The real gain comes from controlling your urge to join in or look on, and training that curiosity to follow reason.

Plutarch advises a person to stop going to the theatre, even for a fine play, and to turn down invitations to see dancers or actors. He also says not to look round at shouting in the stadium or hippodrome, the sports venues. The point is to avoid such public entertainments.

Just as Socrates advised avoiding food and drink that make us eat or drink when we are not hungry or thirsty, we should likewise avoid sights and sounds that control us and draw us in when we do not need them.

Cyrus refuses to look at Panthea, a woman of great beauty. He reasons that the more he is tempted to see her, the more he should avoid her, since a visit might lead to repeated visits that would make him neglect his important duties.

Alexander refused to look at Darius's beautiful wife and instead visited her elderly mother. Plutarch contrasts this with ordinary people, who peek into women's carriages and hang about their windows, excusing their curiosity even though it opens the way to many kinds of vice.

Plutarch advises that a person sometimes give up lawful gains and even abstain from his own wife, so that he becomes practiced at avoiding unjust gains and other women. In the same way, he should sometimes avoid seeing and hearing everything that happens in his own home, and refuse to listen when someone tries to tell him about it.

Plutarch says that Oedipus's own curiosity brought on his terrible misfortunes. He left Corinth to learn who his parents were, killed Laius, took the throne, and married his mother. Even when he was at the height of good fortune, he kept digging into his past, and he forced the old witness to reveal the whole truth.

Curiosity is described as a bitter-sweet itch, like a sore that bleeds when lanced. A person free of this itch, who is calm by nature and does not know many unpleasant things, can say that forgetting human troubles brings wisdom.

Plutarch advises a calm habit toward news. We should not rush to open a letter, tear it open with our teeth, jump up to greet a messenger, or eagerly hear a friend's news. Instead, we should want to hear only what is useful or helpful.

Plutarch describes how, while he was giving a lecture in Rome, a soldier brought a letter from the Emperor to Rusticus, who was in the audience. Plutarch paused so Rusticus could read it, but Rusticus refused and waited until the lecture ended before opening it. The onlookers admired his self-control.

Someone in power who indulges his curiosity until it becomes strong can no longer restrain it. Out of habit, it pushes him into forbidden acts, such as opening friends' letters, spying on private meetings, and prying into the private lives of kings.

Tyrants are disliked most of all for their spies and informers. Darius, the Persian king, was the first to use spies, and the Dionysiuses of Syracuse followed. When the Syracusans overthrew them, they were the first to be tortured and killed. Informers, the author adds, belong to the same family as nosy busybodies.

Informers look only for wicked deeds or plots, but nosy people spread news of other people's accidental misfortunes. The writer gives an example: during a famine in Athens, people who hid their grain and ground it secretly at night were exposed by neighbours who heard the mills, and this is said to be where the name "impious" came from.

The Greek word for informer, "sycophant," is said to come from a word meaning "fig-informer." It arose when people who reported others for exporting figs, which was forbidden, were given that name. The writer adds that curious readers should note this, so they feel shame at any likeness to informers, who are widely hated.

Plutarch says that some faults grow out of a good nature, much as weeds on rich ground show that the soil is fertile. Shyness is one such trait: it is not bad in itself, though it can lead to wrongdoing. Shy people sometimes fall into the same excesses as shameless people, but they feel pain and regret about them instead of pleasure.

The shameless person does not care about disgrace, while the modest person is easily moved, even by the mere look of something shameful. Shyness is too much modesty, and it is called shamefacedness because the face shows what the mind feels. Plutarch also quotes an orator who said the shameless have no modesty in their eyes.

Plutarch says a bashful person's blushing shows a weak spirit, though the weakness is covered by calling it modesty. Cato preferred boys who blushed to those who turned pale, because a person should fear criticism more than hard work or suspicion more than danger. Yet excessive fear of criticism can make people give up good undertakings.

Plutarch says we should not praise a hard, stubborn refusal to feel anything, or a reckless rush forward without thought. He compares that reckless courage to a dog's, citing Anaxarchus. Instead, he argues for a mix of the two qualities that removes both shameless persistence and excessive timidity.

A farmer digs up useless weeds hard and deep, but handles a vine, olive or apple tree with great care, so he does not harm any healthy part. The image contrasts how one treats what is worthless and how one treats what is worth keeping.

The philosopher treats different faults in different ways. He can cut hard to remove harmful traits like envy, greed or excess pleasure-seeking. But with gentle traits such as shyness, he must be careful, because a rough correction might also destroy good qualities like modesty. He compares this to nurses who scrub infants so hard that they hurt them.

Plutarch says that curing a young person of shyness should not go so far that it also destroys the good qualities close to it, such as modesty, meekness and mildness. He compares this to demolishing houses near a temple: the nearby parts must be propped up, not allowed to fall.

The Stoics, a Greek school of philosophy, kept shame and shyness separate from modesty so that the bad feeling could not hide behind the good word. The author allows loose use of the words here, citing Homer's line that modesty harms and helps people. Modesty helps only when reason keeps it from excess.

Plutarch says that a person who is too shy should see his shyness as a harmful illness, and that nothing harmful can be good. He should not be flattered into weakness by being called pleasant and easygoing, nor give in to every request out of fear of being seen as harsh.

Plutarch contrasts two things. He says the Egyptian king Bocchoris, naturally harsh, was given a sacred asp that shaded him so he could judge fairly. Bashfulness, by contrast, makes weak people unable to refuse others, so they give unjust verdicts or say things against their will, and bold people end up controlling them.

Bashfulness is compared to soft ground that cannot hold back an attack, so it leaves a person open to shameful acts and desires. Plutarch says it is a poor protector of young people, since a youth who never learned to refuse has not spent his youth well. It also fails to guard marriage and the women's quarters.

Plutarch argues that shyness, or excessive bashfulness, leaves a person open to vice and manipulation. It makes people easy to seduce, even good ones, and leads them to lend money to doubtful borrowers or act as guarantors against their own judgment. Such shyness, he says, has ruined many people.

Some people were too ashamed to protect themselves against those close to them, and so they were ruined. Dion, for example, knew that his friend Callippus was plotting against him, but he would not guard himself against a friend and host, and he was killed.

Antipater invited Demetrius to dinner, and Demetrius invited him back the next day. Antipater felt it would be shameful to distrust Demetrius when he had himself been trusted, so he went. After the meal, Demetrius had him killed.

Polysperchon had been paid to murder Hercules, Alexander's young son, and invited him to supper for that purpose. Hercules, suspecting a trap, made an excuse and stayed away. Polysperchon then urged him to act like his father, who was generous to his friends, and asked whether he feared them.

The young man, having no good reason left to refuse, went along with a man who invited him, and some of the other guests at the supper strangled him. The passage then turns to a line of Hesiod, the early Greek poet, advising people to invite a friend to supper and not an enemy.

Plutarch says that keeping your guard up against an enemy is wise, not foolish. Do not let false politeness weaken your caution, or the enemy may trust you and take advantage. Returning favors to someone who entertains you can then harm you.

A harmful fault, which the author calls a disease, must be removed through steady effort, beginning with small matters. His example is declining a drink offered at dinner when you have had enough, without feeling shy or forcing yourself to drink.

Do not feel shy about refusing small things. If someone challenges you to dice while drinking, or a talkative person will not leave you alone, you may refuse or walk away. Xenophanes, asked to play dice, simply admitted he was a coward for such things. Practice in these small refusals is said to prepare you for bigger situations.

Demosthenes mocked the Athenians' panic when Philoxenus, Alexander's admiral, appeared at sea. He asked how they would cope with the sun if they could not even look at a lamp, meaning that a small threat had frightened them too much to act.

Plutarch asks how a person can handle important matters, such as a king's demands or a crowd's pressure, if he cannot refuse a friend's invitation to drink or get rid of a chatterbox. He lets trivial people waste his time because he lacks the nerve to say he is busy.

Plutarch says that practice in holding back shyness over small matters helps a person when praise is involved. At a party, when a friend's singer performs badly or a hired actor ruins a play by Menander, he finds it fine to stay silent rather than join the applause against his own judgment.

If you cannot resist praising a friend's bad poem or dull speech, you will end up flattering him. Then you will have no standing to correct him over serious matters such as business, marriage, or public duty.

Plutarch rejects the saying of Pericles that he would be a friend "as far as the altar," meaning he would go as far as perjury for a friend. Plutarch says that is going too far. A man who has trained himself never to praise, applaud or laugh against his own judgment will not reach that point and will not ask others to lie or judge unjustly for him.

Plutarch's point is that we should learn to refuse requests, starting with small ones, so that we can say no when it matters. He gives the example of King Archelaus, who did not hand a gold cup to a man who asked for it, but gave it to the poet Euripides instead. The king judged who deserved gifts by merit, not by how embarrassed he felt about refusing.

People often give to those who keep pressing them, not because they want to, but because they cannot refuse, while deserving friends are overlooked. Antigonus, a king, was skilled at ending such pressure. He answered a begging Cynic philosopher's requests with replies that made each request seem wrong.

Diogenes, a Greek philosopher, begged from statues to train himself to accept refusals. The passage says we should practise in small matters, such as refusing people's requests, so that we can avoid serious failures later. Spending on trivial things leaves nothing for what is necessary, and it brings more shame when we lack what is noble.

Plutarch says that shyness does more harm than wasting money. Because people feel embarrassed, they turn down the best choice in serious matters: they avoid the skilled doctor for a family friend, pick a teacher who pesters them over a better one, and refuse a capable lawyer to help a friend's son gain experience.

Plutarch says many people adopt the views of their friends, such as Epicurean or Stoic teachings, out of shyness rather than real conviction. He advises training yourself in small daily matters to choose the best option, such as a better barber or inn, instead of picking one out of embarrassment or politeness.

Plutarch says that a person should train himself in small habits, as the Pythagoreans did when they avoided certain ordinary acts. At feasts or ceremonies, he should invite a useful friend rather than someone who merely greets him eagerly. Someone who has trained himself this way will be hard to trip up in larger matters.

Plutarch's point is that each harmful passion brings about the very thing it was meant to avoid. Too much love of fame leads to disgrace, too much love of pleasure leads to pain, idleness leads to hard work, and quarrelsome people end up losing lawsuits.

Shyness tries to avoid a small bad reputation and ends up in a worse one. Bashful people cannot refuse those who press them, so they later feel ashamed of the rebuke they earn, and their fear of minor blame often leads to open disgrace.

Some people, when a friend asks them for money, cannot say no out of embarrassment. Soon after, they are shamed when the truth comes out. Others promise to back a friend in a lawsuit, then back down and run away from the other side out of fear.
Many people, out of embarrassment, agreed to a marriage offer for a daughter or sister that was not good for the family. Later they were forced to go back on their word and end the match.

Plutarch says that people who cannot bluntly refuse can still avoid unwelcome requests with a silent gesture, such as raising or lowering an eyebrow. He adds that silence is most useful against foolish people, since reasonable people can be argued out of their position.

The passage advises keeping famous sayings ready to use against people who make demands. It gives Phocion's refusal to be both a friend and a flatterer of Antipater, and his reply to Athenians who wanted him to pay for a festival while he still owed a debt. It ends with a line from Thucydides about poverty and a quotation about having no silver.

Persaeus, a follower of the philosopher Zeno, lent money to a friend but had the loan witnessed by a banker in the marketplace. He did this because he remembered a line from Hesiod saying that even a brother should be given a witness, even when he smiles at you.

Someone asks why Persaeus uses so many legal forms when lending money. He answers that a written, legal agreement lets the money be repaid smoothly, so he never has to sue for it. He adds that many people, too shy to secure a loan, end up in court and lose their friend.

Plato once gave a letter of introduction for a man named Helicon, praising him as good and moderate, yet added a warning that he was changeable by nature. Xenocrates, though strict in character, wrote a recommendation for a man who proved to be bad, because he was too shy to refuse.

A man who had been recommended to Polysperchon, a Macedonian ruler, asked for money and was given a talent, a large sum. Polysperchon then wrote to Xenocrates, the man who had recommended him, advising him to be more careful about whom he recommended in future. Xenocrates had not known the man's true character.

People often know that certain men are bad, yet still give them recommendations and money. They do this without any pleasure, only because they are worn down by the pressure of those who ask. Plutarch says such people act against their own judgment when pressed to perjure themselves, give unjust verdicts, or lend money that will never be repaid.

Plutarch says that regret comes closest to shame, and happens at the moment we act, not later. People feel vexed when they give in or make false promises. Often they promise things they cannot deliver, such as access to a king, because they cannot bring themselves to refuse persistent requests.

Lysander, once out of favour with King Agesilaus, sent away people who wanted his help to reach the king. He said they should go to others with more influence. The point is that failing to do everything brings no shame, while trying to force your way into what you cannot do adds shame and great trouble.

Plutarch says that we should readily grant requests that are proper and modest, but refuse unfair or unreasonable ones. To show this, he recalls Zeno, who scolded a young man for hiding from a friend who wanted him to lie under oath. Zeno asked why the friend was not ashamed to push him toward what was wrong.

Answering vice with vice is wrong, because it only teaches people to copy the bad behaviour. The sensible course is to refuse shameless people what they demand, without giving in out of false modesty.

Plutarch says that turning away low and worthless people who pester you is not hard in itself. He gives Theocritus as an example: when a stranger and a known thief both asked to borrow his bath scraper, Theocritus refused both with a joke, saying he did not know the one and knew the other too well.

Two stories show rulers and officials turning down requests with sharp replies. The priestess Lysimache refuses muleteers a drink because she fears they would make a habit of asking. Antigonus refuses a young man promotion, saying honours go to a person's own courage, not to the courage of his ancestors.

Plutarch says that when a pushy person is famous or powerful, it may not be easy, or even necessary, to act as Cato did toward Catulus when Cato was still a young man. Cato's conduct toward Catulus is not described here, so the example is only named.

Catulus, a senior Roman official, pressed the junior official Cato to excuse a man Catulus had fined. Cato grew impatient and said that having Catulus removed by his officers would be unseemly for him. Catulus, ashamed, left angry.

Agesilaus, a Spartan king, was asked by his father to give a judgment that broke the law. He refused in a polite way: his father had taught him to obey the laws, so he would obey the law and not his father's request.

Themistocles, an Athenian statesman, refused a request from the poet Simonides to act unjustly. He compared it to a poet breaking the rules of verse: just as Simonides could not write good poetry while breaking metre, Themistocles could not be a good magistrate while ignoring the law.

Plutarch says that cities and friends quarrel and suffer not because of poor musical harmony, as Plato put it, but because people break law and justice. Some who care greatly about music and learning still excuse others for neglecting justice in public office and courts. He then asks whether an orator or a politician should expect favours from a juror or council member.

Plutarch suggests a way to turn down a request from a powerful person who asks for something wrong. Make him first do something embarrassing, like speaking bad grammar or dancing in the marketplace. If he refuses, you can ask him which is more shameful: a small social blunder or breaking the law and one's oath.

Nicostratus refused a bribe from Archidamus, a Spartan king, to betray the town of Cromnum. He said Archidamus could not be a true descendant of Hercules, since Hercules punished wrongdoers while Archidamus tried to turn good men into wrongdoers. The passage then applies this: when a respected person pushes us toward wrong, we should say he is acting beneath his noble birth and virtue.

Plutarch suggests that, with people of no standing, you should test whether you can get what you want from them by pressing them. The examples are a miser lending money without a bond (written security), a proud man giving up a better seat, and an ambitious man handing over an office he could have kept for himself.

Plutarch argues that it would be shameful for people who want to be honourable and just to give up their virtue, when their enemies stick firmly to their bad habits. He adds that if enemies push us only to gain glory and power, it makes no sense for us to raise them up while earning shame and a bad name for ourselves.

Plutarch compares people who give out honours or praise just to please others to unfair judges at public games, who lose their own respect and good name. He says it is shameful to spend your own reputation just to fill someone else's purse, and that most people who do this know they are doing wrong.

Plutarch says that a weak mind is like a body that feels heat and cold too easily: it gives way to flattery and gives way to fear of blame. A person should stand firm against both bullying and coaxing. He adds a quote from Thucydides: a person who draws envy while doing important things is acting wisely.

Plutarch says it is hard to avoid envy and blame, so it is better to be hated by bad people than by those who would fairly criticise us for serving their own ends. He also warns against flattery from pushy people, which is insincere, and compares giving in to it to pigs letting someone scratch them.

People who listen to flatterers are no better off than wrestlers who let themselves be tripped up, and their downfall is more shameful. Some hold back from opposing or rebuking bad men so they will look merciful, while others are pushed into pointless and dangerous quarrels by people who praise them as the only honest voices that never flatter.

Bio compared such people to jars that can be grabbed by the handles and turned any way you like, meaning they change their opinions easily. Alexinus spoke badly of Stilpo, then praised him when told so. Menedemus, hearing that Alexinus praised him, said he always criticized Alexinus, because a man who praises a bad man, or is blamed by a good one, is bad himself.

Plutarch describes a man who was immune to flattery. He follows Antisthenes' story of Hercules telling his sons not to be grateful to people who praise them, meaning they should neither be overwhelmed by praise nor flatter the praisers in return. He also gives Pindar's reply to someone who praised him everywhere: he would make that praise true by his own deeds.

Shy people who have been overcome by their weakness, and so acted against their own judgement and been embarrassed, should keep that experience in mind. By recalling the pain it caused, they should stay on guard for a long time.

Just as travellers who stumble on a stone, or sailors wrecked off a headland, learn to beware of that spot and similar ones, a person who recalls the shame, harm and pain that bashfulness once caused will guard against that weakness and not easily let it master them again.

Painters do well, the speaker says, to set a picture aside for a while before final touches. Looking at it again after a break lets them see small faults that constant close looking would have hidden.

Since a person cannot step away from himself for a while and then return to himself as a stranger would, he judges himself worse than he judges others. The next best method is to let friends examine him after some time has passed, checking whether his character has improved or worsened, not his appearance or health.

Plutarch returns to Rome after two years away and finds his friend has grown much calmer. The friend's good qualities have increased, and his once hot and violent temper has become gentle and ruled by reason. Plutarch quotes a line to say how much milder the man has become.

The writer says that this gentleness has not made the person lazy or weak. Instead, like well-worked soil, it has made them calm and steady enough to act, in place of their old rashness and violence. He adds that their tendency to anger was cured by good teaching, not worn away by age or luck.

Plutarch's speaker says that when a friend named Eros reported a change in the listener, he suspected Eros was kind rather than accurate. Eros, the speaker adds, is never willing to say anything other than what he really thinks in order to please someone.

The speaker says that a certain man has now been cleared of the charge of false witness. He then asks the listener, while they travel, to describe the method they used to bring their own temper under control, so that it became gentle and obedient to reason.

Fundanus warns his friend Sylla not to be misled about his true temper, since he may still be quick to anger despite appearing milder. Sylla replies that neither possibility holds and asks Fundanus to do as he requests.

Musonius taught that reason should not be used only as a one-time cure, like a purgative drug that expels the illness along with itself. Instead, reason should stay in the mind as a daily diet, steadily guiding and governing judgement, much as good food supports lasting health.

Scolding and rebuke do little good when anger is at its peak. They are like strong-smelling substances that can revive someone who has fallen in a fit but cannot cure the illness itself. Other passions at their height still take in reason to some degree, but anger does not.

Anger, Plutarch says, drives reason out of the mind and fills it with confusion, so that useful advice cannot be seen or heard. A man in a rage will not listen to others unless his own reason is first ready to listen.

Just as people under threat of siege gather and store food before help fails to arrive, we should collect remedies for anger from philosophy and keep them in the mind. Once the need arises, it will be too late to bring them in.

Plutarch says that a person who is angry either fails to hear outside advice because of the inner noise, unless their own reason is ready to take it in, or hears it and scorns gentle words while harsh blame makes them more angry. Anger is proud and stubborn, like a fortified tyranny, so it can only be overthrown from within by one's own reasoning.

Repeated anger, the passage says, hardens the mind into irritability, leaving it sore and complaining over small things. But when reason stops anger as it rises, the mind is healed for the moment and regains its steady balance for later.

Plutarch says that on a few occasions, when he fought hard against his anger, he won, and so became confident that reason can defeat anger. He also notes that anger can be calmed by cold water, as Aristotle said, and can also be put out by fear.

Plutarch argues that anger can be cured, sometimes by a sudden joy, and that it is not hard to cure for people who want to be cured. He notes that anger often comes not from serious causes but from teasing, jokes, a laugh or a nod. He gives the example of Helen speaking to her niece Electra, whose sharp reply shows how a small remark can stir anger.

Callisthenes angered Alexander by refusing a huge cup of wine. He said he would not drink to Alexander unless he needed the healing god Asclepius (Aesculapius), meaning he would drink only if he were sick or wounded.

Anger is easy to put out while it is still small, like a spark in dry tinder or hair. Plutarch says that if someone notices it rising from idle chatter or silly insults, they can usually stop it simply by staying silent and showing contempt. Once anger takes hold of large, solid things, it becomes much harder to control.

Plutarch argues that anger can be stopped at the start by not feeding it, much as a fire goes out without fuel. He disagrees with Hieronymus, who held that anger cannot be noticed as it begins. Plutarch says anger has a clear birth and growth, and he points to Achilles' sudden rage at Patroclus' death as an example.

Plutarch notes that Achilles grew angry with Agamemnon only slowly, and that his quarrel grew because of the many words the two exchanged. He then describes Socrates: whenever anger rose in him toward a friend, Socrates lowered his voice, softened his face and eyes, and turned against his own anger, like a headland breaking the waves.

Plutarch says the first way to overcome anger is to stay quiet and not obey anger when it urges you to shout, glare, or hit yourself. Shouting and thrashing about only make the feeling stronger, as they would worsen a disease. He adds a light remark about lovers who make a show of their feelings, such as serenades and garlands, which he treats as a mild, pleasant outlet.

Plutarch says that anger grows when a person gives in to it, unlike grief, which eases when a mourner weeps. When anger rises, it is best to stay calm or withdraw to a quiet place. Anger is aimed most often at friends, and it reaches even gods, animals and objects.

Plutarch gives examples of angry acts that look foolish: Pandarus vowing to burn his own bow after breaking it, and Xerxes whipping the sea and threatening Mount Athos. He says anger has both frightening and ridiculous sides, which is why it is the most hated of the passions.

Plutarch says he began to control his own anger by watching how angry people look and sound. He saw that anger changes a person's face, colour, walk and voice, so that they no longer seem like themselves. He was disgusted at the thought of appearing that way to his family and friends.

Gaius Gracchus, a Roman speaker with a harsh manner and a fiery style, used a pitch-pipe during speeches. A slave behind him sounded a soft, low note so that he would lower his tone and calm his voice.

Plutarch says that if a friend held up a mirror to him during an angry fit, he would not mind, because seeing his own twisted face would make him see how ugly anger is. He adds a story where a satyr mocks Athene for puffing her cheeks while playing the pipe.

Plutarch uses the myth of Athena and Marsyas to make a point about anger. Athena threw away her pipes when she saw her swollen face in a river, and Marsyas hid his distorted face behind a mouthpiece. Anger, he says, swells the face and makes the voice even harsher, so it is ugly in both look and sound.

Plutarch says that angry words are like seaweed thrown up from the sea: they dirty the person who speaks them first. Such words show that bad thoughts were already inside the speaker, and anger only brings them out. For a few hasty words, people can end up with a bad name as enemies or slanderers.

Plutarch argues that just as a soft, smooth tongue is good for someone with a fever, it is even more important to keep the tongue calm during anger. He notes that an unnatural tongue in a fever is a sign of illness, not its cause.

Angry people's words are harsh and insulting, and they cause lasting harm. Plutarch says anger shows a person's character worse than heavy drinking does, since drunken talk is merely silly while angry talk is bitter. Silence is the best response to anger, as the poet Sappho advised.

Plutarch says that anger, when we watch ourselves in it, looks base and unmanly. Yet most people mistake its loudness for strength, its threats for confidence, and its stubbornness for force of character. Some even call its savagery greatness of mind and its refusal to forgive firmness.

Plutarch says that angry people show their smallness and meanness of spirit through harsh acts. They lash out at children, women and animals, as the boxer Otesiphon kicked back at a mule. Tyrants show the same weakness in their cruelty, lashing out like a wounded serpent that strikes whoever hurt it.

Plutarch says that anger grows out of weakness, much as a swelling grows from a blow to the flesh. People who are weaker in some way are more ready to lash out. He gives examples: women, the sick, the old, the unfortunate, and men with particular faults, such as a miser angry at his steward.

Plutarch says that men who are too eager for public office or for leading a political faction bring sorrow on themselves. He adds that anger comes mainly from weakness of the soul. Anger is not a kind of nerve in the soul, as some have said, but a strain and spasm when the soul is overly eager for revenge.

Having dealt with harmful examples of anger, the writer now turns to people who handled anger mildly and gently. He finds such conduct pleasing to see or hear about, and he rejects violent sayings like "Put your heel upon his neck" and "dash his head against the ground."

Plutarch argues that manliness is like justice in most ways, differing mainly in gentleness. Controlling anger inside oneself is a greater victory than ruling others, and it takes the power of judgement to govern the passions as firmly as sinews govern the body.

Plutarch says he likes to collect sayings about controlling anger, especially from kings and tyrants, not only from philosophers. He gives an example: Antigonus, overhearing soldiers insult him near his tent, told them to move farther away so he could not hear. The passage then begins a second example about a man who spoke against King Philip.

King Philip of Macedon forgave a man who had insulted him, and sent him gifts. Later, when Philip learned that the man now spoke highly of him to the Greeks, he said he had cured the man better than his advisers could have. The point is that kindness turned an enemy into a praiser.

Plutarch gives examples of rulers who held back their anger when they were mocked. When Philip of Macedon was insulted at the Olympic games, he said that the Greeks would have something to fear if he treated them badly, since they already mocked him while he treated them well. The passage then names other rulers who showed similar restraint, such as Magas, who was jeered at in a comedy by Philemon.

Two anecdotes about rulers who chose mockery over punishment. One king threatens a captured man with a sword, then sends him away with a toy as if he were a foolish child. Ptolemy is insulted by a grammarian, who answers his question with a jibe about the king's own obscure father, Lagus.

Ptolemy argues that a king should not give insults any more than he should take them. Plutarch's examples show the same idea: Porus asks to be treated "as a king," meaning simply that he wants fair treatment, and the passage ends by saying that punishment and torture belong to lesser spirits, not to the gods.

Anger can tear down, but it cannot build, save or spare. Plutarch compares this to Philip of Macedon, who destroyed Olynthus and could not have rebuilt it. Building up and forgiving belong to gentleness and self-control, while biting and stinging belong to insects like ants and horseflies.

Plutarch argues that angry revenge usually achieves nothing. It only produces biting of lips, empty threats and insults, like children who stumble before reaching their goal. He gives an example: a Rhodian told a Roman officer's servant that what mattered was what the officer thought, not what the servant said.

Plutarch argues that courage needs reason, not anger. Some foreign peoples poison their weapons, but true bravery is steeped in reason, while rage is weak and breaks down. The Spartans used music to calm their soldiers' anger before battle and stopped chasing a defeated enemy, so their rage could be called back. Anger, by contrast, kills many before it is satisfied.

Agathocles, a Greek ruler, took insults from the people of a besieged town with good humour and answered them with jokes. Once he captured the town, though, he sold the people who had mocked him into slavery.

Anger makes people fail at their work. Hunters and orators do badly when angry, and a speaker once had his friends plug his ears so that the taunts of his enemies would not make him lose his case. Also, a slave who has done wrong may escape punishment because he runs away in fear of an angry master's threats.

Plutarch compares anger to a child who wants something: calm patience gets the result better than crying or rushing. Just as a father takes a knife from a boy and uses it safely himself, a person should take revenge away from anger and carry out the punishment calmly, so that the wrongdoer is punished and the angry person is not harmed.

Plutarch says that anger toward servants needs more control than any other passion. Envy, fear and rivalry do not arise between masters and servants. Instead, frequent outbursts of anger cause many faults, and because servants cannot resist or check their masters, the master is likely to slip into more wrongdoing.

Plutarch argues that a person with power over others must be gentle, or else anger will break out when they are not in control of themselves. He admits he once grew angry at his household servants for being too lenient with them, and his wife and friends criticized him for it. He later decided that being patient with servants is better than damaging his own character through anger while trying to correct them.

Plutarch observes that some people, when not punished, felt ashamed of their faults and began to reform through forgiveness rather than punishment. Slaves obeyed a mild master more willingly than a harsh one. So reason is obeyed better than anger, and fear does not produce self-respect, as a poet had claimed.

Plutarch argues that harsh, constant beating does not make people sorry for their wrongs; it only teaches them to hide their faults. He suggests that punishment should be given in measured, fitting ways, and that a person to be corrected should be allowed to speak in his own defence and be heard.

Waiting before punishing lets anger cool, so judgement can choose a fitting punishment. A person punished calmly, after guilt is clearly shown, has no fair complaint. Punishing in anger risks the master looking less just than the servant.

Phocion told the Athenians, after Alexander's death, that if Alexander was dead today he would still be dead tomorrow, so there was no need to rush. Plutarch applies the same idea to anger: a person who wants to punish someone in a rage should wait, because a delay costs nothing and an immediate punishment may later look unjust.

Nobody would beat a slave for a small fault, such as overroasted meat or a late errand, if it happened five or ten days earlier. Yet people become harsh over exactly such things right after they happen. Small things look large when anger clouds our view, just as bodies look bigger in mist.

Plutarch says that when anger has faded, a person should still judge calmly whether a wrong deserves punishment, and if it does, carry the punishment out rather than drop it. He warns that people often punish harshly only while angry and then forget the matter once calm, like rowers who rest in harbour in calm weather and then sail out in a storm.

Plutarch says that people wrongly think reason is too soft when punishing, and so they rush to punish while driven by passion. He argues that a punisher should feel no hunger for punishment and no anger spurring it on. Instead, the punisher should act when least desiring it, forcing reason to carry out the punishment.

We should punish wrongdoers calmly, following reason, without eagerly enjoying the punishment and without regretting it afterwards. Plutarch says rushing into punishment with eager pleasure is savage, and feeling sorry afterwards is womanish, so anger should have no part in it.

Plutarch suggests that the real cure for anger is not only to suppress its outward faults but to deal with its cause. Most angry people, he observes, feel they are being despised or neglected. So others should avoid acts that seem contemptuous, and the angry person should see the anger as folly, necessity, emotion, or misfortune.

The angry person should not expect the offender to act humbly, since a humble apology removes any sense of being slighted. Instead, he should take the attitude of Diogenes, who answered mockery by saying he was not someone who could be laughed at. The angry person should not feel despised, but should look down on the offender as acting from weakness, error, rashness, or similar faults.

Plutarch says that servants and friends do not look down on us because we lack ability or energy. They take advantage of our calm and kindness, some because we are gentle and others because they count on our affection for them.

We get angry not only at people close to us, who might seem to slight us, but also at strangers and animals, such as innkeepers, sailors, and barking dogs, because we feel insulted by them too. One man beat his donkey because its driver claimed to be an Athenian and the donkey was not.

Plutarch says that repeated fits of anger build up in the mind, like a swarm of insects, and come from selfishness, fussiness, and a love of luxury. People become gentle with servants, wife, and friends when they are easygoing, content with little, and do not demand many extras. The quoted lines mock someone who complains about his food however it is cooked.

Plutarch describes a man who will only drink snow-cooled drinks, eat bread he did not buy in the market, or use fine plates, and who beats his servants at dinner. He says such a person is a slave to a weak, complaining way of life, and that his readiness to anger is like a constant illness he may not notice.

Plutarch says we should train ourselves to be content with simple food, since people who need little do not lose much. Eating what is set before us quietly, without getting angry, avoids spoiling the meal for ourselves and others.

Plutarch describes how people often lose their temper over small household faults, such as burnt food or cold bread. He then tells of the philosopher Arcesilaus, whose dinner guests had no bread because the servants forgot to buy it. Instead of getting angry, Arcesilaus only smiled and remarked that a wise man makes a poor host.

Socrates takes a friend, Euthydemus, home, and his wife Xanthippe loses her temper and overturns the table, so the friend leaves upset. Socrates answers that a hen once did the same thing in his friend's house and nobody was bothered. The main point is that friends should be welcomed with cheer, not with frowns or fear.

Plutarch says we should get used to any kind of tableware, and not insist on one particular item. He gives examples of people who will drink only from one favourite cup or horn, or who use only one oil-flask or scraper. When such an item breaks or is lost, they become very upset and punish others harshly.

A person prone to anger should avoid owning rare, costly things like fine cups, seals and gems, because losing them drives him out of his mind more than losing ordinary things would. Seneca makes this point to Nero: a costly tent he had built shows he is poor, since he could not easily replace it if lost.

Nero took the loss of his tent in a shipwreck calmly, because he remembered Seneca's advice. The author argues that a man who is relaxed about such losses will also be mild with his servants, and so with his friends and everyone under his command.

Plutarch's point is that a bad temper is the quality people most dread in others. Slaves, he says, care more about whether a new master is short-tempered than about his other faults, and marriage and friendship cannot survive anger, even when the other person is otherwise good.

Plutarch says that the wand of Dionysus, god of wine, deals with a drunk man well enough by itself. But when anger is added to drunkenness, wine stops being a source of cheer and dancing and becomes savage. Likewise, ordinary madness can be cured by hellebore, a plant once used as a remedy, but madness mixed with anger causes disasters like those in Greek tragedy.

Anger should not be let out in any setting. In jest it turns friends into enemies, in debate it turns the love of learning into fighting, and in teaching it makes students hate learning. When a person is in trouble, anger drives away the sympathy of others, as Priam showed when he cursed those who came to comfort him.

Good temper, the passage says, can calm anger and change an angry person's mind. Euclides answered his brother's threat of revenge by promising to persuade him instead, and that softened the brother. Polemo, when insulted, said nothing and simply studied one of his seal-rings closely, a quiet reply that avoided conflict.

Aristippus and Aeschines had quarrelled, and Aristippus chose to end the anger by speaking first. When someone asked where his friendship had gone, he said it was only asleep and he would wake it. He then went to Aeschines, who answered graciously that Aristippus, being naturally superior, was the first to see what was needed.

Plutarch says that people tame wild animals, yet in anger they lash out at children, friends and servants. They try to excuse this as hatred of wrong, but that is a mistake. Anger is a passion like any other, and calling it a virtue does not remove it.

Plutarch compares anger to the seed that Zeno said was made from all parts of the soul: anger, he says, is built from the other passions. It draws on pain, pleasure and arrogance, takes its spite from envy, and contains a desire to harm others, even at cost to itself.

Plutarch says that a house of a spendthrift shows its owner's excess through signs like music, wine dregs and servants hungover at the door. An angry master's house shows his temper in the same way: servants bear marks and chains, and only wailing is heard within.

Plutarch says that people who hate wrongdoing and so often get angry can lessen that anger by trusting their close friends less. Anger grows most when a good man turns out to be dishonest, or when someone we thought loved us turns against us. He admits that he himself trusts people and believes in their goodwill, so he feels deeper hurt when he is wrong.

Plutarch says he cannot stop himself from warm feeling toward others, but he can hold back his trust, using a warning of Plato as a check. Plato praised the mathematician Helicon for being changeable by nature, yet feared the well-educated men of the city, because human beings still show human weakness in some way.

The passage is a fragment, so its exact sense is uncertain. It seems to say that a harsh, fault-finding judgment of people, though it may insult human nature, can still make them calmer in anger. The reason given is that sudden, unexpected events are what drive people out of their minds.

When annoyed, we should remind ourselves of what we already know about people. Like Anaxagoras, who said he knew he had fathered a mortal child, we should tell ourselves that a slave is not a philosopher, a friend is not perfect, and a wife is only a woman.

If a person often asked himself whether he was living as he should, he would be less quick to find faults in others and would see that he needed forgiveness himself. Instead, when angry, people hurl at others the same rebukes that great men once gave, such as "Do not steal" or "Why are you lazy?"

People often scold others for anger while they themselves are angry. They punish faults in a rage, which is the same fault they are punishing. Plutarch contrasts this with doctors, who treat illness without becoming ill themselves.

Plutarch warns that prying too closely into everyday matters, such as a servant's work, a friend's actions, a son's pastimes, or a wife's whispers, causes frequent fits of anger. He says this anger comes from a peevish, harsh character. He also quotes Euripides, who says the god intervenes in great things and leaves small things to chance.

A sensible person should not leave things to chance or ignore them. He should hand over minor matters to his wife, servants and friends, and keep the most important ones for himself. Small details wear a person out and stir up anger, and that habit then spreads to bigger matters.

Plutarch says he admired Empedocles' saying "Fast from evil" and approved of temporary vows, such as giving up wine, sex or lying for a set time. He compares his own vow to these: to avoid anger for a few days, like going without wine as an offering.

The speaker says that after a month or two of deliberate effort, he became more patient. Keeping courteous, calm and gentle, and avoiding angry words and actions, brought him to a view: kindness and gentleness are most pleasant to the person who has them, even more than to those around him.

Plutarch explains why he is sending only a short piece. He had received a request for a letter on contentedness of mind and on some hard points in Plato's Timaeus, but a messenger was leaving for Rome at once. So he copied out notes he had already made on contentedness of mind and sent those instead.

Plutarch tells his friend that he hopes the friend wants practical help for life, not just polished words. He praises him for not being like the tragic king Merops, who forgets human suffering because of public praise. The friend knows that high status cures no ailment: a fine slipper does not cure gout, and a diadem does not cure a headache.

Plutarch argues that wealth, fame, or power can bring calm only if we enjoy them while we have them, without constantly longing for them when they are gone. Trained reason is what keeps us from this longing, holding back strong emotion before it runs out of control. He adds Xenophon's advice to honour the gods in good times so they will be friends in trouble.

Sensible people should think ahead about ways to endure trouble before it arrives, so those ways are ready to use. Just as savage dogs calm down only at a familiar voice, the wild passions of the mind are hard to calm unless well-known arguments are at hand to restrain them.

Plutarch argues that the advice to have little public or private business in order to keep an untroubled mind is too costly. If peace of mind can only be bought by doing nothing, it is like telling every sick person to lie still in bed: the cure is no cure at all.

Plutarch argues that numbing oneself is a poor cure for despair, and that a lazy, soft life that abandons friends, family and country does not truly ease the mind. He also says idleness does not bring peace, since women, who mostly stay home doing little, are not calmer than men. He supports this with a line from Hesiod about the north wind not reaching a soft-skinned maiden.

Plutarch says that worry, jealousy, superstition, ambition and vanity fill the women's quarters of a household with constant trouble. He gives Laertes as an example: even though he lived alone in the country, cared for only by an old woman, he still suffered sorrow and low spirits. Some people, he adds, fall into restless distress simply from having nothing to do.
Plutarch quotes Homer's account of Achilles sulking in his tent, refusing to attend the council or fight. Achilles himself calls his idleness a useless burden on the earth.

Plutarch says Epicurus recommended public life to ambitious people, so they would not be troubled by idleness. He calls this inconsistent, since Epicurus urged only the restless, not capable men. Plutarch's own view is that peace of mind depends on whether actions are good or bad, not on how many actions a person takes.

Some people think certain ways of life are free from trouble, such as farming, being unmarried, or being a king. Plutarch uses a line from the playwright Menander to show this is a mistake: the rich also suffer, and trouble comes with both wealth and poverty.

Plutarch says that changing one's circumstances does not cure the troubles of the soul. A timid person who moves from a small boat to a large ship still gets seasick, because he brings his fear with him. Likewise, these inner troubles come from lack of experience, lack of thought, and not knowing how to enjoy the present, so they affect rich and poor, married and unmarried alike.
Once a sick person recovers and regains health, everything tastes good again. Someone who yesterday refused fine bread and cakes will today happily eat plain bread with olives and cress.

Reason brings contentment and a change of view about every kind of life. Alexander wept on learning there were infinitely many worlds, because he had conquered only one. Crates, who owned almost nothing, lived joyfully, while Agamemnon was weighed down by ruling many people.

Diogenes, when put up for sale as a slave, sat down and mocked the auctioneer, asking if he would tell a fish for sale to stand up. Socrates, in prison, calmly kept talking philosophy with his friends. Phaethon, by contrast, wept after reaching heaven because he was not given his father's horses and chariot.

A person's inner character shapes their life, much as a foot shapes a shoe. Good sense, not habit, is what makes the best life seem sweet, so we should first put our inner state in order. Then outside events can be turned to our benefit, and anger at them does nothing useful.

Plato said life is like a game of dice: we cannot control how the dice fall, but a wise person accepts the throw and makes the best of it. People who live without thought are carried away by good luck and crushed by bad luck, like sick people who cannot bear heat or cold.

Plutarch says that people who handle their circumstances badly suffer, even when their situation looks good. Sensible people, like bees gathering honey from dry thyme, get some benefit even from bad circumstances.

The main point is that when things go wrong, we should train ourselves to find some good in it, as these men did. One man threw a stone at his dog, missed, hit his stepmother, and said "not so bad." Diogenes, exiled, called it good because exile made him a philosopher. Zeno, after losing his only ship, joked that fortune had left him only his cloak and porch.

The speaker is comforting someone who has suffered a setback. Whatever has gone wrong, such as a rebuff from a powerful patron, a burden of work, or slander and envy, can be turned to good use: the person can go to the country, or to study and philosophy, as Plato did after his friendship with the ruler Dionysius ended.

Seeing how famous men bore the same troubles calmly, Plutarch says, helps a person feel more content. He gives examples: Roman kings who had no sons to inherit, Epaminondas and Fabricius who stayed poor, and a king whose wife was unfaithful yet still had a famous monument at Delphi.

Plutarch gives examples of famous men whose families brought them shame, yet who were not harmed by it. Agis, a Spartan king, was not diminished by his wife Timaea's affair with Alcibiades. Stilpo, a philosopher, stayed cheerful when his daughter lived loosely, and when Metrocles criticized him for it, he asked whether the fault was his or hers.

Metrocles tells a man that his wife's wrong was his misfortune. The man replies by asking whether a fault is not a slip, a slip a mishap, and a mishap a misfortune. Step by step, he shows that Metrocles' accusation was empty, a mere barking.

Plutarch says most people get upset not only by the faults of friends but also by their enemies' faults, such as spite, envy and anger. Those who suffer from such faults are a trouble to others, and he suggests the reader is himself disturbed by these things, like the doctors in Sophocles who cure bitter bile with bitter medicine.

Plutarch tells the reader that being bitter about other people's faults is unreasonable. He adds that even one's own affairs are often run by flawed, crooked means, so fixing everything is neither one's job nor easy.

If you accept people as they are, the way a surgeon accepts his tools and a dog simply acts according to its nature, you will be happier than if you dwell on others' faults. Such dwelling fills a small, weak mind like water filling a low hollow.

Plutarch argues that it is unreasonable to get irritated because the people around us are not good or wise. He notes that some philosophers tell us not to pity the unfortunate, and that they also tell people who recognise their own faults to fix them without grief rather than despair over them. If we should not grieve over our own failings, then getting annoyed at others' failings makes even less sense.

Plutarch warns that we may appear to be judging others for their faults, while really acting out of self-interest. Strong wanting or strong dislike of things makes us suspicious and irritable toward the people we blame for taking those things from us or bringing us troubles.

When a sick person tastes everything as bitter, the fault lies in the illness, not the food. Likewise, we should stop blaming circumstances when we see others bear the same things calmly and without grief.

When things go against our wishes, we should look at our many advantages and comforts too, and see that the good outweighs the bad. Plutarch says we wrongly fix our minds on painful things and push away pleasant ones, as a person turns from bright light to look at grass.

Plutarch is asking why someone focuses only on their troubles, making them seem sharp and large, while ignoring the good things they have. He compares this to a Chian who sold fine wine to others but asked for sour wine for his own supper, and to a slave who said his master was asking for bad wine while good wine was right there.

Most people dwell on their troubles and overlook what they still have. Aristippus, a Greek philosopher, did the opposite: after losing a good farm, he pointed out to a sympathiser that he still had three fields while the man had only one, so the sympathiser was the one who deserved pity.

It is foolish to grieve over one loss and forget what is still left. Like small children who throw away all their toys and cry when one is taken, people who lose one thing in life treat everything else as worthless.

The passage argues that people have many blessings if they look for them. Each person has something, such as a good name, a home, a wife, or a good friend. Antipater of Tarsus, a Greek philosopher, counted even a calm sea voyage among his blessings as he was dying.

We should notice the ordinary good things in life and be glad of them. These include being alive and well, seeing the sun, living without war or civil strife, and having freedom to work, rest, speak, or stay silent as we wish.

Plutarch suggests that imagining our blessings as lost makes us content with them now. We then see their worth while we still have them, not only after losing them. He notes that wanting something we lack does not make it more valuable.

Plutarch says we should not hoard the things we value while living in constant fear of losing them, and then ignore them once we have them. Instead, we should enjoy them, so that we can accept losing them more calmly if it happens.

Most people examine other people's poems, paintings and statues closely, but neglect their own lives. They envy others' reputations and fortunes and undervalue their own, as adulterers desire other men's wives.

Contentment comes more easily if a person looks at his own situation, or at people worse off than himself, rather than comparing himself with those who are better off. People always compare upward, so they keep wanting more and never feel thankful for what they have.

Plutarch mocks people from small provinces who are never satisfied with the honours they already have. They complain they lack senators' shoes, then praetorship, then consulship, and then want to be named first consul rather than second. He says this is just a way of finding reasons to be ungrateful for their good luck and to make themselves miserable.

A healthy mind does not sink into sadness because it has less fame or wealth than the countless others in the world. It instead rejoices in its own life, which it counts as better than many others. The last line makes the point that a person cannot win the Olympic games by choosing the rivals they face, so one cannot pick the comparisons that make one look best.

In life we can be proud of out-doing most people, so we are more often envied than envious, unless we compare ourselves to giants of myth. When you envy someone carried past in a litter as more important than you, look instead at the bearers who carry him.

Plutarch urges the reader not to envy powerful rulers such as Xerxes, the Persian king. He points out that the people who suffered under Xerxes' orders, forced to dig through a mountain or punished when a bridge failed, may also have judged the king's life to be happy. The passage then turns to Socrates, who is about to be quoted.
A guide shows a man the prices of wine, a purple robe, honey, meal, olives and a vest. Each time, the man calls the city cheap, even for costly items. The money units are ancient Greek coins.

Plutarch suggests that when someone says our lives are going badly because we hold no high office, we can answer that our situation is good. We do not beg, carry burdens, or live by flattery, so we have reason to count our life as enviable.

People tend to judge their own lives by how others appear, and they envy what looks splendid from outside. Plutarch urges looking behind that show, where others also have troubles. He gives the example of Pittacus, a famous wise man, whose wife upset a dinner table in anger. Pittacus told his guests that everyone has some trouble, and his own was not the worst.

Public opinion calls a man happy when he is respected in the marketplace, but his own home may hold miseries that outsiders never see. Family pride hides these troubles, even in wealthy, famous or royal households. Praise from a distance, based on outward show, does not match what people actually feel inside.
By thinking this way, a person can free himself from dissatisfaction with his own lot. That dissatisfaction comes from admiring other people's situations so much that one's own seems poor and small.

Plutarch says that peace of mind is harmed when people want more than their means allow, and then blame fate or luck for their failure instead of their own foolishness. He compares this to trying to shoot with a plough or hunt hares with an ox: such a person is not unlucky, only foolish in attempting the impossible.

Plutarch says that self-love is mostly to blame for people wanting to be first at everything and to take part in every activity without limit. They want to be rich, learned, strong, popular, friends of kings and rulers all at once, and they even feel dissatisfied without top-quality dogs, horses, quails and cocks.

Plutarch's passage gives examples of rulers and heroes who showed anger or displeasure when they were beaten or thought they should win. Dionysius the elder punished a poet and a philosopher who outdid him in singing and argument, sending one to work in quarries and selling the other into slavery. Alexander was displeased when a runner seemed to let him win, while Achilles, though boasting of his skill in war, is presented as a better model.

Megabyzus, a Persian visitor, started talking about art in the studio of the painter Apelles. Apelles told him that while he stayed silent his gold and purple clothes made him look important, but now that he was talking, the assistants grinding paints were laughing at his foolish remarks.

Plutarch says that some people mock the Stoics for calling their wise man not only prudent, just and brave, but also an orator, general, poet, rich man and king. These critics then claim all those titles for themselves and are angry when they are refused. He adds that even among the gods, different roles belong to different beings.

Different gods are given different jobs. One is called god of war, another god of oracles, another god of gain. Aphrodite, having no part in war, is sent by Zeus to take charge of marriages and weddings.

Some pursuits cannot be combined because they pull in opposite directions. Oratory and mathematics need leisure, while politics and royal friendship need involvement in public affairs. Likewise, wine and rich meat strengthen the body but dull the mind, and seeking money works against philosophy.

Plutarch says that people should accept their own natural character and not try to force their nature into a different way of life. He compares this to animals: a horse suits a chariot, an ox suits a plough, and a hound suits hunting boars. A person who is upset at not being both a lion and a pampered lap-dog is, he says, out of his senses.

Plutarch says it is foolish to want the rewards of several different ways of life at once, such as being a great philosopher while also enjoying a rich marriage, luxury and admiration. He compares this to runners, who do not mind missing the wrestlers' crowns and are glad with their own. The lesson is to make the most of the life one actually has, as Solon advised a citizen of Sparta.

Strato compares crowds of pupils to crowds of people who want a bath rather than an oil rub, implying Menedemus's larger following is no surprise. Aristotle says that Alexander may be proud of ruling many lands, but a man may also rightly take pride in holding correct views about the gods. People who value their own way of life highly, the passage adds, will not envy others.

We expect each plant to bear only its own kind of fruit, yet people expect themselves to have every quality at once, such as wealth and learning, or being both stingy and extravagant. When they cannot, they blame themselves and feel their lives are incomplete.
