Nature gives different creatures different foods, and gives people different ways to earn a living, such as herding, ploughing, hunting birds, or fishing. So each person should choose the work that suits them and do it hard, and leave others to their own work. Plutarch adds that Hesiod's line about potters and smiths quarrelling is true only if people fail to do this.

People envy others close to their own work and way of life, and also those above or beside them in status. The rich envy the learned, the famous envy the rich, and free citizens admire actors, dancers and court attendants. This envy brings them much trouble.

Plutarch says that a person's contentment or discontent comes from within the mind, not from outside forces. Fools ignore the good things they have now, always looking ahead, while wise people call past good things back to mind through memory. The present slips away too quickly for fools to feel it is theirs.

Plutarch compares forgetfulness to a donkey eating a rope that a man is making in the underworld, so the work is always undone. In the same way, forgetfulness erases people's past good experiences and breaks the link between past and present, so each event soon seems as if it never happened.

Plutarch compares people who forget their past to philosophers who say the body is always changing, so no one is quite the same person from one moment to the next. He means that people who let their past slip away treat yesterday and last year as if they had never happened, and so are always starting fresh without the experience they gained.

Plutarch says that a bigger obstacle to peace of mind is when people forget pleasant things, as flies slide off smooth mirrors, and cling instead to unpleasant memories, as flies stick to rough spots or cracks.

Plutarch says that people sink into remembering their troubles and cannot escape, like beetles trapped in a pit they circle until they die. He advises focusing on the bright side of things, as a painter uses bright colours, and keeping the gloomy side in the background, since it cannot be fully erased.

Plutarch says that the world works by opposites, like tight and loose strings on an instrument, so nothing in human life is wholly pure. Just as a musician uses both high and low notes, and a grammarian uses both vowels and consonants, life mixes good and bad in due measure.

Plutarch says we should not lose heart, but should mix the good and bad in life, as musicians cover poor notes with good ones, so that our mixed life becomes balanced. He then rejects Menander's saying that a guardian spirit guides every person from birth.

Plutarch quotes Empedocles, an early Greek thinker, who said that two spirits or guardian powers take hold of each person at birth and rule over them. The quoted lines then name a long list of such female powers, such as Chthonia, Deris and Harmonia.

Plutarch says that people are born with mixed passions, so they should hope for good things while expecting bad ones, and avoid going to extremes. He argues that someone who is not overly anxious about the future enjoys good things more, because excessive desire brings excessive fear of losing them, which makes enjoyment weak and unsteady.

Plutarch suggests that a person can enjoy what he has more fully if he keeps in mind that it can be lost. He points to Anaxagoras, who accepted his son's death by saying he knew he had fathered a mortal, and says this attitude can be applied to every situation, such as knowing wealth, power and a wife can all be taken or fail.

Plutarch says that if a person keeps in mind that a human being is by nature changeable, then bad events that were not wanted but were foreseen hurt less. Such a person does not say "I never expected this," so the heart calms and anger settles quickly. He adds that Carneades, a Greek philosopher, held that surprise makes big misfortunes weigh more.

Aemilius Paulus defeated Perseus, king of Macedonia, and was honored and called happy, even though he had to give up his command. Perseus was seen as deeply unfortunate because he lost his kingdom without expecting it. Aemilius had known from the start that his command would end.
Sudden events hit harder than expected ones. Odysseus grieves more over his dog's death, which he did not foresee, than over his wife's tears, which he had prepared himself to control with reason.

Some things that go against our will cause pain by their nature. Many others only upset us because we have come to think of them that way. So it helps to keep ready a line from Menander, a Greek comic poet: "You suffer no dread thing but in your fancy," meaning that the fear is in the mind.

Plutarch argues that things like a father's humble birth, a wife's adultery, or losing a prize do not harm a person's soul or body, so a man is not made worse by their absence. Painful things such as illness, worry, and the death of loved ones should be met by remembering that suffering is what mortals must expect, as a line from the playwright Euripides says.

Grief is calmed most by remembering that humans are bound to the body and its needs, which is the only thing fortune can reach. The wise person's inner self stays safe from outside loss. Plutarch illustrates this with Stilpo, who said nothing of his was taken, and with a line of Homer about what the Achaeans could not seize.

Plutarch says we should not belittle human nature, since only a small, perishable part of a person is open to misfortune. The better part, made of good opinions, teaching and virtue, cannot be taken away, so we should face the future bravely. He compares this to Socrates saying his accusers could kill him but could not harm him.

Fortune can bring illness, poverty, or false accusations, but it cannot make a good, brave, and noble person bad, cowardly, or envious. Plutarch says that this inner character is worth more to a life than a ship's pilot is at sea.

A ship's pilot cannot calm a storm or choose where the ship lands, and he cannot be sure of his fate. While he has not given up, he uses his skill: he runs before the gale with sails lowered, even though he sits at the helm shaking with fear.

A wise man keeps his body calm mainly by living temperately, eating plainly and exercising in moderation, which prevents most illness. If trouble does come from outside, he avoids it like a sunken rock, and if it becomes overwhelming, he can leave the body behind as a sailor leaves a leaking boat.

Plutarch says that it is fear of death, not love of life, that makes a foolish person cling to the body. He compares this to Odysseus clinging to a fig-tree above the whirlpool Charybdis, held there by fear rather than by any wish to live.

Plutarch says that a person who understands the soul's nature, and believes death brings it something better or at least no worse, is less afraid of death. That calm helps him live at peace. He can enjoy life when good things prevail and leave it without fear when bad things do, trusting that the deity will free him when he chooses.

The speaker is describing a wise man who cannot be troubled by misfortune. He says he has blocked every route by which fortune could reach him. He relies not on physical barriers but on firm purpose and reason, which anyone can choose to develop.

We should not give up on or doubt the sayings Plutarch has just cited. Instead we should admire and imitate them, and test ourselves first in small matters so we can reach greater ones. Excusing ourselves by saying the task may be too hard only breeds laziness and self-indulgence.

A mind that trains itself to face illness, grief and exile, and uses reason to examine each one, finds that much of what seems terrible is false or empty. Still, many people are disturbed by the line from the poet Menander that no one can say they will never suffer this or that.

Plutarch says that it helps us to face hard fortune directly, instead of living on soft hopes that never meet resistance. He answers the saying that no one can promise to avoid suffering by noting that people can promise to refuse wrongdoing, such as lying or cheating. Keeping those promises is within our control and eases the mind, while the memory of wrongdoing does the opposite.

Regret over one's own wrongdoing is said to hurt more than grief from outside events. Shame and self-blame turn inward and torment the mind, much as a fever hurts more than cold or heat from outside. Grief that comes from chance is lighter by comparison.

Plutarch says that shame over one's own wrongdoing makes anger harder to bear. He claims that no amount of wealth, family pride, high office, or skill with words brings as much calm to life as a soul that is free from wrongful deeds and desires.

Good actions bring a lively, cheerful energy and high thoughts, and leave a memory that lasts longer and is sweeter than hope. Plutarch also points out, quoting Carneades, that censers do not keep their sweet smell once emptied.

In a wise person's mind, good deeds leave a lasting, pleasant memory that keeps joy alive. Such a person looks down on those who complain about life and call it a place of suffering or a kind of exile for the soul.

Plutarch quotes Diogenes, who told a man dressing lavishly for a feast that a good man treats every day as a feast. Plutarch agrees, and adds that the world itself is a holy temple where people are brought at birth to see living, moving things like the sun, moon, stars, rivers and earth.

Plutarch says that life itself is the fullest kind of initiation into these things, so it should be lived with peace of mind and joy. He criticizes people who save their happiness for festivals, and who buy their laughter by paying actors and dancers to supply it.

Plutarch says that at religious rites people sit quietly and behave with dignity, but in ordinary life they waste their time in grief, worry and sadness. He adds that people enjoy pleasant music and birdsong and are pleased by playing animals, yet are upset by animals that roar, howl or look fierce.

Plutarch describes people whose lives are full of sorrow and worry, yet who make no effort to find relief. He says they refuse to listen to advice that would help them accept the present without complaint, be grateful for the past, and face the future calmly and without fear.

Plutarch says that envy and hatred look alike and are often mixed together, because vices are linked to one another like hooks and share the same feelings. Both are pained by a prosperous man, and both are the opposite of goodwill. Since they differ more than they agree, he plans to examine each one from its origin.

Hatred comes from thinking someone is bad in general or bad toward oneself, and it is aimed only at people seen as harmful. Envy is broader: it is upset by anyone who seems prosperous, much as an inflamed eye is troubled by any bright light.

Plutarch notes that people also hate some animals, such as cats, beetles, toads and serpents. Some even hate the sight or sound of certain creatures, and some peoples kill mice because they think their gods dislike them. Envy, however, is felt only toward other humans.
Animals, the passage says, probably cannot feel envy. They have no understanding of good or bad fortune, or of reputation and its lack, and those are the things that mainly stir up envy in people.

Plutarch says that some animals hate and fight each other to the death, such as eagles and dragons or crows and owls. He adds that their blood is said not to mix. He also suggests that fear causes hatred between some pairs, such as the cock and the lion, because people naturally hate what they fear.

Envy of others is never fair, because no one harms another merely by being prosperous. Hatred of wrongdoers, by contrast, can be deserved, and hating evil is counted a virtue. Plutarch illustrates this with a Spartan king praised for gentleness, whose colleague replied that he could not be good if he was not harsh toward the bad.

Plutarch notes that Homer described Thersites' bad character in just one line: he was hated by Achilles and Odysseus, the best men. Being hated by the excellent is the worst kind of worthlessness. People who are envious will not admit it. They claim anger, fear or hatred instead, because envy is the one fault of the soul that is seen as shameful.

Envy and hatred are different feelings and do not feed on the same causes. People are hated more as they become worse, but envied more as they become better. Envy attacks the good and those rising in virtue, as insects attack the ripest grain and the roses in full bloom.

Extreme wickedness makes people hated even more. The men who accused Socrates were so despised by their fellow citizens that no one would give them fire, answer them, or touch water they had bathed in, until they hanged themselves. Great success, on the other hand, often puts an end to envy.

Envy does not target people whose success is so great that it is out of reach, much as the midday sun casts almost no shadow. Alexander and Cyrus were such figures, so no one envied them, though many hated Alexander and plotted against him until his death. Misfortune can end envy, but it does not end hatred.

Hatred stays even when an enemy is beaten, but envy is not aimed at the unfortunate. Envy also fades when a person is at either extreme of fortune, good or bad, while hatred does not fade. So the two feelings differ greatly.

Plutarch says people stop hating someone in three cases: when they are convinced they were not wronged, when they come to see the other person as good, or when they receive a kindness. He notes that being convinced of no wrong does not end envy, and the other two cases can even increase it.

Envy is aimed most at people thought to be good, since their virtue is the greatest blessing. When the prosperous show them kindness, envious people are pained, because they envy both the goodwill and the power to do good. For this reason, Plutarch argues, envy differs from hatred: kindness eases hatred but makes envy worse.

Hatred aims to do as much harm as it can, while envy is different. An envious person does not wish his relations or friends ruin or disaster. He only resents their success and tries to block their glory, much as a man removes whatever blocks the light of his house.

Talking about one's own importance or ability is widely seen as tiresome and ungenerous, yet few people who criticise it avoid doing it. Plutarch quotes Euripides, who says that people would not boast of themselves if words cost money, but since words are free, everyone happily speaks about themselves, truthfully or not, without penalty.

Plutarch notes that some writers boast about themselves in their works, even though Pindar said that boasting out of place is a kind of madness. Athletes who win at the games, by contrast, let others praise their victories, so that they avoid the awkwardness of praising themselves.

Plutarch says people rightly dislike Timotheus for boasting in his victory inscription, since praising yourself is clumsy and breaks custom. He adds Xenophon's view that praise from others is pleasant to hear, while self-praise is most sickening to others.

People who praise themselves look shameless, Plutarch says, because modesty would suit them even if others praised them. It is also unfair to give themselves praise that others should give. Yet if listeners stay silent, they seem jealous, and if they fear that, they must praise the speaker against their true opinion, which is closer to flattery than to honour.

A statesman may sometimes praise himself, but not to boast. He may do so when the facts call for it, speaking about himself as truthfully as he would about someone else. If others are praised for good deeds, he need not hide his own. Such self-praise, the passage says, produces more and better praise later, as seed produces a crop.

A statesman wants a good reputation not as a reward or comfort, but because it lets him do more good for others. People who trust him are easier to help, while those who suspect or slander him are harder to benefit. The passage then turns to whether a statesman may sometimes praise himself, as long as he avoids empty boasting.

Vain glory is when a person praises himself so that others will praise him back. People despise it because it comes from ambition and an inflated view of oneself. Plutarch compares this to starving people who eat their own flesh: someone hungry for praise, getting none from others, feeds on his own vanity instead.

When people do more than praise themselves, and compete with others' praise by setting their own deeds against theirs in order to outshine them, they add envy and spite to their vanity. A proverb says that stepping into another's dance is meddling and foolish.

When others are being praised, we should not push our own praise into the moment out of envy or spite, and we should not let others praise us then either. If the honoured person deserves it, we should step aside. If we think they do not deserve it, we should show that by argument and proof, not by praising ourselves.

Self-praise is not blameworthy when it answers an accusation or slander. Pericles, the Athenian statesman, gives an example: he replies to people angry with him by listing his own qualities, such as his knowledge, his ability to advise, his love of his country, and his refusal of bribes.

A man who praises himself without boasting, showing that his virtue is great, can shame envy, since envy cannot lower his virtue. People will seldom blame such a man, especially when his self-praise rests on real achievement, as history shows.

The Theban people put their generals Pelopidas and Epaminondas on trial for staying away from home past their term and invading Laconia instead. Pelopidas, who begged for mercy, was barely acquitted. Epaminondas, who boasted of his deeds and said he would die if they called them wrongs, was admired and freed with joy.
Athena speaks these words to Diomedes, son of Tydeus, in Homer's Iliad. She scolds him for hanging back and watching the battle from a distance, and says he is nothing like his brave father.

Praise of oneself is easier to accept when it answers an attack or a real danger. Plutarch notes that Cicero praised himself over the Catiline affair and angered the Romans, while Scipio, facing danger, was honoured instead, so his self-praise drew no envy.

Plutarch says that self-praise fits misfortune better than good times. In prosperity, a person who boasts seems to be chasing fame for its own sake. In hardship, the same boasting looks like a way to strengthen the spirit against bad luck and to avoid seeking pity.

Plutarch says that holding oneself proud and upright is foolish when walking, but admirable in a fight. A person facing hard times who stands up firmly against fate, even with some boasting, seems strong rather than arrogant. That is why Homer shows Patroclus modest in good times but grand in speech at his death.

Phocion, a Greek statesman, faced his execution calmly and rebuked a fellow condemned man who was weeping. Plutarch says a public man who has been wronged may speak up for himself to those who have been ungrateful to him, and gives Achilles as an example of modest self-description.

Plutarch says that open self-defence can include some self-praise. Themistocles, an Athenian statesman, was not guilty of any wrong, yet when the Athenians grew tired of him he reminded them of the favours he had done them, comparing himself to a tree that gives shelter in a storm and is then stripped of its leaves in fine weather.

People who have been wronged may list their good deeds to ungrateful people. A man who is blamed for his good deeds may be excused for praising himself, because he is defending himself, not scolding. Demosthenes did this in his speech On the Crown, boasting of his embassies and decrees after others had criticised them, and people did not tire of it.

Plutarch describes a rhetorical move: answering an accusation by showing that the opposite of the charge is the shameful thing. Lycurgus, accused of bribing a witness, replies that he would be far more likely to have taken money than given it. Cicero, accused of doing more harm as a witness than good as a lawyer, answers that his honesty is greater than his skill with words.

Plutarch cites Demosthenes' own lines, in which the orator praises himself while seeming to defend himself against attacks. He says the speech On the Crown skilfully works his praise into its contrasts and replies to his critics.

A speaker who praises himself can avoid causing envy by also praising his audience. In this speech, the speaker recalls what the Athenians did for the Euboeans, Thebans, Byzantines and Chersonese, and gives himself only a minor role in those deeds.

Plutarch says that a speaker who praises himself can win the listeners' goodwill by first praising their own successes, since they enjoy hearing about what they achieved and then admire the speaker. He gives Epaminondas, a Theban general, as an example. When a critic said he thought more of himself than Agamemnon did, Epaminondas replied that the credit belonged to the Thebans who helped him defeat Sparta.

People dislike hearing a man praise himself, but they gladly accept praise of others. So a speaker may praise someone with the same work and character as himself. The audience then sees that the praise also fits him, and they warm to him.

When someone praises a good person, he often reminds the listeners of his own faults, so they reply that he is no better himself. Alexander praised Hercules and Androcottus praised Alexander, and each ended up praised in return. Dionysius mocked Gelon and so weakened his own authority.

Someone who must praise himself will sound less offensive if he does not claim all the credit. He should give part of it to luck and part to the gods, as Achilles did when he said the gods had granted him the killing of a hero.

Plutarch gives examples of men who avoided envy by crediting luck or the gods for their success. Timoleon honoured Fortune and a Good Genius, Pytho told Athens that a god had done the work, and Sulla always credited Fortune and claimed Aphrodite's protection.

People prefer to blame defeat on luck rather than on the enemy's courage, because blaming luck spares them from admitting their own faults. In the same way, the Locrians liked the laws of Zaleucus because he claimed the goddess Athene gave them to him, so that none of the laws were his own invention.

Plutarch says that a remedy of talking people round is needed only for those who are very bad-tempered or envious. For reasonable people, it is good enough to tone down excessive praise. If someone calls you learned, rich, or powerful, you should ask him to describe you instead as good, harmless, and useful.

A person who praises himself in the right way does not speak of his own merits directly. He lets others give the praise, and he corrects their praise when it is wrongly based. He hides faults behind better qualities and shows how he should be praised. The example is a man who says he did not build walls of stone, but that his defence lies in his soldiers, horses and allies.

Pericles, dying, rebuked his friends for praising his victories and conquests. He said these were shared by many or owed more to luck than to his own skill. His true achievement, he said, was that he had never caused any Athenian to wear mourning.

When praised for a skill, such as speaking well or winning battles, a good man can turn the praise toward his character and his way of life. If someone offers extravagant flattery, he can answer by saying he is not a god, quoting a line from Homer.

Praise that is modest and believable is accepted even by people who would otherwise envy you, while exaggerated praise provokes envy. Kings who avoided claiming divine titles and took only honours that ordinary men might claim, such as being loved by their brothers or mother, did not stir envy in those who honoured them.

People resent those who call themselves wise, but accept those who modestly say they love philosophy and have made some progress. Showy speech-makers who want loud praise get no praise at all, not even mild approval.

Some people soften their self-praise by admitting a small fault, much as a shade dims strong light for weak eyes, so that others are less likely to take offence or envy them. The example is Epeus, who boasts of his boxing skill but adds that he is poor at fighting.

Plutarch says that a man may praise himself gracefully by admitting his own faults, such as forgetfulness, ignorance, or eagerness to learn. He gives Odysseus as an example, who admits he wanted to hear the Sirens and to see the Cyclops, even though it was dangerous.

Plutarch says that admitting small, forgivable faults or humble beginnings, such as one's past poverty, can soften envy when one is praised. He gives the example of Agathocles, who showed guests earthenware pots and said he once made pots and now had golden cups.

Plutarch says there are inner remedies against self-praise, not just outside ones. He gives Cato's reply that he was envied only because he gave up his own affairs and stayed awake at night for his country. He also quotes two lines where the speaker won't boast of past work and still accepts present hardship.

People tend to envy those who gain fame or respect with little effort or for nothing. They do not envy those who earned it through hard work and danger, just as they would not envy someone who bought a house or farm with great labour.

Plutarch argues that praising oneself can be useful when it is meant to inspire others. He gives Nestor as an example: by recounting his own battle deeds, Nestor spurred Patroclus and others to fight Hector. Such example and deed, he says, rouse people and make them believe their goals can be reached.

Sometimes it is acceptable to speak proudly of oneself, in order to check the arrogant and bold who need taming. The speaker gives Nestor, the old hero of Homer's poem, as an example. He says he once mixed with better men than his listeners, and they never looked down on him.

Aristotle told Alexander that rulers of many subjects, and people with correct beliefs about the gods, have good reason to think highly of themselves. The passage also says a line of verse is useful against enemies: "Ill-starred are they whose sons encounter me."

Plutarch gives two examples of sharp replies to rivals: Agesilaus asks how the Persian king is greater than himself unless he is also more just, and Epaminondas remarks that the Spartans have talked longer than usual. He says such remarks suit enemies, while self-praise can also help friends and fellow citizens, humbling the proud or lifting up those who are afraid.

Plutarch gives examples of leaders who boasted in moments of danger. Cyrus did so in battles, though he was not a boaster otherwise. Antigonus, asked about the enemy's larger fleet, replied, "How many do you make me equal to then?" Homer also shows Odysseus reminding his frightened men of his past skill and courage.

In this quotation, a speaker compares his present trouble to the time the Cyclops, a one-eyed giant from Homer's Odyssey, held the speaker's group captive in a cave. He says that even then they escaped, thanks to his own courage, judgement and wit.

Plutarch separates two kinds of self-praise. The kind meant here is not a show for applause, like that of a political speaker or a clever talker. It is a man stating his courage and experience so that his friends can trust him, since a leader's known ability helps keep people safe in a crisis.

Plutarch says a public man should not usually argue against praise given to others. But when false praise is harmful, it is fine to correct it, by showing the difference between real and false worth. He adds that if vice were praised and rewarded with honour, almost no one would resist it.

Praise of bad actions should be opposed, because it encourages people to copy what is shameful. The best way to answer it is to set a true standard beside it, as in the anecdote where making people weep is said to be less noble than making them forget their sorrows.

Plutarch gives three short examples of people boasting in a way that avoids envy. Zeno says his school is smaller but better taught than Theophrastus' larger one. Phocion says his only achievement is that no funeral speeches were needed, since the dead were buried in their family tombs. Crates turns a line about pleasure into one about learning.

Praising oneself, in the right way, is presented here as good and useful. It shows people to value what is worthwhile and practical rather than what is empty and unnecessary. With this, the question under discussion is considered answered.

Plutarch says that the urge to talk about oneself is strong, even in people who seem to want only modest fame. He compares it to illness: just as a healthy person avoids places where sickness is, or takes great care when they must go there, a person should be wary of the times and places where talk about oneself is likely to slip out.

When others are praised, a person who wants fame is stirred to talk about himself. This is worst when the praised person is credited with the same skills, or lesser ones, that the listener thinks he has himself. Like hungry people made hungrier by watching others eat, such people are inflamed into jealousy.

People who tell of their own successes, such as victories, political achievements, or praise from great men, often slip into boasting without meaning to. Plutarch says soldiers and sailors are especially prone to this kind of self-praise.

People who have held high office and then come home often slip their own praise into talk about great men and kings. They think they are only repeating what others have said about them, not praising themselves.

Some people think they avoid seeming boastful when they recount the honours kings and emperors have shown them, as if the listener only hears praise of those rulers. Plutarch warns that one must take care when praising others, so that it does not look like self-praise in disguise, which he calls praising oneself "under pretext of Patroclus."

Talk that mainly criticises and puts others down is risky, because it gives people who want fame a chance to praise themselves. Old men are especially prone to this when they scold others for their faults and so present themselves as the opposite. Still, for old men of good reputation and merit, such fault-finding is allowed, since it can spur the rebuked to strive and to seek honour.
Plutarch warns against praising yourself by criticising others. Such a person seems to seek credit by showing that other people do not deserve it, which annoys listeners and makes them tired of him.

Plutarch advises that people who care a lot about their reputation should avoid praising themselves, especially when others praise them. Like someone ticklish who must guard against being touched, such a person should blush at praise, stop others who praise them too highly, and never scold them for praising too little.

Many people prompt others to praise them, or steer conversation toward their own deeds, so that the praise they get is weakened by their own self-praise. Some do this to inflate themselves, others to draw out praise with a small bait, and others ask questions only to mock the one who answers.

A soldier shows his wound to others, who ask how he got it. When he tells them he was hit by a javelin while climbing a ladder against a wall, they only mock him instead of taking his wound seriously.

Avoid praising yourself, even when others ask questions that invite it. The best protection is to watch others who boast about themselves, since everyone finds that kind of talk unpleasant and tiring.

Plutarch says that listening to someone praise himself does no direct harm, but people find it tiresome and want to escape it. Even flatterers and hangers-on, who depend on the rich, find a rich man's self-praise hard to bear, and they say it is a heavy price to pay for their entertainment.

Plutarch warns against boasting about oneself. Self-praise brings criticism from others, a bad reputation, and weary listeners who will not believe the speaker is what he claims. A person should stop talking about himself unless it clearly benefits himself or those listening.

Plato's Laws says a person may take water from a neighbour's well only after digging down to clay, which holds water and blocks it from seeping through. Those who cannot dig a well of their own are still allowed to use a neighbour's water, because the law should relieve need.

Plutarch suggests that people should first use their own resources, gathering what they need little by little, before borrowing from others. He says that people today, out of luxury and extravagant spending, borrow at high interest even when they have their own means and do not need to.

Lenders, the passage says, do not lend to people who truly need money. They lend only to borrowers who can offer a witness and sufficient security, meaning people who are already well placed and so are not really in need.

Plutarch suggests that instead of borrowing money from bankers, a person should use the household's own cups, dishes and pots. Cheap earthenware is better than borrowed silver, because it carries no interest, which he calls a rust that spoils one's wealth. Calends, the first day of the month, are called hateful because moneylenders' payment dates make them so.

Plutarch says that people who pawn their goods instead of selling them cannot be saved, even by Zeus, because they feel shame about selling but not about paying interest on what they have pawned. He then points to Pericles, who made Athena's gold statue removable so the gold could be used in war and later replaced.

In hard times, Plutarch says, we should not let a lender put his men inside our affairs like an enemy garrison in a besieged town, or let our property fall into his control. Instead we should cut back on luxuries in food, furniture and travel, so we stay free, planning to get those things back later if fortune allows.
Roman women gave their gold and jewellery to the god Apollo at Delphi, and it was made into a golden cup. Carthaginian women cut off their hair to make ropes for war engines defending their city.

Plutarch says people are ashamed to be independent, so they bind themselves to contracts and debts when they should keep only what is useful and cut back or sell extras. Frugality, or living simply and thriftily, is a refuge open to anyone with a sober mind, offering freedom from debt. Artemis's temple at Ephesus once gave debtors shelter from creditors, but this refuge is available to everyone.

Plutarch compares two kinds of freedom. Just as the Athenians gave up their land and houses to flee to their ships, which the Pythian priestess had called "wooden walls," people who want to stay free should accept simple things like a wooden table, plain dishes, and coarse clothes instead of costly goods.

Plutarch warns against borrowing money. He says a borrower should not ride proud horses and chariots, because interest will soon outrun and overtake them. Instead, the borrower is better off on a plain donkey or nag, fleeing the hostile money-lender, who takes away freedom and status.

Whatever you do, the lender acts against you. If you take him to court, he settles on terms. If you swear at him, he bullies you. If you visit him, he shuts the door, and if you stay home, he keeps turning up at your door.

Plutarch asks what good Solon did for Athenians by ending personal bondage for debtors, since debtors still become slaves to their money-lenders. He adds that the lenders' agents are harsh, savage men, like the torturers Plato describes in the underworld.

Moneylenders turn the marketplace into a place of torment for poor debtors. They tear at them like vultures and stand over others to stop them enjoying their own grapes and crops, like Tantalus, the figure in myth who was kept from food and drink.

Moneylenders are compared to invaders. Like the Persian commanders Datis and Artaphernes, who came to Greece bringing chains for captives, they travel through Greek towns carrying loan contracts that act like fetters. Instead of sowing harmless grain as Triptolemus did, they plant debts that spread and choke cities.

Plutarch says hares were said to give birth, nurse, and conceive again all at once. He claims that the debts of money-lenders are worse: they produce interest the moment they are made, so the lender takes back what he has just given and lends it out again as new debt.

Plutarch mocks moneylenders with a proverb about a place name, Pylos, to say that they charge interest on top of interest, and more interest besides. He adds that they ridicule the natural philosophers who say nothing comes from nothing, because they earn interest on money that neither exists nor ever existed.

Plutarch criticizes lenders who see tax-farming as shameful, though it is legal, while they charge interest, which he says is illegal. He calls this fraud, since a borrower who receives less than the amount named in the loan contract is cheated.

The Persians, according to the passage, see debt as a worse wrong than lying, because debt often leads to lying. Moneylenders lie more than others by falsely recording in their account books how much they have lent. Their only motive is greed, which gives them no enjoyment and harms their victims.

Moneylenders, the passage says, do not use the fields, houses or goods they take from debtors. Instead they ruin one debtor after another, and each ruined debtor lures in the next, so the harm spreads like fire.

The money-lender, Plutarch says, profits from others' debts. Over time he reads his account-book to see how many people he has ruined and how his wealth keeps growing. He adds that he is not speaking as an enemy of money-lenders, since they have not harmed him personally.

Plutarch argues that borrowing money is shameful and foolish. If you have money, you have no need to borrow; if you have none, you will never be able to repay. He ends with a story of Cato rebuking an old man for adding wickedness to the troubles of old age.

Plutarch tells the reader not to add the burden of borrowing and debt to the troubles of poverty. Poverty's one advantage over wealth is freedom from anxious worry, and debt would take that away. Taking on a money-lender is like carrying an ox when you cannot carry a goat.

Plutarch argues that a person with two hands, two legs and a tongue can always earn a living by work such as teaching, portering or sailing. These jobs, he says, are less shameful and less hard than constantly being pressed for repayment of a debt.

Rutilius mocked the philosopher Musonius for being in debt, saying the god Zeus does not borrow. Musonius replied that Zeus does not lend either, since Rutilius was a moneylender himself. Plutarch then argues that nature shows the same lesson, since swallows and ants neither borrow nor lend.

Plutarch argues that people are clever enough to keep useful companions such as horses, dogs, partridges and jackdaws, so a debtor should not despair of finding a friend. He suggests winning someone's affection by serving them and defending them, and he points to the many chances on land and sea. The quotation from Crates, a comic poet, shows a couple working hard together to survive hunger.

King Antigonus asked the philosopher Cleanthes whether he still worked at the mill. Cleanthes said he did, to earn a living, but without giving up philosophy. Plutarch admires this, noting that Cleanthes wrote about the gods and the heavens with the same hands that had ground grain, and he adds that people today consider such manual work to be menial.

Plutarch says people borrow money not because they are poor, since no one lends to the poor, but to keep up a lavish lifestyle and appear free. If people were satisfied with bare necessities, moneylenders would vanish, as creatures of myth do. Luxury, he argues, creates moneylenders just as it creates goldsmiths and perfumers.

Plutarch says people do not run into debt for necessities like bread and wine. They borrow for property, slaves, mules, and lavish entertaining, driven by vain ambition. Once in debt, a person stays there, passed from one creditor to the next like a bridled horse, with no way out.

The lines describe water as it moves in a cycle: the sky drives rain into the sea, the sea sends it back to land, the earth gives it up to the sun, and the sun lifts it back into the sky. Plutarch quotes these verses, which describe the water cycle as an endless passing around, in a discussion of borrowing money.

Plutarch says that a debtor who borrows from one lender to repay another only sinks deeper. He compares this to a man stuck in mud who keeps thrashing about, and to a cholera patient who vomits up every medicine, so the illness grows worse.

Debtors never become free of their debt. They pay interest again and again, with pain and worry, and as soon as one bill is settled another creditor presents his own. They should have cleared their debts completely and regained their freedom.

Plutarch argues that rich people who fear giving up their slaves, home and possessions are like a swollen, dropsical patient who fears that treatment will leave him thin. Losing these things, he says, is the cure for being owned by them. He ends with a fable of two vultures, one of which is willing to vomit up what it has eaten.

Plutarch argues that a debtor, once he borrows, is effectively giving up his property to the creditor, since the law makes the creditor its master. He compares this to inherited things: a father leaves land, but also leaves liberty and standing, which matter more. Like a diseased limb, a debt that cannot be kept should be cut off.

Plutarch compares a debtor to Odysseus. Calypso's gift of fine clothes becomes a burden when Odysseus is shipwrecked, so he throws the heavy garment off to swim. In the same way, the closing question suggests that poor debtors face their own storms when a moneylender demands repayment.
In this quotation from a poem, the sea god Poseidon speaks, and clouds gather and the sea rises into fury. Several winds blow together at once to create a storm.

Debt grows like waves, one interest payment piling on the next, until the debtor sinks and drags down the friends who guaranteed his loans. By contrast, Crates of Thebes, who owed nothing, gave up a fortune of eight talents to live as a poor philosopher, weary of household worries.

Plutarch gives examples of men who gave up wealth rather than let it weaken them. The poet Philoxenus received a lot in a Sicilian colony, with a rich house and many comforts. Seeing that luxury and pleasure were the local fashion, he refused to be undone by them, gave up his share, and sailed home.

Debtors, the passage says, must endure being pressed for payment, treated like tribute-payers, and reduced to slavery, and they are compared to Phineus, who was tormented by Harpies. Lenders seize the debtor's future crops and goods before they are grown or ripe, buying up wine and oil in advance on loan.

Plutarch is mocking a saying that tells people to avoid seeking glory. He argues that the man who said it did so to make himself look wise and win undeserved fame. He adds the line "I hate the wise man for himself not wise," which means that he dislikes a man who is wise only in his own eyes.

Plutarch tells of two greedy men who spoiled dishes others were eating so they alone could eat the best food. He compares this to people who crave glory and run down glory to their rivals, so that they can win it with no one competing against them.

Plutarch compares writers of moral advice to rowers who face backward while moving forward. Such writers seek fame while appearing to reject it. He asks why someone who wanted to be unknown would write down a rule and pass it on to future generations.

Plutarch is saying that the advice "live unknown" sounds like a bad motive, as if one were hiding a crime. He argues that a person should either reform and be seen doing good, or, if the person is wicked, change their ways instead of hiding. He adds that telling a sick, confused person to stay unseen is no help.

Plutarch argues that a person should not hide a vice or a fault from friends who could help. He compares this to a sick person hiding an illness from the doctor. He notes that in early times the sick were openly discussed, and people shared what they had learned from curing similar illnesses, which is how medicine grew.

Plutarch says that people should openly expose their faults and emotional weaknesses, such as anger, jealousy and love, and examine them, warning themselves about each one. He observes that people today deny and hide their vices, which only makes them more deeply rooted.

Plutarch is arguing against the idea that a good man should keep quiet and stay out of public life. He makes the point by listing famous figures and asking whether they should have been told to avoid their great deeds: Epaminondas not to be a general, Lycurgus not to make laws, Socrates not to teach by discussion.

Plutarch is mocking Epicurus for ignoring his own advice. Epicurus told his followers to avoid public life, crowds and showy display, yet he wrote letters and books to many people, took in outsiders, kept a large circle of friends and youths, and gave detailed instructions for his funeral. Plutarch asks what these habits mean.

Plutarch asks why anyone would write thousands of lines about minor figures such as Metrodorus, Aristobulus and Chaeredemus, so they will not be forgotten after death. He argues that this makes little sense if virtue, art, philosophy and success are all meant to be forgotten or left unremembered.

Plutarch argues that if someone hides all knowledge of how they live, as one puts out the lights at a dinner party, so they can move from pleasure to pleasure unseen, then that is a way of living unknown. He says such a life, devoted to physical pleasure and rejecting virtue, needs darkness and forgetfulness, which is why it is right that they are hidden.

Plutarch argues that a man who teaches and defends the gods, justice, law and the constitution should not stay unknown, because being known lets him teach others and set a good example. He points to Themistocles and Camillus, whose public fame helped save Athens and Rome.

Plutarch argues that knowledge does more than bring fame: it makes a person's virtue useful to others. He gives two examples. Dion's study of Plato helped free Sicily, and Epaminondas only helped Thebes and Greece once his merits were known and he gained power.

Plutarch argues that a man who stays out of public affairs and lives quietly in obscurity becomes dull and useless. Just as still, enclosed water goes foul without an outlet, a life of leisure with no activity or influence wears down both body and soul, and its natural abilities waste away.

At night the body grows tired, the mind goes dim, and a person seems barely alive, troubled by confused dreams. At sunrise, light drives these dreams away and wakes people to their daily work, so they set out to their tasks eagerly.

Plutarch argues that people are meant to come to know one another. We enter the world unknown and become known as we grow up and mix with others. He adds that being comes before knowledge: things exist first, and knowing them only reveals what already is. Death, similarly, is not non-existence but the state of becoming obscure.

Plutarch's passage explains names for gods and for humans. The Sun is called Apollo, with the names Delius and Pythius, while the lord of the underworld is called Hades, a place we go into when we die. Humans are said to be named for light, because all people have a strong desire to know and be known.

Some philosophers believe the soul is itself light by nature. They support this by noting that the soul dislikes ignorance and darkness, which cause it fear and doubt, and that it enjoys light so much that nothing pleasant feels enjoyable without it.
A man who hides himself away, cutting himself off from public life, is compared to someone who rejects the life he was born into. Such a man is said to refuse his own existence.
Pindar, an ancient Greek poet, describes the afterlife of the blessed as a bright, flowery meadow with shady trees. There, the blessed spend their time in pleasant talk about past and present.

Plutarch describes a third fate after death, for people who lived wicked and lawless lives. Their souls sink into a dark underworld, where they are punished and then covered by forgetfulness. The image of vultures eating the liver of such people is said to fail, since the liver is gone by then, burned or rolled away.

The passage says the dead have no body left to feel punishment. For people who lived badly, the real punishment is disgrace, being forgotten, and being completely wiped out, sinking into forgetfulness and emptiness.
Good speeches to someone in trouble should comfort him, not simply agree with his sadness. Many who try to help make things worse, like poor swimmers who drag a drowning man down with them.

When someone is in trouble, Plutarch says, they do not need others to wail along with them like a tragic chorus. They need plain speech showing that grief is useless, and that when reason looks at the facts, the trouble is often greater in imagination than in fact. Asking other people to tell you how you feel is foolish; you should ask your own body and mind.

Misfortunes feel heavy partly because of how we judge them, not only because of what they are. A stone is hard and ice is cold by their own nature, but exile, loss of reputation, or loss of honours get their weight from our opinion of them. So each person makes his troubles light or heavy for himself.

Alcman, a Greek poet, imagines that if he had grown up in Sardis he would have been a priest of Cybele dressed in gold. Instead, as a Spartan who writes poetry, he counts himself greater than rich kings. Plutarch uses this to say that one thing can be valued highly by one person and judged worthless or harmful by another, just as coins are accepted or rejected.

Plutarch grants, for the sake of argument, that exile is a painful thing. He then compares it to bitter food, which is made easier to bear by mixing in something sweet, and to harsh colours, which are softened by balance. The point is that hard things can be made easier to bear.

When the eye is strained by bright light, it can be eased by shade or by looking at green. In the same way, a person in trouble can ease it by setting against it the good things still left, such as wealth, friends, leisure, and enough to live on.

Plutarch says that many people from Sardis would prefer the addressee's way of life, even with exile, living as a stranger in a foreign land. They would not want to stay at home in comfort, which he compares to snails that have no home except their shells.

The speaker says that, like a comic character who answers "as a philosopher" when asked how to bear misfortune, we should face bad luck bravely. He compares this to everyday sense: when it rains or the wind blows, we go indoors or put on a coat instead of sitting in the rain and weeping.

Plutarch says that a person can lift their own spirits in hard times by making sensible use of the advantages they already have, without needing outside help. He compares this to a surgeon's cupping-glasses, which draw out harmful fluids to save the rest of the body. Gloomy, complaining people do the opposite: they dwell only on their worst troubles, so even useful things stop helping them.

Plutarch says that the two jars of fortune in Homer are not handled by Zeus, who gives out good and bad in fixed portions. People decide for themselves how much good or bad they receive. Wise people ease their troubles by remembering their blessings, while most people hold on to misfortunes and let good things slip away.

When real trouble comes, Plutarch says we should find comfort in the good things still left to us. Things that are bad only in our imagination should be handled like frightening masks shown to children: examined closely until they lose their power, so that reason shows how empty and exaggerated our fears are.

Plutarch argues that no place, such as a country, house or field, belongs to anyone by nature. Such things get their name from the person who lives in or owns them. He adds that a human being is not an earthbound plant but a heavenly one, and he quotes Hercules saying that all of Greece is his country.

Socrates said he was not just an Athenian or a Greek but a citizen of the world. He did not limit himself to particular places in Greece, and he quoted lines about the sky above and the earth below it.

Plutarch describes a single shared country that belongs to everyone, with no outsiders or foreigners in it. Its common features are the same elements, the same heavenly bodies, seasons and laws, all governed by one god who guides everything according to nature. Justice follows this god to punish wrongdoing, and people naturally call on Justice when dealing with one another.

Plutarch argues that living away from one's home city is not a real problem. He notes that many Athenians, Corinthians and Spartans never lived in the central parts of their own cities, and that Athenians who moved to a new district still treated it as home and celebrated their move with a festival.

The argument is that no place on earth is really far from another, because the whole earth looks like a point next to the heavens, according to mathematicians. People who feel lost when exiled are compared to ants or bees driven from their nest. The writer says we should learn to see all things as our own, since they really are.

Plutarch says we mock someone who claims the moon shines brighter in Athens than in Corinth, yet we behave the same way ourselves. In a foreign land we look at earth, sea, air and sky as if they might differ from what we knew at home. Nature leaves us free, but we confine ourselves to a small, narrow space.

We mock the Persian kings, who (so the story goes) drink only from the river Choaspes and leave the rest of the world without water for themselves. Yet when we travel, we crave the waters of our own home rivers, so we make the whole world feel like no home to us.

Some Egyptians had fled to Ethiopia to escape their angry king. When men asked them to come back to their wives and children, they refused and shamelessly displayed their bodies, saying they would never lack wives or children while they had what they showed.

Plutarch says that a person who has the basic necessities of life is never a stranger or without a home, as long as he also has good sense and judgment. These qualities act like an anchor and a rudder, letting him settle safely in any harbour.

A person who has lost his wealth cannot easily get another fortune quickly. But a wise man can make any city his home and grow prosperous there, as Themistocles and Demetrius of Phalerum did after being exiled. Demetrius, for example, became a close friend of Ptolemy in Alexandria and even sent gifts back to Athens.

Themistocles, an Athenian who had been exiled and was supported by the Persian king, supposedly said that his family would have been ruined had they not been ruined, meaning that their downfall brought the good fortune of the king's favour. Diogenes, told that his home city had banished him, answered that he had banished them to stay where they were.

Stratonicus, visiting the island of Seriphus, joked to his host that exile was the punishment for rogues, so the host must be a rogue too, since he lived there and wanted to leave. He added that the island is so poor it barely has food.

Plutarch argues that a person with one city is like a stranger everywhere else, since it is not fair to leave his own city for another. He says a man must make the best of his native city, even if it is poor or troubled. Only someone who has lost his city is free to settle wherever he likes.

Plutarch says it is sensible to choose a pleasant city, because in time it will feel like home. Such a place spares a man the duties of a citizen, such as paying money, serving on embassies to Rome, or entertaining officials. He adds that a sane person would rather live in exile on a barren island than endure these burdens.

Philip, after being thrown in a wrestling match, looked at the outline his body left in the dust and remarked that he owned only a small part of the earth by nature, though he wanted the whole world. The point is that greed for more land is never satisfied, since even a king's natural share is small.

Plutarch's speaker mentions several places tied to old myths: Naxos, Hyria, and a silted-up spot near the Achelous river. He suggests that Alcmaeon settled there not to escape the Furies of myth but to live quietly, away from political unrest and informers.

Plutarch says that the emperor Tiberius spent his last seven years on the island of Capri, and that the power of ruling stayed with him there the whole time. Still, the constant cares of the empire, reaching him from every side, meant that the island never gave him the calm and complete rest he hoped for.

A man who can escape to a small island and leave his great troubles behind is unhappy if he cannot often repeat to himself Pindar's lines about loving a quiet life on a small plot of land, free from sorrow and political quarrels. These lines are set against the duties of princes, public office and state business that are hard to escape.

Plutarch argues that size does not decide whether a life is good. He says that wisdom is not measured in Persian ropes, a long unit of distance, so happiness should not be measured in land area either. A small island is not a reason for misery, and a large field does not guarantee an easy life.

Plutarch quotes two lines of verse about loss of fortune, saying that a man's wealth has fallen and he should not value worldly things too highly. He then gives the example of Nausithous, who left his home city because of hostile neighbours and lived alone on a remote island, away from other people.

The Cyclades, a group of Greek islands, are shown as pleasant places. They were settled by notable families, and people who think exile there is a punishment are mistaken. Xenophon, after his soldiering, lived a comfortable old age on Scillus, which is no smaller than the islands used for exile.

The passage describes the Academy, a modest school near Athens where Plato and his successors taught and lived. It then recalls a jibe that Aristotle preferred the royal courts of Macedon, with their river Borborus, to the Academy. The ending is a random line of Homeric verse with stuttering "and"s, so it seems to be a broken or unfinished piece.

The passage lists famous men who lived on islands, as named by a writer. Each is given one quality: Aeolus is loved by the gods, Odysseus is the wisest, Ajax the bravest, and Alcinous the most generous to strangers. Aeolus, Odysseus, Ajax and Alcinous are heroes from Homer's poems.

Zeno, a Greek philosopher, lost his last ship and all its cargo at sea, and he thanked fortune for leaving him only a plain cloak and a philosopher's simple life. Plutarch argues that a sensible person could likewise be glad of a quiet life on a small island, free from travel, danger, and the noise of public business, with everything needed close at hand.

Plutarch describes an island retreat where a person can live in quiet, free from the pressures of city life. Nobody there demands money, asks for loans or surety, or calls them to court, and only close friends visit. For anyone who wants a life of leisure, it is a kind of peaceful retirement.

Plutarch argues that people who constantly travel, living in inns and on ferries, are not happier than those who stay put, just as wandering planets are not happier than the fixed stars. He points to Heraclitus, who said the sun keeps to its fixed course, and suggests this kind of reasoning be offered to people who are exiled to an island and cut off from others.

Plutarch is listing reasons a man might give for not having to bother with public life: he holds no office, belongs to no faction, and need not court officials. He compares this to the poet Archilochus, who praised nothing about the fertile island of Thasos and only described its rocky, uneven ground.

People look only at the shame of exile and miss its freedom from worry, its leisure and its liberty. Yet people thought the Persian kings were happy, even though they moved between cities with each season.

The passage asks whether an exile, a person banished from his home city, can still attend the great Greek religious festivals and athletic games. It lists the Eleusinian mysteries, the Dionysia at Athens, and the games at Nemea, Delphi, Isthmia and Corinth, and suggests he could travel to them as a spectator if he enjoys sightseeing.

Plutarch describes a man who owes no money and so is free to rest, walk, read and sleep undisturbed. He can say, like the philosopher Diogenes, that he eats when he chooses, unlike Aristotle, who had to dine when King Philip wished.

Plutarch observes that many of the wisest men did not die in their homelands but voluntarily moved elsewhere, some to Athens and some away from it. He notes that no one has praised their own country as highly as the playwright Euripides did in the lines he then quotes.

The speaker boasts that Athenians are native to their land, not moved in from elsewhere like pieces on a draughts board. He says the city has a mild climate and good goods from Greece and Asia. Plutarch then points out that the poet who wrote these lines moved to Macedonia and spent his later years at the court of King Archelaus, which undercuts the boast.

Plutarch notes that several famous writers moved to other places or were claimed by many cities. Herodotus is said to have moved to Thurii, so some changed his title to "of Thurii," and Homer was claimed by many cities because he praised no single one.

Plutarch says that if someone claims these men sought glory and honour, one should look at the philosophers and their schools. He then lists the founders and leading figures of several Greek schools by their birthplaces, such as Aristotle of Stagira and Zeno of Cittium.

Some Stoic teachers, including the Athenian Archidemus, left Greece for Parthia and Babylon, and no one forced them to go. They went to find quiet, which a famous or powerful person rarely finds at home, so their own lives showed a lesson that their teaching only described.

Many distinguished people, Plutarch says, choose to live abroad of their own free will, to escape business, worries and the lack of leisure that home would bring. He suggests that the Muses helped older writers finish their best works by making exile a kind of helper.

Plutarch lists several Greek historians and writers and the places where each one wrote their work. Thucydides wrote his history of the Peloponnesian War in Thrace, Xenophon wrote in Elis, and the others wrote in Epirus, Athens, Megara and Peloponnesus.

Many famous men were exiled from their homes, yet they did not lose hope or sink into sadness. They saw exile as an opportunity that chance had given them, and it won them lasting fame after death. Those who exiled them are not remembered at all.

Plutarch argues that exile does not bring shame, so anyone who thinks it does is foolish. He gives two examples: Diogenes, the philosopher who lived with almost nothing, and Camillus, the Roman leader who was banished yet is now remembered as a second founder of Rome.

Plutarch argues that exile did not diminish famous men like Themistocles, who gained more fame abroad. He says no one would choose to be the accusers who drove such men out instead of being the exiled men themselves. He then notes that many people are swayed by Euripides' lines attacking exile, and proposes to examine what those lines say.

Keeping quiet about everything you think is not the mark of a slave, Plutarch argues, but of a sensible person. Some times and matters call for silence, and he supports this with a line from the playwright Euripides: "Be silent where 'tis meet, speak where 'tis safe."

The passage argues that a king who takes away an exile's freedom of speech makes a great mistake. As proof, it tells how Theodorus, an exile, answered King Lysimachus, who asked whether his own city had expelled him for his bad character. Theodorus replied yes, comparing it to Semele casting out Dionysus, her son, because she could no longer bear him.

Plutarch gives examples of people who spoke frankly to rulers. A king shows a captive, Telesphorus, mutilated in a cage, as a warning to others. Diogenes calls Philip's ambitions foolish when Philip is about to risk his kingdom and life in battle. Hannibal, an exile, speaks boldly to the king Antiochus.

Hannibal rebukes a seer who advised against an attack because the animal entrails said no, telling him to trust experienced judgment over omens. Plutarch then argues that exiles lose none of their freedom to speak, since teachers of geometry and grammar keep speaking freely; he says only meanness silences a person.

Plutarch argues that the real fault lies in folly, not in exile itself. People who keep waiting for the future and hoping for what they lack never really live in the present, even when they seem to be moving forward. He illustrates this with a short exchange from a play, where Polynices answers that friends and noble birth bring no help in need.

Plutarch argues that Polynices was ungrateful to complain about exile, since his noble birth had won him a royal bride and friends who joined his fight. He also says his mother Jocasta's complaint about her son's marriage was unjustified.

The speaker says a mother should have been glad that her son lived in a fine palace at Argos. Instead she mourned the missing wedding rites and blamed exile for troubles that were really caused by her own pride and foolishness.

Plutarch argues that exile is not shameful in itself. Only foolish people mock exiles, just as they mock beggars and the bald or short. Sensible people respect good men even when they are poor, foreign, or exiled, as people honour Theseus's temple along with the famous temples of Athens.

Plutarch points out that several famous Greek figures were exiles or migrants, yet they were still honored. Theseus was banished from Athens, a city he had founded, and Eumolpus came from Thrace to bring the mysteries to Greece. Codrus, a king of Athens, was the son of Melanthus, who had been exiled from Messene.

Plutarch gives two examples of witty replies to insults about a person's origins. Antisthenes, told his mother was a Phrygian (from Phrygia, a region in Asia Minor), replied that the mother of the gods was also a Phrygian. Asked whether he should answer an insult about exile, Plutarch suggests pointing out that Hercules' father was also an exile.

Plutarch recalls several myths about gods and heroes who left home or were driven out. Cadmus, the Phoenician, left his homeland to search for Europa and settled in Thebes, where he became the ancestor of Dionysus. He then turns to a line by Aeschylus that hints, in an obscure way, that Apollo was an exile from heaven.

Empedocles says that a person who commits murder is punished by spirits and wanders away from the gods for thirty thousand years. He himself is such an exile. Plutarch uses these words to say that all people are strangers and exiles in this world.

The speaker says the soul does not come from blood or a mixed spirit, and that its beginning is not the body, which is made of earth and mortal. Plutarch's point is that calling the soul's arrival from elsewhere a "living in a strange country" is a deceptively gentle way of putting it.

Plutarch says the soul is an exile, pushed around by divine decrees, and it is joined to the body the way an oyster is joined to its shell. It has forgotten the high happiness it came from, and it came from heaven and the moon, not from one earthly city to another. So even a short move on earth makes it feel strange and fade like a dying plant.

A person's happiness, virtue and good sense do not depend on their surroundings, even though a place may suit some people better than others. Anaxagoras worked on his mathematics in prison, and Socrates kept philosophizing and was still thought happy after drinking poison. Phaethon and Tantalus rose high but fell into ruin because of their own folly.

Plutarch quotes the saying that fortune, not wisdom, governs human affairs, and then argues against it. He asks whether justice, fairness, self-control and proper conduct govern human affairs instead. His examples are men whose choices, not luck, decided their outcomes: Aristides refused wealth, Scipio took no spoil, and Philocrates and others lost their cities through greed.

Plutarch asks whether Alexander's self-control and his punishing of others who abused captive women were due to luck. He also asks whether Paris's seduction of his host's wife and the war it caused were due to luck. If all such conduct is due to luck, he argues, then animals' greed and lust would be too.

Plutarch argues that if virtues like self-control, justice and courage exist, then prudence must exist, and so must wisdom. He says these virtues are forms of prudence or depend on it, and that prudence applied to pleasure, danger and dealings with others gets called by different names.

Plutarch argues against the idea that fortune, or luck, controls human life. If we credit fortune with wise acts, he says, we must also credit it with theft and other vices, and then give up reasoning altogether. He adds that if wisdom does not exist, then careful thought and searching for what is useful make no sense either.

Plutarch's point is that if everything depends on luck, then human learning, the advice of city councils and royal advisers, and all planning would have no value. He says people wrongly call Fortune blind when they are themselves blind, since they reject wisdom and let a blind guide steer their lives.

Plutarch argues that it would be absurd to say that seeing and hearing come from luck rather than from the eyes and ears themselves. He says nature gave us our senses as tools for wisdom and good judgment.

Plutarch argues that the mind, or reason, is what makes humans superior to animals, not luck or chance. Without reason, he says, our senses would be of little use, just as the stars would be lost in darkness without the sun. Reason, which he calls Prometheus, is what gives people control over tame animals such as bulls, horses and asses.
Many animals are naturally better equipped than humans. Some have horns, tusks, or stings, others have scales, fur, or tough hooves, while humans are born without any such natural protection.

Plutarch says that humans lack great physical strength, speed or courage, but make up for this with reason, effort and foresight. Because of this intelligence, people can control animals that are stronger or faster than they are, such as horses and dogs.

Plutarch argues that humans rule over other creatures through reason, not through physical strength. Fish and pigs are eaten, and the huge elephant is made to perform for people, which shows how far reason lifts humans above animals. The closing lines admit that people are not strong or fast, so reason is their real advantage.

Humans are weaker than animals in several ways, but they use their experience, memory, wisdom and cunning to get honey and milk from animals, catch them, and control them. The author says none of this comes from luck; it comes from reason and foresight.

Plutarch argues that skilled trades such as carpentry, metalwork, building and sculpture succeed through skill, not luck or chance. He supports this with a line from a poet about craftsmen, who honour the goddess Ergane, a patron of crafts.

The passage says that craftsmen credit their skill, not luck, with their success. It then tells a story about the painter Nealces, who tried to remove some foam from a painted horse's bridle. In anger he threw his sponge at the picture, and by chance the splash made the foam look just as he wanted. The writer calls this the only lucky accident in art that history records.

Craftsmen use rules, weights and measures so their work is never done at random. The arts, the passage says, are small pieces of wisdom spread through everyday life, much as the fire of Prometheus was said to be split up and scattered across the world.

Plutarch argues that ordinary skills such as music, cooking, cleaning clothes, and even good manners need careful training and effort, not luck. He finds it odd that wisdom, the most important art, is said to depend on fortune, which he treats as having no power over it.

Plutarch asks whether the most important things for a happy life can really come about without wisdom, reason and planning. He points out that no one makes bricks by pouring water on earth and leaving it to chance, and no one makes clothes or shoes by simply praying to Fortune for them.

Plutarch says that wealth, slaves and fine furniture do not bring happiness by themselves, unless the owner is also wise. He illustrates this with the Athenian general Iphicrates, who answered a man who mocked him for being neither a soldier nor an archer. Iphicrates said he was the one who commanded and used all those things.

Wisdom is not any of the goods people usually prize, such as gold, fame, health or beauty. It is the thing that makes these goods useful and pleasant when a person has them, and without which they bring harm. The writer adds that Prometheus advised his brother Epimetheus to refuse gifts from Zeus, meaning gifts of outside fortune.

The passage says that a wise adviser would warn a foolish person against seeking office, wealth, or marriage, just as one would warn an untrained person against playing an instrument or riding a horse. Good fortune beyond a person's worth harms those who lack sense, since it makes fools more foolish and the unwise more unfortunate.

The speaker tells a seeker that God is not in any particular place or practice: not in temples, mosques, the Kaaba, Mount Kailash, rituals, or yoga and renunciation. God is close at hand, and a sincere seeker will find God quickly. God is described as the breath within every breath.

Asking what caste a holy person belongs to is pointless, the poem says. Priests, warriors, traders, barbers, washerwomen and carpenters all seek God alike, and so did the named saints Raidas and Swapacha, who came from low castes. Hindus and Muslims also reach the same goal, where no marks of difference remain.

Kabir urges the listener to seek God, know him, and understand him while still alive, because liberation is possible only in this life. Freedom from the bonds of the self cannot be expected after death, since union with God is not gained simply by leaving the body. The final line says that the inner drive to seek is what helps, and Kabir calls himself its servant.

The speaker tells a friend not to look for a garden of flowers outside, because the garden is inside the body. There, sitting on the thousand-petalled lotus, one can see the Infinite Beauty, meaning God.

The speaker asks how to give up Maya, the illusion of the material world. Each time he drops one attachment, another stays behind: giving up ribbons still leaves the garment, giving up passion leaves anger, and so on. Even the detached mind still clings to the letter, meaning outward forms. The true path is rarely found.

The main point is that the divine is already within a person, but people fail to notice it. The moon, sun and cosmic drum are inside the body, yet the blind eyes and deaf ears miss them. Work and ego-attachment are only means: they end once true knowledge comes, as the flower falls when the fruit forms and the deer searches outside for musk it carries itself.

The poem says that the unseen Supreme Being shows itself through all things. It compares this to a seed in a plant, shade in a tree, and void in the sky. The creature and the Supreme are described as distinct yet united, and the Supreme is said to be both limited and limitless.

The poem says that the whole of creation, including the Creator, is found inside the human body, which it calls an "earthen vessel." It names the seven oceans, the stars, the touchstone and the jeweller who tests it, and the eternal sound and spring. Kabir ends by saying his beloved Lord is within.

The speaker says God cannot be fully described. Saying God is inside me is wrong, and saying God is outside me is also wrong, because God is both at once and beyond both. God is neither clearly seen nor hidden, and no words can say what God is.

The speaker says that a holy teacher, called "Fakir" (a Muslim or Sufi religious wanderer, here used as a title for the divine), has drawn his love toward him. He says the teacher woke him from sleep, saved him from drowning in worldly life, and, with a single word, freed him from his bonds. The poem ends with the speaker saying the teacher's heart has joined with his own.

The speaker once played carelessly with friends, but now feels afraid as they approach their Lord's high palace. Still, they must not be shy and must open their whole heart and body to meet Him in love. Kabir adds that only a true lover understands this, and that outward adornment means nothing without real longing for the Beloved.

A speaker addresses a swan, asking where it comes from, where it is going, and what it seeks. The speaker invites it to follow to a land without doubt, sorrow or the fear of death, where the spirit is absorbed in a sense of oneness with the divine and wants no other joy.

Kabir says that people worship a god they have made in their own minds, and that no one seeks the true, perfect God. He argues that the incarnations (Avatars) cannot be the Infinite, since they suffer the results of their actions. Religious teachers argue among themselves, but Kabir says that whoever has seen the radiance of love is saved.

The main point is that a wave and the river are the same water, so a name does not make a wave separate from the water it is made of. In the same way, the many worlds are said to be strung within the one Supreme Brahma, like beads on a rosary. The poem asks the reader to see this with wisdom.

The poem describes a place of spiritual peace where a kind of music sounds on its own and light flows in every direction. Many gods and holy beings are there, and the poet says his Lord is revealed in that place. Few people are able to reach it.

The poem describes the mind as a swing moving between conscious and unconscious states. All beings, worlds, the sun, the moon and the elements hang on this swing and keep moving through endless ages. Seeing this, the poet says he has become a servant of the Lord, who is himself taking form in this motion.

Kabir describes the whole universe as a continuous act of worship, with sun, moon, stars and lightning all joining in a song of love for God, whom he calls the Beloved. He adds that few people truly know this Beloved, while the devout seeker is one who combines love with detachment from the world.
