The passage describes a spiritual inner experience. The heart is like a holy river and a lotus that blooms without water, and the heart's bee drinks its nectar. Those who turn inward find a joy that ends the cycle of birth and death. Kabir urges the listener to dive into this ocean of sweetness.

The speaker describes a state beyond the ordinary world, reached by looking inward. There the senses are satisfied, suffering ends, and life and death are seen as one. Light, music and love fill everything, and opposites such as left and right become the same.

The speaker says the highest truth cannot be learned from scriptures or books. He claims to have reached it through inner meditation, reaching a "sorrowless land" by no ordinary road. He adds that this land is beyond merit, and that only the wise can see it and describe it. Even so, its full taste cannot be put into words.

The passage describes a state of spiritual joy that comes from loving devotion. Once a person has tasted it, the ignorant become wise and the wise fall silent, and the worshipper is filled with ecstasy. Kabir says that merging one's life into the divine "Ocean of Life" brings true bliss.

The speaker, having cast off false show, describes a state of freedom from fear and from the errors of life and death. In this state there is music, joy, and no sorrow, and day and night seem one. Kabir says he has seen the play of one Bliss and has escaped the error of the world.

The speaker feels that inner and outer, the infinite and the finite, have become one. He is overwhelmed by seeing this unity, which he calls the Light that fills the universe. In this state, Kabir says, error cannot enter and the struggle between life and death is no longer felt.

Kabir describes a radiant realm in the middle of the sky, where the divine Lord takes delight. His body shines so brightly that the light of countless suns and moons is outshone, and in a city on that shore nectar rains without end. He invites Dharmadas to come and see the Lord's court.

The speaker calls on the heart to wake up, because the Supreme Spirit, the great Master, is close by. The Beloved, the speaker's Lord, is standing near the head, so the heart should hurry to his feet. The heart has slept for countless ages and is asked whether it will wake this morning.

Kabir asks where the heart could cross to, since that far shore has no road, boat, earth, sky or time. Nothing there can satisfy the soul's thirst. He tells the heart to stay within its own body, where it stands firm, and to drop its imaginings.

Kabir says that the divine is already present in every person's life, but people fail to see it. He criticizes seeking God through rituals, priests, stone idols, yoga, and counting prayer beads. In his view, God is near and sweet, and none of these outward practices count for much with Him.

The speaker longs for a true teacher (Guru) who first drinks the cup of love himself and then offers it to him. Such a teacher removes the veil from the eyes, reveals the divine, makes the speaker hear the inner music, and shows that joy and sorrow are one. The speaker says that whoever has such a teacher has no fear.

Evening darkness has settled over body and mind, and the speaker invites the reader to open the window to the west, enter the sky of love, and drink the honey of the heart's lotus. Kabir concludes that the Lord is present within the body.

The speaker treasures above all a love that lets him live without limits in this world. Like a lotus that blooms in water without being wetted by it, he stays untouched by the world while living in it. Like a wife who enters fire for love, he accepts pain without betraying love. The world is a deep ocean that few have crossed.

The speaker says that God sometimes hides and sometimes shows himself in surprising ways. God also brings both sorrow and joy, and resolves the conflict between them. The speaker vows to give up body, mind and life, but will never forget God.

God is described as formless and beyond decay, yet appearing in countless forms to his creatures. All things come from him, and people are urged to seek union with him. His joy stirs waves of form, and he holds everything within his bliss.

The speaker says that a true Guru (a spiritual teacher) has taught him to know what cannot normally be known. Through this teaching he does things that seem impossible, such as walking without feet, seeing without eyes, and tasting without eating. He ends by saying that the Guru is beyond words and that the disciple is fortunate.
Before the Unconditioned, the Conditioned dances and declares that "Thou and I are one." The passage says that the teacher bows down to the student, and calls this the greatest wonder.

Kabir answers Gorakhnath that his spiritual calling began before the world, before any teacher or student, and before the gods Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva came into being. He says he was taught by Ramananda in Benares and now longs to unite with the Infinite, the One God, in simplicity.

The poet describes an unseen bird that sings inside him. It has no colour or shape, rests in the shade of love, and comes and goes unnoticed. He says the mystery is deep and asks wise people to find out where it rests.

The speaker is in deep longing for her Beloved, so she can neither sleep nor find comfort in her father's house. When the sky opens and the temple is revealed, she meets her husband (the Beloved, meaning God) and gives him her body and mind.

The speaker calls on the heart to dance with joy, because love's music fills all days and nights. Life, death, hills, sea, and the human world all move to this rhythm. The speaker asks why one should wear a monk's robe and live apart from the world in proud isolation, and says the heart delights in many arts while the Creator is pleased.

When love has filled the heart, words are no longer needed. The speaker compares this to a diamond kept safely wrapped, a balance that has tipped fully, and a swan that has reached its lake. Kabir concludes that God dwells within the believer, so outward seeing is unnecessary, and union with God has already happened.

The speaker asks how the love between himself and God could ever be broken. He compares it to a lotus leaf that stays on the water, and to a bird that gazes at the moon all night. He says this love has existed since the beginning of time and can never be put out, and that his heart joins with God as a river joins the ocean.

The speaker longs for the Beloved, God, and feels grieved and restless without Him. They feel ashamed to be called His bride, because their heart has not yet truly reached His heart. They ask who will carry their message to Him, and the speaker says they are dying to see Him.

The speaker urges a neglectful soul to wake up before her life is wasted. Others who woke have gained treasure, while she slept, played foolishly, and missed her divine husband, who has already left. Only the one whose heart is struck by the call of God's music truly wakes.

Light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, love and lust cannot exist together; one drives out the other. The speaker therefore urges a fight against passion, anger, pride and greed inside the body, carried on until death, so that the fighter can stand before the King.

Kabir compares the spiritual seeker to a soldier in a battle fought with the sword of God's Name. He says the seeker's struggle is harder than a warrior's or a widow's sacrifice, because a warrior fights only for hours and a widow's ordeal ends quickly. The seeker's battle lasts day and night for as long as life lasts.
A lock of error keeps the gate shut, and love is the key that opens it. Once the door is opened, the Beloved, meaning God, can be woken, and the speaker urges the listener not to miss this chance.

The body is compared to a lyre, an instrument with strings, and God (called Brahma here) is the player. God tightens the strings to draw out music. When the strings break and the instrument wears out, it turns to dust, and only Brahma can make it sound.

Kabir says that a person should not leave ordinary home life to wander in the forest seeking God. Home is where true union and enjoyment of life are found, and whoever can lead others back home, or find truth within it, is dear to him. He concludes that one should stay where one is, and all things will come in time.

The speaker says that since meeting the Lord, love for him has become a constant joy. Without closing eyes, ears, or punishing the body, he sees God everywhere, and every act, word, and sight becomes a form of worship. He feels united with God beyond all pleasure and pain.

Kabir says that holy bathing places contain only water, which he knows is useless because he has bathed in them. He says idols cannot speak, since he has cried out to them. He says the Puranas and the Koran are only words, and that he has seen past them through direct experience. He holds that only this experience is true.

The speaker finds it funny that a fish in water would be thirsty. In the same way, people look for the Real far away, when it is in their own home. He says that without finding one's own soul, the world seems unreal, wherever one travels, even to holy cities like Benares or Mathura.

Kabir describes a hidden divine presence in the sky, a temple with a blue canopy lit by sun and moon. He tells the listener to quiet the mind before this splendour. He says that whoever has tasted this nectar of spiritual joy behaves like a madman, wandering in ecstasy.

The speaker asks where the divine comes from and how it acts in the world, using the image of fire hidden in wood that is suddenly awakened and then vanishes. He says the true guru teaches that the divine has no limit or end. Kabir concludes that the Supreme God adapts his speech to whatever the listener can understand.

Kabir tells the spiritual seeker (sadhu) to purify the body simply. He says everything, including the elements and the body itself, is contained within the divine and within the soul, much as a tree is contained within its seed. He ends by saying the Word, the Truth, is the essence of the self, and God is both speaker and creator.

A strange tree with no roots, branches or leaves bears fruit, and two birds sit in it: a teacher and a student. The student tastes the many fruits of life while the teacher watches with joy. The closing lines say the formless is found within all forms, and the singer praises those forms.

The speaker has calmed a restless mind and found a joyful heart. Through a spiritual insight, he has seen past ordinary distinctions and found the divine Comrade even among other people. Although bound in ordinary life, he says he has freed himself from narrowness and reached the unreachable through love.

The speaker says the visible world is not the true reality, and that the true reality cannot be fully put into words. Some people worship the formless and others worship visible forms, but the wise see that the divine is beyond both. Whoever combines love with renunciation, Kabir says, never meets death.

The flute of the Infinite, meaning God, plays constantly, and its sound is love. When love gives up all limits, it reaches truth. The fragrance of this love spreads without end and nothing blocks it, and the melody shines and sounds like a vina, a stringed instrument.

The speaker longs to meet the Beloved, whom they feel as a painful separation. Though still wandering among the "alleys of knowledge" without purpose, they have received a message from the Beloved there. This message ends their fear of death, and they say they have gained the Deathless One.
The speaker is sad and restless because they are separated from their Beloved, and they have no comfort by day or sleep by night. Only a meeting with the Beloved can bring them satisfaction.

The speaker asks what flute's music fills them with joy, then lists wonders that happen without normal causes: a flame burning without a lamp, a lotus blooming without a root. The speaker also points to creatures that devote themselves fully to one thing, such as the moon-bird to the moon. The closing question asks what the Lover, meaning God, gives His whole life's love to.

The passage says that music, purity, learning and outward religious marks mean nothing without inner love for God. A teacher of scripture, a yogi in red robes and a person who keeps themselves clean are all judged by whether their hearts are filled with this love. Kabir ends by saying that God takes delight in him in every place and moment.

The path of love is subtle, with no demands made and no refusal to ask. A lover loses himself at his Lord's feet, fully absorbed in seeking, as a fish is in water. He is quick to give his life in service, and Kabir says he reveals the secret of this love.

The speaker describes the true holy teacher, or Sadhu, as one who shows the Formless God in a visible form and teaches a simple way to reach Him. This way needs no rites, no closing of the doors of the senses, no breath control, and no leaving the world. God is found wherever the mind turns, and the seeker stays calm while busy with daily life. God is also present everywhere in nature.

The passage speaks of a sacred "Word" from which the universe comes. The speaker says he heard this Word from his teacher, the Guru, and became a disciple. Many people claim to know it, but few understand its meaning, and the speaker ends by asking where the Word itself comes from.

The speaker tells the listener to empty the cup and drink the divine nectar of God's Name, which means to be filled with devotion. He says that the mind, from foot to head, is full of poison, so it must be emptied before it can take in that nectar. "Sadhu" is a holy man or religious seeker.

Kabir asks why a person takes pride when they do not know their own Lord. He says clever argument and words alone will not bring a person to God. Scripture cannot replace real love, which only the sincere seeker finds.

Having tasted the freedom of wandering in the ocean of undying life, the speaker has given up all asking. Just as a tree is contained in its seed, the speaker says every illness of the mind lies within the act of asking.

Kabir urges the listener to drink the available spiritual water, the nectar of divine love, instead of chasing illusions like a mirage. He warns that death is near and that clinging to desires and deception keeps a person weighed down. He ends by urging truth, detachment, and love.

The speaker asks two questions. No one taught a widow to burn herself on her husband's funeral pyre, and no one taught love to find joy in giving itself up. The implied point is that such things come from within, not from teaching.

The speaker asks the heart why it is so anxious, since the Lord who cares for every bird, beast and insect, and who cared for the speaker before birth, will surely care for them now. The heart has turned away from the Lord, its Beloved, and so its efforts are said to be useless.

Kabir says it is hard to meet his Lord, and he uses three images to show what devotion looks like. The rain-bird longs for rain and will drink no other water, even at the cost of its life. The deer dies listening to music without fearing it. The widow sits on her husband's funeral pyre without fear. The closing line tells the listener to set aside fear of death for the body.

The speaker says that after a guru (spiritual teacher) showed him the true path, he gave up rituals, pilgrimage bathing, temple worship and bodily penances. What pleases God, he says, is a kind and righteous life, caring for all creatures, and humility and pure speech.

The passage mocks yogis who rely on outward signs: dyed robes, pierced ears, long beards, shaved heads, and reading scripture. It says these do not change the mind, which should be dyed in the colours of love. The closing line warns that such people are heading toward death, bound hand and foot.

The speaker says he does not know what kind of God is his, and he questions outside displays of faith. A Mullah (a Muslim religious teacher) cries aloud to God, yet God hears even the faint sound of an insect's anklets. Prayer beads, forehead marks and long matted hair do not bring God near while a harmful weapon lies in the heart.

The speaker hears the call of a divine lover's flute and cannot hold back. Flowers bloom out of season, storms and rain stir the heart, and it longs for God. The poem ends with the paradox that the heart is dying even while it is alive.

Kabir asks what kind of God could be confined to a mosque or a temple image, since then the rest of the world would be left outside God. He says the divine is found within the heart, under names like Ram, Hari, Allah and Karim, and present in all people.

A person who is meek, content, and sees all things as equal, and who has come to know God, is free from fear and trouble. Such a person keeps God in mind constantly, finds joy in nothing else, and spreads love in all they do. Kabir urges the reader to reach toward God, described as one, unchanging, peaceful, and made of love.

Seek out good people who keep the Beloved at the centre of their lives, and learn from them. A gathering where God's name is not spoken is worthless, like a wedding with no bridegroom. Do not turn your heart to other gods or masters, because only the Beloved can be found this way.

A precious jewel has fallen into the mud, and people search for it in many wrong places: east and west, water and stones. The poet Kabir, however, has recognized its true worth and carefully kept it wrapped in the fold of his heart.

The speaker is a bride carried off in a palanquin to her husband's home, but the bearers leave her in a lonely forest, away from everyone she knows. She begs them to wait so she can say goodbye. The singer then tells the holy man to finish his trading, since the land he is going to has no markets.

The speaker tells the heart that it has not understood the deeper purpose of life and will leave the world as it came. It carries a heavy load, and its Friend waits on the far shore, yet it makes no effort to reach him. Kabir warns that no one can help at the end, and each person bears the results of their own actions.

The Vedas teach that the Unconditioned, the divine beyond all limits, lies outside the world. Kabir tells a woman not to argue whether God is beyond everything or within everything. Instead, she should see everything as her home, where pleasure and pain cannot reach, because God is light.

The speaker urges the listener to open their eyes of love and see God, who fills the whole world. A true spiritual teacher (Guru) can awaken this sight and reveal that God is beyond the universe yet present in it. Once this is known, grasping and giving up things no longer trouble a person.

The passage describes a realm of endless joy and beauty where the divine, called the Infinite One, dwells on a throne beyond human sight. Its radiance outshines millions of suns, and creation, with its cycles of birth and death, flows out of it. The speaker says this truth is beyond the reach of philosophy.

The passage says that the infinite, nameless Being cannot be described in words. Only someone who has reached it knows it, and it has no form or measurable shape. Kabir compares this to a mute person tasting something sweet, who cannot explain the taste.

The speaker urges the heart to go to a land where the Beloved lives, a place of endless love, rain, and light. There, love fills its pitcher without a rope, rain falls from a clear sky, and the light of many suns shines. The heart is told to leave its doorstep and bathe in that rain.

Kabir tells the listener, called Sadhu (a holy man), to consider his words carefully, since they lead to real good. He says people have cut themselves off from the Creator they came from, and that all teachings come from Him and grow from Him. God dwells at the heart of all things, so seeking refuge in empty emptiness or placing the Guru (spiritual teacher) at a distance misses Him.

God is not far away but dwells within each person, since He creates the world and fills every part of the servant. Those who think He is absent wander and search in vain, while knowing He is near brings joy. Kabir tells himself to know his own self and stay calm within his heart.

The speaker describes himself by denying every ordinary label: not pious or ungodly, not bound or free, not near or far, not bound for heaven or hell. He acts in the world yet stays apart from all action. Only a few understand this, and the one who does stays calm and unmoved.

The passage says that the true Name, meaning the sacred name of God, is unlike any other name. The divine and the material, called the Conditioned and the Unconditioned, are one reality seen in two ways. Knowledge is like a branch, and the Name is its root. Reaching the root brings happiness, and it leads to meeting God and finding peace.

Before anything existed, the Supreme Being was alone and complete, with no form, no time, no world, no religion and no scriptures. Kabir says that in that state nothing was happening, and God rested hidden within Himself. God, he adds, has no form, name, caste or dwelling-place, so His greatness cannot be fully described.

Kabir says the formless God, who has no caste or country, made the world as a kind of play or joy. Everything, from earth and sky to life, death and rivers, is part of this play. Yet the Player himself stays unknown.

A harp plays and a dance goes on, yet no hands, fingers, feet or ears are needed, because the divine is itself the one who hears and listens. Behind a locked gate there is fragrance, and the meeting is seen by no one. Only the wise will grasp this.

The speaker says that God, here called the Beggar, goes around asking for alms, yet the speaker never even saw Him. Since God gives without being asked, the speaker has nothing to request. The speaker declares belonging entirely to God and accepts whatever happens.

The speaker longs for her beloved, who lives in a distant palace across a great ocean, and she cannot find joy in anything else. She is ready to leave for him, but her parents think she is too eager. She asks a friend to lift her veil, and Kabir ends by asking to be remembered early in the morning.

The speaker is told to honor God, who is present in the body or "temple of life," before the night of death comes. The speaker says God has long waited out of love, and that the speaker only now realizes this closeness. Recognizing it, the speaker feels great good fortune in being loved by God.

Rain clouds gather and the monsoon rain is coming. The poem tells the listener to guard the fences of the fields and prepare the soil so the rain can nourish it. The wise farmer who does this will gather a harvest and feed both wise men and saints.

The speaker rejoices that the Beloved Lord has come as a guest to his home. He welcomes Him by washing His feet, offering himself and all he owns, and feeling that all evil leaves his heart when he sees Him.

The passage says that a divine music sounds in the sky, and that God, the source of this music, fills all vessels while remaining full himself. People in the body are always thirsty because they chase only parts of what they want. Deeper than that, a sound rises saying "He is this, this is He," joining love and renunciation into one. Kabir calls this the Primal Word.

Kabir says that the Beloved cannot be found through abstract ideas or teachings. He compares this to a forest: a person who ignores the individual trees will never find the forest. The divine must be sought in concrete, living things.

Learning Sanskrit and being called wise does not help the speaker, who still feels adrift, thirsty and burning with desire. Pride and vanity are a useless burden. Kabir says to put them down in the dust and go meet the Beloved, that is, God, as one's Lord.

The speaker, a woman separated from her beloved, spins thread and weaves it with love and devotion. The thread stands for her inner life, and she says she will offer her tears to her Lover when He comes to her.

The speaker describes God as a king whose shelter holds all the suns, moons and stars. He calls God the mind within his mind and the eye within his eye, and longs to join his own love with his beloved God. Love is complete, the closing line says, only when the lover and the Lover are united.

The speaker calls out that his land is free of sorrow and open to everyone, from kings to beggars, who seek shelter in the Highest, which is God. He says the land has no earth, sky, moon or stars, because only the light of Truth shines there. The closing line says that Truth alone matters.

The speaker goes to her Lord's home after marriage but never truly lives with him or knows him, and her youth passes like a dream. She leaves him after the wedding rites, and her relatives try to comfort her. Kabir says that he will return to his Lord's house with his love beside him, and then he will celebrate his victory.

Kabir urges a lover of the divine to stop sleeping and to give themselves fully once they have found God. He asks why they keep letting Him go, and why they waste time on comfort. Love, he says, may require giving up even one's life, and it should be done without weeping over the loss.

The poem says God is present in every person, like life in a seed, and that people should drop false pride and look for Him inside themselves. It says that reason, which divides people, cannot reach this presence, and that a poet who finds it sings from within and hears a music that is joyful and beyond ordinary coming and going.

The speaker longs for the Beloved, a divine lover, as the spring season approaches. Because the Beloved is present in all beauty, his colour shows in everything in the world and captivates both body and mind. Kabir says only a few people understand this spiritual truth.

The speaker says that the beloved God is always close. The speaker wakes and sleeps with him, lives where his praise is sung, and follows him wherever he goes. Whoever harms the beloved is ruined at the root. The speaker ends by saying that true love is shown by the lover himself.

The poem urges the listener to give themselves fully to love for the Beloved, a divine figure. It describes hanging body and mind in the Beloved's arms, weeping freely, and speaking one's deepest longings close to the Beloved's ear. It ends by asking the listener to hold the Beloved's vision in the heart.

A king ordered a captive killed. The desperate man cursed the king in his own language, since a man with nothing left to lose speaks freely. The tale compares him to a cornered cat that attacks a dog, or a person who grabs a sword's edge when there is no escape.

A condemned man is brought before a king, and the king asks what he is saying. A courtier softens the reply, saying the man is speaking of forgiveness and mercy, and the king spares his life. A rival courtier then objects that nobles should speak only the truth before kings.

The king prefers a flattering lie to a harsh truth. He says the lie was offered for the sake of good government, while the truth came from ill will. A falsehood that keeps peace is better, he argues, than a truth that stirs up trouble. He adds that a counsellor who gives advice other than good advice is a cause for regret.

The inscription over King Feridun's palace warns that the world does not last for anyone. It tells the reader to fix the heart on God and not to rely on worldly power, since death comes equally to a king and a commoner.

In a dream, a king of Khorasan sees the long-dead Sultan Mahmud, whose body has decayed except for his eyes, which still move and look around. When the learned men cannot explain this, a dervish (a Muslim holy man) says the eyes keep looking because his kingdom and wealth now belong to others.

Many dead rulers are now forgotten, with not even their bones left. Nushirowan, a Persian king long gone, is still remembered for his generosity. So the speaker urges his friend to be generous while still alive, before he too is forgotten.

A king's short, plain son is looked down on by his tall, handsome brothers. He answers that size does not decide worth: a wise short man is better than a tall fool, a sheep is healthier to eat than an elephant, and the small mountain Sinai is greater before God than the larger mountains.

A father compares his sons to horses and asses: one son's worth, like a fine Arab horse, is greater than a herd of asses, and the courtiers agree. The passage then warns that a man's good or bad qualities stay hidden until he speaks, so an empty-looking thicket may still hide a tiger.

A king's son, going out to battle, declares that he will not be the man seen running away. He says he will be seen in the thick of the fight, bloodied and dusty. He then charges the enemy's cavalry and defeats several famous warriors.

A young man, dismissed by the king for his slight body, proves his worth in battle. When the king's small army is about to flee, he shouts that they must stand firm rather than wear women's clothes, and the troops rally and win the day.

A king's favourite is poisoned by his jealous brothers, but his sister sees the plot and gives a warning signal. The boy refuses the poisoned food and remarks that it is hard for the good to die while the wicked take their places. The father learns the truth and punishes the brothers.

Dividing his lands among rival claimants did not calm things; their rivalry grew. The passage says that two kings cannot share one kingdom, while ten dervishes (holy men) can share one rug. A king always wants more territory, unlike a holy man who gives away half his bread.

Officials of nearby districts worry about a band of Arab robbers who have taken a strong mountain fortress and attack travelers. They reason that the robbers must be stopped while they are still weak, since a young tree can be pulled up by one man but a grown one cannot.

The passage uses an image of a leak in a dam: a small hole can be plugged easily, but once it grows, it cannot be crossed even by an elephant. The point is that a small threat must be dealt with early. The rulers then decide to send a spy and hidden troops to a mountain stronghold, timing their attack for when its defenders have gone out to raid another tribe.

Robbers returned from a raid, tired and loaded with loot, fell asleep after putting down their weapons. Soldiers then waited in ambush, seized them one by one as they slept, and brought them to the king in the morning. The king ordered them all executed.
A young man is about to be executed, and a vizier asks the king to spare him because he is young and has not yet lived his life. The king turns away from the request, showing he will not grant it.

A king's minister is told that teaching worthless people is pointless. The speaker argues that good influence cannot reach the basically wicked, so it is wiser to destroy their roots than to spare them. He gives images: walnuts on a dome, a willow that bears no fruit, sugar that cannot come from a common cane.

A courtier flatters the king and agrees with his judgment. He says the king is right that the boy was raised among bad company, and that a child can still be taught to keep good company, since his mind has not yet been corrupted by that gang.

Sa'di's point is that a child's faith comes from upbringing, and that companions can change a person for better or worse. The courtiers plead for a youth's pardon, and the king grants it reluctantly, saying he does not see the benefit.

The passage makes one point with a proverb: a small stream at its source can grow strong enough to carry away a camel and its load, so an enemy should never be dismissed as weak. Then a vizier (a chief minister) takes a boy home and gives him a good education, teaching him logic, rhetoric and courtly skills.

A vizir (a chief minister) boasts that his trained protégé has lost his old savage nature. The king answers that a wolf's cub remains a wolf even when raised by a man. Two years later the young man murders the vizir and his sons and returns to a life of crime, proving the king right.

The king concludes that a base-born person cannot be made noble by education, just as iron cannot become fine steel. He says that kindness shown to the wicked is wasted, and is like wronging the good. Rain falls on all plants alike, but the nature of the ground decides what grows.

Sa'di describes a young officer's son at the Delhi king's gate who was admired for his wit, learning and good sense, despite his youth. The king noticed his abilities. Sages, the author adds, say that worth comes from talent rather than wealth, and that wisdom comes from good sense rather than age.

A courtier tells the king that his rivals' jealousy cannot harm him while the king favors him. He says he has pleased everyone except the envious man, who will never be satisfied unless the courtier falls. He adds that he cannot stop envy, since the envious man carries the source of his own misery inside himself.

Envious people are told to die, since that is the only way they could be rid of their envy. The writer compares them to a bat that cannot see by day: its weakness is its own fault, not the sun's. Better that a thousand such eyes suffer than that the sun's light be dimmed.

A Persian king oppressed his subjects with heavy taxes and violence, so many people fled his realm. With the population shrinking and the treasury empty, his enemies grew stronger. The closing lesson is that whoever wants comfort in hard times should show kindness while times are good.

Sa'di says that a ruler who treats his followers kindly keeps their loyalty, and even strangers can become devoted. To show this, a vizir (chief minister) asks how Feridun, who had no wealth or army, came to hold power. The king answers that people gathered around him out of loyal attachment and helped him win a kingdom.

A vizier (chief minister) tells the king that a king needs an army to hold power, and that the king should win people's loyalty by generosity and mercy. He adds that the king currently has neither quality, so his people have scattered from him.

A tyrant cannot rule a kingdom properly, just as a wolf cannot do a shepherd's work. A minister who warned the king of this was locked in a dungeon, and soon the king's cousins rose in revolt and claimed the throne.

A king who oppressed his people was overthrown when the scattered victims of his cruelty gathered, helped them, and set up a new ruler in his place. The passage warns that a king who tolerates harm to the weak will find that even his friends turn against him in hard times. A just king, it says, has a loyal army in his ordinary subjects.

Hormuz, a Persian king, was asked why he had jailed his father's ministers. He said he had found no fault in them. He jailed them because they respected him only slightly and did not fully trust his promises, and he feared that, fearing for their own safety, they might plot his downfall.

Treat even the weak with care, because a person who is threatened may fight back fiercely, even against someone much stronger. The passage gives examples: a snake bites a herdsman who might hurt it, and a cornered cat tears at a tiger.

A dying Arab king hears that his army has won a victory. Instead of rejoicing, he sighs, because the gains will go to his heirs, not to him. He feels his life has been spent waiting for something that never came to him.

A dying man reflects that even though his hope has been fulfilled, it brings him no benefit, because his life cannot be recovered. Death is calling him, and he bids farewell to his body parts and his friends. He warns the living not to waste their days as he did.

A notorious unjust Arab prince came to pray at the tomb of John the Baptist in Damascus, asking for blessings and his needs. The author then notes that rich and poor alike are devoted to this shrine, and the richer a person is, the more help they seem to need.

A dervish (a Muslim holy man) speaks to a king who asks for prayers against a powerful enemy. He replies that the king should show mercy to his own weak subjects, since a ruler who oppresses the helpless may find no one to help him when he falls.

Whoever plants the seed of wrongdoing and expects a good harvest is foolish. The speaker urges the listener to be just to others, since a day of reckoning will come. He says all people share one origin and should feel each other's pain. Someone who ignores others' suffering does not deserve to be called a man.

A dervish (a Muslim holy man) is asked by the tyrant Hajjaj Yusuf to pray for him. Instead he prays that God take the tyrant's life, saying this is good for the tyrant and for all Muslims. He adds that the tyrant's cruelty cannot last, and that his death would be better than his oppression of people.

A holy man tells an unjust king that the best thing he can do is sleep through midday, so that he cannot harm people during that time. The narrator then sees a tyrant asleep at noon and says it would be better if such a wicked man were dead, since his sleep is better than his waking.

A king, feasting through the night, boasts that he cares for no one and has no worries. A poor dervish (a wandering holy man) outside in the cold replies that the king may have no cares for himself, but should think of others. The king is moved and gives him a purse of gold coins.

A poor holy man (dervish) asks a king for help, and the king gives him money and a robe. The dervish quickly spends it all and comes back in need. The king, who had stopped thinking about him, is annoyed at being reminded and turns away.

Kings are busy with affairs of state and do not like being pestered by common people, so a person should avoid their anger. A king's favor comes only to someone who waits for the right moment. Until that moment comes, a person should not speak up, since useless talk lowers their standing.

A king orders a beggar who quickly spent a large sum from the charity fund to be beaten and driven out, saying the fund is meant to feed the poor, not to fill the wasteful. A wise minister replies that such people should be given their living expenses in small regular payments, so they cannot waste the money they need to survive.

Sa'di's point is that a ruler should not raise hopes and then crush them. He says it is wrong to open the door of greed and then shut it harshly. People gather where generous water is found, just as thirsty travelers gather at a fresh fountain but not at salt sea water.

A king was lenient in collecting taxes from farmers but stingy in paying his soldiers, so when a strong enemy appeared, the soldiers fled. The point is that a soldier who lacks the means to live cannot be expected to fight bravely.

A friend who had withdrawn from service defends himself against the speaker's charge of ungratefulness. He says that if he explained his real reasons, the speaker would forgive him, because his horse had no fodder and his saddle cloth had been pawned to pay for food.

A ruler who holds back his soldiers' pay cannot expect them to serve with enthusiasm. The passage says a prince should pay a brave soldier well so that he stays loyal, since an unpaid soldier will seek service elsewhere. It adds that soldiers fight well when fed and flee when hungry.

A former vizier, after losing his post, joined a group of dervishes (Sufi holy men) and found peace there. When the king offered to restore him to office, he refused. He said wise people prefer to stay out of office, since those in retirement avoid slander, criticism and attacks from others.

A wise official, the ex-minister argues, is one who does not meddle in state affairs. He points to the phoenix, which is honored because it eats only bones and harms no living creature. He also gives the example of the lion-provider, who serves the lion for the leftovers of its prey and for safety under its protection.

Someone advises a man to move closer to a king, who is generous and might make him a chosen courtier. He refuses, because the king's favour can turn to violence without warning. A Guebre (a Zoroastrian) who keeps a fire burning for years is still burned if he steps into it. Courtiers may receive gold one day and be beheaded the next.

Philosophers warn that kings are unpredictable: they may be insulted by a greeting, yet reward rudeness with a robe of honour. So a wise person should stay alert and serious, leaving joking and clowning to jesters and courtiers.

A friend complains that he is poor with a large family and wants to move to another country, where no one would know his circumstances. The bracketed lines add that he often went to sleep hungry and nobody noticed, and that his life was nearly lost without anyone mourning him.

The speaker is asking for a government post. He fears that rivals will mock him and call his care for his family a lack of kindness, so he wants a job to settle his worries. He says he is skilled at accounting and would be deeply grateful.

A man refuses to serve kings. He says the work offers only a hope of support mixed with fear for his life, and that a wise person should not take that risk. The other speaker answers that this does not fit his own case, and warns that someone who helps in a dishonest act will tremble when he must account for it.

A person who keeps honest records and acts righteously has nothing to fear from an inspector or rival. Those who are corrupt, by contrast, are always afraid of being caught and of the people who watch them.

A fox runs in panic because he has heard that camels are being seized for forced labour. Another fox tells him he is no camel, but he replies that if malicious people claimed he was one, no one would check the claim before taking him. The point is that false accusations can harm a man even when he is innocent.

Even a person of knowledge and good character can be ruined before help arrives, because spies and informers can report falsely against them. No one may defend such a person before the king. So the speaker advises seeking contentment and giving up the wish for advancement.

A wise saying holds that a sea voyage has many benefits, but safety is found only on land. The speaker's friend objects angrily, arguing that true friends show themselves in hard times, such as in prison, while enemies may pretend friendship when things go well.

A man who sees a friend in despair and misfortune should help him up, and the speaker does this. He sees that the friend is troubled and impatient with advice, so he speaks to the lord high treasurer on the friend's behalf. The friend gets a small post, and later a much higher one.

A man who had fallen into poverty saw his fortunes rise until he became the king's favorite, and people turned to him for advice. The speaker, glad of the change, tells a friend in hardship not to despair or grow bitter, since hidden mercies are stored up and patience, though bitter, bears sweet fruit.

A man tells the narrator that his misfortune came from a rival group who accused him of wrongdoing. The king would not look into the charge, and his old friends refused to defend him or acknowledge their former ties with him.

When a man falls from favor, everyone turns against him and trample him. When his luck turns, the same people praise him loudly. The speaker says he suffered persecution until news of the pilgrims' safe return freed him from prison, though his family property was taken.

The speaker reminds someone that he once warned them serving princes is like a sea voyage: it can bring great wealth or end in ruin. He compares it to a merchant who either reaches shore rich or is drowned by a wave.

The speaker, who will not add more harsh blame to a poor man's suffering, sums up his advice in two verses. He warns that a man who ignored good counsel will end up in chains, and that he should not put his finger into a scorpion's hole again unless he can bear its sting.

A prince had supported a brotherhood of holy men, but stopped their funding after one of them behaved badly. The narrator wanted to win back the prince's support for them, but the prince's doorkeeper turned him away rudely when he tried to see his master.

A visitor explains that he got past the gatekeeper and the dog only because he had someone to introduce him. The prince's attendants then honor him and offer a high seat. He modestly takes the lowest place, but the great man rejects his humility and tells him it is out of place.

The narrator sits down and talks about many subjects. When his friends' unwise conduct comes up, he says that God, perfect in majesty and goodness, sees human faults yet still supports people. The prince accepts this view.

The speaker thanks a king who has kept paying his friends' allowances and cleared their back pay. He then compares himself and his friends to a fruitless tree, saying the king should tolerate them, since no one throws stones at a tree that bears no fruit. The point is that they are harmless and not worth attacking.

A prince who inherits great wealth from his father spends it freely on his soldiers and people. The point is that a good name must be earned by generosity, just as a plant grows only after seed is sown, and fragrance comes only when the wood is burned.

A narrow-minded courtier warns a king not to spend so freely. He says past rulers saved their wealth carefully, that enemies and emergencies may come, and that the king should instead take a small amount from each family to build a large treasury.

A prince rebukes an adviser who wants him to hoard wealth. He says God gave him the property to enjoy and spend, not to guard it like a miser. He contrasts Qarun, whose great treasure perished with him, with Nushirvan, whose good name lasted after his death.

Nushirowan, a legendary king, orders that salt be paid for at its fair price rather than taken by force. When his advisers call the matter trivial, he replies that small abuses by rulers grow over time: one stolen apple leads guards to uproot the whole tree, and five eggs taken with royal consent lead troops to seize a thousand fowls.

A tax collector seized the huts of poor peasants to fill the ruler's treasury. The passage warns that whoever harms God's favour to win a person's approval will find that person turned against him, and that the sigh of the afflicted is what brings ruin.

The passage says that wise people prefer a working donkey to a man-eating lion, because a beast that carries loads does more good than a man who harms others. It then describes a king who had a cruel official tortured to death after learning of his wrongdoing. It closes with the lesson that a ruler's approval depends on the goodwill of his people.

A man who had been wronged by a ruler spoke to him as he was being put to death. He said that not everyone has the power of high office to take what he likes from people's property. He warned that a bone can be forced down the throat, but when it lodges at the navel it bursts the belly, meaning that excessive oppression ends in disaster.

A dervish (a holy man) was struck on the head with a stone by a spiteful person. He could not take revenge at the time, so he kept the stone. Years later, when that person was thrown into prison by the ruler, the dervish threw the stone back at him. Asked why, he said he had been waiting for the chance.

A poor man, now seeing his former superior held in a dungeon, says he will take his chance to act against him. He quotes a saying: when a powerful enemy is helpless, you should strike while you can, so you do not later suffer for confronting him while he was strong.

A runaway slave is brought back and sentenced to death on the advice of a vizir (chief minister) who dislikes him. The slave accepts the king's right to decide, but says he does not want his death to be counted against the king on the Day of Judgment.

A condemned man, facing execution by a king, argues that the king should first order the vizir (chief minister) killed, so that the execution can be justified as retaliation under law. The king then asks the vizir for advice, and the vizir's reply is cut off at the end of the passage.

A man begs a king to free a reckless servant, and admits his own fault. He says he ignored the wise warning that a man who challenges a skilled opponent, or shoots at his face, exposes himself to being hurt in return.

King Zuzan's minister was kind and spoke well of people even when they were not there. After the king had him imprisoned for displeasing him, the royal officers, remembering his past kindness, promised to repay it.

Those holding a prisoner treated him kindly and did not use force. They quoted a saying: if a rival slanders you, praise him to his face, since a quarrelsome man always wants the last word. The prisoner's debt was partly settled, and he stayed in custody for the rest.

A neighboring prince secretly wrote to a wise man, saying that his own country's ruler had not valued the man's worth and had wronged him, and that the prince's court would welcome him warmly. The minister read the letter and took control of its contents.

A prisoner wrote a short reply on the back of a letter he was sending, and a courtier told the king that the prisoner was secretly writing to a neighboring prince. The king ordered the letter checked. The passage ends mid-sentence, with the prisoner's reply on the back of the letter: a modest statement that the king's favor is greater than his own worth.

A loyal servant refuses to accept the king's favor for a man who has been dismissed, because he owes his whole position to the royal house and will not turn against a long-standing patron over a small change of mood. The king praises his loyalty, rewards him, and apologizes for his own fault.

The speaker says that a hardship has come from God's decree, so it is easier to accept it from a patron he owes thanks to. He tells the listener not to blame other people for troubles, since neither pleasure nor pain comes from other people. Friends and enemies alike act as God directs.
The arrow seems to fly by its own power from the bow, but a wise person sees that the archer is the one who directed it. The point is that the true cause lies behind what appears to be the cause.

A king tells his treasury to pay one courtier double, because that man is always present and ready to obey, while the others are busy with games and neglect their duties. A holy man who overhears this sighs deeply, and when asked why, the story implies he is troubled by the king's reasoning.

The main point is that service to a ruler, like devotion to God, earns its reward. A king's favour comes to those who serve him faithfully, and a person who disobeys shows that he has been rejected. Those who are upright and good will therefore humbly attend the king's threshold.

A tyrant buys firewood cheaply from poor people and sells it dearly to the rich. A holy man warns him that God sees his injustice, and that the poor may complain to heaven against him. The holy man also compares him to a snake and an owl, creatures that harm and ruin the places they live.

A cruel man was warned by a holy man, but he ignored him and turned away. Later a fire burned down his house and all his goods. When he wondered where it came from, the holy man said it came from the sighs of the poor whom he had wronged.

Do not hurt anyone's heart if you can avoid it, because one sigh of pain can set a whole world on fire. The passage then notes that Kai-khosrau's crown bore an inscription: power passes from hand to hand, and rulers will one day be walked over in their turn.
A wrestling master knew 360 tricks and taught his favourite student 359 of them, keeping one back with excuses. The passage suggests his partiality was the reason for holding it back.

A young wrestler, now more skilled than his contemporaries, boasts before the king that he is only deferring to his old teacher out of respect, and that in strength and skill he is his equal. The king is offended by this disrespect and arranges a public wrestling match.

A young wrestler, strong as an elephant, rushes into a public contest before a gathering of court officials and nobles. His master, knowing the youth is stronger, wins by using a trick he had never taught him, since the youth did not know how to defend against it.

A wrestling master lifts a young challenger high and throws him to the ground, and the crowd cheers. The king rewards the master and scolds the youth, saying he betrayed his own patron and was wrong to challenge him. The youth begins to answer the king.

A wrestling master explains that he held back one secret trick from his student, so that the student could not turn it against him. He justifies this by saying a wise person should never give a friend so much power that the friend could harm him if turned hostile. He then adds a bitter remark that either good faith does not exist or no one practices it today.

A dervish, a Sufi holy man who lives without wealth, sits by a desert road and does not look up as a king passes. The king takes offence and calls such beggars like beasts. His vizir, or chief minister, then speaks to the dervish, pointing out that the king has just passed by him.

A man is asked why he did not bow to the king. He replies that the king should expect service only from those who seek his favor. He adds that kings exist to protect the people, not the people to serve the kings, and that a king is only a shepherd of the poor.

A ruler exists to serve his people, not the reverse, as a shepherd exists to tend his sheep. The passage warns that the proud and the suffering will both end in the grave, and at death the difference between king and subject vanishes.

A wise man tells a king that the dust of the dead cannot show who was rich and who was poor. The king is moved and asks for a favor. The man asks only to be left alone, then advises the king to use his power well, since wealth and rule pass from one owner to another.

A king ordered an innocent man executed. The man warned that the king would suffer more from the sin than he would from the punishment, since pain passes quickly but wrongdoing lasts. Moved by this, the king spared him and asked forgiveness.
The other ministers asked the prime minister why he agreed with the king's opinion over the many wise views given in the council. The question shows they thought his choice needed explaining.

The speaker says that when the outcome of a matter is uncertain, it is safer to agree with the king's view, since the right or wrong of it rests with God. Opposing the king could bring ruin, so even if the king said day was night, one should answer that the moon and stars are visible.

A man pretended to be a descendant of Ali, a pilgrim from Mecca, and the author of a poem he presented to the king. The king honored him, until a courtier said he had seen the man elsewhere, on a different date and in a different place, which suggests he was lying.

A man is accused of being a fraud: people say he is not a true pilgrim, that his father was a Christian, and that his verses were copied from another poet's collection. The king orders him beaten, but he asks to speak one more time, promising to accept any punishment if his words prove false.

A king is told by a traveller that a peasant's cup of junket is mostly water, and that a slave's idle talk should be forgiven because travellers tell wonders. The king agrees it is true and rewards the man, who leaves pleased.

A vizier who helped others fell out of the king's favor and was jailed. Friends and officials spoke well of him, and the king pardoned him. A holy man then said that it is worth giving up one's own property to win friends and feed well-wishers. He also said that kindness, even to the wicked, is worthwhile, as a crumb quiets a dog.

Harun-al-Rashid, a caliph, is asked by his angry child what should be done to a man who insulted the child's mother. Several ministers propose harsh punishments, but Harun answers that forgiving the man would be the generous choice.

Sa'di says that a true hero is not the man who fights a dangerous beast, but the man who keeps his temper when provoked and does not speak harshly. He tells of a man who was insulted by a quarrelsome fellow and replied patiently, admitting that he was even worse than the insult claimed.

In a boat accident, a gentleman offers a reward to the pilot to save one of two drowning brothers. The pilot saves one and the other drowns. The speaker remarks that the drowned man's time had come, so the pilot was slow to help him and quick to save the other. The pilot replies that the remark is pure fate, or necessity, which the speaker has stated.

The passage is a tale of repayment: a man helps someone who once did him a kindness, and not the one who once beat him. The writer then says God rewards good and punishes evil. He closes by urging kindness to others, since the same help may one day be needed by oneself.

Nushirowan, a just king, hears that his enemy has died. He does not rejoice, because he knows his own life will also end, and he asks whether the enemy had shown him any mercy that would justify such a reaction.

Abu-zarchamahr, a senior official at the court of the king Kisra, stays silent during a council debate because the other ministers are giving sound advice. He says he would speak only if he saw them heading toward disaster, as one would warn a blind man about to fall into a pit.

Harun-al-Rashid, after conquering Egypt, wanted to show contempt for Pharaoh, who had claimed to be a god. So he gave the rule of Egypt to the lowliest of his slaves, a dull-witted man named Khosayib.

A king is told that rain washed away farmers' cotton plants, and he answers that they should have planted wool instead. A holy man hears this and remarks that if fortune matched knowledge, a fool would get the smallest share.

Wealth and power, the passage says, come from fortune or heaven, not from learning. Ignorant people often rise to honor while wise people are scorned. A fool found treasure by chance under a ruin, while a chemist, a seeker of gold-making, was left disappointed.

A holy man is asked to defend an abid, a monk whose character others have criticized. He answers that he sees nothing wrong in the man's outward conduct and cannot know his inner thoughts. So people should judge by appearance and not pry into what is hidden, since a censor has no business inside a private house.

A dervish (a Muslim holy man) prays at the Kaaba in Mecca and admits he has no claim to God's reward, since his worship is imperfect. He offers only his excuse. Pious worshippers, by contrast, expect a reward for their devotion, as merchants expect profit from trade.

A speaker comes to God not with good works but with hope, asking to be treated with mercy rather than according to what he deserves. He accepts whatever God decides, and he asks only for his sins to be forgiven, not for his obedience to be praised.

A holy man at the Kaaba in Mecca prays that, if God must punish him, he be raised up blindfolded so the righteous will not see his shame. The speaker then says he prays each morning, face in the dust, asking whether God ever thinks of him.

A thief breaks into a holy man's cell and finds nothing to take. The holy man leaves his rug in the thief's path so the thief does not go away empty-handed. The moral drawn is that true holy people do not hurt even their enemies, and the speaker asks how someone who fights with his own friends could reach that high state.
The righteous do not speak ill of you behind your back while praising you to your face. A person who brings you news of others' faults will, in the same way, carry your faults to them.

Sa'di describes wandering holy men (dervishes) who agreed to pool their resources and share the work and comforts of communal life. He asked to join them and they refused. He argues that it is unusual for dervishes to turn away a poor man from their company, and says he would be a helpful companion rather than a burden.

A thief once joined a group of dervishes (Muslim holy men) by dressing as one. Because dervishes were respected, the group did not suspect him and let him in. The point is that a person's outward dress cannot show what he really is.

Holiness is not shown by plain or patched clothing. A holy man may wear any dress, even fine silk, because true holiness means giving up worldly pride and vanity. Clothes alone do not make a person holy, just as armor does not make a coward brave.

A dervish (a wandering holy man) travels with companions and sleeps under a castle wall. He pretends to go wash, then sneaks off to steal from the fort and leaves the others asleep. The point is that a man who looks devout can be a thief.

The narrator says that after a group was jailed, he and his companions stopped taking in new members and kept to themselves. He holds that a small group is safest when united, and that one member's foolish act shames the whole sect, just as one ox can bring disgrace on all the oxen in a village.

The speaker is thankful that he can still learn from dervishes (Sufi holy men), even though he is not part of their company. He then gives an image: one careless person in a gathering can spoil the whole group, just as a dog falling into a tank of rose-water makes all of it impure.

A holy man eats little and prays long while a king's guest, so the king thinks him pious, then eats a full meal at home. The passage warns that his road leads away from the Caaba, and his son notices the pretence.

A boy mocks his father, a dervish (a Sufi holy man), who claims he ate little at the king's feast. The boy says he should then also cut short his prayers. The point is that the father shows off his good deeds while hiding his faults, and such display is false coin that will not help him on judgment day.
The speaker, as a young man, stayed awake all night beside his sleeping father, holding the Koran. He then complained to his father that the others around them were asleep and not rising to pray.

A man is told that the sleepers around him seem dead, and he answers that it would be better for the speaker to sleep than to slander others' faults. He adds that a braggart sees only himself, hiding behind conceit, and would find no one weaker than himself if he could see as God sees.

The narrator preached in a mosque at Balbek to a congregation he found spiritually dead and unwilling to turn from worldly concerns toward mystical devotion. His words seemed to have no effect on them, so he grew tired of trying, though his speech kept flowing.

The speaker is preaching on a Koranic verse saying God is nearer to a person than the vein in his neck. He uses an image of a beloved who is closer to him than he is to himself, yet he is estranged from her. He feels the force of these words strongly, and a passing traveller is drawn in by the effect of his speech.

The speaker says that a listener who cannot understand a sermon cannot expect the preacher to show real skill. He asks that listeners be given freedom to respond, so the speaker has room to express his eloquence. He also notes that people who understand are present in spirit, while the ignorant are far away even when close by.

A traveller, worn out with sleep, lies down in the desert and wants to be left behind to die. His camel-driver urges him to keep going, since Mecca lies ahead and robbers behind, and staying means death. The traveller is told that sleeping under the thorn tree will cost him his life.

A holy man, badly wounded by a tiger and without any medicine, thanks God anyway. His reason is that he was harmed by misfortune rather than by sin. He adds that if God allowed him to die, he would not mind, as long as God was not displeased with him.

A dervish, a holy man with no possessions, stole a rug from a friend and was sentenced to lose his hand. The friend pleaded for him, but the judge refused to cancel the sentence. Then the judge said that a dervish cannot own anything, so what he takes belongs to the needy, and the sentence should not apply.
A thief, caught in a friend's house, defends himself with a saying: take freely from friends, but never approach enemies. In hardship, he adds, take much from enemies and only a little from friends.

A king asked a holy man whether he ever thought of him. The holy man replied that he thought of the king only when he forgot God. Whoever God turns away wanders from door to door, while whoever God guides is kept at God's own door.

A righteous man dreams of a king in paradise and a holy man in hell, and a voice explains why. The king was saved by his love for holy people, and the holy man was damned by his ties to kings. The rest says that outward signs of piety, such as a coarse frock or rosary, count for nothing, and that true holiness lies in good conduct.

A poor, nearly naked traveler joins a pilgrim caravan heading to Mecca. He cheerfully says he owns no camel, no master, and no servants, and he does not dwell on past or present troubles. A rider warns him to turn back or die in the desert, but he ignores the warning and walks on alone.

The point is that life and death do not follow strength or wealth. A rich man dies on the journey while a poor dervish survives, and a weeping friend dies while the sick man recovers. Fast horses die on the road, but a lame donkey arrives safely.

Robbers attacked a merchant caravan in Greek lands and took their goods. The merchants prayed and appealed to God and the prophet, but nothing changed. The point is that a robber who has just won will not care about the travellers' despair.

A traveller asks a wise man to preach to the robbers who took their goods, hoping they might give some back. The wise man refuses. He says that wisdom is wasted on such people, just as a file cannot remove rust from corroded iron.

The passage says a hard heart cannot be moved, as an iron nail cannot pierce flint, and that the fault may lie with the giver, who has not been charitable. It urges giving to the poor, and giving kindly, so that the poor are not forced to take by violence.

Lukman was asked who taught him manners. He said he learned them from rude people, by avoiding whatever in their behavior he saw as bad. The passage adds that a wise person can learn even from a joke, while a fool hears wisdom only as a joke.

A holy man says that a worshipper who ate ten pounds of food each night would do better to eat half a loaf and sleep. Eating too much, he says, fills a person so that good deeds cannot shine and wisdom is lost.

A man who had lived in sinful ways was guided by God into the company of dervishes, and he changed his behavior for the better. Still, critics doubted his sincerity and said he had not really changed. The closing lesson is that repentance can save a person from God's anger, but nobody can escape the tongue of gossip.

A man complained to his spiritual teacher that people's slander troubled him. The teacher answered that he should be glad he is better than the gossip claims. He said it is better to be good and let people speak ill of you than to be wicked and have people think well of you.

The speaker admits he is not as good as people think. Others see him as pious, but he hides his sins behind a closed door. He then argues that this is pointless, since God knows all things, hidden or open.

A man complained to an elder that someone had accused him of lust. The elder told him to answer the charge by living chastely, so the slanderer has no grounds left. He compared this to a harp that is already in tune, which needs no tuning from the player.

The passage contrasts the Sufi brotherhood of the past with its present state. Earlier, Sufis were scattered in body but united in spirit; now they look outwardly well off yet are spiritually poor. It ends by saying that a person with wealth and rank can still be a true hermit if the heart stays fixed on God, while a person living alone can still be impure if the heart wanders.

A traveller tells how, on a night march with a caravan, a companion in a mystical trance cried out at dawn, wandered off into the desert, and rested not at all. The narrator then asks him what state he had been in, which sets up the story's point about his behaviour.

A dervish (a Muslim holy man) explains why he was moved to weep at night. He saw that birds, beasts and other creatures all praised God while he was asleep and forgetful. Then one bird's song, sung near morning, overcame his patience and reason, so he cried out. His friend was surprised that a bird's song could affect him so much.

The speaker replies that it is not the duty of people to praise God just because the birds are singing his praise, and that he therefore should stay silent. In other words, he does not feel bound to match the birds' worship.

Sa'di travels to Hijaz with some devout young men who sing spiritual songs. A worshipper travelling with them mocks dervishes (members of a Sufi religious order) and shows no sympathy for their hardships. When an Arab boy from a tribe sings a mournful song, the worshipper's attitude is challenged.

A camel, moved by a singer's song, kicks up and dances off with its rider, a holy man called an abid (a devout worshipper). The speaker says the song changes the camel but not the holy man, and calls him a brute for lacking the feeling for love that the camel has.

The main point is that everything in creation praises God, but only a receptive heart can hear it. A camel's joy, a breeze moving a tree, and a thorn on a rose-bush all count as voices of praise. The passage says that a man who does not feel this is dull, like an ass, while a heart with an ear hears the divine mystery everywhere.

The dying king left instructions that his crown should go to the first man who came through the city gate the next morning. That man was a beggar, and the ministers carried out the will by giving him the keys to the treasury and the citadel.

A dervish, a Sufi holy man, briefly ruled a kingdom, but his chiefs turned against him, rival princes raised armies, and he lost his troops and several provinces. He was deeply upset, and then an old friend from his days of poverty arrived and saw him in his high position.

A man is congratulated on rising to high rank, with the usual sayings about fortune turning, hardship giving way to ease, and seasons changing. He answers that he wants sympathy, not congratulations, because his new position brings the worries of a whole kingdom, while before he had only worried about getting bread.

Whether life goes well or badly, the mind is troubled, and a prosperous life can enslave a person to its comforts. The author says contentment is the greatest wealth, and the patience of the poor is worth more than a rich man's gift. He compares a king's large gift to a tiny gift from an ant.

A man says he does not need to visit his friend, a royal minister, while the friend holds office. He thinks a visit would be more welcome after the minister loses his post, when he might be glad of company. The point is that a powerful friend may take offence at old acquaintances while in power, but will open up to them in misfortune.

Visiting too often wears out affection, so people should not come every day. The prophet asks Abu-Horairah to visit less often, and a holy man compares this to the sun, which is longed for because it is absent in winter. The closing line says that visits are fine, but not so frequent that people tire of them.

The narrator left his friends in Damascus in anger and went to live alone in the wilderness near Jerusalem. He was captured by the Franks (Western Christian crusaders) and forced to dig ditches in Tripoli with Jews. An old friend from Aleppo saw him there and asked how he had come to such work.

A man who had fled into forests and mountains to live alone is later captured by the Franks (European crusaders). A stranger ransoms him for ten dinars and takes him to Aleppo, where he gives him his daughter in marriage with a dowry of a hundred dinars.

A man describes how his new wife quickly became a bitter, quarrelsome scold who ruined his peace at home. He says a nagging wife is a kind of hell even in this life. In her anger she throws in his face that her father bought him out of captivity among the Franks for ten dinars.

The speaker says a man once freed him from a captor for a small price, then kept him as a slave for a much larger one. In the story, a holy man saves a sheep from a wolf, then that same night cuts its throat himself. The sheep complains that the man turned out to be a wolf to it after all.

A holy man who lived alone in the desert, eating tree leaves, was invited by the king to move to the royal city, where he could pray comfortably and benefit others. The hermit refused and turned away from the offer.

A minister urges a hermit to stay in the city for a few days to see whether its wicked people will spoil his purity, with the option to leave again. The hermit agrees, and they give him a pleasant garden dwelling near the king's palace.

A king sends a beautiful young woman to a garden, and the narrator describes her beauty in florid terms. He says that anyone who saw her would lose the self-control that chaste people normally have. The garden imagery is an ornate setting for the woman's allure.

A beautiful young man follows the woman described earlier, and his looks overpower even pious people. Onlookers thirst for him, but he gives them nothing, and they can never get enough of gazing at him. A hermit then starts enjoying rich food, fine clothes, and the sight of servants.

The speaker says that a beautiful person's curls have trapped his reason and wisdom, as a snare traps a bird. He had devoted his heart and mind to this beloved, and so his years of holy living were wasted. He compares himself to a fly stuck in honey.

The king visits a hermit and finds him comfortable and well-fed, lounging on cushions with a young woman and a servant beside him. The king praises his plump looks, then says he is fond of two kinds of people: the learned and the recluse.

The vizir advises the king to give money to the learned man so he can teach others, and to give nothing to the hermit so he can stay a true hermit. A hermit needs no money, and one who accepts money is no longer a true hermit. A devout person who communicates with God does not need charity to be a hermit.

Sa'di says that beautiful people need no ornaments: a lovely finger and ear need no jewelry, a devout dervish needs no begging, and a handsome woman needs no paint or jewels. The closing lines admit that if he himself covets what belongs to others, he deserves to be judged by them as he judges himself.

A king had promised to give a sum of money to hermits if his important affair succeeded. When it did, he gave a bag of gold coins, not the smaller silver coins he had named, to a servant to hand out to the hermits.

A young man is sent to find sincere holy men and is given money to offer them. After a day of searching he returns with the money untouched, saying he found no true recluses. The king mentions four hundred he knows, and the young man replies that true recluses do not accept money, and those who accept money are not true recluses.

The king smiles and tells his courtiers that, though he honors the holy men, the blunt speaker who criticized them is right. He asks them to find a truly devout hermit, one who does not take money, in place of the one who did.

A learned man is asked whether taking consecrated bread or alms is acceptable. He says it is allowed if the purpose is to calm the mind and aid devotion, but not if monks gather it to build up an endowment or fund. He adds that holy men have accepted such bread to support their withdrawal from the world, and that this is the reason recluses take it.

A hungry dervish, a Sufi holy man, arrives at a host's house where learned guests are telling jokes and stories. Asked to contribute, he says he will recite only a single verse, and the company eagerly agrees to hear it.

A hungry man sits at a rich table and says he is as restless as a bachelor near a women's bath, so he can hardly wait to eat. The host asks him to wait for specially prepared meat, but the man replies that plain bread is enough for someone who has lived in the desert.

A disciple complains that visitors keep interrupting him. His spiritual teacher advises him to lend money to the poor and borrow from the rich, so that they will stop coming. The teacher adds that a beggar is like a scout who drives off enemies, since people flee a persistent beggar as far as China's wall.

A drunk man lies asleep on the road, and a pious worshipper walks past and looks at him with scorn. The drunk man lifts his head and asks the worshipper to pass by him with pity, as the worshipper would want people to treat his own faults. He admits he is no hero in his conduct but asks to be overlooked gently.

A dervish (a Muslim holy man) is beaten and insulted by a gang. When he complains to his spiritual teacher, the teacher replies that a true dervish must accept hardship patiently. A deep river is not disturbed by a thrown stone, but a shallow brook is, so a person who is upset by injury is not yet deep in faith. Bearing trouble brings forgiveness, and since everyone returns to dust, one should be humble.

A standard, a military banner, complains to a roll-up curtain that it works harder. Both serve the same king, but the standard has marched through dust and danger while the curtain has had an easy life. The passage sets up a quarrel between the two servants.

A tent-pole, complaining that it is treated roughly while the tent's curtain is pampered, asks why the curtain should rank above it. The curtain replies that it lies humbly at the threshold, while the pole stands up proudly, and that whoever raises himself in pride will be brought low.

A holy man sees a big, strong man in a rage over some insulting names. He says the man can lift a heavy stone yet cannot bear a single harsh word, so his strength and manliness are false. The man is weak in mind and small in spirit.

A strong man should speak kindly rather than use his fists, since fighting someone proves nothing about courage. Strength without gentleness does not make a man a hero, because people come from dust and must stay humble to be truly men.

A joking old man from Baghdad gave his daughter to a shoemaker, who bit her lip so hard it bled. Her father confronted him, telling him to stop treating her like leather and to behave properly, since a bad habit that has taken root can only be removed by death.

A learned judge's ugly daughter has finally been married to a blind man, since no one else would take her. When a doctor arrives who can cure blindness, the father refuses to have the blind son-in-law treated. He fears that a husband who can see will leave his daughter, so he says a husband of an ugly woman should be blind.

Generosity is shown to be stronger than force. A wise man says that a generous person needs no courage. An inscription on a king's tomb says the open hand is stronger than the arm of power, and that the generous Hatim Tayi is remembered forever. Giving away a tenth of one's wealth is said to bring more gain, as pruning makes a vine yield more grapes.
