A beggar from North Africa stood among shopkeepers in Aleppo and told them that if the rich were fair and the poor were content, begging would end. He then says that contentment is wealth and that patience is the treasure of wise men, so a person without patience lacks wisdom.

Two brothers in Egypt chose different paths: one studied knowledge, the other pursued wealth. The scholar later became the wise ruler of Egypt, and the rich brother mocked him for remaining poor, which sets up the scholar's reply.

A wise man speaks to a king who holds great power. He says he is thankful to God for wisdom, which he calls the inheritance of the prophets, while the king has the lands of Pharaoh and Haman. He compares himself to a small ant that people trample, not a hornet whose sting they fear, and he is grateful he has no power to harm others.

A poor dervish (a Sufi holy man living in poverty) says he prefers to work for his own bread than to owe anything to someone else. A friend answers that a generous man in town would gladly help him, since that man serves holy men and is open to them. The friend is urging him to accept that help.

A poor man is told that a wealthy acquaintance would gladly help him if he knew of his need. He refuses, saying it is better to starve than to reveal his needs to another. He would rather mend an old cloak and stay content than beg the rich for a new one. He adds that getting into paradise through a neighbor's favor would be as bad as the torments of hell.

A Persian king sent a skilled physician to serve the Prophet Muhammad. For years no one among his followers asked for treatment, so the physician came to the Prophet and complained that he had no chance to use his skill.

A tribe eats only when truly hungry and stops while still having an appetite, and a physician says this explains their good health. The narrator adds that a physician advises restraint or indulgence depending on whether the patient risks excess or abstinence, and that health comes from the patient's diet.

A man keeps making vows to give up overeating and keeps breaking them. A wise man tells him his appetite is stronger than any vow, and that it will one day destroy him. He compares this to a man who raised a wolf cub, which later tore its owner apart.

A physician tells the Persian king Ardashir that a small daily amount of food is enough to sustain a person. Eating more is a burden the eater must carry. He adds that people eat in order to live and to praise God, not live only to eat.

Two travelers were locked in a walled-up room for a fortnight. The man who ate little and rarely survived, while the heavy eater died. The story shows that the frugal man outlasted the glutton when both were shut in without food.

A wise man says that a person who is used to simple living can bear hardship and survive it. A person who has indulged the body with comfort and luxury will struggle and may die when times become hard.

A philosopher warns his son not to eat too much, since overeating makes a person ill. The son replies that hunger can kill too, and that it is better to die from overeating than to suffer a constant craving for food.
Eat in moderation, the father says, quoting the Koran: neither so much that you vomit the food, nor so little that your strength fails. Food keeps a person alive, but too much of it harms the body.

Eating a sweet like rose preserve too often makes a person sick of it, while plain bread eaten after a long wait tastes as good as the sweet. The point is that rare simple things give more pleasure than constant luxury.

A wounded young soldier is offered a cure, but only by asking a notoriously stingy merchant. He refuses to ask, because the merchant might refuse and the cure might not work anyway, so the risk of asking seems no better than doing without.

Asking a mean person for favours is harmful, even if it gives the body something, because it costs the soul its dignity. Philosophers say a wise man would refuse even the water of immortality if it cost his reputation. Food from a kind giver tastes better than sweets from a sour one.

A scholar with a large family and little money asked a wealthy man for help, and was refused. The wealthy man thought such begging was shameful for an educated person. The lesson drawn is that a person in trouble should not bring their gloom to a friend, and should ask with a cheerful face, since a friendly appearance helps the request succeed.

A man who receives a larger allowance from a powerful patron loses the patron's regard, and he decides that the money has cost him his good name. He says that going hungry would be better than the shame of depending on charity.

A poor dervish, a holy man living on charity, went to a rich man for money. Seeing the rich man's sour, sullen face, he said nothing and left. He explained that he would not share his need with someone whose look showed no kindness, since such a man would likely meet his request with ill-temper.

Hatim Tayi, a famous generous man, was asked whether he had met anyone more independent than himself. He named a woodcutter who refused his invitation to a feast, saying he would rather eat bread earned by his own work than owe anything to Hatim.

Moses saw a poor dervish (a wandering holy man) buried in sand because he had no clothes. The dervish asked Moses to pray for him to be given provision. Moses prayed, but days later the dervish was led off to punishment after drinking wine, quarrelling and killing a man. The point is that the prayer for relief was answered in a way the dervish did not expect.

God gave each creature a share suited to it, and Sa'di says that if a cat had wings it would destroy sparrows' eggs. A weak man given power would likewise oppress others. Moses, admitting his own pride, quoted the Koran: if God gave people plenty, they would rebel across the earth.

The main point is that wealth and rank are dangerous for a lowly person. A base man who gains power brings trouble on himself, as an ant with wings is quickly crushed. So God, by withholding riches, may be protecting the person from harm he cannot see.

A lost traveller in the desert found a bag he thought held dry wheat, and was glad of it. When he learned it was pearls, he was disappointed, since pearls could not feed him. The point is that to a starving person in the desert, pearls are no more useful than stone or gold.

A thirsty Arab in the desert wishes, before he dies, for just one day with a stream of water to drink from. Another traveller, lost in the same desert with no food left, still has a few coins in his bag, which the passage sets beside the first man's wish.

A man lost in the desert died with coins beside him, and the verses he left in the sand say that gold cannot feed a starving man. A boiled turnip would be more welcome to a thirsty beggar in the desert than a bar of pure silver.

The narrator once complained because he had no shoes, until he met a man in a mosque who had no feet. Seeing this, he felt thankful for what he had and accepted his lack. The passage adds that a hungry person finds a plain turnip as pleasing as a roast fowl is to someone who is full.
A king on a winter hunt, far from his palaces, wants to spend the night in a peasant's cottage. One courtier objects that it is beneath a king's dignity, and suggests pitching a tent instead.

A peasant offers a king and his companions food and shelter, and the king is pleased. The peasant says the king's dignity is not lowered by visiting his humble home, while his courtly companions would not raise a peasant's status. The king rewards him with a robe and gifts.

A peasant walks beside a king's stirrup and tells him that the king's dignity was not lowered by visiting a humble home. Instead, the peasant says his own honor rose high, as if he were lifted to the sun, because the king's shadow fell on him.

A king asks a rich man, who had been a beggar and is still greedy for money, for a loan of some of his wealth. The king promises to repay it with thanks once the public revenue comes in. The story is set up to show what happens next in the tale.

A poor man refuses a king's gift, saying it would be unworthy to take it, since he collected it grain by grain. The king replies that the gift is meant for the Tartars, because impure things suit impure people. He gives the example of dung, which is only good for filling holes in a privy.
A king's officer is said to have refused a royal tax order and argued against it. The king then had the tax collected by force, on the reasoning that when fair words fail, harsher means must be used.

A merchant who had great wealth spent a whole night boasting to the narrator about his goods and property in far-off places. He also said he wanted to visit Alexandria, but thought the rough Mediterranean Sea made it impossible.

A merchant describes one last trading trip he plans before he retires. He will carry goods in a long circle through many lands, from Persia to China, Greece, India, Aleppo and Yamin, and then back home to Persia.

The speaker has been complaining about his restless life of trade, and Sa'di answers with a story. A merchant, dying in the desert, says that only contentment or the grave can fill the greedy eye of a worldly man.

A weak fisherman caught a strong fish, but he could not hold it, so the fish pulled the net from his hand and escaped. A slave went to fetch water and was swept away when the stream rose. Usually the net catches the fish, but here the fish got away with the net.
The fisherman's companions scold him for losing a large fish. He answers that it was not his day of luck, and that what happens to a fish or a fisherman is decided by fate, not by skill or effort.

A man with no hands or feet killed a millipede. A holy man who saw it said that the creature, with its thousand feet, could not escape death at the hands of someone who had none. The point is that when fate comes, speed and strength do not save a person, and no bow or weapon helps.

Sa'di sees a foolish, heavy man dressed in fine clothes and riding a fine horse. When asked why such a fool wears the garments of the learned, he replies that the finery is like a grand letter that describes the man as an ass, a dull beast, dressed up in gold lettering.

The speaker says a man who behaves like a beast is only a man in clothes and appearance, since everything he does is unlawful except what would justify shedding his blood. He also says a noble man who falls into poverty keeps his dignity, and a rich low-born man does not become noble just because he has gold.
A thief mocks a beggar for asking every petty person for a small coin. The beggar replies that asking for a small coin is better than having a hand cut off for a larger theft.

A dervish, a Sufi holy man, lived alone in a cave and looked down on kings without fear or respect. His saying is that whoever takes up begging stays a beggar for life, so one should give up greed and be as free as a prince. Contentment lets a person hold his head high.

A king invites a holy man to share his meal, and the holy man accepts because it follows the prophet's custom. When the king comes the next day to apologize for the trouble, the holy man welcomes him warmly and kindly.

Sa'di's teacher (the shaikh) was asked why he had shown the king unusual humility. He replied that a host should stand up for anyone he has seated or made his guest. He also said that he had arranged his life so he never listened to music.

A man who has learned to do without comforts: he can go without garden flowers, a soft pillow, a companion, or a horse, and sleep on a stone or walk on foot. The one thing he cannot do without is food, since his hungry stomach must be filled.

A friend answers Sa'di's plan to watch his words carefully: rivals only notice faults, so their view of a person is unreliable. The friend says enemies will find fault even with virtue, as a blind mole cannot see the sun. Their judgment says more about the enemies than about the good person.

A merchant lost a thousand dinars and told his son to keep it secret. Asked why, he said that telling people would bring a second harm: the scorn of his neighbors, who would be pleased by his misfortune and would pray for it to continue.

A young man who was learned and well-behaved never spoke in company of scholars. When his father asked why, he said he feared being asked about things he did not know and being shamed. He compared this to a Sufi who, forced by a cavalry officer to shoe a horse, had been stopped only because he was quietly working on his own sandal.

A learned man argued with an atheist, could not win, and left. Asked why, he said his knowledge rests on scripture and tradition, which the atheist does not accept, so arguing from them is pointless. The passage concludes that when someone cannot be persuaded by scripture, the best reply is to give no reply.

Sahban Wabil was said to be so eloquent that he could speak for a year without repeating a word. The passage adds that a good speech, however sweet, should not be repeated, because listeners tire of a pleasure once it has been given to them.

A wise man says that only a person who interrupts someone else before they have finished shows his own ignorance. He tells such a person to wait until a speaker has ended, and says a sensible man waits for a pause before he speaks.

A minister is asked by other courtiers what the king whispered to him. He refuses to say, because the king trusted him to keep it secret. A wise man, he adds, does not reveal what he learns in confidence, since doing so could cost him his life.

The speaker is asked whether a house is a good buy, and a Jewish neighbor vouches that it has no faults. The speaker replies that the house must be poor, since its neighbor is so unpleasant that no house beside him could be worth much. He adds that the house may rise in value once the neighbor dies.

A poet praised a robber chief in a long poem, and was stripped and driven out of the village. Cold and chased by dogs, he tried to throw a stone at them, but the ground was frozen. He then complained that the villagers set their dogs loose and tied up their stones, and the chief heard him.

A learned man is captured by a robber chief. Asked to name a favor, he asks only for his own clothes and to be allowed to leave, and he wants nothing more than to be left unharmed. Moved by this, the chief returns his clothes and gives him a fur robe and money.

Sa'di mocks a preacher with a harsh voice who thinks he speaks well. The passage says his preaching is like the croak of a raven or the braying of a donkey, and it quotes a Koran verse calling the donkey's bray the most unpleasant of noises.

A preacher, out of spite, pretends to tell a fellow preacher about a dream. In the dream, the other man's voice has become pleasant and people are charmed by it. The mocking praise is meant to tease him about a flaw in his speech that his townsmen had avoided mentioning out of respect for his rank.

A preacher, after hearing a dream-vision about his weakness, learns his voice is unpleasant and vows to preach more softly. The narrator then says he is troubled by friends who turn his faults into virtues and see his thorns as roses.

The mosque's manager wanted a man with a harsh voice to stop calling the faithful to prayer, since his singing drove people away. Rather than tell him so directly, the manager paid him ten dinars a month to go elsewhere, and the man accepted and left.

A man complains to a nobleman that he was paid ten dinars to leave his post, when others would have paid him twenty to move elsewhere. The nobleman mocks him: he should refuse, since he might get fifty, and says the man's harsh voice grates on him more than digging rock with a mattock.

A holy man hears a reader with a harsh, loud voice chanting the Koran. He asks whether he is paid for it, and the man says he is not, but reads for God's sake. The holy man replies that reading so harshly will bring shame on Islam.

Sultan Mahmud loved his slave Ayaz far more than his many beautiful slave-women. Asked why, the minister Husan Maimandi answers that whoever the king favors seems good to everyone, and whoever he rejects is ignored, so beauty depends on the viewer's regard, not on the person.

A holy man is so in love with a beautiful person that he cannot hide his feelings or control them, and he will not give up the attraction even though others criticise him. When the speaker asks where his reason has gone, he replies that love overpowers chastity, and that someone deep in such a passion cannot stay pure.

A man has fallen in love and despairs. His friends warn him to give up this useless desire, since many others suffer the same chains of passion. He answers that he will not listen, because his eyes are fixed only on the wish of the beloved.

A lover must not let concern for his own life turn his heart from his beloved. If he cannot reach her by any clever plan, he should keep pressing forward, even under wounds, and if he gets close he will seize her sleeve or die at her threshold.

A young man's relatives advise him and set limits on him, but he ignores them, like a sick man craving sweets instead of the bitter medicine meant to cure him. The passage then turns to a woman he loves, and the people around him tell her about him.
A young man, who is in love, sees the princess who has caused his pain coming toward him on horseback. He weeps and says she has come back, perhaps out of pity for the one she has wounded.

The princess asks the young man who he is, where he comes from, and what his work is. He is so overcome with love that he cannot speak. She then tells him she too belongs to the dervishes, a group of religious ascetics, and is devoted to them.

A young lover, moved by his beloved's kind words, answers that it is strange he can still exist or speak in her presence. He then dies at her tent door. The story suggests that dying there is no surprise, and that surviving such an encounter would have been the real wonder.

The master, who is attracted to a handsome pupil, says he is so absorbed in the boy that he would not even notice an arrow aimed at himself. Although he does not scold or correct the boy like the other scholars, he whispers flattering words to him when they are alone together in a corner.

A young man asks his teacher to point out any faults he can see in him. The teacher replies that he sees only virtue in the young man. He adds that a lover sees only the good in the beloved, even when the beloved has many faults.

A friend asks where he has been, having missed him. He answers that it is better to be missed than to be tiresome through constant presence. The lover then scolds the beloved for arriving late, and says that someone seen rarely is more desired than someone seen too often.

A lover complains that his beloved grows jealous when he visits with others, and that even a brief moment with a rival nearly kills him with jealousy. She answers lightly that she is a torch shining for the whole gathering, so it does not matter to her if the moth burns itself up.

The narrator explains why he sent no message while away. He did not want anyone else, not even a messenger, to see his beloved's face, because he was jealous. He says he would never give up this feeling, even if threatened, and that no one could ever tire of looking at her.

A learned man was deeply attached to a certain person and endured insults and rough treatment from him patiently. The speaker told him that, though his attachment was innocent, it was not fitting for a scholar to expose himself to slander and put up with the coarse behaviour of common people.

The speaker tells a friend to stop scolding him, because he has thought it over and finds it easier to bear public shame for his beloved than to give up her company. He adds that it is harder to stop looking at a beloved than to keep pursuing her. He concludes that anyone who gives his heart to a beloved who deceives him hands his good name over to someone else.

A lover must accept hurt from the one he cannot live without, just as a tethered antelope cannot leap away. The speaker once tried to set terms with his beloved and later regretted it. He now gives his heart over completely, to be drawn near or pushed away as she pleases.

The speaker once had a close bond with a young man he admired for his music and beauty. When the young man's behavior displeased him, the speaker ended the friendship and told him to go his own way, since he would not heed advice.

A speaker overhears a man leaving who says that the bat's dislike of the sun cannot dim the sun's light. The speaker, who has lost the man's company, then begs him to come back. When the man finally returns, his once-beautiful voice and looks have faded.

A young man, whose beauty has faded as a beard grows in, comes back to the speaker hoping to be embraced. The speaker refuses. He reminds the young man that he once turned his lover away, and now that his youth is gone, he has no claim to the same attention.

Sa'di addresses a beloved who has grown a beard. He says the beloved should court only those who want him and charm only those who pay for it, since a young man's fresh beard-growth is what his admirers desire. He compares this to chives, which grow back the more they are cut, and notes the beloved left smooth-faced and returned bearded.

Sa'di speaks with a young man whose beard is just growing in. The young man says that youth will end whatever he does about his beard, and that he wishes he could hold on to life as he controls his beard. Sa'di asks why a beard has appeared on his beautiful face, and the young man replies that his face must be wearing black to mourn its lost beauty.

A parrot is locked in a cage with a crow and is disgusted by the crow's ugliness. It wishes they were as far apart as east from west, and says no one else in the world would be as badly matched with it as the crow is.

The crow, too, has become impatient and deeply annoyed at being kept in the company of the parrot. He complains bitterly about his bad luck and the turning of the heavens, wringing his hands and calling his fate unlucky.

The speaker is complaining that he has been forced to keep company with a conceited, empty-headed chatterbox, which he sees as a kind of imprisonment he does not deserve. He ends with a saying: no one will go near a wall on which a person's portrait has been painted, meaning that such a companion makes others shun him.

A holy man (zahid) sits with wandering singers, and one of them tells him that if he dislikes them he should not look sour, since he is already unpleasant company. He is like a dry stalk among roses and tulips, out of place in their gathering. The point is that the learned man is scorned by the unlearned, and the unlearned are scorned in turn by the learned.

The passage is a fragment of comparisons, likely describing someone or something as cold and harsh. It compares it to an opposing storm, a chilling winter wind, a snowball, and a lump of ice, all images of cold.

A man recalls a long-time travelling companion and close friend. Over some small matter the friend offended him, and the friendship ended. Even so, both men still felt a lingering goodwill toward each other.

A man recites two couplets by the narrator in a gathering, and the friends who hear him praise not the beauty of the verses but his own generosity in quoting them. The verses describe a lover whose mistress's smiles add salt to his wounds, yet he is glad her curls touch his hand, as a generous man's sleeve is glad to be grasped by poor dervishes (wandering Sufi holy men).

The speaker says that a friend, who had once praised him extravagantly, now regrets the end of their friendship and admits his own fault. The speaker, who also wanted to make up, sends verses that accuse the friend of breaking their agreement and of breaking off first. He says he had given up other company and trusted the friend completely.

A man is left with his dead wife's mother, who stays in his house because of the dowry he must return or keep. He says her presence is worse than his wife's absence. He compares it to a thorn left after a rose is taken, and says a rival is worse than losing many friends.

The speaker recalls walking down a street in the hottest days of summer and seeing a beautiful young person. Overcome by the noon heat and his thirst, he sought shelter in the shade of a wall, hoping someone would bring him water.

A narrator sees a beautiful woman in the shadowy entrance of a house. She hands him a cold drink of water with sugar and wine spirit mixed in, and he takes it from her hand. He says her beauty is too great for words to describe.

The speaker says that his thirst cannot be quenched by water, even by oceans of it. He calls happy anyone who sees a beautiful face every morning. He adds that a person drunk on wine lies awake and restless half the night, while one drunk on God, the cup-bearer, will only wake at the day of judgment.

The narrator describes meeting a young man in a mosque at Kashghar who is extraordinarily beautiful. He says the youth has a charming, bold manner, and jokes that he may have learned these ways from an angel.

A young student is reciting a stock grammar example, "Zaid beat Amru," as if it were real news. The speaker teases him, saying the Khwarazm and Khitai rulers have made peace and asking whether this fight between Zaid and Amru is still going on. When the student asks whether the speaker knows Sa'di's poems, the speaker replies with a joke: the grammar student is now attacking him, just as Zaid attacks Amru in the example.

A man who is strict about Arabic vowel marks suggests speaking Persian, since people should be addressed according to their understanding. The narrator replies that the other man's obsession with grammar had left no room for reason in their hearts.

A traveler tells Sa'di that he regrets not knowing earlier that Sa'di was among them, so he could have offered his service. Sa'di replies that in the man's presence he cannot even claim to be himself. The reply is a polite way of saying he feels overwhelmed by the other's greatness or affection.

A holy man who lived alone in a cave refuses to come into the city. He says the city has beautiful people who might tempt him, and that on a muddy road even an elephant could slip, meaning a strong man can fall into temptation there.

The speaker and his friend kiss each other and then part. He says that kissing a beloved's cheek and then saying goodbye in the same breath is pointless. He adds that if he did not die of grief on the day of parting, the beloved would think he was not sincere in his love.

A poor dervish (a wandering holy man) travelling with a caravan was robbed along with everyone else. Unlike the merchants, who wept and complained uselessly, he stayed calm. The narrator asks him whether the robbers had taken his gold too, since he seems so unbothered.

A man says he was not so attached to his pet that losing it would break his heart, and that one should not fix the heart on anything so firmly that letting go becomes hard. The speaker then tells of his own youthful love for a beautiful young man, whom he describes as the centre of his sight and the most desired thing in his life.

After his death, the speaker says, no other loving friendship can be entered into, since no one can compare with him. He grieves at the grave and wishes he had died first, so he would not have to see the world without his friend.

The speaker sits by the grave of a beloved person and mourns. He says that the dead man, who once had rose-like cheeks, now has thorns growing from his grave. After losing him, the speaker resolves to give up pleasure and social life, comparing this to a sea voyage that is profitable but feared for its dangers.

A lover speaks of his pain: once he was proud and joyful in the garden of pleasure, but now he writhes like a snake because his beloved is gone. Then a king hears of Majnun, the famous lover of Laila, who has gone mad and wandered into the desert, and orders that he be brought before him.

A friend asks Majnun why he has left human company to live like an animal. Majnun answers that his critics would understand if they could see Laila, the woman he loves. He wishes they could see her, so that they would excuse him.

The passage is a fragment from a longer tale. Ladies at court, struck by the beauty of a slave, would cut their own fingers while peeling oranges, and the speaker says the reality of her beauty proves the story true. The king then decides to see Laila himself, and she is brought to his courtyard after a search of the Arab tribes.

Majnun, a lover famous for his devotion to Layla, looks at her and sees her as a beautiful woman, while the king sees only a plain, weak woman who seems less lovely than his lowest servants. Majnun tells the king that he would need to see Layla with a lover's eyes to understand her beauty, and that the king cannot share Majnun's suffering.

The speaker says he wants a companion who suffers from the same love-sickness, so he can talk about his beloved all day. Only someone who has felt that pain can understand it, he argues, just as a wound can only be understood by one who is also wounded.

It is pointless to describe the pain of a hornet's sting to someone who has never been stung. Until the listener is in a similar state, the speaker's suffering will seem like a made-up story. The speaker says his pain cannot be compared to another's: the other holds salt in his hand, while he holds it on a wound.

In a shipwreck, a young man was caught in a whirlpool with his beloved. When the pilot offered to save him, he told the pilot to leave him and save his beloved instead. Even as he was dying, he said this, and people admired him for it.

The passage says that a true lover does not abandon the beloved when danger comes. It urges the reader to listen to the lovers' story and to give the whole heart to the one chosen, God, shutting out everything else. The author claims that Laila and Majnun, the famous lovers, could learn about love from this chapter.
A young man asks Sa'di, a Persian speaker, to come to a dying old man who speaks only Persian. The old man may be trying to state his last wishes, and the young man hopes Sa'di can understand him.

An old man, near death, recites lines saying he had only a few moments of enjoyment and only a few mouthfuls at life's table before fate ended it. The narrator translates these lines for some Syrians, who are surprised that an old man still cares so much about worldly life. When asked how he feels, the old man only says, "What shall I say?"

A man in pain is compared to someone losing a tooth, and the speaker tells him not to fear death. He argues that a strong body does not guarantee a long life, and a dangerous illness does not mean death is near.

A sick old man is offered a doctor's medicine, but he refuses, saying his body is already falling apart. He compares himself to a house about to collapse, where only decoration is being done. Once the body's balance is broken, no charm or medicine can help.

An old rich man tells his guest that he had no children for many years. He prayed for a son at a tree in the valley that people visit to ask for their needs, and he got this handsome son only after many nights of asking God there.

The old father hears his son whispering that he wishes his father dead, and the father is pleased by the boy's cleverness. The speaker then turns on the father: he never visited his own father's grave, so why should he expect care from his son? The point is that children copy what parents do.

A young man, proud of his strength, pushed hard on a march and collapsed at the foot of a hill. An old man who had kept a steady pace told him that steady progress beats rushing ahead and breaking down. He compared the fast Arab horse, which tires quickly, with the camel, which keeps going day and night.

A cheerful young man is later found grave and unhappy after marrying and having children. When asked why, he says that becoming a father ended his playfulness, since a man with children must leave merriment to the young.

The speaker laments that youth and strength are gone and cannot return, comparing himself to ripe corn past cutting and a lion that has lost its grip. He then tells an old woman who dyes her gray hair black that she can change her hair by art but cannot straighten her bent back.

A young man speaks harshly to his mother, and she reminds him of how helpless he once was as a baby, clinging to her. Now he is strong and fierce, and she is old and weak, so she asks him to remember how he depended on her.

A stingy rich man's son fell gravely ill, and friends urged him to recite the whole Koran or sacrifice an animal for his son's recovery. He chose the Koran, because it was close at hand, while his herds of animals were far away.

A holy man criticises someone who recites the Koran readily but is unwilling to give money to charity. He says such a person will repeat prayers a hundred times yet struggles to part with even a single coin.

The tale says that teaching only works when a person has good natural ability. A rich man's dull son learned nothing from his tutor, and the tutor said he was making him a fool. The writer compares this to polishing bad iron, washing a dog, and sending an ass on pilgrimage: none of these changes its nature.
A wise man urges his children to seek knowledge rather than wealth. He argues that money and rank are lost on a journey, through theft or gradual waste, while knowledge lasts forever.

Learning is a lasting wealth that cannot be lost the way money can. A learned man is respected wherever he goes, while an ignorant man is looked down on and lives in want. So a son who wants his father's inheritance should gain his father's learning, since money can be spent in ten days.

In this tale, a rebellion in Syria drives everyone from their homes. Learned sons of peasants end up serving kings as ministers, while sons of nobles, lacking real understanding, must beg from village to village. The point is that education, not birth, decides who rises.

A tutor beat a king's son hard, and the boy complained to the king. When the king asked why the tutor treated the prince worse than an ordinary subject's child, the tutor replied that the prince must learn to think before speaking and to weigh his actions before acting, since kings need this most.

Kings are watched far more closely than ordinary people. A king's single foolish word spreads everywhere, while a poor man's many mistakes go unnoticed. So a young prince needs more careful training in manners than other boys. Anyone not taught good manners as a boy, the passage says, will lose good fortune when grown.

A young, flexible branch can be bent into shape, but a dry, hardened one cannot be straightened without fire. The point is that children are easiest to shape when they are young. The king praised this lesson and rewarded the teacher who gave it.

The speaker describes a harsh schoolmaster in West Africa. He is sour, bitter, and unkind, and his reading of the Koran depresses the pious. He rules over the boys and girls in his care so strictly that they cannot smile or speak, and he beats them and puts their legs in stocks.

The parents removed a harsh teacher after learning of his violence and gave the school to a gentle, quiet man. The children, no longer afraid of authority, grew more unruly under him than they had been before.

Children who knew their schoolmaster was lenient stopped studying and played instead, even breaking their tablets over one another's heads. A fortnight later, the narrator found that the children had been forced to make friends with the same master and restore him to his post.

The speaker is angry that a devil has been made a teacher of angels, and an old man answers with a story. A king sent his son to school with a silver tablet bearing the words that a teacher's strictness does more good than a father's indulgence.

A king gave his son to a teacher and expected him to succeed, but the prince did not learn well, while the teacher's own sons did. The teacher replied that the teaching was the same, but the students' abilities differed. He compared this to gold being found only in some stones, and to the same star producing ordinary leather in one place and perfumed leather in another.

A learned elder tells his student that people worry about food more than about God, and that if they cared for God as much, they would do better in Paradise. He argues that God, who already gave them body and mind before birth, will not fail to provide their daily bread.

A father tells his son that on judgment day God will ask what he has done in life, not where his family came from. The passage then compares this to the cloth on the Kaaba in Mecca: it is valued not for being silk but for having been close to something holy.

According to the books of philosophers, scorpions are not born in the usual way. Instead, they eat through their mother's womb and tear open her belly to come into the world. The skin fragments found in scorpion holes are given as proof.

The passage says that people who treat their parents well when young tend to be respected and loved when older. A dying father then warns his son that someone who is ungrateful to his own family cannot expect good fortune.

The scorpion is asked why it does not come out in winter. It replies that it is no different from its summer self, so it has no reason to come out then either. The point is that a creature's nature does not change with the season, so it acts the same way all year.

During a quarrel among pilgrims walking to Mecca, Sa'di overhears a rider in a camel-litter remark to his companion that it is strange how ivory pawns become queens on reaching the end of a chessboard. The passage breaks off there, so its full point is unclear.

The passage is a rebuke to a pilgrim who quarrels with his fellow travelers and hurts them. The speaker says he is not a true pilgrim, and praises the camel instead, which bears its load patiently and eats thorns without complaint. The point is that patient endurance matters more than rank or status.

A philosopher warns an Indian fireworks teacher that the sport is unsuitable for a man whose house is made of straw, since fireworks could burn it. The passage then advises that a person should speak only when his words are sound, and should not ask questions when he already expects a bad answer.

A man with sore eyes asked a horse doctor for treatment, and the doctor used the cure he gave animals, which blinded him. When the man complained to a judge, the judge ruled that he had no remedy, since a sensible man would not have gone to an animal doctor in the first place.

A person who gives an important task to someone without experience will be shamed and seen by wise people as foolish. A sensible man does not trust serious matters to someone of limited ability. Even a mat-maker, though a weaver, would not be hired to work in a silk factory.

A famous religious leader's son has died, and he is asked what should be carved on the tomb. He says Koran verses should not be placed where they could wear away or be trampled or defiled, so a short poem is better. The poem imagines the dead son telling a grieving father to wait for spring, when roses will bloom from his grave.

A holy man sees a rich man beating his slave and tells him that God gave him power over the slave, so he should thank God and not treat the slave so harshly. The point is that power over another person is a gift that calls for gratitude and restraint.

A slave owner is warned not to be so angry with his servant or hurt him in body or spirit. The speaker points out that the owner could only buy the servant, not create him, and that a greater Master, God, has power over them both.

On the day of judgment, a good slave will rise to heaven while a cruel master goes to hell, which would be shameful for the master. The saying urges a master not to vent anger on a slave who obeys him, because the roles could be reversed on that day.
The narrator travelled with a guard who was physically very strong and skilled with weapons. However, he had been raised in comfort and had never travelled, so he had no real experience of the world.
The young man has never seen real war, yet he boasts of his strength. He knocks down old ruins and uproots huge trees, then challenges the world to bring an elephant so he can show his arms.

In this tale, the speaker and his companions are caught on the road when two Hindu robbers jump out from behind a rock. One carries a club and the other a mallet, and the speaker calls to a young man in his group, asking why he has stopped.

A young archer, who thought he could fight off an attacker, loses his nerve when the enemy comes close. The narrator and his companions then have no choice but to give up their weapons and clothes to save their lives. The passage ends by advising that important matters go to someone skilled and experienced.

A strong young man, however big and powerful, will still shake with fear when he meets an enemy in battle. An experienced man is the best choice to scout a battlefield, just as a learned scholar is the best person to explain the law.

The rich man's son boasts that his father's tomb is grander than the poor man's, which is only a few bricks and mortar. The poor man's son replies that his father, unlike the rich man's, will rise to heaven quickly, while the rich man's father is weighed down by his heavy stone.

Death is easier for the poor, the passage says, because they carry less to the grave, much as a donkey walks more easily under a lighter load. A wealthy man who has enjoyed comfort finds dying harder, and a released prisoner is better off than a prince newly taken captive.

A man dressed as a dervish, a holy wanderer, but without their humility, criticizes the rich. He says the poor cannot give because they lack money, and the rich lack the wish to give. The speaker, who depends on the generosity of the great, disagrees and answers him.

The passage praises wealthy people for the good they do with their riches. They shelter the poor, feed the hungry, care for widows and the elderly, and give to charity through endowments, alms, and religious offerings.

The speaker asks how a poor man who can barely manage his prayers could ever reach a rich man's status. He argues that the rich find it easier to be pious and dignified, since comfort and good clothing support devotion. A hungry or ragged person, he says, cannot have much zeal, generosity, or ability to act.

Sa'di contrasts the man who has enough with the man who has nothing. The poor man cannot rest, since he worries about tomorrow and his next meal, while the rich man is calm and free to turn his mind to God. Poverty and peace, he says, do not go together.

Sa'di says that a poor man's mind is as troubled as his purse, so the prayers of the rich are more pleasing to God. Rich people can pray with a settled mind, while the poor are distracted by their needs. He adds that poverty is a hardship in this world and the next.

The speaker rejects a rival's claim that a saying of the Prophet, "poverty is my glory", justifies being poor. He says the saying applies to people who accept hardship patiently, not to those who pose as pious in order to live on charity. He tells such a person to stop begging and stop showing off his devotions.

Sa'di argues that poverty without religious knowledge can lead a poor man to lose his faith. He says that only wealth lets a person do charitable deeds, such as clothing the naked or freeing prisoners, so poor men cannot match the dignity of the rich. He then points to the Koran's promise of provision for the faithful.

Those who spend all their time earning a living are shut out from this share of good fortune, and enjoying what is present is approved by Providence. A thirsty man dreams that the whole earth is a spring. Someone who has suffered hardship will, driven by appetite, take risks.

A greedy man who does not care about consequences or punishment cannot tell lawful from forbidden. He would take a clod of earth for a bone, or a corpse on a bier for a tray of food. The writer contrasts this with the wealthy, who are protected from forbidden things, and then appeals to a judge's fairness.

Sa'di lists the harms that poverty can bring a person: debt and prison, the loss of a good name, punishment for theft, and in some cases sinful desire. He says even brave men have been caught stealing out of need, and a poor man driven by strong appetite may fall into sin.

The rich, the passage says, can have a new beautiful companion each night and day, so they have no wish for forbidden desires or sin. The author asks why a heart captured by such beauties would turn to the beauties of Yaghma, a city known for its lovely people.

People who have enough food do not throw stones at the dates on the trees. Hungry people, however, often turn to theft, and a starving dog grabs meat without asking where it came from. Poverty has led many chaste people into wrongdoing, so self-control does not last when a person is starving.

In this part of the tale, a dervish (a wandering holy man) loses his patience and angrily answers a speaker. He accuses the speaker of praising something so extravagantly that it seems to cure poverty and open the storehouse of God's provision.

The passage describes a group of people who are proud, arrogant and greedy for money and rank. They speak only to insult, look at others only with scorn, and look down on scholars as beggars and on the poor as shabby. They think themselves better than everyone else.

A wise saying is quoted: a man who is less humble than others but richer than them is really a beggar, and a rich fool who insults a learned man should be counted an ass. When the speaker is told not to slander the rich, since they are generous, he replies that they are really slaves to money.

Sa'di says that a person with great abilities or resources is of no use if they do not help others. Such a person gives nothing and acts only when there is something in it for them, or expects thanks in return for every favour.

A miser hoards money in misery, and his heir spends it freely. Sa'di replies that only a beggar, who has needed help, can truly judge a rich man's stinginess, just as only a touchstone, a dark stone used to test gold, can show which gold is pure.

A great man speaks of rulers who keep rude doorkeepers to turn away worthy people and say the master is not at home. He says this is true when the master has no sense or judgment, so the porter is right to say no one is in the house. The narrator replies that such rulers are excused, since they are worn out by demanding petitioners.

The passage argues that greed is never satisfied: a greedy eye can no more be filled with wealth than a well can be filled with night dew, even if desert sand became pearls. It adds a tale about Hatim Tayi, a famous generous man, who would be swarmed by beggars if he lived in a city. The speaker then says that the one who pities the beggars really envies their possessions.

The speaker describes a heated debate in which each side answers the other's moves, like a game of chess, until the rival runs out of arguments. Sa'di then compares a fluent speaker with no real argument to a fort with a showy weapon display over its gate but no soldiers inside. In the end the speaker wins, and the rival falls silent.

When a debate is lost, ignorant people often turn to insults and violence instead, as Azor did with his son Abraham in the Koran. The narrator describes a brawl in which he and his opponent tore at each other's clothes and beards while a crowd watched and enjoyed it.

Two men argued over the merits of the rich and the poor, and they asked a judge to settle it. The judge studied them, thought carefully, and began by saying that every rose has its thorn, meaning that neither wealth nor poverty is without its drawbacks.

Almost every pleasure comes with a matching danger: wine brings a hangover, treasure is guarded by a dragon, and worldly joy hides death. Good and bad things are mixed together, as roses grow among thorns, and the same holds among the rich, where some are grateful and some are not.

Among the poor, some accept their state patiently and some are restless. The passage says that the rich who are humble and the poor who are strong in resolve both stand near a great Judge, and that the best of the rich help the sorrows of the poor. The best of the poor do not seek the company of the rich, because God is enough for those who trust in him.

The judge (cazi) turns his criticism from the speaker to a dervish, a holy man who lives by poverty. He says that some rich people are narrow-minded and stingy with God's gifts. They hoard money and neither use it nor give it away.

The rich, who have plenty, do not care about the suffering of the poor, even if the whole land faces drought or flood. They say that if others die, it does not matter to them, since they are safe. The passage calls such people mean-spirited and says they are the ones who feel nothing for travellers dying in the desert.

The passage describes a second kind of rich man, one who lays out generous feasts, openly announces his generosity, and shows humility. Such men seek a good name and forgiveness, and want the benefits of both this world and the next. The passage then compares them to the servants of a ruler, whose full title it lists in flattering terms.

The narrator describes a judge (cazi) who praised a ruler with extravagant flattery, claiming the ruler's kindness to mankind exceeded even a father's love for his son and that God made him ruler of the world. Having gone so far beyond what was expected, the narrator and his companions felt they had to accept this and offered an apology for their earlier words.

After a quarrel, the speakers made peace, and they ended with two verses. The first tells the poor not to complain about the turns of fortune. The second tells the rich to spend and give generously, so they can enjoy both this world and the next.

Wealth exists to make life comfortable, not for a person to live only in order to hoard it. A wise man said the fortunate person is the one who spends and gives generously, while the unfortunate one dies leaving everything behind, and such a person should not be prayed for.

Moses told Carum to be generous as God had been generous to him, but Carum refused and came to a bad end. The passage concludes that whoever keeps wealth for themselves instead of giving to others loses their future benefit, so one should share wealth with others as God shared it with oneself.

Give generously without attaching conditions, so that the good you do is not turned into a debt owed back to you. Sa'di adds that a generous person should not spoil the gift by expecting a return, and should thank God for the chance to give at all.
Serving a king is not a favor you do for him that he owes you thanks for. Instead, the one to thank is God, who gave you this position of service.

Someone who gathers wealth but never spends it, or who gains knowledge but never puts it into practice, has worked for nothing useful. A person who has read much but does not act on it is ignorant, no better than a donkey carrying books it cannot understand.

Learning should serve to strengthen religious life, not to make money or gain worldly advantage. Someone who sells his self-control, piety, and knowledge for such gain is like a farmer who gathers his harvest into a pile and burns it.

A learned man who lacks self-control is like a blind torch-bearer: he lights the way for others but cannot see it himself. Someone who risks everything on a useless gamble gains nothing and loses what he staked.

Wise people add honour to a kingdom, and pious people add honour to religion. Kings need the company of wise men more than wise men need the company of kings, so the poet advises a king to trust his affairs to learned people, even though government is not their usual work.
Three things cannot last without the things that go with them: wealth needs trade, knowledge needs debate, and rule needs good government. Each one fails to endure when its partner is missing.

Showing mercy to the wicked is described as a kind of cruelty to the good, and forgiving an oppressor as harshness toward the oppressed. Helping a base-born man also leads him to expect an equal share in your fortune.

Do not trust the friendship of kings or the sweet singing of young boys, since both fade quickly, like a dream or a vision. Do not give your love to someone who has many lovers, or else expect to be parted from them.

Keep your secrets to yourself, because a friend may later become an enemy, and an enemy may become a friend. Once a secret is spoken, it cannot be taken back, like water that escapes a dam. Say nothing in private that you would not say in public.

A defeated enemy who offers peace and seeks friendship most likely wants to regain strength and become dangerous again. So a weak enemy should not be ignored, because a small spark can grow into a fire that destroys everything. It is best to deal with him while you still can.
Someone who forms an alliance with your enemies is planning harm to his own friends. So a wise man should cut ties with a friend who has joined forces with his foes.
When you are unsure how to act, choose the option that causes the least offence. Do not answer a gentle person harshly, and do not push someone into conflict when they are seeking peace.

Put simply, a person should not risk their life in any matter while money can still settle it. Only when every clever plan has failed is it right to reach for a sword. The passage explains that fighting is the last resort.
Do not show mercy to a defeated enemy, because if he recovers he will show you none. Do not mock a beaten opponent, since a weakened man still has inner strength and is still a man.

A wicked man's death, the passage says, frees others from his harm and spares him God's punishment. Kindness is good, but it is wrong to soothe a wicked person's wounds, as the story of the man who showed pity to a snake shows: the snake turned out to be a danger to people.

Sa'di advises that you should never take an enemy's advice, though it is wise to listen to it so you can do the opposite. If your enemy points to the straight path, you should take the left one instead.
Two kinds of people harm religion and government: a ruler who shows no mercy, and a holy man who lacks knowledge. A ruler should not govern unless he himself obeys God's will.

A king should control his anger so that his friends do not lose trust in him, because anger burns the angry man first and only sometimes reaches his enemies. Sa'di says that people, made of dust, should not carry pride and passion. When he asks a holy man for teaching, the man tells him to be patient like the earth and to bury his learning.

A bad-tempered person is his own worst enemy and cannot get away from him. Even if a wicked man climbed to heaven to escape trouble, his own evil heart would follow him there and bring him misfortune.
When your enemies are fighting among themselves, stay calm and keep to your own side. If they are united, prepare your defenses, because your own side may be divided.
Do not be the one to deliver bad news if someone else can deliver it first. Let the nightingale bring happy news of spring, and leave the owl, a bird of ill omen, to bring the bad.

Do not trust flattery from a rival or a parasite, and do not pay them for it. Such people flatter in order to gain something, and if they are refused, they will list your faults. A fool who lives on praise is like a corpse that looks briefly full when laid out on a bier.
A speaker's words cannot be judged correct until someone points out their faults. So do not be proud of your eloquence just because a fool praises it or you approve of it yourself.

Everyone believes his own mind is sound and his own child is handsome. The passage shows this with a Muslim and a Jew arguing over a document. Each swears that he is lying if he is not telling the truth, and each says he would become the other's faith. The point is that no one would admit ignorance.

Greed is never satisfied, while a modest person is content with little. A small loaf can fill a hungry stomach, but the whole world cannot satisfy a greedy eye. The father's advice is to control lust now, like putting out a fire, so one does not burn later in hell.

Those who fail to do good while they have the means will suffer when they lose those means. A person who hates people is the most unfortunate of all, because when trouble comes he has no friends to help him.

Those who trade their religion for worldly gain are compared to asses. The passage recalls how the brothers sold Joseph and gained nothing from it. It then quotes God's warning not to serve Satan, and says that by following an enemy's advice people have broken faith with a friend.

Things made quickly are quickly lost, and things made slowly are worth more. The writer compares slow-made porcelain with cheap mass-made cups, and easily found glass with a ruby that is hard to get. He adds that a chicken can look after itself at once, while a human child cannot.

Patience reaches its goal, while haste leads to ruin. The narrator says he saw in the desert a slow, careful traveller overtake one who rushed ahead. A fast horse tires out from its speed, while a camel driver steadily keeps his animal moving until the journey ends.

The main point is that an ignorant person would do best to stay silent, and that speaking without thought shows emptiness. A wise man tells a fool who is trying to teach a donkey to speak that he should learn silence from the animal instead. The passage ends by saying a person should either speak with careful judgment or keep quiet like an animal.

Someone who argues with a person more learned than himself, in order to look wise, only shows others that he is a fool. The quoted lesson is that one should not contradict a superior in conversation, even when one thinks one knows better.

A person who keeps company with wicked people will gain nothing good from them. Even an angel who joined with a demon would pick up the demon's cruelty, deceit and hypocrisy. Just as a wolf tears skins rather than mending them, the wicked cannot teach virtue.
Do not reveal people's hidden faults. If you do, you will shame them and also lose other people's trust in you.
A person who gains knowledge but does not act on it is like a farmer who ploughs his field and then never plants seed. The effort is made, but nothing grows from it.

A handsome appearance does not show good character, because virtue lies in the heart, not the outward look. A person's mind and learning can be judged in a day, but judging the heart's hidden faults may take years.

Whoever picks a fight with powerful people will only hurt himself. The speaker says a man who thinks himself great is like a squinter who sees double, and a man who plays at butting a ram will end with a broken head.

The passage says that fighting a lion or a sword is not what a wise person does. It advises not to challenge an angry person with opposition before they have already overcome you and forced you to submit.
A weak man who challenges a strong man is only ruining himself. Raised in comfort, with no real strength, he is foolish to pit his arm against an iron wrist.
The speaker says that someone who refuses to take advice is still ready to hear criticism. If advice does not reach the listener's ear, then the listener should at least accept a rebuke in silence.
Lazy people cannot bear hard-working people. They behave like street dogs that snarl at and block hunting dogs when they meet them.

A petty person who cannot match someone else in goodness attacks them with spite instead. The envious man will still find a way to insult you, even though in your presence he might be struck speechless.
Taking advice from women is considered a mistake, and being generous to spendthrifts is a fault. Showing mercy to a fierce leopard is unfair to the gentle sheep it may attack.

Whoever leaves a defeated enemy alive is his own enemy, because a wise man kills a snake when he has the chance. Others argue that captives should be held, since they can still be killed later, but a killing cannot be undone. The passage concludes that one should wait before acting, because a shot arrow cannot be called back.

A learned person who argues with an ignorant person cannot expect to keep his dignity. If the ignorant one wins by talking loudly, that is no surprise, just as a worthless stone can chip a gold cup. The wise person's worth stays the same, even when the crude person treats him roughly.

Natural talent without learning is a loss, and learning without natural talent is wasted effort. A person's worth comes from their own qualities, not from their family or origins. Noble ancestry did not help Canaan, the son of Noah, because his character was bad.

A true thing shows itself by its own qualities, not by what others claim for it. As the musk is known by its scent rather than by the perfumers' claims, a skilled person needs no announcement, because their ability is visible in their work.

A wise man is quiet but full of good qualities, like a jar of medicine in a chemist's shop, while an ignorant man is loud and empty, like a war drum. The passage adds that a learned man among ignorant people is out of place, like a beautiful person among the blind or the Koran in a home of unbelievers.
A friend who took years to win over should not be pushed away all at once. Just as a stone slowly turns into a ruby, a friendship built over time can be broken in a moment by a single harsh blow.

Reason is controlled by passion, just as a man who dotes on his wife is ruled by a clever woman. The passage advises shutting the door of joy on any home where a woman's scolding voice can be heard. Word count: about 37.

Good sense without firmness is only cunning, and firmness without good sense is only stubbornness. Power should come after prudence and judgment, because power given to the ignorant is a weapon they use against God.

Someone who gives up physical pleasures just to be well thought of by others has given up a permitted desire and still fallen into wrongdoing. The author asks what a hermit can see in his own dirty mirror, meaning his heart, if he withdraws to a cell for any reason other than God.

A wise man should not forgive the rudeness of common people out of gentleness. If he does, he loses respect and they become more brutal. Kindness toward the lowly only makes them prouder and more arrogant.

Asking a poor, suffering dervish how he is does no good unless you also help him: heal his wound and provide food. The image is of a donkey stuck in mud with its rider; if you feel real pity, help pull it out, and if not, do not come near at all. Asking questions while doing nothing is useless.

Spending more than fate has given us, and dying before our appointed time, are both against reason. Sighs and complaints cannot change what fate has decided. The angel in charge of the winds does not care if his wind puts out an old woman's lamp.

Stop chasing food, since you will eat when you are meant to. Whether you work hard or not, God provides daily bread equally, and nothing, not even a lion, can take your life before your destined time.

Things that are not fated to happen cannot be reached by human effort, while what is fated can be reached in any circumstance. As proof, the passage says Alexander reached the edge of darkness but still did not get the water of immortality.

Nothing happens except by fate: a fisherman catches fish only if it is his destiny, and a fish dies on land only if that is its fate. In the same way, a miser searches the world for wealth while death searches for him.

The envious man is stingy toward the blessings given by fate and hostile to innocent people. The speaker tells such a man that his envy alone is punishment enough, since he carries his own enemy with him, so he needs no one to wish him harm.

A scholar without effort is like a lover without money, a traveller without knowledge is like a bird without wings, a theorist without practice is like a tree without fruit, and a devotee without learning is like a house without a door. Each person needs the missing quality to be complete or to reach his goal.
The Koran was sent down so that people would use it as a guide for how to behave. It was not meant simply to be recited in parts.
Humble sincerity is set against proud idleness. The sincere publican, a tax collector, goes on foot, while the slothful Pharisee, a religious man, rides and sleeps.
A sinner who prays humbly is more pleasing than a worshipper who is proud of his devotion. Likewise, a polite, kind-hearted soldier is better than a learned religious teacher who dislikes people.
A learned man who does no good works is like a bee with no honey. The speaker tells a harsh critic, a hornet, that if he gives nothing useful himself, he should not hurt others with his sting.

Even a fine robe from a ruler is outdone, in the speaker's view, by his own ragged clothes. Likewise, a simple meal he has earned himself, such as salad and vinegar, tastes better to him than the rich food served by a village chief.
It is unwise to take medicine based on guesswork, or to travel a road only when you can follow the tracks of a caravan. Good judgment, the passage says, requires certainty and a known path.

Asked how he became so learned, the scholar Ghazali said he never felt shame in asking others about things he did not know. The passage adds that asking humbly guides a person toward learning, much as a patient trusts a skilled physician with his pulse.

Do not ask about something you can expect to learn on your own, or you may lose respect. Lukman saw iron softened like wax in David's hands, but did not ask how it was done, because he knew he would work it out through his own wisdom.

Good manners mean adapting to your host or companion: if you know the other person shares your feelings, match your talk to what they like to hear. A sensible person in Majnun's company would speak only in praise of Laila, the woman Majnun loved.

Someone who breaks into other people's conversation to show off what he knows only shows how little he really knows. A wise person waits until the question is fully put before answering. Even a correct point will be misread by a fussy listener who is looking for fault.

A lie leaves a lasting mark, like a scar, even after the wound heals. Joseph's brothers, known for lying, were not believed when they told the truth, just as a man known for lying will have his true words called false. Someone who usually tells the truth is forgiven an occasional mistake.
A dog remembers a kindness even after being hurt, so it is judged better than an ungrateful man. Kindness shown to a base person is soon repaid with hostility, the moment he feels slightly provoked.

The passage says that people turn away from God in both conditions. When they are rich they grow proud and careless, and when they are poor they sink into sorrow. So it is hard to say when a person would ever freely do their duty.

God decides who falls and who is saved: he can cast a man down from a throne, and keep another safe even inside a fish. The poet adds that a person who delights in praising God is happy, even if, like Jonah, he spends his time in a fish's belly.

God's anger would frighten even the prophets, and his kindness would reach the wicked as well as the good. Even the prophets could make no excuse if God judged us strictly on the last day. So the speaker asks God to show his mercy, so that sinners may hope to be forgiven.

Someone who does not learn from punishments in this life will face worse punishments in the next, as a Koranic verse says. Sa'di adds that rulers first warn a wrongdoer and, if he ignores the warning, imprison him.

Fortunate people prefer to learn from the warnings and examples of earlier generations, rather than having later generations learn from their own mistakes. A bird that sees another caught in a trap will stay away from the bait. So a person should learn from others' misfortunes, so that others need not learn from theirs.

The main point is that a person cannot help himself or change his fate by his own strength. Only God's mercy can bring good fortune, and no one can lead astray those God guides, or guide those God leaves astray. The speaker therefore has no judge to complain to but God.
A poor man who ends well is better off than a king who ends badly. In the same way, a sorrow that leads to joy is better than a joy that is followed by sorrow.

Rain falls from the sky onto the earth, and the earth gives back dust, so each gives what it has. The Arabic saying "What the vessels have, that they give" makes the same point. The last line tells the listener that if someone else's behaviour seems improper, they should not give up their own good conduct.

God sees and hides a person's faults, while a neighbor does not see them but still loudly criticizes. The speaker says that if people could see what is hidden, no one would be safe from their neighbors' blame.

Gold is dug out of a mine, and it is only taken from a miser when he dies. Misers hoard their wealth and refuse to spend it, hoping for a future use that never comes. In the end the gold stays behind, and the miser dies before he can enjoy it, while his enemies benefit.

Those who treat the weak harshly will in turn be hurt by the strong. Not every strong arm can twist a weak man's hand, so the speaker warns against causing pain to the feeble, lest you fall under the whip of someone stronger.
A wise person works to get past obstacles where they face opposition, but settles and rests where things are calm. Calm places offer safety, and there the wise person can also find enjoyment.

A gambler hopes for three sixes but rolls three aces, which are the lowest. Likewise, a horse in a rich meadow cannot enjoy it because its tether is not under its control. Both show that a person may fail to get what they want even when the chance or the means seems to be there.
A dervish (a Sufi holy man) prays that God show mercy to the wicked. His reason is that God has already been generous to the good, by making them virtuous.

Jemshid, a legendary Persian king, put his ornaments on his left hand, saying the right hand needs no decoration because being right is adornment enough. Feridun, another king, had an inscription placed on his palace urging the wise to make the wicked good, since good people are already great and fortunate.

A holy man is asked why a ring is worn on the left hand, though the right hand is the more honored one. He answers that the best things are often neglected. He adds that fate, which sets a person's fortune and provision, gives either good luck or wisdom.

A person should advise kings only if he does not fear losing his head and does not seek a reward. Whether the king offers gold or threatens death with a sword, such a person is equally unmoved, because his firmness rests on his belief in God's oneness alone.

Each official has a set job: the king removes extortioners, the police chief guards against murderers, and the judge (cazi) settles quarrels. The passage adds that when a claim is genuinely just, it is better to pay willingly than under pressure, though a collector may still force a stubborn taxpayer to pay.

The point is a joke about corrupt judges. Every man's teeth are worn down by sour food, except the judge's, because he eats sweets, which are bribes. A judge who will take a few cucumbers as a bribe will in return grant a claim to ten melon fields.

The passage is cut off, so it gives only the question and the start of the answer. A wise man is asked why the cypress alone is called "free" (azad), though it bears no fruit. His reply begins by saying that every tree has its own fruit and season, and it flourishes only while that season lasts.

The passage is a fragment of advice to be generous when you can and to stay free of worry when you cannot. It uses the date-tree, which gives fruit, and the cypress, which stays green whatever the season. It also says not to set your heart on things that pass away, such as rulers, since the river Tigris keeps flowing after the caliphs are gone.

Two kinds of people die with regret: those who had wealth but did not spend it, and those who knew what is right but did not act on it. The passage also says that a generous man's giving hides all his other faults, even many of them, while a miser's faults are plainly seen.

A man should be very careful before he goes through a gate into a place. He should look around for a long time, because he cannot tell where an enemy may be hiding, even among those already sitting inside.

Hávamál stanza 2 is a greeting to a host when a guest arrives, asking where the stranger should sit. The last lines warn that a man who wants to test his strength with swords will be quickly dealt with, so the stanza speaks of a challenge to a guest's power in the hall. The meaning of "swift" here is quick or soon, as in quickly overcome.
A traveler who comes in from the cold with frozen knees needs a fire. Someone who has come down from the mountains needs food and clothes.
A guest arriving at a feast should be given water to wash with, a towel, and a friendly greeting. If a person wants good reputation and to be welcomed again, he must behave wisely and well.
A traveler needs good wits, because travel is hard, while life at home is easy. A wise man, sitting among fools, should pretend not to notice their folly.
A person should not boast about how clever he is but keep his wisdom to himself. A silent, wise guest seldom comes to harm when visiting a house, and good sense proves the most reliable friend.
A wise guest who comes to a feast sits quietly and pays close attention. He listens and watches carefully, and the stanza says that all wise men behave this way.
Good fortune goes to the one who earns favor and praise for himself. Wisdom held only in another person's heart is described as much less secure.
Happy is the man who, while he lives, has both wisdom and good reputation. Often a man receives bad advice from another's heart, meaning from someone else's mind or intentions.
Wisdom is the best load a person can carry on long journeys, better than wealth when travelling in unknown places. It also offers shelter when a person is in sorrow.
Wisdom is the best load a man can carry on long travels. Drinking too much ale is the worst food to take on a journey.
Less good is found in ale than most people think, the verse says. The more a man drinks, the less control he keeps over his own mind.

Drinking beer makes men forget things, as if a bird of forgetfulness sat on them and took their wits. The speaker then describes himself as bound with heron feathers and held in the house of Gunnlöð, a giantess. The lines are a figure of speech about how drink dulls the mind.

Drunk, the speaker was with Fjalar, a wise man. The point is that drinking is best when a person comes home with more wisdom than he took with him. The speaker is saying that good drinking means gaining knowledge, not just getting drunk.
A king's son should be quiet and wise, and also brave in battle. A man should face life boldly and cheerfully until the day he dies.
The lazy man thinks he will live forever if he avoids fighting. But old age will not bring him peace, even if spears spare his life in battle.
A fool gapes and stammers or sits silent when he arrives at a feast. Once he gets a drink, though, his true character shows.
Only the man who has travelled far and wide knows how much understanding a person gains from wisdom. The stanza suggests that experience of other places is what shows the value of wisdom to a mind.
Do not refuse the mead, but drink only moderately. Speak only when you have something to the point, or stay silent. If you go early to bed, no one can fairly call you rude.
A greedy man with a dull mind eats until he is sick. A coarse man among wise people is mocked because of his appetite.
Cattle know when to leave the pasture and go home. A foolish man, however, does not know how much food is enough for his own belly.
A petty, foolish man mocks everything. He does not know what he ought to know: that he himself is not free from faults.
A foolish man lies awake all night with many worries. When morning comes he is still weary with care, and his troubles are no lighter than before.
The foolish man takes as friends those who laugh at him. He does not notice when wise men speak with hatred of him.
A foolish man takes as friends those who laugh at him. When he comes to the council and hears the truth, he finds that few will speak in his favor.
A person with little wisdom thinks he knows everything while he sits alone. But when other people ask him questions, he does not know how to answer.

A foolish man who meets other men should keep quiet. No one can tell that he knows nothing, as long as he does not talk too much. The last lines say that a man who talks too much does not notice his own ignorance.
A man seems wise if he can ask good questions and also answer them well. Nothing that people say among other people stays hidden.
Someone who talks constantly often says words that no one believes. A chattering tongue, with no restraint on it, often brings trouble on its owner.

A man should not be mocked just because he goes to a feast. A person often seems wise when no one asks him anything, and he sits safely, untouched by trouble. "Dry-skinned" means unharmed, and the stanza seems to mean that silence keeps a person out of harm.
A guest is wise to leave quickly when he mocks someone else. A man who laughs and jeers at a feast, even among enemies, knows little, because he does not see his danger.
Many men seem friendly until they drink at a feast and begin to mock their friends. When guests start fighting with one another, it always brings harm to people.
Eat a meal early so you do not arrive at a feast hungry. A man who comes to the feast starving sits there chewing as if he might choke, and he is too eager to ask for anything.
The road to an enemy is twisted and long, even when his house stands right beside the highway. The road to a friend is wide and straight, even when he lives far away.
A guest should not stay too long in one place or in another person's house. If a visitor sits by someone else's hearth for a long time, the welcome turns into dislike.
A small home is better than a grand one that is not one's own, even if it is only a hut. A man is master in his own house, and a few goats and a patched roof are far better than begging for help.
A man is his own master at home, even if the house is only a hut. Someone who has to beg for food when he wants it suffers deeply inside.
A man should not walk even a short distance away from his weapons while in the open country. He cannot know when he might need a spear on a long road.

A man should not let himself go without when he has earned wealth. Often a person ends up saving money meant for a friend, which then goes to an enemy, because things often turn out worse than planned.
