The speaker says he has never met anyone so generous that they would not gladly accept a gift in return. He has also never met anyone who gave away their wealth so freely that they were not repaid with hatred.
Friends should make each other glad with gifts of weapons and clothing, each giving what he can see is fitting. Friendships between people who give gifts last the longest, if their fates allow it.
A man should be a true friend to his friend, and return gifts with gifts. Mockery is answered with mockery, and deceit with lies.
A man should be loyal to his friend, and to his friend's friend. He should never make friends with the friend of his enemy.
If a man has a friend he fully trusts, and wants good from him, he should share his thoughts with him, give him gifts, and visit him often. The stanza describes how such a friendship is kept up.
If you distrust someone but still want something good from them, the stanza advises speaking kindly to them while thinking falsely about them. It says to repay their deceit with deceit.

It advises caution with a person you cannot fully trust and whose thoughts you cannot read. You may laugh with such a person, but you should not share your real opinions. Your gifts to them should match theirs, meaning you give only as much as they give you.
A young man once travelled alone and did not know the way. He felt rich when he met a companion, because one person is another person's joy.
Brave and generous people live best, because they seldom dwell on sorrow. A coward fears everything, and a stingy person gives grudgingly, without joy.
In this verse, the speaker once gave his clothes to two carved wooden posts standing in a field. Dressed in clothes, they looked like heroes, but a man without clothes counts for nothing.
The speaker compares a lonely fir-tree on a bare hillside to a man whom nobody loves. The fir dies with no use to anyone, and the speaker asks why such a man's life should last long.
Friendship between false friends can burn as hot as fire, but it lasts only five days. On the sixth day the fire cools and all the love is gone.

A small gift can win great praise, and the speaker says that a friend can be made with only half a loaf of bread and a half-full cup of drink. The stanza says a large gift is not needed to make a friend.
Just as a little sand holds only a little sea, human minds are small. Men differ in wisdom, but none is fully wise; everyone is only partly wise.
A person should have some wisdom, but should not think he knows too much. The stanza says the best lives belong to those whose wisdom has grown broad.
A person should have some wisdom, but not too much. The stanza says a wise man's heart is seldom happy when he has gained too great a store of wisdom.
A person should have some wisdom, but not too much. Nobody should try to foresee what fate holds for them, because that way they are freer from sorrow.
A fire is started from another fire, just as one torch lights another. In the same way, people come to know a man by what he says, and they judge a fool by his silence.

A person who wants another's life or property must act early, since a wolf that lies idle gets little food and a sleeping man gets little success. The stanza says that waiting and idleness bring poor results to anyone hoping to gain what belongs to others.
The main point is that someone with few helpers must get up early and go out to find work for himself. A person who sleeps late leaves much undone, and quick action is what brings in wealth.
A person should know in advance what he will need. He should plan how many roofing shingles and strips of bark he needs for the thatch, and how much firewood he will use in a month or in half a year.
Go to the council washed and fed, but do not worry too much about your clothes. No one should be ashamed of his shoes or his clothing, and even less of the horse he rides, even if it is a poor one.

A man who stands among a crowd but has few people to speak up for him is compared to an eagle that comes to the sea and droops its head. The point is that a person without friends to support him feels as lost and downcast as the eagle in that setting.

A person who wants to be seen as wise must be ready to ask and to answer questions. The stanza also warns to share your thoughts with only one person, since once two people know them, and certainly once three do, the matter is known to all.
A wise man uses his strength with restraint. When he goes among brave men, he understands that he may not be the bravest of them.
The speaker says he has arrived at many gatherings either too early or too late. Either the beer was all gone or it was not yet brewed. So a man who is disliked finds little pleasure at feasts.
Men would invite the speaker to their homes, sending him here and there, if he had no need of food at mealtime. He says a true friend would even hang two hams for him, though he had eaten only one.
Fire, the power to see the sun, health, and a life free of wrongdoing are named as the best things a person can have. The stanza lists them as the good gifts of life. (Word count: about 32.)
No man is wholly wretched, however sick he may be. People find joy in different places: some in their sons, some in their kinsmen, some in their wealth, and some in worthy deeds.

A living person can still gain things, such as catching a cow, while the dead cannot. The speaker has seen a rich man's funeral fire, and the rich man lay dead before his own door, so his wealth did not save him.

The lame man can still ride a horse, the man without hands can still herd, and the deaf man can be brave in battle. A blind man is still better off than a man who is burned, and a dead body is of no use at all.
A son is worth more even if he is born late, after his father has died. Stones raised as memorials are rarely seen by the road unless a relative has set them up to honor his kin.

Two people quarrelling is how a fight begins, and harsh words can hurt as much as blows. The speaker says that when someone wears a furry coat, he expects a fist to come out of it, meaning a man may be a fighter and ready to strike.

The stanza says that a man is glad of a night when he has enough food. It adds that a ship's yards (its crossbeams) are short, and that autumn nights are restless. Weather can change many times in a week, and more often in a month.

The stanza says that a person cannot know everything, and that wealth does not always follow from what a man deserves. One man is rich and another poor, so nobody should look down on another for his poverty. "Gold oft apes begets" is an old way of saying that gold often produces offspring, meaning money breeds more money.
Fitjung's sons once had well-stocked sheep pens, but now they carry the beggar's staff. The verse says wealth passes as quickly as a blink, and it is the most false of friends.
Cattle, relatives, and then a person all die. Only a good reputation outlasts them, because a noble name lives on for those who earn good renown.
Everything mortal passes away: livestock, relatives, and eventually oneself. The only thing that does not die is the good name a person leaves behind through their deeds.
A foolish man who wins a woman's love or some wealth becomes prouder, but he does not become wiser. He walks through life full of conceit.

Praise is to be given at evening rather than during the day, and certain things are to be praised only after they have been tested or used. These are a woman after she has been burned on a pyre, a weapon after it has been tried in battle, a bride after her wedding, ice after it has been crossed, and ale after it has been drunk.

Each activity is paired with the time or place where it suits best: cut wood when the wind is strong, go to sea when the wind is fair, seek pleasure with maidens at dusk, and get speed from a ship and safety from a shield. The last line warns that a sword gives wounds while a maiden gives kisses. The lines are a set of practical sayings about choosing the right moment and source for each thing.
Drink ale by the fire and skate on the ice. Buy a thin horse and a sword that has rusted, and feed the horse and the hound at your home.
A man should not trust a young woman's oath or the promises a woman makes. The verse says their hearts were shaped on a spinning wheel and their breasts made changeable, so they cannot be relied on.

The lines list things that break, burn, or churn: a snapping bow, fire, a wolf, a raven, a boar, a torn-up tree, rough seas, and a boiling pot. The list is incomplete, so the point it makes about them is not stated here.
The stanza lists things that are unsteady or unreliable: a flying arrow, falling water, fresh ice, a snake's coils, a bride's pillow talk, a broken sword, bears at play, and kings' sons.

Hávamál 87 is a fragment, so its meaning is only partly clear. It lists things a person should not trust or depend on: a sick calf, a stubborn servant, a flattering witch, and a newly killed enemy. These are the kinds of things it warns against relying on.

Three things are named as not to be trusted: a man who has killed one's brother, met away from home; a half-burned house; and a swift horse with a hurt leg, which is then useless. The stanza says no one has such faith as to rely on all of them.
Do not expect a quick harvest, and do not count too early on your son turning out well. A field needs good weather, and a son needs wisdom, and often neither is given.

The stanza says that the love of fickle women is as hard to hold as a series of hard tasks. It compares it to riding an unshod horse across ice, steering a ship with no rudder in a storm, and a lame man hunting reindeer on slippery rocks. Each image shows a situation that is risky and hard to control.

The speaker says he knows both sides of the matter and that men can be false to women. When men speak most kindly to women, they often mean the opposite, and they act with deceit against what is wise.
A man who wants a woman's love should speak gentle words, offer wealth, and praise her beauty. The one who courts her best is the one who wins her.
Nobody should blame another person for being in love. The stanza says that wise people are often caught by beauty that stirs desire, while fools are left free.
Do not criticise someone for a fault that many people share. Even wise men are often turned into fools by strong love.
A person alone knows what is in his own heart and mind. For a wise man, the worst sickness is not having the joy he longs for.
The speaker says he sat in the reeds and waited a long time for his love. He loved a wise maiden as much as his own life, but he never won her.
The speaker describes finding Billing's daughter asleep on her bed, shining like the sun. Without her beautiful form, even a nobleman's great estate would seem empty to him.
A speaker tells Odin to come back in the evening if he wants to win a woman. He adds that it would be bad if anyone besides the two of them learned of such an affair.
The speaker hurried off in hope of pleasure, ignoring wise advice. He was sure he would soon win great joy with a young woman.
The speaker comes to a place at night where all the warriors are awake, carrying burning lights and torches. Through this he learns about his unlucky fate, or the bad outcome of his journey.

In the morning, the speaker returns and finds that everyone is still asleep. In the woman's place he finds a dog tied up on her bed. The stanza describes the speaker's discovery at dawn, and it is not clear from these lines what the dog's presence means.
The speaker says that many attractive young women prove unfaithful when a man tests them. He tried to win a clever woman through trickery, but she only scorned him and he gained nothing from her.

A man should stay careful and wise even when he is happy at home with guests. A wise person should keep his speech fair. The passage says that someone who cannot say anything is called a fool, since that is how the witless behave.

The speaker, Odin, says he visited the old giant Suttung and came back with little reward from keeping silent. He had to speak many words in Suttung's hall to get what he wanted. Suttung is a giant who guarded the mead of poetry.

Odin describes how he got past danger to win the mead of poetry. Rati, a drill or auger, bored a hole through a stone, making a way for him. He went through the giants' paths, above and below them, and risked his life doing so.

Gunnlöð gave the speaker a drink of magical mead while she sat on a golden stool. He repaid her with a harsh return for her brave heart, and it deeply troubled her spirit. The stanza is about his betrayal of her kindness.
A wise man lacks little when he has gained a well-earned gift. The stanza says that Óðrœrir, a vessel holding the magic mead of poetry, has been brought up among people on earth.
The speaker says he would hardly have gone home from the land of the giants. He only got away because Gunnlöð, the good maiden whose arms had been around him, helped him.
The next day, frost-giants came to Hor's hall. They asked whether Bolverk had returned to the gods or had been killed there by Suttung.

Odin swore an oath on his ring, but then broke it. The verse asks who can now trust his word. Odin betrayed Suttung, the giant, and left Gunnlöth, Suttung's daughter, in grief after he stole the mead of poetry.

The speaker says it is time to recite from the chanter's seat, then describes what he saw and heard long ago at the wells of Urth and in the hall of Hor. He heard talk about runes, the old writing and magic signs, and about advice given there.

Odin advises Loddfafnir, a listener he addresses directly, to listen closely because it will bring him profit. The specific advice is not to get up at night, unless he is going to look for news or needs to go to the outhouse.
Odin advises Loddfafnir to listen closely, since listening brings him profit and gain. The main warning is to avoid falling asleep in a witch's embrace, and not to let her limbs trap him.

Stanza 114 of the Hávamál is a warning about a woman who has been unfaithful or wicked. Its main point is that she has made the speaker's life miserable. Her hold on him has left him unable to take part in public assemblies, leaving him without appetite, joy, or restful sleep.
Odin advises Loddfafnir, the listener, to heed his counsel for his own benefit. The main instruction is never to seek to win another man's wife or to long for her secret love.

The speaker gives advice to a man named Loddfafnir and tells him to listen. If he listens, he will gain something. If he plans to cross mountains or dangerous waters, he should take care to bring enough food for the journey.

Odin, speaking to a man named Loddfafnir, advises him to listen and learn, since this brings him profit. He warns that he must not let an evil man do him harm, because an evil man never repays a good thought with a good deed.
The speaker saw a man hurt badly by a wicked woman's words. A lying tongue struck the fatal blow, and none of what she said was true.
The speaker advises Loddfafnir that if he has a friend he fully trusts, he should visit that friend often. The reason given is that a path seldom walked gets overgrown with brambles and grass.
Odin advises Loddfafnir to listen closely, since listening will bring him profit and gain. The advice is to make a good man a friend and to pay attention to that man's healing charms.

The speaker advises Loddfafnir, a listener named in the poem, to never be the first to break a bond with a friend. He also says that worry wears down the heart when a person cannot speak openly to another person about what they think.

Odin advises Loddfafnir to listen closely, since listening brings profit and learning brings great gain. The main instruction is that he must never exchange words with a foolish person, whom the text calls a "witless ape."
A bad man will never repay you with good. A good man, though, will often show you great love for kind words of praise.
Love is mixed, not pure, when a person cannot say all of his thoughts to another. Being false is the worst thing, and a friend does not speak only pleasant words.

Odin, speaking to a listener named Loddfafnir, advises him not to argue with a lesser man for long. The better man often comes off worse, since the lesser man may turn to violence, here shown as a sword.

Odin, speaking to a listener named Loddfafnir, advises him to be a shoemaker or a maker of spears' shafts, a trade he can practise on his own. If the shoe or shaft is badly made, people will think ill of him for it.

Odin advises Loddfafnir to listen closely, since listening brings profit and learning brings great gain. If he knows of some evil, he should name it openly, and he should not make friends with his enemies.
Odin speaks to a listener named Loddfafnir, advising him to listen and learn, since this brings profit and gain. He says that you will find no joy in evil, while good people will bring you happiness.
Odin, speaking to a man named Loddfafnir, gives him advice: do not look up when a battle is going on. The reason given is that men there go mad, and this madness could cloud his mind.

Odin, speaking to a listener named Loddfafnir, advises that if a man wants a woman's love and her joy in return, he should keep his promises to her well. The stanza's reason is that no one turns against a good thing he has received.
Odin, speaking in the poem, gives Loddfafnir advice: listen, because it will help him. He says to be careful but not fearful. He warns most against drunkenness, another man's wife, and thieves.
The speaker gives advice to a man named Loddfafnir and says he will profit if he listens. The main instruction is that he must never mock or scorn a guest or a traveler.
People often do not know well the character of the man who sits with them in the house. No one is so good that he has no faults, and no one is so bad that he has no worth.
Loddfafnir is told to listen and learn. The main point is not to scorn an old singer, because old people often give good advice, even when their bodies are worn and shrivelled.

Odin, speaking to a man named Loddfafnir, advises him to listen and gain from the advice. The core instruction is to not curse a guest or turn him away from the door, and to treat a needy person kindly.

The stanza is about a door. Its heavy bar must be strong enough to lift so that people can come in, and a ring or handle on it is needed. Without that ring, the speaker warns, ill will would fall on the one who failed to provide it.

The speaker advises Loddfafnir, when he drinks ale, to seek "might of earth." He then lists remedies: earth cures drink, fire cures illness, oak cures stiffness, and so on, each thing curing a particular ailment. The last line says the field soaks up floodwater.
Hor, the speaker of these words, has now said them in the hall. They are kind toward human beings and cursed toward giants. The speaker, the learner, and the listeners are all blessed.
The speaker says he hung on a windy tree for nine nights, wounded by a spear and offered to Odin, giving himself to himself. The tree's roots are hidden, so no one knows what lies beneath it.
The speaker says that no one gave him bread or a drinking horn, and he looked down below. Shrieking, he seized the runes, old writing signs, and at once fell backward.

In this stanza the speaker says he received nine powerful songs from the son of Bolthorn, who is the father of Bestla. He also says he got a drink of fine mead poured from the vessel Othrörir. Bolthorn, Bestla and Othrörir are names from Norse myth, and the stanza does not say more about them.

The speaker says that once he began to gain wisdom, he grew strong and prospered. He describes how one word led to another word, and one deed led to another deed, so his knowledge and actions built up step by step.

Runes are mysterious signs, painted or shaped by a great singer and made by the gods. The stanza says these signs are very strong and powerful, and that the ruler of the gods is the one who writes them.

Odin carved the runes for the gods, Dáinn for the elves, Dvalinn for the dwarfs, and Alsvith for giants and humans. The speaker says he carved some runes himself. The stanza is about who made the runic letters and for whom they were made.

Hávamál stanza 145 asks a series of questions about skills: whether one knows how to write, read, colour (or mark) runes, test them, ask, give, send a message, and make a sacrifice. Runes were the Norse letters, and "tint" likely refers to marking or colouring them. The stanza is a list of knowledge a person should have.

The speaker says he knows songs that kings' wives do not know, and that ordinary men do not know either. The first of these songs is called "help," and it can bring relief in sorrow, pain and sickness.
The speaker says he knows a charm, a third one, that he can use when he badly needs to bind an enemy. With it he makes the enemy's blade dull, so that neither his sword nor his staff can cut or bite.
The speaker says he knows a charm that can free him from bonds. If men tie his legs in fetters, the charm lets him walk out, and the chains fall off his feet and hands.

The speaker says he knows a fifth charm: if he sees an arrow flying toward the people from far away, he can stop it, because it cannot fly so fast that he cannot catch it with his eyes. The passage is a boast about a magic protection against arrows.
The speaker names a sixth charm he knows against harm. If someone tries to harm him with spells made from a sapling's roots, that person will suffer the evil himself before the speaker does.
The speaker says he knows a seventh charm, a song he can sing. If he sees fire burning the hall above his companions' heads, he can put it out. The fire is not so large that he cannot quench it.
The speaker says he knows an eighth charm, one that is the most useful for everyone to learn. With it, he can quickly end hatred when it arises among warriors' sons.
The speaker claims to know a ninth charm, used when a ship needs shelter on the water. With it, he can calm the wind on the waves and put the sea to sleep.

Hávamál 156 is a stanza where the speaker claims a magic skill: he knows a tenth spell, and with it he can see "house-riders" flying through the sky. These are spirits or beings that ride through the air, and he can make them wander wildly until they show their true forms and go back to their own homes.
The speaker knows an eleventh charm, to use if he must lead his dear friends into battle. By singing it over the shields, he makes them go into the fight and come home unharmed.

In this stanza the speaker says he knows a twelfth charm. If he sees a hanged man swinging high in a tree, he carves and paints runes (old writing symbols). Through them the dead man walks away and speaks with him.
The speaker says he knows a thirteenth charm: if he sprinkles a young warrior well with water, the warrior will not fall, even in battle among the army, and will not sink beneath the swords.
The speaker says he knows a fourteenth charm, which he could name to people if he wished, for calling the mighty gods. He claims to know all about the gods and elves, and says few fools know this.

Of the fifteen spells the speaker says he knows, this one is a song sung by the dwarf Thjothrörir before the doors of Delling. It gives might to the gods, glory to the elves, and wisdom to Hroptatyr, a name for the god Odin.
In this stanza of the Hávamál, the speaker claims he knows a magic spell, a sixteenth charm, that lets him win a wise maiden's love. With it he can turn her thoughts and change her mind toward him.
Loddfafnir will look for these songs and try to sing them without success. Still, it would be good for him to get them, learn them, and use them to help.

The speaker says he knows an eighteenth secret charm, which he will never tell to any maiden or married woman. He holds that the best thing is what only one person knows. He would share it only with the woman he lies with, or with his sister.
